The example adopts Kripke’s rigid-designation account of natural-kind identity as a working commitment. Both chests point the same way: coherence in the description is a test the words pass, and passing it settles nothing about what Reality admits.

Real possibility isn’t the same as *conceivability*. Take an ordinary chest: pick any patch of grass in the park, conceive of one buried underneath it, and imagine digging there. The conception is perfectly coherent, and what it conceives is really possible—and none of that settles whether a chest is under that grass. Now the other direction. Imagine a chest that refills itself with treasure every time it is closed. There’s no contradiction in it and the picture comes easily; but coming easily isn’t Reality handing back a capacity. Conceivability fails on both sides, then. It doesn’t reach actuality where real possibility already holds, and it doesn’t establish real possibility to begin with. What thought can entertain is a fact about the reach of imagination, and many conceivable arrangements name nothing real.

There’s a more technical version of this worry. Some philosophers, following Chalmers (2002), ask about a refined, idealized conceivability: what would still seem coherent at the limit of careful reflection, rather than what merely seems coherent at first glance. Might that track a genuine kind of possibility after all? And would it need holding apart from the real possibility fixed here? Nothing in this section settles that. What it fixes is the vocabulary any answer would have to be stated in, and the burden the idealization takes on: an account of why refining a mental operation should track a capacity of Reality. The two-dimensional framework built to handle it is developed at §7.1.2.

Real possibility isn’t the same as *epistemic possibility*. What is open relative to one’s evidence is a fact about a knower, not a fact about the world. Two reasoners with different evidence can disagree about epistemic possibility while agreeing entirely about what could really be. The same chest makes the point. Buried in Central Park, it’s epistemically open—no one has checked every square foot—and also really possible, since a buried chest is the kind of thing Reality permits. Those are two different standings that happen to coincide here, and they come apart the moment somebody digs: the epistemic question closes and the modal one doesn’t move at all. The refilling chest separates them the other way. To a reader who hasn’t worked out the physics it can be epistemically open too, and that openness says nothing whatever about what Reality permits. For now the point is that what is open to a knower’s evidence doesn’t determine what is open to Reality.

A note on register before the last two. The modalities just distinguished (conceivability, epistemic possibility) are doxastic or knower-relative: facts about what a mind can represent or what evidence permits, not facts about modal space. The modal claims throughout this book are *alethic*: they concern what really holds, independently of any mind’s reach. This distinction runs through the argument. Doxastic modality, what a thinker takes to be possible, appears in Chapter 5 as a downstream product of the structural conditions that this argument establishes, not as a ground for those claims. The evidential basis by which the book secures its foundational modal claims is the bilateral performative witness developed at §2.2 (Cartesian Certainty); modal-metaphysical knowledge here isn’t built from doxastic raw material.

Real possibility isn’t equivalent to *nomological possibility* on the standard reading of the laws. *Nomological possibility* means *permitted by the laws of nature*, what some account of the laws says could occur. The refilling chest returns here, and this is the sense that actually bites on it: familiar physics may well rule it out. Set beside it a chest that turns whatever is placed inside to gold. Both pictures come as easily, but they ask different things: the first asks that matter appear where there was none; the second asks only that one kind become another, and transmutation of kinds isn’t excluded in principle, however far the described device sits from any actual means of doing it. Conceivability ranked the two together. The laws don’t. But a law-relative exclusion isn’t yet a metaphysical one, and that alone doesn’t settle whether either chest is really possible. Those laws, as commonly characterized, may rule out things that really could be, and our characterizations of them may fail to rule out things that really couldn’t; the two extensions need not coincide. Whether the deep reading of the laws coincides with real possibility is taken up in §2.6.

Real possibility isn’t the same as *probability*. Objective chance weights outcomes among what really could be the case: nothing has positive objective chance that isn’t first possible. Epistemic probability instead tracks uncertainty; assigning a claim positive credence doesn’t establish its real possibility (§2.9.5). The buried chest in Central Park is wildly unlikely, and being unlikely makes it no less possible. *Possible* settles whether the thing is a candidate at all; *probable* sorts the candidates under the relevant measure.

One more distinction. “Possible” says that something could really be the case, not that the conditions to bring it about are always at hand. The possibility of reading is one thing; the occasion to read is another. One is a standing permission; the other is a particular fact about the world, and nothing in the permission forces the fact either way. Possibility doesn’t promise the occasion. And one consequence: necessary truths count as possible. If something couldn’t fail to be the case, then in particular it could be the case, and that is all possibility requires.

### 1.2.2 Impossibility
Impossibility, possibility’s mirror image, marks what Reality forecloses. Where possibility names what Reality leaves open, impossibility names what it rules out altogether.

**[Definition]**

**Impossibility** · *Definition*

A proposition is impossible when it really could not be the case (¬◇P).

The notation makes the dependence explicit: impossibility is the negation of possibility (¬◇P), so it adds no content of its own beyond what possibility has already fixed. To call a proposition impossible is to say there’s no configuration Reality permits in which it holds: not that it merely fails to obtain, but that it couldn’t be. The plainest cases are the self-canceling ones (a square circle, a proposition both true and false at once), which name no way things could be, because the conditions they state exclude one another. Real impossibility is the outer boundary the remaining statuses are drawn against: necessity is possible truth whose failure is impossible, contingency possible truth whose negation is also possible.

### 1.2.3 Necessity
With possibility and impossibility fixed, call a proposition *necessary* when its failure is excluded across every configuration Reality permits, and *contingent* when both it and its negation remain permitted. The strict defense of the modal machinery that supports these classifications is carried in Chapter 2; the point here is to state the target statuses in the sense the argument will use them.

**[Definition]**

**Necessity** · *Definition*

A proposition is necessary when it really could not fail to be the case (□P).

What is necessary doesn’t lapse. Logical truths are necessary: there’s no configuration with a square circle, no chest that’s both full and empty at the same time. The descriptions cancel themselves; they pick out no object. Arithmetical truths are necessary the same way from the other side: 2 + 2 = 4 in every configuration, so an incompatible equation such as 2 + 2 = 5 is no self-canceling description, only a proposition false in all of them. Metaphysical claims of the form “X is necessarily the case” work the same way: X isn’t just true here, but holds across every configuration there could be.

Necessity can also attach to possibility itself. The form □◇P says that R’s capacity for P doesn’t vary with the local configuration under evaluation, but P must be fixed precisely; the case that follows shows why. Let P be the proposition that some reading occurs. This text will someday be unreadable, as every text eventually will be; sooner or later, the future closes off every occasion to read this token. That loss doesn’t make a reading-instance impossible. Nor does □◇P say that every local configuration contains a reader or readable object. It fixes Reality’s capacity for a reading, not an occasion in every configuration. The permission isn’t the occasion.

The classification sharpens once the possible side is divided. Within what is possible, some propositions hold in every configuration (the necessary), and some hold in only some (the contingent). Set against the impossible, this gives a natural three-way partition (necessary, contingent, impossible) that is mutually exclusive and exhaustive. *Possible* spans the first two: it means *not impossible*.

Necessity marks one half of the possible field, the propositions that hold across all of it. The other half—those that hold in some configurations but not all—is contingency, the next status to name.

### 1.2.4 Contingency
One further status turns on whether a proposition could have been otherwise.

**[Definition]**

**Contingency** · *Definition*

A proposition is contingent when it really could be the case and really could fail to be (◇P ∧ ◇¬P).

Contingency is the modal status that tracks arrangement-dependence: a contingent proposition is one whose truth varies with which configuration obtains. The definition makes two demands, not one: a contingent proposition could be the case (◇P) *and* could fail to be (◇¬P). Possibility by itself doesn’t suffice: a necessary truth is possible too. What singles out contingency is that the negation stays open as well: the matter could have gone either way. This is the status of nearly everything ordinary. That you are reading now rather than asleep, that this sentence stands in these words rather than others, that history took this course rather than another it permitted: each could have been otherwise, and each is therefore contingent. The contrast with necessity is exact: a necessary truth holds in every configuration Reality permits, so its negation is foreclosed; a contingent truth holds in some and fails in others, so neither it nor its negation is foreclosed. Reality’s structure settles both modal statuses: necessity by foreclosing the negation, contingency by leaving both sides open. Actuality settles which side of a contingent proposition obtains in the realized configuration.

### 1.2.5 Actuality
The first four statuses sort how a proposition stands to what Reality permits; the last marks which permitted configuration is actually realized.

**[Definition]**

**Actuality** · *Definition*

A proposition is actual when it is true of the realized configuration.

What is *actual* is what is *real* in the realized sense. That you are reading this is actual. You might have been asleep, or elsewhere, or reading something else. Those alternatives are possible; the actual configuration is the one you are in. Every actual fact is possible (actuality implies possibility), but not every possibility is actual. Conflating actuality with necessity is the *modal-collapse error*: treating what happens to be true as if it couldn’t have failed to be. Actuality also carries no symbol of its own. The two symbols of §1.2 (◇ and □) supply the notation for the other four statuses, but actuality needs none: a proposition asserted outright is already asserted of the realized configuration. What actuality itself consists in (whether it marks an absolute feature of the realized configuration or merely indexes the world one occupies, as on Lewis’s indexical theory) is taken up at §7.2.3, where the indexical reading is answered together with the plurality it belongs to.

### 1.2.6 Statuses Together
The five statuses form a closed modal grammar. Taken pre-formally, in the order §1.1 met them: impossibility is what really couldn’t be the case, and possibility has content only against it. Formally the dependence runs the other way, and the closing paragraphs of this section state it in that direction. Either way round, necessity is possible truth whose failure is impossible; contingency is possible truth whose negation is also possible; actuality is the realized member within the possible field. The grammar therefore includes contingency as a status, but it doesn’t yet establish that some proposition bears that status in every configuration Reality permits. That stronger claim is reserved for §2.9.4 rather than inferred from the vocabulary alone.

This section fixes possibility as the formal primitive (§1.2.1) and impossibility as its negation. Necessity and contingency then divide the possible field by whether the negation is foreclosed or remains open, while actuality marks which permitted configuration is realized. The order is asymmetric: the five statuses don’t each hold their place only because all the others hold theirs, and actuality isn’t derived from the modal operators.

The grammar is closed because these relations exhaust the classificatory work: no sixth modal status is wanted, and nothing outside the five is needed to state a modal claim. That closure is a fact about the vocabulary, not about the world. Whether anything is explanatorily self-subsistent must be earned independently; a vocabulary can’t settle it.

One further principle the argument will use, and Chapter 2 will defend, is this: the modal status of a proposition doesn’t shift with which configuration obtains. In *de dicto* terms the status is invariant: what is possible anywhere is possible everywhere, what is necessary anywhere is necessary everywhere. A *de dicto* claim is about the proposition itself, not about a particular thing the proposition refers to. The literature files this rule under *S5 iteration*, and Appendix A formalizes it under that name. The principle is that what is possible or necessary is itself necessarily possible or necessary.

The name can mislead, so the reading intended here is worth fixing before the rule does any work. The claim isn’t that a box may be stacked on a diamond and the stack evaluated by climbing an accessibility relation between worlds. It is that whatever is possible, *its possibility is necessary*: possibility is a determination Reality settles (§1.2.1), and the rule records that such a determination doesn’t vary with the configuration from which it is reported. Modal status answers to what Reality consists in, not to how any world is arranged (§2.1.3). Both readings validate the same formula. They differ over what makes it true, and therefore over where the rule can be challenged—which is why the defense at The S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5) concerns the scope of real possibility rather than the shape of an accessibility relation.

Two commitments are reserved here rather than discharged.

i. *The modal system.* The choice of S5 over weaker modal systems (T, S4, B, and their variants) is contested; the defense arrives in §2.1.5.

ii. *The quantifier domain.* When the argument deploys these modal statuses across quantified change-claims from the Structural Requirement (§2.4) onward, one further choice becomes load-bearing: whether the same objects exist at every world (constant-domain semantics) or the domains vary across worlds (variable-domain). On the constant-domain option, the Barcan and Converse-Barcan formulas, which link the quantifiers to the modal operators, come out valid. That question is engaged at §7.2.7 against Williamson’s necessitism, with the formal apparatus in Appendix A.2–A.3.

So much for what is reserved. The actual isn’t merely the permitted, not merely what could be, but what *is*: the configuration taken, the one you are in right now. Descartes asked what could survive the most radical doubt: not the senses, not memory, not the external world as ordinarily described. What survived wasn’t a fact about what might be but a fact about what *is*: something is actually happening, something is actually being thought. The cogito doesn’t establish a possibility. It establishes an actuality. And an actuality can’t be doubted away, because doubting is itself an instance of it.

That certainty carries something with it. The actual configuration you are certain of now isn’t the one you were certain of a moment ago. The reading has moved; the thought has shifted. What is undeniably actual has undeniably *changed*. The certainty of the actual doesn’t deliver a static point. It delivers a moving one. What changes is which configuration is actual, not the modal status of anything in it. And what moves isn’t merely possible change, not merely permitted change, but actual change: the fact everything else in this argument runs on.

What change is, and what Reality must be like for it to obtain, is the next question.

## 1.3 Change
The Introduction’s appeal to conceiving was already an appeal to change: to conceive is to pass from one cognitive state to another. **Change** names the concrete transition instantiated in that act and in the reading, doubting, and recognition by which it is noticed. The act fixes the referent; the analysis that follows progressively resolves what that same Change contains.

Change is the most ordinary fact there is. Its certainty is Cartesian: minimal observation that survives doubt, the same kind of certainty the cogito secures. In each familiar case of doubt (dream, illusion, even simulation), something is still *shifting*. That is all the witness needs. The certainty is of the *actuality* of change; from actuality, possibility follows.

The full defense of the witness, and the modal derivation that lifts it into a necessity claim about Reality’s structure, comes in Chapter 2. For now, change supplies the actuality-datum from which the derivation begins.

The Reality analysis extracted three roles (succession, distinction, exchange) from what Reality must provide for possibility (§1.1). The same three are reached from a second direction: what change requires.

**[Definition]**

**Change** · **C** · *Definition*

The concrete transition witnessed here, at minimum resolution: one state, then another.

The phrase fixes one actual phenomenon with the fewest words that identify it; it isn’t an exhaustive analysis of that phenomenon and doesn’t introduce a second, maximally thin object called generic change. At first resolution, “then” marks the ordering displayed by Change: one phase gives way to another. Whether that ordering resolves into Temporality, and what else the witnessed transition contains, are the discoveries the argument now earns without changing what Change refers to.

*Tested against.* The objections to the change-as-primitive thesis developed here are answered in §8.1 and §8.3.

i. *Succession.* If one state follows another, there must be a before and after. “Then” runs in one direction. A bare sequence of labels carries order, but the word *before* doesn’t tell you how long before, or whether anything lasts between the states at all. Whether this bare ordering carries genuine duration (an interval that can be longer or shorter, a moment or a millennium) is what naming Temporality settles at §1.4. At this stage succession requires only the ordering itself: a before and an after.

ii. *Distinction.* If the later phase were simply identical to the earlier one, nothing would have changed. That establishes genuine non-identity at the first resolution; it doesn’t yet turn successive difference into Spatiality. The witnessed Change contains more than successive non-identity: in the recognition of doubt, the standpoint, what it attends to, and the earlier content retained in the recognition are jointly present and differentiated within one episode. Whether that concrete co-present otherness resolves into Spatiality is argued rather than assumed at §1.4.2 and §2.4.7.

iii. *Exchange.* Succession and distinction appear at the minimal resolution of the witnessed Change; exchange requires the closer look, and that is exactly its status. Picture a sequence with succession and distinction and nothing else: one state, then a wholly unconnected other (a cat, then a galaxy, then the number seven). There’s order, and there’s difference, but nothing crosses between them. That is a slideshow, not a change. It’s what Russell’s ‘at-at’ theory of motion says change reduces to: an object at different places at different times, with nothing crossing in between (the frozen-instant picture of Zeno’s arrow). What separates a change from a slideshow is that something is carried across the interval: what the first state held, the second takes up. This is the further requirement exchange names: *what connects departure to arrival*. It isn’t succession (the ordering) or distinction (the difference) but the substitution itself. Think of a wave crossing water: no drop travels with it, yet the wave moves on. Each stretch of water passes its motion to the next, and the wave continues because the motion is taken up, not because anything is carried bodily across. Whether this requirement is genuinely non-optional (whether a bare-succession model is an adequate analysis of the witnessed Change) isn’t settled here by analysis of the word; it’s named now and discharged at §2.4 (and against the Humean reading at §8.2.2). The illustration fixes the structural role exchange picks out and imports neither productive-causation metaphysics nor a persisting thing that does the crossing.

Exchange takes the most unpacking of the three. What holds a change together? Something carries over: the first state doesn’t simply disappear while an unrelated second state arrives.

The carrying can be registered from within an act. Hold a thought across the arrival of the next and the first doesn’t simply lapse; it is borne forward by what is having it. The same structure appears in embodied action: push a door and encounter resistance, grip a railing and feel it bear weight, carry a burden and feel the carrying. These aren’t merely impressions of events that follow one another. They register the exchange from within rather than infer it from outside.

The claim remains limited. Exchange names the carrying-forward that distinguishes change from a bare sequence; it doesn’t yet decide what metaphysical account of that carrying is correct. Any alternative must nevertheless explain how a genuine change differs from an ordered series of unconnected states. (On whether the exchange a change requires is anything more than Humean constant conjunction. Grant the Humean reading at full strength: the phenomenology of resistance isn’t by itself evidence of a persisting medium, and the impression-reading (constant conjunction plus a felt residue) is a live option the argument owes a reply to. Even there, the argument still owes an account of why exchange is a third requirement alongside succession and distinction rather than a projection onto bare succession. That burden isn’t discharged by the definition; it is taken up through the Cartesian-certainty closure on change (§2.2), while Humean constant-conjunction, primitive-asymmetry, and Best System accounts of the persistence-medium requirement are engaged on their own terms at Humean Contingency (§8.2.2).) That is a bill the rivals inherit rather than a claim they can decline: a view may reject every account of carrying on offer and still owes the difference between a change and a sequence. Whether the three-role analysis survives them is tested across §8.1–8.3 and gathered in §8.4.

The definition is descriptive and reference-fixing, not engineered. It isn’t the weakest concept the lowercase word *change* might be made to bear; it fixes Change as the transition Reality demonstrably contains (the reading of this sentence, the doubting across it, the recognition that retains the doubt), named with the fewest words that pick it out unambiguously. Later analysis adds no new subject to Change and changes no meaning mid-proof; it makes explicit the structure the fixed witness already displayed. Alternative concepts engineered to lack succession, or distinction, or exchange describe something else; whatever they describe, it isn’t the change Reality contains. The minimalism is the discipline of the description: no causation imported, no persistence presupposed, no identity-through-time stipulated (no commitment about what makes a thing the same thing across the change). These are what the later derivations must earn from the change itself, not pre-load into the word naming it. Anyone presently reading, doubting, or recognizing the doubt has direct access to its referent and can accept the occurrence, whether they think causation is a law of nature, a habit of the mind, or the work of a creator. The definition commits to none of those positions. It commits only to the occurrence.

Succession and distinction are read off the witnessed Change by analysis, not added to it: its minimal description already carries an ordering and a difference. Exchange is different in status: it is the further requirement that separates the witnessed Change from a bare sequence of unconnected states, named here but defended downstream rather than read off the words. For each role the reader’s check is whether it’s extracted from the fixed phenomenon or imported beside it.

The contestation over what change is runs deep. Process metaphysicians and dispositional realists treat change as primitive and productive; Russellian and Lewisian reductionists treat it as nothing but ordered states; Humean regularity views treat the carrying as a projection from constant conjunction; Aristotelian act-and-potency views treat it as the actualization of a potential. The reference-fixing description stands neutral among them all. It names what Reality contains; the metaphysical reading is reserved for §2.4 and §8.2.2, where the live alternatives are engaged on their own terms. The two priority orderings recur here. On the essence-first reading, the three requirements (succession, distinction, exchange) belong to the real definition of Reality’s change in Fine’s sense: part of what change essentially is. On the modal-first reading, they are necessary for change without an essence prior to modality. The argument takes up the choice at §7.2.1; modal monism requires the second (§2.9.7), while the first remains live only at the price of giving up that result.

## 1.4 Three Conditions
Change displays three things in the concrete witness that fixed its reference: a before and an after to run between, genuinely distinct states to move among, and something that carries across from the one to the next. The previous section began resolving these three roles (succession, distinction, exchange) from the witnessed Change (§1.3); here they take their proper names. Temporality is what makes a change’s sequence irreversible, Spatiality what holds the concrete co-present poles within its recognition genuinely apart, Substantiality what lets each state carry over into the next: the three Conditions on any non-vacuous reality, each defended at full strength in Chapter 2.

Succession, distinction, and exchange don’t come apart. The reading of this page is one activity, not three. It runs forward: each sentence follows the last into a sequence that can’t be reordered. It runs across: the words on the page and the mind reading them are separated by an interval the meaning must cross. And it carries: each word hands off to the next. Imagine the opposite: each word annihilated the instant it is left behind, with nothing connecting the leaving to the arriving. The sentence would collapse behind itself rather than continue forward. You don’t experience the sequence, the separation, and the carrying as three separate features of reading. They are one thing: a line running from the first word to this one. Remove any one and the reading doesn’t weaken; it stops altogether. The reading is offered here as illustration, not as the proof: the load-bearing derivation runs from the bare fact of change, independent of any particular example (§2.4), and is corroborated from below, without leaning on a reader, at §3.2—which reaches the generic role-floor rather than re-running the full derivation.

What the reading shows is why the three don’t come apart *in it*: they aren’t three ingredients that merely combine into an activity. All three constitute the reading of this sentence, and the same inseparability is present in the words used to describe it. Whether inseparability holds of the Conditions themselves, and not only of this illustration, is §2.6.7’s to establish.

Take the word *forward*: temporal (what comes next), spatial (what lies ahead), and physical (each word bringing the next) all at once. The pages behind you are *behind* in both senses (spatially in the binding, temporally already read), and the pages ahead are *ahead* in both. *Behind* and *in front* don’t choose between the dimensions; in the reading, every before is also an elsewhere.

Each Condition is a structural role: what makes succession, distinction, or exchange possible. Paired with each is its *bearer*, the thing that actually has the role: Time for Temporality, Space for Spatiality, Substance for Substantiality. The two are layers of one fact.

### 1.4.1 Time
What any succession runs in is *Time*. A before and an after aren’t yet a genuine order: for the earlier to give onto the later, rather than stand as two labels that could be swapped, there has to be an order that runs one way and that a state can occupy. That occupiable order is Time.

Time bears *Temporality*, the Condition that makes *succession* possible, the first role change named in §1.3. It must do two things on its own: run one way, and reach across the whole sequence rather than only between neighbors. A third feature—that what comes before bears on what comes after—belongs to the sequence as well, but not to Time alone: the bearing is Substance’s contribution (§1.4.3), exercised along Time’s order.

i. *Asymmetry.* The before/after relation runs one way. A-before-B isn’t B-before-A; the two aren’t interchangeable labels for the same relation. The line just read can’t be un-read, not for lack of technology, but because *un-reading* names no act. Asymmetry gives temporal order its direction.

ii. *Transitivity.* The ordering composes. If A precedes B and B precedes C, then A precedes C: the first sentence remains before the last, regardless of how many sentences sit between. Without transitivity, “before” would be a local fact between adjacent states only, and Time would dissolve into a heap of comparisons that cannot be stitched into a sequence.

iii. *Directionality.* What comes before bears on what comes after. Each sentence sets the conditions into which the next one lands. A merely ordered list has first, second, and third items, but nothing about the first constrains the second. Directionality makes the sequence one of settings rather than labels. What Time itself supplies here is only the one-way, composable order the bearing runs along; the bearing itself is carrying, Substantiality’s work (§1.4.3). Directionality therefore belongs to how the role is realized rather than to what the modal proof spends, a split fixed at §2.4: the derivations use Asymmetry and Transitivity alone (§2.4.6), and the causal reading of direction is argued where realization is (§8.2.2, §4.2).

The forward foreclosures in §1.1—you can’t plan for yesterday or remember the future—already displayed Time’s signature. Succession named the same fact from inside Change (§1.3). Time adds duration and—in coordination with Substance—directed weight: a list of labels has order, but no interval and no answer to how the first bears on the second.

What is structural in that addition, and what isn’t, should be fixed while the meaning is being fixed. The order is structural: that states stand one before another, directed and composable, is what Time *is*. The measure isn’t: how much interval there is—the clock, the count, the metric—is content a particular world supplies, and duration rides on succession rather than the reverse. On the account introduced here, a moment is a position in the order of states rather than a vessel that remains when the states are removed; moments are told apart by which state occupies them. That account supports a stronger downstream claim: where nothing differs—no state, no arrangement, no bearing of before on after—multiplying one moment into many requires primitive temporal individuation that the present definition doesn’t supply. It doesn’t yet establish that no rival account can supply such individuation. Shoemaker’s time-without-change case is engaged at §8.1.1 and §4.6.5.

The relation Time secures is *Precedence*: one state genuinely stands before another. Time here names the order in which moments are distinct, directed, and lasting. This chapter fixes that meaning. Chapter 2 asks whether Temporality, together with Spatiality and Substantiality, is merely instantiated in this world or required by any possible reality.

The account doesn’t decide between the A-theory and B-theory of time. Both require an ordered succession. Nor does it treat Time as a self-standing container independent of what occurs; the later philosophy-of-physics discussion takes up those questions on their own ground.

**[Condition]**

**Temporality** · **T** · *Condition*

The Condition that makes succession possible: whatever it takes for before to genuinely give onto after along one directed, lasting order, rather than the two standing as interchangeable labels. Borne in Reality by Time.

### 1.4.2 Space
What any distinction stands in is *Space*. Two states can be called different and still not stand apart: for here and there to be genuinely distinct, rather than one position wearing two names, there has to be a real interval that something can occupy and cross. That occupiable interval is Space.

Space bears *Spatiality*, the Condition that makes *distinction* possible, the second role change named in §1.3. It must do three things at once: set positions a real interval apart, keep complete configurations from coinciding in one position, and allow relation to pass across the interval. These three aren’t deduced from bare distinction—two things can differ without standing apart. They specify the role that separation plays in change, the role the argument will spend: bare numerical difference is the logician’s notion, and what change requires is the stronger, occupiable kind fixed here.

Put in the capacity idiom, Spatiality is Reality’s capacity for a genuine here and there, for this and that to coexist without collapsing into one. Bare numerical plurality doesn’t yet establish the Condition: two numbers or two descriptions may differ without standing anywhere apart. The capacity for more than one concrete relatum to be present together, each accessible as other than the other, does. That capacity isn’t a power waiting behind Space. It is Space at the structural resolution fixed here: the real-separation relation in virtue of which a co-present many can be many at all.

i. *Extension.* Positions are separated by a real interval, not merely by different labels. The text in front of you stands apart from you: separated by air, by the focal distance of the eye, and by whatever medium carries print to the gaze. “Here” and “there” name two places, not one place described twice.

ii. *Exclusivity.* Each position holds one complete configuration at a time. A closed book can’t be read because the page now facing the reader is already occupied by another page pressed flat against it. Without exclusivity, distinct configurations could coincide with nothing to separate them, and their distinction would be distinction in name only. Exclusivity is fixed at the level of complete configurations, not individual occupants: two fields may overlap and two objects may co-locate, but their joint state is then the one configuration that position holds. What exclusivity rules out is two complete rival states of the same position.

iii. *Traversability.* The interval is crossable. It isn’t merely a logical gap between two terms but a distance through which attention, motion, or influence can pass. An interval that nothing could cross would leave its two sides sealed off: no relation could run between them. Traversability is crossability in principle—the interval is the kind of gap relation can span, whether or not anything actually crosses it. Which crossings a world makes available—its metric, dimension, and topology—is content that world supplies, taken up at §4.3.

The examples of §1.1 and §1.3 come together here. Space is what makes separation real rather than descriptive. Extension keeps two places from collapsing into one; exclusivity keeps multiple configurations from collapsing within one place; traversability makes the interval a path for relation rather than a wall.

The relation Space secures is *Separation*: here and there stand genuinely apart. This chapter fixes that meaning. Chapter 2 asks whether Spatiality, together with Temporality and Substantiality, is merely instantiated in this world or required by any possible reality.

The account doesn’t decide whether space is a self-standing structure or nothing over and above relations among bodies. It commits only to the point needed here: the distinction change requires is real separation—an interval something can occupy and in principle cross. Whether every distinction whatsoever demands so much isn’t claimed by the definition; that stronger question is argued, not assumed, where the role is spent (§2.4.7) and where the cross-entailments are tested (§2.6).

**[Condition]**

**Spatiality** · **S** · *Condition*

The Condition that makes distinction possible: whatever it takes for here and there to stand genuinely apart across a real, crossable interval, rather than one position wearing two names. Borne in Reality by Space.

### 1.4.3 Substance
What carries across is *Substance*. The term is metaphysical here, not chemical: it doesn’t mean a material of uniform composition, and it need not be matter. Ordered, distinct states can still sit side by side: nothing yet passes from one to the next. For one state to give something to another, rather than lapse while an unrelated successor arrives, there has to be a real carrying relation. *Substance* names whatever occupies the carrier-role in that relation. This doesn’t yet decide whether the occupant is best understood as a persisting object, a field, a process, a trope, a bundle, or a Humean pattern, or whether the relation is productive causation; those are downstream questions.

Substance bears *Substantiality*, the Condition that makes *exchange* possible, the third role change named in §1.3. The stronger account defended downstream takes exchange to require three things at once: distinct terms, something that genuinely bears and transmits what is carried, and continuity through the transition. Of these, the modal derivations spend Distinctness and Persistence outright (§2.4.8), and Holding only as a role-requirement, the empty case excluded; *Transmission*, the further question whether the occupant carries by productive causation rather than by regularity or process continuity, is argued where realization is (§8.2.2, §4.4). Temporality and Substantiality differ here. Directionality is both a question about realization and one of Temporality’s three properties (§1.4.1); Transmission is a question about realization only, and isn’t one of Substantiality’s three.

i. *Distinctness.* The terms of exchange must be distinguishable: what carries and what takes up the carrying can’t collapse into one undifferentiated state. The same being may occupy both roles at different stages; self-interaction and internal change aren’t excluded. What exchange requires is numerical non-identity between its relata as states or roles, not necessarily between two beings and not merely as spatial separation.

ii. *Holding.* Holding requires that the carrier-role be genuinely occupied: something holds what is carried and makes it available across the transition. The page carries the print: it holds it against erasure and makes it available to the reader’s gaze. A supposed carrier with nothing to hold would be an empty placeholder where carrying ought to be. This is a role-requirement, not an ontology: a persisting object, a process, or a Humean pattern that sustains the regularity occupies the role equally well, and whether the occupant *transmits* by productive causation is a downstream question (§8.2.2, §4.4), not part of the role. What the role excludes is only the empty case, where “carrier” names no occupant at all.

iii. *Persistence.* The carrying remains continuous through the transition. This is a continuity condition on exchange, not yet a theory of which entity persists or what secures its identity through time. The page doesn’t vanish after one word and reappear for the next; without continuity, the page that holds the first word and the page that holds the second would be two pages, and nothing would have been carried forward. Persistence doesn’t require a frozen core untouched by change. It requires an unbroken continuity of carrying.

Holding and persistence are close but distinct. Holding concerns whether something can carry anything at all; persistence concerns whether the carrying runs unbroken across the transition. Together with distinctness, the two features specify what it is for exchange to be real.

The capacity to carry isn’t itself the temporal ordering across which it’s exercised: Temporality supplies the before-and-after order, while Substantiality supplies what has a determinate capacity to be carried or made effective in that order. A physical theory may therefore describe the fundamental realizer in an atemporal vocabulary and still owe an account of how a determinate capacity is realized in the emergent order; removing fundamental clock-time doesn’t by itself erase the carrier-role.

The relation Substance supplies is the causal-bearing role: one state can be connected to what happens in another. Whether that connection is best analyzed as productive causation, Humean regularity, process continuity, or another account is earned downstream rather than built into the role here. This chapter fixes the meaning of Substance as what bears continuity through change. Chapter 2 asks whether Substantiality, together with Temporality and Spatiality, is merely instantiated in this world or required by any possible reality.

The account doesn’t decide what kind of entity a substance ultimately is. The later discussion takes up the disputes among substance, trope, bundle, and process accounts. The point here is prior to those alternatives: if anything is carried through change, there must be a real carrier.

**[Condition]**

**Substantiality** · **Φ** · *Condition*

The Condition that makes exchange possible: whatever it takes for one state to genuinely carry something into the next, rather than lapsing while an unrelated successor arrives. Borne in Reality by Substance.

### 1.4.4 Triconditional Structure
Time, Space, and Substance arrive together. A change requires all three at once: something must persist, through an ordered succession, across real distinctions. Naming them separately doesn’t divide what the change itself requires; it gives three aspects of one fact their three names.

The connection is visible in the concepts as fixed here—visible, not yet proved. Spatiality’s interval was specified as crossable in principle (§1.4.2), and Temporality’s order as one that states occupy in succession (§1.4.1). So each role-specification already mentions the work of the others: an order needs states that can be told apart; a crossable interval is one across which something could pass, and a passage has a before and an after; exchange must carry what is distinct into what comes next. That the specifications interlock is a fact about how the roles were fixed, and it is meant to be—change is one fact wearing three names. Whether the entailments hold independently, whether anything could realize one Condition without the others, isn’t settled by the definitions; it is argued, not assumed, where the cross-entailments are tested (§2.6).

| What change requires | The relation it makes possible |
| --- | --- |
| **Time** | Precedence: one state genuinely stands before another |
| **Space** | Separation: here and there genuinely stand apart |
| **Substance** | Exchange: one state genuinely connects to what happens in another |

Taken together, Time, Space, and Substance compose a single structure. That whole has a name.

**[Definition]**

**Nature** · *Definition*

The joint structure of Time, Space, and Substance: what any genuine change requires.

*Joint* is the word doing the work. Nature isn’t a fourth thing standing alongside Time, Space, and Substance, nor the bare list of them; it names the three in their inseparability, the triconditional structure whose relations the preceding table displays one at a time. Wherever a genuine change occurs, the whole structure is engaged: ordered succession, real separation, and bearing are exercised together or not at all.

Getting from London to Paris makes the same point concretely. The trip requires a route that stays intact for the whole crossing, a duration elapsing in one direction, and a traveler who survives to the far end. No particular way of crossing is required—go by water, by tunnel, by air, or even swim it—but whichever one is actually taken, none of it escapes the three underlying Conditions. Erase the distance and there is no way across; erase the duration and there is no departure followed by arrival; erase the traveler and nobody gets there. Drop any one and the trip doesn’t shorten or become harder. It simply isn’t possible.

Naming Nature settles only what the word means. That Nature must exist, that its three Conditions (Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality) hold of necessity, that there could never have been nothing at all: those stronger claims are Chapter 2’s, reached by asking what follows if change is genuinely possible. Whether the universe, in the widest sense, simply is Nature, and which account of time, space, or substance is ultimately correct, wait just as long. What this chapter needed is narrower: without Time, Space, and Substance together, there is no change for an argument to begin from.

## 1.5 Existence
To say that a thing *exists*, or that a property *is instantiated*, looks like the thinnest claim available: that something is simply there, a positing that commits one to nothing about what it is. Applied to concrete contents, it isn’t thin. To exist concretely, in the sense fixed at §1.1, *is* to instantiate Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: to stand within succession, distinction, and exchange rather than over against them. *Exists* doesn’t stand above the Conditions and reach down to posit a concrete thing apart from them; it carries them with it. This is a definition, not a stipulation: read as mere relabeling it would say nothing. It carries content because its terms are to be earned—and its exclusionary force is wholly deferred to where they are. Nothing here refutes abstracta, atemporal entities, or any rival account of what there is; the definition is the book’s official explication of *concrete existence*, adopted now so the argument has a fixed sense to work with, and cashed only as far as the later arguments carry it. Rival existents are engaged on their own ground in Chapters 8 and 10, not excluded by this sentence. A definition whose definiens is proved necessary is where the substantive claim of the book sits—downstream, where the proving is done, not here.

For formal reference, Concrete(x) means that x exists in this concrete sense: Concrete(x) =df T(x) ∧ S(x) ∧ Φ(x). The predicate doesn’t replace ordinary existential quantification; it records the book’s defined condition for concrete existence.

What holds for *exists* holds for the vocabulary it belongs to. A philosopher writes that one event *causes* another, that distinctness *obtains* between two real states, that a beam *bears* the load above it, that the whole *consists in* its parts in the right relation. Each italicized verb is doing work the sentence can’t do without. They are operators: the working vocabulary of analytic philosophy, how the discipline points at what is the case. Some are uncontested in the field; others are sharply contested. Each, applied to concrete contents, carries the same Conditions *exists* does.

These operators fall into families, and the boundaries between them are blurry: *consists in* and *grounds* overlap; *bears* and *causes* shade into each other in the productive reading. The sections that follow take the families one at a time.

### 1.5.1 Existence and Instantiation
A state of affairs *obtains* when it is the case; a relation *holds* between the things it relates; a property *holds of* its bearer; *is the case* is the most general: propositions assert what is the case, and what is the case is what propositions point at. *Exists* and *is instantiated* belong to the same family, with *exists* attached to particulars and *is instantiated* attached to universals. Take one case across the family: the cat is on the mat. The cat *exists*; the mat *exists*; the property of *being-on* is *instantiated* by the pair; the relation *holds* between the cat and the mat; the state of affairs that the cat is on the mat *obtains*; that the cat is on the mat *is the case*. The family looks transparent and isn’t. Each operator requires something to be there for the operator to apply: a state, the things a relation relates, a bearer, a how-things-are. (Here *exists* carries its ordinary, contingent reading: the cat exists but might not have. On a rival view in the metaphysics of modality, necessitism, the cat necessarily *is something* and is only contingently a concrete cat; that alternative is taken up at §7.2.7.)

**[Definition]**

**Existence** · *Definition*

To exist concretely is to occupy a when, a where, and a what: to stand in Time, Space, and Substance rather than outside them. A concrete thing’s existing just *is* that standing, not something extra added on top of what the thing already is.

The definition’s three demands are the ones §1.4 named: a when is a position in Time’s order, a where a place in Space’s interval, a what a standing in Substance’s carrying. The cat of the family survey exists in exactly this sense: it is sometime, somewhere, something, and its existing isn’t a further fact alongside those three but the three taken together. That is what the definition’s closing clause rules out: concrete existence as an extra ingredient a thing could have or lack while its when, where, and what stayed fixed.

Abstract existence is a different use of the existential vocabulary and not a counterexample to this definition. A number, proposition, set, or relation may be admitted as an abstract object without being assigned a moment or physical location; that admission commits the Platonist to determinate content and identity conditions, not yet to a concrete change-realizer. The fork becomes decisive when a candidate is said to act, change, experience, create, sustain, or cause. Those are concrete operations. A candidate performing one must supply the when, where, and what of the operation, even if the candidate is also described abstractly in another respect. Calling the candidate *abstract* preserves exemption from concrete location only by surrendering the concrete work attributed to it; retaining the work incurs the structural requirements of the work.

Whether anything could stand *outside* the three (whether there is a Null State to fall back to), and whether the Conditions they bear (Temporality, Spatiality, Substantiality, the vocabulary §1.4 fixed) are jointly required in every possible reality, are Chapter 2’s questions; this section fixes the sense in which they are asked.

### 1.5.2 Constitution
The relation isn’t only material; it runs at role level too.

**[Definition]**

**Constitution** · *Definition*

The relation between a thing and what it is made up of, read from either side: the clay *constitutes* the statue, and the statue *consists in* the clay.

*X consists in Y* reads the relation top-down: X is what Y, taken together or in the relevant relation, makes up. *Y constitutes X* reads it bottom-up, the same relation from the other side. The canonical case: the statue *consists in* the clay arranged statue-wise; the clay *constitutes* the statue. The operator also runs at higher levels of abstraction. A role or structural requirement *consists in* what it amounts to: *exchange consists in carrying-forward*; *change consists in succession, distinction, and exchange*. The pattern is the same (X is what Y, in the relevant relation, makes up), applied to roles and structural requirements rather than to material parts. The constitution operator runs across both readings, material constitution among tokens (the statue and its clay) and role-analytic constitution of structural requirements (exchange and carrying-forward), and the survey here covers both.

The two readings differ in their metaphysical commitments. Material constitution is mereological and token-level; role-analytic constitution is hyperintensional, able to tell two notions apart even when they hold of exactly the same things—a distinction finer than mere co-extension. The identity of X as what Y amounts to isn’t merely a matter of co-extension but of what X essentially is, in the sense operative at §7.2.1. The priority question taken up there is this: whether role-analytic constitution bottoms out in an essence prior to modality, or whether the modal field is primitive and role-analytic constitution describes its shape.

### 1.5.3 Inference
Inference is the act; entailment is the relation that licenses it.

**[Definition]**

**Entailment** · *Definition*

One claim guarantees another: *P entails Q* means there is no way for P to be true while Q is false.

Two readings should be distinguished at the outset: the *metalogical* reading (no interpretation or model in which P holds and Q fails, a formal-semantic relation) and the *modal-metaphysical* reading (no possible world in which P obtains and Q fails, an alethic relation). Throughout this book *entails* carries the modal-metaphysical reading unless the context is explicitly formal-logical; the Quinean concern that the slide between the two is illicit is addressed at §7.1.3–7.1.4 and §7.1.6. The textbook case: *Socrates is a bachelor* entails *Socrates is unmarried*. There is no possibility of the first holding while the second fails. *P implies Q* and *Q follows from P* name the same relation in most uses. *P necessitates Q* is the strong modal version: P’s holding requires Q’s holding in the alethic/metaphysical sense fixed at §1.2.1, not logical necessity (truth across all interpretations) and not nomological necessity (consistency with natural law). The operators are read formally as truth carrying over: in any case where P holds, Q holds too. Keeping the three apart matters here because they come apart later, and the reading chosen at this point decides which of them a downstream result is entitled to. How they stand to one another is worked out at §2.6.

### 1.5.4 Supervenience
Supervenience fixes covariation, not direction.

**[Definition]**

**Supervenience** · *Definition*

One range of facts is fixed by another: A *supervenes on* B when there can be no difference in A without some difference in B.

The relation isn’t symmetric, but neither is it asymmetric: as defined it is reflexive and transitive, so the one-way dependence belongs to the canonical case rather than to the operator itself. The names track the morphology: the *supervenient* (A) sits on top, the *subvenient* (B) sits beneath. A varies only as B varies; B may vary without A varying. The textbook case is the mental supervening on the physical: two physically identical configurations can’t differ in their mental states, but the physical can vary in ways the mental doesn’t track.

### 1.5.5 Ground and Dependence
Grounding and dependence are one relation, named from each end.

**[Definition]**

**Grounding** · *Definition*

Non-causal dependence: X *grounds* Y when Y holds *because of* X, where the *because* is metaphysical, not causal or temporal.

*Y depends on X* is the converse; *X is metaphysically prior to Y* names priority. This vocabulary is the working language of a recent literature: grounding emerged as a distinct philosophical category in the early 2000s, with Fine, Schaffer, and Rosen as its principal architects. The canonical case is Fine’s singleton: the set {Socrates} is grounded in Socrates, not the other way around. Socrates doesn’t exist *because of* his singleton; the singleton exists *because* Socrates does. The dependence runs one way only, and that one-way *because of* is what grounding picks out. P and Q together ground their conjunction; the conjunction doesn’t ground either P or Q. Adjacent operators (*fixes*, *makes the case*) name determination: specifying X is enough to settle Y.

Necessary-foundation accounts use the same grounding vocabulary while assigning its terminus differently. Their arguments and the present line are compared where that difference is in scope (§10.1.4). Nothing in this definition selects either terminus.

### 1.5.6 Causation
Of the four classical causes, only the efficient one is meant here.

**[Definition]**

**Causation** · *Definition*

One event brings about another: *X causes Y*. What the *bringing about* amounts to, mere regularity or real production, is the standing dispute.

This definition fixes the efficient or event-causal family—the family in which an effect is attributed to a source’s productive difference. It isn’t offered as a definition of every Aristotelian *aitia*. Material, formal, and final causes answer different explanatory questions, and metaphysical grounding has already been separated as non-causal dependence (§1.5.5). The distinction becomes a proof-scope boundary at §2.4 and a full taxonomy of causal roles at §11.7.2.

Causation is the most contested operator in the family. Hume read it minimally: *X causes Y* reduces to constant conjunction, X-events reliably followed by Y-events, plus a felt expectation projected by the observer. Anti-Humean readings treat causation as a productive relation: one event genuinely makes another happen, and the felt push-and-yield is part of what causation is. The canonical case is Hume’s billiard ball: one ball strikes another and the second moves. The Humean sees only contact, motion, and our expectation of the pattern; the anti-Humean sees one ball *making* the other move. *Produces*, *brings about*, *gives rise to*, *issues from* foreground production rather than regularity. The Humean reads them as habits of speech standing on top of constant conjunction; the anti-Humean reads them as picking out a real productive relation. Either way, the operators are how the field talks about one event making another happen. The book inherits from Hume the methodological discipline he made central (the careful refusal to slide from the felt to the structural without an argument), and disagrees with him metaphysically on whether causation is regularity or production; the metaphysical disagreement is taken up at §2.4 and §8.2.2.

### 1.5.7 Medium of Transmission
*Bears*, *carries*, *transmits*, *supports*, *sustains*: verbs of medium, common in philosophy of physics (the field carries the force) and in ordinary metaphysical prose (the relation bears its term).

**[Definition]**

**Medium** · *Definition*

What carries or sustains something across: a beam *bears* a load, a wire *carries* a current. A medium can bear without producing.

A medium can bear without producing. On productive accounts of causation, production also requires something to bear or transmit what is produced; regularity accounts deny that any further productive relation is needed. Here *medium* names this general transmission operator, not a role-term for Nature or a synonym for the bearer of Substantiality, which is Substance (§1.4.3).

### 1.5.8 Persistence
*Persists*, *endures*, *perdures*, *remains*, *continues*: operators of persistence.

**[Definition]**

**Persistence** · *Definition*

Existing across more than one time or through a change, whether by enduring, perduring, or another continuity relation.

*Persistence* is the generic category. Endurantism holds that a thing is wholly present at every moment of its existence; perdurantism holds that it persists by having temporal parts. The terms also appear in ordinary metaphysical prose to name what survives a transition. Heraclitus’s river is the canonical case: a river persists while its water turns over, and the question of how it does so is what the endurantist / perdurantist split tries to resolve.

### 1.5.9 What the Operators Require
The operators do their metaphysical work when they are applied to concrete contents within Reality, when the discipline reaches for what acts, changes, bears, produces, or persists. That is the claim’s scope. Operator-use considered formally apart from concrete subject matter isn’t what the claim addresses: logic and set theory running their operators over abstract material.

So restricted, the paradigm concrete operators require what any change requires: Time, Space, and Substance. Take *causes*: it links events that are distinct, ordered as before and after, and connected by what runs from one to the other. *Bears* and *persists* wear the same requirements openly. For *obtains*, *consists in*, *entails*, and *grounds* the claim is thinner and staged. Applied abstractly, they require determinate terms and a determinate relation, but that generic floor isn’t yet Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. Applied concretely—to a production, intervention, changing experience, or sustained effect—they inherit the full requirements of the concrete operation. Atemporal entailment between propositions and atemporal grounding among them therefore stand at this point as live rivals rather than casualties of the definition. Whether those readings can ground concrete actuality without an additional point of contact is argued where rival ultimates are engaged (§10), with the priority question at §7.2.1; it isn’t settled here.

This yields the test used downstream. Ask of a proposed entity: *when does it obtain, where is it distinguished from what it isn’t, and what bears its determinate character or activity?* An abstract object may decline the first two questions only while declining concrete activity with them. A concrete entity or operation must answer all three at the resolution its activity requires. A posit that supplies determinate abstract content may remain a live abstractum; a posit that supplies concrete operation incurs Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality; a posit that supplies neither determinate content nor a determinate relation supplies no entity or ground at all. The alternatives are exhaustive because they classify the work attributed to the candidate, not the vocabulary used to protect it.

The claim isn’t a reduction of grounding, essence, or any other operator to Time, Space, and Substance. Grounding as a metaphysical, hyperintensional dependence relation (Fine 2012; Schaffer 2009) remains sui generis. Chapter 7 tests whether an essence- or grounding-prior account can stand before the modal field (§7.2.1). Chapter 2 supplies the formal register for the present claim: it asks whether Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, the Conditions the triad bears (§1.4), are necessary in every possible reality.

With that, the Groundwork is complete: Reality, the modal statuses, Change, the Conditions, and existence are fixed in the senses the argument will use. Chapter 2 doesn’t begin empty-handed. Reality’s no-exteriority has been argued; the global capacity idiom, Change itself, and the role-specifications of the three Conditions have been fixed; and the actual reflective datum has been identified. What hasn’t yet been defended in full force is what the proof must earn from them: bilateral modal invariance, the certainty and necessary possibility of Change, the Structural Requirement, and the necessity and identity results that follow.

# 2. The Argument

Chapter 1 introduced the three Conditions that any genuine change requires: Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, each borne in Reality by Time, Space, and Substance. The question now is stronger: are they merely features of this world, or the necessary constitution of Reality’s complete modal field?

The line begins with ground already in hand, but not with its conclusions assumed. Reality’s no-exteriority, and the meanings of Reality, Change, and the three Conditions, are inherited from Chapter 1. The modal invariance of possibility, the necessary possibility of Change, the Structural Requirement, and the necessity of the Conditions are not. Those are the burdens discharged here.

**[Argument]**

**Necessity of Nature** · *The Cogito–S5 Pipeline*

1. **Whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary**, and whatever is impossible, its impossibility is necessary. The line that separates them is fixed and invariant. *(Necessary Possibility, §2.1)*

2. **Change is possible.** The certainty is in the act of denial itself. *(§2.2)*

3. **The possibility of change is necessary.** (*from 1 and 2*) *(§2.3)*

4. **The possibility of change necessarily requires temporal, spatial, and substantial conditions.** *(The Structural Requirement, §2.4)*

5. **Therefore, Reality is necessarily temporal, spatial, and substantial.** This establishes the Conditions’ joint necessity. The stronger claim that they are internally co-requiring aspects of one operative structure is a further argument *(§2.6)*, not part of this inference. (*From 3 and 4*) *(§2.5)*

The modal proof closes at step 5. It needs the global-capacity account, the witnessed possibility of Change, and the forward Structural Requirement. It does **not** need the converse from structure to change, the pairwise cross-entailments, or the one-fact identity reading. Those stronger results begin at §2.6 and must stand on their own premises.

Each step is defended in the section named beside it, with its formal statement and notation set out where it is earned. There are then two further lanes. **The identity lane** asks what the necessary conjunction amounts to: §2.6 argues for one operative structure, §2.7 closes the Null State, §2.8 tests whether Reality exceeds Nature, and §2.9 gathers the whole line. **The extension lane** develops the result’s consequences for logic at §§2.11.1–2.11.3. Mathematical and physical realization are tested with the convergence accounting at §3.5.6, to which §§2.11.4–2.11.5 provide direct routes; the historical and contemporary neighborhood is mapped at §3.5.7, indexed from §2.10. These are downstream applications and comparisons, not premises of the proof. A reader testing only the central inference can therefore read §§2.1–2.5 and then the formal gathering at §2.9. A reader testing the stronger ontology must also test every added bridge in §§2.6–2.8.

## 2.1 The S5 Pipeline
Around 36,000 to 11,000 years ago, it was possible to cross from Asia to America by foot. Then the ice melted, the sea rose, and the Bering land bridge went with it. Today the same crossing takes a boat or a plane, and no amount of waiting on the shore brings the footpath back. Does that mean possibilities come and go? The coastlines changed, the land bridge vanished, and the walk stalls at the water's edge. But none of those changes make land bridges—or any journey across one—impossible. Land bridges are still possible, and so is walking. What closed was an occasion, not its possibility.

That distinction gets us only partway. It shows that a real possibility can outlast the occasion that makes it available. The stronger claim is that the possibility never depended on that occasion in the first place. The coast supplies the occasion; Reality supplies the capacity. An occasion is just one way Reality expresses. Before it can make anything available, it must itself already be something Reality has the capacity for. It cannot grant the capacity it needs in order to arise. Circumstances can determine which possibilities are actual, or available now; they cannot draw the line between what Reality has the capacity for and what it does not.

Reality is the one whole, and it has no exterior (§1.1); its capacity for a claim is the complete range within which it can admit that claim, and in full extension that range is the modal maximum (§1.2.1). Chapter 1 fixed those meanings without inferring their invariance. The present section carries no-exteriority into the modal question: could an evaluation supply a genuinely different total range, or would any real alternative already fall within the maximum it was supposed to replace?

This is an ontologically one-Reality argument. The possible-world vocabulary used in standard modal logic is retained only as a translation device and as language in which rival views can be answered. A “possible world” in that apparatus represents a complete configuration Reality could admit; it isn’t a second Reality, a container around Reality, or an entity the proof quantifies over as its ground. The proof itself runs on Reality and its capacity.

The section builds that answer in four stages, then meets the central objection to it. Modal Bivalence (§2.1.1) fixes the two verdicts; the Bilateral Frame (§2.1.2) fixes how the modal constraint is identified, by what it permits and what it precludes together; Modal Constitution (§2.1.3) separates occupancy from invariance; Modal Stability (§2.1.4) earns the invariance itself. The objection is that each represented world or local state might own its own horizon of the possible, and the Bottleneck (§2.1.5) is where it is met. A short dispatch at §2.1.6 sends the narrower local Transition Closure to its stress-test home (§3.1.2); it does not replace the Bottleneck or independently establish proposition-wise modal invariance.

What the section reaches is schematic: it fixes a proposition’s modal status once that status is known, and establishes no substantive antecedent. The Cartesian witness supplies the positive content the canonical proof needs (§2.2), and the prohibition-side content used to identify the constraint is made concrete at §2.4. Modal Persistence and Invariance (§2.1.7) separates the diachronic and cross-world indices of the one theorem; Candidate-Ground Convergence (§2.1.8) dispatches candidate-ground applications to Chapter 3; §2.1.9 fixes what necessity transfer requires; and Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10) assembles the result.

*What the proof spends here.* The formal S5 line runs through Modal Bivalence (§2.1.1), Modal Constitution (§2.1.3), the global-capacity derivation (§2.1.4), its defense at the Bottleneck (§2.1.5), and the theorem (§2.1.10). The Bilateral Frame (§2.1.2) does different work: it governs the later identification of what that invariant modal constraint consists in, and is spent at §2.4. Transition Closure (§3.1.2) and §2.1.7–2.1.9 remain auxiliary to both lines.

### 2.1.1 Modal Bivalence
A fair coin is tossed once. Heads and tails are both possible; only one becomes actual. If it lands tails, the claim that this toss lands heads is false. It isn’t therefore impossible. Truth and modal status have sorted the same claim differently.

The difference is between two questions. Truth asks whether a claim obtains in the actual configuration: it holds, or it does not. Modal status asks whether Reality admits what the claim describes at all. For any contentful claim, Reality either has the capacity for it or lacks it: the claim is really possible, or it is not. This is classical excluded middle applied to a modal predicate. It fixes the available verdicts without deciding which verdict any particular claim receives.

Something is either possible, or it isn’t. There is no third option. That is Modal Bivalence. It isn’t ordinary truth bivalence repeated with modal symbols. A proposition can be actually false and still possible, as tomorrow’s rain may be; it can be actually true and contingent, as today’s weather is. Truth and modal status apply the same two-answer grammar to different facts.

**[Premise]**

**Modal Bivalence** · *Premise*

For any contentful claim, either it is really possible or it is not: the two modal verdicts are exhaustive. ∀P: ◇P ∨ ¬◇P.

The premise says *contentful*, and that qualifier isn’t hedging. Vagueness can look like a third answer. It is instead a problem about whether the words have fixed a claim to which either answer can apply. A string that fails to determine a proposition hasn’t acquired a modal status between possibility and impossibility; it has failed to give the modal verdict a subject.

A genuine challenge begins only after a contentful P is in hand. The critic must then reject something in the logical framework: the capacity for truth or falsity, classical negation, exhaustiveness, exclusivity, or a consequence rule used downstream. Each is a live position rather than a verbal confusion.

Consider dialetheism. Graham Priest allows that some propositions are both true and false, challenging truth-value exclusivity. That doesn’t yet produce ◇P ∧ ¬◇P. The second conjunct says that P is impossible, not merely that P is false. A dialetheist who means to reject modal exclusivity here must extend the glut to the modal predicate itself, so that both ◇P and its negation hold. Even then, the disjunction ◇P ∨ ¬◇P may remain true; what fails is the classical claim that exactly one disjunct holds. Paraconsistent positions may instead revise what follows from a contradiction, while intuitionist positions may reject some of the reductios the later argument uses.

The present argument adopts both exhaustiveness and exclusivity. The distinction matters: the displayed disjunction supplies exhaustiveness, while classical negation and consequence supply the claim that both verdicts can’t hold together. The later argument therefore can’t answer a revisionary logic merely by repeating the disjunction. It must meet the revision where the consequence is used. The Incoherence of ∅ argument does that for the Null State (§2.7.2), and the engagement with the catuṣkoṭi tests the four corners separately while leaving open the wider dispute over positive metaphysical thesis-making (§10.3.4).

The disjunction fixes one thing: the two verdicts over which the later invariance theorem ranges. It doesn’t show that either verdict is invariant across worlds, that both sides are occupied, or that any particular proposition is possible. Each requires a further argument.

*Taking stock.* Every contentful proposition receives one of the two modal verdicts under the classical framework used here: really possible, or not. The result is modal exhaustiveness, not yet modal invariance.

*Tested against.* Fictionalism questions whether modal statements bear truth values at all (§7.2.6). Dialetheist and paraconsistent revisions challenge classical exclusivity or consequence; the argument meets them where it spends those commitments, in the Incoherence of ∅ argument and the catuṣkoṭi engagement (§2.7.2; §10.3.4). Dappled-world and deflationist views question whether R has one standing modal capacity (§7.1.6). Quietism doubts that the disjunction is meaningful at all (§7.1.7).

### 2.1.2 Bilateral Frame
Modal Bivalence hands down two verdicts, and the rest of the proof is built on both.

A one-sided reading of Modal Bivalence would emphasize only possibility: there are possibilities, and the question is what underwrites them. The Necessity-of-Nature proof refuses that asymmetry. Possibility and impossibility matter equally. The argument needs witnesses under both statuses because the *modal constraint* is identified by its bilateral work: what permits some change and prohibits other change. A constraint that only permits is a permission, not yet the modal constraint on change. A constraint that only prohibits is a prohibition, not yet the modal constraint on change. Whatever it is about Reality that fixes the modal status of change has to do both, and the proof has to engage both.

This bilateral framing is implicit in Modal Bivalence itself (the modal constraint does permission-work and prohibition-work alike), but it is now made structurally explicit. Its witnesses come from different places. Cartesian Certainty (§2.2) supplies the positive witness: change is actual, and therefore possible. Contradiction and Modal Self-Sustenance (§2.1.3) occupy the negative pole schematically; that pole is given the content the structural identification spends at §2.4, and the specific application to the Null State is earned later (§2.7). Temporality permits succession and prohibits an after preceding its own before. Spatiality permits coexistence and prohibits collapsed positional occupancy, including the square circle. Substantiality permits qualitative change and prohibits an exchange with nothing bearing it. The positive and negative descriptions are not separate laws imposed on the Conditions. Together they specify what each Condition is.

**[Principle]**

**Bilateral Frame** · *Principle*

The modal constraint is identified by its bilateral work: a constraint that only permits is a permission, not yet a constraint on change. Any account that underwrites possibility without equally underwriting impossibility has not described the modal constraint. This is not merely a requirement later premises must satisfy. It is the method by which the invariant constraint is identified with T∧S∧Φ. There is no shortcut through possibility alone.

That identification is carried out at §2.4, the Structural Requirement.

*Tested against.* Chapters 7 and 8 meet the objections to the bilateral reading of Modal Bivalence: the requirement that the modal constraint do permission-work and prohibition-work alike. The canonical one-sided position is the Humean denial of necessary connection, which grants permissions but resists prohibitions as anything beyond regularity (§8.2.2). Lewis presses whether plenitude permits everything and so loses the prohibition side (§7.2.3), and fictionalism presses one-sided modal commitment (§7.2.6). Williamson’s necessitism shares bilateral modal invariance (§7.2.7), and dappled-world accounts ask whether the bilateral reading scales beyond local domains (§7.1.6).

### 2.1.3 Modal Constitution
Modal status answers to Reality’s complete permitting and precluding boundary rather than to how any particular configuration is arranged. One scope limit belongs with that claim rather than beneath it, since it fixes what the later invariance theorem does and doesn’t cover: the invariance is over real, metaphysical modal status—whether P obtains in Reality—not over what remains ideally conceivable under a primary intension, and not over what is epistemically open. The two-dimensional pressure on the invariance claim is engaged at §7.1.2. This fixes the subject of the verdict without yet proving that the verdict is invariant.
