If that boundary is fixed, what is possible can’t lapse into impossibility and what is impossible can’t become possible: ◇P → □◇P, with bilateral companion ¬◇P → □¬◇P. Both directions matter; the bilateral reading fixed in Bilateral Frame (§2.1.2) carries through here.

That conditional marks the work still to be done. The structural ground of possibility *is* what Reality *consists in*, but its invariance across modal evaluation isn’t assumed here. The Bottleneck (§2.1.5) tests whether any candidate alternative can fall outside it; Transition Closure (§3.1.2) separately tests whether local transition-capacity can arise from its own absence. This section fixes the ground to which modal status answers and establishes a separate point: the modal frame is necessarily *occupied* on both sides. Occupancy keeps the frame from being vacuous; the later arguments earn its invariance.

Let ⊤ abbreviate any logical truth and ⊥ any contradiction, Q∧¬Q.

**[Argument]**

**Modal Self-Sustenance** · *The Positive Direction*

1. Under every evaluation of R, ⊤ obtains.

2. Whatever actually obtains demonstrates a corresponding capacity in R.

3. ∴ ⊤ is possible under every evaluation of R: □◇⊤. Therefore necessarily something is possible: □∃P: ◇P.

The performative version remains available: the act of denying that anything is possible is actual, and therefore possible. But the formal proof needs no move from the content of a supposition to its possibility; ⊤ supplies the positive witness directly.

**[Argument]**

**Modal Self-Sustenance** · *The Negative Direction*

1. Under no evaluation of R does ⊥ obtain.

2. So ⊥ is impossible under every evaluation of R: □¬◇⊥.

3. ∴ Necessarily something is impossible: □∃P: ¬◇P.

The two directions rest on different grounds. Logical truth secures the positive pole; noncontradiction secures the negative pole. Neither direction depends on S5, and neither moves from conceivability to real possibility.

Together they establish the theorem. The frame is non-vacuously occupied on both sides—a result
that stands beside the theorem at §2.1.10
rather than inside its derivation.

**[Theorem]**

**Modal Self-Sustenance** · *Theorem*

Something is possible, and something is impossible—necessarily. Both poles of the modal structure are necessarily occupied, not merely kept from going empty. (□∃P: ◇P) ∧ (□∃P: ¬◇P).

**Relation:** stands beside Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10 Necessary Possibility) as the non-vacuity result; neither derives the other.

The bilateral frame also governs the derivative statuses. Necessity, contingency, and actuality aren’t independent additions to possibility and impossibility; each is intelligible only within the same frame. A necessary proposition is one whose failure is impossible; a contingent proposition is possible while its negation is possible; an actual proposition is true of the realized configuration. The theorem doesn’t yet show that the contingent status is occupied in every world, or even supply a particular contingent proposition. It fixes the grammar within which that further question can be asked.

Three limits govern how the theorem may be used. The first is a dependency. The canonical proof depends on the global reading of real possibility defended in §2.1.4–2.1.5. Transition Closure doesn’t replace that premise: it supplies a narrower S5-independent closure on the onset of Change under structural accessibility. Chapter 3 supplies overlapping pressure toward direction, difference, and bearing, supporting each at the level of generic roles without S5, but it neither boxes that generic conjunction nor independently recovers proposition-wise □◇C across silent worlds (worlds with no thinker to token a denial; §3.1.3). The dependencies are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable.

*Tested against.* Humean contingency at §8.2.2, modal collapse at §8.2.5, Williamson’s necessitism at §7.2.7, and refusals of bilateral invariance at §7.3.1. The Reverse-Lift diagnostic at No Reverse Lift (§3.5.4) marks exactly what Chapter 3 reaches without S5 and where □◇C remains upstream.

The second is a matter of scope. The proof’s modal invariance is over the structural conditions that fix modal status, not over the transworld existence of individuals. Neither Barcan formula is load-bearing here, and the quantified modal logic in use neither requires nor forbids constant domains. Williamson’s necessitism runs S5 and modal invariance into a substantive quantifier thesis, extending necessity to every existent. The present argument shares the invariance and diverges on the scope: necessity attaches to T∧S∧Φ as the structural condition on modal status, not to every individual that occupies it. The divergence point is engaged at §7.2.7; the in-chapter scope statement is at §2.9.6.

The third concerns grounding. Modal invariance is a shared theorem with the pluriverse account (Lewis’s plenitude of concrete possible worlds also yields S5) but the explanatory ground differs. The pluriverse grounds invariance in the completeness of the world-collection; the present account grounds it in what structural incapacity consists in. The Transition Closure (§3.1.2) brings out the difference: on the pluriverse view, worlds have their change-incapacity essentially; on the present view, structural incapacity is constitutive. Both groundings are engaged at §7.2.3 (Lewis’s plenitude) and §9.10 (structural realism).

*What the theorem establishes.* The theorem establishes non-vacuity, not proposition-wise modal invariance. The frame necessarily contains at least one possibility and at least one impossibility. It doesn’t yet show that whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary, or that whatever is impossible, its impossibility is necessary. The axiomatic derivation (§2.1.4) and the Bottleneck’s global-capacity defense (§2.1.5) earn that stronger invariance claim. Transition Closure (§3.1.2) supplies a narrower local consequence rather than another invariance proof.

### 2.1.4 Modal Stability
Modal Stability follows from what the modifier *real* contributes to possibility. To say that P is really possible is not to say that P is actual; it is to say that Reality actually has the capacity to admit P. The content may remain unactualized. The capacity can’t be unreal without the attribution of real possibility becoming empty. That attribution concerns R’s complete admissible range rather than a horizon owned by each local state. The negative boundary makes the dependence easiest to see: what no configuration in the complete range admits can’t be admitted by changing which configuration is under evaluation.

**[Definition]**

**Modal Notation** · *Definition*

Let R be Reality, the one whole. For any proposition P:

- Capacity(R,P) means that P belongs to the complete range R has the capacity to admit.
- ◇P means Capacity(R,P).
- □P means ¬Capacity(R,¬P): R has no capacity for P’s failure.

This isn’t the world-indexed operator often introduced first in Kripke semantics. In that apparatus, let Acc name an accessibility relation and let Reach(x,P) mean that some y accessible from x makes P true: Reach(x,P) =df ∃y(Acc(x,y) ∧ P(y)). Reach may vary with x and Acc. The book’s ◇ asks instead what R has the capacity to admit at all: ◇P =df Capacity(R,P). Nothing in the derivation that follows infers Acc(x,y), mutual accessibility, or a plurality of real worlds. Those belong to an optional representation. The argument itself is one-Reality and capacity-first.

The fixed point isn’t the bare numerical identity of R across changing states. It is the exhaustiveness of the range named by Range(R). Suppose an evaluation e is offered at which P is admitted although P was said to be genuinely impossible. If e is a real alternative, then e already belongs to the modal maximum and witnesses Capacity(R,P); P was never excluded. If e isn’t a real alternative, it can’t alter P’s real modal status. The same dilemma applies to an alleged source that changes the whole range: if the source or change can really obtain, it is already within R’s capacity; if it can’t, it supplies no alternative capacity. Reality’s no-exteriority (§1.1) and the modal maximum (§1.2.1) therefore ground the fixity together. The Bottleneck (§2.1.5) defends this exhaustion against world-relative alternatives.

**[Argument]**

**Modal Stability** · *Fixed Capacity*

1. If ¬Capacity(R,P), no real evaluation admits P. An evaluation that admitted P would itself witness Capacity(R,P), contradicting the exclusion. Therefore ¬◇P → □¬◇P (*Negative boundary*)

2. By Modal Bivalence, Capacity(R,P) and ¬Capacity(R,P) exhaust P’s modal status. A change from Capacity(R,P) to ¬Capacity(R,P) would change the fixed exclusion boundary. Therefore ◇P → □◇P (*Complement*)

3. If □P, then R has no capacity for ¬P. If ¬P were actual, actuality would demonstrate that very capacity. Therefore P: □P → P (*T*)

4. Since the incapacity constituting □P is fixed by the negative boundary, □P → □□P (*S4*)

5. If P is actual, actuality demonstrates Capacity(R,P). By the complement result, P → □◇P (*B*)

6. ∴ T, S4, and B over the normal modal base yield the familiar S5 representation of the bilateral result.

The derivation doesn’t use Temporality, Spatiality, or Substantiality, and therefore doesn’t assume the later conclusion that Reality is constituted by those Conditions under every modal evaluation. It uses only the meaning of real possibility fixed in §1.2.1: a modal determination Reality settles over its complete range of permitted ways. The Conditions will later be identified as the permitting and precluding structure of that range; they aren’t a premise in fixing the range’s globality.

**[Corollary]**

**Necessity entails Possibility** · *Corollary*

Whatever is necessary is possible. □P → ◇P.

**Depends on:** the T-Axiom and the Actuality–Possibility Principle (§1.2.5, §1.2.1)

The result composes T (□P → P) with actuality implying possibility (P → ◇P). Contraposed, ¬◇P → ¬□P: what isn’t possible isn’t necessary.

Ordinary Kripke semantics can *represent* this global-capacity result with universal accessibility among possible-world representations. That translation should be stated plainly, but its explanatory order must not be reversed. The argument doesn’t begin with worlds, add Acc, and infer that every world can reach every other. It begins with the unrestricted modal capacity of R. Universal accessibility is therefore one relational rendering of the result, not its premise or philosophical ground. Kripke (1963) supplies that model-theoretic rendering; Williamson (2013) defends S5 for metaphysical necessity on a kindred invariance ground. What the present account adds is a ground for the commitment the form encodes: *real possibility* is what R has the capacity to admit, not a local horizon owned by each world, because Reality has no outside from which its total capacity could be supplemented or revoked (§1.1).

This leaves a precise point of contestation. A critic may insist that possibility is fundamentally world-relative, with each world carrying its own accessible domain. That isn’t a counterexample inside the present operator; it is a rival account of what ◇ means. The Bottleneck takes up that rival directly and asks whether local reachability and real possibility have been conflated.

*Taking stock.* Reality’s no-exteriority and the exhaustive reading of its modal maximum fix the negative boundary; Modal Bivalence fixes possibility as the boundary’s complement. T, S4, B, the Euclidean principle, and S5 then represent the resulting invariance without appealing to the Triconditions. S5 is therefore downstream of global real possibility rather than an independently stipulated axiom: its earned bilateral form is exactly what the Necessity of Nature derivation spends as a premise, not a further assumption introduced for the modal argument’s benefit.

*Tested against.* World-relative and rival-domain readings are engaged through Lewis (§7.2.3), Williamson (§7.2.7), modal collapse (§8.2.5), Sider (§7.2.8), and the source-of-possibility question (§7.2.1).

### 2.1.5 The S5 Bottleneck
Modal Stability (§2.1.4) reaches S5 by joining two pieces of Groundwork: Reality has no real exterior, and real possibility reports its complete admissible range rather than a local horizon. The Bottleneck’s job is to test that inheritance against the world-relative alternative, not to establish in advance that T, S, and Φ constitute the field. A critic may reject the inheritance, but the point of rejection is now exact: either some real alternative stands outside Reality, or *metaphysical possibility* names less than the complete range of what can really be.

*The local-horizon objection.* A critic may hold that P is possible from one world w but not from another world w′ because each world carries its own accessibility horizon. On that semantics, ◇ is indexed to a world-relative relation—using the critic’s own world-indexed idiom here, not the book’s, since the book’s ◇ stays unindexed by design: ◇₍w₎P may hold while ◇₍w′₎P fails.

The reply is a distinction between two modalities. Local reachability can represent what can develop from a state, what laws local to a region permit, or which nodes a model connects. Real possibility, fixed at §1.2.1, asks whether P belongs to R’s complete admissible range at all. If one configuration can’t reach P while another admissible configuration contains it, P is locally unavailable from the first and really possible for R. No local horizon alone is the modal maximum.

The point is capacity, not inter-world travel. The argument posits no plurality of real worlds and infers no accessibility relation among them. Whatever a critic calls multiple worlds, a divine ground, brute contingency, a simulation, a cosmic cycle, or an alternative total history enters at the same gate: if it is really possible, Capacity(R,P); if R has no capacity for it, it isn’t really possible. Renaming an admissible configuration a “world” doesn’t place it outside R, because there is no second Reality for it to inhabit.

*The comparability dilemma.* That reply would be weak if it stopped at a distinction, since the critic can always insist the distinction has been drawn to suit the conclusion. It doesn’t stop there. The pressure comes from the variabilist’s own thesis. To say that Reality’s total capacity is one thing under configuration x and another under configuration y is already to treat x and y as configurations that R has the capacity to admit. Their difference is therefore inside the scope of Range(R), not a difference between two Realities. If the critic instead means two total capacities with no common R, then there is no one subject whose capacity varies and no shared modal claim to evaluate. Either the alternatives are capacities of Reality, R, and globality is granted, or they aren’t alternatives for one Reality at all.

Two dodges are available and neither opens a frame. The variabilist may say the comparison is made from the actual world, using the actual world’s own domain. But then w and w′ are both surveyed from @, their contents are available there, and @’s domain already contains what was supposed to lie outside it. Or the comparison may be pitched at the level of the model rather than the modality: not that the ways Reality permits vary, but that a semantics may assign different accessibility sets to different indices. That is true, and it is exactly the distinction already drawn. Variance at the level of the model is variance in a relative modality, and a relative modality’s varying doesn’t make real possibility vary.

The distinction is therefore earned rather than stipulated, and its ground was laid before any modal machinery was in place: Reality has no outside (§1.1), so there is no standpoint from which a second domain could be specified, and none from which two domains could be compared. This isn’t an exemption-by-definition. It states the exact philosophical choice the operator carries, and locates that choice upstream of the operator. If a critic uses ◇ for local reachability, the critic has changed the subject from global metaphysical possibility to a relative modality. Such relative modalities are legitimate, but their variation doesn’t show that *real possibility* varies. It shows that reachability from a node and Capacity(R,P) are different relations.

**[Argument]**

**Necessary Possibility** · *The Bottleneck*

1. R has no real exterior (*No Exteriority*, §1.1)

2. If a supposedly different total horizon is a real alternative, it already belongs to R’s range. If it shares no Reality within which it can be an alternative, it doesn’t vary one Reality’s capacity.

3. Therefore no real evaluation crosses the exclusion boundary: ¬◇P → □¬◇P.

4. ∴ By Modal Bivalence, possibility is the complement of that fixed exclusion: ◇P → □◇P.

*Scope.* Local reachability may vary within the range; the real modal verdict doesn’t. The notation is the one fixed at §2.1.4.

The proof is schematic and content-neutral. It says nothing about which propositions are possible and imports no claim that T, S, or Φ already hold necessarily. That separation removes the circular line of argument in which the Conditions would be used to derive S5 and S5 then used to necessitate the Conditions.

*Concrete and primitive worlds.* Lewisian modal realism may treat worlds as concrete and mutually isolated; primitivism may treat modal facts as ungrounded. Those are rival translations, not the ontology this proof begins with. If the alleged worlds are really possible, R has the capacity their descriptions express, however isolated their representations may be. If each is assigned a private and incomparable modality, the word *possible* no longer reports one fact about Reality. The dispute then concerns the meaning and ground of real possibility, not a counterexample within Range(R).

A separate structural consequence matters downstream, though it isn’t a premise of Necessary Possibility.

**[Lemma]**

**Parasitic Negation** · *Lemma*

For each of T, S, and Φ, a claim that the Condition begins from its own absence presupposes that Condition in the proposed onset. The ground is general: an onset from domain-external absence is itself a change, and change requires all three Conditions, so the proposed onset presupposes the Condition it claims to introduce. Per Condition: a first moment requires temporal order, a first placing requires positional structure, and a first production requires a bearer across the transition. Domain-internal absence may be coherent; emergence of the domain from domain-external absence is not.

**Feeds into:** Negation Seal (§2.1.5 The S5 Bottleneck)

The analysis of change the lemma runs on is the one fixed at §1.4. In the Φ limb, the bearer across the proposed transition is exactly the criterion named by Substantiality (Φ) (§1.4.3); it is a premise of the onset argument, not merely a later topic of engagement.

The distinction is between absence *within* a domain and onset *of* the domain. “No event occurs during an interval” is internal to Temporality; “Temporality first appears where no temporal order obtains” asks temporal order to precede itself. “Nothing occupies this place” is internal to Spatiality; “the first place is placed where no positional structure obtains” asks placement to precede its domain. The same form applies to production and Φ. The per-Condition readings are illustrations, not the load-bearing step. A critic who declines the placement or production vocabulary—locating the onset of Spatiality purely temporally, as “spatial structure obtains from t₀, not before”—hasn’t escaped: the onset so described is still a transition from domain-external ¬X to X, and a transition is a change, which on §1.4’s fixed analysis runs on succession, distinction, and exchange together. Describing the onset temporally borrows Temporality; the onset’s being a change at all borrows the other two.

*Notation.* In this result and the lemma it rests on, **X** is a variable ranging over the Conditions—X ∈ {T, S, Φ}—and ¬X is the denial of whichever Condition X picks out. The claim is stated once and holds for each.

**[Disjunction]**

**Negation Seal** · *Disjunction*

A candidate history in which X emerges from domain-external ¬X is incoherent. Either the negation is domain-internal, in which case X remains instantiated, or the proposed onset already uses X. No third onset is available.

**Depends on:** Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5)

The scope is exact. Parasitic Negation rules out onset from domain-external absence. It doesn’t by itself show that every possible world instantiates X, and it doesn’t derive proposition-wise modal invariance. Transition Closure (§3.1.2) develops its consequence for the local onset of transition-capacity. The Necessity of Nature is established later by Necessary Possibility, the Cartesian witness, and the Structural Requirement—not smuggled into this Bottleneck.

*Taking stock.* Local reachability may vary, but it is a different modality. What the comparability dilemma forecloses is the claim that a configuration already admitted by the modal maximum can replace that maximum with another one. A proposed second maximum must either be a real alternative within R’s complete range or something outside Reality; the first isn’t second, and the second supplies nothing real by which the range could vary.

One position survives, and naming it keeps the commitment isolated. It is not a variabilist account but a refusal of Modal Constitution itself (§2.1.3): modal facts are brute, answerable to nothing about what Reality consists in, so no comparison of domains and no common frame is owed. This section does not refute that modal primitivism.

The direct engagement belongs to §7.2.1, including the essence-prior version on which real definitions explain modal facts. The pressure there is exact: a real definition may fix the content of a possibility without yet explaining what makes that content possible. A reader who rejects the globality of ◇ is therefore rejecting a named premise with a later defense, not a consequence of the formal derivation hidden here.

The remaining disagreement is therefore clean, located, and small: whether modal status answers to what Reality consists in, and so whether metaphysical possibility is global in the sense fixed at §1.2.1. Chapter 7 engages rival answers rather than treating them as incoherent by stipulation.

*Tested against.* Concrete modal realism and rival accessibility structures are engaged at §7.2.3; invariant-domain and necessitist readings at §7.2.7; primitivist and structuralist alternatives at §7.2.8; the process alternative at §9.6 and the modal-collapse pressure at §8.2.5; and the source of possibility at §7.2.1.

### 2.1.6 The Transition Closure
The global-capacity proof does not need a second route through local transition. A narrower result nevertheless follows from Parasitic Negation: local transition-capacity cannot switch on within a history from a state that lacks it, because its acquisition would itself be a Change available from that state. That temporal closure neither derives S5 nor excludes a silent, isolated world-description. Its office is stress-testing rather than modal premising, and its full argument and theorem are the Unswitchable Capacity (§3.1.2).

Transition Closure supplies no premise of Necessary Possibility. Its role is narrower: once the global-capacity result is in hand, it tests whether a local history could acquire transition-capacity from a state that lacked it.

### 2.1.7 Modal Persistence and Invariance
The Necessary Possibility Theorem has two readings because the standing capacity of R can be tested against two kinds of local variation. The theorem itself is one result: neither a later time nor another represented configuration replaces R, whose capacity real possibility reports (§1.2.1, 2.1.4–2.1.5). It doesn’t rest on a separate world-to-world derivation or on Transition Closure.

*Modal Persistence, the diachronic reading.* A later time doesn’t create a new total capacity for Reality. What becomes locally achievable, ceases to be locally achievable, or is never actualized concerns occasions and configurations; it doesn’t add to or subtract from Range(R). A possibility may lack an occasion at a time without lapsing in modal status.

**[Proposition]**

**Modal Persistence** · *Proposition*

A later time does not create a new total capacity for Reality. What becomes locally achievable, ceases to be locally achievable, or is never actualized concerns occasions and configurations; it does not add to or subtract from Range(R). A possibility may lack an occasion at a time without lapsing in modal status.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility (§2.1.4, §2.1.5), the diachronic reading

The distinction is ordinary before it is technical. From roughly 36,000 to 11,000 years ago one could walk from Asia to America: the Bering land bridge, a plain of dry land, ran from Siberia to Alaska, and people crossed it on foot. The sea rose and the walk closed. What closed is the occasion—where the coastlines sit, what happens to be dry when the traveler sets out. None of it touches whether dry land between two continents is the kind of thing Reality permits, which was settled before the first crossing and remains settled with the sea back over it.

Convergence supplies the converse image. Sharks, ichthyosaurs, and dolphins—fish, reptile, and mammal—independently arrived at similarly streamlined bodies for moving quickly through water. The histories are separate, but the form each realizes isn’t a private possibility of its lineage. Possibility doesn’t promise the occasion; it doesn’t have to. The theorem tracks the standing permission, not the local opportunity.

*Modal Invariance, the represented-alternatives reading.* The same point holds when standard semantics represents alternatives as worlds. If ◇P, then Capacity(R,P); no change of representation replaces R, so ◇P → □◇P. If ¬◇P, then ¬Capacity(R,P), so ¬◇P → □¬◇P. This is the same global-capacity result derived at §2.1.4 and stated formally at §2.1.10 as the Necessary Possibility theorem—named here as its own reading rather than boxed a third time.

The two readings aren’t two causal stories about structural Conditions changing or persisting. They are two indices of one global semantic fact: temporal changes and world-relative accessibility relations don’t replace R or alter Range(R). The same fence holds against neighboring senses of “possible”: what is epistemically open shifts with evidence, what is conceivable shifts with imagination, and what is probable shifts with the odds, while real possibility shifts with none of them (§1.2.1).

Plantinga (1974) develops modal invariance for essentialist claims about individuals. The present theorem generalizes the result to real modal status and grounds it in the standing capacity of R. A critic may instead use a world-relative modality with varying accessibility horizons; that is a different operator, not a counterexample within ◇.

*What binds.* The modal architecture is globally stable: whatever modal status Range(R) assigns a proposition, that status is invariant under local or represented variation. Local opportunity remains local; real possibility belongs to R.

*Tested against.* The global and relative readings of modality are pressed in Chapters 7 and 8: Williamson (§7.2.7), Lewis (§7.2.3), modal collapse (§8.2.5), and the source-of-possibility question (§7.2.1).

### 2.1.8 Candidate-Ground Convergence
Necessary Possibility governs every candidate ground, but applying that discipline to divine, mathematical, brute, apophatic, or otherwise analogical candidates does not help derive the theorem. It tests what survives after the theorem is granted. The three-way burden map—loaded structure, no content, or thin/analogical structure—therefore belongs to Chapter 3’s Candidate-Ground Stress Test (§3.1.4).

Candidate-Ground Convergence therefore supplies no premise to Modal Stability, the Bottleneck, or Necessary Possibility. It asks what candidate explanations can survive once that modal result is granted.

### 2.1.9 What Necessity Transfer Needs
The modal ontological argument turns on the S5 transfer from possible necessity to necessity: ◇□P → □P. Within the present account, that transfer follows from the fixed boundary of R’s complete admissible range. It doesn’t follow merely because an attempted rejection linguistically presupposes the framework.

Like the Euclidean principle before it (§2.1.4), the transfer is schematic. Grant that R’s complete range admits P’s necessity. Since the range’s exclusion boundary is invariant, that modal status can’t be merely local: ◇□P → □P. The inference doesn’t turn on whose proposition P is.

A critic may reject this account only by offering a different semantics of real possibility—one on which modal status doesn’t answer to the standing capacity of R. Merely using modal language to deny S5 doesn’t refute the global-capacity analysis, but neither does it make denial incoherent by itself. It states a competing modal theory that Chapter 7 evaluates in detail.

The theist is therefore bound if the global-capacity account is accepted, and the modal ontological argument itself supplies a particularly clear instance: ◇□MGB → □MGB. Whether that transfer delivers a theistic conclusion, and what it costs to resist it, isn’t adjudicated here; the full engagement with Plantinga’s argument belongs to Chapter 10 (§10.1.1).

*What inverts.* The move the tradition reserved for crowning a necessary being is a structural consequence of Reality’s global capacity. It binds every claim about what R can admit, the theist included; it isn’t a verdict directed against any claimant.

### 2.1.10 Necessary Possibility
Real possibility reports R’s complete admissible range, and the boundary of that range yields a single bilateral result: modal status is invariant across every point of evaluation, a result the rest of the chapter relies on.

The notation is the one fixed in the Groundwork (§1.1, §1.2.1): *R* names Reality, the one whole, and *Capacity(R,P)* names the complete range within which R can admit P. Naming isn’t a premise; what R’s having no exterior establishes is, and it is carried as one below.

**[Argument]**

**Necessary Possibility** · *The S5 Pipeline*

1. Every contentful proposition receives one of the two classical verdicts: ◇P or ¬◇P (*Modal Exhaustiveness*, §2.1.1)

2. R has no real exterior: nothing real stands beyond the one whole, and there is no vantage on Reality from outside it (*No Exteriority*, §1.1). Under the notation fixed above, ◇P means Capacity(R,P), membership in R’s complete admissible range, and ¬◇P means exclusion from it (§1.2.1)

3. Modal status answers to that complete permitting and precluding boundary, not to how any particular configuration is arranged. This fixes what the verdict is *about*; it doesn’t yet make the verdict invariant (*Modal Constitution*, §2.1.3)

4. If an alleged evaluation admits P, it is either a real alternative already within R’s range—so P wasn’t excluded—or not a real alternative. Therefore genuine impossibility cannot vary: ¬◇P → □¬◇P (*Invariant exclusion*, §2.1.4)

5. Possibility is the complement of that fixed exclusion. If P passed from possible to impossible, the exclusion boundary would have changed. Therefore ◇P → □◇P (*Invariant complement*, §2.1.4)

6. Local reachability may vary, but every pair of real alternative horizons is already compared within R’s complete range. No variation in reachability supplies a second real modal maximum (*The Bottleneck*, §2.1.5)

Together, these results close on a single conclusion:

**[Theorem]**

**Necessary Possibility** · *Theorem*

Whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary; whatever is impossible, its impossibility is necessary. The line that separates them is fixed and invariant. No real evaluation can cross the exclusion boundary of R’s complete admissible range, and the possible range is that boundary’s complement. (◇P → □◇P) ∧ (¬◇P → □¬◇P).

The theorem is schematic. It doesn’t say that anything in particular is possible; it says that once a proposition has a real modal status, changing the evaluation point doesn’t alter whether Capacity(R,P) or ¬Capacity(R,P) obtains. The Cartesian witness supplies the substantive input in §2.2.

That the frame isn’t empty is a separate result, and it isn’t a step above. *Modal Self-Sustenance* (§2.1.3) earns the occupancy—necessarily something is possible, necessarily something is impossible—and the theorem earns the invariance. Neither derives the other. The frame needs both: one says the poles are filled, the other says nothing crosses between them.

The derivation is also non-circular with the later Necessity of Nature. No step assumes that Reality is constituted by T, S, or Φ. The global-capacity theorem concerns what real possibility means; the field’s structural content is later identified and necessitated at §2.4–2.5.

The name is conventional. *Necessary Possibility* names the familiar positive S5 form, while the derivational order is negative-first. Genuine impossibility fixes the exclusion boundary; Modal Bivalence fixes possibility as its complement. The two arms are co-equal in the theorem even though the negative arm makes the ground of their invariance easiest to see.

The square circle makes the negative arm concrete without yet doing the structural identification of §2.4. Let SC state that one figure is square and circular in the same respect at the same boundary. R has no capacity to admit SC: ¬◇SC. Therefore its impossibility is invariant: □¬◇SC. This doesn’t say that every local configuration contains squares or circles. It says that Reality’s complete capacity never admits that collapsed positional configuration. Section 2.4 identifies the content-specific boundary doing that work as spatial.

*Taking stock.* Real possibility belongs to R’s complete range, and both modal verdicts hold invariantly. The substantive ground defended here is the conjunction of no-exteriority, modal exhaustion, and Modal Bivalence; the S5 frame represents their bilateral consequence without appeal to the Triconditions it later helps necessitate.

*Dependencies.* The standard objection to modal arguments in this territory is that they purchase their conclusion with an axiom. The Euclidean axiom, ◇P → □◇P, isn’t assumed here: it is the complement-side limb of the theorem just derived. The negative limb, ¬◇P → □¬◇P, states the exclusion with which the derivation begins. Nor is a Kripke accessibility relation stipulated and then redescribed: universal accessibility can *model* the result, while Reality’s no-exteriority and modal maximum ground the one complete range the result records. Modal Invariance (§2.1.7) is likewise derived rather than posited. What the argument assumes is stated in the open: classical Modal Bivalence, the Groundwork definition of real possibility as R’s modal maximum, and the no-exterior result.

This fixes the shape of a refutation, in the way the No-Surplus Criterion does for the identity family (§2.6.9). An opponent who rejects S5 hasn’t yet identified which ground they reject, because the conclusion doesn’t rest on S5 being granted. The live targets are classical Modal Bivalence, real possibility’s exhaustion of the modal maximum, and Reality’s no-exteriority. Rejecting the last requires a coherent sense in which something real stands outside the whole that gives *real* its content; rejecting the second replaces global metaphysical possibility with a relative modality. Those are substantive positions, but they are the positions the argument answers rather than hidden assumptions in an accessibility frame.

## 2.2 Cartesian Certainty
The pipeline closed with a conditional: whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary (the Necessary Possibility Theorem, §2.1.10). Change has yet to supply its antecedent. Take the land bridge again: first walkable, then the water crept in, then not walkable at all—change was doing the work at every stage. But how do we know any of that actually happened, rather than being a story, an illusion, even a simulation? If it’s all fabricated, is there anything left that even a fabrication couldn’t touch? Entertaining that very doubt already required one: a shift from not-doubting to doubting. That is the possibility of change, and it is not merely possible but actual. Trying to deny it only performs it.

**[Premise]**

**Cartesian Certainty** · *Premise*

Change is really possible. No denial can escape it: the act of doubting that anything changes is itself a change, from not-doubting to doubting. ◇C.

The certainty is Cartesian in a precise sense. The witness is the *Cogito*’s structural shadow: any attempt to doubt that change occurs is itself a change, a transition from not-doubting to doubting, performed across a real interval, hosted by a persistent doubter. The doubter here is a functional role: the state constituting doubt is structurally distinct from its absence, and that structural difference is the change the witness requires. The doubt refutes itself in its own performance: no denial of change can be completed without instantiating it. That is Cartesian certainty for the possibility of change, in one exact grade: the performative inescapability of the structural transition, self-defeating to deny, not the phenomenal indubitability the term can suggest. “Cartesian” marks the *Cogito* on the performative reading taken up at §2.2.1, not an introspective luminosity of the doubting.

Two limits hold that grade in place. Phenomenal character isn’t the datum, and the witness doesn’t depend on it (that pressure is taken up at §9.2, where the illusionist’s denial that there is any phenomenal character to have is met on exactly this point). And the change instantiated is intrinsic state change of the doubting system, not duration of time or causal direction per se: what the witness establishes is that change is sufficient to instantiate the structural Conditions, not that temporal structure can’t proceed without intrinsic change, which is Shoemaker’s time-without-change argument and is engaged at §8.1.1.

*Tested against.* The objections that target the change-witness itself are answered in §8.1: the changeless-ground and Shoemaker time-without-change challenges at §8.1.1, emergent-time accounts at §8.1.2.

The argument is given in full at §2.2.1, where change is shown to be actual and certain at three depths—empirically, performatively, and structurally—under the *Cogito*-style closure of §1.3 that no skeptical scenario can undermine.

The input has one job in the canonical proof. Fed into Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10), the possibility of Change carries to its necessitated form. Whether the certainty also reaches past experience to whatever grounds it is a further question rather than a second premise. Chapter 3 tests that extension through level-invariance, the Triconditional Cross-Entailment, and the Encoding Dilemma (§3.1.5).

The argument extends a defended tradition. Hintikka read Descartes’ *sum* as performed rather than inferred (1962): the *Cogito*’s force lies in the fact that any denial of one’s existence re-establishes it in the act of denying. Apel and Habermas extended the move to the presuppositions of argumentation itself (1980; (1983) 1990). Stroud and Taylor formalized the general pattern (1968; 1978): an X is unavoidable if every possible denial of X requires X for its formulation. What is new here is the target: not the presuppositions of reasoning in general but the structural conditions of any concrete, change-bearing state of affairs being the case, regardless of whether anyone argues about it.

Stroud’s own objection sharpens the stakes. Transcendental arguments, taken alone, establish only what must be presupposed for experience or assertion to occur. What entitles the move from a fact about the act of denial to a conclusion about mind-independent reality? Nothing—so long as the performative line stands alone. The reply is a pairing. The performative line shows that the act of denial or conceiving is itself structurally conditioned: anyone running the denial uses what it rejects. The constitutive-definition line (§1.4) carries the metaphysical claim: the Conditions are what it is for any concrete, change-bearing state of affairs to be the case—constitutive of its obtaining, not its subject matter. Neither move alone closes the gap. Cognitive performance alone doesn’t defeat the ideal conceivability of a structureless scenario, and the constitutive definitions alone leave the performance certainty unanchored. The two together do.

*Tested against.* The objections that the cognitive performance serving as the change-witness is itself illusory or eliminable are engaged at §9.2; the argument meets the related objection—that consciousness as substrate stands outside structural exhaustion, the hard problem of consciousness—at §9.1. The input secures the possibility of change without itself answering the hard-problem pressure, which is carried forward rather than discharged here.

### 2.2.1 Change Is Actual
Things change. This sentence is being read; a moment ago it was not. Nothing more elaborate needs to be true for change to have happened, and nothing in what follows assumes more. At the level of ordinary experience, change isn’t a hypothesis but the most immediate and universal feature of inquiry. Ongoing perception changes the perceiving system; measurement compares distinguishable states or values, though not every measurement is spatial displacement; experiment intervenes by producing or registering a difference. The common load-bearing fact is transition, not a premature one-to-one assignment of these practices to the three loaded Conditions.

The sciences don’t first discover that change occurs. They presuppose actual transitions in observing, measuring, intervening, and recording. The later Structural Requirement establishes what any such transition requires: Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality together. Even the denier of change must formulate the denial, and that formulation is itself an actual transition in its realizer.

This empirical certainty is the starting point but not the foundation. It is logically possible (if not coherently imaginable) that our empirical experience is systematically deceived. The foundation of Cartesian Certainty lies deeper, at the level where deception itself can’t reach.

Even granting the radical skeptic—that our experience may be a simulation, a dream, the product of a deceiving demon, or a systematic illusion of any other kind—the possibility of change can’t be coherently denied (Descartes (1641) 1996). The denial is self-refuting at the level of its own performance.

To think is to undergo a succession of mental states: the state of not-yet-having-thought this thought, and the state of having-thought it. To doubt is to transition from a state of not-yet-doubting to a state of doubting. To process this argument is to move through a sequence of propositions, each one replacing its predecessor as the object of attention. Each of these acts instantiates Change in the sense reference-fixed at §1.3: one state, then another, under the ordered, differentiated, cross-interval profile the later analysis makes explicit. The reflective passage is the actual witness for that structural kind, not a restriction of Change to conscious episodes and not a license to thin it into arbitrary succession. To deny that change occurs is to transition from not-denying to denying, a cognitive succession that instantiates what the denial contests. The trying is the change. The denial that change is possible can’t be completed without instantiating the very possibility it denies. Descartes said *cogito ergo sum*, I think, therefore I am. The argument here runs on the same move, with a little change: *cogito ergo muto*. Not certainty of existence alone, but certainty of Change itself.

The witness therefore does three jobs at once. First, it establishes Change: attention moves from the sentence, to doubt about what is read, to recognition of the doubting. Second, it displays the structure of that Change: the phases are ordered, the attended object and the doubt and the recognition are differentiated, and the earlier content is carried into the later recognition. One caution belongs with that middle term and is easier to state here than to repair later. What the episode displays is differentiation, and differentiation is not yet positional distinctness. Red differs from blue without anything lying between them: a real difference, and not a spatial one. The upgrade from displayed differentiation to a spatial interval is argued at §2.4.7, where the reflective episode has to be argued into supplying an interval and a displacement carries one in its own specification; it is not read off the witness here. Temporality and Substantiality take their witness from this episode directly. Spatiality takes its primary witness from movement. Third, it survives the skeptical retreat that produced it. The page may be dream, simulation, or illusion; the turn from outward attention to inward recognition remains an actual, structured performance. Doubt can relocate the object. It can’t remove the structure of the relocating.

The oldest denial that change is possible aims at this target. *Zeno’s paradoxes* of motion conclude that motion, and so change, is illusory. The Dichotomy and the Achilles cut any passage into endlessly many sub-passages that could never be completed; the Arrow freezes flight into instants at none of which anything moves (all transmitted in Aristotle’s *Physics* VI.9 Aristotle (4th c. BCE) 1984). The witness does not adjudicate the paradoxes on their own ground; it refuses their conclusion and names the hidden premise that made it seem forced. What answers Zeno at this stage is the minimal description of Change: one state, then another (§1.3), which commits neither to completing an infinite task nor to finding motion within a durationless instant. The local answer does not change the proposition carried into the modal proof: the same structural kind is witnessed reflectively here and may be instantiated non-reflectively elsewhere.

Against the Dichotomy, the endless task-list isn’t found in the passage but imposed on it—by stopping to mark each halfway point—and stopping to mark isn’t the passage but its interruption. A reader who marks the midpoint of this sentence, then the midpoint of what remains, and again, has stopped reading to measure; the reader who reads reaches the period. The marking that generates the regress is itself one state after another, so the objection is carried out by the very succession it concludes can’t occur.

Against the Arrow, that the arrow fills exactly its own length at an instant isn’t rest but what any extended thing does at any instant, moving or still: it registers the arrow’s extension and its persistence at that time (Spatiality and Substantiality) and is silent about succession (Temporality), which is constituted across instants, not within one. The Arrow reads rest off the mere standing presence of the bearer, mistaking the absence of motion within a slice for its absence across the slices. What the reader who finishes this sentence has just done, the Eleatic says can’t be done—and the finishing is the refutation. (The reading of the subdivisions as *potential*—generated by the act of dividing rather than antecedently completed—is Aristotle’s own (*Physics* VIII.8 Aristotle (4th c. BCE) 1984); the reading of motion as a unity misdescribed when reconstituted from the stationary positions it passes through is Bergson’s (Bergson 1907). The formal dissolution of the divisibility paradoxes in the convergent series (½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … = 1) meets them on their own ground; the witness doesn’t need it, since the Zeno reply needs only Change’s minimally described succession rather than the summed continuum. The reflective transition is the token that supplies certainty, not the intension of Change.)

Hintikka reads the *Cogito* as performative rather than inferential (1962): the certainty of *I am* doesn’t follow from *I think* as a logical inference but is existentially inseparable from the act of thinking; the attempted denial of one’s own existence is self-defeating in the performing, not in the reasoning. The present argument is the performative reading redirected. Where Hintikka’s *Cogito* catches the denier in the act of existing, this one catches the denier in the act of undergoing change. Existence and change aren’t the same target, but the closure is the same move, and Hintikka’s analysis clarifies why it isn’t question-begging: the closure doesn’t derive its content from a premise the denier might refuse; it derives it from the act the denier can’t refuse without ceasing to act at all.

Descartes established that the act of doubting proves the existence of a doubting subject. This argument establishes the actuality of Change in the act of doubting.

The formal claim retains one referent throughout: Change as the structural kind fixed at §1.3. The actual reflective episode is a token of that kind, and its performance displays ordered phases, differentiated poles, and retained content across those phases. It therefore witnesses Reality’s capacity for Change without building consciousness or reflection into what Change means. What the catch does not establish by itself is that every candidate transition instantiates the loaded Conditions. The act’s distinctions are a doubting thought, what is doubted, and the standpoint from which the doubt is made. They do not by themselves complete the proof of Spatiality, and the requirement that a thinker bear the thought does not by itself complete the proof of Substantiality. Those stronger identifications are earned by the Structural Requirement (§2.4); their application to further ontological levels is stress-tested in Chapter 3 (§3.1.5). The witness supplies structured actual Change, not a blank permission the later argument must fill from nothing.

The deceiving demon, simulation architect, and dreaming mind cannot erase the Change instantiated by the doubt. Whether the structure also transfers to the host is a separate level-invariance question, tested in Chapter 3 rather than spent by this witness (§3.1.5).

The skeptical scenarios that are meant to undermine the certainty that change is possible each presuppose it as their own condition of possibility. That Cartesian certainty is therefore not merely empirical certainty that survives scrutiny. It is epistemic inescapability: there is no coherent epistemic position (no possible standpoint of doubt, denial, or inquiry) from which it can be coherently rejected. Any position from which the rejection is attempted instantiates the possibility it attempts to reject.

The move runs parallel to the epistemic-closure literature (Dretske 1970; Nozick 1981; DeRose 1995) but inverts its direction: rather than running closure forward from known premises to their known consequences, the performative catch runs closure backward from the act of denial to the structural Conditions that act already instantiates.

*The token-level reach.* Any particular act of denial instantiates change. But could “change is not possible” still be true in some world where no one denies it? The token catch doesn’t close that type-level question by itself. The constitutive-definition argument of §1.4 does that work: because the structural roles are fully constitutive of the essences they specify, the token catch isn’t a coincidence of the denier’s situation but a structural feature of the proposition’s content. The performative line and the constitutive line are complementary: the first shows that any denial uses what it rejects, the second shows the Conditions are what it is for anything to be the case. In the vocabulary fixed at §7.3.2, the performative line is act-side and the constitutive line object-side; the type-level result rests on the second, since a denial’s using what it rejects is a fact about the denying and not yet about the denied. This distinguishes the argument from Boghossian’s (1998) observation that self-knowledge claims don’t ground substantive metaphysical conclusions. The performative catches here don’t rest on the subject’s self-knowledge. They rest on the structural preconditions of any propositional act, conditions that are constitutive of what propositional content consists in, not merely features of the act of knowing.

What is secured at this point is the actuality of Change. Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10) performs the amplification from possibility to necessary possibility; whether the certainty extends from experience to its ground is taken up at §3.1.5.

### 2.2.2 Actuality’s Reach
The canonical proof needs no inference from experienced Change to a mind-independent or otherwise transcendent ground. Cartesian Certainty supplies one actual Change and therefore ◇C; Necessary Possibility performs the modal lift, and the Structural Requirement identifies what that capacity requires. Questions about what a simulation host, transcendental subject, divine mind, or other ground must instantiate test the witness after it has done that work. The Grounding Conditional and those level-invariance tests are developed in §3.1.5.

### 2.2.3 Witness’s Reach
The witness establishes that Change is actual at the site of any concrete denial and hence that Change is really possible. By itself it establishes no necessity, no particular physical configuration, and no conclusion that experience’s ground is mind-independent. The necessity of the Conditions follows only when ◇C is passed through Necessary Possibility and the Structural Requirement.

The witness reaches whatever concrete realizer hosts the act: distinguishing experience from Reality is itself an act whose realizer changes. That secures structure in cognition and its host, not loaded T, S, and Φ at every noumenal level. The full Kantian, phenomenological, simulation, emergence, and encoding tests belong to §3.1.5.

## 2.3 Necessary Possibility of Change
Change is possible, and certain at the level of its own denial (§2.2). But that witness is actual, and an actual witness does not by itself establish that change stays possible at every modal point. Does the possibility hold only here, or across every world structural Reality admits? One application of the Necessary Possibility Theorem (§2.1.10) settles it: whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary. Cartesian Certainty supplies the antecedent, and the two combine:

**[Argument]**

**Necessary Possibility of Change** · *The Lift*

1. Whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary. ◇P → □◇P (*Necessary Possibility*, §2.1.10)

2. Change is possible, and certain at the very level of its own denial (to deny it would itself be a change). ◇C (*Possibility of Change*, Cartesian Certainty, §2.2)

3. ∴ The possibility of change is necessary. □◇C

Stated formally:

**[Lemma]**

**Necessary Possibility of Change** · *Lemma*

The possibility of change is necessary: it holds not merely in the actual world but in every world within structural Reality, lifted by the Necessary Possibility Theorem from an actual witness of change—the Cartesian certainty of §2.2, or the movement witness of §2.4.9. □◇C.

**Feeds into:** Triconditional Necessity (§2.5 Triconditional Necessity)

*Which witness the lift takes.* The antecedent is the possibility of change, and nothing in the theorem cares how that possibility was secured. Cartesian Certainty supplies it performatively: the denial is itself a change. A second witness supplies it from the other direction, empirically rather than performatively—movement is really possible, and movement is one species of change, so the possibility of movement entails the possibility of change (§2.4.9). A reader who declines the reflective witness, whether as a momentary-instant skeptic or as an illusionist about mental states, still reaches the necessary possibility of change by that route. The redundancy does not buy independence from the theorem applied here. Both witnesses feed the same lift, so Necessary Possibility remains the one premise the chapter does not overdetermine.

The necessity reached here is intermediate in a precise sense: stronger than the unnecessitated possibility of §2.2 (the possibility now holds across all of the modal structure, not only here) and weaker than the conclusion the chapter is reaching for, the unconditional necessity of the structural Conditions, established at §2.5. That necessitated possibility is the antecedent the Structural Requirement (the necessitated conditional from the possibility of change to the structural Conditions, established at §2.4) discharges by modus ponens into that conclusion. Without the lift performed here, only the conditional would be in hand; with it, the chain closes at §2.5.

In the capacity idiom fixed at §1.2.1, the actual witness demonstrates that Reality has the capacity for Change; the Necessary Possibility theorem fixes that standing capacity across the modal structure. Change retains the structural reference fixed at §1.3: one state, then another, progressively articulated as ordered phases, concrete distinction, and cross-interval bearing. The reflective transition displayed in reading, doubting, and recognizing the doubt is the witness for that kind, not part of its intension. The theorem necessitates Reality’s capacity for Change, not this reader, this page, reflection as such, or any particular expression of the capacity.

That capacity is not blank permission, and Change is not thinned after the witness into arbitrary succession. The reflective token displays ordered phases, differentiated poles held within the episode, and earlier content retained in later recognition; the movement token displays the same kind without reflection. The next section argues that ordered succession, positional distinction, and cross-interval bearing are constitutive of Change and identifies them with Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. Because the necessity of Change’s possibility has been established here, that requirement will yield the necessary instantiation of the Conditions, not merely their possible availability.

Nothing needs to be substituted for Change along the way. Its opening formula supplies the least description of one structural kind; the actual episode establishes that kind’s possibility, and the theorem necessitates that possibility, with the same intension throughout. The constitutive identifications established at §2.4 show why Change instantiates Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. Progressive articulation makes those requirements explicit; it neither changes the antecedent nor turns the actual token into a necessary occupant.

*Tested against.* The objections to the lift itself are whether the possibility of change has a source, and whether modal invariance can bear this weight. They are engaged in Chapters 7 and 8: the source of possibility (§7.2.1), the Principle of Sufficient Reason (§8.2.1) (Pruss 2006), and Humean contingency (§8.2.2). The contemporary near-neighbor is Williamson’s necessitism, which accepts the same modal invariance but extends necessity to every existent; the divergence point is engaged directly at §7.2.7.

*Scope of the necessity.* What is necessary is the *possibility* of change, not any particular change. The lemma says that the possibility of change has the same modal standing in every world within structural Reality, not that any specific transition occurs, or must occur, in any world. The theorem therefore leaves which changes occur and their modal status open; positive metaphysical contingency requires the further evidence distinguished at §2.9.4. The lift necessitates the modal standing of change, and stops there.

## 2.4 Structural Requirement
Change is possible, and necessarily so—that much is now established. What that possibility requires is the question here, and Chapter 1 already named the candidates: Temporality, borne by Time (a real before-and-after); Spatiality, borne by Space (genuinely co-present poles held apart); Substantiality, borne by Substance (what carries the exchange). Are they merely how this world happens to be built, or does change need them wherever it is possible at all?

The role-names are inherited; their necessity is not. The Groundwork fixed what counts as satisfying each Condition: ordered succession for T, concrete relational separation for S, and occupied bearing across a transition for Φ (§1.4). The burden here is therefore a satisfaction proof. It must show that the particular Change fixed by the witness meets those criteria, not infer Spatiality from every numerical difference, Substantiality from every abstract relation, or necessity from the definitions alone.

The canonical derivation runs through §2.4.5–2.4.9, and its weight is not spread evenly across that range. The bilateral identification at §2.4.9 is the step that earns the theorem: a reader testing whether the Structural Requirement is established should go there first, and an objection that does not engage it has not reached the argument. The four approaches that precede §2.4.5 are convergent formulations of the Structural Requirement, not additional premises accumulated by the proof.

One contract governs the derivation: Change keeps the single structural reference fixed at §1.3—one state, then another, under the ordered, differentiated, cross-interval profile progressively articulated here. The reflective episode in §2.2 supplies an actual token and therefore the modal antecedent; reflection is evidential, not part of Change’s intension. The movement witness supplies a non-reflective token of the same kind. The Conditions remain at the modal-core resolution fixed before the proof began. Temporality is ordered succession, before and after under asymmetry and transitivity. Spatiality is real relational exteriority, here and there or this concretely apart from that across a crossable interval, under Exclusivity, nonmetric Extension, and crossability-in-principle. Substantiality is real bearing across transition, under Distinctness and Persistence. These are the criteria Change must meet, not thin placeholders awaiting physical completion; □(◇C → T∧S∧Φ) is claimed and proved at that strength. A weaker *generic role-floor*—directed order, difference, and bearing—appears in the independent convergence arguments of Chapter 3 and in diagnostics applied to rival vocabularies. A richer *realization tier* is earned abductively where Nature’s actual configuration is engaged (§4.2–4.4, §8.2.2): particular temporal metrics and causal production, metric and dimensional geometry, fields, material systems, and specific accounts of transmission. The proof spends no realization-tier content. It therefore establishes the Conditions themselves while remaining silent on which determinate physical forms realize them and on the modal status of those forms, which requires separate argument.

The Necessary Possibility of Change was established at §2.3: the possibility of change is invariant across modal evaluation. The claim now is a necessary conditional about the Reality being evaluated: if the witnessed kind of Change already fixed is really possible, then Reality’s modal constitution includes Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. Formally: □(◇C → T∧S∧Φ). T, S, and Φ here predicate the structure of Reality, not the local inventory of a world.

**[Theorem]**

**Structural Requirement** · *Theorem*

Under every modal evaluation, if Change—the structural kind actually witnessed by the reflective episode and by movement—is really possible, then Reality is constituted by Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. □(◇C → T∧S∧Φ).

Read in the capacity idiom, the consequent isn’t one modal step farther away. Reality’s capacity for Change is its standing modal constitution, not a local ability distributed world by world. The capacity for before and after is Temporality. The capacity for here and there, this really apart from that, is Spatiality. The capacity for what obtains in one state to be borne into another is Substantiality. The claim to be earned below is that these aren’t three further possibilities behind the capacity for Change; they are what having that capacity consists in at modal-core resolution. If that claim holds, no inheritance from a local occurrence to a global field is needed, because both sides already concern the same Reality-level capacity.

The objection must be stated without turning it into a quarrel over words. A critic may grant both that every possible displacement has the three Conditions among its constituents and that “P is really possible” is equivalent to “Reality has the standing capacity for P.” Neither concession by itself shows that the permitting constraint *consists in* the structure every permitted realization exhibits. The critic can still say that an otherwise unstructured modal field merely selects structured outcomes.

The capacity idiom therefore does not carry the identification by itself. What matters is the content of this capacity. A capacity for one state and then another of a retained bearer is not a blank permission later supplemented by succession, distinction, and bearing. Remove any of those and a different capacity has been specified: not a capacity for Change under the fixed referent. That secures the conditional’s constitutive direction.

A second question remains. Do the three Conditions merely describe the constraint, or are they the constraint? The bilateral test and no-surplus dilemma at §2.4.9 answer that stronger objection rather than building its answer into the vocabulary here. Discharging the conditional against □◇C therefore yields □(T∧S∧Φ), not the weaker □◇(T∧S∧Φ). The later identity claim carries an additional burden of its own.

Radical doubt can relocate the realizers without removing the criteria they satisfy. If the page is an illusion, the experienced field still presents determinate poles and an apparent interval across which attention passes. If the memory is deceptive, the earlier-seeming content is nevertheless borne as present content into the recognition now occurring. If a demon, simulation, mind, or physical process supplies the episode, that proposal changes what occupies the roles, not whether the episode has ordered phases, concretely separated contents, and retained bearing. The proof requires no external page, human body, metric geometry, or material substance at this stage. It requires the real structure of the occurrence whose actuality the doubt itself certifies.

The conditional isn’t a stipulation, and its necessity isn’t a modal axiom imported from outside. The necessity is *derivative*: the three Conditions are constitutively required by the possibility of change, and a constitutive requirement holds wherever the thing it conditions holds.

**[Corollary]**

**Concrete-Entity Test** · *Corollary*

An abstract object is not a counterexample to the Conditions on concrete change: abstract existence by itself attributes no concrete operation. Any candidate said to change, act, experience, create, sustain, intervene, or efficiently produce a concrete effect incurs the full Structural Requirement at the operation or contact where that work occurs: a when in the order of the act, a where distinguishing its terms, and a what that bears the difference across it. A candidate assigned determinate abstract content but no concrete operation remains an abstractum. A candidate assigned concrete work must supply T, S, and Φ at that work. A candidate assigned neither determinate content nor a determinate relation supplies no entity or ground at all.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

The account of existence and instantiation the test runs on is fixed at §1.5.1. The corollary doesn’t infer that every atemporal entailment is temporal, every numerical non-identity spatial, or every abstract relation physical. Those are generic role-level facts, and the role-to-type bridge isn’t free. The full Conditions enter when the attributed work is itself concrete or change-realizing. This is the boundary Chapters 7–8 apply: abstraction preserves exemption only by declining concrete efficacy; concrete efficacy earns the stronger conclusion.

*The causal-role boundary.* In the Concrete-Entity Test, *cause* means productive or efficient causation, including agent-causal production: a concrete effect obtains because a source makes a difference to it. The corollary doesn’t treat every Aristotelian *aitia* or every *because of* relation as that operation. Material cause answers what something is made from; formal cause answers by what organization or form it is the thing it is; final cause answers for the sake of what a process occurs; metaphysical grounding states non-causal dependence. None is refuted merely for lacking temporal transmission. If a material, formal, final, or grounding role is also assigned creation, intervention, response, or another concrete production, that additional operation—not the causal label—incurs T, S, and Φ at its contact. The full taxonomy matters where divine causality is tested at §11.7.2; here the distinction fixes only which role the corollary governs.

Because the dependence is essential rather than accidental, it doesn’t vary across the modal structure: what essence fixes, it fixes at every world (Fine 1994, essence is prior to modality, not read off from it). Whether that essence is itself prior to the modal field, or names the shape of a field that is already primitive, is the priority question taken up at §7.2.1. The committed essence-prior view is not treated as already closed. The appeal here is to essence in its local role—fixing the necessity of the conditional—not to essence standing prior to ◇.

Four lines approach the requirement, each starting from a different vocabulary and converging on the same constitutive identification. The shape is parallel to Kripke’s *necessary a posteriori* (Kripke 1980): the dependence is secured by reasoning, and once secured it is necessary; the disanalogy is that the discovery here is logical-derivational from change-possibility, not empirical-microstructural.

*Line 1: Modal.* Any possible world at which change is possible already presupposes the Conditions. A plurality of worlds, and the transitions a possible change would range over, require Spatiality’s genuine distinctness, Temporality’s directional ordering, and Substantiality’s carrying pattern of causal-exchange relations. The characterization is relational throughout: Spatiality names the relation of distinctness, not the relata it holds between; Substantiality names the causal-exchange pattern, not a substrate that bears the relations (Ladyman et al. 2007). Modal structure is constituted by T∧S∧Φ, not merely occupied by it; a world that instantiates ◇C instantiates that constitution. Whether this a priori result is prior to and independent of what physics will eventually describe (or requires naturalizing contact with specific sciences) is engaged at §9.10, where Ladyman and Ross’s ontic structural realism is taken up.

*Line 2: Conceptual/Essence.* The Conditions are constitutive definitions, not reference-fixing descriptions. There is no gap between concept and essence at the structural level. Whatever would fill the role of ordered succession *is* Temporality. There is no deeper microstructure the role-specification leaves open; the individual derivations are developed in the subsections that follow. This is a structural-essence variant of Kripke’s natural-kind essentialism (Kripke 1980, Lecture III): the natural-kind machinery doesn’t directly apply at the structural level, but the identity-of-essence-with-role move is the same, and it is what makes the conditional hold of necessity rather than merely in fact.

The two-dimensional objection is that a primary-intension gap may remain even where the secondary/structural identity holds, on which the zombie-style inference from ideal conceivability of a structureless scenario to its possibility would depend. It is engaged at §7.1.2. The conceivability-inversion line at §3.3.4 channels that pressure through the necessary-content reading and points downstream to §7.1.2 for the block.

*Line 3: Grounding.* Any demand for a ground of the Conditions is itself made from inside the framework the demand seeks to stand outside. Grounding is a directed relation (the T-role) between distinct relata (the S-role) whose dependence genuinely obtains in a fact or realizer (the Φ-role). For atemporal grounding, this last role is dependency-stability, not persistence across a temporal interval. The regress can’t get started. The regress-block is a transcendental constraint on access: the demand for the Conditions’ ground already uses the Conditions to pose itself. That rules out the regress from inside. The further question whether a necessary being external to the Conditions could ground them from outside is taken up in the grounding treatment that follows and at §10.1.

*Line 4: Facthood.* The most primitive starting point is that something is the case. Its denial (*nothing is the case*) is itself something being the case, hence self-refuting. Facthood alone secures a generic floor: determinate content, a difference between obtaining and not obtaining, and whatever makes the fact the fact it is. It doesn’t by itself turn identity into Spatiality, obtaining into Temporality, or fact-bearing into Substantiality. The loaded Conditions follow only where the fact is concrete and change-realizing, through the individual derivations that follow. The move from concrete identity-requirement to Spatiality rests on the Relational Distinctness premise—that genuine positional distinctness just is traversable relational extension—defended openly at §2.4.7. With that premise carried there, the S-clause for concrete change is earned rather than assumed. All the more so, any world at which change is possible meets the requirement.

The derivation is modal-structural, not mathematical-structural: it runs through what any obtaining state of affairs requires, not through which mathematical structures independently exist. Whether the formal specifiability of T∧S∧Φ collapses this into the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis is engaged at §9.9; whether the derivation uniquely identifies T∧S∧Φ (only this structure, not other formally consistent alternatives) is engaged at §7.2.6 and §8.2.4.

The four lines converge, but they share a hinge: the role-anchored definitions of the three Conditions and the modal-core derivations that cash them at §2.4.6–2.4.8. A reader may enter through modal, essence, grounding, or facthood vocabulary; none of those entrances substitutes for defending the common constitutive premises. The convergence broadens access to the argument rather than multiplying the warrant for its shared hinge.

One structural note on ideology—in Quine’s technical sense, the primitive predicates a theory takes as basic, not a political program: T, S, and Φ are the book’s fundamental primitive structural predicates, not derived from anything more fundamental, though Lines 1–4 give independent paths to the requirement. Whether T∧S∧Φ is one joint three ways or three independent joints is answered at §2.6. Whether □ itself is primitive or derived from structural incapacity is addressed at §2.11.

The reverse direction T∧S∧Φ → ◇C isn’t needed for the proof to the conclusion. It is defended at §2.4.10 and later read as part of the Modal Identity at §2.6.

The Structural Requirement is the necessary conditional □(◇C → T∧S∧Φ). Discharged against the Necessary Possibility of Change □◇C (§2.3), it delivers the unconditional necessity of the structural Conditions; that step is taken at §2.5. The proof to the conclusion requires only this forward conditional; the biconditional and the identity it grounds do their downstream work later in the chapter.

### 2.4.1 Constituting Modal Structure
The S5 principle fixes how possibility and necessity range across evaluations: whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary, and whatever is necessary, its necessity is necessary. It doesn’t by itself say what any world locally contains. What constitutes the modal field within which world-descriptions can be evaluated at all?

Modal structure presupposes the structural Conditions. Possible worlds aren’t the ground of modal facts; they are descriptions of what Reality permits. The structural Conditions are prior to modal structure, not derived from it. What is necessary is what Reality requires. What is possible is what Reality permits.

The distinction matters. T, S, and Φ aren’t features located *within* modal structure, features that could in principle be subtracted to leave some thinner modal structure behind. They are what makes modal structure something rather than nothing. A natural temptation is the container picture: modal structure is a room, the structural Conditions are features inside it, so one could imagine the room without them. The container picture gets the relation backward. The structural Conditions aren’t contents of modal structure the way furniture is content of a room; they are what would have to be present for there to be any room at all. Vary T, S, or Φ and the result is not a different modal structure. It is none. Modal structure is constituted by T, S, and Φ, not occupied by them.

The temptation has a canonical image, and the book’s habit is to run such images in reverse. Plato’s prisoner takes the shadows on the cave wall for the whole of what is, then is freed into a truer order beyond them; the classical ascent leads *out* of the sensible world toward Forms that stand beyond time and space. Run the other way, the correction isn’t an exit. The prisoner’s mistake was to take a truncated grasp of the one Reality for its whole extent, and what he ascends into isn’t a region beyond Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality but the same Reality grasped without the truncation; his confinement bounded what he took to be possible, not what was. The container picture makes the prisoner’s mistake one level up: it imagines an outside to modal structure as he imagines a world elsewhere, when the three Conditions it would step beyond are what any elsewhere must already instantiate to be anywhere at all.

To introduce a ground of possibility by appealing to a possibility is to concede the possibility-space in advance. The standard theistic reply is that God is necessary: *God exists* isn’t a contingent matter that requires modal structure to be open at the level of God’s existence. The reply shifts where the closure applies. If *God exists* is necessary, the claim *God exists is necessary* is itself a modal claim: it presupposes a modal structure in which necessity and contingency are distinguishable statuses, and a vocabulary in which *necessary* and *contingent* pick out genuinely different statuses for genuinely different propositions. Theism on this reading has to explain how God can be the source of the modal structure already presupposed by the claim of God’s necessity. If theism instead holds *God exists* as contingent, the claim that God is the source of what is possible requires that *God exists* be a live option, which grants the same modal structure at a different level.
