Either reading faces the same pressure: the claim about God’s modal status appears to use the modal structure it was meant to ground. The fuller theistic engagement belongs to Chapters 10 and 11; the point here is what the modal-structure line must carry.

The result has a neighbor in grounding theory. Schaffer’s (2010) priority monism treats the cosmos as a whole as the one fundamental entity, with parts grounded in it rather than composing it, structurally the same claim at the modal level, arrived at from a different direction. Lowe’s (2006) four-category ontology reaches a parallel result through different fundamental categories: objects, kinds, attributes, and modes mutually presuppose one another rather than deriving from any single base. Those categories are equally basic where the present argument treats the modal roles as equally basic.

A more direct path reaches the same conclusion for one family of frameworks: those on which worlds are concrete existents. The path is a conditional critique of concrete modal realism, not a derivation from plurality as such—abstract pluralities are handled by the w′ argument and the abstractist reply that follows, not by this route. For a plurality of concrete worlds to be genuine, there must be a real difference between them—two such worlds must be two, not one world described twice. Whatever makes that concrete difference is differentiating structure. It needn’t be qualitative, relational, or spatial; but if it individuates, it belongs to the complete structure of Reality.

Two concrete things may differ qualitatively, relationally, or through primitive thisness. None of those options escapes structure. A qualitative profile is structure; a relation is structure; and a thisness that genuinely makes this item not that one is nonqualitative differentiating structure. If the alleged individuator makes no difference, it does not make two. The narrower spatial question remains separate: qualitative or haecceitistic difference alone doesn’t supply an interval, just as red isn’t blue yet nothing is traversed in passing from one to the other (§2.4.7). Black’s two spheres make both points vivid: their qualitative indiscernibility is compatible with their relational separation, and any further primitive identity would add nonqualitative structure without replacing the distance between them.

The remaining refusal appeals to primitive thisness while denying that the thisness contributes structure. The fork is exhaustive. If it distinguishes the worlds, it is the differentiating structure by which their plurality obtains. If it contributes no difference, it supplies no individuation. Mere number can’t substitute for what earns the number (§7.2.3; the same pressure applies to Tegmark’s mathematical structures at §9.9).

The point cuts one way only. That two worlds can be told apart presupposes a real differentiator; it does not deliver concrete worlds merely by attaching two labels. A framework that leans on sheer numerical distinctness to secure concreteness reads the arrow backward. One apparent residue the w′ argument doesn’t reach by itself is the determined concrete realist who grants each world its full internal structure and holds only the cross-world plurality primitive. Structural Individuation closes that position deductively within the book’s premise set: whatever makes the worlds two is differentiating structure within Reality; if nothing does, there are not two. The realist can reject the premise, but that is a refusal of the book’s account of concrete individuation rather than a countermodel satisfying it. The cost argument at Modal Realism (§7.2.3) defends the premise against that refusal.

The same verdict carries from the many to the one without turning every individuation into an interval. A haecceity that makes two totalities two contributes differentiating structure. A haecceity invoked to keep one being one across change must likewise contribute to the continuity profile or do no work. What bears identity through change is the persistence of Substance carrying content through Time’s ordering, argued here as Cross-Interval Persistence (§2.4.8) and applied downstream to the changeless-ground dilemma (§3.1.1) and personal identity (§5.7). Primitive thisness may name part of that structure; it can’t both remain outside it and perform its individuating work.

Where worlds of that concrete kind stand in a temporal relation, the relation is already within Temporality in the abstract sense developed at §1.4: simultaneous coexistence places them in one temporal order, while before-and-after orders them asymmetrically. A concrete realist may instead stipulate that causally isolated totalities stand in no temporal relation at all. The temporal line doesn’t refute that option. Structural Individuation carries the separate and more general claim that whatever makes the totalities two is differentiating structure; Relational Distinctness adds only that any *positional* separation among them requires a difference-bearing interval. What Modal Realism (§7.2.3) adds is the cost argument against a primitivist who refuses the general premise. No step of the derivation waits on Chapter 7, which engages refusers of premises Chapter 2 has already argued.

Abstractist frameworks resist this by treating possible worlds as abstract objects rather than concrete existents, but only by conceding that worlds aren’t genuine existents, which relocates the requirement rather than defeating it: whatever hosts the abstract structure must itself be a genuine existent, and the argument applies there. The w′ argument of The S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5) closes this line independently.

For the gap between concrete worlds to be a genuine relation—for their otherness and their temporal situation to be facts rather than labels—something must bear those relations across the interval. A relation nothing bears is not a fact holding between its relata but a label laid across them. And whatever bears a relation across an interval must itself persist across it (the Cross-Interval Persistence premise, defended at §2.4.8, in the bearing sense fixed there rather than production). That bearing is Substantiality.

*Taking stock.* Modal structure isn’t a container standing apart from the verdicts it issues. It is Reality under the bilateral constraint that permits some contents and precludes others. The direct path adds a conditional result: any framework on which worlds are concrete existents rebuilds the structural roles inside its own plurality, and any abstractist framework relocates the requirement to whatever hosts the abstract structure (§2.1.5). This section doesn’t yet identify those roles with the full Conditions by plurality alone; the content-bearing identification is completed by the positive and negative derivations at §2.4.5–2.4.9. Any framework that posits a plurality of possible worlds is already operating within the structure of Reality. Not as one option among others. As the precondition the framework requires.

*Tested against.* Plantinga’s modal ontological argument, which supposes God’s necessity to ground rather than presuppose modal structure (§10.1.1); Tegmark’s mathematical-universe hypothesis, which identifies modal structure with mathematical structure (§9.9); Lewis’s concrete modal realism, which makes possible worlds concrete spatiotemporal manifolds (§7.2.3); linguistic ersatzism, which offers abstract-world surrogates (§7.2.4); and Armstrong’s combinatorialism, which generates modal structure recombinatorially (§7.2.5).

This is Line 1 of four; Lines 2–4 follow at §2.4.2–2.4.4, four access lines converging on one constitutive premise rather than premise-disjoint proofs (§2.4).

### 2.4.2 Structural Gap
The objection against constitutive necessity needs a gap between concept and essence, and that gap can’t open at the structural level.

The standard post-Kripkean picture distinguishes analytic necessity from metaphysical necessity. Water = H₂O is the canonical case: necessary in every possible world, but not knowable from the concept of water alone. The gap opens because *water* fixes reference by surface feature (clear, drinkable) while the essence is discovered elsewhere. The objector to the structural Conditions needs the same gap: perhaps *ordered succession* is to Temporality what *clear drinkable liquid* is to water, a surface description whose deep nature awaits discovery.

The gap can’t open here because structural Conditions have no surface properties distinct from their essential requirements. *Water* picks out a natural kind whose microstructure is left open by the concept: its nature is hidden behind its appearance. *Change* has no place to hide. It picks out a structural requirement: the presence of a before-state and an after-state for a persisting subject. The before/after distinction isn’t a superficial feature that might be explained by a deeper essence. It is constitutive of what change is. The definition just is the specification of the deep nature: the minimum structural requirements any filler must satisfy.

The test is whether anything else could fill the role. *The clear drinkable liquid in our lakes* could have been XYZ rather than H₂O, so the description underspecifies the essence. *Ordered succession* admits no corresponding substitute: whatever fills that role is ordered succession. The same holds of relational extension and cross-interval bearing at the role-resolution fixed in this chapter.

**[Dissolution]**

**Structural Gap** · *Dissolution*

The objection to constitutive necessity needs a gap between concept and essence, and at the structural level no such gap opens. The Kripkean case turns on a surface description whose deep nature is discovered elsewhere: *water* fixes reference by clear-and-drinkable while the microstructure stays hidden behind the appearance. *Change* has no place to hide. It picks out the presence of a before-state and an after-state for a persisting subject, and that distinction isn’t a superficial feature awaiting explanation by a deeper essence; it is what change consists in. The test that separates the two cases is whether the role admits a counterfactual different filler. *The clear drinkable liquid in our lakes* is filled by H₂O here and could have been filled by XYZ, which is what makes the definition descriptive: the role underspecifies the essence. *Ordered succession* admits no such alternative, since anything that would fill the role *is* ordered succession, and the same holds of relational extension and cross-interval bearing. Where role and essence coincide, the definition isn’t a description of the nature but the nature itself, and *outside the Conditions* doesn’t name an undiscovered essence standing behind the role.

*Scope.* The result holds for any realizable essence. It doesn’t by itself reach the reading on which a simple ground holds the dependence-role eminently or virtually rather than filling it, which is engaged as dialectical work in Chapter 10.

**Dissolves:** the concept/essence gap the constitutive-necessity objection requires

To say *ordered succession might turn out not to be Temporality’s core* is to say *what Temporality consists in might turn out not to be what Temporality consists in*, which isn’t a discovery waiting to happen but a contradiction stated in the subjunctive. A possible world in which ordered succession turns out not to require asymmetry or transitivity isn’t a world in which we have discovered something surprising about temporal structure. It is a world in which Temporality isn’t instantiated, by definition. The analytic entailment is already metaphysical.

The identification invites a mislabel. The *Necessity of Nature*, established at §2.9.6, isn’t physicalism. It doesn’t claim that matter exhausts reality and everything else reduces to it. Substantiality is one of three co-equal structural roles, not the basement on which Temporality and Spatiality rest; the claim is instead that any being whatsoever, under any description, instantiates all three Conditions (§2.6). A theist, idealist, or dual-aspect realist keeps their vocabulary descriptively; what they can’t keep is a realizer that escapes the Conditions. Even formulating the charge is an actual propositional performance—a Change in its realizer—so the Structural Requirement, rather than an analogy between words and Conditions, supplies the performative reply.

The constitutive work done by the Conditions is already the work any metaphysical realization performs. *Outside the Conditions* doesn’t name an undiscovered essence behind the role: for any realizer (anything that would fill the structural role) there is no deeper essence the role-specification leaves open. What stays open is a different and narrower question, not a hidden filler: whether a simple ground might hold the dependence-role eminently or virtually (by plenitude rather than by composition) neither filling the role as one more T∧S∧Φ being nor standing as a structureless void. The no-different-filler test doesn’t reach that reading, because an eminent ground is engaged as dialectical work in Chapter 10—not a filler at all. What the Structural Gap settles here holds within its scope: the concept/essence gap the objection needs can’t open at the structural level for any realizable essence. The Necessity-of-Nature position is developed at §2.9.3, which shows why physicalism isn’t the right name for it.

*Tested against.* The classical-theist reading on which a simple ground holds the dependence-role eminently or virtually (by plenitude rather than by composition) is engaged at §10.2.1 (Divine Simplicity), §10.3.2 (Neoplatonism), and §10.2.2 (The Via Negativa).

Fine raises the objection directly (1994). Essence is prior to modality: it is essential to {Socrates} that it contains Socrates, but not essential to Socrates that he be a member of {Socrates}. Applied here: change essentially depends on Temporality, but perhaps Temporality doesn’t essentially depend on change, and if this asymmetry holds, the collapse to metaphysical necessity yields only the right-to-left direction.

The response doesn’t deny Fine’s distinction. It argues that the entailment this line defends is one-way and constitutive, so the distinction has no purchase on it. What the proof spends is the forward direction: change essentially depends on Temporality, because change’s constitutive content—a before-state and an after-state for a persisting subject—just is an instance of the ordered succession Temporality names (§2.4.6). That dependence is written into what change is; no discovery could remove it. Whether Temporality reciprocally depends on change—whether temporal structure could obtain with no possible transition—is a further question, and it isn’t settled here by identity: it is postponed to where it is argued rather than defined, the sufficiency and frozen-world discussions of §2.4.10–2.4.11. Fine’s asymmetry is therefore accommodated rather than resisted: the specifications coincide in the direction the theorem needs, and the direction in which they might come apart is deferred to argument. What this line rules out is only the gap the objector needed: a world in which change occurs without ordered succession isn’t an open possibility awaiting discovery but a contradiction in the specification of change.

A Fine-style reply might press the asymmetry once more. Even granting the inseparability of the specifications, the underlying *items* could still have distinct essential profiles: Temporality essentially temporal, change essentially change-y, in the way Socrates and {Socrates} are inseparable in their existence conditions yet distinct in their essences. The reply doesn’t land against the direction the proof spends. In the Socrates/{Socrates} case there are two items with two essence-yielding specifications, and the asymmetry lives between them. Here, the specification of change already contains the specification of Temporality’s core: one can’t state what change is without stating ordered succession, so on that side there is no gap for a divergent profile to open. If Temporality has a profile that outruns change—temporal structure in a world where nothing could differ—that surplus is real only if the converse fails, which is precisely the question deferred to §2.4.10–2.4.11. Either way the forward entailment the theorem uses is untouched; Fine’s asymmetry, if it obtains, obtains harmlessly.

Fine’s (1995) later distinction between constitutive and consequential essence reinforces the point. The structural requirements are constitutive essences of the Conditions (what they *are*) not consequential properties derivable from a deeper nature that might vary independently. In the forward direction, the distinction between change and the temporal core it spends is a distinction in description, not in entity, like distinguishing the shape of a coastline from the land that makes it; whatever more Temporality may be beyond that core is deferred, not denied. The Conditions constitute modal structure (§2.4.1); they don’t occupy it as entities whose essential profiles could diverge.

Tahko’s *An Introduction to Metametaphysics* (2015) and *The Epistemology of Essence* (2018) develop a neo-Aristotelian essentialist modal epistemology on which modal knowledge derives from knowledge of essences rather than running the other way. The constitutive line here follows that pattern: it reaches necessity through what T, S, and Φ essentially are.

A different kind of gap (Kripkean rather than Finean) requires separate treatment. Pain and C-fiber firing are necessarily connected if identity is true, yet the connection is discovered a posteriori. Perhaps causally structured succession stands to Temporality the same way.

But pain/C-fiber is a case of deeper realization within an already given structure: a phenomenological state realized by a specific physical process. The structural Conditions aren’t surfaces awaiting a hidden realizer. *Ordered succession* specifies what any realizer would have to be like to count as temporal at all. Pain can turn out to be C-fiber firing because both are inhabitants of the same structure. Temporality can’t turn out to be something beneath ordered succession, because anything beneath it would still have to instantiate succession, distinction, and exchange to be anything at all. The Kripkean gap opens within structure. It doesn’t open at structure itself: there is nowhere outside structure from which to pry.

A subtler objection concedes that the definitions are constitutive but argues they may be incomplete: that Temporality’s full constitutive nature includes features beyond what *causally structured succession* captures, and that the gap between concept and essence reopens at the margin of what the definition leaves out.

The objection fails in the direction it needs to succeed. Even granting that a richer constitutive specification of Temporality exists, that specification must include causally structured succession; one can’t arrive at a fuller picture of Temporality that removes the before/after distinction or strips causal directionality. Any additional constitutive features would supplement the structural requirements, not replace them. The proof doesn’t need the definitions to be exhaustive. It needs only that whatever T, S, and Φ fully are, they constitutively include the structural minima the definitions specify. An incomplete constitutive definition still entails what it specifies; what it might leave out are additional requirements, not fewer. The objector needs the gap to run in the other direction: fewer structural requirements than stated. That direction is closed by the constitutive character of the definitions themselves.

Suppose one insists, despite all this, that a gap remains between description and essence: that our conceptual specification of the Conditions might still fail to reach the things themselves.

*Taking stock.* Two closures hold. The first is performative: making and sustaining the insistence is an actual propositional Change in its realizer. The Structural Requirement therefore supplies T, S, and Φ at the level of the performance. The gap between description and essence can’t be asserted from a structureless standpoint.

The second is structural, and it runs through the gap as maintained rather than through bare non-identity, since the interval-requirement of Distinction Requires Spatiality (§2.4.7) governs positional, concrete distinctness rather than every difference whatsoever. A gap between description and essence is maintained in an inquiry that holds the two apart, not held in the abstract. That maintaining is again an actual transition: the inquiry differentiates the description from what it falls short of and carries that contrast through its own course. The gap can’t be maintained without Change in the inquiring realizer, and the forward theorem carries that Change to the Conditions. This closure concerns the performance of maintaining the gap; it doesn’t show that mere semantic non-identity is Spatiality.

*Tested against.* Information-theoretic ontology, on the surface-vs-deep-nature distinction (§8.2.3); Mathematical Platonism, on the abstract essences and the abstract-truth analog of the Kripkean gap (§8.1.5); Finean essence-before-modality, met at strength through the strict/weak-ground fork (§7.2.1); idealism, which reopens the gap at the constituting-mind level (§9.5); and Schaffer’s priority monism, through the constitutive-versus-productive grounding distinction (§8.2.5).

### 2.4.3 Demand Instantiation
A third line follows: any demand for a ground of the structural Conditions must itself be structured. Grounding, explanation, and condition aren’t structureless tools. Each names, in a different register, an asymmetric ordering, a distinction between relata, and a stable standing of dependence.

Those are the generic role-floor—ordering, distinction, and bearing—not yet the loaded Conditions the Structural Requirement spends. Temporality requires genuine ordered succession, Spatiality requires crossable relational exteriority, and Substantiality requires cross-interval bearing. An atemporal or analogically structured grounding relation doesn’t instantiate those stronger roles merely because it has priority, difference, and dependence. The bridge from the generic floor to T, S, and Φ remains a substantive burden, not a verbal consequence of calling something a ground.

The contemporary grounding literature (Fine 2012; Schaffer 2009; Rosen 2010) treats metaphysical grounding as primitive, non-causal, and hyperintensional, distinct from causal grounding precisely by not requiring temporal succession or physical media. The line here doesn’t contest that distinction.

Even on the primitive, non-causal, hyperintensional reading, metaphysical grounding requires asymmetric priority, distinct terms, and a dependence that determinately obtains. A relation stripped of all three—non-directed, between non-distinct relata, with no stable fact of dependence—isn’t a grounding relation but a label without content. This establishes articulation at the generic role-floor. It doesn’t decide whether ontological priority is Temporality, whether distinct terms stand across Spatiality, or whether the obtaining dependence is Substantiality in the loaded sense.

*Taking stock.* The regress can’t reach an absolutely structureless ground: any grounding relation invoked beneath the Conditions already instantiates ordering, distinction, and stable dependence. That is the earned scope. The committed essence-prior theorist isn’t thereby refuted or silently redescribed as T, S, and Φ; the theorist inherits the contact burden of explaining how the thin role-floor grounds concrete change without reinstantiating the loaded Conditions. That dispute is joined at §7.2.1.

**[Corollary]**

**Demand Instantiation** · *Corollary*

Any demand for a ground of Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality must itself be structured. Grounding, explanation, and condition each already name asymmetric ordering, distinct terms, and a stable standing of dependence. These are the generic roles of ordering, distinction, and bearing, not yet the loaded Conditions. A grounding relation stripped of all three is not a grounding relation. The demand therefore cannot terminate in an absolutely structureless ground.

*Scope.* The result does not upgrade ontological priority to Temporality, distinct relata to Spatiality, or stable dependence to Substantiality. A thinly or analogically structured ground remains a live candidate with a contact burden, engaged where that dispute is joined (§7.2.1).

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

The payoff is dialectical rather than an additional premise of the formal proof. The proof earns the loaded Conditions from its witnesses and constitutive premises elsewhere; the corollary here shows that a request for something wholly contentless beneath them can’t even state a grounding relation. A thinly articulated ground survives this corollary and must be tested at the contact it claims to explain.

The broader constitutive point remains. In the forward proof, conceiving change correctly and describing what change must be aren’t operations separated by a gap: ordered succession, crossable distinction, and cross-interval bearing are what the fixed Change consists in. That stronger result is carried by the Structural Requirement’s witnesses and constitutive premises, not by silently upgrading the generic role-floor of grounding.

The form of reasoning has a distinguished recent lineage. Apel’s transcendental-pragmatics (1976) and Habermas’s discourse ethics (1983) 1990 share the deep structure: any speech act that would deny the preconditions of speech instantiates those preconditions in the act of denial. Stroud (1968) remains the canonical analysis of the form and its limits.

The argument here isn’t transcendental-pragmatic in the Apel/Habermas sense: it doesn’t run from the conditions of communication to norms of discourse, but from the conditions of grounding to the structural Conditions any grounding relation requires. What the family of arguments shares is the closure move: the critic’s denial must instantiate the framework the critic purports to step outside. Stroud’s caveat is that transcendental arguments establish only that we must believe the Conditions hold, not that they actually do. It is handled at the ontological level in §3.1.5 by level-invariance; the performative closure here is its complement at the local level.

*Tested against.* The further-grounding demand, run explicitly in the First Cause / cosmological argument (§10.1.5) and in the demand for a rational ground of logic (§10.1.3). Pizzi’s impossibility of nothingness reaches the same modal floor by truth-maker, semantic, and Kripke-frame reductios (§8.2.4), and ontic structural realism approaches the abstract analogues of T, S, and Φ from the relational side via the relations-before-relata line (§9.10).

### 2.4.4 Something Must Be
Something is the case. This is the most primitive philosophical starting point available: prior to the *Cogito*, prior to the possibility of change, prior to any specific claim about the world. Its denial (the claim that nothing is the case) isn’t merely false but performatively self-refuting: the claim *nothing is the case* is itself something being the case. From facthood alone follows only a generic floor—determinate content, a contrast between obtaining and not obtaining, and whatever makes the fact obtain. The loaded Conditions follow on this line only for concrete facthood under the additional tensed, positional, and connection-bearing premises stated below.

For a state of affairs to be real rather than a static description, there must be a before in which it wasn’t yet the case and a now in which it is, or a now in which it obtains and an after in which it either persists or gives way to another. The inference runs on a premise stated here outright rather than carried as a gloss: real obtaining is tensed obtaining—to obtain is to obtain *now*, not merely to be the case in some timeless sense. The Platonist who holds that abstract truths obtain timelessly without being mere descriptions denies exactly that premise; that engagement is carried at §8.1.5, and the premise is used here for the concrete register the facthood line runs in. That asymmetric ordering is what Temporality consists in.

Any state of affairs has identity: it is this rather than that. For the concrete states of affairs this line runs on, that distinctness is positional rather than merely qualitative: there must be a structural fact that distinguishes it—a real interval that makes two things two rather than one thing described twice—where a bare qualitative difference is one description replacing another and marks no interval. That interval is what Spatiality consists in.

For a state of affairs to be part of a world rather than an isolated label, it must stand in connections that something bears across their intervals—bearing in the sense fixed at §2.4.8, not necessarily production. That premise, too, is stated outright rather than smuggled: an utterly isolated fact, related to nothing, is a limiting case this line doesn’t reach, and the isolation challenge is carried at §8.2. What bears those connections is what Substantiality consists in.

The three Conditions are therefore not stipulations about our universe or assumptions imported into the argument. Stated at its earned strength, the result is conditional: any state of affairs that obtains concretely—tensed, positionally distinct, connected to a world—requires all three. Whether every state of affairs must obtain that way is exactly what the named premises claim, and their defenses are carried where each is engaged (§8.1.5 for timeless obtaining, §2.4.7 for merely qualitative difference, §8.2 for isolated facts). The line’s contribution doesn’t outrun those defenses; the theorem’s own weight rests on the within-world route at §2.4.5–2.4.9.

Three challenges to the scope of that claim are taken up downstream. Whether an abstract truth like *2 + 2 = 4* requires the Conditions is engaged at §8.1.5. The Leibnizian demand for a reason *why there is something rather than nothing* is dissolved rather than answered: *nothing* lacks the Conditions that would let it be a state of affairs at all, including the state of affairs that nothing is the case; the Incoherence of ∅ argument is at §2.7.2. The separate ∅ Reductio Boundary (§2.7.4) records why that result cannot supply an independent isolated-world proof of necessary Change-possibility. And the modal contrast space (possible worlds, counterfactual alternatives, unrealized possibilities) doesn’t float free of the Conditions but presupposes them; that engagement is carried at §8.2.

This assertion arrives word after word as an actual performance. That performance is Change in its realizer, so the Structural Requirement supplies T, S, and Φ at the level of the assertion. Something is the case. This is one such thing. The illustration secures the concrete performance; facthood in the abstract remains at the generic floor just distinguished.

*Tested against.* On the abstract-truth case, Mathematical Platonism (§8.1.5). On the modal contrast space, Lewis’s modal realism, which turns plurality-of-worlds into plurality-of-concrete-existents (§7.2.3); linguistic ersatzism, which makes worlds abstract proposition-sets whose distinctness presupposes the structural conditions (§7.2.4); and Armstrong’s combinatorialism, which generates the modal contrast space within the conditions of recombination (§7.2.5). Pizzi’s impossibility of nothingness runs the same nothingness-impossibility argument by truth-maker, semantic, and Kripke-frame reductios to a strictly weaker bare-existential terminus (§8.2.4).

### 2.4.5 Forward Conditional
The four lines converge on the same constitutive identification: the structural requirement T∧S∧Φ. The conditional that does the formal work is **◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)**: if change is possible, the three Conditions are instantiated. The conditional is framework-invariant: it holds across every adequate theory of Reality, not just the one our physics currently provides.

The Conditions aren’t commitments to current physics. They are proposed constitutive minima for any realizer of Change. That is stronger than calling them convenient physical posits and more exact than calling them truths of logic alone: their force depends on the three constitutive premises stated below. Whether the framework is General Relativity, quantum gravity, an informational substrate, or a multi-dimensional manifold, what the theory is called doesn’t matter; what matters is whether its realizers satisfy those premises.

A *timeless* quantum gravity still requires state-transition structure: whether expressed as Hamiltonian evolution under canonical quantization, as constraint-satisfaction in Wheeler–DeWitt approaches where no global Hamiltonian appears, or as relational change between observables in Rovelli-style timeless formulations. The structural Condition the apparatus carries is what counts: ordered transition between distinguishable states. Different timeless-QG programs realize that structure differently; the framework-invariance claim is about the Condition, not about any one program’s preferred mathematical realizer. An *information-only* substrate still requires discrete rules by which informational states are exchanged. A pure relational ontology still requires ordered dependence among relata. Each eliminates a physical posit. None eliminates the structural Condition the posit was filling. And the thought that proposes the replacement is itself one state succeeding another. One version of this objection is that quantum gravity produces a fundamental description in which time doesn’t appear as a variable at all. That version is addressed directly in §8.1.2.

A theory that truly eliminated the Conditions wouldn’t be a superior physics. It would be an incoherent description: change without succession, positional differentiation without relational exteriority, interaction without persistence.

The distinction between a structural Condition and its physical realizer is what matters. The realizer can change. The Condition can’t:

- *T-Invariance:* If Δ describes a transition between states, it must instantiate Temporality’s asymmetry and transitivity.
- *S-Invariance:* If Δ describes concrete positional distinction between relata—an origin and terminus separated by an interval a transition could cross—it must instantiate Spatiality’s relational extension, exclusivity, and crossability-in-principle. Qualitative difference alone does not satisfy the antecedent.
- *Φ-Invariance:* If Δ describes an interaction or a persistence of influence, it must instantiate Substantiality’s cross-interval bearing capacity (§2.4.8).

Any theory that negates these Conditions while claiming to describe a Reality where change is possible is analytically incoherent: an attempt to describe a transition without a sequence, a positional crossing without relational exteriority, or an interaction without persistence. The act of imagining that attempt just performed all three.

What counts as physical isn’t fixed by current scientific vocabulary. It is constrained by what any adequate vocabulary must describe. The labels may change. Structure is what the labels are about.

**[Proposition]**

**Framework-Invariance** · *Proposition*

The Structural Requirement does not depend on which physical theory turns out to be true. The conditional ◇C → (T∧S∧Φ) holds across every adequate theory of Reality **provided the three stated constitutive premises are true**: Ordered Succession, Relational Distinctness, and Cross-Interval Persistence. A timeless quantum-gravity program still needs ordered transition between distinguishable states, however that transition is expressed; an information-only substrate still needs discrete rules by which informational states are exchanged; a pure relational ontology still needs ordered dependence among relata. Each may eliminate a familiar physical realizer. None eliminates the relevant structural role without rejecting the premise that identifies that role. Framework-invariance transfers the premises across theories; it does not prove the premises merely by calling them structural.

*Scope.* The invariance is not uniform across the three Conditions. At role-resolution, Temporality and Spatiality are framework-invariant without qualification, holding under Humean and non-Humean specifications alike, since even bare regularity requires distinguishable states in succession. Substantiality is framework-invariant at the bearing role—even Humean regularities are regularities *of* states of something—but the further, realization-tier strengthening to causal transmission is conditional, and a Humean who rejects that strengthening rejects it without unseating the bearing role or the theorem.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The interaction-definition objection.* The definition in Change (§1.3) specifies causal transmission rather than mere regular correlation, a substantive commitment a Humean will resist at the definitional level. So the Δ argument runs in two tiers, and the scope of the framework-invariance claim differs across them.

The first tier is framework-invariant *without qualification*: any adequate theory of a Reality where change is possible must instantiate T and S, because ordered succession and relational extension are required by change and movement under any non-Humean specification of those concepts, and indeed under Humean specifications as well, since regularity itself requires distinguishable states ordered in succession. T and S survive even if the Humean wins the definitional battle.

The second tier concerns Φ, and the tier policy of Structural Requirement (§2.4) states its scope exactly. At role-resolution—the resolution at which the theorem is claimed—the Φ limb is framework-invariant without qualification, alongside T and S: even the Humean’s regularities are regularities *of states of something*, and the persisting bearer that carriage requires is the whole of what the modal proof spends (§2.4.8). What is conditional is the realization-tier strengthening: Φ as *causal transmission*, production rather than bare bearing. A Humean who rejects causal transmission at the definitional level rejects that strengthening, not the bearing role, and so not the theorem. The stronger reading is engaged on its own terms at §8.2.2, and the pressure is brief enough to preview here. If regularity is restricted to the actual pattern of succession, it doesn’t by itself yield counterfactual stability. If the Humean adds such stability, the account owes an explanation of whether that addition reintroduces the modal necessity the position was meant to avoid. Neither option unseats the bearing role on either horn; the further argument for the productive reading is supplied at §8.2.2. The invariance of all three Conditions at role-resolution isn’t a stipulation. It is a consequence of the definitions the contract at §2.4 makes official, with the causal upgrade left to the tier that earns it (§8.2.2, §4.4).

The Conditions are falsifiable. Produce a coherent account of change without succession and T falls. Distinction without positional differentiation and S falls. Interaction without persistence and Φ falls. The claim stands or falls with whether the definitions hold.

*Taking stock.* The theory and its vocabulary may change, but the requirements don’t, because the requirements are what any coherent description of change must satisfy.

*Tested against.* The framework-invariance claim is engaged in Chapters 7–9: the Principle of Sufficient Reason as an alternative ground (§8.2.1), whether possibility has a source distinct from the structural Conditions (§7.2.1), Tegmark’s mathematical universe as a rival framework (§9.9), and structural realism as an alternative reading of the Conditions (§9.10).

### 2.4.6 Succession Requires Temporality
The three activity-dimensions of change from §1.3 (succession, distinction, exchange) now yield their structural requirements in turn. Succession is first.

Temporality, defined at §1.4.1 and borne in Reality by Time, is the first structural requirement: a relation of precedence among states that is genuinely ordered. Its modal core is two properties, grounded in the Law of Identity rather than stipulated: Asymmetry and Transitivity (§1.4, §2.4). Without Asymmetry, no genuine before/after distinction. Without Transitivity, no globally coherent ordering. Those two are what any succession whatever must instantiate, and they are all the theorem spends. The third familiar property, Directionality (causal structure carrying the succession forward), belongs to the realization tier: it is defended where the causal reading of succession is earned (§8.2.2) and where Temporality’s actual configuration is engaged (§4.2), and no step of the modal proof draws on it.

The argument states this load-bearing commitment openly, as an explicit premise rather than an implicit assumption:

**[Premise]**

**Ordered Succession** · *Constitutive Premise · T-limb*

For one state to come genuinely after another is for the earlier to stand to the later in an ordering that cannot be run in reverse and that composes coherently across states, not merely to be labeled *before* it. Whatever instantiates that ordering satisfies T at modal-core resolution. This spends Chapter 1’s fixing of Temporality as asymmetric, transitive ordering (§1.4.1) rather than re-arguing it.

A stronger reading is the **Causal Succession** thesis, on which genuine succession is moreover a directed relation of *production*, the after-state existing because the before-state existed. That is a realization-tier claim. The book endorses it and defends it against the Humean at §8.2.2, with the abductive case at §4.2; the modal theorem doesn’t spend it.

The premise is cheaper than the classical objection to temporal reality makes it look, and the reason should be recorded where the premise is spent. McTaggart’s contradiction is granted in full at §8.1.3 and still leaves Temporality’s role standing: it falls on one analysis of temporal order rather than on temporal order itself, so if the A-series is incoherent, Temporality is analyzed by the B-series or by a third structure and the choice among them belongs to the philosophy of time. Showing that a role admits no particular specification constrains how the role is specified; it doesn’t show the role unoccupied. A reader who takes McTaggart’s argument to succeed therefore keeps this limb.

What blocks the *labeled order* worry—states merely tagged *before* and *after*, with nothing making the order real—isn’t causal production but the modal core itself: a labeling that could be permuted without loss is an ordering of the labels, not of the states. Where the succession is genuine, the asymmetric, transitive ordering is a fact about the states themselves. What a bare ordering doesn’t yet supply is a subject persisting across the replacement; that requirement is the exchange dimension, carried by Φ at §2.4.8, not an extra content smuggled into T. The stronger causal reading is the realization-tier thesis defended against the Humean at §8.2.2: the *after* state existing because the *before* state existed.

At the modal core, the connection from Temporality to Substantiality runs through change itself: a succession *of states of something* requires that the something stand through the transition, and that standing is Φ’s role (§2.4.8); the cross-entailments are collected at §2.6. On the realization tier the connection tightens: if succession is causally structured, something must carry influence from one state to the next. That tighter entailment runs through the causal reading of succession, so it inherits the conditional scope assigned to the third Condition at §2.4.5: Temporality itself is framework-invariant without qualification, but the causal version of the entailment stands with the reading the Humean contests, secured at §8.2.2.

The impossibility of a reversed ordering isn’t a rule imposed on Temporality from outside. It is what Temporality consists in: Asymmetry is the role, not a constraint added to it. A structure within which *after* could precede *before* wouldn’t be a temporal structure with unusual properties; it would fail to instantiate Temporality at all. (The corresponding impossibility of reversed *causation* is the realization-tier mirror of the same fact, addressed at §8.2.2.) The impossibility and the structure are one structural fact approached from opposite directions.

Temporal logic and Temporality aren’t a model and its target. They are the same structural fact, one described formally, the other instantiated. At the level of the structural Conditions, logical and ontological necessity are one necessity.

The most universal phenomenological anchor for Temporality runs at the level of thinking itself, prior to any measured duration. Any conscious standpoint has succession directly: to think at all is for one state to give way to another—the thought now wasn’t the thought a moment before, and the passage between them isn’t inferred but lived in the having of any standpoint whatever. To doubt that succession is real is to pass from the question to its doubting, a passage that instantiates before-and-after in the very act of denial; the doubter is the successor of the state doubted (the argument of §2.2, run at the level of the bare standpoint). This anchor is offered, like the demonstrations at §2.4.7–2.4.8, as phenomenological confirmation rather than load-bearing proof; the structural argument that follows carries the load.

*The impossibility argument.* Any act that claims to produce Temporality must already instantiate it. There is no prior position from which to generate temporal structure without occupying it, and no moment before Temporality itself. The point can be stated formally:

**[Argument]**

**Structural Requirement** · *The Temporality Reductio*

Let Begin(x) mean *x begins*.

1. Any beginning requires Temporality, since *begins* presupposes a before/after distinction (∀x(Begin(x) → T)).

2. Something has begun: there is at least one beginning, demonstrably the present argument’s own utterance (∃xBegin(x)).

3. So Temporality is instantiated (∴ T; from 1, 2).

4. If Temporality had ever been absent, it would have to begin, since a transition from its absence to its presence is itself a beginning (Begin(T)).

5. **Time cannot have begun, because a beginning needs a before.** Any beginning of Temporality would require Temporality already instantiated on the before side of its own onset, since line 1’s warrant—*begins* presupposes a before/after distinction spanning the onset—applies to T itself (Begin(T) → T-at-or-before-Begin(T)).

6. ∴ So Temporality was never absent: the supposed onset entails T at or before the first instantiation of T—T-prior-to-T, a contradiction (from 4, 5 by reductio).

In plain terms: beginnings can occur within Temporality, but Temporality can’t be one more thing that began from no-Temporality. The transition from no-Temporality to Temporality would already require temporal order.

The move from actuality to necessity runs through lines 4–6 specifically: line 2 supplies actuality (∃xBegin(x)), but the no-absence result doesn’t follow from actuality alone. It follows from the conceptual closure that the candidate alternative—an absence of Temporality followed by its onset—generates a contradiction: the onset would already presuppose Temporality, which the Parasitic Negation rules out. The result follows by conceptual closure of that alternative, not by extrapolation from ∃xBegin(x).

This is the **Parasitic Negation** (§2.1.5) instantiated to T: temporal order can’t emerge from no-time, since any beginning would already instantiate the order it claims to begin. The same move runs against an emergent-time cosmology at §8.1.2. This reductio is an onset closure, not a second road to the necessity of Temporality: it forecloses the emergence of temporal order from its own absence, and doesn’t by itself establish world-wise necessity. The modal line reaches that conclusion jointly at §2.5, where □(T∧S∧Φ) unpacks into the Necessity of Temporality (□T).

*Taking stock.* Succession is established. It must be ordered—asymmetric and transitive—and that is the whole of what the theorem spends; the causal structuring of the order is endorsed and earned on the realization tier. But ordered states that aren’t genuinely distinct aren’t a succession. They are the same state, redescribed.

*Where this is developed.* The composition view of Temporality, the dimension feature (the ordered manifold) and the passage feature (the directed flow through it) as two features Temporality requires, is developed at §4.2, dissolving the A-series/B-series dispute at the level of Chapter 8 confirmation.

*Tested against.* The objections to the temporal Condition are engaged in Chapter 8: McTaggart’s denial of temporal reality (§8.1.3), the block universe and B-theoretic order without becoming (§8.1.4), the changeless ground (§8.1.1), and Platonist atemporality (§8.1.5). The Humean reading of temporal succession without causal direction is taken up at §8.2.2.

### 2.4.7 Distinction Requires Spatiality
Spatiality, defined at §1.4.2 and borne in Reality by Space, is Change’s second structural requirement: the Condition under which here and there stand genuinely apart across a real interval something could cross, rather than one position wearing two names. The claim isn’t that every difference whatsoever is spatial. It is that positional transition requires the stronger separation-relation, while the reflective route must independently earn that its co-present poles satisfy this positional criterion.

Purely qualitative differentiation is insufficient, which is why the Spatiality limb doesn’t infer Spatiality from the successive non-identity of Change’s phases alone. Two contents may differ as red and blue without standing in a relational interval, and a bare sequence of labels supplies no distance.

The reflective token contains more than qualitative succession. Its later recognition retains the earlier content, presents it together with the present act, and passes attention between the retained pole and the recognizing pole without collapsing them into one content. The episode may be externally veridical, illusory, simulated, or wholly mental; in every case the presented separation is a real feature of the occurring episode, because the illusion or thought must have the structured content it has to be that illusion or thought at all. Whether that separation is positional is the explicit burden of Intentional Traversability below; it is not secured merely by calling the episode Change.

Spatiality requires that this concrete positional non-identity be grounded in relational extension: distance between positions as a structural feature, without commitment to a metric or external geometry. Metric, dimensionality, and geometry belong to the realization tier, engaged at §4.3, and no step of the modal proof draws on them.

Unlike Directionality at the T-limb and Transmission at the Φ-limb, the third sub-property named at §1.4.2, Traversability, isn’t itself what the realization tier absorbs. To be crossable in principle is for the interval to be the kind of gap a crossing could span. That is exactly what a non-metric interval consists in, and the S-limb spends it directly, alongside Extension and Exclusivity. What realization leaves open is only which crossings a world makes available: dimension, topology, and the actual metric of any crossing, not whether the interval is crossable at all.

**[Premise]**

**Relational Distinctness** · *Constitutive Premise · S-limb*

For two items to be distinct *as positions* is for them to stand in a relation of extension to one another, not merely to differ in intrinsic properties. The criterion has three parts, and each excludes a different substitute: an interval that could be crossed, an occupiable place to cross from, and an occupiable place to cross to. Bare qualitative non-identity—red is not blue, with nothing traversed—is real but is not the relation at issue; a crossing toward a terminus nothing could occupy arrives nowhere, and a crossing from an origin nothing could occupy never departs. Whatever satisfies that criterion satisfies S at modal-core resolution. All three parts spend Chapter 1’s fixing of Spatiality rather than re-arguing it. Under *Traversability*, §1.4.2 fixes the interval as crossable. Under *Exclusivity*, it fixes the ends as occupiable, each position holding one complete configuration at a time. That is why the Groundwork says in so many words that what change requires is not bare numerical difference but “the stronger, occupiable kind” (§1.4.2). Satisfying the criterion is not a further inference from the word *different*.

The witness supplies co-presence, retained articulation, and selective passage of attention between its poles. Whether that is already *positional* structure rather than only determinate intentional difference is a premise, not something the word *co-present* can settle. State it:

**[Premise]**

**Intentional Traversability** · *Constitutive Premise · reflective S-route*

In the reflective witness, the retained content and the present act are not merely two qualitatively different descriptions. They are simultaneously available as separately selectable poles: attention can take either as its origin or terminus while their non-identity is retained through the shift. A relation with distinct, occupiable poles and a possible passage between them satisfies the modal-core criterion for relational exteriority. Therefore the witness instantiates S at that resolution.

*Scope.* This premise attributes no metric, dimension, bodily location, or physical geometry to thought. It is the disputed bridge from intentional articulation to nonmetric positional structure. A critic may accept every fact about differentiated content while denying this bridge; that refusal blocks the reflective S-route but not the Movement Limb.

An account that grants Intentional Traversability while blocking the spatial conclusion must deny the Groundwork’s role-identification itself. An account that grants only qualitative difference has not granted this premise and therefore has not yet supplied S.

Relational Distinctness plus Intentional Traversability carry the reflective deduction. The Movement Limb below supplies the cleaner route because displacement contains the crossed interval in its specification and does not spend Intentional Traversability. The further co-present, performative, and phenomenological passages are confirmation; the final reductio closes the onset-from-absence alternative without by itself establishing world-wise necessity.

The constitutive claim (that genuine non-identity just is relational non-identity) faces pressure from both directions. From the relationalist direction it is only strengthened: Dasgupta makes individual facts about which object occupies which position non-fundamental and the relational structure itself fundamental, so what grounds distinctness at the most basic level is precisely the relational structure Spatiality consists in (2009).

From the opposed direction, haecceitism (Adams 1979) holds that distinct individuals can share all qualitative and relational properties while being distinct via primitive thisnesses. The position is motivated precisely by the refusal to reduce distinctness to relational structure: the haecceity is offered as a primitive that grounds individuation prior to and independently of any relational facts about its bearer. Granted that primitive thisness supplies numerical individuation, the position looks like a clean exit from the constitutive claim. But the reply that goes through isn’t about articulation but about traversal. That a haecceity must be picked out as *this* rather than *that* is a fact about how it is represented, not about what it *is*; traversal, by contrast, goes to what it is.

One test disposes of every candidate exit at once. Positional distinctness is *traversable* distinctness: for two items to be distinct as positions is for there to be an interval between them that something could cross. (Traversability here is crossability-in-principle, a modal fact about the interval itself; actual traversal, its metric, and its physics are realization-tier matters for §4.3.) A bare qualitative difference delivers non-identity without an interval: red isn’t blue, but nothing is traversed in passing from the one to the other. A primitive thisness delivers a label without an interval: *this* isn’t *that*, but a label isn’t a distance, and nothing is crossed in moving from one thisness to another. Each grants non-identity while withholding the single feature that makes a non-identity *positional*: a crossing. The Constitutive Premise says that withholding the crossing withholds positional distinctness: a non-identity across which nothing could move is a difference of contents or names, not a difference of positions. This is why movement is the cleanest access to the Condition: a displacement is a crossing made explicit, and neither a quality nor a label can be substituted for the interval it traverses. Whatever grounds genuine positional distinctness must supply something crossable, and to supply something crossable is to supply relational extension.

The test has a second edge, and it closes the exit a bare crossing would leave open. A crossing isn’t only a traversal; it is a departure and an arrival. Something leaves one place and reaches another, which means the interval must terminate at both ends in the sort of thing that can be occupied. Neither end is dispensable, and each fails differently if it is missing. Where nothing could stand at the far end, there is no arrival, and what looked like an interval between positions is a gap between labels. Where nothing could stand at the near end, there is no departure, and nothing was ever anywhere to leave; a crossing that begins nowhere hasn’t begun. So the requirement runs in three parts rather than one: an interval that can be crossed, an occupiable place to cross from, and an occupiable place to cross to.

Each part rules out a different escape, which is why stating them together closes the limb. A candidate supplying traversability alone has renamed the qualitative or nominal difference the test already rejects—an approach in a description, with nothing able to stand anywhere along it. A candidate supplying occupiable terms with no interval between them has supplied two contents or two names, not two positions. What makes a distinctness positional is the whole structure: something could be *at* one term, cross, and be *at* the other.

The burden that test imposes is narrower than it first appears. The derivation doesn’t need every numerical distinctness to be relational. It needs the distinctness that a *displacement* crosses to be relational. Whether a primitive thisness individuates concrete particulars, whether two co-located indiscernibles are two, whether trans-world identity is a further fact—none of that must be settled here. What must hold is that positional distinctness, the kind something moves across, is constituted by an interval rather than by a label. That restriction is defended at §8.3.5.

*The movement witness.* So narrowed, the Spatiality limb has a witness of its own, and it isn’t the reflective episode. Change of position is one species of Change: a subject at one location, then at another, with what it crossed lying between. The reflective episode establishes the actuality of the structural kind without confining it to reflection; displacement is a non-reflective token of that same kind. Where the reflective episode has to be argued into supplying an interval, a displacement carries one in its own specification.

**[Premise]**

**Movement** · *Premise*

Movement is really possible: ◇M. Displacement occurs, and what is actual is possible (§1.2.5). Since movement is one species of Change, ◇M entails ◇C; the S-limb spends this narrower witness while T and Φ keep the reflective one.

The premise isn’t offered at Cartesian grade and doesn’t need to be. Soundness requires that a premise be true, not that its denial be self-defeating, and actual displacement supplies it directly. Aquinas opens the First Way with what is *certain, and evident to our senses, that some things are in motion*; Aristotle’s *Physics* takes motion as its subject; the cosmological arguments engaged in Chapter 10 grant motion before they begin. Their broad Aristotelian premise includes alteration as well as locomotion and therefore does not, by itself, entail ◇M. The narrower witness is ordinary displacement itself. Nor does idealism remove that witness merely by relocating it: where the structured world of appearance includes genuine displacement, that admitted configuration witnesses Capacity(R,M) (§2.1.5; §9.5).

The refusal therefore has one exact local form: deny that any displacement is real. That denial blocks the Movement Line and every argument that spends actual locomotion. It does not by itself deny alteration, generic Change, every empirical premise, or the reflective witness for ◇C. Nothing in the theorem depends on claiming otherwise. The Movement Line requires only the truth of ◇M, independently witnessed by actual displacement; the reflective line remains independently available if that premise is refused. A critic can’t grant a genuine change of place and deny the interval that the change of place consists in, but a critic may deny change of place while paying exactly that cost.

The conditional then holds without a bridge. To be displaced is to be at one position and afterwards at another, having crossed what lay between; the crossing isn’t inferred from the displacement but is what a displacement consists in. Read in the capacity idiom fixed at §2.4.9, for Reality to have the capacity for displacement across an interval is for relational exteriority to belong to its constitution—not for a further possibility to stand behind that capacity.

**[Argument]**

**Structural Requirement** · *The Movement Limb*

1. Movement is really possible. ◇M (*Movement*)

2. Whatever is really possible, its possibility is necessary. ◇P → □◇P (*Necessary Possibility*, §2.1.10)

3. From (1) and (2): □◇M.

4. Necessarily, if displacement is really possible, Reality’s constitution includes the relational exteriority a displacement crosses. □(◇M → S) (*Displacement*)

5. ∴ From (3) and (4), by the K axiom and modus ponens: □S.

The limb spends the modal core alone—relational exteriority under Exclusivity, nonmetric Extension, and crossability-in-principle—and selects no metric, dimension, or geometry (§4.3). Traversability is doing exactly the work it was introduced to do, marking off a positional distinctness from a difference of contents or of names, without requiring the reflective episode to establish the interval by itself.

The same premise reaches further than this limb needs, and the fuller result is drawn where the forward conditional is established rather than here. A displacement occupies a before and an after and is undergone by something that persists across it, so ◇M carries Temporality and Substantiality alongside Spatiality; the whole Structural Requirement follows from it by a second and premise-independent route (§2.4.9, *The Movement Line*). What is claimed here is only the S conjunct, on the narrow burden just stated.

*The transition test.* A proposed countermodel can’t merely place two variables on either side of an arrow. It must specify what the states are states of, what makes the latter genuinely later, what makes the states positionally distinct rather than merely differently named, and what makes the latter arise from the former rather than merely accompany it in a list. Directed order supplies the Temporal role; crossable articulation of the distinction supplies the Spatial role; real bearing supplies the Physical role. A model that supplies these roles hasn’t escaped the Conditions by changing their names. A model that can’t do so supplies notation for change, not change.

*The co-present route.* A second route reaches S from the reflective episode, conditional on Intentional Traversability. The retained earlier content and present recognition are successive as phases but co-present as differentiated poles in the later act; Spatiality is not inferred by making before and after simultaneous. A reader granting Movement already has □S, while one declining movement may assess this bridge separately. Necessary Possibility preserves Reality’s capacity for Change, not this reflective token as a necessary occupant.

Co-present content need not be metric or bodily, but it must supply differentiated structural positions: attention can select either pole while their relation holds them apart. With no differentiating relation there is one content under several descriptions; with one, there is nonmetric relational exteriority. Thus an unextended mind, monad, or spirit may relocate Spatiality into an articulated field but does not eliminate its modal core. The result is the spatial *logic* of mutual exteriority—not a metric, dimension, or geometry, whose realization remains open (§4.3).

This structural sense of spatial logic is distinct from the formal discipline of the same name—the mature literature of region, inclusion, and connection surveyed at §3.5.7.5—which regiments inferences over S rather than constituting it.

A determined opponent can still say the co-present states are told apart by a primitive thisness answering to no position; but this is the haecceitist exit already closed above, and it closes faster here. A bare thisness can at most supply the *apartness* of the states; it has nothing to say about their *togetherness*. The togetherness of distinct states in a single standpoint—the *co-* in co-presence—is itself a relation among distinct relata, which is the relational extension the exit was meant to avoid.

*The denial is issued from a standpoint.* Denying co-present differentiation still distinguishes denier from denied content and directs attention between them. The act therefore supplies the criterion’s origin, terminus, and passage—but only **conditional on Intentional Traversability**, the named bridge from differentiated act/content structure to crossable nonmetric exteriority. The catch does not refute claims to be bodiless, metrically unlocated, or outside physical space; those concern realization. It reaches only the modal-core here/there articulation exercised by the denial, and is therefore dialectically weaker than the Temporal witness.

The impossibility of a square circle isn’t a rule imposed on Spatiality from outside. It is what Spatiality consists in. Roundness is a spatial configuration: continuous curve equidistant from a center. Squareness: four equal sides at right angles. Their mutual exclusion at the same coordinate is a consequence of what extension is: the structure that makes positions exclusively and consistently occupiable. A structure within which both could simultaneously occupy the same position would fail to instantiate relational extension at all. The impossibility and the structure are one structural fact.

A familiar parody substitutes the married bachelor, but unpacking it confirms the same point. The words don’t produce the impossibility. *Married* and *bachelor* specify incompatible relational configurations for one person at one time and in one respect. The same person may be a bachelor and later married because Temporality separates the configurations; a married person and a bachelor may coexist because the bearers remain distinct. What is precluded is the collapse of both statuses into one indexed configuration. A square and a circle likewise may occupy different positions, and one figure may change from one configuration to the other across time; what can’t obtain is one boundary completely instantiating both configurations at the same position and in the same respect. Logic expresses the exclusion. The structures supply its content.

The phenomenological anchors confirm rather than prove the limb. At the universal level, a conscious standpoint distinguishes the attending from what is attended—the *me/not-me* articulation—whether embodied or not. Doubting the distinction enacts it. A reader rejecting this illustration but granting Relational Distinctness and Movement retains the conclusion.

For a reader with bilateral haptic differentiation, the same point appears bodily:

Consider the act of reading this sentence. The left hand rests here; the right hand rests here. Two heres, simultaneous, both demonstratively accessible from a single standpoint.

Look at one of them and feel it at once; then let the feeling lead the seeing, then the seeing lead the feeling. The hand has not moved. The standpoint has.

The plural *heres* are given as positions within one standpoint. With no relation differentiating them they collapse into one here; as positions, their individuation is relational. The illustration therefore presents relational extension from inside the standpoint without carrying the proof, which already rests on the constitutive and movement routes.

*The impossibility argument.* Any act that produces spatial extension thereby instantiates the full spatial logic (the foreclosure of square circles, the exclusivity of positional occupancy) constitutive of what extension is, not an addition after the fact. An originating act that produces Spatiality isn’t prior to or independent of Spatiality but an exercise of it; there can be no particular place without Spatiality already in place. The point can be stated formally:

**[Argument]**

**Structural Requirement** · *The Spatiality Reductio*

Let Place(x) mean *x is placed*.

1. Any placing requires Spatiality, since *placed* presupposes a relational interval between positions (∀x(Place(x) → S)).

2. Something is placed: there is at least one placing, demonstrably the plural *heres* of the present standpoint (∃xPlace(x)).

3. So Spatiality is instantiated (∴ S; from 1, 2).

4. If Spatiality had ever been absent, it would have to be placed or introduced, since a transition from its absence to its presence is itself a placing (Place(S)).

5. **Space cannot have been introduced, because introducing needs somewhere to put it.** Any placing or introduction of Spatiality would require Spatiality already in place at its own onset, since line 1’s warrant—*placed* presupposes a relational interval between positions—applies to the placing of S itself (Place(S) → S-at-or-before-Place(S)).

6. ∴ So Spatiality was never absent: the supposed onset entails S at or before the first placing of S—S-prior-to-S, a contradiction (from 4, 5 by reductio).

In plain terms: locations can be assigned within Spatiality, but Spatiality can’t be assigned a location from no-Spatiality. The transition from no-where to where already uses the relation it claims to introduce.

As with the T-limb (§2.4.6), the move from actuality to necessity runs through lines 4–6 rather than from ∃xPlace(x) alone. This is **Parasitic Negation** (§2.1.5) instantiated to S: relational extension can’t emerge from no-extension, since any placing would already instantiate the relations it claims to introduce. The reductio is an onset closure, not a second road to the necessity of Spatiality, and doesn’t by itself establish world-wise necessity; the modal line reaches that conclusion jointly at §2.5, where □(T∧S∧Φ) unpacks into the Necessity of Spatiality (□S).

*Taking stock.* Spatiality’s modal core is derived: Movement is really possible, every displacement includes crossable relational exteriority, and Necessary Possibility therefore yields □S. No metric, dimension, geometry, or physical realization follows here.

*Tested against.* Two sections, in Chapters 7 and 8, **defend the Constitutive Premise** rather than merely engaging a rival, and a reader testing this limb should go to them first.

Haecceitism (§8.3.5) grants Adams’s primitive thisness and Black’s symmetric universe at full strength and shows that neither exhibits a positional distinctness with nothing between its terms. It is also where the narrowing already used—that only the distinctness a displacement crosses need be relational—is worked out against the position designed to defeat it. The premise is spent against Lewis at §7.2.3 and supplies the cost argument for a primitivist who refuses it, stating openly that the deduction is conditional on the premise Lewis remains free to deny.

The remaining engagements test the spatial Condition without bearing on the premise directly: bundle theory and tropes, which deny relational positions as fundamental (§8.3.3), mereological nihilism, which denies extended composites (§8.3.4), Sider’s structuralism on relational extension (§7.2.8), and Platonist aspatiality (§8.1.5). The idealist relocation of extension to the cognitive register, which grants Capacity(R,M) rather than denying it, is at §9.5.

### 2.4.8 Exchange Requires Substantiality
Succession and distinction were derived at §2.4.6–2.4.7. The third Condition is already manifest in the fixed witness: the earlier content is available in the later recognition, so the episode isn’t two unrelated states merely listed in sequence. Something in the occurring episode retains and bears the content across the transition. That occupied bearing-role is Substantiality, defined at §1.4.3 and borne in Reality by Substance. Its modal core is two properties (§2.4): Distinctness (the relata of exchange are non-identical) and Persistence (something remains through the transition it carries). The third role-requirement listed at §1.4.3, Holding—that the carrier-role be occupied rather than empty—isn’t spent as a separate premise here; what remains through a transition it carries is already an occupant of the role. What no step of the modal proof draws on at all is Transmission: the bearer *producing* the next state, carrying influence in the productive sense. That belongs to the realization tier, endorsed and defended at §8.2.2 and §4.4.

**[Premise]**

**Cross-Interval Persistence** · *Constitutive Premise · Φ-limb*

For one state to give way to the next *as a change rather than a bare replacement* is for something to persist across the interval and bear the transition, not merely for two states to be correlated. Whatever occupies that role satisfies Φ at modal-core resolution. This spends Chapter 1’s fixing of Substantiality as occupied carriage across an interval (§1.4.3) rather than re-arguing it. The premise deliberately does not say *causally produce*.

The productive reading is the realization-tier strengthening defended against the Humean at §8.2.2. The witness meets the thinner criterion because recognition contains the earlier content rather than merely following it. An account that replaces retention with unrelated succession has changed the fixed sense of Change rather than supplied Change without Substantiality.

One clarification keeps the premise from claiming more than the theorem needs, and it belongs here rather than in the engagement that defends it. *Persist* names a structural fact spanning the interval, not an endurantist metaphysics of the thing that persists. A perdurantist, for whom the bearer is a four-dimensional whole with temporal parts, and a stage theorist, for whom it is a counterpart relation among numerically distinct stages, each supply that fact under their own decomposition; neither is declining the premise, and the theorem adjudicates between them nowhere (§8.3.2, §8.3.1). What the premise excludes is narrower: that there is no structural fact spanning the interval at all—succession with nothing running across it, which leaves *flux* without a subject. Declining the endurantist type is therefore not declining Φ at modal-core resolution, and a reader who takes the momentarist side of that dispute keeps the limb.

The same neutrality applies to permutation-invariant physics. Φ does not require a further fact of which qualitatively identical particle at the later stage is numerically identical to which earlier particle. Where quantum statistics withholds that trajectory-level identity, the bearer may be the permutation-invariant state, field, conserved quantity, or other continuity structure licensed by the theory. What matters is not a hidden label following an individual through the transition but a real invariant by which the later state is a continuation of the process rather than an unrelated entry. If a proposed theory supplies no such state-, field-, law-, or process-level continuity, it has not supplied a change under the reference fixed here; if it supplies one, that structure occupies Φ without restoring forbidden particle thisness.

**[Lemma]**

**Permutation-Invariant Bearing** · *Lemma*

Cross-Interval Persistence requires a real continuity structure spanning the transition, not numerical identity of a privileged object or particle trajectory. Endurantist objects, perduring wholes, counterpart relations, fields, permutation-invariant states, conserved quantities, and process structures may each occupy the bearer-role if they make the later state a continuation of the same change. The modal proof is neutral among those realizers.

**Depends on:** Cross-Interval Persistence

**Feeds into:** Structural Requirement (the Φ-limb)

*The exclusivity argument.* Suppose exclusive occupancy is a primitive geometric fact: two configurations can’t occupy the same coordinate, and nothing enforces it. What makes the incompatibility real rather than merely described? If nothing prevents double occupancy, the exclusivity is nominal, not structural. If the presence of one configuration forecloses another, the foreclosure is causal in the broad sense: something is doing the excluding, and that cross-interval operation is what Φ names. Either exclusive occupancy is real and underwritten by some cross-interval operation, or it is nominal and not exclusive at all.

A primitivist about exclusion might press a third option: exclusivity is real and primitive, neither causal in the canonical event-to-event sense nor nominal. The reply runs the same way as the response to primitivism about laws (below, with Maudlin 2007). Whatever makes a primitive exclusion *do* exclusion-work must operate across the foreclosure interval: distinguishing the present configuration from the foreclosed alternative, holding the foreclosure stable across the interval where the foreclosed configuration is foreclosed. That cross-interval operation is what Φ names at the level of foreclosure rather than at the level of explicit event causation. The primitivist who keeps the foreclosure stable inherits the medium-work under different vocabulary; the primitivist who strips the cross-interval operation loses what makes the exclusion an exclusion rather than a label. The bridge from exclusivity to Φ is therefore not the claim that exclusion is *the same as* canonical event causation.
