It is the claim that exclusion, to do exclusion-work, requires the cross-interval persistence that Φ names, whether that work is read as causal in the standard sense or as a primitive foreclosure that performs the same structural function.

Causal exchange further requires distinct causal terms or roles. The source-state and uptake-state can’t collapse into one undifferentiated term, but they need not belong to two numerically distinct beings: one persisting system may occupy both roles at different stages. Substantiality requires a real distinction between initiation and reception, not an exclusion of self-interaction or internal change.

*The momentariness reply.* The objection that reality consists of momentary non-persisting events with lawlike relations between them doesn’t eliminate Substantiality; it relocates it. A lawlike relation requires the medium to be configured such that events of type A reliably produce events of type B. That configurational reliability just *is* Substantiality at the level of the medium rather than the object. Dissolve Substantiality at the object level and it reappears at the medium level: what bears the modal force the regularity requires. Hume’s denial of necessary connection between distinct existences doesn’t dispense with the medium; it declines to name what his regularities presuppose.

Primitivism about laws (Maudlin 2007; Beebee et al. 2009) reaches the same result from the other direction. Whatever makes a primitive law govern must itself persist across the causal interval, differentiate its relata, and host the direction from ground to grounded; that is Substantiality, given stronger ontological standing than the Humean was willing to extend.

*The vocabulary case.* Ordinary causal vocabulary carries the three structural conditions in its morphology. Static nouns name the medium: *resistance* and *yielding* (holding under transition or giving way), *consistency* (succession running without lapse), *coherence* (states held in exchange). Verbs name the acts inside change: *cause*, *effect*, *push*, *pull*, *mix*. Each word denotes only the kind of change defined at §1.3; subtract the medium and the words stop carrying meaning.

*Push* and *pull* carry the commitment most concretely. *Push*: to exert force away from the agent. *Pull*: to exert force toward the agent. Each names three relations in a single one-syllable verb: an agent, a patient, and an interval across which force transfers between them. Remove any one and neither verb denotes. No agent: a force without source. No patient: a force with nowhere to go. No interval: two things at the same coordinate, which isn’t a relation at all. Both verbs commit the speaker to T (the force takes a moment), S (agent and patient stand apart), and Φ (something carries the force across) before the sentence finishes. *Resistance* and *yielding* run the same three commitments from the receiving side: what holds against the force or gives way under it. *Cause* runs them abstractly: a producing-relation requires something to produce, something produced, and an interval across which the producing reaches. The vocabulary isn’t neutral evidence of the three Conditions but their signature in the language used to describe and dispute them.

*The deflationary case.* It proposes that *cause* names nothing beyond constant conjunction: events of type A regularly followed by events of type B, with no producing-relation underwriting the pattern (Hume (1748) 1999, §VII; Lewis 1986b; Loewer 1996; Beebee 2006). Declining to posit invisible connective tissue isn’t carelessness but discipline. Three layers of reply are available.

*Statement.* The reduction can’t be stated without what it tries to subtract. *Event B regularly follows event A* requires Temporality (B after A), Spatiality (an interval between them), and Substantiality (an observer persisting long enough to note the regularity). The reduction subtracts the three Conditions in its conclusion and spends them in its premise. The deflationary vocabulary is parasitic on the three Conditions it means to replace.

*Morphology.* The ordinary word *impression* has a historical association with pressing, but etymology doesn’t determine the term’s technical content in empiricist theory. That association may serve as a mnemonic for the experiential contact the word often evokes; it can’t establish that an empiricist is analytically committed to a pressing-relation. The morphology layer is therefore only a non-probative illustration and carries no argumentative weight. The Statement and Inference layers carry the structural point independently.

*Inference.* At a third level, the argument runs on what it denies. Arguments require persistence (premises must hold across the inferential interval) and exchange (premises must yield conclusions in one direction). Persistence and exchange are what Substantiality contributes. To argue against the producing-relation is to deploy producing in the deriving.

The three replies (statement, morphology, inference) establish that the deflationary vocabulary can’t be stated, motivated, or argued for without instantiating T, S, and Φ wherever the case is made. The narrower claim is actuality at the site of statement; the move to necessity across worlds where no case is made is taken up in Chapters 3–5 (Humean modal-contingency at §8.2.2).

The formal derivations already given carry the load; the phenomenological anchor that follows is offered, like the demonstrations at §2.4.6–2.4.7, as confirmation rather than proof. The most universal anchor for Substantiality runs at the level of the thinker holding the thought, prior to any embodied bearing. Any conscious standpoint has the relation directly: a thought doesn’t float free; it is held in being by whatever is having it. The thinker isn’t the thought; the thinker is what bears the thought across the interval of its occurring. Strip out the bearer and what remains is a sentence-shaped description of a thought, not a thought; a thought-without-a-bearer isn’t a thought that happens to lack one, it is the absence of a thought, with only the form of one in language. The relation is undeniable in the strong Cartesian sense: to deny that the thinker holds the thought is to perform a thought that is, in the performing, held; the denier is the holder doing the work the denial would have to escape.

*The impossibility argument.* Any act that would first supply Substantiality must already instantiate it: there is no prior position from which to carry anything across an interval without occupying the role. The predicate here is bearing rather than producing, and deliberately so—Transmission belongs to the realization tier and no step of the modal proof draws on it, so the limb is stated at the resolution it actually spends. The point can be stated formally:

**[Argument]**

**Structural Requirement** · *The Substantiality Reductio*

Let Borne(x) mean *x is borne across an interval*.

1. Any bearing requires Substantiality, since *borne* presupposes something that persists across the interval it is carried over (∀x(Borne(x) → Φ)).

2. Something is borne: there is at least one bearing, demonstrably the thinker holding the present thought across its occurring (∃xBorne(x)).

3. So Substantiality is instantiated (∴ Φ; from 1, 2).

4. If Substantiality had ever been absent, it would have to be borne into presence, since a transition from its absence to its presence is itself something carried across an interval (Borne(Φ)).

5. **Substance cannot have been borne into being, because bearing needs something that persists through it.** Any bearing of Substantiality would require Substantiality already instantiated across its own bearing interval, since line 1’s warrant—*borne* presupposes something that persists across the interval—applies to the bearing of Φ itself (Borne(Φ) → Φ-at-or-before-Borne(Φ)).

6. ∴ So Substantiality was never absent: the supposed onset entails Φ at or before the first bearing of Φ—Φ-prior-to-Φ, a contradiction (from 4, 5 by reductio).

In plain terms: things can be carried within Substantiality, but Substantiality can’t be carried into being from no-Substantiality. Bearing is already the persistence Substantiality names.

A reader who declines the productive reading keeps this limb entire. The reductio spends Distinctness and Persistence and nothing else, so the Humean who refuses causal transmission at the definitional level refuses a realization-tier strengthening (§8.2.2) rather than anything the onset closure runs on.

As with the T-limb (§2.4.6), the move from actuality to necessity runs through lines 4–6 rather than from ∃xBorne(x) alone. This is **Parasitic Negation** (§2.1.5) instantiated to Φ: cross-interval bearing can’t emerge from its own absence, since any act of carrying it into presence would already instantiate it. The same move runs at chapter scope at §3.4; it is deployed for the Φ-incoherence of ∅ at §2.7.1. The reductio is an onset closure, not a second road to the necessity of Substantiality, and doesn’t by itself establish world-wise necessity; the modal line reaches that conclusion jointly at §2.5, where □(T∧S∧Φ) unpacks into the Necessity of Substantiality (□Φ).

*Taking stock.* With Substantiality in place, the three Conditions are derived. Succession, distinction, and the medium that carries them arrived together: each required by the same structural fact, not three independent claims. That they arrived is established. Whether they could have failed to arrive is the remaining question.

*Tested against.* Denials of persistence, the direct stress test of the Constitutive Premise: Yogācāra *kṣaṇabhaṅga*, Sider’s stages, and four-dimensionalism with temporal counterparts (Stage Theory (§8.3.2)). The argument there shows that each supplies a structural fact spanning instants under its own decomposition rather than eliminating one, and concedes precisely what the momentarist gets right about the constructed self. The Lewisian argument that motivates the perdurantist reading is carried at §8.3.1. The remaining engagements test the Substantiality Condition without bearing on the premise directly: Russellian monism (§9.3), idealism (§9.5), bundle theory and tropes (§8.3.3), and mereological nihilism (§8.3.4). The hard problem, as an alleged consciousness-substrate outside structural exhaustion, is taken up at §9.1.

### 2.4.9 Forward Conditional Necessity
The forward conditional is stated as a necessary conditional: **□(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ))**. Not merely true in every possible world: structurally necessary. No possible world could satisfy the antecedent without the consequent. Three aspects establish this, and they converge on the same structural fact. One scope note is restated here: under the tier policy of §2.4, all three conjuncts hold without qualification at role-resolution—the Φ conjunct claims the persisting bearer of §2.4.8, not causal transmission. Only the realization-tier strengthening of Φ (production rather than bare bearing) remains conditional; it is defended at §8.2.2, and no step of this necessity claim spends it.

The *structural aspect:* modal facts are structural facts about Reality. Temporality is ordered succession, Spatiality relational extension, Substantiality cross-interval bearing. These definitions aren’t descriptions of contingent physical processes. They are what it structurally means to host change. A world in which change is possible but succession is absent isn’t a world with unusual physics. It is a world in which change is incoherent, which means it isn’t a world in which change is possible. The Δ argument of §2.4.5 grounds this as framework-invariant: any theory that describes a Reality where change is possible is bound by the same structural constraints.

The *conceptual aspect:* to deny the conditional is to assert that a concept applies in the absence of its own defining conditions. Change without succession. Movement without extension. Interaction without persistence. This isn’t an unusual possible world. It is a contradiction in terms, in the same sense that a square circle is: not because every world happens to exclude it, but because its denial isn’t a coherent description of any world.

The *essential aspect:* the definitions are constitutive of essences, not merely reference-fixing descriptions. There is no deeper essence of change hiding behind the definitions. The concept and the essence coincide, not at the level of language but at the level of structural Conditions. A world where change lacks its essential structural requirements is a world where change is something other than change.

Fine argues that essence is prior to modality rather than derivable from it (1994): the essence of a thing is what that thing is by virtue of its own nature, and necessities about the thing follow from its essence rather than grounding it. The essential aspect already stated endorses Fine’s priority claim for the case of T, S, and Φ. The definitions in §1.3–1.4 aren’t modal stipulations from which the essences of change, Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality follow as a consequence; they are direct specifications of what those phenomena are. The necessity □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)) is derivative: it holds because of what change, T, S, and Φ essentially are, not because a modal axiom has been stipulated to make it hold. This is why denying the conditional doesn’t describe an unusual world: it describes no world, because the antecedent’s own content already requires the consequent.

*Convergence.* The three aspects aren’t independent paths to the same destination. They are the same structural fact viewed from every direction at which necessity has content. The forward conditional isn’t a fact about this universe. It is a fact about what any universe must be. And the fact is level-invariant in the sense established at §2.4.3: whether a given Reality is described physically, as content, or as mental activity, the conditional runs through all three descriptions without remainder, because what it requires (succession, distinction, exchange) isn’t a feature of any description but of what any description is a description of.

*Tested against.* The necessity claim is challenged on several fronts in Chapters 7 and 8. The Principle of Sufficient Reason offers a rival ground of necessity (§8.2.1). Quine denies the analytic–essential distinction the essential aspect relies on (§7.1.3). Conventionalism treats necessity as stipulated rather than structural (§7.1.4). The source-of-possibility question asks whether possibility has an independent source (§7.2.1). And Williamson’s necessitism stands as the over-strong rival (§7.2.7).

*The bilateral identification.* One satisfaction test remains: whether the one invariant constraint that permits and precludes Change satisfies the inherited criteria for the three Conditions. It is not an inference from local occurrence to local inheritance, and it mints no new meanings for them. The Groundwork fixed their roles; the witness shows those roles occupied; and the modal predicates in this chapter have referred to Reality’s global standing from the outset (§1.2.1, §2.1.4). The question is therefore not how a Condition instantiated where change occurs gets carried into a silent world. It is the test just stated.

The answer is bilateral, in exactly the sense proved at §2.1.10. Actual tokens of Change—the reflective episode and, independently, movement—supply the positive edge: Reality permits ordered succession, positional differentiation, and retained bearing across a transition. Necessary Possibility fixes those permissions globally. The impossibility arguments supply the negative edge, and the negative arm fixes them just as firmly: if a configuration is really impossible, ¬◇P → □¬◇P. Temporality precludes an after preceding its own before; Spatiality precludes positional collapse, including the square circle and two complete configurations at one coordinate; Substantiality precludes an exchange with no persisting bearer or connection. These aren’t six independent laws, with three permissions on one side and three prohibitions on the other. Each pair specifies one structural role from both directions. Ordered succession under its asymmetric boundary is Temporality. Relational exteriority under its exclusivity boundary is Spatiality. Cross-interval bearing under the foreclosure of unborne exchange is Substantiality.

That identification is field-level because the modal verdicts it explains are field-level. Let SC be a square circle in the same respect at the same boundary. The negative line is explicit: ¬◇SC; therefore □¬◇SC. A square circle isn’t excluded only at worlds containing circles; its impossibility is a standing fact about what Reality permits. Nor is the exclusion merely a collision between two names. *Square* and *circle* specify incompatible positional organizations, just as *married* and *bachelor* specify incompatible relational configurations at the same time. Logic supplies the contradiction’s formal shape; what is contradicted supplies its content. Here that content is spatial.

The identification uses both edges. The negative edge alone would tell us only that SC is excluded; the positive edge shows that Reality admits coherent positional differentiation and exteriority. The positive permissions and invariant negative boundary jointly identify a non-vacuous positional grammar. The spatial logic doing that permitting and excluding isn’t a non-spatial rule added to Reality from outside. At modal-core resolution, that grammar is what Spatiality means. The same holds for the temporal and physical boundaries. Reality doesn’t first possess a contentless modal field and then receive T, S, and Φ as local occupants. T, S, and Φ are the articulation of the field’s own permitting and precluding work.

*Identity, not merely characterization.* One objection to the identification remains, and it is the one any role-identity claim must answer: grant that Reality’s invariant constraint permits and precludes exactly what T, S, and Φ permit and preclude, and it still seems open that the constraint is only *characterized* by them rather than *consisting* in them—some further modal fact whose profile the three describe without exhausting. Co-extension of profile wouldn’t settle identity. The bridge is individuation itself.

**[Premise]**

**Structural Individuation** · *Constitutive Premise*

Whatever individuates one concrete item from another is a real differentiating structure. If something makes x and y two, there is a fact in virtue of which they differ, and that fact structures Reality differently from there being one. If no differentiating structure obtains, “two” counts the same content twice rather than individuating it. Primitive thisness may name the differentiating structure; it cannot be both nonstructural and individuating. This premise does not say that every individuation is spatial. Relational Distinctness supplies that further conclusion only for positions, where the differentiating structure includes a crossable interval.

Let X name the constraint on the characterization reading, distinct from T∧S∧Φ but sharing its complete permitting and precluding profile. If X and T∧S∧Φ are two, Structural Individuation requires a differentiating structure. If that structure changes what the constraint permits or precludes, the profile was incomplete. If it changes nothing in the complete profile—no permission, prohibition, relation, ground, or operation—then it supplies no structure by which two concrete constraints are individuated. Bare non-identity is not a third option: without a differentiating structure it counts the same constraint twice; with one it returns to the first branch. Neither branch leaves a concrete constraint merely characterized by the three.

The move is the same one made at §2.8 at the level of concrete occupants, where it is stated as a named proposition. It does not broaden Relational Distinctness beyond its positional scope. The S-limb still requires only that the distinctness a displacement crosses be relational; the identity step spends the prior claim that concrete individuation cannot be nonstructural. A critic may refuse Structural Individuation, but then the proposed primitive thisness is being asked to individuate while making no difference by which its two relata are two.

The claim is therefore not “every local configuration contains an extended object,” and it doesn’t infer a local inventory from a global prohibition. It is that Range(R) has invariant rules governing which positional configurations can obtain together: R admits some positional configurations and excludes their contradictory collapses. A content-specific, non-vacuous boundary governing Reality’s total capacity belongs to Reality’s modal constitution rather than to any one local arrangement. Calling that boundary *Spatiality* names its role; it doesn’t turn an abstract logical contradiction into a material object.

**[Lemma]**

**What the bilateral line establishes** · *Lemma*

Reality’s invariant modal constraint is identified at modal-core resolution with T∧S∧Φ by the work it does in both directions: it permits ordered succession, relational exteriority, and cross-interval bearing, and it precludes their contradictory collapses. The Conditions predicate Reality’s modal constitution, not the local inventory of each world.

**Depends on:** Bilateral Frame (§2.1.2); Cartesian Certainty (§2.2); Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5); Structural Individuation

**Feeds into:** Structural Requirement (§2.4 Structural Requirement)

The lemma spends the Bilateral Frame (§2.1.2) as its method, Cartesian Certainty (§2.2) as its positive witness, and Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5) as the closure of each proposed Condition from domain-external absence. Those are its three upstream dependencies; Chapter 7 supplies later tests of the premises, not premises of the lemma.

The Structural Requirement now follows in its original direction. Since the capacity for Change is one permission issued by that constitution, Change can’t be really possible while the constitution that makes it possible is absent: □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)). The claim is at role- and modal-core resolution, not the realization tier; it establishes no particular metric, geometry, causal law, or occupant. Nor does it claim that every world contains an occurring change. It says that under every evaluation, Reality’s capacity for Change is constituted by Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. Triconditional Necessity (§2.5) discharges that conditional against □◇C exactly as stated.

*A second line to the same theorem.* The preceding identification runs on the reflective witness and spends the three limb premises—Ordered Succession, Relational Distinctness, and Cross-Interval Persistence—plus Intentional Traversability at the reflective S-bridge. A second line reaches □(T∧S∧Φ) from movement and does not spend that bridge. It doesn’t re-derive the same conditional: its containment step is □(◇M → T∧S∧Φ), and since ◇M entails ◇C but not conversely, that conditional can’t be traded for the ◇C one. What the movement route delivers is the theorem itself, by a parallel path. The two are stated apart rather than merged, so that a reader can see exactly what each costs and refuse either without the other.

The witness is movement, established at §2.4.7. A displacement is one thing at a position and afterwards at another, having crossed what lay between. Each Condition is a constituent of that specification rather than an inference from it. The passage occupies a before and an after, so ordered succession is instantiated. It crosses an interval between positions, so relational exteriority is instantiated. And what is at the second position is what was at the first—otherwise there is no displacement but a replacement—so bearing across the transition is instantiated. Read in the capacity idiom, Reality’s capacity for displacement isn’t three further capacities standing behind it; it is what having that capacity consists in at modal-core resolution.

**[Argument]**

**Triconditional Necessity** · *The Movement Line*

1. Movement is really possible. ◇M (*Movement*, §2.4.7)

2. Whatever is really possible, its possibility is necessary. ◇P → □◇P (*Necessary Possibility*, §2.1.10)

3. From (1) and (2): the possibility of movement is necessary. □◇M

4. A displacement occupies a before and an after (T), crosses an interval between positions (S), and is undergone by what persists across it (Φ). So necessarily, if movement is really possible, the three Conditions hold. □(◇M → T∧S∧Φ) (*Containment*)

5. ∴ From (3) and (4), by the K axiom and modus ponens: the three Conditions hold of necessity. □(T∧S∧Φ)

The trivialization charge arrives here rather than at the premises, and it should be met plainly: *movement was specified so as to contain the Conditions, so of course it yields them*. That is correct, and it is the line’s advantage rather than its defect. Containment moves the entire weight onto the antecedent. That antecedent isn’t a stipulation: actual displacement supplies it. A critic may deny real displacement, but then the Movement line alone is blocked. Contrast the first line, where the witness is performative and the weight sits on three constitutive premises a critic may decline one at a time.

The two lines are independent at their vulnerable witness: the first has a performative witness but spends the three constitutive premises and Intentional Traversability; the second has an empirical witness—actual displacement—and takes the Conditions from what that displacement consists in. They fail, if they fail, in different places. A reader who declines Intentional Traversability still has □(T∧S∧Φ) if they grant actual displacement. A reader who denies displacement retains the reflective route only if they grant its four stated bridges. Denying the interval and bearer within a granted displacement is not a narrow rejection of Relational Distinctness or Cross-Interval Persistence; it is a denial that the event was a displacement at all.

*Whose premise this is.* Aquinas’s First Way grants motion in Aristotle’s broad sense, which includes alteration as well as locomotion and therefore does not by itself entail ◇M. The narrower witness is actual displacement: anyone—Thomist or otherwise—who grants that bodies really change place grants the antecedent. Nothing else in the tradition’s account of motion, causation, or a first mover is conceded. The Movement Line simply carries that independently available premise through Necessary Possibility to □(T∧S∧Φ), with the theistic consequences assessed where those arguments are engaged at strength (§10.1.5, §10.1).

That use exemplifies the book’s inversion. A tradition insisting that something is necessary, exteriorless, and depended upon has hold of a genuine structural fact; the dispute is where the fact is located. The predicates survive while their proposed bearer may not. Later verdicts therefore differ: some rivals are incoherent, some realize the same roles under another vocabulary, and some are compatible specifications of them (§7.4). Granting a premise from a position to be inverted is not endorsing the position; it preserves what the position gets right and tests what it adds.

### 2.4.10 Sufficiency of Structure
The forward conditional (§2.4.5–2.4.9) established the left-to-right direction: if Change is really possible, Reality’s modal field is constituted by T∧S∧Φ. The converse also holds: **(T∧S∧Φ) → ◇C**. If T∧S∧Φ jointly articulate the field, change is possible. The two together form the biconditional **◇C ↔ (T∧S∧Φ)**. Whether its two sides state one fact rather than two necessarily co-grounded facts is the later identity question of §2.6.6, not something the biconditional alone decides.

*The converse’s scope.* Both directions concern the same structurally specified Change fixed at §1.3: ordered succession between genuinely distinct states with cross-interval bearing. Their evidential routes differ without changing that referent. The forward argument begins from actual tokens—the reflective episode, with Intentional Traversability explicitly priced on its Spatiality limb, and the independent movement witness—and identifies what Change requires. The converse begins from the joint instantiation of those same requirements and shows, through Moment-Individuation, that their order cannot remain wholly without differing states. It therefore reaches the possibility of Change under the same structural description. It does not derive a reflective episode, because reflection was never part of the consequent; it was one source of evidence for the antecedent.

This semantic identity matters even though the chapter’s main theorem does not spend the converse: □(T∧S∧Φ) follows from the forward conditional together with □◇C (§2.3). What the converse adds is the frozen-structure closure. Its dependents may therefore infer Change’s possibility from the jointly instantiated Conditions, but may not infer consciousness, reflection, or any particular token. Those are possible realizations of the structural kind, not hidden content in the symbol.

*The role-level premise.* At the role resolution the theorem spends (§2.4), Temporality is instantiated if and only if ordered succession among states obtains: the succession-condition for change. Spatiality supplies relational extension with exclusivity: the distinction-condition. Substantiality supplies a distinct bearer persisting across intervals: the exchange-condition, in the bearing sense fixed at §2.4.8. The converse claims that wherever those three roles are jointly and genuinely filled, change is possible. The causal readings of the Conditions sit at the realization tier and aren’t spent here; the converse rests instead on one premise introduced at §1.4.1, argued later in this section, and tested against Shoemaker’s case downstream (§8.1.1; cosmological application at §4.6.5): moments are positions in the order of states, told apart by which state occupies them. Call it Moment-Individuation.

The contrast here is with a weaker claim: that structure permits change. *Permits* treats T, S, and Φ as a neutral scaffold compatible with either change or no-change, leaving open a fully-instantiated-but-static structure. The converse denies that the static case is coherent—not by definition, but by derivation. The circularity worry (that the result is definitional) is taken up later.

*The derivation.* Suppose T, S, and Φ are jointly instantiated and change is impossible: no state ever differs from its successor, anywhere, for any bearer, at any point in the history. By Moment-Individuation, instants that no difference distinguishes aren’t many instants: a wholly changeless history, however long it is described as lasting, is a single moment (§4.6.5). A single moment isn’t an ordered succession—succession requires at least two positions, and two positions require a difference that tells them apart. The supposition has therefore removed Temporality while claiming to keep it: it isn’t a description of a frozen world but a contradiction between its first clause and its second. Contraposing: if the order is real, then somewhere across it states differ; with Φ’s persisting bearer and S’s real distinction in place, that difference is a change; and what is actual is all the more possible. T∧S∧Φ can’t obtain while ◇C fails.

What the older, causal-register version of this claim treated as primitive—that causal structure’s instantiation is its activity—survives at the realization tier (§4.2–4.4) as commentary, not premise: nothing in the preceding derivation spends it.

*Four pressure tests.* A challenge to the converse asks whether structure could be fully present yet change still foreclosed. Four objections raise this question: frozen worlds, dispositional masking, definitional guarantees, and the attempt to specify a foreclosing constraint without contradiction. Each fails in a different way.

*The frozen-world objection* (§2.4.11) and *the masking objection* (§2.4.12) press this concern at the level of dedicated subsections. Both fail in the same way: a world in which nothing ever differs has, by Moment-Individuation, no plurality of moments for its alleged order to order; it doesn’t instantiate T in a paralyzed mode but fails to instantiate it at all.

*The trivialization concern.* The old form of the charge said: if the Conditions are defined causally, of course their instantiation entails causal possibility. The role-resolution policy (§2.4) removes the target. The definitions spent here are thin—ordered succession, relational extension, cross-interval bearing—and contain no clause about transition-availability that could smuggle the conclusion in. The work is done by Moment-Individuation, and that premise is independently motivated: it answers what individuates positions in an order, and it was fixed at §1.4.1 before the converse was in view.

Its rival is a genuine position, not a strawman: primitive temporal individuation—bare moments distinguished by nothing but themselves, a substantivalism about instants. The argument grants the rival bare primitive moments and tests whether they can supply temporal order.

Shoemaker’s staggered freeze isn’t resisted at §8.1.1 but granted in full, and granted at no cost. What the scenario establishes is an interval, possibly global, in which nothing happens *while the structure making it an interval is retained*: a frozen stretch within a change-permitting world rather than time without the conditions of time. The freeze is describable as a freeze only because identity persists across it, the regions stay distinct, and the ordering holds. A reader who expects Moment-Individuation to be defended by denying the scenario should expect the opposite; the passage disputes are at §4.2.1.

*Can a foreclosing constraint be specified without contradiction?* The circularity charge can be made precise, and precisely answered. Suppose T, S, and Φ are genuinely instantiated (ordered succession obtains, relational extension obtains, cross-interval bearing obtains) but ◇C is false: no change is possible. What structural feature of such a world forecloses change?

The options are exhaustive. Either the foreclosure empties the history of all difference—in which case, by Moment-Individuation, the succession collapses to a single moment, Temporality is no longer instantiated, and the antecedent is false.

Or the foreclosure permits differences across the order while blocking their counting as change. But a difference between successive states of a persisting bearer just is a change under the §1.3 specification; blocking the label doesn’t block the fact. A constraint that leaves the three roles filled while foreclosing what their joint instantiation entails asserts and denies the same structural fact. It is like asking for a triangle that both has and lacks three sides under the same specification: not a difficult triangle but a contradictory one. No coherent specification of the foreclosing constraint survives: every candidate either empties the order (falsifying the antecedent) or renames the consequent while leaving it true (contradicting the supposition). The supposition isn’t merely false. It is incoherent.

The converse’s honest status is therefore: earned, given Moment-Individuation. A reader who withholds the premise keeps the forward conditional and the chapter theorem untouched: □(T∧S∧Φ) spends neither. What they suspend is wider than the biconditional alone.

They suspend the converse and therefore the Modal Identity (§2.6.6). They also suspend the frozen-world and masking closures (§2.4.11, §2.4.12). The attempted ∅ Reductio is not a dependent result: ∅ Reductio Boundary (§2.7.4) now records why that route stops without a separate field-level co-failure premise. They do not thereby suspend Triconditional Cross-Entailment or the partial-overlap leg of Exclusivity of Nature, which run through the separately priced Operative-Role Bridge and same-realizer pivots at §2.6.2–2.6.4.

Chapter 3 doesn’t add a further role-to-type upgrade: §3.5.3 keeps the bilateral Chapter 2 identification upstream. That is a wide surface for one premise to carry, which is why it is argued rather than left implicit.

*Not a primitive after all.* It is natural to file Moment-Individuation as this framework’s one brute posit for the converse, and earlier statements of the argument did exactly that. It undersells what is available. The claim is an instance of a refusal the chapter has already made and defended, and calling it a primitive concedes ground that was never lost.

The refusal is at §2.4.7, where the haecceitist exit is closed for positions: *a primitive thisness delivers a label without an interval—this isn’t that, but a label isn’t a distance, and nothing is crossed in moving from one thisness to another.* Apply that to positions in an order rather than positions in an interval. Suppose two moments with nothing whatever to tell them apart: no state differs, no arrangement differs, nothing bears differently on anything. What is offered as their distinctness is a label and only a label, since by hypothesis every feature that could have distinguished them is absent. A label isn’t a difference, here for the same reason it wasn’t one there. The two moments are one moment under two names.

Moment-Individuation stands on the same refusal of bare thisness made for positions at §2.4.7, but it does not inherit the whole of that section’s warrant. That is an honest bound, and a bound rather than a weakness. The difference should be marked rather than absorbed.

There the refusal is carried by traversal: a label isn’t a distance, and nothing is crossed in moving from one thisness to another. Nothing is crossed between moments either, so what runs here is the thinner claim that indiscernibles aren’t two. A critic may therefore accept the positional refusal on the traversal argument and still hold that instants are individuated primitively, and that combination isn’t incoherent—substantivalism about instants has motivations the spatial case doesn’t supply.

The dispute is continuous with §2.4.7’s rather than identical to it. What the critic can’t do is grant bare thisness no purchase anywhere else and then reclaim it here. A reader who does decline the premise should be sent to the preceding list of what suspending it costs, rather than told the question was settled upstream.

**[Lemma]**

**Moment-Individuation** · *Lemma*

Positions in an order are distinguished by their occupants, not by a bare thisness attaching to instants as such. Where no state, arrangement, or bearing differs between two alleged moments, there is one moment under two names.

**Depends on:** Spatiality (S) (§2.4.7); Structural Requirement (§2.4)

**Feeds into:** Sufficiency of Structure

The permutation test at No Bare Possibilities (§3.2.2) reaches the same verdict from independent materials and in general form, covering individuals, worlds, and positions together: erase names and coordinates, and no surviving difference means no additional possibility. That is convergence rather than the source, which is what Chapter 3 is for. And what §4.6.5 supplies is neither—it is the cosmological consequence, that a wholly changeless stretch however long it is described as lasting is a single moment, drawn where physics is engaged rather than where the lemma is earned.

The premise is therefore continuous with the book’s verdict on haecceity wherever it appears (§2.4.1, §8.3.5)—bare thisness individuates nothing, one moment no more than one world. And the critic who contests it must occupy successive positions of their own inquiry, before the objection and after, distinguished by exactly the kind of difference the premise names.

The critic who calls the proof circular performs an actual transition from not-asserting the charge to asserting it. That Change falls under the forward Structural Requirement and therefore occurs within T, S, and Φ. The charge is delivered on the structure it contests; this is a performative confirmation, not an additional premise for the converse.

*Result.* Given Moment-Individuation, the converse holds: T∧S∧Φ can’t be jointly instantiated while change is impossible. The biconditional **◇C ↔ (T∧S∧Φ)** therefore stands with one named premise on its right-to-left side, argued rather than assumed, and at full role-resolution strength on its left-to-right side (§2.4.5–2.4.9). The chapter theorem doesn’t wait on it: □(T∧S∧Φ) spends only the forward conditional and □◇C. What the biconditional feeds is the identity ladder of §2.6, which inherits the premise explicitly.

**[Theorem]**

**Sufficiency of Structure** · *Theorem*

The converse of the Structural Requirement holds: **(T∧S∧Φ) → ◇C**. If Temporality, Spatiality and Substantiality jointly articulate Reality’s modal field, Change is really possible. Taken with the forward conditional (§2.4.5–2.4.9), this closes the biconditional **◇C ↔ (T∧S∧Φ)**.

*Scope.* Both legs concern Change under one structural description; neither has reflection in its intension. The forward leg identifies what actual Change requires. The converse establishes Change’s possibility from the joint instantiation of those requirements. Whether the two sides state one fact or two necessarily co-grounded facts is the identity question of §2.6.6, not settled here.

**Depends on:** Moment-Individuation (§2.4.10)

Three pieces are now in hand and should be kept distinct on the path to the chapter-level conclusion.

The Cartesian certainty of change’s possibility (§2.2) grants ◇C as a proposition. The forward conditional ◇C → (T∧S∧Φ), established at §2.4.5–2.4.9, is the left-to-right direction of the biconditional; modus ponens on that certainty and the forward conditional yields T∧S∧Φ.

The converse T∧S∧Φ → ◇C—the right-to-left direction—closes the biconditional ◇C ↔ (T∧S∧Φ). Combined with the necessity of the conditional (§2.4.9) and the Necessary Possibility of Change □◇C (§2.3), the unconditional □(T∧S∧Φ) follows at the chapter level.

What remains is the unconditional necessity of Nature, declared at §2.9.6. That result combines the biconditional, the chapter’s modal-invariance result (§2.3), and the structural identity of T∧S∧Φ with Nature (§2.6.10). The ∅ analysis is not an additional modal-invariance premise: ∅ Reductio Boundary (§2.7.4) explicitly marks why the attempted alternate route does not close. Establishing the converse direction closes the biconditional; the unconditional theorem itself follows only at §2.9.6.

*Tested against.* The converse (that structure suffices for change-possibility) is engaged in Chapters 7–9: Sider’s structuralism (§7.2.8), structural realism (§9.10), Tegmark’s mathematical universe (§9.9), the changeless ground (§8.1.1), and the block universe (§8.1.4).

### 2.4.11 The Frozen-World Test
Suppose a world has the right-looking structure but is permanently frozen: nothing ever changes, nothing can change. It looks like a world that instantiates T, S, and Φ with change ruled out: a standing counterexample to the converse (§2.4.10). The appearance dissolves the moment the Conditions are read as defined.

Take the countermodel at full strength: grant the frozen world its temporal ordering, its geometry, its persisting configuration—grant that nothing about the *description* sounds empty. The question is whether the description can be satisfied. What it needs is a plurality of moments with nothing to tell them apart: every state identical to its successor, forever. By Moment-Individuation, positions in an order are distinguished by their occupants; where no occupant ever differs, the alleged many moments are one moment under many labels. The result is introduced at §1.4.1, argued and spent at §2.4.10, tested against Shoemaker at §8.1.1, and applied cosmologically at §4.6.5. The frozen world doesn’t have a long changeless history. It has no history: a single configuration misdescribed as enduring.

Each Condition then fails in turn, and not by definitional fiat. Temporality fails because a single moment isn’t an ordered succession: the order was real only if its positions were many, and its positions were many only if something differed between them. Spatiality’s relational extension survives in the description as static geometry—the one element the countermodel genuinely keeps—but Substantiality’s cross-interval bearing then has nothing to cross: a bearer persists *across* intervals of a real succession, and the succession has collapsed. The countermodel isn’t a world that instantiates the three roles with change subtracted; it is a world-description whose clauses quietly delete one another. Shoemaker’s staggered freeze, by contrast, is no counterexample here at all: local freezes are timed by changes elsewhere, so the succession stays real, change stays actual somewhere, and ◇C stays true. That’s why the book’s engagement with it (§8.1.1) concedes the local case and disputes only the extrapolation to a global, eternal freeze—the point where Moment-Individuation bites.

*Taking stock.* The consequence for the converse (§2.4.10) is direct: a world that genuinely instantiates the Conditions can’t fail to permit change—not because permitting change was written into the definitions, but because a history emptied of all difference collapses into a single moment and takes Temporality down with it. The frozen-world scenario describes the absence of the Conditions, not their unusual mode. What the reply spends is Moment-Individuation, named and argued, not the causal loading the role policy retired (§2.4).

**[Dissolution]**

**The Frozen World Has No History** · *Dissolution*

A permanently frozen world isn’t a world instantiating T, S, and Φ with change subtracted; it is a description whose clauses delete one another. Positions in an order are distinguished by their occupants, so where no occupant ever differs the alleged many moments are one moment under many labels. Temporality then fails, since a single moment isn’t an ordered succession, and Substantiality fails with it, since a bearer persists *across* intervals of a real succession and the succession has collapsed. Static relational extension is the one clause the countermodel genuinely keeps. The frozen world doesn’t have a long changeless history. It has none.

**Depends on:** Moment-Individuation

**Dissolves:** the frozen-world countermodel to the converse at Sufficiency of Structure (§2.4.10)

*Tested against.* Shoemaker’s canonical staggered-freeze argument for time without change is engaged at §8.1.1.

### 2.4.12 The Masking Test
A dispositionalist (Bird 2007; Mumford and Anjum 2011) might reply that the causal dimensions could be genuine but permanently unmanifested: fragility in a glass never struck. On the dispositionalist picture, masks and antidotes are familiar features of the world: a fragile glass wrapped in foam doesn’t break when dropped, but its fragility isn’t thereby absent. So perhaps the structural Conditions could be present in the world while their characteristic outputs (succession, distinction, exchange) are universally masked.

The disanalogy is structural. T, S, and Φ aren’t localized dispositions within Nature; they are the structural context within which every disposition, masking condition, and interference operates. The stronger reading that T∧S∧Φ *is* Nature in the full Triconditional sense is taken up at §2.6.10; the dialectical foreclosure here requires only the weaker difference between the underlying structure and a disposition within it. A localized disposition (fragility, solubility, irritability) is a property attaching to a Φ-bearer at an S-position over T-succession; the structural context is what makes property-attaching possible at all. The masking machinery operates on properties within the structural context; it has no application to the structural context itself. A masking condition for the Conditions would require a structural outside to structure. There is no such outside. The fragility of the glass is masked by the foam because the foam, the glass, and the dropping all share the structural context that lets a mask be a mask. Strip away that context and there is nothing for the mask to operate within.

The global-constraint variant deserves its own analysis, because it doesn’t need an outside: a necessary law internal to Nature, forbidding every transition, masks nothing local. Analyze it directly. A law that forbids every transition forbids every difference between successive states. Moment-Individuation (§2.4.10–2.4.11) then collapses the succession the law was supposed to range over. A history in which the law leaves nothing ever different is a single moment. A law quantifying over the transitions of a single moment forbids nothing, since there are no successive positions for a transition to connect. The internal mask faces a dilemma. If it leaves differences somewhere, change is actual and the mask has failed as a mask. If it forbids them everywhere, it erases the temporal order it needed to be a law *about* transitions. Either way the specification undoes itself—not because masks require an outside, but because a global mask on succession consumes its own domain.

**[Dissolution]**

**Nothing Masks the Context** · *Dissolution*

The Conditions can’t be universally masked. Masking relates a disposition to an interfering condition, and both operate *within* a structural context: a localized disposition attaches to a Φ-bearer at an S-position over T-succession. T, S, and Φ are that context rather than dispositions inside it, so a mask for them would need a structural outside to operate from, and there is none. The global-constraint variant needs no outside and fails differently: a law forbidding every transition forbids every difference between successive states, and Moment-Individuation then collapses the succession the law was to range over, leaving a law quantifying over the transitions of a single moment—which forbids nothing.

**Depends on:** Moment-Individuation

**Dissolves:** the dispositionalist masking reply to Sufficiency of Structure (§2.4.10), in both its local and global-constraint forms

*Tested against.* Schaffer’s priority monism, through the constitutive-versus-productive grounding distinction (§8.2.5), and ontic structural realism, which takes structure as primitive from the relational side (§9.10).

*Taking stock.* The masking move isn’t rejected because it is theoretically misguided; the dispositionalist literature it draws from (Martin 1994; Bird 2007; Mumford and Anjum 2011) is sound at the level it operates. Localized masks require a structural context and so can’t target the context itself; the global internal mask fails on its own terms, by consuming the succession it would constrain. Neither form leaves a gap between full instantiation of the Conditions and the possibility of change.

## 2.5 Triconditional Necessity
The possibility of change is invariant across modal evaluation (§2.3), and Reality’s capacity for that change is constituted by the three Conditions (§2.4). Together they entail that the three Conditions themselves hold of necessity. They can’t fail to articulate Reality’s modal field. This is the step that makes the joint structure necessary. The stronger identification of that structure as one Nature is established in §2.6, and its identity with Reality is assembled at §2.8.

The result is delivered by a single line that runs the length of the chapter so far. The Cartesian certainty that change is possible (§2.2) is lifted by the Necessary Possibility Theorem (§2.1.10) into its necessitated form, the Necessary Possibility of Change (§2.3). Since the possibility of change means Reality has the standing capacity for change, that capacity doesn’t vary with the local configuration from which it is evaluated. The Structural Requirement (§2.4) identifies that capacity with the three Conditions at the resolution the individual Condition arguments establish.

The two close by a single modal step: the Structural Requirement is a *necessitated conditional* and the Necessary Possibility of Change its *necessitated antecedent*, so necessity distributes over the conditional. That distribution is the K axiom, valid in every normal modal logic and so all the more in the S5 the proof runs in: □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)) → (□◇C → □(T∧S∧Φ)).

The formal shape invites a misreading: that this step is where the argument is won. The distribution is valid, but the weight doesn’t sit there. Since the necessary possibility of change holds, the Structural Requirement’s antecedent is satisfied under every evaluation, so the conditional filters nothing and this step is bookkeeping over a result already earned upstream. What earns it is the bilateral identification at §2.4.9, where Reality’s invariant permitting and precluding constraint is identified with T∧S∧Φ. A reader auditing the chain for soundness should test that identification rather than this modus ponens; a verdict of *formally valid, premises unestablished* returned against this section has looked in the wrong place.

There are two routes to test, and their costs are now explicit. The line assembled below runs on the reflective witness, the three limb premises, and Intentional Traversability at the S-bridge. A second reaches the same theorem from movement, with T, S, and Φ contained in the specification of displacement and with `◇M` as its vulnerable empirical premise (§2.4.9, *The Movement Line*). Either discharges against its own necessitated antecedent and yields the necessary joint instantiation of the three Conditions. A critic who denies displacement blocks the second line only; a critic who rejects Intentional Traversability blocks the first line's S-limb only. The routes therefore reinforce one another without pretending to be premise-disjoint. Assembled end to end, the reflective line runs:

**[Argument]**

**Triconditional Necessity** · *The Full Line*

1. Real possibility is Capacity(R,P), the standing capacity of R, not local reachability. Therefore whatever is really possible, its possibility is necessary. ◇P → □◇P (*Necessary Possibility*)

2. Change is possible, certain at the very level of its own denial (Cartesian Certainty, §2.2). ◇C (*Possibility of Change*)

3. From (1): apply the theorem to change itself. ◇C → □◇C

4. From (2) and (3), modus ponens necessitates the possibility of change. □◇C (*Necessary Possibility of Change*)

5. The possibility of change requires temporal, spatial, and substantial conditions. □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)) (*Structural Requirement*)

6. From (5): the K axiom carries necessity across the conditional. □◇C → □(T∧S∧Φ)

7. ∴ From (4) and (6), by modus ponens: Reality is necessarily temporal, spatial, and substantial. □(T∧S∧Φ)

Step 7 is the result: the three Conditions aren’t features the actual configuration happens to carry, but the invariant articulation of Reality’s modal field. Reality has no capacity for their joint failure. That doesn’t turn each local configuration into a collection of temporal events, extended objects, and causal bearers. The conclusion concerns the role- and type-level Conditions established in §2.4, not particular metrics, geometries, fields, or occupants.

The same line can be checked without abstracting away from the witness that supplied its antecedent. The reflective episode of §2.2 is an actual transition with ordered phases, concretely differentiated poles, and earlier content retained in later recognition. Actuality establishes the real possibility of a transition of that kind; Necessary Possibility fixes that capacity across the modal field. At the modal-core resolution established in §2.4, those aren’t three further possibilities behind the transition: the capacity for ordered phases is Temporality, the capacity for concrete co-present otherness is Spatiality, and the capacity for retention across the transition is Substantiality. The witness-preserving route therefore reaches the same □(T∧S∧Φ). It doesn’t replace the canonical derivation. It shows that the canonical derivation has preserved rather than discarded the structural content of its actual input, while the Structural Requirement establishes the result wherever Change is possible, not merely at the actual token that fixed its reference. Stated as the standing result the rest of the chapter draws on:

**[Theorem]**

**Triconditional Necessity** · *Theorem*

Reality is necessarily temporal, spatial, and substantial, because the possibility of Change is necessary and requires those three Conditions. This stage establishes their joint necessity: □(T∧S∧Φ).

*Where this sits, and why it is also a premise.* The result is a stage, not the terminus. The argument moves in three stages. *Stage 1* established that the possibility of change is necessary: □◇C (§2.3). *Stage 2*, reached here, establishes that the conditions on which that possibility depends are themselves necessary: the Triconditional Necessity. *Stage 3* is the capstone, the stronger claim the whole argument is built toward: that **Reality and Nature are one and the same**, that Nature isn’t a necessary endowment Reality happens to carry, but what Reality consists in, with nothing real lying outside it.

Between Stage 2 and that capstone comes what this result identifies—that Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality aren’t three separate facts but one Nature read three ways. It is taken up at §2.6, establishing the Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10) and earning the full biconditional whose forward leg alone carries this stage.

That’s why the result is a premise as well as a conclusion. It closes Line 1, and Stage 3 takes it up, at §2.8, where the necessity established here is shown to exhaust the real and to leave the Null State (§2.7) as no genuine alternative.

*Scope.* Two limits travel with the premise. The necessity is de dicto with respect to the structural constraint: under every modal evaluation, Reality is constituted by T, S, and Φ. It isn’t a de re necessity of this universe, its constants, any configuration it hosts, or the local occupants of a world. And it attaches to the structural roles, not to their occupants: contingency within necessity is preserved (§2.9.4). Nature is necessary; what fills it isn’t.

*The three, taken singly.* The result is stated jointly because that is how the chain delivers it, but necessity distributes over a conjunction, so each Condition is necessary in its own right—and each under the same de dicto, structural-role scope just fixed. The joint result therefore carries three named consequences:

**[Corollary]**

**Necessity of Each Condition** · *Corollary*

Since □(T∧S∧Φ) is equivalent to □T ∧ □S ∧ □Φ (necessity distributes over conjunction):

- **Necessity of Temporality.** Reality is temporally constituted under every modal evaluation. □T.
- **Necessity of Spatiality.** Reality is spatially constituted under every modal evaluation. □S.
- **Necessity of Substantiality.** Reality is substantially constituted under every modal evaluation. □Φ.

Each follows as a conjunct of the Triconditional Necessity already established.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Necessity (§2.5)

The Parasitic Negation arguments at §2.4.6–2.4.8 supply narrower onset closures: they challenge emergence of a Condition from its own absence, but don’t independently establish world-wise necessity.

## 2.6 Triconditionality of Nature
Time, Space, and Substance can look like three separate ingredients that happen to travel together. Can anything happen with only one? Take the tick of a clock: the first intuition is that it just requires time. But a tick also needs a hand to occupy one position rather than another, and something has to be there, moving, for the tick to be a change rather than a description of one. Take any one of them away, and ask how a tick could occur at all. This section tests that unity three ways. Does one’s possibility require the others’? Does one doing concrete work co-instantiate the other two? And are the three, underneath it all, not separate facts but one? The unity claim is established within the realizer-level structure of genuine change, where operative Condition-instantiation along any one axis co-instantiates the others. It isn’t the unrestricted claim that every abstract order, static geometry, or bearer already instantiates all three.

The Structural Requirement (§2.4) identified the modal constraint with T∧S∧Φ. The strongest reading of ◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ (§2.6.10) is identity rather than accidental co-extension, but that reading has costs beyond the jointly necessary conjunction. This chapter keeps three levels apart: field-level necessity, Operative-Role-Bridge-indexed Triconditional Cross-Entailment within concrete change-realizers, and Ontological Identity under the no-surplus criterion. They converge on one account of Nature only to the extent that their stated premises are granted.

The identity claim isn’t licensed by biconditional form alone. Necessary co-extension between two distinct structural facts would deliver a necessary biconditional without delivering identity. The stock case is the triangle: being three-sided and being three-angled travel together in every Euclidean world, yet what a figure’s sides do and what its angles do are two facts, not one. Identity here therefore has two burdens beyond co-extension. First, each side must be fully specified through the other rather than merely accompanying it. Second, nothing may remain by which the alleged two facts could be told apart. The converse and Mutual Containment arguments discharge the first burden; the No-Surplus Criterion at §2.6.9 discharges the second. Until both are in hand, the chapter has a biconditional, not an identity. If both hold, “change is possible” and “T∧S∧Φ is instantiated” pick out one modal constraint with no individuating remainder—one structural fact under two descriptions. (The identity of Nature with the necessitated co-instantiation of the Conditions is metaphysical-structural: the same modal constraint picked out with no remainder by the two descriptions (change-possibility and T∧S∧Φ). It isn’t a claim about what remains ideally conceivable under a primary intension, and the Modal Identity that follows is secondary / metaphysical necessity: necessity in the real modal structure, not closure of primary conceivability or of what is epistemically open. The two-dimensional question whether the non-identity remains primarily conceivable even where the secondary identity holds is engaged at §7.1.2.)

This is what forecloses Humean recombination **within the change-realizer domain**. Recombination operates on distinct existences that can be varied independently. Where T, S, and Φ are the mutually implicating roles of one genuine change-realizer, deleting one doesn’t leave a thinner change-realizer; it leaves a different kind of abstract structure. The theorem doesn’t forbid recombination among contingent occupants or among thin abstract analogues. Lewis’s mosaic deletes the connection and keeps the structure that the connection was; the Ontological Identity is why the deletion never takes. (Lewis’s concrete-worlds variant of the move is met at §7.2.3.)

*Temporal direction note.* Two resolutions of T run in this chapter, and merging them would let the realizer lines pay for the theorem. What the modal proof spends is T’s modal core alone—asymmetry and transitivity (§2.4)—and that is the T that enters the Modal Identity and the identity sequence. The realizer lines below run at the realization tier, where Directionality is available and where reaching, travel, and causal transmission do their work; they confirm the unity at that tier rather than adding causal structure to the modal theorem, which doesn’t draw on Directionality at any step. On either resolution the ordering is B-series in McTaggart’s terms: asymmetric ordering, not A-series becoming or a moving-now. Whether directed succession requires an irreducibly A-series component, and whether McTaggart’s positive proposal (the C-series, a non-temporal structural ordering from which temporal appearance derives) captures what Temporality consists in without genuine temporal addition, are addressed at §8.1.3 (McTaggart’s unreality of time) and §8.1.4 (block universe / B-theory).

*Notation.* Four formal shapes recur across this section’s preview and should be kept distinct. The plain biconditional ◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ (§2.6.10) is the structural fact change-possibility and the Conditions share: one fact read from two sides. The necessitated biconditional □(◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ), the Modal Identity (§2.6.6), is that one structural fact holding under necessitation. The theorem-level identities N ↔ □(T∧S∧Φ), N ↔ □◇C, and □(T∧S∧Φ) ↔ □◇C identify Nature with the necessitated co-instantiation read along three sides: modal, nomological, ontological. The first form is a biconditional; the second is its necessitation; the third set are the chapter’s central theorem read three ways.

In the theorem that follows, N abbreviates Nature: the joint presence of Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality.

Where the section is going can be said before it is earned, provided it is not claimed yet. Nature is Reality’s necessary structural constitution: to point at any of the three is to point at the others. The joint is the book’s fundamental primitive, derived from nothing more fundamental. The biconditionals that state it, given formally below, carry a necessity this section does not supply: the identity is established in full at §2.6.10, and the necessity predicated of N is earned separately at §2.9.6.

The four lines of §2.4 give independent derivational paths to that identification. Whether necessity itself is primitive ideology or derived is addressed at §2.11, where derived means a consequence of structural incapacity rather than a primitive modal operator.

The Triconditional Identity is the formal spine of the *Necessity of Nature* (§2.9.6) and the foundation on which the Null State Preclusion and the Necessary Occupancy Result are built there.

*What the proof spends here.* Step 6 of the chapter’s line is the Triconditional Identity itself (§2.6.10), and it is the only result in this section the line draws on. Everything before it earns that identity: the three pivot derivations (§2.6.2–2.6.4), their compression into Mutual Containment (§2.6.5), and the three readings that follow from it (§2.6.6–2.6.8). What comes after is scope and consequence rather than premise. Note also that the chapter’s main conclusion □(T∧S∧Φ) is already closed at §2.5 and doesn’t wait on anything in this section: a reader who grants only the forward conditional has the theorem, and what this section adds is the account of *why* the two sides coincide.

**Condition-Individuation** closes the section at §2.6.11: an external methodological screen that closes the easy routes to a fourth Condition and leaves a precise irreducibility burden with anyone proposing one. What it doesn’t do is establish from outside the framework that the three-role analysis is Reality’s privileged carving, and that limit is stated where the screen is built. Condition-Individuation is methodological closure on the substantive work of §2.6.1–2.6.10.

**Conditioned-Nature** closes the section semantically at §2.6.12: a reading of the Triconditional Identity into the genitive *the nature of X*, showing that the chapter title *The Necessity of Nature* and its reverse *the nature of necessity* refer to the same N. Conditioned-Nature is semantic closure on the Triconditional Identity’s identity, paired with the methodological closure on its count at §2.6.11.

### 2.6.1 Three Conditions, One Nature
T, S, and Φ aren’t three independent conditions that happen to co-occur but one structure read along three axes, each, fully unpacked, revealing the others as its own internal requirements rather than as external correlates. It is stated here as a thesis, not announced as a result. What is already banked is joint instantiation: wherever change is possible, the three are instantiated together (§2.4.5–2.4.9), and wherever they are genuinely instantiated, change is possible (§2.4.10, on the Moment-Individuation premise). What §2.6.2–2.6.5 must add—and must earn—is the tighter claim that the co-occurrence is internal co-requirement rather than set-deal correlation.

**Structure.** *A structure isn’t a thing alongside the things it structures. It is the ordered set of relations, constraints, and roles by which anything is intelligible as a thing, field, event, or configuration at all. In this book, structure names Reality under its necessary ordering: Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality together as the conditions any possible item must already exhibit to be anything determinate. Structure is therefore what any existing thing must already have to exist as anything at all, not something added to things from outside or imposed on a prior unstructured stuff.*

Temporality isn’t a finite thing, Spatiality isn’t a locational thing, Substantiality isn’t a material thing. They *are* what finite things, locational things, and material things *consist in*.

T, S, and Φ are introduced at §1.4 and derived at §2.4.5–2.4.10. If change is genuinely possible, the Conditions are already in play (§2.4); the converse—if the Conditions are instantiated, change is possible—is earned at §2.4.10 and spent throughout the sections below.

If the pivots deliver, the consequence follows: not three necessities that travel together but one necessity seen from three sides. Whether they deliver, and at what scope, is decided at the pivots themselves—not here.

*Tested against.* Structural realism (Ladyman & Ross, French), which shares the structural commitment but diverges on what the triconditional structure consists in (§9.10); Sider’s structuralism (§7.2.8); bundle theory and tropes, on the compose-by-relation picture (§8.3.3); mereological nihilism, on whether there is anything for the three to be conditions of (§8.3.4); and Quine’s anti-distinction pressure, on whether the three pivots name a single fact under three readings or three independent facts (§7.1.3).

*The realizer move.* Every relation this chapter names (directed succession, genuine distinctness, causal transmission, exclusive occupancy, persistence, identity through change) admits a thin reading on which it reduces to labeling, self-relation, or coordinate notation, and a real reading on which it requires structural machinery to distinguish it from its deflationary mimic.

The Conditions T, S, and Φ realize one another when any one is concretely operative. To say T ↔ (S ∧ Φ) in this section is to say: under the Operative-Role Bridge, succession doing real work requires both relational extension and persistent bearing, and those two doing change-realizing work require ordered succession. The same holds for S ↔ (T ∧ Φ) and Φ ↔ (T ∧ S). The notation is therefore domain-indexed throughout; it does not assert an unrestricted biconditional among the thin predicates.

Succession alone demands an interval to cross and a medium to carry it; extension alone demands a direction and a being; persistence alone demands a direction to persist through and an interval to persist across—so the realizer move claims. Each clause is tested against its countermodels at its own pivot (§2.6.2–2.6.4), and the price of each direction is stated there line by line: some run unconditionally, some at the role resolution, some for concrete media rather than relational structure as such.

The triconditionals, at whatever scope the pivots earn them, yield the *Mutual Containment Result*, gathered formally at §2.6.5 with its scope stated rather than assumed.

The physical confirmations of these relations (relativistic spacetime unification, conservation laws, thermodynamic asymmetry) are addressed in Chapter 4 as empirical expressions of what is established analytically here.

*A clarification on idiom.* The thin/real reading distinction throughout this section tracks what directed succession *requires* as a matter of structural role, not what directed succession is in its essence prior to modality. ‘Internal requirements’ names structural co-requirements of the primitive modal field, not essence-prior real definitions in Fine’s sense. Whether this role-based use of ‘consists in’ and ‘requires’ can be kept stable against Fine’s pressure (that any such structural identity just is a real definition under a different label) is the question addressed at §7.2.1.

One bridge governs every pivot and prevents a change of resolution from passing unnoticed:

**[Premise]**

**Operative-Role Bridge** · *Constitutive Premise*

When a modal-core Condition is claimed as concretely operative rather than merely represented or formally modeled, its characteristic work must be realized. Operative T orders an actual succession rather than a list; operative S separates occupiable positions across a crossable interval rather than coordinates in a diagram; operative Φ makes one stage a continuation of a process rather than an unrelated entry. The bridge does not assume that all three Conditions are present. It licenses the question each pivot answers: what else must be instantiated for any one of those roles to do that work?

*Scope.* The modal theorem of §2.5 establishes the joint necessity of T, S, and Φ in Reality’s field without this premise. The bridge is spent only by the stronger same-realizer cross-entailments and the identity readings built from them. A reader who grants the necessary conjunction but denies this bridge keeps `□(T∧S∧Φ)` and declines only the claim that any one operative role locally contains the other two.

First: whether succession can stand without extension.

### 2.6.2 Succession’s Two Conditions
*The realizer move, applied to T ↔ (S ∧ Φ).* The claim is not that T’s thin modal-core specification, considered alone, analytically contains S and Φ. It is that **operative** directed succession is biconditional with operative relational extension and persistent bearing in the same realizer. The Operative-Role Bridge carries the move from the modal-core predicate to its concrete exercise; the pivots then ask what that exercise requires. The forward half is local: succession doing temporal work requires differentiated positions across its order (S) and something that bears the order from one to the next (Φ). The reverse half is local too: concrete crossable extension (S) occupied by a bearer that persists across its positions (Φ) supplies an ordered crossing (T). The claim concerns full Conditions at work in a concrete medium, not every abstract order, geometry, bearer, or the field-level predicates merely considered in isolation. The same move is worked from the extension and persistence pivots at §2.6.3 and 2.6.4; the three vantages, with their scopes, are gathered at §2.6.5.

*Direction 1: T→S.* Two lines converge on the same result in the same realizer: genuine directed succession requires relational extension. They locate the differentiated positions across which its direction runs.

*First, operative succession is a reaching, and a reaching needs an interval to cross: that interval is relational extension (the traversability line).* The modal core of T by itself supplies asymmetric, transitive order; it does not yet supply travel. Travel enters through the Operative-Role Bridge when that order is claimed to be the order of a concrete transition rather than a formal list. The after-state is then reached from the before-state, and the reaching must be realized. This is not yet Φ as productive causation. It is the thinner requirement that the transition be borne as one passage rather than two entries, while the passage has differentiated source and terminus positions. If nothing spans A and B, there is replacement rather than one succession; if there are no differentiated positions, there is nothing from which or to which the passage runs. The line therefore derives S and Φ from **T-at-work**, not from the thin T-predicate alone.

*Second, the before-and-after asymmetry has nowhere to reside but the relation between the relata, and that relation is extension (the asymmetry-location line).* A thinner reading: A and B are distinct and A is before B, but the asymmetry is primitive, with nothing to ground it. Ask where the asymmetry resides. Not in A alone (A doesn’t contain the fact that B comes after it). Not in B alone (the mirror problem). Not in a third state floating free (that would need its own grounding). The only remaining location is the relation between them, and a relation with structurally differentiated positions between distinct relata is relational extension. The Bateson (1972) gloss lands in the same place: the causal imprint the after-state carries is a difference that makes a difference, and a difference that makes a difference requires a structure of alternatives among which the signal selected. A structure of alternatives is relational extension.

By PII (the Principle of Identity of Indiscernibles), relata with no relational structure and identical intrinsic properties are one relatum, not two; relata with no relational structure but distinct intrinsic properties are distinguishable but unordered: nothing makes one *after* the other. Directed succession specifically requires a relational carrier for the direction. That carrier is extension.

PII is contested. Black (1952) offers the standard two-spheres counterexample: two qualitatively identical iron spheres in an otherwise empty universe, distinct individuals despite intrinsic indiscernibility. The line’s PII appeal doesn’t require strong PII (individuation by intrinsic properties alone). It requires only the weaker claim that *relata in directed succession* require relational structure to ground their ordering. Black’s spheres themselves stand in a relational structure (each at some distance from the other) which is the kind of structure the line invokes. The line’s PII reading is the relational one, which survives Black; strong intrinsic PII isn’t needed for the line to deliver.

*Direction 2: S→T.* Two lines converge from the other direction. They concern S-at-work under the Operative-Role Bridge: concrete, occupiable extension claimed as a medium of passage, not relational structure or even static concrete geometry merely considered at an instant. Logical order and static geometry are genuine structures outside that claim. Their existence is not denied or reclassified; what they do not supply by themselves is the operative antecedent from which T follows.

*First, an operative interval is one across which a passage can run, and a passage is directed succession (the interval-reality line).* A static interval may be perfectly real without an actual crossing; the theorem does not deny it. The premise here is stronger and explicit: take extension as concretely operative in a change-realizer. Its crossability is then exercised or available as an ordered passage from one occupiable position to another. Strip out every possible ordering of such a passage and S remains a static spatial fact, but it no longer satisfies the operative antecedent of this pivot. The inference is therefore from operative S to T, not from bare spatial reality to time.

*Second, distinct positions are distinct only by sustaining “at x, then at y,” and that takes directed succession (the position-individuation line).* A thinner reading: positions are distinct by stipulation; nothing further grounds their separation.
