An unmanifested disposition doesn’t escape this—its bearer persists, and its manifestation-conditions are specified in the very terms the minimum supplies; a disposition with no bearer, no manifestation-relation, and no possible activation isn’t a disposition at all. The four accounts disagree about why laws hold. They agree (once the structural requirements are made explicit) about what any law requires.

*Taking stock.* The constitutive laws at issue here are the structural requirements T, S, and Φ, not every determinate law of physics. Specific dynamical laws, constants, and nomological patterns aren’t selected by that structure. Their actuality establishes their necessary possibility; variation among alternatives must be established independently (§2.9.4). Nature isn’t a contingent physical universe that happens to exist; it is the necessary structural ground within which any determinate law-pattern can obtain. Any classification of laws already presupposes that minimum.

*Tested against.* The Humean best-systems account (Lewis, the canonical opponent of the constitutive reading) and the governing-law account (Armstrong, Dretske, Tooley), both at §8.2.2, and conventionalism about laws, which shares the contingent-regularities reading the constitutive claim denies, at §7.1.4.

### 2.9.2 Nature Cannot Be Denied
The chapter’s conclusion stands on the derivation, not on a performative catch. The secondary point that no denial can be *performed* from outside Nature is tested with the performative convergence arguments at The Performative Catch (§3.3.1). It confirms a fact about the denial-event, not the truth of the conclusion denied.

The result belongs there because its office is corroborative: the proof is already complete before any denial is performed.

### 2.9.3 No Privileged Floor
Nature (the joint T–S–Φ constitution) is necessary not merely as a modal conclusion but as the precondition for any possible state of affairs. The thesis is the *Necessity of Nature*: the modal-structure claim that Reality’s modal field is necessarily constituted by the structural Conditions, and that this joint constitution is what we mean by Nature.

The position is sometimes mistaken for physicalism, and the correction has to be exact, because one half of the mistake isn’t a mistake at all. What the account refuses is a claim about priority, not a claim about inventory. Physicalism, in slogan form, is the thesis that everything is physical; in its contemporary form it is a thesis about fundamentality: the physical (matter-energy, what occupies Substantiality’s role at the realization tier) is fundamental, and everything else is grounded in or nothing over and above it (*fundamentality physicalism*). It is this basement claim the triconditional refuses. Substantiality is one of three co-equal structural roles, not the floor on which the others rest. The point can be stated formally:

**[Argument]**

**Subsistent Grounding** · *Substantiality Is Not the Basement*

1. **Nature just is the three Conditions taken together.** Nature is the joint structural complex: N ↔ T∧S∧Φ (*Triconditional Identity*, §2.6.10)

2. **No one operative Condition stands under the other two inside a concrete change-realizer.** Under the Operative-Role Bridge, Φ doing bearing-work requires T and S, and each operative Condition likewise co-instantiates the other two (*Triconditional Cross-Entailment*, §2.6.7)

3. **That mutual requirement is symmetric, so it isn’t a grounding relation.** The dependence asserted here is symmetric and co-constitutive, not a one-way grounding relation from Φ to T and S.

4. **A physics-in-the-basement view needs exactly the asymmetry the Conditions don’t have.** Fundamentality physicalism, in the basement form targeted here, requires an asymmetric priority claim: Φ grounds T and S while not being co-grounded or co-constituted by them.

5. **∴ Substantiality isn’t the basement.** That priority claim is incompatible with the Triconditional Cross-Entailment’s co-constitutive structure. Therefore the present view isn’t fundamentality physicalism and cannot privilege Φ as the sole basement.

*Scope.* This doesn’t by itself refute every thesis called *physicalism*; it rejects the specific one-way fundamentality thesis for concrete change-realizers once the Operative-Role Bridge and Triconditional Cross-Entailment are granted. A Φ-basement may refuse the bridge, but it must then explain how bearing does concrete work across differentiated stages without the ordered interval and operative positions that the bridge makes explicit. The result is conditional on that premise rather than analytic from the thin Φ-predicate.

The bare thesis that every entity is physical is left standing by this block, and deliberately so: T and S aren’t entities but dimensional Conditions, so they were never candidate counterexamples to a claim about what things exist. But that survival costs the physicalist the basement. A physicalism that grants T and S as non-physical conditions presupposed by the physical has already conceded fundamentality; what it arrives at is the naturalism defended here: Nature as T∧S∧Φ, with no privileged floor. The only way to keep the physical fundamental is to deny the distinctness the block presupposes, claiming that T and S are themselves Φ; that denial is met at §2.6.4 and the Ontological Identity (§2.6.8).

This places the view on the monist side of an old divide, but not where readers often assume. There is one structured reality, not two kinds of stuff—so a monism. But not substance monism: the thesis that substance is the single basement everything else derives from. That the two names share a root does not make that thesis the book’s. Substantiality is a co-equal structural role, and substance monism promotes its *bearer* to sole basement, privileging Substantiality exactly as physicalism does. The Subsistent Grounding argument refuses both on the same ground. The monism defended here is triconditional: one reality under three co-equal structural readings, none of them the floor. A reader who arrives holding “I am a monist, not a dualist” is already inside the position; the book asks only that the monism not be cashed as the priority of any one Condition.

The position is friendlier to the working physicist than physicalism is. A physicist describes structure: how matter persists, how distance is measured, how succession orders events. Physicalism commits the physicist to a metaphysical claim (that matter is foundational) that no actual physics asserts. The *Necessity of Nature* asks only what physics is already constrained to describe: the necessary structural Conditions under which anything is a being at all. A future physics that revised every current posit would still describe something that persists across distance through time, or it wouldn’t be physics. The thesis is neither empirically hostage nor contentless: its content is modal-structural rather than empirical.

The hard objection is a ground standing in no spatial or temporal relation to what it grounds, with causal power said to operate at the level sustaining space and time. The chapter must not answer by putting ordinary event-causation into that description. It can require only that a real source-role have determinate source and recipient terms and that the dependence genuinely obtain.

If the proposal strips even that articulation, it names the Null State rather than a causal power. If it retains thin ordering, distinction, and standing while denying temporal, spatial, and physical loading, the role-to-type bridge remains disputed. This section does not close it. The operative bridge is priced at §2.6; analogical formulations are tested at §10.2.1 and §10.2.2.

A further consequence sharpens the point. Any existence claim must cash out in obtaining: in something’s being the case. But to obtain is to take place: to be situated temporally (it obtains now rather than never), spatially (here rather than nowhere), and causally (as a result of structural Conditions rather than as a free-floating label). Taking place isn’t a metaphor. It is the literal minimum content of obtaining.

Read univocally—as denying every articulation of taking-place rather than claiming an analogical one—a being defined as placeless, timeless, and immaterial doesn’t merely fail to act within Nature. It fails to obtain as a state at all. To exist *is* to take place. There is nothing outside of reality, because it couldn’t be real. (The analogical reading of such definitions is the §10.2 engagement just flagged; this consequence prices the univocal one.)

A putative purely abstract entity that isn’t proposed as a ground of anything and hosts no causal relations is a different case, addressed in §8.1.5; the claim here targets any entity proposed as the ground of existence, which must itself obtain to ground.

The *Necessity of Nature* isn’t a philosophical position one chooses. It is the modal-structure requirement for choosing. The load-bearing argument is the preceding formal block; the literary closing that follows is a positioning move, not part of the derivation. Plantinga’s modal argument deploys S5 to establish the necessity of a being: the title of that work is *The Nature of Necessity*. The present argument deploys the same machinery to establish the necessity of Nature. The inversion is a tool-and-target reuse rather than a rhetorical flourish: Plantinga’s S5 deployment is valid; the inverted reading is that what S5 establishes the necessity of, when carefully attended to, is the necessary structural ground itself rather than a being separately necessary from it. Plantinga found the tool; the conclusion it yields is Nature.

*Tested against.* Idealism, the inverse position, locating the basement in mind rather than in any of the three Conditions (§9.5); Russellian monism, which posits intrinsic categorical natures behind the relational fabric (§9.3); Plantinga’s modal ontological argument, the tool whose target the present argument inverts (§10.1.1); and classical simplicity, the demanding case, holding a candidate ground to lack Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, with the *analogia entis* reply that causal power applies to a placeless ground only analogically (§10.2.1).

### 2.9.4 Necessity Precedes Contingency
The necessity of Nature isn’t a constraint on contingency. It is its precondition.

A proposition is contingent when it is possible and its negation is also possible (◇P ∧ ◇¬P). Contingency is a property of configurations within Nature (the necessary structure of T, S, and Φ), not of Nature itself; a contingent fact could have been otherwise.

Contingency is a defined modal status, but modal grammar alone doesn’t guarantee that the status is occupied. A trivial modal field could contain only necessary truths. To establish actual contingency, the framework needs at least one proposition P for which both P and ¬P are possible. The claim carried here is therefore conditional and substantive: where Nature permits alternative configurations, contingency is available as their status; which configuration is actual remains contingent.

*The witness and its exact reach.* A proposition can be actually false at one temporal position and actually true at another: that a particular organism exists, that a particular arrangement of relata obtains. The pair establishes occupied variation within the actual temporal field. If modal evaluation ranges over world-time positions, Actuality implies Possibility (§1.2.5) twice, yielding ◇¬P and ◇P. If metaphysical possibility instead ranges over complete worlds or histories, temporal variation alone doesn’t establish that either complete history could have been otherwise; a history containing both positions might itself be necessary. The actual witness therefore establishes temporal occupancy unconditionally and metaphysical contingency only under the world-time indexing stated later. The stronger cross-world claim requires an independent alternative-history premise. Nothing in the Necessity of Nature theorem depends on that further premise.

*From full realization to strict consequence.* A distinct point governs what follows once a configuration obtains. Let P name a configuration and Q its outcome. P is *metaphysically sufficient* for Q only where no possible realization of P lacks Q, equivalently □(P → Q). This is stronger than P’s being reliably followed by Q in the actual world. From □(P → Q) and actual P, Q follows actually by the T axiom and modus ponens; no further selector is left open once the sufficient configuration is complete. Q doesn’t thereby become necessary simpliciter. K yields □Q only from the stronger antecedent □P. The necessity lives in the conditional, the contingency in whether its antecedent obtains.

**[Theorem]**

**Configurational Necessitation** · *Theorem*

Where P is metaphysically sufficient for Q—where no possible realization of P lacks Q—the relation is a structural constraint rather than a local regularity: □(P → Q).

The theorem fixes what is necessary: the conditional itself, not either term. It doesn’t establish that any proposed configuration is sufficient; that burden belongs to the argument identifying P and Q.

**[Theorem]**

**Strict Actualization** · *Theorem*

From □(P → Q) and actual P, actual Q follows by the T axiom and modus ponens. Q is strictly guaranteed by the fully realized sufficient configuration, not merely favored by it; neither P nor Q is thereby necessary simpliciter. If □P is independently established, then and only then does K yield □Q.

**Depends on:** Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4)

*What refusing the world-time reading costs.* A complete-history semantics treats *P-at-t1* and *P-at-t2* as different propositions within one world and therefore withholds cross-world contingency from temporal variation alone. That reading remains available even if passage is real: passage establishes ordered variation, not by itself an alternative complete history. A tenseless reduction may be rejected at §8.1.4 and still owe a separate bridge from actual passage to metaphysical could-have-been-otherwise. The present section doesn’t conceal that bridge inside the witness.

*Contingency is necessarily contingent.* Once metaphysical contingency is established for a proposition, its status is fixed. Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10) gives ◇P → □◇P; applied to each conjunct it yields □◇P and □◇¬P, and normal modal logic licenses collecting them into □(◇P ∧ ◇¬P). Whatever is metaphysically contingent is therefore necessarily contingent on the global-capacity semantics. What it doesn’t yield is □P: the status is necessary, the fact contingent.

*Scope.* What is earned without further modal assumptions is actual temporal variation. What follows under world-time indexing is that the third modal status has an occupant and, by the global-capacity theorem, that its occupancy is necessary. What isn’t earned from temporal variation alone is contingency among complete-history representations. Nor is any account earned of how many configurations are open at a given position. The core theorem requires none of these stronger claims.

This is the stage/play distinction in its exact form. □(T∧S∧Φ) fixes the field-level Conditions under every evaluation; where alternative complete histories are independently established, ◇p ∧ ◇¬p describes which configuration is enacted within that field. The stage theorem neither selects the play nor proves that more than one complete play is possible. Deterministic succession within a history is compatible with modal contingency among histories, and necessity at the level of T, S, and Φ neither requires nor precludes a fixed domain of contingent individuals (Appendix A, *Domain Semantics and the Barcan Question*). Chapter 3 corroborates the structural floor without S5 while openly retaining its shared evaluability premise (§3.2).

**[Proposition]**

**Necessity Permits Contingency** · *Proposition*

The necessity of the structural Conditions does not compete with contingency; it is the condition without which contingency could not obtain at all. Where contingency is independently established, □(T∧S∧Φ) ∧ (◇p ∧ ◇¬p) is consistent, and it is the formal statement of a necessary field hosting contingent configurations: Reality retains its field-constituting Conditions under every evaluation, while which configuration is enacted is left open by the theorem rather than settled by it. The second conjunct is not supplied by the stage theorem, which proves no alternative complete history; that burden is stated in this section’s scope note. A field with no necessary stage has no room in which any play, fixed or open, could occur—so the fear that a necessary ground forecloses contingency inverts: it is the one thing that could not foreclose it, because it is what contingency stands on.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Necessity (§2.5) and Contingency (§1.2.4)

The converse pressure—that possibility-talk requires at least a determinate contrast—runs at §3.2, where Way–Possibility Convertibility establishes difference directly while leaving directed order and bearing conditional on further premises. It isn’t an independent reverse derivation of the full Modal Identity.

A further precision follows from this distinction.

On this framework, contingency attaches to propositions about arrangements rather than to a thing considered without its relations: this arrangement of causal relata at these positions within Nature, rather than some independently possible alternative. Nature itself isn’t contingent. An arrangement within it is contingent only when both that arrangement and its alternative are really possible.

Which laws Nature realizes, which geometry measures its extension, and which constants calibrate its interactions aren’t fixed by the three Conditions. Each is a specification the necessary Conditions don’t themselves require. Whether the alternatives are genuinely metaphysically possible is a further modal question, not a consequence smuggled out of structural underdetermination.

One strand of the argument from contingency asks why this arrangement rather than another. The structural account answers only the part its theorem earns: Nature is necessary, while the theorem doesn’t select the arrangement. If alternatives are independently established, the explanatory question among them is internal to Nature rather than directed at Nature as a whole. A stronger strand, pressed by Rasmussen’s Foundation Argument, asks instead why any contingent concrete reality exists at all. Since Nature is necessary, there is no contingent Reality-as-such left over to demand an external foundation; what may remain contingent is its configuration. The structural-terminus reply meets that distinction at §10.1.

What if the laws themselves evolve?

Smolin (2013; Unger and Smolin 2014) presses this distinction from the opposite direction: not that Nature is contingent, but that Nature is so thoroughly temporal that even the laws of nature evolve. On his temporal naturalism, nothing is timelessly necessary: the laws themselves change over cosmological timescales, and the very idea of timeless necessity is a Platonic holdover. Pressed hard, the challenge targets the necessity operator in □(T∧S∧Φ) rather than the T/S/Φ: if every regularity is local to an epoch, then any putative necessity attaches to whatever happens to be invariant within that epoch, not to a structural ground holding across all of cosmological time.

The challenge is genuine. The structural response is that the evolution of laws is itself Change in the nomological configuration. It therefore falls under the Structural Requirement and presupposes T, S, and Φ jointly; no one-to-one mapping from a before-state, a difference, and a relatum is asked to establish the loaded Conditions by itself. Smolin’s temporal naturalism converges with the structural picture at the level of what makes evolution itself possible. The laws may change. The structural preconditions for change don’t.

Smolin has the direction right (time is more fundamental than the laws) but the structural account specifies what that fundamentality consists in.

*The Third Way pressure.* This resolution answers the pressure behind Aquinas’s Third Way (the argument from contingency), which infers a necessary being from the existence of contingent things. Aquinas’s reasoning, reconstructed: if every being were contingent, then at some past time nothing would have existed; but if nothing had existed, nothing could now exist (since something can’t come from nothing); therefore there must be a necessary being. The inference is valid in form only if its first conditional is granted, and that conditional carries the argument’s famous gap: each contingent thing failing at some time doesn’t yield a time when all fail together. The pressure that something must be necessary nevertheless survives in a corrected form, earned here from the structural materials of §2.5–2.7 rather than from that conditional. The something-can’t-come-from-nothing premise is structural (the Null State admits no transition out of itself, §2.7.2), and the chapter identifies what must be necessary as the triconditional structure (T, S, and Φ together) within which contingency is possible. The Third Way’s contingency pressure therefore reaches a necessary structural terminus without, by that pressure alone, selecting an individual necessary being. Further arguments for such a being retain their own premises and are engaged in Chapter 10.

*Tested against.* Rasmussen’s Foundation Argument and the cosmological-argument-from-contingency family (Avicenna, Leibniz, Clarke, Rasmussen), which meet the structural-terminus reply at full strength (§10.1), the present section having closed Aquinas’s Third Way inline as the historical ancestor; Williamson’s necessitism, which shares universal necessity but applies it at a different scope (§7.2.7); Lewis, on modal realism and contingency across worlds (§7.2.3); and modal collapse, the worry that necessity-as-precondition leaves no genuine contingency (§8.2.5). Modal Exclusivity, what Modal Closure pairs with structurally, is at §7.2.1.

### 2.9.5 Possibility Precedes Probability
Probability isn’t a rival source of possibility. It is downstream of it.

The previous section closed with a boundary it declined to cross: contingency establishes that alternatives are open, not how widely they range. Probability is exactly the discourse that purports to answer the how-widely question, so it belongs here, at the boundary the last section marked and didn’t cross. Two claims are earned about the direction that discourse runs, one metaphysical and one epistemic.

Let Ch be an objective chance function over a possibility-respecting sample space Ω, and let E be assigned positive chance, Ch(E) > 0. Objective chance distributes weight only across outcomes really available for occurrence. E is weighted because E is really possible in the sense **fixed** at §1.2.1: Ch(E) > 0 → ◇E. The restriction matters. Epistemic credence measures an agent’s uncertainty and may rationally assign positive weight to a proposition that is in fact metaphysically impossible because the agent doesn’t know its modal status. No entailment from positive credence to real possibility follows.

A fair twenty-sided die assigns 1/20 to the case that the die comes up seven. That assignment doesn’t make seven possible; it presupposes that seven already is. If seven weren’t a really possible outcome of the roll, no honest weighting could put anything on it, not a small number and not a large one, because there is no outcome there to weight. The figure measures how much of the space seven occupies. It doesn’t open the space seven occupies room in.

A second question is epistemic: given outcomes modeled as draws from Ω, what follows deductively about Ω itself? No sequence sampled under that model entails a wider space Ω′. Evidence may expose model misspecification and rationally motivate revising Ω, but that ampliative inference (one whose conclusion says more than its premises contain) depends on further hypotheses; the sample doesn’t generate a new metaphysical possibility or deductively certify the larger field. Sampling outcomes within Ω never by itself entails ∃Ω′ ⊋ Ω.

*Notation.* **E** is an outcome in the sample space over which the chance function is defined, and **Ch(E)** is its objective chance; **Ω** is that sample space, and Ω′ any wider one a sample might be thought to establish.

**[Theorem]**

**Possibility Precedes Probability** · *Theorem*

*First.* ∀E (Ch(E) > 0 → ◇E): positive objective chance presupposes the real possibility of what it weights; positive epistemic credence does not entail real possibility. *Second.* Sampling outcomes under a model Ω never by itself entails ∃Ω′ ⊋ Ω; expanding the model requires an additional abductive premise.

The two clauses mark one priority without erasing two kinds of probability. Objective chance presupposes real possibility; epistemic probability can guide rational belief without settling modal status. A sample may support revising a model, but only abductively and against additional assumptions. Possibility isn’t manufactured by either weighting or sampling.

*Scope.* What is earned is the direction for objective chance: it presupposes a possibility space and doesn’t manufacture one. Epistemic probability can rationally range over propositions whose modal status is unknown, and data can motivate an abductive revision of the modeled space; neither move deductively settles real possibility. No particular probability calculus is selected here.

*Where this is used.* The theorem is put to direct use wherever probabilistic reasoning is offered as if it could settle a question about an unmapped possibility space on its own. The fine-tuning argument is the case: it infers from the improbability of life-permitting constants to a wider design- or multiverse-space, and is engaged at §10.1.9. The epistemic clause above names the presupposition that inference needs and can’t supply from probability data alone.

### 2.9.6 Necessity of Nature
The chapter’s modal spine arrives here at its named result. Its steps are already in place: the Cartesian witness establishes the possibility of Change, with the movement witness reaching it a second way (§2.4.9); the bilateral modal-closure theorem—derived negative-first from Reality’s no-exterior modal maximum and Modal Bivalence—lifts that possibility to necessity; and the Structural Requirement identifies Reality’s invariant permitting and precluding constraint with T∧S∧Φ. Triconditional Necessity (§2.5) thereby supplies □(T∧S∧Φ). The later Modal Identity (§2.6.6) adds the converse and reads the two sides as one structural fact; it isn’t needed to validate the forward modal derivation. Gathered in order, with each step supported by the section that discharges it, the line runs in full. It is the line previewed at the chapter’s opening (§2, *The Cogito–S5 Pipeline*), carried here with its derivation rather than in outline, and carried one step further: the preview closes at the Necessity of Nature and leaves the identity of Reality and Nature open, where step 7 below takes it up (§2.8).

**[Argument]**

**Necessity of Nature** · *The Whole Line*

1. **Whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary; whatever is impossible, its impossibility is necessary.** R is the one Reality with no real exterior, and Capacity(R,P) reports membership in its complete admissible range. Begin with exclusion: if an alleged evaluation admits an excluded P, it is either real and already within R—so P wasn’t excluded—or unreal and irrelevant to real possibility. Therefore ¬◇P → □¬◇P. Modal Bivalence fixes possibility as the complement of that invariant exclusion, yielding ◇P → □◇P. The conventional theorem-name is *Necessary Possibility*. (*Bilateral Modal Invariance*, §2.1)

2. **Change is possible.** The act of doubt is itself a change, so change is actual and therefore possible. ◇C (*Possibility of Change*, Cartesian Certainty, §2.2). A second witness reaches the same premise: movement is really possible, and movement is one species of Change, so ◇M entails ◇C (§2.4.9).

3. **The possibility of change is necessary.** Necessary Possibility applied to either witness yields □◇C (*Necessary Possibility of Change*, §2.3)

4. **The possibility of change requires temporal, spatial, and substantial conditions.** By the Bilateral Frame and the constitutive arguments of §2.4, the invariant constraint that permits Change and precludes unordered succession, collapsed position, and unborne exchange is identified at modal-core resolution with the three Conditions. □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)) (*Structural Requirement*, §2.4)

5. **Therefore, Reality is necessarily temporal, spatial, and substantial.** □(T∧S∧Φ) (*Triconditional Necessity*, §2.5)

6. **The three Conditions aren’t three requirements that happen to coincide but one structure, and *Nature* is its name.** At modal-core resolution, the possibility of Change and the three mutually implicating Conditions describe one realizer complex (*Triconditional Identity*, §2.6)

7. **Nothing real is left outside Nature’s modal field, so at the level of the whole, Reality and Nature are one.** Reality is maximal, and every real content has its determinate way within that field; no second modal domain remains for a real content to occupy. At that field-and-totality resolution, N = R. Whether a candidate inside that field can claim explanatory priority over it is the narrower question about its grounding role, taken up at §2.9.7 (*Reality–Nature Identity*, §2.8)

8. **∴ Reality is necessarily Nature.** The modal field constituted by T, S, and Φ, without the theorem fixing which configurations occupy it. (N = R) ∧ □(T∧S∧Φ).

Step 8 stands on steps 5, 6 and 7, and those on steps 1 through 4. Every step above is a premise of the conclusion; nothing in the list is carried along without doing work in it. One result of the chapter is deliberately absent for that reason: ¬◇∅ closes the empty alternative (§2.7) and is spent by the Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7), not by this conclusion. The whole-line result can now be stated as a theorem: its modal core comes from step 5, while the identity at step 7 is §2.8’s own result, carried into the line rather than re-earned here.

**[Theorem]**

**Necessity of Nature** · *Theorem*

Reality is Nature at the field-and-totality resolution, and Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality constitute it under every modal evaluation: the structural constraint that permits Change and precludes its contradictory collapses is necessary. Nature—the Triconditional Identity apprehended through three readings—is necessary. (N = R) ∧ □(T∧S∧Φ).

**Depends on:** Triconditional Necessity (§2.5); Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10); Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8)

The theorem reads both ways. *The Necessity of Nature* is also *the nature of necessity*: by the Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10) the modal constraint just is T, S, and Φ, so the genitive collapses in either direction. The Conditioned-Nature (§2.6.12) derives the collapse and generalizes it: every *nature of X* terminates in a structural feature of N, with necessity as the limit case. A third face collapses into the same fact rather than standing beside it: Subsistent Grounding (§2.9.3) is this theorem read structurally instead of modally, T, S, and Φ co-constituting one another with no privileged floor. Necessity, nature, and subsistence aren’t three results but one, seen under three readings of the same genitive.

Two clarifications about the scope of the necessity claim. *Nature* in the Triconditional Identity isn’t a proper name for a concrete individual that exists necessarily. It is a structurally fixed term: its reference is fixed by the joint constitution of T, S, and Φ, and once fixed it holds across modal evaluation because Range(R) is constituted by those Conditions. Possible-world semantics can represent that rigidity, but doesn’t ground it. The comparison is with Kripke’s (1980) machinery of reference-fixing and rigid designation; the refinement here is that the referent is structural rather than concrete (T∧S∧Φ as a constitutive pattern, not a particular individual). The Necessity of Nature theorem is unlike Kripke’s necessary a posteriori identities. Water = H₂O is discovered through empirical investigation of a natural kind; the Necessity of Nature theorem is argued from a Cartesian witness, global-capacity modal semantics, and constitutive structural requirements. Its necessity claim is therefore structural and a priori in the book’s intended sense, while its empirical realizations remain open to investigation. Nature is the structural-condition complex that constitutes Reality’s modal field, not a necessary being among possible others.

And the necessity attaches to the structural Conditions, not automatically to any occupant within Nature. The claim is de dicto with respect to the modal constraint (necessarily, Reality’s modal field is constituted by T, S, and Φ), not a derivation of de re necessity for this universe, configuration, law-pattern, or token state. Nature is necessary; the modal status of what fills it requires further argument. Where genuine alternatives are established, their contingency obtains within the necessary field rather than against it.

The distinction has a classic illustration. Quine (1960) noticed that necessity can appear to shift with description. One person may be picked out as a mathematician or as a cyclist, and predicates central to one description need not be essential under the other. The point doesn’t require the outdated assumption that every cyclist is two-legged; it is that substituting co-referential descriptions inside modal contexts can change the apparent modal claim. Quine drew a deflationary lesson: necessity can look like a feature of how we pick something out rather than of the thing itself.

The lesson is well taken, as far as it reaches. What it leaves unsaid is that under every description the person answers to, whether mathematician, cyclist, parent, or passer-by, something doesn’t vary. To ride at all there must be a surface to ride on, a bike to ride, and the time to ride it: a place, a thing, and a duration, which are Spatiality, Substantiality, and Temporality under other names. Vary the description as often as it will bear and those three remain. Quine showed that necessity floats free of any particular predicate. What his example also shows, once carried a step further, is that it doesn’t float free of everything. Beneath the predicates that come and go lies one set of conditions that no description of anything real can shed. The necessity is de dicto, a necessity of the conditions and not of the bearer, exactly as the cyclist suggests. It isn’t for that reason merely verbal, because these conditions are what any description whatever must already presuppose.

*Against an uncaused initial-state stopping point.* A naturalist may treat the initial condition or causal order as uncaused and decline an explanation beyond the natural order. That is a live rival to the demand for an external necessary ground, but it shouldn’t be attributed to Oppy as a doctrine that a particular concrete initial state exists of necessity. Oppy’s comparative naturalism is assessed on its own total-theory terms in the later engagement (Total-Theory Comparison (§3.5.7.3) (§3.5.7) introduces the comparative framework; Chapters 8–10 conduct the comparison). The present contrast concerns the kind of stopping point at issue: an uncaused or brute initial configuration remains a particular arrangement and so leaves the internal question pressed at §2.9.4, why this configuration rather than another? The Necessity of Nature locates necessity one level down, in the structural Conditions any configuration must instantiate, not in any configuration that instantiates them. The disagreement is between the occupant and the structure, the scene and the stage; it isn’t a claim that Oppy himself necessitates the occupant.

### 2.9.7 Exclusivity of Nature
*The role at issue.* The next question is narrower but decisive. The Necessity of Nature shows that the structural Conditions are necessary. It doesn’t by itself show that nothing else could fill their grounding role. Could a rival stand in Nature’s place? This section closes that space for one exact role: grounding concrete change-realizers within the modal field the chapter has established. The *Reality–Nature Identity* already closes the alleged exterior location; this section asks the further functional question whether any differently described candidate could do Nature’s work. Essence-prior, non-causal, analogically structured, and theological proposals retain their later descriptive and explanatory burdens in Chapters 7–8, but not an unclaimed domain outside Reality.

In the sense fixed in the Triconditional Identity sequence, structure isn’t a thing competing with other things. It is what any candidate ground must already exhibit if it is to be intelligible as anything determinate.

A rival necessary being would survive the proof: one that grounds possible states of affairs without instantiating the structural Conditions. Three moves close that space.

A contemporary defense of the claim that something must exist necessarily (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018) doesn’t settle this question. It sharpens it: their argument establishes that something must exist necessarily, but leaves open what that something is. The present argument identifies the role under its own modal constraint: any candidate offered as the ground of concrete change-realizers either instantiates T, S, and Φ or fails to supply the structure that makes such realizers possible. A candidate that declines that role—an essence-prior, non-causal, or analogically structured ground—doesn’t thereby collapse into the Null State at this stage; by the Reality–Nature Identity it is already confined to the one field. No Unconditioned Essence at §7.2.1 later closes essence-priority as structural priority while preserving it as a direction of explanation.

A subsequent stage of Rasmussen’s argument presses further: whether the necessary ground could bear intentional or personal features. That question is out of scope for Chapter 2. The present chapter’s burden is the structural-modal identification of the necessary ground; intentional or personal features, if they obtain at all, obtain as configurations within Nature rather than as competing structural grounds. Rasmussen’s intentional-foundation move is taken up directly at §10.1.4; Chapter 11 takes up personal-attribute candidates one at a time. The connection to the selection-among-possibilities problem (*why this configuration rather than another*) runs through the level-distinction already established at §2.9.4: selection ranges over what the structural Conditions permit to vary, not over the Conditions themselves.

*First: functional equivalence.* Any proposed alternative *for the role of grounding concrete change-realizers* must fall under one of three descriptions. Either it is functionally equivalent to T, S, and Φ (it satisfies the same minimum structural requirements under different names) in which case it isn’t a genuine alternative but structure redescribed. The functional requirements are what the Conditions consist in; anything that satisfies them instantiates structure regardless of what vocabulary is used.

Role-analog pluralism (the thesis that multiple distinct necessary structures could each discharge the modal-grounding role) collapses to the same point: any structure that actually discharges the role instantiates T, S, and Φ, and the plurality of names doesn’t yield a plurality of necessary structures.

Two candidates are worth naming here rather than left to be found, because Chapter 9 grants each at full strength and both still land inside the first description.

Cosmopsychism may keep its unified, non-discursive phenomenal field: the priority reversal goes through not at the *mode* of cosmic cognition but at the *relation* the cosmic subject must stand in to what it grounds, which requires difference, directed dependence, and real bearing at the level of generic roles (§9.4).

Whiteheadian process metaphysics may keep objective immortality, read as relational inheritance rather than as an entity persisting through an interval. The inheritance from one occasion to the next still carries direction, differentiation, and efficacy across the transition, so the bearer-role is instantiated under a different grammar. The step to a persistent causal being is left to where that type is secured (§2.6.4), and the position is engaged at §9.6.

Neither is refuted by classification; each is conceded its own description and shown to discharge the role by instantiating the roles.

*Second: incommensurability.* Or the alternative is genuinely incommensurable with T, S, and Φ: it hosts no causally structured succession, no relational extension, no causal persistence, and therefore no concrete change, movement, or interaction in the chapter’s defined sense. In that case it isn’t a rival capable of grounding concrete change-realizers. If it also withdraws every thin content by which it differs, stands, orders, or sources, it is a variant of the Null State; if it retains a thin or analogical content while denying the loaded Conditions, it isn’t collapsed here but sent forward as the live rival the later engagements must test.

Ordinary language supplies a useful confirmation of the same pressure. The three negations English uses at the relevant domains (*never*, *nowhere*, *nothing*) are negation-forms built around the positive domains: no-ever, no-where, no-thing (§2.1.5). They don’t name an independent positive item on the far side of the Conditions; they mark the failure of a domain from inside the vocabulary that domain supplies. A rival necessary being that hosts no succession, no extension, and no persistence therefore has to explain how it differs from a *never-nowhere-nothing*: the negation-shape of the three Conditions, which the formal argument identifies with the Null State. The grammar is confirmation, not the proof; the proof is the modal-structural argument around it.

*Third: partial overlap.* A ground might partially satisfy the structural Conditions or satisfy a different but overlapping set, hosting some kinds of change but not others. The partial-overlap option appears to escape the binary. It doesn’t.

The definitions in §1.2–1.3 aren’t one possible characterization of what change-hosting requires: they are the minimum logical content of the concept of change itself. Anything that hosts any transition of any subject from any one state to another instantiates succession, distinction, and exchange in the defined sense, because those are what any such transition analytically consists in.

A partial-overlap ground either hosts genuine transitions or it hosts something that falls short of them. If the former, it fully satisfies T, S, and Φ and is structure. If the latter, it isn’t a ground of change but a ground of something else. There is no coherent intermediate at the level of hosting transitions. What remains open is the third position already noted: a candidate that retains thin or analogical content while denying the loaded Conditions. That candidate isn’t closed here; it carries its burden forward to Chapters 7–8.

The Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7) reinforces the conclusion at the candidate’s operative role. The three thin definitions are not mutually analytic. The stronger result is that, under the Operative-Role Bridge, any one Condition doing concrete change-realizing work requires the other two in that same ground. A ground that claims operative Temporality while denying every differentiated position or bearer therefore fails to explain how its succession is one concrete transition rather than a list. The corresponding tests run from S and Φ. Any ground that genuinely realizes change instantiates all three simultaneously; a candidate that rejects the bridge remains a named premise-denier rather than an unnoticed contradiction.

The partial-overlap leg can be stated formally at the scope the Triconditional Cross-Entailment theorem has earned. Let g be a candidate ground of concrete change-realizers; let T(g), S(g), and Φ(g) abbreviate g’s full instantiation of each Condition. Suppose g instantiates exactly one or two of T, S, Φ. By the Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7), each Condition requires the other two in g by the theorem’s same-realizer routes: T through differentiated succession and bearing, S through ordered crossing and occupancy, and Φ through an ordered interval of differentiated states.

The entailment is therefore derived, not definitional, and it applies where the Operative-Role Bridge and pivot criteria are met. Within that scope, exactly-one-or-two is inconsistent: operative instantiation of any one co-instantiates T∧S∧Φ in the same ground. Outside that role, a thin order, distinction, static extension, or standing is not silently promoted into the operative triad; a proposal built only from the generic role-floor still owes the bridge.

The Exclusivity theorem is relative to that role: for grounds of concrete change-realizers, full overlap is structure under another name and zero modal-core overlap can’t discharge the role. Ontological exhaustiveness comes instead from the *Reality–Nature Identity*: any candidate that is real enough to coexist belongs to Reality and therefore to Nature, whether or not it claims this grounding role.

*The conclusion.* The three moves close the space together, and the exclusivity of structure can now be stated.

**[Theorem]**

**Exclusivity of Nature** · *Theorem*

The necessary structural ground of any concrete change-realizer is uniquely T, S, and Φ together. Any proposed alternative *for that role* is either (i) functionally equivalent to T, S, and Φ, in which case it is structure under another description, or (ii) genuinely unable to supply the full Conditions, in which case it cannot ground concrete change-realization. A zero-content candidate is ∅; a thinly or analogically structured candidate is not thereby ∅, but inherits the independent burden of showing how its claimed grounding role reaches concrete change without reinstantiating the Conditions. Nature is not one change-ground among structural competitors. Nor does declining that role secure an outside: any real coexistent belongs to Reality and therefore, by the *Reality–Nature Identity*, to Nature. Chapters 10 and 11 test whether particular necessary-being descriptions remain coherent within that exhaustive identity.

*What follows—and what doesn’t.* These three Conditions jointly constitute Nature: Reality’s necessary structural constitution, not one structure among possible alternatives. There is no further structure for them to be an instance of.

*A note on “structural constitution” throughout this section.* The phrase “Reality’s necessary structural constitution” is used in the sense fixed by structural role throughout: T, S, and Φ are the co-constitutive requirements of any direction-involving, distinction-involving, and persistence-involving state of affairs, not an essence prior to or independent of the modal field from which modal truths follow. Whether that role-based identity can be kept stable against the pressure that it is a real definition under a different label is the question addressed at §7.2.1.

The result preserves structuralism while denying it a second Platonic domain: every structural fact is a fact about how T, S, and Φ are instantiated. It also corrects physicalism’s over-crediting of Φ as a basement beneath T and S (§2.9.3). The three are co-equal roles fixed modally, not conclusions hostage to future fundamental physics. That closes the structural why-stop question without reducing mind, meaning, or value to physics; it fixes only the minimum any account of them must satisfy.

The role-level rival is foreclosed here, while the *Reality–Nature Identity* separately closes an exterior location for any real candidate. What survives for Chapters 7 and 8 is a candidate within that exhaustive field claiming explanatory priority or a thin, analogical, or essence-prior mode of grounding (§7.2, §8.2).

*Modal monism.* T, S, and Φ are not constraints placed inside an independently given logical space; at modal-core resolution they constitute the one field within which variation occurs. Modality and Nature therefore stand in identity, not isomorphism, since isomorphism would require two domains. Possibility, law, and being are three readings of the same structure (§2.6.9), while possible and actual propositions remain distinct. Chapter 2 earns no rival structural ground of concrete change-realizers outside the Conditions and no second domain for any real referent. It does not yet prove every atemporal, non-causal, analogical, or essence-prior description contradictory; Chapters 7–8 test whether such descriptions relocate, retain content, challenge the role analysis, or collapse. A zero-content ground specifies the Null State; a thinly articulated one still owes an account of the modal field without covertly reinstantiating the Conditions.

Nature, the necessary Conditions, and necessary possibility aren’t three necessities standing in a ring. They are one necessity reached by three routes, and the biconditionals are what record it. N ↔ (T∧S∧Φ); □(T∧S∧Φ) ↔ □◇C; by the Necessity of Nature theorem, both sides hold of necessity. That is the Triconditional Identity, established at §2.6.10.

The component results retain their separate prices: Cross-Entailment uses the Operative-Role Bridge within concrete change-realizers; Modal Identity uses the separately earned converse; Triconditional Identity joins them only at those domains. The unconditional core is §2.5’s jointly necessary field-constitution, and the *Reality–Nature Identity* closes a second modal domain on its own premises.

*Conceivability and possibility.* The standard gap remains between what merely seems conceivable and what is genuinely possible (Kripke 1980; Chalmers 2002; Yablo 1993). The Triconditional Identity does not close it by fiat. Chapter 2 supplies the object-side test: possible worlds are configurations within one structural field, so an apparently conceivable specification may fail by describing the Null State or an incoherent T/S/Φ arrangement. The Conceivability Trap at §3.3.4 adds only an act-side diagnostic; the structured act of conceiving does not itself refute its object. Thus *genuinely conceivable* marks the surviving subset, not a prior domain wider than Nature.

Any percept in view is there because something persists through the distance between observer and observed, something holds them apart, and something carries both forward through the moment. The structural Conditions aren’t a thesis about Reality applied to a world that could have been otherwise. They are the Conditions under which any such encounter takes place: Nature itself, in which *reading*, *sentence*, and *page* have anything to refer to. The proof identifies what any such encounter already requires.

*Occupancy.* If T, S, and Φ constitute Reality rather than furnishing a container inside it, any concrete individual exists by instantiating that structure. A putative entity with no temporal, spatial, or substantial relation would not be an unusual occupant but a failure of concrete occupancy. The *Reality–Nature Identity* closes the transcendent location: anything real belongs to Reality and therefore to Nature. Thin, analogical, essence-prior, and non-causal descriptions proceed only as proposed characterizations of Nature or its articulations; No Unconditioned Essence and No Divine Addition test their further claims.

The fork is limited but firm: any concrete proposed being instantiates T, S, and Φ or fails the occupancy criterion. This does not refute every description called *God* by definition; it fixes where any real referent must belong before later chapters determine whether the description survives, relocates, or collapses.

**[Corollary]**

**Necessary Occupancy** · *Corollary*

For any concrete individual thing to exist is for it to occupy the necessary structure: to be temporally ordered, spatially or relationally situated, and substantially borne as a determinate relatum. This is not an external constraint imposed on beings from outside. It is constitutive of what real concrete occupancy consists in. A putative concrete entity satisfying none of these Conditions is not a thing that exists in an unusual way; it fails to be an occupant. Abstract descriptions remain abstractions of structural features rather than a second concrete domain.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10) and Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7)

**[Corollary]**

**Modal Closure** · *Corollary*

The necessary structural Conditions admit no unnecessary alternative standing apart from them.

**Depends on:** Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8) and Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7)

No parallel substrate, no rival ground, no external addition: everything unnecessary is a configuration within the Conditions, not a competitor to them. Closure constitutes the field within which contingency obtains rather than constraining it from outside. The corollary restates what the Reality–Nature Identity Derivation secured (§2.8) and Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7) completes; it pairs with Modal Exclusivity (§7.2.1): nothing grounds Nature from above; nothing stands alongside it from outside.

*Tested against.* Chapter 10 tests the rival necessary-being families—classical arguments, divine-attribute doctrines, and non-classical ultimates—without treating their mere difference in vocabulary as escape from the structural test (§10.1–§10.3). Chapters 7 and 9 test objections to the modal structure and proposed alternative substrates (§7.2–§7.3; §9). Existential-inertia naturalism is the closest persistence-side case: it treats contingent existence as persisting intrinsically rather than through external conservation, while the present account locates persistence in Substantiality’s structural role. The Schmid neo-classical and existential-inertia literature is engaged at §10.1.6.

## 2.11 Three Logical Strata
The proof remains complete at §2.9; this final section draws out a downstream metalogical consequence. Ask what settles whether one moment comes before another, whether two things share a location, or whether the thing present now is the same thing that was here a moment ago: three different kinds of reasoning, each native to one of T, S, and Φ. Independent inquiries have been converging on the present account from their own directions (§3.5.7). Why is that convergence no coincidence? The reason lies in §2.6.11.

Condition-Individuation supplies a two-clause screen for Condition-status (determinacy plus LEM along an existence-axis, and irreducibility). It shows that T, S, and Φ pass the screen and places a precise burden on any proposed fourth; as clarified in §2.6.11, entailment by the three doesn’t alone prove reducibility, so the screen doesn’t deductively establish that no further irreducible axis is possible. Nor does the screen by itself generate three consequence relations. What it motivates is three axis-specific formal disciplines: temporal logic native to T, spatial logic native to S, and the substantial-logic umbrella native to Φ. Their formal differentiation comes from the operators, axioms, and semantics required by each axis’s upstream structure, together with the independently developed literatures of Prior, Tarski, Leśniewski, Quine, Simons, Lowe, and others. The clustering is downstream confirmation, not a proof extracted from LEM alone.

The Triunity of Nature (§2.6.9) carries three logics native to its three Conditions. Physics is empirical-nomological work conducted within the joint apparatus of those three, the *modal structure*: the fixed structure of what is and isn’t possible that □(T∧S∧Φ) defines. Metaphysics is the root-layer discipline that spells out the logics’ grounding in Reality’s structure. The convergence happens because the three Conditions are real, the disciplines tracking them are the formal logics native to each, and those three logics jointly constitute one modal structure.

The modal structure established here is structural (what any possible Reality must instantiate to be a Reality) not a phenomenal explanation. Whether consciousness fits this structure is the question of §7.2.1 and Chapter 5, not of Chapter 2.

Chapter 3 then tests those results on the terms set at the close of §2.9, recording where its independent lines genuinely separate and where they share the role-level identifications established here.

*Tested against.* Chapter 7 meets the meta-philosophical objections: ontological deflationism at §7.1.6, Wittgensteinian quietism at §7.1.7. The structural-realist alternative is engaged at §9.10.

### 2.11.1 Three Distinct Logics
Condition-Individuation supports three axis-specific formal disciplines, in two stages. First, its determinacy-plus-LEM clause and irreducibility clause distinguish T, S, and Φ as three admitted domains of inquiry. Second, each axis’s native structure motivates its own formal apparatus. The result is three disciplines with different target vocabularies and formal resources: temporal logic, spatial logic, and substantial logic, sharing whatever classical floor this chapter separately defends.

Stage one individuates axes, not consequence relations. Irreducibility means that the content of T-claims doesn’t reduce without remainder to S- or Φ-content. It doesn’t follow that one background logic can’t govern claims from all three domains, or that non-reducible predicates require non-intertranslatable logics. The legitimate conclusion at this stage is weaker: each axis calls for its own theory-specific vocabulary and axiomatization if its native structure is to be represented.

Stage two supplies that differentiation, and each axis carries its own native structure:

- **T** carries temporal modalities: succession, precedence, simultaneity.
- **S** carries spatial relations: region, inclusion, connection, proximity.
- **Φ** carries identity, persistence, and part/whole.

That structure is supplied by the upstream derivations at §1.4 and 2.4–2.6, not by LEM. Formal systems regimenting it can therefore differ in syntax, axioms, and semantics. Temporal logic and spatial logic are established disciplines; *substantial logic* is its synthetic umbrella over several traditions. The claim earned is discipline-level formal differentiation—not a deduction that Reality contains exactly three mutually exclusive logics merely because it contains three irreducible axes.

The distinctness shows in a single ordinary claim. Take *the cup was on the table before it was lifted*. Three inferences run through it at once, along three axes. *Before it was lifted* is temporal: it places the resting earlier than the lifting, licensing inferences of precedence and tense (T). *On the table* is spatial: it locates the cup in contact with and supported by the surface, licensing inferences of region, contact, and inclusion (S). *The cup*—the same one throughout—is substantial: one persisting bearer across both the resting and the lifting, not two cups sharing a name, licensing inferences of identity and persistence (Φ). None of the three cashes out in another’s vocabulary: *before* isn’t a region, *on* isn’t a moment, and *the same cup* is neither a time nor a place. Restating the precedence in the spatial apparatus changes the subject; it does not translate that predicate into a spatial one. That is the axis-level irreducibility Condition-Individuation establishes, met in a single sentence. Three specialized formal disciplines emerge, each with its own target vocabulary. Whether they are non-intertranslatable logics with no broader common coin is a further metalogical thesis—one axis-irreducibility alone doesn’t establish.

The literature delivers exactly this. Temporal logic is a mature formal discipline, with operators F, P, G, H tracking *will sometime*, *was sometime*, *will always*, and *has always been*; branching-time versus linear-time families axiomatize different commitments about T-structure (Prior 1957; Prior 1967; Pnueli 1977; Goldblatt 1992). Spatial logic is similarly mature, with operators for region, inclusion, connection, and proximity (Tarski 1959 on topology in formal language; Randell et al. 1992 on region-connection calculus; Aiello et al. 2007 *Handbook of Spatial Logics*). Substantial logic is different: it is the present argument’s own coinage, not a label any of these literatures use of themselves. It names the umbrella covering the Φ-axis—formal ontology, mereology, classical identity, and substance metaphysics—the *logic of being qua being* in Aristotle’s sense (*Metaphysics* Γ 1003a21). The term is licensed by the role these literatures jointly play, regimenting bivalent inference over the existence-axis of persistence-and-identity, not by any prior unification under the label. Four rubrics sit under that umbrella: formal ontology (Husserl 1900–01 *Logical Investigations*; Smith 2003), mereology (Leśniewski 1916; Simons 1987 *Parts*), classical first-order logic with identity (Quine 1960 *Word and Object*), and substance metaphysics (Wiggins 2001 *Sameness and Substance Renewed*; Lowe 2006 *The Four-Category Ontology*). Each was developed by working logicians and ontologists without its metaphysics in hand.

A second derivation reaches the same threefold carving from the opposite side: the classical laws of thought, taken indexically, rather than Condition-Individuation’s formal screen. Non-Contradiction, applied in turn to position, order, and being, forbids here from being there, before from being after, and this from being not-this. Identity, its flip side, requires that here, now, and this each be only themselves and no other. The three Conditions aren’t three unrelated brute facts assembled into one chapter. Each is the same law of determinacy—identity and non-contradiction read together—instantiated along a different existence-axis, reached from the indexical side rather than from a prior theory of content. Read this way, the three formal disciplines just identified aren’t a list defended one entry at a time. They are one requirement, that a subject can’t be its own negation, read in the registers of position, order, and being.

Space and Substantiality each fail in a single way: here collapsing into there, this collapsing into that—one bearer becoming indistinguishable from another. Time looks like it fails twice. Before equating with after is the parallel failure; before reversing into after looks like a second. But those two are not independent. Bare non-identity is symmetric: here ≠ there and there ≠ here state one fact twice; this ≠ that and that ≠ this do the same; and before ≠ after and after ≠ before do the same. Restating a distinctness in both directions never doubles it. Time’s genuine second collapse is a failure of order, not a second failure of identity.

The difference traces to each Condition’s constitutive relation:

| Condition | Constitutive relation | Symmetry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Time** | Precedence (§1.4.1) | Asymmetric—before conditions after, never the reverse |
| **Space** | Separation (§1.4.2) | Symmetric—here stands apart from there exactly as there stands apart from here |
| **Substantiality** | Identity and non-identity (§1.4.3) | Symmetric—if this isn’t that, that isn’t this |

Reversing either symmetric relation changes nothing; reversing the asymmetric temporal relation yields a genuine alternative, and Time forbids it. That asymmetry, native to Time alone among the three Conditions, is what makes Time the richer axis: not doubly distinct, but distinctly ordered. It is also what secures Time’s direction intrinsically. Being before excludes being after by the identity of the relation itself, with no privileged global direction needed to stamp one order forward.

Each collapse, were it to occur, reaches the same destination by a different route: no space, no time, no determinate thing. The three impossibilities are three roads to the Null State—the positive face of the null-state incoherence argued independently at §2.7. Entertaining the collapse of any one axis already redeploys the very distinctions the collapse would erase. Chapter 3 states the same three failures again from the ordinary side: this rather than that, obtains rather than not, borne rather than merely described (§3.2.1). No logical apparatus is needed there; the two statements are one requirement read at two levels of the same architecture.

That working logicians and ontologists who weren’t consulting this account developed formal work along the three domains it associates with its existence-axes is a suggestive clustering, not a derivation of exhaustiveness or metalogical separation. The clustering is read at §3.5.7 as a partial affinity; the forward derivation explains why these disciplines are grouped here where they are. The three disciplines are modeled as the root layer of the framework-relative scientific architecture at §2.11.2. The metalogical position derived from those three existence-axes (logic as metaphysically grounded, structurally individuated, realist, and foundational to the sciences) is made explicit at §2.11.3.

*Tested against.* Quine, the principal substantial-logic ancestor and the divergence point on whether identity is one discipline among many or part of classical first-order logic *simpliciter* (§7.1.3); conventionalism, on whether axis-individuation is structural rather than chosen (§7.1.4); structural realism (Ladyman & Ross), which agrees that Reality has carvable joints and diverges on whether the joints are these three (§9.10); mereological nihilism, on whether substantial logic has anything composite to regiment (§8.3.4); and Tegmark, on whether the three logics are mathematical structures rather than features of Reality (§9.9).

### 2.11.2 The Stratified Architecture
The three specialized formal disciplines distinguished in §2.11.1 can be modeled as the root of a stratified scientific architecture. On its proposal, temporal, spatial, and substantial formalisms regiment claims along three irreducible existence-axes, and further inquiry operates within their joint constraints. The architecture is therefore framework-relative: a disciplined representation of how the book organizes inquiry, not a uniquely established ordering of every science before the logic-triad thesis receives its independent defense.

The stratification adds no new premise to the proof and contributes no proof of the chapter theorem. It draws out the architecture proposed by the three-discipline result. A discipline occupies a higher stratum by adding distinctive content, vocabulary, and methods to the constraints supplied by the lower strata. Lower strata constrain what can coherently be said at higher ones, but they don’t derive the higher strata’s characteristic claims.

Two practices cross the strata rather than occupying one more rung. Mathematics can abstract and regiment structure at the logical floor, in a physical theory, or in a higher science; it proves what follows once the relevant quantitative or relational profile is fixed. Analytic language can state claims about any stratum; its signs and operators are the vehicle in which a structure is described, not another structure inserted between logic and its subject matter. Physics remains the first empirical stratum because it adds claims about which structures and laws are physically instantiated. The distinctions are therefore differences in role, not four items in a single stack: logic fixes consequence, mathematics fixes invariants within specified profiles, physics identifies empirical realizations, and language carries their description. The mathematical transfer is derived at §3.5.6, which returns to the analytic operators introduced at §1.5; the kind of necessity a physically realized profile carries is then stated at §3.5.6.

*The strata.*

- *Root layer.* LEM applied at existence-axes. The bare logical floor; bivalent existence-claims are determinate at each of the three axes.
- *Layer 1.* The three logics. Temporal, spatial, substantial: each carving its axis’s native structure within LEM-bivalence. Condition-Individuation’s irreducibility clause keeps them distinct.
- *Layer 2.* Physics. Empirical-nomological work within the joint engagement of all three logics. Conservation laws, dynamics, field equations, particles, constants: physics-specific content that operates within the three-logic scaffold but isn’t derivable from it.
- *Layer 3.* Higher empirical sciences. Chemistry (patterns of atomic Φ-beings governed by physics), biology (organized Φ-systems exhibiting metabolism, reproduction), astronomy (large-scale T-S-Φ patterns), each engaging some subset of physics’s content as input.
- *Layer 4.* Human and social sciences. Psychology, sociology, economics, history: patterns within the lower layers’ content.

At each layer the deeper layers act as constraints, not as content. Physics doesn’t derive from the three logics; it operates within them. Chemistry doesn’t derive from physics; it operates within physics’s nomological content. The architecture is stratified rather than reductive: no stratum reduces to the one beneath; each contributes distinctive claims, vocabulary, and methods constrained by but not supplied by the deeper strata.

*Physics is empirical-nomological work within the three logics, not identical to them.* The temptation to identify physics with the three logics is real, and the identification is mistaken. Physics presupposes and uses the three logics: any physical claim is about a Φ-being at an S-position over T-succession, regimented by the inferential apparatus the three logics supply. But physics adds empirical content (specific laws, constants, particles, fields), nomological structure (causation, dynamics, conservation principles), specific mathematical apparatus (calculus, differential geometry, tensor analysis, group theory), and methodology (experiment, prediction, theory-revision). The three logics supply none of this. They supply the framework within which all of this is conducted.

The cleaner, framework-relative formulation: physics is *empirical-nomological investigation regimentable within the joint apparatus of temporal, spatial, and substantial formal disciplines*. Not identity and not a claim that working physics literally derives from three axiom-systems, but a containment model: physics adds empirical-nomological content to claims the three disciplines can jointly regiment. This formulation also tightens the anti-physicalism of §2.9.3: physicalism conflates Layer 2’s content (specific laws, particles) with the root layer and Layer 1 (the three logics that physics is conducted within). The mistake is treating Layer 2’s content as foundational when its foundations lie a stratum below.

*The location of metaphysics.* The stratification places metaphysics correctly. Metaphysics is the discipline whose object is the root layer and Layer 1: the three Conditions and Condition-Individuation’s individuation of them. So it is not a high-level science built on top of physics, not a competitor with physics over the same explanatory territory, and not empty speculation about what physics already settles. Its method is conceptual analysis of LEM-application, irreducibility-testing across candidate axes, and the structural derivations Chapter 2 conducts. That method has its own validity-conditions and its own object, distinct from physics’s.

Critics who treat metaphysics as disguised physics or empty speculation include logical positivists (Carnap 1928 *The Logical Structure of the World*; Carnap 1932 *The Elimination of Metaphysics Through Logical Analysis of Language*), Quine in some moods (1948), and naturalized metaphysicians who locate metaphysics within or below empirical science (Ladyman et al. 2007 *Every Thing Must Go*). Each criticism preserves part of the right discipline while locating it at the wrong level.

Positivism is right that metaphysical claims require clear criteria; Chapter 2 supplies them through explicit conceptual and structural derivations. Quine is right that ontology should track the values of bound variables in our best theories; the further claim is that those values must instantiate the three Conditions. Ladyman and Ross are right that metaphysics should answer to the structure scientific inquiry presupposes; the disagreement concerns where that structure lies.

On the present architecture, physical claims are regimented through the three-discipline root. It can’t investigate that root without employing the very logic under examination. Metaphysics therefore has a distinct object and method. It is neither disguised physics nor speculation unconstrained by physics.

The stratification also explains why the unity-of-science program had the right intuition but the wrong root. The intuition (Carnap 1934 *The Unity of Science*; Neurath 1944 *Foundations of the Social Sciences*; Hempel 1969 *Reduction: Ontological and Linguistic Facets*; Oppenheim and Putnam 1958 *Unity of Science as a Working Hypothesis*) was that there is a single underlying structure that the sciences all rely on. The mistake was putting physics at the bottom. Its proposed correction: model the three disciplines as the root and physics as Layer 2 rather than Layer 0. Levels-of-reality work (Putnam 1967a *Psychological Predicates*; Fodor 1974 *Special Sciences*; Wimsatt 1976 *Reductionism, Levels of Organization, and the Mind-Body Problem*; Kim 1998 *Mind in a Physical World*) comes closer; it recognizes stratification without strict reduction (Kim pressing the reductive challenge from within the same layered picture), but still typically treats physics as the foundational level rather than as Layer 2 above the three logics. Its stratification keeps the levels-of-reality insight while relocating the foundation.

*Tested against.* Structural realism (Ladyman & Ross’s *Every Thing Must Go*), the naturalized-metaphysics position partially shared, parting on where the joints lie (§9.10); Quine, on ontology tracking bound-variable values, which meets the reply that those values must instantiate the three Conditions (§7.1.3); Tegmark, on whether the root is mathematical rather than logical (§9.9); eliminativism, pressing on metaphysics as a legitimate discipline (§9.2); and governing-law accounts, the non-Humean alternative on whether laws govern Layer 2: Armstrong, Dretske, and Tooley on the necessitation relation (§8.2.2).

### 2.11.3 The Metalogical Position
The derivation from the three existence-axes owns a substantive metalogical position: a position *about* logic, not a contribution *within* logic. It proposes no new axioms, no new operators, no new semantic clauses; temporal logic, spatial logic, and the formal-ontology and mereology traditions already exist as developed by Prior, Tarski, Leśniewski, Quine, Simons, Lowe, and others. What it offers is a theory of why there is logic at all, and why these particular logics. The position has four commitments.

*Logic is metaphysically grounded.* Its classical inferential floor is tied here to a joint determinacy-and-LEM commitment along T, S, and Φ. LEM is the Law of Excluded Middle; it doesn’t by itself entail that every claim takes exactly one of two semantic values, so bivalence is an additional commitment rather than a gloss on LEM. The alternative metalogical foundations on offer are rejected. Logic isn’t convention (against Carnap-style pluralism, *The Logical Syntax of Language* 1937, the three logics are dictated by Reality’s axes, not chosen for utility). Logic isn’t transcendental condition of thought (against Kant (1781) 1998 *Critique of Pure Reason*, logic is grounded in Reality, not in mind). Logic isn’t free-floating formalism (against Hilbert 1899 *Foundations of Geometry* on formalist readings, logic has real referents, per the reverse derivation at §2.11.1). Logic isn’t psychological construction for empirical existence-claims (against intuitionist treatments of empirical bivalence, Brouwer 1907; and Heyting 1956 raise legitimate concerns about unbounded mathematical claims, but LEM-application is restricted here to existence-claims along the three Conditions, where the bivalence is empirical not unbounded-mathematical).

Each rejected position gets something right, and this account keeps it. Carnap is right that higher-stratum axiomatic choice has a conventional moment; its anti-conventionalism applies only to the floor LEM and the three axis-logics, not to choices among axiom systems above them. Kant is right that logical structure shows up wherever cognition occurs; what’s added is that the cognizer is a T-S-Φ instantiator, so cognition tracks logic because both track Reality. Hilbert is right that the formal disciplines admit consistent axiomatization independently of semantic interpretation; what’s added is that, for the three logics, the axiomatizations also have real referents per the reverse derivation at §2.11.1.

*Logic is structurally individuated.* Three basic formal disciplines are proposed here, corresponding to the three existence-axes: temporal, spatial, and substantial. That correspondence doesn’t by itself establish that there are exactly three genuinely separate logics rather than three coordinated theories within a broader logic. The modal axis is screened out by Condition-Individuation’s irreducibility clause (§2.6.11): the Modal Identity identifies □◇C with □(T∧S∧Φ), so the modal-axis is the modal-side of the same Nature rather than a fourth independent axis. Not arbitrarily many: the position rejects unrestricted logical pluralism (Beall and Restall 2006 *Logical Pluralism*), according to which any number of logics are correct for any number of domains with no metaphysical privileging. The three logics are axis-individuated, not domain-individuated: what counts as an axis is determined by the Principle’s two-clause screen, not by pragmatic choice. The proposal pressures an undifferentiated one-system treatment at the level of subject-matter, because each axis develops specialized axioms beyond LEM. Whether those systems are formally non-intertranslatable, or instead coordinated branches under one broader consequence relation, remains a further metalogical commitment rather than an output of Condition-Individuation.

*Logic has real referents.* The claims of temporal, spatial, and substantial logic are determinately true or false because they are about real features of Reality. This is realist about the three formal disciplines. This realism extends the realism about Nature established at §2.8: just as Nature is real—not a useful construct, theoretical posit, or regulative ideal—the three Conditions are real, and so are the inferential systems native to them. This is the realism the reverse derivation in §2.11.1 needs to do its work (a formal discipline has determinately true-or-false claims only if its claims have real referents), and it’s owned here as a substantive commitment rather than a methodological convenience.
