The smallest arithmetic case shows what kind of explanation this is. Let *A* and *B* be disjoint pluralities, each with exactly two members, under ordinary finite cardinal addition. Their disjoint union has four members. The left and right sides don’t name two configurations connected by a productive force. *Two plus two* describes the plurality by its composition; *four* describes the same plurality by its cardinality. An overlap between the pairs, a fusion of members, or a change in the operation wouldn’t produce an exceptional case in which 2 + 2 = 3. It would withdraw disjointness, stable membership, or ordinary addition and therefore realize a different profile. Arithmetic necessity is quantitative identity under the operation fixed, not a law imposed on collections from outside them.

That’s why the result doesn’t reverse the explicit limit at §2.7.3: arithmetic necessity isn’t the Necessity of Nature, and mathematical objects aren’t thereby concrete Nature. T, S, and Φ supply the one modal field within which real configurations can realize quantitative profiles; they don’t derive the natural numbers from piles of objects. The mathematical proof establishes the object-side invariant. A concrete act of counting or proving instantiates the Conditions in its performance, but that act-side fact doesn’t make its conclusion true.

Geometry fixes the other edge. In a Euclidean plane, the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees. Spherical and hyperbolic triangles carry different angle-sums because they realize different metric profiles, not because the Euclidean consequence fails in an admissible Euclidean realization. A triangular frame used in engineering adds further conditions still: joint behavior, material strength, loading, scale, and manufacturing tolerance. Mathematics fixes what follows from the idealized profile; physics determines which profile the frame realizes and how the additional physical quantities behave. The theorem transfers the invariant wherever the realization premise holds. It doesn’t supply that premise by resemblance alone.

The result therefore separates four roles that a simple hierarchy would run together. Logic supplies consequence and the determinacy floor. Mathematics specifies abstract profiles and proves their invariants. Physics determines which mathematical profiles and further laws describe actual physical systems. Analytic language supplies the signs, predicates, equations, and operators through which any of those claims can be stated. Mathematics isn’t a rung between logic and physics: it ranges across structures at several strata. Language isn’t a final rung above them: it is the representational practice crossing the stack.

This is the delayed payoff of §1.5’s analytic operators. *Obtains*, *entails*, *grounds*, *bears*, and *persists* can represent abstract or concrete relations; the proposition expressed need not itself occupy a physical coordinate. A token use of the operator—a written proof, a spoken inference, a calculation—is a concrete event and therefore an actual Change in its realizer. The Structural Requirement, not a one-to-one analogy between signs and Conditions, supplies T, S, and Φ at the level of that application. That fact explains how analytic language is possible and how it participates in the structure it describes. It doesn’t validate the sentence, turn its abstract subject matter into a concrete object, or collapse representation into realization. Chapter 5 develops the richer linguistic case, in which self-modeling subjects use signs to transmit propositional content (§5.12); the present result fixes only the thinner formal role on which that practice builds.

Invariant Realization supplies a positive philosophy of mathematical application without deciding every question in the philosophy of mathematics. It doesn’t prove that every consistent formal profile is really possible, identify formal consistency with real possibility, select one ontology of numbers or sets, or rule out uninstantiated mathematical structure. It supplies the bridge the chapter has earned: formal invariance transfers to a real realization because a realization lacking the invariant wouldn’t realize the profile. Platonism tests whether the profile requires a further abstract domain (§8.1.5); Wigner’s puzzle tests why independently developed profiles find precise physical realizations (§9.8); the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis tests whether realization should be strengthened to identity (§9.9); structural realism tests what survives representation and theory change (§9.10). Set-theoretic pluralism presses the prior question, whether a claim about structure that no realization could settle has a determinate answer at all; the theorem is neutral on it, since it fixes only what follows wherever a profile is realized. None is decided by using the word *structure* twice. The theorem fixes the transfer each dispute must preserve or resist.

Invariant Realization permits a precise transformation-profile test, but not a shortcut around the convergence’s modal joints. Let $M_{\Delta}$ be a non-trivial transformation profile: an index set $I$ with an ordering $<$, a state space $X$, and a map $\gamma:I\rightarrow X$, with two indices $i_0<i_1$ such that $\gamma(i_0)\neq\gamma(i_1)$. The profile fixes two consequences before any physical interpretation is supplied. Its indices are directed, and its states are determinately different. Any admissible realization that erased either feature would cease to realize $M_{\Delta}$.

Invariant Realization (§3.5.6) transfers those consequences to every real realization of the profile. It doesn’t make the profile really possible. Nor does the abstract state space by itself supply a concrete bearer: $X$ is a formal domain, not yet Substantiality. Bearing enters when a real configuration is claimed to realize the transformation—when something instantiates the indexed states and carries their difference across the directed mapping. At that point the formal route reaches O and D by profile-preservation and B by real realization. It reaches the generic floor for that realization, not □(T∧S∧Φ) from mathematics alone.

**The transformation-profile route** · *formal corroboration*

1. A non-trivial transformation profile $M_{\Delta}$ contains directed indices and at least two non-identical states: $i_0<i_1$ and $\gamma(i_0)\neq\gamma(i_1)$.

2. Therefore every admissible realization of $M_{\Delta}$ preserves the formally stated consequences $i_0<i_1$ and $\gamma(i_0)\neq\gamma(i_1)$—directed order and determinate difference at the level of generic roles.

3. By Invariant Realization, no really possible real configuration realizes $M_{\Delta}$ while lacking those consequences.

4. A *real* realization is something in which the indexed difference obtains; at the realization level, it therefore supplies bearing, B. The abstract profile alone doesn’t.

5. Therefore every real realization of a non-trivial transformation profile instantiates O∧D∧B at the level of generic roles.

*Scope.* The route establishes neither that $M_{\Delta}$ is really possible nor that it is actually or necessarily realized. It doesn’t identify O/D/B with T/S/Φ, prove □◇C, or replace the Structural Requirement. Because Invariant Realization itself applies Chapter 2’s transfer machinery, this is mathematical corroboration and a precise realization test, not a premise-disjoint proof of the spine.

This also fixes what an allegedly empty mathematical model can show. A formally specified empty domain is still a mathematical profile with identity-conditions fixed in a metalanguage. Its formal availability isn’t yet a really possible null state, and its description isn’t the absence it describes. Mathematics can prove what follows within the profile and what every realization must preserve. It can’t turn a model of absence into the metaphysical actuality or possibility of ∅ merely by calling the domain empty.

*Analytic-language convergence.*

Analytic language reaches the same boundary from the side of the operators surveyed at §1.5. It supplies a family of conditional routes rather than one universal derivation. A claim that *grounds*, *entails*, or *depends on* already states a directed relation and therefore incurs O at the level of its content. Any determinate proposition distinguishes its satisfaction from its failure and therefore incurs D. When the proposition is actually asserted, denied, written, or inferred, the token has a realizer and incurs B at the level of its performance. For the grounding and denial claims Chapter 3 tests, all three routes coincide.

The coincidence remains level-indexed. An abstract proposition’s having truth-conditions isn’t yet Substantiality, and the fact that a sentence about ∅ is tokened by a structured speaker doesn’t show by itself that the sentence’s object instantiates the speaker’s structure. Analytic language therefore strengthens the act-side and operator-side convergence in §3.3 and exposes what a structureless-ground claim must spend merely to state a grounding relation. It doesn’t cross the act/object gap by grammar. The candidate-world and no-residue arguments must still do object-side work.

*Physical realization.*

Invariant Realization reaches beyond mathematics once physics establishes that a real system instantiates the profile from which an invariant follows. The resulting necessity is neither a new source of modality nor the claim that every actual physical law obtains in every possible reality. It is the necessity with which a physically realized profile carries its proved consequences. The profile may fail to obtain; it can’t obtain while lacking what follows from its constitutive structure.

Call *M* a physical-mathematical profile when it specifies the geometrical, dynamical, symmetry, or operational relations relevant to a physical derivation. Calling the profile complete means complete *for that derivation*: enough has been fixed to prove the consequence, not that the desired conclusion has been inserted into the description. That restriction prevents the result from becoming the trivial claim that a law follows from a profile defined as including the law. Physics and mathematics must independently show that *M* is sufficient for *Q*.

Philosophers commonly use *nomological necessity* for truth throughout worlds in which the same laws are held fixed. The present framework can state the relevant content without adding a second primitive box. If *L* names the independently specified law-profile and $Q(x)$ an invariant consequence for a realization *x*, nomological necessity becomes an absolute modal conditional:

$$
\Box\forall x\bigl(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,L) \rightarrow Q(x)\bigr).
$$

The box ranges over the one modal field; the antecedent marks the profile whose realization is being held fixed. This form shows both the strength and the limit. A world can’t realize *L* while violating *Q*. Nothing in that conditional alone establishes $\Box\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,L)$.

Special relativity provides the clean case. Let $M_{\mathrm{SR}}$ include Lorentzian spacetime structure, an invariant speed $c$, the energy-momentum four-vector, and invariant mass. The invariant norm gives

$$
E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4,
$$

and for a body in its rest frame, where $p=0$,

$$
E_0=mc^2.
$$

The relation is special-relativistic rather than a consequence requiring general relativity (Einstein 1905; Minkowski 1908). Inertial frames vary in their decomposition of energy and momentum while preserving the invariant relation. The numerical value assigned to $c$ varies with units; its role as the invariant conversion structure doesn’t. A purported physical configuration with the same relevant Lorentzian profile and a different rest-energy relation wouldn’t be an exceptional realization of $M_{\mathrm{SR}}$. It would either violate the invariant or realize a different profile.

The example also separates *relationality* from *relativity*. Relational Distinctness and the S-limb of the Necessity of Nature establish that determinate physical configurations require relational differentiation. They don’t by themselves establish that every possible reality is Lorentzian. Generic relationality supports $\Box S$ at the book’s structural resolution. Einsteinian relativity adds a particular metric and symmetry profile. Let $E_0(x)$ and $m(x)$ denote the rest energy and invariant mass of an *x* that realizes the profile. The earned result is therefore

$$
\Box\forall x\Bigl(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M_{\mathrm{SR}})\rightarrow E_0(x)=m(x)c^2\Bigr),
$$

not, from relationality alone,

$$
\Box\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M_{\mathrm{SR}}).
$$

Necessary Possibility adds a second grade without collapsing the distinction. If a real realization of *M* is genuinely possible, then its possibility can’t lapse:

$$
\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)
\rightarrow
\Box\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M).
$$

Where $M\models Q$, Invariant Realization fixes the consequence at every relevant realization, so the available profile is available only with its invariant consequence. Thus:

$$
\bigl(M\models Q\ \land\ \Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\bigr)
\rightarrow
\Box\Diamond\exists x\bigl(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\land Q(x)\bigr).
$$

The conclusion is necessary availability, not necessary actuality. If *M* is actually realized, Strict Actualization gives an actual *Q*-bearing realization. If $\Box\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$ is independently established, then the invariant is necessarily instantiated. Neither actuality nor mere possibility supplies that stronger antecedent by itself.

*Notation.* **M** is a physical-mathematical profile: the geometrical, dynamical, symmetry, or operational relations a physical derivation actually uses. **Q** is a proved consequence of that profile, and *Realizes(x, M)* says a real configuration x instantiates it.

**[Theorem]**

**Physical Invariance** · *Theorem*

A complete physical profile cannot vary independently of its proved invariants. If $M\models Q$, every really possible physical realization of *M* carries *Q*: $\Box\forall x(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\rightarrow Q(x))$. If an *M*-realization is genuinely possible, an *M*-with-*Q* realization is necessarily possible. If *M* is actual, *Q* is actual in that realization. Only an independent proof that *M* is necessary licenses the further conclusion that *Q* is necessarily instantiated.

**Dependency routes:** invariant consequence—Invariant Realization (§3.5.6); availability—Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10); actual realization—Strict Actualization (§2.9.4)

Physical Invariance fixes what a profile carries. Necessary Possibility fixes the standing of the profile itself. Let *M* be any physical profile for which a real realization is genuinely possible. Because that possibility belongs to Reality’s capacity rather than to one local arrangement, $\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$ entails $\Box\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$. The profile may never be actual again, and another profile may instead be actual; its availability can’t lapse. Nor can an act, generator, or chooser first make it available. Any such act would already range over alternatives whose modal standing had to be fixed for the selection to be determinate, and any real selector would belong to the Reality–Nature identity rather than supply a stock of possibilities from outside it.

**[Theorem]**

**Modal Availability Cannot Be Tuned** · *Theorem*

For any physical profile *M*, if a real *M*-realization is genuinely possible, an *M*-realization is necessarily possible: $\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\rightarrow\Box\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$. Since actuality entails possibility, every actually realized profile—including the present physical profile—is therefore necessarily available: $\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\rightarrow\Box\Diamond\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$. Its modal availability cannot be conferred, withdrawn, or varied by a selection among profiles. Every genuinely possible physical profile already belongs to Nature’s necessarily stable modal range. A selector may still be proposed to explain why one available profile is actual rather than another; it cannot, as selector, explain the availability of the profiles among which it selects. Necessary availability does not by itself entail actuality at every world.

**Dependency routes:** modal stability—Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10); location of every real possibility—Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8) and Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7)

The result relocates physical contingency. It is misleading to picture a complete physical structure as fixed while its constitutive invariants are freely reassigned, as though laws were labels pasted onto an otherwise unchanged world. Once a profile is shown sufficient for an invariant, changing the invariant changes the profile. What remains unselected is which profile Nature actually realizes, which parameters and boundary conditions fall outside the proof, and which alternative profiles are genuinely possible. Even there, contingency must be earned by warranted alternatives rather than inferred from the modal theorem’s silence.

This distinguishes physical laws by status. A profile-constitutive invariant follows wherever its sufficient structure is realized. An effective law may hold only in a regime or approximation and inherits those boundary conditions in its antecedent. An empirical regularity may lack any proof of sufficiency and so carries no stronger necessity merely because it has held so far. The phrase *physical law* doesn’t settle which category a statement belongs to; the derivation does.

Physical Necessity therefore joins rather than erases the chapter’s distinct roles. Mathematics proves the invariant. Physics establishes the real profile and the domain in which it is realized. Modality fixes the consequence across possible realizations and the stability of any genuine possibility. The result doesn’t derive Lorentzian geometry, Hilbert-space quantum theory, gauge structure, or the values of constants from T, S, and Φ. It states something stronger and narrower about each once independently secured: the same complete profile can’t carry a different invariant while remaining the same profile, and a genuinely possible profile doesn’t await a further source to make it available.

Chapter 4 tests that result against spacetime, fields, symmetries, and conservation at §4.5, then uses it to close the compression-to-expansion consequence wherever a complete boundary profile is physically secured at §4.6. Chapter 9 spends it on the applicability problem at §9.8. The physical-law question is no longer why an external rule compels a neutral substrate to behave one way rather than another. For profile-constitutive laws, the rule spells out what the realized physical structure is; the residual explanatory question concerns the realization of this profile rather than another.

The result isn’t that mathematics or physics independently rediscovers the whole theorem. Mathematics fixes invariant consequence; physics supplies realization; modality fixes the standing of the realized possibility. Their convergence depends on keeping those roles separate. Collapse them, and the proof hides a bridge. Keep them distinct, and each discipline confirms exactly the part of the structure it is equipped to establish.

### 3.5.7 Precedent Convergence
The argument for the Necessity of Nature has neighbors. Spinoza pressed the nearest question, and several modern programs press adjacent ones: necessity, priority, modal jurisdiction, and theoretical cost. Reading them together shows where the pressure driving this argument has been felt before, and it puts the real disagreements where a reader can see them.

Chapter 2 has built the structural case from the inside, and the proof closed at §2.9 spending nothing that follows. None of these positions is the chapter’s theorem under another name, and their proximity is no evidence that □(T∧S∧Φ) is true. The result sits beside a contemporary research landscape of adjacent conclusions rather than at the terminus of a literature-wide convergence.

The historical anchor is Spinoza. The *Ethics* (1677) 1996 makes Nature (*Deus sive Natura*) the single necessary substance, derives modes from it by structural necessity, and grounds the modal field in nothing further. The present argument differs from Spinoza in vocabulary (T∧S∧Φ rather than substance/attribute/mode), method (modal logic over the structural Conditions rather than geometric deduction from definitions), and target (necessary structural Conditions rather than Spinoza’s one necessary substance). Its affinity lies only in locating ultimacy on the Nature-side rather than in an external creator (why contingency survives at the level of configurations despite the shared location of necessity is the question addressed at §2.9.4 and §2.9.6; the full Deus-sive-Natura engagement is at §10.3.1). Four contemporary lines sit beside the structural spine of the present argument, sharing selected pressures while reaching importantly different conclusions: priority monism (§3.5.7.1), the modal limits on necessary-being arguments (§3.5.7.2), the total-theory comparison against necessary-being arguments (§3.5.7.3), and contemporary necessitarianism (§3.5.7.4). A fifth convergence (older but structurally adjacent) is the clustering of independently developed formal work along the three Conditions: two established logics and one synthesized axis (§3.5.7.5).

The affinities matter on four points. *First*, the problem-space isn’t isolated: other inquiries independently press priority, modal limits, theoretical comparison, or global necessity. *Second*, the overlap is partial and must be itemized rather than pooled: Spinoza’s necessary substance is stronger and differently typed; priority monism concerns dependence among concrete entities; modal-limit arguments constrain what modal machinery certifies; Oppy’s method compares total theories without supplying a necessity theorem; contemporary necessitarianism often targets all truths or a concrete cosmos rather than T∧S∧Φ. *Third*, none of those differences is filled in merely by supplying the present architecture, and none of the precedents is evidence for an unresolved bridge in it. Their value is dialectical—they show where the book joins, exceeds, or opposes live programs. *Fourth*, affinity with precedents in the necessity literature isn’t the comparative-total-theories case against naturalism’s rivals. Independent motivation establishes that the move is non-isolated; it doesn’t establish that the move’s total cost (ontological commitments, explanatory loss, tensions against background commitments) is lower than the alternatives. That comparative pricing is engaged at Chapters 8–10 under Oppy’s comparative-total-theories discipline: the necessary-being family in Chapter 10, the modal-variant family at §8.2, the physics/mind family at §9. The present catalog maps literature affinities and disagreements; Chapters 8–10 undertake the separate comparative-cost case.

What the present argument offers beside these programs is its own conclusion and architecture. The modal-invariance bottleneck (§2.1) supplies the fixed modal domain. The bilateral-cogito chain (§2.2–2.4) supplies the structural derivation of Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. The unity of T∧S∧Φ as the Triunity of Nature is supplied at §2.6, identified under three Triconditional readings: Modal, Nomological, Ontological. The Necessity of Nature theorem (§2.9.6) ties the formal result to the named Nature. The affinity is that the contemporary literature reaches neighboring pressure points in its own vocabulary; the longer project must still earn its more specific structural result on its own premises.

Chapter 2 closes at §2.11 by developing what the convergence makes available downstream: the three logics native to the three Conditions, the stratified scientific architecture they ground, and the metalogical position the framework owns. Chapter 3 then stress-tests the result through construction, performance, null-state closure, and grounding. It distinguishes genuinely independent lines from shared hinges, recovers role-level structure without S5, and leaves proposition-wise □◇C with Necessary Possibility unless a separate type-bridge is supplied. The map is therefore evidence only that the pressure points recur, not evidence for the chapter theorem and not a claim of premise-disjoint overdetermination.

*Precedents.* Williamson’s necessitism, the contemporary necessitist complement to the Della Rocca / Karofsky necessitarian line (§7.2.7); Rasmussen’s foundation argument, the contemporary necessary-being program (§10.1); Spinozist pantheism, which carries the Deus-sive-Natura identification (§10.3.1); and Pizzi’s impossibility of nothingness, which shares the reductio method (§8.2.4). The modal-deflationist alternative, modal fictionalism, is engaged at §7.2.6.

###### 3.5.7.1 Priority Monism

Schaffer’s priority monism (2010) holds that the cosmos is the one fundamental object and is prior to its proper parts. Harrop develops a modalized version of priority monism (priority monism enriched with the claim that the priority relation between the cosmos and its proper parts holds with metaphysical necessity) (2024). Harrop argues that this enrichment entails the necessary existence of the actual cosmos and the impossibility of any concrete object not actually instantiated. The argument turns on the grounding-theoretic premise that the prior is fundamental in any world it grounds, combined with the modalization that the grounding relation holds necessarily. Where Harrop reaches a necessary cosmos from grounding-theoretic premises and modal closure, the present argument reaches a necessary Nature from the global-capacity derivation and its Bottleneck defense (§2.1.4–2.1.5) and the bilateral-cogito chain (§2.2–2.4). The two approaches converge on adjacent conclusions, but the theses aren’t identical. Harrop’s thesis is that the *actual concrete cosmos* exists necessarily: a claim about the totality of concrete being. The present argument’s thesis is that the *structural Conditions* T∧S∧Φ are necessary: a claim about the modal structure any cosmos must instantiate. The structural-conditions thesis is implied by the necessary-actual-cosmos thesis under the additional assumption that the actual cosmos instantiates T∧S∧Φ in every world in which it exists; the converse doesn’t hold. A reader who finds Harrop’s concrete-totality move too strong can accept the present argument’s narrower structural-conditions claim without that commitment, and a reader who accepts Harrop’s claim, together with that assumption, accepts the present argument’s conclusion all the more. The structural specification the present argument adds is what Harrop’s *necessary actual cosmos* would have to instantiate on either reading.

###### 3.5.7.2 Modal Limits

Van Hamme (2026) distinguishes three classes of necessity: logical-analytic (Class A), modal-structural (Class B), and existential (Class C), and argues that modal logic’s jurisdiction stops at Class B. Arguments that ask modal apparatus to certify Class C necessity (that a particular being exists necessarily) can’t get that result without admitting Class B structure, which already does the work the proposed existent was supposed to do. Van Hamme reads the result as a limit on a family of necessary-being arguments; the present argument reads it as a relocation of modal force. What modal logic *can* deliver, Class B (modal-structural necessity, the necessity of frame-conditions any possible world satisfies), is the class T∧S∧Φ occupies. The identification is inclusive rather than exhaustive: Class B may include further frame-conditions the present argument doesn’t develop, but T, S, and Φ are Class B necessities on the structural-minimum reading the present argument develops, since they are the frame-conditions any modally specifiable state of affairs satisfies. Fritz, Lo, and Schmid run a structurally distinct reverse-direction modal ontological argument against a necessary-being conclusion, valid in S4 alone, without reliance on the Euclidean Axiom (2026). The relevant comparison is with the global-capacity modal-stability argument and its Bottleneck defense at §2.1.4–2.1.5, not with §2.1.3’s non-vacuity lemma. Any claim that an S4-only reverse argument transfers to the present framework must be assessed against those premises rather than attributed to Modal Constitution. These independent lines converge on the negative result: modal logic doesn’t by itself deliver a particular necessary being. The present argument adds the positive complement: what modal logic does deliver is Nature.

###### 3.5.7.3 Total-Theory Comparison

Oppy’s work (2006) develops the comparative-total-theories framework (assess metaphysical positions by their total cost in ontological commitments, explanatory loss, and tension against background commitments) and applies it to necessary-being arguments (Rasmussen, Pruss, Plantinga-style ontological) as competitors to naturalism. The verdict, on Oppy’s accounting, is that the necessary-being family pays a higher total cost than the naturalist alternative because the necessary-being hypothesis adds a being beyond Nature, whereas the naturalist makes Nature itself the terminus. The present argument relocates the necessity to Nature itself: T∧S∧Φ are necessary, and the question whether anything *further* is necessary (a particular being, a divine reality, a non-natural foundation) is taken up at length in Chapters 10 and 11 (the Theistic Counter-Constructions cluster). Oppy’s comparative framework is the natural discipline for that question. The present argument’s contribution isn’t a rival total theory but the structural specification naturalism’s necessary terminus requires: the Conditions read along three Triconditional axes. Where Oppy’s *naturalism* is structured against the necessary-being alternatives, the present argument supplies what naturalism’s necessary terminus consists in.

A further observation, which Oppy’s own method surfaces, belongs at the level of practice rather than proof. Comparing total theories requires stable-enough logical relations, inferential standards, and pricing criteria for the inquiry to proceed. That is a local presupposition of actual comparison: this inquiry runs within an instantiated reasoning practice and, like every actual practice, within the structured world the chapter describes. It doesn’t follow that the norms couldn’t have been otherwise, or that the structural Conditions are necessary rather than actual; modal necessity must be earned independently by §2.1–2.9. The comparison market is therefore not metaphysically neutral in practice, but neither is its stability an alternative proof of □(T∧S∧Φ). Oppy’s framework supplies comparative discipline. The chapter’s modal spine supplies the necessity claim.

###### 3.5.7.4 Contemporary Necessitarianism

Two related but distinct lines defend strong necessitarian theses. Della Rocca (2010; 2020) revives the Principle of Sufficient Reason and argues that PSR commits its proponent to the necessity of all states of affairs; the conclusion is presented as a consequence of taking PSR seriously rather than as an independently motivated necessitarian thesis. Karofsky’s *A Case for Necessitarianism* (2021) defends the stronger thesis directly: *everything* is necessary, with no contingency anywhere in the modal field. The two lines converge on overlapping conclusions but proceed differently: Della Rocca through PSR-revival, Karofsky through direct necessitarian argument. The present argument doesn’t endorse this stronger thesis (§2.9.4, *Necessity Precedes Contingency*): the modal floor is necessary, while the theorem doesn’t make its contents necessary and permits contingency wherever genuine alternatives are independently established. But the necessitarian’s case leaves the present argument’s narrower claim secure from both directions. If the necessitarian is right that everything is necessary, then all the more the structural Conditions of Nature are necessary, and the present argument’s conclusion is contained in the necessitarian’s stronger one. If the necessitarian is wrong about modal contents, the case for the structural Conditions’ necessity remains untouched, because the present argument never required global necessity to begin with. Della Rocca and Karofsky press from one direction; the present argument fills in the structural specification their general thesis leaves open.

###### 3.5.7.5 Three Formal Logics

Two recognized formal families and one synthetic umbrella align with the three existence-axes identified here as the Conditions. Temporal logic regiments inferences over T, and spatial logic regiments inferences over S. The Φ-axis is distributed across formal ontology, mereology, classical first-order logic with identity, and substance metaphysics. The present argument gathers those traditions under the coined label *substantial logic*: the *logic of being qua being* in Aristotle’s sense (*Metaphysics* Γ 1003a21), read specifically through persistence, identity, and part–whole structure. The convergence is therefore not that three literatures independently adopted the same three labels. It is that independently developed formal work clusters along T and S as established disciplines and along Φ across several traditions synthesized here. *Three Formally Distinct Logics* (§2.11.1) develops that derivation and states the coined status of the Φ-axis explicitly.

The neighborhood confirms recurrence, not truth by company. Mathematics and physics preserve consequences once their realization conditions are independently met; precedent locates adjacent pressures without supplying a missing premise. The dependency ledger therefore closes where it began: Chapter 3 has strengthened the canonical line by showing which conclusions survive local cuts, which receive independent role-level support, and which still stand on shared joints. With those prices visible, §3.6 can state the inversion without making the convergence claim more than it is.

## 3.6 Necessity’s Reversal
The tradition placed the necessary ground *outside* the world: simple, changeless, self-subsistent, the source on which a contingent world depends. The canonical argument inverts that placement, and the convergence pressure-tests the inversion. What is necessary isn’t a particular changing world or a change occurring everywhere, but Nature as Reality’s standing capacity and constraint: succession, distinction, and exchange at modal-core resolution. (Why three necessary aspects rather than one simple necessary being (the question the classical theist presses from divine simplicity, and the aggregation theorist from the other side) isn’t begged here. That the necessary structure is three-in-one rather than a contentless bare simple is earned upstream by the triunity of §2.6.9: one Nature read along three irreducible axes, identity-under-description. The individuation criterion at No Fourth Condition (§2.6.11) supplies the screen any proposed fourth must pass and shifts the burden to the candidate; it doesn’t, by itself, deductively prove that no further irreducible axis is possible.) Reality doesn’t rest in a second modal domain beyond that structure; Reality *is* the field in which change is possible, necessarily. (Self-subsistence here is field-level explanatory non-exteriority, not a proof that physical history has no first moment. The Unswitchable Capacity and Transition Closure block one local story: a transition-capacity can’t arise, within a history, from a state stipulated to lack every transition realizing it. They do **not** show that no first change or first moment is possible, and they don’t turn a silent world into an earlier stage of this one. The positive component is constitutive: Φ names retained bearing across change (§2.4.8); the external-sustainer alternative is tested downstream at §10.1.6. The modal component is that real possibility ranges within Reality’s one field rather than receiving its status from a second domain (§2.8); Chapter 7 tests that Modal Exclusivity downstream (§7.2.1). Both still rely on the disputed grounding claim that Nature isn’t one item awaiting a ground but the field within which grounding relations obtain (§2.4.3). A flaw there would unsettle the self-subsistence reading without undoing □(T∧S∧Φ).) Necessity is only the first of the divine predicates to change hands: Chapter 11 carries the reversal across the rest, taking each in turn. What self-subsistence names here in general is earned as Subsistent Grounding at §2.9.3: the three Conditions co-constituting the field with no privileged floor.

What remains open is left open by design: the metric structure above the role layer waits for *Nature Alone*, the standing rivals wait for the chapters that follow, and the reversal the convergence exposes is opened here, not yet carried through.



# 4. Nature Alone

What would it take for anything to count as metaphysically ultimate?

The question is older and wider than theology. Philosophers have placed the terminus in a first cause, a necessary being, a single substance, a totality of facts, a fundamental law, or a structure that needs nothing outside itself. The candidates differ. The role doesn’t. Whatever occupies it can’t borrow its necessity from something more necessary, receive its modal standing from a wider field, or depend for its operation on conditions it was introduced to explain. A candidate that does any of those things may still be real, powerful, or fundamental in some restricted respect. It isn’t ultimate in the respect it borrows.

The word *greatness* can conceal the distinction. In perfect-being theology, greatness commonly includes personal and evaluative properties: knowledge, power, goodness, life, and presence, each taken to its maximal degree and composed in one subject. Nothing in the argument so far establishes a maximally knowledgeable or morally perfect subject. The present claim is prior to that construction. It concerns **metaphysical ultimacy**: the standing of whatever is necessary, self-subsistent, modally unsurpassable, and exhaustive of the field in which causal power can obtain. Whether personal or moral predicates belong to that same subject is a later question. It can’t be allowed to decide the location of the ground in advance.

The distinction changes the problem. Instead of asking which proposed being possesses the largest collection of great-making properties, ask first what any bearer of such properties would already have to belong to. Knowledge requires determinate content; power requires a real difference between what acts and what is affected; persistence requires something to remain through the relation. Whatever else a candidate may be, it can’t stand outside the conditions under which its own predicates have content. The location question therefore precedes the attribute question.

*Necessity.* A metaphysical terminus can’t be only one fortunate configuration among others. If its absence remains really possible, the candidate doesn’t explain the modal field within which that alternative stands. The necessary level lies elsewhere. What holds under every modal evaluation isn’t this cosmos, these laws, or any particular distribution of matter and energy. It is Reality’s standing constitution as Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: □(T∧S∧Φ). The necessity belongs to the field, not automatically to what occupies it (§2.9.6).

That result meets the necessary-foundation demand without yet making a theological selection. Contemporary necessary-foundation arguments can establish that something exists necessarily while leaving open what that something is (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018). The structural argument supplies the missing identity at the resolution it has earned. Any concrete change-realizer already requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality; any proposed ground of such realizers either supplies those Conditions or doesn’t perform that grounding role (§2.9.7). Necessity isn’t an honor added to Nature after the fact. Nature is what the necessary constraint consists in.

*Self-subsistence.* The usual image of a ground is vertical: contingent things rest on something that doesn’t rest on anything further. The image invites a basement. But a final basement remains one more floor unless it can explain why support stops there, and the Conditions don’t form that kind of stack. Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality co-constitute the field. None stands beneath the other two; each, fully instantiated, requires the others. Their dependence is mutual without being dependence on a fourth term. That is Subsistent Grounding: not independence by isolation, but the absence of an exterior floor because the Conditions hold one another in the one structure Reality is (§2.9.3).

Self-subsistence therefore changes sense at the structural level. It doesn’t mean that Nature is a solitary object capable of existing after every relation has been stripped away. Nature is the relations without which no determinate object, act, or state can obtain. Asking what Nature rests on repeats the grounding relation while trying to place its terms outside the structure that makes relation possible. The question doesn’t reach beneath the ground. It reinstantiates it.

*Non-exteriority.* An ultimate ground can’t leave a second real domain beside or beyond itself. If something stands outside it, either the ground isn’t exhaustive or the word *outside* no longer marks a real relation. The Reality–Nature Identity closes that alleged location: whatever is real belongs to Reality, and Reality is Nature at modal-field and totality resolution (§2.8). No additional thing becomes exterior by being described as transcendent. If it is real enough to differ from Nature, ground Nature, or act on Nature, it is real enough to belong to the one field in which difference, grounding, and action obtain.

This doesn’t yet refute every essence-prior, analogical, or apophatic description. A proposal that retains thin ordering, difference, or dependence while denying loaded Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality carries a contact burden the later chapters must test. A proposal that withdraws every articulation leaves no determinate ground to assess. What is already fixed is the location: neither proposal occupies a second Reality. The later dispute concerns whether its predicates remain coherent within the exhaustive one.

Two corroborative routes meet exactly this seam. The No-Individuating-Surplus (§3.4.3) test excludes a supposed addition that changes no truth, relation, modal profile, grounding fact, or constitution; the Grounding Trilemma (§3.4.4) denies a candidate an *external* grounding role merely for redescribing thin content as outside. Neither route independently upgrades generic order, difference, and bearing into the loaded three Conditions, and neither replaces the Chapter 2 identity theorem. They strengthen the conclusions that there is no individuating surplus and no external grounding role, at the resolution they actually earn.

*Modal maximality.* To be modally maximal isn’t to actualize every possibility. Incompatible possibilities can’t all be actual together, and nothing in the Necessity of Nature selects every configuration, law, or history. Modal maximality belongs instead to Reality’s range: every real possibility is a possibility of Nature, and no further stock of possibility stands outside Reality waiting to be admitted. Nature doesn’t possess the modal field as an object. Nature is the field, read as the complete standing capacity within which possible configurations differ.

That’s why no candidate can enlarge it from beyond. To add a genuinely new possibility would require a real possibility not already in Reality’s range. But whatever is genuinely possible is, for that reason, already within the range whose supposed enlargement it was introduced to explain. The outside possibility defeats its own description. Nature isn’t one maximally capacious member of a larger domain. There is no larger domain in which it could be exceeded.

*Power.* The same distinction prevents a familiar slide from causal exhaustiveness to omnipotence. Nature isn’t an agent supplied with a will, a plan, or a faculty it can exercise at discretion. Nor does structural necessity entail that every describable outcome can occur. Some descriptions are contradictory; others may be excluded by the laws or complete configurations through which the Conditions are realized. The theorem doesn’t erase those constraints.

What it does establish is exhaustive scope. Every real causal power is exercised within Nature. A field propagates, a mass attracts, a star collapses, an organism moves, a person chooses: each operation requires an ordered difference borne across a relation, and so each instantiates the three Conditions (§2.4; §2.9.7). No force arrives from outside those Conditions, because arrival, force, source, and effect already name their work. Every actual power is a configuration of Nature; every possible power belongs to Nature’s modal range.

Nature’s power is therefore maximal in extent, not concentrated as an infinite intensity in one agent. There is no exterior reservoir from which a greater causal capacity could be drawn and no second field from which Nature could receive the capacity for Change. The most violent event in the cosmos doesn’t reveal a power beside Nature; it reveals what one configuration within Nature can do. The weakest interaction does the same. Magnitude varies among configurations. The field within which any magnitude can be real doesn’t.

At the level of metaphysical ultimacy, the properties traditionally sought in an ultimate ground belong to Nature. Nature is Reality’s necessary constitution—□(T∧S∧Φ)—rather than a being that exists necessarily or one contingent arrangement. It depends on no ground outside itself, includes every real being and every real possibility within its scope, and contains every causal power that can be exercised (Necessity of Nature, §2.9.6; Subsistent Grounding, §2.9.3; Reality–Nature Identity, §2.8; Exclusivity of Nature and Necessary Occupancy, §2.9.7; Structural Requirement, §2.4). No real candidate can exceed Nature in any of these respects, because anything real enough to ground, enlarge, or act upon Nature would already belong to the Reality that Nature constitutes.

This concerns metaphysical ultimacy only. It doesn’t make Nature a person or attribute consciousness, will, knowledge, goodness, or omnipotence to it. Those properties require separate arguments.

The inversion is exact. The philosophical demand wasn’t mistaken to seek something necessary, self-subsistent, unsurpassable in modal scope, and answerable to nothing beyond itself. It was pointing at a real structural role. The mistake was to treat that role as though it had to be occupied by a further being set over the field it grounds. Once Reality’s necessary constitution is identified, the properties don’t disappear. They change subjects.

Spinoza reached the same location under the language of one necessary substance, *Deus sive Natura* (Spinoza (1677) 1996). The present argument doesn’t inherit his substance monism or the necessity of every finite mode. It reaches Nature through the possibility of Change, locates necessity in the three Conditions, and leaves particular configurations open wherever alternatives are independently warranted. The affinity is therefore a location, not a borrowed system: ultimacy falls on the Nature-side of the divide.

The remaining uses of *greatness* must now be earned separately. Knowledge may admit of more and less; goodness may be assessed across agents and arrangements; power may name the bounded capacity of an individual rather than the exhaustive causal scope of Reality. A living subject or a political community may realize maxima unavailable to any isolated individual. None of those claims follows merely because Nature is the metaphysical terminus. Each requires the evaluative, experiential, or institutional premises appropriate to its own register.

That separation is what lets the later relocation proceed without equivocation. The constructive chapters can ask what Nature realizes, what life becomes when Nature models itself, and what a shared order can maintain for the subjects within it. The theological chapters can ask whether the personal and moral predicates attached to a divine subject retain determinate content once their structural conditions have been located. Neither inquiry has to carry the other in advance.

The location is already fixed. Whatever else greatness may come to mean, its metaphysical standing belongs first to Nature.

**Nature alone.**

*How the chapter proceeds.* The result has been stated. The sections that follow ask how Nature’s necessary conditions are realized in the physical and biological world. Physics and biology do not supply a second modal proof. They discover actual structures, capacities, and constraints whose agreement with the three roles counts as convergence and whose further modal status must be argued case by case.

The claim is correspondingly limited. No additional **structural** supplement is needed to explain the roles the sciences realize. A determinate supplement that performs concrete work must enter ordered, differentiated, persisting relations; a ground that declines those roles remains a metaphysical posit, not an empirical gap. Later chapters test such proposals on their own terms rather than treating empirical convergence as their refutation.

At the level of the whole, *Reality*, *Nature*, and *the universe* name one referent under different descriptions: what anything real belongs to, its necessary constitution as T∧S∧Φ, and the totality of what there is. Numerical unicity requires a further step. Under Structural Individuation, whatever makes two alleged concrete cosmoses two is differentiating structure and belongs to Reality’s complete account; if nothing differentiates them, there are not two. A primitivist may reject that premise, at the cost engaged by Modal Realism (§7.2.3). Relational Distinctness supplies only the narrower result that positional separation requires an interval. Structural exhaustiveness is already earned. Numerical unicity is not derived from the word *totality* alone.

Religious experience remains first-person and social evidence rather than an exception to structure. Naturalistic mechanisms may explain some interpretations without proving that every reported encounter has one cause. Where an institution makes questioning or doubt costly, its reports are selected before they are counted; *registration-tension* names that evidential failure, not a general claim about which institutions exhibit it or how often. The experiences themselves belong to spirituality (§5.16).

What remains is recognition: the sciences have been describing realizations of the same roles all along. The convergence does not derive physical theory from metaphysics. It asks whether independent inquiry keeps finding temporal order, differentiation, and bearers of determinate capacities wherever concrete change occurs.

## 4.1 Convergence of Method

Four modes of inquiry—logic, metaphysics, mathematics, and physics—approach the structure of reality with different methods and standards. To the extent that they converge on what any concrete world must contain, their agreement provides abductive rather than demonstrative evidence that they address a common subject matter.

The evidence has grades. Logic supplies the necessity claim. Physics supplies the method-independent empirical comparison, although Modal Convergence (§5.4) later identifies scientific observation as the socially pooled form of the first-person registration on which the proof itself begins. Metaphysics and mathematics are less independent: they test whether the result survives translation into vocabularies built for other purposes. Stating those differences makes the convergence stronger, because it asks each discipline to carry only what its method can earn.

Convergence carries evidential weight only after its dependencies are counted. Two arguments that share a premise, a dataset, a model, or a historical source aren’t two independent confirmations merely because they use different vocabularies. A formal derivation is assessed by validity and premise-strength; an empirical identification by discriminating evidence against alternatives; a historical recurrence by transmission, ancestry, translation, selection, and coding controls. Agreement can corroborate, expose robustness, or guide comparison without adding another proof. The later empirical inventory applies these rules claim by claim ([Appendix D](https://inversionofgreatness.org/empirical-predictions)).

The four methods aren’t equally constrained. Logic studies what can’t fail to obtain. Metaphysics studies what is. Mathematics studies what abstract structures permit. Physics studies what the world contains. Their domains overlap at the edges and diverge in the middle.

The claim here isn’t that they say the same thing about every question. They don’t. The claim is narrower: on the question of what conditions any concrete reality structurally requires, they converge on the same answer.

*Logic.* The modal result rests on the invariant standing capacity of R, the Cartesian witness of change, and the Structural Requirement (Chapters 1–2). The Conditions of genuine change are argued as necessary at the resolution the individual Condition arguments establish. The proof doesn’t derive particular temporal metrics, spatial geometries, material substrates, physical constants, or empirical laws. It delivers a structural necessity claim about concrete change-realizing Reality; the specific realizations remain open to inquiry.

That necessity isn’t a restriction imposed from outside. It follows from what the roles are. A reality in which before and after coincide wouldn’t contain Time under different rules; it would lack temporal structure. A structure in which distinct locations aren’t distinct would lack spatial structure. A supposed substance in which distinct somethings fail to be distinct wouldn’t supply Substantiality. The impossibility isn’t a powerful prohibition. It is identity.

*Metaphysics.* Chapters 2 and 3 trace the same necessity claim through the metaphysical literature. Each role—Time, Space, and Substance—has been disputed for millennia. Read against the modal result, however, those disputes largely divide over how a role is composed rather than whether it is instantiated (§4.2–4.4). Tensed and tenseless theories disagree about what Time is, but agree that Time is. Substantivalism and relationalism disagree about what Space is, but agree that Space is. Hylomorphic, monadological, process, and relational metaphysics disagree about what Substance is, but agree that something fills the bearer-role.

Metaphysics therefore functions here as a robustness check, not a fully independent witness. The necessity claim survives translation into conceptual schemes developed for other purposes. That is real support, but it isn’t a second derivation of the result.

*Mathematics.* Linear orders, metric spaces, fields, manifolds, group actions, and dynamical systems provide useful formal realizations and models for the roles the chapter discusses. Invariant Realization (§3.5.6) fixes the exact contribution: where a mathematical profile entails a consequence, any real configuration realizing that profile carries the consequence; mathematics doesn’t supply the realization premise. The mapping must therefore remain qualified: a linear order isn’t by itself temporal succession, a metric space isn’t by itself physical spatial extension, and an abstract field isn’t by itself a causal persistence medium. Mathematics shows that relevant formal patterns are independently studied and available for physical realization; it doesn’t derive the full Conditions from abstract structure alone.

These structures were developed independently of the philosophical argument, in pursuit of internal mathematical questions; that they are also the structures the roles call for is real but limited evidence: the structures were matched to the roles, so mathematics shows the roles are realizable in independently studied structures rather than supplying a wholly independent confirmation. These descriptions also hold at the scales physics probes; whether extension is continuous or, at the Planck scale, discrete (§4.6.2) is left open, and the structural claim is neutral between them.

*Physics.* Its empirical methods—measurement, prediction, and model-fitting—deliver results independent of the philosophical argument, but their relevance must be stated cautiously. Thermodynamics describes robust physical asymmetries; general relativity represents spacetime with metric structure; and conservation laws relate specified symmetries to specified currents within applicable theories. The specific quantities that are conserved in this universe (energy-momentum in appropriate settings, electric charge, and others) depend on its symmetries and on the regime under description; baryon and lepton number are expected to be violated in some beyond-Standard-Model processes (Sakharov 1967; Weinberg 1979). Physics thereby shows that the actual world has rich temporal, spatial, and physical structure. It doesn’t demonstrate that time has a metaphysically fundamental direction, that every possible world must instantiate a metric, or that some universal conservation law holds across every formulation.

The two contributions must remain distinct. The modal derivation argues for necessary structural roles. Physics describes their actual realizations, maps physical invariants, and supplies contingent details; it doesn’t establish the roles’ modal status.

To violate a role isn’t merely to imagine different laws. A world in which nothing persisted across change wouldn’t be a world running unfamiliar laws; it would be a sequence with nothing for the sequence to be *of*. Some persistence is therefore required, while physics determines which symmetries and conserved quantities realize it here. Logic approaches by elimination, ruling out what can’t obtain. Physics approaches by confirmation, mapping what does obtain. The directions differ; the structural roles coincide, while their physical realization remains open.

On the structural-realist reading of quantum ontology adopted here, the fact that the relata aren’t classical objects supports rather than weakens the identity claim. A quantum system, on that reading, *is* its structure (a state space, an algebra of observables, a symmetry group, and a dynamics), and to assert a violation of that structure is to assert something that both *is* and *isn’t* a system of that kind. The dynamics is part of what needs specifying, not a fixed further conjunct: unitary Schrödinger evolution is the textbook case, but collapse theories (GRW, CSL) posit a fundamentally nonunitary dynamics, and on the present reading that is a rival formulation of what the structure is, not a violation of an identity fixed independently of it. Quantum mechanics is therefore an instructive case for the identity reading: much of the theory is formulated structurally, with comparatively little independent content to support a non-structural modality. The identification of a system with its structure remains a contested structural-realist position within philosophy of physics, not a neutral description shared by every interpretation. The identity at issue is structural essence (what a system *is*, on that reading), not the numerical individuality that permutation invariance unsettles; only the former does the modal work. What this secures, for a reader who accepts the structural-realist reading, is the *form*: that any physical reality has a structure whose negation is incoherent. Which structure actually governs (this Hamiltonian, these couplings, this dynamics) is the work confirmation does from within actuality, the other direction of the single approach.

*An older convergence.* The four-method convergence already established is the present case for Nature. A separate convergence, of a different type, runs through the history of structural metaphysics. Philosophers building structural-metaphysical systems on their own terms (without shared authority, vocabulary, or premises) have repeatedly converged on a kindred structural picture: one medium with no outside, configurations within it, finite modes sustaining themselves by participating in what the medium does. Heraclitus articulated the *Logos* (Greek for word, account, ratio, or rational principle; for Heraclitus, the immanent rational ordering that runs through ceaseless change) as the patterning principle that holds change in place (DK 22 B1, B30, B50) (Kahn 1979); the later Stoics extended it into ethics and cosmology (Long and Sedley 1987). Lucretius derived a complete naturalism from atoms in void in *De Rerum Natura* (c. 50 BCE) 1992, with no maker outside the medium. Spinoza reached it most explicitly: *Deus sive Natura* (Latin for God, or Nature: the identification of the single substance with the natural order), one substance, finite modes as its configurations, *conatus* (a finite mode’s striving to persevere in its own being) as what each mode does inside it (1677) 1996. Hegel rebuilt it as the self-articulation of *Geist* (German for spirit or mind; for Hegel, the rational structure that comes to know itself through history) through dialectical unfolding (1807) 1977. Whitehead rebuilt it again as actual occasions composing the consequent nature of God (1929).

The systems differ substantively in what they take the medium to be doing internally; what they share, working on their own terms across twenty-five centuries with no shared authority, is a kindred structural picture. They aren’t predecessors of this argument’s premises, and the resemblance is suggestive rather than probative: their systems differ too much to count as independent confirmations, but their recurrence shows the structural picture is one reflective inquiry keeps finding its way back to.

One part of this convergence isn’t abductive. Every method is itself a reach toward a subject matter, and no such reach can deny the preconditions of its own mapping without performing what it denies. The Performative Witness (§3.1.3) establishes ◇C wherever the question is entertained. A method that rejects the preconditions of its own operation therefore rejects what its dissent performs. Chapter 5 later sets this beside Modal Convergence (§5.4, §5.6); the present point doesn’t depend on that development.

The guarantee is narrow. It establishes that *some* structure conditions every method; it doesn’t identify that structure as T∧S∧Φ. That identification comes from Chapters 1–2. Nor does every discipline explicitly conclude the Conditions. The genuinely evidential question remains whether disciplines that could diverge over the *content* of the structure nevertheless converge on these roles. The performative point explains why some structural convergence is unavoidable without manufacturing the more specific convergence claimed here.

The convergence is suggestive rather than demonstrative. The methods aren’t equally independent, and the physical and mathematical mappings involve interpretive choices. Still, their partial alignment supplies abductive support for treating the structural roles as a useful framework for coordinating modal analysis, metaphysical disputes, formal structures, and empirical descriptions. It doesn’t turn that framework into a result established by physics or mathematics alone.

*The position earned.* The convergence just described is what earns the name given at the outset for the view defended here: **structural naturalism**. Many familiar forms of naturalism hold that the natural world is all there is while taking its existence and structure as brute—contingent, simply given, a matter of how things happen to be. What those forms haven’t supplied is a reason why there is a structured world at all rather than none. That concession isn’t incidental. It is the opening through which every argument for a further ground has entered, since a brute world invites the question of what settles it, and a questioner who is offered no answer will accept one from elsewhere.

The opening is closed from the inside. Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality aren’t read off the world; they are derived as the conditions any world must instantiate for change to be so much as possible (§2.4, §2.5). The natural world is therefore not merely all there is: it couldn’t have failed to instantiate these structural roles. Nothing the sciences observe is revised by this, and nothing is asked of them. What they gain is the ground beneath the regularities they describe—the account of why there must be succession, distinction, and a bearer at all, which every measurement presupposes and no measurement reaches. Metaphysics and physics are two directions on one inquiry, which is precisely what has been argued.

Three neighbors have to be kept off the label, since each would import a commitment the argument rejects. *Physicalism* makes matter basic; the argument makes the three Conditions co-equal structural roles and treats the matter-first reading as over-crediting Φ (§2.9.3). *Pantheism* credits Nature with personhood or divinity; nothing here does (§10.3.1). And Spinozan *necessitarianism* necessitates every fact; this necessitates the structure without thereby necessitating every occupant or configuration. Contingency belongs only where an alternative is independently warranted (§2.9.4). Structural naturalism is naturalism holding the ground it was always missing, and it needs nothing beyond Nature because there is nothing beyond Nature left to need.

## 4.2 Time

Temporal direction is constitutive on this account: having a ‘before’ and an ‘after’ is part of what Time *is*, not a label applied to an otherwise direction-neutral background. No external source is required to initiate or direct it; direction belongs to Temporality itself.

Heat flows from hot to cold. Gas fills a vacuum. Ordinary macroscopic processes don’t spontaneously reverse. The empirical asymmetry isn’t in dispute; the question is how deep it runs. The structural argument answers: deep enough that *before* and *after* aren’t labels a symmetric manifold happens to wear. At the constitutive level, they are what Temporality is.

The empirical arrows don’t follow deductively from that claim. Thermodynamic asymmetry, cosmological expansion, and—on interpretations with real collapse—irreversibility in quantum measurement are convergent physical realizations of temporal direction. The bridge from constitutive asymmetry to particular cosmological endpoints belongs to §4.6. The present claim is only that the underlying tilt belongs to Nature’s T∧S∧Φ unity (§2.6.1–2.6.12; §2.9.6), not that it’s added from outside.

### 4.2.1 The Dispute
McTaggart’s (1908) distinction between the A-series and the B-series has organized the metaphysics of time for over a century. The A-series is time as tensed: past, present, future, flowing. The B-series is time as tenseless: earlier-than, later-than, fixed relations across a manifold. His further argument is that the A-series is incoherent and the B-series can’t by itself deliver real change, so time is unreal. It produced a standing disagreement between A-theorists (presentists, growing-block theorists: Prior 1968; Tooley 1997; Zimmerman 2005) and B-theorists (eternalists, block-universe proponents: Smart 1963; Mellor 1998; Oaklander 2004). Sider (2001) gives the dominant contemporary statement of B-theoretic metaphysics; Dainton (2010) surveys the whole landscape.

McTaggart’s own positive proposal is easy to lose behind the unreality argument. Beneath his critique of the A-series—a critique that remains actively disputed by A-theorists—he posits a C-series: a permanent, non-temporal ordering of positions that carries no direction of its own, the bare array on which an A-series would have to confer pastness and futurity. The structural ordering this chapter defends isn’t that C-series in temporal clothing. It is directed at the root: the arrow of succession is mind-independent and irreducible (§4.2, §4.2.5), so what orders Nature’s states is a genuine earlier-to-later succession, not a direction-neutral array waiting on tense to animate it.

The thesis that temporal structure is tied to change-capacity meets its canonical challenge in Shoemaker (1969). His three-region scenario moves from local freezes to indirect evidence for a total freeze during which nothing changes. The book’s direct modal claim survives at the permission level: temporal structure need not contain an occurring change in every subinterval. A frozen interval may retain earlier–later ordering, cross-freeze identity, and dispositions for resumed change. Shoemaker therefore defeats an uninterrupted-occurrence thesis, not the weaker change-permission thesis used here.

A stronger reply depends on its relationalism about instants. The No Changeless Duration lemma (§4.6.5) holds that a positive global duration with no discernible moment-differences isn’t a further interval. That is precisely what a Shoemakerian substantivalist contests. It is therefore the book’s substantive relationalist answer and cost comparison, not a neutral demonstration that total freeze is incoherent. The live dispute is whether primitive temporal individuation can preserve positive duration without change; the competing burdens are developed at §8.1.1.

### 4.2.2 The Requirement

The standing A/B disagreement (§4.2.1) turns on two demands that shouldn’t be collapsed. The B-series names the ordered dimension along which states stand in earlier-than/later-than relation. The A-series names passage: the stronger claim that states don’t merely occupy ordered positions but give way to one another in a mind-independent directed flow. Ordered Succession (§2.4.6) strictly requires the first demand in an objective asymmetric form: a sequence freely reversible without loss is an ordering of labels, not genuine succession. The second is the realization-tier strengthening defended here. Passage without an ordered dimension would be undifferentiated change without before and after; an ordered dimension without passage is the B-theorist’s live alternative, not something the modal core has already excluded. The composition proposed here takes Temporality to include both.

On that composition, McTaggart’s incoherence charge doesn’t arise in the form he gives it. He argues that the A-series requires every event to be past, present, and future: a contradiction. The composition assigns the ascriptions to different features. Order belongs to the dimension; tense belongs to the passage through it. An event has a fixed position in the B-series and, as the passage advances, is successively future, present, and past from the passage’s own perspective. The account is therefore internally consistent if passage is real. That conditional matters: the reply shows how an A/B composition avoids McTaggart’s contradiction, not that every B-theorist must accept the passage it employs.

The account has a consequence for *now*. Every physical entity or event—everything bearing Substantiality—occupies a position in the dimensional manifold. Passage runs through that manifold whether or not anything registers it; the A-series names passage itself, not its registration.

What distinguishes *now* is registration from within. A physical region integrated enough to track its own temporal position registers the passage as present. *Now* is therefore not a third feature beside dimension and passage; it is passage registered from within a configuration complex enough to track itself. There is no *now* without a *here*, and no *here* without a *this-that-persists-to-register-both*. This is developed as self-modeling at §4.8. The narrower temporal point is that flow can be tracked from within the configuration through which it runs.

Registration from within also prevents a misleading picture. Passage runs along the histories of what bears Substantiality; it isn’t a universe-wide sheet of simultaneity advancing through the manifold.

That distinction answers the immediate relativistic objection. Special relativity denies a frame-independent global present. Rietdijk (1966) and Putnam (1967b) use that denial to argue for the block: if reality can’t vary with an observer’s motion and the present is frame-relative, reality can’t consist in the present. A theory of passage as a moving global present would inherit the objection. This account doesn’t.

Configurations in relative motion may assign different distant events to their respective presents, but they don’t disagree about the order of causally connectable events, which is frame-invariant. Relativity supplies that invariant local ordering. The change-first argument, not relativity alone, supplies the further claim of occurring transition along it. Stein (1968) develops the corresponding reply to Putnam from within the physics; the block universe is engaged in full at §8.1.4.

Presentism and eternalism place the burden at opposite points. Presentism (only the present exists) must recover the ordered extent across which earlier and later positions remain genuinely related rather than reducing the dimension to what no longer and not yet exists. Eternalism (all times are equally real) supplies that extent but, in its reductive B-theoretic form, must explain why objective asymmetric order is sufficient for the occurring transition the Cartesian witness presents. The composition accepts the dimension and passage together. It is stronger than the modal core, which strictly fixes objective asymmetric succession while leaving the metaphysics of passage open.

The composition carries two commitments. First, passage is metaphysically real: directed flow obtains whether or not anything registers it, while registration adds the *now* feature. Second, no moment is uniquely real against unreal past and future moments: the dimension is real along its full extent, and tense-privileging belongs to a configuration’s register rather than to the medium itself.

This isn’t a neutral dissolution of the A/B dispute. It sides with the A-theorist that passage is mind-independent and contradicts the reductive B-theorist who reduces passage to indexical content. The composition claims that dimension and passage are both required; its contested premise is that passage remains real when unregistered.

The defense is the change-first argument already paid for. The Cartesian witness establishes an occurring change, not merely a description of unlike states, and §1.3 analyzes change as a transition from one state to another. A tenseless ordering can index the states and their differences, but the ordering alone doesn’t supply the transition the witness registers. If that analysis of the witness is correct, directed passage belongs to the realized temporal order rather than being added by an observer. A reductive B-theorist can resist by redescribing the witness itself tenselessly; that response contests the book’s upstream account of change rather than exposing an internal contradiction in the composition. The result is therefore defended but openly theory-dependent, not presented as a neutral consequence of physics.

And the question whether the universe *began to exist* admits two readings the composition lets us mark separately: a quantitative reading (how far back along the dimension does the passage run) engaged at §10.1.5, and a categorial reading (a moment-prior-to-T from which T began) foreclosed by Parasitic Negation on T (§2.1.5). Kalām’s traversal argument operates on the quantitative reading; the fall-narrative’s t₀ operates on the categorial reading.

Tensed and tenseless accounts therefore track distinguishable demands on one subject matter. Every adequate account must supply objective asymmetric order. The composition further holds that occurring transition isn’t exhausted by a tenseless description of positions, and so adds mind-independent passage. As in §4.3 and §5.10, the appearance of long-standing division in the tradition need not indicate rival subject matters. It may indicate that one subject matter has distinguishable features whose relation remains contested.

**[Proposition]**

**The Composition of Temporality** · *Proposition*

Temporality at realization tier comprises two demands, and they aren’t the same demand. Ordered Succession (§2.4.6) strictly requires the first: an objective asymmetric order, since a sequence freely reversible without loss is an ordering of labels rather than genuine succession. Passage—states giving way to one another in a mind-independent directed flow—is the second, and it is a realization-tier strengthening defended here rather than a consequence of the modal core. Passage without an ordered dimension would be undifferentiated change with no before and after; an ordered dimension without passage remains the B-theorist’s live alternative.

*Scope.* This is an alignment claim, not a modal result. Nothing downstream of the modal core depends on passage: a reader who declines the strengthening keeps Ordered Succession and everything derived from it.

**Depends on:** Ordered Succession (§2.4.6)

### 4.2.3 Predictions
Succession is one of Change’s three constitutive requirements (§1.3). The states between which a change runs must stand in a definite before–after order, not merely apart. Without that directional *then*, there is no exchange—only a static pair. Temporal asymmetry is therefore not a feature this universe’s initial conditions happen to instantiate. It is a structural feature of Nature. A putative temporal structure with no objective asymmetric order wouldn’t be a universe whose arrow happened to be missing; at the relevant resolution, it would lack Temporality. This is distinct from time-reversal symmetry in particular physical laws.

This is the temporal register of the modal result: if Change is possible, directed succession is required; if the possibility of Change is necessary, directed succession is necessarily instantiated (§1.3–1.5). What this section calls the *Gradient* is then developed at §4.7 and §4.8: the cumulative direction realized under the laws and boundary conditions of this universe. At the cosmic scale it appears as a macro-history from simpler toward more complex arrangements; at the biological scale it appears in evolutionary trajectories. Those realized gradients require further physical premises. They aren’t packed into temporal direction alone.

The structural claim is precise. What it establishes is the constitutive asymmetry of Temporality: that succession runs in one direction, that states stand in ordered relation, that *then* isn’t reversible.
