Whether the thermodynamic asymmetry familiar from physics follows directly from that constitutive fact, or requires supplementation by additional premises such as the Past Hypothesis (the stipulation that the universe began in a macrostate of extremely low entropy) (Albert 2000; Loewer 2007), is a contested question left unsettled here. Price (1996) and Callender (2011) map the space of candidate explanations; the structural account is neutral among them. The arrow itself is settled. What occupies the arrow is a question for physics.

### 4.2.4 Confirmation
The empirical record supplies several physical asymmetries compatible with the structural claim, although it doesn’t by itself establish metaphysically fundamental passage.

Thermodynamics supplies the clearest case. The second law, formalized by Clausius (1865) and given a statistical foundation by Boltzmann (1877), says that an isolated system tends toward maximum entropy. Entropy is the logarithmic count of microscopic configurations compatible with a macroscopic description; “disorder” is only an informal approximation. Spontaneous macroscopic entropy reversal isn’t observed, and the resulting gradient is central to measurement, memory, computation, and life.

Cosmology supplies another asymmetry. Hubble’s recession data (1929) and the accelerating-expansion measurements of Riess et al. (1998) and Perlmutter et al. (1999) describe a directional feature of our observed cosmic history. Expansion alone, however, establishes neither fundamental passage nor a universal cosmological arrow.

Quantum mechanics supplies a third case, though its source must be named carefully. Unitary Schrödinger evolution is formally reversible. Measurement-associated irreversibility enters through decoherence: phase relations disperse into uncontrolled environmental degrees of freedom (Zurek 2003; Joos et al. 2003). Because decoherence is itself thermodynamic, the quantum arrow doesn’t enter as an independent principle. It appears at the same contact as the classical arrow, where a system couples to a much larger one.

Together these phenomena show physical asymmetries the structural account must accommodate; they don’t form a single empirical proof of metaphysically directed succession. Whether cosmic history approaches maximum entropy asymptotically or recurs at the largest scale is the further question taken up at §4.6.

### 4.2.5 Conclusions
The structural claim bears unequally on the standing positions about Temporality. The strict constraint concerns objective asymmetric succession; the stronger conclusions concerning passage follow on the composition defended in this section.

Symmetric-time metaphysics treats temporal direction as a matter of observer perspective rather than an objective part of the structure. It is usually expressed as a block universe: a four-dimensional model on which all times—past, present, and future—are equally real, with the manifold of events laid out as a single static structure. On the account here, that view treats a constitutive feature of Nature as a projection from outside it. The A/B reconciliation above isn’t a vindication of this view. What is preserved is the B-series as a genuine description of structural succession, not as a denial of succession’s direction. A block universe with a real arrow is compatible with the account; a block universe without one isn’t; the block is engaged in its own terms at §8.1.4. A melody makes the difference vivid, though it illustrates the claim rather than proving it. Its tones can be laid out all at once, tenselessly ordered, and the ordering is entirely real—yet played backward it isn’t the same melody heard in reverse but a different melody, and the difference is heard. On the composition’s account, that difference is the arrow: a direction built into the succession, not read into it by the ear that follows. The arrowless block holds that forward and backward are mere labels on an ordering symmetric in itself; the melody doesn’t refute that view outright, since an arrowless-block theorist can grant that the ordering is asymmetric and matters to identity while still denying that the asymmetry amounts to a further, mind-independent directional fact. What the example shows is narrower and still worth having: whatever the ordering’s ultimate metaphysical standing, the direction is doing real work in the notes’ succession, which is what the composition’s account of passage requires and the arrowless view has to explain away rather than simply deny.

Eternal recurrence in the strict Nietzschean sense would require the universe as a whole to return to an earlier macrostate. The observed thermodynamic arrow places that proposal under pressure: a recurrence account must explain how the relevant entropy conditions return as well. The structural result alone doesn’t supply that pressure. Approximate recurrence in finite subsystems, as in Poincaré recurrence on timescales vastly exceeding the age of the universe (Poincaré 1890), is a separate phenomenon and isn’t at issue here. The further question is whether macro-scale recurrence at the cosmological scale is itself entailed by the structural argument or only made probable by it given additional cosmological premises. It is taken up in §4.6, where Reality’s global modal capacity is kept distinct from physical recurrence, and recurrence of a phase-class is kept distinct from return to the same macrostate. Each recurrence claim requires physical premises the modal capacity alone does not supply.

Permanent heat death as a terminal condition requires a distinction the structural result doesn’t itself settle. The Necessity of Nature forecloses Nature’s becoming non-temporal, and □◇C forecloses Reality’s global capacity for Change from lapsing. Neither claim by itself says that every state has a locally available successor. A greatest state could retain its relations to the earlier order while admitting no further transition; excluding that state requires the additional actual-continuation premise stated later. The structural claim therefore leaves three possibilities open merely from □T or □◇C: asymptotic approach to a high-entropy state, an indefinitely differentiated high-entropy regime, or a bare terminal configuration.

The traditional supplementations take several forms: a Prime Mover (the Aristotelian-Thomistic posit of an unmoved mover outside the temporal series, required to initiate or sustain the world’s motion) who imparts the arrow, a creator who winds the clock at t = 0, a transcendent eternity within which the temporal series is set. A supplement introduced solely to supply ordered direction arrives after the role has already been filled. Any determinate act of initiating or sustaining must itself stand in the before-and-after and bearer relations required for concrete work; a posit that declines those relations doesn’t impart an additional temporal structure. This doesn’t settle every account of atemporal grounding, which Chapters 7, 8, and 10 engage in its own terms. It establishes the narrower constitutive result: objective succession is internal to Nature rather than imposed on it from a prior non-temporal state.

Four grades of conclusion must be kept separate.

First, the strict modal result rules out Nature’s origin from non-Temporality and any global lapse in Reality’s capacity for Change. Transition Closure adds the past-directed local result: because Change is actual, the actual history did not emerge from a prior state lacking every C-realizing transition. Neither result rules out a greatest state with no locally available successor. No Changeless Duration (§4.6.5) adds that a supposedly everlasting but wholly undifferentiated rest isn’t an interval at all on its account of moments.

Second, a stronger result is available under an explicit explanatory bridge. Suppose contingent configurations require explanation—the principle later examined at §8.2.1. Explanation need not be temporally prior production. If the productive strengthening is added—every contingent physical configuration is explained by a physically prior configuration—then no contingent physical configuration can be first. The Conditions are necessary, but their necessity doesn’t settle the modal status of the token configuration occupying them. The productive strengthening yields a prior state only for a first token independently established as contingent; without that premise, the argument doesn’t yet rule out a necessary first configuration. This earns a prior physical phase conditionally from premises stated here, not from □T or a later chapter alone.

Third, the future-facing analogue needs its own bridge: actual change never permanently ceases to occur. That premise, together with No Changeless Duration (§4.6.5), excludes both an indefinitely changeless tail and a silent greatest instant. The productive-explanation bridge and the actual-continuation bridge together yield a physical history with neither first nor last state.

Fourth, even that two-sided serial closure doesn’t entail a cycle. A boundaryless history may pass through endlessly many non-repeating configurations. Recurrence requires a further premise—a suitably bounded state space with recurrence-supporting dynamics, a law-governed transition that returns the cosmos to a low-entropy boundary condition, or the premise that a phase the actual history has exercised has no last realization (§4.6.5). Recurrence in kind is argued on that last premise rather than derived; a bounce mechanism and cycle-to-cycle macrostate identity remain successively stronger empirical claims (§4.6). A terminal heat-death configuration with no locally available successor is excluded only at the third grade, by actual continuation; an endlessly differentiated high-entropy regime with no usable gradients requires still more to rule out, including a recurrence premise.

## 4.3 Space

Space is less a thing than a relation: the feature of the world that makes one place genuinely distinct from another. Without it, nothing would separate one arrangement of things from the next, and there would be no sense in which anything was anywhere at all.

Here isn’t there. No two places are the same place, and no place is every place. The empirical fact of extension isn’t in dispute; the question is what extension actually is. The modal framework answers: Spatiality *is* the relational manifold (the connected extent of locations standing in determinate distance and direction relations to one another: the structural arena within which here-and-there distinctions register), not a container within which things are placed, not a catalogue of distances between pre-existing things, but the structural feature by which here and there differ at all. Whether that manifold is continuous or, at the Planck scale, discrete (§4.6.2) is a question physics hasn’t settled; the structural claim (that here differs from there across a determinate interval) holds either way.

### 4.3.1 The Dispute
The most enduring dispute in the metaphysics of Spatiality is between substantivalism and relationalism. Substantivalism (most prominently Newton’s 1687) holds that Spatiality is a real container that exists independently of its contents: an absolute framework in which objects are located and with respect to which motion is objectively defined. Relationalism (most prominently Leibniz’s 1715–1716) holds that there is no Spatiality apart from the relations between bodies: to be somewhere is just to stand in spatial relations to other things; talk of absolute position is without meaning. The contemporary literature (Sklar 1974; Earman 1989; Maudlin 2012; Pooley 2013) continues the dispute in the context of relativistic physics.

The dispute has survived three centuries because both sides are tracking something real. Substantivalism is tracking extension: the fact that there is a where at all, that locations are possible whether or not anything happens to occupy them. Relationalism is tracking relation: the fact that being at a location means standing in determinate connection to other locations. Each side takes its own insight to be the whole story and the other side’s to be superfluous, which is why the dispute never settles.

### 4.3.2 The Requirement

The standing substantivalism-relationalism dispute (§4.3.1) tracks two demands any realization of positional distinction must meet. Extension names the dimensional or topological structure within which positions are available. Relation names the determinate connections by which one position stands apart from another. Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7) fixes their common target: occupiable positions separated by a crossable interval at modal-core resolution. A substantivalist may take the manifold as fundamental and recover relation through its structure; a relationalist may take the relations as fundamental and recover extension from their organization. The role-constraint doesn’t select between those directions of analysis. It requires that the completed account deliver both occupiable differentiation and the relations that make the positions spatially determinate.

General relativity (Einstein 1915) sharpens the composition rather than settling the dispute in one side’s favor. The metric field (the structure assigning spatiotemporal intervals) is a dynamical structure defined on a differentiable manifold, which already carries topological and smooth structure but no metric. Manifold and metric together constitute what relativistic physics treats as spacetime. Earman and Norton’s (1987) hole argument runs as follows. In general relativity, applying a diffeomorphism to the metric and matter fields together appears to produce a distinct assignment of fields to manifold points, even though no observer could distinguish the two. That forces a choice about whether the assignments name genuinely different worlds or only different descriptions of the same world.

The hole argument and the subsequent literature engage exactly this duality without settling it in favor of either side (Sklar 1974; Friedman 1983; Maudlin 2012; Pooley 2013; Dasgupta 2015): sophisticated substantivalists and sophisticated relationalists each have resources to accommodate the puzzle on their own terms. The manifold-plus-metric composition offered here is structural naturalism’s proposed reading of that duality—one further position in the dispute, not the literature’s consensus verdict.

**[Proposition]**

**The Composition of Spatiality** · *Proposition*

Spatiality at realization tier comprises two demands, and any account must deliver both. Extension names the dimensional or topological structure within which positions are available; relation names the determinate connections by which one position stands apart from another. Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7) fixes their common target: occupiable positions separated by a crossable interval. The substantivalism–relationalism dispute is over which half is taken as fundamental and which is recovered from it, and the role-constraint doesn’t select between those directions of analysis. It requires only that the completed account supply both occupiable differentiation and the relations that make positions spatially determinate.

*Scope.* An alignment claim, not a modal result, and not a verdict in the substantivalism–relationalism dispute. General relativity sharpens the composition rather than settling that dispute in either side’s favour.

**Depends on:** Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7)

### 4.3.3 Predictions
Distinction is the requirement that the two configurations a change runs between stand apart from one another. It’s one of the three constitutive requirements of Change (§1.3). If nothing stood apart from anything else, there would be no two states to exchange, no configurations to relate, no where for an event to happen. A universe without extension isn’t a universe whose space happens to be zero-dimensional. It isn’t a universe.

A second presentation arrives from identity rather than change. For A to be what it is, A must stand distinct from non-A; an undifferentiated field contains no configurations capable of self-identity. The relevant distinction isn’t bare numerical non-identity. Co-located, multiply located, and abstract items show that numerical difference need not be spatial. The claim concerns the positional distinctness of physically configured relata, which Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7) identifies with traversable relational extension.

That identification does the load-bearing work, and it isn’t free. Nonspatial individuation by conserved-quantity profile, causal role, or haecceity remains a live alternative against which the premise takes a stand. Given the premise, and restricted to physically configured relata, distinction requires an interval across which A stands apart from non-A. That interval is what Spatiality structurally is.

The change-first and identity-first presentations therefore illuminate one premise from different sides. They aren’t independent derivations: both rely on Relational Distinctness to move from configured difference to spatial interval. Their convergence reinforces the explanation without adding a second proof.

Spatiality is therefore not a stage that might or might not be set. Nature instantiates extension structurally, because exchange requires relata and identity requires interval, and the two requirements converge on the same structural feature.

### 4.3.4 Confirmation
The empirical record converges on the structural claim from the side of space. Geometry isn’t merely a conceptual grid laid over a pre-geometric substrate. Physics measures distances and curvatures, represents them through a metric field, and relates that field dynamically to matter. Relativistic effects such as length contraction, gravitational time dilation, and frame-dependent simultaneity accordingly treat geometric structure as physically significant rather than as bookkeeping.

The Aharonov–Bohm effect (1959) sharpens the point. A charged particle traveling around confined magnetic flux acquires a measurable phase shift even though the magnetic field vanishes everywhere along its path. What registers is the gauge-invariant holonomy—the total geometric quantity accumulated around the closed loop—not a local field strength at a point. The phase depends on the global structure of the gauge connection and the region through which the particle travels. This supports the narrower claim that nonlocal connection-structure is physically detectable; it need not be inflated into the claim that manifold topology as such has been isolated as the cause.

None of this proves the modal conclusion from physics. It shows that geometry, metric structure, and global connection-structure do physical work in our best theories. That is the empirical convergence required by the claim that relational extension isn’t mere bookkeeping.

### 4.3.5 Conclusions
Pure substantivalism in its strong form holds that Spatiality is a container whose existence is wholly independent of every fact of differentiation within it. It can’t discharge the role merely by naming a container. The epistemic observation that an empty container would be indistinguishable from no container doesn’t establish its nonexistence. The constitutive pressure is different: unless the proposed structure provides occupiable positions standing in determinate relations, it hasn’t yet supplied the positional extension Spatiality names. A substantivalism whose manifold intrinsically carries that structure meets the pressure by instantiating the relational role rather than by avoiding it.

Pure relationalism in its strong form holds that Spatiality is nothing over and above actual relations between actual bodies. It carries the complementary burden. A list of pairwise relations isn’t yet a geometry unless its organization recovers occupiable extension, metric or topological structure, and the counterfactual positions required by the physical theory. Sophisticated relationalist programs, including Dasgupta’s algebraic relationalism, attempt exactly that recovery. If they succeed, they realize the extensional role relationally; if they fail, the failure is to supply the role, not a refutation by label. The literature remains contested on whether the recovery succeeds.

Spatial instantiation from nothing—the idea that Spatiality might have come into being from a condition of no-Spatiality—is foreclosed for the same reason as literal emergence of Substantiality from absolute non-being (§4.4): neither no-Spatiality nor no-Substantiality is a condition Nature could have been in and from which it could have departed. Classical creation *ex nihilo*, understood as creation without pre-existing material rather than transition from a prior nothing-state, is a separate grounding claim. Cosmological origin scenarios in which Spatiality emerges describe its emergence within Nature itself (§2.7), not from absolute spatial absence. The cosmological picture this entails is taken up at §4.6.

What is foreclosed strictly here is the elimination of relational distinction itself: a state without here and there isn’t a state Spatiality permits. Permanent heat death as the global thermodynamic endpoint of Temporality is a different question, taken up in §4.6.

Geometric monism is the view that the specific geometry of actual space is itself necessary. It receives no support from the structural claim, because of the level at which that claim operates. Euclidean, hyperbolic, and elliptic geometries exemplify the three signs of constant sectional curvature—zero, negative, and positive respectively—and are consistent specifications of relational extension; global topology and quotient structure introduce further possibilities. What the argument fixes is the structural condition any geometry presupposes (distinguishable regions standing in determinate relation), not the metric by which those relations are measured. The exact result is *nonselection*: extension is necessary, and the theorem doesn’t select a metric. That is weaker than the claim that the metric is contingent, and the difference is that same discipline applied to itself. Mathematical consistency isn’t yet metaphysical possibility; the actual metric establishes its own necessary possibility, and calling it contingent requires an independently warranted alternative rather than a merely coherent one (§2.9.4). By the same standard, the structural argument doesn’t establish geometric monism’s denial either. It is neutral on the metric, and neutrality is what it is entitled to.

The traditional supplement doesn’t supply a missing structural role: a container God first stretches out and then populates with creatures. Extension is already constitutive of every concrete placing, including any determinate act by which a source is said to stretch, contain, or populate a domain. A proposed source performing that work therefore enters the relational structure it was introduced to explain; one described as standing in no such relations doesn’t perform the determinate placing. This doesn’t settle every account of non-causal or constitutive grounding. It establishes that Spatiality isn’t produced from a prior absence of Spatiality and that no additional container is required for positional distinction to obtain.

The specific geometry of actual Spatiality (Euclidean, hyperbolic, elliptic, or some other curvature regime) is an empirical matter, fixed by the metric this universe instantiates rather than by the structural claim, and left open by it in the sense just given. The structural argument fixes occupiable relational extension; whether its physical realization is best represented by a fundamental manifold, an algebraic relational structure, an emergent geometry, or another ontology is for physics and its metaphysics to determine.

How many extended dimensions Spatiality runs is similarly open. The three macroscopic spatial dimensions plus any additional dimensions that contemporary unification programs model as curled into compact shapes (string-theoretic Calabi–Yau compactifications; large-extra-dimension scenarios) are empirical questions, not modal ones. The structural claim entails extension, not dimensionality.

The connection between local relational extension and global structure is also empirically open: whether Spatiality has open, closed, or flat large-scale geometry, and whether it carries non-trivial topology (multiply-connected, wormhole-bearing, or otherwise), is fixed by observation and theory rather than by the structural argument.

And the question of whether the cosmological-scale singularity is a stable zero-extension terminus versus whether *cyclic* recurrence specifically obtains is taken up in §4.6 under separate weights. The role-level claim defended here is strict: a state offering no relational distinction whatsoever isn’t a state Spatiality permits. Whether classical-GR singularities, themselves artifacts of a theory known to break down at those scales, count as instances of that foreclosed state is a further, physics-dependent question this argument doesn’t settle on its own; the cyclic conclusion (§4.6) is explicitly abductive rather than modally forced.

## 4.4 Substance

Through every change, no causal relatum passes into absolute nothingness, and none emerges from it. Two superficially similar claims must be distinguished: an empirical claim of current physics, open to revision, and the book’s structural claim.

A candle burns down; its wax disperses as carbon dioxide, water vapor, and heat. A particle collides; its products carry the energy and momentum tracked by the applicable theory. These cases illustrate conservation, but the empirical and structural claims must remain distinct.

The empirical claim is that particular quantities—energy-momentum, electric charge, and others—are conserved within the domains and precision in which they have been tested. Which laws hold depends on the actual universe’s symmetries and remains corrigible by further inquiry. The structural theorem doesn’t decide whether those symmetries are necessary.

The structural claim is weaker and more exact. It says not that some particular quantity must be globally conserved, but that no causal relatum passes into or out of absolute nothingness. There is no state into which it could vanish and no state from which it could arrive. That claim can remain true even where a physical quantity dilutes or lacks global conservation.

No-passage-to-nothing, not conservation as such, is structurally necessary. Specific conserved quantities depend on this universe’s symmetries. Noether’s theorem (1918) captures the relation: continuous symmetries of an action correspond to conserved currents—time-translation to energy, spatial translation to momentum, rotation to angular momentum. In a generic expanding spacetime, no fixed global energy quantity need exist (§4.4.4).

The modal point survives that result. A process in which causal relata—particles, fields, energies, or configurations—appeared from or disappeared into absolute nothingness wouldn’t merely violate a conservation law. It would require passage through what isn’t a state. The claim therefore survives revisions to the list of conserved quantities.

### 4.4.1 The Dispute
The historical dichotomy between matter (discrete stuff that persists) and energy (dynamic capacity that flows) organized natural philosophy from the seventeenth century through the nineteenth. Matter was the being that bore properties; energy was what matter did. The two were treated as metaphysically distinct categories with different conservation principles, different measures, and different explanatory roles.

The early modern dispute carries forward into contemporary disagreement over how to read the post-Einsteinian unification. Some readings treat mass-energy equivalence (Einstein 1905) as showing that matter just *is* energy, dissolving one category into the other; others treat it as a translation rate between two genuinely distinct categories; still others treat field-theoretic and particle ontologies as mutually irreducible descriptions of layered substrates (Redhead 1982; Cao 1997). The literature on the ontology of quantum field theory (French and Krause 2006; Wallace 2012) continues the dispute in present terms.

### 4.4.2 The Requirement
The standing matter/energy dichotomy was transformed over the course of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Mayer (1842), Joule (1843–1845), and Helmholtz (1847) established the conservation of energy as a unified principle bridging mechanical, thermal, and chemical domains. Faraday’s experimental program (1839–1855) and Maxwell (1873) made the field a first-class physical entity alongside matter. Einstein’s (1905) mass-energy equivalence supplied a precise relation between rest mass and rest energy. $E = mc^2$ states that a system with invariant rest mass has corresponding rest energy; it doesn’t by itself settle whether matter and energy are identical, two ontological categories, or two aspects of a deeper ontology. Nor does it establish a single globally conserved scalar called “mass-energy” in every spacetime. Those remain interpretive and theory-dependent questions.

The structural reading is therefore not a result extracted directly from mass-energy equivalence. It is an interpretive proposal: persistent physical bearers and their changing capacities are both needed for the Substantiality role the book calls Φ. Rest mass, fields, particles, and dynamical energy may realize those functions in different physical theories, but the structural argument doesn’t identify any one of them with Φ or claim that physics has reduced them to two metaphysical aspects. It asks only that an adequate physical ontology provide something that persists through transitions and bears causal capacity across them.

Quantum field theory extends the convergence (Weinberg 1995; Redhead 1982 on QFT ontology; Wallace 2012 on QFT and the Everettian-dynamical reading). It is the framework that recasts particles as quantized excitations of underlying fields defined on spacetime. On a field-ontological reading, particles are quantized excitations of underlying fields, and the apparent dichotomy between localized matter and extended field tracks different states or scales of one field structure. That is one physical realization of a bearer persisting through transformation. Quantum field theory doesn’t by itself establish that every physical ontology contains one numerically identical Substance under two aspects.

The QFT reading already given (fields defined on spacetime, particles as their quantized excitations) is one live reading of what the fundamental physical object is. The alternative, wavefunction realism (Albert 2015; Ney 2021; Ney and Albert 2013), takes the fundamental physical object to be a quantum state defined on a very-high-dimensional configuration space, with 3+1 spacetime as emergent rather than fundamental. Whether the fundamental ontology is fields-on-spacetime or wavefunction-on-configuration-space is a live question in the foundations of quantum mechanics; the structural argument doesn’t need to resolve it. What the argument requires is that the Substance / Φ role be filled across each genuine transition: something bears determinate content from one state into the next. On the fields-on-spacetime reading, fields and their evolving states may fill that role. On the wavefunction-realist reading, the quantum state and the structure from which effective spacetime emerges may fill it. The argument constrains *that* cross-interval bearing obtains; it doesn’t select the bearer, require one cosmic individual, or certify either interpretation’s independent credentials.

A second, structurally adjacent dispute runs one layer up from the physics-foundational one: what kind of thing *bears* causal properties at all, regardless of which physical theory describes it. Four positions are active. Substance ontology (Aristotle, *Categories* 1–5; Lowe (1998); Heil (2003)) takes primary substances as the ontological primitives that bear properties (a horse, a galaxy, a field) with essential and accidental properties standing in dependence on the substance that has them. Trope theory (Williams 1953; Campbell 1990; Maurin 2002) inverts the order: particularized properties (tropes) are the basic items, and what we call substances are compresent bundles of tropes, with no underlying bare bearer behind them. Bundle theory takes substances as bundles of co-instantiated universals (Hume, *Treatise* 1.1.6 ‘Of modes and substances’; Russell (1940); Van Cleve (1985) on bundle-theory variants): same denial of the bare substratum, different account of the property-relata. Process metaphysics (Whitehead 1929; Rescher 1996; Seibt 2017) takes processes (temporally extended activities) as basic, with what we call substances being relatively stable patterns within the underlying flow.

The structural argument is neutral across the four. Distinctness, Holding, and Persistence (§1.4.3) are role specifications (what any Φ-bearer must do), not commitments about what kind of thing plays the role. A primary substance carries causal properties and persists through transitions on the substance reading. A compresent bundle of tropes carries them and persists, by trope-grouping or trope-causation theories, on the trope reading. A bundle of co-instantiated universals carries them and persists, by the co-instantiation relation, on the bundle reading. A relatively stable process carries them and persists, by its own temporal extension and internal coherence, on the process reading. Each is proposed here as saturating the Φ-role. The persistence and causal-capacity credentials specific to each view—how a trope-bundle retains identity through change, how a process’s “stable pattern” counts as a genuine bearer rather than a placeholder for one, and so on—remain internal debates within each ontology. This argument doesn’t adjudicate them and isn’t entitled to assume them settled. The structural argument requires that *something* bear Substantiality; it doesn’t require that the bearer be of one ontological category rather than another, and it takes each candidate’s proponents at their word that their own view can meet its own persistence and causal-capacity commitments. Which of the four is correct—and whether each can, in fact, deliver on those commitments—is a question for argument outside the modal-structural framework: total-theory comparison, parsimony, explanatory virtues, and the empirical fit of each reading with contemporary physics. The argument needs a bearer; it doesn’t itself certify that every candidate bearer succeeds.

**[Proposition]**

**Bearer-Neutrality of Substantiality** · *Proposition*

Substantiality is a role, not a kind of stuff. The dissolution of the matter/energy dichotomy—conservation of energy, the field as a first-class entity alongside matter, mass–energy equivalence—bears on what *realizes* the role, not on whether the role is required. Whatever the carrier turns out to be made of, something must carry: what obtains in one state has to be borne into the next. Rest mass, fields, particles, and dynamical energy may realize that function in different physical theories, and the argument identifies Φ with none of them.

*Scope.* An interpretive proposal at realization tier, not a result extracted from mass–energy equivalence. That equivalence doesn’t settle whether matter and energy are identical, two ontological categories, or two aspects of a deeper ontology, and nothing here needs it to.

**Depends on:** Cross-Interval Persistence (§2.4.8)

### 4.4.3 Predictions
Substantiality is necessarily instantiated by the Necessity of Nature theorem (§2.9.6). It is Φ, the third structural condition of Nature, derived in its exchange role at §2.4.8 and integrated into the Conditions-as-Nature sequence in §2.6. The role can’t be empty wherever genuine change occurs: for one state to give way to another as a change rather than an unrelated replacement, determinate content must be borne across the interval. This isn’t a claim that Substance is a quantity with a forbidden numerical value or that one global individual survives every event. What is structural is narrower than conservation as physics states it: cross-interval bearing obtains, while the bearer and the quantities used to track it may vary with the ontology and symmetry structure of the theory.

A second line arrives from Change. Exchange is one of the three constitutive requirements of Change (§1.3), and exchange requires something to be exchanged. If nothing were borne across a transition, there would be two disconnected states rather than one change: correlation without an occupant of the bearing relation. Succession needs exchange; exchange needs cross-interval bearing; whatever occupies that role satisfies Φ at modal-core resolution. The line remains neutral among an enduring object, temporal parts, linked stages, a field, a process, or another realization. The two derivations—instantiation from §2.4.8–2.6 and exchange from §1.3—converge on the same structural feature without turning it into one conserved cosmic stock.

### 4.4.4 Confirmation
The empirical record converges abductively with the structural claim without establishing it. Noether’s theorem (1918) links each continuous symmetry of a theory’s action to a conserved current within that theory. It shows how conservation follows when physical invariances are represented through a least-action principle; it doesn’t prove a modal conservation law across every possible medium.

Quantum theory and relativity reinforce the distinction. Unitary evolution preserves inner products and total probability, while the preservation of information through black-hole evaporation remains actively disputed (Hawking 1976; Page 1993; Penington 2020; Almheiri et al. 2020). Relativity likewise gives locally covariant stress-energy conservation but, in a generic expanding spacetime without global time-translation symmetry, no globally conserved energy need exist (Wald 1984; Carroll 2004). No single cosmic stock should be inferred from the Φ-role.

What survives is cross-transition bearing: a physical transition carries determinate relata and structure across its interval. Which quantities track that bearing, and whether they are globally defined, depends on the theory’s symmetries and geometry. Their actuality establishes necessary possibility, not the impossibility of alternatives. Standard field theory adds one final convergence: the quantum vacuum is a structured state with correlations and observables, not absolute nothingness, even though its deeper ontology remains contested. These results point in one direction without sharing one mechanism or bearer.

### 4.4.5 Conclusions
Emergence from absolute nothingness is foreclosed because there is no state from which the universe could have emerged. Nature has no coherent prior absence; absolute nothingness isn’t a condition something could have been in and from which it could have departed (§2.8). Whatever cosmological origin scenarios physics ultimately confirms, they can’t be scenarios in which the medium came from no medium. Classical creation *ex nihilo*, however, ordinarily means creation without pre-existing material, not a transition from a prior state called nothing. The Null-State argument doesn’t by itself refute that stronger theological doctrine; it closes only the literal emergence-from-nothing picture.

What is foreclosed by a structural observation is narrower than miracles as such: it is the idea that Substantiality’s persistence—the bearer carrying forward at all—is a contingent regularity a will could suspend. That the medium carries forward at all is what being a medium consists in, and that much is structure-bound rather than a policy the structure enforces. By contrast, the structural argument doesn’t select the specific natural laws of this universe. Those laws exhibit particular symmetries: transformations under which the action functional governing the universe’s dynamics remains unchanged, such as translation in time, translation in space, and rotation in space. The structural argument doesn’t by itself preclude a discontinuity in those laws while the bearer persists throughout. Whether another symmetry-set or a discontinuity in the actual laws is really possible, and whether such a discontinuity could count as a law-violating miracle in the theologically relevant sense is a further question this argument doesn’t settle.

Annihilation of Nature as a total state is Substantiality simply ceasing without a successor structure, and it is foreclosed for the same reason literal emergence from absolute nothingness is. Ordinary annihilation processes don’t instantiate that description: the relata and conserved quantities are transformed into other physical states. The strict result concerns passage into the Null State, which isn’t a state at all. It doesn’t guarantee numerical persistence of every local object or one global bearer. The totality-level cosmological consequence is developed at §4.6.

One traditional supplement is a creator who brings Substantiality into being at t = 0 and could end it at any time thereafter. That temporal picture doesn’t supply a missing bearer role. A determinate act of producing, sustaining, or ending a concrete state must itself connect relata across an ordered transition and therefore instantiate the structure attributed to Nature. Classical accounts of atemporal or sustaining creation deny that production is such a transition; they therefore remain a separate grounding question rather than being closed by this paragraph. A posit that enters no determinate relation doesn’t contribute Substantiality from outside. The strict result is that the bearer role can’t be produced from its own absolute absence.

The specific conservation claims physics supports—energy-momentum where the relevant symmetries and geometry permit it, electric charge, and effective or approximate conservation laws in particular regimes—depend on the structure the actual universe instantiates and remain corrigible against further experimental and theoretical revision. What survives any future revision of that list is narrower than the claim that some conservation law must obtain: it is that some bearer of Substantiality must persist, which the actual symmetries register through the conservation laws physics finds—not a guarantee that every future physical theory must retain a conservation law in that specific form.

The ontological reading of the quantum vacuum is contested in the literature (Saunders 2002; Earman 2003). Standard quantum field theory nevertheless represents the vacuum as a structured state, not absolute nothingness: it has correlations and supports observable effects, while familiar particle-language descriptions of vacuum fluctuations require interpretive care. The structural argument entails only the contrast with the Null State. *Which* ontology the vacuum carries, whether it’s properly described as a bearer, and how vacuum structure relates to the gravitational dynamics of the cosmological constant remain open.

The fine-tuning question at the token level remains an open empirical question. It asks *why* this universe instantiates the specific values of physical constants it does. The structural argument relocates the fine-tuning question (§2.7.3, §4.7) rather than dissolving it: the type can’t have failed to instantiate Substantiality, but the specific values within Substantiality’s parameter space aren’t fixed by the structural claim. Their actuality establishes their necessary possibility; whether other values are really possible, and therefore whether the actual values are contingent, requires further physical and modal argument.

And the question of how matter-energy unification extends into a fully unified quantum-gravitational theory (the open program at the frontier of fundamental physics) is precisely where the conclusions press up against the open work of contemporary physics.

## 4.5 Binding of the Conditions

Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality can’t be instantiated independently on the book’s account: each requires the other two. The earlier argument states this relation abstractly; here the actual physical descriptions of change are tested for its functional counterparts. Successful theories must represent an objective ordering of states, a differentiated domain or configuration structure, and physical degrees of freedom borne through the transition. Spacetime, fields or quantum states, conservation, and symmetry are important realizations and organizing frameworks through which contemporary physics supplies those roles. They aren’t four translations from metaphysical variables into physical nouns.

Each axis first composes within itself: tensed with tenseless time in §4.2, extensional with relational space in §4.3, and bearer with capacity in §4.4. The axes then compose with one another.

Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7) states the cross-axis relation at the law level:

$$
T \leftrightarrow (S \land \Phi), \qquad
S \leftrightarrow (T \land \Phi), \qquad
\Phi \leftrightarrow (T \land S).
$$

Each role obtains if and only if the other two obtain; none is independently instantiated. Ontological Identity (§2.6.8) states the same binding at the level of what Nature is. The question here is whether actual physics describes functional counterparts of that unity under names it developed independently.

The match is role-level. The modal theorem fixes *what must hold together*; it doesn’t select the particular physical theory that realizes the roles. Spacetime, fields, quantum states, conservation laws, and symmetries enter as candidate realizations and interrelations, not as translations that replace the three Conditions.

Dimensional analysis offers a limited illustration of the difference between description and content. The Buckingham π theorem shows that physically meaningful equations can be expressed through dimensionless groups, independent of whether a length is measured in meters or miles (Buckingham 1914; Bridgman 1922). Units are conventional; the represented relations aren’t.

But unit-invariance isn’t the theorem argued here. It separates convention from physical content, whereas the structural/realization distinction runs *within* physical content. Which fields exist, which symmetries hold, and what values dimensionless constants take may all be unit-invariant without being selected by T∧S∧Φ. Their actuality establishes necessary possibility; contingency still requires warranted alternatives. Dimensional analysis illustrates invariance but doesn’t prove the Conditions’ binding. The modal argument does that (§2.6.7). What remains is its physical face: one constraint in three registers (§2.6.9).

### 4.5.1 Spacetime
Temporality and Spatiality don’t obtain independently. Any moment is a moment somewhere; any place is a place at some time. Physics expresses that interdependence through spacetime.

Minkowski’s (1908) reformulation of special relativity treats time and space as one four-dimensional manifold with invariant interval $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$. Inertial frames may disagree about the interval’s temporal and spatial components while agreeing on the interval itself. General relativity (Einstein 1915) deepens the unity: spacetime geometry responds dynamically to mass-energy rather than serving as a fixed stage.

Relativity therefore forecloses frame-independent simultaneity across spatially separated events and the Newtonian treatment of time and space as independently specifiable physical absolutes. It also constrains causal signaling through light-cone structure. Those results don’t settle the further metaphysical dispute between sophisticated substantivalist and relationalist accounts of spacetime.

The invariance also illustrates Physical Necessity (§3.5.6). Once the relevant Lorentzian profile is fixed, its invariant consequences can’t vary while the profile remains the same: the energy-momentum norm $E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4$, and therefore the rest-energy relation $E_0=mc^2$, hold in every realization of that profile. This doesn’t show that Lorentzian spacetime is the only metaphysically possible physical profile. It shows that physical contingency can’t consist in holding the complete profile fixed while freely reassigning its constitutive invariants. The selection of the realized profile and the invariants carried by that profile are different modal questions.

### 4.5.2 Field
Under a field-on-spacetime reading, Substantiality is realized through field structure across spacetime: the bearer of physical capacities is spatially articulated rather than a dimensionless point. That reading is one important realization of the book’s S–Φ binding; it doesn’t establish that every spatial point must carry a nonzero field value, or that all possible physical ontologies must be field ontologies. Maxwell’s (1865) *Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field* unified electricity and magnetism into a single field whose excitations propagate through space at finite speed. Quantum field theory generalizes: particles such as electrons, quarks, photons, and gluons are treated as excitations of underlying fields defined on spacetime (Weinberg 1995). The Aharonov–Bohm effect (1959) shows that gauge-invariant holonomy around a closed path can make a measurable difference even where the classical magnetic field vanishes along that path. It supports the physical significance of global gauge structure, but doesn’t by itself settle every dispute about field ontology or rule out every action-at-a-distance formulation. The structural claim remains role-level: an adequate physical ontology must provide distinguishable configurations and persistent causal capacity; it doesn’t infer a universal field-value at every point from that requirement.

The quantum vacuum is an important test case for a field-on-spacetime reading. In standard quantum field theory, it is the ground state of the relevant fields, with zero-point terms, correlations, and entanglement structure. The ontological interpretation of zero-point energy and vacuum fluctuations is contested (Saunders, ‘Is the Zero-Point Energy Real?’ 2002; Earman, ‘Rough Guide to Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking’ 2003). Straightforward sums of zero-point contributions also generate the cosmological-constant problem (Weinberg 1989). These facts show why no simple identification of “vacuum” with absolute nothingness is warranted within standard field theory; they don’t establish that a physical bearer must exist at every spatial point in every possible ontology. The structural claim remains at the role level, and neutrality is retained here between field-on-spacetime and wavefunction-on-configuration-space approaches.

### 4.5.3 Conservation
Substantiality supplies cross-interval bearing: determinate physical content is carried from one state into the next. *That* bearing is structural; *which* quantities register it depends on this universe’s symmetries and physical theory (Noether 1918). Noether’s (1918) theorem establishes, under its formal assumptions, that every continuous symmetry of an action functional yields a conserved current; time-translation symmetry yields energy conservation, spatial translation yields momentum conservation, and rotational symmetry yields angular-momentum conservation. These are precise theory-internal correspondences, not a metaphysical guarantee that every physical quantity or one aggregate Substance-stock is globally conserved. In a generic expanding spacetime there is no global time-translation symmetry and therefore no global energy budget, while local covariant conservation retains its tensorial form. Baryon and lepton number hold to present experimental limits but may be violated in beyond-Standard-Model regimes; baryogenesis requires departure from baryon-number conservation under Sakharov’s (1967) conditions. Radioactive decay and pair production likewise transform the physical description while preserving the quantities the applicable symmetries protect. The alignment is exact at the level the physics warrants: conservation laws show how specified physical content is borne through transformations under specified invariances. They realize the Φ-role without proving that Φ is one conserved quantity, one enduring cosmic object, or the biconditional T ↔ Φ under a physical name.

### 4.5.4 Symmetry
The three roles bind into one structure in the book’s modal analysis. Physical theories ordinarily represent physical states as localized or otherwise structured in spacetime, and their dynamics relate physical quantities across temporal and spatial relations. This isn’t the empirical claim that every spacetime point must carry nonzero physical content: general relativity permits vacuum solutions, and the book’s role-level claim doesn’t legislate a local field value at every coordinate point. The relevant point is narrower: where a theory describes physical change, it does so through relations among temporal order, spatial or configuration-space structure, and physical degrees of freedom.

That many successful theories are symmetry constrained is an important physical analogue, while the particular symmetries are realization-level features whose modal status must be established separately. Noether’s theorem links continuous global symmetries of an action to conserved currents: spatial translation symmetry yields momentum conservation, rotational symmetry yields angular-momentum conservation, and global phase symmetry yields charge conservation. Local gauge symmetry is a redundancy of field description with a more subtle relation to conserved charge. Variational or action-based formulations are widely used across classical mechanics, field theory, and general relativity, but aren’t a proof that every fundamental formulation must take this form. Lorentz invariance organizes the relation of time and space in special relativity; gauge structures organize Standard Model interactions (Wigner 1939; Gross 1996). These results are compatible with the book’s triadic role analysis without establishing that every possible physics must instantiate the same empirical symmetries or local ontology.

### 4.5.5 Conclusions
The modal argument requires T ↔ (S ∧ Φ), S ↔ (T ∧ Φ), and Φ ↔ (T ∧ S): the three roles hold together under Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7). Physical theories repeatedly describe concrete change through the same integrated demands—temporally ordered states, spatial or configuration-space articulation, and physical degrees of freedom carried through lawful transformation.

The evidential strength of the physical correspondences is uneven. Relativity directly interweaves temporal and spatial measurement. Field and wavefunction ontologies offer rival realizations of articulated physical capacity. Noether’s theorem rigorously links specified continuous symmetries to conserved currents within action-based formalisms. None proves the Chapter 2 biconditionals. Together they establish the convergence needed here: physics doesn’t describe concrete change while dispensing with functional counterparts of succession, differentiation, or cross-transition bearing.

**[Proposition]**

**Binding Realization** · *Proposition*

Every successful physical description of concrete change must represent functional counterparts of objective succession, relational differentiation, and cross-transition bearing, whether those counterparts are fundamental, emergent, geometric, field-theoretic, or defined on configuration space. Relativistic spacetime, field and quantum-state structure, conservation laws, and symmetry principles supply independently developed realizations and interrelations of those roles in current physics. The alignment is abductive and uneven rather than a one-for-one translation: Noether’s theorem rigorously connects specified symmetries and conserved currents inside its formal domain, while the other correspondences depend on the physical ontology adopted. Physics does not prove the Triconditional Cross-Entailment; it repeatedly realizes the integrated role-complex the theorem requires.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7)

The proposition establishes correspondence without multiplying domains. The role-complex and its physical realizations aren’t a metaphysical floor with a physical world laid on top of it. They are one Nature read at two resolutions. Modal metaphysics fixes what any concrete realization must supply; physics determines which complete profiles are actual and which invariants those profiles carry. The first doesn’t choose a metric, field ontology, symmetry group, or set of constants. The second can’t describe concrete change while dispensing with succession, differentiation, and cross-transition bearing. Neither is an external explanation imposed on the other.

**[Theorem]**

**Metaphysics–Physics Continuity** · *Theorem*

Modal metaphysics and physics describe one Nature at different resolutions, not two ontological layers. Modal metaphysics fixes the invariant role-conditions of any concrete change-realizer; physics identifies the actual profiles that realize those conditions and proves the invariants those profiles carry. A physical realization cannot evade Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, while their necessity does not by itself select one physical profile. An alleged explanation placed “above physics” gains no external domain by being called metaphysical: if it makes a determinate difference to physical realization, that difference belongs to the one structured Reality; if it makes none, it does not explain the realization.

**Dependency routes:** invariant role-conditions—Structural Requirement (§2.4) and Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7); one domain—Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8); physical realization—Binding Realization (§4.5) and Physical Invariance (§3.5.6)

The correspondence is hardest to maintain where classical description gives out: at the singularity (§4.6).

## 4.6 Singularity

At the largest scale, the question becomes how cosmic history could begin or end. Classical physics encounters singular boundaries in gravitational collapse and in familiar extrapolations toward the Big Bang. One part of the problem can be settled without a completed theory of quantum gravity: Nature can’t occupy a stable zero-extension state, because Spatiality is one of its necessary Conditions.

The argument then proceeds through five increasingly strong claims:

1. **No Stable Zero-Extension:** no stable zero-extension state is possible.

2. **Structural closure:** Time, Space, and Substance don’t come to be from their prior absence.

3. **Two-sided serial closure:** given productive explanation toward the past and actual continuation toward the future, physical history has neither first nor last state.

4. **Return:** given actual continuation and the premise that an exercised phase of the whole has no last realization (*No Final Exercise*, §4.6.5), the hot, dense phase and its passage into expansion return without end.

5. **Cyclicity:** that return delivered in order rather than by fluctuation; its bounce, turnaround, thermodynamic, stability, and transmission conditions remain for physics.

Only the first two are strict results of the modal framework. The third and fourth rest on named premises, and the fifth adds physical conditions. Keeping them separate allows the chapter to defend a serious cyclic research program without borrowing its conclusion from the modal premises. The two strict results are established before the dispute is taken up, so the physical literature can be granted at full strength and answered rather than resisted.

What the singularity theorems establish is precise. Under specified causal, trapping, and classical-energy assumptions, General Relativity predicts geodesic incompleteness: some timelike or null paths can’t be extended beyond a finite proper time or affine parameter (Hawking and Penrose 1970). The theorems don’t in full generality establish a point of infinite curvature or a physical state located at the end of the path. Curvature divergence occurs in familiar solutions and motivates the ordinary language of “the singularity,” but geodesic incompleteness is the strict theorem-level result. The classical spacetime description has reached a boundary of its applicability. Whether the singularity is a real terminal state of Nature (a region of permanent zero extension) or only an artifact of the current classical description, to be dissolved by a deeper theory, is one of the open questions of contemporary physics.

The argument from §2 already rules out one of the two possibilities. That argument is that anything capable of hosting events at all must have Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality as necessary features. Whatever physics eventually discovers about the interior of a black hole or the moment of cosmological collapse, what it can’t deliver is a permanent total state in which Spatiality has been eliminated. The claim is modal rather than mechanistic: it follows from what Spatiality has to be, not from any particular physical law.

**[Theorem]**

**No Stable Zero-Extension** · *Theorem*

No stable zero-extension state is a state Nature can occupy. ¬◇(permanent ¬S) at cosmological scale. The claim is strictly modal: it holds independently of which specific physics describes the approach to compression.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

The result is immediate from the Necessity of Nature theorem (§2.9.6): the Necessity of Nature gives □(T∧S∧Φ), hence □S, hence ¬◇(permanent ¬S). The same result can be stated in the language of the Null State and at the same totality scale. By the Triconditional Cross-Entailment of the Conditions (¬S → ¬T∧¬Φ; §2.6.7), a *total* state that permanently lacks Spatiality also lacks T and Φ. The no-free-standing-residue thesis then carries this joint modal-core failure to ∅. That step is a separate substantive bridge, not a definition (§2.7.1). The Incoherence of ∅ theorem (§2.7.2) establishes ¬◇∅. A *local* region of vanished Spatiality isn’t reached by this line: carrying the totality result below the totality would need a localization bridge, which the section doesn’t supply and doesn’t use.

*The singularity-resolution constraint.* A complete theory must not represent the classical singularity as a stable state in which Time, Space, or Substance has ceased to obtain. It may instead treat the singularity as a boundary of the classical description or replace it with a configuration that continues to realize the Conditions. The structural result is limited: no stable zero-extension state, no lapse in Reality’s global capacity for Change, and no origination of the Conditions from their prior absence.

One further modal consequence follows for any *genuine* resolution possibility. Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10) yields $\Diamond\mathrm{Resolution} \rightarrow \Box\Diamond\mathrm{Resolution}$: once a resolution is genuinely possible, its availability can’t lapse as a global modal fact (§4.6.3). But availability isn’t actuality. Continuation through a cosmological boundary still requires a premise that actualizes an admissible route there.

The conditional re-expansion argument at Confirmation (§4.6.4) adds the required physical antecedents: an occupied lower bound, continuing nonstationary evolution, and exclusion of branches carried only by topology change or orthogonal degrees of freedom. Under those conditions, greater extension follows by exhaustion. Cyclic history further requires recurrence and premises specifying how later cycles inherit the relevant large-scale conditions. The modal result constrains every stage without actualizing the next one.

*The two directions.* Let $\mathrm{Con}$ be the minimal convergence-proposition: some separated physical trajectories reduce their separation and enter a common region or phase. Let $\mathrm{Div}$ be its minimal directional counterpart: some separated physical trajectories increase their separation. Both are actual. Gravitational aggregation witnesses $\mathrm{Con}$; ordinary separation and cosmic expansion witness $\mathrm{Div}$. The witnesses establish no total cosmic trajectory on their own. They establish the two directional capacities the following theorem fixes.

The derivation is short but its scope matters:

1. $\mathrm{Con}$ is actual, and $\mathrm{Div}$ is actual.

2. Actuality implies real possibility (§1.2.5): $\mathrm{Con} \rightarrow \Diamond\mathrm{Con}$ and $\mathrm{Div} \rightarrow \Diamond\mathrm{Div}$.

3. Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10) gives ◇P → □◇P for any fixed real possibility P.

4. ∴ $\Box\Diamond\mathrm{Con} \land \Box\Diamond\mathrm{Div}$. Reality necessarily retains the global capacities for convergence and divergence.

No early or late cosmological configuration can first supply either capacity or make either cease to belong to Reality’s modal field. Once Reality, Nature, and the universe in the totality sense are identified (§4.9), both capacities are internal to that one totality; neither is imported from beyond it.

**[Theorem]**

**Bidirectional Modal Capacity** · *Theorem*

Reality necessarily retains both directional capacities: $\Box\Diamond\mathrm{Con} \land \Box\Diamond\mathrm{Div}$. Neither capacity can be first supplied or subsequently lost by any cosmological configuration; both are internal to the one totality Reality is. The result is about global modal standing, not local reachability or cosmic scale. It does not entail that every configuration can access both directions, that expansion reverses, that every trajectory meets, or that the whole universe reconverges.

**Depends on:** Actuality (§1.2.5) and Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10)

Combined with No Stable Zero-Extension, the theorem supplies a boundary-closed, two-directional modal architecture. Convergence can’t terminate by eliminating Spatiality, and divergence can’t erase Reality’s capacity for convergence; the converse capacity remains at the compressive side. This is a cycle-shaped constraint, not cyclic actuality.

*The theorem is global.* Gravity and expansion supply actual witnesses, but the conclusion isn’t indexed to the regions in which they were witnessed. $\Box\Diamond\mathrm{Con}$ and $\Box\Diamond\mathrm{Div}$ characterize Reality’s modal field as a whole. An expansive configuration can’t make convergence impossible in Reality, and a compressive configuration can’t make divergence impossible in Reality. This is stronger than the claim that isolated bound systems continue to contract while the distances between them increase. The two directional capacities belong to the one totality and can’t be removed by any configuration within it.

The scope of the operator must still be distinguished from the scope of the proposition inside it. $\mathrm{Con}$ was defined minimally as some separated trajectories entering a common region or phase. Boxing its possibility globally doesn’t silently replace that content with total cosmic reconvergence. The theorem is global in modal standing and minimal in what it fixes as possible. A route to a cycle must therefore either establish a totality-scale convergence proposition independently or show how the actual minimal realizer extends, under the governing dynamics, into the required global phase.

Global modal standing isn’t yet temporal recurrence. In the standard temporal notation already introduced at §2.11, $\mathbf{F}$ means *at some later state* and $\mathbf{G}$ means *throughout the actual history*. A recurrent directional history requires something like $\mathbf{G}\mathbf{F}\,\mathrm{Con}\land \mathbf{G}\mathbf{F}\,\mathrm{Div}$: after every point, convergence and divergence are actualized again. That liveness claim doesn’t follow from $\Box\Diamond\mathrm{Con}\land\Box\Diamond\mathrm{Div}$ merely by changing operators. Possible configurations aren’t thereby later states on the actual trajectory. An unrestricted bridge from necessary possibility to eventual actuality would also be too strong: it would threaten to turn every genuine possibility into an event. The completion must therefore be narrower. It must show, physically or by a further argument about constitutive and continuously operative capacities, why neither of these two directional capacities can remain permanently unexpressed in a temporally unbounded, self-subsistent Nature.

Aggregation, total cosmic reconvergence, and recurrence into a dynamically equivalent phase are therefore different propositions, but the burden has narrowed. Cosmology need not create convergence or preserve a merely local possibility; convergence is actual, and its possibility is fixed globally. It must show that the actual trajectory re-enters a convergence-dominant regime at the required scale. A turnaround law, recurrence-supporting dynamics on a suitably bounded accessible state space, or another mechanism meeting the conditions below would supply that temporal bridge. Cosmology may block or fail to actualize a directional route, but it can’t remove that direction from Reality’s modal capacity. Nothing here says that the two capacities ground or entail one another.

*Temporal closure.* The argument from Modal Constitution through Cartesian Certainty (§2.1.3, 2.2) returns at cosmological scale: Time doesn’t come into being from a prior absence of Time.

The excluded condition isn’t a quiet interval during which no change occurs while change remains available. It is a state of absolute incapacity from which Change later appears. Such a state can’t host the passage into actual Change, because that passage would be the very C-realizing transition it was stipulated to exclude (§3.1.2). Nothing stands “before” or “outside” Temporality as the source from which Temporality arose.

This is categorial closure, not an answer to the temporal order’s bare order-type. It neither proves a past-unbounded sequence nor excludes a least moment with nothing before it. Those remain cosmological and order-theoretic questions.

*Interval and structure.* The oldest form of the question asks whether the series of moments has a first member (a moment with none before it) and treats that as the question of whether time began. The question carries a picture, and the picture is the error. Asking what came *before* the first moment treats time as a line you could stand to one side of, and that picture, not any answer to it, is the mistake. It construes Temporality as an *interval*: a manifold of instants laid out under earlier-than, whose order is then interrogated for a least element, the way one asks whether the integers have a least member. Temporality isn’t that. It is the structural condition, established at §2.3–2.4, that to be at all is to stand in succession; the manifold of instants is represented *within* it, not a container it is laid out inside. Modality has the same relation (Chapter 2): possible worlds are representations within the structure of Reality, not a space Reality sits inside. “Outside the space of worlds” names no further option; it removes the conditions under which an option could be specified (§2.1). The same structural fact—worlds represented within Reality, not concrete relata standing alongside it—does the anti-plurality work at §7.2.3 and is gathered into the unicity of the totality at §4.9. The temporal manifold stands to Temporality as the space of worlds stands to Reality. The parallel is structural, not a verdict on degree of reality: it fixes only that the represented order is no container its condition sits inside, and doesn’t turn past instants into mere possibilia. Past times are as fully obtained as the present; to call the manifold represented within Temporality places it ontologically without demoting it.

That ‘fully obtained’ is the tenseless B-series the account preserves as a genuine description of structural succession, not the symmetric block it rejects: the considered composition (§4.2, §4.2.5) keeps the B-series while holding the arrow mind-independent and irreducible, so a block universe with a real arrow is compatible with the account and one without isn’t. The phrasing is that reconciled tensed-tenseless composition, not a bare B-theory on which ‘the universe began to exist’ would lose its sense, which is why the traversal reply that follows does real work rather than dissolving the dispute trivially.

So “what lies outside Temporality?”, and with it “what came before the first moment?”, isn’t a hard question the argument has left unanswered. It is the modal container fallacy one level down, and it dissolves against the same considerations.

What survives the dissolution is exact. Structural closure, □T, together with the preclusion of the Null State (§2.7) and the parasitic reading of negation (§2.1.5), forecloses any “before” or “outside” Temporality, since each is a domain-external negation already shown to describe no condition at all. That is what rules out a beginning.

A beginning in the categorial sense at issue here isn’t the bare presence of a first moment but time *coming to be*: a passage into Temporality from a state without it; closure denies the “from without” directly. Closure is silent on the manifold’s bare order-type—whether the instants happen to possess a least member—and that silence is the result, not a gap left in it. Should there be a least moment, it is a boundary with nothing on its far side, a pole rather than an edge time crosses from elsewhere, and nothing downstream turns on whether the manifold has one. (That the order-type question is *open* rather than meaningless is shown by its having distinct coherent answers left standing here. At the near end the series may carry a least moment with finite past, [t₀, ∞); no least moment yet finite past duration, (t₀, ∞); or no least moment with infinite past, (−∞, ∞). The far end is open the same way: it may carry a greatest instant (a silent terminus) or none, so each end closes or stays open independently of the other. A senseless question doesn’t come with rival coherent answers like these: none is adjudicated here, which marks a limit of reach, not a collapse of sense. Nor does a possible least moment threaten the *necessity* of Nature’s structure. “Always” divides in two. There is the atemporal sense in which □(T∧S∧Φ), the Necessity of Nature theorem (§2.9.6) holds without being indexed to any moment, much as a necessary truth does (the analogy reaching only that atemporality, not the abstract or stipulated character of mathematical necessity), so that a first moment, were there one, would leave it untouched. And there is the omnitemporal sense in which Nature is present at every moment there is, which a bounded interval [t₀, ∞) satisfies in full. The triconditional structure’s necessity lives at the first level, which the order-type question can’t reach.) The temporal structure has no outside from which it begins or into which it ends. Whether its order has a first or last member remains a separate question.

The boundary that remains is of another kind entirely: not an edge but the closure itself. The constraint is the boundary, bounding not by a limit Temporality arrives at but by leaving nothing beyond to arrive at.

The order-type neutrality must not be made to answer more than it does. Kalām arguments combine two distinct concerns: coming-to-be from a prior absence of Time, and the coherence or traversal of a beginningless concrete history. Structural closure answers the first directly: there is no prior absence from which Temporality emerges. It doesn’t answer the second. A recurrent history remains beginningless if it contains past-unboundedly many cycles, and dividing that history into finite segments doesn’t dissolve the actual-infinity or traversal objections. Whether the represented temporal order has a least member therefore remains open and may still matter to those independent arguments, even though no answer licenses an origin from non-Time. The restraint is principled because the coming-to-be question is settled here, while the order-theoretic dispute is left where it belongs.

*What the closure doesn’t settle.* It is worth being exact about what kind of result the order-type neutrality is, because a principled silence is easy to mistake for an unfinished one. What is earned strictly is narrower than a flat absence of a *last* moment: Reality’s global capacity for Change remains fixed, □◇C never lapses (§2.3–2.4), and no changeless stretch can elapse (§4.6.5, where the relationalism-about-instants premise the floor turns on is shown to be supplied by its own account of Temporality rather than purchased as an extra premise). Neither result says that every state has a locally available successor.

What that floor leaves open is the bare order-type at the far end, exactly as it left it open at the near one. A greatest moment with no locally available successor would close the series even while Reality’s global ◇C remains true: a silent terminus, the far-future twin of the least-moment pole. Foreclosing *that*, unlike foreclosing a changeless stretch, takes more than □◇C: it takes actual change never permanently ceasing, the abductive premise §4.6.5 leans on, not the strict floor.

The strict result doesn’t go untested, and one case tests it. The far-future state physics projects isn’t the zero-extension collapse the No Stable Zero-Extension theorem forecloses but its opposite: heat death, the maximal-entropy equilibrium an expanding cosmos approaches. The No Stable Zero-Extension theorem is silent here: heat death isn’t a region of vanished Spatiality, so the Null-State line that rules out the compressive terminus does no work against the expansive one. Nor does the global modal result by itself show that a heat-death configuration has a locally available successor. The physical description may remain micro-differentiated through quantum or thermal variation even after usable macroscopic gradients disappear, but that is an empirical characterization of the regime, not a consequence of □◇C.

The global proposition ◇C remains true when a heat-death configuration is evaluated, but that says Reality permits Change somewhere in its fixed modal domain; it doesn’t assign a successor to that configuration. Whether a later moment actually *follows* is the bare order-type question again, left open by the strict floor exactly as the least-moment question is. If actual change never permanently ceases, as persistent micro-fluctuation would support, no moment is the last: the series runs on, and heat death is a maximal extension rather than an edge where time runs out. But that step, and with it the cyclic continuation developed later, rests on change continuing to *occur*, not merely remaining globally possible, and so belongs to the additional-premise layer rather than the strict modal floor.

The floor secures two exact results: Reality’s global capacity for Change never lapses (□◇C), and no changeless stretch can elapse (§4.6.5). It takes no position on whether there is a bare first or final instant. A stronger conclusion is available, but only once its additional bridges are stated rather than smuggled into □T or □◇C.

*Productive explanation and the near end.* Suppose contingent facts require explanation—the principle later examined at §8.2.1.
