That requirement alone doesn’t make every explanation a temporally prior producer: a law, a global consistency condition, or a boundary condition may be explanatory without occupying an earlier moment. Add the productive bridge—every contingent token configuration of Nature is explained by a physically prior configuration—and the order-type is no longer neutral at the near end. The Necessity of Nature theorem necessitates the Conditions, not the token arrangement occupying them (§2.9.6). An alleged first physical configuration isn’t thereby contingent. If an independent argument establishes that contingency, the productive bridge gives it a physically prior configuration, contradicting its being first. The conditional result is exact: given premises stated here—productive explanation plus the contingency of any alleged first token—physical history has no first state, and the Big Bang has a physically structured earlier side. What remains conditional is the productive reading of explanation, not the inference once that reading is granted or any premise supplied only by a later chapter.

*Actual continuation and the far end.* The mirror result requires a different bridge: actual change never permanently ceases to occur. □◇C fixes Reality’s global modal standing, and the No Changeless Duration lemma (§4.6.5) rules out an elapsed but wholly changeless tail; neither alone supplies a successor to a silent greatest instant. The actual-continuation premise does. If change continues to occur, then every occupied state gives onto a later differentiated state, so no physical state is last. Productive explanation and actual continuation together yield two-sided serial closure: no first physical state and no last physical state.

That is the boundary result these premises earn, and it is still not yet recurrence. A history ordered like the integers can be predecessor-complete and successor-complete while visiting a different configuration at every position. To derive recurrence in some form requires a further recurrence bridge—a bounded or compact physically accessible state space with recurrence-supporting dynamics, a law-governed boundary process that returns the cosmos to a relevant configuration-class, or an argued premise about phases the actual history has already exercised (§4.6.5). A closed cycle requires more again: a bounce or equivalent relay, a thermodynamic account of the low-entropy boundary, and enough continuity in large-scale conditions for the same kind of cycle to return. The sequence is therefore strict closure, conditional two-sided seriality, physical recurrence, then macro-scale cyclicity. Each stage adds a premise; none may borrow the next stage’s premise while presenting itself as the previous stage’s result.

This symmetry has an independent echo in the critical literature on the Grim Reaper arguments. Schmid (2024) constructs future-oriented Benardete paradoxes and shows them epistemically symmetric with the past-oriented ones the finitist deploys: whatever forbids an infinite past by such reasoning forbids an endless future on the same grounds, a consequence the finitist means to avoid. That symmetry is welcome here; the finitist must resist it. Its strict floor does not decide whether the sequence has a least moment or a silent terminus: global □◇C remains fixed, while no changeless stretch elapses. Where Schmid turns the symmetry into a reductio of the paradox-based case for a first moment, structural closure absorbs it: neither end is foreclosed by the strict result. What closure denies is a categorial beginning or ending as coming-to-be from or passing into a condition outside Temporality, not the bare presence or absence of a terminal instant at either pole.

This is a diagnosis of its reach, not a theorem that the manifold has no least member: it says only that whether the manifold has one isn’t a question the structural apparatus is built to settle, and, by the inertness just shown, not one it needs to. A closure honest about its own reach is the kind worth having.

*Space and Substance.* The closure just run for Temporality isn’t peculiar to Time. It is one reading of a result the proof reaches schematically across all three Conditions: Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5) shows that to negate a Condition from outside itself describes no condition at all, and the schema is indifferent to which Condition fills the slot. Run it for Spatiality and the spatial form of the question dissolves the same way. “What lies beyond the edge of space?” pictures Space as a region one could stand outside of and look back into. It assumes a further place on the far side of Space’s boundary. But such a place would be nowhere in space—an extension that is no extension. This isn’t a hard location the argument has failed to find, only the container fallacy one Condition over. There is no outside of Space for an edge to face, and so no edge in the sense the question needs: not a wall with a beyond, but a closure with nothing past it.

Run it for Substantiality and the oldest creation-question goes the same way. “What brought Substance about from outside it?” asks for an origination of the being through some prior cause or process; but causation and production are among the very operators that presuppose Substantiality to operate (§1.4), and origination from sheer absence is foreclosed already, since ∅ is nowhere Nature can obtain (§2.7). Substance doesn’t come from non-substance: not because some first substance held out against a prior nothing, but because “from outside Substance” names no source.

What each reading forecloses is the “from without,” and only that; on the inside structure of each Condition it stays silent, by the same discipline that kept the temporal closure off the order-type. Spatial closure rules out an edge with a far side; it says nothing about whether Space is finite or infinite in extent, and a boundaryless spatial manifold can be either compact or noncompact. Which one holds is left to physics. Substantial closure rules out substance-from-non-substance and says nothing about how much Substance there is or how it is distributed. The neutrality is again the result and not a gap in it: the argument settles the question that was doing the work (whether a Condition could come to be from a state without it) and declines the questions of extent and quantity that, once that one is settled, were never the difficulty. The three closures are one closure read three ways. Each rests on what the temporal reading rested on, the parasitic reading of negation (§2.1.5) and the preclusion of ∅ (§2.7), now drawing its own conjunct of the □(T∧S∧Φ) the Necessity of Nature secures: □T for the temporal reading, □S for the spatial, □Φ for the physical.

*Notation.* **X** ranges over the Conditions, X ∈ {T, S, Φ}, so *from outside X* means from outside whichever Condition is in question, and the closure is stated once for all three.

**[Proposition]**

**Triconditional Closure** · *Proposition*

The three per-Condition closures are one closure read three ways. A negation of any Condition X ∈ {T, S, Φ} from outside X—a “before” Time, an “outside” Space, a “beyond” Substance—describes no condition at all, and each Condition draws its own conjunct of □(T∧S∧Φ): □T (no coming-to-be of Time from a prior absence), □S (no edge of Space with a beyond), □Φ (no Substance from non-Substance). Each reading forecloses only the “from without” and stays silent on the matching inside question—the order-type of Time, the extent of Space, the quantity of Substance.

**Depends on:** the Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5) lemma and Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6) theorem

The singularity is just the place where the temporal reading meets the physics that made its question feel urgent; the spatial and substantial readings meet that physics elsewhere (in the large-scale geometry of Space and in what conservation secures) and are settled at the structural level before physics arrives.

A figure or two before the constraint lands. The arc from the hot dense state our cosmology calls the Big Bang to the present runs about 13.8 billion years. Compressed to a single calendar year, the solar system forms in early September; multicellular life appears in mid-December; the genus *Homo* arrives in the last two hours; recorded human history fills the final ten seconds. The forward continuation runs through the stelliferous era, the degenerate era, into the black-hole era, extending to something like $10^{100}$ years before the last evaporating remnant emits its final photon. The figures exceed intuitive registration, and that is the point. The full sweep most readers picture when they think *all of time* (beginning to evaporative end) is one history, finite at both ends. Temporal closure is the condition; a cycle is one conditional model of what may play out within it.

*If the resolution is cyclic: the actual-infinity dispute remains.* A past-unbounded sequence of finite cycles would still contain past-unboundedly many events and cycles. Dividing the history into finite segments doesn’t by itself answer the Kalām objections from actual infinity or successive traversal (Craig 1979; Craig and Sinclair 2009). Those objections require independent adjudication: one must determine whether an actually infinite concrete history is coherent and whether traversal language correctly represents a beginningless ordered series. The modal argument doesn’t settle either issue. It establishes only structural closure—no coming-to-be of Temporality from non-Time—while a past-unbounded cyclic history remains a further cosmological model with the same philosophical burdens carried by other beginningless histories.

*No origin from outside the Conditions.* Temporal closure rules out an expansion initiated by a transition from non-Time, non-Space, or non-Substance. It doesn’t show that the particular expansion described by current cosmology has always been occurring, or that an actual prior phase must exist. Those conclusions require a physical account of the boundary and of the token-level conditions under which expansion occurs. If a theory establishes that physical evolution is extendible through that boundary, a bounce may supply the dynamical relay from compression to expansion. If it further establishes repeated contraction and sufficiently stable transmission across successive bounces, a cyclic model may follow. The modal argument excludes an origin from outside the Conditions; it doesn’t actualize one of these physical continuations by itself.

*If the resolution is cyclic, what the model must preserve.* The structural argument doesn’t pick out a cycle or determine how one would close. It constrains what any proposed closure must preserve. Three earlier results do the structural work: Temporality cannot originate from a coherent “before” or “outside” (§2.1.3, 2.2); absolute nothingness, in which any Condition is permanently absent, isn’t a state Nature can occupy (§2.7); and the structural Conditions remain invariant (§2.1.7; cf. §4.5). These results require any admissible cyclic model to preserve the three Conditions. They don’t show that successive compression boundaries are physically equivalent, that the same effective laws govern every high-curvature regime, or that the same macrostate is transmitted across a bounce.

Macro-scale recurrence therefore requires additional physical premises: a theory of the boundary dynamics, specification of the transmitted state variables, stability under perturbation, and enough dynamical invariance to reproduce the relevant configuration-class. In a deterministic model, equivalent laws and complete initial data would reproduce a trajectory; in a stochastic or quantum model, they may reproduce only a probability distribution over trajectories. A reader who grants only the strict modal result retains the preclusion of a stable zero-extension terminus without acquiring a bounce, recurrence, or cycle-to-cycle similarity. Even under a cyclic model, whether each cycle contains the same arrangement-kinds, such as stars, depends on the physical dynamics rather than on the invariance of the three Conditions alone.

The per-cycle low-entropy boundary condition that the macro-trajectory requires is what the philosophy-of-physics literature calls the *Past Hypothesis* (Albert 2000; Loewer 2007). The Past Hypothesis names the philosophical commitment that the macro-scale initial conditions of a thermodynamic history are themselves a load-bearing posit, not a derivable consequence of the laws alone. On the cyclic reading, what the Past Hypothesis names is what each cycle’s bounce-region must deliver: a low-entropy macrostate from which the cycle’s elaboration toward heat-death-as-phase can begin. Any cyclic model of the kind considered here requires that *something* deliver such a state at each recurrence; *which* physical mechanism realizes the delivery (conformal rescaling, ekpyrotic phase transition, horizon dilution, LQC bounce) is for physics to settle. The philosophical posit is named here; physics names the realization.

On the abductive layer just named, recurrence of the same macro-trajectory requires more than preservation of the three Conditions. It requires a physical theory that specifies the boundary dynamics, the transmitted macrovariables, and the relevant stability conditions. Equal laws don’t guarantee equal trajectories unless the pertinent state variables and dynamical conditions are also equivalent. The modal argument supplies none of those details. That no physical continuation may pass into the Null State is structural within the framework; predecessor, successor, recurrence, and cycle-to-cycle similarity each require the additional premises already identified.

*Taking stock.* A bounce or cycle isn’t predicted from modal structure alone. It establishes a constraint any complete cosmology must meet: no physical history originates from or terminates in the absence of Time, Space, or Substance. A classical singularity therefore can’t be the point at which Nature becomes the Null State. Whether its resolution is a boundary, a quantum transition, a bounce, a cycle, or another structure that preserves the three Conditions remains a question for physics. The modal argument constrains the answer without pretending to supply it.

### 4.6.1 The Dispute
The question of whether the cosmological singularity is a real terminal state of Nature (a region of permanent zero extension at the limit of compression) or only an artifact of the current classical description, to be dissolved by a deeper theory, is one of the open questions of contemporary physics. The classical singularity theorems (Hawking and Penrose 1970) establish, under broad classical-energy assumptions, that General Relativity itself predicts geodesic incompleteness: paths of freely falling matter or light that can’t be extended beyond a finite proper time or affine parameter. That is the theorem’s strict content. Curvature divergence is the generic accompanying picture in the physically relevant solutions and is what the informal language of “the singularity” usually points to, but it is a further, boundary-interpretation-dependent claim rather than something the incompleteness theorems alone strictly prove in full generality. Either way, the theory openly declares its own incompleteness at that boundary.

The standing dispute is over how to read this incompleteness. Some interpretations of classical geodesic incompleteness and of the inflationary singularity theorems (Borde et al. 2003) treat the past boundary as evidence that the classical spacetime description can’t be extended further, and some authors interpret that boundary as a beginning of the physical universe. The physics itself doesn’t identify the boundary with a concrete region in which Spatiality is absent. If a terminal reading adds that stronger totality-level gloss—Nature itself occupies a stable state lacking relational differentiation—No Stable Zero-Extension rules it out. A geodesically incomplete description or a local boundary doesn’t acquire that gloss merely by being incomplete. Other programs treat the classical boundary as a point at which a deeper description may supply an extension or successor phase. These include loop-quantum-cosmology bounces (Ashtekar and Singh 2011), conformal cyclic cosmology (Penrose 2010), and ekpyrotic or other bouncing cosmologies (Steinhardt and Turok 2007; Brandenberger and Peter 2017). The modal result constrains interpretations of the total state; physics must determine whether and how that constraint bears on any particular boundary.

BGV develops the terminal-reading pressure. It shows that a spacetime with positive average Hubble expansion along a past-directed geodesic is past-incomplete. Vilenkin reads that result in beginning-language, and Craig’s contemporary Kalām presentation leans heavily on that reading (Borde et al. 2003; Vilenkin 2006; Craig and Sinclair 2009).

Grant the theorem where its condition holds: a classically expanding phase has a past boundary. The further identification of that boundary with Nature’s first moment is denied. A cyclic model pairs expansion with contraction, and a proposed bounce is precisely where the classical spacetime description ceases to be complete. BGV may identify the boundary of an expansion phase without identifying an absolute beginning of Temporality. The dispute concerns what kind of boundary the theorem marks.

Mithani and Vilenkin sharpen the pressure. A cycling model with positive average expansion is itself past-geodesically incomplete, while the emergent-universe alternative is unstable to quantum collapse (Mithani and Vilenkin 2012). Grant that result in full. What is shown incomplete is a classical geodesic congruence—an event-line. Structural closure doesn’t run on an event-line. It denies any “before” or “outside” Temporality from which the geodesic boundary could begin (§2.1.3, 2.2, 2.7).

The result therefore removes past-eternal cyclicity as an easy answer, but the strict argument never depended on that answer. It rejects the terminal reading through No Stable Zero-Extension, not through commitment to any past-eternal cosmology. Mithani–Vilenkin raises the cost of the abductive cyclic layer without overturning the modal floor.

A related dispute concerns past-eternity. *Kalām*-style cosmological arguments (Craig, *The Kalām Cosmological Argument* 1979) treat the Big Bang as evidence of an absolute beginning of Temporality requiring an external cause; standard inflationary and bouncing cosmologies treat the bang as one inflection within a longer (and possibly past-eternal) history. The two disputes are entangled: how one reads the singularity bears on how one reads the bang.

### 4.6.2 The Requirement
The modal argument treats a stable zero-extension terminus as impossible. If that philosophical claim is correct, one might expect physics at extreme compression to require a description beyond classical singularity theorems. This is an abductive expectation, not an independently established physical result of the modal Triconditions (□(T∧S∧Φ), the necessary co-instantiation of Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality (Φ), the three structural conditions).

Several physical programs and conceptual pressures bear on extreme compression. They don’t supply six independent confirmations, and they don’t independently establish that every classical singularity resolves into a bounce.

*Gravity.* Newtonian inverse-square formulas and classical general relativity become singular or geodesically incomplete in idealized collapse limits. This shows the breakdown of the relevant classical description; it doesn’t, by itself, identify the physical state beyond that breakdown.

*Energy.* Gravitational collapse can concentrate matter and energy density beyond the regime in which a classical spacetime treatment is reliable. This motivates a quantum-gravitational description, but classical energy arguments alone don’t show that a singular limit is dynamically unstable or that a bounce follows.

*Quantum mechanics.* Pauli exclusion supplies degeneracy pressure in systems dominated by fermions, and the uncertainty principle makes sharply localized quantum states costly in momentum spread. Neither principle alone rules out every singularity in general relativity or establishes a universal lower bound on cosmic compression. They instead illustrate why matter models and quantum effects matter to any treatment of extreme-density regimes.

*Information.* The *Holographic Principle*, developed by ‘t Hooft (1993) and Susskind (1995), relates the entropy bound of an appropriate gravitating region to the area of its boundary. Its application to an idealized zero-area limit is conceptually delicate: it doesn’t by itself prove that a collapsing system retains a finite, independently specified information content at that limit, nor does it establish a bounce. It does, however, illustrate why classical singular limits sit uneasily with quantum-gravitational accounts of entropy and information.

*Quantum gravity.* *Loop Quantum Gravity* is one active program for addressing classical singularities, alongside string-theoretic, causal-dynamical-triangulation, and asymptotic-safety approaches. In widely studied loop-quantum-cosmology models, effective dynamics replace the classical Big Bang singularity with a bounce near Planck density (Ashtekar and Singh 2011). This is a candidate mechanism within a restricted class of models, not an established result of full quantum gravity and not a proof that extension has a universal discrete lower bound. The structural argument is consistent with this kind of resolution while remaining neutral among candidate mechanisms.

*Empirical cosmology.* The mechanism remains open. Black-hole interiors and the earliest cosmological regime aren’t directly observable in a way that would presently confirm or disconfirm a completed singularity, so the absence of such confirmation isn’t positive evidence for a bounce. Cyclic cosmological models (Penrose 2010; Steinhardt and Turok 2007) and bouncing-cosmology programs (Brandenberger and Peter 2017) each propose concrete resolution mechanisms at total compression. None has been confirmed.

Cyclic and bouncing programs face a standing thermodynamic constraint, often associated with Tolman (Tolman 1934): a naive repeating cosmology must explain how entropy growth and the large-scale conditions required for each new phase are handled. Penrose’s *Conformal Cyclic Cosmology* proposes conformal rescaling at aeon boundaries (Penrose 2010); ekpyrotic and other bouncing variants propose different treatments. These proposals remain theoretically contested and unconfirmed. The structural argument isn’t committed to any particular resolution program. If a philosophical argument rules out a stable zero-extension terminus, that result doesn’t by itself select a bounce mechanism or establish that a viable cyclic model exists.

The considerations can be sorted epistemically. Classical mathematical breakdown identifies the explanandum rather than confirming a resolution. Quantum effects and quantum-gravity models provide candidate resolution mechanisms, none yet observationally established. Information-theoretic arguments identify further conceptual constraints but depend on how entropy and information are defined in the relevant gravitational regime. None of these categories independently warrants the claim that Nature must pass through a singular boundary.

The relevant programs approach extreme compression from different theoretical directions, but overlap substantially in their quantum-gravitational assumptions and shouldn’t be treated as independent confirmations. The modal argument’s conclusion and the physics remain distinct: the former is the book’s philosophical claim; the latter concerns the empirical adequacy of particular high-curvature models. Current work is compatible with non-singular continuations in some models, but it doesn’t establish a general physical theorem that compression must resolve.

The models nevertheless matter to the modal argument in a further, conditional way. If any proposed non-singular continuation isn’t merely mathematically describable but genuinely possible, the Necessary Possibility theorem (§2.1.10) entails that its possibility is necessary: ◇Resolution → □◇Resolution (§4.6.3, *Necessary Resolution Possibility*). The mechanism’s availability then can’t lapse, though its actuality at any boundary still requires a physical selection or actualization premise. The survey therefore supplies candidate witnesses for the antecedent without pretending that theoretical consistency or present evidence has already discharged it.

*Constraints on a physical completion.* The philosophical argument doesn’t dictate equations of motion, but it fixes a target against which candidate cosmologies can be assessed. A physically adequate cyclic completion would have to satisfy all of the following:

1. A maximal-compression phase must remain nonzero in extension and internally differentiated; a literally distinctionless point isn’t a physical state.

2. Any recurrence inference must specify which dynamics remain invariant across the phases it connects. The modal invariance of the three Conditions doesn’t by itself establish invariance of every physical law or parameter. Composite structures may disappear at high density and re-emerge through cooling and symmetry breaking only under the physical dynamics the proposed model supplies.

3. Compression-to-expansion requires an occupied lower bound, actual continuation of the relevant branch, no positive-duration plateau at that bound, and a physical mechanism that makes the net continuation outward.

4. Full phase closure additionally requires an upper turnaround, sufficient causal reconnection, return to the same dynamically sufficient compression-phase class, and stability against cycle-to-cycle drift.

5. Exact microscopic repetition and spatial coincidence are unnecessary. The recurring object is the macro-phase sequence; probabilistic differences may govern its token contents.

6. The outgoing phase must be hot but gravitationally smooth enough to regenerate usable gradients. Concentration energy can power expansion without itself resolving the entropy and information constraints.

7. Any proposal must expose model-specific empirical consequences and remain revisable by cosmology and quantum gravity.

These requirements don’t decide between a patch-based cycle that dilutes inherited entropy beyond the next observable region and a globally reconvergent cycle in which all finite Substance returns to a common compression regime. Existing models develop parts of each architecture; none presently establishes the entire globally reconvergent sequence. The remaining work therefore belongs to physics: supply a turnaround, causal structure, attractor, entropy treatment, bounce, and stability analysis that jointly realize the earned constraints.

*The items on that list aren’t independent.* Counting them as wholly separate debts overstates the burden, but collapsing them into one understates it. Under a strictly constant positive expansion-driving term, the absence of turnaround, the cosmic event horizon, and the cap on further large-scale aggregation arise together. Departure from strict constancy removes that shared source; it doesn’t by itself supply recollapse, causal reconnection, or a common compression phase. Those consequences follow only in models whose evolving component and global dynamics produce them. Stability against cycle-to-cycle drift, entropy treatment, and bounce dynamics remain separate debts at the compressive boundary. The physical program is therefore concentrated rather than discharged: one sector controls several expansive-end obstructions, while each positive bridge still belongs to the model that supplies it.

*The two ends may not be separate either.* The division just drawn between a dilute-end component and dense-end boundary dynamics is how the burden looks when each end is described on its own terms. At least one developed cyclic architecture doesn’t respect it. In the cyclic model of Ijjas and Steinhardt, one scalar field drives accelerated expansion. As its potential enters a steep negative region, the same field governs the ensuing ultra-slow contraction. The field that behaves as dark energy at late times is therefore also the ekpyrotic field that runs the contraction. A non-singular classical bounce, rather than a quantum-gravitational one, completes the transition between phases (Ijjas and Steinhardt 2019). Whatever the model’s independent merits, the architecture is a counterexample to the claim that the two burdens are distinct debts. In it they are one field described at two epochs.

This bears directly on the schema set out at §4.6.3. A model of that kind supplies a candidate antecedent not merely for ◇Resolution but for the conditional □(Cmp → E), since a classical non-singular bounce is precisely a dynamics under which an occupied compression state continues outward rather than terminating or plateauing. The dense end is therefore in better standing than a general handoff to quantum gravity suggests. The accounting already given should accordingly be qualified: two burdens as described, one burden if a single-field architecture of this kind is correct, and no claim is made here that any such model is. What can be said without selecting a model is narrower and still worth recording. The two ends aren’t known to be independent, and the presumption that discharging one leaves the other untouched isn’t a presumption this survey supports.

*What a shared boundary would require.* Supposing the two ends are one mechanism, what would a single quantity have to do to serve at both? The answer is more specific than the supposition suggests. At the dilute end the quantity must sustain accelerated expansion. For a canonical scalar field, whose energy density is $\rho = \dot{\phi}^2/2 + V$ and whose pressure is $p = \dot{\phi}^2/2 - V$, acceleration requires $\dot{\phi}^2 < V$ and therefore a positive potential. At the dense end the same quantity must drive the ultra-slow contraction that does the smoothing and flattening, and in ekpyrotic models this requires a steep negative potential of the form $V(\phi) = -V_0 e^{-c\phi}$. A single field serving at both ends must accordingly carry its potential from positive values into negative ones. The unification isn’t one behavior extended across a longer stretch of history. It is a change of sign.

The crossing isn’t additional structure. When the potential descends below zero the total energy density can fall to zero, and the expansion rate passes through zero with it, so that the turnaround is what the crossing consists in rather than something that happens to the field at it (Andrei et al. 2022). The dilute-end turnaround and the entry into the contracting phase are then one transition described from either side, which is what a shared boundary should look like. Nothing is added at the crossing and nothing external acts on the trajectory: the field continues down the same potential throughout, and what changes is the sign of the quantity it carries. That is already the reading given to the turnaround at §4.6.4, where the rate passes through zero while the acceleration doesn’t.

*A constant can’t change sign.* Constancy is the property of not changing, and a change of sign is a change. If the two ends are discharged by one mechanism, therefore, the expansion-driving component isn’t strictly constant. This reaches by a third route the conclusion that the exemption dilemma at Conclusions (§4.6.5) reaches by pricing a contingent constant, and it reaches it in a different form: not as a cost imposed on constancy from outside, but as a direct entailment of the unification itself. A strictly constant term and a cycle whose two boundaries are the same boundary aren’t jointly available. Nothing here establishes that the component is dynamic, and nothing here selects a model. What it removes is the position that holds both.

*The constancy at issue isn’t automatically the laws’.* The argument just given need not claim that the laws themselves vary between epochs. In the single-field models under discussion, the same specified dynamics govern a field whose value and potential contribution vary by phase: the sign change is in the modeled quantity, not in the equation governing its evolution. That is a feature of those models, not a consequence of Modal Invariance. The structural theorem fixes the three Conditions; a cyclic model separately owes whatever law- or dynamics-invariance its recurrence inference requires.

The same distinction fixes what invariance can and can’t settle here. That the laws don’t change is compatible with a strictly constant expansion-driving term, since a quantity may hold a fixed value under an unchanging law, and it’s equally compatible with a dynamic one. Law-invariance is neutral between them. Whether the component is in fact constant is accordingly a question about a physical quantity, and it stays with cosmology rather than being settled by the structural claim that the laws are the same throughout.

*A ledger against the list.* Since the architecture just described bears on several requirements at once. Requirement (1) is satisfied by construction in a non-singular bounce model: extension doesn’t reach zero. Requirement (3)’s outstanding clause is supplied only if the proposed bounce dynamics make continuation outward. A scalar potential crossing the regime required for turnaround can supply the first condition in requirement (4) within the relevant models; causal reconnection and return to a common compression phase must still be demonstrated from their global dynamics. Requirement (6), a hot outgoing phase gravitationally smooth enough to regenerate usable gradients, is a target ekpyrotic contraction is designed to meet through ultra-slow smoothing. Design isn’t verification, and the complete transition remains model-specific.

Requirement (7) is met in the sense that matters for revisability. Ekpyrotic and bouncing architectures generically suppress the primordial tensor signal, so a detection of primordial gravitational waves at inflationary amplitudes would count decisively against them. The proposal is exposed rather than protected.

What isn’t supplied is what was already identified as separate. Requirement (4)’s fourth condition, stability against cycle-to-cycle drift, and the standing thermodynamic constraint associated with Tolman are untouched by anything above, and they are untouched together, since a cosmology that can’t bound drift across cycles has no stable entropy budget to account for either. Requirements (2) and (5) aren’t debts a model must pay; both clarify what the argument permits rather than naming something a model must supply.

The honest total is therefore narrower than a list of seven and wider than the two burdens already named. One architecture, if correct, would discharge or substantially relieve four of the seven items and expose itself to test on a fifth, leaving one item and one standing thermodynamic constraint. Whether any such architecture is correct isn’t a question this book can settle. The accounting is offered as a measure of the remaining distance, not as a claim to have covered it.

*Which branch, and what it costs.* The requirements already given were stated without deciding between a patch-based cycle and a globally reconvergent one, and that neutrality is no longer free. The entropy treatment developed for this architecture is explicit about what it requires: in the limit of an unbounded universe there is an unbounded reservoir of energy and an unbounded volume to accommodate rising entropy and a rising black-hole count, so no entropic roadblock arises (Ijjas and Steinhardt 2022). A globally reconvergent cosmos, one in which all finite Substance returns to a common compression regime, supplies no such reservoir. The two readings aren’t jointly available, and only one of them is served by a worked entropy treatment.

*What the argument actually requires.* The choice costs less than it appears to, because global reconvergence was never established here. Spatial boundedness is deferred to cosmology: the structural roles don’t by themselves establish that physical space is spatially unbounded, and they equally don’t establish that it’s bounded (§11.2.3). That discussion also keeps apart two claims easily run together. That the conditions admit no *outside* by which they could be bounded is a claim about exterior, not about extent, and an unbounded cosmos has no outside either. The rest of the book has already declined the global-budget premise the reconvergent reading would need: mass-energy equivalence doesn’t establish a single globally conserved scalar in every spacetime (§4.4.2), and in an expanding spacetime energy conservation “holds in its local, covariant form rather than as a global budget” (§4.5.3). Requirement (5) has likewise already released exact microscopic repetition and spatial coincidence. Nothing in the argument requires the reconvergent reading, and this survey proceeds on the unbounded one.

*The obstructions to aggregation are partly enumerable.* Accelerated expansion limits causal access and caps further large-scale binding; angular momentum and pressure support can stall collapse within bound systems; finite accessible material limits what any aggregation process can gather. Removing one obstruction doesn’t establish that no others remain. In particular, loss of a cosmic event horizon enlarges possible contact without proving global capture, merger, or convergence into one phase-class. The value of the enumeration is diagnostic: it identifies physical quantities and scales a reconvergent model must control. It isn’t a completeness proof for aggregation.

The branch therefore yields a research condition, not a terminus theorem. A reconvergent architecture must show that its dynamics overcome expansion, causal separation, angular momentum, pressure, anisotropy, and any further obstruction relevant at the scales it claims to gather. An architecture with net expansion across each cycle also falls within the scope of the Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem (Borde et al. 2003), so past geodesic completeness isn’t among the things it delivers. Structural closure blocks a transition from outside Temporality; it remains neutral on whether the represented temporal order has a first member. A theorem about geodesic extendibility constrains the physical histories available and can’t be set aside by redescribing that order.

*What the branch returns.* The unbounded reading was introduced as a cost, and it is also a resource; the two are one commitment rather than two. The same unboundedness that supplies the reservoir invoked by the model’s entropy treatment also bears on the third obstruction to aggregation. The two jobs aren’t symmetrical: the entropy claim concerns the model’s global volume, while an aggregative stock concerns what a process can causally reach and therefore requires much more than unbounded extent. The proposal’s capacity to describe an unbounded number of cycles (Ijjas and Steinhardt 2022) is likewise not yet stability against cycle-to-cycle drift. A sequence can continue while relevant state variables drift, and the model must separately show that any such drift remains within the phase-class required for recurrence. What changes is only the item’s standing: a contested proposal addresses it; no stability result follows from cycle count alone.

*Recurrence isn’t cyclicity.* The two are easily run together, and they come from different sources. Poincaré-style recurrence is a measure-theoretic consequence only when the dynamics preserve a finite measure on the relevant accessible state space and evolution continues indefinitely; boundedness by itself isn’t enough. Under those conditions, almost every state returns arbitrarily near its prior state. Cyclicity is a stronger dynamical claim: that history traverses the same phase-order and closes. The first doesn’t deliver the second. A trajectory may revisit neighborhoods of its state space without repeating a macrosequence. What recurrence supplies, where its premises hold, is return without ordered phase closure.

The difference isn’t one of degree, and it bears on how the requirements already given are discharged. A strictly constant positive expansion-driving term yields a de Sitter horizon with finite Gibbons–Hawking entropy in the semiclassical description, but inferring a finite-dimensional accessible state space and recurrence from that entropy is a further, contested quantum-gravitational interpretation (§4.6.5). Cyclicity requires still more: dynamics with a tendency under which the phases arrive in the relevant order rather than in whatever order fluctuations deliver. Even an established recurrence result would therefore not partially establish cyclicity. Requirement (4)’s return to a common compression-phase class and requirement (5)’s recurring macro-phase sequence constrain the ordering, not merely the return. A cyclic completion must show not only that the cosmos comes back, but that it comes back by the relevant route.

*The ordering requirement has a candidate mechanism.* Gravitational aggregation is a dominant tendency wherever gravity is locally controlling, and it isn’t a regime awaiting a global contracting phase to appear (§4.6.3). Bound systems can merge and form larger bound structures. Those local dynamics provide a component a cyclic model may extend during contraction. They don’t by themselves constitute a global attractor or establish the ordered return of the whole cosmological state.

What local aggregation lacks isn’t merely scope but the demonstrated global dynamics needed for ordered phase closure. Under a strictly constant expansion-driving term the structures that will ever be bound are limited, and the aggregation ceiling is a final inventory rather than an advancing frontier (§4.6.5). Removing that cap wouldn’t by itself turn local merger into a global attractor. A cyclic completion therefore still owes an ordering mechanism at cosmic scale; ordinary gravitational aggregation is a candidate component of that mechanism, not the completed mechanism already present.

*A modal upgrade doesn’t bridge the distinction.* The Necessary Possibility theorem applies to recurrence as it applies to anything else: if return is genuinely possible, ◇Recur → □◇Recur. That is a global fact about Reality’s modal field, not local access from every configuration. It therefore doesn’t establish that no later state makes return dynamically inaccessible. The gap between recurrence and cyclicity is also not a gap between recurrence being impossible and recurrence being possible. It is a gap between returning and returning in order. An actual recurrence without ordered phase closure wouldn’t by itself constitute a cycle, and necessitating its possibility can’t constitute one either. The modal layer fixes the standing of a possibility once independently established. It doesn’t select or locally distribute the cycle.

### 4.6.3 Predictions
If Spatiality is necessarily instantiated (§4.3), a state of zero relational extension is a state in which Spatiality fails to be instantiated at all. By the *Triconditional Cross-Entailment* established in §2.6.7 (the result that the three roles Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality mutually require each other), the absence of any one of them is the absence of all three. A condition of permanent zero extension is therefore absolute nothingness under cosmological description: not an extreme configuration the universe might occupy, but the point at which the structure for any configuration is absent. It isn’t a condition the universe can persist in. A stable Singularity (maximum density, zero extension) is therefore modally precluded.

The prediction from logic alone is that total cosmological compression can’t persist as a terminal state. The argument doesn’t preclude *asymptotic approach* to such a state; it precludes *permanent arrival*. The constraint depends on Modal Invariance (§2.1.7), the requirement that the structural conditions of Nature hold across all configurations the universe as a totality can occupy, not merely the ones the current cycle has visited: if invariance fails, the preclusion fails with it. General Relativity’s “singularity” isn’t literally a point at zero extension but a boundary at which the manifold’s description breaks down. Black-hole interiors are physically related boundary cases, and some candidate models connect them to cosmological continuation, but the totality-level modal premise doesn’t by itself settle how any local interior resolves.

*Necessary Resolution Possibility.* Let Resolution be the proposition that a history or mechanism preserves T∧S∧Φ through a would-be classical singular boundary. If that proposition is genuinely possible, the Necessary Possibility theorem (§2.1.10) applies directly:

$$
\Diamond Resolution \rightarrow \Box\Diamond Resolution
$$

The possibility of singularity resolution is therefore necessary once its antecedent is secured. It can’t be available only accidentally in one cosmic phase and then disappear at another structurally equivalent boundary. This conclusion is stronger than the observation that current physics contains several speculative models: it fixes the modal status of any genuine resolution possibility. Its scope is equally exact. □◇Resolution isn’t □Resolution. It doesn’t actualize a resolution in this cosmos, prove that mathematical consistency alone establishes metaphysical possibility, or select bounce, branching, conformal rescaling, or any other mechanism. Actualization requires a further bridge—for example, a proof that resolution and a zero-extension endpoint exhaust the options, invariant laws that select a resolution under the relevant boundary conditions, or productive explanation that forbids the boundary from remaining physically unresolved.

*Necessary Aggregation Possibility.* The same schema runs at the expansive boundary with an antecedent that needs no hedging. Let A be gravitational aggregation: the convergence of matter into bound systems under mutual attraction. Where the resolution case must open conditionally, since no resolution mechanism has been observed, the aggregation case opens from actuality. Aggregation isn’t merely conceivable but occurring, at every scale where gravity is locally dominant, throughout the observable cosmos and in every body held to the surface of a planet. From actuality, possibility follows immediately, and the Necessary Possibility theorem then applies:

$$
\Diamond A \rightarrow \Box\Diamond A
$$

The possibility of aggregation is necessary. It isn’t a capacity the present phase possesses and a later phase might lose; its standing belongs to Reality’s modal field as a whole. Within this section it is the one application of the Necessary Possibility theorem whose antecedent requires no argument at all, which is why the result reads as trivial and isn’t.

*Potential for what?* Gravity isn’t itself potential energy. In the Newtonian description, a gravitational configuration carries potential energy relative to the positions of its masses; in general relativity there is no unrestricted global scalar gravitational-energy store for every spacetime (§4.4.2). The physical point survives the correction. Gravitational structure is an actual capacity for work and reconfiguration through reduced separation. Infall converts the configuration’s available energy into motion, heat, radiation, field excitation, and denser organization. A cycle would be a totality-scale actualization of that convergent capacity if the global dynamics carry it into a compression profile sufficient for an outgoing phase. The word *potential* doesn’t establish that global antecedent, but neither does it name an idle abstraction: gravity is already actualizing convergence wherever its attraction controls the motion.

Its scope needs the same discipline as before. □◇A isn’t □A, and fixed modal standing isn’t exercise. A dilute far future in which aggregation is never again actualized at scale is untouched by this result. What the result forecloses is one form of the anti-cyclic position: that the far future makes aggregation *impossible in Reality*. It doesn’t and can’t. Such a future may remove the occasion for aggregation along its actual trajectory; it can’t alter the global capacity, and the two are routinely run together in descriptions of heat death as a condition in which nothing further can happen. The weaker-sounding statement that *something further can always happen at that state* isn’t the same claim and isn’t established here: it asserts a successor available from a particular late configuration, and global capacity doesn’t distribute into local availability (§4.6.2). Whether the occasion returns, by law or only by fluctuation, and whether any given configuration has a successor at all, is the question taken up at §4.6.5 on the actual-continuation premise rather than on the modal floor.

*Two further antecedents are witnessed globally.* Causal contact among regions later separated is part of cosmic history, and low-entropy macrostates are represented in the history from which the present cosmos descends. Their actuality witnesses possibility, and Necessary Possibility fixes that standing globally. Neither result supplies what a cyclic completion needs. It doesn’t show that regions now beyond one another’s horizons can reconnect from their present configuration, or that a future boundary can dynamically realize a low-entropy macrostate. Those are reachability claims about particular physical states, not consequences of □◇.

This is the shape of every application of the Necessary Possibility theorem in this section. The schema converts an actuality into fixed standing within Reality’s global modal field. It never converts that standing into exercise or into accessibility from each physical configuration. A reader who grants every Necessary Possibility result in this section still has no cycle and no trajectory-level return. What has been fixed is the modal status of the witnessed kind; the dynamics, boundary conditions, and reachability relations remain untouched (§4.6.2).

*A second schema: sufficient configuration.* Every application of the Necessary Possibility theorem already established has the same negative shape because □◇P is the wrong form to convert. A necessitated conditional isn’t. Let K name a dynamically complete maximal-compression phase-class: the same governing laws, the same values of every state-variable relevant to the boundary transition, and the same relational organization in every respect on which the outgoing phase depends. Let E name entry into an expanding phase. If physics independently establishes $K\models E$, Physical Invariance (§3.5.6) fixes the relation as □(K → E), and actual K yields actual E. No further selector stands between the complete sufficient configuration and its consequence. The profile may remain physically unestablished; its consequence isn’t optional once it is established and realized.

The gain appears when K returns. A second realization of K isn’t merely another very dense state or another state assigned the same value on one compression measure. It is the same dynamically sufficient configuration-type. The same necessitated conditional therefore applies to it, and the expansion phase recurs without a second origin, restart of the laws, or external trigger. What recurs is the phase-transition type. The galaxies, stars, organisms, and other token contents produced farther along the expanding branch need not repeat.

**[Theorem]**

**Conditional Phase Recurrence** · *Theorem*

Let K be a dynamically complete maximal-compression phase-class and E entry into an expanding phase. If K is metaphysically sufficient for E, then □(K → E). Every actual realization K_n therefore yields an expanding phase E_n. If cosmic evolution later returns to a dynamically equivalent realization K_{n+1}, the same sufficient relation yields E_{n+1}. The recurrence of K is a further physical premise; the recurrence of E given K is not. The theorem fixes recurrence of the phase-transition type, not identity of the token histories formed within the outgoing phases.

**Depends on:** Physical Invariance (§3.5.6), through Configurational Necessitation and Strict Actualization (§2.9.4)

The sufficiency condition carries the precision. If two compression states differ in a variable that bears on whether or how an expanding branch follows, they aren’t two realizations of K at the resolution the theorem requires. Under deterministic dynamics, the same complete state and laws reproduce the same outgoing trajectory until later contingency is introduced. Under stochastic or quantum dynamics, the same state reproduces the same transition structure or probability distribution; necessary recurrence of E follows only if every physically admissible outcome from K enters the expansion phase, while the realized tokens may vary. If some admissible outcome doesn’t expand, what recurs is the distribution rather than E itself. Physics identifies which variables complete K and whether its dynamics satisfy the sufficient conditional. The modal result carries what follows once that antecedent is secured.

*Turnaround prediction.* A cyclic completion adds a reciprocal empirical prediction at the expansive boundary. If accelerated expansion is one phase in a closed sequence, then the contribution presently described as dark energy can’t sustain an eternally positive expansion rate. It must evolve, decay, change effective sign, transfer dominance to another field, or otherwise give way to dynamics that bring expansion to a halt and initiate contraction. This prediction belongs to the proposed cyclic completion, not to No Stable Zero-Extension itself: an eternally expanding, increasingly dilute history remains compatible with the strict modal floor.

The prediction is also its most exposed empirical commitment, and it is currently under test. Some combinations of DESI, cosmic-microwave-background, and supernova data have favored evolving-dark-energy parametrizations over ΛCDM at noteworthy significance, while the July 2026 DESI DR2 Lyα full-shape result shifted toward ΛCDM, its own matter-fraction constraint sitting 1.4σ above DESI BAO. That single probe doesn’t by itself separate a constant term from an evolving one, and the joint analysis still prefers evolution: w₀wₐCDM over ΛCDM at 2.7σ for DESI with the CMB, and 3.2σ once supernovae are included (DESI Collaboration and Adame 2026). The evidence hasn’t moved uniformly. Its force depends on the data combination, parametrization, and treatment of systematics, and model-independent reconstructions have generally reported weaker departures than the standard two-parameter form. The honest statement is therefore narrow: the cyclic completion makes a falsifiable demand on the expansion-driving sector, and current observations have neither established nor closed the required evolution. A candidate mechanism remains available in specified scalar-field models (§4.6.4); observation hasn’t shown that Nature occupies that regime. Should constraints settle onto a strictly positive constant term, the proposed cyclic completion loses its expansive-end turnaround and the strict modal floor is all that remains. The prediction is stated here so that it can be lost.

*Hierarchical convergence under contraction.* Aggregation isn’t a regime that waits on a global contracting phase to begin. It is the present regime wherever gravity is locally dominant: bound systems don’t expand, and every galaxy, cluster, and group is already converging relative to the trajectory it would follow unopposed. What a global contracting phase would supply is therefore not the onset of convergence but its extension to the scales at which expansion currently prevails. The burden on a cyclic completion is correspondingly lighter than it first appears: what must be supplied is a mechanism that removes the obstruction to convergence, not one that initiates it (§4.6.4). Convergence, once global, need not proceed toward a pre-existing center of the universe. Gravitationally interacting bodies form local bound systems around relational barycenters; those systems can merge into larger bound systems, whose barycenters are fixed by their combined contents. Continued contraction predicts an increasingly inclusive hierarchy of aggregation. Black holes would become major concentration sites through accretion and merger, potentially integrating formerly separate pockets into a common trapped or maximal-compression regime. The prediction is conditional on sustained global contraction and restored causal contact. It doesn’t claim that black holes themselves initiate the turnaround.

*The turnaround is a threshold, not an event.* The word suggests a moment at which cosmic history halts and reverses, and nothing in the picture just given requires one. What competes at every scale is local binding against the expansion term, and that competition is already settled in gravity’s favor wherever structures are bound, settled the other way only above the scale at which the expansion term prevails. A weakening of that term doesn’t stop anything and start it moving the other way. It moves the boundary. Structures that were unbound come under the ceiling in order of scale, continuously, as the threshold passes them. There is no interval during which matter is at rest, and no moment at which the cosmos as a whole pauses before reversing.

This clarifies rather than displaces the instantaneous zero described at §4.6.4. The scale factor’s rate may pass through zero at an instant, since that quantity describes the average metric expansion and can change sign. What doesn’t occur is a halt of anything material. Bound systems were never expanding and don’t begin to contract at that instant; unbound systems become bound as the ceiling reaches them, at different times for different scales. The reading also disposes of a question the contracting picture invites, namely where convergence would have to begin. It begins nowhere, having begun already, everywhere gravity is locally dominant. What a turnaround would supply isn’t an origin for convergence but the removal of a limit on its scope. None of this shows that the limit is removed. It fixes what the removal would consist in.

The prediction, then, is that no physical framework can produce a stable zero-extension state. Physics reports exactly that instability, not as six independent confirmations but as several directions that sort into three kinds of pressure (§4.6.2 Requirement), with the mathematical breakdown the explanandum itself rather than a separate witness.

*The classical mathematics breaks down.* The familiar formulas mark their own limits. Newton’s law for the gravitational force between two masses is

$$
F = \frac{G\, m_1 m_2}{r^2}
$$

As the separation r shrinks toward zero, the denominator vanishes and the force F runs to infinity. That isn’t a physical prediction: it is the formula reporting its own breakdown. At zero separation, the quantity the formula was written to compute isn’t defined. General Relativity supplies a sharper example in the Schwarzschild solution. Its *Kretschmann scalar*—a coordinate-invariant curvature scalar formed by contracting the Riemann tensor with itself, which detects curvature even where the Ricci scalar vanishes—is

$$
K = R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = \frac{48\, G^2 M^2}{c^4\, r^6}
$$

which diverges as $r \to 0$. More generally, singularity theorems establish geodesic incompleteness under their stated assumptions, not curvature divergence in every case (Misner et al. 1973; Hawking and Ellis 1973). A geodesic is the curve a freely falling test particle traces through spacetime, the relativistic generalization of straight-line motion. The mathematical description doesn’t produce a state there. It fails to produce one. Divergence in this solution and geodesic incompleteness more generally mark where the classical mathematics gives out; they aren’t themselves empirical evidence for the modal constraint, which is established independently on modal grounds (§4.6, §2.9.6), only the point at which a description consistent with that constraint has to hand off to something else.

*Why nothing in the bare force law halts the collapse.* The same formula, read dynamically, shows why the bare two-body law supplies no stopping point short of its own breakdown. Gravity exists between any two masses separated by any nonzero distance: the Newton formula $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$ is defined and nonzero for every r > 0. Taken on its own, that formula names no distance at which the attractive force is exactly canceled, so nothing in the two-body law itself arrests the approach to r = 0. That is a fact about the point-mass idealization, not a claim that real self-gravitating collapse can never be halted. Pressure gradients—thermal, degeneracy, or otherwise—support actual stars against gravity. Collapse continues only when those pressures can no longer balance gravity. The relevant cause is the failure of pressure support, not merely the persistence of attraction at nonzero separation. The point is about the classical description once pressure support has failed, not a full account of black-hole dynamics (which accretion, merger, and the general-relativistic horizon govern, and which dark-energy-driven expansion eventually isolates rather than feeds): with pressure support absent, the classical law has no last step, and runs the separation down toward the zero at which it fails.

*Where the classical relation stops.* Gravitational attraction isn’t a monadic property a body carries but a relation borne across a separation: its magnitude is a function of r, and that function takes an argument only where two relata stand at some nonzero distance. At r = 0 the classical formula therefore doesn’t describe attraction at its maximum; it ceases to describe a relation at all. That fact locates the handoff without deciding what occurs across it. A process can terminate by eliminating a condition under which its earlier description applied, so no bounce follows merely from the force law’s losing its argument. What follows is narrower: the classical relation can’t itself describe a completed zero-separation state or its successor. A quantum-gravitational account may replace distance with another structural quantity, and the modal constraint then asks whether the replacement still supplies a determinate realization of the Conditions rather than a transition into their joint absence.

What classical physics can’t describe is the terminus of that compression. As r approaches zero, the descriptions break down, not because a physical event ‘at r = 0’ has been observed, but because the mathematical structure they rely on no longer holds. The classical descriptions’ failure at the boundary marks the limit of that description, not an empirical confirmation of the modal constraint: a stable zero-extension state is precluded on modal grounds independent of how or where classical physics happens to break down, and the breakdown is consistent with that preclusion without constituting evidence for it. What replaces the failed description (bounce, repulsion, branching, conformal rescaling) is the empirical question §4.6.2 surveys. The modal argument excludes interpreting a classical boundary as Nature’s transition into the Null State; it doesn’t pick the mechanism or show that every classical boundary has a successor.

*Information preservation is a separate question.* The black-hole information paradox concerns whether unitary quantum evolution is preserved through black-hole formation and evaporation. Hawking (1976) originally argued for information loss; Page-curve calculations (Page 1993) and quantum-extremal-surface methods (Penington 2020; Almheiri et al. 2020) support unitary descriptions in important semiclassical settings. This development doesn’t confirm the modal preclusion. Information loss isn’t equivalent to zero spatial extension or to the absence of every distinction, so no prediction about unitarity follows from □(T∧S∧Φ) alone. At most, this is compatible with information-preserving resolutions. The empirical and theoretical status of information preservation must therefore be assessed within quantum gravity rather than treated as a falsifiable consequence of the structural argument.

### 4.6.4 Confirmation
The modal framework precludes a stable zero-extension terminus on strict grounds (§4.6.1) and precludes the Conditions from originating in their own absence. The stronger boundaryless-history result is conditional: productive explanation supplies a predecessor to every contingent physical configuration, and actual continuation supplies a differentiated successor to every occupied state (§4.6). Neither bridge is contained in □(T∧S∧Φ). Even with both granted, recurrence doesn’t yet follow; a two-sided serial history may remain non-repeating. The programs surveyed later are therefore candidates for the further recurrence bridge and for its cyclic realization. They share overlapping theoretical assumptions and observational anomalies rather than constituting independent empirical confirmations. What this slot establishes is consistency and abductive convergence, not completed verification.

*Bounce models and the structural constraint.* The modal argument and the physical models have distinct evidential roles. The former precludes, within the framework, a stable state in which Spatiality is absent. It doesn’t determine the dynamics at maximal density. In particular, the failure of further contraction doesn’t by itself entail expansion: a bounce requires equations of motion, boundary conditions, and a mechanism that connects a contracting branch to an expanding one. Loop-quantum-cosmology, ekpyrotic, conformal-cyclic, torsion-based, and other programs supply different candidate mechanisms, each with model-specific assumptions and unresolved empirical burdens. The survey that follows therefore bears only on the availability and comparative development of non-singular continuations.

*Conditional re-expansion.* The intended inference can nevertheless be recovered. Let a measure of cosmological extension track a single continuing physical branch, and let maximal compression be an occupied state at that measure’s physically admissible lower bound. Re-expansion follows if four further conditions hold: (i) physical evolution actually continues beyond the boundary; (ii) the measure can’t fall below its lower bound; (iii) the continuation can’t remain on a positive-duration plateau at that bound; and (iv) the model excludes a successor realized solely through branching, topology change, or evolution in degrees of freedom orthogonal to the measure. Under those conditions, some later state must have greater extension. In a smooth scale-factor model, the scale factor reaches its lower bound and subsequently increases.

*Three zeros, distinguished.* Condition (iii) is easily confused with No Stable Zero-Extension, and the two exclude different things. Zero *extension* is the absence of spatial extent as such: the Null State under cosmological description, foreclosed strictly (§4.6.3). Zero *expansion* sustained across a positive-duration interval is a cosmos whose scale isn’t changing and in which nothing else changes either; that is foreclosed by the No Changeless Duration lemma (§4.6.5), and only where the stasis is total, since a stationary scale factor with internal dynamics is differentiated and composes a stretch in good order. Zero expansion at a single instant is neither, and is what the turnaround consists in: the rate passes through zero while the acceleration doesn’t, so no interval of rest is composed and no changeless stretch elapses. The distinction matters because a reader who runs the three together will take the framework to preclude the very transition the conditional argument delivers.

*What maximality doesn’t discharge.* Maximal compression fixes one coordinate of a state: nothing in the tracked measure lies below it. It doesn’t by itself show that the state has no orthogonal degrees of freedom, that evolution continues on the same branch, or that every admissible continuation increases extension. Those clauses belong inside K if K is to be sufficient for E. This is why the four conditions stated in the conditional re-expansion paragraph remain visible rather than being compressed into the word *maximal*. A lower bound forecloses further decrease; the complete dynamics determine what follows there.

*The turning point.* One way a physical model can satisfy the no-plateau condition is by making the lower bound a turning point rather than a resting place. The rate of change of extension then passes through zero at an instant while the relevant acceleration doesn’t, so no positive-duration plateau is composed. That is the middle case of the three zeros already distinguished. The state may remain internally differentiated to any degree, since what carries the transition is its dynamics rather than an exhaustion of every degree of freedom. Calling the state a turning point already includes continuation on both sides; whether the actual boundary is such a point is therefore a physical description to be earned, not a consequence of the mathematical notion of a limit.

*The returning phase.* Suppose those dynamics establish □(K → E), and suppose contraction later returns the universe to K. The return doesn’t place the laws in abeyance and then restart them. It reinstantiates their sufficient antecedent. Conditional Phase Recurrence therefore yields another E. Exact microscopic identity and spatial coincidence are unnecessary where K is a phase-class whose members vary only in respects irrelevant to the K → E relation. If an allegedly differing variable can alter that relation, it was relevant after all and belongs in K’s specification. The theorem consequently permits token variation without purchasing it by vagueness about the configuration that recurs.

*Why the step doesn’t chain.* The same reasoning doesn’t necessitate every later phase or deliver a whole cycle from the boundary alone. A cooling, expanding cosmos reopens degrees of freedom, and no complete later configuration has yet been shown metaphysically sufficient for the entire trajectory back to K. Return to K remains a physical premise assembled from turnaround, contraction, causal structure, entropy treatment, and stability. Once that return obtains, the K → E step runs again. The theorem closes the transition at the repeated antecedent; it doesn’t prove that the antecedent repeats.

The distinction also preserves the type/token result developed in §4.7. Deterministic dynamics may carry a fully identical microstate along an identical trajectory. The weaker and more useful claim requires only that the recurrent phase-class be sufficient for the same outgoing phase-type. The expansion can therefore recur while the galaxies, stars, planets, and lives formed within it don’t.

*The quiescence objection.* If K sat unchanged through a positive-duration interval and later departed without any difference in the state or its governing structure, the question *why then?* would retain its force (Craig 1979; Craig and Sinclair 2009). No Changeless Duration (§4.6.5) forecloses the literally changeless interval within the framework, but it doesn’t by itself prove that a bare boundary instant has a successor. Conditional Phase Recurrence answers the selection question at the resolution where it can be answered: once the physical account establishes K as sufficient for E, nothing further selects the departure. The configuration and its invariant constraint already entail it.

This is a conditional result, not a universal dynamical law extracted from the Necessity of Nature. No Stable Zero-Extension supplies the constraint against a zero-extension terminus. A physical model identifies the occupied boundary configuration, its continuing branch, and the dynamics that make that configuration sufficient for expansion. Once □(K → E) is secured, however, re-expansion isn’t an independent postulate added after K, and its recurrence requires no second cause when K returns. The physical work establishes and returns the antecedent; Strict Actualization carries the consequence each time.

*The energy handoff.* During contraction, decreasing separations and gravitational infall increase density and inward motion. Collisions, turbulence, accretion, magnetic interactions, and other high-density processes convert that motion into thermal, field, pressure, and eventually quantum-gravitational contributions. A non-singular bounce would redirect the contracting state into an expanding branch; it wouldn’t create new content or restart Nature’s laws. The physically meaningful repository is therefore the structured maximal-compression phase that replaces the classical singular boundary, not a singularity treated as a state that stores and releases energy.

The gravitational potential accumulated through convergence is therefore potential for physical work, not by definition potential for a cycle. It becomes cycle-producing where the complete compression profile makes an outgoing phase invariantly follow. At that point Physical Invariance closes the handoff: the same profile can’t retain all of its relevant physics while failing to yield the consequence that physics entails. The new cycle isn’t added after convergence as a second event requiring another source. It is the next phase of the convergent state under its complete dynamics.

Gravity need not disappear at the boundary. Ordinary gravitational attraction generally strengthens with compression, and ordinary pressure doesn’t by itself reverse relativistic collapse. The physical bridge must instead supply a high-density contribution that makes further contraction inadmissible and renders the net continuation outward. At the exact turning state the contraction or expansion rate is zero; positive outward acceleration then carries the solution onto the expanding branch. Loop-quantum-cosmology corrections, torsion-based repulsion, scalar-field dynamics, and other modified high-density models are candidate realizations of that handoff. None is selected by the modal argument.

One distinction becomes important if a structured-bounce model is adopted. Each cycle must deliver a genuine low-entropy boundary condition through the bounce (§4.6, the per-cycle Past Hypothesis), not a chance dip in an equilibrium that otherwise persists. That is what separates these models from the stochastic *eternal return* of Poincaré recurrence or Boltzmann fluctuation, and it is why proponents argue that the *Boltzmann-brain* problem—the objection that fluctuation-generated observers should vastly outnumber ordinary ones, rendering our ordered observations improbable (Albrecht and Sorbo 2004; Carroll 2017)—is substantially defused. The point remains contested: whether rare fluctuation-generated observers dominate over a past-unbounded series of cycles depends on the model’s measure and dynamics, not on the modal floor.

*Candidate non-singular and cyclic programs.* The main programs differ in both mechanism and the kind of recurrence they propose:

- **Conformal Cyclic Cosmology** identifies the dilute future of one aeon with the conformally rescaled beginning of the next.
- **Steinhardt–Turok ekpyrosis** alternates contraction and expansion, originally through higher-dimensional brane dynamics, without occupying a singular state.
- **The Brandenberger–Peter matter bounce** turns a contracting matter-dominated phase into the observed expansion.
- **Loop Quantum Cosmology** uses effective Planck-scale quantum-geometric corrections to replace the classical singularity with a bounce.
- **Pre-Big-Bang string cosmology** uses dilaton-driven evolution and T-duality to relate pre- and post-bang phases (Gasperini and Veneziano 1993).
- **The new cyclic universe** uses ultra-slow contraction to smooth inhomogeneities before a non-singular bounce and is designed to meet Tolman’s entropy-growth objection (Ijjas and Steinhardt 2019; Tolman 1934).
- **Phantom cyclic cosmology** uses dark energy with $w<-1$ to drive a turnaround before heat death, with entropy shed at reversal (Baum and Frampton 2007).
- **Einstein–Cartan models** let torsion coupled to fermion spin generate high-density repulsion; in Popławski’s version, black-hole interiors produce offspring universes (Poplawski 2010; Poplawski 2012), connecting the model to Cosmological Natural Selection (Smolin 1992).

These theories employ distinct mechanisms and don’t constitute independent confirmation of a common result. The structural argument selects none of them; it remains neutral among physically adequate continuations that preserve the three Conditions.

*A turnaround without phantom energy.* The turnaround mechanism already named is the one current data least support. Phantom energy requires w < -1, and recent constraints run the other way: DESI combined with supernova compilations favors a present-day equation of state above −1 with a negative evolution parameter, which is the signature of thawing rather than phantom behavior, at 2.5σ to 3.9σ depending on the compilation (Li et al. 2026). The relevant point is that a finite turnaround doesn’t require phantom energy at all. A quintessence field thawing from a nearly flat potential reproduces near-cosmological-constant behavior at present (Scherrer and Sen 2008); if that potential later runs sufficiently negative, it can cancel the positive contributions so that the total energy density and expansion rate reach zero and the branch turns over into contraction (Andrei et al. 2022). The potential becomes negative; the total density reaches zero at the turnaround rather than passing below it. That is condition (iii) satisfied at an instant rather than on a plateau—the middle case of the three zeros already distinguished—with no violation of the null energy condition and no Big Rip. The substitution bears on the conditional argument rather than on the modal floor. It supplies a candidate turnaround whose parameter regime is the one observation is currently drifting toward, in place of one whose regime observation is drifting away from. Whether the potential in fact runs negative is unsettled, and nothing here decides it.

*A turnaround with no dark energy at all.* The two options just canvassed, phantom and thawing, share an assumption worth isolating: that there is a dark-energy component whose equation of state is the quantity in question. A third program denies it. The timescape cosmology treats cosmic acceleration as an artifact of calibration rather than a dynamical effect, arising because clocks and rods in bound systems are calibrated differently from volume-average observers in a genuinely inhomogeneous geometry. The model is statistically homogeneous and isotropic but departs from average Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker evolution, and it replaces dark energy with kinetic gravitational energy and its gradients (Lane et al. 2025).
