It is materially open and organizationally closed. Its components may change while its identity persists because the reproduced organization, not an unchanging inventory, carries the identity. In dormancy, persistence belongs to the organization that the active process made and left capable, from within its own retained structure, of beginning that work again.

Self-production is therefore not unrestricted self-subsistence. A living configuration makes itself only by drawing on a gradient it neither made nor can guarantee. Internally, its production network may be subsistent in the bounded sense of §2.9.3: its parts hold one another up without a privileged internal floor. Externally, it remains dependent on conditions beyond that network. Life is *boundedly* subsistent; Nature alone requires nothing outside itself.

*Life introduces an immanent better-or-worse gradient.* Once a process produces the conditions of its own continuation, environmental and internal states are no longer neutral relative to it. Some sustain closure, some impair it, some preserve a dormant capacity to resume it, and some terminate it. On this account, that relation is biological normativity: a condition can be good or bad *for* a living being according to whether it sustains or degrades that being’s continued self-production or retained capacity to resume it. It isn’t yet moral obligation, conscious preference, or a command issued by Nature, and it doesn’t rule on whether other kinds of value exist. It is the factual relation from which drive and valence can later develop when the living process becomes capable of registering the difference from within.

*Minimal agency begins as regulation.* In an active phase, a living system must respond differently to conditions that sustain it and conditions that threaten it. At its thinnest, agency is this state-sensitive self-regulation: detecting a departure from viable conditions and acting in ways that tend to restore them. No reflective intention is required at this level. Dormancy can suspend the response without erasing the organization disposed to resume it; the disposition is not an occurrent act. But once continued action depends on registration, error becomes possible: the system can respond to conditions as though they were sustaining when they aren’t, or fail to register a threat that is present. This is the biological root of the later distinction between a representation and what it tracks.

*What three traditions were each tracking.* Schrödinger (1944) approached this structure in *What is Life?* by saying that life “feeds on negative entropy”: it extracts order from its environment by exporting disorder. Prigogine developed the energetic side through the chemistry of *dissipative structures*, configurations that maintain themselves far from equilibrium by channeling energy through themselves (Nicolis and Prigogine (1977)). Maturana and Varela (1980) described the closure side as *autopoiesis*: self-production through the same molecules the configuration uses to maintain itself. Each tradition was tracking part of the same fact, and the joining of the two is itself established: Moreno and Mossio (2015) hold organizational closure together with thermodynamic openness under the name *biological autonomy*, which is what separates an organism from an ordinary dissipative structure. The account here draws the same joint and puts it to a different use. Closure names the production side; throughput names the energetic side. Active life occurs when both are present in one configuration: energy passing through the system sustains its continued self-production. A dormant organism remains the same living configuration only while the organization this activity produced still bears its own capacity to resume the joint operation.

*The NASA definition and what the account adds.* Joyce’s widely used astrobiological definition, adopted by NASA, calls life a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution (1994). Its process-first form allows for life unlike terrestrial chemistry. That advantage is accepted here while separating the two components.

*Self-sustaining* names organizational closure, not independence from energy: the recursion produces itself while drawing on a gradient it can’t guarantee. *Darwinian evolution* is population-level. It requires reproduction, heritable variation, and differences affecting persistence or reproductive success. Closure alone supplies none of those conditions.

For lineage-capable life, §4.8.2 therefore adds heritable specification to closure and throughput. A closed living network may satisfy the proposed minimum while founding no evolving lineage. Once reproduction, heritable variation, and differential persistence obtain, the coupling to evolution is strong; it isn’t a strict consequence of closure alone.

*Cleland and the anti-definitional challenge.* Carol Cleland (2012; 2019) argues that the project of defining life is methodologically misguided: science needs a theory of living things (analogous to the molecular theory that replaced pre-scientific definitions of ‘water’) not a definition that adjudicates borderline cases from the armchair. Definitions, on Cleland’s view, substitute conceptual analysis for the empirically grounded theoretical unification that would actually advance the science. The definition invites this challenge directly, and the first move is to concede its form: the temporally extended closure-and-throughput account is a definition in form (a short necessary-and-sufficient statement, set in a definition box) so the reply can’t be that it isn’t a definition. The reply concerns the *source of its warrant*. The account is offered as a *structural characterization* of what the living configuration is modally: the shape any configuration instantiating life must exhibit across active and genuinely dormant phases. It derives that shape from what the cosmic-evolutionary trajectory (§4.7) must make possible for the biological trajectory to begin. It isn’t a stipulative-conceptual definition that settles whether viruses, prions, or fire are alive by armchair necessary-and-sufficient-condition matching. This is closer to Cleland’s own preferred mode (a theoretical characterization grounded in what the phenomenon structurally requires) than to the definitional projects she criticizes. The definition doesn’t claim to resolve every borderline case; it claims that whatever is alive either actively realizes closure plus throughput or retains the organization and internally grounded disposition to resume that realization across its life history. Cleland’s epistemological complaint (we shouldn’t define life before we have the theory) and the present metaphysical claim (life has this structural shape) are therefore orthogonal: her critique targets the substitution of definition for theory, and the theoretical claim is made here, not the definitional substitution.

*Kauffman and self-organizing criticality.* Stuart Kauffman’s autocatalytic-sets program (1993; 1995; 2008) locates the emergence of life in networks of catalytic polymers that collectively catalyze each other’s production, reaching a phase-transition threshold at which the autocatalytic set becomes collectively self-sustaining. Kauffman foregrounds the network-level phase transition rather than the closure of any individual configuration. The structural account takes closure-and-throughput as the characterization of the configuration once the transition has occurred; Kauffman’s autocatalytic-set dynamics describe the mechanism by which the first closure is reached: the *how* of origin, where the definition names the *what* of the result. The accounts are complementary rather than competitive: closure-and-throughput names the structural shape the self-organizing network instantiates at the phase transition, and Kauffman’s dynamics describe the path to that threshold. Where Kauffman would press that edge-of-chaos criticality is itself constitutive of life rather than merely the path to it, the reply is that the criticality is what sustains the throughput (the self-organizing network maintains its closure precisely by operating at the critical regime) so the structural characterization absorbs rather than excludes Kauffman’s insight.

*The design inference, and what the account does and doesn’t lean on.* Because these are generative claims (that undirected dissipative and autocatalytic dynamics can produce, and not merely redescribe, the specified molecular architecture of the first closure), they meet the design inference head-on: Behe’s irreducible complexity and edge-of-evolution limits (1996; 2007) press that observable mechanisms can describe such architecture without being able to build it. Two things keep the definitional claim clear of that dispute. First, the generative supports invoked here—England’s thermodynamic lower-bound work and Kauffman’s autocatalytic criticality—bear on components of the pathway without establishing an integrated origin; the structural characterization names active closure plus throughput and the retained organization of genuine dormancy, and doesn’t stand or fall with either mechanism for how the first life formed. Second, whether specified complexity licenses an inference to a designer is taken up directly at §10.1.11. Its cosmological-scale counterpart, the fine-tuning argument, appears at §10.1.9. Those treatments, not an appeal to ‘emergence,’ govern the verdict. Section §10.1.9 defers precisely the generative half back to Chapter 4: how the immanent operators of change, composition, and constraint produce form rather than presuppose it. What would bear on the generative question empirically isn’t a gap to be plugged by stipulation but the integrated-abiogenesis frontier of §4.8.4: whether geochemistry, protometabolism, polymerization, compartmentalization, and replication can be run together in one sustained system.

*Jablonka-Lamb and the extended evolutionary synthesis.* Eva Jablonka and Marion Lamb (2005) and the extended evolutionary synthesis (Pigliucci and Müller 2010) broaden the heritable variation driving Darwinian evolution beyond strictly genetic inheritance to epigenetic, behavioral, and symbolic dimensions: chromatin-state transmission, learned behaviors passed across generations, symbolic systems as inheritance channels. The claim that Darwinian evolution is downstream of closure-plus-heritable-variation needs to absorb this extension: if heritable variation encompasses epigenetic marks, learned behaviors, and symbolic transmission, then the coupling from closure to evolution covers all four of Jablonka and Lamb’s dimensions, not only the genetic one. The reply is available and structural: closure-and-throughput generates a self-producing recursion that encodes its own state; any encoding mechanism (genetic, epigenetic, behavioral, or symbolic) that preserves variation across reproduction counts as heritable variation in the relevant sense. Evolution under the extended synthesis is still downstream of closure; what the extension shows is that the heritable-variation channel is broader than the genetic channel alone, which the structural account accommodates by treating heritable variation as any encoding of the recursion’s state that persists across reproduction events.

Killer whales supply a concrete behavioral channel. Stable matrilines preserve group-specific call repertoires across generations, and longitudinal change within those repertoires supports vocal learning rather than a wholly fixed genetic signal (Deecke 2000; Yurk 2002). Distinct ecotypes also maintain specialized prey choices and hunting practices through an interaction of social learning, ecology, and genetic divergence (Foote 2016). The inherited item here isn’t a nucleotide sequence but a socially maintained way of navigating, communicating, and obtaining food. Calling the repertoires *dialects* follows the cetacean literature; it doesn’t imply that they instantiate every syntactic or semantic property of human language. The example fixes the structural point at the right strength: lineage information can persist because later organisms learn from earlier ones, so biological inheritance isn’t exhausted by what enters the zygote.

*The first closure.* The first time this happened in the universe (wherever and however it happened) was the moment life began on the present criterion. It wasn’t a new substance. What was new was an organization: a self-producing recursion materially open to energy exchange. Whether the first instance arose at a deep-sea hydrothermal vent, in a surface pond, on a tidal mineral surface, or elsewhere is an empirical question. Its usable energy source had to be non-biological, but that doesn’t decide between autotrophic and heterotrophic origin families. Heterotrophic models propose consumption of organics synthesized abiotically in the environment; they don’t require prior organisms as food. Autotrophic models propose that the first system fixed carbon using geochemical energy. Photosynthesis as extant biology performs it requires evolved molecular machinery, while simpler prebiotic photochemistry remains a live possibility. Solar-thermal driving, wet-dry cycling, ultraviolet chemistry, and redox gradients therefore remain candidate sources of the disequilibrium an origin model must integrate with closure.

No origin is therefore favored merely by eliminating heterotrophy. It requires a sustained non-biological source of free energy, feedstocks, compartmentalization, and chemistry capable of entering self-production. Alkaline hydrothermal vents (Martin and Russell 2003; Lane 2015), surface environments with wet-dry cycling (Powner et al. 2009; Damer and Deamer 2020), mineral-surface catalysis, ultraviolet-driven chemistry, and organic-rich heterotrophic scenarios supply different subsets of those conditions. Chemoautotrophic vent models remain a serious abductive candidate because they integrate persistent redox and proton gradients with mineral compartments; the structural constraint doesn’t select them before the integrated chemistry does.

Life has retained the chemiosmotic shape ever since. The overwhelming majority of cells pump protons across a membrane to build a charge difference, then let that gradient discharge through the molecular machinery that synthesizes the cell’s own components. Some lineages, such as select anaerobic bacteria and archaea, run the same chemiosmotic shape on a sodium-ion gradient instead. Either way, the cell powers its own production by routing a gradient through itself (Mitchell 1961). The first closure inherited a gradient that geology already maintained; subsequent depths learned to build and maintain their own. It was the first time the universe contained a closure that maintained itself by routing energy through itself.

*Life as evolutionary trajectory.* What the first closure inaugurates is an *evolutionary trajectory*: a directional, asymmetrical sequence of states unfolding under temporal asymmetry, energetic constraint, and the openness named at §4.7. Cosmic evolution is one such trajectory, traced in §4.7: cosmic-scale gradients dissipate through an actual history whose wider recurrence remains conditional. Biological evolution is another, given by what closure-and-throughput configurations do once they appear. Which origin environment first supplied the usable gradient remains open; chemoautotrophic vents are one candidate rather than a threshold the cosmic trajectory is known to deliver. The trajectories don’t require one mechanism shared across their scales. They instantiate the same structural conditions at different scales: the cosmic trajectory is what dissipation looks like across the universe as a whole; the biological trajectory is what dissipation looks like across configurations that have closed into self-production.

That first closure already had what subsequent depths elaborate further. To maintain itself, a self-producing recursion must, at minimum, respond differentially to conditions that sustain or threaten it; this account reads that differential responsiveness as a primitive form of self-tracking, though it is this account’s own philosophical extension toward Chapter 5’s fuller treatment of representation, not a claim the thermodynamic or evolutionary literatures cited here establish on their own. Across four billion years, that recursive organization becomes deeper: bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, multicellular organisms, nervous systems, brains, and finally self-modeling that can represent itself. Ecosystem-level constraints, selection, feedback, and coevolution shape that development. This configuration is *life*. What the organism’s self-modeling amounts to is the next question, and it should arrive only after this account has done its work.

The dialectical engagement with consciousness is at §9.1–9.5 and in Chapter 5’s modal account of experience. At issue there are zombie conceivability, the knowledge argument, the explanatory gap, eliminativism, illusionism, and cosmopsychism.

### 4.8.1 The Dispute
The dispute over what life is has divided natural philosophy from the seventeenth century onward. Vitalism (Bergson 1907; Driesch 1908) posited a non-material *élan vital* without which dead chemistry couldn’t produce living systems. Mechanism, from Descartes through La Mettrie (1747) to the molecular biology revolution, responded that life is just chemistry: extra force is unnecessary. Each captures something the other misses, which is why the dispute never settles in either direction.

The disagreement survives in attenuated form in contemporary disputes over what counts as alive. NASA’s working definition (Joyce 1994) calls life a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. By picking out process rather than substrate, it can cover life that might be nothing like Earth life. Standing disagreement remains over boundary cases—viruses, prions, computer simulations of cells, and synthetic biological systems—and over whether self-sustenance and Darwinian evolution are independent criteria or tightly coupled aspects of one structural fact.

A further dispute concerns how those three twentieth-century traditions stand to one another. (Autopoiesis (Greek for “self-“ + “creation/production”) is Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela’s term for a system that continuously produces and regenerates its own components and its own boundary from within, rather than being assembled or maintained by something outside it. A living cell is the paradigm case: it manufactures the very molecules that make up the membrane and machinery doing the manufacturing. It’s the systems-theory precursor to this book’s own vocabulary of a “self-producing recursion” or “closure.”) The traditions have developed largely in isolation, and the literature hasn’t settled whether they are rival accounts, complementary perspectives on different aspects of life, or partial views of one underlying structural fact.

A fourth dispute, sharpened by recent origins-of-life research, concerns the kind of site at which the first closure formed, alkaline hydrothermal vents (Martin and Russell 2003; Lane 2015), warm-little-pond surface chemistry (Powner et al. 2009; Damer and Deamer 2020), mineral-surface catalysis (Wächtershäuser 1988), or other redox-disequilibrium environments, and whether the first energy source was structurally constrained or contingent.

A fifth dispute, older than these and still live at biological scale, is the design inference: whether the specified, apparently irreducible complexity of molecular architecture can be generated by undirected dissipative and selective dynamics or instead licenses an inference to a designer. Behe’s irreducible complexity and edge-of-evolution limits (1996; 2007), Dembski’s design filter (1998), and Meyer’s information argument (2009) press that observable mechanisms describe such architecture without building it, while the biological mainstream (Sober 2008) holds that they can. The present account takes the naturalistic side and engages the inference directly at §10.1.11, with its cosmological-scale counterpart, the fine-tuning argument, at §10.1.9; the sections here carry the generative half of that reply, how the immanent operators of change, composition, and constraint produce form rather than presuppose it.

### 4.8.2 The Requirement
That configuration (closed self-producing recursion coupled to sustained energy throughput) has two minimum constituents for a living instance: a bounded production network and sustained energy throughput. Lineage-capable life adds a third subsystem, heritable specification, which is required for propagation, Darwinian evolution, and cumulative deepening across generations. Joint sufficiency for an origin system remains the structurally predicted open empirical frontier named at §4.8.1. The structural account is committed to the form, not to the chemistry.

*From configuration to consequence.* Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4) fixes the consequence once metaphysical sufficiency has been established: □(P → Q). Strict Actualization (§2.9.4) then gives actual Q from actual P, without a further selector, where P names the proposed configuration and Q the outcome. It doesn’t establish that closure plus sustained throughput is sufficient for life. The identification offered here is stronger than a claim of correlation: a first living instance consists in a bounded self-producing recursion sustained by throughput. If that constitutive identification is complete, its full realization is already a living instance; if some further condition is required, the proposed configuration was incomplete. Which horn the chemistry occupies remains the empirical frontier already named. The modal theorem keeps the consequence exact. It doesn’t settle the frontier in advance.

*The production network.* The closure side of life is a network of components that produce the components that maintain the network. Maturana and Varela (1980) named the structure *autopoiesis*: a system organized as a network of processes of production whose outputs include the very processes that produced them, and whose collective activity reconstitutes the system that does the producing. Kauffman (1986; 1993) described the same closure dimension chemically as an *autocatalytic set*: a set of catalysts in which every member is produced by some reaction within the set, so the set as a whole catalyzes its own continued existence. The two formulations name the same structural fact at different abstractions: a network is closed when its production cycles back to itself.

Closure is what distinguishes the configuration from a flame or a hurricane (§4.8). Dissipative structures channel energy without producing the components that channel it; the autocatalytic network produces its own producers. The network is necessarily *bounded* (components must remain in proximity to interact) but the boundary need not be a phospholipid membrane. Any persistent constraint that holds the production network together against diffusion will do: a mineral pore at a hydrothermal vent, a coacervate droplet (a liquid droplet that spontaneously separates from a surrounding aqueous solution because the macromolecules inside it associate more strongly with one another than with water, concentrating reactive species without requiring a membrane), a vesicle, a cell wall. Boundary type is parochial; boundedness is constitutive.

*The energy gradient.* The throughput side is the configuration’s coupling to a sustained energy gradient that the network dissipates through itself. Schrödinger (1944) named what life feeds on as *negative entropy*: ordered inputs absorbed, disordered outputs released. Prigogine and Nicolis (1977) gave the result thermodynamic teeth; the fluctuation theorems of Jarzynski (1997) and Crooks (1999) supply the formal nonequilibrium-thermodynamics foundations on which contemporary dissipation-and-self-organization arguments rest. Configurations capable of self-replication are favored outcomes in systems strongly coupled to sustained gradients (England (2013) offers one specific articulation of the claim; §4.8.1, §4.8.3). The gradient doesn’t have to be of any particular kind (chemical, thermal, photic, redox) but it has to be *sustained* over the timescales the closure requires to maintain itself. A transient gradient will fuel a flame; only a sustained gradient will fuel a recursion.

The bonds the gradient acts on are themselves nothing new. Covalent, hydrogen, ionic, and dispersive interactions are all expressions of the electromagnetic force already constitutive of Substance (Pauling 1939); the strong and weak nuclear forces operate at sub-atomic scale, gravity at planetary scale and above, and chemistry (including the chemistry of life) runs entirely on electromagnetic interactions. Life therefore introduces no new force. What it introduces is a *configuration* in which a sustained gradient is enrolled to maintain improbable arrangements of interactions that already exist.

A further temporal asymmetry constrains the *first* gradient. At the moment of the first closure, no prior life exists to be consumed, so its usable free-energy source must be non-biological. That excludes extant photosynthesis, heterotrophy on prior organisms, and any other source requiring already evolved machinery; it doesn’t exclude prebiotic photochemistry, wet-dry cycling, thermal gradients, or abiotically produced organics. Redox couples at sites of sustained geochemical disequilibrium are therefore a developed abductive candidate, not a structurally forced answer. The non-biological-source constraint is strict; selection among redox, photic, thermal, and mixed origin environments belongs to integrated chemistry and evidence. Subsequent life can also exploit gradients produced by earlier life.

The coupling is structural. The production network doesn’t merely sit in the gradient; it routes the gradient through itself, transducing the input form into work that maintains the network’s own production. The energy is *enrolled* in the closure rather than passing alongside it. This is what distinguishes life from any dissipative structure: the energy that flows through life flows through life *because* life uses that flow to keep itself producing itself.

*The heritable specification.* The third subsystem is heritable information: a template that specifies the components of the production network with sufficient fidelity that the network can be replicated. Without heritable specification, a closed network can persist for as long as its components hold together, but the closure can’t propagate beyond a single instance, and selection can’t operate. Eigen’s hypercycle (1971) and Gánti’s chemoton (2003) both identify the information subsystem as a third coupled cycle running alongside the metabolic and membrane cycles, each cycle dependent on the others, none reducible to the rest. Joyce’s NASA definition (1994) names the same component when it requires Darwinian evolution: heritable variation under selection presupposes a template that can vary and be inherited.

What the information subsystem adds structurally is the ability of the closure to *outlast its instantiation*. A single closed network is alive while it persists; a network with heritable specification can persist across lineages. The requirement operates at the level of the lineage rather than the individual instance: an organism that can’t itself reproduce (a sterile worker, a post-reproductive individual, a terminally differentiated cell within a multicellular body) still participates in a lineage carrying the template machinery. Heritable variation is necessary for cumulative evolutionary deepening, but it doesn’t guarantee that deepening occurs, much less that it proceeds toward complexity or cognition. Reproduction, differential persistence, ecological conditions, and time determine which trajectories are actually realized.

A further origin problem concerns the relation between template and catalysis. Modern life separates much of that labor between DNA and protein enzymes, but the protein machinery is itself a product of templated synthesis. An origin account therefore owes a non-circular route by which templating and catalysis become jointly available before the modern division of labor exists. Combining both functions in one molecular class is one parsimonious solution, not the only structure logic permits; co-emergent molecular classes, mineral catalysis, or other scaffolds remain candidates. RNA-world scenarios are prominent because RNA can serve as a readable sequence and fold into catalytic ribozymes (Gilbert 1986; Joyce 2002). That dual capacity is experimentally established; the claim that an RNA world was Earth’s historical first heritable system remains an unresolved hypothesis.

*Three coupled cycles.* The synthesis is Gánti’s: lineage-capable life operates through three coupled cycles, metabolic (autocatalytic production), membrane (self-maintained boundary), and informational (template replication). Remove metabolism and the membrane and template have no source of components; remove the membrane and the metabolism dissipates and the template diffuses; remove the template and the living closure may persist as an individual instance but doesn’t propagate or enter Darwinian evolution. The chemoton is therefore a minimum structural decomposition of an origin system capable of cumulative lineage-level evolution, not an additional requirement imposed on every living individual. Kauffman’s autocatalytic sets, Maturana and Varela’s autopoiesis, Eigen’s hypercycles, Deacon’s autogen (2012), and the NASA–Joyce definition each foreground one or two of these cycles; the structural account proposes that all three are required for lineage-capable life regardless of the chemistry that implements them. Whether this exhausts every conceivable nonreproducing or non-Darwinian mode of life isn’t something the cited literature settles; closure plus throughput remains the individual-level criterion.

This is the structural anatomy. The chain it predicts is traced at §4.8.3, and read against the empirical literature at §4.8.4.

### 4.8.3 Predictions
If Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality are the necessary conditions of any possible medium (§§1–2), they fix the structural preconditions on which any thermodynamic regime must operate: a quantity that persists under transformation (Substance, bearer of Φ), distributed across locations distinct from one another (Space, bearer of S), evolving through successive moments (Time, bearer of T). The modal Triconditions don’t, on their own, entail that such a medium will sustain energy gradients or that dissipation will follow the statistical form of the second law. Those features depend on additional physical assumptions (about initial conditions, energy distributions, and the specific laws this universe instantiates) which thermodynamics, not modal logic, supplies. What the Triconditions establish is the necessary medium; what thermodynamics adds, given that medium, is the dynamics.

The chain traced in the analysis that follows (from gradients through dissipative cycles through self-maintenance through a constitutive inside) isn’t a strict entailment of T, S, Φ alone. Whether a given medium supplies sustained gradients at all is a contingent, empirical matter, not fixed by the Triconditions. If gradients and closure jointly exhaust what a first living instance requires, their realization isn’t merely favorable to life but constitutive of it. Whether they exhaust the requirements is the open empirical burden. The convergent verdict of thermodynamics, evolutionary theory, and predictive processing concerns both that burden and what those conditions select for downstream of a first closure.

Within particular nonequilibrium regimes, dissipation can support the formation and persistence of organized structures. It doesn’t follow that nature universally selects configurations simply because they dissipate more thoroughly; maximum-dissipation principles and their scope remain contested. At low complexity, energy transport can take organized forms: heating a shallow fluid layer from below can generate Bénard cells, and temperature gradients can sustain hurricanes. These are dissipative structures with no biology in them and no self-model (Prigogine and Stengers 1984). Work in nonequilibrium thermodynamics and statistical physics investigates conditions under which driven systems form or maintain more intricate cycles (Prigogine and Nicolis 1977; England 2013). The structural account treats such work as one possible way toward the conditions of life, not as a general theorem that dissipation alone selects complexity.

The chain becomes more demanding at self-maintenance. Some organisms maintain themselves by sensing environmental conditions, regulating exchanges, and coordinating internal processes. Predictive-processing and related approaches offer one framework for understanding this organization, but they don’t establish that every self-maintaining dissipative configuration predicts, represents, or self-models in the same sense. The transition from chemical self-maintenance to cognition and experience is therefore an empirical and philosophical frontier, not a consequence of dissipation alone.

On the model developed here, sufficiently recursive self-maintenance can be described as having an “inside”: a system tracks aspects of its own condition in relation to its environment. Whether even bacterial chemotaxis warrants the language of cognition or an inside is disputed; work on bacterial cognition (Lyon 2015) and minimal cognitive architectures (Ginsburg and Jablonka 2019; Levin 2019) supplies proposals rather than a settled result. The stronger claim, that phenomenal interiority scales continuously with recursive self-modeling, is a positive thesis for Chapter 5 to argue, not a conclusion already delivered by thermodynamics or origins-of-life research.

The proposed chain therefore has conditional scope. Where a medium supplies sustained gradients, suitable chemistry, and the additional conditions for closure, replication, and selection, some forms of self-maintaining organization may emerge. Modal Invariance secures neither gradients nor life across every possible configuration; these depend on contingent physical and cosmological conditions. If the cyclic and macro-transmission premises of §4.6–4.7 hold, comparable conditions may recur in kind while particular histories vary. What any such organization is like from within, and whether recursive self-modeling yields phenomenal interiority, are argued for in Chapter 5, not assumed.

### 4.8.4 Confirmation
Several scientific literatures bear on components of the structural model of life: nonequilibrium thermodynamics, origins-of-life research, and evolutionary theory. They don’t independently establish one agreed definition of life, nor do they converge on a single empirically confirmed way from dissipation to cognition. They provide evidence about the conditions under which organized, self-maintaining, and evolving systems can arise. The book’s closure-and-throughput identification is a philosophical synthesis of that literature, not a result thermodynamics or evolutionary theory establishes on its own. Predictive processing is treated separately at §5.2.2.

*Thermodynamics.* The dissipative-structure account set out at §4.8.2 is where the empirical weight sits. The fluctuation theorems of Jarzynski (1997) and Crooks (1999) establish general relations between work, free energy, and entropy production in nonequilibrium processes; they don’t themselves say anything specifically about self-replication. England (2013) derives thermodynamic lower bounds on the heat produced by self-replication, situating replication within that general framework. Broader claims that driven systems are thereby favored toward self-replication or adaptive organization require further assumptions and remain contested; they aren’t direct consequences of the fluctuation theorems or of the lower bound alone. The second law supplies a constraint under which living structures operate. Living systems persist under that constraint by channeling energy through metabolic cycles rather than relaxing to equilibrium.

Thermodynamics supplies constraints and models relevant to the structural identification §4.8 advances: self-replication and self-maintenance require sustained free-energy throughput and entropy export. Whether such configurations are generally favored outcomes, how likely they are to originate, and whether they are attractors under realistic prebiotic conditions remain open questions. Its modal claims are distinct from these empirical matters. At most, thermodynamics shows that the structural picture is compatible with the behavior of dissipative systems under some specified conditions.

*Chemoautotrophic origin.* The first life, if it arose without earlier biology, required non-biological sources of usable free energy. Alkaline hydrothermal vents are a major and productive hypothesis: Martin and Russell (2007), Lane (2015), Lane and Martin (2012), Sojo et al. (2016), and Weiss et al. (2016) develop arguments concerning natural proton gradients, geochemical disequilibrium, and reconstructions of LUCA. These sources don’t establish the origin site or demonstrate that first life used the same metabolism inferred for LUCA. Surface wet-dry cycling, UV-driven chemistry, and other proposals remain live. The literature supports chemical disequilibrium as an important constraint, not an exact confirmation of a specific origin narrative.

*The RNA world.* The empirical literature also bears on the problem of heritable specification. RNA can both carry sequence information and catalyze reactions, making RNA-world scenarios an important hypothesis. This doesn’t yet constitute an empirical answer for the first heritable subsystem on Earth: the pathway from prebiotic chemistry to sustained RNA replication and integrated protocells remains unresolved. Cech (1981) and Guerrier-Takada et al. (1983) independently demonstrated that RNA can catalyze chemical reactions (the ribozyme discovery, awarded the Nobel Prize in 1989), establishing the catalysis half of the duality. In the ribosome, the peptidyl transferase center that catalyzes peptide bond formation is itself a ribozyme (Nissen et al. 2000). That locates an RNA catalytic core inside contemporary protein synthesis and supports RNA-world scenarios in which RNA catalysis preceded the full protein apparatus. Contemporary translation also depends on essential protein machinery, so the active-site result does not reduce the entire present system to RNA catalysis. Lincoln and Joyce (2009) demonstrated cross-replicating ribozymes in laboratory conditions, showing RNA-only self-replication is achievable. Sutherland’s group (Powner et al. 2009; Patel et al. 2015) has shown that nucleotides, amino acids, and lipid precursors can all be synthesized from a common pool of simple feedstock molecules (HCN, cyanamide, hydrogen sulfide, UV), providing the prebiotic chemistry that bridges geochemistry to RNA. The convergence is close at the level this account predicts: the first heritable medium combined catalysis with template-readability. On Earth, that medium was plausibly RNA before the catalytic role specialized into proteins and the template role specialized into DNA. The integrated demonstration remains an open empirical frontier, so “exact” would overstate how settled the RNA-world picture is.

*Lab-confirmed prebiotic and protocell chemistry.* The component reactions of the chemoautotrophic-origin and RNA-world pictures are increasingly demonstrable in the laboratory. Becker et al. (2019) extended the Sutherland synthesis to a unified prebiotic pathway producing all four canonical RNA nucleotides (purines and pyrimidines) from a common feedstock. Muchowska, Varma, and Moran (2017; 2019) demonstrated non-enzymatic versions of the reverse Krebs cycle catalyzed by Fe⁰ and other transition metals, supplying the non-enzymatic protometabolic chemistry this account requires. Herschy et al. (2014) and Hudson et al. (2020) demonstrated CO₂ reduction to organic molecules in bench-scale alkaline-vent reactors driven by natural pH gradients across thin mineral barriers, instantiating the chemiosmotic-origin hypothesis at laboratory scale. On the protocell side, Adamala and Szostak (2013) demonstrated non-enzymatic RNA template copying inside fatty-acid vesicles, and Wochner et al. (2011) and Horning and Joyce (2016) extended the Lincoln–Joyce work toward general RNA-catalyzed RNA polymerization. The component steps of the structural picture are reproducibly demonstrable; the integrated demonstration (running geochemistry, protometabolism, polymerization, compartmentalization, and replication together in a single sustained system) is the open empirical frontier.

*The metabolism-first / replicator-first debate.* Origin-of-life research remains divided among metabolism-first (Wächtershäuser 1988; Martin and Russell 2003; Lane 2015), replicator-first (Eigen 1971; Joyce 2002), and hybrid or co-emergence approaches. Gánti’s chemoton (§4.8.2) offers a useful model in which metabolic, boundary, and informational cycles are coupled, but it doesn’t make the historical sequencing question malformed. The book’s model favors integrated closure as the target that an origin account must eventually explain; it doesn’t establish that all three cycles began simultaneously or that existing research programs have converged on co-emergence (Damer and Deamer 2020; Smith and Morowitz 2016).

*The early-emergence puzzle bears on the sufficiency reading.* Configurational Necessitation doesn’t fix closure-and-throughput’s sufficiency a priori; the identification carries that burden. Earth’s timing supplies limited abductive evidence relevant to it. Earth became habitable around 4.4 billion years ago, after the Theia impact and the formation of liquid oceans. The earliest accepted biosignatures appear at 3.7 to 3.5 billion years ago (stromatolites; carbon isotopic signatures), with contested earlier evidence from Hadean zircons (Mojzsis et al. 1996; Bell et al. 2015). On the accepted dates, the window from habitability to life is therefore on the order of 700 to 900 million years; the contested zircon evidence would shorten it. That remains geologically rapid. On the present account, sustained gradient conditions make life a reachable attractor on whatever timescale the chemistry permits. The Earth datum is more expected on a high-reachability account than on some rare-accident priors, but one observed biosphere can’t establish metaphysical sufficiency.

Complex observers can only find themselves on a timeline where abiogenesis occurred early enough to leave time for observers to evolve before their star’s main-sequence window closed. This observation-selection effect, Carter’s anthropic argument (1983), predicts an early-looking origin *even if* abiogenesis were rare, so a single datum can’t cleanly separate ‘fast because favored’ from ‘fast because we couldn’t have observed it otherwise.’ Bayesian analyses of the lone Earth datum bear this out: Kipping’s re-analysis (2020) finds that early emergence yields only a modest update toward rapid abiogenesis once the selection effect is folded in. The datum is consistent with the constitutive identification and supplies a modest update at most; its selection-filtered slightness leaves the identification to be earned by structural analysis and integrated chemistry, not chronology.

*Enzymatic completion after LUCA bears on metabolic assembly, not on a second origin of life.* Mrnjavac et al. (2026) reconstruct the metabolic enzymes of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) and argue that its enzymatic network was incomplete: native transition metals and phosphite could have supplied catalytic and energetic functions later carried by enzymes and cofactors. They further infer that bacterial and archaeal lineages completed parts of that enzymatic network independently, in some cases evolving structurally distinct, non-homologous enzymes for the same core reactions. The result supports a gradual internalization of metabolic catalysis after the shared ancestor. It doesn’t establish that LUCA was nonliving or lacked the closure-and-throughput organization defined here; dependence on environmental catalysts isn’t by itself failure of biological closure. Nor does independent enzymatic completion amount to two independent crossings from nonlife to life. The study therefore bears on how an already inherited metabolism was assembled and internalized, not on the frequency with which living closure originates. Its reconstruction is substantial and revisable, and it shouldn’t be counted as a second abiogenesis-like data point.

*Evolutionary theory.* A second line arrives through the evolutionary theory of cognitive architecture and the theory of major transitions. At lower levels of organismic complexity, relatively direct stimulus–response can be sufficient for persistence in some settings. A plant orienting toward light, or a chemotactic bacterium following a gradient, maintains itself through relatively local coupling between sensor and effector. The coupling can be described as the system tracking its own state—the bacterium’s tumble-and-run is, in form, a registration of its gradient position—but the recursive depth attributed to it remains shallow on this account.

This strategy has limits where temporal horizons lengthen, relational complexity increases, and the fitness costs of prediction error grow. In those settings, selection can favor configurations that track not only current inputs but probable future states, and not only external conditions but the system’s own position within them (Godfrey-Smith 1996; Sterelny 2003). Recursive self-modeling is one stable response when shallower coupling no longer supplies enough anticipatory control; distributed variation is another, under the conditions described next. Research on increasingly complex cognitive architectures—from bacterial cognition (Lyon 2015), through unlimited associative learning (Ginsburg and Jablonka 2019), to integrated neural processing in cephalopods and mammals (Godfrey-Smith 2016)—is consistent with the hypothesis that some later systems model their own activity through more layers. It doesn’t establish a universal evolutionary sequence.

*Where the tracking is housed.* Deepening individual self-modeling is one solution to the persistence problem, not the only one, and the alternative is instructive about what the first one costs. A lineage facing variable conditions can invest in an apparatus that models those conditions, or it can forgo the apparatus and distribute the coverage across its own variation, generating phenotypes stochastically at population sizes and generation rates that leave some fraction of them apt whatever the conditions turn out to be (Kussell and Leibler 2005). Bacterial persistence, sporulation, and phase variation are the canonical instances of the second strategy (Balaban et al. 2004; Veening et al. 2008), and clonal selection in the vertebrate immune system runs it inside an organism rather than across one. Which strategy a lineage runs is an economic matter rather than a matter of organism size: modeling pays where cues are reliable and the apparatus is cheap relative to the fitness variance it averts, and randomizing pays where cues are poor or the apparatus is dear. Donaldson-Matasci, Bergstrom, and Lachmann (2010) make the trade-off quantitative, showing that the fitness value of a developmental cue equals the reduction in uncertainty about the environment it supplies. This specifies the conditions under which recursive self-modeling may be the response selection reaches, and it isolates what the apparatus buys. Distributed coverage is limited to the range its variation spans and fails when conditions move outside that range. An interior model can be prospective, representing conditions that haven’t yet obtained. The saturation argument therefore applies where anticipation earns its keep, at lengthening horizons and rising costs of prediction error, and not wherever variation is merely cheap. It identifies a selective route, not an inevitable next stage.

The major evolutionary transitions framework (Maynard Smith and Szathmáry 1995) names the discrete steps in this scaling: replicating molecules to cells, prokaryotes to eukaryotes, single cells to multicellularity, asexual to sexual reproduction, individuals to colonies, primate sociality to language. Each transition is a system-level reorganization in which the unit of selection nests inside a larger unit, and the larger unit’s recursion runs deeper than its parts could individually. Niche construction theory (Odling-Smee et al. 2003) names the reciprocal-causation feedback by which organisms modify each other’s selection environments, deepening the biosphere’s internal complexity over time.

Animal architecture is this feedback made durable outside the body. Spider webs extend sensing and prey capture; beaver dams reorganize water, shelter, and the local habitat; termite mounds regulate a colony’s living conditions; birds assemble structures whose material, geometry, insulation, concealment, and access routes answer recurring environmental problems (Laidre 2021). The point isn’t analogy by courtesy: these are built arrangements that redirect the medium around the organism and alter what the organism and its descendants can do next. Some building variation is culturally maintained as well. Neighboring groups of white-browed sparrow weavers construct measurably different nest and roost forms that remain stable across years, aren’t explained by measured weather, body size, tree height, or genetic relatedness, and persist when birds immigrate between groups (Tello-Ramos 2024). Human architecture is exceptional in cumulative scale, explicit planning, symbolic form, and institutional transmission. The capacity to build complex, adaptive, and even group-styled structures isn’t uniquely human.

*Independent reachability of major transitions.* Several of the major transitions Maynard Smith and Szathmáry name have been reached independently many times across the tree of life, and some have been reproduced under laboratory selection. Multicellularity has originated independently at least twenty-five times, once in animals, multiple times in green algae, independently in red algae, brown algae, and fungi, in several bacterial lineages (filamentous cyanobacteria, myxobacteria, actinomycetes), and in the slime molds, supplying convergent evidence that the unicell-to-multicell transition is reproducibly reachable from substantially different starting points (Grosberg and Strathmann 2007; Bonner 1998). Ratcliff et al. (2012) evolved multicellularity *de novo* in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* in approximately sixty generations of selection for fast settling, the “snowflake yeast” demonstration, and Boraas, Seale, and Boxhorn (1998), with later replication by Herron et al. (2019), evolved multicellular *Chlorella* colonies under flagellate-predation pressure. Eukaryogenesis, by contrast, appears to have occurred once on Earth (Lane 2015). The syntrophy hypothesis of its mechanism is being filled in by Imachi et al. (2020). Their first laboratory cultivation of an Asgard archaeon (*Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum*) showed the kind of obligate metabolic exchange with bacterial partners that the hypothesis requires, building on the genomic bridging work of Spang et al. (2015). The pattern is consistent with this account: several major transitions are reproducibly reachable from independent starting points. It supports a reachability claim for those cases, not a general law that every transition whose conditions persist will be reached many times.

Coevolutionary dynamics complete the picture at the relational level. Predator/prey arms races, host/parasite arms races, signaler/receiver arms races: each is a pairing in which selection on one population creates selection pressure on another, and the ecosystem’s internal information processing thickens as the arms races elaborate. The social intelligence hypothesis (Humphrey 1976) and the Machiavellian intelligence hypothesis (Byrne and Whiten 1988) name the empirical pattern at the cognitive end of the same dynamic: primate cognition evolved primarily under social complexity rather than environmental complexity, because the hardest thing in a primate’s environment is other primates. Theory of mind requires other minds to bear it on; modeling another mind that is modeling you requires depth of recursion no isolated lineage could produce on its own.

The pattern already surveyed—reproducible major transitions, coevolutionary arms races, and recursive self-modeling scaling with social and ecological complexity—is this account’s reading of evolutionary theory as converging with the thermodynamic picture; it draws on selected, well-documented examples rather than a result evolutionary theory establishes as a general law on its own terms. Read that way, under sustained energy gradients recursive self-modeling deepens, the biosphere reorganizes through discrete major transitions, and the directional pressure runs at the ecosystem level rather than at any single lineage.

### 4.8.5 Conclusions
The strict result and the proposed identification now separate cleanly. Every living process must instantiate ordered exchange, relational articulation, and cross-interval bearing across its life history. Active closure plus sustained throughput, with retained organization internally disposed to resume that activity across genuine dormancy, is this account’s proposed minimal physical realization of those roles; its completeness, origin frequency, and evolutionary consequences remain answerable to biology. The implications follow in turn under those different weights.

*Mechanism and the vital supplement.* Vitalism (Bergson 1907; Driesch 1908) posited a non-material *élan vital* without which chemistry couldn’t produce living systems. Mechanistic accounts deny the extra force and explain life through organized physical processes. The structural result establishes a precise constraint on the dispute. Any vital principle that sustains, organizes, or directs a concrete living process must enter ordered, differentiated, persisting relations and therefore instantiate the three Conditions; one that enters none makes no determinate contribution to the process. That removes the explanatory advantage of a structurally external vital force without proving that closure plus throughput is empirically complete. Mechanism still owes the organization, and the proposed identification names the organization it must test.

*The biosphere as a candidate higher-level closure.* Evolutionary theory recognizes selection and feedback at several levels: genes, organisms, kin groups, populations, and, in some accounts, communities or ecosystems. Niche construction and biogeochemical feedback can stabilize conditions compatible with continued life. Gaia-style models (Lovelock and Margulis 1974; Lenton 1998; Schellnhuber 2009) investigate that regulation without requiring teleology. Whether the biosphere itself forms a closed self-producing individual, rather than a network of interacting lineages and environments, is a further claim and remains contested. The structural account may test that possibility with the same closure criterion it applies elsewhere; it can’t assume the higher-level closure from the existence of feedback alone.

*Universality, descent, and structural identity.* The genealogical universality of known Earth life (shared genetic code, shared chirality, shared chemiosmosis) is standardly read as evidence that all extant life descends from a single ancestor (LUCA, the Last Universal Common Ancestor, or a LUCA-like community in the formulations of Woese 1998; and Doolittle 1999). This account requires keeping three claims separate. First, that all life shares a *structural identity*: closure plus sustained energy throughput, with heritable specification added by any lineage-capable instance (§4.8.2). Every organism in the genealogical record is lineage-capable, so all three subsystems are present across known life; the identity claim about *living instances as such* remains the two-part one, and the extant record is evidence about a population of lineage members rather than about the minimum. Second, that known Earth life shares a *chemical instantiation*: DNA, RNA, ATP, L-amino acids, D-sugars. Third, that known Earth life shares a *genealogy*: descent from one ancestor or community. On the present account the first is necessary. The structural criterion doesn’t select the second, but nonselection alone doesn’t prove that another chemistry is metaphysically possible; that requires an independently warranted alternative. The third is empirical. Life elsewhere, if realized through another independently possible chemistry, could share the structural identity without sharing Earth’s chemistry or genealogy.

*Incumbency and the universality of Earth life.* If closure plus throughput is complete, whether and where it’s realized remains empirical. The universality of Earth life’s chemistry is ordinarily explained by common descent from LUCA or a LUCA-like community. Ecological incumbency supplies a further hypothesis: an early lineage can restructure its chemical environment and pre-empt niches, making later independent origins harder to establish or detect. Priority effects (Fukami 2015) and large biological reorganizations such as the Great Oxygenation Event show that established life transforms the conditions later systems encounter. They don’t establish that multiple origins occurred or that incumbency explains the observed universality.

Any later independent origin would face an environment already altered by life and might fail, remain marginal, or be assimilated into existing ecologies. That possibility motivates searches for a shadow biosphere (Davies 2011), but CPR bacteria, DPANN archaea, and giant viruses (La Scola et al. 2008; Forterre 2010) aren’t evidence of independent origins merely because their placement is difficult. Common descent remains the evidentially supported account of known life; many origins under incumbency is compatible with the structural model but presently speculative.

*Lottery vs. attractor: the empirical signature.* Abiogenesis isn’t well represented by multiplying unconditional probabilities for independent stages where earlier products alter the conditions of later reactions. Nucleotides affect polymer formation; polymers affect catalytic networks; networks affect compartmentalized replication. The correct probabilities are conditional on the evolving chemical state. That correction doesn’t make abiogenesis probable. A chain of dependent stages can still contain extremely low conditional transition probabilities, bottlenecks, degradation routes, or incompatible environments. Reproducible component chemistry and repeated evolutionary transitions show that some parts of the larger sequence are reachable from more than one starting point; they don’t establish that the integrated origin of life is an attractor. The empirical discriminator is whether integrated systems repeatedly approach closure under independently varied realistic conditions. Until that demonstration exists, both rare-event and attractor descriptions carry burdens the present evidence doesn’t settle.

*Convergence and non-teleology of cognitive depth.* Cephalopods and vertebrates developed complex nervous systems, flexible behavior, and problem-solving along deeply separated evolutionary lineages. Their convergence shows that some forms of cognitive complexity aren’t confined to one vertebrate architecture. The differences matter as much as the similarities: cephalopod neural organization, extensive A-to-I RNA editing (Liscovitch-Brauer et al. 2017), and genome structure (Albertin et al. 2015) don’t establish that both lineages reached one determinate endpoint or the same kind of self-model. Most successful terrestrial lineages also persist without comparable cognitive depth (Bar-On et al. 2018). The Earth record therefore supports a bounded claim: complex cognition is multiply realizable under some ecological pressures and isn’t a universal evolutionary destination. Whether it is generally reachable in long-lived extraterrestrial ecosystems can’t be inferred from one biosphere and remains an astrobiological hypothesis.

*Abductive preference among origin environments.* Structural neutrality is retained here on chirality, polymer chemistry, and exact catalyst while favoring environments that can jointly sustain disequilibrium, compartmentalization, feedstock production, and coupled reaction cycles. Alkaline hydrothermal vents are a developed candidate because they combine redox and pH gradients with mineral compartments (Martin and Russell 2007; Lane and Martin 2012; Lane 2015; Sojo et al. 2016; Weiss et al. 2016). Warm-little-pond and wet-dry models (Damer and Deamer 2020), ultraviolet-driven cyanosulfidic chemistry, iron-sulfur surface chemistry, and heterotrophic organic-rich environments supply competing integrations. The model that most completely realizes the constraint-set may be preferred here, but current component evidence doesn’t establish one origin site or require every successful rival to converge on chemiosmosis.

*Astrobiology and the structural prediction of life elsewhere.* The three Conditions hold wherever concrete change is realized; particular gradients, laws, and chemical opportunities don’t follow from that necessity. No universal frequency of life is therefore predicted. Its substrate-neutral constraint is narrower: any extraterrestrial living instance must preserve organized identity through ordered exchange across a differentiated boundary, whatever chemistry realizes that work. Active closure plus sustained throughput, with retained organization capable from within of resuming that activity across dormancy, is the proposed minimum; whether the proposal omits a further condition and how often complete realizations assemble remain empirical. Long-lived ecosystems may make complex cognition more reachable by multiplying niches and coevolutionary pressures, but one terrestrial biosphere can’t establish that generalization.

The disequilibrium constraint sharpens astrobiological targets without selecting one terrestrial origin family. Bodies with persistent free-energy gradients and environments capable of supporting complex chemistry are natural candidates: early Mars, Europa, Enceladus, Titan, and chemically active exoplanets. Enceladus, for example, shows silica nanograins consistent with warm water–rock reactions (Hsu et al. 2015) and molecular hydrogen consistent with serpentinization, though no seafloor vent has been directly observed. These observations identify promising conditions, not complete constitutive configurations. Whether any site integrates feedstocks, compartments, catalysis, heredity, and self-maintenance remains empirical.

*Viruses and the boundary of life.* Viruses are a hard boundary case in biology, and this account locates the boundary precisely. A virus has heritable genetic information and evolves by natural selection: it satisfies the Darwinian component of the NASA definition. But it has no self-producing recursion of its own. Outside a host cell, a virus does nothing: no metabolism, no energy throughput, no self-maintenance. That inactivity does not make a free virion equivalent to a dormant organism. The dormant organism retains an organization internally disposed to resume its own self-production; the virion must recruit a host’s closure machinery to be produced at all. It is structured information encoded in Substance, capable of being read by another organism’s closure machinery and causing that machinery to produce copies of the virus. The production is real; what is absent is any closure that belongs to the virus itself. The virus recruits another organism’s self-production without having self-production.

This is why the question of whether viruses are alive isn’t a question about parasitism. Parasitic organisms (tapeworms, ticks, parasitic plants) are fully alive: they have their own self-producing recursions, they metabolize, they maintain themselves, they have an inside. What makes them parasitic is that they draw their energy from a host rather than directly from the environment. The closure is present; only the energy source is borrowed. Under the closure-and-throughput criterion this account adopts, viruses are different in kind, not degree: they lack closure entirely. On that criterion, a virus is structurally closer to a crystal or a prion (a pattern in Substance that causes its own replication under the right conditions) than to even the simplest living cell. This is the boundary the present account’s criterion draws, not an independent resolution of the wider dispute over whether viruses count as alive; the line it draws isn’t at complexity, not at cell membranes, not at the presence of DNA, but at whether a self-producing recursion is present at all.

*Synthetic biology and what counts as alive.* The account also bears on synthetic biology and whether non-natural systems can count as alive. The criterion is structural: active closure plus sustained energy throughput, or the retained organization of that process in a genuinely dormant phase. On that criterion, a computer simulation that runs a model of a self-maintaining cell isn’t alive: the simulation is a model, not a closure. A wet-chemistry artificial cell that genuinely closes its production cycle and dissipates energy through itself counts as alive by that criterion, regardless of how it was assembled. If it later suspends that work, it remains alive only while its own retained organization bears the capacity to resume; an external builder’s ability to reconstruct it would not suffice. The line this account draws is at structural function, not biological history; a framework that individuates life differently could draw it elsewhere. This is consistent with the NASA definition’s process-rather-than-substrate orientation while clarifying what the process consists in.

The site and metabolic mode of the first closure on Earth remain empirically open. This commits to sustained non-biological free energy and an organization capable of approaching self-production. Alkaline hydrothermal vents, surface environments with wet-dry cycling, mineral-surface catalysis, ultraviolet-driven chemistry, and heterotrophic use of abiotically produced organics remain live origin families. Their standing depends on how completely each integrates the required chemistry, not on a modal selection of one site.

The genealogical question, single origin and shared ancestry (LUCA or a LUCA-like community) versus many independent origins under ecological incumbency lock-in, is empirically open. The structural-identity claim doesn’t depend on its resolution, but resolving it remains a live target for paleobiology, comparative genomics, and the search for any surviving shadow biosphere lineages (Davies 2011).

Whether life elsewhere shares Earth’s chemistry or only its structural organization is a central astrobiological question. A substrate-neutral search constraint is supplied here—organized persistence through sustained exchange in active phases, with retained capacity to resume across dormant ones—and that diachronic structure is proposed as its minimum. It doesn’t determine how frequently that organization occurs or which chemistry realizes it. Whether biosignatures are detectable at early Mars, Europa, Enceladus, Titan, or across the exoplanet population remains open.

The deepest open empirical question is whether the cosmic-evolutionary trajectory’s apparent directionality toward cognitive depth is robust across cycles or an artifact of the one history we observe. Any broader conclusion depends on sustained ecological complexity, social-coevolutionary depth, and niche pressure for recursive self-modeling. Cephalopod–vertebrate convergence makes the question tractable but doesn’t by itself settle the cross-cycle generality.

And the boundary between marginal cases (viruses, prions, complex computer simulations, sufficiently sophisticated synthetic-biology constructs) and genuine instances of life is sharpened by the closure-and-throughput criterion but admits practical adjudication only case by case as new candidates arise.

*Forward handoff to Chapter 5.* The outside account of life ends at the active closure-and-throughput configuration, together with the organization that can retain its internally grounded capacity across dormancy, as observed from without. What a sufficiently deep self-modeling configuration is like *from within* isn’t supplied by thermodynamics or by the structural constraint on life. The identification of awareness with the interior aspect (§5.1) of the living organization is argued for once the ground established in §4.1–4.8 is in place. The dialectical engagement with the standard rival accounts of mind (the hard problem and the conceivability arguments, Russellian monism, idealism, eliminativism and illusionism, and cosmopsychism) is the work of §9.1–9.5.

## 4.9 Synthesis

Within the modal framework already derived, Nature is structurally sufficient. The case runs through Time, Space, and Substance; their joint instantiation; singularity constraints and candidate cosmologies; cosmic history; and life, keeping the structural claims treated as settled apart from the constants, mechanisms, and historical particulars that remain open to scientific inquiry.

Taken together, what has been established is the case the title names: within that framework, Nature suffices for the structural and empirical work at issue. No external supplement is required by physics to initiate motion, source extension, or deposit substance—a conclusion conditional on the Chapter 2 modal core rather than free-standing. Some proposed supplements are structurally precluded where they remove the conditions required for the role they claim to perform; others are empirically and explanatorily idle because Nature already supplies the relevant work. A transcendent or essence-prior posit that declines to make a determinate empirical or grounding claim isn’t dissolved by any of this; it remains a further metaphysical proposal, and its credentials are assessed in Chapters 7, 8, and 10.

*Sufficiency isn’t completeness.* To say that Nature is sufficient isn’t to say that Nature has been fully explained, or that the sciences have no open questions. It is to say that the remaining explanations are sought within Nature rather than supplied by an external structural source. Unknown mechanisms, unsettled interpretations, missing observations, and incomplete theories remain genuine unknowns. The sufficiency claim relocates those questions; it doesn’t answer them by declaration.

Three structural commitments come first: Temporality (§4.2), Spatiality (§4.3), and Substantiality (§4.4) are jointly necessary within that framework. Their comparison with the A/B dispute, substantivalism and relationalism, and matter/energy ontologies is interpretive; physics doesn’t deductively establish the modal claims.

The realizations then get more concrete. Spacetime, field and quantum-state structure, conservation, and symmetry are examined at §4.5. Strict preclusion of a zero-extension terminus is separated at §4.6 from continuation and return, which rest on named premises, and from the physical mechanisms a cycle would need. Necessary type is separated from determinate token at §4.7 without settling quantum interpretation. Life’s minimal physical organization is proposed as closure plus throughput at §4.8, with origins and completeness left answerable to biology.

One through-line runs across all of them. Several familiar oppositions can be read as tracking different aspects of a broader structural picture: tensed and tenseless descriptions, extension and relation, persistence and activity, lawful constraint and determinate history, and mechanism and organization. That is a proposed reframing, not a claim that the historical or scientific disputes have been conclusively dissolved. Each comparison keeps the qualifications of its own literature and empirical domain.

The strict constraint is uniform across layers. A supplement that performs concrete work must distinguish before from after, locate its contribution within a differentiated domain, and bear determinate capacities through that contribution. It therefore instantiates the temporal, spatial, and substantial roles whose unity is Nature. If it declines those roles, it performs no determinate physical work.

Two corroborative routes strengthen that no-supplement pressure without repeating the loaded derivation (Chapter 3). The No-Individuating-Surplus (§3.4.3) test removes an idle residue; the Grounding Trilemma (§3.4.4) blocks a merely redescribed external grounding role. Both corroborate closure without substituting for the proof of T∧S∧Φ.

The general result is therefore not that every rival has already been disproved. It is that no concretely efficacious rival stands outside the structural field it purports to supplement. A merely noncausal ground is a different proposal, examined in Chapters 7, 8, and 10.

The stronger realization-level claims remain tiered. A past-eternal cosmology or particular bounce is not established (§4.6.5), token fine-tuning is not settled (§4.7.5), and no origins theory for life is completed (§4.8.5). Each proposal leans on the Chapter 2 modal core without becoming a theorem of it.

What remains open is also uniform. The type is fixed at every layer; the specific tokens are empirical and corrigible. Their actuality establishes their necessary possibility; contingency follows only where alternatives are independently warranted. Whether a bounce occurs and, if so, by what mechanism; the specific geometry of Spatiality; the conserved quantities and physical constants; interpretations of token-level agency; the site of the first living closure; the chemistry of life elsewhere; and particular evolutionary lineages remain open to physics, cosmology, philosophy of mind, and astrobiology. The structural argument doesn’t determine them. What the structural argument supplies is the frame within which their settlement is even possible.

One decisive question is still untouched: what is the living configuration *from within* once its self-modeling becomes deep enough for experience? Closure plus throughput describes the configuration from outside. It doesn’t yet explain subjective character.

That threshold is crossed in Chapter 5, with the *modal field*: the body’s accumulated representation of possibilities, weighted by the body’s stakes in their realization (§5.4). The self-maintaining configuration is in place; what happens when it models itself and its alternatives is the question that follows. The move is from life’s organization to the first-person register, not from physics to an unrelated subject matter.

A promise from the groundwork also comes due. Nature is named at §1.4.4, but its identification is withheld with *the universe* in the totality sense. The exhaustive modal identity is already earned: Reality is Nature, with no real exterior ground or coexistent remainder (§2.8; §2.9.6).

The cosmological usage takes one step more. Once Nature’s necessary structural type is distinguished from this observed arrangement of galaxies and matter, the universe in the *totality* sense is neither Nature’s rival nor its container. *Reality* names the whole to which anything real belongs; *Nature* names that whole’s necessary T∧S∧Φ constitution; *the universe*, in the totality sense, names the whole of what there is. The three descriptions pick out one reality. The particular observed arrangement remains a token within that totality, not the meaning of the identity claim.

**[Theorem]**

**The Identity of the Totality** · *Theorem*

Reality is Nature, exhaustively and without a real exterior remainder, and Nature necessarily instantiates T∧S∧Φ. Separately, the universe in the totality sense is this same Nature, not a container around it and not merely the present observed configuration described by cosmology. Reality, Nature, and the universe in the totality sense are therefore one reality under three names. The particular-arrangement sense of “universe” (this configuration of galaxies and matter) is expressly excluded. The identity stated here is plain identity; the modal theorem governs Nature’s structure rather than separately establishing necessary identity.

*Scope.* This is closure of the totality’s *field*—nothing is outside to enlarge it. It is distinct from Modal Closure (§2.9.4), which says the necessary Conditions admit no unnecessary alternative standing apart from them, and from Modal Exclusivity (§7.2.1), which says no modal item within Reality confers Reality’s capacity from outside. The three are companions and are not interchangeable; cite each for its own claim.

**Dependency routes:** identity and closure—Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6) and Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8); numerical unicity only—Structural Individuation (§2.4.9)

The identity transfers Reality’s modal maximality to the cosmological term. The universe in the totality sense already bears the complete capacity for real possibility: anything that really could be is a capacity of this one natural totality, and no additional real possibility waits outside it to be supplied. This doesn’t say that the universe in the contingent-arrangement sense actualizes every possibility, much less every mutually incompatible possibility at once. It says that the totality’s field can’t be enlarged from beyond, because any genuinely additional capacity would, by being real, already belong to the totality.

The identity has a third, conditional edge. To say Reality is Nature identifies the inclusive structural totality within the book’s modal framework: no second **structural** Nature or container around the global domain can stand outside Reality. Numerical cosmic unicity requires one premise more—Structural Individuation (§2.4.9). Whatever makes two allegedly isolated concrete totalities two is differentiating structure and belongs to the complete account of Reality; if nothing differentiates them, there are not two. Relational Distinctness adds only that positional separation requires an interval. Multiple regions, branches, histories, worlds, or configurations may therefore populate one cosmos without multiplying the totality itself. A primitivist can refuse Structural Individuation by taking cosmic plurality as an ungrounded fact; the cost and cardinality analyses at §7.2.3 answer that refusal. The structural identity and closure already earned are available here. Numerical unicity is a downstream result whose additional premise is made explicit, not something contained in the word *totality* alone.

Nature isn’t a system on which order has been imposed from outside; it is the configuration order takes. Read at the level on which the structural argument operates, that configuration requires no other reading.

# 5. Expanding the Field
