The creature reading this sentence is a living process capable of modeling itself and aware that it is doing so. The question is what that process is like from within.

Chapter 4 described life as a self-producing closure kept open to energy and exchange. The cumulative comparison at §5.1 warrants consciousness as what some living processes deep enough to model themselves are like from the inside, rather than a separate ingredient added to them. Drive, feeling, knowledge, identity, meaning, will, language, morality, art, and spirituality are tested from that starting point, not assumed to be separate faculties bolted onto a body.

The starting point does not settle the identifications. The modal proof strictly requires that any actual register occur through ordered change, differentiation, and a concrete bearer. Functional accounts of what an organism detects, retains, predicts, values, or communicates require their own evidence. Claims about what an operation feels like, what counts as knowledge or meaning, or what anyone owes another subject require arguments of their own.

At sufficient depth of self-modeling, some living configurations register alternatives and their stakes from within. That organized first-person pressure is named *Modal Pressure* and asks how far the account can be carried.

**[Theorem]**

**Modal Pressure** · *Theorem*

Cartesian Certainty establishes an actual first-person episode in which Change is registered; it therefore supplies a strict witness that at least one structured subject can register actuality and possibility from within. *Modal Pressure* names the proposed generalization: where a conscious body represents alternatives as open and weighted by its stakes, those representations exert directional pressure within its modal field. The objective possibility of Change, the body’s local representation of alternatives, and the felt pressure of those representations are three related claims, not one fact established under three descriptions.

*Status: strict as an existential first-person witness; general and naming-level claims remain conditional on the account of consciousness and the empirical fit developed in this chapter. N ↔ □◇C constrains the objective modal structure; it does not by itself describe what any organism represents or feels.*

**Depends on:** Cartesian Certainty (§2.2)

The sections follow two axes. Along the first, a life develops a broader and more finely articulated field: regulation, feeling, retained orientation, reflection, identity, and the ability to represent its own end. Along the second, one subject’s field opens onto others through language, shared knowledge, technology, morality, and art. The sequence is a partial order of dependencies, not a ladder on which each capacity first appears at its named section.

Thin forms may appear far below reflective human life. Bacteria can discriminate and regulate without thereby being shown to have a phenomenal vantage; animals may organize perception and affect without representing themselves as selves. Depth marks how distinct and operable a register has become, not a scale of basic worth and not a settled location at which experience begins.

The chapter remains a research proposal rather than sixteen deductions from one description. Some registers may prove to be operations of one architecture; others may require distinct mechanisms or further normative premises. The question in each case is whether locating the register within living organization explains more than treating it as a separate remainder.

The turn outward prepares the political question without answering it. If subjects are finite lives whose possibilities can be widened, narrowed, shared, and damaged, then the conditions under which they live together matter.

## 5.1 Consciousness

Consciousness is the register the others presuppose. Drive, feeling, knowledge, will, language, and the rest are proposed operations available to a subject, each tested for whether it can be understood as a differentiated operation of one living architecture. The starting point is therefore what the question itself supplies: entertaining it is already a conscious episode, and any such episode instantiates Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. Given the closure-and-throughput account (§4.8), mind need not be introduced as a separate substance added on top of the body. The further identification of consciousness with an aspect of living organization remains the positive thesis to be earned.

*What has to be earned.* Mere responsiveness is too cheap. Molecules change when other molecules bind to them; crystals propagate a pattern; a free virion can undergo receptor-triggered conformational change. None thereby supplies a subject for whom the change matters. Life (§4.8) gives the proposed difference: a living system maintains a boundary, draws energy through itself, and uses the exchange to reproduce the organization doing the maintaining. Conditions can therefore become better or worse *for that system* before they become anyone’s conscious preference. The further step isn’t from no response to response. It is from state-sensitive regulation to integrated registration by the bounded process whose continuation is at stake.

The virus case keeps the distinction honest. A free virion has conditional structure but no metabolic closure of its own, no ongoing comparison performed by its own control system, and no conduct it can redirect under its own power. Once its genome operates inside a cell, sophisticated viral decisions can occur, but the active organization belongs at least to the infected cell–virus system rather than straightforwardly to the particle alone. A virus can therefore carry information capable of reorganizing a living interior without already being an independently maintained experiencer. Sensitivity in the broad physical sense isn’t sufficient.

A bacterium stands on the other side of that boundary. Bacterial chemotaxis couples receptors to a short biochemical memory and changes the probability of continued swimming or reorientation as conditions improve or worsen. Attractants and repellents occupy both poles: the bacterium’s path isn’t mechanically pulled toward a nutrient like iron toward a magnet, but actively biased by a metabolically sustained control loop (Lyon 2015). This establishes discrimination, comparison, approach, avoidance, and the possibility of regulatory error. It doesn’t establish phenomenal awareness. What it supplies is the lower end of the organization the identity proposal must explain without changing subjects halfway through the account.

The vocabulary matters here. *Avoidance* names the observable organization: the system detects a condition and changes its conduct so that contact, damage, or continuation becomes less likely. *Aversion* names the negative condition as lived by a subject. Magnetic repulsion is neither. The magnets don’t detect a threat, compare a trajectory, redirect themselves, or undergo anything as bad. A bacterium plainly exceeds that case in organized avoidance; whether its negative weighting is also aversion is precisely the phenomenological question. Calling every withdrawal aversion would win the identity by definition. Calling even human aversion causally irrelevant to withdrawal would lose the identity by stipulation. The argument must instead ask when organized avoidance and lived aversion are one process under outer and inner descriptions.

*The proposed minimum.* The candidate isn’t motility, complexity, intelligence, or propositional thought. It is the integrated registration of environmental and internal differences as bearing on a bounded organism’s continued self-maintenance, with that registration available to organize what the organism does next.

In the vocabulary of philosophy of mind, the proposal places minimal consciousness at pre-reflective awareness rather than reflective self-consciousness. The organism need not represent the proposition *I am in danger*, still less know that it knows it. It must have a condition that is its own, differences registered relative to that condition, and an integrated way for those differences to alter its activity. Biological weighting supplies favorable and unfavorable poles from outside; attraction and aversion name the proposed inside-aspect of those poles. Temporal retention supplies comparison. Flexible control allows what is registered to guide more than one fixed reaction.

Why call that organization conscious rather than merely functional? The first-person case fixes one end of the comparison. In the one case where consciousness is certain, experience already presents a bounded field, differentiated contents, temporal retention, positive and negative bearing, and activity organized through them. The biological account doesn’t infer consciousness from any one of those features. It identifies the minimal organization that holds them together, then asks whether consciousness is a second fact beyond that organization.

If consciousness is a second fact, it either makes a causal difference that the allegedly complete organization omitted, in which case the organization wasn’t complete, or it makes no causal difference, in which case phenomenal efficacy has been surrendered. A contingent psychophysical bridge remains coherent, but it adds both a further feature and a further law. The identity account instead treats the inner and outer descriptions as two accesses to one operation. That is an explanatory advantage, not a contradiction in every alternative.

*Continuity without a ladder.* Multicellularity can widen the boundary across which regulation is coordinated: many cells differentiate their roles, exchange signals, and contribute to the maintenance of one larger organism. It doesn’t follow that more cells automatically mean more consciousness. What can deepen is the reach of the integrated control—how many distinctions it can preserve, how far across the body and environment it can coordinate, how long it can retain and anticipate, how flexibly it can change course, and whether it can model its own modeling (Levin 2019; Ginsburg and Jablonka 2019). The resulting depth gradient is partial. One lineage may deepen spatial integration while another deepens social prediction, manipulatory control, memory, or reflective monitoring.

Cephalopods make the point visible. Vertebrate and coleoid-cephalopod nervous systems developed their complex organization along deeply separated lineages, with cephalopods distributing much of their processing through the arms rather than reproducing a mammalian cortical plan (Godfrey-Smith 2016; Albertin et al. 2015). Their flexible exploration and problem-solving don’t prove that every similar performance has the same phenomenal character. They do show that deep cognitive organization is multiply realizable: evolution can reach sophisticated integration through architectures that are neither mammalian nor approximations to one. Conscious depth is therefore not well represented as distance up a human-shaped staircase.

Continuity still permits a phase transition. A critic may hold that every bacterial and cellular precursor is wholly nonconscious until a particular integrative architecture appears, just as continuously increasing temperature can cross a genuine phase boundary. The proposal can’t answer that possibility by pointing at a smooth series. It asks the critic to identify the organization that fixes the boundary and explain why interiority appears there.

Unlimited associative learning, global availability, recurrent processing, higher-order representation, and integrated-information thresholds are proposed markers of such a transition (Ginsburg and Jablonka 2019). They don’t all oppose the present account. Some may specify mechanisms or measures by which a living system achieves the integration, availability, or self-relation the account requires. They become boundary rivals only where they locate the first subject differently. None is presently an uncontested measure of the first appearance of experience. Until a breakpoint is independently earned, making functional and evolutionary architecture continuous while making phenomenal existence discontinuous adds a transition the evidence hasn’t yet located.

This is the continuity argument at its proper strength. It doesn’t prove that a bacterium feels, that a white blood cell is a subject, or that every self-regulating system is conscious. It does make the life–consciousness identity more than an analogy. At the near end, first-person awareness is certain and demonstrably admits multiple depths and profiles. At the basal end, living systems already exhibit bounded stake, bipolar regulation, retention, integration, and error. Between them, evolution elaborates those capacities through branching and independently reachable architectures without revealing an agreed point at which a new ontological ingredient enters. Together with multiple realization and explanatory economy, that continuity makes the identity the best-supported explanation developed here. A discontinuity account remains possible, but it owes the missing boundary.

The meta-problem literature asks why reflective beings report a special explanatory gap (Dennett 2018; Frankish 2016). The structural-residue diagnostic (§5.4) offers one explanation of that report: a body searching an external description for the first-person character of its own operation won’t encounter that character as an additional external item. This diagnoses one source of the gap intuition. It doesn’t by itself establish that no phenomenal remainder exists.

The account shares one intuition with Russellian monism, that structural description may leave an inside unexpressed (Goff 2017; Strawson 2006), but it doesn’t posit fundamental phenomenal quiddities behind the structural roles. It proposes instead that some sufficiently organized operations are also inside-aspects. The Russellian reading is engaged at §9.3; the structured zombie is put to the account at §9.1. A separable psychophysical law and epiphenomenal feeling carry explanatory costs, while the identity account owes a non-circular sufficiency argument. Configurational Necessitation sharpens the fork after that argument succeeds, and Strict Actualization spends the actual configuration; they don’t decide the fork in advance.

**[Identification]**

**Consciousness** · *Identification*

Consciousness is actual in at least the present first-person episode, and every such episode is temporally ordered, differentiates content, and is concretely borne. Consciousness is what sufficiently integrated self-producing life is like from within: at minimum, a bounded organism’s integrated registration of its own condition in relation to its environment, where differences bear positively or negatively on it and can alter its conduct. Depth varies along discrimination, temporal reach, flexible integration, and reflective self-awareness, as a branching profile rather than a ladder.

*Status: the first-person witness and the structural constraint are strict; the identity is abductive, warranted by biological continuity, multiple realization, and explanatory economy.*

**Depends on:** Cartesian Certainty (§2.2) and Life (§4.8)

## 5.2 Drive
Every actively living thing must regulate exchanges relevant to its continuation. A dormant organism may suspend occurrent regulation while retaining the organization internally disposed to resume it; its directedness is then borne without being exercised. In conscious animals, some active regulation is lived as appetite, aversion, attraction, restlessness, or felt urgency. *Drive* names the proposed common directional organization beneath those differentiated states. This gives the account a strong external anchor and a first-person instance without assuming that bacteria, plants, and persons all experience regulation in the same way—or experience it at all.

**[Identification]**

**Drive** · *Identification*

In their active phases, living closures exhibit directed regulation: they maintain some conditions, approach or preserve some exchanges, and counter others. A dormant phase can bear that direction dispositionally in the retained organization without presently exercising it. Conscious subjects can register corresponding alternatives as attraction, aversion, or urgency. *Drive* is the proposal that these felt orientations are the first-person aspect of the organism’s integrated regulation before they differentiate into specific object-directed feelings.

*Status: strict for the existence of biological directedness and for the first-person actuality of felt orientation in the witness case. The continuity between them, its distribution across living systems, and the claim that later motives share one underlying organization are defended by fit. Life and Modal Pressure do not by themselves entail felt drive. The felt half inherits the conditionality of the life–consciousness identification at §5.1: cite this result unconditionally for biological directedness, conditionally wherever the interior is at issue.*

**Depends on:** Modal Pressure (§5) and Life (§4.8)

The thermodynamic description and the phenomenological description should be kept distinct long enough to test their proposed identity. From outside, metabolism, foraging, exploration, and regulation are ways an open system maintains itself far from equilibrium. From inside, conscious subjects report pressure, attraction, and aversion. The proposal is that the latter is how some integrated forms of the former are lived. Neither thermodynamics nor outward goal-directed behavior alone establishes where that interior occurs.

*Drive as modal pressure lived from the inside.* Modal Pressure (§5) names alternatives weighted by stake within a conscious field. Drive is its proposed basal directional form: attraction and aversion before a subject has articulated a specific emotion or plan. A living closure can exhibit regulation without the present argument thereby showing that it feels the regulation. Where regulation, conscious registration, and stake-sensitive weighting are independently present together, the identity account offers a unified description of them as one operation from outer and inner sides.

**[Theorem]**

**Living Directionality** · *Theorem*

Any active living closure in the sense established at §4.8 regulates exchanges relative to its continued organization. Closure produces and repairs conditions of continuation; throughput maintains the gradient across which that work occurs. During genuine dormancy the organization retains an internally grounded disposition to resume that regulation, though no regulation or measurable metabolism need then be occurrent. A process that neither performs the joint operation nor retains its own organized capacity to resume it is not a living closure under the account. Biological directedness therefore follows from Life without an additional premise.

The theorem establishes regulation toward continuation. It does not establish phenomenal feeling, felt drive, one experience common to every living system, or the identity between regulation viewed from outside and orientation lived from inside. Those remain the Identification’s explicitly stated burden.

**Depends on:** Life (§4.8)

*Drive belongs to the concrete closure, not to an abstract role.* What is named is the self-producing being coupled to its gradient—the closure-and-throughput Life (§4.8) describes—not a functional organization abstracted from every substrate that might realize it. A description or simulation that doesn’t itself close and metabolize no more bears drive than a description of a storm is wet: it specifies the organization from outside without instantiating the living closure whose inside drive is.

The analogy illustrates the commitment; it doesn’t compel it. A functionalist may hold that a sufficiently rich simulation genuinely closes and metabolizes. Against that position, the storm image carries no argumentative weight. The weight falls on the fit-based proposal defended here: what has an inside is the concrete self-producing life, not the abstract specification considered apart from any realization.

This is where the account parts from functionalism. Functionalism locates mind in the abstract causal role and lets any implementation of that role inherit it. This account locates the inside in the concrete organism that maintains itself against dissolution. The claim isn’t that only carbon can do so—anything that genuinely closes and sustains throughput is a candidate—but that having an inside follows concrete self-production rather than abstract specification.

Life was named at §4.8 as what that structure is from outside: closure, throughput, self-production. Awareness is recovered at §5.1 as what registration looks like from inside the organism at sufficient depth. Drive is what those two facts are when they meet. Awareness without drive would be a registering surface with no stake in what it registered: registration as data without orientation. Life without registration would be metabolism without an inside, gradient-following without anyone for whom the following matters. On the proposal defended here, drive is what awareness is in a being whose continuation depends on what is registered. Drive and awareness aren’t sequenced; they are proposed as two faces of one interiority: the interior aspect of modal pressure, registered as orientation and as fact-of-registration at once.

*Drive and registration may coincide without being definitionally biconditional.* Spinoza distinguished thought and extension as two attributes of one substance (Spinoza (1677) 1996, II); a looser parallel is proposed here between an organism’s directed regulation and its lived registration. In the first-person witness, orientation and registration occur together. Extending that conjunction across species requires independent evidence about experience. Plants without nervous systems discriminate light, water, gravity, chemistry, and damage, signal across tissue and across individuals, and alter growth accordingly (Trewavas 2003; Karban 2015; Calvo 2016; Gagliano 2018). Those findings support sophisticated state-sensitive regulation. They don’t decide whether plants possess phenomenal registration, and calling selectivity an operational mark can’t decide the issue without defining the disputed conclusion into the evidence. The argument may treat plants as a test case for the proposed continuity while leaving their experiential status open.

*Configurational force.* The condition at issue isn’t bare metabolism or outwardly selective behavior. It is the concrete configuration of a self-producing closure, coupled to sustained throughput, that registers its own condition at the depth where modal pressure operates. If that configuration is metaphysically sufficient for interior modal pressure, as proposed here, then Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4) applies: no complete realization lacks drive. Strict Actualization (§2.9.4) then gives drive from an actual sufficient configuration, without a further addition. Drive isn’t thereby necessary simpliciter. The theorem doesn’t establish the naming half’s sufficiency; it fixes the consequence only if the fit-based burden is met.

Drive isn’t yet choice. At shallow depth it is compressed response: tropism, reflex, habit, threat-reaction, the body moving before deliberation has time to occur. At greater depth, the same directedness can hold alternatives apart long enough to model them. This is where will begins to become free (§5.11): not by escaping structure, but by gaining modal distance from the point of action. The more a being can represent live alternatives before one path is actualized, the more its drive becomes deliberative agency rather than automatic response.

When the field shows no sign of a livable continuation, Drive doesn’t go quiet. The ought isn’t *there is no way out*. The ought is *I need to make one*. That is desperation: Drive pushed to its limit, the compressed response already named with the limiter off. It has two directions. In one, continuation is still the pole and the situation is what can’t be borne: the being will do anything that could open a line on which it can go on. In the other, the only possibility still showing is ongoing suffering, and the ought is to prevent that possibility—not the pain already borne, but the branch on which it continues. Continuation then looks like the harder option, not worth the interior that comes with staying, and cessation is the line that has to be made. Both are the same limit. The difference is which side of the field still shows preservation. The collapse can register as no remaining possibility, as only the possibility of suffering, or as never being free again; which precipitant produced the thinning isn’t the mechanism. Those registrations sit on Will’s two pillars and on Aversion, not on three moods: mapping and reach (modal depth) for the first, Aversion for the second, latitude for the third (§5.11). This is spent at the encounter (§6.12), and as the mapping (§6.9, §6.10) and care that can put a livable line back in the field before either direction runs, and as the resourced exit when the only remaining possibility really is ongoing suffering.

Schopenhauer’s Will (Schopenhauer 1818), the blind drive beneath every appearance, strips the pressure to its baseline character. The modal reading accepts the pressure but rejects the blindness once registration is present: a sustained living being orients among represented alternatives rather than merely being pushed by a cosmic substance. This answers only the *blindness* charge. Schopenhauer’s darker claim—that existence carries a standing surplus of suffering over satisfaction—is a separate *suffering-surplus* charge. That suffering-surplus charge is taken up, alongside Benatar’s anti-natalism, at §6.14, which meets the asymmetry at the step it needs.

*Directedness runs a functional gradient; experience may not.* Bacterial chemotaxis, plant tropism, immune-cell migration, animal appetite, and human pursuit all involve state-sensitive orientation toward or away from conditions. That shared abstraction is real and doesn’t require metaphor. It doesn’t follow that every case includes registration in the phenomenal sense or that human vocational pursuit is simply bacterial gradient-following folded more deeply. A continuity in organization is proposed, and tested where conscious drive emerges within it. Evidence for regulation establishes the gradient’s outer form; evidence for experience must be supplied independently.

*The SEEKING system converges with, but doesn’t by itself establish, the neurological correlate.* Panksepp’s work (Panksepp 1998) identified a primary emotional system, phylogenetically ancient and present across all mammals, that drives curiosity, exploration, foraging, and play through dopaminergic activation of mesolimbic circuits. Crucially, the SEEKING system activates not at reward but at the *anticipation* of reward, not at possession but at pursuit. That finding is Panksepp’s own: a claim about neural architecture and behavior. That this activity is the inside registration of a being mobilizing energetic resources toward engagement with the world is the account’s own identification, defended by fit rather than delivered by the neuroscience. What the SEEKING system’s anticipatory profile supplies is convergence: independent evidence, from a different method, that anticipatory pursuit rather than mere metabolic maintenance is a real and phylogenetically deep pattern—exactly what the identification predicts if it is correct, though the neuroscience alone doesn’t adjudicate between that identification and a purely functional description of the same circuitry.

*Play makes the excess visible.* Drive isn’t exhausted by minimal maintenance; it can reach beyond what maintenance immediately requires. Play is the clearest candidate expression of that excess. It is phylogenetically widespread in mammals (Bekoff and Byers 1998), birds (Heinrich 1995), and some reptiles (Burghardt 2005). The invertebrate record is still developing: bumblebees have been observed rolling wooden balls without a food or mating payoff, which Chittka reports as evidence of play (Chittka 2022).

When survival needs are met and surplus energy is available, organisms that model themselves deeply enough may explore, engage, and repeat activities with no immediate survival outcome. Practice accounts describe what play accomplishes from outside. The argument proposes a corresponding inside description: surplus registers as worth spending in play. On that proposal, excitement isn’t a second state merely correlated with energetic surplus but the inside-aspect of surplus running outward in a being deep enough to feel. The dopaminergic anticipatory architecture (Berridge 2007) supplies convergent evidence for the substrate side; it doesn’t establish the identity.

Unused time is the same excess at rest: a field with branches not occupied by maintenance. A being whose every hour is survival-work has no surplus left to play; its practical field has collapsed toward a single demand. Unused time is spent as latitude at §6.7, and rest as care at §6.10. Neither is a right to leisure minted here.

*Modal-field expansion as a primary drive.* Play names one shape of drive’s excess: activity beyond minimum maintenance. Curiosity names a related but distinct shape—the drive to expand the modal field itself by adding conditions and actualities that the body’s own situation hasn’t yet supplied.

The pattern is robust across the animal kingdom: rats explore novel environments at energetic cost without immediate reward (Berlyne 1960); octopuses manipulate novel objects in their tanks (Mather and Anderson 1993); corvids investigate cameras, mirrors, and puzzles in field and lab (Bird and Emery 2009); juvenile chimpanzees devote extensive time to object manipulation; and cetaceans approach novel stimuli. Loewenstein’s information-gap theory (Loewenstein 1994) frames the phenomenology: curiosity occurs when a being registers a structured absence in its field that it has the apparatus to fill. Resolving the absence is then experienced as satisfaction.

Field expansion can clear its evolutionary cost. An incurious being avoids the exposures that curiosity entails, but it also forfeits information about prey, paths, terrains, conspecifics, threats, and opportunities. Whether selection favors curiosity in a lineage depends on that tradeoff; the modal framework alone doesn’t settle it. “Curiosity killed the cat” and “curiosity taught the cat what’s possible” name the two sides of the same operation.

*The cost structure shifts with depth.* At shallow depth, modal-field expansion is physically expensive. The cat has to enter the new alley to discover that it is dangerous and climb the new tree to discover that it can be climbed. Each new branch in the field is paid for in exposure.

At deeper depths, proxy-data channels partially decouple field expansion from physical exposure: gesture, language, narrative, gossip, history, images, recordings, broadcasts, and networked transmission. A being can learn that civilizations fall, that certain people are dangerous, or that certain conditions produce certain outcomes without entering those situations. History (§5.4), reportage (§5.12), anthropology, science, and the persistent appetite for narrative all become channels through which this drive operates. What changes isn’t the basic pull to map what lies beyond present experience but the cost of adding a branch to the field.

Lower exposure costs introduce different risks. An expanded field with unreliable weighting is the structural shape of conspiratorial thinking, news-induced anxiety, informational overload, and paralysis by analysis. Source evaluation, epistemic humility, and deliberate pruning of unconfirmed possibilities answer this deeper cost structure.

*A second deep-cost runs through the satisfaction signal itself.* If the satisfaction of curiosity is the apparatus registering its own field-expansion, then a channel that delivers field-expansion endlessly and near-free can keep that signal firing without the being ever acting on the field it has expanded. The drive’s terminus is enactment, will is the selection that discharges the field into act (§5.11), and a being can be held at the reconnaissance pole indefinitely, its appetite met by the mapping and never carried through to the doing the mapping evolved to serve. This isn’t the over-expanded field of the previous case but an arrested one: a drive fed at the point of registration and starved at the point of discharge. Where over-expansion presents as anxiety and paralysis, arrest presents as a flattened, unmotivated relation to a richly mapped world that no longer issues in action.

*Drive as the substrate.* Drive isn’t proposed as one peer among the registers that follow but as what each of them shapes. On this proposal, Feeling is drive registering pull and aversion. Identity is drive holding itself as a persistent agent in its modal field at sufficient depth. Knowledge is drive stabilizing into structure. Reasoning is drive extending through alternatives. Meaning is drive orienting. Will is drive enacting. Language is drive expressing. Technology is drive externalizing. Morality is drive regulating its own commitments. Art is drive resonating with structure. Spirituality is drive reaching past the organism’s horizon. Each register is proposed as a specific shape of the inside-pressure identified here, a thesis the later registers have to earn rather than one this list establishes.

*Drive’s polarity: aversion and attraction.* Drive runs between two poles, *aversion* and *attraction*. The aversion-pole turns away from what damages, threatens, or negates: harm, suffering, loss, threats to closure, and—at the limit—the closure named as death at §5.9. Death anchors the pole because no being can resist it by continuing to be itself. It isn’t the pole’s only content. A being can be averse to injury short of death, suffering that doesn’t threaten closure, or conditions it registers as not worth living.

At sufficient depth of self-modeling, aversion can also reach the suffering and damage of other beings. A parent steps in front of harm aimed at a child; a soldier covers a grenade to spare comrades; a bystander runs into traffic to pull out a stranger. In each case, another’s threatened field outweighs aversion to the agent’s own death. Death remains the structural anchor, but the field of aversion isn’t confined to self-preservation or kinship.

The moral account draws on this reach (§5.14). Moral theory tracks aversion to suffering in oneself and in others bound to the subject by care, commitment, or recognition of a shared condition. Because the aversion is registered within the beings who bear it, the account remains naturalist rather than transcendent.

The opposite case is equally diagnostic. A being can register its own ongoing conditions as themselves intolerable, and when it does the aversion can override the death-anchor and turn the being toward its own cessation. Suicidality, in the cases where it operates not as impulse but as a being’s settled relation to its own continuation, is that direction of the same limit: aversion working at depth on the far side of the structural floor, the conditions of being alive themselves the thing the being is averted from, with no visible livable line. This confirms what the parent-sacrifice case showed from the other side. Death is the aversion-pole’s structural anchor but not its content. Aversion tracks intolerable states; the death-anchor is the floor past which no being persists, not the field itself. When the field tilts hard enough (when the conditions of continuation have themselves become what the being can’t bear) the anchor can flip from what the creature is averted *toward* to what the creature is averted *from*, and the limit case stops being the worst outcome and becomes the only available direction. The asymmetry that fixes the pole is structural; what populates the pole is everything the being registers as not to be borne.

The attraction-pole runs toward the conditions a being’s continuation, flourishing, and reach require. At the shallow end this is nutrient, water, light, shelter, the metabolic conditions of staying alive. At deeper depths it differentiates: safety, kin and community, the production of other beings (taken up as sexuality at §5.8), understanding (§5.4), meaning (§5.10), expression and resonance (§5.15), and the metaphysical register taken up as spirituality at §5.16. None of these is structurally absolute the way death is; they are open positive content, populated differently at different depths, and each is taken up at its register downstream. What runs through all of them is the same drive-toward, the same forward pressure of a being reaching for what its continuation under its present conditions opens onto. The outer and inner vocabularies must not be collapsed: approach and avoidance name organized trajectories; attraction and aversion name those poles as phenomenally registered. The argument proposes an identity between them in conscious drive, not an equivalence true by definition at every biological depth. A bacterium can therefore exhibit avoidance without the present argument already having shown aversion. In the first-person case, by contrast, aversion isn’t a force added to the control process; it is the negative weighting as lived by the organism whose conduct it organizes.

What drive differentiates into when it encounters specific conditions, fear as drive in the registration of threat, desire as drive in the registration of possibility, grief as drive in the registration of permanent absence, care as drive in the registration of another being’s vulnerability, belongs to feeling (§5.3).

These registrations don’t all have the same temporal object. Threat can be present or anticipated; desire can concern what is absent, present, or continued; grief concerns an actual loss as well as a future without what was lost; care can answer another’s present vulnerability and possible harm. What unifies them isn’t exclusive direction at unrealized branches but sensitivity to how actual and possible conditions bear on a subject.

**[Corollary]**

**Aversion as Modal Weight** · *Corollary*

Aversion may answer a present state of affairs, but it can also persist as a standing weight against that state’s continuation, worsening, or recurrence. In its anticipatory and dispositional forms, it weights represented branches even when the object is absent. Modal weight is therefore one genuine form of aversion, not the exhaustive form of every drive-state.

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2) and Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5)

Three consequences follow.

1. *Anticipatory drive operates on a modal field.* Present-directed pain or aversion requires no represented unrealized branch. Aversion to recurrence, worsening, or loss does: it depends on some representation, however thin, of a condition not presently obtained.

2. *R must be able to admit the object.* Aversion to a really impossible outcome protects nothing, because impossibility doesn’t vary and no arrangement was ever going to deliver the outcome (§2.1.5). Such an aversion isn’t a smaller stake but an empty one: a mapping failure wearing the phenomenology of a stake, and the first of the Three Frustrations of Will (§5.11) met at the level of drive rather than of willing.

3. *A weight can be borne without being felt.* Because the weight is standing rather than currently active, or *occurrent*, a being can hold an aversion it isn’t at that moment exercising, and the line it is averse to can be closed off, or removed from its field, with nothing registering at the time.

The third is what morality requires (§5.14): a wrong against a subject’s registered aversion need not be a wrong the subject notices.

The result is narrow and shouldn’t be widened. It doesn’t establish that a being’s weights are accurate, that what it is averse to is genuinely available to it, or that the strength of a weight tracks anything about the branch beyond the being’s own stake in it. What it fixes is one *form* a drive-state can take, and that form is modal.

### 5.2.1 The Dispute
The literature on motivation, drive, and the forward pressure of life is among the oldest in philosophy and among the most active in the cognitive sciences. A series of standing positions is engaged by name.

*Classical-philosophical accounts of striving.* Spinoza’s *conatus* (Spinoza (1677) 1996, III) names the striving by which each finite mode perseveres in its being. Schopenhauer’s Will (Schopenhauer 1818) names the blind cosmic drive he posited beneath every appearance. Nietzsche’s will-to-power names life’s drive to express and expand itself. Bergson’s *élan vital* (Bergson 1907) names the forward pressure he located in life as such. Each tradition was reaching for a structural fact the framework now names (the first-person perspective on energy-gradient coupling) but each came with metaphysical baggage the structural account can shed. Whether the *conatus*, the Will, the will-to-power, and the *élan vital* refer to one phenomenon or several remains a live exegetical question; they’re read here as four angles on the same structural fact, without the substance-talk each tradition wrapped around it.

*The plurality of drives and the order of rank.* Nietzsche presses a sharper claim than the other striving traditions, and one aimed at its own vocabulary: that the word *drive*, taken in the singular, already falsifies the organism. What a living thing is, on his account (Nietzsche (1886) 2002, §13, §19, §36; Nietzsche (1881) 1997, §129), isn’t one striving but a multiplicity of drives (*Triebe*): hunger, fear, curiosity, the sexual drive, the drive to command, each construing the world from its own angle, each seeking its own discharge, and standing to one another in an *order of rank* (*Rangordnung*): some commanding, some obeying, the configuration shifting as ascending and declining drives gain or lose the upper hand. The unity we call a self is, on this reading, an after-the-fact construction (the temporary expression of whichever drive or coalition currently rules) and will-to-power names not a single appetite but the form the competition among the drives takes. The challenge to any account that speaks of *drive* in the singular is direct: if Nietzsche is right, the singular term names only the surface of a plurality whose real structure is competitive and hierarchical, and the account owes either a defense of the singular or an account of how the plurality is organized. The challenge is met at §5.2.5.

*Drive in psychoanalysis.* Freud’s libido (Freud 1905; Freud 1923), in the broad sense of life-energy seeking expression, and the later distinction between Eros and Thanatos (Freud 1920), name the same baseline as Spinoza and Schopenhauer with a different vocabulary. (Eros and Thanatos are Freud’s later names for two fundamental drives: Eros (Greek, the god of love) is the life drive—self-preservation, bonding, pleasure-seeking; Thanatos (Greek, the personification of death, though Freud himself used “death drive” more often than the Greek name) is the drive toward aggression, destruction, and a return to an inorganic, tension-free state. Freud proposed the pair to explain phenomena libido alone couldn’t account for, like repetition compulsion and aggression, as complementary rather than opposed forces.) Subsequent psychoanalytic traditions (Klein, Winnicott, Lacan) refined the picture in ways that remain contested both within psychoanalysis and at its contact with empirical psychology. Freud’s libido is read as naming that same forward pressure from the inside, accurately tracked under contestable metaphysics.

*Reward, anticipation, and the SEEKING system.* Contemporary affective neuroscience disputes how to carve the territory traditionally called drive. Berridge and Robinson’s distinction (Berridge and Robinson 1998) between *wanting* and *liking* (anticipatory drive versus consummatory pleasure) reorganized the field, with dopaminergic activation now widely understood as tracking the anticipatory side. Panksepp’s SEEKING system (Panksepp 1998) names the mammalian-wide phylogenetically ancient system that drives curiosity, exploration, and pursuit. Whether SEEKING is best understood as one primary emotional system or as a feature of the broader motivational architecture is debated (LeDoux 2012; Adolphs 2017); SEEKING activation is read as the substrate side of the perspective the structural account identifies as drive.

*Optimal-foraging and behavioral-ecology accounts.* The behavioral-ecology literature (Stephens and Krebs 1986; Charnov 1976) treats drive operationally as the variable a foraging organism is optimizing, and predicts species-specific behavior from energetic and informational constraints. The accounts are powerful and predictive but largely silent on the first-person perspective. They’re treated as correct external descriptions whose subjective character is what the structural identification supplies.

*Goal-directedness and teleosemantics.* Millikan (Millikan 1984; Millikan 1995), Papineau (Papineau 1987), and the broader teleosemantic literature locate purpose and goal-directedness in evolutionary function. The account grants that evolutionary function explains *what* the drive is for, and adds that what drive *is* phenomenologically is that same functional fact experienced from within. The two aren’t competitors. The *for* at issue is etiological, not Aristotelian: a drive’s function is what selection built it to do, a fact about past efficient causes, not a final cause drawing the organism toward an end that doesn’t yet exist. The directedness that teleosemantics names is kept here while shedding the forward-pulling teleology Spinoza’s *conatus* wrapped around it.

*Play, surplus, and intrinsic motivation.* Whether play represents excess beyond minimal maintenance or is itself instrumental practice for adult skills remains contested (Bekoff and Byers 1998; Burghardt 2005; Pellis and Pellis 2009). The recent bumblebee ball-rolling results (Loukola et al. 2017; Chittka 2022) press the dispute outward into invertebrates whose architectures weren’t previously thought to support play. Play is proposed here as energy surplus running outward, felt from within at the depth where it can register as such.

*Hedonism and its discontents.* The hedonist tradition (Bentham 1789; contemporary defenders such as Crisp 2006) holds that pleasure and the avoidance of pain are the fundamental motivational variables. Critics (Nozick’s experience machine Nozick 1974; Kraut Kraut 2007) argue that what we want isn’t pleasure as such but engagement with reality. The structural reading is that pleasure and pain are surface registrations of a deeper fact, a being’s flourishing or failing, felt from within, and that the hedonist’s content-level account picks up the surface accurately while missing what the surface tracks.

*Reductionist eliminativism.* A small but persistent literature (Churchland 1986) argues that folk-psychological talk of *drive*, *desire*, *motivation*, and *will* will be eliminated by a mature cognitive neuroscience. The structural response, parallel to the response to eliminativism about consciousness (§9.2), is that drive will be identified rather than eliminated: the underlying activity is real, the folk vocabulary tracks something genuine, and the mature description will refine rather than discard it.

### 5.2.2 The Requirement
*Continuity with thermodynamics.* In its active phases, a living thing is a self-maintaining process coupled to a sustained energy gradient, dissipating that gradient through itself to keep producing itself. A dormant phase may hold the organization and direction of that process without presently running it. Drive is the first-person aspect of the active thermodynamic fact at the depth where a first-person aspect opens. An adequate account has to connect drive to the energetic conditions of life rather than treating motivation as a free-floating psychological variable, deriving directedness from what a living system must do to continue rather than from premises silent on energy.

*Bipolarity.* Drive is bipolar: forward pressure toward what sustains the being and orients its lineage forward, defensive pressure away from what threatens its continuation. The toward-pole and away-pole aren’t two drives but one drive running in two directions from the same thermodynamic fact. An adequate account has to explain why motivation takes this bipolar structure rather than treating approach and avoidance as independent systems requiring separate derivations, deriving both poles from the conditions under which a living thing persists.

*Depth-graded differentiation.* Drive runs from chemical-gradient tracking at the bacterial depth through tropism, appetite, affective motivation, and finally the long-horizon goal-directed pursuits of self-aware beings. An adequate account has to accommodate the gradient (the same forward-pressure activity progressively differentiated and elaborated at deeper depths) rather than assuming bacterial chemotaxis and human vocational pursuit share nothing, while leaving open whether experience runs the same gradient the organization does.

*Excess beyond maintenance.* Drive isn’t minimal maintenance but reach beyond what maintenance strictly requires: play, exploration, curiosity, art, the pursuit of projects whose immediate survival value is negligible. An adequate account has to explain why dissipative currents at sufficient depth reach beyond what their immediate energetic balance requires, explaining the excess from what a dissipative current with surplus throughput does with that surplus rather than from a special faculty added on top of survival.

*Anticipation as well as completion.* The wanting/liking distinction (Berridge and Robinson 1998) separates anticipatory wanting from consummatory liking. An adequate account has to explain why much motivation is future-directed (oriented toward conditions not yet obtained) while some drive-states answer what is presently occurring, locating anticipatory drive in the gap between the present condition and one not yet obtained.

*Connection to feeling without reducing to it.* Drive and feeling (§5.3) are structurally related but distinct: drive is the bare forward pressure pre-differentiation; feeling is what differentiates drive when the organism is deep enough to register valence specifically. An adequate account has to explain the relation without collapsing one into the other, treating feeling as drive made differentiated and reflective, with drive as the baseline forward pressure that feeling specifies.

*First-person aspect as constitutive.* The drive isn’t merely a behavioral variable described from outside; it is the first-person aspect of a being oriented toward its own continuation. An adequate account has to locate drive at the first-person aspect of the activity, not only at its functional or behavioral correlates, preserving the phenomenology rather than describing the substrate while leaving the first-person aspect unexplained.

*Bipolar pair with structural counterparts.* The toward-pole of drive opens onto reproduction and the production of new lives (§5.8 Sexuality); the away-pole opens onto the structural limit of closure (§5.9 Mortality). An adequate account has to accommodate these structural pairings rather than treating sexuality and mortality as separate domains, explaining the pairings from drive’s bipolar structure: what one drives toward includes the lineage’s continuation, what one drives away from includes the individual’s end.

These requirements aren’t neutral conditions every adequate theory must accept. Competing accounts may reject or redescribe some of them, especially the proposed continuity from thermodynamic organization to phenomenology. The framework argues for this set rather than treating it as already established.

### 5.2.3 Predictions
*Drive is the vantage on the thermodynamic fact before differentiation.* Every living system is a self-producing recursion coupled to a sustained energy gradient, reaching for throughput to maintain its own closure. That is the outside description. From inside (at any depth sufficient to have an inside at all) the same fact registers as forward pressure: the basic orientation of the organism toward the world, prior to any particular object, prior to any particular emotion, prior to any specific valenced response. This isn’t yet fear or joy or grief. It is the charge that precedes and underlies all of those, the baseline state of a living system that is, constitutively, not at rest.

Spinoza named it *conatus*: the striving by which each finite thing perseveres in its being. But perseverance understates it. The organism doesn’t merely maintain itself; it presses outward into the environment beyond what maintenance strictly requires. A bacterium follows a chemical gradient toward nutrients it doesn’t need for immediate survival. A well-fed crow investigates a novel object. A satiated otter slides down a riverbank repeatedly. The throughput doesn’t merely sustain the closure; the closure orients toward more throughput and broader engagement with the environment. This forward pressure beyond maintenance is what the structural account predicts: the organism isn’t neutral. It is coupled to an energy gradient, and that coupling isn’t passive: it is active, forward-leaning, seeking. The organism is constituted by reaching for throughput. That reaching, where it is lived from inside, is drive.

The structural account proposes that some forms of self-maintaining organization can be described as an orientation toward conditions of continued organization, and that richer motivational life emerges with greater recursive and neural complexity. This is a philosophical model, not an empirical result establishing felt drive in every living system. At shallow biological levels, approach and avoidance may be described functionally as tropism or regulation; whether they involve any first-person aspect is disputed.

### 5.2.4 Confirmation
Panksepp’s SEEKING system (Panksepp 1998) is an influential affective-neuroscience model of exploratory and appetitive motivation. It links dopaminergic activity with curiosity, exploration, foraging, and anticipatory engagement, while later work continues to debate its precise boundaries and interpretation. The distinction between anticipatory wanting and consummatory liking is an important motivation finding; it doesn’t by itself identify a first-person aspect with energy throughput or establish a single drive shared by every living system. SEEKING is treated here as one possible high-complexity realization relevant to its structural model, not as a direct neurological confirmation of that model.

*Play and excess.* Play is phylogenetically widespread in some animal groups, including mammals and birds, with evidence and interpretation in other groups still debated (Loukola et al. 2017; Chittka 2022). Practice, exploration, social learning, and intrinsic-reward accounts remain active explanations. The proposal is that play may illuminate activity beyond immediate maintenance, but it doesn’t follow that organisms play simply because energy surplus registers as worth playing, or that excitement is identical with the subjective character of energy surplus. Those are further phenomenological claims for the Chapter 5 model to argue.

### 5.2.5 Conclusions
*Drive precedes its objects.* The specific things a subject desires, fears, or cares about are drive encountering specific conditions. Drive itself has no particular object: it is the orientation toward the world prior to any specific thing in the world. This is why desire feels urgent even when its object is absent, why curiosity arises before it has a target, why the restlessness of a subject with nothing to do is the drive with nowhere to go. The object gives the drive direction; the drive doesn’t come from the object.

*The philosophical traditions that named drive were pointing at the same structural fact.* Spinoza’s *conatus* names the striving by which a finite being persists. That directedness is derived here from a thermodynamic and evolutionary substrate rather than from a metaphysical substance theory. A closure presses toward continuation because selection, on a thermodynamic floor, built it to—not because a future end pulls the present toward itself. The *for* in *a drive is for continuation* is therefore the etiological *for* of teleosemantics (§5.2.1). Whether Spinoza’s own *conatus* is covertly teleological remains an interpretive dispute: Garrett and Lin read it that way; Bennett and Curley read Spinoza as a strict anti-teleologist under *Ethics* I Appendix.

Vitalism saw that local mechanical descriptions can omit the system-level closure-and-throughput pattern. Mechanism saw that the pattern requires no extra vital substance and resolves into specifiable physical processes. The structural account preserves both insights. The forward pressure of life is the inside-aspect it proposes for dissipative organization before that pressure differentiates into any specific emotion; no residual *élan* is added to produce it.

*The plurality is granted; the order of rank is explained; the dissolution of the self is refused.* Nietzsche’s challenge to the singular *drive* (§5.2.1) is met by conceding most of it and parting on the last step. Grant the plurality: hunger, fear, curiosity, care, and the drive to expend surplus aren’t one appetite wearing several masks but genuinely distinct drives, each construing the conditions it answers to from its own angle. It grants the competition: they contend, and at any moment one can hold the field while the others fall silent, the hungry organism isn’t curious, the terrified one not at play. And it grants the conditionality the *order of rank* was reaching for: the drives stand in a shifting hierarchy, one commanding while others obey.

What’s added is the ranking principle Nietzsche leaves unexplained. Where he names the ordering principle the will to power and leaves *why this drive rather than that one rules now* without a mechanism, the structural account supplies one: the drives are ranked by *salience-weight*, the valence-and-salience weighting derived at §5.3, and whichever drive carries the steepest weight commands the field. Deficit is the limiting case, not the whole of it: where an unmet condition stands near the closure’s dissolution, its gradient dominates, and the most pressing deficit takes the field because feeling is the reading of that gradient. But the same weighting runs in the surplus regime, where no deficit presses and the ranking falls instead to the positive-valence salience of reach: drive-as-reach, the drive to expend strength on play, curiosity, and field-expansion; there the drive that commands is the one whose opportunity weighs heaviest, not the one nearest to dissolution. Urgency is thus the emergency form of salience-weight, not its definition, which is why the ranking principle doesn’t re-center the self-preservation primacy the aversion-pole already disclaims. The order of rank, in this first and descriptive sense, is therefore not a primitive fact about a will to power but a joint prediction of drive and feeling (§5.3): conditional dominance by salience-weight over a single valenced field, with deficit-urgency as its limiting case.

This explains which drive commands the field, which isn’t yet what Nietzsche’s order of rank most wanted explained. His Rangordnung isn’t a report of which drive is heaviest now but an evaluative axis (ascending versus declining, noble versus base, health versus decadence), and salience-weight, a more-or-less of dominance rather than a higher-or-lower of worth, doesn’t by itself supply it. Nor is that axis the thermodynamic one it is easily mistaken for: ascending and declining aren’t surplus and deficit. A body narrowed to a single demand by genuine need isn’t thereby base; its field is constrained by necessity, and what necessity forces stands off the evaluative scale altogether, neither to its credit nor against it. The evaluative axis lives instead in what a closure does with the room necessity leaves it: a configuration is higher insofar as it widens the modal field it was free to widen (the reach, play, and field-expansion that extent measures, §5.4) and lower insofar as it narrows a field it was free to keep open. Necessity-driven narrowing is the floor, not a low score; decadence, in the one sense worth keeping from Nietzsche, is a field that could reach and doesn’t. This is why Chapter 6 states the political form as maximum possibility under necessities met: the necessities-met clause marks the floor at which necessity stops forcing the ranking, and the maximum-possibility clause is the evaluative axis living above it, the single life and the whole society (Chapter 6) being one structure at two scales.

So located, the account keeps the plurality and the descriptive hierarchy Nietzsche saw and says why that hierarchy takes the shape it does, while parting from him on the measure of rank: worth is scored not by a drive’s power to command but by whether its reach widens the field or devours another’s, so that a magnificent tyrant who narrows the fields around him spends possibility rather than raising it. That verdict draws on the standing of the inter (§5.7, §6), not on will to power alone, so the account claims no clean victory on Nietzsche’s own terrain: it overturns his evaluative picture only by importing a measure of worth he refused.

It parts from him a second time on the self. For Nietzsche the unity is illusory, a story told after the fact by the momentarily-ruling drive; on the structural account the unity is real but relocated: it sits not in any master-drive but in the self-producing closure (§4.8) within which all the drives bid. The drives are *one being’s* drives because they compete inside one field maintained by one closure producing its own continuation; subtract the closure and there is no arena for the competition Nietzsche describes. Grant him the plurality and the competition while refusing his eliminativism about the self: the many drives are real, their contest is real, and the one whose continuation they all serve is real as well.

*Feeling is what drive differentiates into (§5.3).* When the undifferentiated forward pressure encounters specific conditions (threat, opportunity, loss, contact with another subject) the structural account predicts it will read as drive shaped by those conditions: fear as drive in the registration of threat, desire as drive in the registration of possibility, grief as drive in the registration of permanent absence, care as drive in the registration of another subject’s vulnerability. These are claims about kind, not strict identifications, and they are stronger than what current affect science settles (Adolphs 2013; Bonanno 2009; Preston and de Waal 2002). The differentiated forms are taken up at §5.3; what is proposed here is the structural claim those debates leave open to test: drive is what the differentiated registers share, the baseline forward pressure of a being whose continuation depends on what it registers, present prior to and underneath every specific feel.

*Drive compels when thwarted and directs when met.* One feature of this carries past the phenomenology and into political life. A person who can’t find the next meal isn’t weighing how to spend the afternoon; the need consumes the field, and action runs close to reaction. Once that person is fed, housed, and safe, the pressure that had narrowed them to a single demand relaxes, and the same drive that drove them now has somewhere to go: it can be aimed at a chosen project, a person, a curiosity, rather than spent on whatever is most urgent. This aiming of a freed drive is what is taken up as willing at §5.11. Freedom, then, isn’t the absence of drive but the room a drive has to be directed once the most urgent needs are quieted. This is what relaxation is, beneath the everyday word: not the silencing of drive but the lifting of pressure from it, so that nothing urgent forces the next move and the field of what one might do is once again one’s own to choose among. To be relaxed is to drive oneself: to move without being pushed from behind or pulled from ahead.

*Needs and possibility.* In modal terms, a need is a condition whose absence contracts the living being’s modal field: alternatives that may remain objectively possible no longer stand as practical, live routes for that being, because the unmet condition monopolizes attention and action. Meeting the need is therefore not merely adding a good to a life. It removes a field-constraining condition and restores the range of possibilities the being can register, weigh, and enact. The drive toward a need is the living being’s registration both of that contraction and of the route by which it may be relieved. At greater depth, the drive toward a wider field isn’t a separate goal added beside needs; it is the same directional pressure once urgent need no longer occupies the field. What Chapter 6 calls maximum possibility is the collective form of this relation: the widest field of live possibilities a shared order can maintain once necessities have ceased to determine each person’s next move.

*The account theorizes drive from inside drive, and this doesn’t disqualify it.* Schopenhauer’s charge is epistemic: if intellect serves the will, then an intellect theorizing about drive is the servant describing its master. Its verdict may be distorted at the root rather than merely at the edges.

The distinction between a field’s *extent* and its *fidelity* answers the charge (§5.4). Drive shapes cognition by weighting what a body attends to and how urgently; that changes which region of the field is examined. It doesn’t by itself determine whether the resulting map is true. Interest decides what gets looked at, not necessarily whether it is seen accurately.

Interest can, of course, bleed into fidelity. That failure takes familiar shapes—motivated reasoning, confirmation bias, and affective-forecasting error (§5.4)—and corrective practices calibrate a body’s output against what stands outside it (§5.4, §5.6). The theory of drive receives no exemption. The remaining concession is exactly the one made at §5.6: this reasoning runs inside Nature and inside drive, not from a vantage above either. That locates the account without defeating it. A servant can describe the master truly when the description is checked as every other field-claim is checked.

The argument proposes that felt drive isn’t a further fact laid over integrated living regulation but its first-person aspect in conscious subjects. What is settled is narrower: living systems regulate toward and away from conditions, and the first-person witness includes felt orientation. Whether those facts are one operation under inner and outer descriptions, which living systems instantiate the inner description, and whether drive and registration are coextensive remain the account’s explanatory and empirical burdens.

The account doesn’t infer phenomenal registration from selective regulation alone, whether in plants, bacteria, or any other disputed case. Feeling (§5.3) therefore begins with conscious affect where the evidence is firmer and treats extension across the functional gradient as a further question.

## 5.3 Feeling
Feelings are how a living body registers whether things are going well or badly for it: good or bad, urgent or not, worth approaching or worth avoiding. They aren’t a distraction sitting on top of clear thinking, and they aren’t a lower grade of thought. That registration begins before deliberate choice, and practical reasoning never fully leaves it behind. When you feel fear, dread, hope, or relief, your body is reading how the world bears on your continuing and coloring it accordingly. Feeling, on the account here, is that reading: the most direct way a creature takes the measure of its situation from the inside.

**[Identification]**

**Feeling** · *Identification*

Feeling is the conscious registration of a body’s condition and situation with valence, salience, or urgency. It can concern what is actual, remembered, anticipated, imagined, or merely believed possible. Affect is proposed as the lived readout of integrated stake-sensitive regulation rather than a second signal added after valuation has occurred.

*Status: the first-person actuality of feeling and its temporal, differentiated, embodied character are strict in the witness case. Affect’s relation to valuation, attention, interoception (the sensing of the body’s internal condition), appraisal, and action is empirically supported but theoretically contested. Attending to a denial demonstrates selective attention, not affect; that feeling is the proposed integrated readout remains a functional proposal defended by fit.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2)

Drive (§5.2) supplies a proposed directional organization; feeling is the conscious affective registration associated with some such organization. Valence (good or bad, attractive or aversive), salience (this stands out, that doesn’t), and urgency (now, not later) can interact without being identical. Selective attention can occur with little reported affect, and affect can be diffuse without one clear object. The stronger proposal is that integrated conscious feeling reads how actual and represented conditions bear on the subject. That account must accommodate dissociations among its components rather than defining them away.

What this registration is *of* is broader than the current state. A body that only registered what was happening couldn’t feel anticipation, dread, hope, longing, or relief, affects that track what *could* happen rather than what does. Feeling values the body’s field of possibility, not only the actual moment occupying it. The same valence that lands on the present also lands on the imagined landings the body has stored as live (§5.4): a remembered burn shapes the body’s response to nearby flame even when nothing is currently burning, an imagined success steadies the body through preparation for it, an absent friend’s possible illness produces real worry across the distance separating bodies. Valence operates over the *modal field* (the structured space of what a body has registered as possible, defined in §5.4) and the affect a body feels at any moment is the valence-weight of where, in that field, the body currently is and what it currently sees ahead. This is what makes feeling the substrate of empathy, planning, anticipation, and grief, all of which require valence to operate over imagined or remembered possibility rather than only over actual occurrence.

*The field with nothing to weight.* The account also reaches a limiting case: a field that presents no branch salient enough to draw valence at all. Here the forward pressure of drive (§5.2) doesn’t fall quiet for want of an object—it registers its own persistence as an aversive restlessness, the state ordinary language calls boredom (Eastwood et al. 2012; Bench and Lench 2013; Danckert and Eastwood 2020). Boredom isn’t the absence of feeling but feeling with nothing in the field to land on: the standing drive turned back on itself when salience finds no figure. That the drive registers *aversively* rather than lapsing into rest when its field empties fits the claim of §5.2 that the drive is standing and not occasional, never quite at rest: a being whose reach were merely a response to present objects would idle when none were live, whereas a being for which the reach is standing must feel its own reach unmet. This is what separates boredom from calm—calm is the field at rest with its conditions met; boredom is the field at rest with the reach still running.

That feeling values possibility and not only actuality is also what makes it *corrigible*. The bare fact that something is registered is the body’s own, and in that thin sense not mistaken; but *what* a feeling takes the world to be (the dread that fires where nothing threatens, the anticipation that mis-weights a branch of the field, the grief that misreads an absence) can be wrong, because the valence is a proto-prediction and predictions can fail. What corrects a misreading is what corrected it across evolutionary time and what science later institutionalized: coordination of the reading against the world and against other readers. Selection coordinated affect to survival by culling the lineages whose valence tracked badly; science runs the same loop deliberately, pooling registrations across observers so that idiosyncratic error washes out, though shared, systematic bias can survive the pooling, which is why a whole community of coordinated readers can still converge on the same miscalibration. What such coordination reaches is the feeling’s structural content (its causes, its objects, the discriminations it draws), not the intrinsic feel itself, which is approached only through that structural shadow (§5.4, on consciousness and conceivability). A feeling is thus corrigible in what it tracks and public in its structure, while remaining, in what it is from inside, the body’s own.

Corrigibility can now be given its structure rather than left as an observation, because what feeling is a registration *of* is already fixed (§5.2). A drive-state is a standing weight on a branch the body holds as available, not an occurrent response to what is present, and such a weight can be borne without being felt at any given moment. Feeling is where those weights are read out as valence, salience, and urgency. Readout and weight are therefore two things, and once they are two they can fail to match.

**[Corollary]**

**Feeling as Lossy Readout** · *Corollary*

The correspondence between a body’s standing weights and what it feels at a time fails in both directions. A weight can be borne and not registered, so a subject may hold a real stake it is not at that moment feeling. And valence can fire where no weight is warranted, which is the dread that arrives with nothing threatening.

**Depends on:** Feeling (§5.3) and Aversion as Modal Weight (§5.2)

Two consequences follow, and the second is the load-bearing one.

1. *Felt intensity isn’t a measure of standing.* How heavily something registers at a time and how much of a subject’s stake it carries are distinct quantities, so neither can be read off the other.

2. *The readout can’t discriminate its own object’s modal status.* Aversion directed at a line R can’t admit is empty rather than small (§5.2, §2.1.5), but nothing in the registration marks it as empty: dread of the really impossible presents exactly as dread of the avoidable. The distinction is available to reasoning (§5.6) and not to feeling.

The second consequence is why the corrigibility just described isn’t a defect in a particular subject’s feelings but a structural feature of any readout. It also fixes what a felt report can and can’t be used for downstream. Where later sections treat felt states as evidence (§6), the readout is a first source of loss standing upstream of any distortion in the reporting channel, and the two must be kept apart: a subject can report faithfully what it feels while what it feels misrepresents what it holds.

*The field’s two-layer origin.* The modal field a body carries at any moment is loaded from two distinct sources, and non-conscious processing (what is colloquially called the subconscious, what the cognitive-science literature calls the cognitive unconscious or implicit cognition) is largely the processor that runs both. The first layer is genetic: pre-weighted branches installed by the lineage before the individual body encountered anything at all. Loss-aversion, threat-detection, social-bonding circuitry, the startle response: these are the accumulated modal field of the evolutionary lineage, compressed into developmental architecture. The body doesn’t learn them from nothing; it arrives with them partly calibrated, because the lineage ran the selection experiment across millions of generations and pre-set the weights that survived.

The second layer is experiential, what is named here *modal memory*: the accumulated registration of modal access that has occurred across this life, the simulation library built from what foods are available, which situations precede danger, what the consequences of specific actions have been, which people can be trusted. Experience densifies modal memory continuously; its selectivity makes it lossy.

Non-conscious processing is what runs the field as a background processor: running simulations, updating weightings, consolidating the day’s inputs into the field’s structure. Much of what shows up as intuition, expertise, prejudice, and trauma response is this background activity surfacing as pre-conscious modal weighting before deliberate reasoning gets access to the output.

The expert who “just knows” is a body whose field has been densified enough in a specific region that navigation happens below the deliberative threshold; the trauma response is a body whose field was weighted so heavily in a specific aversive direction that the simulation fires and drives behavior before the conscious layer can intercept it. Both are the field operating, not some separate faculty operating alongside it.

This is why affect is structurally prior to practical deliberation rather than a competitor to it. A being that registers no outcome as better, worse, attractive, or aversive has no basis for choosing among outcomes. Damasio’s patients make the distinction visible: they can describe and compare options while struggling to decide among them after affective signaling is damaged. The evidence supports affect’s role in valuation and choice; it doesn’t show that every form of theoretical inference requires occurrent feeling.

Clinical and lesion evidence bears on integration without deciding identity. Congenital insensitivity to pain, affective flattening after damage, and anhedonia can alter both reported feeling and behavior in domains served by damaged or atypical systems. That co-loss is expected if affect and valuation depend on common neural machinery. It doesn’t rule out epiphenomenalism: damage to a common basis can remove a causally efficacious function and a causally idle accompaniment together. Nor does the absence of a clean neurological subtraction establish that none is metaphysically possible. The evidence supports tight dependence and functional integration. The further claim that affect *is* the relevant work registered as the subject’s own state remains an inference to the best account, assessed against rivals rather than delivered by lesion data alone.

The feeling-as-shallow-registration claim has empirical correlates across species. Fish exhibit nociceptive responses with cognitive components that go beyond reflex (Sneddon et al. 2014; Brown 2015). Mammalian fear, attachment, and grief are documented across orders: rats, dogs, elephants, cetaceans (Panksepp 1998; Bekoff 2007).
