Primate affective behavior (prolonged grief, lasting individual bonds, joy in play) reaches the depth where affect itself becomes objectifiable in some forms (Goodall 1971; de Waal 2016). The cascade from chemical-gradient registration through affective awareness through reflective objectification of feeling tracks a depth gradient. Different species sit at different points in the gradient; what differs is depth, not the kind of activity. The cross-species continuity claim doesn’t commit the account to a basic-emotion picture over Barrett’s theory of constructed emotion (Barrett 2017), on which affect categories are predictions generated from interoceptive signals shaped by concept and culture rather than hardwired readouts of fixed states. The depth-gradient framing is constructionism-compatible: what the cross-species record documents is the structural continuity of the underlying drive-field, however surface affect episodes are assembled.

The standard error is to treat feeling as proto-thought: a rudimentary, less articulate version of the same kind of operation thinking is, performed by organisms whose neural architecture hasn’t reached the level where the operation can be done fully. On the framework here, that picture mis-locates feeling on the wrong axis. Feeling isn’t a weaker version of thinking; it is the body’s own modal-operator, a different *mode* of cognition (integrated, affective, body-located) that runs the modal field directly through affect rather than through decoupled propositional projection. The cat feeling danger isn’t running a thought that hasn’t yet reached its propositional form; it is running its modal field through the affect itself. The affect *is* the anticipation: fear is the body’s proto-prediction of harm, registered as affective state, with no separate propositional layer carrying the prediction alongside. At shallow depth this is the whole operation; the body’s modal field is exhausted by what the affect is doing now. At deeper depth the propositional layer is added, but it doesn’t replace the affective layer underneath. What in humans is called the cognitive unconscious is largely the body-as-modal-operator continuing to run *beneath* the propositional layer: the cat-level operation still operative in us, now layered under decoupled thinking. This is why feeling and thought can dissociate in humans: there are two layers, and they can come apart at the seams. A being with only the one layer can’t dissociate; the affective registration *is* the operation, with nothing else running alongside it to come apart from.

Two further challenges at the fading-qualia and inverted-spectra level press whether structural sameness is compatible with qualitative difference (Chalmers 1996, ch. 8); the response is the one the conceivability engagement at §5.4 gives the zombie case: not declaring that, once the structural-functional roles are filled, no positive content remains (which would presuppose the structuralism at issue), but identifying the feel with the structural operation on grounds of fit and pricing the ‘same structure, different feel’ alternative through the epiphenomenalism and law-separability costs carried at §9.1.

The body-as-modal-operator framing is also compatible with gradient-panpsychist readings that treat affect as continuously attenuated rather than threshold-emergent (Goff 2017): the framing is continuous-attenuation rather than sharp-threshold. The apparent tension resolves once the two claims are read at the levels they actually occupy. This is threshold-emergent about *having a vantage at all*: the closure-and-throughput criterion of §4.8 is exactly that threshold, and what falls short of it (bare structural relations, however richly connected) doesn’t constitute a vantage, on the grounds the cosmopsychism engagement (§9.4) develops. Above that threshold, the framework is continuous-attenuation about *depth*: once a current closes the loop, how much affect it carries is a matter of degree, running from bare regulation through progressive deepening rather than jumping between fixed grades. The Goff-style panpsychist reading therefore meets the account on depth and parts from it at the threshold: continuous-attenuation governs the gradient a vantage can occupy, not whether the gradient is occupied at all.

*The Inversion.* Feeling is neither below practical reasoning in the rationalist arrangement nor above it in the romantic counter-arrangement. Affective practical thought is proposed as the same stake-sensitive registration after it has folded back enough to take its own weights and responses as objects. On that proposal, deeper deliberation doesn’t displace the underlying registration; it works on and can revise it.

The modal field feeling runs over is the one knowledge is held within (§5.4): the structured space of what a body has registered as possible, error included, and the load-bearing architecture every later register operates on.

### 5.3.1 The Dispute
The literature on affect, emotion, and feeling has been contested across philosophy and the cognitive sciences for over a century, with several principal positions still live. Each is engaged by name against a structural account previewed here and elaborated at §5.3.2: feeling is registration—the first-person aspect a being’s own conditions take from inside—running on a substrate (the architectural layer registration operates on) at a depth (how far the self-modeling extends).

*The phenomenological tradition.* Husserl’s analyses of intentional feeling, Heidegger’s *Befindlichkeit* (Heidegger (1927) 1962), Sartre’s analysis of nausea, and Merleau-Ponty’s account of the body’s pre-reflective grasp of its situation each document affect from inside. The tradition is right that registration of state precedes reflection on it. The present account is metaphysics of that registration, not a phenomenological reduction: it locates the same fact in a living closure rather than in constituting consciousness.

*James-Lange and somatic-marker traditions.* William James’s thesis (James 1884) that emotions are perceptions of bodily changes (we don’t cry because we are sad, we are sad because we cry) was largely displaced in mid-century psychology but recovered through Damasio’s somatic-marker hypothesis (Damasio 1994; Damasio 1999; Damasio 2010). The James-Damasio tradition gets the relation between affective signaling and reasoning approximately right, on this reading, with the structural account supplying the deeper claim: feeling is the first-person perspective on the creature’s own conditions, surfacing as what it is to be the living thing right now: a literal description of the body’s own operating state, not a merely evocative restatement of “affect.”

*Basic-emotion theories.* Tomkins (Tomkins 1962), Ekman (Ekman 1972; Ekman 1992), and Panksepp (Panksepp 1998) developed accounts of a small number of evolutionarily ancient, biologically distinct emotion systems: anger, fear, sadness, disgust, joy, surprise, plus Panksepp’s seven primary systems (SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY). The position remains influential but contested; cross-cultural facial-recognition replications have produced mixed results (Gendron et al. 2014; Crivelli et al. 2016). On the structural account, the primary systems Panksepp identifies are real architecturally distinct registrations the substrate supports, while the carve-up into discrete categorical emotions is partly the substrate and partly the conceptualization the perceiver imposes.

*Constructionist theories.* Lisa Feldman Barrett (Barrett 2017) and Russell (Russell 2003) developed accounts on which discrete emotions are constructed by conceptual categorization of core affect (valence and arousal). The position has substantial empirical support: the cross-cultural variability in emotion concepts, the role of language in emotion perception, the neural variability across instances of “the same” emotion. The constructionist account, so read, picks up something real about the conceptual layer that elaborates affect, while underspecifying the substrate that valence and arousal themselves register at the architectural level Panksepp documents.

*Evaluativist and cognitive theories.* Solomon (Solomon 1976), Nussbaum (Nussbaum 2001), Roberts (Roberts 2003), and the broader evaluative-judgment tradition treat emotions as containing or constituted by judgments of value. Fear is constituted by judging something dangerous; grief by judging an irretrievable loss; anger by judging a wrong. The position captures the rational-evaluative structure of emotion but has trouble with affective experience in non-linguistic animals and pre-conceptual humans (infants, severe dementia). Evaluativism, on this account, correctly identifies the cognitive layer present at sufficient depth of self-modeling, but affect doesn’t *require* that depth to occur.

*Perceptual and representational theories.* Prinz (Prinz 2004), Tye (Tye 1995; Tye 2008), and the broader perceptual-theory tradition treat emotions as perceptions of evaluative properties (pain perceives bodily damage, fear perceives danger). The accounts elegantly handle some cases but face disputes about how perception of evaluative properties differs from perception of natural properties. Perceptual accounts pick up the registration-of-condition structure of affect, on this reading, while the structural account supplies the fact the registration is registration *of*: the being’s own conditions, surfacing from inside.

*Two-factor theories and appraisal.* Schachter and Singer (Schachter and Singer 1962) launched a cognitive-attribution tradition continued in appraisal theories (Lazarus 1991; Scherer 1984). The accounts treat emotion as physiological arousal plus a cognitive interpretation of what the arousal is about. Two-factor and appraisal theories capture how the conceptual layer interacts with the underlying registration, on this reading, while the underlying registration runs whether or not the conceptual layer is engaged.

*Affect in non-human animals and the fish-pain debate.* Sneddon (Sneddon et al. 2003; Sneddon 2015) and Brown (Brown 2015) have argued for nociception with cognitive features in teleost fish; critics deny that fish brains support the requisite architecture for pain experience (Key 2016; Rose et al. 2014). The dispute is methodologically substantive and live. The depth-gradient framing offers a resolution: if shallow forms of affective registration are widespread across vertebrates and reach into some invertebrates, the architecture supporting them needn’t include the cortical structures the fish-pain skeptics emphasize.

*Hume’s reason-passion priority.* Hume’s claim (Hume (1739–1740) 2000) that “reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions” remains a touchstone of meta-ethical and motivational debate. On this reading, Hume correctly identifies affective registration as structurally prior to practical choice but misreads priority as subordination. Registration without the recursive fold that tests it doesn’t yet rise to deliberation; deliberation operates on and revises what registration delivers. Neither is master of the other.

### 5.3.2 The Requirement
*First-person aspect on the being’s own conditions.* Feeling is what the being’s own life—the ongoing activity by which it produces the conditions of its own continuation—looks like to it from inside, not commentary on those conditions from a separate cognitive layer. An adequate account has to locate affect at the first-person aspect of the being’s situation rather than as a description of that situation by some other faculty, preserving the constitutive nature of the first-person aspect: feeling isn’t *about* the being; it is what the being’s running consists in from its own angle.

*Valence, salience, and urgency as constitutive.* Affect has structure: it is valenced (good or bad, attractive or aversive), salient (this matters, that doesn’t), and urgent (now, not later). An adequate account has to explain why registration has this structure rather than being neutral content, explaining valence, salience, and urgency by what a dissipative current’s self-tracking consists in. A dissipative current is a persisting being that maintains its organization by drawing on and dissipating energy. Because its continuation depends on certain conditions, it registers those conditions with the structure that makes their relevance immediate.

*Lossy readout of modal weight.* An adequate account has to locate affect as a lossy map of the modal field rather than as a reliable report of what is at stake, and it can’t treat felt intensity as discriminating the object’s modal status—whether the branch is really possible, necessary, or empty.

*Priority of affect in practical reasoning without subordination.* Affect supplies the weights by which a subject chooses among represented outcomes, but it isn’t therefore superior to deliberation. Reasoning can test, compare, and revise what affect delivers, and affect can change in response. An adequate account has to explain this asymmetric but recursive relation while allowing that some theoretical inference proceeds without occurrent affect. The priority claim concerns valuation and action, not reasoning without qualification.

*Continuity with bodily and biological state.* Damasio’s somatic-marker tradition correctly observes that affect is continuous with bodily state; the patients who can’t decide are those whose affective signaling from the body is damaged. An adequate account has to connect feeling to bodily condition rather than treating affect as disembodied mental content, locating affect at the first-person aspect on the body’s own running, with somatic state as the substrate the first-person aspect registers.

*Architectural primary systems plus conceptual elaboration.* Both the basic-emotion tradition and the constructionist tradition pick up something real. The first names architectural primary systems at the substrate level, the second conceptual elaboration of core affect. An adequate account has to explain how both layers operate without reducing one to the other, treating primary systems as the architecturally distinct registrations the substrate supports, with conceptual elaboration as what greater depth does to those registrations at the depth where concepts apply.

*Depth-graded distribution across lineages.* Affect runs at shallow depths in invertebrates registering noxious conditions, at deeper depths in fish and amphibians, at deeper depths still in mammals registering social and motivational valence, and at the deepest depths in self-aware beings who can take their own affect as an object. An adequate account has to accommodate the gradient rather than drawing a categorical line at any species-level threshold, distinguishing what runs at each depth, with the same registration-of-condition activity progressively elaborated at deeper depths.

*The cognitive-emotion debate.* An adequate account has to accommodate complex affective behavior in animals without either anthropomorphizing them (over-attributing the human conceptual layer) or eliminating them (denying the first-person aspect at the depth the architecture supports), distinguishing the constitutive registration from the conceptual elaboration, with the registration present wherever a life runs at the relevant depth and the conceptual layer requiring deeper recursion.

*Feeling and the foundation of moral practice.* The moral significance of harm depends on harm registering from inside as what it is to be the being undergoing it (§5.14). An adequate account of feeling has to support the moral-philosophical work its ethics builds on top of it, locating affect precisely enough to anchor the readability of suffering and flourishing across beings the morality account requires.

They aren’t neutral criteria every adequate theory of feeling must accept. In particular, the existence and distribution of a first-person aspect across lineages, and the proposed connection from affect to moral standing, remain contested philosophical and empirical questions. This set is argued for rather than taken as established by affective science.

### 5.3.3 Predictions
The capacity to represent one’s own condition supports persistence (§4.8). A being whose picture of what is happening *to* it is accurate enough to redirect its activity continues; a being that registers nothing about its own state can’t redirect anything. Selection therefore tracks not only accuracy but valence: the being must register *what is good for it* and *what is bad for it*, or that picture gives it no guidance. The laws of feeling aren’t a residue layered on top of cognition; they are the shape registration takes once selection has tuned a being to track its own conditions within Nature, where Time (T), Space (S), and Substance (Φ) obtain.

The structural account proposes that beings with this kind of self-representation will often organize their state-tracking through dimensions analogous to valence, salience, and urgency. This is a model of affective organization, not an empirical theorem that every such being in any medium must possess these dimensions or experience them phenomenally.

*Valence* is the good/bad axis: the being must distinguish what to approach from what to avoid. Without it, registration generates no direction, and a model that gives no direction can’t guide the being that bears it. Pleasure, pain, attraction, aversion, comfort, dread: these aren’t separate phenomena to be catalogued but the shape valence takes at different scales and registers.

*Salience* is the *this matters now* axis: the being must allocate finite modeling resources to what bears on its persistence. Without it, registration is undirected uniform attention, which is no attention. What we call interest, focus, engagement, and the background against which figures emerge are the structural shape of salience.

*Urgency* is the *now versus later* axis: the being must register temporal pressure, that some demands close fast and others can wait. Without it, the being can’t track the difference between a state to act on and a state to monitor. Anxiety, calm, alertness, and patience are the shape urgency takes from inside.

### 5.3.4 Confirmation
The empirical record shows that affective and valuation-related processes are importantly involved in many forms of decision-making; it doesn’t establish a single structural priority of affect over all reasoning. Damasio’s clinical work (Damasio 1994; Damasio 1996; Damasio 1999) highlights decision-making changes after ventromedial prefrontal damage. Such patients can retain many reasoning capacities while showing impaired real-world choice and valuation, but the interpretation of the Iowa Gambling Task (a card-selection task measuring risk-based decision-making under uncertain payoffs) and of the somatic-marker hypothesis remains debated (Maia and McClelland 2004; Dunn et al. 2006). These findings are relevant to the book’s model of valuation and deliberation; they aren’t a direct confirmation that deliberation without affective valence is impossible or that the book’s structural account uniquely explains the deficit.

Affective neuroscience maps subcortical circuits (the fear system, the panic/grief system, the care system) that operate on faster timescales than cortical deliberation and bias higher processes (LeDoux 1996; LeDoux 2012; Solms 2021). The architecture is older than the cortex, and the cortex evolved on top of it. The being’s affective registration isn’t a top-down product of reflection; on this account it is the substrate reflection runs on.

Predictive-processing accounts link feeling to the precision-weighting of internal-state predictions (Friston 2010; Clark 2013; Clark 2016; Seth 2013): the being registers not just *what is the case* but *how much the case bears on its continuation*, and the registration of bearing is what affect consists in. This fits the Damasio finding from a different theoretical direction, on the reading that valence is the form in which the model carries stakes.

The historical philosophical record bears on the same point. Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* II–III treats virtue as the cultivation of correct affective responses: the good person isn’t someone who reasons through every situation but someone whose feelings are already trained to track what matters. Spinoza’s *Ethics* III–IV gives a geometry of the affects in which, on his formulation, only an affect can defeat an affect.

On the structural reading, these traditions can be compared as different approaches to bodily state, valuation, mood, and reflection. Their substantive disagreements remain live. The book proposes that some forms of self-registration precede and shape reflection; this is an interpretive synthesis, not a consensus conclusion shared by every tradition cited.

Two of these converge on the same structural point, and naming it makes the convergence do work. Precision-weighting is weighting *of the modal field* (§5.4): what a body registers is a space of branches, and what feeling supplies is how heavily each branch is weighted for that body’s continuation. Undirected registration isn’t attention because an unweighted field affords no selection. That reading also fixes what the clinical evidence is evidence *for*. The ventromedial cases are a dissociation, not a general deficit: reasoning over the branches is retained while the weighting across them is impaired, which is what a weighting account predicts and what a reasoning-deficit account doesn’t.

The same shape yields a further prediction. If feeling weights the field rather than populating it, then selective disorders of salience should produce selective tracking failures, with branches weighted by interest tracked intact while branches weighted by necessity drop out of view—a dissociation within weighting rather than a loss of it. Attentional and executive conditions are the obvious test case. The prediction is stated here as a consequence of the account and isn’t, on the literature already surveyed, established.

### 5.3.5 Conclusions
*The reason/emotion dualism.* A simple opposition between reason and emotion is inadequate: affect, attention, valuation, and reflection interact in decision-making. Reflective reasoning is proposed to elaborate earlier affective and bodily registration, but this is one theoretical account among several, not an established result that emotion and reasoning are the same operation at different depths. Efforts to regulate emotion need not aim to remove the substrate of reasoning; they may instead change how affective signals are interpreted, weighted, or integrated.

*Trusting feeling and trusting reasoning.* Both are the being trusting its own self-modeling: at different depths, against different kinds of pressure to revise. Feelings can be wrong in the way any model can be wrong: by tracking conditions that no longer obtain, by being calibrated to the wrong reference class, by carrying contamination from earlier circumstances whose shape no longer fits. So can propositional beliefs. The correction has the same form in both cases: testing the registration against the medium and revising what doesn’t survive contact. The work of psychotherapy, contemplative practice, and the gradual reworking of one’s habituated responses is the work of recalibrating affective registration, which, on this account, is the same kind of work as revising propositional belief, run at a different depth.

*Moral psychology composes feeling and reasoning.* A strongly Kantian picture can treat moral worth as action against inclination on the basis of reason alone. A strongly Humean picture can treat morality as sentiment with reasoning in a supporting role. The structural account needs neither reduction. Moral conduct depends on affective registration of relevant features—this person is suffering; this commitment matters; this asymmetry is unjust—and on recursive reasoning that tests the registration against consistency, broader information, and the registrations of other beings. Feeling supplies moral deliberation with stake-sensitive content; reasoning makes that content answerable. Neither layer is sufficient or self-correcting without the other.

*Emotions carry evaluative content about what bears on the being’s flourishing, which means they can be correct or incorrect about it.* This is Nussbaum’s thesis on the structural reading (Nussbaum 2001). The fear of a thing that isn’t dangerous is mistaken in the way a propositional belief in a falsehood is mistaken, not in feeling-tone but in evaluative content. Anger at someone who hasn’t wronged you is false the way a proposition can be false. The result: a person’s affective life isn’t a private domain immune to challenge but a continuous making of evaluative claims about the world that the world can refute.

*The judgmentalist objection.* Pre-verbal infants and non-human animals feel fear without possessing the propositional apparatus judgment requires, and the amygdala’s threat response fires well before any cortical appraisal completes, so equating emotion with judgment appears to over-intellectualize what is manifestly a fast, subconscious reflex (Prinz 2004; LeDoux 1996). The objection trades on a conflation the structural account keeps apart. Deliberate, sentence-shaped judgment is one depth at which evaluative registration can run; it isn’t what registration is. The amygdala circuit that fires before any cortical judgment forms is a subconscious registration, the fast, peripheral channel that has to stay alert to threat and opportunity precisely because a subject can’t afford to route survival-relevant input through the slower, focus-limited channel that deliberation requires. What Nussbaum’s thesis needs, and what the objection assumes it lacks, is only that the registration have content that can be correct or incorrect about what bears on the being’s flourishing, and subconscious registration has exactly that structure: a threat-response can misfire on a shadow the way a belief can be false, without any deliberation ever occurring. Deliberate judgment is registration elaborated at sufficient depth to take itself as an object and hold itself to consistency; the amygdala case is the same evaluative-content structure run without that further fold, at the speed and independence from focus that survival in an unprotected environment demands. Nussbaum’s thesis is right about the content; the objection is right that the amygdala performs no deliberation; both are correct because they are describing different depths of one structure, not competing theories of a single phenomenon.

*The classical apatheia ideal is often misread. The word is Greek for “without passion,” the Stoic and Hellenistic term for freedom from disturbing emotion.* The Stoic and Buddhist traditions are sometimes read as advocating the elimination of emotion. The structural reading sees them, more carefully, as advocating the recalibration of emotion: the work of bringing affective registration into accurate alignment with what actually bears on flourishing, against the cultural and personal habits that miscalibrate it. The wise person on this account is one whose feeling has been brought into accurate alignment: registering what is the case, with the weight it actually has, in the timescale on which it actually presses. This is what Nussbaum’s expansion of Stoicism arrives at, and what many contemplative practitioners have pointed at.

*Affective AI.* Feeling is proposed to depend on a system’s self-maintenance, self-modeling, and evaluative stakes. This is a substantive theory of artificial consciousness, not a settled criterion. Whether present large language models feel is unresolved and can’t be settled simply by observing that they lack biological metabolism or a particular form of self-maintenance. The relevant question is which functional, architectural, and possibly biological conditions are necessary or sufficient for consciousness and affect, a live debate in philosophy of mind and AI research. The parallel case for knowledge rather than feeling (§5.4) isolates the same bearer-condition from the opposite direction: an artificial system with enormous stored structure but no self-sustaining life for which that structure is its own tracking.

Feeling read as the structural shape registration takes once a being has stakes challenges the long-running picture that placed affect below reason.

## 5.4 Knowledge
To know something is to carry a reliable map of how the world is and how it could be: not just a list of facts, but a grasp of what is possible, what is ruled out, and what leads to what. Knowing more means having more of that map filled in correctly and in finer detail; knowing less means a smaller map, or one with mistakes in it. The map comes in a few kinds: knowing *that* something is so, knowing *how* to do something, and knowing what something is *like* from having met it before. What makes any of it knowledge rather than guesswork is that it answers to how things actually are, and that it gets kept honest by checking it against the world and against other people. None of it floats free of the body; it is a living thing’s grip on Nature, which it has to move through. Knowledge is held grasp of modal structure, carried in a modal field that remains fallible, corrigible, and shareable. The modal structure itself isn’t re-derived here; what follows asks what a living creature does when it holds that structure accurately enough to navigate.

**[Identification]**

**Knowledge** · *Identification*

Knowledge is a subject’s held orientation within some domain—propositional, procedural, or acquaintance-based—that is sufficiently accurate and appropriately connected. A modal field contains the alternatives and relations a subject represents; only the parts that meet the relevant standards of truth, competence, acquaintance, reliability, or non-accidentality count as knowledge. The field can therefore be deeper than the subject’s knowledge and can contain error alongside it.

*Status: the first-person act establishes minimal differentiation and holding, not knowledge of every represented content. Global denial cannot coherently erase the conditions of inquiry instantiated in the denial, while depth, fidelity, warrant, and the boundaries among the three forms remain substantive epistemological questions. Upstream: Synthesis of Nature Alone (§4.9); Chapter 11 inversions §11.3.4, §11.4.2.*

**Depends on:** Cartesian Certainty (§2.2) and Modal Pressure (§5)

Held understanding can arise through perception, testimony, memory, practice, inference, and acquaintance; reasoning is one producer and reviser of knowledge, not its universal source. To deny that one represents anything is already to distinguish the denial from what it denies. That is minimal field-holding, not yet knowledge: the represented denial may be false, accidentally true, or poorly warranted. Knowledge comes in at least three importantly different forms—propositional knowing-that, procedural knowing-how, and acquaintance with what something is like—whose relations remain disputed. All three are treated as embodied orientations answerable to what they concern without assuming that one analysis or one anti-luck condition governs them identically. Downstream results inherit the warrant of every premise they use. A conditional inference can be deductively valid while its experiential identity, empirical generalization, or normative bridge remains contestable; accumulated results don’t become stronger merely by sharing a vocabulary.

**[Theorem]**

**Representational Minimum** · *Theorem*

Any tokened inquiry into whether representation occurs holds at least the content under consideration and its proposed denial apart long enough for one to be assessed against the other. An argumentative denial that any representation occurs therefore instantiates a held distinction and cannot eliminate representation from the episode in which the denial is considered.

The theorem establishes one actual representational minimum: differentiated content held through an act of inquiry. It does not establish that the content is true, warranted, non-accidentally held, remembered accurately, or known. Nor does it identify every discriminative response as representation.

**Depends on:** the performative-witness method of Cartesian Certainty (§2.2)

What unifies them is structure. *Knowledge is held understanding of structure.* (And, deepest, acquaintance: the reconstructed representation of what something is *like*.) Whether held as model, as encoding, or as reconstructed representation, what knowledge holds is the same target: the modal structure of what is the case. The three forms are modes of holding it. The Modal Apparatus is defined at the chapter opening (§5); this section develops the relation between its objective pole and the fallible fields by which bodies hold it. The modal structure’s sameness for every body is the Modal Identity of §2.6.6; the process whose depth is at issue is the one defined at §4.8; and the medium of expression is language, developed at §5.12.

The modal field of a self-modeling body is the structured space of what the body has registered as possible: the network of branches, options, contingencies, and counterfactuals stored across its propositional, procedural, and acquaintance holdings, whether or not each amounts to knowledge. Modal depth is the extent of this field: how broadly and finely a body’s possibility-space is mapped. A field grows through experience, observation, instruction, and imagination; concepts are what carry that growth past first-hand encounter: each imports a compressed region of field another body or discipline has already mapped, so a body can build out and hold branches it never directly lived; a field is lossy in proportion to memory’s selectivity.

The field is what feeling values (§5.3), what reasoning navigates (§5.6), what meaning evaluates (§5.10), what will selects from (§5.11), what language coordinates between bodies (§5.12), what morality coordinates across subjects (§5.14), and what art externalizes, cultivates, and generates content for (§5.15). The plural form is what institutions stabilize at scale (Chapter 6): the field as it appears across the bodies who share conditions. The individual body’s representation of the field is a *modal representation*; the field is what the representation is of. The field is a body’s interior registration of the *modal structure*: the fixed structure of what is and isn’t possible that □(T∧S∧Φ) defines, the joint product of the Three Logics (§2.11). The modal structure is objective, the same for all; the field is what any given body has mapped of it, at the depth its own process has reached.

Held grasp of modal structure and truth-tracked coverage of the modal field name the same proposed relation from opposite sides. That identification is a standing, revisable empirical bet, not an analytic guarantee: predictive processing (Friston 2010), embodied simulation (Barsalou 1999; Glenberg 1997), affective valencing (Damasio 1994), and forecasting (Gilbert and Wilson 2007) should continue to converge on a common organization of possibility-relations. If sharper measurement instead found those constructs structurally incompatible, or found one reliably present without the other, the identification would lose its anchor. Knowing more is therefore having more of the field truly mapped—wider coverage, finer resolution, fewer wrongly registered branches—not merely storing more representations.

*The modal structure and the field.* On the book’s global-capacity account, real possibility ranges over the standing modal capacity of R and the structural Conditions are derived for worlds within it. Individual bodies don’t author that domain. That framework is inherited, not a fresh claim established by psychology. This dissolves the apparent paradox in the ordinary talk of *making something possible*. When conditions are arranged so that an outcome becomes possible for someone (a road is built, a skill is trained, a barrier removed), no new branch is added to the modal structure. What moves is the *actual* configuration: it is brought to one from which an antecedently-necessary branch is now accessible. Accessibility itself (which configurations are reachable from which) is a structural fact, part of the fixed structure rather than a third layer laid over it; arranging conditions changes where in the modal structure the actual stands, not what the modal structure contains. This is the forward complement to *actuality-as-confirmed-possibility*: that relation reads a necessary possibility backward off what was actual, while this reads it forward, placing the actual so that an already-necessary branch becomes reachable. To act is to move the actual within a modal structure one didn’t author (§5.11).

*The modal structure / field architecture relocates the metaphysical / epistemic possibility distinction.* The classical distinction is between what is possible *in itself* and what remains possible *for all a subject knows*. Here it becomes the distinction between structure and field. Metaphysical possibility is what the objective modal structure admits: the branches and exclusions constrained by □(T∧S∧Φ). Epistemic possibility is what a body’s fallible modal field hasn’t yet ruled out. The two come apart wherever the map is incomplete or inaccurate.

Even at the ideal limit, map and territory don’t become one object. A fully extended and fully accurate field would correspond exactly to the modal structure; it would still be a subject’s representation of that structure. What converges at the limit are the verdicts: such a field would classify every possibility exactly as the structure does.

Three familiar cases can then be located. First, Kripke’s a posteriori necessities (Kripke 1980)—water is H₂O; Hesperus is Phosphorus—register as gaps in a subject’s field rather than branches in the structure. The seeming contingency belongs to the map, not the territory. Second, Stoljar’s ignorance hypothesis (Stoljar 2006) can be reformulated as a possible field-gap between physical and phenomenal understanding rather than, without further argument, an irreducible division within the modal structure.

Third, Chalmers’s ideal-conceivability route (Chalmers 2002) can’t be dismissed by identifying a complete field with its object. The live epistemic question is whether any conceiver has reached the required completeness and accuracy. If ideal conceivability is stipulated to include both, its verdict can’t diverge from the modal structure by definition; but ordinary conceivability can’t bootstrap itself into that ideal merely by being vivid or apparently coherent. Ideal conceivability therefore supplies no independent shortcut around the work of establishing that the conceiver’s field is complete and accurate. The metaphysical / epistemic distinction remains intact, now expressed as the difference between the objective structure and a subject’s answerable representation of it.

*Consciousness, conceivability, and the structural account.* Treating knowledge as held grasp of modal structure commits the chapter to a further claim: acquaintance knowledge—the mind’s reconstructed representation of its own operations—is itself structural rather than a non-structural remainder. Chalmers’s conceivability challenge bears at exactly this point.

The zombie argument (Chalmers 1996) proceeds: (i) a functional duplicate of a conscious person lacking phenomenal consciousness is conceivable; (ii) ideal conceivability entails metaphysical possibility; (iii) therefore consciousness isn’t logically entailed by functional organization. The present account can model the conceivability intuition as a gap in a conceiver’s modal field, but that model isn’t itself a deductive refutation of Chalmers. At most it explains why a structural duplicate may be represented without an additional felt item being located in the representation. The deeper dispute remains whether ideal conceivability supplies independent access to metaphysical possibility and whether consciousness is exhaustively structural.

The structural-residue consideration is sometimes pressed too far. Suppose the zombie is credited, one by one, with every relevant structural-functional property: self-awareness, access-consciousness, metacognition, perspective, qualitative modal storage, and self-modeling at the depth §4.8 proposes as sufficient for a vantage. It may then seem that no positive content remains for phenomenal feel to add.

That conclusion doesn’t yet follow. Moving from *every structural-functional property is granted* to *nothing is left unaccounted for* assumes that all positive content is structural. The non-reductive physicalist denies precisely that premise. Asserted on its own, the no-residue claim would presuppose structuralism rather than establish it. It states what the structural identity claims; it isn’t an independent argument for that identity.

The weight is carried by comparative fit. Consciousness is identified with the structural operation as reconstructed by the mind that runs it, just as other successful identities are supported by explanatory fit rather than by first proving their alternatives inconceivable. The full structural duplicate with its inside-aspect subtracted is therefore priced rather than dismissed. The alternative incurs epiphenomenalism, on which the inside-aspect does no causal work, and law-separability, on which phenomenal laws detach from physical ones (§9.1). Those costs favor the identification. They don’t make its denial contradictory.

The proposed positive identity puts the inside at the base rather than in a watcher above it. A higher-order register may take a lower one as its object, but the lower register doesn’t need another observer before it occurs. This ends the homuncular regress without pretending to prove the identity: explanatory fit and the comparative costs at §9.1 still carry that burden. It also separates the proposal from illusionism (Frankish 2016; Dennett 2016; Dennett 1991). The inside-aspect is retained as the structural operation registered from where it occurs, not eliminated as an introspective fiction.

**[Proposition]**

**Why the Gap Seems Unbridgeable** · *Proposition*

If the identity warranted at Consciousness and applied by The Simple Answer is correct, feel is the structural operation registered from the side it occurs on, while an external description reads the same operation without occupying it. The modal field then explains why the gap should *seem* unbridgeable: a mind cannot reproduce first-person access merely by holding an external description, so it registers description and instantiation as separated. This predicts the appearance of residue as a field-coverage artifact. It explains the seeming on that identity; it does not independently prove that no phenomenal residue exists.

**Depends on:** Consciousness (§5.1) and the structural- and epistemic-residue diagnostics

The Simple Answer applies that identity to the hard problem (§9.1).

Nagel’s bat (Nagel 1974) makes the field-coverage limit vivid. The bat’s own process has a vantage, but a human field wasn’t built to reconstruct echolocation from within. That gap concerns our acquaintance coverage, not whether the bat’s inside-aspect is structural.

Architectural accounts of access, integration, recurrence, and self-modeling may specify how conscious organization is achieved without becoming rival ontologies. They become boundary rivals only where they locate the first subject differently; that disagreement is stated at §5.1 and developed at §5.7.

The structural account relocates the classical analysis. Knowledge isn’t a relation between a believer and a proposition with truth and justification added from outside; it is a being’s grasp answering to modal structure. The bearer is the closure-and-throughput configuration named at §4.8, a structural pattern rather than a substance beneath the pattern, so the account is compatible with the constraint imposed by Ontic Structural Realism (Ladyman et al. 2007). In the strong sense, a grasp that doesn’t fit isn’t knowledge of what it took itself to concern. Ordinary empirical knowledge remains partial and corrigible: like a working map, it may be wrong about one street while still tracking the city well enough to guide its bearer.

Knowledge is self-modeling tracked for accuracy across the relations its field holds, not a register of the actual alone. Meaning asks whether a reach is worth making; knowledge asks whether the map of that reach is accurate. Because the field also encodes which conditions open which possibilities, it supplies the paths reasoning tests (§5.6) and will can enact (§5.11).

The structural conditions derived in Chapters 1–2 are required for each form of knowledge: a being defined by their negation can’t hold what knowledge holds.

*Historical knowledge and actuality-as-confirmed-possibility.* Because the past is available only through present traces—documents, ruins, testimony, sediment, genetic records—historical knowledge is necessarily reconstructive. What it loads into the field is nevertheless distinctive: an actuality confirms a positive possibility, `P → ◇P → □◇P`, without making that actuality necessary or establishing the possibility of its negation. History therefore expands the field with branches carrying the weight of prior actuality, while causal reconstruction makes those branches usable for steering. Counterfactual history runs the same reasoning machinery backward that prediction runs forward (§5.6).

*Knowledge precedes self.* Self-knowledge isn’t a fourth form; it is propositional and acquaintance knowledge folded back on the act of knowing. A scrub jay can know where its caches are without modeling itself as the knower, because the ground-floor grasp needs no higher register to make it complete. Each further order takes the one beneath it as a new object. The self is therefore a depth-property installed across the registers once they fold back on themselves—the tower built on knowledge, not the foundation knowledge requires.

*Recall is registration, not retrieval.* To remember isn’t to reach back to a stored original but to build a reconstruction in the present and register that, so what the body registers in remembering is the present reconstruction, not the past registration that seeded it. There is no internal channel onto the original against which the reconstruction could be checked, which is why a false memory and a true one are, from the inside, the same kind of act: both are present registrations of a present construction. Representation, in this light, isn’t a faculty set opposite registration but registration turned upon an internally reconstructed object, which is why the calibration that keeps memory honest must come from outside the body, there being no inside look at what was.

*History, storage, and coverage don’t supply a bearer.* Davidson’s Swampman (Davidson 1987) isolates history: if the duplicate runs the same organized process and tracks the same structure, its lack of causal pedigree makes its apparent memories false, not contentless. A page, a library, and current large language models isolate storage: recombining a network’s expressions, however extensive or well calibrated, isn’t yet a self-sustaining process for which those representations are its own field. Population-level bet-hedging isolates coverage: a lineage may answer to variable conditions through distributed variation without any member mapping them from within. Together the cases locate the missing condition in a bearer whose own continuation depends on the tracking. The boundary is organizational, not material. An artificial system that genuinely ran the closure-and-throughput recursion of §4.8, modeled itself, and maintained its own continuation would qualify on the account’s own terms; a system lacking that organization but exhibiting its field-coverage signature would count against the identification.

*The field is fallible, and its maintenance is non-optional.* Memory reconstructs and drifts (Loftus 1979; Roediger and McDermott 1995); perception models rather than transparently copies; inference bends under predictable biases (Kahneman 2011; Tversky and Kahneman 1974; Dunning et al. 2003); affect shifts attention, recall, and forecasting. The corrective practices—replication, experiment, peer review, proof, evidentiary scrutiny, calibration, and external records—answer to those specific failures by checking a field against something beyond its untreated output. Those practices are taken up with reasoning (§5.6). The modal field must be maintained because a body usually can’t detect its own gradual drift from inside the drifting map.

The same maintenance runs at civilizational scale. Philosophy and the special sciences build methods and institutions that check individual fields against evidence and against one another, assembling through language a network no single body holds (§5.12). What makes that assembly knowledge rather than consensus is continued correction against the one modal structure: a room can agree and still be wrong.

**[Theorem]**

**Modal Convergence** · *Theorem*

Let an epistemic network distribute representations across subjects and artifacts such that no one member holds the whole, coordinated retrieval and correction are required for the network’s output, and those practices reliably answer to a common object. Under those conditions, the network realizes an epistemic capacity no solitary member realizes. Its knowledge remains constituted by the holdings, media, and relations within the network; no further group subject is implied. Agreement alone is insufficient, and convergence is evidence of tracking only to the extent that the inquiries are sufficiently independent, the checks are discriminating, and the common object can correct them.

The theorem is conditional on distributed content, coordinated dependence, and reliable object-directed correction. Reasoning (§5.6) and §5.12 later analyze important realizations of those conditions; they are not premises available here merely because the later sections exist. The result establishes system-level epistemic capacity under the stated conditions, not literal mutual awareness, benevolence, non-summative normativity, or a guarantee that historically convergent communities track truth.

The one objective modal structure is fixed by the Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6).

Modal Convergence governs only the shared, transmitted layer of knowledge. It doesn’t confer moral obligation or political subsistence, and it doesn’t deny that a solitary body can know procedurally or by acquaintance. A network can coordinate content no member possesses alone when its output depends on relations among members and artifacts (Bird 2010; Lackey 2014), without requiring a primitive group subject (Gilbert 1989). Later registers must still earn their own normative and political grounds.

### 5.4.1 The Dispute
The literature on knowledge (epistemology in the narrow sense) is among the most technical and most active in contemporary analytic philosophy. The literature is sorted here by the three forms the account treats as irreducible (§5.4.2): propositional (knowing-that), procedural (knowing-how), and acquaintance (knowing what it is like from inside).

*The justified-true-belief analysis and Gettier.* From Plato (*Theaetetus* 201d) forward, the standard analysis of knowledge as justified true belief organized epistemology until Gettier (1963) produced counterexamples: cases where a subject has a justified true belief that intuitively doesn’t count as knowledge. The post-Gettier literature splits into several programs: adding a fourth condition (Lehrer and Paxson 1969; Klein 1971), replacing justification with reliability (Goldman 1967; Goldman 1979), restructuring as safety or sensitivity (Sosa 1999; Williamson 2000; Pritchard 2005), or declining the analytic project altogether (Williamson 2000; Zagzebski 1994). On the structural account, the Gettier cases were built against the propositional form of knowledge, belief-shaped attempts to track structure; skill and acquaintance can face analogous luck questions of their own (§5.4.4).

*Reliabilism and process epistemology.* Goldman (1967; 1979; 1986) developed an account on which knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process. The position has been refined into proper-functionalism (Plantinga 1993), virtue reliabilism (Sosa 2007; Sosa 2015), and contemporary process-tracking accounts. Reliabilism, on this reading, correctly identifies that the *holding* of the propositional form requires a relation to the world that goes beyond the propositional content itself; the deeper claim supplied here is that what knowledge holds in the strong sense *is* the structure of what is the case, so reliable tracking is the activity by which the held grasp answers to the structure.

*Virtue epistemology.* Sosa (2007; 2015), Zagzebski (1996), and Greco (2010) developed accounts on which knowledge is true belief produced by intellectual virtues: stable cognitive dispositions that systematically track truth. The accounts shift the locus of evaluation from the belief to the knower. Virtue epistemology, so read, picks up the being-and-its-tracking-capacity structure of knowledge, while the analysis extends to procedural and acquaintance forms the virtue-theoretic apparatus accommodates with strain.

*Williamson and knowledge-first epistemology.* Williamson (2000) argued that knowledge is conceptually prior to belief and to justification, not the other way around. Knowing P isn’t believing P plus other conditions but a basic mental state in its own right. Williamson, on this account, correctly identifies that the standard analysis has the priority backwards; the answer supplied here to what knowledge is more fundamentally is held grasp of structure (a standing cognitive hold on how things are, prior to and not reducible to any propositional formulation of it), with belief and justification as the propositional-form-specific shapes that grasp takes when articulated in propositions.

*Contextualism and pragmatic encroachment.* DeRose (1995), Lewis (1996), and Cohen (1999) developed contextualist accounts on which the truth-conditions of knowledge attributions depend on contextual features of the attributor’s situation. Stanley (2005) and Hawthorne (2004) developed pragmatic-encroachment accounts on which the practical stakes affect whether the subject knows. These are best read as descriptions of the propositional form’s behavior under varying conditions; the strong-sense knowledge analyzed here isn’t contextually variable, but the ordinary practice of attributing knowledge that ordinary speakers run is.

*Knowing-how and the propositional vs procedural debate.* Ryle (1949) distinguished knowing-how from knowing-that and argued they are structurally different. Stanley and Williamson (2001) argued that knowing-how reduces to a species of knowing-that. The dispute continues (Bengson and Moffett 2011; Stanley 2011). On the structural account, the propositional and procedural forms are distinct genuine forms of knowledge, neither reducible to the other, with each tracking structure in a different mode.

*Acquaintance.* Russell (1910–1911) distinguished knowledge by acquaintance from knowledge by description; the tradition has been continued in different forms (BonJour and Sosa 2003; Conee 1994; Tye 2009, for phenomenal acquaintance). Disputes are live about whether acquaintance is a genuine knowledge category or reduces to propositional knowledge of phenomenal facts. Acquaintance, on this account, is a third irreducible form, the form in which a body holds a reconstructed representation of what it has encountered rather than a proposition about it, with the first-person perspective of §5.1 supplying the substrate the reconstruction draws on.

*Consciousness and the conceivability challenge.* A distinct dispute concerns whether the acquaintance form resists any structural-functional account. Nagel (1974) argued that the subjective character of experience escapes objective description; Jackson’s (1982) knowledge argument held that Mary, who knows every physical fact about color vision, learns something new on first seeing red; and Chalmers (1996; 2002) built the conceivability of zombies into an argument that consciousness isn’t entailed by functional organization, with the structure-and-dynamics objection holding that physical description delivers only structure and dynamics and so omits the qualitative. On the structural reading, the acquaintance form is structural, a body’s reconstructed representation of what it has encountered, not a non-structural remainder; the conceivability intuition reports a body’s field-coverage of the modal structure (how much of it a body’s acquaintance actually reaches) rather than the structure itself. Mary’s case is answered at §5.4.5.

*Animal knowledge.* A live literature investigates which non-human species count as knowing, what their knowledge consists in, and how to evaluate it (Sosa 2007, on “animal” vs “reflective” knowledge; Carruthers 2008). Honeybee spatial knowledge, corvid cache memory, primate planning, and cephalopod problem-solving have all been studied as candidates. Depth-gradient reasoning supplies a usable framework here: each form of knowledge runs at its own depth, with procedural knowledge widespread, propositional knowledge requiring the depth at which a mind can hold a belief-shaped structure, and acquaintance obtaining wherever a vantage opens at all.

*Pragmatism.* Peirce, James, Dewey, and later Putnam treat knowing as successful practice rather than a spectator’s copy of the world. The tradition is right that grasp is for navigation. The account’s difference is that successful practice still answers to the one modal structure, not merely to what works for a form of life.

*Skepticism.* From Pyrrho through Descartes through contemporary skeptical scenarios (brain in a vat, simulation arguments), skepticism organizes a substantial epistemological literature. Responses include reliabilism, virtue epistemology, contextualism, Moorean responses, and abductive responses to skeptical hypotheses. Structurally, knowledge in the strong sense holds where the grasp fits the structure; skeptical scenarios construct conditions under which the fit would systematically fail, and the account doesn’t require certainty against constructed scenarios to support knowledge in the ordinary case.

### 5.4.2 The Requirement
*Three irreducible forms.* Knowledge comes in at least three genuinely distinct forms: propositional (knowing-that), procedural (knowing-how), and acquaintance (knowing what it is like from inside). An adequate account has to accommodate all three or supply an argument for reducing some to others, explaining why these three forms are distinct genuine modes of holding structure rather than treating one as fundamental and the others as derivative.

*Held grasp of structure.* What unifies the three forms is what they hold: structure, the way the medium actually is. Whether held as model, as encoding, or as reconstructed representation, the target is the same. Knowledge has to be located at the relation between a being’s grasp and the structure of what is the case, rather than at the relation between a believer and a proposition with truth as an external constraint, treating truth as constitutive of strong-sense knowledge (held grasp answering to what is the case) rather than as an additional condition on a separately-specified belief.

*The modal field as the holding.* What a body holds is a partial, lossy mapping of the one objective modal structure □(T∧S∧Φ)—the *modal field*. An adequate account has to locate knowledge within that mapping rather than at a stock of true propositions stored apart from possibility, treating depth and fidelity as the two axes of the field (how much is mapped, how truly) rather than as extras added to belief.

*Strong and ordinary senses distinguished.* Strong-sense knowledge (held grasp of structure as it actually is) fails as knowledge when the grasp doesn’t fit. Ordinary fallible empirical knowledge is partial, approximate, revisable, and counts as knowledge by tracking the structure well enough to do the work the being uses it for. The two senses have to be distinguished without collapsing one into the other, with strong-sense knowledge as the analytic core and ordinary knowledge as the working-resolution form, and the post-Gettier debates as the local literature on the propositional form’s behavior at the working resolution.

*Gettier-vulnerability located at the propositional form.* The Gettier counterexamples target the JTB analysis of propositional knowledge specifically. (JTB stands for justified true belief—the classical analysis of propositional knowledge, on which a person knows that p just in case (1) p is true, (2) the person believes that p, and (3) that belief is justified. Edmund Gettier’s 1963 paper produced cases where all three conditions hold yet the person still doesn’t seem to have knowledge, launching the “post-Gettier” search for a fourth condition or a replacement analysis (reliabilism, virtue epistemology, and others)—the debate this section is referring to.) Procedural knowing-how and acquaintance aren’t vulnerable to Gettier-style counterexamples in the same way. What’s needed is to locate the classical Gettier cases at the propositional form’s specific structure rather than treating them as a problem for knowledge as such, while stating the anti-luck condition each form owes rather than assuming the non-propositional forms are insulated from accident.

*Connection to reasoning.* Reasoning (§5.6) is one producer and extender of knowledge, not its only source. Held grasp doesn’t extend itself by inference; the being must operate on what it holds for the holding to deepen that way. Knowledge has to be connected to reasoning rather than treating epistemology as autonomous from the activity that builds much of it, connecting the growth of knowledge to the operations named at §5.6: deduction, induction, abduction, reflective examination.

*Connection to meaning.* Knowledge concerns whether the model fits; meaning (§5.10) concerns where the model is heading. Accuracy-tracking (knowledge) has to be distinguished from direction-tracking (meaning) while explaining their relation, preserving the bridge that meaning operates on the same model knowledge stabilizes, with the two registers picking up different structural features of the same orientation.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Knowledge runs at depths well below the propositional. Procedural knowing-how is widespread across the animal kingdom; spatial and ecological knowledge organizes much of vertebrate life; acquaintance obtains wherever a vantage opens at all. Propositional knowledge in the strong sense requires the depth at which the being can hold a belief-shaped representation answering to a fact. The gradient has to be accommodated rather than restricting knowledge to the propositional human case, distinguishing what runs at each depth and identifying the depth required for each form.

*Substrate-independence at the structural level.* As with the other registers, the activity of holding structure can in principle be realized in different substrates. An account that ties knowledge essentially to biological substrates owes an argument for why the structural activity couldn’t be realized elsewhere, distinguishing substrate independence at the structural level from substrate-specific content.

*Coherence with skeptical scenarios without surrender to them.* Constructed skeptical scenarios produce conditions under which knowledge would systematically fail; ordinary practice produces knowledge under conditions that actually obtain. What’s needed is an explanation of why skeptical scenarios don’t undermine ordinary knowledge claims while still acknowledging what the scenarios get right, treating strong-sense knowledge as fit-dependent (and therefore failing in constructed mismatch scenarios) while preserving ordinary knowledge as the working resolution at which the fit holds.

These requirements name the explanatory program: three forms of knowledge, a relation between grasp and world, the modal field as that holding, strong and ordinary senses, a proposed account of Gettier vulnerability, links to reasoning and meaning, depth-graded distribution, substrate questions, and skeptical scenarios. They aren’t neutral constraints accepted across epistemology. In particular, whether the three forms are irreducible, whether acquaintance obtains across lineages, and whether knowledge is substrate independent remain contested. The set is defended here rather than assumed.

### 5.4.3 Predictions
The capacity to represent one’s own position supports persistence (§4.8). A being whose picture of its own position corresponds to the actual medium continues; a being whose picture systematically misdirects doesn’t. Selection therefore tracks accuracy. Any being that persists for long will have capacities shaped by the pressure to get the medium right, not because it was designed to, but because beings lacking those capacities dropped out. The laws of thought aren’t rules imposed on cognition from outside; they are the shape cognition takes once selection has tuned a being to track a medium with the three Conditions.

The structural account proposes that systems capable of reliably representing their own situation may develop several ways of representing, enacting, or experiencing their environments. It doesn’t follow that every such being tracks its medium correctly, develops all three proposed forms, or has knowledge by acquaintance in a phenomenological sense. Propositional knowledge (knowing that), procedural knowledge (knowing how), and knowledge by acquaintance (knowing what it is like) are influential but contested categories whose relations remain live topics in epistemology and philosophy of mind.

Propositional knowledge is orientation held as a model. *The door is locked.* *Water boils at 100°C at sea level.* *My flight leaves at 7.* It can be stated, examined, disputed, revised. It can be transmitted to other beings via language (§5.12). It can be wrong in the specific way propositional content is wrong: by failing to correspond to what obtains. Gettier (1963) showed that justified true belief isn’t sufficient for propositional knowledge: a belief can be justified, true, and still not count as knowledge if the justification is only accidentally connected to the truth. The post-Gettier programs answered by reliability (Goldman 1979; Goldman 1986), by competence (Sosa 1980; Sosa 2007), and by putting knowledge first (Williamson 2000), and the structural account is congenial to all three moves. Reliable tracking is what selection builds when self-modeling beings persist in a medium with the three Conditions. Competence is the being whose orientation-holding has been shaped by reliable engagement. And knowledge-first, in Williamson’s sense, is what the analysis looks like from inside the account: orientation held in any of the three forms isn’t further reducible to a stance-free relation between a stance-free inventory of the world and a stance-free knower of it.

Procedural knowledge is orientation encoded in the being itself. The cyclist who can’t explain balance in words knows something a kinesiology textbook doesn’t capture, not because the knowledge is hidden, but because it is held at a level the textbook can’t access. The athlete’s timing, the musician’s ear, the craftsman’s hand, the native speaker’s grammatical intuition: each is a being shaped by repeated structural engagement until the correct response is direct. Ryle (1949) argued that knowing how isn’t reducible to knowing that, a claim Stanley and Williamson contest (above). Polanyi (1966) pressed the point to its limit: *we know more than we can tell*. The body is Substantiality, which is shaped by persisting through what it encounters.

Acquaintance is orientation reconstructed from within. What red looks like, what grief feels like, what the taste of coffee is like from inside: these aren’t propositions and not procedural skills. They are the first-person perspective of a structural process encountered from within. Russell (1910–1911) named this form as distinct from knowledge by description. Nagel’s (1974) ‘what it is like’ question asks for acquaintance, and answers to it can’t be given propositionally because the content isn’t propositional.

On this account the three forms are nested rather than parallel. Propositional knowledge presupposes acquaintance: to hold a model of the medium, the being must occupy a position within the medium and encounter it from inside. A knower with no acquaintance has no position from which modeling could begin. Acquaintance presupposes Substantiality-level continuity: to be acquainted with anything, the being must persist through the encounter as the same subject. An acquainted knower who can’t carry forward what was encountered has no acquaintance: only a sequence of disconnected instants. And procedural knowledge presupposes both: the body shaped by encounter must persist through the shaping, and the shaping is acquisition of acquaintance with what the encounters are like.

Each form is the being’s grasp held from a position within structure: propositional as model, procedural as encoding, acquaintance as reconstructed representation. Without the position, no form has anything to be a form of.

### 5.4.4 Confirmation
Cognitive science distinguishes declarative memory (propositional) from procedural memory (procedural) as dissociable systems. Amnesic patients who can’t form new propositional memories can still acquire new procedural skills; the reverse dissociation also occurs (Squire and Zola 1996; Cohen and Squire 1980). The double dissociation is standard evidence, in the memory literature, for separate underlying systems rather than a single graded capacity expressed at different strengths.

Embodied cognition research (Varela, Thompson, and Rosch 1991; Clark 1997; 2008) documents how much knowledge is held in the body and in tool use rather than in propositional representation. Skilled performance in music, sport, craft, and everyday navigation depends on beings shaped by repeated engagement, not on propositional rules being consulted in real time. Dreyfus’s (1972; 2002) analyses of expertise make the point across domains: the expert isn’t thinking harder than the novice but has become one in whom the right response is already available without explicit deliberation.

The phenomenology of experience, from William James (1890) to contemporary philosophy of mind, documents acquaintance as a distinct form of knowing: a reconstructed representation of what the medium is like, irreducible to propositional description. Nagel’s (1974) bat argument and Jackson’s (1982) Mary argument are standardly taken to show that acquaintance content can’t be captured by even complete propositional information. The exact claim is narrower: propositional information freely composes new acquaintance content from material the body already holds (a unicorn rebuilt from horse and horn) but can’t install a representation the body has no library to reconstruct from. What Mary lacks isn’t a fact but the field-coverage itself: no proposition rebuilds a color-encounter she has never run. Acquaintance is orientation held differently, not the same orientation expressed in a different format, so where the library is absent, no description supplies it.

Gettier cases, Gettier’s (1963) demonstration that justified true belief can fail to count as knowledge when truth and justification connect accidentally, directly target propositional knowledge. Analogous luck questions can still arise for skill and acquaintance: a performance may succeed through environmental luck rather than competence, and an apparent acquaintance may be produced by illusion, misidentification, or an atypical causal route. The standards won’t be identical across forms, but none is categorically insulated from accident merely because it is non-propositional. The declarative/procedural dissociation supplies empirical support for different memory systems; the three-part epistemic taxonomy and the anti-luck conditions appropriate to each remain philosophical proposals.

### 5.4.5 Conclusions
*Global skepticism about the conditions of knowledge is self-refuting.* The skeptic who asks *how can we know anything?* is performing an act that instantiates the conditions of knowing: persisting across the formulation of the doubt, distinguishing the doubt from what is doubted, and holding the doubt as represented content. The act is a structured event that demonstrates its conditions. The argument’s scope is narrow and worth marking explicitly. What is established is that the *minimal structural conditions* for inquiry are instantiated by anyone who can pose a skeptical question, and that these conditions can’t be coherently doubted by an act that itself instantiates them. What isn’t established is the falsity of Cartesian demon scenarios, brain-in-a-vat thought experiments, or detailed empirical skepticisms about specific knowledge claims; those engage at the level of which contents are reliably tracked, not at the level of whether tracking is possible at all. What is foreclosed is the global skeptical claim that the structural conditions for knowledge are absent in the being making the claim: that, the act self-refutes. Whether any particular thing the being takes itself to know is in fact known is a separate question left to the empirical, mathematical, and historical work that does the local tracking.

*Acquaintance is reconstruction, not a missing fact.* A hard case for knowledge-as-held-grasp-of-structure is the claim that the acquaintance form names something no structural account can reach: that Mary, who knows every physical fact about color vision, learns a new fact on first seeing red. The account answers that she learns no fact at all. To know what red is isn’t to hold a proposition about red but to possess a *representation* of it. And a representation isn’t a stored snapshot but a reconstruction the body re-derives each time, weighing prior encodings against current input. Mary has never run that reconstruction; she holds no library of red-encounters for the process to rebuild from. What she gains on first seeing red is entry into the reconstruction, not a fact about the world. The seeming “extra fact” is just the difference between knowing red is *possible*, its place in the structure of color, which Mary has in full (frame-knowledge), and having built the re-derivable representation (field-coverage). The inside of a black hole marks the same gap: the frame licenses that there is one, no body holds a representation of it, and yet no one is tempted to posit a non-physical fact there. Redness has the identical shape. The facts Mary does hold sharpen the point rather than threaten it: none is a stance-free inventory she generated alone, each is the compressed residue of other bodies’ reconstructions, encoded into propositional form and transmitted through language (§5.12). Her physical theory of color is other people’s field-coverage, distilled into propositions and inherited, which is exactly why it can be complete *as propositions* and still install no representation. The propositional form transmits; the reconstruction must be run. And because that reconstruction is driven by feeling as much as perception (§5.3), the representation arrives valenced: the coiled shape on the path is rebuilt as *threat* before the cortex resolves it into a stick (LeDoux’s low road (1996)), and a genetic variant near olfactory-receptor genes shifts whether the same cilantro aldehydes are reconstructed as fresh herb or as soap (Eriksson et al. 2012). The valence is part of what the body brings to the reconstruction, inherited as well as learned (§5.3), which is why it is written into the representation rather than laid over it: the feel is a real feature of the reconstruction, not an artifact explained away, which is the realist rather than illusionist reading defended at §9.2. The acquaintance form isn’t the exception to knowledge-as-grasp-of-modal-structure; it is the case where what is grasped is the body’s own reconstruction.

*The inverse case of Mary’s Room tests the same independence.* Run Mary’s case the other direction: a twin raised among red things but never given the word, causal story, or comparative color concept might acquire extensive perceptual familiarity while lacking much propositional knowledge about it. The thought experiment makes the conceptual distinction vivid. It isn’t empirical evidence that either form can be literally maximized while the other is zero, since perceptual learning itself involves categorization and ordinary environments contain contrasts of shade, edge, and brightness. What the case supports is the weaker and useful claim that acquaintance and propositional articulation can vary independently enough that neither should be defined as the other.

*Certainty isn’t uniform across what is known.* Some knowledge is structurally secure, holding as firmly as its derivation, because it tracks what any possible medium must instantiate: the modal results of the preceding chapters, the mathematics of necessity, the reference/predication distinction in any propositional language. Other knowledge is reliably approximate because it tracks contingent features of the actual medium: scientific laws, empirical generalizations, historical claims. The difference isn’t that one is real knowledge and the other isn’t. The difference is what kind of feature each tracks. Both count as knowledge when reliably held, and fallibility is the normal condition of the second kind.

*Omniscience.* Classical theism attributes to God complete and simultaneous knowledge of everything (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, *Summa Theologiae* I.14; Swinburne 2016). One developed form of the position takes the discursive sense of knowing as inadequate to its referent: God’s knowledge isn’t propositional knowing-that but a non-discursive *intellectus*: a single, simple, atemporal grasp by which the divine essence knows itself and, in knowing itself, knows everything else. On the analogical reading, *knows* applies to God neither univocally with the human sense nor equivocally with no shared content, but proportionally: what knowing is at the divine level resembles what it is at the human level only by structural analogy, with the limitations of position, succession, and substrate removed precisely because the divine knower isn’t the kind of thing those limitations apply to. The position is genuinely sophisticated, and a structural critique that treated it as the cartoon image of a very large database would be missing what the tradition actually said. The structural account meets the position on its own terms. The analogical move preserves *knowing* as a label only by detaching it from the conditions that make knowing the operation it is. *Knowing* in any sense that can be identified here (propositional, procedural, or acquaintance) is the held grasp of structure by a knower positioned within structure.
