Calling the I an object in the organism’s own field has a direct consequence, and it supplies a mechanism for the dissociation evidence that follows.

**[Corollary]**

**The Self-Model as Mapped Region** · *Corollary*

If the I is an object in the organism’s own field, it is a mapped region of that field, and a field is a fallible mapping of the modal structure. The self-model therefore stands on the same two axes as any other region: modal depth, how much of the subject is mapped, and modal fidelity, how truly.

**Depends on:** Identity (§5.7), Knowledge (§5.4), and Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7)

Holding the modeled I apart from the modeling process is the co-present content of a single episode—differentiated poles held within one standpoint (§2.4.7)—which is the structure the reflective witness of Change Is Actual (§2.2.1) already displays in distinguishing the doubting awareness from what it takes as its object.

Three consequences follow.

1. *Introspection carries no privilege.* It is a readout of a mapped region (§5.3), so it can be shallow, and it can be false. Sincerity secures neither.

2. *The self-model is corruptible from outside.* A field can be corrupted against mapping by another agent (§5.14), and the region modeling the subject isn’t exempt. That is the structural form of manipulation aimed at what a person takes themselves to be.

3. *Ego dissolution can selectively alter mapped self-content.* Reports and behavioral evidence support attenuation of narrative, bodily, agentive, or perspectival self-representation in varying combinations. Whether minimal awareness persists through every intense phase, and whether it is best described as a bare mapper, remain empirical and philosophical questions.

The third consequence fixes the evidential target narrowly: the organism and substantial processing can continue while some self-representational organization is attenuated. That is evidence for dissociability, not a complete ontology of the subject.

*Parasitism as an agency and control case.* *Toxoplasma gondii*, *Ophiocordyceps*, hairworms, and rabies can alter host behavior through different mechanisms (Berdoy et al. 2000; Vyas et al. 2007; Hughes et al. 2011; Thomas et al. 2002). These cases show that behavior and motivational control can be biased by another organism while host and parasite remain biologically distinguishable. They don’t precisely locate personal identity or establish what the host experiences. Their contribution is narrower: behavioral control, organismic boundary, agency attribution, self-model, and phenomenal subjecthood shouldn’t be treated as one variable.

*Identity extends to identifying others.* Self-modeling deep enough to register the self as an object is also deep enough to register *other* selves as objects of the same kind. Theory of mind (the capacity to model other minds as minds) is what the operation produces when its content domain expands (Premack and Woodruff 1978; Call and Tomasello 2008; Krupenye et al. 2016; corvid evidence at Bugnyar, Reber, and Buckner 2016). This is the inward root of the shared field the outward registers work in: a creature that models others as beings of its own kind can share field-content with them and not merely hold it alongside them—the distributed holding the Modal Convergence theorem (§5.4) describes, here in its self-modeling form, before language (§5.12) makes the transfer explicit. The organism that builds an I builds it relationally (identifying-with, identifying-against, identifying-as) and the moral and political work that begins at §5.14 rests on this. Identifications inherited from family, language, role, profession, gender, ethnicity, and tradition aren’t content added to an antecedently finished I; there is no frozen core for them to be added to, and the construction that holds them is partly made of what it has identified with. The social ontology of these inherited categories is the domain taken up at §5.12, where linguistic transmission is shown to do more than carry content between already-formed constructions. At issue there is how language and practice constitute rather than merely describe gender, role, and kinship, and what the membership conditions for those categories are.

*Identity’s depth gradient.* Not every pull the organism registers becomes identity. Drive’s attraction-pole (§5.2) lights up constantly and indiscriminately: a new hobby, a passing interest, a fixation that lasts a season. Most pass through without residue. What makes one of them identity, rather than merely something that happened to a person for a while, is depth: whether the pull got folded far enough into the self-model’s own organization that the organism now identifies *with* it rather than merely registering it. Someone who cooks doesn’t thereby identify as a cook; a chef does, because the pull was worked into the construction’s own structure rather than left at the surface. The same pull, at two different depths, is a passing interest in one case and a facet of the self in the other; nothing about the pull itself settles which. This is why identity can look, from the inside, like a mix of the chosen and the given: cultivating a pull into a core commitment is real work the organism does on itself (the discipline behind Frankfurt and Watson’s identifying-with, §5.11), while a pull’s arising in the first place isn’t authored by the organism any more than any other content of drive is.

*Identity’s field-shape.* Depth in a single pull isn’t the only variable; the modal field a person’s identifications occupy has a shape, and the shape varies independently of how deep any one column runs. A philosopher or a scientist can be narrow and deep: enormous depth in one column, the curiosity drive (§5.2) digging a single shaft as far as the field permits, often at the cost of reach elsewhere (the same reach-versus-depth trade-off named for externalized fields at §5.13). A field can instead be small and complete rather than narrow and deep: a teenager whose whole identity is one social role has a field limited in scale but fully occupied, which is why it can feel whole rather than impoverished. A field can instead be broad and shallow, many entry points each pushed out before the next one pulls attention away, trading depth-per-column for reach across columns. None of these shapes is identity in a stronger sense than the others; they are different distributions of the same drive over the same kind of field. A further failure is independent of any single column’s depth: two deep columns can simply fail to connect, lacking the modal network (§5.13) that would let either one query the other, which is what a disciplinary divide is, run inward rather than outward.

*Functional depth and the rate of depth.* Depth in a column isn’t a single threshold; there is a difference between depth sufficient to operate a domain’s machinery honestly, drawing on it to reason correctly and build on top of it, and depth sufficient to stand at that domain’s frontier and extend it. Call the first functional depth and the second frontier depth. Frontier depth in a field ordinarily claims most of a life; functional depth in several fields at once is a different resource allocation, not a lesser one, and it buys something frontier depth in one field can’t: because the columns are held by the same organism, the connective tissue between them (the modal network of §5.13, run inward) forms without the translation cost that separate specialists need scaffolding to overcome. What determines how fast a column reaches whatever depth it reaches is a further variable, orthogonal to the column’s shape: the intensity of the pull’s capture multiplied by the duration it holds. A high-intensity pull held briefly and a moderate pull sustained for years can reach comparable depth along different trajectories, because what accumulates is closer to the area under an intensity curve than to the calendar length of the curve. This is also where governance enters: an organism with less top-down control over which column currently holds capture, or for how long, trades duration for intensity more often than it chooses to—reaching real depth in a season rather than a decade, in whichever column the pull currently occupies, rather than failing to reach depth at all.

*Reading and standing.* Not everything the self-model holds is equally revisable, and the reason isn’t always depth. Some identifications are the self-model’s reading of a fact it didn’t construct and can’t construct away: this is made explicit for sexual orientation at §5.8, where what can thin or shift is the narrative self’s reading of itself, not the standing that reading was tracking. The same holds for identity generally. A hobby cultivated into a core commitment can, in principle, be uncultivated; the organism did the folding and can in principle undo it. A standing the self-model only reads, rather than constructs, doesn’t unwind the same way, because nothing in the reading’s revision touches what it was reading. Failing to distinguish these is what makes the claim that a person can always revise their identity sound either trivially true (of the pulls) or false, even cruel (of what the pulls were never in charge of to begin with).

*Why revision isn’t equally available.* Identifications can be revised when the field permits it—and that clause names a further asymmetry that isn’t about the self-model at all. Some identifications are assigned by others organizing the shared field around a person, independently of what that person reads or cultivates. Where that assignment is enforced (the coordination of the field under mutual stake, §5.14, taken up structurally in Chapter 6), the capacity to revise isn’t a fact about the depth of the individual construction but about what the surrounding field will let stand. This is the sense in which identity being something a person is free to explore is true unevenly rather than false: the freedom is real wherever the field permits it, and its absence elsewhere is a fact about the field, not a deficiency in the self-model doing the identifying.

*Identity’s substrate.* In humans, the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, temporoparietal junction) is a leading candidate for the integrative substrate at the depth the narrative I requires (Raichle et al. 2001; Buckner et al. 2008; Andrews-Hanna et al. 2014). Analogous integrative structures may implement the construction in other lineages that have reached the depth—corvid pallium, cephalopod distributed nervous system. The substrate-independence noted at Life (§4.8) holds: the construction is what counts, not the medium it runs in.

*Bridge to §5.9 Mortality.* Identity is what the first-person anticipation of one’s own ending presupposes. Without the I-as-persistent-agent-with-a-future, there is biological closure but no Heideggerian *Sein-zum-Tode*, no Stoic *meditatio*, no *memento mori*. The deep-form mortality of §5.9 is mortality as this construction confronting its own end.

The identifying-with, identifying-against, and identifying-as operations through which the I is built relationally are the structural ground of the identificatory account of the will: Frankfurt’s hierarchy of higher-order desires (1971; 1982; 1988) and, more precisely, Watson’s valuational reading (1975) of what identifying-with consists in—identifying with some valuations and not others as the structure of endorsement and volitional necessity. That engagement, together with Watson’s regress objection to the bare hierarchy, is taken up in full at §5.11.

### 5.7.1 The Dispute
The contemporary literature on the self and personal identity organizes around several live disputes engaged here by name.

*The self-model and ego dissolution.* Metzinger’s self-model theory (2003; 2009) holds that the conscious self is a representational construction the brain runs, not a substrate it is. The position has been sharpened by neurophenomenology (Varela 1996; Thompson 2007), psychedelic neuroscience (Carhart-Harris 2014; Carhart-Harris and Friston 2019), and clinical work on dissociative and depersonalization disorders. The dispute is whether the self-model is the whole story or whether it points at a more fundamental subjecthood that the construction doesn’t exhaust (Zahavi 2005; Strawson 2017). This account sides with the self-model account on the construction: the I is what the organism builds at sufficient depth, not what the organism is, while holding, against the strongest no-self reading, that the construction is real.

*Personal identity over time.* Locke (1689) 1975 identified personal identity with continuity of consciousness; Reid pressed the transitivity objection; Parfit (1984) argued that what matters in survival is psychological continuity, not strict identity, and that the very question of whether a future person is *me* may be empty. Williams (1970), Olson (1997) (animalism), and the narrative-identity tradition (Ricoeur 1992; MacIntyre 1981) all stake out positions on what makes a current person the same as a past one. The principal non-reductionist rival stands apart from all of these. The simple or further-fact view (Swinburne 1997; Lowe 1996; Madell 1981) holds that personal identity is a simple, unanalyzable further fact grounded in a persisting immaterial substance, so that fission has a determinate answer and ego-death is the soul’s bodily access disrupted rather than the self dissolving. It is the account of the persisting self that Parfit’s no-further-fact thesis was built against. On this reading, identity is a construction the organism runs, structurally the same organism across time but constituting different content as the organism proceeds; Parfit’s reductionism comes out broadly correct on the metaphysics, while the narrative tradition is right about what identity *does* for a being of that depth.

*Theory of mind and self-other modeling.* From Premack and Woodruff (1978) forward, the question of which lineages have theory of mind—the capacity to model other minds as minds—has driven comparative-cognition research for half a century. Disputes are live on chimpanzees (Call and Tomasello 2008; Krupenye et al. 2016), corvids (Bugnyar et al. 2016), and the proper interpretation of false-belief tasks across primates. Theory of mind, on this reading, is a specific recursive operation—self-modeling extended to model another being’s modeling—predicted to appear in lineages whose depth of self-modeling supports the operation rather than as a species-specific endowment.

*Mirror self-recognition.* Gallup’s (1970) chimpanzee mirror studies opened a still-running debate about which species recognize themselves in mirrors and what the recognition demonstrates. Elephants (Plotnik et al. 2006), magpies (Prior et al. 2008), and certain cleaner wrasse (Kohda et al. 2019) have produced positive results that remain contested at the methodological seams (Gallup and Anderson 2020). Structurally, mirror self-recognition tracks the depth at which the self-model includes a body-schema mapped to a perceptual exterior—a real and significant depth, but neither the threshold for the self as such nor the deepest level the organism reaches.

*Default mode network and the narrative self.* The discovery of the default mode network (Raichle et al. 2001) and its role in autobiographical self-modeling, mind-wandering, and the construction of narrative identity (Buckner et al. 2008) has reorganized cognitive neuroscience around the self-modeling question. The dispute is whether DMN activity is *constitutive* of self-modeling or merely *correlated* with one mode of it. On this account, the DMN is one implementation, in human brains, of the recursive self-modeling at the depth where narrative identity is constructed; the constitutive activity is broader.

*Social identity and identification.* The twentieth-century sociology and social-psychology literatures on identification (Mead 1934; Erikson 1968; Tajfel and Turner 1979) pulled at the second sense of identity named at the outset: identity as the operation of identifying-with, identifying-against, and identifying-as. The disputes are live on whether social identities are continuous with personal identity or a separate phenomenon, and on the relative weight of inherited identifications versus chosen ones. Social identity, so read, is the same self-modeling operation extended to the relational field the I is constructed within; the two senses of identity name one structural fact at two registers.

*Parasitic mind control and the locus of the self.* *Toxoplasma*, *Ophiocordyceps*, and hairworm cases (Hughes et al. 2012) have driven a literature on what counts as agency, what counts as the boundary of a being, and whether host behavior under manipulation reflects host awareness, parasite agency, or some hybrid (Andersen 2009; Adamo 2013). This account holds that two organisms persist throughout, neither becoming the other; the host’s substrate is biased, not the host’s own process transferred—one position in that dispute.

### 5.7.2 The Requirement
*The narrative self as construction.* The self that ordinary speech assumes—a persistent, unified, autobiographical subject—is buildable, dissolvable, and reconstructable under specific neural conditions (psychedelics, deep meditation, certain pathology). What’s needed is an account that registers the self as something the organism *builds* rather than something it *is*, and that explains why the building is so reliable under normal conditions while remaining dissolvable under specific interventions. The narrative self has to come out as a construction within the organism, not as the substrate of the organism.

*The locus of the registering activity.* Parasitic mind control shows that behavior and motivational control can be biased from outside the being’s body without the being itself being transferred or replaced. The registering activity has to be located precisely enough to distinguish *the host registering under manipulated inputs* from *the parasite registering through the host*, which means separating the organism, whose locus is the being itself, from the inputs and biases that shape what the organism processes.

*Identity over time.* A persistent identity is one the organism holds across change in its content. It has to explain how the same I survives the change in its memories, beliefs, body, and circumstances that any extended life-course produces, without positing a substantial soul or a Lockean memory-thread that fails transitivity. That means locating identity in the continuity of the organism’s own activity, not in any preserved content that activity carries.

*Two senses of identity bound to one life.* Ordinary use of “identity” carries both the I-as-object-in-its-own-field (what one identifies *as*) and the operation of identifying (what one identifies *with*, *against*, *toward*). An adequate account has to explain how the two senses relate without deriving either from the other—the organism that identifies itself as a persistent agent does so by identifying that agent relationally to everything else in its field, so the relational operation is internal to the I-construction, not external to it.

*The self-model as a mapped region.* An adequate account has to treat introspection as a readout of a mapped region rather than as privileged access, so sincerity secures neither accuracy nor completeness.

*Theory of other minds.* Self-modeling beings at the depth where they can model others as modelers extend the identity-construction into the social world. What has to be explained is how the organism that models oneself is extensible to modeling other beings’ modeling: the same recursive operation, when its content domain expands to include other modeling beings, produces theory of mind.

*Substrate-independence at the structural level.* As with the consciousness analysis at §5.1, the self-modeling activity that constitutes identity can in principle be realized in different substrates. Tying identity essentially to specifically biological substrates requires arguing for why the structural activity couldn’t be realized elsewhere, which means distinguishing *substrate independence at the structural level* (the same activity can run in different media) from *substrate-specific content* (what is registered as the I’s contents depends on what is doing the registering).

*Compatibility with depth-relative ethics.* Identity-depth bears on which interests and forms of moral participation are in play (§5.14), not on basic standing. An adequate account of identity has to be precise enough about levels to support the ethical work the moral account (§5.14) and Chapter 6 build on top of it—distinguishing minimal self-presence from reflective self-aware vantage, and locating which level supports which kind of moral participation, delivering a usable level-distinction rather than a binary present or absent.

*Continuity with awareness.* Identity is one level on the depth-axis named as awareness at §5.1, not a separate faculty. What needs explaining is why the I-construction stacks on top of more basic registration rather than appearing as an autonomous addition: the I is constituted by the same self-modeling activity that runs at every level of awareness, at the depth where the organism folds back far enough to register the self as one of the things it registers.

These requirements aren’t neutral requirements accepted across theories of personal identity. Whether identity is reducible to self-modeling, whether a further fact is needed, how identity bears on moral standing, and whether it is substrate independent remain contested. The set is argued for rather than treated as established.

### 5.7.3 Predictions
The following are hypotheses generated by the result just advanced: identity is modeled as a construction that emerges when self-modeling represents the self within its field. They aren’t straightforward empirical consequences, and evidence from psychedelics, meditation, pathology, comparative cognition, and neuroscience admits competing interpretations. Relevant evidence is reviewed at §5.7.4, and the dialectical case developed at §5.7.5.

*The narrative self is a construction, not a substance.* On this account, the *self*—the integrated, persistent autobiographical identity—is predicted to be one specific recursive construction, dissolvable while the underlying organism continues. Interventions that disrupt the integrative process responsible for the self-model should produce phenomenology in which the narrative self thins out or dissolves while bare awareness continues. Psychedelic modulation of the default mode network should produce ego dissolution. Deep meditative practice should produce similar dissolutions over longer timeframes. Certain pathological states (depersonalization, dissociation) should produce partial dissolutions.

*Identity can be biased without being transferred.* The prediction here is that external interventions can alter what identity registers and how that registration is biased—chemistry, neural states, motivational landscape—without transferring the locus of identity to the intervention. The cricket whose hairworm drives it to seek water still has cricket-presence; the rodent whose Toxoplasma reduces fear still has rodent-presence. Two organisms remain throughout. The host’s vantage continues; what changes is its contents and biases.

The same pattern is predicted for less dramatic cases: drugs alter identity contents without transferring the identity; brain damage alters identity contents without transferring the identity; social pressure alters identity contents without transferring the identity. The locus of selfhood is the organism; external factors operate on the substrate the organism runs on.

*Reflexive identity emerges at sufficient depth.* With sufficient depth of self-modeling, the organism is predicted to fold back and register the I as one of the things it registers. Identity isn’t an additional property; it is what awareness becomes when the organism’s own activity is deep enough to model itself modeling. Empirically, this should manifest as metacognition (knowing that one knows or doesn’t know), theory of mind (modeling other modelers), and self-recognition (modeling oneself as a persistent agent).

If reflexive identity emerges in non-human lineages, it should depend on integrative capacities rather than species membership alone. Whether corvids, cephalopods, primates, or humans realize comparable forms of reflexive identity remains an open comparative-cognition question, and neural correlates such as the default mode network shouldn’t be treated as a settled measure of a single identity depth.

*Substrate of deep identity.* In any given lineage, deep identity is expected to be implemented by integrative structures that take other neural processing as their input—the prefrontal cortex, default mode network, anterior cingulate, and temporoparietal junction in humans; analogous integrative regions in other lineages. Targeted intervention on these structures (anesthetics, lesions, electrical stimulation, psychedelics) should produce predictable, dose-dependent changes in the depth and content of identity.

*Identity is relational from the start.* Identity, on this account, is predicted to be relational from the start: the I-construction is co-constructed with the field it identifies itself within. Empirically, this should show as identity development tracking relational development—children’s self-concepts forming alongside theory-of-mind milestones, identity disruption following social rupture (bereavement, exile, role-loss), and the cross-cultural variation in self-concept tracking the relational fields different cultures construct (Markus and Kitayama 1991, on independent vs. interdependent self-construals).

*Identity persists through content change.* The account predicts that identity over time consists in continuity of that self-modeling, not in preservation of content. A person should remain the same person despite turnover of memories, beliefs, and body cells, because identity is what the organism *does*, not what the organism *carries*. Cases of severe amnesia, profound personality change, or radical life rupture should still leave the organism’s locus intact even when the content it carries is largely replaced.

### 5.7.4 Confirmation
The predictions of §5.7.3 meet convergent evidence from neuroimaging, contemplative-tradition phenomenology, pharmacological intervention, comparative cognition, and developmental psychology. None of these literatures was developed in support of the present argument. Each bears, on its own grounds, on part of what the framework predicts.

*Default mode network and reflexive identity.* The neuroimaging literature on the default mode network (DMN) bears out the prediction that deep reflexive identity has identifiable neural substrate (Buckner et al. 2008; Spreng and Grady 2010; Andrews-Hanna et al. 2014). The DMN—medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, and temporoparietal junction—activates during self-referential thought, autobiographical memory retrieval, theory-of-mind tasks, and mind-wandering. It deactivates during external task focus. Lesion studies show that damage to DMN nodes produces specific deficits in self-narrative integration (Philippi et al. 2012). The prediction is that the organism’s reflexive turn on the I will have neural correlates integrating self-modeling activity. That is the pattern the DMN literature reports, though it does not by itself identify the network with the self.

*Ego dissolution under psychedelic intervention.* Psychedelic research provides bounded convergence with the self-as-construction proposal, not a direct identity proof. Psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca, and high-dose DMT modulate DMN activity and connectivity (Carhart-Harris et al. 2012; Pasquini et al. 2020; Tagliazucchi et al. 2016). Reports include weakening of autobiographical or narrative selfhood, altered body ownership, and episodes described as ego dissolution, sometimes followed by reintegration. Carhart-Harris and Friston’s (2019) REBUS model interprets these effects through relaxed high-level priors, including priors supporting a unified self-model, while lower-level sensory and predictive organization remains active. That is evidence for modifiable self-modeling mechanisms. Retrospective reports of experience also support the phenomenological interpretation that some awareness may remain when narrative self-representation is attenuated, but neither DMN modulation nor later report by itself establishes uninterrupted minimal awareness during the most intense phase, still less that one specific recursive mechanism is the identity of the self. Letheby’s *Philosophy of Psychedelics* (2021) develops the model-based interpretation; the evidence is consistent with it without uniquely proving it.

Read in these terms, what the REBUS description reports is a dissociation between a field and its index. Predictive organization continues to register what may follow, which is modal-field activity (§5.4), while the priors that locate a persistent I within that field are the ones that relax. That is the pattern the identification leads one to expect: a construction the organism builds can be built less firmly without the organism ceasing to run, and the registering that survives is what the construction was assembled out of. It also marks why the evidence bears on identity in particular rather than on awareness generally, since what attenuates is the self-locating structure and not the registering as such.

The prediction therefore survives as a supported framework hypothesis: narrative self-organization can be disrupted and reassembled while substantial processing continues. Whether minimal awareness and the proposed underlying process continue throughout is a further empirical and phenomenological question.

*Contemplative phenomenology.* Traditions centered on *anatta* (non-self) provide a long-developed phenomenology relevant to the same distinction without deciding the neuroscience. Advanced contemplatives report attenuation of narrative selfhood, changes in subject–object structure, and experiences interpreted as awareness without an ordinary ego-model (Lutz et al. 2008; Wright 2017). Neuroimaging of long-term meditators reports DMN modulation through practices unlike psychedelic intervention (Brewer et al. 2011; Garrison et al. 2015). The reports are evidence about phenomenology; they don’t independently verify that subject–object structure is wholly absent or identify a unique surviving neural process.

Convergence across pharmacological and contemplative pathways supports a modest claim: self-related processing and self-experience are manipulable through multiple mechanisms, with partially overlapping reported effects and neural correlates. The stronger identity claim remains a framework interpretation to be tested against rival models of minimal selfhood and consciousness.

*Predictive processing and self-modeling.* The predictive-processing framework reinforces the identity-as-construction claim. Friston’s (2010) free energy principle, Clark’s (2013) predictive processing, Hohwy’s (2013) prediction-error-minimization, and Seth’s (2021) interoceptive inference all model the self as the operational running of self-including predictive cycles. The Markov blanket formalism (Kirchhoff et al. 2018), a statistical boundary separating a system’s internal states from its environment, gives the mathematical shape of the being that has a self-model of its environment. Damasio (1999) and Seth (2021) trace selfhood specifically to interoceptive predictive processing—the body’s internal state included in the model. These results are consistent with the prediction that identity is the running of the self-model, not an extra property layered on it, without uniquely establishing it.

*Substrate-independence in non-mammalian lineages.* The comparative-cognition literature supports substrate-independence by finding integrative capacities in different architectures. Corvid pallium implements depth comparable to mammalian cortex through a different organization (Emery and Clayton 2004; Kabadayi and Osvath 2017). Cephalopods have distributed nervous systems and no recent common ancestor with vertebrates; they display problem-solving, individual recognition of humans, apparent play, and chromatophore replay during sleep (Godfrey-Smith 2016). Elephants pass mirror tests through a different brain architecture again (Plotnik et al. 2006). These cases support multiple realization. They do not show without further argument that every architecture implements the same construction.

*Parasitic mind control as biased-not-transferred identity.* The parasitology literature on behavior modification bears out the locus-of-identity prediction. *Toxoplasma gondii* alters rodent fear responses (Berdoy et al. 2000; Vyas et al. 2007); *Ophiocordyceps* drives ants to climb and lock onto vegetation (Hughes et al. 2011); hairworms drive crickets to drown themselves (Thomas et al. 2002); rabies alters mammalian behavior to promote transmission. In the documented cases, the parasite alters the substrate on which the host’s own process runs without transferring it, and two organisms remain. The behavioral record doesn’t establish what the host experiences; what it shows is bias without organismic transfer, which is the pattern predicted.

*Developmental and cross-cultural identity formation.* Developmental psychology shows that identity emerges over years as the organism’s modeling capacity matures, tracking the maturation of integrative neural structure (Damon and Hart 1988). Cross-cultural work on independent versus interdependent self-construals (Markus and Kitayama 1991) bears out the relational dimension: what an I identifies itself with is loaded by the relational field the culture constructs, and the same recursive operation produces different I-contents in different fields.

Taken together, DMN research supports neural implementation of important self-referential functions; psychedelic and contemplative work supports the manipulability of narrative and embodied self-experience; predictive-processing theories supply candidate mechanisms; comparative cognition supports multiple realizability of integrative capacities; parasitology illustrates content-bias without obvious identity transfer; and developmental and cross-cultural findings support the formation and relational loading of self-construal. These are converging constraints on the framework, not six independent confirmations of one uniquely identified process.

### 5.7.5 Conclusions
The implications depend on the identification holding, on the convergence reported at §5.7.4, and on the specific predictions of §5.7.3. They are conditional on those holding—if the identification fails, the implications fail with it. On the convergence as stated, however, several positions in the literature come out differently than they do on their own premises.

*The self-as-illusion debate dissolves.* Eliminativists and illusionists hold that the self is an illusion (Frankish 2016; Dennett 1991). Realists about the self hold that the self is genuinely there (Strawson 1997). The structural account dissolves the dichotomy: the self is real—it is the recursive construction the being runs at sufficient depth, implemented in the activity of specific neural structures—*and* it is a model rather than a substance. Both intuitions are accommodated. The self isn’t an illusion, because it does real work (the being coheres around it; the organism’s outputs depend on its operation). It isn’t a substance, because it is the running of a model rather than an additional ingredient.

*Personal identity over time.* Parfit’s (1984) reductionism comes out broadly correct: identity over time consists in continuity of the right self-modeling, not in strict identity of a substantial self. Against the most aggressive reductionist reading, *the organism itself* is what continues—a real fact, not merely a useful description—and so whether a future person is “really me” isn’t empty so much as locatable: it is the question of whether the organism that is now mine is the organism that will be theirs. In ordinary cases, yes; in extreme thought-experiments (teletransportation, fission), the question reflects the same metaphysical fact Parfit named, that there is no further fact beyond the organism’s continuity to answer to.

*Identity isn’t what matters.* Parfit’s further thesis, that identity isn’t what matters and that what matters is Relation R (psychological continuity and connectedness, which holds by degrees and can hold to more than one future person), is accepted here in a precise and bounded form. What one has prudential reason to care about in one’s own future is the continuation of the organism, its projects, connections, and self-model carried forward, and not a bare identity-badge attaching over and above that continuation. On this the account agrees with Parfit against the simple view: there is no further identity-fact whose presence or absence could matter independently of whether the organism continues. Where the account resists the deflationary reading is on the reality, and in ordinary cases the determinacy, of what carries the mattering. For Parfit, Relation R holds only by degrees and can branch, so the ordinary sense that one’s own survival is an all-or-nothing fact is exposed as a projection. The account grants that the relation can branch, which is exactly the fission indeterminacy already accepted, and that it thins by degrees under radical psychological discontinuity, but holds that the organism is a single determinate continuant in the ordinary, non-branching case, a real fact rather than a useful description, so the concern a self takes in its own future tracks something that is there. The deflationary force applies where the organism actually branches or thins, not to the ordinary case the concern is calibrated to. Parfit’s insight and the account’s realism about the organism are therefore compatible: what matters is the relation and not the bare identity, and in the standard case the relation is a determinate fact about one continuant.

Two classic pressures on this picture are absorbed by the same machinery. Reid’s brave-officer regress shows that memory-connectedness doesn’t chain transitively across a life; connectedness holding in degrees rather than all-or-nothing answers it. Williams’s (1970) body-swap case shows how one operation can read as survival or death depending on the description under which it is presented. The no-further-fact stance answers that pressure: where the descriptions diverge, there is no additional identity-fact, over and above the organism’s continuity, for them to disagree about.

The retorsion against strong self-illusionism is sharper than the constructive accommodation already offered. To recognize this-me as distinct from past-me is to perform a cognitive act that holds two temporally-distinct positions together within a single synthesis. The recognition doesn’t occupy a pre-given continuity between selves; it is the synthesis act in which the continuity is instantiated as a determinate fact. The strong illusionist who calls the persisting subject an illusion is calling that very act illusory—and the act is the one in which the illusionist thesis is held together as a position distinguishable from its negation. The argument refutes itself at the synthesis layer: the recognition’s content presupposes a recognizer who spans both poles, and the spanning is the persistence the illusionist denies. The general result at §9.2 holds that the structural conditions are features of the representing, not the represented. It lands here at higher resolution: the conditions are features of the synthesis act, and the synthesis act is the personal-identity-over-time fact.

This also answers the simple or further-fact view named at §5.7.1. The persisting subject it posits is either this synthesis act itself or a self-substance standing behind the act. If it is the synthesis act, it is the organism’s activity rather than a substance and supplies no further fact beyond the organism’s continuity. If it is a self-substance, it either runs the same structural conditions, making it one more substrate the construction is independent of, or stands outside them and does no identity-work the recognition can register. Either way, the fission indeterminacy stands and the further-fact view gets no purchase.

*The two senses of identity reconcile.* The personal-identity tradition’s I-construction sense and the sociology-of-identification’s relational sense both name aspects of the same structural fact. The organism that builds an I builds it relationally; the I is co-constructed with the field of selves and roles it identifies itself within. What looks like a tension between personal and social identity should turn out to be one operation viewed from two angles.

*Animal cognition and moral standing.* If identity is graded with depth of self-modeling, then nonhuman animals at sufficient depth have genuine self-presence—diminished compared to humans on most dimensions, but real, with content that matters morally. Great apes mourn (de Waal 2016); elephants pass mirror tests (Plotnik et al. 2006); cetaceans maintain individual recognition and culture; corvids manufacture tools and plan for future needs (Emery and Clayton 2004; Kabadayi and Osvath 2017). The traditional Cartesian denial of animal selfhood is structurally incorrect on the framework: if the organism runs deep enough to model the self relationally, identity is present, regardless of species.

Whether this generates moral obligations is a matter for §5.14 Morality. The structural prediction is that identity is present where the organism is deep enough; what follows ethically depends on additional premises about the moral significance of self-presence.

*Artificial intelligence and substrate-independence.* The substrate-independence claim has sharp implications for AI. Closure-plus-throughput is the living configuration defined at §4.8: a recursion that produces its own conditions of continuation (closure), coupled to a sustained energy gradient it dissipates through itself (throughput). If identity depends on it at sufficient depth with self-modeling running, then current large language models and most AI systems don’t have it: they lack closure, they lack throughput-coupling, and their own process, where present, doesn’t run a self-model in the relevant sense.

What the account rejects is any view that makes identity essentially carbon-based or essentially neural. If AI systems were to develop closure-and-throughput at sufficient depth—substrate-engineered, autonomously self-maintaining, with active inference loops over their own operation including self-modeling—the framework predicts they would have identity. Whether such systems are coming, and on what timeline, is an empirical question that isn’t answered here. What the account does is deny the substrate-essentialist objection its premise.

*Fetal development and end-of-life.* The continuous-gradient prediction implies that the I emerges gradually with neural integration, not at any switch-like threshold. Capacities relevant to fetal awareness depend on thalamocortical integration, which develops substantially around weeks 23–28 of gestation (Lagercrantz and Changeux 2009); the narrative self develops over years after birth as integrative structures mature. Principled criteria for when meaningful self-presence is present (closure-and-throughput at integrative depth with self-modeling running) are offered here without committing to a sharp cutoff.

End-of-life cases are symmetric. Anesthesia, coma, persistent vegetative state, brain death—each represents a different point on a gradient of integrative collapse. The I fades with integration. There is no sharp line at which it disappears, only the structural fact that closure-and-throughput at depth supporting self-modeling is required for it to be present.

*Cross-references for adjacent rivals.* The ontological rivals to the consciousness result are taken up across §9: substance dualism, panpsychism, higher-order theories, eliminativism, and illusionism (§9.1–§9.5). That is where the hard-problem dissolution, the higher-order reply, and the panpsychist and idealist responses are worked through. Architectural accounts of conscious access and integration are neighbors rather than opponents merely by being architectural, and the present account doesn’t rest on their exclusion. They enter the dispute only where they place the first subject at a different boundary. The positive account of consciousness as the self-modeling process on which those rivals bear is carried at §5.1. One rival meets this account at its evidence directly. The ego-death record marshaled at Confirmation (§5.7.4) runs to default-mode modulation, narrative-self attenuation, reports of awareness continuing, and the *anatta* convergence. The analytic idealist reads that same evidence in the opposite explanatory direction: not the I dissolving while the organism continues, but dissociation loosening so that an underlying cosmic consciousness shows through. (Anatta (Pāli, “non-self” or “not-self”; Sanskrit anātman) is the Buddhist doctrine that there is no fixed, unchanging self behind experience—what feels like a persisting “I” is really a shifting bundle of processes with nothing permanent running them. The “convergence” named here is that modern ego-dissolution research reports what this doctrine described over two millennia earlier: awareness reported as continuing while the sense of being a separate self drops away.) That re-read is taken up and disambiguated at §9.5. Dissociation is itself a structural operation, requiring a substrate that self-differentiates (S), sustains the alter across the interval (Φ), and, where dissociation is a happening rather than timeless constitution, runs as an event (T), so the idealist relocation instantiates the structural conditions at the substrate rather than escaping them. The two readings don’t divide over the data; they divide over what is fundamental, and the structural conditions hold on either resolution. The identity implications, by contrast, ride on what the organism specifically constructs at sufficient depth—the I, the moral subject, the artificial-intelligence candidate, the developmental and end-of-life cases—and depend on the identity construction rather than restating the underlying vantage.

What the depth-gradient implications do is redescribe these standing debates rather than pick a side within them: each becomes a question about where the organism runs deep enough to construct an I rather than about which faculty switches on.

## 5.8 Sexuality
Sexuality is one branch of the basic pull toward what life reaches for: the embodied and self-modeled register in which attraction, desire, orientation, identity, and coupling—or their absence, conditionality, and variation—take shape. Its evolutionary history includes the reach of one living thing toward another and, in sexually reproducing lineages, toward the making of new life. Its lived content isn’t exhausted by that history. It is the life-continuing counterpart to death at the lineage level, where variation-generating reproduction carries life beyond the individual; at the level of the subject, sexuality is the full register whether or not reproduction, coupling, or sexual attraction is in view. None of its nonprocreative or non-attracted expressions is a lesser case of a procreative original.

**[Identification]**

**Sexuality** · *Identification*

Sexuality is one differentiation of drive’s attraction-pole. In lineages whose variation architecture includes sexual reproduction, the possibility of coupling across distinct organisms shapes this embodied and self-modeled register. At sufficient depth it is registered from inside as attraction, desire, orientation, embodied coupling, and sexual identity, including configurations in which sexual attraction is minimal, absent, or conditional. It is the structural pair to mortality at the lineage level wherever variation-generating coupling is the lineage’s solution; no corresponding reproductive aim is imposed on any individual subject or expression.

*Status: the structural half is Drive’s attraction-pole differentiated; desire is the word Drive already uses once the pull has an object. Thin certainty: some ways of connecting are more intimate than others. There is a depth gradient of how intimate a field feels with different agents—some people you connect with, some you do not. That gradient is this register plus Meaning and Identity, not a Cogito for “sexuality exists.” Sexual identity, a shared encounter, reproduction for those who weight it, can each mean something—that weighting is Meaning (§5.10). Occurrence of sexual reproduction remains contingent on lineage biology. That this differentiated field just is sexuality remains a functional proposal defended by fit.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2)

Mortality (§5.9) names the absolute referent of drive’s aversion-pole. Sexuality is one differentiated register on the attraction side: the inherited field in which drive may take sexual, romantic, embodied, relational, or generative direction, without requiring every subject to occupy each direction. Desire is that pole with an object. What the encounter, the identity, or the making of new life *means* is Meaning running here, including for those who don’t weight reproduction at all.

The thin certainty is the gradient. Some connections run deeper than others. Some agents are felt as intimate, some aren’t, and the difference is registered, not stipulated. That is Identity’s depth (§5.7) run on Drive toward another body. The gradient can be hijacked: a field can be made to feel closer than the coupling warrants, or cut off from a closeness it already holds. Whether the deepest slot can be filled by a hypothesized agent—the unknown judge of §5.16 taking the intimacy form—is the spiritual question, not a third certainty of this register.

Several facts about the kind of being we are converge in sexuality. An individual self-producing life doesn’t continue indefinitely. A lineage can continue beyond its members, but where its environment changes across generations, persistence may depend on generating enough variation to track those changes. The modal commitment to ◇C (§1.3) leaves such environmental variation genuinely possible; it doesn’t guarantee that every lineage faces it or set the rate at which it occurs.

Sexual reproduction is one powerful and recurrent variation mechanism in complex multicellular lineages, but it isn’t the only one and isn’t a modal necessity of life. Where it is absent, mutation, horizontal gene transfer, gene conversion, and alternative repair pathways may carry the load (Gladyshev, Meselson, and Arkhipova 2008; Otto 2009).

Sexuality is therefore a structural pair with mortality (§5.9) only where variation-generating coupling is the lineage’s solution. Mortality closes the individual life; reproduction produces successors rather than extending that individual. The lineage may continue through lives that differ from the one that produced them. That is the precise pairing: closure at the individual scale, continuation with variation at the lineage scale.

Two uses of *asexual* must therefore be held apart. *Asexual reproduction* is a biological mode by which an organism or lineage produces successors without gametic fusion. *Asexuality* is an orientation in which a subject experiences little or no sexual attraction. The first concerns how biological successors are produced; the second concerns how attraction is, or isn’t, organized within a subject’s lived field. Neither entails the other, and the full register isn’t a binary between reproductive coupling and its absence. Attraction, libido, romantic attraction, orientation, identity, behavior, embodied coupling, and reproductive capacity are coupled dimensions that can come apart.

Sexuality carries a second structural fact alongside continuation. Sexuality is also an early and densely embodied form of intersubjective coupling: where attraction forms, the body’s pull toward another body precedes any sign or norm that later mediates it. That dimension draws on the self-model (§5.7) together with the field of subjects meeting subjects (§5.14).

Transfer between subjects (§5.12) and convergence across them (§5.4) presuppose that another subject is represented as distinct. Sexual attraction is one especially embodied form of that registration, but it isn’t where other-registration first appears: caregiving, attachment, rivalry, imitation, joint attention, and ordinary perception of agency can all precede or occur without it.

**[Corollary]**

**Registration Precedes Transfer** · *Corollary*

For one field to take another subject as an object, it must register that subject as an occupant genuinely apart from itself, not as a modification of its own state. That is co-present mutual exteriority—the here that is not the there—obtaining between subjects rather than within a single episode. The corollary inherits Spatiality from §2.4.7’s co-present route, which that section retains as convergent access rather than as what its theorem spends; the inheritance is to the Condition, which the Movement Line establishes independently (§2.4.9), so nothing here rests on the access route being load-bearing.

What the corollary fixes is a logical order: communication or transfer between subjects presupposes some prior discrimination of source, receiver, and otherness. That discrimination need not be conscious, sexual, developmentally earlier than every sign, or sufficient for recognizing another as a subject rather than merely an agent or body. Sexuality is one later domain in which other-registration becomes intimate and self-relevant; it is not the origin of intersubjectivity.

**Depends on:** Sexuality (§5.8), Knowledge (§5.4), and Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7)

Mutual exteriority is fixed in the sense established at §2.4.7. Two consequences follow. The two-subject structure morality operates on (§5.14) is inherited rather than constituted there; what morality adds is the weighting, not the second subject. And the wrongs available here are already the Two Modes in pre-linguistic form, since a body’s broadcasts can misrepresent what a coupling requires or leads to as readily as a sentence can.

The result is narrow. It doesn’t derive Spatiality, which is established independently (Chapter 2); it observes that inter-subject registration is a case of that structure rather than a further one. Nor does it make sexuality the origin of intersubjectivity as such, since registering another subject doesn’t require attraction and occurs wherever a field holds another field. What it fixes is that the containment language and morality spend is in hand before language arrives, and that the pre-linguistic case isn’t a thinner version of the linguistic one—it is the condition the linguistic one operates on.

*A note on scope.* The result offered here—sexuality as the structural pair to death where variation-generating coupling is a lineage’s solution—is conditional on the account (§4.8) of closure-and-throughput. It isn’t a fresh deduction from Chapters 1–2. The biological premise must be supplied in each case: a lineage confronts variation over the relevant timescale, and coupling is among the mechanisms by which it answers that variation.

*Attraction.* The pull toward another, registered as another. Below the depth where attraction is named or chosen, the body registers another body’s broadcasts (the chemistry, the rhythm, the resonance) and a being’s drive (§5.2) shapes itself toward what it has registered. In a being whose inherited architecture includes sexually differentiating coupling, attraction is one way that architecture can register another; its minimal or absent formation is another configuration of the same inherited field, not a failure of drive. The architecture is older than language and runs continuously across mammalian and avian lineages. What human depth adds is reflection on what attracts, or doesn’t: the recursive fold that takes the attraction-pattern itself as an object of awareness.

*Desire.* Drive’s specialization toward another. Where drive (§5.2) is the baseline forward pressure pre-differentiation, desire is drive shaped by attraction toward a particular other. Like all affects (§5.3), it carries valence and salience and urgency, and registers from inside as what it is to be the one oriented toward what they are oriented toward.

*Orientation, including minimal or absent attraction.* An orientation is the standing pattern of a subject’s sexual attraction: whom or what, if anyone, the subject is drawn toward. The familiar heterosexual, homosexual, bisexual, and pansexual labels describe different relations between attraction and sex or gender; none is a claim about reproductive function. Asexuality names the spectrum on which sexual attraction is little, absent, or conditional, while drive (§5.2) and other affiliative or embodied registers may still run. On the structural account this is a variant within the sexual field, not a deficit of drive, and the self-model (§5.7) can construct an identity-position around that pattern as readily as around any other. Aromanticism marks the parallel case at the romantic rather than the sexual register.

*Identity.* The self-model (§5.7) constructed at sufficient depth includes one’s relation to attraction. Gender identity and sexual orientation are features of that self-model: the person’s reading of who they are, including what they are drawn to and how they situate themselves in the field of intersubjective coupling. Gender’s hardware and software aren’t the same layer, and the distinction is load-bearing here. Sex, specified structurally at §5.8.5 by developmental organization toward a reproductive role, is hardware in the sense that matters here: some of it doesn’t bend to self-understanding or to social permission, and nothing in this account pretends otherwise.

Gender identity is software: the self-model’s reading, built on that hardware but not fixed by it, revisable in a way the hardware underneath it need not be. What the self-model carries, at that software layer, is the first-person alignment drawn from socially available categories but not dictated by them. Haslanger’s ameliorative account (2000; 2012) presses further than this and holds gender to be, most fundamentally, a position within a hierarchy of subordination and privilege organized around presumed reproductive role, assignable independently of self-understanding.

This account distinguishes rather than adopts that further claim: the prescriptive roles a culture attaches to gender aren’t merely a separate matter irrelevant to the self-model, but nor are they gender’s constitutive metaphysics. They are an instance of the general fact named at §5.7—that an identification’s field-permitted revisability is a fact about the field, assigned by other people organizing the space around a person, not a fact about that person’s self-model or its depth. A restrictive field around gender expression is therefore not hardware in the sense sex partly is; it is a choice the surrounding field has made, and one it could make differently. Whether it should isn’t a further open question this account defers: standing rests at §5.14 on the capacity for experience under its equal-standing premise, not on category-membership, and morality there on whether a subject is fostered or corroded. A self-model’s gender expression that corrodes no one is exactly the case that standard doesn’t license restricting, which is what recommends maximizing the field’s permission around gender expression and its social acceptance—not a value imported from outside the account, but the fostering standard already in hand, applied to a layer the account develops fully at §5.12.

The available category-set isn’t itself binary: where a culture makes third or non-binary positions available—the hijra of South Asia, two-spirit roles across several Indigenous North American nations, and fa’afafine in Samoa are distinct, culturally specific positions rather than interchangeable tokens of one kind—or where a self-model constructs a position not aligned to either pole of the local binary, the self-model holds that position with the same status any identity-position has. That an individual’s architecture need not be binary merely because the population is bimodal is the structural half (§5.8.5); that the available positions vary across history and culture is the constructed half; non-binary identity is where both halves are visible at once. That the categories themselves (orientation, the normal, even what counts as ‘natural’) have a history, and that naming sexuality natural is itself a move made from within that history rather than from nowhere (Foucault’s scientia sexualis), is granted; the social ontology of the categories is sorted from the structural claim where that work belongs (§5.12).

As features of the self-model they are constructions, not substrates: real, structural, consequential, not chosen, and (like the rest of the self-model’s content) capable of thinning or dropping away when the self-model itself dissolves under the conditions named at §5.7. This is a claim about the self-model’s *reading*, not about the underlying dispositions: that the narrative self can thin or dissolve in ego-death doesn’t entail that an orientation or a gender identity dissolves with it; what dissolves is the self-model’s reading of itself, never the standing that reading was tracking. The self holds a position; the position is held by a self; both are one life.

*Embodied coupling.* The intimate exchange where two people register each other across the full spectrum of registration the body affords: at the chemical, somatic, affective, and reflective levels simultaneously. Morality (§5.14) names the readability of another’s affective broadcasts; sexuality is the register where each person reads the other while simultaneously being read by them, across a single interval, deep enough to know what is happening.

*The dyadic unit and its plural extension.* The base unit of embodied coupling is two-place: distinct subjects reading each other across a single interval (§5.8.2). Plurality—more than two bound in overlapping intimacy—isn’t a new primitive but concurrent two-place registrations, each a full dyad in its own right rather than a fusion into some three-or-more-place organ of coupling. The structural account neither prescribes monogamy nor forecloses plurality; what it fixes is that each bond, however many run alongside it, answers to the same conditions any coupling does: consent on the modal-depth standard (§5.11.4) and the fostering-rather-than-corroding demand of morality (§5.14). Plurality adds one field-level condition the single bond doesn’t face—the bonds must be held so that they don’t corrode one another—which is why disclosure among the parties does structural work here that the single-bond case can leave implicit. Whether a given being’s field is better sustained by one bond or several, the account doesn’t legislate; that is a question of what fosters the subjects involved, answered case by case rather than by rule.

*Reproduction.* The continuation register: closure-and-throughput producing closure-and-throughput. Sexual reproduction is one biological route by which that occurs, not what sexuality must mean in each subject or act. In those deep enough to choose, the choice to bring a new life into being, or not, is the register at which the lineage’s continuation enters the agentive field of the individual. The choice is real, and the structural pair with death persists either way: the life ends; the lineage either continues or it doesn’t. Whether that choice is *good*, whether bringing a new life into existence is to be affirmed or, as the anti-natalist presses (Benatar’s asymmetry of pleasure and suffering; Schopenhauer’s judgment that existence carries a structural surplus of striving over satisfaction), refused, the structural account doesn’t leave wholly open. Benatar’s asymmetry counts the absence of pain as a good while counting the absence of pleasure as no loss to anyone, and that step requires precisely the subject-independent value this account denies throughout: a good that is good for no one, entered in a ledger no subject reads. Where value is constitutively a subject’s own condition surfacing from inside its field (§5.14), an absent pain good for no one isn’t a good at all, and the asymmetry that carried the anti-natalist verdict never forms. Schopenhauer’s pessimism rests on a reading of striving as standing lack that the drive and affect account has already declined (§5.2, §5.3): joy is the being deepening and opening, not the brief quiet between wants.

Schopenhauer’s sharper charge is that sexual attraction is the species-will’s deception of the individual. Pleasure and romantic feeling appear as personal choice while serving an agenda not the individual’s own. There is no species-agent whose interest is served and no one being duped, only individual organisms each pursuing their own drive, statistically shaped by selection toward outcomes selection has no interest in because selection isn’t the kind of thing that has interests. What attraction serves is the subject’s own deepening; that this deepening also, as a statistical regularity across many organisms, sustains the lineage is a consequence of what attraction is, not a hidden agenda smuggled past the individual it operates in.

What this secures is the narrow point that coming into existence is no standing harm, not the stronger claim that more existence is therefore better. That comparative question, how the value of bringing new subjects into being is weighed across whole possible fields of subjects, is population axiology, which Chapter 6 leaves open (§6.14). The account fixes what reproduction is, and that the choice is real; the duties the choice incurs toward the subjects it brings into being are recovered at §5.14.

*The features track the depth gradient.* Attraction operates wherever a being is deep enough to register another at all—present across mammalian and avian lineages, and below them in chemoreceptive forms—while its absence or conditional formation is a standing configuration rather than a lower depth. Desire requires affective awareness sufficient to differentiate baseline drive into a particular orientation; the affective-awareness threshold named at §5.1 is its threshold here too. Embodied coupling at the depth where two beings register each other tracking themselves requires the self-aware level named at §5.1. Identity (the self-model’s reading of what one is sexually) requires the deeper fold that takes the self as an object of awareness. Reproduction is what the lineage’s continuation looks like at every depth simultaneously, since the cellular and somatic processes that produce a new life run underneath whatever affective and reflective registers the deeper depths add.

*The Inversion.* Sexuality isn’t given its meaning by an external authority. Its meaning is structural: the register where one life reaches for another, where attraction shapes drive, where the body becomes legible to another body, where the continuation of the lineage becomes a possibility within a person’s own field. The source is in Nature itself: in living beings, at the depth they have reached.

### 5.8.1 The Dispute
The literature on sexuality is divided across several disciplines that often don’t speak to one another. The principal positions are met by name.

*Sociobiological reductionism.* The sociobiological tradition reads sexual behavior, attraction, and gender difference as fitness-maximizing adaptations to ancestral selection pressures (Wilson 1975; Trivers 1972; Symons 1979; Buss 1989, later evolutionary psychology). Specific predictions include parental-investment-based selectivity asymmetries, jealousy patterns, and preference for cues of fertility and resources. These have generated substantial empirical literature and substantial dispute about replication, interpretation, and cross-cultural generality (Eagly and Wood 1999; Stewart-Williams and Thomas 2013). On this account, the evolutionary pressures the tradition identifies operate on the substrate, but what sexuality *is* phenomenologically—attraction, desire, embodied coupling, identity—is the first-person perspective on those pressures rather than a fitness algorithm running unobserved.

*Social constructionism.* From Foucault (1976) forward, a tradition has held that sexuality—the very category, not only its expressions—is historically and socially constructed: a discourse produced by specific institutions, knowledges, and powers rather than a natural kind. Butler (1990; 1993) extended the analysis to gender, locating gender in performative repetition rather than in biological or psychological substrate. The dispute with the sociobiological tradition is sharp and unresolved. Here, the *content* of sexual categories is significantly constructed—specific identities, scripts, and practices are historical—while the *structural conditions* under which the categories form (attraction, desire, embodied coupling, the self-modeling of one’s position in the field) aren’t constructed but supplied by the recursive architecture sexuality consists in.

*Religious-metaphysical regulation.* The classical religious traditions—Christian, Jewish, Islamic, and others—have regulated sexuality through frameworks that locate its meaning, permission, and direction in a divinely ordained order. Contemporary defenders (Finnis 1980; George 1993, some Thomistic natural-law traditions) refine the position into rational-natural-law arguments.

*Identity discourse and gender philosophy.* Contemporary identity discourse spans sharply opposed positions. The trans-affirmative literature (Bettcher 2014; Serano 2007) holds that gender identity is a robust self-understanding constitutive of who one is. Gender-critical positions (Stock 2021; Lawford-Smith 2022) press against the metaphysics of that position, while intersex perspectives (Karkazis 2008) complicate both. Non-binary identity presses the further question whether a binary exhausts the available gender categories. The status of asexuality is separately disputed: whether the absence of sexual attraction is an orientation in its own right (Bogaert 2004; Bogaert 2012) or, as some clinical framings held, a disorder of desire. The dispute is among the most polarized in contemporary philosophy. Gender and sexual identity, on this reading, are features of the self-model (§5.7)—real, structural, consequential, constructed within awareness rather than substrate of awareness. The reading doesn’t resolve the political disputes but it does locate where the metaphysics is supplied.

*Anti-natalism and the ethics of reproduction.* A tradition from Schopenhauer through Benatar (2006) holds that bringing new beings into existence is morally impermissible because the new being bears risks and harms it can’t consent to. The position is sharpened by the asymmetry between the badness of pain and the goodness of pleasure Benatar exploits. At the structural level: sexually reproducing lineages carry a capacity for producing new beings, but that capacity neither defines each subject’s sexuality nor supplies an obligation to exercise it; whether to exercise the capacity, in agents with sufficient modal depth to choose, is their own ethical question. The structural account makes the act legible without dictating any particular choice, while declining the impersonal value the anti-natalist asymmetry needs: the weight falls on the conditions a new subject would enter, not on being born.

*The variation-and-reproduction question.* A live biological dispute concerns why sexual reproduction is so widespread given its substantial costs (the two-fold cost of sex, Maynard Smith 1978). The variation-and-recombination hypothesis (Hamilton, Axelrod, and Tanese 1990; Otto 2009), the Red Queen hypothesis, and Muller’s-ratchet-based accounts each press the question from different angles. This account treats sexuality as a recurrent solution to the lineage variation-generation problem in eukaryotic lineages, not as a modal necessity of life as such—one position in that biological dispute, consistent with the bdelloid-rotifer and bacterial-recombination cases the field continues to investigate (Gladyshev et al. 2008) (The two-fold cost of sex (named by biologist John Maynard Smith) is the puzzle at the center of this debate: an asexual female passes on 100% of her genes to every offspring, while a sexual female passes on only 50% (the rest coming from the male) and must also produce sons, who don’t themselves bear offspring. All else equal, an asexual lineage should out-reproduce a sexual one roughly two-to-one every generation. Explaining why sex persists anyway, despite this steep cost, is the puzzle the Red Queen hypothesis and Muller’s-ratchet accounts are competing to solve.).

*Pornography, commodification, and the limits of consent.* A series of contemporary disputes—over pornography (MacKinnon 1987; Dworkin 1981) vs. liberal accounts, prostitution and sex work, surrogacy, and the commodification of intimacy—turn on whether and how consent under economic, social, and developmental conditions counts as full consent. The modal-depth account of consent (§5.11.4) supplies a usable test—whether the will behind the word had enough mapped possibility to understand the act—without resolving the political and policy questions specific cases raise.

*Relationship structure.* Independently of orientation, the number and configuration of simultaneous intimate bonds is contested: whether monogamy is a structural norm, a cultural institution, or one option among several, and whether ethically negotiated non-monogamy differs in kind from both serial monogamy and the plural-marriage structures the ethnographic record documents. The structural reading is that the dyad is the base unit of coupling and plurality is concurrent dyads under the same consent and non-corrosion conditions, which locates the structural claim without settling the cultural and normative dispute.

### 5.8.2 The Requirement
*Connection to the lineage’s continuation.* An individual self-producing life doesn’t persist indefinitely. Where a lineage faces environmental change across generations, an adequate account should explain how its reproductive architecture supplies or preserves the variation needed to continue. Sexuality, where it occurs, can answer that lineage-level problem without exhausting the lived sexual register or becoming a requirement imposed on each subject.

*Connection to intersubjective coupling.* Where mutual sexual coupling occurs, it can become among the deepest forms of embodied intersubjective coupling—two beings tracking each other tracking themselves at the full depth of registration the bodies afford. This intersubjective register has to be accommodated rather than treated as a one-place biological or psychological state, preserving the two-being structure where it is present: distinct subjects, mutual registration, shared exchange across an interval that conditions what the exchange consists in. It doesn’t exhaust the wider sexual register, which also includes solitary desire, non-attraction, orientation, identity, and forms of intimacy not organized around sexual coupling.

*Registration precedes transfer.* A field can contain another subject before any sign is exchanged. An adequate account has to locate the other in the modal field as already mapped—another closure with its own stakes—rather than treating recognition as beginning only when language or gesture arrives.

*Both poles of drive’s bipolarity.* Sexuality is a field differentiated from the attraction-pole of drive’s bipolar structure (§5.2), while its lineage history includes the production of other beings that share the recursive architecture. What’s needed is a connection between sexuality and drive’s structural bipolarity without turning that evolutionary connection into the definition or aim of every lived expression. Coupling for variation-generation is one lineage’s solution to its continuation problem; attraction, non-attraction, desire, orientation, identity, and intimacy are the subject-level differentiations that history can support without each being ordered toward reproduction.

*Multiple registers operating simultaneously.* Sexuality runs at the chemical, somatic, affective, and reflective levels simultaneously in beings deep enough to register at all of them. How the registers stack has to be explained, rather than treating sexuality as one level: attraction at the depth where another being is registered as such, desire as drive shaped by registered attraction, embodied coupling at the depth where mutual reading becomes possible, and identity at the depth where the self-model includes its position in the field, each located at its depth in the life.

*Self-model construction in the sexual register.* Gender, sexual orientation, and sexual identity are features of the self-model constructed at sufficient depth of self-modeling. Their constructed status has to be registered without making them merely arbitrary or merely fictional: sexual self-modeling comes out as a real construction within awareness—consequential and structurally sustained—with the same status the narrative self has in §5.7.

*Depth-graded animal and human spectrum.* The depth gradient of attraction, coupling, and identity has to be registered rather than treating sexuality as one categorically unified phenomenon, distinguishing what runs at each depth from what requires greater depth to obtain.

*Consent at the modal-depth standard.* Sexual encounter between beings of sufficient depth requires consent on the modal-depth standard named at §5.11.4. What has to be accommodated is the structural fact that what counts as consent depends on the modal capacity of the will behind the act, preserving the bridge between sexual ethics and the modal-depth account of will, with consent as the operational form autonomy takes in the sexual register.

*Non-reduction without supernaturalism.* Sexuality is neither reducible to fitness maximization (the sociobiological story understates the phenomenology) nor decreed from outside Nature (the classical religious story locates the source incorrectly) nor merely culturally constructed (the constructionist story understates the structural conditions). What’s needed is an account that locates sexuality as the first-person embodied register emerging from a lineage history that includes attraction, coupling, and continuation, without making any one of those the definition of the whole. That gives sexuality its phenomenology, its structural conditions, and its constructed contents without reducing one to another.

These requirements aren’t neutral criteria every adequate account of sexuality must accept. In particular, the proposed relation to drive, the account of gender and sexual identity, and the modal-depth account of consent are substantive philosophical claims that require independent argument.
