### 5.8.3 Predictions
The following are hypotheses generated by the proposed account of sexuality as embodied intersubjective coupling and, in some contexts, reproduction. They aren’t direct consequences of the modal roles or established conclusions of evolutionary biology, psychology, or gender studies:

*Variation under changing conditions; sexuality as a powerful recurrent solution.* Where conditions change across generations, a long-running lineage needs enough heritable variation to remain viable across those changes.

Sexual reproduction is one recurrent solution. Across many complex multicellular eukaryotes, meiotic recombination can generate combinations faster than mutation alone. It isn’t the only solution, and not all life depends on it. Bacteria and archaea draw on horizontal gene transfer alongside mutation. Bdelloid rotifers appear to have persisted for long periods without conventional sex, using alternative repair and gene-acquisition pathways (Gladyshev et al. 2008). Parthenogenetic and clonal lineages persist over shorter ranges. Whether sexuality benefits or is required by a particular lineage depends on mutation rate, environmental volatility, existing diversity, and access to other variation channels. Sexuality is therefore identified as a recurrent biological answer under specified conditions, not as a modal necessity of life (Maynard Smith 1978; Otto 2009).

*Recurrent prevalence among complex lineages.* Among complex multicellular eukaryotes—animals, fungi, and land plants—sexual reproduction recurs across many lineages without being universal in every lineage, life stage, or organism. The architecture supporting it varies; the recurrence is at the level of the structural problem recombination helps solve, not at the level of any particular mechanism. Where asexual reproduction persists over long evolutionary spans, the account predicts that variation must be supplied by other pathways—mutation, gene conversion, horizontal acquisition, or another mechanism—carrying the load recombination otherwise would.

*Affective registration at depth.* Sexuality takes affective form at the depth that registers attraction. Below that depth it is mechanism (gametic fusion, mating tropisms); at that depth and above it is felt. The depth gradient traced at Feeling (§5.3) applies here as it does to other registers—chemical-gradient registration, perceptual registration, affective registration, reflective registration—each elaborating what the shallower depths already do.

*Identity construction at self-aware depth.* Some forms of sexual and gender identity involve a person’s reflective sense of themself in relation to others. Identity construction, on this account, becomes possible with sufficient self-awareness. It doesn’t establish that gender and sexual orientation are universally constructions of one specified depth, and their ontological status remains a live philosophical and social question.

*Orientation variation, including minimal or absent attraction.* If orientation is the standing direction desire takes—drive (§5.2) shaped by attraction toward another—the prediction is that this direction can vary in kind, intensity, conditionality, and presence. Asexuality doesn’t imply absent drive, libido, affection, romantic attraction, intimacy, or reproductive capacity, since these are distinct registers on the account. Because sexual reproduction is a lineage-level solution to the variation problem rather than a demand on any individual subject, these configurations should occur without being deficits of drive, and the self-model (§5.7) can construct stable identity-positions around them. The dissociability of sexual attraction, romantic attraction, libido, affiliation, behavior, and reproduction is itself the prediction: they should come apart in documented cases, which is what asexuality and aromanticism, together or separately, display.

*Coupling structure.* Dyadic mutual registration is the base unit of embodied coupling, with plural bonds read as concurrent dyads. That structural claim doesn’t settle the ethics of monogamy, non-monogamy, marriage, or other relationship structures. Those questions also depend on culture, law, consent, power, and the preferences of the people involved.

*Sexual ethics as a special case of morality.* What one being owes another in intimate exchange is morality (§5.14) where registration of one being by another is among the most complete. The same conditions that ground Morality apply with full force where the registration is among the most direct—consent, the readability of the other’s affective broadcasts, the asymmetric vulnerability the body affords.

*Reproduction-choice as agency.* Reproduction-choice emerges as agency at the depth where a being can take the production of new lives as an object of its own reflection. Below that depth, reproduction is what coupling does; at that depth, it is what coupling can be chosen for, against, or differently. Reproduction-choice is an instance of modal depth in operation: the act becomes agency when the subject can hold possible futures open long enough to decide whether, when, and under what conditions another subject should come into being.

### 5.8.4 Confirmation
*Sexual reproduction and variation.* Sexual reproduction is widespread across many eukaryotic lineages, while asexual and mixed reproductive strategies also occur. The evolutionary maintenance of sex remains an active research problem: recombination, parasite coevolution, mutation load, ecological conditions, and lineage-specific histories can all matter. Bdelloid rotifers, parthenogenetic vertebrates, and other asexual lineages require explanation, but they don’t simply function as exceptions that confirm a single rule. Muller’s ratchet and Red Queen models are influential proposals, not a settled proof that sex is the dominant solution to one universal variation-generation requirement. (Muller’s ratchet (named for geneticist Hermann Muller) describes how, in a population that reproduces asexually, harmful mutations can only accumulate over generations—there’s no way to recombine with a better copy of a gene to remove them—so genetic quality can only click downward, like a ratchet that turns one way. It’s one of the leading proposed explanations for why sexual reproduction, which lets genomes shuffle and recombine, persists despite its costs.) (The Red Queen hypothesis (named for the character in Through the Looking-Glass who must keep running just to stay in the same place) proposes that species are locked in a constant evolutionary arms race with parasites, predators, and competitors—each side’s adaptations cancel out the other’s gains, so lineages must keep evolving just to hold their current ground rather than to get ahead. It’s a leading proposed explanation for why sexual reproduction, which speeds up the generation of new genetic combinations, persists despite its costs.) These literatures motivate questions about variation and lineage continuity; they aren’t confirmation of the modal-structural account.

*Affective registration.* Across mammalian and avian lineages, courtship behaviors involve sustained affective registration (Bekoff and Byers 1998; Bagemihl 1999). The neurochemistry of attraction (dopaminergic mesolimbic circuits, oxytocinergic bonding circuits) is shared across mammals and traces to the architecture named at §5.2—the SEEKING and pair-bonding systems Panksepp (1998) identified as primary emotional circuits. Carter (1998) on oxytocin and pair-bonding extends the same picture into the social-affiliative register that adjoins sexual coupling.

*Identity construction.* Cross-cultural anthropology documents both the universality of gender as a structural feature of human social organization and the variability of its specific construction. Self-aware identity-positions in sexuality—orientation and gender—are documented across cultures with significant variability in how they are named and lived (Herdt 1994; Roughgarden 2004). Same-sex sexual behavior is documented across hundreds of vertebrate species (Bagemihl 1999), foreclosing the assumption that orientation maps cleanly onto reproductive function. Asexuality is the stable absence of sexual attraction, distinguished in the empirical literature from low desire and from sexual dysfunction. It is documented as a distinct orientation at roughly one percent of the population (Bogaert 2004; Bogaert 2012): the predicted case in which the sexual-attraction register doesn’t form while drive and, in many individuals, libido remain.

*Variation across the animal kingdom.* The substrate-variation pattern extends well beyond same-sex behavior, as the account expects. Sexual reproduction is deeply conserved and widespread across eukaryotes, but it isn’t the active mode of every lineage or organism; the architectures that support it vary still further. Sex determination has multiple structural implementations—XY in placental mammals, ZW in birds and many reptiles, haplodiploidy in hymenoptera, temperature-dependent in many reptiles, environmental in some fish. Sequential hermaphroditism is widespread: clownfish change from male to female (protandry), many wrasses and parrotfish change in the other direction (protogyny), with the transition triggered by social-structural cues. Simultaneous hermaphroditism is the norm across many invertebrate phyla and obtains in some fish; the chalk bass trades egg-laying and sperm-donating roles with a partner within a single spawning bout, switching roles as often as twenty times in an evening (Fischer 1984; Hart et al. 2016). Sustained same-sex pair-bonding, courtship, and coupling is documented in over 1,500 species (Bagemihl 1999; Bailey and Zuk 2009; Monk et al. 2019): roughly one-third of Laysan albatross pairs in some Hawaiian colonies are female-female (Young et al. 2008); bonobo female-female sexual contact is integral to social cohesion; bottlenose dolphins, Japanese macaques, and many other species show extensive same-sex coupling; sheep show stable male-male partner preference in approximately 8% of rams (Roselli et al. 2004) with corresponding hypothalamic correlates. Within-species role-morph variation is widespread: side-blotched lizards have three male morphs running rock-paper-scissors reproductive strategies (Sinervo and Lively 1996); ruffs have three male morphs including female-mimicking faeders; bluegill sunfish have parental, sneaker, and satellite male types (Gross and Charnov 1980); Mozambique tilapia have three stable male morphs, one of which recruits a subordinate male into cooperative courtship of females (Roughgarden 2004, citing Oliveira and Almada 1998). Hyena females have a pseudo-penis and female-dominant social organization. What earlier observers read as a male-active, female-passive default has been extensively revised by a generation of evolutionary biologists working on female sexual selection, female-female competition, female promiscuity, and matriarchal social organization, with Cooke (2022) surveying the empirical reversal across taxa. Extended postreproductive female lifespan—menopause—has evolved independently in humans and in several toothed-whale lineages (orcas, belugas, narwhals, short-finned pilot whales), in each case coupled with grandmother-mediated kin support rather than continued reproduction (Ellis et al. 2024): a second architecture for allocating female reproductive investment across the lifespan, not a deviation from a single mammalian default. Across all of this, what the current human-centric framing calls “the standard arrangement” is one stable architecture among many—what is expected if sexuality consists in attraction and coupling shaped by underlying architecture rather than in a single canonical type the lineage either instantiates or fails at.

*Biological and neural correlates of orientation and identity.* Large genetic work supports polygenic contribution to same-sex sexual behavior without a single determining locus (Ganna et al. 2019), while twin, developmental, hormonal, and birth-order findings indicate multiple probabilistic influences rather than one pathway. Neuroanatomical and diffusion-imaging studies have reported group-level associations involving INAH-3, BSTc, and white-matter measures (LeVay 1991; Byne et al. 2001; Zhou et al. 1995; Kruijver et al. 2000; Rametti et al. 2011; Rametti et al. 2011). These literatures are heterogeneous, often based on small or selected samples, and don’t supply a robust individual neural marker of sexual orientation or gender identity. Group associations can’t establish an individual’s identity, fix causal direction, or show that the self-model merely reads a fully specified prior substrate. The defensible convergence is broader: orientation and identity develop through interacting biological, developmental, psychological, and social processes, with substantial individual variation. The substrate–self-model distinction must remain compatible with that complexity rather than anchored to any one correlate.

*Sexual ethics.* Cross-cultural moral codes invariably regulate sexuality, and the structural features the codes track—consent, fidelity, harm, the production and care of children—are everywhere recognized as morally weighted, even when specific rules differ. Brown’s (1991) human universals catalog includes multiple sexuality-related entries; the universality of regulation is itself the empirical face of the prediction (§5.14) that intersubjective coupling at this density requires structural maintenance.

*Reproduction-choice.* In cultures with reliable contraception, reproduction has shifted from default to chosen, and the consequences for individual life-course planning, gender relations, and demographic structure are now the subject of substantial empirical literature. This bears out the expectation that, at sufficient self-modeling depth and given the technological conditions, the agentive field expands to include reproduction itself.

### 5.8.5 Conclusions
*What the reduction gets right, and what it collapses.* The sociobiological reading stated at §5.8.1 rests on the explanatory power of selection: sexual behaviors that didn’t aid reproduction wouldn’t be reliably present in the biological record, and tracing observable patterns of attraction, mate choice, parental investment, and intersexual conflict back to selection pressures has yielded a substantial body of testable predictions, some of which have survived contact with the data while others remain disputed. Any account of sexuality that ignored that substrate would be missing the structural floor on which the rest stands. This account keeps the evolutionary substrate intact, and the explanatory power of selection within that frame. What the structural account adds is a distinction the reductive form collapses: between *reproductive function*, which the evolutionary substrate captures well, and *sexuality’s broader embodied/intersubjective register*, which it doesn’t. Sexuality isn’t exhausted by reproduction. Its operation as one of the densest registers of intersubjective coupling—affect, attraction-as-registration-of-another-being, identity construction at self-aware depth, the production of new subjects as agentive choice rather than as biological default in beings capable of choosing—runs continuously alongside the reproductive function but isn’t reducible to it. Affect is real because registration is real; reducing affect to replication-strategy mistakes the substrate for the phenomenon, and treating same-sex coupling, post-reproductive sexuality, contraception-mediated reproduction, and sexual coupling as ends in themselves as anomalies-to-explain rather than as features the broader register makes immediately legible is one place where the reduction shows. The same substrate hosts both bacterial gradient-following and the deepest human intimacy; what differs is depth, not the kind of activity.

*Social constructionism.* Foucault (1976), Butler (1990), and the constructionist tradition read sexuality and gender as productions of historical discourse. The position rests on the variability of how sexuality is named, organized, regulated, and experienced across cultures and historical moments: what counts as sexual at all, who is permitted to do what with whom, which identity-positions are even available to the subjects who construct themselves around them, which forms of attention are sexually weighted versus unmarked, and how desire and constraint are jointly produced by power, language, and institution all vary in ways that resist substrate-only explanation. The constructionist’s central observation—that identity is held in language, transmitted by institution, and shaped by power—is correct as far as it goes, and any account that treated identity-positions as substrates rather than as constructions would miss precisely what makes those positions historically and culturally located. Here, the constructed character of identity-positions is preserved—they are self-model constructions in the sense named at §5.7, not substrates—without dissolving the substrate they are constructed against. The body is real, attraction is real, the affective architecture is shared across lineages and predates discourse, and the neural-correlate findings (§5.8.4) on orientation- and identity-architecture aren’t optional. What discourse constructs is how a particular being takes up its position in the field; the field itself is structural.

*Sex-binary reductionism.* Contemporary sex-realist arguments—Stock (2021), Joyce (2021), Soh (2020), and the broader gender-critical literature—correctly insist that sexed embodiment is materially real, that reproductive biology isn’t a discursive artifact, and that institutional handling of identity categories has policy consequences that can’t be wished away. All three claims stand on this account. What it forecloses is the move from “one biological layer is real” to “that layer is the whole structure of sex and gender.” Five recurring inferential collapses drive the argument past what its substrate supports.

The gametic collapse moves from anisogamy—that sexually reproducing species use two gamete types—to the conclusion that sexed embodiment, development, attraction, and identity must therefore be binary in the same way; but anisogamy is one structural layer, not the whole architecture documented at §5.8.4. The chromosomal collapse moves from XX/XY’s prevalence to the conclusion that sex is settled by chromosomes; but development is multilayered—genes, gonads, hormones, morphology, neural development, self-model—and atypical patterns at every layer are documented. The statistical collapse moves from population dimorphism to the conclusion that every token person is binary in the same way; but average differences between groups don’t determine the architecture of the individual being. The policy collapse moves from “some institutions handle gender identity poorly” to “gender identity is therefore not real in the relevant sense”; but bad institutional handling doesn’t falsify the phenomenon being handled. The construction collapse, running in the opposite direction, moves from “gender is socially constructed” to “gender is therefore arbitrary”; but self-models, languages, laws, and identities are constructed and causally real at once.

The structural account avoids all five by holding what each register tracks at its proper level: gametic polarity, chromosomal pattern, endocrine development, morphology, attraction, identity-position, and political standing are coupled registers, not interchangeable names for the same thing. Beneath the gametic and statistical collapses in particular lies a single distinction the reductions elide: at the substrate layer, sex-category membership tracks developmental organization toward a reproductive role, not the realized exercise of that function. The infertile, the post-reproductive, the prepubescent, and the celibate aren’t thereby removed from the category—which shows the category was never a per-token functional test but a claim about the developmental pathways a body’s development instantiates, holding whether or not the function is ever exercised or succeeds.

Both collapses trade a type- or population-level fact for an individual functional criterion; the organization/function distinction forecloses that trade at its root. Two limits keep the distinction honest. First, the organization at issue is the typical bimodal pattern the chromosomal collapse already qualified, not a re-assertion of clean binary development: where organization is itself atypical—the documented intersex and disorders-of-sex-development conditions—category standing is genuinely intermediate rather than settled by a hidden exercised-function test, exactly as the multilayered account requires. Second, this is a claim about the substrate layer alone; it carries no verdict on social-category membership or on the self-model identity a person holds, which are the questions taken up at §5.12 and §5.7, and the organizational reading of sex-as-substrate licenses no inference to them. Adopting the developmental reading of sexed embodiment therefore concedes nothing to the move from substrate to identity that the gender-critical inference requires: the registers stay separate.

*Religious-metaphysical regulation.* Augustine, Aquinas, and the natural-law tradition, with cross-cultural variants in Confucian, Brahmanic, and Islamic ethics, did more than issue commands from outside Nature. They identified four real features of sexuality that thinner accounts tend to omit. First, sexual coupling has in-built structural directionality and isn’t metaphysically inert. Second, the norms tracking it aren’t arbitrary divine fiat but constraints latent in what coupling is. Third, what is done sexually leaves enduring effects on the beings involved that mere consent or contract doesn’t exhaust. Fourth, sexuality participates in an order larger than the individual life, a kinship-and-generations order across which subjects are produced and sustained.

Each of these phenomena is real, and a recreational-signaling or contractual-exchange account of sexuality can’t capture them. The structural account agrees with the tradition on the phenomena and corrects only the metaphysics. The directionality is what coupling is at the substrate level, with attraction-architecture, hormonal coordination, gestational physiology, and pair-bonding circuitry all converging on it; the norms tracking the directionality are structural-moral constraints (§5.14) on registration at high density, not divine fiat; the enduring effects are what registration in a recursive self-model does over time; the kinship-and-generations order is what intersubjective coupling at the density named at Morality (§5.14) already is, with no relocation above Nature required. The traditions accurately identified the weight, the directionality, the duration, and the order. They misidentified only the location of the source.

*Contemporary identity discourse.* Both poles of the public argument flatten one half of the substrate–self-model pair held together here. The “gender is just biology” position collapses the self-model construction (§5.7) into the substrate, missing that the construction is real, person-specific, and consequential—that the self-model holds the position, and what the self-model holds is what it is to be that subject. The “gender is purely social construction” position collapses the substrate into discourse, missing that the body and its attraction-architecture are real. The political weight derives from morality (§5.14): identity-positions are the beings subjects construct of themselves in the field of intersubjective coupling, and the structural account of moral standing applies to them as it applies to subjects in any other intersubjective register. Manne’s (2017) distinction between sexism (the role-ascribing belief system) and misogyny (the enforcement mechanism that punishes deviation from the ascribed role) gives the framework (§5.14) analytic purchase here: misogyny is structural-moral violation directed at one being of the substrate-and-self-model pair, operating through the language register (§5.12) to constrain the self-model (§5.7).

*The scope of the claim, stated once and directly.* This account asserts two things and declines a third. It asserts that every subject at issue has moral standing at §5.14 on the capacity for experience under its equal-standing premise, not on category-membership, so the moral verdict is invariant across the realist and constructionist readings alike. It asserts that the substrate architectures those identities construct around are empirically real and variable (§5.8.4). It declines to adjudicate the contested specifics of contemporary policy and etiquette debate. The account will be misread from both directions—as biological essentialism on one reading, as gender ideology on the other—and both misreadings collapse a register it holds apart: substrate (§5.8.4), self-model identity (§5.7), social category (§5.12), and moral standing (§5.14) are coupled but distinct, and no claim at one level settles a question at another.

*Sexual violation.* The structural account names sexual coupling as morality (§5.14) at one of its highest densities, where registration of one being by another is among the most direct. Sexual violation is the inversion at that density: structural-moral failure at a register where the structural-moral demand is among the densest. This isn’t read as an ordinary harm scaled up, but as a violation targeted at a position where the depth of registration is among the greatest. This is why the harm can’t be accounted for by injury-metrics alone—somatic recovery doesn’t retire it—and why traumatic registration persists at depths the language register (§5.12) can’t fully reach (Herman 1992; Walker 2013). Manne’s (2017) reading of misogyny as enforcement-mechanism extends here: the prevalence of sexual violation as an instrument of role-enforcement, war, and political subordination is structural-moral failure operating systematically rather than incidentally. Nothing here explains why violation occurs—that is a question about substrate, history, institution, and agent—but the account locates the wrong it represents at a point where intersubjective coupling is among the densest, and gives the framework (§5.14) analytic purchase on what the wrong consists in.

*The boundary between variation and violation.* Across the practices this section hasn’t enumerated—commercial exchange, the range of kink and fetish, the configurations consenting adults arrive at in private—a single line does the work, and it is the same line drawn throughout: consent on the modal-depth standard (§5.11.4), the standing of every party (§5.14), and, where more than one bond is in play, non-corrosion. What falls on the permitted side is variation, and variation isn’t the account’s to moralize; what falls on the forbidden side is violation, and the account names it without hedging. The two verdicts are asymmetric by design. Where valid consent can’t be given, or where a party lacks the standing the act presupposes, the coupling is ruled out, and no appeal to preference, custom, or privacy reopens the question. Consent fails where a party can’t map the possibility the act requires, whether through immaturity, incapacity, or coercion. Where consent is real and standing is intact, the account issues no verdict beyond that one, and declines to convert its silence into either endorsement or prohibition. Commodification is the instructive case. The introduction of payment doesn’t itself alter the consent analysis: an exchange of money between consenting adults whose consent meets the modal-depth standard isn’t structurally distinct, at the register this account speaks to, from the same act unpaid. What the word exploitation names isn’t the payment but the defeat of consent by the conditions around it—coercion, deception, or a desperation severe enough that the will behind the word lacked the mapped alternatives real consent requires; the wrong is a person used and mistreated, their consent hollowed out, not the presence of a price. The account locates the wrong there and leaves the policy question—how a shared structure should permit, regulate, or restrict such exchange—to Chapter 6, where institutional questions belong. One further distinction keeps the boundary honest: whether a practice is publicly acceptable is a question of the social register (§5.12), not of structural-moral standing, and the two must not be run together. That a practice offends public norm isn’t itself a structural wrong, and conducting it in private discharges the separate concern of not implicating non-consenting witnesses—but privacy addresses only that concern. It can’t launder a consent-or-standing violation into a permitted act: what is done to a non-consenting party, or to a party without standing, is no less a violation for being done unseen. The boundary is consent and standing, not visibility.

*Reproduction-choice.* Pregnancy gives the structural account its hardest application because one subject’s body is the site where another possible subject is produced. The developmental-gradient result (§5.9) is therefore load-bearing here but not settled here: consciousness emerges as the neural architecture capable of integrated registration comes online, and standing comes into view by degrees rather than by binary switch. The decision whether, when, and under what conditions to produce another subject belongs to the agency of the already-existing subject whose body bears the process. The developing being’s emerging standing matters once the developmental threshold (§5.9) begins to be reached; the pregnant subject’s standing is already present throughout. From there the question becomes institutional (Chapter 6): how should a shared structure protect an existing subject’s bodily autonomy while registering the developing standing of another being as it comes into being?

Sexuality read structurally as one of the densest registers of intersubjective coupling preserves what each rival tradition was tracking while refusing each collapse it forced. Its structural counterpart is drive’s aversion-pole at its limit (§5.9).

## 5.9 Mortality
Every living thing we know of eventually dies. The narrower phenomenon is what it is like, from the inside, for a creature to grasp that *it itself* will end. A bacterium dies without ever knowing it will; a mind must at least model itself as one person stretched through time before it can register its own coming death as a fact about itself. Once available, that awareness can change everything else in a life, because feeling, knowing, meaning, and will can now all run against a limit the mind sees ahead of it. What biologically ends (the living process and, on the identity proposed here, its inside view) is separate from what outlasts it, like the memories, works, and children a person leaves behind. Those continuations are real without by themselves establishing that the person survives.

Drive runs in two directions, and the defensive one has a structural limit: not the moment-to-moment threat-responses and homeostatic corrections, but the fact that the closure each defense was oriented against isn’t contingent. Every organism that lives is organized against its own closure. The effort not to die is already Drive. Leaving something behind—staying in the field after a life closes—is Meaning running at that horizon. What is death, structurally, for beings of the kind we are? Every philosophical tradition treats mortality as a discrete subject: Epicurus’s anodyne argument, Lucretius’s image of the vanished candle, the Stoic *meditatio mortis*, Montaigne’s essay on learning to die, Heidegger’s *Sein-zum-Tode* (being-toward-death), Becker’s *Denial of Death*, the Buddhist contemplations of impermanence, the Christian *memento mori*. Mortality is given here a specific structural meaning, and in that meaning, what the traditions have been pointing at is recovered.

*What gets bundled under “death.”* The question needs sharpening before it can be answered. There is the *structural fact*: what a closed self-producing life is organized against is its own failure to keep producing itself, and that orientation isn’t contingent—it is what being organized that way consists in. This much is universal: every bacterium, every plant, every animal, every human is so organized. That every such process in fact reaches that failure is a further and empirical matter, about organisms in finite conditions rather than about the structure; neither the Conditions nor ◇C supplies a finite upper bound on a living process, and the account doesn’t need one. It is already named in §5.2 Drive, where the closure-threshold is the absolute structural anchor of the aversion-pole, operative at any depth and not requiring self-modeling. And there is the *phenomenon*: what it is like, from inside, for a creature to grasp its own ending as a structural fact about itself. This second thing is what is at issue here. The phenomenon requires that the organism have folded back deeply enough to model itself as a persistent subject in time and to project that subject toward its terminus. A bacterium dies but doesn’t grasp its own dying. The structural fact operates everywhere; the phenomenon is what mortality becomes from inside at the depth where it can become anything at all. Conflating the two has been a persistent source of confusion in the literature: treating Heideggerian *Sein-zum-Tode* as if it claimed something true of every living thing, or treating the universal biological fact as if it carried the phenomenological weight only the deep form actually carries. They’re kept distinct here: Drive (§5.2) carries the universal structural anchor; the phenomenon is carried here at the depth where it emerges.

What we are was identified at §4.8 as a closed self-producing recursion coupled, in its active phases, to a sustained energy gradient. Death, on this account, is not a mere pause in self-production: dormant life can suspend measurable metabolism while retaining the organization internally disposed to resume it. Death occurs when that organization and its capacity to resume are irreversibly lost. The vantage that opened with sufficient depth of self-modeling closes when the organism does. Death isn’t an external event imposed on the person; it is the structural condition of the person coming apart.

*A note on what is and isn’t closing.* Several distinct things are usefully separated here. *Biological closure* is the irreversible loss, at the cellular and organismic scale, of both active closure-and-throughput and the retained organization internally capable of resuming it; it is the structural event the main argument is about. *Ordinary-consciousness closure* is the irreversible loss of the organized activity on which every measured instance of ordinary personal consciousness depends. The identity account proposed here reads that dependence constitutively: when the organization ends, its vantage ends rather than migrating elsewhere. *Surviving effects* (the dead person’s models held by others, the social patterns their life shaped, the artifacts their making produced, the children they raised) persist after biological closure and are real, but their persistence alone isn’t personal survival. A survival account therefore owes an independently specified bearer or continuity relation; the effects themselves don’t supply one.

*What death takes, and why it remains a loss.* The account at Conclusions (§5.7.5) draws Parfit’s consequence that identity isn’t what matters: what one has reason to care about in one’s own future is the continuation of the person, not a bare identity-fact laid over it. Carried to mortality, this fixes what death takes and blocks two opposite errors. Against the survival traditions, death takes exactly the person’s continuation, the projects, connections, and self-model that would have been carried forward, and not some further self-substance that might have gone on elsewhere, for on the identity account there is no such further thing to survive. Against the fully deflationary reading, the loss is nonetheless real and, in the ordinary case, determinate, because the person whose continuation matters is a single real continuant rather than a relation that only ever held by degrees. Parfit’s softening of the badness of death has purchase where the life is already thin or branched, where little of what matters was going to be carried forward in any case, and not against the standard case, where a determinate continuant with a future is what ends. What Epicurus and Lucretius saw is that there is no post-closure vantage for death to be bad for; what they missed is that the badness was never located there but in the foreclosure of the continuation the living process was oriented toward.

Mortality is constitutive of the finite biological organization described here; *awareness* of mortality isn’t automatically constitutive of every deep first-person perspective. Self-modeling requires sustained activity under conditions it doesn’t guarantee, but a subject can possess a temporally extended self-model without explicitly representing its own death. What sufficient depth makes available is the further fold: the person can register, from inside, that its continuation depends on conditions that can fail.

*Mortality-awareness as a possible reorganization of the living process.* Crossing the threshold at which mortality registers as a first-person structural fact can reorganize rather than merely supplement the modalities already in play. Feeling can become the feeling of being a current that will end; knowledge, knowledge held by a mind that can’t guarantee its own persistence; meaning, meaning for a life bounded at both ends; will, will against a horizon; art, resonance with what its maker may not outlast. How completely this reorganization occurs is an empirical and biographical question, not something the structural account settles. The precise claim is that an explicit representation of one’s own ending becomes available only once the self-model can extend through time and include its own absence, and that such a representation can become a limit-condition carried through the rest of the field.

The depth-gradient framing applies to mortality as it does to other registers. Some social animals exhibit responses to the deaths of group members: comparative thanatology, the study of how nonhuman animals respond to death, documents elephants revisiting remains for years and touching bones with their trunks (Douglas-Hamilton et al. 2006; McComb et al. 2006); cetaceans carrying dead calves for days; chimpanzees and other primates carrying or attending to deceased infants; corvids gathering around dead conspecifics in what some researchers call funerals (Swift and Marzluff 2015). These are shallow forms (recognition of others’ death, grief response, behavioral changes around the dead) present in species without robust self-awareness in the strong sense. *Awareness of one’s own mortality* as a structural fact about one’s persistent self in time is the deep form, requiring the organism folded back far enough to model the self as a temporally extended subject who will end. The structural threshold for the deep form sits at the self-aware level named at §5.1. The shallow forms exist below it; the deep form is what mortality becomes from the first-person perspective of the depth registered there.

**[Corollary]**

**Mortality** · *Corollary*

Mortality, in its deep form, is the living process registering its own ending as a structural fact about itself: the closure every living current is organized against, folded back into a self-model deep enough to project itself toward its terminus. (The universal fact of closure is the aversion-anchor of Drive; the phenomenon here is that fact registered from inside.)

*Status: the structural half is Drive’s aversion-pole: the effort not to die is already running. The catch is not “you will die.” It is that the being who will not go quietly has already weighted continuation. The deep form—grasping that ending as one’s own—requires the self-model. That this registration just is mortality remains a functional proposal defended by fit.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2) and Identity (§5.7)

The aversion-anchor is Drive (§5.2); the structural backdrop is the Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2).

*The bookend at the other side.* Closure has a structural counterpart: emergence. The current that ends is the same current that earlier came into being, and neither boundary need be one instantaneous event for every property under discussion. Biological life is present before birth; capacities associated with sentience, memory, temporal self-modeling, and agency depend on structures that develop along different trajectories. The argument therefore blocks the simplification that biological life, sentience, subjecthood, moral standing, and political standing must all arrive at one moment. It doesn’t by itself say when any contested capacity is sufficient, whether subjecthood is graded, or what moral and political standing follows. Those require the relevant empirical evidence and the normative premises of §5.14 and Chapter 6. The structural point is only that the life has a developmental history at its opening boundary just as its organized capacities can be lost along different trajectories at its closing boundary.

The body that can map possibility can’t map its own non-existence as a first-person possibility, because there is no first-person body to run the simulation from. The organism can register its own *ending* (that is what mortality, in the deep form, just is) but it can’t occupy the *state* of its non-existence from inside, since occupying anything is itself something the organism does only while it lives. What is unmappable isn’t the fact of the terminus but the territory past it. This offers a structural reason for the asymmetric appetite the contemplative traditions have always noticed: the body’s modal field is hungry for data about its own end, and there is no data of the kind it most wants, so the body borrows. Other bodies’ deaths (witnessed, narrated, depicted, rehearsed in religious imagery) are the proxy training data the body uses to extend its modal representation of the only territory it can’t natively occupy. On this account, what ordinary speech calls morbid curiosity is the empirical face of this: the body deliberately seeks aversive simulations of death and serious harm because storing the possibility expands modal coverage of what could go wrong, and the survival value of that coverage can outweigh the affective cost of running the simulation. The same logic operates whether the proxy is a horror film, a true-crime story, a *memento mori* image, a Buddhist *maranasati* practice, or a funeral. The body is engaged in extending its modal representation toward its own terminus through whatever proxy material the culture makes available, because that extension is what the body can do given the structural fact that the territory itself is unmappable from inside.

*The general operation, of which this is the limit case.* The proxy borrowing just described (using other beings’ actualities as proxy training data for one’s own modal field) is one instance of the general modal-field-expansion drive named at §5.2. Beings at depth load actualities from outside their own situation through whatever proxy channels are available: a child learning what neighbors are like through family stories, an adult studying historical catastrophes through documentary and book (§5.4), a culture maintaining its repertoire of social cases through gossip (§5.12), a discipline accumulating its corpus of empirical findings through publication. Mortality is the limiting case of the operation, not its only instance, because the territory it maps is the only one structurally unmappable from inside the organism that draws the map. Where other proxy-data acquisition has the option of being verified later by the body’s own experience (the body may eventually visit the country it read about, meet the kind of person it heard about, encounter the kind of failure it studied) mortality has no such option. The appetite is one extreme of a continuous drive operating across every register where the body can borrow into its modal field. This is the mortal inversion of the outward spine: where the other registers have the organism sharing field-content with other beings (the distributed holding the Modal Convergence theorem describes, §5.4), mortality is the register where it must borrow *from* them. Even at the horizon it can’t cross, the field a being draws at that horizon is borrowed from others rather than private.

*Legacy: continuation after personal continuation.* Once a self-model can represent its own terminus, it can also represent the world continuing without it and ask what of its present direction will remain active there. The drive toward continuation can’t carry the same experiencing creature through closure, but at sufficient depth it can differentiate into a wish that the life not vanish without remainder: that someone remember it, that something it made continue to work, that a person it cared for carry possibilities the relation opened. The wish varies in strength and form and isn’t a universal occurrent desire. Its structural availability follows from the conjunction already in hand: identity supplies a person represented as this one, mortality supplies the future in which this one is absent, knowledge supplies a model reaching into that future, and relation supplies other subjects and structures capable of carrying effects into it.

**[Corollary]**

**Legacy** · *Corollary*

Legacy is the continuation of a person’s effects after the person’s own life has closed: the representations other subjects retain, the possibilities a relationship opened, the practices and artifacts a life set in motion, and the institutions or living subjects it helped shape. It is real causal and relational continuation, admitting of degrees. It is not numerical or experiential survival of the person whose effects continue.

*Status: the structural half is Drive’s weighting carried to Mortality’s horizon: a standing weight that something remain after one’s own life closes. The fuller account of how such weightings are held and criticized is §5.10’s, and is not presupposed here. That this continuation just is legacy remains a functional proposal defended by fit. Not a fresh derivation from the modal proof and not the claim that every subject seeks remembrance. Builds on the account of Mortality already given.*

**Depends on:** Mortality (§5.9), Identity (§5.7), and Knowledge (§5.4)

The result says legacy is real causal and relational continuation without experiential survival. What is already in hand is an account of what continues, and it is more specific than influence. A body’s field is a partial, lossy mapping of one objective modal structure, and field-content is conveyed between bodies; that transfer is one of the conditions the Modal Convergence theorem states (§5.4). Transfer isn’t a metaphor for remembrance. It is the same operation language runs on (§5.12), and it doesn’t require the source field to persist.

**[Proposition]**

**Legacy as Transferred Field-Content** · *Proposition*

A closure ends one mapping of the modal structure. It does not retrieve what that mapping had already transferred into others. What continues is therefore neither the person nor a trace of the person, but field-content now held in fields that remain open: possibilities other subjects can register because this one registered them first, and dependencies they can navigate because this one mapped them.

Two consequences follow. Legacy admits of degrees by how much transferred and into how many fields, not by how well the person is remembered, so an unremembered life whose mappings propagated widely has more of it than a remembered one whose did not. And the content is fully alienated from its source: once held elsewhere it is subject to the same lossiness as any other mapping, so a legacy is revisable, corruptible, and improvable by others, and never by the one whose it was.

**Depends on:** Legacy (§5.9) and Modal Convergence (§5.4), Knowledge (§5.4)

This also fixes what the mortal case does *not* soften. The transferred content isn’t the subject, and its continuation isn’t a diminished form of survival; the person who registered it has closed, and nothing in the proposition bears on that closure. What the result establishes is narrower and worth having on its own: that the continuation the result names has a mechanism already established, rather than resting on the ordinary sense in which anything influences anything.

Knowledge and legacy are inverse holdings. In knowledge, the subject carries what exceeds it within its modal field. In legacy, what exceeds the subject—the fields of other subjects and the shared structures between them—continues to carry something of the subject. Close relationships are a clear case. Each person builds a working representation of the other into the field by which they interpret and navigate the world. At death the reciprocal updating ends on one side, but the surviving model and the changes the relationship made don’t disappear. To be remembered is to remain causally present in another subject’s field after one’s own field has closed. The presence is partial and revisable: the good and the bad, the accurate and idealized, are held by a living subject whose own development continues. The wish to be remembered need not be a wish to burden that subject with grief. Its minimum content is the wish to have been real enough to someone that the relation leaves a shape.

Parenthood separates the forms of continuation cleanly. Reproduction brings another organism into being. Parenting sustains a developing subject and helps furnish the conditions under which its modal field can widen. Legacy is what remains active in that subject and in what the subject later carries forward. Adoption demonstrates that the second and third require no genetic transmission: care, language, security, knowledge, and remembered affection can pass between lives without ancestry. The child is never the parent continuing under another name. A child is a new center of possibility, able to revise, reject, and transform what was received. Loving formation widens that field; domination tries to narrow it into a copy. The parent’s most defensible continuation through the child is therefore not the child’s resemblance to the parent but the child’s enlarged capacity to become itself.

The afterlife wish is the maximalized form of the same pressure. Ordinary legacy asks that effects, representations, or relations continue. An afterlife asks that the same experiencing subject continue: still this one, at further moments, somewhere, with possibilities remaining open. In these terms, it asks for identity, Temporality, Spatiality, Substantiality, and a live modal field beyond biological closure. That the wish is structurally intelligible supplies no evidence that its object obtains. It helps explain why the religious proposal is recurrent: a finite field can model its closing and desire continuation, but it can’t model from inside what its own nonbeing would be, so the desire is projected across the boundary it can’t cross.

*The Inversion.* The standard religious response locates what answers mortality outside Nature: an immortal soul, a world to come, a vantage that survives the closure of the current. On the identity account there is no such vantage. What remains to describe is the self-modeling activity while it runs, and the person’s relation, from inside, to the closure that conditions it. What the inversion forecloses (the upward exit) isn’t what mortality calls for. Mortality calls for a different orientation: the deep first-person perspective taking its own finitude as constitutive rather than as something to be escaped. The contemplative traditions that practice this orientation directly are doing structural work: the Stoic *meditatio*, the Buddhist *maranasati*, the Christian *memento mori*.

Sexuality (§5.8) is the most legible lineage-level structural pair to death: one differentiation of the attraction-pole named at §5.2, historically shaped in sexually reproducing lineages by continuation through producing other organisms without imposing that function on each subject or expression. Death is the absolute referent of the aversion-pole at its structural limit; sexuality is one attraction-pole register through which life can reach beyond the individual being.

*Structural responses to the horizon.* Sexuality isn’t the only register at which the organism is organized against the death-horizon; it is one of several. *Sexuality (§5.8)* answers at the lineage register: where sexual reproduction occurs, the organism produces other organisms, and the lineage continues even where the individual being can’t. *Legacy* answers at the relational and causal registers: other subjects, artifacts, practices, and institutions continue to carry effects after the originating person closes. *Art (§5.15)* answers in its aesthetic register: the organism resonates with structures of the same kind as itself, registers its own situation through vehicles whose persistence outlasts its making, and finds in that resonance an orientation that doesn’t depend on individual continuation. *Spirituality (§5.16)* answers by orienting toward what exceeds the organism: registering the limit of its own model, the organism may construct representations of what would lie past its horizon if the structural limit weren’t absolute, and orient itself by them, even though no first-person vantage can verify them from inside the organism that draws them. These aren’t alternatives but parallel structural responses to the same limit-condition, operating at different registers of the organism’s reach. A creature that has crossed the threshold finds itself, in varying proportion across lives and cultures, organizing all of them. The Inversion doesn’t erase them; it forecloses spirituality’s claim, where it makes one, to terminate at a substantive transcendent and refers each of them back to what they structurally are: the creature’s situation under an absolute horizon, expressed at different registers of its own reach.

### 5.9.1 The Dispute
The literature on mortality is among the oldest in philosophy and continues to organize work across philosophy, theology, psychology, and bioethics.

*Epicurean dissolution arguments.* Epicurus (Letter to Menoeceus) and Lucretius (*De Rerum Natura* III) argued that death isn’t bad for the one who dies because at the moment of death there is no subject for whom it could be bad. Death isn’t an experience; the dead don’t suffer; the symmetry between pre-existence and post-existence shows that neither involves the subject. The argument continues to organize contemporary work on the badness of death (Nagel 1970; Bradley 2009; Feldman 1992; Kagan 2012), with deprivation accounts (death is bad because it deprives the subject of future goods) the principal contemporary response. On this reading, the Epicurean argument identifies a real structural fact—there is no subject after closure—and underspecifies the inside-vantage of the subject *while alive* who registers mortality as structural condition.

*Stoic and Christian meditatio mortis.* The Stoic *meditatio mortis* (Seneca, Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus) and the Christian *memento mori* tradition both treat sustained contemplation of mortality as constitutive of practical wisdom or spiritual discipline. The frameworks differ sharply on what survives death—the Stoics naturalistic, the Christian tradition committed to an immortal soul—but converge on the practical claim that orienting toward finitude shapes how the life is lived. The practical convergence is affirmed here, while siding with the Stoics on the metaphysics: on the identity account, no vantage survives the closure.

*Heideggerian being-toward-death.* Heidegger’s (1927) 1962 account of *Dasein* as *Sein-zum-Tode* (being-toward-death) makes mortality constitutive of authentic existence rather than an external limit. The position has been extended in existentialism (Sartre, de Beauvoir) and contemporary phenomenology (Critchley 2009). Heidegger’s claim, so read, names what mortality structurally is for a being that has come to register its own finitude—not a peculiarity of human existence, and not a theorem that every sufficiently recursive vantage already registers it. What Heidegger located in *Dasein* is located here in recursion at sufficient depth, once the terminus is represented.

*Becker, terror management, and denial of death.* Becker’s (1973) *Denial of Death* argued that much of culture is organized around the management of death anxiety—a thesis subsequently developed empirically as terror management theory (Greenberg, Pyszczynski, and Solomon 1986; Pyszczynski, Solomon, and Greenberg 2003). Hundreds of studies report defensive responses to mortality salience; whether the effect generalizes is contested, and the confirmation below sets out where the replication record now stands (§5.9.4). This account holds that the Becker-TMT tradition correctly identifies a structural feature of self-modeling at sufficient depth: a being that models itself as a temporally extended subject who will end can have psychological resources organized around that fact.

*Buddhist impermanence and the Hindu doctrines.* The Buddhist traditions (Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana) treat *anicca* (impermanence), *maranasati* (mindfulness of death), and *anatta* (non-self) as related practical-philosophical commitments, with sustained attention to mortality as part of the dissolution of self-clinging. Hindu and Jain traditions develop different metaphysics of survival, rebirth, and liberation. The Buddhist practical convergence—mortality contemplation as constitutive of insight—is affirmed here, and the structural support for the *anatta* claim is located in the self-model account developed at §5.7, while remaining neutral on rebirth-related metaphysics that depend on substantive afterlife commitments.

*Survival, soul, and personal identity.* A substantial literature from Locke (1689) 1975 forward through Parfit (1984), Williams (1973b), Lewis (1976), and Olson (1997) investigates what survival across time consists in and whether anything like a soul, a continuing self, or a person-stage can survive bodily death. Contemporary metaphysics of personal identity remains highly contested. On this account, the closure of the organism is the closure of the subject, with surviving effects in others and in the structure the life shaped but no vantage that persists—a specific position in this debate, one that depends on the life–consciousness identification (§5.1) holding.

*The permanence argument for ultimate meaning.* William Lane Craig (2008) argues that a life isn’t merely difficult but *ultimately* meaningless without a permanence that only survival past death could secure: a purposeful existence that ends isn’t, on this view, different in the end from one that was never purposeful. This is a distinct claim from the theistic prescriptive accounts taken up at §5.10, which locate meaning’s authority in a divine command; this version locates meaning’s permanence in the subject’s own survival, and makes survival the variable that turns a finite purpose into an ultimate one. This account holds that the argument is best tested by holding theism fixed and varying only whether the created subject’s own continuation ends at ordinary death or persists into the promised afterlife; that test is run at §5.9.5.

*Bioethics, euthanasia, and the right to die.* The bioethical literature on end-of-life decisions (Buchanan and Brock 1989; Battin 2005; Velleman 1992) divides over whether and when terminating a life can be permissible, on the relation between bodily and biographical death, and on the structure of advance directives across dementia and other identity-disrupting conditions. The modal-depth account of will (§5.11) supplies a usable framework for thinking about consent under contracted modal depth, without resolving the policy questions specific cases raise.

*Comparative thanatology.* A growing literature documents responses to death in non-human species—elephants revisiting remains (McComb et al. 2006), cetaceans carrying dead calves, chimpanzees attending to deceased infants, corvids gathering around dead conspecifics (Swift and Marzluff 2015), and increasingly invertebrate cases. Disputes are live on what counts as mortality awareness, what counts as grief, and which lineages reach the depth required for either. On this reading, response to others’ death is widespread (the depth gradient supports it), while awareness of one’s own mortality as a structural fact about one’s persistent self requires the self-aware level named on the depth axis at §5.1.

### 5.9.2 The Requirement
*The breakdown of self-maintenance.* Death is what happens when a living process can no longer keep producing and sustaining itself and no longer retains the organization internally capable of resuming that work. Death has to be located in that breakdown rather than in an external or supplementary event: mortality follows from the failure of self-maintenance, with the point of view ending because the organization that made it possible has been lost.

*Distinction between three closings.* Biological closure, ordinary-consciousness closure, and surviving effects have to be kept apart—confusing the third for the first or second is a recurring structural error—with an explanation of how they relate: the vantage closes with the organism, surviving effects persist after closure, and the person is what closes, not what the closure leaves behind.

*Constitutive rather than incidental mortality.* Active self-modeling requires sustained energy throughput it can’t guarantee. The depth at which self-modeling folds back on itself is also the depth at which the person becomes capable of registering, from inside, that its activity and the organization capable of resuming it depend on conditions that can fail. Mortality has to come out as constitutive of the finite biological organization in view, not as an unfortunate addition to an otherwise immortal substrate, while leaving open whether every possible conscious architecture must end; registering finitude is one of the operations the depth makes possible.

*No vantage surviving the closure.* On the identity account, vantages that survive the organism’s closure are ruled out, because the vantage is what the organism is from inside, not a separate thing keyed to it. The alternative is to supply the supplementary substance, property, or law that would carry a vantage past closure, with an argument for why the supplement does work this account can’t. Absent that, supplementary survival posits earn no place: they matter only if they do work nothing else does, and no such work remains outstanding here.

*Depth-graded responses across species.* Comparative thanatology shows continuous variation across lineages in response to others’ death and in awareness of mortality. The gradient has to be registered rather than drawing a sharp categorical line at the human case, distinguishing response to others’ death from awareness of one’s own mortality (§5.1) and locating each at its depth in the process.

*Structural pair with sexuality.* Death and sexuality stand as structural counterparts at the lineage level wherever sexual reproduction is the variation-generating solution: the attraction-pole’s generative capacity and the aversion-pole at its structural limit are one continuation-problem running in two directions. The pairing has to be accommodated without turning lineage function into an aim imposed on each subject or expression. What makes the individual finite at the individual scale and permits continuity with variation at the lineage scale is the same structural problem under two angles; the lived register of sexuality remains broader than its reproductive history.

*Practical and contemplative implications.* Mortality, registered as constitutive, has practical and contemplative implications the contemplative traditions have long worked. What has to be explained is why orientation toward finitude shapes how the life is lived—not merely as psychological response but as a structural feature of self-modeling at the depth where mortality can be registered as such, making the practical traditions intelligible as structural work rather than as cultural curiosities.

*Coherence with consent and modal depth.* End-of-life agency and advance directives raise a later question about consent under contracted modal depth (§5.11.4). The mortality account identifies the organism and the closure in view; it doesn’t by itself decide whose authorization governs, how present and prior wishes should be weighted, or whether an irreversible intervention is permissible. Those conclusions require the account of will and the normative premises developed later. Closure cannot simply be said to “satisfy” revocability: it eliminates the future agent who might revoke, which is precisely why authorization before an irreversible act requires unusually careful independent justification.

These requirements aren’t neutral conditions every adequate account of mortality must accept. In particular, the no-surviving-vantage claim, the proposed structural pairing with sexuality, and the account of consent under modal depth are substantive philosophical and ethical positions requiring independent argument.

### 5.9.3 Predictions
Living systems are finite self-maintaining processes, and mortality follows when the processes sustaining an organism irreversibly fail. This doesn’t depend on establishing a recurrent cosmology, nor does present-day science establish that every sufficiently complex medium produces consciousness. What is developed here is a philosophical account of finitude rather than an empirical theorem about all possible conscious beings.

A current is the closure of a self-producing recursion coupled to sustained energy throughput (§4.8). The closure is what makes it a current rather than a flame or a clock. The throughput is what keeps the closure going. Neither is permanent; both depend on conditions the current can’t guarantee. The organism requires the throughput to keep producing itself, the throughput requires a gradient to dissipate, and the gradient requires a source the current can’t replenish without exhausting it. The eventual failure of living self-maintenance is treated as a central feature of terrestrial biological life. Whether mortality is metaphysically constitutive of every possible self-maintaining or conscious system is a further philosophical claim, not an established consequence of thermodynamics or biology. The account has three components.

*Closure failure is the structural definition of death.* Death isn’t the current ceasing to exist—the matter persists, the energy persists, the three Conditions continue without interruption. Death is the closure of a self-producing life coming apart: it stops closing on itself to produce its own conditions, the throughput’s coupling ends, and what was a self-producing current is no longer that. The matter the organism was made of is redistributed into other currents; the medium is undisturbed; the process is over.

*Mortality conditions the deep first-person perspective; mortality-awareness is a further capacity.* How the vantage opens at sufficient depth of self-modeling was traced at §4.8. Any biologically realized vantage described here depends on conditions its organism doesn’t guarantee. A temporally extended self-model can then acquire a representation of that dependence and its terminus. The dependence is built into the life; explicit awareness of the ending isn’t. The latter requires enough temporal, self-referential, and conceptual capacity to represent the same subject as later absent.

*The identity account leaves no surviving vantage.* A current whose self-production has irreversibly come apart isn’t that current in a different state. If the conscious person is identical with the organized living process, as proposed here, its closure leaves no further bearer to which the vantage transfers. That conclusion is stronger than the empirical dependence claim and inherits the identity premise: a dualist, resurrectionist, or transfer account can resist it only by specifying and supporting a bearer or continuity mechanism that the present account denies. Epicurus’s formulation—where we are, death isn’t, and where death is, we aren’t—holds on the structural reading conditional on that identity account.

The generalization from biological finitude to a broader claim about self-producing life is conjectural. Mortality in known organisms depends on contingent biological, ecological, technological, and historical conditions. The account offers one interpretation of why finitude is central to the human and animal forms of life we know.

### 5.9.4 Confirmation
The empirical record strongly supports the dependence of organismic life and known consciousness on continuing biological organization. It documents closure failure; it doesn’t directly observe every metaphysical possibility of transfer or continuation. The non-transfer conclusion is an inference from its identity account—identity is the running self-producing organization—not an empirical result supplied by biology alone. The systems-biology account (Maturana and Varela 1980; Thompson 2007) treats life as autopoiesis—the closed self-producing system—and death as autopoietic failure. The thermodynamic account (Schrödinger 1944; Prigogine 1980; Schneider and Sagan 2005) treats life as a dissipative structure maintaining itself against the gradient toward equilibrium, and death as the structure ceasing to maintain itself. Evolutionary theories of senescence (Williams 1957; Hamilton 1966; Kirkwood 1977) explain why aging evolves in many lineages through declining late-life selection, antagonistic pleiotropy, and maintenance tradeoffs. They don’t establish universal senescence for every competitively reproducing organism; negligible-senescence and unusual-regeneration cases constrain that generalization. Mortality remains widespread, but its mechanisms and life-history profiles vary. Three independent biological frameworks converge on the same structural conclusion: death is the failure of the self-producing system that constituted the organism.

Neuroscience locates the first-person dimension. The default-mode network’s role in self-modeling (Raichle et al. 2001; Northoff and Bermpohl 2004; Buckner et al. 2008) and predictive-processing accounts of the conscious self (Friston 2010; Seth 2013; Solms 2021) identify the architecture by which the organism folds back deeply enough to model itself. The same literature documents graded loss and alteration of self-modeling and consciousness as the relevant architecture is disrupted. No accepted measurement has observed a vantage migrating to another bearer. Near-death-experience studies (van Lommel 2010; Parnia et al. 2014) document reports associated with extreme physiological crisis, but temporal localization, residual activity, memory construction, and instrument sensitivity remain live questions. These studies neither establish post-closure persistence nor prove its metaphysical impossibility.

The contemplative traditions document the first-person side directly. The Stoic *meditatio mortis* (Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*; Marcus Aurelius, *Meditations*) treats the contemplation of mortality as a structural exercise—a person registering their own finitude against what surrounds them, to clarify what the finitude makes available. The Buddhist contemplations of impermanence and the *maranasati* meditation on death (Nyanaponika and Bodhi 1999) work the same architecture from a different cultural register. The Christian *memento mori* tradition, from desert monastics through medieval *ars moriendi* manuals, does the same. Heidegger’s *Sein-zum-Tode* (being-toward-death) (Heidegger (1927) 1962) gives the modern philosophical statement: *Dasein* is the being for whom its own being is at issue, and the issuing-character is constituted by orientation toward an ending that can’t be deferred indefinitely. The traditions diverge in their metaphysical accompaniments; the finitude each is registering is the same.

Psychology tests what happens when mortality is made salient. Becker’s *Denial of Death* (1973) reads the being’s relation to its own ending as deeply shaping behavior—heroism, ideology, denial—whether or not the influence is explicit. Terror management theory (Greenberg, Pyszczynski, and Solomon 1986; Solomon, Greenberg, and Pyszczynski 2015) operationalized parts of that claim, reporting effects on worldview defense, in-group bias, and related behavior; the core mortality-salience effect failed to replicate in a large preregistered multi-lab study (Klein 2022) (Many Labs 4). The experimental generalization is therefore contested. Becker’s broader interpretation remains a philosophical and psychological proposal, not a residue established after the failed replication.

What converges is an observed dependence claim: living self-production and every measured form of personal consciousness require functioning organization, and mortality awareness can shape behavior and meaning. On the identity account, irreversible loss of the constitutive organization is the closure of that person rather than a transfer. The evidence supports the premises of that inference; the non-transfer verdict remains philosophical and could be challenged by an independently evidenced continuity mechanism.

### 5.9.5 Conclusions
This account doesn’t treat mortality as a problem solved merely by adding a soul, an afterlife, or a resurrection. It begins with the finite organized life and asks what would have to continue for *this person* to continue. On the identity proposed here, the deep first-person perspective is the organized life from inside; its persistence after that organization closes would therefore require either the restoration of that organization or a defended continuity relation to another bearer. It can’t be obtained just by redescribing surviving effects as the person. A consciousness realized in some deathless structure might be possible, but it wouldn’t establish the survival of this finite person without that continuity argument (cf. Williams 1973b; Parfit 1984, Part III). Death remains the person’s loss because it forecloses the projects, attachments, and categorical desires that supplied reasons to continue. How a finite life orders those into meaning is taken up at §5.10.

The Epicurean premise is structurally sound, and the registration of mortality is also structurally appropriate. Epicurus’s premise—where we are, death isn’t, and where death is, we aren’t—is correct on this reading: there is no subject to whom the closure is suffered, because the vantage requires the life that has ceased. But the same life that opens the vantage also lets the person register, while still alive, that their life will end. Fear of death, grief before death, and the orientation of a finite life toward its ending aren’t category errors corrected by the Epicurean argument. They are a person’s registration of their own finitude, performed while they are still alive. The premise and the registration operate at different levels; both are correct.

The denial of death isn’t merely a failure of nerve, but neither does the present evidence license one invariant behavioral profile. Traditions that engage mortality directly—Stoic, Buddhist, Christian *ars moriendi*—don’t free a person from finitude. (Ars moriendi (Latin, “the art of dying”) refers to a genre of Christian devotional texts, popular from the 15th century on, that gave practical and spiritual guidance for facing death well—how to prepare, what temptations to expect at the deathbed, and how to die in a state of grace. It’s cited here as one of several traditions, alongside Stoic and Buddhist practice, that treat facing mortality directly as a discipline to be cultivated rather than a fact to be denied.) They are practices for making one’s relation to finitude explicit; whether and how they improve that relation must be assessed rather than built into the definition.

The grief response is veridical at the level of the surviving model. When someone dies after years of contact with the bereaved, the model the bereaved built across that relationship doesn’t close when the other person’s life closes. The model continues to run, and its outputs register as presence. The phenomenology—that the deceased is somehow still there, that the room still holds them, that they will walk in at any moment—isn’t delusional. It is the model’s continued activity in the absence of its referent (Field and Filanosky 2010) (the religious case is at §5.16.5). Mourning is the gradual reworking of the model’s predictions under the new condition: the referent no longer arrives. Grief is a person recalibrating after a sustained relationship has ended, not weakness or a failure of acceptance.

*Legacy without survival.* This account distinguishes personal survival from the real continuation of a person’s effects. The standard religious posit is that a person persists past death as the same self in a different medium. The identity account defended here rejects that posit because it identifies the person with the organized life whose closure is in view; it doesn’t pretend that biological closure alone proves every rival bearer impossible. The surrounding practices remain intelligible without deciding that dispute: the surviving community holds the deceased in mind, the deceased continues to affect the people they shaped, and mortality orients the life that remains. This continuation is legacy. On the reductionist consequence drawn at §5.7.5, models, works, influence, and altered possibilities are partial preservations of connectedness, real and admitting of degrees. They don’t become this life merely by being causally descended from it. The afterlife also pictured a secured and unconstrained life. How closely a shared structure could approximate that condition within the world, without treating the approximation as personal survival, is a political question (Chapter 6).

Craig’s argument that life without God isn’t merely difficult but *ultimately* meaningless (Craig 2008) is answered most directly on its own ground. The argument responds to something real: a purpose secured only for a finite stretch and then gone can feel, from within the wish for permanence, indistinguishable from no purpose at all. But a controlled version of Craig’s own comparison shows where that feeling actually originates. Hold theism fixed—God exists, creates the subject, and assigns the subject a purpose—and vary only whether the subject’s own continuation ends at ordinary death or persists into the promised afterlife. If a divine ground were what secured *ultimate* significance, the two lives should come out equal: both are created, purposed, and valued by the same God on the same terms.
