They don’t come out equal on the intuition the argument itself trades on; the annihilated life reads as the lesser one, God and purpose held fixed. What the variation isolates is that the intuitive loss tracks the subject’s own continuation, not the presence of a designer—the same variable identified here as the structural anchor of mortality-registration, independent of any theistic gloss. A parallel case confirms the isolation from the other side: what it would mean to a subject, theist or not, that it isn’t presently suffering some catastrophic and final loss tracks what that subject stands to keep or lose, not whether a designer named the stakes. One reply relocates the claim rather than defending it: that a permanent God could go on loving and remembering a subject whose own life has closed, so that the subject’s meaning is secured in God’s continuing regard rather than in the subject’s own continuation. But regard for someone has never required that the person still exist to receive it—the bereaved go on loving those who have died, and a person can go on cherishing a period of a life without any expectation of returning to it—so a continuing regard held on one side of a relation doesn’t restore the *other* side’s continuation. Either the regard does no more work than any love for something finite and complete already does, in which case the *ultimate* claim has become the ordinary one this account already recovers, or it is asked to stand in for the very afterlife the variation removed, in which case nothing has been isolated that wasn’t already on the table. Run this way, Craig’s argument tracks the wish for permanence rather than a dependency on a divine source—the same diagnosis developed throughout, reached this time by testing the theist’s own comparison rather than assuming the structural account from the outset.

Cosmological recurrence doesn’t restore what closes. The §4.6 strict claim is that a stable zero-extension terminus is foreclosed. On a named premise, it adds that the hot, dense phase returns without end (§4.6.5). Even granting full cyclic recurrence of macro-conditions, the result doesn’t entail that any particular person is restored across cycles. The cycle returns the conditions under which life and consciousness can arise. It doesn’t restore the particular consciousnesses the previous cycle hosted. What recurs is the occasion for life and consciousness, not the specific lives and consciousnesses the medium hosted last time. A reader who hoped the account would underwrite a Nietzschean eternal recurrence of the same self is reading more than even the argued return permits.

The orientation toward death shapes what the deep first-person perspective can do. A person who registers their own finitude accurately can prioritize what bears on the time they have: what the contemplative traditions called wisdom and the existentialists called authenticity. A person who suppresses the registration spends their time on the structures the suppression generates. The account developed here doesn’t prescribe one orientation over the other. It identifies what each does. Traditions that engage mortality directly take up the work finitude makes available. What follows from that engineering—the kind of orientation it produces, the kind of art and spirituality it makes available—belongs to art (§5.15) and spirituality (§5.16).

Mortality, read this way, is a condition of the finite organized life under examination; awareness of mortality is a further capacity that can reorganize a person’s field once it appears.

## 5.10 Meaning

Meaning is the sense that what you are doing matters and points somewhere: that some things are worth pursuing, some worth protecting, and some worth avoiding. It is close to knowledge but does a different job: knowledge tracks whether your picture of the world is *accurate*, while meaning tracks where that picture is *heading* and what the heading costs you. Meaning isn’t stamped onto life from outside, by a command or a cosmic decree; it is what a creature registers from the inside once it is deep enough to notice the direction of its own life. The heaviest meanings are the ones you can’t give up without ceasing to be who you are. What stays open is the particular content (which projects and which people carry the weight) even after any external source is set aside.

**[Identification]**

**Meaning** · *Identification*

At its minimal first-person level, meaning is a subject’s field *weighted* as worth pursuing, protecting, or avoiding: which branches matter and what their loss would cost. Intersubjective meaning adds a different relation—the ways projects, practices, signs, and lives acquire significance among subjects across time. Where knowledge concerns accuracy, meaning concerns significance and direction.

*Status: Drive supplies weighting, and a held field supplies something that can be weighted. That combination makes significance-to-a-subject available; it does not strictly derive every richer sense of “meaning,” prove that every inquiry is existentially meaningful, or determine which ends deserve pursuit. The proposed identification of lived meaning with weighted orientation is defended by fit. Its intersubjective forms require the relations developed later rather than being smuggled into the first-person result.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2) and Knowledge (§5.4)

To ask whether anything means anything normally weights the inquiry: the answer is treated as worth having. That modest catch establishes concern for the question in the episode; it doesn’t refute global nihilism or show that the person’s life has meaning in every disputed sense. A nihilist may value accuracy, refusal, or intellectual honesty while denying cosmic purpose. Likewise, the care with which someone avoids overclaiming is a weighted discipline without becoming, by that fact alone, an answer to the meaning of life. What can’t be denied while inquiry is actually under way is the local structure of concern: this answer, method, or refusal matters to this inquirer then. Which further projects matter, to whom, and why remain open.

**[Corollary]**

**Inquiry Carries Local Weight** · *Corollary*

Where a subject sustains an inquiry as an inquiry, some answer, method, clarification, or warranted refusal is treated as worth the attention the episode gives it. The inquiry therefore instantiates local weighting even when its conclusion is that life has no cosmic purpose or that no answer is presently available.

This establishes episode-relative concern only. It does not show that every compelled response is meaningful to the respondent, that an entire life has meaning, that the inquiry’s object exists, or that what the subject weights ought to be weighted by anyone else.

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2) and Representational Minimum (§5.4)

Two nearby registers must not be collapsed into this one. That the words mean is Language’s catch (§5.12): transfer across an interval. That the asking *matters* is this register: the same interval, now with stake. Wanting to understand and to be understood is the crossing, weighted. Reciprocal sexuality is the same operation on an embodied interval: two fields weighting one encounter as worth sharing, opened by registering another subject as a distinct occupant (§5.8). Meaning doesn’t absorb those registers. It is what they are when the field isn’t merely mapped or crossed but cared about.

Two levels should remain separate. *Significance-to-a-subject* is first-personal: the subject registers an orientation, cost, attachment, or stake. *Intersubjectively constituted meaning* is relational: projects, practices, signs, and lives matter within patterns held among subjects across time. The first doesn’t require that every stake be socially authored; the second can’t be reduced to one person’s private weighting. The proposal is that the two are connected without being identical: weighted subjects generate, inherit, contest, and sustain meanings together.

The modal results about Change (§2.2–§2.3) supply actual change and available alternatives; they don’t supply significance. A self complex enough to represent its own direction can weight some transitions differently from others. What §4.8 called self-maintaining direction becomes, on this proposal, significance only when it is registered as mattering to a subject. The transition from objective modal structure to meaning therefore runs through Drive and a subject’s representation, not directly from ◇C.

The relation between knowledge and orientation (§5.4) clarifies the contrast without deriving one register from the other. Knowledge concerns whether a representation fits; meaning concerns what directions and objects matter to the being that holds it. A self-modeling being can possess accurate representations without reflecting on the direction of its life, and it can find something significant while misunderstanding it. The proposed connection is that a sufficiently integrated model lets stakes be organized across time, not that knowledge automatically becomes meaning.

Meaning’s content and minimal structure are distinct. The content—what a being values, which projects it weights, which others it seeks relation with—is contingent and revisable. The minimal structure proposed here is weighting within a represented field: some branches carry stake for this subject. At greater depth, a care can organize the will so strongly that surrendering it would alter who the person is; Frankfurt’s (1988) “volitional necessity” names that strong case, not every instance of meaning. Knowledge can improve the map; reasoning (§5.6) can navigate it; meaning weights it. This doesn’t make every weighting motivating enough to act, or every meaning intersubjectively valid. It identifies the first-person difference between a possibility-space one can merely describe and one in which something is at stake, while leaving the relational constitution of shared meaning as an additional layer.

Identifying meaning as the field weighted raises a question the result doesn’t by itself answer: whether a weighting can be *wrong*. The answer has to be careful in both directions, because ends aren’t ranked here, and no pretense is made otherwise.

**[Corollary]**

**Derivative Corrigibility of Meaning** · *Corollary*

A weighting is not true or false in the way a mapping is. That some branch matters to a subject is not a misrepresentation of the modal structure, and nothing here supplies a standard by which one end is the right end.

Weightings are nonetheless defective in two ways, and neither requires ranking ends.

1. *A false dependency.* If a weighting treats one thing as required for another, it inherits the defect of that requirement when the dependency does not hold.

2. *A line that is not there.* If a weighting reaches toward a line the structure cannot admit, or toward a possible object that the world does not contain, its felt force does not supply the missing object.

The upshot is a criticism that can be made here and a criticism that cannot. One can show that a life is organized around a requirement that does not hold, or oriented toward a line that is not there. It cannot show that what the life was reaching for was not worth reaching for.

**Depends on:** Meaning (§5.10) and Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5)

The second limb needs a restriction, or it will be read as concluding more than it does. That a weighting is empty follows only where the line it reaches toward is genuinely not something R can admit, and the argument establishes preclusion for specific candidates under specific sets rather than for whatever a subject might mean by its object (§11.10; the scope limits are priced at §11.1). More importantly, emptiness attaches to the line *under the description the subject holds it by*, and a weighting can track a real branch under a failed description. What such a life reaches through—the continuity, the awe, the moral seriousness, the belonging—isn’t thereby empty, and those are recovered on structural terms rather than dismissed (§5.16). So the finding isn’t that such a life was wasted. It is that some of what it took itself to be reaching for wasn’t there to reach, while much of what it was actually reaching through was.

The clearest cases of the second limb have nothing to do with religion, and stating one first keeps the limb from being mistaken for a claim about it. A life organized around demonstrating that the earth is flat is weighted toward something not there. The orientation is real, the attention is sustained, the community is genuine, and the meaning is felt exactly as meaning is felt by anyone; what is missing is the object. That is the general shape, and it covers any life built around a claim that doesn’t hold—a conspiracy, a vindication that won’t arrive, a reconciliation with someone who was never going to offer it.

One variant of the first limb has a collective rather than an individual scale. A weighting can attach to something real and reachable while the *consequence* attributed to it is false—the mirror of the requirement case, not *X is necessary for Y* but *Y will follow from X*. How the two differ under action is fixed at §5.14: consequence claims generate their own disconfirming evidence and are in principle self-limiting, where requirement claims don’t and are self-sealing. Where the weighting is held by a population and its object is a shared arrangement, the correction is available in principle and slow enough in practice to matter, which is a political condition rather than a feature of meaning as such; it’s taken up at §6.4.

The religious case is an instance of that shape rather than its subject, and it is worth working through only because it shows the phenomenon must be conceded by everyone. Where two traditions make incompatible claims about what there is, at most one is right, and each already holds of the other exactly what the limb states: that an enormous population orients a life toward something not there while experiencing the orientation as fully meaningful. The Christian says it of the Muslim and the Muslim of the Christian, with equal force and on the same evidence. Nor can the point be contained by retreating to what the two share, since the disagreement doesn’t stop at the boundary of theism: non-theistic worldviews weight meaning in directions incompatible with theistic ones, and the incompatibility runs in every direction across the whole set. Whatever is the case, some very large population is oriented as the limb describes. Nothing in the structural account is needed to generate that verdict; every party has already conceded the phenomenon and merely locates it elsewhere.

Two things follow. The first is that felt meaning isn’t evidence of its object. That is §5.3 at population scale: the readout can’t discriminate its own object’s modal status, so an orientation toward a line R can’t admit presents from inside exactly as an orientation toward a line that is there. The disagreement between traditions isn’t a disagreement about whether the experience is genuine, and treating the experience as its own credential is a move none of them can afford, since it certifies their rivals equally.

The second is that the framework is one more entry in this structure and not an exception to it. It holds weightings of its own, and they are corrigible on both limbs like anyone’s; showing that a rival orientation runs toward an empty line is a result about that line, never a credential for the position that showed it. The inclusivist reading, on which rival traditions track one reality under different descriptions, isn’t excluded here either—that is the failed-description case already considered, and where it holds the weighting isn’t empty at all.

The distinction matters most where the two are easiest to confuse. A subject whose orientation runs through a false requirement isn’t mistaken about what they care about; they are mistaken about what caring about it demands of them. That’s why the correction, when it lands, doesn’t feel like being told one’s ends were wrong—it feels like being given back a range of ways to pursue them.

A life that treats labor as the whole field is the same shape. If continuation, or remaining free, is held to require this job, these hours, this term, when R admits other lines and they are reachable, the weighting inherits a false dependency: work is taken as necessary for what the floor was supposed to hold open. The correction doesn’t rank rest above contribution. It returns the range (§6.7). That is Derivative Corrigibility spent on a field collapsed to one branch, not a right to leisure.

It also explains why such errors persist. Complying with a supposed requirement may never test whether the requirement held, since only a route not taken would have supplied the contrast. A manufactured purpose can therefore become self-sealing in the same way as a manufactured impossibility. Where another agent installs the false dependency, the epistemic point established here is that a life can be directed through a false modal claim without any simple falsehood about an occurrent fact. When doing so constitutes wronging is a moral question (§5.14), and that verdict isn’t a premise of the present result.

*A note on scope.* This result (meaning as orientation registered from inside) is offered as a structural account of what meaning is, not as a strict derivation from the proof of Chapters 1–2. The proof establishes the necessary structure; the structural half is a conditional consequence of Cartesian Certainty via Modal Pressure and Life. That this interior just is meaning remains a functional proposal defended by fit, in the sense flagged at the head of Chapter 5. A reader can grant the proof and still take the first-person perspective of orientation differently without putting anything earlier at risk; what the naming lives or dies by is its own fit to the phenomenon.

### 5.10.1 The Dispute
The literature asks at least three questions: what makes a life meaningful, what makes a project matter, and what significance itself consists in. Its traditions often work past one another. Existentialism, nihilism, absurdism, and hermeneutics form the continental meaning-of-life literature; Wolf and Metz mark the contemporary analytic field. What follows stays metaphysical: the structure of orientation, not a phenomenological reduction. The standing positions are addressed individually.

*Theistic prescriptive accounts.* A long tradition holds that meaning is conferred on a life by its relation to a divine source (Augustine, Aquinas, contemporary defenders Craig 2008; Swinburne 2004; Cottingham 2003): the meaning of a life is what God commands, decrees, or designs it for. The position has the explanatory virtue of making meaning robustly objective; it has the structural difficulty that, with the inversion (Chapters 10–11) foreclosing the supernatural source, the architecture loses its anchor. The theistic tradition, so read, correctly identifies that meaning carries genuine weight—the gravity is real—while locating the source incorrectly: the gravity comes from the depth of the subject registering its own direction, not from an external authority commanding it.

*Existentialist constructivism.* Sartre ((1943) 1956; 1946), de Beauvoir (1947), and the existentialist tradition more broadly hold that meaning is constructed by the self through its projects, with no external ground supplying content. The position has the structural virtue of locating meaning in the activity of the self-modeling subject; it has the difficulty that, taken to its limit, it makes meaning purely contingent on what the self happens to project, with no constraint on the projecting. Existentialism, on this account, correctly identifies that the *content* of meaning isn’t given to the subject from outside, while missing the structural fact it understates: the orientation having direction at all isn’t constructed; what is constructed is which directions get pursued.

*Nihilism and absurdism.* Nietzsche’s (1882; (1886) 2002) diagnosis of nihilism, Camus’s (1942) absurdism, and Nagel’s (1971) argument about the absurdity of human life share the claim that, once external grounds for meaning are withdrawn, the meaning the tradition supplied is gone. The positions differ on what follows—Camus’s revolt, Nagel’s irony, Nietzsche’s transvaluation—but converge on the diagnosis. They correctly identify that the *content-as-given* is gone once the inversion forecloses the supernatural source, but they miss a structural fact: what survives the withdrawal isn’t nothing but the subject still oriented, still registering direction, with the structural fact intact and the contingent content open.

*Hybrid and objectivist-naturalist accounts.* Susan Wolf (1997; 2010) developed a hybrid account on which meaning requires both subjective engagement and objective worth—“meaning is loving the right things,” or in Wolf’s more precise formulation, *fitting fulfillment*: the subjective engagement must meet a genuine standard of worth independent of the feeling. Wolf’s hybrid picks up something real—meaning has both a subjective registration component and an objective fit-to-structure component—and the structural account supplies a further reading: subjective engagement is the first-person perspective on orientation; what Wolf calls objective worth divides into separate questions of accuracy, relational sustainability, and moral standing. That division isn’t Wolf’s irreducibly normative criterion, and the disagreement is staged at §5.10.5 rather than resolved by absorbing one account into the other. Metz (2013) surveys and refines the contemporary analytic field, cataloging accounts from fundamentality-based to supernaturalist to naturalist; the structural account sits within the naturalist-objective wing and inherits its dispute with both purely subjective and purely prescriptive alternatives.

*Volitional and caring accounts.* Frankfurt (1988; 2004) asks not which objects are worth attending to but what it means for a subject to *care* about something at all. A subject that cares about a person or project isn’t simply one that has judged those things to be worth caring about; it is one whose will has organized itself around them—invested in their continuation in a way that isn’t freely revisable from moment to moment, because the investment has become part of what the will is. Meaning accrues, on Frankfurt’s account, to the exercises of volitional caring; the subject’s own caring is what gives weight to what it cares about, not the independent worth of the objects. Frankfurt, on this account, identifies a necessary registration condition the structural account honors: what registers as meaning heaviest to a given subject isn’t the set of objectively maximally coherent directions but the set the subject has formed itself around, the weights it can’t give up without ceasing to be who it is. Frankfurt’s volitional account and the structural account are climbing the same structure on different sides; the convergence is made explicit at §5.10.3.

*Narrative-identity and hermeneutic accounts.* MacIntyre (1981), Taylor (1989), and Ricoeur (1990) developed accounts on which meaning is structured by the narrative the self constructs of its life—the story that makes its sequence intelligible as a unified life. Gadamer’s hermeneutics (1960) is the same line under another name: a life made intelligible by interpretation, as a text is. The position has been influential across philosophy, psychology (McAdams 1993), and theology. Narrative and hermeneutic accounts, so read, pick up the self-modeling structure of meaning at the depth where a person holds themselves as a temporally extended subject, with the narrative being one form the orientation takes when a mind is deep enough to register a life as a whole.

*Pragmatist accounts.* James, Dewey, and the pragmatist tradition treat meaning as what a life can use: significance as successful orientation rather than a property of objects. The tradition is right that meaning isn’t a spectator’s extra. What it understates is the structural fact of weighting a field at all, which is already running before any success is scored.

*Naturalist deflationary accounts.* A position from Hume forward (and developed in contemporary form by Joyce 2006; Garner 1994; Hinckfuss 1987) holds that meaning is a kind of projection—a feature the mind imposes on neutral facts and then mistakenly takes to be a property of the facts themselves. The deflationary tradition, on this reading, correctly identifies that meaning isn’t a mind-independent property of objects, while underspecifying what meaning *is* on its own account: the first-person perspective of a self-modeling subject registering its own direction isn’t a projection onto neutral content but a constitutive feature of what the subject’s activity consists in.

*Anti-natalism and the meaning of bringing new lives into existence.* Benatar (2006) and the anti-natalist tradition raise specific meaning-related questions about whether new subjects should be brought into existence and what meaning their lives could have. The position interacts with meaning theory and with the ethics of reproduction (§5.8). The anti-natalist tradition, on this account, raises a real question about consent and harm, without foreclosing the structural fact that a subject brought into existence registers direction and meaning at the depth its own mapping supports.

*Meaning across species and across substrates.* A growing literature investigates whether non-human animals have meaningful lives, what their meaning would consist in, and whether artificial systems could have meaning in the relevant sense. The depth-gradient reading developed here supplies a usable framework: meaning runs wherever the self-modeling subject can register its own direction, with the depth required for human-style meaning available only at a depth sufficient to model a life as a whole.

### 5.10.2 The Requirement
*First-person perspective on orientation.* Meaning is the internal registration of orientation: the recognition, by a being that can take its own life as an object of thought, that what it is doing reaches forward through a world that doesn’t end with it. Meaning belongs in the subjective character of orientation, not as an external property of objects or projects; it is part of what such a being’s activity consists in, with registering direction as the activity meaning *is*.

*Structural fact distinct from content.* Meaning’s content and meaning’s basic form are distinct. The content is what a being is oriented toward; the form is that there is direction at all, felt from inside, with weight. Collapsing one into the other loses the distinction that matters: the *that* of orientation arises once a life can reflect on itself, and so isn’t contingent on any particular object of orientation, while the *what* is supplied by a person’s history, situation, and projects.

*Connection to consciousness and self-representation.* Once consciousness has been identified (§5.1) as the inner aspect of a system representing itself (§4.8), meaning can be read as the next register: what consciousness is when it registers its own direction within the world. Meaning isn’t a separate domain grafted onto consciousness; it sits at the depth where a mind has folded back far enough to register its own direction as direction.

*Connection to knowledge.* Accuracy-tracking (knowledge, §5.4) and direction-tracking (meaning) need to stay distinguished even as their relation is explained: meaning operates on the same model knowledge stabilizes, the two registers picking up different structural features of the same orientation.

*Connection to drive.* Meaning operates on what drive (§5.2) supplies as forward pressure. Drive is the baseline forward pressure pre-differentiation; meaning is the registration of where that pressure is heading once a mind is deep enough to register direction. Meaning isn’t autonomous from motivation; it has to be connected to drive, at the depth where the registering becomes possible.

*Robustness to the withdrawal of supernatural anchors.* The inversion (Chapters 10–11) forecloses the supernatural anchors theistic accounts of meaning have relied on. Meaning has to survive the withdrawal of those anchors rather than collapsing into nihilism, which means locating its source in features of the subject and the medium that need no supernatural supplementation: a mind at sufficient depth, registering direction within the structure it is part of.

*Non-arbitrariness within the account.* While meaning’s content is contingent, not all directions fit equally well. Some projects cohere better than others with a person’s bodily needs, social situation, and real possibilities. This has to be explained without treating all projects as equally meaningful or imposing a single mandatory project on everyone.

*Distinctness from happiness and moral worth.* Wolf’s (2010) central contribution is the identification of meaning as a third evaluative dimension—not reducible to happiness (the condition of feeling good) or to moral worth (the condition of doing right)—that has its own structure and its own demands. This distinctness has to survive rather than collapsing meaning into either of the other two dimensions: orientation-at-depth constitutes a register neither identical to valenced-feeling (§5.3) nor to the reciprocal-coupling norm (§5.14), even though all three draw on the same modal field.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Meaning at the level of registering one’s life as a whole requires the self-aware depth named at §5.1. Shallower forms of direction-registering run at shallower depths—the cricket oriented toward water, the elephant oriented toward its herd, the chimpanzee oriented toward its current task. The gradient has to be accommodated rather than restricting meaning to the human case: what runs at each depth needs distinguishing, along with the threshold at which life-as-a-whole meaning becomes available.

*Coherence with mortality.* Meaning belongs to a life that will end, and this finitude has to be accommodated rather than treating meaning as if a person were immortal. Its weight, urgency, and directedness arise from a life that can understand its own limits.

They aren’t neutral requirements accepted across theories of meaning. Whether meaning is grounded in self-modeling, how it relates to moral worth and happiness, and whether non-human or non-biological systems have meaningful lives remain contested. The case is made for this set rather than treating it as settled.

### 5.10.3 Predictions
If Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality are the necessary conditions of any possible medium (Chapters 1–2), and if self-modeling is constitutive of persistence at sufficient integration (§4.8), then any self-modeling person must orient itself within the medium they navigate. Orientation isn’t optional for someone whose persistence consists in modeling their own position. To model one’s position is, already, to be oriented—to track not only where one is but what one is moving toward, what one is moving away from, and what exchanges one participates in across the manifold. The phenomenological tradition named this structure under different vocabularies (Heidegger (1927) 1962; Merleau-Ponty 1945): being-toward, embodied intentionality, the tacit directedness of a body already in its world. The modal argument here locates the same phenomenon inside the self-modeling function self-persistence requires.

Integrated self-modeling, on this proposal, can support an experience or registration of direction within a medium. Whether every integrated self-model has a phenomenological aspect, and whether orientation has the three components the account identifies, are substantive philosophical claims rather than empirical necessities. Spatial distinction, continuity over time, and temporal ordering are structural features the model uses to explain orientation; the model doesn’t establish that they yield the same kind of meaning in every possible system.

It doesn’t follow that every self-modeling person will find the same things meaningful. The proposal is that some self-modeling persons register their causal reach and commitments as direction and significance. This shouldn’t be read as an established claim that self-modeling always entails phenomenological stakes or that no self-modeling person can experience a lack of meaning.

What is at stake isn’t abstract. Self-modeling exists in the first place because it supports persistence (§4.8): selves whose models track what sustains them continue, and selves whose models misdirect don’t. Meaning is therefore not a free-floating registration of any direction whatever. It is the internal aspect of the orientation that bears on a person’s continued existence and on the continued existence of the exchanges they participate in. Directions that extend their causal reach and their integration with the surrounding medium tend to register as meaningful because they are, constitutively, what persistence at this level *consists in*. Directions that corrode reach or sever integration tend to register as meaningless, or worse, because they erode the conditions under which the person is there to register anything. Meaning tracks survivability—not as a prudential calculation added to the orientation, but because persistence is the condition the orientation arises under. The modal framework predicts the presence of orientation, not its content: a self-modeling person orients, and characteristically registers some direction as mattering, but which direction (which persons, practices, places) remains a function of where they stand in the medium, not of the framework. The content belongs to the life lived; the structural account is silent on the particulars by design. The link to §5.14 is direct: the conatus (Spinoza (1677) 1996, III) that grounds morality is the same persistence-pressure that grounds meaning, registered from inside the self whose persistence it is. The link to the theist is the same pressure, pushed to its limit: the afterlife is Drive’s attraction-pole refusing a last state, subsistence weighted as unbounded (§5.16). That weighting is already registered. It isn’t a second purpose imported from outside.

*Tracks* survivability isn’t *reduces to* survivability, and the distinction carries real weight. Survival, on this account, is the condition under which a subject is present to register anything at all; meaning is one of three things that registration can track, not a relabeling of fitness. A subject can persist robustly and find little meaningful; it can find much meaningful while its well-being suffers—the gripped life that costs the one living it; it can orient toward what sustains others at cost to its own persistence, the parent-sacrifice case (§5.2). Meaning, well-being, and moral orientation are three registrations a self-modeling subject runs on its own direction, and survival is the shared precondition of all three rather than the content of any one. The survivability framing names why the capacity for meaning was selected—subjects that register direction toward what sustains them persist—without claiming that what any particular subject finds meaningful reduces to what keeps it alive.

*Ground and Content.* Meaning has two components, kept separate throughout.

The ground is constitutive. It is the set of necessary conditions under which anyone can reach toward anything at all. Without the three Conditions, there is no relational interval to reach across, no persistent self to do the reaching, and no unfolding through which the reach can extend. These aren’t features meaning happens to have. They are what meaningful orientation *consists in*. The ground is therefore not optional, not invented, and not contingent on any particular person’s attitudes. It is what the medium already provides.

The content is contingent. Which direction a given person’s causal reach most fully expresses (what they find meaningful, which exchanges they are particularly positioned to extend) depends on who they are, where they are placed, and what the medium around them permits. Meaning isn’t the same for every person because no two people occupy the same position in the manifold. The content is shaped by history, body, culture, and circumstance. It isn’t given from outside.

Three categories of content recur across nearly every human life, and it is no accident which three. Relationships extend a person’s reach into other people—the exchanges that most directly sustain survival in a social species and that most directly give survival its texture. Within the relationships category a further normative register operates that the structural account marks rather than absorbs: what a person owes their particular others (this child, this friend, this partner) isn’t fully captured by the connection constant the structural account supplies. The partiality of that owed concern isn’t a defect to be corrected against a universalist baseline; it is the proper shape of moral weight along the actual depth of commitment (Frankfurt 2004, cf. §5.14).

Work extends that reach into the surrounding medium—the material, institutional, and conceptual environment they shape and are shaped by. Hobbies extend the reach along directions they have chosen for their own sake, where the alignment between who they are and what they are doing is unusually tight. Each category is meaningful for the same double reason. Each supports survival: relationships supply the cooperative fabric a social species is evolved to depend on, work supplies material resources and standing within the medium, hobbies maintain the cognitive and affective integration a complex organism requires. And each supplies what bare survival alone can’t: the experience of survival as worth sustaining. A person who persists without anyone to persist with, without anything to do, and without anything they do for their own sake still meets the minimum conditions of biological continuance; but they don’t tend to continue well or long. Surviving and enjoying surviving aren’t two separate goods stacked on top of each other. Enjoyment is itself a constitutive feature of robust persistence—the internal aspect of a life whose orientations are integrated rather than strained, reaching rather than retracting, extending rather than enduring. The eudaimonic tradition identifies this directly (Aristotle NE I.7, Ryff 1989; Ryff and Singer 2008): flourishing isn’t a second good added on top of survival, it is the form survival takes when it is going well. The people who most fully find meaning in relationships, work, and hobbies are those whose persistence those exchanges most fully constitute.

Beneath the three categories is a single underlying constant: connection. Relationships are connection with other selves. Work is connection with the surrounding medium through productive exchange. Hobbies are connection with a domain, a practice, a tradition, or a material someone returns to for its own sake. The purpose self-modeling persons characteristically seek (the direction that, when found, registers as meaning most unmistakably) is connection. This isn’t a separate claim added to the modal account; it is what the modal account leads one to expect once the role of Space is taken seriously. Spatiality is the relational interval across which selves stand; connection is what happens across that interval without collapsing it. A person who has reach but no connection is extending into a void; a person whose connection has collapsed the interval is connecting to nothing other than themselves, which isn’t connection. Meaning consists in the middle case: a reach that lands on something genuinely other and holds the interval open while it does. The three categories are the three main kinds of landing humans are structured to seek. Searching for meaning and searching for connection are the same activity described two ways.

The relationships category carries a feature the other two don’t, and it is worth naming as such rather than folding into connection-in-general. What a person finds in another subject, at sufficient depth, isn’t only an interval reached across but a direction they come to care about for its own sake—and the caring, once formed, isn’t held at will. Frankfurt (1988; 2004) named this the structure of love: to love is to be bound by reasons that are reasons *because* one loves, not to love because one judged the reasons sufficient. Wolf’s “loving the right things” sits at the same juncture from the evaluative side. In the structural vocabulary, this is analogous to the mutual-holding pattern Modal Convergence (§5.4) formalizes at the knowledge register, now at the relational register of love (the subjects the field can’t release without dissolving) and registered from inside as the special weight of the persons whose loss would cost the subject part of what it is. Reasons of love aren’t a separate faculty; they are what the weighting operation becomes when its heaviest weights land on other subjects. The relationship is meaningful not merely because it connects, but because the connection has become load-bearing for the identity of the one who holds it.

Two further threads bear on meaning. First, the cross-generational reach of meaning (directions a subject orients toward that bear on persons not yet in existence) raises Parfit’s non-identity problem (1984): the persons our present orientations affect are, in part, persons whose very existence those orientations determine, so the meaning of reaching toward them can’t be cashed out as benefit to antecedently fixed individuals. Its institutional form is taken up at §6.5, and what remains open is recorded at §6.14. Second, and more delicate: identity was taken at §5.7 to be constructed rather than substantial, and Parfit’s argument that identity isn’t what matters (that what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can hold without strict identity) sits naturally with that reading. Meaning travels with the continuity of the self-modeling subject, not with a fact of identity over and above it: what a subject finds meaningful is carried forward by whatever continues its psychological organization, whether or not that continuant is “the same person” in any further sense.

The distinction dissolves a long-running false dichotomy. Meaning is neither invented wholesale by a sovereign self imposing value onto a neutral universe, nor prescribed in advance by a designer inscribing purpose from outside. Both pictures miss the structure. The ground is found, because it was always already structurally available. The content is one’s own, because each person reaches from their own position. The ground isn’t robbed of authenticity by being found; the content isn’t fabricated by being authored.

### 5.10.4 Confirmation
Research on meaning-in-life provides several findings and theoretical proposals relevant to the structural account, but it doesn’t converge on a single account of meaning. Philosophical accounts remain divided. Wolf’s (2010) ‘fitting fulfillment’ view holds that meaningful lives involve active engagement with projects of genuine worth; Metz’s (2013) ‘fundamentality’ account emphasizes orientation toward what is comparatively fundamental. These accounts share some broad themes of engagement and value while disagreeing about their ground. The structural account offers another interpretation of those themes; empirical or philosophical overlap doesn’t by itself confirm its structural model or settle whether meaning is an irreducible third evaluative dimension.

Empirical psychology bears on the shape from a different angle. Baumeister and colleagues (2013) find that meaning, distinct from happiness, tracks integration across time, connection to others, and orientation toward projects larger than the self—the three coordinates the structural account names, and features evolutionary psychology has also linked to persistence and reproductive fitness in social organisms (Tooby and Cosmides 1990; Buss 2019). On this account, meaning and survival correlate because they share a structural ground—the persistence of a self-modeling subject whose continuation depends on integrated orientation toward what sustains it. This doesn’t reduce meaning to reproductive fitness: the persistence at issue is the persistence of the subject’s exchanges with its medium, not narrowly its gene-propagation, and the empirical correlations track the broader structural fact rather than the narrower evolutionary one. Reproductive success is one specific subset of the broader persistence-pressure; meaning tracks the broader pressure.

Frankl’s (1946) observations in the Nazi concentration camps make the link vivid. In conditions where starvation, cold, forced labor, arbitrary violence, and systematic dehumanization had collapsed every other component of wellbeing, meaning persisted wherever orientation persisted, and Frankl reports that those who kept a future to live toward were likelier to endure. On this account the association isn’t accidental. Meaning is the internal aspect of the orientation that sustains a person against what threatens them: a model of a future that hasn’t yet arrived, a relational interval between the self and what the self reaches toward, and a substrate that continues under conditions designed to erode it. Meaning tracked the three Conditions (the three structural roles derived through Modal Identity and Conditions-as-Nature, §2.6–2.7) before the framework was named, and tracked them in their role as conditions of persistence.

Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan 2000) reaches the same structure through motivational psychology: autonomy (an agent with causal reach), competence (the reach connecting to what matters), and relatedness (a relational interval between self and other). The three basic psychological needs can be read as the three structural conditions of orientation, restated in motivational vocabulary.

Comparative cognition extends the prediction across species. Animals reach toward what sustains them through orientations that involve real relational intervals—mate selection, territory maintenance, bond formation, the long-running attachments documented across mammals, birds, and cephalopods. Meaning in the structural sense obtains wherever a self-modeling subject registers its own reach: the internal registration of one’s direction within the medium. What human meaning adds isn’t the registration but the depth at which the registration takes itself as an object: spelling out directions, naming projects, transmitting purposes across generations through language and culture. Birds returning to last season’s nest and humans returning to a vocation are running the same operation at different depths.

These literatures offer partial points of contact with the structural account, but their methods, constructs, and normative commitments differ. Their overlap is suggestive background for the model rather than confirmation that the structural argument predicts the settled shape of meaning.

### 5.10.5 Conclusions
*Constructivism*—the view that meaning is imposed by sovereign subjects onto a universe indifferent to value (Sartre 1946)—rests on the insistence that without some imposing subject, no meaning would obtain anywhere; meaning is the kind of thing that exists only where someone meant something, and any account that locates it elsewhere either smuggles in a subject under another name or equivocates on what *meaning* is. The structural account shares that much: meaning requires a self-modeling subject to register direction, and no meaning lives in the medium prior to the subjects that hold it. Where constructivism then misidentifies the locus of meaning is in the imposition image itself. Any imposition presupposes a ground on which it lands. No one can impose direction onto a medium that lacks the conditions for direction, any more than a hand can press onto a surface that lacks extension. The structural ground isn’t optional for the constructivist either. What constructivism correctly identifies is the contingency of content. What it mistakes is the necessity of the conditions under which any content can be meant at all.

*Theistic prescription* is the view that meaning requires a transcendent lawgiver to inscribe purpose from outside (Craig 2008; Swinburne 2004). It rests partly on the experienced weight of moral and meaningful demands: some commitments don’t feel withdrawable at will. A voluntarist picture on which the subject simply chooses what matters struggles to capture that phenomenology. That constraint is preserved here without pretending to have derived normativity from modal structure: a subject inherits biological stakes, relationships, histories, and commitments it didn’t individually author, and these can organize the will from inside. Whether a transcendent source additionally grounds them is a rival-account question. The structural proposal shows that external prescription isn’t required to explain why meaning can exceed present preference; it doesn’t establish, merely from the three Conditions, that every further theological ontology is false.

The same point explains how religion produces genuine meaning while getting its metaphysics wrong. Religious communities connect people to each other across real relational intervals and orient them toward shared outcomes sustained through time—the structural conditions of meaning, met whether or not the outcome exists as named. A congregation oriented toward a heaven that isn’t real still connects: to each other, across the interval the community holds open; to a direction that organizes collective life across time; to a tradition whose persistence exceeds any single member. The meaning isn’t imaginary; the connection is actual. The terminus of the shared reach is imaginary; the reach itself isn’t. Religion has been one of the most effective meaning-producing technologies humans have built (Durkheim 1912; Geertz 1973; Atran 2002), and the modal account inherits the phenomenon without inheriting the ontology. What the tradition’s metaphysics located beyond Nature wasn’t where it claimed to be; what the gathering itself produced—connection across the relational interval, shared orientation across time, communities held open by what they reached toward—was real all along.

One heuristic sharpens the contrast. Meaning under theistic prescription works like a paint-by-numbers kit: the subject traces a fixed scheme whose authority is pre-supplied; the picture is right when it matches the template. Meaning under the structural account is more like the open studio where the curriculum has been genuinely absorbed—the medium, tools, tradition, and the constraint that some marks are technically incoherent are all real—but what gets made within them is authentically the maker’s own. The studio version isn’t emptier than the kit. The constraints are found, not invented; the expression is genuinely one’s own; the tradition is shared; the conversation with other makers continues across the making. What the kit supplies that the studio doesn’t isn’t richer meaning but fewer choices—and the fewer choices, not the meaning, is what its adherents sometimes mourn when they leave.

The concession is mortality. Religion didn’t only host meaning; it hosted meaning eternalized—security against all contingency, survival without end, a witness that never looks away. The structural account can relocate meaning because the arrangements that secure possibility are real, and the connections they hold open are real. It can’t relocate the fantasy that those arrangements can’t be lost. Meaning returns to the finite world intact but without the guarantee against loss. That isn’t nihilism; it is the mature cost of the relocation. The full burden of that cost is carried at §5.9, because mortality is where the wish for permanence has to be faced directly.

*Nihilism and absurdism* insist that no consolation prize be smuggled in once external prescription is withdrawn. They hold that the universe is silent on the question of meaning, and that the human demand for meaning confronts a neutral or indifferent cosmos (Camus 1942; Nagel 1971). The structural account should accept that discipline. It establishes that living subjects can have stakes and orientations without receiving prescribed content from the universe. It doesn’t thereby answer the nihilist’s stronger question about cosmic or “ultimate” meaning. The activity of asking shows local concern for the answer; it isn’t itself a proof that the universe answers. The disagreement is therefore narrowed rather than declared over: the nihilist may deny external purpose while granting significance-to-subjects, whereas this account argues that the latter is already a real and non-arbitrary phenomenon worth calling meaning.

A fourth position deserves separate treatment—Wolf’s hybrid (1997; 2010), which shares its combination of subjective engagement and objective constraint. Wolf holds that meaningful activity requires subjective engagement with something objectively worth caring about: *fitting fulfillment*. The need for discrimination can be accepted here without pretending that Spatiality or directedness alone supplies an inventory of worthy objects. It instead separates three questions Wolf’s formula joins: does the activity matter to the subject, does it connect accurately and sustainably to its objects and other subjects, and is it morally permissible? The first belongs to meaning in the minimal sense developed here. The second exposes it to factual and modal correction. The third requires the independent moral argument of §5.14.

This separation handles the cases that motivate Wolf without erasing their differences. A life organized around a harmless activity outsiders find trivial can be deeply significant to its subject and community; an external ranking isn’t established merely by disdain. A cohesive cruelty-project can also be meaningful *to its participants* in that first-person and social sense while being false in its representations, destructive in its relations, and morally wrong. Calling it meaningless doesn’t perform the moral argument. The account therefore refuses to use “meaning” as a single all-purpose verdict: significance, accuracy, relational sustainability, and moral standing can come apart.

Worth also needs indexing. The pilot in a cockpit has unusual instrumental importance within that frame because many lives route through the pilot’s functioning. It doesn’t follow that the passenger is worth less as a subject. Positional importance can vary; equal moral standing, if established, belongs to another layer. Drive supplies each subject’s own stake in continuation, but the move from many self-stakes to equal standing is precisely the bridge morality must earn (§5.14). Meaning shouldn’t claim it in advance.

The moral-sainthood observation (Wolf 1982) tightens the disagreement. A perfectly virtuous agent who devotes every moment to morality loses the engaged particularity that makes a life feel meaningful—loses the projects and persons they have *their own* stake in, the directions that carry *their* weight rather than the universal weight of what morality assigns. The observation sits uncomfortably inside Wolf’s own hybrid account—on her view, morality is one of the items of objective worth, so more devotion to it should be better for meaning, not worse. Its reading dissolves the discomfort: morality is what the inter requires of a subject among subjects; meaning is what that subject’s own weighting of its modal field produces. A subject can honor what the inter requires and still have a life that is, in terms of the weighted field, particularly *theirs*. The three evaluative dimensions are distinct: meaning (internal direction-registration), happiness (affective quality of integration), and moral worth (what the inter requires of one subject among others). Wolf’s moral-sainthood observation is the diagnostic that shows why they must be kept that way.

The convergence just traced isn’t an accident of selective reading—though the right way to take it isn’t quite Parfit’s. Parfit (2011) argued that Kantian ethics, contractualism, and consequentialism—traditions that spent the twentieth century in apparent opposition—were each converging, in their most defensible forms, on substantially the same verdicts; and that the agreement was itself evidence about the moral terrain rather than a coincidence of three independent projects happening to err in the same direction. The traditions of meaning don’t agree in that way—they divide over meaning’s very source—and so the pattern here isn’t shared verdicts but shared ground, each holding one face of a single meaning-relation. Existentialism tracked the contingency of content—the fact that what a given person finds meaningful is authored, not received. Theism tracked the genuine weight of meaning—the fact that the mattering doesn’t feel like something the subject could simply revoke. Nihilism tracked the discipline of honest refusal—the fact that no cheap consolation can replace what the withdrawal of external prescription removed. Each built its metaphysics around its own face. The inference is weaker than Parfit’s, but real. What makes it evidence is the common source they all stand on. Before any of the three gets a vote, some things already matter to a being of this kind, because it has conditions to meet; and those conditions are, in the first instance, negative—survival, health, safety, and protection aren’t yet a structure of significance but what a subject registers on the way away from its own dissolution, the aversion identified as structurally prior at §5.2. Meaning is that aversion read forward—on the moral side, “not the absence of pain but the optimum the avoidance points at” (§5.14.3)—the field held maximally open once the floor is secured and the freed drive has somewhere to go (§5.2.5). That three traditions built from incompatible starting points each preserved a distinct genuine component of one relation is what would be unlikely if that relation weren’t real, and what is expected once meaning is read as the forward face of a persisting subject’s aversion to its own dissolution. The same logic is applied to morality at §5.14.

Meaning collected against constructivism, theistic prescription, nihilism, religion, and Wolf’s hybrid is proposed here at two levels: significance registered by a weighted subject, and significance sustained or contested among subjects. The first is neither arbitrary invention nor cosmic inscription; it grows from a life with inherited stakes that can represent its own directions. The second depends on actual relations, practices, and transmissions rather than on private registration alone. Religion tracks the production of durable shared orientation, and Wolf the intuition that subjective grip isn’t the whole story, alongside the three faces already named. This convergence is explanatory evidence for the two-level account, not a derivation or a verdict that every rival metaphysics has been corrected. Language (§5.12) develops one medium through which shared meaning is constituted; it is downstream support, not a premise silently used to prove the first-person result here.

## 5.11 Will
Will is the capacity to select and act through represented alternatives. The proposal here is compatibilist in shape: freedom doesn’t require escape from cause and effect, but it requires more than seeing options. It varies with the field’s breadth and depth, its fidelity to the actual situation, the agent’s identification with the valuation governing the act, and the latitude to enact or refuse the selection. Knowledge, upbringing, education, reflection, treatment, and changes in material or social conditions can alter different parts of that structure; none guarantees freedom by itself.

**[Identification]**

**Will** · *Identification*

Will is a living being’s capacity to select and act through represented alternatives. It draws on what the other registers supply—direction from drive, valence from feeling, a corrigible map from knowledge, comparison from reasoning, weighting from meaning—and is the selection itself, insofar as it issues through the agent’s organized capacities. Freedom (*modal freedom*) is not standing outside causation. On the proposed account it varies along four distinguishable dimensions. **Depth and coverage**: how much of the alternatives and consequences are represented. **Fidelity**: how well that representation matches the situation. **Endorsement or identification**: whether the governing valuation is the agent’s own, rather than merely the strongest passing impulse. **Latitude**: the practical room to enact or refuse the selection.

*Status: Drive plus a represented field makes selection possible but does not strictly derive thick will, freedom, responsibility, or this four-part analysis. The analysis is a compatibilist proposal defended by its treatment of ignorance, deception, compulsion, weakness of will, and coercion. Each dimension is gradable, and gains in one can coexist with losses in another. Chapter 11 application: §11.7.2.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2) and Knowledge (§5.4)

Directedness appears before thick will. A bacterium moving up a gradient, an animal orienting away from threat, and a person trying to hold attention all exhibit regulation toward outcomes, but calling all three “will” would erase the distinctions the section needs. Thick will begins where action is mediated by represented alternatives and organized valuation. Refusal or inaction can be selected, imposed, habitual, or merely what occurs when no selection controls behavior; it isn’t automatically a third-person proof that thin will was exercised. The argument therefore treats Drive as an evolutionary and functional precursor rather than a Cartesian-grade instance of will.

That’s why will belongs here in the cascade: after drive, feeling, knowledge, reasoning, and meaning. A choice is only as free as the modal field (§5.4) through which the agent understands it. Thin will operates on a sparse field, thick will on a dense one, which is why parenting, education, and the cultivated breadth made available through language and art bear directly on the freedom of the resulting agent. Each is, mechanically, the deliberate installation of modal-field content the agent will later select from.

If will is selection among the options a field presents, and that field is a partial, lossy mapping of the one objective modal structure (§5.4), then a willing can fail to reach what it is directed at in three structurally distinct ways, and the difference between them isn’t a matter of degree.

**[Corollary]**

**Three Frustrations of Will** · *Corollary*

1. *R cannot admit the line.* What is willed is not really possible. The frustration is structural and permanent: impossibility does not vary, so no change of circumstance, effort, or arrangement makes the line available.

2. *R can admit the line, but it is not locally reachable.* What is willed is really possible and unavailable from where this being stands. Global standing and local reachability are different relations, and the second varies while the first does not; the frustration is real, contingent, and in principle answerable by a change of position.

3. *R can admit the line, and it is locally reachable, but it is absent from this field.* Nothing outside the being forecloses it. It has not been mapped, so it is not among the options selection is running over. The frustration is a mapping failure rather than a modal one.

What could answer them differs. The first admits no answer that leaves the object as described. The second answers to a change of position or circumstance, sometimes through the agent’s action and sometimes through other agents or institutions. The third answers to a change in representation, which may come through reflection but also through inquiry, education, testimony, treatment, or another person’s disclosure. Will alone guarantees none of these.

**Dependency routes:** all three frustrations—Will (§5.11); impossible-line branch—Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5); unmapped-line branch—Knowledge (§5.4)

That impossibility doesn’t vary is the S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5).

The trichotomy also fixes what freedom-as-depth is for. Depth can’t alter what R can admit, and it doesn’t by itself move a being to a position from which an unreachable line becomes reachable. What it does is close the gap between what is available and what is registered as available, which is the one gap interior work reaches. A life can be constrained by all three at once, and mistaking which is operating is its own failure: treating a structural impossibility as a personal deficiency, or an unmapped option as a closed one, are errors the distinction is meant to prevent.

The collapse Drive names at its limit (§5.2) is this trichotomy plus latitude, felt from inside. *No remaining possibility* is usually the second or third limb: a line out of reach, or admitted by R and reachable but unmapped. *Only the possibility of suffering* is Aversion weighting the branches that remain. *Never free again* is latitude at zero: time, a refuseable exit, room not to take the next term. Depth can’t restore that. Chapter 6 spends mapping and reach as education, subsistence, and care; it spends latitude as time in the floor (§6.7) and as a remaining field after sanction (§6.13).

### 5.11.1 The Dispute
The literature on will is organized around a small number of standing positions, each of which is engaged directly here. The engagement runs on three terms formally specified at §5.11.2—the modal-mapping network (the structure that holds an agent’s live alternatives), modal depth (how far that structure extends), and the modal field it presents—introduced here in their working sense.

*Libertarian free will.* The classical libertarian tradition (Chisholm 1964; van Inwagen 1983; Kane 1996; O'Connor 2000) argues that responsibility requires more than ordinary causal determination, though libertarian theories differ over event-causal indeterminism, agent causation, and sourcehood. The structural account presses a familiar luck objection: insofar as a selection is explained by the agent’s character, reasons, and organized capacities, it is causally continuous with structure; insofar as the outcome is left unexplained by the agent, indeterminacy alone doesn’t add control. Agent-causal theories propose that the agent as substance supplies the missing source. The identity account in §5.7 resists that proposal by identifying the agent with an organized living subject rather than a further substance behind it. This is a conditional incompatibility, not a modal proof that every libertarian act-description is impossible: a libertarian can reject the identity account or offer a richer account of how irreducible agent causation explains control without collapsing into event randomness. The present model’s positive alternative is depth, fidelity, endorsement, and latitude within causal structure.

*Hard determinism and hard incompatibilism.* The hard-determinist tradition (Pereboom 2001; Caruso 2012; Strawson 1994) holds that because every act is caused by prior conditions the agent didn’t author, no one is ever ultimately morally responsible for what they do. No agent authors itself from nothing—the structural account grants that much freely—but the inference that responsibility therefore disappears doesn’t follow. Responsibility, on this account, tracks modal depth—the capacity to hold alternatives open, model consequences, inhibit response, and revise the field—together with the conditions that make a selection the agent’s own, not ultimate metaphysical sourcehood. Hard incompatibilism is right, on the identity account, that libertarian sourcehood is unavailable; what the account denies is that anything moral practice cares about depended on it.

*Classical compatibilism.* Compatibilist accounts from Hume forward (Hume (1748) 1999; Hobbes 1654; Frankfurt 1971; Watson 1975; Fischer and Ravizza 1998; Wolf 1990) hold that free will is compatible with determinism because what matters is the right kind of internal cause—desires endorsed by higher-order desires, reasons-responsive mechanisms, sanity-relative reasons-tracking. What the structural account offers is this thought carried to its conclusion, not a rival to it. The internal structure that does the work is a modal-mapping network: its depth supplies the alternatives a higher-order desire or a reasons-responsive mechanism would range over, while the agent’s identification with one of the valuations the network holds is, on this account, what those criteria track. Compatibilism named the location; the structural account proposes what is there.

*Frankfurt cases and the principle of alternate possibilities.* Frankfurt (1969) argued by counterexample that responsibility doesn’t require the ability to have done otherwise: an agent who acts on their own reasons, while unbeknownst to them a counterfactual intervener would have forced the same act had they tried to deviate, is still responsible despite lacking genuine alternatives. The literature has multiplied increasingly elaborate versions (Fischer 1994; Widerker and McKenna 2003; Pereboom 2001). On the structural reading the dispute eases once what alternatives consist in is distinguished. Frankfurt cases manipulate the external-world branching while leaving the agent’s modal-mapping network—the inside of the act—intact. What matters is the internal map, not the count of metaphysically open branches.

*Hierarchical will and volitional necessity.* A second strand locates freedom not in how many alternatives lie open but in the agent’s relation to their own desires. Frankfurt (1971) gives the hierarchical version. A wanton, moved by whichever first-order desire is strongest without caring which one moves them, is unfree with options to spare; an agent is free when the desire that moves them is one they endorse by a higher-order desire.

Watson (1975), routinely filed alongside Frankfurt but in fact the locus classicus critique of him, presses the objection the hierarchy invites. A higher-order desire is only another desire, with no standing to confer authority, so ranking desires by order begins a regress rather than ending it. Watson substitutes a valuational reading: what makes a desire the agent’s own is that it expresses what the agent values, the deliverance of a valuational system distinct from the mere strength of the motivational one. Bratman (2007) develops the same identificatory thought in terms of self-governing plans.

The distinction is load-bearing here. The endorsement criterion adopted here is Watson’s valuational one rather than Frankfurt’s higher-order-desire one, and the account answers Watson’s regress worry rather than inheriting it. A later refinement (Frankfurt 1982; Frankfurt 1988) adds that one form of such endorsement—volitional necessity, being unable to act against what one cares about most—is a height of freedom rather than a limit on it, and supplies an analytic reply to the demand for open alternatives. These positions press the modal-depth framing from a direction the alternatives-based disputes don’t, since they turn on which valuation governs rather than on how many alternatives lie open.

*The Eden story.* The classical reading of the Genesis narrative—present in Augustine and Aquinas, refined in the contemporary Catholic tradition—holds that Adam and Eve were created with perfectly oriented wills and full modal competence by divine endowment, so that the choice they faced was a free turning of an already-competent will rather than a choice that lacked the depth to count. This reading meets its own commitments awkwardly: a will competent to choose moral evil already requires a modal field rich enough to contain the alternative as live, and the field’s structure is what the present account calls Nature; the endowment view relocates rather than removes the modal-depth requirement. And the endowment cuts against what the defender needs from it. A will acting on an *infused* map—competence conferred whole, as Aquinas’s original justice and infused knowledge have it—is acting on modal-field content it did not author, so its selections are grounded in that installed structure: freedom in precisely the structural, modal-depth sense, not the contra-causal one. That modal content can be *installed* at all is no concession against this—education, language, and art install it piecemeal, divine infusion all at once, and in neither case does the will that acts on the map act independently of the map. Infusion therefore yields, on this account, a structurally free will, not a contra-causally free one, and cannot rescue the libertarian reading of the first choice; the only question it leaves open is whether the infused map was *deep* enough for the choice to count as fully responsible—a question internal to the structural account, and one its account of accumulated, lived modal depth answers in the negative. On the structural reading—modal depth as accumulated terrain—the first humans are placed before a morally decisive choice before they have accumulated the modal depth required to understand it. They have no history of deception, no developed map of death, no prior moral failure, no experience of shame, alienation, guilt, punishment, or irreversible consequence. The act is formally voluntary, but formal voluntariness isn’t freedom. Freedom requires a modal network deep enough to understand what is selected. On that standard, Eden isn’t the origin of fully responsible rebellion. It is the exposure of undeveloped will to a consequence it couldn’t yet understand.

*Divine will.* The same analysis returns to divine will. The classical reading holds that divine willing isn’t the operation of selection across alternatives but a single, simple, eternal act in which what God wills and what God is aren’t distinct; on this view divine simplicity is preserved without surrendering the language of will, and the apparent absence of modal depth isn’t a defect but a higher-order feature of the divine mode of being. (*Actus purus* (Latin, “pure act”) is Aquinas’s description of God as fully realized being with no unactualized potential left in it—nothing left to become, only pure being-in-act. The dilemma named here is that a being with no potential left to actualize (*actus purus*) has, by that same description, no open possibilities left to choose among—and modal depth, on this account’s own terms, is what freedom is made of.) The reading is Aquinas’s *actus purus*, pure actuality with no unrealized potential, refined in Stump (2003) and the contemporary Thomistic tradition. The picture leaves a dilemma intact. Classical God can be assigned modal status, but not modal depth. If God is pure actuality, there are no live alternatives, no delay, no unrealized possibilities, no selection, and no distance between willing and obtaining. That isn’t will; it is necessity wearing the grammar of will. If God has maximal modal depth instead, then God stands within a modal field rich enough to contain alternatives, contingencies, unrealized possibilities, and distinguishable possibilities. But to stand within such a field is to instantiate the structure God was supposed to transcend. The first option gives no will. The second gives Nature.

### 5.11.2 The Requirement
*Distance.* There must be distance between the willing and what is obtained by willing. The obtained state isn’t yet actual; possible lines toward it must be distinguishable; and a persisting medium must carry the transition from present condition to obtained condition. Where willing and obtaining are identical, will disappears into identity. Where they differ, the structure of the difference is already in play.

*The three modal axes.* The distance just identified decomposes into three conditions that map onto Time, Space, and Substance (T, S, Φ—the three roles derived through Modal Identity and Conditions-as-Nature, §2.6–2.7). *Time* supplies the not-yet: a state not yet actual, so that what is willed differs from what is. *Space* supplies the distinction among lines: more than one path from present to obtained, so that selecting one displaces the others. *Substance* supplies continuity: something holds together across the transition, so that the agent who acts and the agent who obtains the result are the same agent. Strip any of the three away and willing collapses. A timeless agent has no not-yet to will toward. An agent without distinct lines has nothing to select among. An agent without persistence can’t be the same one at the moment of willing and at the moment of obtaining. The three Conditions aren’t philosophical categories grafted onto agency from outside; on this model they are what willing requires.

*Modal depth.* The bare three-axis distance is necessary but not sufficient for what the literature has called *free* will. Free will, on this proposal, begins with the depth of the distance—not libertarian exemption from causation but modal depth within a causal field: the expanded capacity to hold alternatives open, model their consequences, inhibit immediate response, and revise the map. Whether the agent can then enact the line it selects—participate in which possibility becomes actual—is a further condition, *latitude*, external to depth rather than part of it (§5.11.5). At shallow depth, life is responsive. A bacterium follows a nutrient gradient or avoids a toxin; that is directed responsiveness, not free will in the relevant sense. At greater depth, response becomes mapped line. At still greater depth, mapped lines can be held open before action. The more alternatives an agent can hold, compare, and revise before one path runs, the deeper the field the will runs over; depth is one dimension of freedom, not the whole of it. A bigger mind, in the sense relevant here, is a modal-mapping system with greater depth, broader integration across modules, more capacity to inhibit immediate response, and longer reach into both modeled futures and accumulated pasts—not a brain with more storage.

*Asymmetric freedom.* The depth of will is asymmetric across the present moment. The forward side of will is the field of possible futures ahead: what can be done, what can be avoided, what can be obtained, what may follow. The back side of will is the accumulated modal network behind: memory, experience, learned consequence, social pattern, emotional calibration, bodily habit, and prior encounter. A person’s freedom depends on both. Two agents may face the same external option while not possessing the same freedom toward it, because they don’t bring the same modal map to the choice. The structural requirement is therefore not just that a modal field be present at the moment of willing but that the agent bring sufficient accumulated depth to register what the field affords.

*Two kinds of registered constraint.* A modal-mapping system deep enough to support will must register constraint of two kinds. Some constraint distinguishes possibilities from one another—the wall isn’t the doorway, the closed door isn’t the open one, the past isn’t the future, this object isn’t that one.
