Some constraint settles which possibility becomes actual—the line taken excludes the line not taken, the door once opened can’t also be left closed in the same moment, the chosen action displaces its alternatives. Both are required: conditions that keep possibilities distinct, and conditions under which one possibility comes to occupy the place the others could have.

*Placement in the cascade.* These conditions explain why will belongs after meaning in the cascade. Drive supplies direction (§5.2). Feeling supplies valence (§5.3). Knowledge stabilizes the map (§5.4). Reasoning navigates alternatives (§5.6). Meaning weights the map as worth pursuing or avoiding (§5.10). Will acts through it. The willing subject isn’t outside causation but is the point at which causation has been internally mapped deeply enough for the agent to participate in which possible line becomes actual.

Willing is modeled here through temporal, spatial, and persistent dimensions of action, and freer action through a capacity to represent alternatives, consequences, and prior learning. This is a philosophical account of agency, not an established result that free will requires the book’s specific modal-depth architecture. Other accounts of agency, responsibility, and consent remain live.

### 5.11.3 Predictions
Willing, on this proposal, involves a system capable of representing alternatives, constraints, and anticipated consequences before action. In humans and other animals, neural systems are relevant to this work, but the relation between neural architecture, conscious access, and agency remains actively debated. The following are hypotheses generated here, not a specific cognitive architecture established wherever willing occurs.

*A note on scope.* The empirical sketches that follow are offered as structural correspondences consistent with cognitive-neuroscience practice, not as load-bearing empirical premises of the structural argument: the brain as modal-modeling network, modular sensory architecture, the subconscious as accumulated modal terrain. The load-bearing claim is the modal architecture itself; the empirical realizations name what that architecture looks like in the human case. Wherever willing occurs in other substrates, the same structural features must obtain, though their implementation will differ.

*The brain as modal-modeling network.* The brain is the organism’s modal-modeling network. It doesn’t merely represent what is actual. It models actuality as possibility-space: what can happen from here, what can’t happen from here, what must happen for another state to obtain, what blocks a line, what opens a line, what threatens continuation, what enables it, and which response-pathways remain available. At reflective depth that map can take propositional form: *if I do this, that may follow; if that follows, this future closes; if I wait, another line may open.* Beneath reflective depth the same operation is embodied, affective, spatial, temporal, and procedural. The organism maps condition, response, consequence, and constraint before it names any of them.

*Three modal dimensions of the map.* The map is structured by the same Triconditions that organize Nature itself (Time, Space, and Substance: the three Conditions). Temporal modal mapping registers sequence, delay, what must come before what, what is ripening, what is closing. Spatial modal mapping registers distinction, reach, separation, what blocks passage, what opens onto what. Substantial modal mapping registers persistence, identity, capacity, what holds together under change, what a thing can and can’t do given what it is. The dimensions aren’t chosen by the brain; they are the modal dimensions a living current must map to act at all.

*Modularity.* That modeling is modular. A subject doesn’t build one undifferentiated map of everything at once. The work is distributed across specialized modules that map regions of possibility-space at different scales and through different channels. Each sense is a modal-mapping module rather than a passive sensor. Vision builds a navigable visual possibility-space rather than recording pixels—what is present, what is reachable, what blocks what, what is likely to move next, what is hidden but inferable. Hearing builds a directional, source-attributing acoustic possibility-space. Proprioception builds a possibility-space of available bodily motion. Memory, language, social recognition, threat-detection, and future-simulation are likewise modular: each maps a kind of modal structure the organism must navigate. Will and reasoning operate on the integrated field these modules produce, which is why damage to a module doesn’t merely subtract data; it subtracts a region of livable possibility from the subject’s world.

*Concepts, language, technology, institutions.* Concepts are portable modules of this kind. A concept like *door* isn’t a label for an image. It is a stable modal map: passable when open, blocking when closed, separating inside from outside, available through handle or push or key, changing what lines are live. Language (§5.12) is the sharing of such modules between agents. Technology (§5.13) is their externalization into the world. Institutions are modules for coordinating recurring modal problems across many subjects at once. Each is a structural extension of the same predicted architecture beyond the boundaries of any single brain.

*The subconscious as accumulated modal terrain.* The subconscious is the accumulated modal network operating beneath reflective attention. It isn’t a hidden second self but the stored terrain of prior condition-response-consequence pairings: habit, skill, aversion, trauma response, bodily anticipation, social recognition, procedural memory. Autopilot isn’t irrational in itself. It is the map running where the system doesn’t reopen the whole field. Beneath even this stored terrain lies a faster layer that doesn’t run through the field at all: the withdrawal of a hand from a hot surface is run by a protective reflex arc that fires before the field is consulted and before the act could be selected or refused, so that the body executes it *for* the current rather than through it. Such a movement isn’t a shallow exercise of will but the absence of will—directed, adaptive, and wholly involuntary, which is why it’s felt as something that happened rather than something done. Will begins above both layers, where the current can delay, inspect, inhibit, or redirect the stored line before it becomes action—predicting a specific functional architecture in which prefrontal inhibition, working-memory holding, and conscious access selectively reopen subconscious channels for revision.

*Depth gradient across lineages.* Richer capacities for foresight, delay, learned revision, and counterfactual reasoning may correlate with more complex integrative cognitive systems. This is a graded hypothesis about agency, not a settled cross-species measure of free will or responsibility.

### 5.11.4 Confirmation
*Premeditation and passion in criminal law.* Legal distinctions among purpose, knowledge, recklessness, negligence, premeditation, provocation, and impairment track capacities relevant to the proposed account: foresight, inhibition, reasons-responsiveness, and practical control. Premeditation can indicate time to model the act, foresee consequences, revise intention, abandon the line, or continue anyway; intense affect can sometimes narrow those capacities without eliminating agency. But legal categories are normative and jurisdiction-specific compromises, not an empirical calibration proving one psychological variable called modal depth. Hart’s (1968) analysis of mens rea and the wider Anglo-American literature (Moore 1997; Robinson 1997; Husak 2010) supply points of comparison. They support the importance of differentiated mental capacities while leaving the book’s four-part architecture as a philosophical model.

*Consent.* Consent depends on modal depth. Consent requires more than verbal selection: it requires a subject whose modal network is developed enough to understand what the option means—what is asked, what consequences may follow, what alternatives exist, whether refusal is safe, whether power is asymmetrical, and what future self-states may be affected. A choice can be formally available while the agent lacks sufficient modal competence for the choice to count as consent. The relevant question is whether the will behind the word had enough mapped possibility to understand the act as a choice, not whether a word was spoken. Contemporary work in bioethics (Beauchamp and Childress 2019; Faden and Beauchamp 1986) and sexual-consent law arrives at a related structure from clinical and legal directions: informed, voluntary, and competent consent are the three conditions, and they map onto the account’s dimensions (information to the forward map and its fidelity, voluntariness to latitude, competence to accumulated depth). Read through the account’s two pillars, depth and latitude, consent is the exercise of will over one’s own field: knowing what a decision makes possible—*if I do this, these outcomes; if I do that, those*—and weighing those outcomes oneself, with the latitude to act on the weighing. Its two failure modes follow directly. Deception and immaturity corrupt the field, so that the outcomes weighed aren’t the real ones—the lied-to and the child assent to a decision whose scope they can’t map. Coercion ordinarily leaves the field intact and removes the latitude, so that the outcomes are understood but can’t be freely acted on—the threatened assent to what they would otherwise refuse, though pressure severe enough to contract the field as well returns the case to the impairment analysis already given. The child is the limiting case of the first: a real selection over a field too shallow to hold the decision, which is consent in form without consent in substance.

*Impairment.* Impairment cases show why the modal-depth test must remain general rather than scenario-bound. Intoxication, panic, coercive pressure, dissociation, developmental immaturity, and other contractions of the modal field can narrow the subject’s capacity to understand the act as a choice. The principle isn’t that one external marker mechanically settles consent or blame. The principle is that consent requires enough modal depth for self-rule, and responsibility intensifies where one will knowingly uses another subject’s contracted agency as the medium for its own end. Where impairment is shared, ambiguous, or symmetrical, the analysis can’t simply assign predatory asymmetry by formula; it must ask whether one subject’s will actually governed, exploited, or overrode the other’s. What follows is therefore a general structural test, not an endless catalog of moral or legal scenarios. Forensic and clinical practice has been refining related tests across more than a century of case law, from the *M’Naghten* rules forward through *Durham* and the Model Penal Code.

*Developmental neuroscience.* Capacities relevant to will don’t mature at one switch-point. Executive functions, inhibitory control, working memory, planning, reward sensitivity, and social learning follow partly distinct trajectories through adolescence and early adulthood (Casey et al. 2008; Steinberg 2008; Giedd 1999). Some executive measures approach adult levels earlier than the popular “brain matures at twenty-five” formula suggests, while context-sensitive judgment can continue changing later. This record supports a graded, multidimensional treatment of agency and cautions against assigning one neurological birthday to competence. It doesn’t confirm the book’s modal-depth construct or mechanically determine legal and moral responsibility.

*Pathology.* Damage to prefrontal cortex (Damasio 1994; Bechara et al. 1994), severe addiction (Volkow et al. 2016), and certain dissociative and impulse-control disorders can narrow the modal field in measurable ways, producing behavioral patterns consistent with the structural account: contracted future modeling, weakened inhibition, line-locked responding, and impoverished alternative-holding. The phenomenology, the neuroscience, and the legal-clinical assessment bear on related capacities from different directions.

*Decision neuroscience and predictive processing.* Computational accounts of action selection—model-based versus model-free reinforcement learning (Daw et al. 2005), active-inference frameworks (Friston 2010; Hohwy 2013), and the role of prefrontal cortex in deliberate line-comparison versus habitual response (Miller and Cohen 2001)—describe a comparable gradient from another direction. Model-free responding is the modal-mapping system running its accumulated lines without reopening the field; model-based deliberation is the system holding alternatives open, simulating consequences, and revising before action. The literature doesn’t name the variable modal depth; on this account the variable it tracks is closely related.

Criminal law, bioethics, forensic practice, developmental neuroscience, neuropsychology, and computational decision research all address capacities relevant to deliberation, control, and consent. Their constructs and purposes differ, and they don’t independently confirm the book’s modal-depth architecture. What follows is one way of integrating these literatures, while the philosophical debates about free will and responsibility remain live.

### 5.11.5 Conclusions
*The reframing.* The dispute between libertarianism, compatibilism, and hard determinism has been organized for centuries around a single load-bearing question: does free will require exemption from prior causation, or is some form of causally embedded freedom sufficient? The structural account proposes to relocate the variable. Freedom is neither metaphysical exemption nor any single compatibilist criterion (higher-order endorsement, reasons-responsiveness, sanity); on this proposal it is modal depth, with fidelity, endorsement, and latitude, achieved within the field that the modal pressures (T, S, Φ—see §2.7) make available. Libertarianism, on this reading, named depth and called it exemption. Compatibilism named ownership and called it the right kind of cause. Hard determinism noticed that exemption was unavailable and concluded freedom must therefore be illusory. Each tracked a real feature of the same architecture from an incomplete angle.

*Depth is necessary but not sufficient: fidelity and endorsement.* Modal depth names the space freedom requires but not the whole of its structure, and the cases that follow show why. A wanton is Frankfurt’s (1971) agent, moved by whichever first-order desire is strongest without caring which one moves them. Such an agent can command an enormous field and still fail to be free, because nothing in the agent settles which mapped line counts as their own. The agent under volitional necessity runs the other way: Luther’s *Here I stand, I can do no other* (Frankfurt 1982; Frankfurt 1988) has the field collapsed to a single option by the depth of what is cared about, and isn’t thereby less free but more.

Depth points the wrong direction in both—the wanton has it without freedom, the resolute agent has freedom without it—which points to freedom as the degree to which an act is governed by the valuation the agent identifies with, operating over a field that is both deep enough and uncorrupted.

This is the point at which Watson’s regress must be stopped rather than relocated. Were the valuation the agent identifies with authoritative merely by being a higher-order desire—one more want ranked above the rest—the question would simply climb a level: what confers authority on that desire, and why not one higher still? The structural account doesn’t rank desires at all.

Identification, on the identity account (§5.7), isn’t a further-order preference the agent happens to hold. It is the operation by which the self-model is constituted. The self’s identifying with some valuations and against others is the same operation by which it builds the I. A valuation the agent identifies with is authoritative not because it wins a contest among desires but because it is partly constitutive of who the agent is. There is no higher tribunal to appeal to, because the identifying is the self any appeal would be made to.

This is the move that resists agent-causation earlier in the section—on the identity account, the agent is the structured recursion, not a substance behind it (§4.8, §5.7)—applied to endorsement.

The modal-mapping network must therefore meet several conditions, each of which fails recognizably. Its *depth* can be too shallow: an agent who doesn’t know an option exists isn’t free with respect to it, however available it is in the world—the diner who never learns the kitchen will prepare a dish that isn’t on the printed card has exactly the freedom the card’s depth allows and no more, which is why part of the relevant competence is knowing that one’s field has edges and can be probed. Its *fidelity* can be compromised: a field that misrepresents what an act makes possible defeats freedom even where depth is intact, which is why honest disclosure expands freedom without adding any new act—the consumer who learns a product carries a lethal long-term risk gains freedom over the identical choice once the consequence-branch is installed, and why the law counts consent obtained by concealment or fraud as no free consent at all (the competence-and-consent variable tracked at §5.11.4). Knowledge feeds the field directly at this point: since whatever is actual is possible, every fact an agent holds is already an entry in the modal field, and inference projects from those entries to the further possibilities they license—the precise sense in which knowledge (§5.4) is a condition of will.

Corruption can also be internal rather than external: where the salience-weighting that decides which valuation governs is set so that it reliably under-serves the agent’s endorsed priority—as in conditions of executive-function dysregulation such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder—the endorsed valuation can remain wholly intact and still lose, which marks the seam where a corrupted field shades into a defeated endorsement. Its *endorsement*, finally, can simply be overridden in the moment: judging one course best and being carried by the stronger immediate pull into another is the weakness of will the tradition has named since Aristotle and sharpened in Davidson (1970)—the episodic form of the wanton’s standing failure. Beneath all three, will rides on a substrate it doesn’t author. The thick will of this section is the thin directedness of drive (§5.2) brought under a field that is deep, faithful, and owned, and like all drive it stays embodied: a current can override a standing drive such as hunger by the valuation it endorses, but only to the limit the body itself permits. Depth, fidelity, and endorsement work together, instantiated by a living current—none alone suffices, and the tradition’s single-criterion accounts each foregrounded one of them.

These conditions concern the field and the agent’s ownership of the act made over it; freedom needs one thing further, external to them all. It also requires *latitude*—the standing room to act on the selection once made—which coercion removes without touching depth, fidelity, or endorsement: the coerced agent can map the field truly, endorse the refusal, and still be made to act against it. Depth, fidelity, and endorsement settle whether a selection is genuinely the agent’s; latitude settles whether the agent can enact what has genuinely been selected. So *modal freedom*, on the proposed account, resolves into two pillars: modal depth (the grasp) and latitude (the room to enact). Fidelity and endorsement are the conditions under which the depth-side selection is truly the agent’s own.

*Frankfurt cases reconsidered.* The proliferation of Frankfurt-style counterexamples in the late twentieth century revealed that something about responsibility was decoupled from metaphysical branching, and the literature offered several accounts of what. The structural account proposes one. What the cases preserve while removing external alternatives is internal modal depth: the agent’s mapping network, the alternatives the network holds open at the time of action, and the agent’s participation in which mapped line runs. Branching in the world matters less than branching in the map. The Frankfurt literature was right that responsibility survives the loss of external alternatives; the modal-mapping variable is offered here as one explanation of why, alongside reasons-responsiveness accounts (Fischer and Ravizza 1998).

*The Eden challenge revisited.* The reading developed in §5.11.1—that Eden subjects undeveloped will to morally decisive choice—doesn’t depend on rejecting the classical endowment view’s conceptual coherence; it depends on the structural-depth account being the correct read of what freedom is. If freedom is modal-mapping depth accumulated through encounter, no act of divine endowment can substitute for the encounter. A perfectly oriented will with no developed modal terrain has the form of a will and lacks the substance the form requires. The endowment view answers a structural-depth requirement with a metaphysical decree, and the decree can’t do what the depth would.

*The divine-will dilemma revisited.* The dilemma at the end of §5.11.1—*actus purus* has no modal depth, maximal modal depth gives Nature—admits no escape, on the account of will as selection given here, that preserves the classical view of divine will as both transcendent of structure and genuinely will-shaped. Stump’s (2003) refinement secures simplicity at the cost of the modal architecture *will* names; alternative refinements that secure the modal architecture surrender the transcendence. The dilemma is structural, not rhetorical.

*The inversion at the level of will.* What the inversion of greatness names at the level of consciousness (§5.1) returns at the level of will. The freedom traditionally located above Nature—exempt from causation, prior to creation, transcendent of structure—is what modal depth within Nature looks like at sufficient depth. The motion is again inward, not upward. On this account, free will isn’t what we have despite being natural creatures. It is what being a sufficiently deep natural creature, with room to act, consists in.

*Responsibility, asymmetry, and moral practice.* The structural account doesn’t collapse responsibility into determinism. Two agents facing the same external option may bring different modal maps to it, and the moral practice that tracks responsibility—praise, blame, punishment, gratitude, resentment, forgiveness—calibrates against those maps. Strawson’s (1962) reactive-attitudes account, the Hart-Honoré tradition in legal philosophy, and the bioethical apparatus of competence and consent can be read as calibrations of related variables. The account offers an explanation of why the calibrations work that needs no commitment to libertarian sourcehood and no surrender of moral practice to hard-determinist deflation.

Will is modeled here as action mediated by a representation of alternatives, accumulated experience, valuation, and practical latitude. It proposes that richer modal mapping supports more reflective forms of agency. This doesn’t dissolve the standing debate between libertarian, compatibilist, and hard-determinist accounts; it supplies one compatibilist-leaning framework for interpreting it. The relation between reasoning, knowledge, valuation, will, and responsibility remains a substantive philosophical question. The medium through which such an agent makes itself legible to others is taken up at §5.12.

## 5.12 Language

Language is a family of learned practices through which subjects coordinate across their separation. It can report, ask, promise, command, joke, point, name, express, and reshape attention. Shared words don’t place one identical chunk of map in every mind; they support sufficiently convergent uses, references, expectations, and inferences for people to correct one another and go on together. Teaching, writing, and specialist jargon can greatly extend that coordination without reproducing one interior inside another.

**[Identification]**

**Language** · *Identification*

Language is a structured social practice for coordinating signs and acts across subjects. Its vehicles can be propositional, indexical, expressive, interrogative, imperative, performative, iconic, or ostensive; often one utterance does several jobs. Understanding is not reproduction of an interior but sufficient practical alignment in use, reference, inference, response, and correction. The interval between subjects is not a barrier to that coordination but its condition.

*Status: an addressed denial already performs a communicative act across an interval, establishing only the local fact of attempted coordination. Cartesian Certainty does not derive linguistic conventions, semantic content, propositional form, or successful understanding. The broader account is a functional proposal defended by fit with public criteria and linguistic practice. Chapter 11 application: §11.8.3.*

**Depends on:** Knowledge (§5.4) and Cartesian Certainty (§2.2)

Three results elsewhere run on this operation without naming it. Modal Convergence gives a network of subjects and artifacts an epistemic capacity no single member has, and communication is one way that network’s representations are distributed and corrected (§5.4); Legacy holds that what continues after a closure is content that had already transferred (§5.9); and the mapping-mode of wronging corrupts a subject’s field by what is externalized into it (§5.14). Each is a use of the single operation identified here, and putting that plainly shows what the three share. A denial of language, addressed to a reader, is already an attempted transfer: content presented for uptake across the interval. The trying is the crossing. That is the catch. What it doesn’t settle is that this operation just is the technology of shared interiority, or that understanding is sufficient practical alignment rather than identity of copies. Those remain the naming half.

**[Theorem]**

**Addressed Denial Instantiates Communication** · *Theorem*

A denial addressed through signs to another subject presents content for uptake across their separation. Whatever its success, truth, conventional form, or eventual interpretation, the act is an attempted coordination of signs and response. An addressed denial that communication occurs therefore instantiates communication at that minimal level.

The theorem establishes attempted communication, not shared conventions, successful reference, accurate transfer, mutual understanding, or language’s complete functional identity. A private mark, involuntary signal, or uninterpreted event falls outside the conclusion unless it is addressed for uptake.

**Depends on:** Representational Minimum (§5.4)

The theorem secures the minimal occurrence. The broader operation already traced across knowledge, legacy, and deception now supports a separate consequence about what one communicative channel can carry.

**[Corollary]**

**One Channel** · *Corollary*

The same communicative capacities can transmit knowledge, preserve a person’s representations beyond that person’s life, and mislead a receiver. Deception requires no separate linguistic faculty: it recruits ordinary capacities for assertion, implication, attention-direction, and trust toward a false or strategically incomplete representation.

Lossiness alone does not make communication deceptive: understanding never requires identical internal representations. Deception adds an intention or function of inducing or preserving a representation the communicator takes to be false, misleading, or materially incomplete.

*Scope.* This corollary distinguishes communicative uses; it does not derive a moral norm of truthfulness from communication itself. Strategic concealment, fiction, play, privacy, error, compression, and culpable deception must be kept apart. The later argument about when misleading another subject constitutes wronging is supplied at §5.14.

**Dependency routes:** shared communicative channel—Language (§5.12) and Knowledge (§5.4); deceptive or aversive use—Aversion as Modal Weight (§5.2)

That second point closes an objection the result would otherwise invite. If every transfer is partial, and a corrupted transfer is also partial, it can look as though the difference between speaking truly and deceiving is one of degree, with honesty the limiting case of low loss. It isn’t. A speaker who compresses badly and a speaker who supplies a false dependency are doing structurally different things, and the difference isn’t how much of the field arrived but whether what arrived was built to serve the receiver’s navigation or to serve someone else’s at the receiver’s expense. Fidelity is a separate axis, and a perfectly faithful transfer of a false necessity is the most damaging case rather than the least.

The corollary fixes what one channel can carry. It doesn’t yet fix what the operation requires of the receiver, and the limit that condition names isn’t a defect in the channel but a consequence of what the forms of knowledge are.

Some linguistic instruction arrives primarily as propositional content. Other communication is demonstrative, affective, practical, iconic, or ostensive and can guide the receiver’s own encounter. Acquaintance is nonetheless not exhausted by a description: it depends on the receiver undergoing or exercising the relevant relation (§5.4). A transfer can therefore deliver everything a speaker can state while the receiver still lacks the encounter needed to recognize, discriminate, or apply it firsthand.

That is the structure of Mary’s case (§5.4.1), and seeing it as a transfer-condition shows why the case establishes less than it appears to. Mary’s exhaustive propositional coverage fails to deliver acquaintance not because acquaintance is a further fact her propositions omit, but because it is a different form of holding, constituted by reconstruction from encounter. No volume of transfer supplies encounters. What she gains on first seeing red is a form, not a fact, and the knowledge argument reads the change of form as the arrival of new content.

The same condition fixes what teaching can and can’t do, which is the practical weight of the point. Instruction guides the construction of representations of regions of the modal structure no single life is long enough to encounter firsthand, and that is what makes the accumulated network worth more to a body than its own field (§5.13); education (§6.9) is that operation run deliberately. What instruction can’t do is install acquaintance where there has been no encounter. A curriculum of transferred propositions with nothing anchoring them yields a field dense in claims and thin in what the claims are about—true content the holder can’t verify, weigh, or correct—which is a mapping deficit rather than an education, and is exactly the condition a corrupted transfer exploits.

A will acting through its modal field (§5.11) eventually has to make the field legible to other actors. Language is the first technology of that making. The central question isn’t how sound, gesture, posture, or marks become meaningful, but how the structural content of one mind’s model can be reliably conveyed (imperfectly but systematically) into another’s.

Language and art (§5.15) overlap. Poems, songs, novels, performances, diagrams, ritual speech, and ordinary conversation can carry claims, feelings, attention, rhythm, social action, and forms of acquaintance together. Propositional articulation is one power of language, not its outer boundary; art isn’t whatever remains after propositions run out. The later distinction is functional and graded: artworks characteristically organize an experience for uptake, while linguistic practices characteristically stabilize publicly correctable uses, but neither owns an exclusive kind of content.

Language doesn’t mechanically transfer a region from one mind into another. Signs prompt hearers to interpret, infer, attend, remember, respond, and correct within public practices. A shared vocabulary supports enough convergence in use and inference for coordination without requiring the same internal map under each label. Specialist jargon compresses procedures, distinctions, and inferential commitments for people trained in a practice; the term alone doesn’t install the expertise. Teaching and documentation can guide the construction of representations across time, while testing, encounter, correction, and practice determine what the receiver actually acquires.

*Communication’s expressive and referential functions.* Communication runs on a continuum from pure expressive function (direct externalization of the sender’s drive-state) to referential function: externalization of modeled objects in the sender’s modal field, displaced from the immediate context. A cat backed into a corner rearing itself, a dog snarling, a bird’s alarm call, a baby’s cry, a wince at unexpected news: these are expressive; they make the sender’s drive-state public so other beings can register and respond. Symbolic language carries the expressive function all the way up; “stop that” is functionally a snarl with words, “I love you” is functionally a purr with grammar, and a great deal of everyday speech is more articulated drive-state externalization than referential transmission. What symbolic language adds at sufficient depth is referential function: the capacity to externalize content that *isn’t* the sender’s current drive-state, referents displaced from the here-and-now, other times, other places, hypothetical states, abstract types, counterfactual branches, the absent friend, last week’s meeting, next year’s plan, the square root of two. A cat can’t rear at the threat that was here yesterday or at the threat its modal field is projecting forward; the cat’s body has no apparatus for that displacement. The modeling that permits displacement is the same modal-field machinery reasoning runs on (§5.6), applied to externalize modal-field content rather than to operate on it internally. Referential function doesn’t replace expressive function (almost all human utterance carries both), but it is the structural addition that emerges as the depth gradient deepens, gradually rather than at a sharp break. Vervet predator-calls have a thin form of reference (type-of-predator, not just here’s-something-bad). Bee waggle dances have thin displacement (food at a location not currently visible). Toddler pointing at an absent ball is fuller displacement. Adult abstract reference is the upper end. The specific work here is on the deep-form referential capacity; its expressive function remains continuous with the signaling that runs all the way down the depth gradient.

Two self-modeling configurations persist, occupy genuinely different positions, and remain in causal exchange across the interval between them. Distinction, persistence, succession (Spatiality, Substantiality, Temporality) aren’t features the linguistic situation happens to require. They are what propositional transmission consists in. Without distinct positions, there is no separation for a claim to cross. Without persistence, there is no speaker whose claim remains the same claim a hearer can take up. Without succession, there is no before-and-after to the act of saying or the act of being understood. A proposition is a structure that can survive the journey between minds because the journey passes through the same three conditions every other concrete transition passes through. The exchange can hold content mutually across the interval: each speaker contributes to what the other can take up, rather than merely passing an asymmetric signal. The Modal Convergence theorem (§5.4) remains the narrower epistemic theorem of collectively held knowledge; language is one means by which such knowledge can be formed and transmitted, not an automatic application of the theorem.

This relocates the standing positions in philosophy of language. Saussure’s conventional signs, Chomsky’s generative competence, Wittgenstein’s meaning as use, Frege’s sense and reference, Kripke’s rigid designation, and Davidson’s truth-conditional semantics were each tracking real features of how minds reach each other through propositional form. What the structural account resists is an assumption several of them invite, though Davidson and the later Wittgenstein reject versions of it: that language is a system separable from Nature, a layer of signs or rules or uses that coordinates with reality through some external relation. Language isn’t separable. Its own form carries Nature’s form because there is no other order for it to carry, and what each tradition was tracking is what propositional transmission looks like from the angle that tradition approached. That there is a mind-independent structure for language to carry, rather than a scheme the mind lays over a formless content, is the realism defended once at §5.6.

The charitable readings sharpen the point. Wittgenstein (1953) is right that meaning is bound to use: a proposition that doesn’t function in the practice of any community of speakers doesn’t transmit, because there are no shared procedures by which a hearer can recover its content. Kripke (1980) is right that names refer through causal-historical chains rather than through descriptions speakers can articulate, because reference must survive disagreement and error about what is referred to. Davidson (1967; 1973) is right that systematic compositionality helps make indefinite production from finite resources possible: speakers can build new propositions without learning a new convention for each one. Quine (1960) is right that translation underdetermines: no observable behavior fully fixes the model in another speaker’s mind; the gap between minds is real, and what closes it sufficiently is alignment under shared conditions rather than identity of internal representation. Chomsky (1965; 1986) is right to place generative embedding near the center of linguistic competence. Whether every language realizes that capacity through syntactic recursion is the further question, not something the structural requirement decides. Each position locates one face of the same structural fact: a configuration capable of modeling itself, modeling another, and modeling what passes between them must coordinate across distinct positions, across time, and across whatever sustains the exchange. Where the literature has competed over which face is fundamental, the structural account reads them as views of one transmission from different angles.

*The private-language pressure.* One charitable credit isn’t yet an answer to Wittgenstein’s private-language challenge, and the account’s own vocabulary is what stands exposed to it. If “shared interiority” named a private inner sample each speaker checks a word against, the private-language argument (Wittgenstein 1953, §§243–315) would apply in full: nothing could count as using the label correctly, and “the same chunk of possibility space under the same label” would carry exactly the confusion the argument diagnoses. The concession is total: there is no private sample. The interior on the closure-and-throughput account (§4.8) isn’t an object held up against a word but a self-modeling process whose contents are individuated by what they let a configuration do: coordinate, correct, predict, and go on. So the criteria for two speakers having loaded the same region are public, where Wittgenstein placed them: convergence under shared conditions and continued success in use, not an inward comparison no one could check. Rule-following and forms of life are then not pressures the account must absorb from outside; they name the same fact from the side of practice: a region of modal field counts as shared when, and only when, the practice of using it holds up across the interval. Family resemblance operates by the same standard: concept boundaries are fixed by overlapping use rather than shared essence, so whether a modal-map region coheres is judged by whether use holds together, not by whether a common property subtends it. The structural account doesn’t posit an inside the criteria fail to reach. It locates the inside as the publicly-criterioned thing Wittgenstein’s own argument requires.

*A test case: acquaintance without articulation.* Consider a child raised in total isolation from language, encountering water directly, with no interlocutor and no word ever offered. Such a child registers the wet/dry distinction: the same thermal-and-mechanical inference apparatus that produces the sensation in any human body runs whether or not a word exists for its output, and a dog or a fish, with no language at all, plainly responds differently to being wet and being dry. What the isolated child lacks isn’t the sensation but the shared criterion: a public practice of using a label reliably enough that another speaker could correct a misuse. This is a thin registration, in the depth-gradient sense running through this chapter: a real discrimination, held by the system, that hasn’t yet been articulated, named, or folded into a practice checkable by anyone else. The private-language argument’s target was never the existence of that thin registration; it was the idea of a private sample a word could be privately checked against. The isolated child has the registration and no word; what would be incoherent is a claim to have privately named it in a sense no one, including a later-taught version of the same child, could ever get right or wrong. Helen Keller’s own account (1903) of the moment at the water pump makes the transition vivid: the sensation of water over her hand was already fully present long before language, and what broke open at the pump wasn’t a new feeling but the discovery that the finger-spelled pattern named the thing she had been feeling all along—the folding of a thin registration into the public, checkable practice a word requires.

Language has structure because that is what language describes. The claim is about the deep conditions of propositional transmission (reference, predication, and composition across an interval), not about surface grammars, lexicons, idioms, or inflectional systems, which are shaped by historical contingencies the structural account doesn’t track. The conditions any language must meet to carry propositions across the interval between speakers are the same conditions a self-modeling being must meet to register anything at all. If consciousness is a self-modeling process registering itself from inside, and language is the practice by which that self-registration is structured and shared, then the structure of language is the process’s own logical form, made communicable. The proof required all three roles to state itself; language requires the same three to carry any statement at all. The derivation and linguistic practice arrived at the same grammar. Every sentence that successfully says anything (in any language, by any species capable of uttering one) runs on the same structural conditions the argument has named, from whatever position within them the speaker happens to occupy.

The depth-gradient framing applies to language as it does to other registers. Many species transmit information via signals: pheromone trails (ants), referential alarm calls (vervets, Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler 1980), waggle dances (bees), individual signature whistles (dolphins), prairie-dog calls apparently encoding predator type, size, and color (Slobodchikoff 2002). These are shallow forms of language: signaling without the depth of displacement, embedding, or theory-of-mind dependence human language permits. Deep propositional language emerges most fully in humans, who can model others as modelers and externalize that modeling symbolically. The shallow forms exist below the self-aware threshold named at §5.1; the deep form requires it.

*Gossip as a primary social use of language.* Among the deep-form referential uses of language, gossip (talking-about-other-people, especially people in proximity, especially regarding their conduct) has structural prominence. Dunbar’s (1996) *Grooming, Gossip, and the Evolution of Language* argued that the small-group social-information-sharing function predates and underwrites the more abstract referential uses humans developed; he ties it to a social-information-management scale of roughly 150 people, Dunbar’s number. Read in the modal-field vocabulary, gossip is *distributed modal-field maintenance* for a social network. It delivers actualities about specific people in the listener’s proximity (what they did, how they responded, what they value) at higher proximity-weighting than distant or fictional cases, because the modal apparatus treats nearby actualities as more applicable to the body’s own field than far ones. It maps consequences as well as actualities: shame, ostracism, reputational damage, social cost (the visible consequences of conduct gossip names) are what make gossip an effective norm-enforcement mechanism. It is also a distributed predator-detection system: a body that has heard the right gossip can recognize an exploitative neighbor, a manipulator, or an untrustworthy partner without being burned individually. Reputation, the social map gossip lays down, is itself a feature of the social modal field (everyone’s prediction of how a given person is likely to behave), and gossip is the substrate by which that structure is built and updated. This is plausibly one reason gossip is reflexively pleasurable across cultures: the modal apparatus is fed exactly what it is hungry for, in a domain it cares about deeply (immediate social possibility), at evidential weight high enough to be useful. Reality TV, true crime, celebrity coverage, and social-media commentary are extensions of the same operation at scale, mediated by technologies that broaden the proximity-circle the apparatus treats as relevant; the underlying drive is the modal-field-expansion drive named at §5.2, here flowing through the referential function of language at the social register where Dunbar located its evolutionary purpose. Beyond the evolutionary register Dunbar names, gossip is also where social categories are constituted and enforced: reputations, roles, and standings are the ameliorative kinds of §5.12.1 maintained in distributed talk, and to gossip about how someone occupied a role is to keep updating the social modal field that says what the role demands.

*Pronouns and the register collision.* A pronoun is the most compressed referential device a language has for a person: in a single syllable it installs, in the hearer’s modal field, a minimal re-identifiable position for the referent—a shared region of map at its smallest. In gendered languages that installation bundles a social-category assignment into the act of referring, which is why the pronoun becomes a site of dispute out of all proportion to its size: three registers meet in one word. Using a pronoun is a referential-and-social-category act (§5.12.1); the identity it points at is a self-model position (§5.7); the body it may or may not track is the substrate (§5.8). Much of the contemporary argument is a register collision—parties who take the pronoun to report a substrate fact, parties who take it to register a self-model position, and parties who take it to maintain an ameliorative social kind aren’t contradicting one another about a single thing but speaking across three. What the structural account settles is narrow and firm: whom the pronoun refers to is a subject, and on the equal-standing premise defended at §5.14 that subject’s standing doesn’t turn on category-membership, so the referring-verdict—that there is a someone here, owed what any subject is owed—is invariant across the readings. What it doesn’t settle is the contested etiquette and policy specifics of who is owed which term under which conditions; that adjudication isn’t the structural account’s to make. The deeper point answers the natural puzzle of why anything has a pronoun at all: reference across the interval requires re-identifiable positions, since distinction, persistence, and succession are what let a claim about a someone survive the trip between minds, and a pronoun is the minimal such re-identifier. In that sense a pronoun is structural. Its gender-marking isn’t: gendered pronouns are surface grammar, among the historical contingencies this section has already set aside as untracked by the structural claim. But contingent at the grammatical layer isn’t trivial at the personal layer: the self-model position a pronoun references (§5.7) is real and consequential even where the grammatical gender-slot that carries it is arbitrary. The deep fact, that reference needs a re-identifiable position, is invariant; the gendered packaging of that position is contingent. Much of the heat around pronouns, like the older habit of assigning the ungendered a default gendered term, is a contingent grammatical slot being mistaken for a substrate verdict.

*In-group vocabulary and modal-field narrowing.* Not every installation a shared vocabulary performs is expansive. A term can install a region of social possibility by closing a hearer’s field rather than opening it: labeling one’s own group *the elect*, *the remnant*, or *the light of the world* installs a favorable self-location that need not be argued for each time it is invoked, and labeling disagreement *worldliness*, *hardness of heart*, or *suppression of the truth* installs an unfavorable location for the response before its content is examined. Maxims that foreclose a line of inference before it opens—*God works in mysterious ways*, *who are we to question*, *just have faith*—do compressed referential work the way a pronoun does at smaller scale, loaded once and then spent without argument on every later occasion. What is distinctive about this class is the direction of the installation: most vocabulary opens a region of the hearer’s field for use, the way jargon makes a decade of a discipline’s mapping available in one syllable; this class installs a boundary against further mapping, marking a region closed rather than making one available. The pattern isn’t specific to any one tradition or doctrine. Structurally identical devices recur across independent religious and political traditions wherever a group’s boundary needs maintaining at lower cost than argument supplies, which is what makes the convergence a corroboration rather than an argument in its own right: it is what the account of language predicts language will be recruited to do wherever groups form and hold boundaries, not a separate case against whichever group happens to be doing it.

Successful communication isn’t merely the transfer of information; it is the convergence of two minds’ models on a shared claim about Nature they both inhabit. The interval between speakers isn’t a barrier to that convergence but its condition: there must be a gap for a claim to cross. Understanding is sufficient practical alignment: the two models needn’t match, but they converge enough in use, reference, and correction for coordination to go on. That alignment is what the structural account of language predicts and what the experience of being understood reports.

*A note on scope.* This result is offered as a structural account of what language is, not as a strict derivation from the proof of Chapters 1–2—the result being language as the structured practice by which propositional content crosses the interval between self-modeling persons. The proof establishes the three necessary structural Conditions; the claim that those conditions are what propositional transmission consists in at the depth a self-modeling configuration reaches is the naming half, in the sense flagged at the head of Chapter 5. That a reader might accept the proof while reading the linguistic case differently (assigning more weight to convention, to use, to neural architecture, or to social practice) leaves nothing earlier disturbed; the naming carries weight just to the degree it fits the phenomenon.

### 5.12.1 The Dispute
The literature on language is among the most technical in twentieth-century philosophy and among the most active in the cognitive sciences.

*Saussurean structuralism.* Saussure’s (1916) *Cours de linguistique générale* established the modern study of language with the distinction between *langue* and *parole*, the arbitrariness of the sign, and the structural relations among signs as the locus of linguistic meaning. The position has organized continental linguistics and semiotics for a century. Saussure is right that language is a system rather than a list; what is added here is why the system has the structure it has, tracking the structure of what language is about, with arbitrariness operating at the surface and structural fit operating beneath.

*Chomskyan generativism.* Chomsky (1965; 1986; see also 1957; 1995) developed the generativist tradition on which linguistic competence requires an innate language faculty supplying universal grammatical structure. The position has been refined through government-and-binding theory, the minimalist program, and the broader cognitive-linguistic enterprise; it has been challenged by usage-based and construction-grammar approaches (Tomasello 2003; Goldberg 2006). Chomsky correctly identifies the pressure to explain generative embedding. The deeper claim is what that capacity is for: propositional transmission must carry propositions about propositions. Whether its grammatical realization is universally recursive remains part of the dispute rather than a consequence settled here.

*Wittgensteinian meaning-as-use.* Wittgenstein’s (1953) *Philosophical Investigations* developed the position that meaning is constituted by the use of words in shared practices, with rule-following grounded in form-of-life rather than in private mental content. The position has been refined through Kripkenstein (Kripke 1982), Wright (1980), and the broader use-theoretic tradition. Wittgenstein is read here as correctly identifying that meaning is bound to use—a proposition that doesn’t function in the practice of any community of speakers doesn’t transmit—while supplying the deeper claim: the practices succeed in transmission because they coordinate on the structural conditions transmission requires. The later work’s distinctive moves bear directly on its own vocabulary. Language-games and forms of life locate meaning in patterned shared activity rather than in inner ostension; family resemblance denies that a general term needs a common essence to function; and the rule-following considerations deny that meaning is fixed by any private act of interpretation. These are taken as constraints that must be met, not positions that must be defeated: a shared region of modal field counts as shared only where there is a public practice of correction—speakers who can be brought back into line when they use a term wrongly—which is what use in a form of life supplies and what a private inner sample couldn’t.

*Frege and the sense-reference distinction.* Frege (1892) distinguished sense from reference and located meaning in a third realm of abstract objects. The position has been refined through Russell, Carnap, and contemporary semantics. Frege’s distinction correctly identifies that propositional content has both a referential and a presentational aspect. On the structural reading, the sense-reference split is what propositional content has when it carries a claim about structure to another mind; the abstract-objects metaphysics is dispensable.

*Kripke and direct reference.* Kripke (1980) *Naming and Necessity* developed the direct-reference tradition on which names refer through causal-historical chains rather than through descriptions speakers can articulate. The position has been refined and contested across forty years (Soames 2002; Kaplan 1989; Stalnaker 1997). Kripke correctly identifies that reference must survive disagreement and error about what is referred to. What makes causal-historical chains succeed, on the structural reading, is that they preserve the structural connection between the speaker using the name and the person or object the name picks out.

*Davidsonian truth-conditional semantics.* Davidson (1967; 1973; 1984) developed the program of treating semantics as the specification of truth-conditions, with compositionality as the structural feature that makes infinite production from finite resources possible. Davidson correctly identifies systematic compositionality as what makes propositional language possible at scale. It works, on the structural reading, because the medium itself supports the embedding of structure within structure. Davidson’s (1974) objection cuts toward this framework rather than away from it. In *On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme* he argued that the picture of a conceptual scheme that organizes, fits, or carves an uninterpreted reality—what he called a third dogma of empiricism—is unintelligible, since there is no standpoint outside both language and world from which scheme and content could be lined up and checked against each other. A framework that speaks of a Reality all description answers to, and of the three Conditions as what carves it, is exactly the kind of view that objection targets. Davidson is read here as correctly identifying that any scheme-against-content dualism is hopeless; the account meets the charge not by defending such a dualism but by denying it has one.

*Quinean indeterminacy.* Quine (1960) argued that translation is underdetermined: no observable behavior fully fixes the model in another speaker’s mind. The position has been refined and contested across decades (Davidson (1973); Soames (1999)). Quine is right that the gap between minds is real. What closes it sufficiently, on the structural reading, is alignment under shared conditions rather than identity of internal representation; translation succeeds to the extent the structural features align.

*Searle’s Chinese Room and the symbol-grounding problem.* Searle (1980) argued that symbol manipulation isn’t understanding: a system implementing a syntactic program doesn’t thereby grasp the semantic content the symbols are about. The position has been refined and contested across decades (the systems reply, the robot reply, Searle (1984)). Searle correctly identifies that propositional transmission requires something mere syntactic manipulation doesn’t supply. That something, on the structural reading, is the self-modeling that runs on both ends of the transmission, with the structure of the proposition mapping onto structure on each end.

*Large language models.* The recent emergence of LLMs (OpenAI’s GPT family; Anthropic’s Claude; Google’s Gemini) has reorganized debates about whether and how computational systems engage in language. Disputes are live: some hold LLMs demonstrate that language can be mastered without semantic understanding (Bender et al. 2021); others argue LLMs may have rudimentary forms of understanding (Bowman 2023). LLMs are read here as engaging in a structurally interesting subset of linguistic activity: they manipulate the surface structure of language with substantial success and instantiate parts of the compositional and sequential structure transmission requires, while what they share with self-modeling mind-to-mind transmission remains an open empirical and conceptual question.

*Whorfian relativity.* The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis—that language shapes thought—has been refined through decades of cross-linguistic cognitive research (Lucy 1992; Levinson 2003; Boroditsky 2011). The empirical record shows real but generally moderate language-thought interactions. The moderate Whorfian results are read here as picking up real conceptual-elaboration effects, while denying the strong-Whorfian claim that language constitutes thought: the underlying registration runs whether or not specific languages are imposed on it.

*Haslanger and the constitutive dimension of social kinds.* Haslanger (2000; 2012) developed the ameliorative-analysis project: rather than asking what our concepts *do* mean or what their referents *naturally* are, it asks what a concept *should* mean given the legitimate purposes it serves, and argues that for social categories—gender, race, role—language partly constitutes which categories are practically available rather than merely labeling kinds fixed independently of it. This is placed between the Whorfian and conventionalist poles already located: stronger than moderate Whorfian content-effects, since social kinds are partly brought into and held in existence by the classifying practice; weaker than constitution of thought as such, since reference and predication run whether or not any particular social vocabulary is imposed. Read in modal-field terms, an ameliorative category is an exterior modal map maintained across a community: classifying a person under it installs a region of social possibility—what is expected, permitted, withheld, or owed—in every speaker trained to the term. This is the social-ontology work relational identity (§5.7) calls for, met here where social categories are actually built and policed.

*Brandom, Lewis, and the social-pragmatic tradition.* Brandom (1994) developed an inferentialist account on which meaning is constituted by the role expressions play in giving and asking for reasons, and—extending the line that runs from Sellars—a modal expressivism on which modal vocabulary doesn’t describe a special class of facts but makes explicit the material-inferential commitments already implicit in ordinary concept-use. Lewis (1969) developed a convention-based account on which language is coordinated through community-level conventions. Both are read here as picking up real social-coordinative features of language; the question this tradition puts to the account is whether the inferential and expressivist reading displaces the structural conditions or instead makes them explicit.

### 5.12.2 The Requirement
*Propositional transmission across the interval between minds.* Language transmits propositional content from one self-aware person to another across the interval that separates them. How the structural content of one mind’s model gets reliably transferred, imperfectly but systematically, into another’s has to be explained. The conditions of transmission have to be derived from the structure of what is transmitted (propositional content) and what is doing the transmitting (self-aware beings in a shared medium).

*Transfer of field-content.* What crosses the interval is a partial transfer of one body’s modal field into another’s, never the field itself. An adequate account has to locate language as that transfer rather than as a second structure alongside the field, so a corrupted transfer is the same channel turned against the receiver’s mapping, not a different kind of speech.

*The three structural conditions.* Distinct positions, persistent reference-bearing entities, and successive utterance and uptake—Space, Substance, and Time—aren’t features the linguistic situation happens to require. They are what propositional transmission consists in. The three have to be accommodated, or an argument supplied for why one can be dispensed with, and the necessity of each has to be derived: without distinct positions, no interval for a claim to cross; without persistent reference-bearing entities, no speaker or hearer remaining the same across the utterance; without succession, no before-and-after to the act of saying or being understood.

*Reference and predication minimum.* Any proposition combines reference (picking out what is talked about) with predication (saying something about it). Reducing language to reference alone, or to predication alone, won’t do; the minimum has to be accommodated. Reference and predication are the irreducible structural pair propositional content consists in, reference relating to entities and predication ascribing structure to them.

*Compositionality and embedding.* Propositional language must support propositions about propositions, claims about claims, and the indefinite extension Frege and Davidson identified. Restricting language to flat predication won’t accommodate that content; a capacity for structure-within-structure has to be available. The requirement fixes what speakers must be able to express. It leaves open whether every grammar supplies that capacity through syntactic recursion.

*Convention without arbitrariness all the way down.* Saussure correctly identified that the relation between specific signs and their referents is conventional at the surface. The surface conventionality has to be accommodated, but so does what is *not* conventional: what is conventional (which sounds or marks carry which meanings) has to be distinguished from what isn’t (the structural conditions any language must meet to carry propositions across the interval between speakers).

*Practice and form-of-life.* Wittgenstein correctly identified that meaning is bound to use in shared practices. That dependence has to be accommodated without reducing meaning to use, which means preserving what use does—coordinates a practice, calibrates speakers’ uptake, and supports rule-following—while explaining what use is for: tracking what is the case so that people can communicate successfully.

*Connection to consciousness, self-modeling, and meaning.* Language operates on what awareness (§5.1), self-modeling (§4.8), and meaning (§5.10) supply. Language has to be connected to these earlier capacities rather than treated as autonomous. Language grows from what self-aware beings need to do when they share a world and reach one another through propositions.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Shallow forms of signaling—pheromone trails, alarm calls, signature whistles, waggle dances—run below the depth of propositional embedding at issue here. Deep propositional language requires the self-aware threshold named at §5.1. Language isn’t one categorically unified phenomenon, and the gradient has to be accommodated: signaling is widespread, partial propositional structure may be available in some non-human lineages, and the deepest compositional capacity emerges most fully in humans.

*Substrate-independence at the structural level.* As with the other registers, the activity of propositional transmission can in principle be realized in different substrates. The recent emergence of LLMs presses the question concretely. What is substrate-essential has to be distinguished from what is substrate-independent: the compositional structure (substrate-independent) from the self-modeling that anchors transmission to a vantage (currently realized only in biological minds, with the structural status of LLMs an open question the account makes legible without prejudging).

*Surface-vs-deep distinction.* The structural conditions any language must meet to carry propositions aren’t the same as the surface grammars, lexicons, and inflectional systems of specific languages. Treating linguistic surface as constitutive collapses a distinction that has to be preserved, conditions deep, instantiations contingent.

They aren’t neutral constraints on every theory of language. In particular, whether propositional content has the proposed structural minimum, whether non-human communication is propositional, and whether language is substrate independent remain contested. This set is defended rather than presupposed.

### 5.12.3 Predictions
Self-modeling configurations that share a world must coordinate about what is the case. Where food is. Whether a partner is reliable. What threatens the group. What happened yesterday, what will likely happen tomorrow, what another mind is thinking. The content at stake is *propositional*: it has truth conditions, it can be confirmed or disconfirmed, and it persists across speakers such that those who weren’t there to witness what the proposition reports can still inherit it.

The structural account proposes that coordinated self-modeling systems may develop richer communication systems, including propositional transmission under some conditions. This isn’t a theorem that self-modeling and coordination always yield language, or that no other forms of communication can support coordination. The following features are proposed conditions for the book’s model of propositional transmission, not universal predictions for every possible communicating system.

It must have *distinguishable signs*. Different meanings must be carried by different signals, because one signal carrying every meaning would carry no meaning at all. Distinction is Spatiality: signals must occupy different positions in the space of possible signals.

It must have *sequential ordering*. Meaning must unfold across a before and after, because simultaneous delivery of all signs is indistinguishable from silence. Order is Temporality: which sign comes first, second, third affects what is said.

It must have *causal transmission*. The signal must move from speaker to receiver through something that carries it without dissolving it. Transmission is Substantiality: something persists from utterance to reception, or no reception occurs.

These three features are central to its analysis of transmission, but they don’t by themselves settle whether a system carries propositional content. Communicative systems can use sound, sign, gesture, chemical signal, or electrical pulse, and the status of bees, whales, non-human animals, and artificial systems as propositional communicators remains contested. The structural account offers a model of what would make transmission proposition-like; it doesn’t resolve every empirical classification. The return argued at §4.6.5 extends the reach on its named premise: the Conditions never lapse, and wherever a return of the occasion produces coordination-capable life under the relevant social and ecological pressures, propositional transmission, where it develops, runs on the same three structural axes.

Grammar recapitulates the three conditions at the level of parts of speech. Nouns name what persists at a position—Substantiality at Spatiality. Verbs name transitions—the motion of Temporality. Prepositions and case markers name the relations between positions—Spatiality and Temporality made explicit. Adjectives and adverbs modify what the noun and verb pick out. Every natural language ever documented has means for the functional distinctions that map onto the structural conditions, however its word classes are drawn, because a language lacking those means couldn’t carry the content those conditions make possible.

Propositional content has two components the grammar of every natural language distinguishes. Both are needed; neither alone makes a proposition.

The first is *reference*. A proposition must point to what it is about. Nouns, pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, and definite descriptions all do reference: they identify an entity persisting in Spatiality that the claim is to be made *about*. Without reference, a predicate floats free and says nothing, because there is nothing for it to be true or false of.

The second is *predication*. A proposition must say something about what it refers to. Verbs, adjectives, and predicate constructions all do predication: they ascribe a feature, an action, a relation, a state. Without predication, a referring term is a label, not a claim. *The sky* says nothing. *Is blue* says nothing. *The sky is blue* is a proposition, because reference has been joined to predication and the joint construction now has truth conditions.

A proposition is the minimum unit of propositional content because it is the minimum combination of reference and predication that has truth conditions. Anything less can’t be true or false. Anything more is built out of propositions. This isn’t an incidental feature of how language happens to work. It is what propositional content structurally is, and any system that carries propositional content must have it.

The same structural requirement explains a cross-linguistic fact otherwise puzzling. Evans and Levinson (2009) argue that many alleged linguistic universals are softer than once claimed, a sharp noun/verb distinction among them; yet no known human language lacks a way to refer and a way to predicate, despite enormous variation in morphology, phonology, and surface syntax. The reference/predication distinction survives their scrutiny because it isn’t a contingent universal but what having propositional content consists in. Languages differ wildly in how they mark the distinction, in what else they encode, in how rigidly parts of speech are separated. But a language without any way to refer and any way to predicate couldn’t carry propositions, and wouldn’t be a language.

Reference has one further structural feature every language must instantiate: it must include terms that point back to the occasion of utterance itself. The speaker, the hearer, the present moment, the shared surrounding space aren’t separately nameable the way ordinary referents are—they are where the utterance is coming from and going to, not what it is about. Deictic or indexical terms (*I*, *you*, *here*, *now*, *this*, *that*) fill this role, anchoring the transmission to the specific positions the two parties occupy. Without deictic reference, propositions could be transmitted but couldn’t hook onto the occasion that produced them. With it, the abstract reference-predication system becomes usable by speakers and hearers at particular positions in T and S. Every natural language has a deictic system because every language is used by speakers and hearers who must refer back to themselves, each other, and the situation they share in order for propositions to land at all (Peirce 1931–1958; Bühler 1934; Kaplan 1989; Levinson 2004).

A simple case shows what deictic reference does by showing what fails when it can’t land. Imagine a slip of paper found decades later, reading *Meet me here tomorrow at noon.* The proposition is grammatically complete and lexically unambiguous; reference and predication are both performed. Yet the note as found can’t tell anyone what it once told its addressee—which speaker is *me*, which place is *here*, which day was *tomorrow*. Spoken face-to-face, the same words land effortlessly because the speaker, the location, and the day are all present at the occasion of saying. Deictic reference is what lets a proposition ride on the structural specificity of the T–S position the utterance occupies; strip the occasion away and the proposition keeps its form but loses its grip.

*A note on scope.* The three structural features predicted here—distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, causal transmission—together with the reference/predication minimum and the deictic anchor follow from what propositional transmission consists in given the three Conditions at the depth a self-modeling configuration reaches. They are predictions of the structural account in the two-half sense flagged at the head of Chapter 5, not theorems derived from the proof of Chapters 1–2.

### 5.12.4 Confirmation
The structural argument predicts that any system carrying propositions must instantiate the same three structural features. The empirical record can’t prove that unrestricted claim by induction, but every studied linguistic case gives it a demanding test: cross-linguistic typology finds the same structural skeleton across thousands of unrelated languages. Greenberg (1963) identified word-order universals that correlate with how languages mark argument structure. Comrie (1989) and Croft (2003) documented recurring patterns in how languages encode tense, aspect, modality, and grammatical relations. Surface features vary: some languages are head-initial, others head-final; some mark case morphologically, others syntactically; some grammaticalize evidentiality, others handle it lexically. The deep structural features recur. The variation is on what structure already affords; structure itself is what makes the variation intelligible as variation within the same kind. The universal claim rests on the structural argument, not on induction; the typological record corroborates it across the human cases presently available.

Non-human communicative systems instantiate the same three structural features on their own terms. The waggle dance of honeybees encodes spatial information (direction and distance to food) through a temporally ordered sequence of body movements that causally influences receiving bees who then fly along the encoded vector (von Frisch 1967; Seeley 1995). Cetacean signature whistles identify individuals and coordinate group behavior across distances in a medium where vision is useless (Janik and Slater 1998; King and Janik 2013). Vervet monkeys use distinct alarm calls for distinct predators, and conspecifics respond with predator-appropriate behavior (Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler 1980). In each case the system has distinguishable signs, temporal ordering, and causal transmission, because nothing else could do the coordinating work these species need done.

The Chomsky/Tomasello debate about whether grammatical constraints are innate or emergent from communicative practice (Chomsky 1965; Tomasello 2003; Goldberg 2006) is a live dispute about the proximate source of human linguistic universals. The structural account is neutral on it. Wherever the specific constraints originate, the deeper requirement is located in what any communicative system must be—distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, causal transmission. Whether human brains come pre-equipped with those requirements or discover them again each generation through use, they obtain either way.

A sharp test comes from spontaneous language genesis. When speakers without a shared language are thrown together, they generate pidgins, which their children, on Bickerton’s account, expand into fully grammatical creoles (Bickerton 1981; Bickerton 1984). Deaf children in Nicaragua, brought together in schools in the 1970s and 1980s without a pre-existing sign language, spontaneously generated Nicaraguan Sign Language—and the children generated a grammar more complex than their first teachers used (Kegl et al. 1999; Senghas et al. 2004). The grammatical features that emerged weren’t taught and not copied from any existing language. On the structural reading, they emerged because anyone who needs to be understood by anyone else will, given a community and time, invent the features being understood requires—even when nothing outside them supplies those features. This offers a structural reading of what linguists call the poverty-of-the-stimulus argument (the claim that children’s linguistic input is too sparse to determine the grammar they end up with): the grammar children converge on needn’t be derived from insufficient input, because it is what propositional coordination structurally requires, and minds generate it whenever coordination is at stake.

### 5.12.5 Conclusions
