*Linguistic relativity is real at the surface and bounded at the depth.* Languages carve up the world differently at the level of content: color terms, evidentiality, tense granularity, and grammatical gender are famously variable (Boroditsky 2001; Lucy 1992; Deutscher 2010), and what a language forces a speaker to specify measurably shapes habitual attention and memory. But the effect is bounded by what every language must do anyway—distinguish referent from predicate, before from after, speaker from hearer; express negation, question, command, conditional. What varies is content; what is shared is structure. Sapir and Whorf correctly identified that languages shape thought within the space the structure permits; their critics correctly identified that the shaping can’t reach the structure itself. Each position is correct at its own level.

*Translation between languages.* The structural invariants make translation possible at the level of reference, predication, and relation; they do not guarantee an exact sentence-for-sentence equivalent. Concept boundaries, morphological economy, register, and sound can resist the rendering even where the proposition travels. This is why good translation is a genuine art, not a mechanical operation. The structure gives the translator something to carry. It does not carry everything for them.

*The overlapping domains of language and art.* Translating a legal contract carries the propositions forward with little loss; translating a poem carries the propositions but loses the sound and rhythm that constitute much of the work. Content that survives paraphrase is where propositional language is strongest; content destroyed by paraphrase is where art characteristically works. A single utterance can do both at once—poetry in any language is exactly this—but the two operations remain distinguishable, and understanding why is understanding why some things are said and others sung.

*Mathematical and logical languages place extreme constraints on what their notation is asked to carry.* Once a syntax, semantics, and background interpretation are fixed, formal notation can preserve selected relations with unusual precision: variables and constants refer, equations and propositions predicate, and operators and connectives mark relations. That’s why a proof or equation can travel across natural languages with relatively little change in its formal role. It does not follow that mathematics retains every feature of natural language, or that its content is independent of notation, interpretation, and practice. Mathematics gains its cross-linguistic reach by controlling those dependencies, not abolishing them. What travels most reliably is the specified relation.

*Propositional content must compose and permit embedding.* Coordination includes talking about other propositions: what someone said or believes, what would follow from what, what would be the case if some other proposition held. A language restricted to atomic propositions couldn’t carry everything self-modeling minds need to coordinate about one another’s modeling. This establishes a capacity to compose content and represent embedding (Frege 1892; Hauser et al. 2002; Pinker and Jackendoff 2005; Szabó 2022). It does not decide whether every grammar realizes that capacity through a syntactic operation properly called recursion, or whether iterative, paratactic, pragmatic, or other representational resources can sometimes do the work. Propositional transmission requires the capacity; its grammatical realization remains a live question.

*Writing gives temporal sequences a persistent spatial form and extends transmission across generations.* The three features can be instantiated in any substrate that preserves distinction, ordering, and causal transmission. Spoken language orders signs in time. Writing arranges persistent marks in space, while their production and uptake still unfold in time. T and S are not interchangeable; writing coordinates them differently. A language becomes writable when a usable system maps its distinctions and order into durable marks, and once written its transmission chain can extend across generations the speakers never meet. Law codes, scriptures, treaties, scientific results, and accumulated culture all ride on that coordination. The cognitive transformations Ong, Goody, and Havelock describe—abstract reasoning, historical consciousness, recursive self-criticism in literate cultures—are, on their accounts, downstream effects of letting propositional content persist at Substantiality across far more Temporality than speech alone could reach (Ong 1982; Goody 1977; Havelock 1986; DeFrancis 1989).

*Lying and the truthfulness baseline.* Reference and predication can be combined to produce propositions that don’t match the features they purport to describe. This separability is what lets language carry claims about what isn’t yet the case, what isn’t present, what is hypothetical—and the same separability lets it carry claims about what isn’t true. But deception is parasitic on reliability. If most propositions were unreliable, there would be no reason to attend to any proposition, and the coordination medium would collapse. Functional propositional transmission therefore requires a default of truthfulness, against which deception registers as deviation. Grice’s cooperative principle and Lewis’s convention of truthfulness name the coordination baseline; the structural account grounds why the baseline is required rather than merely customary (Grice 1975; Lewis 1969; Sperber and Wilson 1986; Williams 2002).

*Propositional content is used not only to describe but to do.* Austin (1962) distinguished constatives from performatives—utterances that perform actions (*I promise*, *I name*, *I pronounce*, *I apologize*) rather than describing states of affairs. The structural account covers both: propositional transmission is a coordination medium, and coordination includes reporting features of the world as well as instantiating new features of the coordination itself. *I promise to X* registers a commitment in the speaker’s model and is received into the hearer’s as a mutual commitment—a coordination feature that didn’t exist before the utterance. This is why speech act theory (Austin 1962; Searle 1969; Bach and Harnish 1979) has a natural home here: the medium was never only for description, because the coordination it serves was never only about the world as it stands.

*Language isn’t what makes a mind conscious, but it radically extends what consciousness can model.* Consciousness, on the identity argued at §5.1, is what sufficiently integrated self-producing life is like from within, and it needs no language—pre-linguistic infants and cats are the ordinary cases, and a language-less mind of that organization on another world would be another. But a mind with language can model what isn’t present, what hasn’t yet happened, what another mind is thinking, what would happen under conditions that haven’t obtained. Language externalizes the modeling capacity into a shared medium where minds can build models together that no single one could build alone. Science, mathematics, law, philosophy, and literature are precipitates of this extension. What a linguistic community can think isn’t the sum of what its members can think unaided; it is the sum plus everything the shared medium lets them construct in common.

*Analytic philosophy and the medium’s standards.* Reference pinned, predication precise, inference tracked across propositions—syntax, operations, semantic function, and inferential role audited at the strictness the structure permits. The discipline is internal to the medium: every analytic move is made *in* language, on the same three structural features any language must have, sharpened until the medium’s constraints become a method. The argument now in progress is itself an instance—the structural features the proof requires to state itself are the structural features language has, and the analytic practice auditing propositions is language being audited within itself.

Several positions in the analytic tradition of philosophy of language stand in specific relation to the account.

*Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, and teleosemantics.* Frege (1892) and Russell (1905) made the reference-predication distinction foundational to the analysis of propositional content; the structural account inherits it and adds the derivation—reference and predication are what propositional content structurally *is*, given T, S, Φ, and self-modeling minds coordinating within the medium. Wittgenstein’s (1953) private language argument receives a narrower structural grounding here: a sign whose correct application could in principle be checked only against one speaker’s private impression cannot acquire its standard of correctness from that impression alone. A code with only one actual user is not private in that sense; its signs can remain governed by repeatable or publicly specifiable criteria. Meaning-as-use (Wittgenstein 1953; Kripke 1982) and biological teleosemantics (Millikan 1984; Papineau 1987) both locate meaning in the practices and functions of using signs. (Teleosemantics (Greek telos, “end” or “purpose,” + semantics, “meaning”) is the view that a sign’s meaning is fixed by the biological function it evolved to serve—what the signal is for, in the sense that natural selection shaped it to carry that information—rather than by convention, causal history, or use alone. On this view, a frog’s neural response to a moving dot means “prey” because producing that response is the function the mechanism was selected for, whether or not the frog gets it right in any given case.) The structural account grounds those practices and functions in what coordination structurally demands, rather than in contingent features of any particular community or species-history.

*The criteria question, turned on its own vocabulary.* Wittgenstein’s criteria challenge isn’t met by grounding the private-language argument; it is met only when the same criteria pressure is turned on the terms this chapter itself uses. What are the criteria of application for *shared interiority*, or for two speakers having *the same region of modal field loaded under one label*? The answer is public and behavioral, exactly as the *Investigations* demands: two speakers share a region of field to the degree that they can be brought into agreement and correction across cases—sorting the same instances together, drawing the same inferences, repairing the same misunderstandings, recognizing the same uses as mistaken. Sameness of loaded possibility-space isn’t an inner comparison of two private samples, which is the move PI shows to be idle; it is the convergence of two public sorting-and-correcting practices, which is the only thing that ever counted as sameness of meaning. This also fixes what disagreement with the central claim would consist in—Wittgenstein’s test of whether a sentence has gone “on holiday.” To deny that language is inseparable from the structure it describes is to predict a working language some community could use—referring, predicating, understood—while lacking distinguishable signs, ordering, or causal transmission. The disagreement has cash value: produce the practice, or the claim stands.

*Quine on translation indeterminacy.* Quine (1960) argued that radical translation is indeterminate even at the level of gross reference—rival translation manuals can be equally compatible with all behavioral evidence. The account accepts the content-level indeterminacy Quine’s argument establishes and rejects its extension to structure. Fine-grained content (what exactly *gavagai* picks out) is Quine-indeterminate; structural features (that *gavagai* refers, that other terms predicate, that the language marks relations) aren’t, because those features are what having propositional content consists in. Quine was right about what translation can’t pin down and wrong if the indeterminacy is extended to the structure translation rides on. Some structural alignment can therefore survive precisely where an exact translation manual remains underdetermined.

*Searle’s Chinese Room.* Searle (1980) argued that a system manipulating signs according to rules can pass for linguistic without understanding. If so, the three structural features would be sufficient for sign-manipulation but insufficient for meaning-bearing language. The account agrees with Searle’s verdict and proposes the missing ingredient. Propositional transmission requires not only distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, and causal transmission, but self-modeling minds at both ends—minds for which the signs have content because they correspond to features the minds are already modeling from inside (§4.8). A sign-manipulating system without self-modeling has no content of its own, however well it mimics speakers who do; what its signs carry, they carry for the minds that read them, as a found note or a written law does. Searle was right that the room doesn’t understand, and the structural account offers a reason: understanding, on this account, requires a self-modeling interior, which the room lacks.

*Large language models, specifically.* Current systems trained on human text produce output in propositional form with remarkable fluency, passing many of the surface tests linguistic competence admits of. On the structural account, that fluency establishes successful sign-manipulation with distinguishable form, sequential ordering, and causal transmission. It does not by itself establish a self-modeling interior for which the signs have content. Current LLMs therefore remain compatible with the Chinese Room diagnosis rather than proven instances of it. Whether a current or future architecture has the relevant interior is an empirical and conceptual question the account doesn’t settle. If a system were built with it, the same structural features would carry content for that system as they do for any self-modeling mind. What the account rules out is only the claim that fluency alone is sufficient. Something has to be modeling something from inside for signs to become language §4.8, Bender and Koller (2020); Bender et al. (2021); Mitchell and Krakauer (2023); Chalmers (2023)].

*Kripke, Davidson, Brandom, Lewis.* Kripke’s (1980) causal theory of reference grounds naming in a causal chain from an initial baptism forward through a community—Substantiality persisting across Temporality through a linguistic practice, and the structural account explains why a causal-historical chain is available to carry a name.

Davidson’s (1984) truth-conditional semantics and principle of charity fit naturally once coordination across self-modeling minds is the frame: interpretation must assume shared structure because without it there is no translation to do. His deeper challenge is that to posit a scheme which organizes or carves an uninterpreted reality is to revive a third dogma, an unintelligible scheme-content dualism (Davidson 1974). It is met head-on by the inseparability argued above: the account sets no scheme over against a content, because language’s structure *is* the structure it carries, there being no other structure for it to carry. There is no uninterpreted Reality on one side and a carving framework on the other, waiting to be lined up from some vantage outside both; there is one structure, met under language from within. The dualism Davidson rightly rejects is one the account never had—what looks like a scheme answering to a content is a single structure registered in the medium that shares it. This answers the local charge about language, but Davidson’s pressure has a global edge the reply must also take: the book’s foundation speaks of a Reality all description answers to—the phrasing conceded at §5.12.1 (‘is exactly the kind of view that objection targets’)—and an *answers-to* can look like precisely the scheme-tracking-a-content the third dogma forbids. The edge is blunted once the register of the book’s realism is made explicit. What description answers to isn’t an uninterpreted content lying on the far side of the account, inspected from a vantage outside language and world; it is the single a posteriori datum the whole argument rests on—that change occurs, delivered with Cartesian certainty from within (§2.2.1)—together with everything the S5 lift of that datum makes constitutive (§7.1.7). The necessity of T∧S∧Φ is therefore not a mind-independent joint the account tracks across a scheme/content gap but a constitutive truth in the register §7.1.7 owns: it states what counts as there being an act, or a reality, at all, its only alternative being ∅. A realism of that register revives no dogma, because there is no neutral content for a scheme to organize and no standpoint outside both from which to line them up—the point pressed at §9.9 against Tegmark’s plenitude, that the account terminates inside Reality, not above it. What is discovered is discovered from within; the *answers-to* answers to what any act constitutively involves, not to a content held apart from the describing.

Brandom’s (1994) inferentialism locates meaning in inferential role, and coordination among self-modeling minds does require tracking propositions in their relations to other propositions—a demand the recursive, compositional structure already established meets. His sharper challenge is the modal expressivism running from Sellars: modal vocabulary, on that view, doesn’t describe a special class of facts but makes explicit the material-inferential commitments implicit in ordinary concept-use, so that *Reality is necessarily T∧S∧Φ* would be the explicitation of an inferential rule—from change-talk one may non-optionally infer time-talk—rather than a discovered feature of the world. The account doesn’t resist this by insisting the conditions simply run underneath; it grants the pragmatics and locates the disagreement precisely. Expressivism is right that the modal claim isn’t one more descriptive report ranged alongside empirical ones, and right that asserting it makes an inferential commitment explicit: from the presence of any act one may infer distinction, ordering, and persistence, and may not withhold the inference. But making-explicit and being-constitutive aren’t rivals here, because what the inference makes explicit is itself the constitutive structure—the rule holds, and holds non-optionally, only because its alternative is ∅ (§2.7, §7.1.7). The core vocabulary can then be given exactly the inferential articulation Brandom demands: to call something an act commits one downstream to its involving distinction, ordering, and persistence—what Space, Time, and Substance respectively do—and licenses upstream the inference to those same conditions from any act whatever; to call the structure necessary is to mark that these commitments can’t be discharged, their only release being that nothing is an act at all. That is a descriptive claim earned in the constitutive register (§7.1.7), not asserted in the special-fact register expressivism rightly deflates—the account grants Brandom the shape of concept-use and keeps its necessity, because the very commitment his articulation makes explicit is the structure the argument derives.

Lewis’s (1969) convention-theoretic account roots language in coordination equilibria; the structural account explains why those equilibria take T/S/Φ-shaped forms and not others.

*Universal grammar and usage-based accounts.* The Chomsky program presses that human brains come equipped with something strongly predisposing them to acquire language in the patterns languages take. The Tomasello program presses that the patterns are learnable from communicative practice given the right cognitive substrate. What neither side emphasizes enough is that the patterns are what they are because propositional transmission structurally requires them. Whatever pre-equipment the brain has would be for what the medium demands, and that it evolved by natural selection on a species living in a medium with the three Conditions wouldn’t be surprising. The structural requirement is upstream of both accounts, and neither is complete without it.

The structural conditions of linguistic communication are specified here; not every object-level question those conditions raise is decided. Which theory of reference—descriptivist, causal-historical, hybrid—best captures how particular terms attach to particular things; how pragmatic inference combines with semantic content; what individuates a language from a dialect; whether a given animal system rises to propositional language or sits below it—these remain questions for linguistics, philosophy of language, and further empirical work. Naming the structure of propositional transmission isn’t naming every feature of any particular language that instantiates it.

## 5.13 Technology
Technology begins wherever a creature or community recruits a repeatable arrangement to redirect what its unaided activity could do. It need not begin with an explicit or accurate theory: trial and error, imitation, embodied skill, inherited technique, and partial models can all produce working tools. More developed technologies externalize representations and procedures into writing, notation, instruments, computers, and networks, where other people can store, test, share, and recombine them. This is reach turned outward, not a rising above nature: the builder remaking the world remains part of the world and works through its constraints.

**[Identification]**

**Technology** · *Identification*

Technology is the organized use of materials, processes, skills, or representations to extend or redirect practical capacity. Its developed forms can externalize models and procedures into shared substrates—notation, instruments, machines, computers—making them persistent, queryable, transmissible, and recombinable beyond one body. The artifact stores a configuration that users can exploit; it does not contain objective modal structure itself or guarantee that the representation embodied in it is accurate.

*Status: Drive, learning, and practical reach make tool use intelligible but do not strictly entail technology. Successful technique may precede explicit understanding, and specific tools remain contingent on materials, transmission, history, and opportunity. The identification of technology with organized outward reach is a functional proposal defended by fit.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2), Knowledge (§5.4), and Language (§5.12)

Language (§5.12) was already a technology: the technology of shared interiority. Technology in the broader material sense generalizes that operation past the communicative register. Drive supplies the reach; a field accurate enough to predict an alteration supplies the map; Will commits to the alteration as a project. There is no third thing required, and no fork between speaking and writing. One can chip flint, speak, write, or not. The structural half is the availability of redirection once the field and the drive are deep enough, not a denial-trap for “technology exists.”

A self-modeling being with sufficient awareness has a model of Nature, which it inhabits. The model serves navigation and redirection. *Navigation*: anticipating what Nature will do, aligning action with what is possible, taking what Nature offers. *Redirection*: using the model to alter what Nature produces. Reasoning, knowledge, meaning, will, and language all involve navigation, while language already begins redirection in the communicative register. Technology generalizes redirection into the material register.

The depth at which the second function opens is the depth at which the being has, jointly, a model accurate enough to predict consequences of alterations and the agentive self-modeling required to commit to alterations as projects rather than as impulses. Both are reached at roughly the same depth of self-modeling: where the self-model integrates anticipatory simulation with goal-directed planning.

Animal tool use exists in shallow forms that lack one or both of these. Sea otters use stones to crack shellfish through learned association without sustained planning. Chimps termite-fish through behavioral routines that involve some anticipation but limited innovation across generations. New Caledonian crows manufacture and modify tools (Emery and Clayton 2004), closer to deep technology in planning and innovation, though without language to transmit refinement cumulatively. *Cumulative cultural technology* is tools used to make tools, refined across generations, taught between members and inherited. It emerges most fully in humans, who have both the depth of self-modeling required for cumulative refinement and the linguistic capacity to transmit knowledge across time. The depth gradient runs from learned association through planning through cumulative culture, and what tracks it is the level of awareness the organism has reached.

Technology is therefore a recurrent possibility for beings able to learn regularities and organize action through tools, not a structural consequence of consciousness as such. Accurate explicit models greatly expand what technology can do, but workable alteration can also arise through embodied know-how, imitation, selection among variants, and retained practice. Opportunity, materials, social transmission, and time remain independent conditions. The convergence claim is correspondingly modest: where agents can retain and improve successful interventions, technological repertoires can accumulate; no proof requires every sufficiently aware lineage to develop them.

*The Inversion.* The standard reading treats technology as instrumental: a tool of survival extending biological needs into the social-historical realm. On the account here, technology is the being’s outward operation: the inside model turned operative on Nature. The being redirecting Nature is itself a being within Nature, operating from no exterior position and using its model to alter what Nature produces, which is what dissipative beings have always done, now at a depth that includes itself in what it modulates.

*Externalization and the modal network.* Philosophy of technology and cognitive science describe external representations (Zhang and Norman 1994), cognitive artifacts (Norman 1991), distributed cognition (Hutchins 1995), extended cognition (Clark and Chalmers 1998), and material inscriptions (Latour 1986). The present framework groups these by a shared function: an artifact can preserve marks, procedures, measurements, or transformations that help users represent and navigate what is actual, conditional, or possible. What is externalized is therefore a *representation or usable procedure*, not the objective modal field itself. It may be accurate, inaccurate, incomplete, or uninterpretable without a trained practice. Notation, writing, instruments, and computers differ in what they preserve and what operations they support; together they can make knowledge materially durable and distributed without becoming a single knowing subject. Their portability rests on reliable causal and interpretive relations among substrates, users, and targets, not merely on every substrate instantiating the three Conditions. Computers are unusually flexible participants in this gradient, extending what people and institutions can store, calculate, search, and coordinate beyond what one unaided body can hold.

*Standardization as interoperability.* Externalized knowledge coordinates action only where different people, instruments, and systems can read one another’s representations. Shared technical standards reduce the translation work required at those boundaries. Measurement is a clear case. A decimal system allows many conversions to be inferred from one rule, while a system built from unrelated ratios requires more separate facts to be learned and retained. In mechanics, manufacturing, medicine, science, and transportation, incompatible standards can also duplicate tools, complicate training, and create opportunities for conversion error. The specialist can master that complexity, but mastery doesn’t show that the complexity is necessary; expertise is better spent on the real complexity of the object than on avoidable friction in the language used to describe and maintain it. This supports interoperability, not cultural uniformity. A common public standard can govern the domains that must coordinate while customary units remain available in ordinary life. Whether a particular standard reduces errors, training time, and duplicated equipment is an empirical question; the argument identifies the function to test, not the answer in advance.

*The internet and AI as modal network.* Two contemporary configurations of the modal network warrant marking by name. The internet is the modal network at civilizational scale: substrate configured to store, simultaneously, representations drawn from the modal holdings of very many bodies, readable and queryable across them—many individual fields pooled and interlinked without becoming one knowing subject. Where individual writing and individual instruments extended a single body’s modal representation, the internet extends the aggregated modal holdings of a civilization. The accuracy of what it represents depends entirely on the filtering apparatus between contributing bodies and shared substrate. With no filtering, the field carries the noise of every body that contributes, including lines the field never actually contained, dressed as lines it does. With strong filtering, it approaches what its best contributors hold. Social-epistemology accounts (Goldman, *Knowledge in a Social World* 1999; Origgi, *Reputation* 2018; Coady, *Testimony* 1992) describe the filtering apparatus a modal network requires if it is to function as knowledge rather than as noise. Large language models, trained on substantial slices of that aggregated substrate, are compressions of the modal network: they surface lines the inquiring body wouldn’t have hit alone and aggregate across more contributors than any individual could survey, while inheriting the underlying field’s noise and adding compression artifacts of their own: confident assertions on contested questions, generated lines the field never contained, smoothed-out disputes that look like consensus only because the training process flattens them (Bender et al. 2021; Ji 2023). The structural point is that AI is continuous with the prior gradient of externalization, not a break from it, and the user’s filtering apparatus must do work on AI output that it wouldn’t have to do on a direct corpus query.

*Responsible use constrains amplified reach.* The ethical problem isn’t intelligence or technical power as such. It is amplified reach detached from purpose, restraint, review, and answerability. A responsible use identifies what the system is asked to accomplish, limits what it may decide or do, preserves ways to inspect and correct the result, and leaves a person or institution answerable for the consequences. These requirements increase with the use’s scale, stakes, authority, and irreversibility. A playful image made for friends and an automated decision governing healthcare, employment, political speech, or physical force don’t require the same level of constraint.

*Assistance and substitution differ.* AI assists inquiry when it expands a person’s ability to ask, compare, verify, revise, or create. It substitutes for inquiry when it supplies a result the nominal author cannot reconstruct, evaluate, or answer for. Play remains a legitimate use; purpose need not mean economic productivity. The relevant failure is unattended generation at scale: output produced without proportionate judgment or responsibility whose costs of evaluation, correction, storage, and attention are shifted onto everyone who encounters it. Cheap generation becomes information-environment extraction when the generator captures the benefit of volume while the public bears the work of determining whether anything produced is reliable or worth receiving.

*The device paradigm and the disburdening ledger.* Borgmann (1984) names a distinction the exterior-modal-maps gradient leaves implicit, not one it can’t carry. A *device* delivers a commodity while concealing the machinery that produces it; a *focal thing* delivers it through visible engagement that carries skill, attention, and relation as constituents of the activity rather than as overhead to be eliminated. A microwave meal and a meal cooked from scratch both deliver food; only the second is a focal practice. But both are externalizations of the field, and the distinction Borgmann marks isn’t between technology and something outside it; it is between two things an externalization can do to the practice that held the modeling: retire it or preserve it. That is a real axis the gradient as stated doesn’t register, and the structural account gains rather than loses by marking it: the gradient measures reach, and Borgmann’s distinction measures what a given gain in reach retires. Read through the drive (§5.2), the two aren’t opposed. Disburdenment frees a subject from spending itself on already-met needs and so opens modal-field reach, which is gain; but reach and depth are distinct axes, and an externalization that delivers the commodity while retiring the focal practice expands what is available to the body without deepening what the body can itself do. The curiosity drive named at §5.2 persists through disburdenment rather than lapsing with it, which is why the device-form *captures* engagement rather than abolishing it: the same SEEKING orientation that would deepen a skill can instead be fed cheap proxy-data that simulates field-expansion without delivering a well-weighted field: the structural shape already flagged at §5.2 as an over-expanded field with unreliable weighting. Whether externalization becomes a gain or a hollowing depends on two things, neither supplied by the technology alone: first, whether capability and control are broadly distributed rather than concentrated in hidden machinery; second, whether people retain the practices named at §5.2—source evaluation, deliberate pruning, and focal practice—that turn expanded reach into deeper understanding rather than passive dependence on a device. *Holding On to Reality* (1999) carries the point into the digital register: read structurally, it identifies a real transformation in the texture and cost of engagement that digital externalization brings, not a break in the continuity of what technology is. The continuity claim survives as an account of what technology structurally *is*; what Borgmann adds is the ledger the celebratory reading omits: that every externalization disburdening a body of some modeling also retires the practice that held it, and whether the trade is gain is settled by arrangement and cultivation, not by the fact of continuity alone.

That same book sharpens the device/focal-thing distinction into a trichotomy worth engaging directly: natural information (a thing disclosing its own structure), cultural information (structure carried through skilled practice and tradition), and technological information (structure detached from any particular referent, freely substitutable, apt to be treated as reality’s replacement rather than reality’s report). The worry generalizes the disburdening ledger into a metaphysical substitution: a civilization saturated in technological information comes to treat the sign as the thing. On the framework here that substitution can’t go all the way down, because technological information is never a replacement *for* structure: it is a representation of structure held in a different substrate, as the externalization account above describes. What the trichotomy tracks correctly isn’t a threat to structure’s reality but a threat to a practice: natural and cultural information carry engagement as a constituent of accessing structure, while technological information can be consumed without any of that engagement, which is the disburdening ledger’s point restated at the register of information itself, not a further metaphysical cost beyond it.

The methodological result, stated for probability at §10.1.9: within a fixed modal frame, externalizations amplify the resolution at which the frame can be searched, simulated, and computed; they don’t fix the frame. Frame-fixing remains a conceptual operation. A being armed with a very powerful modal network can compute very precise answers within whatever frame is supplied; whether the frame is well-formed for the question isn’t something the network can settle.

### 5.13.1 The Dispute
The literature on technology has reorganized substantially across the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, with several principal positions still live. Each of these is engaged by name.

*Heideggerian critique.* Heidegger’s (1954) 1977 “The Question Concerning Technology” developed the most influential twentieth-century philosophical analysis: modern technology is *Gestell* (enframing) that reveals all of nature as *Bestand* (standing reserve), available for extraction and use. The position has been refined through Borgmann (1984), Dreyfus (1992), and the broader phenomenological-critique tradition. Heidegger is read here as identifying a real structural feature of how modern technology relates the subject to what it operates on, while supplying the structural reading: technology is the subject’s outward operation on structure it tracks, and the Heideggerian critique picks up the specific shape this operation takes when it loses contact with the wider structural conditions that constrain it.

*Borgmann’s device paradigm.* Borgmann (1984) is often filed as a refinement of Heidegger, but his distinctive contribution stands on its own: the *device paradigm*, on which modern technology systematically replaces *focal things and practices*—activities that gather skill, attention, and relation around a center, like the hearth, the table, or the played instrument—with *devices* that deliver the same commodity while making the underlying machinery disappear. Borgmann is read here as marking a real axis the exterior-modal-maps gradient leaves implicit—whether an externalization retires or preserves the practice that held the modeling—and that axis is engaged above rather than dissolved into the enframing critique.

*McLuhan and the extension-of-man tradition.* McLuhan (1964) treated technologies as extensions of human capacities—wheel as extended foot, writing as extended memory, electronic media as extended nervous system. The position has been refined through media-studies traditions (Postman 1985; Carr 2010) and through Stiegler’s tertiary-retention account of technical externalization (1998; 2011). The extension tradition is read here as correctly identifying that technology externalizes capacities of the subject, with the modal-map analysis supplying the specific structural reading: external maps extend the modal-modeling reach of the subject beyond what any single body can hold.

*Instrumentalism.* The instrumentalist account treats technology as a means: a tool extending biological functions, evaluated by what it accomplishes for the organism that wields it. The position is widely held both popularly and in much philosophy of technology (Bunge 1985). Instrumentalism correctly describes the means/end structure at the level of a single tool, while the structural reading supplies the conditions that make instrumental use available at all: the depth of self-modeling required for a subject to model the gap between what is and what could be, and to commit to closing the gap as a project.

*Social-constructionist accounts.* The social-construction-of-technology (SCOT) tradition (Pinch and Bijker 1984; Bijker 1995) and Latour’s (1987; 2005) actor-network theory developed accounts on which technologies aren’t neutral instruments but socio-technical assemblages shaped by, and shaping, the social relations they are embedded in. The position has been highly influential in science-and-technology studies. Constructionist accounts are read here as correctly identifying that specific technologies are conditioned by their social context, while supplying the structural reading: the *that* of technology—subjects at the relevant depth operating outward on structure they track—isn’t socially constructed, while the *what* of specific technologies is significantly so.

*Ellulian autonomy of technique.* Ellul (1954) developed the influential thesis that *la technique*—the rationalized organization of means—has become autonomous from human ends, with its own developmental logic that humans no longer control. The position has been refined through Mumford (1934; 1967), Winner (1977), and the broader critical-theory tradition. The autonomy thesis is read here as identifying a real structural feature—cumulative cultural technology develops along trajectories that exceed any single subject’s intentions—while supplying the structural reading: the trajectories aren’t autonomous from subject-level activity, but emerge from the accumulated outward operations of many subjects on the structure they jointly track.

*Marxist and political-economy accounts.* Marx (1867) and the Marxist tradition treat technology as embedded in modes of production, with productive forces and productive relations conditioning what technologies develop and how they are used. The position has been refined through Frankfurt School critical theory, Braverman (1974), and contemporary political-economy approaches. Marxist accounts are read here as correctly identifying that the social relations under which technology is developed condition its specific character, while supplying the structural reading: the underlying activity—subjects operating outward on structure—is what political economy conditions and channels.

*Existential-risk and longtermist accounts.* A contemporary literature (Bostrom 2014; Ord 2020; MacAskill 2022) treats certain emerging technologies—AI, biotechnology, geoengineering—as posing existential risks to humanity and emphasizes the long-term consequences of present technological decisions. This literature is engaged without endorsing all of its specific predictions: the structural fact that exterior modal maps amplify within-frame search without fixing the frame (stated above, and for probability at §10.1.9) supplies a usable framework for thinking about powerful tools applied within underdetermined frames.

*Posthumanist and transhumanist accounts.* Posthumanism (Haraway 1985; Hayles 1999) and transhumanism (Bostrom 2005; More and Vita-More 2013) develop sharply different accounts of what technology does to the human—destabilizing the human/non-human boundary versus extending and improving human capacities. The depth-gradient reading supplies a structural framework: technology is what subjects at the relevant depth do; what counts as human is one designation along the depth gradient; the relation between technology and the boundary of the human is structurally legible without prejudging the normative questions both positions raise.

*The AI-as-tool vs AI-as-agent dispute.* A contemporary dispute concerns whether sufficiently capable AI systems are best understood as tools (extensions of human capacities) or as agents (independent participants in a shared field). The structural reading is that the question is empirical at the limit: an AI system instantiating the self-modeling structure consciousness consists in (§4.8, §5.1) would count as an agent; one instantiating only the outward-operation structure of technology would count as a tool. Whether and when the threshold is crossed is currently underdetermined.

### 5.13.2 The Requirement
*Outward operation on tracked structure.* Technology is the subject’s outward operation: the inside model turned operative on the structure it tracks. Any account must locate technology at this structural fact rather than at any specific class of artifacts. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish navigation (tracking what structure does) from redirection (using the model to alter what structure produces), with technology constituted by the second function.

*Joint conditions of accuracy and agentive depth.* The second function opens at the depth where the subject has, jointly, a model accurate enough to predict the consequences of alterations and enough reflective agency to commit to alterations as projects rather than as impulses. Any account must accommodate both conditions rather than treating technology as the product of either alone. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish modeling accuracy (the subject’s grasp of structure) from agentive commitment (the subject’s capacity to hold alterations as sustained projects) and identify the joint depth at which technology becomes available.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Any account must accommodate the gradient from shallow tool use to cumulative cultural technology rather than treating technology as one categorically unified phenomenon. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish what runs at each depth.

*Exterior modal maps.* One form of technology externalizes the subject’s modal map—substrate configured to represent modal structure outside the body, persistent across the reasoning interval, queryable, recombinable, transmissible across subjects. Any account must accommodate the modal-mapping function rather than treating technology as merely instrumental in the narrow sense. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish ordinary tools (extending bodily capacities) from exterior modal maps (extending the subject’s modeling reach), with notation, writing, mathematical formalism, instruments, and computers forming a gradient of exterior modal maps.

*Substrate-portability.* Interior maps (in the subject’s body) and exterior maps (in shared substrate) are configurations of the same medium; a computation in silicon can substitute for one in neurons where reliable causal and interpretive relations carry the representation across substrates, not merely because both instantiate the same structural conditions. Any account must accommodate the substrate-portability rather than treating biological and artifactual modal mapping as essentially different. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish substrate-independence at the structural level (the same modal-mapping activity can run in different media) from substrate-specific implementation (specific brains, specific computers).

*Fixing the modal structure remains conceptual.* Any account must accommodate this limit rather than treating sufficiently powerful tools as solving every problem they can be applied to. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the methodological result (stated for probability at §10.1.9 and in general above).

*Cumulative cultural transmission.* Cumulative cultural technology requires subjects that can both refine inherited tools and transmit refinements to other subjects. Any account must accommodate the social-transmission dimension rather than treating technology as the achievement of individual subjects alone. The structural requirement is that the account explain cumulative technology from the joint conditions of self-modeling depth (for refinement) and linguistic transmission (for inheritance), with both conditions required for the cumulative-cultural phenomenon human technology centrally consists in.

*Connection to consciousness and self-modeling.* Technology operates on what awareness (§5.1), self-modeling (§4.8), and reasoning (§5.6) supply. Any account must connect technology to these upstream registers rather than treating it as autonomous. The structural requirement is that the account connect technology to what self-modeling subjects do when their modeling has become accurate enough to support alteration of what they model.

*Convergence claim without strict modal entailment.* The structural claim is that the mind turning operative on what it tracks is what the depth gradient makes available; specific instantiations of technology remain conditional on lineage history and circumstance. Any account must accommodate this convergence-without-necessity reading rather than overpromising strict modal entailment. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the structural availability of the technology-function (made available by depth and conditions) from the historical contingency of specific technologies (not entailed).

*Coherence with morality and political life.* Technology operates in fields of subjects whose conditions either sustain or starve continued participation (§5.14). Any account must accommodate the moral and political stakes rather than treating technology as ethically neutral. The structural requirement is that the account make the bridge between technology and morality legible: the subject’s outward operations on structure include operations that affect other subjects, and what counts as legitimate operation is what morality (§5.14) and the political extensions in Chapter 6 supply.

*Form-of-life under device conditions.* The modern device paradigm (Borgmann 1984) exhibits a characteristic form: outward operation that delivers a commodity while disburdening the user of engagement with the focal practice that once produced it—the furnace displacing the hearth, the recorded performance displacing the concert, the processed meal displacing the household kitchen. Any account must accommodate this form-of-life dimension—distinguishing focal practices (where engagement with the thing is the point and requires skill, attention, and communal form) from devices that commodify the output and conceal the machinery—while locating both within the same structural account. The structural requirement is that the account identify when and why the device-form predominates.

*Accountable deployment.* The greater a technology’s scale, stakes, authority, and irreversibility, the stronger the requirements on its use. An adequate account must distinguish technical capability from legitimate authority and preserve purpose limits, review, correction, and responsibility wherever a system acts on other people’s conditions. Execution can be delegated without automatically delegating judgment: the party that selects an objective, authorizes deployment, and receives its benefits remains answerable for what the system sets in motion.

*Repairability, resilience, and retained control.* A technology doesn’t fully extend a person’s or community’s capacity if continued use depends entirely on a provider that alone can inspect, repair, alter, or recover it. An adequate account must therefore include maintainability, interoperable records and contact, access to competent repair, and resilience against foreseeable failure. This doesn’t require every user to master every device. It requires that specialized knowledge, parts, documentation, and legal authority remain sufficiently available for the technology to be maintained without permanent dependence on the seller that supplied it.

### 5.13.3 Predictions
Technology emerges as a structural tendency wherever those structural conditions obtain. A subject who persists in a structure, has needs, and can understand that structure will encounter gaps between their present state and what they need. That is a problem. A subject with sufficient depth who understands the structure and encounters a problem will use that understanding to close the gap, given opportunity, materials, and time. That is technology—understood here as a convergence claim about what reflective subjects with drives do when they inhabit a structure they can understand and have what is required to act on that understanding, not as an occasional achievement.

The prediction is one of recurrence under conditions, not strict modal entailment from the proof of Chapters 1–2. Wherever subjects of the relevant depth exist in sufficient proximity to structure—and have access to materials, social transmission, and the time required to elaborate what they understand—technological elaboration will occur. The specific forms technology takes are contingent tokens; the elaboration itself follows reliably under the conditions named, with the qualifier that lineages lacking opportunity, materials, or transmission may be unable to instantiate it even where the recursion-depth condition is met.

Technology therefore belongs to the emergence arc framed at §4.7 and traced in biology at §4.8. It is a threshold: the point at which a subject’s understanding turns outward and the subject begins redirecting structure rather than merely navigating it. The structural account also predicts the form externalization takes under conditions of rapid scale: where cumulative externalization advances faster than focal engagement deepens, the device-form predominates—technology delivering commodified outputs while concealing the means of production (Borgmann 1984). This isn’t a failure of the technology function but a predictable attractor state within it, following from the same dispersion and transmission conditions the availability prediction names.

The same account predicts an information-environment pressure from low-cost automated generation. Where producing an item becomes much cheaper than evaluating it, and where the producer gains from volume while the audience bears the costs of checking and sorting, unattended output will tend to proliferate. The prediction isn’t that abundant generation is intrinsically bad: play, experimentation, accessibility, and inexpensive creation can widen possibility. The failure appears where generation is detached from judgment and distributed at a scale that exports its costs of attention, verification, and correction onto others. Systems that preserve provenance, review, rate limits, and responsibility should produce less of that cost-shifting than systems optimized for volume alone.

### 5.13.4 Confirmation
The empirical record across independent disciplines supplies convergent support for the prediction across multiple temporal scales. Comparative cognition bears on the depth threshold identified above. Animal tool-use is widespread—sea otters cracking shellfish on stone anvils carried between feedings, chimpanzees stripping twigs to fish termites, New Caledonian crows manufacturing hooked tools and remembering which tools worked on which kinds of larvae, octopuses carrying coconut shells across the seafloor to assemble shelter (Goodall 1968; Hunt 1996; Finn et al. 2009; Rutz et al. 2010). What none of these cases demonstrates is *cumulative* culture in the strong sense—the modification of inherited tools across generations such that later cohorts build on improvements they didn’t invent. Chimpanzee termite-fishing has remained essentially the same across the decades it has been observed, and evidence for cumulative refinement of corvid tool techniques across cohorts is limited and contested. Cumulative culture is a practice that *gets better* across generations, because each cohort inherits not raw technique but a tradition already under modification. It is rare-to-absent below the depth of self-modeling that lets a subject model not only the tool but the practice of tool-modification, the reasoning that produced the modification, and the transmission that carries it forward (Tomasello 1999; Boyd et al. 2011; Henrich 2015; Laland 2017). The threshold named above is the one below which redirection of the medium doesn’t compound, and above which it does. Below it, redirection occurs at a single level; above it, redirection itself becomes subject to redirection, and the lineage’s reach into structure begins to compound.

The archaeological record shows the threshold being crossed. Tool use in the hominin lineage predates anatomically modern humans by over two million years—Plummer et al. (2023, *Science*) secure Oldowan tools (the earliest stone-tool tradition) at 2.9 million years from Nyayanga, Kenya; the earlier Lomekwi 3.3-million-year claim (Harmand et al. 2015) has been contested on dating and assemblage grounds (Domínguez-Rodrigo and Alcalá 2016), but Plummer et al. (2023) secure the broader claim independent of that dispute. The threshold for some redirection is well below *sapiens*. Fire control appears by at least 400,000 years ago. Agriculture emerges independently across at least seven distinct regions between roughly 10,000 and 5,000 BCE (Diamond 1997)—what the emergence account expects: not a single invention diffusing outward but a threshold reached independently where the conditions were met. Writing emerges independently in Mesopotamia, China, and Mesoamerica. On this account each emergence is the same threshold crossed under independent conditions, a feature of what self-modeling deep enough to redirect is rather than of any particular cultural lineage. The pattern supports recurrence under similar pressures rather than strict necessity: which subjects cross the threshold first, in what form, and at what timing remain shaped by historical contingencies—geography, available materials, climate, demographic scale, neighboring traditions, sequencing of prior crossings. The structural prediction is that the threshold gets crossed wherever the conditions hold long enough; the contingencies determine the path each crossing takes.

The acceleration of technological elaboration over the past three centuries is consistent with the recurrence the account predicts once people model their conditions explicitly and acquire the material and social capacity to act on those models at scale. The Industrial Revolution developed through increasingly precise control of energy gradients; the digital revolution through the representation and manipulation of information in new substrates; artificial intelligence through attempts to model and reproduce increasingly complex forms of inference and self-modeling. These histories don’t show that any particular revolution, timing, or technical form was necessary. They support the narrower claim that technological reach compounds when inherited representations, instruments, and institutions allow later work to operate on the products of earlier work. Historical contingencies determine which developments occur, where they occur, and who controls them.

### 5.13.5 Conclusions
*Technology is internal to Nature.* It is what living beings do when they understand enough about their conditions to alter them. A wheel extends a person’s reach through Space. A vaccine redirects causal processes in Substance. An algorithm automates a sequence of inferences. None of these tools comes from beyond Nature; each is Nature acting through living beings that have learned how its conditions work.

This opens rather than settles the standard ethical question. Technical reach and economic productivity don’t by themselves establish that an arrangement is good. Evaluation requires further premises about whose interests and standing count, how benefits and risks are distributed, which forms of participation matter, and who may authorize exposure to the consequences. The technology account supplies the descriptive variables—amplified capacity, externalized cost, dependence, control, reviewability, and reversibility. Morality (§5.14) and Chapter 6 supply the normative and political arguments. Ownership and control are therefore central downstream questions, not verdicts derived from the definition of technology.

*Some technologies become conditions of participation, not merely optional tools.* Writing extends memory beyond one person’s lifespan; mathematics extends calculation; networks can extend access to knowledge and coordination. Where institutions route education, work, public services, or communication through a technology, lack of access can exclude a person from those practices. The descriptive dependence is real. The conclusion that access is owed requires the standing and participation premises argued later. The 4E cognition tradition (embodied, enacted, embedded, and extended, Clark and Chalmers 1998; Clark 2008) supplies one account of how thinking can extend into tools, records, and practices while remaining attributable to the person or organized system using them.

Access without retained control is incomplete. A tool that becomes indispensable while remaining inspectable, repairable, or recoverable only by its provider extends capability and creates dependence at once.

This also identifies a descriptive sustainability constraint. A technological system that irreversibly depletes materials it requires, destroys the institutions and skills that maintain it, or concentrates control until cooperation fails undermines its own continuation. That is enough to call it self-undermining relative to its continued function. It isn’t enough, without further normative premises, to establish duties to future subjects or a complete environmental ethic. The temporal argument from §4.7 clarifies the irreversibility risk; §5.14 and Chapter 6 determine what present subjects owe in response. Borgmann’s device analysis adds a separate empirical question: whether expanded reach retires practices and capacities worth retaining.

*Responsible AI use keeps amplified reach answerable.* Current AI systems can extend inquiry, composition, accessibility, and play. They can also generate claims, decisions, and public material faster than users or audiences can evaluate them. Ethical use is therefore purpose-bound, constrained, reviewable, and attributable.

Transparency is necessary but not sufficient. Disclosing that AI was used establishes provenance; it doesn’t establish understanding or responsibility. In education and authorship, the relevant test is whether the person can reconstruct the reasoning, verify the claims, explain the revisions, and answer for the final result. The assistance/substitution distinction applies to automation more generally. Removing unnecessary labor expands possibility only where the time, safety, or productive capacity released by the technology reaches the people whose work and shared infrastructure made the gain possible; otherwise technical disburdenment can coincide with a loss of practical freedom.

A system may calculate, classify, recommend, simulate, or draft without thereby acquiring authority to determine which objectives should govern, whose interests count, or which risks other people must bear. At the institutional register, the automated system can participate in the bearer’s procedure without becoming the bearer (§6.3): attribution runs through the offices, authorization, records, and review structure that selected and maintained the system. If an artificial system eventually satisfies the conditions for genuine agency, its standing becomes a further empirical question; uncertainty about that future threshold doesn’t dissolve responsibility for present deployments.

*The AI question is internal to the framework.* Whether artificial systems can have an inside-vantage of their own remains open to further confirmation (§5.4); what technology adds is that *humans building AI represents mind attempting to instantiate its own conditions in another substrate*.

A scope clarification is needed at exactly this point. The conditions for *life* were named at §4.8—a closed self-producing recursion coupled to sustained energy throughput, instantiated in the biological case by membrane-bounded chemistry that produces the components that produce the membrane. The depth at which awareness becomes operationally registered was named at §5.1. The claim is that *the structural conditions*—closure, throughput-coupling, self-modeling at sufficient depth—are what matter, not the *substrate-specific* implementation in which biology happens to instantiate them.

Whether silicon systems can instantiate the conditions is the open empirical question, and it has two readings kept separate here. On the *literal* reading, an AI system would need to be *biologically alive* in the sense that follows the biological substrate to its detail—membrane-bounded autopoiesis, metabolic self-repair through chemistry; on this reading, present-day AI systems aren’t candidates and the question reduces to whether artificial life in the strict autopoietic sense is possible. On the *functional* reading, what is required isn’t the biological substrate specifically but the *structural conditions*—closure of the recursion against the medium, sustained energetic throughput coupling, recursion that folds back deeply enough that the recursion registers itself from inside; on this reading, silicon isn’t ruled out in principle, but no system has yet been demonstrated to instantiate the combination of closure, sustained throughput, and self-registration those conditions require.

The account isn’t neutral between the two. The account of life at §4.8 fixes the constraint as structural rather than chemical—closure, throughput-coupling, and self-modeling by whatever mechanism realizes them—so the literal reading is a rival the account rejects, not a branch it leaves open. What stays genuinely open is the empirical question inside the functional reading: whether any system, silicon or otherwise, instantiates closure, sustained throughput, and self-registration together. What the account forecloses is the imprecise version that elides the distinction. Whether silicon-substrate systems can instantiate either is an empirical question that the engineering will eventually answer; whether the question is structurally well-formed isn’t—it is, and the conditions under which the answer would be yes are supplied here.

The methodological result applies directly (for probability, §10.1.9): exterior maps—including the most capable AI systems available today—amplify the resolution at which an existing modal frame can be searched and computed, but don’t fix the frame.

Technology read structurally is mind elaborating through subjects that have learned enough about the medium to direct it, never standing outside Nature even when the elaboration externalizes itself into substrates the subject didn’t produce.

## 5.14 Morality

Morality is about what subjects owe one another once they meet as beings with welfare, agency, relationships, and stakes of their own. The descriptive facts matter: another creature’s distress can be evidence of what an action is doing to it, and its authorization can be evidence of how it understands its own interests. But facts about aversion and possibility don’t yield duties by themselves. The bridge defended here is a reciprocity and equal-standing premise: like stakes receive like consideration unless a relevant difference justifies unequal treatment, and no agent’s first-person access gives its interests a moral privilege merely because they are *its* interests. Non-maleficence, beneficence, autonomy, and justice are developed as implications of that bridge under different conditions, not as deductions from distress alone.

The recurrence of aversion to pain, terror, coercion, deprivation, abandonment, and being treated as property helps identify a common practical floor. The moral presumption against imposing them follows only once subjects’ comparable stakes are granted comparable standing. Consent can then alter what would otherwise be impermissible within limits of information, competence, voluntariness, scope, effects on third parties, and revocability; it isn’t the sole source of legitimacy in every emergency, dependency, or incapacity case. An aversion to what is done to oneself is evidence for a claim under the reciprocity premise. An aversion to how others live doesn’t by itself confer authority over them. If this moral bridge holds, the political version is developed at §6.14.

**[Identification]**

**Morality** · *Identification*

Morality is the domain of reasons and claims governing how agents may treat subjects with welfare, agency, relationships, and stakes of their own. The account’s positive orientation is fostering: accurately attending to those dimensions and sustaining or enlarging them where one has reason and standing to act. Its limiting orientation is non-corrosion: not damaging, commandeering, or disregarding another’s protected interests without adequate justification.

*Status: Drive and Meaning supply first-person stakes and instrumental “oughts” relative to ends. They do not entail obligations to anyone else. The two-place moral result requires the explicit reciprocity/equal-standing premise: relevantly similar stakes count alike regardless of whose they are, unless a relevant difference justifies different treatment. That bridge is defended through consistency, mutual exposure, and the instability of claimed self-exemption. Readers who reject the bridge can accept the upstream metaphysics without contradiction. The account rests on two premises it does not derive, and they are independent: this bridge, and the life–consciousness identification at §5.1, whose conditionality the felt side of the moral relation inherits.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2), Meaning (§5.10), and Life (§4.8)

Shared exposure is the closure-and-throughput account of §4.8; the field-expansion drive is taken up at §5.2. The Chapter 11 inversion is taken up at §11.9.1.

Drive supplies directed activity, and Meaning supplies weighted ends. Conditional on an end, means can be better or worse suited to achieving it: if the organism is to eat, keep warm, or survive, some actions are required. This is practical or instrumental normativity. Calling it a one-place “ought” is useful only if the register remains explicit; the fact that an organism pursues an end doesn’t prove that it morally ought to pursue it, much less that another agent owes assistance. Honor, consequence, standing, and principle are therefore not merely disguises of biological compulsion. They are candidate accounts of the bridge from stakes and action to moral reasons.

Around other subjects, practical compulsion doesn’t automatically widen. Each subject can remain organized around its own ends. The two-place ought therefore begins only when a further standard is accepted: first-person location alone isn’t a relevant difference between like stakes. Consistency then forbids an agent from treating its own aversion, agency, or claim as decisive while treating the relevantly similar stake of another as nothing. This is the reciprocity bridge argued below. What institutional consequences follow if it succeeds is a further question (Chapter 6); those consequences aren’t packed into the metaphysical description of Drive.

*Configurational force.* Harm isn’t a label stamped on from outside. Where a complete configuration of exposure is metaphysically sufficient for an aversive interior—this subject, this act, this field, at this depth—Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4) applies: no complete realization of that configuration lacks the outcome. Strict Actualization (§2.9.4) then gives the actual distress from the actual configuration, without a further addition. The distress is the configuration showing through. The theorem doesn’t make any particular harm necessary simpliciter, and it doesn’t establish sufficiency on its own; that remains the fit-based burden. What it does fix is the arrow. Different subjects are affected in different ways because they are different complete configurations: different trained environments, different depths, different standing weights already in the field. Some outcomes are occurrent and pass; some persist as long-lasting or traumatic standing weights, the field after the event still carrying what the event installed. That persistence is why a wrong is no less a wrong for going undetected, and why the aversion at issue is the standing kind.

**[Proposition]**

**Wrong** · *Proposition*

A wrong is an unjustified failure to give a subject’s protected welfare, agency, relationships, or standing the consideration the reciprocity bridge requires. A subject’s own aversion is important evidence of its welfare and will, but it is neither necessary nor sufficient for every wrong: undetected injury, exploitation, betrayal, discrimination, and status degradation can wrong without an occurrent aversion, while some aversions concern conduct a subject has no authority to control. Severity can vary with the magnitude, duration, reversibility, and kind of interest impaired; cognitive or self-modeling depth does not by itself determine how much the subject morally counts.

*Status: Drive identifies stakes and aversions; the moral binding force comes from the equal-standing/reciprocity premise, not from aversion alone. This is a substantive normative account defended by its fit across welfare, agency, relational, and standing cases. It is not a corollary of the modal proof.*

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14) and Drive (§5.2)

The modal account clarifies two mechanisms without fixing the whole moral domain. A subject navigates a partial representation of what is possible (§5.4), and another agent can alter what that subject can reach or what it takes to be available. The S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5) means the wrongdoer doesn’t rewrite objective possibility itself. It doesn’t mean every welfare, relational, status, or distributive wrong reduces without remainder to the two frustrations named at §5.11.

**[Corollary]**

**Two Modes of Wronging** · *Corollary*

No agent alters whether R can admit a line merely by wronging someone. Two especially important mechanisms of wronging can nevertheless be distinguished without treating them as an exhaustive moral theory.

1. *Against reach.* A really possible line is made unavailable from where the subject stands. Coercion, confinement, deprivation, and exclusion work here.

2. *Against mapping.* The field the subject navigates by is corrupted, along any axis it registers. A real line is concealed; a line that is not there is supplied; what a line requires is misrepresented (X is necessary for Y when it is not); or what a line leads to is misrepresented (Y will follow from X when it will not). Deception, concealment, and the manufactured field work here.

These mechanisms often overlap and can help explain coercion, confinement, deprivation, deception, and manufactured necessity. Other wrongs may be best described through welfare, relationship, status, or fair-distribution concepts even where “reach” and “mapping” can be applied at a high level.

**Dependency routes:** both modes—Wrong (§5.14) and Will (§5.11); unchanged modal admission—Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5)

The false dependency deserves separating from the others, because it is the form that recruits rather than blocks. Concealing a line removes an option; supplying a false necessity leaves every option in place and reroutes the subject’s own willing through a condition that was never required. The subject then selects freely, by its own lights, within a field built to return one answer. That’s why a manufactured necessity does more work than a manufactured impossibility, and why it is harder to detect from inside: nothing is missing from the field, and the route it reports is the one the subject would have chosen had the dependency been real.

A false contingency behaves differently again, and the contrast explains which corruptions last. To say that if you do X then Y will follow is to assert a consequence the subject can test by doing X. The claim generates its own disconfirming evidence, and compliance is what exposes it: the subject acts, the promised consequence fails to arrive, and the field corrects itself. A false necessity generates no such evidence. Complying with a requirement never tests whether the requirement held, because only the route not taken would have shown it, and the subject who believes the route foreclosed has no occasion to take it. Corruptions of the contingency axis are therefore self-limiting under action, while corruptions of the necessity axis are self-sealing: obedience furnishes no counter-instance, and the absence of a counter-instance reads from inside as confirmation. A promise can be broken and known to be broken. A requirement can be false for a lifetime and never once be caught at it.

Two further consequences are worth drawing out, because each is easy to get wrong in the other direction. Deception isn’t the lesser wrong for leaving the world untouched: it attacks a frustration a subject could often answer for itself, since a line unmapped is a line selection never ranges over (§5.11). And neither mode requires that the subject notice. The aversion at issue is a standing weighted branch rather than an occurrent response (§5.2), so a reach quietly closed or a field quietly narrowed is a wrong on Wrong’s own terms, undetected.

This also names one part of what the political chapter inherits. Where wronging operates by reducing another’s reach or corrupting its mapping, arrangements assessed by how far they extend reach answer to that same structure rather than to a separate standard imported for politics (§6). Welfare, relational, status, and distributive wrongs retain the broader scope fixed by Wrong.

Beings that can share what is the case with each other (§5.12) come available to each other as more than information channels, as subjects: exposed, vulnerable, mutually registering. What they owe each other in that exposure is what morality names. Moral wrongness goes beyond preference violation. The experience of being wronged carries the form of a claim: one that persists regardless of whether the agent who acted acknowledges it, and one that demands a response Nature itself doesn’t supply. That claim-pattern is diagnostic: it reveals features of the moral domain that any adequate naturalist account must accommodate.

Two subjects persist, occupy genuinely different positions, and meet across an exchange that can’t be undone. One acts; the other is acted upon. Distinction, persistence, succession (Space, Substance, Time) aren’t conditions moral life happens to require. They are what morality’s subject matter consists in; what makes the encounter moral is the bridge.

The same fact, in the native vocabulary: morality’s positive orientation is fostering another being. A being is a life met from the inside (§5.2): one that drives, registers its own condition, and feels (§5.3); the closed self-producing life (§4.8), met as the one whose life it is. Fostering is the choice, made from inside one’s own life, to act on real attunement to what would sustain another and let it deepen. *Foster* carries the anti-paternalism: one can’t foster what one hasn’t seen clearly. And it covers the full range, from gentle nurture to fierce defense, according to what the other being actually requires. Its negative axis is corrosion: damaging another being, or acting on one’s projection of what fosters it rather than attending to what does.

This attunement has a phenomenological floor. Beings read themselves, and the readings are what we call feeling. The structural account predicts a reductive identification of the major affects with the dimensions along which a being registers its own condition: *pain* with damage as it lands; *fear* with anticipated damage not yet landed; *anxiety* with ongoing registration without resolution; *grief* with damage already done; *joy* with deepening—flow opening, the recursion taking on more capacity.
