These are stronger identifications than contemporary affect science endorses (each affect remains contested among representational, evaluative, and sensory accounts, Tye 2008; Klein 2015; Kurth 2018; Ratcliffe 2008), and the section doesn’t require the strong reading to do its moral work. What it does require is the weaker unifying claim those debates leave intact: each affect is the being’s own situation surfacing as what it is to be that being right now, not commentary on the situation from outside it. Each being is therefore continuously broadcasting its own conditions. To foster another is to read those readings: the fear showing where the current is unstable, the grief what it has lost, the joy where it is opening.

What ordinary speech calls *feeling someone’s energy* is this kind of reading across beings. The empathic-accuracy and thin-slicing literatures (Ambady and Rosenthal 1992; Ickes 2003) document that observers recover information about another’s state from brief integrated impressions of face, voice, posture, breath, and movement-rhythm at rates above chance, with effect sizes that scale with attention and exposure. What folk vocabulary calls *energy* is the actual physiological and informational state of the being those signals emerge from, not a second substance flowing alongside the physical, but the physical state the broadcasts make legible. The phrase tracks something real, even though the implied metaphysics (auras, fields, fluids) is mistaken.

Given the reciprocity bridge, the standard categories of moral philosophy follow from this structure rather than entering as unrelated primitives. Non-maleficence (the duty not to harm) begins from another subject’s affective broadcasts as evidence of what an act is doing to them; harm isn’t merely a value an external observer projects. Beneficence (the duty to foster) applies the same equal standing to the fact that beings persist by throughput, not inertia, and that one being can genuinely deepen another’s life when the action is read accurately.

Autonomy is the consequence of a structural epistemic asymmetry: a subject ordinarily has access to its own conditions that external observers can’t match (though that readout is lossy, §5.3), which makes the subject’s own authorization the most reliable available proxy for what would foster it. Consent is autonomy’s operational form—the authorization made public and verifiable, with *informed*, *voluntary*, and *competent* naming the conditions under which the subject’s self-knowledge can be trusted as the basis for action by others. (Consent’s authorization is directed, not merely aligned. It runs from a subject to a specific act by a specific agent; it isn’t two independent preferences that happen to coincide. A subject who privately wants what an agent goes on to do hasn’t thereby authorized the agent to do it, since the agent couldn’t have verified that private alignment and didn’t act on the subject’s own say-so. What releases the claim the reflexive aversion protects is the directed relation itself—this subject authorizing this act by this agent—not a coincidence between an unspoken preference and an act performed without reference to it.) Read against the will account (§5.11), these conditions are the axes of free will turned outward: to corrode another being’s field of possibility is to attack either its *field* (by deception or miseducation, so that the outcomes it weighs aren’t the real ones) or its *latitude* (by coercion or force, so that outcomes correctly weighed can’t be acted on); consent fails under either, the first defeating informed competence and the second voluntariness. The field-attack prohibition is scoped the same reflexive way the claim against being wronged is. What deception corrodes is a subject’s grip on its own possibilities, so the claim to a true field reaches only as far as the field the subject navigates for itself. A truth sought as an instrument to dissolve another subject’s possibilities falls outside that claim: the murderer at the door, demanding to know where the hidden victim is, has no claim to the information he would use to seize a latitude that isn’t his to take. The lie that turns him away corrodes nothing the moral relation protects, because the only interest it crosses is his interest in committing the wrong. Information isn’t owed as such; it is owed as a condition of a subject navigating its own life, never as a weapon against another’s.

Slavery is the limit case of the latitude-attack: not a single coerced choice but the standing seizure of another being’s entire latitude (the whole field of outcomes it might weigh held permanently beyond its power to act on), one being treating another, whose refusal is owed exactly the respect its own is owed, as though that refusal carried no weight at all.

Mill’s harm principle (Mill 1859) captures one implication: a subject’s freedom to direct its own course extends until that course begins to corrode another’s, because freedom and the limits on it both answer to distinct subjects in shared exchange.

Once equal standing is granted, the dyadic form of the relation is symmetric. Each subject’s refusal receives the same consideration unless a relevant difference justifies otherwise; what one being may not do to another without authorization is what no being may have done to it on merely indexical grounds. Reciprocity is therefore not a second fairness constraint added after the bridge but the bridge expressed between two subjects. It has a mutual-holding shape, but its normative ground is the explicit equal-standing premise applied to shared exposure, not the Modal Convergence theorem (§5.4), whose formal scope is collectively held knowledge.

This mutual subsistence has embodied forms that predate the signs and norms later used to articulate it. Sexuality (§5.8) is one early site: the attraction-pole’s reach of one being toward another, registered before language or principle mediates it. The more mediated couplings—language (§5.12), art (§5.15), and explicit moral exchange—extend embodied intersubjectivity without making sexuality the universal origin of recognition.

Distinct operations carry this reciprocity from the dyad outward, and each rests on machinery already developed. One is empathy: the body running another’s situation as a counterfactual on its own valence field (§5.3), where the simulation lands as feeling on the other’s behalf because, mechanically, it lands as feeling about a possible-self. The reach of empathy is bounded by the modal depth of the body running it (the breadth of stored possibility from which counterfactual situations can be drawn), and that depth is modal memory in the sense of §5.3, with all of memory’s selectivity and partial coverage. What we can simulate is what we have stored as possible; what we have stored as possible is what experience and inheritance have left in the network; so the empathic reach of any body is necessarily narrower than the field of subjects to whom morality must answer.

Another operation is shared exposure. When bodies share a modal field densely enough—a family, a household, a community—what happens to one can register in the others because their simulations include one another. The collective-protective response is the felt form reciprocity can take at the communal scale: *how do we prevent this from happening to any of us?* It may fire before argument or codification, though domination and exclusion show that overlap never guarantees it. This helps explain why grief is communal, why family and home concentrate moral weight, and why the dread of being alone can be the dread of unshared exposure.

A further operation extends judgment past the community boundary. The same evolved machinery that makes solidarity easier inside a group can make wariness easier outside it; communal reciprocity doesn’t, on its own, scale past those whose bodies feel like *us*. The extension depends on the section’s explicit equal-standing commitment: relevantly similar exposure carries the same moral weight whether or not empathy fires. Another being’s conditions matter because the bridge assigns comparable standing to the comparable feature, not because an agent happens to resonate with it. Where recognition fires, the mattering is felt; where it doesn’t, the premise still governs.

*The prudential egoist doesn’t escape by changing the grammar of their demand.* The earlier formulation needs a limit. An agent can treat resentment, protest, and retaliation as nothing more than prudential responses: *don’t deceive me because I will impose costs if you do*, not *don’t deceive me because I have a claim against it*. That posture doesn’t yet contradict itself. A conditional threat is intelligible as a preference backed by power, and there is no warrant here to pretend that every expression of resistance secretly contains a normative assertion. The performative argument therefore does not establish that a subject’s standing depends on every agent acknowledging it, nor does it turn the pure prudential demander into a wanton merely because they refuse moral vocabulary.

What the prudential gloss can’t establish is an exemption from the relation. It can explain why the egoist resists being corroded; it cannot make corrosion cease to be what it is for the subject on its receiving end. The agent’s preference and retaliatory capacity change the expected consequences of acting against them, but neither changes the fact that the same act uses another exposed subject against that subject’s own registered aversion. Standing is fixed by that relation, not conferred by the agent’s willingness to speak its name. The ground of the claim is negative and reflexive, exactly as Wrong scopes it: a subject’s registered aversion to what is done to *it*, never anyone’s positive preference about what to do toward another. Preferences about others’ conduct or others’ lives ground nothing; the aversion to one’s own corrosion grounds everything the relation protects. And the only release from a subject’s claim is the one the subject itself provides: consent, autonomy’s operational form (above). A claim belongs to the exposed subject, not to the agent who would act against it, so nothing on the agent’s side (prudential posture, indifference, hostility, or refusal of moral vocabulary) can waive it; only the subject’s own authorization can. The egoist may decline to *recognize* the standing, and may in that sense remain unmoved by its claim; that is a failure of moral alignment, not a discovery of a space outside morality.

The performative line accordingly has a narrower but firmer role. Where an agent presents their demand as a demand for justified treatment, condemnation, blame, or respect, they already invoke the reciprocal standing they deny to another, and the denial is performatively unstable in the sense made precise at §3.3. Where they instead present only a threat-backed preference, no such contradiction follows, but neither does a justification: force can explain compliance without supplying a reason why corrosion is permissible. Three things the earlier dichotomy compressed are therefore distinguished: the moral claimant, whose claim presupposes reciprocity; the prudential egoist, whose preference may be coherent but doesn’t discharge or defeat another’s standing; and the wanton, who lacks the formed second-order will from which full moral agency operates. *Status: fit on the structure (§4.8) identifies what mattering and wrong are; the performative argument exposes the inconsistency of normatively voiced denial; neither makes a pure prudential preference into a moral premise.* Where empathy supplies the affective engine and shared exposure supplies the natural generalization, structural reciprocity supplies the rule that carries the verdict across difference, distance, and unfamiliarity. Consent operationalizes the reciprocity at the dyadic scale; communal practice operationalizes it at the field scale; institutional structure operationalizes it past the community boundary. The same exposure logic appears across all of them; only the means of honoring it change with scale.

These operations carry reciprocity outward universally, but they don’t exhaust the moral relation, and a position that should be kept apart here rather than absorbed is the partial register Frankfurt named. Frankfurt (2004) argued three things. *First*, that what one agent owes its beloved isn’t derivable from the impartial principles owed to subjects in general. *Second*, that a parent’s reasons toward this child, a friend’s toward this friend, a partner’s toward this partner are reasons because the caring has formed, not because impartial reflection has endorsed them. *Third*, that their partiality is not a defect to be corrected against the universalist baseline, but the proper shape of moral weight along the actual depth of an agent’s commitments. The structural account agrees and locates the phenomenon: where shared exposure runs through one being’s modal field densely enough that the simulation of another’s situation lands not as a possible-self among many but as a possible-self the being cannot release without losing what it is, the felt-best branches it tracks for that other carry weight no impartial accounting can match or substitute. Partial reasons aren’t exceptions the universalist framework tolerates, but neither are they derived from it, and the distinction to hold is between what the field *locates* and what it *grounds*. The structural field predicts and locates the phenomenon at the level of kind: that intense partial attachments will arise, and where, since the densest regions of mutual modal exposure are both where their affective mass collects and where a history capable of forming such an attachment can run at all. What the field doesn’t do is ground the attachment at the level of the particular. Why this child, this friend, this partner rather than another isn’t read off any regularity, impartial or structural, but fixed by the particular history through which the caring formed; that history is the caring’s own ground in Frankfurt’s sense, not a value the field assigns. The field marks the conditions under which a particular caring can take hold without deriving which caring does, and it is the latter that Frankfurt calls irreducible. Locating a phenomenon isn’t absorbing it, and it is only the locating the account claims.

The verb leaned on so far (*foster*) points to the same strand from another angle, and Frankfurt’s account of caring and volitional necessity is what names it. To care about another being is, on Frankfurt’s reading (1988; 2004), not to have judged that one ought to care but to be the kind of being whose will is now shaped around the caring: invested in a way that isn’t freely revisable from moment to moment because the investment has become part of what the will is. The fostering described so far is this kind of investment surfaced as action: not impartial benevolence executed by a being that could just as well not have, but the doing that follows from a will already organized around the other’s continuation. Frankfurt’s *volitional necessity* (Luther’s *here I stand, I can do no other*) names the limit case: the agent who can’t betray what they care about is differently situated, morally, from the agent merely required not to. A being whose modal field has integrated another’s persistence into the conditions of its own continued integration can’t release that other without releasing part of itself; the impossibility isn’t weakness of will or compulsion from outside but the shape the will has taken from the inside. *Foster*, restated, is the action of a will so shaped, and marking it as volitional rather than merely structural supplies a register for the moral weight caring itself carries, beyond and through whatever structural reciprocity also requires.

Frankfurt’s wanton presses on a real boundary here. The wanton is a creature who acts on first-order desires without ever stepping back to ask whether those desires are the ones it wants to be moved by: no second-order will, no commitment, no caring as a structural feature of the will. The wanton meets the mutual-exposure conditions structurally: it is a being, it broadcasts its conditions, it can be harmed and helped. The structural rule binds *toward* the wanton (it is owed non-corrosion like any other subject), but the question Frankfurt presses is whether the wanton can be a full moral agent *from* whom such treatment is owed in return. The structural account’s answer is that the wanton is a subject for whom the impartial rule applies as patient but only marginally as agent, because the volitional strand is what carries the agent-side weight: a being that has formed no caring has nothing in its will the moral relation can grip from inside. This doesn’t strip the wanton of moral standing; it locates the asymmetry exactly. Patiency follows from being one that registers its own conditions; full agency follows from being one whose will has taken the shape caring imposes. The structural and volitional strands run together for ordinary agents and come apart precisely at the wanton, which is why Frankfurt’s case is diagnostic rather than peripheral.

The field’s weights are asymmetric in a way that may help explain a recurring moral priority. Catastrophic harms can’t always be recovered from; smaller gains can often be deferred or replaced. Loss aversion is one empirical index of that calibration: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) identified the asymmetry, and Tversky and Kahneman (1992) estimated a coefficient near 2.25 in the conditions they studied. The magnitude isn’t universal: it varies with context and may attenuate or disappear for small, symmetrically framed stakes (Gal and Rucker 2018). Moral cognition need not inherit the coefficient directly for the broader asymmetry to matter. The medical maxim *primum non nocere*, negative formulations of reciprocity, deontological prohibitions, and the comparative intensity of blame all place avoiding serious harm before producing a comparable benefit. That pattern is consistent with, though not proved by, a modal field calibrated in a survival regime where catastrophic branches demanded special weight.

Justice extends the picture from pairs to fields. Subjects exchange inside a shared field of further subjects whose conditions either sustain or starve continued participation; the maintenance of those conditions (food, shelter, safety, time, and access to learning and exchange) is the field-level analogue of throughput. None of these standard categories enters as a primitive. Each is the structural account projected into the standard analytic vocabulary.

Read this way, morality admits empirical investigation in the way a science does. Cross-cultural anthropology, evolutionary biology, developmental psychology, and primatology have been investigating its conditions for decades, finding, provisionally, not a cultural accident but a recurring pattern tied to the conditions under which subjects meet subjects. That empirical work has always rested on metaphysical commitments (that subjects genuinely persist, that their exchanges connect them, that harm and care are tracked rather than projected), and the structural argument makes those commitments explicit. As in §4.8, what looks like philosophy arriving alongside science is science absorbing metaphysics as a guiding constraint on its own further discovery.

The *ought* isn’t derived from the *is*, because the *is* of a feeling body reading its own possibility space is never value-neutral: the body’s modal field (§5.4) is always already valenced (§5.3), every stored possibility carrying the body’s own stake in that branch, and the *felt-best branch* within it is what the body registers as its own one-place ought. The functional/biological normativity of any living being upgrades to specifically moral normativity through the structural one-place→two-place move developed in detail at §5.14.3: once mutual registration between beings of the same kind comes online and the equal-standing premise is granted, the felt-best branch ceases to be only the felt-best for the body running the simulation and becomes the felt-best for the field of bodies the simulation reaches.

*A held disagreement.* A robust non-naturalist such as Parfit holds that normative truths are irreducible facts not constituted by any attitudes or structural relations, however universal or mutually recognized (*On What Matters* III 2017). Nothing here refutes that view. The grounding offered here instead joins real stakes among mutually exposed subjects to the explicit reciprocity/equal-standing premise traced at §5.14.3. If that premise is accepted, the robust-realist alternative isn’t needed for the moral work that follows. The book’s objective₂ is therefore a structural-relational account with a stated normative bridge rather than an overlooked robust non-naturalism; Chapter 12’s entries on the Moral Gap (§12.3.9) and Divine Command Theory (§12.3.11) inherit this same stance.

To feel wronged, then, is the recognition that a vulnerability has been exploited: one subject’s exposure used against them by another in an exchange neither can take back. The heat isn’t illusion. It is the affective register of the structural fact: Substance has met Substance, and the conditions of mutual exposure that any genuine encounter requires were violated rather than honored.

### 5.14.1 The Dispute
The literature on morality is among the most active in contemporary philosophy, with disputes running across metaethics, normative theory, moral psychology, and practical ethics.

*Moral realism and its varieties.* Robust moral realism (Boyd 1988; Brink 1989; Shafer-Landau 2003; Enoch 2011) holds that moral facts exist mind-independently, as objective features of reality. Naturalist realism identifies moral properties with natural ones; non-naturalist realism (Parfit 2011; Scanlon 2014) treats moral facts as a *sui generis* category. Moral realism is right that morality isn’t purely conventional. What grounds that on the structural reading isn’t a separate normative realm but facts about distinct subjects in shared exchange, grounded in the structural conditions of intersubjective coupling.

*Anti-realism, error theory, and expressivism.* Mackie (1977) developed error theory: ordinary moral discourse presupposes objective moral facts, but no such facts exist, so the discourse is systematically false. Blackburn (1984; 1993) and Gibbard (1990; 2003) developed expressivist alternatives on which moral discourse expresses non-cognitive attitudes rather than describing facts. The positions remain influential. Error theory correctly identifies how hard it is to sustain stance-independent, intrinsically prescriptive moral properties, but the further claim that no moral facts remain doesn’t follow: the structural facts about subjects meeting subjects aren’t eliminated with those properties. Expressivism picks up real features of moral psychology while underspecifying what the expressed attitudes are tracking.

*Constructivism.* Korsgaard (1996; 2009), Street (2006; 2012), and the constructivist tradition hold that moral norms are constructed through procedures of practical reason rather than discovered as mind-independent facts. Constructivism correctly identifies that moral norms emerge through agent-level activity rather than from a Platonic realm. What the structural reading adds is that the activity through which norms are constructed is itself constrained by structural facts about what subjects need to do to remain subjects in shared exchange.

*Parfit on reasons and persons.* Parfit’s *Reasons and Persons* (1984) and *On What Matters* (2011) develop positions canonical to contemporary normative theory. *Triple Theory*: that the best formulations of Kantian contractualism, Scanlonian contractualism, and rule-consequentialism converge on a common set of fundamental moral principles, with moral progress as the progressive discovery of that convergence. Parfit correctly identifies the convergence pressure at the level of best-case formulations. On the structural reading, the reciprocal-coupling floor defended here on the equal-standing premise is one candidate explanation of what the three traditions converge toward.

*Virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism.* The three principal normative-theory traditions organize most contemporary normative debate: virtue ethics (Aristotle; MacIntyre 1981; Hursthouse 1999; Annas 2011), deontology (Kant 1785; Korsgaard 1996; Scanlon 1998; Kamm 2007), and consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Sidgwick, contemporary defenders Singer 1979; Kagan 1989; Norcross 2020). Each captures real features of moral practice; each generates counterintuitive results in specific cases. These are read as three operations on the same modal field (§5.4) that the moral case coordinates across subjects.

Virtue ethics tracks the *cultivated-field* operation: a body whose modal field is dense enough and accurately calibrated enough that the morally relevant features of a situation come into view before deliberation begins—what older traditions called wisdom and what virtue ethics formalizes as character. Deontology tracks the *structural-reciprocity* operation: the floor of non-corrosion that follows when mutual registration is governed by equal standing—what the account treats as the negative-rule core and what deontology formalizes as rules and rights. Consequentialism tracks the *trajectory-comparison* operation: the forward-running of modal branches the field already contains, with the body’s valenced weights assigned across each branch—what the modal account treats as one mode of practical deliberation and what consequentialism formalizes as outcome aggregation.

The same body runs all three operations simultaneously, because the field carries cultivated content (virtue), structural floor (deontology), and forward-running branches (consequentialism) at once. Where the three converge, ordinary cases settle without effort; where they diverge, the traditions disagree about which operation should govern. On this reading none is fundamental; each partially articulates one of the operations the moral case runs on the modal field. The trolley problem and its relatives are the cases built so those operations come apart.

*Moral particularism and prima facie pluralism.* Dancy (1993; 2004) argues for reasons-holism: a consideration that favors an act in one configuration of surrounding features can oppose it, or drop out of relevance entirely, in another—pleasure taken in another’s suffering doesn’t favor the act the way ordinary pleasure does, and no feature carries a fixed valence assignable independently of what else is present. Moral judgment, on this reading, is a form of situational perception rather than the application of a codifiable rule, and the demand for exceptionless general principles that deontology and consequentialism both presuppose is a demand particularism denies can be met by any moral theory whatsoever. Ross (1930) reaches a related but weaker conclusion from the opposite direction: a plurality of genuine, non-derivative prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, self-improvement) can conflict in a given case, with no algorithm ranking them in advance; what one’s actual duty is, all things considered, is fixed only by judgment exercised on the case at hand, never read off a governing formula. Grant the holism at the level Dancy and Ross are describing: which of the three operations a case calls for, and how the structural-reciprocity floor actually cashes out given the configuration of facts present, is exactly the work of the cultivated-field operation virtue ethics already names, not a mechanical output the structural floor delivers in isolation from judgment. What isn’t granted is the further claim that the floor itself carries no fixed content beneath the case-by-case variation: non-corrosion of another subject’s field of possibility is invariant across every configuration particularism’s holism ranges over, exactly as the structural-reciprocity operation requires, even though which specific act counts as corrosive in a given case is precisely the situational question Dancy is right to say no advance valence table can settle. Particularism is right about how the floor is applied and wrong, pressed to full generality, about whether there is a floor to apply.

*Frankfurt’s reasons of love and volitional necessity.* Frankfurt’s work (1971; 1982; 1988; 2004) develops a position that cuts across the three-traditions division rather than occupying a place within it. *Reasons of love*—the partial reasons one has for a beloved’s good simply in virtue of loving them—are, on Frankfurt’s account, irreducible to the impartial considerations shared by virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism. This tradition is read here as tracking a real axis the three traditions leave underspecified—the first-person normative weight of what an agent has identified with most fully, operating alongside the reciprocal-coupling norms defended here on the equal-standing premise—and Frankfurt’s hierarchical account is engaged in full at §5.11.

*Evolutionary debunking and moral nativism.* Joyce (2006) and Street (2006) developed evolutionary debunking arguments: moral beliefs are products of selection pressures unconnected to moral truth, so even if there are moral truths, our beliefs aren’t reliably connected to them. Haidt (2012) developed moral-foundations theory on the moral-psychology side. Debunking arguments raise a real challenge to specifically realist accounts. The structural response is that morality isn’t a separate normative realm vulnerable to evolutionary debunking but the structural shape of subjects meeting subjects, with the evolutionary pressures producing moral psychology operating on the same structural conditions morality’s subject matter consists in; what selection doesn’t supply is the equal-standing premise.

*Hume’s is/ought gap.* Hume (1739–1740) 2000 argued that one can’t derive ought from is: normative conclusions don’t follow from purely descriptive premises. The position has been refined and contested across centuries. The structural reading agrees. A feeling body supplies one-place stakes rather than value-neutral description, but the move to duties between subjects still depends on the reciprocity/equal-standing premise.

*Moral relativism.* Cultural and individual moral relativism hold that moral truth is relative to the cultures or individuals that produce it. Harman (1975; 1996) developed influential relativist positions; Wong (2006) developed pluralistic accounts that combine relativist and universalist elements. Relativism correctly identifies real cross-cultural moral variation. Variation in moral *content*, on the structural reading, is consistent with universality of moral *structure*: the structural fact of subjects meeting subjects operates everywhere, with specific norms being culture-conditioned articulations of how the meeting is to be conducted.

*Care ethics and feminist moral philosophy.* Gilligan (1982), Noddings (1984), Held (2006), and the broader care-ethics tradition developed accounts on which moral relations of care and dependency are central to moral practice rather than peripheral. Care ethics correctly identifies real moral relations the dominant traditions have understated. The cross-current reading of affect above supplies the structural support: fostering another subject includes care for it, which requires reading its conditions accurately.

*Ubuntu and relational personhood.* Southern African moral philosophy in the Ubuntu tradition (Tutu 1999; Menkiti 1984; Gyekye 1997; Metz 2007; Metz 2011) holds that personhood isn’t a given but an achievement realized through relationship with others—captured in the Nguni aphorism *umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu*, a person is a person through other persons. Menkiti’s strong formulation holds that moral status itself accrues incrementally through a lifetime of participation in community norms and obligations, so that personhood is ontologically, not merely developmentally, a social product. Metz’s more moderate formulation locates rightness in the promotion of harmony, understood as a combination of identity (a shared way of life, a sense of common purpose) and solidarity (mutual goodwill, disposition to aid), and reads wrongness as whatever produces discord between persons or degrades an individual’s communal way of relating. The convergence with the structural account is real and substantial: both read morality as constituted through the relation between persons rather than residing in an isolated individual’s private states, and both name a self that is only fully itself in relation to others as the moral achievement worth pursuing. The frameworks part where Menkiti’s version presses furthest. On the structural account, what grounds moral status—being a subject with welfare, agency, or stakes of its own, under the equal-standing premise—is already fully present in a subject prior to any relational achievement. So an infant, a stranger encountered for the first time, or a person a community has failed to integrate is already owed the structural floor, regardless of what relational history has or hasn’t yet accrued. What Ubuntu’s lifetime-achievement reading correctly identifies isn’t the threshold for moral status but the trajectory of the cultivated-field operation virtue ethics already names, extended to its properly social register. A person’s cultivated capacity to read and be read by a community deepens across a life. But that deepening is growth in what an already-existing moral subject can do, not the constitution of the subject’s standing to begin with. Metz’s harmony-as-identity-plus-solidarity reading fares better against this seam: identity and solidarity name relational goods the structural account already locates as fostering, scaled to the community register, not conditions on standing itself.

*The is-of-life and biological-functional normativity.* A tradition from Aristotle through contemporary work (Foot 2001; Hursthouse 1999; Thompson 2008) holds that biological functions supply a kind of normativity—a heart that fails to pump is malfunctioning, a creature whose flourishing is impaired is *worse off* in a sense not purely descriptive. This tradition identifies the functional-biological normativity already named. The structural upgrade is that moral normativity proper requires the two-place mutual registration that turns one-place functional norms into structures binding distinct subjects.

*Animal moral status and bioethics.* A live literature investigates the moral status of non-human animals (Singer 1975; Regan 1983; Korsgaard 2018), the bioethics of medical decisions (Beauchamp and Childress 2019), and the standing of subjects with different capacities. Standing shouldn’t track one scale of self-modeling depth. Sentience may ground welfare interests; agency may ground autonomy claims; relationships and dependency may generate further duties; equal standing constrains how those differences may be used. Cognitive depth can change which interests a being has and how an action affects them without turning greater cognition into greater basic moral worth.

### 5.14.2 The Requirement
*Distinct subjects in shared exchange.* Moral life consists in distinct subjects—living beings meeting one another across exchanges that can’t be undone. Moral structure has to be built on this fact, with its normative bridge stated, rather than on premises silent on intersubjective coupling. Distinction, persistence, and succession, Space, Substance, and Time, aren’t conditions moral life happens to require but what its subject matter consists in.

*Two-place mutual recognition.* Moral normativity goes beyond biological function when one subject can recognize another as a subject. How one-place functional norms become two-place moral norms has to be explained. Mutual recognition supplies the relation and the evidence; the reciprocity/equal-standing premise supplies the normative bridge between beings able to grasp what their actions would do to another who experiences from within as they do.

*Overlapping modal fields.* When bodies’ fields overlap densely enough, what happens to one can register as potential harm to each body whose simulation includes the others, though overlap never guarantees it. An adequate account has to explain collaboration, reciprocity, trust, and rule-following as responses generated within that overlap rather than as posits added to pair-relations, and it has to treat harm as a contraction of live possibility the other is averse to, not only as occurrent damage.

*Reading another’s condition.* What ordinary speech calls *feeling another’s energy* tracks the physiological and informational state of the being whose signals are being read. Treating moral cognition as mere projection or inference from purely external signs misses this readability. Moral perception begins in reading another’s condition, with affective expression as direct evidence of what an action is doing to its subject.

*The fostering-vs-corroding axis.* The account’s positive orientation is the choice to foster another being; its negative orientation is corrosion, including action based on a projection of what fosters rather than attention to what actually does. Treating moral evaluation as the application of decontextualized rules won’t accommodate this axis. What has to be preserved is the anti-paternalist condition—one can’t foster what one hasn’t seen clearly—and the full range of fostering, from gentle nurture to fierce defense, according to what the other being actually requires.

*Derivation of standard moral categories.* Non-maleficence, beneficence, autonomy, consent, the harm principle, and justice should follow as derivations rather than enter as primitives. Treating these as foundational posits skips the derivability that has to be shown. Given the equal-standing bridge, each has to be derived from the underlying structural facts: non-maleficence from affect-broadcasts as direct evidence of what is being done; beneficence from currents persisting by throughput; autonomy from the epistemic asymmetry of self-access; consent from autonomy’s operational form; the harm principle from one subject’s course corroding another’s; justice from field-level maintenance of throughput conditions.

*The is/ought distinction.* The *is* of life already contains one-place functional normativity: outcomes can be better or worse for the organism relative to its persistence. That observation doesn’t close the specifically moral gap by itself. An adequate account must explain why descriptive premises silent on life miss the first kind of normativity and why the upgrade to two-place obligation still requires mutual registration plus the reciprocity/equal-standing premise.

*Depth-graded interests, equal basic standing.* Different capacities generate different welfare, agency, relational, and autonomy interests; sentience may ground claims against suffering while deeper self-modeling supports more extensive claims about authorship and consent. Cognitive depth can therefore change what harms a subject and what consideration its interests require without determining how much the subject basically counts. An adequate bioethics must track those differences without either drawing a simple species boundary or turning cognitive depth into a hierarchy of basic moral worth.

*Field-level extension.* Subjects exchange inside a shared field of further subjects whose conditions either sustain or starve continued participation. Treating morality as pair-relations alone won’t accommodate this field extension. Justice has to be derived from field-level analogues of throughput—food, shelter, safety, time, learning, exchange—with the maintenance of those conditions as the field-level extension of fostering.

*Coherence with the rest of the chapter.* Morality (§5.14) is one register among others (§5.2–§5.17), connected to feeling (§5.3), the modal-depth account of will (§5.11), and language (§5.12). Treating ethics as autonomous from moral psychology and moral metaphysics won’t accommodate these connections. Moral practice has to be derived from features developed elsewhere in the chapter: feeling as the cross-current readable register, language as the medium of moral discourse, modal-depth will as the basis for consent and responsibility.

*Robustness to supernatural withdrawal.* With the inversion (Chapters 10–11) foreclosing the supernatural anchors classical religious accounts of morality have relied on, morality has to survive the withdrawal rather than collapsing into relativism, nihilism, or error theory. Its account must combine natural facts about distinct subjects in shared exchange with an explicit normative bridge that doesn’t require supernatural supplementation.

### 5.14.3 Predictions
Morality concerns the world from one particular angle rather than a separate domain added to it: the angle at which one parcel of Substance registers another as something that persists, is distinct from itself, and can be affected across an exchange that can’t be undone. Persisting subjects meeting persisting subjects supply morality’s subject matter before any code is written. Moral obligation appears only when that relation is taken up through a normative standard such as the reciprocity/equal-standing premise defended here.

The constituents are real: persistence, distinction, asymmetric exchange, and the welfare and agency of the subjects involved. Moral codes don’t invent that subject matter, though they can organize and evaluate it well or badly. The stronger claim—that these facts bind agents under equal standing—depends on the normative bridge rather than on encounter alone. Wherever subjects can meet and that bridge governs their treatment, moral reasons arise without a further supernatural or Platonic addition.

*The anchor isn’t merely relative.* A stance-involving morality invites the worry that it is true-for-me or true-for-you with nothing underneath. The first-person anchor is narrower than a Cartesian retorsion. An occurrent aversive episode is given to the subject as aversive: if I am now suffering in the relevant sense, denying the experienced recoil doesn’t make that recoil disappear. But merely asking whether I care doesn’t prove that I care, and sincere indifference to future suffering or even to one’s own continuation is coherent. Inquiry-interest isn’t aversion.

The witness still has structural content. Where aversion is present, it establishes a subject for whom an experience or represented outcome bears negatively. Suffering, in the clean psychological case, is an occurrent form of that capacity: experienced recoil as live possibilities contract and modal depth, one of the dimensions of freedom at §5.11, falls. The experiencing and aversion matter, not contraction alone. A field narrowed during dreamless anesthesia isn’t thereby an experienced harm, while a physically uninjured subject who registers the foreclosure of important possibilities may have a genuine stake.

Reading aversion forward into maximum possibility requires another step. The witness establishes recoil from a registered outcome; it doesn’t by itself establish that the positive optimum is a maximally open field. That interpretation is defended by fit with §5.11, which counts modal depth among the dimensions of freedom. The reach to other subjects requires a further bridge again. I don’t know your suffering by acquaintance, but evidence about shared phenomenology, biology, and conatus supports treating you as a subject with comparable capacities. The equal-standing argument below then asks whether the feature grounding my claim—being a subject capable of aversive experience—can consistently be denied weight when it occurs in you. Objectivity here comes from the feature, the evidence, and the reciprocity bridge, not from a performative contradiction in the act of asking.

The question is then what grounds the encounter in the first place—what it means for there to be subjects capable of meeting subjects at all.

*The conatus structure of life.* Before there are subjects meeting subjects, there is life persisting. A living system is the active avoidance of dissolution, not a current that merely happens to avoid it. A system that didn’t pursue its own continuation wouldn’t persist long enough to count as alive. The avoidance is what being an organism structurally consists in—it isn’t added on as a preference. Spinoza (*Ethics* III (1677) 1996) named this the *conatus*—the striving by which each finite mode perseveres in its being. Hans Jonas (1966; 1984) and Evan Thompson (2007), working from biology rather than metaphysics, reached the same result: self-maintaining systems generate their own norms because self-maintenance establishes a perspective from which outcomes are better or worse *for the system itself*.

Critics have pressed whether this move dissolves the is/ought question too quickly. Bedau (1992) argues that biological self-maintenance licenses at most a weak functional normativity—what is good-for-the-organism in the teleological sense, not yet what is good full stop. Philosophers of biology (Godfrey-Smith 1996; Di Paolo 2005) have raised parallel worries about the Jonas/Thompson line in particular—whether *self-maintaining* carries the normative weight the argument places on it. The response consolidates these: the conatus structure isn’t yet morality. It is the material from which morality becomes possible, as *Vulnerability registers* below makes explicit. What the *is* of life delivers is constitutive normativity at the organism’s own level of persistence; mutual registration supplies another subject’s stakes, and the equal-standing premise determines their moral relevance.

The bridge from functional to moral normativity has a specific shape. Functional normativity is *one-place*: it concerns what is good for system S relative to S’s own persistence-conditions. The norm is internal to S and doesn’t yet bind anyone else. Moral normativity is *two-place*: it concerns what subject A owes subject B, given the way A’s conduct bears on B’s persistence-conditions and B’s conduct bears on A’s.

Mutual registration supplies the additional content. Once A can accurately model B as another closure-and-throughput process with stakes of its own, B’s persistence-conditions become part of the relational field A is deliberating within. A theory that still describes the situation only by reference to A has left out something A’s own model now contains. But accurate representation alone doesn’t yet generate equal weight. The normative bridge enters here.

The bridge is that indexicality supplies *access* to a reason, not its *ground*. A encounters aversion first as *my* aversion, but what makes the episode weight-bearing is the general feature *being a subject capable of aversive experience*. If that feature grounds A’s claim, then the same feature in B supplies a reason of the same kind. A who weighs the feature only when indexed to A mistakes the way the ground was encountered for what the ground is.

This is the argument’s load-bearing normative premise, not a stance-free theorem. A committed agent-relativist can deny that reasons must generalize across structurally similar subjects. The premise is defended here by fit with reciprocity, equal standing, and the evidence that A and B share the relevant capacity. The occurrent first-person witness fixes an actual case of aversion; it doesn’t prove the generalizing premise or establish B’s experience without evidence.

On that premise, the move from one-place to two-place normativity is a constraint of consistency rather than an inference directly from biological function. The limit case is the structurally insulated egoist who makes no generalizable claim even on its own behalf and accepts its own collapse when the index changes. Others may protect themselves from it through withdrawn consent and a cooperative order; argument alone can’t force it to accept a premise it explicitly refuses.

**[Theorem]**

**No Arbitrary Self-Exemption** · *Conditional Theorem*

Assume the reciprocity/equal-standing premise: relevantly similar stakes receive relevantly similar consideration unless a relevant difference justifies unequal treatment. If feature F grounds A’s claim against treatment X, and B bears F in the relevantly similar respect, A cannot count F as claim-grounding only when indexed to A. First-person location explains A’s access to the reason; by the premise, it does not supply a difference in the reason’s ground.

The theorem is conditional on the equal-standing premise and on evidence that A and B bear the relevantly similar feature. It neither derives that premise from biology nor proves that every pair of stakes is alike. An agent-relativist may reject the premise; a threat-backed preference that makes no claim to justification does not contradict it from within, though it supplies no justification either.

**Depends on:** the reciprocity/equal-standing premise defended in §5.14.3 and the subject-side stakes identified at §5.2

Bedau is therefore right that biological self-maintenance delivers only functional normativity. Godfrey-Smith and Di Paolo are right that *self-maintaining* can’t carry the moral load alone. The additional content arrives when one subject accurately registers another and accepts that the feature grounding a claim in one case has the same relevance in the other.

This locates rather than erases the is/ought distinction. *Life wants to avoid dissolution* describes one structural fact from two sides: from outside, the system maintains itself; relative to its own persistence, some outcomes are better or worse for it. No further premise is needed for that one-place functional normativity. The two-place moral *ought* still requires the reciprocity/equal-standing bridge. Intersubjective registration supplies the other subject and the evidence about its stakes; the bridge supplies the reason those comparable stakes must receive comparable consideration.

Thermodynamic selection underwrites the universality. The default of any medium with the three Conditions is dissolution—gradients flatten, organization decays, exchange disperses. Prigogine and Nicolis (1977) showed how far-from-equilibrium organization can produce self-maintaining systems that dissipate gradients; Schrödinger (1944) had already named the point by calling life a process that feeds on negative entropy. Any persistent self-maintaining system is therefore, by what *self-maintaining* structurally means, actively resisting that default. The claim isn’t biological and doesn’t depend on Darwinian mechanisms specifically; natural selection as we know it is one sorting mechanism among possible others, an Earth-specific instantiation of a deeper principle: only avoidance-pursuing currents persist, because persistence *is* avoidance of dissolution. The reach the argument needs is narrower than a cosmological one, and should be taken at that width. The three Conditions aren’t contingent features of this epoch (§2.9.6); whether the occasion returns is argued separately, on its named premise, at §4.6.5, with the physical mechanism of a return left open there. Nothing here needs it. What generalizes is conditional and sufficient: wherever a self-maintaining organization obtains, its persistence is avoidance of dissolution, so the shared aversions cooperation generalizes are features of any life so organized rather than parochial to terrestrial biology.

Shared aversion doesn’t make cooperation inevitable; vulnerable agents can defect, dominate, exclude, or attack first. It does make durable mutual exposure a practical problem none can solve alone. Where agents seek stable continuation without domination, cooperation is the warranted response: it reduces shared exposure, requires reliable coordination, and therefore generates norms of reciprocity, non-defection, and restraint. Morality isn’t what shared vulnerability mechanically produces. It is the answer agents can justify to one another when life pursuing its constitutive avoidance encounters other life doing the same.

The question is then how one parcel of life comes to register another—how Substance, meeting Substance, comes to register itself as such.

*Self-modeling and the registration of vulnerability.* For the encounter to come into view within a subject, the subject must be able to model itself. A subject that registers its own exposure to harm—its own persistence as the kind of thing that can be broken, its own position as the kind of thing that can be reached—is also the kind of subject that can register another subject as standing in the same kind of relation to harm. Empathy, before it is a feeling, is this second registration: another subject’s exposure, internally tracked (Hoffman 2000; Batson 2011; Decety and Jackson 2004; Singer and Lamm 2009; de Waal 2008). It isn’t yet morality. It is the material from which morality becomes possible—the moment at which one parcel of Substance begins to model another as persisting, distinct, and reachable. Vulnerability in this sense is positional, not metaphorical: to be reachable is to occupy a position within Space, at a moment in Time, as Substance that persists through the exchange. It isn’t a cultural ornament added to an otherwise indifferent structure.

That registration gives morality its vocabulary. To *draw a boundary* is a spatial act (this side, not that side), made at a moment (from now on), by someone who persists as the one who drew it—Space, Time, Substance, already named in the verb. To *hold* a boundary requires persistence against the pull to violate it; to *cross* a boundary is to violate a limit that was supposed to hold. Morality, before it is codified in any system, is the practice of drawing, holding, and honoring the limits that register the reality of another subject.

A consequence follows for a question that has organized meta-ethics for three centuries.

*The is/ought question and moral uptake.* No valid inference from purely descriptive premises to a moral conclusion follows here. Hume’s boundary remains: the reciprocity/equal-standing premise does normative work that facts about life and aversion cannot do alone. A separate question is how a justified moral reason becomes motivationally effective. Arguments can direct attention toward another subject’s stake and show what consistency with the premise requires, but they cannot make every agent care. When the reason engages a field already weighted to register it, the ought is felt as compulsion; when it does not, the obligation may remain while motivational uptake fails.

That makes motivation an alignment problem. A moral reason becomes felt only when it is articulated at a level the subject’s uptake can register. A four-year-old and a philosopher don’t receive the same argument the same way; a subject whose empathic equipment has been blunted by trauma, ideology, or structural neglect may not receive it at all. Failures of moral uptake—psychopathy, dissociation, radicalization, trauma, severe self-interest—sit between articulated reasons and the compulsion they would ordinarily produce, not in the disappearance of the affected subject’s claim. Moral progress often proceeds through attention to features previously ignored: abolition, expansions of the moral circle, recognition of harms to those who can’t complain.

*Moral motivation has more than one grip.* What matters for uptake isn’t that one argument reach everyone but that morally relevant features find some purchase on the subject—and there is more than one surface they can catch on. Four subjects are moved four ways. One because an authority it trusts has spoken. Another by consequence: the aversion to penalty or loss the valenced field (§5.4, §5.3) registers when a branch is run forward. Another by standing among others whose regard it needs. And another by a principle it has made its own, so that violation would break with what the subject has identified with: the self-legislated grip Frankfurt’s volitional necessity (§5.14.1) names. These aren’t rungs in a contest of moral dignity, and no grip is disqualified for being the one that reaches a particular subject. They do differ in reach: as registration widens from self to intimates, community, society, and strangers, motivation can shift toward principles that hold for everyone the subject has learned to count. Most subjects remain reachable through several grips at once, in proportions that change with the stakes and the breadth of their registration.

*The grips aren’t equal in what they can correct.* Consequence, reputation, and principle each carry an internal check: a subject moved by them can ask whether the penalty is real, whether the regard is deserved, whether the principle survives being made general—and can revise the verdict against the answer. The authority grip carries no such check. Its content is exhausted by *someone entitled to command has spoken*, so the only question it can raise from the inside is what was in fact commanded, and that is settled by interpretation rather than by anything the situation itself supplies. A morality anchored solely in authority therefore has no court of appeal within itself: when its directives are unclear, conflict with one another, or run against what its adherents have otherwise come to register, it can move only by disputing the text, never by testing the directive against the subjects it governs. This is a structural property of the grip, not a verdict on the truth of any particular authority, and it predicts what the record shows—that moral traditions anchored in a fixed ancient command remain perennially contested over what their own morality requires, carry directives their later adherents come to judge indefensible and must reinterpret or explain away, and can’t close those disputes from within, the only internal resource being a return to the same underdetermined source. “Because God said so” is the limit case: it places the whole of moral weight in the fact of the command, and inherits the limitation entire. What a recognition- or principle-grounded morality can do that an authority-grounded one can’t is check a directive against the registered reality and standing of the affected subject—a standard no text can revoke—which is why moral progress has tended to run by re-grounding inherited commands in the subjects they concern rather than in the authority that issued them. What they share is the phenomenology: each delivers the same felt *I ought to*, because each is the valenced field reading its own possibility space through a different one of its channels. This is why the alignment problem is really many problems—to move a subject one must articulate the feature at whatever surface its uptake registers—and why moral formation is less the supplying of a correct argument than the finding, in a given subject, of which grip the compulsion still has.

Morality must therefore be cultivated. Family, punishment, attachment, reciprocity, education, imitation, narrative, and institutional design hone the rough equipment biology supplies. Which grip takes hold most readily varies from subject to subject—one most responsive to empathy, another to reputation, another to consistency, another chiefly to consequences—and formation works by strengthening whichever a given subject already has. The hard cases fit this picture better than a stronger realism does: they don’t show that the exposure of subjects is unreal; they show that uptake can be blunted, fragmented, or severed.

Because modal depth is one dimension of freedom (§5.11), that blunting also narrows the agent’s field of live options. Agency is reduced by degree, not removed through an all-or-nothing exemption. Such failures therefore modulate the response a breakdown calls for without dissolving responsibility. The agent’s contribution to causal history is degraded, not erased, and the harm done to the subjects on the other side remains fully real (the Modally Compatibilist Responsibility corollary, §6.12).

Cultivation isn’t a dispensable afterthought. The conditions under which a justified reason comes to motivate are part of a complete moral psychology, even though they do not constitute the obligation itself. An account that delivers the structure of the moral relation but stays silent on how its reasons acquire motivational grip has explained binding without explaining uptake; a meta-ethics complete on paper can still leave the reasons it describes inert in practice.

The shape of moral norms is visible in a nearby case: language (§5.12). No one designed English. It emerged from speakers-in-relation, constrained by what coordination among speakers necessarily requires—phonemes distinguishable from one another, utterances ordered in time, meanings persisting across the utterance long enough to be received. No Platonic entity decrees that English plurals take *-s*, and yet within a linguistic community there are genuinely right and wrong ways to speak. Errors miscommunicate. Ungrammatical constructions fail. Misleading usages damage coordination. A speaker who declares that *water* henceforth means *fire* hasn’t redefined the word; they have stepped outside the coordination that makes speech work. The grammar didn’t bend to accommodate them.

Two features of this case matter. Language is *stance-involving*: grammatical facts are facts about speakers and hearers, not about a speaker-less reality. Remove all speakers and there are no grammatical facts left—not grammatical facts stripped of observers, but no facts at all, because grammar’s content is exhaustively about coordination among stance-bearers. And language is *not stance-determined*: no individual speaker, and no collective consensus, can unilaterally redefine what English is. The linguistic system is real, binding, teachable, enforceable, answerable to facts about how communication works among creatures like us—and none of that reality depends on the existence of stance-independent linguistic properties. There are no such properties. There don’t need to be.

Morality works the same way. Moral facts are stance-involving because their content is exhaustively about agents-in-relation—what one subject does to another, what persists across exchange, what one owes another who is vulnerable in the ways one is oneself vulnerable. There is no moral fact left once the stances are removed, any more than there is a grammatical fact left once the speakers are removed. But moral facts aren’t stance-determined either: no individual agent, and no collective consensus, can unilaterally declare that betrayal is fine or that gratuitous cruelty is acceptable. The structure of coordination among mutually exposed subjects generates determinate content that individual stances can violate but can’t dismiss.

This is the answer to the robust realist who holds that real moral facts must be *stance-independent* in the strong sense—independent of all stances, collective as well as individual. Language shows that stance-independence isn’t what distinguishes real standards from fake ones: the standards of a living language are genuinely binding, objective within their domain, answerable to facts—and entirely constituted by the coordination of stance-bearers. The same possibility is available for morality. Stance-involving doesn’t mean unreal; it means real in the way standards about coordination among stance-bearers are real: objectively, bindingly, without needing stance-free Platonic backup. The normative pull the realist takes as evidence for stance-independent facts is the pull the intersubjective structure produces, and can be accounted for without the further posit.

Two specific patterns follow as predictions falsifiable against the empirical record. The negative formulation of reciprocity—*don’t do to others what they wouldn’t have you do*—should recur across genealogically distant cultures after transmission and coding are taken into account, because it carves the structural floor of non-corrosion that any encounter between persisting subjects requires; the positive formulation, which depends on attunement to throughput conditions that vary across forms of life, should appear later and be more variable. Harm-symmetric reciprocity—refusal of mistreatment, punishment of defectors, consolation of distress—should be biologically broader than flourishing-symmetric prosociality, because the affect-family registers damage more legibly across currents than it registers deepening: pain, fear, and grief broadcast in forms more reliably shared than the forms in which joy opens.

If this is how morality comes into view and how it spreads, then wherever its conditions obtain, its characteristic pattern should obtain with them.

### 5.14.4 Confirmation
The record supports the prediction provisionally. Wherever subjects meet subjects, moral life appears as a stable pattern rather than an optional cultural feature. The evidence comes from several disciplines, but their agreement counts only to the extent that their samples, codings, and causal assumptions aren’t inherited from one another.

Cross-cultural work finds recurrent prohibitions against unprovoked killing, theft within the group, and betrayal of cooperative ties—exactly where persistence and distinction are most acutely at stake (Brown 1991; Curry et al. 2019). The negative formulation of reciprocity—*don’t do to others what they wouldn’t have you do*—is a particularly persistent instance, appearing in Confucian, Hebraic, Vedic, Hellenic, Buddhist, and Egyptian sources and predating its positive formulation by centuries in most traditions (*Analects* 15.23; Hillel in *b. Shabbat* 31a; *Mahābhārata* 5.1517; Isocrates *Nicocles* 49–61; *Udānavarga* 5.18). Recurrence isn’t yet independence: contact, shared ancestry, translation, selective preservation, and the coding of unlike norms under one category have to be assessed case by case. The asymmetry between negative and positive formulations is what the structural account predicts: non-corrosion is the minimum condition of any encounter between persisting subjects, while fostering depends on attunement to throughput conditions that vary across forms of life. The emotional architecture matches: empathy, shame, indignation, and guilt all track positions within a field of mutually exposed Substance (Haidt 2012; Bloom 2013), reporting the exchange from within the subject. Evolutionary biology explains how that architecture came to be stable. Reciprocal altruism, kin selection, and indirect reciprocity (Trivers 1971; Hamilton 1964; Nowak and Sigmund 2005) select for agents that can navigate other agents without destroying them—cooperation among persisting, distinct agents whose interactions extend across time. Game-theoretic formalization of iterated exchange (Axelrod 1984) reaches the same result through mathematics: strategies enacting non-initiation of harm and reciprocity-with-forgiveness perform robustly under noise.

The ancient Near East offers a regional case. Across roughly fifteen centuries—from the Laws of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BCE) and Lipit-Ishtar (c. 1930 BCE) through the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), the Hittite Laws (c. 1650 BCE), the Middle Assyrian Laws, and the Covenant Code of Exod 21–23—legal traditions in distinct languages, polities, and theologies converge on the same floor: prohibition of unprovoked killing within the polity, of theft, of false witness, of oath-violation, and of abuse of the structurally dependent (widow, orphan, resident foreigner). The wisdom literature shows the same pattern at the level of conduct rather than statute. The Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope* (c. 1300–1100 BCE) and the Thirty Sayings of Prov 22:17–24:22 share thematic content, structure, and specific phrasings closely enough that documented transmission is the standard explanation (Erman 1924); the Negative Confession of the Egyptian Book of the Dead enumerates the same prohibitions in the form of a posthumous ledger. Where borrowing can be shown—Wright (2009) argues the Covenant Code is a deliberate reworking of Hammurabi—it weakens the recurrence as independent confirmation while supporting a different claim: communities can recognize, retain, and adapt the floor across political and theological change. The regional case therefore tests transmission and uptake more directly than independent convergence. Independence has to be supplied by cases for which contact and common descent are less plausible.

Classical China supplies a parallel test under different conditions. Across the Warring States and early Han period (c. 500–200 BCE), four traditions in deep metaphysical disagreement converge on the same floor within a shared language and political space. Confucian *ren* (humaneness) and *shu* (reciprocity) articulate the negative Golden Rule directly (*Analects* 15.23). Mohist *jian’ai*, impartial concern, derives the harm-prohibition floor from an explicitly consequentialist calculus that rejects Confucian role-ethics at the root—a calculus akin to Western utilitarianism without being identical to it. Daoist *wuwei* arrives at non-interference by way of metaphysical quietism that rejects the Mohist calculus and the Confucian ritual program alike. Even the Legalist tradition, which is officially anti-moralist and grounds rule in coercive efficiency (Han Feizi), retains the harm-prohibition floor as a precondition for state cohesion. Four traditions disagreeing about virtually everything else—the nature of persons, the standing of ritual, the metaphysics of the way, the basis of authority—agree on the floor (Graham 1989; Hansen 1992; Van Norden 2007). Where the ancient Near East isolates convergence across distinct languages and theologies in a shared region, the Chinese case isolates convergence across rival metaphysical systems in a shared linguistic and political space.

Mesoamerica supplies a more independent historical test. The Aztec *Huehuetlatolli*—the “ancient discourses” recorded by Sahagún in Book VI of the Florentine Codex—and the Nahua ethical tradition organized around *neltiliztli* (rooted truth, groundedness) enumerate the same prohibitions: theft, deceit, cruelty, abuse of dependents, and the obligations of host to guest and elder to young. The reciprocity formulations parallel Old World wisdom literature closely, in a civilization without plausible contact with Eurasian moral traditions before the sixteenth century (León-Portilla 1963; Maffie 2014; Read 1998). That separation gives the recurrence more evidential weight than a documented borrowing case, while the post-contact recording, translation, and selection of the sources remain live controls. The floor of non-corrosion isn’t shown to be a Eurasian export; where contact was absent, a recognizably similar architecture appeared.

Taken together, the three regional cases provide different comparative contrasts. The ancient Near East holds region roughly constant while varying language and theology and exposing transmission; classical China holds language and political space roughly constant while varying metaphysics; Mesoamerica reduces the plausibility of pre-contact Eurasian transmission while leaving source-recording questions visible. The cases aren’t experimental controls, but their differences let the prediction be tested against more than bare recurrence.

Developmental and comparative work shows precursors relevant to moral life without establishing an innate moral floor in the strong form once claimed here. Early helper–hinderer studies reported infant preferences for helpers, but a preregistered 37-lab replication with 567 included infants aged 5.5–10.5 months found no helper preference in the hill paradigm (Lucca et al. 2025). Likewise, the famous capuchin unequal-reward result (Brosnan and de Waal 2003) can’t now be stated as a settled inequity-aversion effect: a preregistered meta-analysis of 23 accept/reject studies, 60,430 observations, and 18 species found no evidence of inequity aversion overall or in the capuchin and chimpanzee subsets (Ritov et al. 2024). Consolation, cooperation, social preference, protest, and sensitivity to others’ distress remain active comparative literatures, but none can simply be renamed morality. The evidence supports evolved and developing capacities from which moral cognition may be built; the reciprocity/equal-standing bridge remains philosophical and culturally articulated rather than empirically read off one infant or animal task.

The pattern also appears where a tradition locates moral authority beyond ordinary life. Christian heaven and hell, Buddhist samsara and nirvana, Hindu karma, the Zoroastrian Bridge of the Separator, and the Egyptian weighing of the heart all connect post-mortem outcomes to harm, conduct, or forms of flourishing, though they construe those relations differently (Boyer 2001; Norenzayan 2013). These eschatologies frequently build their motivational force out of differential exposure to suffering and flourishing—the conatus structure of §5.14.3 extended to another horizon. The recurrence is consistent with the claim that religious moral vocabularies elaborate an intersubjective normative currency already available in life. It doesn’t establish that every eschatology uses only that currency or that the traditions are historically independent.

The record runs in time, not only across it. While cross-cultural and developmental evidence shows the floor present wherever the conditions obtain, the historical record shows uptake of that floor deepening over the long run. Rates of interpersonal violence have fallen by roughly an order of magnitude from prehistoric and tribal baselines to modern state societies, with further sharp declines across the European homicide record from the medieval period to the present (Pinker 2011; drawing on Eisner 2003; Gurr 1981). Across the same span, judicial torture, chattel slavery, public execution, dueling, and warfare-as-default have been progressively delegitimized. Recognition of standing has been extended successively to commoners, to women, to children, to ethnic and religious out-groups, and—incompletely but trackably—to the structurally dependent across species (Pinker 2018; Inglehart and Welzel 2005). Self-reported life satisfaction tracks the same direction in cross-national data, rising in step with the conditions that lower coercion and widen participation (Helliwell, Layard, and Sachs 2020; Inglehart 2018). The gradient is asymmetric and directional: increased recognition of subjects as subjects and reduced corrosion of the conditions under which they persist—not monotonic at every scale, but the long-run signal these sources report across the controls the data permit. That is what the structural account predicts as the historical signature of the floor coming into reflective view; read against the fall-theodicy frame (§10.1.9), the same gradient counts against what that frame requires.

The sciences find the descriptive and psychological conditions of morality in subjects meeting subjects rather than in a value-neutral abstraction. The empirical record can support the account’s claims about vulnerability, registration, cooperation, and uptake; it cannot derive the equal-standing premise. Conditional on that bridge, morality needs no further supernatural or Platonic layer: it is the normative ordering of real relations among exposed subjects, at no stronger level than the premise supports.

Once the mechanism, the conceptual structure, and the empirical record point the same way, a number of familiar positions about morality come under structural pressure rather than remaining merely optional.

### 5.14.5 Conclusions
*Popular positions.* *Platonic moral realism* is the view that obligations exist as stance-independent cosmic facts awaiting discovery in the way a law of motion awaits discovery (Shafer-Landau 2003). It has no place here. But the alternative isn’t deflation. Moral facts are as real as the Substance they concern. What the account denies is a register of obligations floating above the subjects; what it affirms is that morality is as real as the persistence, distinction, and exchange it consists in. The cosmic inventory is absent; the reality isn’t.

*Divine command as the foundation of morality* (Adams 1999; Quinn 1978) fails for a different reason. A command that licenses atrocity doesn’t become persuasive by acquiring theological authorship. Believers themselves rely on prior aversions, sympathies, and judgments of proportionality in deciding which commands to affirm, reinterpret, or reject (cf. Maitzen 2009)—which means the intersubjective evidence remains in operation beneath the theology. On this account, the equal-standing premise applied to that evidence does the grounding work; a command may guide uptake but cannot replace the bridge. The failure sharpens against the compatibilist structure stated as Modally Compatibilist Responsibility (§6.12): responsibility lives at the token-level contribution an agent makes to causal history, while divine command can ask that agent to outsource judgment to an external authority. A command licensing atrocity is therefore not vindicated by authorship, and deferral does not erase the agent’s contribution.

*Moral nihilism* (Joyce 2001; Garner 1994) isn’t established by rejecting Platonism. Subjects genuinely persist, remain distinct, and meet across asymmetric exchange. Practices, norms, and codes are answerable to real facts about outcomes, psychology, and social design; some arrangements work better for creatures like us than others. The further moral conclusion depends on equal standing: once comparable stakes are granted comparable consideration, those differences become reasons and claims rather than matters of taste alone. A nihilist may reject that premise, but cannot derive nihilism merely from the absence of a cosmic moral register.

One practical objection bridges the popular positions and the professional ones: the agent who grants that cruelty makes some worlds worse but asks what *reason* they have to participate. Self-interest rightly calculated and moral participation converge for any agent who remains exposed to the costs of defection. Anyone who helps build a society that benefits everyone is among the people who benefit. Over any reasonable time horizon, the self-interested agent and the moral agent tend to choose the same actions, because both depend on the conditions that let people live and cooperate together. Hobbes (1651), Hume (1739–1740) 2000, and Gauthier (1986) saw parts of this convergence; the structural account explains it by noting that the person doing the calculation depends on the very conditions morality spells out. But the convergence is the on-ramp, not the ground, and it must not be asked to carry more than it can. For most agents it is decisive—pure egoism isn’t a rival framework but a miscalculation about one’s own exposure.
