It doesn’t reach the agent with asymmetric protection from the harms their defection produces—the tyrant, the structurally insulated elite—and the account doesn’t pretend it does; the political account meets the same limit of the insurance argument and declines to lean on self-interest to cover it (Chapter 6). That agent isn’t a counterexample, because the obligation never rested on the payoff. Given equal standing, his exemption is simply groundless: the feature that licenses his own stake—being a subject with the capacity to be averse to particular experiences and outcomes—is equally present in those he exempts himself from, so the only thing distinguishing his case is an indexical, and an indexical isn’t a ground (§5.14.3). What binds him is therefore not a calculation he can defeat but the recognized standing of the others whose conditions are still at stake (§6.3)—expressed as the field’s claim against any pair, the consent constraint the procedure below makes operational, and, where he acts on his exemption, the enforcement and restorative-justice institutions (§6.11, §6.12). The floor binds every participant, and the one apparent exit doesn’t open. Genuine exit would mean drawing nothing from the social and material conditions that sustain one’s life—but a person who relies on language, legal protection, exchange, and the biosphere can’t meet that condition. What the insulated elite achieves isn’t exit but insulation: they draw on those conditions as fully as anyone while reducing only their own exposure to the harm caused when others lose them. That makes him the maximal free-rider, not an escapee, and the field’s claim against him is strongest precisely where his felt stake is weakest. The floor is left only by leaving the field altogether, never by prospering within it.

*Meta-ethical challenges.* Four challenges press from different directions—debunking (Street 2006), queerness (Mackie 1977), the amoralist (Brink 1986), and the open question (Moore 1903)—but the responses share a common structure: because the account posits no stance-independent moral properties, each one either misses its target or relocates to the equal-standing premise.

*Debunking.* Street’s (2006) Darwinian Dilemma poses a serious challenge to robust moral realism: natural selection shaped evaluative attitudes for fitness rather than truth-tracking. Contested responses exist (Enoch 2011; Wielenberg 2014). The evolutionary shaping is conceded here: it can explain why subjects register exposure, dependence, cooperation, and harm, all real features of social life. It does not independently vindicate the equal-standing premise. The account therefore uses evolutionary explanation for the reliability and limits of moral uptake while leaving the normative bridge to its stated philosophical defense.

*Queerness.* Mackie (1977) argued that moral properties, if they existed, would be metaphysically *sui generis*—intrinsically motivating, categorically prescriptive, utterly unlike anything else in the natural world—and that the best explanation of their persistent strangeness is that there are no such properties. This challenge does not directly target an account that posits no stance-independent moral properties. What occupies the room Mackie empties is a practice among mutually exposed subjects, answerable to their real conditions and normatively ordered by the equal-standing premise. Mackie can still reject that premise or deny its categorical reach, but the queerness argument against a special moral property doesn’t settle that further dispute.

*The amoralist.* Brink (1986) pressed the separability of moral judgment and moral motivation: a person can sincerely judge an action wrong and feel no inclination whatsoever to refrain. The judgment may therefore lack motivational force without changing its content. This is exactly the distinction between binding and uptake: indifference does not by itself refute a norm, but neither does the mere intelligibility of calling someone an amoralist prove that the norm is valid. Validity rests on the equal-standing argument; motivation is a further fact about how, or whether, the agent’s field responds.

*The open question.* G. E. Moore (1903) observed that for any natural property N—pleasure, fitness, social utility—it remains intelligible to ask *but is N good?* If goodness were identical to a natural property, the question would close as trivially as *is water H₂O?* The openness is real. It persists because prescribing isn’t describing, even when what is prescribed tracks what is described. The gap between *is* and *ought* isn’t evidence of a separate moral reality. It is the distance between registering a pressure and responding to it.

The post-Moorean sharpening fits rather than threatens this reading. Horgan and Timmons (1991) imagined a Moral Twin Earth where ‘good’ tracks a different natural property—and showed that our moral terms would still diverge from theirs, because moral concepts aren’t rigidly fixed to any single natural kind. Moral vocabulary isn’t a label for a natural property. It is a tool for coordinating responses among subjects who can wound and be wounded. The Twin Earth intuition holds—and points exactly where this account already stands.

*Realist revivals.* These press from different directions; the responses converge: what each revival invokes can be carried by the medium itself and the equal-standing premise, without stance-independent properties.

*Indispensability.* Enoch (2010; 2011) presses from the opposite direction. Where Mackie and Street challenge the existence of moral properties, Enoch argues that robust moral realism is explanatorily indispensable—that the best explanation of our taking the normative seriously, of the striking coincidence between our moral beliefs and what we have reason to do, is that there are stance-independent normative truths. The coincidence is real; his explanation isn’t required. We take the normative seriously because exposure is real, because the consequences of ignoring it are severe, and because the capacities that register it were selected for reliability in tracking the conditions that matter. Convergence between moral belief and reason to act is evidence that norm-construction within the field of mutually exposed subjects works, not evidence of a moral reality beyond us. This isn’t evolutionary debunking recast: evolution shaped the capacities that register the exposure, but what those capacities register—persistence, distinction, asymmetric exchange among mutually exposed subjects—is a structural feature of the medium itself, not a contingent feature of our lineage, so any subject capable of modeling others would track the same content for the same structural reason.

*Non-ontological realism.* Parfit (2011) presses a more sophisticated version of the realist line. His reasons-fundamentalism takes reasons rather than obligations as the normative primitive, and his *non-ontological* realism holds that there are truths about what agents have reason to do without reasons being entities in a Platonic register—a move that concedes Mackie’s queerness worry at the level of ontology while preserving the mind-independence of normative truths. The diagnosis is shared; the parting is on what supplies the reason. Exposure is real, but its normative significance here is fixed by the equal-standing premise rather than by exposure alone. Parfit’s *Double Error* argument (2011, vol. 2) presses that a non-realist must hold both that suffering doesn’t really matter and that this first error itself doesn’t matter. The present account avoids nihilism by granting the premise that comparable stakes matter comparably and locating those stakes in subjects who genuinely persist, remain distinct, and can be reached across exchange. Parfit can deny that this relational grounding is sufficient; nothing here converts that disagreement into a contradiction.

*Reduction.* Railton’s (1986) reduced moral naturalism identifies moral goodness with what a fully informed, ideally rational version of an agent would want the agent to want—a natural property picked out by its causal-explanatory role the way *water* is identified with H₂O. Moral knowledge is then a posteriori, and the Moorean open question reflects semantic access to the property rather than a metaphysical gap between *is* and *ought*. Railton’s naturalism and his rejection of Moorean skepticism are shared; the parting is on the property assignment. The natural fact morality tracks isn’t what an idealized agent would want but the constitutive relation among mutually exposed subjects that any such agent’s wanting would itself be responding to—the idealization pushes the grounding question back one step without changing what eventually grounds it.

*Homeostatic cluster.* Boyd’s (1988) homeostatic property-cluster account sharpens Cornell realism in a different direction: moral kinds, like many natural kinds, are identified not by a single essential property but by clusters of properties that co-occur because homeostatic mechanisms causally sustain the co-occurrence. *Goodness* or *justice* picks out such a cluster the way *species* picks out co-occurring morphological, behavioral, and reproductive traits held together by ecological mechanisms. The homeostatic structure and the causal sustaining are shared with Boyd; the homeostasis is located precisely: the cluster of moral features—harm, care, fairness, trust, proportion—co-occurs because the same structural conditions (persistence, distinction, asymmetric exchange among mutually exposed subjects) sustain all of them together. Boyd’s account identifies the right pattern; the modal argument identifies what holds the pattern in place.

*The third factor.* Wielenberg’s (2014) *robust ethics* defends non-natural moral realism without God: moral facts are stance-independent and non-natural but require no theistic backup, and the coincidence between evolutionarily shaped moral beliefs and such facts is handled by a *third-factor* explanation—a common cause that makes belief and fact co-vary without either tracking the other directly. Wielenberg’s atheism is shared, and the third-factor diagnosis is shared at the level of structure. What plays the role of Wielenberg’s common cause here is the medium itself—the field of mutually exposed subjects—rather than a separate non-natural fact: belief and fact co-vary because both are shaped by the same structural conditions among mutually exposed subjects. Where the accounts part company is on the non-naturalness. Wielenberg treats the moral facts as *sui generis*; the modal account treats them as facts about a natural structure—the field of mutually exposed subjects—that doesn’t reduce to any lower-level description but isn’t for that reason non-natural. The *sui generis* posit was doing the work of keeping moral facts from collapsing into arbitrary social construction; the structural necessity of the three Conditions, with the equal-standing premise, does that work without leaving the natural order.

*Nearby relatives.* A different challenge must also be answered: not that the account is wrong, but that it isn’t new. Four established positions occupy nearby territory.

*Constructivism.* Korsgaard’s (1996) constructivism grounds normativity in the reflective endorsement of practical identities—the agent who asks *what should I do?* is already committed to norms by the act of asking. Schroeder (2007) and Boghossian (2006) have pressed constitutivism from different angles: Schroeder questions whether reflective endorsement yields genuinely normative reasons rather than merely hypothetical ones, and Boghossian challenges the constructivist family for conflating the conditions under which norms are taken up with the norms themselves. The present account likewise rejects a Platonic register but does not derive normativity from reflection. Vulnerable subjects in a shared field provide the objects and conditions of moral concern; the equal-standing premise provides the bridge. The Schroeder/Boghossian worry therefore becomes a direct test of that bridge’s sufficiency rather than something structural necessity alone answers.

*Contractualism.* Scanlon’s (1998) contractualism grounds morality in principles no one could reasonably reject. The overlap is real—both locate normativity in what agents owe each other under conditions of mutual exposure. The conditions of exposure are derived here from the necessary structure of the medium; their equal moral standing remains the explicit normative commitment rather than a consequence of structure alone.

*Expressivism.* Blackburn’s (1993; 1998) quasi-realism and Gibbard’s (1990; 2003) expressivism share the denial that moral claims are descriptions of stance-independent facts. Quasi-realism is the project of earning the right to realist-sounding moral talk from expressivist foundations. The resemblance is genuine. What distinguishes this account is its claim that the conditions under which moral life is possible—subjects persisting, distinct, and meeting across asymmetric exchange, within a necessarily instantiated medium—are themselves structurally necessary. Expressivism offers no such structural necessity. This account isn’t expressivism with a metaphysical garnish. The structural necessity of the conditions, with the stated bridge, is what makes the expressions non-arbitrary.

*Neo-sentimentalism.* D’Arms and Jacobson’s (2000) neo-sentimentalism analyzes moral concepts through fitting sentiments—an action is *wrong* when guilt would be the fitting response, *admirable* when admiration would be—and their moralistic-fallacy argument distinguishes a sentiment’s *fittingness* to its object from the separate question of whether having the sentiment would be good. The overlap with the present account is substantial: both locate moral life in sentiments that register features of exchange among subjects—empathy, indignation, guilt, aversion—and refuse to treat those sentiments as mere projections. The difference is where the binding force comes from. Here, real features of mutually exposed subjects explain what sentiments answer to, while the equal-standing premise explains why comparable features carry comparable normative weight. Selection may explain reliable uptake without itself supplying that bridge. The moralistic fallacy D’Arms and Jacobson diagnose is what happens when evaluation of having a sentiment overrides the sentiment’s answerability to its object.

Once rival metaphysics are cleared, the question turns practical.

Parfit (2011) argued that Kantian, contractualist, and consequentialist ethics, built on different foundations, converge in their strongest formulations and that this agreement is evidence about the moral terrain. The present account offers one explanation of that convergence. Kantian universalizability resembles the impartial constraint supplied by equal standing; contractualism articulates what mutually exposed subjects can justify to one another; consequentialism compares branches across affected subjects. Each may therefore track a different operation within one moral field. That proposal does not recover every commitment of the three theories or dissolve every conflict among them, but it explains why their best formulations can converge without sharing a foundation.

The intergenerational reach of the framework—duties carrying across generations, conditions one subject’s choices set for subjects not yet in existence—raises Parfit’s non-identity problem (1984), and the hand-off should be marked rather than absorbed. The persons our present choices affect across generational distance are, in many cases, persons whose very existence those choices determine, so the wrong done by setting their conditions poorly can’t be cashed out as harm to *them* against a counterfactual in which they exist better off—there is no such counterfactual; either they exist under these conditions or different people exist instead. The structural account carries the problem cleanly to §6, where institutional reciprocity scaled past face-to-face exchange is developed in detail, but it can say what the structural register adds before handing off: the duty doesn’t need a determinate future patient to bind, because what reciprocity rules out is the setting of conditions a subject wouldn’t authorize for any of the subjects it might bring into them. Person-affecting accounting is one register the structural relation operates in; an impersonal register that ranks possible fields of subjects by the conditions of exposure they would constitute is another. Both track what the structural fact already requires; the non-identity case is where that has to be said explicitly, and worked through institutionally (§6). The nearby *repugnant conclusion* is that a vast population of barely livable lives ranks above a smaller flourishing one on a pure count (Parfit 1984). It is the same stacking, not a separate puzzle: adding lives that sit on the floor isn’t “more” if necessities are the first unit and possibility is the maximand above it. Population ethics is Chapter 6’s to carry; what this section owes is that the count isn’t the floor.

Two further Parfitian distinctions, operating implicitly alongside the non-identity hand-off, should be marked. First, what one subject owes another isn’t the same as what one subject has reason to want for itself or others impersonally—Scanlon and Parfit’s “what we owe to each other” and Parfit’s “what matters” track different operations on the moral field, and they should be kept apart rather than let one swallow the other. Second, what carries the moral relation forward across time isn’t the strict identity of the patient but the psychological continuity that is the substrate of the self-modeling current (§5.7)—what makes future-directed duties bind to *this* future subject isn’t that the subject is “the same person” in any further sense but that this continuity suffices to make the relation hold. Person-affecting and impersonal registers, what-we-owe and what-matters, identity and continuity: no member of a pair has to be elected fundamental, and the account operates on the second member of each, as it does for identity (§5.7) and cross-generational meaning (§5.10).

Given equal standing, the policy turn can be stated with the moral architecture already developed. The moral field has a better/worse gradient relative to the subjects in it—not an objective₁ ought written into a value-neutral world, but an objective₂ ordering among the subjects governed by the bridge. That gradient is layered, and the order is lexical. Necessities are met first, because a current that can’t persist isn’t present to value anything at all. Possibility is maximized second, because once persistence is secured what subjects owe each other is the field of further possibility their exchanges hold open—the same field the fostering named here, scaled into the political maximand developed at §6 as *maximum possibility*. Structural conflict is minimized third, not as an independent goal but as the multi-subject form possibility-maximization takes when many subjects share one field. The stacking matters because it forecloses the *peace-of-the-grave* objection—a regime that minimizes conflict by destroying possibility fails the first two tiers before the third applies. Conflicts generated by an arrangement, largely occupant-independent, and dissolved by changing the arrangement rather than the agent are structural; poverty is the paradigm. Responsibility isn’t eliminated by the structural reading. It is relocated upstream, to those with power over the arrangement, and earlier in time—to design and foresight—where it can weigh more heavily than blame allocated downstream to the agents the arrangement produced.

*The trolley problem is a picture of this relocation.* The standard dilemma stages a runaway trolley and a bystander at a lever: divert onto a track where one person dies, or do nothing while five die. A whole literature’s energy goes into weighing the act of diversion against what the outcome deserves, or into which operation should govern when they pull apart—count, non-use as a means, the special relation when the one on the track isn’t a stranger. The footbridge variant makes the same split sharper: pushing one person to stop the trolley is the deontological operation refusing to use a subject as a means, against the same count. Those weights are real. They are the three operations already named, plus the reasons of love located with Frankfurt at §5.14.1. None of them is the whole picture, and none of them is wrong for being partial. What the construction doesn’t get right is the grain. The morally load-bearing question isn’t which way the bystander pulls the lever, or whether they push. It is why anyone was ever positioned on a live track with a runaway trolley bearing down and no third option.

The same miss is the mother who steals bread to feed a child. Drive is running where the field has collapsed; the storekeeper’s aversion is real too; the event is that a society left only those two branches live. Singer’s pond is live for a different reason. A child drowning in reach, and a child drowning far away, share the same aversion; distance is a grip problem, not a proof that the far child doesn’t count (Singer 1972). If you can reach, some surface should catch. Treated as the whole of morality, the construction still substitutes the passerby’s rescue for the floor. Why the child is in the water is the Chapter 6 question. Charity at the edge isn’t it.

Canonical moral-dilemma theory takes the agent’s moment-of-choice as the fixed frame and asks what they ought to do inside it. The account here fixes the arrangement as the object and reads the moment-of-choice dilemma as evidence that the upstream work was left undone. The person at the lever isn’t thereby excused. Their contribution to causal history remains real. The larger share of responsibility sits earlier, with whoever left the field with only those branches. This is spent at the docket (§6.13).

**[Proposition]**

**Manufactured Dilemma** · *Proposition*

When a situation has been reduced to a forced choice among harms, the morally load-bearing question is the arrangement that left only those branches live. The agent’s remaining choice is real; it is not what the moral account is primarily of. Canonical dilemma constructions take the moment of choice as the fixed frame. They picture competing weights on one field, with a shared aversion underneath, and locate the problem at the wrong grain.

*Status: a reading of what the two-place account and the structural-conflict relocation require of forced-choice constructions. Not a corollary of the modal proof, and not a unique verdict for any given lever.*

*Scope.* This is the moral relocation. Justice (§6.13) spends it at the docket; it does not by itself derive a justice-system architecture.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14) and Wrong (§5.14)

One further fact bears on the policy turn. Given the equal-standing premise, the cooperative ought binds as a reason; it becomes effective motivation only for agents able to reason past the immediate horizon. The empirical record on scarcity-cognition (Mullainathan and Shafir 2013) indicates that precarity can narrow that horizon. Securing the floor is therefore both a tier-one moral target and an enabling condition for sustained moral deliberation. Its political face can be stated as a principle—*converge on the floor, truly individual above it*: collective convergence at the level of necessities, genuine individuation in the possibility-field above. The floor enables individuality rather than merely exacting its price, because a person governed by immediate necessity has less practical latitude. Specific mechanisms—a guaranteed material baseline, progressive financing, prevention of rent-seeking—belong to the policy literatures taken up in §6.

*Practical output.* Given equal standing, non-maleficence, beneficence, autonomy, and justice aren’t independent rules to balance but aspects of a single move: act on the other subject’s own readings rather than the actor’s projection. Where a subject expresses what they want done, informed, voluntary, and competent consent ordinarily licenses the action within its scope. Where a subject refuses, the action is ordinarily forbidden, subject to the claims of non-consenting third parties. Where the actor doesn’t know, action waits on inquiry when circumstances permit. Where the subject can’t respond—incapacity, unconsciousness, immediate crisis—non-corrosion is the default while the actor works toward conditions under which authorization can resume. This yields a defeasible negative guarantee rather than an exceptionless formula: intentional intervention requires the subject’s authorization or an adequate justification grounded in the protected interests of that subject or another.

What that guarantee protects, beneath the vocabulary of consent and harm, is each subject’s capacity to generate and direct its own possibility. So the measure of this violation isn’t only the welfare it costs but the possibility it forecloses against the will the subject could form. A benevolent dominator who provides for a subject in every material respect while enclosing what that subject may become commits a paradigm wrong of this kind: welfare left intact doesn’t redeem a possibility-field seized. Nozick’s experience machine (1974) is the same enclosure from the other side—pleasure intact, the field of live possibility seized. Drive already reads it against hedonism (§5.2); here it is the two-place form of that reading. Domination is therefore not exhausted by inflicted suffering or direct command. It consists in acquiring unanswerable control over the possibilities another subject may realistically pursue. This carries morality forward into the politics—the wrong at the individual scale and the maximand at the political scale (§6, *maximum possibility*) are one currency, and foreclosing a subject’s possibility against its formable will is what, scaled across a shared field, the political order exists to prevent. Measuring against the will the subject *could* form, rather than the will it happens to hold, also disarms the contented-captive objection: an enclosure that reaches into the will itself and quiets all protest is the most complete violation, not the absence of one.

This fixes the one limit consent can’t cross, and fixes it structurally rather than by hand. Consent can license almost anything—binding commitments, vows, lifelong arrangements—because a commitment is an exercise of the capacity to author one’s possibility, not a surrender of it. What consent can’t reach is the arrangement whose content is the *effective* destruction of that capacity: to consent away the standing power to revise and exit one’s commitments is to use present authorship to extinguish the feature that licenses authorship at all—the egoist’s groundless self-exemption turned inward. Inalienability is therefore not an added axiom but the consent constraint applied to its own precondition.

The deeper reason is temporal. Consent reaches into the future—it authorizes what is going to happen, pinned to a particular arrangement of time, place, and act—but it reaches forward as a *standing* authorization, the live approval of the subject whose act it is, not a token transferred out of them. What licenses an act at the moment it occurs is therefore that it is still authorized at that moment; a past consent can’t govern a present act any more than yesterday’s appetite can be eaten today. So consent carries forward as a default that holds unless withdrawn, never as a lock immune to its own withdrawal—and an arrangement purporting to bind a subject after their consent had lapsed wouldn’t be their authorization governing the act at all, but their earlier self overriding their present one. Revocability isn’t a permission added on top of consent; it is what consent, being the live state of the one whose act it is, already is.

**[Proposition]**

**Consent’s Conditions** · *Proposition*

Consent that licenses what may be done to a subject must be informed, voluntary, competent, specific, and revocable: absent those conditions, the purported modification is not the subject’s rule for what may happen to them, but another party’s rule imposed through the grammar of permission. Informed, voluntary, and competent are the axes of free will turned outward: the subject’s self-knowledge can be trusted as the basis for another’s action. Specific names the directedness of the authorization: this subject, this act, this agent. Revocable names what consent already is as a live state rather than a token transferred out of the subject.

*Scope.* This is the dyadic standard. Institutional design of protected domains applies it at scale in §6.1; it does not by itself derive a political rights architecture.

**Depends on:** Two Modes of Wronging (§5.14) and Will (§5.11)

Thomson’s violinist (1971) is the live case for unauthorized use of a body. A dependent with standing still has no claim-ticket on another subject’s person: they can be wronged; standing isn’t occupancy. The violinist was reaching for the structure that Consent’s Conditions states. What the case doesn’t settle, and what this section already splits rather than collapsing, is the further question of responsibility for a dependency one has already set in motion.

Inalienability turns on effective foreclosure, not formal: a commitment merely costly to leave remains revisable, but one engineered toward inescapability—debt bondage, a ruinous exit penalty—destroys revisability as surely as a chain. And because commitments are often joint, the protected core is unilateral *exit*, not unilateral *amendment*: each subject always retains departure, while none may force a shared arrangement to reshape around them or conscript another into it. Exit preserves the door, not freedom from what was set in motion behind it—the responsibility an agent bears for its contribution to causal history (§6.12) survives the departure.

Two distinct relations are doing the work here, and keeping them apart dissolves what would otherwise look like a single tangled obligation. Consent governs what may be *done to* a subject going forward—its body, its presence, its participation—and that authorization is the live, revocable state just described. Responsibility governs what a subject *owes for what it has already set in motion*—its contribution to causal history—and that is backward-looking, so withdrawing consent ends the authorization without erasing the responsibility.

The two divide along a structural seam: consent attaches to the inalienable latitude a subject has over its own person; responsibility attaches to the external, substitutable performances a subject’s choices produce in the shared world. What sorts a case is whether the thing relied upon can be made good by substitution without reaching the promisor’s body. Where it can—goods, payment, the product of labor—withdrawal is permitted but carries *reparative* responsibility for the reliance it induced: bounded by what repair requires, tracking the withdrawing subject’s actual contribution to the other’s loss, never a penalty added to make leaving irrational.

Where it can’t—where the only thing that would satisfy the reliance is the subject’s own body or intimate participation—no reliance interest can attach at all, because to price the withdrawal would be to price the body, the standing seizure of latitude named in the slavery case above; and a conviction doesn’t dissolve it, the point carried into the confinement case at §6.12.

A bodily commitment is therefore never specifically enforceable and never carries a withdrawal penalty; what was exchanged for it, if anything, settles on the external track as a return, while the body itself stays beyond the reach of the debt. This is why a personal-service promise yields damages but never compelled performance, and why one may always leave an intimate arrangement at no charge to the leaving while remaining answerable for the external entanglements—shared property, created dependents—the arrangement produced.

One loss this leaves deliberately unrepaired: where what the other wanted was itself the freely-given participation now withdrawn, no substitution can restore it, and no attempt is made here, since the only available remedy would be to commodify the inalienable. That loss is borne, not transferred; bearing it is the price of keeping the body beyond purchase, and the account marks it as a cost it accepts rather than a gap it has closed.

The procedure operationalizes the account under its equal-standing premise rather than adding another metaphysical layer. Its terms—*consent*, *authorization*, *third party*, *capacity*—are the standard vocabulary moral and political philosophy already use. Consent gives public form to autonomy because subjects ordinarily have privileged access to their own conditions; the harm principle limits one subject’s course where it unjustifiably corrodes another’s; justice extends the same consideration to the conditions that sustain or starve continued participation. The structural account connects that vocabulary to one relational picture while keeping its normative bridge visible.

Read through the equal-standing premise, morality as a relation among mutually exposed subjects can recover insights distributed across its rivals without claiming that all were tracking one theory. It retains realist answerability without a Platonic property, the motivational force emphasized by command and sentiment without making either the ground, Mackie’s queerness diagnosis without nihilism, and constructivist and contractualist attention to agents in relation without treating individual endorsement as sufficient. Non-maleficence, beneficence, autonomy, and justice then become aspects of one operational demand: attend to the other subject’s protected interests rather than substituting one’s projection for them.

## 5.15 Art

Art characteristically organizes a perceptible form for attention and uptake. It can carry claims, feelings, stories, gestures, practices, and ways of seeing together; language can do many of those things too, especially in poetry, song, drama, and narrative. What paraphrase leaves behind is therefore not a content owned exclusively by art but the experience of this form, sequence, medium, and encounter. The receiver doesn’t get a copy of a maker’s experience. The work affords a reading of its own, shaped by the work, the receiver, and the practice in which they meet. Beauty names one kind of resonance in that meeting; art also ranges through ugliness, dissonance, instruction, play, protest, ritual, and inquiry.

**[Identification]**

**Art** · *Identification*

Art is a socially situated practice: making, selecting, framing, performing, or sustaining forms—for uptake that is aesthetic, expressive, imaginative, commemorative, critical, or ritual. A work can occasion perspectival and affective understanding that no paraphrase reproduces, while also carrying propositions and actions. Its reception is constrained without being copied: different warranted readings can emerge from the same work, and some readings can still be poorly supported by its form, history, or context. Resonance (beauty) is one possible event, not the definition of the register.

*Status: Drive, imagination, feeling, language, and technology supply capacities art recruits; none strictly derives art or an exhaustive definition of it. Deliberate transmission is one important case, not a necessary condition: improvisation, collective practice, found objects, ritual inheritance, and works whose effects outrun their makers remain possible. The account is a functional proposal defended by range and fit.*

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2), Imagination (§5.5), Feeling (§5.3), and Language (§5.12)

The desire is already named. Drive reaches past maintenance into curiosity, play, surprise, the pull to express (§5.2); imagination loads what hasn’t been made yet (§5.5); feeling reads a non-normative showing-up as worth undergoing. Art is exploring what those operations can create, then making a vehicle that carries the feel across an interval, whether or not it also carries a claim. Preferring the surprise to the familiar is already a weighted branch. Looking, tasting, hearing, standing in front of the work is the encounter. The account starts from those capacities, not from the bare fact that art exists.

*The result is medium-neutral.* Nothing in it privileges the eye. What it names is a way of carrying—a perspectival reading borne by a medium and not reducible to a stated proposition—and that criterion is indifferent to which sense the medium addresses, or whether it addresses a single sense at all. Music, dance, film, narrative, theater, architecture, a meal, a liturgy, the shape of a garden, the timing of a joke: each carries a reading in the way the result specifies, and none is a derivative case of painting. A list of forms would need revising every time a new medium appeared, and would have to arbitrate whether the newcomer counted; the functional test needs no such revision, because the question is never what the work is made of but whether it carries a reading through a medium, whatever it also asserts.

*Two intervals, not one.* The result already given is stated across the interval between minds, which is the interval language also crosses. But a vehicle that carries a perspectival reading has to persist to carry it, and once it persists it crosses a second interval as well: the one between times. That second crossing is the whole point of a great deal of art, and it isn’t a variant of the first. A portrait of someone dead, a photograph kept in a drawer, a name cut into stone, a song that outlives the people it was written about: each holds a reading available to be undergone long after the mind that made it has stopped. Language stores facts about the dead; these store how the dead showed up.

So art has a memory function alongside its transmission function, and the two run on different Conditions. Transmission crosses Spatiality, the interval between one standpoint and another. Storage crosses Temporality, and does it the only way anything crosses Temporality, by a bearer that persists (§1.4.3)—which is why the memory function always has a physical object at its center and why losing the object loses the memory in a way losing a copy of a text doesn’t. It also marks where art meets knowledge (§5.4) without collapsing into it. Knowledge is orientation held accurately enough to act on, and a memorial is orientation held: not the casualty figures, which a record keeps better, but what the loss was like to those who carried it. That’s why a record can’t replace a memorial and a memorial can’t replace a record. They are storing different things, and only one of them is replaceable by a more accurate copy.

The two functions then distribute across media rather than concentrating in any of them. The arts that unfold—music, dance, film, the run of a narrative—are the clearest cases of transmission, since a reading delivered in sequence is a reading undergone in the receiver’s own time. The arts that stand—the carved, the built, the painted, the inscribed—are the clearest cases of storage, since they persist as objects and can wait for a receiver who isn’t born yet. Most work does some of both, and the difference isn’t two definitions of art competing but the two intervals one vehicle can cross.

*Where the effect is.* The storage function invites a reading it must not be given: that the experience sits inside the object, waiting. It doesn’t. A progression arrives at its crescendo and someone is in tears, and nothing in the sound is grief—the same interval played into an empty room does nothing, and played to someone who has no ear for that idiom does very little. What moves is a meeting. Attention was given in the making, attention is given now, and the vehicle is the only thing that passes between them; the maker isn’t present, and the tears aren’t a copy of anything the maker felt. This is what the result means in saying the receiver undergoes a reading of their own, set going rather than transmitted, and it is what *resonance* names: not the vehicle matching a feeling already there, but the vehicle and the attending mind falling into a shape together. So nothing here stores an experience. What persists is a vehicle that can start one, and it goes on being art for exactly as long as there is someone left who can be started by it.

The relation to language can now be stated exactly, because language has a limit (§5.12) that art is standardly read as evading and in fact satisfies.

**[Corollary]**

**Art as Encounter** · *Corollary*

Description alone does not reproduce acquaintance, though linguistic and nonlinguistic communication can both guide and partly constitute encounters. Artworks characteristically supply organized things or events for a receiver to undergo, not merely reports about them.

Art is therefore not a clean second channel running beside language. The two overlap in poetry, narrative, performance, song, film, ritual, and ordinary expressive speech. What distinguishes the artistic function in these mixed cases is the organized encounter and attention the work solicits, not the absence of propositions or the necessity of a deliberately encoded feeling.

**Depends on:** Art (§5.15) and One Channel (§5.12)

Three consequences follow.

1. *Paraphrase-resistance is structural rather than mysterious.* To paraphrase a work is to convert an encounter back into the one form that can’t install acquaintance. Nothing is lost to ineffability; what is lost is the form.

2. *Non-identity of reading is expected, not failure.* Reconstruction runs on the receiver’s own materials, so what the receiver undergoes isn’t a copy of the maker’s reading, and no fidelity requirement is breached when it differs.

3. *The vehicle is a third thing.* It must persist to carry anything, be distinct from both minds, and be undergone in some order. That is Substantiality, Spatiality, and Temporality instantiated by an object between subjects—the Ontological Identity (§2.6.8) applied to the work itself rather than to either party—and it’s why the same vehicle crosses the interval between times as well as the interval between minds. A perspectival reading that stayed inside one mind would cross neither.

The second consequence is worth drawing out, because it is easily mistaken for a concession that reading is arbitrary. Reconstruction runs on the receiver’s own prior encounters, and those are neither random nor private: they are the receiver’s accumulated registration (§5.4) with its weights (§5.2) already attached. So divergence in reading is systematic rather than noise, and the clearest cases are the ones where a public disagreement can be traced to what the disagreeing parties had already encountered.

Maya Lin’s Vietnam Veterans Memorial is the standing example. The same wall—cut into the ground, black, bearing names in the order the deaths occurred—was received by some veterans and commentators as a wound, a refusal of the honor a memorial owes, and by others as a structure that placed the dead before the cause and let grief stand without argument. The dispute was severe enough that a figurative sculpture was added nearby. Neither reading need be dismissed merely because it differs from the other: each can be reconstructed from the wall and a different history of encounter. That doesn’t establish that no reading could misread the work. Its design, inscriptions, historical setting, genre, and public use constrain interpretation even though no proposition fully arbitrates among readings.

An inkblot isolates the mechanism most cleanly because the vehicle is emptied on purpose. It carries almost no reading of its own, and what a viewer reports is correspondingly almost all reconstruction: the figures found in it are drawn from what that viewer has already registered, and nothing can be found there for which no prior encounter supplies material. Whatever is to be said about the diagnostic use such tests were put to, which is contested on its own grounds and isn’t relied on here, the ordinary observation holds and is the present point in unusually pure form. The richer the vehicle, the more it constrains the reconstruction; strip the vehicle toward nothing and the reading approaches the receiver’s own stock. Works sit between those poles, which is why they can be genuinely about something and still read differently by different people.

The point isn’t confined to objects one can look at. Shostakovich’s Fifth ends in a major-key march that has been heard as an affirmation and heard as a coerced affirmation, rejoicing performed under a gun; the disagreement turns on what a listener brings concerning the year, the composer’s position, and the cost of the alternative, and the notes are identical either way.

Three things follow. Divergence can often be explained partly by what receivers have encountered, so interpretation is open to study rather than sealed off as taste. Convergence may reflect shared histories, conventions, features of the work, or common perceptual capacities. And warranted plurality doesn’t imply interpretive immunity: a reading can conflict with salient features of the vehicle or context, or be false about what the vehicle represents, without there being one complete paraphrase against which all readings are measured.

The result also fixes where art’s liability sits. Because an encounter can be manufactured, it can be manufactured to install a reading that misrepresents what it is a reading *of*, and the receiver has no paraphrase to check it against—the very feature that makes the form work. That is the against-mapping mode (§5.14) operating through a channel with no propositional surface, which is what propaganda in artistic form is, and why it isn’t a misuse of some faculty adjacent to art but the same operation run against the receiver.

*Beauty before art.* Before there is art there is *beauty*: the structural relation a being’s art will draw on and carry a reading of across the interval. Beauty is the resonance a being that models itself deeply enough experiences when its self-modeling registers fit with the structures of the field it is in. It isn’t a property the field carries on its own and it isn’t a projection the mind lays onto an inert field; it is the mutual registration of a self-modeling being and a structure of the field when the two are configured to register one another. A face, a phrase of music, a landscape at evening, a proof, a turn in a film, a season’s first cold: these are beautiful when the structures they present and the mind attending to them resonate, and the resonance is real on both sides. Beauty is what the mind’s coupling to the field is, in the moments where the coupling is registered as fit rather than as pressure. Art is the practice that follows from this: the making of vehicles that carry the maker’s perspectival reading of such a coupling across the interval that separates self-modeling beings, so that the resonance the maker registered is occasioned anew in the receiver, who undergoes a reading of their own, not a copy of the maker’s. Resonance is what art works from and what it occasions at the far end; what the vehicle itself carries is the reading.

*Beauty without an artist; art through practice.* Beauty doesn’t require an artist. A sunset, landscape, storm, face, proof, or season can occasion resonance whether or not anyone designed it. Nature is therefore not art merely by being beautiful. Art begins when a form is made, selected, framed, performed, or sustained within an artistic practice. Intention can matter without being sovereign: works can emerge through improvisation, collaboration, accident, inherited ritual, found objects, cameras, synthesizers, or generative systems, and their significance can exceed what any maker meant to render. Authorship and classification then depend on contribution, adoption, framing, practice, and reception rather than on a hidden feeling that must have been encoded at the start.

*Beauty and the agreeable.* Kant’s third Critique drew the line the resonance account has to honor. He separated the *agreeable* (das Angenehme), what merely gratifies a particular sense and about which each person speaks only for themselves, from the *beautiful*, which is disinterested (not the discharge of a want) and yet claims what he called a universal voice: to call a thing beautiful is to speak as if others ought to find it so, even though no concept and no listed property of the object compels the agreement. The resonance account keeps both marks without the apparatus Kant thought they needed. Resonance isn’t the agreeable, because gratification discharges an appetite the body brought to the encounter, while resonance is the registration of fit with a structure the current wasn’t using for anything, which is why it can be undergone at no advantage and often at cost (the requiem, the storm). And resonance carries the universal voice without making beauty a property the object holds on its own: because the coupling is between a structure that is really there and a mind configured as other minds are configured, the maker builds the vehicle expecting the fit to be occasioned again in another current, and that warranted expectation (not a concept, and not an object-property) is what the claim to shared assent amounts to. Kant’s subjective universality reads here as the shareability of a coupling across minds similarly configured to a common field: subjective because it lives in the registration rather than in the object alone, universal because the presented form and the receiver’s configuration are held in common. The judgment of taste is then neither a report of private sensation nor the detection of a quality the thing carries by itself, but the claim that a coupling available to one is available to the similarly configured many.

Art is how one mind’s perspectival reading of some structure is made available to another, across Space and Time, through a made vehicle. Art transmits *how* a particular structure (death, a face, a city, autumn, or Nature itself) shows up to a particular mind, across the interval language also crosses (§5.12), through a different technology.

What language transmits distinctively is propositional content: claims that can be assessed for truth, repeated without distortion, and understood in the abstract. What art transmits distinctively isn’t propositional. Propositional content can ride along: a poem asserts, a protest song claims, a history painting argues. But what makes the register art is what paraphrase doesn’t preserve: the felt shape of a particular mind’s reading of what the work is about. Strip the perspectival reading from a poem and only the claim remains; that claim isn’t what made the poem art.

*The shared root with language.* Although the distinction so far has emphasized what art and language transmit *differently* (perspectival reading versus propositional claim) the two practices share a root in *symbolic externalization*: the act of taking something held in the maker’s modal field and giving it external form so that another current can register it. At the developed end of the gradient, the specializations diverge cleanly. Wordless music is pure art, externalizing resonance with no referential content; a mathematical proof is pure language, externalizing referential content with little or no resonance-work. But the divergence is recent in evolutionary and developmental terms. At the early end of the gradient, the two functions weren’t separated. Cave paintings depict animals and hunt-scenes; their specific cultural functions remain contested across the interpretive literature, with hunting-magic, shamanic-neuropsychological (Lewis-Williams 2002), ritual, and identity-marking accounts all in play, and whatever the function, the marks do referential work (depicting subjects) while also externalizing the maker’s perspectival reading of those subjects (resonance); hieroglyphic scripts begin as pictorial reference and conventionalize into linguistic signs over generations, with the resonance and the reference held in the same marks. Music probably begins as affective vocalization undifferentiated between proto-art (expressive resonance) and proto-language (referential signaling), specializing later into song and speech. Children’s drawing, gesture, mark-making, and humming are pre-specialized in the same way: the same externalization operation performed across both functions before either has separated out. What language and art are, then, are two specializations of the same underlying capacity for symbolic externalization, diverging as the mind’s depth permits each function to be developed in its own direction. The linguistic specialization is treated at depth at §5.12; the shared root is why every developed culture has both, why the boundary between them remains porous in poetry, in protest song, in graphic novels, in calligraphy, and in the many art forms that do referential and resonance work simultaneously.

The reading is *of* some structure (a subject) and is rendered *through* a structured medium. The subject can be anything sufficient to occasion a stance: death, politics, technology, a person, a season, or, as in much music and abstract painting, the medium itself. The medium has its own internal grammar (tonal harmony and meter, prosody, perspective and color, framing and cut, line and weight) and this medium-structure constitutively shapes which readings are even renderable. A composer’s reading of grief is rendered through tonal structure; the same reading attempted in another musical grammar would yield a different work, not because the reading is different but because the medium-grammar yields different angles. This is why mastery of a medium matters, why traditions develop their own expressive capacities, and why different art forms aren’t interchangeable.

The reading is perspectival, not subjective. It is genuinely of the structure, but *from somewhere*: bound to one mind’s current, history, and emphases. And the rendering isn’t a faithful transcription but a *creative distortion* of the structure (selecting, heightening, compressing, recombining) so that what the vehicle expands on another current’s modal field (§5.4) is possibility rendered impressionistically rather than stated exactly. The distortion isn’t a lapse of fidelity but the mechanism of the register: it is calibrated, consciously or not, to the angle from which the structure resonates: with the maker first, and through the vehicle with whoever reads it after. Two perspectival readings of the same structure don’t compete the way two propositional descriptions do; they are different angles, both real, both about the same thing. This is why ten poems on death don’t refute each other, and why a single artwork keeps yielding new readings across receivers and across time: receivers, themselves perspectival, are set resonating with what the work holds, in registers shaped by their own lives.

What this transmission accomplishes for the receiver is more than reception of one mind’s reading. Art operates at three levels on the modal field (§5.4) traced so far. First, externalization: the made vehicle is a stable occasion for shared simulation, and when many receivers encounter it independently they each run the simulation it occasions on their own field. The audience in a horror theater watching characters split up is each, separately, running a simulation that concludes they shouldn’t; the work’s externalization is doing what no individual body could do alone: coordinating private simulations across many bodies onto the same modal target. That shared target is one region of felt modal field held across the many beings the work reaches: language may hold a shared *claim*, while art holds a shared *reading*. Art can therefore contribute to the material from which collectively held knowledge is built, but the Modal Convergence theorem (§5.4) remains the narrower epistemic theorem of that knowledge rather than a theorem of aesthetic transmission. Second, cultivation: a serious work installs into the receiver’s modal field regions the receiver had not lived through. A hero arc rehearsed and worked through under narrative pressure leaves the receiver with the protagonist’s hard-won possibilities loaded into their own field, available later when the receiver faces analogous conditions. The reach of any single life is finite; literature, drama, and film extend the modal coverage of any body that engages them well past what the body’s own experience would have laid down. Third, generation: art can install possibilities that have never occurred, including possibilities that strictly can’t. Dystopias, ghost stories, counterfactual histories, science fiction, horror: these are pure modal generation, and the body stores their content the same way it stores observed and lived possibility, because the network doesn’t care whether the input came from experience, observation, or imagination. Morbid curiosity is the legible appetite for this third operation: the body deliberately seeks aversive simulations because storing negative-possibility content expands its modal coverage of what could go wrong, and the survival value of that coverage outweighs the affective cost. The three operations aren’t three different art forms; they are three modes of the same operation, layered in every work to different degrees.

The structure of transmission therefore involves three terms: the maker, the made vehicle, and the receiver. The maker’s perspectival reading is registered in how the vehicle is built: what is foregrounded, what is held back, what the medium-grammar is made to do. The vehicle carries those registrations across Space and Time as a stable occasion for attention. The receiver, encountering the vehicle, has their attention shaped by what it does, and undergoes a reading that resonates with the maker’s without copying it. The made vehicle need not persist: it may be a recited poem, a sung phrase, a danced figure, an utterance, as well as a painting, a manuscript, or a recording. What is required is the *act of making* (the instantiation of a reading in something a receiver can attend to), not the persistence of a thing. Persistent vehicles extend transmission across longer Time intervals than ephemeral ones; both register as art.

This account treats art as a structural register of beings of sufficient depth, not as a category of objects defined by institutional consensus or aesthetic theory. Once self-modeling beings have perspectival readings of structures and need to transmit them, the conditions for art are met. The specific traditions, conventions, and forms art has taken across human cultures are contingent (shaped by available materials, technologies, and historical moments) but the structural fact that perspectival readings of structure require a made-vehicle medium for transmission is what makes those traditions possible at all.

*The sublime and the death-haunted: content versus act.* The account so far raises a question that has to be answered. If beauty is resonance with structure, and art is the practice of making that resonance shareable, why is so much of art bound up with what damages, ends, or negates the lives the work is shared among? Tragedy, war painting, requiems, gothic and horror traditions, lament poetry, the entire literature of grief and finitude: all of it is art, and much of it is among the work the tradition treats as its most serious. Two facts can be distinguished here. The *content* of a work is what the work is about: what the perspectival reading registers and the vehicle conveys. The *act* of the work is what the maker does in making it and what the receiver does in receiving it. A requiem’s content is death; the act of composing the requiem and the act of listening to it are continued exercises of the current that knows it will end. A funeral lament’s content is loss; the act of singing it is an organized response of the surviving currents to that loss. Burke and Kant, treating what the eighteenth century called the sublime, had hold of a piece of this: the experience of confronting a structure that exceeds or threatens the person (a storm, a vast space, a chaos) is registered as beauty rather than as bare terror because the act of registering it from inside the life that registers is itself an affirmation of that life’s continuation in the act. Schopenhauer’s account of tragedy and Nietzsche’s of the tragic art form name the same thing at greater historical depth. Death-haunted art isn’t a counterexample to beauty as resonance with vitality. It is the structural case in which the content is negation and the act is affirmation, and the asymmetry between content and act is what the receiver registers as sublime rather than as merely beautiful. The mind can resonate with what it knows it won’t survive, because the act of resonating is one of the things a mind does while it is still running.

*Resonance precedes mortality.* That beauty is the resonance of a mind with the field, rather than a death-anchored response, is confirmed at the pre-mortality end of the developmental arc as well as at the death-anchored end. Children resonate with structure long before they have grasped mortality as a structural fact about themselves: a song, a face, a painted animal, a sunset, a story. The resonance is genuine and the engagement is genuinely aesthetic; the death-horizon hasn’t yet reorganized anything. The mortality threshold (§5.9) reorganizes beauty *after* it into the three death-anchored responses (sexuality, art, spirituality), but it doesn’t create beauty. The pre-threshold form of aesthetic engagement isn’t a precursor to art in the way that babbling is a precursor to language; it is already art’s operation, run by a current whose modal field hasn’t yet been rearranged by the absolute horizon. Dutton (*The Art Instinct* 2009) and Chatterjee (*The Aesthetic Brain* 2014) confirm the same point from the evolved-aesthetic-capacity angle: aesthetic responsiveness is a feature of the current at depth, not a derivative of mortality-awareness.

*A note on scope.* The account of art isn’t a strict derivation from the proof; rejecting it doesn’t propagate backward.

### 5.15.1 The Dispute
The philosophy of art has organized around several principal positions across the analytic and continental traditions. All of them are engaged by name.

*Institutional theory.* Dickie (1974; 1984) and Danto (1964; 1981) developed institutional accounts: a work is art if it has been conferred art-status by the artworld (Dickie) or interpreted as a candidate for appreciation within an artworld-supplied theoretical framework (Danto). The position handles avant-garde and conceptual works elegantly but is widely criticized for its circularity and for its inability to explain art before the institutional apparatus existed. Institutional theory is read here as picking up real features of the contemporary artworld, while supplying the structural reading: art is the made-vehicle transmission of perspectival readings of structure; the institutional apparatus is one of many cultural contexts within which this transmission has been organized, neither necessary for art’s existence nor constitutive of its nature.

*Formalism.* Bell (1914), Greenberg (1960), and the broader formalist tradition treat significant form as constitutive of art—the arrangement of formal elements (line, color, mass, sound, rhythm) being what art *is*, with content as either secondary or constituted by form. The position handles abstract and non-representational work elegantly but struggles with representational art’s clear engagement with subjects beyond its formal arrangement. Formalism is read here as correctly identifying that the medium-grammar of art is constitutive of what art can transmit, while supplying the structural reading: form is the medium through which perspectival readings are rendered, not the content the readings are *of*.

*Expressivism.* Collingwood (1938) and Tolstoy (1898) developed expressivist accounts on which art is the expression of emotion: the artist spells out an emotion through the work, and the audience reconstructs the emotion in response. The position captures something real about art’s affective dimension but has trouble with art whose content isn’t primarily emotional. Expressivism is read here as correctly identifying that perspectival reading carries affective register, while supplying the structural reading: emotion is one register a perspectival reading can carry, with perspective on structure being more general than emotion alone.

*Aesthetic-experience accounts.* Dewey (1934), Beardsley (1958), and the broader aesthetic-experience tradition locate art’s defining feature in the kind of experience it produces in suitably situated receivers. The position captures something real about art’s reception side but faces the difficulty that aesthetic experience can be produced by non-art (a sunset, a face) and that some art (challenging modern works) produces little of what is traditionally classified as aesthetic experience. Aesthetic-experience accounts are read here as picking up real features of art’s transmission to receivers, while supplying the structural reading: what the receiver undergoes is a resonating reading shaped by the vehicle, not a separate aesthetic-experience kind.

*Heideggerian and continental accounts.* Heidegger’s (1935–36) 1971 “The Origin of the Work of Art” developed an influential account on which the artwork sets up a world and lets truth happen in its work-being. Gadamer (1960), Adorno (1970), and Merleau-Ponty (1964) extended the continental tradition. These accounts are read here as identifying real features of art—art’s capacity to disclose and to challenge—while supplying the structural reading: what is disclosed is a structural feature of the medium the perspectival reading registers, with the work as the made-vehicle holding the disclosure available to the receiver.

*Analytic aesthetics.* Walton (1990), Levinson (1990; 2006), Currie (2010), and the contemporary analytic-aesthetics tradition refine specific questions—the ontology of artworks, the role of imagination, the structure of fictional truth, the relation between art and morality. This literature develops the local logic of specific art-related phenomena, and the structural account supplies what the local debates can be located within.

*Critical theory and ideology critique.* From Marx and Benjamin through the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse) to contemporary critical theory, a tradition treats art as inseparable from the social conditions of its production and reception, with ideology critique as a central task. The account here reads critical theory as correctly identifying that art is socially conditioned—specific works arise in specific historical situations, with the social conditions shaping what can be made and what can be transmitted—while supplying the structural reading: the social conditions condition the *what* of specific artworks; the *that* of art (made-vehicle transmission of perspectival readings) isn’t socially constructed.

*Adorno and negative dialectics.* Beyond ideology critique, Adorno’s (1970) *Aesthetic Theory* presses an objection a structural account of art must face. Its core is the non-identical: conceptual thought subsumes the particular under the universal and always leaves a remainder, and art’s truth-content is its capacity to hold precisely that remainder—what the concept can’t. A metaphysics that derives everything from one necessary structure invites the charge that treating art as just one more structural register is itself an act of subsumption, dissolving the particular work into an instance of a kind.

Three further objections follow. First, art bears truth exactly where the concept fails, so explaining art *as* transmission threatens to explain away what makes it truth-bearing. Second, letting suffering speak is itself a condition of truth, so a system that smooths the negative away falsifies itself: a whole that erases its own negative is to that extent false. Third, a system claiming to have demonstrated the necessity of all things can revert to the myth and fate enlightenment was meant to escape. The account here reads Adorno as correctly identifying that any account which subsumes the particular and affirms the whole stands condemned. It meets the charge not by resisting the non-identical but by claiming it, the reply taken up at §5.15.5.

*Reductionist evolutionary and cognitive accounts.* Dutton (2009), Bloom (2010), Boyd (2009), and the broader evolutionary-aesthetics tradition treat art as an adaptation, by-product, or culturally evolved phenomenon explicable through cognitive and selection pressures. The account here reads them as identifying real features of art’s psychological architecture, while supplying the structural reading: the perspectival-reading transmission art consists in is what subjects at sufficient depth do when they need to share what language can’t carry; specific cognitive and selection pressures condition how the activity is realized but don’t constitute it.

*The art/non-art boundary.* A live dispute concerns what distinguishes art from non-art—craft, design, entertainment, propaganda, decoration. Various proposals (institutional, formal, intentional, functional) have been advanced. The structural reading supplies a usable distinction: art is the made-vehicle transmission of perspectival readings of structure, with works whose function is restricted to information-transmission (propositional argument), to utility (craft, design), or to mere stimulus (entertainment) sitting outside the structural core, while admitting that hybrid works are common and the boundary isn’t sharp. Entertainment isn’t thereby dismissed as idle: on the account developed at §5.5, it is a manufactured case of branch-loading, field-expansion with the exposure cost engineered down, so most entertainment carries some perspectival load and most art supplies some traversal; the boundary was never going to be sharp because the two draw on the same operation.

*Authenticity, reproduction, and the digital question.* Benjamin (1936) and the subsequent literature on mechanical reproduction raised questions about authenticity and aura. The recent emergence of generative AI art presses similar questions in new form: what is the perspectival reading transmitted by an artwork whose maker is a generative model? The structural reading supplies a framework: art requires a perspectival reading to be transmitted; whether a generative model has perspectival readings (and what they would consist in) is structurally the same question as whether LLMs engage in propositional understanding (§5.12.1), currently underdetermined.

### 5.15.2 The Requirement
*Form-specific uptake.* Propositional paraphrase doesn’t preserve every feature of an organized encounter, but language and art are overlapping practices rather than exclusive channels. An adequate account should explain why a poem, song, novel, painting, proof, performance, or film can combine assertion, affect, action, and form, and why changing the medium changes what can be taken up. The relevant contrast is graded and functional, not “language carries the claim while art carries the feel.”

*Encounter rather than field-transfer.* Propositional transfer can’t install acquaintance, which is reconstructed from the receiver’s own prior encounters (§5.4). An adequate account has to locate art as the manufacture of an encounter the receiver undergoes, not as a second channel of modal-field transfer beside language, so paraphrase-resistance is structural rather than a failure of description.

*Three-term transmission structure.* Any account must accommodate the maker, the made vehicle, and the receiver rather than reducing art to maker-intention or receiver-experience alone. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the maker-vehicle-receiver structure, with the vehicle as the persistent (or repeatable) occasion that bridges the interval.

*Perspectival without subjective.* Any account must distinguish perspectival from subjective rather than collapsing one into the other. The structural requirement is that the account treat perspectival readings as different angles on the same structure, both real, with two perspectival readings of the same subject not competing the way two propositional descriptions do.

*Medium-grammar as constitutive.* Any account must accommodate medium-grammar rather than treating media as interchangeable. The structural requirement is that the account explain why mastery of a medium matters, why traditions develop their own expressive capacities, and why different art forms aren’t interchangeable.

*The act of making rather than the persistence of a thing.* Any account must accommodate ephemeral art (recited poems, sung phrases, danced figures) alongside persistent art (paintings, manuscripts, recordings). The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the instantiation (necessary) from the persistence (extending transmission across longer Time intervals but not constitutive of art’s structure).

*Connection to language and meaning.* Art is the next structural register after language (§5.12) and depends on the meaning-orientation named at §5.10. Any account must connect art to these upstream registers rather than treating it as autonomous. The structural requirement is that the account derive art’s transmission structure from what self-modeling subjects need to do when their perspectival reading of structure exceeds what propositional content can carry.

*The reading-is-of-some-structure condition.* Any account must accommodate this *of-structure* condition rather than treating art as expression without aboutness. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the directedness of perspectival readings: they reach toward the structure they are readings of.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Art requires the depth of self-modeling at which a subject can hold a perspectival reading and intend a vehicle to transmit it. Shallow forms—ritualized display, marking, decorative behavior—exist in non-human lineages. Any account must accommodate the gradient rather than treating art as uniquely human. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish what runs at each depth, with full perspectival-reading transmission requiring the self-aware threshold named at §5.1.

*Substrate-independence at the structural level.* As with the other registers, the activity of perspectival-reading transmission can in principle be realized in different substrates; whether generative AI systems engage in it is structurally legible without prejudgment. Any account must distinguish what is substrate-essential from what is substrate-independent. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the substrate-independence of the structural activity while flagging the open question of which substrates currently support it.

### 5.15.3 Predictions
Given the structural conditions the chapter has assembled, art isn’t an optional cultural embellishment. Under those conditions it is what the account predicts.

A person registers their own orientations (§5.2, §5.8). That registration has a feel—the internal aspect consciousness consists in. Some of the feel is propositionally expressible: someone can state what they have registered, and language will carry the statement across the interval to others (§5.12). But much of the feel isn’t propositional. The specific quality of grief at a particular loss, the specific texture of joy in a particular encounter, the specific weight of a particular memory—these aren’t paraphrasable. A paraphrase loses precisely what was to be transmitted. The content is the feel itself, not a description of the feel.

The prediction is conditional and sharp. Wherever sufficiently self-modeling social beings with non-propositional content needing transmission persist together in a medium with the three Conditions—and have materials and time enough to instantiate forms—the conditions for art are met, and this predicts that some form of made-object vehicle will arise to carry the content. The argument is conditional on those antecedents (depth of self-modeling sufficient for non-propositional registration; sociality sufficient for the transmission demand; materials and time enough to instantiate forms), and is a structural-tendency claim under those conditions, not a bare entailment from T/S/Φ alone. Once the conditions obtain, propositional transmission can’t carry the content without destroying it. Something else must do the carrying. That something is art.

Art therefore requires all the conditions assembled so far. It requires Time because the form persists across a before and after, and because the feel unfolds rather than appears instantaneously. It requires Space because artist and audience occupy different positions, and the artifact crosses the interval between them without collapsing it. It requires Substance because the form must be made of something that holds its shape long enough to be encountered. It requires self-modeling in the artist, because only a being with an internal aspect has a feel to externalize. It requires self-modeling in the audience, because only a being with an internal aspect can have a feel occasioned in it. Remove any of these and art becomes structurally unavailable. Keep all of them, in beings that model themselves deeply enough and are sufficiently social, and art becomes structurally predictable—what such beings do with non-propositional content given materials and time.

*Making and uptake.* Art has two components, kept separate throughout. Both are needed; neither alone is art.

The first is making. A person whose inside registers a particular orientation—a grief, a joy, a wonder, a terror, a tenderness, a recognition—shapes Substance into a form that answers to it. The artist doesn’t transcribe the feel; transcription is description’s operation, and description can’t install this content. The artist instead builds a thing whose structure, when encountered, produces the feel in someone capable of receiving it. The craft of art is the craft of building such things.

A song is a structure of sound in Time; a symphony or instrumental composition, the same operation at larger architecture. A painting is a structure of color and shape in Space; a drawing, of line and tone; a sculpture, of mass and surface in three dimensions; a photograph, of light caught at an instant; a work of architecture, of inhabited Space organized for the people who pass through it. A poem is a structure of language used for its sound, image, and rhythm rather than its propositional content; a novel or short story unfolds language across narrative Time; a piece of theater gathers bodies, voices, and language into one place for the duration of a performance. A dance is a structure of body moving through Space in Time.
