Craft—pottery, weaving, woodworking, glass, garment, tattoo, the well-shaped tool—works Substance into forms someone lives with daily, and remains art wherever the form is built so a feel can land in whoever takes it up. Comedy times sound, image, and silence so a recognition arrives as release. A film is a structure of many of these at once; an interactive medium like the video game folds the audience’s own choices into the form.

The materials differ; the operation doesn’t. In each case the artist has taken something internal, a feel that was theirs alone, and built an external form that will, if the craft succeeds, no longer be theirs alone—composer, painter, sculptor, photographer, architect, poet, novelist, playwright, dancer, choreographer, actor, craftsperson, comedian, filmmaker, designer.

The same operation runs at scales the canon doesn’t always honor. A curated social presence, a styled feed, a hosted dinner, a chosen wardrobe, a room arranged for a guest, the cadence of someone’s everyday self-presentation—each *can be* the operation art consists in, but only when two conditions are jointly met. First, the making must be shaped for *resonance*—for a non-propositional feel landing in whoever encounters the form—rather than only for utility, status, persuasion, identification, or compliance with convention. Second, the form must hold together as a current in its own right, not merely as the sum of its functional parts; what it presents has to be a structured whole whose unity is what carries the feel.

A wardrobe chosen for warmth and price is styled, but it isn’t yet art; a wardrobe chosen so a particular feel of selfhood can land in the people who encounter the wearer, and composed as a current whose unity carries that feel, is the operation, even if the result isn’t what gallery-and-museum aesthetics has historically named. The criterion separating art from styled-but-non-art presentation isn’t whether the maker has been licensed by an institution or the form ratified by a tradition; it is whether the form is built so a non-propositional content can land. By that criterion most curated social presence is *not* art—most is styling for status, identification, persuasion, or compliance with platform convention. Some of it is. The operation, not the medium, is what determines which.

The second is uptake. Someone else, elsewhere in Space or later in Time, encounters the form and undergoes an experience shaped by it. That experience need not reproduce the artist’s, and the work need not please, move, or “resonate” successfully with every receiver to remain art. Resonance names one strong mode of uptake. Confusion, resistance, estrangement, boredom, analysis, and delayed recognition are others. The form makes an encounter available; the artistic practice doesn’t require one invariant effect to complete an encoded arc.

Art isn’t identical to self-expression. A private scream can express without being art, while conceptual, procedural, found, or collaborative art need not externalize one person’s prior feeling. Craft matters because forms constrain uptake, but craft can be exploratory rather than engineered toward a known response. Art is better identified by its place in practices of making, framing, attention, and interpretation than by expression successfully transmitted.

### 5.15.4 Confirmation
The structural account predicts that wherever subjects can externalize and transmit non-propositional orientation through made forms, art will recur. The anthropological record gives that conditional a demanding test across documented human cultures: no society has been documented without artistic practices in such forms as music, visual representation, narrative, or bodily performance (Brown 1991; Dissanayake 1995; Dutton 2009). The record therefore corroborates recurrence across the available human cases. The universal conditional rests on the structural account rather than by projecting a finite sample onto every possible culture.

The antiquity is older than our species in its modern form. The oldest known figurative art dates to at least 40,000 years ago (Aubert 2014; Aubert 2019), with geometric markings and pigment use extending much earlier. The Hoffmann et al. (2018) claim that Neanderthals produced Iberian cave art at least 64,000 years ago is contested on dating methodology (White and Bosinski 2020; Hoffmann 2020); the broader picture of Neanderthal symbolic activity—pigment use, ornament, deliberate burial—is supported across multiple independent lines. Ochre was being deliberately processed 100,000 years ago at Blombos Cave (Henshilwood et al. 2011). Musical instruments—bone flutes—appear at least 35,000 years ago, with later recalibrations of the Aurignacian sequence pushing the dates earlier still (Conard et al. 2009; Higham 2012). Whatever art is, it isn’t a late refinement of civilization. It appears early in the record of beings of our kind, and possibly before them.

Affective neuroscience identifies the neural substrate of the resonance. Music engages the brain’s reward, motor, and affective systems in coordinated patterns that track the structural features of the composition (Koelsch 2014; Zatorre and Salimpoor 2013), and encountering depicted emotion activates affective circuitry overlapping with directly undergoing emotion. The strong mirror-neuron interpretation of this overlap (Gallese 2003; Keysers 2011) has been substantively contested (Hickok 2014); the broader neural-overlap finding doesn’t depend on which mechanistic account explains it. Narrative transports listeners into simulated experiences whose affective consequences mirror lived ones (Mar and Oatley 2008; Zunshine 2006). The mechanism by which a form occasions a feel in a receiver is the same self-modeling machinery found in life (§4.8), operating on externally supplied input—nothing mysterious about it.

The fact that art can’t be fully paraphrased confirms the prediction from the other direction. A summary of a poem counts as a different thing altogether, one that has lost what the poem was for, rather than simply a shorter poem. A description of a piece of music isn’t the music; the description doesn’t produce the feel the music produces. Translation across art forms is always partial and always loses content that was specific to the original form: novelizations of films, film adaptations of novels, orchestral arrangements of songs. If what a work carries were independent of its form, these losses would be incidental. They aren’t incidental. They are constitutive, because what a work supplies is an encounter with this form, and neither a description nor another medium reproduces it.

Aesthetic display extends below the human threshold. Bowerbird males build elaborate decorated structures that serve no direct survival function, selecting and arranging objects by color, symmetry, and visual arrangement to attract females, with younger birds learning by observing the structures of older males (Borgia 1985; Madden 2003). Lyrebirds and mockingbirds incorporate complex vocal mimicry into elaborate displays. Across the courtship literature, what recurs is made forms whose structure is shaped to produce a response in another self-modeling subject—the resonance half of art’s arc, instantiated below the depth at which making becomes deliberate craft transmitted as cultural inheritance. What human art adds isn’t the made-thing-shaped-to-produce-feel—that is widespread—but the depth at which both the making and the resonance become objects of awareness, modeled by the subject that performs them, and transmitted across generations as cultural form (Dissanayake 1995; Dutton 2009).

Religion confirms the prediction from a third direction. Sustained religious traditions have characteristically developed elaborate artistic practices—liturgical music, architectural space designed for affective resonance, ritual performance, narrative scripture read aloud, iconic visual representation—because each needed to transmit non-propositional content (reverence, awe, belonging, dread, consolation) across generations, and propositional transmission alone couldn’t do it. Theological propositions about a tradition survive translation; the feel of the tradition survives through its art. That religion and art so often developed together isn’t coincidence. They share a constitutive function: the transmission of shared orientation across the interval that separates one person from another.

### 5.15.5 Conclusions
Several long-standing debates resolve once art is understood structurally. Beauty is neither in the eye of the beholder nor in the object. The subjectivist holds that beauty is whatever a viewer happens to find beautiful. The objectivist holds that beauty is a property of the object itself, awaiting detection. Both misidentify the locus. Beauty is the name for successful resonance—the structural event in which a form and someone capable of taking it up resonate together. It requires both the object (with structural features that afford the resonance) and the subject (with structural capacity to resonate). It isn’t a property of either alone, because it is an event between them. This dissolves the apparent disagreement between the traditions without splitting the difference: the objectivist was right that the form has real structural features, the subjectivist was right that the receiver is essential, and neither saw that beauty is what happens when the structural features meet a receiver structured to take them up.

Propaganda is art weaponized. The same mechanism that transmits tenderness across generations transmits hatred across a population. A film that builds affection for a character uses the same resonance operation as a film that builds contempt for an out-group. This isn’t a flaw in the structural account; it is what the account predicts. Art is a transmission technology. Technologies can be used to transmit content that serves or corrodes the exchanges among those who receive it. What distinguishes art from propaganda isn’t the mechanism but what the content does to the receiver’s relations with others. Morally corrosive resonance is resonance engineered to narrow and harden—to foreclose the receiver’s capacity for the mutual registration that grounds morality (§5.14). This is distinct from merely persuasive or partisan art: art with a position, even a strongly partisan one, can leave the receiver’s capacity for moral attention to others intact, because taking a position isn’t the same as foreclosing the receiver’s capacity to register others as subjects of the same kind. Propaganda fails the criterion (§5.14) specifically—it is resonance designed to corrode the very mutual-registration capacity the receiver would need to recognize the corrosion as such. The morality of art is the morality of what art does to those it lands in, evaluated against the structural account (§5.14) of what corrodes intersubjective registration.

Art and religion share machinery because they share a structural function. Both bind communities around a feel too specific to paraphrase. This is why secular art has absorbed so many religious functions in societies where religion has receded—the structural need the machinery met doesn’t disappear when the metaphysics does.

AI-generated art poses a genuine structural question, not a merely technological one. The question isn’t whether a non-self-modeling process can produce an artifact that triggers feels in receivers; clearly it can, because the resonance operation runs on the receiver’s own architecture, not the producer’s. The question is whether an artifact produced without a feel on the making side is art in the structural sense developed here, or something else that happens to use art’s mechanism. The account here suggests the latter for art’s central case. There, a reading passes from one self-modeling inside into another, and the internal aspect on the making side is a component of the operation rather than a definitional add-on. An AI-produced image that moves a viewer is doing resonance without making in this structural sense—half the arc. Concealing that origin adds a harm the half-arc description alone doesn’t name. A receiver who takes a work to be made has formed exactly the belief identified as recognition’s first condition at §5.14 and §6.2.2: that a genuinely other position is present in the exchange. When the work has no maker, that belief is false, and its collapse on discovery is a recognition failure rather than a mere factual disappointment, which is why it registers as betrayal rather than demystification. The mechanism is distinct from misrepresenting a real other’s identity (as in catfishing) or violating a condition assumed between two correctly-recognized others (as in infidelity): in both of those cases the other is genuinely there and the recognition condition holds; here it doesn’t, which is what makes the concealed half-arc case the sharper one. Whether to extend the term ‘art’ to cover the half-arc is partly a terminological question and partly a question about what the practice of art is for, not a question the structural account settles by itself. What the account does settle is that the two halves are distinct operations, and collapsing them loses something important about what art has been.

Censorship of art is a distinctive kind of harm. Suppressing art doesn’t merely restrict expression in the way suppressing speech does. It severs a transmission interval that people separated by Space and Time rely on for non-propositional connection. A community whose art is censored loses access to the feels its members would otherwise share with each other and with those who came before. The harm reaches the conditions of connection (§5.10) rather than only the content of any particular work.

Adorno’s objection is met by claiming the non-identical, not resisting it. The account doesn’t subsume the particular work under a concept; it identifies art as the register built to carry what the concept must drop—the perspectival reading that survives no paraphrase. Art and language are both representations, and every representation leaves a remainder; what distinguishes art is that the remainder is its content. Where a paraphrase (§5.12) keeps the claim and lets the encounter fall away, the work holds precisely what the paraphrase discards—Adorno’s non-identical named as a structural function rather than feared as a vulnerability. And the perspectival reading is genuinely *of* what the work represents, real on both sides and not mere projection, so art breaks the formula of literal realism without forfeiting the truth-content Adorno prizes. The suffering objection is met by a distinction Adorno’s own demand requires. Letting suffering speak is a condition of truth, and art is where it speaks; but to register suffering as real isn’t to justify it. The account holds suffering as an inevitable, only-mitigable feature of existing, never as a necessity redeemed by the whole: the triconditional structure is necessary, the suffering within Nature isn’t thereby affirmed, and making art from suffering takes the side of the living without endorsing the wound—the requiem’s content is death, its making an act of life. This is why, here, the whole isn’t the false. The account demonstrates the necessity of the *structure* while leaving the negative un-recuperated, and that is the one move that keeps a necessitarian metaphysics from reverting to the myth and fate Adorno warns of: necessity shown, not suffering sanctified.

Art isn’t decoration added to meaning. It is the structural technology by which the inside of one person’s orientation becomes recoverable in another. Every cave painting, every lullaby, every love poem, every film, every dance is the same operation performed with different materials: someone reaches inward, shapes Substance into a form the reach can live in, and sends the form across the interval to others who complete the exchange by resonating with what the form carries. The feel doesn’t travel directly between people; nothing does. It travels through the made thing. That a 40,000-year-old handprint on a cave wall can still move someone today isn’t a sentimental fact about the durability of human connection; it is the structural fact that self-modeling, externalization, and resonance together constitute a technology by which the feel of being a particular kind of creature in a particular kind of world can be preserved across the entire history of our species and occasioned anew in someone who wasn’t there. Art is how a person expresses what it feels like to experience the world. The register the made thing was reaching for when the reach exceeds what any made thing can hold is taken up at §5.16.

## 5.16 Spirituality

Spirituality, on the naturalist interpretation developed here, is a finite mind registering dependence, finitude, salience, or the excess of reality over its models. Awe and mystery can track real limits in knowledge and control without settling what, if anything, their intentional object is. Some religious traditions interpret such experiences through gods, revelation, liberation, ancestors, sacred places, practices, or communities; some don’t center an “excess” encounter at all. The proposal is therefore neither that every tradition was secretly reaching for Nature nor that every theological specification is false by definition. It asks how much of the phenomenology and practice can be explained within Nature before any further metaphysics is added.

**[Identification]**

**Spirituality** · *Identification*

On the naturalist interpretation proposed here, spirituality is a family of practices and experiences in which subjects orient toward dependence, finitude, ultimacy, sacredness, belonging, transformation, or what exceeds ordinary control and representation. One important form is a field registering the limits of its own model. Such registration can be accurate about the limit without settling whether its source is impersonal structure, another agent, a deity, a practice-shaped construction, or some combination.

*Status: finitude and model-incompleteness are secure; their identification with spirituality and the genealogy offered for religious interpretation are abductive. Imagination can render the unknown as gods, powers, or favoring wills without certifying those objects, but the existence of cognitive and social mechanisms does not by itself disprove a theological referent. This is a structural-naturalist account among rivals, not a corollary that closes philosophy of religion. The no-outside argument is developed later at §11.10.*

**Dependency routes:** subject-side orientation—Drive (§5.2), Knowledge (§5.4), Will (§5.11), and Imagination (§5.5); realization constraint—Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4) and Strict Actualization (§2.9.4)

The others keep their catches. Drive, knowledge, reasoning, thin will: denial already is the operation. Spirituality has two certainties and then a stop. You can be certain that something is bigger than this. You can be certain that the world is influenced in two ways: by your will, and by what happens to you beyond your will—lines that become actual by selection (§5.11), and lines that become actual because the configuration delivers them (Strict Actualization, §2.9.4). What you can’t be certain of is why the bigger thing is in front of you: whether it is an agent’s cause, a will, or not-will. That is the uncertainty that drives the register.

Imagination hypothesizes into it: renditions of a god, an ultimate power, a favoring will. Loading isn’t fidelity (§5.5). Drive wants the loaded answer to be a will that has your favor, because the pull to subsist is already running, and if the bigger thing is a will, you want to be doing right by it. That want takes the authority grip of §5.14.3: the unknown judge, the unknown authority. Authority cannot check itself against the affected subject; “because God said so” is that grip at the limit. The grip is how the ought catches here, not a second moral ground, and not evidence that the judge exists. The catch isn’t “God exists.”

Art (§5.15) carries what language can’t. The turn outward that language (§5.12), morality (§5.14), and art (§5.15) each trace (every one a being’s reach toward another) has a limit case: the reach carried to where no second being answers, where what it meets isn’t a second subject but Nature, which exceeds any model it can form. Spirituality is what happens when a person’s reach presses past what any vehicle could carry at all: against what they can’t contain. Nature is always larger than any model of it, not as a contingent limitation of undeveloped minds but as what finite modeling within Nature structurally consists in. The encounter with that excess isn’t rare, not specially induced, not the province of mystics. It is the default condition of being a person: available whenever the reach notices its own boundary, which is whenever the reach is deep enough to notice anything at all.

Comparative behavior supplies possible precursors without licensing spiritual attributions. Elephants investigate conspecific bones (McComb et al. 2006); chimpanzees display at waterfalls and in heavy rain and have been reported stacking stones at particular trees (Goodall 1986; Kühl 2016); corvids gather around dead conspecifics (Swift and Marzluff 2015). These behaviors may involve grief, arousal, attention, social learning, display, or site fidelity. The evidence doesn’t show that the animals represent ultimacy, non-self-grounding, sacredness, or an excess their models can’t contain. Human spirituality may recruit older affective and social capacities, but the transition to reflective interpretation remains an empirical and conceptual question.

*The wish to remain held.* Mortality’s legacy account (§5.9) supplies a second route into the spiritual register. A person knows that other subjects can hold a representation of them after death, and also knows that every such holder is finite. The wish for remembrance can therefore press toward an imagined limit: an awareness in which nobody is finally forgotten, a knower able to hold the person completely when the last human memory is gone. The personal God functions here as an ultimate witness, and the afterlife as the promise that the witnessed person remains available to be held. The two wishes must still be separated. Divine remembrance, even if granted, would continue a representation on the knower’s side; it wouldn’t by itself continue the dead subject’s own vantage. An afterlife adds the stronger claim that the same subject remains to experience further possibilities.

That stronger claim is Drive’s attraction-pole taken to its limit. A living closure is oriented toward continuation (§5.2); the afterlife is that orientation refusing the closure Mortality names—subsistence without a last state, the field held open, as far as weighting can push it. The theist doesn’t import a second purpose from outside Nature. The drive to subsist is already registered; what theology adds is the unbounded form of a weighting the body already has. Maximal subsistence is Drive, not a rival source of meaning. The recurrence of both beliefs is structurally intelligible from identity, mortality, grief, legacy, and that drive. Their intelligibility is a genealogy of the belief, not evidence that the projected witness or surviving vantage exists.

The composition isn’t sapiens-distinctive. Neanderthals built ringed structures from broken stalagmites 336 meters into the dark of Bruniquel Cave 176,000 years ago (Jaubert 2016) and deliberately buried their dead at Shanidar and La Ferrassie (Pomeroy 2020; Balzeau 2020). Red-ochre marks in Iberian caves dated to over 64,000 years ago pre-date the arrival of *sapiens* in Europe (Hoffmann 2018). About half a million years ago, *Homo erectus* engraved a deliberate zigzag onto a freshwater shell at Trinil (Joordens 2014). What hominin minds deep enough to compose did with the encounter, in the cases the archaeological record retains, was register it materially: at specific places, in specific acts, with specific marks. (The Hoffmann et al. 2018 dating of the Iberian red-ochre marks remains contested in the literature; the broader pattern across Bruniquel, Shanidar, La Ferrassie, and Trinil is more secure.) These materials are precursors and structural materials of religion, not religion in the developed sense; the reflection that takes the encounter as an object (modeling it, transmitting the model as obligation, addressing it in language) is what religion adds. The threshold for such registration may predate the species; the reflection that codifies religion proper is later and human.

What the pressing actually is, in structure, is a wondering. Not a percept: there is no sensory channel for it. Not a hypothesis: no claim is yet being made. A question, held open as a question: whether anything lies beyond what the reach can model. And here the grammar matters, because *beyond* is a relation drawn from inside Nature (one thing lies beyond another only from some vantage within the world) so the question is never whether something stands outside Nature, which would borrow an internal relation and apply it where it can’t reach, but whether what is exceeds the model any finite reach can form of it. It always does. Felt as awe, as mystery, as the sense of something more, as the feeling of being part of what exceeds you. The wondering is what reach does at the depth where it can notice its own boundary as a boundary and ask about what lies past it. Below that depth, no wondering is possible; reach can’t ask about what it can’t reach. Above it, the reach is held open by the question itself. What the wondering reaches toward is real: what no model can capture, Nature exceeding every model the reach can form. Named at the load-bearing register, spirituality is the modal field (§5.4) registering its own dependence: the body’s modal representation encountering the boundary of what its current depth and inheritance can register, and holding open the question of what lies past that boundary, Nature, without which there would be no field for the body to hold. Knowledge holds the field; reasoning (§5.6) navigates it; meaning (§5.10) weights it; spirituality is the field registering that no field is self-grounding: folding back not on the field’s content, as self-knowledge does, nor on the worth of its reach, as meaning does, but on the bare condition that there is a held field at all. The non-self-grounding the register names isn’t a further application of the Modal Convergence theorem (§5.4), whose formal scope is collectively held knowledge. It is the limit condition on every field: what beings hold for and through one another is itself enabled by what exceeds any one being’s reach. The dependence is a part’s, not the whole’s: each being genuinely fails to ground itself and is held by what exceeds it, but the totality that holds every being isn’t one more thing needing a ground; it is the immanent whole in which all grounding takes place. So the register reads a real dependence, and the cosmological reading takes it as a debt owed to something outside the series, where on this account the magnitude that impresses is the series entire (§11.10). The God-hypothesis is a sustained answer-attempt human reach has formed, but it is an answer-attempt, not the wondering. The wondering precedes and exceeds every answer formulated about it.

Individuals and traditions vary both in whether they report such an encounter and in the vocabulary applied to it. Some theological systems may interpret dependence or awe; others organize primarily around covenant, ritual obligation, ancestry, revelation, liberation, purity, communal identity, or historical narrative. The structural-naturalist account can test where an excess model fits and where it distorts. It shouldn’t infer from the persistence of a tradition that its practitioners encountered one common referent, nor treat disagreement as proof that every specification is merely a culturally limited translation.

The historical-critical record traces the arc through its best-documented case. The pre-Israelite West Semitic substrate, attested at Ugarit, seated El at the head of a divine council with Asherah his consort and Baal his storm-warrior (Smith 2002). The earliest layers of Israelite religion show Yahweh inside that pantheon: identified with El, paired with Asherah (attested at Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom, Dever 2005), seated among other gods in council (Cross 1973). The deity had a face, a body, a footstool. He walked with Abraham, wrestled with Jacob, ate with the elders on Sinai (Stavrakopoulou 2022; Sommer 2009).

Across the exilic and Persian-period redactions the body recedes (Römer 2015); in Hellenistic absorption the deity is fused with Greek philosophical abstraction and declared simple, incorporeal, impassible (Boyarin 2004). The Yahweh of the early text and the *ipsum esse subsistens* of Maimonides and Aquinas no longer share a recognizable referent. The trajectory, on this reading, isn’t from a primitive misreading toward a refined understanding. It is an encounter receiving the vocabulary each generation’s models could carry. Where the layers answer to the excess, what they kept reinventing (body, council, presence, Logos, simplicity, sephirot, sacrament) is what Nature is. The theology drifted; the encounter stayed.

One historical pattern moves from more local and embodied agents toward abstraction, and cognitive accounts of agency detection (Barrett 2004) and minimally counterintuitive concepts (Boyer 2001) may help explain parts of it. But the record isn’t one unidirectional scale: abstraction, embodiment, ritual presence, personal devotion, iconoclasm, immanence, and transcendence recur and recombine. The roughly first-millennium-BCE transformations grouped under the contested “Axial Age” label (Jaspers 1949; Bellah 2011) occurred amid unequal contact and distinct local histories. They can’t be assigned to depth of self-modeling alone.

Abstraction can intensify until a tradition speaks of a simple or incorporeal absolute, but later layers often re-embody, personalize, localize, or ritualize the divine. Incarnation, devotional images, saints, relics, sacred presence, revival movements, and popular practice aren’t mere failures to preserve a ratchet. They show that religious change is multidirectional and that abstractness isn’t a reliable proxy for cognitive depth. The historical material can support a genealogy of particular concepts; it doesn’t establish one necessary arc for religion as such.

Apophatic and mystical currents sometimes arise within highly elaborated traditions—Pseudo-Dionysius’s divine darkness, Eckhart’s Godhead beyond God, Sufi *fana*, Advaita’s *neti neti*, the Zen of the unspoken (McGinn 1991; Sells 1994). (Fana (Arabic, “annihilation” or “passing away”) is the Sufi concept of the dissolution of the individual ego in union with the divine—the self’s boundaries dissolving into God rather than being negated through argument. *Neti neti* (“not this, not that”) is the Advaita Vedanta formula of negation.) They don’t all share one chronology, metaphysics, or corrective function, and negative or ineffability-oriented practices need not wait for an abstraction “terminus.” The structural account can compare them as techniques for limiting concepts and transforming attention without declaring them instances of one universal reaction.

*The structural diagnosis: divergence and inherited transmission.* One pattern in the empirical history of religion bears on the structural account from a different angle than the history of abstraction: *divergence*. Within each tradition and across traditions, religion doesn’t converge over time in the way domains that track external reality do. Where the sciences converge on specific findings (despite local controversies), where mathematics converges, where engineering converges, where the literal-empirical historical record converges, religion *branches*: into sects, denominations, mystical schools, esoteric currents, reform movements, schisms, syncretic fusions. The pattern is diagnostic. Convergence is what happens when investigators are constrained by something external to their own claims; divergence is what happens when the claims have no convergence-pressure from outside. The encounter the reach meets is real, but the inherited content the tradition transmits isn’t constrained by it: there is no decisive feedback from the referent that prunes incompatible claims. Bodies receiving the content load it into their modal fields at whatever weight their inherited transmission and individual discernment assigns. What reaches them is the long-form, generationally stabilized version of the social-information channel named at §5.12: tradition is an inherited transmission practice operating across generations rather than within a small group. The same proximity-weighting and norm-enforcement structure runs. The same source-evaluation problem applies. Where specific empirical claims internal to a tradition are exposed to source-evaluation discipline (through formal education, critical reading of source histories, comparative study, the developmental cultivation of discernment named at §5.2 as the operational suite’s response to the cost-structure of curiosity at depth) their weight in the modal field drops, sometimes sharply. This would supply one mechanism for the reported inverse correlation between formal education and credulous-literal religious belief across Pew, Gallup, and World Values Survey data; it is also the structural shape of the demographically growing “spiritual but not religious” category, where the structural drive named at the outset persists while the inherited content is no longer credulously installed. The drive is universal; the content is inherited through transmission and remains sensitive to discernment.

*A distinction worth marking: content versus operations.* The gossip-channel analysis applies to the *content* of theological claims: what gets transmitted as inherited tradition. Religious traditions also developed substantial *epistemic operations*: medieval Christian Scholasticism applied Aristotelian logic to theology and natural philosophy; the Islamic *kalam* tradition developed rigorous systematic argumentation; the Buddhist epistemologists Dignāga and Dharmakīrti produced formal accounts of perception and inference; Talmudic reasoning evolved a dialectical methodology over centuries of commentary. Those operations belong to the reasoning-register treated at §5.6: civilizational work of reasoning calibrating itself against its own failure modes, conducted inside religious traditions but not reducible to their content-transmission. The *content* propagates through the gossip channel and is discernment-sensitive in the way the preceding analysis names; the *epistemic operations* developed inside those traditions are continuous with the broader operational suite that Reasoning (§5.6) describes.

*The encounter’s epistemic standing.* A reflexive objection presses here, and it is owed an answer rather than a wave-past. If the personified God is debunked by showing that survival-shaped cognition would produce the belief whether or not anything answered to it (agency over-detected, the minimally counterintuitive maximally transmissible) then why does the same suspicion not dissolve the structural reading this section affirms, since the faculties that deliver *no field grounds itself; Nature exceeds every model* were selected by the same blind pressures? The objection is Plantinga’s, turned reflexive (the evolutionary argument against naturalism, engaged at §10.1.1) and the reply isn’t that these faculties are specially exempt but that the two claims aren’t the same kind of claim.

A debunking explanation applies where a belief’s truth is idle to the mechanism that fixes it: the personal deity is produced by agency-detection whether or not anything answers to it, which is exactly why divergence, not convergence, is its signature. The structural recognition isn’t contingent content of that sort. It is read off the conditions of there being any modeling at all (that any reach presupposes a structure exceeding the model it forms) and a claim of that form can’t be coherently denied from inside a reach, since the denial would have to be modeled too (the performative line, §3.3; consolidated as the central defense at §5.6). Selection shapes the vehicle; what the vehicle here registers is the precondition of there being a vehicle, and no survival story reaches behind that to make its truth idle.

The exemption is narrower than it may look: it certifies the bare structural recognition, not the particular vocabulary. The cross-cultural convergence already traced earns no more than that: it is architecture-explained, what the same depth of self-modeling yields when it meets the same structural feature, not a report of unmediated access to Nature; and since the apparatus that measures the convergence imports interpretation of its own, the convergence is offered as defeasible convergent support, never as instrument-free perception (the constructivist caution (Katz 1978)).

Katz’s point, more precisely, targets one of two claims this section makes, not both. The structural claim (that any sufficiently deep self-model runs into a boundary it can’t itself model past) is a claim about the architecture of self-modeling as such, established independently of what any tradition’s mystics report, and Katz’s mediation thesis doesn’t touch it: an architectural feature of modeling isn’t itself a mediated experience requiring an unmediated check to underwrite it. What Katz’s caution correctly disciplines is a different, weaker claim this section doesn’t make: that cross-tradition convergence in mystical report establishes one shared unmediated datum beneath the traditions’ different vocabularies. The universality asserted here is universality of the boundary’s structural presence, not universality of how it is phenomenologically reported.

What is being done here should be owned: this is a belief-forming practice about Nature, and like every foundational practice (perception, logical inference, empirical science) it can’t step outside itself to ground itself without circularity (Alston 1991b). The honest claim isn’t a view from nowhere but a practice answerable from inside: to coherence with the structural account built elsewhere, to its own defeasibility, and to the same source-evaluation discipline turned on the inherited content. The circularity is universal, conceded, and survivable; what is unavailable (to this account as to every other) is the external standpoint the projected God was the wish for.

*Swinburne’s rival explanation, run on his own metric.* A further rival explanation of the same data is owed the same courtesy as Plantinga’s. Swinburne holds that theism is the simplest substantive hypothesis able to explain the encounter—one personal being of unlimited degree, whose properties compose a single set rather than a set of independent stipulations—and that simplicity is itself evidence of truth. On that account a self-disclosing God explains the cross-cultural reach, cognitive limitation and sin explain the divergence in content, and agency-detection explains only the form the encounter takes, not whether anything answers to it. So debunking the form doesn’t by itself lower theism’s prior. The reply has to be run on Swinburne’s own metric, not past it. Simplicity, on the measure his argument needs to do this work, tracks the number of independent, freely-specifiable parameters a hypothesis must fix, not felt intuitive unity (Sober 2005). On that metric theism isn’t simple: a personal being with libertarian freedom, complete knowledge, and perfect goodness is a bundle of independently-fixable properties, each carrying its own why-this-value question—why omniscient rather than merely vast, why perfectly good rather than merely benevolent—the same parameter-proliferation pressure that makes a designer’s own design demand explanation in turn (Dawkins 2006), aimed here at Swinburne’s specific set rather than at cosmological fine-tuning generally. The structural terminus reached here posits no such set: it adds no agent-like property—no intention, no knowledge-state, no moral psychology—beyond what any coherent structure already requires for something to be capable of failing to ground itself. On the parameter-count sense of simplicity Swinburne’s own argument relies on, the structural account scores as the simpler hypothesis, not as a different assertion competing on unstated terms. That is a win on the rival’s own metric, and one input to comparative fit rather than its verdict.

*The via negativa as one response to pressure.* Empirical and philosophical scrutiny can make particular positive theological claims harder to sustain, and some traditions respond by qualifying, analogizing, or negating divine predicates. This is one route into apophatic theology, not a necessary terminus of increasing knowledge. Positive and negative theologies coexist; sophisticated traditions continue to make affirmative claims; and negation can arise from devotional discipline or doctrines of transcendence rather than eliminated “gaps.” Spinoza’s *Deus sive Natura* (*Ethics* I, propositions 14–15) is one important naturalizing response, not the destination toward which every theology tends. The present framework can argue independently that an outside-standing entity conception fails its constraints and that Nature is enough for its own explanatory work. It should not recast that conclusion as what apophatic mystics had reached all along or claim to know what every religious experience was “actually touching.”

### 5.16.1 The Dispute
The literature on religion, spirituality, and the encounter with what exceeds finite modeling has organized across philosophy, theology, anthropology, cognitive science, and the historical-critical study of religions. Every one of these is engaged by name.

*Theistic realism.* Plantinga (1967; 1974; 2000), Swinburne (1979; 2004), Alston (1991b), and the contemporary analytic-theology tradition develop accounts on which the central religious referents—God, divine action, religious experience—are mind-independent realities that religious traditions track with varying success. The position has been refined into reformed epistemology (Plantinga), natural theology (Swinburne), perceptual epistemology of religious experience (Alston 1991b), and other variants. Theistic realism is read here as correctly identifying that the religious traditions are tracking something real, while supplying the structural reading: where they track something real, what they track is the structural fact that Nature is always larger than any model of it—the encounter is real; the metaphysics each tradition formed about its referent is the vocabulary its practices could carry, not the referent itself.

*Cognitive science of religion.* Boyer (2001), Atran (2002), Barrett (2004), and the broader cognitive-science-of-religion tradition develop accounts on which religious belief and practice are explained by features of evolved cognitive architecture: hyperactive agency detection, minimally counterintuitive concepts, theory-of-mind extension to non-human agents. CSR is read here as correctly identifying the cognitive architecture that shapes how the encounter is registered and articulated, while supplying the structural reading: the architecture conditions *how* the encounter is registered and what concepts get applied to it; what is registered is the encounter with what exceeds finite modeling, which exists structurally whether or not the architecture is in place.

*Religious-experience epistemology.* James (1902), Otto (1917), Stace (1960), and contemporary refinements (Alston 1991b; Forman 1999; Yandell 1993) developed accounts on which religious experience is a distinctive epistemic category that warrants belief in specific religious propositions. Religious-experience epistemology is read here as correctly identifying that the experience is real, while supplying the structural reading: what the experience tracks is the structural encounter with what exceeds modeling; the specific theological propositions experiences are taken to warrant are vocabulary-bound rather than directly justified by the experience.

*Perennial philosophy.* Huxley (1945), Schuon (1953), and the perennial-philosophy tradition hold that the world’s religious traditions converge at their mystical core on the same underlying truth, with surface differences reflecting cultural translation of the common substance. The position has been refined and contested (Forman 1999, in defense; Katz 1978, in critique). Perennialism is read here as correctly identifying a real convergence at the structural level (finite models meet the same kind of limit across traditions) while denying the further claim that mystical content converges on a specific positive metaphysics: what converges is the *structural feature* of the encounter; what diverges is the conceptual articulation of what is encountered.

*Social-constructionist accounts of religion.* Asad (1993; 2003), Smith (1998), and the broader genealogical-critical tradition argue that *religion* as a category is a Western academic construction projected onto disparate cultural phenomena that don’t naturally form a kind. Constructionist accounts are read here as correctly identifying that *religion* in the academic sense is a partly-constructed category, while supplying the structural reading: what is *not* constructed is the encounter with what exceeds finite modeling and the reflection that takes the encounter as an object; the category *religion* picks out a culturally-specific subset of the larger structural phenomenon.

*Apophatic and mystical traditions.* Pseudo-Dionysius, Eckhart, Sufi traditions (Ibn Arabi, Rumi), Advaita Vedanta, Zen, and contemporary refinements (McGinn 1991; Sells 1994) develop accounts on which the encounter with the divine exceeds any positive theological articulation—the only adequate response is negation (via negativa, *neti neti*). Apophatic traditions are read here as picking up a structural fact: the encounter exceeds any model a mind can form, so any positive theological articulation under-describes it.

*Religious pluralism.* Hick (1989) developed an influential pluralist account on which the world’s religions are equally valid responses to the same underlying transcendent reality, with their differences reflecting human cognitive variation. Heim (1995), DiNoia (1992), and others developed alternative pluralist positions. Pluralism is read here as correctly identifying that traditions track something real and that their differences reflect variation in the tracking, while supplying the structural reading: what is tracked, where something is, is the structural encounter; the limit is available to every tradition, while traditions differ in whether and how they articulate it.

*New Atheism and naturalist critique.* Dawkins (2006), Harris (2004), Hitchens (2007), and the broader naturalist-critique tradition argue that religious belief is unwarranted, harmful, and should be replaced by naturalistic alternatives. New Atheist critiques are read here as correctly identifying that the supernatural-metaphysics of classical religion fails (the inversion forecloses it), while denying the further claim that what religion has been responding to is illusory: the structural encounter with what exceeds modeling is real; what fails is specifically the tradition’s metaphysical articulation of what the encounter was *of*.

*Archaeological and historical-critical evidence.* A growing literature documents the deep prehistory of religious behavior—Neanderthal burials (Pomeroy 2020), Bruniquel cave constructions (Jaubert 2016), Iberian red-ochre marks (Hoffmann 2018, contested), the Trinil engraving (Joordens 2014), the historical-critical reconstruction of the ancient Near Eastern religious context (Smith 2002; Stavrakopoulou 2022; Sommer 2009; Römer 2015).

*Religious naturalism.* A position from Spinoza through Dewey to contemporary developments (Crosby 2002; Stone 2008; Goodenough 1998) holds that the religious response is appropriate but that its object is Nature itself, properly understood. Religious naturalism is the account’s nearest relative, and the structural account supplies its grounding: the encounter is with Nature in its modal depth, with the religious response appropriately responsive to what Nature actually is rather than to a supernatural source.

### 5.16.2 The Requirement
*The encounter with what exceeds modeling.* Any account must locate the religious response at the encounter with Nature’s excess over every model rather than at a separate supernatural reality. The structural requirement is that the account derive the religious response from what finite modeling within Nature consists in: the reach noticing its own boundary.

*The field’s own horizon.* The excess is the modal field noticing that it is a partial mapping: some of what is possible, and the structure that makes it possible, outruns what this body has registered. An adequate account has to locate the encounter at that horizon rather than at a second field behind this one, and it must not treat agency-attribution (a will behind the excess) as a catch: that filling is Imagination and Drive, not a third certainty.

*Wondering as the structural phenomenon.* Any account must accommodate the wondering’s structural shape rather than treating spirituality as either ordinary perception or ordinary belief. The structural requirement is that the account derive the wondering from what reach does at the depth where it can notice its own boundary as a boundary and ask about what lies past it.

*Default rather than rare.* Any account must accommodate the encounter’s universality at sufficient depth rather than treating spirituality as exceptional. The structural requirement is that the account derive the spiritual response from features of self-modeling at sufficient depth, with the wondering available whenever the reach notices its own boundary.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Forms of the encounter run across non-human lineages—elephants at bones, chimpanzees at waterfalls, corvids at the dead. What human spirituality adds isn’t the encounter but the reflection that takes the encounter as an object. Any account must accommodate the depth gradient rather than restricting spirituality to species-specific human behavior. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the *encounter* (widespread at sufficient depth) from the *reflection that takes the encounter as an object* (specific to human-level self-modeling) from *religion in the developed sense* (requiring the conceptual and linguistic apparatus that gives that reflection durable form).

*Vocabulary-bound articulation.* What varies across individuals, cultures, and traditions isn’t whether the encounter happens but what vocabulary gets applied to it. Any account must accommodate this distinction rather than treating cross-cultural variation as evidence of the encounter’s unreality. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the reach (accurate where it registers a real limit of modeling) from the metaphysics (each tradition’s best available articulation, never adequate to what was touched).

*Coherence with the historical-critical record.* Some traditions move from bodied local deities embedded in pantheons toward incorporeal absolutes, best documented in the Hebrew Bible; others re-embody, personalize, or never follow that sequence. Any account must accommodate that record rather than treating theological development as random or arbitrary. The structural requirement is that the account say where depth of self-modeling contributes to abstraction without assigning the pattern to depth alone or reading one arc into religion as such.

*Apophatic counter-currents.* Apophatic and mystical currents use negation to discipline claims about what exceeds ordinary concepts. Any account must accommodate these currents rather than treating them as eccentric byways. The structural requirement is that the account compare them as practices of concept-limitation without assigning them one chronology or one corrective function.

*Coherence with the inversion.* With Chapters 4 and 11 foreclosing the upward exit—no supernatural source, no realm beyond Nature—any account of spirituality must support a religious response that survives the foreclosure rather than collapsing into either atheist dismissal or covert supernaturalism. The structural requirement is that the account locate spirituality’s source in Nature’s structural depth: the encounter with what exceeds finite modeling is an encounter with Nature itself, not with anything outside it.

### 5.16.3 Predictions
A reflective creature builds a picture of its position within Nature. That picture is always partial; Nature is always larger. Our basic condition is to live inside something vaster than any account of it. The return argued at §4.6.5 extends the point on its named premise: Nature’s excess isn’t a feature of this particular cosmological epoch but of every return. Whatever the universe passes into next, the relationship between finite creatures and infinite ground will be the same.

The defeasible prediction is that sufficiently reflective people will encounter limits to their own models. That cognitive-limit registration is structural in the modest sense that finite models remain partial. Its phenomenological interpretation isn’t fixed: it may be registered spiritually, philosophically, scientifically, aesthetically, anxiously, indifferently, or not made salient at all. Spiritual encounter is one possible identification of the boundary, conditional on attention, affect, culture, and interpretive practice—not a consequence every reflective person must undergo.

When the boundary is registered spiritually, reports often describe presence, vastness, belonging, awe, dread, or self-transcendence. These are candidate phenomenological signatures, not a universal feel entailed by finite cognition. Other subjects may register the same epistemic limit as uncertainty, curiosity, abstraction, or silence. Where it is registered as presence or belonging, that is because the encountered excess isn’t negative space but active Nature—the same three Conditions that ground a person’s existence, extending past what anyone can understand. A person meets that excess through continuity with it: the Nature they are made of extends beyond their boundary, and so it appears as something they belong to rather than something facing them from outside.

The encounter is the first component of spirituality. The second is the reach toward that excess. A person doesn’t merely notice it passively, but turns toward it. That turn can take many forms: reverence, awe, surrender, prayer, meditation, contemplation, wonder, dread, gratitude. What these share is a reaching past the limits of one’s own understanding while remaining a distinct person. Spirituality isn’t self-dissolution into the excess—that would collapse the interval that makes relation possible. It is a person’s orientation toward what exceeds their self-understanding, across an interval they can’t close.

The historical proposal is correspondingly testable rather than universal. Some traditions may move from personified agents toward abstraction and later apophatic currents as institutions, literacy, intercultural contact, political structure, and reflective practices change. Depth of self-modeling is one candidate cause among these. The hypothesis is weakened by durable traditions that don’t follow the sequence, early apophatic evidence, independent abstraction without the proposed precursors, or better cultural and ecological explanations. No claim is made that every sufficiently old tradition must reproduce one trajectory.

The traditions have named this reach in many vocabularies. *Spiritus*—breath. The most immaterial concept in the religious vocabularies is the most physical word. Breath is a directed exchange of Substance through a medium, unfolding in Time across a relational Space between the person and what surrounds it. The word the tradition chose for what transcends the body is a description of what the body does.

### 5.16.4 Confirmation
Several evidence streams are consistent with the proposal that deep self-modeling can support experiences interpreted as spiritual, but they don’t establish a universal mechanism independent of culture. Archaeology, comparative religion, psychometrics, contemplative reports, psychedelics, neuroscience, and cultural evolution answer different questions and must not be merged into one confirmation. The evolutionary-historical arc is a framework hypothesis, not a recovered law. Below the recursion threshold, the components show up unjoined in non-human animals (McComb et al. 2006; Goodall 1986; Kühl 2016; Swift and Marzluff 2015). At the threshold, the composition is older than *Homo sapiens*: Neanderthal cave structures (Jaubert 2016), deliberate burials (Pomeroy 2020), and Iberian cave art (Hoffmann 2018, dating contested) all pre-date the species. With sustained cultural transmission the composition is bodied and personified—the Ugaritic divine council and its Israelite reception (Smith 2002; Dever 2005). With deepening textual recursion the abstraction trajectory follows, in several of the traditions grouped under the contested Axial Age label (Jaspers 1949; Bellah 2011); in the cases these literatures examine, apophatic counter-currents emerge after that abstraction rather than before it (McGinn 1991; Sells 1994)—an ordering claimed for the traditions studied, not as a law holding of every tradition. These materials are compatible with increasingly elaborated symbolic and ritual cognition, but their dating, function, and religious interpretation remain contested. Burials, cave structures, or art don’t by themselves identify the phenomenology, theology, or sequence proposed here.

Mystical and contemplative experiences have been reported across many religious and nonreligious settings (James 1902; Stace 1960; Hood 1975; Forman 1990). Reports show recurring themes—unity, presence, boundary alteration, ineffability, sacredness—but also substantial differences in doctrine, attentional training, expectation, and interpretation. Instruments such as the Mysticism Scale identify cross-population common factors under particular operational definitions; measurement invariance, sampling, translation, and perennialist assumptions remain disputed. The recurrence supports comparative phenomenology, not the conclusion that T/S/Φ plus self-modeling uniquely generate one culture-independent encounter.

Neuroscience of mystical experience locates the mechanism without explaining it away. Psilocybin studies at Johns Hopkins (Griffiths et al. 2006; Griffiths et al. 2008) produced in naive subjects experiences that, weeks later, a majority rated among the most meaningful of their lives. Neuroimaging during some meditation and psychedelic states reports altered DMN activity and connectivity (Brewer et al. 2011; Carhart-Harris et al. 2012). Those changes support modulation of self-related processing; they don’t show that the person encounters the medium more directly, that ordinary subject–object mediation disappears, or that the experience is veridical. Reliable induction establishes a reproducible psychophysiological phenomenon, not its metaphysical interpretation.

Cross-cultural variation supplies evidence that religious concepts are culturally and ecologically shaped, while leaving the causal mixture disputed. Botero et al. (2014, *PNAS*) found across 583 societies that environmental harshness and resource scarcity predict the prevalence of moralizing high gods; Henrich (2009) and Norenzayan et al. (2016) develop the cultural-evolutionary account by which ecological conditions shape religious cognition. Botero et al. (2014) and the cultural-evolution literature test associations among ecological harshness, social complexity, and moralizing gods, but causal direction, coding, regional dependence, subsistence form, warfare, and institutional transmission remain contested. General-reader syntheses can illustrate hypotheses but don’t bear the load of a desert-versus-forest law. The supported conclusion is plural causal shaping of religious representation, not that all traditions project one independently established excess through a single ecological mechanism.

The decline of institutional religion in developed societies, doesn’t undercut the structural reading and is compatible with it at the population scale. Religious affiliation, weekly attendance, and confessional identification have fallen sharply across high-income societies over the past four decades, with the steepest drops where economic security and educational attainment rose fastest (Inglehart 2020, *Religion’s Sudden Decline*; for the United States, Pew Research Center 2015; 2022). Across the same span, self-reported interest in spirituality, mystical and peak experience, contemplative practice, and the category *spiritual but not religious* has risen or held steady (Lipka and Gecewicz 2017). One framework interpretation is that institutional disaffiliation and continued spiritual identification reflect vocabulary change rather than disappearance of all self-transcendent experience. Alternative explanations include cohort replacement, trust decline, political sorting, individualization, education, welfare security, and survey-category change. The trends may interact, but they aren’t established as one mechanism—the proposed population-scale analogue of apophatic revision. On that reading, the answer-attempt is what falls away while the wondering persists, and the tighter its binding to a single answer-attempt had been, the more visible the loosening becomes.

The pressure cuts in a second direction. Where the encounter pressed from inside and the answer-attempt couldn’t carry it, the loosening runs from the experiential side. From outside, the natural sciences converged on the age of the Earth, common descent, deep time, and the brain dependence of mental states (§4.1). The answer-attempts traditions had built around those questions could then be dropped or insulated from the converging evidence. The resulting fragmentation of positions on origins, the historical Adam, and soul-body relations runs opposite to the convergence-on-truth the sciences register.

The two pressures point the same direction: the vocabulary stops responding to what the encounter touched, and its answer-attempts stop cohering with the rest of what the population knows. The most disaffiliated societies in the cross-national record—the Nordic states, the Netherlands, post-confessional Czechia—sit consistently at the top of subjective-wellbeing rankings rather than the bottom (Helliwell, Layard, and Sachs 2020; Inglehart 2018), in a pattern the structural reading allows and a simple deficit model doesn’t expect: the encounter doesn’t require the institution; the institution requires the encounter. The same gradient is read against the fall-theodicy frame at §5.14, where it constitutes evidence in the opposite direction from what that frame (§10.1.9) requires.

Swinburne (2004) argued that religious experience constitutes evidence for God: its widespread, cross-cultural occurrence is more probable on theism than on naturalism. The structural account accepts the evidential weight of the experience and inverts its direction. What’s offered is a naturalistic model under which self-transcendent experiences are expected from modifiable self-modeling, affect, attention, and culture. Theism offers different likelihood claims depending on its revelation and religious-experience theory. Without specified rival models and likelihoods, the evidence doesn’t establish that the experience is more probable on one account. Its evidential force lies in comparative explanatory fit, independent predictions, and discriminating traces, which remain open.

### 5.16.5 Conclusions
*What the encounter is like.* Most people have felt it. A landscape that opens past where the eye can follow, and what registers isn’t the view but the reach—the awareness that what lies out there doesn’t end. A mathematical result arriving with the sensation not of triumph but of contact, as if structure was always there and the proof found it. Music resolving into something that feels less like composition than inevitability—as if the sound was always going to land exactly there. The death of someone close, and the absence so total it reveals that the presence had edges you never noticed because you were never outside them. These aren’t the same experience. They share a structure: in each, the reach has pressed against what exceeds it, and what it meets isn’t blankness but more—something real that the model can’t hold. The encounter doesn’t require tradition, initiation, or special states. It requires only that the reach be deep enough to notice its own boundary. That capacity is universally met: any reach of sufficient depth meets the boundary whenever conditions bring it to notice. Its activation isn’t: whether a given person registers the encounter, how often, and in what terms, is conditioned by depth, attention, habituation, and the interpretive vocabulary available for naming it—the same standing-capacity/occurrent-registration split the chapter already relies on for curiosity (§5.2: a standing drive, not a constant activity) and boredom (§5.3: available whenever a field goes unweighted, not constantly occurring). A reflective, sincere naturalist who reports no such encounter hasn’t thereby shown the capacity absent; the report tracks activation, which the same variables that govern every other occasioned state also govern. Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument, read against this distinction, targets a relational, self-disclosing deity who would choose to secure the encounter’s activation; it has no equivalent foothold against a non-agential structural feature, since there is no agent whose reticence needs explaining—only an occasioned capacity like any other named in this chapter.

The excess isn’t a gap to be filled by better thinking. It is the constitutive difference between a finite person and the infinite Nature they are inside of—between a model and the thing it models, where the thing is always larger than any model of it. Awe, reverence, the feeling Schleiermacher called absolute dependence, the *numinous* Otto named—these register a structural fact: the person is inside something they can’t contain. Understanding Nature better doesn’t dissolve the feeling. It makes the excess more precise.

Where a tradition’s “God” answers to the excess, it is the excess, personified. Minds that evolved to detect agents in ambiguous signals show a robust agency-detection bias whenever the excess presses, because missing a predator cost more than imagining one. Whether this bias amounts to a dedicated *hyperactive agency detection device* in the strong modular sense remains contested (van Leeuwen and van Elk 2019); the broader observation that agency-detection runs liberally under uncertainty is well-supported. The architecture that kept the species alive on the savannah delivers its default verdict—someone is there—whenever an unidentifiable pressure registers, and the inheritance of these verdicts across generations supplies the agent-shaped form religious traditions take (Guthrie 1993; Barrett 2000; Atran 2002; Boyer 2001). Grief phenomenology supports the mechanism from an adjacent direction: the bereaved sense the deceased as present for months or years afterward, because the self-model built across years of contact continues to run after the departed is gone, and the absence registers with the phenomenology of presence (Rees 1971; Datson and Marwit 1997; Field and Filanosky 2010). Inherited across generations and stabilized by ritual and narrative, these verdicts congeal into the personified God the tradition hands down—and a tradition built around ancestors, saints, or a continually-present divine person is the same mechanism run at cultural scale (Boyer 2001; Norenzayan 2013).

These mechanisms don’t by themselves debunk a reported encounter. Agency detection and grief phenomenology can help explain why ambiguous or emotionally charged experiences take agent-shaped forms; that causal availability is neither proof nor disproof of a divine agent. The structural account’s independent argument is narrower: spatial and temporal terms such as *beyond*, *above*, and *before* cannot be applied uncritically to the whole as though it occupied another location in its own field. A person’s dependence on what exceeds it is clear; whether the totality requires, is identical with, or is created by a further ground remains part of the rival metaphysical dispute. Religious concepts are shaped by cognitive, ecological, textual, and institutional histories. That genealogy undercuts automatic inference from experience to one theology without establishing that every named god is a misdescription of the same natural excess.

The structural encounter isn’t equivalent to any tradition’s theology, and no claim is made that every contemplative tradition points to one thing. The naturalist proposal recovers a subset of experiences as veridical registrations of finitude, dependence, salience, and model-limitation while suspending or disputing further theological interpretation case by case. This is stronger than dismissing all religious experience as illusion and weaker than declaring it universally veridical at one level and universally false at another. The experience, its interpretation, and its alleged object must be assessed separately.

Contemplative practices train attention, affect, bodily regulation, interpretation, and social identity in different combinations. Meditation, prayer, fasting, ritual attention, silence, wilderness exposure, and artistic engagement can’t be assigned one mechanism or aim merely because each can alter ordinary self-focus. Some studies associate particular practices with changes in default-mode-network activity and attentional processing, but the direction and meaning vary by task, expertise, and method. The practices are real forms of human self- and group-shaping; “registering Nature’s excess” is this account’s interpretation of some outcomes, not a neuroscientifically confirmed universal function (Kabat-Zinn 1990; Wallace 2006; Goleman and Davidson 2017).

Reverence, awe, and wonder are structural phenomena. They are what the encounter with excess feels like at different scales and registers. Reverence is the reach toward what exceeds held with acknowledgment that the person is smaller than what it reaches toward. Awe is the same reach registered as overwhelming—the person’s ordinary self-model temporarily unable to scale. Wonder is the reach registered as curious, inviting, continuing—the person drawn further into what they can’t model. These aren’t sentimental leftovers from a pre-scientific age; they are the internal aspect of structural encounters. Their fading from a life or a culture is a capacity going unused, not a childish feeling outgrown by maturity (Keltner and Haidt 2003; Monroy and Keltner 2023).

*Comparative positions.* Several positions in theology and philosophy stand in specific relation to the account.

1. *Classical theism (Anselm, Aquinas).* The scholastic tradition defined God through divine simplicity, infinity, omnipresence, and necessary existence (Anselm (1078) 1998; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947). The structural account can read these as descriptions that fit the medium—the three Conditions fit each attribute once God is read as the infinite ground a person is inside of rather than the personal agent above nature. On that reading, what the scholastics were formalizing was structure, expressed in the personal vocabulary their culture supplied, and the formalism survives the removal of the mythic frame. The reading is the account’s, not a report of what the scholastics took themselves to mean.

2. *Process theology (Whitehead, Hartshorne).* Process theology (Whitehead 1929; Hartshorne 1948) rejects the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary)’s timelessness and places the divine within the process of actualization, making the referent relational and temporal. This is a partial convergence: the structural account agrees that whatever warrants the vocabulary is inside the process rather than above it. Where the structural account goes further is in declining to keep the personal framing after the metaphysical revision. What is inside the process is the process itself—Nature iterating through its living forms—not a personal being with preferences.

3. *Schleiermacher, Otto, Eliade.* Schleiermacher’s feeling of absolute dependence ((1799) 1988; (1830–31) 1928), Otto’s (1917) numinous, and Eliade’s (1957) distinction between sacred and profane describe the structural encounter from inside theology. Each names a real feature: the person’s registration of its own finitude against something larger (Schleiermacher), the phenomenology of the encounter with the excess (Otto), and the pattern by which people mark places, times, and objects that register the encounter more strongly (Eliade). The descriptions are accurate at the phenomenological level and detach cleanly from the theological commitments their authors wrapped them in.

4. *Apophatic and mystical traditions.* Pseudo-Dionysius (c. 500 CE), Meister Eckhart (c. 1300), the *Cloud of Unknowing* (c. 1375), Sufi negative theology, and Kabbalistic *Ein Sof* use negation to discipline claims about what exceeds ordinary concepts. Their chronologies and functions differ, and no “never before, never absent” law is supported. The structural account treats them as important comparative cases in concept-limitation and transformed attention, without claiming they all correct one abstraction trajectory or converge on the naturalist interpretation (McGinn 1991; Sells 1994).

5. *Non-dual traditions (Buddhist śūnyatā, Advaita Vedanta).* Nagarjuna’s (c. 150 CE) emptiness and Shankara’s (c. 800 CE) identification of *ātman* with *brahman* point past the personal-agent framing toward a structural claim: a person isn’t a separate thing from Nature but a local mode of it. The structural account shares the insight that the interval between current and medium is real but not separating. Where it differs is in preserving the interval rather than collapsing it—the warning (§5.10) that collapsing the interval ends the person rather than uniting it with what it reaches toward. The non-dual traditions were closer to the structural point than the theistic traditions were, and still overcorrected in the direction of dissolution (Stace 1960; Forman 1990). One form of the tradition presses past dissolution-as-practice to a metaphysical claim, and it is owed a hearing at full strength. On the two-truths reading, the world of appearance is real only conventionally (vyavahārika), while what is real without qualification is *nirguna* Brahman, an objectless awareness that hosts no world; the structural conditions would then reach the appearance and never the ground (Deutsch 1969; Forman 1990). (Ātman (Sanskrit) names the individual self or innermost essence of a person; brahman names the single, unconditioned reality underlying the whole universe in Vedanta philosophy. Advaita (“non-dual”) Vedanta’s central claim is that these aren’t two things that merely resemble each other but one and the same reality: the self, examined closely enough, turns out to be identical with the ultimate ground of everything. That’s the move the book compares to its own structural picture in what follows.) The reply is twofold. First, the doctrine’s own apparatus is structured through and through: the distinction between conventional and ultimate truth is itself a distinction (S), holding it along the path is a succession of states (T), and superseding each lower truth by a higher one requires something that persists to undergo the supersession (Φ). The non-dualist can grant this and relocate the whole apparatus to the conventional level, leaving the ultimate untouched. Second, the ultimate is still offered as awareness, and awareness carries its own condition. The pure-consciousness-event literature supplies the retreat directly: a wakeful episode with no object, no thought, and no felt subject, known only in retrospect (Forman 1990). Grant the episode, and a dilemma follows. Either it retained some minimal over-against, if only the bare difference between the awareness and its own occurring. In which case there is still a distinction, and distinction is Spatiality in the structural sense derived at §2.4.7, not a metric manifold—holding at the very place the ground was meant to be conditionless.

Or it retained none. In which case nothing is set over against anything, and no feature marks the episode as awareness rather than as nothing. What is called thin objectless awareness is then indistinguishable from ∅ (§2.7), and can’t be the sole reality the doctrine needs, since structure necessarily obtains (§2.8). The introspective deepening the traditions actually train doesn’t reach the second horn: awareness turned inward at depth is awareness holding itself as its own object, the reflexive fold the Yogācāra tradition analyzes as *svasaṃvedana*, and a fold is a distinction sustained. One narrow foothold remains: because the episode is reported only in retrospect, memory can’t certify which horn obtained, so the dilemma constrains what the episode could have been without settling it from the inside. That residual is genuine, and it isn’t enough to carry an objectless ground. *The idealism form of this objectless-awareness gate is raised at §9.5.*

1. *Freud, Durkheim, and projection accounts.* Freud (1927) argued religion is projection of the infantile father-relation; Durkheim (1912) argued religion is society worshipping itself. Both are partially right. Agency detection and grief phenomenology supply a cognitive basis for projection; ecological shaping (Sapolsky 2017) supplies a social basis for the variation across cultures. What both miss is the underlying encounter the projection and the social structure are shaping into their specific forms. The excess is real before any projection reaches it, and a person registers the excess whether or not their society has supplied an interpretation.

2. *Nietzsche and the new atheists.* Nietzsche (1882; (1883–1885) 2006) announced the death of God and asked what remained. Dawkins (2006), Dennett (2006), Harris (2004), and Hitchens (2007) pressed the case against the classical God on empirical and moral grounds. What dies is the personification. What survives is the infinite medium a person is always already inside of, which can’t die because it isn’t an object. The question Nietzsche asked about what remains has an answer: structure remains, and with it, the encounter.

3. *Hick’s pluralism.* Hick’s (1989) pluralism converts cleanly from Kantian to structural footing once the veil drops.
