He argued that the world’s major religious traditions are equally valid responses to the same ultimate reality—the Real—cognized differently through culturally-conditioned conceptual schemes that produce *personae* (Yahweh, Allah, Vishnu, the Trinity) and *impersonae* (Brahman, Tao, Nirvāṇa, *śūnyatā*), which aren’t the Real itself but the Real as humanly experienced. The structural account converges on the pluralist thesis and sharpens it. On this account the Real, where the traditions answer to it, is the medium—the three Conditions—and the reason the traditions arrive at different *personae* and *impersonae* isn’t Kantian noumenal opacity but the ecological and cognitive shaping already described: agency detection delivers the agent-shaped forms, and environment selects which features get amplified into the infinite. Hick kept the Kantian veil between the Real and its appearances. The structural account lets the veil drop. What they encounter, where they encounter it, isn’t the Real behind a screen but the medium itself, encountered from inside a person whose architecture shapes what it registers into the forms the tradition supplies.

4. *James and perennialism.* James’s (1902) varieties of religious experience, Huxley’s (1945) perennial philosophy, and the mystical-monism thesis (Stace 1960; Forman 1990) all point at a common core underneath tradition-specific surface. The structural account supplies what the perennialists lacked: a non-theological explanation of why a core would be common. What is common, where a common core is found, isn’t the shared content of distinct divine revelations; it is the shared structural encounter that distinct cultural inheritances dress differently.

*What follows.* The encounter does not decide the metaphysics by itself. It can be real while its interpretation remains disputed, and the comparative positions above survive or fail by what they add to it.

The tradition projected not only a *someone* beyond the world but an *outcome*: security without threat, life without suffering, care without limit. Remove the supernatural venue and the personal dispenser, and the image becomes a standing to be maintained from within—the widest field of live possibility a shared structure can keep open.

## 5.17 Synthesis
Drive, feeling, knowledge, will, language, and the rest need not be separate mysteries joined back together afterward. They may be differentiated operations of one living process, a life becoming more capable of registering itself and its world. Where tradition set mind, morality, and spirit *above* nature and then wondered how they could reach down into bodies, the test is whether they are what living nature looks like from within at different depths. The motion proposed is inward, not upward, and from this inner deepening the question moves to how such beings live together.

*The cascade reconstructed.* A living being first meets its world as drive (§5.2): an outward polarity of approach and avoidance, set against what self-maintenance requires, with attraction and aversion proposed as its conscious aspect. That identity is defended in conscious cases and investigated toward the biological boundary; it isn’t built into the terms.

When the same forward pressure becomes valenced, salient, and urgent, it is lived as feeling (§5.3): Modal Pressure—the directional pressure that open alternatives, weighted by a body’s stakes, exert within its modal field, answering to the necessary structure (§2.6.10) without being identical to it—encountered before the being has folded back deeply enough to call its own folding *thought*. This is an identity proposal between affect and an integrated organism’s stake-sensitive operation, not an inference from regulation alone.

What a body has registered as possible gathers into its modal field, and knowledge (§5.4) is the sufficiently accurate and appropriately connected orientation held within it, in a field that can run deeper than what is known and hold error alongside it. Where representations are distributed across subjects and artifacts and reliably corrected against a common object, the Modal Convergence theorem gives the network an epistemic capacity no solitary member has, without implying a further group subject.

Imagination (§5.5) carries the field past the body’s own history, the one operation in the cascade that reaches what hasn’t been met: it loads a possibility without proving it and leaves the evaluation of what it loads to reasoning. Reasoning (§5.6) makes the field navigable, extending the held grasp across possibilities not yet tested; its failure modes (memory’s reconstructive drift, perception’s constructive distortions) and the practices that correct them make up the operational suite the deeper registers draw on. Folded back far enough, the being constructs an identity (§5.7), an *I*: the self-model that takes the body as a persistent agent in its own modal field, real at the depth where it operates and dissolvable under the conditions ego death and contemplative practice document, one construction among many that a being can hold of itself. That embodied, self-modeled field is also where sexuality (§5.8) lives: attraction, non-attraction, desire, orientation, identity, and coupling, with sexual reproduction as one lineage-level variation architecture rather than the definition or aim of every subject’s sexuality. Its lineage function is structurally paired with mortality wherever that architecture occurs; its lived register remains broader than reproduction.

Once a temporally extended self-model can represent its own terminus, the being can make its closure an object of its field, and mortality (§5.9) enters. Legacy then separates personal survival from the real continuation of effects: models held by other subjects, possibilities opened through relationships, care transmitted through parenting or adoption, and works or institutions carried after the originating life closes. Meaning (§5.10) divides between significance to a subject and meanings constituted and sustained among subjects. Will (§5.11) is choice among represented alternatives, made through a field whose coverage, fidelity, endorsement, and practical latitude can each vary.

In language (§5.12), subjects coordinate signs and acts across their separation. Technology (§5.13) extends practical reach through skills, processes, representations, and artifacts. Where stakes run among subjects, they come under morality (§5.14) by the explicit reciprocity/equal-standing bridge. Art (§5.15) lives in practices of making, framing, attention, encounter, and interpretation that overlap language without reducing to it. Spirituality (§5.16), read structurally and naturalistically, is orientation toward dependence, finitude, ultimacy, sacredness, or what exceeds ordinary control and representation, a reading that isn’t a verdict over every religious rival.

*The unified proposal.* These registers are different phenomena, not synonyms, but the test is whether many can be explained through interacting capacities of living subjects rather than through independent substances or realms. Some relations are developmental or constitutive; others are functional, empirical, social, or normative. The cascade is therefore a dependency-shaped research program, not a strict ladder on which every later register is entailed by an earlier one. Its gain is explanatory economy if the local identifications and bridges hold. Its risk is collapse if common vocabulary such as *field*, *depth*, or *registration* is allowed to substitute for the missing evidence in any one register.

*Pre-established harmony, made unnecessary if the identity holds.* Leibniz proposed that mind and body run in parallel (never causally interacting), coordinated by God’s pre-established harmony. Psychophysical harmony is needed once two substances have been posited and their coordination requires explanation. The present framework instead proposes one living operation under inner and outer descriptions. Its advantage is that no further coordination is needed; its burden is to earn that identity rather than assume it.

*The space of reasons, preserved rather than displaced.* Sellars’s distinction between the manifest image (persons, reasons, oughts) and the scientific image (particles, causes, structure) presses a version of the same worry from the normative side: if reasoning, meaning, and morality are identified with a mind operating on modal structure, does the space of reasons collapse into the causal order it was meant to be autonomous from? The identification here is a theoretical identity, not a reduction of one vocabulary to another: water is identical to H₂O, and the identity doesn’t retire water-talk in favor of chemistry, because the vocabularies track the same referent at different levels of articulation, each doing work the other can’t do without loss. The vocabularies don’t even carve alike. Ice and steam are both H₂O, and neither is what ordinary speech calls water: everyday talk sorts by phase and use where chemistry sorts by composition. The everyday term isn’t a coarser rendering of the chemical one. It answers a different question. The normative registers traced here—reasoning’s warrant, meaning’s worth, morality’s obligation—are, on the proposal defended here and on the same grounds, identical to structural facts about a mind operating on the modal field. That identity does not make them *reducible* to a causal vocabulary that could state what they state without remainder. The space of reasons isn’t a second, spooky arena alongside the causal order; its autonomy from causal vocabulary survives the identification exactly as water’s autonomy from chemical vocabulary survives being H₂O. Sellars’s manifest image isn’t displaced by the scientific image here. Both are readings of one natural process, and the fusion traced here is identity with the manifest image’s vocabulary intact, not identity that trades the space of reasons away.

*The local results, gathered.* They have different warrant. Drive and Feeling relate directed regulation, valence, salience, and urgency. Knowledge and Reasoning describe corrigible representation and reasons-responsive transformation. Imagination separates loading a possibility from proving it. Identity distinguishes self-models from every fact about subjecthood and persistence. Sexuality separates communicative other-registration from the richer sexual register. Mortality distinguishes closure from survival of effects. Meaning separates subjective significance from intersubjective constitution. Will distinguishes objective possibility, local reach, representation, endorsement, and latitude. Language broadens coordination beyond propositions. Technology distinguishes objective structure from external representations and procedures. Morality adds an explicit equal-standing bridge. Art permits overlap, plurality, and warranted interpretation. Spirituality remains a naturalist interpretation among rivals. Read together, these are a coordinated account, not thirteen theorems of one grade.

Six strict cores can nevertheless be separated from the richer register identifications, alongside the chapter’s strict Modal Pressure witness and the conditional Modal Convergence theorem. Living Directionality follows from closure-and-throughput without establishing felt drive. Representational Minimum fixes the held distinction any argumentative denial of representation instantiates. Reason-Giving Instantiates Reasoning fixes the inferential operation any reason-giving denial performs. Inquiry Carries Local Weight fixes episode-relative concern without yielding existential meaning. Addressed Denial Instantiates Communication fixes attempted coordination without deriving conventions or understanding. No Arbitrary Self-Exemption is deductive only after the reciprocity/equal-standing premise is granted. These results strengthen the cascade exactly where its performative or premise-conditional cores permit it; none converts the organization/interiority bridge, the full functional identifications, or the normative premise into a theorem.

Taken together, three of those performative cores yield a result stronger than any one alone. An argument addressed to another and offered for a reason can’t coherently remove every instance of the operations by which it is being made: it holds content apart, treats a consideration as bearing on a conclusion, and presents signs for uptake. Where the exchange is sustained as inquiry, it also carries local weight. The result concerns what the discursive token instantiates, not whether its conclusion is true or its communication succeeds.

**[Theorem]**

**The Discursive Minimum** · *Theorem*

Any addressed, reason-giving argument instantiates at least a held distinction, an inferentially answerable transition, and attempted communication. If it is sustained as inquiry, it also instantiates episode-relative weighting. No argument of that form can establish the global absence of representation, reasoning, communication, or—where inquiry is sustained—all local concern, because the argumentative token is a counterinstance.

The theorem establishes only those minimal operations. It does not establish truth, warrant, knowledge, successful reference, shared understanding, existential meaning, or normative binding.

**Depends on:** Representational Minimum (§5.4), Reason-Giving Instantiates Reasoning (§5.6), Addressed Denial Instantiates Communication (§5.12), and, for the local-weight clause, Inquiry Carries Local Weight (§5.10)

Three threads run through the whole set, and naming them is more useful than the list. *Standing and registration come apart*: a weight can be borne unfelt, a mapping corrupted unnoticed, a wrong done without a grievance to record—which is why the felt signal can misreport, in either direction, at every level from drive to politics. *R’s capacity isn’t negotiable*: no agent, arrangement, or devotion moves what is really possible, so every defect in view is a defect of reach or of mapping and never of the domain. And *the map isn’t the mapper*: fields, selves, weightings, and works are all mapped things, corrigible on depth and fidelity, while the mind holding them is the mapping and survives their revision. The thirteen results are those three facts meeting the fifteen registers above.

*Where the account remains exposed.* The necessary modal constraints of Chapters 1–2 don’t supply the sufficiency of any biological configuration for consciousness, the identity of experience with regulation, the distribution of subjecthood, the four-part analysis of freedom, the reciprocity/equal-standing premise, or the naturalist interpretation of spirituality. Those are empirical, identity, functional, or normative claims defended locally. A reader can accept the strict modal core while rejecting any of them without contradiction.

*What the modal field organizes, and what it doesn’t.* Read across §5.3–5.15, many registers concern an organism’s local representation of actual and possible conditions. “Modal field” is useful when it names that representation and its limits. It shouldn’t be literalized into one stuff that feeling, identity, morality, language, technology, and art merely manipulate. The Modal Convergence result remains epistemic and conditional; it neither creates a group subject nor supplies the later moral and political relations. Depth and intersubjectivity are useful axes of comparison, not guarantees that every register emerges once a threshold is crossed.

*Why this set of registers and not some other.* The list isn’t arbitrary but it is also not closed. The registers traced are the registers a sufficiently deep self-modeling being produces *in coordination with other such beings in a world that admits T, S, and Φ*. Each is what the mind is doing when it has enough depth to do it. A shallower lineage won’t produce them all; a deeper one might produce registers we haven’t yet named. The claim isn’t that consciousness, drive, will, morality, and the rest exhaust what self-modeling can do, but that they are what self-modeling at our depth, on a world like ours, in a coordination field like ours, structurally produces. Any sufficiently deep self-modeling lineage anywhere in Nature should produce the same registers, not the same particular cultures, technologies, languages, or moralities, but the same structural categories under which those particulars sort. This is a prediction in the full sense rather than a flourish: it is in principle testable, and the places it would be tested can be named. Comparative cognition tests it now, at the near end—the registers should appear in other deep lineages on this world to the depth each lineage reaches, which the animal cases already begin to trace (knowledge at §5.4, feeling at §5.3, reasoning at §5.6). Artificial systems, and astrobiological contact should it ever arrive, would test it at the far end: a sufficiently deep self-modeling lineage with a wholly alien substrate, chemistry, and history should still sort its life under these same structural categories—drive, valence, held possibility, selection, transfer, coordination—and a deep lineage that produced a genuinely different set would count against the account. The account stakes itself on the categories, not the particulars. The ordering carries the same double character. Some of it is fixed by dependence: knowledge precedes the identity that folds back on it (§5.4 → §5.7), and identity precedes the mortality that takes the self as its object (§5.7 → §5.9), because each later register operates on what an earlier one must already have laid down. But registers not joined by such dependence (sexuality among them: rooted in drive’s attraction-pole, it presupposes none of the inward chain, though its lived forms draw on the self-model) are sequenced for exposition rather than by a finer gradation of depth. The cascade is that dependency-fixed partial order traced as a line, not a claim that each register sits at a strictly deeper fold than the one before it.

*Cross-lineage epistemic convergence.* The same prediction applies to what cumulative inquiry discovers, with an important limit. Independent lineages need not produce our proper names, concepts, sequence of discoveries, or exact theories. An Einstein-like role isn’t the historical Einstein repeated, and a modal-core-equivalent result need not be this book repeated. The prediction is narrower and stronger: to the extent that different lineages preserve results, correct error, reach the same domains, and continue inquiry, one Reality should force convergence at its invariant structural nodes. Their representations may remain unlike while what those representations successfully track becomes increasingly the same. A mature lineage that could reliably navigate the same Reality while requiring an incompatible deep modal structure would therefore count against the framework; a lineage that reached the same constraints by an unrecognizable route would support it.

*The inversion itself.* The cascade traced here—inward—is what the book’s title names from a different direction. The classical picture located the higher-order phenomena (consciousness, reasoning, will, morality, spirituality) above Nature and asked how they could descend into bodies, matter, and causation. If the local bridges hold, the direction is wrong: phenomena ranked above Nature are what living Nature does when its organization includes increasingly deep registration of itself. This is the unifying identity claim, warranted only as strongly as its local bridges.

*The two halves of the inversion meeting.* The inversion was carried in its outward form at §4: the structural pressure that sustained dissipative life already exemplifies. The inward form is the proposal here: what traditions elevated above the natural may be living organization registered from inside at the depths a life reaches. The identity view reads these as third-person and first-person access to one structural fact. The rival further-feature view agrees that both occur within one mind-independent Reality but denies that they are identical. The evidence developed favors the first reading without deriving it from the modal core.

*Continuity with what follows.* What self-modeling beings do when they organize institutions (Chapter 6) is a downstream application and further argument, not evidence for the identity or normative premises reached here.

*Proved, and proposed.* The strict modal core establishes constraints within which any adequate account must operate. The proposal is then that drive, feeling, sexuality, knowledge, imagination, reasoning, identity, mortality, meaning, will, language, technology, morality, art, and spirituality can be investigated as capacities and relations of natural subjects without first positing a second realm. Their unity is explanatory and conditional, not numerical identity or strict entailment. The inversion of greatness is the research claim that much of what traditions placed above Nature may be recoverable within living, embodied, social processes; each recovery stands or falls on its local argument.

*The political consequence.* A person isn’t first a fully formed knower, chooser, and moral participant and only afterward placed inside institutions. These capacities are sustained or narrowed by the conditions in which a life develops: care, safety, education, truthful shared information, material latitude, and relations in which refusal remains real. The inner and the political are therefore continuous. Maintenance, in the political sense (Chapter 6), isn’t the delivery of benefits to agents already complete; it is the collective preservation of the conditions under which agents can know, consent, reason, revise themselves, and hold one another to account at all.

Where illness, coercion, immaturity, disability, or acute crisis narrows a person’s field, the political task is neither abandonment in liberty’s name nor substitution of another’s direction for theirs. It is support calibrated to restore the conditions of self-direction while preserving the person’s standing and voice throughout. Capacity may change what assistance or protection is warranted; it doesn’t turn the person into an object of administration.

# 6. Maximum Possibility

When people live together, they come to depend on the same handful of things: a roof, food, wellness, safety, schooling, a say in what happens to them, and a way to get around. This holds at every scale—a household, a town, a country, or a planet.

The question is what political life becomes when those are treated as conditions under which real possibilities remain open rather than as rewards, charity, or permissions granted from above. The convergence is not automatic. It depends on recognizing other people’s standing, on institutions remaining answerable to them, and on empirical conditions that make cooperation durable.

*Recognition* is acknowledgment of another person as a subject whose conditions count. *Maximum possibility* is the political aim of keeping more real possibilities open to more people without letting choice collapse into survival-response or domination. It does not enlarge Reality’s modal range; it changes which possibilities people can actually reach and recognize. Participation is evidence of that effective access, not the final aim and not something a person must perform to qualify for the foundation. *Structural extraction* names the contrary pattern: drawing benefit from a shared arrangement while shifting an inadequately justified share of its costs or risks onto others.

An arrangement can’t make an impossible state possible or erase a real possibility. It can open or close routes within that field, and it can help or hinder a subject’s ability to see the routes that remain.

**[Proposition]**

**The Two Axes of Participation** · *Proposition · conditional political result*

An arrangement can’t alter what Reality can admit. It can alter two things directly relevant to a subject’s participation: *reach*, which alternatives are locally available, and *mapping*, which alternatives the subject can recognize and compare. A reachable but unmapped option is unavailable for selection; so is a mapped option that can’t be reached. Maximum possibility therefore concerns both institutional axes without claiming that every moral wrong reduces to them.

*Scope.* This is a foundation and a non-domination constraint, not a formula for ranking every arrangement that satisfies them. It supplies no cardinal measure of possibility and no automatic aggregation rule for tradeoffs between the axes.

**Depends on:** the Two Modes of Wronging (§5.14) and the Three Frustrations of Will (§5.11)

Maximum possibility is therefore not the instruction to produce the largest sum of options regardless of who receives them or what they cost. The foundation blocks gains purchased by foreseeably collapsing another person’s agency beneath it; non-domination blocks gains purchased by making one person’s field answerable to another’s arbitrary power. Above those constraints, widening reach and improving mapping are genuine gains, but they need not move together and cannot always be reduced to one quantity.

Material provision also consumes rival goods. When two adequate claims compete for land, labor, care, money, time, or ecological capacity, the metaphysical account does not choose a coefficient or make the conflict disappear. An acceptable decision must state the scarcity, identify who gains and who bears the foreclosed possibility, protect comparable standing, include affected people in the authorization, and remain open to evidence and correction. This yields a priority shape—secure the foundation, prevent domination, then widen the field—not a complete decision procedure. Conflicts within the foundation, and choices among designs that satisfy it, remain matters for proportionate judgment, empirical comparison, and publicly answerable institutions.

Reach and mapping are properties of an arrangement, and an arrangement has to be something that lasts longer than the people staffing it.

A [polity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) is the organized political relation among people living under shared institutions. The people remain the subjects. The polity is neither a collective consciousness nor a creature with one will, but its arrangements can carry decisions and obligations beyond the tenure of any officeholder.

**[Definition]**

**Institutional Bearer** · *Definition*

An institutional bearer is a persisting arrangement of offices, rules, records, procedures, and material capacities through which changing persons can make and carry publicly attributable commitments. The persons remain the subjects; the arrangement is not a collective consciousness. Offices specify who may act for it, procedures specify how an act becomes its act, and records allow its obligations to survive turnover among officeholders.

Formal permission is not effective agency when hunger, untreated illness, insecure shelter, threat, or unanswerable power consumes the distance in which a person can attend, compare, refuse, and revise. The conditions that sustain participation therefore also bear on whether rights can be exercised as informed judgment rather than held only in name.

Shared institutions already distribute conditions on which each subject’s continuation depends. A subject has reason to maintain what their continuation relies on (§5.2), and the same claim extends to other subjects exposed to the arrangement (§5.14). The result supports common maintenance without making cooperation automatic or reducing every continuing obligation to present self-interest.

**[Proposition]**

**Mutual Sustenance** · *Proposition · conditional political result*

Subjects can’t escape dependence on shared conditions while they live within them. Where their continuation remains exposed to those conditions, they have reason to sustain them together. Mutual sustenance is the warranted response to that interdependence, not its inevitable outcome: durable convergence requires institutions that preserve recognition, representation, and cooperation without domination. For a subject whose immediate exposure has lapsed, any continuing obligation rests on recognized standing and political judgment, not on self-interest alone.

**Depends on:** Drive (§5.2) and Morality (§5.14)

Those results converge on one political proposal, and what follows is a test of it.

**[Principle]**

**Convergent Individualism** · *Principle*

A political proposal in which distinct subjects retain separate ends and wide latitude above a common foundation of effective possibility, while converging on maintenance of that foundation through shared institutions they can hold accountable.

That proposal turns on one ordinary word used in a narrower sense than usual.

**[Definition]**

**Subsistence** · *Definition*

*Subsistence* ordinarily names continued existence or the means by which it is maintained. Here the noun is used in a stipulated political sense for a relation in which members and institutions maintain the shared conditions of agency-bearing life and effective participation. The stipulation is explanatory shorthand, not an inference from etymology and not a claim that a polity is literally an organism or a single subject.

The sections that follow test this proposal domain by domain. They inherit the foundation and non-domination constraints without pretending those constraints settle every policy design, tradeoff, or empirical question in advance.

Each application has three layers, and nothing that follows may slide between them. **Shape** is what the argument derives: the direction of a relation, the conditions that must be maintained, and the failure a design must avoid. **Prediction** is what should be observed if that shape is correct and a proposed arrangement actually realizes it. **Coefficients** are the numbers that fill the shape in a place and time: costs, rates, thresholds, elasticities, capacities, and measured effects.

The derivation fixes the shape. The shape generates predictions. Evidence then tests those predictions and supplies the coefficients. A country, program, or institution can show that one implementation works under stated conditions; it can’t turn its own settings into necessary features of the framework. When the evidence changes, the coefficients and sometimes the chosen design should change with it. The foundation and non-domination constraints remain the standards the new design must meet.

## 6.1 Rights

Before a community can work out how to run anything else, it has to say what its institutions are *for*, and that is what rights do. Rights spell out what a person must be able to count on to take part in political life as a full member, not merely survive inside it. The pillar’s central political claim is that the right to life can be read more substantively than “do not kill me.” A life lived one illness or one missed paycheck from ruin may preserve biological survival while leaving agency severely constrained. On the participation-condition interpretation, food, shelter, healthcare, and an effective political voice aren’t optional welfare additions but conditions required for the right to life to be politically meaningful. This is a normative interpretation defended through fit to agency and subsistence, not a semantic truth settled by the modal proof alone. That is why rights come first: every other pillar is this same commitment worked out in one domain.

Rights articulate the foundation that the rest of the chapter is structured to maintain. A political community that doesn’t articulate the rights its institutions are for can’t derive what those institutions must do; an institution that doesn’t know what it is structured to protect can’t tell when it is failing.

The derivation runs at the readerly register before any framework apparatus has to do its work. The key to political life that lasts is to build a [polity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) that people want to protect and invest in because it protects and invests in them. The wanting isn’t added from outside as duty, altruism, or solidarity; it is what each subject’s wanting-to-be-well and not-wanting-to-be-harmed becomes once generalized across everyone who shares those wantings. A polity that protects everyone protects me. A polity that invests in everyone invests in me. A polity that protects and invests in me is one I have reason to support, to protect, and where it falls short, to change.

The principle first appears in three compressed faces (provision, protection, and reform), but those faces unfold into a fuller grammar. *Provision / investment*: the system builds, maintains, develops, equips, and cares for the people who live inside it. *Protection*: the system shields them from preventable harm, coercion, deprivation, predation, and arbitrary power. *Restraint / consent*: the system doesn’t make people the objects of its projects without authorization; it respects refusal because the same respect is owed in return. *Recognition / voice*: the system hears people’s reports, needs, fears, aspirations, and direction as evidence about what maintenance requires. *Repair / accountability*: the system answers injury, violation, negligence, corruption, and institutional failure by making the harmed party and the damaged relation answerable to repair. *Reform / learning*: the system changes when its pattern is wrong, because a system that does to anyone what I would refuse to have done to me is a system that could do it to me. *Contribution / stewardship*: the system gives people real ways to sustain what sustains them, through work, taxes, voting, care, maintenance, criticism, invention, public service, and local knowledge.

These aren’t new domains and not a second table of contents. They are dimensions of the same subsistence relation. Every domain in Chapter 6 contains all of them, though one or another becomes most visible depending on the material at issue. Environment has provision, protection, restraint, recognition, repair, reform, and stewardship; so do representation, community, education, healthcare, economy, defense, enforcement, and justice. The domains are the sites where subsistence becomes institutionally concrete. The faces are the recurring operations subsistence has to perform wherever it lands.

*Subsistence as equation, not account.* Subsistence (the Subsistence definition in §6) names this relation in noun form. The noun doesn’t name an account that participants pay into and from which benefits are drawn down. It names the equation itself: *members invest in the political community because the political community invests in them, and the political community invests in members because members invest in it*. The reciprocity is the thing, and the noun *subsistence* names that reciprocity at the political scale.

The principle operates at three scales of the same form. *Dyadic*: each subject’s refusal is respected because the same respect is owed in return; this is what consent names, in the modern register that emerged once subjects’ aversions and refusals were taken as load-bearing rather than as private preferences the surrounding social order could override. *Institutional*: organizations act only on what their participants authorize: informed consent in medicine, democratic legitimacy in politics, voluntary association in civil society. *Political*: a system that protects and invests in people is a system that people want to protect and invest in. The same reciprocity runs from two subjects across a table to a population of millions; what changes is scale, not structure.

The connection to Chapter 5 isn’t a loose analogy, but the register has to remain explicit. Each Chapter 5 register has two halves. The structural half is a conditional corollary of Cartesian Certainty via Modal Pressure and Life: Drive’s continuation-pressure, Consciousness as a living closure’s vantage, and the thin one-place ought. The two-place upgrade takes a further step, granted rather than derived: modeling another subject as the same kind supplies its stakes, and the equal-standing premise supplies the reason they count comparably (§5.14.3). The structural half is derivation; the upgrade rests on that premise.

Consciousness’s organization–interiority identity is separately warranted at §5.1 as the best-supported explanation in its cumulative comparison, though not deductively demonstrated. Each later identification of a lived operation is a functional proposal defended at its own strength. Chapter 6 can inherit the structural half as structure. When a political conclusion depends on the consciousness identity, a later naming, a thick will, or a particular institution, it inherits that conditionality.

The constraint-following form comes from Reasoning; the shareable and correctable representation from knowledge; direction from meaning; agency moving through live alternatives from will; and mutual recognition, consent, non-maleficence, beneficence, autonomy, and justice from morality. Equal standing at this scale is the two-place ought of §5.14.3, not a second moral ground. Subsistence is what those reciprocal capacities become when the subjects who must foster, refrain, authorize, repair, and learn together are no longer two subjects in a single exchange but millions of subjects living inside the same inherited institutions.

### 6.1.1 The Dispute
The standing dispute turns on what the right to life is *for*. The negative-rights tradition reads it as a side constraint: others may not kill, confine, or dispossess the rights-bearer, but the right generates no general claim on anyone else’s labor or resources. The social-rights and capabilities traditions answer that formal protection is hollow when a person lacks the material conditions needed to exercise agency at all. The disagreement is not over whether non-interference matters. It is whether protected biological survival exhausts the right, or whether life-as-agency requires a feasible material foundation.

Nozick (Nozick 1974) and Hayek (Hayek 1960) press the strongest objections. Separate persons may not be used as instruments of an aggregate project, and a right without an identifiable duty-bearer is not yet a right. Roosevelt (Roosevelt 1944), the UDHR drafters (United Nations General Assembly 1948), Marshall (Marshall 1950), Shue (Shue 1980), Sen (Sen 1992; Sen 1999), and Nussbaum (Nussbaum 2000; Nussbaum 2006) press the reply: subsistence, healthcare, education, and effective access are conditions under which the familiar liberties become exercisable. The requirement that follows accepts the objections’ constraints and asks whether public institutions can bear bounded duties of provision without erasing separate lives, protected domains, or the need for public authorization.

*The principle’s place in the literature.* Rawls’s original position (*A Theory of Justice* Rawls 1971) reaches universalizability through a veil of ignorance that suppresses agents’ actual identities so the worst-off case carries weight in their deliberation. Rawls has universalizability right, and is right to ground political commitments in something each agent has reason to endorse. The parting is on the veil: the principle runs through *actual modal exposure to the same system* rather than through *counterfactual ignorance about which person one is*. The agent doesn’t have to imagine not knowing who they are. They only have to notice that what the system does to anyone is what the system is willing to do, and that they share the system.

Scanlon’s contractualism (*What We Owe to Each Other* Scanlon 1998) reaches the same symmetry through what no one could reasonably reject. I grant the symmetry and part on grounding it in structural co-exposure rather than idealized reasonable rejection. Habermas’s discourse ethics (*Moral Consciousness and Communicative Action* Habermas (1983) 1990) reaches it through ideal speech. Again, I grant the universalization and part on the grounding. All three counterfactual moves—veil, reasonable rejection, ideal speech—do work that the framework derives more directly from actual shared conditions.

That parsimony claim needs a defense. The counterfactuals supply a standpoint from which actual discourses, contracts, and arrangements can be measured for distortion, coercion, hierarchy, and exclusion. My reply is that actual exposure to shared conditions can supply the same standpoint. The question is what an arrangement would have to look like to maintain the participation conditions of every subject inside it. The structural conditions already established answer that question without counterfactual scaffolding. Where they leave the answer indeterminate, the counterfactuals remain available as auxiliary tools. The narrower claim is that they aren’t necessary at every step, not that they have been eliminated.

Hume’s account of justice (*Treatise of Human Nature* III Hume (1739–1740) 2000) as the artificial virtue that emerges among agents with limited generosity, moderate scarcity, and mutual interdependence is a foundational ancestor of the principle. The convergence is on deriving institutional commitments from interest under shared conditions. The parting is on positive provision: Hume thought positive duties couldn’t be made determinate enough to be requirements of justice, and the principle’s *provision* face commits to positive provision. Its reply is that the body and the conditions of agency give positive duties the determinacy Hume thought they lacked; what *life* requires when read at *bios* rather than *zoē* (the derivation that follows) is determinate in a way Hume’s eighteenth-century examples couldn’t yet make visible.

Honneth’s recognition theory (*The Struggle for Recognition* Honneth 1995) grounds institutional life in struggles for mutual recognition; the recognition-foundation is shared; the parting is by deriving the institutional shadow from generalized self-interest rather than from recognition struggles directly. Iris Marion Young’s structural-injustice work (*Responsibility for Justice* Young 2011) reaches its *reform* face on independent grounds: participation in a structural system generates responsibility for the system’s outputs. Young’s social-connection model is granted what it claims; the parting is only on grounding, since the reform face here runs through self-interested generalization rather than through identification with the harmed party. Hirschman’s *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty* (Hirschman 1970) names the dynamics the *wanting* clause describes: loyalty as the wanting that compounds under sustained reciprocity, voice as its expression under stress, exit as what happens when reciprocity fails irrecoverably. The principle’s claim is that the conditions under which loyalty is structurally available are the conditions of mutual investment developed here; voice and exit are the responses when those conditions fail. Mill’s harm principle (*On Liberty* Mill 1859) is the dyadic-scale analogue of its reciprocity, and the modern consent-as-foundational-category development (from Locke’s *Second Treatise* (1689) 1988; through Beauchamp and Childress’s *Principles of Biomedical Ethics* 1979) operationalizes the dyadic scale in medical, legal, and political institutions. Pettit’s non-domination (*Republicanism* Pettit 1997), already cited in §6, gives the *protection* and *reform* faces their republican formulation; convergence with Pettit is very close; what is added is the structural derivation Pettit assumes rather than gives.

The principle’s contribution is the synthesis. Universalizability is Kantian; generalized self-interest is Hobbesian-Humean; mutual vulnerability is Hobbesian; non-domination is Pettit’s; capabilities-as-precondition is Sen’s, Nussbaum’s, and Shue’s; recognition-as-institutional-grounding is Honneth’s; reform-from-structural-exposure is Young’s; loyalty-from-reciprocity is Hirschman’s; consent-as-foundational is Mill’s, Locke’s, and the modern biomedical-ethics tradition’s. What is offered is holding these together in one derivation, running across these recurring faces and at three scales, where the existing literature has held them apart. One role-distinction the synthesis depends on has to be marked, since the partings already traced all locate its ground in co-exposure or generalized self-interest: that language names what *binds and scales* the obligations, not what *confers the standing* they answer to. The standing is settled upstream: that another subject’s conditions matter, and so are something an arrangement can fail to maintain, is a fact about that subject, holding whether or not anyone’s self-interest registers it (§5.14.3); this is why §6 root extends rights by capacity rather than by exposure. Generalized self-interest is the motive that sustains the political arrangement and carries the obligation past the subjects whose exposure happens to be felt; capacity is the ground that makes the obligation owed at all. Where an institutional commitment is grounded in self-interest, the grounding names the binder a polity runs on, not a relocation of standing into the wanting: the wanting stays downstream of the fact rather than constitutive of it (§5.14).

### 6.1.2 The Requirement
The argument here draws on Morality (§5.14), the agency analyses at Drive (§5.2), Will (§5.11), Identity (§5.7), and Reasoning (§5.6.4), and the chapter opener’s account of mutual exposure. The political conclusion requires an explicit normative bridge: **equal standing forbids an institutional order from protecting formal agency while foreseeably allowing avoidable collapse of the minimum capabilities needed to exercise it, where coordinated provision is feasible without violating comparable standing.** A duty-allocation premise then identifies public institutions as primary duty-bearers because they coercively set the common rules, pool resources, assign responsibilities, and possess coordination capacities individuals lack. Duties remain limited by feasibility, proportionality, role, and protection against using particular people merely as means. Conditional on those premises, three results follow: rights articulate participation conditions; the right to life protects agency as well as biological survival; and subsistence can be included as a precondition of effective exercise. These are defended normative conclusions, not semantic or modal entailments from T/S/Φ alone.

Throughout Chapter 6, the argument moves in one direction: the rights tradition reached for protected existence and located the right at the formal register of non-interference. This chapter spells out the same commitment where existence is actually maintained or undermined.

Consider concretely a parent working two part-time jobs with no health insurance and no paid sick leave. The legal right to life is intact: no one is threatening to kill them. The right to liberty is intact: no one is detaining them. But a serious diagnosis makes treatment impossible without medical bankruptcy; a flu makes work impossible without rent becoming impossible; a child’s emergency forces a choice between earning and caretaking. The rights are formally present and substantively absent. The argument’s claim isn’t that the legal rights are wrong but that they are incomplete: a right to life that leaves a parent in this position has been articulated at the wrong register, naming the formal protection while leaving the conditions of life to luck. Add accessible healthcare, paid sick leave, and stable housing, and the parent now has what the right to life was always meant to name. The legal form hasn’t changed. What changed is whether the right has substantive content where life is actually maintained. The failure-mode the case describes is unevenly distributed: in the United States, uninsured rates, scheduling-precarity exposure, medical-bankruptcy rates, and eviction rates all stratify along race and gender lines, and the participation-conditions denial therefore lands disproportionately on populations the substantive-rights commitment is disproportionately owed (developed at §6.10 and §6.13).

**[Proposition]**

**Wanting Downstream** · *Proposition*

Where the subsistence conditions for life-as-agency have not been met and a person wants to end their life as a result, provision of an exit can’t substitute for fulfillment of the obligation the right to life already required. The claim is about what the political community owes, not about what the person is doing: a wanting formed under deprivation the community was obliged to prevent indicts the arrangement whether or not it’s autonomous, and the obligation is not discharged either way. Nothing here rules that such a wanting fails to be the person’s own. A choice can be both a response to unjust conditions and genuinely the chooser’s, and treating deprivation as by itself voiding agency would withdraw standing from the very people this result is defending.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14) and the Chapter 6 participation-foundation and duty-allocation premises

The result follows from the participation-foundation and duty-allocation premises. Where deprivation contributes to a wish to die, the unmet obligation remains an indictment of the arrangement even if the wish is also genuinely the person’s. Providing an exit can’t substitute for housing, food, care, or support already owed. It doesn’t follow that terminal illness guarantees autonomy or that deprivation negates it: capacity, causation, coercion, values, prognosis, pain, disability, and alternatives require individual assessment. Population rates can trigger investigation of institutional conditions, but they can’t classify any individual case. The political and clinical questions concern different objects, and neither settles the other.

**[Proposition]**

**Government Work** · *Proposition*

Given the Chapter 6 equal-standing, effective-exercise, and duty-allocation premises, a central function of public institutions is to maintain participation conditions and protect people against coercion and avoidable collapse. This does not exhaust legitimate government purposes or prove that one agency must directly provide every condition. Culture, administration, discovery, public goods, and other functions may have independent justification, while private, local, associative, and mixed arrangements may discharge bounded roles where access and accountability remain secure.

**Depends on:** Right to Life (§6.1)

The obligation isn’t a posture; it is delivered through work. That work is done by people acting on behalf of the political community: civil servants, public educators, public-system clinicians, public-works infrastructure workers, enforcement officers, judicial officers, military personnel, elected representatives, and their administrative staff. At the foundation, government work discharges the right-to-life obligation in two parts. Economy (§6.7), Housing (§6.8), Education (§6.9), and Healthcare (§6.10) maintain the conditions of life. Defense (§6.11), Enforcement (§6.12), and Justice (§6.13) protect life from threat.

A government function that doesn’t trace to this foundation isn’t thereby illegitimate. As the Government Work box holds, culture, discovery, public goods, and other functions may have independent justification beyond this derivation. The narrower result is that each function that *does* trace to the right-to-life obligation is either one of the commitments above or subordinate to one.

This bears on civil-service hiring, training, evaluation, and professional formation; on the recognition-bearing identity of public-service work (§6.7); and on the implementation role developed at §6.15. The people implementing the framework are the people whose work delivers what it derives. Structural correctness and institutional legitimacy remain distinct. The derivation supplies the first; affected parties’ ratification through representation supplies the second (§6.3). The Habermasian distinction between facticity and validity names this directly (*Between Facts and Norms* Habermas (1992) 1996).

*Scope of the derivation.* The derivation fixes the obligation and the categorical scope of what it covers. It doesn’t fix how much provision discharges that obligation in a given context. That requires welfare-economics measurement, public-health infrastructure analysis, political deliberation, and capabilities assessment. Nussbaum’s central-capabilities list, for example, covers life, bodily health, bodily integrity, senses–imagination–thought, emotions, practical reason, affiliation, other species, play, and control over environment (*Women and Human Development* Nussbaum 2000, ch. 1). Raworth’s *Doughnut Economics* (Raworth 2017) combines a social foundation derived from the UN Sustainable Development Goals with an ecological ceiling derived from planetary-boundaries science (§6.5). Cities including Amsterdam, Brussels, Copenhagen, Portland, and Glasgow have used it in implementation as of writing. The derivation establishes the categorical commitment. Institutional work has to calculate what satisfies it.

*Three results.* *Rights as participation conditions.* Morality (§5.14) grounds the moral framework in the mutual recognition of subjects who persist, occupy distinct positions, and can be reached across asymmetric exchange. Rights at the political scale articulate the conditions under which such mutual recognition can continue across the population: the institutional protections that keep subjects able to keep meeting one another as recognized subjects. A rights-violation, correspondingly, is the political-scale instance of what §5.14 defines a wrong to be: an arrangement corroding a subject against its own registered aversion, treating that subject’s stake in what befalls it as though it carried no claim. A right isn’t a metaphysical possession the subject brings to the political community from outside. It is what mutual recognition at population scale requires when written as institutional commitment. The framework converges on the participation-condition reading reached on independent grounds in the capabilities tradition (Sen 1992; Sen 1999; Nussbaum 2000; Nussbaum 2006), Shue’s basic-rights argument (Shue 1980), the social-rights tradition Marshall (Marshall 1950) historically describes, and the republican-citizenship tradition (Pettit 1997).

*Why a want isn’t a claim.* The account invites an obvious objection. If rights are the conditions of participation, and subjects are the ones who register what their participation requires, then any sufficiently insistent preference can be presented as a condition and there’s no principled way here to refuse it. It has two, and they are independent of each other.

The first is that a participation condition is a reachability claim, not a preference. To say that X is a condition of subject $s$’s participation is to say that participation is unavailable to $s$ without it: the means–end dependency a field registers (§5.4). Claims of that form are truth-apt and can be false, which preferences can’t be. So the demand to own persons isn’t refused merely for being repugnant; it is refused because the dependency it asserts doesn’t hold. No subject’s capacity to persist, hold a position, and meet others as recognized subjects requires the ownership of anyone.

That also names what such a demand is on its own terms. A misrepresented dependency—X asserted as necessary for Y when it isn’t—is one of the four ways a modal field is corrupted (§5.14), and corruptions of the necessity axis are self-sealing: complying with a false requirement furnishes no counter-instance, so the requirement is never caught at it. That is a prediction about how such claims behave over time, and the record set out later bears it. The proprietors and enslavers who articulated the participation-conditions framework while denying those conditions to specific populations sustained the necessity-claim across lifetimes without its failing any test they were disposed to run.

The second block holds whether or not the dependency obtains. A condition whose satisfaction requires corroding another subject against its own registered aversion is a wrong on the two-place account of §5.14.3, and participation conditions are precisely what keep subjects able to go on meeting one another as recognized subjects. A demand that removes another from that standing can’t be a condition of it. So a subject who did somehow depend on the ownership of others would have a dependency, and still not a claim.

One thing the account can’t do is let registration constitute the condition, and the distinction is worth keeping sharp. A modal field is a fallible mapping and can misrepresent what it maps (§5.4). If a right were whatever a subject registered as necessary, then a corrupted field would manufacture rights, and the false-necessity mode would be a generator of them rather than a corruption of the field. What registration supplies is how subjects locate their conditions and come to recognize them in one another. What makes a condition a condition is the dependency itself.

*The right to life is already a right to agency.* Jefferson’s “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness,” derived from Locke’s “life, liberty, and property” (Locke (1689) 1988, II, §9), names one underlying commitment at progressively explicit registers: protection of the subject’s agency. The historical contradiction the bios/zoē derivation makes legible deserves naming directly: Locke’s Carolina-proprietorship and Royal African Company investments, and Jefferson’s lifetime enslaving, are the canonical instance of the participation-conditions framework being articulated in language while its articulators denied those conditions to specific populations through the legal apparatus they constructed. The bios/zoē move is exactly the depth at which the contradiction becomes legible. Mills’s *The Racial Contract* (Mills 1997) develops the canonical analytic engagement with this articulation-vs-application gap. The relevant distinction is between *bios* (lived life, life-as-mode-of-living) and *zoē* (bare biological substrate). A subject can be biologically alive and legally unconfined while still lacking the real conditions for agential choice. The right to life, properly understood, therefore protects life-as-agency, not mere biological continuation.

**[Right]**

**Right to Life** · *Right*

The right to life protects life-as-agency (*bios*), not bare biological continuation (*zoē*). Participation is unavailable to subject $s$ without the conditions that make agency real. Owed by membership, not earned by performance. Form of provision stays open.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14), Consciousness (§5.1), and The Chapter 6 Premises (§6.1)

That is the right the rest of this chapter spends.

*The foundation of liberty.* In classical philosophical vocabulary, the foundation of liberty is the set of conditions under which life-as-agency is exercisable rather than reduced to bare biological continuation. The foundation isn’t held at a minimum and stepped over toward whatever is supposed to come next; it is *maximized*, because the conditions that make life-as-agency possible just are the conditions that make liberty real. They aren’t stacked, with liberty above and the foundation below. They are the same condition seen from different angles, and the deepest happiness and the truest liberty turn out to name the same thing. The Jeffersonian formula gets half of this right and half of it wrong. The half right: life and liberty are foundational, and political institutions exist to maintain them. The half wrong: the *pursuit of happiness* framing makes happiness the destination of pursuit rather than the substantive content of what is foundationally secured. The classical sense the formulation drew on—Aristotle’s *eudaimonia* (*Nicomachean Ethics* I.7, 1098a16)—isn’t a destination at all but the activity of well-functioning life, which is what *bios* names when its pursuit-capacity is intact. The argument restores this sense: the foundation just is the conditions of life-with-pursuit-capacity-intact, which is what the older eudaimonic tradition meant by happiness. What is *pursued from* the foundation is whatever directions a subject recognizes as their own: meaning, contribution, relationship, knowledge, work, art, family, whatever the subject lives toward. Pursuit happens *from* the foundation, not *toward* it. The compressed form: the foundation is happiness, the foundation is liberty, and the truest happiness is the truest liberty; ambition, on this account, is structurally available to everyone, because everyone is already on the foundation that ambition requires.

*The foundation has no underside.* Because the foundation is maximized rather than held at a minimum, it isn’t a line some members clear and others fall beneath. A threshold has a below; a foundation doesn’t. To be a member of the political community is already to stand on it, and there is no register at which a person drops out of the conditions of agency into some lower place the arrangement keeps available but empty, because that place isn’t a place.

A polity organized around maximum possibility can’t contain such a register, and not merely as a humanitarian preference. A person who has fallen below the conditions of life-as-agency has had their field of live possibility collapsed into the survival response that this chapter exists to prevent (§6). A trapdoor in the foundation is therefore not a gap in an otherwise sound structure. It is the point where the field the whole arrangement exists to widen goes to zero. No-place-to-fall is the negative face of maximum possibility; subsistence-as-precondition is its positive face. To maximize live possibility for every member is to allow no register in which that field is foreclosed for any of them.

Liberty is the political name for the field that opens above the foundation; and the foundation isn’t a floor, because a floor is one of a series and has something under it. That is the point of the word: what a member stands on is terminal, not the lowest story of a building that keeps a basement available. There was never a legitimate lower status waiting beneath the foundation, only the withdrawal of conditions that shared life already consists in.

The image marks a political limit, not a claim that food, land, care, or labor are non-rival or costless. Holding the foundation everywhere requires material provision, and material provision consumes rival resources. The commitment is that scarcity must be faced as a shared constraint—through contribution, priority, and openly governed tradeoffs—rather than silently converted into a class of people whose exclusion is treated as normal. When the foundation is held everywhere, what remains is the field: open, and open to everyone standing on it, because the arrangement no longer keeps anywhere to fall.

“No privileged floor” names the same shape in two registers. In the metaphysical register, Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality have nothing beneath them because each is held up by the other two rather than by some deeper Condition (§2.9.3). In the political register, there is no lower rung beneath the members of a community. Each is held by the arrangement the others maintain. The first register runs through Conditions; the second runs through persons.

*The foundation isn’t conditioned on participation.* The same no-underside logic denies the foundation a gate. If membership already places a person on the foundation, participation can’t be the price of admission. Nor can participation make the person forfeit it. The foundation is owed by membership rather than performance, and it isn’t withdrawn when a member performs.

This is the maximized-not-minimal logic on the participation axis rather than the depth axis. A floor that drops as a member earns isn’t a floor but a ceiling wearing a floor’s name. It makes the member trade the conditions of agency against the exercise of agency, restoring the trapdoor at the point where capacity was supposed to be drawn out. The worked case is developed at §6.9: accessibility owed by membership rather than demonstrated deserving, and earnings-cap benefit designs that withdraw the foundation as capacity is exercised.

A right establishes that a domain is protected: body, attention, privacy, property, medical treatment, sexuality, representation, movement, speech.

**[Definition]**

**Consent as Right Modifier** · *Definition*

Consent is the subject’s authority to modify the default rule governing a protected domain: the rights-bearer’s act of specifying what may happen within that domain, by whom, under what conditions, and for how long. It does not erase the right; it exercises the right. Refusal leaves the default protection in force, and consent changes the permitted relation only to the extent the competent subject has authorized it. Consent must therefore be informed, voluntary, competent, specific, and revocable: absent those conditions, the purported modification is not the subject’s rule for what may happen to them, but another party’s rule imposed through the grammar of permission.

**Depends on:** Consent’s Conditions (§5.14)

*Two commitments, and neither is subordinate.* Two commitments govern the chapter at once, and the temptation at every hard case is to buy one with the other. The first is that the foundation is owed unconditionally: no being has to earn the conditions of its own continuation, and no failure of circumstance, capacity, or conduct converts those conditions into a reward. The second is that a being’s standing to decide about its own life isn’t contingent on its circumstances being just. Those pull apart in the cases that matter most—someone deciding under conditions the community was obliged to prevent—and the two easy exits are refused here. It doesn’t say that because the conditions are unjust the decision isn’t really theirs, which would strip standing from the people the foundation exists for. It doesn’t say that because the decision is theirs the conditions are no longer the community’s problem, which would let an exit discharge an obligation. Both hold. The community owes the foundation whether or not the person wants it, and the person’s refusal is theirs whether or not the foundation was met. Where a later section seems to settle such a case by dropping one of the two, that is a defect in the section rather than a resolution of the tension.

The definition above gives consent its technical rights meaning. Its five conditions come from Consent’s Conditions at §5.14; here they determine whether a person has actually modified a protected domain. The same reciprocal relation also holds between two people, where each respects the other’s refusal because the same respect is owed in return.

Both scales fail in the same way. The form of authorization may be present while structural deprivation destroys the substance of free refusal. What remains has the grammar of permission without the freedom that permission requires.

*A right to life that a subject must fight the arrangement to actualize is hollow at its foundation.* A formal right to life that leaves a person without secured access to food, shelter, healthcare, and the material conditions of bodily continuation preserves the legal form while undermining the right’s substance. The right to life, taken at the depth where life actually subsists, already includes subsistence as the precondition for the agency the right protects. The later sections spell out the operational architecture: Adequate Living Cost in §6.7, the housing floor in §6.8, the healthcare floor in §6.10, the educational foundation in §6.9, and the caregiving infrastructure crossing them.

Adequate Living Cost is a non-domination floor in Pettit’s sense (Pettit 1997; Pettit 2012): the income below which a worker can’t effectively refuse exploitative terms. It isn’t a distributive threshold. Its treatment of subsistence as a precondition corresponds to Rawls’s difference principle (*A Theory of Justice* Rawls 1971), but reaches it through participation conditions rather than the original-position procedure.

This upstream structure also answers Walzer’s objection to a single principle of distribution (*Spheres of Justice* Walzer 1983). Participation conditions aren’t a master distributive principle competing with the separate principles proper to medical care, office, recognition, or security. They are the foundation beneath them. No sphere may distribute its good so as to run a member below the conditions of agency. Once the foundation is held, distribution within each sphere remains for that sphere and the recognition mechanism of §6.3 to decide.

The structural reason the negative/positive rights distinction has felt foundational deserves naming explicitly. The modal field on which moral cognition operates (§5.14) appears to be asymmetrically weighted — stored aversive possibilities carrying more affective mass than stored appetitive ones at equivalent magnitude, with the magnitude contested and context-dependent — and the rights tradition inherits that calibration. Negative rights (against being killed, tortured, enslaved, confined arbitrarily) track the field’s most heavily weighted branches; positive rights (to healthcare, education, housing) track less affectively dense branches even when their substantive importance is comparable. The asymmetry is real and is doing work the structural account doesn’t deny. What it is an asymmetry *in* can now be stated precisely, and the precision matters for what follows. A drive-state was established at §5.2 as a standing weight on a branch the subject holds as available, not an occurrent response to what is present, and such a weight can be borne without being felt at any given moment. Affective mass and standing weight are therefore separable, and the calibration the rights tradition inherited is an asymmetry in the first. That’s why it can’t by itself license a difference in the second: a branch can carry full standing while registering little, and a subject reporting no distress isn’t thereby a subject whose stake is smaller. What the structural account does deny is the inference, common to the libertarian wing, that the asymmetry licenses treating positive rights as a categorically different kind of moral claim. Subsistence shows up on the negative side of the asymmetry once *life* is read at *bios* rather than *zoē*: a person without healthcare, food, shelter, or stable conditions of bodily continuation isn’t currently in possession of the life the negative right to life was protecting. The aversion-asymmetry then runs in its favor rather than against it: where the substantive content of *life* includes the conditions of life-as-agency, withholding those conditions registers on the same heavily-weighted aversive side that *don’t kill* and *don’t torture* register on. The asymmetry is kept, while correcting where it falls.

The contemporary opposition to the subsistence-as-precondition reading runs through Nozick (*Anarchy, State, and Utopia* Nozick 1974) and Hayek (*The Constitution of Liberty* Hayek 1960). Nozick treats rights as side constraints that can’t be overridden for any aggregate good. On his account, positive welfare rights are a category mistake because no person has a claim on another’s productive labor simply by naming it a right. Hayek presses a different objection (*Law, Legislation and Liberty*, vol. 2, *The Mirage of Social Justice* Hayek 1976). A right must name a specific duty-bearer, and “society” isn’t one. So the move from negative civil rights to positive social rights looks like a category shift that rights-language can’t absorb.

Grant the central point in each objection. Separate lives aren’t instruments of other people’s projects, and a duty without a specific bearer isn’t yet a right. The disagreement is over what subsistence is. On the side-constraints reading, it is an added positive duty that competes with negative protections. On the reading defended here, it is what the right to life requires once *life* means *bios* rather than *zoē*.

The duty-bearer isn’t society as an undifferentiated whole. It is the institutional structure the political community already maintains: legislatures, executives, courts, administrative agencies, and the civil-service workforce. The Government Work result above names them directly. The disagreement is therefore about what *life* in *the right to life* means, not about smuggling welfare rights in under another name.

Nozick’s separateness-of-persons constraint remains intact. The argument doesn’t aggregate liberty across persons. It maintains the conditions under which each person’s liberty is actual. What the side-constraints account treats as a trade between people is, on this reading, maintenance of the conditions that must hold before such trades can be free.

*The foundation binds against intermediate authorities.* Rights as participation conditions apply anywhere a person could be dropped below the conditions of agency, including inside the political community. Religious institutions, families, employers, communities, and other intermediate authorities have legitimate authority within their domains. That authority doesn’t include the power to drop someone below the participation threshold.

A religious institution may organize the religious life of its adherents and hold its own beliefs. It may not use doctrine to justify medical neglect, deny education, shelter sexual or physical abuse, or close off the capacity (§5.6.4) for analysis that participation requires. A family may organize its own life. Parental authority doesn’t license the denial of food, shelter, education, or medical care, or exposure to abuse. An employer may organize work. It may not hold subsistence hostage to coercive conditions or extract below the substrate (§6.7).

This preserves religious liberty, family autonomy, and associational life as exercises of liberty above the foundation: faith, tradition, custom, and shared practice remain for subjects to pursue as their own. What intermediate authorities can’t do is use their standing to override the foundation of the people under their care. A subject reduced to mere biological persistence by an intermediate authority no more possesses life-as-agency than one reduced that way by the political community.

The same limit applies at the household scale. Forced marriage, marital-rape exemptions where they exist, and domestic violence sheltered by family authority preserve a legal form while denying equal participation in substance. They violate the result in the same way as the child-protection cases. Anderson’s *Private Government* (Anderson 2017) develops the workplace version, taken up at §6.7 and §6.12. At the racialized substate scale, policing, schools, redlining, and neighborhood-level enforcement disparities have withheld the foundation from specific populations under state-aligned authority (§6.12; §6.13). These are instances of the same structural failure, not separate political questions.

The relocation parts ways with the rights tradition’s libertarian wing (Nozick, Hayek) and converges with its participation-conditions wing (Roosevelt, the UDHR drafters, Marshall, Shue). The negative rights the tradition foregrounds remain protected. The argument adds that the positive conditions under which negative rights are exercisable already sit inside what the participation-conditions wing articulated, and that treating those conditions as supplementary welfare obscures the unity its deepest formulations already saw.

The following are **conditional design requirements**, not a structural-necessity inventory derived from T/S/Φ alone. They follow if three premises are accepted:

*One word about the phrase, since later sections use it in the other direction.* §6.5, §6.6, and §6.13 each set out what they call a *structural-necessity inventory* for their domain. That isn’t a contradiction of the sentence above, and the difference is the whole architecture of the chapter: what is denied here is necessity derived from the Conditions **alone**, and what those sections assert is necessity **given the three premises below**. Nowhere in the chapter does an institutional requirement descend from the three Conditions without passing through them.

**[Premise]**

**The Chapter 6 Premises** · *Premise · conditional, not derived from T∧S∧Φ*

**Equal-standing.** Each person’s agency and basic capabilities count comparably in the justification of common institutions.

**Effective-exercise.** Formally protected liberties are inadequate where avoidable deprivation predictably removes the capability to exercise them.

**Duty-allocation.** Institutions that coercively set shared rules and possess distinctive taxing, coordinating, and enforcement capacities bear primary duties to secure a sufficient participation foundation, with burdens limited by feasibility, proportionality, role, and side constraints.

These three carry the chapter. Every per-domain reform cites the same three, and the shared grounding is what makes the domains interlock (§6.14). They are premises of political theory accepted here, not results the modal core delivers.

**What they add, and what they do not replace.** They are not the source of the rights. The subject a right is owed to—a being that registers its own continuation, can be wronged, and holds a field that another can foreclose or corrupt—is Chapter 5’s, and each domain section names the registers it draws on: Morality above all, with Consciousness, Drive, Feeling, Will, Knowledge, Language, and Technology entering where the domain requires them. What these three premises license is the further step from *a subject can be wronged in this way* to *institutions bear the primary duty to prevent it, and each subject’s claim counts comparably*. That step is political theory and does not follow from the account of the subject alone, which is why every Right in this chapter declares both: the Chapter 5 register that says what is at stake, and these premises that say who owes what about it.

The equal-standing premise remains a premise, but its repeated applications don’t each require a new normative assumption. The conditional consequence established by No Arbitrary Self-Exemption is that, once equal standing and relevant similarity are granted, first-person location can’t by itself make a feature claim-grounding for one subject but not another. The open commitment is the premise and the relevant-similarity judgment; the consistency of its application is earned.

*What a Right box states.* Each of the twelve boxes that follow in this chapter is typed **Right**, and the type marks a derivation rather than a declaration. A Right is an entitlement that follows from the three premises above together with Morality (§5.14) and Consciousness (§5.1), and it holds conditionally on them. That conditionality isn’t a hedge: the premises are premises of political theory, marked here as not derived from the three Conditions, so a reader who rejects equal-standing, effective-exercise, or duty-allocation is entitled to reject what the boxes conclude. What the type doesn’t mean is that a right has been posited and then defended.
