The gate is circular: the only way to become legible to the allocation function is to consume its products, so the arrangement manufactures demand for the very thing it gates, a scarcity of standing rather than of goods. The gate is unanswerable: what counts as creditworthiness is decided by privately held scoring institutions whose measurement choices answer to no one they measure, a subset directing allocation. And the asymmetry widens the divide between renting and owning by measurement alone: the renter’s housing payment builds no legibility while the owner’s mortgage payment builds it, so the line between them widens without any difference in conduct (the housing side of the divide is developed at §6.8). An allocation function answerable to the recognition mechanism reads the evidence of dependability a member’s participation actually produces, whatever ledger it sits in. Rent, utilities, and other standing obligations are that evidence.

*Capture compounds.* Financial holdings converted into unanswerable political direction have already been named as extraction; what makes finance the chief vector of that conversion is that the capture compounds. Rent-seeking gains advantage by controlling rules or access rather than by creating corresponding value. Captured allocation goes further: it directs resources toward whatever deepens the capture, so the drift becomes self-financing. The repair isn’t a new mechanism. It is the same recognition-and-answerability architecture derived here, applied to the allocation function itself.

*Income isn’t contribution.* Income and wealth can be poor proxies for what an activity adds or costs: unpaid care can sustain participation without appearing as income, while rent-seeking or harm-repair can increase measured activity without improving the underlying conditions. The phrase *net subsistence generated* names the evaluative question—what an arrangement adds to shared maintenance after its costs—but it isn’t a directly measurable unit and shouldn’t be treated as one. GDP’s familiar limits illustrate the problem; they don’t supply a replacement scalar.

*The evaluative target isn’t the tax base.* Any attempt to certify each actor’s total contribution would combine contestable value judgments, severe information limits, and Goodhart effects. Tax systems therefore operate on administrable bases—income, consumption, property, land value, transactions, externalities, estates, or combinations—whose incidence and avoidance profiles differ. The argument can require that financing preserve the foundation and avoid domination; it can’t infer that income and flows must remain the base or that one authority could neutrally measure contribution.

*Tax bases should answer to the burden they are meant to address.* Land rents, externalities, resource use, transactions, estates, and income are measurable only through institutions and never without contestable baselines. Land-value and Pigouvian taxes can target rents or harms more directly than a general income tax, but each requires valuation, causal attribution, enforcement, and an account of incidence. Estate and financial-transaction taxes rest on partly different arguments. The constraint supplies reasons to compare these tools by how well they finance the foundation, reduce unjustified cost shifting, preserve productive activity, and avoid new domination; it doesn’t derive them as interchangeable instances of one metric.

*The same principle bears on categorical exemptions from taxation generally, of which religious tax exemption is a clear case.* A categorical exemption, granted because of what an institution is rather than what it generates, decouples an institution’s tax status from any accounting of its net subsistence contribution—precisely the coupling the sources-of-taxes principle exists to enforce. Many religious institutions plainly do generate net subsistence: food banks, shelters, disaster relief, hospitals, and schools run under religious auspices are contribution by its own test, and nothing here revises that. The pressure falls on the mechanism, not the category. Current exemption is granted by what an organization is—a religious body, as such—rather than measured against what it generates. The accounting is weakened further by resting on individual congregants’ charitable behavior rather than institutional accountability. So an institution can hold an exemption while directing negligible resources toward subsistence and considerable resources toward property accumulation, political activity, or compensation, with no mechanism tying the exemption to the generation it would be required here to demonstrate. The fix implied isn’t an identity-based rule run the other direction (tax religious institutions because they are religious institutions), which would repeat the same category error with the sign flipped; it is applying the sources-of-taxes test itself, uniformly, to every institution regardless of category—rent, externalities, resource draw, and harm taxed, genuine contribution relieved, and exemption an accounting status an institution earns and re-earns rather than a status its category confers.

*The dependence on institutional agency is itself the tell.* An accounting gap that closes only when an institution chooses well isn’t closed at all, on its own terms: a structural fix doesn’t stay contingent on an occupant’s goodwill, it changes the arrangement so the outcome no longer depends on who is running it. Charitable relief—religious or otherwise—filling the gap the exemption leaves open is downstream relief for an upstream failure, in the same sense those terms already have elsewhere, and the more of it a society structurally requires, the less its upstream architecture is doing the job the sources-of-taxes principle assigns it. The measure of the tax structure’s success is how little need is left for downstream relief to meet, not how well downstream relief meets the need it leaves behind. A society doesn’t need a specialized institution to root out the poverty its own structure produces—the goal is a structure that doesn’t produce it, so that the institution built to catch what falls through has less, and eventually nothing, to catch.

*Firms are institutional bearers, not additional subjects by legal declaration.* A corporation already has the continuity structure defined at the Chapter 6 bridge: offices may turn over while contracts, records, assets, liabilities, and authorized procedures remain attributable to the continuing organization (Institutional Bearer). Legal personality is one device for making that attribution administrable. It doesn’t by itself establish consciousness, moral patiency, or standing equal to the living persons whose conditions the firm can affect. The distinction cuts both ways. An executive can’t dissolve personal responsibility into the corporation where their own conduct meets the relevant responsibility standard, and a corporation can’t dissolve an institutional obligation merely by replacing executives, shareholders, or a brand. Merger, bankruptcy, dissolution, and successor-liability rules remain legal design questions, especially where assets and control genuinely change; the constraint is that organizational form may not function as a laundering mechanism by which the continuing beneficiaries and operations preserve the gain while the bearer of the corresponding obligation disappears.

*The same reframing fixes the aim of transparency without pretending to derive a disclosure code.* The governing obligation was established at §6.4: “The right to accurate information has a positive face: what power conceals, it owes.” Here it applies to the economy. Extraction can’t be detected unless the relevant flows are visible.

That does not make *net subsistence generated* a number an institution can simply report. The phrase names an evaluative question, not a directly measurable scalar, as the preceding qualification states. What must be made visible are the inputs needed to answer that question responsibly: rents taken, externalities shifted, harms imposed, public privileges received, and contributions made. Income remains one relevant record; it can’t stand in for the whole account. Which disclosures, measurements, and auditing institutions provide adequate visibility is an empirical and legal design question. The structural conclusion is narrower: opacity may not be the mechanism by which an accountable flow is kept from the people who bear its costs.

*The function of the social structure is to put distance between subjects and vulnerability.* Hunger, untreated illness, homelessness, coercive dependence, and physical danger force choices to happen too close to collapse. Maintenance widens the interval: time to think, safety to refuse, stability to compare alternatives, and enough protected standing for action to become choice rather than survival-response. Subsistence isn’t generosity. It is the resource-condition for the social possibilities the society claims to offer.

The same fact was named (§5.11) from the inside as modal depth. Precarity doesn’t merely remove external options; it collapses the internal distance between condition and response. A subject acting under untreated illness, panic, hunger, threat, exhaustion, or survival pressure has fewer live alternatives available for reflective mapping before action. Upstream maintenance therefore protects agency itself. It keeps action from collapsing into reaction.

*Subsistence isn’t assistance.* The vocabulary in which subsistence is normally discussed is the vocabulary of government assistance: a benefactor with discretion, a recipient in need, an asymmetric relation in which something is given by some to others. That vocabulary mislocates the structure. Subsistence is a quantification of what it costs to maintain a person within the shared structure at a given place and time: housing, food, healthcare, transit, communication, the basic conditions of participation. Calling that subsistence rather than assistance isn’t euphemism. It is the correction of a category error. The political question shifts with the vocabulary. *Should we give you this* is contested moral territory whose contests aren’t resolvable from inside the vocabulary that frames them. *What does it cost to subsist here* is empirical, administrative territory, decidable by the same regional cost-of-living measures the shared structure already maintains for other purposes. The participation conditions the previous passages identified don’t require a benefactor to deliver them. They require a vocabulary that names what they actually are.

*Earning may not open a hole in the foundation.* A benefit designed as temporary relief may disappear as income rises. That is not automatically a defect; the relevant question is what the withdrawal does to actual access. A hard cliff, a steep phase-out, or an earnings cap fails when earning a little more leaves a member unable to secure the conditions the benefit had supplied. The structural requirement is not a universal cash payment at every income. It is that participation not be punished by the sudden loss of its own foundation. The rate and form of any phase-out are coefficient questions, tested by net resources, prices, access, and behavior. Healthcare and disability provide the clearest worked cases (§6.10).

*Liberty is organized across a shared structural space.* The conditions of remaining alive are normatively prior to discretionary accumulation because without them liberty is merely formal for the person below the foundation. They are not materially costless. Financing food, shelter, care, and security uses rival resources and can constrain what remains available above the threshold. The chapter root supplies the order, not an aggregation formula: secure the participation foundation and prevent domination, then widen liberty across the admissible arrangements that remain. Above that floor, decentralized markets retain their informational and choice-preserving work; where claims still conflict, incidence and comparative evidence decide among designs rather than the word *liberty* deciding the tradeoff twice.

*Why the aim can be positive-sum.* Freedom is modal freedom (§5.11): modal depth, the alternatives a subject can model and grasp, together with latitude, the room to enact them. One person’s increased understanding need not reduce another’s, and many forms of latitude grow through shared institutions. But the material means of action remain rival, and some liberties conflict. It doesn’t therefore follow that every gain aggregates without cost. People designing an arrangement must expand each person’s live field where possible and expose the tradeoffs where it is not.

These two pillars are the two axes under their freedom-side names: latitude is reach, and modal depth is mapping (§6). Neither can simply substitute for the other. The first is latitude—the maintained conditions that hold the interval open: subsistence, safety, time. Those conditions are shared in purpose but rival in provision, so extending them requires resources and can generate real conflicts. The foundation prevents those conflicts from being resolved by pushing some participants below the conditions of agency. The second is modal depth, the reach of a subject’s modal representation. Coordination with other subjects’ specialized coverage can extend it (§5.4): the surgeon’s mapped region, shared, can widen the carpenter’s field rather than subtracting from it. The information shared may be non-rival even where the labor, attention, and institutions that transmit it are not.

A scarce material good is rival: one person’s use forecloses another’s. Live possibility, mapped against a modal structure no one consumes by accessing, isn’t. This is why the feeding loop runs both ways at once rather than trading one subject’s gain against another’s. What grows on each side isn’t a fixed stock being divided but modal freedom across a shared structure. The structure is non-rival in the single sense Samuelson named (1954): one subject’s access forecloses no other’s. The analogy carries that property of non-rivalry in access down to the level of possibility itself, not the rest of the public-goods apparatus.

Aggregating the conditions under which liberty is actual is on that account aggregating something non-rival, which expands the field for each subject without conscripting any subject’s possibility to fund another’s.

The denial of conscription is a claim about possibility, not about dollars: what is aggregated is the non-rival access to conditions, while the rival resources used to maintain them remain rival and must be accounted for openly. Nothing in the non-rivality claim determines how those resources are raised.

The separateness of persons is preserved not despite the aggregation but because what is aggregated was never the kind of good that pits one person’s share against another’s, honored at the layer where the conditions are maintained, not denied at the layer where they are funded. (Convergence (§6.14) carries this non-rivalry forward into the convergence: it decomposes each economic act into a non-rival possibility-expanding component and a rival access-capturing one, reads the accumulation cap derived here as the requirement that the capturing component approach zero, and grounds the political Subsistence definition in the non-rival structure at its base.)

Housing is where this result meets land, the one good in which a rival material asset and a non-rival structural value share a single object; it is developed at section length in §6.8.

*The question is who can do the most for the bottom, not who can make it to the top.* The legacy of a society, on this framework, is measured not only by the height the highest reached but by what held the lowest. Whether a specified population can secure the participation foundation is an empirical question bounded by productivity, demographics, prices, ecological limits, administrative capacity, and political choice. Comparisons with Nordic, continental European, and other arrangements can test feasibility under their conditions; they can’t establish a universal budget or transplantable design. The structural claim is conditional and exact: where the foundation is materially feasible, refusing to secure it requires a justification other than impossibility. Where it is not yet feasible, the obligation is directional—to expand the capacity that would make it so without pretending the missing resources already exist.

*Proportionate shape, open coefficients.* Maintaining the foundation consumes rival resources, and those resources must come from within the arrangement being maintained. Greater stake in that arrangement—greater holdings protected by its law, contracts, currency, infrastructure, workforce, and stability—carries greater contribution back into the foundation. The direction can’t be inverted so that smaller-stake participants bear the larger effective burden while larger-stake participants retain the larger protected benefit. That is the tax shape the derivation supplies. It does not supply the curve. Ability to pay, benefit received, harms imposed, risks shifted, behavioral response, and actual incidence still determine how the shape can be implemented without defeating itself. Rates, brackets, bases, exemptions, and the choice between a proportional and a more steeply progressive schedule remain open wherever more than one design preserves the required direction.

Avoidance, exemptions, preferential treatment, and inheritance rules are therefore questions for the same test, not violations by definition. Ask what burden the rule shifts, what benefit or reliance is offered to justify it, who can answer for the rule, and what happens to the foundation after incidence. A tax haven used to conceal an otherwise owed liability and an exemption justified by a public contribution are not the same case. Neither the label nor the instrument supplies the verdict in advance.

*Intergenerational non-domination.* The legacy structure developed at Mortality (§5.9) distinguishes continuing a person’s effects from continuing the person, and the distinction becomes institutional when accumulated wealth outlives its holder. Ordinary inheritance can widen a descendant’s field by securing shelter, education, care, or room to choose; that transmission isn’t precluded. The limit is reached when inheritance, perpetual trust, foundation governance, or another posthumous vehicle transmits unanswerable command over the conditions of subjects who didn’t authorize it. The dead holder’s preferences may continue as a contribution available to the living; they may not become government over the living merely because assets can preserve an instruction after its author no longer participates in recognition. Acceptable estate and foundation architectures must therefore preserve revision, accountability, and democratic voice among the living subjects affected. This is a design constraint, not a derivation of a particular estate-tax rate, inheritance ceiling, trust duration, or philanthropic form.

*Statutory assignment isn’t economic incidence.* The condition binds on who actually bears an instrument’s cost, not on whom a schedule nominally names. Corporate-tax incidence falls partly on workers through wages and on consumers through prices. How that burden is divided depends on market structure and labor mobility rather than on the statute; the public-finance incidence literature, from Harberger (1962) onward, treats the split as an empirical question. Payroll-tax incidence likewise falls substantially on workers regardless of the statutory division between employer and employee. A levy that reads proportionate-to-stake on paper but shifts economically onto lower-stake participants fails the condition it was written to satisfy.

Satisfying proportionate-to-stake contribution therefore requires incidence analysis specific to each instrument and market context, not a proportionate-looking statutory schedule alone. Where that analysis shows a nominally progressive instrument shifting its burden downward, a different instrument is required to meet the condition.

*Shared maintenance has a resource side.* Institutions can’t maintain material conditions with words alone. Labor, materials, land, knowledge, and administrative capacity must come from somewhere inside the population and economy being maintained; there is no costless outside source. That is the structural point. Taxation is one current mechanism for assembling those resources. Public ownership, insurance, regulated private provision, voluntary institutions, and mixed arrangements organize them differently. The argument does not decide among those forms. It requires each proposal to show that the foundation is actually maintained, that its costs remain visible, and that people who bear those costs retain an answerable political relation to the decision.

*Foundation non-substitutability.* No financing or delivery instrument may substitute a nominal entitlement for actual access. Insurance, cash, direct public provision, regulated private provision, mutual provision, or a hybrid can satisfy the condition only if people can reliably reach the care, shelter, food, and security the foundation names. Profit is not disqualifying by definition, and public administration is not adequate by definition. A design fails where denial, price, exclusion, scarcity, or administrative breakdown leaves the protected condition unavailable in practice.

*Adequacy tracks circumstances.* What maintains participation varies by place, household, time, health, and circumstance. No universal amount can therefore be supplied. Cost-of-living measures, household data, medical evidence, and observed access can help an implementation locate adequacy, but the selection and weighting of those measures remain corrigible. The foundation reaches the conditions of participation; it does not promise replication of every prior standard of living or specify the discretionary holdings above it.

*What people need to participate.* *Societal needs* are the conditions under which a person can be a live participant in the political community. Without them, real possibility collapses into survival-response and a person loses access to the field of action described throughout this chapter. People do not earn these conditions by participating, and nobody grants them as permission to participate. The political community maintains them so that formal rights become real alternatives.

Concretely, people need shelter sufficient for sleep, hygiene, and rest; food sufficient to feed themselves; and healthcare that does whatever it can without bankrupting the patient. Children need education and care. People who can’t care for themselves at a given life-stage—the very young, the very old, the seriously ill, and the disabled—need care from others. Everyone needs public safety, mobility, access to information, clean air, clean water, a livable environment, and enough time not working to be a person rather than an output.

The list isn’t exhaustive, and a societal need takes more or less specific institutional form across societies and eras (Marshall 1950). But its structural function is fixed: whatever people need to be the people they are. The threshold doesn’t specify how each condition is delivered, how far provision rises above the bare minimum, or what sits in the discretionary territory above. It says that maintaining the conditions of participation is what the system exists to do. The list converges with the central capabilities Nussbaum develops in *Women and Human Development* (2000) and *Frontiers of Justice* (2006): both lists pick out conditions whose absence reduces a subject below the threshold of participation rather than ranking goods to be distributed. Sen’s *Development as Freedom* (1999) develops the same threshold from the capability-development side, and the chapter-opener convergence-with-capabilities paragraph at §6 root locates the operationalization toolkit (HDI/IHDI, Doughnut Economics, OECD Better Life, Bhutan GNH) its categorical commitments hand to implementation.

*A foundation uniform in name can be unequal in effect.* Some conditions of participation fall on only part of the population and aren’t thereby discretionary. Menstrual products are the clearest instance: a recurring, non-optional cost of the hygiene already named among the conditions above, borne by roughly half the members across several decades of life, whose absence produces exactly the participation loss the threshold is defined by, in the documented form of missed school and missed work. A foundation nominally identical for everyone, under which one category of member meets a recurring necessity cost the other doesn’t, isn’t an equal foundation but an equal figure laid over an unequal incidence—the distinction adequacy after accounting for incidence (§6.8.2) is used elsewhere to mark. The same incidence test governs how such goods are taxed: a schedule treating them as discretionary while exempting other necessities assigns the burden by category rather than by what the sources-of-taxes principle measures. The same structure runs at other unequal incidences. Diapers and infant formula are the concrete goods that the care of the very young—already named above among the conditions—actually consists in, and they fall on households at one life-stage rather than across the population; their standing cost is among the material conditions treated at §6.10 at the reproductive threshold. Classifying such goods as conditions of participation doesn’t convert every good into a public one, and it leaves the threshold’s silence on delivery and on generosity above the bare minimum exactly where the paragraph above sets it: what the classification fixes is that the cost falls inside the maintenance obligation the political community already holds, not that any particular good must be free. Which instrument corrects it—direct provision through schools, clinics, workplaces, and public facilities, exemption, allowance, or some combination—is underdetermined in the usual way. That the cost is a condition of participation rather than a personal expense isn’t.

*Certain social possibilities require necessary resources.* Deliberation requires time and stability. Meaningful consent requires information, maturity, safety, and freedom from coercion. Free labor requires enough security that employment isn’t survival-hostage. Law-abiding participation requires viable means of survival that don’t run through desperation. Mutual sustenance requires subjects whose own minimal survival isn’t consuming the whole field. These conditions are what makes the social possibilities just named live alternatives rather than nominal ones: what maximum possibility requires of the structure that maintains it.

*Universality concerns standing, not one delivery formula.* Every member holds the same claim to the foundation. That does not entail that every member receives an identical payment or service. Universal provision, means-tested provision without punitive cliffs, automatic enrollment, and mixed designs can all be assessed against the same question: does the arrangement keep the foundation available without making a person perform humiliation, remain poor, or surrender agency to receive it? Equal standing and continuity of access are established here. Comparative evidence must decide which design secures them with the least exclusion, capture, and administrative failure.

*Judge the foundation where it reaches the person.* A nominal transfer or service does not satisfy the foundation if price changes, fees, withdrawn compensation, exclusion, or an intermediary’s capture leaves the protected condition unavailable. How much pass-through occurs is specific to the market and design; housing-allowance studies, for example, report different results across reforms and supply conditions. The structural test is actual access after those effects. What must be measured, how often, and whether cash, direct provision, regulation, supply expansion, competition, or a mixed design answers a failure remain empirical questions.

*Public amenities not participation-conditioned.* Access to public goods (libraries, parks, transit, public health resources, civic spaces) may not be conditioned on work-participation status. Conditioning would reintroduce, at the level of amenity, the coercion subsistence maintenance exists to eliminate at the level of survival; it would create a class of participants who can subsist but can’t participate in the public commons of the configuration they belong to. Amenity access is a participation condition the configuration provides for itself, not a reward for performing the configuration’s preferred forms of activity.

*Structural extraction is actor-neutral.* An institution and an individual can each take a benefit while shifting its cost or risk onto others without adequate justification. That common form does not equalize their power, magnitude, intent, or remedy. The same question must be asked at every scale, with the response left to evidence: what was taken, who bore the cost, what relation made the shift possible, and which intervention can stop it without creating another unanswerable power?

*Corruption is a structural infraction against everyone.* The derivation already established that any arrangement that redirects the shared structure’s maintenance toward a subset’s preferred conditions isn’t maintaining the social structure but the subset’s position within it. Corruption is this failure at the level of the individual officeholder: a person in a position of political maintenance who redirects the shared pool or the direction-setting mechanism for private gain isn’t committing an offense against an abstraction called *government*. The victim is every person whose conditions depend on what was taken: the healthcare not funded, the school not staffed, the infrastructure not built. The resources were drawn from the shared pool that everyone contributes to; their diversion is a direct subtraction from everyone who depends on what they were supposed to maintain. Corruption is cheating in the exact game-theoretic sense: defecting from cooperation while continuing to take its benefits. This is true at every scale. A local official who redirects municipal funds, a legislator who writes rules for a paying client, a regulator who clears the way for an entity they will later work for, each is doing the same structural thing: converting a position of maintenance into a position of private extraction. The social structure they were entrusted to maintain degrades in proportion to what they take.

*Regulatory capture is the same failure operating from outside.* An entity that extracts value from the shared structure while externalizing costs onto it is doing precisely what the derivation identifies as political failure: taking the benefits of the shared structure (infrastructure, educated workers, contract enforcement, currency, stable markets) while offloading the costs of its activity onto others who bear them without compensation. The word “regulation” misleads here, because it sounds like government constraining free activity from above. But if the people control the social structure (which the derivation requires), then regulations are the people collectively setting the terms under which entities operating within the shared structure must operate. Regulation isn’t government versus market. It is the participants in a shared structure deciding what counts as fair participation in something they collectively maintain. An entity that poisons a river to reduce its production costs hasn’t exercised a freedom. It has taken a cost it should bear and placed it on everyone downstream, a structural taking, not a market transaction. The regulation that prevents it is the people enforcing the terms of participation in the structure they share, not an imposition on the entity. Corruption inside government and under-regulation outside it are the same structural failure: the mechanism that is supposed to maintain the shared structure for everyone is used to maintain a subset’s position within it. The only difference is where the capture occurs.

Consider concretely a planning board reviewing a chemical-plant permit upstream of a residential watershed. Two failure modes lead to the same outcome through different mechanisms. *Inside the board:* a board member receives an undisclosed consulting retainer from the applicant and covertly steers the review past the watershed objection. *Outside the board:* the applicant successfully lobbies the legislature to weaken the rule the board enforces, so the rule no longer requires watershed review at all. Different mechanism, same structural result: the downstream community absorbs a cost the applicant should have borne, and an institution whose function is maintenance of the shared structure has been converted into an instrument of private extraction. The first form is illegal in most jurisdictions and the perpetrator can be prosecuted; the second is currently legal in much of the regulatory landscape and the rules themselves get rewritten. They’re treated as one structural infraction with two implementations. Closing one channel without closing the other leaves the failure open.

*Extreme inequality can threaten the social structure itself.* The danger isn’t only deprivation at the bottom. Concentrated wealth can become a threat to everyone where it converts into political direction-setting through campaign finance, lobbying access, media ownership, regulatory capture, or comparable channels. At that point, a subset can direct mechanisms that are supposed to register the direction of all. The threat is predictable where those conversion channels remain open, but concentration alone doesn’t prove that the conversion has occurred. That distinction makes the claim testable. Piketty’s comparative wealth-income series (2014), Piketty, Saez, and Zucman’s distributional national accounts (2018), and related administrative-data work document large changes in ownership and concentration; they don’t make an inequality statistic a definition of extraction. A return on capital above aggregate growth can amplify inherited concentration under specified saving, ownership, taxation, valuation, and transmission conditions, but it is neither necessary nor sufficient for political capture. The stronger prediction is conditional: where durable concentration is converted into unanswerable direction, democratic voice will deteriorate. Stiglitz’s *The Price of Inequality* (2012) develops that political-economy mechanism, while Atkinson’s *Inequality: What Can Be Done?* (2015) develops design alternatives.

*Concentration can threaten the field without purchasing political control.* Capture is one channel: wealth converts into unanswerable direction. A second channel is material. Land, attention, infrastructure, and productive capacity are finite enough that some holdings can narrow what remains available to others even where no campaign contribution or lobbying contact occurs. That observation doesn’t derive a ceiling or make the size of a holding its own verdict. It identifies a further inquiry: did the activity enlarge the shared field, draw a return proportionate to what it added and risked, or secure a scarce position by shifting costs and foreclosing access? A firm, technology, or investment can enlarge the field and justify a very large return; a smaller holding can still be extractive. Because *net contribution* isn’t a ready-made scalar, the conclusion remains diagnostic and evidence-dependent. Capture and material foreclosure are two ways extraction may appear, not two shortcuts around showing it.

*The same test reaches the firm.* Compensation, control, risk, and the benefits of firm performance may be distributed through many architectures: conventional ownership, cooperatives, profit sharing, employee ownership, trusts, or codetermination. Neither one of them nor a permissible pay ratio is derived. The question is whether the arrangement makes contribution and risk visible, leaves workers genuine room to refuse, and prevents control from becoming unanswerable extraction. Mondragón, Lincoln Electric, John Lewis Partnership, Employee Stock Ownership Plans, and German codetermination are comparative cases for that inquiry, not proofs that one architecture follows from the structural premise.

*The classical-liberal economic-tradition objection, engaged directly.* The three objections set out at §6.7.1—Hayek’s knowledge problem (*The Road to Serfdom* 1944; *The Constitution of Liberty* 1960), Friedman’s minimal-state position (*Capitalism and Freedom* 1962), and public-choice on endemic regulatory capture (Buchanan and Tullock, *The Calculus of Consent* 1962, Tullock on rent-seeking)—are each granted their central concession here. Hayek’s knowledge problem is granted at the production side: production isn’t centrally planned, prices aren’t set, and nothing substitutes for the informational function of markets above subsistence; the discretionary economy operates on market mechanisms throughout, and its substantive constraints sit at the participation-conditions foundation and at the ecological substrate (§6.5) rather than at the price-formation contact. Friedman’s preference for cash transfer over bureaucratic provision is granted as a design principle: universal maintenance on the tax-side architecture derived here converges with the negative-income-tax form Friedman defended. Public-choice’s diagnostic on capture is granted in full. It is the foundation of the *Corruption is a structural infraction* and *Regulatory capture is the same failure operating from outside* derivations already given. The parting from the tradition is not on the diagnostic but on the conclusion drawn from it—that the diagnostic licenses minimal regulation rather than dual-channel closure of capture. Both channels are already derived from the same premise: legal closure of the inside channel through anti-corruption enforcement, and structural closure of the outside channel through campaign-finance and lobbying limits. The parting from the classical-liberal tradition is also on what subsistence is: subsistence isn’t redistribution from autonomous market participants but the participation conditions without which the market doesn’t operate as a market among rights-bearing-equals; the same §6.1 derivation that engages Nozick and Hayek at the rights level applies here at the economic-architecture level. There is convergence with the classical-liberal tradition on the price-formation function of markets, the cash-transfer preference over bureaucratic provision, and the structural reality of capture; it parts from the tradition on whether subsistence is the precondition of market participation or a redistribution from it.

Together, these claims fix the participation foundation and the tests applied above it. They do not compose a financial program. Equal standing, effective access, answerability, visible incidence, and protection against domination constrain the field. Tax systems, provider forms, benefit formulas, firm structures, and numerical thresholds remain candidates to be compared within it. The predictions at §6.7.3 state what evidence should look like if the constraints are doing the work claimed.

### 6.7.3 Predictions
The account of economy as recognition-and-distribution infrastructure, read through the structural-extraction derivation, generates predictions that distinguishable empirical patterns should confirm or refute. Each prediction therefore states an observable comparison and a failure condition; the empirical literature is reviewed against them in §6.7.4.

*First.* Reported reliance on public and institutional infrastructure should fall as wealth rises even where objectively measured reliance—use of corporate law, enforceable contracts, currency and payment systems, intellectual-property protection, regulated markets, and publicly formed labor—rises. The test compares reported reliance and tax preferences across wealth groups while holding the relevant institutional exposure constant. The prediction fails if high-stake participants recognize that exposure at least as accurately as lower-stake participants, or if opposition to contribution doesn’t increase once ideology and expected personal incidence are controlled.

*Second.* Where profit-seeking insurance is the primary gate to subsistence coverage, matched systems should show higher administrative cost per covered person, more coverage denials or underinsurance, and weaker access or financial-protection outcomes after differences in population health, prices, and benefit generosity are controlled. The prediction fails where a private or mixed insurance architecture supplies equal or better full-cost access, protection, and outcomes without extracting rents at constitutive vulnerability.

*Third.* In longitudinal or matched-jurisdiction comparisons, greater tolerance of identifiable extraction channels—regulatory capture, uncompensated externalities, monopoly rent, wage theft, corruption, and evasion of proportionate contribution—should predict worse avoidable mortality, mental-health distress, social trust, and civic participation after productivity, demographics, baseline institutions, and prior outcomes are controlled. The causal claim is earned only where changes in those channels precede changes in outcomes or a credible quasi-experiment isolates the mechanism. The prediction fails if the association disappears under those controls or runs in the opposite direction.

*Fourth.* Improvement-inclusive property taxation should, where assessments respond to investment and no offsetting credits or deferrals apply, discourage marginal improvement relative to taxes concentrated on land value; rapidly rising assessments can also burden liquidity-constrained owners. The test compares investment, vacancy, land use, displacement, and revenue stability across matched standard-property, split-rate, and land-value regimes, including transition rules. Not every property tax fails on this account: the prediction fails where improvement disincentives and displacement aren’t observed, or where circuit breakers, deferrals, assessment design, and service benefits offset them without increasing land speculation.

*Fifth.* Where labor’s bargaining and ownership position weakens while productivity rises, median compensation and labor’s income share should grow more slowly than net productivity, with a larger share accruing to profits, top compensation, or capital income. The test must use consistent deflators, distinguish average from median compensation, include benefits, and compare net rather than gross productivity. This isn’t a definitional result: the prediction fails where compensation continues to track productivity under those measures, or where divergence is better explained by depreciation, sector composition, technology, or relative-price changes than by a shift in capture.

*Sixth.* Large reductions in taxes on top incomes or wealth, when not tied to new productive investment, should raise top income shares more reliably than they raise broad employment, median real income, or productivity relative to matched jurisdictions or pre-policy trends. The prediction concerns the policy configuration, not every supply-side reform. It fails where such a change produces durable, broadly distributed gains large enough to offset the foregone contribution and where the pathway from the tax change to those gains is empirically identified.

*Seventh.* Crises should enlarge extraction where emergency discretion, concentrated asset ownership, weak oversight, and public downside guarantees expand together. The test compares excess profits, emergency-contract margins, asset-price gains, and top income or wealth shares with pre-crisis trends and with crises subject to stronger oversight and broad-based transfers. The prediction is conditional, not universal: it fails where crisis policy prevents disproportionate capture or where distributional changes are explained by productivity, sector composition, or temporary valuation effects rather than the named channels.

*Eighth.* Holding wealth magnitude constant, perceived contribution should increase admiration and perceived extraction should reduce it. The appropriate test uses matched survey vignettes, repeated public-opinion measures around identifiable changes in conduct, or comparative reputational data rather than selected biographies alone. The prediction fails if absolute wealth dominates evaluation after contribution, extraction, ideology, publicity, and prior reputation are controlled.

Three further hypotheses carry the same constraints past the aggregate economy: to recoverable capacity, to the firm, and to public safety. They are stated as candidates, and the record reviewed in §6.7.4 bears on them only in part.

A common objection to foundation-and-infrastructure architectures is that they presuppose resources an economy may not have. That objection can’t be answered from structure alone. It predicts where to look: productive capacity alongside unmet foundation needs, gains whose incidence is concentrated, rents, externalized costs, and public inputs whose returns are captured narrowly. Whether enough recoverable capacity exists in any jurisdiction is an empirical question.

The relevant empirical signature is a gap between productive capacity and population access to it. Concentrated gains alongside survival-precarity, productivity growth without corresponding compensation growth, rents in protected sectors, and costs shifted onto workers or the public are evidence to examine. None proves extraction by itself. The inquiry has to identify the contribution, the public or private inputs, the risks borne, the costs displaced, and the destination of the gain. Where that accounting finds extraction, redirection is warranted; where it finds proportionate contribution, the holding is not condemned merely for being large.

*The constraint is closure.* Greater stake in a political economy carries greater responsibility for maintaining the foundation that makes the stake possible. The tax shape therefore runs from greater stake toward greater contribution, never the reverse. That is the derived direction. How steeply it runs, what counts as the base, and how much capacity is available are coefficient questions for evidence and public judgment.

Artificial intelligence sharpens the question because its gains can draw at once on private investment, public research and infrastructure, purchased or licensed data, human labor, and material that was never supplied on negotiated terms. Calling those inputs universal doesn’t settle their ownership, and no dividend is inferred from the technology’s name. Who supplied the inputs, who bore the costs and risks, who can answer for harms, and who captures the gain? If that inquiry finds broadly distributed stake and narrowly captured returns, the closure constraint applies. A dividend, taxation toward the foundation, public investment, negotiated compensation, or a hybrid may answer it. Which one does is an empirical and institutional question.

The diagnosis is structural, not adversarial. None of this requires *billionaires are villains* or *AI is bad*. What is named is a structural mechanism: institutions can permit gains whose costs are shifted outward, whose public inputs go uncounted, or whose control becomes unanswerable. The political community’s task is to close that mechanism, not to punish people merely for occupying the positions it created. The error is in the institutional design; showing that a particular gain is extractive still requires the accounting described above.

A familiar trickle-down claim is also turned here into a testable comparison. If concentrated gains reliably improve the foundation without a specified return channel, that pattern should appear in the incidence data. If they do not, an appeal to eventual diffusion has not supplied the missing mechanism. A different shape is specified here: contribution flows into the political community in proportion to stake, and the political community maintains the foundation. Whether a given design realizes that shape remains to be shown.

The directional image is simple. Contribution flows *into* the political community according to stake; the maintained foundation and shared infrastructure flow back to its participants. Greater stake means greater contribution. Nothing in that shape says what a worker owes, what a billionaire owes, or whether income, wealth, rents, inheritance, consumption, or some mixture supplies the best base. Those are the numbers and instruments that evidence must fill in.

The pathway is at least named. That makes its prediction inspectable: after taxes, transfers, prices, and provider behavior are counted, the foundation should be more secure without the burden being shifted downward. If it is not, the chosen mechanism has failed even if its announced purpose was correct.

How recovered capacity is allocated is underdetermined and is picked through recognized direction. It may strengthen the foundation, reduce contribution demands while preserving it, expand shared investment, fund a dividend, or combine these. Existing dividends and social funds are useful cases, not templates the derivation can generalize without further argument. Only an allocation that recreates the same failure is excluded: an insecure foundation, an inverted burden, hidden incidence, or unanswerable capture.

*Rollout is a design problem under the same constraint.* A transition need not install every mechanism on one day, but it may not protect the eventual foundation by making a disposable class during the move toward it. People displaced by automation, infrastructure change, or the closure of extractive arrangements present an especially clear test because the shared transition has removed conditions on which they relied. That can justify priority protection. It does not prove that one cohort-first sequence is feasible everywhere, or that a pilot should precede universal standing. The destination and the non-abandonment constraint are derived; the path is not.

*The proportional-income firm is a candidate, not a theorem.* The proportionate-stake principle has a firm-level question: how closely do contribution, risk, control, and capture track one another inside the company? A proportional-income firm is one possible answer. The question and the failure conditions are derived here; that architecture isn’t.

The candidate model links part of each participant’s income to collective performance and makes the rule apply at the top as well as the bottom. Its prediction is comparative: when participants can see a credible connection among their contribution, the firm’s performance, and their share, cooperation and recognition should improve without destroying accountability. But contribution is difficult to measure, firm outputs are jointly produced, and incentives can be gamed. The model therefore has to earn its case against alternatives; the convergence theorem does not settle it in advance.

The experiential side supplies a further hypothesis. Mutual recognition is derived (§5.14) as constitutive of being the kind of subject political life consists in; the deepest registration of meaning is located (§5.10) in orientations bearing on persistence and thriving. At firm scale, a wide and unanswerable divergence among contribution, return, risk, and voice should make participants more likely to experience themselves as labor inputs rather than as participants in the arrangement. The cog-in-the-machine experience may then be evidence of a real structural relation rather than merely a private complaint. It isn’t infallible: the contribution and the experience both need independent evidence.

The diagnostic here converges with the diagnostic portion of Marx’s alienation theory, not with Marx’s premises or prescriptions. Marx identified, from different premises, the same structural pattern derived at §5: alienation from the product of labor, from the labor process, from species-being, and from other workers names a structural-recognition-failure the mutual-recognition commitments (§5) derive on independent grounds. The diagnostic territory is shared; the dialectical materialism, the class-warfare logic, the revolutionary prescription, and the abolition of markets aren’t. The alienation diagnosis is confirmed here as a structural observation, while declining the surrounding doctrine. The honest accounting is to name the convergence rather than to obscure it.

The flip side is a prediction. Where participants have credible voice and a defensible share in gains they help produce, work should be less likely to register as mere use. That can be tested across cooperatives, profit-sharing firms, employee ownership, codetermination, trusts, and conventional firms. A secure foundation outside the firm makes exit less coercive. What happens inside still depends on governance, measurement, bargaining power, and the actual distribution of risk and return.

Mondragón, Lincoln Electric, the John Lewis Partnership, Employee Stock Ownership Plans, and German codetermination supply different comparison cases. They vary too much in ownership, governance, compensation, legal setting, and selection effects to count as one confirmation. The useful question is narrower: which arrangements make voice, risk, contribution, and return track one another more closely, and with what effects on productivity, resilience, pay dispersion, retention, and worker freedom? Those answers belong to comparative evidence, not to the derivation.

What is carried to the firm is a constraint, not a pay formula: labor, capital, risk, control, and public support must all be counted, and none may disappear from the account merely because one party already holds the governing power. Cooperatives, profit sharing, employee ownership, trusts, codetermination, conventional compensation, and hybrids are candidates. A large pay ratio is a reason to inspect the account, not proof by itself that the account fails. The failure is unanswerable capture: return or control that can’t be defended by the contributions, risks, costs, and dependencies that produced it.

The architecture is predicted to reduce several within-firm mechanisms contributing to the gender pay gap, not to close them automatically. Transparent contribution bands can reduce negotiation-based differences, title accumulation, and unequal pay for comparable work; broad-based profit sharing can also widen the stake captured by workers. But a contribution metric can reproduce gender-coded valuation, biased performance assessment, occupational sorting, unequal assignments, and promotion barriers unless those inputs are separately constrained and tested. Blau and Kahn’s surveys (e.g., 2017) treat the pay gap as multi-causal, and no compensation architecture makes the unexplained remainder disappear by definition. The earned claim is therefore comparative: against an otherwise matched discretionary-pay system, a transparent and independently reviewed proportionate-contribution system should reduce specified within-firm gaps without reducing performance or retention. If it doesn’t, or if its measurement imports the same discounting under a new label, the architecture fails this prediction.

The inquiry does, however, force a question current arrangements often hide: how is contribution being measured? Market compensation is evidence about scarcity and bargaining, but it is not a neutral readout of contribution. It can also carry historical discounting, occupational segregation, unequal bargaining power, and network effects. A candidate architecture can’t answer the question by renaming the prevailing wage its contribution metric. It must defend what the metric counts, what it misses, and how affected participants can contest it. Constructing that metric is a design problem exposed here rather than solved.

Comparable-worth scoring, activity-based measures, role tiers with collective bonuses, and negotiated profit sharing are possible instruments. Each measures a different thing and can hide a different error. The tests supplied here: the metric must be public enough to contest, sensitive to forms of contribution the old arrangement discounted, and corrigible when its predictions fail. Evidence must decide whether any particular method narrows unjustified disparities without creating worse distortions.

Above the constraint, markets may still coordinate prices, hiring, investment, and movement among firms. They do not guarantee that a bad metric will be competed away: exit can be costly, employers can share the same distortion, and information can remain hidden. Nor does public specification guarantee a good metric. Neither laissez-faire correction nor a central pay formula is therefore committed to. It requires contestable rules, real exit, visible incidence, and revision against outcomes.

Nothing in the constraint abolishes performance judgment, promotion, removal, role changes, or variable pay. It changes the burden: those practices must be answerable, and their measures must be open to challenge. No architecture removes bias or capture by definition. Its claim is earned only if the observed arrangement reduces them while preserving the work the firm must do.

Components of the gender pay gap that arise upstream of the firm aren’t closed by firm-level architecture alone. Four causes require treatment beyond compensation architecture: occupational segregation, the motherhood penalty, gender-coded educational steering, and workplace harassment and discrimination. Education (§6.9) addresses capacity-building without gender steering. Healthcare (§6.10) addresses caregiving infrastructure. Justice (§6.13) addresses anti-discrimination enforcement. The household-configuration passage that follows addresses whether survival dependence makes labor configuration a genuine choice. The gap is a multi-domain pattern, so the response must be tested across domains rather than declared complete in any one of them.

The same test therefore has to reach more than one scale: economy, firm, household, and community. A foundation at the political-economic level can coexist with extraction inside a firm; the first doesn’t cancel the second. Applying the contribution, answerability, and genuine-exit tests at firm scale is what keeps convergence from remaining merely aspirational.

*Welfare is also crime policy.* Healthcare, housing, nutrition, early-childhood support, education, and treatment for addiction and mental illness don’t merely compete with crime and safety spending. They can change conditions under which theft, violence, neglect, or domination becomes more likely or appears locally rational to a person whose options have narrowed. An untreated psychosis, an unsheltered person in winter, a child whose first five years lacked a reliable adult, a community whose nearest work is hours away: these can be upstream contributors to cases police and courts later receive. The categories therefore overlap without becoming identical. Which investment prevents which harm, and at what rate, remains an empirical question developed further at §6.13.

A secure foundation should reduce a stratum of derivative anxieties. Its effects are predictions, not definitions. If access to care, shelter, food, education, and security is reliable through job loss, illness, caregiving, old age, or a failed venture, fewer people should have to privately insure every transition against ruin. More household and work arrangements should become live options. Exit from an employer or partner should become less dangerous. Productive risk should become less confined to people already able to absorb failure. These gains can be measured, and a nominal benefit that disappears through prices, waiting lists, debt, eligibility cliffs, or provider capture has not secured the foundation. Markets and private providers may operate above or within it; whether they do so well is an empirical question. The structural claim is only that survival may not depend on accepting one otherwise-refusable arrangement.

### 6.7.4 Confirmation
The predictions at §6.7.3 are matched against an existing body of empirical and theoretical literature. The question is how far the record supports them.

*Confirmation standard.* Descriptive association supplies provisional support; longitudinal and matched comparisons test temporal order and rival explanations; quasi-experimental designs can support a causal mechanism; replicated findings across jurisdictions establish transportability. No single correlation or illustrative case counts as causal confirmation. The language that follows tracks those levels, and heterogeneous or contrary findings count against a prediction rather than being treated as exceptions by definition.

*First.* Wealthy under-recognition of reliance isn’t yet directly confirmed. Bartels (2008), Page, Bartels, and Seawright (2013), and Gilens and Page (2014) document preference divergence and disproportionate political responsiveness at the top of the distribution. Those findings support the political-influence part of the account, but a preference for lower taxation doesn’t by itself measure whether a respondent misperceives institutional reliance. Direct confirmation requires pairing reported reliance with objective exposure to contracts, corporate law, public research, currency, infrastructure, and workforce formation. The present record is therefore suggestive, not decisive, on Prediction 1.

*Second.* Insurance-substitution pathologies receive comparative support, with causal scope still limited. Akerlof (1970) and Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976) establish the information problems analytically; they don’t by themselves show that any particular public design will outperform. US administrative-cost, underinsurance, medical-debt, and cross-national health-system comparisons show higher spending with weaker performance on several access, equity, and outcome measures. That pattern supports Prediction 2, but countries differ in prices, provider markets, population health, benefit design, and regulation, so the record doesn’t isolate private insurance as the sole cause. The evidence supports the narrower claim that profit-seeking insurance at the foundation can generate the predicted pathologies and must be compared on full-system outcomes, not the universal claim that every private or mixed architecture does so.

The mechanism behind the aggregate pattern is concrete at the level of a single participant. Consider a person with type-1 diabetes in a market that permits health-status underwriting—the pre-2014 US individual market, or any regime without guaranteed issue and community rating. The insurer’s underwriting models them as a high-cost participant and prices them accordingly: premiums, deductibles, and coverage limits are set to recover expected payouts plus a margin. Where underwriting on health status is prohibited, as it is in ACA-regulated markets, cost and access may still be sorted through deductible and out-of-pocket design, formulary tiering, narrow networks, or prior authorization. Those instruments can perform legitimate functions—managing utilization, negotiating prices, coordinating care, and preserving a risk pool—or they can operate chiefly by moving cost and nonaccess toward chronically ill participants. The provider-neutral test asks which function a design is actually performing and what its full-system outcomes are. A private insurer that pools risk and administers care without making the foundation unreachable can satisfy it; a public program can fail through scarcity, exclusion, or administrative breakdown. The charge is therefore not that private provision or profit adds nothing. It is that a margin earned through avoidable denial, opaque sorting, or cost shifting isn’t justified merely by calling the mechanism insurance.

*Third.* Extraction tolerance correlates with several forms of aggregate suffering, but the causal inference remains partial. Wilkinson and Pickett (2009) report cross-national associations between inequality and multiple social outcomes; Case and Deaton (2020) document rising deaths of despair in the United States; Mullainathan and Shafir (2013) and Haushofer and Fehr (2014) identify mechanisms through which scarcity affects cognition and action. These findings are consistent with Prediction 3, but inequality isn’t identical to extraction tolerance, and cross-sectional association doesn’t isolate the political-community-failure mechanism. The prediction is provisionally supported; causal confirmation requires longitudinal or quasi-experimental evidence connecting changes in identified extraction channels to subsequent outcomes.

*Fourth.* Property-tax design produces mixed, mechanism-specific evidence. Henry George’s *Progress and Poverty* (1879) and the Henry George theorem supply an analytic case for separating land value from improvement value. Empirical work on split-rate and land-value taxation supports the possibility of reducing the marginal penalty on improvements, while studies of assessment increases and tax delinquency identify liquidity pressure for some fixed-income owners. The evidence doesn’t establish that every standard property tax produces displacement or speculation: assessment rules, service benefits, deferrals, circuit breakers, supply constraints, and transition design matter. Prediction 4 is supported only in the conditional form stated in §6.7.3 and remains open to reversal where those mechanisms are absent or offset.

The comparison does not yield a categorical verdict on either base. A standard property tax may discourage improvements or strain a cash-poor owner, but it may also finance local services, reach otherwise hidden wealth, or offset benefits capitalized into property values. A land-value tax may capture part of a collectively produced location value while reducing the marginal penalty on improvement, but assessment, transition, development incentives, and incidence still matter. The derived shape asks whether greater stake contributes more toward the foundation without shifting the burden downward. Evidence decides which base, or mixture of bases, realizes that shape under local conditions.

The contrast is concrete in two adjacent parcels in a city neighborhood. The first holds a single-family home whose owner has improved it over twenty years: a new roof, a finished basement, an updated kitchen, a carefully tended garden. The second holds a similar plot the owner has held vacant, waiting for the surrounding neighborhood’s improvement to raise its resale value. Under standard property tax, the improving owner pays more each year than the speculating owner, even though the speculating owner is capturing infrastructure-driven appreciation without contributing back. Under land-value taxation, both parcels are taxed on the value of the land (the value the schools, transit, regulatory protections, and surrounding neighbors have created), and the improvements the first owner made aren’t penalized. The improving owner’s bill drops; the speculating owner’s bill rises to match what the land has already captured from collective investment. Same neighborhood, same tax dollars in aggregate, different distribution of who pays what, and the difference tracks its distinction between value created by collective investment and value created by individual contribution.

*Fifth.* The distributional divergence is real under several measures, but a mechanical extraction claim isn’t. Piketty, Saez, and Zucman’s distributional national accounts (2018) document strong divergence in income growth across the US distribution. Autor, Dorn, Katz, Patterson, and Van Reenen’s firm-level work on superstar firms (2020) links part of the labor-share decline to rising concentration. And Stansbury and Summers’s primary analysis of productivity and pay (2017) finds divergence between productivity and typical compensation—while also finding that productivity growth still transmits to compensation, and that measurement choices (net versus gross productivity, average versus median pay, benefits, and deflators) change the size and timing of the gap. Bebchuk and Fried (2004) document executive-compensation mechanisms that can disconnect pay from performance. Together the record supports the observable distributional pattern and several capture mechanisms, not the claim that every productivity-pay gap is extraction by definition. Prediction 5 is supported where the consistent-measure gap remains and the destination and mechanism of the displaced share are identified.

*Sixth.* The tested top-tax-cut configuration receives comparatively strong contrary evidence. Hope and Limberg (2022) examine major tax cuts for the rich across 18 OECD countries over five decades and find higher top income shares without significant aggregate growth or employment effects. Romer and Romer (2010) and related tax-shock studies show that growth effects depend on the kind, timing, and financing of a tax change; the IMF comparative record also shows that progressive tax-and-transfer systems can coexist with growth. This supports Prediction 6 for large untargeted top-end tax cuts. It doesn’t show that every supply-side measure fails, and the prediction remains reversible if a specific reform produces identified, durable, broadly distributed gains net of its fiscal cost.

*Seventh.* Crisis-period distribution is heterogeneous rather than uniformly extractive. Asset-price recoveries after 2008 and 2020 generated large gains for households holding concentrated financial wealth, and emergency procurement and rescue programs created identifiable capture opportunities. But broad transfers, wage support, unemployment insurance, and temporary regulation also reduced or reversed disposable-income inequality in some jurisdictions and periods. The evidence therefore supports the conditional mechanism in Prediction 7—weak oversight plus concentrated asset exposure plus socialized downside—not the original universal claim that crisis accumulation must exceed its steady-state rate. Comparative event studies across different crisis responses are required for causal confirmation.

*Eighth.* The biographies illustrate the recognition hypothesis but don’t confirm it. Carnegie’s reputation changed across the Homestead and library-foundation phases; Rockefeller, MacKenzie Scott, Chuck Feeney, and Yvon Chouinard provide further cases in which visible contribution and public regard appear together. Selected cases can’t hold wealth, publicity, ideology, prior reputation, and extraction history constant, and contrary cases may be omitted by selection. The record is suggestive. Direct confirmation requires matched survey or experimental evidence showing that perceived contribution changes admiration while wealth magnitude is held fixed.

*Convergent feasibility and association: the shared-conditions record.* The comparative cases show that strong foundations and market economies can coexist and that several predicted outcomes move together. They establish feasibility and convergent association, not by themselves the causal sufficiency of the framework.

*The Nordic countries.* Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden consistently rank at or near the top of the World Happiness Report (Helliwell, Layard, and Sachs 2020, and annually since 2012), the Human Development Index, and cross-national measures of social trust and institutional confidence. They also maintain market economies alongside comparatively strong social foundations. That combination establishes feasibility and matches the predicted association: securing a foundation needn’t crowd out industry, and the conditions named here can move together. It doesn’t show that the foundation alone caused the outcomes, that every relevant threshold is met, or that the same institutional package transports unchanged. The cases matter because the coexistence is real, not because four countries complete the causal argument.

*Costa Rica.* Costa Rica’s long investment in education and health alongside the abolition of its standing army is a useful comparative case. Its outcomes can’t be assigned to that choice alone, and regional rankings vary by measure and year. The case supports inquiry into whether sustained social investment can secure participation conditions at modest income levels; it does not by itself confirm the framework or supply a transferable budget.

*Germany: the social market economy and Bismarckian social insurance.* Germany’s *Soziale Marktwirtschaft* was explicitly designed as a foundation-plus-market architecture, with the Bismarckian social insurance system (originating 1883, Hennock 2007) as the oldest surviving example of collective pooling structured around contribution and universal coverage.

*Bhutan: Gross National Happiness.* Bhutan’s GNH index illustrates a national-accounting attempt to track what members are able to be and do rather than treating output alone as the measure of success. It is a neighboring design, not independent confirmation that this account has selected the right dimensions or weights.

*The World Happiness Report findings.* The report’s cross-national models associate life evaluation with several variables the present account derives as conditions of maximum possibility under necessities met: income sufficient for material security, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom to make life choices, generosity, and confidence in public institutions. Their joint predictive contribution is evidence that these aren’t decorative additions to a prior notion of happiness: populations’ own evaluations vary with the shared conditions the account identifies. Because the models are observational and the variables interact, this record confirms the predicted association and the practical relevance of the conditions; it doesn’t by itself establish that any one variable is independently sufficient or reproduce the book’s first-principles derivation.

Finance and credit depend on public law and can generate systemic risk, discrimination, and rents. They also supply liquidity, screening, payments, maturity transformation, and risk allocation. The evidence supports regulation and accountability, not the conclusion that all private financial returns are capture of a public function.

*Divergence.* The evidence reviewed here bears against specified empirical claims: that large untargeted top-end tax cuts reliably produce broad gains, that private insurance necessarily lowers total administrative burden, or that market prices by themselves reveal every public input and shifted cost. It does not empirically refute a moral entitlement theory, because that dispute turns on premises about property and obligation. Nozick’s pre-political premise is rejected here for reasons given in the derivation; evidence then tests the consequences of the institutional shapes that follow. Keeping those disputes separate prevents a policy result from being written as a metaphysical proof, or a moral disagreement as a failed forecast.

### 6.7.5 Conclusions
The implications of the derivation for institutional design are a shape and a set of constraints, not a financial program. Contribution runs from greater stake in the shared arrangement toward maintenance of the participation foundation. A design must also keep its burdens visible and protect participation against domination and cost shifting. The derivation does not supply rates, thresholds, bases, or an institutional mix. Those coefficients belong to the comparative evidence examined in §6.7.3–6.7.4 and remain revisable with it.

*Financing constraint.* An acceptable design must secure the foundation, and greater stake in the arrangement must carry greater contribution toward doing so. That direction is derived. Its numerical expression is not. Reliance on shared institutions, ability to bear a contribution, benefit received, rents, harms, and market power help determine whether a proposed instrument preserves the shape in practice. Flat and graduated rates, capital-gains treatment, inheritance rules, exemptions, and anti-avoidance measures must therefore be tested by incidence: who finally bears the burden, and whether the result maintains the foundation without domination or concealed cost shifting. No instrument is validated by its political label, but no design that reverses the contribution direction satisfies the constraint.

Intergenerational non-domination is the matching legacy constraint. An acceptable inheritance, trust, foundation, endowment, or other posthumous vehicle may carry resources, works, and proposed directions forward; it may not make a deceased holder’s direction unanswerable to the living subjects whose conditions it governs. Designs must preserve revision, accountability, and recognized direction among those affected. This leaves ordinary family provision intact and leaves multiple estate and philanthropic architectures open. It precludes the limit case in which legal persistence converts a finite person’s former ownership into indefinite political authority.

*Non-substitutability of the foundation.* A nominal benefit does not satisfy the right if price, exclusion, denial, or administrative failure leaves the needed condition unreachable. That is a constraint on outcomes and access, not on provider identity. Public, private, mutual, nonprofit, regulated, or mixed provision may qualify if the foundation remains universal, adequate, answerable, and independent of a person’s ability to pay at the point of need. The derivation does not preclude private insurance or establish public provision merely by naming either form.

*Adequacy is concrete and bounded.* The foundation has to meet the actual conditions of participation where a person lives; a nominal amount that can’t secure them is not adequate. Costs vary by place, household, time, and circumstance, so no number can be stated here. Nor does the foundation entail public provision of every preferred holding. It reaches what participation requires and stops where discretionary choice begins. Drawing that boundary and selecting the evidence used to update it are administrative and political tasks open to revision, not deductions from the structural argument.

*Extraction is tested symmetrically.* An arrangement fails when an actor can shift costs or risks onto others while keeping the corresponding benefit and escaping answerability. The actor may be an institution, officeholder, firm, intermediary, provider, or claimant. Similar structure does not make the cases equal: magnitude, power, intent, incidence, and remedy still have to be established. Regulation, taxation, transparency, enforcement, competition, or institutional redesign may answer a demonstrated failure. The failure and the test are identified here; evidence selects the remedy.

Protection runs in two directions. Smith’s *proportion to the revenue which they respectively enjoy under the protection of the state* (Bk V Ch 2) has been read almost exclusively from the wealth side: more assets, more protection, more contribution owed. The symmetry is completed by reading the same phrase from the other end.
