Ordinary participants are also protected, but on a different axis: not in their assets primarily, but *from extraction by those whose stake is larger*. Labor law, consumer protection, antitrust enforcement, regulatory foundations, public courts that don’t run on who can pay better lawyers, antifraud institutions at institutional scale, housing protections from real-estate consolidation, and healthcare not tied to employer leverage each close an avenue through which large-stake actors could otherwise extract from small-stake actors. The wealthy contribute proportionately more because more of *their stake* is protected; ordinary participants receive proportionately more because more of *their not-being-extracted-from* is protected. The two readings are the same protection-relation observed from opposite ends.

This also turns the protection axis into an evaluative dimension, not a single metric. How effectively a small-stake participant is protected from extraction is part of what the political arrangement delivers. A society in which labor law is captured, consumer protection gutted, antitrust dormant, and regulatory capture licensed is delivering less even when nominal infrastructure (roads, schools, courts) is unchanged. The dimensions won’t always move together, so their incidence must be examined rather than collapsed into one score. What the account establishes is that protection from extraction belongs in the evaluation at all.

*Legacy un-inversion gives the title thesis an economic application.* A tax design can reduce the return to extraction without capping what anyone contributes. The sources-of-taxes principle supplies that direction; it does not supply a marginal-rate schedule, and progressive taxation by itself does not make accumulated wealth an asymptote. The narrower inversion survives: admiration can track what a person generated for the shared foundation rather than treating the size of what they retained as the achievement. Honor of that kind is non-rivalrous—remembering one contribution does not prevent another from being remembered—even though the resources and institutions through which contributions are made remain finite.

The greatness-drive therefore need not be suppressed; its object can change. Institutions can stop using accumulation as their only public score and make contribution easier to see and honor. Legacy, on this reading, joins the opening and closing claims across a lifetime rather than a single balance sheet: success is recoupled to contribution “where admiration actually follows,” and a society is measured “not by the height the highest reached but by what held the lowest.” The individual-scale mirror is concrete: ask what a life added to the foundation, not only how high its private pile became. Tax design can help separate those measures. It can’t determine whom a society will admire.

The pattern is already half-true historically: Salk’s declining to patent the polio vaccine was declining to convert generated subsistence into a pile, and it is exactly that refusal, not the vaccine alone, that the historical record reveres him for. The guardrail needed here is the same one needed everywhere a metric risks becoming a target: legacy has to stay plural and adjudicated only in the long run, never collapsed into a single “most subsistence ever generated” leaderboard, which would reintroduce the arbiter and Goodhart problem the design-target result already given was built to preclude, one level removed.

*Power, legacy, and the redirection orientation.* Legacy survives the account developed here, pointed at maintenance. It is not the dead person’s survival but the continuation of that person’s effects through the subjects and structures that remain (§5.9). Wealth gives that ordinary human continuation-pressure exceptional reach. Insofar as a holding confers durable control, it functions as stored direction: the capacity to determine which projects continue, which institutions bear a name, which descendants receive command, and how many other subjects’ conditions remain affected after the originating holder is gone. The political question is therefore not whether wealthy people may leave a legacy. Everyone leaves effects. It is what kind of continuation the accumulated reach is made to carry.

Four forms come apart. *Monumental legacy* preserves the name. *Dynastic legacy* preserves a lineage’s command. *Controlling legacy* preserves the founder’s preferences through institutions able to direct living subjects without remaining answerable to them. *Generative legacy* converts accumulated reach into conditions through which future subjects can form and pursue directions of their own. The distinction isn’t between private and public giving as labels: a privately founded hospital can be generative, and a nominally public institution can become controlling. The test is what the arrangement does to the field and who can revise it. A legacy is generative insofar as it widens the possibilities of the living without requiring the living to remain governed by the will of the dead.

That test separates inheritance without treating family care as a defect. Passing shelter, education, security, or discretionary room to a child can continue the parental work identified at §5.9: sustaining a new center of possibility. Passing unaccountable control over unrelated subjects is a different operation. Philanthropy divides the same way. Relief, research, education, art, and infrastructure can remain genuine contributions regardless of whose name they bear; a foundation becomes politically problematic where the gift’s legal shell preserves unilateral priority-setting after the giver can no longer participate in the reciprocal recognition by which priorities are corrected. Contribution may outlast the contributor. Command can’t acquire legitimacy merely by outlasting its author.

The deepest registration of meaning was located (§5.10) in orientations that bear on persistence and thriving. At the scale where one person’s decisions affect many people’s conditions at once, maintenance of those conditions is among the most far-reaching orientations available. *What better way to be remembered than as the one who contributed the most possible to society?* The question is an invitation, not a prediction that every powerful person must find their deepest meaning there. It offers a way to redirect resources already in motion without treating the holder or the economic system as an enemy. Capitalism figures here as one structure under examination, not as the target named in advance. Protection of others can converge with legacy and meaning; whether it moves a particular person remains open.

The miracle-impulse relocates without deflation. What earlier framings attributed to divine intervention names a category of relief whose felt force is unchanged when its source is relocated: curing the sick, feeding the hungry, lifting the broken. Resources oriented toward maintenance can deliver such relief at scale, within the limits of knowledge, institutions, and the resources actually available. The impulse the tradition named was real, and the relief it points toward is real. What changes is the agent and the practical burden of choosing where finite help can do the most.

Power is nothing without an affect. A position that touches no lives isn’t power but inert holding; meaning has already been located where the touching happens, and power, on the same account, is the capacity to land such touches at scale. There is a kind of power that allows its affects to enjoy the wielder’s having it. The people touched by such power don’t merely tolerate the position: they reach for it, are glad it exists, wouldn’t unmake it even if unmaking were on offer. The miracle-impulse, the legacy-impulse, and the redirection-orientation all name forms of this kind of power. The legacy a position of power leaves is the kind its affects would protect.

*Benevolence inverts.* This inverts a long-standing picture of benevolence. Generosity, welfare, and care for strangers are usually framed as virtues directed outward, extensions of the self toward others who lie beyond its proper concern. The argument reverses the direction. A person isn’t sealed off from the conditions around them; the strangers whose conditions they help maintain are part of the world that keeps them alive. Benevolence was never extension but maintenance: what felt like reaching outward was the self recognizing how far its own conditions reach. Healthcare for the uninsured, housing for the unhoused, education for other people’s children: these aren’t acts of reaching past the self. They are acts of tending to the self, whose borders turn out to include more than the skin suggested.

*Subjects subsist one another.* Run intransitively, *to subsist* names what each subject does individually: continue to exist. Run transitively, in the form the argument requires, the verb names what subjects do to one another: act on one another to keep one another in being. *Humanity is a subsistence: the noun-form of what the verb already names.* The chapter root calls this *Subsistence*: humanity is the singular kind of collective entity that mutual subsisting constitutes, the way *a community* or *a commonwealth* names a kind of singular entity its constitutive activity makes. The fund is contributed to by everyone, distributed to everyone, structurally guaranteed to each as a condition of being part of the configuration. The state apparatus is the vehicle of mutual subsistence, not its agent. Subjects aren’t subsisted by the government. They subsist one another through the mechanism the government provides. Grammar carries the structural fact: there is no asymmetric agent and patient, no benefactor and beneficiary, no giver and receiver. There are co-subsisters doing the same thing to one another.

*The providential function relocates.* Here the inversion applies to a political object. Classical theism projected the providential relation upward: God provides. Applied consistently to its own derivation, the argument returns the function to where it actually structurally lives: *the mutual subsistence of subjects*. Same providential structure, different subject. The providence the tradition was tracking was real (a person’s continuing existence depends on conditions no one person produces, conditions that arrive from elsewhere and that one neither earns each morning nor can secure single-handedly), but the mistake was placing those conditions outside the political community. They are inside it. What benevolence-inverts named at the level of the individual agent, that the strangers whose conditions one helps maintain are part of what keeps one alive, *subjects subsist one another* names at the level of the structure: the community provides those conditions, member to member, through the institutions it maintains. The longing to be taken care of is answered by the fact that the community already does, when it is organized to. Subjects don’t receive subsistence from above. They subsist one another.

*Neighbors.* The legacy reframe concerns the very wealthy, and it takes nothing from what they built: no claim is made that historic accumulators—a Carnegie, a Rockefeller, a Musk, a Bezos—didn’t accomplish anything at scale. What is disputed is whether further accumulation by itself adds to that accomplishment or just enlarges the holding. Andrew Carnegie’s *The Gospel of Wealth* (1889) made the distinction from inside great wealth, and his libraries, universities, and other public works put it into practice. The Giving Pledge places a similar legacy-versus-accumulation choice inside the contemporary billionaire class. Neither example proves a motive, a tax schedule, or a universal status response. They show that contribution can remain a recognizable measure of success even when retained wealth stops being the measure.

The positive theory of success follows. Success survives intact, recoupled to contribution rather than abolished. The image is reciprocal flow: productive activity feeds the system, the system feeds back, proportionally, with substantial returns to the productive actor and a significant flow to collective investment, simultaneously. Taxation functions here as the feedback mechanism itself, not a cost extracted from earnings. The image has a deep lineage: Quesnay’s *Tableau économique* (1758) first formally modeled the economy as circular flow; Marshall and Schumpeter develop the structure dynamically; Ford’s 1914 five-dollar day is its supply-side proof of concept (Ford roughly doubled wages and the company expanded faster, not slower). Under proportionate-to-stake contribution, higher earnings literally mean higher collective investment, so the chronic critique of capitalism (*the more successful you are, the more you take from society*) inverts into its opposite. A precision: the feeding-loop image lands cleanly for genuinely value-creating activity (entrepreneurship, manufacturing, services, scientific work). It doesn’t legitimize extractive activity disguised as productive: rent-seeking, externality-shifting, regulatory arbitrage, monopoly extraction remain structural extraction whatever the actor’s self-description. Recognition follows from contribution per the derivation (§5.14): current resentment of billionaires structurally consists in failure-of-mutual-recognition at scale, not resentment of wealth as such. Smith made this side explicit (*The Theory of Moral Sentiments* 1759, part I, section III, ch. 2): *to deserve, to acquire, and to enjoy the respect and admiration of mankind, are the great objects of ambition and emulation.* *Wealth of Nations* Bk V Ch 2 grounds the contribution mechanism; *Theory of Moral Sentiments* grounds the recognition payoff. The empirical pattern matches the derivation, as §6.7.4 documents: wealthy contributors are widely admired, wealthy extractors widely resented, and the same individual can move from one category to the other across the arc of a career.

And the yacht stays within the permissible field. Is this communism in disguise? It isn’t. The economic form of the worry is settled here; the tradition-level form of it, where Marxism is met as a body of theory rather than as a set of economic prescriptions, is taken up as a departure at §6.14. The framework doesn’t prohibit discretionary above-foundation holdings—a yacht, mansion, art collection, second house, personal jet, or wine cellar—or infer their confiscation from their names. Their acquisition, use, transfer, and inheritance remain answerable to the same contribution, incidence, and non-domination constraints as other holdings.

What is actually adjusted versus left alone separates cleanly:

| Adjusted | Left alone |
| --- | --- |
| Returns traceable to extraction rather than contribution | Permissibility of personal holdings above the sufficiency foundation |
| Mechanisms that invert burdens or preserve unanswerable control | Personal use, enjoyment, and transfer within the contribution and non-domination constraints |
| Extraction patterns at every scale (institutional and individual) | The yacht. The mansion. The Picasso. |

On the account of property used here, a contribution proportionate to the institutions protecting and enabling a holding isn’t classified as expropriation. That conclusion is exactly as strong as the account it rests on. Property here is stewardship over collective-investment output rather than a pre-political holding the polity merely respects (§6.13). A reader who declines that premise will see a transfer and will be reasoning correctly from a different account of property; what the section owes them is the argument for its premise, not the assurance that nothing moves. Nor does the claim say that no one is worse off than under present arrangements: incidence changes, transition costs, and a redrawn line between holding and stewardship all fall somewhere, and these proposals put them there.

The class-warfare deflection is the load-bearing political move. Progressive-taxation framings have a chronic vulnerability: sliding into class-resentment politics where “the rich pay more” becomes “the rich deserve worse,” and tacit license follows for vandalism, sabotage, and rhetoric of personal destruction. The collective-investment frame forecloses that slide *at the derivation level*. The same logic that grounds proportionate-to-stake contribution also grounds the wrongness of property destruction in §6.13 (Justice), on the same premises, at the same time. There is no line of derivation within this framework that gets to “stick it to the rich” as policy or practice. The cross-domain consistency is what makes the framework politically distinctive among progressive frameworks: it is unusable as a class-warfare lever by construction.

A further objection runs: “I could protect my own stuff with private security and contracts.” Private security operates within a legal system that recognizes property, prosecutes theft, and enforces contracts. Private contracts likewise rely on courts or other institutions whose decisions the surrounding order will recognize, alongside currency stability, banking, infrastructure, and a trained workforce. Private alternatives can be additive within that infrastructure; they don’t show that the protected stake is independent of it. An opt-out claim therefore has to identify which shared conditions it can actually replace rather than merely purchase within.

*The public case for extractive accumulation is self-undermining.* Legacy, safety, and status all depend on a social field no private holding creates alone. Where accumulation degrades that field—by shifting costs, purchasing unanswerable direction, or withdrawing support from the conditions on which others depend—it can erode the audience, security, and freely given regard invoked to justify it. That is a conditional argument against extraction, not a claim that every large fortune produces isolation or that wealth supplies no private safety, status, or choice. The case turns on the demonstrated mechanism and its incidence. Contribution can support both a large holding and the field around it; extraction makes the two diverge.

Income and well-being don’t display one universal saturation point. Kahneman and Deaton (2010) reported a plateau in experienced well-being under their measure; Killingsworth (2021) found continuing gains above that income; and the Killingsworth, Kahneman, and Mellers (2023) adversarial collaboration reconciled the results by finding a flattening chiefly among the least-happy group, while well-being continued to rise with log income for many others. The evidence therefore doesn’t support the categorical claim that resources past a finite threshold cease to improve felt experience, or that the richest and the merely comfortable must report the same quality of life. What it supports is narrower: income has heterogeneous and often diminishing marginal associations with well-being, and an additional private benefit doesn’t by itself establish that the mechanism producing it is contributive or that its externalized costs are justified. The structural case against extraction stands or falls on contribution, incidence, and effect on the shared field, not on a disputed universal happiness ceiling.

The descendant case presents the same comparison. An inheritance depends on banking, currency, jurisdiction, and the inheriting party’s continued standing; investment in a healthy society supports the wider conditions within which any inheritance remains usable. Neither is a complete substitute for the other. The structural claim is narrower: provision for descendants doesn’t exempt a holding from contributing to the institutions that make the provision durable or from the non-domination constraint on posthumous control.

*Once lifestyle is held fixed, the mechanisms can be compared.* No universal saturation threshold was established. But two holdings can fund materially similar lives while having been built through very different relations to the shared field. One may expand what others can reach; another may capture a larger share of what the field already produced or shift its costs outward. Holding lifestyle constant doesn’t make mechanism the only morally relevant variable, but it keeps private consumption from answering the institutional question by itself. The comparison still turns on contribution, risk, cost, incidence, and effect on the field—not on an assumed ceiling in felt well-being.

*The fortress can subtract from the one who builds it.* Private security, gated enclosure, and other forms of insulation can preserve options within the enclosure while reducing a holder’s practical access to the shared life outside it. Economics names part of this chase *positional goods* (Hirsch, *Social Limits to Growth* 1976): goods whose value depends on others lacking them. At social scale, Reich’s *secession of the successful* (Reich 1991) and Lasch’s *revolt of the elites* (1995) describe withdrawal from public goods on which everyone else still depends. The effect isn’t an inverse quantitative law between wealth and freedom. It is a risk to *real freedom* (Van Parijs, *Real Freedom for All* 1995): insulation can buy formal options while making parts of the shared field less usable, including for the person who withdrew from it.

Each justification therefore points back at the field rather than away from it. Accumulation can deliver optionality, insulation, position, provision for descendants, and sometimes power over others. Those are real goods, and naming them is more honest than pretending every additional holding is either socially useless or automatically contributive. The public question is whether securing them depends on asymmetric protection, shifted costs, or unanswerable direction—the exception to self-interest/morality convergence identified at §5.14.5 and §5.14.3, and the threat to democratic voice developed at §6.3. Where that mechanism is shown, the justification fails on the account’s own terms. Where it isn’t, size alone supplies no substitute verdict.

The argument operates at three different levels. It *binds*: the indexical exemption is groundless, and the standing of others remains whether or not their claim persuades the holder (§5.14.5, §6.3). It supplies a test for institutions: holdings must not purchase unanswerable direction or leave the foundation unfunded. And it can still *move*, where admiration follows contribution and withdraws from extraction. The first is a moral conclusion. The second needs laws and institutions capable of enforcing it. The third is a possible motive, not a guarantee.

*The foundation is a condition of freedom, not freedom’s completion.* A common objection holds that its maintenance restricts freedom: what it gives one participant it takes from another. Two burdens must be counted together. Contribution constrains the contributor; deprivation and dependency constrain the person whose refusal carries the threat of ruin. The derived tax shape answers that conflict by requiring more from greater stake while forbidding an inverted burden. A secure foundation does not let everyone contribute exactly as they want or receive exactly what they want. It does something prior: it widens the range within which refusal and choice are real. Whether a given design achieves that without producing a different domination is a question of incidence and institutions. The structural conclusion converges with Rawls’s difference principle (*A Theory of Justice* 1971, §14), that permissible inequality is constrained by the position of the worst-off, on different grounds: Rawls derives it through the original-position procedure; a participation condition is derived here under which liberty can become more than formal.

The reason is modal freedom. The foundation is meant to give a subject distance from immediate need: time to think, safety to refuse, stability enough to compare alternatives, education enough to understand consequences, and protection against deprivation as the price of refusal. When it does, it supports both pillars at once: latitude to act and the conditions of modal depth. Political maintenance is therefore not merely external option-creation. Its success is whether people actually gain the room to understand and choose among options.

Work, on its account, should be for opportunity rather than the price of bare survival. A lifetime with no time, rest, or refusable exit collapses the field to a single branch. Maximum possibility isn’t maximized labor. The foundation includes time because latitude is half of freedom (§5.11); work that occupies the whole field can collapse possibility from the other side. Decoupling care, education, old-age security, and subsistence from any one job should make work more available as a route to meaning, ambition, contribution, and developed capacity. It will not make every job meaningful, erase bad management, or ensure that each person finds the work they want. The test is more concrete: can a participant refuse, leave, retrain, care for someone, or try another path without losing the conditions of participation? The relational-egalitarian outcome Anderson develops (*Private Government* 2017)—workplace freedom requiring not just exit-rights but conditions that make exit genuine rather than a survival risk—is the same outcome this foundation is meant to make possible.

*Consumer participation is one lateral channel through which work runs.* Many subjects have preferences past subsistence: particular foods, kinds of housing, travel, entertainment, fellowship, and the artifacts of culture. For them, discretionary income supplies a reason to work without making deprivation the price of refusal. The alternative is no longer not subsisting; it is forgoing some discretionary participation they prefer. This is an incentive the foundation leaves intact, not a motivation that may be assumed every subject shares.

That distinction matters for the objection critics will reach for first: that a guaranteed foundation produces dependency because participants will sit on it and stop contributing. The subject’s directed persistence was established at §5.2, not a structural guarantee of paid employment, consumption beyond the foundation, entrepreneurship, ambition, or contribution in one public form. The results in Chapter 5 explain why subjects often pursue meaning, recognition, capacity-development, care, creation, and projects beyond immediate survival. They don’t license the stronger claim that every subject must do so, or must do so through markets.

The foundation therefore doesn’t stand or fall with a prediction of universal productivity. It is owed as a condition of participation, including to a subject who contributes little, contributes outside paid work, or needs a period in which recovery is the whole task. The empirical question is narrower: how a particular foundation changes paid labor, caregiving, education, risk-taking, creative work, and other forms of contribution under actual institutional conditions. Removing survival coercion can redirect those activities rather than extinguish them, and discretionary rewards remain available above the foundation; whether a design succeeds on those terms must be measured rather than read off the metaphysics. The inversion survives the qualification: survival pressure isn’t what makes contribution possible. For many subjects, it is what prevents their contribution from taking the form they would otherwise choose.

And further: the foundation itself isn’t a dividend earned by prior contribution, so choosing a foundation-only life isn’t by definition benefits fraud. A participant who works more still receives more discretionary income, capacity, experience, and recognition; survival pressure isn’t needed to create that difference. But it would be false to conclude that no gaming opportunity remains. Gaming can occur in eligibility administration, false claims, provider billing, employer substitution, contractor pricing, or intermediary capture. A landlord may absorb part of a housing transfer through rent, a concentrated healthcare provider may absorb coverage through price, and a nominal beneficiary may receive less than the appropriation records. The empirical incidence of such pass-through is mixed and design-specific, which is why the requirement is adequacy after accounting for incidence rather than confidence in any one delivery form. Universal maintenance reduces the eligibility and cliff channels; it doesn’t close the provider, price, or market-power channels. An acceptable design therefore audits the recipient’s net position, supply response, price movement, and intermediary margins, and changes cash, direct-provision, public-option, competition, or price-setting components where capture materially erodes the foundation. Free-riding and capture remain symmetric infractions at every scale; neither is assumed away.

*Politics, on this view, should widen the connective tissue for meaningful exchange rather than reduce everything to winning or losing.* Once the threshold holds, more of the political question can become how many subjects can reach one another on terms each could freely endorse, and how much of what each contributes returns as something they actually value. The evaluative target is connective, not a single metric. The exchange is commercial as well as non-commercial: labor for wages, goods for money, services for services, alongside attention, care, ideas, and time. Markets above a secured threshold can be a primary form of that connective tissue. A society in which more subjects can engage across a wider surface, on terms less distorted by survival pressure or position-asymmetry, performs the function more fully than one in which the surface is compressed. Conflict over rival goods doesn’t disappear when maintenance holds, but fewer conflicts need take the form of survival contests.

*Comfort, contribution, and the principle of proportionate exchange.* Politics should be organized around principles most people already accept when stated plainly. People’s problems are worth solving. Whatever helps people live comfortably is worth doing. If someone wants more than comfort, they are free to earn it: the baseline isn’t the ceiling, and ambition isn’t suspect. People seek more than comfort anyway: purpose, novelty, experience, the chance to contribute something, to be recognized, to follow their curiosity, to express what they find inside themselves. These aren’t demands on the system. They are what subjects do when the conditions are right. A person who needs time to recover from illness, loss, or exhaustion should have that time: organizations that depend on people should build contingency for that, because a system with no slack for human recovery has designed the human out. Pay people based on what they contribute. Build the baseline so that contribution is a choice rather than a survival mechanism. These aren’t radical propositions. They are what shared life looks like when it is organized around people rather than around the extraction of people.

So long as the comfort doesn’t come at the expense of disproportionate exchange. The baseline isn’t funded by extracting more from those who have less, and it isn’t earned by prior contribution. Above it, compensation should remain answerable to contribution, risk, control, and the public conditions supporting the exchange. The minimum-wage debate is a proxy for two questions too often collapsed: whether survival is secure and whether compensation is defensible. The baseline answers the first unconditionally. The contribution test addresses the second without pretending that one number resolves every case.

A society collectively values convenience. The people who provide it (in every form, at every hour) shouldn’t have to worry about their survival or health in exchange for doing so. A person who works anywhere (or nowhere, for whatever reason) is owed the same baseline. The baseline isn’t a reward for labor. It is what the political community maintains for every subject inside it.

What is left underdetermined is left to the design literatures: marginal-rate schedules; capital-gains, estate, land-value, and transaction-tax treatment; single-payer, multi-payer, public-option, regulated-private, or hybrid delivery; universal basic income, negative income tax, jobs guarantees, or combinations; and specific competition policy. The governing tests are adequacy after accounting for incidence of the foundation, accountability, access, fiscal and administrative feasibility, effects on productive activity, and protection against domination or capture. Provider profit and private delivery aren’t disqualifying labels; neither is public delivery self-validating. Where more than one arrangement clears the tests, the choice belongs to comparative evidence and the recognized direction of the population through §6.3.

All told, the argument turns on a political commitment to secure the participation foundation without allowing its costs, risks, or governing power to be shifted unanswerably onto others. Protection of holdings, ability to pay, benefit, rent, harm, and market power can support financing obligations through different arguments; they shouldn’t be compressed into one proportionate-to-stake equation. The empirical record can test trickle-down claims, insurance performance, productivity-pay divergence, tax incidence, and provider capture only in specified jurisdictions and designs. Economic reform is therefore assessed as a set: whether the foundation is adequate after incidence, whether financing is defensible, whether provision is accountable, and whether the arrangement preserves room for productive and voluntary exchange above it.

## 6.8 Housing
Subject $s$ can’t participate without a base from which the other conditions can be taken up. Housing draws on §6.7’s account of the shared and rival conditions of liberty and of collective investment, and on §6.1’s treatment of stable shelter as a condition of life-as-agency. Land is where those results meet their hardest case: a rival material asset and a non-rival structural value occupy one object.

**[Right]**

**Housing** · *Right*

Participation is unavailable to subject $s$ without a base from which the other conditions can be taken up. Tenure instrument stays open. Manufactured scarcity does not.

**Depends on:** Right to Subsistence (§6.7), Right to Life (§6.1), and The Chapter 6 Premises (§6.1)

*Land is the rival good that foundation has to face on its own terms.* The positive-sum result holds because what liberty aggregates across—latitude and modal depth—is non-rival, while the rival material goods that finance the foundation are handled openly on the contribution side. Land is the limiting case because contributed improvement and scarce location value occupy one asset. The improvement a holder builds or maintains is contributed value, theirs on that logic. Site value has several sources: natural amenities, expectations, permitted use, scarcity, nearby private activity, and the roads, transit, utilities, schools, law, and population that collective investment supplies. What follows therefore earns a narrower and more defensible conclusion than the claim that every dollar of unimproved value is public creation: the portion traceable to shared investment or publicly manufactured scarcity can’t be represented as the holder’s contribution alone. An acceptable architecture must account for that collectively generated rent and must not let scarcity be deliberately intensified for private gain while others are excluded from the housing floor. Land-value taxation or capture in the Georgist tradition is one unusually direct way to do so while leaving improvements untaxed; it isn’t the only possible instrument, and its rate, base, incidence, valuation method, and transition remain empirical design questions. The Lockean proviso that appropriation leave *enough and as good* supports the anti-exclusion constraint under scarcity, but it doesn’t by itself select one tax mechanism.

*Housing is the spatial precondition the other conditions are exercised from.* Shelter already sits on the necessities list, so the subsistence floor already includes housing. The land result explains why housing is more than one line item among others.

A home is the reliable base from which the other conditions of participation are used. Reliability means continued access, safety, and an address, not necessarily permanent residence in one place. Without secure shelter, a person can’t reliably hold the address political representation runs through, get the rest healthcare presupposes, or keep the base from which education and work begin. Without that security, action becomes a response to survival rather than a choice.

Homelessness is the economic collapse of modal distance described at §6.7 made literal: there is nowhere to stand back from necessity. Losing shelter thins the field in the same way as losing work or having work occupy the whole field (§5.2). Housing must therefore be treated as maintained [infrastructure](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary), whether provision is public, private, cooperative, or mixed, rather than as a market outcome corrected only after access fails. Shelter comes first for the same reason prevention comes before correction.

*Exclusion is how scarce land can become foreclosure.* No one can make more of a particular location, but the number and kind of dwellings it supports can change. Control over that capacity creates a standing relation vulnerable to domination. Exclusionary zoning, minimum-lot requirements, single-use rules, and incumbent restrictions can prevent housing supply from responding where demand is high. Where those rules exclude newcomers in order to protect incumbent scarcity rents, extraction and exclusion happen together. Not every land-use rule has that function; safety, infrastructure capacity, ecology, and other imposed risks remain legitimate constraints.

The historical record supplies direct cases. FHA and HOLC redlining (1930s–1968), urban-renewal demolition, and the racial sorting of residential geography developed at §6.2 show extraction in the register of land. The reparative obligation they raise belongs at §6.13.

Sandel and MacIntyre are right that home and place can constitute a life rather than function as commodities someone merely holds. That point supports secure tenure. It parts from the argument only when attachment to place becomes a warrant for shutting others out.

*Security of tenure is indexed to access, not to place.* The foundation protects against arbitrary eviction, foreclosure, or removal. It does not require permanent residence in one location. A person or community moving among sites meets the requirement when access to the site currently held remains secure for as long as they hold it. That is the same standard applied to a fixed dwelling. The portable, person-attached allowance specified at §6.8.2 travels with such an arrangement rather than assuming a fixed address. Requirements that force Traveller, Romani, and other itinerant communities into one location apply the domination of zoning and exclusion to movement itself.

The form remains open. Collectively generated site rent might be addressed through land-value taxation, split-rate taxation, public or trust ownership, development charges, leasehold recovery, or another instrument. The transition path for households whose savings are held as home equity also remains open (§6.15), as do the zoning and tenure systems used to secure the foundation. Where several designs work, the choice remains with the population. What is ruled out is deliberate scarcity or a privatized public windfall alongside insecure housing access.

*The anti-displacement and incidence principle.* Housing policy is assessed at the household after prices, rents, taxes, fees, supply responses, and benefit withdrawal—not at the statute or appropriation. No reform satisfies the foundation if it predictably pushes a person below secure, adequate housing without an available replacement that preserves continuity, safety, and access. Renters, mortgaged owners, debt-free owners, and land-rich but cash-poor households can bear different burdens from the same instrument; incidence must therefore be reported separately by tenure, income, age, and liquidity. Deferral, circuit breakers, renter credits, replacement housing, community land trusts, supply expansion, and person-attached support are possible protections rather than a jointly necessary set. The categorical result is the housing floor after accounting for incidence and the prohibition on avoidable displacement below it; the mechanism remains corrigible.

### 6.8.1 The Dispute
The housing dispute begins with one fact: no one makes more land, but roads, schools, businesses, public services, and neighbors all help determine what a site is worth. May an owner keep the whole increase when the surrounding community produced part of it? And may zoning exclude newcomers from that fixed supply in the name of property or local self-government?

Land is the hard case because a rival material asset—the site—and a non-rival structural value—housing as a condition of participation—occupy the same object. Land-value capture returns the community-created share while leaving the owner’s improvements untaxed. Limits on exclusionary land use keep owners and municipalities from turning fixed supply into a means of foreclosure. Protection against displacement keeps the remedy from forcing current occupants out. Three traditions in property theory and land-use governance reject this account from different directions.

The propertarian entitlement tradition presses from one direction (Nozick, *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* 1974; Rothbard, *For a New Liberty* 1973; Epstein, *Takings* 1985). Once a title has been justly acquired through purchase, inheritance, or first appropriation meeting the Lockean proviso, it covers the parcel as a whole. A levy on unimproved site value is therefore a taking like a levy on any other justly held asset, whatever collective investment made the location valuable.

On that view, separating site from improvement invents a division the entitlement does not recognize. The market values the parcel as one thing. If collective contribution licenses taking part of that value, the same argument appears to reach every asset dependent on infrastructure, network effects, or favorable regulation—which is nearly every asset.

The homevoter tradition presses from a second direction (Fischel, *The Homevoter Hypothesis* 2001; and the broader municipal-finance and local-public-goods literature). Homeowners often hold most of their wealth in one illiquid asset. Local land-use control lets them protect that asset against negative externalities, and zoning makes local government answerable to the people who bear the cost of decline. On this view, exclusionary zoning is not extraction disguised as governance. It is democratic control exercised by people with a durable stake in the outcome, and abolishing the instrument abolishes their self-government.

The land-decommodification tradition presses from a third direction (Engels, *The Housing Question* 1872; Harvey, *Social Justice and the City* 1973; *Rebel Cities* 2012; and the broader Marxist urban-political-economy literature). Any system in which land and housing remain individually held and sold at market prices reproduces the rent relation at the center of extraction. The holder keeps a monopoly over the use of a fixed resource and gains from appreciation produced by the community.

On this view, land-value capture merely redistributes part of the rent. It leaves land as a commodity that an individual can hold, sell, and profit from. Only deprivatizing land and allocating housing through use rights answers the diagnosis implied by collective investment.

A fourth pressure runs inside its own communitarian engagement rather than against its premise. Sandel (*Democracy’s Discontent* 1996) and MacIntyre (*After Virtue* 1981) press the constitutive-community reading: home and place are constitutive of a life rather than commodities a person merely holds. That direction largely converges with the security-of-tenure protections here. The residual pressure is narrower—whether attachment to place can ground a community’s standing to exclude newcomers whose presence would alter that place’s character. The account grants the attachment as a real interest but not as a self-validating warrant. The standing of present residents enters the decision; it doesn’t erase the standing of those excluded, and the rule still has to answer for its effects on access, scarcity, infrastructure, and the character it protects.

The argument compares four accounts of land. The propertarian account treats land as an ordinary asset whose full value belongs to its titled holder. The homevoter account treats it as a local public good governed by the people whose wealth it constitutes. The decommodification account holds that land’s commodity form is itself extractive and must be abolished rather than adjusted. These views are pressed, respectively, by the Nozick–Epstein, Fischel and municipal-finance, and Engels–Harvey traditions.

The fourth account begins from land’s unusual structure: a rival site and a non-rival participation value occupy the same object, while the site’s market value comes from natural features, private activity, scarcity, permitted use, expectations, and shared investment in different proportions. The answer developed here makes the collectively generated portion answerable while limiting exclusionary foreclosure. It draws on the Georgist land-value-capture tradition (George, *Progress and Poverty* 1879), the classical-liberal convergence on land taxation (including Friedman’s 1978 “least bad tax” remark (1978)), the fair-housing and anti-redlining record developed at §6.2, and research on community land trusts and inclusionary zoning. The dispute is answered at §6.8.2. There, the Chapter 6 political premises apply the account of collective investment from §6.7 and the shelter requirement from §6.1 to housing and land use. The question is what housing institutions must provide if they are not to become mechanisms of extraction and foreclosure around a scarce, non-substitutable location.

### 6.8.2 The Requirement
Under the Chapter 6 political premises, categorical constraints must be separated from the instruments that satisfy them. The constraints are secure and adequate housing access, no avoidable displacement below that foundation, no deliberate manufacture of exclusionary scarcity for private capture, accountability for the portion of site rent created by shared institutions, adequacy after accounting for incidence, and administratively equal valuation wherever assessed value is used. Deferral, land-value taxation, community land trusts, allowances, public or non-market supply, zoning reform, and rent regulation are candidate mechanisms. Their necessity is conditional on being chosen; no one set follows merely from housing’s status as a participation condition.

*Site-value accountability without a foundation breach.* Where a design recovers the portion of site value traceable to shared investment or publicly created scarcity, it must distinguish that portion from contributed improvements and must not collect in a way that deprives an occupant of adequate housing. Collection at transfer is one strong solution for liquidity-constrained owner-occupants; annual collection paired with income-sensitive circuit breakers, automatic deferral, renter protection, or other safeguards can also satisfy the same constraint. The application therefore requires accountable recovery and housing security after accounting for incidence, not transfer-only collection in every case.

*Liquidity and transition protection.* If deferral is used, it attaches to an occupied home rather than an investment parcel and must have transparent interest, a bounded claim on equity, simple enrollment, and a repayment event that doesn’t trigger involuntary loss of the foundation. Those are conditions on a deferral design, not reasons every household must use deferral or every jurisdiction must collect only at transfer. Circuit breakers, installment plans, homestead credits, renter credits, and replacement-housing guarantees can perform the same structural work where they better protect the relevant population. Each design must report take-up, non-take-up reasons, foreclosure, forced mobility, equity loss, and fiscal recovery by income, age, race, disability, and tenure.

*Durable affordability where community land trusts are used.* A trust that promises permanent affordability must use a resale or ground-lease formula that preserves affordability across transfers while leaving residents a stated share of improvement and appreciation value. Community land trusts are a demonstrated way to separate site stewardship from dwelling ownership; they aren’t the uniquely required tenure form. Their performance must be compared with other shared-equity and permanently affordable designs on resale affordability, household wealth formation, default, mobility, maintenance, and administrative cost.

*Portable access and meaningful choice.* The foundation belongs to the person, but it need not always be delivered as cash. A portable allowance, public or social housing with genuine choice and transfer rights, ownership assistance, emergency placement followed by stable tenure, or a mixed system can satisfy the requirement. Adequacy must track locality and household need, support may not create a benefit cliff through the foundation, and a person must have a usable route between arrangements rather than being trapped in one assigned unit or one provider. A person-attached allowance is one especially portable design, not a structural necessity.

*Post-incidence adequacy and supply response.* An allowance or tax credit doesn’t satisfy the foundation to the extent that landlords, lenders, sellers, or intermediaries absorb it through rents, prices, fees, reduced quality, or reduced compensation. Pass-through isn’t fixed by theory alone: it varies with vacancy, supply elasticity, market power, tenant mobility, benefit design, and the time horizon. Every implementation must therefore measure the recipient’s net housing gain, rent and price response, quality, vacancy, construction, conversion, and displacement against a credible comparator. Provision-cost indexing, land-value recovery, zoning liberalization, direct construction, public options, acquisition, tenant protection, and rent stabilization can be combined in different ways. Rent regulation can reduce displacement for protected tenants while some designs also reduce rental supply or shift costs to unregulated tenants; it is neither categorically required nor categorically excluded. The structural requirement is that the chosen set preserve adequacy after accounting for incidence and adequate supply without transferring the foundation to incumbent asset holders.

*Code compliance scoped to imposed risk, with rescue unconditional and recovery bounded by the foundation.* The housing foundation applies to dwellings people actually occupy. Its requirements can’t become a reason to withdraw shelter from someone whose dwelling violates them.

One criterion governs which building rules follow from the foundation. The rule must address a risk imposed on someone who did not authorize it: a neighboring household, a later occupant, a responder, a tenant, a child, or a successor. A rule addressing only a risk the holder bears is not thereby invalid, but it is not imposed by the housing foundation.

Rescue remains unconditional either way. Firefighters, ambulances, and police reach a noncompliant dwelling exactly as they reach a compliant one because the foundation protects people, not structures. Withholding rescue to enforce a building standard would revoke a person’s subsistence over a property defect.

Compliance affects recovery, not rescue. If the violated rule caused the loss, the fund restores the person to the housing floor rather than their previous holdings. The allowance continues, but the destroyed structure is not rebuilt at collective expense. If the choice imposed risk on someone else, liability attaches afterward under the same asymmetry used at §6.11.2. Once children, tenants, or successors occupy the dwelling, the risk was never the holder’s alone to waive.

*Assessment integrity wherever assessed value is used.* A site-value or property-value instrument is only as fair as its valuation. Better-resourced holders can win larger assessment reductions, and reassessment lag can produce systematically higher assessment-to-value ratios on lower-valued parcels. Any assessed-value design therefore requires a public and reviewable methodology, regular reassessment, error testing by value band and neighborhood, accessible appeals, and published post-appeal ratios. This condition is categorical for valuation-based instruments, not for housing architectures that use no assessed-value base.

Together, the categorical constraints are these: secure and adequate access; no avoidable displacement below the foundation; no deliberate scarcity manufactured for exclusionary capture; accountability for collectively generated site rent; adequacy after accounting for incidence and supply; risk-protective habitability; and equal administration wherever valuation is used. The listed instruments are conditionally governed applications of those constraints. A jurisdiction may satisfy the architecture through different combinations, and the mechanisms are tested separately at §6.8.3 rather than treating one preferred set as definitionally necessary.

### 6.8.3 Predictions
The requirements at §6.8.2 generate testable predictions distinct from the political premises supporting them. Confirming or disconfirming those predictions against the empirical record is the task of §6.8.4; this section states what the account predicts before that record is read.

*A shift from taxing improvements toward accurately assessed site value predicts less penalty on marginal construction and greater capitalization of the tax into land prices, with incidence varying through the transition.* Fixed land supply supports the long-run expectation that a pure, anticipated site-value tax is capitalized mainly into the land asset rather than passed through like a tax on newly supplied structures. Existing leases, reassessment shocks, credit constraints, market power, mixed tax bases, and transition rules can nevertheless shift short- and medium-run burdens among sellers, buyers, landlords, renters, and lenders. The test therefore compares construction, density, vacancy, land prices, rents, tenure transitions, and after-housing-cost income across matched jurisdictions and population groups. The prediction fails if the shift doesn’t reduce the marginal penalty on improvements, produces no utilization response, or persistently burdens renters and liquidity-constrained occupants without compensating protection.

*Exclusionary zoning predicts rising site values for incumbents and falling access for newcomers moving together, not separately.* Exclusion and extraction happen in the same act. Municipalities adopting larger minimum lots, single-family-only zoning, or restrictive permitting should therefore show two changes together: rising property values for incumbents and falling household formation or in-migration among newcomers. The prediction is that the trends track each other rather than move independently.

*Liquidity protection predicts lower tax-induced mobility and foreclosure among otherwise comparable cash-constrained owners, with a measurable fiscal trade-off.* Deferral, circuit breakers, and related protections should reduce involuntary moves and delinquency relative to a credible eligibility-boundary or policy-change comparator. The test must report take-up and selection, accumulated liens, equity remaining, administrative cost, and eventual recovery. The prediction fails where protection doesn’t reduce tax-induced displacement, where complexity prevents the exposed population from using it, or where accumulated obligations consume an excessive share of household equity.

*Community land trusts predict durable affordability and resistance to the price cycles that erode other subsidized-housing stock.* A resale formula removes the appreciation windfall that would otherwise go to a departing resident. Community land trust units should therefore remain affordable near the original qualifying income band through repeated sales and market cycles. Income-restricted units without such a formula should instead become less affordable as each resale occurs near market price, shown by rising qualifying incomes and declining representation of the original target group.

*Housing support predicts heterogeneous pass-through rather than one universal capitalization rate.* More of an allowance or credit should appear in rents or prices where ownership is concentrated, vacancies are scarce, and supply barely responds to price. Recipients should keep more of the benefit where supply responds, rents track costs, bargaining power is dispersed, or direct and non-market options discipline the market. Combining a provision-cost index with adequate supply may reduce pass-through, but that package has not been tested directly. The prediction fails if capture does not vary with the named market conditions or if the proposed package is captured at the same rate in matched comparisons.

*Racially exclusionary credit and land-use history predicts persistent differences in homeownership, house values, rents, credit access, and segregation near historical redlining boundaries.* The strongest test uses boundary or policy designs that compare otherwise similar locations rather than inferring historical causation from a present racial appraisal gap alone. Persistence after current structure, location, and neighborhood controls supports a reparative question at §6.13; the prediction fails where credible designs find no long-run discontinuity attributable to the historical intervention.

*Assessment integrity predicts elimination of assessment regressivity wherever methodology is standardized and appeals access is equalized; its absence predicts the regressive pattern already documented in conventional property-tax administration.* A land-value system can reproduce private capture at the valuation stage if it leaves assessment methods, appeal access, or reassessment timing ungoverned. Standardized assessment with equal access to appeals should produce assessment-to-value ratios that do not vary systematically with parcel value. Discretionary assessment or unequal appeals should reproduce the documented regressive pattern: higher-valued parcels assessed at lower ratios than less valuable ones.

*Distributional incidence predicts different effects by tenure, income, age, liquidity, and market structure.* Owner-occupants may lose capital value. Highly leveraged owners may face refinancing risk, and cash-poor owners may face immediate liquidity pressure. Existing renters may face pass-through or displacement, while prospective buyers may gain from lower land prices. Landlords may bear more where rents already sit at the market ceiling. Any instrument that looks progressive in aggregate but leaves a protected group below the housing floor fails unless another measure closes the gap.

Each prediction is falsifiable in the ordinary sense. No construction or utilization response, no reduction in tax-induced mobility from liquidity protection, affordability erosion in a trust or shared-equity design, pass-through invariant to supply and market power, persistent assessment regressivity after standardization, or unremedied foundation breaches concentrated among renters or low-liquidity owners count against the relevant mechanism. The record is read against each separately (§6.8.4).

### 6.8.4 Confirmation
The predictions stated at §6.8.3 meet an uneven empirical record. Descriptive comparisons establish feasibility and association; policy discontinuities, boundary designs, and matched longitudinal studies support stronger causal claims. Because most housing instruments operate in sets and induce transitions, no jurisdictional example confirms the entire framework at once. The record that follows therefore distinguishes supported mechanisms, mixed incidence, and still-untested designs.

*Land-value and split-rate evidence is consistent with a construction response but doesn’t establish a universal effect or incidence.* Oates and Schwab’s analysis of Pittsburgh (1997) found that the building boom had a major independent demand driver and that the split-rate reform played a supporting role by avoiding higher taxes on improvements. Reviews of the broader Pennsylvania record find some credible positive estimates, some null findings, and substantial identification limits. Cross-country land-tax cases further differ in assessment, exemptions, municipal finance, credit, and planning. The evidence supports feasibility and the direction of the marginal-incentive mechanism; the size of construction, land-price, rent, and distributional effects remains open and must be measured by property type and transition cohort.

*The land-use record strongly supports a scarcity mechanism, with effect size and local trade-offs still empirical.* Metropolitan comparisons and regulatory-restrictiveness studies repeatedly associate tighter land-use constraints with less construction and higher prices in high-demand locations. Houston, Tokyo, coastal California, and other comparisons illustrate the mechanism but aren’t matched experiments: transport, demand, national institutions, geography, and building rules differ. The evidence supports the conditional claim that binding exclusionary controls can raise incumbent values by suppressing access; it doesn’t show that every land-use rule is exclusionary or that liberalization alone guarantees affordability.

*Liquidity protection is plausible and partly supported, but the strong no-displacement claim isn’t yet established.* Household-panel evidence indicates that higher property-tax burdens can increase mobility among older homeowners, supporting the need for relief. Existing deferral and circuit-breaker programs demonstrate an administratively workable response, but take-up is often very low and enrolled households are selected. The record doesn’t yet justify the claim that deferral eliminates forced sale or guarantees full recovery across a generalized population. Those are direct outcome tests for pilots and expansions, not assumptions licensed by the existence of current programs.

*Community land trusts establish durable-affordability feasibility, not single-mechanism causation.* The Champlain Housing Trust and the broader multi-decade trust record show that resale-restricted ownership can preserve affordability across transfers. Thaden’s study (2011) reports substantially lower delinquency and foreclosure among surveyed community-land-trust owners than in the conventional market during the financial crisis. Resale price, stewardship, counseling, underwriting, selection, and intervention all differ, so the record can’t attribute the full outcome to the resale formula alone. The earned result is that the architecture can preserve affordability and resilience; comparative performance, household wealth effects, and scalability remain empirical.

*Housing-support incidence is mixed and design-specific.* Susin’s US analysis (2002) found rent spillovers from voucher expansion in constrained markets. Finnish quasi-experimental studies have produced different estimates across reforms: some find substantial landlord capture, while others find little or no rent response and benefits accruing mainly to recipients. That variation supports the revised prediction that pass-through depends on design, tenant response, supply, vacancy, and market structure. It doesn’t confirm a universal market-rent-indexing mechanism, and the full provision-cost-indexed set hasn’t been directly tested.

*Historical redlining has stronger causal support than the prior appraisal-gap formulation stated.* Perry, Rothwell, and Harshbarger’s Brookings study (2018) documents a large contemporary devaluation of homes in majority-Black neighborhoods after observed home and neighborhood characteristics are controlled; it doesn’t by itself identify HOLC maps as the cause of that entire gap. Aaronson, Hartley, and Mazumder’s boundary and propensity-score designs (2021) more directly find that HOLC maps caused persistent reductions in homeownership, house values, and rents and increased segregation. The combination establishes a live reparative question at §6.13 while keeping contemporary racial devaluation and historically identified redlining effects analytically distinct.

*Assessment regressivity is well documented; the corrective mechanism remains provisionally supported.* Berry’s work (2021) documents higher assessment-to-value ratios for lower-valued properties and advantages associated with appeal capacity. Standardized mass-appraisal reforms, including Cook County’s post-2019 changes, provide evidence that methodology can reduce disparities, but reform evaluation must include post-appeal ratios, model error by neighborhood and value band, and persistence across cycles. No land-value-specific implementation yet supplies direct confirmation at that register.

*Distributional incidence remains the principal open confirmation domain.* Evidence on property-tax pass-through, housing-allowance incidence, owner mobility, and capitalization shows that statutory assignment doesn’t determine economic burden. Renters, current owners, prospective buyers, and low-liquidity households can be affected differently, and aggregate gains can conceal a foundation breach in one group. No existing record confirms one universal incidence pattern or the full instrument set. Overall, the evidence supports the scarcity and valuation mechanisms and the feasibility of several protections; it doesn’t establish the normative housing floor, which rests on the chapter’s political premises. It also falsifies any claim that one instrument has invariant effects. The full institutional result remains conditional on matched, distributional performance after accounting for incidence.

### 6.8.5 Conclusions
*Structural constraints.* Housing is constitutive infrastructure because secure, adequate shelter is a spatial condition of participation. Individual tenure and contributed improvements remain legitimate. What is precluded is avoidable deprivation below the housing floor, deliberate manufacture of exclusionary scarcity for private capture, representation of publicly generated location rent as wholly private contribution, and valuation or collection systems whose net burden after accounting for incidence predictably displaces protected occupants without secure replacement. It doesn’t preclude every private receipt of site appreciation, require transfer-only collection, or select one land-tax, allowance, tenure, zoning, or rent-regulation design. Those instruments are judged by incidence, supply, access, administrative equality, and transition performance.

*Cross-domain couplings.* Housing couples to the economy (§6.7) because taxes, transfers, credit, rents, and land prices must be evaluated by economic rather than statutory incidence. It couples to rights (§6.1) because stable shelter is the spatial precondition from which other participation conditions are exercised. It couples to justice (§6.13) as well, and causal evidence of redlining’s persistent effects raises a reparative question the argument names rather than decides. It couples to implementation (§6.15) because any change in land taxation, tenure, subsidy, or land-use rules creates transition gains and losses that must be measured across renters, owners, debt positions, income groups, and neighborhoods. The shared logic is the foundation and anti-capture constraint, not an inference that every neighboring economic instrument is independently necessary.

*Neighbors.* This isn’t a prohibition on private land tenure. Individually held and improved land remains licensed by the contribution logic. What is precluded is capturing site value that the holder didn’t produce. That places the account beside Georgist land-value capture and the classical-liberal view of land taxation as comparatively undistorting. It rejects both the propertarian treatment of unimproved site value as an ordinary contributed asset and the decommodification demand to abolish individual tenure where the site/improvement distinction already answers the extraction.

The account also predicts organized opposition where homeowners’ asset interests benefit from local controls that an anti-exclusion reform would limit. Resistance to land-use liberalization or site-value capture should be strongest where expected losses are concentrated, salient, and politically organized. That resistance remains legitimate to voice, and not every objection is reducible to asset protection; attachment, infrastructure, ecology, and transition risk can supply independent reasons. Implementation must distinguish those reasons rather than treating opposition as confirmation by definition.

Non-market construction and community land trusts provide another route. They can expand supply without first winning every zoning fight. Pairing site-value capture with non-market supply may therefore deliver more housing per unit of political effort than relying on zoning liberalization alone.

Several choices remain open. The argument does not set the rate or base of land-value capture, the zoning or tenure system, or the formulas for deferral caps, interest, and resale restrictions. It does not choose the transition path for households whose savings are held as home equity. Nor does it choose among community land trusts, non-market construction, or the forms of repair addressing the redlining-era site-value gap confirmed at §6.8.4. Multiple designs can satisfy the constraints. The choice belongs to the relevant design literatures, the evidence, and the population acting through §6.3.

The argument here earns four conclusions. Every member must retain secure and adequate housing access. Contributed improvements and legitimate tenure remain protected. Collectively generated location rents and publicly manufactured scarcity remain answerable to the public. Every housing instrument must preserve the foundation after incidence, supply response, administration, and transition are counted.

The evidence strongly supports supply constraints, the lasting effects of redlining, assessment regressivity, and the feasibility of durable-affordability mechanisms. Estimates remain mixed or incomplete for construction under land taxes, tax and subsidy pass-through, generalized deferral, and the full provision-cost-indexed design.

Land-value capture, zoning reform, liquidity protection, community land trusts, allowances, public or non-market supply, and tenant protections are corrigible mechanisms under common constraints. They are not one indivisible obligation. The maximal claim is stronger than a policy preference and narrower than a manifesto: no design succeeds unless it keeps people housed without shifting the burden invisibly onto another protected group.

## 6.9 Education

Education is the work of helping a child become an adult who can function in a world no one can specify in advance. The durable thing to build isn’t a stock of facts alone but the capacity to use knowledge: to distinguish what is possible from what isn’t, understand what depends on what, navigate unfamiliar conditions, and solve problems. Those capacities don’t float free of content. They are built through language, mathematics, science, history, art, and other bodies of knowledge whose concepts and examples give thought something to work with. A school can move a great deal of content past a student and still fail when little becomes durable understanding or transfers beyond the assessment. Because every future citizen passes through some educational arrangement, education is shared [infrastructure](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) the way courts and public health are. The political community can’t outsource responsibility for the foundation: public, private, religious, cooperative, home-based, and mixed providers must all be judged by whether they develop the required capacities without systematic exclusion, stratification, or extraction. Profit isn’t disqualifying by itself; profit obtained through public subsidy, information asymmetry, or credential dependence without proportionate educational contribution is. And the foundation has to reach everyone, because a community that asks its people to help steer it can’t first deny some of them the capacity to do so.

A political community depends on members able to understand, deliberate, and take part in common life. Formal education develops those capacities, but it begins from care, safety, nutrition, and stable recognition. It can’t replace that prior work; it extends it into the public conditions of knowledge, judgment, and participation.

The derivation draws on §5.4, §5.10, and §6.2, with Reasoning (§5.6) and Will (§5.11) naming capacities involved in navigating a modal field. The upstream condition for the later AI discussion is supplied at §5.13 and tool-use discussion. Education develops those capacities across the population because *direction from all* requires everyone to be able to engage.

The right to education is therefore the mapping-and-depth participation condition. Reasoning is already running wherever the question is entertained, and thin will wherever selection occurs. Education doesn’t add a second Cogito; it densifies the field without which political direction has no effective occupants. Subject $s$ can’t participate without cultivated capacity to model the [polity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary). That capacity includes recognizing possibilities, dependencies, and routes through them—the Three Frustrations of Will taught as life rather than as a list. Curriculum and provider remain questions of fit and design. The foundation is capacity, not a stock of facts.

**[Right]**

**Education** · *Right*

Participation is unavailable to subject $s$ without cultivated capacity to model the polity. That capacity includes what is possible, what is necessary for what, and how to navigate. Reasoning’s catch and thin will are already running; education densifies the field. Curriculum and provider stay open.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14), Knowledge (§5.4), and The Chapter 6 Premises (§6.1)

The forward-facing aspect of that foundation is structural, not preference. The kid being educated will be an adult later—sometimes much later—and the culture they will operate inside isn’t yet fully fixed. Some specific knowledge remains indispensable; some will date or be forgotten. What survives the gap is a combination of durable knowledge and the capacity to learn, test, and reorganize it. Education prepares people both to receive a culture and to participate in shaping it, since the citizens being educated are the ones who will later direct the polity through the recognition mechanism of §6.3. Additional cognitive and lived perspectives can surface recognition-relevant knowledge that existing institutions miss. They don’t guarantee improvement merely by being added; the institutions must be able to hear, test, and use what those perspectives disclose.

Consider a worked case: a student takes federal loans of forty thousand dollars to enroll in a for-profit certificate program promising a career in medical billing. The program receives the loan dollars on enrollment; the student receives a certificate that the local hiring market doesn’t recognize and that doesn’t place them in the promised work. Two years later the student is in debt, the school has its revenue, and federal taxpayers will cover much of the default. Where that pattern persists after completion, placement, instructional cost, student preparation, and local labor demand are counted, the financing channel can reward enrollment and marketing while shifting failure onto students and the public. Restricting loan eligibility, requiring risk sharing or refunds, enforcing outcome and disclosure standards, or redirecting funds to stronger providers are possible repairs. The result selects the failing mechanism, not public provision by name.

### 6.9.1 The Dispute
Educational policy turns adversarial over what education is *for*, and over whether the political community has structural obligations to develop the capacities its participants need to take up the participation conditions derived at §6.1. The recognition tradition reads education as the shared infrastructure through which the political community prepares the population that is going to participate in it: capability development covering the full range of capacities participation actually requires, organized around bringing every participant to the modeling threshold rather than around credential issuance. Three contemporary traditions in education theory deny this framing at its premise from different directions.

The disagreement is sharper with one child in view. A ten-year-old isn’t reading at grade level. Her school is underfunded, her parents both work, and by the time she is eighteen the difference between her and a classmate who reads fluently will show up in what she can earn, what she can refuse, what contracts she can understand, and whether a ballot measure means anything to her. Everyone in the dispute below agrees this is bad. They disagree about whose failure it is: a monopoly provider with no reason to improve, a state that took the decision away from her parents, or an institution that was never really built to teach her in the first place. Each of the three positions is one of those answers pressed to its conclusion.

The Friedman voucher tradition (Friedman 1962; Friedman and Friedman 1980, the contemporary school-choice movement through Caroline Hoxby and the charter-school empirical literature) presses the financing-versus-provision distinction, and its answer to the ten-year-old is that her family should be able to take the money elsewhere: universal access can be delivered through state-financed vouchers to families who choose among competing providers, and its collapse of state-financing into state-provision misreads the actual policy question. The market-discipline-through-choice mechanism is on this reading the structurally-sound delivery architecture for an educational foundation otherwise granted here as required.

The libertarian parental-authority tradition (Rothbard 1971, the contemporary Home School Legal Defense Association literature, the broader homeschool and unschooling movement) answers that the state took the decision from her parents, and presses the domain claim: education is the parental-authority domain, not the political community’s, and compulsory state schooling overrides a family-formation function the family is structurally placed to perform.
