Where education is treated here as shared infrastructure, this tradition reads it as state-overreach against a constitutive private sphere.

The Illich deschooling critique (Illich 1971; Freire 1968, on credentialing; Bourdieu and Passeron 1970, on cultural-capital reproduction) answers that the school was never built to teach her, and argues that credentialing functions as extraction from the opposite political direction: schools function structurally as credentialing apparatuses reproducing class hierarchy rather than as developers of the participation conditions named here, and its defense of public education-as-infrastructure underestimates how much of the institution operates as extraction.

*The three objections, engaged directly.* Grant the central concession in each case. Financing-vs-provision is granted: voucher architecture with adequate quality-foundation regulation and structural anti-extraction safeguards can satisfy the participation-conditions constraint, and the for-profit-education analysis explicitly names the failure mode voucher design has to guard against. Parental authority is granted above the foundation (homeschooling, religious schooling, alternative-pedagogy schooling operate as the qualified-preserve of §6.2) and not below it (denial of basic literacy, denial of socialization, indoctrination that closes off the capacity-for-analysis at §5.6.4). Credentialing-as-extraction is granted in full and is the foundation of the for-profit-education analysis and of its broader anti-extraction architecture. The parting is on the deschooling conclusion: modal-field development at population scale requires institutional structure that the deschooling alternative doesn’t reliably deliver. Education-as-shared-infrastructure is a claim about what the political community is obligated to ensure every participant receives, not a claim about which entity holds the provider license; financing, provision, and pedagogical design remain underdetermined where the participation-conditions foundation is met. On the traditionalist side, E.D. Hirsch’s cultural-literacy line (*Cultural Literacy* 1987) presses that capabilities-oriented pedagogy underweights canonical-content transmission and the shared reference base civic participation depends on; the shared reference base is granted as a real desideratum (supporting §6.2 belonging and §6.4 information-environment participation) and is located as a developmentally early scaffold for the work of developing capabilities rather than a competing telos.

The positive case begins from democratic participation, capability, development, and relational competence.

The common-school tradition located universal access in democratic-republican premises, but it tracked a real structural obligation to develop civic-and-cognitive capacities for participation. It runs from Mann (1848) through the universal-public-education lineage of Jane Addams and the Settlement movement. The Deweyan democratic-education tradition (Dewey 1899; 1916) reaches the same view of education as shared infrastructure through the question of which capacities democratic participation requires. Freire (1968) reaches capability development through critical-consciousness pedagogy, against banking-model education.

The capabilities tradition (Sen 1999; Nussbaum 2011) supplies the structural-foundation architecture: institutions are constrained to maintain the capabilities participation requires across the full population. The sociology-of-education tradition (Bowles and Gintis 1976; Bourdieu on cultural capital, Lareau 2003) documents the stratification patterns its anti-extraction architecture is designed against.

Its work of developing capabilities engages four of the central capabilities Nussbaum develops directly (*Women and Human Development* 2000, ch. 1; *Frontiers of Justice* 2006): senses, imagination, and thought; emotions; practical reason; and play. The threshold-not-aggregation commitment asks whether each student has effective access to each relevant capability rather than whether aggregate output is high. In educational terms, that means usable knowledge and judgment rather than either content retrieval or a free-floating capacity to think. Nussbaum’s capability-by-capability assessment in *Frontiers of Justice* (2006) Part I also supports differentiated provision in disability cases: students may need different supports to reach substantively comparable opportunities, without uniform output becoming the aim. Where capabilities conflict, the tragic-dilemma framing makes the conflict a design constraint rather than permission to pretend every capability can be maximized at once. Tracking into vocational and academic streams, and the later college-versus-trade decision, are concrete cases. Relational-capabilities refinements by Goering, Kittay, and Lindemann add that flourishing can depend on relationships rather than belonging to an isolated individual alone.

The developmental-psychology tradition supplies the capability-development account at the cognitive-architecture level: Vygotsky on the zone of proximal development (1978), Piaget on developmental stages, and Erikson on developmental periods (1968). The Heckman early-childhood-economics tradition (Heckman 2006; Heckman 2013; Heckman and Masterov 2007, on the return-on-investment curve) documents the structural-priority case for early-childhood investment.

The capabilities-oriented framing lands close to several pedagogical traditions, and the convergence is worth naming. Dewey’s experiential education in *Democracy and Education* (1916) emphasized inquiry; Vygotsky’s developmental work in *Mind in Society* (1978) located learning at the edge of what a learner can manage with support; Freire’s *Pedagogy of the Oppressed* (1968) centered dialogue; Montessori’s *The Absorbent Mind* (1949) placed the child in developmentally appropriate cognitive work. Problem-based, inquiry-based, and constructivist approaches develop related commitments. They do not become uniquely required pedagogies because they converge with the participation aim. What is required is the function—durable capability development—and each pedagogy must earn its place through learning, transfer, inclusion, developmental fit, and cost. The structural argument fixes what the political community must ensure, not how every classroom must teach it.

The Finnish National Core Curriculum tradition (Finnish National Core Curriculum 2016 on transversal competencies, Sahlberg 2011) is the operational instance of an integrated transversal-competency architecture. The relational-competence research tradition supports teaching relational capacities as part of the curriculum: Gottman on relational-pattern identification (1994), Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication framework (2003), and Bowlby and Ainsworth on attachment (1969; 1978).

The dispute has two sides. On one, educational obligation reduces to something narrower: a financing-mechanism question, a parental-authority defense against compulsory schooling, or a critique of credentialing that ends in deschooling—positions pressed by Friedman, the Rothbard-tradition literature, and Illich respectively. On the other, education is shared infrastructure for capability development. Stratification and unrecoverable debt can then become failure modes where they leave participants below the foundation. Mann, Dewey, Freire, Sen, Nussbaum, Heckman, the Finnish operating example, and developmental research reach parts of that wider view from different premises. Under the Chapter 6 political commitments, the question is what functions education must perform (§6.9.2); answering it does not convert agreement among those traditions into a structural-necessity proof.

### 6.9.2 The Requirement
The argument derives that education isn’t *merely* a private good measured by the participant’s future earnings. It is also the shared infrastructure through which the political community prepares the population that is going to participate in it. That conclusion fixes responsibility for universal capability development without uniquely fixing the provider. Public provision, regulated vouchers, nonprofit or cooperative schools, private schools, and home education can satisfy or violate the constraint. The failure occurs when a financing or provision arrangement converts public subsidy, information asymmetry, or credential dependence into returns unsupported by educational contribution while leaving participants below the capability foundation. The same logic that makes regulatory capture problematic therefore applies to the documented for-profit-education channel without treating every private provider or every earned return as extraction.

The infrastructure includes the teachers who do the cultivation. Teacher capacity to hold the standards, ask the follow-up questions, evaluate the cognitive work, and lead the subject-specific inquiry is itself a structural condition the political community is obligated to develop, not an implementation detail treated as given.

*Education has to make knowledge usable in participation.* The conditions of maximum possibility include cognitive conditions: enough knowledge and judgment to model the polity, understand options and consequences, recognize manipulation, and make refusal more than a nominal right. In the vocabulary of §5.11, education helps build the modal field (§5.4) through which selection becomes informed action. The Three Frustrations of Will name the job: a person needs to distinguish what is really possible, what is blocked, what could make it reachable, and what remains unmapped. That is why content and capacity can’t be opponents. Without knowledge there is too little to reason with; without practice in transfer and evaluation, remembered content may never become usable outside the setting in which it was tested. The educational threshold is therefore not a choice between what students know and whether they can think. It is whether they can use what they know to understand and navigate conditions they haven’t simply rehearsed.

A child’s modal field, structurally, is sparse. The body hasn’t yet stored the possibilities experienced bodies have laid down across decades; what fires in the child’s simulations is whatever has been installed so far, with the limitation that implies. Education is the structured densification of that field: installing possibilities the child wouldn’t encounter through unmediated experience, examples of conditions and outcomes the field wouldn’t generate on its own, ways of organizing what is present that experience doesn’t supply unprompted. The arts are among the chief instruments of that densification, not enrichment added once the core subjects are covered: Art (§5.15) establishes that literature, drama, film, and music install into a receiver’s modal field regions the receiver hasn’t lived through and couldn’t reach by direct experience alone, which is the same field-densification education is structurally for. An arts education is therefore a [maximization condition](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) relative to the threshold at §5.4, not a mere ornament layered on top of one: it doesn’t by itself set where that threshold lies, but cutting it narrows the modal coverage available for building the capacity the threshold requires as richly as the field-densification task allows. The developmental-psychology literature tracks the densification process from outside—Piaget on stage-dependent moral judgment (1932), Kohlberg on the progression from pre-conventional to post-conventional reasoning (1981)—while the modal-field account is what its mechanism is from inside. *Wisdom* in the older sense is what an unusually dense and accurately calibrated field looks like from the inside: the practically and morally relevant features of a situation already in view by the time deliberation begins, because the field has stored enough comparable cases that the situation reads as a case of something. An educational system brings subjects to genuine participation when it supports field densification across the population, not when it merely transfers content.

A common failure mode is content transfer without durable understanding: information moves from curriculum into short-term memory for assessment, then disappears or remains inert. A student who has memorized procedures without being able to recognize when and why they apply hasn’t reached the problem-solving threshold. Critical evaluation matters across domains, but it isn’t one content-free meta-skill that makes every other threshold reachable. Evaluating a historical claim, a medical study, a loan, and a mathematical proof requires different background knowledge and methods. The structural failure is to leave students without either the knowledge or the domain-sensitive habits needed to identify a problem, evaluate evidence, recognize a bad inference, and update a model when the evidence requires it.

*The curriculum question follows from the participation aim, but no syllabus follows directly.* A participant needs resources for judging possibility and dependency, evaluating claims, navigating institutions and technology, and managing practical decisions whose terms can otherwise remain opaque. Financial and legal literacy, evidence evaluation, household and health knowledge, civic understanding, and technological judgment are candidate applications of that aim. They are taught through substantive domains—mathematics, literature, science, history, art, vocational study—not instead of them. Which content belongs at which stage, how much common reference knowledge is needed, and how transfer should be tested remain questions for educational evidence and public judgment. The governing question is durable: *what does this subject need to become a genuine participant?* The answer isn’t fixed in advance.

*The inversion-frame recurs under AI.* Education has long described itself as cultivating thought while often grading artifacts taken to evidence thought. AI makes the two easier to separate: a student can produce a polished essay without possessing the judgment the essay is meant to display. The response needn’t be a categorical ban, but provenance can still matter where the task is expressly designed to observe unaided recall, composition, or developmental progress. Where tool use is permitted, output quality alone is also insufficient. Assessment may need the student to represent opposing positions, explain why the argument is ordered as it is, defend the evidence, identify what the tool got wrong, or reproduce the relevant reasoning in another form. Equal access becomes a structural concern when an institution requires or builds assessment around the tool; it doesn’t follow that every student must receive every tool at every stage. The standard is whether the arrangement develops and can verify the capability it claims to assess.

When AI is used well, some thinking is relocated rather than eliminated. The student may frame the question, specify constraints, evaluate the return, push back, revise, and decide what they would stake their name on. But relocation isn’t guaranteed by tool use, and those supervisory abilities usually depend on knowledge and practice acquired without outsourcing the same judgment. Assessment must therefore register what cognitive work the student actually performed rather than infer it from either the artifact or the presence of a tool.

What school is for, under that relocation, is the constraints of the form: why a proof can’t skip a step, why an argument is ordered, why a journal entry is dated. An outside instrument can now produce the artifact without those constraints. The student who has them can use AI as a problem-solving tool inside a field they already understand. The student who skipped them can prompt for outputs they can’t check. This isn’t a fresh derivation. It is the genuine-participation test spent on a solver that will never hold the standards for itself.

Implementing capabilities-oriented pedagogy at scale faces real institutional obstacles: standardized-testing infrastructure built around output-shape rubrics, credentialing systems that reward content-coverage, teacher-evaluation systems that select against the skills required here. These obstacles are handled at the implementation level by the sequence, measurement, reversibility, and audit requirements of §6.15; in education, that means treating testing, credentialing, and teacher-evaluation reform as implementation problems rather than as objections to the educational requirement itself.

*Relation-capacity is foundational, and formal education can neglect it.* Cooperative life depends on what happens when subjects share conditions. Communication, conflict navigation, recognizing manipulation, setting and respecting limits, repairing ruptures, and grieving what has ended are therefore participation-relevant capacities. How much formal instruction students currently receive, which methods help, and what belongs to schools rather than families or other institutions vary by setting; the structural point is that the capacity can’t be treated as irrelevant merely because it isn’t a conventional content domain.

*Consent belongs here.* Consent amounts to will operating at a threshold of modal competence, not mere verbal selection. A subject must understand what is asked: what consequences may follow, what alternatives exist, whether refusal is safe, whether power is asymmetrical, and what future self-states may be affected. Relation-education is therefore not etiquette. It is education in what makes participation a live possibility, at the site where vulnerability is most immediate.

These aren’t soft skills supplementary to real education. They are capacities used throughout political, economic, and cooperative life. Their absence can contribute to conflict, isolation, workplace dysfunction, or susceptibility to domination, but education is neither the only cause nor the complete remedy for those outcomes. The claim here is a curricular burden of relevance: where reliable teaching can develop relational competence without overstepping evidence or family and cultural plurality, an educational architecture should not dismiss it as ornamental.

*Neurodivergence isn’t a deviation from equal standing.* ADHD, autism, dyslexia, and other forms of neurodivergence can involve disabling impairments, distinctive capacities, or both, with wide variation among people carrying the same label. Educational and occupational structures can intensify those difficulties when they treat one cognitive profile—compliant, sequential, patient with repetition—as the measure of intelligence itself. Accommodation doesn’t require romanticizing every trait as an advantage or denying support for real impairment. It requires identifying which barrier belongs to the person’s condition, which is imposed by the environment, and which design lets the student develop and demonstrate capability without lowering the substantive standard.

The ADHD case makes the interaction visible. Hyperfocus, novelty-seeking, restlessness with repetition, or rapidly connecting several threads can be useful in some contexts and impairing in others. A student with ADHD in a rote, sit-still-and-repeat curriculum isn’t simply failing education; education may also be failing them. ADHD is associated with significantly elevated rates of accidents and all-cause mortality (Dalsgaard et al. 2015; Barkley 2015), but that association doesn’t by itself divide causal responsibility between the condition, comorbidities, treatment access, and environmental mismatch. It raises the upstream question the chapter asks elsewhere: which harms persist under better-fitting conditions, and which are amplified by avoidable design?

The conditions of maximum possibility are for everyone. If the polity is designed around one cognitive template, people whose architecture diverges from it can be denied the conditions needed to develop or display their capacities. Cognitive diversity can also widen the repertoire of perspectives and problem-solving strategies available to a community. It doesn’t guarantee that every cognitive profile fits every task or that diversity solves more problems by itself. The institutional requirement is narrower: don’t mistake fit with one inherited classroom design for intelligence, and test whether alternative supports preserve standards while opening genuine participation.

*Racialized educational inequality is the same structural failure read along the race dimension.* The conditions-before-population diagnostic applied to neurodivergence applies with equal force to the racial stratification of educational outcomes.

Where school funding depends heavily on local property values, segregated residential geography can reproduce resource disparities without an explicit racial rule. Resegregation, tracking, ability grouping, and disciplinary differences can add further sorting, though their magnitude and causes vary across systems and require separate evidence. The diagnostic from §6.2 therefore applies: before an achievement gap is attributed to a population, examine the conditions for developing capability—funding, teacher capacity, access to demanding instruction, constructive intergroup contact, and the chronic-stress load of under-resourced or over-disciplined schooling. Conditions don’t explain every difference by definition; they are variables that must not disappear from the account.

Mills’s white-ignorance analysis (*The Racial Contract* 1997; *Black Rights / White Wrongs* 2017) presses the further point that the curriculum and canon are themselves not racially neutral: what counts as the shared reference base (the desideratum the Hirsch exchange already considered takes up) has historically been specified in ways that encode whose knowledge counts, and a capabilities-oriented pedagogy that doesn’t examine that specification reproduces the ignorance structurally rather than correcting it.

The *direction-from-all* commitment bears against systematic racialized differences in access on the same logic that applies to any required educational tool: a population whose conditions for developing capabilities are under-maintained can’t participate in recognized direction on equal terms (§6.3). Where an institution makes AI or another tool part of instruction or assessment, access to that use must not reproduce the same disparity. The structural claim concerns equal access to the educational function, not identical equipment in every classroom.

At political scale, education has to develop the capacities on which participation depends across the population. The floor is functional: durable knowledge and judgment, genuine access, protection against stratification and extraction, accommodation compatible with substantive standards, and the ability to evaluate rather than merely repeat. These functions may be combined and implemented differently; the list doesn’t turn one competency taxonomy into a constitution. Evidence-sensitive priorities such as early-childhood investment govern expected effectiveness and sequence. They don’t become categorical merely because an average return is high.

*Universal access to capability development at the foundation.* Every participant in the political community has access to the developmental conditions necessary to take up the participation conditions derived at §6.1. The condition holds at the foundation: small-scale private alternatives (private schools, religious schools, micro-school cooperatives, homeschooling) remain legitimate within the educational ecology; what is precluded is stratification at scale or any architecture that routes the educational foundation through profit-extracting substitutes that fail to deliver the capability-development the foundation requires. Specific schooling-design among permissible alternatives (public-school monopoly; public-school-with-charters; voucher systems with strong quality-foundation regulation; hybrid public-private architectures) is underdetermined.

*Develop capability, not credentials alone.* The system must develop the capacities, not merely issue credentials that signal them. Designs that optimize issuing credentials over developing capability violate the condition at scale. The condition doesn’t preclude credentials (signaling has legitimate functions); it precludes credentials without capability as the system’s primary output. Assessment regimes have to register whether participants have crossed the modeling thresholds the capacities require, not merely whether they have moved content through short-term memory for retrieval.

*Curriculum coverage of participation-relevant capacities.* Six useful domains can be distinguished: cognitive, informational, financial, technological, relational, and civic. They name functions an education may need to perform, not six freestanding courses or a claim that every capacity is equally teachable at every age. The cognitive domain concerns modeling and problem solving; the informational concerns evaluating claims; the financial concerns navigating consequential economic decisions; the technological concerns understanding and judging tools; the relational concerns communication, limits, conflict, and repair; and the civic concerns political recognition and collective decision-making (§6.3; §6.1). Their boundaries overlap, and a different curriculum may organize them under other names. Coverage is adequate when participants develop the relevant capabilities in durable, transferable form; pedagogy, sequence, content, and developmental staging remain open to evidence.

*Anti-stratification at scale and anti-extraction at the financing contact.* Educational architectures that produce systematic stratification at scale (capability disparities between tiers propagating into downstream representation, economic, and civic disparities) are precluded. Higher-education financing primarily through individual debt at scales the empirical record displays (above earnings-recovery capacity for substantial subgroups) is structural extraction at the developmental contact and is precluded. Various financing models satisfy the alternative constraint (free public higher education; income-share agreements with structural protections; collective-investment funding through general taxation); the debt-extraction model is precluded at scale, with no pick made among the alternatives. For-profit-education channels that route public-loan dollars through marketing-as-instructional-value architectures with low completion and high default are precluded on the same logic.

*Early-childhood investment priority (a maximization condition, not a foundation gate).* The developmental account and the Heckman literature (Heckman 2006; Heckman and Masterov 2007; Heckman 2013) support giving early capability development strong priority because plasticity is high and benefits can compound across a long horizon. But the priority attaches to effective, developmentally appropriate support, not to every program carrying the label *pre-K*. Perry and Abecedarian show that intensive, high-quality programs for disadvantaged children can produce durable returns; the Tennessee Voluntary Pre-K randomized follow-up (Lipsey et al. 2018; Durkin et al. 2022) shows that a scaled program can yield fadeout and later null or adverse outcomes. Skipping effective early support may therefore secure the foundation less efficiently, but front-loading an ineffective design doesn’t satisfy the priority. Specific architectures (universal pre-K, home visiting, integrated family support, subsidized high-quality childcare, or combinations) remain underdetermined and answer to measured quality, counterfactual care, subgroup effects, durability, and downstream return.

*Cognitive-diversity accommodation as design constraint.* The conditions of participation are for everyone. Classroom architecture, pacing, assessment, and credentialing therefore have to distinguish substantive capability from fit with one inherited cognitive template. Neurodivergence can include variation, impairment, or both; equal standing requires reasonable routes to develop and demonstrate capability without assuming that every difference is advantageous or that every standard must change. The elevated accident and mortality associations reported for ADHD (Dalsgaard et al. 2015; Barkley 2015) establish serious outcomes, not school-design causation. The structure-mismatch hypothesis must be tested by whether accommodations improve capability and downstream outcomes relative to comparable unsupported settings.

*Procedural neutrality on contested normative and political questions.* The capacity the curriculum is required to build is the capacity to evaluate, not a specific evaluation delivered as settled fact. On questions genuinely contested within the polity’s own recognized plurality (contested political, economic, religious, and moral questions, as distinct from questions of empirical or scientific consensus), the foundation requires that curriculum expose students to genuine live disagreement and to the reasoning on more than one side, rather than teach a single contested position as the settled conclusion the work of developing capabilities was building toward. A curriculum that develops the critical-thinking capacity derived here while directing that capacity toward one contested conclusion has substituted indoctrination for the capacity it claims to cultivate, whatever the political valence of the conclusion. This condition gives the parental-authority boundary named at the chapter root its adjudicating test directly: an above-the-foundation choice (religious schooling, alternative pedagogy, homeschooling) stays above the foundation exactly as long as it doesn’t foreclose the student’s later capacity to encounter and evaluate the contested question at all; it crosses below the foundation when it does, regardless of which side of the question the foreclosure favors. The condition binds its own curriculum-relevant claims to the same standard it applies to any other institution: where its own positions on contested political-economic questions enter classroom material, they are subject to the same live-disagreement requirement as any other contested position, not exempted from it by the derivation’s own confidence in its conclusions.

*Tool-use registers the genuine-participation distinction.* As technology extends the cognitive reach available to participants, educational architectures must register the distinction between participants doing the modeling themselves while using tools to extend their reach (still modeling the problem, evaluating the solution, and understanding what it means) and participants who have handed the cognitive work to the tool while claiming credit for its output. The condition is genuine participation in the cognitive work, not a rule about which tools are permitted. That work includes the constraints of the form: why this artifact is shaped as it is, so the tool’s return can be judged against that shape rather than accepted as an output. Assessment regimes have to register that distinction at every developmental stage where tools are part of the cognitive environment. As tools extend further (AI; future cognitive-extension technologies), the condition extends with them.

Together, these conditions specify the work capability-development infrastructure has to do. Universal access, durable capability rather than credential issuance alone, protection against stratification and extraction, cognitive-diversity accommodation, procedural neutrality on genuinely contested questions, and verifiable participation when tools are used are floor functions. They don’t all require separate institutions, and a design may satisfy one function through several routes. Early-childhood investment is an evidence-sensitive maximization priority instead. Its strength, sequence, and form must change when comparative evidence shows a later intervention or different design produces more durable capability per unit of cost. The set remains open to correction by the measurements and failure conditions at §6.9.3.

### 6.9.3 Predictions
The account of education as capability development, paired with the anti-extraction constraint, predicts differences that must be visible in outcomes rather than inferred from institutional labels. Each prediction therefore specifies a comparison, measures, and a failure condition. Jurisdictions should pre-register the relevant capability foundation and time horizon; disaggregate results by income, race, disability, neurotype, language, provider type, and prior attainment; and count administrative, fiscal, and transition costs.

*First.* Effective educational investment should reduce later costs in justice, healthcare, and lost earnings. Compare otherwise similar cohorts differentially exposed to exogenous school-finance reforms, program eligibility thresholds, lotteries, or phased implementation. Measure completion, earnings, poverty, health, incarceration, and public expenditure over a stated horizon, together with the full cost of the intervention. The prediction is supported when credible causal estimates show durable capability gains and downstream savings or gains that justify the upstream cost. It fails as a general claim if well-powered, transported replications show no durable gains, if benefits are confined to outcomes mechanically targeted by the program, or if total costs exceed downstream benefits under reasonable discount rates.

*Second.* Stratified educational tiers should reproduce capability and participation gaps when access to effective instruction, peers, teachers, or credentials tracks family resources. Measure within- and between-provider gaps in demonstrated capability, completion, civic participation, earnings, and mobility, while separating selection into providers from provider effects through lotteries, boundary changes, or matched longitudinal designs. The relevant variable isn’t whether a provider is public or private but whether the architecture produces unequal effective access to the foundation. The prediction fails if a plural-provider system preserves universal foundation attainment and doesn’t widen downstream gaps after selection and compositional effects are addressed.

*Third.* School resources and family or neighborhood conditions should each matter, with their interaction determined empirically rather than assumed. Estimate the effect of exogenous changes in per-pupil resources across differing baselines of housing stability, health, income, and neighborhood exposure. Measure both average effects and whether complementary supports amplify, merely add to, or substitute for school spending. The prediction fails if credible designs repeatedly show one side contributes no independent effect, or if integrated programs don’t outperform their separately measured components where complementarity was predicted.

*Fourth.* Credential systems should become extractive when required credentials rise without corresponding growth in task requirements or demonstrated capability. Track degree requirements for stable occupations, tuition and time costs, validated job-task measures, wage returns, completion, and employer performance. Distinguish legitimate upskilling from screening: rising requirements count as inflation only when the work hasn’t changed and the credential adds no validated capability. The prediction fails if requirement growth is explained by changing tasks, if credentials reliably add the relevant capability, or if capability-based hiring doesn’t achieve comparable performance with lower exclusion and cost.

*Fifth.* Higher-education finance should breach the foundation where payment obligations are predictably unrecoverable from the education they financed. Measure completion, debt-to-income and payment-to-income ratios, delinquency, default, wealth, occupational choice, and consumption by institution, program, income, race, and completion status. Compare conventional debt with grants, income-contingent repayment, public provision, and other protected designs after administrative burden and taxpayer cost are counted. Debt itself isn’t the predicted failure; the failure is a net burden after accounting for incidence that blocks participation without proportionate educational return. The prediction fails if protected debt designs preserve access and repayment capacity as well as or better than alternatives, or if claimed harms disappear after completion, selection, and earnings are addressed.

*Sixth.* Effective early-childhood support should often yield high returns, especially for children facing the largest developmental constraints, but the size and ordering of returns should vary with program quality, counterfactual care, later-school quality, and subgroup. Compare randomized admission, eligibility cutoffs, or credible phased rollouts; measure cognitive and social-emotional capability, grade progression, health, earnings, and justice involvement through long follow-up. Perry and Abecedarian motivate the prediction; Tennessee Voluntary Pre-K supplies a contrary case that prevents universalizing it. The prediction fails in a jurisdiction when early gains fade without later benefit, adverse effects persist, or a later-stage investment produces more durable capability per dollar.

*Seventh.* Institutional extraction and individual credential fraud should share incentives but need not move symmetrically. Measure public subsidy retained per completion, instructional spending, earnings value added, defaults, deceptive marketing, cheating, and credential fraud. Test whether weak verification, high-stakes credentials, and information asymmetry predict both forms after opportunity and enforcement differ. The shared-mechanism claim fails if the two patterns don’t covary under comparable incentive changes or require materially different explanations.

*Eighth.* A capability-centered and procedurally neutral system should produce transfer: participants should be able to reason through unfamiliar problems, represent strong opposing positions, detect manipulation, revise beliefs when evidence changes, and use tools without surrendering evaluation. Use novel-task assessments, blinded argument evaluation, delayed retesting, and oral or process-based verification rather than output shape alone. On genuinely contested questions, audit whether recognized live positions receive accurate steelmanning and whether students can later encounter and assess alternatives. The prediction fails if capability-centered designs don’t improve transfer over content-retrieval controls, if neutrality becomes false balance against settled evidence, or if the curriculum predictably produces rigid assent without independent evaluative competence.

These predictions engage the voucher, parental-authority, and deschooling objections in §6.9.1 without deciding among providers in advance. They test whether an architecture delivers universal, durable capability after selection, incidence, subgroup effects, and total cost are counted. A favored institution that fails those tests isn’t rescued by its label; an unfavored one that passes them isn’t excluded here.

### 6.9.4 Confirmation
The predictions at §6.9.3 are read against the empirical and theoretical literature on education-system performance. The confirmation standard is graded: descriptive association establishes a pattern; longitudinal or matched comparison narrows alternatives; lotteries, discontinuities, court-ordered finance changes, and randomized programs support causal attribution; replicated effects across settings support transportability. A feasibility case can show that an architecture is possible without showing that it caused the observed outcome, and theoretical convergence can corroborate a result without empirically confirming it.

*First.* Educational investment can produce durable downstream gains. Jackson, Johnson, and Persico (2016) use court-induced school-finance reforms to identify effects of sustained K–12 spending on completed education, adult wages, and poverty, with larger effects for children from low-income families. Perry and Abecedarian follow randomized intensive early-childhood programs into later education, earnings, health, and justice outcomes. These designs strongly support the proposition that effective investment can matter beyond test scores. They don’t establish that every expenditure, curriculum, or early-childhood program pays for itself, and the cost-saving claim remains program-, population-, and horizon-specific.

*Second.* Resource and access stratification are well documented; privatization isn’t by itself the identified cause. Reardon (2011) and related work document income-achievement gaps, and school-finance research identifies unequal resources and gains from equalizing reforms. Putnam (2015) describes the broader opportunity gap, while Bowles and Gintis and Bourdieu supply influential reproduction theories rather than clean causal estimates. Voucher and charter evidence is heterogeneous across programs: rigorous studies include negative, null, and positive outcomes depending on provider quality, regulation, selection, and outcome measured. The record confirms the danger of tiered effective access, not a universal public-versus-private ranking.

*Third.* Outcomes track both school resources and conditions beyond school. Jackson, Johnson, and Persico identify effects of exogenous spending changes; Chetty and collaborators identify neighborhood and mobility effects (e.g., Chetty and Hendren 2018). This supports independent contribution from both channels. The stronger claim that they always compound non-additively, or that every holistic program outperforms every targeted one, isn’t established by those citations alone. Interaction, substitution, and implementation quality must be estimated in each design.

*Fourth.* Credential inflation is descriptively supported but incompletely identified. Collins (1979) supplies the theory; job-posting studies document degree requirements rising in some occupations whose recorded tasks didn’t rise proportionately, and employer surveys report perceived readiness gaps. Those findings support testing for screening and unnecessary exclusion. They don’t by themselves prove that credentials added no capability, that the underlying jobs were unchanged in every relevant respect, or that readiness surveys measure performance without bias. The joint claim is therefore provisional until task change, worker selection, and validated performance are measured together.

*Fifth.* Student-debt burdens are sharply heterogeneous. Aggregate balances and tuition growth describe scale, not extraction by themselves. The strongest evidence concerns incidence: non-completers and low-return programs face high repayment risk; Armona, Chakrabarti, and Lovenheim (2022) find that for-profit attendance relative to local public alternatives increases borrowing and default risk and can worsen labor-market outcomes; Cellini’s work (e.g., Cellini and Turner 2019) documents high prices and weak returns in important for-profit segments. Income-driven repayment can reduce short-run delinquency, though administrative burden and longer-run disconnection complicate the result. This confirms a distributional risk after accounting for incidence at particular institutions and for particular borrowers, not a universal analogy between student lending and health insurance and not the claim that every educational loan is extractive.

*Sixth.* High-quality early-childhood programs can produce large and durable returns, but universal dominance isn’t confirmed. Perry and Abecedarian are unusually intensive randomized programs serving disadvantaged children and support long-horizon benefits under those conditions. The Tennessee Voluntary Pre-K randomized follow-up found initial gains followed by fadeout and later null or adverse outcomes through sixth grade (Lipsey et al. 2018; Durkin et al. 2022). The earned conclusion is an early-development priority conditioned on quality, counterfactual care, subgroup, later-school environment, and durable measured return—not that any early dollar necessarily beats every later dollar.

*Seventh.* Institutional extraction is documented in specific channels; cross-scale symmetry remains a hypothesis. For-profit default and completion evidence supports the institutional case where subsidy and credential dependence aren’t matched by educational value. Testing, preparation, and textbook markets establish prices and incentives but require evidence of excess return, capture, or blocked alternatives before they count as extraction. Cheating and credential fraud are real individual failures, yet the present record doesn’t show that they covary symmetrically with institutional extraction. The common-incentive mechanism is plausible and testable, not confirmed merely because examples exist at both scales.

Three registers of the comparative record converge here: Finland, relational-skills evidence, and ADHD outcomes.

*Finland and other comparators.* Finland’s National Core Curriculum organizes learning around transversal competencies including learning to learn, daily life, critical and creative thinking, and participation in a sustainable future (Finnish National Core Curriculum 2016). Financial and social-emotional learning are integrated across subjects rather than treated only as add-ons. Other Northern European systems and Australia organize some of the same capacities differently. These cases establish feasibility, not causal superiority. Outcomes covary with teacher preparation and status, funding, selection, social trust, population, and institutions a cross-country comparison can’t separate. The comparison therefore shows that capability-oriented curricula can operate at scale; whether a particular curricular feature produces transfer requires stronger designs.

*Relationship-pattern evidence.* Gottman’s research identifies contempt, criticism, defensiveness, and stonewalling as correlates of relationship breakdown across longitudinal samples (Gottman and Silver 1994; Gottman and Levenson 2000). The widely circulated *over-90%-accuracy* figure has been criticized as retrospective overfitting rather than out-of-sample prediction (Heyman and Smith Slep 2001), so no curricular claim rides on that number. Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication (2003) offers one practical framework, while attachment research (Bowlby 1969; Ainsworth et al. 1978) examines how early relational patterns can affect later relationships. These literatures make some relational capacities plausible teaching targets; they don’t establish that every pattern is learned, that one program reliably changes it, or that schools are always the best provider. That stronger case requires intervention evidence.

*OECD on social-and-emotional implementation gaps.* The OECD’s 2023 survey found that more than 90 percent of school leaders describe developing social and emotional skills as a core objective alongside academic achievement, while implementation and teacher preparation remain uneven (Coleman et al. 2024). That gap establishes a difference between stated priority and reported capacity; it doesn’t show which curriculum closes it or that every older student faces the same unmet need. Finland supplies an operating illustration. Intervention and transfer evidence must establish whether particular instruction produces durable relational competence.

*ADHD outcomes and the structure-mismatch hypothesis.* ADHD is associated with elevated accident and mortality risks (Dalsgaard et al. 2015; Barkley 2015), especially from unnatural causes. That association establishes the seriousness of the outcome but doesn’t identify how much is caused by school design, accommodation, treatment access, comorbidity, discrimination, or cognitive architecture. The structure-mismatch account is compatible with the evidence and generates a test: accommodation changes should improve capability and reduce downstream harm relative to comparable unsupported settings. Until such designs identify that pathway, the causal share remains open.

*On theoretical convergences.* These conclusions are independently reached in: capabilities-approach educational theory (Sen 1999; Nussbaum 2011 on capability-development through education), critical pedagogy (Freire 1968), Deweyan progressive education, sociology-of-education research (Bowles and Gintis (1976); Bourdieu and Passeron on cultural capital (1970)), and developmental psychology (Vygotsky on the zone of proximal development; Piaget on developmental stages). Agreement reached from these independent starting points corroborates the conclusions without supplying their grounding.

*What the record rules out—and what it doesn’t.* The evidence rules out two universal claims: that market delivery reliably supplies quality without strong foundation, information, and anti-extraction constraints, and that educational investment generally can’t change durable outcomes. Poor for-profit outcomes and negative voucher estimates refute universal market superiority; positive, null, and negative choice results also prevent the opposite claim that every plural-provider design fails. School-finance reforms and intensive early-childhood programs show that investment can matter; heterogeneous and adverse pre-K results prevent treating spending or timing as sufficient. The record therefore supports its design-neutral foundation and its demand for causal, subgroup, and incidence tests. It doesn’t empirically settle every parental-authority, provider, pedagogy, or heritability dispute named in §6.9.1.

### 6.9.5 Conclusions
*Structural constraints.* Education develops capacities the political community presupposes participants to have, so responsibility for a universal capability foundation can’t be privatized away. That fixes the outcome owed, not the provider: public schools, regulated vouchers, nonprofit or private schools, cooperatives, religious schools, home education, and mixed systems can satisfy or violate the constraint according to effective access, capability development, plurality, stratification, and extraction. Credentials remain legitimate signals when they track real capability; credential dependence without capability doesn’t. Higher-education finance fails when its net burden after accounting for incidence is predictably unrecoverable for substantial groups and blocks participation without proportionate educational return; debt isn’t categorically precluded where completion, earnings, protected repayment, and administrative access keep the foundation intact. Early-childhood support is a strong maximization priority where program quality, counterfactual care, and durable effects justify it, not a categorical rule that every early dollar outranks every later intervention. The maximal categorical result is universal capability development under procedural neutrality and genuine access; financing, provision, sequence, and pedagogy remain corrigible instruments.

*Cross-domain couplings.* Education couples to representation (§6.3), economy (§6.7), healthcare (§6.10), justice (§6.13), and the information environment (§6.4), but the size of each coupling is empirical. Capability disparities can impair recognition and economic mobility; credible school-finance and intensive-program evidence shows that some educational investments affect earnings, poverty, health, or justice outcomes. Those findings make education a plausible upstream intervention in several domains without making every healthcare or justice burden an educational failure or every educational expenditure an equally effective remedy. Resistance to disinformation likewise depends on media systems, incentives, identity, and trust as well as evaluative capacity. Cross-domain claims therefore require measured mediation and can’t be inferred from correlation alone.

*Neighbors.* No specific schooling design is endorsed: public systems, charters, vouchers, private or religious schools, cooperatives, home education, and hybrids can each satisfy or violate the constraint depending on access, capability, stratification, accountability, and extraction. Nor is one curriculum or pedagogy selected; the implementation question—what knowledge and capacities, at which developmental stages, through which methods—belongs to educational research and recognized public direction. Higher-education finance requires reform where debt is predictably unrecoverable for substantial groups and blocks participation without corresponding educational return. That conditional finding doesn’t classify every feature of one national system as extractive or choose among public provision, grants, protected repayment, restructuring, risk sharing, and mixed designs. Provider size and identity don’t decide the case in advance; demonstrated outcomes and incidence do.

*Cognitive diversity, relational capacity, and AI-tool use.* A system designed around one cognitive template can mistake environmental fit for capability. It should test accommodations and alternative assessment routes against the same substantive standards, without denying impairment or assuming every difference is advantageous. Relational capacities likewise warrant curricular attention where evidence shows that instruction produces durable transfer and where schools are an appropriate provider; no single therapeutic or communication framework is derived. AI sharpens the genuine-participation test. Tool use can extend reach or bypass the modeling the task was meant to develop. The relevant questions are whether the student can explain the problem, evaluate the solution, identify failure, and understand why the form is constrained as it is. At some developmental stages that may require unaided work; at others it may require supervised tool use. Assessment should register the cognitive participation actually at stake rather than treat either use or nonuse as proof of competence.

What remains open is a specific schooling-design among permissible alternatives, the curricular content beyond the capability-development constraint, the pedagogical methods, higher-education financing beyond the bar on extractive debt at scale, the testing-and-assessment systems beyond the bar on credentialing without capability development, the calibration of public-school, charter, voucher, and private-alternative components in any given polity, the teacher-credentialing, certification, and compensation architectures, and the reform paths from current configurations to permissible alternatives. Where more than one design will do, the choice is handed here to the design literatures, the empirical record, and the recognized direction of the population through §6.3 (Representation).

Boiled down, the argument holds one maximal earned thesis: education is capability development for participation, and every participant is owed access to the cognitive, informational, financial, technological, relational, and civic capacities required to understand and direct a life shared with others. The foundation includes cognitive-diversity accommodation, genuine participation when tools are used, and procedural neutrality that equips students to evaluate live disagreement rather than delivering one contested conclusion as settled. Evidence strongly supports that effective resources and some intensive programs can improve durable outcomes, that stratified access and low-return institutions can impose serious harms, and that debt burdens concentrate among non-completers and low-return programs. It doesn’t support a universal provider ranking, automatic early-childhood dominance, or the classification of every credential, loan, or private return as extraction. The book therefore keeps that conclusion while making every institutional instrument answer to transfer, durability, incidence, subgroup, and total-cost tests.

## 6.10 Healthcare
Everything else in political life assumes the people in it are alive and well enough to take part, which makes health care not one more service a society offers but part of the foundation the rest of society stands on. Even the most limited view of government grants that a community must not let its people be killed or left to preventable violence; untreated illness, injury, and unmanaged pain can remove participation through the same body, so excluding healthcare from the maintenance foundation requires a distinction the outcome itself doesn’t supply. The obligation is universal effective access to adequate care, not one uniquely required payer or provider. Public, nonprofit, regulated private, savings-based, social-insurance, and mixed systems must be judged after premiums, taxes, cost sharing, waiting, denial, quality, and fiscal sustainability are counted. Profit becomes extraction when it is obtained through vulnerability, information asymmetry, gatekeeping, or public privilege without proportionate contribution while people are left below the foundation; an earned return that improves access or capacity isn’t condemned merely because it is private. Questions about one’s own body land here too—what to take, whether to continue a pregnancy, how to meet the end of life—but their exact answers require additional premises about autonomy, standing, risk, and harm rather than following from universal access alone.

The people whose direction a political community is meant to recognize must be alive and well enough for that recognition to mean anything. Healthcare derives from Consciousness (§5.1), §5.3 (Feeling), and §5.9 (Mortality), read at the institutional scale established in §6.2. Consciousness is the vantage of a living closure, a corollary of Cartesian Certainty and Life. If that vantage is what being a participant *is*, then maintaining conscious participants isn’t one good among many that the political community might or might not provide. It is what makes political participation possible in the first place.

Feeling and the proximity of death give the point its urgency. A person in pain or danger isn’t merely uncomfortable; their capacity to take part in civic life is at stake. The modal field (§5.4) the person holds collapses toward crisis-management whenever the body holding it is in pain, threatened, or breaking down. That field is the structured space of action-possibility within which any meaningful participation occurs. Pain and crisis collapse the field toward one line. A body that never stops is the same collapse by another route. Rest, time off, and parental leave are care: they restore the vantage participation requires. They aren’t a Right to Rest. Healthcare is how some preservation-lines get back into the map before Drive hits the limit (§5.2, §6.12).

In a suicidal crisis, ongoing suffering can look like the only possibility left. Care isn’t merely a command to stay. It is an attempt to put a livable line back in the field—therapy, someone who can talk, pain relief, material support, and time enough to register exits the person may not yet see. A wish formed under deprivation or illness isn’t non-agentive by category, but neither does its sincerity establish that the field has been mapped or that capacity is intact. The residual end-of-life question comes later and rests on additional premises.

Healthcare maintains the conditions under which that person can participate at all. Participation is unavailable to subject $s$ without that maintenance. The obligation is the right to life at *bios*, not a welfare add-on.

**[Right]**

**Healthcare** · *Right*

Participation is unavailable to subject $s$ without effective care. That care includes mental-health care that can put livable lines back in the field, and rest: time off and parental leave. Rest is not a further right. Consciousness as vantage is the standing-gate, not the autobiographical I. Payer form stays open.

**Depends on:** Consciousness (§5.1), Feeling (§5.3), Mortality (§5.9), and The Chapter 6 Premises (§6.1)

The Healthcare right therefore sits on the side of the aversion-asymmetry (§6.1) the libertarian frame already concedes. Political community has uncontested obligations on the aversive-prevention side: don’t let participants be killed, don’t let them be unjustly imprisoned, don’t let them be subjected to violence the [polity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) could have prevented. Healthcare is the maximum-force case of that conceded obligation: the conditions whose failure dissolves bodily participation directly, on the side of the asymmetry Subsistence is placed on at §6.1 through the *bios* reading. The frame’s selective acceptance of negative-aversive obligation for harms enemies and criminals could cause, while denying it for harms disease, injury, and unmanaged pain produce, is internal incoherence rather than principled distinction. Both work the same way structurally: they dissolve the body’s modal field below the threshold required for participation. The asymmetry doesn’t care about the proximal cause; it cares about the outcome the polity is committed to preventing.

The argument places healthcare *upstream* of agentive participation rather than parallel to it. A political community that fails to maintain its participants’ baseline health isn’t failing at one of its tasks; it is failing at the precondition of having tasks. Where it was derived at §6.7 that mechanisms substituting for subsistence maintenance are structurally precluded, healthcare is the case where that derivation lands at maximum force: the foundation is the participants themselves, in the constitutive vulnerabilities that make them participants in the first place. The bodily-health and bodily-integrity capabilities Nussbaum develops in *Women and Human Development* (2000) and *Frontiers of Justice* (2006, Part I) directly engage healthcare as a constitutive capability: Part I’s disability-case analysis bears directly on the disability-rights critique passage, and the capabilities-approach methodology of starting from concrete cases that dominant theories have marginalized converges with the wanting-downstream result (§6.1) applied here.

A working person who breaks an arm and skips the emergency room because they can’t afford the deductible is recognizing the failure the foundation exists to prevent: their participation capacity has been narrowed by structural cost rather than by the injury itself. A society in which that calculation never has to be made is what the healthcare derivation calls for; whether single-payer, multi-payer-with-foundation, or hybrid is the architecture that delivers it is left to design literatures and recognized direction.

A genuine participation foundation covers health needs as people actually have them, not a neutral-looking average that silently undercounts one body’s costs. Menstrual products, reproductive care, disability supports, and recovery time aren’t special pleading added to a general list; they are tests of whether the list was general in the first place. Parental leave belongs here insofar as bearing, recovery, bonding, and infant care are health and participation conditions. The exact benefit, duration, and institutional channel remain design questions shared with Economy.

*Accessibility and the earnings trap.* Mobility aids, personal assistance, adaptive equipment, and navigable settings maintain participation rather than reward it. Programs that withdraw those supports at an earnings threshold can turn the floor into a ceiling, forcing a person to choose between the support that makes participation possible and the work it enables. The §6.1 result names the form: the foundation is neither earned by participation nor forfeited by it. Partial capacity is ordinary; a constraint on one axis doesn’t erase agency on the others. A foundation that competes with the participation it exists to enable contradicts its own purpose.

*Insurance and structural extraction at the foundation.* Risk pooling isn’t structurally redundant merely because the foundation is collectively owed; Beveridge, Bismarck, single-payer, regulated multi-payer, and Singaporean systems all pool catastrophic risk through different institutions. What the derivation precludes is making effective access depend on an intermediary’s ability to profit by leaving necessary care uncovered or unaffordable. Claim denial, risk selection, opaque pricing, administrative duplication, and margins unsupported by contribution are therefore tested after incidence and outcomes rather than classified by institutional label. A public payer can ration badly, a private or nonprofit insurer can administer a foundation successfully, and either can fail through waiting, underpayment, capture, exclusion, or waste. The categorical constraint is that no architecture may leave participants below adequate care because of payment status or extract returns from a gatekeeping position without proportionate value.

The symmetry note from Economy (§6.7) applies in full force here: individual-scale fraud (staged accidents, false claims, gaming benefits) is a structural infraction on everyone who contributes to the pool, on the same logic. Neither party is moralized against preferentially; the structural form is identified here, and the form is left to do the work. Employer-sponsored insurance in particular operates as Private Government extension (Anderson, *Private Government* 2017): healthcare access tied to employment converts at-will employment into something stronger, since dismissal now revokes healthcare with it: a deeper domination structure than the wage relation alone, and the workplace-authority register (§6.7) applies directly at the healthcare contact.

*Race-stratified healthcare tests recognition at maximum force.* Maternal mortality, pain undertreatment, race-adjusted clinical tools, and the record running through Tuskegee, Henrietta Lacks, and J. Marion Sims show that nominal access can coexist with unequal recognition and care (Hoffman et al. 2016; Vyas et al. 2020; Roberts, *Killing the Black Body* 1997). The foundation must therefore be measured not only at the front door but in diagnosis, treatment, outcomes, trust, and whose testimony clinicians believe. The current disparity record is tested under Confirmation rather than made to carry the derivation here.

### 6.10.1 The Dispute
*Engaging the classical-liberal health-policy objection.* Three counter-traditions press directly on the foundation just derived: Friedman’s medical-licensure and consumer-directed-care critique (*Capitalism and Freedom* 1962, ch. IX), the Cato-tradition Singapore medical-savings-account and catastrophic-coverage architecture, and Pauly’s moral-hazard analysis, which asks how insurance changes behavior and cost (*The Economics of Moral Hazard* 1968). Grant the central concession in each case.

Licensure-rent capture is granted in the form the licensure-economics literature has confirmed; its anti-extraction architecture (§6.7) applies symmetrically.

Singapore-style medical savings plus catastrophic coverage is one permissible institutional arrangement alongside single-payer and regulated multi-payer systems, but it isn’t evidence for a minimally governed cash market: Singapore combines mandatory savings, national catastrophic insurance, direct subsidies, public provision, price and capacity management, and a final safety net. Its contribution is to show that universal responsibility can coexist with cost sharing and plural finance when the foundation is protected.

Moral hazard is granted in its empirical form: RAND and later insurance experiments show that lower out-of-pocket prices increase use. They also show that patients reduce effective and ineffective care together, so cost sharing isn’t a reliable clinical sorter. Price signals can therefore be compatible with the foundation only when exemptions, caps, income adjustment, and clinical safeguards keep necessary care genuinely accessible.

The parting from the consumer-directed account is not because every price is coercive, but because a price that predictably deters necessary care below the foundation fails the outcome the architecture is obligated to secure. Convergence with the classical-liberal tradition holds on price signals above the foundation, on opposition to licensure-rent capture, and on Singapore-MSA as a permissible design alternative; the parting is on whether the foundation is a market contact or the precondition of having markets at all.

Daniels’s *Just Health Care* (1985) and *Just Health* (2008) extend Rawlsian political-liberalism to healthcare through the normal-opportunity-range argument (that healthcare is constitutive of fair equality of opportunity rather than additive to it) converging with its upstream-of-agentive-participation derivation on different grounds. The parting from the Daniels/Rawls grounding is on grounding: normal-opportunity-range grounds healthcare standing in fair-equality-of-opportunity (which the original-position procedure delivers), while this grounds it directly in §5.14 mutual recognition and the participation conditions that recognition presupposes.

The care-ethics tradition reaches the healthcare-as-precondition conclusion on a third set of grounds. Kittay (*Love’s Labor* 1999), Held (*The Ethics of Care* 2006), and Tronto (*Moral Boundaries* 1993) ground moral and political obligation in the dependency relation itself: every subject is, across the lifespan, both a recipient and a giver of care, and the caregiving relation, not the contract among independent equals, is the relation political theory has to take as basic.

The central claim is granted and treated as convergent: healthcare on its account is the institutional form the care-relation takes once the subjects who depend on one another number in millions, and the dependency the care-ethics tradition makes central is the same constitutive vulnerability recognition is grounded in at §5.14. The parting is on grounding (healthcare standing is derived from the participation conditions mutual recognition presupposes rather than from the dependency relation taken as primitive) but the care-ethics tradition supplies something the recognition argument under-develops: caregiving labor, paid and unpaid and disproportionately performed by women and by racialized and migrant workers, is itself collective investment in the root sense (§6): infrastructure the political community depends on and has historically declined to recognize or resource as such. The collective-investment concept brings that labor inside the account rather than leaving it as the unpriced substrate on which the priced system runs.

Care isn’t merely a service delivered after someone has become a participant in public life. It is part of how participants are sustained and formed in the first place: pregnancy, infancy, disability, illness, and old age all make dependence a normal condition of human life rather than an exceptional failure. A political community that relies on care while treating its labor as private, invisible, or freely supplied offloads a constitutive cost onto the people who perform it. Public support for care is therefore required as a condition of participation, while leaving the household forms through which care is given open.

*Drugs and bodily autonomy.* The healthcare floor includes evidence-based prevention and treatment for substance-use disorders, mental illness, and crisis. Substance use can be coping, recreation, compulsion, dependence, social practice, or several of these at once; deprivation or addiction doesn’t make every act non-autonomous by category. The policy question therefore adds premises about bodily autonomy, public risk, criminalization harms, dependence, third-party injury, and comparative institutional performance. A layered approach can distinguish personal use, supply, clinical administration, and harms to others: competent-adult use may be decriminalized; distribution may be regulated by evidence about dependence and acute and population harm; therapeutic administration may require clinical safeguards; and impairment-driven negligence remains answerable under ordinary third-party-harm principles. These are defended policy conclusions if comparative evidence supports them, not consequences of the healthcare floor alone. The enforcement side is developed at §6.13.

*End-of-life access and the subsistence floor.* Universal care requires palliative care, pain treatment, mental-health support, disability accommodation, social support, and careful assessment of capacity and coercion. It also means that access to an assisted death, where legally and ethically permitted, can’t substitute for services the political community already owes. Neither causal direction settles autonomy by itself. A wish formed amid deprivation can remain genuinely the person’s; a wish formed amid terminal illness can be affected by depression, coercion, misinformation, untreated symptoms, or burdens the person feels imposed on others. Population-level increases can trigger investigation of social conditions, while every individual case still requires person-specific assessment. Whether assisted dying should be available adds premises about autonomy, medical role, irreversibility, error, disability justice, eligibility, and safeguards. The foundation constrains that debate; it doesn’t decide it.

*Taking stock.* Single-payer, multi-payer-with-foundation, and hybrid implementations remain design questions. The fixed claims are that the subsistence floor is constitutive, that mechanisms substituting for the foundation are precluded, and that the foundation must cover conditions producing failures of agentive participation, including mental health and substance-related conditions. Where multiple institutional designs satisfy those constraints, the choice remains open.

Reproductive autonomy is political because pregnancy joins the established bodily agency and welfare of the pregnant person to contested questions about developing sentience, subjecthood, potentiality, and standing. The structure of life (§4.8) doesn’t settle when fetal consciousness begins. Neuroscience can constrain the inquiry by examining the development required for integrated processing, but evidence about thalamocortical connectivity, arousal, nociception, and organized experience remains indirect and doesn’t by itself supply moral standing or a legal rule (Lagercrantz and Changeux 2009; Koch 2019). Institutions must therefore make decisions under empirical and normative uncertainty while protecting the pregnant person’s bodily autonomy and health throughout.

If experiential subjecthood is treated as sufficient for direct welfare standing, the developmental question becomes when the evidence warrants attributing experience. That remains a conditional application of §5.1’s fit-defended account, not a second Cogito and not a threshold the modal proof locates. Other accounts may give potentiality, organismic life, relationships, viability, or community recognition independent weight. The argument can therefore state its own conditional: as evidence for experiential subjecthood strengthens, the developing being’s welfare claims strengthen; the pregnant person’s already-established welfare, agency, health, and bodily claims remain present throughout. How competing claims should be balanced additionally depends on risk, burden, medical circumstances, feasibility, and the institutional harms of enforcement.

The account shouldn’t convert gradual and indirect evidence into a metaphysical switch. Basic moral worth isn’t graded by intelligence, autobiographical complexity, or the richness of experience; this protects disabled people, infants, and people with diminished cognition from a hierarchy of worth. But whether any experience is present at a developmental stage is still uncertain, and unconsciousness isn’t equivalent to permanent absence of the capacity for experience. The appropriate policy posture must therefore combine the account’s standing criterion with evidential humility, precaution, and the independent bodily claims already in the case.

Consent can’t do all the work in this dispute. A being unable to authorize treatment can still have interests, as infant, incapacity, and emergency cases show; the absence of consent capacity neither proves nor defeats standing. Before experiential subjecthood there is no experiential will to consult on this account, but whether and when that condition obtains remains the empirical question just identified. The pregnant person is the competent authorization-bearer whose body and medical risk are present throughout.

This precludes both binary simplifications that dominate the public debate. A conception-as-full-standing view treats biological life as already equivalent to a subject with a first-person perspective, collapsing the developmental-consciousness gradient (§4.8). A birth-as-full-beginning view treats the developing configuration as politically irrelevant until separation, collapsing the same gradient from the other side.

Three intermediate positions deserve direct engagement. *Potentiality* arguments (Marquis 1989; Stone 1994) hold that what matters is what the developing being is becoming rather than what it is at any moment, and that the standing of the eventual person extends backward to the inception of the developmental sequence. The argument grants what potentiality tracks—the developing organism is becoming a subject of experience—but locates direct experiential standing when that becoming reaches integrated consciousness rather than at the process’s inception.

*Viability* arguments, central to the *Roe v. Wade* (1973) and *Planned Parenthood v. Casey* (1992) frameworks, locate a legal line where survival outside the pregnant person’s body becomes possible. Viability can be evidence and can alter bodily dependence without being identical to consciousness. *Personhood-as-conferred-by-community-recognition* arguments (Warren 1973; English 1975) instead locate standing in the recognition a community extends. The account grants that mutual recognition is constitutive of moral standing (§5.14) while denying that a community can settle who has standing merely by withholding recognition. The threshold remains conditional on the developmental and consciousness arguments already stated.

The *disability-rights* critique of selectionist regimes (Saxton 2000; Kafer 2013; Garland-Thomson 2012) tracks the same concern developed at §6.10.5 at the genetic-medicine and end-of-life thresholds: that the slide from threshold-permission to existence-selection is real and partly socially produced. The same response applies: address the social conditions that drive the slide through the upstream commitments above. Hold the critique as ongoing pressure on policy design rather than as resolved by structural reform alone.

The *religious and natural-law* traditions articulate stances toward existence and contingency respected here as stances: Aquinas on delayed animation (*Summa Theologiae* I.118), Catholic magisterial teaching from *Humanae Vitae* (1968) onward, Orthodox Jewish threshold positions in the rabbinic tradition (Mishnah *Ohalot* 7:6), and Sandel’s (2007) openness-to-the-given orientation. Where parents hold these orientations, its autonomy commitments protect the exercise of those commitments.
