That those positions function as structural constraints on what reproductive healthcare may be made available to others isn’t derived here; the disagreement runs at the level of personal moral commitment expressed through autonomous choice, not at the level of architectural design pressure.

The argument doesn’t make these debates disappear. It offers a conditional sentience-based account while acknowledging that neither the onset of fetal experience nor the complete moral and legal significance of that onset is derived upstream. The resulting political position must therefore be defended through reproductive autonomy, health, standing, potentiality, risk, enforcement effects, and empirical evidence together—not presented as the automatic application of two earlier results.

Health policy comes to dispute over what the political community owes its members at the point where bodies, minds, and the proximity of death meet institutional structure. The recognition tradition reads healthcare as constitutive infrastructure upstream of agentive participation: the foundation at which participants are themselves maintained in the constitutive vulnerabilities that make them participants. Four things follow. It precludes profit-extraction at the foundation. It routes mental-health and substance-related conditions through care rather than punishment. It treats population-scale public-health infrastructure on the same logic as the legal system. And it extends the foundation, in option-not-mandate form, to reproductive healthcare, therapeutic genetic medicine, and end-of-life autonomy for capacity-confirmed wellness-irretrievable cases. Three contemporary traditions in the classical-liberal lineage deny this framing at its premise from different directions.

The Friedman medical-licensure and consumer-directed-care critique (Friedman 1962, ch. IX; Friedman and Friedman 1980) presses two claims: occupational licensure of physicians produces monopoly rents that elevate cost without proportionate quality gains, and the insurance-against-catastrophe plus cash-purchase-for-routine-care architecture (the health-savings-account / consumer-directed-care form) delivers maintenance without bureaucratic intermediation. Its collapse of state-financing into state-provision, on this reading, misreads the actual policy space.

The Cato-tradition classical-liberal health-policy position presses the architecture claim, drawing on the Cato Institute’s health-policy work through Michael Cannon and successors and on the comparative-health-policy literature reading the Singapore medical-savings-account architecture: Singapore-style medical-savings-accounts with catastrophic coverage satisfy universal access without the purchasing power of a single-payer system that mainstream universal-coverage frameworks require. Framework critiques of privatized insurance overgeneralize, on this reading, from the United-States-style market-failure case to architectures that don’t share its failure modes.

The Pauly moral-hazard analysis (Pauly 1968, the wide subsequent literature on cost sharing) presses the consumer-incentive claim: lower marginal prices increase utilization, some of which supplies little clinical value, and a foundation with no demand discipline can raise cost and crowd out more valuable care. RAND and later insurance experiments support the utilization response while also showing that patients reduce effective and ineffective care together. Deductibles and copayments are therefore possible demand instruments, on this reading, but their distributive and health effects have to be compared with clinical triage, reference pricing, supply-side budgets, and value-based payment.

A systems objection is broader than financing. Every architecture rations: markets by price and coverage, budgeted systems by queues, capacity, formularies, and clinical thresholds. Universal coverage can still fail through long waits, workforce shortages, political underfunding, provider exit, geographically unequal supply, or public capture. Conversely, fragmented markets can finance rapid access for some while excluding others. Innovation is likewise a real tradeoff rather than a slogan: high expected returns may support research and diffusion, while monopoly pricing, me-too development, and weak comparative-effectiveness incentives can waste the same resources. A healthcare floor must therefore be tested simultaneously for access, waiting, quality, health gain, innovation, administrative load, provider capacity, fiscal durability, and distribution. No payer label resolves those variables in advance.

The disability-rights critique of selectionist regimes in genetic medicine and end-of-life policy (Parens and Asch 2000; Saxton 2000; Kafer 2013; Garland-Thomson 2012) registers from a different political direction as cross-pressure on its commitments: that the slide from threshold-permission to existence-selection is real, well-documented, and partly socially produced.

The categorical-against tradition on end-of-life autonomy holds that human life carries inviolable weight independent of wellness or agency, and that medical assistance in dying corrupts medicine’s healing role even in hard cases. Kass (1989), Pellegrino (1992), and the Catholic line through *Evangelium Vitae* (1995) supply versions of that objection. The slippery-slope tradition adds an empirical concern: case law, professional norms, and legislation can widen eligibility after a regime is installed (Keown 2002; Pereira 2011).

The disability-rights critique presses differently. A formally voluntary option can become pressure against disabled lives when care, income, accommodation, and social standing are missing; procedural competence may not detect that soft coercion. Coleman (2010) and the Not Dead Yet tradition, Stainton (2022), Saxton (2000), Garland-Thomson (2012), and Kafer (2013) make this cross-pressure central. The objection can’t be answered merely by restating autonomy, because the dispute includes the conditions under which autonomy is exercised and recognized.

The prohibitionist tradition on substance policy (DuPont’s policy-track work (1997); Sabet on the institutional-prevention case (2013); and, from outside prohibitionism, Kleiman’s case for “grudging toleration” against substance-specific harm escalation (1992)) presses one claim: that normalization of substance use produces population-scale wellness damage through use-rate elevation, dependence-rate elevation, and aggregate cost externalization, and that decriminalization or legalization regimes (whatever their harm-reduction architecture) produce systemic harms that prohibition’s downside costs don’t exceed. Treating substances on the alcohol-or-tobacco model under-counts the substance-specific harms, on this reading. The strict-libertarian tradition on substance policy presses the symmetric counter-claim from the opposite direction—Szasz (1992) on the right to drugs, Block on the legal and economic case against prohibition (1993): that any restriction on substance use, including the distribution-regulation its three-layer architecture incorporates, is paternalistic intrusion on the user’s bodily autonomy, that supervised-administration and maintenance regimes are soft prohibition, and that the political community has no standing to regulate what a competent adult ingests beyond the harm-to-others case standard recklessness doctrine already covers. Its three-layer architecture, on this reading, retains prohibition’s substantive form at the distribution layer while gesturing at autonomy at the use layer.

Public health, capabilities, care, and autonomy each offer a route to a protected healthcare foundation.

The WHO social-determinants-of-health framework (Marmot 2004, WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health 2008) locates aggregate health outcomes in upstream structural conditions rather than in downstream clinical inputs alone. The capabilities tradition (Sen 1999; Nussbaum 2011 on bodily-integrity as a central capability) supplies the structural-foundation architecture: institutions are constrained to maintain bodily-integrity capability across the full population. Daniels (2008) reaches the just-health-distribution conclusion through Rawlsian fair-equality-of-opportunity reasoning.

The Beveridge social-medicine tradition and the Bismarck social-insurance tradition supply the two principal universal-coverage lineages along which contemporary OECD systems operate. Beveridge runs through his 1942 report (1942) and the NHS founding with its operational record; Bismarck through the 1883 German social-insurance establishment and its successor architectures across continental Europe.

The public-health-and-sanitation lineage supplies the population-scale-infrastructure case: Snow’s Broad Street pump investigation (1855), Chadwick (1842), Virchow’s nineteenth-century social-medicine writings (1848) 2006, and the WHO smallpox-eradication record.

The mental-health-as-healthcare reform tradition reaches the routing claim from independent premises: the community-mental-health movement following Action for Mental Health 1961, the WHO Mental Health Atlas series, and the Lancet Commission on global mental health. The harm-reduction tradition—G. Alan Marlatt on harm reduction (1996), the Portugal decriminalization record from 2001 onward (Hughes and Stevens 2010; Greenwald 2009), the Swiss heroin-assisted-treatment program, and the Vancouver Insite supervised-injection-site evaluation literature—grounds the case for treating substance-related conditions through care.

The reproductive autonomy tradition contributes the reproductive-healthcare-as-foundation case—Faden on biomedical ethics (Faden and Beauchamp 1986), the women’s health movement through *Our Bodies, Ourselves* and successors, and capabilities-based bodily-autonomy work—alongside the *Roe v. Wade* (1973) and *Planned Parenthood v. Casey* (1992) jurisprudential lineage.

The end-of-life autonomy lineage provides the case for a resourced exit where wellness is irretrievable, under procedural safeguards: the Oregon Death with Dignity Act 1997 operational record, the Netherlands Termination of Life on Request Act 2002, the Belgian 2002 euthanasia legislation, the Canadian Medical Assistance in Dying regime from 2016, and the supporting bioethical work of Battin (2005) and others.

The dispute is therefore not single-payer versus markets in the abstract. It is whether the political community owes every participant effective access to an adequate healthcare floor, and, if it does, which combination of public responsibility, private or public provision, risk pooling, cost sharing, capacity planning, and innovation incentives secures that foundation with the least exclusion, delay, waste, and capture. Friedman, the Cato-Singapore tradition, Pauly, public-choice critics, and innovation and waiting-time objections show why universal responsibility can’t be converted into confidence in one bureaucracy or zero-price design. Beveridge, Bismarck, capabilities, social-determinants, and public-health traditions show why price and voluntary purchase can’t by themselves secure a population foundation. Reproductive, genetic, substance, and end-of-life applications then add their own autonomy, consciousness, disability, and harm premises. The requirement (§6.10.2) closes only what the shared derivation can close, and leaves payer, provider, rationing protocol, and contested bodily applications open to their additional arguments and evidence.

### 6.10.2 The Requirement
For healthcare to obtain at the scale of a political community whose participation conditions presuppose maintained, capacitated participants, the universal foundation is separated here from additional application rules. The foundation fixes outcomes every architecture must secure: timely effective access to adequate care, population-health protection, and scarcity allocation that doesn’t substitute wealth or status for clinical criteria. Financing, provision, cost sharing, capacity planning, and exact triage protocols are corrigible designs. Substance, reproductive, genetic, and end-of-life conclusions draw on further premises specified later and don’t become categorical merely by appearing in the same domain.

*Sufficiency-foundation non-substitutability at constitutive vulnerability.* The political community is structurally obliged to maintain effective access to care adequate for bodily and mental participation. Rest belongs on that foundation: time off and parental leave restore the body whose field constant work collapses. They are care, not a Right to Rest; duration and instrument stay open. It may contract, regulate, insure, subsidize, or provide directly, but it can’t discharge responsibility by pointing to a nominal market in which necessary care remains unaffordable, unavailable, dangerously delayed, or clinically inadequate. Single-payer, regulated multi-payer, Singapore-style mandatory savings plus catastrophic pooling and subsidy, Beveridge provision, Bismarck social insurance, and hybrids are candidates rather than conclusions. Returns at the foundation count as extraction when vulnerability, information asymmetry, denial, or public privilege yields gain without proportionate contribution while access fails; private status or profit alone isn’t the criterion.

*Risk pooling and cost sharing are subordinate to the foundation.* Insurance is one form of collective risk pooling, not the structural failure by definition. The failure is an arrangement in which claim denial, risk selection, opaque pricing, administrative duplication, underfunding, or cost sharing predictably leaves participants without necessary care. Public payers can fail through queues, low capacity, political rationing, or capture; private and nonprofit payers can satisfy the foundation under strong guarantees and can fail through financial gatekeeping. Cost sharing is permissible only where income adjustment, exemptions, caps, and clinical safeguards prevent deterrence of necessary care. Institutional denial for unsupported gain and individual fraud both burden the pool, but their magnitude, power, and remedy must be measured rather than declared symmetric.

*Mental-health and substance-related conditions begin in healthcare rather than justice; exact substance policy requires further premises.* A crisis, dependence, or cognitive condition doesn’t become a penal condition merely because it has behavioral effects. Care, treatment, and harm reduction therefore come before punishment. For substances, a plausible layered architecture distinguishes competent-adult possession and use, distribution, clinical administration, and injury to others: user-side decriminalization protects bodily autonomy; distribution rules track evidence about dependence, contamination, acute harm, and population effects; therapeutic administration can carry clinical safeguards; and impairment-driven injury remains answerable under ordinary harm-to-others principles. The healthcare foundation fixes the priority of treatment over punishment. It doesn’t by itself fix where decriminalization ends, which distribution rules work, or how substance-specific and population harms should be balanced. Those conclusions depend on the comparative record (Portugal: Hughes and Stevens 2010; Greenwald 2009; Swiss heroin-assisted treatment; CAHOOTS; Housing First: Tsemberis 2010) and on the autonomy and third-party-harm premises engaged here and at §6.13.

*Population-scale public-health infrastructure is constitutive infrastructure.* Vaccination programs, communicable-disease control, sanitation, environmental-health monitoring, and pandemic preparedness aren’t discretionary subsidies but constitutive infrastructure on the same logic as the legal system or the public-education system. Privatizing or dismantling such infrastructure violates the condition at the structural level. Specific institutional housing is underdetermined: a national public-health agency, sub-national public-health departments, multilateral coordination through WHO and successors within the constraint.

*Triage and scarcity allocation, need- and prognosis-based rather than payment- or status-based.* Genuine scarcity is a condition the foundation has to specify an allocation principle for, not a gap it can leave silent: organ allocation, ICU capacity under surge conditions, a pandemic-scale ventilator or vaccine shortfall. The structural requirement is that allocation under genuine scarcity runs on clinical need and prognosis (likelihood and magnitude of benefit, urgency) rather than on ability to pay, social status, or contribution history: the same anti-extraction logic that precludes profit margins at the foundation precludes a scarcity-rationing system that lets payment or status substitute for clinical criteria. This doesn’t resolve every contested triage protocol: age-based tiebreakers, disability-adjusted prognosis scoring, and first-come-versus-lottery allocation among clinically-equivalent candidates remain contested within the clinical-ethics literature, and the disability-rights critique of prognosis scoring that discounts disabled patients’ quality of life (Saxton 2000; Kafer 2013) applies here with full force and isn’t resolved by naming need-and-prognosis as the axis. What the condition fixes is the axis allocation has to run on and the axes it may not run on; the specific protocol is left to the clinical-ethics and public-health design literatures.

*Reproductive healthcare is part of the foundation; contested standing requires an additional argument.* Contraception, prenatal and postpartum care, fertility care, and care for pregnancy loss belong to adequate healthcare when clinically indicated. The pregnant person’s health, agency, and bodily integrity carry direct weight throughout. Abortion and later-pregnancy conflicts add questions the healthcare foundation doesn’t settle: when the evidence supports attributing fetal experience, what standing follows, how competing bodily claims are weighed, and what enforcement itself does. The sentience-based account developed above rejects easy switches at conception or birth, but it remains conditional on the Chapter 4 account and on indirect developmental evidence.

*Therapeutic genetic medicine: option, not mandate; standards rise with irreversibility.* The healthcare floor supports access to interventions that prevent or treat serious suffering, while autonomy protects refusal. Somatic interventions face the ordinary standards of therapeutic medicine; heritable and difficult-to-reverse interventions require stronger evidence, oversight, and authorization (the He Jiankui 2018 case is the clearest record of failed standards, Cyranoski and Ledford 2018). State-directed selection, disability-as-defect framing, and biological class advantage trigger separate recognition, disability, and sanctioned-disproportion objections. The foundation alone doesn’t draw the therapeutic/enhancement boundary or settle every parental and future-person conflict.

*End-of-life autonomy is a conditional application, not part of the universal-access proof.* The foundation directly requires palliative care, pain relief, mental-health treatment, disability accommodation, material security, and protection against coercion. If the book’s further premises about bodily autonomy, the medical role, irreversibility, error, and durable authorization hold, a tightly scoped assisted-dying option may be justified for a capacity-confirmed person whose suffering remains irremediable after relevant supports are genuinely available. Capacity assessment, repeated confirmation, freedom from coercion, and an opportunity to withdraw are therefore integral rather than decorative. The foundation rules out offering death in place of care; it does not, without those additional premises and evidence, require that the option exist.

*These conditions don’t all rest on the same premises.* The participation derivation directly supports universal effective access, population-scale public-health capacity, mental-health and substance treatment as healthcare, and allocation that doesn’t let payment or status displace clinical need. It doesn’t uniquely derive one insurer, cost-sharing rule, delivery system, capacity budget, or triage formula. The exact substance architecture additionally invokes bodily autonomy, harm to others, dependence evidence, and comparative policy results. Reproductive standing, therapeutic genetic medicine, and end-of-life autonomy additionally inherit the Chapter 4/8 account of consciousness and agency, together with further premises about autonomy, disability, whether the loss can be reversed, risk, and coercion. A reader can therefore accept the universal foundation while disputing one or more applications without inconsistency. That stratification keeps each result within the premise set that carries it.

Together, the direct foundation and the conditional application rules form the healthcare architecture argued for here, but they don’t stand or fall as one set. The direct foundation is tested at §6.10.3 across access, delay, quality, health gain, incidence, administrative burden, innovation, capacity, and fiscal durability, and tests each additional application under the premises specific to it.

### 6.10.3 Predictions
The account of healthcare as upstream of participation generates predictions about outcomes, not institutional labels. Every comparison should report access, delay, clinical quality, health gain, financial protection, administrative burden, provider capacity, innovation, distribution, and total fiscal cost; disaggregate by income, race, disability, geography, age, and clinical need; and distinguish selection from treatment effects.

*First.* A financing architecture fails when premiums, cost sharing, denial, network limits, or waiting predictably block necessary care below the foundation. Compare systems and reforms using unmet need, delayed treatment, preventable hospitalization, treatable mortality, financial strain, continuity, and risk-adjusted outcomes. Private and public payers can each pass or fail. The prediction is falsified as a categorical criticism of private administration if regulated private or nonprofit systems preserve universal timely access without excess burden, and falsified as a categorical defense of public payment if budgeted systems leave comparable need unmet through queues or capacity shortage.

*Second.* High spending shouldn’t guarantee strong outcomes when prices, administrative complexity, low-value care, or weak primary and public-health capacity absorb the difference. Decompose spending into prices, quantities, administration, prevention, primary care, long-term care, and social determinants before comparing life expectancy or mortality. The prediction is supported when reforms shifting resources toward effective upstream care improve risk-adjusted outcomes per unit of total cost. It fails if downstream spending consistently produces greater health gain after population risk, nonmedical determinants, innovation spillovers, and measurement differences are addressed.

*Third.* Cost sharing should reduce utilization, but not reliably separate low-value from necessary care. Measure both categories, health effects, and financial burden across income and illness risk. RAND and later experiments predict lower use under higher prices; the foundation predicts exemptions and caps are necessary where reduced use harms access. The claim fails if carefully designed cost sharing persistently removes low-value care without reducing necessary care or worsening outcomes among vulnerable groups.

*Fourth.* Routing mental-health crises and substance dependence toward treatment and harm reduction should improve health and reduce avoidable criminal-justice burden relative to punishment-dominant regimes, conditional on implementation and substance. Use phased reforms, geographic discontinuities, or matched longitudinal comparisons; measure overdose, infection, treatment engagement, crisis resolution, incarceration, victimization, public disorder, family stability, and total cost. The prediction fails where credible comparisons show no health or justice gain, or where commercialization and increased use create harms exceeding the benefits.

*Fifth.* Expanding effective coverage to excluded populations should improve access and financial protection; mortality and downstream-cost effects should vary by baseline risk, benefit design, provider supply, and time horizon. Use lotteries, eligibility thresholds, and difference-in-differences designs. The prediction fails if coverage doesn’t increase effective care, if provider scarcity converts coverage into nominal entitlement, or if total downstream savings and health gains don’t justify costs under the stated objective. The foundation doesn’t require every expansion to be budget-saving; it requires adequate care, with fiscal cost counted honestly.

*Sixth.* Population public-health measures should outperform atomized purchase where transmission, sanitation, surveillance, or herd effects create collective-action problems. Test vaccination, outbreak control, environmental monitoring, and preparedness against credible counterfactuals while measuring liberty costs, adverse events, trust, compliance, and distribution. The claim fails where decentralized arrangements achieve equal coverage and control, or where a centralized response produces net harm through error, coercion, or capture.

*Seventh.* Systems face real rationing and innovation tradeoffs. Budgeted universal systems may produce queues, restricted formularies, or provider shortages; market-heavy systems may ration by price, insurance status, and network. Compare time to clinically indicated care, outcomes while waiting, workforce retention, adoption of cost-effective innovation, research output, diffusion, prices, and access. No universal winner by payer type is predicted: an acceptable architecture must ration transparently by clinical value and preserve sufficient incentives for useful innovation without allowing monopoly return or scarcity to breach the foundation. Any claim that one architecture automatically solves waiting, cost, or innovation is falsified by contrary performance on those measures.

*Eighth.* Political and administrative capture should follow concentrated stakes rather than public or private status alone. Measure lobbying, revolving-door appointments, reimbursement distortions, denial rules, procurement favoritism, underfunding, and regulatory barriers. The prediction is that concentrated actors will seek rents in every architecture and that transparent rules, contestability, audit, and outcome accountability reduce capture. It fails if capture doesn’t respond to those institutional safeguards or if one sector is assumed immune without comparative evidence.

The classical-liberal objections in §6.10.1 therefore remain inside the test. Singapore is evidence for a heavily governed mixed architecture, not for unregulated purchase; RAND confirms utilization response without showing that patients can clinically sort care by price; universal systems demonstrate feasibility while their queues and fiscal constraints remain failures to measure. The maximal prediction is that secure effective access can be achieved through multiple designs, but no design succeeds unless it preserves the foundation after incidence, delay, quality, capacity, innovation, and transition are counted.

### 6.10.4 Confirmation
The predictions at §6.10.3 are read against a graded evidence standard. Cross-sectional system rankings establish descriptive differences; longitudinal and matched comparisons narrow alternatives; lotteries, eligibility discontinuities, and plausibly exogenous policy changes support causal attribution; replication across populations supports transportability. Feasibility doesn’t identify a mechanism, and no country comparison controls the full set of demography, prices, behavior, social policy, and institutions.

*First.* The United States combines unusually high spending, substantial administrative expense, fragmented coverage, affordability barriers, and weaker average outcomes than many peers. Contemporary estimates commonly place administrative activity around 15–25 percent of US health expenditure depending on definition; billing, coding, insurer operations, and provider administration all contribute. This supports the prediction that fragmentation and financial intermediation can be costly, but the older 25–30 versus 10 percent contrast isn’t one stable apples-to-apples measure, and administrative cost isn’t all insurer profit. Commonwealth Fund and OECD comparisons establish the high-cost/access/outcome pattern. They don’t by themselves prove that one payer structure caused every gap.

Medical debt and bankruptcy supply stronger incidence evidence than rhetoric alone, though estimates of how many bankruptcies are *caused* by medical events vary with survey wording and causal definition. The earned conclusion is that illness-related bills and income loss create distinctive financial risk in the United States and are much less prominent where coverage and income protection are stronger—not that one uncontested percentage settles the case.

*Second.* Coverage causally improves some outcomes, but effects differ by measure and horizon. The Oregon Medicaid lottery increased care use, diagnosis and treatment of diabetes, financial protection, and self-reported wellbeing and reduced depression, while producing no statistically significant improvement in the measured physical-health outcomes over two years. Quasi-experimental Medicaid-expansion studies often find improved access and financial protection and several find mortality reductions, including among higher-risk groups, but estimates are heterogeneous and mortality is difficult to identify over short periods. This supports effective coverage as a [floor condition](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) while refusing the claim that every expansion immediately lowers total spending or every measured mortality rate.

*Third.* Moral hazard exists in the empirical sense. RAND and later studies show that higher out-of-pocket prices reduce utilization. RAND also found that cost sharing reduced effective and less-effective care together and posed greater risk for low-income participants with health needs. The evidence therefore supports Pauly’s utilization mechanism and its warning that price is a poor clinical sorter. It favors calibrated caps, exemptions, reference pricing, or supply-side value controls over either universal zero price or indiscriminate deductibles as an automatic solution.

*Fourth.* Mental-health and substance-policy evidence supports treatment and harm reduction, but not every broad causal claim previously attached to it. Portugal’s 2001 reform combined decriminalization with treatment and public-health changes; subsequent declines in HIV, criminal penalties, and several harm measures are consistent with the combined approach, while attribution to decriminalization alone is limited by concurrent reforms, trends, and measurement changes. Swiss heroin-assisted treatment and supervised-consumption evaluations support benefits for selected high-risk populations under clinical conditions. They don’t establish that every substance, legalization model, or commercial market improves population health.

Housing First has strong evidence for housing stability and important health and service-use benefits. Cost offsets vary by population and study design; reviews note that rigorous cost studies are fewer and that programs need not pay for themselves to be justified. CAHOOTS and related mobile-crisis models demonstrate feasibility and report low per-incident costs, but the record is largely observational and doesn’t yet isolate their causal effect against comparable police or clinical alternatives. These cases support testing care-first routing rather than declaring all downstream savings confirmed.

*Fifth.* Public-health infrastructure has some of the clearest confirmation. Sanitation, vaccination, surveillance, and communicable-disease control address externalities and collective-action problems that individual purchase can’t reliably solve. Historical and quasi-experimental evidence strongly supports large health gains. Yet implementation matters: mandates, risk communication, adverse-event monitoring, trust, and state capacity affect net outcomes. COVID-19 is broadly consistent with the value of preparedness and population response, but density, age, prior immunity, policy timing, behavior, and measurement prevent a simple national ranking from isolating the mechanism.

*Sixth.* Mixed systems demonstrate underdetermination rather than one universal architecture. Taiwan and Japan achieve universal coverage at far lower cost than the United States with stronger population outcomes, establishing feasibility. Singapore combines mandatory savings, national catastrophic insurance, direct subsidy, public provision, price and capacity management, cost sharing, and a final safety net. Its success confirms that universal responsibility can coexist with personal accounts and plural payment; its active state architecture prevents treating it as a clean test of laissez-faire medicine. Beveridge and Bismarck systems likewise show multiple routes to a foundation.

*Seventh.* Waiting, capacity, and innovation objections remain empirically live. OECD evidence documents long waits for some specialist and elective services in several universal systems, while the United States also rations through price, network, geography, and insurance status. Comparative records show that policy can reduce queues, but no financing label eliminates scarcity. The United States contributes disproportionately to some pharmaceutical and medical innovation, yet the causal share attributable to high prices rather than public research funding, market size, scientific institutions, and global demand is unsettled. The evidence supports preserving innovation incentives and measuring diffusion and access, not granting monopoly pricing immunity or assuming public payment has no innovation cost.

*Eighth.* Political capture isn’t confirmed as uniquely or maximally private-insurance behavior. Lobbying and regulatory influence by insurers, pharmaceutical firms, hospitals, professional associations, and device manufacturers are documented. Public systems can also be captured through budgets, procurement, licensing, and provider bargaining. The earned prediction is that concentrated stakes invite capture and require audit, transparency, and contestability; ranking one industry’s resistance as “the most ferocious” needs a comparative metric the current record doesn’t supply.

*Cross-national, state, and disparity records.* US state life-expectancy differences are large and correlate with income, education, healthcare access, public policy, race, urbanization, industry, migration, and behavior. Shared federal law and currency don’t make the states a controlled experiment. The comparison is useful for hypothesis generation and can be strengthened with policy discontinuities or longitudinal reforms; it can’t assign the residual difference mainly to “stronger foundations” by inspection.

Black maternal mortality remains a severe and well-documented disparity: current CDC summaries report roughly a threefold Black–White difference, with most pregnancy-related deaths considered preventable. Evidence implicates variation in quality of care, chronic-condition exposure, maternity-care access, social determinants, implicit bias, and structural racism. Hoffman et al. (2016) demonstrate false biological beliefs and pain-assessment bias in a specific clinical context; Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) document race correction in algorithms. Those findings support institutional mechanisms, but no single study assigns the entire mortality gap to one cause. The maximal claim is multi-causal structural exposure with identifiable, testable healthcare pathways.

*What the record rules out—and what it leaves open.* The evidence rules out confidence that voluntary purchase and lightly regulated competition alone will secure universal adequate access, and it rules out the claim that coverage, public health, or upstream investment generally can’t improve participation. It also rules out complacency about public systems: waiting, capacity, taxation, prioritization, innovation, and capture are real design constraints. The record supports universal responsibility with design pluralism and incidence analysis. It doesn’t empirically select single-payer, abolish all insurance, prove every expansion budget-saving, or settle the reproductive, genetic, substance, and end-of-life arguments whose premises extend beyond system performance.

### 6.10.5 Conclusions
The derivation here carries three kinds of implication for institutional design: structural constraints, transitions, and neighboring positions.

*Structural constraints.* Non-substitutability of the sufficiency foundation reaches its greatest force in healthcare because untreated illness, injury, severe pain, and mental crisis can remove the participant from participation through the participant’s own body. The political community therefore retains responsibility for timely effective access to adequate care. It may provide directly or secure the foundation through regulated public, nonprofit, private, savings-based, social-insurance, or mixed institutions; it may not treat nominal availability as success while payment, delay, denial, geography, or low quality leaves necessary care inaccessible. Profit is precluded as extraction only where vulnerability, information asymmetry, gatekeeping, or public privilege yields return without proportionate contribution while the foundation fails. Public systems remain equally accountable for queues, undercapacity, capture, and poor outcomes.

Mental health and substance-related conditions belong in healthcare, not in justice. Healthcare is upstream of agentive participation (per the root of this section and the structural requirements in §6.10.2) and couples upstream into the justice domain developed at §6.13. Conditions producing failures of agentive participation are therefore healthcare-domain conditions whatever their downstream behavioral manifestations. Routing mental-health crises through criminalization rather than through crisis healthcare, routing substance dependence through prohibition rather than through treatment, and routing developmental and cognitive conditions through penal rather than therapeutic systems are each a domain misallocation precluded at the design-pressure level.

Substance policy is best treated in layers: possession and use, distribution, clinical administration, and injury to others. The foundation requires that dependence and crisis remain reachable through care; it doesn’t make one regulatory boundary self-executing. User-side decriminalization, regulated supply, clinical safeguards, and ordinary liability for impairment-driven injury form the defended package here only insofar as the autonomy, dependence, population-harm, and comparative-evidence premises support it.

The strict-libertarian objection to distribution-regulation operates at layer (ii). The strict-libertarian tradition (Szasz 1992; Block 1993) rejects the three-layer architecture there: any restriction on what a competent adult ingests, including supervised-administration and maintenance regimes, is paternalistic intrusion on bodily autonomy.

Grant the central concession at layer (i): user-side decriminalization on the same logic the libertarian tradition runs. Also grant at layer (iii) that harm to others through impairment-driven negligence remains answerable under standard recklessness doctrine. The disagreement is at distribution. Layer (ii) operates on the same structural logic that governs food safety, pharmaceutical quality, and licensing of professional service-providers. The strict-libertarian position would have to reject all of these to be consistent, and the strong-form Rothbardian register does, at substantial downstream cost that isn’t accepted here.

Informed consent depends on accurate information about what is consumed, and unregulated retail systematically undermines that condition. Distribution-regulation against agency-capture and aggregate population-scale harm therefore protects the autonomy the libertarian position invokes rather than violating it. The residual disagreement over standing remains real and foundational: the political community has standing to regulate against those harms; the strict libertarian holds that it doesn’t. The reply runs through the structural derivation rather than through a direct refutation of the libertarian axiom on its own ground.

Population-scale public-health infrastructure is constitutive infrastructure. Cooperative infrastructure includes the conditions for participants to remain participants. Public-health infrastructure (vaccination programs, communicable-disease control, sanitation, environmental-health monitoring) is therefore not a discretionary subsidy but constitutive infrastructure on the same logic as the legal system or the public-education system. Privatizing or dismantling such infrastructure violates the constraint at the structural level.

*Transition.* The derivation fixes where the transition must arrive, but not how it gets there. A political community currently configured around privatized insurance doesn’t reach a sufficiency-foundation-non-substitutable architecture by decree. The transition is its own engineering problem: existing employment relationships, financial structures, patient-provider relationships, and institutional capacities all have to be brought to a new equilibrium without producing transitional collapse. The destination of insurance-occupies-the-foundation is precluded; the path from the present to a non-substitutable-foundation arrangement is left open. That work belongs to the implementation literatures and to the political processes §6.3 (Representation) and §6.2 (Belonging) constitute.

Concentrated resistance is predictable but not unique to one industry. Insurers, hospitals, pharmaceutical firms, professional associations, public employees, taxpayers, and patients can each resist reforms that threaten income, autonomy, access, or expected benefit. Transition design must map those stakes, protect continuity of care and useful capacity, compensate or retrain where justified, and distinguish rent defense from legitimate warnings about taxes, waiting, provider supply, and innovation. No claim that one lobby is structurally “most ferocious” is needed.

*Neighbors.* The argument concerns institutional performance, not the character of any executive, employee, clinician, patient, or shareholder. Risk pooling, administration, utilization review, and innovation can be genuine contributions; denial, selection, opaque pricing, fraud, and capture can be extraction. Institutional denial for unsupported gain and individual false claims both burden shared resources, but their power and scale differ and must be measured. The political community’s nondelegable role is guaranteeing the foundation and correcting failures, not necessarily performing every administrative or clinical function itself.

Illness isn’t pathologized. The healthcare-as-constitutive-infrastructure derivation explicitly precludes any reading in which sick people are burdens on the political community. Sick people are participants in the constitutive vulnerabilities that make them participants, and the political community maintains them because doing so is part of what being a political community consists in. Any rhetoric that frames healthcare provision as charity-from-the-healthy-to-the-sick mistakes the structural relation, which is constitutive, not charitable.

*Reproductive autonomy.* The pregnant person’s health, agency, bodily integrity, and access to reproductive healthcare carry direct weight throughout pregnancy. Treatment of developing standing is conditional on the sentience-based account stated earlier and on an empirical record that doesn’t yield one sharp threshold. Contraception, prenatal and postpartum care, fertility care, and care for pregnancy loss belong within the healthcare floor when clinically indicated and adequately specified. Abortion law and later-pregnancy conflicts require additional judgments about fetal standing, bodily burdens, medical risk, viability, enforcement, and emergency exceptions. The argument can oppose careless binary descriptions without claiming that the modal proof has already resolved those judgments.

*The upstream relocation at this threshold.* Material security, accessible contraception and healthcare, parental leave, childcare, housing, education, and protection against coercion can change the conditions in which pregnancy decisions are made. That is a reason to act upstream, not a proof that any particular decision is non-autonomous or that provision will eliminate it. Finer and colleagues (2005) found that respondents commonly reported several intersecting financial, educational, caregiving, and relationship reasons; the Turnaway Study (Foster 2020) found worse economic outcomes among women denied abortions. Those findings make material conditions relevant without settling fetal standing or the legal rule. The narrower convergence is enough: anyone concerned with reducing abortions has reason to support the conditions that make wanted pregnancy and parenthood more livable, while the remaining disagreement about standing, bodily authority, and enforcement stays real.

*Genetic medicine.* Genetic intervention belongs on a continuum with other preventive and therapeutic medicine, but its standards rise with heritability, irreversibility, uncertainty, and effects on a future person. Five questions organize the case: expected welfare benefit, proportionality, authorization, reversibility, and fair access. The healthcare foundation supports access to genuinely therapeutic interventions and protects the choice to refuse them; it doesn’t by itself settle the therapy–enhancement boundary or authorize decisions on behalf of future persons.

Treating a condition needn’t deny the personhood of people who have it. That distinction holds only if accommodation and full standing remain unconditional: care can target suffering without treating an existing kind of person as a mistake. The disability-rights critique remains pressure on what counts as therapeutic, how options are presented, and whether a nominal choice is being made under avoidable social abandonment.

The secular core of the playing-God objection—humility about irreversible intervention, unintended consequences, and hyperagency—is answered by graded standards rather than dismissal. Somatic interventions can be judged much like other therapies; germline interventions demand substantially stronger evidence and oversight, as the He Jiankui case demonstrates. State-directed selection and coercive eugenics are independently precluded by mutual recognition and Justice. Positional enhancement raises the sanctioned-disproportion problem from §6.7, but whether every enhancement is positional or impermissible remains a further question.

The governing form is option, not mandate, under conditions that don’t punish refusal or make access a class marker. Structural support can reduce coercive background pressure, but it can’t be assumed to neutralize disability critique or make every parental choice unproblematic.

*End-of-life autonomy.* The universal floor settles the obligation to provide care, palliation, material support, disability accommodation, and protection against coercion. It does not alone settle whether medicine may help a person die. The affirmative case additionally depends on autonomy, medical role, prognosis, irreversibility, error, and the possibility of reliable safeguards.

The categorical-against tradition is right that life under suffering carries weight and that accompaniment, palliation, and the healer’s role aren’t formalities. The dispute begins after those obligations have been honored and a competent person’s suffering remains irremediable. At that point, prohibition is also state action: it enforces continuation against a registered will. That burden-flip matters, but it doesn’t settle the case unless the additional premises hold and institutions can identify the residual case reliably.

The resulting claim is conditional but substantive: if the person has decision-making capacity, the request is informed and durable, relevant supports are accessible, the suffering is medically irremediable, and safeguards can detect coercion and error with acceptable reliability, enforced continuation may override the agency care is meant to sustain. Opponents can contest any of those premises without contesting the universal healthcare floor.

Homeostatic and allostatic regulation help explain why healthcare is oriented toward functioning and relief rather than biological continuation considered in isolation (Cannon 1932; Sterling 2012; Damasio 2018). They don’t, by themselves, yield a rule for assisted dying. The normative work still belongs to the account of agency, suffering, authorization, and the obligations owed to a person whose condition cannot be relieved.

Whether suffering can be relieved is the residual question after the foundation operates. Pain, isolation, depression, financial fear, and social abandonment can shape a request without automatically nullifying it. Making care and support available should reduce the share driven by remediable conditions; how much is an empirical question. What remains is not whatever a system labels “irretrievable,” but the person-specific case in which relevant interventions have been offered, understood, and found unable to restore a tolerable line of life.

Drive names the phenomenology without deciding capacity: the field can collapse until continued suffering appears to be the only line. Sometimes care, time, material security, or another person can put a livable line back. Sometimes they cannot. The first obligation is therefore exploration rather than automatic approval or categorical disbelief. A request formed under unjust conditions can still be agentive, and a sincere request can still be distorted by treatable illness, misinformation, transient crisis, or pressure.

If the additional premises hold, denying a competent person access after relevant supports are genuinely available doesn’t merely preserve life; it forces continuation of the suffering the person has durably refused. No one can be required to exhaust every imaginable intervention, and an unwanted treatment isn’t support. The requirement is meaningful access, informed consideration, and a process capable of distinguishing remediable collapse from the residual case. Forced endurance can’t be called care, but neither can abandonment be called autonomy.

The subject has phenomenological access observers lack (Scarry 1985; Nagel 1974), but self-report isn’t the only relevant evidence when capacity, prognosis, coercion, and treatment response are disputed. The person’s account receives presumptive authority without becoming institutionally unreviewable. Family grief is real and deserves support; it cannot simply substitute the family’s will for the patient’s.

Safeguards are therefore integral: capacity assessment, repeated confirmation, freedom from coercion, adequate time, clinical review, and a real opportunity to withdraw. Their exact form and reliability remain empirical questions. They must protect against error without becoming an indefinite delay designed to defeat a competent refusal.

Existing jurisdictions establish feasibility and reveal the disputed edges rather than fully confirming the framework. Oregon’s Death with Dignity Act operates at a small share of deaths under terminal-prognosis and capacity requirements, and some recipients never use the prescription; that supports the possibility of a tightly scoped option. The Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, and Canada use materially different eligibility and administration rules, so their rates can’t be treated as one experiment. Canada Track 2 and psychiatric or nonterminal cases show that scope expansion and structural soft coercion aren’t imaginary concerns. The evidence doesn’t show “mass euthanasia,” but neither does it prove safeguards infallible. Terminal, capacity-confirmed, support-complete cases are therefore treated as the operational fit supported here, and broader eligibility must answer to separate evidence and renewed authorization.

Harm reduction is relevant but not decisive. Some people denied medical assistance will attempt suicide by more dangerous means; others won’t, and legal availability can itself affect behavior, clinical practice, family pressure, and social expectations. The policy comparison therefore concerns prevention, substitution, error, trauma, palliative alternatives, and effects on vulnerable populations under particular eligibility rules. Evidence that a regulated option can reduce some harms supports considering it; it doesn’t establish that prohibition never prevents death or that assisted dying is structurally identical to drug policy.

The *bios*/*zoē* distinction clarifies one value in dispute without settling it (*Politics* I.2, 1252b30, Agamben 1998). Agency, relationships, experience, and projects can matter to what a right to life protects beyond biological continuation alone. It doesn’t follow that life without a specified degree of agency has lost standing, that wellness has one irretrievable threshold, or that continued existence protects nothing once a person can’t pursue earlier projects. The end-of-life argument must therefore rest on the person’s informed and durable authorization, relief options, prognosis, present interests, and safeguards rather than a declaration that *bios* has departed.

The revocability condition neither automatically clears nor bars the resourced exit. A consent-based account owes an answer to an objection its own structure raises: valid authorization holds only while it remains revocable (§6.1.2), while death is the most irreversible act a subject can authorize.

The objection mistakes what revocability protects. Revocability doesn’t require that an authorized act be undoable, since many authorizations licensed here are irreversible in their effects; it requires that the authorizing agent never be permanently bound by a past authorization its present self can no longer reach. A waiver that leaves a living agent in place while stripping that agent of all standing to revoke is void at the structural level, because it preserves the very thing (an agent with a present will) whose authority it claims to have canceled and overrides that will at every later moment.

Death isn’t a case in which revocability is vacuously satisfied. It is the case in which error or later revision becomes impossible, which increases rather than removes the burden on authorization. Revocability can be protected only up to the act itself through contemporaneous capacity, repeated confirmation, freedom from coercion, adequate time, and a genuine opportunity to withdraw. Whether those safeguards are sufficient is an empirical and ethical question. The inalienability principle neither automatically bars nor clears the exit.

Advance directives raise a different problem from contemporaneous choice. A directive may preserve an earlier competent authorization, but it can also bind a later person whose present interests or wishes the author didn’t anticipate. That precedent-versus-current-interests dispute applies to feeding tubes and dialysis as well as assisted death, and it isn’t settled here. Documentation, fit to the actual condition, capacity when the directive was written, and any evidence of present interests all matter.

The disability-rights critique is strongest where an assisted death is available while ordinary life remains unsupported. Secure income, care, accommodation, and equal standing reduce that pressure but don’t prove it gone; soft coercion can survive formal choice and procedural compliance. The framework therefore converges with the critique against substituting an exit for the foundation and leaves open the empirical disagreement over whether safeguards can identify coercion reliably enough even after the foundation operates.

If an assisted-dying option is justified under the additional autonomy, medical-role, risk, and safeguard premises, it must remain an option rather than a mandate and must not displace palliative care, hospice, disability support, or community accompaniment. Access and protection against pressure both matter. The universal healthcare floor itself doesn’t require that the option exist; it requires that no person’s eligibility or refusal be driven by lack of ordinary care or material support.

A reliable foundation can reduce several sources of health-related financial insecurity: exposure to medical debt, loss of coverage with employment, catastrophic caregiving costs, and inadequate support in old age. It can’t guarantee that none will occur. Adequacy, waiting, uncovered services, labor supply, housing costs, family needs, and fiscal design remain consequential. The prediction is comparative: systems that maintain effective access and social insurance should reduce these risks relative to otherwise similar systems that leave them to private capacity, with the size and distribution of the effect established empirically.

The argument leaves the payer and provider mix, capacity planning, mental-health delivery, pharmaceutical pricing, public-health administration, and transition path open. Drug policy still requires comparative judgment among treatment, harm reduction, decriminalization, legalization, and enforcement. End-of-life policy still requires decisions about eligibility, prognosis, waiting, capacity review, and the medical channel. Where several designs satisfy the constraints, research, operating evidence, and democratically recognized direction through §6.3 decide among them.

At bottom, a layered conclusion is earned here. The categorical core is that every participant must have timely effective access to adequate healthcare and public-health protection, with scarcity governed by clinical criteria rather than wealth or status. No payer or provider model is uniquely derived; every architecture must be judged after payment incidence, waiting, quality, health gain, administrative burden, capacity, innovation, fiscal durability, and capture are counted. Mental-health and substance treatment belong within care, while exact drug regulation adds autonomy, harm, and comparative-evidence premises. Reproductive, genetic, and end-of-life conclusions remain substantive but additionally depend on the book’s consciousness, agency, disability, risk, and coercion arguments. This separation doesn’t gut the applications. It prevents disagreement with one application from reaching the universal foundation and prevents the foundation from doing argumentative work only those additional premises can perform.

## 6.11 Defense

A hard case for treating other people as real is the one where they live on the far side of a border, under another government, and may even be on the other side of a fight. The argument’s answer is that the rule doesn’t change with distance: a civilian abroad is as real as a neighbor, so the same recognition owed a fellow citizen sets limits on what may be done across a boundary. Defending a community against being coerced from outside is legitimate on exactly the grounds that fund courts or public health. What isn’t legitimate is a permanent war industry that needs conflicts to keep going, or force that treats a foreign population as an object of coercion rather than as people still owed protection. So the test for any use of force is whose foreclosed standing it actually protects, kept honest by how it is fought rather than by what it is called.

The political community isn’t the only political community. Different communities interact under conditions where mutual recognition is harder, slower, and more contestable.

Defense derives from §5.14 (Morality) and §5.13 (Technology). If mutual recognition grounds the moral framework within a political community, the question is how that recognition reaches people governed by other communities—people with the same basic vulnerabilities but different institutions for coordinating their lives. International relations aren’t exempt from the recognition-failure-as-wrong logic; they simply make recognition harder to achieve.

Technology (§5.13) matters because a population’s weapons and [infrastructure](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) determine which other populations it can affect, and at what stakes. A population with nuclear, cyber, biological, or orbital reach therefore has recognition obligations across that reach, on the same logic applied across time at §6.5. The civilian across the border holds the same two-place standing (§5.14.3); Technology scales the obligation to reach, as Environment scales it to time.

Defense doesn’t mint a right to force. It spends the right to life already earned at §6.1 on the external boundary: participation is unavailable to subject $s$ where the community remains unprotected against foreseeable coercion from outside. Force that makes a population itself the coercive object attacks subjects the obligation still runs toward. Procurement form stays open; a permanent extraction industry doesn’t follow from the protective floor.

**[Right]**

**Protection** · *Right*

Participation is unavailable to subject $s$ if the community is left open to foreseeable coercion from outside. This spends the right to life at the border; it does not mint a right to force. Procurement form stays open.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14), Technology (§5.13), and The Chapter 6 Premises (§6.1)

The protective obligation isn’t exhausted by war. Trade can shift environmental and labor costs onto people outside a [polity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary)’s borders; migration policy can treat displaced people as burdens rather than as subjects whose conditions are at stake; climate policy can consume a shared atmosphere while leaving others with its consequences. The argument doesn’t derive a world state or a single global program. It does derive a constraint: a political community may not secure its own conditions by systematically offloading their costs onto people beyond its border. Where cross-border problems require common institutions, those institutions must recognize the affected populations rather than merely aggregate the interests of the states with the most power.

A defense procurement system has to preserve enough standing capacity, skilled labor, supply resilience, and reserve capability to answer threats before a new industrial base could be built. Permanence is therefore not itself evidence of extraction. The diagnostic case is narrower and stronger: contractor returns, lobbying, concentration, and revolving-door movement grow while independently assessed protective contribution stagnates or declines; programs survive failed performance tests because cancellation would impose concentrated political costs; or conflict-continuation incentives influence the assessment that is supposed to justify the spending. A compatible budget may rise before an imminent threat materializes and may decline only after procurement lags and alliance commitments are counted. What it must do is remain answerable to independently reviewable changes in adversary capability, demonstrated intent, imminence, probability, expected magnitude, and the least harmful sufficient response. That responsiveness pattern is fixed here, not a dollar number or a public-versus-private label.

Three results follow.

*Defense is shared infrastructure when it protects the political community; it is extraction when it turns against the people and institutions it is supposed to protect.* The argument isn’t pacifist. It derives the legitimacy of adequate protective capacity directly from the political community’s obligation to maintain itself against external coercion, on the same logic as the legal system or public health. The constraint doesn’t decide in advance between public production, competitive contracting, regulated private specialization, alliance pooling, or mixed provision. Compensation and profit are supported where they track necessary contribution under transparent prices, contestable procurement, enforceable performance, and public control. They become extraction where monopoly, information asymmetry, cost shifting, lobbying, or conflict-continuation incentives produce returns unsupported by protective contribution and insulate programs from review. Eisenhower’s January 1961 farewell address articulated the risk; the empirical question is where the risk is instantiated, at what magnitude, and against which less captured comparator.

Defense also has a workplace register. Military command is among the strongest forms of authority Anderson analyzes (*Private Government* 2017): service members surrender substantial civilian discretion under the UCMJ, while contractors can exercise delegated public power. Necessary delegation doesn’t transfer responsibility for constitutional control, labor conditions, performance, or remedy. Nor are defense burdens distributed neutrally: the US record includes segregated service, Vietnam-era deferment inequities, unequal exposure to military risk, and the racially unequal domestic incidence of equipment and doctrine transferred through the 1033 Program. Mills’s *The Racial Contract* (1997) and *Black Rights / White Wrongs* (2017) sharpen that recognition problem. Defense is public work the community may delegate but cannot alienate.

*The balance between deterrence investment and nonmilitary engagement is a [maximization condition](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) layered on the foundation each secures separately.* Each secures something the other can’t: nonmilitary engagement is how mutual recognition scales across arrangement boundaries at all, and deterrence investment is how the political community maintains its standing when recognition fails. A community that maintains neither fails the protective obligation already established at §6.1. Their relative weighting, worked out at §6.11.2, is a prediction rather than a derivation: political communities whose deterrence investment systematically outruns their nonmilitary engagement are predicted to over-produce conflict, on the same logic that engagement-extraction over-produces information-environment degradation in §6.4. Getting the proportion right doesn’t change whether the foundation is met; it changes how much conflict the arrangement avoids beyond it.

*Cross-boundary recognition-failure follows the same logic as within-arrangement recognition-failure, located at greater distance.* Civilians of other arrangements, refugees, populations under occupation, and future participants of any arrangement currently being put at risk are participants whose constitutive vulnerabilities were already established. What that precludes, and how the just-war tradition’s discrimination, proportionality and last-resort constraints recover structurally from it rather than arriving as a separate moral system grafted on, is set out at §6.11.2.

This yields a diagnostic at the level of cause: any use of force across the boundary must answer whose foreclosed standing it protects. A war of annexation or resource seizure extends the aggressor’s reach by foreclosing the seized population’s standing and is unjust on its face. Halting enslavement, extermination, invasion, or comparable mass foreclosure can answer the protective obligation directly, but the severity of the wrong doesn’t by itself establish that a proposed operation will reduce it.

Authority requires a public showing that can be independently reviewed. First, an actor must have both the capability and demonstrated intent to impose the harm. Second, the threat must be imminent and probable enough to make coercive action necessary. Third, the defensive objective must be tied to ending that threat. Fourth, less harmful means must have been exhausted or shown inadequate. Fifth, the operation must have a reasonable prospect of leaving the protected population better rather than worse off. Sixth, its conduct must discriminate and keep expected harm proportionate. Seventh, it must have conditions for termination once the threat is removed.

Classified particulars may be withheld from general release while still being tested by independent civilian bodies. Cause and conduct remain distinct axes. A war can pass at the level of cause and fail in its conduct. A just cause launders no atrocity.

That diagnostic follows from where the obligation lands. The vulnerabilities Morality (§5.14) governs are borne by individuals, not regimes; recognition therefore belongs to the person at every scale from the household to the political community. Where another political order forecloses its own population, the first-line response is nonmilitary engagement: protection, diplomacy, materially effective aid where it can be delivered without strengthening the coercive machinery, refugee and migration capacity, sanctions designed around civilian incidence rather than expressive punishment, and support requested by the affected population. Force remains residual. Even precision force can’t literally strike a regime without risking the people and institutions around it, so the relevant requirement isn’t the fiction of costless targeting but the least harmful sufficient means under a comparative forecast that includes civilian death, displacement, institutional collapse, retaliation, escalation, and post-conflict vulnerability. The ought that force enforces is fixed independently by the recognition obligation; the offending regime’s conduct supplies evidence that the obligation is breached, not the norm itself.

The same individual-locus fixes where liability to force ends: liability tracks the active threat, so a genuine surrender withdraws it and force pressed past that surrender inverts the moral position. Its full account of combatant liability—surrender and its terminus, perfidy, and the limits that hold the line—is derived in §6.11.2, where the in bello conditions are worked out; its staging against the moral-equality-of-combatants tradition belongs to §6.11.1, where that debate is joined.

The just-war tradition reached for what is recovered here structurally. From Augustine through Walzer, it placed the authority to use force in divine authorization, natural law, or a cosmic moral order behind political life. The dispute below takes that lineage up in full (§6.11.1).

The same Inversion appears in §11. Just cause, discrimination, proportionality, last resort, and legitimate authority were traditionally grounded beyond the world. Here they arise inside political life once people on both sides of a boundary are recognized as subjects with the vulnerabilities established at §5.14. The constraints are real and binding. They answer to Morality and to the reach established at §5.13, not to a backup ontology.

### 6.11.1 The Dispute
*International-relations-tradition objections.* Pacifism argues that organized lethal force reproduces the recognition-failure it claims to resist. Realism argues that recognition cannot bear the weight assigned to it under international anarchy. Cosmopolitanism agrees that standing crosses borders but disputes the political community’s privileged role. Just-war revisionists divide over combatant equality and liability, while public-choice critics question whether any defense institution can reliably judge its own necessity. Grant the central concession in each case before testing the conclusion.

The pacifist tradition presses the legitimacy claim from one direction: the use of organized lethal force is itself the recognition-failure the framework derives against, and any architecture that licenses defense reproduces at the political-community level the recognition-failure it precludes at the within-community level. The tradition draws on Tolstoy (1893) 1894, the historic peace churches’ Mennonite and Quaker witness, Gandhi’s *satyagraha* (truth-force) writings (1951), and Hauerwas (1983). Its licensing of defense as constitutive infrastructure, on this reading, fails the structural derivation it claims to follow.

The realist tradition presses from the opposite direction (Thucydides, *History of the Peloponnesian War* c. 400 BCE, book V on the Melian Dialogue; Hobbes, *Leviathan* 1651, ch. XIII; Morgenthau 1948; Mearsheimer 2001; and the broader neorealist and offensive-realist literature). On this view, mutual recognition across boundaries is unavailable under anarchy. Making nonmilitary engagement load-bearing imports a moralism the record of state behavior has never sustained. Capabilities and interests, not an obligation to engage, set the proper level of deterrence.

The timing objection sharpens the point. A credible defense can’t be improvised after hostile intent becomes certain. Industrial capacity, trained personnel, alliances, intelligence, logistics, and technological development take years to build, while an adversary can exploit visible weakness. Spending above the current threat estimate may therefore purchase resilience against uncertainty rather than prove capture. Secrecy may protect sources, operations, and deterrent ambiguity rather than merely evade accountability.

The cosmopolitan tradition presses the boundary claim from a third direction: its arrangement-bounded recognition is itself the structural failure mode. The political community whose obligations stop at its own boundary can’t meet the recognition obligation the framework derives at full scope, and the answer is to dissolve the boundary by building transnational institutions, not to optimize the within-boundary recognition proportions. The tradition draws on Kant (1795), Held (1995), the modern transnational-institutionalist literature through Held and Slaughter (2004), and the cosmopolitan-democracy strand through Archibugi (2008) and beyond.

A fourth dispute concerns conduct rather than the authority to use force, and it remains inside the just-war frame. Walzer’s conventionalist account holds that combatants on both sides fight with equal right and are equally liable to attack regardless of which cause is just (*Just and Unjust Wars* 1977). The accumulated practices governing war bind both sides symmetrically on their own interpretive authority. *Jus in bello* therefore stands independently of *jus ad bellum*.

McMahan’s revisionist account denies that equality (*Killing in War* (2009)). Liability tracks responsibility for an unjust threat, so those prosecuting an unjust cause do not occupy the same moral position as those resisting them. But liability to necessary defensive force must still be separated from blame or deserving. A coerced or deceived combatant can pose an active threat without bearing full blame. A culpable planner may bear blame but cease to be targetable once they pose no active threat.

The deeper question is whether the war convention gets its force from shared practice, as Walzer argues, or from something prior to that practice, as the recognition account argues. The choice can’t be avoided. But necessity, liability, culpability, and punishment still can’t be collapsed into one category.

A fifth dispute concerns institutional competence rather than the legitimacy of force. Public-choice critics grant that civilian control, review, and anti-capture rules are valuable while denying that any review body escapes its own incentives, information deficits, and partisan pressures. Procurement specialists add that private contractors can supply innovation, surge capacity, and specialized knowledge that an exclusively public system may not reproduce; military professionals add that operational autonomy and secrecy can be necessary when deliberative delay would cost lives. The answer can’t be that one institutional label is safe. It must specify which decisions require speed, which require prior authorization, which may be secret from adversaries but not from cleared oversight, how failed forecasts are audited afterward, and what evidence would show that an anti-capture reform weakened protection rather than improving it.

The constructive case for defense begins with a harder question: how can protection remain protection rather than turn against the community? Just-war, security, peace, and arms-control traditions each supply part of the answer.

The just-war tradition identified five conditions on the legitimate use of force: just cause, discrimination, proportionality, last resort, and legitimate authority (Augustine, *De civitate Dei* book XIX; Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, q. 40; Vitoria’s lectures on the Indies (1539) 1991; Suárez’s reworking (1612) 1944; Grotius, *De Jure Belli ac Pacis* (1625) 2005; Walzer, *Just and Unjust Wars* 1977). Here those constraints are recovered from the same recognition-failure logic applied across political boundaries.

Dwight D. Eisenhower’s January 17, 1961 farewell address articulated the structural prediction, warning that the same defense apparatus could be turned against the arrangement it was built to protect.

The security-dilemma branch of realist theory (Jervis 1976; Glaser 2010, and the broader defensive-realist literature) supplies the apparatus for explaining how deterrence investment can increase reciprocal fear and conflict even when each side describes its posture as defensive. The security-community institutionalist literature (Deutsch on pluralistic security communities 1957; Adler and Barnett 1998) supplies the countervailing case for how recognition and dependable cooperation can scale across boundaries under conditions realism treats as difficult but not always impossible.

The peace-studies and structural-violence tradition supplies the analytic vocabulary for naming defense political-economy capture as structural extraction: Galtung on structural violence (1969), and the broader peace-research literature. The defense-political-economy literature supplies the operational evidence on which the structural-extraction prediction rests: Bacevich (2008; 2010), the SIPRI Yearbooks documenting global defense spending, and the empirical literature on revolving-door Pentagon-to-contractor career flows.

The arms-control tradition supplies the empirical case for cross-border nonmilitary engagement that the realist tradition treats as structurally unavailable: the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, and the broader nuclear-arms-control empirical literature through Wezeman and Wezeman at SIPRI.

Four positions set the first dispute. Pacifism rejects defense as organized recognition-failure. Realism governs it through capabilities and interests under anarchy. Cosmopolitanism moves it into transnational institutions. The position defended here treats defense as legitimate public infrastructure constrained by adequate protection, cross-boundary recognition, discrimination, necessity, proportionality, civilian control, and resistance to capture.
