Two further disputes cut across those positions. Walzer and McMahan disagree about whether liability as an active threat coincides with responsibility for an unjust cause. A second dispute asks whether democratic review can constrain force without disabling the secrecy, speed, expertise, and standing capacity protection may require. The analysis at §6.11.2 must answer all five pressures without treating either force or restraint as self-validating.

### 6.11.2 The Requirement
Defense has to discharge the political community’s obligation to protect people against external coercion while remaining answerable to the equal standing of people beyond its boundary. That yields a categorical protective floor, governance constraints on any institution that supplies it, and design questions that evidence must settle. A permanent military establishment, a particular budget, and one procurement system don’t follow from the existence of the obligation.

*Effective protection against external coercion is the foundation.* The argument isn’t pacifist. Sufficient capacity to deter, resist, and recover from external coercion follows from the rights-protection result at §6.1. That capacity may be supplied through national forces, alliances, reserve systems, diplomacy backed by credible enforcement, civil defense, cybersecurity, or mixed institutions. An architecture that leaves people predictably defenseless fails the obligation. Which combination is sufficient depends on adversary capability, demonstrated intent, imminence, probability, expected magnitude, alliance reliability, mobilization time, and the comparative effectiveness of less coercive means.

*Protective capacity is foundational; the balance between deterrence and nonmilitary engagement is a maximization question.* Diplomacy, trade, cultural exchange, joint scientific work, migration capacity, treaties, and arms control are ways recognition scales across boundaries. Deterrence preserves room to act when recognition fails. The argument derives neither a fixed ratio nor the claim that every instrument must be funded at every moment. It predicts that a posture whose marginal deterrence gains are outweighed by reciprocal fear, arms competition, or foregone cooperation can increase expected conflict. The balance remains comparative and corrigible: under some threats additional capability will dominate, under others reassurance or cooperative engagement will.

*Cross-boundary recognition obligation is binding (just-war constraints).* Civilians, refugees, occupied populations, and future participants beyond the border retain the vulnerabilities and standing already established. An adversary’s wrongdoing therefore supplies no blank check: any operation must distinguish active threats from protected persons, compare foreseeable civilian and institutional harm with the harm prevented, use the least harmful sufficient means, and stop when its protective purpose ends. The just-war constraints of discrimination, proportionality, necessity, and last resort reappear here as recognition applied across technological reach (§5.14; §5.13).

The *in bello* dispute staged in §6.11.1 turns on four questions that must remain distinct. Is force necessary to stop an active threat? Is the person legally targetable under a workable convention? Are they culpable for creating or sustaining the threat? What punishment or accountability is deserved afterward?

McMahan is right that an aggressor and a defender need not occupy the same deep moral position. Walzer is right that combatants can’t reliably judge individual moral responsibility during battle and that symmetric rules can protect everyone better under radical uncertainty. The underlying constraint comes from recognition, while status-based conventions remain where they best implement discrimination and reciprocal restraint. Targetability does not establish culpability.

The active-threat principle fixes its own terminus. Necessary defensive force lapses when the threat does: a surrender that is manifest and genuine withdraws the forward-looking basis for attack, because the basis was the threat being posed, not an enduring moral status of the person. Perfidy remains prohibited because feigned surrender exploits the protection genuine surrender must receive. A coerced or deceived combatant may be subject to necessary force while the threat is live and still bear diminished backward-looking responsibility. Quarter, safe custody, due process, and eventual release or lawful accountability restore the distinction between stopping a threat and punishing a person.

The coerced conscript is doubly a subject. They may be liable to necessary defensive force while posing an active threat, yet bear diminished blame because coercion narrowed the live alternatives from which their conduct emerged. That is the Modally Compatibilist Responsibility result (§6.13) applied across the boundary. Threat-liability is forward-looking; culpability and deserving are backward-looking. The first need not fall merely because the second does.

Deception can narrow the field epistemically as coercion narrows it practically. A soldier who reasonably believes they are defending others may pose the same immediate threat as one who knowingly prosecutes aggression while lacking the knowledge full culpability requires. Participation alone proves neither informed endorsement nor innocent deception. Adjudication must ask what information was available, how credible it was, what inquiry or refusal would have cost, what authority the person exercised, and whether contrary evidence was deliberately avoided.

Willful ignorance is not mitigating merely because it is ignorance. Responsibility turns on whether evidence was genuinely within reach and deliberately refused. Wartime information systems are often built to close that reach (§6.4), so one scrap of contrary information doesn’t establish culpable knowledge. The soldier who grasps what they prosecute and the soldier deceived into prosecuting it may be equally targetable while the threat is live and unequally answerable after it ends.

Two limits hold the result in place. Surrender ends the forward-looking license to use force against the one who has laid it down; it doesn’t extinguish backward-looking accountability for the recognition-failures already committed, which survives the cessation of the threat. But the register that survives isn’t the within-community adjudication of §6.13: it is the cross-boundary accountability marked at §6.14 as a determinate but not-yet-fully-derived extension. What the surrender line fixes is that register’s lower edge: liability for the threat ends with the threat, while answerability for what was done under the license persists into the cross-boundary register rather than dissolving with the license that occasioned it. And force pressed past a genuine surrender inverts the liability it claims: the party continuing to prosecute force against the non-threatening becomes the responsible recognition-failure threat, and the just cause that licensed defensive force expires at the line the surrender draws.

**[Proposition]**

**Surrender Terminus** · *Proposition*

The license to use defensive force tracks the active threat, not an enduring status of the person. A surrender that is manifest and genuine withdraws that threat, so the forward-looking license ends there. Backward-looking accountability for recognition-failures already committed survives the cessation of the threat, in the cross-boundary register rather than dissolving with the license. Force pressed past a genuine surrender inverts the liability: the party that continues to prosecute force against the non-threatening becomes the recognition-failure threat.

*Scope.* This does not uniquely specify a tribunal, a world state, or a particular convention of quarter. Perfidy remains prohibited because feigned surrender exploits the protection genuine surrender must receive.

**Depends on:** Protection (§6.11) and Morality (§5.14)

*Surrender transfers a person from the active-threat register into protection and accountability.* The license to attack ends; humane custody, medical care, protection from reprisal, and due process begin. Repatriation, asylum, resettlement, release, or trial then depend on the person’s safety, status, conduct, and the governing law rather than following from surrender alone. Coercion and deception may mitigate responsibility without erasing it, while perfidy remains prohibited because feigned surrender exploits the protection genuine surrender must receive. The point is narrower than a migration rule: once the threat ends, the surrendered person can’t be treated as an enemy status made permanent.

*Unsupported returns and captured judgment are precluded at the protective floor.* Public production, competitive contracting, regulated private specialization, alliance pooling, and mixed provision can each contribute to protection. Profit isn’t disqualifying where it compensates necessary contribution under contestable procurement, transparent cost, enforceable performance, and public control. Extraction occurs where concentration, information asymmetry, cost shifting, lobbying, or revolving-door incentives produce returns unsupported by protective contribution, preserve failed programs, distort threat assessment, or favor conflict continuation. That incidence pattern is precluded; the corrective instrument is left open: public production, competition policy, independent cost testing, contract reform, recusal and cooling-off rules, concentration limits, or other effective designs.

*Capability and spending must answer to a reviewable threat test.* No threat estimate is self-validating, and spending can’t move one-for-one with a contemporaneous indicator when training, procurement, alliance commitments, replacement cycles, and industrial resilience operate across years. The required test separates adversary capability, demonstrated intent, imminence, probability, and expected magnitude; compares military and nonmilitary responses; counts procurement lag and the option value of reserve capacity; and states what evidence would permit expansion or require contraction. Multiple independent assessments, external red teams, disclosed uncertainty ranges, industry-recusal rules, and retrospective scoring of forecasts are compatible safeguards. Exact institutions remain open, but the burden for sustained expansion must not be controlled by the institutions or firms that benefit from it.

*Emergency authority, secrecy, and mission expansion answer to one abuse-resistance standard.* Speed and secrecy can protect a polity. It need not disclose operational plans to an adversary or wait for ordinary procedure while an attack unfolds. But secrecy from an adversary doesn’t entail secrecy from cleared civilian oversight, and temporary speed doesn’t create permanent authority.

Any compliant system needs the equivalent of five controls. Emergency and war-making powers must expire or face affirmative periodic renewal. Classified decisions must remain reviewable outside the chain of command that made them and should enter a declassification process once the protective reason lapses. Threat forecasts need independent challenge and retrospective scoring. Military command must remain subordinate to civilian institutions accountable through §6.3. Expansion into domestic policing, domestic political surveillance, or force projection unconnected to a live protective purpose requires separate legal authority and justification.

Particular timelines and bodies remain design questions. The binding requirement is that no institution can invoke its own secrecy, urgency, expertise, or mission success as the final test of powers from which it benefits.

*Veterans care is a non-substitutable foundation with heightened remedial responsibility.* Veterans care is healthcare for people who accepted distinctive risks and constraints on behalf of the political community. The §6.10 foundation therefore applies in full, while service-connected injury creates an additional duty of repair proportionate to the burden imposed. Public, nonprofit, contracted, and hybrid delivery remain candidates; a design fails when it produces avoidable delay, discontinuity, denial, or financial exposure below the foundation. The relevant empirical comparison is need-adjusted access, quality, continuity, and recovery, not a presumed inverse relation between contractor spending and veterans budgets.

The direct foundation therefore has three parts: effective protection against external coercion, binding limits against imposing equal or greater foreclosure on people across the boundary, and adequate repair for those burdened or injured in providing the protection. Threat review, anti-capture rules, civilian control, emergency renewal, secrecy review, and mission limits are governance constraints: every architecture must supply effective equivalents, but no single committee, deadline, procurement form, or ownership model is uniquely derived. The balance among deterrence, diplomacy, and international cooperation is a maximization condition judged by conflict, security, and human-incidence outcomes. The predictions of §6.11.3 put all three layers to test.

### 6.11.3 Predictions
The account developed here predicts differences among defense systems, not results from the label attached to them. Each comparison must specify the threat, the protective contribution, the human incidence, the time horizon, and the institutional alternative. A favored architecture that fails the protective floor isn’t rescued by being public, private, restrained, or heavily armed.

The second prediction is the one worth holding concretely, because it is where the difference between a defense budget and an extraction becomes visible. A threat assessment concludes that an adversary’s capability has fallen. If assessment is genuinely independent, procurement should fall too, and some program should end. If instead the assessment changes and the budget doesn’t—if capability only ever ratchets upward, and every reassessment finds new reasons for the same line items—then the assessment isn’t driving the spending and something else is. That asymmetry is measurable, it is the test the predictions that follows are built to run, and it is the reason the account refuses to read a large defense budget as either evidence of prudence or evidence of capture without checking which way it moves when the threat recedes.

*First.* Adequate protective capacity should reduce expected loss from external coercion relative to a feasible less-capable alternative. Compare similarly exposed political communities, alliances, or policy changes using adversary capability and intent, successful deterrence and defense, territorial and civilian loss, alliance reliability, cyber and infrastructure resilience, fiscal cost, and recovery time. Account for geography, alliance guarantees, technology, procurement lag, and adversary adaptation. The prediction fails where lower capacity or slower mobilization produces greater coercion or harm without an offsetting gain from nonmilitary engagement.

*Second.* Where threat assessment is independent, capability and spending should respond in both directions to changes in adversary capability, demonstrated intent, imminence, probability, and expected magnitude after modernization cycles, inflation, alliance obligations, and reserve requirements are counted. Compare assessment changes with later budget, posture, and procurement decisions, then compare those decisions with district dependence, lobbying, concentration, and revolving-door measures. A persistent political-economy effect after the strategic controls supports capture; disappearance of the effect, or better threat responsiveness in industry-dependent systems, counts against it.

*Third.* Captured procurement should produce more noncompetitive awards, cost and schedule growth, requirements drift, program survival after failed tests, and returns unsupported by delivered capability than matched procurement with contestable suppliers and independent cost review. Program complexity, technical novelty, quantity changes, inflation, and deliberate resilience spending are confounders rather than evidence of capture. The claim fails where ownership, lobbying, concentration, and revolving-door exposure don’t predict performance after those differences are controlled.

*Fourth.* Weakly reviewed war powers and conflict-continuation incentives should be associated with deployments that outlive their stated objective, repeated authorization by inherited emergency language, expanding mission definitions, and termination decisions more responsive to concentrated beneficiaries than to civilian and strategic outcomes. Compare otherwise similar operations by authorization, renewal, objective clarity, independent review, contractor exposure, civilian harm, duration, and exit performance. The mechanism is weakened if stronger oversight doesn’t improve termination discipline or if captured systems end unsuccessful operations as readily as their comparators.

*Fifth.* Veterans systems should be judged against need-adjusted access, clinical quality, continuity, disability recovery, financial protection, and geographic variation. The predicted failure isn’t a mechanical inverse relation between procurement and veterans budgets. It is a political community willing to finance exposure while leaving the resulting injury untreated. The claim is defeated where service-connected need is met comparably across burden levels and procurement configurations, or where the alleged tradeoff disappears after caseload and severity are counted.

*Sixth.* Defense-to-domestic mission expansion should increase where external equipment, personnel, surveillance capacity, or doctrine lacks a separate domestic authorization and incidence test. Compare changes in transfers and missions with crime, officer safety, use of force, civilian injury, racial incidence, public trust, and displacement into ordinary policing. Because existing 1033 research is mixed and data quality matters, neither equipment receipt nor withdrawal by itself settles the mechanism. The prediction fails where expansion improves relevant safety outcomes without increasing coercive incidence or weakening civilian accountability.

*Seventh.* Deterrence, diplomacy, and international cooperation should be tested jointly. Across rivalries and policy changes, compare military capability, arms-control verification, diplomatic contact, trade and scientific ties, crisis frequency, escalation, proliferation, and war onset. The prediction isn’t that arms always produce war or diplomacy always prevents it. It is that a posture adding marginal capability while worsening reciprocal fear can increase expected conflict, whereas credible defense paired with verifiable reassurance can reduce it. Evidence that additional deterrence consistently reduces conflict without escalating arms competition counts against the proposed gradient; evidence that nonmilitary engagement fails under comparable threats does the same.

*Eighth.* Abuse-resistant civilian control should improve both protection and correction. Compare emergency renewal, war-powers reporting, classification review, declassification, forecast accuracy, mission expansion, retaliation against oversight, and post hoc remedy across institutions with stronger and weaker external review. Secrecy that protects operations while remaining accessible to cleared oversight is compatible with the prediction. Persistent error, abuse, or mission growth hidden from every independent body supports it. If stronger review predictably destroys necessary speed or leaks protective information without improving accountability, the proposed safeguard has failed and must be redesigned.

These predictions engage pacifism, realism, cosmopolitanism, just-war theory, public-choice criticism, and the defense-industrial-base objection developed in §6.11.1. They leave force structure, ownership, alliance design, treaty architecture, procurement form, and budget level open. What they don’t leave open is the performance standard: protection, recognition, incidence, accountability, and correction are measured together.

### 6.11.4 Confirmation
The predictions of §6.11.3 require an evidence hierarchy. A speech, chronology, budget series, or cross-sectional association can identify a mechanism worth testing. Matched comparisons and longitudinal changes can narrow alternatives. Natural experiments, policy discontinuities, and well-identified procurement studies can support causal claims. No single national history establishes transportability across threats, alliances, and institutions. The record that follows is graded accordingly.

*First.* The military-industrial-complex record strongly establishes the existence of capture risks, not their presence in every permanent defense institution. Eisenhower’s January 17, 1961 farewell address states the hypothesis; it isn’t evidence for itself. SIPRI time series establish the scale and movement of military inputs, while SIPRI’s own method cautions that expenditure isn’t a direct measure of capability or security. US consolidation, noncompetitive procurement, cost and schedule growth, lobbying, and Pentagon-to-contractor movement supply mechanism-consistent evidence, with some procurement research identifying worse contracting outcomes where product-market concentration increases. The earned conclusion is that concentration and political access can degrade contestability and shift risk to the public. Permanent capacity, contractor use, and profit don’t by themselves confirm extraction.

*Second.* Spending responds to both threats and political institutions. US spending did contract after the Cold War, which defeats the categorical claim that it didn’t scale down at all; it remained above some proposed post-Cold-War baselines and later expanded after 2001. Cross-national research likewise treats external threat, alliances, regime type, fiscal capacity, public opinion, ideology, and domestic interests as joint determinants. A spending-versus-threat gap can’t be read directly from SIPRI inputs because threat assessments are contested and readiness has long lags. The record supports testing political distortion after strategic controls rather than treating every residual as capture.

*Third.* The post-2001 US record confirms long deployments, inherited authorizations, shifting objectives, and very high human and fiscal costs. It doesn’t by chronology alone identify contractor capture as the cause of continuation. Bacevich’s analysis, contractor exposure, lobbying records, and concentrated district interests make the mechanism plausible; presidential strategy, alliance commitments, bureaucratic inertia, public threat perception, and conditions in theater remain rival explanations. The forever-war pattern is established descriptively. Its attribution to industry is supported but not isolated across the whole period.

*Fourth.* Veterans-care failures are real, but the proposed inverse signature was overstated. The 2014 VA wait-time scandal established serious access and reporting failures. Later administrative and comparative studies show substantial geographic and specialty variation, and some find VA care timelier or better coordinated than community alternatives. Veterans spending has also risen substantially over time. The evidence supports a non-substitutable need-adjusted care standard; it doesn’t establish that contractor spending mechanically causes veterans underfunding or that private delivery necessarily performs worse.

*Fifth.* The 1033 Program, post-9/11 surveillance expansion, and military-derived domestic tactics establish mission transfer as a real phenomenon. Balko (2013) and ACLU compilations document its scale and incidence. Causal claims are less settled. Studies have reported no average reduction in crime or officer harm, reputational costs, and associations with coercive outcomes; other analyses have found benefits or have shown that results change when transfer data are corrected. The evidence supports separate domestic authorization and outcome testing. It doesn’t yet isolate defense-industry overcapacity as the general cause of police militarization.

*Sixth.* Arms races, proliferation, and arms-control erosion have multiple causes. The ABM withdrawal, strain on New START, failed negotiations, and domestic constituencies show that arms-control architecture is politically vulnerable. Security competition, verification problems, alliance commitments, technological change, leadership beliefs, and domestic distributional interests all matter. Industry influence is a credible contributing mechanism in particular cases, but the record doesn’t confirm that it is generally the most powerful force against arms control. Nor does the evidence support the opposite universal: arms control has sometimes improved stability, while credible deterrence has sometimes prevented coercion.

*Seventh.* The institutional record shows concentrated resistance to particular demobilization decisions. The US base-closure process was removed from ordinary congressional decision-making and handed to an independent commission whose recommendations were voted up or down as a set. That design was adopted because district-level protection had made closure on the merits unreachable. The institution itself thereby acknowledges the pattern. But *maximal* resistance isn’t established without a common measure across industries, reforms, and periods. Demobilization can also impose real local transition costs and destroy capacity that can’t be restored quickly. The record supports predicting organized resistance and requiring transition plans. It does not support treating every objection as rent protection or every retained base as waste.

*Eighth.* Emergency and secrecy institutions exhibit the predicted accountability risk. Long-lived emergencies, broad executive delegations, incomplete war-powers reporting, overclassification, and delayed correction show how temporary authority can persist and prevent public assessment. At the same time, intelligence sources, operational plans, cyber capabilities, and deterrent uncertainty can require secrecy and speed. The evidence supports independent cleared review, renewal, retrospective forecast scoring, and eventual declassification presumptions. It doesn’t derive one universal sunset period or require contemporaneous public disclosure of every protective fact.

*Theoretical convergence.* Jervis’s security dilemma, Glaser’s variation in the prospects for cooperation, Adler and Barnett’s security communities, Galtung’s structural-violence vocabulary, and Eisenhower’s institutional warning reach overlapping mechanisms from different premises. That convergence supports the test architecture; it doesn’t substitute for causal confirmation.

*Counterevidence and transportability.* Permanent forces, alliances, nuclear and conventional deterrence, private technological specialization, and classified operations have sometimes protected political communities. Procurement reform can also trade lower price against resilience, innovation, or surge capacity. These cases rule out the universal claims that standing capability is extraction, that more deterrence always increases conflict, that public production is always superior, or that transparency is costless. They don’t rule out the bounded conclusion: each increment of force, secrecy, emergency authority, and protected return remains answerable to independently reviewable protective contribution and comparative human incidence.

### 6.11.5 Conclusions
*Structural constraints.* A political community must maintain sufficient capacity to deter, resist, and recover from external coercion. That is the categorical result. It doesn’t uniquely require a permanent national military of one size, public production, private contracting, a particular alliance, or one doctrine. Those are candidates judged by whether they deliver protection without imposing equal or greater foreseeable foreclosure on people beyond the boundary. Discrimination, necessity, expected-harm proportionality, a reasonable prospect of protective success, and termination when the threat ends are therefore constitutive limits on the use of force, not optional restraints added after defense has been licensed.

*Governance and design.* Capability and spending must answer to a threat test that separates adversary capability, demonstrated intent, imminence, probability, and expected magnitude while counting procurement lag, alliance reliability, modernization, and reserve capacity. Public, nonprofit, competitive private, alliance-pooled, and mixed provision can satisfy the result. Compensation and profit are legitimate where they track necessary contribution under contestable procurement, transparent cost, enforceable performance, and public control. Concentration, information asymmetry, lobbying, revolving-door influence, or conflict-continuation incentives become extraction where they produce unsupported returns, preserve failed programs, or control the assessment that justifies their own expansion. That incidence pattern is precluded, not every contractor.

Emergency authority, secrecy, and operational autonomy are likewise judged by function rather than label. Speed can be necessary during attack, and secrecy can protect sources, plans, cyber capabilities, and deterrent ambiguity. Neither is self-validating. Emergency powers must expire or face affirmative renewal. Independent cleared officials must be able to review classified decisions, and those decisions should enter a declassification process when the protective reason lapses. Threat forecasts need external challenge and retrospective scoring. Military command remains subordinate to accountable civilian institutions. Domestic policing, political surveillance, and force projection unrelated to a live threat require separate authority. Exact bodies and timelines remain open, but no institution may be the final judge of a power from which it benefits.

*Cross-boundary conduct and responsibility.* Active-threat liability, legal targetability, culpability, and punishment are distinct. Necessary defensive force may be used against an active threat without presuming that every person posing it is fully blameworthy. Coercion, deception, authority, available evidence, and willful ignorance govern backward-looking responsibility. A genuine surrender removes the forward-looking basis for attack; it doesn’t erase lawful accountability for prior acts. This preserves McMahan’s insight that aggressor and defender need not occupy the same moral position while preserving Walzer’s insight that symmetric conventions can protect everyone when individualized moral adjudication is impossible in battle.

*Cross-domain couplings.* Veterans care joins defense to healthcare (§6.10): the ordinary care floor applies in full, and service-connected injury adds a duty of repair proportionate to the burden imposed. Delivery remains open among public, nonprofit, contracted, and hybrid systems that meet need-adjusted access, quality, continuity, and financial-protection tests. Civilian control joins defense to representation (§6.3), since review fails where decision-makers answer principally to military, contractor, or district interests. Procurement and transition join defense to the economy (§6.7), because reform that closes a program or base without protecting workers and dependent communities converts a public correction into concentrated private harm. Diplomacy, arms control, environmental cooperation, migration capacity, and joint scientific work connect defense to the wider architecture of nonmilitary engagement; they are protective investments, not sentimental substitutes for it.

*Neighbors.* Pacifism correctly identifies every use of force as a grave recognition cost, but refusing all protective capacity can leave others exposed to coercion. Realism correctly identifies uncertainty, anarchy, and the need for credible capability, but those facts don’t make threat assessments infallible or erase cross-boundary standing. Cosmopolitanism correctly extends concern beyond borders, but a world state isn’t uniquely derived. Public-choice criticism correctly denies that public ownership, review bodies, or civilian officials are immune from capture. The defense-industrial-base objection correctly insists that skilled capacity can’t always be rebuilt after intent becomes certain. Each objection therefore sharpens the conditions rather than defeating the foundation.

The evidence supports a calibrated conclusion. Consolidation, noncompetitive procurement, cost growth, lobbying, revolving-door movement, long deployments, mission expansion, and persistent emergency powers establish serious and recurrent risks. They don’t prove that all standing capacity is waste, that contractor influence caused every intervention, that veterans spending moves inversely with procurement, that industry is the dominant cause of proliferation, or that resistance to demobilization is greater than every other organized resistance. Deterrence, alliances, permanent capacity, private specialization, and classified operations have sometimes protected people. Those successes remain answerable to comparative security, civilian incidence, fiscal durability, accountability, and correction.

Treaty design, alliance architecture, force structure, doctrine, posture, weapons policy, budget level, procurement form, oversight bodies, sunset periods, industrial transition, and veterans-care delivery therefore remain open. Where multiple designs satisfy the constraints, the choice belongs to the strategic and empirical literatures and to the recognized direction of the population through representation under §6.3.

The maximal earned result is that adequate defense is legitimate and required, while every increment of force, secrecy, emergency authority, protected return, and mission expansion carries an independently reviewable burden to show that it reduces expected coercion and human harm more effectively than less coercive alternatives. Existing defense systems contain documented protective achievements and documented extractive configurations. The same obligation that licenses their protective work requires correction where the latter displaces the former.

## 6.12 Enforcement
Where defense guards a community against threats from outside, enforcement guards people against coercion by one another inside it. The direct obligation is effective protection: credible capacity to answer violence, restrain imminent harm, investigate serious wrongdoing, and preserve the rights of victims, witnesses, bystanders, and the person subjected to authority. A substantial share of preventable demand arises before any encounter—in untreated illness, material precarity, lost options, and failed channels of dispute—but adequate prevention doesn’t eliminate every predatory, impulsive, organized, or otherwise residual threat. The institution must therefore be able both to prevent where prevention can work and to act quickly where delay would expose someone to grave harm.

The second claim concerns how that authority is exercised. An enforcement agent is there to protect rights, including the rights of the person being stopped, and a person ordinarily makes better decisions when given time to understand and respond. Combat posture used as the default for a traffic stop or welfare check can erase that time and defeat the protective purpose. Yet time-preservation isn’t a command to wait through an active assault: where an independently assessable threat is imminent, proportionate time-compression may be necessary to protect the person endangered. The point is neither against police nor against force as such. It is that every exercise of coercive authority must answer to the protective function it serves and to the rights-bounded authorization that makes this institution and this officeholder entitled to exercise it. Duty Does Not Confer Authority: the existence of a protective obligation doesn’t supply that authorization by itself.

The political community requires internal protection against coercion within its own perimeter. Defense protects against external coercion; enforcement protects against internal coercion. The two domains share the protective register but address different threat-sources, and the account of each derives from a different upstream stretch of the argument.

Enforcement draws on §5.6, §5.11, and §5.14 to emphasize agency, reasons, and standing. Time, information, and visible alternatives can improve a person’s ability to understand and respond, but their importance varies by institutional stage. A fair trial protects understanding and answer before adjudication through notice, counsel, evidence, an impartial tribunal, and review. A street encounter instead requires lawful grounds, communication where feasible, necessity, proportionality, and preservation of decision-time unless delay would increase an independently assessable threat. These protections share values without becoming one right or one procedure.

The officer in any interaction has to see the possible causes of that felt ought, even in the thin sense of morality (§5.14): the person feels they ought, or they don’t. Panic, psychosis, intoxication, grief, a language the officer doesn’t share, or a reason the person takes as binding: each can make the same surface look like defiance. Time to answer is wasted if the encounter has no way to hear those causes as causes.

Where a person perceives few safe alternatives, threat display can further narrow attention and increase panic, flight, resistance, or self-harm. A welfare check or suicide call therefore ordinarily calls for a clinical and de-escalatory orientation rather than an assumption of defiance. It can also present danger to the person, responders, or third parties, so dispatch and responders must assess weapons, behavior, medical need, communication, and available distance rather than classify every call by diagnosis alone. A visible path toward safety can help; it isn’t guaranteed to resolve the crisis. The care side is supplied at §6.10, while necessity and proportionality govern any protective force.

**[Right]**

**Fair Trial** · *Right*

A fair trial requires meaningful notice, an opportunity to understand and answer the case, adequate assistance, an impartial decision-maker, and review appropriate to the stakes. Pretrial detention, police encounters, crisis response, and use of force are governed by related but stage-specific protections: lawful grounds, necessity, proportionality, communication where feasible, and remedy. They share the standing of the person subjected to authority; they are not all instances of the trial right.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14), Will (§5.11), and The Chapter 6 Premises (§6.1)

That is the foundation at the encounter. Education is what keeps preservation-lines in the field before the limit is reached (§6.9); subsistence and care are what make a mapped line reachable (§6.7, §6.10). The domains are one mechanism.

The conventional articulation locates enforcement at the reactive-punitive register: police respond after harm, arrest after offense, deter through the threat of consequence. The same institution is spelled out at the upstream-prevention register: enforcement exists to prevent the conditions and de-escalate the moments where coercion within the political community would otherwise materialize. The legitimacy of any encounter rests on its preservation of the agency the encounter is supposed to protect. This is the validity-redemption-of-facticity logic Habermas develops (*Between Facts and Norms* (1992) 1996) applied at encounter-level: the coercive facticity of law is legitimate only when redeemable through the discursive justification the affected community can endorse, ratified continuously through the recognition mechanism (§6.3). The symmetric question is when citizens may legitimately resist enforcement that has failed its derived purpose. That is the civil-disobedience question Habermas develops at the result register (‘Civil Disobedience: Litmus Test for the Democratic Constitutional State’ 1985), developed downstream at §6.13. The Inversion runs the same direction as the rest of Chapter 6. The protective tradition reached for safety understood as the absence of coercion and located the institution at the reactive-punitive register; the same commitment is spelled out at the level where coercion is prevented before it becomes the kind of event reactive force has to manage.

Consider a 911 call reporting that a man on a downtown sidewalk is shouting at no one and sometimes lunging at passers-by in an apparent psychiatric crisis. One response sends patrol officers whose principal tools are command and force. A differentiated system first assesses violence, weapons, medical need, and bystander exposure; when the call is reasonably triaged as non-violent, a behavioral-health responder leads, with police backup available if the risk changes. The architecture can materially change the path from contact to treatment, arrest, injury, or death, but it can’t guarantee a benign outcome: dispatch information can be incomplete, crises can escalate, and civilian responders need training, communications, withdrawal protocols, and timely backup. The records from CAHOOTS, Denver STAR, and related programs support testing this differentiated-response prediction rather than treating one program label as decisive. Co-responder and alternative-response systems instantiate *Integration without assimilation* at the institutional register when enforcement, clinical care, and crisis response coordinate without collapsing their distinct functions into one tactical playbook. That architecture is the thick clinical case. The thin requirement still runs on the traffic stop: the officer has to see possible causes of the person’s felt ought even when no one has labeled the call psychiatric.

*The upstream-prevention thesis.* A substantial but not exhaustive share of coercion-demand is shaped by conditions the argument addresses in earlier domains: untreated mental illness and substance disorder (§6.10), poverty and material precarity (§6.7 and §6.10 jointly), educational gaps and under-formation of capacity (§6.9), and failed public channels for resolving disputes before they become physical (§6.1, §6.3, §6.4). Adequate upstream investment should reduce the component of harm and call volume causally responsive to those conditions. It won’t erase coercion rooted in organized predation, acute conflict, opportunism, or causes not altered by the intervention, and it can’t substitute for prompt protection when harm is underway. Upstream institutions and enforcement are therefore complements whose marginal contributions must be tested separately. Systematic under-investment can overload enforcement and worsen its performance, but that claim is empirical and fails where comparable investment doesn’t reduce victimization, crisis demand, or coercive encounters.

*The rights-protection inversion.* Enforcement is for the third parties whose rights the encounter is protecting, not a crackdown on the enforcement-target. A speed-limit stop isn’t punitive toward the speeder; it is protective of every other driver’s right to navigate the road without elevated risk. The person being stopped isn’t the institution’s adversary. The institution exists to change behavior that is harming other people who share the same civic conditions. The same orientation appears in §6.10 Healthcare (the patient isn’t a cost center; healthcare exists for the patient) and §6.9 Education (the student isn’t a credential-sorting target; education exists to develop the student). The enforcement-target remains a participant in the political community throughout the encounter; the institution isn’t licensed to treat them as an adversary even when their behavior has produced the encounter. This is the relational-equality test (Anderson, ‘What Is the Point of Equality?’ 1999) applied at the enforcement encounter: standing as a participant in the political community is what the encounter must structurally preserve. The §6.1 ‘Government work discharges the obligation’ result names the foundational form this section inherits: enforcement is one of the ways the political community discharges the obligation (§5.14), not a function each citizen separately discharges in private capacity.

*De-escalation as an agency-preserving commitment.* Reasoning navigates a field of possibilities (§5.4; §5.6), and will acts through the alternatives a person can register (§5.11). An enforcement encounter puts that agency under unusual pressure: a decision to comply, explain, move, or speak can alter a person’s liberty or life. Where danger permits, distance, clear communication, time, and a visible path toward safety protect the capacity the institution is meant to preserve. They don’t guarantee compliance or safety, and the philosophical argument doesn’t establish the effect size; training and operational evidence must do that. But default combat posture can compress thought and erase mapped exits before the threat requires it. De-escalation is the defeasible rule against that avoidable compression, not a prohibition on rapid protective action.

De-escalation and upstream prevention work at different horizons. One preserves possibilities within an encounter; the other changes conditions that make some encounters more likely. Removing deprivation, untreated illness, or an inaccessible dispute channel won’t make coercion impossible, and those conditions never prove why a particular person acted. It can reduce the portion of harm causally responsive to them. That is why prevention and residual protective capacity are complements rather than rival absolutes.

This yields a sharp structural critique of conventional tactical doctrine when it is applied as the default posture for routine encounters rather than reserved for independently assessable danger. Rapid intervention is appropriate where an active threat is underway—a drawn weapon, an in-progress assault, an immediate danger to life—and the necessity and proportionality of compression can be reviewed afterward. The critique targets generalized escalation in traffic stops, welfare checks, mental-health calls, and other encounters where there is time to create distance, communicate, reassess, and call specialized help. In those settings, avoidable compression of the citizen’s analysis-time can destroy the agency the institution exists to preserve.

The boundary with §6.11 Defense is therefore functional rather than genealogical. Equipment isn’t disqualified merely because a military has also used it: medical supplies, protective equipment, communications, rescue vehicles, and specialized tools may reduce harm in narrowly defined circumstances. What requires justification is the capability, deployment rule, and induced posture. Enemy-identification, indiscriminate threat display, routine tactical deployment, and acquisition that creates pressure to use a capability violate the boundary where less harmful sufficient means exist; protective equipment or specialized armed response may satisfy it where the expected-risk record supports the use.

### 6.12.1 The Dispute
The enforcement debate turns on two questions that must remain separate: whether a political community needs an effective function for protection against internal coercion, and which institutions can discharge it without becoming coercive themselves. Abolitionists press the historical and institutional record; order-maintenance traditions press the protective value of presence; libertarians press monopoly and incentive failures; anarchists press the danger of standing hierarchy. The first question is answered by the protective obligation. The second remains open to those objections and to comparative evidence; no familiar department, private market, or decentralized council is legitimate by name.

The police-abolitionist tradition presses the historical and institutional objection at strength (Davis 2003; Gilmore 2007; Kaba 2021; Vitale 2017). Racialized origins, strike-breaking and colonial functions, repeated reform cycles that leave coercive patterns intact, budget crowd-out, and the tendency of a force monopoly to reproduce its own demand give reason to doubt that a department can be refounded merely by changing its mission statement. The objection isn’t answered by showing that protection is necessary; it requires mechanisms that can withdraw authority, reallocate functions, expose records, provide remedy, and replace an institution that repeatedly fails.

The broken-windows and order-maintenance traditions (Wilson and Kelling 1982, Bratton, Mac Donald, Weisburd) press a different protective objection. Visible presence, rapid response, focused attention to high-harm places, and credible consequences can prevent victimization, improve clearance, and reassure people whose neighborhoods bear concentrated violence. Hot-spots evidence supports modest crime reduction under some focused strategies. That result doesn’t establish indiscriminate low-level enforcement, stop saturation, or adversarial contact as the mechanism: place concentration, problem-oriented intervention, social services, and procedurally fair presence can produce different incidence. The crime-prevention result must be preserved while rejecting methods whose marginal benefit is outweighed by error, displacement, humiliation, distrust, or unequal exposure.

The libertarian minimal-state tradition (Nozick 1974; Rothbard 1973, Benson, Friedman) presses the monopoly objection. State agencies face weak competitive discipline, diffuse liability, and political incentives that can protect poor performance. Contracted security, insurance, and arbitration may sometimes specialize, innovate, or scale faster. Yet contract doesn’t by itself protect a person who can’t pay, didn’t consent, or is subject to another party’s provider. Any private contribution must therefore preserve universal access, independent adjudication, public standards, transparency compatible with safety, and authority that can’t be purchased against a less-resourced party.

The anarchist tradition (Kropotkin 1902; Bakunin 1883; Rocker 1938; Ward 1973; Graeber 2004) presses the objection further: mutual aid, federated councils, restorative practices, and direct community action may prevent and resolve conflict without a standing professional force. Grant these as eligible designs rather than treating a centralized department as definitional. It parts only where a proposal leaves no institution capable of binding a person who is actively violating another’s standing. A recallable council, emergency team, or communal process that restrains an assailant or enforces a remedy is performing the protective function in decentralized form.

The standpoint and intersectional feminist tradition (Crenshaw 1989; Crenshaw 1991; Hill Collins 1990) shows why formally equal rules can still fail. Domestic-violence response, antiracist practice, disability response, immigration exposure, poverty, gender identity, and other positions can interact so that an aggregate improvement conceals concentrated harm. The participant-throughout requirement must therefore be tested across intersecting positions, including victims who are underserved as well as people overexposed to enforcement.

A further operational objection comes from the work itself. Dispatch information is incomplete; some low-risk calls turn violent; response delay can cost lives; focused presence can deter coercion; investigations require specialized skill; and responders, including civilian responders, have legitimate safety and labor interests. Officer due process isn’t the same as immunity, and review can’t become predetermined punishment. Personal civil liability may also over-deter reasonable action if indemnification, insurance, and institutional responsibility are badly designed. Nor does the military origin of equipment decide its domestic use: protective, medical, communications, rescue, and specialized-response tools must be judged by function, deployment rule, alternatives, and incidence rather than provenance alone.

The recognition tradition answers with a conjunction rather than a label. The §5.6 and §5.11 agency derivation supports preserving decision-time where time is available; §5.14 supports equal participant standing; public-health and collective-efficacy work supports upstream prevention; reform-criminological evidence tests doctrine and supervision; CAHOOTS, STAR, B-HEARD, CIT, and related programs test differentiated response; Camden and other reforms provide informative but non-randomized institutional comparisons; and Stuntz (2011) and Forman (2017) explain historical and political-economic pathways. None alone proves a complete architecture. Together they specify what rival designs must be compared on: victimization and harm prevented, response and clearance, force and injury, lawful resolution, error and reversal, trust, unequal incidence, cost, responder safety, and recurrence.

The dispute is therefore not police or no police in the abstract. It is whether protection requires a familiar standing monopoly, can be discharged through plural and decentralized institutions, or can disappear as an institutional function altogether; whether proactive presence protects or becomes low-level coercion; whether private specialization disciplines or reproduces power; and how authority remains effective without becoming self-protecting. The Requirement (§6.12.2) resolves only the structural part: some effective protective function is required, while every concrete architecture must earn its authority under the same independently reviewable constraints.

### 6.12.2 The Requirement
The §6.1 protective obligation requires an effective function for protection against internal coercion. It doesn’t by itself require one department, responder type, liability regime, or ownership form. The maximal earned result separates the direct protective floor, the constraints governing every exercise of coercive authority, the cross-domain conditions that reduce preventable demand, and the institutional choices that remain empirically underdetermined.

*Effective protective capacity is required.* A political community must be able to receive calls for help, reach people facing imminent harm, restrain active coercion, investigate serious wrongdoing, preserve evidence, locate dangerous actors, and secure lawful orders and remedies. Capacity includes availability, competence, geographic and temporal coverage, surge capability, and coordination. Upstream prevention can’t replace this foundation, because some threats remain after adequate prevention and delay can enlarge their incidence. The function may be distributed across conventional departments, specialized agencies, community institutions, contracted technical services, or mixed systems, but it may not be left undisclosed or unavailable.

*Participant standing binds every encounter.* The person subjected to authority remains a participant in the political community, not an enemy by default. The same is true of victims, witnesses, bystanders, responders, and people whose harms have historically been ignored. Equal standing doesn’t prohibit restraint. It requires the institution to identify the person or right being protected, distinguish an active threat from noncompliance or disrespect, and stop coercion when the protective reason ends. Resistance, flight, intoxication, disability, mental crisis, prior record, or offense severity may alter risk assessment; none substitutes for evidence of the threat presently justifying a particular intrusion.

*Necessity, proportionality, discrimination, and termination govern coercion.* A search, seizure, detention, or use of force must pursue a lawful protective objective, be no more intrusive than the least harmful sufficient means reasonably available, discriminate between the source of danger and others, have a reasonable prospect of achieving the objective, and terminate when the threat, lawful basis, or necessity terminates. Proportionality is comparative expected incidence, not a judgment that an offense makes whatever follows deserved. Emergency judgment can occur under uncertainty, but the asserted facts, alternatives, timing, and result must remain reviewable afterward.

*Due process, correction, and remedy are part of the foundation.* Notice and a meaningful opportunity to contest must precede final fines, forfeitures, license restrictions, or comparable consequences except where a temporary emergency measure is necessary. Review must be independent of the person and chain of command whose action is contested, accessible to enforcement targets and complainants, timely enough to matter, and empowered to correct records, reverse consequences, compensate unjustified harm, and identify recurrent institutional causes. Responders retain fair notice, representation, evidence access, and neutral adjudication; equal accountability doesn’t require arbitrary discipline.

*Time-preservation is the default, with an active-threat exception.* The §5.6 and §5.11 account of agency supports distance, communication, explanation, reassessment, and time where these don’t expose someone to added danger. The encounter should also make a safe path visible where one exists; a person who sees only capture, injury, or humiliation may panic, flee, resist, or try to create an exit (§5.2), though no response is guaranteed. Delay isn’t required during an active assault or independently assessable imminent threat. Training, dispatch, supervision, and force policy must distinguish routine or containable encounters from cases in which rapid intervention is the least harmful sufficient response. A doctrine fails if it preserves time for one party by abandoning the person endangered, or compresses time where no comparable danger required it.

*Differentiated response capacity is required; one routing rule isn’t.* Mental-health, substance, housing, medical, family-conflict, traffic, investigative, and violent-threat calls present different competencies and risks. A sound system must have civilian, clinical, mediation, investigative, and armed capabilities sufficient to match those differences; it must also have triage standards, shared communications, escalation and withdrawal rules, and timely backup. Civilian-led response is presumptively appropriate for calls reasonably assessed as non-violent and primarily clinical or social, but it doesn’t follow that every such call is safe, that police may never assist, or that one program model fits every jurisdiction.

*The defense boundary is functional.* Domestic enforcement may not adopt enemy-identification or battle-space control as its ordinary relation to fellow participants. Yet provenance doesn’t decide function. Medical supplies, communications, protective equipment, rescue vehicles, and specialized weapons may be justified for defined hazards. Each acquisition and deployment requires a stated use case, expected-risk comparison, training and authorization rule, public reporting compatible with operational safety, review of actual deployment, and retirement when marginal benefit no longer exceeds cost and incidence. Routine threat display, indiscriminate tactical use, and acquisition-driven mission expansion fail that test.

*Financing must not reward coercion.* Budgets, compensation, contracts, fines, fees, forfeitures, citations, detention, and service volumes must be arranged so that the institution or provider doesn’t gain by increasing unjustified encounters or making protection conditional on ability to pay. Ferguson-pattern revenue targets and direct departmental retention of encounter-generated proceeds fail structurally. The same incidence test applies to public, nonprofit, and for-profit providers. Private specialization isn’t excluded by its label, but coercive judgment, universal access, evidence custody, conflicts, profit, performance, and termination must remain under public standards and independent review.

*Accountability must be effective without predetermining one liability design.* Civilian control, transparent policy, auditable encounter records, independent investigation of serious harm, conflict-free prosecution or adjudication, meaningful remedies, pattern detection, and authority to change practice are mandatory functions. Qualified immunity, indemnification, departmental liability, insurance, collective bargaining, licensing, and individual discipline are design variables to the extent different arrangements can still deliver those functions. A regime that leaves established violations without a realistic route to remedy fails; so does one that denies responders ordinary labor protections or predictably deters reasonable protective action without improving public safety.

*Upstream conditions are required by the chapter and coupled to enforcement, but not internal substitutes for it.* Healthcare, housing, education, economic sufficiency, representation, public space, and dispute-resolution institutions should reduce the portion of coercion causally responsive to illness, deprivation, exclusion, and unmanaged conflict. Their contribution must be measured against victimization, crisis calls, repeated contact, and distributional incidence rather than assumed from spending alone. Enforcement remains responsible for the residual protective floor, while its demand and performance can’t be evaluated honestly without those surrounding conditions.

The categorical result is effective internal protection under participant standing, necessity, proportionality, discrimination, termination, due process, remedy, anti-extraction financing, and abuse-resistant civilian control. The governance layer requires functional equivalents for triage, differentiated response, recordkeeping, independent review, correction, and recurring evaluation. The design layer remains open among arrangements that meet the foundation and perform best under the tests in §6.12.3. That layer is department structure, responder mix, provider form, equipment, liability, bargaining, funding source, and transition path.

### 6.12.3 Predictions
The enforcement argument generates comparative predictions, not a presumption that one institutional label will perform well. Each prediction requires a defined comparator, measures of protection and incidence, relevant confounders, a time horizon long enough to distinguish transition from steady performance, and a condition under which the claim fails.

*First.* For comparable encounters, a time-preserving default with a defined active-threat exception should reduce unnecessary force and injury without increasing injury to victims or responders. Compare units or periods facing similar call types and assessed threat levels; measure force frequency and severity, civilian and responder injury, compliance without force, time to resolution, complaints, and repeat calls. Account for firearm prevalence, call mix, staffing, reporting rules, body-camera coverage, local law, and simultaneous reforms over at least one training-and-supervision cycle. The prediction fails if better-implemented time-preservation produces no reduction in avoidable force, or secures that reduction only by increasing serious harm or abandoning lawful protection.

*Second.* Upstream investment should reduce the component of coercion-demand responsive to the conditions addressed. Compare matched places or phased changes in housing stability, behavioral healthcare, education, employment access, community organizations, and dispute-resolution capacity; measure victimization, crisis calls, repeat contact, serious violence, emergency detention, and demand by neighborhood and intersecting social position. Account for demographic change, migration, policing intensity, reporting willingness, economic cycles, drug markets, firearm access, and regression from unusually high baseline periods across multiple years. The claim fails if credible improvements in the relevant conditions don’t reduce the predicted demand or merely displace it to another population or jurisdiction.

*Third.* For calls that can be reliably triaged as non-violent and primarily clinical or social, civilian-led or co-response should outperform police-only default response on resolution without force or arrest, treatment connection, repeat-call reduction, client and responder safety, and full-system cost. Compare like call categories under phased, randomized, threshold-based, or carefully matched routing; count transfers to police, delayed escalation, adverse events, service completion, and downstream health and criminal-legal outcomes over months rather than only at scene clearance. Account for dispatch selection, hours and neighborhoods served, workforce capacity, caller behavior, and concurrent service expansion. The prediction fails where civilian routing can’t be performed safely or reliably, doesn’t improve outcomes, or shifts hidden costs and risk to another system.

*Fourth.* Accountability systems with independent review, accessible complaint routes, reliable records, correction, and enforceable remedy should reduce repeated unjustified conduct more than systems in which the reviewed institution controls the full process. Measure complaint access and disposition, investigation time, reversal and reinstatement, recurrence, civil payouts, policy correction, employee retention, and legitimate-action delay. Union contracts, civil-service rules, prosecutorial conflicts, indemnification, supervision, and political control are mechanisms to test rather than proxies that decide the result. The claim fails if stronger independent review doesn’t reduce recurrence or improve justified confidence, or if it predictably destroys fair employee process and protective capacity without offsetting benefit.

*Fifth.* Militarized posture, rather than the mere military origin of equipment, should predict agency compression and domestic mission expansion. Separate acquisition from deployment, protective from offensive equipment, specialized from routine use, and material from doctrine. Measure tactical deployments, weapon presentation, force, civilian and responder injury, crime and clearance, trust, protest incidence, maintenance cost, and whether acquisition precedes expansion into lower-risk missions. Account for preexisting threat, disaster exposure, jurisdiction size, selection into transfer programs, grants, and specialized-unit need. The claim fails if narrowly governed capabilities improve safety or rescue without increasing coercive incidence, or if provenance has no independent effect once function and deployment are counted.

*Sixth.* Encounter-linked revenue dependence should change institutional behavior at the margin. Compare jurisdictions or reforms that vary in retention of fines, fees, forfeitures, citations, detention payments, or contract volume; measure stops, citation and seizure rates, amounts extracted, offense mix, budget dependence, contest success, public-safety outcomes, and incidence by income, race, disability, and neighborhood. Account for law, tax base, crime, traffic volume, enforcement priorities, and reporting over several budget cycles. The prediction fails if removing the financial stake doesn’t change behavior, or if observed differences are fully explained by lawful demand and don’t burden vulnerable groups disproportionately.

*Seventh.* Necessity, proportionality, termination, and due-process rules that are trained, supervised, documented, and reviewed should outperform rules that exist only on paper. For comparable threats, measure intrusion severity, duration, escalation, evidence of alternatives considered, charges sustained, seizures returned, appeal reversals, time to remedy, victim protection, and recurrence. Account for case severity, evidentiary strength, local law, judicial capacity, counsel access, and changes in reporting. The claim fails if implementation leaves outcomes unchanged, if review can’t identify overshoot, or if reduced intrusion is purchased through lower protection against serious harm.

*Eighth.* A compliant enforcement system should jointly improve protection and liberty rather than optimizing one by sacrificing the other. Compare whole systems on serious victimization, response time, investigation and clearance, force and injury, wrongful arrest and reversal, resolution without arrest, trust and willingness to report, responder safety, unequal incidence, recurrence, and total fiscal and human cost. Use matched jurisdictions, staggered reforms, natural experiments, and replicated results over several years; model firearm prevalence, inequality, urban form, demographics, law, drug markets, staffing, and baseline trend. The composite claim fails if an arrangement lowers visible coercion only by leaving victims unprotected, or raises clearance and deterrence only through unjustified, unequally distributed intrusion.

These tests don’t rescue an arrangement because it is public or private, centralized or federated, police-led or civilian-led, restrained or assertive. Nor does one failed program refute the structural foundation. The relevant question is whether a design delivers effective protection while meeting the independently measured constraints, with counterevidence and adverse incidence counted rather than classified away.

### 6.12.4 Confirmation
The predictions in §6.12.3 meet an uneven evidence base. Descriptive records can establish that a pattern occurred; longitudinal and matched comparisons can test whether it moved with an institutional change; natural experiments and randomized or credible quasi-experimental designs can better isolate cause; replication across places tests whether the effect travels. No cross-national contrast, celebrated program, or reform narrative carries the same weight as replicated causal evidence, and no input—spending, training hours, equipment acquisition, or program adoption—stands in for protection or reduced incidence.

*Doctrine and de-escalation.* The Louisville evaluation of ICAT provides unusually strong evidence within this field: randomized rollout was associated with lower force and fewer civilian and officer injuries. PERF’s *Guiding Principles* and reforms in Las Vegas, Camden, and other departments are consistent with the mechanism. But much of the surrounding record is pre/post, bundled with supervision, policy, staffing, reporting, or leadership change, and the wider de-escalation literature hasn’t produced uniform effects. The evidence supports a trained-and-supervised time-preservation mechanism; it doesn’t establish that a course label alone works everywhere or that rapid intervention is never necessary.

*Upstream conditions.* Collective-efficacy, concentrated-disadvantage, public-health, education, housing, and community-organization literatures support pathways from social conditions to violence, crisis demand, and enforcement contact. Sampson, Raudenbush, and Earls (1997); Sharkey, Torrats-Espinosa, and Takyar (2017); Stuntz (2011); Forman (2017); and the violence-prevention literature make the upstream hypothesis serious. Yet communities differ simultaneously in inequality, firearm prevalence, drug markets, age structure, migration, service quality, policing intensity, and willingness to report. Cross-national welfare-and-policing comparisons are descriptive convergence, not causal confirmation of the entire set. The record supports particular interventions and pathways; the claim that adequate upstream provision will reduce all or most enforcement demand remains broader than what has been isolated.

*Differentiated crisis response.* CAHOOTS demonstrates long-running operational feasibility and substantial call diversion, but its reports aren’t a randomized comparison and the program’s local ecosystem matters. Denver STAR supplies stronger quasi-experimental evidence for appropriately triaged low-risk calls, including reduced low-level criminal-legal involvement and lower response cost without a detected rise in serious crime during the study period. Other programs show varied implementation and outcomes. The earned result is that civilian-led response can outperform police-only default for a bounded call class when dispatch, staffing, referral capacity, communications, and backup work. Universal superiority across crises, jurisdictions, or time horizons isn’t yet confirmed.

*Accountability and labor institutions.* Contract provisions, record sealing, short investigative windows, arbitration, civil-service law, prosecutorial dependence, supervision, and political control can obstruct accountability. Rushin and the developing police-union literature document mechanisms and associations; reinstatement records show that discipline can be reversed. The causal literature is still comparatively young, and union membership or bargaining alone isn’t proof of capture. Collective representation can protect fair process, safety reporting, and lawful refusal of improper orders. Evidence therefore supports testing specific rules by recurrence, correction, fairness, and protective performance rather than treating labor organization itself as the causal variable.

*Military equipment and posture.* The 1033 and SWAT records establish large transfers and expanded tactical deployment. Balko and the ACLU document the institutional history and visible incidence. They don’t by themselves show that defense-industry overcapacity caused each acquisition or that every transferred item induces harmful conduct: the program includes ordinary, medical, protective, communications, and rescue equipment, departments select into acquisition, and higher-threat places may seek more capability. Empirical studies of acquisition, crime, officer safety, force, and public trust have produced mixed results sensitive to measurement and design. The record supports a functional review of capability and deployment and a concern about routine enemy-style posture; it doesn’t confirm a blanket provenance rule.

*Revenue-linked enforcement.* The 2015 Department of Justice Ferguson investigation is direct administrative evidence that municipal revenue targets shaped court and police practice and imposed racially disparate burdens. The civil-forfeiture, private-probation, bail, fine, and fee records support the conflict-of-interest mechanism, while jurisdictional studies increasingly connect fiscal dependence to enforcement behavior and harm. The conclusion concerns retention and marginal incentive: when the enforcing institution or municipality benefits directly from additional coercive transactions, behavior and incidence require heightened scrutiny. This doesn’t show that every fine is extraction, that public general-fund financing is automatically sound, or that every contracted service is captured.

*Cross-national and place comparisons.* Low police-shooting rates in the United Kingdom, Norway, Iceland, New Zealand, and Japan are compatible with time-preserving doctrine, different weapon posture, and stronger surrounding conditions. They are also confounded by civilian firearm prevalence, violent-crime composition, law, training, reporting, urban form, healthcare, and institutional history. Cross-national gaps can’t isolate doctrine. Hot-spots systematic reviews, moreover, find modest crime-control gains from focused presence and often little displacement, which is counterevidence to any claim that proactive enforcement is inherently ineffective. The open question is which focused strategies preserve legitimacy and equal standing rather than whether presence can ever protect.

*Camden and composite reform.* Camden’s post-2013 record includes lower violence, revised force policy, increased staffing and foot patrol, organizational replacement, and broader community and economic change. It is an important institutional case but not a clean natural experiment isolating de-escalation: the reform bundled county takeover, labor and staffing changes, proactive order maintenance, leadership, later use-of-force policy, and wider trends. Similar caution applies to before/after narratives elsewhere. Composite reform may work precisely because components interact, but bundled success can’t identify which component was necessary or transportable.

*Counterevidence and boundary conditions.* Rapid response can improve apprehension and clearance in time-sensitive cases. Focused deterrence and hot-spots approaches can reduce some violence when concentration is accurate and implementation is procedurally sound. Armed specialists and protective equipment can save victims, responders, and bystanders during active threats. Civilian programs can suffer triage error, workforce shortages, weak referral networks, and hidden transfers. Public agencies can be bureaucratic, secretive, under-resourced, or captured; private and nonprofit providers can contribute specialization but also create conflicts. Lower force doesn’t prove adequate protection, and higher enforcement activity doesn’t by itself prove extraction.

The evidence therefore supports the central mechanisms at different confidence levels: encounter-linked revenue can distort behavior; doctrine and supervision can affect force; differentiated crisis response can improve a bounded class of calls; upstream conditions matter through identifiable pathways; and independent review can expose and correct abuse. It doesn’t establish one universally superior architecture, a categorical equipment rule, universal civilian-response superiority, or the claim that doctrine and political economy govern outcomes far more strongly than individual conduct in every setting. Those stronger propositions remain comparative and falsifiable under §6.12.3.

### 6.12.5 Conclusions
*The protective floor.* A political community is categorically obliged to maintain effective protection against internal coercion. That includes accessible calls for help, timely intervention in imminent harm, investigation and evidence preservation, restraint of active threats, protection of victims and witnesses, and enforcement of lawful remedies. Adequate healthcare, housing, education, economic security, representation, and dispute resolution should reduce preventable demand, but no upstream achievement licenses abandoning the residual person facing violence now. The protective function is therefore not abolished here, even though centralized professional policing is left open to replacement, division, or radical reconstruction.

*The encounter constraints.* Every person remains a participant throughout: victim, witness, bystander, responder, and person subjected to authority. Search, seizure, detention, and force require a lawful protective objective, discrimination, necessity, the least harmful sufficient means reasonably available, comparative proportionality, a reasonable prospect of success, and termination when the threat or legal basis ends. Time-preservation is the default where distance, explanation, reassessment, and specialized help can be used without increasing danger. The encounter must also display a sign of preservation: at least one non-threat line in the person’s field.
