Utilitarianism, libertarianism, Marxism, and Rawlsianism each begin from a different normative or explanatory device; this account begins from the conditions under which actual subjects share and maintain political life. The comparison is about grounding and constraint, not a claim that every version of a tradition yields one policy.

*Not utilitarian.* Sophisticated indirect or rule utilitarianism (Hare 1981; Brink 1989), and threshold-deontology hybrids that incorporate rights-protections instrumentally, accommodate much of what maximum possibility requires by recognizing that long-run aggregate welfare is best served when basic conditions for everyone are protected from case-by-case calculation. That conclusion is granted; its grounding is not: the maximum-possibility criterion isn’t a constraint vindicated because it maximizes welfare on net, but a structural condition of political maintenance. A society that maximized aggregate welfare by cutting some people off from the conditions of live possibility would be failing structurally, not succeeding at a different kind of justice. The criterion’s force doesn’t depend on the empirical claim that respecting it always maximizes aggregate welfare.

*Not libertarian.* Libertarian and left-libertarian theories begin from stringent rights over persons and resources and ask what coercion can be justified (Nozick 1974; Otsuka 2003; Vallentyne and Steiner 2000). This account shares their suspicion of domination but rejects a pre-political baseline. Actual autonomy is self-direction within relations of dependence, not self-sufficiency outside them. Public conditions can widen liberty by turning formal permissions into live alternatives, but this doesn’t make every public intervention freedom-enhancing; authority, burden, exit, and outcome still have to be shown.

The off-grid case makes the distinction concrete. A person may reasonably seek minimal entanglement and protection from institutional failure. Yet seed stock, tools, medicine, energy systems, roads, and inherited knowledge reveal dependence even at the point designed to minimize it. That fact defeats a claim of literal self-sufficiency, not a claim to privacy, exit from particular institutions, or low-contact life. The foundation must therefore protect minimal entanglement without pretending that shared dependence authorizes unlimited demands.

The anarchist tradition reaches part of this on independent grounds: Kropotkin’s mutual aid relocates maintenance to voluntary and federated forms rather than denying dependence (Kropotkin 1902). The remaining dispute concerns which coercive functions, if any, are necessary and how their authority is earned.

A subject who wants minimal entanglement is neither exempted from harms imposed on others nor penalized merely for wanting little of public life. The housing rule at §6.8.2 illustrates the boundary: regulate risk that crosses to others, keep rescue unconditional, and limit recovery claims to what the shared obligation actually covers.

*Not Marxist.* Marxism diagnoses extraction and alienation as structural rather than the work of a few bad actors (Marx and Engels 1848; Marx 1867; Luxemburg 1913; Cohen 1978; Cohen 1995). This account agrees that a participant can be reduced to an input by the arrangement itself. It parts over the institutional conclusion: matching stake, contribution, and control constrains ownership without deriving common ownership as the only permissible form. Cooperatives, codetermination, profit-sharing, employee ownership, and other designs must be compared by how well they meet that constraint (§6.7.5).

Markets above a secured foundation remain available because exchange can widen participants’ options, though the foundation does not magically remove bargaining power or coercion. Revolutionary and vanguard routes face the same test as incumbent power: a transition may not treat the people it claims to liberate as expendable inputs or deny them a correctable voice (§6.3).

The error is located in the relation, not assigned by class in advance. Regulatory capture, wage extraction, corruption, and fraud can all shift costs onto others; their scale, power, and incidence differ and must be measured rather than made symmetrical by slogan.

The positive line runs between maintained conditions and the varied products people make through them. Roads, courts, currency, knowledge, health capacity, and the foundation require shared maintenance; what people own, make, and trade above that line is not thereby collectivized. Wright’s participatory designs and Roemer’s market socialism show that the boundary cuts across familiar ideological labels (Wright 2010; Roemer 1994).

*Not Rawlsian, though substantially convergent.* Rawls’s basic structure, concern for the least advantaged, public reason, and stability for the right reasons overlap with this account (Rawls 1971; Rawls 1993; Rawls 2001). The grounding differs. This book is a comprehensive framework, not a freestanding political conception, and it argues from actual subjects in shared arrangements rather than hypothetical choice behind a veil. Representation provides continuing public correction, but it is not a substitute for overlapping consensus and cannot by itself show that citizens affirm an arrangement for the right reasons.

Periodic or continuous ratification can reveal durable acceptance, strategic accommodation, or a temporary balance of power. Distinguishing them requires evidence about inclusion, reasons, information, contestability, and the distribution of leverage. The recognition mechanism is therefore a way to test stability, not proof that stability is already justified.

*Moral disagreement is intelligible without threatening the account.* Moral disagreement (Doris and Plakias 2008; Wong 1984; Prinz 2007) becomes intelligible without threatening the account. Different groups and persons occupy different positions within the social field, inherit different histories, undergo different forms of moral training, and become responsive to different levers. They may share the same basic vulnerabilities while disagreeing sharply about which norms best answer to them. That is exactly what is to be expected if morality is intersubjective, socially cultivated, and constrained by the requirements of cooperative life. Across societies the alignments are often similar without being identical: social species require a workable spectrum of trust, reciprocity, restraint, care, and coordination to avoid internal collapse, but there remains wide room for variation in how those pressures are interpreted, weighted, and enforced. Disagreement doesn’t show that morality is unreal. It shows that norm construction, like every other social achievement, is partial, contested, path-dependent, and shaped by the environments through which groups try to survive: the same ecological-shaping pattern documented for religious vocabulary at §5.16 applies here to moral vocabulary.

*Convergence-skeptical objections.* Berlin’s value pluralism denies that all goods fit one ordering (Berlin 1958; Berlin 1969). Hayek’s knowledge problem denies that a designer can know enough to coordinate the whole (Hayek 1945). Foucault warns that a totalizing framework can become an instrument of discipline (Foucault 1975). Mouffe argues that every settlement is politically achieved, excludes alternatives, and cannot present itself as neutral ground (Mouffe 2000; Mouffe 2005; Laclau and Mouffe 1985). These objections strike the chapter precisely where *convergence* could become a license for synoptic control.

The concessions are substantial. Personal values and life-forms remain plural; institutional knowledge is partial; spontaneous coordination can outperform design; administrative categories can entrench power; and this framework is a participant in political contestation, not a view from nowhere.

The reply is correspondingly limited. Convergence operates at the level of conditions for political participation, not one ranking of every good. It supplies constraints within which decentralized and spontaneous arrangements may operate, not a central plan. Public audit, appeal, revision, and exit can reduce the risk of governmentality, but no procedure proves itself immune to capture. Implementation (§6.15) therefore has to treat reversibility and error correction as safeguards rather than certificates of innocence.

Against Mouffe, the account claims no neutral procedural standing. Its constraints exclude some designs, and those exclusions remain politically contested. What it owes is not a denial of that fact but an account of who can challenge the boundary and how it can be revised.

The boundary should fall between permissible actions and institutional designs, not between admissible and inadmissible citizens. No doctrine loses its bearer’s standing. Conduct and arrangements that breach others’ standing can still be prohibited, and the dispute about what counts as a breach remains open to evidence and contestation.

Mouffe’s distinction between an enemy to destroy and an opponent to contest names the hoped-for political register. Secure conditions and answerable institutions may make agonistic conflict easier to sustain, but they do not automatically convert enemies into opponents. Democratic ethos, historical memory, organization, and enforcement remain part of the explanation.

The exchange fixes how every neighboring tradition should be read. Agreement at the level of result can be suggestive and can reveal that the book is not inventing its policy concerns from nothing. It is not evidence that the modal derivation is true unless the independent route bears on the premises or inference at issue. Convergence should therefore be reported as convergence, not promoted into confirmation.

The traditions remain distinct in grounding, empirical assumptions, and theoretical machinery. Naming the level of agreement is what keeps an ecumenical survey from manufacturing consensus.

One objection carries more than the others and deserves separate treatment. A framework pitched at the level of structural design is open to the charge, pressed most sharply by Charles Mills (2005), that it commits the signature evasion of ideal theory: it describes an arrangement in which domination has no place and thereby falls silent on the domination that actually exists. The charge has force, and the response is to divide it rather than deny it. At the level of design, supremacy is granted no standing at all. A racial order is an arrangement that places a group below the foundation and treats its members as lesser, which is the very treatment a near-universal aversion to which is established at §5.14 and which the foundation-holding criterion of §6.3 precludes; there is no permissible design in which supremacy occupies a legitimate position. But granting supremacy no standing in the design isn’t the same as ending it in the world. Supremacy is sedimented (carried in the distributions, advantages, and disadvantages laid down by the order being replaced) and a clean architecture inherited by a society shaped for centuries under the old one doesn’t dissolve that sediment merely by being clean. Mills is right that this is where ideal theory tends to stop; this doesn’t stop there, but owes the non-ideal, reparative work of dismantling what the prior architecture built, and carries that as a structural obligation rather than a hope.

This is also where its universalism must be stated with care, since the wrong form of it reproduces the very erasure Mills attacks. The foundation is universal, but breaches of it aren’t interchangeable: racial marginalization isn’t financial marginalization under another name, and treating them as a single generic harm would lose precisely the specific architecture Mills insists must be seen. The foundation is universal in what it guarantees and positional in how its violations are recognized. That positional recognition isn’t bolted onto the theory; it follows from the theory’s own evidential commitments. If first-person experience is the primary political evidence, as the felt-evidence chain holds (§6 root; §5), then those who live a given marginalization have access to its specific texture that an outside designer structurally lacks. The §6.3 recognition mechanism is the channel through which that evidence enters, which is what makes it epistemically mandatory rather than optional: there is no armchair from which the content of every position’s breach could be derived in advance.

Universal protection has position-sensitive implications. The same threshold may require different resources or remedies because people face different barriers and inherit different harms. That supports giving greater urgency to severe breaches without making priority strictly lexical or pretending one metric can rank every repair. The relevant comparisons include distance below the foundation, preventable harm, feasibility, time, spillovers, and whether helping one group installs a new breach for another. Equality lies in the standing and threshold protected, not identical inputs or outcomes.

This doesn’t require equal holdings or outcomes above the foundation. It requires that accumulation not proceed by pushing others beneath it or buying unaccountable control of shared direction (§6.7; §6.13). Progressive contribution is one way to finance the shared base and answer differentiated capacity, not a tax instrument deduced without fiscal or institutional premises.

*The universal foundation and rival resources.* The modal structure described in Chapter 5 may be equally available in the abstract; land, labor, care, energy, time, and ecological capacity are not. Nothing about non-rival possibility makes material provision costless or proves one distributive schedule. The political obligation instead rests on recognized subjects sharing institutions and being exposed to their decisions. Scarcity therefore remains inside the problem: priorities must be publicly justified, burdens counted, and rival claims compared.

Some goods—knowledge, standards, designs—can be reproduced at low marginal cost, while their implementation still consumes rival resources (Romer 1990). Other goods are positional by design (Hirsch 1976), and ecological actualization is bounded by replenishment and cumulative harm (§6.5). The useful economic distinction is consequently empirical: an activity can widen others’ options, capture access, shift costs, or do several at once. Institutions should measure those effects and prevent accumulated stock from purchasing unaccountable public direction; no single tax or ownership form follows from that constraint alone.

*The argument applies to every person regardless of identity.* The upstream-conditions argument, the requirement of maximum possibility, and the rule of law aren’t abstract principles that apply in general but not in particular. They apply to every person who participates in the shared arrangements. The history of political life is substantially a history of systematically violating these requirements for specific groups: shaping the shared arrangements so that some people’s participation conditions were degraded, their directions unrecognized, and the rules applied to them differently based on race, gender, or identity. Each of these isn’t a separate political question requiring a separate derivation. Each is the same structural failure applied to a specific population: upstream conditions systematically narrowed, the conditions of live possibility selectively withheld, democratic decision-making processes designed to exclude, and rules applied unequally. Structural racism, patriarchal arrangements, and the legal exclusion of people based on gender identity or sexual orientation from participation conditions others take for granted are each instances of the same structural failure the account has been describing throughout: the mechanism being used to maintain a subset’s preferred conditions rather than the conditions of all. These aren’t added as special cases. They are the most prominent historical and ongoing applications of what has already been derived.

*Consent and the aversions that ground the foundation.* Consent can transform the normative character of an act: a strike can be assault on the sidewalk and sport under accepted rules. The relevant authorization must be informed, voluntary, competent, specific, and revocable (§6.1.2). It modifies a protection for the consenting subject within its scope; it doesn’t authorize unconsented harm to others or erase public effects.

That separates infringement from distaste. Disapproval of another’s consensual life does not by itself establish injury or a political claim against them. Neutrality is useful evidence—a rule that can only be stated by naming the identity it burdens is suspect—but formally neutral rules can still be discriminatory in purpose or incidence. The full test asks about consent, harm, external effects, equal standing, and application, not the number of people offended.

Where capacity for the decision is absent, authorization must come through a separate protective standard; incapacity is not consent and does not erase standing. That standard must be specific to the decision, attentive to the subject’s will and welfare, and guarded against conflicts of interest (§5.11.4).

Some authorizations are not practically revocable once acted on. The revocability rule therefore governs continuing relations and future participation; it cannot make every completed act reversible. Irreversible choices require heightened capacity, information, voluntariness, and safeguard analysis rather than the fiction that revocation remains available afterward.

*Better never, or better tended?* Benatar’s asymmetry (2006) presses a limit on the language of maximum possibility: if absent pain is good even without a beneficiary while absent pleasure is not bad without someone deprived, existence cannot be assumed a benefit merely because it creates a field of possibilities. The criterion is not a population maximand. It governs how existing and foreseeable subjects are treated; it does not imply that producing more subjects is better.

That blocks a pronatalist inference. It also meets Benatar at the step his asymmetry needs. Absent pain counts as good without a beneficiary only if value can be good for no one, and value on this account is always a subject’s own condition (§5.14), so coming into existence is no standing harm (§5.8). A defender of impersonal value rejects that premise, and the disagreement lands there rather than on whether a life can be good. Consent is unavailable before existence, and the non-identity problem and permissible procreative risk still require premises this chapter has not supplied.

What the challenge does secure here is where the weight falls: not on being born but on the life a subject is born into. That means caution about bringing a subject into foreseeably severe and unavoidable suffering, plus a duty to improve the conditions future subjects may enter (§5.14). It does not show that exclusion of likely sufferers is the answer, that every risk is justified once support exists, or that environmental repair resolves every tragic case.

Schopenhauer’s suffering-surplus challenge (1818) also remains. The standing of a self-modeling subject is not a proof that the subject’s life contains more good than suffering (§5.7; §5.2). Evidence that a settled wish to die is uncommon, and may change when depression, pain, loneliness, or isolation is treated, is relevant to particular interventions but cannot settle the value of existence (Briggs et al. 2021; Rodríguez-Prat et al. 2024).

Self-report remains indispensable evidence about a person’s experience, but it cannot bear that metaphysical conclusion alone. Optimism bias, adaptation, selection for continued living, question framing, and reporting context all complicate the inference. Those limits counsel triangulation; they do not license disbelieving a person’s report about their own life.

The convergence with pessimism and antinatalism is therefore narrow: foreseeable suffering matters, and politics owes future subjects conditions fit to enter. Whether existence itself wrongs them remains open.

*Patchwork implementations.* Existing jurisdictions supply comparisons and illustrations, not a set of interchangeable natural experiments. Each case bundles institutions, history, wealth, demography, baseline conditions, selection effects, and measurement choices. The question is whether a specified reform changes a specified outcome under a design capable of separating those influences.

The per-domain sections at §6.2.4–6.13.4 examine the evidence at the level where its comparator and outcome can be specified. Nordic welfare states, Costa Rica’s demilitarization, German social insurance, East Asian health systems, Portuguese drug reform, voting-system variation, austerity episodes, and US state differences are relevant because each contains outcomes the hypotheses concern. None identifies the full mechanism by inspection. They differ on background institutions and typically change several variables together. Their warranted use is to generate bounded comparisons and falsifiable mechanisms, not to confirm “maximum possibility” as one set.

Taken together, the cases provide varying degrees of support, tension, or illustration for domain-level predictions. They don’t confirm three chapter-scale structural predictions or establish that joint implementation will produce more than the sum of independent effects. *Interlocking* is therefore a research hypothesis: one reform may alter the resources, incentives, trust, administrative capacity, or political coalition on which another depends. The hypothesis earns strength only where those mechanisms are specified and joint effects are compared with isolated and alternative sets.

No existing society instantiates the chapter’s full proposed configuration. Existing jurisdictions supply pieces, counterexamples, and comparisons; they do not supply a finished model to copy.

The earned structural observation is that the domain proposals share a foundation, an equal-standing constraint, and a legitimacy requirement. That explains their thematic unity and lets contradictions among them be tested. Interlocking, joint reinforcement, rollback resistance, and reduced identity-coded friction don’t follow merely from premise-sharing. They are empirical hypotheses about mechanisms, coalitions, administrative capacity, media environments, and historical context. Specific implementations, transition paths, and cross-domain priorities under scarcity remain open. Implementation (§6.15) therefore treats coordinated sequencing as a strategy to test rather than the analytic completion of the derivation.

Several limits remain. Multiple designs can satisfy the constraints, and transition paths must be compared rather than inferred. Adoption is not inevitable; incumbent interests, administrative weakness, public disagreement, and unintended effects can defeat it. Reduced cultural friction is only a hypothesis, not a promise that conflict moves onto one axis. Convergence with other traditions supports particular conclusions without validating this framework’s grounding. The environmental technology condition also remains unsettled (§6.5.3 Prediction 7).

*This aligns with an outcome, not a party.* No existing party or tradition owns the criterion. A conservative concern for the fragility of working institutions can identify how the possible is lost; a progressive concern for people excluded by existing arrangements can identify what the structure has failed to do. Those orientations can also disagree about ends, rights, evidence, and who counts—not merely about whether an institution works. The criterion adjudicates none of that by political label.

The goal of political progress is a polity that takes care of everyone. That is the progress the derivation points toward, not toward any particular party’s platform, but toward the structural outcome. Once a polity genuinely maintains the conditions of maximum possibility for all subjects, it is worth conserving. Not because change is bad, but because what actually works is genuinely valuable and genuinely fragile. The conservative impulse, properly directed, is the impulse to protect what is doing the structural work. The progressive impulse, properly directed, is the impulse to close the gap between where the structure is and where it needs to be. Properly directed, they are less opposed ends than successive phases of one project.

The argument yields a criterion more demanding than either tradition has fully met and more neutral than either is comfortable with. To apply it, ask whether an arrangement maintains the conditions of maximum possibility for all subjects: the live field of action, refusal, contribution, and self-direction available to the people who share it. Where the answer is yes, the arrangement is worth conserving. Where the answer is no, it is worth changing. The political labels are orientations toward the criterion: useful, limited, and not to be confused with it.

*Tradition is a legitimate choice, not self-validating public authority.* A subject may organize their life around inherited family forms, religious practice, hierarchy, and cultural continuity. Public policy may also overlap with a tradition’s commitments. What it may not do is treat the tradition itself as sufficient reason to subordinate people who do not share it. Coercive rules still owe a public justification in protection, rights, and shared conditions.

This isn’t a mandate for any particular way of life. It is a structural foundation beneath which no way of life can fall, and above which every way of life is free to operate. A person who lives by tradition within a polity that holds the foundation is exactly what the account makes room for. A political system that uses the shared mechanism to enforce traditional values on those who haven’t chosen them is doing exactly what it must not: converting the maintenance system into an enforcement system. The same structural argument that protects traditional subjects from having secular values imposed on them protects secular subjects from having traditional values imposed on them. The protection is symmetrical, and the structural foundation holds for everyone.

*Religious-political separation cuts in both directions.* Religious belief is outside the present account’s political reach, and that isn’t a concession but a consequence of the derivation itself. The structural argument is that the metaphysical claims of religious traditions are mislocated: the structures those traditions attributed to God actually live in Nature. That argument, if correct, doesn’t give any political authority the right to act on it coercively. A political system that enforced secular belief (or any belief) would be violating the structural requirement it exists to maintain. Direction must come from all. A subject whose orientation toward Nature is expressed in religious terms is participating in the polity no less than one who holds secular views. Their belief is their own reading of what Nature is. The political structure has no mandate to correct it.

This follows directly from the derivation rather than from reluctant tolerance. The account holds that the encounter with what exceeds the self-model is real, universal, and available to every subject. What traditions have built around that encounter (the practices, the communities, the vocabularies of meaning) are what subjects do with their inner lives. A political system that trespasses on inner lives has confused its function. Its function is to maintain the conditions of participation, not to determine the orientations subjects bring to participation.

What the political system owes subjects in this domain is education (honest, accurate, and complete) and the freedom to reach their own conclusions. What it owes is the conditions under which subjects can think for themselves, not enforced conclusions and not insulation from challenge. A subject who has been honestly educated and remains religious hasn’t failed; a political system that substitutes enforcement for education is what fails.

The structural separation of religious and political authority cuts in both directions. Religious institutions may not govern the polity: that would narrow participation to those who share the institution’s beliefs, violating the derivation’s first requirement. And the polity may not govern religious belief: that would violate the same requirement from the other side. Both directions of violation are the same structural failure: the polity being used to enforce orientation rather than maintain conditions. The separation preserves political contestation across religious/secular orientations rather than resolving it through stipulated reasonableness-conditions—the agonistic register Mouffe develops (*The Democratic Paradox* 2000).

Comparative work by Norris and Inglehart associates existential security, institutional confidence, and secularization across societies, while Zuckerman’s study of Scandinavia documents settings in which high cohesion and moral life coexist with little religious governance (Norris and Inglehart 2004; Zuckerman 2008). These cases show compatibility, not a one-way causal law: history, selection, wealth, institutions, and religious change move together. The political claim does not require religion to decline. It requires that religious authority, like secular authority, remain answerable to people who do not share its premises.

*Belief is protected, not despite its content but because of what believing is.* Whatever orientation this argument points away from, it doesn’t ask anyone to stop believing. Belief is how subjects model what exceeds their current understanding: reflexive awareness reaching toward what it can’t yet derive. It is how we collectively hypothesize. It is how subjects work out what there is. God has long been a convincing hypothesis: a way of modeling the encounter with scale, with depth, with the fact that there is something rather than nothing. That encounter isn’t an error, and this framework doesn’t explain it away; it relocates its referent. What the tradition reached for was real, and it was here all along, not beyond the world but built into the fact that there is one. The name was provisional, but the pointing wasn’t wrong.

Belief is shielded for what believing is, not for what is believed: a self-model reaching beyond what it can yet derive. Protecting belief protects the inner life’s freedom to inquire, interpret, and orient itself. When belief is expressed through conduct that harms or coerces others, the conduct enters political assessment; the inner conviction is not thereby made an offense. On this account, Nature Alone doesn’t foreclose the sacred; it relocates its referent into Nature.

*A political structure can perform some functions people also seek religiously.* Protection, care, belonging, and participation in something larger than one household can be supplied by a population through its institutions. That doesn’t establish that religious longing is nothing but displaced politics, that no transcendent referent exists, or that a polity can replace worship, ritual, salvation, or ultimate meaning. The political claim is functional and limited: people can organize care for one another without waiting for an external agent to perform it. The population remains many subjects rather than one larger subject, and the shared foundation protects variation in how they understand and pursue the sacred. (Laclau and Mouffe’s chain-of-equivalence apparatus 1985 describes one way distinct political identities can be linked without being dissolved.)

What remains is a disciplined convergence. The domain proposals share premises and can therefore be tested for mutual consistency. Some may reinforce one another; some may compete for resources, create new burdens, or fail under local conditions. Independent traditions can corroborate a concern or reveal a blind spot without proving its grounding. The close is a unified political research program: a foundation and non-domination constraint applied across domains, with causal interlocking left to evidence rather than declared by architecture.

## 6.15 Implementation

*From derivation to implementation.* Each prior section applied one condition to one domain. The remaining question is practical: how can people make those changes together, against what resistance, and at what transitional cost?

This isn’t a finished blueprint. The argument derives political constraints and proposes practical hypotheses. Communities still have to test them against local conditions through institutions answerable to the people living under them. Incremental and locally measured reform is one strategy because it permits learning and, where possible, reversal. The argument doesn’t establish that incremental reform is always sufficient, that property relations never require deeper restructuring, or that one sequence fits every jurisdiction.

Representation reform is a strong practical hypothesis because it may protect later reforms against capture. It isn’t a theorem about what must come first. Nor does the argument authorize any class to own the process. A community must secure public answerability through the recognition mechanism of §6.3, and how it does so remains a political question.

The task is to sequence conditions already earned. No new right is minted here.

A mid-sized democratic jurisdiction may sequence healthcare, electoral, tax, or crisis-response reforms rather than attempt one comprehensive enactment. Ranked-choice voting, automatic registration, a land-value-tax pilot, a public-option expansion, and a co-responder program illustrate separable interventions, not a universally recommended order. Each needs its own justification and audit, and an earlier reform may ease, obstruct, or leave untouched the politics of the next. Costa Rica’s post-1948 demilitarization and Portugal’s post-2001 drug-policy changes illustrate long transitions with bundled causes; they don’t establish one implementation sequence for other jurisdictions.

*What gets implemented.* Rights require effective conditions of participation as well as formal protection (§6.1). Representation needs continuing channels of direction, contest, and correction rather than depending only on periodic choice among finished platforms (§6.3). Belonging and information policy support the face-to-face and mediated infrastructure through which people encounter one another and test public claims (§6.2; §6.4).

Economic policy has to protect the foundation, finance it sustainably, and keep accumulated wealth from buying unanswerable political power (§6.7). Land-value, estate, income, consumption, wealth, and financial-transaction taxes are candidate instruments with different incidence, avoidance, growth, and administrative effects. No label settles the choice. The package must be tested by who actually bears it, what it funds, what behavior it changes, and which avoidance channels remain.

Healthcare may be single-payer, regulated multi-payer, or hybrid. Whatever the form, foundational access may not depend on avoidable denial, exclusion, or incentives that profit by withholding necessary care (§6.10). Education develops civic and practical capacity (§6.9); agriculture must count life, nutrition, labor, and ecological sustainability (§4.8; §6.6); environmental policy must count delayed and cross-generational effects (§6.5).

Defense maintains credible protection while comparing force with diplomacy, alliances, deterrence, and prevention rather than fixing one universal order among them (§6.11). Enforcement matches responder and force to the encounter, preserves time where danger permits, and remains independently accountable (§6.12). Justice combines protection and responsibility with repair where possible, while testing upstream interventions for the populations and harms to which they are causally relevant (§6.13).

These are constraints, not one institutional package. More than one arrangement may satisfy them, and some problems cross local or national boundaries. The relevant public must be able to direct, contest, and correct the choice through institutions appropriate to the scale of its effects (§6.3).

The argument doesn’t provide an economic equation. It fixes what an acceptable equation has to preserve: real liberty as agency, freedom from immediate survival-capture, a foundation that doesn’t extract profit through necessity, and protection for people whose livelihoods depend on roles being phased out. Political economy solves within those limits.

The relevant curve isn’t equality for its own sake, revenue for its own sake, or punishment of surplus. It distributes the burden of funding real liberty while minimizing agency-loss across the arrangement. The numbers aren’t arbitrary. The modal proof doesn’t announce them either. Evidence does that work.

*Sequence, measurement, and stop rules.* Derivation order is not implementation order. Sequence should follow dependency, urgency, feasibility, administrative capacity, reversibility, and the risk that one step blocks or captures the next.

*Representation often comes first or alongside.* Public answerability can protect later choices from capture, making early representation reform a strong practical hypothesis. But an acute health, housing, environmental, or safety failure may have to be addressed before electoral redesign can mature. The reason for a sequence must be stated in the case, not inherited from the chapter’s table of contents.

*Measurement comes early.* A locality-adjusted foundation needs Adequate Living Cost data (§6.7). Representation needs participation data and accessible public channels (§6.3). Healthcare needs public-health data (§6.10). Environmental policy needs emissions and ecological monitoring (§6.5). Those systems are shared infrastructure and have to be funded early.

Without measurement, a reform can’t be audited. Without audit, the population can’t correct it. An arrangement insulated from correction isn’t an implementation of this account. It is a substitute for it.

*Patchwork permits learning. It doesn’t guarantee success.* Costa Rica, Nordic welfare states, German social insurance, Portuguese drug policy, voting-system variation, wellbeing budgeting, and Doughnut-Economics dashboards (Raworth 2017) supply cases for comparison. A result can travel only after its comparator, background conditions, outcome, and transfer limits are known. Partial reform may work, conflict with an unreformed domain, or be captured and reversed. That uncertainty is why the process measures and learns. It doesn’t prove that patchwork always beats comprehensive reform.

*Failure is specified before institutions acquire a stake in redefining it.* Each step should name its intended outcome, baseline, comparison, schedule, distributional safeguards, and evidence that would trigger review. Capture also needs observable indicators: who controls appointments, information, appeals, contracts, funding, and rule changes. These terms should be public before implementation, while remaining corrigible if the original metric proves perverse or incomplete.

Outcomes should be disaggregated across affected groups rather than judged only by an average or a best-case projection. A program can meet its headline target while shifting serious burdens onto a minority, excluding hard cases, or giving its provider control over the audit.

Failure triggers a decision, not one automatic off-switch. A harmful or captured feature may need suspension, replacement, redesign, or in an emergency immediate termination. The response depends on severity, confidence, dependencies, and the cost of interruption. What cannot happen is allowing the institution that benefits from continuation to define success alone.

Stopping a failed form doesn’t always mean returning to the old one. People organize their lives around institutions once they exist. Habitats can’t be restored on demand, and medical treatment can’t always be interrupted without consequence. Property, ecological, medical, and life-course changes can all be path-dependent.

Returning to the old baseline may therefore harm the same people the reform was meant to reach. The stop rule says what must stop, not what must be restored. Reversion, suspension, replacement, or continuation under redesigned terms depends on what reversal would now cost. Reversibility is a design aim where it’s available. It isn’t a property every reform has.

*Resistance and transition.* No single path follows from the argument. Ordinary reform may be enough in one jurisdiction and inadequate in another. Constitutional revision, property restructuring, or a deeper break may sometimes be required. Those are strategic and empirical questions requiring democratic authorization, legal analysis, and local history. Revolutionary rupture, institutional continuity, expropriation, and market preservation all have to make their own cases. None is automatic.

Some problems require international coordination. Others don’t. The argument rules out domination and unaccountable extraction. It does not promise that transition can avoid conflict or material redistribution.

*Who has something to lose?* Reforms alter revenue, authority, status, employment, and organizational survival. Insurers may lose profitable products or gain new administrative roles; fossil-fuel firms face stranded assets and liability; wealthy holders face changed tax treatment; media firms face altered attention incentives; carceral contractors face reduced demand; established parties face electoral uncertainty. The effect varies by design, and some incumbents may adapt or support reform. Mapping the stake identifies likely pressure points without deciding anyone’s motive in advance (§6.3–§6.13).

That locates an incentive. It doesn’t prove why anyone resists. Opposition may reflect extraction, competing interests, a legitimate dispute about causes, or disagreement with the foundation itself. Resistance is evidence only after those possibilities are tested. It can’t confirm the account merely by occurring.

*Workers aren’t the arrangement.* Reform may displace people employed inside extractive institutions. That doesn’t make the workers extractive. Their expertise is real, and much of it transfers to the institutions that replace their employers.

Actuaries, claims investigators, loss assessors, and underwriters possess skills that may transfer to public, nonprofit, or differently regulated systems. Transfer is not automatic: the replacement institution must need the work, recognize the credential, and provide a viable job.

Some carceral workers may move into supervision, reentry, treatment, or restorative programs; some fossil-fuel workers have skills relevant to renewable infrastructure, monitoring, or remediation (§6.5). Geography, wages, licensing, working conditions, identity, and actual labor demand can still block transfer. Campaign and ideological-media roles may have fewer direct equivalents. A just transition has to measure those frictions rather than infer a new job from an adjacent skill.

That displacement is real. The political community owes workers the foundation during transition and should compare wage insurance, bridge income, training, relocation support, credential recognition, regional investment, and job creation by whether they make redirection genuinely available.

The transition isn’t punishment. Anderson’s account of workplace authority (*Private Government* 2017) makes the agency problem visible: retraining offered under threat of destitution isn’t a genuine choice. Workers need funding, time, support, and a secure foundation after the change.

The just-transition literature also asks who bears the cost. Extractive industries, including coal and the carceral system, have concentrated working-class employment in particular regions and communities. The people displaced often benefited least from the prior extraction. The race-stratified record across §6.4–6.13 therefore matters to transition design, including in the environmental register developed at §6.5. The Just Transition Alliance, the Climate Justice Alliance, and Movement Generation carry that work in practice; Bullard’s *Dumping in Dixie* (1990) and Mills’s *Black Rights / White Wrongs* (2017) supply the analytic engagements.

*Revision and institutional memory.* A political order also has to survive its own success. Public attention fades. Officeholders become insulated. Rules become ritual. Institutions built for public purposes can be redirected toward private advantage without announcing the change.

Capture is most dangerous when it disables the checks that would expose it. Durability therefore requires recurring public review, transparent records, independent checks on concentrated power, rotation where offices become insulated, and practical routes for correction. The point isn’t permanent instability. It is an order that can notice drift before drift hardens into capture.

Rotation changes the officeholders, not the institutional bearer (§6.3). Commitments, duties, reasons, evidence, and the record of failure have to survive the handoff in forms the public and the next officeholders can inspect. Otherwise a change of personnel launders an old obligation. Institutional memory also lets responsibility attach to a continuing pattern without pretending every present official personally caused it.

An institution that can’t preserve why it acted can’t later show that it learned.

No implementation is final or insulated from revision. Ask the direct question: does this arrangement deliver the condition it was adopted to secure? If not, the population corrects it through §6.3. Designs may be revised, replaced, or extended as evidence changes and people change direction. This isn’t a closed system.

Explicit aims, measurement, revision, and attention to unintended consequences answer part of the objection to comprehensive design. They don’t prove incrementalism sufficient. Some increments compound. Others are neutralized, captured, or made incoherent by domains left untouched. A reform may make sense on its own and still fail to last on its own.

Coordinating reforms is therefore a hypothesis about survival and interaction, not a condition of their meaning. Habermas’s problem of validity and facticity (1992) 1996, together with Rawls’s and Habermas’s treatments of civil disobedience (Rawls 1971, §55; Habermas 1985), frames the remaining questions of authorization, resistance, and correction. The recognition procedures proposed here are answers to test, not guarantees.

Mills’s “Ideal Theory as Ideology” (2005) identifies the practical silence ideal theory often leaves behind: it describes the destination without saying what a participant may do before the destination exists. The ordinary answer is democratic: a population legitimately directs implementation through institutions it can hold answerable (§6.3).

But what happens when that channel is captured or unavailable? The obligation doesn’t disappear because its ordinary route is blocked. Civil disobedience can become democratic voice operating through a route capture has left open, appealing to the political community’s own commitments.

Publicity and accountability help civil disobedience function as an appeal rather than an unexplained exercise of power. They are not exceptionless requirements. Whistleblowing, underground publication, and resistance under severe repression may require anonymity or secrecy to remain possible at all. The relevant questions are what the act communicates, whom it burdens, what risk publicity creates, and what avenues for accountability remain.

The limit on force comes from §6.1 and §6.11–Enforcement (§6.12), not from nonviolence treated as an exceptionless virtue. Defensive force may be justified against an ongoing unlawful threat, but necessity, proportionality, alternatives, and incidence still govern it. Blocking a road, occupying a building, or refusing an order cannot be classified by tactic alone: emergency access, notice, duration, target, and burdens on uninvolved people matter. Resistance does not acquire a general license to coerce merely because authority acted unjustly first.

Private coercion doesn’t become legitimate by calling itself resistance. The same argument against extraction applies whoever runs it. Political change is therefore not a fifteenth domain. It is the recognition and protective obligation of §6.1 operating under capture instead of ordinary institutional function.

*Four objections to implementation.* The account faces opposition from four directions.

*The revolutionary critique* holds that existing institutions absorb incremental reform and leave relations of extraction intact. Only revolutionary rupture changes those relations (Marx, “Critique of the Gotha Program” 1875; Lenin, *State and Revolution* 1917; the contemporary revolutionary-left literature broadly).

*Burke and Oakeshott* warn from the other direction. Explicit institutional design produces consequences no designer anticipated, while inherited practices contain knowledge the design may not see (Burke, *Reflections on the Revolution in France* (1790) 1987; Oakeshott, *Rationalism in Politics* 1962). People implementing a reform can therefore repeat the hubris of rationalist engineering.

*Public-choice theory* predicts rollback. Concentrated interests reverse distributive reform unless institutions can resist them (Buchanan and Tullock, *The Calculus of Consent* 1962; Olson, *The Rise and Decline of Nations* 1982). A patchwork strategy may underestimate the pressure back toward extraction.

*Mouffe’s agonistic objection* reaches the position of the implementer itself (*On the Political* 2005; *The Democratic Paradox* 2000). Any attempt to implement the framework is a hegemonic articulation with a constitutive outside: the people who reject it and the commitments it excludes. A political community implementing these conditions is making a political move. It isn’t occupying neutral ground.

Grant each objection what it establishes. Some arrangements can’t be reformed without restructuring property relations, and that restructuring is permitted (§6.7). Explicit design produces unforeseen consequences, and inherited practices carry tacit knowledge reformers ignore at cost. Concentrated interests resist reforms that threaten them. And this framework enters political contestation rather than standing outside it. Its position has to be achieved politically, and its claims remain contestable through the recognition mechanism they specify.

The disagreement with revolutionary critique is about means, not whether property relations may need to change. Tax architecture, representation reform, and property redefinition can pursue restructuring within democratic and constitutional institutions. Nordic, Costa Rican, Portuguese, and German cases show that incremental reform can move meaningful distance; they don’t show that it is always sufficient. A revolutionary strategy must still answer for coercion, concentrated authority, transition risk, minority protection, and whether the institutions replacing the old order remain publicly correctable.

Burke and Oakeshott are answered by the position of the reformer. The conditions in §6.14 already operate inside political life. A community revises its own arrangement with measurement, stop rules, and attention to inherited knowledge. No theorist stands outside society and constructs it from nothing.

Public-choice theory identifies a pressure the account expects. Electoral finance rules, transparency, competition, review, rotation, and renewed public authorization may constrain different routes of capture (§6.3). None is sufficient alone, and each can be gamed. Without effective barriers and monitoring, reforms that impose concentrated losses while distributing benefits diffusely face a serious rollback risk.

Mouffe is right that implementation is agonistic. The reply doesn’t claim neutrality. It makes the excluded alternatives visible and leaves the derivation contestable through §6.3. What distinguishes this position from the authority of an outside engineer is not neutrality. It is the community’s continuing power to revise it, developed at §6.14.

No single group is appointed to implement the account. Reformers, activists, policymakers, civil servants, business leaders, and ordinary participants may all shape it. None owns it by default. Reform remains answerable to the political community through recognized direction.

The proposal is contestable and revisable through public institutions. It is not a design the community has already endorsed without knowing it. The foundational form was fixed by the Government Work corollary at §6.1: implementation is one way a political community discharges the obligation established in §5.14. It is not a private project assigned separately to every citizen.

Nothing here commands the reader to adopt a finished program. The argument supports a baseline of political concern and a way to test what follows from it. Communities acting through accountable political processes must decide whether to implement, criticize, revise, or reject each proposal.

# 7. Modality

With the positive argument in place, the rival accounts come up for test. The question put to each is the same: does it eliminate Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, or does it preserve their work under another description?

A rival can deny the Conditions, place something prior to them, grant them while finding them insufficient, or challenge the semantic, logical, or epistemic apparatus by which the conclusion was reached. The fourth need not describe an alternative world or ground. It may qualify the argument without disputing what obtains.

These are not four versions of one objection, and they do not receive one answer. A denial carried through to absolute structural absence meets the ∅ result; a priority claim must specify a grounding relation; an insufficiency claim identifies content the Conditions allegedly leave out; an apparatus objection must be answered at the point where its own premises place the pressure. Each engagement begins there and follows the position to what it costs, preserves, or leaves open.

One test recurs across the chapter. If an objection’s standard would also reject logic, mathematics, the past, other minds, or the objection’s own articulation, those companions must go with it unless the objector can state the relevant difference. The comparison does not settle the objection. It fixes the price of applying its standard consistently.

## 7.1 Modal Semantics and Its Skeptics
This cluster gathers accounts of how modal language works, together with the skeptics who would deflate it.

Rigid designation (§7.1.1) fixes reference across worlds and makes necessary a posteriori truths available. Two-dimensional semantics (§7.1.2) splits meaning into an epistemic and a metaphysical dimension and asks which one modal intuition tracks. De re necessity is necessity attaching to the thing itself, rather than to how a statement describes it. Quinean modal skepticism (§7.1.3) doubts that it is intelligible at all.

The next three accounts offer ways of thinning the commitment. Modal conventionalism (§7.1.4) makes necessity a product of our linguistic rules. Modal expressivism (§7.1.5) treats modal claims as expressions of attitude rather than descriptions of fact. Metaontological deflationism (§7.1.6) holds that existence questions are shallow or merely verbal. Wittgensteinian quietism (§7.1.7) goes further and declines the enterprise altogether as a misuse of language.

The question put to each is the chapter’s: does the account show that the argument’s modal vocabulary is confused, dispensable, or misapplied, or does it preserve the relevant work under another description? That question bears most directly on §2.1–2.6 and the Modal Identity of §2.6.6. A semantic challenge need not describe a world without Temporality, Spatiality, or Substantiality to matter. It may instead defeat the inference, change what its operators mean, or show that the conclusion cannot be stated with the claimed force. The individual engagements must decide which pressure each view actually supplies.

One pressure runs across the deflationary part of the cluster and is best stated once. The retorsion run against an opponent—that articulating the thesis presupposes the structure the thesis deflates—is deliberately scope-limited: it establishes the conditions’ actuality where the objection is articulated, not their necessity across worlds where no content occurs (§7.1.1). The engagements mark that limit as the act side of a result, and the rule holds for every one of them: an actual assertion, stipulation, inference, framework-comparison, or refusal exhibits the structure in the performing of it, and only the independent modal and role-to-type arguments carry that across worlds. Where a reply below reaches further than the performance, it is spending those arguments and says so. A second pressure bears on content rather than performance. When a restricted semantic or linguistic claim is extended into a global account of modality, that global account owes an account of its own modal status.

**[Theorem]**

**The Self-Application Fork** · *Theorem*

A global deflation of modality owes a coherent account of its own modal status. Contingent, and the theory may still be true of the actual world; what it then owes is why a configuration at which it fails does not unmake it as an account of what modality actually is. Necessary, and the object-language/meta-theory distinction must be drawn before treating that necessity as an exception that unmakes the thesis: the theory’s own standing may be a further claim, not automatically another piece of the deflated object language. The restricted claim survives. The global one is not thereby refuted; it carries a meta-level burden it has not discharged.

The fork doesn’t touch the restricted theses, and the following sections should not ask it to. Selected analyticities can be stable (§7.1.4); contingent descriptions behave as Quine’s examples show (§7.1.3); necessary co-extension doesn’t entail identity (§7.1.1). The pressure begins only when one of those claims is made to explain or deflate modality globally.

A note on alethic and doxastic modality. The engagements operate in alethic modality—what is possible or necessary—rather than merely in what a thinker can conceive or believe. Oppy argues that conceivability-to-possibility inferences are unreliable because conceivability tracks cognitive limitations, and remains agnostic about whether broadly logical and metaphysical modality are genuinely distinct (Oppy 1995; Oppy 2006; Oppy 2013). Both points press arguments that move from a doxastic premise to an alethic conclusion without a bridge.

The present route begins instead from an actuality claim: change occurs in the act of doubt. Actuality entails possibility (§1.2), so that witness establishes ◇C. The later necessity claim does not come from conceivability or from actuality alone; it requires the separately defended modal-stability and global-capacity premises of §2.1. This is enough to avoid the simple conceivability inference without proving that alethic facts are epistemically prior to every doxastic state.

Oppy’s agnosticism about broadly logical and metaphysical modality also survives the Condition-Individuation Criterion (§2.6.11). Distinguishing temporal, spatial, and physical subject matters doesn’t itself derive separate consequence relations. The book proposes differentiated disciplines or readings; whether logical and metaphysical modality are distinct remains a substantive semantic question.

### 7.1.1 Rigid Designation
The Kripkean challenge separates necessary co-extension (two terms applying together in every possible world) from necessary identity (two terms picking out the same thing as a matter of what it is). It presses that the argument has established only the former. Wherever change is possible, the three Conditions may be required; that alone doesn’t show that the possibility of change and the Conditions are one structural fact. The reply therefore grants Kripke’s narrower point and returns the burden to §2.6, especially the Modal Identity at §2.6.6 and the Triconditional Identity at §2.6.10. If those arguments establish identity rather than mere accompaniment, the wedge doesn’t separate their relata. If they don’t, rigid designation won’t repair them.

Necessarily, if something is water, it is H₂O. But water itself might not have existed: on another planet, or in a world with slightly different chemistry, there could have been no water at all. The necessity belongs to the identity of water with H₂O; it doesn’t secure that water exists in every possible world. Kripke (1980, Lecture I) draws the distinction: some necessities are de dicto, holding of the description, while others are de re, holding of the thing. Putnam presses the same point with Twin Earth (1975): the same words can pick out different substances in different worlds. Necessity lives in reference, not in existence.

The distinction exposes a common failure in arguments for necessary existence. Rigid designation can help state a de re conclusion, but it supplies neither a justified possibility premise nor a valid modal bridge. The live question is whether this argument has earned those claims without sliding from the necessity of a description to the necessary existence of its referent.

If the necessity is merely verbal—a consequence of how ‘change’ is defined rather than a fact about what change requires—the argument collapses into conditional necessity. Section 2.6 (§2.6) instead claims that change-possibility and T ∧ S ∧ Φ are one structural fact disclosed from two directions. Three versions of the objection test that claim.

*First.* The sparse-world move stipulates w′, a world in which the words for the Conditions apply but pick out no causally structured succession, relational extension, or persistence—only verbal placeholders. If w′ counts as a countermodel, the argument’s necessity is a truth about descriptions rather than what worlds contain.

But a placeholder isn’t yet a countermodel. If w′ has no content beyond the words, it describes no world; §2.7 classifies that limit as ∅. If it has content, the objector must say whether that content supports change. If it does, the question is whether it realizes the operative roles of the Conditions under another description. If it doesn’t, w′ falsifies neither the Structural Requirement nor the identity claim restricted to change-possibility. This answer blocks the merely verbal case. It does not yet prove that every metaphysically substantive specification must resolve into the book’s loaded types; that is the work of the realizer and no-surplus arguments in §2.6.

*Second.* Exempting the preconditions from S5 grants the ∅ result but restricts S5’s reach. The refinement concedes that the three Conditions obtain in every change-permitting world but denies that S5 licenses the further step to their obtaining in every world *simpliciter*. S5 governs inferences within the space of possibilities; it doesn’t settle the status of that space itself. So the modal behavior of the preconditions can be governed by S5 while S5 still fails to bridge the conditional.

The refinement sharpens the problem rather than loosening it. There may be worlds without actual change that are nevertheless structured and distinct from ∅; a frozen or silent world is the obvious test case. What is ruled out (§2.7) is absolute structural absence, not every world in which change fails to occur. The Kripkean therefore isn’t forced into a simple change-or-∅ dichotomy. To close the exemption move, the argument needs the separate claim that every possible world retains the capacities or role-structure required for change, and the role-to-type bridge must not be assumed in stating that claim. The local retorsion doesn’t supply this cross-world result. The modal core does, and at full type-resolution rather than at role-resolution: Necessary Possibility carries the witnessed Change to □◇C (§2.1.10), the Structural Requirement supplies □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)) (§2.4), and the two discharge to □(T∧S∧Φ), with the role-to-type bridge earned by the realizer lemmas (§2.6.2–2.6.4) rather than assumed. The role-level convergence of §3.2–3.3 corroborates that result without the Euclidean axiom; it doesn’t replace it, and it doesn’t independently box even the generic conjunction (§3.5.4). The dependency stays visible at §3.5.3.

*Third.* The objection can grant the prior replies while denying the underlying identity of §2.6. Necessary co-extension isn’t identity (Kripke himself distinguishes necessary identity, water = H₂O, from mere necessary biconditionals) and so the possibility of change and the instantiation of the three Conditions may be necessarily co-extensive without being one fact. Fine’s (1994) distinction between essence and necessity cuts the same way: Socrates and {Socrates} are necessarily co-present without the singleton being part of Socrates’s essence. The wedge would hold, and the structural conditions would be necessarily co-present with change-possibility without being what change-possibility essentially consists in.

Within this argument’s commitments, necessary co-extension between change-possibility and T∧S∧Φ isn’t yet a rival account of their relation. Both sides have already been argued necessary (§2.3, §2.5), and any two necessary truths are co-extensive across worlds regardless of subject matter. “Necessarily together but distinct” is therefore a coherent warning, not an explanation of what distinguishes the facts.

Fine’s own case shows what a successful distinction can look like. {Socrates} essentially contains Socrates, while Socrates bears no corresponding essential relation to the singleton. One side carries content the other lacks. A parallel objection here should identify some asymmetry or surplus between change-possibility and T∧S∧Φ. Mere co-extension doesn’t supply one—but the absence of a proposed surplus is not by itself a proof of identity either.

Fine’s point therefore fixes the standard rather than deciding the result. A necessary biconditional leaves open whether two distinct facts always obtain together; an identity claim says that two descriptions disclose one fact. Water/H₂O is offered as the latter after an empirical identification. The Modal Identity of §2.6 must reach the same strength by constitutive analysis.

Section 2.6 analyzes change as a succession (Time) of states (Substance) across a structured interval (Space). Its bidirectional entailments establish more than one-way dependence, but bidirectionality alone still doesn’t yield identity. The additional No-Surplus Criterion argues that neither side contains a fact left out by the other. In Fine’s terms, the intended result is an essence claim: T, S, and Φ spell out what change-possibility consists in. The strength of the reply rises or falls with that constitutive analysis.

The water/H₂O case permits a two-description gap because Twin Earth is specified using space, time, and chemistry before it asks which substance the surface concept picks out. A parallel diagnostic for the Conditions is harder to construct. An inquiry in which “causally structured succession” turns out to pick out something other than Time already uses succession, a distinction between concept and candidate referent, and persistence from setup to verdict. The machinery of the diagnostic is drawn from the domain in which it is supposed to open a gap. That limits this particular test; it doesn’t make every non-epistemic distinction impossible by fiat.

**[Dissolution]**

**No Twin Earth for the Conditions** · *Dissolution*

Twin Earth is assembled from resources outside what it targets: space, time, and chemistry presuppose neither water nor H₂O. A Twin-Earth diagnostic aimed at the Conditions has no equally neutral platform. Exhibiting the gap already requires succession, differentiation, and persistence—the very roles under dispute. The diagnostic therefore can’t establish independence without first assuming it.

**Dissolves:** the direct transfer of the Twin Earth diagnostic to the Conditions

The objector can answer that this is only an epistemic limit: *we* can’t represent the counterexample, but the metaphysical distinction may remain. The Cartesian argument establishes something narrower. Denying change is itself a transition (§2.2.1), and imagining Nature away instantiates the Conditions in the act (§3.3.1). Any performed denial therefore witnesses their actuality. It does not, by itself, survey worlds in which no denial or imagining occurs. The cross-world conclusion still depends on the modal bridge stated above; the failure of the diagnostic supports the constitutive reading without independently proving it.

The book accordingly uses the three Conditions not as loose descriptions but as names for the irreducible existence-axes individuated at §2.6.11. ‘Reality’ is likewise reference-fixed at §2.9.6 as their joint complex. Reference-fixing states which structures the terms target; it does not manufacture the metaphysical identity. That remains the job of the analyses that identify the roles, their realizers, and the absence of surplus.

A kindred deflationary move drops rigid designation in favor of modal conventionalism (Sidelle 1989; Cameron 2010; Sider 2011): necessary truths are consequences of our classificatory conventions rather than discoveries about reality. The practice of classifying still instantiates persistence, differentiation, and succession. That establishes the Conditions in the practice; it doesn’t yet refute the conventionalist’s account of modal truth. The broader dispute therefore belongs to the adjacent semantic sections rather than serving as another proof here.

Adjacent modal deflations are engaged in their own sections: two-dimensionalism (§7.1.2), the Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR) demand (§8.2.1), modal collapse (§8.2.5), and the changeless-being objection (§10.2.3).

*Taking stock.* Three forms of the Kripkean wedge receive different answers. A merely verbal sparse-world placeholder supplies no countermodel; a genuinely structured frozen or silent world, however, isn’t forced into a change-or-∅ dichotomy. The S5-exemption move is answered by the Chapter 2 modal line and its realizer lemmas, as set out above, not by the retorsion. Fine’s essence/necessity distinction then fixes the remaining burden: the argument at §2.6 must establish one fact under two descriptions rather than a necessary biconditional between distinct facts. The argument therefore records a closure dependent on those bridges, not a result delivered by §2.7 alone.

One pressure isn’t so qualified, because it doesn’t run through the retorsion at all. Pressed to a global thesis, the wedge owes its own modal status and can’t pay it without a meta-level account: the Self-Application Fork (§7.1) presses that ascent independently of the preceding bridges. The global thesis is that no necessity is ever *de re*, that modal force always belongs to description. What the fork leaves standing is exactly what Kripke himself asserted and this section concedes in full: the narrower, restricted point that necessary co-extension doesn’t entail identity.

Nor is □(T∧S∧Φ) presented as a necessary a posteriori discovery on the water/H₂O model. The derivation begins from the actuality of change, treated as Cartesian rather than ordinary empirical evidence because skeptical counterhypotheses still occur as changing acts (§2.2.1). It then requires two further pieces: the modal ascent through Necessary Possibility and the constitutive analysis at §2.6. Calling the result “a priori” must preserve that structure: it is reached from an inescapable actuality-premise, not from meaning alone. The two-dimensional bookkeeping is taken up at §7.1.2.

Kripke’s causal-historical picture of reference traces a name through transmissions from a naming event, across time, among persisting speakers, in uses differentiated enough to preserve reference. Its actual deployment therefore instantiates succession, differentiation, and persistence. It provides no structure-free standpoint from which to formulate the objection. But this is again a retorsive point about the theory’s use, not a derivation of what reference must be in every possible world.

The water/H₂O case likewise remains formulated within ordinary chemical and spatiotemporal theory. It supplies no counterexample to the structural framework, but neither does it establish that every possible referent must instantiate the book’s full loaded types. Its lesson is methodological: rigid designation can preserve an identity once the identity is earned; it cannot turn necessary co-extension into identity.

### 7.1.2 Two-Dimensional Semantics
Two-dimensional semantics promises a wedge between what a concept picks out when a world is considered as actual and what it picks out across possible worlds. If that wedge holds at the constitutive level, the Modal Identity of §2.6.6 (□(◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ) read as one fact under two descriptions, connecting change-permission with co-instantiation of the three structural roles) won’t survive. The challenge presses at three points: the two-intensions machinery itself, the water/H₂O analogy that exhibits it, and the indexical anchor on which primary intensions depend. Chalmers is right on a narrower point, conceded here without qualification: the primary/secondary distinction is a genuine feature of natural-kind terms, and arguments that ignore it routinely overstate what necessary co-extension delivers. The claim contested in the analysis that follows is narrower and specifically targeted: that the structural role definitions are natural-kind terms, and that the two-intension machinery has purchase where the appearance/nature separation it exploits doesn’t exist.

Chalmers (1996; 2010) distinguishes two intensions. The primary intension tracks what a concept would refer to in a world considered as actual; the secondary tracks its reference across possible worlds once its actual referent is fixed. For natural-kind terms they can diverge: ‘water’ may pick out the clear drinkable stuff under the first evaluation, while rigidly designating H₂O under the second. The framework thereby represents a gap between epistemic appearance and counterfactual reference that rigid designation alone doesn’t display.

Jackson (1998, chs. 2–3) develops an allied account in terms of A- and C-intensions. Chalmers and Jackson (2001) connect reductive explanation to a priori entailment from an appropriately specified base; failure of entailment marks an explanatory gap. Chalmers’s scrutability program (2012) and his account of ideal a priori conceivability (2002) extend the machinery beyond natural-kind terms. The challenge is therefore general: does an ideal primary-intension scenario separate the book’s role language from its claimed metaphysical referents?

Applied to the present account, the framework presses a precise threat. The argument at §2.6 holds that ‘causally structured succession’ and Time aren’t merely co-extensional descriptions but the same structural fact under two modes of presentation: that the role definitions are constitutive rather than descriptive. The two-dimensionalist replies that even for terms the argument labels constitutive, primary and secondary intension can diverge: what ‘causally structured succession’ picks out when a given world is considered as actual may differ from what it picks out across possible worlds. The Modal Identity of §2.6.6 would then fail, and with it the step from □◇C to □(T∧S∧Φ): from the necessary possibility of change to the necessary co-instantiation of the three structural conditions. A wedge between description and reference at the constitutive level would leave the structural roles necessarily co-extensive with change without being identical to it: the exact space the classical theist needs to reassert an uninstantiated ground.

*First.* The argument may illicitly collapse the two intensions at its constitutive terms. A primary intension captures how a world might turn out under ideal a priori evaluation, while a secondary necessity can remain fixed by actual reference (2002). The objector therefore asks whether ‘causally structured succession’ could pick out something other than Time when a world is considered as actual. Scrutability (Chalmers 2012) broadens the pressure: unless the appropriately specified base a priori entails the target, the claimed constitutive identity leaves an explanatory gap.

The reply runs on the analytic/a posteriori distinction the 2D framework itself respects, but it must keep two resolutions apart. At role-resolution, a constitutive definition fixes what counts as directed order, relational differentiation, or real bearing. At type-resolution, further arguments identify temporal succession, spatial extension, and causal persistence as the relevant realizers in genuine change. The Modal Identity doesn’t treat the names alone as settling those richer types.

The Kripkean cases 2D was built to accommodate are a posteriori identities: ‘water is H₂O’ was discovered, not defined, and the primary/secondary gap tracks exactly what the discovery added. The structural claim is different at role-resolution: ‘causally structured succession’ specifies the role T plays in a genuine change-realizer rather than reporting a discovery that two independently identified things coincide. Where that role specification is analytic, primary and secondary intensions have no independent residue to track. A critic may still contest the type-level realization, but that is a dispute over the realizer arguments, not a primary/secondary gap generated by the role definition itself.

The 2D matrix is a function from possible worlds to extensions, and functions require a domain. In the present account, real possibility is fixed by the standing capacity of the one Reality, R: ◇P means Capacity(R,P) (§2.1). Two-dimensional semantics may offer a different representation of modal evaluation, but it must say whether its primary-intension scenarios represent that same standing capacity of R, a relative accessibility relation, or an epistemic space. Only the first is the book’s alethic operator ◇. The semantic tool therefore doesn’t by itself overturn the global-capacity account; it either represents the same real possibilities at another level or shifts to a different relative modality. The structural roles become relevant where a scenario is offered as a genuine change-realizer, not merely because any semantic matrix is described.

The disanalogy with the paradigm case can be stated directly. The water/H₂O primary intension is evaluable without presupposing water or H₂O: the evaluation is built from chemistry, sense-perception, and an ordinary spatiotemporal setup, none of which is the disputed term. No parallel construction is available here.
