Evaluating the primary intension of ‘causally structured succession’ requires exactly the apparatus in question: a scenario individuated from its alternatives (Space), a reasoner who carries the evaluation from premises to verdict (Time), and content held fixed long enough to be compared against the secondary intension it is meant to diverge from (Substance). The act of running the semantic tool is structured, but that act-side fact doesn’t show that every scenario represented by the tool instantiates the loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types. The object-side question remains whether a scenario is admitted as a genuine change-world or only as an epistemic representation.

*Second.* The water/H₂O analogy sharpens the pressure. Scientists discovered water is H₂O a posteriori: the identity holds necessarily but wasn’t analytically given. Chalmers and Jackson generalize the pattern (2001): every necessary a posteriori identity admits a corresponding primary-level contingency, and the identity’s modal weight is confined to the secondary level. If ‘causally structured succession’ and Time stand in this relation, the objector presses, their identity is a discovery rather than a definition, and a discovered identity is necessary only in the restricted secondary sense that leaves the primary-level gap open, which is the gap the theist needs.

The analogy works in the natural-kind case precisely because ‘water’ and ‘H₂O’ pick out different levels of description: surface features on one side, microstructure on the other. The gap opens because a world could present the surface features while hosting different microstructure (Twin Earth’s XYZ). The structural role definitions don’t operate at two separable levels. ‘Causally structured succession’ names nothing except asymmetric directed succession among states: the full specification of what Time *is*. There is no surface/microstructure distinction to exploit, no layer of appearance hiding a different metaphysics underneath. The 2D gap requires exactly the appearance/nature separation the role definitions are designed to eliminate.

The water/H₂O example operates within an ordinary physical setting, but that doesn’t dissolve the semantic distinction it illustrates. The relevant reply is narrower: role specifications and natural-kind identifications have different logical forms. Whether the book’s type-level identifications behave more like definitions or discoveries must be defended by the realizer arguments rather than inferred from the physical setting in which semantic evaluation occurs.

*Third.* The indexical anchor presses the objection furthest. The primary intension is evaluated from the perspective of a world considered as actual, and ‘considered as actual’ is an indexical that depends on the evaluator’s position rather than any mind-independent fact. The indexicality drives the 2D framework, the objector concludes, and if it survives so does the gap.

The indexical objection establishes an act-side point, not immediately an object-side result. The object-side issue is semantic: whether the scenario is offered as a configuration R can really admit or merely as an epistemic representation. In the first case, it answers to the Structural Requirement; if it is merely an epistemic representation, its variation doesn’t by itself yield a metaphysical possibility.

Two lines support the claim rather than asserting it. First, Lewis individuates worlds as maximal fusions of spatiotemporally interrelated things (*On the Plurality of Worlds* 1986a, section 1.6). That criterion requires the relevant worldmate relations where there are multiple inhabitants, but it doesn’t by itself prove asymmetric temporal ordering in every sparse or changeless world. Lewisian individuation therefore supplies a concrete-world constraint without independently establishing the book’s full T-type. Second, the Chalmers/Jackson scrutability framework requires an idealized a priori reasoner conducting the evaluation exercise from within a world considered as actual (*Constructing the World* 2012, Ch. 2). That idealization strips cognitive limitations (bounded memory, finite inferential steps) while preserving the structural conditions of reasoning: directed inference from premises to conclusions (T), distinction among propositions being evaluated (S), and persistence of the cognitive state across the derivation (Φ). Any actual token of idealized reasoning is performed through an ordered cognitive practice. That establishes an act-side condition on evaluators; it doesn’t place a temporal coordinate inside every scenario they evaluate or settle whether an abstract ideal inference is itself temporally extended.

The indexical reading of ‘actual’ is itself contested. Van Inwagen (1980) argues that Lewis’s formulations don’t sustain a reading that is both genuinely indexical and correct; Adams (1974) treats actuality instead as a primitive property of one world. Neither result decides the inventory of worlds. If ‘actual’ is indexical, a token evaluation may be centered on an evaluator without imposing one temporal frame on every scenario. If actuality is primitive, its application need not depend on a standpoint within the actual world. In either case, the act-side constraint is not an essence claim about actuality.

A kindred deflation drops the 2D apparatus for conceptual-role semantics. On accounts associated with Block (1998) and Harman (1987), meaning is fixed by inferential role within a conceptual system, so §2.6 may appear to establish an inferential equivalence rather than a metaphysical identity. Actual inference still instantiates ordered steps, distinct contents, and persistence across a derivation. That retorsion secures the Conditions in the practice, not the further claim that inferential-role semantics has merely renamed them or that its account of meaning is false.

The Kripkean challenge (that necessary co-extension isn’t necessary identity) is handled at §7.1.1, which states the modal-epistemic route and defers its two-dimensional bookkeeping here.

*The bookkeeping, made explicit.* Section 7.1.1 locates the intended result as constitutive rather than a necessary a posteriori identity, while preserving its dependence on an inescapable actuality-premise and substantive modal bridges. Two-dimensional accounting should display that mixed route rather than relabel the whole derivation analytic.

Run the derivation through the 2D matrix and the actuality of change (§2.4) is its world-indexed input. It doesn’t enter as ordinary empirical discovery: skeptical counterhypotheses still occur as changing acts (§2.2.1). The role definitions may be analytic at thin resolution, but the role-to-type bridges and the claim that they exhaust genuine change-realizers remain substantive metaphysical premises. They are not consequences of vocabulary alone.

If the constitutive analysis succeeds, ◇C ⟷ T∧S∧Φ leaves no primary/secondary gap at role-resolution. ‘Causally structured succession’ is then not scrutable from an independent base but states part of that base under another description. By contrast, ‘watery stuff’ retains a surface profile while its microstructure varies to XYZ. The objector’s opening is therefore precise: identify an independently held feature of the change-role that can remain fixed while its alleged structural referent varies.

The Modal Identity and No-Surplus Criterion are meant to remove that handle: the role definitions of §1.3–1.4, the converse at §2.4.10, and the realizer arguments claim that neither side contains a differentiating fact. Two-dimensional semantics shows what those arguments must accomplish; it does not independently verify them. If no surplus remains, an ideal reasoner has no profile along which the primary intension can diverge. If the objector supplies such a profile, the claimed identity—not merely its semantic bookkeeping—has failed. The reply is therefore non-circular only because its support is external to this section and open to challenge at those earlier steps.

**[Dissolution]**

**No Surplus, No Divergence** · *Dissolution*

A primary intension can diverge where a concept keeps an individuating feature fixed while its referent varies, as “watery stuff” retains a surface profile while microstructure shifts to XYZ. The book’s no-surplus argument denies any corresponding handle between the change-roles and the Conditions. If that prior argument succeeds, the 2D wedge has no feature on which to turn; if such a feature can be supplied, the Modal Identity fails.

**Dissolves:** an independent 2D wedge after no-surplus is established

*Convergence.* The three pressure points produce differentiated results. The two-intensions machinery doesn’t itself choose between the book’s global-capacity operator and an epistemic or relative modality. The water/H₂O analogy identifies the needed appearance/constitution seam but does not show that the role terms possess one. The indexical anchor structures actual acts of evaluation without placing a Time coordinate in every represented scenario. None independently defeats the argument; each clarifies a burden the constitutive and modal bridges must bear.

Chalmers’s natural-kind point stands. Its transfer to the structural identities is conditional. At thin resolution, the role definitions are not natural-kind terms waiting for an empirical essence; at full type-resolution, the book still owes the claim that those roles have unique realizers and exhaust what genuine change requires. Two-dimensional semantics does not create a new gap once those claims are earned. It gives a disciplined way to expose one if they are not.

### 7.1.3 Quinean Modal Skepticism
Quine’s modal skepticism is a thoroughgoing rejection of the modal vocabulary, and the position hasn’t been refuted so much as outlasted by the literatures that find ways to work around it. “Two Dogmas of Empiricism” (1951) attacks the analytic/synthetic distinction on which much prior modal regimentation depended; “Reference and Modality” (1953) shows that quantifying into modal contexts produces the notorious failures of substitutivity that de re essentialism is supposed to license; *Word and Object* (1960) turns the screw further with the indeterminacy of translation, on which essential properties cannot be picked out across translation manuals. The proposed cure is austerity: keep the language of regimented science (extensional first-order logic, logic sensitive only to reference and truth-value, not to meaning or modal force, plus the working vocabulary of physics and biology), drop the language of necessity, get on with the work.

Føllesdal and Burgess carry the position forward in modal logic (1986; 1997); Gibbard develops the contingent-identity wedge that presses against essentialism from within (1975); Williamson’s *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* (2013, ch. 2) is the contemporary acknowledgment that the position remains the floor any modal account must clear. Where the present argument needs de re necessities (that the structural roles obtain in virtue of what they are, not in virtue of how we describe them) Quine’s apparatus stands in the way.

The concession runs in full. Quine is right that mid-century modal regimentation imported analyticity as if Carnap had not been answered; right that quantification into modal contexts requires more than its proponents had supplied; right that translation doesn’t pick out essences in any extensionally regimented way. The position closes more loose modal arguments than it opens, and any argument for necessary structural conditions has to clear the Quinean floor before it earns its conclusion. The Quinean tool has tracked something real about how modal vocabulary had been used; the question is whether it tracks something real about the structural conditions established at §2.6. Three forms of the Quinean move press the objection at three resolutions, each closing where it doesn’t reach: classical analyticity, which holds that modal claims trade on hidden synonymies; de re / de dicto substitutivity, which catalogues the failures that follow from quantifying into modal contexts; and extensional regimentation, which relocates necessity into how reliably the predicates of our best science extend to new cases.

*First.* The classical analyticity form runs against the present account directly. Necessities, on this reading, are analytic in disguise: “Time is causally structured succession” is a stipulative truth about how we use “Time,” not a discovery about what any change-permitting world contains. Modal claims trade on hidden synonymies, and once the synonymies are exposed there is nothing left for necessity to track. Gibbard’s (1975) contingent-identity wedge sharpens the pressure: even paradigm de re identities can be analyzed as description-relative if essentialism is given up, and the a posteriori necessities the Kripkean apparatus delivers (water = H₂O) are recast as terminological decisions about which features fix reference.

The reply runs on the distinction between stipulative definition and structural specification. The role definitions of §1.3–1.4 aren’t synonymy claims about how the English word “Time” relates to the English phrase “causally structured succession”; they are specifications of what any medium hosting transitions must instantiate, derived from what a transition consists in. The derivation doesn’t depend on the term “Time” picking out anything in particular; it shows that succession, distinction, and exchange are the conditions on transition under any vocabulary in which the conditions can be stated. Quine’s analyticity critique cuts against synonymy claims dressed up as discoveries; it leaves untouched discoveries that hold in any vocabulary capable of stating them. Gibbard’s wedge cuts against essentialism construed as a discovery about which descriptions a thing satisfies; the present account isn’t in that business. It doesn’t claim that *Time* picks out the same role across worlds; it shows that any world containing transitions instantiates the role, by whatever name.

*Second.* The de re / de dicto form presses where the first leaves off. Even granting that the structural conditions aren’t synonymy claims, the Quinean denies that the de re reading on which they obtain “of the world rather than of a description” is intelligible at all. Quantifying into modal contexts produces the failures Quine catalogues (1953): “necessarily, 9 is greater than 7” appears true, “9 = the number of planets” is true, “necessarily, the number of planets is greater than 7” is false. The de re reading on which a structural condition obtains *of* the medium, independent of how we describe it, is exactly the reading the substitutivity failures rule out. Føllesdal and Burgess extend the point (1986; 1997): modal logic is a useful instrument for organizing inferences but can’t, on Quinean grounds, be read off as picking out language-independent modal facts.

The reply concedes the substitutivity point and presses where it doesn’t reach. The de re readings Quine’s catalogue dismisses are readings on which a contingent description (“the number of planets”) is treated as if it picked out its referent rigidly across modal contexts. The Kripkean apparatus (§7.1.1) answers the catalogue by distinguishing rigid from non-rigid designators; the present account doesn’t depend on the answer. Ask what Quine’s pair actually is. Two singular terms for an object, independently graspable in sense, co-referring in one world and coming apart in another. The structural roles aren’t that kind of term. They are specified by what a transition requires (§2.4), and the specification is invariant across any vocabulary that can state the work (§2.4.5).

The remaining reconstruction is the Fregean one the Modal Identity already met (§2.6.6): two independently graspable senses of one fact, so that substituting one specification for the other inside a modal context would fail even if the referent were shared. Morning star and evening star. The Modal Identity’s reply is that the two readings aren’t independently graspable. To grasp that change is possible is already to grasp directed succession among distinct persisting states; to grasp those Conditions is already to grasp the availability of transition. There aren’t two senses that could be entertained singly. The No-Surplus Criterion (§2.6.9) is what that identity consists in: specifying either side already specifies the other, with nothing left over to mark them as two. Essence-Description (§2.6.12) blocks the last reconstruction, on which the role-specification would be a nominal essence sitting in front of a hidden real one to which a second sense could attach. Descriptions that pick out the conditional profile are descriptions of the essence, not approximations to an inaccessible one behind them.

So the substitutions the argument actually uses aren’t substitutions of co-referring object-terms into an opaque context. They run between change-possibility and the three Conditions, and among the Conditions themselves under Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7). They are identity-substitutions of one fact. Quine’s catalogue remains where he established it, against descriptions mistaken for essence claims. It doesn’t reach individuation by role. Whether the identity remains primarily conceivable as false even where the secondary structural identity holds is the two-dimensional question at §7.1.2, not a second substitutivity pair.

**[Proposition]**

**Role-Specifications Admit No Substitution** · *Proposition*

Quine’s substitutivity failures need two singular terms that co-refer while remaining independently graspable in sense: “9” and “the number of planets.” The book’s role-specifications are not that pair. They are individuated by constitutive job, and the Modal Identity has already shown that change-possibility and the three Conditions are not independently graspable senses of one object but one content approached from either side. The No-Surplus Criterion is what that identity consists in; Essence-Description blocks reconstructing a hidden sense behind the role. The substitutions the argument actually uses are therefore identity-substitutions of one fact, not opaque-context substitutions of co-referring object-terms. Quine’s catalogue stands against descriptions mistaken for essence claims. It does not reach individuation by role.

The instrumentalist reading Burgess defends is consistent with this: modal logic is a useful instrument, and the structural conditions are what the instrument has to track to be useful. The instrument’s utility on Burgess’s own terms is the data the modal account explains.

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6); No-Surplus Criterion (§2.6.9); Essence-Description (§2.6.12); Framework-Invariance (§2.4.5)

*Third.* The extensional-regimentation form grants that the role-specifications hold in any vocabulary but denies that the holding is *modal* in any sense that escapes extensional logic. What looks like necessity is instead a pattern our best science can reliably extend to new cases; what looks like de re essentialism is the privileged status of certain natural-kind classifications within that science. The work modal vocabulary did before is now done by what regimented science treats as nomological (law-governed, a matter of the laws of nature) and the question whether that treatment tracks something modally robust is exactly what Quine refuses to answer outside the framework. Williamson (2013, ch. 2) presses the contemporary form: the position survives as a methodological stance even where its first-order claims have been answered, and any necessitarian account has to show that the necessities it posits aren’t artifacts of the science that names them.

The reply distinguishes scope, and it answers the burden cumulatively rather than resting on any single bridge. The Quinean is right that much of what passed for modal claim at mid-century was talk about which predicates science could reliably extend to new cases dressed up; right that natural-kind classifications carry methodological privilege within a science without thereby carrying language-independent modal weight; right that the burden is on the necessitarian. What the reply does *not* do is the thing the Quinean would be entitled to reject: assert that reliable extension to new cases simply *is* structural necessity renamed. Quine has a fully naturalized account of why some predicates extend beyond observed cases (entrenched quality-spaces, “Natural Kinds,” 1969); answering it by relabeling would beg the question. The conditions identified at §2.6 earn their standing instead by what any nomological practice must presuppose to be one at all, and several independent considerations converge on the same commitment.

*The transcendental consideration.* Actual projection occurs through succession and comparison among distinguishable cases, and Quine’s naturalized story invokes persistence and causal selection. This establishes the structure of the actual scientific practice. It doesn’t show that reliable extension to new cases requires productive law-like causation rather than Humean regularity, or by itself establish the full loaded types in every possible world.

*The indispensability and invariance considerations.* Quine’s own criterion fixes ontological commitment by what our best science must quantify over, and what keeps the conditions from being artifacts of the science that names them (Williamson’s 2013, ch. 2 standing worry) is that *every* nomological practice presupposes them, not one.

**[Argument]**

**What the Variables Range Over** · *The Quinean Inversion*

1. **Ontological commitment is fixed by what our best science must quantify over.** This is Quine’s own criterion, not one imported to embarrass him (§2.9.3).

2. **Any nomological practice quantifies ineliminably over a structured succession of distinguishable, causally interacting items.** The structural conditions aren’t an optional modal overlay laid on the science; they are what its bound variables range over.

3. **No nomological practice can decline them.** Rival sciences, future regimentations, and Quine’s own meta-theory alike must range over them. Which predicates can be extended to new cases varies from science to science; the structural conditions don’t, because they are the conditions under which any predicate can be extended that way at all.

4. **∴ Quinean indispensability commits the practice to whatever temporal, relational, and physical ontology its best regimentation genuinely quantifies over.** The skepticism is about modal vocabulary; the commitment is read off the variables, and the variables were never modal vocabulary.

*Scope.* Identifying that ontology exactly with T, S, and Φ requires the independent role and realizer arguments; the criterion alone doesn’t supply the identification. The framework-independence earned here is the thin kind of §7.1.6—conditions no framework can refuse, not a privileged carving lying behind every framework.

The three considerations support a cumulative reply; none alone converts actual scientific practice into an unrestricted cross-world necessity.

A kindred move drops Quine’s program for Williamson’s necessitism (2013), which keeps the modal vocabulary while denying that contingency is fundamental; that position is engaged at §7.2.7. A different skepticism keeps both the vocabulary and ordinary modal knowledge while denying that the modal faculty is reliable at metaphysical distances (van Inwagen 1998); because it concedes everything the present section vindicates, it is engaged separately at §7.3.2. The adjacent deflationary tradition, modal conventionalism (§7.1.4) and metaontological deflationism (§7.1.6), runs parallel deflations at neighboring resolutions, and the structural reply takes the same form across the family. The regimentation of the structural claims in formal terms that satisfy Quine’s extensionalist constraints is carried out at §3.5.7.1–2.10.3, showing that the role-specifications are statable without the analytic/synthetic distinction and without quantifying into modal contexts in the way Quine’s (1953) catalogue targets; the bound-variable ontology that licenses the existential commitments is laid out specifically at §2.9.3.

*Taking stock.* None of the three forms of Quinean austerity opens the gap. The Quinean refuses the modal vocabulary; the present account shows what the vocabulary picks out, and what it picks out is unaltered by the refusal. What none of the three forms reaches is the constitutive register where □(T∧S∧Φ) is claimed, and what carries the argument to that register is the global-capacity lift together with the separate Structural Requirement and role-to-type premises rather than anything settled here.

What the austerity hasn’t produced is a configuration of reality in which the structural conditions fail to obtain, and what the catalogue hasn’t produced is a substitution failure that touches role-specification rather than description. The skepticism, taken seriously, narrows to the claim that necessity is an unnecessary word. The argument concedes the possibility and asks what remains when the word is gone. What remains is structure.

The narrowing is itself the Self-Application Fork (§7.1) doing its work. Austerity as a *methodological stance* survives everything here and isn’t contested: drop the word, see what the science still needs. Austerity as a *global thesis* about what there is to be necessary doesn’t, because the thesis owes a coherent account of its own modal status: stated as contingent it may still be true of the actual world, and then owes why a configuration at which it fails doesn’t unmake it as an account of modality; stated as necessary it must distinguish object-language from meta-theory before the necessity is treated as the de re necessity it was raised to deny. The global thesis carries that burden; the restricted methodological stance doesn’t.

### 7.1.4 Modal Conventionalism
If necessity is something we make, then the conclusion of this book is a fact about our descriptive habits wearing the grammar of a fact about Reality—and the rival need not dispute a single step of the derivation to say so. That is the shape of the threat here, and it’s why the reply cannot consist in restating the derivation more firmly.

Alan Sidelle’s *Necessity, Essence, and Individuation* (1989) develops the contemporary case for the view that necessity is a feature of how we describe the world rather than of the world itself. The argument descends from logical positivism (Ayer’s *Language, Truth and Logic* 1936 on analyticity; Carnap’s “Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology” 1950 on framework-relativity; Quine’s 1951 “Two Dogmas” as the critical pressure the tradition had to absorb). Sidelle’s contribution is to extend the analyticity treatment to de re modal claims (necessities about a thing itself rather than about its description). Saying water is necessarily H₂O is, on this picture, a decision about how to use “water” as a natural-kind term rather than a discovery about water.

The position has been pressed in different directions since. Sidelle’s “Modality and Objects” (2010) develops the view in response to its critics. Ross Cameron’s “On the Source of Necessity” (2010) and his subsequent work argue that necessity is grounded in linguistic and conceptual practice without being reducible to it. Amie Thomasson’s *Norms and Necessity* (2020) defends an adjacent modal normativism on which modal claims express norms governing concept-use rather than describing language-independent facts. Bob Hale’s *Necessary Beings* (2013) develops a contemporary critique of the conventionalist tradition, while Jonathan Schaffer’s necessitarian counter (“Laws for Metaphysical Explanation,” 2017) presses from a different direction.

The argument here doesn’t contest the analyticity of selected modal claims. It contests the claim that all of them are. The three structural Conditions aren’t stipulated into necessity by linguistic decision; they are the conditions any stipulator must operate within to stipulate. (The formal regimentation of these structural claims in terms that satisfy Quine’s extensionalist constraints is carried out at §3.5.7.1–2.10.3; the bound-variable ontology is at §2.9.3.) Any actual proposal and comparison is a structured cognitive and linguistic performance. That secures an act-side point about actual convention-making, not yet the object-side conclusion that every possible world instantiates the full temporal, spatial, and causal types. The global conventionalist still owes an account of the non-conventional resources used to formulate and apply the thesis. Three forms of the conventionalist move sharpen the reply at three resolutions, each refining the last to escape a regress: classical Sidelle, on which de re modal claims are analytic stipulations in disguise; Cameron’s grounding refinement, on which necessity is grounded in linguistic practice without reducing to it; and Thomasson’s modal normativism, on which modal claims express norms for concept-use rather than facts.

*First.* The classical Sidelle (1989) form treats de re modal claims as analytic in disguise. “Water is necessarily H₂O” isn’t a discovery about water; it is a stipulation about how “water” is to be used in modal contexts, with the analyticity hidden by the de re surface grammar. The argument generalizes: every necessity is, on examination, a hidden analyticity, and the appearance of language-independent modal fact is the product of unrecognized linguistic decision.

The reply is internal. Stipulations are themselves entities, sequences of marks, sounds, or mental events whose individuation depends on extension, persistence, and contrast with other stipulations. Conventions are configurations within Reality, not grounds prior to it. To say “necessity is conventional” is to use a medium whose conditions aren’t conventional in any sense the position can recover. Sidelle anticipates the move and replies that the medium itself is conventional all the way down, but the regress closes the position rather than vindicating it. If “medium” is conventional, then the convention that fixes “medium” as conventional is itself a configuration, requiring the very conditions it purports to deflate. Quine’s regress presses that conventions can’t alone generate all logical consequence, since applying them requires inferential resources. The structural account may use this against a global conventional reduction, but specifying those resources as the full types of the three Conditions requires further argument rather than following from the regress itself. Hale’s *Necessary Beings* (2013, ch. 4) presses this point at length: the conventionalist account requires modal vocabulary to state, and the modal vocabulary it requires isn’t stateable in the conventionalist’s preferred terms.

*Second.* Cameron’s (2010) refinement concedes the medium’s structural conditions and presses the thesis at a higher level. Necessity is grounded in linguistic and conceptual practice in the sense that what makes modal claims true is the practice of using modal vocabulary in the way we use it, not in the sense that modal claims are reducible to claims about the practice. The grounding relation is asymmetric: modal facts hold in virtue of practices, but modal facts aren’t identical to facts about practices. The position survives the regress because it doesn’t deny that practices have structural conditions; it grounds modality in practices and is silent on the structural conditions of practices.

The concession is real. The reply is that Cameron’s position succeeds at the cost of being consistent with the present account at the level where the present argument’s claim applies. A concrete discursive practice ordinarily involves continuing practitioners, distinguishable acts, and temporal ordering. Those are conditions on such practices; calling them unrestricted modal conditions, and identifying them with the full loaded types, depends on the book’s separate structural derivation. The grounding Cameron offers (modality grounded in practice) terminates at conditions on practice that are themselves necessary in every world in which practice exists. The present account names those conditions; Cameron’s account leaves them implicit. The remaining disagreement is about whether the structural conditions are best described as conditions on linguistic practice in particular (Cameron) or on any configuration capable of hosting practice or anything else (the present argument).

*Third.* Thomasson’s (2020) modal normativism is a refined version. Modal claims don’t describe modal facts; they express norms governing concept-use. “Water is necessarily H₂O” doesn’t say anything about water; it endorses a norm about how the concept *water* is to be applied across counterfactual cases. The position is genuinely deflationary about modal facts without being committed to the regress-prone claim that modal claims are reducible to claims about language.

The reply tracks Thomasson’s own framework. Actual norm-governed practices distinguish applications and often maintain standards across time. An abstract norm need not itself persist as a physical bearer or be applied in temporal sequence, so the practice-side structure shouldn’t be transferred automatically to the norm as an abstract object. Thomasson’s normativism doesn’t deny these conditions; it is silent on them, treating them as background to the normative analysis rather than as the locus of modal commitment. The present account makes them explicit. The conditions of a norm’s being in force (proposed, applied, maintained in a practice) are what the structural roles secure, and any normativist account that disowns those conditions disowns the apparatus the account requires.

A kindred move presses from outside conventionalism entirely. Schaffer’s (2017) necessitarianism argues that the laws governing metaphysical explanation are themselves necessary, but the necessity isn’t conventional: it is grounded in the structure of explanation itself. The present account agrees with Schaffer that the necessity isn’t conventional, and adds a constructive specification of what the necessity is grounded in: the structural conditions any configuration capable of being something must instantiate. Where Schaffer leaves the grounding at “the structure of explanation,” the present account specifies the structure.

Two adjacent positions live elsewhere. Carnapian framework-deflationism is engaged at §7.1.6 (Metaontological Deflationism). Modal fictionalism, which deflates modal commitment by relocating it to a fiction rather than to convention, is engaged at §7.2.6.

**[Proposition]**

**The Register Does Not Match** · *Proposition*

Every form of modal conventionalism—analyticity-extension, grounding-asymmetry, normativism—locates the source of the necessity in a derivative register: convention, practice, or norm. The register at which the necessity is claimed is constitutive, and the argument reaches it through the global-capacity lift together with the Structural Requirement and the role-to-type premises, not through anything about conventions. The mismatch is the whole reply, and it does not require showing that conventions are unreal or that practice does no work. A convention is a practice, a practice has structural conditions, and those conditions are the ones at issue; so the account that would explain the modality away is already running on it. What the practice-side point secures on its own is act-side: that conventions are made under the conditions, not that every world instantiates the loaded types.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10) and the Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*Convergence.* The conventionalist tradition has refined itself since 1989, from Sidelle’s classical analyticity-extension (unstable on its own articulation, since stipulations have structural conditions it can’t recover) through Cameron’s grounding-asymmetry (consistent with the structural account at the level of conditions on practice) to Thomasson’s normativism (consistent at the level of conditions on norms). Each form locates the source of □(T∧S∧Φ) in a derivative register, which is the mismatch *The Register Does Not Match* records.

Sidelle’s 1989 book was written when the analyticity treatment of modality looked, after Quine’s “Two Dogmas,” like a project that had not survived the mid-century. The intervening decades have been a long argument that selected analyticities can be defended even if Quine’s general critique stands. The argument has succeeded in part: there are conventional necessities, and the analyticity of selected modal claims is a stable position. What the long argument hasn’t produced is a global conventionalism that survives examination of its own articulation. The conditions for the convention aren’t conventional. The structural roles are what any convention presupposes.

The cluster-level form of that last point is the Self-Application Fork (§7.1), and it reaches conventionalism at the level of content rather than of assertion. Ask what modal status “all necessity is conventional” itself carries. Contingent, and the thesis may still be true of the actual world; what it then owes is a meta-level account of why a configuration at which it fails doesn’t unmake it as an account of what necessity is. Necessary, and the object-language/meta-theory distinction must be drawn before treating that necessity as an exception that unmakes the thesis: either the necessity is itself conventional (the convention that establishes conventionalism, question-begging at the one point it can’t afford to be) or it isn’t, and a non-conventional necessity has been admitted by the thesis that denies there are any. The global thesis therefore carries a burden it hasn’t discharged; the restricted claim about selected conventional necessities is left standing.

### 7.1.5 Modal Expressivism
Expressivism doesn’t deny what the argument concludes. It denies that concluding it was ever a case of describing anything. The pressure is therefore not a premise-level contradiction: agreement with every modal sentence can remain agreement in attitude rather than agreement about a modal fact.

Modal expressivism, defended by Blackburn (1986; 1993) and developed by Brandom (2008) and Thomasson (2020), denies that modal sentences express propositions about modal facts. Saying *necessarily, water is H₂O* is, on this view, expressing a stance (a commitment to a certain inferential pattern, a certain way of treating the claim) rather than describing a feature of reality. Modal vocabulary is a tool for organizing thought, not a window onto modal reality. The position parallels expressivism in ethics (Gibbard 1990; Gibbard 2003) and in mathematics, and it aims to deflate modal ontology without giving up modal practice. We can keep saying *necessarily, P* while denying that there are modal facts for *necessarily, P* to be true of.

The argument’s reply turns on what expressing a stance requires. Stances are states. They have content. They are distinguishable from other stances. They are sustained by a thinker who persists from the formation of the stance to its expression. The expressivist’s framework operates on the structural conditions the argument identifies, and the operation isn’t a marginal feature of expressivism: it is the mechanism by which expressivism replaces descriptive ontology.

The Frege–Geach problem (Geach’s (1965) sharpening of a worry traceable to Frege: how can sentences that merely express stances figure as components in logically valid inferences when embedded in conditionals and other complex contexts?) deserves full engagement. Modal claims figure in valid inferences (*modus ponens*, from *if P then Q* and *P*, conclude *Q*, and conditional reasoning more broadly) that look like inferences over propositions, not over stances. Schroeder (2008) gives the expressivist response its logical machinery, building stances out of “being for” attitudes (mental commitments toward propositional contents, treated as a basic stance-type with logical structure) whose logical relations are engineered to mirror propositional logic. Gibbard’s quasi-realism (1990; 2003) takes a parallel line: the expressivist earns the right to talk as if modal sentences had truth-conditions by showing that stance-talk supports the same inferential structure realist talk supports.

These responses recover the inferential behavior the Frege–Geach problem demands. Their actual deployment requires structured agents and inferential practices, but this act-side requirement doesn’t by itself establish that modal vocabulary describes mind-independent modal structure. Stance-composition requires that one stance be distinguishable from another, that combinations of stances yield further stances with determinate inferential properties, and that a thinker can navigate the network of stance-relations over time. Schroeder’s “being for” attitudes are states with content, sustained by a subject and distinguishable from other states. The structural conditions belong to the practice through which expressivism operates; that isn’t yet a claim about an abstract inferential relation considered apart from its use.

Two variants of the family require engagement on their own terms, since neither rests its case on the stance-bearing the preceding reply targets. Brandom (2008) constitutes modal content not by a speaker’s stance but by inferential role: the material inferences a claim licenses within a discursive practice, which modal vocabulary makes explicit. The Brandomian can grant everything said above about stances and still hold that content is fixed by inference, not by any condition on stance-formation. Actual inferring and deontic scorekeeping involve ordered acts, differentiated commitments, and continuing practitioners. That establishes the structural conditions of the discursive practice at act-side resolution. Inferential relations considered abstractly need not themselves be temporal processes or physical bearers, and the expressivist can still deny that modal sentences represent independent modal facts.

Thomasson, in *Norms and Necessity* (2020), locates modal claims differently again: neither stances nor descriptions but object-language expressions of the semantic rules constitutive of our concepts. An abstract semantic rule need not itself be a temporal process or a physical bearer. What does instantiate the three roles is the rule’s institution and application: cases are distinguished as correct or incorrect, applications are ordered, and competent users and practices persist across them. The claim is therefore about the concrete rule-governed practice, not an automatic transfer of its conditions into the abstract normative relation.

A second front opens at the level of scope. Expressivism can be localized to a particular fragment of vocabulary: *this* part of language is expressive, *that* part is descriptive. The local form requires a fact about which sentences fall on which side, and the local expressivist can admit such facts at the metalinguistic level while denying them at the object level. Globalizing expressivism—the thesis that all assertion is stance-expression—generates a different problem. The claim *modal sentences express stances rather than facts* is itself either a fact about modal sentences, in which case the global thesis has admitted descriptive content, or a stance about modal sentences, in which case it lacks the descriptive force needed to classify modal discourse. Dreier (2004) names the “creeping minimalism” worry from the realist side: as expressivism succeeds in recovering the surface features of realist talk, it becomes harder to tell what the disagreement was about. This is the Self-Application Fork (§7.1) in expressivist currency: the global thesis carries the burden, while the local thesis remains available.

The present argument’s intervention is orthogonal to that debate. It doesn’t press the realist demand that modal sentences correspond to modal facts. It presses the prior point that any assertion (descriptive, expressive, or quasi-real) operates on the three Conditions. Local expressivism faces this point at its metalinguistic level, where the demarcation between expressive and descriptive vocabulary is drawn. Global expressivism faces it at every level, since the structural conditions are exhibited by stance-formation as decisively as by description.

*The one modal claim the position must also handle.* The replies so far are act-side, and their limit was stated with them. One further point isn’t act-side, though it stops short of refutation. Expressivism requires that expressing be possible, and *expression is possible* is itself a modal claim. On the account fixed at §1.2.1, for something to be really possible just is for Reality to have the capacity to admit it, so read that way the claim reports Reality’s admissible range rather than anything about a speaker, and the stance-relocation has nothing to relocate.

The expressivist needn’t read it that way, and saying so is the honest statement of where the two accounts part. What isn’t in dispute is the occurrence: stance-taking happens, and that is a non-modal fact the expressivist asserts as readily as anyone. The dispute is over the step from the occurrence to the possibility. Treating *what is actual is possible* as a report of Reality’s capacity is the semantics fixed at §1.2.5; an expressivist may instead treat it as licensing an inferential pattern, on which *expression is possible* voices a commitment rather than describing a range. Pressing the realist reading at this point would assume what the position denies, which is not how it is pressed here.

What the case establishes is a burden, and it has the shape of the Self-Application Fork. The expressivist treatment now has to be given for a claim whose warrant is not an attitude anyone takes but something that simply happened: whatever *expression is possible* expresses, what makes it warranted is the occurrence of the expressing, so the account owes conditions of correctness that answer to an occurrence rather than to a practice. Exempting the claim instead concedes that one modal fact isn’t constituted by expression, which yields a local semantic proposal rather than an account of what modality is. Both branches are live, and neither is free.

**[Proposition]**

**Off Description Is Not Off the Conditions** · *Proposition*

Every concrete vehicle through which expressivism operates—stance-taking, actual inference, rule-institution, and rule-application—instantiates T, S, and Φ. Abstract inferential or normative relations need not inherit those loaded conditions merely from being used. Relocating modal content from description to expression therefore does not relocate the practice of modal talk off the structural conditions. The result is act-side: it does not show that modal vocabulary describes mind-independent modal structure. It shows that no reinterpretation of modal talk escapes the conditions under which the reinterpretation is proposed and applied.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*Taking stock.* Each vehicle expressivism works through—stance-taking, inferring, instituting and applying a rule—instantiates the three Conditions, and the local and global forms both meet the point, the one at its metalinguistic level and the other everywhere. The result is act-side. It does show that reinterpretation of modal semantics isn’t by itself an escape route, because the argument never ran through the semantics.

### 7.1.6 Metaontological Deflationism
A family of contemporary metaontological positions argues that disputes in fundamental ontology are verbal rather than substantive. Different ontological vocabularies are different languages, equally adequate to the world; the choice between them is pragmatic, not factual.

The lineage runs from Rudolf Carnap’s “Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology” (1950) through Eli Hirsch’s quantifier variance (*Quantifier Variance and Realism* 2011, collecting work from 2002 onward) to Amie Thomasson’s easy ontology (*Ontology Made Easy* 2015). Carnap distinguishes internal questions answerable within a linguistic framework from external questions of pragmatic framework-choice; Hirsch’s variance is the view that different ontological frameworks have different quantifier-meanings, each equally adequate to reality. David Chalmers’s “Ontological Anti-Realism” (in *Metametaphysics: New Essays on the Foundations of Ontology*, ed. Chalmers, Manley and Wasserman 2009) develops a more refined version on which there is no fact of the matter about absolute existence, while internal-to-framework existence is unproblematic. Matti Eklund’s “The Picture of Reality as an Amorphous Lump” (in Sider, Hawthorne and Zimmerman’s *Contemporary Debates in Metaphysics* 2008) defends a related but distinct position on which different carving-schemes are equivalent descriptions of a structurally underdetermined reality. On this picture, asking whether the three Conditions are necessary is asking the wrong kind of question; there is no language-independent fact of the matter for an answer to track.

The deflationist’s neutrality isn’t neutral. Different ontological vocabularies are put forward as vocabularies *of something*: different ways of carving up a shared reality. If there were no common reality, there would be nothing for distinct vocabularies to be alternative descriptions of. A deflationist may decline that picture and hold that rival schemes stand in no relation to a common something, and the price of declining it is the verbal-dispute diagnosis itself, which needs the parties to be talking about one subject matter before their disagreement can be called a difference in how they talk about it. (“Configuration” throughout this reply names whatever jointly instantiates the three structural roles as derived at §2.6; it is shorthand for that joint-instantiation condition rather than an additional ontological category.) Three forms of the deflationary move sharpen what each version commits to.

*First.* The Carnapian framework form treats ontological questions as internal to a chosen linguistic framework. “Are there numbers?” is well-formed inside the framework of arithmetic and answerable trivially in the affirmative; outside the framework it is a pragmatic question about whether to adopt the framework. Hirsch’s quantifier variance generalizes the move: different frameworks have different quantifier-meanings, each equally adequate to reality. There is no privileged sense of “exists” against which framework-choice can be assessed.

The reply is internal to the position’s own apparatus. For two frameworks to be alternative carvings of a shared reality, the shared reality must have whatever properties license distinct alternative carvings: at minimum, sufficient extension to be carved differently (S), persistence across the alternative carvings (Φ), and the temporal ordering of carving-events that lets one framework be adopted, then another, then evaluated comparatively (T). Hirsch concedes that frameworks must be alternatives of something but holds that what they are alternatives of can be specified only within some framework. The concession is enough. If the something has whatever properties are required to be the something the frameworks are alternatives of, those properties are the structural conditions, and they obtain whether or not any framework names them.

This is the thin claim, not the heavyweight one: not that some framework-transcendent carving is metaphysically privileged, but that whatever a framework must quantify over to be a framework at all already instantiates the roles. On Quine’s bound-variable criterion (§2.9.3; with the later formal discussion at §3.5.7.2), the commitment is read off what any framework-comparison must range over; the conditions are framework-independent in the sense that no framework can decline them, not in the sense of a privileged carving lying behind every framework and reachable from none.

Carnap’s “external questions” are pragmatic only on the assumption that there is no fact of the matter outside the framework. The assumption is the position’s central claim, and the assumption is what the present argument contests. It is a contest whose founding form is Quine’s, who rejects any principled internal/external distinction in “On Carnap’s Views on Ontology” (1951) on the strength of the ontological-commitment criterion of “On What There Is” (1948). What the present account adds to that Quinean realism is the specification of the conditions a substrate must satisfy to be the something rival frameworks are alternatives of.

*Second.* Thomasson’s (2015) easy ontology develops the contemporary application-conditions version. Existence questions are answerable trivially given conceptual competence: “Are there tables?” follows from “There are particles arranged tablewise” plus the application conditions of “table”; “Are there numbers?” follows from “There are five apples” plus the application conditions of “number”. The position is deflationary about ontology while remaining committed to the trivial truth of ordinary existence claims. There are no hard ontological questions because the apparent hardness reflects only confusion about application conditions.

The reply tracks Thomasson’s own framework. Application conditions are themselves features that must be specified: a concept’s application conditions persist across applications (Φ), distinguish cases of application from cases of non-application (S), and operate across the temporal succession of applications (T). Thomasson’s account is consistent with the present account at the level where the present account’s claim applies: the application conditions are themselves features of a configured reality, and the conditions of their being application conditions are the structural roles. Thomasson’s deflationism succeeds at deflating ontology in the sense she means; it doesn’t deflate the conditions on which the deflationary apparatus operates. The remaining disagreement is whether the structural conditions are themselves substantive ontological commitments (the present view) or further easy commitments derivable from concept-use (a possible Thomassonian reply). The present argument takes the Triconditional machinery of §2.6 (especially the Mutual Containment Result at §2.6.5) as the case for the first reading: the structural roles mutually require one another and can’t be derived from any prior conceptual base.

*Third.* The Chalmers (2009) and Eklund (2008) positions occupy philosophically refined ground. Chalmers’s ontological anti-realism distinguishes lightweight quantifiers (used in ordinary discourse, indifferent to deep ontological commitment) from heavyweight quantifiers (used in fundamental ontology, subject to framework-relativity). The position holds that heavyweight ontological questions have no determinate answer while lightweight ones have trivial answers. Eklund’s position treats reality as a structurally underdetermined “amorphous lump” that admits of multiple equivalent carvings, with no carving privileged over others. Both positions sharpen the deflationary tradition by making it consistent with the trivial truth of ordinary existence claims.

The reply concedes the lightweight/heavyweight distinction and presses where the heavyweight claim sits. Chalmers’s position requires that there be lightweight-but-real configurations (otherwise lightweight existence claims wouldn’t be trivially true) and that no heavyweight fact about absolute existence obtains. The present account’s claim isn’t a heavyweight claim about a privileged absolute carving; it is a claim about what any configuration capable of being something (at any weight) must instantiate. If Chalmers’s lightweight configurations include extension, persistence, and temporal succession, then the structural conditions obtain at the lightweight level Chalmers grants. Eklund’s amorphous lump faces the same pressure. Read as *underdetermined by privileged carvings* rather than structureless, the lump admits multiple equivalent carving-schemes without privileging one. That reading doesn’t escape structure. Framework-comparison requires different carvings to be distinguishable from one another and from the lump they carve; applying a scheme requires something that persists as its target; adopting, evaluating, and replacing schemes requires ordered acts. Those are conditions on the comparison and application of carvings. The further claim that the lump itself instantiates the full loaded types depends on the book’s object-side arguments, not on the act of carving alone. The ∅ fork therefore reaches a lump stipulated to contain no differentiable content at all; it doesn’t by itself turn every framework-invariant constraint into mind-independent ontology.

The position can be sharpened across all three forms into the claim that every ontological commitment is internal to a framework. The sharpening is unstable. The claim itself is either internal to a framework (in which case it is one ontological commitment among others, not the metalevel verdict it presents itself as) or external, in which case it asserts a framework-independent fact about the relation between frameworks and the world, contradicting its own deflationism. There is no third position from which the verdict can be issued without using the apparatus the verdict denies. This is the Self-Application Fork (§7.1) in metaontological currency, arrived at here independently and by the position’s own internal/external distinction rather than imported from the cluster. Thomasson’s reply (2015, ch. 3) (that the metaontological claim is itself trivially true given the application conditions of metaontological vocabulary) relocates the instability rather than dissolving it: the application conditions of metaontological vocabulary are themselves features of a configured reality, and the conditions of their being application conditions are what the present argument names.

*The retreat to the framework.* One reply remains. Grant everything so far: that no framework can decline the three roles, that every carving and every comparison of carvings already deploys succession, distinction, and exchange. The deflationist can still say this fixes only a fact about frameworks (about what any scheme must presuppose to be a scheme) and not a fact about Reality. That the roles are presupposed by all our descriptions is one thing; that they are Reality’s own structure, owing nothing to the describing, is another, and the transcendental result delivers only the first. The line is Stroud’s: that we can’t think past a structure shows how we must think, not how things stand.

The retreat has no ground to stand on, and the reason is internal to the position once more. The deflationary apparatus rests on a single criterion of what it is for something to be objective rather than framework-relative: to be objective is to be invariant under the choice of framework, and to be merely framework-relative is to vary with it.

Quantifier variance is the thesis that what exists varies with the quantifier-meaning a framework supplies; the lightweight/heavyweight distinction is the distinction between what holds inside a chosen scheme and what would hold across all of them; the verdict that no carving is privileged just is the claim that every candidate joint varies across admissible frameworks. Strip the position of the invariance-criterion and it cannot state its own thesis: “privileged” means framework-transcendent, and framework-transcendence is measured as invariance. The criterion isn’t optional equipment; it is what gives the deflationary verdict its content.

Apply it. The three roles don’t vary across frameworks; they are what every framework presupposes, the fixed point under the operation *adopt a different scheme*. Framework-invariance supplies evidence that the roles aren’t artifacts of any one scheme. It doesn’t, without a further bridge, entail that they are mind-independent features of Reality; a deflationist may treat them as constraints on every admissible framework. The dispute therefore narrows to whether invariance is merely transcendental or genuinely ontological. The present account argues for the latter, but it shouldn’t present that bridge as forced by deflationism alone. The transcendental fact, read through the criterion the deflationist must hold to speak at all, counts as objective by the deflationist’s own measure, which is a weaker result than mind-independence and is the one claimed.

**[Proposition]**

**The Invariance Turn** · *Proposition*

Deflationism measures objectivity by invariance across admissible frameworks, and cannot state its thesis without that criterion. The structural roles do not vary across frameworks, and no ascent escapes them, since ranging over frameworks is itself carving. By the deflationist’s own measure they fall on the objective side. That earns their status as more than a framework artifact, not the further step from transcendental to ontological.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

This is the heavyweight claim in the only sense the opening allows it. *Reality* is fixed at §1.1 as a structural-role term (what any content presupposes, its reference set by what the role requires and not by which thing fills it). The constitutive language there names the structural shape of the primitive modal field, not an essence prior to it. The present conclusion claims exactly that and no more: the roles belong to Reality in that they are invariant across every scheme in which anything is configured at all, not in the sense of an essence lying behind all configuration and reachable from none.

The deflationist who demands the second sense before conceding the first asks for a target the account declines to posit (§1.1). The demand purchases nothing: a structure that does no work in any framework and is reachable from none is, by the ∅ fork, indistinguishable from the absence of structure (§2.7). What Reality Precludes (§1.1.1) leaves conditional is supported here but not discharged by invariance alone: what is invariant across languages is internal to no single language, yet may still be characterized by a deflationist as a universal condition on representation rather than as mind-independent ontology.

One regress is owed an answer. The deflationist can lift the retreat a level: the claim that the roles are invariant across all frameworks is itself advanced within a framework (a meta-framework that individuates schemes and ranges over them) so what is shown is invariance within that meta-framework, not invariance as such. But the trilemma is indifferent to level. The meta-claim that one has shown only invariance-within-M is itself either internal to some further scheme, in which case it varies across schemes and is, by the criterion, non-objective, and so can’t deliver the objective verdict it pronounces; or it is external, a framework-transcendent fact about the relation between meta-frameworks and the roles, which is the thing the position forbids itself.

Nor does the regress escape the roles by climbing: any meta-framework that individuates frameworks and ranges over them is itself carving. It requires distinction to hold its frameworks apart, exchange to compare them, succession to adopt one and then another. Each ascent instantiates the roles it is meant to rise above. The invariance is therefore not invariance at a level but invariance the hierarchy can’t exit, and the regress doesn’t undercut the result so much as exhibit it again at every rung.

A kindred move worth marking. Modal conventionalism (§7.1.4) runs a parallel deflationary argument at the level of modal claims rather than existence claims; the structural reply takes the same form. Modal fictionalism (§7.2.6) deflates modal commitment by relocating it to a fiction; again the structural conditions return at the level of the storytelling. The deflationary family across these three sections shares a common structure and a common vulnerability: each version succeeds at deflating its target only by leaving the conditions on its deflationary apparatus implicit, and each, on examination, presupposes the structural roles at the level its deflation operates.

*Convergence.* Three forms of metaontological deflationism (Carnapian framework-relativity, Thomassonian easy ontology, Chalmers–Eklund refined deflationism), and each, fully developed, is consistent with the present account at the level its claim applies: the Carnapian form requires a substrate frameworks are alternatives of, Thomasson’s form requires application conditions, and the Chalmers–Eklund form requires lightweight-but-real configurations or a structurally non-trivial lump. Each of these already has the structural conditions, and each denies □(T∧S∧Φ) any framework-transcendent standing. What answers all three is one fixed point: the roles are what a framework must range over to be one, so they don’t vary when the framework does.

The deflationist who presses anyway operates within the structural conditions while declaring them undecidable. The declaration is a configuration within Reality, and so is the framework that hosts it. Both fall within the scope of the argument they contest.

### 7.1.7 Wittgensteinian Quietism
Wittgensteinian quietism comes in distinct varieties that share a common stance: philosophical theses, including metaphysical theses about the structural ground of reality, aren’t properly to be argued for or against but to be diagnosed. The varieties differ in what diagnosis amounts to.

The Tractarian Wittgenstein (1921) 1961, and the resolute reading developed by Diamond (1991) and Conant (2002) on which the *Tractatus*‘s philosophical sentences are themselves nonsense to be climbed and discarded, holds that metaphysical sentences fail to express propositions. They aren’t false; they lack truth-conditions. The proper response is silence: to climb the ladder of philosophical analysis and then throw it away.

The later, *Investigations*-derived varieties operate differently. Hacker (with Baker, 1980; 1985; Hacker, 2001) defends the orthodox Wittgensteinian view that metaphysical claims are grammatical confusions: when we ask whether time is real, we have misread the grammar of *real* and projected an answerable question where none lives. McDowell develops a therapeutic quietism in epistemology and philosophy of mind (1994): philosophy’s task isn’t to construct theories but to dissolve the appearance of problems by clarifying the conceptual framework that generated them. Cavell goes further (1979): skepticism can’t be refuted by argument but only acknowledged, and the criteria for our concepts come from forms of life rather than from any standpoint outside them. On all three readings, a sustained metaphysical argument like the present one isn’t engaging a question the quietist takes to be live; it is exhibiting a confusion the quietist takes its task to clarify.

The challenge shifts the target from truth to assertibility. The quietist doesn’t argue that the present argument is wrong. The quietist argues that it isn’t the kind of thing that can be wrong, because it isn’t the kind of thing that can be right.

*First.* The Tractarian framework distinguishes saying from showing: certain features of the world can’t be stated within language but can be exhibited by what language does. Time, Space, and Substance, on the present argument, are precisely such features. Every act of language exhibits them, ‘exhibits’ here in the sense fixed by the ∅-fork at §2.7: any act that isn’t ∅ instantiates the structural conditions, their joint instantiation being what counts as there being an act at all. The argument isn’t the proposition *the three Conditions are necessary*; the argument is the structural exhibition of what utterance, distinction, and persistence require. A Tractarian who grants showing has granted that structure is exhibited rather than stated, which is the register the argument is working in. What showing alone hands over is the role and not the loaded type, and nothing about necessity across worlds: logical form exhibited in use is not yet Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality as the book fixes them, and the upgrade belongs to the arguments that earn it. The resolute reader, who discards showing along with the rest of the ladder, is met not here but by the performative point that follows, since the climbing and discarding are themselves enacted.

*Second.* The Hacker–Baker line says metaphysical questions are misuses of language; McDowell says they are appearances generated by a conceptual framework whose clarification dissolves them. Both readings require a coherent distinction between misuse and use, or between confused appearance and clarified perception. Drawing the distinction is itself an activity. It occurs over time, differentiates one form of words from another, and persists through the diagnostician. The diagnostic activity exhibits the three Conditions no less than any first-order metaphysical claim does. The therapy doesn’t undo what makes the therapy possible.

*Third.* Cavell holds that philosophical claims rest on criteria that come from forms of life, and that a form of life isn’t a thesis but a way of being-in-language. The present argument doesn’t contest this. It identifies what any form of life (any way of using criteria, any practice of acknowledgment) requires. The structural conditions aren’t criteria offered from a standpoint outside the form of life. They are what occupying any form of life involves. Cavell’s acknowledgment of skepticism is itself a sustained activity; the activity has the structure the argument identifies; the acknowledgment doesn’t float free of what makes acknowledgment possible.

*The grammatical reading, owned.* The quietist presses one step further: if the only thing that would count against ‘every act exhibits T, S, and Φ’ is ∅ (the absence of any act at all) then the claim has no contrastive use among actual cases, and a claim with no contrastive use is grammatical rather than substantive. The response isn’t to resist this but to accept it, on one condition. The claim is indeed constitutive: it doesn’t report a feature some acts have and others lack; it states what *counts* as there being an act at all. The therapeutic charge is narrower than the concession, and answering it means saying what work the grammar does rather than insisting that it does some. The charge is that a claim drawing no contrast among cases is idle: nothing turns on it, so the appearance of a discovery is an artifact of the grammar. What turns on this one is stated at §2.7, where the boundary it marks does inferential work: it is what rules out ∅ as an alternative, and a claim that rules something out isn’t idle, even when what it rules out is the only thing it could. The boundary falls not between cases but between there being cases and there being nothing at all.

A quietist can hold the line one step further back and say that marking such a boundary is grammar functioning well rather than metaphysics succeeding, and at that point the disagreement is over what would count as a discovery rather than over what the claim says. That is a real disagreement and it is left standing here. The claim earns a constitutive register precisely because its proposed countercase is absolute structural absence rather than another ordinary act. Still, the exhibition of the roles in actual speech or diagnosis establishes an act-side result. The cross-world □(T∧S∧Φ) conclusion depends on the modal and role-to-type arguments developed elsewhere; quietist performance alone doesn’t supply it.

**[Dissolution]**

**Constitutive, Not Confused** · *Dissolution*

Either the sole countercase, ∅, is a case that fails to obtain, in which case a claim drawing no contrast against it is confused; or it is the absence of any case, in which case the boundary falls between there being cases and there being none, and drawing no contrast there isn’t confusion but the register the claim was always operating in. ∅ is the second, not the first: the diagnostic meant to dissolve the claim instead locates it. Act-side, this fixes register rather than cross-world scope.

**Dissolves:** the confusion-charge

That ∅ is the absence of any case, rather than a case that fails to obtain, is established at §2.7. Quietism is also the one position in this cluster the Self-Application Fork (§7.1) doesn’t reach, and the exemption is principled rather than an oversight. The fork asks a global thesis about modality to account for its own modal status; the quietist advances no thesis to be asked. That is why the engagement here runs through performance and register instead, and why the reply is correspondingly narrower.

*Convergence.* The dialectical point extends across all the varieties considered here. Where refusing to articulate an objection is itself a performed act of declination, it involves persistence, distinction, and an ordered episode. Mere absence of speech, however, isn’t automatically such an act and doesn’t by itself instantiate the full triad. The performative point applies to enacted quietism, not to silence considered simply as no tokened response. Enacted quietism exhibits the structure while declining to state it.

## 7.2 The Grounds of Modality
This cluster questions the modal machinery the argument rides on: necessity, possibility, and possible worlds. If the semantics of possibility differed, the canonical lift might not follow.

The reply begins with a distinction. The argument’s operator ◇ means *real possibility*: the standing capacity of the one Reality, R: ◇P just when Capacity(R,P) (§1.2.1, 2.1). A theory may instead model local reachability, epistemic openness, or world-relative accessibility. Those are legitimate relative modalities, but variation in them doesn’t by itself vary what R can admit.

The source of possibility (§7.2.1) asks what makes the modal facts hold at all. Dispositionalism about modality (§7.2.2) grounds them in the potentialities of actual objects. Modal realism (§7.2.3) makes other worlds concrete. Linguistic ersatzism (§7.2.4) replaces them with maximal consistent descriptions.

Combinatorialism (§7.2.5) builds possible worlds by recombining actual elements. Modal fictionalism (§7.2.6) treats world-talk as useful pretense. Necessitism (§7.2.7) holds that everything exists necessarily and only qualitative contingency remains. Sider’s structuralism (§7.2.8) locates modality in the world’s joints rather than in a plurality of worlds.

The engagements that follow ask whether a rival has offered a different account of real possibility or only a different relation within or alongside what R can admit.

The objections of §9 press whether something is left out here: experience, intrinsic nature, mathematical applicability, mind itself. The objections gathered here press instead on the modal apparatus the argument runs on. If the modal logic is wrong (if necessity, possibility, and counterfactual reasoning don’t behave as the argument assumes) then □(T∧S∧Φ) doesn’t follow even if T, S, and Φ (Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, the three structural Conditions the book’s argument derives, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) are exhaustive.

The literature here is dense, technical, and inconclusive on most of the central questions, and each position is taken up where it is engaged rather than surveyed twice.

The argument’s strategy across the section is to distinguish three questions that modal theories often run together: what R can admit, the semantics used to represent that capacity, and the ontology assigned to worlds or domains. The canonical proof depends on the first, not on Lewisian concreteness, transworld identity, Barcan formulae, or a particular local accessibility relation. Structural roles enter only where a candidate world or ground is offered as a realizer of genuine change. A thin abstract representation need not instantiate temporal succession, spatial extension, or causal persistence; a theory that offers it as physical reality, a ground of experience, or a complete change-realizer inherits the richer burden. The sections that follow therefore test each framework at the resolution it claims.

### 7.2.1 The Source of Possibility
The PSR demand is met at §8.2.1 by showing that Nature isn’t a thing that grounds itself but what grounding consists in. A residual question remains: can an entity **within the modal domain** be explanatorily prior to real possibility, conferring content on what R can admit? The answer runs by disjunctive elimination on the candidate’s own modal status. It is deliberately narrower than the claim that every possible essence-prior or primitive grounding account has been refuted by contradiction.

Two questions are kept apart throughout, because they take different arguments and reach different strengths. The first is whether a candidate’s own modal status could source the field; that runs by elimination and reaches a diagnostic. The second is whether an essence could stand prior to the structure of every determinate way of being; that needs the structural results of Chapter 2, and it is where the essence-prior proposal is actually met.

The position pressed against is the family of grounding accounts that take possibility as a derivative phenomenon: neo-Fregean abstractionism on modal grounds (Hale 2013), Lewisian reduction of modality to concrete possible worlds (Lewis 1986a), Williamsonian necessitism (Williamson 2013), dispositionalist grounding of possibility in the potentialities of actual objects (Vetter 2015), engaged on its own terms at §7.2.2, and the theistic moves that locate modality in a divine intellect or divine nature (Adams 1983; Pruss 2011; Leftow 2012).

That last family, pressed as an argument from modality’s need of a ground to God’s existence, is engaged on its own terms at §10.1.2.

*Definition.* Let *source of possibility* name any X such that ◇p (for some non-empty range of p) holds in virtue of X. The “in virtue of” relation is left maximally general: causal, metaphysical, conceptual, intellectual, or explanatory grounding all qualify. The argument doesn’t turn on which grounding relation is in view.

One distinction narrows the target before the trilemma begins. Necessary Possibility and its diachronic reading, Modal Persistence (§2.1.7), already exclude the *production* of modal status. If ◇p, then □◇p, so no event first makes p possible and none removes its possibility; if ¬◇p, then □¬◇p, so no event converts p from impossible to possible. Events may actualize p, make it locally reachable, or bring it within an agent’s map without changing its standing in Range(R). An essence-prior theorist can accept all of that and claim instead that p’s invariant standing holds *in virtue of* an essence. The trilemma tests that explanatory claim. It isn’t needed to rule out a temporal or volitional onset of possibility, which the bilateral theorem has already closed.

**[Premise]**

**The Modal Trilemma** · *Premise*

1. If X is a source of possibility, then ◇p holds in virtue of X (Definition).

2.
