Every modally classifiable candidate X has exactly one modal status: ¬◇X (impossible: true in no world), ◇X ∧ ¬□X (contingent: true in at least one world but not in every world), or □X (necessary: true in every world). These cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive within modal classification. A candidate stipulated to stand beyond modality is not classified by this premise and must be tested through its alleged grounding relation instead.

*The impossible case.* ¬◇X. If X is impossible, X has no instances and no relata. Nothing is the case in virtue of what isn’t the case. The impossible isn’t a source but the absence of one.

*The contingent case.* ◇X ∧ ¬□X. If X is possible without being necessary, ◇X is itself a fact within the modal field. A contingent X can coherently ground a restricted range of possibilities while presupposing the wider field. What it can’t do is ground the field as a whole: a source of some possibilities isn’t yet a source of possibility *as such*. The field isn’t grounded by one of its own features.

*The necessary case.* □X. Necessity doesn’t by itself bar X from explanatory priority: grounding priority and modal status are distinct, an item may be necessary without being explanatorily inert, essence need not reduce to modal fact (Fine 1994), and a necessitist may hold X necessary yet grounding (Williamson 2013). Once that orthogonality is granted, modal classification alone doesn’t close the case. Describing X as necessary uses □, but it doesn’t follow from that description alone that X’s nature or grounding activity is ontologically posterior to the modal field; a Finean essentialist may hold that □X is true because of X’s essence. What the classification shows is narrower: the modal description □X can’t itself explain the content of ◇ without circularity. The additional theory needed to test essence-priority is supplied later by Conditioned-Nature, Reality–Nature Identity, and No Non-Configurational Remainder. The point here isn’t that necessity precludes explanatory priority, but that priority *to ◇* is unavailable to anything whose own status is already modal.

**[Proposition]**

**Modal Exclusivity** · *Proposition*

No candidate’s modal status by itself explains the modal domain: impossible and contingent candidates fail as global sources, while a necessary candidate requires an additional, non-modal account of how its essence or grounding activity confers modal content. The trilemma exposes a circularity burden; it does not by itself refute every essence-prior source. The structural and identity results applied below supply the further argument.

**Depends on:** the Modal Trilemma, scoped

*The self-grounding rejoinder.* A defender may concede the trilemma and posit that possibility grounds itself, that ◇ is its own ground. Two readings exhaust the move. On the deflationary reading, “self-grounding” is a notational variant of primitivism: ◇ isn’t derived from anything more basic, and Modal Exclusivity stands. On the substantive reading, grounding is a reflexive relation on ◇, and the field grounds itself. Here the analytic literature on ground divides the relation in two (Fine 2012). *Strict* ground is irreflexive: nothing strictly grounds itself (Schaffer 2009; Fine 2012). So if the rejoinder means that ◇ strictly grounds ◇, irreflexivity rules it out directly. *Weak* ground is reflexive by construction (every fact weakly grounds itself) so ◇ does weakly ground ◇; but weak self-grounding is just the absence of any strict ground, which is primitivism stated in the grounding idiom rather than an alternative to it. Either way ◇ has no strict source. This is also what accommodates the minority dissent that admits reflexive or non-well-founded grounding (Jenkins 2011): that dissent is a thesis about weak ground and the failure of well-foundedness, not a denial of strict-ground irreflexivity, so it is absorbed by the fork rather than set aside as a bare commitment. The substantive reading doesn’t escape the trilemma; it renames its floor.

*The classical-theism rejoinder.* Aquinas-style classical theism doesn’t propose God as a source of possibility distinct from God; on divine simplicity, God *is* the modal field (*ipsum esse subsistens* applied to modality). The move sidesteps the trilemma by collapsing the source/sourced distinction. The collapse delivers one of two results. On the relabeling reading, *God* renames “the primitive modal field,” in which case Modal Exclusivity stands and the relabeling is theological vocabulary rather than a modal-foundations counterexample. On the predicate-bearing reading, the modal field carries predicates classical theism attributes to God (will, intellect, agency), which is the engagement taken up at §10.2 and §10.1, not a counterexample to the present result.

Nor does the presupposition improve on iteration. Let the defender universalize: every possibility is sourced. Then the sourcing (itself a modal fact) is a further possibility, and by the defender’s own thesis it requires a source; so, in turn, does the possibility of that. The chain forks. Either some link goes un-sourced, which concedes Modal Exclusivity outright, or none does, and the sourcing relation never steps outside the field it was meant to ground. The regress is vicious not because it fails to terminate but because no stage of it is ever prior to ◇; the explanatory debt the account incurred is never discharged. Its one exit, a loop in which ◇ grounds its own possibility, is the self-grounding rejoinder already met. What stands is a dilemma whose floor is the one-step presupposition: primitivism, or a regress that never leaves the field.

*Taking stock of the diagnostic.* No candidate whose own status is stated in modal terms can be a thing-style source of the modal capacity its own status already presupposes, if what is at issue is a source of the field as a whole. What the diagnostic doesn’t reach is the proposal whose explanatory direction was never a modal classification in the first place. That is the second question, and it needs the structural results rather than the trilemma.

*The transcendence rejoinder.* A defender may place X beyond modality altogether: neither possible, necessary, nor impossible. Repeating the trilemma doesn’t answer that proposal, because the trilemma classifies candidates whose modal status is already in view.

The relevant pressure comes instead from the Grounding Conditional at §3.1.5. Any grounding relation Grounds(x,y), at any level of an ontological stack, requires asymmetric priority, real differentiation of x from y, and a real fact or realizer in which the relation obtains. Those are the three Conditions at role-resolution, reached by what a grounding relation is rather than by assigning X a place in the trilemma. If X explains R’s capacity by grounding R, X is already role-level structured once that relation is granted, on the same footing as the demon, simulation substrate, and other candidate grounds considered at §2.2.2.

A classical theist or Finean essentialist may regard the grounding relation as primitive or essence-prior. The Grounding Conditional doesn’t refute that explanatory direction by itself. What is already unavailable is treating the ground as innocent of structure until a later argument imposes it: proposing the grounding relation already proposes a role-level structured ground. What the combination with Reality–Nature Identity and Essence-Description adds below is that neither the relation nor an essence bearing it supplies an independently constituted remainder outside or inside Nature.

Role-resolution must not be confused with concrete realization. Thin ordering, differentiation, and bearing in an abstract or atemporal relation need not be metric space, temporal succession, or material composition at that same resolution. They nevertheless remain articulations of the three Conditions within the one Nature; nothing is exempt from the Conditions merely because it realizes them abstractly. The theological version is engaged at §10.1.2, where concrete intellectual or causal operation incurs the loaded Conditions at the operation while an atemporal relation remains an internal structural articulation rather than an exterior source.

*The real-definition rejoinder.* The essentialist need not place the ground beyond modality at all. The claim may be simply that essence is real definition—what it is to be the thing—and that real definitions are prior to and explanatory of modal facts, so that □X holds in virtue of what X is (Fine 1994). Grant the notion at full strength, including the gap that motivates it: Socrates belongs necessarily to his singleton without that belonging being any part of what Socrates is, so essence is finer-grained than necessity and isn’t reducible to it. The question here is narrower than whether essences exist. It is whether a real definition, once given, has explained what makes the defined kind possible. Let the essence of *human* be *rational animal*. Then *rational animal* must be possible, and what makes it so isn’t stated by saying what the kind is. A real definition fixes the content of a possibility; it doesn’t supply the possibility whose content it fixes.

That demand doesn’t turn qualitative distinctness into metric extension. The determinacy of an essence—that *human* isn’t *horse*—is qualitative distinctness, and qualitative distinctness alone is expressly insufficient for concrete Spatiality at §2.4.7, which requires relational extension rather than mere non-identity. An objectual essence may therefore be abstract in its mode of articulation, as may the structures examined at §9.9 and §9.10. Abstractness doesn’t place it beyond Nature: by Reality–Nature Identity, it is an abstraction of structural articulation rather than a second realm or an extra ingredient within the first. The essentialist may still hold that modal truths terminate explanatorily in what a thing is. What is closed is the further picture of that essence as an independent source behind the configuration it specifies.

The same closure bears on the question §2.6.1 defers to this section: whether the realizer biconditionals, □(T↔(S∧Φ)) and □(Φ↔(T∧S)), state a structural-functional necessity or a Finean real definition under another name. The Closed Seam (§3.5.3) doesn’t defer here and shouldn’t be read as doing so: it closes the role-to-type seam upstream at the Structural Requirement (§2.4), and notes besides that the Movement Line (§2.4.9) reaches the theorem without passing through that joint at all. What follows therefore bears on §3.5.3’s *type-upgrades* without being owed to them. The two readings must be prised apart from what depends on them. The *type-upgrades* of §3.5.3 need only that the biconditionals are necessary, and they are necessary on either reading—a real definition is necessary if anything is—so □(T↔(S∧Φ)) transmits its necessity to the spatial and persistence types under modus ponens whichever reading is correct. The type-layer therefore closes even for a reader who keeps the Finean essence-prior gloss; nothing in the structural conclusion is hostage to the outcome.

A committed essentialist can keep the Finean gloss; if so, the disagreement is over the gloss on a necessity both sides grant, not over the necessity the biconditionals transmit. The structural-functional reading is the one this account adopts and the one the modal monism of Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7) requires: the biconditionals record what any medium hosting succession must be, the structural feature reality *is* rather than an essence some entity *has*.

What the structural-functional reading underwrites is the *further* claim the modal-monist commitment (§2.9.7) makes: that this necessity isn’t seated in the essence of an item standing prior to the modal field. The modal trilemma alone doesn’t secure that claim. The Finean is entitled to hold that essence explains modal truths rather than being explained by them, and assigning an essence-bearing candidate a modal status doesn’t by itself reverse that explanatory direction. The further result comes from combining the trilemma with what is already established about the field in which any real candidate belongs (Chapter 2). The Reality–Nature Identity closes both alleged locations for an independent essence: nothing real occupies a second modal domain outside Nature, and no content within Nature supplies an independently constituted addition to it. The question is therefore not whether essence may be prior to modal truths—it may—but whether an essence can be prior to the structure of every determinate way of being. That stronger claim is what the rest of this section closes.

*What an essence is, on the account already given.* Before the contact question comes a prior one: what is posited when an essence is placed prior to modality? Two readings must be separated, because the book endorses one of them and the posit needs the other. Fine’s priority claim is that necessities about a thing follow from its essence rather than grounding it. It is accepted here for the case of the three Conditions (§2.4.9). What that acceptance rests on is an account of essence with nothing hidden in it: the definitions are constitutive specifications of what the phenomena *are*, and there is no deeper essence standing behind them. An essence, so understood, is the configuration something must have for a description to apply to it. The essence of a circle is its spatial configuration; the word *circle* is a shared representation laid over that configuration so it can be communicated about, and nothing is left over once the configuration is given. Being human is likewise not a hidden ingredient behind a human; it is the configuration without which nothing is described as one.

What the argument takes from Fine, on that reading, is a claim about the direction of derivation: necessities about a thing follow from what it is rather than from a modal axiom stipulated to produce them. Priority in that sense isn’t priority over structure. The specification comes first, and the modal facts read off it.

The distinction that matters is therefore not between essence and modality but between essence prior to *modality* and essence prior to *structure*. The first is available and is used. The second is what a transcendent ground requires, and it is unavailable on the account of essence just described: an essence that specifies no configuration hasn’t been specified at all. Strip the configuration and there is no description left to apply; a name with no configuration answering to it hasn’t picked anything out. That isn’t a further burden added to the contact burden. It is the same burden appearing earlier, at the point where the candidate is stated rather than at the point where it is asked to do work.

*What the essence-prior intuition is tracking.* The real-definition rejoinder concedes the field to the essentialist further than it needs to, because it never asks what the essence is an essence *of*. Take the case where the essentialist’s picture is least comfortable: not *human*, whose kind has always had instances, but an artifact. Was there an essence of *computer* before any computer existed?

Three answers are available and each concedes what the structural account needs. The first says yes: the essence was timelessly there and merely uninstantiated, and what arrived in the 1940s was our knowledge of it together with the first thing satisfying it. That answer is available only on the real/nominal picture that Essence-Description collapses (§2.6.12): there is no essence standing behind the conditional profile for our descriptions to approximate. It is also a heavier commitment than the natural-kind case disguises, since it populates the structure, before Earth and before any describer, with a determinate essence of *computer* awaiting satisfaction. The second says no: the essence of an artifact kind comes into being with its instances, or with the practices and intentions of makers. Then whatever was permanently available before the 1940s wasn’t an essence, and what it was still needs saying. The third makes the essence conditional: not an item awaiting satisfaction but a real definition of the form *whatever is a computer is thus and so*. A conditional real definition is a profile, and a profile is a configuration.

The structural account doesn’t need to pay for the first, and it doesn’t need the second’s deflationary corollary either—that artifact essences are merely posterior and conventional, which would owe a principled account of why natural kinds differ. What was permanently available before any computer existed isn’t an essence but a modal standing: the possibility of that configuration, necessarily (§2.3, §2.6.6). Nothing had to hold the content of *computer* in reserve for computers to become buildable; the structure permits the configuration, and permits it necessarily, which is what the essentialist’s *always there* was reaching for. The intuition is tracking the permanence of a possibility and mislocating it as the permanence of an essence.

Two scope limits keep the reading exact. Necessary possibility is global modal standing, not local availability: that Capacity(R,P) doesn’t entail that it is reachable from every state, which is the Bottleneck’s distinction (§2.1.5), and computers weren’t buildable in the Hadean. And the essence, once there is something to have one, is the conditional profile rather than a residue beneath it. *Computer* names a function, and functions are configurational; the multiplicity of computers isn’t a failure to locate the essence but a sign of what the essence is.

The tradition’s own paradigm invites the same reading. *Animal* carries a bearer that persists (Φ), and *rational* carries inference run across an ordering (T) among distinguished contents (S). That reading isn’t forced on the essentialist by the formula alone; it is the configurational analysis an essence-prior theorist disputes. What the case fixes is where the dispute has to be settled. A remainder that isn’t a configuration has to be specified, and specifying it is exactly what Essence-Description says can’t be done, since any specification offered is a description and every description answers to a configuration. The essence-prior theorist is therefore not merely choosing a terminus for explanation; he owes that specification, and the burden the trilemma records has a specific address at §2.6.12 rather than resting on a general preference about where grounding stops.

**[Proposition]**

**No Non-Configurational Remainder** · *Proposition*

The essence-prior intuition is tracking something real and locating it wrongly. What was permanently available before any computer existed is not an essence held in reserve but a modal standing: the structure permits that configuration, and permits it necessarily. The permanence belongs to the possibility, and the essentialist reads it as the permanence of an essence. Pressed on the artifact case, the position must either populate the structure, before Earth and before any describer, with a determinate essence of *computer* awaiting satisfaction, or let artifact essences arrive with their instances and their makers, or make the essence a conditional profile. The first is available only on the real/nominal picture Essence-Description collapses; the second concedes that what stood permanently available was a possibility rather than an essence; the third is a configuration under another name. The tradition’s own paradigm reads the same way—*animal* carries the bearer that persists (Φ), *rational* carries inference run across an ordering (T) among distinguished contents (S)—and an essentialist who resists that reading owes a specification of the remainder that is not itself a configuration. Finean essence-priority survives as a direction of explanation: modal truths about a thing may follow from what it is. What it does not supply is a non-configurational item standing behind what the thing is.

**Depends on:** Structural Gap (§2.4.2), Essence-Description (§2.6.12), and Modal Identity (§2.6.6)

*The distinctness the ground would need.* An essence-prior ground is offered as something really distinct from what it grounds: not a redescription of N but another item standing to N in an asymmetric grounding relation. That claim cannot be discharged by a numeral alone. Under Structural Individuation, whatever makes the proposed ground concretely distinct is differentiating structure and belongs to the complete structural account; a primitive thisness may be nonqualitative or nonrelational, but if it individuates, it is not nonstructural (§2.4.9).

The resulting fork concerns what makes the two terms genuinely two. If the ground is a real item distinct from N, their two-ness must be constituted. If a relation differentiates them, they belong to the one structural order in which it obtains. If a primitive thisness differentiates them, that thisness is itself part of the structure of Reality–Nature. If nothing differentiates them, there are not two terms for the grounding relation (§11.2.2, §4.9). If the ground isn’t a real item in that sense, its distinctness from N reduces to a difference of names, which supplies no second term either.

The essence-prior theorist may reject Structural Individuation. That is the standing refusal identified at §2.4.9 and defended against at §7.2.3, and the fork above is conditional on it. What the present argument denies is that the ground’s distinctness from N can be made costless by calling it abstract, since abstractness removes the concrete two-ness the grounding relation was supposed to hold between.

*What the contact can’t be.* Suppose the proposed ground reaches concrete actuality, and something is the case that wouldn’t otherwise have been. Then the reaching makes a difference, and the difference-making fork at §3.4 applies to it directly—what makes a difference is *this* rather than *that*, the dependence has a direction, and the difference is borne. Those are the three roles at thin resolution. The relation is therefore an articulation within Nature, not a contact from something exterior to it. If it performs concrete work, the Concrete-Entity Test supplies the loaded Conditions at that operation. If it remains abstract or atemporal, it may relate one resolution of Nature to another, but it doesn’t become a source standing structurally clear of the field it explains.

The type distinction remains important without reopening an exterior. A thin grounding relation isn’t thereby a concrete event, and its direction, difference, and bearing shouldn’t be redescribed as metric location, temporal succession, or material composition at the same resolution. What closes is the claim of structural exemption: at its own resolution the relation and its relata are determinate articulations of the one field. A defender may keep the ground abstract and inert with respect to concrete actuality; that gives up the explanatory role the posit was introduced to fill. Or the defender may assign it concrete effects, in which case the Conditions are incurred at the operation. Neither option supplies an unconditioned essence outside or additional to Nature.

**[Theorem]**

**No Unconditioned Essence** · *Theorem*

Any essence real enough to ground modal truth must have a determinate way to be. That way belongs to Reality’s one modal field, which is Nature; within that field it is the field itself, a determinate content of T, S, and Φ at the resolution appropriate to what it is, or an abstraction of such an articulation. Conditioned-Nature and Essence-Description then leave no independently constituted essence behind the configuration. Essence may be explanatorily prior to modal truths about a thing, but no essence is structurally prior to Nature or additional to it. An alleged essence with no determinate configuration specifies no possible ground.

**Depends on:** Way–Possibility Convertibility (§3.2.5), Conditioned-Nature and Essence-Description (§2.6.12), Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8), and No Non-Configurational Remainder (§7.2.1)

*The impossibility pole.* Let a *source of impossibility* be any X such that ¬◇p holds in virtue of X. The trilemma on X’s own modal status is unchanged. An impossible X has no relata in virtue of which anything could hold. A contingent X is a fact within the field and presupposes the modality it would confer. A necessary X can’t explain impossibility merely by being described with □. If its essence is invoked, No Unconditioned Essence applies: the essence may state the configuration whose contrary has no determinate way, but it isn’t an additional source that confers the exclusion from beyond Nature.

The claim that both poles admit no exterior source comes from the structural-functional thesis that modal content is a feature Reality is, together with the Reality–Nature Identity and No Unconditioned Essence. A voluntarist may still say that a divine intellect represents necessary truths or that modal truths follow from divine essence. What the voluntarist can’t retain is a divine item additional to Nature that confers possibility or impossibility from outside the field.

The result established here has two layers, and they are unequal. No candidate’s *modal status alone* explains either pole: that is the diagnostic, and it blocks divine intellect, concrete worlds, abstractions, or necessary entities from conferring R’s capacity from a position the trilemma can classify. Beyond it, Way–Possibility Convertibility records that possibility is a determinate way within Nature and impossibility the absence of one; Reality–Nature Identity and No Unconditioned Essence close the proposal that a second essence-bearing item supplies those ways, and Modal Closure (§2.9.4) records that no unnecessary alternative stands alongside it from outside. Essence can articulate why a configured way has the modal consequences it has. It can’t add the way, its exclusion, or itself to the field whose articulation it is.

### 7.2.2 Dispositionalism about Modality
Dispositionalism grounds possibility in actual reality rather than in a plurality of worlds. Where Lewis makes ◇p true by the existence of a concrete world at which p obtains, the dispositionalist makes ◇p true by a property of something actual (1986a): a potentiality, a power, a disposition. Vetter gives the position its book-length statement, grounding modality in object-level potentialities and dispensing with worlds as explanatorily basic (2015); Borghini and Williams and Jacobs develop article-length versions (2008; 2010); Pruss develops a related actualist grounding (2011). Behind them stands the dispositional essentialism of Bird and Mumford, with Mumford and Anjum on the causal side (2007; 2004; 2011). The resulting question isn’t whether the actual can ground the possible—the two accounts agree that it can—but whether object-level powers can supply the whole modal field without presupposing the structural capacity in which those powers obtain.

A distinction has to be drawn before the engagement starts, because two different theses travel under one name. Dispositionalism about *laws* holds that laws are the structural expressions of the dispositional essences of natural kinds. That thesis is engaged at §2.9.1, where it is one of four law-accounts the constitutive claim survives, and the engagement there is complete. Dispositionalism about *modality* is a different and more ambitious thesis: not that laws are grounded in powers, but that ◇ itself is. It is that thesis at issue here, and it presses where the source of possibility is defended (§7.2.1).

The concession runs in full. The dispositionalist is right that a plurality of concrete worlds is an extravagant truthmaker for a modest claim; right that modal truths should answer to what is actually the case rather than to what is elsewhere the case; right that the possible-worlds apparatus is a formal convenience whose metaphysical reading was never obligatory. On the negative program the present account and the dispositionalist are allies, and that alliance does its work against modal realism (§7.2.3). The disagreement is entirely about the positive one.

*First.* The reduction form runs directly at the Convertibility. Its claim is that ◇p holds if and only if some actual object has a potentiality for p, so possibility isn’t a structural feature of reality but a summary of what things can do. The Way–Possibility Convertibility (§3.2.5) is then a redescription of the powers facts rather than a rival to them, and the structural triad is read off potentialities rather than presupposed by them.

The reply is that a potentiality already exhibits the triad, and the exhibition should be taken at the strength the position itself requires rather than at the strength a familiar example suggests. Two commitments are minimal, on any version. A potentiality is *of* something: there is no potentiality that is nobody’s and nothing’s, which is the Φ-role at its thinnest. And a potentiality is *for* something distinguishable from its present state, since a directedness that doesn’t mark off what it is directed at hasn’t directed at anything, which is the S-role. Both hold for a static power, an unmanifested one, a multi-track one, and an atemporal one alike; none of them requires that anything happen.

The T-role is where care is owed, because the causal-powers picture supplies it too easily. A fragile glass breaking, the standard case, runs from latency through an interval to manifestation, and there the ordering is plain. A dispositionalist who posits potentialities with no temporal profile at all isn’t refuted by that case; what such a theorist owes is an account of manifestation, since a potentiality whose manifestation is not so much as ordered with respect to its latency has lost the asymmetry that distinguishes a power from a mere property. Where manifestation is concrete, the interval falls due with it. The point is already made on the laws side at §2.9.1. The dispositionalist hasn’t produced an alternative to the way-structure. A potentiality is a way, individuated as one, and taking it as primitive doesn’t remove what individuates it.

The reply doesn’t identify necessitation with directional production or say that the manifestation relation supplies the content of T. That would give the structural conditions a second, analogical sense, which Block Universe (§8.1.4) forecloses. The claim is the deflationary one: the potentiality is described in the structural vocabulary because it instantiates the structure, not because the structure is a species of causal production.

*Second.* The primitiveness form concedes the exhibition and contests the direction of explanation. Grant that potentialities display direction, difference, and bearing; the dispositionalist may hold that potentiality is metaphysically primitive and the triad is a true description of primitives rather than a condition on them. Description doesn’t establish priority.

The reply asks which side survives the removal of the other. A potentiality stripped of its directedness isn’t an undirected potentiality but no potentiality; strip the distinctness of latency from manifestation and there is nothing the potentiality is *for*; strip the bearer and there is nothing whose potentiality it is. The triad is therefore not a description that happens to fit but the individuation-condition of the primitive, and an individuation-condition isn’t posterior to what it individuates. The structural claim also takes a weaker form than the dispositionalist’s own. The Convertibility runs as a convertibility, with neither *possibility* nor *way* reducing to the other, whereas dispositionalism is a reduction in one direction and therefore owes an account of its reduction base. What sits in that base is a property of an actual object, and a property of an actual object is specified from within the modal field in exactly the sense the Modal Exclusivity trilemma identified at §7.2.1.

*Third.* The coverage form makes the disagreement with the present account visible rather than verbal. Wang presses that dispositionalism can’t reach possibilities for which nothing actual seats the relevant potentiality (2015): alien properties, radically different physical regimes, possibilities concerning how things stood before there was anything with powers of the requisite kind. Vetter answers with iterated and joint potentialities, extending the base by chaining what actual things can bring about (2015).

The reply is that the internal dispute is settled, whichever way it goes, by asking whether there is something actual to seat the potentiality, and that question concedes the structural point rather than answering it. Both parties agree that possibility must be seated in actual reality. They differ only over whether the seat is a property of an object or the conditions any object-involving state already instantiates. At ordinary scope the difference is hard to see, because objects are available to bear the powers. At global scope the difference is decisive.

**[Proposition]**

**The Bearer Problem** · *Proposition*

1. Dispositionalism about modality: for any p, ◇p holds in virtue of the potentiality of some actual object (Reduction).

2. A potentiality is borne. There is no potentiality that is not the potentiality *of* something (Bearing).

3. Consider the possibility that there be objects at all.

4. By (1) and (2), that possibility holds in virtue of the potentiality of an object.

5. So the possibility that there be bearers presupposes a bearer, and the account has supplied its own manifestation-condition as its ground.

6. The dispositionalist must therefore either accept the circle at (5) or exempt the limit case from (1), which concedes that not all possibility is dispositionally grounded.

Neither horn is available at low cost, and the structural reading takes the second one without paying. What seats the possibility that there be objects isn’t a further object but the conditions any object-involving state instantiates: succession, distinction, and exchange aren’t properties an item has but the structure any item-involving state is. The dispositionalist’s seat runs out at precisely the scope the argument of Chapter 2 operates at, and it runs out for a reason internal to the position rather than imported against it: powers are borne, and the global case has nothing to bear them.

A rejoinder is available and should be recorded. The dispositionalist may deny that *there being objects at all* is a genuine possibility requiring a ground, holding instead that it is necessary, so that no potentiality need seat it. That reply isn’t obviously wrong, but it is a concession in the relevant sense: it grants that something is necessary without being dispositionally grounded, and once one such necessity is admitted the reduction is no longer general. It also moves the dispositionalist onto the terrain of §2.9.4 and §7.2.1, where the question is no longer what powers ground but what a necessity that grounds nothing further can be. Williamson (2013) reaches a structurally similar place from the opposite direction, and the answer given at Necessitism (§7.2.7) applies here.

*Taking stock.* Dispositionalism isn’t refuted as an account of laws, and Laws as Constitutive (§2.9.1) already grants it what it is owed there. As an account of modality it doesn’t bypass the structural requirement but instantiates it, since a potentiality is individuated as a directed, differentiated, borne thing and is therefore a way rather than an alternative to ways. The order of explanation runs from the individuation-condition to the primitive, not the reverse. And the reduction doesn’t reach the global case, because the possibility of there being bearers can’t itself be seated in a bearer. What the position establishes, and what the present account keeps, is that modality answers to actual structure rather than to a plurality of worlds. Where it locates that structure in the powers of things, the account locates it in what any thing with powers already presupposes.

### 7.2.3 Modal Realism
David Lewis began with counterpart theory in the 1960s, added the analysis of counterfactuals in the early 1970s, and over the following decades built an ontology of concrete possible worlds. On counterpart theory an individual is represented in other worlds by sufficiently similar individuals rather than by strict transworld identity. When you say “I could have taken the other job,” Lewis holds, you are saying truly that somewhere, in a universe spatiotemporally isolated from this one, a person who resembles you in the relevant respects took that job. The universe is concrete: just as concrete as this one. It contains stars and tables and chairs. You will never causally interact with it. But it exists, full stop, in exactly the sense this one does. Modal language isn’t abstract after all. It is a report on a plurality, and the plurality is the ontology.

Lewis developed Modal Realism across two decades, in *Counterfactuals* (1973b) and *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986a), a systematic landmark of late analytic metaphysics. The position remains his alone: its orbit has structured a generation of work on modality without persuading others to adopt the concrete plurality unchanged. Divers (2002) and Nolan (2002) develop Lewisian variants with modified commitments. Bricker (2020) gives the standard contemporary taxonomy of how Lewisian worlds individuate. Against the concrete variant stand the abstract or ersatz realists: Plantinga (1974) defends worlds as maximal states of affairs; Stalnaker (1976; 1984) treats worlds as maximal properties; Adams (1974; 1981) as maximal consistent sets of propositions; Kripke (1980) operates with primitively stipulated worlds rather than discoverable ones. Van Inwagen (1986) presses the central internal critique: the plurality is ontologically exorbitant without being explanatorily adequate. Rosen (1990) develops modal fictionalism as an explicit alternative: the plurality as useful fiction, not reality. Armstrong (1989) pushes combinatorialism: possibilities are recombinations of actual constituents, no alternative universes required.

Like Armstrong’s combinatorialism, the present reply rejects the concrete plurality. It also specifies which structural roles any recombination must preserve. Why they can’t be recombined apart is supplied not here but by the cross-entailment among the three roles (§2.4.8, §2.6): they aren’t distinct existences for recombination to separate.

Modal Realism presses directly against the necessity claim of the argument. What Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6) establishes is □(T∧S∧Φ): in every represented world corresponding to a configuration R can admit, the structural Conditions obtain. S5 is earned from the global-capacity reading of real possibility (§2.1), not assumed as an axiom. Transition Closure is a narrower result about the local onset of transition-capacity within a history; it isn’t an independent derivation of S5 applied separately to each proposition. If possible worlds are concrete universes, the question is what every concrete universe R can admit contains. Lewis’s plurality admits concrete worlds without requiring them to be configurations of this world. If even one such world lacks T, S, or Φ, the argument’s necessity claim is false. (ET) is false on the same condition: the Exhaustion-of-Existence claim that T, S, and Φ exhaust the forms of real existence.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute isn’t with Lewis’s counterfactual semantics or with the usefulness of possible-world talk. The question is whether the concreteness criterion Lewis himself requires (the feature that distinguishes Lewisian realism from ersatz alternatives) permits radically sparse worlds to qualify as concrete. The move comes at several resolutions: the bare sparse-world move and its sharpened recombination form, the isolation-thesis variant, and the primitivist fallback.

*First.* The sparse-world move holds that among the plurality there is a world w₁ containing a single unchanging state: no succession, no spatial extension, no causal activity. Such a world is conceivable, and the move needs conceivability of a coherent description to entail concrete existence of the corresponding world. w₁ contains no T, no S, no Φ, and it concretely exists.

For Lewis, worlds are maximal sums of spatiotemporally interrelated things, with worldmates unified by the relevant natural external relations. This gives Lewisian worlds a spatiotemporal criterion where such relations obtain, but it doesn’t by itself prove that every world contains both temporal succession and spatial extension. A sparse or changeless world remains a live test of the book’s independent type-level arguments. The present argument need not claim that every abstract representation of a world has those types; it claims that a concrete world proposed as a real change-realizer can’t lack them. A world with no temporal succession hosts no change, so whatever else it is, it isn’t a change-realizer. A world with no causal persistence has no bearer across which content could be sustained. A world lacking all three can’t be the change-realizing concrete world it was proposed as; whether it is a concrete world of some sparser kind is the live test just named, and Lewis’s concreteness criterion doesn’t by itself settle it.

*Recombination.* The sparse-world objection doesn’t require an empty world. Lewis’s principle of recombination permits extensive recombination of distinct existences, subject to its own constraints; it doesn’t license every arbitrary description as a world. Recombination needs only a selective deletion of what the Humean treats as distinct. Take a spatiotemporally extended world and deny necessary connections between its distinct local states; the resulting Humean mosaic retains Time and Space while rejecting a necessary productive connection between distinct existences. The issue is whether the mosaic can retain the structural work the present account assigns to Φ without thereby retaining Φ under another description.

The reply must not answer it by saying the mosaic “has no bearer,” since whether a world requires a persisting bearer is precisely what the Humean denies; to assert it here would beg the question.

The reply turns instead on what the mosaic already grants. A mosaic is a distribution of local states across a spatiotemporal manifold: Lewis (1986b, pp. ix–xvi), introducing Humean supervenience in *Philosophical Papers, Volume II*, exempts the spatiotemporal relations from it and takes them as primitive, so the manifold is conceded, not constructed. The manifold grants differentiation and spatiotemporal arrangement. It doesn’t follow merely from exclusion or Best-System regularity that a productive cross-interval causal operation exists: the Humean denies exactly that inference. The remaining question is whether the mosaic realizes Φ’s broader bearing or continuity role without accepting productive necessary connections. A regular mosaic may remain a substantive rival at the type level rather than collapsing into ∅.

*Second.* The isolation thesis presses from a different angle. Lewis’s worlds are spatiotemporally isolated from one another: no causal or spatiotemporal connections between them. A world in the plurality need not be internally rich; it needs only to be isolated from other worlds. A single unchanging state, isolated from all other such states, qualifies as a world by isolation alone.

Lewisian worlds are isolated in the sense that no spatiotemporal relations connect their inhabitants; isolation isn’t an additional between-world relation requiring a common surrounding manifold. The thesis therefore doesn’t establish any particular world’s internal richness. Whether a sparse candidate qualifies as a world turns on Lewis’s worldmate criterion and the candidate’s contents, not on reifying non-connection as a structural relation. The isolation thesis is a structural criterion applied to structured worlds, not an alternative to structure.

*Third.* The primitivist version denies that worldhood requires a constitutive analysis. Being a world is a primitive fact, irreducible to any further ontology. Worldhood is fixed by the modal role ‘world’ plays: as the primitive truthmaker for modal claims. This is a coherent rival semantic proposal, but it carries a cost: it declines a constitutive account of what makes a world concrete or a genuine realizer of change.

The present argument can’t close primitivism by retorsion alone. At most, it can show that any primitive world introduced as a concrete universe or as a realizer of change inherits the relevant role- and type-level burdens. A primitivist who treats worldhood as primitive while refusing those burdens has replaced structural explanation with an additional primitive. That is a theoretical cost, not a contradiction.

A further Lewisian pressure targets the Modal Identity directly rather than the concreteness of worlds. Lewis’s counterpart theory denies strict trans-world identity. What you would have been had you taken the other job is your counterpart in another world: qualitatively similar, numerically distinct. The Modal Identity of §2.6.6 (□(◇C ↔ (T∧S∧Φ)), where ◇C is the possibility of change) appears, under counterpart semantics, ambiguous between a claim about the same T, S, and Φ across worlds (requiring trans-world identity Lewis denies) and a claim about qualitatively similar structural roles in each world (a weaker claim counterpart theory permits but insufficient to ground the necessity the argument needs). Either the Modal Identity assumes identity Lewis rejects, or it retreats to similarity that can’t carry the argumentative weight.

The dilemma turns on what the Modal Identity of §2.6.6 asserts. It doesn’t claim that a numerically identical token of any of the three Conditions recurs across worlds. It claims that any world containing change contains the structural *roles* change requires: whatever plays Time’s role in w and whatever plays it in w′ are instances of one role-type. Counterpart theory forecloses strict trans-world identity for worldbound particulars. A structural role isn’t such a particular.

Lewis (1986a, §1.5) treats properties as classes of their actual and possible instances. That is an across-world specification his semantics permits for types while forbidding it for tokens. “Whatever plays Time’s role” can therefore pick out the class of actual and possible role-players without smuggling a trans-world individual into the theory. On Lewis’s own regimentation, the role-type is an abundant property, identified through its instances across the plurality.

The Modal Identity therefore operates at a level counterpart semantics already allows. Whether that level is rich enough depends on the independent claim that the role specification is constitutive rather than merely similar across worlds; counterpart theory itself neither supplies nor defeats that claim. A second counterpart-theoretic pressure targets the transfer principle instead. The chained-origin cases of Chisholm, Chandler, and N. Salmon are engaged at §7.3.3.

A kindred move drops Lewis’s concrete realism for Stalnaker’s (1976) moderate realism: possible worlds are abstract maximal ways the world could be, not concrete alternative universes. That variant raises the Platonist challenge answered at §8.1.5. In modal-realist vocabulary, abstract maximal ways can be distinguished and compared, directly supporting only a thin difference-role. They need not thereby instantiate temporal succession, spatial extension, or causal persistence. The richer roles apply when a way represents or realizes a concrete change-world, not merely because it is an abstract modal surrogate.

*Convergence.* The sparse-world move first meets Lewis’s own criterion for worldhood: a candidate with no spatiotemporal structure isn’t unified as a world by the relation Lewis unifies one with, and a candidate with no change isn’t a realizer of change. Whether anything sparser still counts as concrete is left to the type-level arguments. The recombination refinement isn’t closed by that definition. Its conceded mosaic nevertheless includes a differentiated manifold, arrangement across it, and local states in which that arrangement obtains. Bearing is therefore granted at role-resolution by the mosaic’s own description rather than imposed from outside.

The type-level question stays live: can Best-System regularity discharge the bearing role without productive connections among distinct existences? At that point the mosaic relocates Φ at role level and contests its loaded realization. The disagreement is substantive, but narrower than a world without any bearer.

The isolation thesis is different. Isolation is a spatiotemporal criterion, so any candidate satisfying it already carries the structure in which isolation is defined. That gives a structural criterion for each world, not yet a ground for counting several. On Structural Individuation, whatever makes the count real is differentiating structure within Reality (*Isolation Is Not Separation*, below). A primitivist can refuse that premise and take world-plurality as an unstructured primitive. The result is an additional primitive and the explanatory cost that comes with it, not a contradiction.

*The unity of the frame.* The replies so far grant Lewis his plurality and show only that each member of it must instantiate the structure. A further reply asks what individuates the plurality itself. Structural Individuation (§2.4.9) states the governing premise: whatever makes two concrete totalities two is real differentiating structure. It needn’t be qualitative, and it needn’t be a spatiotemporal interval. But it can’t both individuate the worlds and be absent from their complete structure. If the differentiator is a relation or ordering, the alleged worlds belong to the one wider structure that contains it. If it is primitive thisness, that thisness is itself the differentiating structure and likewise belongs to the complete account of Reality. If nothing differentiates them, there aren’t two. Lewisian isolation can deny spatiotemporal and causal relations between worlds; it can’t turn the structure that fixes their plurality into no structure at all. Isolation is therefore not a second ontological frame. At most it is how multiple concrete configurations stand within the one all-inclusive Nature whose differentiating structure makes them many: the combinatorial rather than ontological reading of modal plurality already reached at §2.6.6 and developed at §3.2.

**[Proposition]**

**Isolation Is Not Separation** · *Proposition*

Two concrete totalities are two only if their non-identity is concretely grounded. Whatever supplies that ground is differentiating structure: relational structure if a relation separates them, primitive nonqualitative structure if thisness individuates them. Either way the ground belongs to the complete structure of Reality, so the alleged worlds are multiple configurations within one all-inclusive Nature rather than alternatives to it. If nothing differentiates them, there aren’t two. Isolation removes causal and spatiotemporal connection; it does not remove the structure that makes plurality obtain.

**Depends on:** Structural Individuation and Reality–Nature Identity

A second pressure on the isolation thesis shows in the very act of pointing, and its status should be marked rather than assumed: to single out a world as *that* one is to set it off from *this* one, and this-and-that is here-and-there in other clothes. “That world” says “not here,” and “not here” asks after a where—either a location standing off from this one, which is a relation and undoes the isolation, or no where at all, in which case “that” has singled out nothing. This is diagnostic and not load-bearing. A defender may answer that how a world must be *referred to* is a fact about the order of description while the plurality is a claim about the order of being, and that answer is available (§8.3.5 declines the same bridge for the same reason; the act/object ruling is at §3.3.4). The proposition above does not run through it. What the pointing shows is where the difficulty is felt; what closes the position is that a label is not a distance.

The narrower real-interval requirement for *positional* distinction remains established by Relational Distinctness at §2.4.7. The plurality result does not convert every individuation into a spatial one; it spends the more general Structural Individuation premise.

A further question follows. The primitivist might concede the demonstrative point—that “that world” borrows the here-and-there it was meant to outrun—and insist instead that bare thisness simply is, at the level of being, prior to any pointing or description. The question is what the thisness is being asked to do. If it is a feature of the world it individuates, then it is a differentiating feature and belongs to the complete structural account, which is the first horn of the fork already stated. If it is bare in the strict sense, carrying no qualitative, relational, or structural content whatever, then nothing about it is available to make one world differ from another: “bare thisness makes them two” and “nothing makes them two” are, on every dimension that could tell them apart, the same description. The posit hasn’t located bedrock below structure; it has named the absence of a differentiator and kept the numeral.

Stated precisely, the argument reaches structural and numerical unicity together. The one all-inclusive frame is therefore the one concrete cosmos: positions, regions, branches, worlds, and configurations may multiply within it without multiplying the Reality whose structure individuates them (§11.2.2). Reality isn’t the winner of a headcount among external rivals; its all-inclusiveness absorbs whatever could make the headcount real.

The deduction is conditional on Structural Individuation, as deductions are conditional on their premises. Lewis can deny that concrete numerical distinctness requires any differentiating structure, or insist that a primitive thisness individuates while adding none. That denial doesn’t supply a model in which the premise is true and the conclusion false. It rejects the load-bearing premise and thereby blocks this route.

Blocking this unicity route doesn’t, by itself, block the necessity of the Conditions. The Movement Line (§2.4.9) begins from actual displacement, finds the Conditions in what displacement is, and discharges against its necessary possibility. A reader who rejects Structural Individuation has therefore declined the identity and unicity results that spend it, not the independent Movement derivation of the three Conditions.

The cost analysis therefore has a precise task: defending Structural Individuation against the primitivist refusal. Lewis needs the numeral’s economy and the worlds’ concreteness together; the premise requires him to say what in the concrete ontology earns the count (§2.4.1; §8.1.5).

The resulting intervalless plurality is a positive existential posit with no access and no causal trace, carried for a modal-semantic payoff the structural account already supplies from a ground independently necessary (§2.9.6).

The cost ledger carries one more line, and it is quantitative. Grant the primitivist bare distinctness, and the plurality still owes an answer: how much of it is there? Forrest and Armstrong (1984) showed that unrestricted recombination over the totality of worlds generates a world containing duplicates of all the worlds—a world bigger than any world, itself included—so neither the aggregate nor the set of all worlds survives the principle’s own closure.

Lewis replies (1986a, §§1.8, 2.2) by restricting recombination to what “size and shape permit,” without independently fixing the restriction’s content. Nolan (1996) argues that the proviso is unmotivated on Lewis’s terms and defends unbounded recombination, with more possible entities than any set can contain. The alternatives leave the plurality without a determinate size: a finite tally would lack a reason for ending where it does, while the unrestricted alternative doesn’t stabilize at a cardinality.

This doesn’t by itself prove unicity; it prices the primitive plurality. A posit whose quantity its own machinery can’t determine carries the pattern the unity reading predicts: number fails at the level of totalities. What appears inside the theory as a bookkeeping problem is, on the structural reading, the quantitative face of the interval problem—*how many?* can’t be answered where the frame supplying numerical distinction is itself what is counted.

The shape of the mistake can be put more plainly. Each Lewisian world is internally rich—intervals throughout, a full spatiotemporal interior, exactly like the interior of a fiction, which stipulates its own distances freely. What carries no interval is the relation *between* worlds. That relation is a seam—world-to-world as fiction stands to reality—and every seam we have uncontested access to is interval-free precisely where it is non-concrete: there is no distance from Sherlock Holmes to Hamlet, not an unknown distance but no such fact. The photograph in your hand sits a foot away, while the person it pictures, held now as pictured, is at no distance from you at all; the only way to recover a distance is to switch back from the representation to the living worldline—from the seam to a concrete interior. Lewis is thus a concretist about each world and, without owning it, an ersatzer about the many: he imports the interior’s concreteness across a seam that bears none of concreteness’s marks.

Lewis has an answer, and it is his thesis rather than a repair: worlds stand in no spatiotemporal relation at all, and on his view that is what their distinctness consists in, so a missing interval is what the position predicts rather than an anomaly it must explain. The comparison doesn’t refute him. What it prices is the novelty. Every interval-free seam we have uncontested access to is non-concrete, so the plurality asks for a relation between concrete things with no precedent outside representation, and it asks for it at the one place where nothing can be checked.

**[Proposition]**

**Concrete Relata, Non-Concrete Seam** · *Proposition*

Each Lewisian world is internally rich, with intervals throughout. What carries no interval is the relation between worlds, and every seam we have uncontested access to is interval-free exactly where it is non-concrete: there is no distance from Holmes to Hamlet, not an unknown distance but no such fact. Lewis is therefore a concretist about each world and, unowned, an ersatzer about the many. The plurality is a set of concrete relata related as if they were not concrete. Lewis predicts the missing interval rather than conceding it, since standing in no spatiotemporal relation is what he takes distinctness of worlds to be, so what the comparison prices is a relation without precedent outside representation rather than an inconsistency.

And the intuition that makes the picture feel forced—that the worlds are *obviously* many—leans on distinguishability, which is downstream of the structure and confers no actuality of its own: that two worlds can be told apart no more makes them two concrete existents than telling Holmes from Hamlet makes either one a man. The arrow runs from the Conditions to distinguishability, never back.

**Depends on:** Structural Individuation; the seam comparison is diagnostic support

*A further thesis: actuality as indexical.* One Lewisian commitment travels with the plurality without being identical to it, and it is the one §1.2.5 reserved. On Lewis’s analysis, *actual* is indexical, in the way *here* and *now* are: it picks out the world of whoever utters it, and the inhabitants of every world say it as truly of theirs as we say it of ours, with no world actual *simpliciter* (1986a, §1.9). The thesis isn’t decoration. It is what keeps the other worlds from being second-class, merely possible things standing alongside one real one, and without it the plurality would concede at the level of standing the asymmetry it was built to deny.

Granted at full strength, the analysis is right about the word. An indexical takes its value from the position of its utterance, and if there are many concrete totalities, which one is *actual* is settled by which one the utterance occurs in, with nothing further to say. What the analysis needs is the range the index runs over. *Here* works because there is a there: the word selects from a field of positions it doesn’t itself supply. At the level of totalities the proposed range must itself be individuated. Whatever makes its members many is differentiating structure within Reality; absent such structure, the index has no plurality to select from (*Isolation Is Not Separation*, *Concrete Relata, Non-Concrete Seam*). An index with one value in its range isn’t an index but a name.

The thesis therefore need not be met on its own ground. It stands or falls with the plurality it serves, and the premise that decides the one decides the other. What is left when it falls is already fixed (§1.2.5): actuality is which configuration among those Reality admits is the realized one, a fact about Reality rather than about the standpoint a report is made from. The unrealized configurations aren’t distant places wrongly denied a title; they are ways the one Reality could have been and isn’t. None of this touches the indexicality of *here* and *now*, which range over positions inside the frame and have their field. What is denied is that *actual* is one of them.

*On the Plurality of Worlds* defends concrete realism against what Lewis called “the incredulous stare”: the reaction he expected from any reader encountering the view for the first time, and which he thought no sufficient response to a working modal semantics. What Lewis left behind isn’t the plurality but a diagnostic: any modal ontology powerful enough to do the work has to specify what makes a world a world, and whatever does the specifying instantiates the structure the argument names. Ersatz worlds individuate by property or proposition; concrete worlds individuate by spatiotemporal aggregation. Either specification is a structural fact. What the plurality purchased in modal expressive power it paid for in ontological commitment, and the ontological commitment, examined for what it requires, confirms the structural conditions the argument derives.

### 7.2.4 Linguistic Ersatzism
Ersatzism keeps Lewis’s modal apparatus and declines his bill. A rival that spends less isn’t thereby claiming less, and the discount is taken in exactly the currency this chapter audits. If a world is an abstract object rather than a concrete manifold, then nothing in a world is obviously required to instantiate anything. What, then, requires every represented world to contain the structural conditions rather than merely to describe them?

Ersatzism (from German *Ersatz*, “substitute”) holds that possible worlds aren’t concrete spacetime manifolds, à la Lewis’s Modal Realism (on which every possible world is an equally concrete, equally real spatiotemporal manifold), but abstract surrogates. Other worlds are abstract objects: surrogates rather than rivals. The position retains the modal apparatus while avoiding Lewis’s ontological extravagance.

The label covers three importantly different positions, and the reply that follows must hold across all of them. Adams (“Theories of Actuality” 1974) treats worlds as world-stories: maximal consistent sets of propositions, with the actual world represented by the set all of whose members are true. Stalnaker (“Possible Worlds,” 1976) instead treats worlds as abstract ways the world could have been—maximal properties it might have had—and his later *Mere Possibilities* (2012) refines this into a contingentist account with no robustly existing merely possible individuals. Plantinga (1974; 1976) treats worlds as maximal possible states of affairs, abstract objects that exist necessarily and, on his wider theistic view, have their being in the divine intellect. Those differences matter to the metaphysics of abstracta. The pressure here is narrower: propositions, ways, and states of affairs are distinguishable, content-bearing items standing in consistency relations, so what must obtain for any of those ersatz constructions to be distinguishable and consistent at all?

The argument’s relation to ersatzism is broadly friendly. Ersatzism doesn’t require Modal Realism’s commitment to a plenitude of concrete worlds; it doesn’t commit the user of modal vocabulary to the existence of donkeys that talk in some other concrete reality. Ersatzism’s worlds are abstract objects, and the question of what abstract objects depend on is a question for the metaphysics of abstracta, addressed in §8.1.5 (Platonism) and adjacent.

Ersatz worlds contain distinguishable propositions, ways, or states of affairs standing in logical relations. This directly secures thin differentiation at the level of the representation. It doesn’t make an abstract surrogate temporally successive, spatially extended, or causally persistent. Those richer burdens belong to the concrete world represented, or to any surrogate proposed as its physical realizer.

A second observation. On Adams’s world-story version, actuality privileges the maximal consistent set all of whose members are true. Stalnaker’s ways and Plantinga’s maximal states of affairs require their own actuality relations rather than this exact set-theoretic formulation. In each case, truth or obtaining is assessed against how things actually are. How things are *is* Reality: with its three Conditions. The actual world’s privilege is parasitic on Reality being a particular way. Ersatz worlds are alternative description-sets relative to Reality; they aren’t ontological rivals to it.

**[Proposition]**

**Actuality Is Conferred, Not Contained** · *Proposition*

Each abstract form privileges the actual world by a relation of its own: for a world-story, that every proposition in the maximal consistent set is true; for a maximal property, that Reality has it; for a maximal state of affairs, that it obtains. In none of the three does the privilege come from a feature of the surrogate. What makes the set true, the property had, or the state of affairs obtain is how Reality stands. Actuality is therefore conferred on the apparatus from outside rather than found within it. The ersatzist supplies a semantics for modal talk and inherits, rather than displaces, whatever Reality must be for one set to come out true.

**Depends on:** Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8)

*Convergence.* Ersatzism is a successful theory of what we mean by talk of possible worlds. It isn’t a theory that displaces the present argument’s necessary structure. The two operate at different levels: ersatzism at the level of modal semantics, the present argument at the level of the structural conditions any modal semantics describes.

### 7.2.5 Combinatorialism
Dispositionalism (§7.2.2) and combinatorialism meet the present account on different axes. Dispositionalism agrees that modality is grounded in something actual rather than conferred by a plurality of worlds. Combinatorialism agrees that modal plurality consists in configurations of one actual base rather than alternatives to it. The disagreement is therefore exact: what among the things there are anchors admissible recombination, and can that constraint remain distinct from the structured capacity the present account identifies?

Armstrong (1989; 1997) defends a combinatorial theory of modality. Possibility, on this view, is the combinatorial space generated by recombining the actual world’s fundamental constituents, particulars and universals (the concrete individuals and the repeatable properties they instantiate, in Armstrong’s technical sense), in all possible ways consistent with their adicity (the number of argument-places a universal takes) and type. Possible worlds aren’t concrete (Lewis) or abstract (ersatzism); they are constructions out of actual elements. The space of possibility is wholly determined by what actually exists.

The combinatorialist’s modality is grounded in the actual. The argument here is consonant with this in its commitment to the actuality of the three Conditions. Where the two part ways is on the source of the recombinatorial range. Armstrong takes the actual particulars and universals as primitive and lets recombination do the rest. The present argument identifies the three Conditions as necessary features of the actual, which means that recombination can’t generate worlds in which any of the three Conditions fail to obtain, since their failure isn’t a configuration of the elements but the absence of the conditions for any configuration.

This is a constraint on combinatorialism, not a refutation of it. Combinatorialism is consistent with the argument provided it acknowledges that the recombinations operate within the structural conditions, and that acknowledgment can be extracted from the combinatorial operation itself, without first granting the structural argument’s conclusions. Combinatorial generation requires distinguishable constituents and admissible arrangements, so it directly presupposes a thin difference-role. But the modal construction isn’t itself a temporal process: possible combinations need not be produced one after another, and the constituents need not persist through an act of recombining. Temporal succession and causal bearing must be established within any concrete change-world represented by a combination, not inferred from the theorist’s operation on the base. The structural conditions are therefore not items in the actualist base awaiting recombination: the difference-role is presupposed by any combinatorial generation, and the richer roles fall due wherever a combination is offered as a concrete change-world rather than a description.

*Where the kinship runs.* The debt to Armstrong belongs here rather than in an aside to §7.2.3. Both accounts refuse the concrete plurality; both hold that modal facts answer to what actually is; and the reading of modal plurality reached at §2.6.6 and developed at §3.2 is combinatorial in Armstrong’s own sense—what are called possible worlds are alternative configurations within one necessary natural ground, not alternative grounds. On the question his theory was built to answer, the two accounts agree. They part over a question it doesn’t pose: what any configuration must preserve to be a configuration at all. Combinatorialism about the plurality and combinatorialism about the conditions are separable theses, and the present account holds the first while denying the second.

*The gap shows in what does the constraining.* Armstrong’s own machinery already carries a restriction: recombination runs subject to adicity and type, so a universal can’t be recombined into an arrangement its argument-places don’t admit. The constraint is not itself one of the recombined elements, which is the point worth pressing, and it is worth pressing without borrowing a problem aimed elsewhere. The Forrest–Armstrong result—that unrestricted recombination over the totality of worlds generates a world containing duplicates of all of them, itself included (1984)—was an argument against *Lewis*, and it is used against Lewis’s plurality at §7.2.3. Armstrong’s base is actual and fixed, so he doesn’t inherit that paradox. What the episode shows is the shape of the standard repair: Lewis answers with a proviso, “size and shape permitting,” whose content he leaves unspecified, and Nolan (1996) argues the restriction is unmotivated on Lewis’s own terms. A qualification of that form concedes that something other than the recombining does the constraining: permission is granted or withheld by what the domain admits, not by the operation performing the admitting. Armstrong’s adicity-and-type restriction concedes the same thing in a tidier form, and neither position has supplied a principled account of what the constraint is grounded in. The three Conditions are a candidate answer of exactly the right type—not further elements awaiting recombination, and not a proviso fastened on from outside, but the conditions under which recombining is an operation on anything at all. The offer isn’t a correction of combinatorialism. It is the missing clause the position has been carrying a placeholder for.

That the fit isn’t coincidental can be said more exactly than “the right type.” Whatever supplies the missing clause has to do three things: stand in an asymmetric relation to what it constrains, so that the constraint governs the arrangements rather than the arrangements the constraint (a priority role, and not a temporal one—nothing here requires that admissions occur in a sequence), differentiate admissible arrangements from inadmissible ones by something more than a label (a role of real differentiation), and be realized in some actual fact rather than left a free-floating restriction (a role of real bearing). Any constraint capable of doing that work already satisfies the Grounding Conditional earned at §3.1.5: any relation of constraint, at any level of any possible ontological stack, requires asymmetric priority, real differentiation, and a real realizer—the three Conditions at role-resolution, on exactly the footing that closes the demon, the simulation substrate, and every other proposed ground. A restriction lacking any one of those roles couldn’t do the constraining that adicity and type are asked to do for Armstrong; nothing “size and shape permitting” leaves unspecified could do it for Lewis either, which is the precise defect Nolan presses. What “exactly the right type” was reaching for is therefore not a happy resemblance: any adequate answer to the constraint problem has to instantiate these roles.

**[Proposition]**

**The Missing Clause** · *Proposition*

Recombination runs under a constraint the recombined elements don’t supply: adicity and type for Armstrong, “size and shape permitting” for Lewis, whose content he leaves unspecified. Whatever supplies it must stand asymmetrically to what it constrains, which is a relation of priority rather than a sequence in time, differentiate admissible arrangements by more than a label, and be realized in some actual fact rather than float free. Those three are T, S, and Φ at role-resolution. The combinatorialist may still hold the admissibility relation as an unnamed primitive of that same shape, at the cost Nolan already charged against the proviso.

**Depends on:** The Grounding Conditional (§3.1.5)

A second observation. Combinatorialism faces a familiar pressure: it can’t easily generate alien properties, properties that no actual entity instantiates. If recombination is restricted to the actual, the modal range is narrower than most modal intuitions allow. Various extensions have been proposed (Armstrong himself, then Sider 2003): typically by admitting alien properties as primitive possibilities not generated by recombination, or by allowing modal primitives beyond the actualist base. The combinatorialist will call these workable refinements, but they aren’t free, and naming the cost precisely is what the objection requires. The appeal of combinatorialism was exactly its strict actualism (the thesis that only actually existing things exist, with no real merely-possible entities): the promise that the entire space of possibility is fixed by what actually exists, with nothing modal taken as primitive. An alien property admitted as a primitive possibility is, by definition, a possibility not fixed by the actual base, so the extension purchases modal adequacy by conceding the very reduction that made the position attractive. And the resulting view is no longer the actualist economy it advertised but a base of actual elements supplemented by free-floating modal primitives. The dilemma is stable: stay strictly actualist and the modal range is too narrow to capture ordinary modal intuition; widen it and the actualist motivation lapses.

Either horn is consistent with the present point, because the three Conditions aren’t candidate alien properties at all: not properties an entity might or might not instantiate, but conditions on there being entities, properties, or recombinations in the first place. The present argument doesn’t turn on the resolution of this debate. What it offers is a fixed point: whatever combinatorialism includes or excludes, the three Conditions aren’t in the recombinable set. They are what the actual base must already instantiate for there to be anything to recombine.

*Convergence.* Combinatorialism is, like ersatzism, a theory of how modal vocabulary is grounded. The present argument is a theory of what modal vocabulary describes. The two are compatible if the former locates its grounds within the structural conditions the latter identifies.

What remains open is the move the combinatorialist can make without contradiction: take the admissibility relation itself as a modal primitive, leave it unidentified with T, S, or Φ, and accept the resulting explanatory remainder. The Grounding Conditional shows what any adequate constraint must be structured like; it doesn’t force the combinatorialist to identify that constraint with T, S, and Φ rather than posit a primitive answering to the same structure. Nolan’s criticism of Lewis’s proviso fixes the cost: the account now contains a primitive with the shape T∧S∧Φ already fills, held apart from it without a further differentiating ground. The position remains live. Its remaining disagreement with the present account is the refusal of that identification, not a different account of the work the constraint must perform.

### 7.2.6 Modal Fictionalism
Gideon Rosen’s “Modal Fictionalism” (1990), a short paper in *Mind*, proposed a middle path: accept the expressive power of Lewis’s plurality, reject its ontological commitment. When you say “I could have taken the other job,” Rosen holds, you are saying truly that according to the fiction of possible worlds, some world contains a counterpart of you who took that job. The fiction does its work without the worlds needing to exist. The plurality becomes a story we tell about modality, not a plurality we discover. On Rosen’s account, Lewisian semantics can be retained without Lewisian ontology.

Rosen’s paper set the terms for two decades of debate. Brock (“Modal Fictionalism: A Response to Rosen” 1993) pressed the dilemma that fictionalism threatens to reduce modal claims to claims about what the fiction says, which presupposes a non-fictional fact about the fiction. Divers (*Possible Worlds* 2002) and Nolan (*Topics in the Philosophy of Possible Worlds* 2002) canvassed Lewisian and fictionalist variants side by side. Hale (“Modal Fictionalism: A Simple Dilemma” 1995) and Noonan (1994) sharpened Brock’s dilemma. Sider (*Writing the Book of the World* 2011) moved the tradition toward pragmatic deflation: modal talk as a useful tool whose commitments don’t penetrate metaphysics. Woodward (“Is Modal Fictionalism Artificial?” 2011) defended Rosen’s account against the charge that the fiction is hopelessly artificial; Rosen himself later partially distanced himself from the no-correspondence form of the view.
