What the literature preserves is a test case: how far can modal talk be deflated before the deflation undermines the level at which talk itself happens?

Modal fictionalism presses directly against the necessity claim of the argument. The current proof chain separates the relevant work. Necessary Possibility / S5 comes through the S5 pipeline (§2.1), the structural roles required by change are identified at §2.6, the Modal Identity follows at §2.6.6, and the Necessity of Nature theorem is declared at §2.9.6: □(T∧S∧Φ), the necessary obtaining of the three structural Conditions borne by Time, Space, and Substance. On the fictionalist picture, that claim is true only insofar as the fiction of possible worlds licenses it. But the fiction is a story, not a feature of reality. If the argument’s necessity claim is a claim about a story, its ontological weight dissolves. The argument has proved something about the fiction we use to talk about modality, not something about reality. The structural-exhaustion claim suffers in parallel: if exhaustion is fictional, no actual alternative was ever excluded.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute isn’t with the usefulness of fictionalist semantics for counterfactual reasoning. The question is whether the fiction can be told without the structural conditions the fiction is meant to deflate. If telling the story requires the three Conditions, the three conditions aren’t what the fiction is about. They are what make the fiction tellable. Three forms of the move press the answer at three resolutions: the bare story-element move, the meta-level refinement, and the no-correspondence move.

*First.* The story-element move holds that modal claims are true according to the fiction, not true *simpliciter* (Latin: “absolutely,” without qualification). “Possible world w₀ lacks the three Conditions” is a coherent story element; the story is part of the fiction; therefore the fictionalist can say w₀ is possible without committing to its ontology. The argument’s individuation conditions for concrete possible worlds don’t apply to story elements.

The relevant world-fiction must be disciplined enough to support the fictionalist’s translation scheme, though fictional discourse can represent contradictions without thereby collapsing. The key question isn’t whether the act of telling is structured, but whether the fiction licenses the target modal claim under the adopted analysis. A story of w₀ can be coherently represented even if the act of representation occurs in a structured actual world; fiction routinely represents what its production doesn’t instantiate. Individuating the story element and attributing a property to it therefore establish only that the act, inscription, or reasoner has differentiation and persistence. They don’t establish that w₀ itself contains the loaded T/S/Φ types or is metaphysically possible.

*Second.* The meta-level refinement concedes the first reply and still preserves the move. The fictionalist can accept that storytelling instantiates the three Conditions and still insist that w₀’s properties are fictional. The story requires the three conditions at the meta-level; it doesn’t require them within the story. w₀ can lack the three conditions as a story element even if the act of telling the story about w₀ requires them.

The meta/story distinction blocks any inference from the structure of telling to the structure of the represented world. At most, the actual performance supplies act-side evidence that the actual world is structured. It doesn’t establish that every real possibility instantiates the loaded types. The remaining dispute is therefore about the non-fictional modal resources needed to state which world-fiction is correct, not about storytelling as a cross-world proof. The story can contain structureless worlds, but fictionalism still needs resources for deciding which world-fiction correctly translates modal discourse and why. Brock’s dilemma presses that non-fictional semantic or representational basis. The actual conditions of storytelling may constrain that basis, yet it establishes only actual-world roles. To reach □(T∧S∧Φ), the book must show that the correctness conditions for modal representation commit the fictionalist to the invariant standing capacity of R and exclude structureless candidates for reasons independent of the act of telling.

*Third.* The no-correspondence move denies that modal claims have truth conditions beyond what the fiction specifies. There is no fact of the matter about whether w₀ is possible beyond what the story says. The argument’s claim that w₀ is incoherent is itself just another story about stories: a meta-fiction whose ontological weight is no greater than the fiction it critiques.

The no-correspondence version is unstable at the meta-level. If modal claims have no truth conditions beyond what the fiction specifies, the fictionalist still owes a non-circular account of the translation’s correctness and of which fiction is privileged. The meta-claim about that semantics isn’t automatically itself modal, so self-defeat doesn’t follow merely from its formulation. What the move can’t do is extend the no-truth-conditions treatment to that meta-claim itself: the account of the translation’s correctness and of which fiction is privileged must hold non-fictionally, or the position dissolves into a fiction about fictions with nothing to recommend it. This is the Self-Application Fork (§7.1) in fictionalist currency. Asked whether “modal claims have no truth conditions beyond the fiction” itself has truth conditions beyond the fiction, the no-correspondence version answers no and owes a non-fictional standing it has just declined, or yes and admits a meta-level exception whose status it hasn’t accounted for. The position therefore requires a level of non-fictional fact.

A kindred move drops full-blown fictionalism for Sider’s (2011) pragmatic deflationism: modal talk serves practical purposes and carries no deep ontological commitment, but neither does it require a full-scale fiction. The reply follows the same path. Pragmatic deflation evaluates modal statements by their utility for reasoners whose reasoning instantiates the roles; the pragmatic frame is Nature’s tool for modal reasoning. Deflation doesn’t escape Nature; it describes Nature’s modal practice from within.

*The telling, and what it does and doesn’t secure.* One point stands outside the act-side concession and reaches the analysis rather than its practitioners, though it falls short of refuting it. Fictionalism translates *P is possible* into a claim about what holds according to the fiction. Apply that translation to the fiction’s own telling. The telling isn’t a story about a telling; it occurs, and on the semantics fixed at §1.2.5 what is actual is possible, where being possible is Reality having the capacity to admit it (§1.2.1). Read that way, at least one modal fact—that the fiction can be told—is secured by an occurrence rather than by anything holding according to a story.

A fictionalist can decline that reading, and it is worth being exact about what gets declined. The occurrence isn’t in dispute. What is in dispute is the step from the occurrence to a modal fact of that kind, since actuality-to-possibility is one of the very inferences the translation was built to analyze, and nothing bars applying it to *the telling is possible* merely because the telling happened. So the pressure is a burden rather than a contradiction, and it is the burden the literature already presses. The translation has to be given for a claim whose warrant is an occurrence rather than anything the story says, and its correctness is what Brock’s dilemma asks the fictionalist to supply non-fictionally.

The alternative is to restrict the analysis to the modal claims made *within* the practice, leaving the practice’s own possibility outside it. That restriction is available and it isn’t free: the thesis was that modal talk needs no real modal commitment, and the restricted version concedes one at the foundation. What remains is a translation scheme operating inside a modal fact it doesn’t analyze.

**[Proposition]**

**The Fiction Owes Non-Fictional Resources** · *Proposition*

The act-side result is granted and is not the pressure: that actual representations, reasoners, and inscriptions are structured does not establish the structure of what is represented. Two pressures remain. The first is that the translation must be given for the fiction’s own telling, which occurs rather than holding according to a story, so a claim the analysis has to cover is made warranted by an occurrence and owes conditions of correctness answering to one. On the semantics fixed at §1.2.1 and §1.2.5 that occurrence secures a modal fact outside the analysis; a fictionalist who declines that reading still carries the burden. The second is semantic. The fictionalist owes non-fictional resources for translation correctness, fiction selection, and modal consequence—an account of which fiction is the right one, and of what follows from it, that is not itself told inside the fiction. Those resources either inherit the global-capacity constraints, in which case the modal conclusion is not evaded, or they are supplied from somewhere the position has not identified.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10)

*Convergence.* Modal fictionalism concedes an act-side result: actual representations, reasoners, and inscriptions are structured. That doesn’t establish the represented world’s structure or cross-world necessity. What remains are the two pressures *The Fiction Owes Non-Fictional Resources* states: the translation owed for the fiction’s own telling, and the non-fictional resources for translation correctness, fiction selection, and modal consequence.

Rosen’s paper responded to the concern that Lewisian plurality imposed excessive ontological commitments. Fictionalism sought to retain possible-worlds semantics without those commitments. Subsequent debate has clarified the difficulty: dispensing with concrete worlds doesn’t dispense with the actual representational conditions under which the fiction is formulated and assessed. Rosen’s central insight—that modal discourse need not commit us to a concrete plurality—remains defensible. The broader conclusion doesn’t follow. Modal discourse commits us at least to actual representational structure; whether it also commits us to the book’s global modal constraints remains the substantive semantic and metaphysical dispute.

### 7.2.7 Necessitism
Timothy Williamson published *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* in 2013, a book whose title names exactly what the project is. His argument (developed across two decades of papers and consolidated in the book) is that modal logic isn’t a regional formalism for talking about possibility but the central apparatus of metaphysics itself, and that its quantifiers, when interpreted with the seriousness the formalism deserves, range over a constant domain across worlds. Necessarily everything is necessarily something. Whatever there is belongs to the same unrestricted domain at every world, including merely possible objects that are non-concrete at the actual world. Contingency concerns which objects are concrete and which properties they instantiate, rather than variation in the unrestricted domain itself. The Barcan formula and its converse, which together express the commutativity of quantification and modality, are validated. The view is ambitious—everything whatever exists necessarily—and the case for it draws on the simplicity, generality, and explanatory reach of constant-domain QML (quantified modal logic).

Williamson (*Modal Logic as Metaphysics* 2013) is the systematic statement; “Bare Possibilia” (1998), “Necessary Existents” (2002), and “Everything” (2003) develop the apparatus. The position descends from Barcan Marcus (1946), who first proved the formula that bears her name in a quantified modal logic and pressed its philosophical consequences. Against necessitism stands a cluster of contingentist responses: Stalnaker (*Mere Possibilities* 2012) defends the contingent-domain alternative by arguing that the apparent simplicity of constant-domain quantification is purchased at the cost of a domain populated by “merely possible” entities whose existence-status is obscure; Fine (“Necessity and Non-Existence,” 2005) develops an essence-based account on which Socrates can be necessarily Socrates without necessarily existing; Adams (“Actualism and Thisness” 1981) defends actualism against the Barcan-formula consequences; Hale (*Necessary Beings* 2013) develops a structured-necessity account on which different kinds of necessity have different scopes. Plantinga (1974) had in effect pressed the objection in advance: such a position misreads modal claims about objects as modal claims about haecceities (individual thisnesses, the property of being *this very individual* and no other). The contemporary higher-order modal logic literature (Linnebo, *Thin Objects* 2018; Linnebo and Rayo, “Hierarchies Ontological and Ideological,” 2012) extends the dialectic into plural-quantification frameworks where the Barcan formula’s status is again disputed.

On the contingentist question, the present reply agrees with Stalnaker that some entities exist contingently and adds what his account alone doesn’t specify: where contingency may enter the structural account, and why the argument for the necessary Conditions doesn’t wait on it.

The challenge to the structural argument is double-edged. On one hand, necessitism would seem to make the necessary being trivially available: every possible thing exists necessarily, so the necessary being is among them. On the other hand, necessitism eliminates the explanatory work the necessary being is supposed to do. If everything exists necessarily, there is no explanatory contrast between the necessary being and contingent beings at the level of unrestricted existence, because there are no contingent beings in that sense. The argument’s modal conclusion is □(T∧S∧Φ): the necessary obtaining of the three structural Conditions T, S, and Φ, borne by Time, Space, and Substance. It may then appear to land trivially in a framework where every member of the domain exists necessarily. The pressure isn’t that Chapter 2 secretly requires a world without change or a contingent choice of which world is actual. It requires neither. The pressure is whether ◇C remains a substantive capacity-claim rather than a disguised constant-domain existence claim, and whether □(T∧S∧Φ) identifies constitutive structure rather than merely repeating that its relata belong to the fixed domain.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute isn’t with quantified modal logic, the Barcan formula’s formal validity in S5, or the ambition of modal logic to do metaphysical work. The argument shares with Williamson the commitment that modal logic isn’t a regional formalism but the apparatus through which metaphysical structure is structured. The dispute is whether the move from formal validity in constant-domain QML to ontological necessitism preserves the difference between necessary domain-membership and necessary structural constitution. Three forms of the move press that question at three resolutions: constant-domain compatibility, preservation of the Cartesian witness, and the place of contingency once structural necessity is established. The first two bear on the proof itself. The third tests what the proof permits but doesn’t independently establish.

*First.* The constant-domain compatibility move presses that the structural argument’s modal conclusion lands trivially in Williamson’s framework. □(T∧S∧Φ) is a necessity claim, and necessitism makes every existence claim a necessity claim. The conclusion is therefore consistent with necessitism but undistinguished by it. If the structural argument’s distinctive contribution is the modal status of T, S, and Φ, and necessitism flattens all modal-status differences at the existence level, the argument hasn’t earned anything Williamson’s framework doesn’t already deliver. The conclusion would be true but not informative.

The reply distinguishes the structural sense in which the three Conditions are necessary from the necessitist sense in which everything is necessary. Necessitism’s necessity is *constant-domain*: the same things exist in every world. The structural argument’s necessity is *constitutive*: the three Conditions are conditions any world must instantiate to be a world. The two are compatible but not equivalent. A necessitist can accept that the things which exist in every world include configurations satisfying the three Conditions, and the structural argument adds that the satisfaction of the three Conditions is what makes the constant domain a domain of any kind rather than a featureless plurality.

The Barcan formula and its converse fix that the domain is the same at every world. They say nothing about what that domain’s members instantiate, so they don’t deliver what the argument independently derives (that every world’s domain instantiates the three Conditions), still less explain *why* it does. Appendix A’s *Domain Semantics and the Barcan Question* records that the structural argument quantifies over Conditions rather than individuals, so Barcan and Converse Barcan are orthogonal to the proof’s load-bearing claims at the structural level.

The structural argument proposes a metaphysical explanation Williamson’s formal framework doesn’t itself provide. This shouldn’t be attributed to a general truthmaker requirement on Williamson’s part: the narrower point is that constant-domain semantics alone doesn’t establish the book’s constitutive account of the three Conditions. On the structural account, the quantifier’s range across that domain is the formal shadow of the constitutive fact. The constant-domain framework is exactly the framework the structural argument’s conclusion describes, with the constitutive content filled in.

*Second.* The Cartesian-Certainty preservation move asks whether the argument’s witness has been translated into the wrong key. The central premise (◇C, the possibility of change) is secured at §2.2 from the actuality of change in the act of doubting. Its force doesn’t depend on the further claim that a no-change world is possible. If ◇C is read as the claim that change-events belong to the unrestricted domain, necessitism makes that membership necessary and leaves the occurrence of change untouched. If it is read as the claim that change can occur, the operator ranges over qualitative configurations rather than over which entities exist. The objection must therefore show that the capacity-claim has been reduced to domain-membership; denying contingency alone doesn’t undermine the premise.

The collapse doesn’t occur, because the premise’s modal weight doesn’t sit at the level necessitism flattens. ◇C isn’t a claim about which entities exist in modal space; it is a claim about which configurations the structural roles permit. The Cartesian datum isn’t ‘a change-event exists’ but ‘the act of thinking now occurring is itself a change’, and the modal scope of the premise is over configurations of the roles, not over the existence of relata. Necessitism leaves the configuration-level intact: even if every entity exists necessarily, the question of which configuration any entity is in remains a qualitative-contingency question, and qualitative contingency is precisely what Williamson preserves. ◇C marks a substantive possibility at the level Williamson’s framework licenses: configurations vary across worlds, the configuration-of-change is one configuration among others, and the Cartesian certainty is that *this* configuration is instantiated.

The distinction is explicit at §2.9.4. Configurational Necessitation fixes a conditional where a complete configuration is metaphysically sufficient for an outcome; it doesn’t make the antecedent or outcome necessary simpliciter. Necessity Permits Contingency then adds that, *where contingency is independently established*, □(T∧S∧Φ) is consistent with ◇p ∧ ◇¬p. The Cartesian witness supplies actual C and therefore ◇C without supplying ◇¬C. Fine’s (2005) essence/necessity distinction sharpens the point: that change is occurring is a datum about the actual configuration; that change-events exist necessarily, if Williamson is right, is a claim about the domain. The proof spends the first and not an unearned alternative-history premise.

*Third.* The contingency-preservation move asks what remains open once the proof succeeds. The structural line decomposes into four elements. *Cartesian Certainty* supplies ◇C from actual change (§2.2). *Necessary Possibility* lifts ◇C to □◇C. *Modal Identity* states □(◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ) (§2.6.6). The theorem-level conclusion □(T∧S∧Φ) follows. No step requires a world at which ¬C or ¬(T∧S∧Φ) obtains. The necessitist challenge is therefore downstream: if the domain and every admissible configuration were fixed without alternative, the structural theorem would still hold, but the book couldn’t infer configuration-level contingency from it. That is precisely the boundary now marked at §2.9.4.

The reply runs at the level necessitism itself leaves open. Constant-domain quantification fixes what belongs to the unrestricted domain; it doesn’t by itself fix which properties those entities instantiate or which configurations are concrete. Williamson therefore preserves qualitative variation even while rejecting contingent existence. Where such variation supplies both p and ¬p possibilities, Necessity Permits Contingency shows how they coexist with the necessary Conditions. Where it doesn’t, the proof of the Conditions still stands and the stronger contingency claim remains unearned. Necessitism is compatible with the argument either way; what it doesn’t supply is the constitutive explanation of why every concrete configuration must instantiate T, S, and Φ.

Adams (1981) is helpful here as a foil: Adams holds that the qualitative-contingency level is itself unstable, but his argument depends on the haecceitist reading Williamson explicitly rejects. Hale’s (2013) structured-necessity account makes the cleaner point: necessities at different levels do different work, and the structural argument’s necessity at the constitutive level is compatible with qualitative-contingency at the configuration level. The stretch from □◇C to □(T∧S∧Φ) is non-trivial because the configuration-of-change is one qualitative possibility among others, and the actual configuration’s instantiation of that possibility is what the proof’s first premise records.

Williamson’s positive defense of S5 in *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* rests on considerations the structural argument finds hospitable rather than threatening. The present proof likewise reaches S5 from a different ground: real possibility is the standing capacity of the one Reality, R, so whether Capacity(R,P) obtains doesn’t change with a represented point of evaluation. This is distinct from Williamson’s constant-domain thesis about **individuals**. Reality’s invariant capacity doesn’t by itself entail a constant domain of entities across those worlds.

The Brouwer axiom (p → □◇p) then follows for the present operator because actuality entails Capacity(R,P), and that standing capacity doesn’t vary. The Cartesian datum establishes ◇C through actuality; the global-capacity account, not a prior claim that T, S, and Φ are everywhere instantiated, yields □◇C.

The disagreement is therefore precise. Williamson uses constant-domain QML to motivate ontological necessitism. The structural argument uses an invariant standing capacity of R to establish modal invariance, then separately derives the necessary Conditions that any world in that domain realizes. The shared formal result doesn’t settle the ontological reading.

Fine, engaged as dialectical opponent rather than as authority, presses the structural argument from a complementary direction. Fine’s “Essence and Modality” (1994) and “Necessity and Non-Existence” (2005) establish that necessity derives from essence: what makes a modal claim necessary is that it follows from the essence of some entity. Applied to the structural argument: what makes □(T∧S∧Φ) necessary? If it follows from the essence of T, S, or Φ themselves, the argument is circular: T, S, and Φ must already exist and have essences to generate the necessity, which is what the argument is trying to establish. If it follows from the essence of *change*, Fine will press that conceptual essence generates analytic necessity rather than unrestricted metaphysical necessity. The structural reply is that the argument’s modality is neither essence-based in Fine’s sense nor merely analytic. It is role-necessity: the necessity that anything being a *something* at all instantiates the structural conditions, grounded not in the essence of T, S, or Φ as entities but in the role-structure that any entity’s being anything at all requires. Role-necessity is proposed as an alternative explanatory basis, but Fine’s framework is flexible enough to ask whether structural roles themselves have essences or are grounded in more basic essences. The challenge therefore remains substantive: the priority of role-structure has to be defended rather than treated as outside Fine’s apparatus by definition.

A kindred move drops Williamson’s necessitism for Linnebo’s higher-order modal logic, where the Barcan formula is reformulated in plural-quantification terms and the necessitism/contingentism dialectic re-emerges at the level of pluralities rather than individuals. This form of the necessitist challenge can’t be turned aside by the observation that the structural roles are conditions rather than individuals. The first-order replies bank configuration-level contingency as the residue necessitism leaves free, and they can do so because first-order necessitism rigidifies only the domain of individuals. Higher-order and plural necessitism rigidify properties and pluralities as well, and configurations live at exactly that level. Plural logic isn’t silent where configurations operate; it is a logic of that level. The reply must therefore be earned at the higher order, not asserted to lie beneath it.

It is earned by lifting Williamson’s own distinction to the plural level, and the lift needs stating carefully rather than assuming that *concreteness* means at the higher order what it meant at the first. Necessitism separates *being* from *concreteness*: whatever exists, exists necessarily, but what is concrete is contingent; a thing has its being in every world and is concrete in only some. The higher-order analogue of that distinction isn’t concreteness but instantiation. A property, plurality, or configuration may exist necessarily and still fail to be instantiated at some world, and higher-order necessitism as Linnebo and Williamson develop it rigidifies the first without rigidifying the second. That residue is what the proof draws on. The first premise doesn’t record that some plurality exists; it records that the configuration-of-change is the one instantiated here.

The lift therefore holds unless a further thesis is added: that every configuration whose being is necessary is also instantiated at every world. That thesis isn’t necessitism, at any order. It is the modal collapse engaged on its own terms at §8.2.5, and a necessitist who declines it leaves the configuration-level residue standing. Linnebo’s apparatus extends the dialectic to pluralities without changing that structural issue, which was already present at the level of individuals.

**[Proposition]**

**Being, Not Concreteness** · *Proposition*

Necessitism separates being from concreteness: whatever exists exists necessarily, while what is concrete varies by world. At the higher order the analogue of concreteness is instantiation: a plurality or configuration may exist necessarily and still not be instantiated at every world. Higher-order necessitism rigidifies being at whichever order it is run, leaving instantiation free, and the proof’s first premise records an instantiation rather than a being. The residue therefore survives the ascent unless every necessarily-existing configuration is also instantiated everywhere, which is modal collapse rather than necessitism.

**Depends on:** Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4)

*Convergence.* Each of the three forms of the necessitist threat operates at a level the structural argument either accommodates or doesn’t depend on. The constant-domain compatibility move is correct that □(T∧S∧Φ) is consistent with necessitism, but it underestimates what the structural argument adds: the constitutive account of what makes the constant domain a domain. The Cartesian-Certainty preservation move targets the proof’s first premise by denying that an occurring change-event establishes an ontological addition to the domain; ◇C survives because it concerns Reality’s capacity to admit a configuration, not whether a change-event belongs to the unrestricted domain. The contingency-preservation move reaches a downstream question rather than a missing premise: qualitative variation is available within necessitism, and where it supplies genuine alternatives, Necessity Permits Contingency shows why the necessary Conditions don’t collapse them. The structural theorem itself doesn’t wait on that further result.

Williamson draws the conclusion that the formal apparatus deserves to be taken at face value: the quantifiers range over a constant domain, the Barcan formula and its converse are validated, and what looked like ontological contingency dissolves into qualitative variation across a fixed plurality. What Williamson left behind isn’t a refutation of the structural argument but a cleaner statement of the level at which the argument’s necessity claim operates: not at the qualitative-contingency level where Williamson preserves modal variation, but at the constitutive level where the variation is hosted.

### 7.2.8 Sider’s Structuralism
Theodore Sider published *Writing the Book of the World* in 2011, and the title is a job description for metaphysics. His argument is that the world has a privileged structure (a set of joint-carving notions) and that the project of metaphysics is to identify which notions those are. Existence quantifiers, mereological parthood, fundamentality, even logical operators: Sider is willing to ask of each whether it carves at the joints or merely tracks our practical interests. Modality is among the notions whose structural status Sider’s methodology invites us to assess. His project shouldn’t be reduced to the blanket claim that necessity is merely a relation between structure and language. The rival considered here is a Siderian or Humean extension on which modal ideology isn’t fundamental and modal truths supervene on non-modal joint-carving structure.

Sider (*Writing the Book of the World* 2011) gives the systematic statement; “Ontological Realism” (2009) supplies the methodologically central earlier paper. The position belongs to a broader structuralist family: Ladyman and Ross (*Every Thing Must Go* 2007) and French (*The Structure of the World* 2014) in philosophy of physics, both engaged at §9.10; Quine’s structuralism in philosophy of mathematics; and the line from Russell through Worrall (“Structural Realism: The Best of Both Worlds?” 1989) in philosophy of science. Sider extends the project into general metaphysics: logical, mereological, and existential structure, not only physical structure, may be fundamental. Schaffer (*Monism* 2010), Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds* 1986a), Williamson (*Modal Logic as Metaphysics* 2013), and Fine (“The Question of Realism,” 2001) supply nearby alternatives about grounding, modality, and structure. The present account agrees that metaphysics seeks structure the world has rather than a merely chosen scheme. The pressure is modal: can Sider’s privileged structure explain claims about every possible cosmos while remaining silent on the scope across which that privilege holds?

Sider’s structuralism presses the central claim of §1.5 from a direction §7.2.3, §8.2.5, and §7.2.7 don’t. Lewis multiplies the modal ontology; Modal Collapse worries about its propagation; Williamson endorses its scope. Sider deflates it. Modality, on his picture, is a way of speaking about what the privileged structure looks like through the lens of various linguistic frameworks, not a feature the structure itself possesses. T, S, and Φ might be perfectly real, perfectly joint-carving features of the actual world without being necessary features in any deeper sense. They are the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance—the trio the book’s argument derives. The argument’s necessity claim (□(T∧S∧Φ), read as “necessarily, T and S and Φ obtain together”) is, on the structuralist’s reading, a claim about how the world’s joint-carving organization looks under a particular modal idiom rather than a claim about anything that organization itself contains. The threat is precise: if modal scope is deflated, □(T∧S∧Φ) becomes an actual-world structural claim rather than a global-capacity necessity.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute isn’t with structural realism as a methodological program. The argument shares with Sider (and with Ladyman & Ross’s naturalistic structural realism, engaged at §9.10) the commitment that fundamental ontology is given by structural relations rather than by hidden quiddities (intrinsic natures beyond any structural or causal role). The dispute is with whether the structural ontology can be specified without modal scope. Three forms of the move press the deflation at three resolutions: the bare deflation move, the redundancy move, and the no-modal-realism move. The replies test whether any form can deflate modal scope without requiring it to specify what the joint-carving ontology consists in.

*First.* The bare deflation move holds that modal claims aren’t joint-carving. There are facts about what is the case (Sider’s privileged structure, the actual configuration of the world) and there are facts about what would have been the case, but the second class of facts is derivative. Possible-worlds talk tracks something useful; what it tracks isn’t modal reality but the relations between linguistic frameworks and the privileged structure. The argument’s modal claims, on this reading, are linguistic claims with structural correlates rather than structural claims about modal space.

The deflation requires specifying what the privileged ontology consists in. Sider’s account answers in joint-carving notions—those that track reality’s own fundamental divisions rather than merely our practical interests: existence, parthood, fundamentality, identity, predication, plus whichever physical and logical primitives the final theory turns out to require. Two readings of joint-carving status are available. On the first, joint-carving status is exegeted modally: what the joint-carving ontology would recommend across counterfactual variation in our descriptive vocabularies. On the second, developed across the Sider–Fine–Schaffer hyperintensional-structuralist line (Fine, “The Question of Realism,” 2001; Schaffer, “On What Grounds What,” 2009), with Lewis’s perfectly-natural-properties as the precedent for a non-modal structural primitive in even the arch-modal-realist’s metaphysics, joint-carving status is primitive structural-fundamentality, hyperintensional, not analyzable modally.

The argument’s reply doesn’t require the first reading. Grant Sider the second: joint-carving is primitive structural-fundamentality, ontologically prior to modal facts. The argument’s modal scope, if earned, comes from the global-capacity and structural arguments of Chapters 2–3, not from later empirical or cross-substrate applications. The redundancy move next asks whether that prior modal commitment adds content beyond actual-world joint-carving status.

A note on the target, because the strongest deflationary rival here is a constructed one. Sider’s own commitment is that modal ideology isn’t joint-carving; that is a claim about what belongs in the fundamental book of the world, and it doesn’t by itself say what makes modal claims true. The Humean extension that does say so is the position worth engaging: modal truths supervene on the actual-world mosaic of non-modal joint-carving patterns, so what makes a modal claim true is whether the pattern it describes is carved in that mosaic. That is richer than bare deflationism, since it grounds modal claims in structural fabric rather than dismissing them, and it is the form the reply below addresses. It is attributed to the position, not to Sider.

The reply presses one question: does the mosaic’s joint-carving character hold necessarily or contingently? Suppose it is contingent: a different cosmos could have entirely different joint-carving patterns. Modal grounding then bottoms out in a contingent mosaic and doesn’t capture the structural argument’s necessity claim. Suppose it is necessary: any mosaic must have these patterns simply to be a mosaic with causal joints. The extension then approaches the structural conclusion instead of deflating it. The argument offered here takes the second route. The three Conditions are joint-carving across any cosmos because they are conditions on there being a fabric with causal joints at all.

A third answer is available and worth stating, since it is the one a best-system Humean will give. The carving may be contingent while modal truths are fixed by a consequence relation over it: what is necessary is what follows from the system that best balances simplicity and strength for the actual mosaic. That answer is coherent, and it relocates the question rather than settling it. The necessity it delivers is necessity relative to one mosaic, and the structural claim quantifies over the mosaics there could be; asked what fixes the range of admissible mosaics, the best-system theorist either answers with a further non-modal fact about the actual world, which doesn’t reach the range, or with a constraint on what any mosaic must be, which is the second horn under another name.

**[Proposition]**

**The Mosaic’s Own Modal Status** · *Proposition*

Positive Humeanism grounds modal truth in the actual mosaic’s joint-carving patterns. Ask whether that carving holds necessarily or contingently. Contingently, and the grounding bottoms out in a contingent mosaic, capturing no necessity of the kind in dispute. Necessarily, and the patterns any mosaic must have to be a mosaic are what the structural account names, so the position endorses the conclusion rather than deflating it. A best-system answer, on which necessity is what follows from the system best fitting the actual mosaic, delivers necessity relative to one mosaic and returns the question as what fixes the range of admissible mosaics. The target is the Humean extension rather than Sider’s own thesis that modal ideology isn’t joint-carving.

**Depends on:** The Self-Application Fork (§7.1)

*Second.* The redundancy move asks whether the later applications require modal scope at all. Where the present argument makes modal predictions, the cycle (§4.6), substrate-independence of consciousness (§4.8), the preclusion of absolute nothingness (§2.7), Sider’s structuralism delivers them as descriptions of how this world’s structure works. The cycle is what the actual cosmic dynamics deliver; the argument’s modal apparatus is metaphysical surplus. The substrate-independence claim is what neuroscience plus the physics of information processing delivers; the argument’s “in any world where T, S, Φ obtain...” formulation is bookkeeping. The preclusion of absolute nothingness is what cosmological inflation plus the structure of quantum field theory delivers; the modal scope adds nothing physics can’t say more carefully without it.

The redundancy diagnosis turns on the prior modal proof. Actual-world joint-carving status says that this mosaic instantiates its fundamental patterns. The book’s stronger claim says that every world in the invariant standing capacity of R instantiates at least T/S/Φ. That difference is genuine, but later applications don’t establish it. Substrate-neutral consciousness claims are conditionals whose scope is inherited from the structural account; cyclic recurrence isn’t a consequence of □T and remains a separate cosmological hypothesis. The reply to Sider must therefore stand or fall with Chapters 2–3’s independent case for global necessity, not with the success of §4 predictions.

Whether this broader generality matters depends on what the structural argument is for. If only our actual universe is at stake, Sider’s deflation may suffice. If the structural conditions are genuinely necessary across any cosmos, as §2.6–2.7 argue, then the modal scope isn’t surplus but constitutive; it is the difference between describing what this world happens to do and identifying the conditions any world must satisfy to be a world at all.

*Third.* The no-modal-realism move denies that modal facts concern a modal reality. They concern how the privileged structure relates to descriptive frameworks. The structural argument’s “necessarily, T∧S∧Φ” can be rewritten as “in the privileged structure, T∧S∧Φ are joint-carving features of the actual world’s fundamental ontology,” with no modal claim left over. The argument’s content is preserved, its modal commitment dissolved.

The rewriting fails to preserve content. “In the privileged structure, T∧S∧Φ are joint-carving features of the actual world’s fundamental ontology” is true if T, S, Φ obtain in the actual world and the ontology carves at the joints. It doesn’t entail that T, S, Φ obtain in any other world. But the argument needs the entailment. The foreclosure of absolute nothingness and the global-capacity structural claim are presented in Chapter 2 as holding across worlds. Sider’s rewriting eliminates the across-world reach. What it preserves is the actual world’s organization; what it loses is the necessity that makes the three conditions load-bearing. Joint-carving features can be contingent; structural conditions of any cosmos aren’t. The bold rewriting trades the second for the first and calls the trade a translation.

A kindred move drops Sider’s full structuralism for the more cautious naturalistic structural realism of Ladyman & Ross. NSR holds that physics gives us structural facts about the actual world without committing to whether those facts are necessary across worlds. The reply runs as it does at §9.10: NSR is a methodological constraint on physics that is silent on the modal question; it isn’t a positive metaphysical alternative to the present argument. The argument welcomes NSR’s empirical structuralism and adds the modal architecture NSR’s caution declines to address. The two positions aren’t competitors but layered.

*Convergence.* Structural deflation can accept actual T/S/Φ while withholding □(T∧S∧Φ). The translation from necessity to actual joint-carving status therefore loses content if the prior global-capacity argument succeeds. Nothing in §4 independently restores that content: substrate-neutral applications inherit the scope, and cyclic recurrence remains conditional. The dispute with Sider is consequently clean and upstream—whether Chapters 2–3 have earned a global modal floor—not an empirical confirmation supplied by later cosmology or consciousness claims.

The agreement between Sider’s structuralism and the argument is real and worth naming explicitly. The structural-realist insight that physics names the constraints rather than discovers properties hidden behind them is already endorsed at §4.5. The Triconditional Cross-Entailment of §2.6.7 and the Ontological Identity of §2.6.8 operate within a framework that is recognizably continuous with Sider’s. What the argument adds (and what is made explicit here) is the modal floor under the structuralism. Joint-carving features can be contingent; necessary structural conditions can’t—the same distinction the Necessity Permits Contingency result names directly (§2.9.4): the necessity attaches to the structural floor, never automatically to what stands on it.

Sider’s defense of joint-carving structuralism holds that there is a privileged structure, that metaphysics aims to identify it, and that the identification is revisionary: we discover the world’s joints rather than choose among equally legitimate frameworks. The defense answers critics for whom general metaphysics had begun to look like terminological housekeeping rather than discovery. The present argument shares that project. What it adds is the modal commitment on which its across-substrate claims depend: not only that this world has its particular joint-carving organization, but that any possible cosmos must instantiate at least the three conditions to be a cosmos at all. Sider’s joint-carving claim concerns which structure is privileged; the argument’s necessity claim concerns the range across which some structure must obtain. The book of the world has more pages than one cosmos can fill.

## 7.3 Modal Logic and Modal Knowledge
The rivals in this section attack the apparatus rather than the claims made with it. Impossible worlds and relative modality (§7.3.1) press whether one absolute space of possibility can be sustained, or whether modality is always indexed to a standard; the remoteness objection (§7.3.2) asks how anyone could know what holds at possibilities far from the actual; Chisholm’s paradox (§7.3.3) chains small variations in an individual’s properties or origin until the chain arrives somewhere no single step could reach, and demands to know which link breaks; and Gasking’s parody (§7.3.4) reproduces the argument’s form to derive an absurdity, charging that the form proves too much to prove anything.

These are objections to method. If they reach the machinery the argument actually uses, repeating the earlier conclusions can’t save them: the means of establishing those conclusions has failed. The question in each case is therefore exact—does the objection touch its commitments, or a further commitment the framework never made?

### 7.3.1 Impossible Worlds and Relative Modality
Two pressures are often filed together and should be separated, because they attack different parts of the same sentence. One enlarges the space of worlds to include impossible ones (Priest 2005; Berto and Jago 2019; Nolan 1997). The other relativizes the quantifier to a contextually supplied background (Kratzer 2012). The first asks whether □(T∧S∧Φ) has been quantifying over too little. The second asks whether its □ means anything absolute at all.

*First.* The non-normal-worlds objection targets the S5 derivation rather than the structural conclusion. Non-normal worlds invalidate necessitation by allowing logical truths to fail and modal formulas to be evaluated by stipulation rather than by the accessibility clause. On that semantics, ◇C may hold at the actual world while □◇C fails at a non-normal one. If the book’s lift were licensed by accessibility among worlds, the device would block it directly.

The reply has two stages, and the first locates the target. The book does use a lift from ◇C to □◇C, but it doesn’t derive that lift by climbing an accessibility relation between worlds. The rule reads as invariance in a determination made by Reality’s standing capacity (§1.2.6): what R can admit doesn’t change with the configuration from which that capacity is reported. The S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5) therefore defends the scope of real possibility rather than the geometry of accessibility. The same limit is stated from the formal side at §2.1.4: the derivation infers no Acc(x,y), mutual accessibility, or plurality of real worlds. A device that alters accessibility semantics reaches the book only if it also shows that R’s standing capacity varies by configuration. The non-normal stipulation alone doesn’t establish that further claim.

The second stage is the substantive one. An impossible world is admitted as a *representation* of an inconsistent content, not as a genuine alternative way for reality to be. Nolan makes the point in defending the modest approach (1997): impossible worlds earn their keep as representational devices for reasoning about inconsistent scenarios, and admitting them carries no commitment to their being possibilities. But a representational device is an item with content, and content is structured. The reply developed against linguistic ersatzism at Linguistic Ersatzism (§7.2.4) applies here without modification: distinct representations must be distinct (the S-role), must be evaluated in an ordered succession of acts (the T-role), and must be borne by something that carries the content (the Φ-role). Enlarging the space of representations enlarges the space of representations. The □ in □(T∧S∧Φ) ranges over genuine alternatives, and no number of additional representations adds one.

A further point closes the limit case. An impossible world at which the three Conditions all fail isn’t merely an inconsistent scenario but the null state, and the argument of §3.2.6 is that the null state is unspecifiable rather than merely inconsistent. The distinction matters exactly here, because the impossible-worlds theorist is professionally in the business of hosting inconsistent contents. A round square is hostable: it has parts to describe, and the description can be given and then found contradictory. The null state has no parts to describe, and the corresponding point is made against the fictionalist at §3.3.3. An impossible-worlds semantics can host any content that can be stated. What it can’t do is supply a content where none can be stated, and that is the case the necessity claim turns on. An impossible-worlds theorist who assigns content to it by stipulation rather than by specification is disputing that premise rather than evading it. The dispute is worth having in those terms: the question is whether a semantics may assign a content to a description that specifies nothing, and it is settled where the null state is argued, not by the inventory of worlds a semantics admits.

*Second.* Hyperintensionality supplies a central motivation for the literature, and the response here is concession rather than denial. Berto and Jago argue that necessity is too coarse a sieve for many of the distinctions metaphysics needs (2019): necessarily equivalent contents aren’t thereby the same content, and a framework whose finest grain is necessary equivalence will misdescribe the differences between them.

That is granted without reservation, and the concession is smaller than it looks because the argument doesn’t merely tolerate the point—it relies on it. Two distinct claims are in play, stated at two different grains, and the objection reaches only the coarser one.

The *necessity* claim is that the three Conditions obtain at every genuine alternative. It is stated at the grain of necessity, it needs nothing finer, and hyperintensional distinctions cut below it without cutting into it. Berto and Jago are right that necessarily equivalent contents aren’t thereby the same content; nothing in that observation bears on where the Conditions obtain.

The *identity* claim is hyperintensional and says so. It is established at §2.6.9 that once both relata are necessary their modal co-extension follows for free and distinguishes nothing, since it would hold between any two necessary truths whatever; what makes the Modal Identity a result rather than a triviality is the absence of individuating content on either side, which is a claim about what specifying each side consists in and not about where the two are jointly true. That is precisely a grain finer than necessity, adopted deliberately, and it commits the argument to the objection’s own thesis rather than against it. A framework whose finest grain were necessary equivalence couldn’t state the book’s central identity at all, which is why the book doesn’t use one.

So the relation is convergence rather than concession, and a worked instance is supplied: an identity claim whose whole content survives at the finer grain and vanishes at the coarser. What remains genuinely open is narrower—whether the no-surplus criterion the identity runs on is the *right* hyperintensional notion, or whether some more discriminating account of essence is needed to state what the Conditions are. That is the essence-prior question, engaged at §7.2.1 rather than settled here.

*Third.* The relative-modality form runs from linguistic semantics. On the standard account (Kratzer 2012), a modal expression is interpreted relative to a contextually supplied modal base together with an ordering source, and the many flavours of necessity (epistemic, deontic, nomic, metaphysical) are one machine supplied with different backgrounds. If that is right, metaphysical necessity isn’t a privileged absolute but one setting among many, and □(T∧S∧Φ) reduces to a claim about what follows given a particular background. Another background, another verdict.

The reply is that context-relativity in this framework operates on the *restriction*, not on the *domain*. A modal base selects which worlds a claim quantifies over; it doesn’t introduce genuine alternatives that weren’t there. Some bases do reach beyond the genuine alternatives—an epistemic base holds open what a speaker hasn’t ruled out, including things metaphysically ruled out already—and those bases quantify over representations rather than over ways Reality could be, which is the distinction the reply to impossible worlds has just drawn. The structural claim is field-level—about Reality’s complete modal constitution, not any world’s local inventory (§2.4)—so what every member of the domain *inherits* is answerability to that one field, not a local copy of T, S, and Φ each world separately contains. A subset of a set whose members are all so answerable has no member that fails to be. Varying the background varies which necessities are salient and which are worth asserting. It can’t vary what a world is.

**[Premise]**

**Restriction Adds Nothing** · *Premise*

1. A modal base selects, from the worlds available to the semantics, the ones a modal claim quantifies over (Kratzer semantics).

2. □(T∧S∧Φ) states that every represented world corresponding to a genuine alternative is answerable to Reality’s one structural field, not that each such world locally realizes the conditions as its own separate inventory.

3. Where the base is drawn from genuine alternatives, it selects a subset of the configurations R can admit, and a subset introduces no member the domain lacked.

4. Where the base admits worlds that are not genuine alternatives—an epistemic base includes worlds ruled out metaphysically, since what might be so for all a speaker knows need not be so much as possible—it quantifies over representations, and representations are not what □(T∧S∧Φ) ranges over.

5. So no choice of modal base delivers a genuine alternative lacking the conditions. Context-relativity varies which necessities are asserted, not what an alternative is.

The conclusion generalizes past Kratzer’s framework specifically. Any relativization that proceeds by restricting a domain inherits the argument, because restriction is a subset operation and a subset operation can’t manufacture a configuration R can’t admit. A relativization that instead *replaces* the domain, supplying worlds that don’t represent configurations R can admit, is no longer a restriction and owes an account of where the new worlds came from and in what sense they are alternatives. That account is the one already pressed for at §7.2.3 and §7.2.4, and the demand is unchanged by relabeling the framework as semantic rather than metaphysical.

One clarification of scope is owed. Nothing in this argument denies that there are genuinely relative modalities, or that most ordinary uses of *must* and *can* are relative in exactly Kratzer’s way. The §7.2 overview grants this already. The claim is narrower: that a relative modality is a restriction on the field rather than a rival to it, and that the field is what the structural conclusion describes.

*Taking stock.* Non-normal worlds block accessibility-based derivations of S5. The book’s derivation instead treats real possibility as R’s standing capacity, so the live objection must show that this capacity varies with the reporting configuration; stipulating non-normal evaluation doesn’t yet do so. Impossible worlds otherwise multiply representations rather than alternatives, and the representations are themselves structured. Hyperintensionality is shared: necessary equivalence is too coarse for identity, which is why the central identity is stated at the finer no-surplus grain (§2.6.9). Kratzer-style relativization restricts a domain it doesn’t populate, and restriction can’t produce a world the domain lacked. Each apparatus changes how the field is represented or restricted; none, without the further argument just identified, changes what R can admit.

### 7.3.2 Modal Epistemology and the Remoteness Objection
Quine denies that the modal vocabulary is intelligible. Van Inwagen grants it and denies something else: that the faculty by which we reach modal verdicts is reliable at the distances philosophy asks it to work at. Van Inwagen is the canonical statement (1998). Ordinary modal knowledge is secure, on this view, because it operates by small variation on the actual: the table could have stood two feet to the left, the meeting could have run long. Remote modal claims (that there could be a being than which none greater can be conceived, that there could be a physical duplicate of a person lacking consciousness, that transparent iron is possible) are cases where the faculty has been carried far past anything that calibrates it, and the confident verdicts philosophers return aren’t knowledge.

This isn’t the skepticism of §7.1.3, and the two must not be run together. The Quinean refuses the vocabulary. Van Inwagen keeps the vocabulary, keeps ordinary modal knowledge, and refuses the extension. A reply that vindicates the intelligibility of *necessarily* leaves his objection entirely untouched, which is why it needs its own address. Its compositional half is discharged at §8.3.4; the half taken up here is the one that section explicitly defers.

The objection lands with more force here than almost anywhere, because □(T∧S∧Φ) is about as remote as a modal claim gets. It quantifies over every world, including worlds bearing no resemblance to anything experienced, and it returns a verdict of necessity rather than mere pervasiveness. By van Inwagen’s own criterion of similarity to ordinary life, no claim in the book is further from the calibrated range.

The concession runs in full. Van Inwagen is right that a great deal of analytic metaphysics has run on brute intuitions about distant scenarios; right that no one has produced a credible account of a faculty that would deliver such verdicts reliably; right that the modal ontological argument and the zombie argument both turn on exactly this move; right that the burden falls on whoever wants a remote modal conclusion. That is already granted at §3.3.4, and the agreement isn’t tactical. On conceivability, the book accepts van Inwagen’s warning and therefore owes a route that doesn’t rely on remote modal intuition.

*First.* The remoteness form runs directly. Ordinary modal knowledge proceeds by imaginative variation from the actual, the reach of that method is short, and □(T∧S∧Φ) lies far outside it. So whatever warrant the conclusion has, it can’t be the warrant ordinary modal claims have.

The reply is that the conclusion isn’t an output of that method, and the point is methodological rather than defensive. The argument nowhere asks the reader to imagine a world and report what is found there. It asks the reader to *specify* one and observe what the specification requires. Those are different operations, and only the second is publicly checkable. The S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5) is a clear case: it doesn’t invite the objector to picture a world lacking the structural conditions, it invites the objector to describe one, and the argument turns on what the description turns out to contain. An invitation to describe can be accepted or declined in a way an invitation to imagine can’t, and its results can be inspected by someone who doesn’t share the imaginer’s phenomenology. Van Inwagen’s skepticism is calibrated against a faculty; the derivation doesn’t run on that faculty.

The inversion is the book’s general shape. Where the standard method treats *I can conceive of it* as evidence for possibility, the method here treats *a specification whose own conditions consume what it denies* as evidence for impossibility. The first is a report about the person; the second is a result about the specified object.

*Second.* The parity form presses that the reply hasn’t escaped anything. The premises of the derivation are themselves modal claims (that a way must have direction, difference, and bearer; that no world can lack the conditions), and modal claims are what the skepticism targets. Relocating the warrant from imagination to specification changes the vocabulary of the defense without changing what is defended.

The reply distinguishes two ways a modal verdict can be reached. One surveys possibilities and reports what is found among them, and that method requires epistemic access to the possibilities surveyed, which at remote distances is exactly what van Inwagen denies is available. The other analyzes a proposed scenario and asks whether its object-side conditions contradict one another. That method requires no survey of distant worlds, but it requires a discipline the argument can’t waive: structure used by the act of description isn’t thereby structure in the described object. A temporal sentence can concern an atemporal object; a structured model can represent an empty domain. Only a contradiction among the proposed object’s own conditions supports impossibility. Failure of the act supports, at most, a burden on the offered route.

*Third.* The reliability form presses from both directions. Roca-Royes argues that conceivability-based methods don’t deliver de re modal knowledge of the kind essentialist conclusions require (2011). From the other side, Hawke argues that van Inwagen’s own similarity-to-ordinary-life criterion is unstable, either permitting too much or forbidding the ordinary knowledge it means to protect (2011). Applied here, the question is why an inability to complete a specification indicates impossibility rather than a limit on the specifier. Every inference from failure to construct risks becoming an argument from ignorance.

The worry is granted in general and answered by separating two diagnoses. If the proposed object must itself instantiate what it denies—if, for example, a concrete change is specified while every before/after, real separation, or bearer is removed—the object-side clauses contradict one another. If only the thinker, sentence, or model instantiates what the object denies, the diagnosis is act-side: this attempt hasn’t supplied the object, but the represented scenario hasn’t thereby been disproved. Bare inability remains evidence only about the specifier. The distinction between *the object consumes what it denies* and *the representation uses what the object denies* is the whole of the revised test.

**[Principle]**

**The Specification Test** · *Principle*

1. For a remote candidate p, distinguish the representing act from the represented object.

2. If p’s own satisfaction conditions require and deny the same feature, p is incoherent.

3. If only the representing act deploys what p denies, the result is act-side: that representation has not established p, but p is not thereby impossible.

4. If specification merely stalls, the result is an unmet epistemic burden, not an impossibility result.

5. Negative modal results are claimed only under (2); results under (3) and (4) are marked at their narrower strength.

The standard cuts against the book as well as for it, which is the reason to adopt it. It commits the argument to marking which of its negative results are diagnosed and which rest on nothing better than an unproductive search, and any result of the second kind is owed a downgrade rather than a defense.

The distinction applies across the load-bearing negative results. The masking test (§2.4.12) is object-side if the proposed world both instantiates and globally forecloses the same change-conditions. The fictionalist and conceivability replies are act-side where they show only that representation is structured (§3.3.3–3.3.4). The null-state argument must likewise stand on the claimed absence of any object-side satisfaction conditions, not on the temporal or cognitive structure of our attempt to imagine absence. Chapter 7’s verdict ledger (§7.4) records these differences rather than treating every retorsion as one kind of proof.

*The problem being answered has a name.* Vaidya and Wallner (2021) call it the *problem of modal epistemic friction*, and stating it in their terms sharpens what the Specification Test is for. Imagination can’t be applied without restriction on pain of delivering the impossible—water without hydrogen is the clear case, and transparent iron is the instructive one, offered by van Inwagen precisely because nobody can say whether it is possible while imagination returns a verdict anyway—so any modal epistemology owes an account of what supplies the friction, and of how a reasoner comes to deploy the friction creators correctly. They further separate two questions that this section has been running together: an *Access* question, how modal knowledge is acquired at all without leaning on prior modal premises, and a *Navigation* question, how one moves between kinds of modality once some modal knowledge is in hand (the remoteness objection is an Access question; the alethic/doxastic separation at §7.1 and the global-capacity restriction at §2.1.5 are Navigation questions).

Read that way, the Specification Test is a proposed friction creator, and a deliberately austere one. It doesn’t appeal to grasp of essence, to conceptual competence, or to any faculty whose calibration van Inwagen could question, since those are precisely what is in dispute. The friction it supplies is internal to the candidate: a proposal’s own satisfaction conditions either contradict one another or they don’t, and that is inspectable by anyone without a survey of remote worlds. The test earns its keep exactly where Vaidya and Wallner say friction is needed, and it purchases that with a correspondingly narrow yield—negative verdicts only, and only under object-side contradiction.

What isn't supplied here is a general theory of friction creators. Vaidya and Wallner leave the question open, and nothing here closes it; the claim is only that one such creator is available, doesn’t presuppose the faculty under attack, and is enough to carry the book’s negative results at the strength they are marked. The survey by Mallozzi, Vaidya, and Wallner (2021) is the point of entry for the wider literature this section doesn’t attempt to settle.

An ally inside the book is recorded on the same terms, with the disclaimer doing more work than usual. A structural account of why conceiving behaves this way is given at §5.5: imagining loads a branch into a modal field by recombination from what the field already holds, and nothing internal to the composing checks the result against the domain. Recombination is free by construction, so the operation raises modal depth without touching modal fidelity, and an unrestricted imagination is structurally over-generative rather than accidentally unreliable. That is a mechanism for the asymmetry already asserted—why *I can conceive of it* is a report about the conceiver while a specification that consumes what it denies is a result about the specified object—and it predicts the pattern rather than restating it, since conceivability tracks an accumulated representational stock that grows while what R can admit doesn’t. The disclaimer: that identification is defended by fit to the phenomena rather than derived, so a treatment here that leaned on it would inherit the conditionality and end up weaker than it is. The dependence runs the other way, and should: the Specification Test constrains what §5.5 may claim, not the reverse.

An ally in the literature is available and should be recorded, though the argument doesn’t depend on it either. Williamson (2007, ch. 5) argues that modal knowledge isn’t the deliverance of a special faculty at all but a byproduct of the ordinary capacity to evaluate counterfactuals, which is exercised constantly and isn’t obviously less reliable at metaphysical distances than at everyday ones. If that account is right, van Inwagen’s skepticism loses its target, because there is no distinct modal faculty whose calibration range can be exceeded. The present reply is deliberately weaker and doesn’t require Williamson’s account to be correct. It requires only that specification is a different operation from imagination, and that its failures can be diagnosed.

*Taking stock.* Van Inwagen’s challenge isn’t answered by producing confidence at the relevant distance. Object-side contradictions can support negative modal verdicts without a remote survey; act-side failures can’t. What remains is a standing demand that the book distinguish contradiction in the proposed scenario from structure in its representation and from inability to find a model.

### 7.3.3 Chisholm’s Paradox: Chained Origins
Roderick Chisholm asked a question in 1967 about Adam and Noah (Chisholm 1967). Adam lived 930 years, Noah 950. Surely Adam could have lived a year longer, and Noah a year less: nothing in either man’s essence hangs on a single year. Grant the concession once and a world opens in which Adam lives 931 and Noah 949. Grant it again from there, and again, and let the rest go the same way, one small exchange at a time: the lifespans, then everything else that marks each man out. The chain ends in a world in which Adam has every property Noah actually has and Noah every property Adam has, which is to say a world in which each is the other. Every step was innocent. The destination isn’t. Chisholm’s Paradox is the ancestor of every later argument that possibility is *chained*: that what is possible depends on where the question is asked from, and that iterating small admissible variations carries one somewhere no single leap could have reached.

Hugh Chandler (1976) ran the same pattern on artifacts rather than patriarchs and aimed it at the machinery the present derivation uses. A bicycle assembled from a given set of parts could have been assembled with one part swapped; from *that* world, another swap is admissible; and the chain terminates in an assembly too distant from the original to have been possible for the original bicycle. His title, “Plantinga and the Contingently Possible,” marks the target: Plantinga’s modal apparatus (1974) turns on the same transfer principle the present argument uses.

Nathan Salmon develops the case through Kripke’s table. A table made from hunk of wood H could have been made from the slightly different H′, and a table made from H′ could have been made from H″—although H″ wasn’t a possible origin for the original table (N. Salmon 1981; 1989; Kripke 1980). Salmon draws the conclusion the others resist: metaphysical accessibility isn’t transitive. If so, S4 can’t collapse a two-step modal chain into a single step, and the S5 transfer fails with it. Salmon is careful about what fails. A table made from H″ is possible on his view; what isn’t possible is that *the original table* was made from it.

The available replies preserve different parts of the case. Graeme Forbes keeps the logic and locates the trouble in vagueness, through degree-theoretic and then counterpart-theoretic treatments (Forbes 1984; Forbes 1985). Lewis appeals to the inconstancy of counterpart relations: modal properties are read from resembling individuals in other worlds, and the respects of resemblance shift with context (Lewis 1968; Lewis 1986a). Timothy Williamson supplies an epistemicist option on which the series has a sharp but unknowable cutoff (Williamson 1994). Kripke’s origin essentialism stands behind the dispute: a thing couldn’t have come from a wholly different origin and still be that thing (Kripke 1980). The literature therefore disagrees about whether the chain revises the logic, exposes vagueness, shifts counterpart relations, or crosses a boundary that exists even though we can’t locate it.

Brought to bear on the present argument, the objection targets the logic directly rather than the ontology. Necessary Possibility is established at §2.1.10: whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary (◇P → □◇P), with the bilateral companion that whatever is impossible, its impossibility is necessary (¬◇P → □¬◇P). It is packaged into S5 at §2.1.4; the move from the actuality of change to its necessary possibility at Necessary Possibility of Change (§2.3) runs on it, and so does the Modal Identity of §2.6.6. If possibility is chained, the transfer is unsound in its unrestricted form, and no amount of care about T, S, and Φ—Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality, the three structural Conditions—repairs it. The objector grants the framework, possible-worlds semantics, and origin essentialism, then supplies cases in which stepwise admissibility outruns admissibility for the original object. The reply must explain those cases without assuming the transitivity they contest.

A clarification before the moves, and a distinction the replies turn on. The argument’s ◇ means *real possibility*: ◇P just when the one Reality, R, has the standing capacity to admit P, Capacity(R,P) (§1.2.1, §2.1). Two kinds of proposition must then be kept apart. A *qualitative* proposition says what kind of thing obtains without fixing which individual is involved: “some table is made from H″,” or “change occurs.” A *singular* proposition concerns a particular thing: “*this* table is made from H″.” Both are propositions, and the theorem as stated at §2.1.10 ranges over both, so the distinction doesn’t move the singular cases outside its scope. What it does is locate them. Every case in this literature generates its pressure through the identity of an individual across the variations: the chain is harmless until someone asks whether the thing at the far link is still *this* one. Three forms of the objection press at different resolutions: Chisholm and Chandler’s chained-origin move, Salmon’s rejection of transitivity, and counterpart-theoretic inconstancy. The replies must preserve the intuitions driving the series while explaining why they do or don’t reach the book’s global-capacity operator; merely contradicting the cases would explain nothing.

*First.* The chained-origin move holds that the series of small variations is individually innocent and jointly unacceptable, so possibility must be relative to a starting point. Each link is possible relative to its predecessor; the endpoint isn’t possible relative to the origin; therefore what is possible varies with where the question is asked.

The reply begins with the qualitative propositions, because there the chain has no case at all. “A table made from slightly different wood” is among the least exotic possibilities ever entertained in philosophy: furniture workshops witness it by the thousand daily. Every such table is already among the ways Reality permits, and no act of carpentry puts it there—the carpenter never once consults an accessibility relation. Salmon agrees, and the agreement generalizes link by link. Whatever configuration obtains at the far end of the chain obtains at a world that differs from it only in which table is which, and nothing in an origin constraint excludes that world, because an origin constraint restricts which individual can have which origin, not which configurations can obtain. Chisholm’s case runs the same way with essence in place of origin. The non-transitivity, if it is real, is confined to singular propositions about individuals that carry their origins or essences with them.

That confinement protects what the derivation actually spends. The lift at §2.3 applies the theorem to ◇C, and C there is change of the witnessed kind, not “this reader, this page, or any particular expression of the capacity.” ◇C is qualitative. However the singular cases are resolved, they supply no failure of transfer for it.

**[Proposition]**

**The Chain Stops at the Individual** · *Proposition*

Chained-origin cases generate their pressure only through an individual’s tolerance for variation in its origin or essence. Whatever configuration obtains at any link obtains at a world differing only in which individual is which, and a constraint on which individual can have which origin doesn’t exclude that world. Even granting the non-transitivity the cases are offered to show, it is confined to singular propositions, and the transfer the lift spends, on the qualitative proposition ◇C, is untouched.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility of Change (§2.3)

*Second.* Salmon’s version refuses to leave the theorem its unrestricted form. His ◇, he insists, is the metaphysician’s own unrelativized operator and not a disguised accessibility relation; the cases show that operator to be non-transitive for singular propositions, and a theorem stated over every proposition inherits the failure.

For singular propositions the reply can’t take the qualitative route, and shouldn’t pretend to. Ask of the far link: is *this table’s* originating from H″ among the ways Reality permits, or not? On the reading fixed at §2.1.10, the question admits one answer. If yes, Capacity(R, this table from H″) held all along, and what varied along the chain was never modal standing but tolerable distance from a shifting anchor—a fact about the essentialist premise, not about the logic. If no, then no sequence of intermediate represented worlds confers that capacity, since traversing representations doesn’t alter R. Salmon declines the question in that form. When he says the far origin wasn’t possible for the table *originally*, the adverb carries the weight: his possibility for singular propositions is indexed to a starting point. That is one of the positions Necessary Possibility names as a live target (§2.1.10), the replacement of global real possibility by a relative modality, and it is met there, at the premises of no-exteriority and modal exhaustion, not dissolved here.

What can be weighed here is how much support the cases lend the relativization, and the point is abductive. They don’t force it. The same data—every step tolerable, the endpoint not—are explained by Forbes’s vague counterparthood, by supervaluation over admissible sharpenings, and by Williamson’s unknowable cutoff, and each of those keeps one range and its S5 logic. The cases underdetermine the choice between a non-transitive operator and a tolerant, vague essence. The global reading, meanwhile, isn’t introduced to handle modal puzzles; it is derived from no-exteriority and modal exhaustion. An underdetermining case doesn’t outweigh a derivation, though a failure of the derivation’s premises would.
