The dispute stays where it was, at those premises, and the chain adds no independent pressure to them.

On the global reading, the chain also can’t travel without paying. To move from H to H′ to H″, the argument must concede at every link that the intermediate origin is possible; that concession is what licenses the step. But a conceded possibility, run through the transfer, is a necessary possibility: each step certifies its own destination as something R can invariantly admit. Meanwhile no step removes anything, because unreachability isn’t eviction—that an origin can’t be reached from a given anchor is silent on whether it is in the range at all. So the chain deposits members and withdraws none. Pursued to its end, the argument has populated the range of configurations R can admit that it set out to fragment, and the only thing still varying at the far link is the singular label: which of those necessarily possible tables counts as *this* one.

**[Proposition]**

**The Chain Populates What It Means to Fragment** · *Proposition*

On the global-capacity reading of possibility, moving from H to H′ to H″ requires conceding at every link that the intermediate origin is possible, and a conceded possibility, run through the transfer, is a necessary possibility: each step certifies its own destination as something R can invariantly admit. No step removes anything, since unreachability from a given anchor is not eviction from the range. The chain therefore deposits members and withdraws none, populating the range of configurations R can admit that it was supposed to fragment. Against a theorist who relativizes possibility for singular propositions, this states what the chain costs rather than refuting the relativization.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10)

One further point bears on the relativist’s own picture. If “possible for this table relative to one world, impossible relative to another” states a fact, the rule fixing which origins are tolerable relative to which anchors must itself hold whichever world one evaluates from. What varies is an individual’s reach under a fixed rule, not the rule. That is all the variation hypothesis needs, and it sits comfortably with a single range of configurations standing behind every anchor, which is the range the lift uses.

The candor kept elsewhere is owed here too. Salmon can plant on the disputed point and hold that the unrelativized operator simply is non-transitive, taking the cases as primitive data about it rather than as evidence to be diagnosed. Against a philosopher who does that, nothing here is a formal refutation of his account of singular modality, because its load-bearing premise is the global-capacity reading he declines. What the reply secures is narrower and still worth having: the proof’s own transfer, on ◇C, doesn’t wait on the dispute, and the chain can’t be run against the unrestricted theorem without conceding, link by link, the very possibilities whose global standing is at issue.

*Third.* The counterpart-theoretic version drops non-transitivity in favor of inconstancy. On Lewis’s treatment, a de re modal claim about the table is made true by what happens to the table’s counterparts—the objects in other worlds that resemble it most in whatever respects the conversation is weighting. Weight origin heavily and the H″-table is no counterpart of this table; weight function or appearance instead and it is. So “possibly made from H″” comes out true in one conversation and false in another, and any transfer principle stated over such claims inherits the instability.

The reply is that inconstancy of this kind is variation in representation, not variation in the domain. What shifts with context is which similarity respects a de re predication tracks—a fact about the semantics of counterpart talk. Nothing shifts in which worlds are among the ways Reality permits, and the whole plurality remains available to every context that draws on it. The inconstancy defense is also an awkward ally for the objector, since it concedes that the chained-origin data are produced by a context-sensitive representational device rather than discovered in the logic of possibility. A phenomenon that varies with conversational salience isn’t the sort of thing a modal axiom is answerable to.

A kindred move presses the vagueness directly rather than through counterpart semantics. Each origin-swap is tolerable, the endpoints aren’t, and no step appears to be the step at which identity lapses. This is a sorites on essence: a chain of individually admissible changes whose endpoints differ in a way no single link seems to introduce.

The present account need not choose among Forbes’s degrees of counterparthood, supervaluation over admissible sharpenings, and Williamson’s unknowable cutoff. Each treats the series as evidence that the identity predicate is tolerant across small changes, not by itself as evidence that Reality’s modal capacity varies from world to world.

The status reading that makes this diagnosis available is fixed at §1.2.6 and §2.1.7: the claim isn’t that a necessity operator scopes over a possibility operator by climbing an accessibility relation, but that whatever is possible has its possibility as a settled status. The Bottleneck at The S5 Bottleneck (§2.1.5) marks the single point at which a rival can disagree. Lewis’s concrete plurality, whose counterpart theory supplies the third move’s machinery, is engaged at §7.2.3.

*Convergence.* Each of the three forms turns on an individual’s identity across worlds rather than on the range of configurations the worlds compose. The chained-origin move has no qualitative case, and the transfer the proof spends is on a qualitative proposition. Salmon’s principled version, pressed on singular propositions, meets the argument at a premise rather than at a diagnosis: it relativizes real possibility, which §2.1.10 answers from no-exteriority, and the cases that motivate it are equally served by a tolerant, vague essence that keeps one range. The counterpart-theoretic version relocates the variation into context-sensitive representation, where it is no longer the sort of fact a modal axiom answers to. Underneath all three is a sorites on essence, and tolerance isn’t world-relativity without a further premise the cases don’t supply.

The chain never has to settle whether Adam and Noah could trade places. What the series shows is that “same man” bears a great deal of counterfactual stretching without anyone being able to say where it snaps, which is a fact about the elasticity of identity under supposition and not, by itself, a discovery about the range of ways Reality permits. The lives at every link were always in that range. The question the chain makes vivid is only ever which of them we are still entitled to call Adam’s.

### 7.3.4 Gasking’s Parody of the Ontological Argument
Gaunilo, a Benedictine monk of Marmoutiers, replied to Anselm’s *Proslogion* in the late eleventh century: the ontological argument’s form, if sound, would prove the existence of a perfect lost island (an island than which no more perfect could be conceived), and since no such island exists, the argument’s form can’t be sound. His parody was the first great demonstration that an argumentative form can be tested by seeing what else the form delivers. Nine centuries later, Douglas Gasking extended the tradition in a manuscript circulated in the late 1970s and published after his death: the greatest conceivable achievement, he argued, would be creating the universe while not existing, since creation from nothing without resources or powers is a greater feat than creation by an omnipotent being. If maximal greatness entails necessary existence in the Anselmian tradition, parody-greatness entails necessary non-existence. The parody is deliberately absurd. Its point is methodological: an argument whose form licenses its own *reductio* never really licenses its conclusion.

Gaunilo’s *Pro Insipiente* (c. 1078) set the template. Gasking’s “Proof of the Non-Existence of God” (commonly cited 1978; published posthumously in *Language, Logic and Causation* (1996)) modernized it. Mackie (*The Miracle of Theism* 1982) and Oppy (*Ontological Arguments and Belief in God* 1995; *Arguing About Gods* 2006) developed the parody tradition into a general diagnostic: an argumentative form that delivers one impressive conclusion can usually be adapted to deliver its opposite, revealing that the form’s apparent productivity rests on hidden premises about greatness, predication, or modal reasoning. Plantinga (*God, Freedom, and Evil* 1974) responded that the modal ontological argument survives parody because the parody premises aren’t genuinely possibly instantiated in the way the original premises are. Grim (“There Is No Set of All Truths,” 1984) opened a different parody-adjacent front via Cantorian diagonalization (the powerset technique that, given any proposed totality, generates an element outside it) against omniscience. Adams (“Flavors, Colors, and God,” 1987) and van Inwagen (“Ontological Arguments,” 1977) canvassed the conditions under which a parody does and doesn’t mirror its target. The tradition’s shared assumption is that arguments with modal conclusions are particularly susceptible to parody because modal space is abundant enough to contain mirror-image premises the original argument can’t exclude.

Brought to bear on the present argument, the parody tradition tests whether □(T∧S∧Φ) (the necessity of Time, Space, and Substance together) is earned by content or by form. The argument’s machinery is the Modal Identity from §2.6.6, S5 / Necessary Possibility from §2.1 (the modal-logic system in which whatever is necessary or possible at any world is necessary or possible at every world), and the ∅ result from §2.7 (the null state, the absolute absence of being). If that machinery could be redeployed to produce inverted or absurd conclusions, it is suspect. A parody that successfully mirrored the argument’s form would deliver a structural result the argument can’t accept, revealing the necessity claim rests on hidden premises rather than on the form the argument presents. The question is whether the formal structure is neutral between its intended conclusion and a parody-conclusion, or whether the content of T, S, and Φ does work the form alone can’t carry.

A clarification before the moves. The argument’s conclusion isn’t ‘the three Conditions are great and therefore necessary.’ It is ‘the three Conditions are the structural requirements of any change, any extension, any persistence, and therefore no medium can be without them.’ The content is functional, not evaluative. A parody that substitutes an evaluatively defined alternative (‘maximal Non-Being,’ ‘greatest achievement of non-existence’) isn’t running the argument’s form with new content. It is running a different form entirely, one the present argument never uses. Three forms of the parody; each breaks at a point where the present argument differs from the Anselmian one.

*First.* The inversion move runs Gasking’s exact trick on the present argument. The greatest conceivable being, the objector presses, is one whose existence isn’t presupposed by the categories of existence: a being that grounds Nature without instantiating the three conditions. This is the exact move classical theists make for God. By parallel reasoning, there must be a maximally great Non-Being that grounds Nature while instantiating none of its structural roles. If the ontological argument’s form is legitimate, the parody’s form is equally legitimate.

The parody fails before it reaches the machinery, and the reason is simple enough to state in one line: there is no greatness premise in the argument for the parody to invert. Anselm’s argument runs on a superlative—*that than which no greater can be conceived*—and every parody in the tradition works by holding the superlative fixed and changing what fills it. Gaunilo fills it with an island, Gasking with an achievement. The structural derivation contains no such premise at any step: it runs from an occurring change to what change requires, and nothing in it ranks candidates by how impressive, perfect, or admirable they would be. A parody that supplies a maximally great Non-Being is therefore not this argument with new content. It is Anselm’s argument with new content, and it inherits whatever the Anselmian form is worth.

The point can be put in the parody’s own currency for a reader who wants to keep the greatness-talk. Greatness in the ontological tradition is measured by impressiveness, by what it would be more impressive for a being to be, and on that measure creating a universe while not existing outdoes creating one while existing. Measure instead by what a candidate can do—its capacity to act, cause, and affect—and non-existence has none of it. A non-existent cause produces no manifest effect, so ‘necessary non-existence’ names maximal causal inertness, which is what ∅ names. The inverted measure, not the argument, generates the absurdity. That reply is available, and it isn’t what the section rests on; where greatness itself is examined at strength is §11.1, which the parody question doesn’t wait on.

**[Dissolution]**

**Impressiveness Is Not Potency** · *Dissolution*

The parody needs a superlative premise to invert, and the derivation has none: it runs from an occurring change to what change requires, ranking no candidate by how impressive it would be. So the parody mirrors Anselm’s form rather than this one. Pressed in its own currency the inversion still fails: read “greatness” as impressiveness and creating while not existing outdoes creating while existing, but read it as what a candidate can do, and non-existence has no capacity to act, cause, or affect, so necessary non-existence names maximal causal inertness, which is what ∅ names. The inverted measure generates the absurdity, and the argument never used a measure at all.

**Dissolves:** the Gasking inversion

*Second.* The S5 symmetry move targets the logical machinery directly. The argument moves from ◇C to □◇C via S5, applied to change-permission. By parallel reasoning, ¬◇C should yield □¬◇C: the necessary impossibility of change. If the logical machinery licenses the first move, it licenses the second. But the second contradicts the first. The S5 system powers both, so the argument’s conclusion rests on a prior decision about which modal premise to start with.

The parallel fails because the two premises aren’t symmetric. ◇C (change is possible) is defended by the Cartesian certainty that change is occurring in the very act of doubt and the subsequent derivation that change requires T, S, and Φ. ¬◇C (change is impossible) has no equivalent step. There is no Cartesian certainty that change is impossible, because the certainty of doubting would itself refute the certainty of impossibility. The parody’s starting premise conflicts with the book’s Cartesian datum if doubting is correctly analyzed as change. That is a substantive premise about the act, not an analytic truth and not yet a freestanding cross-world proof. S5 preserves whichever modal premise is supplied; it doesn’t establish the asymmetry by itself. The machinery is the same. The inputs aren’t. This is where the present reply converges with Plantinga’s (1974): a modal argument survives parody only when the parody’s mirror premise isn’t genuinely possibly instantiated. On the book’s act analysis, ¬◇C is dialectically unstable because asserting or considering it occurs through an ordered cognitive performance. The force of that reply remains act-side and depends on the argument connecting the performance to real change.

*Third.* Oppy’s general indictment presses the crispest version. Any argument attempting to derive substantive ontological conclusions from conceptual premises is suspect in principle, because conception doesn’t deliver existence. The structural argument is such an argument: it conceives change and derives structural necessity. The parody argues, equally validly, that it conceives non-existence and derives structural absence. Both conclusions rest on the same epistemic error: confusing what can be coherently thought with what must ontologically obtain.

The argument doesn’t derive existence from conception. It derives structural conditions from what any occurring thought requires. The Cartesian datum (that thought is occurring) isn’t a conceptual premise but a phenomenally given fact. The subsequent derivation proceeds from what any thought-event structurally requires, not from the conceptual content of any particular thought. Oppy’s indictment applies to arguments of the form ‘there is a concept of X; therefore X exists.’ The argument has a different form: ‘there is a phenomenally given fact F; F requires structural conditions T, S, Φ; therefore T, S, Φ obtain.’ The parody can’t be reformulated in the same way because there is no phenomenally given fact of non-existence: non-existence isn’t a fact that can be phenomenally given, because phenomenal givenness requires the very structural conditions non-existence is defined as lacking. The parody can be conceived. It can’t be given. Oppy’s indictment targets the wrong kind of argument.

A kindred move drops Gasking’s inversion for Grim’s Cantorian diagonalization. In its original form (Grim 1984) the target is omniscience: if there is a set of all truths, the powerset argument generates a truth outside it, so the set (and the omniscience that would survey it) is incoherent.

*The Incomplete Universe* (Grim 1991) generalizes the result past omniscience to any totality of facts: if a world is conceived as a maximal consistent collection of truths, the same diagonalization shows there is no such collection, and the universe considered as a totality of facts is essentially open and incomplete.

The Grim-style form bears directly on the present argument because the exhaustion claim can look like just such a totality. Applied here rather than to theism, it argues: if the three Conditions exhaust necessary existence, there is a fact about that exhaustion standing outside Nature, and the exhaustion claim is incoherent.

The reply turns on what the exhaustion claim quantifies over, and the diagonalization is answered by saying so rather than by the retorsion that serves against Gasking. Grim’s argument bites on a *collection*: give it a set of all truths and it produces a truth outside the set. The exhaustion claim is not a collection of truths but a universally quantified conditional over beings—for anything real, T, S, and Φ obtain of it—and a universally quantified conditional needs no completed totality to be true, any more than “every prime has a successor” needs a set of all numbers. Nothing in the argument assumes a set of all truths, a maximal consistent collection, or a survey of the facts from outside them, and where a world is treated as maximal, it is a way things could be rather than an inspected inventory.

That is the whole answer, and it holds only while the book keeps to it. An account that did quantify over a completed totality of truths would inherit the Cantorian problem, and observing that the diagonal fact is itself one more instance of the three Conditions would not resolve it: a truth generated outside a collection is a problem about the collection, not about who states it. So the meta-statements point—that facts about exhaustion are made by reasoners instantiating the roles, inside Nature rather than from beyond it—answers the charge of a view from nowhere, and is left to do that narrower work.

*Convergence.* Each of the three parodies breaks at a point where the present argument differs from the Anselmian one. Gasking’s inversion needs a superlative premise the derivation never makes. The S5 symmetry move fails because the two premises aren’t symmetric: ◇C is defended by a Cartesian certainty that change is occurring, and ¬◇C is dialectically unstable because asserting or considering it occurs through an ordered cognitive performance. Oppy’s indictment targets arguments that move from concept to existence; the present argument moves from a phenomenally given fact of change to its structural conditions, and the parody can’t be reformulated in the same way because non-existence can’t be phenomenally given.

Gaunilo’s island vanishes beneath a wave the moment it is conceived: not because islands can’t be perfect, but because an argument that proves an island by its mere conceivability has confused what is contained in a concept with what is contained in the world. Gasking’s non-existent creator performs an identical trick, translated into the idiom of twentieth-century analytic theism. The argument survives both because it never performs the trick either parody is designed to expose. It doesn’t move from the concept of change to the existence of structure. It moves from the phenomenal fact of change—the thinking now going on—to the structural conditions that make the thinking possible. Constructing the parody supplies an actual structured performance and therefore rebuts a denial aimed at the performance itself. It doesn’t alone establish that every possible world realizes the same loaded types; that broader result depends on the separate modal and role-to-type arguments.

## 7.4 What the Rivals Carried
The rivals gathered here divide into two kinds, and the division matters more than any single verdict. One kind proposes a source: a ground of possibility, a plurality of concrete worlds, a fixed domain of individuals, a power borne by actual objects. The other contests no source at all, but the semantic, logical, or epistemological machinery used to reach the conclusion. The verdicts aren’t uniform. Some rivals relocate structure, some remain compatible with it, some expose an explanatory cost, and some leave an open seam or impose a discipline on the argument. The ledger records each result at that level rather than converting the chapter into one general refutation.

*1. Grounding and source accounts.*

**Source-of-possibility accounts.** No candidate whose own status is stated in modal terms can ground R’s standing capacity when its own status already presupposes that capacity. Finean essence-priority may still reverse the explanatory direction—modal truths following from what a thing is—but No Unconditioned Essence closes the proposed essence as a primitive external ground. Any essence real enough to ground has a determinate way within Reality–Nature and is the configuration, an articulation of it, or an abstraction of such an articulation. **No exterior source of possibility**, without the further claim that essence can’t explain modal truths about what something is (§7.2.1).

**Dispositionalism about modality.** The position locates modality in actual reality rather than in a plurality of concrete worlds, and its objections to Lewis overlap with those developed here. It grounds possibility in powers borne by actual objects. The pressure arises at the global case: iterated and joint potentialities extend what existing bearers can bring about, but the possibility that there be bearers can’t itself be grounded in a bearer without circularity. **Agreement on actual grounding, with the bearerless global case left to the structural capacity account** (§7.2.2).

**Lewisian plurality.** Concrete Lewisian worlds must meet concrete spatiotemporal burdens internally. Their numerical plurality, if treated as primitive, remains a coherent but costly posit rather than a contradiction. **Structured realization plus explanatory cost** (§7.2.3).

**Linguistic ersatzism.** World-stories, abstract ways, and maximal states of affairs can represent modal alternatives without a concrete plurality. Their distinguishability and consistency directly establish only thin structural roles; the loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types belong to what a surrogate represents when it represents a concrete change-world, not automatically to the surrogate itself. **A viable representational apparatus whose actual use is structured, with object-side realization still governed by the represented world** (§7.2.4).

**Combinatorialism.** Recombination makes modal plurality configurations of an actual base. Actual elements and admissibility constraints therefore do real work. Alien possibilities force a choice: restrict the range to what the base generates, add primitives, or leave admissibility primitive. The final option is coherent and remains open. Its cost is a primitive constraint with the structural shape the present account already identifies. **Convergence on configured plurality, with primitive admissibility as the residual disagreement** (§7.2.5).

**Modal fictionalism.** A fiction can preserve possible-worlds discourse without commitment to concrete worlds. Actual storytellers, inscriptions, and evaluations are structured, but that act-side fact doesn’t determine the represented world’s structure. The further pressure is semantic: translation correctness, fiction selection, and modal consequence require non-fictional standards. **Successful deflation of concrete-world commitment, with non-fictional semantic resources still owed** (§7.2.6).

**Necessitism.** Fixed domains of individuals are compatible with the invariant standing capacity of R. Necessitism neither refutes the structural conclusion nor automatically supplies its metaphysical content. **Formal compatibility with a competing ontological reading** (§7.2.7).

**Sider’s structuralism.** Joint-carving structure supplies a mind-independent target for metaphysics and converges with the book’s rejection of framework-relative ontology. Sider’s own thesis is that modal ideology isn’t joint-carving; the position engaged is the Humean extension that adds an account of what makes modal claims true. The remaining question concerns modal scope: a privileged structure in this world doesn’t by itself establish what every possible cosmos must instantiate. **Shared structural realism with the global modal range still requiring an account** (§7.2.8).

*2. Semantic, logical, and epistemic accounts.* A second kind of objection accepts the proposed ground but challenges the semantic or epistemological methods used to establish it. It offers no rival world, source, or realizer. Its claim is instead that the argument’s methods don’t support the conclusion assigned to them. These verdicts are correspondingly narrower, and two require substantive qualifications.

**Rigid designation.** Necessary co-extension doesn’t entail identity, and the Kripkean warning remains in force. The book’s reply therefore depends on the separate no-surplus and essence arguments showing that change-possibility and T∧S∧Φ are one constitutive content rather than two rigidly coextensive terms. **Kripke’s wedge preserved, with its application made conditional on whether the constitutive identity has been earned** (§7.1.1).

**Two-dimensional semantics.** Primary and secondary intensions separate appearance from underlying nature in cases such as water and H₂O. The book denies that its role definitions contain the same seam, while conceding that the role-to-type bridges are substantive metaphysical premises rather than analytic consequences of vocabulary. **The two-dimensional distinction retained for natural-kind and conceivability cases, with the structural identity defended at constitutive rather than discovery register** (§7.1.2).

**Quinean modal skepticism.** Quine’s objections discipline analyticity, quantification into opaque contexts, and essentialist vocabulary. Extensional scientific practice nevertheless quantifies over ordered, differentiated, persisting items, while identifying that ontology with the book’s loaded Conditions requires the independent realizer arguments. **Modal vocabulary deflated without removing the ontology over which the extensional practice ranges** (§7.1.3).

**Modal conventionalism.** Selected necessities may be conventional, grounded in practice, or normative. A global conventionalism still relies on concrete acts of stipulation, comparison, and application and must account for the status of its own universal thesis. **The local conventional claim retained, with the global reduction carrying an act-side and self-application burden** (§7.1.4).

**Modal expressivism.** Stances, actual inferences, and rule-governed practices require structured agents and acts; abstract inferential or normative relations don’t inherit the loaded types merely by being used. Expression’s actuality also puts one modal claim in an awkward place for the account: *expression is possible* is warranted by an occurrence rather than by any stance, so the expressivist treatment must either cover a claim answering to an occurrence or exempt it and become local. **A live local semantics, with global expressivism carrying a burden at its own foundation** (§7.1.5).

**Metaontological deflationism.** Framework comparison requires invariant constraints, and the structural roles don’t vary with the scheme used to describe them. That earns status as more than a framework artifact by the deflationist’s own invariance test. It doesn’t, without a further bridge, force the move from universal conditions on representation to mind-independent ontology. **Framework invariance established, with the transcendental-to-ontological bridge kept open** (§7.1.6).

**Wittgensteinian quietism.** Saying, diagnosing, withholding, and acknowledging are structured performances. Mere silence isn’t automatically a performed refusal, and act-side exhibition doesn’t supply cross-world necessity without the modal and role-to-type arguments. **Constitutive structure exhibited by enacted quietism, with silence and the cross-world lift outside the retorsion’s reach** (§7.1.7).

**Impossible worlds and relative modality.** Impossible worlds multiply representations rather than genuine alternatives. A Kratzer-style base drawn from genuine alternatives restricts a domain rather than populating it, and a base that reaches past them, as an epistemic base does, quantifies over representations instead. Hyperintensionality is shared: necessary equivalence is too coarse for identity, which the book states at the finer no-surplus grain. Non-normal worlds block accessibility-based S5 derivations. The book’s lift is instead a claim about the invariance of R’s standing capacity, so the objection reaches it only if non-normal semantics supplies the further metaphysical claim that this capacity varies by configuration. **Representational or semantic variation without a demonstrated variation in what R can admit** (§7.3.1).

**Chained-origin counterexamples.** The tolerance chaining that generates Chisholm’s paradox makes what is possible for an individual vary from world to world, which is genuine pressure on S4 and S5 and isn’t dismissed here. It generates that pressure through singular claims about individuals carrying their origins or essences, while the transfer the proof spends is on a qualitative proposition, ◇C. Against the theorem in its unrestricted form the objection is met at a premise rather than by a diagnosis: Salmon relativizes real possibility, which is one of the positions Necessary Possibility already names as its live target (§2.1.10). **Live pressure on the unrestricted theorem, none on the instance the proof spends** (§7.3.3).

**The remoteness objection.** The claim that modal judgment becomes unreliable at substantial metaphysical distance is accepted. A failed specification can expose an equivocation, an illicit bridge, or a missing account; the structure of the specifying act alone can’t establish that the represented object shares that structure. **The faculty conceded and a disciplined burden incurred**: object-side impossibility requires an object-side contradiction, while an act-side failure establishes only that the offered route hasn’t specified its target (§7.3.2).

**Gasking’s parody.** The parody works by inverting a superlative premise, and the derivation has none: it begins from the occurring fact of change and argues to its structural conditions, ranking no candidate by greatness at any step. The parody also supplies no corresponding phenomenal fact of non-existence. That difference protects the route only if the actuality datum and the role-to-type bridges succeed independently. Grim’s diagonalization is a separate matter and is answered separately: it bites on a completed collection of truths, and the exhaustion claim is a universally quantified conditional over beings rather than a collection. **A valid parody of concept-to-existence reasoning that doesn’t reproduce the form of the argument used here** (§7.3.4).

# 8. Metaphysics

Chapter 7 (§7) took up the rivals that contest the argument’s own semantic and modal machinery before any question of a rival ground is on the table. The family taken up here is different: rivals that grant the machinery and press instead on what change, contingency, and objecthood themselves require. The question is the same one asked throughout Part III—does the rival eliminate Time, Space, and Substance as conditions, or only redescribe them?—but here it is asked of accounts that engage the world’s own structure directly rather than the apparatus used to describe it.

Three clusters organize the engagement. Time, change, and the changeless (§8.1) asks whether a real world could be one in which nothing happens, from Shoemaker’s frozen intervals to the block universe’s tenseless spread. Contingency, necessity, and nothingness (§8.2) asks what the world’s contingency actually demands, from the Principle of Sufficient Reason to the charge that a necessary ground leaves no contingency standing at all. Objects, parts, and identity (§8.3) asks what a persisting thing is, from temporary intrinsics to haecceitism’s primitive thisness. What the pattern across these three reveals is drawn together at §8.4.

The positions don’t all oppose the argument in the same way. Some deny a Condition; some relocate its realization or place something prior to it; some argue that necessary structure overgenerates necessity; some dispute the inventory of objects while retaining the arrangements among them; and Pizzi independently converges on the exclusion of absolute nothingness. The question therefore changes with the proposal: does it eliminate a structural role, realize it differently, expose an excess in the argument, or reach part of the same result by another route?

## 8.1 Time, Change, and the Changeless
This cluster asks what remains of temporal structure when actuality, fundamentality, passage, or concreteness is withdrawn. Shoemaker’s time without change (§8.1.1) argues that empty intervals could be inferred without anything happening in them; emergent time (§8.1.2) makes succession a derived feature of a fundamentally atemporal substrate; the unreality of time (§8.1.3) denies that passage is a feature of reality at all; the block universe (§8.1.4) retains tenseless temporal order while treating flow as perspectival; and Platonism (§8.1.5) posits abstracta outside concrete change. The tests differ accordingly: absence of actual transition isn’t absence of capacity, a tenseless ordering isn’t no ordering, and abstract existence isn’t automatically a concrete change-realizer.

The cluster bears most directly on the proof’s claim that any concrete Reality permits change and on the identification of change-possibility with T∧S∧Φ. The subsections distinguish denial from relocation, alternative realization, and exemption; only the first would supply a change-realizing counterexample without the Conditions.

A preliminary note before the named engagements. Two general intuitions support the positions taken up later. The first is that change might be denied at the limit: that some level beneath, above, or beside the changing world is itself unchanging, and that the unchanging level is the truer one. The second is that the appearance of change might be misleading: what looks like succession may be juxtaposition, what looks like persistence may be pattern. The argument grants the intuitions as intuitions and contests what they license: the structural conditions are derived at §2.4–2.7 from the actuality, possibility, and impossibility profile of change. Clearing the temporal candidates turns on the permission side alone. A frozen interval, a timeless base, a temporal error theory, and a block are each offered as a reality from which change, or its passage, is absent, and the test for each is whether the capacity goes with the occurrence. Platonism is not that kind of candidate and isn’t tested that way: robust abstracta aren’t proposed as concrete change-realizing realities at all, so what is at issue there is scope—whether a conditional about concrete change-realizers reaches them—rather than permission. That a candidate permits change suffices to answer it, and that sufficiency is the load-bearing claim for the cluster. The Frozen-World Test at The Frozen-World Test (§2.4.11) argues that fully typed structure makes change possible; it doesn’t show that every world must contain an actual transition or that every changeless interval is ∅. A frozen or silent world may retain the capacities and role-structure required for change. The cluster therefore tests whether the candidates remove those capacities. The subsections press the weaker, sufficient point and leave the stronger result standing behind it.

### 8.1.1 Shoemaker’s Time Without Change
Sydney Shoemaker, writing at Cornell in 1969, constructs a universe built on local freezes: a region in which nothing moves, decays, or interacts for a stretch of time, then resumes exactly where it left off, displaced from the ongoing world by the length of the freeze. He multiplies the case into three rooms subject to periodic freezes on staggered intervals, a universe built to let observers in one region infer the freezes of another by clock comparison. The periodicities eventually coincide: once every sixty years, all three regions freeze at once. During that year, by Shoemaker’s construction, nothing changes anywhere in the universe. And yet, the argument runs, time still passes.

The inference is staged with such care that the paper became the canonical modern defense of time-without-change in the analytic literature, the standing objection to every Aristotelian who thinks time requires motion. The objection is serious. Grant the global interval: nothing changes anywhere, and time still passes. But Shoemaker’s universe retains change-capacity and a continuity role held across the freeze. The case separates time from uninterrupted change, not time from the structure that makes change possible.

Shoemaker (“Time Without Change,” *The Journal of Philosophy* 1969) offers a carefully constructed defense of time without change. Local cessation is coherent: a region can freeze while the rest continues, then re-enter the ongoing temporal order when it resumes. So is the global case. What does the global interval show? Either it removes the capacity for change, or it remains an interval within a change-permitting world. Shoemaker’s own construction supplies the test.

The literature on time-without-change runs back to Aristotle’s *Physics* (Aristotle (4th c. BCE) 1984, IV.10–14), where time is defined as the number of motion with respect to the before-and-after, and an unchanging universe therefore fails the conditions for time’s obtaining. Newton’s *Principia* (1687) develops the opposing substantivalist position: absolute time flows uniformly without regard to anything external, and its passage is independent of whatever change happens to take place within it. McTaggart (“The Unreality of Time,” 1908) poses the foundational question of what change itself consists in, the A-series/B-series distinction that structures the modern debate. Prior (“Changes in Events and Changes in Things,” 1968) sharpens the change-theoretic tradition. Shoemaker’s 1969 paper supplies the argument that has carried most weight for that side since. It is designed to show that time without change is at least possible, and that inhabitants of such a world could have inductive grounds for concluding a global freeze had occurred. That supports the substantivalist position without asserting it: the paper argues for the possibility, not for time as an independent substance. Newton-Smith (*The Structure of Time* 1980) defends the Shoemaker conclusion at length.

Against the substantivalist line, three objections bear on the argument made here: Le Poidevin (*Change, Cause, and Contradiction* 1991) presses the verificationist worry about the global-freeze extension, Forbes challenges the inferential structure of the thought experiment (1993), and Mellor (*Real Time II* 1998) defends a change-theoretic view from the B-theoretic side. Lombard (1986), Craig (2000), Horwich (1987), and Sider (2001) develop the surrounding positions, and Dainton (*Time and Space*, 2nd ed. 2010) gives the standard survey. The present reply draws on the change-theoretic tradition represented here by Mellor and Le Poidevin, and adds what neither specifies on its own: Shoemaker’s inference runs on persistence, which his scenario leaves in place and which he himself grants, and that persistence is named explicitly by the structural-role apparatus of §2.6.

The challenge bears directly on §2.6. The Modal Identity established there is bidirectional: necessarily, change-possibility obtains if and only if T ∧ S ∧ Φ obtains, and the two are one structural fact under two descriptions. Shoemaker’s argument exhibits, if successful, time during an interval in which no change is occurring. That doesn’t by itself break the book’s Modal Identity, whose left side is the *possibility* of change rather than its continuous actuality. A globally frozen interval bracketed by change may still belong to a world in which change is possible. The relevant question is therefore whether the case preserves change-capacity and structural continuity, not whether a transition occurs during every interval. What follows is narrow by design. The reply locates the substantivalist move as a relocation rather than an elimination.

A clarification before the moves. The local freezes are coherent. Given three regions freezing on staggered intervals, one can calculate when they coincide and infer a global interval from the periodicities bracketing it. The question is narrower: whether that global interval removes the structural capacity for change, or retains the ordering, distinction, and persistence by which it is one interval in the history of a world. Three claims must be separated: that the global interval is inferable from the local freezes, that the analysis survives a change in descriptive level, and that the absence of occurrence defeats the book’s possibility claim.

*First.* The inference is always from observed change, not to time-without-change. Shoemaker’s observers reconstruct A’s frozen interval by reference to B’s and C’s ongoing change: by counting B’s cycles while A is frozen, by watching the clock. When all three regions freeze simultaneously, no such reconstruction is available from inside the freeze. The claim that time still passes during the global freeze isn’t a direct measurement but an extrapolation from the periodicities on either side of the gap, underwritten by the assumption that the pattern continues across it. That assumption is cross-freeze identity: the same periodicity, resumed. Without something carrying it across, the post-freeze regions aren’t the pre-freeze regions resumed; they are new regions with coincidentally similar patterns, and the inference collapses into correlation. Shoemaker’s reasoning works because the universe stays the same universe across the pause, and a universe that doesn’t stay the same across it can’t underwrite the reasoning.

What that establishes should be stated at its own strength. The inference needs a continuity role occupied across the interval; whether the occupant is the loaded Φ of §2.6 rather than some thinner cross-time relation is settled by the independent role-to-type argument, not by the freeze. Nothing in the case turns on winning that point, because Shoemaker grants persistence outright: his target is the linkage between time and change, not the bearer. The scenario is therefore a relocation of the structure rather than a concession extracted from an opponent who meant to deny it.

**[Proposition]**

**Resumption Requires a Bearer** · *Proposition*

The inference to time across a global freeze extrapolates from the periodicities bracketing it, and holds only if the pattern on the far side is the same pattern resumed. Without something persisting through the interval, the post-freeze regions are new regions with coincidentally similar behavior, and resumption degrades to correlation. Shoemaker’s construction therefore runs on a continuity role held across the freeze, which he grants rather than contests; whether that role is occupied by the loaded Φ is a question the independent role-to-type argument settles. The frozen interval is real, and so is the continuity by which it belongs to one continuing world.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

*Second.* Level-invariance (§2.1.7) applies to the containing universe, not just to each region. The regions are genuinely distinct (S). The freezes occur in a determinate order relative to one another (T). The containing frame persists across the freezes to underwrite each region’s re-emergence with preserved identity (Φ). The simultaneous freeze is global in occurrence but remains an interval within a structured universe. Shoemaker has described a universe whose history includes change and a global interval without it, not a universe without the capacity or conditions for change.

*Third.* Pushed to the global limit, the scenario contains no internal clock or observer during the freeze. That creates an epistemic and verification problem, not an immediate metaphysical contradiction: a thought experiment may specify unobserved structure, and observers before and after may infer a duration from the wider history. The construction preserves cross-freeze identity, periodic dispositions, and the possibility of resumed change. The fully extended scenario is therefore a universe with time and an interval during which no change occurs. The Modal Identity survives because the scenario never removes the possibility of change or the structure in which that possibility consists. Shoemaker defeats an uninterrupted-occurrence thesis. The book’s modal claim is not that thesis.

A kindred move drops the Shoemaker apparatus for classical Newtonian absolutism: time is an independent substance whose passage doesn’t depend on any change within it. The reply is the same in older vocabulary, with one dependency made explicit. An absolute time independent of change must still be individuated (this moment of absolute time distinct from that moment), and, on the change-theoretic conception of Temporality defended at §1.4.1 (Directionality as structural, not imposed) and abductively at §4.2, that individuation is the structural fact identified at §2.6. Absolute-time substantivalism relocates the structural roles into the substance of time itself rather than eliminating them; the substance of time contains distinctness of moments (S), directed ordering (T), and persistence across the ordering (Φ) as the conditions of its being a time at all. (The reply that absolute-time substantivalism relocates the structural roles rather than eliminating them isn’t neutral between conceptions of time. A purist who takes time to be bare duration (mere ordering, with influence occurring within time rather than constituting it) can decline the identification of a moment’s individuation with T ∧ S ∧ Φ. Two costs attend the exit, and the relational account pays neither. First, individuating the moments of an empty, changeless absolute time without relational extension requires primitive thisness: the haecceity Leibniz’s identity of indiscernibles and the hole-argument literature press, which sophisticated substantivalism can absorb only by surrendering haecceitism; the relational individuation supplied at §2.6 (S) needs no such posit. Second, by the lights of the change-theoretic conception defended here (a cost the purist won’t grant is one) a duration stripped of all influence is ordering without succession, the ordered-set structure (§2.6.7) rather than Time. The position remains coherent, but it incurs commitments to primitive identity and to a conception of time separated from succession. The relocation reply identifies those commitments; it doesn’t provide a neutral refutation.)

Another kindred: a deflationary verificationist move (Le Poidevin 1991; earlier Ayer 1936) that the global-freeze scenario is meaningless because no possible observation could confirm or disconfirm it. The structural reply accepts the verificationist point for the specific purpose for which it was introduced while declining the broader verificationism: the scenario isn’t meaningless; its global interval is unobservable from inside, which is an epistemic limit rather than a failure of sense.

*Taking stock.* The global extension holds. The universe remains structured even when the freeze is global. Shoemaker therefore establishes a changeless interval within a change-permitting world, not time without change-capacity or without the Conditions in which that capacity consists.

Unlike the emergent-time, momentariness, and changeless-ground objections, the Shoemaker objection grants that time is real and that persistence obtains, and contests only the bidirectional linkage of change and time. The reply is therefore correspondingly narrow: the target is the global extension of the local scenario, not the coherence of time or of persistence in general.

One clarification for the Shoemakerian reader. The argument addressed here is the 1969 time-without-change paper, not Shoemaker’s signature causal theory of properties (*Causality and Properties* 1980; *Identity, Cause, and Mind* 1984, expanded ed. 2003), on which properties are individuated by their causal powers. That broader thesis isn’t a further counterexample to §2.6 but an instance of it: causal individuation presupposes the very structural roles the account names, since a causal power is exercised across an ordering (T), among distinct relata (S), and is borne by what persists long enough to exercise it (Φ).

The paper establishes something narrower than a universe without change, and something the account can grant at no cost: an interval, possibly global, in which nothing happens while the structure making it an interval is retained. What it doesn’t establish is time without the *conditions* of time. The freeze is describable as a freeze only because identity persists across it (Φ), the regions stay distinct (S), and the ordering holds (T). Granted in full rather than resisted, Shoemaker’s scenario instantiates the three conditions throughout the very interval it was built to empty.

### 8.1.2 Emergent Time
Suppose time isn’t fundamental. Suppose what we call time is a feature that emerges from a deeper, timeless level of reality: the way temperature emerges from molecular motion, or the way solidity emerges from atomic lattices. The fundamental description of the world, on this proposal, makes no reference to time; time is a useful approximation at our scale, a coarse-grained feature that drops out of the deeper physics in the appropriate limit. If this is right, then the structural account of §2.6 is at best a description of the emergent layer, not of fundamental reality. The classical theist, sensing again an opening, can locate the changeless ground at the timeless fundamental level and the structural roles at the emergent surface.

The move isn’t idle. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation, the canonical equation of quantum gravity, contains no time variable; the wavefunction of the universe is timeless, and the appearance of time in our experience is to be recovered (somehow) from a fundamentally timeless formalism. Page and Wootters develop a correlational proposal (1983): time emerges as a correlation between subsystems of a timeless universe, with one subsystem serving as a clock for the rest. Barbour’s *The End of Time* (1999) develops Platonia: a timeless configuration space from which temporal experience emerges as “time capsules,” configurations that happen to encode apparent memories. Rovelli’s *The Order of Time* (2018) offers a relational account: time is the structure of correlations between physical systems, not a fundamental backdrop. Smolin’s *Time Reborn* (2013) takes the opposite line, defending time’s fundamentality, but the position the present reply targets is the timeless-fundamental position, not Smolin’s.

In the philosophy of time, kindred views include Albert’s *Time and Chance* (2000), which derives temporal asymmetry from the past-hypothesis and statistical-mechanical considerations; Price’s *Time’s Arrow and Archimedes’ Point* (1996), which argues that the apparent directedness of time is a perspectival feature; Reichenbach’s *The Direction of Time* (1956), the classical mid-century treatment of time’s arrow; Maudlin’s *The Metaphysics Within Physics* (2007), which defends time’s fundamentality against eliminativist readings. Anderson’s *The Problem of Time* (2017) gives the technical state of play in canonical quantum gravity. The literature is vast and the technical questions are subtle. The present reply targets the structural claim: that time is derivative rather than fundamental, and therefore that the structural conditions of §2.6 obtain at most at an emergent layer.

The proposal has three relevant forms: strict emergence from an atemporal basis, Page–Wootters correlation with a clock subsystem, and relational time constituted by correlations among systems. They incur different burdens and shouldn’t receive one verdict in advance.

*First.* The strict-emergence form claims that the fundamental level is timeless and that time is a phenomenon of the emergent layer only, in the way that temperature is a phenomenon of bulk thermodynamics and not of individual molecules. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation, on this reading, describes a fundamentally timeless universe, and the appearance of time at our scale is a coarse-grained illusion.

The analogy with temperature doesn’t carry the weight the position needs. Temperature is emergent in the sense that it is a statistical property of an underlying dynamics that is itself temporal: the molecules move, collide, and exchange energy in time, and the bulk property of temperature is a statistical summary of that temporal dynamics. The molecular dynamics isn’t itself temperature, but it is itself temporal; the emergence is from a more fundamental temporal description to a less fundamental temporal description. For time itself to be emergent in the analogous sense would require a more fundamental description that is itself non-temporal but supports the emergence of time, and that is the one thing the analogy doesn’t model. This doesn’t discredit the program. An emergent-time theorist need not offer temperature as a strict model of temporal onset, and may appeal to constitutive or synchronic notions of emergence in which nothing is produced from anything. What it shows is that the familiar analogy isn’t doing the work it is usually asked to do, and that the recovery question has to be answered on its own.

**[Proposition]**

**The Analogy Runs on Time** · *Proposition*

The thermodynamic analogy runs from a temporal base to a temporal surface: temperature is a statistical summary of molecules moving, colliding, and exchanging energy in time. Time’s own emergence would require a base that is not temporal, which is the one case that analogy does not model. Other notions of emergence—synchronic, constitutive, mathematical—are not production stories and are not answered here; what fails is the appeal to temperature, which therefore cannot license the program it is offered to motivate. That leaves the recovery question standing on its own merits, where the physics is genuinely open.

The Wheeler–DeWitt equation does not describe a non-temporal dynamics from which time emerges; it describes a wavefunction satisfying a constraint, and the recovery of time from the wavefunction is the open problem the field has been working on for decades. To call the formalism “timeless” is to describe the constraint, not the dynamics; the dynamics, if there is to be one, is what the recovery program is meant to produce.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

One version of the recovery claim is closed more strictly (Chapter 2). If the fundamental level is described as a state with no local transition-capacity that later produces or enters a state with such capacity, Transition Closure applies: the production is already a transition, so the proposed onset spends the capacity it says hasn’t yet appeared (§3.1.2). Parasitic Negation gives the same result at the domain boundary: a first temporal order can’t begin from domain-external non-temporality without the beginning itself supplying a before-and-after (§2.1.5). This closes local onset from temporal incapacity. It doesn’t classify the Page–Wootters construction or an atemporal grounding relation as a local transition; those proposals face the separate realizer question that follows.

The structural question is what resources the recovery requires. A formalism may contain distinguishable variables, correlations, constraints, or an ordered clock spectrum without thereby containing fundamental physical Temporality or a persisting substantial bearer. Moving from those formal features to the book’s loaded Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality types requires the independent realizer bridge of the pivot derivations (§2.6.2–2.6.4), with §3.3 supplying only role-level corroboration. The emergent-time program is challenged only if recovery can’t be specified without a structure that functionally realizes those roles; the conclusion doesn’t follow from the notation alone.

*Second.* The Page–Wootters form recovers time through correlation: time emerges as the correlation between two subsystems of a timeless universe, with one subsystem (the clock) serving as a reference relative to which the other subsystem (the rest) appears to evolve. Mathematically, the global wavefunction is timeless; the conditional wavefunction (conditioning on the clock state) evolves in the clock variable. The conditional evolution is what we observe as time.

The Page–Wootters construction yields relational evolution of one subsystem conditional on states of another while the global state is stationary. It requires a clock/rest factorization (dividing the total state into a clock system and the remainder), correlations, and an ordered clock observable. Those are formal and physical resources from which effective evolution can be recovered. Whether they already *instantiate fundamental T*, or instead realize an ordered structure from which temporal physics emerges, is the metaphysical question; a stationary global wavefunction isn’t shown to “persist through” an external time merely because the conditional construction is defined. The book may identify the functional realizer with T/S/Φ through its separate role-to-type argument, but the physics itself doesn’t make that identification.

*Third.* The relational-time form, developed by Rovelli, claims that time isn’t a backdrop in which physical systems evolve but a structure of correlations between physical systems. There is no absolute time; there is only the relative evolution of one system with respect to another. Each system is a clock for the others, and the appearance of a universal time is the coarse-grained agreement of many such relative clocks.

Relational time is a metaphysics of temporal relations rather than an absolute backdrop. It supplies correlations and relative evolution among physical systems. That is compatible with the book’s functional account, but it isn’t simply identical to the loaded triad by inspection. The required bridge asks whether the relations realize causal ordering rather than bare parameter ordering, relational differentiation rather than merely formal non-identity, and maintained causal capacity rather than a sequence of indexed descriptions.

A kindred move is the past-hypothesis style derivation (Albert, Price): the apparent directedness of time is derived from a low-entropy initial condition plus statistical mechanics, with no fundamental time-asymmetric law. The reply is the same. The derivation requires distinctness of microstates (S), an ordering across them sufficient to define entropy increase (T), and a dynamical evolution that preserves the relevant structural facts across the increase (Φ). The asymmetry of time is derived from the past-hypothesis, but the symmetric temporal structure is presupposed by the derivation, not eliminated by it.

Another kindred is the eternalist/B-theoretic position that the appearance of temporal becoming is a perspectival feature of conscious experience while the world itself is a four-dimensional manifold without genuine becoming. This is treated separately at §8.1.4 (the B-theoretic block). The B-theoretic eternalist accepts the temporal extension of the manifold and contests the metaphysical reality of passage. That is the one feature of Temporality the account takes a side on, not a dispute over whether the ordering obtains.

*Convergence.* None of the three programs establishes the book’s metaphysical conclusion by physics alone. Wheeler–DeWitt supplies a Hamiltonian constraint and a problem of recovering temporal phenomenology or dynamics; Page–Wootters supplies conditional relational evolution in a stationary global state; relational approaches treat temporal facts as correlations among systems. Each provides candidate realizers—ordering, correlation, differentiation, dynamical dependence. The book’s conclusion that fundamental T/S/Φ obtain is conditional on the independent claim that these candidates realize the loaded roles and that no weaker formal structure can do the recovery work. “Timeless” isn’t by itself an incoherent external negation; it is a technical and metaphysical proposal whose success depends on the recovery account.

The emergent-time literature establishes this much: the time of our experience isn’t the time of fundamental physics in any direct mapping. The clock-based time of relativity isn’t the conditional time of canonical quantum gravity, the entropic arrow isn’t the light-cone structure, and the phenomenal flow of experience isn’t the parameter of the Schrödinger equation. The structural roles aren’t the time of any particular physical theory; they are what any theory must instantiate to have time-like structure at all.

Half a century of work on the Wheeler–DeWitt equation has produced no consensus on the recovery of time, and the fundamental level may turn out to be very different from the time of our experience. A recovery account stated through atemporal correlation or grounding remains live only if its formal resources can perform the work of distinctness, ordering, and persistence without realizing the loaded roles. That is the seam the physics leaves open and the role-to-type argument must carry.

### 8.1.3 The Unreality of Time
In 1908 J. M. E. McTaggart published a paper in *Mind* titled “The Unreality of Time.” The argument is short, the conclusion is shocking, and the influence has been deep. Time, McTaggart claims, is unreal. The paper became one of the most cited works in twentieth-century philosophy of time, with well over a century of subsequent literature responding to it. If McTaggart was right, the present account of §2.6 has, in its first condition, named something unreal, and the bidirectional identity collapses on the temporal side.

The argument is concise enough to state in a paragraph. McTaggart distinguishes two ways of describing temporal events: the A-series (past, present, future, with the present moving) and the B-series (earlier than, simultaneous with, later than, fixed across the manifold). Time, McTaggart argues, requires the A-series: without becoming, there is no genuine temporality, only a static array of events with relations of earlier and later. But the A-series is contradictory. Every event is past, present, and future (these properties are mutually incompatible) and any attempt to remove the contradiction by relativizing (event E is future relative to time t1, present relative to t2, past relative to t3) generates a regress: the relativizing times are themselves events, each of which is past, present, and future, and so on. The A-series is incoherent; the B-series alone is insufficient for time; therefore time is unreal.

The argument has divided the philosophy of time ever since. Broad’s *An Examination of McTaggart’s Philosophy* (1938) gives the first sustained reply, defending A-series becoming against the contradiction charge; the moving-spotlight theory (the view that a four-dimensional manifold of events is timelessly arrayed and a privileged ‘now’ moves across it) is the image Broad had earlier introduced in *Scientific Thought* (1923) only to reject it. Prior’s *Past, Present, and Future* (1967) develops tense logic to formalize A-series claims. Mellor’s *Real Time* (1981) and *Real Time II* (1998) accept the contradiction in the A-series and develop a B-theoretic alternative on which tensed claims are reduced to tenseless truth-conditions. Tooley’s *Time, Tense, and Causation* (1997) defends a growing-block theory (on which the past and present are real but the future isn’t, with the block growing by addition as time passes). Dummett (1960, reprinted in *Truth and Other Enigmas*) reads McTaggart as a reductio of the assumption that the description of reality must be perspective-independent. Dainton (*Time and Space*, 2nd ed. 2010) gives the standard survey. The contemporary positions (presentism, eternalism, growing-block, moving spotlight) are largely structured by which side of McTaggart’s argument they accept and which side they reject.

The target here is McTaggart’s conclusion: that time is unreal. The A-series/B-series question, at the level it operates within the philosophy of time, is largely orthogonal to the present account. The dispute is already bracketed at the structural level by §2.6–2.7: the present account requires temporal ordering of states sufficient to support change, and the composition view the account prefers is developed at The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2) by holding A-series passage and B-series dimension together as two features Temporality requires rather than rival specifications of one. The reply here is narrower: McTaggart’s argument, granting its details, doesn’t establish what its conclusion claims. It establishes at most a thesis about how to describe time, not a thesis about whether the structural conditions of temporality obtain.

The argument supports three distinguishable readings: strict temporal error theory, incoherence of the A-series with a B-theoretic remainder, and a claim that complete description must be perspective-independent. The first carries an act/object burden; the latter two are compatible with directed order and therefore require different verdicts.

*First.* The strict-unreality reading: McTaggart’s argument shows that time itself is unreal, full stop. There is no time, only the appearance of time, generated by some non-temporal feature of reality. This is the eliminativist reading and the one McTaggart himself sometimes seems to endorse.

McTaggart’s writing and publication occurred within the apparent temporal order, so the performance of the argument instantiates temporal structure at the act level. The 1908 paper is itself an event with structural conditions: it is distinct from the 1907 draft and from the 1909 reception (S), it stands in temporal relations to those events (T), and it persists as a paper across the century of subsequent commentary (Φ). Its publication in *Mind* presupposes that the paper was first written and then published, not that the writing and the publication are non-temporally co-present in some atemporal mode. What that establishes is narrower than the date 1908 might suggest: the argument can’t dispense with temporal representation in its articulation. It doesn’t by itself refute an error theory on which the apparent order is grounded in non-temporal reality. The object-side account must be tested separately, and the burden it carries is to explain the indispensable structure without real time.

The structural point is this: the A-series/B-series dispute is internal to the analysis of T. If one of the two series is incoherent, then T must be analyzed in terms of the other series, or in terms of some third structure. McTaggart’s own C-series (the permanent, direction-neutral ordering of positions that survives the A-series’ collapse) is one such third structure, and the structural account partially vindicates it: the C-series’ bare ordering is real, the genuine residue of McTaggart’s positive view. What the structural T-role adds is precisely what the C-series withholds (asymmetric direction) supplied not by the contradictory A-series but by the self-exclusion the account grounds independently. So the affinity is the ordering and the difference is the asymmetry: the account preserves McTaggart’s positive residue while supplying the direction his negative argument leaves ungrounded.

That is also the answer to the premise the reply would otherwise leave standing, and it should be stated rather than passed over. McTaggart doesn’t merely offer the A-series as one optional analysis; he argues that time requires it, so that a B-series without it is a bare ordering and not a temporal one. Granting the contradiction while answering that another specification remains available would be no answer at all if the premise held. What the premise needs is that direction can come only from the tensed properties—past, present, future, predicated of events and shifting—whose joint attribution generates the regress. The account denies exactly that. Direction is grounded at §2.4 in self-exclusion: a state that gives way to another is not available alongside it, and the asymmetry of before and after falls out of that exclusion rather than out of any event’s being present. So the A-series is essential to McTaggart’s own construal of passage and not to directed order as such, and the incoherence he demonstrates, granted in full, reaches the construal. An A-theorist who holds that passage must be the shifting of tensed properties will find this unsatisfying, and the disagreement is then over what passage is rather than over whether McTaggart’s regress runs. What the dispute doesn’t show is that T fails to obtain. Whether a tenseless analysis alone supplies the whole of Temporality is the further dispute the B-theoretic form raises, and the choice among analyses is the topic of the philosophy of time, not a refutation of the existence of T.

**[Proposition]**

**Specification Is Not Obtaining** · *Proposition*

McTaggart’s contradiction, granted in full, falls on one analysis of temporal order rather than on temporal order itself. If the A-series is incoherent, T’s directed ordering is analyzed by the B-series or by a third structure, and the choice among them is the topic of the philosophy of time; whether that analysis also supplies passage, which Temporality requires alongside dimension, is a further dispute. Showing that a role admits no particular specification constrains how the role is specified; it does not show the role unoccupied.

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6)

*Second.* The A-series-incoherence form retains the B-series. McTaggart’s argument shows only that the A-series is incoherent, and a B-theoretic analysis of time is the proper response: time consists in the B-series, and the apparent reality of becoming is to be explained as a perspectival or psychological feature rather than as a metaphysical fact. Mellor’s *Real Time II* develops this position with full rigor.

The self-undermining argument above closes the strict-unreality reading only; the B-theoretic tradition (Mellor, Williams, Sider) operates at this level and is engaged here and at §8.3.1. The B-series (earlier than, later than, simultaneous with) supplies the dimension feature of Temporality. The four-dimensional manifold of B-series events is distinguishable into events (S), ordered (T), and persists across the manifold as a unified four-dimensional whole (Φ). On The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2), Temporality requires both the dimension and the passage; the B-theorist who supplies the dimension cleanly and reduces passage to indexical content gives one feature where the composition requires two, and the disagreement lives there. The Mellor reading is one specification of Temporality’s dimension feature, not the complete metaphysics of T.

*Third.* The perspective-dependence reading (Dummett, Sider, the early-twentieth-century Cambridge reading) takes McTaggart’s argument as showing not that time is unreal but that any complete description of reality must be from no perspective (perspective-independent in the strong sense) and that the A-series, which is irreducibly perspectival, can’t figure in such a description. This is a thesis about the metaphysics of description rather than about the metaphysics of time directly.

The perspective-dependence reading is structurally interesting and partly correct. The A-series claims are perspective-dependent in a sense the B-series claims aren’t: ‘the present moment’ picks out different moments depending on when the claim is made; ‘earlier than 1908’ picks out the same moments regardless of when the claim is made. What the present account requires is that whatever specification of T is offered, the structural fact of directed ordering obtains. Whether the metaphysical description that captures the ordering is perspectival or perspective-independent is a separate question. The B-theorist offers the perspective-independent version; the A-theorist offers the perspectival version; both supply the directed ordering T requires. McTaggart on the present reading, like Dummett, raises a question about the metaphysics of description; the question is genuinely open, and the present account is consistent with either resolution.

A kindred move is the radical eliminativism (some readings of Parfit, some readings of Buddhist analyses): time is unreal because the relations it requires (between selves, between events, between moments) are themselves unreal. The reply combines the present reply with §8.3.2 (the momentariness reply): the relations are exactly the structural facts named at §2.6, and their elimination either collapses on its own description or relabels the structural facts under another vocabulary.

Another kindred is the McTaggart-via-presentism position: only the present is real, and the past and future aren’t, so the A-series can’t generate the contradiction because there is only the present moment. Presentism is a metaphysical thesis with its own challenges (the truthmaker problem, the cross-time relations problem, the problem of historical reference); the present account is consistent with presentism in the sense that the structural conditions can be specified at each present moment as a fact about what reality contains. Whether presentism is the right metaphysics of time is a separate question that the present account doesn’t adjudicate.

*Convergence.* Three forms clarify the dispute: strict unreality faces an act/object burden because its argument uses temporal representation but may still propose a non-temporal ground of appearance; A-series-incoherence is consistent with the present account, which admits a B-theoretic specification of T’s dimension and locates the remaining disagreement at passage; and perspective-dependence is a thesis about the metaphysics of description, not about whether T obtains. Across the three forms, McTaggart’s argument either leaves the error theorist a burden it has not discharged or is consistent with the present account.

McTaggart’s argument belonged to a broader idealist program, and the natural worry is that the present account’s necessary, empirically unencounterable structure is itself a covert idealism rather than a neutral structural claim. The question is taken up directly at §9.5: whatever is taken as fundamental (a cosmic mind included) instantiates the three Conditions once it is structured enough to do the work the position needs of it, so the structural conditions are mind-compatible without being mind-derived. The idealist setting is engaged there, not set aside here.

The McTaggart literature does secure one point: pre-analytic temporal vocabulary doesn’t settle the relation between A-series and B-series descriptions. That question isn’t adjudicated here, and needn’t be. Its claim is invariant across the dispute: the structural fact of directed ordering obtains on either description. A-series and B-series accounts, the hybrid views (growing-block and moving-spotlight), and presentism each carry the structural conditions in different vocabulary, which is precisely why T’s necessity doesn’t wait on the winner. The book’s own positive view, on which tenseless order and tensed passage are two features Temporality jointly requires rather than rival readings of it, is developed at §4.2.2. That is where the account states a preference, not where the present result is secured.

The 1908 argument survived its tradition: the British Hegelian idealism that gave it its broader setting was largely abandoned by the 1920s, but the distinction between A-series and B-series became a permanent landmark of analytic philosophy of time. The argument survives because the question it raises is real, even if the conclusion it draws isn’t. Time is real on the present account, but its proper analysis remains disputed. McTaggart made that dispute unavoidable, and the structural account of §2.6 inherits the distinction his argument forced into view.

### 8.1.4 Block Universe
The B-theorist of time (Mellor, Smart, Williams, Sider) holds that the world is a four-dimensional manifold in which all events, past, present, and future, are equally real. There is no objective becoming; the apparent flow of time is a feature of conscious experience or of the indexical content of tensed claims, not a metaphysical fact about the manifold. The block-universe view is an influential metaphysical interpretation of relativity: the relativity of simultaneity makes a privileged present problematic, and the four-dimensional manifold is a natural setting for relativistic physics, though the interpretation remains contested. If the B-theorist is right, the present account of Triconditionality of Nature (§2.6) must be reinterpreted: T is the temporal extension of the block, not the directed flow of becoming, and the structural conditions obtain across the block as a whole rather than as a feature of a moving present.

The move is influential and the position is widely held. Smart’s “The River of Time” (1949) and *Philosophy and Scientific Realism* (1963) give the position its mid-century analytic articulation. Williams’s “The Myth of Passage” (1951) is the canonical statement of the case against objective becoming.
