Mellor’s *Real Time* (1981) and *Real Time II* (1998) develop a careful contemporary defense, on which tensed claims are reduced to tenseless truth-conditions and the apparent flow of time is a perspectival feature. Sider’s *Four-Dimensionalism* (2001) defends the block as the proper setting for ordinary objects, with persistence cashed out as having temporal parts at different times. Putnam’s “Time and Physical Geometry” (1967b) and Rietdijk’s (1966) argue that special relativity forces the block. Maudlin’s *The Metaphysics Within Physics* (2007) defends time’s fundamentality against the standard B-theoretic readings. Price’s *Time’s Arrow and Archimedes’ Point* (1996) argues for a thoroughgoing block view on which temporal asymmetry is a perspectival illusion.

The target here is the structural claim: that the block universe is a static four-dimensional manifold without genuine becoming, and therefore that the structural conditions named at §2.6 (if they obtain at all) obtain in a sense compatible with the absence of becoming, and possibly in a sense weaker than the present account requires. The reply isn’t that the B-theory is incoherent (it isn’t) but that the block supplies the ordering and distinctness the structural conditions require, and supplies candidate realizers for the continuity role, while the passage feature remains genuinely in dispute. The block isn’t a counterexample to the present account; it is one of the available metaphysics of how the structural conditions are instantiated, and the one point of real disagreement is named rather than absorbed.

The position can be separated into a strict-static-block thesis, an interpretation of relativity, and an account of becoming as perspectival. Each preserves the ordered manifold; the live disagreement concerns whether passage is an additional feature of Temporality.

*First.* The strict-static-block reading: the four-dimensional manifold is static in the sense that no genuine becoming obtains. The events of the manifold are timelessly arrayed, and the appearance of becoming is illusory. This is the eliminativist reading and is sometimes endorsed by readers of Williams or by readers who take the relativistic argument to its eliminativist limit.

The strict-static-block reading must distinguish two senses of ‘static.’ In one sense, the block is static in that the manifold as a whole doesn’t itself change: there is no super-time in which the four-dimensional manifold is arrayed and across which it evolves. In this sense, ‘static’ is correct and uncontroversial. In a second sense, ‘static’ would mean that the events within the manifold don’t stand in temporal relations: that no event is earlier or later than any other event, that there is no directed ordering. In this second sense, the block isn’t static; the temporal extension of the manifold is what makes it a four-dimensional manifold rather than a three-dimensional one. The events within the block stand in B-series relations (earlier than, later than, simultaneous with) and these relations supply the directed ordering T requires. The B-theorist who denies becoming in the metaphysical sense (no objective A-series flow) doesn’t deny temporal relations in the structural sense (B-series ordering across the manifold). The ordering T requires is the latter; whether Temporality also requires objective passage is a further question, and the one place the account takes a side.

**[Dissolution]**

**Two Senses of Static** · *Dissolution*

Either “static” means no super-time hosts the block and no evolution runs across it, in which case the charge is true and bears on nothing here; or it means the block’s events stand in no temporal relations at all, in which case it is the sense that would actually reach T—and no B-theorist asserts it, since events in the manifold stand in earlier-than relations, the very ordering that makes it four-dimensional rather than three. The objection trades on the first sense while requiring the second.

**Dissolves:** the static-block objection to Temporality, which reaches T only on a sense of *static* no B-theorist asserts

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6)

The events within the block are distinguishable from one another (S). They stand in temporal relations of earlier and later (T). The manifold is a unified four-dimensional whole, but it doesn’t itself persist through a further time. Within it, worldlines, temporal parts, or other cross-time relations may realize the bearing and continuity role associated with Φ. The block’s unity shouldn’t be redescribed as temporal persistence of the whole. The B-theoretic block instantiates the dimension feature of T cleanly. On The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2), Temporality requires both the dimension and the passage as two features held together; the block-only reading without objective passage gives one feature where the composition requires two. The B-theorist who reduces passage to indexical content (Mellor, Williams, the perspectival-becoming form that follows) is in disagreement with the composition view on the metaphysical status of passage rather than consistent with it; the disagreement lives there. The B-theorist who allows objective passage through the manifold is the composition view in B-vocabulary.

*Second.* The relativistic form is the central motivation for the block. Special relativity’s relativity of simultaneity is incompatible with a privileged objective present: different inertial frames disagree on which events are simultaneous, and there is no frame-independent fact of the matter. The four-dimensional manifold of Minkowski spacetime is the natural setting; events stand in the light-cone structure (causal past, causal future, elsewhere) rather than in a frame-independent A-series (the tensed past/present/future ordering with the present moving); the block is what relativity gives us.

The relativistic argument is correct as far as it goes, and it is accommodated here without revision. T (directed ordering of states) doesn’t require a frame-independent global present. It requires that events stand in temporal relations sufficient to support change, and the light-cone structure of Minkowski spacetime supplies exactly that: every event has a determinate causal past (events that can have influenced it) and a determinate causal future (events it can influence). The ordering is partial rather than total (events in each other’s elsewhere don’t stand in a determinate temporal relation) but partial ordering is sufficient for the present account. Change is local; the structural conditions named at §2.6 are conditions on local processes of change, not on the existence of a global frame-independent present. Relativity makes the present account more careful, not less correct.

A note on the contested status of the inference itself. The move from special relativity to the four-dimensional block isn’t a settled physics result. Neo-Lorentzian interpretations, Bell, Maudlin’s *Quantum Non-Locality and Relativity* (1976; 2002, ch. 7), and Craig’s *Time and the Metaphysics of Relativity* (2001a) most directly, preserve a privileged frame consistently with the empirical content by treating Lorentz contraction and time dilation as dynamical effects on rods and clocks rather than as features of the spacetime structure itself; the Putnam–Stein exchange (Stein 1968; Stein 1991) and Balashov–Janssen (2003) press the orthodox four-dimensionalist reading against these alternatives. The dispute is genuine, and the present account doesn’t contest either reading: on the orthodox reading T is supplied by light-cone partial ordering across the manifold, on the neo-Lorentzian reading T is supplied by a privileged dynamical frame, and on either reading the directed ordering the structural conditions named at §2.6 require is instantiated.

*Third.* The perspectival-becoming form (Mellor’s mature position; Williams’s “Myth of Passage”; Price’s perspectival arrow) accepts the block at the metaphysical level and locates becoming at the perspectival level: the apparent flow of time is a feature of conscious experience, of indexical content, of the perspective of an observer embedded within the block, not a fact about the manifold itself.

The perspectival reading is consistent with the present account on the dimension feature of T and in tension with it on the passage feature. The structural conditions are instantiated by the manifold; the Mellor account preserves the dimension feature of T (B-series ordering), preserves S (event-distinctness), preserves a cross-time continuity or temporal-parts structure capable of realizing the Φ-role, and offers a story about how perspectival experience of becoming arises from the structural facts. On The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2), the passage feature of Temporality is metaphysically real rather than indexical, and Mellor’s reduction is what the composition view declines. The story about perspectival becoming is consistent with the present account where it explains how the metaphysically-real passage registers from within a configuration that tracks its own position; it isn’t consistent where the becoming is the whole of what passage names. The disagreement is local to the passage feature; the rest of the Mellor architecture stands.

A kindred move is the growing-block theory (Tooley, Broad’s earlier position): the past and present are real, the future isn’t, and the block grows by addition as time passes. Growing-block is structurally a hybrid: it accepts B-series relations among the past-and-present events, accepts a privileged present (the leading edge of the block), and posits an objective process of addition. The present account is consistent with growing-block in the sense that the growing block instantiates T (across the past-and-present), S, and Φ; the disputes between growing-block and the strict-block (and between both and presentism, on which only the present moment is real, the past having ceased and the future not yet existing) are internal to the metaphysics of which structures are instantiated, not whether the structural conditions obtain.

Another kindred is the moving-spotlight theory (Cameron, Skow): the block is timelessly there, and a privileged present moves across it. The present account is consistent with the moving-spotlight in the sense that the spotlight obtains within an already-structured block; the spotlight is one structural feature among others, supported by the underlying structure.

*Convergence.* Three forms and each is consistent with the present account at the level it operates: the strict-static-block reading distinguishes two senses of ‘static’ and yields the ordering T requires; the relativistic form replaces a global present with light-cone structure and supplies T as a partial ordering; and the perspectival-becoming form locates becoming in conscious experience while preserving the ordering at the metaphysical level. Across the three forms the block supplies S and the dimension feature of T cleanly, and worldlines or temporal parts stand as candidate realizers of the continuity role. What it doesn’t supply, on the strict reading, is the passage the composition view holds Temporality requires alongside dimension, and that is where the disagreement sits.

A consequence for the Kalām engagement (§10.1.5). On The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2), the passage feature of Temporality is metaphysically real; *began to exist* therefore has determinate structural content. What the composition view marks is two readings of the begin-question: a quantitative reading (how far back the passage runs along the dimension) engaged at §10.1.5 and a categorial reading (a moment-prior-to-T from which T began) foreclosed by Parasitic Negation. The strict-B-theoretic reduction of passage to indexical content is a separable issue that doesn’t absorb the begin-question in the way Craig’s pressure assumes; the composition view’s commitment to objective passage is what the engagement at §10.1.5 runs on.

The B-theoretic literature gives powerful reasons to question naïve assumptions about a frame-independent present, objective passage, and the metaphysical privilege of the present moment. B-theorists commonly locate apparent flow and presentness in conscious experience or the indexical content of tensed claims; A-theoretic and neo-Lorentzian rivals contest that interpretation. These are live philosophical disputes, and what follows is meant to hold across them. What is added here is that the four-dimensional manifold the B-theorist describes isn’t an alternative to the structural conditions but a particular specification of them. The block is what the dimension feature of T looks like when it is described by the metaphysics of relativistic physics.

The block is the standard backdrop now in a way it wasn’t in McTaggart’s day. The block’s events are distinct and ordered, and its cross-time structure is what would bear the persistence Φ names; that much is what the block consists in, and the argument over passage is a dispute about one feature within that structure rather than about whether there is any (§2.6).

### 8.1.5 Platonism
What of mathematics? Numbers seem to be the paradigm of changeless objects. The number 7 isn’t somewhere; it doesn’t move; it doesn’t decay; it doesn’t depend on anything for its existence; it stands in eternal mathematical relations with the other numbers and with the structures it figures in. If anything is a counterexample to the present account, it is the realm of mathematical objects: abstract, atemporal, aspatial, immaterial, and indubitably real (or at least real enough that mathematical practice across cultures and millennia has converged on remarkably stable conclusions about them). The Platonist about mathematics has the natural candidate for objects exempt from the structural conditions of §2.6.

The move is venerable. Plato’s Forms, the original Platonist proposal, are paradigmatic of changeless reality: the Form of the Triangle, of Justice, of the Good, each eternal and unchanging, the temporal world of becoming a degraded copy of the timeless world of being. Frege’s *Grundlagen der Arithmetik* (1884) revives mathematical Platonism in modern dress: numbers are objective abstract objects, and arithmetic is the science of their structure. Gödel (1944; 1964) defends a robust Platonism on which mathematical objects are perceived through a faculty analogous to sense perception. Quine and Putnam’s indispensability arguments (1971; 1979) make mathematical realism respectable to naturalists who would otherwise have shied away from abstract objects. Shapiro’s *Philosophy of Mathematics: Structure and Ontology* (1997) develops structuralism, on which mathematics is the science of structures rather than of particular objects. Maddy’s *Naturalism in Mathematics* (1997) and *Defending the Axioms* (2011) move from her earlier set-theoretic realism to a naturalism on which the justification of axioms answers to mathematical practice rather than to Platonist metaphysics. Balaguer’s *Platonism and Anti-Platonism in Mathematics* (1998) gives the comprehensive survey. The classical theist sometimes adopts a Platonism-plus theology: God’s mind contains the abstract objects, and the realm of Forms is the divine intellect.

The target here is the structural claim: that mathematical objects are abstract entities exempt from the structural conditions of §2.6, and therefore that the Modal Identity of §2.6.6 (the result that the necessary possibility of change entails the necessary co-instantiation of Time, Space, and Substance) holds at most for the concrete world while a wider reality contains entities that violate it. The reply isn’t that Platonism is incoherent, and the scope is worth fixing once, here, because everything below stands inside it. The result the structural argument delivers against this rival is a scope result: the necessity claim concerns concrete change-realizing worlds, and abstracta as the Platonist describes them are not offered as one, so a Platonist may keep the abstracta entire and will not thereby have exhibited what the objection needs, which is a concrete change-realizing world lacking the conditions. That much is settled and is all that the chapter’s argument requires.

What follows the scope result is an interpretation, offered as one and not forced by anything above it: that mathematical objects are descriptions of what structured reality, actual and possible, affords, rather than residents of a separate realm that must be shown to satisfy the conditions after all. Because the conditions govern the *possible* and not merely the actual (§2.6.6), those descriptions reach as far as the possible reaches—to collections larger than anything the actual world contains, and to the infinite—without positing a single abstract object. A robust Platonist is free to decline the interpretation and keep the objects; nothing in the necessity claim rests on his accepting it. What the reply never does is claim that mathematical objects possess their own time-like, space-like, and substance-like structure in some rarefied mode, which would relocate the exempt object and stretch Time, Space, and Substance into a second, analogical sense.

That reading has a name and a literature. Treating mathematics as the science of quantity and structure instantiated in the world rather than resident in a separate realm is *in re* or Aristotelian realism, developed most fully by Franklin (2014) against Platonism and nominalism alike. The reading available here belongs to that family and departs from it in one respect worth marking. An *in re* account is only as secure as the instantiation it presupposes: it holds that mathematics is about structures the world contains, and has no resources of its own for saying why the world must contain them. Modal Identity supplies that floor—Time, Space, and Substance are not found to be instantiated but derived as necessarily co-instantiated (§2.6.6), so the structures the reading describes cannot fail to have bearers.

*First.* Classical Platonism (the Plato–Frege–Gödel line) holds that mathematical objects are particular abstract entities, each numerically distinct from the others, standing in eternal relations of mathematical structure. The number 7 is a particular object, distinct from the number 6 and from the number 8; the natural numbers stand in the successor relation; the relation is eternal and changeless.

Platonic Forms presuppose form. The word *form* (English *form*, Latin *forma*, Greek εἶδος) carries both the verbal sense (to take shape, to come into being) and the nominal sense (the eternal pattern, the abstract universal). εἶδος descends from ἰδεῖν, *to see*: it named originally what something looks like as it takes shape, the seen aspect of something undergoing process. Plato’s move is to read the seen-aspect as an eternal pattern that prescribes the shape the process takes. We observe trees taking shape, mammals developing, planets accreting; the Platonist infers Forms of Tree, Mammal, and Planet prescribing what those processes converge on. The inference trades on the equivocation between the verbal sense (formation) and the nominal sense (the eternal Form): what follows from the observation is that formation-processes occur, and that the conditions of reality are such as to permit them, not that there is an eternal pattern prior to them prescribing what they must produce.

Three pressures on the classical-Platonist line are worth naming before the math-Platonist refinements. *The natural-kind pressure.* Trees vary across species, climates, and life-stages; mammals span the spectrum from blue whale to shrew; the Form of Tree or Form of Mammal that would be at the same explanatory level as the Form of the Triangle becomes indeterminate across borderline and heterogeneous cases. Plato himself hesitates on this point in the *Parmenides* (130c–d), where Socrates flinches over whether there are Forms of hair, mud, and dirt. The modern reactivation runs through Wittgenstein’s family-resemblance critique (Wittgenstein 1953, §§65–71), Dupré’s species pluralism (Dupré 1993), and Boyd’s homeostatic-property-cluster account of natural kinds (Boyd 1991), each pressing the point that the kinds the world contains aren’t the kinds the Platonist’s Form-talk requires.

*The process pressure.* A tree isn’t a static form: it is seed, sapling, mature, senescent, snag, and across seasons evergreen or deciduous. The Form of Tree would have to be either the form of a static cross-section (which isn’t what a tree is) or the form of the developmental sequence. An atemporal Form can specify a temporal sequence without itself changing: a sequence can be represented timelessly, the way a function can specify a trajectory. Neither horn shows that an abstract Form must occupy time. What they press is whether the Form of Tree, so specified, still supplies a concrete change-realizer exempt from the conditions. Aristotle presses the explanatory uselessness of Forms for change and coming-to-be in *Metaphysics* A.9, 991a8–b9, and develops the immanent, hylomorphic alternative in *De Anima* II.1, 412a19–28; the process-philosophical tradition from Heraclitus through Whitehead (1929) and Bergson (1907) develops the point systematically.

*The reflexive-substrate pressure.* The Platonist standing on Earth is held by what they describe (a planet) and owes an account of the Form of Earth that supports them. Retreat to property-universals (Armstrong, Tooley) abandons Forms of individuals; retreat to the *Timaeus* elemental geometries (53c–55c) confuses earth-the-element with Earth-the-planet; retreat to Plotinian emanation (*Enneads* V.9, VI.9) substitutes a Neoplatonist theology for the Platonist analysis; retreat to Lewisian modal realism (Lewis 1986a) changes the ontology under discussion. Each retreat concedes that the Form of the individual thing supporting the Platonist wasn’t available.

The pressures share a structural diagnosis. The Platonist treats Forms as prescriptive: the Form of Tree explains why trees take the shape they do; the Form of Triangle explains why triangles have the angle-sum they have; the Form of Justice explains what just acts have in common. The structural account inverts the direction. That trees take the shape they do follows from the structural conditions of §2.6 being such as to permit trees: the necessary co-instantiation of Time, Space, and Substance yields a Reality in which tree-formation is among the possible processes. The descriptive content the Platonist reads as the Form of Tree is the description of what those conditions afford for that kind of configuration. The 180° angle-sum of a Euclidean triangle isn’t prescribed by a Form of Triangle; it is a structural consequence of the metric specification of the relevant space (the metric-as-contingent-specification point is developed at §2.4.7) and spherical and hyperbolic geometries produce different angle-sums under different metric specifications, all licensed within the structural conditions.

**[Argument]**

**The Form Runs Downstream** · *The Platonic Inversion*

1. **The Platonist treats Forms as prescriptive.** The Form of Tree explains why trees take the shape they do; the Form of the Triangle why triangles have the angle-sum they have.

2. **To be a Form at all is to be a determinate *this* rather than *that*.** The Form of the Triangle isn’t the Form of the Circle, and a Form with nothing it is rather than isn’t fixes nothing.

3. **That determinacy is borrowed, not native.** The Form of the Triangle is determinate because triangles, actual or possible, are determinate; its distinctness from the Form of the Circle is the distinctness of the configurations it describes.

4. **∴ The prescriptive direction reverses.** What the Platonist calls a Form runs downstream of actuality plus the structural conditions, never upstream: what looks like a prior pattern prescribing actuality is a description of what actuality, under those conditions, produces.

*Scope.* The reply isn’t that Platonism is incoherent. A robust Platonist may keep the abstracta, and what the four forms test is only whether those abstracta supply a concrete change-realizer lacking the conditions. The inversion bears on the prescriptive reading, not on mathematical existence.

**[Proposition]**

**Borrowed Determinacy** · *Proposition*

A Form is a Form only by being a determinate this rather than that: Triangle and not Circle, Justice and not Beauty. Ask what fixes the determinacy. If it is the configurations the Form describes, then determinacy runs from structure to Form, and the Form does not supply a concrete change-realizer that lacks the conditions; it need not thereby be reduced to a description. If it is native to the Form instead, the position owes an account of differentiation within an order carrying no distinction, ordering, or bearing to supply it.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

Take the number 7. What is 7 apart from seven of something? The classical Platonist’s answer is: a particular abstract object, distinct from 6 and 8, sitting in the eternal successor relation. The present answer is that *7* is the count-structure of any seven-membered plurality there could be, the way any such collection is when it is enumerated. Its distinctness from 6 and 8 is the distinctness of those collections (one fewer thing, one more); the successor ordering is the ordering of the collections under the operation of adding a unit; the stability of “7 is the successor of 6” across every time, person, and culture is the stability of what *any* possible seven-membered collection would be.

These can be represented as facts about actual or possible pluralities. Actual concrete pluralities have concrete members, but merely possible, infinite, or abstract pluralities can’t simply be assumed to occupy Space, stand in temporal order, or be made of Substance. The modal-structuralist analysis must explain those cases rather than treating concreteness as automatic.

On the modal-structuralist reading, the number needs no private time, space, and substance of its own, because it was never an object over and above the things; it is the description of their count. And because the count is a count of *possible* collections, it reaches numbers larger than all the things that happen to exist, and the transfinite, without any object’s being conjured to bear it. Classical Platonism doesn’t exhibit a counterexample to the account developed here, and on the reading just given the apparent counterexample dissolves rather than being defeated.

The smallest nontrivial case fixes the ontology. *Two* is neither a particular pair nor an additional member standing beside every pair. Different pairs share no material content: two stones and two stars contain different things at different places. What they share is cardinal structure. Each plurality can be placed in one-to-one correspondence with the other, enumeration terminates after the second member, and the addition or removal of a member changes the cardinality represented. The written numeral *2* is a sign; the concept *two* represents this invariant *how many*; a particular pair instantiates it. None of those roles requires a further object, *the Two*, over and above the sign, the representation, and the structured pluralities represented. A Platonist may posit that object as the ground of the invariant, but the invariance doesn’t by itself establish the posit: correspondence already specifies what the pluralities have in common.

Two homely cases make the reading concrete. First, measure. No one is tempted to house “1.5 meters” in a realm of abstracta; it is how long a thing is, a magnitude borne by the rod that has it. Number belongs to the same family: *7* is a *how many* in the way a length is a *how long*, a feature of a plurality rather than an object standing beside it. The Platonist’s temptation is to treat the one magnitude we happen to reach by counting as though it were unlike every other magnitude, a thing rather than a measure. Second, matching. A shepherd who can’t count can still keep his flock exactly: he drops a pebble into a sack as each sheep leaves the fold and removes one as each returns, and a pebble left over at dusk is a sheep unaccounted for. He has tracked the number without ever naming it, and the sheep and the pebbles share nothing beyond standing in one-to-one correspondence with none left over. That correspondence is what *7* records, and it’s why collections with nothing else in common can be identical in number: sameness of number is sameness under pairing, not joint participation in a shared object. This is the content of Hume’s principle (Frege 1884, §63): the number of *F*s equals the number of *G*s just when the *F*s and *G*s correspond one-to-one; on the present reading the principle fixes a fact about pluralities rather than introducing a name for an abstract particular.

*Second.* Structuralism (Shapiro, Resnik, Hellman) refines the classical position by holding that mathematical objects aren’t particular entities but positions in structures. The number 7 isn’t a particular abstract object but the seventh position in any ω-sequence (any infinite sequence ordered like the natural numbers, with a first element and a successor for every element); what mathematics studies is the structure of ω-sequences, not particular sequences. This is meant to handle the multiple-reductions problem (3 can be reduced to {{{{}}}} or to {{},{{}},{{},{{}}}}) by holding that any reduction that preserves the structure preserves what 7 is.

Structuralism makes the structural-conditions reply more direct, not less. The structures mathematics studies are constituted by determinate elements or positions and relations, directly supporting a difference-role. Some structures include asymmetric order; many don’t. Their abstract stability doesn’t by itself amount to temporal persistence or physical bearing. Upgrading the mathematical roles to T and Φ therefore requires a realization premise. The reply isn’t that Shapiro is wrong about mathematical structure: positions individuated by their relations to other positions in the same structure are the difference-role in the mathematical case. The structural-conditions account is, on the present reading, structuralism extended to non-mathematical reality, the same insight applied to the wider domain of which mathematics is one structured region.

*Third.* The naturalized form (Maddy, Quine, Putnam) drops the strong realism about abstract objects and holds instead that mathematical objects are whatever the indispensability argument requires, the entities that are quantified over in our best scientific theories. The ontological commitment is to whatever is needed to make the science work; the metaphysics of the entities is left open.

The naturalized form doesn’t aim to exhibit a counterexample to the structural account; it aims to deflate the metaphysical question. As deflation, it is irrelevant to the structural reply: whatever the indispensable mathematical entities turn out to be, they will be whatever the science requires, and the science requires distinctness, ordering, and persistence of mathematical facts. If the naturalist insists on a stronger reading (that mathematical entities have some metaphysical status that exempts them from the structural conditions) then the reply to the classical Platonist applies. If the naturalist remains deflationary, then the position isn’t in tension with the structural account.

*Fourth.* Plenitudinous Platonism (Balaguer) holds that every consistent mathematical theory describes a real domain of mathematical objects: the universe is mathematically plenitudinous, with every possible mathematical structure instantiated somewhere. This is meant to dissolve the access problem: we don’t need a faculty for picking out particular abstract objects, because every consistent description picks out something.

Plenitude is a stronger claim than the classical Platonist makes, and the structural reply applies more straightforwardly. The plenitude of mathematical structures isn’t itself a further structured object but a description, at maximal extent, of what the structural conditions afford. To speak of the totality of consistent theories is to describe how such theories stand: individuated by their consistency conditions, ordered by relations of inclusion or interpretation, stable across all considerations of which structures exist. Each of those is a description of the distinctness, ordering, and persistence any possible structure would have, not a Time, Space, or Substance instantiated by some super-object ‘the totality.’ If the present account is right, plenitudinous Platonism is its mathematical correlate, not its refutation.

A kindred move is the divine-intellect Platonism: the abstract objects exist in God’s mind, and their atemporality is the atemporality of the divine intellect. The reply combines the present reply with §10.2.3 (the changeless-ground reply): the divine intellect that contains the structured realm of abstracts is itself structured, and that structuredness is the triconditional structure itself (§2.6). The classical theist’s Platonism-plus-theology faces the structural reply twice over.

The modal-structuralist position (Hellman) is, on the present reading, not one more Platonism to absorb but a mathematical statement of the reply itself: mathematics isn’t about actual abstract objects but about possible structures. That is precisely the account given here: *7* is the structure of any possible seven-membered collection, and arithmetic is the study of what such possible structures are like. The only adjustment is the ground: the modality isn’t a primitive realm of its own but is fixed by the structural conditions of §2.6, which govern the whole space of the possible (§2.6.6). Invariant Realization (§3.5.6) adds the transfer: a proved invariant binds any real realization of its mathematical profile without turning the profile into a second concrete domain. Mathematics describes the possible; the possible is structured by Time, Space, and Substance; so mathematics, far from naming exceptions to the conditions, is a general description of what they afford.

*Convergence.* Four forms and none exhibits the counterexample the position needs: classical Platonism’s particular abstract objects are read here as descriptions of structured possibility rather than exceptions to it; structuralism’s structures are constituted by exactly the relational facts the account names; the naturalized form is either deflationary (and not in tension) or stronger-than-deflationary (and faces the classical reply); and plenitudinous Platonism describes the full range of structures it admits, not a counterexample to it. Across the four forms, no mathematical view by itself supplies a counterexample to the necessity of structure in concrete change-realizing worlds. The nominalist conclusion, that mathematical objects aren’t objects at all but descriptions of possible structure, remains one proposed interpretation, not a result forced on Platonism by §2.6 alone.

What the Platonist tradition genuinely captures is worth preserving. There is a sense in which mathematical truths aren’t merely conventional, not merely useful, not merely about marks on paper or sounds in the air. The persistence of mathematical truth across cultures and millennia, the convergence of independent investigations on the same theorems, the resistance of mathematical structure to revision in ways that empirical theories are revised, each speaks to something real about the subject matter of mathematics. The account of §2.6 is consistent with that sense. Mathematical structures are real structures; their reality is the reality of what the structural conditions afford, the count and pattern of every possible collection, described maximally and changelessly. The stability is the stability of the possible, not the serenity of an abstract object.

Frege’s *Grundlagen* (1884) was printed on paper that has decayed in the intervening century and a half. The arithmetic he was investigating did not decay. What did not decay, on the present reading, isn’t a timeless object exempt from §2.6 but a truth about every possible collection: that seven of anything is the successor of six of it. The number 7 isn’t somewhere because it isn’t the kind of thing that could be anywhere: it is the count any seven-membered plurality has, and pluralities are where their members are. It doesn’t move or decay because descriptions of what is possible don’t move or decay; the possibilities they describe are fixed by the structural conditions that govern the possible. The Platonist’s number isn’t a counterexample to the present account, and it isn’t a hidden instance of it either. It is a description of what reality, under the conditions of §2.6, makes countable.

## 8.2 Contingency, Necessity, and Nothingness
The rivals gathered here contest what the world’s contingency requires.

The principle of sufficient reason (§8.2.1) presses the demand that every fact carry an explanation. Humean contingency (§8.2.2) answers that the demand is unmotivated, and that regularities need no ground beyond their holding. Information-theoretic foundationalism (§8.2.3) relocates the base from substance to information.

Pizzi’s impossibility of nothingness (§8.2.4) argues that the absence of everything isn’t a genuine alternative to be explained away. The modal collapse objection (§8.2.5) turns the question back on the framework itself, charging that a necessary ground leaves no contingency standing.

The accounts press different questions. PSR asks whether structural necessity leaves an explanatory debt; Humeanism denies that regularity needs a governing bond; information-first views reverse the order of priority; Pizzi independently closes modal space against nothingness; and modal collapse asks whether the necessary floor makes every occupant necessary. Their verdicts therefore range across open burden, relocation, convergence, and non-propagation rather than one common failure to eliminate the Conditions.

### 8.2.1 The Principle of Sufficient Reason
The rationalist demand for sufficient reason is an exacting standard any necessary-existence argument has to meet on its own terms. Applied to the three Conditions, the demand takes three forms (a contrast demand, an origin demand, and Pruss’s modal refinement). The replies that follow grant the Leibnizian point freely. A rationalist argument that terminates in a brute fact has betrayed its own standard, and a conclusion terminating in brute necessity would betray the standard this argument was raised under. The argument doesn’t so terminate, and the verdict divides. Where the demand asks for a contrast, it runs out of one; where it asks for a beginning out of a prior absence, it asks for a transition before transitions are possible. Pruss’s version is not disposed of on either count: the demand for an explanation of the whole contingent conjunction stays live, and is answered, so far as it is answered here, by declining the Hume–Edwards inference rather than by closing the question.

Leibniz gives the demand its canonical form (1714) 1989: nothing exists without a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise. Pruss develops a rigorous contemporary defense (2006): if every contingent fact has an explanation, the chain must terminate in something whose existence isn’t contingent. The demand isn’t parochial; it is the demand that reality be intelligible all the way down.

Applied to this argument, it presses that T∧S∧Φ obtaining necessarily is itself a fact about reality, and facts about reality are subject to the PSR. If the necessity is brute, the argument has violated its own commitment. If it is grounded, whatever grounds it stands outside or beneath Nature as the true necessary ground.

*First.* The contrast demand presses that without a reason why the three conditions obtain rather than not, the argument has merely relocated bruteness from physics to metaphysics, and a brute necessity isn’t more intelligible than a brute contingency, only more deeply hidden.

The demand presupposes a contrast the argument has already foreclosed. ‘Why the three conditions rather than not?’ supposes that ∅ is a coherent alternative whose non-obtaining requires explanation. As established at §2.7, ∅ isn’t: nothing individuates it, nothing distinguishes its obtaining from its non-obtaining, nothing for any description to attach to. The PSR demands a reason for obtaining rather than not obtaining; where the ‘not obtaining’ side is incoherent, the demand doesn’t find a gap but fails to articulate one. The question presupposes a contrast its own terms can’t sustain.

*Second.* The origin demand grants the ∅ result but presses for a beginning: even if ∅ is incoherent as a state, Nature must have begun, and there must be some account of why the three Conditions obtain now rather than a prior arrangement.

The demand, on this analysis, isn’t unanswered but unaskable in the form it was issued in. A beginning in that sense, out of a prior absence, is an event: a transition from non-existence to existence. Such a transition requires the three Conditions to take place: a temporal succession in which the prior state doesn’t contain the three conditions and the subsequent state does, within a Space that can host both, carried by Substance. To propose that kind of beginning for Nature is to propose a transition before transitions are possible, which is to describe nothing at all. A least temporal boundary, with no prior state behind it, is not a transition of this kind (No Stable Zero-Extension). The word ‘prior’ has no application outside the succession it names. The demand uses the three Conditions in its own formulation and then asks why they obtain, using the very conditions of the asking.

*Third.* Pruss’s modal refinement drops the demand for explanation of necessary facts and confines the PSR to contingent facts. The modal PSR doesn’t require ∅ to be coherent as an alternative. It simply notes that every contingent fact admits of explanation, and asks whether the three conditions’ instantiation in this world is such a contingent fact.

The refinement survives, but it survives by conceding the conclusion. A PSR confined to contingent facts leaves the necessity of the three Conditions unchallenged: that is what ‘confined to contingent facts’ means. The necessary conditions aren’t in its scope. What the modal PSR captures are the causal sequences and events within Nature: why this reaction rather than that, why this memory rather than another. The present account (necessary structural conditions plus contingent investigation of everything within them) leaves every such question open to investigation. A theist who adopts the modal PSR is no longer arguing against the three conditions’ necessity but engaging contingent facts within Nature, the domain the present account is designed to accommodate.

One further engagement is owed at this site. Pruss’s central deployment of the modal PSR isn’t the abstract form already addressed (why T∧S∧Φ rather than ∅) but the *Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact* argument (*The Principle of Sufficient Reason* 2006; *Necessary Existence* with Rasmussen 2018): the conjunction of all contingent facts (the BCCF) is itself contingent and by modal PSR requires an explanation outside it.

On the book’s framework the BCCF is the conjunction of all contingent configurations of Nature: this cosmos, these initial conditions, this particular sequence of events. Each contingent fact within Nature has a contingent cause or explanation within Nature’s causal structure; the modal PSR is satisfied at that level. This is compatible with genuine chance and doesn’t quietly presuppose determinism. Where a transition is governed by an objective probability distribution rather than a deterministic law, the distribution itself, fixed by the prior state and Nature’s causal structure, is what the modal PSR is owed. It is a reason why the outcome falls within a determinate range of possibilities, weighted in a determinate way, not a further hidden fact that secretly settles which member of the range is realized. To demand the latter is to demand that chance covertly be non-chance, which begs the question against genuine indeterminism rather than pressing a live PSR violation. This is exactly the room the reply to modal collapse (§8.2.5) draws on when it invokes quantum indeterminacy: an open token outcome isn’t a PSR debt left unpaid but the kind of contingent fact the modal PSR was always going to leave open once explanation is distinguished from determination.

The reply doesn’t, however, rest on the Hume–Edwards principle that explaining each contingent conjunct thereby explains their conjunction, the very inference Pruss’s BCCF argument is built to reject. Its load-bearing move is instead the foreclosure of the external demand itself. The demand for an explanation *outside* the BCCF commonly motivates a necessary explainer, but the three candidates considered here—∅, Nature itself, and a necessary being whose free act selects the BCCF—don’t exhaust every theory of explanation by logic alone. They organize the principal options the structural account engages. ∅ is foreclosed. Nature doesn’t explain the BCCF *necessarily*; if it did, the BCCF would be necessary, and contingent facts would collapse into necessities (the modal-collapse risk addressed at §8.2.5). The third candidate is the theist’s actual proposal—a necessary agent whose libertarian choice explains a contingent outcome without necessitating it, escaping the modal-collapse horn. It is engaged, not ignored: Nothing to Consider (§2.7) forecloses ∅, while the external-ground proposal is tested at §10.1 and §10.2.3, with No Supernature (§11.10) stating the downstream boundary. What this section settles is narrower—the modal PSR doesn’t by itself convert the demand for an external explainer into a demand for a *necessary personal* one; that inference is what those sections test, not one the PSR delivers here. Nature explains the structural preconditions under which contingent configurations obtain; the contingent selection among configurations is internal to Nature.

The selection-among-possibilities question (why this configuration rather than another) is addressed at §2.9.4 and §10.1: contingency is a property of configurations within Nature, not of Nature itself, and the demand that selection receive an external necessary explanation posits a grounding framework outside Nature.

This is the disambiguation the reply turns on. The BCCF isn’t *granted* an internal sufficient reason for the conjunction as a whole; that would be the Hume–Edwards move Pruss is right to reject. Nor is the totality-level demand declared incoherent merely because its proposed answer would stand outside Nature. What this section establishes is that modal PSR alone doesn’t identify that answer as a necessary personal explainer. Each contingent conjunct keeps its contingent explanation within Nature’s causal structure; whether their conjunction incurs a further totality-level debt, and whether any external candidate can pay it, remains for the dedicated engagements in Chapters 10–11.

The dissolution carries further than the deflection of three demands, but only for one starting point. If ∅ isn’t a coherent alternative to Nature (§2.7), then Nature’s contingency can’t serve as a starting point for the argument to a necessary divine cause, because the structure has been shown to be not contingent but necessary. Its necessity renders that demand incoherent rather than redirecting it toward a divine answer. Contingency of the framework is where Leibniz and Clarke standardly begin, and started there, it isn’t answered by the Necessity of Nature but dissolved at its foundation. Pruss’s BCCF argument doesn’t take that starting point. Its premise is that the conjunction of all contingent facts is itself contingent; it doesn’t require the structural framework or Nature itself to be contingent. Showing Nature necessary therefore doesn’t dissolve that route.

**[Dissolution]**

**Dissolved, Not Answered** · *Dissolution*

Either the PSR route to an external necessary ground takes its framework-contingency form—Leibniz and Clarke’s, starting from Reality’s contingency—in which case it is not answered by the Necessity of Nature but dissolved one step earlier: if ∅ isn’t a coherent alternative, that starting point is unavailable, the structure is necessary rather than contingent, and no framework-level contingency remains for the demand to take hold of; or it takes Pruss’s BCCF form, beginning from the contingency of the conjunction of contingent facts, in which case the necessity of Nature doesn’t touch that premise and the demand isn’t dissolved. A totality-level demand raised on the second horn stays live here; modal PSR doesn’t by itself identify a personal external explainer, and the demand is engaged at §10.1 and §11.10.

**Dissolves:** the contingency-premised theistic PSR demand

A further move deserves naming. The Thomist may press that structural necessity isn’t the right kind of necessity: that classical theism demands the necessity of essence possessed by a being whose essence is its existence (Feser 2017; Koons 1997; Rasmussen 2019). The observation is correct and the counter-construction is live, but it isn’t a fourth variant of the PSR; it is taken up on its own terms in §10.2.3 (a being outside Nature) and §10.1 (a being beneath it).

Another move presses a structural parallel rather than a PSR variant. If Nature is self-grounding, why is the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) not equally so? The *causa sui* construction holds that the divine nature is its own sufficient reason, requiring no external explanation, and the suggestion is that the present reading must concede the same status to whatever it proposes as the necessary ground.

The setup is incomplete on its face. Nature doesn’t need an outside ground in the way that objects within Nature need their grounding conditions, because Nature isn’t an object that occupies anything outside itself. Nature *is* what occupying-anything consists in. The question ‘what makes Nature possible?’ assumes something outside Nature within which its possibility could be grounded, but that outside doesn’t exist. To be possible is to be permitted by Nature. Nature doesn’t permit itself from some external vantage point; it is what permission consists in.

The parallel fails because the two cases are structurally different in a precise way. Nature isn’t self-grounding in the sense that it is an entity which happens to satisfy the conditions for grounding from the inside. It is self-grounding in the stronger sense that it just is the conditions under which grounding operates: the logical space within which any explanatory demand, any sufficient reason, any grounding relation first becomes possible. There is no grounding framework outside Nature within which the question of Nature’s own ground could be posed, because the framework is Nature.

The distinction is sharp, and it isn’t neutral. God, on the *causa sui* construction, is proposed as a thing that grounds itself. Nature isn’t a thing; it is what things are in, so a self-grounding thing still requires the conditions in which self-grounding is possible, and those conditions are Nature. A classical theist will deny the premise that does the work here, holding that God is not one entity inside a prior framework of conditions but subsistent being itself, in which case the thing/conditions contrast doesn’t apply to the candidate as described. That denial is where the disagreement actually sits, and it is answered, if at all, by Reality–Nature Identity together with the exterior-ground analysis of §10.2.1 and §7.2.1, not by the contrast alone.

**[Proposition]**

**Thing Versus Conditions** · *Proposition*

The *causa sui* God is proposed as a thing that grounds itself, an entity satisfying the conditions for grounding from the inside. Nature is not a thing but what things are in, self-grounding in the stronger sense that it is the conditions under which grounding operates at all. A self-grounding thing still requires conditions in which self-grounding is possible. The parallel therefore fails on the divide between an entity meeting grounding conditions and what those conditions consist in. A classical theist who holds that God is subsistent being itself, not an entity inside a prior framework of conditions, denies that premise rather than the parallel; that denial is met by Reality–Nature Identity and the exterior-ground analysis, not by this contrast.

**Depends on:** Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8)

A constructive complement is available only conditionally from §4.6. The modal core establishes neither past-unbounded time nor cyclic cosmology. □T says that Temporality obtains at every world in the invariant standing capacity of R; it doesn’t specify whether a world’s temporal manifold has a least boundary, what occurs near that boundary, or whether its dynamics recur. No Stable Zero-Extension distinguishes a least temporal boundary from a domain-external transition out of ∅: if a least boundary exists, asking what happened temporally before it misuses the temporal ordering. That result doesn’t show that no first moment is coherent or that every event has a sufficient reason. Event-level explanation remains a further causal or PSR commitment, and cyclic recurrence remains conditional on §4.6’s independent cosmological premises. Neither may be used here as an additional derivation of structural necessity.

*Fourth.* The three forms already stated run the PSR toward a ground beyond Nature: the demand is that T∧S∧Φ be explained by something more basic. Della Rocca (Della Rocca 2010; Della Rocca 2020) runs it in the opposite direction. Take the PSR without exemptions and apply it to distinctness itself. Why is *a* distinct from *b*? Any answer either invokes some further difference, which raises the same question about that difference, or terminates in a distinction that simply obtains, which is a brute fact of exactly the kind the PSR forbids. Della Rocca’s conclusion is that the demand, honestly pressed, doesn’t stop at a necessary being; it consumes distinction as such, and terminates in strict monism—not Schaffer’s priority monism, which keeps the parts and orders them (§3.5.7.1), but the denial that there are many things at all.

This bears directly on the present argument. Spatiality is relational extension with exclusivity (§2.4.7): a *here* that isn’t the *there*. If nothing is distinct from anything, S isn’t merely ungrounded but empty, and by the cross-entailment T and Φ go with it (§2.6.7). The haecceitist exit closed at §2.4.7 is a different challenge and doesn’t cover this one: haecceitism grants distinctness and disputes what grounds it, while this position denies there is distinctness to ground.

The reply available is the one run elsewhere, and its strength has to be marked rather than overstated. Stating the monist conclusion requires distinguishing it from its denial, distinguishing the premises from one another, and distinguishing the position from the rivals it is offered against; the PSR itself, as a principle *about* facts and their explanations, requires facts to be many enough to stand in explanatory relations. The companions-in-guilt cost is total, since a standard that voids distinctness voids logic, mathematics, the argument’s own inferential steps, and the distinction between the PSR holding and failing.

But by the Specification Test (§7.3.2) that reply is **act-side**. Everything it establishes concerns the representing: what the monist must deploy to state, argue, and be understood. The strict monist has an answer, and it is the same answer the temporal error theorist gives at §8.1.3—that discourse is unavoidably articulated while reality isn’t, and that the appearance of manyness is precisely what the view predicts and explains. Nothing in that act-side argument exhibits a contradiction among the proposed object’s own conditions, which is what an object-side verdict would require. The verdict is therefore **act-side incoherence with the object-side error theory open**, the same shape strict temporal unreality receives at §8.4, and not a refutation.

What the argument does hold against it is narrower and worth stating exactly. A view on which nothing is distinct from anything can’t be a *change-realizer*: change requires one state and then another, which is two, and the monist’s own explanation of why manyness appears is itself a story with stages. So the position doesn’t supply the thing Chapter 2’s conditional needs an antecedent for; it denies the antecedent instead. That is a coherent place to stand, at the cost of denying ◇C—and denying ◇C is what the Cartesian witness rules out (§2.2), not because manyness is obvious but because the denial is performed in stages. That reply, too, is act-side. The honest summary is that strict monism is closed to anyone who grants ◇C and open to anyone prepared to treat their own reasoning as unreal.

*Taking stock.* Four forms of the demand, three of which find no gap: the contrast demand presupposes ∅ as a coherent alternative foreclosed at §2.7; the origin demand uses the three Conditions in the very act of asking why they obtain; and Pruss’s modal refinement, confined to contingent facts, leaves structural necessity outside its scope. The fourth isn’t deflected and isn’t claimed to be: Della Rocca’s monist deployment is answered only act-side, and is recorded at that strength in the ledger. Two further results follow once the deflections are in place. The dissolution removes the contingency-of-Reality starting point that would otherwise carry the PSR to an external necessary ground, and the *causa sui* parallel fails on the thing-versus-conditions distinction: Nature isn’t a thing that grounds itself but what grounding consists in.

The narrower Leibnizian point (that contingent facts admit of explanation) isn’t what the argument denies. What the argument denies is that the structural necessities are contingent facts in need of explanation against an available alternative.

### 8.2.2 Humean Contingency
Hume’s challenge is a generous and disciplined attempt to thin Time. He grants that states follow states. He just doesn’t see anything holding them together: one state, then the next, and the “then” does no work. No necessary connection, no causal arrow. Just sequence.

The replies here grant his narrowest claim (constant conjunction doesn’t by itself entail necessity) and contest the broader one by testing whether each form can state succession without handing over directional succession through Substance. The structural-level engagement (defending the producing-relation against eliminativist pressure) is carried by §2.6.8; this section takes up the modal-contingency arm.

Hume (1748) 1999, §VII argues that our impression of causal necessity is a psychological habit projected onto the world, not a feature discovered within it. His contemporary inheritors (Lewis (1986b, pp. ix–xvi), Loewer (1996), Beebee (2006)) sharpen the point into the Best System Account: laws of nature are the axioms of the simplest, strongest systematization of the pattern of events, not constraints that govern it. Succession without enforcement—order that simply obtains.

Time, as §1.4.1 defines it, is different. Not bare sequence: directional, asymmetric, productive, with the earlier state grounding the later, an arrow running through. Hume grants the sequence and denies the arrow.

*First.* The bare-succession form holds that states can follow one another without any carrying medium. States follow states, the ordering is all Time needs, and nothing about Substance makes the next state follow the previous. Indexed order, not enforcement.

That concession is already enough, but note where it is enough. Try thinning succession further. Read “indexed order” as a block universe (B-theory, Mellor 1998, *Real Time II*): time-slices arranged by index, all moments equally real, ordered by a tenseless before/after, no privileged now. On this reading, “persistence” just means qualitative similarity across slices; nothing is carried through. Can the thinner reading hold?

Consider what the thinning requires. An ordering of slices by index is one of two things. Either it is a function from integers to qualitative profiles applied to the manifold, in which case the manifold itself has to have enough structure to be indexable at all, an intrinsic distinction of positions that the arithmetic is tracking, not supplying. Or the ordering is free-floating abstract, a function unattached to any manifold, in which case it isn’t a time-series anymore, just a set of profiles paired with numerals, two disjoint structures sitting next to each other.

The first reading borrows the structural fact it is trying to replace. The second yields an abstract set of profiles paired with indices rather than a concrete temporal manifold. It doesn’t collapse into ∅: the set still has members and formal structure. Its limitation is instead that the abstract pairing doesn’t by itself realize temporal succession or causal persistence. Grant succession at any strength sufficient to state the position, and the Mutual Containment Result (§2.6.5) takes over: succession requires something that persists (Substance) across a structured interval (Space). Whether it is called “produced” or “enforced” isn’t the hinge; that something is sequenced at all is.

The bare-succession form is the wager that replacement is never more than mere sequence. Put exactly: replacement isn’t bare succession. It requires something that can be replaced, something that replaces it, and structure in which the replacement counts as replacement rather than mere juxtaposition. Strip the being, the interval, and the relation, and the Humean hasn’t described thinner succession. They have removed the conditions under which succession is describable at all.

*Second.* The asymmetric-before form grants more ground than the first and tries to hold a thinner line. Sequence is real. Co-instantiation is real. But before-and-after is treated as a brute relational fact between states: the ordering is there, causation isn’t. Tim Maudlin (*The Metaphysics Within Physics* 2007) holds the same line on the arrow from the opposite side. He rejects the Humean mosaic, so his view is no form of Humean contingency, but he makes time’s arrow a fundamental primitive of the manifold, asymmetry that needs no further grounding, and it meets the same reply.

Consider what this does. An asymmetric relation between states is either a label applied from outside (a convention we impose, with nothing in Nature answering to it) or a structural fact about Nature itself. If it is a label, it is a label for one of two things. Either it removes the ordering along with the arrow (leaving co-present states with nothing to index, which is no succession at all) or it keeps the ordering and imposes only the direction: the direction-conventionalist’s line, on which the series is real but no fact of Nature settles which way it runs. The second reading doesn’t thin Time; it relocates the arrow to a mind-independent gradient, the thermodynamic move taken up at §8.1.2. Neither branch yields an asymmetry that is real, in Nature, and not already Exchange under another name. If it is structural (whether read as a consequence of deeper machinery or as a Maudlin-style primitive) then “asymmetric relation” and “Exchange” are doing exactly the same work. Two names, one relational fact.

Maudlin’s primitivism is the view that time’s directionality is a fundamental feature of the world, not reducible to anything more basic. It refuses reduction in any direction. Time’s passage isn’t to be analyzed via entropy gradients, nor reduced to tenseless B-theory relations, nor deflated to psychological flow; it is a fundamental directional structure of the world that fundamental physics already presupposes whenever its laws are stated as differential equations evolving an initial state forward (*The Metaphysics Within Physics* 2007, ch. 4). Take the position on its own terms. The directionality is real, primitive, ontologically irreducible. It still attaches to states standing in directional relation across a manifold that bears the primitive. The primitive is the directionality of something: three structural conditions the primitivism can’t dissolve. Maudlin’s primitive is what the three Conditions jointly amount to once a defender insists on irreducibility. The role analysis doesn’t refute the primitivism. It states what the primitivism describes.

*Third.* The Best System Account (BSA) offers a deflationary form of the challenge. On BSA, laws of nature are the axioms of the simplest, strongest way to describe the total pattern, not constraints that govern it. Regularities get described, not enforced. The picture is the Humean mosaic: a distribution of local matters of fact, no necessary connections between them (Lewis 1986b; Loewer 1996).

The standard non-Humean replies in the contemporary literature treat laws as relations among universals (Armstrong 1983, *What Is a Law of Nature?*) or as primitive necessitating relations between properties (Dretske 1977; Tooley 1977). The reply here is structurally different. It isn’t that something enforces the regularity already described and beyond the distribution; it is that any vocabulary capable of stating the regularity already runs on the structural conditions the Humean meant to deflate.

Lewis’s doctrine of Humean supervenience says everything supervenes on the distribution of local qualities together with the spatiotemporal relations among their instances. Those relations belong to the supervenience base rather than being derived from the qualities alone. The mosaic is therefore distributed across an already structured manifold, not used to construct that manifold (Lewis 1986b, pp. ix–xvi). This is the load-bearing concession, and it runs under the whole account.

Consider what a regularity actually is. For events of type A to be reliably followed by events of type B, the Humean has already granted a distribution across a spatiotemporal manifold and a pattern stated over that distribution. That concession is enough. If the regularity is brute, the Humean offers systematization rather than a governing explanation; that is a deliberate feature of the view, not an internal contradiction. If the regularity is grounded in an invariant feature of the manifold, the account moves toward a non-Humean structure. The present argument can therefore claim that BSA presupposes spatiotemporal structure, but it can’t infer a productive causal arrow from regularity alone. A mosaic without a manifold isn’t a mosaic: it is a set with no ordering.

The Humean wants regularity without necessity. Strip Nature and regularity has nothing to regulate.

Physical Invariance (§3.5.6) sharpens the boundary without withdrawing the Humean concession. It doesn’t infer $M\models Q$ from a history of repeated $Q$-events. Physics and mathematics must first specify a profile *M* with enough structure for *Q* to follow and establish that a real system realizes it. Only then does the theorem say that the same complete *M*-realization can’t lack *Q*: $\Box\forall x(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\rightarrow Q(x))$ doesn’t make an *M*-realization necessary. The Humean may deny that laws govern, challenge the profile’s sufficiency, or hold that a different mosaic realizes a different profile. What the view can’t coherently describe is the very same complete profile with its constitutive consequence freely reassigned, since that changes the profile rather than merely redescribing its regularity. Which profile Nature realizes remains open.

A kindred deflationary move drops causal vocabulary entirely in favor of symmetric functional relations between variables: Russell [“On the Notion of Cause”] argues causation has no place in mature physics (1913); Norton carries the case forward (2003). The reply is the same, shaped differently: functional relations between variables presuppose the variables’ distinctness (Space) and persistence (Substance), and any functional relation with a privileged direction of dependency presupposes Time’s asymmetry. Thermodynamic variants (that temporal asymmetry emerges from entropy gradients rather than obtaining structurally) come up in §8.1.2.

One narrower point, stated exactly. The self-refutation charge is that a denial of the structural conditions presupposes them in the act of denying. It establishes the conditions’ actuality wherever the denial is performed, not their necessity across worlds where no such performance occurs. The move from actuality to necessity is the work of Chapter 2 and doesn’t rest here. The result is narrower: the deflationary vocabularies are parasitic on the three conditions they are meant to replace, wherever they are stated.

One rejoinder remains. A Humean might grant the dependence and insist that it reflects only the conditions of description: any vocabulary capable of saying anything relies on structure supplied by its subject matter, and that fact doesn’t refute deflationism. The rejoinder is partly correct. The relevant question isn’t whether the vocabulary uses spatial or temporal metaphors, but whether the Humean ontology can state succession, regularity, and transmission without the roles the account identifies.

The historical transmission of Hume’s *Enquiry* illustrates the act-side point. Its content has remained identifiable through ordered material transmissions over time. This establishes that stating and preserving the Humean position requires succession, differentiation, and persistence in the actual world. It doesn’t by itself establish necessary connections among all events and therefore doesn’t refute Hume’s narrower claim.

The same reply reaches an agential case. Hume’s account of necessity runs from observation through habit to projected expectation: repeated conjunctions, formed habit, projected necessity. There is a class of cases where that order is reversed: cases where the regularity is *established*, in a single act, by an agent who specifies it. The Anscombean and interventionist traditions (Anscombe 1971, “Causality and Determination”; Woodward 2003, *Making Things Happen*) have pressed a kindred line against the spectator’s epistemology for half a century: an agent who establishes a regularity by an intervention has first-person access to causal efficacy that no abstraction-from-conjunctions can supply. A programmer who specifies a function settles in advance what the function will return on inputs it has never been called on: no series of conjunctions, no time for habit to form, just a stipulation that holds because the system bears it. The constant conjunction is *fixed in advance* by the stipulation, not abstracted from a history of it. Hume’s habit-formation story has no machinery for that order, and the cases where the order runs that way aren’t exotic. What follows from them, though, is narrower than an anti-Humean metaphysics, and the narrowing is owed. The specification makes nothing conform on its own: it takes effect through implementation, execution, and a machine that runs, and a Humean is entitled to count all of that as further pattern in the mosaic rather than as a governing bond. What the case does establish is epistemic—a regularity known before any series of instances—and, on the metaphysical side, a realizer burden: what the stipulation requires to take effect is the same triple the descriptive case required to be statable, a structural setting, a domain across which the stipulation ranges, and something the regularity holds across. The same conditions appear from the agent’s side as from the describer’s side.

**[Proposition]**

**The Reversed Order** · *Proposition*

Hume’s account runs from observation to habit to projected necessity. A class of cases runs the other way: an agent specifies a regularity in a single act, and a programmer settles what a function returns on inputs it has never been called on, with no series of conjunctions and no interval for habit to form. A regularity is therefore known before any series of instances, which Hume’s habit-formation story doesn’t cover. The metaphysical conclusion doesn’t follow with it: the stipulation makes nothing conform on its own, it takes effect through implementation and execution, and a Humean may count those as further pattern in the mosaic rather than a governing bond. What the case delivers is an epistemic asymmetry and a realizer burden—a structural setting, a domain across which the stipulation ranges, and something the regularity holds across—not an anti-Humean metaphysics.

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6)

*Convergence.* Time is the Condition defined at §1.4.1, bearing the succession role extracted at §1.1, and each deflationary form fails to remove it.

Bare succession can’t be indexed without borrowing the manifold it meant to replace, or else it thins into an abstract pairing that realizes no succession at all. Asymmetric before-and-after is either a label applied from outside, which removes the ordering or relocates the arrow (§8.1.2), or a structural fact about Nature, which is Exchange under another name. And the Best System Account admits the spatiotemporal manifold into its own supervenience base rather than deriving it, describing the structure in Humean vocabulary rather than replacing it.

Each form therefore retains structural conditions that its deflationary description doesn’t eliminate. The narrower Humean point—that constant conjunction doesn’t entail necessity—isn’t contested. The argument accepts that constraint: it doesn’t infer necessity from regularity, but from structural analysis together with the Cartesian datum that change occurs; the two are compatible in exactly the way Necessity Precedes Contingency states at §2.9.4, where the necessity of the structural conditions carries none of the contingency of what regularly occurs within them. The causal-transmission point is correspondingly limited. It establishes the actual conditions under which the Humean position is stated and preserved, not the necessity of a productive bond in every possible world.

### 8.2.3 Information-Theoretic Foundationalism
Wheeler’s *it from bit* proposes that reality is informational all the way down: binary distinctions are fundamental, and spacetime and matter emerge from the relational structure of information processing. The picture has real purchase in physics (Shannon’s (1948) formalism, Landauer’s (1961) thermodynamic cost of erasure, information-theoretic reformulations of quantum mechanics) and none of it is in dispute. What is contested is the priority claim: the claim that information is more fundamental than the structural roles, that the three Conditions are emergent features of an information-processing substrate rather than conditions of what information consists in. The three Conditions are the three structural conditions whose necessity the Necessity of Nature theorem (§2.9.6) declares, borne by Time, Space, and Substance. The thesis under test is specific: that concrete information and its processing are ontologically prior to the roles, so that the roles are features of an informational substrate rather than conditions on there being information at all. Three forms of it follow. Two neighbouring views appear along the way because each makes a version of the same priority claim, and each is a different position with different primitives: Tegmark’s mathematical identity thesis is engaged on its own terms at §9.9, and relation-first ontic structural realism at §9.10. What they are tested for here is only the priority claim they share with Wheeler. The replies test whether each can sustain the priority without handing over what it meant to deflate.

*First.* The bit-first move holds that reality at the most fundamental level consists of bits (yes/no distinctions) with spacetime and matter emerging from their relational structure (Wheeler 1990).

A bit requires difference to be a bit. Bateson’s (1972) phrase names the contrast at the core: information concerns a difference that can matter within some system.

But Shannon’s (1948) formalism is deliberately abstract. Its sender, receiver, channel, and signal are formal roles in a communication model; the formalism by itself doesn’t establish that every bit must have a physical bearer, spatial manifold, or temporal transmission. The stronger claim belongs only to physically realized information processing: where a difference is registered, propagated, or acted upon in a concrete system, there must be a persisting realization, distinguishable states, and an ordered process. That is a claim about realization, not a consequence of information theory alone. Information-theoretic foundationalism must therefore show how an abstract informational base is physically realized without already relying on the structural roles it proposes to derive.

*Second.* The Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (Tegmark 2014) goes further: reality doesn’t resemble mathematics but is a mathematical structure, and all mathematically consistent structures equally exist.

For a mathematical structure to be a structure at all, its elements must stand in determinate relations. That directly supports a role of differentiation. It doesn’t follow from determinate relatedness alone that the relations are asymmetric, temporally ordered, continuous, or borne by a concrete substance. Those further roles enter only when the mathematical structure is claimed to be concretely realized or dynamically operative. Tegmark’s own account requires the mathematical structure to be the kind of thing whose elements stand in determinate relations; this concedes the difference-role at the level of what a mathematical structure consists in. The plenitude reading compounds the concession: every mathematically consistent structure supports that role under abstraction. The Platonist hasn’t escaped differentiation, and the temporal and bearer roles fall due wherever the structure is claimed to be concretely real.

What the account requires Tegmark to give up isn’t the mathematical-identity thesis as such but its unrestricted plenitude complement. The Mathematical Universe Hypothesis at Level IV holds that all mathematically consistent structures equally exist (*Our Mathematical Universe* 2014). If T∧S∧Φ are necessary conditions for a mathematical structure to be concretely real rather than merely abstractly consistent, then the Level IV plenitude is structurally bounded: only T∧S∧Φ-consistent structures are candidates for physical instantiation. The claim isn’t that MUH is false but that it requires the structural conditions as a constraint on plenitude. Tegmark’s account can absorb T, S, and Φ as specifying what it takes for a consistent structure to be physically instantiated; the cost is giving up the claim that mathematical consistency alone is sufficient for physical existence.

*Third.* The computational-universe move presses the case directly. Lloyd holds that the universe is a quantum computer (2006): physical processes are computations, particles are data, interactions are logic gates.
