Deutsch and Wolfram develop parallel variants (1997; 2002). The common commitment is that computation precedes the structural roles ontologically.

A physically realized computation instantiates each of the three roles at the level of the computing. For a bit to be processed in a concrete machine, there must be an ordered transition between states through a medium capable of realizing it; this supplies the relevant temporal role. An abstract computation, considered only as a mathematical mapping, doesn’t by itself establish physical succession. For information to be held, maintained, and updated, something must persist as the being that bears the informational state, which is the role Substance names. For bits to be distinct from one another, there must be relational non-identity among them, which is the role Space names. A computation lacking any of the three isn’t a computation but something weaker: a static set of symbols (no Time), a dynamic flux with no being (no Substance), or a homogeneous stream with no distinguishable units (no Space). Landauer’s (1961) principle cuts the same way from physics: erasing a bit costs kT ln 2 of energy (the Landauer limit, where k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is temperature, the minimum thermodynamic cost of erasing one bit), and thermodynamic cost requires a physical substrate with temporal evolution, spatial distinctness of states, and persistent beings.

A kindred deflation drops the computational framing entirely for ontic structural realism: Ladyman et al. argue that only relational structure is fundamental and relata are ontologically dispensable (2007). Structure, on this view, goes all the way down, with no bearer beneath it. This form of the priority claim has to be met head-on rather than deflected, because the case against it is the case for Φ.

Eliminative OSR denies the grammar on which the quick “pattern of something” reply relies. Pressed all the way, relations or relational structure are ontologically primary; ordinary objects are derivative representational conveniences, not omitted thick relata waiting beneath the network. Building and blueprint analogies can’t decide that dispute, because both import object ontology into the example.

The exact issue is functional realization. Can a relation-first fabric maintain causal capacity and identity conditions across transitions without primitive object-relata? If it can, the fabric may realize the book’s thin Φ-role even though no independently existing bearer sits beneath it; “Substance” would name maintained causal bearing at the network level, not a thick particular. If it can’t, the account owes a realizer for that diachronic bearing—no fact would then distinguish persistence of the network from replacement by an isomorphic successor. The argument here is for the latter burden, but it may not win it by defining a node as an object. The live disagreement is whether relational structure itself realizes Φ, not whether eliminative OSR has forgotten the ordinary noun after the relation.

*The Concession Move.* One last move remains to the opponent: not denial, but concession, that information is the substrate, and what the argument calls Time, Space, and Substance are already informational through and through. Look at the words information theory reaches for when it needs to name where information lives. Channel. Bearer. Register. Substrate. Carrier. Medium. Every one is a word for something. Information is descriptive. It needs something to describe.

**[Proposition]**

**Information Is Descriptive** · *Proposition*

Every term information theory reaches for to name where information lives is a term for something: channel, bearer, register, substrate, carrier, medium. Information requires distinction to be information, transition requires succession to be transition, and processing requires persistence to be processing. Information is descriptive, and needs something to describe. What that earns is a realizer burden on concrete information processing, not a completed defeat of relation-first ontology.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

Strip the roles from concrete information processing and what remains isn’t a more fundamental informational substrate but no processing at all. Wheeler’s slogan, on the present account, runs in both directions: it comes from bit only where bit is already the output of the three Conditions doing their work. The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in describing physical structure is taken up directly at §9.8. *It from bit* implicitly trades on it.

*Convergence.* The information-theoretic proposals separate by realization level. Abstract information and mathematical consistency establish differentiation but don’t by themselves establish the loaded temporal or bearer types. Physically realized computation requires ordered transition, distinguishable states, and maintained causal capacity; the independent role-to-type bridge determines whether those realizers count as the three Conditions. Eliminative OSR remains a type-level rival: it grants relational fabric while disputing that Φ requires primitive relata. The earned result is a realizer burden for concrete information processing and diachronic causal bearing, not five definitional concessions or a completed defeat of relation-first ontology.

### 8.2.4 Pizzi’s Impossibility of Nothingness
David Pizzi’s *The Impossibility of Nothingness: A Foundational Argument for Necessary Existence* (Pizzi 2025) runs a contemporary parallel to the impossibility-driven recovery this argument runs across the lines of §3.2–§3.3 and the convergence tallied at §3.5, and at §10.1.4. The dialectical situation is symmetric and instructive: Pizzi and the present account converge on the same modal floor (that absolute nothingness is impossible and that something must exist necessarily) by closely related performative and self-refuting machinery. They diverge on what sits at that floor. Pizzi concludes that something exists necessarily (□∃x x) and explicitly declines to decide among the candidates that could occupy the necessary slot. The present account concludes that the three structural conditions T ∧ S ∧ Φ obtain necessarily (□(T ∧ S ∧ Φ)) and names the necessary content Pizzi leaves open. The same final move (closing modal space against ∅) yields a bare-existential conclusion in Pizzi and a determinate-content conclusion here.

Pizzi’s argument runs three reductios against the metaphysical possibility of total absence and bridges them through a single theorem. The first reductio targets the truth-maker logic of *nothing exists*: given truthmaker maximalism, if that proposition were possibly true it would need a truth-maker; the proposed absence can’t stand in the truth-making relation without being something. The result therefore depends on the truthmaker requirement rather than following from the proposition alone. Quantification over absences therefore collapses. The second reductio targets representations of the proposition: actual assertion and formal modeling presuppose syntactic and semantic resources. That is a strong act-side or model-side result, though an opponent may deny that resources used to represent a scenario must exist inside the represented scenario. The third reductio targets empty-domain semantics. Whether actuality operators force non-emptiness depends on the quantified modal semantics adopted, so this line constrains particular formalisms rather than settling every empty-world model by definition. The bridging theorem assembles the three: since each path forecloses the possibility that nothing exists, by the modal duality ¬◇¬X ≡ □X it follows that something exists necessarily. The argument runs at the same logical strength as the convergence of lines catalogued at §3.2–§3.3 and tallied at §3.5: classical modal duality, no S5, no positive theology, no conceivability premise outside the structural-self-defeat asymmetry the conceivability-inversion line develops at §3.3.4.

A note on formalization for the Pizzi-mode reader. Pizzi’s three reductios run in formal modal-logical mode and converge on □∃x x via classical modal duality. That result is significant but deliberately thin: it establishes necessary existence without identifying the necessary content.

The present argument reaches □(T∧S∧Φ) by a different line. It needs the global-capacity modal theorem, the Cartesian witness of change, and the Structural Requirement that any change-permitting world realizes the Conditions. The move from □∃x x to □◇C isn’t licensed by modal duality alone, and the present account shouldn’t attribute such a T-completeness lemma to Pizzi’s result. A nonempty world might contain abstract or otherwise thin content without thereby realizing genuine change. The structural conclusion therefore requires the independent role- and type-level arguments of Chapters 2–3.

The boundary shows in the object language as well: the □ in □(T∧S∧Φ) ranges over worlds, while T is a within-world structural condition, so the box governs whether the three conditions obtain at each world, not any temporal ordering internal to one of them.

The methodological convergence is close enough to require an account of what the present argument does that Pizzi doesn’t. Two answers. First, Pizzi’s three paths each target the assertion or modeling of ∅: what happens when one tries to *state* or *represent* the empty case. The negation line of The Negation Trap (§3.3.2) closes a parallel gap by targeting the *operation* that would produce ∅ from a populated case: stripping the three conditions away. This line isn’t among Pizzi’s three; he doesn’t run an introduction-by-subtraction argument, since his framework treats ∅ as a candidate state whose semantics must be evaluated, not as a state that would have to be reached by subtracting structure from somewhere. The negation line therefore complements rather than duplicates Pizzi’s three. Second, Pizzi’s three reductios establish ¬◇∅ at the level of the bare-existential conclusion; the present argument runs that same closure across the convergent lines of §3.2–§3.3 (tallied at §3.5) and then *names the necessary content*. The naming is the work Pizzi’s §4 leaves open.

Pizzi’s §4 surveys the candidates for the necessary existent his argument has established: abstracta (Platonism), substratum (priority monism), modal-realist plurality, theistic models, and Vedāntic Brahman. He notes that the argument is silent on which candidate occupies the slot, and treats that neutrality as a virtue, which for an argument built to secure a minimal floor it may well be.

**[Proposition]**

**The Bare Existential Underdetermines** · *Proposition*

The proof reaches □∃x x and stops. That conclusion is satisfied alike by classical theism, Spinoza’s substance, Platonic abstracta, priority monism, modal realism, and the present account: a result six incompatible positions all meet has not selected among them. Naming the necessary content is therefore further work, and the bare existential doesn’t supply it.

That the argument *to* □∃x x is silent on the slot’s occupant is granted here. Whether the silence is a virtue depends on the project: for an argument aiming at a minimal, widely acceptable floor it may be exactly the point, and what is claimed here is only that the floor leaves the question this book is asking unanswered.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

The candidates require different verdicts. Abstracta may be coherent as abstracta; the present argument doesn’t infer from their atemporality that they are impossible. The relevant question is whether they can ground R’s standing capacity or the concrete, change-realizing world. That requires an additional grounding relation, and the abstracta theorist must supply its content. Priority monism may identify the cosmos as a partless whole prior to its parts. The present account can grant that priority while asking whether the whole, insofar as it realizes change and grounds configurations, instantiates the structural roles. The verdict isn’t that every candidate simply collapses into T∧S∧Φ, but that none receives automatic entitlement to the grounding role merely from Pizzi’s □∃x x conclusion.

Modal-realist plurality supplies concrete worlds subject to Lewis’s worldmate criterion. Change-rich Lewis worlds realize the structural roles, while sparse or changeless candidates remain tests for the book’s independent necessity and type-level arguments; and the fictionalism line in §3.3.3 picks this up against modal fictionalism’s milder cousin. Theistic models split on the classical/temporal distinction taken up at §10.2.1 and §10.3.3. A classical model that denies the loaded types may still posit determinate grounding or dependence roles; whether those can remain wholly outside the three conditions is tested in Chapters 10–11, rather than settled by defining the model as ∅. Temporal, process, and open-theist models more directly instantiate the roles. Vedāntic Brahman likewise divides into nirguna and saguna readings at §10.2.2; the burden is to determine whether the former is genuinely contentless or instead carries thin determinacy, while the latter more openly carries the three conditions. In each case the structural account adds a further question Pizzi’s result leaves open: does the candidate realize, ground, or merely coexist with the structural roles required by a concrete change-realizing Reality? Some candidates may be compatible abstracta or metaphysical pictures; none is selected as the necessary ground by □∃x x alone. The Chapters 10–11 engagements supply differentiated verdicts rather than a simple reduction of every candidate to one option.

The closing chapter of *The Impossibility of Nothingness* (Pizzi’s own §5.4) places his conclusion in a theist-friendly axiological frame, citing Adams (Adams 1999) on the goodness of the existence of God as the contemporary anchor for the move from “something exists necessarily” to “the necessary existent is divine.” Pizzi flags this as a gesture rather than an argument, and is explicit at his §5.3 that the formal result of that book is silent on theism. The present account takes the disclaimer at face value. The contemporary necessary-existence cluster (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018; Pizzi 2025) is already engaged at §10.1.4, as a methodologically continuous neighborhood that nonetheless doesn’t reach this account’s conclusion. The axiological gesture is a separate move from the modal-existence argument, and one this account doesn’t run. T ∧ S ∧ Φ aren’t maximally great in the value-theoretic sense; they are necessary because nothing else is a *something*. The axiological closing is available to anyone who has reached □∃x x and wants to identify the necessary existent with a value-maximal being; the present account reaches the stronger and value-neutral □(T ∧ S ∧ Φ), and the axiological move doesn’t gain traction on it.

*Taking stock.* Pizzi’s position is therefore distinctive. The positions engaged in Chapters 10–11 disagree with the argument about the *form* of the necessary ground: classical theism (§10.2.1), Swinburne’s personal-God theism (§10.1.8), Spinozism (§10.3.1), Neoplatonism (§10.3.2), Plantinga’s modal ontological argument (§10.1.1), and so on. Pizzi disagrees with none of the formal commitments. He runs the same kind of argument to a strictly weaker conclusion and leaves the further question open by design. The reply is correspondingly cooperative: the convergence is real, and the only question is where he stops. *Necessary Existence* (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018) shares Pizzi’s bare-existential terminus and runs by formal-modal apparatus. Rasmussen’s *How Reason Can Lead to God* (Rasmussen 2019), engaged at §10.1.4, pushes past the bare-existential terminus by stage-by-stage construction toward a personal necessary being. The cluster shares the present argument’s bare-existential starting point while leaving its occupants to further argument. The gap between □∃x x and □(T ∧ S ∧ Φ) is already closed in Chapters 2–3, at the Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6). Chapters 10–11 do a different job: they test the candidate occupants Pizzi leaves unnamed.

### 8.2.5 The Modal Collapse Objection
The modal-collapse objection holds that a necessary ground generates necessary outputs: an argument that makes the structural conditions of reality inescapable thereby makes everything that happens within them inescapable too. Spinoza reached this conclusion by tracing out the consequences of substance monism, and drew it as a triumph: every mode follows with the force of geometrical demonstration, and the appearance of contingency is a mark of ignorance. Most of his successors reached the same conclusion and tried to find a way to block it. The present account, the objector presses, appears to rebuild the same trap from a different direction: with the three Conditions (the three structural conditions the book’s argument derives, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) in the place of *Deus sive Natura* (Spinoza’s identification: “God or Nature”) and the history of the world in the place of the modes.

The modal-collapse objection has a long lineage. Spinoza (*Ethics* (1677) 1996) drew it as a positive conclusion: substance is necessary, its modes follow with geometrical necessity, and contingency is an illusion of perspective. Leibniz (*Theodicy* 1710) reached a softer form: God necessarily chooses the *best possible world*, and the specific history of this world is therefore fixed with a necessity one step removed from Spinoza’s. Modern defenses: Pruss (*The Principle of Sufficient Reason* 2006) presses the Leibnizian version against necessitarian accounts of grounding. Van Inwagen (*An Essay on Free Will* 1983) supplies the deterministic relative, the Consequence Argument: if determinism is true then, since no one has any choice about the laws or the remote past, no one has any choice about what follows from them. Rasmussen (*How Reason Can Lead to God* 2019) applies the modal-collapse worry to necessitarian alternatives to classical theism. Against the collapse, the contemporary literature runs thick: Plantinga (*The Nature of Necessity* 1974) deploys the de dicto/de re distinction in ways that block various propagation moves; Swinburne (*The Christian God* 1994) defends a libertarian space within theism; the open theists (Hasker, Sanders) reject the collapse by denying the necessity of the antecedents.

The contemporary grounding literature establishes the framework the present reply uses. Fine (“Guide to Ground,” 2012) and Rosen (“Metaphysical Dependence: Grounding and Reduction,” 2010) set out grounding as a relation of constitutive determination and defend the principle that a full ground necessitates what it grounds; Schaffer (*On What Grounds What* 2009; *Monism* 2010) and Dasgupta (2014) develop the apparatus the present reply turns on: above all the distinction, owed to Fine, between full and partial ground. On grounding the structural account runs with Dasgupta’s line, and adds: the specific grounds at issue are the three Conditions, and their necessity is compatible with the contingency of what they ground because they are only a partial, structural ground of any particular change, never its full ground.

The objection bears on two of the argument’s central theses. The Modal Identity is established at §2.6.6: the necessity of the structural conditions (□(T∧S∧Φ)) entails □◇C, the necessary *possibility* of change, not □C, the necessity of change itself. The Necessity of Nature theorem is then established at §2.9.6: the specific character of the natural order is constrained by, but not reducible to, the structural conditions. If the modal-collapse objection succeeds, one of two things goes wrong: either the distinction between □◇C and □C dissolves (collapsing the stage into the play), or the grounding relation between structure and specifics is productive (collapsing the contingent specifics into the necessary structure). Both collapses entail Spinozism.

A clarification before the moves. The objection isn’t that contingency is difficult to square with the argument: it is that contingency is incompatible with it. Three forms of the move press that incompatibility at three resolutions: the deterministic version, the Leibnizian best-of-all-worlds version, and the Spinozan propagation version.

*First.* The van-Inwagen-style propagation move presses the deterministic version. Necessary laws plus necessary initial conditions yield necessary outcomes. If the three Conditions are necessary, and the laws of physics follow from the structural roles, the laws are necessary too. Necessary laws plus a fixed past fix the future, so every event is necessary. The Consequence Argument is the nearest familiar model for that propagation step, but it establishes something weaker: its conclusion is that no one has a choice about what follows, not that what follows is metaphysically necessary. The objector needs the stronger reading and owes it separately.

The Modal Identity (§2.6.6) draws a line the objection ignores. What the argument establishes is □◇C (the *possibility* of change is necessary), not □C (change occurs necessarily).

**[Proposition]**

**Necessity of Change (□C)** · *Proposition*

The argument establishes □◇C (Modal Identity, §2.6.6), not □C. Structural necessity fixes what is structurally possible, not which possibilities are actualized.

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6)

A necessary stage doesn’t, by itself, script the determinate play. The necessity of the three Conditions constrains the *type* of physical law (any law must be expressible as a structural relation among the roles), but it doesn’t fix the specific content. Which symmetry groups govern, which constants obtain, which particles compose the physical domain: these are determinate facts within the necessary architecture whose actuality establishes necessary possibility, but whose contingency requires independently warranted alternatives. Quantum theory supplies interpretations on which token history is genuinely open, while deterministic interpretations remain live; the reply therefore doesn’t presuppose that every token is contingent.

Physical Invariance (§3.5.6) states the same boundary at the level of a determinate physical profile. If $M\models Q$, then $\Box\forall x(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\rightarrow Q(x))$: any realization of that complete profile carries its proved invariant. But the boxed universal conditional isn’t $\Box\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$. An actual *M*-realization yields an actual *Q*-bearing realization; only an independently established necessity of *M*-realization would make *Q* necessarily instantiated. The theorem therefore prevents an opposite error without licensing collapse: one may not hold the complete profile fixed while varying its constitutive consequence, but nothing in the theorem selects that profile as the necessary physical history.

*Second.* The Leibnizian best-possible-world version adds a necessary ranking of outcomes. A necessary, perfectly good ground must produce the best possible outcome. If the structure is necessary and it generates a universe, that universe must be the best possible one. Anything less contradicts the ground’s perfection. So the specific universe is necessary after all. Modal collapse returns through the back door.

The Leibnizian move presupposes a necessary evaluative subject: something that ranks possible universes and selects the best. The present account posits no such subject. The three Conditions are structural roles, not agents. They permit contingency; they don’t rank it. The Leibnizian version gets traction against classical theism, where a necessary perfect Being must choose the best; it loses traction against a structural account with no such Being to rank outcomes. An impersonal version of the same demand needs a different answer, since the reply just given was aimed at a chooser. Axiarchism (Leslie, *Value and Existence* 1979) drops the chooser and grounds the demand in value itself: ethical requirement, on this view, is creatively effective, and the good tends toward its own actuality with no one selecting it. Nothing in that requires a subject, and treating it as a disguised act of choice would answer a position nobody holds. What it does require is a selection principle: some determinate configuration obtains rather than the alternatives it leaves unactualized, and an account on which value explains that has to say how value discriminates among them—which configurations rank higher, on what measure, and why the measure is answerable to nothing further. Axiarchism supplies such a principle as a primitive. The structural account declines to, and the difference is an added premise rather than a defect: structure permits contingency without ranking it, and an axiarchist who adds the ranking owes its content.

*Third.* The Spinozan propagation version asserts transmission through grounding. Necessity propagates through grounding relations. If the ground is necessary and the relation is grounding, the grounded is necessary. A necessary structural base can’t ground contingent content, because grounding transmits modal status. The argument has smuggled in contingency it has no right to.

*Notation.* Where this section invokes Physical Invariance, **M** is a complete physical profile and **Q** a proved invariant of it, in the sense fixed at §3.5.6; *Realizes(x, M)* says a configuration x instantiates that profile.

**[Lemma]**

**Constitutive Grounding Non-Propagation** · *Lemma*

Two relations must be kept apart. □(T∧S∧Φ) and □◇C are not ground and grounded but one fact under two readings: by the Modal Identity, the necessity of the structural conditions just is the necessary possibility of change read modally, so □◇C carries its necessity by identity, not by transmission across a grounding relation. The structural conditions also ground particular changes, but only in part: to be a change at all is to instantiate T, S, and Φ, while what makes a given change occur rather than another—its initial conditions or outcome—lies outside the three roles. Configurational Necessitation fixes the full-ground conditional, □(P → Q); Strict Actualization yields actual Q from that conditional and actual P. Physical Invariance applies that boundary to complete physical profiles: $\Box\forall x(\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)\rightarrow Q(x))$ fixes what follows of an *M*-realization without establishing $\Box\exists x\,\operatorname{Realizes}(x,M)$. Only an independently established □P permits K to yield □Q. The necessary Conditions therefore constrain every change without making the complete antecedent of every change necessary. □(T∧S∧Φ) ⊢ □◇C, not □C.

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6), Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4), Strict Actualization (§2.9.4), and Physical Invariance (§3.5.6)

**Feeds into:** The Sustenance Fork (§10.1.5 The Cosmological Argument)

Spinozan propagation holds only if the three Conditions are the *full* ground of each particular change: only if fixing the structural conditions fixes which changes occur. They aren’t. The roles ground the *possibility* of change and enter each actual change as a necessary structural constituent, but they are never the whole of what grounds a given change: which change occurs turns on contingent specifics (initial conditions and, on indeterministic interpretations, the quantum outcome of §4.7) that the roles leave undetermined. Grant the grounding-necessitarian principle, that a full ground necessitates what it grounds; a merely partial ground doesn’t, and the three Conditions are at most a partial, structural ground of any particular change. That the three Conditions are necessary entails any actual change instantiates them; it doesn’t entail any particular change had to occur.

A kindred move presses through mereology. Schaffer’s (2010) priority monism holds that the cosmos is the fundamental object and all its parts derive from it by ontological grounding. If grounding transmits necessity, every part is necessary. The reply is the same in mereological vocabulary. Priority monism by itself doesn’t decide whether the cosmos fully or only partly grounds each configuration of its parts. Blocking collapse requires the additional thesis that the necessary structural base underdetermines those configurations; it can’t be read off monism alone. Priority monism doesn’t generate modal collapse unless the cosmos is the full ground of each configuration of its parts.

*Convergence.* Each of the three forms misreads what the argument establishes and what grounding does. The Consequence Argument targets determinism, which the present account isn’t committed to: □◇C fixes what is structurally possible, not which possibilities are actualized, and the structural roles don’t by themselves fix laws, initial conditions, or outcomes, whichever quantum interpretation obtains. The Leibnizian best-world version presupposes a necessary evaluative subject the present account doesn’t posit, and applies to classical theism because that view posits the evaluative subject the present account doesn’t. Spinozan propagation holds only if T, S, and Φ fully ground each particular change rather than partly. Configurational Necessitation and Strict Actualization show the exact boundary: a sufficient configuration fixes its outcome when actual, but the outcome becomes necessary only if the complete sufficient configuration is independently necessary. The three Conditions don’t supply that complete configuration.

Spinoza wrote the *Ethics* *more geometrico* (Latin: “in the geometrical manner”, his method of presenting metaphysics in the form of definitions, axioms, and propositions). The necessitarian conclusion he reached (God is nature, nature is necessary, every mode follows with the force of geometrical demonstration) has haunted rationalist metaphysics ever since. Most of his successors tried to restore contingency by loosening the grounding relation between substance and mode. The structural account restores it by a different line: by clarifying what was grounded in the first place. The three Conditions ground the *possibility* of change, not the necessity of any particular change. The stage may be necessary without the argument thereby making every detail of the play necessary. Spinoza saw what happens if the necessary base fully grounds its modes, so that necessity transmits unrestricted; he saw correctly. The mistake wasn’t in following the logic. It was in assuming the base must be the full ground of what follows from it.

Necessity at the base permits contingency at the leaves.

## 8.3 Objects, Parts, and Identity
The positions in this section contest what an object is and what it takes for one to persist. The problem of temporary intrinsics (§8.3.1) asks how one thing can bear incompatible properties at different times; stage theory (§8.3.2) replaces endurance (persistence by being wholly present at each time) with relations among momentary stages; bundle and trope theory (§8.3.3) rejects an underlying substrate; mereological nihilism (§8.3.4) denies that arrangements compose further objects; and haecceitism (§8.3.5) locates numerical identity in a primitive thisness not exhausted by qualitative description.

These are chiefly disputes about realization and inventory, not five attempts to eliminate the same thing. Temporary-intrinsics theories specify cross-time predication; stage, bundle, and trope theories propose realizers for continuity without an enduring substrate; nihilism removes composites while retaining arrangement-facts; haecceitism challenges the qualitative and relational analysis of individuation. The structural question is what each proposal must preserve for change, arrangement, or displacement to remain intelligible—and where the proposal instead contests the bridge from a thin role to the book’s loaded type.

### 8.3.1 The Problem of Temporary Intrinsics
David Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds* 1986a) names the problem of temporary intrinsics; a simple case makes it vivid: a banana is green at t1 and yellow at t2, and the banana can’t be both green and yellow simpliciter (in the unqualified, unrelativized sense), since those properties are incompatible. Some way of relativizing the predication is needed, and the analysis one chooses for it is largely determinative of one’s metaphysics of persistence and change.

The problem is sharp because the available solutions all carry costs. Presentism (only the present is real) avoids the contradiction by holding that the banana is yellow simpliciter at t2 (t2 is the present) and there is no greenness for the contradiction to obtain with. But presentism faces difficulties about cross-time relations and historical truth. Four-dimensionalism (perdurance) holds that the banana is a four-dimensional object with temporal parts; the t1-stage is green, the t2-stage is yellow, and there is no contradiction because the green and yellow are properties of distinct stages. But four-dimensionalism faces the standard objection (Lewis himself raises it) that ordinary objects don’t seem to have temporal parts in the way they have spatial parts. The relational-properties account holds that ‘green at t1’ and ‘yellow at t2’ are time-relativized properties that the banana has wholly and simpliciter; the contradiction is dissolved because the properties have time-indices built in. But the relational-properties account makes intrinsic properties relational, which Lewis argues is to misdescribe what ‘intrinsic’ means.

The target here is the structural claim that the temporary-intrinsics analysis, in any of its three forms, undermines the account of §2.6. The argument the objector might run: change, on every available analysis, turns out to be either the difference of intrinsic properties at different times (presentism, with cross-time relations as a separate problem), or the difference of intrinsic properties of different temporal parts (perdurance), or the relational property of the same object at different times (relationalism). On none of these analyses is change a single thing standing in different conditions across time, the picture named at §2.6. So the present account is, at best, a description of one of these analyses, and likely a description of none of them.

The reply is that the present account is consistent with all three analyses of temporary intrinsics, and is the structural fact each of them is an analysis of. Ordering, distinctness, and cross-time continuity sit at a level above the metaphysics of how persistence is realized: they are what any analysis of persistence must supply, and each of the three supplies them in a distinct way. Whether a given analysis’s continuity surrogate also meets the loaded Φ type is a further question, settled by the role-to-type argument rather than by the banana. The dispute among the three is internal to the metaphysics of persistence; the present account is what the disputes are disputes about.

The temporary-intrinsics problem yields presentist, perdurantist, and relationalist analyses. Each supplies a different account of cross-time predication; the structural question is what continuity each analysis retains.

*First.* Presentism (Prior, Bigelow, Markosian) holds that only the present is real. The banana is yellow simpliciter at the present moment t2; the banana was green at the past moment t1, but that past moment isn’t now real, only its having-been-real is now real. Tensed truths are taken as primitive: ‘the banana was green’ is true now, but its truth-maker isn’t a present-tense fact about a past entity but a primitive past-tense fact.

Presentism is consistent with the present account at each present moment. The banana at t2 is distinct from the seed it grew from and from the compost it will become (S). Presentism can’t straightforwardly relate the present banana to presently nonexistent past and future stages. It instead invokes primitive tensed facts, ersatz times, or another truthmaking account. Those resources may realize the ordering role, and the reply assumes no literal relations to non-real relata. The banana persists across changes (the banana that is now yellow is the same banana that was green) and the persistence is the structural fact that the cross-time identity obtains, however the metaphysics of cross-time relations is specified (Φ). Presentism’s specific contribution to the metaphysics of temporary intrinsics is to hold that the cross-time relations are tensed primitives rather than relations to wholly-real past or future entities.

*Second.* Four-dimensionalism (Lewis, Sider, Heller, Hudson) holds that the banana is a four-dimensional object with temporal parts. The t1-stage of the banana is green; the t2-stage of the banana is yellow; the four-dimensional banana itself, the whole, is partly-green-and-partly-yellow in the way a striped flag is partly-red-and-partly-white. There is no contradiction because the green and yellow are properties of distinct temporal parts.

Four-dimensionalism is an explicit candidate realization of T ∧ S ∧ Φ. The temporal parts are distinct (S). They stand in temporal relations of earlier and later (T). The four-dimensional whole doesn’t endure from one time to another; it has temporal parts at different times. Its perdurance and the relations unifying those parts offer one realization of the Φ-role, but calling the timelessly extended whole persistence without qualification would beg the question against endurantism. The four-dimensionalist hasn’t eliminated the continuity role; they analyze it through temporal parts and their unifying relations.

*Third.* Relationalism (Mellor, Lowe in some moods, Wasserman) holds that ‘green’ and ‘yellow’ aren’t strictly intrinsic but covert relations to times: ‘the banana is green-at-t1 and yellow-at-t2.’ The contradiction is dissolved because ‘green-at-t1’ and ‘yellow-at-t2’ are compatible properties; the banana has them both wholly and simpliciter, in the way it has the property of being-three-feet-from-the-window and the property of being-five-feet-from-the-door wholly and simpliciter without contradiction.

Relationalism is consistent with the present account. The relations to times require times for the relations to be relations to (T). The relations distinguish the banana’s condition at t1 from its condition at t2 (S in the relational structure). The persistence of the banana (the same banana having both relations) is the structural fact that one entity stands in both (Φ). The relationalist’s specific cost (making intrinsic properties relational) is a cost internal to the metaphysics of properties, not a cost to the structural account.

A kindred move is the adverbialist account (Johnston, Haslanger): the banana is green at t1 in the sense of being t1-ly green, where ‘green’ is modified adverbially by the time. The adverbialist hopes to keep intrinsic properties intrinsic by relocating the time-relativization from the property to the manner of having the property. The reply is that the structural conditions are satisfied either way: the manner of having the property at t1 is distinct from the manner of having the property at t2 (S in the manners), the manners stand in temporal relations (T), and the entity persists across the manners (Φ).

Another kindred is the soft-presentist combination (Crisp, Markosian’s later work): only the present is real, and tensed truths are primitive, but the structural fact that the world has been and will be in determinate ways is itself a primitive feature of present reality. The reply is that the structural facts the soft-presentist takes as primitive are the structural facts named at §2.6, taken as primitive. The present account is consistent with primitivism about the structural facts.

**[Proposition]**

**A Problem One Level Down** · *Proposition*

Presentism, four-dimensionalism, and relationalism each supply an ordered continuity structure, at a level the derivation operates above: presentism at each present moment with cross-time relations carried by tensed-fact primitivism, four-dimensionalism in the manifold existing timelessly, relationalism in properties indexed to times. The temporary-intrinsics problem is therefore a dispute about how cross-time continuity is realized rather than about whether it is required. What each supplies is a candidate occupant of the continuity role; whether the occupant meets the loaded Φ type is settled by the independent role-to-type argument, and none of the three analyses is refuted by that question being asked.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10)

*Convergence.* Three forms, and each supplies ordering, distinctness, and a candidate continuity structure at a level the account operates above (§2.6). The level-above placement is a deliberate trade, worth stating in Lewis’s own cost-benefit idiom. What it buys: neutrality, the structural conditions are secured without adjudicating the persistence dispute, and what all three rivals share is made explicit rather than left implicit. What it costs: discriminating power, the account doesn’t, and doesn’t try to, settle which of presentism, perdurance, or relationalism is correct, and it commits to structural facts of ordering, distinctness, and persistence whose own individuation is specified at §2.6 rather than here. For the present argument the purchase is the right one: the thesis of §2.6 needs only what every analysis of persistence must satisfy, so buying neutrality at the price of adjudication costs the argument nothing it required and secures exactly what it did.

The temporary-intrinsics literature gets one thing right: pre-analytic talk of an object changing doesn’t determine how that object is related to its earlier state. The banana that ripens requires either a metaphysics of temporal parts, or a metaphysics of relational properties, or a metaphysics of tensed primitives, or some other specification of how cross-time identity is sustained. The present account doesn’t adjudicate among these. It makes a weaker claim: whatever specification of cross-time identity is correct, the cross-time continuity itself is a structural fact of the kind Φ names. The banana that ripens is analyzed differently across the views: as one enduring object, as a four-dimensional whole with differently qualified parts, or as appropriately related stages. What survives neutrally is an ordered continuity structure, not strict numerical identity on every account. The neutrality is the same one that Arrangement, Not Composition states against the nihilist (§8.3.4), run here on persistence rather than on composition: the three analyses settle how cross-time identity is realized, not whether the continuity they each analyze obtains. The present account is the level at which that continuity holds regardless of which specification is correct.

Lewis introduced the temporary-intrinsics problem in 1986, in the brief passage on endurance and perdurance in *On the Plurality of Worlds* (pp. 202–204) that has occupied subsequent metaphysics for decades. Lewis’s own resolution was perdurance, but the problem outlived his answer; presentism, perdurance, and relationalism remain the three dominant analyses, and the dispute among them is one of the central debates of contemporary metaphysics of persistence. The banana ripens, on the present reading, by standing in successive conditions across an ordering of times, with the metaphysics of how the standing-across is realized to be specified separately. The standing-across is the structural fact. The metaphysics of its specification is the topic of the dispute. The former is named by §2.6; the philosophy of persistence elaborates the latter.

### 8.3.2 Stage Theory
What if there is no persistence? What if the world is a sequence of momentary flashes: each instant a complete fact unto itself, each one followed by another that isn’t it, each connected to the next by nothing but resemblance and causal succession? Buddhist philosophers call this *kṣaṇabhaṅga*, momentary destruction. Its nearest analytic relative is stage theory, or four-dimensionalism with temporal counterparts. The traditions differ in aim and in machinery; what they share is a structural proposal: persistence is illusory, and what we call a continuing thing is a series of distinct stages bound only by relations of similarity and causal continuity.

The move is radical and the consequences are drastic. If it succeeds, the structural account of §2.6 collapses at Φ, the persistence condition. Without persistence, there is nothing across which Change can occur. Without persistence, the bidirectional identity of change-permission and T ∧ S ∧ Φ has no third leg to stand on. The classical theist, sensing the opening, sometimes adopts a momentarist line: God’s relation to the world is a sequence of momentary creative acts, each instant freshly produced, with no need for persistence running through them. Pratītyasamutpāda (dependent origination) supplies the metaphysical scaffolding. Sider supplies the contemporary analytic version. The objection deserves a careful answer.

Buddhist Abhidharma and Yogācāra thought develop *kṣaṇabhaṅga* in detail: every existent (*bhāva*) is a *kṣaṇa* (momentary instant), arising and ceasing in the same instant, replaced by a successor that is causally continuous but numerically distinct. Vasubandhu (4th–5th c.) and Dharmakīrti (7th c.) elaborate the doctrine; the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness, itself a stream of moments rather than an enduring self) and the *santāna* (the continuum a series of momentary existents composes, in the mental case the *citta-santāna* or mind-stream) do the explanatory work that ordinary persistence would otherwise do. Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (2nd c.), earlier and from the Madhyamaka school rather than Yogācāra, comes at the question from another side: nothing has *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), momentary existents included, and *śūnyatā* (emptiness) is the proper analysis of every apparent persistent.

In analytic philosophy, the structurally similar position is stage theory: Sider (*Four-Dimensionalism* 2001) develops a rigorous version, on which ordinary objects are momentary stages bound by genidentity (Lewin’s term, taken up by Carnap and Reichenbach, for cross-time identity-by-causal-continuity rather than strict numerical identity) or counterpart relations. Hawley (*How Things Persist* 2001) defends a closely related view. Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds* 1986a; *Philosophical Papers* II 1986b) supplies the perdurantist framework. Quine’s stage-theoretic readings of ordinary objects in *Word and Object* (1960) and Russell’s logical-construction program are ancestral. Heller (*The Ontology of Physical Objects* 1990) and Hudson (*A Materialist Metaphysics of the Human Person* 2001) develop the position in different directions.

The target here is the structural claim: that the world is a sequence of momentary stages bound by external relations only, with no persistence operating across them. The philosophical opponents of stage theory, endurantists like van Inwagen (*Material Beings* 1990a), Wiggins (*Sameness and Substance* 1980), Lowe (*The Possibility of Metaphysics* 1998), who hold that ordinary objects are wholly present at each moment of their existence rather than composed of momentary stages, have written extensively against perdurance. The present reply is narrower than their full case: it locates the structural commitment that any momentarism must make to be the position it claims to be, and shows that the commitment instantiates the structural roles the position is defined as denying.

The position has three relevant forms: strict momentarism, causal continuity among momentary existents, and counterpart or genidentity relations among stages. The first denies persistence; the latter two offer candidate realizers of a thinner continuity role.

*First.* Strict momentarism (a stripped-down form of the doctrine) claims that each instant is a complete fact unto itself, with no relations to any other instant. Each *kṣaṇa* arises and ceases in the same instant, and what we call succession is a cognitive imposition on what is in fact a sequence of unrelated complete facts.

Strict momentarism can’t describe its own claim. To say that there are many *kṣaṇa*s, in succession, is to relate them, and the relation of succession is exactly what is denied. The position requires either that the *kṣaṇa*s be related or ordered, in which case a cross-stage structural fact is admitted, or that they be wholly unrelated, in which case the theory can’t recover succession. Wholly unrelated plurality doesn’t literally collapse to one fact, but it can’t constitute a sequence without an ordering relation. The strict-momentarist version of the doctrine collapses on its own description: either the position is false because succession obtains, or the position is empty because nothing in it can be a succession of anything.

*Second.* The causal-continuity form weakens the claim: each moment is distinct, but moments are bound by causal relations. The *santāna* (the continuum) is a causal stream, not a persistence condition; the appearance of a continuing self or object is the cognitive trace of the causal continuity, not the deliverance of an underlying substance.

A causal relation between distinct *kṣaṇa*s requires a structural fact connecting them. That supplies directed dependence and cross-stage bearing, but it doesn’t by itself establish numerical identity or persistence of one bearer. The momentarist may accept causal continuity while denying strict persistence; the structural account must therefore distinguish the thin Φ-role from an endurantist persistence type. *Santāna* is offered for the work the thin Φ-role names: the structural condition that makes A’s effect on B a real relation rather than a coincidence of pattern. If the doctrine is read as eliminating Φ, then the causal continuity it appeals to has nothing to run on and no force; if the doctrine is read as preserving Φ under a different name, then it hasn’t eliminated persistence, only relabeled it. The Yogācāra thinkers saw the need clearly. The *ālaya-vijñāna* carries karmic seeds across instants, and it is built as a stream of moments rather than an enduring substance, so that the cross-moment work gets done without reinstating what the doctrine denies. That makes it a candidate realizer of the thin Φ-role: a continuity that bears content across instants without strict identity. The design is honest about the explanatory need; what it doesn’t show is that the structural role has been eliminated.

*Third.* The counterpart-theoretic form analyzes ordinary persistence-talk through relations among stages: stages are momentary, but the genidentity relation (or the counterpart relation, or the appropriate cross-time similarity-plus-causation relation) ties them into the unified entities ordinary discourse names. The claim that this stage is the same person as that earlier stage is true under genidentity even though strict numerical identity doesn’t obtain. Sider develops the position with full rigor; the technical apparatus is sophisticated and the resulting metaphysics is internally coherent.

The genidentity or counterpart relation is one proposed surrogate for persistence, not strict persistence under another vocabulary. For genidentity to obtain between this stage and that earlier stage, there must be a structural fact (not internal to either stage, since each is momentary, but extending across them) that makes the relation hold. Whatever fact it is, it is a structural fact spanning instants, and is therefore a candidate realizer of the thin Φ-role.

Sider’s stage theory is distinct from perdurance: stages aren’t temporal parts of a four-dimensional whole but the primary objects, with persistence analyzed as a counterpart relation among numerically distinct stages (*Four-Dimensionalism* 2001, §7.2). On stage theory, the persistence structure is the counterpart-genidentity relation itself, which may realize the thin Φ-role as cross-stage continuity. Stage theory nevertheless denies that the later stage is numerically the same entity as the earlier stage; the relation supports survival-talk without restoring strict identity.

On perdurance, the persistence structure is the four-dimensional whole of which stages are temporal parts. Both posit a structural fact spanning instants; they differ on whether that fact is a relation among stages or a whole of which they are parts. The question of which account is fundamental isn’t settled here. Neither view refutes the thin continuity role: each supplies a candidate realization of it. Whether either candidate satisfies the loaded Φ-type requires the independent role-to-type bridge rather than a stipulation from cross-stage relatedness alone. The endurantist holds that a thing wholly present at each moment persists; the perdurantist holds that a thing has temporal parts at each moment and the four-dimensional whole persists. Where they differ is on the metaphysics of the parts, not on whether the thin continuity role obtains.

A kindred move is the bundle theory variant: the world is a bundle of tropes or property-instances, with no underlying substance. Each instant is a co-presence of tropes; the apparent persistence of an object is the resemblance and causal connection between successive bundles. The reply is structurally identical: either the bundles are unrelated (no succession, no persistence, no anything) or related (the relations are the structural facts named at §2.6). A bundle theorist who explains cross-time identity thereby proposes a realizer of cross-time continuity; whether it reaches the loaded Φ-type depends on the same role-to-type bridge.

Another kindred is the radical Heraclitean: nothing persists; everything is in flux; the river is never the same river twice. The reply is the same. To say that the river is in flux is to say that something stands in the relation of being-the-changing-pattern across the flux: the bed, the volume, the channel, or the whole spatiotemporal manifold of the river-event. Without structural persistence of some kind, ‘flux’ has no subject and the claim has no content. Heraclitus needs more structure than his slogan announces, and the more careful presocratic readings (Kahn, *The Art and Thought of Heraclitus* 1979) acknowledge as much.

*Where the momentarist is right, and it is worth conceding precisely.* The replies already considered defend Φ against the general elimination of persistence. They don’t defend the persisting *self*, and the book doesn’t have one to defend. The narrative I is a construction the recursion runs rather than a substrate it is, and it is a mapped region of the subject’s own field like any other, corrigible on depth and fidelity and releasable without the mapping ceasing (§5.7). On that point the momentarist tradition—the Yogācāra analysis of the self into a *santāna*, Sider’s stages, Hume’s bundle—isn’t being refuted but joined. What the structural account denies is narrower and is where the traditions come apart: that there is nothing across which the succession of states runs. Something persists, and what it is in the living case is named at §4.8, a closure coupled to sustained throughput that continues while its material composition turns over entirely. The recursion persists; the self-model it builds doesn’t have to, and demonstrably sometimes doesn’t. A momentarist who rejects the persistence premise rather than joining at this point has declined one route to the same conclusion. The Movement Line carries the necessity of the Conditions from the real possibility of displacement, on the premise that a displacement is undergone by something there across it (§2.4.9). A stage theorist contests exactly that premise, holding displacement to be a relation among stages, so the Movement route isn’t a second argument that answers momentarism; it is the route momentarism declines, and it stands or falls with the premise where that premise is argued.

The concession above is an alliance rather than a load-bearing step. The strict engagement runs on cross-stage ordering and causal relation alone, and needs neither the account of the self nor the criterion for life it draws on here; whether the cross-stage relation meets the loaded Φ type remains the upstream role-to-type question.

Keeping those two apart is what lets the reply be as narrow as it is. A momentarism aimed at the constructed I meets no resistance here and gains an ally. A momentarism aimed at the bearer meets the preceding arguments. The distinction matters because the evidence usually offered for it—the dissolution of the sense of self, the absence of an inspectable ego—is evidence about the first and silent about the second.

**[Proposition]**

**Self-Model, Not Bearer** · *Proposition*

There is no persisting self here to defend: the narrative I is a construction the recursion runs, corrigible and releasable. A momentarism aimed there meets no resistance and gains an ally. What the account denies is narrower, that there is nothing across which the succession runs. The evidence usually offered for momentarism, the dissolution of the sense of self and the absence of an inspectable ego, bears on the model and is silent on the bearer.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

*Convergence.* Three forms and none lets the structural elimination stand. Strict momentarism can’t describe a succession of wholly unrelated moments, because succession is itself a relation across them. Causal-continuity accounts answer that problem with the *santāna* or an analogue, thereby supplying a candidate cross-moment continuity realizer rather than strict endurance. The counterpart-theoretic form is internally coherent and supplies a candidate realizer of thin cross-stage continuity, whether through counterpart-genidentity or, on perdurance, a four-dimensional whole. It doesn’t by itself settle the loaded Φ classification. The endurantist and the perdurantist agree on the structural fact; they disagree on its metaphysics of parts. The question of which description supplies the fundamental analysis (the four-dimensional whole, the momentary stages in counterpart relations, or the wholly-present enduring object) is a question within the structural framework and answerable within it. It doesn’t bear on whether the thin continuity role obtains, though the loaded Φ classification still depends on the independent bridge. The meta-position held here is that fundamentality questions of this kind are downstream of the instantiation question: once Φ is established as a necessary structural condition, further questions about its realization (by temporal parts, by counterpart relations, or by simple endurance) remain open to metaphysical investigation without threatening the structural conclusion.

The momentarist insight, carried to its conclusion, is one the structural account preserves rather than denies: there is something importantly correct about the observation that nothing in the world is fixed, that every object is in some sense an event, that what we call a thing is the persistent pattern of its becoming. The structural account names that pattern Φ (the persistence condition) and locates it as one of three structural roles whose joint instantiation is what change consists in. The momentarist who pushes the insight to the elimination of Φ has gone too far: persistence isn’t a substance behind the pattern but *is* the pattern itself, the structural fact that there is a pattern at all rather than a sequence of unrelated fragments.

### 8.3.3 Bundle and Trope Theory
Take away the substrate and ask what is left to do the persisting. Two positions press that question at Φ from opposite directions—one dissolving the bearer into the properties it was supposed to carry, the other dissolving the properties into particulars that need no bearer to be shared—and the structural account owes an answer to both, because Φ is the condition it can least afford to hold by assertion.

Bundle theory, developed in different forms by Hume, Russell, and more recently by Paul (2017), holds that objects are bundles of properties without underlying substrates. Trope theory, developed by Williams (1953), Campbell (1990), and Maurin (2002), holds that properties are particularized (this redness here, that hardness there) rather than universals shared across instances. Both positions challenge the substance role of Φ (causal persistence across temporal change, the third structural Condition alongside T and S, borne by Substance just as T and S are borne by Time and Space): if there are no underlying substrates, what does causal persistence inhere in? If properties are particularized tropes, what bundles them into the persisting configuration the structural account requires?

The reply distinguishes the metaphysics of property-bearing from the structural role of Φ. The substance role is the role of causal persistence across temporal change: whatever obtains in such a way that the same configuration is causally connected from one moment to the next. Bundle theory and trope theory are accounts of how property-bearing works at a fine grain; they aren’t denials that something persists. Where a bundle persists across time, that persistence is, for the present argument, an occupant of the Φ-role; where a collection of compresent tropes (tropes co-occurring at the same location) maintains its compresence across temporal succession, so is that. The conditional matters: not every bundle or trope theory supplies diachronic unity ready-made, and one that doesn’t owes an account of it rather than inheriting one. The present argument isn’t committed to the substrate metaphysics that bundle and trope theories deny; it is committed to the structural role those metaphysics still have to fill, however they fill it.

Two finer questions the bundle and trope theorist press don’t change this. The first is Bradley’s old regress: if the tropes are bound into one bundle by a relation, and that relation is itself a trope, it requires its own binder, and the bundle never closes. The regress is a real pressure on bundle theory’s internal economy. Renaming compresence as S holding across Φ doesn’t by itself solve it; the bundle theorist still owes an account of what unifies the tropes, whether primitive compresence, a non-relational tie, or another device. The structural account can remain neutral on that account while requiring any successful proposal to realize differentiation and continuity. The second is whether the bundle endures, wholly present at each moment, or perdures through distinct temporal parts. Φ is neutral between them: it asks only that the configuration be causally connected from one moment to the next, a demand the endurantist meets through identity and the perdurantist through genidentity among temporal parts. The persistence-metaphysics dispute (pressed in its perdurantist form at §8.3.1) settles how Φ is realized, not whether it is.

**[Proposition]**

**Downstream of the Role, Not Rival to It** · *Proposition*

Bundle theory, trope theory, substance theory and process theory are competing answers to a question that arises only once the Substantiality role has been specified. The derivation identifies the roles any configuration must instantiate; how the roles are filled is a further question, and every one of these accounts that succeeds fills them rather than replacing them. None is refuted here and none needs to be: a dispute about what occupies a role presupposes the role, so the necessity claim is untouched whichever account wins.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

*Taking stock.* The reply matches the reply to ontic structural realism (§9.10) in shape. The roles any configuration must instantiate are identified at §2.6.8 and §2.7; metaphysical accounts of how the roles are filled are downstream of the necessity claim. The move is the one that Arrangement, Not Composition states for the nihilist (§8.3.4) and haecceitism meets again at §8.3.5: each settles the inventory rather than the structure any inventory’s items must instantiate to obtain at all.

### 8.3.4 Mereological Nihilism
Van Inwagen’s *Material Beings* (1990a) answers the special composition question from one step short of mereological nihilism. There are no chairs, no tables, no planets, no stones: only simples arranged chair-wise, table-wise, planet-wise, stone-wise. The single exception is living organisms, whose self-maintaining causal activity Van Inwagen takes to ground a unity mere arrangements lack. The position shrinks the ontology where Lewis’s plurality (§7.2.3) multiplies it, and it does so with the same systematic care. Sider’s “Against Parthood” (2013) presses one step further: even the organism exception is rejected, and what remains is only simples in arrangements.

Mereological nihilism (also called compositional nihilism or compositional eliminativism) has a precise lineage. Classical mereology (Leśniewski 1916; Tarski 1929) supplies the formal vocabulary of parthood, and Lewis’s *Parts of Classes* (1991) systematizes the contemporary defense of unrestricted composition the nihilist most directly opposes. Van Inwagen (*Material Beings* 1990a) develops the organism-exception version in detail. Merricks’s *Objects and Persons* (2001) extends Van Inwagen’s exception to persons and presses the overdetermination argument against composite objects more broadly. Sider’s “Against Parthood” (2013, *Oxford Studies in Metaphysics* vol. 8) develops the strictest nihilist version: no composites at any level, organisms included. Dorr’s “What We Disagree About When We Disagree About Ontology” (2005) defends compositional nihilism through paraphrase: nihilist and non-nihilist sentences can be made true under the same conditions. Cameron’s “Truthmakers and Ontological Commitment” (2008) develops a kindred deflationary line. Against the nihilists: Markosian’s “Brutal Composition” (1998) treats composition as a brute fact admitting no further criterion; Schaffer’s “On What Grounds What” (2009) and the monist literature (Schaffer 2010) defend the cosmos as the fundamental composite from which parts derive; classical mereology (Goodman 1951; Simons 1987) defends unrestricted composition. On composition the structural account runs with the moderate-OSR line of §9.10: neutral on what composes, specific about what any arrangement must instantiate.

The nihilist pressure bears on Φ specifically and on the architecture (§2.7) more generally. If composite objects don’t exist, then the persistent configurations the argument has been describing (patterns of features held together as one substantial bearer across temporal succession) have no bearer to inhere in. T and S might survive as relational facts among simples, but Φ, the persistence of structured pattern, would require a pattern that is something over and above its constituents. The nihilist position, in its strict form, dissolves the Substance role into arrangements of underlying simples and denies that the arrangement composes anything further.

A clarification before the moves. The nihilist isn’t denying that the world contains the arrangements ordinarily called “chairs” and “tables.” Van Inwagen and Sider both grant the arrangement-facts; what they deny is that the arrangements compose further objects. “Simples arranged chair-wise” describes a real configuration on every nihilist account; what it doesn’t describe, on the strict version, is a chair as an additional ontological item. The question turns on whether the structural argument requires composite objects beyond the arrangements, or whether the arrangements themselves carry the structural roles. Three forms of the move press that question at three resolutions: the basic eliminativist version, Van Inwagen’s organism-exception version, and Sider’s strict version.

*First.* The basic eliminativist move denies composition wholesale. There are no composite objects (chairs, tables, planets, organisms), only simples in various arrangements. The structural argument, in describing the persistence of configurations across time, has been describing composites the nihilist rules out. Without composites, no Φ; without Φ, the Triconditional fails.

The argument doesn’t need composites in the sense the nihilist denies. What it needs is that the arrangements themselves instantiate the structural roles. A pattern of simples arranged chair-wise that persists across a temporal interval instantiates Φ at the level of the arrangement, whether or not the arrangement composes a further object called “the chair.” Persistence is a feature of the pattern, not a posit beyond it. The nihilist who grants that the arrangement obtains, and obtains across time, has granted the structural role; what they have refused is the additional ontological commitment to a composite as a further item. The argument is neutral on that further item. The three Conditions specify what arrangements consist in, not what arrangements compose. Compositional nihilism leaves the structural roles where they are.

**[Proposition]**

**Arrangement, Not Composition** · *Proposition*

The nihilist denies that arrangements compose further objects while granting the arrangement-facts. The structural roles attach to the arrangements. *Arranged* is itself a structural predicate: simples arranged chair-wise must be individuated from one another, and where the arrangement lasts across an interval and is maintained by its own causal activity, it obtains in order and something holds across it. Whether arrangements additionally compose objects is a question the argument leaves open, because it operates one level below it.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

*Second.* Van Inwagen’s organism exception holds that living things compose but artifacts and inanimate aggregates don’t. The criterion is unity: the activities of an organism’s parts are coordinated in service of the organism’s life in a way that the parts of a chair aren’t coordinated in service of the chair. Living things therefore qualify as composites; chairs and tables don’t. The structural argument, on this reading, gets purchase only where Van Inwagen’s exception holds.

The criterion Van Inwagen invokes is itself Φ at the appropriate resolution. Causal persistence of a configuration across temporal change, where the configuration’s persistence is constitutively maintained by its internal causal activity: that is what Substance names in the structural argument, and it is what Van Inwagen identifies as the mark of organic unity. The argument generalizes the criterion rather than restricting it. Any arrangement whose obtaining is constitutively maintained across time by its own causal activity instantiates Φ; the question is whether the maintenance is real, not whether the arrangement is biological. Crystalline lattices maintain themselves through electromagnetic binding; weather systems maintain themselves through fluid dynamics; the argument applies wherever maintenance obtains. Van Inwagen draws the line at the biological case; the argument follows the maintenance wherever it goes.

*Third.* Sider’s strict version denies even Van Inwagen’s exception. There are no composites at any level, organisms included; only simples in various arrangements, including the arrangements ordinarily described as living. The arrangement-facts obtain (Sider doesn’t deny that simples are arranged organism-wise), but no further composite organism exists. The structural argument, on this version, must run entirely on arrangement-facts, without the resource of any composite bearer.

The recasting is the right one for the strict nihilist, and the reply is correspondingly cleaner. Arrangement-facts that obtain across time, with patterns maintained by causal activity among their constituents, instantiate the structural roles whether or not they compose further objects. The argument operates at the level of what arrangements consist in. Sider’s strict version concedes the arrangement-facts; it denies the further composite. The three Conditions specify what such arrangement-facts are: relationally distinct and, where they last and are maintained, temporally ordered and causally borne. The argument’s necessity claim runs at the arrangement-fact level. Whether the additional composite is also there is a separate ontological question the structural argument leaves open. Sider’s nihilism is compatible with the structural argument: it constrains the inventory of composites without contesting the structure of arrangements. Sider’s nihilism is only one of two commitments he brings to bear here; the other (his joint-carving structuralism, on which the live question is whether the three Conditions belong to the fundamental ideology rather than sit above a deeper structure) is the subject of §7.2.8, where that question is engaged on its own terms.

A kindred move runs through priority monism (Schaffer 2010). Where the nihilist denies composites by eliminating them, the monist denies composites as fundamental by absorbing them into the cosmos: only the whole cosmos fundamentally exists, and the apparent composite objects are derivative aspects of it. The reply runs in the same direction. Whether the cosmos is fundamental and its parts derivative, or the simples are fundamental and the apparent composites eliminated, the structural argument operates at the level of the arrangements that obtain (at whatever ontological level the arrangements are located) and on the structural conditions any obtaining arrangement must instantiate. The composition question is orthogonal to the structural-role question. The same applies to the bundle/trope alternatives canvassed in §8.3.3: those answers, like nihilism, address what the inventory contains rather than what the inventory’s items must be like to obtain.

*Convergence.* Each of the three forms misreads what the argument requires. The basic eliminativist move denies composites the argument doesn’t need; the structural roles attach to the arrangements, not to the composites the arrangements may or may not constitute. Van Inwagen’s organism-exception invokes a unity criterion that just is Φ at the level of organic maintenance; the argument generalizes the criterion to any arrangement constitutively maintained by causal activity. Sider’s strict version concedes the arrangement-facts while denying the composites, and the arrangement-facts are exactly where the structural argument operates. Nihilism, at every resolution, leaves the structural roles where they are.

One clarification of scope is owed, because Van Inwagen’s signature pressure isn’t compositional but modal-epistemic. His modal-epistemic question is how one knows that the three Conditions are *necessary* rather than merely pervasive, given how far that claim sits from the conceptual and near-by possibilities the modal faculty handles reliably. It isn’t answered by the compositional reply already considered, and isn’t meant to be. That pressure is upstream of this section, and the book’s answer to it is methodological rather than intuitive: the necessity verdict is claimed as the output of the derivation of §2.6–2.7, not of a modal intuition about distant scenarios, which is precisely the non-intuitive line Van Inwagen’s own modal skepticism leaves open. The argument here discharges the compositional half of the Van Inwagen inheritance; the modal-epistemic half is engaged on its own terms at §7.3.2, and paid where the necessity is derived, not where composition is discussed.

What Van Inwagen saw clearly, and Sider sharpened, was that the modern compositional tradition had multiplied entities far past anything the world’s structure demanded. The classical-mereology pedigree runs from Leśniewski’s plenitudinous parthood through Lewis’s *Parts of Classes* to contemporary unrestricted-composition defenses. It produced an inventory the nihilist refuses on grounds of austerity. What the nihilist tradition hasn’t always seen as clearly is that the world’s structure doesn’t consist in that inventory either. It consists in what arrangements (composite or not) must be like to obtain. The composition debate is real; it runs on a level the structural argument leaves open. Wherever simples are arranged in patterns that obtain across time, are distinct from other patterns, and are maintained by causal activity, the three Conditions are there. The argument is for the structure of what obtains, not for the inventory of what composes.

### 8.3.5 Haecceitism
A great deal of the book depends on this engagement, and the debt is better shown than discovered. The haecceitist exit is closed in the derivation itself, at §2.4.7, and Moment-Individuation is derived from that closure at §2.4.10. What happens here is the defense of that closure against the position’s contemporary form. The stakes are therefore inherited rather than local: Moment-Individuation carries the converse, the frozen-world and masking tests, and the role-to-type upgrades drawn on in Chapter 7, and its security is exactly the security of the anti-haecceitism—no greater. It does not carry an ∅ reductio: the ∅ Reductio Boundary (§2.7.4) records the additional field-level bridge that route would need. A reader who leaves this section unconvinced should carry that doubt to each actual dependent rather than to none of them.

Haecceitism holds that the facts about which individual is which aren’t exhausted by the qualitative and relational facts: two situations can agree on every qualitative and relational property and still differ over which individual is which. Adams’s *Primitive Thisness and Primitive Identity* (1979) gives the position its canonical analytic statement: a thisness is the non-qualitative property of being this very individual, grounding numerical identity prior to and independently of any qualitative or relational characterization. The motivating case is older: Black’s “The Identity of Indiscernibles” (1952) describes a symmetric universe of two qualitatively indiscernible iron spheres, two and not one, with nothing qualitative to tell them apart. Lewis’s *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986a) is the locus of the contemporary debate, rejecting non-qualitative differences between worlds in favor of a counterpart-theoretic treatment, on which an individual figures in other possible situations not literally but through its qualitatively closest counterparts there, so that qualitative character fixes all there is to fix. The subsequent literature (Skow 2008) separates a deflationary form, which grants haecceitistic possibilities without positing primitive thisnesses, from the robust Adamsian form, which grounds them in genuine non-qualitative properties. What unites the family is the refusal to reduce individuation to qualitative or relational structure. That leaves two questions apart: whether the individuator may be nonqualitative or nonrelational, and whether it may be wholly nonstructural. The first remains open. The second is what Structural Individuation denies.

The position bears on two premises that must not be merged. Structural Individuation at §2.4.9 says that whatever individuates concrete items is real differentiating structure; Relational Distinctness at §2.4.7 says the narrower thing needed for Spatiality, that positional non-identity is constituted by relational extension across a traversable interval.
