Necessary Occupancy applies to the concrete observers the hypothesis invokes; the structure identical with their reality must therefore contain, as internal relations and not as a further substrate, the order, differentiation, and determinate bearing their processes require. This does not show that every mathematical structure is inhabited, concrete, or T-S-Φ-bearing. It shows that the anthropically selected structure cannot be the one we inhabit while leaving those roles behind.

**Dependency routes:** structural identity—Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10); observer-containing realization—Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7)

*Convergence.* What the MUH offers, on its observer-containing branch, is a mathematical formalization of the necessary ground rather than an alternative to it. Necessary Occupancy fixes the scope: concrete observers occupy the three Conditions, so any mathematical structure identical with their entire physical reality must realize those roles. Invariant Realization does less—it transfers proved invariants after realization is established—and Conditioned-Nature describes mathematics as Nature’s quantifiable articulation rather than asserting Tegmark’s identity. The three positions therefore converge on realized structure without becoming interchangeable. Nothing here establishes that every member of the Level-IV plenitude is concrete, inhabited, or triconditional.

## 9.10 Structural Realism
In a 1989 paper in *Dialectica* titled “Structural Realism: The Best of Both Worlds?” (1989), John Worrall proposed that what survives across theory change in physics isn’t the entities science postulates but the structural relations encoded in its mathematics. The Fresnel equations survived the abandonment of the luminiferous ether; what was preserved was the relational form, not the substance. Worrall’s epistemic structural realism holds that we can know the relational structure without knowing the natures of the relata.

James Ladyman developed the position in an ontic direction. In “What is Structural Realism?” (1998) and then with Don Ross in *Every Thing Must Go* (2007), the claim became that there are no relata with intrinsic natures awaiting our knowledge; reality is structures all the way down. French’s *The Structure of the World* (2014) gave the view a book-length defense. Esfeld and Lam retain objects as nodes within the structure while denying them independent intrinsic natures (Esfeld 2004; Esfeld and Lam 2008). Chakravartty’s *A Metaphysics for Scientific Realism* (2007) retains structures and detectable causal properties, with dispositional natures grounding the latter.

The result is a family of adjacent positions rather than one view at several strengths: epistemic structural realism, ontic structural realism in a radical, object-eliminating reading and a moderate, object-retaining one, and Chakravartty’s semirealism, which is a neighbour of OSR rather than a form of it. Its challenge is that the three Conditions may be a parochial selection from a richer relational fabric. If so, the Necessity of Nature theorem at §2.9.6, supported by the Modal Identity and Triconditional machinery of §2.6–2.7, may identify the wrong features as necessary.

The challenge sits closer to the present account than to its standard rivals, and the reply is correspondingly cooperative. The present argument doesn’t posit the three Conditions as objects with intrinsic natures; it identifies role-level conditions of genuine change-realizers. OSR’s claim that the world is fundamentally relational is compatible with directed order, relational differentiation, and real bearing. Whether a given physical relational fabric also realizes temporal succession, spatial extension, and causal persistence is a further type-level question, not something settled merely by calling every relation Time, Space, or Substance. The disagreement concerns both the modal status of the roles and the step from roles to their realizers. OSR is typically silent on whether the relational structure it describes is necessary or contingent; the present argument fills in the modal claim. Epistemic structural realism makes no ontological claim for the reply to engage and stands as the family’s starting point; the three ontic positions below—radical OSR, moderate OSR, and semirealism—sharpen what the family can commit to and what each commitment costs.

*First.* The radical or eliminative reading of OSR is associated with Ladyman and Ross (Ladyman et al. 2007) and French (French 2014), though how far either actually eliminates objects is disputed, and French’s own formulations are more cautious than the label suggests. On that reading there are no things; there are only patterns of relation. The challenge is that any pattern of relations might constitute a world, leaving the three Conditions as a parochial choice from the space of relational fabrics. The reply runs through §2.6–2.7: any pattern offered as a realizer of change must include the three roles at the appropriate resolution. Bare obtaining directly supports determinacy or difference, but doesn’t by itself entail temporal extension or causal persistence. Those loaded types require the separate change-realizer arguments.

French’s *The Structure of the World* identifies group-theoretic symmetries, gauge structures, and permutation invariance as fundamental relations among distinguishable items or positions. In familiar dynamical formulations, they are structured through an order of states or events and through constraints or capacities that hold determinate physical differences in place. A thoroughgoing atemporal-structure reading need not concede that the formal parameter in an equation is fundamental time. It instead owes an account of how the atemporal structure grounds an emergent order in which real differences occur and determinate capacities become available. Merely calling the base structure doesn’t discharge those obligations; neither does the present argument certify every timeless structural proposal in advance. This is the Realizer Fork (§8.4) in relational form: abstract structure can specify a pattern, while a concrete change-realizer must perform the work.

The division matters. T is the order of before and after; Φ is the determinate capacity or bearing condition that is exercised in that order. They are mutually required for real change but not the same role. The eliminativist version therefore doesn’t by itself undermine the role-level claim. It reformulates ontology in relational terms and can resist objects with intrinsic natures. But it remains a live challenge at the type level: an eliminative structuralist may deny that relations require persistent causal bearers in the book’s richer sense. The present account can reply that a relational fabric proposed as physical reality or as a realizer of change must meet the relevant type arguments; it doesn’t treat eliminative OSR as defeated merely because relations are named. The three Conditions are roles; the configurations satisfying the roles need not be objects with intrinsic natures in the sense OSR rejects.

*Second.* The moderate form (Esfeld 2004; Esfeld and Lam 2008) retains objects as nodes within the relational structure but denies them independent intrinsic natures. The position is compatible with the present account wherever those nodes are configurations in a physical fabric. Esfeld’s claim that nodes are exhausted by their relational profiles directly supplies thin difference. Where such nodes participate in actual change, their physical profiles must also realize order and cross-transition bearing. The moderate OSR theorist and the present account therefore converge in denying that fundamental ontology requires objects with hidden intrinsic natures. The remaining disagreements concern whether current physical structure exhausts what is fundamental, whether the roles are necessary, and whether the book’s role-to-type bridges succeed. The present argument takes its case from §2.6–§2.7 rather than building those conclusions into the word *relation*.

Ladyman’s Principle of Naturalistic Closure presses the modal claim on methodological grounds: no metaphysical hypothesis should be accepted unless it unifies well-confirmed hypotheses from more than one specific science. The present account aims to meet that constraint by identifying roles that recur across sciences rather than deriving a metaphysics from one favored theory. Dynamical formalisms use ordered states; field theory, topology, and network science use relational differentiation; conservation laws and accounts of development track determinate features or capacities across change. Experimental inquiry also instantiates order, distinction, and bearing on the act side. That act-side recurrence doesn’t prove that every object described by science has the loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types.

The modal claim instead rests on the argument of §2.6–2.7, especially Triconditional Cross-Entailment at §2.6.7. Its science-facing payoff is unificatory: any *law-governed structure* proposed as a concrete change-realizer must explain ordered states, real differentiation, and determinate capacities borne through the order. Naturalistic Closure doesn’t prove that triad, but it gives a methodological test the triad must pass. The case succeeds only if the independent derivation and its physical realizations do.

*Third.* Semirealism (Chakravartty 2007), a neighbouring realism rather than a form of OSR, retains both structure and detectable causal properties, treating dispositional natures as the ground of causal-property detectability. Chakravartty’s detectable causal properties supply a direct candidate for the Φ-role: dispositions manifest under differentiated stimulus conditions and retain a determinate manifestation profile across relevant changes. The present account doesn’t adjudicate between that dispositionalism and the more austere ontologies of moderate OSR. It requires any physical version to explain the same role-complex while allowing different accounts of its bearer.

A kindred move worth marking. The structuralist tradition in philosophy of mathematics runs a parallel argument in the mathematical case (Resnik, *Mathematics as a Science of Patterns* 1997; Shapiro, *Philosophy of Mathematics: Structure and Ontology* 1997): mathematical objects have only relational properties, and the structures themselves are what is real. The reply parallels the OSR reply: a mathematical structure contains distinguishable positions or relational differences, directly supporting the S-role. Stability across mathematical instances isn’t automatically physical persistence, and the temporal course of our inquiry is an act-side feature rather than a property of the abstract structure. Mathematical structuralism therefore supports the thin relational point while leaving T- and Φ-realization open. Invariant Realization (§3.5.6) transfers a proved consequence across realizations of a mathematical profile. Physical Invariance (§3.5.6) supplies the next step once physics establishes that a real system realizes a sufficiently complete physical profile: the system can’t instantiate that profile while lacking its proved invariant. Neither theorem establishes physical realization, makes the profile necessary, or turns a thin mathematical relation into temporal succession or persistence.

Two adjacent positions live elsewhere. The Tegmarkian “mathematical universe” hypothesis (Tegmark 2008; Tegmark 2014) runs a parallel ontological-monism move with mathematics rather than relational structure as the fundament; it’s engaged at §9.9. The information-theoretic ontology that treats reality as fundamentally informational is engaged at §8.2.3.

**[Proposition]**

**Structural Realism Converges Without Closing the Dispute** · *Proposition*

The structural-realist family overlaps substantially with the account. Radical OSR rejects objects with intrinsic natures, which the account does not require; moderate OSR treats nodes as structurally individuated; semirealism, a neighbour of OSR, supplies dispositional candidates for causal bearing. Two questions remain live: whether T, S, and Φ are necessary rather than contingent features of the physical fabric, and whether the thin roles require the loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types. Those questions are argued upstream rather than settled by the word *structure*. Invariant Realization transfers proved consequences across realizations of a mathematical profile; Physical Invariance carries them into a physical system once its realization of the profile is established; Triconditional Cross-Entailment supplies the further burden for a nomological change-realizer. None of these routes makes the profile itself necessary or makes bare mathematical structure temporal or persisting by description alone.

**Dependency routes:** nomological structure—Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7); mathematical consequence transfer—Invariant Realization (§3.5.6); physically realized invariants—Physical Invariance (§3.5.6)

*Convergence.* The present account converges with each of the three ontic positions in the family (radical OSR, moderate OSR, semirealism) at increasing levels of ontological commitment. Radical OSR rejects objects with intrinsic natures, which the present account doesn’t require. Moderate OSR retains nodes as structurally exhausted, which the present account already affirms. Semirealism retains dispositional natures, which the present account is consistent with without requiring. The disagreement, where there is one, is about whether the trio T, S, Φ is necessary at a level prior to the relational fabric current physics describes, or merely one description among others of that fabric.

Structural realism was proposed to reconcile the no-miracles argument for scientific realism with the argument from the repeated replacement of successful theories (the pessimistic meta-induction). Its ontic forms disagree about objects but converge on structure, and the present argument takes that convergence seriously.

Its claim is restricted to a relational fabric proposed as *nomological* and change-realizing: one in which laws hold, states succeed one another, and determinate capacities are borne through the succession. A bare mathematical structure directly supports the relational point without thereby realizing temporal succession or causal persistence. Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7) supplies the further argument for structures that do real physical work. An ontic structural realism about the actual changing world therefore meets the role-complex; whether it also accepts the book’s loaded realizers remains open.

## 9.11 What the Rivals Carried
The rivals don’t divide into one verdict. Some deny that there’s anything here to explain; some add a phenomenal or categorical bearer; some replace a classical physical realizer; some identify physical reality with mathematical or relational structure. They don’t begin from the same concession, and they don’t leave the same question open. What recurs is narrower: whenever a position supplies a determinate representation, a concrete change-realizer, an observer, or a contact that makes a difference, order, differentiation, and bearing reappear at the relevant resolution. Whether those thin roles exhaust reality, require the book’s loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types, or leave further phenomenal and categorical facts is recorded separately below.

**Eliminativism and illusionism.** The Churchlands’ eliminative materialism centrally targets propositional attitudes; stronger illusionist views deny that phenomenal consciousness exists as it seems. Neither move removes the conditions on the representing process that formulates, distinguishes, and sustains the denial, and the illusionist never proposed to; neither view is refuted by that observation. **Compatibility: deflation of the represented, not removal of the representing conditions**. The positive question of what consciousness is remains downstream (§9.2).

**Hard problem of consciousness.** Experience doesn’t establish a structureless domain. Even irreducible qualitative features would be features of a structured ground. The structured zombie—the same complete functional organization with consciousness withheld—separates two accounts. If the interior is identical with the organization, Configurational Necessitation forbids withholding it, and Strict Actualization gives the actual interior from an actual sufficient organization (§2.9.4). If it is a further feature, the account adds a phenomenal property and psychophysical law while the duplicate stipulation makes phenomenal character causally idle. Consciousness (§5.1) favors identity through biological continuity, multiple realization, and explanatory economy; it doesn’t prove the sufficiency premise. **No escape from structure; the zombie priced here, with its closure conditional on the Chapter 5 identity** (§9.1).

**Russellian monism.** A categorical or phenomenal realizer can’t do concrete work from outside all structure: if it bears capacities, differentiates realizations, or carries transitions, the Realizer Fork (§8.4) places it within the thin roles. That doesn’t prove role exhaustion. A complete causal profile may still leave categorical character underdetermined unless the No-Individuating-Surplus and constitutive identity arguments succeed. **Necessary Occupancy secured; categorical residue constrained but not independently eliminated here** (§9.3).

**Cosmopsychism.** A cosmic subject that grounds differentiated finite minds must stand in directed dependence relations to them and bear the differentiation it grounds. Calling the ground a subject therefore doesn’t place it prior to all structure. The stronger claim is that subjecthood is itself a self-modeling configuration and so can’t be fundamental. That claim depends on the account defended in Chapters 4–5. The decombination problem and the possibility of a cosmic subject remain questions for cosmopsychism. **Priority reversal at role-resolution; the subject-type conclusion conditional on the positive consciousness account** (§9.4).

**Idealism.** Berkeleyan and phenomenological idealisms relocate the roles to perception or constitution; Kant posits no mental fundamental and meets the ∅ fork’s challenge to a characterless noumenon instead, which Kantian humility can resist; analytic idealism, the principal target, must have its cosmic field differentiate and maintain its alters—temporally if dissociation is a happening, at thin resolution if it is timeless constitution. A mind that hosts a differentiated world must realize order, distinction, and bearing, so the relocation doesn’t remove the roles. Placing consciousness at the bottom doesn’t forbid asking what makes experience possible; it leaves idealism owing a derivation, a comparative explanation, or an openly held primitive. Acosmic nondualism and contentless awareness deny the relevant world-hosting premise and are routed to §5.16.5 rather than declared closed here. **Mind-compatible structure, not structure derived from mind; the objectless-awareness case remains separately engaged** (§9.5).

**Whiteheadian process.** Prehension and the superject can carry efficacy without an enduring subject. They thereby realize directed inheritance, difference between donor and recipient, and cross-transition bearing. This establishes the roles without deciding that the bearer is a persistent causal being in the book’s loaded sense. **Process realizes the bearer-role; role-to-type dispute deferred to the independent realizer argument** (§9.6).

**Bell non-locality.** Bell-inequality violations exclude Bell-local/factorizable hidden-variable accounts under the relevant independence and experimental assumptions. They don’t deny that the correlated outcomes are distinct, and they don’t by themselves select a metaphysical interpretation or eliminate every possible common-cause account. **Differentiation and relational structure retained at thin resolution; permissible relations constrained more finely; loaded spatial extension left to the role-to-type question** (§9.7).

**Everettian branching.** Physically realized branches contain ordered, differentiated histories with determinate capacities. At the universal level, unitary evolution and decoherence supply thin order and difference, while whether the wavefunction is itself a concrete Φ-realizer depends on the ontology adopted. **Branch-level recurrence of the roles; universal bearer left interpretation-dependent** (§9.7).

**Quantum field theory.** Interacting relativistic QFT removes any entitlement to assume a universal exact particle ontology. It doesn’t remove the need for an ontology—fields, algebras, excitations, dispositions, or another candidate—that makes determinate physical capacities available across ordered changes. **Classical particle realizer rejected; Φ-role retained without prejudging its bearer** (§9.7).

**The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics.** Shared structure explains broad applicability and makes dependence among the anticipations the natural hypothesis, undercutting a cumulative case that multiplies their improbabilities without defending their independence; the dependence is a hypothesis rather than a probabilistic result, and doesn’t by itself exclude a designer or a common origin. The thin roles don’t derive SU(3), Hilbert-space quantum theory, Lorentzian geometry, or the contingent laws those formalisms represent. **The external-fit picture reduced; the high-resolution likelihood comparison between theism and naturalism left open** (§9.8).

**Mathematical Universe Hypothesis.** Tegmark’s identity thesis and the Level IV plenitude are separate claims and receive separate replies. Pure mathematical structures need not instantiate temporal succession or causal persistence. A structure identified with an observer-containing physical reality must, however, contain as internal relations—not as a further realizing substrate, which the identity thesis denies—the order, differentiation, and bearing its observers require. That conclusion doesn’t show that every member of a Level-IV plenitude is concrete, inhabited, or triconditional. **Observer-containing identity inherits the realizer burden; plenitude’s object-side ontology remains open** (§9.9).

**Structural realism.** Bare relational or mathematical structure directly supplies thin difference; it doesn’t become temporal or persisting merely by description. An ontic structural realism about the actual changing world must explain order and concrete bearing as well. Radical and moderate OSR, and neighbouring semirealism, offer different bearers and may dispute both the necessity claim and the role-to-type bridges. **Substantial convergence at role-resolution; modal status and loaded realization remain live** (§9.10).

The positive finding across these three chapters isn’t that every objection secretly proves the full Necessity of Nature. It is more exact: no rival surveyed supplies a fully articulated alternative that both avoids the relevant structural roles and performs the determinate concrete work for which it was introduced. Some positions deny that there is anything to explain. Many relocate roles. Several remain compatible specifications. Others remain coherent at a price or leave explanatory questions carried forward.

The claim remains falsifiable conjunct by conjunct. A defeater to the full Structural Requirement need only specify a real change-realizer that performs its stated work while lacking one of the three Conditions; it need not lack all three. A proposed abstract ground poses a different test: it must explain how abstract structure reaches concrete actuality without silently importing the missing operation at the contact. Producing either case would defeat the corresponding claim. None of the positions considered here supplies the first. Several leave the second as a live dispute.

That contact dispute is live but constrained. A contact that does determinate work makes a difference to what is the case. The difference-making fork at §3.4 then applies at thin resolution: the result is this rather than that, the dependence has direction, and the difference is borne. The Realizer Fork (§8.4) states the resulting choice. An abstract or formal specification may leave the concrete realizer unsupplied; a concretely operative contact incurs the roles. This doesn’t identify every concrete realizer with the loaded types of the three Conditions by definition. It fixes the burden the independent role-to-type arguments must meet.

What counts as failure is now fixed rather than left to judgment. The Specification Test (§7.3.2) distinguishes act from object. Where an account deploys in its proposed object the very condition it denies, it has contradicted itself. Where only the act of representing uses that condition, the result is act-side: the representation hasn’t yet delivered the object-side conclusion. A stalled specification is therefore evidence of an unmet burden, not by itself evidence of impossibility.

The result is therefore differentiated rather than a single verdict. Denying that there is anything to explain doesn’t remove the conditions on representing it. Relocation doesn’t eliminate a role. Compatibility doesn’t amount to refutation. Explanatory cost isn’t incoherence. Abstract structure isn’t concrete realization merely by being specified. Thin roles don’t become loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types merely by being renamed. What no surveyed rival did was avoid the roles while performing the determinate concrete work it was introduced to do. That isn’t a comprehensive defeat and isn’t offered as one. It is the narrower result this chapter set out to test; the surviving content, type, realizer, and comparative-likelihood questions remain visible for the chapters that bear them.

# 10. Rival Ultimates


The positions tested so far contest the account of Time, Space, and Substance (Chapters 7–9). Next are proposed ultimates more fundamental than structure: candidates asked to occupy the ground the tradition reserved for God.

Each candidate is pressed on one question: can it be specified as prior to the structural conditions without merely relocating the roles those conditions play? Some grounding proposals fail for want of determinate content. Some preserve the structural roles under another vocabulary. Others remain open while carrying an explanatory burden the chapter cannot close by contradiction. An open burden is not a proof of possibility, and a formulation that meets it remains answerable here.

Classical-theistic arguments and doctrines receive the most space because their grounding accounts have been developed in the greatest detail. They are one family among others, not a category apart. The same structural moves recur in Islamic and Jewish philosophy and in non-classical accounts of the ultimate; each meets the position at the resolution and with the commitments its defenders supply.

## 10.1 Theistic Arguments for a Divine Ground
This first cluster gathers theistic arguments that reach for a divine ground, arranged by how they claim to know it.

Modal and transcendental arguments come first (§10.1.1–§10.1.3). Foundation, causal, and metaphysical explanations follow (§10.1.4–§10.1.8), then arguments from empirical teleology (§10.1.9–§10.1.11).

The next group argues from morality, prudence, non-skepticism, and moral knowledge (§10.1.12–§10.1.14), followed by beauty (§10.1.15). The cluster closes with apparent encounter rather than a feature of the world: religious experience and miracles (§10.1.16).

Each proposes God as a ground prior to and more fundamental than time, space, and substance.

Two of those sections are read together, since they share what needs explaining—a dependent order and whatever holds it in being—and divide the labor rather than repeating it. The inference from dependence to a first or necessary term, with the concurrent rather than prior dependence that would let an atemporal source ground a temporal order without entering its time, is taken up at §10.1.5; the claim that the order requires holding in being moment by moment rather than merely starting, at §10.1.6. The neighboring sections are grouped with them by epistemic route rather than by subject: The Necessary Foundation Argument (§10.1.4) argues from the need for a terminus rather than from causation, and §10.1.7 and §10.1.8 aren’t causal arguments at all.

Each is assessed by a single question: can the argument be completed without presupposing the structural roles from which its proposed ground is said to be independent? The recurring finding is often relocation rather than semantic collapse. A ground that acts, knows, creates, sustains, or explains must bear directed dependence, relational differentiation, and real grounding content. Those roles articulate Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality at the resolution appropriate to the proposal; concrete operation realizes them concretely. No Unconditioned Essence closes essence-priority as a route to an independent source behind the field while preserving it as a direction of derivation. The argument therefore asks whether a proposed articulation earns its explanatory and personal predicates, not whether it occupies an exterior left open by the structural argument.

### 10.1.1 The Modal Ontological Argument
Some existence claims ask for almost nothing. A mountain of gold is possible not because anything exotic underwrites it, but because gold is possible, a mountain-sized quantity of matter is possible, and nothing about combining the two calls for more than ordinary mining piled high enough. The concession costs nothing beyond what’s already been granted about gold and mountains separately. Plantinga’s wager is that a [maximally great being](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) belongs to that same modest family: not something you have to prove exists, only something you have to admit isn’t incoherent. Anselm’s original version couldn’t collect on a concession that small, because Kant’s objection—existence isn’t a predicate a definition can confer—cuts a purely definitional argument off at the root. The modal route was built to survive exactly that complaint: trade the definition for a possibility claim, let S5 do the rest, and what follows is just valid logic doing what valid logic does. It is, on its face, a remarkably economical bet. Whether the bet is actually that cheap, built the way the golden mountain is built, out of parts already known to be possible, is the question the rest has to answer.

Plantinga’s modal ontological argument (Plantinga 1974) runs as follows. An entity possesses *maximal excellence* just in case it is omniscient, omnipotent, and morally perfect in a given world; an entity possesses *maximal greatness* just in case it possesses maximal excellence in every possible world, so that maximal greatness already entails necessary existence.

**[Argument]**

1. *Possibility premise.* Possibly, a maximally great being is instantiated: ◇□MGB.

2. *S5.* Possible necessity yields necessity: from ◇□MGB, □MGB.

3. *Conclusion.* A maximally great being exists in every possible world, the actual one included: □MGB, and so MGB.

The crux is the possibility premise: is maximal greatness coherent?

The argument has antecedents and successors that sharpen what is claimed. Hartshorne (Hartshorne 1962) develops an earlier modal version of the argument from Anselmian materials, and Adams (Adams 1971) defends the broader thesis that the modal-ontological strategy survives the Kantian objection that existence isn’t a predicate. Plantinga’s own assessment in *The Nature of Necessity* is more modest than the argument’s later reception: the argument aims to show that belief in a maximally great being can be rational, not that disbelief is irrational. The objection developed later preserves that dialectical scale. S5 doesn’t support the possibility premise, and classical enrichments of the candidate incur additional coherence burdens; the argument doesn’t thereby show that Plantinga’s thinner maximal-greatness predicate is semantically empty.

The argument’s modal core relies on the same global-capacity S5 framework the present book operates within. The present account doesn’t contest the transfer rule; it contests whether the classical possibility premise supplies a determinate candidate among the configurations R can admit.

*Try to conceive of an atemporal, aspatial, immaterial being.* The conception fails not because the being is alien or unlike anything in experience but because the description subtracts from its object the conditions of statehood itself: temporal location, spatial-relational differentiation, substantial bearing. The collapse of the conceiving act (succession of imaginative acts, distinction of the imagined being from background, sustained representational substance, each withdrawn by the very content entertained) is the symptom of that subtraction rather than what drives the argument; the load is carried by what the description withdraws from its object, made exact in what follows. The general result has already been pressed at §3.3: structural absence can’t be coherently conceived, because every attempt to represent it instantiates what it denies, and the asymmetry between conceivability-to-possibility and inconceivability-to-impossibility favors the downward direction when the inconceivability is of this structural kind. The maximally great being, enriched with the full set of classical negations, is the case where structural absence would be dressed in classical-theistic predicates. What follows works the same point through Plantinga’s machinery directly.

Plantinga’s possibility premise concerns maximal excellence—omniscience, omnipotence, and moral perfection—instantiated in every world. Atemporality, aspatiality, immateriality, and strong divine simplicity are additional classical-theist doctrines, not premises of the modal ontological argument itself. Coherent possibility, in the relevant sense, requires that the conjunction’s content be specifiable in a way that doesn’t contradict itself or contradict the conditions on which content is possible. If a defender adds negative classical attributes in their most expansive form, the book can press whether a personal being so characterized retains determinate cognitive, volitional, and grounding roles. That pressure doesn’t show that Plantinga’s thinner maximal-greatness predicate is contentless; it challenges one theological development of the candidate.

A defender may attempt the Plantingian reply: vehicle and content come apart. One can conceive a colorless object using a colored display; conceiving an atemporal being doesn’t require the thought itself to be atemporal. The reply works for ordinary properties and also blocks a categorical inference from description to concrete instantiation. What is established is narrower (Chapter 2): Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7) places every concrete individual within temporally ordered, relationally differentiated, substantially borne structure. It doesn’t make an abstract proposition or an atemporal grounding relation concrete by definition. The question is therefore which role the maximally great being is asked to occupy.

If the maximally great being is a concrete person, Necessary Occupancy applies to the subject, and its knowing, willing, creating, and acting incur the Concrete-Entity Test at the operation. If it is instead an atemporal abstract ground, the occupancy inference doesn’t apply; the proposal owes determinate content and an account of how its grounding relation reaches concrete actuality. The colorless-object analogy therefore doesn’t settle the dispute in either direction. It protects the difference between the thought’s vehicle and its object, while leaving the candidate’s mode of being and attributed work to be specified.

The claim is scoped to concrete existents. Abstract objects (numbers, propositions, the possible worlds Plantinga’s actualism treats as abstract) bear properties without instantiating any of the three Conditions, and nothing here denies it; the status of abstracta is treated at §8.1.5. But the maximally great being is proposed as a person who knows, wills, creates, and acts. If those predicates name concrete operations, they incur succession, distinction, and a bearer under the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4). If they name one atemporal explanatory act, that reply blocks a direct inference to succession in God but inherits the semantic and abstract-to-concrete contact burdens developed at §10.2.1 and §11.1. Calling the being *sui generis* chooses neither answer by itself.

If the enriched description withdraws every determinate cognitive, volitional, relational, and bearing role, it risks failing to specify the personal candidate it invokes. That is a coherence and specification burden. It doesn’t follow merely from the negative attributes that Plantinga’s thinner maximally-great predicate lacks truth-evaluable modal content.

The diagnosis shouldn’t be placed automatically before truth-value. Standard semantic treatments can assign falsehood, presupposition failure, or undefinedness to defective descriptions. Here the safer verdict is dialectical: the defender owes a coherent account of how the added classical attributes combine with personal agency; semantic emptiness doesn’t follow merely from their negations. Its earned conclusion is that a defender who enriches maximal greatness with atemporality, aspatiality, immateriality, strong simplicity, and personal agency owes a coherent account of their joint realization before ◇□MGB is warranted.

**[Proposition]**

**Possibility-Premise Burden** · *Proposition*

S5 validates the transfer from ◇□MGB to □MGB but supplies no warrant for ◇□MGB. Plantinga’s thinner maximal-greatness predicate is not shown semantically empty here. If it is enriched with the full classical conception—atemporality, aspatiality, immateriality, strong simplicity, and personal cognitive, volitional, and causal powers—the defender owes a coherent joint-realization account. Until that burden is discharged, the modal-ontological inference has no established possibility premise. The stronger specification trilemma is developed in Chapter 11, without treating this local result as its proof in advance.

**Dependency routes:** modal transfer—the Modal Transfer Analysis; enriched concrete-person branch—Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7) and the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)

*The criterion, turned around.* Anselm’s argument runs on a comparative: God is that than which no greater can be conceived, and the conception is then ranked against a rival that exists only in the understanding. The ranking is what does the work, and a ranking needs a scale. What the preceding analysis shows is that the scale has a floor, and that the floor isn’t where the argument assumes it is. Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality aren’t one more item to be ranked. They are what any item must already have to be a candidate for ranking at all, since a description that withdraws them leaves nothing determinate to compare.

**[Argument]**

**The Floor, Not the Ceiling** · *The Ontological Inversion*

1. **Anselm’s criterion ranks conceptions, so it presupposes that there’s something determinate to rank.** *That than which no greater can be conceived* is comparative, and a comparison requires candidates with content.

2. **A description that withdraws time, place, and bearing leaves its object with no determinate content.** The subtraction is on the object side, not merely a failure of the conceiving act (§10.1.1 above; §3.3.4).

3. **So the strictly withdrawn subject isn’t the top of Anselm’s scale but its floor**—not that than which no greater can be conceived, but that than which no *lesser* can be, since nothing determinate remains to be conceived at all (§2.7.2).

4. **∴ Anselm’s own criterion, applied consistently, selects the Conditions rather than a subject described by their withdrawal.** What cannot be surpassed is what any candidate must already instantiate to be a candidate.

*Scope.* The inversion bears on the strictly withdrawn description, in the same range as §11.10’s scope note: an account that supplies determinate content—analogically, or on an essence-prior proposal—isn’t touched here and carries its burdens forward rather than being refuted at this step. Nor does the argument show that Nature is great in any evaluative sense; the inversion set out at §4 concerns metaphysical ultimacy only.

The reversal borrows nothing from Chapter 11. Its two load-bearing steps are the Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2) and the object-side reading established above, both upstream of this chapter, so the result stands here on its own and converges with the later attribute-by-attribute treatment rather than depending on it. What it adds to the assessment is narrow and worth stating exactly: not a further objection to the possibility premise, but the observation that the argument’s ranking criterion, taken at its word, doesn’t point where the tradition has taken it to point.

The standard objection remains central: S5 transfers the possibility premise but doesn’t support it. The structural critique adds that some classical enrichments create tensions with personal agency and therefore increase the burden of defending that premise.

The present objection should also be distinguished from the symmetry objection developed by Oppy (Oppy 1995) and Sobel (Sobel 2004). The symmetry objection observes that the same modal apparatus generates a parody: possibly there is no maximally great being, therefore necessarily there is no maximally great being. The objection’s force is that the argument and its parody share a form, so neither tells us which possibility actually obtains. The present objection doesn’t rely on parody. It holds that the starting premise remains unsupported and that an enriched classical candidate bears additional coherence burdens. The symmetry objection and the structural objection therefore converge on the same problem of insufficient support by different routes; neither requires the claim that Plantinga’s thinner premise is meaningless.

The diagnosis isn’t special pleading against Plantinga; it catches the objection tradition built to embarrass him too. Gaunilo’s reply to Anselm argued that if the ontological form is valid, it equally proves a perfect lost island (Gaunilo of Marmoutiers c. 1078), and later informal descendants swap in other superlatives—a greatest possible mountain, a greatest possible pizza—offered as parity refutations rather than serious commitments. Each trades on the same move the possibility premise itself makes: define a superlative predicate, then assert that something answering to it is possible. That move is no more reliable run backward, to embarrass the argument, than it is run forward, to establish it, so a stipulated maximally great island earns no more entry into a possible world than a stipulated maximally great being does. This same parody tradition is taken up at length at §7.3.4, aimed there at the book’s own necessity argument rather than at Plantinga’s.

The S5 inference and modal framework remain intact. What is missing is independent warrant for the input. A valid transfer rule yields no sound conclusion until ◇□MGB is defended, and adding the full set of classical attributes makes that defense more demanding.

A second front is available, independent of the possibility-premise rebuttal just completed. Can the same transfer rule certify a person? Van Hamme (van Hamme 2026) argues that modal logic alone doesn’t supply a substantive account of a necessary *personal* God. This should be stated precisely. S5 can transfer necessity to any determinate proposition P for which Capacity(R,P); it doesn’t restrict its scope to structural vocabulary. What it can’t do by itself is establish that personhood-attributing predicates—omniscience, omnipotence, moral perfection—form a coherent necessary set or that they apply to the candidate described. The modal-ontological argument therefore needs more than the transfer rule: it needs an independently supported, determinate possibility premise for a personal being.

This front constrains the present account too, harmlessly: the book doesn’t derive the personal or the axiological from S5 alone. Claims about value, agency, and greatness must be grounded in the structural and dialectical arguments specific to them (Chapter 11). The two rebuttals therefore do different work. The first challenges the classical candidate’s content; the second blocks the inference from a bare modal rule to the full personal-theistic conclusion. Together they show that S5 neither repairs an empty specification nor substitutes for an argument about the attributes.

*The formal derivation.* A more rigorous version of the modal ontological argument doesn’t assert the possibility premise but derives it. Gödel’s ontological proof lays down that every property is positive or its negation is, that positive properties are closed under entailment, and that necessary existence is positive. From these it proves as a theorem that a God-like being—one bearing every positive property essentially—is possibly instantiated; S5 then delivers necessary existence. The proof runs on his axiomatization of *positive properties*, sharpened in Anderson’s emendation against modal collapse and analyzed in Hájek’s formal treatment. Deriving the possibility premise looks to answer the present objection at its root: the premise is no longer left unsupported but established by proof.

It doesn’t answer it. Gödelian derivations shift the burden to the positive-property axioms, their consistency, and the definition of God-likeness. Those axioms don’t by themselves encode atemporality, aspatiality, or immateriality, so the earlier structural critique can’t simply be transferred to them. Formal derivability manufactures no more modal content than the axioms supply: the proof is valid, and whether its input carries the intended theological content is exactly what the axioms leave unsecured.

The personhood front closes the same gap from the other side: the positive properties are meant to include personhood-attributing predicates—omniscience, omnipotence, moral perfection—though the axioms don’t themselves say which properties are positive, so even granting the axioms their domain the apparatus doesn’t independently warrant those axioms or show that the formal predicates carry the intended theological interpretation. Modal logic can entail a personal conclusion when personhood is encoded in the axioms; what it can’t do is certify that encoding. The Gödelian formalization raises the rigor of the derivation; it leaves untouched the status of what is derived.

A respondent may revise maximal greatness to drop the classical attributes, making the maximally great being temporal, extended, and embedded. The revision changes the subject in two respects. First, the present argument doesn’t dispute such a being’s possibility, only the inference from possibility to necessity by S5: the inference depends on the being’s maximal greatness across worlds, which the revision has redefined and which now requires independent argument. Second, the revised being instantiates the three Conditions rather than grounding them, and a being so embedded depends on structure for its existence. The aseity—independence from anything else for existence, treated fully at §11.3—the modal-ontological tradition was specifically trying to secure (necessary existence as a feature of the being rather than of its conditions) is the property §11.1 and §11.10 (Horn 3) establish the [embedded deity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) can’t have. The revised argument may go through to a different conclusion, but the conclusion is no longer the conclusion the classical modal-ontological project was constructed to deliver.

**[Proposition]**

**No Rescue by Changing the Modal Logic** · *Proposition*

A defender may keep the classical candidate and reject S5, so that possible necessary existence no longer transfers to necessary existence. That is a coherent position and is not self-undermining merely for being stated in modal vocabulary—it is a rival account of what fixes real possibility. It is self-defeating for this argument, because the transfer it rejects is the inference that makes the modal ontological argument go. So the fork closes on both sides: grant S5 and the argument still needs a determinate classical candidate the possibility premise has not supplied; reject S5 and the transfer is unavailable, leaving a different argument that owes its own modal semantics and its own defense of the same premise.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10)

*Taking stock.* S5 validates the transfer from possible necessary existence to necessary existence, but it doesn’t establish the possibility premise or the coherence of the full theological conception. Structural tensions arise when strong negative classical attributes are added to a personal agent; those tensions qualify the candidate without making Plantinga’s thinner premise semantically empty. The personhood front closes the same line from the inference side: modal logic doesn’t warrant the personhood axioms or their intended interpretation even where the structural conditions are present. Revising the maximally great being to drop the classical attributes preserves the inference at the cost of what the classical project was specifically trying to secure: aseity as a feature of the being rather than of its conditions.

*A parallel epistemological line.* Pascal’s wager is taken up at §10.1.14, where the temptation to run the same possibility-of-classical-necessary-being premise through a probability claim is closed off and the wager is returned to its own decision-theoretic ground.

*Plantinga’s reserve: de re/de dicto and EAAN.* Plantinga would press two further questions on the present account. First, the modal-scope question: □(T∧S∧Φ) can be read de dicto (necessarily, whatever constitutes the modal constraint on change instantiates the three roles) or de re (these specific structural occupants necessarily exist). The two readings differ on whether contingent states of Nature inherit necessity from Nature’s necessity. The de dicto reading is the intended scope: what is necessary is that the roles be instantiated, not that any specific instantiator is necessary. Where alternative states are independently warranted, their contingency remains within a necessary structural framework (§2.9.4); the scope-limit argument at §2.5 (‘the necessity attaches to F, not to every item within the field F makes possible’) is the relevant disambiguation; and the co-instantiation claim at Mutual Containment (§2.6.5) secures the de dicto reading without collapsing into de re necessity for contingent occupants. Second, Plantinga’s Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism (*Warrant and Proper Function* 1993): the present argument is delivered by cognitive faculties selected for survival; whether such faculties can reliably track necessary structural conditions is the EAAN question. The structural account’s response (that any functioning cognitive faculty operates within T, S, and Φ by the transcendental conditions on operation itself) lives in Chapter 5.

### 10.1.2 The Modal-Grounding Argument
A rulebook doesn’t write itself. Ask why chess lets a knight move in an L and not any other shape. The answer traces back to a decision someone made: the rule didn’t have to come out that way, and something fixed it so that it did. Modality can look the same way from the inside. The boundary between what’s possible and what isn’t seems too orderly for an accident, too rule-governed to have arrived at random. That’s the shape a decision leaves behind. A decision-maker isn’t the only place to look, but it’s an intuitive one.

Arguments of this kind reason toward a divine being. The modal-grounding argument reasons toward God as the explanation of modality itself: of why there are necessary truths and real possibilities at all, rather than nothing modal to speak of. It leans on the same modal facts the present account is built from and therefore meets the book’s own grounding of necessity directly; it warrants engagement on its own terms rather than as a restatement of the ontological argument handled at §10.1.1.

The argument’s most developed form is Leftow’s. Historically, theist modal theories based all necessary truth on God’s nature; Leftow (*God and Necessity* 2012) argues instead that necessary truths about possible creatures and kinds are fixed by God’s unconstrained imagination and choice, with the broadly logical modalities reduced to causal modalities seated in God and events in God’s mind. The distinctive move is a *global economy* argument: theists are committed to some theist modal theory, and the explanatory merits of a good one (its economy against the heavy ontologies of Lewisian modal realism and abstracta-laden ersatzism) are offered as an argument for God’s existence. Adjacent constructions press the same thought from other directions: Plantinga’s suggestion that propositions are best construed as divine thoughts, since there are far more of them than finite minds could entertain (“Two Dozen (or So) Theistic Arguments” (Plantinga 2007)); and the theistic activism, or absolute creationism, of Morris and Menzel (Morris and Menzel 1986), on which abstracta (modal truths among them) depend for their existence on God’s intellectual activity. The shared argumentative form is an inference to the best ground:

1. *Grounding demand.* Modal and necessary facts are real and can’t be brute: they require a ground.

2. *Mind as ground.* A mind is the best or only adequate ground for them.

3. *Conclusion.* A divine mind exists as the ground of modality.

Whether that closes the gap turns on a comparative judgment: is a mind really the best available ground for modality, or only the most familiar one?

Grant the demand in full. The argument is right that modal facts aren’t free-floating: that “possibly P” and “necessarily P” cannot be ungrounded surds, true with nothing about Reality to fix them. Grant, too, that a plurality of concrete non-actual worlds (Lewis), or a Platonic heaven of modal abstracta, is a heavy and contestable ontology. The demand for a ground for modality is legitimate, and the dissatisfaction with possible-worlds Platonism is one the present account shares rather than resists.

Here, structure does the fixing instead of a decision-maker. What the argument adds to that demand is a mind to satisfy it, and Reality’s modal constitution satisfies it first. Reality’s standing capacity grounds modal status at §2.1: Modal Stability derives S5 from Capacity(R,P), while the Bottleneck distinguishes that global modality from local reachability. Transition Closure is a narrower auxiliary result concerning the onset of local transition-capacity from a state lacking it, not a third derivation of proposition-wise S5. Necessary Possibility makes the production point bilateral: if p is possible, it is necessarily possible; if p is impossible, it is necessarily impossible. An intellect may represent, discover, locally realize, or actualize a possibility, but no intellectual act first confers or later withdraws p’s real modal standing. Modal status is fixed by the global modal structure the account spells out. The explanatory work Leftow credits to God’s imagination and choice, and Morris and Menzel to God’s intellectual activity, is already discharged one level down, by the conditions any possibility presupposes. This bears directly on the global-economy form: the theist theory is advanced as the *best* ground precisely because its rivals are taken to be Lewisian realism and abstracta-Platonism. A structural account is a third option that grounds the modal structure without a mind and without a plurality of worlds, so at that level the inference from “best available ground” to God is blocked at the comparative step it depends on.

Modal Closure (§2.9.4) states the corresponding economy result: the necessary structural Conditions admit no unnecessary alternative standing apart from them. Its contribution here is exact and limited. A divine mind that merely duplicates the already discharged role of fixing modal structure is unnecessary as a second ground. Modal Closure alone doesn’t identify every essence-bearing candidate with an aspect of Nature or settle Leftow’s further question about the specific de re contents of creaturely possibility. The independent bridge is No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1): essence may explain modal truths about a determinate configuration, but it supplies neither a second modal domain nor an independently constituted ingredient within the first.

This front must be drawn at its real scope. What §2.1 grounds is the modal *structure*: modal status is determinate and determined by structure. That result is existence-silent about which contingent configurations are actual; it doesn’t enumerate a roster of creaturely kinds. Leftow’s theory reaches further, aiming to explain why *these* creaturely kinds are possible. But a possible kind isn’t content waiting for a mind to admit it. By Way–Possibility Convertibility it is a determinate way to be; by Reality–Nature Identity that way belongs to Nature’s one modal field; and by No Unconditioned Essence its essence is the configuration specified rather than a second item that supplies the configuration’s possibility. A divine intellect may represent or comprehend the content. It doesn’t make the kind possible.

The argument’s deeper trouble is independent of how much of modality the structural account claims to ground: the proposed ground can’t do the grounding without carrying a structural articulation of its own. That isn’t a special demand made of theism. It is the Grounding Conditional earned at §3.1.5: any grounding relation, at any level of any possible ontological stack, requires asymmetric priority, real differentiation of its terms, and a real fact or realizer in which the relation obtains—the three Conditions at role-resolution, by what a grounding relation is rather than by anything owed to the present account. A divine mind proposed as the ground of modality incurs those roles the instant the grounding relation is granted, on the same footing as the demon, the simulation substrate, and every other candidate ground closed there. A classical divine intellect is typically described as atemporal, non-spatial, and immaterial. Those thin roles need not be redescribed as metric extension, temporal succession, or material composition at the same resolution. But they aren’t exempt from the Conditions: they are the abstract or atemporal articulation of them. Actual finite imagining realizes the Conditions concretely; the classical theorist proposes one timeless intellectual act. Even on that proposal, determinate contents and asymmetric dependence remain within Reality–Nature, and no independently constituted mind stands behind them as an additional ground.

Creation sharpens the burden into a modal fork. If the divine mind has no capacity for anything genuinely distinct from itself, then no creature is really possible and the proposed ground can’t supply creaturely possibility. If it has that capacity, Reality already admits a determinate this and that: ground and possible creature as genuinely distinct relata. Bare numerical difference wouldn’t be enough, since the theory needs a real grounding or creation relation rather than two unrelated labels. The admitted capacity is therefore the capacity for relationally articulated otherness, Spatiality at the role-resolution the Structural Requirement fixes. This doesn’t assign God a metric location or material parts. It establishes the narrower priority result the modal-grounding argument needs: an allegedly aspatial mind can’t ground the possibility of distinct creation from a condition in which the distinction-enabling structure is absent, because its capacity to ground that possibility already uses the structure.

**[Proposition]**

**The Creation Fork** · *Proposition*

A divine mind with no capacity for anything genuinely distinct from itself cannot ground creaturely possibility, since no creature is really possible for it. A divine mind with that capacity already admits a determinate this and that, ground and creature as genuinely distinct relata, and bare numerical difference will not do, since the theory needs a real grounding relation rather than two unrelated labels. The admitted capacity is therefore relationally articulated otherness, Spatiality at role-resolution, prior to any act of creating.

**Depends on:** The Grounding Conditional (§3.1.5)

A defender might relax the ground to an embedded, temporal mind, one that realizes the Conditions concretely. Then it is no longer the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) whose aseity the theory was built to secure. Nor is it an extra ingredient inserted into Nature: like every concrete occupant, it is the three Conditions in a determinate operation. Such a mind may explain or select an internal configuration, but it can’t be modality’s independently constituted ground. The revision keeps an internal grounder by giving up exterior ultimacy.

The argument points at something real: modality isn’t explanatorily idle. Modal structure is located in the standing capacity of the one Reality and the structural Conditions later derived for every configuration R can admit. Ask what makes it possible for a mind to make anything possible at all, and the regress the argument was built to stop reappears one level up: the mind’s own capacity to confer modal status is itself a modal fact, one that would need grounding by the argument’s own lights. Modal Exclusivity establishes that no candidate’s modal status confers the field; No Unconditioned Essence closes the proposed relocation into an essence structurally prior to it. A mind can represent, discover, or reason from modal content. It can’t be an additional item that confers R’s capacity from outside or from a surplus position within.

*Taking stock.* The modal-grounding argument is right to refuse free-floating modality, and the structural account supplies the ground for the standing modal capacity of R. That blocks the global-economy inference to God at the comparative step. A classical divine mind stripped of every structural role supplies no intelligible grounding relation. An essence-prior mind may retain Finean explanatory priority—modal truths following from what the mind is—but what the mind is must itself be a determinate content of Reality–Nature. It can’t confer the field’s possibility from an independent exterior or interior surplus. What the argument sees—the need for modal explanation—Reality’s modal constitution supplies; what it adds—a specifically divine mind—remains an unearned personal description of that structure, not a second ground of it.

### 10.1.3 The Transcendental Argument for God
Call something a law and a lawgiver seems to follow: someone had to write the rule, or nothing would hold it in place. But the law of falling bodies has no author standing over the world with a rulebook. Drop two objects of different mass and they accelerate at the same rate, not because a legislator decreed it and stands ready to punish violations, but because that is simply what falling is. One word, “law,” names two different things: a rule someone lays down, and a regularity someone merely describes.

The transcendental argument for God presses logical necessity. The Laws of Identity, Non-Contradiction, and Excluded Middle are absolute, universal, and not plausibly derivable from any contingent feature of the world; something must secure their status, and a purely structural account can seem too thin to carry that weight, so on this argument the securing ground is God. The claim can widen past logic to intelligibility as such—the very possibility of making sense of anything—but logic is where it bites, and that is where the engagement begins. Pressed for the relation that ground bears to logic, the argument divides into three genuine positions: classical presuppositionalism (Van Til 1955; Bahnsen 1998)—the transcendental argument in the strict sense—places logic outside God, as externally grounded by a necessarily rational being; theistic conceptualism (Morris and Menzel 1986; Plantinga 1980; Leftow 2012; Welty 2014) places logic inside God, as a structural feature of divine thinking; Cartesian voluntarism places logic downstream of God, as the free output of divine will. The three moves cover the principal theistic grounding strategies considered here (logic external to and grounded by God, logic internal to divine nature or thought, and logic dependent on divine will) and none secures a distinct theistic ground without unpaid burdens: voluntarism appears to presuppose the alternatives it would decree, presuppositionalism owes a non-circular account of its Author, and conceptualism converges on the structural conditions under a theistic description.

Regimented, the argument runs:

1. The laws of logic (Identity, Non-Contradiction, Excluded Middle) are absolute, universal, and necessary.

2. Their necessity can’t derive from any contingent feature of the world; something must secure it.

3. Only a necessarily rational being can secure necessary rationality.

4. Therefore a necessarily rational being, God, grounds logic.

The presuppositionalist move is, in its contemporary form, the most philosophically developed of the three. Van Til’s *The Defense of the Faith* (Van Til 1955) and Bahnsen’s *Van Til’s Apologetic* (Bahnsen 1998) stand at the head of the presuppositionalist tradition, which argues that any non-theistic worldview can’t account for the preconditions of intelligibility (logic, induction, morality) without borrowing from the theism it purports to reject.

Morris and Menzel (Morris and Menzel 1986) reframe the tradition with the view that has dominated the last three decades: theistic activism, on which God’s necessary thinking constitutes the realm of abstract objects, including logical truths. Plantinga’s *Does God Have a Nature?* (Plantinga 1980) had earlier pressed the companion question whether God stands subject to the logical laws or is identical to them, and settled on a version of the conceptualist reply. Leftow’s *God and Necessity* (Leftow 2012) is a systematic contemporary treatment: defending a modal conceptualism on which the modal facts are grounded in God’s nature. Welty (Welty 2014) develops a theistic conceptualist position that locates logic inside God rather than outside.

Craig’s *God Over All: Divine Aseity and the Challenge of Platonism* (Craig 2016) presses the same aseity motive to a different destination: surveying divine conceptualism among the realist options and finding it wanting, Craig concludes that abstract objects (propositions, properties, logical truths) aren’t entities of any kind, so the apparent Platonic realm is dissolved by anti-realist deflation rather than relocated into divine intellection. The voluntarist position runs through Descartes’s letters to Mersenne (Descartes 1630) and has few contemporary defenders, though Frankfurt (Frankfurt 1977) and Curley (Curley 1984) give it sympathetic reconstructions.

The present account is closer to Sher’s realism than to any of the theistic positions, but the reason is specific: logic describes formal constraints on determinate contents and relations. Where a manifold is offered as a concrete change-realizing reality, the structural Conditions identify the roles it must realize. Logic alone doesn’t derive the full types of the three Conditions from any arbitrary manifold of relata.

The challenge bears directly on §2.6 and §2.7. The three Conditions are identified at §2.6 as the Triconditional Identity. Questions of the form “why is there something rather than nothing?” are dissolved at §2.7, which argues that ∅ (the Null State: the configuration in which none of the three Conditions is instantiated) is incoherent on multiple independent grounds. The divine-logic objection presses both: against the structural account, that logical necessity is a distinct domain requiring its own ground; against §2.7, that the positive necessity of the laws ruling out ∅ requires a ground of its own, and the ground must be a necessary rational being. The reply grants the necessity and universality of the core logical laws. The three Conditions can supply concrete instances of determinacy, difference, and ordered dependence, but logic is more general than any particular physical manifold. The structural account therefore offers an interpretation of logic’s application; it doesn’t derive all logical truth from the loaded types alone.

The three moves share a prior assumption worth naming: each treats the laws of logic as prescriptions, edicts that hold because something with the authority to lay them down has done so, which is why a legislator seems required to account for their force. But the “law” in “laws of logic” is descriptive, not prescriptive. It issues no command that a manifold of distinct relata could obey or flout; it states what being such a manifold already comes to. A description needs something to describe, not someone to enact it, and once the laws are read this way the role of lawgiver the three moves compete to fill stands empty before any of them is assessed.

**[Proposition]**

**Descriptive, Not Prescriptive** · *Proposition*

All three theistic strategies treat the laws of logic as edicts, holding because something with authority laid them down, which is why a legislator seems required. But “law” in “laws of logic” is descriptive: it states what being a manifold of distinct relata already comes to, and issues no command a manifold could obey or flout. A description needs something to describe, not someone to enact it. The role of lawgiver stands empty before any candidate is assessed.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

The distinction can be put as one of prepositions. What holds necessarily of God, that a given act is necessarily open to him or that his nature is what it is, is a law *of* God, not a law *from* God: it describes him rather than issuing from his authority, and he couldn’t have prescribed it to himself, since to prescribe anything already presupposes the modal space in which the prescription would hold. A lawgiver who must stand under the laws to legislate them hasn’t grounded them but exemplified them, and the appeal to divine authority regresses at the very point it was meant to terminate.

The same three options are forced by any necessary truth of the sort, and it is worth seeing the range before pricing them, because the trilemma is usually run on logic alone and looks narrower than it is. Arithmetic is the familiar case: two things and two things make four things, and no account of creation makes room for a world where the count comes out otherwise. Geometry is the same. There is no creatable world in which a triangle’s interior angles fail to sum to two right angles, or in which the ratio a circle’s circumference bears to its diameter is some other ratio. These aren’t restrictions imposed on a maker from outside. Counting requires items held distinct, persisting through the count, and borne; a triangle requires three distinguishable positions with determinate separation between them, and the angle sum falls out of what having three such positions in a plane is. The truths are locked from the inside, by what it takes for there to be anything to count or to lay out. That is why the trilemma below can’t be escaped by narrowing its subject: whatever is said about the ground of logic must be said about these too, and the conceptualist and voluntarist horns get harder rather than easier as the subject widens (§2.6, the Wigner Dissolution; applicability is engaged at §9.8).

*First.* The classical presuppositionalist treats logic as externally grounded. On Van Til and Bahnsen’s view, logical truths require something outside themselves to secure their necessity, and the only candidate is a necessarily rational, necessarily existent being whose nature underwrites the laws without being reducible to them. Every argument presupposes logical laws; every use of logical laws presupposes their ground; every ground of necessary rationality must itself be necessary; and the only necessary thing that can ground necessary rationality is a necessarily rational being. Call this the *authoring relation*: God authors logic by being the kind of being whose existence makes logical truth possible.

The authoring relation generates a modal dilemma at its own level. If the necessarily rational being (call it the Author) is the source of logical possibility, then the counterfactual “were the Author not to exist, logic would not obtain” must be true. But ‘were the Author not to exist’ is itself a logical possibility, a consistent hypothesis about what could fail to obtain, and its being a logical possibility presupposes the laws of logic holding. If the Author’s non-existence is logically possible, logic can’t depend straightforwardly on the Author’s actual existence. If it is logically impossible, the theist may say that logical necessity is grounded in the Author’s essence rather than externally governing it. That answer faces a circularity or explanatory-priority burden, but it isn’t formally inconsistent merely because logical predicates apply to their proposed ground.

The regress completes the point. If logic is grounded in the Author’s existence, what grounds the fact that the Author’s existence has the relevant logical character? The presuppositionalist’s candidate is the Author’s necessary nature, but “necessary nature” is itself a logical characterization, and the grounding runs in a circle. Bahnsen’s transcendental formulation (“the impossibility of the contrary”) exhibits the point: “the impossibility of the contrary” is a logical modal claim, and the impossibility it invokes is the very kind of necessity the argument is trying to ground. The presuppositionalist account, pressed for substance, supplies a name for what underwrites logical necessity rather than an independent grounding of it.

Van Til’s distinctively Christian refinement is meant to answer the underdetermination charge: the Trinity’s one essence and three persons are said to resolve the one-and-many problem, which concerns how universals and particulars can both be real. This deserves to be distinguished from merely naming a generic rational ground. But the bridge remains unargued. A doctrine about one divine essence and three divine persons doesn’t, without further premises, explain how one universal applies across many particulars or why logical laws govern every domain; and the Trinitarian specification is itself part of the conclusion the argument was supposed to establish. It doesn’t select Christianity over Platonist, nominalist, or other metaphysical accounts merely by being stipulated as the solution (Van Til 1955; Bahnsen 1998).

*Second.* The contemporary conceptualist relocates logic inside the divine mind. On the conceptualist view (Morris and Menzel 1986; Plantinga 1980; Leftow 2012; Welty 2014), logical truths aren’t external to God and grounded by God; they are constitutive of God’s thinking. The Law of Identity isn’t a law God obeys and not a law God creates; it is a structural feature of how God necessarily thinks. Logic is God thinking. The view is a substantial improvement on the classical presuppositionalist version: it eliminates the authoring relation (which the previous move showed to carry an unpaid circularity burden) and replaces it with an identity-style grounding that avoids the regress. Leftow’s *God and Necessity* develops this position carefully, and it is genuinely resilient to the reply given to move one.

The concession is real. The reply is that the position succeeds only by locating structured content inside the divine mind. The point shouldn’t be put as though divine thinking must be discursive in the creaturely sense. The conceptualist explicitly denies that God reasons through logical truths one after another. The pressure is weaker and harder to evade: if logical truths are grounded in divine intellection, then divine intellection must contain determinate logical content. The Law of Identity requires determinacy of content; the Law of Non-Contradiction requires the distinction between a content and its negation; the Law of Excluded Middle requires an exhaustive contrast between a proposition and its negation. T doesn’t enter because Excluded Middle is itself a temporal sequence. It enters through the asymmetric grounding and inferential roles the conceptualist needs: ground to grounded, premise to consequence, alternative-space to exhausted alternatives. These aren’t temporal episodes in a divine psychology. They are structural features of the content the conceptualist places in God.

Leftow (Leftow 2012, chs. 10–12) is explicit that the divine modal activity isn’t temporally successive and doesn’t involve distinguishable mental states. But if the content of that activity is genuinely modal (if it fixes the space of possibilities and the laws governing it) it must still be determinate, internally structured, and capable of grounding asymmetric entailment relations. That is structure. Plantinga (Plantinga 1980) entertains exactly this worry under the heading “the bootstrapping objection”: if God’s nature grounds logic, and logic applies to God’s nature, then the grounding relation runs in a circle. The standard conceptualist reply distinguishes the explanatory priority of God’s nature from its logical priority, but the distinction requires logical apparatus to state, and the apparatus is what the account is trying to ground. The conceptualist account converges on the same structural conditions the argument names; the remaining disagreement is whether those conditions are best described as features of a divine mind or as features of structure as such. The same debt recurs from a wholly non-theistic direction: analytic idealism’s dissociation of one fundamental consciousness into many minds requires the differentiating and persisting structure its monism was meant to forestall, as argued at §9.5.

*Third.* The Cartesian voluntarist makes logic the free output of divine will. On Descartes’s letters to Mersenne (Descartes 1630), the eternal truths (including the laws of logic and mathematics) are established by God as a king establishes laws in his kingdom. God could have decreed otherwise; the fact that God decreed these laws rather than others is what makes them necessary; and the modal force of the laws traces entirely to the divine will. Frankfurt (Frankfurt 1977) reconstructs the view as genuinely coherent: a position on which God’s omnipotence extends to the logical as well as the natural order. Curley (Curley 1984) gives a more cautious defense, reading the Cartesian view as a limit position rather than a settled doctrine.

Voluntarism faces the deepest difficulty of the three: the act of decree appears to presuppose what it was meant to create. A temporal decree would involve succession, distinction, and persistence. Cartesian voluntarists can instead construe God’s willing as eternal.
