The remaining objection is that free selection among alternative logics appears to presuppose determinate alternatives, identity, and consequence relations already available to the will; this yields a logical-priority problem without assuming a temporal divine psychology. The source of logic must already be inside logic to perform the act of sourcing. The objection is sharper than the parallel regress in move one, because voluntarism is committed to the contingency of the decreeing (God could have willed otherwise) and contingency is the mode of choice between alternatives. For there to be alternatives, there must be a space of distinct options; for a choice among them, an asymmetric dependence of outcome on selection; for the choice to hold, a chooser distinct from and stable across what is chosen. Voluntarism demands every structural condition the theory is trying to explain, in the very act of explaining it. This is why contemporary theism has largely abandoned the position: not because the motivation is wrong (the motivation is to protect divine omnipotence from external constraint) but because the machinery is self-defeating at a level even the conceptualist can see. Leftow (Leftow 2012, ch. 4) devotes an entire chapter to showing why voluntarism can’t be the theist’s fallback, precisely because it presupposes what it tries to ground. The present reply agrees with Leftow’s diagnosis and presses the point one level further: the conditions voluntarism presupposes are the three Conditions, and once they are secured, no further appeal to divine will is needed to underwrite logical necessity.

A kindred deflationary move presses from outside theism entirely. Sober (Sober 1993) argues, in a Humean spirit, that logical truths need no grounding at all: their status as truths is a matter of their formal character, not of any metaphysical relation to a ground. Sher’s *Epistemic Friction* (Sher 2016) develops a logical realism on which logic is objective but not grounded in any further entity; logical truths track formal features of reality the way mathematical truths track quantitative ones, and no rational author is required. The structural account agrees with Sober and Sher that no being is required to ground logic, and adds a constructive account of what does underwrite logical necessity: the structural roles. Where Sober stops at the formal character of logical truth and Sher stops at objective formal features of reality, those features and why they obtain necessarily are specified here. The convergence is on denying the theistic grounding; the divergence is on whether anything positive can be said about what logic describes. The structural account says yes, and says it is what the present book has been defending from §2.1 on.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Three Grounds Trilemma** · *Disjunction*

Can a theistic account ground logic without using logic to ground it?

- **If logic holds independently,** then God isn’t grounding it. The account concedes a necessary order God doesn’t ground, and the transcendental argument is left without its conclusion.
- **If logic is the content of God’s thought,** then the thinking already has structure in it. To be logic at all, that content has to be genuinely modal and genuinely articulated. Articulation of that kind is differentiation, ordering, and bearing. So the structural Conditions turn up inside the very being that was offered as prior to them.
- **If logic is decreed by divine will,** then the decree already uses what it was supposed to create. Choosing takes alternatives to choose between, deciding takes identities to tell apart, and decreeing takes consequence for anything to follow from it. Logic is in use before it is made.

Each pays in the same currency. The first surrenders the argument; the second and third presuppose T, S and Φ in the act of grounding them. Once those Conditions are secured, no further appeal to a divine mind or will is needed to underwrite the necessity.

*Scope.* The trilemma prices the grounding options for necessary truth; it doesn’t claim that theism is incoherent, that the conceptualist position is unmotivated, or that no fourth option could be formulated. Divine simplicity as the identity of God with the divine attributes, which bears directly on the conceptualist horn, is engaged at §10.2.1. What divine necessity amounts to as an attribute, and the cost of indexing omnipotence to logical possibility, is engaged at §11.3.1.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Identity (§2.6)

Swinburne’s case that the necessary ground must be a mind rather than a set of roles is engaged at §10.1.8. The present section confines itself to the positive claim that logic requires a rational ground, and contests it on the three strategies available for what that ground could be.

*What the three moves show.* The three strategies receive different verdicts. Voluntarism faces an internal difficulty: an act of decree appears to presuppose the logical and modal alternatives it is meant to create. Presuppositionalism must explain how a necessarily rational Author grounds logic without merely describing that Author through logical predicates. The conceptualist view may coherently locate logical content in a divine intellect, but then it becomes an interpretation of one aspect of Nature rather than an escape from structural constraints. Retorsion alone doesn’t establish that no essence-prior or conceptualist interpretation could be coherent. No Unconditioned Essence supplies the further location result: the proposed intellect can’t be an independent source behind the field. The remaining question is whether attributing intellect explains the necessity and applicability of logic without adding unearned personal predicates.

*The widened claim.* Pressed on logic, the presuppositionalist widens the target: the claim becomes not that logic requires a divine ground but that *intelligibility itself* does—that the very possibility of making sense of anything (logic, induction, the uniformity of nature, the fit between mind and world) presupposes God (Van Til 1955; Bahnsen 1998, whose 1985 debate with Stein ran the demand for logic, induction, and moral standards together). The widening looks like a strengthening. The reply is that it mistakes a relation for a substance.

Intelligibility isn’t a substance that something must supply; it is a relation, the fit that obtains when a tracker converges on a structure already there. A text is intelligible to a reader who has acquired its language and opaque to one who hasn’t, though the text is unchanged: what varies isn’t a quantity of intelligibility resident in the ink but the match between an acquired competence and an antecedent structure. The relation has two terms, and each is already accounted for. The objective term is structure—that there is something with determinate identity, distinction, and exclusion to be tracked at all—and that is what the three Conditions secure, the burden this chapter has already discharged. The subjective term is a competence that converges on the structure, acquired the way any tracking is acquired, through exposure and adjustment. Neither term, and so not the relation they compose, requires a further being to supply it.

The presuppositionalist’s demand—*what grounds intelligibility?*—therefore mislocates its object. To ask what supplies the fit between a competence and a structure is to treat a relation as though it were a thing, on the model of asking what grants a key its fit to a lock: nothing grants it, the cut of the one matches the cut of the other, and the matching isn’t a third item in need of a donor. Once intelligibility is seen as the convergence of a tracker on a structure rather than a gift bestowed from above, the question that seemed to demand God as its answer turns out not to require an answerer.

**[Proposition]**

**Nothing for an Omniscient Ground to Make Sense Of** · *Proposition*

Intelligibility is not a substance but a relation: the fit between graspable structure and a grasp of it, the way a text is intelligible to a reader who has learned its language. Finite *coming to understand* is one form of that relation, a competence closing a gap it did not already hold. Omniscience rules out that acquisitive form; it does not rule out eternal non-acquisitive grasp of determinate logical content. The widened claim therefore does not show that nothing is intelligible *to* an omniscient ground. What it shows is that logic and intelligibility do not by themselves require a divine author, and that conceptualism remains a comparative grounding interpretation with its own bootstrapping burden.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

The demand fails from the other side as well, once the relation is turned on the being the argument offers as its ground. On the acquisitive reading, to make sense of something is an achievement: a competence closing a gap, gathering a structure it didn’t already hold. That reading of the relation runs in a direction, from not-yet-tracking to tracking, and it presupposes a knower who lacked the structure before acquiring it.

An omniscient being holds all structure already, so it has no gap to close and nothing it *comes to* track. That rules out *making sense of* as a finite tracker’s acquisition; it doesn’t rule out timeless grasp of determinate content. Conceptualism remains exactly that proposal, and it still owes its own grounding account rather than being eliminated by the acquisitive reading. The second reading of the phrase fares no better: if *to make sense of* the world were to *make* it, to author the structure rather than converge on it, that is voluntarism, and it collapses under the act of decree exactly as the third move showed. On the first reading there is nothing for an omniscient ground to *acquire*; on the second the making already presupposes the structure it would produce. Intelligibility is left as nothing a divine being must supply, not as nothing such a being could grasp.

The same dissolution handles the induction prong the presuppositionalist presses through Hume. That the future’s resemblance to the past can’t be justified without circularity is a real problem, but a divine guarantor doesn’t solve it: the belief that a sustaining God will keep nature uniform rests on exactly the inductive habit under examination, so the guarantor relocates the circle rather than closing it. The three Conditions provide conditions under which ordered inquiry and stable comparison are possible, but they don’t entail that the contingent laws or regularities of nature remain uniform. The Humean problem of induction therefore survives the bare structural floor; a divine guarantor may not solve it without circularity, but the triad alone doesn’t solve it either. The direction of support then runs opposite to the one the argument needs: we hold nature uniform because we meet it as uniform, not because anything announces its uniformity to us.

*The reliability rejoinder.* Grant that intelligibility is a tracker converging on structure—what makes the tracking *reliable*, apt to latch onto what is there rather than to misfire? The demand repeats the category error one level in. Reliability isn’t a further substance the relation must be given; it is the success-condition that individuates something *as* tracking. Tracking admits degrees of reliability: a competence can correlate with a structure while misfiring in some conditions. Reliability therefore requires an account of error rates, calibration, and the processes that sustain successful representation; it isn’t guaranteed by the definition of tracking alone. At the structural floor, though, the demand thins: whatever competence tracks the three Conditions at all already operates within them, as a key that opens the lock is already cut to it. The fallible work of exposure and adjustment is just the process by which non-converging candidates fall away; what the word “competence” picks out is what survives. Nor does the evolutionary debunker’s wedge—selection tracks fitness, not truth—find purchase here, for the structure tracked isn’t a contingent regularity from which fitness could come apart but the precondition of there being distinct representational states to select among at all: any competence operating on distinct states already operates within the three Conditions. The wedge bites on contingent first-order content, never on the structural floor.

*Convergence.* The close has two prongs. The first, developed through the three moves, is that the structure logic describes is necessary and no theistic strategy has shown it to require a rational author. The second is that intelligibility—the broadened target to which the argument retreats once the first prong holds—is a relation between grasp and structure, not a substance any being must provide; learned acquisition is its finite form, not its exhaustive form. The first removes the demonstrated need for a divine ground of logic; the second removes the demonstrated need for a giver of intelligibility while leaving non-acquisitive conceptualism as a comparative grounding account. Together they block a quick inference from logic or intelligibility to God. The comparative question remains whether a theistic, realist, conventionalist, or structural account best explains logical necessity, induction, and cognitive reliability without circularity.

*The variant that targets knowledge and reasoning rather than logic.* A related move widens the transcendental argument’s target from logic to the operations of knowing and reasoning themselves, claiming that God is a precondition for knowledge (that knowing anything at all requires a divine source that grants it) and, in a parallel form, that God is the precondition for reasoning (that the capacity to weigh possibilities and draw conclusions is a gift underwriting an otherwise inexplicable rational faculty). Both forms misdescribe the operation they are trying to ground. Knowledge, on the structural account developed at §5.4, is something a knower *acquires*: held grasp of structure, built and re-derived by a body doing the holding, not a substance projected onto a person from outside. Cases that look like knowledge being *granted* are cases of causal enablement of that acquisition, not exceptions to it. A bank teller who supplies a customer’s forgotten account number hasn’t projected knowledge into the customer; the teller’s utterance is a causal input the customer’s own mind takes up, checks, and comes to hold as its own grasp. The acquisition is still the customer’s; the teller merely supplied an input to it, the way any testimony, textbook, or perception does. Generalizing this to God changes only the source of the causal input, not the structure of knowing, and so establishes nothing that a further, more ordinary explanation doesn’t already cover.

The reasoning form of the variant fails on the same grounds and more directly still, because what the operation requires is already specified (§5.6), and it isn’t much: two or more live possibilities and some grasp of what accepting or denying each would entail, with the mind weighted toward one by that grasp. That is what reasoning is; nothing beyond structure holding possibilities apart and a knower’s grasp of their consequences is called for. The transcendental claim that a necessarily rational being must underwrite this capacity repeats the error the logic-grounding version made: it treats an operation, something a mind does, as though it were a substance requiring an external donor. A mind that can hold two possibilities apart and register what follows from each already has everything reasoning needs; positing a divine source adds a step the operation never asked for.

*The fallback to God as maker of the knowable.* Pressed further, the position often retreats to a different claim: not that God grounds the act of knowing, but that God is a precondition of knowledge as the creator of the things there are to be known. This trades a claim about the operation for a claim about the causal history of its object, and it fails a simple test. Hold the knower and the known fixed, subtract God as the thing’s causal origin, and put any other origin in its place, or none. Nothing about the knowing relation changes. Whatever caused the known thing to exist is a question about the thing’s history, external to what makes the knower’s grasp of it count as knowledge. The fallback also turns on itself. If being created is what makes a thing knowable, the premise strips knowability from the one being the argument most wants to preserve it for: God, on classical theism, is uncreated, and so would be the one thing the fallback’s own criterion rules unknowable. The theist can’t have it both ways, that createdness is the precondition of knowability and God, who has no creator, is nonetheless known or knowable. Either createdness isn’t really the precondition of knowability, which surrenders the fallback, or it is, and God falls on the wrong side of the very line the fallback draws.

*The argument form, kept.* The replies above decline the presuppositionalist’s conclusion, and the trilemma prices the grounding options that might have secured it. Neither disputes the argument’s *form*. A transcendental argument identifies what must hold for some undeniable activity to be possible at all and establishes it by the impossibility of the contrary, and that form is sound. What follows isn’t a further objection but the same argument run to its own terminus.

**[Argument]**

**The Ground Fails Its Own Preconditions** · *The Transcendental Inversion*

1. **There are preconditions of intelligibility.** Features that must obtain for anything to be thought, said, or reasoned about at all.

2. **They cannot be coherently denied.** Any denial is itself an act of thinking and saying, and so supplies an instance of what it denies (*The Self-Refutation*, §3.3.1).

3. **Among them is determinacy on the side of the object.** For a subject to be thought or said *about* is for it to have content distinguishing it from other subjects and from nothing at all.

4. **Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality are what supply that determinacy.** Their joint absence is ∅, the state in which no content is held one way rather than another (§2.7.1).

5. **A description may withdraw all three at once.** Atemporality, aspatiality, and insubstantiality together, while denying every thin or analogical content that might supply determinacy in their place.

6. **∴ Such a description fixes no possible subject.** It leaves nothing to distinguish its subject from ∅, and ∅ isn’t a possible state (§2.7.2). The preconditions of intelligibility exclude a ground described by their withdrawal.

*Scope.* The line bears on a description withdrawing all three Conditions while refusing every replacement articulation, and on nothing weaker. A determinate atemporal ground, an analogical account that states what its proportion preserves, or an essence-prior proposal supplying content by another route isn’t declared empty by this argument; the later No Unconditioned Essence and No Divine Addition results locate any possible referent as Nature or an aspect of Nature (§10.2.1, §10.4, §11.10). The premises are the transcendental argument’s own, and the conclusion converges with *The Contentless God Has No Referent* without depending on it: steps 4 and 6 run on §2.7 directly, so nothing here is borrowed from Chapter 11.

The premises are the transcendental argument’s own. That there are preconditions of intelligibility, and that they can’t be denied without being employed, are exactly what the presuppositionalist establishes, and the second is proved rather than assumed here (§3.3.1). The turn comes at the third step, which is a further premise rather than a consequence of the second: the preconditions include determinacy on the side of the object, not only the conditions of the act that thinks it. That distinction is kept deliberately, since an inference running straight from a structured act to a structured object is the one §3.3.4 declines to make. What carries the line isn’t the conceiving but what the description withdraws from the thing described.

Stated that way the argument is the presuppositionalist’s method applied without exception. If the preconditions of intelligibility can’t be suspended for the sake of a denial, they can’t be suspended for the sake of a ground either, and a description purchased by withdrawing all three has spent what any subject needs to be a subject at all.

Where the strict form widens into the worldview version, a further claim carries the weight: that no account other than the theistic one can supply the preconditions, since it is by eliminating the alternatives that the argument arrives at a personal ground at all. The internal critique that does that eliminating presses that no *contingent physical arrangement* yields universality, invariance, or normativity. The preconditions identified across this chapter aren’t a contingent arrangement but Reality’s necessary structural constitution (§2.9.6), from which invariance follows directly and universality from there being no evaluation at which the constitution fails. The elimination therefore passes the account by rather than answering it, and what the widened argument requires at that step is the impossibility of the contrary.

*What a rational ground costs.* The argument’s third premise asks the ground to be a *necessarily rational* being, and rationality isn’t a bare label. Knowing is knowing of something; a relation of any kind holds between relata; and inference moves from one content to another. Each of these requires an object distinct from the act that takes it. The demand is therefore not that the ground be complicated, but that whatever it knows, relates to, or reasons about be distinguishable from its knowing, relating, and reasoning. That requirement can be met in one of two ways, and the argument’s own commitments make each of them expensive.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Nothing-to-Know Problem** · *Disjunction*

With nothing other than itself, is there anything for the ground to know?

- **If it knows something other than itself,** then it stands in a real relation to something it isn’t. Its rationality is then conditioned by what that other thing supplies. The same holds for relating and for acting. Whatever the direction of dependence in existence, the ground doesn’t hold these predicates independently: it holds them by there being something else to hold them toward.
- **If it knows only itself,** then the distinction between knower and known falls inside it. A distinction that makes no difference isn’t a distinction (§2.4.7), so the differentiation must be real—and real internal differentiation is what a simple, partless subject is defined to exclude.

Rationality doesn’t become free by being placed in a necessary being. It costs an object either way, and the argument must say which cost it is paying.

*Scope.* The dilemma bears on the ground’s possession of rational and relational predicates, not on whether a first cause exists or whether logic requires grounding. A doctrine that accepts internal differentiation, or that declines to attribute determinate rational predicates at all, escapes it by paying elsewhere.

**Depends on:** Distinction (§2.4.7)

The result isn’t that a necessary being is impossible but that the third premise isn’t free. What made *only a necessarily rational being can secure necessary rationality* attractive is the thought that necessity and rationality sit together in one subject at no cost. They don’t. Rationality is a relational achievement wherever it occurs, and locating it in a necessary being doesn’t exempt it from needing something to be rational *about*. The premise that was supposed to close the argument turns out to owe an account of its own.

A final consideration, offered as illustration rather than argument: the case that logic requires a rational ground is itself made in logic, and even the logician’s vocabulary is borrowed from the structure it evaluates. “Therefore” is *there + fore*, space and time fused; “necessarily” renders the Latin *ne + cedere*, not to withdraw, and withdrawal is a structured act: a succession of positions across a relational distance by something that persists. The etymology settles nothing; it only shows the structure surfacing in the very words built to describe it.

### 10.1.4 The Necessary Foundation Argument
What does any shape actually need to count as a shape at all? Erase every edge in the name of making it as expansive as possible, and the result isn’t the most spacious shape there could be; it is no shape, because having an edge was never the defect shapes labor under, it is what makes something a shape rather than nothing at all. Arguments that trace contingent reality back to an unlimited foundation reach for the same move at the far end of a very long regress: strip a candidate of every determinate feature in the name of maximal supremacy, and the stripping risks removing the very thing that let it be a something in the first place. Among contemporary arguments for a divine ground, Rasmussen’s foundation program (Rasmussen 2019) presses the case without appeal to revelation or scriptural authority, but the case doesn’t rest on the PSR alone. It moves from the value and reliability of explanation-seeking to a foundation of contingent reality, then uses a no-arbitrary-limits premise and conceptual analysis to argue for *supreme existence*. Further arguments from value, productive ability, maximal knowledge, and goodness are required to approach a personal God. It belongs to a lineage running from Avicenna’s contingency argument (*burhān al-ṣiddīqīn*) in the *Kitāb al-Shifā* (Avicenna (c. 1020) 2005), through Leibniz’s *Monadology* (Leibniz (1714) 1989, §32) and Clarke’s demonstrative cosmology, to its contemporary reconstructions in Pruss (Pruss 2006) and Koons (Koons 1997). Because it stakes everything on explanatory principles the present account also accepts, it earns engagement at full strength before any reply.

The reconstruction separates three stages and makes each additional premise visible.

1. *Foundation.* Explanation-seeking is reliable for contingent reality; reality as a totality has no outside explanation; therefore contingent things ultimately depend on a foundational, independent layer whose basic nature isn’t explained from outside.

2. *Supreme existence.* The foundation lacks arbitrary, unexplained limits in its basic uncaused attributes. Conceptual analysis is then invoked for the further premise that anything less than supreme existence would contain such a limit. Supremacy—and, on one formulation, necessary existence derived from a supreme nature—follows only if both premises hold.

3. *Toward a personal God.* Rasmussen offers additional routes: unlimited productive or explanatory power is treated as valuable; a nonmaximal degree of value would be an arbitrary limit; and the greatest conceivable ability is argued to include maximal cognitive and moral abilities. These bridges aim at power, knowledge, goodness, and personhood, but they aren’t restatements of the PSR and Rasmussen presents them as further considerations with live burdens.

The resulting program is cumulative rather than a three-line derivation of classical theism from explanation alone. Its strength is precisely that it supplies separate premises at the disputed transitions, which lets the reply ask where each transition succeeds rather than attributing the whole result to the PSR.

What the argument gets right is granted from the start: explanatory regress doesn’t terminate in a brute fact. Where it goes wrong is the identity of the terminus. The terminus is located by §2.7 in the structural roles themselves: the three Conditions (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) as the conditions under which anything is coherently a something-rather-than-nothing. Rasmussen accepts the PSR and rejects that terminus: the roles, he would say, are facts, facts require reasons, and the reason must be something outside them that can ground them without itself requiring grounding. The dispute isn’t about whether the PSR generates pressure; both accounts agree that it does. It is about where that pressure comes to rest. If the structural roles are themselves the conditions of coherent fact-hood, they don’t stand in line with other facts awaiting a reason; they are what allows anything to be a fact waiting for one. The argument reaches its Foundation by three lines, and each is followed here to what it has to keep: the Argument from Limits, the bridge toward a personal God, and the direct appeal to the PSR.

*First.* The argument from arbitrary limits doesn’t run from the PSR alone. It combines an explanatory premise—the foundation has no arbitrary, unexplained limits in its basic nature—with a conceptual premise: a less-than-supreme foundation would exhibit such a limit. The conclusion is supreme existence, not immediately every classical divine attribute. The reply must therefore distinguish legitimate resistance to arbitrary stopping points from the stronger claim that every nonmaximal determination is arbitrary.

The move risks treating every determination as a limiting defect. At role-resolution, a proposed Foundation must at least be determinate, distinguishable from what it grounds, and stand in a real asymmetric dependence relation to it. None of that yet proves clock-time, spatial extension, or ordinary causal persistence in an atemporal ground. It does show that maximality can’t be obtained simply by subtracting every form of order, difference, and bearing; a wholly indeterminate posit supplies no intelligible grounding content. Read as shedding every determination, the Argument from Limits mistakes the conditions for existence for restrictions on a hypothetical limit-free existent, and concludes by describing ∅ under a greatness-theoretic heading.

A theist will object that this describes ∅, not the infinite plenitude classical theism intends: a Foundation lacking every limitation is maximally full, not empty. But the objection trades on an equivocation the reply can refuse. The limit at issue isn’t *privation*, some perfection the Foundation lacks, but *determination*: to be anything at all, even infinite fullness, is to be this and not that, full and not empty, being and not nonbeing. The principle descends from Spinoza’s *determinatio negatio est* (determination is negation, Letter 50), generalized by Hegel into the *omnis determinatio est negatio* since quoted in his name, and pressed here to its theological conclusion. Determination isn’t a defect to be maximized away; it is what being a something costs, and a candidate that sheds it entirely doesn’t rise above the roles but falls beneath them into ∅.

**[Disjunction]**

**Determination Is Not a Limit** · *Disjunction*

The Argument from Limits treats every determination as a defect a maximal foundation must shed. But the limit at issue isn’t privation, a perfection lacked, it is determination: to be anything at all, even infinite fullness, is to be this and not that. Either the foundation keeps its determinacy, and it is a structured ground, the floor already conceded, or it renounces determinacy, and the plenitude is ∅ under a superlative name.

**Depends on:** Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2)

Answering that the Foundation merely can’t be empty, since emptiness is no perfection to lack, guards it against privations it never faced and leaves untouched the determinacy it can’t shed. A bolder theist welcomes the second horn: the God of the via negativa is “beyond being,” so naming it ∅ merely fails to rise past determinate categories. But “beyond being” either marks something determinate, this and not that, and falls back into the first horn, or it marks no determination at all, which Null State (∅) (§2.7.1) establishes isn’t eminence beyond being but ∅, nothing under the honorific “beyond.”

*Second.* The bridge toward a personal God isn’t simply that consciousness is one positive property and must therefore be maximized. Rasmussen offers value-and-ability arguments: the foundation’s unlimited capacity to produce or explain valuable dependent things is itself treated as valuable; arbitrary limitation of that value is rejected; and the greatest conceivable ability is argued to include maximal cognitive and moral abilities. The live questions are whether productive ability is intrinsically value-bearing, whether dimensions of value are comparable and monotonic, and whether maximal causal or explanatory ability entails knowledge, goodness, or personhood rather than merely permitting them.

A discursive mind that entertains a proposition carries that proposition across its articulation (Time), distinguishes it from neighboring propositions (Space), and persists as the same mind across the act (Substance). A mind that remembers, compares, deliberates, learns, responds, or changes its attention therefore incurs the full Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4): those are concrete operations with a when, a where of differentiated content, and a bearer.

The classical reply is deliberately stronger. The divine intellect, it says, doesn’t reason from one thought to another but knows all truths timelessly in one simple act. That reply blocks the direct inference from cognition to succession in God. It doesn’t yet explain how the simple act has determinate content, how necessary knowledge differs from knowledge of contingent truths, or how the act grounds a changing order. Atemporal grounding supplies a generic floor—asymmetric dependence, non-identity of source and grounded, and a real grounding fact—but those thin roles aren’t by themselves Time, Space, and Substantiality. The loaded Conditions enter only if the alleged intellect performs concrete cognitive or causal work. If the personal bridge establishes literal knowing, intending, responding, or producing, that work must pass the Concrete-Entity Test. If it establishes only an abstract explanatory relation, personhood hasn’t followed. This separation strengthens both results: discursive or active mind earns the full Conditions; timeless grounding retains an exact contact burden without being redescribed as clock-time by definition.

*Third.* The direct appeal to the PSR skips theistic content altogether and invokes the PSR unadorned: the structural roles are facts, facts require reasons, and the reason must be a necessary being that grounds them without itself requiring a ground. This version is difficult to answer without appearing to abandon rationalism, because refusing the PSR’s demand at the structural level looks like allowing a brute fact at the foundation.

The PSR has no purchase against the structural Conditions if the proposed contrast class is simply their total absence: ∅ isn’t a coherent alternative state, as argued at §2.7. That result blocks a demand for a cause of the Conditions construed as an ordinary contingent fact. It doesn’t, by itself, eliminate an essence-prior proposal that takes the Conditions to depend on a primitive metaphysical ground; such a proposal incurs a further explanatory burden rather than being answered merely by the absence of ∅. The present reply is that Rasmussen hasn’t yet shown why a necessary structured ground requires an additional personal Foundation, not that every possible grounding gloss is already contradictory.

The move trades on two senses of *necessary*. The word carries a monadic sense, □X, obtaining in every possible world regardless of what else is the case, and a relational sense, X is necessary for Y, □(Y→X), obtaining in every world in which Y does. The two aren’t interchangeable. Whenever X is monadically necessary, X is necessary for every Y whatsoever in the relational sense, trivially and at zero explanatory cost, since a proposition true in every world stands in that conditional relation to any other proposition no matter what does the explaining. A necessary structured ground therefore already qualifies as ‘necessary for’ contingent reality the instant it is granted necessary, but only in the vacuous sense that costs nothing and explains nothing. What the Foundation argument needs is the strong reading, on which the ground’s necessity is itself doing the grounding work, standing in the asymmetric source relation the reply develops next, not merely co-obtaining with whatever it is asked to found. Trading on the monadic sense to help itself to the relational one is the additional premise Rasmussen hasn’t supplied.

**[Proposition]**

**Two Senses of Necessary** · *Proposition*

“Necessary” carries a monadic sense, true in every world regardless of what else holds, and a relational sense, necessary *for* something, true in every world in which that something holds. Whatever is monadically necessary is trivially necessary-for anything whatsoever, at zero explanatory cost. A necessary structured ground qualifies as “necessary for” contingent reality the instant it is granted necessary, but only in the vacuous sense. The Foundation argument needs the strong reading and has not supplied the premise that gets there.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

The Foundation, moreover, inherits a structural burden. Rasmussen can press that the relevant explanation need not be causal or temporal: the Foundation may ground without producing, explain without sustaining through time, or source without performing a causal act across an interval. Grant that distinction. Any intelligible source/ground relation must still distinguish source from grounded, order the dependence asymmetrically, and obtain as a real explanatory fact rather than as a bare label. These are generic structural roles, not yet the loaded Conditions. They establish that the proposed explanation is determinate; they don’t establish that an atemporal Foundation occupies clock-time, spatial extension, or causal persistence.

To predicate analogically is to attribute a property to a subject, but only by way of analogy. That is the classical theist’s natural recourse at exactly this point: God grounds not univocally but analogically, so the relation is retained in an eminent, non-creaturely mode. The answer isn’t that analogy secretly means Time, Space, and Substantiality. It is that an analogy doing explanatory work must fix a determinate respect in which source, grounded, and dependence are related. If it does, the generic structural floor is conceded and the remaining question is how that abstract relation reaches concrete actuality. If it doesn’t, the analogy supplies no grounding content. The full pressure on the classical via negativa runs at §10.2.2 and §10.4.

The distinction between floor and Conditions isn’t a retreat from the fuller three Conditions defended elsewhere; it prevents the conclusion from being purchased by equivocation. The Structural Requirement establishes the loaded Conditions wherever Change is possible and wherever concrete operation occurs. The generic floor establishes only that a proposed atemporal grounding relation is determinately a relation. A Foundation that refuses even source/grounded distinction, dependence direction, and real obtaining fails as a Foundation: nothing in the proposal explains anything. A Foundation that grants them remains a structured-ground competitor and faces the contact question. If it then creates, responds, deliberates, intervenes, or otherwise performs concrete work, the stronger Concrete-Entity Test applies and the full Conditions enter at the work. This is the exact boundary carried forward at §10.4.

The classical admission that God can’t make a square circle was always a concession that coherence binds the Foundation. At the generic level, coherence requires determinate content and noncontradictory relations. At the concrete level, an act requires the when, where, and what of the act. A Foundation isn’t released from either requirement by being called ultimate.

The abductive variant on these arguments reaches the same terminus by inference rather than demonstration: best-explanation reasoning rather than deductive PSR application, as in Koons (Koons 1997). The reply is parallel. A posit must be able to do the explanatory work attributed to it; doing that work requires determinate ordering, differentiation, and bearing at role-resolution. An abductively posited Foundation therefore carries structural commitments. Whether those commitments reduce the Foundation to the book’s structure or remain features of a distinct personal ground is the live abductive comparison, not something the role-floor alone decides.

Two objections press at this site. The selection-among-possibilities challenge asks: if Nature is the necessary structural foundation, what selects which contingent configuration it realizes? The question is internal to Nature: which configuration obtains within the necessary structure, not a question about Nature itself. The modal PSR as applied to contingents within Nature (§8.2.1) answers the explanatory pressure without an external intentional selector, while the absence of a coherent contrast class for Nature’s non-instantiation (§2.7) blocks projecting the question back onto the Conditions; the level-distinction at Necessity Precedes Contingency (§2.9.4) fixes why, since contingency is a property of configurations within Nature, not of the necessary structural ground. Configurational Necessitation (§2.9) supplies the positive half of that reply. Where one configuration is metaphysically sufficient for another, the relation holding between them is a structural constraint rather than a local regularity, □(P → Q); the theorem fixes the conditional, not either term. A contingent fact is therefore explained by two things that are both internal to Nature: the configuration it obtains in, and the structural constraint under which that configuration necessitates it. No external selector is required for the explanation to be complete at the level the question is asked.

Pressed once more—*but why this configuration rather than another?*—the reply either lands on a prior configuration, still inside, or reaches a point where the series isn’t further explained. That is a real cost. What it isn’t is a cost the theistic alternative avoids. A necessary being that produces this configuration rather than another inherits the identical question about its own act, and inherits it in a sharper form: a being whose nature is necessary and whose act is identical with its nature owes an account of how a contingent output issues from it at all (§11.3.1, Q5). The demand doesn’t reach outside Nature. It reaches at a level where every candidate ground pays the same price, which is why paying it here purchases nothing there.

The aggregation challenge asks: if T, S, and Φ are each necessary, why are they not three independent necessary foundations that aggregate to one, the structural form of monotheism? Because T∧S∧Φ isn’t a conjunction of three independently necessary grounds but one structural fact under three logical-categorical readings. The Triunity of Nature (§2.6.9) and Condition-Individuation (§2.6.11) establish that instantiation of any one Condition requires the others, so there is no coherent specification of T, S, or Φ as a foundation prior to their conjunction. Rasmussen’s aggregation move, which correctly collapses multiple independent necessary foundations to one, doesn’t reach T∧S∧Φ, because the Triconditional identity forecloses the independence it requires.

*Convergence.* Rasmussen’s program now meets the reply at its actual joints. The foundation stage may leave open whether modal truths follow from structure directly or from the essence of a structural ground, but No Unconditioned Essence closes that essence as a distinct source behind Nature. The arbitrary-limits stage requires both that unexplained basic limits are objectionable and that every less-than-supreme determination is such a limit; the structural reply denies the second where determination is constitutive rather than arbitrary. The personal stage requires separate value-and-ability bridges to power, knowledge, goodness, and personhood; if those bridges succeed, the resulting cognitive and grounding relations articulate the Conditions, while if they establish only productive capacity the personal conclusion remains unearned. Essence-priority therefore survives as an explanatory ordering within Nature, not as an additional foundation.

Rasmussen is right that explanatory regress must terminate somewhere, and right that the terminus can’t be an indeterminate blank. The divergence concerns its identity. Chapters 1 and 2 establish T∧S∧Φ as the necessary conditions of concrete Change; the Foundation program seeks a further necessary being that explains why those Conditions and their contingent configurations obtain. The role floor alone doesn’t identify that being with Nature, and Rasmussen’s explanatory premise alone doesn’t identify it as personal. The result is reciprocal: the book owes its argument that the Conditions need no external ground, while the Foundation program owes both an abstract-to-concrete contact and the further bridges to knowledge, goodness, and personhood.

For neighboring contemporary positions in the same methodological cluster, the engagement runs at §3.4, §3.5, and, for Pizzi, §8.2.4, rather than here: Pruss and Rasmussen (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018), and Pizzi (Pizzi 2025). The cluster reaches □∃x x; the five-domain convergence reaches □(T∧S∧Φ). Pizzi (Pizzi 2025) explicitly leaves the identity of the necessary existent open in his §4. The present argument narrows that opening by fixing what every concrete change-realizer must instantiate; it closes it entirely only if the independent Exclusivity of Nature argument succeeds. Divine simplicity is taken up at §10.2.1. Rasmussen’s personalist last stage is engaged directly in Chapter 11: whether awareness, knowledge, and agency are genuine additions to the necessary structural ground or configurations it realizes is tested at §11.4.1, §11.4.2, and §11.7.1. The modal-collapse risk remains foreclosed by the level-distinction established at §2.9.4: necessity attaches to the Conditions, not to the configurations they permit to vary.

### 10.1.5 The Cosmological Argument
The demand for a first cause is a longstanding organizing move in natural theology: if the three Conditions are necessary, what caused them to be? Time, as defended at §2.1–2.6, is a necessarily instantiated structural role, derived without PSR machinery and without any external originating cause; the First Cause objector grants that necessity and asks what started it. The demand comes in four forms carrying three burdens. The Kalām and its kin carry a *temporal-beginning* burden; Koons’s contingency argument and Pruss’s sufficient reason carry a *totality-explanation* burden; and Aquinas’s *per se* series carries a *simultaneous-dependence* burden, which receives the longest treatment because a purely temporal reply doesn’t reach its distinction between logical and temporal priority.

The argument concedes at the outset that the Leibnizian tradition is correct on a narrower point: causal series within the structural conditions do admit, and often require, further explanation. The claim pressed here is weaker than the target that tradition is built to refute. The order through which causal series run isn’t itself a series. Causal vocabulary applies to what occurs within the order, not to the order itself. A framework that makes causation possible isn’t among the candidate effects causation explains.

The cosmological tradition offers a resilient natural-theological resistance to the sufficiency of structural necessity. Its core commitment is simple: something must have started things. The universe is a vast succession of causes and effects extending backward in time; either that succession is infinite or it has a first member. An infinite past, the objector contends, is incoherent: actual infinities can’t be traversed, and we could never have arrived at the present if infinitely many prior moments had to elapse first. A finite past therefore requires an originating cause, and such a cause can’t itself lie among the events it initiates. The argument’s classical roots run through the Islamic *kalām* tradition (medieval speculative theology that pressed dialectical-rational defenses of revealed doctrine): Al-Kindi’s *On First Philosophy* (al-Kindī c. 850) gives the earliest systematic case for the impossibility of an infinite past, and Al-Ghazali’s *Tahāfut al-Falāsifa* (al-Ghazālī c. 1095) develops the mature premodern version that the contemporary recovery directly invokes.^(Craig 1979, ch. 1; Davidson 1987 traces the Islamic transmission.) Its contemporary inheritors refine it into the Kalām appeal to traversal, the Koonsian appeal to mereological contingency, and the Pruss appeal to the Principle of Sufficient Reason (Craig 1979; Koons 1997; Pruss 2006; Pruss and Rasmussen 2018; Rasmussen 2019), and the Thomistic *per se* series stands beside them as the older fourth form. Each converges on the same conclusion: a necessary being outside the causal order, identified with God. The present account lands next to the Leibnizian wing of this tradition—□(T∧S∧Φ) and their necessary ground being adjacent endpoints—and diverges from it only on the line taken and the commitments incurred along the way.

The empirical case deserves stating at its strength before it’s answered. There is evidence that this cycle had a beginning, and it isn’t a theological inference but a measurement: an expansion history that runs backward to a boundary, a background radiation carrying the imprint of an early dense state, and light-element abundances matching what that state predicts. The premise is right in the sense that matters here. Something began, and it can be dated.

That concession is larger than it looks, and it doesn’t run in the direction the argument needs. The measurement of a beginning is itself evidence of succession. A world produced complete into a static void would leave nothing to measure: no expansion to run backward, no cooling to leave a residue, no sequence of states to read off. That there is a boundary to find is evidence that the order runs, which is what this account already claims. Taken at full force, the empirical prong establishes Temporality before it establishes a first cause.

*First: the temporal-beginning burden.* The Kalām traversal argument, regimented, runs:

1. *Causal principle.* Whatever begins to exist has a cause.

2. *Finite past.* The universe began to exist: an actual infinite sequence of past events can’t be traversed, for if infinitely many moments had to elapse before now, now could never arrive, so the past is finite.

3. *Conclusion.* The universe therefore has a cause; and a cause not itself in time must be a timeless agent, which is God.

The first premise sounds self-evident because its ordinary cases already contain an arrangement, a transition, and prior conditions. A house begins when materials are assembled; an organism begins through reproduction and development; a storm begins when atmospheric conditions organize into one. In each case *begins to exist* means that a particular configuration becomes instantiated within an existing causal field, and its cause is an earlier or sustaining configuration in that field. The theological inference then changes the subject while keeping the sentence. It applies the warrant earned from configurational instantiation to Nature as a whole, but removes the prior configuration, temporal transition, and causal field that made instantiation causal in the first place. Nature is asked to begin in the same sense as a house while being denied every surrounding condition under which a house begins. The premise therefore licenses causes for beginnings *within* Nature. It doesn’t, without a further bridge, license a beginning of Nature with no configuration doing the instantiating.

*The premise, turned around.* The observation that the ordinary cases carry an arrangement, a transition, and prior conditions can be pressed further than a diagnosis of where the premise loses its warrant. Those cases supply Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality more directly than they supply a cause. A house begins at a time, in a place, out of materials; the causal reading is an interpretation laid over what is already there, while the three Conditions are simply a description of it. The Kalām’s own examples therefore license a premise its defender has no reason to refuse, and that premise runs the other way.

**[Argument]**

**A Beginning Needs What It Would Begin** · *The Cosmological Inversion*

1. **Whatever begins to exist begins at a time, in a place, and from something that persists through the beginning.** This is what the Kalām’s own ordinary cases display before any causal reading is imposed on them (§10.1.5).

2. **There is no time, place, or persisting substance outside Nature.** Nature is Reality’s necessary constitution, and no real content occupies a modal domain outside it (*Reality–Nature Identity*, §2.8).

3. **So if Nature began, its beginning would have a when, a where, and a what—all of them internal to Nature.** Nature would have to obtain already at its own beginning.

4. **∴ Nature did not begin.** The categorial beginning the argument requires—a moment prior to T from which T departed—is foreclosed, and what remains available is a chronometric boundary within T (§2.4.6).

*Scope.* This establishes that Nature has no categorial beginning. It doesn’t establish that Nature is necessary, which the modal line argues separately (§2.9.6), and it doesn’t touch the simultaneous-dependence burden, which asks for moment-by-moment sustaining rather than for an origin (§10.1.6). A defender who grants the conclusion may still press that Nature is held in being without having begun.

The reversal’s force is dialectical rather than additional. It introduces no premise the chapter hasn’t already earned: step 2 is the Reality–Nature Identity, and step 4’s distinction between a categorial and a chronometric beginning is the one drawn at *A Boundary Is Not an Outside* below. What the reversal supplies is a route to that boundary result which runs through the Kalām’s own first premise instead of around it. Where the reply given above declines the inference from finitude to an external cause, this one accepts the premise about beginnings and finds that it excludes the beginning the argument needs.

Two features of the trade are worth marking. The first premise, in this form, has better warrant from the ordinary cases than the causal version does, since a beginning’s time, place, and material are present in the examples while its cause is supplied by interpretation. And the reversal survives the standard reply that the universe began *with* time rather than *in* it: that reply addresses the temporal limb alone and leaves the spatial and substantial limbs untouched, since a beginning still requires somewhere for it to occur and something to undergo it. The trilimb structure is what makes the argument harder to slip than a purely temporal one.

The traversal argument trades on a spatial metaphor. ‘Traverse’ treats the past as a finished road Now had to travel down, a road whose length must be completed before the traveler arrives. But in a successional order, Now isn’t a traveler reaching a destination. It is the current coordinate of the order’s state. You don’t need to ‘finish’ infinity to be at a specific point within it, any more than you need to visit every point on an infinite plane to be at coordinate (0,0). Oppy (Oppy 2006) formalizes the point: the absurdities of Hilbert’s Hotel require the simultaneous rearrangement of discrete objects, a spatial and substantial paradox that doesn’t map onto temporal succession. You can’t shift past moments aside to make room for the present. The rearrangement tools that generate Hilbert’s absurdities don’t obviously apply to temporal succession.

Craig (Craig and Sinclair 2009, §3; Craig and Moreland 2000) has pressed a generalized version of the point in reply: the absurdities follow from the actuality of the infinite itself, not from any rearrangement procedure; Hilbert’s Hotel is a vivid illustration of a more general impossibility rather than its only form. Granting actual-infinite-absurdity in general, the question is whether a temporal past counts as that kind of completed-collection-accessed-as-a-totality. The general cases involve completed infinite collections accessed as totalities, and whether a temporal past is one depends on the theory of time.

On a tensed or passage-centered theory, the past need not be treated as a completed collection accessed from outside; on a tenseless block theory, the past can form a completed ordered totality. The traversal objection therefore depends partly on the theory of time and cannot be dismissed by one model alone. The tensed/tenseless question is the standing pivot of the Kalām dialectic, but the account need not settle it here: on The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2), tenseless order and tensed passage aren’t rival readings of Temporality but the two features it jointly requires, and the reply holds on each.

Taken as ordered dimension, the traversal worry doesn’t arise: there is no formation to complete, only an ordered manifold at whose interior Now sits. Taken as directed passage, grant the finitist the point in full—successive addition, if it establishes anything, establishes that the past is finite; that much is conceded below, since the account is compatible with a finite-past cosmology. A finite past is a chronometric boundary within T, the earliest coordinate the passage has reached from within, not a moment-prior-to-T from which T departed. So the theological inference fails on both features alike: what it needs isn’t a boundary but a cause outside the order, and the boundary is a feature of the order (§4.2.2). The Kalām’s own conclusion about finitude is granted; only the step from finitude to an external cause is refused.

Craig’s stronger reply keeps open the question whether a beginningless temporal order can be actually infinite without anyone traversing it from an external vantage. Oppy’s response weakens the traversal metaphor; it doesn’t by itself settle every argument against an actual infinite past.

Craig’s empirical prong is separable from the conceptual one. The Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem (Borde et al. 2003) is standardly cited as proving the universe had a past boundary, and Craig treats it as empirical confirmation of Kalām’s second premise. Two points cut the weight. First, BGV establishes only that geodesics with positive average Hubble expansion are past-incomplete, not that the universe as such began. Aguirre and Gratton (Aguirre and Gratton 2002) and Carroll (Carroll 2010; Carroll 2016) describe eternal cosmologies in which past-incompleteness of inflating geodesics is compatible with an eternal ambient spacetime. Craig and Sinclair’s *Blackwell Companion* reply (Craig and Sinclair 2009, §7) presses that Aguirre–Gratton requires a quiescent low-entropy past boundary that itself functions as a beginning, and that Carroll’s eternal cosmologies require thermodynamic time reversal at a past boundary that operates likewise; the 2014 *Greer–Heard Forum* exchange with Carroll restates the point.

Granted: the quiescent boundary, where one is required, is a beginning in the chronometric and thermodynamic senses. It isn’t a beginning in the categorial sense the Kalām requires. The chronometric beginning is a feature within T (§2.4.6, §8.1.2); the categorial beginning, which the Kalām needs and the cosmological model doesn’t deliver, is foreclosed by Parasitic Negation on T (§2.1.5, §10.1.6).

Second, even if the universe has a finite past boundary in its own time-coordinate, that boundary is a feature within the three Conditions: the first chronometric coordinate of the successional order, not an event caused by anything outside it. A boundary of the order doesn’t transport the order’s explanation outside the order. The argument concedes the empirical finding and denies the theological inference it is supposed to underwrite.

A newer wave of anti-infinite-past work has migrated away from actual-infinity absurdities toward paradox-based causal finitism. Koons (Koons 2014) presses Grim Reaper cases (scenarios in which an infinite staggered sequence of potential killers generates contradiction) as evidence that infinite causal sequences are metaphysically impossible even when mathematically coherent. Pruss’s *Infinity, Causation, and Paradox* (Pruss 2018) generalizes the point into a systematic case. These arguments aren’t touched by Oppy’s Hilbert deflation, because they don’t turn on Hilbert-style rearrangement; they target the supposition that infinitely many prior events could each causally produce the next. The present reply doesn’t contest causal finitism in general (the account is compatible with a finite-past cosmology) but denies that causal finitism, even if sound, establishes what Kalām requires.

A finitely-extended past is still a past within T; its first chronometric coordinate is the earliest position the passage has reached from within, not an event caused by something outside the order it would initiate. The Kalām framework presents this as a forced choice between (i) the first moment of T has no cause (denying Premise 1) and (ii) the cause isn’t within T (and so outside T). A third position is taken. The first chronometric coordinate is treated as a boundary of the temporal order rather than automatically as an effect of something outside it. The Kalām defender can contest that category assignment and argue that the universe’s beginning is an event falling under the causal principle.

The dispute therefore turns on the scope of causation, not on a contradiction generated merely by asking for a cause. The categorial-vs-chronometric distinction is drawn at *A Boundary Is Not an Outside* below: what is foreclosed is a moment-prior-to-T from which T departed; what is admitted is a chronometric boundary as the first coordinate of T itself. Grim Reaper considerations constrain the shape of causal series; they don’t relocate causation to the order’s exterior.

A further reply is available, though the categorial response doesn’t require it. Grim Reaper cases idealize location, propagation, and mechanism to isolate a causal-structural paradox. The idealization can’t be rejected merely because it omits ordinary physical realization; the relevant question is whether the causal stipulations are jointly satisfiable and whether their contradiction generalizes from the constructed series to every beginningless causal past.

Substantiality is taken here on the realization-tier reading defended at §8.2.2 and §4.4—a substance carrying causal power across T-succession through S-extension (§1.4, §2.4.11). It is the right register for this reply, since the objection itself trades in physically located causes; the modal core of Φ spends only the thinner bearing role (§2.4.8), and nothing in the present paragraph feeds back into the modal theorem. A putative cause that occupies no region and transmits nothing across one isn’t a faint or limiting-case cause but no cause at all.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Reaper-Cause Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

Put the reapers back into the world. If they are genuine causes, they need somewhere to be, something to carry causal power, and time for it to travel.

- **Let the reapers be causes,** and the converging series drives their separation toward zero and their energy density without bound. The machinery breaks, not infinity or causation as such.
- **Make them spaceless triggers instead,** and nothing travels, nothing bears the power, and no cause has been supplied on the present account. A causeless paradox cannot prove that an infinite causal past is impossible.

The reapers lose the causal-finitist inference either way.

*Scope.* The dilemma concerns the causal-finitist use of Grim Reaper cases, not every argument for a finite past.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

A beginningless past is untouched on either horn: it isn’t a staggered swarm of located conditional agents racing to act inside a shrinking window, but the past-directed order of T itself, whose earliest coordinate is a boundary rather than an effect. The Grim Reaper thus constrains, at most, the arrangement of embodied causes; it doesn’t reach the successional order those causes run within, which is the only thing the Kalām needed it to reach.

This verdict converges with the critical literature rather than standing alone. The unsatisfiable-pair diagnosis—Shackel’s demonstration that Benardete constructions merely encode two jointly unsatisfiable conditions (Shackel 2005), pressed against causal finitism by Schmid and Malpass (Schmid and Malpass 2025)—locates the contradiction in the stipulation rather than in the infinity, and observes that purely non-causal Benardete variants (in which each reaper’s action brutely correlates with its predecessors’ rather than being caused by them) generate the paradox with no causal chain for finitism to sever. That non-causal variant is decisive here: if a swarm carrying no causal power at all yields the same contradiction, the impossibility was never a fact about causation reaching infinitely back. The present account agrees on the diagnosis and adds only that the past-directed order of T isn’t a Benardete series to begin with, so nothing in the family bears on whether that order has a first coordinate.

Loke (Loke 2017) presses a further refinement: the only coherent transition from a timeless cause to a temporal effect is free agential initiation, so the first cause must be personal. The refinement inherits the structural reply already given. A ‘timeless cause’ stands outside T by hypothesis, and standing outside T is standing outside the conditions under which causing has content; a free agent who initiates temporality must persist as the same agent across the initiation (the bearing role), distinguish its pre- and post-initiation states (the differentiation role), and stand in a before-and-after relation to the effect it initiates (the order role). The personal-agent refinement doesn’t escape the structural roles; it concentrates them. Loke’s argument is a contribution to the personalist question, not a distinct way past the present response.

Morriston presses two further objections the account can absorb. The first is inductive: the causal principle that anchors the Kalām, that whatever begins to exist has a cause, draws its support only from cases of rearrangement within the order, so its warrant doesn’t extend to an absolute beginning of the order itself (Morriston 2000; Morriston 2002). The account doesn’t lean on this objection, since its own reply is categorial rather than inductive, but the objection reinforces from a second direction that the causal idiom is at home within the order and strains when lifted outside it. The second objection is sharper against the personalist fix: a timeless agent’s producing a first effect is itself a transition from not-creating to creating, and a transition is a succession, so the agential initiation Loke and Craig invoke reintroduces the very order it was meant to precede (Morriston 2000; Morriston 2013). That is the structural reply already given, reached from the opposite side: the transition presupposes the structural roles rather than delivering them from outside.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Timeless Choice Problem** · *Disjunction*

How does a timeless agent begin anything without the time that beginning takes?

- **If nothing changed between not creating and creating,** then nothing was begun. Calling the relation free agency adds a word rather than a transition.
- **If something changed,** then time was already there at the point of beginning. The agent persists across a distinguishable difference, and creating stands after not-creating in the order of the effect: persistence, differentiation, and succession appear at the point of initiation.

Freedom doesn’t remove the structure an exercised choice requires.

*Scope.* The dilemma bears on the transition, not on whether a first cause would be personal. It assumes only that initiation distinguishes nonproduction from production.

**Depends on:** The Grounding Conditional (§3.1.5)

A corollary follows if the theist absorbs Morriston’s point rather than resisting it. The standard absorption denies the transition outright: God’s willing of the world is timeless and immutable, so there was never a state of not-creating for the first effect to succeed. The absorption then leaves one exit from necessity: a willing immutable in fact yet able to have been otherwise, the necessity of supposition Aquinas distinguishes from absolute necessity (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.19.3, I.19.7). The exit keeps the world contingent, but at the price of a modal contrast (a possible circumstance in which the changeless willing is absent) that nothing in the timeless picture grounds; whether that contrast survives divine simplicity is the modal-collapse question pressed at §8.2.5 and engaged at §10.2.1. The theist who declines the exit, identifying the timeless willing with the necessary divine essence so that no modal distinction remains between what God is and what God wills, delivers the present account’s conclusion in theological dress: there is no vantage, temporal, volitional, or modal, at which God exists and the world doesn’t, and obtaining in every circumstance is necessity under its ordinary modal name. Those premises yield a necessary natural order directly: □(T∧S∧Φ) with a divine will attached. And that will contributes nothing to the necessity itself, since it is the modal closure of the willing, not any further feature of the agent, that closes off every circumstance lacking a world. What remains in dispute on that horn isn’t whether the order is necessary but whether its necessity needs an owner, and that is the personalist question, which the fourth form below takes up directly.

**[Proposition]**

**A Boundary Is Not an Outside** · *Proposition*

Grant the Kalām its finite past outright. A past boundary is the first chronometric coordinate of the successional order—the earliest position passage has reached, viewed from within—not a moment prior to that order from which it departed. The beginning the cosmology delivers is therefore a feature *inside* T, and the beginning the argument needs is categorial: an origination of the order as such. A boundary of an order does not transport that order’s explanation outside it. So the empirical finding can be conceded in full while the theological inference it is meant to underwrite is declined, and conceding it costs nothing, because what a first coordinate marks is where the dimension starts being measured rather than where it came from.

**Depends on:** Parasitic Negation (§2.1.5)

*Second: the totality-explanation burden, by contingency.* The contingency-of-the-whole move grants, with Koons (Koons 1997), that an infinite past is possible. The series still consists entirely of contingent beings, events that didn’t have to happen. A series of contingent beings, even an infinite one, is itself contingent. The contingency of the whole demands a necessary cause outside the series. That cause is God.

The move trades on two senses of *contingent*. Individual events may be contingent even if the structural possibility of an order is necessary. It doesn’t follow that this particular total history is necessary. Koons’s argument gets traction if the Big Conjunctive Fact or total series is itself a contingent fact requiring explanation, whether or not it is an additional concrete object over and above its members. But a succession isn’t a thing over and above what succeeds; it is just the parts in the order they take. And that order obtains within a necessary framework whose conditions are what make succession possible at all. Member-level contingency is real. Whole-level contingency, treated as a further concrete object over and above the members, is a misattribution.

Hume’s *Dialogues* IX (Hume 1779) and Paul Edwards (Edwards 1959) diagnosed the underlying slip as a fallacy of composition, treating a property of the parts (contingency) as a property of the whole, and the diagnosis is sound and worth crediting where the whole is treated as a further thing. The reply doesn’t, however, rest on the Hume–Edwards explanatory principle that explaining each member thereby explains the conjunction, the very inference Pruss’s contingency argument is built to reject.

Its load-bearing move is narrower: the necessary framework doesn’t make this particular total history necessary, and neither does it convert the remaining totality-level demand into a personal ground outside Nature (§8.2.1). Koons’s mereological premise is precisely what is supposed to rescue the argument from the composition charge; denying that the whole is an entity over and above its members withholds that premise without leaning on the Hume–Edwards inference. What Koons locates at the top of his derivation (necessary ground) is already present at the bottom, as the three Conditions, for the framework itself. This one arrives without the mereological premise that the series is an entity additional to its elements, a premise Koons himself flags (Koons 1997, §3) as load-bearing and contestable.

**[Proposition]**

**The Whole Isn’t a Further Contingent Thing** · *Proposition*

The contingency-of-the-whole move needs the total series to be a contingent fact over and above its members, requiring a ground of its own. A succession is not a further concrete thing beyond what succeeds; it is the parts in the order they take. Member-level contingency is real and is not in dispute—individual events did not have to happen. A conjunction can still be contingent because one conjunct could differ, so this particular total history isn’t made necessary, and the totality-level question isn’t dissolved. What doesn’t follow is that the question automatically identifies an external personal explainer.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

*The same burden, by sufficient reason.* The PSR appeal presses, with Pruss (Pruss 2006), that every contingent fact requires a sufficient reason. The entire sequence of contingent events is itself a contingent fact: it could have gone differently in countless ways. Its sufficient reason must be a being whose existence isn’t itself contingent, and whose nature explains why this history rather than another obtains. That being is God.

The PSR question splits into two the reply must keep apart. Read as ‘why an ordered history rather than none at all?’, it presupposes ∅ as the contrast, and ∅ is no contrast: that is closed on independent modal and temporal grounds at §2.7.2, and sufficient reason bottoms out where alternatives run out, which is at the roles that make alternation possible. Read as ‘why this configuration rather than another?’—Pruss’s Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact, the conjunction of all contingent configurations of Nature—the alternatives are genuine and the PSR does real work: rival configurations compete within the structural conditions, and each contingent fact keeps its contingent explanation there.

What doesn’t follow is the further step, that the conjunction as a whole requires a necessary explainer outside Nature. But the alternatives aren’t exhausted by ∅ and a Nature that necessitates every configuration: a theist may posit a necessary personal ground whose contingent intention explains one history without necessitating it. That proposal must face the grounding, freedom, and modal-collapse burdens developed in §10.1.4 and §8.2.1 rather than being eliminated by the PSR split alone, including the two-senses-of-*necessary* burden pressed directly at §10.1.4: a necessary personal ground is ‘necessary for’ this history only in the trivial, cost-free sense every necessary being bears to every proposition, unless the stronger explanatory relation is independently secured. The dissolution doesn’t run through the Hume–Edwards principle that explaining each conjunct explains the conjunction, the inference Pruss’s argument is built to reject; it denies that the external demand has an automatic target, as developed in full at §8.2.1.

Hume anticipates the move in *Dialogues* IX (Hume 1779): Cleanthes’ reply to Demea is that if a necessary being must be posited at all, the material universe itself is a candidate, and the theist offers no non-theological ground for disqualifying it. The present argument completes Cleanthes’ gesture. The ‘necessary material universe’ Cleanthes floated wasn’t specified enough to bear the weight; □(T∧S∧Φ) specifies it. The Humean cosmological option the *Dialogues* left undeveloped is the one the structural account takes up. Pruss’s own defense of the PSR against Humean attack (Pruss 2006, chs. 2–7) is uncontested here; the present argument simply doesn’t conscript the principle into service outside the domain where it has purchase. The standard critical literature presses harder, rejecting the principle rather than confining it: Rowe (Rowe 1975) argues that the PSR isn’t rationally compelling and can be denied without irrationality, and Mackie (Mackie 1982) presses both the causal principle and the demand for an explanation of the totality as unmotivated once every member has been explained. The reply here needs neither rejection. It grants the PSR full force within the structural conditions and withholds only its application to them, a narrower and less contestable claim than the outright refusal Rowe and Mackie mount.

A kindred deflationary move presses from the opposite side: the call for a first cause is a pseudo-question, Rundle (Rundle 2004) and Grünbaum (Grünbaum 1998) argue; ‘why is there something rather than nothing’ has no grip because no coherent answer-space exists. The role account agrees with half of this and rejects the other half. It agrees that ‘what caused the structural order?’ terminates, because the idiom of causation applies within that order rather than to it. It rejects the dismissal of the further question ‘why is the order necessary rather than absent?’, because that one does have an answer, given at §2.1–2.8. The cosmological demand isn’t empty; it is a question with a structural answer where theism has given a theological one. Rundle and Grünbaum close the inquiry without resolving it; the present argument resolves it without closing it.

Kant’s critique presses furthest. The cosmological argument extends causality beyond the field of possible experience, where alone the concept has warrant, and so misapplies a category whose jurisdiction is the world of appearances (*Critique of Pure Reason* Kant (1781) 1998, A603/B631); Kant presses further that the argument covertly relies on the ontological proof it claims to do without. The First Antinomy sharpens the impasse (*KrV* Kant (1781) 1998, A426/B454): equally compelling cases can be built for a first beginning in time and against one, which for Kant shows the question has outrun the conditions under which causal reasoning stays legitimate.
