The account agrees that causation doesn’t apply to the order as a whole, and for a recognizably Kantian reason: the idiom belongs to what occurs within the field, not to the field itself. It parts from Kant on the status of the conclusion. His verdict is epistemic, that reason can’t settle the question and must fall silent; the verdict here is metaphysical, that the question is malformed, because the order is necessary (§2.1–2.6) and its necessity has a structural ground rather than a causal one. Where Kant reaches a limit of knowledge, the account reaches a categorial boundary.

One objection cuts across all three forms and is the family’s most resilient. Schopenhauer (Schopenhauer 1813) named it the Taxicab objection: the Principle of Sufficient Reason is hired to carry the argument as far as a first cause and then waved off once the destination is reached, the terminus exempted from the very demand that powered the regress. Oppy (Oppy 2006) presses the contemporary form as a symmetry: whatever explanatory privilege the theist claims for the divine terminus, whether necessity, self-explanation, or brute factuality, the naturalist can claim with equal right for the universe or its fundamental laws, so the demand for a cause of the order underdetermines the theological answer. The objection lands against any account that stops by fiat. It doesn’t land here. The account exempts nothing: it grants the structural order no standing waiver from a demand that otherwise applies, but denies that the demand was ever well-formed against the order, since causation relates elements within the order and the order isn’t one of its elements. The symmetry Oppy exploits is real, and it is conceded rather than resisted, because it isn’t met by making the necessary ground simpler or more unified than a physical candidate. It is met by locating necessity in the three Conditions themselves (§2.1–2.6), which are neither a divine terminus nor a rival physical one but the conditions any candidate terminus, divine or physical, would have to instantiate. The taxicab is never hired, so there is no fare to dodge.

**[Dissolution]**

**The Taxicab Never Hired** · *Dissolution*

The Taxicab objection charges that the PSR is dismissed the instant it reaches its own terminus, exempting the destination from the demand that powered the trip. The charge lands against any account that stops by fiat. It doesn’t land here, because nothing is exempted: the demand was never well-formed against the order in the first place, since causation relates elements within an order and the order isn’t one of its own elements. Locating necessity in T, S, and Φ answers Oppy’s symmetry the same way—not by out-explaining a rival terminus, but by being what any terminus, divine or physical, would have to instantiate.

**Dissolves:** the Taxicab objection, as pressed against an order whose necessity is constitutive rather than stipulated

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

Aquinas’s Third Way (from possibility and necessity, *ST* I.2.3) is the scholastic ancestor of the contingency argument treated here and at §10.1.4.

A final consideration turns the objection back on the conditions of its own statement, a move called retorsion: the call for a first cause presupposes what it is calling on to be caused. The asking unfolds across moments, the words occupy relational positions, and the thought persists across its articulation and transmission: an objection to the necessity of the three Conditions raised within the three Conditions. The obvious reply is that enacting the three conditions while demanding their cause shows only their actuality in the world where the demand is issued, not their necessity. Granted, but modal necessity doesn’t need to be closed here; it is closed at §2.1–2.6. The argument defends the sufficiency of that closure against calls for an additional explanatory step. What the retorsion shows is that every idiom in which the call can be issued (temporal succession, spatial articulation, substantial persistence) is parasitic on the very order the call purports to require a cause for. Causation explains moves inside the field. It can’t explain the field: not because the field is mysterious, but because ‘cause’ is a relation between elements of the field, and the field isn’t one of its own elements.

*Third: the simultaneous-dependence burden.* The remaining form isn’t a claim about how the order began but about what holds it up now. Aquinas’s *per se* series runs vertically rather than backwards: a stack of concurrent dependencies, each member causing only insofar as it is itself being caused, terminating in a source that depends on nothing. The move matters because it sidesteps the traversal question entirely. Even granting an infinite past, a *per se* series is held to require a first term at every moment, and the source is atemporal rather than early. Simultaneous causation is the mechanism the form needs, and it deserves treatment at length, because if it fails the first two forms lose a premise rather than an illustration.

The order of cause-before-effect isn’t the only order causation admits. A hand moving a stick that presses a stone illustrates concurrent dependence: while the contact and applied force obtain, the stone’s acceleration is produced without a temporal gap between the applied force and its effect. Releasing the hand need not stop all motion instantaneously, because inertia remains. Simultaneity is a causal structure too, and Aquinas sees in it the template he needs: an eternal God could simultaneously ground every moment of a temporal world without entering the time of what it grounds. The *per se* causal series runs through a stack of concurrent dependencies rather than a sequence of prior ones. Cause at the top, effect at the bottom, no temporal interval between them. Remove the top and the whole column falls in the same moment. If the picture works, the stack can be finite upward while terminating in an atemporal source, and the atemporal cause at the summit never needs to enter the time of the stones it moves.

Aquinas (*ST* I.2.3) deploys simultaneous causation in the First Way, the *per se* series that stops at an Unmoved Mover. The Second Way uses the same concurrent structure for efficient causation: a series of causes that cause only insofar as they are caused, terminating in a first uncaused cause. Aquinas’s *De Aeternitate Mundi* addresses explicitly the coexistence of eternal cause and temporal effect. Avicenna’s continuous-creation doctrine in the *Kitāb al-Shifā* develops the parallel position in the Islamic tradition: God is the necessary, atemporal cause whose causing of contingent existents is itself eternal even though the existents are temporally extended (McGinnis 2010; Adamson 2013). The continuous-creation model isn’t a separate escape but the same atemporal-sustaining picture in Islamic dress, and it meets the reply given in the analysis that follows to the occasionalist and conservationist kindred: a continuously creating cause must still individuate what it sustains (S), order it (T), and carry it across (Φ).

Kant’s *Critique of Pure Reason* refines the concept in the Second Analogy, distinguishing logical from temporal priority and illustrating with the ball resting on the pillow. Stump and Kretzmann’s “Eternity” (Stump and Kretzmann 1981) proposes ET-simultaneity as a relation between the eternal present and each temporal moment. Craig’s *God, Time, and Eternity* (Craig 2001b) develops a contemporary version keyed to biblical-theism commitments: God timeless without creation, temporal with creation.

Against the doctrine: Wolterstorff’s “God Everlasting” (Wolterstorff 1975) presses the case for divine temporality against Boethius and Aquinas. Padgett’s *God, Eternity, and the Nature of Time* (Padgett 1992) defends a relative-timelessness alternative. Mullins’s *The End of the Timeless God* (Mullins 2016) presses a sustained contemporary argument that timelessness is internally incoherent. Morriston (Morriston 2002; Morriston 2010) has pressed the simultaneous-causation move specifically for two decades: if the cause is eternal, the effect must be equally eternal.

The present reply agrees with the Mullins–Wolterstorff wing that timeless grounding doesn’t cohere, and adds what that wing doesn’t specify: the failure isn’t primarily biblical or doctrinal but structural; the logical priority the doctrine requires is itself a structured relation, and the three conditions are what were supposed to be escaped.

Applied here, the move offers the theist a path to concede that the three conditions govern the created order while preserving God as external ground. The argument holds that any ground of the three conditions must itself instantiate their roles. The simultaneous-causation theorist counter-claims that grounding need not be temporal, spatial, or substantial: it can be purely logical, a relation of eternal dependence that places the effect within T, S, Φ (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) without placing the cause there. On this picture, the demand that grounds instantiate what they ground fails at the central claim: God grounds the three conditions atemporally, the three conditions ground creatures temporally, and the argument’s reach stops one level short of fundamentality.

The move bears directly on the Cartesian Certainty for change of §2.2, the Intermediate Necessity of §2.3, the identification in §2.4 of the modal constraint with the three Conditions, and the Triconditional account in §2.6 of the Conditions as Nature. Simultaneous causation is the specific mechanism by which classical theism tries to exempt God from the structural conditions while accepting their application to creatures. If the exemption holds, a changeless ground is possible after all, provided the ground relates to change by logical rather than temporal priority. Three forms of the move take up the objection: the *per se* causal series, Kant’s logical/temporal distinction, and Craig’s modal refinement. The replies that follow argue that each still owes the thin roles inside the logical priority it was supposed to replace.

*The per se series.* The first form, regimented, runs:

1. *Two series.* A *per accidens* series (events in time) differs from a *per se* series (grounding relations that hold at every moment).

2. *The First Way.* Aquinas’s First Way holds that a *per se* series of causal dependencies requires no temporal extension: it is a relation of ontological priority rather than temporal sequence.

3. *Conclusion.* So God can be the *per se* cause of the world without being in time: the world depends on God at every moment, and the dependence relation isn’t itself a temporal event.

A sufficient cause guarantees its effect: wherever C obtains, E obtains too, with no room for the effect to lag behind—the general form of this necessitated-conditional move is Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4). The will of the Maximally Great Being (MGB) is held to be eternal, changeless, and sufficient. An eternal sufficient cause entails an eternal effect. Morriston (Morriston 2002) presses the point: if the cause is eternal, the effect must be equally eternal; if the effect is finite, a simultaneous cause must be equally finite. (The Stump–Kretzmann ET-simultaneity reply to this eternal-cause/eternal-effect point is engaged at §10.2.3.)

The *per se* series doesn’t dissolve the structural question, which reappears within it: how can an eternal, changeless ground produce a finite, changing effect without the ground itself being modally or structurally differentiated between its producing and its non-producing state? The doctrine gestures at logical priority while still requiring the asymmetric directionality it was supposed to avoid. If temporal priority is denied, the causal relation must still supply asymmetric dependence; otherwise the remaining relation is structurally indistinguishable from simultaneous coexistence, two things obtaining together without one producing the other.

The issue isn’t whether every cause must come earlier in clock-time. The issue is whether “cause” has determinate content without ordered priority, distinguishable relata, and a stable dependence relation. Those are the structural roles in non-clock form.

That identification isn’t stipulated here. The minimal floor was established independently at §10.1.4, showing that even a timeless grounding intellect must exhibit asymmetric grounding-order, relational distinction, and identity-retention across the relation to count as a ground at all. Asymmetric ontological priority isn’t being relabeled temporal by fiat; it is being held to the floor that any grounding relation must clear, and that floor is source/recipient, direction, and bearing at role-resolution, not yet loaded Time, Space, and Substantiality. The simultaneous-causation theorist can’t keep the priority while refusing the floor, because the priority is precisely what the floor spells out.

The deeper problem cuts across all three forms: whatever the priority relation is called, simultaneous causation turns the contingency of creation into a dilemma. If God is necessarily creator or sustainer, and the sustaining relation is sufficient, then the sustained order follows necessarily from God. The only way out is to make the sustaining relation itself contingent—a necessary, sufficient sustainer otherwise locks in a necessary result. But if the sustaining relation is contingent, creatorhood isn’t necessary in God; and if the sustaining relation is necessary, the particular order God sustains is necessary with God. It won’t do to answer that Nature is necessary in any case: the necessity of the structural conditions is affirmed here (□(T∧S∧Φ)), and why the necessity of the three conditions doesn’t necessitate any particular configuration within them is shown at §8.2.5. That reply is available for the three conditions and unavailable for a contingent created world. A necessary complete sufficient cause would necessitate its effect. The classical theist therefore distinguishes God’s necessary existence from a contingent free willing or from the contingent obtaining of the creation relation. Whether that distinction is coherent under timelessness and divine simplicity is the modal-collapse question; simultaneous causation alone doesn’t settle it. The doctrine alone hasn’t preserved a free creator beyond Nature; it has purchased the atemporal ground at the price of leaving in dispute the contingency it was meant to protect.

A second pressure compounds the first. Creation considered as an atemporal dependence relation has generic structural requirements: source and recipient are nonidentical, dependence runs asymmetrically, and the relation determinately obtains. Those thin roles aren’t yet Time, Space, and Substantiality. Eternal creation therefore avoids a first temporal moment without contradiction at this stage, but it inherits a contact question: how does the atemporal relation ground a concrete changing order? If *creation* names a concrete production, sustaining, selection, or intervention, the operation incurs the full Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4). If it names only abstract dependence, the concrete effect requires the additional bridge. If neither relation is determinately specified, no creating relation has been supplied. The pressure is exact without redescribing explanatory priority as temporal succession.

Feser’s defense of the per-se series through the act/potency distinction merits direct engagement at this point. The per-se causal series is, on Feser’s reading in *Aquinas* (Feser 2009) and *Five Proofs* (Feser 2017), not merely a sequence of concurrent dependencies but an analysis of what it is for one thing to be the *actualizer* of another: the cause supplies actuality that the effect has only potentially, in the very instant of causation. The causal series terminates in *actus purus* (pure act without potency) because any cause that retains potency is itself in need of actualization.

The structural reply doesn’t contest the act/potency analysis on its own terms; it shows that the three Conditions are what the analysis describes. Actualization supplies asymmetric dependence and distinction between actualizer and actualized, directly yielding thin order and difference roles. Thomistic concurrent actualization need not be a temporal transition from an earlier potential state, and dependence need not by itself be spatial extension. The richer types of the three Conditions require the separate realizer arguments. Feser’s act/potency machinery, taken on its own terms, is an analysis of what asymmetric causal dependence consists in, and the structural roles are what that analysis bottoms out in. The conclusion is the same as the main reply: the per-se series, whether described in the language of actualization or in the language of asymmetric dependence, presupposes the structural conditions at the terminating cause rather than exempting it from them.

The engagement with the *actus purus* form of simplicity and with the analogy-of-being machinery that underwrites it lives at §10.2.1; the structural question raised there and here is the same: whether a fully-actualized being can bear the causal roles the doctrine requires without bearing the structural conditions those roles presuppose.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Sustenance Fork** · *Disjunction*

Is the sustaining relation between God and creation necessary or contingent?

- **If that sustaining relation is necessary,** then this order is as necessary as God is. God couldn’t have been without it, and the freedom to have made it otherwise is gone.
- **If that sustaining relation is contingent,** then the order may remain contingent, but God isn’t necessarily a creator.

The book’s necessity of Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality doesn’t supply a third branch: that structural necessity doesn’t propagate to particular configurations, while no parallel non-propagation has been shown for this sufficient sustaining relation.

**Depends on:** Constitutive Grounding Non-Propagation (§8.2.5)

*Logical priority without temporal priority.* Kant’s distinction pushes the case further. A cause and its effect can be simultaneous in time (the ball resting on a pillow creates the indentation at the moment it rests there) while the cause is logically prior: the indentation depends on the ball, not vice versa. Classical theism uses this template for God’s relation to the world.

Kant’s distinction is real and doesn’t rescue the move. Logical priority without temporal priority requires a structural relation that holds between simultaneous states, a relation of asymmetric dependence between distinct elements within a single moment. Such a relation requires distinguishable relata, asymmetric dependence, and determinate obtaining at role-resolution. Logical priority within one moment isn’t thereby temporal asymmetry, and relation-stability isn’t automatically ordinary persistence. The ball-and-pillow analogy illustrates this vividly: the indentation depends on the ball because mass, resistance, and gravity are structurally active between them. The analogy works because ball and pillow are both in time, both in space, both substantial. Remove the structural roles and the analogy collapses: there is no ball and no pillow, only two labels with nothing between them. Kant’s distinction describes the asymmetric relation that carries the logical priority; it doesn’t supply an escape from the conditions that relation runs on.

*The modal refinement.* Craig’s version goes furthest. God exists timelessly without creation and temporally with creation; the transition isn’t an event in God but a relational change: God stands in new relations to creatures without changing intrinsically. Simultaneous causation on this reading is what timeless grounding looks like at the temporal contact.

The refinement concedes the point while renaming the concession. If God stands in new relations to creatures with creation, then God’s relational profile changes from no-relation-to-creatures to standing-in-relation-to-creatures. A change in relational profile is a change, and a change requires before-and-after, a prior state differing from a subsequent state.

Here the strict-timelessist will invoke the distinction between real and merely Cambridge change: God’s coming to stand in relations to creatures is, on this reply, an extrinsic Cambridge change (as Socrates comes to be shorter than a growing Theaetetus without himself altering), not a real change in God, so timelessness survives untouched. The distinction is genuine; the Mullins–Padgett objection is that it doesn’t cover this case. Becoming temporal, on that objection, changes the subject’s mode of existence rather than merely adding an external predicate; Craig denies this and treats the change as relational, and the move from real to Cambridge change requires defense rather than mere assertion. Cambridge change is the correct description of “shorter than”; it is the wrong description of “timeless, then temporal.” (The kindred ET-simultaneity reply, which relates the eternal present to each temporal moment without either term changing, is engaged at §10.2.3.) Timelessness-without-creation plus temporality-with-creation requires God to occupy two distinct modal-relational states and a transition between them. That transition is itself a structural event. Craig accepts that God is temporal from creation on, and the view makes God’s atemporality conditional on not-creating and God’s temporality conditional on creating, a structural description of a being whose modal status varies with its relational context. The result isn’t a being outside Nature, but a being whose structural position depends on which relational role it occupies.

Mullins (Mullins 2016) pushes the critique further: if God’s atemporality is contingent on God’s non-relations, then God’s atemporality isn’t a necessary feature of the divine nature but a contingent fact about the divine’s relational profile, and classical theism was supposed to deny exactly that. Padgett (Padgett 1992) presses from a different direction: the transition Craig posits (from timeless-without-creation to temporal-with-creation) isn’t coherent unless God was already in some temporal frame within which a transition could occur, which is why Padgett opts for relative-timelessness from the start rather than trying to combine strict atemporality with a creative act.

A kindred variant is Malebranchean occasionalism: God is the sole genuine cause, and what appear as natural causal relations are divinely ordained regularities holding between occasions rather than mechanisms. The reply is the same in thinner vocabulary. For God to occasion distinct events, the creaturely occasions must be differentiated and ordered, and the decree must supply determinate explanatory bearing. Occasionalists may construe the divine intention as one timeless decree rather than a persisting mental episode, so the move secures the minimal roles while leaving the loaded divine types contested. Occasionalism hasn’t eliminated the structural conditions; it has relocated them into the divine willing itself. Another kindred: the conservationist account (Freddoso 1991), on which God continuously sustains creatures in existence without directly causing their operations. The sustaining relation holds at every moment the creature persists, so the contact question returns at each of them.

**[Proposition]**

**Logical Priority Keeps the Asymmetry It Was Meant to Replace** · *Proposition*

The exemption needs a priority that is not temporal: the ball and the indentation are simultaneous, yet the indentation depends on the ball and not conversely. Each of the three forms still owes asymmetric dependence, distinguishable relata, and a determinate obtaining. Those are thin source/recipient, direction, and bearing roles—not yet loaded Time, Space, and Substantiality. Simultaneity removes the interval between cause and effect; it does not remove the ordering that makes one of them the cause. The timeless contact therefore inherits a contact burden rather than a contradiction: how the atemporal relation grounds a concrete changing order remains to be explained, and a concrete operation would incur T, S, and Φ at the operation.

**Depends on:** Ordered Succession (§2.4.6)

Plato set the problem in the *Timaeus*: time is the moving image of eternity. The formulation gave Western metaphysics its longest-running project: to describe a relation between the eternal and the temporal that didn’t collapse one into the other. Augustine inherited the project; Boethius articulated eternity as the complete and simultaneous possession of illimitable life; Aquinas formalized simultaneous causation as the mechanism; Kant sharpened the logical-temporal distinction; Craig, Stump, and Kretzmann refined the apparatus across the last half-century. What simultaneous causation loses across the refinements is the still point: the eternal ground from which the world was supposed to hang. Two and a half millennia of work on the eternity/time contact converge on the same structural conditions the doctrine was designed to hold at arm’s length: simultaneity, relational priority, and donation of being are all structured relations, and the three conditions are what the doctrine was attempting to transcend.

*Convergence.* Each of the four forms concedes the very order it means to extend.

The Kalām traversal treats the past as a finished road Now had to travel down, a spatial metaphor that doesn’t map onto successional order. Oppy’s Hilbert deflation weakens the rearrangement absurdities without settling every argument against an infinite past, and any finite past boundary is a feature within T rather than an event outside it.

The contingency-of-the-whole move concedes a necessary framework and then misassigns member-level contingency to it, committing, where the whole is treated as a further thing, the fallacy of composition Hume and Edwards diagnosed.

The PSR appeal either presupposes ∅ as a contrast Nature forecloses or, in its Big-Conjunctive-Fact form, demands an external necessary explainer the PSR split alone doesn’t deliver (§8.2.1). That leaves the personal-ground variant to the burdens of §10.1.4 and §8.2.1, with sufficient reason bottoming out where alternatives run out.

The *per se* series relocates the demand from the beginning of the order to its present dependence, and inherits the contact question in place of the traversal one: simultaneity removes the interval between cause and effect but not the ordering that makes one of them the cause, and Morriston’s point stands that an eternal sufficient cause entails an eternal effect.

What the argument contests is only the step beyond that opening concession: the assumption that the order through which sequences run is itself a sequence, that the language of causation lifts from elements to their ground, and that the call for a first cause can be satisfied by anything other than what makes calls, causes, and sequences possible in the first place. The regress objector runs on Nature while asking what Nature rests on. It doesn’t rest on anything; it is what makes resting on possible at all.

### 10.1.6 The Divine Conservation Argument
Two traditions agree that things persist and disagree about why. The classical theist holds that no contingent thing keeps itself in being for an instant: existence must be conserved, moment to moment, by a being that holds it there, on pain of annihilation. The existential-inertia theorist denies the dependence: a thing that exists tends to remain in existence on its own, absent a sufficient destroyer, and needs no concurrent sustainer to persist. This book sides with the inertialist on the narrower conclusion that mere continuation doesn’t itself establish a concurrent actualizer, while rejecting brute persistence as an explanation. Φ (the retention of identity across an interval) states what persistence consists in. That constitutive account closes the supposed gap in persistence itself; whether a further sustaining explanation is required is a distinct grounding question, not something Φ settles by definition.

The conservationist case is Thomist in origin. Aquinas holds that God’s causality is required not only to bring things into being but to keep them there: creatures stand to God as the air stands to the sun’s illumination, ceasing the instant the influx ceases (*ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.104.1; *De Potentia* (1265–1266) 1932, q.5 a.1). Freddoso (“God’s General Concurrence with Secondary Causes,” 1991; and the 1994 sequel 1994) reconstructs the medieval taxonomy and defends the concurrentist reading on which divine sustaining is required for every created effect. The taxonomy runs three ways: mere conservationism (God conserves things in being but creatures produce their own effects), concurrentism (each created effect is produced by God and creature together), and occasionalism (God is the only real cause, creatures mere occasions for his acting). Feser (*Aquinas* 2009; *Five Proofs of the Existence of God* 2017) presses the demand through act and potency: a thing’s existing at each moment is a potency that must be actualized by something already actual, terminating in Pure Act. Against the demand stands the existential-inertia thesis. Beaudoin, Schmid, and Schmid and Linford argue that persistence is the default state of concrete objects, and that the conservationist owes a positive argument the tradition hasn’t supplied (“The World’s Continuance: Divine Conservation or Existential Inertia?” 2007; “Existential Inertia and the Aristotelian Proof,” 2021; *Existential Inertia and Classical Theistic Proofs* 2022). Kvanvig and McCann (“Divine Conservation and the Persistence of the World,” 1988) hold the conservationist line with a counter-challenge: what grounds a thing’s continuing to exist from one moment to the next, they ask, if not a sustaining cause? The structural account answers that question without adopting either side’s location for the ground.

*First.* The conservationist argument runs on a hidden premise: that continued existence is a kind of change, a fresh actualization at each moment, a coming-to-be repeated. Feser’s act/potency version makes the premise explicit: existence-now is a potency, and a potency requires a concurrent actualizer. Grant the framework and the conclusion follows; the demand is only as strong as the premise that persistence is a transition. It isn’t. A transition is a passage from one state to another. Mere continued existence need not be a fresh transition, although a persisting thing may undergo many qualitative changes while remaining the same thing. The conservationist must therefore argue that existing at a later time is a continuously derived effect, not simply infer that persistence as such is the absence of all change. The act/potency machinery earns its concurrent cause where there is becoming to account for; applied to mere continuation it manufactures a becoming that isn’t there and then requires a cause to sustain the manufactured becoming. Continuation isn’t continuous becoming. Nothing crosses from potency to act in a thing’s simply remaining what it is, and so nothing is required to drive the crossing.

**[Proposition]**

**Continuation Is Not Becoming** · *Proposition*

The act/potency demand for a concurrent sustainer is only as strong as its hidden premise: that continued existence is a fresh actualization repeated at each moment, a transition. It is not. A transition is a passage from one state to another; mere continuation need not be one. The sun-and-illumination analogy imports exactly this picture and holds only if continued being is an effect of the relevant kind. Illumination is a process; existence is not, and nothing is required to sustain what was never becoming.

**Depends on:** Ontological Identity (§2.6.8)

The simultaneous-causation machinery the Thomist offers to make the sustaining concurrent rather than prior is taken up at §10.1.5. The point here is upstream of it: mere continuation supplies no transition-effect that requires concurrent actualization. Whether existence is nevertheless a continuously derived effect remains the next question.

This defeats the act/potency form of the demand, but not every form of it. The concurrentist need not say that persistence is a becoming at all. Freddoso’s continuous-creation reading (1991; 1994) treats created existence as a continuously-derived *effect*: dependent at every instant on a sustaining cause, yet with no transition, nothing crossing from potency to act, no becoming to drive. So construed, the demand never leans on the transition premise and survives its denial, but it survives as a demand for a *ground*, in virtue of what the thing exists now, not for a cause of change, and a grounding demand is met later rather than here.

Two replies converge on it. The ground the concurrentist places in an external sustainer is given a constitutive analysis one level down by Φ (the second move below), but a continuously-deriving sustainer isn’t thereby shown redundant: excluding it requires an additional argument that the constitutive account exhausts the relevant explanatory demand.

And independently, whatever fills the deriver role is bound by what that role requires. A continuous derivation is a way something stands to something else: source-direction, a source/recipient distinction, and a carrier across which the deriving holds. Way–Possibility Convertibility (§3.2) fixes the determinate difference of that way. Its asserted asymmetry supplies directed order, and a derivation that actually obtains requires a bearer or realizer. The immediate burden is therefore generic order, difference, and bearing—not yet, from the word *way* alone, full T∧S∧Φ. The Chapter 2 structural arguments carry that further type-level attribution wherever the sustaining relation is claimed as concrete operation.

That doesn’t eliminate the sustainer, and doesn’t need to: it places the sustaining claim under the generic content the classical specification was built to hold it beyond. Where the claim is one of concrete continuous operation, the Chapter 2 structural bridge places its operation within the Conditions; where it is instead recast as a merely atemporal dependence, the account still owes the contact by which that dependence reaches concrete effects. This is the section’s own inversion run a second time, now on the deriver rather than on the persisting thing. Whether anything answers to that specification at all is a further question, taken up at §11.1; the present result doesn’t wait on it and isn’t weakened if that verdict is resisted. The transition form fails here; the continuous-effect form is relocated here and pressed there.

*Second.* Conceding that persistence isn’t a transition doesn’t end the matter, and the most precise opponent presses past it. Schmid’s question isn’t “what changes a persisting thing?” but “in virtue of what does it persist rather than not?”, a demand for a ground, not for a cause of change. Schmid and Linford (2022) are right that the demand can’t be waved off: a thing’s continuing to exist is a fact about it, and facts about what is have grounds. The existential-inertia theorist who answers “it just does: persistence is the default” has named the fact to be explained and called it an explanation. The structural account doesn’t take that exit.

Φ provides a constitutive analysis of persistence: persistence consists in the relevant retention or continuity of identity across an interval (§2.6). That answers what persistence is. It doesn’t, merely by definition, answer the conservationist’s distinct explanatory question of why this particular thing continues rather than ceases; treating the constitutive analysis as a sufficient sustaining explanation would beg that question. This is deeper than any contingent disposition the object carries (deeper than a tendency-to-persist that might be present or absent, masked or triggered) because Φ is the condition under which the object is a determinate something at all, at either moment.

The conservationist is right that persistence is grounded and not brute; the inertialist is right that mere continuation doesn’t require a concurrent sustainer. Both put the ground outside the persisting thing: the theist in a sustaining cause, the inertialist’s critics in a missing one. The constitutive ground is one level down, in the structural condition any persisting thing already instantiates by being a thing across time. This is the book’s inversion performed at the site of conservation: the feature the tradition reaches for (a sustaining ground beneath contingent existence) is real, and isn’t what the tradition takes it to be.

*Third.* Schmid’s modal-collapse instinct supplies a reply available to the opponent. If persistence is grounded in Φ, and Φ is necessary (the book argues exactly this) then is the persistence of every particular thing necessary too? If the ground can’t fail, and the ground is what holds the thing in being, then the thing can’t fail to persist, and the contingency of the world collapses into necessity. The worry is the existential-inertia analogue of the modal-collapse argument Schmid presses against divine simplicity, and it is the one objection a structural ground must answer or forfeit the field.

It doesn’t go through, and the reason is a distinction the book has already drawn. The necessity of Φ is the necessity of the condition (that whatever persists does so by retaining identity across an interval), not the necessity of any particular persister’s retaining it. The level-distinction is fixed at §2.9.4: that the conditions of contingency are necessary doesn’t make the contingent facts they condition necessary; the framework within which things come and go can’t itself come or go, while the things within it still do. The Constitutive Grounding Non-Propagation lemma (§8.2.5) is the grounding-theoretic statement of that same distinction rather than a second defense: a constitutive ground hands its modal status to the *condition* it grounds, never to the particular actualizations that satisfy it. It is established there for the necessity of change: there □(T∧S∧Φ) and □◇C aren’t ground and grounded but one fact under two readings, so the necessary possibility of change carries its necessity by identity, not by transmission across a grounding relation. What the conditions ground *constitutively, not productively* are the particular changes, with the necessity propagating to none of them (□◇C, not □C). The persistence case runs that constitutive half of the schema once more, with one shift worth marking: at §8.2.5 the constitutive ground bears on each particular change, whereas here it bears on persistence under a constitutive *condition*, leaving the contingent de re fact (*that any particular thing persists*) outside the reach of the necessity.

Φ grounds persistence *constitutively*, not productively: it doesn’t produce each thing’s continuation as an effect produces its output, which is the only way necessity would propagate Spinoza-fashion; it is what continuing-to-be *consists in*, the identity-retention condition any persister instantiates simply by being a thing across the interval.

So the □ attaches to the conditional, read de dicto (a claim about the proposition, not the thing), □(if x persists, x persists by Φ): necessarily, whatever persists does so by retaining identity across an interval. It doesn’t attach to the de re □(x persists): no particular thing’s continuing is thereby made necessary. Φ’s being necessary no more makes this oak’s persistence necessary than the necessity of the conditions of value makes any particular thing valuable of necessity. The oak persists by Φ while it persists, and ceases when its identity-retention fails.

**[Proposition]**

**Necessity Passes to the Condition, Not the Persister** · *Proposition*

The reply available to the conservationist is a modal-collapse worry: if persistence is grounded in Substantiality and Substantiality is necessary, then every particular thing persists necessarily, and the contingency of the world is gone. It does not go through, and the reason is a level-distinction already drawn. What is necessary is the *condition*—that whatever persists does so by retaining identity across an interval—not that any given persister retains it. What things come and go within cannot itself come or go, while the things within it still do. Substantiality grounds persistence **constitutively rather than productively**: it does not produce each continuation as a cause produces an effect, which is the only route by which necessity would propagate Spinoza-fashion. It is what continuing-to-be consists in.

**Depends on:** Necessity Permits Contingency (§2.9.4)

*Related positions.* Three positions also locate persistence in what the thing is, and the account must not blur into any of them. Dispositional essentialism grounds persistence in a first-order power to persist: a disposition the object carries, one that could be present or absent, masked or triggered. Φ isn’t such a power: a disposition is a further feature of an already-individuated thing, whereas Φ is the condition under which there is an individuated thing at all, at either end of the interval, to bear features.

Beaudoin’s naturalist inertia (2007) reaches the right conclusion (no sustainer) by treating persistence as a brute default; it differs from the structural account exactly as the brute inertialist of the second move does, by leaving ungrounded what the structural account grounds.

And Spinozist necessitarianism grounds persistence in the necessity of substance, paying for it with the collapse just blocked: it runs the ground’s necessity straight into the persister, making every continuation necessary. The structural account takes the necessity of the ground together with the level-distinction, so the ground is necessary while the persister isn’t. The difference from each neighbor is one difference told three ways: Φ is a condition, not a first-order feature; the ground is structural, not brute; and the necessity in play is the necessity of that condition, not of whatever satisfies it.

The result feeds back into the case against the classical sustainer. The conservationist demand is supposed to deliver a being that does the sustaining. Once persistence is grounded constitutively, continuation isn’t automatically a fresh actualization, and Φ’s necessity doesn’t necessitate any particular persister. Whether an additional sustaining explanation is still required remains open: constitutive analysis answers what persistence is, not why this thing continues. The argument takes up the being the conservationist names; it doesn’t close a determinate atemporal contact merely by showing that mere continuation isn’t re-creation. The conservation argument needs a becoming to sustain, and that half fails here. The fuller engagements with the being the conservationist names are at §10.2.1 (the simplicity that is supposed to make it the unconditioned ground), §10.1.5 (the simultaneous causation supposed to make its sustaining concurrent), and §10.1.4 (the foundation argument that reasons toward it). The narrower result those depend on is that continued existence doesn’t, by itself, hand the theist the fact the argument needs explained.

*What holds.* The existential-inertia debate is run between a conservationism that grounds persistence in a sustaining God and an inertialism that grounds it in nothing at all. The same move answers both. Persistence isn’t a transition, so it needs no concurrent actualizer of a becoming that isn’t there (against the conservationist); but it isn’t brute either, so the inertialist’s default isn’t the last word (against its critics). Persistence is grounded in Φ, the retention of identity across an interval, which is deeper than any disposition and which doesn’t, by its own necessity, necessitate what it grounds (§2.9.4; Constitutive Grounding Non-Propagation lemma, §8.2.5). The local result is that Φ states the constitutive condition under which persistence counts as persistence and that its necessity doesn’t necessitate any particular persister. Whether a further sustaining explanation is required remains a separate grounding dispute; this section blocks the inference from mere continuation to continuous re-creation but doesn’t settle every conservationist formulation by definition alone.

### 10.1.7 The Degrees of Perfection Argument
A fire is hotter than a stone in the sun, and the stone is hotter than the earth beneath it. Heat comes in degrees, and the degrees aren’t a projection: one thing really is warmer than another. Aquinas reads that kind of gradation as already pointing past the things that have it. Among beings some are more and some less good, true, noble; more and less are said of different things according as they resemble, in their different ways, something which is the maximum; there is therefore something truest, best, noblest, and consequently something which is uttermost being; and this maximum is the cause of all that is, of all goodness, and of every other perfection (*ST* Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.2.3). The Fourth Way isn’t a ranking of creatures with a gold medal at the top. It is an inference from participation. A thing that has a perfection only by sharing in it can’t be what makes that perfection available to be shared; limited instances require an unlimited source.

The argument inherits its causal step from Aristotle: the maximum in a genus is the cause of all that belongs to the genus (*Metaphysics* Aristotle (4th c. BCE) 1984, II.1). Wippel (Wippel 2000) reconstructs the Way as a proof from transcendental gradation—being, goodness, and truth convert, so a maximum of goodness is a maximum of being, and that maximum causes the participated instances rather than merely topping their scale. Feser (*Aquinas*, Feser 2009; *Five Proofs*, Feser 2017) presses the same participation structure through act and potency: a limited act of being is the actualization of a potency, and a potency is actualized only by what is already actual in that respect, terminating in *ipsum esse subsistens*. Kerr (Kerr 2015) develops the *De Ente* form of the move, on which the real distinction between essence and *esse* in creatures requires a cause whose essence is its *esse*. Oppy (Oppy 2006) and Sobel (Sobel 2004) treat perfection-arguments as failing to license the step from a scale of degrees to a separately existing maximum that causes them. The present section grants the scale and asks what the causal step still owes.

Applied here, the argument concedes graded being and asks what the grades are grades of. If they are grades of a perfection whose maximum lies outside the three Conditions (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance), the account has missed a ground. Three forms of the move take up that claim: the scale-and-maximum, participation in *esse*, and the Augustinian intellect that holds eternal truths. The replies that follow argue that each still specifies the maximum as a cause of the grades, and that causing grades is already a grounding relation.

*First.* The scale-and-maximum form, regimented, runs:

1. *Gradation.* Some beings are more and some less good, true, noble, real.

2. *Maximum as measure.* More and less are said by reference to a maximum: a thing is hotter insofar as it approaches fire.

3. *Maximum as cause.* The maximum in a genus is the cause of all that belongs to the genus; therefore there is a maximum of being that causes whatever has being by degree, and this is God.

The fire illustration is Aquinas’s own, and it does real work. Heat has a paradigm, and nearer approaches to the paradigm are hotter. What the illustration also shows is that fire, the warmer body, and the cooler body occupy one thermal order. They are distinct; the ranking has a direction; each persists as the bearer of the heat it has. Remove those roles and “more hot” has no content: there are no relata to compare, no order in which one exceeds the other, and nothing that *has* the degree. Gradation isn’t evidence of a cause outside comparison. It is comparison at work.

A defender of the Way will say that fire is only a genus-maximum, a hottest among bodies, whereas the Fourth Way wants a maximum of being itself, not of heat. The distinction is real, and it doesn’t remove the structural demand. Even a maximum of being is specified, in the proof, as the *cause* of graded beings. Causing those grades is a relation: source and recipient are nonidentical, dependence runs one way, and the relation determinately obtains. Those are the thin roles the necessary-foundation floor already required at §10.1.4. The proof can’t keep the causal step while refusing the floor, because the causal step is what the floor spells out. A maximum that measured without causing wouldn’t be the Fourth Way’s God; it would be a top mark on a scale, and a mark isn’t a ground.

*Second.* Participation in *esse* is the form on which the Way’s defenders rest the causal step. Creatures have being by participation; God has being by essence. A participated act is received, contracted, limited by the essence that receives it; an unreceived act is unlimited, and only an unreceived act can be the source from which the received acts derive (Wippel 2000; Kerr 2015; Feser 2017). The analysis of limited instances is granted. A thing whose being is really distinct from its essence does need an account of why it is, and the tradition’s account is that it receives *esse*.

What participation names, so specified, is a grounding relation between participant and source. The source donates being; the participant receives it; the donation is asymmetric and determinate, or it isn’t donation. The floor at §10.1.4 is exactly that demand: a ground must exhibit asymmetric grounding-order, relational distinction from what is grounded, and identity-retention across the relation. Participation-in-*esse* meets the demand by occupying it. It doesn’t yet prove clock-time, spatial extension, or ordinary causal persistence in the source; those loaded types wait on independent arguments. It does show that the existence-proof’s own causal vocabulary incurs the role-level floor rather than exempting the source from it.

A further pressure, already drawn at §10.1.4, bears on the attempt to keep the source extra-structural by subtracting determination. The Argument from Limits treats every determination as a defect a maximal foundation must shed. Determination isn’t a privation. To be the cause of *these* grades rather than of nothing is already to be this and not that: source rather than recipient, donor of being rather than of its absence. A maximum stripped of every such determination isn’t a more perfect cause. It is no longer specified as a cause at all, which is the ∅ the section on limits named under a superlative heading.

*Third.* Feser’s Augustinian proof (Feser 2017) is a cousin rather than a restatement. It infers from eternal truths, numbers, universals, and graded being to a divine intellect in which they subsist: the degrees of truth require a maximum of truth, and abstract objects require a mind that isn’t itself an inhabitant of the changing order. The Fourth Way’s transcendental convertibility (being, goodness, truth) is what makes the cousinship real. The intellect that holds those truths still stands in a determinate relation to what it knows. Omniscience covers what-is-the-case, and what-is-the-case has distinguishable contents; the knowing relation is asymmetric, or it isn’t knowing. That is the role-level floor again, not yet a claim that a timeless knower intrinsically instantiates loaded Time. The mode of cognition can be non-discursive, a single act rather than a sequence of thoughts, and the represented contents and the knowing relation remain articulated. The *tota simul* and ET-simultaneity variants of that act are engaged at §10.2.3; the *actus purus* form of the intellect’s simplicity is engaged at §10.2.1. What this section needs is only that an existence-proof from graded truth still specifies a knower-of-grades, and that specification is a grounding relation rather than an escape from one.

The a priori cousin of the same maximum is the modal ontological argument at §10.1.1: there the maximum is reached from the possibility of maximal greatness, not from observed degrees. The two proofs share a destination and not a route. Perfection as a divine attribute, once a bearer is already claimed, is engaged at §11.2.4.

**[Proposition]**

**The Maximum Inherits the Scale** · *Proposition*

The Fourth Way infers from genuine degrees to a maximum that causes them. Gradation is already comparison among distinct bearers in a directed order, and the causal step specifies a source–recipient relation with those same roles. The maximum therefore inherits the scale it was meant to explain rather than standing outside it. Subtracting every determination to keep the source extra-structural removes the content that let it be the cause of these grades. Loaded Time, Space, and Substantiality are not established here; the role-level floor is.

**Depends on:** Determination Is Not a Limit (§10.1.4)

Aquinas’s Five Ways are five arguments, not one, and each is met where it actually reasons. The First and Second Ways—from motion and from efficient causation—are the *per se* series of §10.1.5; what it would be for God to cause, as an attribute, is engaged at §11.7.2. The Third Way—from possibility and necessity—is the contingency wing of §10.1.4 and §10.1.5, with its modal step met at §2.9.4. The Fourth Way is this section. The Fifth Way—from the governance of natural things toward ends—is the teleological ancestor of §10.1.9 and §10.1.11, and the teleology of living systems is also the terrain of §4.8. Swinburne’s probabilistic comparison is a different kind of argument and is engaged at §10.1.8.

*Convergence.* Each form grants the degrees and spends them on a causal relation.

The scale-and-maximum form treats more and less as evidence of a paradigm outside comparison, while the fire illustration works only because the paradigm and the instances already share an order of distinct, ranked, persisting bearers.

Participation in *esse* supplies a genuine analysis of limited instances, and the analysis is a grounding relation: donor and recipient, asymmetric dependence, determinate obtaining. That is the floor already required at §10.1.4 of any foundation specified as a cause.

The Augustinian intellect holds graded truth by knowing it, and knowing is still a relation to distinguishable contents. The mode of the act can be denied its sequence; the relation can’t be denied its terms.

The Fourth Way therefore doesn’t fail as a description of graded being. It fails, at the role level, as an existence-proof of a maximum specified as extra-structural cause. The grades are real. The cause of the grades, as the proof itself writes it, already occupies the comparative order those grades are.

### 10.1.8 The Simplicity Argument
The Swinburnean case concedes more ground than any other contemporary theist move: not a denial that the structural roles are present, but a bet that a simpler hypothesis explains them better. Richard Swinburne develops a mathematically precise case for theism in the analytic tradition. *The Coherence of Theism* (Swinburne 1977) establishes that the concept of God is internally consistent. *The Existence of God* (Swinburne 1979; 2nd ed. Swinburne 2004) argues that, given the evidence of the natural order, consciousness, religious experience, and the moral phenomena, the posterior probability of theism (its probability after the evidence is taken into account, in the technical Bayesian sense) exceeds one-half. *Simplicity as Evidence of Truth* (Swinburne 1997), his Aquinas Lecture at Marquette, spells out the underlying epistemology: simpler hypotheses have higher prior probability as a matter of methodological necessity, not sentimental preference. The argument differs in kind from the Five Ways: Swinburne doesn’t present a deductive demonstration of God’s existence; he offers a probabilistic comparison. On his proposed metric, the evidence favors a single infinite mind.

Swinburne doesn’t deny the structural roles are present, doesn’t deny they admit coherent formulation, doesn’t deny the argument for their necessity has some force. He argues rather that a divine mind is a simpler, more probable explanation for why the structure obtains at all. The argument is probabilistic rather than structural, and comparative rather than exemptive. Swinburne (Swinburne 2004) argues that a single infinite mind, a being with a single, infinite degree of each positive property (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness), constitutes a simpler hypothesis than the complex, multi-component physical universe. By Occam’s razor, the simpler hypothesis has higher prior probability as an explanatory ground. The physical universe, with its many particular constants, particles, and forces, is highly complex by comparison. The theistic hypothesis is therefore assigned greater comparative parsimony.

Applied to the present argument, this becomes a challenge to its explanatory sufficiency. Swinburne doesn’t deny the three Conditions are present; he argues they are better explained by positing a simpler posterior ground than by accepting them as brute or self-grounding. If the structural proof is valid and its premises are true, comparative simplicity can’t lower its conclusion’s probability. Swinburne’s case instead pressures the premises or explanatory sufficiency of the structural account: it argues that, given contested background assumptions and evidence, theism is the better overall explanation. The move requires a simplicity metric that operates across ontological levels and favors infinite-mind posits over structural-role posits. If that metric is justified, comparative probability would favor theism without directly refuting the structural derivation.

The contemporary literature on simplicity runs thick, and the picture is less favorable to Swinburne than his standing in the field might suggest. On simplicity as a truth-indicator: Sober’s *Ockham’s Razors* (Sober 2015) develops a sustained philosophical analysis of simplicity’s role in scientific inference, and concludes that simplicity functions only relative to background assumptions, never as an unconditional criterion. Huemer (Huemer 2009) presses the deflation further: the standard rationales for parsimony hold in scientific settings but fail to transfer, leaving ontological simplicity without evidential value in typical philosophical contexts.

The objections to Swinburne then divide. Mackie’s *The Miracle of Theism* (Mackie 1982) presses the Bayesian prior-assignment problem: prior probabilities are stipulated, not derived, and Swinburne’s stipulations do the theological work before the calculus runs. Philipse’s *God in the Age of Science?* (Philipse 2012) presses the scientific-methodology angle: Swinburne’s criterion is alien to the actual practice of inference in physics. Oppy’s *Arguing about Gods* (Oppy 2006) catalogs the failures of the probabilistic arguments across their range. Dawkins’s *The God Delusion* (Dawkins 2006) offers the rhetorical version of the deflation (a God who continuously monitors and controls every particle in the universe cannot be simple) whose analytic substance was already present in Mackie and later refined by Philipse. The present reply agrees with Sober on simplicity’s background-relative operation and with Philipse on the scientific-methodology point, and adds what neither alone specifies: the background relative to which Swinburne’s simplicity claim would have to be evaluated is the three Conditions themselves, and that constrains what the comparison can rank.

The argument turns against the necessity claim of §2.5 and the exhaustion claim of §2.6. If simplicity favors theism over structural necessity, the modal conclusion of the argument is pressured through its premises by comparative probability even if its logic is sound. The reply runs on two levels, and the order matters.

The load-bearing level concerns the *candidate*, not the comparison. Whatever wins the parsimony contest is offered as the ground of the structural order, and being a ground of any kind requires the minimal floor established at §10.1.4: asymmetric grounding-order, relational distinction from what is grounded, and identity-retention across the grounding relation, which is T∧S∧Φ read at the structural level. A single infinite mind that grounds the roles thereby instantiates them; it can’t be the simpler thing the roles reduce to, because it already presupposes them. This level says nothing about who performs the comparison, so it’s untouched by the rejoinder that the book’s own case for the roles is equally an exercise of embedded reasoning.

The second level concerns the comparison itself, is genuinely weaker, and is placed second for that reason: comparative parsimony ranks candidates within a fixed background of alternatives, and it has no purchase on a background weighed against its own absence, because there is no coherent contrast class in which the roles fail to obtain (§2.7). Without an articulable alternative, the razor has no candidate against which to compare the roles. This doesn’t exempt the roles from rational support; the transcendental case of §2.1–2.6 is offered as that support. The narrower claim is that comparative parsimony is inapplicable here because it requires a set of alternatives among which the structural roles aren’t candidates.

Three forms of the move take up the objection: one-mind parsimony, cross-level simplicity, and Bayesian refinement.

*First.* The one-mind parsimony move holds that an infinite mind has a single unified essence (one being with one set of infinite properties) while the present account posits three distinct roles each requiring separate grounding. Occam’s Razor, the objector presses, favors the one over the three: infinity in a single subject is simpler than multiplicity across structural roles.

The objection misapplies Occam’s Razor by confusing ontological levels. The razor governs explanatory entities within a background of structural possibilities: it operates by comparing candidate explanations of contingent facts against a stable background against which simplicity judgments have meaning. It is coherent to ask whether electrons or fields are the simpler posit for explaining electromagnetic phenomena, because both are candidates within structure and the simplicity comparison has a stable background. It isn’t coherent to apply the same criterion to structure itself: structure isn’t a candidate explanation within a background of structural possibilities; it is the background.

**[Proposition]**

**Background, Not Candidate** · *Proposition*

Occam’s Razor compares candidate explanations against a stable background of structural possibilities, which is why it can weigh electrons against fields. It cannot weigh structure itself against its absence, because there is no coherent contrast class in which the roles fail to obtain. With no alternative to compare against, the roles are not one posit among rivals but the condition any posit, mind included, already occupies.

**Depends on:** Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2)

The proposed comparison between one mind and three roles also doesn’t apply: §10.1.4 presents the three Conditions not as three independent posits but as one structural fact under three categorial descriptions.

Actual simplicity comparisons are structured cognitive acts, but that act-side fact doesn’t prevent them from evaluating hypotheses about the structure of reality. The stronger reply must concern the candidate and the metric: whether the divine-ground hypothesis already incurs structural commitments, and whether any background-neutral simplicity measure favors it. Occam’s razor compares entities within a shared background; it doesn’t independently evaluate that background against its absence.

*Second.* Cross-level simplicity extends the proposed comparison across ontological levels. On this version, a single infinite mind is simpler than the structural conjunction even as an ultimate explanation, and the question is whether the mind or the structural conditions constitute the better ultimate posit.

The candidate-side problem remains. To rank the mind against the structural conditions is still to offer the mind as an ultimate ground, and any ground carries the role-level requirements identified at §10.1.4: asymmetric grounding order, relational distinction from what is grounded, and identity-retention across the relation. A grounding mind can’t lack those roles while remaining a determinate ground. The cross-level comparison therefore treats as an alternative to the structural conditions a candidate that already instantiates them. Swinburne’s proposal specifies a configuration of the roles rather than an alternative to them. The additional fact that the comparison is performed by a structurally embedded reasoner is secondary; the principal issue concerns the commitments of the proposed ground.

*Third.* The Bayesian refinement turns the comparison probabilistic. The prior probability of the theistic hypothesis, given its internal simplicity and explanatory scope, exceeds the prior probability of a necessary structural architecture; updating on the evidence of a contingent-looking, complex physical universe, the posterior favors the infinite-mind hypothesis. The inference is probabilistic rather than deductive, and its conclusion depends on the assigned priors and likelihoods. That dependency runs into the theorem sharpened at §2.9.5, Possibility Precedes Probability: distributing a prior across “theism” and “necessary structural architecture” as rival possibilities already presupposes both are live members of one possibility space, and no amount of Bayesian updating over that space substitutes for showing the space was rightly drawn.

The Bayesian refinement’s real weakness isn’t that priors are computed by embedded reasoners; pressed that way the point would prove too much, sweeping in the book’s own reasoning along with Swinburne’s. The weakness is that the prior assigned to “the theistic hypothesis” is already doing the theological work before the calculus runs, as the comparison-class problem addressed later makes plain.

Set the prior-assignment problem aside and the candidate-side reply still binds: for an infinite mind to be a coherent posit, that mind must stand in determinate cognitive and grounding relations to what it knows and what it grounds. Its omniscience covers what-is-the-case, and what-is-the-case has structural content: distinguishable objects, temporally structured states of affairs, persisting carriers of becoming.

The mind’s mode of cognition need not be discursive (running through premises and conclusions in succession, the way a finite intellect does) for the point to bind. Even non-discursive cognition, where the divine intellect grasps all things in a single timeless act rather than thinking them through step by step, cognizes content that is structurally articulated; and the grounding relation a mind bears to what it grounds is itself asymmetric, sustained, and obtaining between distinguishable relata. Aquinas’s intuitive cognition, the Boethian *tota simul*, and the Stump–Kretzmann ET-simultaneity are engaged at length in §10.2.3, which shows each variant requires structural conditions through the relations it bears to what it knows and what it grounds even where it denies them in the *mode* of cognition. The represented contents and the grounding relation are structurally articulated even if the mind’s mode of cognition is non-discursive.

That result must not be shifted into a claim about the mind’s intrinsic constitution. From the fact that a timeless knower represents temporal, spatial, or physical contents, it doesn’t follow that the knower intrinsically instantiates any of the three Conditions in loaded form; representation, represented content, and instantiation are different relations.

What does follow is the role-level floor: the hypothesis includes determinate contents and an asymmetric grounding relation between distinguishable relata, and it must explain how a simple subject bears those contents and that relation. This doesn’t yield a theory-neutral numerical simplicity ranking, because Swinburne counts properties and laws under a different metric. It does undercut any claim that the divine hypothesis is *automatically* simpler before the metric, the treatment of relational commitments, and the background assumptions are defended. The classical rejoinder that the divine mind has no intrinsic composition at all is the *actus purus* line; it’s taken up at §10.2.1. The reply here needs only the conceded content-and-relation floor and leaves any stronger constitution claim to that site.

The infinite-mind hypothesis is therefore not shown cheaper merely by counting one subject. It carries articulated representational and grounding commitments whose weight depends on the defended simplicity metric. The present argument doesn’t redescribe the timeless cognizer itself as a maximally rich T/S/Φ configuration.

One underlying premise of Swinburne’s cumulative case deserves direct engagement in this section. Swinburne holds that personal explanation (explanation in terms of an agent’s intentions) is an irreducibly distinct form of explanation, not reducible to structural or scientific explanation, and at least as fundamental as structural explanation (*The Existence of God*, Swinburne 2004, ch. 2; *Mind, Brain and Free Will*, Swinburne 2013, ch. 1). The premise carries weight independent of the simplicity comparison: even granting the structural-conditions reply already considered, if personal explanation is irreducibly distinct from structural explanation, then an irreducibly personal ground remains a live explanatory terminus. The book’s reply concedes the irreducibility claim while denying the entailment. That personal explanation is irreducible to the vocabulary of physics is true: intentions aren’t fully translatable into particle velocities or field configurations. Ordinary personal explanation involves an agent, an intention directed toward a distinguishable outcome, and continuity between intending and acting. A timeless theist will deny that intention is formed across time. The role-level point survives—content, direction, and explanatory bearing remain—but the loaded temporal and persistence types can’t be inferred from personal explanation alone. The irreducibility of personal explanation to physics is compatible with the three Conditions being necessary conditions for personal explanation to occur. Swinburne’s canonical examples (the agent who freely decides, who selects among possibilities, whose intentions cause outcomes) each instantiate the structural conditions in the act of being a personal explanation. The irreducibility claim survives; what it doesn’t establish is that the irreducible personal level is free of the three Conditions or prior to them. A personal explanation that instantiates the three Conditions in its own performance isn’t an alternative ground to the structural conditions but a high-order configuration of them.

A separate line of pressure runs through the comparison class itself. Swinburne ranks one infinite mind against the complex physical universe and concludes the mind is simpler. The comparison class is incomplete relative to other alternative forms of theism. Process theism (Whitehead 1929; Hartshorne 1948) posits one dipolar deity whose abstract pole carries fewer essentially distinct attributes than the classical theist mind. Panentheism (Clayton 1997; Peacocke 2007) posits one substance with internal differentiation rather than a divine substance externally related to a created one, reducing the number of fundamental ontological categories. Open theism (Hasker 1989; Pinnock et al. 1994) drops the strong omniscience condition that does heavy work in the Swinburnean parameter count. On Swinburne’s own metric (fewer essentially distinct properties scoring as simpler) several sibling theisms score equal or better than the Swinburnean theism his prior assignments single out, and the calculus doesn’t settle among them without theological commitments that precede it. The simplicity case, pressed honestly through its full class of rivals, narrows to a contest among theisms rather than a contest between theism and structural necessity. Mackie’s (Mackie 1982) prior-assignment objection sharpens here: the priors Swinburne assigns to “the theistic hypothesis” elide which theism, and the elision does the disputed theological work before the Bayesian calculus runs.

A related argument replaces the Bayesian framework with an appeal to aesthetic simplicity: simpler ultimate posits are treated as intrinsically more credible than complex ones, independently of probability calculus. Huemer (Huemer 2009) argues from within the parsimony literature that this aesthetic rationale has no evidential value in ontological disputes. The structural reply explains why the judgment may nevertheless appear compelling. Aesthetic simplicity is an assessment made by embedded reasoners, structurally configured to find the simpler posit more satisfying because structural cognition naturally compresses. The aesthetic judgment isn’t a view from outside structure; it is a feature of how structure evaluates itself. Another kindred is Dawkins’s (Dawkins 2006) inverse parsimony argument: a mind capable of monitoring every particle can’t be simple. It arrives at an adjacent conclusion by a different way. The present reply sharpens it: not only is the mind not simple in the information-theoretic sense, but its simplicity is uncomputable without the structural background, and the structural background is what the simplicity claim was meant to explain.

*A note on direction.* The reply doesn’t depend on which direction the parsimony comparison is run. Oppy (*Arguing about Gods*, Oppy 2006; *The Best Argument against God*, Oppy 2013; *Atheism and Agnosticism*, Oppy 2018a) develops the naturalistic counterpart: where Swinburne argues theism wins on parsimony, Oppy argues naturalism wins on the same metric, one ontological category, no additional minds, a necessary-or-brute natural terminus reached without theological posits.

The difference from Oppy’s is at the structural level. Any appeal to parsimony presupposes standards of comparison, and the argument identifies those standards with T∧S∧Φ. The distinction between comparisons within the structural conditions and comparisons of those conditions themselves applies equally to Swinburne’s theistic and Oppy’s naturalistic uses of parsimony. On this account, parsimony can’t settle between the structural conditions and their alleged alternative because the comparison already requires those conditions.

The reply runs at a second layer as well. The candidates being compared are themselves causes (Swinburne’s mind that grounds structure, Oppy’s structure that grounds phenomena), and being-a-cause carries the structural roles at the level claimed throughout: a directed order in which the grounding runs one way rather than the other (T), distinguishable relata for it to run between (S), and something across which the influence is carried (Φ), their co-instantiation following by the Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7). This is the role-level floor rather than the loaded types, and the difference matters here as it did above: the point doesn’t require that either candidate intrinsically instantiate temporal succession or material persistence, and it therefore survives a defender who denies both of the candidate. Neither candidate can be specified as a cause without bearing those roles.

Swinburne’s case is cumulative by design (simplicity sets the prior, and fine-tuning, the existence of consciousness, and the moral phenomena are aggregated toward a posterior exceeding one-half), so dismantling the simplicity wing in isolation would leave the aggregate standing if the other weights did. Each component must therefore be assessed at its own site (fine-tuning at §10.1.9, the PSR at §8.2.1, consciousness and moral awareness elsewhere). Weakening one component lowers the cumulative case, but it doesn’t establish that every remaining evidential weight is zero. The replies are reckoned together at §10.4.

**[Proposition]**

**Parsimony Cannot Weigh Its Own Standard** · *Proposition*

The reply does not depend on which direction the comparison is run: it answers Swinburne, for whom theism wins on parsimony, and Oppy, for whom naturalism does, at the same joint. Any appeal to parsimony presupposes standards of comparison, and those standards are the structural conditions themselves, so parsimony cannot settle between the conditions and an alleged alternative to them—the comparison already runs on what is compared. A second layer closes the same move again. Both candidates are offered as *causes*, and being a cause carries a directed order, distinguishable relata, and something across which influence is carried, at role level rather than as loaded types. Neither candidate can be specified as a cause without bearing the roles. The metric and the things it would weigh run on the same conditions.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7)

*Convergence.* The three forms of the simplicity argument encounter related limitations. Occam’s razor compares candidates against a stable structural background and therefore doesn’t independently compare that background with its absence. Cross-level comparison doesn’t establish the structural conditions as optional, because a grounding mind already carries the asymmetric order, distinction, and identity-retention identified at §10.1.4. The Bayesian refinement depends on a prior assigned to “the theistic hypothesis,” while an infinite mind specified through articulated contents and an asymmetric grounding relation isn’t automatically simpler before the metric and those commitments are defended.

Swinburne’s work is the kind of work only a theist who takes secular philosophy with complete seriousness could produce: at every juncture he accepts the standards of the field and argues the theistic hypothesis wins on those standards. The precision is what lets the reply be precise too. The simpler hypothesis the objector recommends is specified through structured content and a determinate grounding relation, not established as a background-free alternative to structure. Comparative parsimony therefore presupposes the conditions required for the comparison to be formulated and assessed. Hume gives the move its final form in *Dialogues concerning Natural Religion* (posthumous Hume 1779): if a necessary being must be posited at all, the material universe itself is a candidate, and no non-theological consideration disqualifies it. Cleanthes’ suggestion was underspecified in 1779. The specification supplied here: □(T∧S∧Φ). The necessary being Cleanthes proposed as an alternative is identified here with the structural ground that Swinburne’s simplicity comparison was intended to explain.

### 10.1.9 The Fine-Tuning Argument
