Precision is the fine-tuning argument’s wedge. Several fundamental parameters appear to lie in ranges compatible with complex structure that are narrow relative to commonly discussed comparison ranges. The often-cited 10¹²⁰ figure for the cosmological constant primarily expresses the discrepancy between observed vacuum energy and a naive Planck-scale estimate, not straightforwardly the width of a life-permitting interval. The tradition reads the broader sensitivity evidence as evidence of selection and the selection as evidence of a selector. The resulting inference challenges the structural account to say exactly where physical contingency remains once the three Conditions (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) are necessary. The answer can’t be that every physical quantity is fixed by those Conditions; the book derives no such thing. It must distinguish selection of a physical profile from consequences already fixed within that profile. The fine-tuning argument is a single inference (from narrow-window precision of the constants to selection) with two extensions the theist presses when the core inference meets resistance. The reply follows this shape rather than treating the three versions as independent objections.

Beneath all three forms lies a prior question: what alternative configurations and comparison class the probability model is licensed to range over. And beyond the bare inference lies a stronger reading (that the universe isn’t merely life-permitting but life-intended) which separates cleanly from the core argument.

The observation behind the argument isn’t in dispute. The constants of this universe do sit within narrow ranges compatible with complex structure. The account contests the inference from the observation to selection, not the observation itself.

The fine-tuning tradition is the empirical wing of natural theology’s design inheritance. Where Paley’s watchmaker reasons from biological complexity to a designer, the post-Paley inheritors (Collins 2009; Barnes 2012; Swinburne 2004; Plantinga 2011 at selective points) reason from the values of the fundamental physical constants to the same conclusion. Substantial changes in the effective cosmological constant relative to the observed value can prevent galaxies and other complex structures from forming; the exact life-permitting range depends on the model and on which parameters are varied together. Vary the strong force coupling by a few percent and stable atomic nuclei don’t form. The quantitative sensitivities have been catalogued with professional care. What is contested is whether precision of this kind, against the background of no further specification of the alternatives, is genuinely evidence of selection. The naturalist reply has two heads. Anthropic reasoning (Carter 1974; Bostrom 2002) notes that observers can only observe observer-permitting conditions. This supplies a selection effect, not by itself a complete explanation of why any observer-permitting universe exists; its force depends on the cosmological ensemble and observation-selection model adopted. The probabilistic critique (McGrew et al. 2001) argues that the likelihood calculations the theist runs presuppose a measure over an unbounded parameter space for which no canonical measure exists. The present account absorbs both replies and adds a third: the structural Conditions aren’t themselves settings selected from the constant-space, while the physical profile and its profile-defining parameters remain a separate explanatory target.

The challenge bears on §2.4 most directly. T and S, defended there as necessary structural conditions, admit no variation: not because the values of physical constants are fixed at a particular numerical setting, but because the roles T and S discharge are logically prior to anything a numerical setting could register. Fine-tuning compares this configuration to alternative configurations. The comparison is coherent only at a level where ‘configuration’ has content, which is within the structural order. Every alternative configuration the tradition actually proposes bears this out: adjust the cosmological constant, the strong-force coupling, or the mass ratios, and the result is still a configuration with time, space, and substance, merely reset to different values. No fine-tuning proposal on record varies the constants into a setting that lacks one of the three outright—a materially structured, spatially extended world with no temporal dimension at all, say. The tradition’s own imagination never leaves the three Conditions even while treating their numerical settings as free to vary; that silent restriction is itself evidence for where the actual contingency lies.

*The prior question.* Objective chance is downstream of possibility, the direction earned at §2.9.5: positive objective chance presupposes the real possibility of what it weights, and sampling under a model doesn’t by itself deductively establish a wider one. Before assigning a physical chance distribution, one must establish a genuine space of alternative outcomes. A Bayesian confirmation argument can instead use epistemic probabilities over rival hypotheses, but it must still justify its comparison class, priors, and likelihoods. Mere ignorance about whether the constants are necessary doesn’t by itself provide a canonical distribution over their values. This question sits upstream of whether the proposed probabilities can be normalized—made to add up to one: McGrew, McGrew, and Vestrup (McGrew et al. 2001) show that even granting a space of alternatives, no canonical measure over it exists; the prior question asks whether the space has been shown to exist at all.

The proponent has a practiced escape. Probability, they note, need not wait on metaphysics; rational agents assign credences to propositions whose modal status is fixed but unknown all the time. Goldbach’s conjecture is either necessarily true or necessarily false, yet a mathematician may rationally hold it to 0.99 on inductive grounds; so (the move runs) one need not first prove the alternative constants metaphysically possible to spread a credence across them and call the actual values surprising. The escape shows that a Bayesian design argument can use epistemic probabilities without positing an objective chance process that sampled the constants. Rational credences can be evidentially responsive even when the proposition is necessarily true or false. The remaining burden is comparative: the proponent must justify the likelihoods and priors under theism and its rivals, rather than infer an ontic selector directly from an objective frequency distribution. Epistemic probability can support an abductive conclusion, but only through defensible comparative likelihoods; it can’t be treated as if it revealed a literal sampling process over constants.

A second escape runs the other way: perhaps the alternatives only seem possible. Kripke (Kripke 1980) shows that some truths are necessary but knowable only a posteriori (that water is H₂O, that Hesperus is Phosphorus) so that what presents itself as a contingent setting can be a necessary one wearing the appearance of contingency. If the constants are necessary a posteriori, the apparent space of alternatives is an illusion of contingency, and the fine-tuning improbability never gets started. The present account doesn’t lean on this claim, and notes the standing counter: Chalmers (Chalmers 2002) argues from modal rationalism that ideal conceivability does track genuine possibility, so the appearance of contingency can’t be dismissed so cheaply. The dialectic is unsettled, and the account doesn’t rest on settling it. It rests only on the asymmetry the prior question fixes: the burden lies with the proponent to establish that the alternatives are possible in the sense the measure requires, and that burden hasn’t been discharged. The account’s own positive footing is narrower: the three Conditions secure the structural availability of Change, not the necessary actuality of a life-permitting physical profile. Fine-tuning may therefore leave a question about which profile is realized. Whether the observation is evidence for a selector remains to be established; the structural Conditions and the modal availability of every genuine profile aren’t products of selection.

One discipline must be observed in pressing this. The claim isn’t that the numerical values of the constants are necessary: that is a separate and stronger thesis, argued elsewhere and not needed here. The claim is that the three structural Conditions are necessary, while the contingency of the particular numerical settings within them is unestablished. The argument requires that contingency as a premise and hasn’t earned it. The conclusion isn’t ‘the values are necessary’ but ‘the values haven’t been shown to be contingent in the sense the inference needs’, and an inference that presupposes an unestablished premise doesn’t transmit its conclusion.

Physical Invariance (§3.5.6) adds a separate discipline. Let *M* be a sufficiently complete physical profile and *Q* a proved invariant of that profile. Where $M\models Q$, a real *M*-realization can’t lack *Q*. In a fine-tuning comparison, *Q* is therefore not a second independently adjustable datum once *M* is held fixed; counting the selection of *M* and the occurrence of *Q* as two independent coincidences double-counts one structural fact. The theorem doesn’t show that *M* is necessarily realized, that its profile-defining constants couldn’t differ, or that every observed regularity is constitutive. It instead forces each alleged tuning datum into the right column: profile selection, invariant consequence of the selected profile, or empirical regularity whose dependence remains to be shown. Fine-tuning retains whatever evidential force belongs to the first and third columns after their alternatives and likelihoods are defended. It gains no additional force by recounting the second.

The remaining profile question is narrower than the original inference. Modal Availability Cannot Be Tuned establishes more than the stability of profiles admitted only hypothetically. This physical profile is actual; actuality entails possibility; and its possibility is therefore necessary. The actual profile is necessarily available within Nature’s modal range without thereby being actual at every world. Metaphysics–Physics Continuity (§4.5.5) establishes that the modal conditions and their physical realizations belong to one Nature rather than to stacked domains. The observation can therefore concern why this necessarily available profile is actual here. It can’t show that a selector supplied the possibility space, made the profile possible, attached its invariant laws, or stood outside Nature to do so. A move from the actuality question to a personal selector must independently establish genuine alternatives, a comparison measure, comparative likelihoods, a specified intention, and a coherent relation by which the proposed selector makes one profile actual.

**[Theorem]**

**Fine-Tuning Leaves an Actuality Question** · *Theorem*

After modal availability and profile-relative invariance are separated, fine-tuning leaves at most the question why this necessarily available physical profile is actual here rather than another. Its actuality already secures its possibility, and Necessary Possibility secures that possibility throughout the modal field; neither result makes the profile actual at every world. Fine-tuning does not by itself identify a selector, supply a space or measure of alternatives, explain a profile’s constitutive invariants, or establish an intention directed toward life. Multiple consequences entailed by one profile are not independent tuning data. An inference from the residual actuality question to a transcendent personal tuner therefore requires independent bridges to genuine alternatives, comparative likelihood, agency, intention, and realization.

**Dependency routes:** licensed alternatives and probability—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5); stable profile availability—Modal Availability Cannot Be Tuned (§3.5.6); consequence within a profile—Physical Invariance (§3.5.6); one metaphysical–physical domain—Metaphysics–Physics Continuity (§4.5.5)

A third escape concedes the modal point and tries to survive the concession. The measure, on this version, was never a claim about real possibility at all: what the argument needs is only that alternative constants are conceivable—compatible with what can be known a priori, from the armchair—and epistemic credences are then spread across that conceivable range. This form of the argument states its basis directly and is worth taking at its word, because taking it at its word is what costs it. A range of armchair-compatible descriptions isn’t yet a range of alternatives. Conceivability under an incomplete description yields a set of specifications whose modal standing is exactly what remains unsettled; laying a measure across them assigns weights to items not yet shown to be weight-bearing, and the resulting figure reports the resolution of the describer’s modal map rather than any feature of the constants (§2.9.5). The objection isn’t that conceivability is an unreliable guide to possibility, which is a separate and contested thesis this account has already declined to lean on. It is that a conceivability-defined range isn’t the sort of thing a probability is a probability over.

The same concession disarms a reply frequently made at this point. Faced with the suggestion that the constants might be necessary, the proponent forks it. Either the necessity is generic—whatever the values are, they hold necessarily—in which case it gives no reason to expect life-permitting values and leaves the comparison untouched; or it is specific—the values necessarily fall within the life-permitting band—in which case whatever predictive power it buys is paid for in prior improbability, since a necessity locating them anywhere else is equally conceivable. The fork is well constructed against the position it describes. The position it describes isn’t the one held here, and neither prong is asserted. What is claimed, as the discipline above states, is that the structural Conditions are necessary while the contingency of the particular settings is unestablished—a claim about what has been shown, not about where the values necessarily fall. The pricing argument charges for a hypothesis adopted to absorb the data, and declining to concede a premise adopts nothing. The pricing also runs on the currency the escape has just handed over: that a necessity locating the values elsewhere is ‘equally conceivable’ is a statement about armchair compatibility, offered as a distribution over the ways a world might necessarily be.

A third prong of the same objection tries to reverse the burden by analogy. Cutter and Crummett ask us to picture arriving at an island of boulders, holding beforehand that boulders of that size can’t be moved by hand, and finding them laid out in a great circle. The right response, on their reading, isn’t to keep the prior about immovability and write the circle off as coincidence, but to become confident of a conjunction: someone was here, and they could move the boulders. Transposed, an initial confidence that the constants are necessary should give way, on observing that they are life-permitting, to confidence in the conjunction that theism is true and that the values are contingent and controlled.

The analogy repays attention, and what it displays isn’t quite what it is offered to display. The uncertainty it trades on is of the wrong kind. Nobody doubts that the boulders could have lain otherwise; alternative arrangements are uncontroversially available, and geology supplies them without assistance. What is in question is the causal route—whether an agent was present with the capacity to bring about an arrangement everyone already grants was possible. Transposed to the constants, that becomes uncertainty about whether the alternative arrangement is available at all, which is a different question, and the one the prior question raises. The intuition the island pumps is calibrated on the first uncertainty and is spent on the second.

Two further features of the island do quiet work. The circle is striking against a baseline of how boulders lie when nothing arranges them, and the visitors didn’t make the boulders—they moved what was already there. The observation draws its force from a contrast between an arranged region and an unarranged one. On theism there is no unarranged region, since the boulders are made as well, and a contrast holding across the whole of what there is has stopped being a contrast. The circle also reads as intentional because a great deal is independently known about what human beings do and like: Stonehenge is evidence about us before it is evidence about design as such. Withdraw that independent specification and a circle is one arrangement among many, no more expected than another. The analogy therefore supplies itself with both the baseline and the specified intention that the fine-tuning case is asked to provide, which is why it feels decisive on the island and doesn’t transfer.

Behind all three prongs sits an assumption worth surfacing: that appealing to necessity is a way of avoiding an explanation rather than giving one. The assumption founders on a case the objector already grants. Almost no one in the contemporary literature holds that God selected the truths of arithmetic. Voluntarism, which did hold it, has been largely abandoned—and abandoned for a structural reason rather than a pious one, since the decree presupposes the alternatives, identities and consequence relations it was supposed to establish (§10.1.3). What remains is the ordinary position, and it is the Thomistic one: omnipotence is indexed to what is logically possible, so two things and two things make four things in every world God could make, God didn’t choose this, and God couldn’t have chosen otherwise. The cost of that restriction—that necessity becomes a condition on divine action rather than a product of it, which moves the locus of the deepest necessity beyond the being—is reckoned at §11.3.1 and isn’t re-argued here. That is a necessity, affirmed without embarrassment, holding of every creatable world, and selected by no one—held by the same position that treats the naturalist’s appeal to necessity as a dodge.

Nothing follows from this about whether the constants are necessary; that isn’t the point being made. What follows is that necessity-without-selection isn’t a naturalist evasion but shared ground. Both parties already hold that some features of any world God could make aren’t up to God, and both already accept that where a feature falls on that line is settled by modal argument rather than by whether the placement is convenient. The disagreement is entirely about where the line runs. The fine-tuning argument needs the constants on the contingent side of it and hasn’t established them there; observing that the other placement would be useful to the naturalist doesn’t put them on this side, any more than observing that arithmetic’s necessity is useful to the theist puts arithmetic on that one.

On the account developed here the arithmetic case isn’t a separate domain to begin with, which sharpens what the comparison shows. Two things and two things make four things because counting requires items held distinct, persisting through the count, and borne—arithmetic spells out the quantifiable aspect of Nature rather than describing a second realm that Nature is fortunate to match (§2.6, the Wigner Dissolution; the applicability question is engaged at §9.8). The reason no creatable world lacks it isn’t that an external constraint was laid on the making of worlds, but that there is nothing it would be to make a world with distinguishable contents in which the count came out otherwise. Whether the constants belong to that class is precisely what the prior question asks, and it isn’t answered by finding it surprising that they might.

*The core verdict, and what follows it.* The theorem above is the section’s governing result, and it doesn’t wait on anything below. Once modal availability and profile-relative invariance are separated, fine-tuning leaves an actuality question, and any Bayesian inference from it still owes a comparison class, a measure, priors, and likelihoods. What follows are independent extensions of that result. Discoverability and lawfulness ask whether further data beyond life-permission add evidence; nomological harmony is the same prior question asked of laws rather than constants; the three forms test the Bayesian, multiverse, and cumulative routes; and the teleological reading, with its hell, malfunction, and waste problems, targets one specified design hypothesis rather than fine-tuning in general. Each can fail without disturbing the core verdict, and none is needed for it.

*Discoverability.* A further version holds life fixed and asks why living observers receive unusually good epistemic access to the world they inhabit. The case presented by Collins appeals to parameters that could allegedly vary across a life-permitting range while making important evidence much harder to recover. The baryon-to-photon ratio is offered as one example: within a range compatible with observers, its actual value is claimed to make the cosmic microwave background intense enough to disclose the early universe. If such cases are robust, anthropic selection alone doesn’t remove them. Observers need conditions compatible with observation; they need not inhabit conditions especially favorable to reconstructing cosmic history. A good creator may have reason to provide the intellectual goods of inquiry, understanding, and the discovery of an intelligible order. Discoverability would then add evidence beyond bare life-permission rather than redescribe the same datum.

The additional datum has to be specified before it can bear the additional weight. A parameter may improve one evidential channel while degrading another, and a value identified after investigators know which signals their sciences use is vulnerable to selection from a large field of possible discoveries. The argument therefore needs a measure of discoverability fixed independently of the actual scientific route: which truths and observers count, how improvements across methods and epochs are aggregated, what tradeoffs are permitted, and where the actual configuration ranks across the relevant alternatives. Showing that one actual parameter enhances one important signal doesn’t yet show that the configuration is globally or nearly maximally discoverable. The modal and measure burdens also remain. A modeled interval of life-permitting values isn’t by itself a space of really possible alternatives with a licensed distribution over them.

The likelihood under theism requires an intention model of its own. A creator could favor direct revelation, creaturely dependence, epistemic struggle, different cognitive powers, or discoveries unrelated to cosmology; generic perfect goodness doesn’t assign comparative weights among those possibilities. Conversely, lawful Nature supplies standing regularities that embedded investigators can exploit, while cultural accumulation and instrument-building widen access far beyond unaided perception. That doesn’t make deep discoverability inevitable on naturalism. It means the comparison is between specified hypotheses, not between “God intended knowledge” and “knowledge happened for no reason.” If a defended discoverability metric placed this configuration unusually high, the observation could favor purposive or value-sensitive selection. It wouldn’t yet distinguish a classical creator from a finite designer, axiarchic bias, or another value-directed selection principle, and it wouldn’t identify a religious tradition.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Discoverability Fork** · *Disjunction*

What does the tuning optimize?

- **If it optimizes one particular sign,** then that sign counts for less the more signs there were to pick from. The fit itself is real, and local. But its evidential weight has to include every parameter, signal, method, and tradeoff the fit was selected out of.
- **If it makes the universe easier to discover,** then what counts as easier has to be settled before the measurement, not after it. The argument gains a datum beyond life-permission. But it owes three things: that independent measure, the range of worlds this one is compared against, and how likely the result is on naturalistic, axiarchic, and theistic hypotheses alike.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t deny the reported physical sensitivity or reduce inquiry to observer selection. It separates local signal enhancement from the wider claim that the universe is tuned for scientific discovery.

**Dependency routes:** both routes—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5); global-discoverability route—Modal Convergence (§5.4)

*Lawfulness itself.* A prior version of the design inference holds the constants and their particular values out of view. Grant only contingent initial conditions. Why should there be stable laws under which those conditions develop, rather than a condition that goes nowhere or a sequence with no regularity that could support prediction? Swinburne treats the existence of simple, pervasive natural laws as evidence for personal explanation: an agent intending embodied knowers, rational action, relationship, and inquiry has reason to produce an orderly world in which states develop intelligibly, while a purposeless initial state supplies no comparable reason (Swinburne 2004). This isn’t yet the question whether the laws fit the contents, or whether their constants permit life. It asks why there is law-governed development at all.

The argument changes with the metaphysics of law. On a governing conception, laws are further facts constraining what states do, so a lawless condition can be proposed as a genuine contrast. The proposal still owes a specification: a condition that persists, changes, or fails to change already has a determinate modal profile, and calling it *lawless* can’t mean that anything whatever follows from it without contradiction. On a powers conception (Bird 2007; Mumford 2004), what a thing can do belongs to what it is; removing every disposition while keeping the complete thing fixed doesn’t describe the same initial condition without laws. On a Humean best-system account, laws are the simplest and strongest summary of the mosaic rather than additions governing it. A highly irregular mosaic may then lack a simple informative system, but the evidence has shifted from the existence of a second governing item to the degree of order in the history itself. That remains available to an argument from order. It isn’t an argument from the bare existence of laws.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Law-Free Condition Fork** · *Disjunction*

Strip the laws away. Is the same starting condition still there to compare against?

- **If it is,** then the laws are a further fact needing explanation—but explaining them isn’t yet naming an agent. If laws are additional governing facts, their presence is something further to explain. The contrast may support a law-supplying principle, but identifying that principle as a personal God requires a separate bridge from governance to agency and intention.
- **If it isn’t,** then there was never a lawless rival to compare ours against. If the powers and modal profile belong to the complete condition, or if laws describe the history rather than govern it from outside, removing the law changes or incompletely specifies the condition. The purported lawless alternative hasn’t been held fixed.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t decide among Humean, powers, and governing accounts of law. It fixes what each account leaves for the lawfulness argument to explain.

**Dependency routes:** constitutive-law branch—Why the Laws Are Constitutive (§2.9.1); governing-law branch—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5)

*Nomological harmony.* Fine-tuning asks why the constants sit in a life-permitting band. Cutter and Saad (Cutter and Saad 2024) press a prior pairing: why the laws of this universe match the contents they govern at all. A world might have Newtonian laws and initial conditions those laws don’t engage; it might have laws for charged particles and an inventory of only ‘schmarged’ ones; it might, in their image, run Monopoly rules on a Go board. The result would be stillborn: states, and laws, and no evolution of the one under the other. They treat the actual match as a striking outcome, epistemically improbable on a purposeless pairing of independently variable laws and states, and therefore as calling for a designer, an axiarchic meta-law, or some other coordinating principle. The construction isn’t a third form of the constant-tuning inference. It is the same prior question, asked of law-content matching rather than of numerical settings.

The Monopoly image generates a mismatch only if a scientific law is being read as a statute: a prescription issued for a board that might have been a different game. In the scientific sense the word doesn’t work that way. A law of nature is a description of how the contents behave. Gravity isn’t a rule laid onto masses that might have missed them. It is what massive bodies do. Ask what gravity would be if it didn’t behave gravitationally, and the question doesn’t name a nearby world. It names a failure to have specified gravity. Precision of description isn’t tuning. A circle isn’t fine-tuned because the equation that describes it is exact. The strikingness of the match is generated by sliding from the scientific sense—the precision with which the behavior can be written down—to the statute sense, a rulebook that might have missed the pieces. Cutter and Saad aren’t naive about Humeanism; they note that versions of the puzzle survive several non-governing conceptions. The game analogy still does the slide.

Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5) requires a licensed space of alternatives before a match can be scored as lucky. Conceiving a Monopoly rulebook laid on a Go position shows that two descriptions can be written side by side. It doesn’t show that Reality admits a world whose dynamical laws and whose states fail to determine one another. On the constitutive reading of laws (§2.9.1), a law isn’t an independent instruction set that might or might not fit the pieces. Under a powers account (Bird 2007; Mumford 2004), what a thing is determines what it does; a mismatch of law and content isn’t a second genuine world but a failure to specify one. Under a governing-law account the pairing can look independent, because that account treats laws as something more than the description of the contents, and the Humean mosaic can look more independent still if the best-system axioms are imagined as one inventory and the mosaic as another; those are live options, engaged at §8.2.2, and they are the options on which nomological harmony has purchase. The present reply doesn’t need those versions to fail as puzzles for every law-metaphysics. It needs only that the inference from a conceived mismatch to a sampling space of real worlds, and from that space to an exterior coordinator, hasn’t been earned until the alternatives are shown to be really possible—and that the precision of a scientific description doesn’t, by itself, license reading the description as a prescription that might have missed.

The stillborn universe is then not a nearby rival that failed to be selected. It is a description that hasn’t yet been shown to name a configuration Nature admits. Where the pairing of law and content isn’t independently variable, there is no combinatorial luck left to explain. If the contents are already metaphysically sufficient for the behavior they exhibit, Configurational Necessitation forbids a complete realization that behaves otherwise, and Strict Actualization (§2.9.4) gives that behavior from the actual contents. That isn’t Armstrong’s governing relation *N*(F,G): the theorems don’t add a further item that makes the pairing obtain; they say that once P is complete, no extra selector is required. Where the pairing is independently variable, the coordinator the argument reaches is still a principle operating on Nature’s inventory, not a demonstration that Nature itself is contingent. The leap from an in-Nature match to an outside tuner is the same leap the constant-tuning inference makes, and it meets the same prior question. The mind-side analogue is a different pairing, and why phenomenal states pair with physical ones as they do is taken up at §10.1.10.

*First.* The precision argument, in its contemporary form, runs from likelihood ratios rather than intuition. Collins and Barnes don’t rely on intuition; they rely on comparative probabilities. If life is extraordinarily rare across the space of possible constants under naturalism, and non-rare under theism, then the narrow-window observation confirms theism. The form of the argument is Bayesian: P(tuning | theism) / P(tuning | naturalism) is large, and observing tuning updates credence toward theism.

The calculation requires a probability measure over the space of possible constants. McGrew, McGrew, and Vestrup (McGrew et al. 2001) press a serious measure problem: an unbounded parameter space admits no uniform normalizable measure, and the ratio of life-permitting to life-forbidding regions is undefined without additional constraints. Defenders answer with restricted ranges, scale-sensitive priors, or direct likelihood comparisons, so the objection imposes a burden rather than refuting every Bayesian formulation. ‘One part in 10¹²⁰’ presupposes a flat measure over an interval that extends to infinity in both directions; a log-uniform measure would yield a different ratio; a measure weighted by physical plausibility another; and the argument offers no principled reason to prefer any of them. The sensitivity of the conclusion to the measure chosen is as large as the purported fine-tuning itself. Stenger’s *The Fallacy of Fine-Tuning* (Stenger 2011) observes that many of the ‘fine-tuned’ constants are only fine-tuned relative to a particular parameterization; under different but empirically equivalent parameterizations, the apparent precision dissolves. Carroll (Carroll 2016) notes that whether the tuning is ‘fine’ depends on what set of possible universes one is comparing the actual one to, a set the theist hasn’t specified.

A developed reply on the theist’s side is Collins’s (Collins 2009), which concedes that the full parameter space admits no canonical measure and restricts the comparison to an *epistemically illuminated* range: the interval of values across which the life-permitting effect of variation can actually be assessed, within which, Collins argues, a normalizable measure is available and the life-permitting sub-region is vanishingly small.

The restriction relocates the problem rather than resolving it. An epistemically illuminated range is bounded by what inquirers can currently model, not by what is metaphysically possible, so a measure defined over it is a measure over the reach of present physics, and confidence drawn from it is confidence about that reach, not about a space of ways the constants could have been. This is the objective-epistemic conflation the prior question already isolates, reappearing one level in: Collins secures a normalizable measure by substituting an epistemic boundary for a modal one. And even granting the illuminated range as a genuine space of alternatives, the measure over it is still unfixed, since a uniform and a log-uniform measure on the same finite interval deliver different ratios and the argument supplies no principled reason to prefer either. The coarse-tuning observation that the life-permitting band is narrow on any reasonable measure survives the restriction, but it establishes only that the band is narrow relative to the illuminated range, which is a fact about the range our physics can survey, not evidence that the constants were drawn from a wider space and selected from it.

Anthropic reasoning makes a complementary point that doesn’t duplicate the measure problem. Carter (Carter 1974) and Bostrom (Bostrom 2002) argue that observers can only find themselves in observation-permitting conditions: not because observation causes the conditions, but because the selection effect is built into what it is to be an observer making an observation at all. Were the constants otherwise, no one would be measuring them. The present account extends the anthropic point rather than replacing it: the three Conditions aren’t conditions that happen to be observer-permitting; they are conditions that make observation possible in the first place. An observation that these conditions obtain is made from within them. That fact requires an observation-selection correction, but it doesn’t by itself show that the observation has no evidential bearing beyond the conditions.

*Second.* The multiverse-insufficiency extension presses the design inference up one level. Conceding everything naturalist cosmology asks for (a universe-generating mechanism, an ensemble of universes, a stochastic process sampling parameter space) the theist (Collins 2009, §9; Barnes 2012) argues that the fine-tuning demand reappears at the meta-level rather than dissolving. Any universe-generating mechanism must have its own structure: laws governing what universes it produces, a range of constants it can assign, a probability measure over outcomes. Those higher-order parameters are themselves either contingent (so the fine-tuning demand reappears at the meta-level) or necessary (so the theist concedes the destination of the present account). The regress of designers, the theist argues, doesn’t terminate in the multiverse; it terminates in whatever fixes the multiverse.

Two replies. Hacking’s inverse-gambler objection (Hacking 1987) warns that observing one apparently unusual outcome doesn’t automatically support many unobserved trials. Contemporary multiverse arguments often add independent cosmology and an observation-selection rule, so the objection constrains naive inferences rather than every multiverse explanation.

The sharper reply is available within the modal framework defended in §2.1–2.6 rather than from the fine-tuning dialectic’s neutral empirical register; conditional on that framework, S5 preserves the necessity of any genuinely necessary higher-order parameter. It doesn’t identify the parameter or explain its high-resolution content. Necessary meta-parameters would be invariant features of the ensemble theory, but the three Conditions are too coarse to determine their specific values or probability law. The structural roles constrain any genuine universe-generating realizer; they don’t identify every higher-order parameter or meta-tuner with the triad. Readers unconvinced by the prior modal framework can rely on McGrew’s point about the absence of a canonical probability measure alone: that burden is framework-neutral, and the S5 point is a further sharpening available only on top of it.

*Third.* The Bayesian cumulative case, pursued most carefully by Swinburne (Swinburne 2004), takes the argument in a more restrained probabilistic direction, retreating from entailment to confirmation. Swinburne doesn’t claim the fine-tuning observation entails a designer; he claims it raises the probability of theism relative to naturalism by a non-trivial factor, and that when combined with other probabilistic considerations, the cumulative case for theism becomes compelling: simplicity (the prior-from-simplicity wing of Swinburne’s case, engaged at §10.1.8), the existence of consciousness, and the phenomenon of moral awareness. Fine-tuning is one weight on a larger scale.

Monton (Monton 2006) isolates the structural problem with the fine-tuning weight specifically. If God is omnipotent, God can instantiate conscious beings in any logically possible configuration. The present configuration isn’t therefore necessary for the existence of conscious beings. But if it isn’t necessary for the existence of conscious beings, the theist can’t explain why God selected this one rather than another except by appeal to divine preference, which does no Bayesian work: preference is compatible with any observation and discriminates between no hypotheses. The probability P(this configuration | theism) is as free as divine preference allows; which is to say, unanchored; which is to say, unable to contribute a determinate likelihood ratio.

A sharper version presses on the theist’s own commitments rather than on Bayesian bookkeeping. God is held to be a conscious being not in this universe. If the constants of this universe are necessary for the existence of conscious beings, no conscious beings exist outside this universe, and God doesn’t exist as characterized. If these constants aren’t necessary for consciousness simpliciter, the fine-tuning argument must be stated more narrowly in terms of embodied observers or life of our general kind. That limits the conclusion but doesn’t make the observation evidentially null; comparative likelihoods may still differ over how readily rival hypotheses produce such observers. The fine-tuning premise concerns embodied life or observers generated by physical laws, whereas God is proposed as an unembodied mind. That isn’t a simple equivocation, but it narrows the evidence: the likelihood comparison must explain why theism predicts a physically life-permitting cosmos of this sort rather than merely the existence of consciousness somewhere.

*The teleological reading.* This isn’t a fourth form of the inference to a tuner; it is a further claim that can be laid on top of any of the three that precede it, evaluated on its own because it can fail even where the three succeed. The inference examined so far concludes only that the constants were selected; it is silent on what for. A stronger reading is almost always present in the tradition and rarely separated out: that the universe isn’t merely life-permitting but life-intended, tuned for life, with life as the purpose the tuning serves. This reading is separable from the bare inference, and it can fail on its own terms, independently of whether the bare inference succeeds. It is also the reading that carries the argument’s rhetorical force, so how it fares matters.

*The problem of any-tuning.* The reading forces a fork the argument hasn’t faced: is God bound by the tuning already present in this configuration, or not? If bound, this configuration is required rather than merely permitted, and the fine-tuning proponent has conceded, without quite intending to, that Nature’s structural order isn’t open to alternative tunings at all—which secures a necessity of the configuration rather than a designer’s discretion. If bound instead to a *range* of life-permitting configurations while free to choose among them, the concession runs at the boundary rather than at the profile: the life-permitting constraint still binds, and whatever discretion is left concerns which admissible profile obtains, which is evidence only given the account of intention the unbound horn also lacks. If not bound at all, an omnipotent being could realize conscious life through any coherent configuration whatever, and the narrow-window observation carries no evidential weight unless something beyond omnipotence favors this window: the same being achieves the same result regardless of which window the constants sit in, so learning that the actual window is this one says nothing about why it rather than some other. A designer model that specifies an intention for orderly, law-governed means, or for this kind of physics, could change that; the burden is to state the intention and defend it independently of the data, not to assume that none can be stated.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Any-Tuning Problem** · *Disjunction*

Is an omnipotent designer bound by the tuning that conscious life needs?

- **If the designer is bound by that tuning,** then it wasn’t chosen, so no chooser is explained. The configuration is required rather than selected at divine discretion, so the designer doesn’t explain why it obtains instead of another.
- **If the designer isn’t bound by it,** then this configuration wasn’t the only way, and its narrowness proves nothing. God could produce the same result under other coherent configurations, so this configuration’s narrowness doesn’t favor a designer without an independently specified account of divine intention.
- **If the designer is bound to a range of life-permitting configurations but keeps discretion within it,** then the boundary of that range is the life-permitting constraint itself—which is exactly what the narrowness names—and the designer is bound by it as in the first horn. Discretion may survive over which admissible profile is actual, but a selection claim about that is evidence only on the independently specified account of divine intention the second horn already found missing. Either way the narrowness isn’t what the choice explains.

Narrowness can mark a constraint or a discretionary selection. It cannot explain the chooser in both roles at once.

*Scope.* Narrowness alone doesn’t establish a discretionary omnipotent tuner. The dilemma doesn’t exclude a Bayesian fine-tuning argument with an independently licensed comparison class.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

Pressed on the second horn, the reading has one retreat left: insist that consciousness itself, not merely embodied life of our kind, requires this configuration—that an environment has to look something like this one to sustain a being capable of observing its own state. Test the retreat on its own terms. Suppose you wake up in a world infused with violence, suffering, torture, rape, and the like. Conscious as you are, would it be fair to say the world was finely tuned for you or anyone there? If we accept the retreat’s own premise—that an environment counts as fine-tuned for conscious life as long as it sustains a being capable of observing its own state—then yes: the presence of violence, suffering, and heartache does nothing to disqualify it.

Push the criterion to its limit and it yields a proposition no theist wants to hold: hell is finely tuned for life. Hell is, on the traditional commitment, exactly such an environment—conscious beings, aware of their own condition, sustained in it indefinitely. If the criterion is thin enough to certify hell, the theist has to either accept that hell was finely tuned or abandon the criterion. Almost no one accepts.

The natural reply is to reject the fork itself: whatever else is true of tuning, a place like the one just described—violence, torture, anguish without relief—is plainly not the kind of place anyone would call finely tuned for the beings in it, and a criterion that says otherwise has simply been stated wrong. That reply is available, and it costs the argument the thing it was for.

The environment described at the outset was never hell, and was never a hypothetical. It was Nature all along: violence, suffering, and heartache are observable in the world already being lived in, the very world the fine-tuning argument was invoked to certify. To reject the fork by holding that no such place counts as finely tuned for its occupants is to hold that this place doesn’t, which is precisely the conclusion the argument exists to deny. The two moves are therefore not an escape and a cost but the same criterion read at two settings. Set it thin enough to certify this world, and it certifies hell in the same breath. Set it strict enough to exclude hell, and this world goes out with it. Nothing in the retreat distinguishes them, because the description that fits one fits the other, and the fine-tuning argument needs a criterion that separates them.

Nor does any of this turn on the fiery hell of the popular picture, which many Christians have never held. The horn needs only that someone continues after death in a condition worse than this one, on whatever description a branch prefers; if they do, something sustains them there, and on theism that environment did not arrive on its own—every environment there is was made.

A branch may decline even that, holding that no one persists in a worse condition at all, as conditional immortality and universal restoration both do (§12.1.8, §12.3.12). The declining costs something too. If no sustained condition anywhere is worse than the worst this world contains, then this world is the floor of the actual created order: the most severe conscious condition ever occupied, anywhere in it, for its whole duration. The claim is about the actual, not the possible—no one has to say this is the worst world there could be, only that among the conditions ever occupied, this one is the bottom. That isn’t a conclusion the argument can hold at arm’s length, because this world is its exhibit.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Hell Is Fine Problem** · *Disjunction*

If awareness of one’s own condition is evidence of tuning, is the tuning of hell fine?

- **If the criterion is loose enough to call this world tuned,** then hell is tuned too—and tuned better. Hell is traditionally understood as conscious beings sustained indefinitely, which is more sustaining than this world manages for anyone.
- **If it is strict enough to say hell isn’t tuned,** then this world isn’t either. This world contains violence and unrelieved anguish, and it is the case the argument was built to certify.

The retreat supplies no feature that separates the two environments. The horns are exhaustive only so long as none is supplied: a criterion that admitted this world while excluding hell would need some further difference between them, and naming one is the open route out.

*Scope.* The dilemma targets this sustaining criterion, not fine-tuning arguments generally. Conditional-immortality and universal-restoration branches may deny that anyone persists in a worse condition; they then treat this world as the floor of the actual created order rather than as the worst possible world.

**Depends on:** The Any-Tuning Problem (§10.1.9)

The retreat fails a second way as well: that only configurations near ours could host conscious beings at all is precisely what the argument hasn’t shown. For all that is known, most configurations might support life of some kind; our inability to imagine it reflects the limits of our physics, not the limits of the possible (Ikeda and Jefferys 2006). Nor is the theist’s own ontology any help here: God is a conscious being with no physical parameters at all, and angels, on the traditional commitment, are conscious without bodies. If consciousness can obtain in God and in angels with none of this configuration in place, then this configuration isn’t necessary for consciousness on the theist’s own accounting, and the ‘tuned for conscious life’ reading contradicts the metaphysics it is meant to serve. The example isn’t a hostile construction; it is drawn from the proponent’s own creed. The criterion also runs one step past the case it was built for. If an environment counts as tuned wherever it sustains a being aware of its own condition, the criterion asks what sustains a God so aware, and the tradition has an answer ready: nothing does, because God depends on no conditions and is composed of no parts. The answer is available and it isn’t evasive—it is the doctrine of aseity and divine simplicity, engaged on its own terms at §11.3 and §10.2.1. What the answer can’t do is halt the regress and leave the criterion usable, since the exemption covers exactly one case and rests on a further doctrine about that case’s nature. The weight then sits on that doctrine rather than on the tuning observation, which is where the present section hands it over.

The retreat fails a third way, and this one turns on the conceivability the argument leans on. If the space of alternatives is generated by what can be conceived from the armchair, then the faculty that conceives the constants otherwise conceives them better just as easily: a setting with the same hospitality to conscious life and less of the hostility, fewer of the mechanisms that destroy the beings the tuning is said to be for. Conceivability doesn’t merely open a range of different configurations. It opens a range of better ones, and the narrow-window figure locates the actual configuration nowhere in particular within that range: the precision measures a band, not an optimum. Here again the proponent’s own commitments arrive ahead of the objection. The tradition asserts a conscious environment better than this one, and asserts it not as an imaginable alternative but as an actual destination—the redeemed conscious, aware of their condition, sustained in a state without death or suffering or the mechanisms that produce them. Taken at its word, that is a better setting for conscious life than this one, held to obtain, by the proponent’s own lights. Whether such a state can be specified coherently is a separate question pressed at §12.2.5, and nothing here turns on the answer. What follows without it is narrow and enough: a tradition committed to a better conscious setting can’t also hold flatly that this configuration is the finely tuned one, and the reading owes an account of why a maker with the better setting available built the beings it was for into this one instead.

*The problem of insufficient need.* Scoped to the reading rather than to the bare inference, the fine-tuning observation runs the other way. If God is omnipotent, the space of means by which conscious life could be realized is enormous: God could sustain life in any configuration, or with none, or by direct fiat. A universe that must be threaded through a needle’s eye of constants to permit life is therefore a strange choice for a being to whom all means are open: it is exactly the expedient a maker without options would be forced into, not one a maker with every option would prefer. The likelihood reversal makes this precise (Ikeda and Jefferys 2006): once observability is taken as background, learning that the universe is naturalistically life-permitting can’t raise the probability of a supernatural tuner, and on the for-life reading specifically it lowers it, since an omnipotent intender had no need of a delicately balanced mechanism at all. The positive thesis follows: life that needs no apparatus to be created, yet is given a vast and precarious one, is evidence against the apparatus being for it.

*The problem of malfunction.* The objection turns on how teleology is individuated. A thing made for a purpose is identified as such by its serving that purpose: the test of ‘made for X’ is ‘succeeds at X.’ An omnipotent maker can’t fail to realize what it intends, but omnipotence alone doesn’t specify the intention. The reversal therefore targets a determinate design hypothesis: that abundant, secure, broadly distributed life is a primary end rather than one good among others or a means subordinated to some different end. On that hypothesis, a universe made for life should be unmistakably, abundantly, securely hospitable to it; the observed scarcity then counts against the hypothesis rather than against generic theism. What is observed instead is a cosmos in which life clings to a vanishing margin, sustains itself against constant threat, and is extinguished with ease. A product that barely and precariously discharges its supposed function is, by the only test teleology affords, not made for that function. This wing is immune to the ‘precious because rare’ reply: rarity is evidence of difficulty, and difficulty is exactly what omnipotence doesn’t face.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Malfunction Test** · *Diagnostic*

The target is the design hypothesis that abundant, secure, broadly distributed life is a primary intended end of an omnipotent maker. The test is teleological success: a product offered as evidence of an intention should succeed at the function that intention specifies, and an omnipotent maker cannot fail through lack of capacity. The observed outcome is instead life clinging to a vanishing margin, sustained against constant threat and extinguished with ease. Under the stated hypothesis, that mismatch counts against abundant, secure life being the product’s primary intended end. The diagnostic doesn’t determine every purpose the maker might have had, and it doesn’t by itself count against generic theism without an independently specified intention model.

*The problem of disproportion.* Suppose you are seated at a restaurant advertised as the work of a maximally great chef, and the plate set before you holds a single grain of rice, presented as fine dining. Is the grain evidence of a fine meal? Would you hold it to the standard fine dining is supposed to meet? Would you say the plate was specifically prepared to feed someone? A single grain doesn’t feed anyone, and no honest answer to any of those questions is yes. So on what basis would the grain still count as evidence of a maximally great chef at all? The presence of a little nourishment somewhere on the plate doesn’t make the plate a meal, and a maximally great chef who could have set a feast and instead set only the grain has, if anything, made the case against fine dining rather than for it. Nothing in that verdict turns on the word ‘chef.’ Swap it for ‘designer,’ the plate for a cosmos, and the grain for the terrestrial biosphere, and the same verdict holds for the same reason: a lone, hard-won pocket of nourishment isn’t evidence of a feast, whoever is credited with setting the table. 

Three observations reinforce the functional point. 

*Qualitatively,* life doesn’t find a hospitable world; it engineers itself against a hostile one. Survival is a labor of building shelter, regulating temperature, and defending against an environment that isn’t arranged for the organism; cities are monuments to how much must be done to make a patch of the world habitable.

In the human case the labor isn’t merely reactive but deliberate, cumulative, and still under way: agriculture, sanitation, medicine, climate control, seismic monitoring, and weather forecasting are a sustained program of retuning local conditions toward what the environment doesn’t supply on its own, and the scale of that program is a measure of the distance between the world as found and a world that would suit its occupants. A species that must build all of this to occupy its own planet safely isn’t reporting that the settings are already right for it.

A defender may answer that the capacity to build it is itself part of the design, but the reply concedes the point at issue: it relocates the tuning from the constants to the ingenuity of one species that has to correct for them, which is a different and weaker claim than the one the fine-tuning argument advances.

There is a further consequence for how the for-life reading gets its plausibility. The apparatus is now so complete that almost no one arguing about it has lived outside it: the environment a modern arguer actually inhabits is already the corrected one, heated and plumbed and policed, provisioned against famine, insured against weather, medically defended from birth. Even the deliberate excursion out of it is conducted from within—the savanna viewed from an enclosed vehicle, the summit approached on bottled oxygen, the seafloor through a pressure hull. A judgment that the world suits its occupants, formed from inside all of that, is a report about the correction rather than about what was corrected for.

What the uncorrected environment delivers is recorded in the demographic baseline it held for nearly the whole human past, in which roughly half of the born died before reaching any age of accountability (Volk and Atkinson 2013). That is the hospitability of the world as found. The point is directed at the for-life gloss and at the intuition that sustains it in popular presentation, not at the likelihood-ratio arguments of Collins and Barnes, which don’t run on felt hospitability and are answered on their own ground above. The relation runs opposite to the gloss: life is tuned to its environment by adaptation, not the environment to life by design.

*Quantitatively,* the life-permitting region is a vanishing measure of a cosmos overwhelmingly lethal to life: near-absolute vacuum, lethal radiation, temperatures at both extremes, durations and distances on scales that dwarf anything life occupies. (The scale disparity, quantified. The observable universe spans roughly 93 billion light-years and roughly 13.8 billion years; a single known planet has hosted life for about 4 billion of those years, and reflective life occupies a fraction of a percent of that span. The precondition compounds the disparity: the mammalian radiation that eventually produced humans followed directly from the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction roughly 66 million years ago, in which an asteroid impact eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs and most other species then living; the ecological niches that opened were what primates, and later humans, expanded into. A universe built for a species that arrives this late, by way of a mass extinction, and occupies this little of it, is a strange one to have spent 13.8 billion years preparing, most of it filled with sterile voids.) 

*Structurally,* the narrowing recurs one level down inside that vanishing region: the fraction that is habitable isn’t itself one hospitable environment but a partition of mutually exclusive niches, where crossing from one into another is lethal rather than merely difficult, an ocean drowns what land life requires, open air suffocates what ocean life requires, and each further subdivision (pressure band, temperature range, salinity, atmospheric composition) forecloses what its neighbors permit. There is no environment hospitable to life as such, only a fractal series of disjoint environments each hostile to whatever isn’t already fitted to it.

The fracturing recurs even inside a single generalist species. The Bajau of maritime Southeast Asia carry a genetic adaptation, an enlarged spleen serving as an oxygen reservoir, that lets them free-dive to depths and durations unadapted humans cannot match, while Tibetan and Andean highlanders meet the same challenge of high-altitude hypoxia by two different physiological routes: lower hemoglobin concentration in the one population, higher in the other. Ethiopian highlanders answer the same hypoxic pressure a third way, holding hemoglobin at sea-level norms while still reaching oxygen saturation levels neither of the other two groups matches by their own route. Inuit and Yup’ik populations carry a variant of the gene *CPT1A* that lets a near-zero-carbohydrate, fat-heavy diet fuel the body without the metabolic cost that same diet would impose on someone without it. The Haenyeo free-divers of Jeju evolved their own route to breath-hold diving in cold water, independent of the Bajau’s.

None of this is a claim of lethal incompatibility of the ocean-and-land kind; it is a claim about differential fit. Even the species most often cited as Nature’s generalist exception has already sorted into sub-populations locally optimized for extremes the rest of the species only tolerates. A universe that is for life is, on inspection, almost entirely against it.

*The problem of gratuitous waste.* A being capable of speaking a finished, life-sustaining world into existence directly had no need of any process at all to reach that result. What the actual history shows instead is a long, costly, and largely blind one: several generations of stellar nucleosynthesis over billions of years to produce the heavier elements life requires, then some four billion years of evolutionary trial and error on a single planet, the overwhelming majority of it ending in extinction rather than descendants. Partway through, a mass-extinction event eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs and the ecological order they had held for roughly one hundred fifty million years, clearing the niches mammals needed before that lineage could diversify toward primates and, eventually, the species the design hypothesis is meant to center on. None of this is doctrine-specific; it costs any designer, under any tradition, who is credited with having humanity as an end and every means available to reach it directly. A path this long, this wasteful, and this indifferent to the vast majority of lives spent traveling it isn’t what foreknowledge executing a settled plan looks like. It is what an unplanned process that arrived somewhere in particular, and was retroactively read as aimed there, looks like.

What unifies these wings isn’t omnipotence alone but omnipotence joined to a specified intention. Each observation suggesting poor or purposeless design invites the reply that the hostility is instrumentally necessary: that a universe capable of producing life must be large, old, and governed by laws that are lethal elsewhere. Omnipotence removes inability, but it doesn’t by itself remove every instrumental or value-ordering explanation; a defender may claim that the history, scarcity, or risks serve independently specified goods. Such a reply succeeds only if those goods and their connection to the chosen means are defended rather than introduced after the evidence. Against a life-maximizing or flourishing-centered design hypothesis, hostility, scarcity, and precariousness remain unforced features and therefore evidence about purpose; against generic theism, they leave the likelihood underdetermined. This is the cosmological specialization of the evidential structure Draper (Draper 1989) presses for pain and pleasure: the distribution of good and ill in the world is more expected on indifference than on a specified benevolent intention centered on flourishing, and the gap is evidence.

Three replies are available to the reading, and each carries a stated cost. The instrumental-necessity reply binds the process, not the agent: an omnipotent agent isn’t bound by the process unless the goods it serves are independently specified, which is the burden just stated. The minimalist-masterpiece reply (that a great maker might sign a single, spare, improbable work) does no Bayesian work, since ‘a great maker would do this’ is compatible with any observation whatever, and it collides directly with the suffering the spare work contains. The soul-making reply (that hardship is the point) concedes that the universe isn’t made for life’s flourishing but for its testing, which is a different purpose, post-hoc with respect to the fine-tuning data, and which reactivates the problem of evil rather than answering it.

*The tuning fork.* A last rescue holds that the tuning was once benign and was broken: that the world’s hostility postdates a fall, an original sin, a derangement of nature. The rescue lands on a fork before its own trilemma even opens: either the present configuration is the tuned state, in which case nothing relevant to the fine-tuning inference has changed and the fall does no explanatory work, or it is the untuned, broken state, in which case the present configuration isn’t evidence of a tuner at all, and the fall rescues the argument only by conceding that the observation it was built on is no longer the observation of a tuned world.

Which conditions changed determines which horn applies, and neither is free. If the physical constants changed, the claim is a physical hypothesis with no physical evidence, and one that runs against the very constancy the fine-tuning argument relies on. If only the biological or moral order changed, the cosmic hostility (vacuum, radiation, scale) was there from the start and is unexplained; the constants stayed tuned, and the fall changed nothing that bears on the inference. If the change is purely spiritual, it does no work against the physical dysteleology at issue, for the same reason. And the rescue forfeits the project: an inference licensed only by an ancient text is no longer natural theology, which was the genre the fine-tuning argument entered to occupy.

The collective form of the doctrine compounds the cost. A penalty visited on all conscious beings for the act of two, through a headship none of the penalized consented to or could have refused, is a moral structure an omnipotent maker had every means to avoid, who could, for instance, have created each pair on its own world to stand or fall for itself, with no representation imposed. That the collective arrangement was chosen when non-collective ones were available isn’t a necessity to be excused but a choice to be assessed, and it’s assessed under the problem of evil, engaged in its own right elsewhere.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Tuning Fork** · *Disjunction*

Is the present tuning built in from the start, or is it out of tune?

- **If it was built in from the start,** then the Fall was irrelevant to the tuning. The Fall changed nothing relevant to the fine-tuning inference and cannot explain the vacuum, radiation, scale, and physical precariousness the rescue was introduced to answer. Every feature catalogued above stands as intended: the hostility, the disjoint niches, the waste.
- **If it is out of tune,** then we aren’t measuring the tuned world at all, and that reading owes what changed. Measurements of the present configuration aren’t observations of the allegedly designed tuning and cannot serve as evidence for its tuner. Each answer carries a different cost: a change in the constants is a physical hypothesis with no physical evidence; a biological or moral change leaves the original cosmic hostility untouched; a spiritual change does no work against physical dysteleology.

The Fall cannot both explain away the present configuration’s hostility and preserve that same configuration as evidence of benevolent tuning. Either branch fixes what kind of Fall could still be claimed. *Feeds into* The Fall-Event Fork (§12.1.4).

*Scope.* The dilemma concerns the Fall as a rescue of the fine-tuning inference, not the doctrine of the Fall generally or a narrower biological, moral, or spiritual change proposed for another purpose.

The eliminativist wing of the fine-tuning debate presses harder than the present argument does. Stenger (Stenger 2011) argues that the appearance of fine-tuning is a statistical artifact: that under a full accounting of the possible parameterizations, no remarkable precision remains to be explained. (The Ikeda–Jefferys reversal, a distinct claim, is already engaged against the for-life gloss rather than against the bare observation.) The present account doesn’t commit to the eliminativist’s stronger claim. Some sensitivity is real; the question is what the sensitivity is of. The eliminativist answers: of nothing in particular, once the parameterization is normalized. The present account answers by classification: some data concern why the realized physical profile is actual, some are invariant consequences once that profile is fixed, and some remain empirical regularities whose dependence hasn’t been established. The two answers converge on rejecting naïve multiplication of tuning claims and diverge on whether the remaining actuality question can acquire evidential force. The present account preserves that question without treating it as a selection datum or declaring the design comparison settled.

*Probability rides on modality.* The three forms share a structure worth stating directly: every probability is conditional on the modal frame that fixes its sample space, so probability questions are asked within a structure, never of it. That cuts against the tuner from two sides. Tuning requires a standard to tune toward, and the standard admits no tuner: if it is contingent, fine-tuning collapses into preference-matching and a regress of standards opens; if it is necessary, there is nothing to tune, since what holds necessarily holds in virtue of its necessity, not by being selected for. And the precision of any probability assignment tracks the resolution of the modal map beneath it, so a coarse map that under-distinguishes necessity from contingency inflates apparent contingency and, with it, apparent improbability. The narrow-window number is calibrated against what, at the structural level, isn’t itself a probability-bearer; precision against an unsettled structure is precision about the map, and the argument presents it as evidence about the very structure it was conditioned on.

**[Proposition]**

**Probability Rides on Modality** · *Proposition*

Every probability is conditional on the modal frame fixing its sample space, so probability questions are asked within a structure, never of it. Tuning requires a standard to tune toward, and the standard admits no tuner: contingent, and fine-tuning collapses into preference-matching with a regress of standards behind it; necessary, and there is nothing to tune, since what holds necessarily holds in virtue of its necessity, not by being selected for.

**Depends on:** Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5)

The cumulative structure doesn’t rescue the fine-tuning weight: Swinburne’s method aggregates several individually-weak considerations toward a posterior above one-half, but each faces the same structural-presupposition reply and its own comparative burdens wherever it is pressed (fine-tuning here, simplicity at §10.1.8, the PSR at §8.2.1), so the contribution of this weight must be reassessed before the cumulative posterior can be claimed. The replies are reckoned together at §10.4.

The problem of evil has its own treatment, to which the present section defers. The for-life reading and the appeal to a fall have already reactivated it. The present section confines itself to the direct inference from narrow-window observation to a tuner, to the law-content pairing and discoverability claim that share that inference’s prior question, and to the for-life reading laid on top of the constant-tuning case; the companion moves are handled where they belong.

*Convergence.* A prior question, three forms, and separable discoverability and teleological extensions converge on a qualified verdict. Fine-tuning can enter a Bayesian case only after its comparison class, priors, measure, and observation-selection effects are defended. Even then, the sensitivity data leave an actuality question; they don’t carry the bridges from that question to a transcendent personal selector.

Physical Invariance then prevents a proved consequence of an already-fixed profile from being counted again as an independent tuning datum; it doesn’t explain why that profile is realized. Nomological harmony inherits that same division: a conceived mismatch of laws and contents isn’t yet a licensed alternative world, and an invariant law-content fit within a profile isn’t an additional external coincidence. Why this profile is actual remains open. That is an actuality question, not an unexplained remainder already bearing the marks of agency.

Finally, the for-life reading is separable from the bare inference and must be evaluated at the level of the intention it specifies. On the theist’s own ontology consciousness obtains without this configuration; where abundant, secure, broadly distributed life is posited as a primary end, the world’s overwhelming hostility is evidence against that design hypothesis. Generic omnipotent theism, without a defended intention model, leaves the likelihood underdetermined rather than reversed.

A final consideration: the argument for a tuner is delivered within the configuration it calls tuned. The precision of the constants is measured across moments, in laboratories configured in space, using instruments that persist through measurement; the inference from precision to selection is run by minds that instantiate the very structural roles whose contingency the argument is trying to leverage. The observation ‘these constants are precisely set’ is a report from within a world where the constants obtain; the inference ‘therefore a setter’ imports the idiom of selection from domains where selection has content (domains where unselected options also obtain) into a domain where no such options are available to compare against. The actual measurement and argument are structured acts, but a classical theist denies that divine selection is a temporal engineering process using pre-existing space and material. Retorsion establishes the structure of inquiry, not the absence of an external selector. The stronger objections remain the comparative-likelihood, measure, and grounding burdens already developed. The precision is a feature observed from within one structured configuration. Whether it is also evidence of selection remains a comparative explanatory question rather than something retorsion settles. Even if that comparison eventually supported selection, it wouldn’t yet support an exterior selector of total actuality: No Outside Selector at What the Rivals Carried (§10.4) establishes that any real selector and operative selection relation belong to Reality–Nature. The evidence could discriminate among internal actualization accounts; it couldn’t, without contradiction in the totality claim, place a real selector outside the total actuality.

### 10.1.10 The Psychophysical Harmony Argument
The psychophysical harmony argument’s wedge isn’t that consciousness exists. It is that phenomenal states pair with physical states, and with one another, in ways that look fortunate once those two inventories are treated as independently variable. Pain tracks damage and drives avoidance; visual presentation tracks the scene and licenses belief; reports of what it is like come out true of the states they report. Cutter and Crummett (Cutter and Crummett 2025) name that fortunate pairing *psychophysical harmony* and argue that it confirms theism (or at least disconfirms atheism in its standard naturalistic form). The construction has a recent literature of its own: Pautz (Pautz 2020) isolates *normative* harmony; Chalmers (Chalmers 2018) isolates the luck in the meta-problem reports; Goff (Goff 2018) isolates *cognitive* fine-tuning for those who take occurrent thought to be phenomenal. Cutter and Crummett gather these into a Bayesian comparison: the overwhelming majority of conceivable psychophysical mappings would be disharmonious, theism has reason to prefer a harmonious mapping, and so P(harmony | theism) >> P(harmony | naturalistic atheism).

This is a different argument from Swinburne’s (Swinburne 2004, ch. 9) case from the mere existence, or the alleged complexity, of psychophysical laws. Cutter and Crummett are explicit about the difference: complexity without value wouldn’t favor theism, and what they need explained is the *fortunate* pattern, not the length of the list. It is also a different argument from the hard problem and the structured zombie, which ask whether the interior can be withheld from a complete physical duplicate (§9.1). Harmony grants the pairing and asks why *this* pairing rather than a disharmonious one. A reply that only closes zombies hasn’t yet met it. A reply that only notes that dualist residue still instantiates the three Conditions hasn’t yet met the luck claim either, though that floor will matter for what the luck, if luck it is, could be luck *of*.
