The physical sibling is nomological harmony: the match of dynamical laws to the contents they govern (Cutter and Saad 2024). That pairing is already treated with the constants, at §10.1.9. What remains is the mind-side pairing.

*The datum, at strength.* Two families do most of the work. *Normative* harmony (Pautz 2020) is the match between an experience’s essential reason-giving role and the functional role of the physical state it’s paired with. A damaging stimulus produces physical state X; X produces avoidance; the psychophysical laws map X onto pain, which essentially gives reason to avoid. The laws could, the argument runs, have mapped X onto pleasure, or onto a buzz. Then we would systematically flee what we have reason to pursue, or pursue what we have reason to flee. *Epistemic* harmony is the same shape for belief: the state that drives round-object-reaching is mapped onto a phenomenal presentation of roundness, which essentially justifies the belief that something round is there. Goff’s cognitive fine-tuning (Goff 2018) is a further instance for those who take thoughts themselves to be phenomenal: of all the ways cognitive phenomenology, sensory phenomenology, and function might have been matched, they tend to be matched in rationally appropriate ways. Cutter and Crummett remain officially neutral on that last antecedent; they don’t need it.

*Semantic* harmony is the match between reports and the states that make them true (Chalmers 2018; Cutter and Crummett 2025). Given causal completeness, there’s a complete physical explanation of the utterance “this hurts” that doesn’t mention the hurt. That the psychophysical laws nonetheless pair the speaker with a state that makes the utterance true looks, on the dualist setup, like a further coincidence. Spectrum inversion can be absorbed by a shift in what the color-words pick out. Pleasure/pain inversion, and a mapping of every physical state onto the same buzzing noise, can’t: the reports would then be false, or empty, in a way the inverted-spectrum case isn’t.

Two concessions belong on the table before any reply. First, if the inventories really are independently variable, evolution doesn’t explain the pairing. Selection can explain why a damage-tracking, avoidance-producing state is common. It can’t explain why the extra phenomenal law maps that state onto an experience whose essential normative role matches the function, because selection doesn’t rewrite fundamental psychophysical laws. Cutter and Crummett are right about that conditional. Second, interactionism doesn’t make the luck free. If phenomenal states push the physical, there are still countless ways they might push; most of them don’t yield avoidance-when-it-hurts or truth-when-we-report (Cutter and Crummett 2025, §3.1). Saad’s (Saad 2019) teleological law—experience causes the physical state it most rationally warrants—does explain the match, but only by writing value into the fundamental dynamics. That is already a departure from purposeless naturalism, and Cutter and Crummett treat it as theism-adjacent rather than as a rival they need to beat. Nagel’s (Nagel 2012) teleological laws and Goff’s (Goff 2023) pan-agentialism sit in the same neighborhood: purpose is relocated into Nature’s inventory, not shown to stand outside it.

The argument is also offered as not needing dualism up front. Cutter and Crummett (Cutter and Crummett 2025, §3.2) claim that even identity physicalism leaves a large space of *epistemically* possible psycho-functional identifications, most of them disharmonious, so P(harmony | atheism & functionalism) is still low unless one already treats the actual pairing as background. The Boulder Island analogy is meant to carry the point: an apparently designed arrangement should raise credence in visitors *and* in their ability to move the stones, even if one began fairly confident that boulders can’t be moved. Harmony, they say, should likewise raise credence in a designer *and* in the designer’s control over the pairing—hence against a functionalism on which God couldn’t have chosen otherwise. The analogy is examined where it’s first deployed, against the constants, at §10.1.9; the short form is that the island’s uncertainty concerns a causal route to an arrangement nobody doubts was available, while the transposed uncertainty concerns whether the alternative arrangement is available at all.

The challenge bears on the necessity claim for the three Conditions, and on the identity proposed at §5.1, in different ways. If harmony requires an exterior selector, Nature’s structural order isn’t the last word about why this configuration looks as it does. If the pairing isn’t a selection from a licensed space of alternatives, the argument never starts.

*The prior question.* Objective chance is downstream of possibility (§2.9.5): a sampling model doesn’t by itself manufacture a wider modal space. Before scoring the actual pairing as lucky, one must establish a genuine space of alternative mappings. Cutter and Crummett are careful here. They often speak of *conceivable* mappings and of *epistemic* probability, not of physical chance over psychophysical laws. That is the same escape already granted at §10.1.9: a Bayesian design argument can use epistemic probabilities without positing a lottery over genuinely possible outcomes. The remaining burden is still comparative, and it still includes the comparison class. Conceiving a pleasure/pain inversion shows that a mind can write two descriptions side by side. It doesn’t show that Reality admits a world in which the complete configuration that is this nociceptive-motor organization is paired with a hedonic polarity the organization doesn’t have. Ideal conceivability may be a guide to possibility; the book doesn’t rest on settling that (see §9.1 on phenomenal transparency). It rests on the asymmetry the prior question fixes: the burden lies with the proponent to show that the disharmonious mappings are possible in the sense the measure requires. That burden hasn’t been discharged by listing them.

*First.* For the pairing to be combinatorially lucky, two inventories must be independently sampleable. Either they are, or they aren’t.

If the identity proposed at Consciousness (§5.1) holds—if the interior is the living organization registered from the side it occurs on—then there aren’t two inventories. Pain isn’t a second item mapped onto the avoidance-organization; it is that organization as undergone. Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4) then forbids a complete realization of the sufficient configuration from which the interior is withheld, and Strict Actualization (§2.9.4) gives the actual interior from an actual sufficient organization. The mapping space collapses because there is nothing left to map. Neither theorem proves the identity. It is defended abductively (§5.1), by biological continuity, multiple realization, and explanatory economy against an extra phenomenal property or contingent bridge law; the structured zombie is priced at §9.1 if the identity is refused. Harmony can’t treat the identity as already refuted without doing the hard problem’s work over again, and Cutter and Crummett don’t claim to have done that work. What they claim is that even functionalists face a space of epistemically possible identifications. That claim returns to the prior question: an epistemic space of labels (“pain = F1,” “pain = F2”) isn’t yet a space of real worlds. If only one complete configuration is really possible, the “lucky” identification is the only identification there is.

If the identity doesn’t hold, the inventories can come apart. Consciousness is then a further feature, linked by a further law. That is a coherent dualism, and it is the setup on which harmony has its cleanest reading. Two costs follow, neither of them a contradiction. The first is the cost already priced at §9.1: under causal completeness the further feature is idle in the production of the very reports and avoidances the argument treats as fortunate; interactionism avoids the idleness only by writing a special pushing-law, which is the luck again. The second is the floor of that same section: the extra ingredient is still temporally ordered, differentiated, and borne. Dualism crowds Nature. It doesn’t supply a ground outside it. McKee (McKee 2025) presses a further crowding inside the dualist setup itself: if the psychophysical laws attach to intrinsic physical properties, overlapping realizers multiply subjects in the immediate vicinity of every person. The dualist can restrict the laws to maximal properties, as Cutter notes in related work; the restriction is another special form the laws have to take. None of this shows that God selected the mapping. It shows that the view on which the mapping looks selectable has already added an in-Nature inventory and then has to police it.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Inside-Out Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

Is the inside the interior of the outside, or is it a further thing?

- **If it is the interior of the outside,** then there aren’t two inventories, and nothing was ever there to pair. If the interior is identical with the complete living organization specified at §5.1, Configurational Necessitation leaves no independent mapping space for a selector to tune.
- **If it is a further thing,** then that thing and the law linking it are additions inside Nature. The additional phenomenal feature and the law linking it to physical configurations remain items in Nature: temporally ordered, differentiated, and borne. Dualism crowds Nature; it doesn’t supply a ground outside it.

*Scope.* The dilemma targets the inference from psychophysical harmony to an exterior selector. It doesn’t prove the identity (§5.1) or exclude a Bayesian case built on an independently licensed comparison class.

**Dependency routes:** interior-of-the-outside branch—The Simple Answer (§9.1); further-thing branch—Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10); Bayesian scope—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5)

*Second.* Even granting independent inventories, the licensed sample space hasn’t been shown. Most of the argument’s force is carried by a count: the overwhelming majority of conceivable mappings would be disharmonious, and the simplest mappings (every physical state onto the same buzz) look disharmonious too (Cutter and Crummett 2025, §2.4). Conceivable mappings are cheap. The reason is explained at §5.5: conceiving loads a recombined branch into a modal field without certifying that Reality admits it. The buried-chest distinction of Modal Status (§1.2) applies here as it applies to the zombie. Writing “map X onto pleasure” is a successful construction of a representation. Whether that construction names a real possibility is the disputed object-side question. Mørch (Mørch 2017) and Langsam (Langsam 2011) try to shrink the space from inside dualism, by taking some phenomenal-to-mental powers as a priori; Cutter and Crummett reply that phenomenal-to-*physical* powers remain wide open. The present account doesn’t need their a priori powers. It needs only that openness in conception isn’t yet openness in Reality.

The functionalist half of their §3.2 inherits the same demand. “Pain might have been identical to some other functional property F*” is an epistemic possibility relative to a conceiver’s map. If identity is necessary, at most one of those identifications is a world. Treating the whole list as the atheist’s sample space is the objective-epistemic conflation already isolated for Collins’s illuminated range at §10.1.9: a measure over what inquirers can currently tell apart is a measure over present concepts, not over ways the pairing could have been. Harmony can still enter a Bayesian case. It can enter only after the comparison class, and the claim that disharmonious identifications are really possible, are defended rather than read off the list.

There’s a further difficulty in treating the pairing as observed. Ask what disharmony would present as. The argument needs a further phenomenal feature, with the physical order causally complete. On that setup, a disharmonious creature is behaviorally indistinguishable from a harmonious one. Its damage state still drives avoidance, because avoidance is physically caused; its mouth still forms the words *this hurts*, because utterances are physically caused. What differs is only which experience the law pairs with the state, and that difference doesn’t reach the report. Such a creature couldn’t tell anyone it was disharmonious, and couldn’t tell itself in any channel that issues in speech. The consequence is awkward for the datum rather than for the creature: *we observe that our states are harmoniously paired* is a sentence a disharmonious being would produce in the same circumstances and with the same conviction. The observation therefore doesn’t discriminate between the two cases it’s introduced to distinguish. This doesn’t show the pairing isn’t harmonious, and it isn’t an argument that we are secretly disharmonious. It bears on evidential standing. A datum whose presence and whose absence are consistent with the same total evidence is doing less confirmatory work than the argument requires of it, and the harmony proponent who reaches for interactionism to restore the difference has reached for the special pushing-law again.

*The problem of a gradient.* The argument treats harmony as a clean achievement, and its Bayesian shape needs that: a mapping either lands in the fortunate region or it doesn’t. What is actually observed is a gradient. Pain persists after tissue has healed and in limbs that are no longer attached; referred pain locates injury in the wrong organ; battlefield analgesia suppresses the signal precisely when damage is greatest; congenital insensitivity removes it altogether; pain asymbolia delivers the sensation while removing the badness that was supposed to be essential to it. On the hedonic side, appetite is tuned to scarcities that no longer obtain, and addiction is the pairing pulling steadily against the function it’s said to match. Perception is systematically and catalogably wrong in ways vision science has mapped in detail.

None of this refutes harmony, and the proponent has a fair reply available: a mapping can be fortunate in the main and ragged at the edges, and the raggedness may be damage to the physical side rather than disorder in the law. The reply is reasonable and it has a price. It concedes that the observed pairing is approximate, locally miscalibrated, and in some presentations inverted—which is what one expects of an organizational property maintained under selection pressure, and not what one expects of a mapping chosen by a being optimizing for fit. The test applied to teleological claims at §10.1.9 applies here unchanged: a product offered as evidence of design is assessed by how well it serves the end it’s offered as designed for. Applied to the constants that yields the problem of malfunction. Applied to the pairing it yields the same question, and the harmony literature has largely not been asked it, because the datum is usually stated in its idealized form—pain with damage, sight with the scene—rather than in the form the clinic reports.

*The problem of many harmonies.* The pairing is also not one achievement but a great many, and they differ. A bat’s world is built from returning sound, a mantis shrimp’s from more photoreceptor classes than our own vocabulary has words for, a shark’s from voltage gradients in seawater, a migratory bird’s from a magnetic field none of the others detect. Each of these is harmonious in the sense the argument cares about: the interior fits the apparatus and the apparatus fits the animal’s life. If harmony were the needle’s eye the count requires, one wouldn’t expect to find it independently achieved in echolocation and in vision and in electroreception and in chemical gradient-following. What the comparative record shows is a wide and repeatedly realized region, not a narrow target hit once.

The pattern also has a direction that bears on the two horns of the inventory dilemma. Phenomenology varies with organization, tightly and without exception: change the apparatus and the interior changes with it, across every lineage that has been examined. A law pairing physical states with experiences has no particular reason to shift as body plans shift; it could as easily have held one mapping fixed while organisms changed around it. An identity between the interior and the living organization (§5.1) has no choice but to shift, since the organization is what the interior is. The comparative data therefore sit more comfortably with the first horn than with the second. This is evidential rather than demonstrative, and it doesn’t close §9.1; a dualist may hold that the psychophysical laws are themselves organization-indexed. That is another special form the laws have to take, and the tally of such forms is by now not short.

*Third.* An in-Nature correlation isn’t yet an outside tuner. Suppose, for the sake of the horn, that the pairing is contingent and the space is licensed. Theism then raises P(harmony) only given an independently specified divine intention to realize the values harmony realizes. Cutter and Crummett grant that divine psychology is hard and that P(harmony | theism) need not be high in absolute terms—only higher than P(harmony | atheism). That is formally correct, and it is the same comparative structure Swinburne runs for the constants. Two pressures already developed at §10.1.9 transfer.

The Any-Tuning Problem transfers as a constraint on the intention, not as a proof that no likelihood ratio could move. If God is bound by this pairing as a condition of producing valuable conscious life, the pairing is required rather than selected, and the designer doesn’t explain why this mapping obtains instead of another. If God isn’t bound, an omnipotent being could realize valuable consciousness under other coherent pairings, or with none of this physical apparatus at all—the theist’s own ontology already includes an unembodied mind. Narrowness of this pairing then doesn’t favor a designer without a further account of why *this* valuable form was chosen. Pautz’s (Pautz 2020) cheese-god and suffering-god barbs aren’t a refutation; Cutter and Crummett answer them with simplicity and the claim that a perfect being would be motivated by value rather than by cheese. The answer helps against arbitrary designer-hypotheses. It doesn’t yet specify why a value-directed being would choose *this* harmony, in *this* physical world, with the suffering the hedonic pairing also includes. The existence of evil isn’t the work. It is a comparative-likelihood cost the harmony argument must eventually face, and Cutter and Crummett themselves flag theodicy as live background rather than as already settled.

*A mind with no pairing at all.* One further asymmetry belongs here, and it is drawn from the proponent’s own commitments rather than constructed against them. God, on classical theism, has a complete mental life and no physical states whatever: knowledge, will, love, and beatitude (complete blessedness), with nothing for a psychophysical law to map. Two things follow. The first is the point already made about need—if a mental life of the highest value requires no pairing, the pairing isn’t what valuable consciousness demands. The second is less often noticed. That divine mental life is itself harmonious. Knowledge answers to what is the case, will answers to what is good, beatitude answers to what God is. Set the argument’s own combinatorial reasoning going on it, and the conceivable arrangements of a mind’s contents are no less numerous than the conceivable pairings of feel with function; most arrangements one can write down aren’t coherent in that way.

The theist has two replies and they aren’t equally cheap. The first is that divine harmony has an explanation of the same kind—something arranged it—which begins a regress the doctrine of aseity exists to stop (§11.3). The second, and the one the tradition actually gives, is that God’s mental life is harmonious because God’s nature is necessarily what it is, so no arrangement was selected and none could have been otherwise. That reply is available and it is the right one. What it can’t also do is treat necessity as an illegitimate explanation of harmony when a naturalist offers it. If a necessary nature accounts for the coherence of a mind’s contents without a tuner and without luck, then the question at issue isn’t whether necessity can explain harmony—both parties agree that it can—but which harmonies have a necessary nature standing behind them. That is the prior question again, and it is where this section has been pointing throughout.

Pressing the necessity-answer one step further changes what it is an answer of. Harmony is a relation, and a relation needs terms held apart: for knowledge to answer to what is the case, the knowing and the known must be distinguishable, and the answering-to runs in a direction. Ask whether the divine attributes are distinct in that way and the tradition divides against itself in a familiar place. If they are—if knowledge, will and beatitude are genuinely distinguishable and genuinely match—then there is differentiation inside God, something bearing the terms, and an ordering among them, which is the structural inventory of §2.6 appearing in the being offered as prior to it. That is the same result the transcendental argument (§10.1.3) reaches for logic relocated into the divine mind, and it is pressed there against the same commitment. If they aren’t distinct—if divine simplicity is taken at full strength, so that God’s knowledge is God’s will is God’s essence—then nothing in God matches anything else, because matching takes two, and there is no divine harmony to cite as a model. What there is instead is an identity: not two features that fortunately agree, but one thing described more than once.

The second horn is worth dwelling on, because it is the tradition’s own considered position and it has an unnoticed consequence. On divine simplicity the theist’s account of why the only unpaired mind in their ontology hangs together is an identity account. That is the form of §5.1’s answer for the interior and the organization: not a second item mapped onto the first, but the first undergone. The harmony argument is thus offered against an identity solution by a position whose own explanation of unpaired mental coherence is an identity solution. This doesn’t show the identity (§5.1) is true, which is argued on its own grounds and abductively. It shows that the identity strategy can’t be treated as the desperate move, since it is already in use on the other side of the table, doing the same work.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Divine Harmony Trilemma** · *Disjunction*

How does God’s own mind hold together?

- **If it was arranged,** then a regress begins at the point aseity is meant to stop.
- **If it follows from God’s nature and the attributes are distinct,** then their matching introduces differentiation, bearing, and ordering within God.
- **If it follows from God’s nature and the attributes aren’t distinct,** then nothing is matched to anything. Identity explains the coherence, not harmony—and identity is the strategy the harmony argument was raised against, already in use on the other side of the table, doing the same work.

Necessity explains harmony without a tuner and without luck. If it can do that for God, it cannot be refused to the naturalist.

*Scope.* The trilemma targets the inference from harmony to an exterior selector, not the coherence of divine simplicity or aseity. It neither calls God’s mental life disharmonious nor proves the identity (§5.1).

**Dependency routes:** comparison-class constraint—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5); identity parallel—Consciousness (§5.1); distinct-attributes consequence—Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10)

Minds that report the pairing, and that run the Bayesian update on it, already instantiate the structural roles whose contingency the argument is trying to leverage. Retorsion establishes the structure of the inquiry, not the absence of an external selector. The stronger objections remain the inventory dilemma, the prior question, and the intention-model burden.

*Convergence.* The argument is a serious empirical-teleology chip, and it isn’t answered by noting that consciousness occurs. If two inventories can vary independently, the fortunate pairing is something that genuinely needs explaining, evolution doesn’t explain it, and interactionism doesn’t make it free. The identity proposed at §5.1 collapses the mapping space if it holds; it is abductive, and this section doesn’t upgrade it. If the identity is refused, the further feature remains in Nature, and the leap from that in-Nature pairing to an exterior selector inherits Possibility Precedes Probability and the intention-model burden already pressed against the constants.

Three further pressures are comparative rather than modal. The observed pairing is a gradient rather than a clean achievement, so the test of teleological success that yields the problem of malfunction for the constants applies here unchanged. The pairing is many pairings, independently realized in echolocation, vision, electroreception, and magnetoreception, which is a wide region rather than a narrow target—and it varies with organization in the way an identity requires and a bridging law doesn’t. The tradition’s own unembodied mind is coherent with no mapping at all: explained by a necessary nature, and, pressed on whether the attributes it relates are distinct, by internal differentiation or by identity. Both are explanatory forms the luck claim asks the naturalist to give up.

Harmony can still enter a Bayesian case after its comparison class is defended. It doesn’t, by itself, finish an argument for a ground outside Nature. Even if the comparison supported selection of a psychophysical pairing, No Outside Selector (§10.4) confines the result to an internal selector or selection principle: the selector, the relation, and the paired inventories all belong to the total actuality. Harmony could therefore discriminate among in-Nature explanations without establishing an exterior source of Reality’s total configuration.

### 10.1.11 The Design Argument
The intelligent design argument is the biological-scale version of the design inference engaged at cosmological scale in §10.1.9. Its proponents, Behe (Behe 1996; Behe 2007), Dembski (Dembski 1998; Dembski 2002), Meyer (Meyer 2009; Meyer 2013), and Plantinga (Plantinga 2011, ch. 9) at selective points, argue that biological complexity exhibits features (irreducible complexity, specified complexity, information content) that no unguided process can produce, and that the inference to a designer is the best explanation of those features. The Discovery Institute has carried the position into legal and pedagogical fora, and the *Kitzmiller v. Dover* (2005) decision held that teaching it in public-school science classes violated the Establishment Clause, but the underlying philosophical structure is what concerns the present argument. Aquinas’s Fifth Way (*ST* I.2.3) reads the governance of natural things toward ends as requiring an intelligence that directs them; the contemporary design inference is that argument’s empirical heir, and the teleology of living systems is taken up at §4.8.

ID isn’t simply fine-tuning at biological scale. Its core commitment is the forward design inference from specified or irreducible biological complexity to intelligent agency. Some religious deployments add special creation, an initially perfect order, or Fall-based explanations of dysteleology, but these aren’t commitments of ID as such and should be treated as optional extensions rather than the defining set. The Fall-based extension is what makes the religiously extended set self-sealing in a way the bare fine-tuning inference isn’t. Fine-tuning claims forward tuning of constants and faces straightforward probabilistic and structural rebuttals. ID has a built-in absorber for every poor-design rebuttal: the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the human spine, the ichneumon wasp, the long catalogue of biological inefficiencies and cruelties (The catalogue extends to reproduction itself. Two distinct losses are involved, and the argument doesn’t need the larger one. The first is clinically recognized loss: roughly one in ten recognized pregnancies ends in miscarriage (the clinically-recognized estimate, cited in Deshpande and Kucirka, *StatPearls*, 2023). The second is separate and additional: a substantial further share of fertilized eggs are lost before implantation is ever detected, a quantity estimated much higher but on far weaker evidence, since the losses are by definition unobserved. Take only the conservative, clinically documented figure and set the second aside entirely. A designer credited with intending the birth of every child still inherits a design in which roughly one attempt in ten fails before term, before any undetected loss is counted at all. The point doesn’t turn on which number is right; it turns on there being a large failure rate in the process the designer is credited with intending, and every candidate figure is large.): these are read not as evidence against design but as evidence of *fall from* design. The argument flips dysteleology into confirmation. The present reply engages the core inference and both extensions, not just the core.

*First.* Against the design inference, the present reply draws on the four probability–modality couplings developed at §10.1.9, named here for ease of reference: the standard-side dilemma (a tuner needs a standard, contingent or necessary, and both options foreclose the tuning), the consciousness self-application (the designer can’t be exempted from the constraints that motivated the inference), the modal-structure mask (improbability claims at the structural level are modal questions disguised as probability questions), and the resolution bound (modal-map coarseness inflates apparent contingency). Where §10.1.9 reads “constants” the argument reads “biological configurations.” Where it reads “tuning,” it reads “designing.” The transfer isn’t automatic, because the two scales don’t pose the improbability in the same key. Cosmological fine-tuning is a claim about the modal status of the constants, whether they could have been otherwise. Biological improbability is pressed as something nearer a first-order probability over a space of chemical and genetic configurations, and that is where the argument’s intuitive force actually sits.

The biological case can’t be closed merely by transferring the cosmological objections. It turns on empirical models of mutation, selection, drift, developmental constraint, and the causal history of particular systems. Modal and probability questions still matter, but the decisive comparison is whether evolutionary mechanisms or design better explain the evidence under defensible likelihoods.

One further point belongs here rather than with the couplings already specified, because it concerns not the modal status of the improbability but what the improbability figure is a figure *of*. The numbers most often quoted for abiogenesis or for a given protein fold measure the odds of the relevant components arriving at a functional configuration by unconstrained combinatorial search: every possible arrangement weighted equally, the target arrangement being one point in a very large space. That is a measure of P(outcome), computed as though no chemistry were operating and nothing about the setting favored any arrangement over any other. It isn’t what the actual process is a claim about. The live empirical question is P(outcome given the prebiotic conditions), and where those conditions channel the search rather than leaving it uniform, an outcome can be probable, even close to certain, under conditions that are themselves rare. Rarity of the conditions and improbability of the outcome given the conditions are different quantities, and a figure computed for the second by imagining the first away isn’t evidence about either one on its own. This doesn’t make abiogenesis probable; whether prebiotic Earth in fact supplied channeling conditions, and how common such conditions are, remains open empirical territory the present argument doesn’t settle. What the point secures is narrower and entirely about what a number is allowed to measure: the standard combinatorial figure has never been evidence against unguided chemistry succeeding, because it was never a measure of the process unguided chemistry actually runs. The diagnosis is object-side in the sense the Specification Test names (§7.3.2): the defect is in what the calculation represents, not in a failure of anyone’s imagination.

A further pressure bears on the inference from within its own founding image. Paley’s (Paley 1802) watch is recognized as designed only against a backdrop that isn’t: the artifact stands out because the heath it lies on doesn’t bear the same marks. The local analogy therefore reads “designed” off a difference between the worked object and the unworked ground. That contrast licenses the local step; it doesn’t, by itself, license extending the same verdict to everything, the watch and the heath alike. A property can apply universally without losing content, and an inference may compare design with counterfactual non-design models even when no actually undesigned backdrop is available. Paley’s image can’t by itself carry the theistic generalization; the comparison that can is the one run below, between full historical models and the traces they predict.

**[Proposition]**

**Local Contrast Does Not Establish Universal Design** · *Proposition*

Paley’s watch is recognized as designed only against a heath that isn’t: the artifact stands out because its surroundings don’t bear the same marks. That local contrast does not, by itself, license extending the same designer to the heath. A property can apply universally without losing content, and design can still be compared with non-design models even when no actually undesigned backdrop is on hand. What Paley’s image cannot do is carry the global generalization unaided; the comparison that can is of full historical models and the traces they predict.

The analogy that anchors the inference also marks where it fails. A watch can’t produce another watch, and it is that incapacity, not the watch’s intricacy alone, that makes an external maker feel mandatory: nothing about a watch could bring a second watch about. Living things have exactly the capacity the artifact lacks. They reproduce, vary, and are filtered, so the inference can’t be carried from the watch to the organism without importing the watch’s sterility as a silent premise, which is to assume rather than show that life, like a watch, couldn’t have come about unaided.

The point can be put as a controlled comparison. A kennel holds a hundred dogs. In the first case a breeder selects two of them whose cross yields an animal well suited to a particular hunt: the mating is intended and the result is designed. In the second case the same two dogs are simply the last pair left together and breed as dogs do, with no one intending anything: the litter is identical to the breeder’s. Set the two animals side by side. Nothing in either records which history produced it. One was designed and one wasn’t, and the designed one carries no mark of the fact. What the comparison demonstrates is that agency is the sole variable differentiating the two cases; all product-level features are held constant.

That result grounds a general claim about the domain the design inference operates in. Design is a prospective process: the designer models a function and selects for it. Selection is a retrospective process: the environment tests against function and retains what fits. Both are function-tracking processes; they differ only in whether the specification precedes or follows the production. For any functional product a designer can yield—any product whose distinguishing features consist in fitness to a function—a sufficiently calibrated selective filter operating on that same function can yield the same, because the features the designer specified-for are precisely the features selection retains.

Functional similarity alone may underdetermine whether a trait was designed or selected, because different histories can converge on similar products. But causal histories can leave traces in genealogy, constraint, redundancy, and error-patterns. The design inference must therefore compare full historical models rather than assume either that function uniquely reveals agency or that products can never contain evidence of their origin.

This bears directly on the appeal to specified complexity. A specification is a function-profile: the set of functional properties an object must instantiate to serve its purpose. Selection is differential reproduction based on fitness to the environment. Fitness to the environment is a function-profile. Selection can cumulatively retain variants that function better in a given environment, but it isn’t literally intentional specification: fitness landscapes emerge from organism–environment relations rather than from a prior semantic target. Dembski’s design filter claims to detect specifications that are improbable under the relevant non-design process but more probable under design. Functional convergence doesn’t make design and cumulative selection *equally probable*: comparative likelihoods require specified models of mutation supply, population dynamics, selection strength, developmental constraint, search time, historical contingency, and designer goals. The defensible conclusion is underdetermination at the product level. A functionally apt trait doesn’t uniquely identify agency, because cumulative selection can also retain function-tracking variants; whether design or evolution better explains the trait depends on the full historical models and the traces they predict. Genealogy, nested hierarchy, path dependence, redundancy, constraint, error patterns, and independent evidence of intervention can discriminate histories. The core of Sober’s reply is therefore not probability equality but the need for an explicit likelihood comparison rather than an inference from specification alone (Sober 2008).

The empirical critique of ID’s specific apparatus, Behe’s irreducible complexity, Dembski’s design filter, Meyer’s information argument, lives in evolutionary biology and isn’t the structural argument’s burden; that work has been done there, notably by Sober (Sober 2008). One strand of Behe’s case isn’t purely empirical, however. The *Edge of Evolution* claim (that specified biological information is a quantity the unguided process can generate only within narrow limits) is a thesis about what generates structural information, not only about what the biology shows; the structural reply to it, how the immanent operators of change, composition, and constraint generate form rather than merely presuppose it, is developed where the operators are (§4.8), and the information-theoretic features are taken up at §8.2.3. The couplings at §10.1.9 and the comparative-history burden already identified bear on the design inference here, however that generative question is settled. The present argument shows what the inference must establish before it runs; the biological literature contests the empirical premises themselves.

*Second.* A historical Fall narrative posits an earlier condition within temporal history from which later corruption proceeds. It need not posit a moment outside T or a structural origin of time. The relevant objections are empirical and theological—whether there was such an initial condition, what changed, and whether it explains the evidence—not Parasitic Negation alone.

There is no moment-prior-to-T from which the first change departed, no temporal position at which “perfect creation” was instantiated as an initial condition outside the order it would initiate (§2.6.6, §8.1.2). The duration question of how far back along the dimension the passage runs (whether the past is finite or infinite in duration) is a separate question within T, engaged at §10.1.5 against the Kalām’s traversal and BGV arguments.

Parasitic Negation applied to T (§2.1.5, §2.6.6) is the move a privileged-t₀ reading of the Fall can’t survive: any beginning would already instantiate the order it claims to begin. The question “when did time begin?” admits two readings. The duration reading (how far back does succession run) has a numerical answer within whatever cosmology one is asking from. The structural-origin reading (what moment yielded T) is malformed: a moment is what T provides, not what produces T.

A moment of perfect creation followed by decay is structurally describable as an event within time. Its difficulty is that ID evidence doesn’t establish such a moment and the biological and cosmological records may count against particular versions of it. The structural-origin closure dispatches the fall narrative’s t₀; it doesn’t dispatch the Kalām’s duration question, which is the work of §10.1.5.

*Third.* The asymmetric decay vector, the third commitment, reads observed imperfection as evidence of fall from initial perfection. The reading conflates two distinct phenomena: entropy increase (a structural feature of T running) and moral or teleological decline (a normative feature attributed to history). The conflation is what gives the fall claim its empirical footing: every ad hoc construction, vestige, inefficiency, and cruelty in the biological record is reabsorbed as evidence of a perfect prior state from which the present has departed. Entropy increase shouldn’t be identified without argument either with moral decline or with Temporality itself. Thermodynamic arrows depend on physical laws and boundary conditions; a Fall theology that links them to corruption owes an additional empirical and doctrinal account. Reading entropy as moral-teleological decline imports a normative direction located nowhere here. T running isn’t T falling. The fall reading also lacks a historical anchor. It requires a moment at which a first human moral agent acted in a way that initiated decay, but roughly half a billion years of metazoan suffering predate any organism that could be such an agent, and contemporary population genetics rules out descent of *Homo sapiens* from a single founding pair within the recent timescales such narratives usually require (Venema and McKnight 2017). Plantinga’s *O Felix Culpa* (Plantinga 2004) relocates the fall into a privileged theological moment whose empirical anchorage is set aside; the move preserves the theological structure at the cost of giving up exactly the historical fall the original argument needs. Without the entropy-as-fall reading, and without a historical fall to anchor it, the dysteleology cases revert to what they were before being absorbed by the theodicy: evidence against the design inference, not evidence for it.

A note on scope. The fall claim also makes a directional empirical prediction (that observed history runs away from an initial perfection), and there are aggregate gradients in human social life and in religious demand that appear to run the other way. Those gradients are contested empirical terrain, and the present section doesn’t rest on them, because the fall claim is already foreclosed in one form and burdened in the other, on independent grounds. In its privileged-t₀ form it is foreclosed structurally, by the no-privileged-origin argument: any beginning would already instantiate the order it claims to begin. In its historical-within-T form it isn’t foreclosed structurally at all—that version is empirically and theologically assessable, and it carries its burden there instead, for want of an anchor: the entropy misreading supplies no normative direction, and no moment is available at which a first moral agent could have initiated the decay. Neither difficulty turns on the long-run social data, whatever those ultimately show. The substantive case that these gradients positively confirm the structural account is made where that work belongs (§5.14.4 on the moral arc and §5.16.4 on declining religiosity) and is left to stand or fall there on its own evidence.

**[Diagnostic]**

**T Running Is Not T Falling** · *Diagnostic*

The asymmetric decay vector reads observed imperfection as departure from an initial perfection, and it does so by conflating two unrelated things: entropy increase, which is a structural feature of the order running, and moral or teleological decline, which is a normative direction attributed to history. The conflation is what lets every vestige, inefficiency and cruelty in the biological record be reabsorbed as evidence of a prior perfect state. Thermodynamic arrows depend on laws and boundary conditions; nothing in them carries a normative direction, and a theology that links them to corruption owes that account separately. The reading also lacks a historical anchor: roughly half a billion years of metazoan suffering predate any organism that could have been the first moral agent. Without the entropy-as-fall reading and without a historical fall to anchor it, the dysteleology cases revert to what they were before the theodicy absorbed them—evidence against the design inference rather than for it.

**Dependency routes:** structural/non-normative T—Modal Identity (§2.6.6); historical-anchor limb—the thermodynamic, paleontological, and population-genetic record established in this section

*Taking stock.* The core inference and its two extensions are assessed separately, and each carries its own burden once separated. The design inference carries the couplings at §10.1.9 and the comparative-history burden already developed. Even a successful identification of biological agency would establish a designer of a subconfiguration within Nature; it wouldn’t by itself establish an exterior selector of Nature’s total actuality. That further limit is stated as No Outside Selector at §10.4. The privileged origin moment is foreclosed by the present argument that T has no exterior or prior origin moment, a structural-origin closure that leaves the duration question of a past finite in duration to §10.1.5 and Chapter 4. The asymmetric decay vector misreads entropy as moral decline. A Fall-based absorber can make a religious design theory resistant to evidence of poor or purposeless design, but it is an optional theological auxiliary rather than part of ID’s core. It incurs empirical and explanatory burdens concerning the initial condition, mechanism, and scope of corruption. Without the absorber, the design inference at biological scale inherits the burdens of the design inference at cosmological scale, which The Fine-Tuning Argument (§10.1.9) leaves undischarged.

### 10.1.12 The Moral Argument
The moral argument reasons from the reality of objective moral facts to God as their necessary ground. It has proved resilient precisely because it leans on a premise few want to deny (that some things are genuinely right or wrong, independent of what anyone believes or desires) and asks what could underwrite it. It must be engaged where it actually pushes, not as a restatement of the ontological argument taken up at §10.1.1: its force is axiological, not conceptual, and turns on the authority of obligation rather than the content of a concept.

The argument’s contemporary forms tie moral obligation specifically to a personal will. Adams (Adams 1999) identifies moral goodness with resemblance to God and obligation with God’s commands; Evans (Evans 2013) argues that obligations bear marks (authority, universal scope, inescapable bindingness) that only the commands of a personal, loving God adequately explain. Hare (Hare 1996) presses the “moral gap” between the demand morality makes on us and our capacity to meet it, a gap divine assistance is needed to close. Craig (Craig 2008) presses the argument in its most widely debated deductive form (if God doesn’t exist, objective moral values and duties don’t exist; objective moral values and duties do exist; therefore God exists), the popular syllogism that fixes the argument’s public profile, with all the philosophical weight resting on its first premise: that authority of the relevant kind requires a personal commander. Baggett and Walls (Baggett and Walls 2011; Baggett and Walls 2016) give the argument a contemporary form, recasting it as an abduction rather than a deduction: theism is offered as the best explanation of the full moral landscape at once, its values, its obligations, its knowability, and the possibility of moral transformation, so that no single premise carries the inference and the cumulative fit is what is offered as evidence. Behind these stands Mavrodes’s (Mavrodes 1986) point that objective moral facts sit awkwardly, are “queer”, in a world with no more than nature in it; and even Mackie (Mackie 1982), no theist, allows that objective values, were there any, would fit more easily in a theistic universe than a naturalistic one. The shared argumentative form is an inference to the best ground: moral facts are real and categorically binding; only a personal will supplies authority of that kind; therefore God.

Grant the realism in full. Moral facts aren’t projections, conventions, or sentiment got up as fact; that gratuitous cruelty is wrong is true, and no individual’s attitude and no collective’s consensus can make it otherwise. Grant, too, that bindingness is the crux: an obligation that bound no one wouldn’t be an obligation, and a naturalism that reduces value to preference or fitness-tracking does struggle to recover the authority that genuine obligation carries. The argument’s animating worry is legitimate, and the present account shares it rather than dissolving it.

*The compulsion is real; what differs is where it takes hold.* A believer who reports being bound by God’s command isn’t reporting an illusion, and nothing here requires them to be mistaken about being bound. The authority grip (§5.14.3)—a feature arriving with the standing of someone entitled to command—is one of the surfaces the same compulsion catches on, and it delivers the same felt *I ought to* that principle or consequence delivers; a morality weighted toward reward and away from punishment is running the consequence grip, no less genuinely. The disagreement isn’t over whether the ought is felt but over what the bindingness consists in, and over what each grip can correct against. Authority alone carries no internal check: its content is exhausted by the fact that someone entitled to command has spoken, so a directive that runs against the registered condition of the subjects it governs can be reinterpreted but never tested.

*First.* The ground the argument seeks is real but mislocated. What the argument adds to that worry is a personal will to supply the authority, and the dependence of morality on such a will is exactly what the book contests. The ground of moral bindingness is located at §5.14 in the structural constitution of persons and their standing toward one another, not in commands issued from outside that order; obligation is grounded in what persons are and how they stand to one another, under the reciprocity premise that section defends, not conferred by a will above them. If that identification holds, the argument’s central premise (that objective morality depends for its existence on God) is false, with the ground already supplied structurally and no further person required to issue it.

This front must be drawn at the register Chapter 5 actually licenses. The argument of §5.14 proceeds by structural *identification*, not strict derivation: it exhibits where moral bindingness is seated, but doesn’t derive the full content of obligation the way modal status is derived in Chapter 2. A determined moral realist can decline the identification (holding that authority of the relevant kind still requires a commanding will, however well morality maps onto the constitution of persons) and so keep the dependence premise alive. Taken alone, this front shifts the burden; it doesn’t discharge it.

**[Proposition]**

**Real, and Mislocated** · *Proposition*

The moral argument is right twice over: moral facts are not convention, projection, or preference, and their bindingness needs a ground. What it adds to those is a personal will to supply the authority, and that addition is the contested step rather than the shared premise. Obligation is grounded in what persons structurally are and how they stand to one another, under the reciprocity premise defended at §5.14, not conferred on them by a will issuing commands from outside that order. If the structural identification holds, the argument’s central premise—that objective morality depends for its existence on God—is false, not because morality is unfounded but because the ground was already supplied and no further person is required to issue it. The argument locates a real need and fills it with something the need did not call for.

*Status: the identification is structural, not a derivation from the modal proof, and it rests on the reciprocity/equal-standing bridge defended at §5.14 rather than following from the structural facts alone. A moral realist who declines that bridge can hold the dependence premise open. This front shifts the burden; it does not discharge it.*

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

*Second.* The commanding will the argument names can’t be had for free. The argument’s deeper trouble doesn’t wait on Chapter 5. Grant, for the sake of the argument, that moral authority does require a personal ground: the ground the argument names still can’t supply it. The classical commanding will is typically described as atemporal, non-spatial, and immaterial. The revised §10.1.1 result doesn’t make such a being semantically empty by definition. The pressure is whether a timeless divine nature or will can ground directed obligations to distinct persons while preserving determinate authority and content. Ordinary commands are temporal acts. Divine-command theorists may instead ground obligation in God’s eternal nature or standing will. That move avoids a temporal issuing event but still owes an account of the directed relation between commander, content, and obligated persons. Each is a condition of succession, relation, or persistence, and a ground precluded from time, space, and substance hasn’t been shown able to supply any of them. Adams’s resembling goodness, Evans’s loving commander, Hare’s assisting God each presuppose a personal agent doing personal things: willing, relating, sustaining. Pressed to name the will that obligates, the moral argument points at a ground whose standing to command is exactly what remains unexplained.

**[Proposition]**

**A Commanding Will Cannot Be Had for Free** · *Proposition*

Even granting that moral authority requires a personal ground, the ground the argument names cannot supply it. Ordinary commands are temporal acts; grounding obligation in an eternal nature instead avoids the issuing event but still owes an account of the directed relation between commander, content, and the persons obligated. Each is a condition of succession, relation, or persistence, and a ground precluded from time, space, and substance has not been shown able to supply any of them.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

A defender might relax the ground to a personal agent that does instantiate the conditions: temporal, related, present to those it binds. Then the proposal departs from strict classical timelessness. It may still claim ultimacy, but it must explain how an agent participating in temporal and relational moral life grounds rather than merely exemplifies moral authority. The revision keeps a commander by giving up the commander’s ultimacy.

*Third.* Grant the commander outright, and the word the argument leans on has still not been earned. The premise is that *objective* moral values and duties exist, where objective means what the robust realist means by it: not constituted by anyone’s attitudes, holding independently of any stance taken toward it. That is the property the argument says naturalism can’t supply. Ask, then, what in God does the grounding. If it is the will—commands, decrees, a standing intention to bind—then what grounds obligation is a directed relation running from one subject to another: a commander, a content, an addressee. A relation of that form is constituted by the standing of one party toward another, which is precisely what stance-independence was introduced to exclude. The theist hasn’t escaped a stance-involving morality; they have proposed one with an asymmetrically powerful party. If instead it is the divine nature, unchosen and not an attitude, that horn survives the first—but a nature doesn’t command. What grounds obligation is then a standard that obtains, and willing, commanding, and relating do no grounding work; the commander has become a criterion, which is the concession traced through the Euthyphro navigation at §12.3.11. And if the ground is something independent of God altogether, the argument’s own central premise is false as stated.

The point isn’t that a stance-involving morality is defective. The argument defends one (§5.14), and holds that moral facts are stance-involving without being stance-determined, real in the way the standards of a living language are real. The point is that the moral argument’s leverage was comparative: naturalism was said to be unable to deliver an objectivity theism could. If the theistic ground is stance-involving too, that leverage is gone. The live question stops being which account escapes stances and becomes which stance-involving account better explains what obligation is—and that is a question to be settled on the merits, not by the inference from objectivity to a person.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Obligation Problem** · *Disjunction*

Is obligation grounded in the divine will, the divine nature, or neither?

- **If obligation is grounded in the divine will,** then morality is held to a stance. It is constituted by a directed relation among commander, content, and addressee, with one asymmetrically powerful party, rather than a standard independent of every stance. *Feeds into* The Command-Authority Specification (§12.3.11).
- **If obligation is grounded in the unchosen divine nature,** then the personal features do no grounding work. A standard obtains independently of command, and the claim that moral authority requires a personal will is surrendered.
- **If neither grounds obligation,** then the premise that objective morality depends for its existence on God is false.

No branch supplies a ground that is both stance-independent and personal.

*Scope.* The trilemma targets the inference from moral objectivity to a personal ground. It doesn’t deny that God could command, that commands could specify obligations grounded elsewhere, or that a theistic metaethics could be stated.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

*Where a ground can be located.* The preceding fork asks whether a will can supply stance-independent objectivity. A prior question decides how many candidates there are to fork between. Euthyphro is normally run as a two-way choice—an act is forbidden because it is wrong, or wrong because it is forbidden—and both branches share an assumption that goes unexamined: that what makes the act wrong is something other than what it does to the one it is done to. Naming that third possibility changes the shape of the question, because it is the branch on which the other two become unnecessary rather than merely mistaken.

The three grounds aren’t symmetrical in a respect the trilemma doesn’t itself settle. On the first, someone is worse off: a subject with stakes has been harmed, and the wrong is that harm. On the other two, the thing violated has no stakes at all. A command isn’t injured by being broken; a norm isn’t injured by being violated. Whatever the wrong consists in there, it doesn’t consist in anything’s being worse off. The natural reply relocates the injury, to the community or to the agent’s own character, and both forms of that reply concede the asymmetry rather than answering it: each names a subject with stakes and locates the wrong in what happened to it, which is the first branch reached from inside the other two.

The exhaustiveness claim is modest and worth stating exactly. Every candidate ground must locate the wrongness somewhere, and the available somewheres are the party affected, an authority whose directive settles the matter, and a standard the act falls under. A proposal that appears to name a fourth is asked what makes *it* authoritative, and the answer returns one of the three. What the trilemma doesn’t do is decide between them; it establishes that the choice is among three, that the third has a positive occupant rather than a bare denial, and that a defender of either theistic branch is choosing it against a live alternative rather than for want of one.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Wrong Problem** · *Disjunction*

Is an act wrong for the harm it does, the command it breaks, or the standard it violates?

- **If an act is wrong because of the harm it does,** then the wrong consists in what is done to a subject with stakes of its own. Welfare, agency, relationship, and exposure are the materials, and they yield claims on other agents once comparable stakes are granted comparable standing—a premise this account states rather than assumes (§5.14). No commander appears in the ground, and what is owed for defense is the standing premise.
- **If an act is wrong because a command forbids it,** then the wrong consists in the command being broken, whatever happens to the subject. The position must then accept that the same act, done to the same subject with the same effects, differs in moral status with the directive alone (§12.3.11, §12.4.3). *Feeds into* The Command-Authority Specification (§12.3.11).
- **If an act is wrong by an independent standard,** then the wrong consists in violating a norm that holds independently of anyone. The norm’s authority is then not derived from any agent, including a divine one, and this reading owes a reason why a standard binds agents rather than merely describing them (§11.2.4).

A fourth proposal doesn’t add a fourth ground. That an act is wrong because it expresses a defective character postpones the question rather than answering it: asked in virtue of what a trait counts as a virtue, the reply names what the trait does to those affected, a standard it conforms to, or a command it obeys. Moral intuition is likewise not a candidate here, being an account of how wrongness is recognized rather than of what it consists in.

*Scope.* The trilemma fixes where a ground can be located and shows that the familiar fourth options reduce. It doesn’t price the horns: the costs of the command and standard branches are assessed above and at §12.3.11, and the standing premise the first branch requires is defended at §5.14 rather than here.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

The epistemic companion of this argument is taken up at §10.1.13: it grants the moral facts and presses instead on our access to them. The two are independent: the present section’s replies don’t answer the access question, and that section’s replies don’t settle where bindingness is seated.

The argument tracks something real. Moral facts are binding, and their bindingness isn’t self-standing: it is grounded. On the account at §5.14, the mistake is the location: what grounds obligation isn’t a will behind the world but the structural constitution of persons within it, the same inversion run throughout, fixing on a genuine feature and mislocating its bearer. The doctrines this argument carries with it (divine-command theory as an account of where obligation is grounded, §12.3.11, and Hare’s moral gap, §12.3.9) are taken up in their own right in Chapter 12, where the structural account is in hand to reconstruct what survives of them without the existence argument.

The abductive form needs separate handling, since it rests not on the single commanding act the second front dismantles but on a comparative claim: that theism explains the moral landscape better than any rival. The comparison fails at both ends. On the theist’s side, an explanation is only as good as the standing of what is proposed to explain it, and the classical proposal enters the comparison owing the relation problem already identified: a ground precluded from time, space, and substance must account for the explanatory, sustaining, and commanding relations the abduction credits to it before its explanatory fit can be scored.

On the rival side, the inference is run against a strawman naturalism that reduces value to preference or fitness-tracking. The genuine rival is robust non-naturalist realism, worked out most fully by Wielenberg (Wielenberg 2014): objective moral facts as brute necessary truths standing in non-causal *making* relations to their base properties, requiring no commander and no reduction to preference. That account is the near-twin of the structural identification at §5.14, obligation seated in what persons are and how they stand to one another, and it blunts Mavrodes’s queerness charge: necessary moral facts are a serious rival to divine-command accounts, but their normativity isn’t explained merely by analogy with necessary structural conditions. The non-naturalist still owes an account of authoritative reasons and their relation to natural persons.

Against that rival the abductive inference hasn’t yet cleared its comparative step, as the modal-grounding argument hasn’t cleared its own (§10.1.2): a personal ground wins the comparison only where the field of rivals omits the structural and non-naturalist ones.

*Taking stock.* The moral argument is right that moral facts aren’t convention or preference and that they bind, and right that their bindingness must be grounded. It is wrong about the ground, on three fronts that don’t depend on one another. Where Chapter 5’s identification holds, obligation is seated in the structural constitution of persons rather than in a will above them (§5.14). Independently of that identification, the classical ground faces a substantive relation problem: its timeless nature or will must ground determinate obligations to distinct persons without relying on an unexplained command relation. And independently of both, the objectivity the premise asserts can’t be had from a will at all, since a command is a relation between subjects and what it grounds is stance-involving—leaving the argument without the comparative advantage over stance-involving accounts that motivated it. What the argument sees (that morality is grounded) the constitution of persons supplies. What it added (that the ground is a divine will) names a being whose capacity to will and command is the very thing still owing an account.

### 10.1.13 Non-Skepticism and Moral Knowledge
Two epistemic arguments meet here. The first asks why Reality is hospitable to knowledge at all: why rational subjects aren’t predominantly deceived by simulations, misleading appearances, or environments systematically disconnected from what they believe. The second grants an ordinarily hospitable environment and asks why particular faculties track moral, modal, mathematical, or other facts that didn’t straightforwardly shape their development. Both seek an explanatory connection between belief and truth. They differ over its scale. Non-skepticism asks for a connection between a subject’s beliefs and the distribution of deception across Reality; moral knowledge asks for one between a faculty and its subject matter. They are taken as two movements with a verdict each, because an answer to one doesn’t carry over to the other: the first ends at the global-census question, the second at the difference between tracking what harms and tracking what binds. The two meet again only where both invoke a ground that must itself make contact with the knower.

*First movement: the global argument.* Pittard’s inhospitable-world argument begins from internal duplicates: subjects whose total internal perspective is just like one’s own while their beliefs are radically mistaken. Among the conceivable worlds containing such duplicates, he argues, worlds in which most are deceived appear to predominate. If one also holds that one’s warrant would be defeated by learning that almost every relevant duplicate was wrong, then rejecting radical skepticism requires some reason why Reality isn’t arranged that way. Axiarchism supplies one: fundamental concrete reality is necessarily ordered toward the good, and epistemic hospitality is among the goods it favors (Pittard 2024). A theistic extension makes the ordering personal. A good ultimate agent can intend rational creatures to know, and an ultimate agent—unlike a simulator, demiurge, or regional designer—can exclude deceptive observers in every causally isolated domain because nothing exists outside the scope of its permission.

The argument earns its pressure from a familiar fact about defeat. Learning that a process generates overwhelmingly false outputs can defeat confidence in one’s own output even before a particular error is located. It also makes the move to ultimacy intelligible rather than ornamental: a finite designer may calibrate this environment while lacking control over duplicates elsewhere, whereas the proposed bodyguard must explain absences throughout Reality. The claim isn’t merely that God could make reliable thinkers. It is that only an ultimate source can secure the global distribution on which anti-skeptical confidence is said to depend.

Two questions determine whether that global requirement transfers to ordinary knowledge. First comes the comparison class. Conceivable internal duplicates don’t arrive with a measure showing how many worlds contain them or which observers are relevantly similar. Possibility Precedes Probability blocks treating a describable range as a sampled population without an additional premise about its modal standing and weighting. Second comes the scale of warrant. A belief may be connected appropriately to its local object even if remote or causally isolated duplicates are deceived. If that local connection is enough, the global census is unnecessary. If it isn’t enough, the subject’s belief about the census is itself formed inside one local causal network and can’t become sensitive to the distribution merely because a hypothesis capable of controlling the distribution has been described.

The Discursive Minimum fixes a floor beneath the disagreement without deciding it. Any addressed, reason-giving skeptical argument instantiates representation, reasoning, and attempted communication, so it cannot establish their global absence. Radical skepticism here concerns whether the represented content is true or warranted, however, and the theorem establishes neither. It prevents the argument from erasing the activity in which the dispute occurs; it doesn’t certify that activity’s outputs.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Global Census Problem** · *Disjunction*

Does warrant come from your own connection to the world, or from a head count of everyone in it?

- **If a local connection is enough,** then what happens to causally isolated duplicates elsewhere is irrelevant. A belief is warranted through an appropriately reliable connection to its object. The global preponderance isn’t a condition of ordinary knowledge, so the epistemic-bodyguard argument loses its premise.
- **If the global count is required,** then warrant depends on a census no one can take. The distribution is one the local subject cannot survey or causally track. Axiarchism or theism may explain why the distribution is favorable, but that explanation can certify the subject only after the ordering principle, its reach, and its truth-directedness are warranted without relying on the anti-skepticism they were introduced to secure.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t settle the dispute between internalist and externalist theories of warrant, assign a measure to observers, or establish radical skepticism. It identifies the further premise required to move from possible deception to an ultimate epistemic protector.

**Dependency routes:** local-warrant branch—Knowledge (§5.4); global-distribution branch—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5)

The theistic proposal remains relevant on either account. A good creator may raise the expected reliability of local faculties even if no global census is required, and a defender may argue that knowledge need not include reflective access to the source that makes a process reliable. Those are ordinary comparative claims about the likelihood of epistemic agents under competing hypotheses. They require an intention model—why theism predicts truth-directed cognition rather than merely finite cognition—and they inherit the record of error, disagreement, cognitive variation, and alleged divine permission of deception considered at §12.3.6. The global argument therefore adds a live evidential consideration without establishing ultimacy from anti-skepticism alone. That is the first movement’s verdict.

*Second movement: the domain argument.* The argument from moral facts to a divine ground is taken up at §10.1.12; the turn here is from global epistemic hospitality to its domain-specific companion, which grants the facts and targets our access to them. The argument isn’t that naturalism can’t supply moral facts but that it can’t supply moral *knowledge*: a naturalist who is a full-blooded realist about moral facts still owes an account of why the faculty delivering our moral beliefs should track those facts, when the process that installed it was selecting for reproductive fitness and nothing else. Street’s Darwinian dilemma (Street 2006) and Joyce’s genealogical argument (Joyce 2006) put the pressure in secular form; Crummett and Swenson (Crummett and Swenson 2019) press it as a comparative argument for theism, and Bogardus (Bogardus 2016) sharpens which version survives, arguing that most debunking arguments rest on principles that fail, while one—the argument from symmetry—threatens naturalists specifically, forcing a choice among abandoning moral realism, accepting a rationalism uncomfortable inside naturalism, or abandoning naturalism.

The driving premise is an explanationist principle about defeat, developed most carefully by Korman and Locke (Korman and Locke 2023; Korman and Locke 2020): if your beliefs in a domain rest ultimately on something that isn’t explained by the facts that domain is about, those beliefs are defeated. The principle earns its plausibility from cases where it plainly bites. Someone who learns that the travel book she believed was written by an author with no contact of any kind with the country described has acquired a defeater, and the defeat doesn’t wait on showing that any particular claim in it is false. Someone who learns that a powerful mathematical intuition was installed by a hypnotist who flipped a coin over which intuition to install should suspend the belief, however the coin landed. What defeats in each case isn’t falsity and not unreliability in the abstract, but a conceded absence of explanatory connection between the belief’s source and the subject matter. Applied to morality, the argument’s second premise says naturalism concedes exactly that absence: bedrock moral intuitions were installed because they were fitness-enhancing, and moral facts aren’t the kind of thing that reaches into a genome. As the argument’s proponents observe, an evolutionary biologist explaining why we find infant torture abhorrent never cites the fact that infant torture is abhorrent. If moral beliefs rest on intuitions unexplained by moral facts, they are defeated; we do have moral knowledge; so naturalism is false. The argument then extends past morality: the same reasoning is applied to intuitions about modality, composition, mathematics, and theory choice, on the ground that abstract facts in those domains no more shape selection pressures than moral facts do, and the naturalist who accepts the principle in the moral case owes an explanation of why it stops there.

Grant the force of the principle. Something has genuinely gone wrong in the travel-book and hypnosis cases, and it is what the principle says has gone wrong. Grant also that the extension is fair rather than opportunistic: a naturalist who accepts explanationist defeat for moral intuitions and then exempts modal or mathematical intuitions owes a reason, and Bogardus is right that the versions of the debunking argument turning on unreliability alone are the weaker ones. Nothing below treats the argument as a trick or the worry as manufactured.

*First.* The argument’s second premise describes a naturalism, but not this one. That premise needs moral facts to be the kind of thing incapable of explaining a creature’s dispositions—abstract, causally inert, on the far side of a gap that selection pressures can’t cross. Read that way the premise is plainly right, and the argument goes through. It is the reading the book’s account of morality doesn’t supply. What a moral fact is, at §5.14, is a fact about how agents may treat subjects who have welfare, agency, relationships, and stakes of their own. Facts of that shape aren’t on the far side of any gap. A creature’s distress, on the account given at §5.14, isn’t an inert abstractum reporting on a configuration from outside it: under Configurational Necessitation (§2.9.4) and the identity defended at §5.1, no complete realization of a configuration of exposure lacks the aversive interior, and the distress *is* the configuration showing through. Whether an action damages a subject’s welfare, commandeers its agency, or severs its relationships is therefore a fact about the very configurations selection has always had to answer to. An organism that couldn’t register what harms conspecifics and what sustains them wasn’t tracking a separate normative realm badly; it was tracking the configurations of its own environment badly, and paid for it.

That is what closes the explanatory gap the premise requires. The connection runs through the subject matter itself rather than through a lucky correlation: the properties that make an act wrong on this account—that it damages, commandeers, or disregards a subject with stakes—are properties an organism embedded among such subjects has been under continuous pressure to detect. The intuitions are explained by the facts they are about, in the only sense the principle asks for.

**[Proposition]**

**The Explanatory Connection Is Available** · *Proposition*

The explanationist defeat argument requires that naturalism concede no explanatory connection between moral intuitions and moral facts. The concession is forced only where moral facts are causally inert abstracta standing outside the configurations organisms respond to. On the account at §5.14, a moral fact is a fact about how an act bears on a subject with welfare, agency, relationships, and stakes, and, given the identity defended at §5.1, under Configurational Necessitation a subject’s aversive interior is the configuration showing through rather than a separate item correlated with it.
