Facts of that kind are among the facts selection has always had to answer to, so the intuitions responding to them are explained by what they are about. The argument’s second premise is therefore not a consequence of naturalism as such but of a particular metaethics the book does not hold.

*Status: the connection secured here is to the descriptive layer—that an act damages, commandeers, or disregards a subject with stakes. It does not by itself secure a connection to the normative fact that such acts bind, which on §5.14’s account rests on the reciprocity and equal-standing bridge that section defends by argument and does not derive. The objection can therefore be pressed again one level up, and the passage following states it at strength. A moral realist who holds that moral facts are stance-independent abstracta of the debunked kind faces the argument in full force; what is shown is that the argument’s premise requires that metaethics, not that the premise is false on every naturalism.*

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

The reply is bounded in a further way worth stating. It closes the gap for the properties that make acts wrong; it doesn’t thereby vindicate any particular moral intuition, and it shouldn’t. That a faculty is responsive to a domain is compatible with its being badly calibrated within it, and the historical record of moral belief is a record of severe miscalibration alongside genuine correction. What the reply removes is the *global* defeater—the claim that nothing in the domain could be tracked at all. Local defeaters remain, and the account at Morality (§5.14) supplies the standard against which local correction runs. A tradition that revised its judgment about who counts as a subject with stakes wasn’t merely changing its preferences; it was correcting toward a fact about which beings have welfare and agency, which is the kind of correction the bridge licenses and the debunking picture can’t describe.

The objection to that reply isn’t that the explanatory connection fails but that it reaches the wrong facts, and it should be stated in full because the answer to it is partial. Grant everything the front claims: an organism embedded among subjects with welfare has been under continuous pressure to detect damage, commandeering, and disregard, and its aversive registrations are those configurations showing through rather than representations correlated with them. What has been explained is sensitivity to the *descriptive* facts—that this act damages, that this subject is exposed. The moral claim is that such acts are *wrong*, and wrongness on the account at §5.14 doesn’t follow from the descriptive facts alone; it follows from them together with the reciprocity and equal-standing bridge, which that section defends by argument and explicitly declines to derive. An explanationist can therefore accept the whole of the first front and press again one level up: the intuition that harm occurs is explained by harm, and the intuition that harm is *binding on me regardless of whose harm it is* hasn’t been shown to be explained by anything the configuration contains.

This is where Bogardus’s symmetry argument bears, and it is the version of the debunking case taken most seriously. His trilemma offers the naturalist three exits: abandon moral realism, accept a rationalism uncomfortable inside naturalism, or abandon naturalism (Bogardus 2016). The position here takes the second and disputes the discomfort. The bridge isn’t a faculty of non-natural apprehension and doesn’t require one; it is a principle defended in the ordinary way philosophical principles are defended—by consistency, by the mutual exposure of the parties it governs, and by the instability of a self-exemption that can’t be stated without abandoning the standing it claims. A naturalist who reasons isn’t thereby a rationalist in any sense naturalism forbids, and no step in that defense requires a mode of access the natural world doesn’t supply. What the position can’t claim is that the bridge is *derived*. The account says so in its own voice (§5.14), and the Status of the front above inherits it. No Arbitrary Self-Exemption nevertheless fixes what follows once the bridge and relevant similarity are granted: first-person location alone can’t make a feature claim-grounding for oneself but not for another. The dispute therefore comes to rest at a definite place. Whether equal standing has normative authority remains open; whether one may grant it and then reserve an unsupported indexical exception doesn’t. That is narrower than the question the argument began with, and pointing at evolution doesn’t reopen it.

*Second.* The counterfactual the argument runs on isn’t as open as the wind-and-tides image suggests. Street’s analogy asks us to picture selection as a force whose direction has nothing to do with the destination—wind and tides on a boat set out for Bermuda—and the illustrative cases are meant to show how far off course it could have pushed us. Darwin’s hive-bees are the oldest of them: reared under their conditions, unmarried women would think it a sacred duty to kill their brothers. The case repays a closer look than it usually gets, because the behavior it describes isn’t arbitrary. Worker bees favor sisters over brothers as a consequence of haplodiploid relatedness asymmetries (Hamilton 1964): the reproductive economics of the lineage fix the outcome. That isn’t wind. It is a structural constraint operating on a differently constituted creature.

The counterfactual then forks, and neither reading delivers what the argument needs. Read it as changing the creature—bees really are bees, with their own relations of stake, exposure, and reproductive interest—and the subjects whose welfare the moral facts concern have changed along with it. On the account at §5.14 a moral fact is a fact about how an act bears on subjects with welfare, agency, relationships, and stakes; alter what the subjects are and one has altered which facts obtain, so no case of a faculty getting the facts wrong has yet been exhibited. Read it instead as Darwin wrote it—“if *men* were reared under precisely the same conditions as hive-bees”—and the human constitution is held fixed while the social conditions are imported. That reading does describe error, since creatures with human stakes would be systematically misjudging them. But the scenario is then not a product of selection at all: selection never placed human-constituted creatures in hive conditions, and the thought experiment did, by stipulation. The pump draws its force from holding fixed exactly what an actual change of evolutionary course would have altered.

The same structure shows in the formal results. Axelrod’s analysis of iterated exchange finds that strategies enacting non-initiation of harm and reciprocity-with-forgiveness do well under noise across a wide range of environments (Axelrod 1984), a result about the game rather than about any species: among agents that persist, are mutually reachable, and interact repeatedly, the strategies that fare well are constrained. Selection operating on such agents is better pictured as a channel with banks than as wind on open water. This doesn’t show that selection aims at moral truth, and nothing here claims it does. What it removes is the assumption that the alternatives were freely distributed across the whole space of logically possible evaluative judgments, which is the assumption that makes the actual outcome look like a fluke of luck requiring a lucky coincidence to explain.

The point can be put without the counterfactual at all. What the debunking argument needs is variation in the stakes, not variation in belief, and the stakes aren’t a free parameter. Any lineage that persists faces damage, depends on others, and meets the same others repeatedly; those conditions are what make a creature the kind of thing that can be harmed. A creature indifferent to harm isn’t a differently calibrated version of us but a thing with nothing at stake, and selection doesn’t run on such things.

The actual world already supplies variation of the only kind available, and it doesn’t deliver what the argument needs. Human constitutions differ, sometimes sharply, and moral response differs with them. But those are differences in access to stakes, not differences in the stakes themselves. Someone whose capacity for moral response is impaired still has a life that can go badly, still depends on others, still can be wronged; the impairment doesn’t hand them a different set of things to lose. The pattern that results is the one a stake-tracking account predicts, convergence where the stakes are shared and divergence where access to them is damaged, and it isn’t a pattern a lucky calibration has any reason to produce.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Debunking Counterfactual Fork** · *Disjunction*

What would a different evolutionary history actually have changed?

- **If the creature itself changes,** then its stakes change with it, and the moral facts are about a different kind of creature. Its relations of exposure, dependence, and reproductive interest move together with its constitution. Correctly tracking that configuration isn’t an instance of error.
- **If only the circumstances change,** then the scenario may describe error. But it is stipulated by the thought experiment rather than produced by a different course of selection.

The case gets its force by holding fixed precisely what a different evolutionary course would have changed.

*Scope.* The dilemma targets the motivating counterfactuals, not the explanationist defeat principle. It neither denies possible miscalibration nor claims that selection aims at moral truth.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

*Third.* The extension past morality meets a different obstacle, and it is the one the book is best positioned to answer. Applied to modal intuitions, the argument holds that facts about what is possible can’t explain our beliefs about what is possible, since a merely possible purple cow exerts no influence on anything. That framing treats modal facts as inhabitants of a realm adjacent to the actual one, reachable only across a bridge naturalism can’t build. On the account at §2.9.6, the modal structure isn’t adjacent to the actual world; it is the structure of the world the organism is embedded in and made of. Knowledge (§5.4) accordingly describes a body’s modal field as built from contact with that structure and corrected against it, and the Modal Convergence theorem states the conditions under which agreement among independently built fields is evidence of tracking rather than of shared error—independence of inquiry, discriminating checks, and an object able to correct them. A creature that misjudges what is possible in its vicinity walks into what it took to be passable. The explanatory connection here isn’t a bridge to a separate realm but embedding in the only one there is.

The mathematical case divides at the ontology of its subject matter. For arithmetic and mathematics understood structurally, access doesn’t require a faculty causally struck by the number 7. A proof is an actual, rule-governed sequence in which the conclusion preserves relations fixed by its premises and operations; its warrant comes from that inferential connection. Its content concerns the invariant structure of pluralities, orderings, magnitudes, transformations, and possible configurations. On the articulation thesis defended at §2.6.12 and developed against Platonism at §8.1.5, mathematical reasoning is therefore performed by a configuration within Nature upon structures Nature affords. The connection is constitutive and inferential rather than a causal signal sent by an abstract object.

That answer doesn’t cover every philosophy of mathematics. A robust Platonist who holds that mathematical truths concern irreducibly abstract objects independent of every actual and possible concrete structure retains Benacerraf’s access problem (Benacerraf 1973): what explains the reliability of beliefs about objects that enter no causal relation? Theism can propose that a designer knows those truths and calibrates finite reasoners toward them, but the proposal owes two connections rather than removing the first—between abstracta and the divine intellect, and between that intellect and a material cognizer. If mathematical truths are instead constituted by divine thought, the view has changed the subject from access to truthmaking and must explain why those truths are necessary rather than selectable. Neither problem is manufactured by naturalism, and neither is solved merely by adding a knower.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Mathematical Tracking Fork** · *Disjunction*

What is mathematical reasoning tracking?

- **If mathematical reasoning tracks invariant structure,** then no access to a separate realm is required. Proof supplies an inferential connection to the consequences of specified axioms and operations, and application requires evidence that a concrete system realizes the relevant structure.
- **If mathematical reasoning tracks independent abstract objects,** then the access problem remains for any knower. A divine calibration proposal must specify both divine access to the objects and the contact by which a material reasoner is made reliable about them.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t establish nominalism, validate every axiom or intuition, or reduce pure mathematics to current physical application. It separates the structural mathematics for which the book supplies an access relation from robust Platonism, where the access problem remains live.

**Dependency routes:** structural route—Conditioned-Nature (§2.6.12) and Invariant Realization (§3.5.6); separate-realm route—the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)

Abstract composition principles require the same division but aren’t settled merely by naming it. Where a principle spells out determinate relations among possible wholes and parts, the structural route is available; where it is treated as a truth about an independent abstract domain, the access burden remains. The argument’s extension is therefore answered for structural and conditional knowledge while remaining live for the stronger independent-realm ontology.

*Fourth.* Grant the principle and grant the defeat, and the theistic side has still to satisfy the same principle it invoked. A God who underwrites moral knowledge must stand in a determinate relation to the believer’s cognition: the divine intention that the creature’s moral faculty deliver truths has to explain the faculty’s actually delivering them, or the explanatory connection the argument demands is missing on the theistic side too. That relation is a concrete operation—it produces an effect in a temporally extended, materially constituted cognizer at a particular point in that cognizer’s history—and the Concrete-Entity Test of Structural Requirement (§2.4) applies at the operation. The requirement isn’t marginal to the argument but built into the development, on which the explanatory constraint is satisfiable only by a ground with sufficient ultimacy to explain absences as well as presences, which is a demand for exactly the concrete grounding relation §10.4 later gathers under the Grounding-Contact Trilemma. The classical ground can meet the demand by accepting the structural conditions at the operation, which revises it, or by declining them, which leaves the explanatory connection unspecified in precisely the way the principle counts as defeating. What it can’t do is invoke the principle against the naturalist and stand outside its reach.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Bodyguard Problem** · *Disjunction*

Does the ground itself have the conditions it says our knowing requires?

- **If it has them,** then the connection is specified—but the ground now sits inside the structure it was meant to explain. That is a revised theism, not a ground classically outside the structure.
- **If it doesn’t have them,** then the position is defeated by its own standard. The connection remains unspecified in the very way the explanationist principle counts as defeating.

The principle cannot be applied to the naturalist while its proponent’s own ground is exempted from it.

*Scope.* The dilemma tests the theistic account’s standing to use the principle, not the principle itself. A revised theism can take the first horn without contradiction.

**Depends on:** the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)

*Fifth.* The positive proposal has a second cost, and it falls out of how the argument is motivated rather than from any premise it states. The theistic solution is that a good God has reason and means to bias the mechanism producing our cognitive faculties toward moral truth. Call that the calibration claim. It isn’t a bare posit: it is offered as explaining why our moral beliefs are largely accurate, and its evidential work depends on our being able to tell that they are. The argument therefore relies twice on the same faculty—once to register that fratricide-as-sacred-duty would be monstrous, which is what makes the counterfactual a case of *error* rather than of difference, and again to register that our actual moral beliefs are largely right, which is what the calibration claim is invoked to explain. A calibrated faculty’s deliverances are, on this account, evidence about moral truth.

That is a commitment with reach the argument doesn’t control. The same faculty, turned on the legal and narrative material the Abrahamic traditions hold to be divine legislation or divine command, returns the same kind of recoil: at a statute permitting a father to sell his daughter (Exod 21:7–11), at one under which beating an enslaved person to death carries no penalty if the victim survives a day or two, “for the slave is his money” (Exod 21:20–21), at a command distinguishing within a defeated population to keep the virgin girls (Num 31:17–18). Whether those texts can bear the readings their defenders give them isn’t a question this section takes up; it is argued at §12.4.2 and §12.4.3, where the accommodation, hyperbole, and misattribution defenses are each stated and priced. What matters here is narrower and doesn’t wait on how that is settled. The recoil isn’t manufactured by critics: the sustained apologetic literature on these passages—the regulation-not-endorsement reading, the redemptive-movement hermeneutic, the accommodation doctrine running back through Calvin—is itself evidence that the recoil is felt within the traditions, since defenses are written where a moral response has already registered an objection.

Three positions are available and each carries something. A defender may hold that the recoil is unreliable in this application, which preserves the texts but withdraws the faculty’s standing at the point where the argument’s own counterfactuals need it, since those counterfactuals are cases of error only if the recoil reports truly. A defender may hold that the recoil is reliable and the texts nonetheless carry defensible readings, which is the burden set out at §12.4.2 and §12.4.3. Or a defender may hold that the recoil is reliable and that these attributions are human rather than divine—the branch both of those sections already carry, and the one a great many theists occupy. That third position is consistent, it keeps the calibration claim intact, and it isn’t a concession of theism; what it gives up is the inerrancy premise, which the moral-knowledge argument never needed and doesn’t assert.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Moral Recoil Problem** · *Disjunction*

What happens when the faculty God supposedly calibrated recoils at what God supposedly commanded?

- **If the recoil is unreliable here,** then the faculty loses the standing on which the argument’s own counterfactual examples depend.
- **If the recoil is reliable and the texts have defensible readings,** then those readings have to be defended, not assumed.
- **If the recoil is reliable and the attribution is human,** then the position remains theistic but surrenders inerrancy.

The calibration claim cannot license the faculty only when it confirms the source credited with calibrating it. It must accept the recoil, defend the attribution, or narrow the doctrine.

*Scope.* The trilemma states what the calibration claim commits its user to. It decides neither the explanationist principle nor any exegetical question.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

*The damaged-faculty reply.* A tradition may run the calibration claim in the opposite direction. Rather than holding that the moral faculty is divinely tuned to track moral facts, it may hold that the faculty is impaired—that sin darkens the intellect and disorders the appetites—and use that impairment to explain why a sincere inquirer finds some of the tradition’s moral teaching intuitively unacceptable. The objection is then not answered but accounted for: the intuition is what the tradition predicted a damaged instrument would produce, so it isn’t evidence against the tradition.

The reply is made carefully by those who make it. It isn’t offered as global skepticism about moral judgment, and its defenders anticipate the charge that it undercuts the reasoning that reached the tradition in the first place. The damage is presented as directional rather than uniform: it is said to track disordered appetite, so that a person underrates the gravity of what they wish to keep doing and overrates their own desert, while leaving empirical and historical reasoning substantially intact. That confinement is what the reply needs, and it is a real distinction rather than an evasion.

What the confinement doesn’t supply is a control group. The traditions that make this claim also hold that the impairment is universal—that no one is without sin—so the differential the reply requires can’t come from the presence or absence of the damage. It has to come from degree, or from repair. Both routes are available, and each transfers the burden somewhere it is harder to discharge. If the differential is degree, then the mark of a less impaired faculty is needed, and the mark ordinarily offered is agreement with the tradition’s own moral conclusions: the witnesses cited as clear-sighted are those who arrived where the argument is heading. Their convergence is evidence of reliability only if reliability was fixed some other way. If the differential is repair by grace, the question becomes the distribution of that repair, and an appeal to inward aid can’t simultaneously leave the unaided evidence sufficient for everyone in the same respect (§12.3.6).

The repair route carries a further difficulty, and it is the one that decides how much the reply can carry. The evidence that any faculty has been repaired is first-person report—the convert who says they had not grasped the gravity of their own sin, the ascetic whose sense of desert deepens. Those reports are produced by the faculty at issue, by people the tradition still counts as sinners, after adopting the framework that predicts the report. The direction of the change was specified in advance by the hypothesis the change is offered to support. A report of that shape shows that the output moved; it doesn’t show that the instrument improved.

Nor can the intensity of the new conviction close the gap, because the reply has already spent that resource. The discounting of the objector’s contrary intuition proceeds by noting that strength of seeming is weakly correlated with the absence of distorting factors. If that holds, it holds symmetrically: the depth of the converted conviction isn’t itself a mark of restored sight, and can’t be counted as one while the objector’s certainty is being discounted for exactly that reason.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Self-Reported Repair Problem** · *Disjunction*

If sin impairs everyone’s moral judgment, what tells an impaired judgment from a repaired one?

- **If the difference is one of degree,** then some mark of the less impaired faculty is owed. Agreement with the tradition’s own conclusions cannot be that mark. The witnesses offered as clear-sighted are selected by having reached the position in question, so their convergence establishes reliability only if reliability was fixed independently.
- **If the difference comes from repair through grace,** then the question passes to who receives that repair, and those who sought it without receiving it aren’t thereby shown to have resisted.

On either branch, the evidence that repair occurred is a report by the repaired faculty, made by someone the tradition still counts as a sinner, in the direction the framework predicted in advance. That the output changed isn’t yet evidence that the instrument improved.

The intensity of the new conviction cannot supply what the report doesn’t. An argument that discounts the objector’s contrary intuition on the ground that strength of seeming tracks distortion poorly has thereby given up citing strength of seeming on its own side.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t deny that moral formation is real, that conscience can be dulled by what one repeatedly does, or that conversion changes what a person sees. It doesn’t impugn anyone’s sincerity or their account of their own history. It fixes what the impairment claim can be used to establish about the standing of an objector’s judgment relative to a believer’s.

**Depends on:** Morality (§5.14)

*Taking stock.* The two arguments identify a genuine constraint: belief-forming processes owe some account of their connection to truth. On the first movement, the global argument doesn’t establish that ordinary warrant depends on a census of causally isolated duplicates, and without that premise it doesn’t establish an ultimate epistemic protector. It does identify a comparative question the naturalist can’t answer merely by pointing to this one reliable subject: what licenses the relevant comparison class, and why should its distribution be epistemically hospitable?

On the second movement, the moral-knowledge argument applies the same demand within particular domains, and its verdict has two layers that must not be merged. It doesn’t establish that naturalism as such can’t supply the connection. Where the identification at Morality (§5.14) holds, moral facts are facts about the configurations of subjects with stakes, and those are among the facts an embedded organism has always been under pressure to track—so the explanatory connection the principle requires is present at the descriptive layer, and what remains there is the ordinary work of local correction rather than a global defeater. The connection to the normative layer isn’t secured by the same move, and the section says so: it rests on a bridging principle defended by argument rather than derived at §5.14, which is where Bogardus’s trilemma genuinely bites and where the position takes the rationalism horn while disputing that reasoning of that kind is foreign to naturalism. That question is live and is left live.

The counterfactuals that motivate the argument equivocate between changing what a creature is and changing only its circumstances, and only the second describes error while only the first describes something selection would have done. The extension to modal intuition meets the same answer through embedding in the one modal structure. Mathematical and compositional knowledge divide: proof and realization supply the connection for structural and conditional truths, while robust independent-realm versions retain an access problem for natural and divine knowers alike.

Independently of all of these, the principle reaches the ground offered to replace naturalism: an intention that explains a creature’s cognition is a concrete operation, and the account owes the contact every other concrete-acting classical ground in this chapter has been asked for. And the calibration claim that makes the theistic solution explanatory commits its user to the faculty’s deliverances more widely than the argument’s chosen cases, at a cost that can be paid but should be paid explicitly.

What both arguments see—that knowledge requires a connection to what is known—the structural account answers by placing the knower inside what there is to know, rather than by positioning a mind outside it to install the connection from there.

### 10.1.14 Pascal’s Wager
Pascal’s *Pensées* (Pascal 1670) advances a prudential argument for theistic belief that has shaped the apologetic literature for three and a half centuries. The wager doesn’t claim that the God of classical Christian theism exists, nor that the evidence weighs in favor of existence. It claims that, under uncertainty, belief is the rational choice: finite costs are evaluated against an infinite expected return. Where the cosmological and ontological arguments engaged earlier in this cluster purport to establish a conclusion about what is the case, the wager purports only to settle a question about what to do under irresolvable uncertainty. Its appeal is that it appears to bypass the metaphysical disputes the other arguments inherit. Whether it does turns on what its payoff presupposes, and what that presupposition invites and costs must be assessed on the wager’s own decision-theoretic terms.

Contemporary reconstructions sharpen the wager’s defended form. Jordan (Jordan 2006) develops the canonical analytic treatment, treating the wager as a many-gods-robust decision under genuine option in the William James (James 1896) sense, and argues that the wager survives several classical objections when properly reconstructed: the principle of insufficient reason, the mixed-strategies dilemma developed by Hájek (Hájek 2003), and the symmetric-payoff parodies. Lycan and Schlesinger (Lycan and Schlesinger 1989) press the dominance argument: granted any non-zero credence in the classical Christian God, no available strategy dominates belief. The load-bearing premise across these reconstructions is the same: *P*(God exists) > 0, where the God in question is the necessary-being God of classical Christian theism whose existence underwrites the infinite expected payoff.

*The modal distinction.* The wager’s prudential framing may invite a modal interpretation that its premises don’t establish. Non-zero *objective chance* would require a genuine possibility, but Pascal’s wager ordinarily uses epistemic credence. A rational agent may assign non-zero credence to a proposition that is in fact impossible because its modal status is unknown. Thus *P*(God exists) > 0 doesn’t by itself entail metaphysical ◇(God exists)—the asymmetry that Possibility Precedes Probability states directly at §2.9.5: an objective probability requires an antecedently established possibility, but an epistemic credence isn’t thereby an objective probability, so no entailment runs from credence to metaphysical modal status. The wager therefore need not assert a metaphysical possibility premise; it needs a defensible epistemic credence. The God on whose existence the wager’s infinite payoff depends (the God of classical Christian theism, omniscient and omnipotent and morally perfect across worlds) is a necessary being on the tradition’s own commitment: Anselm (*Proslogion* (1078) 1998, III); Aquinas (*Summa Theologiae* (1265–1274) 1947, I.2.3); Plantinga (1974). The classical conception forecloses a contingent reading: *God exists* is therefore equivalent to □(God exists), with no contingent witness available. If metaphysical possibility of a necessarily existing God were independently established, S5 would yield necessary existence. The wager’s epistemic credence doesn’t establish that modal premise. The argument and its S5 defenses are carried at §2.1.5, and the parallel line through the modal ontological argument’s explicit possibility premise is closed at §10.1.1.

The wager resembles Plantinga’s argument only if epistemic probability is conflated with metaphysical possibility. Kept distinct, the wager is a decision-theoretic argument under uncertainty, not a disguised S5 proof. Plantinga explicitly uses a metaphysical possibility premise and S5. Pascal uses credence and expected utility. Conflating the two would be an error; the wager must be assessed on decision-theoretic rather than modal-transfer grounds.

*The epistemic reading.* A defender may reply that the wager’s probability is epistemic rather than metaphysical: Pascal is reasoning under uncertainty, not assigning probabilities to metaphysical alternatives. This is the wager’s standard interpretation, not a retreat. Decision theory routinely operates with epistemic credences under uncertainty. The harder problems are different: assigning coherent probabilities across rival religions and payoff schemes, handling infinite utilities, accounting for mixed strategies and finite costs, and determining whether belief is voluntarily controllable. The epistemic reading therefore preserves the wager while exposing it to the standard decision-theoretic objections.

*A further pressure.* The classical-Christian-God specification isn’t optional for the wager: it is what underwrites the infinite payoff. The payoff structure requires that the wagered-for being be such that its existence settles eternity in the manner the wager presupposes: omnipotent enough to deliver infinite reward, omniscient enough to recognize the wagered belief, morally engaged enough to honor it. A god whose attributes fall short of that specification doesn’t deliver the payoff structure the wager needs. The many-gods objection identifies one difficulty: too many candidates fit the prudential framework, and the calculation can’t select among them. The present objection identifies another: only a being meeting that specification supplies the stipulated infinite payoff.

*The wager’s aim.* The wager has force because the loss of possibility isn’t a trivial risk. Heaven gathers images of a life no longer exposed to final foreclosure: continuing existence, security, reunion, abundance, and a future that doesn’t close. In that register, the wager identifies a real drive: the current reaches toward a wider field of possibility. But it privatizes that drive and projects its fulfillment beyond the world. The wagerer is asked to treat God not first as true or worthy of love, but as the insurer of an individual future; belief is recommended as a strategy for securing the wagerer’s own outcome. If the promised relation requires sincere faith rather than strategic self-protection, the wager can’t supply what it needs: it may motivate religious performance or an attempt to cultivate belief, but it can’t make the instrumental motive truth-directed or turn it into the relation its payoff presupposes.

Maximum possibility (§6) relocates the same pressure: it isn’t a post-mortem reward allocated to a successful bettor, but the shared task of maintaining the widest field of live possibility for persons under necessities met. The heaven-image registers that aim in projected form; the wager mistakes it for a private insurance policy.

**[Proposition]**

**The Bypass Presupposes What It Bypasses** · *Proposition*

The wager is offered as a way past the metaphysical disputes the other theistic arguments inherit: not a claim about what is the case, but about what to do under uncertainty. It does not get past them. Its infinite payoff is underwritten by one specific being—powerful enough to deliver the reward, knowing enough to recognize the belief, engaged enough to honor it—and that specification carries the whole metaphysical burden the prudential framing was meant to avoid. A vaguer god does not pay. Nor can the wager be converted into a modal proof to recover the difference: it runs on epistemic credence, and a credence is not an objective probability, which is what would require an antecedently established possibility. Kept distinct, the wager remains a decision-theoretic recommendation under contestable credences; conflated, it becomes an argument Pascal did not make.

**Depends on:** Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5)

*Taking stock.* The wager doesn’t establish God’s existence and shouldn’t be converted into an S5 derivation. As prudential reasoning, it depends on contestable epistemic credences, utility assignments, and a treatment of the many-gods problem. The classical-Christian specification supplies one payoff model but doesn’t receive probability merely from being describable. The wager can remain a pragmatic recommendation for some agents under some credal states; it doesn’t settle the rival-ultimate question. A second strand of the wager (Pascal’s counsel that one may *cultivate* belief by acting as if, until assent follows) meets the account of the will at §5.11, which shows the will can’t install a conviction its field withholds. The strong claim that belief is uniquely rational doesn’t survive without further decision-theoretic and theological premises.

### 10.1.15 The Argument from Beauty
The argument from beauty runs the same evidential form as §10.1.9 and §10.1.10: some pervasive fact is said to be antecedently surprising on naturalism and unsurprising on theism, and the disparity is offered as evidence. Here the fact is aesthetic rather than nomic or phenomenal.

Tennant catalogued its range across a whole book: nature isn’t beautiful in isolated places but, as he puts it, “sublime or beautiful” from “the starry heaven to the siliceous skeleton of the diatom,” in structures large and small, and “the exceptions do but prove the rule” (Tennant 1930). The catalogue is easy to extend past what any one survey attempts: proteins, cells, and ecosystems; galaxies and geological time; mathematical proofs and physical law; architecture, music, and narrative.

On the older form of the argument, the wager was that beauty is an objective property and that its objectivity itself needs a ground. Tallon’s treatment surveys several versions and develops one derived from Plantinga, drawing on the *Mozart Argument* in support of beauty’s objectivity, and extends the case beyond beauty to play, holding that both sit naturally within a theistic picture and awkwardly within a naturalistic one (Tallon 2018).

McKay’s version declines the objectivity wager. It targets our capacity for aesthetic *experience* rather than the standing of the beauty that experience responds to, and holds that the nature and range of such experience are explained neither by standard Darwinian selection nor by the more elaborate sociobiological mechanisms offered to extend it, sexual selection and between-group selection among them; he presents the formulation as improving on others in depending neither on contested probability judgments, nor on analogies between natural phenomena and human artefacts, nor on objectivism about aesthetic value (McKay 2023).

A third form, the one presentations most often reach for and which non-theist philosophers have sometimes granted, is conjunctive: a world containing beauty *and* beings able to appreciate it is held to be likelier on theism than on naturalism, and the combination rather than either conjunct is offered as the thing wanting explanation.

The standard reply to the counter-evidence of ugliness isn’t to deny it but to relocate its significance: on the classical aesthetic theodicy, an ugly part can be integral to a beautiful whole exactly as a discordant passage serves a resolving one, or as painted hands too arresting to be beautiful in isolation serve a composition that needs the eye to move past them (Augustine of Hippo (413–426) 1998). And the argument is said to survive even a thoroughgoing aesthetic subjectivism: if there is no fact about what is beautiful apart from what appreciating minds register, the existence of minds so extensively calibrated to register it is still the thing to be explained, and explained better by a maker with reason to produce such minds than by chance variation across an indifferent process.

Grant what should be granted. The world isn’t sparingly or occasionally beautiful; on any honest inventory it is saturated with it, in exactly the sense Tennant meant. The capacity to register that beauty, across senses and across abstractions with no sensory form at all, is a striking fact about the creatures that have it. Nothing in what follows treats either fact as small or waves it off as illusion.

Three arguments have been described and they aren’t one argument, so what answers one may leave another untouched. The **indicative** version, Tennant’s and, on the objectivity side, Tallon’s, holds that the world’s beauty is evidence of the character of what made it, and that beauty’s standing as a real feature is itself something naturalism accommodates poorly. The **conjunctive** version holds that a beautiful world together with minds able to appreciate it is a combination unlikely on naturalism, the pairing rather than either half carrying the weight. The **capacity** version, McKay’s, sets the world’s beauty largely aside and asks about us: whether the nature and range of our aesthetic experience is explained by selection or its sociobiological extensions. The three carry different commitments, and the capacity version carries the fewest by design, since it declines objectivism about aesthetic value and the artefact analogy that the others draw on. Any reply that leaves it standing hasn’t finished. The order below is set by that: the first two fronts are addressed to the conjunctive and capacity versions, since those are the demanding ones; the later fronts bear on the indicative version and on the defenses the tradition has built around it, and aren’t offered as reaching McKay’s.

*First.* The argument treats beauty as a further fact standing over and above a structured world and a feeling creature—a third thing, distributed across both, whose pervasiveness is then a separate coincidence to be priced. On the book’s own account of what beauty is, that isn’t the right unit of analysis. That account establishes that a work’s resonance—the very phenomenon the tradition calls beauty—isn’t a property residing in the form nor a private state residing in the receiver, but the event between them: a structured thing externalizing what a receiver’s feeling, imagination, and language can take up, with the fit itself doing the work neither party does alone (§5.15).

Once that identification is granted, Tennant’s catalogue isn’t one surprising fact needing one explanation. It is the intersection of two independently motivated facts already derived without any appeal to beauty: that Nature’s structural order is everywhere patterned, recursive, and law-governed rather than everywhere-uniform (the very order shown at §10.1.9 not to be the free-standing coincidence the fine-tuning reading needs), and that feeling, imagination, and drive are widespread among conscious life, deriving from the same naturalistic apparatus, established independently of any aesthetic payoff (§5.2, §5.3, §5.5).

Given structured form and receivers so equipped, resonance events aren’t a further low-probability draw stacked on top of two other unlikely facts; they are what the intersection of two already-explained facts predicts. The claim should be held at the strength it has. It rests on the resonance account of §5.15, and it reduces the surprise the argument trades on rather than exhausting aesthetics: it doesn’t explain why these forms rather than others strike us as beautiful, settle whether beauty carries objective value, or account for every convergence in judgment across subjects. What it needs to do, and does, is remove the pervasiveness of beauty as a separate coincidence requiring a composer. The “world didn’t have to be this way” framing prices the joint fact as if it were a single throw, when it is the product already priced twice, on separate grounds, in earlier chapters.

**[Proposition]**

**Resonance Absorbs the Aesthetic Surprise** · *Proposition*

Beauty is not a third fact distributed across a structured world and a feeling creature, over and above them; on the resonance account of §5.15 it is the event between them. Given that identification, the pervasiveness of beauty is not a separate fact needing explanation but the predictable intersection of two facts the book derives on separate grounds: that Nature’s order is everywhere patterned rather than uniform, and that feeling, imagination, and drive are widespread among conscious life. An argument that prices the pervasiveness of beauty as a single surprising coincidence has priced the same joint fact already explained twice. The result is conditional on that resonance account and reduces the surprise rather than explaining every aesthetic fact; what it removes is the pervasiveness of beauty as evidence that uniquely indicates a transcendent composer.

**Depends on:** Art (§5.15)

*Second.* The subjectivist retreat is meant to make the argument coincidence-proof: even if there is no beauty in the world apart from what minds register, the reach of the registering is still surprising. That retreat assumes only two positions are on the table—an objective property in things, or a private response in minds—and locates the explanatory burden wherever the naturalist is forced to stand. The resonance account occupies neither slot, and the reframing changes what needs to be surprising. Aesthetic experience isn’t, on this account, an independent faculty aimed at a target called beauty, requiring its own dedicated tuning to hit that target across so wide a range of forms; it is what feeling and imagination already do whenever either engages a structured thing, and the account at Art (§5.15) identifies no further mechanism beyond the capacities those sections independently derive. What would need to be surprising, then, isn’t a purpose-built aesthetic sense but the existence of feeling and imagination at all, and the existence of structured forms at all—both addressed on independent grounds already, neither addressed here for the first time. Observing that the two resonate whenever both are present adds nothing further to explain; it restates the identification rather than supplying a new datum.

The capacity version needs one thing more, and it is where the front bears. McKay’s case rests on the *breadth* of aesthetic responsiveness: it reaches deep-space dust clouds, fractals, set-theoretic structure, and proofs, none of which any ancestor was selected to appreciate. That breadth is surprising if the capacity is special-purpose—a faculty aimed at beauty, which would then have to have been aimed remarkably well, across domains it never encountered. It isn’t surprising if the capacity is general-purpose. A system that responds to structure responds to whatever structure it can parse, including structure with no bearing on survival whatever; that is what makes it general rather than a collection of special detectors. On the account at §5.15 that is precisely what is on offer: beauty is registered wherever a self-modeling being’s field and a structure of the world are configured to register one another, and the account names a proof alongside a face and a landscape at evening as things that can occasion it. The reach into fitness-irrelevant domains is then the default behavior of a general capacity rather than evidence of aim, and no separate tuning has to be explained.

The spandrel concession can be pressed the same way. McKay grants that aesthetic experience may be an evolutionary by-product but holds that the by-product thesis conjoined with naturalism is improbable given how much beauty the world contains. That inference needs the two conjuncts to be independent, since a conjunction of correlated facts isn’t improbable merely because each is unlikely on its own. They aren’t independent here. If beauty is the resonance between structured form and a receiver equipped to register structure, then a world dense with structure and creatures built to parse structure will be a world dense with beauty as a matter of course, and the by-product is a by-product *of the same fact* that makes the world beautiful. The improbability the argument computes is the improbability of a joint draw that was never drawn jointly.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Aesthetic Faculty Fork** · *Disjunction*

Is the sense of beauty a faculty aimed at beauty, or just a system that reads structure?

- **If it is aimed at beauty,** then its reach beyond anything an ancestor met is what needs explaining. Its accuracy across domains no ancestor encountered remains to be explained, and the faculty should be dissociable from ordinary structure-parsing in a way not yet shown.
- **If it just reads structure,** then breadth is exactly what generality predicts. A system that parses structure parses fitness-irrelevant structure too, so no separate tuning is left for a designer to supply.

The spandrel argument inherits the same fork: on the general account, the by-product thesis and the world’s beauty are consequences of one fact about structured worlds and structure-responsive receivers.

*Scope.* This addresses the capacity version, not the indicative argument from beautiful objects. It doesn’t claim that aesthetic response is fully explained.

**Depends on:** Art (§5.15)

*Third.* The reply to ugliness borrows more than an analogy. Treating an ugly part as earning its place by service to a beautiful whole—the discordant passage resolved, the hands positioned so the eye moves past them—requires an artist who orders, weighs, and places parts relative to a whole across a structure that unfolds: the resolution has to come after the discord for the discord to be heard as discord resolved, and the hands have to be composed in relation to a canvas extended around them. That is exactly the kind of concrete operation §10.4’s Grounding-Contact Trilemma tests. Either the composing act is itself temporally and relationally extended—an ordering of parts, a placing of one thing before another, a weighing of position against the whole—in which case it instantiates the three Conditions at the operation and the composer isn’t the classical timeless ground the doctrines of §10.2.1 and §10.2.3 describe; or the act isn’t so extended, in which case it isn’t composition in the sense the reply needs—an ordering and a weighing—but a decree that a result will *look* composed, which is a different and weaker claim carrying none of the reply’s force. A classical ground barred from succession, relation, and extension hasn’t been shown able to compose a whole in the sense its own reply to ugliness requires.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Composer’s Contact Burden** · *Disjunction*

Does composing cost the composer anything?

- **If the act is spread across the structure it orders,** then composing costs time, difference, and persistence. Ordering parts before others and weighing position against a whole instantiates succession, relational distinctness, and persistence; the composer isn’t the classical timeless ground.
- **If it isn’t spread across it,** then it isn’t composing at all—only decreeing that the result look composed. The act isn’t composition in the sense the reply needs, but a decree that the result will look composed.

Neither branch returns the holistic reply to aesthetic evil intact. The choice fixes whether the composing role is concrete or has ceased to be composition. *Feeds into* Grounding-Contact Trilemma (§10.4).

*Scope.* The dilemma targets that reply, not the positive argument from beauty. A revised, temporally embedded theism can take the first horn.

*Fourth.* There is a class of case the ugliness reply isn’t built to reach, and the argument doesn’t take it up. The reply above concerns beauty and ugliness as separable parts of a whole: the discord, the badly drawn hands, the dump. It answers by relocating the ugly part into a composition that needs it. But some of the world’s beauty isn’t a part standing beside a harm; it is the instrument of one. The *Photuris* firefly mimics the flash-response of a *Photinus* female and eats the males that answer (Lloyd 1965). The orchid mantis resembles a flower well enough that field experiments found it attracting wild pollinators at a higher rate than the flowers themselves, and taking them as prey (O'Hanlon et al. 2014). Aposematic coloring runs the same machinery honestly rather than deceptively, and the pitcher plant’s nectar guides run it on insects. In each case what draws is what kills, and the drawing isn’t incidental to the killing but its mechanism.

The holistic reply has no purchase here. That reply requires an ugly part whose ugliness earns its place within a beautiful whole. In a lure there is no ugly part. The lure is the beautiful part, and its beauty isn’t serving as contrast, texture, or a rest for the eye on its way somewhere better. It is functioning as bait. A defender may of course say that predation itself belongs to a larger good, but that is the ordinary problem of natural evil answered on its ordinary grounds, not the aesthetic theodicy, which was supposed to be the easier case precisely because no one was treated as a means. Here something is.

The same decoupling holds in the case nearest to hand. A person’s beauty isn’t evidence of their character, their intentions, or what they are capable of doing; the appearance and the interior vary independently, and everyone knows this well enough to have proverbs about it while still, reliably, drawing the inference anyway. The aesthetic argument asks us to draw exactly that inference at cosmic scale—from the beauty of a made thing to the character of what made it. In the one domain where we have extensive independent access to both terms, the inference isn’t merely fallible but is a known and recurrent error. A proponent may answer that God isn’t a person about whom we could be so mistaken, which is available; what it costs is the analogy to craftsmanship and artistry that gives the argument its intuitive pull in the first place.

The pattern isn’t confined to what one organism does to another, and the case nearest to everyone is the one the argument most often reaches for. Sunlight breaking through a bank of cloud and falling in visible shafts across the land, a sky going red at evening: these are the images the case is made with, and the response they draw isn’t an error to be corrected. They are beautiful, and the response is the resonance the account describes. What the images can’t do is carry the inference. The shafts are sunlight scattered by particulates in the air, made visible by contrast where cloud blocks the rest; the rays are parallel, and the appearance of their radiating from a point is an artefact of perspective. The evening color is Rayleigh scattering, the same process that makes the midday sky blue, running longer through more atmosphere at a low sun angle. Nothing in either is unexplained, and the beauty is undiminished by that—but neither is a signature.

The intensification is where the point sharpens, because the most spectacular skies of this kind are frequently produced by particulate loading: dust, wildfire smoke, industrial haze, volcanic aerosol. The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa killed some thirty-six thousand people and threw enough material into the upper atmosphere to circle the globe repeatedly, and for more than a year afterward the world’s evening skies were more vivid than anyone living had seen. They were painted, reported, and finally published by the Royal Society with color plates of the Thames at sunset (Symons 1888); in November of that year fire brigades in New York and in several European cities turned out to extinguish what proved to be the sky. The most celebrated skies of the age were the residue of a catastrophe, and were beautiful because of it rather than in spite of it. Nor is this the exceptional case: a wildfire season delivers the same effect on a smaller scale and is reliably remarked on while it does.

Set beside the sunset, the supercell makes the structural point without the historical detour, since the rotating updraft that gives the storm its sculpted appearance is the same organization that produces the tornado and the hail. In each the beauty isn’t adjacent to the harm and not a consolation offered alongside it; it is what the harm looks like from outside. The features that make a landscape draw human settlement are frequently the features that make it lethal. River valleys are fertile, watered, navigable, and among the most reliably admired things there are; they are also floodplains, and they flood. Glacier-fed valleys in high mountain country are more striking still, and the color and the hazard have a common source, since both follow from active glaciation: the suspended rock flour that gives meltwater its color, and the impounded water held behind unconsolidated moraine that can release without warning. What draws people to build there isn’t separable from what periodically destroys what they build. This isn’t the observation that the world contains dangers alongside its beauties. It is that in a large class of cases the same feature does both jobs, which is the configuration the argument’s premise about what beauty is *for* doesn’t anticipate.

On the account in use here, both are one phenomenon. If beauty is the resonance event between a structured form and a receiver equipped to take it up, then a lure is that event exploited: the same responsiveness that makes a display beautiful is what makes a mimic effective, and a perceptual system that can be moved by form is for that reason a system that can be moved by a form which isn’t what it advertises. One mechanism yields the beauty and the trap together, and needs no further premise to do it. The aesthetic argument owes the harder account here—not why a good world contains some ugliness, which it has answered, but why a maker who instils beauty to draw creatures toward what is good also built the machinery by which beauty draws them onto a hook.

**[Proposition]**

**What Draws Is What Kills** · *Proposition*

The classical reply to aesthetic evil relocates an ugly part into a beautiful whole. A distinct class of case is not reached by it: aggressive mimicry, aposematism, and lure structures generally, where beauty is not a part standing beside a harm but the mechanism of it, and where there is accordingly no ugly part to relocate. The same structure recurs outside predation, in skies and landscapes whose drawing features and lethal features are the same features. Resonance is constituted on the receiver’s side (§5.15), so a capacity to be moved by form is a capacity to be moved by a form that is not what it presents; beauty and the lure are then one phenomenon under two descriptions, and no premise beyond that already established is required to predict both. The aesthetic argument’s premise that beauty tends toward the good therefore owes a treatment of the cases in which its tendency is the harm.

*Status: this bears on the inference from beauty’s pervasiveness to a benevolent aesthetic intention, not on whether beauty is real or valuable, and it is not a version of the problem of natural evil, which is engaged on its own grounds elsewhere. It addresses the indicative version of the argument and is not offered as reaching the capacity version, which the second front takes up. A defender may fold predation into a wider theodicy; the point here is that doing so surrenders the aesthetic argument’s advantage of being the easier case.*

**Depends on:** Art (§5.15)

*Fifth.* A related case presses on the catalogue itself rather than on the inference from it. The shrike impales prey on thorns and barbed wire, and the resulting larder isn’t only a store. Males impale in conspicuous places far more often than females, place the larder at territory borders where it will be seen, build it up before mating rather than after, and leave much of it uneaten; females assess males by it, so the larder functions as an extended phenotype under mate choice (Antczak et al. 2012). Here is a display: constructed to be looked at, made more conspicuous than function alone requires, and successful in the response it elicits from the receiver it is for. It is also a rack of corpses.

The case matters because of what the argument’s opening move takes for granted. “Almost anywhere you look, there’s beauty” is a claim indexed to a looker, and the indexing is doing work that goes unremarked. If what the catalogue counts is aesthetic organization—form elaborated beyond function, produced for and assessed by a receiver—then displays are everywhere in nature and a great many of them are built out of, or oriented toward, killing; the shrike’s larder qualifies on every criterion except our reaction to it. If instead what the catalogue counts is what human beings find beautiful, then the premise has become a claim about the responses of one species, which is a considerably weaker thing to build an inference on than the mind-independent saturation the argument advertises. The dilemma isn’t answered by observing that human aesthetic response might itself be God-given, since that is what the appreciating-minds half of the argument already asserts and so can’t also be the reason the catalogue is drawn where it is.

This isn’t a demand that the argument treat every display as beautiful. It is a request that the criterion be stated, since on the resonance account of §5.15 the question *which receiver* is constitutive rather than incidental: beauty is the event between a form and something equipped to take it up, so a display that works for shrikes and repels us hasn’t thereby failed to be one. The proponent is entitled to say that human response is the relevant one and that it tracks something real. Saying it explicitly is what makes the resulting premise assessable, and it prices the inference at a level the informal survey doesn’t.

*Sixth.* The tradition on whose behalf the argument is usually run has its own doctrine about beauty, and the doctrine is a warning against the inference the argument makes. This isn’t a matter of reading a pattern into narratives. It is taught directly. Proverbs states that “charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (Prov 31:30), the first term the ordinary Hebrew word for a falsehood and the second the vapour-word Ecclesiastes uses for what doesn’t last. Elsewhere the same literature warns against desiring beauty in the heart or being captured by it (Prov 6:25), and compares a beautiful person without discretion to a gold ring in a pig’s snout (Prov 11:22). Ezekiel’s oracle against the prince of Tyre—read through most of the tradition’s history as describing a primordial fall—makes beauty the cause rather than the ornament of the ruin: “your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendour” (Ezek 28:17). The New Testament continues it, directing that adornment be inward rather than outward (1 Pet 3:3–4).

One passage has God as speaker and inference as subject. Samuel, sent to anoint a king, is on the point of choosing Eliab on the strength of his appearance, and is stopped: “the LORD does not see as mortals see; they look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Sam 16:7). The verse isn’t a general caution about vanity. It corrects a prophet in the act of reasoning from how something looks to what it is, and it does so by contrasting that procedure with God’s. The aesthetic argument’s move is an inference from how the world looks to the character of what stands behind it. Its own scriptures identify that move as the characteristically human error and disclaim it of God.

The narratives run the same way. David sees that Bathsheba is “very beautiful,” and adultery, the arranged death of Uriah, and a dead child follow from the seeing (2 Sam 11:2–27). Absalom receives the most lavish description of beauty in the corpus—“from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him,” the vocabulary of an unblemished offering—immediately before the account of fratricide, usurpation, and revolt; the following verse weighs his hair, and he dies caught by the head in an oak (2 Sam 14:25–26, 18:9). The pattern recurs with Tamar, with Joseph, and with Sarah, in each case as danger to the one described. And the founding narrative has it already: the fruit of the one prohibited tree is “a delight to the eyes,” and that delight is given as one of three reasons it was taken (Gen 3:6). The exegetical questions there are argued at §12.1.4 and aren’t reopened here: what the tree was, what the prohibition presupposed, whether the will facing it was competent to the choice.

None of this makes the tradition anti-aesthetic, and the argument’s proponent can point to the other strand with equal justice: the heavens telling the glory of God (Ps 19:1), the worshipper asking to behold the beauty of the Lord (Ps 27:4), the beauty of holiness, and Augustine’s address to Beauty ever ancient and ever new. The tradition holds both. That is precisely the difficulty. A corpus that contains a positive theology of divine beauty *and* a developed warning literature against reasoning from appearance doesn’t hand the argument a premise; it hands it a question about which strand governs, to be settled on grounds other than citation. The Augustinian reply is available here as before—beauty is a real good, and these are its disorderings—and it is coherent. What it doesn’t supply is what the argument needs. A good whose own scriptures call it deceitful, treat it as the occasion of the primordial fall, and instruct a prophet not to reason from it hasn’t been shown to point anywhere in particular.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Tradition Warns Against the Inference** · *Diagnostic*

The aesthetic argument infers from the world’s beauty to the character of what made it. The scriptural tradition on whose behalf it is generally advanced contains a developed teaching against inference of that form. Beauty is called deceitful and fleeting (Prov 31:30) and identified as the cause of a primordial fall (Ezek 28:17). In the one passage where God corrects a prophet’s reasoning directly, appearance is contrasted with what God attends to: “they look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Sam 16:7). The same corpus also carries a positive theology of divine beauty, so the point isn’t that the tradition forbids the argument. It is that the tradition speaks on both sides, and the argument draws on one strand while the other is aimed at precisely its inferential move. Which strand governs is a question to be settled on independent grounds, and until it is, scriptural support for the premise cannot be assumed.

*Status: this bears on whether the tradition supplies the argument’s premise, not on whether the premise is true, which the preceding fronts address on other grounds. It addresses the indicative version and isn’t offered as reaching the capacity version. It takes no position on the disputed exegesis of any passage cited, and the doctrines built on these texts are engaged at §12.4.2 and §12.4.3.*

Two of the preceding fronts converge, and they reach it from opposite directions. Proverbs calls charm *sheqer*, the ordinary word for a falsehood, and that is precisely the term a biologist would use of an aposematic or mimetic display: a signal, and signals can be dishonest. The wisdom literature warns that beauty isn’t a reliable indicator of what stands behind it; signaling theory says the same thing about why, and supplies the mechanism—a receiver that can be moved by form is a receiver that can be moved by a form which isn’t what it advertises. The tradition’s cautionary strand and the evolutionary account aren’t in tension here but in agreement, and what they agree on is that appearance isn’t a reliable indicator of what stands behind it, which is the inference the aesthetic argument’s governing premise needs.

A further difficulty meets the argument even where it clears the preceding fronts, and it arrives before the question of degree. The argument concludes to a maker whose aesthetic character the world’s beauty is said to manifest—“a magnificent display,” on one formulation, of intelligence, power, craftsmanship, and majesty. Ask what makes that maker beautiful.

Every instance in the catalogue is a temporal, spatial, material thing: proteins and galaxies, birdsong and rivers, architecture and music and proofs. Music requires succession; visual beauty requires extension; the beauty of a proof requires steps standing in order. Strip time, space, and substance and it isn’t obvious what remains for the predicate to attach to, and *display* and *manifestation* are themselves relational notions requiring something shown, a medium, and someone shown to.

The tradition has an answer and it isn’t a naive one: beauty is treated as convertible with being and goodness, God is beautiful *per essentiam* rather than by having a beautiful appearance, and creaturely beauty is beautiful by participation. Aquinas gives three requisites—wholeness, due proportion, and radiance (*ST* Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.39.8). But two of the three sit awkwardly with the classical description the argument’s God is meant to satisfy. Proportion is a relation among parts, and divine simplicity denies parts; radiance is a shining-forth, which is a manifestation relation and so raises the contact question pressed at §10.4 on every classical ground said to do concrete work. Wholeness survives intact.

The participation account then inherits exactly the burden The Degrees of Perfection Argument (§10.1.7) already sets out for participation generally: a maximum specified as the cause of the graded instances occupies the comparative order those grades constitute. On the account used here, the difficulty is sharper still, since beauty is the resonance event between a structured form and a receiver equipped to take it up, and the classical ground is offered as neither—not a structured form, having no parts or extension, and not a receiver embedded among forms.

Only after that question is settled does the question of degree arise, and it has its own answer. Suppose a personal ground with maximal aesthetic excellence is granted outright: beauty is already among the great-making properties without an evident maximum, on a par with love and wisdom rather than with omnipotence. “A maximally beautiful being would actualize maximal beauty” then either stipulates a maximum by narrowing which aesthetic properties count as great-making—a move already priced (Chapter 11) as converting the driving premise from *select the great-making properties and maximize them* into *select the maximizable properties and call those great-making*—or the premise has no determinate content to run the inference from. The argument’s own conclusion, that this world is what a maximally beautiful being would produce, needs the maximum it hasn’t been shown to have.

*Taking stock.* The argument from beauty is right about the phenomenon: the world isn’t occasionally but pervasively beautiful, and the capacity to register that is a striking fact rather than a footnote. What doesn’t follow is that the phenomenon is a single further coincidence needing a personal explainer. Where the resonance identification at Art (§5.15) holds, the pervasiveness of beauty is the predictable intersection of two facts already derived on other grounds, not a separate fact needing explanation—a result that reduces the surprise without claiming to explain every aesthetic fact. Independently of that identification, the subjectivist retreat trades one target for a description the book’s own account has already reframed, adding nothing the two prior derivations had not covered.

Independently of both, the argument’s standard answer to ugliness borrows a temporally extended composer the classical ground hasn’t been shown able to be, inheriting the contact burden pressed against every other concrete-acting classical ground in this chapter. And that answer, whatever its success, doesn’t reach the cases where beauty is the instrument of harm rather than a part standing beside it—where there is no ugly part to relocate, and where the resonance account predicts the lure and the beauty together from one mechanism.

On the governing premise, that beauty tends toward the good and points beyond itself, the two bodies of thought with the most direct claim on the question converge against it from opposite directions: signaling theory explains why a display need not be honest, and the tradition’s own wisdom literature calls charm a falsehood and instructs a prophet not to reason from appearance.

Whether the predicate even applies to the maker the argument concludes to is a further question, and the classical answer to it—beauty by essence, with creaturely beauty by participation—inherits the burdens set out at §10.1.7 and §10.4.

What the argument sees, that the fit between a structured world and a feeling mind is remarkable, is real. The resonance account makes that fit expectable without a maker positioned outside either term to arrange it, and so beauty doesn’t single out a transcendent composer—which is all the argument’s conclusion needed beauty to do, and more than the resonance account needs to deny.

### 10.1.16 Religious Experience and Miracles
Religious experience and miracles approach a divine ground from the side the preceding arguments have largely left untouched. The cosmological and modal arguments begin with dependence or possibility; fine-tuning, psychophysical harmony, morality, and beauty begin with features of the world available to public inquiry. The present arguments begin with apparent encounter. In religious experience, a subject seems to encounter a divine or transcendent reality directly. In a miracle claim, an event seems to disclose the action of an agent whose power exceeds the ordinary causal order. The two arguments can overlap—a healing may occur during prayer and be accompanied by an experience of presence—but they don’t have the same evidence. The experience is first-person. The event, if sufficiently public and preserved, may be assessed by others.

Neither argument needs the crude premise that anything unusual proves God. The experiential argument begins from the ordinary epistemic standing of appearances and testimony. The miracle argument begins from a comparative explanation of an event whose occurrence has first been established. Their shared claim is that an encounter should not be redescribed as a mistake merely because its apparent object is divine. If perceptual seemings are innocent until defeated, if testimony normally transmits warrant, and if intentional action sometimes explains an otherwise improbable conjunction better than the available non-intentional alternatives, then religious evidence cannot be excluded by a rule imposed only after the evidence becomes religious.

The two cases are taken as two movements, each at its strength and then each reply, because they carry different evidence and, where they fall short, fall short at different places. The movements meet again only where both face the same questions of accumulation and selection, and then at the question of what success would establish.

*First movement: the case from religious experience.* The experiential argument has three forms. The first is personal and non-inferential. A subject who seems to be addressed, loved, judged, forgiven, or held in the presence of God may not reason from an experience to a conclusion. The belief can arise within the experience as perceptual belief arises within seeing. Plantinga’s account permits belief in God to be properly basic when produced by a functioning *sensus divinitatis*, and permits specifically Christian belief to receive warrant through the internal instigation of the Holy Spirit (Plantinga 2000). The believer need not possess an argument from religious experience any more than a perceiver needs an argument from colored surfaces before believing that a red object is present.

The second form is a parity argument. Swinburne’s principle of credulity holds, roughly, that if it seems to a subject that something is present, the subject should accept that it probably is present unless there is a reason for doubt. His principle of testimony extends a corresponding presumption to reports by others (Swinburne 2004). These aren’t special permissions created for religion. Refusing all appearances until their reliability is independently proved would disable ordinary perception, memory, and much of what anyone knows through other people. A religious seeming therefore begins with defeasible standing. Its privacy, singularity, or resistance to laboratory repetition may limit what it warrants without reducing its prior standing to zero. Historical events and interpersonal encounters are likewise unrepeatable, and many remembered events leave no surviving public trace.

Alston’s account gives the parity claim an institutional form. Christian mystical perception belongs to a socially established belief-forming practice: subjects learn how to identify, interpret, test, and correct apparent manifestations of God within a community that has accumulated procedures for doing so. Sense perception also operates as a belief-forming practice whose reliability can’t be certified without eventually relying on its own deliverances. If Christian mystical practice is internally coherent, socially established, practically fruitful, and not shown unreliable by an independent defeater, dismissing it while trusting perception risks an unsupported asymmetry (Alston 1991b). The point isn’t that every deliverance of either practice is true. Perception misfires. It is that fallibility is compatible with rational use, and that a practice need not attain infallibility before its deliverances may warrant belief.

The third form is public and abductive. Across periods and cultures, people report experiences as of presence, unity, overwhelming goodness, command, forgiveness, judgment, deceased persons, angels, saints, particular deities, or an ultimate reality that exceeds ordinary representation (James 1902; Otto 1917; Stace 1960; Yandell 1993). Some are solitary; some occur in groups; some are followed by predictions, conversions, durable moral change, or information the subject is said not to have possessed. The datum on this form isn’t merely that human beings possess religious concepts. It is that experiences bearing an apparent interpersonal or transcendent character recur, sometimes with a noetic quality—a felt presentation not merely as an emotion but as knowledge received.

The abductive comparison then asks what each hypothesis predicts. A personal ultimate who values relationship with finite persons has reason to make itself experientially available. Naturalism predicts altered self-modeling, sensed presence, agency attribution under uncertainty, culturally shaped imagery, and experiences induced by grief, contemplative practice, sleep transition, neurological disturbance, fasting, ritual, expectation, or psychoactive compounds. It doesn’t follow that every experience generated through such conditions is illusory. Every ordinary perception also has a neural realization, and a divine agent could act through the ordinary causal order.
