The relevant question isn’t whether a neural process occurred but whether the naturalistic and theistic hypotheses differ in what they predict beyond that process: the content’s specificity, the acquisition of otherwise unavailable information, independent corroboration, the temporal relation to petition or need, durable fruits, and the distribution of experiences across persons and traditions.

Religious diversity doesn’t end the argument at the opening. Reports from different traditions often share a thinner phenomenal content—presence, dependence, unity, love, terror, command, an encompassing reality—while differing in the concepts used to identify its object. A Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, or religiously uncommitted subject may interpret an experience through the categories available to them. Some apparent contradictions can therefore arise at the interpretive layer rather than within the experience itself. A theist can also allow that finite subjects encounter one source under incomplete descriptions, or that some experiences concern created spiritual agents rather than God. Diversity then limits doctrinal identification more readily than it eliminates a common theistic contribution to the evidence.

Nor does uneven distribution reverse the argument by itself. Not experiencing an object is different from experiencing its absence. A person who has never encountered another person supplies no testimonial counter-instance to those who have. A divine agent may also have reasons not to make its presence equally vivid to everyone: preserving a field for trust and inquiry, avoiding psychological compulsion, working through the testimony and care of other persons, or meeting subjects under different forms and conditions. These replies don’t remove the problem of divine hiddenness. They block only the inference from *some subjects don’t report the experience* to *the reports of those who do are thereby defeated*.

The case is cumulative. A private sensation with content supplied by expectation carries less than an experience that is unexpected, shared, independently described, informationally specific, temporally connected to a prior request, and followed by a publicly checkable event. None of those features is indefeasible. Together they can make a religious explanation compare better than it would against the bare proposition that somebody felt something unusual.

*Second movement: the case from miracles.* A miracle is likewise more than an event whose cause is unknown. Aquinas distinguishes events nature couldn’t produce, events of a natural kind occurring outside their natural sequence, and events nature could produce but which divine agency is alleged to have produced on this occasion (*SCG* III.101; *ST* I.105.7). Swinburne describes a miracle as a non-repeatable counter-instance to a law of nature brought about by God; enough repetitions would instead be evidence that the proposed law had been stated incorrectly (Swinburne 1970). On either account, an effect may have a kind that sometimes occurs naturally while still being divinely caused in this token. Recovery after illness isn’t disqualified from being providential because recovery is biologically possible. The proponent’s claim may concern the cause, timing, completeness, or signifying context rather than the bare type of outcome.

Hume’s evidential objection therefore can’t be stated as a prohibition on miracle evidence. His maxim asks whether the falsehood of the testimony would be more extraordinary than the event reported and concludes that religious miracle reports haven’t met that comparison (Hume (1748) 1999, §X). The comparison is demanding, not incoherent. Antecedent theism changes the prior. Multiple independent witnesses are better than one. Contemporary records are better than a late report. Preserved medical images, pathology, laboratory samples, and measurements can bear on occurrence in ways testimony alone can’t. A prediction recorded before an event is different from a fit noticed afterward. A case whose investigators were able to expose fraud, retained contrary evidence, and applied criteria fixed in advance is different from a collection containing only favorable reports.

The cases offered in a Catholic cumulative argument occupy several evidential classes.

*Healing claims* include sudden or lasting recoveries associated with intercessory prayer, shrines, relics, the Eucharist, or candidates for canonization. Lourdes maintains a medical assessment process that gathers pre- and post-recovery records, consults specialists, and distinguishes a declared cure from an unexpected or medically confirmed one before a diocesan judgment is considered. (Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, “Recognition of a Miracle,” describing the stages from a declared cure through medical confirmation and an assessment of its exceptional character under present knowledge: <https://www.lourdes-france.org/en/recognition-miracle/>.) Canonization inquiries can likewise ask whether a serious condition was accurately diagnosed, whether the recovery was complete, durable, and rapid, and whether the treatment received was insufficient to explain it. The point of these procedures isn’t that a committee can assay divine causation. It is that some of the ordinary exits—misdiagnosis, temporary improvement, incomplete recovery, or expected treatment response—can be tested rather than assumed.

*Apparition claims* add public coordination. At Fátima, the case includes an announced date for a sign, a large gathered crowd, reports of unusual solar phenomena, and claims of observations beyond the apparition site. At Zeitoun, reports concern a luminous figure seen repeatedly over a Coptic church by crowds over an extended period, with photographs and witnesses from more than one religious background. Lourdes joins apparition and healing claims within one continuing site. The proponent need not claim that the sun left its astronomical position or that every witness saw the same display. The evidential point is that expectation, mass perception, meteorology, retinal effects, journalistic transmission, and deliberate production must explain not one remembered vision but a coordinated body of reports with a prior religious frame.

*Saintly and bodily phenomena* include stigmata, unusual wounds or bleeding, odor claims, apparent knowledge of concealed facts, bilocation reports, abnormal temperature reports, incorruption, and healings associated with a person such as Padre Pio. Contemporary cases such as Myrna Nazzour add recurring stigmata, oil exudation, ecstasy, reported messages, and observations by physicians or visitors. These reports vary sharply in documentation. Taken at their evidential ceiling, however, their force lies in conjunction: a persistent bodily sign, observation under some degree of control, information not plausibly available by ordinary means, and an explicit devotional context are harder to explain together than one feature is alone.

*Eucharistic claims* concern consecrated hosts alleged to have changed into blood or human tissue. Reports associated with Lanciano, Buenos Aires, Tixtla, Sokółka, and other sites include histological identifications of cardiac or myocardial tissue, blood typing, inflammatory or trauma-related features, and in some cases claims that laboratories received samples without being told their proposed origin. Blinded pathology, if the blinding was real, bears on what the submitted material was. The further claims—that the material came from the host in question, that no substitution or contamination occurred, and that the transformation occurred after consecration—depend on provenance and chain of custody. A cumulative Catholic argument treats the recurrence of a Eucharistic context and similar tissue findings as evidence once those links are supplied.

*Demonic and exorcistic claims* concern patterned aversion to sacred objects, apparent knowledge of concealed information or unlearned languages, unusual strength, levitation, temperature changes, and behavioral responses that are alleged to discriminate blessed from outwardly identical unblessed objects. Their evidential advantage, where controls exist, is semantic and agentive. An unknown physiological process might produce convulsion or analgesia. It doesn’t as readily predict a response that tracks concealed religious meaning. Their principal liabilities are the vulnerability of distressed subjects, suggestion, retrospective narration, uncertain linguistic assessment, and the rarity of records produced under independent controls.

*Resurrection and artifact claims* extend the case historically: the resurrection appearances and empty-tomb tradition, the Shroud of Turin, the Sudarium of Oviedo, and claims of incorrupt bodies. These require their own source, dating, contamination, dependence, and alternative-explanation analyses. They shouldn’t be used as if their inclusion in a miracle inventory supplies those analyses. Their relevance here is architectural. The Catholic cumulative case isn’t one inference from one recovery. It proposes convergent signs across medical, perceptual, historical, material, and agentive evidence, some tied only to generic theism, some to Christianity, and some to Catholic devotional or sacramental claims.

A content-neutral inventory is wider than the religious inventory. Unexpected remission, anomalous perception, sensed presence, striking coincidence, apparently precognitive dreams, sudden changes in ability or personality, and events whose available records don’t yield an adequate causal reconstruction are also reported without prayer, shrine, sacrament, or theological interpretation. The secular cases aren’t automatically natural merely because no religion claimed them, just as the religious cases aren’t automatically divine because a tradition did. Until some feature discriminates their causes, both belong to the same evidential class: events or experiences whose occurrence and explanation require case-specific assessment. Restricting the numerator to anomalies already preserved by a religious community would make that community appear evidentially distinctive before the comparison began.

The breadth of the record has evidential force of its own. When the same repertoire appears in incompatible religious systems and outside religion, the deed-type supplies less support for any one system than an in-tradition inventory suggests. The repertoire is healing, apparition, presence, warning, hidden knowledge, bodily anomaly, answered petition, meaningful coincidence. This doesn’t establish that every tradition’s cases are equally numerous or equally documented. It establishes that supremacy can’t be inferred from possession of the repertoire. It requires a comparative corpus gathered under common standards, including cases that failed, cases that received no religious interpretation, and cases whose content points elsewhere. Without that comparison, a cumulative case may show that a tradition has accumulated miracle narratives more effectively than it shows that miracles accumulate uniquely around the tradition.

The modal conclusion must be stated at the resolution the evidence earns. The occurrence of rival *reports* establishes that report-production is actual, and therefore possible, outside the Catholic interpretive community; it doesn’t establish that every reported event occurred. If subjects in incompatible traditions genuinely undergo the same phenomenal type—presence, command, unity, apparition, answered petition—then that experience-type is actual, and therefore possible, under more than one inherited interpretation; it doesn’t establish that the experiences share an external cause. If a relevantly similar recovery or anomaly is independently shown to arise through natural processes, then natural production of that event-type is actual, and therefore possible, at that level of description; it doesn’t identify the cause of the Catholic token. Each actuality establishes its corresponding possibility. Under Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10), a real possibility once established is necessarily possible: Reality’s capacity to admit that report-production, experience-type, or natural production doesn’t disappear under a different configuration. This doesn’t make the event necessary, make it available under every local law-set, raise its probability, or identify the cause of any token. None of the actualities licenses a stronger actuality than the one observed.

One consequence does follow across all three levels. Where the same evidential type is jointly possible with incompatible interpretations, the type alone can’t entail one of them. Healing by itself can’t entail that a Catholic invocation caused it if healing is possible without such an invocation; sensed presence can’t entail a Christian identification if the same phenomenology is possible under mutually incompatible identifications; an unexplained event can’t entail divine action if unexplained events are possible without evidence of agency. The proponent can restore discriminating force only by adding a feature not shared across the comparison—antecedent prediction, source-specific content, controlled response, or another trace—and showing that the conjunction is less expected on the alternatives. That is the source-identifying case. The bare event-type has already been shown not to do the identifying work.

**[Proposition]**

**The Outcome Alone Does Not Identify Its Cause** · *Proposition*

Where the same outcome-type is possible under more than one causal account, occurrence of that type does not identify which cause produced this occurrence. Identification requires a discriminating feature not shared across the live comparison: antecedent prediction, source-specific content, controlled response, or another trace whose presence is less expected on the alternatives. The event may still have the proposed cause. The outcome alone does not establish it.

*Scope.* This proposition concerns identification of a token cause from a shared outcome-type. It does not assign probabilities, deny that a cumulative case can discriminate among causes, or infer natural causation from natural possibility.

**Depends on:** Necessary Possibility (§2.1.10)

The Latter-day Saint witness tradition is a comparative case of the same evidential form. The Book of Mormon was published with a joint testimony from three witnesses who reported that an angel showed them the plates and that a divine voice authenticated the translation, and a separate testimony from eight witnesses who reported seeing and handling the plates. (“Testimony of Three Witnesses, Late June 1829” and “Testimony of Eight Witnesses, Late June 1829,” *The Joseph Smith Papers*, <https://www.josephsmithpapers.org/paper-summary/appendix-4-testimony-of-three-witnesses-late-june-1829/1> and <https://www.josephsmithpapers.org/paper-summary/appendix-5-testimony-of-eight-witnesses-late-june-1829/1>. The statements establish what was formally attested; judging the experiences and later recollections requires the wider historical record.) Several witnesses later broke with Joseph Smith or the institutional church while continuing to affirm some form of their testimony. For a Latter-day Saint argument, persistence through estrangement is evidence of sincerity and of an experience not reducible to institutional loyalty. Competing interpretations distinguish physical inspection from visionary experience, attend to kinship and prior commitment among the witnesses, and dispute what the later affirmations preserved. The present point requires no verdict on that history. A rule that counts multiple testimony, persistence under cost, and continued affirmation after institutional rupture in a Catholic or early Christian case must count the same features here; a psychological explanation invoked here must likewise be available there. The comparison prevents one tradition from treating a shared evidential form as self-authenticating only when it supports that tradition.

That final distinction is the Catholic case’s governing reply to miracle reports elsewhere. Healings are reported in Protestant, Orthodox, Muslim, Hindu, Indigenous, and nonreligious settings. Apparitions, possession, mediumistic information, sacred-object phenomena, and extraordinary recoveries aren’t Catholic-exclusive categories. The Catholic argument need not deny any of this. It distinguishes events that don’t identify a doctrine or source from signs that do. A healing may be an act of compassion, an answer to imperfectly understood prayer, or divine action that authenticates no doctrine beyond the possibility of divine care. A sign identifies a source when its content and context connect it to a discriminating claim: an apparition identifies itself and announces a checkable event; a Eucharistic transformation occurs specifically under consecration; a healing follows the invocation of a named saint in a canonization inquiry; an experience supplies information bearing on a disputed practice. The relevant datum is then not merely *an extraordinary event occurred among Catholics*. It is *an event occurred under conditions that would be expected if this Catholic claim were true and less expected if the relevant alternatives were true*.

The result is a layered cumulative argument. Religious experience gives prima facie first-person and testimonial evidence of encounter. Healings and apparitions add publicly assessable effects. Eucharistic and exorcistic claims add sacramental or semantic specificity. Historical claims connect the contemporary pattern to Christianity’s originating events. Institutional investigation supplies selection against at least some false reports. If each category raises the likelihood of Catholicism by even a limited amount, and if the categories are sufficiently independent, their conjunction may carry more than any case considered alone.

*The replies.* They begin by granting the epistemic starting point. A religious experience can rationally warrant belief for its subject. Testimony about it is evidence for others. A medical recovery may be real, sudden, complete, and without a presently adequate explanation. A public apparition report may preserve a real perceptual event. A submitted sample may genuinely be cardiac tissue. None of those concessions should be withheld merely to secure a naturalistic verdict.

*The reply to the miracle case.* The inferences nevertheless cross distinct thresholds. The first concerns occurrence: whether the experience or event happened with the features attributed to it. The second concerns natural reach: whether the event exceeds what the relevant natural systems can produce or only what is presently explained in this case. The third concerns agency: whether the evidence favors intentional action over unknown or incompletely modeled non-intentional causation. The fourth concerns source: if agency is established, what identifies the agent as God rather than a finite, deceptive, unknown, or differently interpreted agent. The fifth concerns message: if the source is identified, what proposition, institution, or practice the event authenticates. Evidence at one threshold can contribute to the next. It can’t silently replace it.

*Occurrence.* The central question isn’t whether a witness is sincere. Sincere subjects can misperceive, remember through later interpretation, repeat a source they take to be independent, or report accurately what happened to them while misidentifying its cause. For healing claims, the record needs a diagnosis fixed before recovery, the natural history and prognosis of the condition, treatments received and their expected lag, objective measures before and after, duration of follow-up, and a reason the selected case isn’t one survivor extracted from an unknown denominator. For physical specimens, the laboratory result begins only after provenance is secured: who collected the material, when, under what observation, how it was sealed, who handled it, and whether the investigators who knew its claimed origin could have substituted or contaminated it. Blinding a pathologist answers the question *what tissue was submitted?* It doesn’t answer *where did the tissue come from?*

This isn’t a demand for laboratory repeatability from singular events. It is a demand that the evidence discriminate occurrence from its live alternatives. The standard can be met by records, independent testimony, fixed predictions, custody, and traces that the alternatives don’t predict. Its precise form changes with the case.

*Natural reach.* Three modalities are easily conflated. An event may be **epistemically unexplained**: no available account is presently adequate. It may be **nomologically impossible**: the actual laws and powers of nature don’t permit it under the relevant conditions. It may be **metaphysically impossible**: no possible reality admits it. Medical review ordinarily bears on the first and sometimes supplies evidence toward the second. It doesn’t issue a direct finding about either impossibility.

At the first level, the miracle inference is the God-of-the-gaps argument at finer grain. Instead of placing divine action in the present absence of a cosmological explanation, it places divine action in the present absence of an explanation for one recovery, specimen, perception, or event. Reducing the size of the unknown doesn’t change the form of the inference: *no adequate natural explanation is now available; therefore the cause is divine*. The conclusion remains stronger than its premise. A smaller gap may permit better records and a more disciplined search for alternatives, but unexplainedness alone supplies no positive discriminator between divine action, an unknown natural process, an incorrectly specified history, and an evidential defect in the case.

This diagnosis reaches only the inference from absence of explanation. A miracle argument can take another form. Antecedently recorded prediction, semantically specific coordination, response to a concealed variable, or information unavailable through the ordinary channels can be positive evidence of agency rather than vacant space into which agency is inserted. Whether any reported case possesses those features under adequate controls is an empirical question. The conceptual difference is exact: a gap argument asks what hasn’t been explained; an agency argument asks which available hypothesis predicted the features that occurred.

The distinction matters most for healings. Spontaneous regression and remission are rare but documented in several diseases, including malignancies. (Gudapureddy Radha and Manu Lopus, “The Spontaneous Remission of Cancer: Current Insights and Therapeutic Significance,” *Translational Oncology* 14, no. 9 (2021): 101166, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tranon.2021.101166>. The article is a review, so it establishes a documented class of spontaneous regression rather than a natural cause for any particular recovery.) Their occurrence establishes that natural recovery of those types is possible. The frequency may be low; the mechanism may be incomplete; a particular recovery may remain unexplained. None of those qualifications restores the claim that recovery of the type is naturally impossible. Once a relevantly similar recovery has occurred through natural processes, *nature can’t produce this result* is no longer available at that level of description.

This doesn’t settle the cause of the token. A recovery that can occur naturally may still have been produced by God, exactly as Aquinas’s third class permits. Nor may every case be assimilated to a broad outcome such as *the patient improved*. A defender can specify a narrower type: immediate restoration of missing anatomy, elimination of a well-documented lesion within a period no known process permits, or recovery conjoined with a prior precise prediction. The narrowing must track an independently relevant feature of the evidence. If the type is refined after a natural analogue is found merely to preserve uniqueness, the argument has changed what needs explaining rather than defended the first account of it.

The same discipline applies in reverse. A critic hasn’t explained a healing by naming spontaneous remission in general. Showing that natural recovery is possible defeats an impossibility claim; it doesn’t show that spontaneous remission caused this recovery or that the evidence fails to favor divine action. Possibility, probability, and token causation are three questions. The first constrains the second. It doesn’t answer the third.

Living systems enlarge the natural comparison without supplying that missing token explanation. Evolution is one source of novelty: lineages reproduce with heritable variation, and selection preserves variants that maintain themselves under the pressures they encounter. But an unprecedented recovery within one person need not be an evolutionary change in the human lineage. An organism is already a layered adaptive system containing interacting cell populations and microbial communities, with selection among immune and other cell lineages, redundant and compensatory pathways, tissue repair, phenotypic plasticity, treatment effects with variable lags, and feedback that can cross a threshold abruptly after gradual change. These sit within life’s more general organization toward continued self-maintenance, with population-level variation distinguished from clonal selection within an organism (§4.8). No one mechanism guarantees recovery, and biological adaptation isn’t an upward march summoned by need: available variation may be insufficient, pathogens coevolve, repair can fail, and one locally successful response can impose costs elsewhere. The narrower consequence is enough. A recovery can be novel in the medical record without introducing a new kind of causation, and rare biological success isn’t foreign to natural systems merely because it lies far from the average response or appears first in one observed case.

The symmetry becomes important when adaptation is read as favor. An antibiotic may leave one resistant bacterial lineage to proliferate while susceptible competitors disappear; a tumor-cell lineage may survive a therapy that kills the rest; a host immune lineage may discover an effective response. The selective form is shared even though the human value of the outcomes is opposite. The providential attribution therefore forks. Providence may name divine governance of the whole biological order, with its repair and predation, immunity and autoimmunity, host adaptation and pathogen adaptation. That general attribution is coherent, but because it accommodates both directions of the mechanism, a favorable outcome isn’t by itself a discriminating sign of special favor. Or providence may name a special act selecting this favorable token beyond the general order. That claim need not treat every harmful counterpart as divine negligence: a defender may distinguish positive willing from permission and appeal to stable causal order, creaturely goods, or reasons not exhausted by the patient’s immediate outcome. But the favorable valence of the result doesn’t establish that selection. The case requires a feature that differentiates special action from the same mechanism operating without it—an antecedent specification, a response pattern, semantic content, or another token-level trace. If both intervention and nonintervention can be accommodated after the fact without any expected contrast, selected successes can’t themselves supply the missing evidence of special providence.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Natural-Reach Fork** · *Disjunction*

Could this kind of event have happened naturally?

- **If it could,** then the kind of event cannot pick out its cause. The outcome-type alone cannot identify a divine cause, although the particular occurrence may still have been divinely caused. *Priced by* The Outcome Alone Does Not Identify Its Cause.
- **If it couldn’t,** then that impossibility has to be proved—and proving it still only reaches *not natural*. That natural impossibility must be established rather than inferred from the absence of a present explanation. Even when established, it crosses only the natural-reach threshold; agency, source, and message remain further conclusions requiring further evidence.

Epistemic unexplainedness occupies neither horn. Both branches continue to the question of agency; neither identifies a source or message. *Feeds into* The Sign–Source Dilemma (§12.3.3).

*Scope.* Natural possibility doesn’t establish natural causation in this case, and rarity doesn’t establish natural impossibility.

**Dependency routes:** horn 1 (a shared outcome-type does not identify its token cause)—The Outcome Alone Does Not Identify Its Cause; horn 2 (impossibility must be established, not inferred from an absence of a present explanation)—Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5)

The Netherlands assessment of reported prayer healings illustrates the evidential middle. An independent medical team evaluated twenty-seven selected reports, classified eleven as medically remarkable, and classified none as medically unexplained; the positive effects were nevertheless often durable and the experiences transformative. (C. van der Kooi et al., “Can You Be Cured If the Doctor Disagrees? A Case Study of 27 Prayer Healing Reports Evaluated by a Medical Assessment Team in the Netherlands,” *Journal of Religion and Health* (2022), PMID 35987685, <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35987685/>.) That finding neither dissolves the experiences nor identifies a divine cause. It shows why *medically remarkable*, *medically unexplained*, and *naturally impossible* must not be used as synonyms even in a sympathetic investigation.

Controlled intercessory-prayer trials supply the denominator that selected healing narratives don’t. In the STEP trial, 1,802 coronary-bypass patients at six hospitals were randomized among two groups uncertain whether they would receive organized intercessory prayer—one prayed for and one not—and a third group told with certainty that it would be prayed for. Complications occurred in 52 percent of the uncertain patients who received prayer and 51 percent of the uncertain patients who did not, a null comparison. They occurred in 59 percent of patients certain they would receive prayer, against 52 percent of prayed-for patients who remained uncertain; major events and thirty-day mortality did not differ. (Herbert Benson et al., “Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer (STEP) in Cardiac Bypass Patients: A Multicenter Randomized Trial of Uncertainty and Certainty of Receiving Intercessory Prayer,” *American Heart Journal* 151, no. 4 (2006): 934–942, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ahj.2005.05.028>.) The result doesn’t show that prayer harms patients or that no petition is ever answered. It shows no therapeutic effect of the assigned prayer in that population and an adverse association with certainty of being prayed for, possibly through the burden or anxiety that certainty introduced. MANTRA II likewise found no significant improvement from masked off-site prayer in its primary clinical outcome, and a Cochrane review of ten randomized trials involving 7,646 participants found no clear effect on death, general clinical state, coronary-care readmission, or rehospitalization. (Mitchell W. Krucoff et al., “Music, Imagery, Touch, and Prayer as Adjuncts to Interventional Cardiac Care: The Monitoring and Actualisation of Noetic Trainings (MANTRA) II Randomised Study,” *The Lancet* 366, no. 9481 (2005): 211–217, <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(05)66910-3>.) (L. Roberts, I. Ahmed, and A. Davison, “Intercessory Prayer for the Alleviation of Ill Health,” *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews* 2009, no. 2: CD000368, <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000368.pub3>. The review judged the evidence equivocal and the trials limited; it didn’t support recommending for or against prayer as a health intervention.)

These trials don’t test every theological account of prayer. A divine agent isn’t a treatment mechanism compelled to produce an outcome by random assignment, and a theology may hold that answers depend on goods, intentions, relationships, or reasons the protocol doesn’t model. That reply is coherent. It limits the empirical prediction. If petitionary prayer is offered as producing a population-level improvement detectable under controlled comparison, the trials bear directly on it and haven’t found the improvement. If prayer is said to work only under conditions unavailable to randomized study or according to reasons that predict no stable difference between assigned groups, the null result is expected, but selected recoveries can’t then be counted as though the same view had predicted those outcomes in advance.

*Agency.* Suppose occurrence is secure and no natural account presently explains the event. The remaining alternatives aren’t exhausted by *known natural cause* and *God*. Unknown natural causation, an incorrectly specified diagnosis or law, an unusual interaction among known processes, finite nonhuman agency, and divine agency remain conceptually distinct. Ignorance alone distributes probability poorly among them. Positive evidence of agency comes from features non-intentional processes don’t predict as readily: semantically specific information, a risky prediction recorded in advance, selective response to concealed conditions, coordination with a petition, or a sequence organized toward an intelligible end.

A case capable of carrying the inference through all five thresholds would combine rather than substitute those features. The event would be specified before it occurred; the relevant records or specimen would remain under continuous independent custody; the outcome would exceed a natural capacity defined at a non-arbitrary level; investigators with different commitments would obtain the same measurements; unsuccessful predictions, petitions, and comparison cases would be registered under the same rule; and the event’s timing or content would identify an agent and message without relying on the institution whose claim was being tested. A restoration of missing human anatomy announced in advance, continuously observed, independently measured, and coupled to information unavailable to the claimant wouldn’t be evidence merely because no natural explanation had yet been proposed. Its positive conjunction would be much more probable on some intentional hypotheses than on mistake, spontaneous remission, retrospective selection, or an unknown process indifferent to semantic content. Even then, the source and message would require comparison with finite or deceptive agency. But the argument would have crossed the gap form before reaching that question.

Here the Catholic case improves as a sign identifies its source more specifically. A recovery following prayer is temporally meaningful but vulnerable to the fact that many prayers and illnesses supply many opportunities for coincidence. A recovery following a named invocation fixed in advance, under an inquiry that also retains unsuccessful invocations, supplies a better comparison. An announced public event with a narrow date is stronger than a retrospective association. A response that discriminates concealed blessed from unblessed objects would be more agentive than a response to visible ritual cues. These features don’t prove divine agency. They are the kind of features an agency inference needs.

*Source and message.* Even an intentional anomaly doesn’t identify its author by magnitude alone. The religious traditions themselves preserve the point. Deuteronomy warns against following a wonder-worker toward other gods even when the announced sign occurs (Deut 13:1–5). The Gospel tradition acknowledges rival exorcists and warns of signs produced by false prophets (Matt 12:27; 24:24). Catholic demonology supplies the possibility of non-divine spiritual agency from inside the worldview, not as a skeptical addition to it. If a deceptive finite agent can produce an apparition, bodily effect, or piece of hidden knowledge, the move from agency to God requires moral, doctrinal, contextual, and comparative identification.

The source-identifying distinction answers part of this. A semantically specific sign can favor one message over another. It also makes the case comparative. Catholic-associated signs must be assessed alongside apparently source-identifying signs, answered prayers, healings, apparitions, predictions, and experiences in rival traditions. It isn’t enough to classify the Catholic cases as doctrinal and the others as compassionate by looking only at whether their messages fit Catholicism. The classification needs criteria that could identify a non-Catholic event as source-identifying if its evidence and content had the relevant form. Otherwise Catholicism is built into the coding rule and then recovered from the coded data.

The Church’s own current discipline is more restrained than many popular presentations imply. Under the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith’s 2024 norms, a *nihil obstat* normally authorizes prudent devotion without declaring the phenomenon supernaturally authentic; even canonization doesn’t authenticate every extraordinary phenomenon reported in a saint’s life. (Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, “Norms for Proceeding in the Discernment of Alleged Supernatural Phenomena,” May 17, 2024, §§11–17, <https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/bollettino/pubblico/2024/05/17/240517h.html>.) That restraint doesn’t count against Catholicism. It is an institutional acknowledgment that pastoral fruit, permission for devotion, verified recovery, supernatural causation, and doctrinal authentication are different judgments.

The identification problem itself isn’t new to this section. Exodus tests the same structure directly, from the side of doctrinal authentication rather than positive evidence: the Sign–Source Dilemma (§12.3.3) shows that an extraordinary deed can’t identify its own source, since the shared deed-type supplies no discrimination among rival agents and traditions that report the same kinds of signs.

*The reply to the experiential case.* The same ladder clarifies religious experience. An experience is an occurrence. Its phenomenal content is what seemed present within it. Its cause is what produced the experience. Its object, if any, is what the subject encountered. Its interpretation is the proposition the subject or tradition takes the experience to disclose. These may coincide. They aren’t identical by definition.

Swinburne’s principle of credulity is defensible as a starting presumption and insufficient as a complete public argument. Appearances receive default standing in part because perceptual practices possess continuing calibration: other senses, other observers, prediction, action, instruments, and recurrent contact with the object expose error. Alston is right that no basic practice can certify itself from nowhere. It doesn’t follow that all practices have equal error-correcting resources. A practice whose apparent objects are public, recurrent, measurable, and able to frustrate expectations earns a different resilience from a practice whose deliverances are largely private and interpreted within the same community that identifies their source.

That difference limits warrant; it doesn’t erase it. A solitary experience of overwhelming love may rationally reorganize a person’s life even when it can’t compel an outsider. A shared experience, a fulfilled prediction, or information unavailable to the subject adds public purchase. Conversely, sleep-transition phenomena, grief-related sensed presence, temporal-lobe disturbance, suggestion, fasting, psychedelics, and trained contemplative absorption aren’t global defeaters. They are local causal alternatives whose force depends on whether they predict the particular profile of the case. The fact that an experience has a neural correlate is expected on every hypothesis under which a living person has it.

Religious diversity is likewise evidentially double-edged. Convergence on a thin content may support the reality of some shared object or condition while divergence limits what the shared content identifies. If subjects across traditions encounter an overwhelming presence and only afterward identify it as Christ, Krishna, an ancestor, emptiness, or undifferentiated consciousness, the convergence may support *something encountered* while the disagreement weakens the inference to any one theology. If the tradition-specific content occurs within the experience itself—if the apparent speaker names itself, supplies unknown information, or issues a checkable prediction—the experience becomes more discriminating and inherits the historical questions governing that information.

The position at §5.16 occupies the resulting middle rather than dismissing the evidence. A finite mind can veridically register dependence, salience, finitude, and the excess of Reality over any model it can form. Awe, presence, unity, and self-transcendence are then not illusions merely because a tradition’s interpretation outruns what the phenomenology identifies. Natural cognitive and social mechanisms explain why the encounter takes culturally available forms; their availability doesn’t prove that no agent was present. Experience, interpretation, and alleged object remain separately assessable. The experiential argument bears on the second and third only to the degree that its discriminating features cross that separation.

*Where the two cases meet: accumulation, selection, and testimony.* The cumulative case survives the failure of any demand that one event prove the whole. Several modest likelihood shifts can together matter. But accumulation depends on conditional independence. Ten reports copied from one source aren’t ten independent witnesses. Ten medical cases investigated by one advocacy network under one selection process don’t multiply as though the institutional assumptions were reset in each case. Eucharistic samples handled by overlapping investigators, apparition reports shaped by a common published narrative, canonization cases selected from successful petitions, and experiences elicited by one practiced vocabulary may share evidential causes.

Shared causes don’t make the reports worthless. They determine how much multiplication is licensed. Evidence accumulates most where the vulnerabilities differ: a preserved medical record isn’t vulnerable in the same way as a visionary narrative; a prediction fixed before a crowd gathers isn’t vulnerable in the same way as a retrospective fit; a laboratory classification isn’t vulnerable in the same way as testimony, although it may depend on testimony for provenance. Heterogeneity can therefore strengthen a case precisely where the links between the categories are documented rather than assumed.

Denominators matter for the same reason. If thousands of petitions generate a small number of remarkable recoveries, the relevant comparison includes the unrecovered patients and the base rate of comparable recoveries without the selected invocation. If many announced apparitions fail and only one successful date is preserved, the prediction is less surprising. If all cases, favorable and unfavorable, were registered under criteria fixed beforehand, a surviving conjunction carries more. A miracle dossier built only from numerator cases can’t by itself establish the likelihood on either hypothesis.

The comparison must also range over the whole live explanatory space rather than a sequence of individually selected rivals. Catholicism may fit the preserved evidence better than Protestantism, Islam, Hinduism, or any other named alternative considered one at a time while still fitting it less well than all non-Catholic alternatives taken together. Those alternatives include ordinary recovery, error, fraud, unknown natural processes, generic divine action, finite nonhuman agency, and religious interpretations not yet represented in the comparison. They can’t be counted as equally weighted possibilities; their prior standing and their likelihoods must be argued. The relevant distinction is nevertheless exact. Being the strongest single member of a comparison class isn’t the same as receiving most of the support distributed across the class.

Catholic institutional rigor enters both sides of that comparison. Medical review, centralized procedures, archives, and a long investigative tradition can make retained Catholic cases more reliable than loosely preserved reports elsewhere. The same machinery also makes it more likely that an unusual event arising in a Catholic setting will become a detailed, durable dossier. That advantage in ascertainment and preservation is predicted whether the underlying event is miraculous or not. It may improve the evidential quality of each retained case while introducing common selection and classification dependencies across the collection. The cumulative argument must therefore separate evidence supplied by the event from evidence supplied by the process that found, filtered, and preserved it.

**[Proposition]**

**The Plurality–Dominance Gap** · *Proposition*

A religious hypothesis may fit the preserved evidence better than every individually named rival without fitting it better than the disjunction of all its rivals. Superiority within a selected comparison class establishes at most a plurality position. A more-likely-than-not conclusion requires comparison with the full complement of live alternatives under a justified probability model, not a count of metaphysical possibilities. Institutional rigor can increase the reliability of retained cases while also increasing the probability that favorable cases will be detected, classified, documented, and preserved within that institution. Its contribution must therefore be divided between evidence about the event and evidence about the machinery that produced the dossier; common machinery must also be conditioned on before the cases are treated as independent confirmations.

*Scope.* The gap assigns no probability to Catholicism and does not deny that a Catholic cumulative case can succeed. It identifies what must be shown before an advantage over particular rivals becomes dominance of the total comparison.

**Depends on:** Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5) and the conditional-independence and denominator requirements established in this section.

Geography adds an ascertainment condition. A medically documented miracle requires two infrastructures to overlap: a religious network that identifies an event as a candidate sign and a medical network that diagnosed the prior condition, preserved records, measured the outcome, and supplied specialists for later review. Canonization procedure makes that overlap explicit by requiring a petitioner, diocesan inquiry, documents, witnesses, and medical expertise before an alleged healing reaches Roman review. (Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, *Sanctorum Mater: Instruction for Conducting Diocesan or Eparchial Inquiries in the Causes of Saints* (2007), including the collection of documentary proof and the preparation of a medical expert’s report for an alleged miracle, <https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/csaints/documents/rc_con_csaints_doc_20070517_sanctorum-mater_en.html>.) Catholic populations are distributed across Latin America, Europe, sub-Saharan Africa, North America, and the Philippines, whose healthcare coverage and record systems vary substantially; no simple inference from Catholic predominance to superior healthcare follows. (Pew Research Center, “The Global Catholic Population,” February 13, 2013, <https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2013/02/13/the-global-catholic-population/>. The figures are dated and are used only to establish wide geographic distribution, not current country shares or a healthcare correlation.) (World Health Organization, “Universal Health Coverage Service Coverage Index,” country-level indicator under SDG 3.8.1, <https://data.who.int/indicators/i/9A706FD>. No Catholic-share correlation is inferred from the index here; it identifies the healthcare variable a comparative analysis would need.) But the subset that becomes a medically certified Catholic dossier may be concentrated where Catholic institutional density and evidential infrastructure coincide. Better healthcare can increase prior diagnosis, imaging, survival, follow-up, and documentary continuity, thereby increasing the number of recoveries capable of being called medically inexplicable even if it doesn’t increase the underlying anomaly rate. The event’s geography and the geography of its validation may also differ when specimens or records travel to foreign specialists.

This bias can’t be estimated from the celebrated cases alone. A comparative test would need rates of candidate events relative to Catholic population, healthcare access, diagnostic intensity, disease mix, record retention, petition volume, shrine attendance, and institutional resources, together with parallel rates from other religions and from cases receiving no religious interpretation. Without those denominators, geographic clustering is compatible with divine concentration, medical ascertainment, ecclesial collection, or an interaction among them. The dossier can’t decide among those explanations by displaying the cluster it was built to collect.

Motivation enters the same model without requiring fraud. A subject who hopes for healing attends closely to improvement and has reason to connect it to prayer. Witnesses who share the expectation have reason to notice agreement, resolve ambiguity toward the expected interpretation, repeat convergent details, and preserve the report. A devotional community has reason to solicit candidate cases, connect them to a saint or shrine, fund investigation, and transmit the cases that survive. An institution seeking converts, recognition for a candidate, or confirmation of a practice has reason to make favorable cases public; failed petitions and inconclusive inquiries have no comparable narrative career. The same structure occurs outside Catholicism—in charismatic healing ministries, mediumistic and New Age communities, secular therapeutic movements, and skeptical organizations that select exposed failures. Motivation changes search, classification, preservation, and publicity before it changes anyone’s honesty.

Crowd testimony introduces separable pressures before, during, and after the report. Before reporting, expectation and visible reactions from others can organize an ambiguous stimulus. In Sherif’s autokinetic experiments, subjects judging the apparent movement of a stationary point of light under perceptual uncertainty converged toward a group norm. (Muzafer Sherif, “A Study of Some Social Factors in Perception,” *Archives of Psychology* 27, no. 187 (1935), especially the group convergence under the autokinetic effect, <https://brocku.ca/MeadProject/Sherif/Sherif_1935a/Sherif_1935a_4.html>.) The experiment doesn’t show that a religious crowd invents an event. It shows that agreement among people exposed together isn’t equivalent to independent perception when the stimulus is ambiguous and their judgments are mutually available. During reporting, Asch’s conformity studies showed that a unanimous majority can draw public answers away from an unambiguous visual judgment; informational uncertainty is therefore not the only route, since avoidance of isolation and distrust of one’s own dissent also matter. (Solomon E. Asch, “Studies of Independence and Conformity: I. A Minority of One against a Unanimous Majority,” *Psychological Monographs* 70, no. 9 (1956): 1–70.) After reporting, co-witness discussion can alter the memory later retrieved. In Gabbert, Memon, and Allan’s experiment, witnesses saw different versions of an event and then discussed it; 71 percent of those who discussed it later reported at least one item acquired from the co-witness rather than from their own video. (Fiona Gabbert, Amina Memon, and Kevin Allan, “Memory Conformity: Can Eyewitnesses Influence Each Other’s Memories for an Event?” *Applied Cognitive Psychology* 17, no. 5 (2003): 533–543, <https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.885>.)

The sequence matters for apparition evidence. A person may initially register an uncertain light or movement, hear nearby witnesses supply an interpretation, assent publicly because dissent is costly or embarrassing, discuss the event afterward, and later remember the interpreted event with sincere confidence. At no stage must the person decide to lie. The resulting convergence is evidence, but its independence is lower than the headcount suggests. Reports recorded separately before discussion, descriptions fixed before a public narrative forms, observers unable to monitor one another, instrument traces, and witnesses who had no expectation of the event answer these mechanisms better than retrospective estimates of how many people were present.

Public commitment continues after the event. A person who announced that a sign would occur, traveled to witness it, testified before family or congregation, or reorganized a life around it faces more than correction if the evidence later disappoints: status, relationships, sacrifice, and self-understanding are exposed at once. Cognitive dissonance can be reduced by withdrawal, admission of error, reinterpretation of what was predicted, spiritualization of the event, or recruitment of new believers whose agreement supplies social confirmation. Festinger, Riecken, and Schachter’s study of a small UFO group made increased commitment after failed prophecy the classic case, but the effect was proposed under restrictive conditions—deep prior conviction, costly commitment, recognizable disconfirmation, and continuing social support—and later studies of prophetic movements show divergent responses rather than a universal law. (Leon Festinger, Henry W. Riecken, and Stanley Schachter, *When Prophecy Fails* (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1956). The case generated the disconfirmation model; it doesn’t establish that failed predictions generally strengthen belief. Subsequent field research has emphasized leadership, ideology, organization, and the social circumstances of disconfirmation as variables governing whether members reinterpret, proselytize, fragment, or leave.) Persistence after disappointment is therefore compatible with sincerity and can be evidentially relevant; it isn’t a transparent measure of truth, because the social cost of revision may itself predict persistence.

Exit costs sharpen the point. Private belief, public profession, institutional affiliation, and willingness to disclose a change are four different variables. A person may cease believing while remaining publicly Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Latter-day Saint, or a member of another inherited community because disclosure threatens parental relationships, marriage, access to children, housing, employment, education, friendship, ritual belonging, or standing as a good and trustworthy person. The feared consequence need not be formal shunning. A parent’s grief, repeated attempts at reconversion, suspicion that the person is morally lost, or fear for their eternal fate can be enough to make silence protective rather than deceptive. Research on deconversion and high-cost religious exit records identity disruption, ostracism, family strain, and the problem of reconstructing social ties after disaffiliation. (Heinz Streib, “Leaving Religion: Deconversion,” *Current Opinion in Psychology* 40 (2021): 139–144, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2020.09.007>; Nicholas B. C. Elnakouri et al., “You Can’t Reason with Them: Dismissing Religious Defectors as Irrational,” *Asian Journal of Social Psychology* 26 (2023), <https://doi.org/10.1111/ajsp.12546>. The literature spans traditions and exit regimes with very different sanctions; it supports treating disclosure and affiliation as socially conditioned, not assigning one consequence to religious exit generally.)

These costs can preserve public unanimity after private agreement has already eroded. Each quiet dissenter observes a community in which almost nobody admits doubt, takes the apparent consensus as evidence that others remain convinced, and has still less reason to disclose. Continued membership then measures the cost structure partly alongside conviction. The same problem applies to witness persistence. “They never recanted” has evidential force only after asking what recantation would have cost, whether a private qualification could have been recorded, and whether those who withdrew remained visible to the tradition preserving the testimony. Conversely, a witness who left the institution, accepted the costs of rupture, and continued to affirm a narrowly specified experience has answered part of the institutional-pressure explanation. Even there, the separate costs of retracting a public testimony—reputation, self-conception, and admission of having misled others—remain. The evidence is strengthened by costly institutional departure and weakened by costly recantation; neither cost can be omitted merely because the same person bore both.

The resulting correction isn’t that enduring communities consist of secret unbelievers or that continued testimony is worthless. It is that retention and profession are selected behavior. Where exit is punished or disclosure is relationally dangerous, they can’t be used as direct measures of belief prevalence, sincerity, or evidential confidence without an account of those pressures. The comparison must also include those who left, those who stayed silently, and those whose later qualifications weren’t preserved by the institution whose public record is assessed.

Belief can also affect the event rather than only its report. Expectation, stress, social support, treatment adherence, willingness to seek care, pain appraisal, and placebo or nocebo effects can alter experienced symptoms and some clinical pathways without distant intervention. The STEP result’s higher complication rate among patients certain they were receiving prayer is relevant at this layer: whatever produced the difference, knowledge of the religious intervention was itself a possible causal input distinct from the assigned intercession. A prayer-associated improvement can therefore be real, causally connected to the religious setting, and naturally mediated. That possibility isn’t equivalent to fabrication and doesn’t establish that every recovery has such a cause.

These motivations cut in more than one direction. A Church that certifies a false miracle risks reputational and doctrinal damage; medical reviewers have professional reasons to reject weak claims; and a process that discards most candidates contains a genuine error-control mechanism. Skeptical investigators also have reputational and ideological incentives. Motive alone therefore proves nothing about a case. Its evidential role is to identify pathways by which the same underlying events could generate different observed records. The relevant question is whether the procedure blocks those pathways through prospective registration, preservation of failures, independent or blinded judgment, continuous custody, fixed criteria, and access to the complete case pool. A rigorous filter can improve the reliability of cases submitted to it while leaving selection into the filter unresolved.

The resulting causal picture has at least three inputs: the underlying rate of unusual events, the capacity to document them, and the motivation and institutional capacity to turn them into claims. Observed miracle dossiers are downstream of all three. A high dossier rate therefore can’t be attributed to the first until healthcare and the religious-social production of the record have been modeled rather than treated as background.

This also constrains the appeal to doctrinal specificity. A Catholic event linked to a Catholic practice is evidence for Catholicism only against alternatives that predict the conjunction less well. Catholic communities perform Catholic rituals, retain Catholic testimony, investigate candidates for Catholic canonization, and interpret religious material through Catholic categories. Catholicism therefore predicts the context whether or not the event is miraculous. The additional evidence lies in what the alternative doesn’t already predict: the event’s independently secured anomaly, its semantic fit beyond ordinary expectation, the absence of corresponding failures under the same registration rule, and comparative performance against rival traditions.

*What success would establish.* Grant the experiential and miraculous cases more than the reply has required. Suppose some subjects genuinely encounter a nonhuman personal agent. Suppose a healing occurs that no created process could produce. Suppose the timing and content identify intentional action. Suppose the source is morally and doctrinally discriminated from rival agents. None of those concessions conflicts with the Necessity of Nature.

The Necessity of Nature establishes the necessity of Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. It doesn’t establish that this universe’s particular laws admit no exception, that every cause is human, or that every concrete agent is embodied in the way terrestrial animals are (§2.9.6). Necessity Permits Contingency (§2.9.4): necessary structure admits contingent laws, configurations, and events within it, so even a genuine law-anomalous event wouldn’t contradict the modal result. An unfamiliar event remains an event: it occurs in an order, differs from what surrounds it, and carries a change from one state to another. A spiritual agent capable of encounter or intervention remains differentiated from what it encounters, bears powers or information through the operation, and stands in a directed relation to an effect. Miraculous content can enlarge Nature’s inventory. It doesn’t supply an outside from which the structural Conditions are absent.

The pressure begins when the evidential conclusion is asked to establish the classical ground. If the divine source responds to a petition, appears at a time and place, selects this tissue or body for intervention, communicates this rather than that content, or causes an effect that wouldn’t otherwise occur, the source is determinately related to a concrete configuration. The Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) applies at that operation, while Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7) locates any concrete agent within Nature. A temporal responder therefore can’t be an exterior, self-subsistent ground of the Conditions it bears, where self-subsistent means existing in itself rather than in another. An atemporal single act avoids sequence in God but inherits the Grounding-Contact Trilemma: the account must specify how one undivided act is determinately related to this effect, here, rather than another, without borrowing the structural differentiation it removes from the cause (§10.4).

Concurrent and sacramental accounts can deny competition between divine and created causation. God may cause an event through natural processes, sustain every created cause, or make one event specially revelatory without interrupting a law. Those accounts preserve the possibility that a naturally possible recovery is divinely caused. They also make anomaly less central. If ordinary and extraordinary recoveries alike depend on God, what distinguishes a miracle as a sign must come from timing, context, content, and intention—the same independent features the Sign–Source Dilemma identifies.

Religious experience reaches the same contact from the other direction. If God produces or participates in a subject’s experience, the divine act bears a determinate explanatory relation to a temporally extended, materially realized cognizer. If the experience is instead the subject’s natural registration of a God who does nothing distinct on that occasion, the evidence may still concern God, but the hypothesis must say why that registration is truth-tracking rather than only the subject’s culturally shaped response to dependence and excess. The experience is real on either account. The disputed work lies in identifying its object and explaining the contact.

The resulting verdict isn’t that miracles are impossible or that religious experience has no warrant. Law-anomalous events aren’t excluded by the modal argument. Naturally possible outcomes may be divinely caused. First-person experience can rationally warrant belief for the subject, and public traces can transmit part of that warrant to others. A well-preserved, semantically specific, independently corroborated sign could supply evidence for agency and for a message within a cumulative case.

What these arguments don’t establish by themselves is a ground prior to Nature’s structural Conditions. At their evidential ceiling, they establish an encounter or intervention within the concrete order and then face the same question as every other rival ultimate: whether the source can be specified without retaining the relations, distinctions, and carrying powers through which it is said to encounter and act. If those are retained, the result is a personal power within Nature or a revised theism that accepts structural embedding. If they are withdrawn, the experiential and miraculous effects remain while the proposed relation to their source loses the content that made them evidence of that source.

*Taking stock.* Religious experience and miracle reports are evidence, not exemptions from evidence. The experiential argument is right that religious seemings should receive defeasible standing rather than a presumption of falsehood, and that a neural realization isn’t a debunking argument. The miracle argument is right that Hume’s comparison can in principle be met, that prior theism affects the comparison, and that records, independent witnesses, predictions, custody, and doctrinally specific context may together favor intentional action. Catholic reports need not be the only reports in order to contribute to Catholicism; the source-identifying claim rests on discriminating context rather than denominational exclusivity.

The limits enter at the transitions. At the level of unexplainedness alone, a miracle is a finer-grained God-of-the-gaps inference: the unknown is local rather than cosmological, but the missing explanation is still being asked to identify its replacement. An unexplained recovery isn’t a naturally impossible recovery; a naturally possible recovery isn’t thereby naturally caused in this token; an event without a current natural explanation isn’t thereby an act; an act isn’t thereby divine; and divine action isn’t thereby authentication of a doctrine.

The cumulative case can cross those stages only to the extent that it adds positive discriminators and its evidence is independent, comparative, registered against denominators, and source-discriminating. An advantage over every individually named rival is still not dominance of the total comparison unless Catholicism also outweighs their full complement under a justified probability model.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Concreteness Ceiling** · *Disjunction*

If the case succeeds, what has it shown about the cause?

- **If the case succeeds on its own terms,** it adds an agent or act to Nature rather than establishing a ground outside it. The features that give such a case its evidential force are concrete: a recovery in a body, a wound under examination, an announced event at a place and hour, a specimen under custody, a response coordinated with a petition. A cause credited with producing them is credited with concrete work. The result is an agent within the Conditions, which is a substantive conclusion and not a deflationary one. *Priced by* Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4).
- **If the case is asked to reach a ground outside Nature,** the concreteness that carried it doesn’t travel. Evidence about an encounter is evidence at the level of the encounter. The proposal then owes the relation between an atemporal or analogical ground and this effect here, rather than discharging it. *Feeds into* Grounding-Contact Trilemma (§10.4).

Strengthening the evidence doesn’t move the case between horns. Better records, tighter custody, and earlier specification make the first horn firmer, because each of them is a further concrete feature.

*Scope.* The dilemma grants occurrence and may grant divine causation. It assigns no probability to any tradition, decides no question of historicity, and doesn’t claim that empirical evidence is generally powerless against a structural result. It fixes only what this kind of evidence, when it succeeds, is evidence for. The separate question of what an extraordinary event authenticates is engaged at §12.3.3.

**Depends on:** Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)

*The asymmetry tie-breaker.* A defender who concedes that first-order considerations deadlock may offer an asymmetry between what the competing views predict about *misleading* evidence. The claim is that a religion predicts its adherents and critics will find some of its teachings intuitively hard to accept, and so predicts the contrary intuitions; while rival views make no comparable prediction that the evidential record would come to favor that religion in particular. If both halves hold, the asymmetry breaks the tie.

The first half is a claim about the tradition and belongs with the doctrines that make it. The second half is a claim about the subject matter, and it isn’t available for free. The processes canvassed above—ascertainment where institutional and medical infrastructure coincide, selection of candidate cases by the bodies that investigate them, retention of favorable and not unfavorable outcomes, common investigators and a shared published narrative, motivated attention and preservation short of any dishonesty—aren’t a religion-specific posit. They are ordinary and they predict a favoring, well-preserved dossier concentrated where one tradition’s collecting machinery is densest. Whether they predict *this* record at *this* strength is the substantive question. What can’t be assumed is that no rival view predicts a favoring record at all.

**[Proposition]**

**Both Halves Must Be Earned** · *Proposition*

An argument from asymmetric prediction of misleading evidence requires two claims, not one: that the favored position predicts the contrary evidence its critics report, and that no rival position predicts the favorable evidence its adherents report. The second is a claim about ascertainment, selection, retention, and shared evidential causes, and the conditional-independence and denominator requirements bear on it directly. An asymmetry established only by arguing the first half assumes the second.

*Scope.* The proposition does not deny that an asymmetry may hold, or that a tradition may have principled grounds for predicting resistance to its teachings. It fixes what the second half costs.

**Depends on:** the conditional-independence and denominator requirements established in this section; The Plurality–Dominance Gap (§10.1.16)

## 10.2 Doctrines of the Divine Nature
This cluster gathers the doctrines of the divine nature: the constructions built to keep the divine ground ultimate without regress, simple without composition, and independent of Nature, which it is supposed to ground. Divine simplicity (§10.2.1) holds the ground free of all composition; the via negativa (§10.2.2) secures it by denial, saying only what it isn’t; and the changeless ground (§10.2.3) places it outside time, space, and matter.

The question is the one the chapter presses throughout: can the doctrine hold its ground apart from the three conditions without relying on them to do so? The finding is again relocation rather than refutation. Each doctrine, where it asserts the ground’s independence in determinate terms, incurs the structural roles it was meant to set the ground above.

### 10.2.1 Divine Simplicity
Divine simplicity is the doctrine that God has no parts, not only no physical parts, but no metaphysical composition of any kind: no distinction between God and God’s attributes, none between God’s essence and God’s existence. Where the other classical counter-moves contest how structure applies to God, simplicity denies that it applies at all. The doctrine is run end-to-end here, against the nine forms of its defense, and on one question: whether simplicity secures an ultimate ground—whether a simple being can be distinct from what it grounds, really related to it, and carry the positive operations a ground performs. Whether simplicity is a *perfection*—whether a being is greater for being simple, and whether wisdom, goodness, and power stay distinct predicates on strict identity—is a different question, taken up at §11.2.1, which draws on this treatment rather than repeating it. Where the two touch, the grounding question is settled here and the predicate question there.

It isn’t austerity for its own sake. It is meant to secure divine ultimacy by ruling out composition, dependence, and metaphysical parts in God: were God assembled from features more basic than itself, aseity would already be lost, for the more basic features would ground God rather than vice versa. The doctrine has two tightly linked expressions, simplicity proper and *actus purus* (pure act without potency), which classical theism treats as mutually entailing. Strict Thomistic simplicity takes both to their limit: *Deus est suum esse*, God’s essence just *is* God’s existence, without distinction.

The doctrine has a long history and a contested one. Augustine (*De Trinitate* VI) spells out an early form: God’s attributes are identical to God’s being. Maimonides (*Guide of the Perplexed* I.50–60) presses an austere version: the divine attributes are equivocal with creaturely attributes, and positive predication of God is strictly impossible. Avicenna (*Metaphysics* VIII) develops the essence-existence identity later inherited by Aquinas. Aquinas (*ST* I.3–I.4) gives both doctrines full rigor and argues their mutual entailment. The doctrine was contested even within its home tradition: Duns Scotus (Duns Scotus (c. 1300) 1987) introduces the formal distinction as a middle ground, arguing that God’s attributes are formally distinct though really identical, an internal concession that the strict reading generates problems.

Contemporary defenders: Dolezal’s *God Without Parts* (Dolezal 2011) defends strict simplicity; Brower (Brower 2009) and Stump’s *Aquinas* (Stump 2003) refine it through truthmaker and phased-identity variants; Feser’s *Aquinas* (Feser 2009) defends the act/potency distinction as the metaphysical basis of simplicity; Kerr’s *Aquinas’s Way to God* (Kerr 2015) reconstructs *esse* as the central Thomistic category; Pruss (Pruss 2006) supplies contemporary PSR groundwork; Leftow’s *God and Necessity* (Leftow 2012) develops an alternative modal-theistic framework preserving key simplicity commitments; Rogers’s *Perfect Being Theology* (Rogers 2000) defends a contemporary Anselmian simplicity.

Against the doctrine: Plantinga’s *Does God Have a Nature?* (Plantinga 1980) presses the charge that strict simplicity either identifies God with a property (ontologically incoherent) or abandons the doctrine; Hughes’s *On a Complex Theory of a Simple God* (Hughes 1989) develops the analytic critique at length; Mann’s “Divine Simplicity” (Mann 1982) is sympathetic but catalogs the unresolved problems; Mullins’s *The End of the Timeless God* (Mullins 2016) presses the combination of simplicity and timelessness as internally inconsistent; Wolterstorff’s “Divine Simplicity” (Wolterstorff 1991) rejects the doctrine in favor of a richer divine psychology.

The structural account agrees with the Plantinga–Mullins wing that strict simplicity and active divine predicates stand in deep tension. Its narrower claim isn’t that every simplicity doctrine is immediately contradictory, but that any account on which a simple God grounds, donates, sustains, knows, or wills must explain how those relations acquire determinate content without the structural roles the account identifies.

Against the structural account, simplicity is the counter-move with the longest pedigree. The canonical line is run end-to-end at §2.1, which defends Necessary Possibility and S5 invariance; Cartesian Certainty for change’s bilateral witnesses is supplied at §2.2; the necessary modal constraint, tying the possibility of change to the three Conditions, is established at §2.4; that constraint is lifted to the unconditional Triconditional Necessity of the three Conditions at §2.5; and those Conditions are identified with Nature through the Triconditional machinery at §2.6. Simplicity, in its strict form, denies the application of that whole structure to God.

The classical theist answers that a maximally ultimate being is precisely one that doesn’t instantiate the structural roles: a being with no composition can’t be assembled from parts the way structured entities are. One coherent being lacking relational non-identity, causal persistence, and temporal succession is all the position requires.

Pressure turns on whether that one being is coherently specifiable. Nine questions take up the objection: one at the level of the commitment, eight across its forms. They test three connected matters: whether the divine subject can be distinctly specified, whether it can stand in a real relation to creation, and whether its predicates retain differentiated content. The replies test whether any form avoids dissolving into ∅ or reinstating the roles under a different name.

Chapter 2’s Conditioned-Nature (§2.6.12) begins conditionally: where X spells out a structural feature of Nature, the nature of X terminates in that feature. The later Reality–Nature Identity closes the alleged locations from which a real essence could evade that scope—there is no second modal domain outside Nature and no independently constituted ingredient added within it. No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1) applies the combination directly. If the divine predicates articulate Nature’s structure, their nature terminates in N and the proposal is a structural identification or revision. If they supply no determinate content, they specify no possible independent ground. What remains to test is the divine description’s content and whether its predicates establish personality, cognition, or agency rather than merely renaming structural roles.

*First.* The commitment question asks what simplicity delivers beyond its negative specification. Simplicity names the absence of composition without naming the activity the doctrine performs with it. Negatively specified, the doctrine rules out parts, composition, potency, and any distinction between essence and existence. A position that did nothing beyond negation would be inert. Simplicity earns its place because the theist uses it to affirm: that God grounds creation, donates existence, sustains the created order, and is fully actualized without potency. Each operative verb is a positive predicate. *Ground* requires an asymmetric dependence relation and a distinction between grounder and grounded; *donate* requires directed source–recipient content, though not necessarily a temporal transition in the donor; *sustain* requires an enduring or counterfactually stable dependence relation; *fully actualized* must retain content beyond bare self-identity.
