These are thin role-level demands, not yet an identification with loaded physical Time, Space, and Substance. The doctrine is specified by negation and cashed out by positive structural operations. The remaining eight questions test whether any form of the doctrine can accommodate the affirmations the doctrine is used to make.

*Second.* The relational-extension form tests whether a being with no spatial extension can be a distinct existent. Strict Thomistic simplicity holds that God has no parts, no composition, no distinction between essence and existence. God isn’t assembled from features; God is God’s features, wholly and undividedly. Structural categories (distinction, succession, persistence) apply to creatures, not to the ground of creatures.

The absence of spatial extension doesn’t by itself prevent numerical distinctness: abstract objects, if admitted, supply an obvious countermodel. The sharper question is whether the simple being has enough determinate identity and relational content to be distinguished from creation and to ground it without composition. Pressed to this limit, the worry is whether the doctrine leaves in place the structural conditions under which a distinct existent can be picked out at all.

The capacity for creation makes the question unavoidable before any creature is actual. The point doesn’t equivocate between passive potency and active power. The Thomist may coherently deny that God can be completed or changed while affirming that God can create. The pressure concerns the modal contrast active power must carry if creation is free: God creates rather than refrains, or creates this order rather than another. If the simple being has no capacity for a genuinely distinct creature, creation isn’t really possible and *creator* names no power the being has. If it has that capacity, Reality already admits the distinction between source and possible recipient. The second horn doesn’t infer ordinary distance from bare numerical plurality. A creature must be genuinely other than its source and stand in a determinate creation relation to it, or “God and creature” is one item under two labels. The capacity for that relationally articulated otherness is Spatiality at role-resolution. The doctrine may still deny metric location, extension by parts, or a real relation inhering in God; it can’t make the possibility of a genuinely distinct creation do grounding work while treating the distinction-enabling structure as absent from Reality.

Strict simplicity then faces a three-way result. If the alternative effects are grounded by different intentions, selections, or exercises of divine power, there is differentiated content in God and strict simplicity is qualified. If God is intrinsically identical while the effects differ and nothing grounds the difference on the divine side, the difference remains logically available but God no longer supplies its contrastive ground; the appeal terminates in a brute *this rather than that*. If no real alternative obtains, the one necessary divine act has its one necessary terminus and contingent creation collapses into necessity. The second option isn’t a formal contradiction, and the argument doesn’t manufacture one: it is the surrender of the sufficient-grounding work for which God was introduced. Active power therefore survives the denial of passive potency only by paying one of three prices—internal differentiation, brute selection, or modal collapse.

**[Disjunction]**

**Three Prices for Active Power** · *Disjunction*

Strict simplicity faces a three-way result once creation is granted possible. If alternative effects trace to different divine intentions or exercises, there is differentiated content in God and simplicity is qualified. If God is intrinsically identical while the effects differ with nothing grounding the difference, the difference remains logically available but unexplained: a brute *this rather than that*. If no real alternative obtains, the one necessary act has its one necessary terminus and contingent creation collapses into necessity. None is a contradiction; each simply spends something the doctrine needed to keep.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

Chapter 11 presses the consequences for Power (§11.7.1) and creature-directed love (§11.8.2).

Pressed to strip every distinction, a simple being would collapse the architecture required for causal power. For any being to be a causal agent (to ground, sustain, or relate to creation), it must be a distinct relatum capable of entering into relationships. Interaction requires a between. Strict simplicity, read that way, removes the between. The result is a *Point-State*—a would-be existent contracted to a dimensionless point, with no extension across which anything could be held apart from anything else: no relational manifold to host distinct coordinates, no gap between divine will and divine act, no distinction between divine subject and object of knowledge. Without Space in its distinction-grounding role, no distinct relata; without distinct relata, Substance’s interaction has nothing to connect. The advocate who strips all distinction performs one in the act of stripping: individuation (what makes one entity numerically distinct from another) requires exactly what absolute simplicity removes.

The classical theist has one reply left here: God’s distinctness from creation is transcendent, not positional; numerical, not at a distance; God distinct as Being Itself rather than as one relatum standing off from another. Grant the reply for distinctness taken statically; it still can’t be purchased for the verbs the doctrine refuses to drop. To *ground*, *donate*, or *sustain* is more than merely to differ from the recipient: it requires determinate asymmetric dependence. Metaphysical grounding need not involve motion or transit across a spatial interval. The burden is therefore to explain the direction and content of the relation without introducing composition, not to supply a literal crossing. The move that rescues the static distinctness forfeits the active verbs, and those verbs were the doctrine’s entire reason for asserting the distinctness to begin with.

*Third.* Brower’s truthmaker simplicity and Stump’s phased-identity simplicity refine non-compositional distinctness. Simplicity doesn’t require God’s properties be strictly identical in the strong Thomistic sense; it requires only that no composition grounds God. The properties may be distinct in some sense but not compositional; what is ruled out is metaphysical dependence, not distinctness as such.

The refinement concedes the structural point while relabeling the relation. If God’s properties are distinct in some sense but non-composite in another, then some relational structure holds among them: a structure that distinguishes the properties while unifying them. That is exactly what relational non-identity within a unified manifold consists in. Space at the role-definition level doesn’t require a unified whole be dissolved into its parts; it requires parts be distinct within the whole. Brower’s truthmaker simplicity and Stump’s phased-identity simplicity both concede distinct relata within a unified divine being, a description of a structurally unified substance with distinct aspects. The structural conditions the argument names are retained in the refinement; what changes is the vocabulary under which they are described.

*Fourth.* Dolezal’s apophatic form pairs strict simplicity with the claim that creaturely concepts can’t fully articulate what it amounts to, and holds that structural categories don’t apply to the uncreated ground. The categories of our thought (including the structural roles the argument invokes) apply to creatures, not to the uncreated ground. Simplicity is a truth affirmed of God even though the categories we use to describe God fall short; the structural objection applies a creaturely measure to a non-creaturely reality.

Apophatic simplicity makes the position immune to objection only at the cost of making it immune to assertion. If the structural categories don’t apply to God, neither do the categories of existence, power, will, or ground, each of which the theist affirms. The apophatic move is selectively applied: negation is invoked against the argument’s categories but suspended for the categories the tradition wants to preserve. Either the negation is global, in which case the doctrine says nothing about God at all, or it is selective, in which case its selectivity requires a justification apophaticism was meant to avoid. Selective apophaticism does work the doctrine needs done while exempting itself from the obligation to justify where the negation stops. The structural analysis doesn’t apply a creaturely measure. It applies the measure any affirmation of existence requires.

*Fifth.* The *actus purus* form presses simplicity through its metaphysical architecture. God is pure act: the complete actualization of all perfections with no unrealized potential. Whatever has potency is partly not actual; whatever is pure act has no potency. God is therefore pure act and the unconditioned ground of everything partly actual.

Pure actuality generates its difficulty more specifically than the crude charge that “no potency” means “no power.” The Thomist is right to reject that formulation: potency in the act/potency scheme isn’t active power, and pure act is meant to be fully actual causal power rather than inertness. The problem isn’t active power as such. The problem is the transition from not-exercising to exercising, from no creaturely effect to creaturely effect, from source alone to source-related-to-recipient. If the effect is contingent, the exercise of power must be related to that effect in some determinate way; if the exercise is eternal and unchanged, the effect seems eternal with it; if the effect isn’t eternal, some relational asymmetry has entered the account.

Feser’s refinement distinguishes pure act from static immobility: pure act isn’t absence of causal capacity but fully realized causal capacity, a being whose power is entirely actualized. The refinement sharpens the structural question rather than removing it. An act that genuinely produces, sustains, or donates being is an exercise of causal capacity. It requires determinate source–effect difference, asymmetric dependence, and a bearer of the causal role. Those thin requirements don’t by themselves establish spatial extension, temporal succession, or physical substance; the stronger identification needs the independent arguments supplied elsewhere. *Sustains* is itself a maintenance relation: to sustain is to hold something in being across the relevant interval or dependence-structure. An atemporal pure act can be asserted; what remains missing is how it produces, sustains, or donates without the structured relation those predicates require.

What the Way–Possibility Convertibility (§3.2) makes inescapable here is the way-side of the predicate. Pure act forecloses potency, and the Thomist can refuse the potency framing without contradiction: the act/potency scheme is internal Thomistic vocabulary, and *actus purus* declines the predicate on the Thomist’s own terms.

The way-predicate isn’t declinable. *Ipsum esse subsistens* is subsistent being itself, a determinate manner-of-being rather than dependent or composed. The Thomist’s own characterization of God in those terms is itself a *way* of being. To say God’s mode of being is *subsistent rather than dependent*, *simple rather than composed*, *necessary rather than contingent* is to specify determinate content by contrast with alternatives. By the Convertibility, that supplies difference at role-resolution. Where the account further says that God grounds, sustains, or produces concrete effects, those asserted relations supply directed order and bearing only insofar as they are genuine, obtaining relations; the Chapter 2 structural bridge, not Convertibility alone, carries any full T/S/Φ attribution. The exit *actus purus* offers against potency isn’t available against way: the Thomist commits to positive determinate content, and can’t then withdraw every structural burden that content and operation incur.

**[Proposition]**

**The Way-Predicate Is Not Declinable** · *Proposition*

Actus purus can decline the potency framing as internal Thomistic vocabulary the doctrine never accepted. It cannot decline this: calling God subsistent rather than dependent, simple rather than composed, necessary rather than contingent is itself specifying a determinate way of being. By the Convertibility, that specification incurs difference at role-resolution. Where the doctrine additionally predicates concrete grounding, sustaining, or producing, the asserted relation incurs directed order and bearing; the independent Chapter 2 bridge carries the resulting full-condition attribution. The doctrine’s own positive content and operation are what reintroduce the structural burdens it set out to escape.

**Depends on:** Way–Possibility Convertibility (§3.2.5), the operator requirements (§1.5.9), and the Structural Requirement (§2.4)

Two Thomist replies deserve direct hearing. Dolezal’s *God Without Parts* (Dolezal 2011) apophatic move holds that *way* is creaturely vocabulary, predicated of God only analogically and not univocally, so the way-predicate doesn’t carry its structural conditions across the analogy. The Fourth preceding question answers this in the general case: selective apophaticism can’t disqualify *way* while retaining *subsistent*, *simple*, *actus purus*, and *ipsum esse* as positive content. Either all the positive predicates the doctrine asserts of God fall under the apophatic disqualification (in which case the doctrine asserts nothing), or none of them do, in which case *way* stands with the rest. Brower’s (Brower 2009) and Stump’s *Aquinas* (Stump 2003) truthmaker-identity reply holds that one simple truthmaker can ground distinct predicates (*subsistent rather than dependent*, *simple rather than composed*) without those predicates introducing real distinctions in the truthmaker. The general form of that reply is met at the Seventh question that follows; the point that bears here is way-specific: as soon as the truthmaker is the condition under which *way of being* is correctly predicated, the truthmaker bears a way under the Convertibility, regardless of whether the multiplicity of senses is located on the creaturely-concepts side.

The same wedge applies to creation specifically. Classical theism reads creation as either a way *from* God (efficient donation outward, source-to-recipient) or a way *through* God (sustaining medium across which created being is held). Both readings require God to occupy a way-role: the former states source-direction and source/recipient distinction; the latter states a carrier of the sustaining relation. Convertibility secures the determinate-content burden of either reading. When either is asserted as concrete operation, the operator and realizer arguments carry directed order and bearing, and the Chapter 2 structural bridge bears the further T/S/Φ conclusion. Neither way-from nor way-through can therefore be asserted as concrete divine operation while being held wholly outside the structural conditions its operation requires. Nor can the doctrine drop both readings, since dropping both abandons creation as a relation between God and creatures, which it is constructed to maintain. What results is the shape the Three Prices already named rather than a fresh refutation: keep the relation and accept its structural burden, or keep absolute exteriority and forfeit the relation. The cost is exacted either way, and neither branch is a contradiction the Thomist can be convicted of.

The underlying critique (that classical simplicity is in tension with creation as a real relation) is well-trodden ground: Mullins’s *The End of the Timeless God* (Mullins 2016) presses it as the modal-collapse argument; Schmid’s “From Modal Collapse to Providential Collapse” (Schmid 2022) sharpens the tension for atemporalist simplicity by showing that avoiding modal collapse forces providential collapse; Wolterstorff (Wolterstorff 1991) rejects simplicity partly on the ground that it cannot accommodate God’s responsive relation to creatures. The standard Thomist reply invokes the doctrine of mixed relations (real on the creature side, conceptual on the divine side, *ST* I.13.7) together with simultaneous causation (treated at §10.1.5); the atemporalist’s further resource is the Stump–Kretzmann eternal-present account (Stump and Kretzmann 1981), whose ET-simultaneity is offered to dissolve the modal-collapse and timelessness tensions by denying the temporal sequence they presuppose; its eternal-present mechanism is handled at §10.2.3, where the Boethian eternal present and ET-simultaneity are met directly.

The way-foreclosure framing isolates what these replies must still concede: even a relation merely conceptual *quoad nos* requires *some* way-role on the divine side to terminate the creaturely relation, and a pure terminus with no way-role at all is ∅ articulated in classical vocabulary rather than an alternative to it.

Feser’s *Aquinas* (Feser 2009) and subsequent work extends the *actus purus* defense through the Thomistic doctrine of the analogy of being (*analogia entis*): predicates like “ground,” “donate,” and “sustain” apply to God not univocally (importing creaturely conditions) nor equivocally (as mere homonyms) but analogically: in a mode proportioned to the divine being, tracking a real divine attribute without importing the full creaturely profile. This is a refined attempt to hold the positive predicates and the simplicity negations simultaneously: the analogy licenses the affirmations while the simplicity doctrine strips the structural conditions those affirmations normally presuppose.

The structural reply addresses the analogical mode directly. Analogical predication requires a real proportion grounded in something real about the divine subject: the predicate must track a real divine correlate that stands in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely counterpart. A feature that distinguishes God-sustaining from God-not-sustaining is a relational position, Space in its distinction-grounding role. To be the *source* rather than the *recipient* of sustaining is to occupy a directed role, Time in its ordering sense. To be the *medium* through which sustaining propagates is Substance’s persistence role. The analogical mode doesn’t eliminate these structural conditions; it reasserts them under a mode of predication that is itself a structural fact about the proportion between divine and creaturely attributes. The doctrine of analogy, taken seriously, presupposes the structural conditions it is designed to moderate. The same cluster recurs at §10.1.6 (Feser’s act/potency machinery under direct scrutiny) and §10.2.2 (the analogical-apophatic complementarity); the structural question at each is whether an analogical-relational claim can be grounded without the structural conditions any relational claim presupposes.

*The eminent-containment retreat.* One form of the analogical reply isn’t yet exhausted. Pressed past predication to its ground, the classical theist may hold that the perfections are present in God not as ways God is (not as direction, difference, or link) but *eminently*: as the positive plenitude in which every perfection pre-exists in a higher mode than its creaturely realization (Aquinas, *ST* I.4.2). On this retreat God is neither a being among beings exhibiting the structural roles nor bare being, but positive fullness *containing* what creatures have in structured form, without the structure. The retreat concedes that *way*-talk carries the conditions the Convertibility names, and for that reason declines to predicate *way* of God at all: what is affirmed is content, not a way of being.

The Convertibility reaches the retreat through what positive content is. Content that is genuinely positive is determinate: it is thus and not otherwise, the fullness of being rather than its privation or limit. Determinacy is contrastive: to be the fullness rather than the privation is to exclude the privation, and a content that excluded nothing (compatible with every state, including its own absence) wouldn’t be content but an idle word (*omnis determinatio est negatio*, in its minimal logical form). That contrast secures generic non-identity, not Spatiality by itself. Spatiality enters only if the content performs concrete sustaining or production, where source and recipient stand in a real operational separation under the Concrete-Entity Test.

A defender may resist the step from determinacy to Space by pointing to abstracta: the number seven is fully determinate yet stands in no spatial relation. The example is granted (the status of abstracta is treated at §8.1.5 and conceded at §10.1.1). Determinacy alone therefore secures only the generic floor. The eminent content the retreat needs is also said to ground, donate, or sustain concrete actuality. If those verbs name an atemporal dependence relation, the account owes the contact by which abstract grounding reaches concrete effects. If they name concrete production or sustaining through change, the operation reinstates Space together with Time and Substance under the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4). The abstract example blocks the automatic inference and sharpens the remaining one.

Eminent content is therefore not a *tertium quid* beside way-of-being and bare being. Either it is determinate, in which case it is contrastive and reinstates the structural condition under the name *eminence*; or it excludes nothing, in which case it is content-free and is ∅ after all. The *tertium quid* the retreat needs would have to be positive content that is neither contrastive nor empty, and there is no such option to occupy.

Before that premise is named, its reach is far narrower than the result it secures: it is load-bearing only here, against the eminent-containment retreat. Every form of the doctrine that keeps the active verbs (*ground*, *donate*, *sustain*) was already closed by the way-foreclosure, which needs no truthmaker premise at all; only the retreat that drops the verbs for pure content reaches this far, and only it forces the question of what then distinguishes that content from ∅. The closure rests on one premise worth making explicit: that what bears no feature discriminating it from ∅ is ∅, a discernibility principle for being. The classical theist’s only coherent refusal is to hold that divine positive content is really distinct from the Null State while bearing no discernible differentiator from it, a primitive positivity distinct from nothing by no feature at all. That refusal isn’t free here, because the Null State is precluded on exactly this ground (§2.7): a putative something with no feature to distinguish it from nothing is nothing described as if it were something. The eminent-containment retreat and the Null State stand or fall together; the doctrine can’t reject the principle for ∅ and keep it for God.

The principle isn’t a stipulation the argument helps itself to; it is the truthmaker demand the doctrine already honors. *God isn’t nothing* is either true in virtue of something on the divine side (a *fundamentum in re*, some feature answering to the distinction), or it is a distinction drawn in our concepts alone, with nothing in God answering to it. The seventh question that follows presses the first horn for the attribute-predicates: *good* and *omnipotent* are true of God only if they track something real about him. The existence-predicate isn’t exempt. If a *fundamentum* distinguishes God-existing from the Null State, determinacy has been conceded. That generic difference isn’t yet Spatiality; it establishes only that the candidate isn’t wholly indeterminate. If nothing answers to it, then nothing on the divine side makes *God isn’t nothing* true rather than false, and the positive existential lacks the foundation in re the tradition invokes for the divine names.

So the primitive-positivity refusal is an exemption, and a local one: it asks that a single predication (*God is*, *God isn’t nothing*) be released from the truthmaker demand the doctrine accepts for everything else it says of God, and the release falls exactly where the doctrine needs it.

The exemption is neither free nor Thomist. A reader who rejects truthmaking outright can decline the demand; the classical theist, having already grounded the divine names in what is real about God, cannot withhold it for the one predication on which the simplicity of God and the reality of the Null State are made to part.

What stays genuinely open is one premise, and it is worth scoping exactly, because it is narrower than full truthmaker commitment. The closure needs no truthmakers for all truths, and none for negative or general truths, the contested precincts of truthmaker theory. It needs only that a single positive existential (*God is*, *God isn’t nothing*) be true in virtue of something on the divine side: that there be a difference in re between God-existing and the Null State.

Nor can the Thomist slip the demand by recasting this as a negative truth: *God isn’t nothing* read as the bare denial of a competitor, exempt the way negative and general truths are exempt. That recasting is foreclosed by the doctrine’s own center: *Deus est suum esse*, God’s essence is God’s existence. On that thesis *God is* is made true by the divine *esse* itself, the most positive *fundamentum* the tradition recognizes, the act in virtue of which anything whatever exists; it is the one existential the doctrine can least afford to make costless. A theist who downgrades *God is* to an exempt negation hasn’t reached for the negative-truth exemption but denied that God’s essence is *esse*, which is to abandon simplicity at its root. That is the least controversial corner of the doctrine, and it is one the classical theist already occupies. Aseity is the claim that God’s existence is grounded in God rather than in another; a theist who denies that *God is* has an ontological ground hasn’t escaped the argument but abandoned aseity, the classical project’s load-bearing commitment. So the closure holds as firmly as aseity, and no more firmly: which is as firmly as the doctrine needs, since aseity isn’t negotiable for the position under examination.

**[Disjunction]**

**No Third Option Between Contrastive and Empty** · *Disjunction*

The eminent-containment retreat holds that God’s perfections are present not as ways of being but as positive plenitude, containing without structure what creatures have in structured form. Content that is genuinely positive is determinate, thus and not otherwise, which is contrastive: it excludes its own privation. So the content is either determinate and contrastive, reinstating the structural condition under the name *eminence*, or it excludes nothing, in which case it is ∅. There is no positive content that is neither.

**Depends on:** Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2)

*Sixth.* The *ipsum esse subsistens* form holds that being itself precedes structural characterization. *Ipsum esse subsistens* is the version of the doctrine that goes deepest: the sheer act of existing, prior to any structural characterization. God isn’t a being among beings but Being itself, the unconditioned ground in virtue of which beings are. The three Conditions are features of creatures, of beings that have existence. The source of that existence isn’t itself a being with structural features; it is the pure act of existing, which precedes every structural distinction. The stratification proposal makes this precise: created being exists within the three Conditions; uncreated being stands at a prior level; the two levels are related by the act of *esse*; God donates existence to creatures, and the donation is neither a structural event (which would place God in the structure) nor a non-event (which would leave the donation inexplicable). It is a transcendent act that stratifies being itself.

The stratification relocates the question to the relation. For God to donate existence to creatures, there must be a determinate relation between source and recipient. (The simultaneous-causation mechanism classical theism offers is engaged at §10.1.5.) If donation names an atemporal grounding relation, the proposal incurs the generic roles—distinct terms, dependence direction, and real obtaining. Those roles are an abstract structure within Nature, not an exemption from its Conditions. If donation names concrete production or sustaining through change, the operation has a when, a where distinguishing its terms, and a bearer across the effect; the Concrete-Entity Test then supplies the three Conditions at the operation (§2.4). Read charitably, the Thomist’s insight—that being isn’t a property added to an essence but the act making anything real—isn’t refuted by the word *act*. The disagreement is whether the claimed act remains an internal abstract grounding relation or performs concrete work, and whether either reading establishes a personal ground additional to Nature. Neither does so merely by being called divine.

*Seventh.* The multiple-descriptions form tests whether a strictly simple being can ground distinct true predicates. Strict simplicity holds that God has no real distinctions: God’s goodness, power, and knowledge aren’t separate properties but identical with God’s simple essence. The multiplicity is in our creaturely concepts, not in God.

This generates a genuine predication burden, but not the false dilemma that distinct predicates require corresponding parts in their referent. One simple truthmaker can ground several nonsynonymous truths; the truthmaker-identity reply (Brower 2009; Stump 2003) is therefore coherent as far as numerical identity goes. The remaining question is semantic and explanatory: what fixes the different correctness conditions for *good*, *knowing*, and *omnipotent*, and how does one undifferentiated actuality non-arbitrarily ground their different modal profiles and contingent exercises? Answering that question need not divide God into spatial or material parts. It must, however, supply enough determinate content to explain why one predicate applies rather than another and how the corresponding concrete operations differ. If the distinctions remain entirely on the concept side, the account owes their truth and non-arbitrariness; if something on the divine side grounds them differently, strict identity must explain how without merely denying the difference it is asked to ground.

What bears on the grounding question is the second half of that burden: a ground performs differentiated operations, and one undifferentiated actuality has to supply them. Whether wisdom, goodness, and power remain distinct perfections on strict identity—the attribute-level form of the same pressure, including whether aspects or analogy (§10.2.2) can keep them non-interchangeable—is pressed at §11.2.1 and isn’t re-argued here.

*Eighth.* The softenings (Leftow, Scotus) preserve assertability by allowing distinctions the strictest formulation resists. Leftow’s (Leftow 2012) divine-modality framework, for example, distinguishes God’s nature and will. Such distinctions concede determinate structure and therefore articulate the three Conditions at the resolution appropriate to the distinction; they don’t automatically amount to metric extension, temporal succession, or material composition. Those concrete realizations follow where the account adds temporal duration, genuine response, changing knowledge, or concrete production, as open theism does most explicitly. A formal or explanatory distinction incurs the predication and internal-relation burdens; a concrete divine operation incurs the full Concrete-Entity Test. The cost to simplicity therefore varies with the distinction admitted and shouldn’t be stated as one verdict across all softenings.

*Ninth.* The essence/energies form is the Eastern counterpart to the softenings, and it concedes the structural point while insisting it hasn’t. Gregory Palamas (*Triads* III.2), systematizing the hesychast tradition, distinguishes within God the imparticipable essence (*ousia*, utterly unknowable, beyond participation) from the uncreated energies (*energeiai*), the divine operations in which creatures genuinely participate: the deifying grace and the light of Tabor through which theosis occurs. The distinction is held to be real, *in re* and not merely in our concepts, yet to introduce no composition: the energies are God wholly in act, not parts of God, so simplicity is claimed to stand. Lossky’s *The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church* (Lossky 1957) and Bradshaw’s *Aristotle East and West* (Bradshaw 2004) develop the position as the one account securing both divine transcendence (the essence withdraws absolutely) and real communion (the energies are genuinely God and genuinely shared), the pair strict Western simplicity is pressed on at the Fourth and Fifth questions. It affirms distinction in God and asks to keep simplicity anyway; that is the direct point of contact with the structural account.

That affirmation supplies determinate structure rather than evading it. If the essence–energies distinction is merely nominal, the account inherits the truth and non-arbitrariness burden of strict simplicity. If it is real, God carries a real non-identity and an ordered explanatory relation. Those are thin structural commitments, not yet Spatiality and Temporality. Where participation is a concrete activity conveyed to changing creatures, however, the contact incurs the three Conditions. The Palamite account therefore makes the book’s distinction visible inside theology itself: real distinction secures content; concrete participation supplies the stronger structural burden.

The defender answers that this is a distinction *sui generis*: neither real as between two things nor merely logical, but the Palamite middle. That middle is the formal distinction of the Eighth question pressed one tradition over: Scotus’s formal distinction and the essence/energies distinction are, on this reading, the same concession made in two tongues, and the structural conditions never required separability; a real but inseparable distinction, with a directed order and a carried activity, is the paradigm of a structured structure rather than an exemption from one.

The plurality of the energies presses the point a second time, more bluntly. The energies are many (wisdom, power, foreknowledge, providence, deifying grace) and each is held to be uncreated. Either they depend asymmetrically on the essence, which is a thin directed dependence-order within the divine and an internal structure simplicity was meant to exclude, or they are co-primitive, in which case the uncreated is an irreducible manifold at the level of generic differentiation and the unity that secured aseity requires further account. Neither branch by itself establishes loaded T or S. Nor does that dilemma exhaust the Palamite position. The defender denies that the energies are effects produced by the essence or independent co-primitive entities: they are really distinct without separation, parts, causal production, or numerical multiplication of uncreated beings. The narrower pressure is role-level. If deifying grace and the other energies are genuinely communicable operations through which creatures really participate in God, the account owes determinate source–recipient articulation and a real communion relation. Those roles establish distinction and bearing at the contact; any upgrade to the full three Conditions depends on the independent role-to-type arguments. The point isn’t that Palamism multiplies uncreated things, but that real distinction and real communion can’t be made explanatorily idle while doing the work the doctrine assigns them. Read at its most careful, the essence/energies distinction doesn’t bypass the structural conditions classical simplicity strips from divine being: it supplies generic content itself and incurs the loaded Conditions wherever the communion is a concrete operation.

A being denied every determinate distinction, dependence direction, and stable bearing role couldn’t support simplicity’s positive predicates. Mere lack of spatial extension or temporal succession, however, doesn’t establish that stronger absence.

*Convergence.* The nine questions return to a common burden: the doctrine is specified by negation and cashed out through positive predication, grounding, or action. Strict identity leaves the differentiation of divine truths and activities to be explained. Non-compositional distinctions retain determinate structure without automatically becoming spatial composition. Selective apophaticism must explain why some positive predicates remain contentful. Pure act owes the relation between necessary source and contingent actuality. *Ipsum esse subsistens* relocates the question to the donation contact. The softenings concede different degrees of differentiation, and the essence–energies distinction makes the difference between generic structure and concrete participation explicit. The eminent-containment retreat is closed on its own terms: determinate content is contrastive and reinstates the structural condition under the name *eminence*; content that excludes nothing is ∅. What isn’t claimed is the loaded reading: that a simple atemporal ground is clock-temporal, or spatial in the metric sense. What is closed is narrower and harder to refuse—the *tertium quid* the retreat required. Nor does the narrower result leave strict identity untouched. The differentiation of divine truths and activities still has to be explained, and every softening that explains it concedes some measure of the differentiation simplicity was introduced to deny. That is a burden the doctrine hasn’t discharged rather than a contradiction it has been shown to contain, and it is the burden it is held to from here on.

One further constraint applies to the doctrine’s identity claims themselves, and it is the same one this account accepts for its own. Simplicity asserts identities among items each held to be necessary: God’s essence with God’s existence, God’s mercy with God’s justice, each attribute with the divine being. The No-Surplus Criterion (§2.6) fixes what such an assertion can’t rest on. Where both relata of a claimed identity have already been established as necessary, their modal co-extension is uninformative: it follows from the necessity of each, it holds between any two necessary truths whatever, and it therefore distinguishes nothing. Sameness across every world is what any two necessary items share, so it can’t be what makes these two one. An identity claim between necessaries has to be carried by what specifying each side consists in, not merely by the fact that both are necessary. This isn’t a demand imported for the occasion. It is the bar the Reality–Nature Identity is held to at §2.8, where co-extension is explicitly refused as sufficient and the identity is earned instead from the absence of individuating content on either side. The difficulty for simplicity is that the resource the bar requires is the one the doctrine has most thoroughly renounced: an apophatic theology that denies positive individuating content to the divine attributes has, by that same denial, given up the means of distinguishing its identity claims from the trivial co-extension that holds among all necessary truths. The doctrine isn’t refuted by this. What it loses is the option of establishing its central identities cheaply, and the via negativa (§10.2.2) is where the cost is paid.

All the ways necessary for possibility are held in place by the structural conditions strict simplicity strips from divine being. Read that strictly, the doctrine asks the reader to grant every condition possibility requires while denying every one of them to the being possibility was supposed to terminate in.

What the doctrine calls simplicity may preserve a minimal structural floor whenever it retains determinate active predicates or real relations to creation. Calling the ground essence-prior doesn’t place it before structure: No Unconditioned Essence permits modal truths to follow from what a thing is while denying an essence independently constituted behind its configuration. An apophatic formulation that retains a determinate ground or relation likewise remains an aspect of Nature at its appropriate resolution; one that withdraws every articulation supplies no specified ground. Strict simplicity therefore doesn’t deliver a structure-free source, and versions retaining active predicates or real relations must still discharge the relation and predication problems developed here without treating their subject as an addition to Nature.

### 10.2.2 Via Negativa
The via negativa is the “negative way” of approaching God by denying predicates. It’s among the oldest theistic responses to the structural pressure made general at §3.5. Three traditions all approach God by stripping predicates away until what remains is supposed to exceed every structural category: Pseudo-Dionysian unknowing (*Mystical Theology* 1; *Divine Names* 1), Maimonidean predicate-denial (*Guide of the Perplexed* I.50–60) (Seeskin 2000; Stern 2013), and the later apophatic tradition (Eckhart, *Sermons*) (Marion 1991; Turner 1995; Davies and Turner 2008). Contemporary reconstructions (Sells 1994; Turner 1995) argue that apophatic discourse doesn’t merely deny predicates but performs a linguistic self-subversion that transcends the predicate/denial framework altogether.

The general point has already been pressed at §3.5: the act of negating the structural conditions instantiates them in the very performance of the negation. The apophatic application brings the abstract pressure to ground. An apophatic move that subtracts time from divine being uses time to make the move, distinguishes what is subtracted from what remains, and persists as a negating act. The successive negation of T, S, Φ (Pseudo-Dionysius’s ladder of unknowing, Maimonides’s series of attribute-denials, Eckhart’s *abyss beyond God*) doesn’t reach a standpoint outside Nature; it traces Nature’s contour from the inside, marking each condition by the act that tries to remove it.

The contemporary self-subversion reading marks a necessary distinction. Sells’s *Mystical Languages of Unsaying* (Sells 1994) and Turner’s *Darkness of God* (Turner 1995) argue that the apophatic move isn’t a simple negative proposition but a recursive undoing of its own enunciation. Granted in full: the practice of self-subversion is an activity unfolding through succession, distinction, and a continuing practitioner. That establishes an act-side structural fact. It doesn’t by itself establish that the intended referent of apophatic discourse is structured, because the apophatic theorist may deny that the discourse represents a determinate object at all.

*A parallel front: the immutable-thinker dilemma.* The apophatic discipline pressures classical theism from one direction: every act of negation instantiates what it negates. A parallel pressure runs along the divine attribute of immutability itself. The classical-theistic God is, on the standard view (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.9; Anselm, *Proslogion* (1078) 1998, 18–22), immutable, atemporal, and omniscient.

The three attributes pull against one another when the question is whether God thinks. Either divine knowledge involves successive cognitive episodes, or it is one timeless act. The first option conflicts with strict immutability. The second is the classical answer and can’t be dismissed merely by assuming that every instance of thought must be episodic.

The classical responses to this horn, Boethian eternity (*Consolation of Philosophy* (524) 1969, V.6); the Stump and Kretzmann ET-simultaneity reconstruction (a relation of co-presence between eternity and time without temporal succession on the divine side) (Stump and Kretzmann 1981); Leftow’s *Time and Eternity* (Leftow 1991); Helm’s *Eternal God* (Helm 1988), all attempt to dissolve the succession by relocating divine cognition outside time. The relocations preserve immutability by separating the mode of divine knowing from creaturely succession. They face a burden of explaining how one timeless act bears differentiated, tensed, and contingent content, but the proposal isn’t closed simply by redescribing that mode as non-successive.

If God has no cognitive state or relation at all, omniscience is lost. But dispositional and non-occurrent models of knowledge show that knowing need not consist in a stream of episodes. The live issue is what positive cognitive relation remains and whether it can distinguish its contents.

The Thomistic *actus purus* names fully actual actuality without potency rather than activity-as-transition; on a reading that preserves that distinction (the eternal-present and actuality-potentiality discipline is developed at §10.2.3; the classical divine simplicity case at §10.2.1), the conditions established at §3.5 are instantiated not in the *mode* of divine cognition (which is unitary act, not succession) but in the *content* divine cognition cognizes. ‘Eternal knowledge’ (Aquinas, *ST* I.14) is content-bearing: omniscience predicates determinate content over articulated objects (S-distinguishability); divine knowing of what-is-the-case inherits the temporal structure of what-is-the-case (T at the level of what is known); the unity of the eternal act sustains its content (Φ as the structural carrying of the act, not the duration of a process).

Nor does recasting divine omniscience as second-personal knowledge (acquaintance with persons rather than grasp of propositions) lift the result clear of the conditions: the persons known are themselves distinct from one another and from their knower (S) and articulated across the times of their lives (T), so personal knowing bears determinate content no less than propositional knowing, and the content it bears carries the temporal and relational articulation the relocation of mode was meant to escape. The Aristotelian and Thomistic frameworks (*Metaphysics* Λ 1072b14–30; *ST* I.3) shift where the three Conditions are instantiated; they don’t extract divine cognition from the structural conditions any cognition’s content requires. The classical-theistic account therefore faces a mode–content tension rather than a deductively closed dilemma: succession in the divine mode threatens immutability, while a timeless unitary mode owes an account of differentiated and temporally structured content.

Feser’s *Aquinas* (Feser 2009) and *Five Proofs* (Feser 2017) develop a contemporary integration of the apophatic and analogical modes: apophasis disciplines the excess of positive predication, and the analogy of being (*analogia entis*) supplies the positive content that apophasis alone cannot provide. On Feser’s reading, “God is not composite” (apophasis) pairs with “God is subsistent being itself” (analogy), the two modes functioning as complementary faces of a single theological discipline.

The structural reply tracks both poles. The apophatic pole has already been addressed: every act of negation instantiates the three Conditions in the performance. The analogical pole is addressed in the engagement with the analogia entis at §10.2.1: analogical predication requires a real proportion grounded in something real about the divine subject: the predicates must track a real divine correlate that stands in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely counterpart, and such a correlate must at least support determinate difference, direction, and stable bearing. Whether those roles warrant the stronger labels Space, Time, and Substance is a further step rather than a consequence of analogy alone.

The word choice at the pairing’s positive pole isn’t incidental, but it can’t be cashed as a lexical concession. Aquinas’s *subsistens* names existing in itself rather than in another; it doesn’t, by itself, mean a composition of mutually supporting parts (*De potentia* (1265–1266) 1932, q.9 a.7). The book’s own account of persistence argues that determinate subsistence runs through Φ, with the three Conditions each holding the other two up, with no privileged floor (§2.9.3; §1.2.6). That is a further argument, not something the Thomist’s phrase already grants. What the pairing still owes is narrower. The apophatic pole subtracts Substance among the rest, and a referent stripped of Φ has then withdrawn the persistence-conditions the book’s account requires, while Aquinas’s own sense of subsistence remains standing as a distinct claim. The two faces don’t cancel by sharing a word; they leave a burden about whether subsistence without Φ still specifies a determinate persisting ground.

**[Proposition]**

**Subsistens Owes What It Subtracts** · *Proposition*

The positive pole names God *ipsum esse subsistens*, existing in itself rather than in another, not a composition of parts holding each other up. The book’s Φ-account of persistence is a further argument, not a meaning the word already concedes. The apophatic pole still subtracts Substance among the rest along its ladder of unknowing. What survives is then without Φ on the book’s terms, and the pairing owes an account of how subsistence without that condition still specifies a determinate persisting ground.

**Depends on:** Triconditional Cross-Entailment (§2.6.7)

The complementarity places structural conditions on the act side and a determinate-content burden on the object side. The object-side question doesn’t have to be answered in the form it invites, and stating why narrows what is owed. Nothing here needs to prove that the apophatic referent instantiates the structure of the discourse used to approach it. What has to be shown is narrower: that, for a discourse making claims, there is no position between saying something determinate about the referent and saying nothing.

There isn’t. Withdraw every predicate, including the predicate of *being what the discourse is about*, and no object-level claim has been made—there is nothing to evaluate, and nothing has been asserted that the account would need to contest. Retain any determinate claim, and it is a claim about something distinguished from other things, standing in some relation to them, and holding rather than lapsing; those are the conditions at issue, and retaining the claim incurs them. The discipline can’t both point at a referent and decline every predicate that would make it one. That fork binds the assertoric use, and it binds without the act-side result having to reach across to the object side.

The same fork is run against a specific ultimate at §10.3.2, where the One is asked to be a structured ground while declining the predicates that would make it one. What is added here is only that the fork doesn’t depend on which ultimate is named: it follows from what a negation needs to be a negation *of* something.

*Convergence.* The argument’s stance on the via negativa is disciplined rather than eliminative. The apophatic tradition tracks the inadequacy of univocal projection from creaturely concepts to divine being. The tradition is doing two different jobs, however, and the result differs by which. Used to make an assertion—as a doctrine about what God isn’t—it is answerable to the retorsion (the self-undermining reply that turns a denial against its own performance): each negation is a determinate act that discriminates this from that, and a content excluding nothing is ∅. Used contemplatively, as the unsaying Sells and Turner describe, it advances no proposition for the retorsion to reach, and nothing here refutes it. What the two can’t do is cover for each other. The contemplative register survives precisely by not asserting, and so can’t discharge the doctrinal burden classical theism needs the via negativa to carry; the assertoric register can carry that burden only by taking on the determinate content it was introduced to avoid. So the act-side fact that apophatic negations are structurally conditioned doesn’t settle whether apophatic discourse refers beyond determinate predication. That question isn’t refuted by retorsion; it is a burden of apophatic semantics and theology. The general structural result sets the terms of that burden, while the religious and existential significance of the apophatic remainder is carried forward to §11.8.3.

### 10.2.3 The Changeless Ground
The classical theist proposes the most important exception to the claim that change pervades reality: a changeless ground (atemporal, aspatial, immaterial) exempt from all of it. Not frozen in time but outside time altogether. The doctrine has two tightly linked expressions. The first is static-being: God as timeless in the sense of possessing being without temporal instantiation. The second is eternal-present: God as timelessly simultaneous with every temporal moment, possessing life *tota simul*, whole and all at once. The question here is whether a changeless thing can be the *ground*—whether either expression specifies an ultimate that stands prior to the structural conditions. Whether an unchanging God can also *do* what the tradition says it does, beginning to create, answering one prayer rather than another, becoming incarnate at a moment, is the attribute question, and it is tested separately at §11.3.3.

Aquinas develops both (1265–1274) 1947: God is *actus purus*, pure act without potency, entirely without temporal or spatial extension; God is also eternal in the Boethian sense, possessing illimitable life in complete simultaneity. Boethius introduces the eternal-present doctrine to resolve the foreknowledge problem (524) 1969: God knows all temporal events not by foreseeing them but by perceiving them as simultaneously present. Plantinga (1974; 2000) defends a modern version: the Maximally Great Being is a necessary, immaterial mind whose changelessness grounds rather than instantiates the changing world. Stump and Kretzmann refine eternity through their doctrine of ET-simultaneity (eternity–time simultaneity), a non-temporal simultaneity relation between God and temporal events (1981). Leftow develops a quasi-temporal eternity (QTE) variant (1991). Barbour proposes a physical analogue (1999): Platonia, a timeless configuration space from which the experience of time arises as an illusion. The intuition is ancient, the defenders are serious. If any such being is coherent, it grounds the three conditions without being subject to them.

The counter-construction bears on the argument’s most ambitious reach. The argument claims that wherever change is possible, Time, Space, and Substance obtain. The classical theist counter-proposes a being for which change isn’t possible (for which T, S, and Φ are strictly inapplicable) and which grounds the three conditions rather than participating in them. If such a being can exist, then □(T∧S∧Φ) as a claim about all of reality fails. Structure obtains wherever there is change, but something else obtains changelessly, and that something else is the ground.

A clarification before the moves. The argument’s intermediate conclusion is □◇C: Reality necessarily permits change, not that change must always be occurring. A being in which no change occurs bears on the second claim, not the first. Permission isn’t a fact about whether change happens in a being. It is a fact about what Reality structurally allows. A static being that exists within Reality exists in a Reality that already permits change, and that permission is fixed by the triconditional structure. The objector is proposing something stronger: a being that exists outside Reality-as-structured. The shared structural failure has a name in advance. *Changeless* is a parasitic negation of Change, a quantifier internal to the domain of transitions, not a state outside it (§2.1.5, Parasitic Negation). A ground specified as changeless either reduces to that quantifier and grounds nothing, since a quantifier isn’t a substrate, or smuggles in determinate features that instantiate the very domain the construction was meant to escape. Five forms of the move test that dilemma.

*First.* The Maximally Great Being move proposes a being atemporal, aspatial, and immaterial that possesses being without instantiating any of the three roles, grounding Nature without being part of it. A changeless being can’t be identified with ∅ merely from atemporality, aspatiality, or immateriality. At most, its being determinate rather than nothing supplies a thin difference-role. The further step from qualitative or logical distinctness to Spatiality’s loaded type—relational extension within a manifold—requires the independent bridge argued elsewhere (§2.4.7); it can’t be assumed against the classical theist at the outset.

Now consider grounding: the static being is proposed as the ground of existence, something that produces or sustains structure. Any grounding relation, whether construed as causal production or as metaphysical/explanatory dependence, requires determinate relata, asymmetric direction between them, and real obtaining. An atemporal grounding theorist will deny that it must persist through a temporal interval; the simultaneous-causation move is taken up in detail at §10.1.5. The conclusion therefore divides. Where the ground is credited with producing or sustaining concrete structure, the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) places the full Structural Requirement at that contact. Considered apart from concrete production, the conclusion is role-level: a wholly indeterminate ground can’t ground, while a determinate grounding relation instantiates difference, direction, and bearing. Whether those roles require the fully temporal and physical types, in that abstract case, is the separate role-to-type question. The proposal seeks a ground with none of the roles grounding requires, and so leaves itself with no determinate way to specify that ground at all.

*Second.* The Aristotelian non-temporal priority move refines the claim: the static being is prior to Nature in the order of explanation, not in the order of time. Formal causes (what a thing essentially is) and final causes (what a thing is for) involve non-temporal ordering; a changeless being can stand in formal or final priority to Nature without standing in temporal priority. Non-temporal priority is still structural priority. Formal priority requires the ground to be structurally distinct from what it grounds, requiring the difference-role to hold ground and grounded apart. Final priority isn’t temporal succession, and the Aristotelian point should be granted in full. But it is still an asymmetric ordering relation: source and end, potency and actuality, orientation and fulfillment. The structural argument doesn’t need to redescribe final causality as clock-time. It needs only the weaker claim that final priority isn’t structureless priority. To ground Nature, the static being must stand to what it grounds in some determinate ordering relation (formal, final, logical, or temporal) and a determinate ordering relation already requires distinguishable relata, asymmetric priority, and a stable relation between them. The defining feature of the static being, its non-instantiation of the roles, is exactly what disqualifies it from standing in any grounding relation at all.

*Third.* The Boethian eternal present presses a different line: God exists not in time but in an eternal present, a timeless simultaneity from which the whole of temporal history is present at once, as a landscape is present to an observer on a hill. From eternity, all temporal moments are equally present, not as a series God remembers or anticipates but as a totality God possesses, *tota simul*. This isn’t static immobility but complete, simultaneous, perfect possession of illimitable life.

The eternal-present view shouldn’t be caricatured as requiring God to track a moving present from inside an A-series (McTaggart’s term for the tensed past/present/future ordering, distinct from the tenseless B-series of earlier/later relations, a distinction developed at §8.1.3). Its point is exactly the opposite: God knows each temporal event in its temporal location without occupying one moment rather than another. The pressure arises when the doctrine is asked to preserve more than tenseless total knowledge. Classical theism also wants divine responsiveness, providence, answer to prayer, and knowledge of creaturely events as events to which God stands in determinate relation. Those commitments require more than the passive possession of a static array. They require asymmetric dependence between prayer and answer, between creaturely event and divine knowledge, between what is asked and what is given.

If the Boethian account gives only B-series access to the whole temporal order, it hasn’t yet supplied response in the operative sense; prayer and answer stand as correlated elements of the array rather than in a response relation. If it supplies genuine response, it has introduced ordered asymmetry, distinguishable relata, and a stable relation between them, the structural roles in the very place the doctrine was meant to exempt from them. The objection isn’t that God must know “currently” in the creaturely mode. It is that the theological predicates the doctrine wants to preserve require a structured relation that mere eternal co-presence doesn’t by itself provide.

**[Proposition]**

**Co-Presence Is Not Yet Response** · *Proposition*

The Boethian eternal present secures tenseless total knowledge of every temporal moment at once, but classical theism also wants responsiveness: providence, answered prayer, knowledge as standing in determinate relation to what happens. If the doctrine gives only B-series co-presence, prayer and answer sit as correlated elements of one array, not as response. If it supplies genuine response, it has introduced the ordered asymmetry between relata the doctrine was built to exempt God from. Total presence and active response are not the same purchase.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*Fourth.* Stump and Kretzmann’s ET-simultaneity offers a technically refined version: a non-temporal simultaneity relation between God and temporal events. God is simultaneous with every temporal moment, not in the sense of being at the same time as each, but in the sense of standing in a “simultaneity in the mode of eternity” relation to each. This relation is neither temporal nor non-existent; it is a third kind, definable precisely.

ET-simultaneity replaces ordinary temporal simultaneity with a sui generis relation between eternity and temporal events. That relation supplies determinate relatedness, but relatedness alone doesn’t entail spatial extension. The live objection is instead whether ET-simultaneity can support asymmetric response and agency without importing temporal succession; the doctrine shouldn’t be rejected simply by redescribing every relation as Space. McTaggart argues that genuine change requires the A-series (1908); if divine agency involves change, it inherits that requirement, and ET-simultaneity then owes an account of how agency survives the trade.

*Fifth.* Barbour’s Platonia offers a radical version, physical rather than theistic: a timeless configuration space with the experience of time an illusion arising from “time capsules”, configurations that happen to encode apparent memories. No being, just the static configuration space.

Platonia’s configurations must be individuated (each is this configuration rather than that), which spends the difference-role, and the configuration space must hold together as one whole that bears its configurations, which spends the bearing-role. Distinguishing one configuration from another takes cognitive succession from one to the next. The act of describing Platonia occurs in time, but that establishes only an act-side fact about the describer. It doesn’t by itself show that Platonia’s represented content is temporal. The object-side question is whether the configuration space contains an intrinsic ordering or dynamical structure adequate to recover time; that must be argued from the model rather than inferred from the description event.

A kindred softening worth naming is Leftow’s (1991) QTE (quasi-temporal eternity) which allows God to stand in quasi-temporal relations to creatures while remaining intrinsically timeless. QTE concedes explicitly that relations to temporal creatures require some structural analog of Time. The position is honest about the cost: intrinsic atemporality is preserved only by distinguishing intrinsic from relational structural features, and the relational features do the work that the structural roles require. Open-theist softenings (Hasker, Sanders) concede still more (temporal duration, genuine response, real relation to creatures) and concede the structural commitments most explicitly.

*Convergence.* The five forms don’t exhaust every atemporal-ground theory, and they don’t fail alike. Each incurs a differentiated burden. The Maximally Great Being has no foothold for specification: a wholly indeterminate ground can’t ground, and a determinate grounding relation instantiates difference, direction, and bearing.

Non-temporal priority is still structural priority, since formal and final precedence require the very roles they were meant to escape. The Boethian eternal present either supplies only B-series co-presence, which isn’t yet response, or supplies genuine response and with it the ordered asymmetry it was meant to exempt. ET-simultaneity supplies determinate relatedness but owes an account of asymmetric response and agency. And Platonia’s configurations are individuated in a space that bears them, while the succession its description deploys poses a question the model has yet to answer.

Two neighboring constructions in this chapter carry the rest of the doctrine: the simultaneous-causation mechanism classical theism uses to connect the eternal God to the temporal world is answered in §10.1.5, and the divine-simplicity construction of the eternal God’s internal metaphysics in §10.2.1.

## 10.3 Non-Classical Ultimates
This cluster gathers competing accounts of ultimacy that aren’t classically theistic, and they don’t all make the same bid: Spinozist pantheism (§10.3.1), Neoplatonism (§10.3.2), process theology (§10.3.3), Madhyamaka emptiness (§10.3.4), and axiarchism (§10.3.5). Each names or reconceives ultimacy—one infinite substance, the One beyond being, creative process, emptiness, or value ordered toward actuality—and they do so in different ways. Neoplatonism places the ultimate beyond being; Spinozism makes it immanent, one substance whose modes the natural order is; process theology makes it a process within the order rather than prior to it; Madhyamaka declines to posit an ultimate at all, so that emptiness is a dialectical result rather than a ground; axiarchism makes value, not a being, the explanatory bottom. Only Neoplatonism is a bid to stand free of the structural conditions; the others revise what ultimacy is.

The single question therefore has to be asked with that difference in view: where an account places its ultimate prior to the conditions, can it reach it without leaning on them; and where an account identifies ultimacy with an immanent, processual, or dependent order, what does that revision leave for the conditions to constrain? The finding is relocation rather than refutation. The candidates divide: articulated priority claims incur determinate-role burdens; immanent and process accounts may be compatible with the structural floor while revising ultimacy; strict apophatic and anti-thesis positions leave an open semantic or dialectical seam.

### 10.3.1 Spinozist Pantheism
Spinoza’s *Ethics* (Part I) identifies God with Substance: the single, infinite, necessarily existing reality of which all finite things are modes. Spinoza’s God isn’t a person standing outside Nature but the totality of what is, expressed under the attributes of thought and extension (and infinitely many other attributes we don’t access). On this view, God is the one necessary substance expressed through attributes and modes. That makes Spinozism a close comparison for the book’s necessary structural ground, but not an automatic identification with it.

The Spinozist position is a non-classical counter-construction that shares several of the argument’s commitments. Unlike the classical theist, the Spinozist doesn’t place God beyond Nature. The Spinozist can therefore regard the three Conditions as necessary features of the one substance’s modal order. This is compatibility, not identity: Spinoza’s attribute theory, necessitarian derivation of modes, and parallelism go beyond the book’s structural result.

The alliance should be scoped, though. Spinoza’s attributes are thought and extension expressed co-equally (the order and connection of ideas the same as the order and connection of things) whereas the account holds the three Conditions co-equal and derives mind downstream, as recursive structural depth yields phenomenal interiority (Chapters 4–5). That downstream derivation of mind is a commitment this account owes rather than a result it can claim here: the defensive case that experience requires no non-structural ingredient is made at §9.1, and the positive account of how structural depth yields interiority is earned, not assumed, in Chapters 4–5.

On the immanence-and-necessity axis the convergence is genuine; on the attribute taxonomy the present account isn’t a parallel-attribute substance monist, and it isn’t physicalism either (§2.4): every being, minds included, instantiates all three Conditions rather than belonging to one attribute that runs parallel to another, so the parallelism that is Spinoza’s third distinctive demand is precisely what it doesn’t inherit.

*The half-necessitarian pressure.* A sharper Spinozist challenge presses not the identification but the prior consistency of the necessity verdict. The driving premise behind the argument is the derivation in §2.6–§2.7 that closes the necessity of the three Conditions. If it carries any modal force, Spinoza’s own reasoning suggests it should close modal space at the level of the modes as well.

Spinoza holds that finite modes follow from infinite Substance with the same logical necessity as theorems follow from axioms; contingency, on his view, is an epistemic effect of partial perspective, not a structural feature of reality. A half-necessitarian reading (necessary structure, contingent particular configurations) appears to split what Spinoza holds together.

This isn’t a worry read off the primary text alone: Melamed (*Spinoza’s Metaphysics* Melamed 2013), the most careful contemporary reconstructor of Spinoza’s substance monism, defends the strict-necessitarian Spinoza against the moderate readings that would soften the modal claim, holding that on Spinoza’s system there is no genuine contingency anywhere, the finite modes included, and that the appearance of contingency is wholly an artifact of inadequate ideas. The challenge is therefore pressed directly: if the argument’s modal engine carries the force claimed for it, the natural reading of Spinoza says it should leave no contingency standing at the level of the particular configurations either.

The reply is that the argument’s modal engine isn’t a rationalist PSR that cascades from necessary ground to necessary consequence. It is a more confined demonstration: that the three Conditions are conditions on any concrete existent, derived from the incoherence of ∅ (the maximally undifferentiated configuration in which none of the conditions obtains), not from a principle requiring that whatever follows from the ground must follow necessarily. The modal PSR is confined at §8.2.1 to the existence of contingents as a class, and the necessity claim is located at the structural level alone by §2.8.

What is necessary is that there be a reality satisfying the three Conditions; what particular reality satisfies them isn’t determined by the necessity of the conditions.

The half-necessitarian position is therefore stable: the necessity runs to the conditions, not to the configurations meeting them. Spinoza’s deeper necessitarianism requires a further principle (that the specific attributes and modes are uniquely determined by Substance) that the present argument doesn’t need and doesn’t accept.

The argument grants the Spinozist’s structural commitment. What it contests is the identification. *Deus sive Natura* (God-or-Nature: Spinoza’s formula identifying the two) is offered as a term-substitution. If “God” is just another name for the necessary ground, the substitution is harmless and the disagreement is verbal.

But the historical theological work the term *God* is asked to do (providing an object of worship, a source of moral obligation, a being to whom prayer is addressed, a guarantor of cosmic justice) doesn’t transfer to the structural ground. The structural ground isn’t a being to whom one prays, a moral agent, or a loving person.

**[Proposition]**

**Cheap Substitution, Expensive Word** · *Proposition*

*Deus sive Natura* offered as a term-substitution costs nothing at the level of the necessity claim: if “God” just names the necessary ground, the relabeling is harmless. What it does not carry over is everything the term historically did—an object of worship, a source of moral obligation, a being who hears prayer, a guarantor of cosmic justice. The substitution is cheap where it changes nothing and expensive exactly where the tradition needed it to change something.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

*Taking stock.* The Spinozist who accepts this pares the divine vocabulary down to something closer to reverence for what is. That position is coherent and may be theologically valuable; it isn’t what the analytic theology literature means by classical or personal theism. The argument’s verdict is that Spinozism avoids the specific burden of locating God beyond structure because it identifies divinity with immanent Nature. The cost is the abandonment of most of what the term *God* was historically asked to deliver.

### 10.3.2 Neoplatonism
Plotinus (*Enneads* Plotinus c. 270 CE) and the Neoplatonic tradition place the ultimate ground beyond being itself. The One (τὸ Ἕν) isn’t a being among beings, not even the supreme being; it is the source from which being emanates, lying beyond all predication, including the predicates of existence and unity in the strict sense. Plotinus is willing to push apophasis (the via negativa: approaching the divine by denying predicates rather than affirming them) past where classical theism stops. Where Aquinas’s God is being-itself (*ipsum esse*), Plotinus’s One is prior to being and to *esse* alike.

Articulated as emanation, the position relocates the challenge rather than escaping it. If the One is the source from which Reality emanates, the account posits an ordering or dependence relation between source and derivative. Plotinian emanation isn’t ordinarily a temporal process, so succession can’t simply be assumed. The sharper burden concerns determinate sourcehood, derivative difference, and asymmetric dependence: how these obtain without turning the One into one relatum among others.

Nor does the henological motive for positing the One (that a manifold of conditions must derive from a prior unity to be one structure rather than a heap) find purchase here: the three Conditions (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) aren’t an aggregate awaiting an external unifier but one Nature, identical under the Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10), so the unity the One is invoked to supply is already internal to the structural ground.

The same analysis covers the inward arm of the Neoplatonic cycle. The reply to this point runs on procession (the outward emanation from the One) but the reversion by which all things turn back toward their source fares no better: reversion likewise expresses an ordered dependence of the derived upon its source, not necessarily a clock-time journey. It requires intelligible difference and direction, while the Neoplatonist owes an account of how those roles apply analogically without compromising the One’s priority.

Plotinus is alert to the difficulty, and the difficulty has able contemporary defenders, so the apophatic reply must be taken at full strength. Gerson (*Plotinus* Gerson 1994) reconstructs the language of emanation as systematically analogical rather than literally predicative, and Perl (*Thinking Being* Perl 2014) reads the One not as a further being standing behind beings but as the sheer intelligible presence in which beings consist, so that talk of a source names a relation of dependence internal to appearing rather than a process undergone by some super-entity.

The *Enneads* insist that the language of emanation, derivation, and procession is improper: that nothing can really be said about the One, including that it is the source of anything. The strategy of strict apophasis preserves the One’s transcendence by withdrawing every predicate, including the predicate of being a ground.

The consequence should be stated with care. If the One isn’t asserted to stand in a determinate grounding relation, then the present argument has no object-level ground claim to refute. It can register that the philosophical practice of unsaying is structurally enacted, but that act-side point doesn’t establish the One’s structural character. If a Neoplatonist instead retains determinate claims of emanation, sourcehood, or dependence, those claims incur the grounding-role burden developed in this chapter. The engagement therefore yields a fork: apophatic silence leaves a theological or contemplative stance outside the positive grounding claims; articulated emanation enters the dialectic and must explain its relation.

The contemporary readings don’t escape this. Analogical predication is still predication: an analogy holds between two terms in a respect, and to sustain it is to deploy distinction and relation, the very conditions at issue. And Perl’s immanentist reconstruction concedes the point rather than evading it, for a presence in which beings consist, a dependence internal to appearing, just is a structural-dependence relation described from the inside, the structural roles under another name, not a way past them.

*Taking stock.* The argument closes only the structured priority claim: a One described as emanating, grounding, or standing in determinate dependence relations incurs the structural burden of those relations. Strict apophatic silence isn’t thereby contradicted; it declines to supply the kind of ground claim at issue. The remaining disagreement is whether such silence can support the explanatory work Neoplatonism often asks of the One.

**[Disjunction]**

**Silence or Speech, Not Both** · *Disjunction*

Strict apophasis preserves the One’s transcendence by withdrawing every predicate, including the predicate of being a ground. If no determinate grounding relation is asserted, there is no object-level claim here to refute, but nothing has been said either. If emanation, sourcehood, or dependence are retained as determinate claims, they incur the grounding-role burden the rest of the chapter presses.
