The One cannot both stand as a structured ground and decline every predicate that would make it one.

**Depends on:** Necessity of Nature (§2.9.6)

### 10.3.3 Process Theology
Process theology, developed by Charles Hartshorne (*The Divine Relativity* Hartshorne 1948; *A Natural Theology for Our Time* Hartshorne 1967) from Whitehead’s metaphysics in *Process and Reality* (Whitehead 1929), abandons the classical attributes in favor of a God who is temporal, related, and changing. Hartshorne’s central technical move is dipolar theism, developed from Whitehead’s distinction between two natures in God: a primordial nature that grasps the eternal possibilities and a consequent nature that grows with the world’s becoming (in Hartshorne’s own terms, God’s abstract and concrete poles). [Divine perfection](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) is reconceived. Omniscience is knowledge of all that has become, not of what will be (which is genuinely indeterminate). Omnipotence is the maximal persuasive power compatible with creaturely freedom, not coercive control. Eternity is everlastingness within time, not timelessness outside it.

John Cobb and David Griffin’s *Process Theology: An Introductory Exposition* (Cobb and Griffin 1976) gives the tradition a systematic statement, and the position has been extended by Marjorie Suchocki (*God–Christ–Church* Suchocki 1982; *The End of Evil* Suchocki 1988), Joseph Bracken (*The Triune Symbol* Bracken 1985; *Society and Spirit* Bracken 1991) on social-trinitarian process theism, Roland Faber (*God as Poet of the World* Faber 2008) on theopoetics, and Thomas Jay Oord (*The Uncontrolling Love of God* Oord 2015) on essential kenosis.

The position’s significance for the present argument lies in shared commitments: both reject the classical attributes of timelessness, immutability, simplicity, and impassibility (the inability to be affected or undergo suffering); both insist on the reality of time, change, and relation as features any adequate metaphysics must accommodate.

Where they part is over personhood and grounding. The process theist holds that the supreme exemplification of process is itself a person (the divine consequent nature is conscious, loving, and responsive) and that this person is the necessary ground of the world’s becoming. The present argument is silent on the first claim and supplies a limited structural challenge to the second. Two distinct questions need separating, and each requires a distinct reply.

The first question is whether, within Nature, there exists a maximally inclusive person who experiences every event and to whom every event matters. On this the present argument is silent. It establishes Nature’s necessary features; it doesn’t settle which configurations within Nature actually obtain.

The choice between a process-theistic Nature (with a maximally inclusive divine person) and a non-process-theistic Nature (without) is downstream of what the argument settles, and turns on substantive empirical, phenomenological, and theological considerations rather than structural ones.

The phenomenology of religious experience, the problem of evil and theodicy, the coherence of divine consequent-nature consciousness, the question whether anything in nature exhibits the universal-prehension structure Whitehead’s metaphysics requires (prehension being Whitehead’s technical term for the non-cognitive grasping by which each occasion of experience takes up its predecessors): these are the considerations that bear on the first question, and the present account doesn’t settle them.

Hartshorne’s argument from divine relativity, Cobb and Griffin’s case for the religious adequacy of process theism, Suchocki’s development of the eschatological consequent nature can stand or fall on their own terms. The present account neither requires nor forbids them.

The second question is whether such a being could be what classical theism wanted God to be: the necessary ground of the three Conditions (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) rather than a configuration within them. On this the present argument isn’t silent, but its conclusion is limited: a process-theistic God clearly realizes temporal, relational, and active roles; whether those roles preclude every sense of divine ultimacy depends on the further theory of grounding and aseity the process theist offers.

Hartshorne’s dipolar theism is the test case. The primordial nature grasps the eternal possibilities timelessly; the consequent nature grows with the world’s becoming. The question is which nature is supposed to ground the world’s structural conditions.

If the primordial nature grounds them, the process theologian must explain how an abstract pole that orders possibilities grounds concrete becoming; this doesn’t by itself collapse into classical theism. If the consequent nature grounds them, its growth with the world raises a circularity or mutual-dependence concern, though a process theorist may explicitly reject one-way classical grounding.

Cobb and Griffin’s reply (Cobb and Griffin 1976, ch. 2) is that the dipolar God is the ground of the *order* of becoming rather than of the structural conditions of becoming, but the distinction relocates the classical role rather than recovering it. Order presupposes the structural conditions, and a God who grounds order while presupposing the conditions isn’t the necessary ground the classical project required.

The dilemma tightens into a single result. What makes the two poles *poles of one God*, on Hartshorne’s own account, is a relation between them: the consequent nature prehends, includes, and grows from the primordial nature, and the primordial nature is the abstract ground the consequent nature concretely actualizes.

That relation isn’t static co-instantiation but a directed dependence: grounding and prehension run from the primordial ordering of possibilities to the consequent nature’s concrete inclusion of the world.

The pole relation requires determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer that unifies the poles. These are the book’s thin structural roles. Where the concrete pole does what dipolar theism says it does—receive, respond, and grow with the world—those roles are the loaded Conditions at that operation, by the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) and Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7). Identifying them with loaded spatial interval, temporal succession, and physical substance for the abstract pole is what requires further argument; on neither reading does dipolar theism describe a wholly structureless ultimate.

**[Proposition]**

**What Makes the Two Poles One God** · *Proposition*

The primordial and consequent natures are poles of *one* God only by standing in a relation: the consequent nature prehends and grows from the primordial, which is the abstract ground the consequent concretely actualizes. That relation is a directed dependence, not static co-instantiation, and directed dependence requires determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. Dipolar theism secures coherence by instantiating exactly the roles a structureless ultimate would have to lack.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

The same role-floor applies to the dipolar reconception of perfection as responsiveness. Perfect inclusion of and affectedness by the world require determinate receptivity and relation. This locates the divine consequent nature within a structured process, but it doesn’t by itself settle whether that process can be metaphysically fundamental.

Hartshorne’s God avoids the classical tensions of timeless simplicity by instantiating the structural roles at both poles and in their relation. The remaining question is whether such instantiation makes God merely an inhabitant or instead a necessary, co-constitutive feature of the process order.

Process theology avoids the charge that its divine candidate lacks determinate temporal, relational, or active roles. It carries a serious aseity burden: a temporal, relational God appears dependent on the conditions of the process it inhabits. Process theists may respond by revising aseity rather than denying dependency; the present account records that cost without treating the revision as a contradiction.

Suchocki’s eschatological development of the consequent nature doesn’t change this: an eschatological consummation is still a temporally extended event, and a God consummated in it still realizes temporal roles. Bracken’s social-trinitarian extension multiplies the divine persons but doesn’t relocate them outside Nature. Oord’s essential kenosis specifies the modality of divine action without altering the metaphysical embedding. Each contemporary development of process theology preserves the central commitment (God is temporal, related, changing) and each, on the present analysis, preserves the consequence: such a God instantiates the three Conditions and owes the same account of whether its relation to them is dependence, identity, or co-constitution.

A kindred position worth marking is open theism (Pinnock et al., *The Openness of God* 1994; Hasker, *God, Time, and Knowledge* Hasker 1989). Open theism shares with process theology the rejection of timeless omniscience and the affirmation of genuine creaturely freedom, but typically retains creation ex nihilo and divine independence in ways process theology doesn’t. The present reply raises the same question: an open-theist God who exists in time and knows the past while leaving the future open is structurally embedded, and the theorist must explain how that is compatible with the proposed grounding role. The aseity question is the same question for both positions.

Process theology is the theistic position best positioned to accept the argument’s structural commitments without contradiction, but the cost is a substantial revision of classical aseity (the divine attribute of existing from oneself alone, independent of anything else for one’s being), and aseity is the load-bearing commitment of the classical project. Process theology provides a coherent way of being a theist after the present account; it doesn’t provide grounds for accepting theism, and it doesn’t preserve what the classical project was distinctively trying to secure.

Whether the further commitments of process theology are independently warranted (whether the consequent nature exists, whether divine persuasion is the right account of God’s action, whether eschatological consummation is the right account of history) are questions for the philosophy of religion rather than for the present account. The first question is left open; on the second, it establishes the structural instantiation and records the aseity cost.

*Taking stock.* The process theologian who accepts the structural argument has a coherent position: a God who realizes temporal, relational, and active roles at maximum scope. This isn’t the classical aseity claim, and it requires either treating God as a configuration within Reality or spelling out a revised account of ultimacy compatible with divine process. Hartshorne’s move is therefore a genuine theological revision, not a mere preservation of the classical project. The present account records the cost: process theology doesn’t straightforwardly preserve the grounding role classical theism assigned to God. Whether its revised religious and metaphysical picture is independently preferable remains a live philosophy-of-religion question.

### 10.3.4 Madhyamaka Emptiness
Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (c. 150 CE) (Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd c. CE) 1995) develops the doctrine of *śūnyatā* (emptiness) as a sustained critique of any view that attributes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to anything whatever. Nothing exists from its own side; everything arises in dependence on conditions. The tetralemma (A; not-A; both A and not-A; neither A nor not-A) exhausts the options and refutes each. The result isn’t nihilism but the rejection of ultimately established intrinsic nature, including substance, time, and space conceived as existing from their own side. What conventional positive claims a Mādhyamika may retain, and in what register, is an interpretive dispute rather than something the word *emptiness* settles by itself.

The challenge is radical in a way no other challenge the argument faces is, but the contemporary attribution map isn’t a single anti-Tsongkhapa front. Garfield’s interpretation is substantially informed by Tsongkhapa and Gelug accounts of the two truths: emptiness denies ultimate establishment while conventional truth remains indispensable. Siderits develops a reductionist and semantic reading with a different account of conventional truth, and Westerhoff analyzes the no-thesis and anti-foundational pressures without thereby turning every conventional assertion into silence (Garfield 1995; Garfield 2002; Siderits 2003; Siderits 2007; Westerhoff 2009).

The precise Prāsaṅgika challenge is therefore not a blanket refusal to utter any positive sentence. It is that the Mādhyamika advances no thesis as *ultimately established* from its own side, and uses *prasaṅga* to expose the consequences of an opponent’s reifications. Dependent arising and the two truths can still function conventionally. The present argument becomes a target insofar as □(T∧S∧Φ) is offered as a final, scheme-independent metaphysical structure rather than as a conventionally indispensable description.

Two replies must be distinguished, because they engage Madhyamaka at different scopes.

The narrower reply concerns *svabhāva*. *Svabhāva* in the technical sense is intrinsic, independent, self-existing nature. Nāgārjuna’s arguments are devastating against the claim that any phenomenon has nature in that sense. They aren’t directed against (and don’t refute) the claim that phenomena exhibit structural conditions that obtain dependently. The present argument here has never claimed *svabhāva* for any of the three Conditions (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance). The triconditional structure is mutually constituting: each role requires the other two, and none has independent existence apart from the others. In the technical Mahāyāna vocabulary, the three Conditions are empty of *svabhāva* and dependently arisen with respect to one another.

The narrower reply observes the convergence: the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent arising) Nāgārjuna names is structurally isomorphic to the present argument’s mutual requirement.

The wider reply must engage a strong anti-foundational reading on which even “structural conditions that obtain dependently” risks becoming *svabhāva* in disguise if the assertion is treated as ultimately established, scheme-independent, and immune to conventional revision. This isn’t usefully described as Garfield versus Tsongkhapa. The live issue across the disputed readings is the status assigned to the positive thesis: whether the Triunity is claimed ultimately, or whether it functions as a conventionally indispensable account whose terms remain empty.

The present argument resists the wider critique only at a limited point. It doesn’t depend on assimilating Madhyamaka to a conciliatory reading; it distinguishes the practice of *prasaṅga* from the object-level thesis the Mādhyamika declines to assert.

*Prasaṅga* is a dialectical method: the Mādhyamika draws absurd consequences from an opponent’s premises. The drawing-of-consequences is an activity. It occurs through succession, differentiates premises from conclusions, and persists through a reasoner or practice. *Prasaṅga* therefore exhibits the three Conditions at role-resolution in its operation.

That act-side fact doesn’t force the Mādhyamika to accept an object-level thesis that the structural conditions exist inherently or independently. It establishes instead that the conditions of the dialectical practice aren’t dissolved by the practice. The structural account may claim those conditions are necessary; the Prāsaṅgika may deny that this is a final metaphysical description. Their dispute remains over the status of the positive structural thesis, not over whether the practice of reasoning takes place in a structured manner.

*The four corners, run explicitly.* The catuṣkoṭi is built to exhaust the options for any thesis and refute each in turn; run against □(T∧S∧Φ), it reaches no exit.

To affirm the first corner (that the conditions hold) is to perform an assertion that unfolds over time, distinguishes what is affirmed from what isn’t, and persists through the one affirming: the affirmation instantiates the three Conditions.

To affirm the second corner (that the conditions don’t hold) is to perform a denial carrying the same three features, so the denial instantiates what it denies.

The third corner, both, must differentiate the respect in which the conditions hold from the respect in which they don’t (Space), hold the two together in one bearer (Substance), and articulate them in sequence (Time); it presupposes the conditions to state its two conjuncts.

The fourth corner, neither, is itself a configuration: the withholding unfolds over time, sets itself apart from assertion, and persists through the one who withholds. That corner is the refusal to occupy any corner, and the Prāsaṅgika’s own dwelling.

The tetralemma closes the space of positions one might take toward the modal claim; it doesn’t close the space of conditions on taking any position at all. Each corner, the empty fourth included, is occupied by an activity that exhibits the very triconditional structure the corner was meant to dissolve: the catuṣkoṭi can’t be turned against □(T∧S∧Φ) except from within it.

**[Proposition]**

**No Corner Is Empty of Structure** · *Proposition*

The catuṣkoṭi is built to exhaust every stance toward a thesis and refute each. Affirming, denying, affirming-and-denying, and refusing all three are each an activity: unfolding over time, distinguishing itself from its alternatives, persisting through the one occupying it. The fourth corner, the refusal to occupy any corner, is no exception—the withholding is itself a configuration. The tetralemma closes the space of positions; it cannot close the space of conditions on taking any position at all.

**Depends on:** The Performative Catch (§3.3.1)

*Taking stock.* Tsongkhapa/Gelug readings, including the major line developed by Garfield, distinguish the negation of *svabhāva* from the negation of conventional existence: the structural conditions may be conventionally affirmed while remaining ultimately empty of intrinsic nature. Other Madhyamaka reconstructions place different pressure on how much positive conventional metaphysics survives. The present account can establish that Madhyamaka practice is structurally enacted; it can’t settle the ultimate-status dispute by treating enactment as a contradiction. Accommodation is available if the Triunity is read as conventionally indispensable and dependently constituted; a genuine disagreement remains if the book claims it as an ultimately established structure.

### 10.3.5 Axiarchism
Axiarchism gives value explanatory priority. On John Leslie’s formulation, the world has the configuration it does because that configuration is ethically required or favored: goodness isn’t merely a property the actual configuration possesses, but part of why this configuration rather than another is actual (Leslie 1979). Contemporary versions need not say that only the uniquely best possible world exists. They may hold that fundamental concrete reality is necessarily ordered toward goodness, that value raises the probability of better outcomes, or that value constrains which outcomes are eligible without fixing one uniquely. The shared claim is impersonal. No divine subject first recognizes the good and then chooses it; value itself belongs in the explanation of which configuration Nature actualizes.

The view gathers several pieces of the cumulative case without inheriting every feature of classical theism. If consciousness, knowledge, relationship, beauty, and moral agency are goods, an order directed toward value has reason—in the explanatory rather than psychological sense—to admit them. Pittard extends the proposal to non-skepticism: if fundamental reality is ordered toward goodness, epistemically inhospitable worlds in which most internal duplicates are deceived need not be treated as equally eligible with hospitable ones (Pittard 2024). Fine-tuning and psychophysical harmony can be read the same way. Their life- and knowledge-permitting character is explained by a value-bias in actualization rather than by a mind standing outside Nature. On that comparison axiarchism isn’t naturalism with an unexplained coincidence added. It is a rival account of why the coincidences aren’t coincidences.

Its economy is also its pressure on theism. A personal explanation requires a subject, knowledge of the relevant goods, an intention directed toward them, power to select, and a relation between the selection and the selected configuration. An impersonal value principle appears to remove those additions while retaining much of their explanatory output. The axiarchist need not personify goodness or treat it as an efficient cause. The claim is one of metaphysical explanation: ethical requiredness or favoring helps explain which configuration is actual. The theist can answer that a fact about goodness describes or ranks outcomes but is explanatorily inert until some agent responds to it. That answer can’t be assumed. It is the question between the views: whether there is a direct value–actuality relation, whether value merely describes what results, or whether value supplies a reason that an independently existing chooser may act upon.

The vocabulary must remain exact. Reality is the totality of what is; it doesn’t stand outside itself waiting to obtain. If goodness is real, it and any connection it bears to actualization belong to Reality. If it isn’t real, it can’t explain anything. Because The Identity of the Totality (§4.9) identifies Reality with Nature, an internal axiarchic proposal remains available: necessary Nature includes a value-sensitive feature that bears on which of its contingent configurations is actual. That proposal can rival personal selection without becoming a rival totality.

The direct version does incur a specification burden. To say that goodness favors actuality is to posit some determinate connection between comparative value and what obtains. If the connection necessitates the uniquely best outcome, contingency is threatened, and the no-best-world problem arises wherever every candidate can be improved (Adams 1972; Rowe 2004; Kraay 2010). If the connection merely weights outcomes, the view owes a measure and a rule for how value changes the weights; Possibility Precedes Probability applies before the distribution can be treated as given. If the connection constrains outcomes without ranking them completely, the remaining contingency is preserved, but the constraint explains only what it excludes. None of these costs makes the view empty. They identify the work hidden inside the phrase *ordered toward goodness*.

The personal version pays elsewhere. Once value supplies a reason rather than an actualizing relation, the explanation requires something capable of representing alternatives, recognizing their value, selecting among them, and making the selection obtain. A limited or temporally embedded agent can perform those operations, but doesn’t thereby become an ultimate ground. A classical agent claimed to stand prior to the modal field inherits the contact burden gathered into a trilemma at §10.4: the reason, the alternative, the act, and the outcome must form a determinate explanatory relation without quietly reinstating the structure from which the agent was exempted. Adding a subject may explain how value becomes a motive. It doesn’t make the subject structurally free.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Value-Contribution Fork** · *Disjunction*

What work does goodness do in making one configuration real rather than another?

- **If value describes the configuration,** then calling a configuration good records its value once subjects, stakes, or stance-independent value facts are already in place. The description doesn’t select or actualize what it describes.
- **If value disposes Nature toward the configuration,** then impersonal axiarchism remains a live rival to personal selection. It must specify whether the value–actuality relation necessitates, weights, or constrains outcomes; because that relation is real, it is a feature of Nature rather than a source prior to it.
- **If value supplies a reason for a chooser,** then the chooser is a further posit that brings its own costs. The chooser must be established independently, and its recognition, selection, and actualization of the good incur the cognitive, agential, and grounding relations the personal hypothesis adds.

No branch places goodness before Reality. The first is descriptive, the second locates a value-sensitive disposition within Nature, and the third adds a subject there as well.

*Scope.* The trilemma doesn’t decide whether stance-independent value facts exist, whether a value–actuality relation can explain, whether this configuration is favored, or whether axiarchism outranks theism. It identifies the work assigned to goodness and distinguishes an internal impersonal principle from a personal extension.

**Dependency routes:** descriptive route—none; dispositional route—The Identity of the Totality (§4.9) and Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5); chooser route—The Grounding Conditional (§3.1.5) and the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)

One proposed collapse from axiarchism into theism therefore moves too quickly. If value favors whatever is best, and a maximally perfect personal being would be the best possible being, the proposal concludes that axiarchism favors or entails God. The inference requires both that such a being is genuinely possible and that the axiarchic principle ranges over beings in the relevant way. The first is the possibility premise examined at §10.1.1; the second is a substantive rule about how value bears on existence. Restricting the principle to finite or physical goods may be ad hoc, but refusing a restriction doesn’t itself establish that every sufficiently valuable description has an instance. Axiarchism may entail theism under added premises. The added premises, not the word *good*, carry the entailment.

The world’s mixed value creates a further comparative problem without settling it. A value-directed order can allow local suffering where it contributes to a better whole, where the goods can’t be ranked on a single scale, where no best world is available, or where value biases rather than necessitates. Theism has parallel resources in freedom, soul-making, stable laws, redemption, and unknown reasons. Both views can absorb counterevidence by loosening the connection between value and outcome; both lose predictive force as they do. The comparison therefore requires a defended value ordering and a likelihood model, not the observation that this world contains both goods and evils. The theodicy questions remain at §12.5, where the relevant justifying relations are tested rather than presumed.

*What survives.* Axiarchism doesn’t displace the structural conditions or stand prior to Reality. A direct value–actuality principle is a determinate feature of Nature’s modal order: it distinguishes outcomes, bears a direction of favoring, and must obtain in some way if it explains anything. A personal extension adds a subject whose recognition and selection require more structure, not less. The view therefore survives as a genuine competitor to personal selection within Nature, not as a rival ultimate outside it. Where the cumulative case reaches only the claim that actualization appears biased toward life, knowledge, beauty, or value, it hasn’t yet distinguished value-sensitive Nature from a good designer. That further discrimination must be earned by evidence for agency rather than supplied by the conviction that value can’t explain on its own.

## 10.4 What the Rivals Carried

The rival ultimates don’t all end with one verdict. Some descriptions subtract the conditions under which a determinate ground or relation can be specified, and on the book’s analysis dissolve into ∅. Some preserve directed dependence, relational non-identity, and real grounding content under analogical, process, or apophatic vocabulary. Those articulated proposals may remain coherent as accounts of relations or configurations within Nature, but No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1) closes their use as independently constituted grounds outside or additional to it. Here and throughout this synthesis, *unprecluded* means only that a description may specify some aspect of Nature; it doesn’t establish a transcendent bearer, an exterior grounding role, or a positive case for calling that content God.

The claim isn’t that theistic philosophers reasoned carelessly. The traditions considered here contain some of the literature’s carefully developed accounts. The question is which verdict each proposal warrants: incoherence, relocation, compatibility, explanatory cost, or an unresolved question.

A recurrent pattern from Chapters 7–9 also appears here: some constructions presuppose structural roles they were intended to transcend, while others revise their account of ultimacy or leave an explanatory question unresolved rather than becoming incoherent.

- The Spinozist identified God with immanent Nature and accepted structural articulation rather than classical transcendence—*Cheap Substitution, Expensive Word* (§10.3.1) prices what the relabeling keeps and what it loses.
- The Neoplatonist placed the One beyond being and described emanation; pressed on whether apophasis can be applied selectively, the position has only silence or speech, never both (§10.3.2).
- The process theologian made God temporal and embedded: the revised theist’s option, named differently, and *What Makes the Two Poles One God* (§10.3.3) is the further question a dipolar deity owes once aseity is the cost of staying coherent.
- Plantinga’s maximal greatness raises a compossibility and possibility-premise burden; negative classical attributes are additional commitments rather than part of that definition (§10.1.1).
- The Madhyamaka (Nāgārjuna’s middle-way Buddhist school) emptied *svabhāva* (Sanskrit: “own-being” or self-existence) and left the dependent-arising structure intact—*No Corner Is Empty of Structure* (§10.3.4) names what dependent origination still requires.
- The axiarchist made value rather than a subject explanatory of actuality; where value directly weights outcomes, the weighting remains a structured principle within the modal field, and where value supplies reasons to a chooser, the personal grounding burdens return—*The Value-Contribution Fork* (§10.3.5) is what prices the two routes apart.
- The Pascal’s-Wager reasoner makes no grounding claim at all: the wager recommends belief under uncertainty rather than asserting what is the case, but the infinite payoff it trades on is underwritten only by the classical specification, so the prudential framing relocates the metaphysical burden the other arguments in this cluster carry rather than escaping it (§10.1.14).

The resulting verdicts differ: compatibility for some immanent accounts, a grounding burden for articulated transcendence, relocation for the prudential wager, and an open dialectical seam for strict apophasis or anti-thesis positions.

Three interlocutors require separate treatment because they respond in different ways: the revised theist accepts the structural conditions while retaining the term *God*; the Thomist identifier accepts the result but claims that the tradition already identified it; and the Kalām objector grants the structural conditions as actual while seeking a cause beyond them.

Consider the revised theist. A philosopher who rejects the classical attributes and defines God as temporal, extended, and causally embedded—a necessary person who realizes the structural roles—avoids the reduction to ∅. That much the argument grants. The revision doesn’t place an additional being into Nature as a box receives another content. By the constitutive non-addition of the Reality–Nature Identity, the proposed person is Nature in a determinate operation. The revised theist may still propose that this configuration is necessary, co-constitutive, or locally priority-bearing and must defend that account. What can’t be recovered is an independently constituted bearer that grounds the whole from an exterior or surplus position.

Consider the Thomist identifier. Distinct from the revised theist, this interlocutor doesn’t modify the classical attributes. The identifier accepts the argument’s structural result and identifies it with God under the classical description intact: Thomas’s *ipsum esse subsistens*, Feser’s Pure Act, Dolezal’s being-itself: these, the identifier says, just are □(T∧S∧Φ) under another name. If the argument proves a necessary structural ground, Thomism was right. The ground exists and deserves the name the tradition gave it. The book hasn’t refuted classical theism; it has renamed it.

The direct identification requires what the classical description denies. *Ipsum esse subsistens* was specified by Thomas as being without temporal succession, spatial extension, or material composition. The structural account specifies concrete Change by what it instantiates: succession, relational exteriority, and real bearing across transition. These are opposing type-level specifications, not two descriptions of one fact. If the identifier says the classical ground literally is T∧S∧Φ at modal-core resolution, the classical denials have been revised. If the identifier instead says that God bears only analogous or atemporal counterparts of the roles, the claim is no longer identity with T∧S∧Φ but a distinct-ground proposal whose contact with concrete actuality requires defense.

Analogical predication doesn’t supply a non-T/S/Φ articulation. The Thomist reply at this junction is that the “requires” in the preceding reduction smuggles in *univocal* predication: it treats the source–recipient relation as if it had to be structured in the same kind of temporal, spatial, and physical terms that creaturely causal relations require, whereas the Thomist insists on *analogical* predication for God-talk.

Suppose that divine predication is analogical and that the divine act isn’t an additional event within the world.

The structural claim isn’t that every divine relation must be *creaturely* T/S/Φ. Any determinately contentful source–recipient relation must carry a dependence direction, a non-identity between its terms, and a fact of obtaining that makes it this relation rather than a label. Those are generic structural roles. They become the loaded Conditions only where the relation performs concrete work: creating a change, sustaining a changing bearer, responding, intervening, or producing an effect.

If the Thomist denies every determinate term, direction, and obtaining relation, the proposed “grounding” supplies no grounding content. If the Thomist grants an atemporal relation with determinate content, a structured but nonconcrete grounding proposal remains available only as an abstract structure within Nature; if it is invoked to explain concrete actuality, the cross-resolution relation must be stated. If the proposed ground is itself a concrete individual, Necessary Occupancy identifies it as the three Conditions in determinate operation rather than as an additional occupant. If it remains nonconcrete while being credited with concrete action, cognition, response, or production, the Concrete-Entity Test applies at that operation and the Conditions are incurred there.

The analogical/univocal distinction therefore doesn’t exempt the proposal from articulation, but neither does articulation by itself turn analogy into concrete type-identity. It fixes the remaining internal question: whether an abstract structure of Nature can explain a concrete articulation and, if so, what that dependence consists in. It no longer leaves open a relation arriving from beyond Nature.

**[Disjunction]**

**Grounding-Contact Trilemma** · *Disjunction*

What does an ultimate ground supply that Nature doesn’t already?

- **If it supplies only abstract or atemporal grounding content,** then it is an abstract structure within Nature, not an exterior ground. If it is invoked to explain concrete actuality, the relation between those resolutions is still owed.
- **If it is concrete, or does concrete work,** then it is T, S, and Φ in determinate operation; neither route adds an independently constituted item to Nature. *Priced by* Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7) for a concrete ground; Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) for a concrete operation.
- **If it supplies neither determinate content nor a determinate grounding relation,** then it supplies no ground at all.

So the direct Thomist identification of classical *ipsum esse subsistens* with □(T∧S∧Φ) cannot be sustained while the classical type-level denials remain intact. Retaining determinate analogical content yields an internal abstract-grounding proposal, not a second source behind Nature. Dropping the denials yields a revised aspect of Nature.

**Dependency routes:** exhaustiveness of the three horns—Ground-Candidate Partition (§3.5.5); abstract or atemporal grounding—The Grounding Conditional (§3.1.5) and No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1); concrete ground—Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7) and Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8); concrete operation—the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4); no determinate ground—Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2)

The trilemma draws on the account of existence and instantiation at §1.5.1, the Structural Requirement at §2.4, and the greatness analysis at §11.1.

*Proof (Grounding-Contact Trilemma).* Let g be proposed as the ground of concrete actuality.

1. g’s attributed role is either abstract/atemporal only, concrete in its bearer or operation, or not determinately specified.

2. If abstract/atemporal only, the Grounding Conditional supplies a thin dependence direction, differentiated terms, and a fact of obtaining. No Unconditioned Essence and Reality–Nature Identity locate that relation as an abstract structure of Nature; if it explains concrete actuality, the cross-resolution relation remains to be stated.

3. If g is concrete, Necessary Occupancy identifies the ground as T∧S∧Φ in determinate operation. If a nonconcrete g performs concrete work, the operation has a when, a where distinguishing its terms, and a what bearing its effect; the Concrete-Entity Test therefore places T∧S∧Φ at the operation.

4. If not determinately specified, g supplies no grounding relation and fails as the proposed ground.

5. Classical *ipsum esse subsistens* retaining the type-level denials can’t be identical without remainder to T∧S∧Φ; granting the loaded Conditions revises the classical specification.

∴ Every proposed ground is an abstract structure of Nature, a concrete aspect of Nature, or no specified ground; and the direct classical identifier fails while the denials remain intact. An abstract structure invoked to explain a concrete one additionally owes the relation between those resolutions. ∎

Consider the psychophysical-harmony objector (§10.1.10). Either the interior is the living organization registered from its own side, as the book’s account of consciousness holds, and there was never a second inventory to pair; or it is a further feature linked to the physical by its own law, and feature and law are additions inside Nature. The theist’s account of the divine mind meets the same fork. Granting every comparative cost the argument presses, the result is confined to an internal selector or selection principle rather than an exterior source of total actuality, which the theorem below states in general form.

The actuality question now turns back on selection itself. Let a selector be proposed to make one available configuration actual. If the selector and the selection relation are real, they belong to Reality and therefore to Nature. If they are concrete, they fall under the Concrete-Entity Test; if they are only abstract or atemporal, they remain internal articulations whose relation to concrete actuality must be stated. In neither case does calling the relation *selection* make the selector an additional ingredient or place it outside the actuality it is meant to explain.

The scope distinction matters. An internal selector can explain why one subconfiguration obtains rather than another: a person can choose one action, an environment can select one trait, a dynamical process can select one attractor. But once what needs explaining is the total actual configuration, the selector and its operative relation can’t be omitted from that totality. Include them, and selection is one fact within the total configuration rather than its exterior source. Exclude them, and only a subconfiguration needed explaining. Deny that either is real or determinately related to the result, and no selection explanation has been supplied.

**[Theorem]**

**No Outside Selector** · *Theorem*

No real selector stands outside Nature or constitutes an independently formed addition within it. A real selector and any determinate selection relation are aspects of Reality–Nature. They may explain which subconfiguration obtains, conditional on the selector and relation, but they cannot explain the actuality of the total configuration from an exterior or surplus position. A concrete selector or operation is T, S, and Φ in determinate operation; an abstract or atemporal selector remains an internal structure and must state its relation to concrete actuality; an unspecified selector supplies no selection. Selection can therefore be an internal explanation of configuration, not an external source of total actuality.

**Dependency routes:** one totality—Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8); no external metaphysical layer—Metaphysics–Physics Continuity (§4.5.5); concrete selection—the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4); abstract or atemporal selection—Grounding-Contact Trilemma (§10.4); prior modal availability—Modal Availability Cannot Be Tuned (§3.5.6)

An identifier who nevertheless maintains strict equivalence applies the traditional term to a ground characterized by features the classical account denies in type. An analogical identifier may remain coherent, but it has changed the claim from identity to correspondence and inherits the internal relation and predicate-realization burdens. That conclusion follows from the distinction and prevents the classical account from claiming the book’s theorem as a result it had already established under another name.

Consider the transcendental arguer (§10.1.3), who presses a ground for logic itself. Authored logic owes a non-circular account of its Author, decreed logic presupposes the alternatives it would originate, and conceptualism—the position that survives longest—converges on the structural Conditions described as a feature of a divine mind. Pressed to a necessarily rational being, the cost recurs one level up; widened to a ground specified by withdrawing time, space, and persistence, the description loses the determinacy its own method invokes. **Grounding burden for the conceptualist rescue; specification failure for the content-denying limit.**

Consider the moral arguer (§10.1.12), who reasons from stance-independent bindingness to a personal will. The worry that morality needs a ground is shared. Three independent fronts contest the rest: where the book’s account holds, obligation is already seated in persons and their standing toward one another; a classical will still owes the directed relation among commander, content, and obligated; and a will grounds by a stance-involving relation while a nature doesn’t command. **Relocation, not refutation: morality is grounded, conditionally on the Chapter 5 account, in the persons the will was meant to bind.**

Consider the Kalām objector. The Kalām is the contemporary research program dedicated to denying necessity-of-T on independent grounds: the conceptual impossibility of an actual infinite past (Hilbert and traversal arguments), the empirical claim that the universe has a past boundary (BGV), and the cosmological inference from beginning to a transcendent personal cause.

It fits the pattern differently from the deflationary, change-skeptical, and modal-variant clusters of Chapters 7–9: the Kalām doesn’t arrive at the structural conditions by presupposing them in its denial; it accepts the three Conditions as actual and contingent and asks for an originating cause outside the order.

The argument raises a different objection to the Kalām. At §10.1.5, objections to an actual infinite past, evidence for a finite cosmic boundary, and the further inference to a timeless personal cause are kept apart. A first temporal boundary need not be a moment prior to T, and §10.1.11 doesn’t treat an ordinary historical Fall as requiring such a categorial origin. The composition view of Temporality is set out at The Composition of Temporality (§4.2.2), separating the quantitative question of how far the past extends from the metaphysical question of what grounds the order.

The Kalām and the structural argument both seek a necessary ground for the contingent series. The disagreement concerns the argument used to reach that ground and its further specification as a personal cause.

The same structural ground constrains accounts of miracles without establishing their impossibility. An intervention’s effect has temporal, spatial, and bearing conditions; whether its cause must share that mode is the contact question, not a premise the analysis may assume. **A burden on the causal contact and on identifying an event as divine intervention, not a foreclosure of miracles from the classical attributes.**

Consider the objector who presses religious experience and miracle reports directly (§10.1.16). An outcome-type that could arise through unremarkable causes doesn’t identify this occurrence’s cause (the Natural-Reach Fork); a best-fitting hypothesis among named rivals isn’t yet dominance of the full comparison class, and institutional rigor improves ascertainment as well as reliability (the Plurality–Dominance Gap; Both Halves Must Be Earned). Where the case succeeds, the Concreteness Ceiling states what has been shown: a concrete agent or act inside Nature, since the features that made the evidence forceful are concrete work, and better records firm up the concrete identification rather than the transcendent one. **Evidence for an agent or act can succeed and still fall on the concrete side of the Grounding-Contact Trilemma.**

The difficulty pressed here is chiefly structural, though several arguments also carry evidential burdens: classical claims must retain determinate content and explain their relation to the structured domain.

Consider the two epistemic objectors (§10.1.13). The global argument meets its own dilemma: if warrant runs through a local connection, the census of deceived duplicates is irrelevant; if it needs the census, no subject can take it, and a ground invoked to secure the distribution borrows the confidence it was meant to supply. The domain argument meets, where the book’s account of morality holds, an explanatory connection at the descriptive layer, with the bridge to bindingness argued rather than derived and left open. The theistic alternative pays a matching contact cost, and a calibrated faculty must be trusted wherever it recoils. **The demand for a connection between belief and truth is real and met from inside Nature; the normative bridge stays an open question.**

These proposals therefore leave a narrowed internal question, not an open ontological field. A ground defined by the absence of every determinate condition dissolves on the book’s analysis. The direct identification of classical *ipsum esse subsistens* with □(T∧S∧Φ) fails while the type-level denials remain intact. A ground that grants determinate roles is an aspect of Nature, and No Unconditioned Essence blocks essence-priority from turning that content into an independent source behind the field. What remains is whether an abstract structure explains a concrete one, and whether anything in that account establishes the personal predicates attributed to God. Those questions are tested in Chapter 11. It doesn’t inherit a possible exterior ground waiting for a contact.

A defender may answer a narrowed question by widening it again, and the maneuver deserves stating in its own right because it recurs across the chapter and isn’t always illegitimate. Rather than defend any one account, a defender observes that the literature contains several that aren’t obviously hopeless, declines to choose among them, and concludes that their disjunction is enough to relieve the pressure. Nothing is asserted; the latitude does the work. Where the objection was that *no* account has been offered, this answers it, and answers it fairly: a position isn’t obliged to settle every internal question before it may be held, and an open research program isn’t refuted by being open.

The maneuver changes character when the objection isn’t that an account is missing but that the position’s own commitments generate the difficulty. Then the disjunction must contain some member that is both available to that position and actually resolves the conflict rather than relocating it, and neither can be shown of a member left unspecified. What follows isn’t that mutually exclusive candidates fail to aggregate as credences—for exclusive members, confidence in the disjunction is exactly the sum of the confidences in each, and that arithmetic is untouched here. It is narrower: aggregate confidence that *some* member resolves the conflict is confidence in a disjunction, not yet possession of a resolution, and reasoning by cases licenses only a consequence every member shares. Where the members share no such consequence, nothing beyond “some resolution or other exists” follows from the disjunction, and a defender who relies on a specific member’s resolution has selected that member and owes its distinctive costs, which aren’t discharged by the confidence spread across the others. Credence spread across a disjunction is in any case a measure over a space, not a demonstration that the space has an occupant (§2.9.5).

**[Disjunction]**

**The Unselected Disjunct** · *Disjunction*

What burden is a list of undefended options supposed to discharge?

- **If the burden is existential—that some workable account exists—**the disjunction may discharge it, provided at least one member is specified enough to be tested and is consistent with the position’s other commitments. Neither can be established of a member that remains unspecified.
- **If the burden is a consequence every member shares,** it follows validly by reasoning by cases without selecting a branch—that is not in dispute here.
- **If the burden is specific to one member—a cost, a mechanism, a particular resolution not shared by the others—**the disjunction doesn’t discharge it. A defender who relies on that resolution has thereby selected the member and owes what it costs, rather than the confidence distributed across the set.

A list can establish only what its members jointly entail or that a specified live member exists. It cannot borrow one member’s solution while leaving that member and its cost unselected.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t deny that confidence in mutually exclusive candidates aggregates as ordinary credence, require a defender to settle every internal question, treat unresolved options as failure, or deny that a plurality of live accounts can be a sign of a healthy research program. It fixes only what a disjunction may be cited *for*: a bare menu, a warranted disjunction with a shared consequence, and reliance on one member’s distinctive consequence are three different things, and only the last incurs that member’s cost.

**Depends on:** Possibility Precedes Probability (§2.9.5); Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)



# 11. Reclaiming Greatness


Everything the tradition most wants to say about God is active: God knows, acts, creates, sustains, answers, and loves. Everything classical theology most wants God to *be* is withdrawn from the conditions under which those words acquired their content—outside time, outside space, without composition, susceptibility, or change.

*Apophasis* is theology’s discipline of unsaying: the withdrawal of positive predicates so that no creaturely condition is mistaken for the divine. The chapter inverts that discipline by asking whether, after the unsaying, anything can be said at all.

A representation need not resemble its object, and its object need not be actual. It must still contain enough to distinguish what it represents from nothing and enough to say what would make the representation accurate. Reference can outrun actuality; it can’t outrun every condition of reference.

God-language makes the distinction unusually visible. Devotional imagination supplies a figure who speaks, intends, judges, hears, intervenes, and stands in personal relation to worshippers. Classical theology may call that picture analogical, accommodated, or creature-side. The reply can be coherent, but once the natural chassis is disowned, something must still make it a picture *of this subject* rather than a projection with no specified subject behind it.

Metaphysical necessity, self-subsistence, non-exteriority, modal scope, and the exhaustive field of causal power have already been relocated to Nature (Chapter 4). That relocation didn’t establish that Nature is conscious, loving, righteous, or personal. The tests here ask what those further predicates retain after the conditions of their natural use are withdrawn.

The answers need not be uniform. A predicate may name a structural role already shown to belong to Nature; it may retain recognizable content and incur structural commitments; it may survive only through revision; or it may lose every discriminator, truth condition, and relation that could fix a referent. An unanswered burden is not yet the last of these. Inability to picture a subject is not proof that none exists.

The Christian-Scholastic synthesis is the primary case because it assembles simplicity, atemporality, aseity, creation, and providence in one developed account. The pressure is not confined to Christianity. It arises wherever an alleged ultimate is given determinate active predicates while placed outside the conditions that make their application intelligible.

Each test therefore asks where the relevant articulation occurs: in the alleged bearer, the predicate’s content, its object, or the contact through which it makes a difference. The chapter does not send every attribute toward one verdict. *Knows*, *loves*, *creates*, and *reveals* incur different debts, and the sections keep those differences in view.

## 11.1 Greatness

The analysis begins by granting the perfect-being construction on its own terms. [Perfect-being theology](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) attributes each great-making property—knowledge, power, goodness, presence, and life—to God at its maximal degree: not extensive but complete knowledge, not great but unrestricted power, and goodness without defect. God, on this measure, is that than which no greater can be conceived (Anselm, *Proslogion* (1078) 1998, II), every great-making property held to the maximal degree at once, the maxima taken to compose into a single being who has them all together and has them of necessity. That is the standard set by the tradition, and this chapter adopts it for purposes of analysis.

The decisive move, made before any single attribute is named, is to treat these maxima as a *starting ground*: possessed complete and from the outset, as pure actuality, with nothing in the being left unrealized. A maximum with no unrealized passive potency is the classical doctrine of pure actuality, not nothing by definition. Knowledge, power, and goodness are properties or capacities whose exercises have determinate content. The pressure is whether one immutable act can ground contingent, differentiated knowing and action—not whether the grammar of the predicates already refutes the doctrine.

This is the inversion the book is named for, taken at its root. The tradition seeks greatness by subtracting creaturely conditions—temporal succession, spatial extension, material composition. Those denials don’t by themselves state ∅. The limit is reached only when every determinate feature and every determinate relation is subtracted while active predicates are retained: then nothing remains to make the predicates true of their proposed subject (§2.7.1). The same maximization run the other way, toward the fullest concrete exercise of knowledge, power, presence, and relation, is what the political argument develops as maximum possibility (§6). What the tradition placed in the evacuation of creaturely limitation, the inversion relocates in the plenitude of concrete capacity. Nothing divine is moved into Nature. The claim is about predication, not ownership: concrete exercises of *knowing*, *acting*, *powerful*, *present*, and the rest draw their content from operations that instantiate the Conditions. An atemporal or analogical use isn’t eliminated by this point alone, but it must fix its own content and explain its contact with those operations; non-elimination doesn’t establish its formal possibility.

At the limit the loss is total. A predicate said of a subject stripped of every determinate feature doesn’t name some further thing it might have named; it fails to name at all (§11.8.3). Short of that limit the verdict is graded rather than binary. The inversion is therefore not a transfer of greatness from God to Nature. It is the recognition that the concrete content of greatness is realized within Nature, while any proposed transcendent analogue owes the relation by which it applies. The inversion de-deifies the predicate rather than sanctifying its subject. This isn’t the positivist thesis that theological language is meaningless: the argument is that a predicate stripped of every determinate correlate has nothing left to discriminate among, a demonstrated failure of application rather than a rule about significance. Nor is it conventionalism about necessity (§7.1.4): Reality, not linguistic practice, fixes the application conditions. Greatness so relocated changes category: it isn’t a completed actuality but a self-maintaining standing, held open in its exercise, and so achievable, losable, and deepenable rather than finished.

**[Definition]**

**Greatness** · *Definition*

The gradable dimension along which anything that exists in its own right—a *subsistence*—may stand. Great-making properties such as knowledge, power, goodness, presence, and life admit of more and less, so one subsistence may stand higher on a given property than another. A *maximum possible* degree is the most of a property that could actually be held, whether by one individual or by a subsistent collective; it is not an absolute stipulated in advance. The ceiling at which every property reaches the greatest degree compatible with the others is what the tradition calls *maximal greatness*.

Plantinga’s modal form of maximal greatness is developed at §10.1.1: maximal excellence in every possible world. The Floor, Not the Ceiling turns the earlier Anselmian criterion at that joint. A comparison among conceptions needs determinate candidates to compare, so removing every condition of specification doesn’t maximize a candidate. It removes the candidate from the ranking. What the criterion reaches before any evaluative maximum is the structural minimum anything must retain to be something at all. That result does not make Nature evaluatively perfect; it keeps metaphysical ultimacy and great-making value apart before the attribute tests begin.

The [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) is defined by three denials: outside time, outside space, not made of anything. The structural difficulty arises when such a God is also said to act, be present, affect the world, know, create, or sustain. Those predicates require determinate relations and therefore at least the role-level floor of directed order, relational non-identity, and real bearing. The argument doesn’t infer creaturely clock-time, metric extension, or material composition merely from these roles; it asks how a classical account makes its active predicates intelligible while withdrawing the roles they appear to require.

To act at one moment rather than another is to be in Time. To be present here rather than there is to be in Space. To affect the physical world is to exercise Substance. The theist who describes God as responding to prayer, directing influence, knowing what is currently the case, or creating at a moment has already committed to a God that instantiates the structural roles, not because the argument forces this conclusion from outside but because the theist’s own descriptions of divine activity presuppose it from within.

The classical God is defined by the negation of creaturely temporal succession, spatial extension, and material composition. Those denials reject the loaded types; they don’t automatically reject every thin ordering, differentiation, or grounding relation. The argument must therefore show where positive divine predicates introduce concrete operations rather than define that conclusion into the negative attributes. By the Modal Identity (§2.6.6), the instantiation of the three Conditions is analytically equivalent to the possibility of Change. A purported subject from which every determinate feature and relation has been removed is ∅-like under the Null State analysis (§2.7.1); a classical ground retaining determinate atemporal relations instead faces the contact burden developed in §10.4.

The preclusion at issue concerns concrete operation outside the three Conditions; it tests classical theism as a set of aseity, active predicates, and structural withdrawal across fundamental ontologies; and it doesn’t treat a contentless essence-prior posit as refuted merely by naming it (§2.6.5, §2.6.6, §2.9.6). A determinate atemporal ground isn’t made impossible by it; such a ground is left with the contact burden developed in §10.4.

One caution governs the attribute tests. Simplicity, *actus purus*, and immutability converge on the claim that God has no alternative way to be. That alone doesn’t yield impossibility: a necessary being has exactly one way to be, and *Necessity entails Possibility* (§2.1.4) makes what is necessary thereby possible. The diagnosis attaches not at the level of *way* simpliciter but at the level of *possible*, and it reaches impossibility only for a strict formulation that denies every thin and analogical content, leaving no stated conditions of satisfaction.

This is the foundational move at the level of the conjunction. What runs next, one attribute at a time, is the inversion at the level of the predicate. Take any classical attribute (creation, will, goodness, providence, revelation) and unpack what the predicate requires. A temporal creative episode requires succession; a directed reaching relation requires distinct terms; knowing requires a knower and determinate content. Classical accounts may construe creation and knowledge as one timeless act, leaving a relation and contingency burden rather than conceding succession in God. Each *concrete* unpacking points back at Nature: responding, intervening, deliberating, and producing already contain the Conditions their exercise requires. A timeless analogue may be proposed, but it owes both determinate content and an account of how that content reaches the concrete operation.

The inversion runs farthest at the predicate that doesn’t merely operate within Nature but purports to install it. A temporal creative episode requires succession, distinction, and bearing, so a creator acting in that mode already incurs the Conditions the act was supposed to install. A classical account may instead construe creation as an atemporal grounding relation; then succession in the source doesn’t follow, but the account inherits the contact burden. The target-side result remains stronger and independent: Reality’s capacity for Change is necessary (§3.2.5; §2.3), and what is necessary can’t have depended for its modal standing on a contingent creative episode. It isn’t possible to create possibility. What remains open is an essence-prior explanation of why that necessary standing obtains, not a temporal production of it.

The theist who maintains the classical attributes alongside divine action faces a serious coherence burden: the account must explain how an immutable, non-spatial, immaterial subject bears determinate causal relations without importing creaturely modes. That isn’t yet a contradiction until the proposed analogical or timeless account is assessed. The apologetic that most relies on divine action (miracles, revelation, answered prayer, creation) is the apologetic that puts the classical attributes it invokes under the most direct strain. Every miracle is an event in Time, Space, and Substance. The classical attributes and the active God of religious practice stand in a well-known tension that requires a worked account of timeless action, relation, and responsive practice (Mullins 2016).

*Framework invariance.* The preclusion holds across every fundamental ontology on offer, not naturalism alone.

Under physicalism, the structural roles are instantiated by physical fields and spacetime geometry; a being defined by the negation of physical structure is defined by the negation of what it was supposed to create.

Under idealism, the fundamental medium is mental, and the roles survive the relocation intact: any experience that unfolds requires succession (T), any experience that differentiates requires relational distinction (S), and any experience that persists requires a substrate of continuity (Φ). Berkeley’s God must perceive, and perception is a T/S/Φ event; the idealist renames Nature without eliminating the roles.

Under the Kantian transcendental framework, Time and Space are forms of intuition any cognitive act presupposes, and Strawson’s reconstruction (*The Bounds of Sense* 1966) argues that succession, coexistence, and persistence are conditions of self-conscious experience (§2.4). The modal argument extends the Kant–Strawson line from the conditions of any possible experience to the conditions of any possible ground of experience.

Under panpsychism, the roles are instantiated twice (once in the physical exterior, once in the experiential interior) since proto-experiential combination requires a relational manifold, a succession, and a persistence medium all over again. The preclusion isn’t relaxed under the richer ontology. It is doubled.

Under ontic structural realism (Ladyman et al. 2007), structure is fundamental and what physicalism treats as bearers are nodes in structural relations. A dynamic physical structure incurs the three Conditions; a purely abstract structure doesn’t become a concrete world merely by being called fundamental. This is where the henological worry bears: if the Conditions are three, what makes them one ground rather than three coordinate relations—and must their unity not derive from a prior One? By the Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10) Time, Space, and Substance are one Nature read three ways, not three ingredients awaiting an external unifier. A henological One with determinate emanative or grounding relations remains an essence-prior competitor with a contact burden; a One denied every determinate feature and relation supplies no unity-producing ground. The unity-priority reading is engaged on its own terms at §10.3.2.

Under Russellian monism, the intrinsic categorical base of physical structure is phenomenal; the dual aspect specifies the first-person perspective on the three Conditions rather than escaping them.

Under analytic idealism (Kastrup, *The Idea of the World* 2019), the cosmic mental field whose dissociated alters constitute individual minds is itself structured: dissociation requires distinguishable contents (S), persistence of the field across the dissociations (Φ), and temporal differentiation between the alters’ arising and dissolution (T). The relocation doesn’t eliminate the roles; it specifies them at the cosmic-mental level rather than the physical level.

Each framework locates the three Conditions in its own register. None of these frameworks removes the structural difficulty for the classical God.

*The embedded-deity concession.* The argument doesn’t rule out every conceivable theology. Process theism, open theism, and some forms of panentheism posit a temporally [embedded deity](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) with genuine causal power operating within Nature; such a being instantiates the three Conditions and therefore doesn’t collapse into ∅. Hartshorne’s dipolar theism warrants naming as a distinct sub-position within this family: God’s abstract pole (the necessary, eternal, essential nature) is held to be atemporal and immutable, while the concrete pole (God’s actual, contingent states of experience and response) is held to be temporal, cumulative, and genuinely affected by creaturely events (*The Divine Relativity* Hartshorne 1948; *Man’s Vision of God* Hartshorne 1941). The abstract/concrete bifurcation is designed precisely to retain classical honors at the level of essence while accepting temporal embedding at the level of actuality. Whether a single subject can coherently sustain both poles under the structural constraints developed here (and in particular whether the abstract pole, if genuinely atemporal and immutable, can stand in the act-relations the concrete pole requires) is the live question the relevant attribute sections (§11.3.1, §11.3.2, §11.3.3, §11.3.4, §11.7.2, §11.7.4, §11.9.1) carry. What the argument does establish is that any such being forfeits classical exterior aseity—existence *from itself*, dependent on nothing more basic for its being (Latin *a se*, ‘from itself’)—because the Conditions are constitutively prior to the embedded being. Whether a revisionary priority or co-constitution relation can be defended is a further question; it doesn’t restore the classical grounding claim.

**[Theorem]**

**Aseity Forfeiture** · *Conditional Theorem*

Any deity embedded in temporal, relational, and active roles escapes the ∅-like specification problem but thereby forfeits *classical exterior aseity*: it depends constitutively on the structural Conditions required for its existence and operation and therefore cannot be their independent ground. That consequence is categorical once the embedding is granted. Such a being may still be uncaused within Nature, or may retain a revisionary use of *aseity*, but neither restores independence from Nature’s Conditions. It is a configuration within Nature, or else the name *God* is applied to Nature itself; the latter relabeling does not by itself establish personhood, agency, or intentionality. The result does not make every revised theology contradictory. It fixes exactly which classical claim the revision has surrendered.

**Dependency routes:** concrete embedded bearer—Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7); one-Nature classification—Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10)

Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7) supplies the concrete-bearer route: anything concrete occupies the structural field. The Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10) supplies the classification route: the three roles jointly constitute one Nature rather than three exterior containers. Together with the structural analysis developed across this chapter, they place an embedded deity within the Conditions on which its concrete existence and operation depend. The priority isn’t temporal, as if the Conditions preceded the being in a sequence, but constitutive: they are preconditions of the embedded being’s existence rather than effects of its concrete activity.

If God is real, God is part of Reality; if God is part of Reality, God is inside Nature, and a God redefined to instantiate the structural conditions isn’t the classical target but a configuration within Nature, subject to the same structural constraints as any other. The Spinozist or panentheist relabeling (the necessary structure is God rather than Nature) doesn’t alter the result. It establishes, at most, that what is ultimate is necessary, all-encompassing, and explanatorily basic. The God of theism is supposed to be personal, agential, provident, and in some sense capable of care; Nature, as the argument establishes, is the necessary condition of all possible occupancy and exchange, not thereby a person, not thereby a center of concern, not thereby an object of worship. Re-labeling Nature as God changes the word while conceding the substance. What survives isn’t classical theism repaired but theology thinned into a metaphysical honorific for Nature.

*The eternalist reply.* The answer aimed most directly at the temporal horn doesn’t deny God’s timelessness but reconciles it with real relations to time. Stump and Kretzmann (1981; developed in Stump’s *Aquinas*, 2003) posit *ET-simultaneity*: an eternal-temporal simultaneity on which God’s single unextended eternal act is simultaneous with every temporal moment at once, in the mode proper to eternity. God therefore acts, knows, and answers without succession, standing in a simultaneity relation to each time from the standing present of eternity. Leftow (*Time and Eternity* Leftow 1991) develops a kindred account on which temporal events are present within an eternal reference frame. The reply grants that acting requires a relation to time and claims to secure the relation without placing God in time. It relocates the difficulty rather than escaping it. A simultaneity relation is still a relation: it requires relata distinct from one another (S), it persists as the relation it is (Φ), and where a single act is simultaneous with a succession of moments the ordering of those moments is exactly what the act must answer to (T).

An eternal present that genuinely stands in the ET-relation bears determinate relational roles and must explain their compatibility with simplicity and aseity. An eternal present that stands in no relation to temporal events can’t perform the explanatory work for which ET-simultaneity was introduced. And the deeper line doesn’t wait on the temporal question at all: grant a coherent atemporal standing-present, and the eternal act is still *actus purus* with nothing unrealized and nothing internally differentiated, so on the strict formulation its subject is left with no determinate way to be at all—not merely with one way rather than several, which would be no defect. ET-simultaneity, even if it worked, would show only how a timeless God might relate to time; it supplies none of the modal room the being lacks, answering the temporal horn while leaving the no-way-possible horn untouched.

*The subsistent-being reply.* The classical answer refuses the framing the result rests on. On the Thomist account God isn’t a being among beings but *ipsum esse subsistens*: the subsistent act of being itself, that by which everything else is, of which created time, space, and substance are analogical participations rather than constituents (Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* (1265–1274) 1947, I.4.2, analogy at I.13.5). To show that a concrete being can’t perform concrete work outside the three Conditions isn’t yet to refute Being Itself construed as an atemporal ground. The reply can’t be dismissed as relabeling.

The reply nevertheless divides cleanly by the work attributed. If Being Itself supplies only a determinate atemporal grounding relation, the proposal has content but owes the contact by which that relation grounds concrete Change. If it sustains changing things, knows contingent events, responds, intervenes, or causes in a concrete mode, those operations incur the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) and instantiate T, S, and Φ at the contact, forfeiting classical exterior aseity. If every determinate feature and relation is denied, nothing remains to perform the grounding work. The first position remains an unsettled essence-prior competitor, not a positively established possibility; the second incurs the Conditions and loses the classical grounding status; the third fails as a ground. What can’t be maintained is strict identity between the classical type-level denials and □(T∧S∧Φ) without revising one side of the identification (§10.4).

The preclusion isn’t a contingent fact about how the argument defines its terms; it is a necessary consequence, established at the level of the conditions of Change (Chapter 2), of what any possible medium must be. The survey already given is eliminative confirmation, not the ground of the result, and the ground is exhaustive in a way no survey could be. The Chapter 2 derivation doesn’t enumerate the fundamental ontologies on offer and eliminate them one by one; it derives the three Conditions from the conditions of Change as such, from what it is for anything to be possible rather than ∅ (§2.6.5, §2.6.6, §2.9.6). A genuinely novel ontology is therefore not an unsurveyed gap in a list but an already-decided case: whatever it nominated as fundamental would still have to make room for the possibility of Change, and to make room for the possibility of Change is to instantiate the three roles. The survey illustrates the result for the live contenders; the derivation secures it for any contender there could be.

Perfect-being theology supplies the method by which the attributes examined in this chapter are derived (Morris 1991; Murphy 2017); those attributes are assessed without defending or rejecting the method itself. Whether the maxima compose coherently into a single being is taken up at §11.2.4, and the cumulative case closes at §11.10 (What Remains of God?). Swinburne’s theistic personalism rejects strict atemporality and strong Thomistic simplicity while retaining aseity, necessity, and omnipotence (*The Coherence of Theism* 1977; *The Existence of God* 1979; 2004). Its everlasting God preserves recognizable personal agency and so occupies the revisionary branch. The question for that account isn’t whether its predicates are empty, but whether a temporal agent can remain the independent ground of the structure in which it acts.

## 11.2 Constitution
The first cluster gathers the attributes that specify what God is made of—the constitution the tradition assigns to the divine essence itself: simplicity (§11.2.1), unity (§11.2.2), infinity (§11.2.3), and perfection (§11.2.4). Each is a claim about internal makeup: that God is without parts, without division, without limit, and without defect.

Together they fix the static apex the attribute tests start from—The Discriminating-Content Burden of §11.2.1, which the remaining three draw on. Pressed, each owes the structure it was defined by denying: a being with no internal differentiation and no alternative truth conditions can’t be distinguished, sustained, or characterized at all, and the line to that result runs through the three Conditions rather than around them.

### 11.2.1 Simplicity
