Simplicity is the claim that God has no parts: no inner distinctions of any kind, so that each divine attribute, the divine essence, and the bare fact that God exists are one and the same undivided reality. The strain is that telling one true claim about God apart from another (even telling its wisdom from its goodness) owes discriminating content: either something on the divine side answers to the difference, or the predicates differ only in the speaker. A being for which every such content is denied, and no alternative truth conditions are supplied, isn’t the most unified being but the one whose identity has lost the structure identity tracks. What *subsistent being itself* reaches for, fully stated, isn’t the absence of structure but the structural role already earned for Nature. The further claim that one simple personal subject knows, wills, and loves doesn’t follow from the role.

Divine simplicity holds that God has no parts and no inner distinctions at all: God’s power just *is* God’s knowledge just *is* God’s existence, with nothing to tell apart. The classical tradition makes this identity definitive of God in a register the structure can’t host: no real composition, no distinction between essence and accidents, no distinction between essence and existence, no distinction among the divine attributes themselves: a stripping of internal differentiation from the divine being (Augustine, *De Trinitate* (400–428) 1991, VI; Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.3). *Ipsum esse subsistens* (*ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.3.4) identifies God’s essence with God’s existence. God *is* being rather than *has* it, and therefore depends on nothing beyond God for what God is.

The doctrine of the Trinity (Athanasian Creed, Augustine, *De Trinitate* (400–428) 1991; Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.27–43) holds three persons in one substance, distinguished only by relations of origin (paternity, filiation, procession), preserving distinction without composition. Necessary being (Anselm, *Proslogion* (1078) 1998, II–III; Plantinga 1974) extends self-sameness modally across every possible world, so that divine identity is preserved not just within a world but across the space of worlds.

Each formulation tries to keep divine identity from being one more identity among identities, and each is defended in contemporary form (Stump 2003; Stump 2016; Dolezal 2011; Dolezal 2017; Pruss and Rasmussen 2018; Leftow 2004; Leftow 2012; Brower and Rea 2005) as expressing not a property but the condition under which a being can be without dependence. Taken at the tradition’s own fullest formulation, the doctrine names the deepest unity philosophical theology has reached for: a being whose identity rests on nothing prior, because there is no internal structure to rest on and no external structure to depend on. Classical simplicity isn’t the only target in the neighborhood: the temporalist repair (drop simplicity and keep a temporal, personal God) is engaged at §11.7.3, and the embedded-deity concession at §11.1, so the pressures developed later aren’t aimed as if strong simplicity were the sole option. The doctrine’s full treatment, run end-to-end against the nine forms of its defense, is at §10.2.1; the present section presses simplicity specifically as a great-making attribute and draws on that treatment rather than re-litigating it. The division is exact: whether a simple being can be an ultimate ground—distinct from, really related to, and operative upon what it grounds—is taken up there; whether simplicity is a perfection, and whether the predicates it identifies stay distinct, is the question here.

The doctrine isn’t a Latin peculiarity, and Aquinas’s isn’t its only demanding form. Maimonides holds that the divine attributes are equivocal with creaturely ones, that no positive attribute may be predicated of God at all, and that what look like ascriptions of goodness or knowledge are to be understood either as negations or as descriptions of God’s effects (*Guide of the Perplexed* (c. 1190) 1963, I.50–60). Islamic *kalam* runs the same austerity through the dispute over whether the divine attributes are distinct from the essence, with the Mu’tazila denying it precisely to protect the unity (al-Ghazālī c. 1095; Griffel 2009), and the shared difficulty across all three traditions has been treated as one problem rather than three (Burrell 1986). What follows therefore tests a doctrine held in its strictest form well beyond the tradition that gave it its Latin vocabulary, and the pressures below apply wherever that strictness is maintained.

*The interrogation.* Six questions press the points at which simplicity owes an answer.

**Q1.** *If God has no parts, then how are his wisdom and goodness distinct?* Plantinga’s (1980) pressure on strong simplicity hasn’t been answered in the form it was put. If God’s wisdom is identical with God’s power, and God’s power with God’s goodness, transitivity gives wisdom-is-goodness, and these are clearly distinct properties on any predicative reading. The contemporary defenses (Stump 2003; Dolezal 2011; Dolezal 2017; Pruss and Rasmussen 2018) recast simplicity as non-composition rather than strict property-identity. That recast is already granted at §10.2.1, Seventh: one simple truthmaker can ground several nonsynonymous truths, and the objection isn’t “many predicates, therefore many parts.” What this section spends is the further claim the doctrine adds: God’s wisdom *is* God’s goodness *is* the essence, each necessary.

The book’s own identity theorem shows what that form of claim requires. Necessary co-extension isn’t identity. Being three-sided and being three-angled travel together in every Euclidean world, yet they remain two facts (§2.6). The licensing condition is stronger: the two sides have no independent ground, so that specifying either already specifies the other (No-Surplus (§2.6.9); Modal Identity (§2.6.6)). Reality–Nature Identity is held to that bar at §2.8: co-extension is refused as sufficient, and the identity is earned from the absence of individuating content on either side. Wisdom and goodness are advertised as having remainder. They have different inferential profiles, different creaturely analogues, and they are different things the believer is saying. That remainder is exactly what an identity of necessaries is forbidden to rest on unless hyperintensional specifying content carries it. Role-Specifications (§7.1.3) is the contrast case, not the application: change-possibility and the Conditions aren’t independently graspable senses of one object. *Wise* and *good* are. Essence-Description (§2.6.12) blocks parking the remainder behind an undescribed real essence to which a second sense could attach.

One developed form of the recast invokes the analogy of being (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.13): *wisdom*, *power*, and *goodness* pick out distinct content at the level of signification, grounded in diverse creaturely perfections eminently contained in the one undivided essence, without internal differentiation in God and so without composition. Grant the Thomist the superabundant actuality. Then ask, in virtue of what does *wisdom* apply rather than merely *goodness*? If something on the divine side answers, that is the specifying content No-Surplus requires. It isn’t yet composition, and it isn’t yet any of the three Conditions in loaded form: §10.2.1, Eighth, already prices a formal or explanatory distinction as a predication and contact burden rather than as clock-time, metric space, or physical parts. If nothing answers, the predicates differ only in the creaturely speaker, and the identity of the perfections is the cheap co-extension No-Surplus refuses. Eminence as positive plenitude without contrast is already closed by No Third Option Between Contrastive and Empty (§10.2.1): determinate content is contrastive or empty. Abstracta block the inference from determinacy to Spatiality, as granted at §10.2.1; they don’t supply a remainder-free identity between *wise* and *good*.

The most refined Thomist names the relation precisely here: the perfections are *virtually* distinct, a *distinctio rationis ratiocinatae* in the Cajetanian idiom, distinct neither really nor by any relation in God, but by a distinction of reason carrying a foundation in the thing. Ask what the *foundation in the thing* is. If it has a *fundamentum in re*—some specifying content in virtue of which *wisdom* applies rather than *goodness*—that is the hyperintensional remainder the identity of necessaries owed. The distinction is virtual only in that two concepts read off one essence; the specifying content is still what No-Surplus asked for. If it has no foundation in the thing (a *distinctio rationis ratiocinantis*, purely in our minds), then *wisdom* and *goodness* track one undifferentiated point under two names, the identities are uninformative co-extension, and the attribute-tradition has kept the words without the content that made them two. The Cajetanian middle wants a foundation that grounds discriminating application without being a real or relational feature. No-Surplus doesn’t care what it is christened. Either specifying either perfection already specifies the other, with nothing left over to mark them as two—then the predicates aren’t two—or there is leftover content, and that leftover is what the account owes. Dissolution follows only where every such content is denied and no alternative truth conditions are supplied, while the identities and the distinct profiles are both retained.

A last Thomist resort relocates the diversity from the foundation to the manner of signifying. On Aquinas’s distinction between the *res significata* and the *modus significandi* (*ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.13.3), *wisdom* and *goodness* signify one undivided *res* under diverse *modi significandi* grounded in diverse creaturely effects. The reply is given in full at §11.8.3. In brief, the modes must themselves be carried by specifying content or they are speaker-side only: diverse creaturely effects taken back to the essence as variously imitable either name the remainder No-Surplus required or leave the identities cheap. The same bar reappears at the level of signification (Mullins 2013).

The same pressure is pressed against omniscience in §11.4.2: a being that knows a differentiated manifold needs an account of how one actuality non-arbitrarily grounds differentiated content. That is the discriminating-content and No-Surplus bar again, not a proof that the knower is composed. A being whose essence has no specifying content for its predicates, and no alternative truth conditions, isn’t a being whose identity has been preserved more strictly than ours; it is a being whose identity claims have been left unearned.

**Q2.** *If there’s nothing in God to tell apart, what tells the Father from the Son?* Trinitarian distinction has to be real distinction or there is no Trinity, and real distinction requires determinate non-identity between the persons. It doesn’t by itself require a spatial interval. The patristic and Thomistic reply locates the distinction in relations of origin (paternity, filiation, procession, Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.27–43) rather than in real composition. But relations of origin are themselves structured: paternity and filiation aren’t interchangeable, procession is a directed relation of source and term, and origin-order is asymmetric even when it is explicitly denied to be ordinary temporal before-and-after. That is the book’s Temporality role in non-clock form: directed order, not a sequence of divine moments. Latin trinitarianism (Leftow 2004; Leftow 2012; Brower and Rea 2005) keeps distinction-without-extension by treating the persons as distinct only by relation within a single divine consciousness; social trinitarianism (Swinburne 1994; Hasker 2013) keeps distinction-with-extension by treating the persons as distinct centers held in *perichoresis* (their mutual indwelling in one another). The first preserves unity by attenuating distinction toward modalism (collapsing the persons into mere aspects of one God); the second preserves distinction by attenuating unity toward tritheism (three separate gods). The intermediate position sought by the tradition requires what the three Conditions identify: three relata distinguished by asymmetric origin-order and held in a persisting substance. The doctrine affirms origin-order and one substance while denying that either is temporal or composite, and that denial is where the account is owed.

**Q3.** *When we call God necessary, are we saying something about God, or just about every possible world?* Kant’s (1781) 1998 objection (existence isn’t a real predicate) is sharper than Plantinga’s modal reframing acknowledges. Plantinga (1974) reads necessary existence as instantiation in every possible world and so escapes the Kantian objection at the level of the predicate. Instantiation in every possible world can be expressed either as a de re modal property of a thing or as a fact represented by the modal structure. Plantinga’s reframing therefore can say something about God. The remaining issue is whether the relevant individual and cross-world identity conditions are coherent and whether the possibility premise is warranted. What modal-structure necessity comes to is taken up at §11.3.1; the present concern is more local. The predicate the doctrine wants (necessarily existing as a way of being self-same across modal space) is preserved, on the structural reading, by relocating its referent from a being to a feature of how worlds are structured. What is necessarily instantiated across every possible world is the three Conditions; what isn’t necessarily instantiated is a being defined by not instantiating any of them.

**Q4.** *If all we can say is that God is, have we said what God is?* *Ipsum esse subsistens* (subsistent being itself) closes the gap that, in creatures, makes existence contingent on something other than essence. The closing preserves aseity; what it doesn’t preserve is identity in a sense the predicate could pick out. Every creaturely being is a particular kind of being, and being-this-kind is what makes the being identifiable as the being it is. A being whose essence is its existence isn’t the most identifiable being but the one whose identity has thinned to the bare fact that it is, a fact with no kind-content for identity-talk to track. Stump (2016) and Dolezal (2017) defend the position as expressing divine non-contingency rather than as a determinate metaphysical claim, and the move is genuinely available. The doctrine survives, on that reading, by narrowing the work the predicate is asked to do: *ipsum esse subsistens* names God’s non-dependence rather than supplying a determinate kind-description. That isn’t a mere retreat; it is the most defensible Feser-style way to keep the doctrine from becoming one entity inside a wider genus. The structural cost remains that the believer who calls God *the Holy One of Israel* isn’t invoking the bare fact that something is; they are invoking a determinate being with a determinate kind. *Ipsum esse subsistens* preserves the term while leaving the being without determinate content.

**Q5.** *If God isn’t a being among beings, what makes God anyone at all?* The post-Heideggerian critique (Heidegger (1927) 1962; Heidegger 1957; Marion 1991; Marion 2002) puts the dilemma sharply. If God is a being among beings, divine transcendence collapses into supremacy within a category; if God is being itself, divine identity loses the structural conditions any identity requires. The Thomistic reply (Burrell 1979; Westphal 2001) reads *ipsum esse subsistens* as precisely the move past being-among-beings. Plotinus gives the older and more radical version of the same pressure: the One is prior to being and to number, the source of intelligibility rather than an intelligible item within it (*Enneads* c. 270 CE, V.5, VI.9) (§10.3.2). The reply trades one structural concern for its mirror image: a being among beings has identity but loses transcendence; being itself, or the One beyond being, has transcendence but loses identity. The analysis here doesn’t pick a horn. What *being itself* names, when fully stated, is the conditions under which any being can be individuated, distinguished, and sustained across the time within which it persists. The three Conditions aren’t a being among beings, and they do the work *being itself* was meant to do without leaving the structural side of identity unprovided.

**Q6.** *If God is the greatest in every way at once, what makes God this being and not another?* [Perfect-being theology](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) (Anselm of Canterbury (1078) 1998; Morris 1991; Murphy 2017) generates the divine attributes by maximizing each great-making property. The methodological assumption is that maxima compose: that maximally wise, maximally powerful, maximally good, maximally simple, maximally eternal can be jointly predicated of one being without internal contradiction. Swinburne’s use of simplicity is different: it is a theoretical virtue in a cumulative explanatory case, not the strong ontological identity of attribute and essence the Thomistic doctrine asserts (Swinburne 1979; 2004) (§10.1.8). The cumulative case is developed from the joint side at §11.2.4; this section presses the same point from the individuating side. Sobel (2004), Martin (1990), and Everitt (2004) press incompossibility (the impossibility of the maximized attributes being jointly instantiated in one being) from a different angle. What individuates an identity is the structured content the maxima have been defined to exclude. There is no determinate identity for a being whose individuation has been removed at the level of every great-making property at once.

*The burden.* What the six pressures together surface is the structural inventory identity actually depends on. Identity depends on six conditions.

(i) Discriminating content, and where the predicates are necessary and identified with the essence, the No-Surplus bar on that content: specifying either already specifies the other, or leftover content remains to be named. Sharing one truthmaker doesn’t by itself collapse them; denying every divine-side articulation while retaining both the identities and the distinct profiles does.

(ii) Asymmetric relational ordering: distinct relata require non-identity (S), and ordered relata a directionality (T) between them, without which “distinct” is a verbal claim with no structural correlate.

(iii) A structure-grounded locus of necessity: what is necessary across modal space is necessary because the modal structure is configured a particular way, and that configuration is where the necessity lives.

(iv) Determinate kind-content: a being is the being it is by virtue of being *a kind of being*, and identity-talk tracks the kind, not the bare fact that something is.

(v) Structural individuation: what makes a being identifiable isn’t the withdrawal of all dependence but the structural conditions under which the being can be individuated, distinguished, and sustained.

(vi) Structured content sufficient to support each great-making property: the maxima can’t compose into a coherent identity unless the structured content the maxima predicate is preserved rather than negated.

These six conditions aren’t extrinsic to identity; they are what the predicate *identity* names when its referent is examined. Concrete identity across moments runs on the three Conditions. A simple atemporal identity still owes discriminating content for its predicates; the upgrade from that burden to the loaded three Conditions remains a further step.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Discriminating-Content Burden** · *Diagnostic*

Several predicates can share one truthmaker without dividing that truthmaker into parts. Predicative plurality therefore doesn’t by itself refute simplicity. Where the perfections are also identified with one another and with the essence, and each is necessary, modal co-extension cannot be what makes them one (No-Surplus (§2.6.9)). The virtual distinction must supply hyperintensional specifying content, or the identities are uninformative and the predicates differ only in the speaker. Supplying that content is a predication and contact burden, not composition, and not yet loaded T, S, or Φ. Dissolution follows only where every such content is denied and no alternative truth conditions are supplied, while the identities and the distinct inferential profiles are both retained.

**Depends on:** No-Surplus Criterion (§2.6.9) and §10.2.1

*The reclamation.* The genuine inversion concerns subsistence, not every predicate attached to the alleged subsistent. Nature supplies the necessary field within which anything can be individuated, persist, differ, or compose; it isn’t itself assembled from an exterior stock. *Ipsum esse subsistens* reaches toward that structural role. The further claim that one simple personal subject knows, wills, loves, and creates doesn’t follow from the role and can’t be protected merely by identifying every predicate with one divine act. Those identities, where each relatum is necessary, aren’t earned by co-extension; they owe specifying content, which is the bar Q1 spends. The account must still discriminate those truths. Nature’s necessary possibility of change isn’t an unrealized potency awaiting actualization from without (§2.9.6); the personal and cognitive enlargement remains a separate specification.

The role isn’t this tradition’s alone, and neither is the seam. Plotinus places absolute simplicity at the head of everything precisely because a One with parts would require something prior to compose it (Gerson 1994), and Avicenna’s necessary existent is simple for the same structural reason (Avicenna (c. 1020) 2005). Each reaches the role by the same route this section grants, and each meets the same step at the same place: a simplicity strong enough to need nothing prior isn’t yet a subject who knows, wills, and loves. The difficulty is therefore not an in-house Christian one. It meets whoever takes the role, by the same route.

Nor is a structureless Pure Act available as the other horn: *pure act* is itself a structural predicate. It is marked off from impure act by a distinction, and a distinction is contrastive content, the generic floor Q1 already presses rather than Spatiality by itself; and it is *act* only as the actualizing of what it affects, a directed relation of actualizer to actualized across the interval between them, exercised by what persists as the agent of the actualizing. An actuality that causes an effect must stand in a determinate causal relation to it. Thomistic pure act forecloses passive potency in God, not active causal power; the seam at §11.7.1 is whether an unchanged necessary act can explain contingent effects without modal collapse.

What structures whatever it touches can’t itself be structureless, and proportionate causality, the doctrine’s own principle, says as much from the effect’s side: a cause produces only what it contains, so a structured world needs a cause proportioned to structure, and the retreat to eminent containment either supplies the specifying content Q1 asked for or is empty. No Third Option already closed the attempt to have plenitude without contrast. The terminus is therefore neither horn the objection offers, neither a composite item within the order nor a bare actuality above it, but the conditions any actuality meets in being one; strip even the structure by which *pure act* differs from empty actuality and what remains isn’t a supreme simple but ∅ (§2.7). *Actus purus*, when used to support differentiated causal and cognitive predicates, incurs the thin role-floor of determinate order, difference, and bearing, and wherever those predicates are cashed as concrete production in the world the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) places the three Conditions at that operation. The upgrade remains a further argumentative step only for the act considered in itself. And the triad the doctrine would press as a many is no aggregate: by the Triconditional Identity (§2.6.10), Time, Space, and Substance are one Nature read three ways, co-instantiated so completely that to lack any one is to lack all three (§2.6.5). The unity a henological One is summoned to supply is therefore not added to the triad reached by the negative route but is what the triad is; closing the regress needs neither a fourth relation binding the three nor a One beyond structure standing over them. It is necessarily what it is because there is no second vantage from which it could be otherwise.

Read in the structure that supports the phrasing, *subsistent being itself* reaches toward what the three Conditions are. The properties classical theism assigns to *ipsum esse subsistens*—atemporality, aspatiality, and priority to composition—correspond to those assigned to the Null State at §2.7; where the doctrine excludes Nature and denies every determinate content, its remaining specification is ∅. This is the same claim Subsistent Grounding (§2.9.3) states formally: none of T, S, Φ a privileged floor the others rest on, each subsisting only because the other two do. Pressed through the tradition’s own six questions, the phrase classical theism reserved for a simple, partless God points toward a co-constituted triad instead, subsistent by mutual dependence rather than by having nothing to depend on.

The one premise this verdict turns on is the one the doctrine can’t surrender: that *God is* (*God isn’t nothing*) is made true by something on the divine side rather than by nothing at all. That is aseity, read as a truthmaker demand; a being whose existence answered to nothing in it would exist from nothing, the one thing aseity forbids. The discernibility principle the inversion uses isn’t imported against the doctrine: it is the doctrine’s own first commitment, turned on the bare predicate *is*.

The doctrine of divine simplicity, pressed through these questions, either supplies a determinate account of differentiated predication and relation or leaves the structural burden unresolved; it isn’t thereby identical to Nature by definition.

### 11.2.2 Unity
Monotheism’s core is that God is one, not merely one being among others, but uniquely and indivisibly one. Counting something as one, or telling it apart as *this* being rather than another, takes the very distinctness that space and structure provide. Applied to a being placed beyond all structure, “one” has nothing to fix it as one. The oneness the argument can actually secure is the unity of the framework within which occupancy and exchange occur. That isn’t yet the personal God of monotheism.

The classical doctrine of divine unity holds that there is exactly one God, not as a contingent count but as a necessary feature of what divinity is. Distinct from simplicity, which concerns God’s internal lack of parts (§11.2.1), and from necessity, which concerns God’s modal status (§11.3.1), unity is the cardinality claim monotheism rests on (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.11; Swinburne 1994, ch. 8) (Anselm, *Monologion* III). The classical argument runs from the great-making properties to the count: a being than which no greater can be conceived must be unique, since two such beings would either be indistinguishable (and hence one, by the identity of indiscernibles) or distinguishable (and hence each lacking some perfection the other has, contradicting maximal greatness).

Aquinas’s parallel line argues from simplicity: a being identical with its essence can’t be one among others sharing that essence, since *one among others* requires a principle of individuation outside the shared essence, and a simple being has no such principle (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.11.3; Stump 2003; Dolezal 2017). The claim is also pressed outside the Latin tradition. Islamic *tawhid* holds not merely that there is one God but that God admits no partner and no internal composition whatever, so that associating anything with God is the one unforgivable offense; the doctrine is a claim about the structure of the divine being and not a headcount. The consequence the Islamic theologians drew is the one this section is testing: if God is one in that sense, what becomes of the many attributes scripture ascribes? The Mu’tazila answered that the attributes can’t be entities distinct from the essence without compromising the unity, and so read them as identical with it; their Ash’arite opponents held the attributes real and distinct-yet-not-other, which the Mu’tazila regarded as multiplicity readmitted under a hedge. That dispute states the unity problem directly, and was argued for centuries by parties who took the stakes to be the difference between monotheism and its denial (al-Ghazālī c. 1095; Frank 1992; Griffel 2009). Maimonides presses the same austerity from the Jewish side, holding that no positive attribute can be predicated of God univocally and that the attributes are to be read negatively, since any positive ascription introduces the composition unity forbids (*Guide of the Perplexed* (c. 1190) 1963, I.50–60; see also Burrell 1986 on the shared problem across the three traditions).

The Christian tradition complicates the picture at the Trinitarian level: one divine being in three persons, with the unity preserved at the level of *substance* and the threeness located at the level of *persona* or *hypostasis* (the Greek theological term for a divine person or individual subsistent reality) (Augustine of Hippo (400–428) 1991, V; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.29–43; Rea 2009). The unity claim survives the Trinitarian complication in the sense that the divine substance remains one; the multiplicity is *internal* to the one God, not a multiplicity *of* gods. The position the doctrine, fully stated, holds is that the count *one* is fixed at the level of the divine essence and that no metaphysically possible world contains two distinct divine beings.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test how the doctrine fixes the count once ordinary structural principles of individuation have been withdrawn. What lies underneath them is structural, what fixes the count: if the conditions that could pick out a divine being are satisfiable at all, what prevents their being satisfied more than once?

**Q1.** *What makes God one rather than two, if God has no place, time, or matter to be told apart by?* Two beings of the same kind are distinguished by some principle of individuation: spatial location, temporal trajectory, material constitution, qualitative difference, or haecceity. A divine being on the classical bundle has none of the first three: God is non-spatial, atemporal, immaterial. Qualitative difference between [maximally great beings](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) collapses to indiscernibility (Anselm’s argument already given). Haecceity—primitive thisness without further principle (Adams 1979; Plantinga 1974)—is what remains.

The classical reply is that the divine being’s uniqueness rests on the impossibility of two beings each maximally exemplifying the great-making properties: two such beings would collapse into one (Anselm) or would each lack a perfection (Swinburne 1994). The concern here is that the collapse-or-lack argument runs through *distinguishability*, and distinguishability is what the structural conditions provide. Where the structural conditions are absent, the question *are these two beings or one?* has no resource on which to settle either way. The argument’s force, on the classical bundle, depends on the very structural distinctness the bundle denies the divine being.

Plotinus offers a dissolution at the root of Q1’s individuation problem. The One doesn’t require a principle of individuation, because it is beyond being and hence beyond the entire domain in which individuation questions arise (*Enneads* V.5, *That the Intelligibles Are Not External to the Intellect*; VI.9, *On the Good, or the One*) (Plotinus c. 270 CE). The individuation question—*what makes this being one rather than two?*—presupposes enough structure for the question to get purchase; the Plotinian One is prior to all structure, all relation, all multiplicity, and hence prior to the individuation question itself. The One isn’t *one* in the numerical sense—the source of all number is itself beyond number—and the Anselmian collapse-or-lack argument, which quantifies over indistinguishable or distinguishable divine beings, doesn’t reach the One’s level. The concern for the Plotinian dissolution is that *beyond being* terminates the individuation question by terminating the domain of predication entirely: §11.8.3, Q5 traces the convergence between the Plotinian ascent and the structural analysis at that same terminal point.

Spinoza’s *Ethics* (Spinoza (1677) 1996, I.5) offers a complementary argument within the framework of attribute-individuation: there can’t be two or more substances sharing the same attribute, since substances are individuated by their attributes; if God is the substance possessing all attributes, there can be only one such substance. The argument is simpler than the Anselmian line and settles Q1 from within substance-metaphysics without requiring the via negativa. The concern here is Spinoza’s own conclusion: once the one-substance result is reached, the particular modes—individual temporal events, spatial configurations, creaturely substances—are modes of the one substance. The *deus sive natura* identification follows, and the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary)/world distinction has already been collapsed.

**Q2.** *How is God exactly one, if a being without parts gives nothing to count?* Aquinas’s individuation argument holds that a simple being is identical with its essence, and so can’t be one among others sharing that essence (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.11.3). The concern here is that *one among others* is a cardinality claim, and cardinality presupposes the very structural distinctness simplicity refuses. A being identical with its essence isn’t less enumerable than a non-simple being for any structural reason; it is unenumerable in the sense that *enumeration* presupposes distinguishable members, and a simple being has no distinguishable features by which to be a member. The argument secures *exactly one* by removing the resource on which *exactly two* could be coherent, which secures uniqueness at the cost of removing the cardinal predicate itself. The reply that *one* applies to the simple being as a transcendental rather than as a number (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.11.1; Wippel 2000) preserves the count by treating it as analogical; the concern here is that the analogical *one* is consistent with *no others of the kind* and with *no further determinable count of the kind*, and the doctrine of monotheism needs the determinate count, not the indeterminate transcendental.

**Q3.** *What tells the three persons apart, if nothing in God divides one from another?* The Christian tradition holds one God in three persons: a unity at the level of *ousia* / *substantia* (essence or substance), a threeness at the level of *hypostasis* / *persona*. The classical reply distinguishes the levels and locates the multiplicity at the personal level while preserving the unity at the substantial level (Augustine of Hippo (400–428) 1991, V–VII; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.29–43; Swinburne 1994, ch. 8). The contemporary literature is divided: social trinitarians (Plantinga 1986; Swinburne 1994) emphasize the threeness; Latin trinitarians (Leftow 2004; Rea 2009) emphasize the oneness; constitution accounts (Brower and Rea 2005) provide a metaphysical apparatus for both. The concern here is that *three persons in one substance* requires a principle of individuation at the personal level that doesn’t run at the substantial level. The traditional reply is that the persons are individuated by their relations of origin: the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten of the Father, the Spirit proceeding from the Father (and the Son, in the Western tradition). The concern here is that *relations of origin* are directional relations (*begotten of* and *proceeding from* are asymmetric) and asymmetry is the structural feature of T (§1.4). The reply that these are eternal relations of origin preserves the asymmetry in a non-temporal register, and divine atemporality then owes an account of directed order without succession (§11.3.2). The Trinitarian complication doesn’t merely sit alongside the classical bundle; it reaches into the structural features the bundle was preserving God from.

**Q4.** *What makes two ultimate frameworks two, if telling them apart takes a wider frame over both?* The structural reasoning run so far treats Nature as the necessary condition of any possible world (§2.6.6, §2.6.10). The question presses whether *more than one* such Nature is coherent. By Structural Individuation, whatever makes two concrete frameworks two is differentiating structure. If a relation or ordering supplies the difference, it is the more comprehensive frame in which both stand. If primitive thisness supplies it, that nonqualitative individuator is still part of the complete structure of Reality. If nothing supplies it, there aren’t two frameworks. The argument is parallel to the cosmological-isolation case (Kraay 2010; Almeida 2008) at the level of worlds, but runs at the level of modal-structure conditions rather than world-content: plurality either contributes differentiating structure, which the all-inclusive frame contains, or contributes none, in which case the cardinality is unearned.

The concrete-world form of this reductio is deployed at §7.2.3. Given Structural Individuation (§2.4.9), the conclusion is deductive: whatever makes a second concrete totality second is differentiating structure and belongs to Reality’s complete account; if nothing makes it second, there is no second totality. The determined primitivist can deny the premise, but premise denial doesn’t turn the valid inference into an abductive one. On the structural reading, the count is fixed with the unity: exactly one all-inclusive frame and, as its concrete totality, one cosmos. Relational Distinctness remains separately responsible for the narrower claim that positional separation requires an interval.

**Q5.** *What makes many gods divine, if no one of them is the ground of the rest?* The contemporary literature on theological pluralism (Hick 1989; Heim 1995; Knitter 2002) and the historical literature on polytheism (Versnel 2011; Pakkanen 1996) have pressed alternatives. The concern here is that each alternative either treats the multiple divinities as multiple conditioned beings within a single structural frame (in which case the frame is the genuine ground and the divinities are particulars within it) or treats them as ungrounded multiples (in which case the question of what holds them together is unanswered). The pluralist reading registers, rather than resolves, the structural concern. On the structural reading, the *something common* across the multiple divine names would be Nature itself, and the *plurality* across the names the multiplicity of particulars within Nature. Where monotheism collapses the multiplicity into one being, pluralism preserves it by treating no one of them as the ground; the structural reading places one ground and reads the names as tracking particulars within it.

*The burden.* Followed to the end, the five pressures pin down what the predicate *one* actually depends on. Cardinality presupposes distinguishability, and concrete distinguishability requires differentiating structure; an *exactly one* claim about a being lacking all such structure depends on the very resource it withdraws. Simplicity secures uniqueness by removing what *exactly two* would have needed, but the move converts the *one* into a transcendental consistent with no determinate count of the kind. Trinitarian threeness-with-substantial-oneness requires asymmetric relations of origin, and asymmetry is the structural feature of T; the eternal-relations reply preserves the asymmetry in a non-temporal register the classical bundle must show can carry directed order. Two distinct modal structures raise a meta-level individuation problem: whatever differentiates them—relation, order, or primitive thisness—is structure within the complete account of Reality; if nothing differentiates them, there are not two. The inference is deductive within Structural Individuation. A pluralist may reject that premise, but can’t retain it while positing a concrete plurality with no differentiating structure. Theological pluralism registers the multiplicity at the level of names while leaving the *what makes the names answer to many concrete ultimates* unaddressed. What the predicate *one* survives as, after the five pressures have run, is at least the integrated unity of the modal frame—not the cardinality of a being lacking the structural conditions of cardinality, but the unity-of-structure that *frame* names.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Cardinality Presupposes Distinguishability** · *Diagnostic*

*One* is a cardinality claim, and a cardinality claim presupposes distinguishability: to fix a being as exactly one is to hold the resource by which a second would have differed. Location, temporal trajectory, and material constitution are ordinary resources, and primitive thisness is a proposed nonqualitative one; whichever does the work is differentiating structure. Simplicity secures *exactly one* by removing what *exactly two* would have needed, which buys uniqueness by converting the count into a transcendental consistent with no determinate count of the kind. The frame meets no such difficulty. Whatever makes a second concrete structure second belongs to the complete structure of Reality; if nothing does, there is no second. That inference is deductive given Structural Individuation, and a primitivist may decline the premise, but declining it withholds assent rather than furnishing a countermodel.

**Depends on:** Structural Individuation (§2.4.9)

*The reclamation.* Unity genuinely applies to Nature as the integration of its structural conditions. Numerical uniqueness follows within the independently defended Structural Individuation premise: whatever differentiates candidate concrete totalities belongs to the complete structure of the all-inclusive Reality, while an alleged plurality with no differentiator is no plurality. A primitivist who denies that premise remains a premise-level rival. *One Nature* therefore names the unity of the framework within which occupancy and exchange occur. It doesn’t identify that framework with the personal God of monotheism, since agency, cognition, and value would still have to be added and defended. Spinoza’s *deus sive natura* (*Ethics* Spinoza (1677) 1996, I, Props. 14–15, 29) marks one way to make that further identification; the structural account doesn’t inherit it merely by reaching one necessary frame. The remaining question is how a necessary structure hosts contingent configurations, which is taken up at §4.7.

### 11.2.3 Infinity

The tradition calls God *infinite*: unlimited, unbounded, without measure. Quantitative infinity is always infinity along a magnitude, number, degree, or intensity. Classical divine infinity is offered instead as non-quantitative absence of ontological limitation, so that analogical sense has to be assessed, without assuming the quantitative one exhausts the term. In its familiar uses, infinity is a fact about a magnitude with no greatest, a series that doesn’t terminate, a scale that runs on without end. The [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary), though, has no magnitude (it is immaterial), no number (it is one and simple), no parts to be many, no degrees of more-and-less (simplicity admits no composition of intensities). Strip away every dimension along which a thing could be unbounded, and the question presses: infinite in *what*?

Classical theology makes infinity a [divine perfection](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary): God is *infinitus*, without limit, and the tradition is careful about the sense. God isn’t infinite in magnitude or quantity: Aquinas follows Aristotle in holding an actual infinite magnitude impossible, so divine infinity is neither spatial nor numerical bulk (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.7.1–4; cf. Aristotle, *Physics* (4th c. BCE) 1984, III). Divine infinity is infinity *of being*: God’s act of existing (*esse*) is unlimited because it isn’t received in, and so not contracted by, any matter or essence that would bound it, a form unlimited by reception. Where a finite being’s existing is limited by the essence that receives it, God’s existing is its essence and is subject to no such limit; God holds the whole perfection of being without restriction. Infinity, so understood, is the negative face of the divine fullness: *in-finite*, not-bounded, because there is nothing outside God to bound God. The doctrine keeps the believer’s intuition that God exceeds every creature without measure, and binds it to the unlimited perfection of being rather than to any quantity.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test what the doctrine means by *infinite* once it must specify what the infinity is of. What presses beneath them is that unboundedness has content only relative to a dimension, and the classical God is defined to have none.

**Q1.** *If God has no magnitude, no number, and no degree, what is God infinite in?* To be infinite is to be unbounded along a dimension: a magnitude with no greatest, a count with no last, a scale with no ceiling. The classical God is defined without any of them, so with every dimension of unboundedness removed, *infinite* has no variable to range over. If no positive account of unlimited *esse* is supplied, the predicate risks becoming merely negative. That is a determinacy burden, not yet a category mistake, because the Thomist explicitly denies that divine infinity is a magnitude.

**Q2.** *If God’s infinity is unlimited being rather than unlimited size, what is the more-and-less of being along which God is the maximum?* The tradition’s best move relocates infinity from quantity to *esse*, and refuses to concede that this names a scale at all. Infinity of being, on the Thomist account, is a *negative* determination: God’s *esse* is unlimited not because it tops some dimension of intensity but because it is unreceived, not contracted by an essence that would bound it (*ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.7.1). Unboundedness here is the *absence* of a limiting receiver, not a maximal rung on a ladder of more-and-less, so the demand “unbounded along what?” is said to misfire. It is the reply the doctrine leans on here, and it has already been run to its end (§11.2.1).

*Esse* unreceived by any essence is *ipsum esse subsistens*, and what that construal delivers is fixed at §11.2.1: an act of existing with no receiving essence has no determinate kind-content, no what-it-is, nothing but the bare that-it-is. Press the infinity-claim through that result. Either the unreceived *esse* has determinate content (it is *this* plenitude and not another, full in *these* respects rather than those) and that content is contrastive, a being thus-and-not-otherwise, which reinstates the contrastive differentiation the negation was meant to avoid; or it has no determinate content, and then its property-list is the one assigned to the Null State at §2.7, so “infinite being” names not the maximum of being but ∅. The negative determination doesn’t slip the fork; it inherits it. What is unbounded in the one respect the structural account secures (limited by nothing outside because there is no outside) is Nature, within which bound and measure are defined at all.

**Q3.** *If infinity is a positive intrinsic mode rather than a negation, what is a mode a mode of?* Duns Scotus declines the account the second question has just pressed, and what he puts in its place is the more resilient position. Where the Thomist reads *in-finite* as a negative determination, unbounded because unreceived, Scotus holds divine infinity to be *positive*: intensive infinity is a perfection in its own right rather than the absence of a bound (Scotus, *Ordinatio* I.2.1.1–2) (Duns Scotus (c. 1300) 1987; Cross 2005). Nor is it a further form added to being, which would cost simplicity, but an *intrinsic mode* (*modus intrinsecus*), the manner or degree in which being is had, as the intensity of a whiteness isn’t a second form laid over the whiteness but the way that whiteness is. *Infinite being* is on this account the simplest and most perfect concept available of God, more proper than *first cause* or *highest good* because it is absolute rather than relative to creatures, and the division of being into finite and infinite runs prior to any division into categories.

The move is a real advance on the negative route, and it advances by diagnosing correctly: a merely negative *infinite* leaves the predicate without content, and Scotus supplies content instead of resting on the negation. What it doesn’t do is pass outside the fork, because it takes the first horn deliberately and says the horn is habitable. An intrinsic mode is contrastive by construction. The division of being into finite and infinite is a division, and the model offered for it is *intensive degree*, which is a more-and-less as stated. The Scotist therefore secures determinate content for divine infinity by seating infinity within an ordering: a respect along which infinite and finite being stand, a difference between positions along it, and a being whose existing is had in this mode rather than another. Determinate order, difference, and something bearing them are what the account spends to get its content. Whether those thin roles upgrade to the three Conditions in type is a further step and isn’t taken here; what the question settles is narrower and enough, that the determinacy the Scotist rightly demands is purchased structurally rather than granted free of structure.

The compatibility with simplicity carries the same charge. Intrinsic modes sit alongside a partless essence, for Scotus, only through the formal distinction, and what that distinction concedes has already been weighed (§10.2.1): a distinction real but inseparable, holding a directed order between what it distinguishes, is the paradigm of a structured structure rather than an exemption from one. Scotus is right that infinity has to be positive if it is to say anything. The positive content arrives with structure attached.

**Q4.** *If no completed actual infinite is possible, how is God an actual infinite, and if God’s is merely potential or qualitative, in what does it exceed the finite?* The theistic tradition that presses the impossibility of a completed actual infinite to argue for a beginning of the world (Craig 1979) can’t then help itself to a completed actual infinite in the divine being without strain. The charge must be stated precisely or it equivocates: what that tradition forbids is an actual infinite *magnitude or multitude* (an infinite of quantity), and the actual infinite is defended on exactly that quantitative terrain against the Kalām at §10.1.5. Divine infinity, the Thomist rightly answers, was never quantitative (the first question), so the prohibition doesn’t reach it directly. The remaining question is whether “unlimited being” has intelligible non-scalar content; failure to provide it would make the predicate obscure, but it wouldn’t revive the mathematics of completed multitudes. If it is merely potential, it is a never-completed limit, the infinity of a process rather than of a perfect being. And if it is “qualitative,” the second question returns unanswered: qualitative along what?

**Q5.** *If God’s infinity just is God’s simple essence, what tells it apart from finitude?* On simplicity (§11.2.1), infinity isn’t a feature added to the essence but the essence itself. Yet the marks by which the infinite is told from the finite (the finite can be exceeded, added to, bounded; the infinite can’t) are all marks along a dimension, and a partless essence standing on no dimension of more-and-less bears none of them. Where there is no scale at all, *infinite* and *finite* lose their contrast together, exactly as §11.2.1 finds a simple essence admitting no internal differentiation losing the contrasts identity needs. An infinity that differs from finitude in no specifiable respect is *infinite* in name only.

*The burden.* Taken in order, the five pressures settle what *infinite* depends on. Infinity is unboundedness along a dimension; remove every dimension and the predicate has nothing to range over. Relocating infinity from magnitude to being doesn’t escape this: *more-and-less of esse* is itself a scale, and the negative-determination reply forks, by §11.2.1, into contrastive content or ∅. The positive route does better and pays openly: reading infinity as an intrinsic mode rather than as a negation supplies the content the negation lacked, and supplies it by seating infinity in an ordering of degree, with the formal distinction that reconciles the mode with simplicity conceding a structured structure of its own (§10.2.1). The tradition’s own anti-infinitism forbids a completed actual divine infinite of quantity, and the retreats to potential or qualitative infinity either reintroduce process or reopen the demand for a dimension. And an infinity identical with a partless, scaleless essence loses its contrast with finitude altogether. What *infinite* survives as, once the pressures have run, is unboundedness along some specified respect. Nature’s non-exteriority is one such respect; it isn’t thereby metric infinity, temporal unboundedness, or qualitative plenitude, and it isn’t the infinite personal God.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Unboundedness Requires a Dimension** · *Diagnostic*

Infinity is unboundedness along a dimension, so the predicate carries content only where there is something for it to range over. The classical God is specified as having no magnitude, no number, no parts, and no degrees, which withdraws every dimension at once. Both relocations available to the doctrine restore what was withdrawn or lose the content. The negative reading, taking infinity as unreceived *esse*, forks into determinate contrastive content, which reinstates differentiation, or into no determinate content at all. The positive reading, taking infinity as an intrinsic mode, secures the content by seating infinity within an ordering of degree and holds it compatible with simplicity through a distinction that concedes a structured structure. What is bounded by nothing outside, in the respect the structural account secures, is the conditions within which bound and measure are defined.

**Depends on:** The Discriminating-Content Burden (§11.2.1) and §2.7

*The reclamation.* Infinity requires a respect in which something is unbounded. Nature has no spatially external container, but that non-exteriority doesn’t establish that physical space is metrically infinite, that time has no first or last moment, or that Nature possesses the qualitative plenitude classical theology attributes to God. A positive account of divine infinity may remain coherent if it specifies the respect and truth conditions involved; it then carries determinate order and contrast rather than escaping all articulation. What genuinely relocates is only non-exteriority: no boundary can place Nature inside a more comprehensive concrete Nature. Calling that *infinity* is an analogy, not an identity between Nature and the infinite personal God.

### 11.2.4 Perfection

The inference from graded creatures to a maximum as an existence proof is engaged at §10.1.7; perfection is taken up here once a divine bearer is already on the table. Perfection is the attribute behind all the others: God as the greatest conceivable being, each good quality maxed out. Two problems surface. If God is the *standard* of perfection, nothing else can be perfect in the same sense; but a *perfect maker* should produce perfect work, and creation isn’t perfect. And the maxed-out qualities resist composition—each proposed fix must show it can reconcile two of them without weakening a third. If the broad classical bundle isn’t possibly co-instantiated, the ontological argument’s possibility premise is blocked at the point of entry for that bundle; Plantinga’s narrower definition of maximal greatness is a further question.

Classical theology assigns God the meta-attribute of perfection: that-than-which-no-greater-can-be-conceived, with each great-making property held to apply to maximum degree (Anselm of Canterbury (1078) 1998, II; Morris 1991; Murphy 2017). Perfect-being theology functions as the methodological engine producing the attributes the chapter has examined (§11.1). The doctrine binds *perfectus* to *completus*: that which lacks nothing it could have, that which has every property the having of which would constitute a greater being (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.4; Anselm of Canterbury (1078) 1998, V). On a contemporary refinement, perfection is the meta-attribute by which the great-making properties are selected and assembled: each property is included if having it constitutes greatness; the maximal assembly is the divine essence (Morris 1991; Hoffman and Rosenkrantz 2002; Speaks 2018). Perfection is also, on the tradition, the *standard* of perfection in lower beings: a creature is perfect insofar as it participates in the [divine perfection](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary), which it does in the analogical sense Aquinas’s *analogia entis* develops (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.4.3) and Cajetan after him (Velde 1995; Long 2011). The doctrine preserves the believer’s intuition that God is what greatness names by binding the standard and the bearer in one being: God is perfect by being what perfection is.

*The interrogation.* Five questions draw the doctrine up short of what it can answer. What sits underneath them is structural, the bind between standard and bearer: if God is the standard of perfection, then perfection is by-reference-to-God; if God is also the perfect creator, then the creator’s perfection should propagate into creation.

**Q1.** *If God is a perfect maker, why is creation not perfect?* If God is the *standard* of perfection (that against which all perfection is measured) then perfection is by-reference-to-God, and nothing outside God can be perfect *in the same sense*. A perfect creator need not produce a creation perfect in every respect: the aim may be a finite order, valuable freedom, or goods requiring vulnerability and development. The sharper question is whether this particular creation is proportionate to the creator’s stated aims and whether its evils are compatible with perfect goodness and competence. No simple propagation principle settles that issue. The classical analogical move (creation is perfect “in its way,” not God’s way) either collapses into homonymy (the two senses share only a name) or smuggles in a univocal core (in which case the exclusivity horn revives).

The *analogia entis* machinery Cajetan inherits (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.13; Velde 1995) runs into exactly this dilemma; it doesn’t escape it. Hartshorne’s dual-transcendence doctrine (Hartshorne 1941) dissolves the standard/bearer dilemma at the level of the framing: God transcends all creatures in the abstract pole’s invariant excellence, and surpasses God’s own prior states in the concrete pole’s growing actualization. Neither horn of Q1 applies straightforwardly, because the abstract pole isn’t a bearer that propagates perfection into creation, and the concrete pole isn’t a static standard but a growing excellence that always exceeds its prior state. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3: the two forms of transcendence (invariant excellence over creatures; growing excellence over prior states) are attributable to one subject only through the relation between the poles, and that relation is shown at §10.3.3 to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles.

The single perfection-predicate is borne, if at all, by a subject whose pole-relation instantiates those conditions rather than escaping them. Swinburne’s theistic personalism offers a different handle on Q1 (Swinburne 1979; Swinburne 2004): divine perfection isn’t the metaphysical attribute of a being at the apex of the *analogia entis* but the feature that makes theism the simplest explanatory hypothesis. An infinitely powerful, omniscient, free person is the simplest causal explanation for the universe’s existence because a person without physical complexity, spatial location, or temporal constraints on the will is the least arbitrary explanatory posit. On Swinburne’s account, *perfect* is as much a methodological as an ontological term: it names the simplicity-of-nature that makes the theistic hypothesis maximally parsimonious. The concern for the Swinburnian recasting is whether simplicity-of-nature for an explanatory agent escapes the analysis of what any possible explanatory ground requires.

**Q2.** *How do God’s maxed-out qualities fit together, if reconciling any two weakens a third?* Perfect-being theology assembles God’s attributes by selecting each great-making property and holding that God has each to maximum degree. Whether the maxima compose coherently into a single being has been the central battleground of the literature: Mackie (Mackie 1955), Sobel (Sobel 2004), and Oppy (Oppy 1995; Oppy 2006) press the incompossibility cases. These include: omnipotence vs. omniscience (the freedom-and-foreknowledge problem); omnibenevolence vs. omnipotence (the problem of evil); immutability vs. responsiveness (the prayer problem); aseity vs. relatedness; and the stones-too-heavy-to-lift classics. The classical replies attempt either to refine the great-making properties so that the alleged incompatibilities dissolve (Plantinga 1974 on free will and foreknowledge; Stump 2010 on suffering and love) or to argue that the apparent incompatibilities reflect inadequate understandings of the properties (Adams 1999; Murphy 2017). Some refinements relax a traditional property; others clarify its content or deny a contested entailment. The dialectical task is to test each repair rather than assume that every reconciliation is a weakening: the maximally-knowing being on the open-theist refinement doesn’t know what creatures will freely do until they do it; the maximally-loving being on Stump’s refinement is constrained by what creaturely natures can receive; the maximally-good being on the free-will-defense refinement permits suffering its omnipotence could prevent. The three repairs just named each purchase composition by relaxation, and each relaxation moves the bearer further from what the driving premise was designed to produce.

Hartshorne’s dipolar account addresses the composition problem directly: the great-making properties do compose for the dipolar God, because the abstract pole handles the invariant, necessary great-making dimensions (formal omniscience of necessary truths, necessary existence, eternal simplicity) while the concrete pole handles the relational and growth-admitting dimensions: responsive knowing of contingents, cumulative benevolence, aesthetic agency. On the dipolar account, the apparent incompatibilities that drive the classical composition problem dissolve, because each horn of each incompatibility (immutability vs. responsiveness; aseity vs. relatedness; impassibility vs. love) is assigned to a different pole. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3: the relation between the poles is a directed dependence, requiring an ordering between abstract and concrete aspects, a carrier of both, and the relational structure in which they are aspects of one being. The composition problem the dipolar God was meant to solve reappears at the level of the composite.

Swinburne’s cumulative-case framework (Swinburne 1979; Swinburne 2004) reframes the composition question: the relevant test for the composition of great-making properties isn’t metaphysical co-instantiation in a single infinite being but whether the composite makes theism simpler and more explanatorily powerful than the naturalistic alternative. Swinburne argues that a perfectly free, omniscient, omnipotent person is a simpler hypothesis than the initial state of a purely physical universe, because simplicity for a person is the absence of constraints on the will, and a person unconstrained by physical complexity, spatial location, or temporal structure is as simple as any explanatory posit can be. The concern here is whether the absence of physical constraints constitutes the kind of simplicity relevant to the analysis: a person unconstrained by physical structure still requires the structural conditions that make personhood (agency, knowledge, will) coherent predicates.

**Q3.** *What is the most loving or most beautiful, if there is no greatest such thing to reach?* Some great-making properties admit a clear notion of maximum (e.g., omnipotence as the property of being able to do every possible thing). Others don’t: maximal beauty, maximal love, maximal wisdom. What is the maximum of these? Morris (Morris 1991), Murphy (Murphy 2017), and Plantinga (Plantinga 1974, ch. 10) defend the notion of *intuitive maxima*: the maximum is whatever the great-making property’s content requires; if the content doesn’t admit a maximum, the property isn’t strictly great-making. The concern here is that this defense secures the maxima by stipulating that any property without a clear maximum is excluded from the great-making list, which converts the driving premise from *select the great-making properties and maximize them* into *select the maximizable properties and call those the great-making ones*. The exclusion is the structural concern: a perfect being on the resulting account is perfect in the maximizable dimensions only, which leaves open whether the bearer is perfect *simpliciter* or perfect *in those respects in which perfection admits a maximum*.

**Q4.** *How can the greatest possible being hold every perfection, if each one needs conditions God is said to lack?* The attributes examined so far each carry structural conditions the classical bundle places outside the divine being. The driving premise that produces the attribute list is the perfect-being engine. The concern here at the level of the driving premise is that the very procedure for selecting the divine attributes produces, when run consistently, an attribute set the bearer can’t bear: the great-making property *necessary existence* requires structural necessity, the great-making property *omnipresence* requires position, the great-making property *omniscience* requires tensed knowledge, the great-making property *creative power* requires directed transition. The driving premise is faithful to what greatness names; the bearer is defined as lacking the structural conditions of every great-making property the driving premise produces. Running the driving premise to completion is what produced the inversions.

Hartshorne agrees that running the classical perfect-being engine to completion produces contradictions, and proposes an alternative dipolar engine: start not with the negation of all structural conditions but with a bifurcated attribution (invariant formal excellence to the abstract pole, maximal responsive creativity to the concrete pole) and let each pole’s great-making properties be selected relative to its pole’s structural register. The dipolar engine is designed to produce a being that doesn’t generate the inversions; it selects its great-making properties with the composition problem in view. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3: a being with two poles standing in irreducible relation is, on structural analysis, two relata in a directed dependence, and that relation is shown at §10.3.3 to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. The dipolar engine produces an entity that instantiates the structural roles rather than one beyond them.

**Q5.** *By what standard is God perfect—God’s own, or one beyond God?* The tradition has resisted this move on the ground that any standard external to God would be a constraint on God, which is incompatible with aseity. The contemporary literature has pressed alternatives. Murphy (Murphy 2017) and Speaks (Speaks 2018) defend a methodological perfect-being theology that takes the great-making properties as what the religious life requires of a worship-worthy being, rather than as what the bearer is the standard of. The *Euthyphro*-style move locates the standard in something other than God’s will: Adams (Adams 1999), Murphy (Murphy 2002), and Wielenberg (Wielenberg 2014) explore the options for moral perfection. The concern here is that each move that locates the standard outside God admits the structural feature the classical doctrine refused: a standard outside God is a feature of Reality not identical with God, which is what aseity denies. The methodological refinements register, rather than resolve, the structural concern: the standard against which the great-making properties are great is a structural feature of what greatness *is*, and *what greatness is* is a fact about the structure of value within Reality rather than a property of any one bearer.

*The burden.* Worked through, the five pressures spell out what the predicate *perfect* actually depends on. Perfection is either by-reference-to-the-bearer (in which case nothing else can be perfect in the same sense, and the perfect maker’s perfection can’t propagate into creation) or by-reference-to-a-standard (in which case the standard is structural and the bearer is at most an instance of it). The analogical reply collapses into homonymy or smuggles in a univocal core. The surveyed reconciliations compose the great-making properties only by relaxation, and each relaxation moves the bearer further from what the driving premise was designed to produce. Maximal degrees are specifiable for some great-making properties and not others, and the resulting engine selects the maximizable properties rather than the great-making ones. Running the driving premise to completion produces an attribute set the bearer can’t bear, since the structural conditions of each great-making property are what the bearer is defined as lacking. Locating the standard outside the bearer admits the structural feature aseity refused. After the five pressures, perfection remains a value-laden completeness notion whose compossibility and standard require defense. It can’t be reduced without argument to the modal property of being necessary.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Maximizing Leaves No Bearer** · *Diagnostic*

Perfect-being theology fixes each attribute by maximizing a great-making property, and the attributes the chapter has examined are its output. Two demands fall on the driving premise and aren’t met together. The standard has to be located, and both placements cost: by reference to the bearer, nothing else is perfect in the same sense, and the perfect maker’s perfection doesn’t propagate into the making; by reference to a standard, the standard is a structural fact about what greatness is, and the bearer is an instance of it rather than its source. The maxima then have to compose, and the reconciliations surveyed compose them only by relaxation, each relaxation carrying the bearer further from what the driving premise was built to deliver, while maximal degrees are specifiable for some great-making properties and not for others, so that the driving premise selects the maximizable rather than the great-making. Run to completion it yields an attribute set whose structural conditions the bearer is defined as lacking. The bearing on the modal ontological argument is conditional and no wider: if the bundle isn’t possibly co-instantiated, the possibility premise is blocked and the S5 inference doesn’t run. Objections to the broad classical bundle don’t by themselves reach the narrower maximal greatness Plantinga defines.

**Depends on:** Greatness (§11.1) and Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* One component genuinely relocates: Nature is structurally complete in the sense that no exterior condition remains for it to borrow. That is necessity and non-exteriority under another description. It isn’t moral perfection, excellence, beauty, fitting activity, or worship-worthiness. Calling Nature *perfect* would therefore obscure more than it clarifies unless the restricted structural sense is stated each time. Perfect-being theology adds the evaluative claim that the maximized bundle is good and compossible in one subject. The modal core supplies neither premise. The result is a burden on the bundle and its standard, not a proof that Nature is the standard of every lesser perfection. Nor does it strand the evaluative sense. Excellence, fitting activity, and the judgment that a thing has been well made are exercised by beings who can tell better from worse and care which of the two they produce. Perfection in that sense isn’t a possession but a direction, and the ones facing it are us.

The analysis carries a direct implication for the modal ontological argument. Plantinga’s (Plantinga 1974) S5 argument moves from the possibility of maximal greatness to its necessary instantiation in every world: if it is possible that maximal greatness is instantiated, and maximal greatness includes necessary existence, then by S5 maximal greatness is instantiated in every possible world. The argument’s pressures challenge the compossibility of a broad classical-theist bundle. Plantinga’s modal ontological argument itself defines maximal excellence through omnipotence, omniscience, and moral perfection, with maximal greatness adding necessary existence; atemporality, impassibility, and immutability are additional doctrines. Objections to the broader bundle therefore don’t by themselves establish that Plantinga’s narrower definition is impossible. If the bundle isn’t possibly co-instantiated, Plantinga’s first premise is blocked at the point of entry, and the S5 inference doesn’t run. The result is carried forward at §11.10.

## 11.3 Aseity and Modal Standing
This cluster gathers the attributes that fix God’s self-existence and modal-temporal standing: necessity (§11.3.1), eternity (§11.3.2), immutability (§11.3.3), and impassibility (§11.3.4). Each says how the divine being stands to time, change, and dependence: that God exists of itself, outside succession, beyond alteration, and unaffected from without. Whether a necessary, changeless, or timeless being can be the *ground* of Nature has been asked already (§10.1.4, §10.2.3). What is asked here is what these attributes contribute to *greatness*: whether necessity, eternity, and changelessness, said of such a being, leave the predicates of knowing, acting, and responding any determinate content.

Pressed, each owes an account of the structural conditions it was meant to escape: necessary existence, timeless standing, changelessness, and unaffectedness, said of a being that knows, acts, and responds, can’t be specified without accounting for the succession, persistence, and exchange that the three Conditions name. Impassibility (§11.3.4) is a boundary-crossing: classified here by attribute-type, its inversion runs on the reach-arm, where contact between God and Nature is tested (§11.8).

### 11.3.1 Necessity
God, the tradition says, doesn’t merely happen to exist. God exists necessarily: in every possible world, unable to be otherwise. Necessity of that kind is first a feature of the modal structure any world must have, not something that can be pinned to a being defined as standing apart from that structure. What the earlier argument has shown to be necessary is Nature itself: the conditions under which any world could count as a world. That doesn’t by itself prove that no further necessary being exists, and the frame’s status doesn’t transfer to a personal inhabitant. The question is what *necessary* still means once those two moves are refused.

The classical doctrine of divine necessity assembles several reinforcing claims. God exists in every possible world (Anselm of Canterbury (1078) 1998, II–III; Plantinga 1974; Hartshorne 1962). God exists *a se*: not depending on anything else for divine being (Anselm, *Monologion* 6) (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.3.4; Pruss 2011). God is the *ens necessarium*, the being whose non-existence is incoherent (Leibniz (1714) 1989, §§38–45; Leibniz 1710). The same modal status is developed in the Islamic *falsafa* tradition by Avicenna’s distinction between *wajib al-wujud* (necessary existence) and *mumkin al-wujud* (possible existence) in the *Kitab al-Shifa* (McGinnis 2010; Adamson 2013), with the *wajib*‘s necessity made the ground of the *mumkin*‘s possibility. On a contemporary refinement, God grounds the modal structure itself: there are no possibilities prior to God for God to range over (Leftow, *God and Necessity* 2012; cf. Morris and Menzel 1986 on theistic activism). Each move tries to keep necessity from being a feature borrowed from elsewhere by a being whose excellence might otherwise have been contingent. Carried to its limit, the doctrine reaches for a being whose non-existence is held to be incoherent precisely because the being’s existence is held to be what makes coherence possible to detect at all.

*The interrogation.* Eight questions test what an account of divine necessity must explain. What runs underneath all eight is structural, modal invariance (§2.1.4–§2.1.5): modal status doesn’t vary across worlds. What is necessary is necessarily necessary; what is possible is necessarily possible; what is impossible is necessarily impossible. A modal structure isn’t the kind of thing whose status another agent or being could fix. The S5 framework on which the necessity operator runs here is defended for metaphysical-modal scope at §1.1 and §2.1.3. The possible worlds the operator ranges over are read here in actualist terms: ways the one actual Nature could be configured, the alternatives grounded in the three structural Conditions rather than in concrete Lewisian worlds standing alongside it, in merely abstract ersatz constructions, or in primitive potentiality; the alternatives are alternatives of Nature, not parallel universes beside it. The eight pressures run three at the level of the predicate, five at the level of the conditions necessity-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *In which possible worlds does the ground of all possible worlds exist?* Modal predicates can apply non-trivially to an invariant subject: necessary beings, propositions, and mathematical objects are standard candidates. The sharper issue is whether God is represented within the modal domain or proposed as its ground, and how those two roles relate. A modal subject is a coordinate of modal space: existing in some worlds and not others (contingent), in every world (necessary), or in no world (impossible). The classical doctrine wants God to be a modal subject as necessary in every world while defining God as outside the modal structure, as the being whose existence makes that structure possible at all (Leftow 2012; Pruss 2011). Wanting both at once is the structural difficulty itself.
