If God is constitutive of the modal structure, then God’s existence isn’t a coordinate over which the operator ranges; it is a part of the apparatus that makes ranging possible.

The verdict the operator returns is then degenerate: trivially-true (every world is God-grounded) or trivially-false (no world contains God as an element of its furniture), with neither tracking the informative modal claim the believer’s intuition reaches for. The believer who says *God could have existed* (or its negation, *God couldn’t have failed to exist*) is making a modal claim about a being whose existence is alleged to be the precondition of any *could*. The claim can’t be both a substantive modal predication and a claim about the precondition of modal predication without trading on the very ambiguity the predicate was supposed to settle. The mathematical analogue is instructive: *possibly 2+2=4* collapses harmlessly into the truth claim itself because mathematical truth is itself the abstract overlay of what quantitative event-modality supports, and the operator’s trivialization preserves the content. For God’s existence the trivialization is the cost: the believer wants the operator to do substantive work, and the doctrine has removed what the operator could substantively track. The line of treating divine necessity as ontological independence (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018) preserves the verbal *necessary* by relocating it to aseity (Q4); the line of grounding modality in God (Leftow 2012; Morris and Menzel 1986) applies the predicate at the level whose conditions it presupposes (Q6). The present pressure runs prior to both: before asking whether necessity-as-aseity or necessity-as-frame-grounding can do the work, the question is whether the modal predicates apply to God at all. The seven pressures that follow proceed under the assumption (granted for the sake of the argument) that the predicates do apply, and test what each application still tracks.

**Q2.** *If all the proof shows is that something exists in every world, what makes it a being rather than the structure?* Anselm’s *id quo maius cogitari nequit* (*Proslogion* II) reasons that the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality, since existence-in-reality exceeds existence-in-the-understanding alone. Gaunilo’s island and Kant’s predicate-objection are well-known; Plantinga’s (Plantinga 1974) modal recasting, anticipated by a decade in Hartshorne’s revival of the modal ontological argument (*Anselm’s Discovery* Hartshorne 1965), the structural ancestor of the modern form, answers them at the level of the predicate by treating necessary existence as instantiation in every possible world rather than as a real property added to a thing. The recasting is genuinely available, and the formal validity of S5 ontological arguments isn’t in question. What is in question is the being the argument’s conclusion picks out. Plantinga’s premise (it is possible that maximal greatness is instantiated) entails, in S5, that maximal greatness is instantiated in every world. Maximal greatness doesn’t name whatever is instantiated in every world; it includes maximal excellence—omniscience, omnipotence, and moral perfection—across every world. Showing that the three Conditions are invariant wouldn’t show that they satisfy those personal predicates. The argument has shown that something modally invariant must obtain. It hasn’t yet shown that the modally invariant something bears the personal predicates maximal greatness includes; invariance alone fits Nature as readily as the being the doctrine names.

**Q3.** *If ‘exists in every world’ is a fact about the worlds, what has it told you about God?* Kant’s (Kant (1781) 1998) objection has been treated as resolved by the modal recasting. The resolution is only partial. Existence in every possible world can be treated as a de re modal property of a subject as well as represented by a fact about the modal landscape. The live question is whether the subject is coherently specified and whether its necessity is explained rather than whether the grammar permits de re predication. Pruss and Rasmussen (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018) and Leftow (Leftow 2012) argue that necessary existence is properly construed as ontological independence rather than as cross-world ubiquity, and so escapes the Kantian concern at a different level. The reply rephrases necessity as aseity (treated at Q4) and so shifts the locus rather than answering the original question. Even granting the de re reading, the informative content of the predicate lies not in an additional way the being is but in the relation between the being and the modal structure. The distinction is de re / de dicto: the modal-structure necessity affirmed here is de dicto of Nature (necessarily, Nature obtains) and de re of its conditions (each of the three Conditions is such that it necessarily obtains) while no de re necessity attaches to a being specified apart from the modal structure. The same point is pressed from the side of identity at §11.2.1, Q3; here it returns from the side of necessity itself.

**Q4.** *If aseity just means depending on nothing, what can it ground?* The classical reading of divine aseity (being-from-itself, *a se*) holds that God depends on nothing for divine being (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.3.4). The doctrine is sometimes pressed into service as the ground of divine necessity: God exists necessarily because God exists *a se*. The concern here is that aseity, fully stated, is the negation of every dependence, not a positive ground from which existence flows. To exist *a se* is to fail to depend, and a failure to depend isn’t yet a positive explanatory base. What grounds the necessity, on the doctrine, is asked for and not delivered: aseity tells us what God isn’t (dependent), without telling us what makes God’s existence not-otherwise. The analysis here points, in answer, to Nature: the three Conditions don’t depend on anything else, because there is no anything-else for them to depend on: Nature is the condition for there being something rather than nothing for any subsequent dependence to obtain within. Aseity, on this reading, is the negative shadow of Nature’s positive role, the same fact Subsistent Grounding (§2.9.3) states from the positive side: not one thing failing to depend, but three holding each other up.

**Q5.** *What makes creation contingent, if God’s act is God’s necessary nature?* If God’s nature is necessarily what it is, and God’s act is identical with God’s nature (divine simplicity read strictly), then God’s act is necessarily what it is, and what God’s act produces is necessarily what God’s act produces (Mullins 2013; Mullins 2016; Tomaszewski 2019). Creation collapses into necessity.

The classical reply distinguishes God’s act-in-itself from the act’s *terminus ad extra*, holding the act necessary while leaving the terminus contingent (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.19; Stump 2003; Dolezal 2017). The reply preserves the contingency of creation by introducing a structured relation between act and effect that the doctrine of strong simplicity is supposed to disallow. The concern here is that the more strictly simplicity is held, the more sharply the modal collapse follows; the more relaxedly simplicity is held, the more the doctrine has surrendered the ground from which divine necessity was supposed to flow. The doctrine wants both—strict enough simplicity to ground necessity, loose enough simplicity to let creation be contingent—and these are two incompatible commitments joined only by the shared term.

Hartshorne’s dipolar account addresses the modal-collapse pressure directly: God’s abstract pole is necessarily and immutably what it is; the concrete pole actualizes contingently, responsive to the open alternatives creaturely co-creation supplies, and so provides the modal contrast creation requires without implicating the abstract pole in contingency. On the dipolar reading, the modal-collapse concern targets the abstract pole alone, and the concrete pole’s contingency is the structural resource the doctrine needed. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3 against dipolar theism generally: the abstract pole sustains the concrete pole’s act-relations only across the directed dependence between them, and that relation requires determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. The modal-collapse question doesn’t dissolve; it migrates from the necessity predicate to the abstract/concrete relation, where Process Theology (§10.3.3) records it as a standing account rather than a solution.

What makes the dilemma sharp also shows why the structural account isn’t caught by it. Necessity Permits Contingency (§2.9) holds that the necessity of the Conditions doesn’t compete with contingency but is the condition without which contingency could not obtain at all: □(T∧S∧Φ) ∧ (◇p ∧ ◇¬p). Reality retains its field-constituting Conditions under every evaluation while which configuration is enacted remains genuinely open. Necessity and contingency aren’t rationed against each other there, because they are predicated of different things—the frame, and what is arranged within it.

The doctrine’s trouble is that simplicity forces both onto one item. Necessity and contingency must attach to God’s single act, since strong simplicity leaves no second thing for either to attach to, and no distribution of one act between two modal statuses is available once the act is identical with the nature. Hartshorne’s dipolarity is precisely an attempt to buy back the second locus, which is why it works to the extent that it abandons simplicity. Relocating necessity to the structure doesn’t solve the problem for classical theism; it locates the problem in the insistence that the necessary ground be an individual rather than a structure.

**Q6.** *How do you ground possibility by an act, when acting already needs it?* Leftow’s (Leftow 2012) theistic activism presses this reply furthest. What is possible is grounded in divine activity; there are no possibilities prior to God for God’s selection to range over. The doctrine preserves divine sovereignty over the deepest layer the doctrine could reach. The structural concern is the one §11.7.2, Q7 raises at the level of agency: to ground a modal structure is to stand in an asymmetric explanatory relation to it. The relation requires determinate ground, grounded content, and direction; it need not be a temporal transition from ungrounded to grounded. To remove those conditions while preserving ground is to keep the verb and lose the structure that gave it its content. Pruss (Pruss 2011), Mullins (Mullins 2016), and others have raised structural concerns from inside the literature. The point added here is that the doctrine at that extension, when its predicates are read in the structure that supports them, points toward Nature rather than a being beyond it. Modal invariance is a structural fact about how possibility works, not a contingent product of any agent’s exercise. Pruss’s positive argument presses from the other side: that only an agent freely selecting among possibilities explains why one contingent cosmos is realized rather than another. Granted in full, the selecting it posits must distinguish alternatives and explain the contingent realization. A timeless-selection model avoids a temporal transition in God but still owes an account of differentiated alternatives and contingent effects. The contingent realization it seeks to explain is Nature’s own: the actual configuration among those the structure permits, which, on the structural account, calls for no selector standing outside the conditions any selecting would presuppose.

**Q7.** *By what logic does God author logic?* Descartes (Letters to Mesland Descartes 1644) extends divine sovereignty to the eternal truths themselves: God could have made 2+2=5, and God’s not having done so is a free divine choice. The Thomistic mainstream rejects the move (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.25.3) by indexing omnipotence to logical possibility—God can do whatever doesn’t involve contradiction, and *square circle* names no candidate for divine action because it names no candidate for anything. The contemporary literature (Swinburne 1977; Wierenga 1989; Plantinga 1980) sides decisively with the Thomistic restriction. The cost is that logical necessity is treated as a condition on divine action rather than a product of it, and the locus of the deepest necessity has moved beyond the being. The options include external constraint, grounding in divine nature, identity between divine rationality and logical truth, and voluntarist authorship. The latter faces the presupposition problem; the nature and identity accounts instead face explanatory circularity and content burdens.

**Q8.** *What makes one being necessary, if necessity belongs to the frame it sits in?* The phrase *necessary being* presupposes a contrast with contingent being and a category broad enough to contain both. Beings, on the contrast, range from those that might not have been to those that couldn’t fail to be, with the necessary case at one limit. The concern here is that the limit isn’t a maximally exalted being. It is a structural condition.

What can’t fail to be, when the modal verb is taken seriously, is what would have to be in place for any *could-have-been-otherwise* to be a coherent thought. Possibility presupposes a frame within which alternatives can be set against each other. The frame requires differentiation among alternatives, modal relations among them, and a domain or bearer of modal content, the roles the earlier machinery identifies as Space, Time, and Substance. Treating one being within the frame as the being of necessity in its highest form tries to import the modal status of the frame into one of its inhabitants. The status doesn’t transfer.

A second constraint holds whether or not the transfer is attempted, and it is separate from the first. Necessary Occupancy (§2.9) fixes what existing as a concrete individual consists in: to be temporally ordered, relationally situated, and borne as a determinate relatum. That isn’t an external requirement laid on beings from outside, and it is indifferent to whether the being in question is necessary or contingent—a necessary concrete individual occupies the structure exactly as a contingent one does, because occupancy is what concrete existence *is*, not a liability contingency incurs. So even a defender who resists the frame-to-inhabitant diagnosis, holding that this being’s necessity is intrinsic rather than borrowed, still owes concrete occupancy for it. The two moves close different exits: the first denies that the frame’s modal status can be inherited, the second denies that inheriting it would exempt the inheritor from occupying the frame.

Hartshorne’s dual-transcendence doctrine (*Man’s Vision of God* Hartshorne 1941) attempts to escape the transfer problem by bifurcating the necessity: the abstract pole carries modal invariance; the concrete pole carries contingent, responsive actuality; the same subject bears both by being the single reality whose abstract dimension is invariant and whose concrete dimension is what creaturely events contingently make it. The structural concern is the one pressed at §10.3.3: a single subject bears two irreducible modal statuses only by way of the relation between its poles, and that relation is the directed dependence shown at §10.3.3 to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles, the roles of the very frame whose status the transfer problem found couldn’t pass to an inhabitant. The bifurcation relocates the transfer problem into the pole-relation rather than escaping it.

*The burden.* Eight pressures surface what the predicate *necessary* actually runs on. Before it substantively applies at all, its subject has to be a coordinate of the alternation the operator ranges over: a being defined as a constituent of the modal structure rather than as a value within it isn’t a candidate for the modal verb. Invariance can characterize both a modal framework and entities represented as existing throughout it. The structural account must argue comparatively for Nature as the best ground of necessity rather than infer that no invariant entity can be necessary. The frame requires differentiation among alternatives, modal relations, and a domain or bearer of modal content. Calling these roles Space, Time, and Substance is a substantive identification that depends on the earlier machinery; possible worlds need not themselves be temporally ordered. Necessity is the modal status of these three in their joint operation. Two further conditions follow negatively. The not-otherwise of the necessary is what is in place, not what fails to obtain, so aseity construed as the bare negation of dependence doesn’t do the grounding work the doctrine asks of it. And whatever could author the modal structure appears to presuppose structural conditions only the frame itself can supply, which leaves agent-authored modality facing a presupposition problem at the level the doctrine’s modal extension reaches. The structural form of this reasoning replaces the Principle of Sufficient Reason rather than running through it: where strong PSR demands a sufficient reason for every contingent fact and weak PSR a possible one, the present account reads necessity from the conditions any *otherwise* presupposes. These aren’t optional supports the predicate could trade among. They are what the verb *necessarily* picks out when its referent is examined.

One rival reading of this result must be met, since it grants that something is modally invariant and presses only on its number. Aggregation arguments (Rasmussen 2009; Pruss and Rasmussen 2018) hold that multiple necessary foundations collapse into one, and so ask why the three Conditions aren’t three necessary beings whose constant co-occurrence requires a single ground to bind them (the structural form of monotheism) rather than one Nature. The first reply blocks binding understood as holding separable items together. There is no seam to bind: the three Conditions aren’t three separable necessities that happen to co-occur but are mutually constitutive (succession with nothing persistent to undergo it isn’t time, a persistent something with no interval to stand in isn’t substance, an interval with no succession across it isn’t a manifold), so their co-instantiation is internal and analytic, one structure under three descriptions rather than an arrangement an external ground maintains (§2.6.5). To ask what holds them against separation is to ask what holds a figure’s three-sidedness to its three-angledness: nothing does, because they are one fact differently stated.

A grounding refinement makes a different claim: the proposed ground need not act temporally or prevent the Conditions from coming apart, but may instead explain why their one structure obtains necessarily. That proposal isn’t identical with Nature merely because it is non-acting. It divides according to the relation it specifies. If the ground acts concretely, it operates in the three Conditions, a denizen of the Conditions rather than a ground above them, and by the transfer result (Q8) can’t simply inherit the frame’s necessity. If it supplies no determinate asymmetry, content, or explanatory relation beyond the Conditions’ standing co-obtaining, then it adds only a second label to Nature. If it supplies a determinate atemporal grounding relation, the proposal remains live at this step and inherits the grounding-contact burden: it must state how that relation confers or explains necessity without presupposing the modal structure being explained, and how any personal or intentional predicates attributed to the ground connect to the relation. A contingent ground can’t confer necessity merely by being invoked; a necessary ground must give independent content to its necessity rather than borrow the status of the frame. This is where the naturalist and monotheist readings finally diverge (§11.2.2): the present account reads the unity of the necessary as the triconditionality of one structure, while the monotheist proposes a further ground and assumes the corresponding contact burden.

A second rival reading presses not on the number of the necessary but on the contingent. Pruss’s cosmological argument from the Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact (the conjunction of all contingent truths, the actual cosmos with just these features and no others) holds that this conjunction is itself contingent and, on the Principle of Sufficient Reason, demands an explanation that can’t lie within it, terminating in a necessary being whose act explains why this conjunction obtains rather than another (Pruss and Rasmussen 2018). The argument is distinct from the aggregation just met: it asks not why the necessary foundations are one rather than three, but why the contingent whole is this one rather than another. The reply is the restricted Principle of Sufficient Reason already named. What the argument needs is the strong PSR (every contingent fact has a sufficient reason) and that is the principle the present account replaces rather than honors.

The necessary frame of the three Conditions is no member of the contingent conjunction and so isn’t among what the argument asks after: it is the type, it is necessary, and against the necessary the explanatory demand runs out of contrast, exactly as Q4 and §8.2.1 found. The particular configuration the conjunction records (this cosmos, these constants) is the token. The structural theorem doesn’t select it, but that nonselection alone doesn’t establish its contingency; the BCCF argument must independently warrant the alternative configurations it invokes. Its explanation is the cosmic-historical one developed at §4.7, not a selecting act by a being outside the frame, since any such selecting (Q6) runs on the very conditions the frame supplies. Pruss’s charge that a brute contingent whole is intolerable has force only against the strong PSR that generates it; under the restricted PSR any genuinely contingent token isn’t a necessity-demanding brute fact but a configuration the necessary frame permits and cosmic history fills in, and the regress of contingent explanation terminates not in a necessary being but in the necessary frame whose modes the token varies. The stopping point is marked, not helped to: the type is necessary, the token’s further modal status isn’t fixed by the type (§4.7).

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Not-Otherwise Is What Is in Place** · *Diagnostic*

Before *necessary* substantively applies to anything, its subject has to be a coordinate of the alternation the operator ranges over; a candidate defined as a constituent of the modal structure rather than as a value within it isn’t yet a candidate for the modal verb. The alternation itself requires differentiation among alternatives, modal relations among them, and a domain or bearer of modal content, and calling those three roles Space, Time, and Substance is a substantive identification resting on the earlier machinery rather than a reading off the roles. Two results then fall out negatively and hold on their own. The not-otherwise of the necessary is what is in place, not what fails to obtain, so aseity taken as the bare negation of dependence doesn’t perform the grounding the doctrine assigns it. And whatever could author the modal structure appears to presuppose structural conditions only the frame supplies, which leaves agent-authored modality facing a presupposition problem at the depth the doctrine’s fullest extension reaches. What isn’t established here is the stronger comparative claim: that no invariant entity could be necessary. Invariance can characterize a modal framework and can characterize an entity represented as existing throughout one, and choosing between them is an argument still owed.

**Depends on:** Modal Identity (§2.6.6)

*The reclamation.* Here the relocation is genuine. Necessity is the modal status of T, S, and Φ jointly: no possible world lacks the conditions under which it could count as a world. The etymological image of non-yielding illustrates the result but doesn’t derive it; □ still means truth throughout the relevant modal range. Nature’s necessity doesn’t by itself prove that no further necessary being exists, nor does the frame’s status transfer to a personal inhabitant. A God proposed as the ground rather than an inhabitant of modal space therefore faces a different task: to state what *necessary* means at that level and how the alleged ground relates to the structure whose necessity the earlier derivation has established.

### 11.3.2 Eternity

Classical theism places God wholly outside time, living all of time “at once.” But the things the believer’s God does (knowing what is happening now, responding to a prayer, acting at a moment) all need a before and an after. Placing God outside time keeps the word “eternal” but owes an account of how those acts reach the temporal order.

The classical doctrine of divine eternity assembles three reinforcing claims. God is *aeternus* in the strict Boethian sense: *interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio*, the simultaneous and complete possession of unbounded life (Boethius (524) 1969, V.6). God is atemporal: outside time, with no before, no after, no succession in the divine being itself (Augustine of Hippo (397–400) 1991, XI; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.10; Stump and Kretzmann 1981). On a contemporary refinement, the eternal life stands in eternal–temporal (ET) simultaneity with every temporal moment alike, with the eternal *now* equally adjacent to every creaturely *now* (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991; Rogers 2000; Helm 2010).

The competing tradition (divine sempiternity, everlastingness, omnitemporality) keeps God within time but extends the divine duration without limit (Wolterstorff 1975; Wolterstorff 2001; Hasker 1989; Mullins 2016; Craig 2001c; Craig 2001b). Craig combines the everlasting position with A-theoretic tense-realism (the tensed view on which the *now* is ontologically privileged and time genuinely passes) and with the Kalām cosmological argument’s reliance on a temporal beginning of the universe (“The Kalam Cosmological Argument” in *The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology* Craig and Sinclair 2009). The Kalām’s premise that the universe began to exist is taken up at §10.1.5, and the structure of the cosmological *beginning* in Chapter 4. Each move tries to keep eternity from being a feature borrowed from time, with one party preserving transcendence by removing the temporal conditions and the other preserving relation by retaining them.

Hartshorne’s dipolar theism (Hartshorne 1948; Hartshorne 1984) proposes a third line: God’s abstract pole (the invariant, necessary, essential nature) is atemporal and immutable in the Boethian sense; God’s concrete pole (the cumulative, responsive actuality in which God genuinely experiences and responds to creaturely events) is temporal, successive, and grows with the world’s creative advance. The dipolar account is designed to buy classical atemporality for the essential register while preserving genuine temporal responsiveness for the relational register. Q3 (whether duration is coherent without extent) presses the abstract pole. Q4 (whether sempiternity preserves transcendence) presses the concrete pole. Whether the bifurcation itself can be held together is pressed against dipolar theism generally at §10.3.3, where the abstract/concrete pole-relation is shown to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles.

In its classical formulation, the doctrine asks for a life whose unboundedness is preserved by removing every dimension along which duration could be tracked.

*The interrogation.* Six questions test what an account of divine eternity must explain. The six pressures run one at the level of the predicate itself, five at the level of the conditions eternity-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *When is a timeless life possessed all at once?* The Boethian formula is the most enduring formulation in the tradition, and it bears more argumentative weight than its length suggests. *Tota simul* (wholly at once) is the move under pressure. Possession-at-once requires a possessor and a possessed; if the possessed is unbounded life, the life in question must have temporal extent, since unboundedness is the modifier of an extent. The eternal *tota simul* possesses an extended life all at once, which isn’t yet a coherent description until we ask what the *at* anchors. The Boethian defender’s primary reply is that the dilemma misreads the doctrine: eternity isn’t a quasi-temporal manifold but a *sui generis* mode of being whose *at* isn’t a temporal index. Nothing in the present reading insists on a temporal construal of *aeternitas*, and the distinction stands as the doctrine draws it. The concern reformulates. Even granting the *sui generis* mode, the doctrine wants the eternal life to be in operative cognitive and causal contact with temporal events: to know creatures, to act in history, to respond to prayer, to sustain in being from moment to moment. Each of those predicates requires a determinate asymmetric relation between the eternal pole and the temporal event. If the *at* of eternity supplies that relation, eternity has structural content of its own; if it doesn’t, the *tota simul* preserves co-presence at the cost of losing the operative predicates the doctrine wants the co-presence to carry. Leftow (Leftow 1991) develops a careful contemporary defense; the present reading is that the formula succeeds at marking what the doctrine wants and leaves open, on either disambiguation, how it supplies the structural relations the predicates downstream require. 

A parallel concern attaches to the doctrine’s principal alternative formulation. The Augustinian–Thomistic phrasing of divine timelessness as *being outside time* (Augustine, *Confessions* (397–400) 1991, XI; Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.10) trades on a predicate whose ordinary content is spatial-positional: to be *outside* X is to be at a location not enclosed by X, with the relation running along S. The doctrine wants *outside* to do non-spatial work; the classical reply, that the term is meant analogically rather than literally, preserves the verbal gesture by emptying the relation of the spatial content that gave the term its force. *Outside X* requires X to be a region, the subject to be not-in-the-region, and the not-in relation to track containment; when X is time and the subject is non-temporal, the analogical use preserves the verbal form and reduces the substantive content to *not-temporal*, which is the predicate the formulation was supposed to non-vacuously specify.

The objection that *outside* has unproblematic non-spatial uses—outside the set, outside the law, outside the genus—is granted; the point doesn’t rest on the spatial etymology. Take a contentful reading, on which *outside time* asserts a determinate content: that the divine being is a member of no temporal order and bears no temporal property intrinsically. That reading isn’t vacuous, but its content is purely privative, and the privation is the difficulty rather than its avoidance. A being that bears no temporal property intrinsically stands in no intrinsic before-and-after relation. Classical eternalists can nevertheless posit extrinsic relations to temporally ordered events and tenseless knowledge of their locations. The burden is to explain indexical knowledge and responsive agency without importing intrinsic succession, not to assume that every such relation is intrinsic. So the contentful reading of *outside* doesn’t escape the first horn; it reaches it by another line: the spatial reading empties the relation of structure, while the privative reading keeps the relation contentful only as a denial, and a denial supplies none of what the downstream predicates run on—that supply is the burden the extrinsic-relations account still owes. *Tota simul* and *outside time* are the doctrine’s two principal verbal moves: the first preserves co-presence at the cost of the asymmetric relations the doctrine wants the co-presence to carry; the second preserves transcendence at the cost of the structural relation *outside* implicitly relies on.

**Q2.** *By what shared time is a timeless life simultaneous with a temporal one?* Stump and Kretzmann (Stump and Kretzmann 1981) define ET-simultaneity as a *sui generis* relation between eternal and temporal entities: the eternal life is simultaneous with every temporal moment without itself being temporal, and without the temporal moments thereby being simultaneous with one another. The relation does the structural work the doctrine asks of it: keeps eternal causation, eternal knowing, and eternal love in operative contact with temporal events without temporalizing the eternal pole. The concern isn’t that *simultaneous with* must mean clock-simultaneity. The defender is right that ET-simultaneity is a defined technical relation, not the ordinary relation. The concern reformulates: a defined technical relation is operatively contentful only insofar as it preserves the asymmetric structure the believer’s reports require. The believer’s prayer at 3 PM Tuesday was offered after their morning confession and before their evening weeping; the asymmetry is part of what the prayer is. ET-simultaneity can preserve the prayer’s place in the creaturely temporal order without reproducing that succession intrinsically in God. The challenge is whether one timeless act can explain different responses to differently located events while remaining simple and unchanged. Leftow’s (Leftow 1991) formal development sharpens the position, and Mullins (Mullins 2016) presses the sustained published case against ET-simultaneity—that the relation either collapses into a temporal mode or fails to secure the asymmetric contact it was introduced to provide; the question the present reading presses is which disambiguation the doctrine takes, not whether the technical relation is well-defined.

**Q3.** *How long is a life that takes no time?* Boethius keeps *life* in the formula. Creaturely life has duration, while the classical doctrine proposes a non-successive mode of life; the coherence of that analogical extension is what must be tested. Aquinas (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.10) takes the further step of identifying divine eternity with divine being itself, so that God’s being and God’s life are the same eternal *now* without succession or extension. The doctrine preserves divine immutability by removing every dimension along which duration could be tracked. The concern here is that what remains is a *now* with no internal differentiation: not the eternal life of a being but the bare instant of an event. An unextended instant isn’t an everlasting duration. But the eternalist doesn’t identify eternity with a temporal instant; the proposal is a distinct mode of existence, which faces a relation and content burden rather than this simple limiting-case objection. Stump (Stump 2003) and Helm (Helm 2010) defend the position by treating *now* as analogically rather than univocally applied, and the move is genuinely available; the cost is that the predicate the doctrine wanted (life in its fullest form) now attaches to a mode that has yet to show it can host the conditions life requires.

**Q4.** *How does endless time put a being beyond time?* Wolterstorff (Wolterstorff 1975), Hasker (Hasker 1989), and Mullins (Mullins 2016) develop the alternative tradition: God is everlasting, not timeless. God exists through time, with infinite duration, and the divine being is genuinely affected by, and responsive to, what occurs at each temporal moment. The position preserves the relational vocabulary the doctrine performs (Causality (§11.7.2) takes this up directly) at the cost of placing God within the temporal manifold the classical doctrine had placed God beyond. The concern here is parallel to those raised in §11.3.3 and §11.4.2: a being within time has temporally located acts and knowledge. This revises strict atemporality but need not surrender every form of transcendence or ultimacy; it shifts the burden to aseity and temporal dependence. The two positions (timeless and everlasting) are best read as the doctrine splitting along a structural incompatibility, with each branch keeping one half of what the unified doctrine had wanted.

**Q5.** *How does a theory of time deliver a being out of time?* Recent defenses of divine atemporality (Leftow 1991; Leftow 2012; Helm 2010) sometimes appeal to the B-theory of time: the tenseless view on which all moments are equally real and the *now* is indexical rather than ontologically privileged. On the B-theory, the move from divine atemporality to divine simultaneity-with-every-moment becomes more tractable: the eternal pole stands in tenseless relation to a tenselessly extended manifold, and the modal asymmetry the A-theory introduces is set aside. The concern here is that the B-theory doesn’t remove temporal structure; it relocates it. Tenseless before-and-after relations are still T, and a being eternally adjacent to a tenseless manifold is still a being whose adjacency requires the manifold to be the manifold it is. Craig’s A-theoretic objection presses the dilemma from the other side: if tense is fundamental rather than indexical, divine atemporality has to stand in tenseless relation to a manifold whose primary facts are tensed, and the doctrine’s reach for B-theoretic support trades one structural cost (the tenseless adjacency the eternal pole still requires) for another (the disjunction between the eternal pole’s tenseless relations and the temporal pole’s tensed facts), with the cost on the A-theoretic side sharper than the doctrine’s B-theoretic refinements register (Craig 2001c). The B-theory clarifies the doctrine without dissolving the structural difficulty. T’s standing on either A- or B-theory is taken up at §2.6.6; the present concern is that whichever theory of time is correct, eternity-talk that carries relations to creatures presupposes the temporal order rather than transcends it.

**Q6.** *What does “unchanging” add to a being with no time in which to change?* The classical bundle ties eternity tightly to immutability: God is eternal because God doesn’t change, and God doesn’t change because God is eternal. Mullins (Mullins 2016) presses the dependency from the inside: the doctrines don’t require each other in the form the tradition holds them, and a more relaxed immutability (God’s character doesn’t change, though God’s relations to creatures do) can survive without strict atemporality. The concern added here is that the relaxation removes the motivation for the strict atemporalist moves: if God can change in some respects, the question why God can’t change in temporal respects becomes a question about which respects rather than about temporality as such. The doctrine of strict atemporality, on the present reading, stands or falls with the doctrine of strict immutability, and the contemporary moves that loosen one have already loosened the other.

*The burden.* What the six pressures jointly surface is what *eternal* actually runs on. The Boethian formula keeps *life* in it, and life is the modifier of an extent; remove every dimension along which extent can be tracked, and there is nothing for the modifier to modify. The relational predicates the doctrine asks the eternal life to carry (knowing creatures, acting in history, responding to prayer, sustaining in being from moment to moment) each require an ordering between not-yet and now without which the verbs lack determinate content. *Simultaneous with* is a relation, and a defined technical relation is operatively contentful only insofar as it preserves the asymmetric structure the believer’s reports turn on. A temporal moment with no extent isn’t an everlasting duration, while a proposed timeless mode must be assessed on its own relational semantics. The B-theory clarifies the doctrine without dissolving the difficulty, since tenseless before-and-after relations are still T. And the classical bundle of eternity-with-immutability doesn’t survive its own loosening: the tradition has held the doctrines as if they entailed each other, and the contemporary moves that relax one have already relaxed the other. Temporal relations structure creaturely events and every everlasting model. A timeless model must explain its contact with that order. This doesn’t by itself identify eternity with T’s modal status.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Life Is the Modifier of an Extent** · *Diagnostic*

The Boethian formula keeps *life* inside it, and life modifies an extent: it is had all at once only where there is something whose all-at-once it is. Withdraw every dimension along which extent can be tracked and the modifier has nothing left to modify. The relational predicates the doctrine asks the eternal life to carry—knowing creatures, acting in history, answering prayer, holding in being from moment to moment—each need an ordering between not-yet and now, without which the verbs lack determinate content. *Simultaneous with* is a relation, and a technical relation defined for the case is operatively contentful only so far as it preserves the asymmetric structure the believer’s own reports turn on. The B-theory clarifies the doctrine without dissolving the difficulty, since tenseless before-and-after relations are still T, and a being eternally adjacent to a tenseless manifold is one whose adjacency requires that manifold to be what it is. The classical pairing doesn’t survive its own loosening either: the tradition held eternity and immutability as though each entailed the other, and every contemporary move that relaxes one has already relaxed the other. What follows is that a timeless model owes an account of its contact with the temporal order, not yet that eternity is to be identified with T’s modal status.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Durational continuity and presence-throughout belong to T. That doesn’t make Nature a life possessing its duration *tota simul*, and it doesn’t refute a timeless mode merely by contrasting it with creaturely duration. Strict timeless eternity remains a rival proposal whose coherence depends on the positive content of its mode and its relation to temporal life. Everlastingness, by contrast, retains duration and places its bearer within temporal order. The argument therefore distinguishes three claims that the word *eternal* can hide: temporal unboundedness, invariant presence throughout an order, and timeless existence. The first two require T; the third owes a contact with it.

### 11.3.3 Immutability
The doctrine is engaged twice. Whether a changeless thing can be the *ground*—static-being and eternal-present as candidate ultimates—is asked at §10.2.3. What is asked here is narrower and concerns the attribute: whether a being that never changes can also do what the tradition says it does.

Immutability is the claim that God never changes in any way. The strain is that the things the tradition also says God does (beginning to create, answering a prayer, becoming incarnate) are all transitions from one state to another. Keeping the action-language while denying God any transition leaves the verbs owing an account of how their direction and contingency arise from an unchanging source.

Classical theology holds that God is immutable: God doesn’t change, can’t change, and doesn’t undergo any sort of intrinsic variation across time, situation, or relation (Aquinas, *ST* I.9.1; Augustine, *Confessions* XI; Anselm, *Proslogion* XXII). The doctrine has Aristotelian roots in the unmoved mover (*Metaphysics* Λ.7) and binds tightly to simplicity (§11.2.1), necessity (§11.3.1), and pure actuality: a simple, necessary, fully actual being has no potency to be otherwise, and so doesn’t change. Contemporary defenders include Dolezal (2017), Feser (2017), Weinandy (2000), and Stump (2003); the doctrine has been refined into *weak immutability* (Mullins 2016; Pawl 2020) that distinguishes intrinsic from relational change. The position immutability has traditionally held, fully stated, is that God’s intrinsic state (essence, knowledge, will, relations to creatures) is invariant across any possible difference in creaturely state, and that the apparent changes in God’s relations to creatures (becoming the creator of *this* world rather than another, becoming incarnate, responding to prayer) are *Cambridge changes* (mere shifts in how God stands related to a changing world, involving no alteration in God) rather than real changes in God.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test how immutability can preserve the action-language joined to it. What underlies the five is structural: the difference between *acting* and *being acted upon* depends on directed transition, and the doctrine’s strategy is to deny directed transition of the divine being while preserving the action-language the believer’s life rests on.

**Q1.** *How does a being that can’t change begin to create?* Pure actuality (the property of having no unrealized potential) is the metaphysical floor of immutability (Aquinas, *ST* I.3.1). Creation requires a transition in the creature from not existing to existing. Whether it also requires intrinsic transition in the cause is precisely what the classical timeless-causation model denies. The classical reply locates the transition entirely in the creature: God eternally wills the creature; the creature comes to be in time; God doesn’t undergo any change in the willing (Aquinas, *ST* I.46.1; *SCG* II.35). The concern here is that the eternal willing of a temporal creation is the relational structure the believer’s prayer life and providence rest on: prayer at t_1 that affects God’s relation to the world at t_2. The Cambridge-change reply preserves God’s intrinsic invariance by relocating the variance into the creature, but religious language of deliberation and response can suggest intrinsic change. The issue is whether that language is literal, analogical, or accommodated to creaturely perspective; intuition alone doesn’t settle it.

**Q2.** *How does a mind that never changes know that the present has changed?* If God knows that *Caesar crosses the Rubicon* before, during, and after the crossing, the *knowledge-content* differs by tense even if the *fact* is timeless. The classical reply is that God knows the timeless fact and that the tensed truths are creaturely modes of access to the same fact (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.13, Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Helm 2010). The concern here is that a being who knows *that Caesar crosses the Rubicon* without knowing *that Caesar will cross* or *has crossed* either lacks information the creature has (in which case omniscience fails) or has the tensed information by some mode the timeless-fact reading doesn’t deliver (Prior 1959; Kretzmann 1966; Mullins 2016). The Boethian reply (eternal vision of all times at once) preserves immutability by relocating God outside time, which makes the tense-bearing structure of knowing about a temporal world the structural feature the doctrine forecloses.

**Q3.** *How does the maker undergo no transition, when making is the transition?* The creature comes from non-being to being. The classical reply treats the transition as entirely in the creature: it is the creature that transitions; God neither pre-exists the act in any tensed sense (atemporality) nor changes by performing it (immutability). The concern here is that *bringing-into-being* is the paradigm of directed transition (§2.6.2): the act has a *from* (nothing) and a *to* (the creature), and the directedness is what the act consists in. To attribute the act to an unchanged agent requires an account of how causal direction and contingent effect arise from one invariant intention. It isn’t semantically empty merely because the transition occurs in the effect. The reply that God is the *terminus a quo* (the starting point *from which*) of the transition without undergoing it makes the *acting* into a structural feature of the world’s hosting of the act, not of the agent’s performing it.

**Q4.** *How does the unchangeable become flesh?* The doctrine of the incarnation holds that the second person of the Trinity *became* man (*ho logos sarx egeneto*, John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined the union as one person in two natures, fully divine and fully human. The classical reply is that the incarnation is a change in the human nature, not in the divine nature: the divine Word doesn’t become human in the sense of acquiring a property, but human nature becomes the Word’s nature in the sense of being assumed (Aquinas, *ST* III.16; Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Unity of Christ*). The concern here is that *assumption* is itself a directed transition: there is a *before* the assumption (in which the human nature doesn’t exist as the Word’s) and an *after* (in which it does). The reply that the assumption is eternal in the divine register and temporal in the human register locates the directedness in the human register only, which makes the *becoming* of John 1:14 a structural feature of the human side. Chalcedon doesn’t treat the human nature as a second person who becomes in the Word’s place. The remaining burden is personal unity: how one subject is the subject of that becoming without the divine nature itself undergoing it.

**Q5.** *How is a change in God’s relations not a change in God?* Pawl (2020) and Mullins (2016) develop *weak immutability*: God doesn’t change in essential properties or intrinsic state, but does change in accidental or relational properties (e.g., becoming-the-creator-of-this-world, being-prayed-to, becoming-incarnate). The concern here is that *change in relational properties* is what *real change in relations* names, and the classical doctrine’s whole strategy has been to deny real relations between God and creatures (Aquinas, *ST* I.13.7; *SCG* II.12). The weak-immutability refinement admits variance back into the divine being’s relations, which is what the strong doctrine refused. The refinement is honest about what the believer’s intuition requires; the concern here is that what the refinement admits is the directed transition the strong doctrine was preserving against.

The temporalist repair pressed from inside the literature (drop strong immutability but keep a temporal, personal God, rather than continue to the dipolar terminus) is the live alternative engaged at §11.7.3 (with the temporality structure at §11.3.2); the concern this section presses is that weak immutability’s *internal* logic, once relational variance is admitted, runs on to the dipolar assignment taken up next. Hartshorne’s dipolar theism occupies the logical terminus of the weak-immutability move and gives it a principled stopping point: the abstract pole is strictly immutable in the classical sense (no intrinsic change, no relational change, no variance of any kind) while the concrete pole is genuinely responsive, growing with the world’s cumulative creative advance and bearing the directed transitions the believer’s life rests on (*The Divine Relativity* 1948; *Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes* 1984). The dipolar account doesn’t blur strong and weak immutability; it assigns each cleanly to a different pole of a single subject. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3: the relation between the poles is a directed, asymmetric crossing, and the abstract pole enters a determinate relation with the concrete pole. That creates a differentiation and dependence burden, though a relation need not be a transition undergone by both relata. The relation requires determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles, as shown at §10.3.3; the dipolar assignment relocates the immutability problem into the pole-relation rather than resolving it.

*The burden.* Taken together, the five pressures expose what *immutable* requires. Pure actuality relocates the transition into the creature and construes divine agency through invariant causation. The burden is to explain contingent effects and real causal asymmetry without intrinsic divine change. Tensed knowledge of contingents requires either the tense-bearing structure the doctrine forecloses or a Boethian timeless vision that makes the believer’s intuition of God-as-responding to temporal events a feature of the creature’s access, not the divine knowing. Creatio ex nihilo is a directed transition in the effect; an immutable-agent account must explain how its source grounds that directedness without undergoing it. The Chalcedonian incarnation requires a *becoming* that the strong doctrine relocates into the human nature. The remaining burden is personal unity: how one subject is the subject of the becoming without either making the divine nature a second agent of the action or treating the human nature as a second person who becomes in the Word’s place. Weak immutability admits relational variance, which is the variance the strong doctrine was preserving against. The five pressures leave a distinction between invariance of character or essence, strict absence of intrinsic change, and invariance of structural conditions. These shouldn’t be collapsed into one predicate.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Three Invariances, One Word** · *Diagnostic*

Each pressure is answerable, and each answer relocates rather than removes. Pure actuality moves the transition into the creature and reads divine agency as invariant causation, leaving the burden of explaining contingent effects and real causal asymmetry without intrinsic divine change. Tensed knowledge of contingents needs either the tense-bearing structure the doctrine forecloses or a timeless vision on which the believer’s sense of God-as-responding is a feature of creaturely access rather than of the divine knowing. *Creatio ex nihilo* is a directed transition in the effect, and an immutable-agent account owes how its source grounds that directedness without undergoing it. The Chalcedonian *becoming* is relocated into the human nature. That isn’t yet a second subject beside the Word; the remaining burden is how one person is the subject of the becoming without the divine nature itself undergoing it. Weak immutability admits relational variance, which is the variance the strong doctrine was holding out against. What the five pressures establish is therefore a distinction rather than a verdict: invariance of character or essence, strict absence of intrinsic change, and invariance of the structural conditions are three different claims, carrying three different burdens, and the doctrine’s force has depended on their traveling under one word.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* The word *immutable* covers at least three claims: invariance of character, absence of intrinsic succession, and invariance of the modal frame. Only the third genuinely relocates. The three Conditions remain the conditions under which change is possible; their modal status isn’t one more changing configuration within the field they constitute. That doesn’t make Nature a changeless agent, and it doesn’t show that a personal subject can’t retain stable character through changing relations. Concrete creation, providence, and response remain temporally ordered operations. A timeless account may redescribe them as one invariant grounding act, but then it owes the differentiated contact by which that act bears differently on contingent effects. What the analysis doesn’t put in doubt is the constancy the word was reaching for. Holding to a character across changing circumstances is something a person can do, and doing it through change rather than in its absence is what makes it steadfastness rather than mere fixity. A personal subject can retain stable character through changing relations; so can we, and that is where the constancy anyone has actually admired has been found.

### 11.3.4 Impassibility
Impassibility says God is never acted upon: never moved, never affected, never made to suffer or respond by anything outside. The pressure is that loving someone, hearing a prayer, or suffering on the Cross all involve being affected by another. Removing every trace of “being affected” keeps the words *love* and *mercy* while leaving disputed whether anything responsive remains for them to name.

Classical theology holds that God is impassible: God isn’t acted upon, doesn’t suffer, doesn’t undergo emotional disturbance, and doesn’t receive anything from creatures (Aquinas, *ST* I.20.1; Augustine, *De civitate Dei* IX.5; Anselm, *Proslogion* VIII). The doctrine binds tightly to immutability (§11.3.3), simplicity (§11.2.1), and aseity (§11.3.1): a being that can’t be acted upon is also one that doesn’t change, has no parts to be moved, and depends on nothing outside itself. The classical reading locates the affective language of Scripture (God’s anger, grief, compassion, jealousy) in the creature’s relation to God rather than in God’s reception of the creature (Aquinas, *ST* I.20.1 ad 2, Gavrilyuk 2004; Weinandy 2000). The twentieth-century *passibilist* turn (Moltmann 1974; Fiddes 1988; Bauckham 1984) pressed in the other direction: a God who doesn’t suffer with creation can’t love it, and the Cross is the central revelation of divine passibility: God’s capacity to be affected by, and to suffer with, creation. The position the classical doctrine, fully stated, holds is that God’s intrinsic state is invariant under creaturely action: nothing the creature does adds to, subtracts from, or modifies the divine being; God’s love, knowledge, and providence are entirely a function of God’s own being and not of what God receives.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test what impassibility must explain. Beneath the five runs one structural fact: *reception* is a structural feature of substances persisting through time (§2.6.4), and the doctrine’s strategy is to deny all reception of the divine being while preserving the relational language the believer’s life depends on.

**Q1.** *How does a being love what can’t move it?* The classical reading of divine love is that God’s love for the creature is the act by which God wills the creature’s good, and that this act is identical with God’s own being (Aquinas, *ST* I.20). Many accounts of interpersonal love include receptivity and affective response, while classical accounts define divine love primarily as willing the beloved’s good. The dispute is substantive: whether perfect love requires intrinsic affective change, not a truth fixed by the concept alone. The classical reply removes the *affected by* component and identifies love with willing the good. The passibilist reply (Moltmann 1974; Fiddes 1988) is that willing another’s good without responsiveness doesn’t preserve the full content of love. The dispute is therefore whether willing alone suffices for what the believer means by *God loves us*, a central question in twentieth-century theology.

**Q2.** *Who hears a prayer, if nothing can reach the one it’s prayed to?* The believer prays to God for the healing of a sick friend. The classical reply is that God eternally wills the friend’s healing in response to the eternally-foreseen prayer; the prayer doesn’t move God in time, but figures eternally in the divine plan that includes the healing (Aquinas, *ST* II-II.83). Response to prayer names a counterfactual and explanatory dependence between petition and outcome. In creaturely cases this often involves acts at t_1 and t_2; a classical account instead posits one timeless intention whose effects are temporally ordered. The reply that the figuring is eternal in the recipient relocates the directedness into the petitioner-creature side and leaves the recipient as the *terminus ad quem* (the end point *toward which*) of the figuring without being the *receiver* of the prayer. The believer’s intuition that the prayer is *heard* (received by an attending recipient) is what the classical reply replaces with the prayer’s *being-figured-in*. What the reply suppresses isn’t the intuition itself but the structural feature it tracks—reception by an attending recipient, which the eternal-figuring model must either supply in another register or explain away.

**Q3.** *How does an impassible God suffer on the Cross?* The crucifixion of Jesus is, on the Chalcedonian definition, the suffering of the second person of the Trinity in the human nature he has assumed. The classical reply is that the suffering is real in the human nature and that the divine nature doesn’t suffer; the unity of person is preserved by predication-of-the-person rather than by attribution-to-the-nature (Aquinas, *ST* III.46, Weinandy 2000; Gavrilyuk 2004). The passibilist objection is that this preserves impassibility by locating the suffering in a nature distinct from the divine being, which converts the Cross from the revelation of God’s love into the dramatic event of a human nature’s pain. The concern here is that *the suffering of the person* requires the person to bear what the nature undergoes (to be the *whose* of the *what*) and the impassibilist reading locates the *bearing* without the *being-affected*. What is at stake here isn’t only Moltmann’s (1974) reading of the Cross as the suffering of God but the central event of Christian revelation that reading interprets.

Hartshorne’s dipolar account offers a principled reply to Q3: the suffering on the Cross is borne by the concrete pole (the cumulative, responsive divine actuality that is genuinely affected by creaturely events, including the event of the crucifixion) while the abstract pole remains invariant. Moltmann’s (1974) intuition that the Cross reveals a suffering God traces its process-theological ancestry to Hartshorne (*The Divine Relativity* 1948), whose systematic account of divine receptivity is the direct predecessor of the twentieth-century passibilist revival. The pressure here is the one raised at §10.3.3: if the single subject suffers, its abstract dimension stands in relation to a temporal event across the pole-relation, and that relation is shown at §10.3.3 to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. The concrete pole’s reception of the Cross is sustained only by drawing the abstract pole into those roles.

**Q4.** *What does a being receive, if it has no potency to receive?* Reception requires the potency to receive. A being that is pure act (with no unrealized potential) has no potency to receive (Aquinas, *ST* I.3.1, Feser 2017). The concern here is that the doctrine of impassibility is *what pure act entails at the relational level*: a being that can’t be moved can’t be received-from, because reception is being-moved by what is received. The reply that God receives in the order of intention (knowing, willing) without being moved in the order of being (Aquinas, *ST* I.20 ad 2) preserves impassibility by introducing a distinction between intentional and ontological reception. The concern here is that *intentional reception* is what *being affected by what is known and willed* names, and the doctrine’s strategy is to keep this in a register that doesn’t modify the being’s intrinsic state—which the believer’s intuition resists keeping apart.

**Q5.** *How does God respond to creatures without being acted upon?* The twentieth-century passibilist tradition (Moltmann 1974; Fiddes 1988; Bauckham 1984) has argued that divine love requires divine suffering. The contemporary refinements (Weinandy 2000; Gavrilyuk 2004; Mullins 2016) distinguish *strong impassibility* (no affective variance) from *qualified impassibility* (affective responsiveness without ontological diminishment). The concern here is that *affective responsiveness* is the variance the strong doctrine refused, and the qualified-impassibility move admits the variance the strong doctrine was preserving against. The qualified move is honest about what the believer’s intuition requires; the concern here is that what the qualified move admits is the structural feature Φ (substance persisting through events) carries: the persisting substance is the *bearer* of the events, and, on the passibilist reading, *being the bearer* is *being modified by* the events as they occur in the bearer.

The qualified-impassibilist and full-passibilist positions developed within personal theism (Mullins 2016) are substantive alternatives in their own right—a temporal, personal God genuinely affected by creatures, engaged at §11.7.3 and alongside §11.3.3—rather than transitional positions on the way to dipolar theism. The concern is that admitting affective variance introduces the same structural commitments that dipolar theism makes explicit. Dipolar theism provides a systematic development of the commitments introduced by passibilist refinements: Hartshorne’s abstract pole isn’t weakly impassible but strictly impassible, and the concrete pole isn’t qualifiedly passible but fully receptive, growing with the world’s cumulative experience. The abstract/concrete bifurcation assigns impassibility and passibility to two poles of a single subject rather than qualifying both within one nature. The pressure here is the one raised at §10.3.3: the two poles constitute one subject only through the directed dependence between them, which imports the structural roles the abstract pole was supposed to avoid.

*The burden.* Run to their end, the five pressures show what *impassible* finally rests on. Love without intrinsic affective change is the classical proposal; the disputed question is whether willing another’s good suffices for perfect love or whether receptivity is essential. Petitionary prayer requires a recipient whose receiving is part of the prayer’s structure; relocating the receiving into the eternal-figuring register must supply the structural feature *being heard* there or lose it. The Cross requires a suffering of the person. Classical impassibilism locates the suffering according to the human nature while denying that the divine nature is affected; that is a live proposal, not a juxtaposition of two sufferers. The remaining burden is how the one person is the subject of the suffering without intrinsic alteration of the divine nature, and what *the person suffered* still names if the divine nature is unaffected. Pure act has no potency to receive; the intentional-vs.-ontological distinction preserves impassibility by allowing reception in a register that doesn’t modify the receiver, which requires a clarified distinction between intentional relation and intrinsic alteration. Qualified impassibility admits the variance the strong doctrine refused, which is the variance Φ carries: the persisting substance is the bearer of the events, and being the bearer need not entail intrinsic modification by every relational event. After the five pressures, impassibility remains a claim about the mode and limits of divine receptivity. Φ can describe the persistence of affected bearers, but impassibility isn’t thereby identical with Φ.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Being Heard Is a Structural Feature, Not a Register** · *Diagnostic*

Love without intrinsic affective change is the classical proposal, and whether willing another’s good suffices for perfect love or whether receptivity is essential is genuinely disputed. What the relocations cost can be stated. Petitionary prayer needs a recipient whose receiving is part of the prayer’s structure; moving the receiving into an eternal-figuring register must supply *being heard* in that register or lose it. The Cross needs a suffering of the person. Classical impassibilism locates the suffering according to the human nature while denying that the divine nature is affected; that is a live proposal, not a second sufferer beside the Word. The remaining burden is how the one person is the subject of the suffering without intrinsic alteration of the divine nature, and what *the person suffered* still names if the divine nature is unaffected.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Reception and affective persistence occur through bearers within Nature; impassibility isn’t another name for Φ. The live dispute is whether divine love requires intrinsic receptivity, whether a mixed relation can preserve being heard without change in God, and whether the suffering attributed to Christ belongs to the person without affecting the divine nature. The structural analysis fixes what creaturely reception costs and what devotional responsiveness appears to promise. It doesn’t settle those theological questions by transferring the negative predicate *impassible* to Nature. What it does return is the positive term the negation was built on. Being moved by another—receiving, and being altered in the receiving—is something bearers within Nature do, and the devotional weight of *being heard* rests on that capacity rather than on its denial. Whatever is settled about the divine nature, receptivity isn’t a limitation awaiting exemption. It is what makes being heard possible, and it is ours.

## 11.4 Cognition
This cluster gathers the two attributes of divine knowing: awareness (§11.4.1) and knowledge (§11.4.2). The tradition holds that God is conscious of all that is and knows it perfectly, without acquiring, losing, or revising any content.

Pressed, both require the structural conditions of any cognition whatever: to be aware is to stand in a distinction between knower and known, and to know is to bear content in the act of knowing. Where the awareness is an actual experiencing rather than a representation of one, all three Conditions are co-instantiated in it (Constitutive Instantiation, §2.6.7); where the knowing attends, modulates, or meets another as another, the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) places the full Structural Requirement at that operation. Neither is a faculty exempt from the conditions.

### 11.4.1 Awareness

Aristotle’s phrase still sets the standard: God is “thought thinking itself”: consciousness and self-knowledge complete in a single act, taking in nothing from outside. The problem this raises is how one undifferentiated act bears phenomenal and intentional content. Many theories require a subject, perspective, and some self-relation; not all require a temporally extended higher-order registration. Collapse all of that into one changeless point, as the doctrine does, and what is left must show how it keeps the name of awareness without the structure that makes anything aware.

The classical doctrine of divine awareness assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *vita perfecta*, perfect life, with the fullness of self-presence the term implies (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XII.7; Aquinas, *ST* I.18). God is *noesis noeseos noesis*, thought thinking itself: the eternal self-cognition in which knower and known are the same act (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XII.9; Aquinas, *ST* I.14.2). On a contemporary refinement, divine awareness is sui generis: not a creaturely state of consciousness writ large, but a primitive divine cognition of which creaturely awareness is a faint analogate (Stump 2013; Stump 2016; Plantinga 2000; Alston 1991a). Each move tries to keep the qualitative dimension of awareness from being a feature only creatures have. Carried to its limit, the doctrine names a divine being whose self-cognition is one eternal act in which the asymmetry between knower and known has been collapsed into identity at the highest register.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test what the doctrine of awareness must supply. What these pressures turn on is a burden weaker than any single temporal higher-order theory. Awareness requires at least determinate subject–content articulation and something that bears the awareness. The subject and content may be simultaneous; their distinction need not itself be a temporal interval, and a perspective may be indexical rather than metrically spatial. Loaded T and S enter only for awareness that modulates across states, tracks changing objects, or stands in second-personal encounter; Φ enters first at the thinner level of a real bearer or realizer, with causal persistence requiring a further upgrade. One result already earned tightens this, and it turns on a distinction the doctrine itself insists on. Constitutive Instantiation (§2.6.7) holds that where one of the Conditions is actually present in an experiencing—instantiated, and not merely represented in the content of that experiencing—all three are co-instantiated in it; and because an experiencing is a state its ground is *in* rather than a content the ground merely represents, the ground instantiates all three as well.

The qualifier is doing the work: the corollary reaches actual experiencing, not represented structure. That is precisely the ground the classical doctrine claims. *Vita perfecta* and *noesis noeseos noesis* aren’t descriptions of a representation of self-presence; they assert self-presence as fully actual, an experiencing complete in a single act. The doctrine can’t take the representational escape without abandoning the thesis that divine awareness is a life rather than a description of one. What the corollary then delivers stays at role-resolution—articulation and bearing, not a metric interval or a material part—and the loaded upgrades remain where the paragraph above leaves them. The classical doctrine must therefore explain how one absolutely simple act carries determinate subject–content structure. The five pressures test that burden and then identify where the stronger temporal, positional, and persistent roles are incurred by the richer claims.

**Q1.** *What relates to itself, where the knower and the known are the same act?* The phenomenal tradition from Brentano (1874) through Husserl (1900–01) to recent higher-order theorists (Rosenthal 2005; Kriegel 2009) treats some form of self-relating as constitutive of awareness, not as a contingent feature of certain awarenesses among others. First-order representational accounts (Tye 1995; Dretske 1995) can treat awareness as representational content available to a system without a distinct higher-order self-relation. The structural burden therefore concerns determinate subject and content, not one theory of consciousness imposed on every rival. The classical reply is that divine awareness isn’t analyzable along these lines: God’s self-cognition is one eternal act in which knower and known are identical, and the *self-relation* isn’t a structural condition but a creaturely shadow of the unified divine act (*ST* I.14.2, Stump 2013). The distinction does the work the doctrine asks of it.

Its exact form is Aquinas’s *distinctio rationis*: knower and known differ in God by a distinction of reason (a conceptual distinction with no answering distinction in the thing) so the asymmetry awareness seems to need is preserved in our way of conceiving God without importing real composition into the divine act (*ST* I.14.2; I.13.4). The concern this section adds is that a *distinctio rationis* secures the asymmetry at precisely the register that can’t do the structural work. A distinction that holds only for the mind conceiving God, and not in God, leaves the divine act itself with no internal asymmetry between the registering and the registered, and an act with no such asymmetry isn’t the upper limit of self-relation but its absence. A perfectly identical knower-and-known isn’t a more vivid awareness than the believer’s; it is a static relation with the same name as self-relation and none of the structure that made self-relation phenomenal.

**Q2.** *How does an awareness that never varies attend to one thing rather than another?* For an awareness to be the awareness of *this* rather than *that*, the being must be in a state-of-being-aware-of-this that is distinguishable from the being’s state of being aware of something else. Distinguishable contents require differentiation, but they need not occur successively; one awareness can simultaneously include several distinct objects. Aquinas’s eternal self-cognition (*ST* I.14) forecloses the registering deliberately: God’s awareness is one eternal act that doesn’t modulate as creaturely circumstances change. The doctrine preserves divine immutability. The cost is the same one raised at §11.4.2 for knowledge and raised at §11.8.2 for love: an awareness that doesn’t modulate when its object varies isn’t a heightened form of attention but a constitutive feature of a static relation. The believer who comes to a moment of grief feels the difference between being-attended-to-in-grief and being-attended-to-in-ordinary-times. Stump’s (2010) second-personal experiential knowledge is a contemporary attempt to preserve modulation while keeping atemporality, and the present analysis registers the position as a resourceful defense of the doctrine. The concern raised here is whether the modulation Stump preserves can do the work without the temporal index whose role she has factored out.

**Q3.** *From what point of view is a being aware, if it has no point of view?* The phenomenal tradition treats perspective as constitutive of awareness, but a perspective need not be a metric spatial location; it may be an indexical or subject-relative standpoint. Nagel’s (1974) bat is aware *as a bat is*, with the perspective doing structural work in what the awareness-of-echolocation is like. The classical reply is that divine awareness is non-perspectival: God’s cognition is from no point of view, equidistant from every point of view alike. The concern here is one raised at §11.8.1 for presence: *equidistant from every point alike* keeps the language of perspective and removes the contrastive structure perspective requires. An awareness from no perspective isn’t the most encompassing form of awareness but the limiting case of an awareness with no positional anchor for its content to take hold in. The reply that divine awareness is anchored in divine essence rather than in spatial position (Helm 2010; Rocca 2004) preserves the term by relocating the anchor; what *anchor* names, on the relocation, is doing primitive work the doctrine hasn’t specified.

**Q4.** *What bears the awareness, if there is no being to bear it?* Self-relation runs on a being. The being holds the doubling, sustains it across the moments of the registration, and is what the registering is *of itself* in the relevant sense. The classical doctrine of divine immateriality denies matter and extension, not metaphysical subsistence; Aquinas explicitly treats God as subsistent being. The pressure is whether such a bearer can host differentiated awareness under simplicity.

A defender can press further with Stump’s hylomorphic reading of Aquinas (Stump 2003): the divine being is *esse* itself—being itself—and her configurational account of substance offers a bearer that owes nothing to matter or extension, a substance-without-composition fit to hold the self-presence. The concern here is that the bearer this supplies is a substance with exactly the features of substance subtracted: a configuration sustains a doubling only by holding distinguishable elements in a determinate arrangement, and divine simplicity removes the differentiated content any configuration arranges. What remains isn’t a being with a fuller form of self-presence but a bearer that has yet to show it can hold what *self-presence* names.
