Stump’s second-personal defense isn’t the bare positing of a primitive. On Stump’s account (*Wandering in Darkness* 2010), divine awareness is *knowledge of persons*: the irreducible, non-propositional knowing-by-acquaintance the believer has in mind when they say God *knows* them, distinct in kind from knowledge *that* such-and-such holds. The present analysis registers it as a positively structured knowing rather than a place where analysis stops. The concern here is that second-personal knowledge, taken at the strength Stump gives it, is *more* structurally demanding than the propositional knowing it’s contrasted with, not less.

To know a person second-personally is to attend to *this* one, as they are, from the standpoint of one present to them: a relation indexed at both poles, running across the interval between the attender and the attended, and borne by a being that sustains the attending as the encounter unfolds. The richness that distinguishes second-personal knowing from propositional grasp is supplied entirely by the three Conditions: the temporal index that makes the attending *now*, the positional standpoint that makes it *to this one*, and the substantial bearer that holds the encounter together. Invoked to defend a being without those conditions, the second-personal account doesn’t exempt awareness from the structural requirement; it intensifies it. What the believer means by *God attends to me* is precisely the second-personal relation Stump describes, and that relation, described faithfully, is the structure the classical definition has removed. The defense rescues the believer’s intuition only by reintroducing the conditions the doctrine was formulated to deny: the move §11.4.2, Q8 makes for knowledge.

**Q5.** *Once awareness is stripped of all self-relation, what is left to conceive?* The conceivability question for predicates of God in general is taken up at §11.8.3; the present concern is local. Chalmers (2002) registers the relevant asymmetry: conceiving something coherent is some evidence for its possibility, conceiving something with structural self-defeat licenses no such inference. To conceive of awareness without self-relation is, on the analyses surveyed at Q1, to conceive of awareness with the structural condition for awareness removed. To conceive of *vita perfecta* without temporal differentiation, spatial perspective, or substantial being is to conceive of life with the structural conditions of life removed. The reply available to the doctrine is the analogical-and-apophatic one (predicating of God by analogy, or by negation alone; §11.8.3, Q1–Q2): the predicates apply analogically, and the conceivability concern dissolves under the analogical reading. Analogical predication is weighed on its own terms at §11.8.3. What this section adds is that the conceivability concern doesn’t require univocity to apply. Even on the most generous analogical reading, the predicate has to share enough structure with its creaturely paradigm for the analogical relation to obtain, and the structural conditions removed at the three Conditions are precisely what the creaturely paradigm consists in.

One classical argument seems to cut beneath all five pressures at once. Avicenna’s *Flying Man* (Avicenna (c. 1020) 1959) asks you to imagine a person created in an instant, full-grown, suspended in still air, blindfolded, limbs held apart so nothing is felt—no sensation, no perceived body, no world. Even so, the person would affirm *that they are*: self-awareness given with no body to give it, so awareness is no debtor to the structural conditions. Grant the intuition its full force; it still concedes the point. What the scenario subtracts is *outer* sensation and the *perceived* body—not the conditions the self-affirmation runs on. Awareness as creatures have it isn’t a static having but a registering: to be aware is to be modulated by what one is aware of, to occupy a state that responds to its object and is thereby distinguishable from the states one isn’t in. If the Flying Man is asked a question, the scenario gains relational content not present in Avicenna’s original thought experiment.

Even without it, the self-affirmation supplies a minimal subject–content structure. His affirming *I am* is the barest form of the same loop, a self registering itself. Feedback of this kind isn’t one feature of awareness among others; it is what remains when everything else is stripped, and it is already the three structural roles at work: the modulation runs across an ordering (T’s role), the registrant stands over against the registered (S’s role), and a persisting bearer is what the difference makes a difference to (Φ’s role). The tableau concedes as much before the argument begins, suspending him *in air*, creating him *at an instant*, having him *affirm*. The Flying Man supports awareness without outer sensation or perceived embodiment. It supports a bearer and determinate content, but it doesn’t by itself establish temporal duration, spatial placement, or the loaded T/S/Φ types. The intuition that self-presence outlasts the senses is sound; the inference that it outlasts the three Conditions removes the very structure the affirmation instances.

*The burden.* The universally earned burden is determinate subject–content articulation plus a bearer: awareness must be awareness *by* something and *of* something, even where knower and known are numerically one and the contents are simultaneous. That doesn’t yet prove a temporal interval or spatial manifold. The stronger roles enter conditionally. Attention that modulates when its object varies incurs temporal ordering; second-personal awareness incurs distinct relational poles and a standpoint; awareness realized in an ongoing cognitive process incurs persistence in its bearer. The classical account can therefore resist loaded T or S only by keeping divine awareness at the thin, non-modulating self-cognition level—and then owes an account of how absolute simplicity supports determinate content rather than bare identity. And the analogical defense the tradition leans on requires shared structural scaffolding with the creaturely paradigm to obtain at all: exactly what is conceded at the three Conditions is exactly what the paradigm consists in. Awareness is what self-relation does when the relation is doubled across a manifold. The predicate names that structure wherever a subject realizes it. It doesn’t make the modal field itself aware, and it doesn’t license treating every awareness as a loaded temporal and spatial process.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Awareness Needs a By and an Of** · *Diagnostic*

One burden is earned universally and survives every refinement: awareness has to be awareness *by* something and *of* something, with determinate subject–content articulation and a bearer, and this holds even where knower and known are numerically one and every content is simultaneous. That much doesn’t yet establish a temporal interval or a spatial manifold, and the section doesn’t take it to. The heavier roles enter conditionally instead, each with its own trigger: attention that modulates as its object varies incurs temporal ordering; second-personal awareness incurs distinct relational poles and a standpoint; awareness realized as an ongoing cognitive process incurs persistence in its bearer. The classical account can decline the loaded readings of T and S, but only by holding divine awareness at the thin, non-modulating level of self-cognition, and it then owes an account of how absolute simplicity supports determinate content rather than bare identity. The analogical defense doesn’t relieve that debt, since analogy obtains only where structural scaffolding is shared with the creaturely paradigm, and the shared scaffolding is what the paradigm consists in.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Awareness doesn’t belong to Nature simply because conscious organisms arise within Nature. It belongs to subjects wherever the life–consciousness identity of §5.1 is realized. The divine predicate therefore owes a subject, determinate content, and an account of what makes the awareness more than the bare identity of knower and known. Modulating attention, second-personal awareness, and ongoing cognitive processing incur additional structural commitments; timeless self-cognition may refuse those richer readings, but then it can’t quietly borrow their devotional content. The verdict is a specification burden, not the claim that the modal structure itself is aware. What the section doesn’t leave in doubt is where awareness is found. A subject, determinate content, and a bearer holding the two together are met in every waking moment of every creature that has one. Whatever is settled about a timeless self-cognition, the awareness anyone has actually encountered is the kind they are having now, and it needed no bearer beyond the one having it.

### 11.4.2 Omniscience
The doctrine of omniscience holds that God knows every truth in one timeless act. The recurring question is how one timeless act bears differentiated, contingent, and temporally indexed content. Knowing requires a knower, content, and epistemic fit; whether it must itself be temporally extended is disputed. A knower with no time of its own can grasp tenseless facts but loses the believer’s “you know me, *now*”: the very contact the doctrine was meant to secure.

The classical doctrine of divine omniscience assembles several reinforcing claims. God knows every true proposition (Anselm, *Proslogion*, Aquinas, *ST* I.14, Swinburne 1977): every truth past, present, future, contingent, necessary, modal, and counterfactual. God’s knowing is one eternal act of comprehension, not discursive succession (*ST* I.14.7).

On contemporary refinements, the eternal act stands in ET-simultaneity (a sui generis relation in which the eternal life is cognitively simultaneous with every temporal moment without itself being temporal) with every temporal moment alike (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991; Leftow 2012; Rogers 2000; Helm 2010). The totality of truths forms a proper class rather than a set, escaping the Cantorian closure pressure (Plantinga 1993; against Grim 1991). Divine knowledge is propositional rather than acquaintance-based, deflecting the worry about phenomenal grasp that Jackson’s knowledge argument (1982) raises when applied to omniscience. Divine middle knowledge encompasses every counterfactual of creaturely freedom, dissolving the foreknowledge–freedom dilemma (de Molina 1588; Flint 1998; Craig 1987). Or, on the open-theist alternative, divine knowledge ranges only over what is determinately the case, leaving genuinely open futures genuinely open (Hasker 1989; Boyd 2001; Mullins 2016).

Each move tries to keep omniscience coherent under the doctrine’s other commitments. Carried to its limit, the doctrine names a knower whose contact with every truth is held in one comprehensive act and whose scope reaches what creaturely knowers can at best approximate.

*The interrogation.* Eleven questions test what the doctrine of omniscience must answer. At bottom the worry is structural. Knowledge, in its creaturely form, is a triconditional relation: a subject (Φ), a holding across time (T) of differentiated content (S), and a fit between the held and the case. The eleven pressures run three at the level of the predicate, eight at the level of the conditions knowledge-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *How does a timeless knower keep contact with every moment, if contact runs through time?* The classical doctrine answers without qualification (Anselm, *Proslogion*; Aquinas, *ST* I.14). God knows every truth in one eternal act, and the *ever* the question places at the verb is, the defender will say, the wrong frame: God knows not at every moment but eternally, in a single act that stands in cognitive contact with each moment alike (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991; Leftow 2012). The reply preserves the doctrine on its own terms, and the present analysis registers it. The concern isn’t lexical but structural, and it survives the careful distinction the tradition draws between *aeternitas* (the Boethian *interminabilis vitae tota simul possessio*, the complete and simultaneous possession of unending life) and *sempiternitas*, mere everlasting duration. Grant the strict timeless reading of *aeternitas* in full. The doctrine still wants the eternal knower in comprehensive cognitive contact with every moment alike: knowing what is the case at each time, sustaining each creature through its time, answering each prayer in its time. Contact-with-every-moment is the temporal scope the predicate can’t shed: whether or not the knower is *located* in time, the content known ranges over every time, and the relation of knowing has to reach each of them. The atemporalist retreat relocates the knower out of time without relocating the known out of time, and it is the temporal structure of the known (not a temporal location of the knower) that the section will press. Contact with truths about every moment imports temporal structure into the content. It doesn’t by itself show that the knower’s act is temporally successive; the burden is to explain the content–mode relation.

**Q2.** *When does a timeless knowing itself occur?* The interrogative sharpens the previous question by demanding a temporal anchor rather than a yes-or-no on temporal reach. The defender’s available reply is the same atemporal one (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 2012): God knows in no *when*; the eternal act has no temporal location at which it occurs, and the question’s presupposition doesn’t apply. The reply is candid, and the present analysis registers it. The concern is the structural condition the predicate runs on. Creaturely episodes of knowing arise and persist in time. A standing disposition or proposed timeless cognitive state need not take a moment to come into being, so the section can’t assume episodic temporality as part of the predicate. The *when* the question asks for is the temporal anchor at which the holding occurs: not the *when* at which the holding’s content is indexed, but the *when* of the holding itself. To answer “in no *when*” is to deny that knowing has a time at which it obtains, which removes the temporal anchor creaturely holdings supply. The doctrine can’t supply a *when* without temporalizing God, and can’t deny one without explaining what does the anchoring instead. The proposal instead owes a positive account of timeless cognitive bearing and epistemic fit.

**Q3.** *How does a knower with no now of its own know the present as present?* The *Kretzmann–Prior puzzle* (Kretzmann 1966; Prior 1962) raises a question the doctrine has answered with care. The defender will grant that an atemporal knower can’t host the indexical *now* in the first-person way a temporally located knower hosts it, and will reply that an atemporal knower can know all token-reflexive facts as facts indexed to whoever occupies a given temporal location: God knows that *the believer at t says or thinks ‘now’*, that *t is Tuesday at 3 PM in the temporal manifold*, and that the manifold contains the moment so indexed. The indexing works as described, and the present analysis registers it. The concern reformulates. The believer’s confession that God *knows me now* isn’t the confession that God knows the indexed proposition *the believer at t thinks ‘now’*. It is the confession of being attended to *as* the believer is at the moment they are. The devotional vocabulary (*known, attended to, heard, responded to, present with*) turns on a relation that is itself temporally indexed at both poles, not on a tenseless registration of a fact about an indexical token. Aquinas’s eternal single act (*ST* I.14) preserves comprehensiveness; what it doesn’t preserve, on the present analysis, is the temporal index that makes the believer’s *now* the believer’s, in any sense distinguishable from the eternal act’s tenseless grasp of every *now* alike.

**Q4.** *From when does a timeless God foreknow?* The question asks for the vantage from which the *fore* operates: a position relative to which the foreknown is later, the cognitive contact prior to the contacted. The available reply on the strict atemporal reading is candid (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991; Leftow 2012): there is no *from when*; the eternal pole stands outside the temporal manifold and contacts every moment alike. The reply concedes that *foreknowledge* on this reading doesn’t name an antecedent grasp; it names tenseless cognitive contact relabeled. The present analysis registers the concession and asks what the doctrine is left holding. *Foreknowledge* in the tradition’s load-bearing uses isn’t a relation that incidentally involves time. Those uses include Boethius’s reconciliation of divine knowing with creaturely freedom (*Consolation* V), Molina’s middle knowledge antecedent to creation (de Molina 1588; Flint 1998), and the prophetic literature’s *I knew you before I formed you in the womb*. It is a temporally-asymmetric relation in which the knowing is prior to the known and the prior is operative as prior. Strip the asymmetry and the doctrine retains the word and discards the relation it names. The believer who is told that God *foreknew* their prayer is being told that the divine attention to the prayer was anterior to its making. The atemporal defense preserves attention without anteriority. What remains is contact, not foreknowledge.

**Q5.** *What makes foreknowledge “fore,” if the knower comes before no moment?* Stump and Kretzmann (1981) define ET-simultaneity as a sui generis relation in which the eternal life is cognitively simultaneous with every temporal moment without itself being temporal. Leftow (1991; 2012) gives a detailed contemporary development. The doctrine does the work the tradition asks of it: keeps God in operative cognitive contact with every moment without temporalizing the divine pole. The concern here is the one §11.3.2, Q2 presses: ET-simultaneity is introduced precisely as a cross-mode relation and doesn’t presuppose ordinary shared time by definition. Its burden is whether the technical relation explains cognition and causation without covertly temporalizing God. The believer’s prayer at 3 PM Tuesday was offered after their morning confession and before their evening weeping; the temporal asymmetry of the offering relative to the surrounding life is part of what the prayer is. ET-simultaneity preserves God’s contact with the prayer by setting the asymmetry aside on the divine side. The prayer’s own temporal structure can remain in the content. What the doctrine still owes is how that ordered content is registered without the registering itself being ordered: the contact the result names, not a proof that the correlate has been flattened into an undifferentiated token.

**Q6.** *Where is a knowledge held, if there is no being anywhere to hold it?* The question asks for the locus of the holding: the being in whom omniscience persists. The doctrine answers without spatial commitment. God’s knowledge is held *in God*: not in a region, not at a place, but in the divine essence that grounds the knowing without itself being a containing thing (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.4). The reply denies the question’s spatial presupposition and relocates the holding from a spatial being to an essential ground. The present analysis registers the relocation and notes its cost. The being the predicate runs on (the Φ among the structural conditions of §1.4) is what stands under the persisting and lets it persist. Bearing knowledge need not require spatial location: minds and abstract informational states are commonly modeled non-spatially. The relevant requirement is a determinate subject or ground of cognitive content, not a literal where. Grounding identifies what makes something the case; it doesn’t perform the holding the predicate names. The divine essence as ground stands as that on which the grasp depends, not as that which stands under it. The doctrine’s available answer denies the *where*; whether the essence-as-ground can also stand under the grasp is the open question, and until it is answered what remains is grounding, not holding.

The coordinate question must be divided between the act, the concrete object, and formal content. A concrete event is the event it is partly by where it falls in temporal, spatial, and causal structure; exhaustive knowledge of it must register those coordinates, even if the knower is alleged not to occupy them. An abstract or formal truth need not itself occupy a physical coordinate. *2 + 2 = 4* isn’t an event at a place. But coordinate-free conceptual content supplies no coordinate-free existent. On the modal-structural reading defended at §8.1.5, mathematical content describes what actual and possible structured pluralities afford; logical and modal content likewise describes relations and constraints across the possible. Its coordinate-freedom is the coordinate-freedom of a concept or structural description, not evidence for a second, aspatial realm populated by concrete knowers.

The resulting claim is narrower than *whatever is known has a coordinate* and stronger than the theological alternative it replaces. Concrete knowledge is knowledge of configurations within the three Conditions. Formal, modal, negative, and general knowledge conceptually describes the structures, limits, absences, and invariances of what Reality affords; it doesn’t add a second class of concrete objects for the knower to encounter. Once the *Reality–Nature Identity* is earned (§3.4), these exhaust the positive subject matter available to knowledge: configurations of Nature and structural truths about their actual or possible organization. A supernatural object of knowledge isn’t excluded by the grammar of *know* alone; it would require an independently established referent outside that exhaustion. If *God* is offered only as coordinate-free conceptual content, the concept is available but the concrete divine subject has been surrendered. Divine self-knowledge can’t restore that subject without circularity, since treating *God* as the extra-natural object already assumes the referent whose availability the appeal to divine knowledge was meant to establish.

**Q7.** *How does a single act hold all truths at once, if the truths form no whole to be held?* Grim (1991) raises the *Cantorian difficulty*: the truths form no set, since for any set of truths *K* the power set ℘(*K*) contains more truths than *K*. No unified cognitive grasp of every truth is therefore available as a totality. Plantinga (1993) replies that divine knowledge is proper-class: not bounded by the power-set limit because not a bounded object at all. The reply is a contemporary response to the Cantorian pressure, and it turns on a distinction the present concern has to honor rather than run past: *comprehending* isn’t *containing-as-totality*. A proper-class grasp can be read distributively (for each truth, that God knows it) without positing a completed whole, *all truths*, that some single act holds as one object. Read that way, Plantinga’s reply doesn’t need the totality the Cantorian result denies, and pressing it as though it did would miss it. So the concern is put to the comprehending mode directly.

Distributing the grasp truth-by-truth relieves the set-theoretic bound but not the structural condition the predicate runs on: each severally-known truth is still a holding, and the believer’s prayer, known severally, is still something that has to be *held* by a knower if *known* is to keep the devotional sense the doctrine trades on. Omniscience is commonly defined distributively—for every truth, God knows it—and need not require all truths to form one set-like object. A separate simplicity question remains about how one act grounds all those differentiated knowledge relations, returning the pressure in the Eleventh interrogation’s form: registering a manifold *as* the differentiated manifold it is requires differentiation within the knowing itself (§11.2.1). Whether the grasp is read as a totality or as distributive comprehending, the believer who hopes to be known is hoping to be held in mind: not to be a member of a class, and not to be one more value over which their knower’s quantifier ranges.

**Q8.** *How does a being that knows everything know what it is like to know nothing?* Jackson’s (1982) *Mary* distinguishes propositional knowledge from acquaintance: a knower may know every true proposition about red without ever having seen it, and may know every true proposition about pain without knowing what pain is like. The difference appears in ordinary cases that require no sin, error, or imperfection. Exhaustive information about an anxious interval of waiting isn’t yet acquaintance with waiting as lived: inhabiting a duration whose relevant future hasn’t arrived, under anticipation, uncertainty, bodily tension, and sustained attention. Exhaustive information about sustained perception of an open horizon isn’t yet occupation of the viewpoint from which it opens: a visual field with orientation, distance, embodiment, and a here from which the there is seen. Those phenomenal characters aren’t decorative additions to the propositions. They are what the experiences are like for the subject undergoing them.

The doctrine therefore forks by what *omniscience* is taken to mean. If omniscience ranges over propositions alone, the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) can know every truth *about* waiting, seeing, pain, surprise, discovery, and ignorance without knowing any of them by acquaintance. The position is coherent at that narrowed scope, but it can’t infer from propositional completeness that God knows what creaturely life feels like or that the believer is known in the sympathetic sense the devotional claim carries. If maximal knowledge includes acquaintance with every mode of consciousness, the classical attributes conflict with its range. Waiting requires temporal duration and an unarrived future; staring into an expanse requires a situated perspective and spatial orientation; pain and vulnerability require affectability; discovery requires passage from not knowing to knowing. To instantiate those phenomenal modes is to instantiate structural conditions atemporality, aspatiality, impassibility, and immutability deny.

The Incarnation is a Christian answer: the Son knows hunger, waiting, pain, abandonment, and death through an assumed human nature, so the divine person possesses creaturely acquaintance without the divine nature changing (Chalcedon; Heb 4:15). The answer genuinely supplies the experience, but only by supplying the very temporal, spatial, embodied, and affectable nature required to undergo it. If the acquaintance belongs only to the human nature, classical divine omniscience considered in itself still lacks it. If it belongs to the divine person in a way that enriches divine cognition, the person bears creaturely experiential content through a real temporal life and the strict exclusion of the Conditions is qualified. The communicatio idiomatum permits the person to be truly predicated through either nature; it doesn’t make the human experience occur without the human nature’s structure. Incarnation therefore doesn’t show that a structureless knower has phenomenal knowledge. It shows how the tradition gives God phenomenal knowledge by union with a structured knower.

The consequence is relational as well as epistemic. A God may possess complete third-person information about a person’s anxiety—its causes, bodily character, thoughts, intensity, and effects—without knowing the anxiety as the person undergoing it. That yields cognitive comprehension and may support benevolent action, but not acquaintance from within the sufferer’s condition. The distinction matters to the confession that God *knows how I feel*. On the propositional reading, God knows exhaustively *that* and *why* the person suffers while never knowing *how it feels* to be that suffering subject. What remains may be perfect beneficence, but not experiential solidarity or *compassio* in its suffering-with sense. The classical effect-only account of mercy accepts this cost explicitly: God relieves misery without being moved by it (§11.9.2). The relational consequence is pressed at §11.8.2: the action runs toward the sufferer, while the sufferer’s state never enters the divine life as something felt.

The same result inverts the argument from design. Grant for the moment that the experienced order is intentionally designed. If its designer lacks phenomenal acquaintance, then anxiety, grief, pleasure, waiting, terror, relief, and bodily vulnerability are designed through complete propositional and causal representation without ever being felt by the designer. The design isn’t uninformed in the propositional sense; it is experientially uninhabited. Its subjects know a dimension of its effects from within that its author knows only by description. It doesn’t follow from this fact alone that the design is bad: that verdict would require the further normative premise that responsible design must include first-person acquaintance with its imposed or permitted effects. What does follow is the epistemic inversion. The supposedly derivative creature possesses acquaintance the perfect designer lacks, and the claim that God alone knows creation completely fails unless *complete* has already been narrowed to exclude how creation feels to the beings living through it. The further moral question is taken up at §11.9.1: whether an act can be called perfectly benevolent when its valuation of creaturely suffering is made without acquaintance with the suffering it permits.

Nor does one incarnate life straightforwardly supply acquaintance with every creature’s phenomenal life. It supplies genuine human vulnerability and particular experiences of hunger, waiting, pain, abandonment, and death. It doesn’t follow that one situated human perspective instantiates what pregnancy, dementia, panic disorder, every form of bodily pain, or every historically and personally particular anguish feels like. The doctrine may treat Christ’s assumed humanity as representative of human nature; phenomenal acquaintance, however, is indexed to the perspective actually lived. Incarnation therefore answers the claim that God has no creaturely acquaintance at all. It doesn’t by itself establish omniscience as acquaintance with every mode and token of creaturely consciousness.

Propositional omniscience doesn’t by itself include every phenomenal acquaintance or ability. Whether perfect divine knowledge must include those modes is a theological and conceptual question. The concern invoked by Heb 4:15 is that the high priest who is *able to sympathize with our weaknesses* is doing more than holding propositions. The pastoral and devotional vocabulary the tradition has performed for two millennia turns on a sense of being known closer to acquaintance than to propositional grasp. Nagasawa (2008) and Stump (2010) develop contemporary positions that try to preserve some experiential dimension of divine cognition; the present analysis registers those attempts and notes that each preserves the experiential dimension by reintroducing structural conditions the strict atemporalist reading had removed.

**Q9.** *How is a free future act known, before there is any fact of it to know?* The dilemma is ancient (Boethius, *Consolation* V; Aquinas, *ST* I.14.13). If *the believer will pray on Tuesday at 3 PM* is true antecedently, then antecedent truth fixes the action, and the action’s freedom in any libertarian sense (the freedom to have done otherwise) is hard to recover. Four positions, each well-developed, address the dilemma. Molinism introduces *middle knowledge* of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom (de Molina 1588; Flint 1998; Craig 1987) and faces the grounding objection: what makes the counterfactuals true antecedently to the actions whose ground they are (Adams 1977; Hasker 1986)? Ockhamism holds that only hard facts about the past are accidentally necessary; the past fact of what God believed about a future free act is soft, because its truth depends on the act (Plantinga 1986). The strategy doesn’t give the creature causal control over the past; it recasts the relevant past fact as future-dependent.

Atemporalism removes the *fore* by removing the temporal location relative to which the foreknowing would be antecedent; the structural concern is Q1’s. Open theism (Hasker 1989; Boyd 2001; Mullins 2016) accepts that genuinely open futures aren’t yet there to be known. Each preserves a different commitment by surrendering another, and each has serious defenders. Ockhamism adds a distinctive burden: it must say why a particular past divine belief isn’t fixed independently of the later act it predicts. If the belief’s content is fixed at the earlier time, calling the fact soft doesn’t show how the agent can do otherwise; if its content varies with the later act, the account makes the past mental state future-dependent. The present analysis is that the dilemma reflects a real tension in the doctrine, and the four positions are the four ways the tension can be relieved given the classical bundle. None of the four preserves the bundle intact.

**Q10.** *What determines that God determines all facts, if that itself is one of the facts?* Pressed to the modal level, the doctrine extends divine knowledge to every modal fact: God knows what is necessary, what is possible, what is impossible. Modal Constitution / S5 invariance (§2.1.3) establishes that modal status doesn’t vary across worlds and isn’t a product of any agent’s exercise (§11.3.1). Divine knowledge of the modal structure is, accordingly, knowledge of a structural fact about how possibility works—not a sovereign reach into a domain the knower has authored. Leftow’s (2012) modal grounding is a contemporary attempt to make the modal frame a product of divine activity; it’s addressed from the necessity side at §11.3.1, Q6. The point added here is that even granting the comprehensiveness of divine knowledge, what omniscience reaches at the modal level is the structure that conditions any knowing whatsoever: Nature that omniscience operates within rather than over.

**Q11.** *How does a partless knower hold a manifold of truths as the differentiated manifold it is?* The pressure is internal to the classical bundle, where omniscience stands beside divine simplicity (§11.2.1): the God of classical theism is without composition, and the divine knowing isn’t an attribute added to the divine being but is identical with the divine essence (Aquinas, *ST* I.3; I.14.4). The doctrine has a developed answer. God knows the manifold of creatures not by being informed by them but by knowing his own essence as the imitable source from which each derives, so that the multiplicity falls on the side of what is known and not in the simple act or the simple knower (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.5–6, I.15, Dolezal 2011). The reply is developed within the tradition, and the present analysis registers it in full: a simple knower can know many things, the defender holds, because the manyness is in the objects while the knowing stays one.

Three cognitive acts must be distinguished before that reply is tested. Knowledge of the arithmetical proposition *2 + 2 = 4* doesn’t require belief in, or even occurrent entertainment of, its negation. Immediate knowledge need not be the product of inference. But to know the proposition *as true* requires its content to be determinate enough to differ from its negation and requires the fit by which the former is true and the latter false. To reason to the proposition is stronger: premises and conclusion must be held apart and ordered so that one is reached through the others. To know that one knows is stronger in another direction: the knowing must take its own act and fit as content without losing the first-order truth it knows. A reflexive act can close that loop without generating an infinite regress, but it can’t close it without articulation among knower, known, knowing, and fit.

The non-discursive reply blocks only the temporal inference. An omniscient God need not reason from premises to conclusion because there is no truth not already known; atemporality is therefore compatible by stipulation with standing comprehension, though not with deliberation, discovery, inference, or learning. It doesn’t follow that the one act can be internally undifferentiated. If *God knows that two plus two is four*, *God knows that two plus two isn’t four is false*, and *God knows that God knows the first truth* are all true, the single act must ground their different contents and their logical order. If nothing in the knowing answers to those differences, the predications collapse into one indiscriminate state and no longer specify what is known or whether it is known as true. If something in the knowing answers to them, the divine cognition contains real articulation even if it contains no temporal succession and no separable parts.

The question is whether *knowing the manifold as the manifold it is* can be had on the doctrine’s terms. To know every truth is to know, among the truths, that this one is distinct from that: to register the differentiation, not the items alone. That is the discriminating-content bar now spent at §11.2.1: the identities of necessaries owe specifying content, not a proof that the knower is composed. Either something in the knowing answers to the distinctness among truths, in which case the account has supplied that content, or nothing does, in which case the distinctness among the known isn’t registered. The eminent-containment move is the same bar again: plenitude without contrast is already closed; leftover content is what the identity of the perfections owed. A partless essence isn’t thereby shown incapable of hosting a manifold. It owes how one actuality non-arbitrarily grounds differentiated known content. Either that account is given, or omniscience hasn’t been specified. The classical bundle can’t keep both the identities and the distinct profiles without the specifying content; it isn’t forced to surrender simplicity or omniscience by composition.

*The burden.* Across the eleven pressures, what *know* runs on becomes visible. They don’t carry equal weight. The result rests on the pressures of time, bearer, and differentiation (Q1–Q6, Q11); the Cantorian, acquaintance, foreknowledge, and modal pressures (Q7–Q10) are real tensions in the classical bundle that reinforce it without being needed for it. Grant the strict timeless reading of *aeternitas*: omniscience still ranges over temporally structured content. The scope sits in the known, but it doesn’t follow without further argument that the knower instantiates the content’s temporal mode.

There’s an argument available at exactly this joint, though it has to be applied with its scope marked. The Encoding Dilemma (§2.6.7) is stated for candidate *grounds* of an actually structured experience: either the ground instantiates the experienced Conditions outright, or it merely encodes them, and an encoding that grounds a live experience is a tokened activity, carried in a medium across distinct vehicle-elements and processed across steps. A timeless knower is a bearer of structured content rather than a ground of experience, so the dilemma doesn’t transfer by simple substitution; what transfers is its fork. Either the knowing instantiates the temporal structure it knows, or it holds that content in some borne mode that isn’t instantiation. The second horn is the one the doctrine needs, and it isn’t free: a mode of holding that is doing real work is a mode with a bearer, and the dilemma’s price falls on the bearer.

The dilemma carries one exemption, and it is the reason this bites here rather than elsewhere. Its limit is the temporal step, which restricts it to *actual, ongoing* cases: a frozen, never-read encoding isn’t covered. That exemption is exactly what omniscience can’t claim. A divine knowing held to be inert, an inscription no one is reading, isn’t the doctrine anyone defends; the knowing is supposed to be fully actual, complete, and live. The doctrine’s own commitment to the actuality of the divine act forecloses the one escape the result leaves open.

What follows isn’t the loaded temporal mode—that would overreach the derivation, and the paragraph above is right that it needs further argument—but the thinner claim that the borne mode is borne, which is the Φ-role at role-resolution, and that the articulation borne is structured, which is the S-role. *Know* also asks for a temporal anchor at which the holding obtains—not the time the holding’s content indexes, but the time of the holding itself—and a knower that denies the anchor still owes the positive account of timeless bearing. The believer’s *known now* is a relation indexed at both poles; an atemporal grasp of an indexed token reaches the correlate and leaves the index unattended. The *fore* in *foreknowledge* operates from a temporal vantage, and ET-simultaneity preserves the term by setting aside the frame the term presupposes: contact without anteriority is contact, not foreknowledge. The holding needs a bearer: grounding is what makes something the case, and bearing is what stands under the persisting, so relocating the holding from the second to the first preserves the word and hasn’t yet shown the relation.

A unified cognitive grasp differs from both distributive comprehending and open-ended class-membership: the believer hoping to be known is hoping to be held in mind, not to be a truth their knower commands severally and not to be a member of a proper class. Pastoral acquaintance does more than propositional grasp: the high priest *able to sympathize* is doing more than holding propositions, and propositional-only omniscience keeps the word by trading away the experiential dimension the tradition has performed for two millennia. The compatibility of foreknowledge with the freedom of the foreknown is real tension, and each of Ockhamism, Molinism, atemporalism, and open theism preserves one commitment of the classical bundle by surrendering another.

Modal knowledge operates *within* the modal structure rather than over it: what is known at that depth is a structural fact about how possibility works, not a proof that Nature is the knower. And the partlessness the classical bundle prizes still owes how one actuality grounds a differentiated manifold: that is the bar spent at §11.2.1, not a proof that either simplicity or omniscience must be surrendered. Knowing, finally, is reflexive in form: taking up what is the case in a way that holds, where the taking requires content differentiated enough for what is taken to be the case it is.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Scope Sits in the Known** · *Diagnostic*

Grant the strict timeless reading outright: omniscience still ranges over temporally structured content, since what is known includes what happens before and after what else. That much is settled by the scope of the knowing rather than by the mode of the knower, and it does **not** follow without further argument that the knower instantiates the temporal mode of what it knows. The pressure therefore doesn’t run from the content back to the knower by itself. What it does establish is narrower and harder to set aside: a knowing whose content is temporally ordered owes an account of how that ordering is registered without the registering being ordered.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Natural knowers provide the paradigm: a bearer holds differentiated content with some degree of epistemic fit. Acquired knowledge is temporally ordered; standing knowledge need not be. Temporally structured objects of knowledge don’t automatically place the knower in time, so the section stops at the contact question: how is the ordering in the known registered by an allegedly unordered knower? Divine omniscience remains determinate only if the account supplies an answer and distinguishes knowing from the bare obtaining of every truth. The positive account of natural knowledge (Chapter 5) doesn’t turn Nature itself into a knower or establish that omniscience was always a disguised predicate of Nature. What it does establish is that the knowing is real wherever it occurs. Holding differentiated content with some degree of epistemic fit is something natural knowers do, and the reaching for more of it is ours: the curiosity that won’t leave a question alone, and the long collective work of answering it, which is unfinished and known to be. Omniscience names the limit of that activity rather than its source. The activity was never on loan.

## 11.5 Intrinsic Value
This cluster gathers the attributes of divine worth taken in itself: holiness (§11.5.1) and beatitude (§11.5.2), God as set apart in value and as complete in self-sufficient blessedness.

Pressed, each owes an account of the conditions it claims to transcend: to be set apart is to stand in distinction, and to be blessed in relation to goods is to be a subject that persists in its own act. Where either is cashed as something done—consecrating, keeping pure, receiving what is given—the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) places the full Structural Requirement at that operation; the intrinsic-purity and self-sufficient readings then owe their own specifying content rather than an intrinsic value floating free of the conditions.

### 11.5.1 Holiness
Holiness includes set-apartness, moral purity, and fittingness for worship. The relational analysis bears most directly on the first strand and shouldn’t be treated as exhausting the attribute. But being set apart is a relation: you are apart *from* something, standing distinct within some field. A being with nothing to stand apart from and no field to stand in isn’t supremely set apart; it is simply indistinct, with the word “holy” laid over it.

The moral strand of the injunction *be holy, for I am holy* has a conduct-form the set-apart reading doesn’t exhaust: *be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect* (Matt 5:48), the *imitatio Dei* the devotional tradition presses into the *imitatio Christi* (à Kempis, *De Imitatione Christi*) and contemporary exemplarist ethics recover as moral modeling on a perfect exemplar (Zagzebski 2017). To imitate an exemplar’s conduct is to reproduce a pattern of acting—to track a way of doing and approximate it—so the injunction to imitate presupposes that the exemplar acts, that there is conduct with determinate content to copy. Causality (§11.7.2) and §11.9 press the conditions of concrete agency and moral exercise: a being defined without those conditions has no creaturely pattern of acting to copy.

That doesn’t yet prove that no analogical or timeless operation remains; it does mean the *imitatio* demand, addressed to conduct, finds its imitable content in a life lived in time. What the devotional tradition in fact imitates is Christ—and the imitable content of Christ is the human life’s: the Sermon’s teacher, the washed feet, the conduct that runs in time through a body. Chalcedon doesn’t treat that life as a second subject’s. The remaining burden is how that conduct is the Word’s, the unity-and-predication question identified at §12.2.3 and §11.3.3, where the imitable content appears exactly where the three Conditions are present. Holiness gives the creature what it can—the set-apartness—and none of the conduct it can’t: the moral exemplar the believer imitates is a T/S/Φ-bearing life, not the wholly other of the set-apart strand.

The classical doctrine of divine holiness assembles several reinforcing claims. Holiness is the attribute under which the others are confessed: the believer’s God is holy before it is simple, and the perfect-being maxima are received as the holiness of God made specific. God is *qodesh*: set apart, separated from the common and the profane (Lev 11:44–45; 19:2; Isa 6:3, the seraphic *trisagion*). Holiness is the first predicate the worshipper reaches for and the one the liturgy repeats: *hagios, hagios, hagios*—holy, holy, holy—the Sanctus.

On the phenomenological refinement, holiness is *sui generis*: Rudolf Otto’s numinous (1917), the *mysterium tremendum et fascinans*—the awe-inspiring and fascinating mystery—a category irreducible to the ethical or the rational, encountered as the *wholly other* before which the creature knows itself as creature. The phrase has a henological precedent older than the phenomenology in the Plotinian One beyond being (*Enneads* V.5; VI.9), whose absolute set-apartness it echoes.

Even so, the numinous is no unmediated given. With Katz (1978), the *wholly other* is itself constituted by the tradition that receives it, not a datum prior to all mediation. Eliade (1957) supplies the comparative record the phenomenology was drawn from, and it is a record of distinctions drawn *somewhere*: the sacred is met as sacred ground, sacred season, sacred object, marked off from profane ground and ordinary time by hierophanies that fall at a place and a moment. The evidence is descriptive, bearing on how the holy is encountered rather than on what holiness must be, so nothing modal follows from it directly. What it does establish is that the tradition’s own inventory of the sacred is an inventory of positions, intervals, and bearers.

In the dogmatic tradition, holiness is God’s transcendent separateness as such. Aquinas treats *sanctitas* as purity together with the firmness by which the mind is fixed on God (*ST* II-II.81.8), and the broader scholastic settlement reads divine holiness as the incorruptible separateness of pure act from every creaturely admixture. Barth (*CD* II/1) develops holiness as the form of the divine love that simultaneously gives itself and resists, judges, and sets apart. Contemporary dogmatics (Webster 2003) recovers holiness as the mode in which each of the other perfections is God’s own.

The doctrine carries two strands the tradition holds together: ontological set-apartness—God’s categorial separateness from everything creaturely—and moral purity—God’s separation from sin and defilement, of which the demand *be holy, for I am holy* is the creaturely echo. Carried to its limit, the doctrine names a being set apart not by degree but by category: the wholly other, separate from all that isn’t God by the very kind of being it is.

*The interrogation.* Four questions test what the doctrine of divine holiness must explain. What underlies them is that set-apartness is a relation before it is a perfection. To be holy is to be set apart, and to be set apart is to stand distinguished from what one is apart from, within a manifold in which the distinction can obtain (S), maintained as the same set-apart being across what would erase the distinction (T and Φ). The classical God is defined without the three Conditions. The four pressures run one at the level of the predicate, two at the level of the conditions holiness-talk runs on, and one at the level of what is left to revere when the conditions are gone.

**Q1.** *What is set apart, when nothing stands over against it to be set apart from?* Set-apartness is contrastive: the holy is holy in distinction from the common, as the sacred is sacred against the profane. The contrast requires a field of the not-holy for the holy to be marked off within. The classical reply is that divine holiness isn’t the relational set-apartness of one item marked off from others but the intrinsic perfection of the divine nature—holiness as the purity of pure act, not a standing-apart from creatures (*ST* II-II.81.8; the simplicity tradition of §11.2.1). It does what the doctrine asks of it, shifting holiness from relational apartness to intrinsic purity. That is a legitimate change of strand; the remaining question is how intrinsic purity is specified and related to moral value. On the relational strand, a wholly other with no manifold to be other within isn’t supremely distinct but indistinct; the intrinsic-purity reading escapes that verdict only by carrying the specification burden just noted. That burden is dischargeable, and Adams’s theistic Platonism discharges it (1999): the purity is specified as the transcendent Good, and the tie to value is resemblance to it. What the specification costs is weighed at §11.9.1, where the resemblance-base meets the same fork in the register of goodness. The local point is narrower: intrinsic purity becomes specifiable at the price of a paradigm determinate enough to be resembled in stated respects.

**Q2.** *From what does the wholly other stand apart, if it stands in no position relative to anything?* Otto’s numinous and Barth’s holy God are encountered as *wholly other*, and otherness is a standing-over-against, a positional-relational predicate that requires S, the manifold within which two stand distinguished as the ones they are. The same point is pressed for presence at §11.8.1: a being equidistant from every point alike has no position from which to stand apart. The classical reply relocates the otherness from spatial standing to the analogical transcendence of the Creator–creature distinction. The concern here is the one raised at §11.8.3 for analogy: the Creator–creature distinction, if it is a real distinction and not a verbal one, is itself a structural relation—directed, asymmetric, obtaining within a manifold that holds the two terms apart. Levinas’s absolutely Other (*Totality and Infinity*, 1961) is borne by the face and indexed to the encounter; strip the indexing and the otherness loses the contrast that made it other. The comparative pattern runs the same way: on Eliade’s survey (1957) the sacred is never encountered unlocated, but always as a *this place, not that one* and a *this time, not that one*, so that the religions’ own practice of marking the holy is a practice of drawing positions within a manifold. That reports how the holy has been met, not what it must be. A defender remains free to hold that the encounter is structured while its object isn’t, and what that leaves standing is the contact burden the third question presses rather than a result settled here.

**Q3.** *How is anything made or kept holy, if both consecration and purity require a being that stands in time to bear them?* Holiness in the scriptural register is verbal before it is adjectival: *qadash* is to consecrate, to set apart, and what is consecrated is then kept pure: the sabbath, the temple, the people are *made* holy and *guarded* holy. Both moments are structural. Consecration is a transition from the common to the set-apart, and a transition requires T, a before and an after across which the same thing is first common and then holy. Purity is the maintained integrity of a being that could be defiled and isn’t, a property with a bearer (Φ) and a standing across what would compromise it. The classical God is the source of all sanctification yet is immutable, atemporal, and immaterial, and on strong simplicity sustains no real relation to what it sanctifies; its purity, likewise, is the purity of a being with nothing to keep intact and no defilement so much as possible.

The classical reply is that God sanctifies eternally and without change in God (the change is in the creature, the immutability settlement of §11.3.3) and that divine purity isn’t the contingent cleanness of a defilable being but the impossibility of defilement in pure act. The concern here is the one §11.3.3, §11.4.1, and §11.9.1 reach from their own sides: a sanctifying that terminates on the creature at a moment is a temporally located effect, though a classical theorist can posit a timeless cause. Impossibility of defilement is a modal purity claim, not by itself an ∅-like absence. Both moments take their content (the transition and the maintained integrity) from the temporal side of the relation; the timeless-sanctifier model faces a contact burden there, not yet a semantic failure.

**Q4.** *What is left to revere, once the wholly other is conceived without the otherness that made it holy?* The conceivability question for divine predicates in general is taken up at §11.8.3; the local form concerns reverence. The numinous, conceived without the three Conditions, terminates at the point reached at §11.8.3: a referent for which *holy* retains no determinate content, only the affective residue of an encounter the conditions of encounter have been removed from. The reply is Otto’s own: holiness is the very category that exceeds conceptual capture, and the demand for determinate content mistakes the numinous for a concept. The concern here is that exceeding conceptual capture is consistent with the set-apartness belonging to the modal structure rather than to a being beyond it. The mystic’s silence before the Holy is the honest terminus of refusing to predicate; the worshipper who goes on to address, revere, and stand before the Holy One re-enacts, in every act of address, the positional and relational structure the encounter requires.

*The burden.* The four pressures lay out the structural shape of holiness. Holiness, on its set-apartness strand, needs a field of the not-holy for the holy to be marked off within; an apartness apart from nothing is indistinction, not the maximum of distinction. It needs a manifold in which the wholly other can stand over against what it is other than; otherness with no position is the language of distinction without its content. Creaturely consecration involves transition. A timeless sanctifier model retains an asymmetric causal relation while relocating transition to the creature, and therefore faces a contact burden rather than semantic failure. It needs a bearer whose integrity is maintained across what would defile it; purity with no possible defilement and no bearer risks collapsing into ∅’s immunity rather than a being’s holiness; the modal-purity reading owes the difference. The set-apartness strand can be analogically relocated to the categorial difference between a modal structure and its occupants: the way Time, Space, and Substance stand to every inhabitant as that which isn’t itself one of the inhabitants.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Set-Apartness Is a Relation Before It Is a Perfection** · *Diagnostic*

The doctrine holds two strands together, and they come due differently. On the set-apartness strand *holy* is contrastive and positional: the holy is marked off from the common, within a manifold that holds the two apart (S), kept the same holy thing across what would erase the distinction (T and Φ), and the tradition’s own inventory of the sacred—sacred ground, sacred season, consecrated object—is an inventory of positions, intervals, and bearers. Withdraw every condition of position and persistence and what is left isn’t the maximum of distinction but indistinction, with the word laid over it. On the intrinsic-purity strand the relational demand lapses and a specification demand takes its place: what the purity consists in, and what ties it to value. That demand is answerable, and the answers available supply a paradigm determinate enough to be resembled in stated respects. Either strand can be held. What the four pressures don’t turn up is a way of holding either one that doesn’t spend the conditions it was introduced to do without.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Nature isn’t holy. Set-apartness is a contrastive relation within Nature, and structural non-exteriority isn’t moral purity or worship-worthiness. The divine predicate therefore divides. If *holy* means set apart from the common, the account must specify the contrast and the field within which it obtains. If it means intrinsically pure or supremely valuable, it must specify the purity or value standard and why the alleged subject satisfies it. Calling God “wholly other” while withdrawing every contrast condition doesn’t maximize set-apartness; it removes the content by which the holy was distinguished from the common. What remains is either a revised evaluative predicate with stated truth conditions or an empty honorific. That dichotomy is the doctrine’s to settle, and settling it doesn’t touch what the word was tracking. Set-apartness is felt from one side. What a person meets in it is the distance between what they are and what they could be, and that recognition is exercised by the one who has it rather than conferred by what it is directed at. The weight is accurate about the distance and mistaken only about where the far end stands. Whatever grounds the standard, the seeing of the shortfall is ours, and it was never held elsewhere.

What the word keeps isn’t nothing, and what it keeps isn’t parochial. The pull toward what is set apart is a real orientation: a creature weighted toward something it registers as standing out from the rest of its field. Traditions sharing none of this doctrinal bundle reach for the same protective move—Maimonides withdrawing every positive predicate (Maimonides (c. 1190) 1963), the *Tao Te Ching* opening on a name that can’t be the thing named (Laozi (c. 4th c. BCE) 1963)—and each inherits the same question, which is what remains specified once the withdrawal is complete. The orientation isn’t the error. It is doing what orientations do, and doing it accurately: something here is set apart from something. What the doctrine adds is a claim about where the weight points, and that claim is what the contrast conditions were needed for.

### 11.5.2 Beatitude

Beatitude is God’s perfect blessedness: the fullness of self-sufficient joy in which God, lacking nothing, wants nothing it doesn’t already have. The pressure is that the same tradition calls God a lover who wills the good of creatures, a giver whose goodness pours outward, a will that creates what need not have been. Desire and hope ordinarily concern an unattained good, but willing and giving need not arise from lack. The classical distinction between desire and beneficent willing is therefore central rather than something the section may erase. And once God is said to will goods that the world’s history may not deliver, a further question opens that the doctrine can’t close: can such a being be satisfied?

Classical theology assigns God beatitude: the perfect and self-sufficient blessedness of a being that possesses the complete good and so lacks nothing it could want. The doctrine inherits the eudaimonist conception of blessedness as the self-sufficient life (*makária*, the life of one who, having every good, needs nothing further, Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* (4th c. BCE) 1984, I.7, X.6–8) and locates that life in God as its unqualified instance. Aquinas treats the attribute directly: beatitude (the perfect good proper to an intellectual nature) belongs to God supremely and essentially, one with the act of divine self-understanding, so that God isn’t made blessed by anything beyond it but *is* its own beatitude, with every other beatitude contained eminently in the divine (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.26).

The doctrine binds beatitude to the attributes already examined: a being that is *actus purus*, with no unrealized potential (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.3.1), and *perfectus* in the sense of *completus*, lacking nothing the having of which would make it greater (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.4), is a being for which nothing is left to want; its blessedness isn’t the satisfaction of a desire but the eternal possession of the good it is. Yet the same tradition holds that God loves (wills the good of the creature, Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.20) and that the divine goodness is diffusive, pouring outward in creation. The contemporary literature divides on whether blessedness so understood survives as a coherent predicate of a personal God. Theistic personalism takes God to be everlasting rather than timeless, a person whose perfect well-being is lived through time (Swinburne 1977; Swinburne 2004; Mullins 2016); the dipolar tradition assigns invariant blessedness to an abstract pole and a growing, world-enriched joy to a concrete pole (Hartshorne 1941; Hartshorne 1948); and the account of love as union and desire for the good of the beloved (Stump 2010) makes the beloved’s good internal to the lover’s own flourishing. The position the classical doctrine, fully stated, holds is that God’s blessedness is complete, invariant, and underived: nothing the creature does or fails to do adds to or subtracts from the divine joy, which is God’s eternal possession of its own infinite goodness.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test what the doctrine must answer. Underneath them the concern is structural: blessedness, in the sense that distinguishes it from bare self-identity, is the *satisfaction* of a being that could have wanted, and wanting, satisfaction, and the rest that follows attainment are features of substances oriented through Time toward states not yet actual.

**Q1.** *How does a being that lacks nothing desire, will, or hope?* To desire is to be oriented toward a good not yet possessed; a temporal act of willing an end may be directed at a state of affairs that doesn’t yet obtain; to hope is to lean toward a future not yet actual. Each predicate carries, in its ordinary sense, a reference to the not-yet: the temporal order Time names (§1.4). The classical reply removes the not-yet: God doesn’t desire the good as absent but possesses it eternally, and God’s will isn’t a motion toward an end but the eternal act by which the end is willed (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.20). The concern here is that this empties the predicates of the content that made them predicates of a *blessed* being rather than of a bare fact: a timeless will needs an account of contingent objects and effects, but willing another’s good need not involve frustrated desire, and joy need not be analyzed solely as desire-satisfaction. The orientation-toward-the-not-yet-actual that *desire* and *hope* name is the structural feature Time carries; the doctrine keeps those words only by removing it, and the non-deficient willing that remains must be specified without them.

**Q2.** *Can a being that lacks nothing want anything—and if it can’t want, can it love or create?* Perfection in the classical sense is *completus*: God has every property the having of which would constitute a greater being, and lacks nothing it could have (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.4). Pressed from the property-side to the want-side, completeness entails that God lacks no state of affairs it could want, because wanting is the relation of a being to a good it doesn’t have. But a being that is *actus purus* has no potency to be actualized (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.3.1), and wanting is precisely the potency to be moved by an unattained good. The reply that God *wills* the good of creatures without *wanting* it (willing as pure act, not as desire, Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.20) preserves plenitude by distinguishing the willing of an end from the wanting of it. The concern here is that the distinction, pressed, leaves creation and love without the feature that made them acts of a blessed will: to will the creature’s good and bring about a contingent state requires intentional direction, but it isn’t therefore wanting under another name. A beneficent agent can choose an outcome without needing it for completion. The dilemma is therefore conditional: either God wants the goods it wills, and isn’t complete, or the willing is non-deficient beneficence, in which case the doctrine still owes an account of why *this* outcome is chosen that never borrows the orientation wanting supplies.

**Q3.** *Can God be satisfied?* Three commitments the tradition holds together generate the question. First, God loves universally—wills the good of every creature (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.20). Second, on orthodox eschatology, not every creature attains the good God wills for it; some are finally lost. Third, God’s blessedness is complete, invariant, and impassible—not added to or diminished by what creatures do (§11.3.3, §11.3.4). Add the contestable value-theoretic premise that divine love includes a desire whose satisfaction contributes to divine well-being. Classical theorists reject that premise, and traditions also differ over whether God wills every creature’s final salvation in the same sense. The three commitments and the premise can’t all hold. If some willed good is finally unattained, a being whose blessedness tracked its loves wouldn’t be fully satisfied, but the doctrine says God is fully blessed. If God is fully satisfied regardless of whether its loves attain their goods, then the willed goods aren’t goods God wanted attained, and universal love is emptied. And if the divine satisfaction varied with the world’s history (full where its loves are attained, less than full where they aren’t), beatitude would change, which immutability and impassibility forbid. The trilemma therefore arises only under a desire-satisfaction model plus a specific account of universal salvific will; it isn’t internal to every doctrine of beatitude. The trilemma is the beatitude-register form of the composition pressure developed at §11.2.4: perfect love, perfect blessedness, and invariance don’t compose without relaxing one of them.

**Q4.** *Which gives way: universal love, complete satisfaction, or impassibility?* The tradition’s resources for the trilemma are systematic, and each resolves it by relaxing one of the three commitments. The atemporal-eternalist holds that God’s beatitude is timeless, so there is no before-and-after of satisfaction to vary, but this relaxes the sense in which God wills goods *for* a history whose outcomes aren’t yet actual, the pressure of Q1. The pure-act Thomist holds that *satisfied* and *unsatisfied* apply to God not univocally but only analogically, but this concedes that beatitude-as-enjoyment isn’t literally predicated, and the analogical move faces the homonymy-or-univocal-core dilemma pressed at §11.2.4 (Q1). The open theist and the theistic personalist hold that God’s blessedness genuinely tracks the world and can be less than it would otherwise be—God grieves what is lost (Swinburne 1977; Swinburne 2004; Mullins 2016)—but this relaxes immutability and impassibility (§11.3.3, §11.3.4) and concedes a temporal, affected God.

The dipolar theist assigns invariant blessedness to the abstract pole and world-tracking joy to the concrete pole (Hartshorne 1941; Hartshorne 1948), but, as §11.3.4 and §11.2.4 press, the two poles are one subject only through the directed dependence between them (§10.3.3), which imports the structural roles the abstract pole was meant to escape. The Reformed-Edwardsian holds that God’s last end is the manifestation of its glory (Edwards (1765) 1989), so that the finally lost manifest divine justice and no willed good goes unattained, but this relaxes universal love, narrowing what God wills the good of. The Aristotelian-Thomist returns beatitude to its eudaimonist root: God’s blessedness is the self-contemplation of its own goodness, *makária* in the strict sense, and doesn’t consist in the attainment of any creaturely good, but this relaxes the diffusiveness of the good and the love of Q2, severing blessedness from the willing of creaturely goods altogether. Every exit pays in one of the three commitments; none holds all three.

**Q5.** *By what is God blessed—by its own goodness, or by the attainment of what it wills?* The eudaimonist root makes blessedness self-sufficient: God is *autarkēs*, blessed in the contemplation of its own complete goodness, needing nothing outside itself. The relational commitments make blessedness include the good of what God loves: a God whose joy is wholly indifferent to whether its loves attain their goods doesn’t love them in the sense the believer’s life rests on. If blessedness is self-sufficient, then creation, love, and the creature’s good add nothing to it, and the diffusiveness of the good is a giving that costs and returns the giver nothing: beatitude sealed off from the history it is said to govern. If blessedness includes the attainment of willed goods, then it depends on what is received and brought about (on states of affairs realized through Time, in Space, by the persistence of substances) and is conditioned by the three conditions the doctrine placed beatitude beyond. The concern here is that *blessed* is either self-sufficient, in which case it names not a relation to any good but a completeness Nature’s non-exteriority already supplies, or relational, in which case it is conditioned by the three Conditions. The doctrine wants both: the self-sufficiency of a being that needs nothing and the responsiveness of a being whose loves are answered.

*The burden.* Carried through, the five pressures bring out what the predicate *blessed* actually depends on. Desire and hope are ordinarily oriented toward the not-yet-actual, while will can be construed as non-deficient intention; a beatitude that removes the orientation keeps the words only if joy can be specified apart from desire-satisfaction, and that specification is still owed. Wanting is the potency to be moved by an unattained good, which pure act excludes; plenitude and the diffusiveness of the good compose only through a non-deficient willing whose account of directed choice remains open. The satisfaction-trilemma, under its desire-satisfaction premise, can’t be answered while all three commitments stand: universal love, complete blessedness, and invariance then don’t compose, and every classical exit relaxes one of them. And blessedness is either self-sufficient (in which case it revises beatitude into the non-exteriority already established for Nature, which isn’t yet joy) or relational, in which case it is conditioned by Time, Space, and Substance. What survives is a disputed distinction between non-deficient self-sufficiency and relational joy. Structural completeness may illustrate the first, but it doesn’t itself possess joy.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Blessedness Trilemma** · *Conditional Disjunction*

If God desires creaturely goods, and some are finally unattained, which of universal love, complete blessedness, and invariance goes?

- **If universal love and complete blessedness are kept,** then invariance relaxes. Divine well-being answers to creaturely outcomes.
- **If universal love and invariance are kept,** then love is no longer desire. Some loved goods go unattained without diminishing blessedness, which requires a non-desire account of love.
- **If complete blessedness and invariance are kept,** then creature-directed love narrows. Creaturely attainment contributes nothing to divine well-being.

All three can be retained only by changing at least one operative sense. Under the stipulated desire model, no branch preserves universal love, complete blessedness, and invariance together.

*Scope.* The trilemma is conditional on the desire-satisfaction model and the relevant universal-love claim. Doctrines rejecting either premise don’t fall within it, but owe the alternative account their rejection invokes.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Self-subsistence genuinely belongs to Nature at the structural level; blessedness doesn’t. *Blessed* describes a subject’s relation to goods, wants, satisfaction, or flourishing. A subject that literally desires nothing, receives nothing, risks nothing, and undergoes no satisfaction may still be called complete, but the affective and eudaimonic content has been surrendered. The classical account must therefore choose what *divine beatitude* contributes beyond aseity. If it names joyful self-possession, the cognitive and phenomenal predicates require specification. If it names only dependence on nothing outside, it revises beatitude into the non-exteriority already established for Nature. The revision may be coherent. It should not be presented as evidence that Nature is blessed. Nor does it leave blessedness unlocated. Relational joy—wanting, receiving, and being satisfied in what is received—belongs to subjects who could fail to have it, and that vulnerability is what distinguishes joy from mere completeness rather than falling short of it. Whatever aseity secures, the flourishing the word points at is the kind that can be lost, and it is the only kind anyone has had.

## 11.6 Life

The tradition calls God *the living God*, not merely existent but supremely alive, life in its highest instance. The difficulty is what *life* has meant since the tradition’s own founding texts: to be alive is to possess immanent operation—to act from within, as a source of activity rather than a thing merely held in being. In Aquinas this isn’t simply locomotion or creaturely alteration, and it need not mean passage from potency to act in God. The pressure must therefore be stated more carefully: if divine life is pure, changeless immanent operation, what determinate content makes it an operation rather than the bare standing of the essence? Temporal transition is one realization of living activity, especially in responsive life; it isn’t presupposed by the Thomistic predicate.

Scripture’s God is *the living God*, and the philosophical tradition makes life a divine attribute of the first rank. Aristotle’s unmoved mover is itself life: the actuality of thought is life, and God is that actuality. The divine life is the eternal self-contemplation of *noēsis noēseōs*, thought thinking itself (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* (4th c. BCE) 1984, XII.7, XII.9). The definition the attribution runs on is set out elsewhere in the same corpus: to be ensouled is to hold within oneself the principle of one’s own activity (*De Anima* (4th c. BCE) 1984, II.1–2), so that *living* names a source of operation rather than a kind of stuff. Aquinas systematizes the attribution: life belongs to God most properly of all, because those things are most properly called living that move themselves. Life is immanent self-activity, operation that proceeds from the agent and remains within it, and God, as pure act, is the highest instance of such immanent operation, the act of self-understanding (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.18.1–4). To live is the highest grade of being; God, as the fullness of being, is alive in the fullest sense: *vita Dei*, the life identical with the divine essence. The doctrine keeps the God of the covenant from collapsing into an inert principle by binding life to actuality: God is most alive because most fully in act.

*The interrogation.* Four questions test what the doctrine must supply once *life* is required to carry its own content. The pressure beneath them is that the tradition’s own definition of life (immanent self-movement) must be told apart from bare standing without the transition the classical attributes forbid.

**Q1.** *If divine life is immanent operation without change, what makes it operation rather than inert standing?* Aquinas defines living things through self-motion (*ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.18.1), but orders the notion analogically (Wippel 2000): in intellectual life the relevant perfection is immanent operation, and in God that operation is pure actuality rather than a passage from potency to act. Grant the steelman. The objection isn’t that every operation must be creaturely locomotion or temporal alteration.
