It is that *operation* must have determinate content—an exercising subject and an intelligible operation distinguishable at least in account from bare existence—if *living* is to mark anything. If no such distinction is available even at the level of real content, life adds nothing to essence; if it is available, simplicity owes the specifying content that makes the operation tellable from the essence’s standing. Temporal transition enters only when the doctrine also claims response, attention, choice, or action toward changing creatures.

**Q2.** *If God’s life is the pure actuality of self-understanding, what does that understanding do that bare being doesn’t already do?* Aristotle and Aquinas locate the divine life in contemplation: the changeless act of thought thinking itself. The Thomist anticipates the obvious pressure (that an act which never passes from considering to considered is an act in name only) and blocks it on the doctrine’s own terms: *life* and *operation* are predicated of God not univocally but analogically (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, I.13), naming *immanent operation*, activity that remains wholly within the agent and needs no transition, in a mode proper to the divine being. It is the reply the doctrine leans on here, and it has to be met on the same ground as at §10.2.1.

Analogical predication earns its content only if the predicate tracks a real correlate in the divine subject, standing in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely instance (§10.2.1, on the criterion) (McInerny 1996; Rocca 2004; Burrell 1986); a predicate that tracks no such correlate isn’t analogical but empty. Ask what the correlate of *operation* is. The Thomist denies at the outset that divine understanding is a taking-up that runs from understanding to understood: in God knower and known coincide, the operation remaining wholly within, with no interval to cross and no order to run. Grant exactly that. The pressure isn’t that God’s self-understanding *must* be a directed crossing, but that it must be *something* if it is to be operation at all: an exercise the divine subject performs, tellable apart from the bare standing of its essence. At minimum, such an exercise costs determinate content and a bearer; where it is responsive or directed toward a changing term, it also incurs order and relational distinction. The dilemma is therefore not whether the divine act must cross a creaturely interval the Thomist has already denied, but whether, stripped of every distinction between operation and bare essence, anything is left that *operation* still names. The horns are the ones drawn for *actus purus* (§10.2.1) and now spent as specifying content (§11.2.1): either the divine operation is a genuine way of being-in-act, tellable apart from the essence’s standing, or it is no way at all (an act with no exercise, no relatum, no passage) and then it is indistinguishable from the bare standing of the essence, and *life* has added nothing to *existence*.

**Q3.** *If God is alive only by being responsive to what happens, how can the living God be the ground of happening rather than a participant in it?* The process tradition presses exactly this: the immutable, impassible God is *dead* (affected by nothing, responsive to nothing) and only a God who genuinely changes with the world is alive (Hartshorne 1948; with the metaphysics at Whitehead 1929 and the systematic statement at Cobb and Griffin 1976). The dipolar God is alive because responsive. But responsiveness has a cost (§10.3.3): to receive and respond is to stand in a directed dependence ordered toward a changing term, and a being alive by such responsiveness instantiates the structural conditions rather than standing beyond them. Life understood through responsiveness therefore requires the structural conditions. The resulting dilemma is that an unresponsive God preserves aseity at the cost of responsive life, whereas a responsive God preserves life at the cost of classical aseity.

**Q4.** *If God’s life, knowledge, will, and being are one undivided act, what does calling God living add to calling God existent?* On divine simplicity (§10.2.1), God’s life isn’t distinct from God’s understanding, willing, or being: God *is* the divine life, without composition. But then *living* marks no feature that could be present or absent, and where that leads has already been traced (§11.2.1). Either *life* picks out a determinate content distinct from bare existence, an operation tellable apart from the mere standing of the essence, and the identities of those necessaries owe specifying content; or it picks out nothing distinguishable, and *the living God* says no more than *the existing God*, the predicate emptied of the vitality it was asserted to carry. That is the discriminating-content bar, not a proof that simplicity has already failed by composition.

*The burden.* The four pressures isolate two levels. At the minimal Thomistic level, life as immanent operation requires determinate operative content and a bearer; it doesn’t follow merely from the word *operation* that every divine act passes through temporal stages. At the richer level of responsive, attentive, choosing, or creature-directed life, the operation differentiates states or terms, is ordered toward an outcome, and is sustained by an agent—there the T/S/Φ burdens arise. Contemplation counts as life only where it is exercised, and an exercise stripped of interval, order, and carrier has yet to show what *operation* still names. Responsiveness counts as life only at the cost of embedding in the structure the response crosses. And life predicates something of its bearer only where it is distinguishable from bare existence, which is the specifying content simplicity still owes. What *life* survives as, once the pressures have run, isn’t a grade of being a static essence could hold but, at the richer level, directed activity in a bearer; at the minimal level it remains a revision burden on what *operation* still names.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Operation Must Be Tellable From Standing** · *Diagnostic*

The tradition defines life as immanent operation, activity proceeding from the agent and remaining within it, and predicates it of God most properly of all. The predicate holds only where the operation can be told apart from the bare standing of the essence, since that is the whole of what *living* was added to *existing* to mark. Two levels come due separately. At the minimal level the demand is content and a bearer: an exercise the divine subject performs, distinguishable in real content from its simply being what it is, which is the specifying content the identities of necessaries owe, or isn’t distinguishable, and then *the living God* says what *the existing God* already said. At the richer level, where the life is responsive, attentive, or directed toward creatures, the operation also differentiates states, runs in an order, and is sustained through them, and those are the structural conditions rather than an alternative to them. The two levels aren’t answered by one reply: what secures aseity leaves the minimal demand outstanding, and what secures responsive life meets it by taking the conditions on.

**Depends on:** No Third Option Between Contrastive and Empty (§10.2.1)

*The reclamation.* Living systems are natural bearers that maintain and reproduce their organization through ordered, differentiated activity. Nature hosts life; Nature isn’t thereby one organism. A Thomistic account may revise life into changeless immanent operation, but then it owes positive content distinguishing that operation from the bare actuality of an abstract truth. A devotional “living God” ordinarily contrasts a responsive agent with an inert abstraction. The stricter the account makes divine life changeless, nonresponsive, and without metabolic or developmental activity, the less of that contrast survives. The argument therefore exposes a revision burden; it doesn’t transfer biological life to Nature as a whole. Nor does it leave *life* unclaimed. Ordered, differentiated activity sustained by a bearer is what the living are doing while the doctrinal question stays open, and it is what the word has named all along. Whatever a changeless immanent operation turns out to be, the paradigm the word was learned from is the one we are inside.

## 11.7 Agency
The active arm opens with agency: the attributes of divine doing: power (§11.7.1), causality (§11.7.2), interaction (§11.7.3), and sovereignty (§11.7.4). Each says that God acts: brings about, causes, engages, and governs.

Here the structural analysis bites most directly: any act that brings something about runs from cause to effect along an asymmetric ordering, through distinct relata, with an agent that persists across the doing, which is what the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) places at any concrete operation. A being defined as lacking every such role can’t perform an act; a concrete act instantiates the three Conditions at the operation.

### 11.7.1 Omnipotence

Omnipotence is “all-powerful,” but the same tradition calls God “pure act”: without any unrealized potential. Those pull against each other, since power is usually the capacity to do what isn’t yet done. And whatever power comes to, exercising it (creating, sustaining, intervening) is an act, and acting runs through time, place, and substance. The argument presses both seams.

Theists call God omnipotent and gloss the word as *all-powerful*. *Omnipotens* is *omnis* + *potentia*: all-potency, every capacity. But in the Aristotelian frame the tradition inherits, potency is the unrealized side of act: the capacity not yet exercised, what could be otherwise but isn’t yet. And the same tradition defines God as *actus purus*: pure act, entirely without potency. Aquinas is explicit that in God there is no potentiality, no unrealized capacity, no movement from what isn’t yet actual to what is (ST I.3.1–2; I.9.1). The central attribute is therefore held in two directions at once. The standard Thomistic resolution distinguishes active power from passive potency: God has unlimited active power without unrealized passive potency (ST I.25.1, Stump 2003; Dolezal 2017), so that the gloss *all-powerful* reads *omnipotens* against active power rather than against unrealized capacity.

Around this resolution the classical doctrine assembles a set of reinforcing claims about how that power operates. God created the universe ex nihilo, with no antecedent matter, time, or space (Aquinas, ST I.45; cf. Gen 1:1). God conserves all things in being moment by moment (ST I.104). And God concurs with creaturely action, so that creaturely causation occurs through divine causation rather than alongside it (ST I.105, Flint and Freddoso 1983). God also acts in history through miracles, in which divine causation overrides ordinary causal regularity (Hume (1748) 1999; Swinburne 1970; Larmer 2014). Ash’arite occasionalism is the parallel development in the Islamic tradition (Al-Ghazali, *Incoherence of the Philosophers* XVII, Frank 1992; Griffel 2009). It holds that God is the sole genuine cause, creaturely events being only the occasions of God’s acting.

The tradition then refines the scope of the power itself. On Aquinas’s canonical refinement, omnipotence is the capacity to bring about whatever doesn’t involve contradiction (ST I.25, with Mavrodes 1963; and Frankfurt 1964 on the stone-paradox). On Geach’s reading, the more theologically traditional term is *almighty* (Geach 1973). Wierenga (1989) develops the contemporary analytic account. And on the most ambitious reading, divine power extends to the modal structure itself (Leftow 2012). Taken at that most ambitious reading, the doctrine names a being whose power is comprehensive enough to author what is possible, sustained moment-by-moment in everything that obtains, and unrestricted by any condition external to itself.

*The interrogation.* Six questions test what an account of omnipotence must supply. The structural pressure here has two layers. First, the active-power refinement preserves the gloss but not the work: active power is power-*to*-actualize-this-rather-than-that, and what divine power is asked to do (create, conserve, govern, intervene, answer) has its content in the actualization of one determinate state rather than another. Without a contrast between the state actualized and the state not actualized, the verb *actualize* loses determinate content; the doctrine of pure act, taken strictly, must say where that contrast lies. Second, concrete efficient causation, on the analyses developed at §2.4, carries influence from a bearer (Φ) across a relation between distinct terms (S) in a temporal direction (T), and the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) is defined as without temporal succession, spatial extension, or material composition. The six pressures run one at the level of the predicate, five at the level of the conditions causation-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *How does creation cause a world, if there is no state it brings the world out of?* *Creatio ex nihilo* holds that God brought the universe into being with no antecedent matter, time, or space. Aquinas (ST I.45) develops the doctrine carefully: creation isn’t a change, since change requires a subject that undergoes the change, and prior to creation there is no subject. Creation is the production of being itself, with nothing antecedent for the production to occur in.

The reply preserves the doctrine against the classical objection that nothing comes from nothing. The concern here is the cost of the preservation. Causation, on the analysis given, is a transition from a state in which the effect doesn’t obtain to one in which it does. If creation isn’t a transition—if there is no antecedent state for the transition to be from—then creation, on the classical reading, isn’t a case of the structural relation the analysis examines. The classical reply is that *cause* applies to creation analogically rather than univocally, and the analogical application preserves what the term performs. What analogical predication can carry is measured at §11.8.3. The point added here is that what *create* names, on the doctrine fully stated, is closer to a primitive of divine doing than to an analyzable case of causation, and the difference is precisely the structural conditions the doctrine has placed beyond divine being.

There is a further pressure on the modal side. If creator-status is essential to God—if God is necessarily a creator—then in every world where God exists, God creates; if God exists necessarily, creation is necessary. The Thomist’s standard distinction between God’s act-considered-in-itself (necessary) and the act’s *terminus ad extra*—its outward effect toward creation, which is contingent—requires a real ground for the distinction in God, which strict simplicity disallows. Mullins (2013; 2016) and Tomaszewski (2019) press this from inside the literature. The doctrine has wanted necessary creator-status and contingent creation simultaneously, and these are two commitments joined only by the term *one act*.

Pruss and Rasmussen’s necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction (*Necessary Existence*, 2018, ch. 5) offers a middle position: God necessarily creates *some* world—creator-status is essential—but creates this particular contingent order among alternatives. The necessity attaches to the creator-status, not to the specific creation. In the power register, the distinction deflects the modal-collapse concern by locating contingency in the terminus of the creative act rather than in the act itself. The concern for the Pruss/Rasmussen reply at Q1 is whether the selection among contingent termini itself requires the directed-act structure creation-as-power consists in: the being must differentiate the termini it selects among, order the selection toward one of them, and bear both the creator-status and the selecting act. The distinction shifts the modal-collapse concern from the level of creator-status to the level of selection, where the structural analysis applies.

The active-power reply should be granted exactly as stated before it is tested. Pure Act denies passive potency—the capacity to be completed, improved, or changed—not active power, the capacity to actualize an effect. Needlessness therefore doesn’t by itself entail powerlessness. What active power can’t surrender is a real modal contrast: to be able to create freely is to be able to create rather than refrain, or to actualize this terminus rather than another. That yields a trilemma. If different possible termini answer to different content in the divine intention or act, strict simplicity has admitted differentiation. If the divine reality is intrinsically identical across the alternatives and nothing on the divine side grounds which terminus obtains, the selection is brute: logically possible, but no longer contrastively explained by God. If there are no genuine alternatives, the necessary act fixes its terminus and modal collapse follows. A defender may choose the brute-selection horn as a primitive libertarian act; that blocks a contradiction, but it also relinquishes the sufficient explanation of *why this creation rather than another*. Thus the earned result isn’t that Pure Act is verbally incapable of action. It is that active power with contingent effects costs the doctrine either differentiation, brute selection, or modal collapse.

**Q2.** *How does power make a thing possible, when making it already takes its being possible?* Aquinas (ST I.25.3) restricts omnipotence to what is logically possible: God can’t make a square circle, not because divine power is limited but because *square circle* names no possibility for power to range over. Descartes (Letters to Mesland 1644) takes the opposite turn: God’s power extends to the eternal truths themselves, including logical and mathematical necessity. The contemporary mainstream sides with the Thomistic restriction (Swinburne 1977; Wierenga 1989; Flint and Freddoso 1983). The modal-frame question is worked from the necessity side at §11.3.1 and from the logic-grounding side at §10.1.3; the concern returns here in the form §3.4 revisits. The Thomistic restriction either makes logical necessity a condition on divine power, in which case the deepest modal facts aren’t products of divine activity (§11.3.1), or extends divine power to the modal structure itself (Leftow 2012), in which case the conditions any exercise of power presupposes are themselves the products of an exercise. The first horn keeps coherence by surrendering scope; the second keeps scope at the cost of self-grounding the doctrine hasn’t made structurally tractable.

**Q3.** *What is unlimited in a power confined to possibilities it never authored?* Frankfurt (1964) raises the puzzle directly: can God create a stone too heavy for God to lift? The Thomistic resolution is well-developed (Mavrodes 1963; Plantinga 1967): omnipotence is the capacity to bring about logically possible states of affairs, and a stone too heavy for an omnipotent being to lift isn’t a logically possible state of affairs. The resolution is correct as far as it goes. The concern here is what that reveals: omnipotence is defined relative to a modal space whose status is already in question (§3.2.6). The paradox dissolves under the Thomistic restriction; what the restriction leaves is a doctrine of omnipotence indexed to the modal structure, with the being’s authorship over the modal structure either denied (collapsing scope) or affirmed (making the authorship circular). The pattern generalizes.

The *stone paradox* is one of three structurally analogous cases the tradition treats under the same restriction: the immovable stone (Φ-logic), the square circle (S-logic), and the past-altering act (T-logic). The three are analogous rather than identical (the immovable stone fails by modal-conceptual necessity, the square circle by geometric necessity, the past-altering act by temporal-logical necessity) but the Thomistic restriction dissolves each the same way, by declaring it not a possibility for power to range over; what the restriction concedes, taken across the three together, is that what *power* can do is indexed to the three structural logics §3.5.7 isolates: the modal structure any exercise of power presupposes. The limit the theist concedes so readily in logic, that omnipotence reaches neither the immovable stone nor the square circle nor the altered past, was a limit of structure all along: what logic forbids in the three cases is what the structural logics of substance, extension, and succession forbid. The paradox is a symptom; the concern is the condition the symptom registers.

**Q4.** *How does a cause come before its effect, if it stands at no time at all?* Causation runs in a temporal direction: the cause precedes or is simultaneous with the effect, and the effect doesn’t precede the cause. The analyses developed at §2.6 are explicit on this point, and even the most permissive contemporary accounts (Lewis 1973a; Salmon 1984; Dowe 2000) preserve the asymmetry as constitutive. The classical God, defined as atemporal, has no temporal location relative to which the *from*-state of any causal act is before and the *to*-state is after. The doctrine of eternal causation addresses the difficulty by setting aside temporal direction, treating God’s act of creation, conservation, and governance as one eternal act (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991; Leftow 2012). The concern here is the one pressed at §11.3.2 for eternity and §11.4.2 for knowledge: setting aside the temporal asymmetry preserves the term *cause* and removes the temporal asymmetry that distinguishes causation from a static relation between abstracta. A logical entailment between premises and conclusion doesn’t *cause* the conclusion in the sense the doctrine of providence trades on. The doctrine wants the relation between God and creation to be more than logical entailment, and on the efficient-causal reading the more is T.

**Q5.** *By what power does a being produce the very conditions its power runs on?* Q2 raises the modal-scope question; Q5 returns to it directly. Carried that far, the doctrine extends divine power to the conditions any exercise of power presupposes: God authors what is possible, not merely what is actual (Leftow 2012). The concern here is the one pressed again at the level of agency (§11.7.2): to author the modal frame is to do something whose conditions appear to require the three Conditions—a transition between not-having-authored and having-authored, a position from which the authorship is exercised, and a substantial being through which the activity runs.

The pressure runs equally on the target side. Creating X presupposes that X is possible to create, since *create* names the actualization of what is antecedently possible: the verb has no determinate target where the target has no modal standing, and the actualization-relation runs from a possibility into an actuality of that possibility. Necessary Possibility fixes the order without turning it into a temporal sequence. If X is possible, then X is necessarily possible; if X is impossible, no act makes X possible. And if X is actualized, that actuality itself witnesses ◇X and therefore □◇X. Divine creation can’t first confer X’s real modal standing and then—or in the same act—actualize X, because the standing doesn’t admit an onset. The classical reply can instead be recast as an atemporal grounding claim: X is necessarily possible in virtue of the divine essence. That claim no longer describes an act altering the modal range. It enters the essence-prior dispute at §7.2.1 and inherits the grounding-contact burden rather than escaping it through simultaneity.

Agent-side and target-side conditions converge on the same modal field: the field that realizes the act and the field that supplies the target are one field, and a field that realizes and supplies the exercise of power can’t be the exercise’s product. To preserve *author* while removing those conditions is to keep the verb and lose the conditions that gave it content. Pruss (2011), Mullins (2016), and Mullins and Byrd (2022) raise structural concerns from inside the literature. The point added here, from the side of power specifically, is that the doctrine’s modal extension—omnipotence over modality—reaches for what Nature is and locates it in a being beyond Nature. Nature is what underwrites possibility because Nature is what possibility is the modal status of. No Unconditioned Essence blocks the relocation of modal legislation into a divine essence structurally prior to the field. No Outside Selector (§10.4) supplies the actuality-side limit: a divine selector may be a personal articulation explaining a subconfiguration, but can’t stand outside or constitute a surplus within total actuality to select the whole.

Pruss’s PSR pressure runs symmetrically against the inversion. If Nature underwrites possibility because it is the necessary modal structure, the PSR demand returns at the level of Nature itself: what grounds Nature’s having the specific structural conditions it has—the three Conditions in their particular constitutions—rather than other conditions or none (*The Principle of Sufficient Reason*, 2006; *Infinity, Causation, and Paradox*, 2018)? The argument’s terminus (*Nature has them as a necessary fact*) is what Pruss identifies as the PSR-violating move: treating brute structural necessity as the terminus of explanation without asking what grounds the necessity’s specific character. The asymmetry the inversion requires is that Nature’s structural necessity is less explanatorily objectionable than a God’s. It depends on a reply to Pruss’s PSR demand that the book’s positive account carries at §4.7 (resting on §2.8).

**Q6.** *How can a creature do otherwise than God moves it to do?* If divine causation conserves all things in being moment by moment (ST I.104) and concurs with all creaturely action (ST I.105, Flint and Freddoso 1983), the question is whether creaturely actions retain the not-being-determined-by-divine-causation that libertarian freedom requires. The Banezian–Molinist debate (Báñez vs Molina, 16th–17th c., Garrigou-Lagrange 1936; Flint 1998) is the classical site. Banezian physical premotion holds that God moves the will to its act in such a way that the act remains genuinely the creature’s own; Molinism holds that divine concurrence (God acting with a creaturely cause without replacing it) operates through middle knowledge of what the creature would freely do. Both positions are serious; both face well-developed contemporary objections: the grounding objection against Molinism, the question of how physical premotion preserves freedom against Báñez. The concern here is parallel to those raised at §11.3.4 and §11.7.2: the doctrine wants comprehensive divine causation and genuine creaturely freedom, and the standard refinements partition the explanatory contributions in ways that preserve the verbal predicates without resolving the underlying tension.

*The burden.* The six pressures, considered together, reveal what the predicate *power* commits to. Power consists in actualizing this rather than that, and active power without a this-rather-than-that for the act to be the actualization of preserves the term while removing the modal contrast power consists in. *Creation* read as production without transition is closer to a primitive of divine doing than to the analyzable causal relation *cause* names, and the analogical defense registers the distance from causation rather than closing it. The carrying of influence runs through a bearer; a divine essence as ground stands as what exercise depends on, not as what performs the carrying. It runs across a relation between distinct terms, since without that distinction there is nothing for the influence to pass between. And concrete efficient causation runs in a temporal direction: eternal causation preserves the term *cause* while removing the temporal asymmetry that distinguishes causation from logical entailment, while the doctrine of providence requires the relation between God and creation to be more than entailment. At the deepest layer the doctrine reaches, power that authors the modal structure is power exercising the conditions it authors, and the account becomes circular; the comprehensive-providence/creaturely-freedom partition preserves the verbal predicates without dissolving the underlying tension. *Potens*, read against the conditions of its application, is the capacity of some configuration within Nature to issue its potency into act; the three Conditions are what makes the issuing possible. That doesn’t make Nature an omnipotent agent.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Power Is a This-Rather-Than-That** · *Diagnostic*

Power consists in actualizing this rather than that. Active power with no this-rather-than-that for the act to be the actualization of keeps the term while removing the modal contrast the term consists in. *Creation* read as production without transition is nearer a primitive of divine doing than the analyzable causal relation *cause* names, and the analogical defense registers that distance rather than closing it. Carrying influence runs through a bearer, and a divine essence specified only as ground hasn’t thereby been given one under another name.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Every real power is a capacity of some configuration of Nature, and no exterior reservoir enlarges Nature’s modal range (§4.9). Necessary Possibility fixes the range; No Unconditioned Essence closes essence as an exterior legislator; No Outside Selector fixes the location of any selecting operation. Together they leave actualization and arrangement as operations of Nature while excluding a power that expands Nature’s real possibilities or selects total actuality from an exterior or surplus position. This doesn’t make Nature an omnipotent agent. Omnipotence attributes selection and actualization to a personal articulation; pure actuality adds the denial of unrealized potency in that bearer. The classical account must explain how those claims coexist and how one unchanged act produces contingent rather than necessitated effects. The structural conditions don’t concentrate all power into a cosmic will. What they do secure is that power is a capacity of some configuration, and that some of those configurations are people. Being able to do a thing and then doing it is what *potens* names in the only case anyone has met. Such power is distributed rather than concentrated, and exercised rather than held in reserve, but it isn’t thereby a lesser quantity of the same thing. It is where all of it has ever been.

### 11.7.2 Causality

Scripture’s God causes: creation, providence, miracle, judgment, and answer to prayer are presented as effects obtaining because of divine activity. The governing question here is therefore causal, not merely agential: what distinguishes *God causes E* from the static claim that E follows from the divine nature, and what relation connects cause to effect? Intention, choice, and freedom matter as features of the personal-cause model, but they are species-level commitments inside the larger causality question, not substitutes for it.

The classical doctrine of divine agency assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *actus purus*, pure act, with no potency, no transition, no movement from could-be-willing to is-willing (Aquinas, *ST* I.3, I.19). God’s willing is identical with God’s being; the willing and the willed are one eternal act (Augustine, *De Trinitate* XV; Aquinas, *ST* I.19). God acts in history (election, exodus, incarnation, resurrection) and answers prayer, and works miracles in which divine causation overrides ordinary causal regularity (Hume (1748) 1999; Swinburne 1970; Larmer 2014).

Contemporary refinements place the eternal divine act in ET-simultaneity (eternal-temporal simultaneity: the relation by which an eternal being is present, in full, to every temporal moment alike) (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991; Leftow 2012). Divine causation is *primitive* rather than a special case of structural causation (McCann 2012; Stump 2016). Divine sovereignty extends to the modal structure within which acts are intelligible at all (Leftow 2012). Open theism takes the reverse turn and pulls God back into time, allowing genuine response to creaturely action (Wolterstorff 1975; Hasker 1989; Mullins 2016).

*Which kind of cause?* The distinctions matter because the structural costs aren’t uniform. Aristotle’s four *aitiai* are four kinds of explanatory answer: material cause is what something is made from, formal cause is the organization or form by which it is the thing it is, efficient cause is the source of a production or change, and final cause is the end for the sake of which a process occurs (*Physics* II.3; *Metaphysics* V.2). Contemporary metaphysical grounding adds a non-causal dependence relation—one fact obtains in virtue of another—whose priority need not be temporal (§2.4.3). Agent-causal theories add a sourcehood claim: the substance or agent, not merely an event, causes the action (§5.11). Efficient-causal history is already distinguished from final causation in the account of biological function (§5.2) and causal from non-causal grounding in the Structural Requirement. Divine creation, miracle, intervention, and answer to prayer ordinarily require efficient or agent causation; conservation requires an asymmetric sustaining dependence; the Aristotelian unmoved mover operates as a final cause; exemplary and participation accounts can resemble formal causation or grounding. One causal sense can’t answer for all the others. The questions below therefore don’t demand physical transmission of every dependence. They ask which sense is claimed, whether it can carry the particular theological work assigned to it, and what distinguishes that relation from mere entailment or co-obtaining facts.

Each move tries to keep agency from being a creaturely capacity writ large. Carried to its limit, the doctrine names a being whose every doing is one eternal act, whose sovereignty extends to the modal structure within which doing is intelligible at all, and whose creatures’ acting is held within the divine causing without compromising its being theirs.

*The interrogation.* Seven questions test the causal claims at their proper levels. Q1–Q2 examine the personal-cause species—intention and choice. Q3 asks how a non-spatial cause discriminates its target. Q4 distinguishes immediate efficient causation from non-causal grounding rather than assuming that every cause needs a physical medium. Q5 asks whether final causation can carry the productive and responsive work assigned to divine agency. Q6 tests how one timeless act explains temporally differentiated effects. Q7 examines claimed authorship of modal possibility. Concrete efficient causation has the clearest structural profile: a source produces a difference in a determinate effect across an ordered relation borne by real terms. That profile incurs the three Conditions under the Concrete-Entity Test. Final causation and metaphysical grounding need not involve transmission or temporal succession, so they aren’t refuted by failing that test; their burden is to show that the thinner relation can perform the work for which creation, providence, miracle, judgment, or answer to prayer invoked *cause*. Personal agency adds a further issue. Alternative-possibilities theories locate agency in a live modal contrast, while compatibilist and actual-sequence theories locate it in a reasons-responsive process owned by the agent. Strict Pure Act supplies neither familiar resource, which creates a specification burden rather than a definition-level impossibility. Analogical and apophatic replies are taken up in the form they have in the literature at §11.8.3.

**Q1.** *How does God intend this rather than that, if there is no “that” left undone?* On an alternative-possibilities account, intending *this rather than that* requires a live contrast: a determinate state the agent doesn’t actualize set against the state the agent does actualize. *Actus purus* (Aquinas, *ST* I.19) forecloses that contrast deliberately: in God there is no passive potency, no unrealized alternative, no movement from could-be-willing-otherwise to is-willing-this, only the single eternal act in which willing and being are identical. The Thomistic distinction between active power and passive potency therefore answers one formulation of the worry but leaves the agency-making question: what within the eternal act makes it an intention rather than the static entailment of effects from essence? The believer who prays “let this cup pass” is asking for a difference between an actualized and an unactualized alternative. A compatibilist or actual-sequence account may deny that the difference is required; that route is tested below rather than excluded here. Stump (2003) and Dolezal (2017) treat *intention* analogically. The present burden isn’t that analogical predication is illicit, but that the analogue must identify what plays the role that modal contrast or an agency-producing process plays in familiar cases.

Hartshorne’s dipolar account addresses Q1 by locating agency in the concrete pole: the concrete pole’s acts are genuine intentional acts, involving directed transition, modal contrast, and responsive selection among the open alternatives creaturely co-creation supplies. The abstract pole provides the invariant structure within which the concrete pole’s agency runs; the concrete pole provides the modal contrast Q1 requires. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3, in the local form of an agency dilemma: if the composite subject’s acts belong to the concrete pole, the concrete pole is a temporal, T-instantiating being whose acts have all the structural features Q1 identifies; if the concrete pole’s acts aren’t the composite subject’s acts, the abstract pole bears an acting subject at one remove across the pole-relation: the directed dependence shown at §10.3.3 to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. Either way the agent the doctrine’s predicates are about instantiates the structural roles rather than escaping them.

**Q2.** *What does God choose in willing the best, if the best leaves nothing else open to will?* On a libertarian account, willing isn’t fixed by the inputs that supply its content: the ranking over options permits divergence, the selection rule doesn’t return a unique output, or the agent contributes something not already fixed by the ranking and option set. The classical doctrine appears to fix all three. The ranking is the divine nature, identified with the good (Aquinas, *ST* I.19.1; Augustine, *De Trinitate* VIII). The option set is the modal landscape (§11.3.1; §2.3). The selection rule is *wills what is best*, formalized in Leibniz’s claim that God selects the *best of all possible worlds* (*Théodicée* 1710). If those elements uniquely determine one world, the defender must say what distinguishes the willing from the output of a function.

Spinoza recognizes that the doctrine, taken to its logical extreme, collapses Leibnizian optimism into necessitarianism (*Ethics* I, prop. 33). Adams (1972), Rowe (2004), and Kraay (2010) develop the no-best-world variant, in which the selection rule has no unique optimum to track; Aquinas himself allows that God could create no world or a different world (*ST* I.25.6, ad 1). That variant preserves modal openness but owes a non-arbitrary selection account. The compatibilist reply—divine freedom is action from God’s own nature without external constraint—is a genuine alternative to the libertarian premise, not a verbal failure by definition. Yet action from nature alone is too weak: a thermostat also operates from its constitution, while robust compatibilist accounts add reasons-responsiveness, self-governance, or an actual process owned by the agent. Applied to Pure Act, the reply must identify the analogue of that difference within an eternal identity of essence and willing. Hartshorne proposes an aesthetic-creativity alternative: God necessarily exemplifies the highest aesthetic order (abstract pole), but the specific content of the best isn’t fixed in advance. The concrete pole’s willing is the best responsive integration of creaturely contribution rather than selection from a predetermined set (*Man’s Vision of God* 1941; *Creative Synthesis and Philosophic Method* 1970). The remaining question is whether the abstract pole’s necessary order uniquely determines each response; if it does, the function-output concern returns, and if it doesn’t, the account has supplied the openness strict Pure Act lacks.

A Frankfurt-style reply blocks any inference from the absence of alternatives alone: genuine agency need not require that the agent could have done otherwise (Frankfurt 1969); the same point for creaturely freedom is developed at §12.5.2. Frankfurt cases instead hold the actual sequence fixed. A reasons-responsive process runs from the agent’s antecedent state to the act, and that process, not a live alternative, grounds responsibility; the counterfactual intervener is idle because the actual mechanism already suffices. Strict Pure Act supplies no such sequence: no antecedent state and no transition from could-be-willing to is-willing, since willing and being are numerically one eternal act rather than the terminus of an unfolding history. The argument therefore identifies a two-route burden rather than a universal impossibility proof. Alternative-possibilities accounts need a live contrast; familiar compatibilist and actual-sequence accounts need an agency-producing process. Pure Act supplies neither. A defender may propose a third, atemporal ground of agency, but must state what makes the eternal fact an act or choice rather than static entailment.

**Q3.** *What makes this effect the target of a cause that has no position relative to it?* Causal direction doesn’t generally require the cause to occupy a metric location. A non-spatial cause could discriminate its target through intentional content, and omnipresence could remove distance without removing aboutness. The sharper question is what supplies that discriminating content. If the divine act is identical at every point and wholly simple, what makes it productive of this effect here rather than another effect elsewhere? Inman (2017) and Hudson (2009) develop careful accounts of divine presence and action without bodily position. They relocate target-direction to primitive divine intention. That is a coherent strategy, but it routes the burden back to Q1–Q2: the intention must contain enough differentiated content to select this target without acquiring the internal structure strong simplicity denies. The issue isn’t that action literally needs a launch coordinate; it is whether the theory specifies an asymmetric cause–effect relation with a determinate target.

**Q4.** *What makes an immediate dependence causal rather than merely grounding or entailment?* Efficient causation need not always transmit influence through an intermediate physical medium. A direct cause may relate immediately to its effect, and metaphysical grounding is expressly non-causal and non-temporal. McCann (2012) treats divine causation as primitive rather than as a special case of ordinary event causation; Pruss develops a parallel account in *Actuality, Possibility, and Worlds* (2011), retaining metaphysical dependence without an intermediating medium. The live burden is therefore discriminative, not mechanical: what makes *God causes E* different from *E is grounded in God*, *E follows from God’s nature*, or the bare conjunction of God and E? Calling the relation primitive can be legitimate, but the primitive must still have truth conditions that distinguish causal production from those neighboring relations. If the account supplies asymmetric dependence alone, it may have specified grounding. If it also assigns creation, intervention, or response, it must explain what adds the productive or agential content those claims require.

**Q5.** *Can a final cause create, intervene, or answer prayer—or only explain what draws things?* The question separates two causal senses that the older vocabulary can make look continuous. Concrete efficient causation produces a difference in an effect; final causation explains a process by the end toward which it is directed. At the Aristotelian origin, the Prime Mover (*Metaphysics* XII) moves the celestial spheres as the object of desire: the spheres’ orientation toward the good supplies the motion, while the mover remains unchanged. That is genuine final causation within Aristotle’s explanatory scheme, so its lack of transmitted motion isn’t a defect by its own standard. Aquinas’s First Way (*ST* I.2.3), however, terminates a regress of movers in a first unmoved mover, while the wider doctrine also assigns God efficient production, conservation, providence, miracle, and response. Final causation can explain why an ordered process tends toward an end. It doesn’t by itself specify the productive act by which a world begins, a contingent effect obtains, or a petition is answered. The choice is therefore not “change or no cause.” It is: which causal role is claimed, and can the unchanged final cause carry the efficient-causal and personal functions the theology also assigns?

At the contemporary end, the pressure concerns responsive efficient agency rather than final causation as such. Wolterstorff (1975) gives the alternative its canonical form: God is everlasting, not timeless; Hasker (1989) and Mullins (2016) extend the move into open theism. The repair responds to the concern because a God who undergoes states can differ between not-yet-responding and responding. Its cost is structural: a being whose acting occurs through changing states instantiates T, and the directed relation to a creature incurs the accompanying S- and Φ-roles at the operation. Strict *actus purus* keeps changelessness but must explain responsive efficient action without any difference at the source; divine everlastingness supplies the difference by locating the acting subject within the conditions the classical doctrine had placed it beyond. This is a dilemma for the responsive efficient-cause set, not an argument that an unchanged final cause is unintelligible.

*The premise the First Way spends.* Both replies already considered bargain over what a mover must undergo. A separate consideration reaches the same doctrine without entering that bargain. The First Way opens on motion, and the Movement Line (§2.4.9) carries that same premise, through Necessary Possibility, to □(T∧S∧Φ): if movement is really possible, the structural Conditions hold necessarily. The argument from motion therefore grants at its first step what its conclusion needs to be false, since a mover standing outside T, S, and Φ requires there to be an outside to stand in. The point doesn’t turn on whether an unmoved mover could move, and so doesn’t contest the moving-without-being-moved distinction the doctrine is built on; it denies the location rather than the capacity, which is why the final-causation reply already considered doesn’t reach it. A Thomist may of course decline ◇M, but declining it costs the First and Second Ways together (§2.4.7). What survives here is what survives throughout the chapter: not a mover outside Nature, but a determinate atemporal ground carrying the grounding-contact burden (§10.4).

**Q6.** *Why does one timeless act produce this effect now rather than earlier?* Boethius (*Consolation* V.6) describes eternity as the simultaneous and complete possession of unbounded life. Stump and Kretzmann (1981) refine this into ET-simultaneity; Leftow (1991; 2012), Rogers (2000), and Helm (2010) develop and defend atemporal models. A timeless cause need not itself acquire a new state when a temporal effect begins, so the effect’s date doesn’t automatically temporalize the cause. The explanatory question remains: what in the one unchanged act accounts for the difference between the effect’s obtaining at 3:14 PM on Tuesday and its not obtaining a minute earlier? An eternal intention can contain tensed or indexed content only if the account explains how that differentiation is present without succession in the knower or will. ET-simultaneity supplies a relation between the eternal act and every temporal moment; it must additionally explain why one moment is the terminus of this effect. The point isn’t that the cause must share the effect’s clock time, but that temporal specificity belongs to what must be explained.

**Q7.** *Can an act ground the possibilities it must already be possible to perform?* Theistic activism holds that God grounds what is possible rather than selecting from a modal landscape independent of God (Leftow 2012). The view need not posit a transition from “not possible” to “possible”; an atemporal grounding relation can be invariant. Its pressure is instead reflexive. Divine activity is described as possible, necessary, free, or capable of producing alternatives, and those descriptions already use modal structure to characterize the act said to ground modal structure. §11.3.1, Q6 and §11.7.1, Q5 engage that circularity from the necessity and power sides. Leibniz avoids authorship of possibility by having God select the best among independently available possibles (*Théodicée* 1710), but then divine sovereignty operates within a modal field it doesn’t create. The stronger activism route owes a non-circular account of how divine nature fixes modal facts without presupposing the alternatives, capacities, and counterfactuals it is invoked to ground.

The creation question then divides. If creator-status is essential and God exists necessarily, God necessarily creates something; if creating this order follows necessarily from the same simple act, contingency collapses. The Thomist distinguishes God’s necessary act considered in itself from its contingent *terminus ad extra*, while Pruss and Rasmussen distinguish necessary creating from the contingent order created (*Necessary Existence*, 2018, ch. 5). That distinction blocks the inference from necessary creatorhood to the necessity of this world. It leaves a selection question: what grounds the difference between possible termini when the divine act is simple and invariant? A libertarian answer needs modal openness; a compatibilist answer needs an agency-making structure that explains why this terminus issues from the act. The doctrine need not surrender necessary creatorhood or contingency by definition, but it owes the bridge between them.

The same pressure appears when creation is considered as a whole. A creator who brings about a reality genuinely other than itself must stand in a determinate relation to the created term. If created reality is external to God, creatorhood is a real outward relation—the directed relation the preceding questions analyze. If created reality is within God, creaturehood becomes a differentiation or modification in divine reality, pressing against simplicity and the Creator–creature distinction. If the relation is real only on the creature’s side, the remaining question is what makes *God creates* a determinate explanatory claim rather than a formula for creaturely dependence. The point isn’t that creatures make an infinite God quantitatively larger; infinity isn’t a quantity. It is that a genuinely other creation can’t be related to a simple, atemporal God without either restoring a structural relation or withdrawing the positive content of creation.

*The burden.* Seven pressures yield, between them, the structural commitments of determinate causation, with personal agency as the relevant application here. Concrete actualization differentiates a before from an after and one realized condition from another. Alternative-possibilities accounts of choice require modal contrast; familiar compatibilist and actual-sequence accounts require a reasons-responsive process owned by the agent. Strict Pure Act supplies neither, so an atemporal agency account owes a distinct agency-making difference rather than being excluded by stipulation. Where an act lands depends on directional structure: action identical at every point lacks the asymmetric agent–target relation along which influence is reckoned, and relocating directedness to a primitive of intention shifts rather than answers the specification burden. A concrete act runs through a structural relation between cause and effect. A primitive immaterial cause can remain a live proposal only if it specifies enough of that dependence for *cause* to distinguish explanation from co-obtaining facts.

Responsive causation bears differential change; the open-theist response preserves responsiveness by locating God within the conditions the classical doctrine had defined God against. The believer’s reported moment of grace has temporal specificity; ET-simultaneity must explain what on the divine side answers to that specificity without importing succession. Concrete doing also has a bearer in whom it originates. The unmoved mover and final-cause models may describe a different kind of dependence, but neither is automatically the concrete act devotional language attributes. Finally, the modal structure the doctrine wants to author functions as a condition on every concrete exercise of power. For concrete, directed causal action, the three Conditions are the structural conditions the cause–effect relation runs on. A determinate analogical or atemporal cause isn’t excluded by being non-temporal; it bears the narrower burden of specifying why the effect obtains because of this source rather than merely co-obtaining or following by stipulation.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Pure Act Owes an Agency-Making Difference** · *Diagnostic*

Concrete actualization differentiates a realized condition from what preceded it; strict Pure Act contains no such transition. That fact doesn’t by itself disprove atemporal agency. It divides the familiar routes: alternative-possibilities accounts require live modal contrast, while compatibilist and actual-sequence accounts ground agency in a reasons-responsive process issuing in action. Strict Pure Act supplies neither. A proposed atemporal agency therefore owes a distinct account of what makes the one eternal fact an act or choice rather than the static entailment of effects from essence.

**Dependency routes:** concrete actualization—Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4); concrete bearer—Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7)

*The reclamation.* In its productive sense, causality is what occurs when one configuration makes a difference to another; agency is the self-modeling, selecting species of that wider relation. Final causation and metaphysical grounding are different explanatory relations and aren’t defective merely because they lack physical transmission or temporal succession. The decisive question is which relation a theological claim needs. Creation, miracle, intervention, judgment, and answer to prayer present God as an efficient or personal cause; conservation presents an asymmetric sustaining dependence; the unmoved mover can operate as a final cause; participation and exemplary-cause accounts may state formal or grounding relations. A thinner relation may be coherent while failing to carry the thicker work. The positive natural account of agency as directed change is developed at §5.11. Concrete agency belongs within Nature’s causal order and incurs the Concrete-Entity Test. What *God causes* must name, if it is to remain a determinate explanatory claim, either a specified cause–effect relation bearing the costs appropriate to its causal type or an analogical primitive whose relation to efficient, final, formal, or grounding explanation is independently defended. The argument establishes that burden. It doesn’t define every causal relation as temporal action. What isn’t in question is that the productive relation obtains, or that some of its instances are ours. Making a difference to how things go—weighing options and then bringing one of them about—is the self-modeling species that Will (§5.11) describes, and it is the case from which *cause* was learned. Whatever the theological use turns out to require, causing is something we are doing.

### 11.7.3 Interaction

Scriptural narratives present repeated interaction: God speaks, Israel answers, and God responds. Sequence, reciprocal influence, and two parties that persist through the exchange are what those narratives report. The classical doctrines put every one of those features on the creature’s side only. That still leaves an asymmetric relation. What it doesn’t leave is interaction in the responsive sense the stories appear to name.

The doctrine of divine interaction holds that God acts upon, communicates with, and is responsive to creatures while remaining timeless, immutable, impassible, and absolutely simple. Aquinas treats the relation as one of pure asymmetry: creatures are really related to God, but God is only logically related to creatures (*Summa Theologiae* I.13.7), so that what scripture calls God’s “turning toward” or “drawing near” is a change in the creature rather than in God. Boethius secures the same point through eternity-as-*tota simul*: God’s act of providence is a single, undivided gaze on the whole temporal order, and what appears to us as sequential response is, in him, one timeless willing (*Consolation* V.6). Anselm and the Reformed scholastics inherit this picture and harden it: the impassibility tradition (Augustine, *City of God* IX.5; Aquinas, *ST* I.20.1 ad 1; Turretin, *Institutes* III.xi) treats every scriptural ascription of grief, anger, or change-of-mind as anthropopathism: accommodation to creaturely modes of speech rather than literal predication.

Yet the same tradition affirms that Yahweh struck Egypt, spoke from Sinai, walked the wilderness with Israel, took flesh in the womb of Mary, ate fish on a shore, wrote in the dust, and at every point bilaterally engaged particular creatures at particular times. The doctrine therefore affirms divine interaction while locating every constitutive feature of interaction—sequence, responsiveness, persistence of relata, affect, change of mind, and physical contact—exclusively on the creaturely side.

*The interrogation.* Eight questions ask how a being defined by timelessness, immutability, impassibility, and simplicity can be the subject of any of the predicates that make scriptural narrative legible as encounter. The eight pressures run two at the level of the predicate (responsiveness and affect), two at the level of the conditions interaction runs on (sequence and change of mind), two at the level of the bearer (the persisting relatum and the incarnate subject), and two at the level of contact (physical engagement and petitionary dependence).

**Q1.** *How can a being whose life is one timeless, immutable act be the subject of sequence—acting, then being acted upon, then acting again?* The back-and-forth is constitutive of interaction, not incidental to it. Boethius’s *tota simul* eternity collapses this sequence into a single timeless act. Stump and Kretzmann’s ET-simultaneity (1981) attempts to recover bilateral structure within timelessness, but the recovery requires that distinct temporal beats register as distinct in God, which is what the doctrine of immutability was meant to deny: the objection Mullins develops at length in *The End of the Timeless God* (2016). Mullins (2016), Wolterstorff (1975), and Hasker (1989) argue that the scriptural picture (Moses pleading, God relenting, the conversation continuing) is unintelligible without temporal sequence in God himself. Tradition’s reply preserves the doctrines by locating on the creature’s side every feature that could make the narrative interaction rather than monologue.

**Q2.** *How can a being that is acted upon by nothing be bilaterally responsive, as interaction requires?* The wilderness account is structured by call and answer: Israel cries, God responds; Israel rebels, God grieves; Moses intercedes, God turns. Impassibility (Weinandy 2000; cf. Helm 2010) denies that God is acted upon. Open theism (Pinnock et al. 1994; Boyd 2001; Sanders 1998) accepts the bilateral structure and surrenders the doctrine. The classical tradition retains the doctrine and reads the bilateral structure as unilateral accommodation, but accommodation is a mode of divine action, not of divine *inter*-action, and the *inter* is what the predicate names.

**Q3.** *How can two things relate across time when divine simplicity grants a real relation on only one side?* The forty-year engagement with Israel isn’t a series of unrelated acts but a continuous relation. Divine simplicity (Dolezal 2017) holds that there are no real relations in God—every relation is on the creature’s side only. A one-sided dependence is still a relation. An interaction whose relata persist only on one side isn’t interaction in the sense the wilderness account reports.

**Q4.** *How can an impassible being track engagement affectively, as the wilderness narratives mark it?* The wilderness narratives mark engagement by registers of divine feeling: wrath at the calf (Exod 32:10), kindled anger at Kibroth-hattaavah (Num 11:33), and the appearing of the glory with the plague at Korah (Num 16:42–45). The Korah verses report *kābôd* as manifested weight and presence, not as an emotion; the affective register in that episode is the judgment that follows, not a lexical slide from *kābôd* to *kābēd*. Impassibility (Helm 2010; Dolezal 2017) reads each of these as anthropopathism; open theism (Pinnock et al. 1994; Sanders 1998) reads them as literal divine affect. Tradition can’t have both the literal text and the doctrine: it must subtract one.

**Q5.** *How can an immutable being change his mind, as the texts repeatedly say God does?* *Nāḥam* (to repent, relent, or grieve into a different course) is used of God at Exod 32:14 (Yahweh relents after Moses’s intercession), Gen 6:6 (Yahweh regrets making humanity), 1 Sam 15:11 (Yahweh regrets making Saul king), and Jonah 3:10 (Yahweh relents from destroying Nineveh). Each is the verbal form whose literal sense is a turning. The impassibility tradition reads each as anthropopathism, but the texts aren’t merely emotive: they record a different downstream course of divine action contingent on a creature-side act. Either the divine course is genuinely contingent on the creature-side act (and strict immutability must place the contingency wholly in the effect), or the contingency is illusory (and the text is false at its surface). The classical model takes the first route with one timeless intention whose effects are ordered to the petition, and then owes what varies at the divine pole (§11.3.4, Q2).

**Q6.** *How can an incorporeal being engage the physical world by contact, as interaction with it appears to require?* The doctrine of omnipotence (Mavrodes 1963; Plantinga 1967; Wierenga 1989; Hoffman and Rosenkrantz 2002) holds that God can do anything logically possible. But interaction with the physical world appears to require physical contact: the burning bush burns, the pillar of fire heats, the Red Sea parts. (The writing in the dust and the broken fish are acts of the incarnate Word, taken up at Q8.) Tradition’s reply (that these are instrumental acts mediated through created causes) concedes that *God doesn’t himself interact physically*; he occasions physical events from outside the physical, which isn’t the picture the texts present.

**Q7.** *How can petitionary prayer be efficacious—God’s act depending on the petition—when immutability and timelessness forbid that dependence?* The tradition (Stump 1979; Murray and Meyers 1994; Davison 2017) treats petitionary prayer as efficacious: God answers, sometimes by granting, sometimes by withholding, in a way that depends on the petition having been made. But efficacy requires that God’s act be contingent on the creature’s act, which strict immutability must locate wholly in the effect; and if the contingency must be temporally located, timelessness denies it. The doctrine of efficacious prayer is functionally interactionist while the metaphysical doctrines owe an account of the interactionism that would underwrite it.

**Q8.** *How can the incarnation, the paradigm of interaction, be the act of a God who as God doesn’t interact?* The two-natures doctrine (Hick 1977; Morris 1986; Crisp 2007; Pawl 2016; Pawl 2019) holds that the Logos took on a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. Chalcedon locates eating, sleeping, tiring, weeping, and dying in the human nature of one person, not in a second subject beside the Word. The remaining burden is personal unity and the communication of idioms: how those human interactions are truly the Word’s without the divine nature itself undergoing them, and how they remain the Word’s without collapsing into a second agent. The tradition wants both: God interacts as the man Jesus *and* God as God doesn’t undergo creaturely passion. That is a unity-and-predication burden, not a proof that the incarnation is two beings. It is at the incarnation, more than at any other point, that the doctrinal structure and the narrative structure of interaction have to be shown to be the same subject’s.

*The burden.* Relation, unilateral causation, reciprocal causal influence, affective responsiveness, and second-personal exchange must be kept apart. Only the last three require the creature’s state to make some difference at the other pole. Concrete interaction between changing relata occurs within the three Conditions. A timeless ground may stand in an asymmetric dependence relation without intrinsic alteration; that possibility isn’t excluded by the word *relation*. The pressure arises when the doctrine also claims that God answers, grieves, relents, or encounters a creature in a way for which the creature’s condition matters. The account must then state what varies, where the responsive difference is borne, and how the relation remains more than unilateral dependence.

Divine temporalism and open theism take the responsive branch directly (Wolterstorff 1975; Hasker 1989; Mullins 2016; Pinnock et al. 1994; Sanders 1998; Boyd 2001). They place before and after in the divine life so that God can respond, relent, and be affected by creatures. This preserves recognizable interaction while revising strict atemporality and impassibility. It doesn’t reduce the God so described to Nature, nor does temporal occupancy alone refute that God’s necessity. It does place the divine exercises within the temporal and relational order and shift the question to aseity: how a responsive participant is also the independent ground of the order in which response occurs.

**[Diagnostic]**

**One-Sided Interaction Is Not Interaction** · *Diagnostic*

Not every relation is reciprocal, and an asymmetric grounding relation isn’t incoherent merely for lacking mutual alteration. The stronger burden attaches to responsive interaction: answering, grieving, relenting, and second-personal encounter require the creature’s condition to matter at the divine pole. A mixed relation can preserve dependence without that responsiveness, but it then revises what the devotional predicate appeared to promise.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Interaction occurs among relata within Nature; Nature isn’t itself the interacting subject. Nor does every relation require reciprocal alteration. The stronger bilateral content enters when believers say God answers, is affected by suffering, responds differently under different conditions, or participates in a genuinely second-personal exchange. Classical impassibility and immutability can preserve unilateral causation or a creature-side relation of reason, but those are revisions of interaction in the responsive sense. The issue is therefore not whether the word belongs to Nature. It is whether the divine use retains the *inter-*—a determinate between in which the creature makes any difference at the alleged divine pole. That determinate between isn’t scarce. It obtains wherever two subjects meet and each is altered by the meeting, which is the exchange the responsive sense of the word was drawn from. The open question is what the divine use retains of it, not where it is to be found.

### 11.7.4 Sovereignty

Sovereignty is God’s rule over everything: providence, election, the eternal decree. To govern a domain requires epistemic and causal access to it: the capacity to know it and act upon it. So sovereignty inherits all the difficulties the knowledge and power sections already raise, now at the level where God is said to rule. The eternal decree and its unfolding in history add a further strain on a God who is supposed never to change.

The classical doctrine of divine sovereignty assembles several reinforcing claims. God is king (Ps 47, 93, 96; Isa 6; Rev 4–5), with kingship the central political-theological metaphor for divine authority. God exercises providence, ordering all things to their proper end (Aquinas, *ST* I.22), and governance, the execution of providence in time (*ST* I.103). God elects: God has chosen some creatures for salvation, with the choice grounded in divine sovereign will rather than in any feature of the creatures (Augustine, *De Praedestinatione Sanctorum*; Aquinas, *ST* I.23; Calvin, *Institutes* III.21–24). Reformed scholasticism develops the architecture of decree theology: a single eternal decree determines every event in creation (Turretin (1679–1685) 1992–1997; Owen 1648; Helm 1993; Feinberg 2001). On a contemporary refinement, divine sovereignty grounds the modal structure itself: not merely what is actual but what is possible (Leftow 2012). Each move tries to keep divine governance from being one regional jurisdiction among others. Carried to its limit, the doctrine reaches for a king whose decree is meticulous, eternal, and comprehensive, whose election constitutes those it falls upon, and whose reach extends to the modal structure within which any decree is intelligible at all.

*The interrogation.* Six questions test what an account of divine sovereignty must supply. What drives them is local to sovereignty and cumulative across the chapter. Governance, on the analysis given, is the holding of a domain under determinative authority such that what occurs within the domain occurs by the authority’s decree. The holding requires a jurisdictional being structurally related to the domain, and §11.4.2 (Knowledge) and §11.7.1 (Power) have already examined that relation. If the conditions for divine knowing and divine causing have been hard to reconcile with the doctrine of divine simplicity-and-atemporality at every step, the conditions for divine governing inherit those difficulties at the level where governance is exercised through knowing and causing. The six pressures run one at the level of jurisdictional grip, five at the level of the conditions sovereignty-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *How does a being keep its hold on a world it is no part of?* For a jurisdiction to extend, the being who holds the jurisdiction must stand in some real relation to what falls under it: must be able to know the domain, hold it within a determinative frame, and effect what the jurisdiction decrees. Helm (1993), Feinberg (2001), and Leftow (2012) develop rigorous contemporary defenses of comprehensive divine governance. The concern here is that the difficulties run together: whether the conditions of divine knowing are coherent with the doctrine of divine simplicity-and-atemporality is raised at §11.4.2, and the parallel question for divine causing at §11.7.1. Sovereignty exercised through knowledge and power inherits both. The reply that divine governance is direct rather than mediated by knowledge and power is the account McCann (2012) develops as primitive divine causation; it preserves governance while leaving its mode unanalyzed. The present analysis records the move and its cost: a primitive relation whose conditions can’t be examined isn’t a more comprehensive form of structural governance but a distinct relation described by the same term.

**Q2.** *What does history add to a decree already complete in eternity?* Reformed scholasticism holds that the divine decree is one eternal act in which God determines every event that will ever occur (Turretin (1679–1685) 1992–1997; Owen 1648). The execution of the decree unfolds in time. The concern here is the relation between the two. If decree and execution are one act, the temporal unfolding adds nothing the decree didn’t already contain, and the temporal world is a representation of an eternally complete decision. If decree and execution are distinct, divine immutability is pressured: God’s decreeing is eternally complete, but God’s executing is temporally extended. Stump and Kretzmann’s (1981) ET-simultaneity addresses the difficulty by treating decree-as-eternal and execution-as-temporal as eternally simultaneous. The structural concern with the relation is pressed in other contexts at §11.3.2, Q2 and §11.4.2, Q2. The point this section adds is that decree-and-execution is the doctrine’s signature pairing, and the pairing is intelligible only if both terms have determinate content. Eternalizing the decree preserves immutability; temporalizing the execution preserves history; the doctrine has wanted to do both at once, and these are two commitments joined only by the term *one act*.

**Q3.** *How does God choose some over others, with no one yet there to be chosen?* The doctrine of election holds that God has chosen some creatures for salvation, with the choice grounded in God’s sovereign will rather than in any feature of the creatures (*De Praedestinatione*; *Institutes* III.21). For election to discriminate, the elector must stand in a position from which the elected can be picked out and the unelected passed over. The classical reply is that God’s election isn’t a temporal choosing-among but an eternal act in which the elect are constituted as such (Aquinas, *ST* I.23). The concern here is whether constitution-without-position is the form the doctrine of election asserts. If God’s eternal decree constitutes who counts as elect, the elect aren’t picked out from a prior class but defined by the decree; the doctrine preserves the believer’s sense of having been chosen by setting aside the *from-among* the choice ordinarily presupposes.

Barth’s (*CD* II.2) reframing of election as universal in Christ and Stump’s (2018) narrative reading register the difficulty from inside the tradition; the modal reading agrees that the difficulty is real and locates it in the constitution-without-position move the classical position depends on. Stump’s (*Atonement*, 2018, ch. 6) narrative-relational reading of election offers a richer alternative: election isn’t primarily the selection of individuals for a soteriological status (a standing with respect to salvation) by an eternal decree, but the irreducibly particular character of God’s second-personal relating to Israel-in-Jacob-and-his-descendants in a narrative whose particularity is what makes it election rather than general divine benevolence. On Stump’s account, the *from-among* the classical doctrine needs isn’t secured by a positional distinguishing act but by the thisness of the relation: what it is in the relating, not in a prior act of positional picking-out. The concern for Stump’s narrative election is whether the *thisness* of a second-personal relation has individuating content in the absence of spatial and temporal distinguishability: a narratively irreducible relation between God and Israel requires that the relata be distinguishable as the relata they are, and relational thisness at the narrative level trades on the same structural conditions of individuation found constitutive of any relation at all.

**Q4.** *How does God decree what is possible, if decreeing already needs the possible in place?* Carried past the actual, the doctrine extends divine sovereignty beyond the actual world to the modal space within which actuality is selected. Leftow (2012) develops the position that what is possible is grounded in divine activity: there are no possibilities prior to God for God to range over. The position is engaged from the necessity side at §11.3.1, Q6, from the power side at §11.7.1, Q5, and from the agency side at §11.7.2, Q7. The point sovereignty adds is that *governance*, carried that far, extends to the conditions any governance presupposes. To govern a domain is to exercise authority within structural conditions the domain provides. To govern the conditions themselves is to exercise authority over what makes any exercise intelligible.

Modal invariance (§2.1.4–§2.1.5) presses the same difficulty from the opposite direction: modal status isn’t a product of any agent’s exercise. The modal account agrees that the deepest structural facts aren’t subject to anyone’s decree. The doctrine that places them under decree, when its predicates are read in the structure that supports them, is reaching for the modal status of Nature and naming a sovereign beyond it.

The same difficulty runs through the doctrine of necessary creator-status: if creating belongs essentially to God, then in every world in which God exists God creates; if God exists necessarily, creation is necessary. And creation, if coherent, can only be creation of an order instantiating the three Conditions (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance). The dichotomy is binary, not gradient. Whatever God could be said to create either has temporality, spatiality, and substantiality, or it has none. In the first case, the creature is Nature or part of it. In the second case, there is no duration over which the creature persists, no location at which it stands distinct from its creator, and no being that carries the property of having been created. The second branch doesn’t describe a different kind of creature. It describes the absence of any feature by which a creature could be there to have been created. There is no third option. Sovereignty over a necessarily sustained domain is therefore not the elective decree the doctrine performs; what remains at that level is Nature’s non-exteriority, which isn’t rule. The modal-collapse concern is developed from the sides of power and agency at §11.7.1, Q1 and §11.7.2, Q7; the same concern surfaces here as the pressure on sovereign election.

Pruss and Rasmussen’s necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction (*Necessary Existence*, 2018, ch. 5) carries to the sovereignty register: God necessarily creates *some* order (essential sovereign creator-status), but the content of the order is contingent on God’s free selection among possible orders (the necessity attaches to the creator-status, not to the specific created order). On this reply, the dichotomy between a necessary creator that necessarily creates and a contingent creator that creates freely is dissolved.
