The concern in the sovereignty register is that the selection among contingent orders is itself a sovereign act: it requires a being that differentiates the alternatives it selects among, an ordering of the selection toward one of them, and a sovereign who bears both the creator-status and the act of selection. The necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction preserves sovereign freedom at the level of what is created; the structural conditions of sovereign action apply at the level at which freedom is now located.

**Q5.** *How does a creature freely do what God decreed it would do?* The Augustinian-Calvinist tradition holds that God’s eternal decree determines every event, including every creaturely free action. The Pelagian, Arminian, and Molinist traditions develop alternative positions on which creaturely freedom remains genuinely libertarian (Arminius 1608; de Molina 1588; Flint 1998). Compatibilist positions (Edwards 1754; Helm 1993) hold that determined actions can be free in a sense compatible with moral responsibility. Libertarian positions (Plantinga 1974; Flint 1998) hold that genuine freedom requires alternative possibilities the decree must not foreclose. The concern here is parallel to §11.4.2, Q9 (foreknowledge) and §11.7.1, Q6 (concurrence) at a different level: the question at §11.4.2 is whether divine knowing fixes the future; the question at §11.7.1 is whether divine causing leaves room for creaturely doing; the present question asks whether divine *decreeing* can determine creaturely action without precluding it. Each of the three positions (compatibilism, libertarianism, Molinism) preserves one commitment at a price the doctrine had been holding the others against. None preserves the full classical bundle.

**Q6.** *What does a creature add, if God decrees the falling of every leaf?* Meticulous providence is a thoroughgoing version of the doctrine: every event, down to the falling of every leaf, is decreed by God (Calvin, *Institutes* I.16) (Helm 1993). The concern here is whether the doctrine leaves room for any genuinely creaturely contribution to what occurs. If every event is meticulously decreed, creaturely action is at best the executed expression of a decree creatures had no part in making. The classical reply is the concurrence-and-secondary-causation move §11.7.1, Q6 engages: divine sovereignty operates *through* creaturely agency rather than around it. The concern here parallels the earlier ones: whether the through-not-around relation has determinate content on a non-analogical reading, or whether the relation is doing primitive work the doctrine asks of it. Pruss (2013) and Furlong (2019) develop contemporary attempts to give the relation more determinate content; the modal reading registers them as developed attempts and notes that each preserves the through-not-around relation by reintroducing structural conditions the doctrine of strong simplicity had removed. Hartshorne’s process alternative presses from the other side: divine sovereignty is persuasive rather than coercive, the concrete pole genuinely responsive to the creaturely contributions meticulous providence can’t accommodate (*The Divine Relativity*, 1948), and the coherence of that responsive sovereignty is pressed against dipolar theism at §10.3.3 and §11.7.2, Q1.

*The burden.* Governance adds more than exhaustive scope. It requires a governor, a domain, norms or intentions by which outcomes count as governed, and some relation between decree and execution. Nature supplies the domain and its lawful structure; it isn’t thereby the governor. A timeless decree can be proposed as the invariant ground of temporally differentiated effects, but it then owes the contact by which one act explains these outcomes rather than others. Election and providence add further discriminating content, while compatibility with creaturely freedom remains a separate problem. The structural result is non-exteriority: nothing governs Nature from a second concrete domain. Sovereignty, understood as purposive rule, doesn’t relocate without an argument for a ruler.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Grip Requires a Domain** · *Diagnostic*

Governance is a relation to a domain, and each element of it has to be determinate. Sovereignty exercised through knowing and causing inherits the burdens of the prior sections, and a relation left primitive isn’t thereby a more comprehensive form of governing. Decree and execution have to make a determinate pair: eternal-decree-with-temporal-execution wants both terms at full content, and the *one act* formula holds them together verbally rather than structurally. Election has to discriminate from-among, and the constitution-without-position move sets aside the choosing-among that election asserts, while the believer’s sense of having been chosen depends on a prior class to have been chosen from. The modal frame operates as a condition on governance rather than as its product, since the deepest structural facts are subject to no one’s decree. And decree and creaturely freedom have to hold together without flattening either, where compatibilism, libertarianism, and Molinism each keep one commitment of the bundle by surrendering another, and through-not-around concurrence keeps the verb by relocating the through-relation to a primitive whose work is left unspecified. What *governs* picks out, examined, is the condition under which jurisdictional grip obtains at all.

**Depends on:** Pure Act Owes an Agency-Making Difference (§11.7.2) and One-Sided Interaction Is Not Interaction (§11.7.3)

*The reclamation.* Nothing stands outside Nature to govern its modal constitution. That is non-exteriority, not sovereignty in the agential or political sense. A structure doesn’t command, deliberate, legislate, or rule merely because every event occurs within its constraints. Divine sovereignty adds precisely those personal contents to exhaustive scope. The account must therefore distinguish lawful invariance from governance and identify what makes histories products of authoritative selection rather than configurations within an uncommanded field. Nature answers to no higher frame; it doesn’t follow that Nature reigns.

Four of the attributes now converge. Necessity, immutability, sovereignty, and perfection have each, run to completion, pressed the same structural role under a different description: necessity on the structure’s reach across every world, immutability on its constancy across all time, sovereignty on its answering to no higher frame, perfection on its lacking nothing the frame requires. These are four angles on one role, the modal standing of the three Conditions, not four separate perfections of a being. That four major divine attributes press one structural fact isn’t redundant. It expresses the inversion thesis at its earned strength: the classical account assigns several names to what the argument identifies as one role and distributes them across a being. The role is the invariance and non-exteriority already earned. It doesn’t make Nature a king, a moral agent, or a perfect being; the personal enlargements remain unpaid.

## 11.8 Reach and Contact
This cluster gathers the attributes by which God reaches and is reached: presence (§11.8.1), relatability (§11.8.2), describability (§11.8.3), and revelation (§11.8.4)—being present to, standing in relation to, being truly described by, and disclosing itself to creatures.

Each is a contact-attribute: to be present is to occupy a standpoint relative to another, to be related and described is to be distinguished and carried in thought, and to reveal is to transmit across an interval. The reach the tradition assigns to God is the reach the three Conditions make possible, and where the contact claimed is two-way, the test cuts in both directions.

### 11.8.1 Presence

Omnipresence is God’s being wholly present everywhere at once, present to every place while occupying none. The two halves pull apart: “present at every point” quantifies over places, but “no spatial extension” denies there are any places for God to be at. A presence that cannot tell here from there isn’t a more intimate presence; it is the loss of the very contrast the word “present” depends on.

The classical doctrine of divine omnipresence assembles three reinforcing claims. God is present everywhere by being everywhere intimately and substantially: *Deus est in omnibus rebus*, God is in all things, by power, by presence, and by essence (Aquinas, *ST* I.8.3). God is present *totus in toto et totus in qualibet parte*: wholly in the whole and wholly in every part (*ST* I.8.2; Augustine, *Confessions* I.3). On a contemporary refinement, presence is an act in which God is operatively present at every point alike, with no point favored over any other (Wierenga 1989; Hudson 2009; Inman 2017). The doctrine preserves the believer’s intuition that God is here and not absent at any *there* by extending the *here* without limit. It does so, on the doctrine fully stated, in a being defined as having no *here* of its own. Pressed to its limit, the position holds that divine presence is unrestricted precisely because the being has nowhere of its own from which any restriction could be a restriction *from*.

*The interrogation.* Five questions test what the doctrine of omnipresence must specify. The difficulty beneath them is structural: God is said to be wholly present at every spatial point while having no spatial extension. *Wholly at every point* quantifies over positions; *no spatial extension* denies that God occupies the manifold over which the quantifier ranges. The questions determine whether *presence* keeps positional content, relocates its content into another predicate, or loses the contrast that made it presence. They don’t assume in advance that every account fails.

**Q1.** *At what place is a placeless being present?* The classical doctrine treats omnipresence as the universal of position: God is at every point. Hudson (2009) develops the contemporary defense by treating divine presence as *occupation* of every spatial region, with the divine being filling space without being divided by it. Inman (2017) argues for a *grounding* construal: God is present at a region by grounding what occurs there. Wierenga (1989) and Hoffmann and Rosenkrantz (2002) treat presence as a function of divine knowledge and power: God is wherever God knows and acts. The concern added here is that each construal trades positional content for something else: occupation without division, grounding without location, knowledge-and-power without where. The believer’s *here* is positional. *Wholly at every point* is positional. Treating divine presence as non-positional preserves the universal at the cost of removing what the *at* in the universal was supposed to track. To say God is present-by-knowledge-and-power is to say something true about what knowledge and power require (as developed at §11.4.2 and §11.7.1); on the doctrine taken in its strong form it is to substitute one predicate for another.

One test applies to the non-positional construals together, and it doesn’t assume what the defenders deny. Grant each its own terms: occupation without division (Hudson 2009), grounding of what occurs at a region (Inman 2017), presence-by-knowledge-and-power (Wierenga 1989). Each is still the claim that God is present *at this region rather than that one*: present at the burning bush in a way God isn’t present at the next shrub on Sinai, present at A in whatever way occupies or grounds or knows A and not identically at B. Strip that out and the construal no longer yields omnipresence but a single undifferentiated relation to everything at once, and the nearness and directedness the doctrine insists on (the fourth and third questions that follow) go with it. So the construal must individuate presence-at-A from presence-at-B. But to individuate A from B is to hold them apart as distinct positions standing in relational non-identity, and a manifold of positions held apart by relational non-identity is what S is (§2.6.7). The defender’s *at every region* is a quantifier, what it ranges over is a field of mutually distinct locations, and a field of mutually distinct locations isn’t an alternative to spatial structure but an instance of it. Occupation, grounding, and knowledge-and-power don’t remove S from presence; they presuppose S as the manifold across which their *at* is indexed.

One construal doesn’t trade position away, and so doesn’t fall to the disposing test as stated: *ubiquitous entension* (Hudson 2005; Hudson 2009). The entension theorist concedes location rather than substituting for it: God is *wholly* located at every region and at every subregion alike, an extended occupant present in its entirety at each part of what it occupies and divided by none. This is the contemporary cash-out of *totus in qualibet parte*, and it meets the disposing test head-on: it doesn’t preserve the universal of presence by removing the *at*; it affirms the *at* at full strength and denies only that being wholly-located-at-each entails being partitioned. The preceding test assumes the defender purchases omnipresence by trading position for occupation-without-division, grounding, or knowledge; the entension theorist refuses the trade, so the construal must be met on its own ground. Grant entension everything it claims: an undivided whole wholly located at every region and subregion.

It remains that the regions it is wholly located *at* are many, and many *as positions*: the occupant is wholly at A and wholly at B only if A is a position distinct from B and held apart from it, so that being-wholly-at-A isn’t already being-wholly-at-B. Entension doesn’t dispense with the manifold of mutually distinct positions; it is *defined over* it: *wholly at each* is a quantifier whose field is a plurality of locations held apart by relational non-identity, and that plurality is what S is (§2.6.7). The occupant isn’t thereby identified with the manifold (that would help itself to the thesis rather than earn it) but the entended occupant can’t so much as state its *wholly at each* without presupposing the manifold as the field across which the *each* is indexed. Entension locates the predicate *present* in S all the more firmly for affirming location instead of trading it away: it needs the differentiated field of positions to have anything for its undivided whole to be wholly at.

This is why the aspatial defender’s most ambitious move (that God is present to creation in a manner needing no spatial structure at all) doesn’t relocate presence to a higher register but dissolves it: a relation that can’t tell *here* from *there* isn’t a more intimate presence than the believer’s, but the negation of the contrast the word *present* names. The differentiation of positions isn’t an imperfection in creaturely presence that divine presence improves on; it is the condition under which there is any *there* for God to be present *to*.

**Q2.** *How is a being with no extension wholly present at every point?* The formula is *totus in toto et totus in qualibet parte*. To be wholly in the whole is one claim; to be wholly in every part of the whole is another; to be both at once, when the whole has parts and the parts are spatially distinct, is to be reduplicated at every part without thereby being divided. The classical reply is that divine non-extension makes the reduplication unproblematic: only an extended being could be divided by being placed in extended regions. The concern here is that *wholly at* presupposes spatial location for whatever is wholly at the place, since *wholly* contrasts with *partly* and the contrast is positional. A non-extended being isn’t wholly at any point in the contrastive sense the formula trades on. *Totus in qualibet parte* keeps the language of part-by-part presence and removes the structure that makes part-by-part presence different from no-part presence. The formula performs the doctrine’s deepest work by deploying terms whose ordinary content has been suspended.

**Q3.** *In what direction does a being act, if it is no nearer one point than another?* For an action to be directed at a target (for a divine intervention to land on this object rather than that one, on this body rather than the body next to it) there must be a structural relation between the agent and the target along which the action runs. The question for agency is pressed at §11.7.2; the present concern is closer in. If God is at every point identically, with no point preferred to any other, the divine standing-at-A-and-not-at-B that would distinguish acting on A from acting on B is unavailable. The reply that divine action is mediated by divine intention rather than by spatial direction is the same one examined at §11.7.2: it preserves directedness by relocating it from a structural relation to a primitive of will. The concern added here is that omnipresence in its strong form removes the spatial asymmetry directionality requires, and the doctrine’s preservation of directedness through divine willing must supply, in the will, the differentiated content the positional relation would have supplied (§11.7.2, Q3). The two commitments of the doctrine are in structural tension at the point of contact between presence and act.

**Q4.** *How is a being near to one place, if it is no farther from any other?* Scripture and devotional theology repeatedly emphasize divine nearness in particular places and moments: the burning bush (Exod 3), the tabernacle (Exod 40), the holy of holies (1 Kgs 8), the incarnation as the *tabernacling* of the Word (John 1:14), the indwelling of the Spirit in the believer (Rom 8). Each presupposes a contrast between *here in this place* and *not-here in some other*. The classical reply distinguishes ordinary presence (everywhere alike) from special presence (here-and-now in a way that elsewhere isn’t), with special presence understood as a heightened mode of divine action rather than as a positional difference. The reply preserves the devotional vocabulary by treating *nearness* analogically (Aquinas, *ST* I.8.3 ad 1, Pruss 2013). The concern here is that the analogical reading preserves the term by removing the contrast the term tracks. Nearness is a positional contrast; the divine special presence at the burning bush is *not at* every other shrub on Sinai in the sense that mattered for Moses to remove his sandals at this one. Omnipresence-in-its-strong-form leaves no resource for reading the contrast structurally, and the analogical reading registers the cost.

**Q5.** *Can panentheism, panpsychism, or pantheism make God present without giving God a place?* The contemporary literature has pressed alternatives that retain the spatial intuition while modifying the doctrine. Panentheism (Clayton and Peacocke 2004; Cooper 2006; Pfeifer 2016) holds that the world is in God without being identical with God, preserving immanence by giving God a quasi-spatial relation to creation. Panpsychism in its theistic forms (Goff 2017; Mathews 2003) treats consciousness as ubiquitous in nature, with divine consciousness as the unifying fact about the manifold. Pantheism (Spinoza, *Ethics* I, Levine 1994; Buckareff and Nagasawa 2016) identifies God with the world. Each move concedes some classical commitment to preserve another. The present analysis agrees that the doctrine of strict transcendence-with-omnipresence is unstable, and treats the contemporary alternatives as registering the instability rather than resolving it. What each alternative reaches for, in different directions, is a way of relocating the *here* of divine presence into the structure that makes *here* a coherent predicate at all. The relocation, taken to its limit, is the analysis offered here: position and spatial availability belong to S; S isn’t a subject present to anyone. Nature isn’t thereby an omnipresent person.

*The burden.* The five pressures gather into one requirement: the *at* of presence is positional. Occupation, grounding, and knowledge-and-power keep the universal only by trading what the *at* was holding; *totus in qualibet parte* needs the contrast between wholly and partly at; directed action needs a standing-at-A-and-not-at-B; nearness needs the *not at* every other shrub on Sinai. The contemporary pan- alternatives register the same destination from different directions, each relocating the predicate into the manifold that makes *here* coherent. S is what the positional conditions require, which locates the content without renaming Space as God or as an omnipresent person. Asked of any one spot, the requirement leaves three answers.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Present Trilemma** · *Disjunction*

Is God here, right now?

- **If in some places and not others,** then God is somewhere in particular, which isn’t being everywhere—and whether *here* is one of those places is now a question with an answer.
- **If everywhere,** then here, at this spot; and this spot is one position among the ones *every* is ranging over. Ubiquitous entension may keep God undivided, but it doesn’t remove the positions.
- **If nowhere,** then *presence* is no longer naming presence. It has become knowledge, power, grounding, or availability, and whichever one it has become owes that relation’s burden instead. *Feeds into* Which Relation Is Being Claimed? (§11.8.2).

No branch gives you a God who is everywhere and also outside space.

**Depends on:** Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7)

**[Diagnostic]**

**The At of Presence Is Positional** · *Diagnostic*

The *at* of presence carries positional content, and substituting occupation, grounding, or knowledge-and-power for location clarifies what the doctrine commits to while trading away what the *at* was holding. The contrast between *wholly at* and *partly at* is positional in the only sense that lets *totus in qualibet parte* mean presence part-by-part rather than presence at no part, and that contrast obtains only across an extended spatial manifold. Directed action, read positionally, presupposes spatial asymmetry: a being identically at every point lacks the standing-at-A-and-not-at-B that distinguishes acting on A from acting on B, and relocating the directedness to a primitive of will owes, in the will, the differentiated content that asymmetry supplied. Nearness is a contrast in the same way, since special presence at the burning bush is *not at* every other shrub on Sinai in the sense that made Moses remove his sandals, and the analogical reading registers what removing the contrast costs rather than absorbing it. The believer’s *here* is positional throughout, which makes presence-everywhere the universal of position rather than its negation.

**Depends on:** Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7)

*The reclamation.* Position and spatial availability belong to S; S isn’t a subject present to anyone. The divine predicate divides into several claims that must not be merged: occupation of every place, causal power at every place, knowledge of every place, and second-personal availability to creatures. The first is positional. The next two may be stated without divine spatial occupation but inherit the power and knowledge burdens. The last requires more than universal scope: it requires an addressable and responsive relatum. Replacing all four with “not absent from anywhere” preserves a negation while leaving the positive mode of presence unspecified. The argument locates the content; it doesn’t rename Space as God or as an omnipresent person. What it fixes is what the word runs on. *Present* requires a where, and a where is one place and not another. That isn’t a deficiency in the concept but its content, and the content is routinely satisfied: occupying a place, reachable from it, addressable by whoever is also there. That is the ordinary case for us. Presence isn’t a property waiting on a bearer wide enough to hold it. It is had by anyone who is anywhere.

### 11.8.2 Relatability

Religion lives on a God who can be related to: one who loves, hears prayer, and draws near in answer. The classical safeguard is the “mixed relation”: creatures are really related to God, but God is related to creatures only in our way of speaking, with nothing added on the divine side. That is still a relation. The trouble is whether it is the two-sided love, hearing, and drawing-near the believer reports.

The classical doctrine of divine relation assembles several reinforcing claims. God loves creation (1 John 4; Rom 8); God is present to the believer (Ps 139; Matt 28:20); God hears prayer (Ps 65; Matt 7); God grieves and rejoices over creaturely action (Gen 6; Luke 15). At the same time, God is immutable (Mal 3:6; Jas 1:17), impassible (§11.3.4; Aquinas, *ST* I.9), aseitous (§11.3.1, Q4; *ST* I.4), and simple (*ST* I.3): lacking parts, dependencies, or any feature whose obtaining requires anything outside God. Aquinas’s resolution: the relations between God and creatures aren’t mutual. The creature has a *real* relation to God, grounded in the creature’s actual ontological dependence; God has only a *relation of reason* to the creature, a relation that obtains only from the creature’s side and adds nothing to the divine being (*ST* I.13.7; cf. *ST* I.28) (for contemporary defenses, Stump 2003; Dolezal 2017). On contemporary refinements, divine simplicity entails that God’s loving the creature, knowing the creature, and creating the creature are all identical with God’s being and add nothing relational to it (Pruss 2008; Bergmann and Brower 2006; Dolezal 2011). Open theism, process theology, and panentheism take the reverse turn and grant God real relations at the cost of immutability and aseity (Hartshorne 1948; Wolterstorff 1975; Hasker 1989; Pinnock et al. 1994; Mullins 2016). Each move tries to keep the believer’s experienced relation to God from collapsing. Pressed to its limit, the position holds a relation in which the creature’s real dependence on God is meant to preserve the believer’s experiential reports while the divine end remains untouched by what the creature is or does.

*The interrogation.* Six questions test what the doctrine must supply for its relational predicates. What presses here is structural—local to the relational predicates and explicit in the tradition’s own concession. Two things stand in a relation when something obtains *between* them: the cup is on the table; the child loves the parent; the planet orbits the star. In each case the relation has two relata and a structural connection that holds them in the configuration named. Reciprocal alteration is a further claim, not the definition of relation: greater-than, caused-by, and known-by don’t require both ends to change. The classical tradition reaches for a relation between God and creation that exceeds any creaturely relation in depth and intimacy, and reaches, simultaneously, for a doctrine of divine immutability and aseity on which the deeper end of that relation contributes nothing to the divine being. The two reaches pull against each other, and the doctrine of *mixed relation* (Aquinas, *ST* I.13.7) is one of the most explicit resolutions in the history of metaphysics: the classical tradition holds the two reaches together by giving the relation a real end only on the creature’s side. On the analyses developed at §2.6, a relation is a structural connection between relata. The stronger burden attaches when one relatum’s state is supposed to make a difference at the other. The [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) is defined as sharing none of the three Conditions with the creature. The six pressures run two at the level of the relational predicates themselves, four at the level of the conditions relation-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *Can a relation that exists only in our thought make God responsive to us?* Aquinas’s *mixed relation* (*ST* I.13.7) is the central resource: the creature is really related to God, but God is related to the creature only by *relation of reason*, a relation that obtains in our concepts and predicates rather than in the divine being. Stump (2003), Dolezal (2017), and Bergmann and Brower (2006) defend the doctrine carefully. The concern here is what the relation of reason is positioned to do. The believer who reports being loved by God isn’t reporting a relation that holds only in the believer’s concepts of God; the believer is reporting a relation in which God is the lover and the believer the beloved, with the loving running from God to the believer. The doctrine of mixed relation preserves divine immutability by relocating the divine end of the relation from the divine being to the creature’s concepts of the divine being. What this preserves is the term *love*; what it surrenders is the structure on which the believer’s report depends: the running-from. The Thomistic doctrine is honest about the cost in a way the contemporary refinements often aren’t: Aquinas doesn’t pretend the doctrine leaves the believer’s experiential reports unchanged. The present analysis registers the candor and presses the cost.

**Q2.** *Does God love the world, and can the unaffected love?* The believer’s confession that God loves the world (1 John 4:8) is among the most central claims of the tradition, and the relational reports that surround it (of being loved, heard, attended to, grieved over, rejoiced over) are reports of an affecting relation: God’s state is held to be partly determined by the believer’s state. For loving to be the relation the confession reports, the lover must respond to the beloved: the loving must take its character, in some structural sense, from what the beloved is and what the beloved does. Two classical commitments foreclose this together. On love, the reply is that God’s love is wholly active rather than responsive; it bestows rather than receives; it is identical with God’s being and is therefore eternal, immutable, and unaffected by what the beloved does (Aquinas, *ST* I.20), whose classical form Nygren (1932) states in the *agape*-vs-*eros* contrast.

On affection, impassibility holds that God can’t be acted upon by anything outside God (§11.3.4; *ST* I.9), and the *real-but-not-mutual* doctrine has God affect the creature without the creature affecting God (Lewis 1940; Stump 2003; 2010; Helm 2010). Needlessness alone doesn’t answer the question: the tradition can distinguish acquisitive desire, which seeks a lacked good, from benevolent willing, which gives without deficiency. The stronger pressure concerns creature-directed love in particular. If God could love this creature, another creature, or no creature while remaining intrinsically identical, then nothing differentiated on the divine side explains which beloved is loved; the relation is real only at the creaturely end. If a differentiated divine intention explains the beloved and the manner of loving, simplicity is qualified. If no alternative is real, the beloved and the loving follow necessarily from the divine essence. The same three prices recur as under Power (§11.7.1): differentiation, brute selection, or modal collapse. The concern is therefore not that fullness semantically excludes love, but whether love deprived of responsive or selective difference remains the relation the believer’s confession reports. A love that doesn’t respond to the beloved isn’t, in the structural sense, a relation jointly determined by two relata. An affective relation that operates from one relatum to another without reciprocal determination is unilateral: the doctrine preserves divine action toward the creature while excluding the creature-to-divine responsiveness reported by believers. The doctrine preserves divine immutability by relocating the responsive structure from God to creation; the believer who reports having been heard in a moment of distress is reporting a responsive structure factored out at the divine pole.

The mystical literature (Eckhart, *Sermons*; Teresa, *Interior Castle*) is full of reports the present analysis isn’t positioned to dismiss; the question is what the reports presuppose about the structural conditions of encounter. Stump (2010; 2018) and Wolterstorff (2015) develop attempts to preserve the responsive structure within the classical frame, and each does so by reintroducing structural conditions divine immutability had removed. The dipolar account is the principled terminus of those attempts.

Hartshorne’s *The Divine Relativity* (1948) proposes that divine love is genuinely bipolar: the abstract pole’s love is the invariant, bestowing, formal commitment to the creature’s good and is strictly impassible, the creature’s state making no difference to it; the concrete pole’s love is constitutively responsive and fully receptive, growing with the beloved’s joys and sufferings. The two sides of love (bestowing and responsive) and the two sides of affection (impassible and receptive) are assigned to two poles of a single subject, supplying the bidirectionality the reports require while the abstract pole keeps the aseity the classical doctrine demands. The concern here is the one pressed at §10.3.3: the abstract pole and the concrete pole are one subject only through the relation that unites them, and that relation is shown at §10.3.3 to require determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. The unity of the loving agent therefore depends on structural roles obtaining between its poles, while the abstract pole retains the same absence of reciprocal determination identified in the classical account.

**Q3.** *Where do the relata meet?* Two relata stand in a structural connection only if they share enough conditions for the connection to obtain. The cup and the table share spatial position; the child and the parent share temporal extension and embodied presence; the planet and the star share the gravitational structure of the solar system. The classical God shares none of the three Conditions with the creature. The relation between God and creature must therefore obtain across a difference at every structural level. The classical reply is that divine relation is *sui generis*: a relation of a kind no creaturely relation matches, holding between God and creature in a way no creaturely framework can capture (Pseudo-Dionysius, *Mystical Theology*; Aquinas, *ST* I.13). The apophatic non-relation strategy originates with Plotinus: in *Enneads* VI.9 the One is related to nothing and to no one, since relation presupposes a dyad and the One precedes all dyadic structure; Pseudo-Dionysius transmits the Plotinian strategy to Aquinas via the Neoplatonic inheritance. §11.8.3, Q5 and §11.2.2, Q1 trace the apophatic ancestry more fully. The reply is honest. The concern here is what makes the *sui generis* relation a relation in the structural sense the relational predicates trade on. Whatever connects God and creature, on the doctrine fully stated, lacks the shared conditions that make creaturely relations relations. The term *relation* is doing work the doctrine hasn’t specified.

**Q4.** *Can the believer be heard?* Petitionary prayer presupposes that the believer’s request reaches God and that God responds. For the request to be heard, the petition must make some difference at the divine pole — and a receiving is an operation, so wherever one is claimed the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) places the full Structural Requirement at it. For God to respond in the ordinary temporal sense, there must be a difference between God’s not-yet-having-responded and God’s having-responded; that difference is a transition; transitions require T. The classical reply is that God’s response is eternally complete in a single act, and what unfolds in time is the temporal expression of that eternal act (Aquinas, *ST* I.23) (Stump and Kretzmann 1981). §11.7.2, Q6 presses the concern with the relation between an eternal act and a particular temporal *when*; the present concern is closer in. The believer in distress at 3:14 PM on a Tuesday is asking for a difference between the world before 3:14 and the world after; ET-simultaneity preserves the divine end of the answering by setting aside the temporal asymmetry that, on the structural analysis, is constitutive of an act’s being a response to anything in particular.

**Q5.** *Can the Trinity be a relational solution?* The doctrine of the Trinity gives the classical tradition a resource: God is internally relational (the Father loves the Son in the Spirit) without depending on anything outside God. Trinitarianism preserves divine relationality without compromising aseity (Augustine, *De Trinitate*; Boethius, *De Trinitate*; Aquinas, *ST* I.27–43) (for the contemporary social-vs-Latin debate, Plantinga 1989; Swinburne 1994; Cross 2002). The concern here is what the divine processions are, on the doctrine fully stated. If the relations within God are real relations (each Person’s being depending on the relations to the others) the Persons are individuated by relational properties, and those properties require structural conditions for relation. The Latin tradition since Augustine has worked to give the relations content without giving the Persons separable being; the Cappadocian tradition has worked the converse problem. Both run on relational structure that, on the present analysis, requires the structural roles the three Conditions name. The doctrine of immanent Trinity buys internal relationality at the cost of locating relational structure within the simple, atemporal divine being, which is precisely the structural difficulty divine simplicity was intended to foreclose.

**Q6.** *What does immanence relate?* The contemporary panentheist and process traditions, with Hartshorne (1948) the systematic process progenitor, developed by Cobb and Griffin (1976), Clayton (2004), and Peacocke (2007), attempt to preserve the relational depth the believer’s experiential reports require by placing creation *within* God or treating God and creation as mutually constitutive. This panentheist *creation-within-God* must be distinguished from Plotinian emanation: in emanation the One’s procession reaches even matter without the One being *within* what proceeds from it (§10.3.2), so the source keeps its non-relational transcendence, whereas panentheism surrenders exactly that transcendence to secure mutual constitution. The move responds to the concern. The cost is symmetrical to the open-theist cost named at §11.7.2: a being whose relations to creation share creation’s structural conditions is a being who instantiates those conditions. Panentheism preserves relationality by relocating God within the modal structure the classical doctrine had defined God against. The two positions (mixed relation and panentheism) are best read as the doctrine splitting along a structural incompatibility. One preserves the predicate by relocating its referent; the other preserves the structure by surrendering the referent.

*The burden.* Taken in sum, the six pressures show what *related* depends on once the term is held to the conditions of its application. Two things stand in a bilateral relation when their states are jointly determined by a structural connection between them, and the relation of reason preserves the term while surrendering the running-from on which the believer’s report of being loved depends. Love runs through responsive structure: love-without-response is a one-sided pouring whose target’s state makes no difference to the pouring, and the doctrine of divine immutability factors that responsive structure out at the divine pole. Relata meet by sharing structural conditions; the *sui generis* relation lacks what creaturely relations have, and the term *relation* is doing work the doctrine hasn’t specified. Prayer, as the believer reports it, reaches God along a temporal channel: ET-simultaneity preserves the divine end of the answering by setting aside the temporal asymmetry constitutive of being a response to anything in particular. Affecting relations in the devotional sense are bidirectional: asymmetric affection can still be a relation, and the half the believer’s reports require is precisely what the doctrine doesn’t give. Internal relationality can’t be secured without affecting simplicity: the Trinitarian account preserves internal relations by locating relational structure within the simple, atemporal divine being, thereby reintroducing the structural difficulty simplicity was intended to exclude. And the panentheist preservation of relational structure revises the transcendent referent specified by classical doctrine. Each option splits the doctrine along the same structural incompatibility rather than holding it together. The three Conditions are the conditions of bilateral connection where that is what is claimed. Relation as such is wider; the test is which kind is claimed.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Which Relation Is Being Claimed?** · *Diagnostic*

Relation simpliciter doesn’t require reciprocal alteration. Causation, representation, exemplification, dependence, comparison, and creature-side relations of reason may all be asymmetric. Devotional relation makes stronger claims: that a subject is heard, answered, loved, forgiven, resisted, or met, and that the subject’s concrete condition figures in what occurs at the other pole. The section must test those claims at their own resolution. A mixed relation can preserve dependence without preserving mutuality; it cannot be treated as though it had preserved both merely because the word *relation* remains.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Real relations occur within Nature; Nature isn’t thereby the relatum believers address. Classical mixed-relation theory coherently preserves a real change in the creature without a corresponding intrinsic change in God. Its cost is semantic and devotional, not the contradiction of relation as such. If prayer, love, and encounter require that the creature’s condition make a difference at the divine pole, the mixed relation doesn’t supply what those predicates appeared to promise. If no such difference is required, the doctrine has revised responsiveness into unilateral dependence. The argument should name that revision plainly rather than define every relation as bilateral in advance. What isn’t in question is that bilateral relation occurs. Being changed by someone who is changed by you is the ordinary condition of a friendship, and it is the relation the devotional vocabulary was modeled on. Whatever the divine case turns out to require, the thing anyone means by being in relation is available, mutual, and already had.

### 11.8.3 Describability
The apophatic route is treated at length as a doctrine of the divine nature at §10.2.2, where it is pressed on whether a ground described only by negation remains a ground. The present section asks the attribute question instead: whether the being so described can be described at all.

The standard reply to everything before it is that words like *knows* or *good* were never meant to apply to God in the plain, ordinary sense: they apply by analogy, or only by negation. Yet any genuine analogy must preserve some common structure with the ordinary meaning, and the account must say what that shared content is. Identifying it with loaded Time, Space, and Substance is one further step, not the definition of analogy. Negation and analogy relocate the problem; they don’t dissolve it.

The classical tradition assembles several reinforcing positions on religious language. *Univocal* predication holds that the term means the same whether goodness is applied to God or to Socrates. Aquinas rejects it (*ST* I.13.5); Scotus (*Ordinatio* I.3) defends a restricted version. *Equivocal* predication (the term means something altogether different in the two cases) is rejected by both. *Analogical* predication, the middle path, holds that divine and creaturely predicates share content via a structured proportion: God’s goodness stands to God as creaturely goodness stands to creature, with the *as* doing structural work the merely equivocal lacks (*ST* I.13.5–6, with refinements by Cajetan (1498) 1953) (McInerny 1996; for contemporary discussion Burrell 1986; Rocca 2004; White 2016).

*Apophatic* or negative theology (we know what God isn’t, not what God is) was developed by Pseudo-Dionysius (*Mystical Theology* 1; *Divine Names* 1) into the central method of mystical-theological reflection, taken up by Maximus, Eriugena, and Eckhart, and continues in contemporary form (Marion 1991; Turner 1995). The method’s philosophical origin lies with Plotinus: *Enneads* V.3 (*On the Knowing Hypostases and That Which Is Beyond*) and VI.9 (*On the Good, or the One*) develop the ascent-through-negation procedure in its first systematic form: the One is beyond intellect, beyond being, beyond any predicate that would make it an object of thought; what can be said of the One is said by stripping away every determination, and the stripping terminates in silence. Pseudo-Dionysius transmits the Plotinian method into the Christian theological tradition; from Pseudo-Dionysius it passes to Maximus, Eriugena, Eckhart, and the contemporary apophatic forms Marion and Turner develop. The citation gap isn’t merely genealogical: what Plotinus names as *the One beyond being* is the philosophical ancestor of the Pseudo-Dionysian *cloud of unknowing*, and naming the ancestor changes the doctrinal assessment at Q5.

Maimonides’s negative theology in the *Guide for the Perplexed* I.50–60 (Seeskin 2000; Stern 2013) is the parallel Jewish-tradition development; the doctrine of attribute-by-attribute negation receives a classical statement there. *[Perfect-being theology](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary)* holds that God is the being than which none greater can be conceived (Anselm, *Proslogion* 2–3), with each attribute the perfection of its kind; it supplies the methodology for deriving the classical attributes (Morris 1987; Leftow 2012; Speaks 2018).

Each tradition tries to keep divine description from being either flat creaturely projection or empty piety. The meta-doctrine, at its most disciplined, asks for a register in which divine predicates are neither univocal projections from creaturely experience nor empty equivocations, and in which the apophatic, analogical, and perfect-being resources together preserve the believer’s confession against both flattening and dissolution.

*The interrogation.* Seven questions test what the meta-doctrine must supply. What surfaces beneath them is the reply deferred so far through eleven sections. Eleven sections of pressing the classical attributes have so far proceeded as if the predicates *exists*, *is one*, *is necessary*, *is eternal*, *is present*, *is aware*, *knows*, *can*, *acts*, *governs*, *relates* applied to God in the same sense they apply to anything else. The classical tradition itself hasn’t made that assumption. Aquinas’s doctrine of analogy (*ST* I.13.5) is a developed theory of religious language, and the Pseudo-Dionysian tradition of apophasis is older still. The believer who confesses that God is good isn’t, on the classical position, predicating goodness of God univocally with the goodness of a friend or a deed; nor is the predication merely equivocal, with no shared content between the divine and creaturely cases. The third option, *analogy*, has done the work of making divine description intelligible for the better part of a millennium. The full reply is that every structural pressure registered so far concerns the predicates read univocally, and the classical tradition has been telling its readers since at least Aquinas not to read them that way.

The concern isn’t whether analogy and apophasis are coherent doctrines of religious language; they are. The concern is what content remains when these qualifications are considered together. The eleven preceding sections have argued that the classical attributes, taken at face value, presuppose the three structural Conditions, which the doctrine has placed beyond divine being. The doctrine of analogy responds: the predicates were never meant to apply at face value. The doctrine of apophasis responds: the predicates negate creaturely limitations rather than affirm divine features. The doctrine of perfect-being theology responds: the predicates are derived from the very property of being maximally great, which neither structural analysis nor creaturely experience constrains. Each reply preserves the doctrine by relocating where its content is carried. The seven pressures ask what remains when these relocations are taken seriously and the structural conditions removed from the predicates are considered together: one at the level of the doctrine of analogy (Q1), four at the level of the conditions divine description runs on (Q2–Q5), and two at the level of competing doctrines of religious language (Q6 univocity, Q7 revelation).

**Q1.** *How is God’s goodness like ours, if in God there is nothing for goodness to belong to?* Aquinas’s doctrine of analogy (*ST* I.13.5–6) holds that divine and creaturely predicates share content via a structured proportion: God’s wisdom stands to God as creaturely wisdom stands to creature. The concern here is what the proportion preserves. For *as* to do structural work, the two sides must share something the proportion can be a proportion *of*.

The doctrine of *analogy of proper proportionality* (Cajetan (1498) 1953) holds that the shared content is the constitutive relation between attribute and bearer; the doctrine of *analogy of attribution* holds that creaturely attributes are derivative from divine ones. McInerny (1996) and Rocca (2004) develop contemporary refinements. The concern here is that the doctrine of strong divine simplicity (*ST* I.3) entails that there is no real distinction in God between the attribute and the bearer, and the *as* of the proportion requires precisely that distinction on the divine side. The doctrine of analogy preserves the predicates by appealing to a constitutive relation that the doctrine of simplicity has eliminated at the divine pole. White (2016) acknowledges the difficulty and develops a contemporary defense; the present reading registers the defense and presses the cost.

Feser’s act/potency grounding (*Aquinas: A Beginner’s Guide*, 2009, ch. 4) offers a developed defense of the causal-grounding side of Q1’s second pressure. On Feser’s account, the analogical proportion is primarily a metaphysical grounding relation rather than a semantic proportion between predicate-tokens: creaturely perfections are *participated* forms of an act that God, as *ipsum esse subsistens*—subsistent *esse*, the act of being itself—possesses without any act/potency composition. The *esse*/essence distinction in creatures—*esse* is real and distinct from *essentia*—grounds the asymmetry. In God *esse* and *essentia* are identical, so God’s perfections are possessed eminently and without restriction, and the proportion tracks metaphysical participation rather than linguistic similarity.

The concern for Feser’s grounding is that *participation* is itself a structural relation: for the creature’s participated act to be grounded in God’s subsistent act, the creature must stand in a reception-relation to a source, and that relation is a directed, asymmetric dependence of the participated on the subsisting source. Those are role-level demands, not yet the loaded three Conditions. Feser’s reply is that *esse* isn’t a temporal-causal relation but the metaphysical grounding of participated-being in being-itself. The remaining question is whether the grounding relation—*creature receives esse from God*—requires the structural conditions of any reception, including direction, distinction, and a substantial bearer.

A second pressure on the analogy doctrine runs through its grounding rather than its compatibility with simplicity. Aquinas’s own grounding of analogical predication (*De Potentia* q.7 a.7; *Summa Contra Gentiles* I.34) takes the semantic fact of analogy to rest on a metaphysical fact: a real causal relation between Creator and creature, in which creatures derive their perfections from God as effects from their source. That causal relation is structurally constituted. Production is asymmetric, cause and effect are distinct relata, and the productive act is carried across the distinction it spans. Those are role-level demands: directed dependence, distinct terms, and a bearer of the relation. They don’t by themselves establish clock-time, metric space, or physical substance; that upgrade is owed only where the operation is independently shown to be concrete. The doctrine that was supposed to insulate divine predicates from the structural conditions enlists those conditions at the level of grounding. The two analogy concerns are complementary: the first locates the cost at the divine-pole side of the proportion; the second locates it at the metaphysical grounding the proportion rests on. Both press in the same direction.

A third resource within the analogy family locates the shared content not in the proportion but in the manner of signifying. Aquinas’s distinction between the *res significata* and the *modus significandi* (*ST* I.13.3) holds that a perfection-term (*good*, *wise*, *living*) said of God signifies a perfection, the thing signified, that belongs to God properly and indeed pre-eminently, while the creaturely *mode* of signifying it (the way the perfection is held by a composite, dependent, time-bound knower) is what falls short and isn’t affirmed of God. On this account the predicate’s determinate content survives on the side of the *res significata* even as its creaturely mode is set aside; the difficulty is supposed to lie only in the mode, not in the thing signified. The concern is what the *res significata* retains once the *modus* is subtracted. The perfections the believer predicates are given as determinate only in a mode: goodness as a settled orientation among alternatives, wisdom as the holding-together of a differentiated manifold, life as a duration.

Subtract the mode and the move forks. Either the thing signified keeps a determinate content, or the subtraction takes the content with the mode, and the *res significata* thins to the bare *is* found at §11.2.1 without individuating content and that Q2 and Q5 below reach as the apophatic terminus. On the first horn it keeps the specifying features the mode was carrying—the orientation, the manifold, the duration—and those features still owe an account of how they are held without collapsing into the mode the doctrine set aside. The distinction draws the line in the right place; it doesn’t relieve the pressure, because the features that made the perfection determinate are exactly what the *modus significandi* supplied and the divine pole is required to shed. Whether those features upgrade to loaded Time, Space, and Substance is a further step, owed only where the operation is independently shown to be concrete.

**Q2.** *What is left to confess, once every word for God has been negated?* The Pseudo-Dionysian tradition of negative theology (*Mystical Theology* 1; *Divine Names* 1) holds that we know what God isn’t, not what God is. The doctrine has been the central resource of mystical theology for fifteen centuries (Maximus, *Ambigua*; Eriugena, *Periphyseon*; Eckhart, *Sermons*) (for contemporary form Marion 1991; Turner 1995; Davies and Turner 2008). The concern here is what the negations leave for the believer’s confession. *God isn’t finite*, *God isn’t temporal*, *God isn’t embodied*, *God isn’t changeable*: each negation rules out one structural condition the corresponding affirmative predicate would have required. When the negations are summed, what remains is a being defined by the absence of every structural condition affirmative predication has been found to require. The Pseudo-Dionysian tradition is honest about this: the via negativa terminates in the *cloud of unknowing*, in silence, in the surrender of every conceptual handle on the divine. The present reading agrees that the apophatic tradition has been more honest about its terminus than the cataphatic (affirmative) refinements that build atop it. The question added here is what *God exists* affirms when every structural condition for existence has been negated. The honest answer the apophatic tradition itself gives is: not what *exists* affirms in any case the structural analysis examines.

**Q3.** *What is the greatest possible power, if it has no conditions left to be powerful within?* Anselm’s perfect-being methodology (*Proslogion* 2–3) derives the classical attributes by taking each attribute as the perfection of its kind: God is most powerful, most knowing, most good, with each *most* taken to its limit. Morris (1987), Leftow (2012), and Speaks (2018) develop contemporary versions. The concern here is the projection. To project an attribute to its limit is to extend a creaturely scale beyond any creaturely instance. The scale extends within the structural conditions of the attribute: powerful-within-T, knowing-within-T-and-S, good-within-relations-with-other-bearers. To extend the scale beyond any creaturely instance while removing the structural conditions of the scale isn’t to find a maximal point on the scale; it is to leave the scale. The doctrine projects the predicate beyond the modal structure the predicate is intelligible within. The result isn’t the predicate at its maximum but a being defined by the predicate’s having no modal structure to be at any value within. The methodological reply is that perfection just means *unlimited by structural conditions*. The present reading registers the reply and presses what is left of the predicate when its structural conditions are *the limitation* perfection negates.

**Q4.** *How does calling something a mystery make a contradiction cohere?* The classical tradition has long held that the divine nature exceeds creaturely comprehension and that the limits of creaturely comprehension entail no limit on divine being. The doctrine of *mystery*, properly understood, isn’t the surrender of reason but its acknowledgment of the bounds of analogical predication (Pseudo-Dionysius, *Mystical Theology*; Aquinas, *ST* I.12.7) (Wittgenstein (1921) 1961; for contemporary defense Plantinga 2000; Stump 2010). The concern here is what mystery accommodates and what it excludes. A doctrine that contains apparently incompatible commitments (say, divine immutability and divine response to prayer) can preserve coherence by appeal to mystery: the apparent incompatibility holds only at the level of creaturely understanding, not at the level of divine being. The structural reading doesn’t exclude it. The question this section presses is what mystery is positioned to do. Mystery, properly understood, is the recognition that creaturely concepts may not capture divine reality. It isn’t the recognition that contradictions cease to be contradictions when applied to a sufficiently elevated subject. The concern here is that the eleven preceding sections haven’t turned on creaturely conceptual limits; they have turned on structural conditions the doctrine has placed beyond divine being. Whatever mystery accommodates, it doesn’t accommodate the running-of-predicates outside the constitutive modal structure the predicates require for application.

**Q5.** *If God is beyond every word, what have the words been describing all along?* Apophasis at full extension (Eckhart, *Sermons* 22, 52) (Marion 1991) takes the negations to their limit: God is beyond being, beyond goodness, beyond every category, beyond beyond. The position isn’t nihilism but a rigorous form of theological humility. The present reading registers the position and notes its symmetry with the conclusion pressed throughout. To say of God *exists*, *is one*, *is necessary*, *is eternal*, *is present*, *is aware*, *knows*, *can*, *acts*, *governs*, *relates* (with every predicate qualified to remove the structural conditions of its application) is to terminate at the same point as Eckhart’s *abyss beyond God*: a referent for which no predicate the believer would recognize has determinate content. The mystical tradition arrives at this terminus by faithfulness to the apophatic method; the present chapter has arrived at it by faithfulness to the structural conditions of predicate application. The two paths converge.

The Plotinian origin makes the convergence structurally intelligible. In *Enneads* VI.9, Plotinus’s ascent terminates in the One *epekeina tēs ousias* (beyond being) which is beyond intellect, beyond goodness as a property, beyond every predicate that would make it an object of thought. The present chapter arrives at the same terminus from the structural side: the predicates applied to God, when their structural conditions are removed, no longer have determinate content. The Plotinian mystic arrives there by faithfully stripping predicates; the structural analysis arrives there by faithfully examining what makes predicates contentful. The question the convergence raises is which path has been tracing the right referent: the Plotinian One-beyond-being, or the structural conditions whose removal the negations name. The question is what the convergence shows. On the apophatic reading, what the predicates have been reaching for is the divine being itself, beyond all categories. On the present reading, what the predicates have been reaching for is the structural conditions of any reaching at all.

The convergence doesn’t leave the two readings symmetrically poised. The Plotinian One is the honest terminus of *refusing to predicate*: the ascent ends in silence, and silence is consistent with the One-beyond-being precisely because no predicate is asserted of it. But the believer’s God isn’t silent. The tradition doesn’t stop at the *cloud of unknowing*; it goes on to confess a God who creates, knows, loves, judges, and answers. Every such confession is an act of predication, and an act of predication is governed by the conditions of predication this section has been tracing. The apophatic terminus is therefore available only to a theology willing to follow it all the way down into silence: to surrender the acting, relating, worshipped God along with the predicates. The theology that keeps predicating has already declined the One-beyond-being; what it is left reaching for, every time it predicates, is the structural conditions any predicate requires. On the present analysis, continuing positive predication still owes determinate content and a referent-fixing relation; it doesn’t by itself track Nature rather than a referent beyond being. The One-beyond-being is available only where predication ceases; where positive predicates remain, their determinate content depends on what is preserved across the proportion or what is denied by the negation.

**Q6.** *If “being” means the same for God as for us, how is God’s being not structured like ours?* Duns Scotus, against Aquinas, holds that *being* (*ens*) applies univocally to God and creatures: the same concept of being, with the same content, predicated in the same sense across the Creator–creature divide *Ordinatio* I.3 (Cross 2005; Williams 2005). The semantic motivation is sharp: if creaturely concepts shifted in meaning when applied to God, theological speech couldn’t refer at all. Univocity of being is what makes theological discourse contentful. Grant the position in full. Univocity doesn’t flatten God into a being among beings; the formal distinction (Cross 2005, ch. 4) preserves the qualitative gap between infinite and finite being while keeping the concept of being itself constant across the divide. The Scotist Creator is still uniquely sovereign, uniquely necessary, uniquely the source. The cost surfaces at the level of what the constant concept *is*. If *being* applies univocally to God and creatures, then whatever being is for creatures it is also for God. Creaturely being is structured being—being-in-Time, being-extended-in-Space, being-as-what-bears-its-own-persistence. Univocity preserves theological speech by paying for it in the coin of structural commitment: the feature that makes God-talk contentful for Scotus is the feature that places God within structure. The Scotist Creator–creature distinction is real, but it is now a distinction *within* structure, not a distinction between structured being and something outside it.

Scotus’s is the medieval form of the position; a developed contemporary form is Swinburne’s (*The Coherence of Theism*, 1977, ch. 4, “The Words of Theology”). Swinburne grants neither full univocity nor analogy but a controlled stretching of ordinary-language terms: a word keeps its ordinary meaning while the conditions of its application are loosened just far enough to reach the divine case without importing the creaturely limitations. The motivation is Scotus’s (speech that doesn’t refer isn’t speech) but the mechanism is meant to preserve reference at lower structural cost than univocity of being. The concern here is what the stretching can loosen without losing the term. Either the loosened conditions still include the structural frame the predicate runs on, in which case the controlled stretch still incurs the role-level demands univocity incurred, only less visibly; or the stretching loosens the structural conditions themselves, in which case it hasn’t stretched the term’s content but cut it loose from what gave the term determinate application, sliding toward the equivocity Swinburne means to avoid and the apophasis Q2 has already weighed. Controlled meaning-stretching preserves reference only on the first branch, and the first branch is univocity’s structural commitment under a softer name. The upgrade from those roles to loaded Time, Space, and Substance is a further step for a timeless subject; for an everlasting God who acts in time, as Swinburne’s does, the Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) has already taken it at the acting.

**Q7.** *How does the hidden God become the disclosed God without changing?* Karl Barth ((1932) 1975, I/1; cf. McCormack 1995; Hunsinger 1991; Webster 2004) refuses analogy in favor of revelation: we know God not by extending creaturely concepts upward, but only in the act in which God reveals Godself. That act is dialectical (*Realdialektik*): in revealing Godself, God remains hidden, disclosed as the One who isn’t exhausted by what is disclosed. Barthians press this as the move that protects God’s transcendence without giving up theological speech. A dialectic between hiddenness and disclosure that is *real*, and not just a conceptual contrast, requires three things: a distinction between what is hidden and what is disclosed, an act in which the one becomes the other, and one and the same God who is both the hidden one and the disclosed one. Those are role-level demands: distinct terms, directed becoming, and a persisting bearer. They don’t by themselves establish metric space or clock-time. The Barthian rejoinder (that revelation isn’t a worldly event but God’s eternity breaking into time) restates the point in stronger language without removing it. Eternity that breaks *into* time still has direction. Hiddenness that endures *through* disclosure still has a being. Transcendence revealed *as* immanent still has relational structure. The *Realdialektik* is the act in which those role-level demands operate at maximum intensity, not the act in which they are left behind. Whether they upgrade to loaded Time, Space, and Substance is owed only where the disclosure is independently shown to be a concrete worldly event. Between univocity (Q6), equivocation (rejected by both Aquinas and Scotus), and analogy (Q1), no semantic option preserves a Creator outside structure. Revelation as the alternative to analogical predication preserves it by *enacting* those demands rather than predicating them.

*The Word at the beginning.* Two of the traditions pressed here place divine speech not at the far end of the difficulty but at the very start of what they confess, and it is worth reading those confessions closely, because the escape route runs through them. John’s prologue opens *in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God* (John 1:1). The Islamic doctrine of *kalām Allāh* makes the Qur’ān the uncreated speech of God, not a created report about God. Neither is a marginal formulation. Each is a founding formulation, and each says that the divine isn’t merely describable but that something word-like is what the divine *is*, or is inseparably of.

Take *Word* in its ordinary sense and the demand is already met, in the tradition’s own opening sentence. A word isn’t a bare presence. It is *of* something, which requires the word and what it names to be distinguishable; it says something rather than something else, which requires exclusion among alternatives; and it is uttered, received, or held, which requires a bearer. Those are the structural roles, arriving before anything has been argued about them. The prologue’s own grammar is stricter still: *with* God and *was* God together require a relation and a term, and a relation between the wholly undifferentiated and itself isn’t a relation.

Take *Word* as analogical instead, and the escape route rejoins the road it left. If the Word isn’t a word in any sense continuous with words, the term has been withdrawn just as *knows* and *good* were, and the diagnostic above applies to it unchanged: an analogy that shares no structure with its ordinary use hasn’t extended a meaning but retired one. The difficulty is that this is a costlier withdrawal than the others, because the doctrine isn’t using *Word* to describe God from outside. It is using it to say what God is. A tradition may hold that its central term is analogical; it can’t hold that and also hold that the term tells us what stands at the beginning. The point is that the confessions were never reticent about description in the first place, not that they are confused—the reticence is a later doctrine, and it is in tension with the sentence the tradition opens with.

*The burden.* The seven pressures register the structural conditions divine description depends on. Analogy requires a constitutive relation between attribute and bearer on the divine side for the proportion to be a proportion *of*; the doctrine of strong simplicity has factored that relation out at the divine pole. The causal grounding the analogy rests on is itself structurally constituted (asymmetric production, distinct cause and effect, a productive act carried across the distinction), so analogy preserves the predicates by enlisting at the level of grounding the very structure it tries to set aside at the level of the proportion. Those are role-level demands, and the upgrade to loaded Time, Space, and Substance is owed only where the production is independently shown to be concrete—where it is, a cause terminating in creatures, it has already been taken there. Apophasis, summed, removes every condition affirmative predication has been found to require, and the tradition’s terminus in *cloud of unknowing* and *abyss beyond God* is honest about what its method leaves standing. Perfect-being theology projects creaturely scales past the limit of their own modal structure; extending an attribute beyond any creaturely instance while removing the structural conditions of the scale is leaving the scale, not finding a maximal point on it.

Mystery accommodates conceptual humility, but it doesn’t accommodate predicates running outside the structural frame their application requires: the eleven preceding sections turned on structural conditions, not on creaturely conceptual limits. Mystical apophasis and the present chapter’s structural reading converge on the same referent for which no recognizable predicate retains determinate content; the question is which referent the predicates have been reaching for. Univocity preserves the content of theological speech but thereby incurs structural commitments: if *being* applies univocally to God and creatures, whatever being is for creatures it is for God, and creaturely being is structured being. Revelation as the alternative to predication enacts the same role-level demands at maximum intensity rather than transcending them: hiddenness through disclosure has direction, hidden-and-disclosed needs a being, and *Realdialektik* is the act in which those demands operate at full force, not the act in which they are left behind. What divine description names, when its referent is examined, is whatever content the analogy preserves or the apophasis denies. Silence is a coherent religious posture. It can’t simultaneously deliver the positive claims that God knows, acts, loves, creates, or relates.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Analogy Enlists the Structure It Was Built to Avoid** · *Diagnostic*

Analogical predication needs a constitutive relation between attribute and bearer on the divine side, or the proportion isn’t a proportion *of* anything—and strong simplicity has factored exactly that relation out at the divine pole. The causal grounding analogy rests on is itself structurally constituted: asymmetric production, distinct cause and effect, a productive act carried across the distinction. Those are role-level demands, not yet clock-time, metric space, or physical transmission. So the device preserves the predicates by recruiting, at the level of its own grounding, the structure it was introduced to let the subject do without. It doesn’t fail by saying too little. It succeeds only by quietly requiring what it denies.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Description need not picture its object, and successful reference need not disclose an object’s intrinsic nature. It does require content that distinguishes accurate from inaccurate application and some account of how the words are about their alleged referent. Analogy can supply that account if it states what is preserved across the proportion; apophasis can discipline overdescription by stating what is denied. The failure arrives only when every positive similarity, discriminator, and referent-fixing relation is withdrawn while the original confession is retained as though nothing had changed. What the section leaves standing is the ordinary achievement the difficulty is measured against. Words that distinguish accurate from inaccurate application, about objects they in no way resemble, are used successfully all day. Describing works, and the discipline of saying carefully what something is belongs to whoever undertakes it. The pressure here falls on a particular referent, not on description.

Nor is the discipline parochial. Withdrawing positive predicates to protect a transcendent referent is a shared method rather than a local expedient: Ibn-Sina, Maimonides, and Aquinas are studied together precisely because they run it in parallel (Burrell 1986), and Advaita proceeds by the same subtraction, *neti neti*, not this, not that (Deutsch 1969). The question this section presses isn’t an embarrassment peculiar to one theology. It arises from the method itself, and arises at the same point wherever the method is practised: after the last denial, what fixes the reference.

### 11.8.4 Revelation

Revelation is the claim that God has made himself known—at Sinai, in Christ, in scripture, creation, conscience, or an event of the Word—but traditions disagree about to whom, for what purpose, and at what evidential strength that disclosure is sufficient. The historical disclosures are local in time and place, culturally marked, and transmitted through ordinary human channels. That pattern creates an abductive problem for formulations that assign them universal epistemic clarity or decisive public evidence; it doesn’t by itself refute doctrines that claim only salvific availability, moral accountability, covenantal address to a community, or divine self-disclosure without universal evidential decisiveness.

The doctrine of divine revelation holds that God has made himself known (his nature, his will, his redemptive purpose) through specific historical disclosures (Sinai, the prophets, the incarnation of the Word, the apostolic witness) and through the standing testimony of creation and conscience. The medieval and Reformed traditions distinguish *revelatio specialis* (special revelation: scripture and incarnation) from *revelatio generalis* (general revelation: the natural order and the *sensus divinitatis* implanted in every human being). Aquinas treats the specially-revealed articles as suprarational truths necessary for salvation (*ST* I.1.1; cf. Rom 1:20 and the Five Ways for the naturally-knowable preamble), and Calvin grounds the *sensus* in *Institutes* I.iii.1 as a universal seed of religion. The Reformed scholastics tighten the structure: scripture is self-authenticating (*autopistia*) and clear in the matters necessary for salvation (*perspicuitas*); the natural knowledge is sufficient to convict but insufficient to save (Turretin, *Institutes* I.iv). Barth’s twentieth-century reformulation collapses the special–general distinction by treating *all* revelation as the dialectical event of the Word’s own self-disclosure (*Church Dogmatics* I/1), so that natural theology is rejected as a category-mistake. Across these formulations one common claim remains—that God is genuinely disclosed—but the sufficiency predicates divide. Aquinas distinguishes naturally knowable preambles from specially revealed salvific articles; Reformed accounts often treat general revelation as sufficient for accountability but not salvation and scripture as clear in matters necessary for salvation; Plantinga’s properly-basic warrant concerns justified Christian belief under a design plan; Barth resists treating revelation as a generally available evidential deposit. No single formulation should be charged with all of assent-sufficiency, salvific sufficiency, moral-accountability sufficiency, and decisive public evidence at once.

*The interrogation.* Twelve questions test different doctrinal targets, and their conclusions are limited accordingly. Q1–Q2 and Q7 test claims of universal reach or non-resistant availability; Q3–Q5 and Q8–Q9 test strong inspiration or source-transcendence claims; Q4 and Q6 test text-mediated and public-evidential sufficiency; Q10 tests Barthian self-disclosure; Q11 tests general revelation; Q12 tests Reformed epistemology’s properly functioning *sensus*. *Sufficient* isn’t one demand, and no answer—or shortfall—automatically transfers among salvific, epistemic, moral, covenantal, and public-evidential registers.

**Q1.** *How does a revelation delivered at one time reach people in every time?* Sinai occurred at one place in one millennium; the incarnation occupied a thirty-year window in a single Roman province; the Quranic recitations span twenty-three years of seventh-century Arabia. A being whose nature is to-be-known by every temporal cross-section of the rational creation can’t deliver his self-disclosure at a temporal point and expect the disclosure to bear universal weight. Either the disclosure is for that location only (and the universal claim fails), or it reaches later locations by transmission, which Q2 and Q4 take up, or it must be re-delivered to each location (and it hasn’t been).

**Q2.** *How does a revelation from one place become a disclosure to everyone?* Sinai is in the Sinai; the incarnation in Galilee and Judea; the Quran in the Hijaz.
