The actual propagation pattern of each tradition follows the contours of empire, trade-route, migration, and conquest, that is, the contours of human cultural diffusion. The pattern of dissemination is indistinguishable from the pattern any merely-human cultural production would exhibit. If revelation were sourced in the omnipresent ground of being, we would expect its distribution to look unlike, not exactly like, the distribution of human cultural artifacts.

**Q3.** *If revelation bears its culture’s fingerprint, what marks it as coming from outside that culture?* The texts are written in the literary genres of their period; they encode the cosmologies, legal institutions, and rhetorical conventions of their producing cultures; the variants and redactional layers track the practices of the scribes who transmitted them. Ehrman (2005; 2009), Allison, Walton, and Collins document the pattern in detail (2010; 2009; 2006). A revelation issued by a being whose standing is outside Φ wouldn’t bear Φ’s fingerprint at every level of its delivery; one issued from inside Φ would. The available disclosures exhibit the characteristics expected of culturally situated productions.

**Q4.** *Even granting a genuine source, how can a written text be the right instrument for a disclosure meant for every person?* Scripture reaches anyone only across a chain of human relays (composition, transcription, canonization, transmission, translation, interpretation) and each link is a point of loss, open only to the literate, the linguistically matched, and the textually trained. Paine presses the structural form: a revelation fixed in writing and carried by human hands is, after its first hearer, no longer revelation but report: testimony about a revelation, with no more reach than the fallible chain that conveys it (Paine 1794). A source whose standing is universal wouldn’t entrust its universal message to the least universal of media; one working from inside human culture would have nothing else to use. The deliveries use exactly what a from-within-Φ production would use, and nothing a from-outside-Φ source could distinctively command.

**Q5.** *Setting the question of error aside, why does a disclosure supposedly from outside human culture never carry content its era couldn’t yet have reached?* A source from outside Φ has every opportunity to exceed its century; none of the deliveries does. Where the deliveries speak of nature, law, or history, they speak with exactly the reach, and exactly the limits, of the era that produced them: the otherwise-inaccessible truth a from-outside-Φ source could supply, and a from-within-Φ source couldn’t, never appears. The point isn’t that the content errs, which Q8 takes up, but that it never exceeds its century: a failure of the prediction that an external source would supply content unavailable to the originating culture.

**Q6.** *What good is a delivered message if its evidence can’t identify its source?* The tradition often equivocates between the two: between *God has made himself available* and *what God has made available is decisive*. Habermas’s completed four-volume treatment now supplies the fullest version of his case: historical method and positive evidence, answers to alternative explanations, a survey of the scholarly field, and the event’s theological implications (Habermas 2024a; Habermas 2024b; Habermas 2025; Habermas 2026). Alongside Licona, Wright, Craig, and Davis, it presses the resurrection as a sufficient evidential ground for the central claim (2010; 2003; 2008; 1993): not merely *some witnesses reported X*, but a cumulative case from early testimony, transformed communities, explanatory fit, and the claimed irreducibility of the resurrection to ordinary legendary development. Pressed that far, the case isn’t dismissible as naïve evidentialism. The concern here is narrower and sharper: even if the historical case is granted as stated, the inference from historically serious testimony to *this is the load-bearing public ground for cosmic moral allegiance* runs through a probabilistic gap that the doctrine of sufficient revelation can’t tolerate without supplementation by the very *sensus* or interior witness it was meant to supply from outside.

**Q7.** *Why isn’t revelation clearest to the people most sincerely open to it, as a loving discloser would seem to require?* Schellenberg (1993; 2007; 2015) formalizes the divine hiddenness problem: a perfectly loving God would ensure that no capable, non-resistant rational creature is, by their own lights, without sufficient ground for relationship with him; many such creatures are, by their own lights, without such ground; therefore no perfectly loving God exists. Howard-Snyder and Moser (2002) collect the responsive literature, and Hick (1966) offers the epistemic-distance defense. But the defenses retain the fact that needs explaining: the actual distribution of revelatory clarity doesn’t track the distribution of sincere openness. The revelation is delivered, on the tradition’s own terms, less clearly than its purpose appears to demand.

**Q8.** *How can deliveries marked at every turn by the empirical errors of their era have a source outside that era?* Gen 1’s cosmology, Josh 10’s stayed sun, Luke 2’s Quirinian census, the Matthean and Lukan birth narratives’ incompatible geographies, the genealogical disagreements, the parallel-pericope contradictions in the synoptic record: each is documentable, and each is the kind of artifact a delivery from within Φ would exhibit and a delivery from outside Φ wouldn’t. Gen 1 describes a solid dome with waters standing above it, and openings through which those waters fall (Gen 1:6–7; 7:11; 8:2)—the ancient Near Eastern picture of the sky, not a description anyone reading it today would recognize. Ehrman (2005; 2009), Allison, Walton, and Collins catalog the artifacts (2010; 2009; 2006). The tradition’s reply (that these are accommodations to the original audience’s idiom) concedes the data and relocates the burden onto a doctrine of accommodation strong enough to absorb anything the texts contain, which is to say strong enough to absorb falsifying content.

**Q9.** *How can one source deliver two claims when each one denies the other?* Mary’s location at the tomb (Matt 28 vs. John 20), the death of Judas (Matt 27 vs. Acts 1), the genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1 vs. Luke 3), and the timing of the crucifixion (synoptic Passover vs. Johannine Preparation) can’t all be true on any reading that respects Aristotelian non-contradiction (*Metaphysics* Γ.3) or its scholastic inheritance (Aquinas, *ST* I.85.5). The accommodation move available for empirical errors is structurally unavailable for contradictions in revelation’s own content: a being who delivers revelation can’t deliver, as the content of revelation, a pair of propositions one of which entails the negation of the other.

**Q10.** *If revelation is reframed as a self-disclosure that carries its own veiling within it, what surface feature of the delivery could still count for or against its having occurred?* Barth’s dialectical move (Barth (1932) 1975, I/1; McCormack 1995; Hunsinger 1991; Webster 2004) attempts to absorb these pressures by reframing revelation as the event of God’s self-disclosure that bears within itself its own veiling: a *Realdialektik* in which the Word makes himself known precisely by remaining hidden in his disclosure. The move is theologically powerful but evidentially evacuating: if the dialectical structure is internal to revelation, then no surface feature of the delivery (clarity, accuracy, distribution, evidential adequacy) can count for or against revelation having occurred, which is to say no feature can count.

**Q11.** *Can general revelation supply what special revelation doesn’t, or does it exhibit the same marks of cultural production?* Rom 1:20, the Five Ways, Paley’s *Natural Theology* (1802), and Plantinga’s *sensus divinitatis* (2000) furnish standing creaturely access to God that doesn’t depend on a particular historical delivery. But each construal of general revelation either runs against the same Φ-fingerprint critique (the natural theologies are themselves cultural artifacts of particular philosophical traditions) or relocates the work to an interior faculty whose universality is empirically contested.

**Q12.** *Why does the belief Reformed epistemology calls properly basic track where the believer was born rather than what is true?* Reformed epistemology (Plantinga 2000) treats Christian belief as properly basic (justified without being inferred from other beliefs) when produced by a properly functioning *sensus* in a congenial environment with the truth-aimed cognitive design plan of the IIHS (Internal Instigation of the Holy Spirit). The epistemic system is internally coherent, but it has no resources for explaining why the *sensus* delivers, in the actual cultural-distribution data, beliefs that track the religious tradition of the believer’s geographic origin rather than tracking the truth-conditions of the propositions believed. The cultural-distribution argument is, on Plantinga’s own framework, a defeater-deflector candidate, and the deflector isn’t in hand.

*The burden.* These pressures constitute convergent abductive evidence rather than formal entailments, and only against the formulations each question engages. Taken individually, each is answerable. Collectively, the culturally mediated pattern weighs against the strong claim that the historical deliveries provide universally distributed, unambiguous, and decisive public evidence of an extra-natural source. It doesn’t establish that no revelation occurred, that no community was addressed, or that no account of salvific or moral sufficiency can survive. The world’s standing availability to inquiry supplies a natural contrast case: public orientation can emerge through corrigible investigation without a punctual transmission from outside Nature. That contrast doesn’t turn discoverability into revelation, since revelation additionally claims a discloser, an intention, and communicated content.

Revelation isn’t merely information-transfer; it is intentional disclosure. Its reception requires a field in which content can become available, subjects for whom it becomes available, and media through which marks, reasons, memories, and practices persist. Those conditions locate the delivery within the three Conditions. They don’t establish that the proposed source contains those conditions intrinsically; a source-transcendent account instead owes the contact by which determinate content enters a culturally mediated delivery. The availability of the world to inquiry is therefore a control case, not the relocated meaning of *revelation*.

*What the relocation doesn’t concede.* The relocation invites a symmetry charge from the side of the hiddenness argument itself. Schellenberg’s mature position doesn’t rest with the denial of personal theism; it offers *ultimism* (the bare commitment that there is a reality ultimate in being, in value, and as the source of our deepest good) as the standing alternative the honest inquirer should adopt once revelation fails (Schellenberg 2007). The charge presses a symmetry. Dissolving revelation into the availability of the world to inquiry, the objection runs, doesn’t refute revelation so much as rename its absence. To say that the personal self-disclosing God is nowhere clearly given, and that what is universally given is instead the world’s openness to inquiry, simply restates Schellenberg’s own conclusion—that the personal discloser is unavailable—under a friendlier description. The concession is only apparent, and seeing why turns on which side of the disclosure relation carries the variation. The availability the relocation names isn’t response-dependent—it doesn’t wait upon, and isn’t constituted by, anyone’s act of inquiry.

The world’s discoverability is a standing, mind-independent, T- and S- and Φ-spanning structural fact, one that reality exhibits at every cross-section whether or not an inquirer is present to exploit it, exactly as the necessity of Nature requires (§2.9.6). What emerges (with life, and deepening with cognitive complexity) isn’t the world’s discoverability but the *capacity* to discover it; emergence sits on the subject side of the relation, not the object side. The hiddenness datum (that revelatory clarity doesn’t track sincere openness) then receives the explanation a hidden personal discloser could supply only by positing some further reason for the silence: an unevenly developed, contingently distributed capacity to read an always-open world is just what an emergent capacity predicts. The asymmetry Schellenberg presses is real, but it is an asymmetry of access, not of availability; the universal standing-ground (the world’s intelligibility) is never absent, and only the capacity that reads it is uneven, which is precisely what needs no hidden person to explain.

Nor does the contrast recover ultimism under another name. Nature’s discoverability isn’t a personal disclosure and doesn’t warrant trust, hope, or devotion toward an underdescribed ultimate. If a divine discloser is retained, that personal and intentional content must be supported independently. If it is withdrawn, discoverability remains, but revelation hasn’t been redescribed; it has been replaced by a different epistemic relation.

**[Diagnostic]**

**What Is Needed Moves, Not the Delivery** · *Diagnostic*

The pressures here are convergent abductive evidence rather than entailments, and they bear only on the formulations each question engages. Taken singly each is answerable; taken together the culturally mediated pattern weighs against the strong claim that the historical deliveries supply universally distributed, unambiguous, decisive public evidence of an extra-natural source. **It doesn’t establish that no revelation occurred, that no community was addressed, or that no account of salvific or moral sufficiency can survive**, and it isn’t offered as establishing any of those. What the pattern indicates is the same relocation found at Righteousness and Interaction: what is wanted isn’t a more universal delivery or a better-distributed set of them, but the standing ground for orientation that a delivery was supposed to carry.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* The strong public claim is evidentially burdened: the deliveries are historically and culturally located, and their clarity doesn’t track sincere openness in the way universal decisive disclosure predicts. Nature’s discoverability supplies a wider and corrigible route to knowledge, but it isn’t revelation because it supplies no personal discloser or communicative intention. Weaker event, covenantal, salvific, and moral-accountability claims remain to be assessed on their own standards. The outcome is comparison and possible replacement, not relocation of the divine predicate to Nature. What the concept requires is nevertheless within reach. A discloser, an intention, and communicated content are met whenever one person tells another something true about themselves that couldn’t have been worked out from outside. That is the case the word was built on, and it isn’t rare. What is disputed is a further and much larger claimant, not whether disclosure of that kind occurs.

## 11.9 Moral Act
The active arm closes with the moral attributes: benevolence (§11.9.1) and righteousness (§11.9.2), God as good in will and just in act. Both are act-attributes before they are value-attributes: to will the good and to render justice is to do something, directed at an object, across the relation between agent and recipient.

Pressed, each exercise-claim incurs the full Structural Requirement at the act itself (Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4)): a moral act has an agent, a recipient, and a directed doing between them, and the conditions of that doing are the three Conditions at the operation. The character and standard claims owe truth conditions of their own.

Before the machinery, the worry can be put in a breath. To be just or benevolent, cruel or kind, righteous or wicked is to conduct oneself some way toward someone—to behave, and to behave one way rather than another. Behaving is something a being does: it takes a transition from not-yet-acting to acting (T), a field holding another party to act toward (S), and a doer the conduct is of (Φ). A being defined without time, space, and substance doesn’t behave well or badly; it doesn’t behave at all, because behaving isn’t among the things such a being is positioned to do. And what cannot behave cannot misbehave. The moral predicates come in contrasting pairs—just and unjust, merciful and cruel, righteous and wicked—and a pair gets no grip where neither term could apply.

This is why the tradition’s proudest moral claim, impeccability, the impossibility of divine wrongdoing, isn’t the summit of character the doctrine takes it for: a being that can’t sin because it can’t act hasn’t achieved the refusal of evil, it is simply the wrong kind of thing to be virtuous or vicious, as a number is the wrong kind of thing to keep a promise or break one. The point cuts on both sides of the ledger at once, and disarms the objector in the same motion it deflates the devotee: the God who can’t be cruel or unjust for want of any conduct to be cruel or unjust in is, by that same want, unable to be kind or just in the conduct-sense either. *God is good*, if it is to survive, can’t mean *acts well*; it must be re-seated as something God is said to be rather than something God is said to do—the being-to-structure relocation run on agency (§11.7.2), carried one step further into moral character. And the verdict is reached here without touching any of the disputes the subsections take up—skeptical theism, penal substitution, original sin, the conquest texts, the demographics of belief—so it stands however those are settled: an opponent who won every one of them would still be left with a subject outside the conditions under which just and unjust carry differential content.

### 11.9.1 Benevolence

Divine goodness isn’t merely that God is good but that God can’t be otherwise: benevolent, loving, incapable of evil. The key observation is grammatical, but the grammar isn’t one grammar. Words like “benevolently” or “justly” can describe a *way of acting*, and those uses need an act to attach to, and acting needs time, a recipient, and an agent. A being defined without those can’t *act* in the relevant sense, and so can’t be good or bad *as an agent of those acts*. Character and standard uses remain live until they are given their own truth conditions; they aren’t refuted by showing that an adverb needs a verb.

The classical doctrine of divine goodness assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *summum bonum*: the highest good, the good itself rather than a good among goods (Augustine, *De Trinitate* VIII.3; Aquinas, *ST* I.6.2; Anselm, *Monologion* 1–4). God is *bonitas ipsa*, goodness itself, identical with the divine nature on classical simplicity (*ST* I.6.3). God wills the good of creation: *bonum diffusivum sui*, the good is self-diffusive, and God’s creative act is the overflow of divine goodness toward what isn’t God (Pseudo-Dionysius, *Divine Names* IV; Aquinas, *ST* I.19; *ST* I.44.4). God is essentially benevolent toward creation: *amor benevolentiae*, the love of willing-good-toward (Aquinas, *ST* I.20) (Stump 2010). God is impeccable: incapable of sinning, of doing moral evil (*ST* I.25.3 ad 2) (Morris 1991; Pawl 2016 on Christological impeccability). The same cluster includes divine justice (*ST* I.21; Anselm, *Cur Deus Homo* I.12), divine mercy (*ST* I.21.3; the mercy–justice relation is worked at §11.9.2, Q1), and divine love construed as more than benevolence: *amor amicitiae*, friendship-love (Aquinas, *ST* I.20.2) (Stump 2010 develops the contemporary form). The Islamic tradition develops parallel claims: *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim* (the Compassionate and the Merciful) among the divine names (Q1:1, 1:3); God’s mercy as *wajib* (obligatory) in the Mu’tazilite reading, as gracious-overflow in the Ash’arite (Frank 1992). The doctrine, carried to its limit, names a being whose moral character is essential to its being (whose goodness isn’t a property had alongside other properties but constitutive of what the being is) and whose every act toward creation is therefore necessarily good.

*The interrogation.* Seven questions identify limitations in the doctrine of divine goodness as stated. What runs beneath them is grammatical before it is metaphysical, but the grammar isn’t one grammar. *Benevolent*, *just*, *merciful*, *loving*, *patient*, *faithful*, *gracious* can name a manner of acting, a standing character, or a standard. The adverbial uses require the verb, and the conditions of acting are what makes the verb available: succession from not-acting to acting (T), a target distinct from the actor (S), a substantive agent who acts (Φ). Those uses can’t attach to a being defined without any of the three Conditions. Character and standard uses aren’t thereby empty; they owe a value profile, a relation to actual conduct, and a discriminator that keeps *good* from collapsing into self-identity. The seven pressures run at both levels. A methodological note is owed before they begin. Stump’s narrative theodicy (*Wandering in Darkness* Stump 2010) presses that abstract goodness-talk misses what the doctrine of divine goodness is for; the argument here doesn’t compete with that project but runs prior to it for the *exercise* claims. The claim isn’t that the [classical God](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary)’s goodness fails to console but that commanding, judging, forgiving, protecting, and permitting need an acting before any narrative about the acting can begin. Character and standard claims face a different burden, and they aren’t settled by the adverb.

**Q1.** *How does God do good, if doing means acting in time upon something other than oneself?* Before the question can be answered, the question of what *do* means for the being the doctrine names has to be settled. To do is to act, and to act is to transition from a state in which the action doesn’t obtain to one in which it does (T), to bear on something distinct from oneself (S), through a substantive being that performs the action (Φ). Omnipotence (§11.7.1) works the doing-question for the predicate *power*; the present pressure returns the worked result. The Thomistic resolution distinguishes God’s act from creaturely acts and applies the verb *do* analogically rather than univocally (Aquinas, *ST* I.45) (Burrell 1986). The analogical reply preserves the verbal predicate by registering that what *do* names in God isn’t what *do* names in creatures. What it doesn’t preserve is the contentful relation between the doing and any manner-of-doing descriptor. If *do* applies analogically rather than univocally, then *do well* and *do badly* apply analogically rather than univocally, and the contrast that gives the manner-of-acting predicates their content has been displaced by the analogical move. The question whether God can do good things dissolves into the question of what *do* means for God, and the analogical answer to the second leaves the first without a univocal sense to apply. The moral predicates depend on the doing-predicate’s univocity for their differential content; the doctrine’s analogical resolution preserves the predicate’s name at the cost of the contrast that makes the predicate’s modification informative.

**Q2.** *How is one timeless act good, if it sustains the world’s evil no less than its good?* The classical doctrine holds God as *actus purus*: pure act, without potency, without unrealized capacity (*ST* I.3.1–2; I.9.1). The most thoroughgoing reading takes God’s act as one eternal, all-encompassing, all-sustaining act in which the distinction between creating, conserving, and concurring collapses into a single divine doing (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991). The concern here is what this does to moral differentiation. Goodness, in the contentful sense the doctrine wants, requires the differential preference of one outcome over an alternative: an act is benevolent because it prefers the good of its target over the not-good. Pure act, taken strictly, has no alternatives to prefer among, since alternatives are differentiations within the modal field the doctrine has placed beyond the divine being (§11.3.1). The pressure sharpens at the consequence side. One eternal act that sustains all things sustains them indiscriminately; what is sustained includes what the doctrine elsewhere calls evil: the suffering of creatures, the disorder of the natural world, the moral failures of finite agents.

If divine sustaining is one pure act, the same act sustains the good things and the bad things, and the doctrine has no resource for differentiating the act’s relation to the good consequences from its relation to the bad. The classical reply distinguishes God’s permitting evil from God’s directly willing evil (Aquinas, *ST* I.19.9) (Stump 1985; Stump 2010 on the theodicy literature). The reply preserves God from authorship of evil at the cost of partitioning the single pure act into a willing-part (the good) and a permitting-part (the evil). Strict simplicity disallows the partition; loose simplicity surrenders the unity of the act on which the impeccability claim rested. The doctrine wants pure-act unity *and* moral differentiation *and* impeccability simultaneously, and these are three commitments joined only by the term *one act*. The ordinary-morality form of this pressure is that our duty to intervene in preventable suffering doesn’t lapse when the sufferer’s greater good is invoked. It is run against divine non-intervention at §11.9.2 (Q7).

**Q3.** *Does inability to do evil limit omnipotence?* The question turns on what the power claim ranges over. Creatures’ actual evil establishes that evil action occurs and is therefore possible-simpliciter. It doesn’t establish that every agent has the capacity to perform every possible act-type. Nor does omnipotence ordinarily mean that God can instantiate every action some differently constituted creature can instantiate. The claim is usually that God can actualize every broadly possible state of affairs within the scope of power. On that reading, God may be able to actualize a world in which a creature freely does evil without God thereby doing the evil. Impeccability and omnipotence don’t conflict by operator logic alone. The live question is whether the proposed restriction belongs to the nature of the agent, to the scope of power, or to an independently structured modal field. The classical replies divide there.

The privation-of-evil reply (Augustine, *Enchiridion* III–IV; Aquinas, *De Malo* I) holds that evil isn’t a positive capacity but a defect of right action, and God’s incapacity for evil is the absence of a defect rather than the absence of a capacity. The reply faces three independent pressures, each at a different theoretical level, and each forcing a concession the doctrine elsewhere refuses.

*The modal-priority pressure.* Commitment B already treats possibility as a condition on divine action rather than its product. If God creates the universe, universe-creation must be possible; its modal standing can’t be produced by the very act whose availability it conditions. That is the externality result established at §7.2.1. Impeccability doesn’t add the further result that divine capacities form a proper subset of creaturely capacities, because the capacities belong to differently constituted agents and aren’t typed merely by act-description. It instead forces the account to specify the range of omnipotence. If the range is possible states of affairs, God may actualize a world containing creaturely evil without being its evil agent. If the range is actions available to God given the divine nature, the nature-index is part of the power claim rather than an exception discovered afterward. In either case possibility constrains what power can actualize; neither case by itself shows that God lacks a power some creature possesses.

*The doctrinal-interlock pressure.* A tempting reading of the privation account against other classical attributes would run as follows. The doctrine holds (i) God is goodness itself: *bonitas ipsa*, identical with the divine nature on simplicity (*ST* I.6.3); (ii) evil is the privation of due-good (the present reply); (iii) God is omnipresent: present whole in every place (*ST* I.8). If (i) and (ii) together meant that evil is the numerical absence of God, then wherever there is evil God would be absent, and (iii) would yield that there is no evil anywhere. That reading misstates the target. Privation of a *due* good is the absence of a good that belongs to a creature in its kind, not the numerical absence of God; invoking *due* doesn’t concede a positive evil entity, and it doesn’t identify every due good with the divine being. The conjunction of (i)–(iii) therefore doesn’t by itself produce “no evil anywhere.” What remains of the pressure is narrower: if *bonitas ipsa* is identified with every due good a creature can lack, the identification still has to be argued, and the omnipresence claim still has to say what presence-of-goodness amounts to in a region of privation. Those are discriminating-content and presence burdens, not a three-way contradiction already in hand. The inversion of omnipresence at the structural level is developed at §11.8.1; the present pressure works the converse direction only so far as the identification of goodness with every due good is actually made.

*The internal-structural pressure.* The privation account, examined as a representation of the moral domain, is structurally binary: it divides acts into *good* (positive instantiation of due-being) and *not-good* (privation, deficiency, the absence of due-being read as evil). The moral domain, as it actually shows up, is at least ternary. There is *maintenance*: acts that positively contribute to other subjects’ subsistence-conditions (the contentful good). There is *non-engagement*: acts that bear on no other subject’s subsistence-conditions, neither contributing nor violating (the vast bulk of human action, and the morally neutral region). There is *violation*: acts that positively interfere with other subjects’ subsistence-conditions (the contentful evil, structurally distinct from neutral non-engagement). The privation account can represent maintenance and the absence of maintenance, but can’t distinguish non-engagement from violation. Both look like *not-(maintenance)* on the binary scheme. The forks the account takes to recover the distinction each cost a load-bearing commitment.

*Fork A.* Treat all *not-(maintenance)* as evil. Then every act that fails to maintain another subject’s subsistence is evil, most of life becomes evil, and the result is one the doctrine elsewhere refuses. *Fork B.* Appeal to *due-good*—privation is the absence of *due-good*, where some goods are due and others aren’t. The fork relocates the explanatory work to the *due* structure, but the *due* structure is a positive moral fact: it says *X is owed to Y in conditions Z*. That need not make evil a positive entity. It does mean the privation analysis isn’t yet an analysis of what is due; it depends on one. *Fork C.* Distinguish non-engagement from violation by the agent’s positive intent or willing-toward-harm. The positive act and intention can be the bearer of a disorder without the disorder becoming a positive entity, so this move doesn’t contradict privation theory. It relocates the explanatory burden again: the account must say which order the willing fails to realize and why that order is due. The phenomenological point remains useful but limited. Moral attribution commonly tracks the agent’s willing-toward-violation, while the victim’s deficiency is its consequence. A privation theory can represent that structure only by locating the privation in the act’s due order as well as in the victim’s resulting condition.

The remaining pressures are independent and narrower than a contradiction. Commitment B admits modal externality because possible creation conditions the act of creation. The privation account can distinguish non-engagement from violation, but only by supplying the positive order under which a good is due and an act or condition can fail to realize it. That structure may be available; it isn’t furnished merely by calling evil a privation. The doctrinal-interlock reading likewise doesn’t, as stated, force a three-way give-up.

The essentially-good reply (Morris 1991; Plantinga 1980 on God’s nature) holds that *possible-for-God* is indexed to God’s nature. That indexing isn’t a concession that possibility-simpliciter has been overwritten; it distinguishes an agent’s capacities from the unrestricted possibility of states of affairs. The account still owes a precise formulation. If omnipotence ranges over actualizable states of affairs, impeccability restricts which agent performs the evil, not whether a world containing evil can be actualized. If omnipotence ranges over actions available to God, the nature-index fixes that range. The modal field remains external on Commitment B for the earlier creation reason, not because creaturely and divine capacities must coincide. Swinburne’s theistic personalism (*The Coherence of Theism*, 1977, ch. 11) takes a different line to impeccability than either the privation or the essentially-good account.

On Swinburne’s analysis, divine goodness is a simple, non-relational property of the divine person’s nature: not a complex formed from a privation of evil, nor a restricted modal profile over the possibility-space, but a basic feature of a perfectly rational personal agent, analogous to the way an ideally rational agent’s character is simply good without that goodness requiring a contrastive range of evil alternatives. The concern for Swinburne’s simple-property line is that a *basic property* of a person that explains why the person acts well without ranging over alternatives is either a disposition (a structure of tendencies to act certain ways in certain situations, which imports the directed-transition structure the three Conditions supply) or a categorical property with no dispositional content (in which case it is unclear how it generates the moral differentiation the believer’s confession requires). Swinburne’s reply is that personal simplicity (the absence of physical constraints on the will) is what makes the property basic rather than compositional; the structural concern is whether personal simplicity, on the analysis, escapes the conditions its exercise of will presupposes.

**Q4.** *Whom does God will good toward, if the one willed exists only by being willed?* Benevolence, in the classical formulation, is *amor benevolentiae*: the love of willing-good-toward (*ST* I.20). To will *toward* requires a target distinct from the willer; willing-toward-nothing-distinct isn’t willing-toward at all. The doctrine places God as the only being whose existence is necessary in itself; creatures are dependent products of divine willing rather than antecedently distinct beings the divine will reaches toward (*ST* I.44) (Pruss 2011). The concern here is the order of dependence. If the target of divine willing-toward is itself a product of divine willing, then *willing-toward* names a relation whose target the willing constitutes, and the *toward* is doing different work from what the predicate ordinarily picks out. In the creaturely case the willer encounters an antecedently distinct target and bears willing-toward it.

In the divine case the willer constitutes the target in the willing, and the toward-relation is internal to the willing-act rather than reaching across an interval to something antecedently other. The reply that divine love is more than the willing-toward of *amor benevolentiae* (that it is *amor amicitiae*, friendship-love (*ST* I.20.2) (Stump 2010)) doesn’t relieve the pressure. Friendship-love presupposes two distinct loci who bear the friendship; the structural concern at *amor benevolentiae* is the one at *amor amicitiae* in stronger form, since friendship has tighter relational requirements than mere willing-toward. Hartshorne’s dual-transcendence account presses here from the concrete side: the concrete pole’s love is *amor benevolentiae* and, in its fuller form, *amor amicitiae* borne toward creatures the divine encounters as antecedently distinct rather than constitutes in the willing: genuinely responsive love, growing with what the world contributes (*The Divine Relativity*, 1948). The dipolar account supplies the antecedently distinct target that Q4 finds absent from the classical account of willing-toward; the concern is that doing so introduces the three structural conditions from which the classical account sought independence. A willing that reaches across an interval to a distinct creaturely target (S), borne by a substantive concrete actuality (Φ) genuinely moved by what it encounters (T), is the manner-of-acting relation this analysis requires, and a concrete pole bearing it instantiates the structural conditions of a subject among subjects rather than standing beyond them. The full account is assessed at Q6, and the pole-relation is examined at §10.3.3.

**Q5.** *How is God just or merciful, if there is no act for the justice or mercy to shape?* Moral predicates don’t all have one grammar. *Good* may characterize a person, disposition, institution, act, or state of affairs; *benevolent* can name a stable orientation before it names an occurrent exercise. Justice and mercy nevertheless acquire much of their determinate content through characteristic acts: judging a claim, rendering what is due, withholding a penalty, forgiving an offender, protecting a vulnerable subject. Classical theology may locate the relevant character eternally in God and treat its exercises as temporal effects of one timeless act. That is coherent as a proposal. It owes two distinctions: what makes the standing character benevolent rather than indifferent, and how that invariant character explains differentiated exercises toward particular creatures. The active predicates incur the conditions of their exercises; the character predicate faces a counterfactual and evidential burden rather than a grammatical refutation.

**Q6.** *What does calling God good rule out, if God couldn’t have been otherwise?* Goodness, on the classical reading, is what God is: *bonitas ipsa*, goodness itself, identical with the divine nature on simplicity (*ST* I.6.3). Essential predication isn’t empty merely because its predicate can’t be withheld: *triangles have three sides* is informative despite being necessary, and the book’s own structural necessities would otherwise collapse into pledges. The concern must therefore be more exact. What fixes the evaluative content of *good*, and what makes identification with God an explanation of that content rather than a stipulation? The classical reply says that God *is* the standard against which goods are measured, not a being who instantiates the standard among other instantiations (Stump 2010; Adams 1999 on the divine command tradition). That proposal can be substantive if it supplies independently intelligible respects of resemblance, dependence, or right action by which candidate goods can match or fail to match the standard. Without those respects, *God is good* reduces explanatorily to *God is the standard fixed by God*: the identification preserves the affirmation but doesn’t yet tell us why kindness rather than cruelty, fidelity rather than betrayal, or mercy rather than indifference resembles the standard. The issue isn’t whether God could lose an essential property. It is whether the account gives the property discriminating content that isn’t exhausted by identity with its bearer. The *Euthyphro dilemma* (is an act good because God commands it, or commanded because it is already good?) marks the same fork from the command side; the present point is its predication-side form. A contentful standard may be necessary and still rule things out. What it can’t do is use its own label as the whole account of what it rules out.

Adams’s resemblance account (Adams 1999) is the reply built precisely to keep *God is good* contentful without a contrastive range, and it must be met rather than passed over. On Adams’s theistic Platonism, *good* names resemblance to God, the transcendent Good in which finite goods participate, so that *God is good* isn’t the tautology *God is God* but the substantive claim that God is the paradigm the resemblance-relation is fixed to: a claim with content, on Adams’s telling, because the respects in which finite things count as resembling are drawn from our independent grasp of the goods we already recognize. The reply turns on what fixes those respects, and the fork is the section’s. Either the resemblance-base is the determinate features our paradigm goods actually exhibit—kindness shown, debts rendered, mercy borne—in which case the respects are manner-of-acting features, and a paradigm that exemplifies them is a being that acts well: one that does good, borne by a substantive agent (Φ) toward a distinct recipient (S) across the vector from not-done to done (T), which is a subject acting within Nature rather than a being beyond it. Or the resemblance-base is left formal—resemblance to God in whatever respects the divine goodness consists in, respects not specifiable in advance from the finite side—in which case *resembles God* supplies no failure-condition after all: nothing determinate is fixed that a candidate good could be found to match or fail to match, and the contentful predication the account promised slides back into the avowal the tautology charge identified. The resemblance account doesn’t escape the fork between manner-of-acting content and empty self-identity; it restates the fork in the idiom of participation.

Swinburne’s cumulative-case framework (*The Existence of God*, 1979; 2004) challenges Q6’s modal analysis directly. On Swinburne’s account, divine goodness need not be grounded in a contrastive range; it is a probability-raiser for theism: the fact that God is perfectly good makes the existence of a morally ordered universe more probable than it would be on any naturalistic hypothesis, and the goodness of the God who explains the universe is assessed by its explanatory power rather than against a contrastive range of bad-alternatives. The concern for the Swinburnian reframing is whether the probability-raising relation is itself a structural relation: for the hypothesis *God is perfectly good* to make the existence of a morally ordered universe more probable than its rival, the hypothesis must have content (it must specify what a good God would produce) and specifying what a good God would produce requires ranging over the alternatives the modal field provides, which is the contrastive range Q6 identified as the condition of the predicate’s informativeness.

Hartshorne’s dual-transcendence account challenges Q6’s analysis at its foundation by denying the Anselmian account of how divine goodness is grounded. Where the classical account defines perfection as *actus purus* (the good a being *is*, complete and unsurpassable), dual transcendence redefines perfection as surpassing all others while remaining surpassable only by oneself (*Man’s Vision of God*, 1941; *Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes*, 1984): the abstract pole is the invariant standard of value, and the concrete pole is good by *responsively* willing the richest integration of what the world has actually contributed, surpassing every other and surpassable only by the divine self at a later, fuller moment. The account is designed to restore the failure-condition absent from the standard-bearing reading: the concrete pole *could* love less responsively than it does, and is good rather than merely self-identical because it doesn’t. The concern is that the restoration concedes the result in the idiom of process.

A goodness that ranges over alternatives, prefers the richer integration to the poorer, and grows in responsive love is a manner of acting borne by a substantive concrete actuality (Φ), reaching toward antecedently distinct creaturely targets (S), across the temporal vector from not-yet-responded to responded (T); the concrete pole is good in exactly the sense the manner-of-acting grammar requires, and in being so instantiates the structural conditions of a subject acting on subjects, not those of a being beyond them. The abstract pole, meanwhile, inherits Q6’s standard-bearing verdict unchanged: an invariant standard of value presupposes the range of alternatives the measurement applies to, and the live result of Necessity (§11.3.1) holds here in moral form; the modal status of being the standard belongs in the first instance to the range within which standardhood is exercised, not to an abstract pole that bears no responsive acting and is therefore no candidate for a manner-of-acting predicate at all. Binding the unsurpassable standard to the responsive lover into one good God is the pole-relation examined at §10.3.3: a directed dependence requiring determinate difference, asymmetric order, and a bearer unifying the poles. The dual-transcendence account doesn’t relocate divine goodness beyond Nature; in process-theological terms, it describes goodness as the responsive mutual maintenance of subjects within Nature.

**Q7.** *How is God incapable of evil, if evil is never a possibility for God to begin with?* Impeccability is the doctrine that God can’t sin (*ST* I.25.3 ad 2) (Morris 1991; Pawl 2016). The concern here follows from Q3’s fork. If impeccability means *God’s nature excludes the evil-region of the modal field*, then the modal field has structure that includes evil as a region, and the doctrine has admitted modal externality with extra structure (Q3 fork option 1). If impeccability means *evil isn’t possible-for-God in the sense relevant to omnipotence*, then either evil isn’t really possible (which is empirically false, since humans do evil constantly) or *possible-for-God* is distinct from *possible-simpliciter*, which is the same fork in different vocabulary. Beyond Q3’s structural concession, impeccability faces an internal-coherence problem at the conditions of the predicate. To be incapable of evil is to be in a structured relation to evil—namely, the relation of incapacity. The relation requires that evil be a candidate the incapacity-relation could in principle hold of; a being to whom evil is in no sense a candidate isn’t *incapable* of evil but simply *outside the range within which evil is a candidate*. Impeccability either names the structured relation of nature-restricted incapacity (admitting the externality of the modal field’s evil-region) or names the absence of the range within which evil could be a candidate (in which case the being is amoral rather than impeccable, and the doctrine has changed register without admitting the change).

*The burden.* The pressures divide the divine moral claims into character, standard, and exercise. A character claim must specify the counterfactual orientation that distinguishes benevolence from indifference or cruelty. A standard claim must say what fixes rightness without reducing *God is good* to self-identity or placing every possible history beyond moral discrimination. An exercise claim—judging, forgiving, commanding, protecting, permitting—must identify its bearer, recipient, content, and mode of realization. Concrete exercises occur within the three Conditions; an invariant divine character or atemporal standard isn’t eliminated by that fact, but it owes the contact by which it bears on those exercises. Nature hosts moral subjects and the relations in which moral predicates are applied. Nature isn’t thereby good, benevolent, or righteous.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Character, Standard, and Exercise** · *Diagnostic*

Moral predicates don’t all have one grammar. They may describe character, disposition, standard, agent, institution, state of affairs, or manner of acting. Concrete claims that God commands, judges, forgives, protects, permits, or responds are actional and relational; they incur the conditions of those exercises. Claims about perfect character or an unchanging disposition need not describe a transition, but they owe a value standard, counterfactual profile, and relation to actual conduct. The section must keep bearer, standard, disposition, and exercise apart rather than deriving them all from an adverb.

**Depends on:** Structural Requirement (§2.4)

*The reclamation.* Nature has no moral status merely by hosting moral subjects. *Benevolent* can describe a stable disposition as well as an occurrent act, so timelessness alone doesn’t empty it. The divine claim must nevertheless say what makes the disposition benevolent, how its counterfactual direction differs from malevolence or indifference, and how that character bears on the actual suffering and goods of creatures. Specific predicates—commanding, judging, forgiving, protecting, permitting—add identifiable exercises and relations. The argument can test those without reducing goodness itself to action. Where every possible history is declared equally compatible with perfect benevolence, the predicate loses differential evidential content; that is the earned pressure. None of that touches where benevolence is presently found. Willing another’s good, and acting on it at cost to oneself, is something moral subjects do, and it is the case the word was drawn from. Its differential content is available in exactly the place the doctrine labors to supply it: someone who could have done otherwise, and didn’t. Goodness of that kind isn’t held in trust for a later bearer. It is exercised, unevenly and often, by us.

### 11.9.2 Righteousness

To be just is often to render to each what is owed: a manner of *giving*, which needs a giver, a recipient, and a before-and-after. With those removed, the *acts* of justice lose their ordinary grip. Character, standard, and verdict uses remain live until they are given their own truth conditions; they aren’t refuted by showing that a giving needs a giver. The doctrines built on the predicate (atonement, inherited guilt, final judgment) inherit whichever sense they actually use.

The classical doctrine of divine justice assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *iustus* (just) and *iustitia* is among the divine names, identical with the divine essence on classical simplicity (Augustine of Hippo (400–428) 1991, VIII.6; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21) (Anselm, *Monologion* 16). Justice in the classical sense is *suum cuique tribuere*, the rendering to each of what is owed (Ulpian, *Digesta* I.1.10, taken up into Christian moral theology at Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, II-II.58.1). The doctrine extends the predicate eminently across commutative, distributive, and retributive senses (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, II-II.61), and pairs it with the doctrine of impeccability: God is *incapax peccandi*, incapable of injustice as of any other moral evil (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.25.3 ad 2; Morris 1991; Pawl 2016).

Divine justice co-instantiates with divine mercy without contradiction (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.3–4; Anselm of Canterbury (1098) 1998, I.12, II.20; Stump 2018 develops the contemporary form). Mercy itself is among the divine names: *misericordia*, the heart-toward-misery, identical with the divine essence on simplicity (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.3; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, II-II.30) (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 102.8). The Islamic tradition opens every Qur’anic surah but one with *al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm* (the Compassionate, the Merciful) and reads the names as *dhātī*, essential rather than accidental (al-Ghazālī, *al-Maqṣad al-Asnā*) (Murata and Chittick 1994). The Hebrew Bible pairs *ḥesed* (covenant-loyal love) with *raḥamim*, the visceral compassion whose noun-root is *reḥem*, the womb (Sakenfeld 1978; Trible 1978). The doctrine holds mercy as a [divine perfection](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) co-essential with justice rather than its competitor: the Anselmian and Thomist tradition explicitly denies that mercy diminishes justice or that justice limits mercy (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.4; Anselm of Canterbury (1078) 1998, 9–11), and the classical impassibility doctrine reads mercy not as God’s *being moved* by misery (the affective pole the predicate carries in its ordinary use) but as the divine *effect* of relieving misery, identical with the divine act (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.3; Pawl 2016; Creel 1986).

The classical atonement extends justice’s reach across persons: Christ’s death satisfies the demands of divine justice on behalf of the guilty (Anselm of Canterbury (1098) 1998, II; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, III.46–49; for contemporary defenses, Swinburne 1989; Crisp 2020; Stump 2018). The doctrine of original sin extends justice’s domain backward through generations: humans inherit guilt and corruption from Adam’s act (Augustine of Hippo (413–426) 1998, XIII.14; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I-II.81; Edwards 1758; for contemporary discussion, Rea 2007; Couenhoven 2013). Each covenant is a distinct dispensation of the same eternal justice (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I-II.107; Calvin (1559) 1960, II.10–11). The eschatological judgment renders the same justice across all who have ever lived (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, Suppl. 88; for contemporary form, Walls 1992).

The Jewish and Islamic traditions develop parallel claims: the Hebrew *ṣedeq* / *ṣedāqāh* names the right-ordering of communal life under covenant (Koch 1955; Weinfeld 1995); the divine name *al-ʿAdl* (the Just) is held in the Muʿtazilī reading to be *dhātī*: essential to the divine being (Hourani 1985). The doctrine, carried to its limit, names a being whose moral character renders the moral order itself (whose justice isn’t a property had alongside other properties but the structural truth about how moral reality is constituted) and whose every act toward creation, including those acts the believer finds difficult, is therefore necessarily just.

*The interrogation.* Eight questions identify the limits of the doctrine of divine justice once it is stated in a form suitable for structural analysis. Underneath, the concern is structural: the one pressed through the preceding attributes. *Just*, *merciful*, *equitable*, *fair*, *righteous* can describe standards, characters, institutions, verdicts, or acts. *Iustitia* in the classical sense, *suum cuique tribuere*, is often a manner of giving; and giving requires the conditions of action: a substantive agent who gives (Φ), a target distinct from the giver who receives (S), and a temporal direction from not-giving to giving (T). Those *exercise* uses can’t attach to a being defined without any of the three Conditions. Standard and character uses aren’t thereby empty; they owe a discriminator that keeps rightness from collapsing into what is commanded, and a relation to the particular judgments they are said to govern. The eight pressures run at both levels, and at the level of what the auxiliary doctrines of atonement, original sin, covenant, and final judgment commit when the sense they actually use is taken seriously.

**Q1.** *Can justice give each their due while mercy withholds it?* The classical doctrine holds God as perfectly just and perfectly merciful, with no diminution of either by the other (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.3–4; Anselm of Canterbury (1098) 1998, I.12, II.20). The concern here is the content of the two predicates. Justice, in the sense the doctrine wants, renders to each what is owed; mercy suspends or remits what is owed in favor of unearned good. The two predicates name opposed directions of moral motion on the same input: justice tracks what is owed; mercy gives what isn’t. The Anselmian reply is that mercy operates within justice, since Christ’s satisfaction pays the debt justice requires. It preserves co-instantiation by relocating mercy from *suspension* of justice to *means* of justice. The relocation costs the predicate’s ordinary grammar. Mercy, on the reframing, is no longer the unearned remission of debt; it is the redirection of debt to a third party. The structure of *gift against what is owed* has been replaced by the structure of *transactional substitution*, and the substitution’s evaluation as just is the very question Q4 takes up. Stump’s contemporary development (Stump 2018) handles the tension by identifying mercy with second-personal love that, in seeking the beloved’s good, includes the work of restoring what the beloved owes and has withheld. The structural concern returns: second-personal love, on the analysis run at §11.8.2, requires the relational structure between distinct loci the doctrine elsewhere has factored out. The two attributes co-instantiate at the cost of relocating one or both of them past the contrast that gave them informative content. Three further pressures on mercy-predication sharpen the same concern.

*The impassibility pressure.* *Misericordia*, on its ordinary grammar, is *cor ad miseriam*: heart-toward-misery, the structure of being-moved-by another’s suffering. The classical doctrine of divine impassibility holds God as *actus purus*, not subject to being moved by anything outside the divine essence (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.9; Weinandy 2000; Dolezal 2017). The two grammars conflict on the affective pole: mercy in its first-person human use names *being affected by* the other’s state, and impassibility denies the affective structure. Aquinas’s reply (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.3) preserves co-instantiation by reading divine mercy as the *effect* alone—God produces the relief of misery without undergoing the being-moved that constitutes mercy in the creaturely case. The relocation costs the predicate’s content: mercy without the affective pole is the verbal predicate without the affective relation that gives it content; what remains is a class of effects classified after the fact as merciful, not the manner-of-being-moved the predicate ordinarily reports. The reply parallels the move identified at §11.8.2 on *love* (the second-personal structure factored out) and the move Q7 below identifies on *just* (the discernment factored out): preserving the verbal predicate by removing the relational condition the predicate’s content runs on. Mullins develops the contemporary form of the impassibility-mercy tension (2016); the contemporary defenses (Dolezal 2017; Helm 2010) preserve impassibility by accepting Aquinas’s effect-only reading, which is to accept that *mercy*-predication, on the doctrine, names something different from what it names in the cases that gave the predicate its content.

*The grace–mercy distinction.* The tradition often treats mercy and grace as overlapping divine acts toward the unworthy, but the structural difference matters for predication. Mercy responds to misery: its target is the suffering subject, and its act is the relief of suffering. Grace, in the strict sense, is unmerited favor whose ground isn’t the recipient’s state at all but the giver’s free generosity (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I-II.110–111; Barth (1932) 1975, IV/1). If divine mercy is genuinely mercy in the substantive sense, it requires the relational structure of object-in-misery; if it collapses into grace (gift-without-precondition) then *mercy* is the wrong name for what the doctrine picks out, and the contentful relation between the predicate and the structural feature its vocabulary tracks has been silently swapped. The doctrine can’t have both a strong mercy whose object-of-misery structure runs and a strong grace whose ground is the giver alone without admitting that what the tradition calls *mercy* is, at the level of structure, grace operating on a recipient who happens to be in misery: a different relation under a borrowed name.

*The necessity-of-misery horn.* If mercy is a necessary divine attribute and mercy requires recipients-in-misery, the field horns from Q2 sharpen further on the mercy side. The intra-Trinitarian construal that handles justice (Q2, horn three) can’t run for mercy: the Trinitarian persons aren’t in misery, and the predicate’s object-condition isn’t met. The field-co-necessity horn that conflicts with creation-ex-nihilo on the justice side conflicts more sharply on the mercy side, because what becomes co-necessary with the attribute isn’t merely *recipients-with-dues* but *recipients-in-misery*: the doctrine inherits a necessary field of suffering as the ontological condition of the divine attribute, which the standard theodicy literature treats as the result to be avoided rather than embraced. The horns that remain (contingency of exercise or mere disposition) weaken the necessary-attribute claim on the mercy side in the same way they do on the justice side, and more directly, because mercy without recipients in misery has no corresponding intra-Trinitarian application.

**Q2.** *Who can be owed anything if no creatures necessarily exist?* Justice, in the classical sense, is *suum cuique tribuere*: the predicate is structurally tri-place, requiring an agent who renders, a recipient to whom rendering is owed, and the due that is rendered. The doctrine holds justice as a *necessary* divine attribute, identical with the divine essence on simplicity (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.1). The concern here is the modal status of the field.

The necessity has to be pinned down before the horns bite. Read de dicto—necessarily, justice-if-instantiated requires recipients-with-dues—the claim is the conditional the horns work on. Read de re—there is a field of recipients-with-dues that exists necessarily—it is horn one. If justice is necessary and its content requires recipients-with-dues, four locations for that field remain.

*Horn one.* The recipients are external and necessary: the field is co-necessary with the attribute. This collapses creaturely existence into necessity and conflicts with creation ex nihilo, the doctrine’s standing position on contingent creation (Pruss 2011); the unity-side correlate is developed at §11.2.2.

*Horn two.* The recipients are external and contingent: the exercise of justice is contingent on them, while what is necessary is the disposition or character from which just acts issue. This preserves contingent creation and a necessary divine character, but it distinguishes necessary character from contingent exercise—the distinction the account must then reconcile with strong simplicity.

*Horn three.* The field is internal and necessary: the Trinity renders dues among its persons, and the modal status of justice rides on the necessity of the intra-Trinitarian relations rather than on any external recipient. The construal Aquinas in places suggests (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I.21.1 ad 3) preserves the necessary relation. It still owes an account of whether *due-ness* among consubstantial persons retains the contrastive structure on which *suum cuique* runs, since the persons’ shared essence may undercut the asymmetry between owing and being owed.

*Horn four.* Justice requires no recipient-field because the necessary predicate names intrinsic character or a standard rather than an exercised tri-place relation. This preserves necessary divine justice without necessary recipients. It also revises the opening sense of *justice as rendering each their due*, so any inference from the intrinsic standard to concrete verdicts or acts requires a further bridge.

The horns exhaust the relevant placements of the recipient-field: external and necessary, external and contingent, internal and necessary, or unnecessary to the revised predicate. None is dismissed merely for being revisionary; each identifies which further commitment the account must defend. The live result of Necessity (§11.3.1) applies in justice form: invariance can belong to a framework and to entities represented throughout it; the modal status of a tri-place relational structure belongs in the first instance to the field within which the relation obtains, and locating that status in a relatum stipulated outside the field is a further claim, not a transfer already in hand.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Missing Party Problem** · *Disjunction*

If God is necessarily just, who is owed?

- **If those owed are outside God and had to exist,** then they are as necessary as God is.
- **If they are outside God but might never have existed,** then being just by nature has to be told apart from ever actually doing justice.
- **If they are inside God,** then one divine person is owed something by another, and that has to be made out.
- **If no one is owed, because *justice* now names a character or a standard,** then something still has to carry that standard to an actual verdict.

Those four exhaust whether anyone is owed, who they are, and whether they had to exist. None of them is incoherent. Each has its own price.

**Depends on:** Relational Distinctness (§2.4.7) and Necessity Permits Contingency (§2.9)

**Q3.** *If everyone deserves punishment, what work is justice still doing?* The Christian doctrine of universal sinfulness (Rom 3:23) (Augustine of Hippo (413–426) 1998, XIV; Calvin (1559) 1960, II.1; for contemporary discussion, Couenhoven 2013) holds that every human, from the fall onward, stands in a state of culpable corruption. The doctrine has structural consequence for justice-predication. If every human deserves condemnation, then every act of divine condemnation (from natural death to plague to flood to eternal punishment) is the rendering of due. The verdict, in the doctrine’s strong form, is uniform across input. The concern here is what *justice* picks out under a uniform-verdict regime. A predicate that returns the same value across every input isn’t tracking the structural feature the predicate is supposed to track; it is a constant function whose name still carries the appearance of differential content. The classical reply is that justice operates within the *category* of the deserved, and that mercy is what differentiates outcomes within that category. It relocates the differential work from justice to mercy, and concedes that justice itself isn’t the locus of moral information about divine action. What *justice* does, on the relocation, is set the categorical floor against which the only contentful moral attribute (mercy) operates; what *justice predicates* is the floor’s universal applicability rather than any differential rendering. The doctrine has preserved the predicate’s name and surrendered its informative content. The structural cost compounds when the move is paired with Q7: the believer who can’t discern divine reasons can’t discern *which* punishments fall within universal deserving as opposed to outside it, and the floor’s name is the only thing the predicate carries.

**Q4.** *Can guilt transfer across substantive bearers?* The doctrine of penal substitution requires guilt to move between persons: Christ’s death satisfies divine justice on behalf of guilty humanity. Five moves license the transfer; each has structural cost. *The imputation move*, federal-Reformed (Murray 1955; Crisp 2020), treats guilt as a legal property reckoned to Christ and righteousness as a legal property reckoned to the believer. The concern here is what *reckoning* names. In the human case, reckoning is a courtroom procedure whose justice depends on the reckoning tracking the substantive moral relation between agent and act; reckoning that doesn’t track (that imputes a property whose substantive ground is absent) is what the predicate ordinarily marks as miscarriage. The doctrine preserves transfer by emptying the reckoning of substantive tracking. *The participation move*, mystical-union (Stump 2018) (compare Athanasius, *De Incarnatione*, on incorporation), treats believers as ontologically united with Christ such that guilt becomes genuinely Christ’s and righteousness becomes genuinely theirs.

The fork sharpens: either union is metaphysically sufficient to transfer the moral properties (in which case Christ becomes genuinely guilty during the union, and the impeccability claim of Q3-at-§11.9.1 fails for the duration), or union is metaphorical (in which case reckoning has returned in disguise). *The consent move* (Anselm of Canterbury (1098) 1998, II.11) treats Christ’s willing submission as licensing the substitution. Consent licenses some transactions—gifts, contracts—but consent doesn’t manufacture *deserving*, which is the property justice tracks. A judge who accepts a willing volunteer in place of the convicted hasn’t done justice; the judge has substituted a willing victim for a deserved one, and the substitution’s voluntariness doesn’t change the verdict’s miscarriage. *The satisfaction move* (Anselm of Canterbury (1098) 1998, I; Swinburne 1989) treats the cross as paying a quantitative debt owed to divine honor or moral order. The reframing shifts justice from punishment-of-the-guilty to debt-payment-on-behalf-of-the-guilty; the two aren’t equivalent moral structures, and treating them as equivalent equivocates on the predicate. *The Christus Victor move* (Aulén 1931; Boersma 2004) treats the cross as defeat of cosmic powers rather than satisfaction of justice. The justice-language drops out: the cross is rescue, not a tracking of what is deserved. The concern across the five moves is the same. Guilt, on the moral phenomenology, is a property of substantive agents whose acts the property tracks; it attaches at Φ. Transfer across Φ-distinctions is what the predicate ordinarily marks as injustice in every other application. The doctrine preserves transfer by relocating *guilt* from agent-tracking property to bookkeeping-property, to courtroom-fiction, to debt-token, or to rescue-narrative. Each relocation preserves the term while surrendering the substantive relation that justice was supposed to track.

**[Proposition]**

**Five Relocations, One Missing Act** · *Proposition*

Guilt, on the moral phenomenology, is a property of substantive agents whose acts it tracks; it attaches at Φ, and transfer across Φ-distinctions is what the predicate ordinarily marks as injustice in every other application. Five atonement constructions preserve transfer by relocating guilt itself—the imputation move to a bookkeeping-property, the participation move and the consent move to a courtroom-fiction of union or agreement, the satisfaction move to a debt-token, and the Christus Victor move to a rescue-narrative from which the justice-language drops out. Each relocation preserves the term while surrendering the substantive relation justice was supposed to track. What none supplies is the act the predicate needs: an agent whose own doing the guilt evaluates.

*Status: a reading of what the five constructions cost the predicate, not a demonstration that no atonement account can succeed. It grants the doctrine’s God and texts throughout and turns on the ordinary grammar of guilt-attribution, which a defender may contest at that point rather than at the transfer.*

**Depends on:** Character, Standard, and Exercise (§11.9.1)

**Q5.** *Can culpability attach without action?* The doctrine of original sin (Augustine of Hippo (413–426) 1998, XIII.14; Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I-II.81; for contemporary discussion, Rea 2007; Couenhoven 2013) holds that humans are culpable, from conception, for an act they didn’t perform. The concern here is the relation between culpability and action. Culpability, on the moral phenomenology, tracks the agent’s action: A is culpable for X just in case A performed X under conditions of knowledge and freedom that license the attribution. The doctrine relocates culpability past the conditions of agent-action: A is culpable for B’s act in virtue of A’s metaphysical, biological, or representational relation to B. Three accounts try to license the relocation. *The federal-headship account*, Reformed (Edwards 1758; Murray 1959), treats Adam as legal representative. The disanalogy with human representation is decisive against the move: representation in human politics requires either consent of the represented or exit-availability under the system the representative acts within; Adamic representation supplies neither.

Representation without consent or exit is conscription, which is the moral structure the relocation was supposed to avoid. *The seminal-realism account* (Augustinian-Traducianist) treats human beings as metaphysically present in Adam at the time of the act. The account requires (i) the metaphysical claim that potential persons share in actual persons’ acts, which generalizes to make every descendant complicit in every ancestor’s act, and (ii) the moral claim that seminal presence licenses culpability, which is just to redefine culpability away from the action-condition the predicate ordinarily tracks. *The inherited-corruption account* (some Arminian and Orthodox readings) treats humans as inheriting a *condition* (concupiscence, mortality) but not *guilt*; subsequent acts under the condition generate the culpability. The account is the most morally defensible, but it (a) shifts the doctrine substantially from its Augustinian-Reformed form, and (b) leaves a different injustice in place: why is *the condition itself* just, if no act of the condition’s bearer brought it about? The critical case is the death of children without an attributable action: in flood, plague, famine, or eternity. Strong original-sin makes the death deserved; weaker original-sin makes the death undeserved suffering of a condition the sufferer didn’t author. Either horn is an injustice on the standard moral phenomenology; the doctrine selects the horn by selecting the version of the doctrine, not by removing the structural problem. The abstract-versus-narrative question this case raises is addressed methodologically at §11.9.1: the preclusion runs prior to narrative theodicy and holds however it fares. The question is whether the dead-children horn is met by structural analysis or owes theodicy-through-narrative.

**Q6.** *Does the predicate retain identity across the covenants?* The Hebrew Bible records, and in places commands, acts the New Testament’s ethic and contemporary moral intuition classify as deeply unjust: the *ḥērem* (the ban: total destruction devoted to God) warfare of the conquest (Josh 6, 10; Deut 20), the destruction of Amalek including women and children (1 Sam 15), the slaughter of Midianite captives (Num 31), capital punishment for Sabbath violation (Num 15:32–36) and for cursing parents (Exod 21:17). The doctrine holds the same God, with the same justice, at work across the Old and New Testaments (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947, I-II.107; Calvin (1559) 1960, II.10–11). The concern here is whether *just* names the same property at both temporal indices. Four moves try to preserve identity-across-time. *The progressive-revelation move*, developed in different forms by Origen and Wesley (for contemporary versions, Copan 2011; Copan and Flannagan 2014), holds that God’s commands accommodate the moral capacity of the age.

If the underlying moral facts are eternal, the move forks: either the OT commands were unjust by the eternal standard (and God commanded injustice), or the NT ethic is a leniency relative to the eternal standard (and Christ countermanded what justice required). Either horn surrenders the moral character of one of the Testaments. *The dispensational move*, covenant-administrative (for contemporary versions, Saucy 1993), holds that the standard is constant but its administration differs by covenant. The reply rescues immutability of the standard at the cost of the means question: an omnipotent agent had alternative means to the pedagogical or covenantal ends, and the chosen means (mass killing including non-combatants) require positive justification beyond the dispensational frame. *The accommodation-rhetorical move*, developed in ancient-Near-Eastern–contextual readings (for contemporary form, Lamb 2022; Earl 2010), holds that the conquest narratives are ANE military rhetoric rather than literal command. The move dissolves the most acute cases at the cost of a general result: the texts long held as divine commands are conceded not to have been divine commands, and the selection criterion for which texts are accommodation and which aren’t can’t be *the ones we find morally tolerable* without making the reader the authority over the text. *The prerogative move* (God, as creator, has authority over creaturely life that humans lack) is the discernment-collapse horn (Q7) in another form. If *just*, predicated of God, tracks compatibility-with-divine-prerogative rather than the structural feature the predicate ordinarily tracks, then the predicate’s content has been emptied; the predicate now reports something trivially true given the definition. The four moves together cover the available options, and each costs a load-bearing commitment elsewhere.

**Q7.** *If we can’t recognize divine justice, how can we affirm it?* A standard reply to moral pressure on divine action runs through skeptical theism (Wykstra 1984; Bergmann 2001; Howard-Snyder 2009; and its contemporary development, Bergmann 2012). The believer concedes that some divine actions appear unjust by creaturely standards and explains the appearance by appeal to limited epistemic access: we can’t see the divine reasons. The reply can therefore undercut an inference from *I see no justifying reason* to *there is no justifying reason*.

The concern here is what the reply commits at the level of affirmation. The affirmation *God is just* is contentful only if the believer can, in principle, discern justice well enough to identify it as a recognizable claim with definite truth-conditions. If the skeptical reply is extended from ignorance in some cases to incapacity for moral evaluation at the relevant level generally, then *God is just* exceeds creaturely capacity for evaluation at that same level. The unrestricted reply rescues the predicate from counter-evidence at the cost of removing the discernment by which the believer applies it.

That isn’t the only position available. A local skeptical theism may hold that moral judgment remains reliable while particular cases exceed it. Its burden is to state a principled defeater: why limited access discounts these apparently unjust cases without discounting the apparently just cases appealed to in support of the predicate. If the skeptical discount is applied only where moral discernment would disconfirm divine justice, while the same faculty is accepted where it confirms divine justice, the application is asymmetric. The issue isn’t falsifiability as a general criterion of truth. It is whether the account supplies a non-question-begging rule for when creaturely moral evidence is permitted to bear.

*The local turn.* Bergmann’s contemporary skeptical theism doesn’t run globally.
