Bergmann’s local thesis (Bergmann 2012) grants the believer ordinary moral knowledge intact and confines the skepticism to a single defensible claim: that our sample of the goods, evils, and entailment-relations in the total economy of value isn’t known to be representative of the whole, so the inference from *we discern no justifying reason* to *there is none* is blocked. Conceded at full strength, the local thesis survives the global fork already given—it doesn’t render *God is just* contentless, because it leaves first-order moral discernment standing and withdraws only the inference from non-discernment to the non-existence of reasons. The concern here is what magnitude the representativeness gap is a gap about. *Just*, in the *suum cuique* sense held throughout, is fixed by what is owed to the affected party, the manner in which the act is rendered to the subject who receives it (Φ acting on S), not by the act’s standing in the all-things-considered economy of value across the whole.

The representativeness gap is a gap about the latter magnitude; granting it in full leaves the act-as-rendered-to-the-party exactly where it stood. To make the local skeptic’s gap bite justice-predication, the reply must add that justice-to-a-subject *supervenes on* all-things-considered global value: that whether the child’s death is rendered justly to the child depends on goods elsewhere in the economy the child has no part in. That addition is the relocation diagnosed at every prior attribute: it moves *just* from the agent–recipient relation on which its content depends to an assessment of aggregate value, and a predicate that tracks aggregate value rather than what is owed to the affected party identifies a different structural feature. The central cases therefore remain: Q3’s universal deserving, Q5’s death of children, and Q6’s *ḥērem* each concern what is owed to the affected party, which the representativeness concession doesn’t address.

*The intervention parallel.* Maitzen’s other signature argument presses the same point from the opposite epistemic end (Maitzen 2009). Where the demographic argument (Q8) and the local skeptic turn on what the believer can and can’t discern, this one stipulates the favorable epistemic case and still bites: grant that the outweighing good is real *and* that the believer has access to it. Ordinary morality (the morality the believer relies on everywhere else) still obliges the bystander who can prevent a child’s death from meningitis to prevent it, and doesn’t release the bystander on the ground that the suffering may secure a greater good; the doctor who withholds treatment so that the ordeal may build the patient’s character, or another’s compassion, has acted wrongly by the standard the believer applies without hesitation in every non-theological case. So the greater-good defense of divine non-intervention forks: either ordinary morality is mistaken about the bystander’s obligation (in which case the doctrine rests on overturning a moral datum more certain than any premise of the theodicy that overturns it) or the human/divine parallel breaks, and *just*, said of God’s non-intervention, isn’t *just* in the sense said of the bystander.

The fork is the fork in intervention form. *Just* is either univocal across the parallel (in which case the obligation that binds the bystander binds the divine agent, and non-intervention is unjust on the shared sense) or equivocal, in which case the predicate said of God has been cut loose from the sense that gave it content. The one principled way to break the parallel without bare equivocation is the prerogative move (that the creator holds an authority over creaturely life the bystander lacks) and that move routes directly back into the prerogative horn of Q6 and the discernment-collapse this question presses: an authority that converts what would otherwise be a failure to render what is owed into a rightful withholding empties *just* of the differential content the predicate reports. The reply generalizes across every *perfect-X* predicate the doctrine applies to God; the treatment of apophasis in Describability (§11.8.3) identifies the structural form, and the present section identifies its specifically *justice*-form, where the form is most acutely self-undermining because justice is the predicate whose content the difficult-case literature presses on most directly.

*The demonstrated-mechanism sharpening.* The intervention parallel is ordinarily met by conceding that direct intervention on a resistant will might not be available to a being committed to preserving creaturely freedom, an empirical hedge the tradition’s own narrative material removes. Exodus states, repeatedly, that God produces Pharaoh’s resistance to the request Moses is sent to deliver (Exod 4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8; see §12.1.5, Free-Will Defense). Paul generalizes the mechanism into standing doctrine (Rom 9): “he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Rom 9:18). It raises the fairness objection itself, then overrules it rather than answering it (9:19–21). Once a tradition’s own text reports the mechanism in successful use for a demonstrative purpose against a single ruler, the freedom-preserving hedge is no longer available to explain non-intervention at any later, larger scale: the question is no longer whether direct intervention on a human will is metaphysically available to this God, but why it was exercised for that stake and withheld at every greater one.

*The four-cell breakdown.* Where two human wills stand in live moral conflict—a perpetrator’s and a resister’s, at any scale—the same mechanism admits exactly four dispositions, and each conflicts with another commitment of the doctrine. God may shape the perpetrator’s will alone, which is Pharaoh’s case at whatever scale the conflict runs, and makes God the direct author of the harm rather than its permitter. God may shape the resister’s will alone, leaving the perpetrator’s genuinely free, which requires an unstated selection principle for who receives the intervention and who doesn’t, and cannot consistently credit the resulting courage as the agent’s own without also crediting Pharaoh’s resistance as his own, since both are installed by the identical mechanism; crediting one as authentic while discounting the other introduces an asymmetry not grounded in a difference between the cases. God may shape neither, leaving both wills free, in which case the intervention parallel already drawn applies at full force, sharpened rather than softened by the demonstrated mechanism: the bystander obligation the believer honors everywhere else binds a God shown willing and able to intervene at far smaller stakes. Or God may shape both, determining the entire conflict while its participants experience the terror and resolve as their own. In that case the good invoked by the free-will defense—genuine creaturely agency—is absent rather than merely outweighed, and can’t justify the resulting suffering.

*What recurrent correction concedes.* Independent of which cell obtains in a given case, that the mechanism is exercised at all concedes something about the object it is exercised on. A creation whose ordinary operation reliably produced acceptable outcomes wouldn’t require recurrent corrective intervention by its maker. Where the doctrine affirms such intervention, it raises a question about the standing adequacy of the created order rather than only about the isolated crisis being averted. The point mirrors the one already made of the fall’s necessity (§12.1.4, The Fall): a transgression that had to happen has no author but the design that required it; a creation that has to be periodically seized and corrected to avert catastrophe has no author, for that recurring fact, but the design that made the seizing necessary.

**Q8.** *Does morally arbitrary distribution of eternal stakes count as just?* Stephen Maitzen’s argument from the demographics of theism (Maitzen 2006; cf. Schellenberg 2007 on hiddenness; Marsh 2008) starts from the empirical fact that the distribution of belief in any particular religious tradition tracks geography, era, and family of origin more strongly than it tracks rational inquiry, moral character, or evidential examination. If salvation is gated on belief in specific propositions, and the distribution of belief tracks morally arbitrary facts, then eternal-stakes outcomes are determined by morally arbitrary facts.

The tradition’s own practice concedes the distribution. A standing Great Commission—the centuries-long project of carrying the message to those who haven’t received it—is an admission, made in action, that the message hasn’t in fact reached everyone, and that whether a person receives it turns on the contingent arrival of a messenger rather than on anything the person is or does. A ground adequate to a universal task wouldn’t depend on contingent human transmission to reach its intended recipients; the need for such transmission shows that the message isn’t universally available without it. The concern here is the fit between *arbitrary distribution of eternal stakes* and the classical predicate *just*.

Five responses are available; each carries cost.

*The Molinist response* (Plantinga 1974; Craig 1991) holds that God knows what each person would freely do under any circumstance and arranges history so that all who would respond receive opportunity. The response imports the contested metaphysics of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom—the grounding problem (Hasker 1989)—and entails the conclusion that those born outside the gospel’s reach are condemned for *what they would have done* under different conditions: a counterfactual structure of deserving whose justice is itself open to the present question.

*The inclusivist response* (Rahner 1976; for contemporary form, Sanders 1992) holds that those who respond to whatever light they have are saved by Christ’s work without explicit knowledge. The response revises the New Testament’s apparent insistence on explicit faith (Rom 10; Acts 4:12), transforming *salvation by faith in Christ* into *salvation by responsiveness*.

*The postmortem-opportunity response* (for contemporary defense, Reichenbach 1982; Lindsell 1949) holds that those who never heard receive opportunity after death. The response has thin biblical support (1 Pet 3:19 is opaque and contested), qualifies the New Testament’s stress on this-life response, and raises the question why this-life epistemic conditions are so asymmetric if postmortem opportunity is the real decision-point.

*The universalist response*, Origen, *De Principiis* III.6 (for contemporary defense, Hart 2019), dissolves the eternal-stakes asymmetry by removing the eternal-stakes verdict; the cost is departure from the historical mainstream and a substantial revision of the doctrine of judgment.

*The hard-exclusivist response*—those who don’t hear are lost, and this is just because all deserve condemnation—is the universal-wickedness defense (Q3) deployed at eschatological scale. It carries the same structural cost: under uniform deserving, *just* tracks nothing differential.

Each response preserves the predicate by paying a doctrinal cost the standard set doesn’t pay in full. The cumulative result isn’t that every response is internally incoherent. It is that the set can’t retain all of explicit-faith exclusivism, this-life urgency, universally available opportunity, libertarian freedom, and non-arbitrary eternal judgment without revising at least one commitment. The argument’s force lies in making that price visible.

*The burden.* Run together, the eight pressures register what divine-justice predication depends on once the senses are kept apart. *Just*, *merciful*, *equitable*, *fair*, and *righteous* can describe standards, characters, institutions, verdicts, or acts. The adverbial uses require the verb—to give *justly*, to render *mercifully*, to judge *fairly*, to act *righteously*—and the verb requires a substantive agent, a target distinct from the actor, and directed action. Concrete exercise therefore incurs the relevant Φ-, S-, and T-roles. Standard and character uses aren’t thereby empty; they must specify the content by which the standard or character differs from its alternatives and connects to concrete acts. Each relocation must be marked.

The pressures cluster in three groups. *Transfer.* The mercy-vs-justice tension (Q1), penal substitution (Q4), and hereditary guilt (Q5) require moral properties to cross distinctions the predicate’s substantive structure depends on: between attributes and between substantive bearers. The relevant account must explain whether this is transfer of guilt, representation, participation, assumption of penalty, or something else; treating every route as bookkeeping would erase differences among the replies.

*Dependence and consistency.* The dependence problem (Q2) asks where the recipient-field of exercised justice stands modally; the cross-covenant identity problem (Q6) asks what keeps one standard constant across temporal indices and different administrations. Neither question by itself proves that the predicate changes or empties. Each requires an account of what remains invariant and what varies.

*Discernment and arbitrariness.* Universal deserving (Q3), skeptical access (Q7), and demographic distribution (Q8) test whether *God is just* retains differential content and evidential vulnerability. A global denial of creaturely moral access threatens the affirmation’s warrant; a local skeptical reply owes a principled defeater; an eternal-stakes distribution that tracks morally arbitrary conditions owes an account of opportunity and deserving.

What the local argument earns positively is narrower: justice and mercy require differential content within an agent–recipient field when they are exercised. Justice must track what is owed to affected subjects rather than return a constant verdict or migrate guilt by an unspecified transfer; mercy must track restoration or remission responsive to misery rather than merely rename any favorable effect. No grammatical argument alone establishes that every moral predicate requires a new divine transition. The further identification of justice with mutual subsistence under symmetry-of-extraction is the book’s Chapter 6 political proposal. It isn’t derived by the destructive pressure on divine predication and is deferred to the sections that define and defend its normative bridge.

**[Diagnostic]**

**What Makes the Verdict Right?** · *Diagnostic*

*Just*, *merciful*, *equitable*, *fair*, and *righteous* can describe standards, characters, institutions, verdicts, or acts. The divine application must identify which is meant, what makes the standard right rather than merely commanded, how particular judgments answer to it, and what mercy contributes when no possible response alters the divine subject. Moving between these senses may be legitimate, but it is a revision that must be marked. No grammatical argument alone establishes that every moral predicate requires a new divine transition.

**Depends on:** Character, Standard, and Exercise (§11.9.1)

*The reclamation.* The justice and mercy vocabularies are deeply relational. *Iustitia*, *dikaiosynē*, and *ṣedeq* concern right order, fit, obligation, or the giving of what is due; *misericordia*, *eleos*, *ḥesed*, and *raḥamim* concern response to suffering, covenantal loyalty, compassion, and restoration. Their histories don’t prove that only embodied institutions can be just or merciful. They do show what the theological predications must preserve. A divine standard must discriminate right from wrong independently of the bare fact that God wills it. A divine verdict must answer to the differentiated subjects and harms it judges. Divine mercy must contribute something beyond the same outcome redescribed after the fact. If the doctrine supplies those truth conditions, the predicates remain live and incur their relational commitments. If every possible command, distribution, punishment, and nonintervention is made compatible with perfect righteousness, the words cease to distinguish their alleged subject from one with contrary character. Nature isn’t righteous; natural subjects and institutions are the domain in which the relevant contrasts are presently identifiable. The divine application stands or falls on whether it specifies another. That domain isn’t a fallback. Giving what is due, answering to the harmed, and letting a wrong be repaired rather than merely recorded are things people do to one another, and they are where the vocabularies were learned. The pull anyone feels toward justice done and mercy shown is accurate about something real and already practised. What the doctrine adds is a claim about a further bearer. What the words carry, they carry already.

## 11.10 What Remains of God?

The attribute analyses from §11.1 through §11.9.2 repeatedly reach the same division: a divine predicate either retains enough determinate content to be assessed at the resolution claimed, or loses the truth conditions by which its affirmation could differ from its denial. The closing dilemma collects that earned division without deciding by stipulation whether any articulated theism is true.

This division produces four local results. Structural roles already earned of Nature, such as necessity and self-subsistence, relocate. Predicates of natural subjects, such as knowledge or life, may characterize determinate aspects of Nature without making the whole their subject. A theological use may revise ordinary or devotional content while remaining coherent. Only where every content-bearing articulation is withdrawn does the divine name dissolve from specification. The closing keeps those results apart.

*Content retained: application.* If the theist accepts Time, Space, and Substance as the preconditions of concrete Change, then every divine act described as occurring in history, responding, intervening, deliberating, or producing a concrete effect incurs those Conditions at the operation. A being defined by their absence can’t perform such work in the same concrete mode. A classical theologian may instead construe divine causation and cognition as atemporal grounding; that blocks the inference to concrete succession in God, but not structural inclusion. The Reality–Nature Identity establishes that every real determinate way belongs to Nature and that no content supplies an independently constituted addition within it. No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1) permits essence to explain modal truths while closing the stronger claim that an essence stands structurally prior to Nature. Atemporal grounding therefore remains assessable as an internal abstract relation, not as a contact from a second source.

*Premise challenge: reject the role analysis.* A defender may deny that concrete Change requires the roles identified as Time, Space, and Substance. That challenge must supply an alternative analysis of ordered occurrence, real distinction, and persistence across difference. Contemporary cosmology doesn’t itself furnish such a denial. BGV establishes past geodesic incompleteness for the relevant classical spacetimes, not an absolute beginning of every temporal structure; no-boundary and quantum-cosmological models revise the earliest physical regime while retaining determinate mathematical and physical relations (Carroll 2012; Carroll 2016; Hartle and Hawking 1983). Those models matter to cosmological arguments, but they don’t decide the constitutive analysis prosecuted here. Rejecting that analysis remains a live premise dispute, developed at §4.7.

*Content retained through revision.* If God is redescribed as a being who exists temporally, enters reciprocal relations, and performs concrete acts, the personal predicates retain recognizable application. The account has revised strict classical atemporality and exterior aseity, but revision isn’t dissolution. Such a being is the three Conditions in a determinate personal operation—an aspect of Nature, not an extra constituent placed inside it. The pantheist who identifies deity with Nature makes a different proposal: Nature is necessary, all-encompassing, and explanatorily basic, but those roles don’t by themselves establish personality, agency, intention, or worship-worthiness (§10.3.1).

A pantheist or cosmopsychist may add that the triconditional structure is conscious. No such inference follows from the three Conditions alone (Chapter 5). Consciousness appears where organization realizes the relevant integrated sensitivity, and its character depends on that organization (§5.1). A cosmic subject therefore requires an additional unity and realization argument. Even if supplied, it wouldn’t yet establish the intentional, responsive, or second-personal predicates of a devotional God.

Process theism and open theism escape the ∅-like specification charge. They thereby forfeit classical exterior aseity: a God who exists in time and acts is a determinate operation of Nature and can’t be its independently constituted ground. A theologian may still propose that this personal configuration is uncaused, locally priority-bearing, or co-constitutive rather than simply dependent. Those are internal structural claims requiring their own arguments; none restores an extra bearer behind Nature or the classical independence already surrendered.

Swinburne’s theistic personalism is a developed revisionary candidate (*The Coherence of Theism*, 1977; *The Existence of God*, 1979; 2004; *The Christian God*, 1994): God is an everlasting person whose simplicity is freedom from physical constraint rather than strong Thomistic non-composition. Many of the pressures therefore don’t apply to Swinburne’s God. The remaining question is comparative. His proposal attributes knowledge, will, freedom, and purposive selection to a configuration of Nature; the structural account doesn’t infer those personal features from the necessary frame. Bayesian comparison can rank articulated hypotheses within a fixed possibility space; it can’t establish that space without presupposing some modal structure. That limitation doesn’t make the personal description incoherent. It means each attributed feature and its explanatory work must be earned; none is an ontological addition to the modal field.

*Content withdrawn.* The Conditional Closure reaches the zero-content result without assuming that every theology already places God inside modal space. A faster line reaches the same limited conclusion directly, at the cost of one added assumption. Simplicity, *actus purus*, and immutability converge on one claim: that God has no alternative way to be. *Actus purus* is sheer actuality, with nothing in it awaiting realization. By the tradition’s own description, God couldn’t have been otherwise.

**[Argument]**

**The No-Way Argument** · *Argument*

1. God has no alternative way to be: by the tradition’s own commitment to simplicity, *actus purus*, and immutability, God couldn’t have been otherwise.

2. The absence of alternatives isn’t by itself the defect, and the argument must not be run as though it were. A necessary being has exactly *one* way to be, and *Necessity entails Possibility* (§2.1.4) gives □P → ◇P: what couldn’t fail to be the case could, in particular, be the case. Uniqueness of way is therefore compatible with possibility, and an inference straight from *no alternative* to *not possible* would contradict the book’s own modal grammar (§1.2.1).

3. What does the work is the *strict formulation’s* further denial of every thin or analogical content by which the divine predicates could have determinate content. Simplicity and pure actuality alone don’t yield that denial. Where it is added, what remains isn’t one determinate way with alternatives foreclosed but a description with no stated conditions of satisfaction.

4. To be possible is to have a determinate way to be: ◇P ↔ ∃way(P) (Way–Possibility Convertibility, §3.2.5). An analogically structured account satisfies this step only if it supplies a determinate divine correlate. That correlate is then an aspect of Nature and inherits the predication and realization questions at §10.2.1 rather than being declared impossible here.

5. ∴ The classical theist’s God, on the strict content-stripped formulation, isn’t possible. *(3, 4)*

6. What isn’t possible is impossible.

7. ∴ The classical theist’s God, on that formulation, is impossible.

*Scope.* What is shown impossible by this fast line is the strict, fully content-stripped set, not every doctrine that calls God necessary. Essence-prior, apophatic, or analogically structured proposals remain assessable only where they supply enough content to distinguish their alleged referent. Once they do, the No Divine Addition result below locates that content as Nature or an aspect of Nature rather than an independent divine remainder.

The argument doesn’t add a new premise. It makes explicit what the role-definition mapping of §11.1–Righteousness (§11.9.2) establishes: the classical commitments, pressed to the strict formulation, leave no determinate way for their subject to be; and the predicate *is possible*, applied substantively, requires exactly such a way. The descent runs: *no determinate way → no possibility → not possible → impossible*. Note what the descent does **not** run on. It doesn’t run on the absence of alternatives, which would prove far too much—every necessary truth lacks alternatives and every necessary truth is possible. De-articulation carries the load, so the conclusion reaches the strict, zero-content conception and not every doctrine that calls God necessary. This is the conjunction-level line: the quickest road, and the one that runs on the substantive-modal-subject assumption isolated in the analysis that follows. Its advantage over the Conditional Closure is speed; its cost is that the assumption can be refused, which is why the Conditional Closure, not this faster line, is the theorem’s proof of record.

The faster argument can now discharge its apparent presupposition. A classical theist may hold that God grounds modal structure rather than being explained by it (Leftow 2012; Morris and Menzel 1986; Pruss 2011). That reverses explanatory direction; it doesn’t exempt God from modal classification. If God is actual, God is possible. If God is necessary, Necessity entails Possibility. By Way–Possibility Convertibility, either claim requires a determinate way God is. By Reality–Nature Identity, that way belongs to Nature’s one modal field. The theologian may therefore deny that modality explains God, but can’t deny that *God is possible* applies while continuing to assert actuality or necessity. A concrete grounding act realizes the three Conditions concretely; a determinate atemporal relation realizes them at abstract role-resolution. Neither supplies an exterior subject.

*The necessity rescue.* A second classical reply concedes the strict set’s impossibility but holds that God’s *necessity* puts God beyond it. The reply runs against the *Necessity entails Possibility* result derived at §2.1.4: □P → ◇P, falling out of the T-axiom composed with the *actuality implies possibility* result of §1.2. Contraposed: ¬◇P → ¬□P—what isn’t possible isn’t necessary. An analogically structured or essence-prior God avoids the specification failure only by supplying a determinate way to be. That saves possible content by locating the candidate in Nature; it doesn’t recover modal or structural exemption.

*The cumulative case.* The concrete exercises of the classical attributes repeatedly require Time, Space, and Substance, while their timeless formulations repeatedly incur predication, contingency, and contact burdens. The arguments aren’t independent: many run through divine simplicity and the analysis of directed action. Their cumulative force is therefore concentrated rather than additive, and a successful account of timeless differentiated action would propagate across the attributes that depend on it. The closing synthesis records that dependency instead of treating each local diagnostic as an independent proof.

*The higher-order objection.* A critic can grant every displayed inference provisionally and still press a different concern: philosophers using the same methods divide sharply, so confidence in any long speculative derivation should fall even before its error has been found. That is genuine higher-order evidence, and the literature divides over how far disagreement should move a reasoner who has inspected the first-order case (Christensen 2007; Kelly 2010; Elga 2007). Nothing in a deductive form makes the reasoning immune to that evidence. A conclusion whose costs become independently incredible gives reason to return to its premises, its inferences, or the way its terms were held fixed.

What the objection cannot do by itself is select the place where the return should end. The line here exposes its joints: the actuality and real possibility of Change, the Structural Requirement, the identity steps, and the modal principles that carry their consequences. Evidence against any one of them bears there; a demonstrated invalid step closes the route; an independently supported counterexample tests the premise it contradicts. But “one of these must go wrong somewhere” is only the disjunction of those possible defeats. It doesn’t establish any member, and disagreement about the conclusion doesn’t acquire more first-order content by leaving the disputed joint unnamed. Appendix C lays the joints out so that none can hide behind the length of the line.

The contrast with empirical evidence is therefore not a ranking of methods. A photograph, laboratory report, or body of testimony may establish that an event occurred and may bear strongly on its token cause. The evidential thresholds at §10.1.16 and the occurrence–cause–authentication division at §12.3.3 say exactly where that evidence enters. If a well-established occurrence conflicts with a claimed structural result, the derivation must be reopened. What the occurrence cannot establish without the further bridge is which modal premise failed, or that its cause stood outside the Conditions under which the occurrence and its evidence obtained. Higher-order evidence can lower confidence and demand a new audit. It cannot finish the audit anonymously.

What is secured after the audit is broader than the concrete work. Time, Space, and Substance condition every determinate way at the resolution appropriate to it; concrete change, intervention, experience, and act realize them concretely. A determinate atemporal ground is therefore an abstract structure of Nature, not a distinct source behind it. The remaining question is whether that content explains any concrete configuration and whether the further predicates establish personality. Essence-priority no longer supplies an exterior candidate.

*The epistemic form of the inversion.* Inquiry often begins from the richest causal model immediately available to a self-modeling being: agency like its own, projected beyond its own scale. As inquiry supplies determinate natural relations, some explanatory work once assigned to transcendent intention is replaced. That history isn’t a proof that no transcendent ground exists, and one more natural explanation isn’t one more deduction against God. Its force is discriminating. Where necessity, self-subsistence, or non-exteriority has already been established of Nature, repeating the role under a divine name adds no explanation. Where personal content is added, the account must state what realizes it and what difference it makes. Where all such content is withdrawn, the residue approaches ∅. Nature hasn’t thereby become a cosmic agent; it becomes locally self-modeling in the subjects through whom the distinction is learned (§5.4).

The creator claim now receives an exact upper bound. Reality’s capacity is the complete field of real possibility (§1.2.1), and the identity of Reality, Nature, and the universe in the totality sense is earned at §4.9. Even granting a creator for the sake of the argument, no act could add a real possibility beyond that field: if the added capacity were real, it would already belong to Reality; if it didn’t, nothing would have been added. At most, *creation* could name the actualization or arrangement of a configuration Reality already permits. God could therefore create no more, in modal extent, than the universe already has the capacity to contain. Nor is the creator itself an ontological addition: if real, it is Nature in a determinate operation or an abstraction of such an articulation. No Outside Selector (§10.4) confines creation-as-selection to an internal explanation of a subconfiguration. The proposed creator neither enlarges possibility, adds a second bearer to Reality, nor externally selects total actuality.

The standard incompossibility-of-maxima objection, that the perfections, even granted individually, can’t coherently obtain in a single being (Sobel 2004; Martin 1990; Everitt 2004), surfaces here as the cumulative form of the concern pressed throughout: each attribute has already been pressured at its individual point, and the question the cumulative case raises is whether the failures, taken jointly, leave any coherent residue for the perfect-being-theology engine to have produced. 

The No Supernature theorem bears directly on the modal ontological argument without pretending that every description called God is semantically empty. Plantinga’s (1974) S5 argument advances from ◇(maximal greatness is instantiated) to □(God exists). The strict zero-content conception can’t satisfy that possibility premise. A concretely active [maximally great being](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary) is a determinate operation of T, S, and Φ; an analogically structured atemporal candidate, if possible, is an abstract structure of the same field. Either candidate must still show that its predicates are compossible and that personality, cognition, and causality are realized. The argument blocks an unsupported entry into S5 and rules out a transcendent addition; it doesn’t rule out every natural articulation to which a theologian may apply the name *God*.

Plantinga’s de re reading asks whether the entity itself could exist; the de dicto reading asks whether the description *maximally great being* is possibly satisfied. The Concrete-Entity Test applies de re wherever the entity performs concrete operations and de dicto wherever the description includes them. A timeless reconstruction remains an abstract structure and must state how the personal and causal predicates are realized. The distinction therefore doesn’t recover an exterior subject, but neither does the structure of the description alone make every natural articulation called God impossible.

*Mysterious ways.* “God’s reasons exceed our understanding” can properly mark an epistemic limit. It can’t by itself supply the truth conditions of *God is love*, *God is just*, or *God creates*. Those claims may retain analogical content without becoming exhaustive descriptions, but the content must still distinguish their affirmation from denial and explain their bearing on the histories invoked as their effects. Mystery therefore doesn’t form a third side of the dilemma. It either protects a partly specified predicate, which remains assessable at the stated level, or withholds specification, in which case no conclusion about that predicate has yet been supplied.

*Refusing the classification.* A theorist may refuse to classify the divine predicates as abstract, concrete, or indeterminate. The refusal is itself a structured discursive act, but that establishes only the act side. On the object side, the proposal remains unassessed until it states what work the predicates perform. Silence doesn’t prove that every religious use of the name is empty; it supplies no possible competing ground. The Grounding-Contact Trilemma (§10.4) classifies articulated proposals by their attributed work, while Way–Possibility Convertibility and No Unconditioned Essence prevent a contentless essence from functioning as an unnamed fourth option.

A single image collects the concrete side of the argument. An author begins writing, directs marks toward a surface, persists from first stroke to last, distinguishes the order of a plot, and reaches readers through a medium. Concrete authorship therefore instantiates the three Conditions. Calling God the Author may be analogical rather than a claim that God performs those creaturely motions. The analogy remains informative only if the account states what correlates with selection, production, ordered content, and relation to the work on the divine side. The image establishes the structural cost of concrete authorship and the content burden of its timeless analogue; it doesn’t collapse the two by definition.

The closing results escalate in three steps. The first fixes location: any possible divine candidate stands within Nature, not beside or behind it. The second fixes operation and domain: what a candidate at that location can do concretely, and what selection it can perform. The third fixes the strict limit: what follows when every content-bearing articulation is withdrawn.

**[Theorem]**

**No Divine Addition** · *Theorem*

Any God claimed to be actual or necessary must be possible; any possible God must have a determinate way to be. Every determinate way belongs to Reality’s one modal field, which is Nature. By constitutive non-addition, the candidate is therefore Nature itself, Nature in a determinate operation, or an abstraction of such an articulation—not an independently constituted being inserted within Nature or standing outside it. An alleged divine essence does not reopen either location: essence may explain modal truths about the configuration, but No Unconditioned Essence establishes that it is not structurally prior or additional to Nature. If no determinate content answers to the description, no possible divine candidate has been specified.

**Depends on:** Actuality and Necessity entails Possibility (§2.1.4), Way–Possibility Convertibility (§3.2.5), Reality–Nature Identity (§2.8), and No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1)

No Divine Addition closes the candidate’s location. The attribute tests of §§11.1–11.9, the no-way argument above, and Chapter 10’s grounding-contact and No Outside Selector results now determine what work any candidate at that location can perform. Their conjunction earns the closure theorem.

**[Theorem]**

**No Supernature** · *Theorem*

Given the Structural Requirement, no concrete act, change, experience, intervention, causal production, or selection occurs outside Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality. A proposed deity performing such work is T, S, and Φ in determinate operation and cannot be the concrete exception to Nature the classical exterior picture requires. A determinate atemporal or analogical ground is an abstract structure of Nature, not an exterior source; if it is invoked to explain concrete actuality, the relation between those articulations must be stated. A strict set withdrawing every determinate feature, truth condition, and relation supplies no specified subject or ground. No Divine Addition closes both alleged remainders: no independently constituted deity stands outside Nature or is added inside it. No Outside Selector adds that selection may explain an internal subconfiguration but not total actuality from an exterior or surplus position. There is therefore no supernature: no second domain, exempt concrete agent, additional divine bearer, exterior selector, unconditioned essence, or exterior source of determinate effects beyond Nature.

**Dependency routes:** any divine candidate—No Divine Addition (§11.10); concrete operation—Concrete-Entity Test (§2.4) and Necessary Occupancy (§2.9.7); total actuality and selection—No Outside Selector (§10.4); no determinate content—Incoherence of ∅ (§2.7.2); determinate atemporal ground—Grounding-Contact Trilemma (§10.4) and No Unconditioned Essence (§7.2.1)

The theorem draws on the account of existence at §1.5, the Structural Requirement at §2.4, and the Grounding-Contact Trilemma at §10.4.

*Proof (Conditional Closure).* Let g be proposed as the ground of concrete actuality, and grant the Structural Requirement.

1. If g is actual or necessary, g is possible; if g is proposed only as a possibility, that standing is already granted.

2. If g is possible, g has a determinate way to be (Way–Possibility Convertibility).

3. Every such way belongs to Reality–Nature, and constitutive non-addition leaves no independently constituted item outside or inside the field (Reality–Nature Identity).

4. If g is concrete or performs concrete work, the bearer or operation is T∧S∧Φ in determinate operation (Concrete-Entity Test; Necessary Occupancy).

5. If g supplies a determinate atemporal relation only, it remains an abstract structure of Nature; if credited with concrete explanatory work, the relation between those resolutions must be stated (Grounding-Contact Trilemma).

6. Essence-priority doesn’t reopen an exterior: modal truths may follow from what g is, but what g is has no non-configurational or unconditioned remainder (No Unconditioned Essence).

7. If g isn’t determinately specified, no possible subject or grounding relation has been supplied (Incoherence of ∅).

8. Therefore every specified divine candidate is Nature or an aspect of Nature; every unspecified candidate fails as a possible ground. No supernature remains. ∎

Rejecting the universal application of the Conditions challenges premises 3–6. Defending an atemporal ground preserves a distinction of resolution, not a position outside Nature; assigning that ground concrete explanatory work requires the relation identified in premise 5.

**[Theorem]**

**The Contentless God Has No Referent** · *Theorem*

Suppose a God is defined as outside time, outside space, and without substance, and at the same time as a determinate agent who acts, knows, and wills. Suppose also that every thinner or analogical reading of those active predicates—any reading that might have supplied their truth conditions—is refused. Then nothing at all answers to the description.

Call that exact description CG₀: not classical theism as such, but a stipulated conjunction of atemporality (¬T), aspatiality (¬S), and denial of any bearer-role (¬Φ) with determinate active predicates whose every thinner or analogical truth-condition is then refused. On CG₀ the definitional line reaches ∅; ∅ is precluded by Exclusivity of Nature, so ¬◇CG₀, and □¬CG₀ follows by modal duality.

*Scope.* □¬CG₀ holds for that description and nothing broader. Classical, apophatic, analogical, essence-prior, and revisionary proposals that supply determinate content are not made impossible by this theorem. No Divine Addition places any possible referent within Nature: as Nature, a determinate operation of Nature, or an abstraction of such an articulation—never an independent remainder.

**Depends on:** Exclusivity of Nature (§2.9.7), No Divine Addition (§11.10), and No Supernature (§11.10)

This is specification failure, not a mirror-image ontological argument: no ◇□¬CG₀ premise is asserted. S5 remains neutral between Plantinga’s ◇□MGB and its schematic mirror ◇□¬MGB (§2.1).

In ordinary terms: no one acts concretely outside the conditions of action, no wholly indeterminate blank grounds anything, and no determinate timeless ground stands behind Nature as an additional source. A timeless articulation may still be proposed as internally explanatory of concrete actuality, but the relation and the personal predicates must be earned within the one field.

The classical traditions have joined two projects that have to be separated. Their modal language reaches for the necessity, self-subsistence, and non-exteriority already established of Nature. Their personal and devotional language reaches for a subject who knows, wills, loves, judges, and answers. The first project doesn’t establish the second. When the second is protected by withdrawing every condition under which its predicates are intelligible, the words remain joined to the modal role while the personal referent disappears from specification.

Oppy’s total-theory framework (*Arguing about Gods*, 2006; *Naturalism and Religion*, 2018b) gives the closing result its comparative test: the relevant standard isn’t whether classical theism can be described in isolation, but whether a total theory containing it is simpler, more comprehensive, and more explanatorily powerful than the naturalistic rival. Both accounts may use the words *necessary ground*. The principled difference isn’t a preferred label. Nature is the modal structure, and structural necessity alone doesn’t make it personal, agential, intentional, or a subject in the second-personal sense the believer’s confession requires—not because those predicates are excluded, but because nothing argued here establishes them. A God must add those contents. The question is whether they have been specified and what explanatory work remains for them once the structural role is already filled.

The PSR-symmetry objection asks why Nature’s necessity may stop explanation when God’s necessity allegedly may not. The first distinction is between *modal-structure necessity* and the necessity of a particular articulation of that structure. The frame’s status doesn’t automatically transfer to any configuration it permits. A theistic activist may propose God as the essence from which modal truths follow. That explanatory direction isn’t refuted by applying a modal operator alone; it is closed as an *additional source* by the combination of Reality–Nature Identity and No Unconditioned Essence. Divine intellect or will may represent alternatives or select an internal configuration, but it can’t fix possibility from an independent position without presupposing the determinate ways and relations it’s said to supply (§7.2.1; §10.1.2).

The difference between Nature and a god is therefore not an ontological addition. Nature is the modal structure already derived; it isn’t thereby a person. Calling some articulation *God* attributes knowledge, will, value, intention, and second-personal relation to it. Those predicates require evidence and realization, but their bearer—if there’s one—is an aspect of Nature rather than another ingredient beside it. Calling Nature itself *God* likewise doesn’t establish those predicates. Neither personality nor transcendence follows from calling the structure *necessary*.

Concrete existence, in the sense used here, need not mean point-location in metric space. It is the three Conditions in determinate operation. Abstract existence and atemporal grounding aren’t denied by aspatial vocabulary alone; they articulate the Conditions at a different resolution and remain within Nature. A posit with no determinate standing, relation, or content can’t perform the assigned grounding work. A posit with determinate atemporal content may remain intelligible as an abstract structure, but any claimed relation to concrete Change and any personal predicate must be stated and defended. What remains of God is therefore not an extra being behind Nature. It is whatever theological description can be earned of Nature or one of Nature’s articulations.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Predicate-Content Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

Ask the divine predicates to pick out their subject. What makes *wise* true rather than false, or *good* apply rather than not apply?

- **If something answers,** then it has retained determinate content: something borne by a concrete subject, specified through an atemporal grounding relation, or articulated some other way. That answer can be assessed—and whatever has a determinate way to be is already located inside the one field. *Feeds into* No Divine Addition.
- **If nothing answers,** then the predicates cannot identify the subject they are said to describe, or distinguish their affirmation from their denial.

Mystery can leave part of the answer dark. It cannot do the work of an answer after every condition for one has been withdrawn.



# 12. Exodus


Classical theism is not a single claim. It comes with a body of doctrine: how creation begins, how evil is permitted, how guilt is inherited and lifted, how a hidden God can still be believed in, and how prayer is heard. Those doctrines are taken one at a time, each tested for whether it holds together.

Grant what the doctrines need: a personal, transcendent, sovereign creator, and leave the existence question closed. Two lines of pressure can then be kept apart. An internal argument asks whether a doctrine sits with its own commitments and texts. An imported-result argument applies an earlier account of time, will, knowledge, identity, morality, or divine predication. Rejecting an imported result exits that line; it does not erase an internal pressure running beside it.

The distinction matters because doctrine makes claims about creatures throughout: what they can believe, choose, know, inherit, answer for, and survive. Those claims can be tested without pretending that every branch of Judaism, Christianity, or Islam shares every doctrine. Each section names the tradition and commitments it actually addresses.

**[Principle]**

**The Explanatory Burden** · *Principle*

A defense shows that evidence does not compel an adverse conclusion. An explanation does more: it gives some reason to expect one outcome rather than another. A reply compatible with every outcome may succeed as a defense, but that same compatibility prevents it from counting as evidence for the position it protects.

*Scope.* The principle governs what a defense may be cited *for*. It does not make unfalsifiable claims meaningless, settle any doctrine by itself, or presume that a particular reply fits every outcome.

The distinction between a *theodicy* and a *defense* is one application. A theodicy claims to give the reason God permits an evil. A defense claims only that some reason is possible and answers the narrower charge that God and evil are incompatible. A defense can succeed while leaving the world unexplained; defeating a theodicy need not defeat the defense.

The sections begin with origins, fall, and salvation, pass through messianic and eschatological claims, then take up divine governance, revelation, moral standing, and theodicy. The order follows dependencies where they exist without pretending that every branch inherits every burden. Nothing here opens a new metaphysical foundation. The work is to see what survives when each doctrine is held to its own commitments and to whichever earlier results it spends.

## 12.1 Origins, Fall, and Salvation

The first cluster takes the tradition’s account of what the human creature is before God, what then goes wrong, how it is repaired, and how the repair reaches anyone. It opens with creation (§12.1.1), the doctrine that supplies the world the rest of the arc presupposes. Genesis as primeval history (§12.1.2) then fixes what kind of human past Gen 1–11 may hand forward. Only after that interpretive price is stated does the cluster turn to the claim that the creature bears God’s own image (§12.1.3), before the arc proper runs from a first transgression (§12.1.4) through original sin (§12.1.5), inherited guilt (§12.1.6), and atonement (§12.1.7). Salvation (§12.1.8) then asks what applies the repair: explicit faith, obedient response, sacrament, grace or election, conscience, universal restoration, or some stated conjunction.

The arc is cumulative, but it isn’t a row of dominoes. An eternal-dependence account may preserve creation after surrendering a first moment; a functional image may survive the absence of a sharp species boundary; ancestral corruption may survive after inherited culpability is abandoned; a universalist may retain salvation after permanent loss is denied. Each move keeps a doctrine by changing what the next doctrine has to work with. One pressure is inherited from Chapter 11: the account must specify the personal, acting God its claims require. The other is internal to the cluster: fault, guilt, rescue, death, and restoration must remain predicates of the same responsible persons the doctrine begins with. The record of branches matters because neither pressure licenses this chapter to answer a position the reader no longer holds.

### 12.1.1 Creation
Creation is the doctrine everything after it leans on. Before a creature can bear God’s image, fall, inherit corruption, or be brought back, there has to be a world, and a human history, for those things to happen to. In its classical form, creation says a personal God freely brought everything else into being out of nothing, not shaping material that was already there, but giving reality to the whole created order in the first place. Genesis tells that as a story with an ordered beginning, and Christian theology turns it into the sharper metaphysical claim, creation from nothing, drawing on Gen 1:1–2:3 and Aquinas’s *Summa Theologiae* I.45 (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947). The real question isn’t whether the world has a history that makes sense. It’s whether that history can actually be the work of a being outside it, acting the way the doctrine says it does.

The strong version bundles four things together. The world has a first moment. It depends on a personal agent, not on Nature itself. The act that brought it about was free, not some automatic unfolding. And the Genesis account, read as history, gives the human story its actual starting point, the one the Fall narrative later needs. A defender can loosen any of these: reading Genesis theologically rather than as a timeline, treating creation as an eternal dependence rather than a single act, or stepping back from a determinate personal creator altogether. But each time one of these commitments is loosened, the doctrine hands down something different to everything built on top of it.

Those are positions defended within Christian philosophy, not alternatives invented for the fork. Craig joins creation to a temporal beginning and argues for that beginning as part of a Christian apologetic (Craig 2008). Aquinas distinguishes creation from temporal beginning: reason can establish the creature’s dependence on God, on his account, but not that the world began rather than having been created eternally (*ST* I.46.2) (Aquinas (1265–1274) 1947; see also the contemporary Thomist presentation in Feser 2009). The branch structure therefore follows a disagreement inside the tradition about what creation itself entails.

The Chapter 11 results don’t apply to *creation* merely because the doctrine uses causal language. The causal role has to be fixed first (§11.7.2). A free temporal origination is productive or efficient work: a creator brings about a concrete order that didn’t obtain before, so the operation must have determinate terms and make a difference. Eternal creation or conservation may instead be offered as metaphysical grounding: the world depends on God without a prior moment or a transmitted change. That branch isn’t refuted for lacking temporal transmission; it inherits the Grounding Conditional and must specify a determinate directed dependence and explain how it bears the thicker doctrinal work assigned to creation. Exemplar or final-causal readings may supply form or purpose without yet supplying either efficient production or a historical beginning. The branches therefore incur different burdens and hand different inheritances to the Fall.

Two Chapter 10 results bear on those branches without collapsing them. *The Creation Fork* (§10.1.2) asks what makes creaturely possibility genuinely other than the creator rather than content already identical with the divine essence. *The Sustaining Relation’s Own Dilemma* (§10.1.5) asks whether a sustaining dependence is necessary and sufficient for this particular order or contingent in its terminus. The Grounding-Contact Trilemma (§10.4) then keeps the options separate: no determinate content fails to specify a ground, concrete productive work incurs the Conditions at its contact, and a determinate atemporal ground remains available with an explanatory-contact burden. What follows tests what each doctrinal branch can actually pass downstream.

The temporal branch also inherits A Beginning Needs What It Would Begin from the cosmological argument. Every ordinary beginning named by the premise has a when, a where, and something whose state is different across it. A beginning of Nature would therefore spend Nature at the point said to produce it. That closes a categorial beginning from outside T, S, and Φ; it does not close an earliest coordinate within a temporal history, or the eternal-dependence branch that declines temporal production altogether.

*The first-moment problem.* Consider an ordinary case first: a carpenter building a chair already presupposes an order in which there was no chair and then there was one, and the making sits inside that order rather than producing it. A beginning isn’t merely an earliest date on a timeline. It is a transition: the beginning obtaining rather than not obtaining is already an order of before and after. If time begins from no time, the move from no-time into time needs the very temporal order it is supposed to be originating. The classical doctrine is careful to say creation isn’t a change, which does avoid attributing change to God, but it still doesn’t supply the directed relation the doctrine needs. If nothing precedes the created order, there is no condition for an act to proceed from, no recipient to receive it, and no interval across which a cause could make a difference. The word *creation* is retained, but the structure that would distinguish an act of creation from an unexplained standing fact about Nature has been withdrawn.

The other familiar route is to make the created order eternally dependent on God rather than temporally initiated. That avoids the first-moment problem precisely because grounding isn’t efficient production. It also changes what later doctrines may inherit. Eternal dependence by itself supplies no pristine historical state, first human pair, or datable rupture for the Fall; those require additional historical premises. The relation must still be determinate—this order depends on this ground in this direction—and the doctrine must say whether personal choice, providential selection, or continuing conservation adds an efficient or agent-causal role to the grounding claim. The atemporal dependence isn’t dismissed for failing to transmit a change. The thicker operations attached to it are tested according to the roles they are claimed to perform.

There is a further problem behind the first-moment problem, one about necessity itself. Even granting a free creative act, the bare possibility of creating, the fact that a world could be brought about at all, isn’t itself something God’s agency produces. That possibility has to already stand, necessarily, prior to any choice God makes to actualize it. God doesn’t author the space of what is possible; God, if there is a God, only selects within it. Necessity therefore runs beyond agency: the framework a free act operates inside isn’t itself a product of that freedom.

What, then, would the productive branch’s act amount to? Ordinary making rearranges what is already there into a configuration it did not previously have. *Creatio ex nihilo* expressly denies that model: neither a prior material nor a prior created interval is available. That denial doesn’t make grounding incoherent, but it leaves efficient-production language with a specification burden. A productive difference requires an ordered act, distinguishable source and effect, and something bearing the difference at the contact; those are the roles the Concrete-Entity Test identifies. If the reply relocates all directedness into the effect and describes the divine side only as an atemporal ground, it has selected the grounding branch and must not silently recover a temporal first act from it. If it retains a free act producing this concrete order rather than another, it owes the productive contact the doctrine invokes.

Composition doesn’t by itself close either creation branch. A composite created order has distinguishable aspects and relations, and those must be modally intelligible before they can be actualized. But modal availability isn’t a stock of material or structure already existing outside the creative act; from the fact that an arrangement was possible it doesn’t follow that the creator merely rearranged an ontological ingredient. A simple created entity isn’t thereby indeterminate either. It may lack internal parts while possessing a distinct essence and standing in external relations to its creator and to other things. Simplicity therefore doesn’t deprive creation of a target unless every individuating essence and external relation has also been withdrawn. The productive branch retains the earlier contact burden—what makes this source bring about this effect rather than another—and the grounding branch retains its directed-dependence burden. Composition changes how those burdens are answered; it doesn’t furnish an independent dilemma against creation.

Creation and primeval history therefore hand off different questions. The question here is whether a world could begin through a free productive act or stand in eternal dependence on a determinate ground. The next asks what the early chapters of Genesis contribute as history once that metaphysical question has been separated from the text’s chronology. A creation doctrine may survive a nonchronological Genesis; a first pair, first transgression, global Flood, or historical Babel requires further premises the creation claim doesn’t supply by itself (§12.1.2).

The branches leave different creation claims standing. A free temporal origin owes a coherent productive contact and a first-act relation; eternal dependence avoids that problem but doesn’t, by itself, supply the historical stage the Fall requires; exemplar and final-causal accounts may preserve form, vocation, or purpose without yet establishing efficient origination. Non-literal dependence, meaning, and orientation remain open, as does a determinate atemporal ground under the Chapter 10 contact burden. What none of those branches may do is surrender temporal beginning or personal selection here and silently recover it as a premise later.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Doctrine-of-Creation Fork** · *Disjunction*

What does a doctrine of creation hand down?

- **If the doctrine claims a free temporal beginning,** then it owes a coherent first act, and a relation between creator and created order. *Feeds into* The Timeless Choice Problem (§10.1.5).
- **If it claims eternal ontological dependence,** then a first temporal transition is avoided. But this relation doesn’t by itself supply the historical origin later Fall doctrines require. *Feeds into* The Fall-Event Fork (§12.1.4).
- **If it claims a theological or symbolic Genesis,** then dependence, vocation, and meaning may remain. But the text no longer supplies a straightforward chronology of cosmic and human beginnings. *Feeds into* The Age-Old Problem (§12.1.2).
- **If it claims only a generic source,** then later doctrines may not silently recover personal agency, biblical history, or a freely selected plan.

**Applies to:** any account on which the created order begins, depends, or receives its meaning from a source

### 12.1.2 Genesis as Primeval History

Creation asks how the world could begin or depend. Genesis as primeval history asks what kind of past the text gives the doctrines that follow. The unit runs from the ordered creation accounts through the first pair, genealogies, Flood, and Babel. Those stories can orient a community, name a vocation, diagnose a human condition, or narrate judgment without functioning as one continuous modern chronicle. They can also retain historical cores without making every feature a surveyed report. The question isn’t whether only literal history matters. It is which historical claims each reading is entitled to pass forward.

Three readings have to be kept apart. A straightforward-chronicle reading treats the narrated sequence and scope as history at the level the surface account states. A historical-core reading retains one or more actual events while taking their chronology, universality, or literary shaping as theological narration. A literary or theological reading doesn’t require a recoverable event behind each episode. These aren’t different levels of seriousness. They are different accounts of what happened, and every doctrine downstream must inherit the account actually selected.

Genesis lays creation out in days, grounds Sabbath observance directly in that order (Exod 20:11), and places humanity at the start of creation’s human story. Each day is marked by evening and morning (Gen 1:5). Jesus locates the pair there too: “from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female’” (Mark 10:6). The empirical cosmic and evolutionary history isn’t that chronology (Young and Stearley 2008). A literal young-world reading has to reject the same history that gives many contemporary cosmological arguments their evidential force in the first place. A concordist or historical-core reading keeps it by treating some combination of the days, genealogical frame, first-human setting, and universal scope as literary or theological rather than as a single chronicle of cosmic and human origins (Collins 2006; Walton 2009). That may preserve real events. It can’t preserve every surface feature as a straightforward report of them.

The text’s own composition compounds the chronology problem. Gen 1 and 2 give two creation sequences that don’t agree with each other: a structured seven-day account in which humanity arrives last, after plants and other land animals, and a second account in which a man is formed first, then plants, then animals, then a woman drawn from his side. Historical-critical scholarship attributes the two accounts to distinct literary traditions later redacted together—the Documentary Hypothesis, in its classic and successor forms—rather than to a single author recounting one event twice (Smith 2002; Cross 1973; Dever 2005; Sommer 2009; Römer 2015; Boyarin 2004). The flood narrative that follows enters a Mesopotamian literary field already occupied by older flood traditions. The eleventh tablet of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* has the boat rest on a mountain, releases birds in sequence to test for dry land, and recounts a divine decision to destroy humanity by flood; the correspondences with Gen 6–9 are part of a broader, well-attested interaction between Judean scribes and Mesopotamian traditions about primeval origins (Finkel 2014; Carr 2020). That supports literary inheritance. It doesn’t, by itself, recover the scribes’ exact intention. A monotheistic recasting in which Israel’s God takes the place occupied by a Mesopotamian divine assembly is a plausible account of the story’s theological work; the more specific claim that exilic writers adopted it to answer Babylonian rivals remains a historical hypothesis, not a premise this argument needs.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Age-Old Problem** · *Disjunction*

Is Genesis a literal chronicle, a history told theologically, or a literary one?

- **If it is read as a straightforward chronicle,** then the reading has to reject the same empirical history that gives many contemporary cosmological arguments their evidential force. *Feeds into* §10.1.5, whose empirical prong runs on that history.
- **If it retains a historical core under theological narration,** then the empirical history may remain. But the reading must identify which events and persons are historical, which features belong to the narration’s enlargement, and why later doctrines may inherit one rather than the other.
- **If it is read as literary or theological without a required historical core,** then the empirical history is kept, but the days, genealogical frame, and first-human setting are no longer a report of how the world and humanity began. *Feeds into* The Fall-Event Fork (§12.1.4).

Each reading preserves something. None may hand later doctrine more history than it kept here.

**Applies to:** doctrines that require a datable first pair, a first transgression, a genealogical line running back to it, a historical Flood, or a historical Babel

**Still open:** which persons and events remain historical on the middle reading, and what downstream doctrines may inherit from them

*The Flood.* The recurrence of flood stories has an ordinary environmental and epistemic explanation as well. The narrative itself imagines an inhabited land between waters: the *raqia* separates the waters above from those below (Gen 1:6–8), and the flood begins when the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven open together (Gen 7:11; 8:2). The event is an undoing of that narrative’s habitable world, not a report written from a surveyed globe. From inside an inundated alluvial plain, an observer whose horizon shows only water has no observational route from *everything we can reach is flooded* to *the entire planet is submerged*. Local and seasonal flooding in Mesopotamia therefore supplies a sufficient setting for stories that enlarge a destroyed experienced world into a destroyed whole earth (Walton 2009; Lang 2026). This doesn’t prove that every flood tradition arose independently. It does show why their recurrence is expected without one globe-spanning event, so recurrence alone can’t carry the global reading’s evidential burden.

Other nations’ flood stories, offered as corroboration, consequently cut the other way. If “only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark” (Gen 7:23), there is no other lineage left to remember it; if there was, the verse is wrong on the global reading. A historical-local reading takes a different route. It can retain a real Noah, warning, boat, inundation, rescue, and covenant while reading the destroyed *earth* as the inhabited land within the narrator’s horizon and the universal language as the experienced world’s enlargement into a narrated whole. That is neither a global flood nor a myth. It is a historical event carried in theological narration.

The route is coherent, but it has to state what it keeps. The covenant after the flood sounds on its face like a promise that no flood will again destroy the earth (Gen 9:11), while local floods haven’t stopped. The local reader can restrict the promise to no repetition of this covenantal judgment, but then *this kind of judgment*, not geographical extent, does the limiting work. The pairs of animals can be read as local fauna or the household’s dependent stock, but populations beyond the inundation already preserve their kinds, so the ark is no longer needed as a zoological reset. Matthew’s comparison between Noah’s days and the coming of the Son of Man (Matt 24:37–39) requires sudden judgment and unprepared hearers; it doesn’t by itself require the same geographical scale. These replies preserve a historical core by surrendering the planetary census, exhaustive animal mortality, and straightforward universality of the surface narration. The price is real, but it isn’t myth.

A historical-local event leaves a further question that interpretation alone can’t answer: why an ark was selected as the means of rescue when the threatened region had an outside. That proportional-means problem belongs to divine judgment rather than to the genre of Genesis and is carried at The Ark-or-Exit Problem (§12.3.12).

**[Disjunction]**

**The Global Flood Problem** · *Disjunction*

If flood stories corroborate Noah, where did they come from?

- **If they came from peoples outside Noah’s household,** then other lineages survived, contrary to Gen 7:23.
- **If they came from Noah’s descendants,** then the traditions aren’t independent confirmation, and their divergence requires a non-circular reason to identify Genesis as the uniquely preserved account.
- **If they came from distinct local floods,** then recurrence is expected without one global event. *Feeds into* The Age-Old Problem (§12.1.2).

The plurality can corroborate a global Noahic flood only by surrendering either the sole-survivor claim or the independence and canonical control the corroboration requires.

**Still open:** the historical reading must identify which transmission branch it accepts and may not cite the same traditions as both independent witnesses and corrupted descendants of Noah.

*Babel and the later commission.* The tower narrative adds a second transmission problem, but only for a specific doctrinal conjunction. The Babel narrative presents one language as enabling a centralized project and divine confusion of speech as the means of scattering its builders. A literal reading may understand the act as judgment on pride, imperial concentration, coerced uniformity, or refusal to fill the earth. On those readings the target isn’t communication as such, and linguistic plurality may carry genuine cultural goods. The later salvation economy nevertheless introduces a new stake: if restored relation comes to depend on receiving a historically situated message, the division of language becomes one of the conditions determining who can receive it, how quickly, and through how many interpreters.

Pentecost supplies an internal answer (Acts 2:1–11). It makes the gospel intelligible across languages without erasing their plurality, and therefore can be read as a repair that preserves difference rather than a reversal of Babel. But it is a local miracle at the beginning of the mission, not a permanent removal of the barrier. Ordinary hearers still depend on translators, teachers, institutions, travel, literacy, and the uneven arrival of a message. A direct or universally repeated Pentecost would answer the access problem; ordinary translation accepts the fallible chain later examined in §12.3.4 and §12.3.7. Natural revelation, conscience, inclusivism, or access-relative grace can protect those whom the chain doesn’t reach, but then receipt of the translated historical message isn’t an exceptionless gate. A literary or etiological reading can instead deny that God historically introduced linguistic difference at one moment; it preserves the story’s critique of human concentration while withdrawing the literal act that generates the tension.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Babel–Mission Problem** · *Disjunction*

Why scatter the languages, then require a message that must cross them?

- **If the barrier is answered by direct or miraculous understanding,** then the same power that supplies the understanding to some withholds it from others at no cost to itself, and an unevenly distributed remedy needs a reason the remedy cannot supply. *Feeds into* The Uniform Requirement Problem (§12.3.6).
- **If the barrier is answered by ordinary translation,** then the message inherits delay, unequal reach, and fallible human mediation from a barrier God knowingly introduced. *Feeds into* The Delivery Tradeoff (§12.3.4). *Feeds into* The Four Insufficiencies (§12.3.8).
- **If it is answered by natural revelation, conscience, inclusivism, or access-relative grace,** then the unreached may be protected. But explicit receipt of the proclamation isn’t universally necessary, and the account still owes what grades access to God relative to each mind’s differing capacity to register it—the same problem in its softer form. *Feeds into* The Uniform Requirement Problem (§12.3.6).
- **If Babel is nonhistorical,** then the access charge against a divine act falls away. But so does Babel as the literal origin of linguistic difference. *Feeds into* The Age-Old Problem (§12.1.2).

Every branch gives up one member of the original conjunction: a historical divine barrier, universally necessary proclamation, or equal access. No route keeps all three without a further remedy.

**Applies to:** salvation accounts combining a historical Babel judgment with a message-dependent creature-side condition

**Still open:** the value assigned to linguistic plurality, the remedy for unequal access, and whether explicit proclamation remains necessary

This isn’t an objection to symbolic or theological readings simply because they are symbolic or theological. Such readings can preserve orientation, ritual meaning, or a community’s sense of its own dependence. What they give up is the historical work later doctrines need when they appeal to a first pair, a first transgression, or an original created condition the human story fell from. A historical-core reading may retain some of that work, but only by naming the retained event and distinguishing it from the narration’s scope. A story that supplies no determinate historical beginning can’t underwrite, on its own, the historical sequence built on top of it.

The next two sections receive that branch rather than reopening it. Imago Dei may retain a vocation, relation, or standing without a datable first pair; a historical Fall may not. Neither section may treat Genesis as literary when avoiding its chronology and literal when recovering an ancestral event. The history handed forward is the history kept here.

### 12.1.3 Imago Dei
*Imago Dei*—the “image of God”—is the claim that the human creature is made, uniquely among creatures, in God’s own image and likeness (Gen 1:26–27). It names whatever makes the human creature a real image of God: a resemblance, a role received from God, a bodily form, or a standing in relation to God. The doctrine grounds every station after it. Before there is a fall to fall from, or a guilt to inherit, there is a claim about what the human creature already is.

The claim is repeated after the flood, as the reason human blood may not be shed with impunity (Gen 9:6), and carried into the genealogies as something itself heritable, with Adam fathering Seth “in his own likeness, after his image” (Gen 5:3). Judaism reads the same claim as *tzelem Elohim*. Islam’s *fitra* names a cognate but not identical idea, an innate disposition toward God rather than a resemblance to him. What the three traditions share, and what the argument that follows addresses whichever vocabulary is in view, is the demand for some real point of resemblance, role, or relation between God and the human creature, not a bare title.

A bare title is in fact the one reading the doctrine can’t afford. If “image” names no actual similarity or relation, only an honorific attached to the human species by fiat, then the doctrine carries no more content than an assertion of preferred status. That is useless for grounding the claims later doctrines rest on it: the special dignity that forbids killing, the rational soul the fall will damage, the nature the incarnation will assume. The tradition has never been willing to leave it there. Across its long commentary, it has offered four ways of cashing the resemblance out.

On a *substantive* reading, the image is a capacity the human creature has and other creatures lack: reason, will, a rational soul capable of knowing and loving God (Augustine, *De Trinitate* XIV.8, Aquinas, *ST* I.93.4, locating the image specifically in the intellectual nature, (1265–1274) 1947).
