On a *functional* reading, the image is a delegated role rather than a possessed faculty: humanity stands in creation as a king’s statue stood in a conquered province, marking a rule exercised on another’s behalf. Middleton defends this royal reading from the ancient Near Eastern image idiom and the dominion language of Gen 1:26–28 from within Christian biblical scholarship (Middleton 1994).

A *morphological* reading takes the resemblance to be, at least in part, literally bodily. A *relational* reading takes the image to name no resemblance at all but a standing conferred: humanity as the creature God addresses, calls, and enters covenant with. These are alternatives, not four claims every defender must hold. Each carries a different burden because each hands a different human status to the Fall.

Before taking the readings one at a time, separate the work each asks God to perform. A substantive image requires determinate attributes in the exemplar; a functional image requires a role with content and recipients; a relational image requires a directed standing between God and creature. Classifying them as relations doesn’t erase all three (Chapter 11). It asks what makes each determinate while simplicity, infinity, impassibility, and exterior aseity are retained (§11.1, §11.8.2). A relation of reason may express creaturely dependence without a reciprocal change in God, but then it supplies dependence rather than the responsive address some relational accounts claim. A real conferral, command, or response adds agent-causal or efficient work and incurs the corresponding contact burden; an exemplar, final-causal, or grounding account may avoid temporal transmission while still owing the content of the resemblance, end, or dependence (§11.7.2). These are conditional costs to the selected doctrine, not a prior result that leaves every image account with nothing to say.

Set those inherited results aside for the moment. Even if a determinate, relatable God is granted—whatever that costs the tradition’s other commitments—the substantive reading still faces a different problem on its own terms.

*Breadth.* The reading needs a qualitative break: some capacity humans have that draws a line under the rest of the animal kingdom, sharp enough to carry a difference in kind rather than degree. Comparative cognition research hasn’t supplied one. Great apes use tools and transmit techniques socially. Corvids plan for future states they don’t currently want. Cetaceans and elephants show grief behavior, mirror self-recognition, and long-term social memory. Several primate and cetacean species pass some version of the mirror test taken to mark self-awareness. Reason, tool use, self-awareness, moral sensitivity, and communication each admit of substantial cross-species continuity, even where their human forms remain exceptional (Hull 1976 makes the general point that biological kinds resist exactly this kind of sharp-boundary treatment). The evidence therefore burdens a simple all-or-nothing capacity boundary; it doesn’t establish that no derived cognitive profile is uniquely human.

The cultural case presses a different boundary from individual tool use. Resident killer-whale matrilines and pods maintain group-specific repertoires of stereotyped calls—described in the literature as vocal dialects—and changes in those repertoires track social learning and cultural transmission across and within lineages (Deecke 2000; Yurk 2002). Orca populations also sustain specialized diets and hunting practices, with ecological, genetic, and culturally transmitted differences interacting across generations (Foote 2016). These findings establish socially inherited vocal and practical traditions; they don’t by themselves establish human-like language, open-ended syntax, or the scale of cumulative symbolic culture. A defender may therefore relocate uniqueness to that stronger set. But the original line can no longer be drawn at tool use, communication, social learning, or the passage of acquired knowledge to descendants. The candidate image must be specified at the stronger level and then carried through evolutionary gradualism and marginal cases.

*Depth.* The same problem recurs across time rather than across species. Homo sapiens didn’t appear as a finished kind. The capacities nominated as image-bearing—language, abstract reasoning, shared intentionality (Tomasello 1999)—accumulate gradually across the hominin lineage, with every proposed marker present in partial, ancestral form in earlier hominins and absent in full in some populations of Homo sapiens itself. Shared intentionality shows the pattern: Tomasello develops it as itself a matter of degree, built up over developmental and evolutionary time rather than switched on at once. A doctrine that needs a sharp break owes an account of where, in a continuous lineage with no natural joint, the break falls. The traditional answer, a soul or rational capacity inserted at some point in that lineage rather than accumulated by it, trades a biological gradualism problem for a metaphysical one. On that account one hominin population received the image and its immediate ancestors didn’t, though the two are indistinguishable in every observable respect. The fossil and genetic record supplies no principled place to locate that difference.

*Marginal cases.* The substantive reading also has to explain infants, the severely cognitively disabled, and the permanently unconscious, all of whom the tradition wants to count as full image-bearers despite lacking, temporarily or permanently, the very capacities the doctrine locates the image in. The reply that the image is borne by the kind rather than the individual capacity, that a human lacking reason still images God by belonging to a reasoning kind, concedes the point rather than escaping it. The doctrine is no longer locating the image in a possessed capacity but in kind-membership, which is a different and weaker claim than the one the substantive reading advertised, and one that owes its own account of what fixes kind-membership independent of the very capacities just conceded not to be doing the work (an argument from marginal cases run to the same structural point, though aimed at a different target, by Singer, Rachels, and Regan against capacity-based moral status generally).

*Kind-membership.* Even granting the shift to kind rather than capacity, biology doesn’t supply the sharp kind-boundary that shift needs. Species boundaries in an interbreeding, evolving lineage are themselves populations shading into one another over time, not the discrete natural kinds folk biology assumes. Human populations outside sub-Saharan Africa carry measurable Neanderthal ancestry from historical interbreeding between what were, on any reasonable species concept, two distinct kinds, and hybridization across the hominin lineage appears to have been the rule rather than the rare exception. A doctrine that needs “the human kind” to name a sharp, principled boundary is borrowing folk-biological confidence that the biology behind the folk category doesn’t return.

The morphological reading faces two separate problems. The first is inherited: a literal divine body sharpens the determinacy problem already in view. The second is internal: a bodily image must explain why this particular body plan, and the variations within it, could constitute the divine image. The move to a literal, bodily reading looks, at first, like it escapes the gradualism just pressed against the substantive reading, by relocating the resemblance from a shared capacity to a shared shape, and the text supports this reading better than commentators sympathetic to the substantive reading generally admit. God is described walking in the garden in the cool of the day (Gen 3:8), wrestling a man through the night (Gen 32:24–30), eating a meal with Abraham (Gen 18:1–8), and permitting Moses to see his back, though not his face (Exod 33:20–23): a body doing bodily things, not a metaphor doing figurative ones. Stavrakopoulou develops the historical and anatomical case for reading this embodied portrait as prior to later abstractions of God (Stavrakopoulou 2022). The argument is collected elsewhere rather than re-derived here.

But the move sharpens the inherited determinacy problem rather than escaping it. A God with a specific anatomy isn’t merely determinate but concretely, contingently shaped, and the realization pressure Chapter 11 brings against a mind with no medium applies with at least equal force in the other direction, against a body with no history or medium to realize it. The textual body looks, on the evidence available, like the ordinary human form projected onto the divine rather than an independently discovered anatomy. And on top of that inherited problem, it reintroduces gradualism internally, now at the level of the body rather than the mind. Bipedal, forward-facing, five-fingered morphology is one convergent outcome among the many stable body plans evolution has produced, shaped by terrestrial locomotion, tool manipulation, and stereoscopic hunting vision, not a privileged form that a body-plan-free God would have had any reason to select in advance of the evolutionary history that produced it here.

And it reproduces the marginal-cases problem in a new register, since bodies vary continuously in exactly the morphological respects the doctrine would need fixed, congenital difference, developmental variation, injury and disability, with no principled way to say how much deviation from the paradigm form a body can carry before it stops counting as an image of the divine shape, a question the substantive reading’s appeal to kind-membership could at least defer to biology and the morphological reading can’t defer at all, since shape is exactly what is on the table.

**[Proposition]**

**No Break Where the Image Would Have to Sit** · *Proposition*

Grant for argument that some determinate, relatable God survives everything argued earlier, so that there is something for a creature to resemble, be delegated by, or stand in relation to. The doctrine still needs a break—a place where the human creature differs in kind rather than degree, since an image held uniquely among creatures has to sit somewhere the other creatures are not. The substantive reading looks for that break in species or in time and comes back empty against comparative cognition and the fossil record, which return differences of degree along every axis examined. Its fallback to kind-membership borrows a sharp biological boundary that population genetics does not supply. The morphological reading inherits the same determinacy problem in sharpened form, and adds to it a gradualism about body plans and a disability problem it cannot defer, since a bodily criterion for bearing the image sorts living human beings by how far their bodies depart from the type.

*Scope.* This result addresses substantive and morphological accounts that require a uniquely human break in capacity, kind, or bodily form. It concedes a determinate, relatable God for argument and does not claim that human beings lack distinctive capacities. Functional, relational, and status accounts do not fall merely because biological capacities are gradual; they instead retain the conferral, identification, and content burdens stated in the branch dilemma.

The readings therefore leave different sets. On the imported line, §11.1 and §11.8.2 pressure the determinate target, delegation, and real relation these models require. A reader who rejects those prior results remains on the internal line. There, substantive and morphological accounts still face the break result just stated. Functional, relational, and conferred-status accounts remain available, but what they carry forward is a role or standing whose source, scope, recipients, and content must be specified—not a damaged cognitive faculty that may be silently assumed by the Fall.

With the substantive and morphological routes tested, the alternatives can now be collected without treating their different burdens as interchangeable.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Image-Bearing Problem** · *Disjunction*

What is the image of God drawn from?

- **If the image is a capacity,** then the capacity view must say why creatures sharing that capacity don’t share the image. It must also handle the gradual arrival of the capacity, and the humans who don’t have it.
- **If it is a functional or royal role,** then capacity objections recede. But the role view owes the role’s source, scope, recipients, and conferral.
- **If it is a relation to God,** then the relational view must say what makes the relation real and how its bearers are identified. *Feeds into* §11.8.2.
- **If it is kind-membership, soul, or conferred status,** then infants and cognitively marginal cases are preserved. But a principled boundary and a contribution beyond an honorific are still owed.
- **If it is bodily resemblance,** then the resemblance view must say which features resemble, how precisely, and what to do about the variation among bodies.

The later Fall may inherit only the model selected here.

**Applies to:** any account on which human beings uniquely bear the divine image or an analogous conferred standing

### 12.1.4 The Fall

On the historical-rupture reading, the fall is the claim that a first pair, created upright in a world without death, transgressed one command and thereby introduced sin, mortality, and the disordering of nature into a creation that until then had none—a rupture, a before and an after with a single act between them. Other readings retain a corporate, developmental, existential, or necessary-passage account instead: not a rupture but a passage, a stage a creature of that kind was always going to cross. What later doctrines may inherit depends on which reading survives.

Two independent lines of pressure bear on it. The first is structural: if there is no privileged first moment from which a perfect creation could decline, and no will competent to grasp the stakes of its first decisive choice, then the fall lacks both the origin and the agent it requires. The second is internal: even granting a first pair in an uncorrupted state, the doctrine faces problems in its own texts and commitments. The two lines don’t depend on one another; a reader who rejects the structural theses still faces the internal case.

On the strong reading (Augustine, *De Civitate Dei* XIII–XIV; Aquinas, *ST* I-II.81–82) (Edwards 1758), Adam and Eve are created with rightly ordered wills in a world without suffering or death. Their free transgression forfeits that original state and propagates a fallen condition to all who follow.

The Qur’an tells substantially the same story of a first pair and a forbidden tree (Qur’an 2:35–39; 7:19–25; 20:115–123), but stops well short of the inheritance. Adam’s transgression is a lapse forgiven on repentance (“Then Adam received some words from his Lord and He accepted his repentance,” Qur’an 2:37), not a fall that propagates guilt or a corrupted nature to his descendants. Judaism carries no counterpart doctrine of a propagating fall either. Ezekiel states the later non-transfer principle directly: the person who sins is the one who shall die (Ezek 18:20). These branches therefore don’t enter the later inherited-guilt test merely by sharing a first-pair narrative. What the narratives share—and what the two structural pressures that follow address—is the narrower pattern of a claimed perfect origin in time and a will held competent to depart from it.

The narrative does double duty. It locates the origin of evil in creaturely will rather than divine design, and it supplies the corrupted starting point every doctrine downstream of it requires. The cosmic version extends the claim, reading the imperfection of the natural order as decay from an initial perfection (the design form engaged at §10.1.11).

Two preliminary objections arise before the doctrine’s internal test. First, the historical-rupture account needs an identifiable uncorrupted interval from which the decline occurs; neither an earliest cosmological coordinate nor an evolutionary population history supplies that interval by itself. Second, culpable choice requires an agent able to understand the alternatives, losses, consequences, and irreversibility attached to the choice, while the narrative assigns the first pair no prior experience from which to acquire that depth. Both objections are substantive and contestable, so their application is conditional rather than a direct refutation. Everything after them is the doctrine-internal track, and it doesn’t rest on either. That track runs in two movements. The first asks who authors the test: what the first pair could know and were told, who spoke against the command, how long the trial ran and for how many, and whether a fall that had to happen has any author but the design. The second asks what kind of event the Fall was, and by what mechanism one act could become a standing condition.

*No moment to fall from.* The fall requires a privileged origin: a perfect t₀ from which the decline is measured. Temporality supplies no such moment. Any “beginning” already instantiates the order of succession it claims to begin, so the demand for the instant at which perfect creation was set going isn’t unanswered but malformed.

*Succession isn’t decline.* The cosmic version reads entropy and the long catalogue of natural imperfection as evidence of a fall from perfection. But entropy is the structural condition of any host of succession, not a departure from a prior unfallen state. To read it as moral or teleological decline is to import a downward normative direction Nature locates nowhere. What looks like a world fallen from perfection is succession running. The retreat to *necessity* doesn’t recover the fall: nature is contingent, so no aspect of it is fundamentally necessary, not entropy, not predation, not death. Where such features are nonetheless called necessary, their necessity is only ever relative to some chosen goal of the creation in question. A feature necessary only relative to a goal isn’t one a world *fell into* but one a design selected; a feature necessary to nothing is no corruption either. On neither reading is there a descent to read off the natural order.

*No will competent to fall.* The fruit itself gives no warning: it looks, feels, and tastes like any other fruit in the garden. Nothing marks it off but a decree, and a will that has never faced a war, a grief, or a broken trust has no way to weigh what that decree is actually asking—a point taken up again later. Nor could the first pair have sorted what kind of statement the decree even was. Suppose “you shall surely die” was meant as a warning, not a moral decree. Death follows the eating causally, the way it follows touching a manchineel. Spanish explorers named that tree *la manzanilla de la muerte*, “the little apple of death”: its sap blisters skin on contact, announcing the danger before any words are needed. Or suppose the opposite: death as a penalty attached to the disobedience itself, carried by nothing in the fruit at all. Which is it? Genesis gives its tree no physical signature to settle the question; the fruit is described only as “good for food” and “a delight to the eyes” (Gen 3:6), so there is nothing a will could read as a natural warning even if it had the experience to read one. A warning and a threat are different things to weigh, and a will with no concept of death has no way to tell which one it is facing, or whether the tree itself was ever the danger at all.

That ambiguity isn’t something later interpretation introduces; it is what the inspired text itself hands down. Genesis isn’t a bystander’s uncertain report. It is the account tradition holds God caused to be written, in words God judged sufficient. Suppose the underlying situation was actually just, a real distinction between warning and threat, resolvable if only the record said which. An inspiration adequate to that situation could have said which. That it instead leaves the two readings open, on a point this consequential, isn’t a minor omission. So the ambiguity forces its own fork. Either the situation itself was unjust, and the text’s silence on what kind of statement “you shall surely die” was simply reports that unjust ambiguity faithfully. Or the situation was just, and the inspiration that produced Genesis rendered a just event in terms that read as unjust once carefully unpacked, an inspired text misrepresenting the very justice it existed to convey. Nothing available here lets both the inspiration and the justice of the underlying event stand together.

A later reading tries to save the calendar rather than sort the speech-act: they did die that day, but spiritually. That isn’t the sequel Genesis writes. The narrative’s own consequence is exile from the tree of life and a return to dust (Gen 3:19, 22–24). Spiritual death is a later save. It also replaces a consequence a novice will might conceivably weigh—stopping—with one they have no concept of at all.

The disclosed stake was their own death. “In the day that you eat of it you shall die” (Gen 2:17) names one consequence, for the eaters, on that day. Gen 3 then delivers more than that sentence contains. The woman is given pangs in childbirth and rule by her husband; the man, a cursed ground, thorns, toil, and a return to dust; both, exile from the tree of life (Gen 3:16–19, 22–24). None of that is in the command. If “you shall die” named only their dying, the choice wasn’t made under the stakes the doctrine later charges to it. If it was already a name for that whole set, a novice will was asked to weigh an inherited curse under a one-word label, which is the competence problem just run. The doctrine doesn’t get a disclosed, limited penalty and an undisclosed, standing curse.

*The serpent’s standing.* The speech that interrupts the command has to be read before the speaker is named. The serpent says they will not surely die, that their eyes will open, and that they will become like God in knowing good and evil (Gen 3:4–5). The narrative then confirms the opening of their eyes (3:7) and places the knowledge claim in God’s own speech (3:22); Adam’s death is reported centuries later (5:5). A defender can answer that the serpent used true or technically defensible claims in order to deceive about God’s motive, or that death began that day as mortality, alienation, or spiritual death. Those are real readings. The first locates the deceit in implicature and purpose rather than in the two contents the narrative expressly confirms. The second inherits the disclosure burden already identified: the announced consequence was not available to the first pair in the sense later required to make the warning plain.

Genesis itself calls the speaker the serpent, not Satan. The identification develops in later Jewish and Christian reception: Wisdom 2:24 assigns death’s entry to the devil’s envy, and Revelation identifies “the ancient serpent” as the Devil and Satan (Rev 12:9; 20:2). If that identification is retained, the founding speech must be assessed in the narrower way just stated: two textually confirmed contents, a disputed death claim, and a deceptive purpose. If it is declined, Satan is not an actor in the narrated Fall, and the later soteriological role cannot be read backward into Genesis without an additional interpretive bridge. Neither branch shows that the narrative is worthless or that no deception occurred. It fixes where the deceit and the adversary’s identity must be argued instead of supplied by the label.

Take the story on its own terms. Eden sets a morally decisive choice before an agent who hasn’t accumulated the depth to understand it: no map of death, no experience of deception, shame, or irreversible consequence. Formally the act is voluntary; voluntariness of that kind isn’t yet freedom. Freedom begins with depth in the field, and the field isn’t yet there. So read, Eden isn’t the origin of fully responsible rebellion but the exposure of an undeveloped will to a consequence it couldn’t yet understand.

Two further features sharpen the same point without depending on how the libertarian/Thomist dispute addressed later is resolved. First, on any reading where Eden is a stable state that persists across time rather than a single instant, the forbidden tree remains a recurring option for as long as the state lasts. Finite options plus unbounded time don’t by themselves entail that every option will be selected; a settled refusal is logically possible. The pressure begins when the test’s exploration process is made explicit.

Stated plainly: the longer the test runs, the less the eventual failure looks like a personal flaw, and the more it looks like something the process was always going to produce. If Edenic exploration is exhaustive, if every live object is eventually investigated, the forbidden option is eventually reached, and the outcome follows from the process the design sustains rather than from a first pair’s special preference for evil. If exploration isn’t exhaustive but every still-open occasion carries a conditional probability of transgression bounded below by some positive value ε, then after n occasions the probability of continued obedience is at most (1 − ε)ⁿ, which approaches zero as the occasions continue. This doesn’t make transgression logically necessary on any particular occasion, and it requires no assumption that the choices are independent; it makes failure almost sure under the stated lower bound. If neither condition holds, because refusal can become settled and drive the risk to zero, then that settled state is the natural success condition for the test. Continuing the exposure after that point would add no evidence of an unsettled will; it would merely preserve an opportunity for eventual breakdown. The doctrine therefore owes one of three things: an exhaustive-search rule, a recurrent-risk model, or a criterion by which stable refusal counts as passing. On the first two, the design makes eventual failure structural or almost sure. On the third, the test must be capable of ending in success rather than leaving obedience permanently provisional.

The adversary sharpens the authorship question without replacing it. “The wages of sin is death” (Rom 6:23) is addressed to human sin, so it cannot simply be assumed as a separately revealed sentencing rule for Satan. The wider tradition does assign the adversary a final sentence, but postpones its execution until the final judgment (Rev 20:10). That answer removes a bare exception and makes the interim the issue: the condemned adversary retains agency, access, and a role in temptation while human lives are tested under that pressure.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Adversary’s Wage** · *Disjunction*

What follows if the adversary’s sentence is deferred while the trial continues?

- **If the adversary is simply exempt from the penal rule applied to human sin,** then the rule is not universal and its unequal application needs a reason.
- **If the sentence is fixed but deferred,** then the exception disappears. But continued permission of the adversary’s work belongs to the design of the trial, and the account must say what good requires that added pressure and why a safer test would not secure it.
- **If the adversary is required for genuine choice,** then temptation is not an external difficulty the design merely encounters. The examiner has retained the condition said to make the examination necessary, and must explain why freedom needs an active deceiver rather than available alternatives, ordinary uncertainty, or a test that can end in settled refusal.
- **If the adversary is read symbolically,** then no personal sentence is waiting. The same question remains wherever the testing conditions themselves are attributed to divine creation or permission.

Deferral can preserve a future sentence or an adversary’s present function. It cannot make the function costless to the design that knowingly retains it.

*Scope.* The disjunction does not infer a doctrine of Satan from Rom 6:23, require a literal serpent-adversary identity, or deny every free-will defense. It asks only who authors and justifies the conditions under which creaturely wills are tested.

**Feeds into:** The Victimless-Agency Dilemma (§12.5.2); A Duty-Bearer Need Not Have Designed the Harm (§12.4.1)

Second, and independent of that trilemma, the fruit is modally identical to every other object in the garden from the only vantage the first pair have: it can be reached, held, and eaten exactly as any other fruit can. Nothing internal to the field distinguishes it in kind, only a decree that it is off-limits, and a will with no map of death, betrayal, or loss has no resource for converting that decree into a difference it can weigh as such. Asking such a will to treat “forbidden” as a morally decisive category is asking it to register a distinction it has been given no experiential means to register: the prohibition supplies a label, not a stake, and a will without a concept of consequence cannot be expected to tell the two apart.

The tree is named for that missing competence. It is “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen 2:9, 17). The command not to eat of it is a moral prohibition, while the fruit is said to confer the knowledge needed to recognize good and evil; God confirms afterward (Gen 3:22) that they have “become like one of us, knowing good and evil.”

**[Disjunction]**

**The Edenic Competence Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

The first command asks Adam and Eve to know what the fruit is supposed to give them.

- **If they already knew good and evil,** then the tree did not confer that knowledge, and their becoming “like one of us, knowing good and evil” needs a different reading.
- **If they did not know,** then they lacked the moral competence to understand the prohibition as a test of good and evil, or to bear the culpability later assigned to failing it. *Feeds into* The Inheritance Problem (§12.1.5).

The account needs them to know enough to be guilty and not know enough for the fruit to matter. It cannot have both.

**Applies to:** literal-first-transgression accounts in which the tree confers knowledge of good and evil

This second removal is more contested than the first. In plain terms, both replies try to give Adam and Eve a ready-made will, not one built up through experience. Two defenders refuse the structural reading at its root. The libertarian (Plantinga 1974) holds that a created agent can have contra-causal competence from the first moment, owing nothing to an accumulated field. The Thomist (Stump 2003) holds that Adam was given infused knowledge and original justice, competence conferred whole rather than developed, so that the first sin is a deficient turning (*aversio*) of an already-competent will from rightly ordered reason, not a failure of modal depth. Against both, the rebuttal reaches all the way down, because the fork below is argued here rather than assumed from outside.

To the contra-causal competence the libertarian claims, the fork is the familiar one and needs no importing: pressed for its content, contra-causal freedom resolves into either determination by the agent’s own structure or sheer luck, with agent-causation relocating the question rather than answering it. There is no will free in that sense for the first pair to have been given, and a defender who insists otherwise owes an account of what the third option is. To the infused competence the Thomist claims, the answer is internal to the proposal: a will acting on an infused map is acting on content it did not author, so its choices are grounded in that installed structure. Infusion confers a *structurally* free will, not a contra-causal one, and the “installation” point, that education, language, and art install modal content piecemeal while divine infusion installs it all at once, is no longer an opening but the very reason infusion cannot deliver contra-causal competence. What is left is the one question internal to the present account: whether the infused map was *deep* enough. Here the Thomist presses twice, so the answer must be argued, not assumed.

The first press is that the criterion is rigged: if depth just means accumulated, traversed mapping, then infusion lacks it by definition, and the verdict that the infused will is too shallow is true by stipulation rather than by argument. But the depth at issue isn’t traversal as such. It is whether the will grasps what is at *stake* in the choice, and grasping a stake like death isn’t the same as assenting to the proposition that death will follow. Infusion can install the proposition (*disobedience brings death*) as held content. What it can’t do, merely by installing a proposition, is supply the field that gives that proposition its force: the networked weight of loss, finality, the irreversible. To understand death as a stake is to have it bound into a map of consequence, not merely entered as a true sentence, and that binding is what a field is. The requirement is therefore not stipulated against infusion but follows from what understanding-as-stake consists in: the content can be conferred whole, but the modal grasp that makes it understood as a stake is constituted by the field, not by the act of assertion, and is thus not the kind of thing the infusing of a proposition can deliver.

The second press is that the criterion proves too much: if responsible choice required lived acquaintance with the very act, the first murderer, who has never killed, would be excused, which is absurd. But the criterion isn’t acquaintance with the specific act; it is richness of field. The ordinary first offender is fully responsible because his field is dense: he has seen death, carries a moral history, has mapped deception and irreversible loss across a lifetime, and brings all of it to an act he commits for the first time. Eden’s agent, on the doctrine’s own terms, has essentially no field at all: no observed death, no traversed loss, no accumulated map of consequence of any kind. The first offender fails against a rich field; the Edenic will lacks the field as such.

So the leg no longer stands merely conditional on an unargued thesis. It stands on the fork just stated, and the two defenders are met rather than set aside. Even where a libertarian digs in at that frontier, the first removal still stands: there is no perfect origin for any such will, competent or not, to fall from.

*No population size the doctrine can specify.* The doctrine also assumes, without ever defending it, that exactly two agents ever faced the choice, and that the choice was resolved almost immediately. Nothing in Eden’s own terms secures either assumption. The forbidden tree remains a live option for as long as Eden persists, and Eden’s duration is nowhere fixed short of the transgression. If the first pair could have children before eating, the number of wills facing the identical undeveloped choice grows for as long as the state holds, and grows faster than ordinary history does, since the doctrine’s own premises remove every ordinary check on population: no war, no famine, no death. This forces a further fork, independent of the two preceding removals.

If procreation before the transgression is possible, the doctrine needs a rule for how one descendant’s act, out of an arbitrarily large and branching population, converts the condition of everyone else, and only two rules are available. Restrict the fallen condition to the transgressor’s own line, and a large unfallen population produces a permanently forked humanity, some branches fallen and others not, in perpetuity. That isn’t the universal corruption the doctrine requires, and nothing in the tradition anticipates or wants it. Extend the fallen condition to the whole population regardless of descent, and the mechanism is no longer inheritance in any sense recognizable from its every other application: the moral and metaphysical status of every already-living person, however many generations removed and however blamelessly they have lived, is made to hinge on an act performed by one member of a large population they may never have met and to whom they stand in no closer relation than to any other branch of the same ancestry. This is the transfer burden the sequence tests explicitly at §12.1.6, but here it arises for the fallen condition before any verdict about culpability is assumed: the account must explain how one person’s act changes the standing of already-distinct persons. The larger and longer-lived the unfallen population, the more visibly arbitrary this becomes: a single descendant’s choice, on one ordinary day among centuries of ordinary days, retroactively fixes the condition of a planet.

If procreation before the transgression isn’t possible, the population problem is avoided only by producing a different one. “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen 1:28) is given to the first pair as blessing and command in the same continuous narrative, prior to the forbidden-tree episode. If procreation is genuinely unavailable until the transgression occurs, the first command is satisfiable only by first breaking the second: God’s opening instruction to humanity is fulfillable exclusively through humanity’s first sin.

Either branch of that fork is a real cost, and nothing in the setup determines which branch obtains. Restricting the account to exactly two people who fail almost immediately, the reading every version of the doctrine in fact relies on, isn’t a default drawn from the premises. It is the single narrowest branch out of every duration and population size compatible with the same starting conditions, and a doctrine that builds providence and foreknowledge into its account of God doesn’t get to treat one specific historical branch as a brute given. Either that branch was the one God selected as best among the alternatives, or it was simply the branch that occurred, unselected and unprivileged, and the two options are the same fork already used above, now run on the doctrine’s account of history rather than its account of nature. If selected as best, the selection is strange to credit: every longer-lived, more populous unfallen alternative would have realized strictly more of the state the doctrine treats as the uncomplicated good, an existence without suffering or death, before any transgression whatsoever, making the branch that in fact occurred one of the worst-performing branches available by the doctrine’s own measure of value, not the best. If merely the branch that occurred, the no-privileged-origin problem returns in a new register, aimed now at a branch of history rather than an instant of time: nothing in Eden’s terms explains why this branch, out of every population size and duration equally compatible with the same premises, is the one that became actual history rather than any of the others.

Nothing in a free-willed obedience test requires that it be run once, on a shared ancestral pair, with the verdict transmitted to everyone born after. The same test could instead have been individualized: one trial per person, with each person’s accountability confined to that person’s act. That design would avoid inherited guilt and any collective curse whose sole basis is an ancestor’s transgression. It would therefore sharpen the comparative question: why select a shared transmissible condition rather than individualized accountability if both preserve a genuine creaturely test?

The alternative doesn’t dissolve everything that follows. Individuals might still transgress; interpersonal sin, social disorder, governance, and law could still arise; and a doctrine of rescue or reconciliation might still be proposed for those who fail. Nor does individualized testing by itself show that a Flood, covenantal law, or atonement could have no role. What it removes is the need to make those institutions answer for liability transmitted from one ancestral act. The internal burden is correspondingly narrower: the tradition must explain what good required the shared, hereditary design and why that good couldn’t be secured while each will answered for itself, and show that the imposed cost is proportionate to it. The free-will-testing good alone can’t carry that additional load.

The private design also exposes what “passing” the test could ever have meant, on either version. Where the forbidden option remains a standing, permanently live possibility, true of Eden on any reading where the first pair’s nature is unchanged and the tree is never removed, “not yet having eaten” isn’t by itself the achievement the doctrine needs. Under an exhaustive-exploration rule, failure follows from the rule. Under a recurrent positive risk bounded away from zero, failure becomes almost sure across unbounded exposure. If neither model applies, because a will can settle into permanent refusal, then the settled refusal must be recognizable as success; otherwise the test has a failure condition but no completion condition. The claim isn’t that every possible free will must eventually transgress. It is that the Edenic test as specified either builds eventual failure into its process or withholds the point at which obedience becomes a completed result. Whether the trial is shared by two people or run privately for each person, no one can be certified as having passed until the doctrine supplies that missing success condition; without it, the most anyone achieves isn’t yet having failed.

*A fall that had to happen has no author but the design.* Grant what the soul-making reading needs: that the fall was no contingent lapse but a required passage, the first necessary step of a program God meant to run. The doctrine’s central transfer then fails on its own terms. A transgression that *had* to occur doesn’t lodge the origin of evil in creaturely will; it lodges it in the design that required the transgression and built the agents fit to perform it. On that reading the first pair aren’t the free authors of the fall but its trigger: the mechanism by which a predetermined outcome was discharged. The story was meant to absolve the designer by interposing a free creaturely choice between him and the ruin; a *necessary* choice interposes nothing. Either the fall was avoidable, and the appeal to its necessity is idle, or it was unavoidable, and the will it was built to indict was only running the design.

**[Dissolution]**

**No Author but the Design** · *Dissolution*

The fall narrative exists to absolve the designer by interposing a free creaturely choice between him and the ruin. A *necessary* choice interposes nothing. Either the fall was avoidable, in which case the appeal to its necessity is idle and the soul-making reading forfeits the passage it needed; or it was unavoidable, in which case the will the story was built to indict was only running the design, and the origin of evil lodges in whatever required the transgression and built the agents fit to perform it. The doctrine cannot have the fall be both freely authored and structurally required, and it needs both.

**Dissolves:** the free-creaturely-choice interposition

*What kind of event, and by what mechanism.* The bind generalizes past the soul-making reading, but it doesn’t reduce every act-to-nature account to two mechanisms. Grant, for argument, a first pair in an uncorrupted state and a transgression after which a fallen condition obtains. Three causal families are immediately available. God may directly transform nature in response to the act. The created order may contain a standing disposition or trigger whose manifestation follows the act. Or creaturely secondary causation may produce a new emergent condition under the powers and laws already given to creatures. The third route genuinely locates efficient causation in the creature and can’t be collapsed into direct divine transformation merely because God created the causal field.

Each route bears a different burden. Direct transformation attributes the new condition to divine action. A pre-installed trigger attributes the relevant disposition to the original design. Secondary or emergent causation must explain how one localized act generates the pervasive biological, moral, and environmental condition the doctrine calls the Fall, which powers mediate that propagation, and why later subjects inherit its effects. The designer’s responsibility for creating those powers isn’t identical to the creature’s responsibility for exercising them. The doctrinal question is therefore not settled by a two-horn authorship claim; it is to specify the act-to-nature mechanism and allocate responsibility across source, law, creaturely act, and inherited effect.

**[Diagnostic]**

**Transformation, Trigger, or Secondary Cause** · *Diagnostic*

Grant a first pair in an uncorrupted state and a transgression after which a fallen condition obtains. A direct divine transformation, a pre-installed disposition or trigger, and a creaturely secondary or emergent cause are distinct mechanism-families. The first locates the change in divine response; the second in the original design; the third in created powers exercised by the creature. The third is a genuine exit from the original two-horn argument. It still owes the propagation bridge from one act to a pervasive inherited condition and an allocation of responsibility among designer, causal law, acting creature, and later bearer.

**Still open:** the act-to-nature mechanism, its propagation range, and the allocation of causal and moral responsibility

One reply locates the transition in withdrawal: God endows the first pair with a gift beyond bare nature, and the transgression’s effect is that God withdraws it, letting nature return to its baseline. This is a determinate version of the mechanism question rather than a refutation of every alternative. If the baseline nature isn’t corrupted, disordered, or liable to death, bare resumption doesn’t yet supply the fallen condition, so the account must identify what further change does. If the baseline already carries the mortality or disorder later called fallen, then the transgression explains the loss of the gift rather than the origin of those baseline liabilities. A mixed account may distinguish natural mortality from moral disorder and assign them differently. The withdrawal proposal therefore clarifies what the act removes; it must still state which later features are privations of the gift, which are positive consequences mediated by created causes, and which belonged to the baseline from the start.

Animal nature makes the mechanism question sharper. If predation is treated as a post-Fall acquisition, the account must explain what changes in animals that aren’t morally responsible agents. Direct divine alteration and a pre-installed disposition remain available; secondary ecological consequences are available as well, if human action can alter habitats, resource relations, or other conditions from which predation emerges. The last route can’t explain pre-human predation and the fossil record without further historical premises. Because animals don’t author a moral transgression on the doctrine’s own terms, any account must distinguish the cause of their changed condition from responsibility for it. The point isn’t that two mechanisms exhaust the options, but that the animal case makes the propagation and responsibility bridges impossible to leave implicit.

There is a second form of the same bind, internal to the doctrine of the curse. A literal set can hold three things at once: that the original creation was “very good” and complete as God intended it (Gen 1:31); that suffering and death entered only as the *curse* consequent on the transgression; and, where the fall is read as the soul-making program’s required first step, that suffering is *necessary* for the central good creation was meant to yield. With *complete* read as already finished, the three can’t stand together. If the “very good” creation was complete and yet suffering-free, then the good for which suffering is said to be necessary was either already secured without it, so the necessity claim is false, or absent from the creation God called complete, so that creation wasn’t complete as intended after all. The Irenaean reading takes a genuine exit: creation was good as a beginning, not as a finished state. That keeps the three consistent only by placing the developmental route before the Fall, and then either the route was originally harmless, so suffering isn’t necessary to it, or the Fall introduced the suffering the route now runs on, so a contingent violation has been made the necessary means for every later life. The remaining way to keep suffering *necessary* is to deny that it was the curse: to grant that it was built in from the first, intended, and no penalty the creature incurred. That concession unmakes the fall’s whole role, which was to lodge the origin of suffering in creaturely will rather than divine design. A suffering always required can’t also be the wage of a sin; the curse can’t be both the design’s penalty and its precondition.

A literal fall doctrine bears several burdens: reconciling a perfect historical origin with current empirical and cosmological accounts, explaining how an originally innocent pair could bear the competence required for their decisive act, and specifying how a localized transgression produces a pervasive natural and inherited condition. The argument here is that its temporal and agency accounts make the doctrine difficult to sustain, but those accounts are themselves contestable. The internal track remains: the population fork, the be-fruitful-and-multiply tension, the individualized-trial comparator, the act-to-nature mechanism burden, and the very-good-versus-necessary-suffering bind press the doctrine on its own terms. None establishes that every symbolic, non-literal, secondary-causal, or revisionary reading has been eliminated.

What remains is the event the doctrine asks later claims to inherit.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Fall-Event Fork** · *Disjunction*

What event does the Fall describe, and what would it transmit?

- **If the Fall was a literal first transgression,** then there is an originating act. That reading still needs three things: agents competent to weigh the choice, a choice they could have avoided, and a mechanism carrying that act to later conditions. *Feeds into* The Inheritance Problem (§12.1.5).
- **If it was a federal or corporate event,** then a community may be bound. But representation has to be explained, and so does the difference between shared consequence and shared culpability. *Feeds into* Guilt Does Not Travel (§12.1.6).
- **If it was a developmental or secondary-causal transition,** then the rupture may be placed within evolutionary and social history. But a pristine first pair is surrendered and the transition must be identified.
- **If it was a nonliteral or existential condition,** then a universal human condition may be described without a datable event. But inherited liability cannot later be recovered from one ancestral act. *Feeds into* The Age-Old Problem (§12.1.2).
- **If it was a necessary passage or soul-making trigger,** then its place in the intended history may be explained. But authorship returns to the design that required it. *Feeds into* The Soul-Making Dilemma (§12.5.3).

**Applies to:** any account on which an original good order is ruptured, lost, or represented by a standing human condition

### 12.1.5 Original Sin

Original sin is the Fall’s proposed inheritance, but traditions disagree about what is inherited. The Augustinian-Reformed branch includes culpability: every human arrives already guilty in virtue of Adam’s act. Federal accounts may instead emphasize an imputed juridical liability. Eastern ancestral-sin accounts retain corruption, mortality, or proneness without Adamic guilt. A further revision treats the condition as universal but not historically transmitted from one pair. The difference decides what the next doctrines are entitled to assume.

Inherited guilt is, among the Abrahamic traditions, distinctively Western Christian. Judaism and Islam reject that branch rather than merely relocating it, so the culpability analysis that follows tracks a debate internal to Christianity—most sharply between the Augustinian-Reformed line and the Eastern church’s ancestral-sin alternative—not a live three-way dispute across the wider Abrahamic family.

On the Augustinian-Reformed account (Augustine, *De Civitate Dei* XIII.14; Aquinas, *ST* I-II.81) (Edwards 1758), every human is, from conception, both corrupted in nature and *culpable*: guilty before any act of their own, in virtue of Adam’s transgression. The remedy the tradition builds (regeneration, baptism, grace) is addressed to a liability already in force before the infant has done anything at all.

On the account of §11.9.2, *just*, *guilty*, and *culpable* are manner-of-acting predicates: culpability tracks the agent’s action; A is culpable for X just in case A performed X under the conditions of knowledge and freedom that license the attribution. It attaches to the substantive agent whose act it marks. The doctrine relocates it past the action-condition: A is culpable for B’s act in virtue of A’s biological, metaphysical, or representational relation to B. That relocation is exactly the move the predicate marks as injustice in every other application.

For branches that retain culpability or imputed guilt, three accounts try to license the relocation; each meets the same structural point. Corruption-only and nonhistorical-condition branches bypass this particular test.

Federal headship: Adam is our appointed representative (Edwards 1758; Murray 1959), so his act counts as ours. Representation can impose consequences without each represented person consenting or retaining an exit: children, citizens, and corporate members can be bound by authorized decisions made on their behalf. What it can’t do merely by being representation is transfer the representative’s culpability. That predicate remains indexed to who performed the act under the relevant knowledge and freedom conditions. A representative’s treaty may bind a population; the representative’s private assault doesn’t make every represented person guilty of assault. To cross that boundary, federal headship must show not only that Adam’s act affected his descendants but that they themselves satisfy the action-condition for his transgression. Biological descent and appointment supply consequences and relations, not performance. Without that further identity-of-act argument, Adamic headship can transmit a condition or liability imposed by the scheme, but calling the descendants *culpable* for Adam’s act is conscription into a verdict, not representation of an act they performed.

Seminal realism: we were metaphysically present in Adam and so really performed the act. The account needs both that potential persons share an actual person’s acts (which generalizes ruinously, making every descendant complicit in every ancestor’s act) and that such presence licenses culpability, which simply redefines culpability away from the action-condition it tracks.

Inherited corruption: we inherit a *condition* (mortality, concupiscence) but not *guilt*; culpability arises only from our own later acts under that condition. This is the position the Eastern church marks off as *ancestral sin* (*propatorikon hamartēma*) (Romanides 2002), a corrupted inheritance from Adam, but not his guilt, declining the Augustinian identification at exactly the point now in dispute. Contemporary analytic theists who affirm a Fall take the same line: Swinburne holds that what is inherited is a proneness to wrongdoing, not Adam’s guilt (*Responsibility and Atonement*)(Swinburne 1989), and Plantinga distinguishes the inherited corrupt condition from any imputed culpability (*Warranted Christian Belief*)(Plantinga 2000). It is a defensible version, and it concedes the doctrine’s central claim: it abandons inherited *guilt*, and still owes an account of why the condition itself is just, imposed on bearers who didn’t author it. That debt is real but no longer this doctrine’s to carry: once guilt is dropped, what is inherited is a condition rather than a verdict, and the question of why such a condition is imposed on the innocent is the general problem of evil, pressed where this chapter presses it, not a surviving form of original sin. The debt doesn’t go unpaid: a duty-bearer with unlimited capacity and no scarcity constraint owes a participation foundation by capacity alone, whether or not it authored the specific harm withheld from that foundation, and owes it unconditionally rather than as something earned or inherited into (§12.4.1, *A Duty-Bearer Need Not Have Designed the Harm*; §12.5.3, *No Scarcity Excuse for an Omnipotent Duty-Bearer*). A condition imposed at birth, prior to any performance, is the participation-axis trapdoor those two results independently preclude—each argued at its own station further along the sequence, and neither presupposed here.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Inheritance Problem** · *Disjunction*

What drops from the Fall?

- **If descendants inherit culpability, imputed guilt, or juridical liability,** then blame is detached from what an agent did and reattached to whom they descend from—and desert that survives that detachment is no longer desert. *Feeds into* Guilt Does Not Travel (§12.1.6).
- **If they inherit corruption, mortality, disorder, or proneness without guilt,** then the transfer test at Guilt Does Not Travel (§12.1.6) doesn’t apply. The justice and authorship of the imposed condition enter the problem-of-evil sequence instead.
- **If what they bear is a universal condition not transmitted from one act,** then ancestral inheritance is surrendered, and Adamic liability cannot later be recovered.

Consequence, condition, culpability, and verdict must remain distinct throughout.

**Applies to:** any account on which the Fall leaves descendants with guilt, liability, corruption, mortality, disorder, or alienation

The switchboard therefore sends different sets forward. Culpability, imputation, and juridical liability enter §12.1.6. Corruption-only accounts bypass its guilt conclusion while retaining the question of why descendants bear the condition. A nonhistorical universal condition bypasses ancestral transfer altogether. None may later borrow a verdict from a branch it left here.

### 12.1.6 Inherited Guilt

Inherited guilt is load-bearing only within sets that retain it. On those branches, Adam’s guilt must reach descendants; on penal-substitution branches of atonement, human guilt must later reach a substitute. Both rely on moral transfer. The book’s account of justice (§11.9.2) challenges that transfer on agent-responsibility grounds; this is a substantive moral theorem within the book’s moral account, not a result settled by modal structure alone. The present section establishes it once so later penal branches may use it without making Original Sin depend backward on a later station.

Across its uses the tradition treats guilt as transferable: reckoned from Adam to his posterity, and from the guilty to a willing substitute, with righteousness reckoned back the other way on the federal-Reformed account (Murray 1959; Crisp 2020). Guilt and righteousness are entries in a moral ledger that can be posted to accounts other than the one that incurred them.

On §11.9.2, guilt is a property of the agent whose act it tracks, and it attaches to that agent. That needs no particular theory of what makes a person the same person over time. It needs only that agents are distinguishable one from another, which every doctrine of individual judgment already assumes and which no branch of the tradition disputes: what individuates the bearer is the continuity of that life, and deserving stays with the one whose act incurred it. Transfer across the boundaries between distinct bearers is precisely what the predicate marks as injustice everywhere it is ordinarily applied.

The intuition isn’t local to this framework: Kant fixed it as a principle of practical reason; moral guilt is the most personal of liabilities, and can be made over to another neither by inheritance nor by substitution (Kant 1793). Nor is it local to a philosophical framework read into the traditions from outside: two other Abrahamic scriptures state the identical principle in their own canonical voice, independently of any argument this book makes. The Qur’an holds that no soul bears the burden of another and that each person answers only for what they themselves have done (Qur’an 17:15). The Hebrew Bible holds it in as many words: “the person who sins is the one who shall die… the righteousness of the righteous shall be his own, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be his own” (Ezek 18:20).

The same corpus already runs the transfer in narrative. The Lord strikes David’s infant son dead for David’s sin (2 Sam 12:14–18), and seventy thousand Israelites die by plague for a census David ordered, a cost David himself names as misplaced: “I alone have sinned… but these sheep, what have they done?” (2 Sam 24:17). The tenth plague is the same assignment at a further remove. The Lord strikes “all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the prisoner who was in the dungeon” (Exod 12:29; cf. 11:5). Pharaoh’s refusal is the named offense; the mill-slave’s child and the prisoner’s aren’t parties to it. Hardening—the will that produced the refusal—is a different pressure, and is taken up at §12.5.2. What this section needs is only where the cost lands: a child who originated none of the act bears the penalty for it. The Decalogue states the transfer as standing policy: “punishing children for the iniquity of parents, to the third and the fourth generation of those who reject me” (Exod 20:5). Ezek 18:20 isn’t a foreign principle imported against the tradition. It is the tradition’s own refusal of a practice the tradition’s own law already announces and its stories already perform. The doctrine under examination here isn’t, on this point, a working-out of what Abrahamic theism as such requires; it is a departure two of its three traditions already refused to make in their own scripture. The question is therefore not whether the transfer is licensed by this or that mechanism, but whether *guilt* can survive being made transferable at all.

One qualification keeps the principle from proving too much. What is non-transferable is *culpability* (guilt as blameworthiness, what would license punishing its bearer) not every answerability persons bear for what they did not severally choose. Williams’s moral luck is granted rather than resisted: the agent whose guilt is in question is itself shaped by constitution and circumstance it did not author, so the boundaries of the self are less pristine than a pure agent-tracking picture implies (Williams 1981). But that bears on how one comes to be the agent one is; it doesn’t make deserving portable across agents, and so doesn’t reopen the inheritance. Shared condition, relational or remedial liability, answerability for what one is caught up in: these the account leaves standing; what it refuses is the transfer of blame away from the agent whose act incurred it.

Five moves (the inventory is in §11.9.2) try to license the transfer; each preserves the ledger by emptying guilt of the agent-tracking that made it guilt.

Imputation: guilt is *reckoned* to another. But reckoning is just only when it tracks the substantive relation between agent and act; reckoning that doesn’t track is the paradigm of a miscarriage, not its remedy.

Participation: union makes the guilt genuinely the other’s—not presence in an ancestor, as the seminal-realist move in the original-sin section has it, but union with a substitute. The fork: either union really transfers the moral property (in which case the substitute becomes genuinely guilty, and the spotless-victim claim fails) or it is metaphor, and imputation has returned under another name.

Consent: the substitute’s willingness licenses the swap (Anselm, *Cur Deus Homo* II.11). But consent manufactures permission, not deserving. A judge who lets a willing volunteer stand in for the convicted has substituted a victim, not done justice.

Satisfaction: guilt is a quantitative debt any payment can discharge. This silently converts *punishment of the guilty* into *payment on behalf of the guilty*: two different moral structures treated as one.

Christus Victor: the cross defeats hostile powers rather than satisfying justice (Aulén 1931). Here the justice-language drops out altogether: the event is rescue, and the transfer it was invoked to license is no longer in view.

**[Theorem]**

**Guilt Does Not Travel** · *Theorem*

Culpability is blameworthiness indexed to the bearer whose act it evaluates. Consequence, inherited condition, remedial responsibility, corporate answerability, and harm may cross relations between persons; culpability does not cross merely because one of those does. Imputation calls the verdict transferred without supplying the agent’s performance; participation either makes the substitute genuinely culpable and abandons innocence or leaves the transfer figurative; consent permits bearing a cost but does not create deserving; satisfaction converts punishment of the guilty into payment by another. Two Abrahamic scriptures state the same agent-indexing principle in their own canonical voice: no soul bears the burden of another (Qur’an 17:15), and the person who sins is the one who shall die (Ezek 18:20). Any account that treats guilt as portable therefore owes an additional identity-of-act relation strong enough to make the recipient the acting bearer, not merely a mechanism for moving consequences.

**Depends on:** Five Relocations, One Missing Act (§11.9.2)

The carried result is exact. Corruption, mortality, shared consequence, relational responsibility, and remedial obligation remain available; transferred culpability doesn’t. Original-sin branches that retained guilt lose that component unless they supply the required identity of act. Penal and satisfaction accounts at §12.1.7 inherit the theorem because they require a substitute to bear what the acting bearer incurred. Rescue, restoration, moral-influence, theosis, and direct-forgiveness accounts don’t inherit that transfer premise merely by being theories of atonement.

### 12.1.7 Atonement

The atonement is supposed to resolve what came before it, but what came before need not be guilt. The set arriving from Original Sin may contain culpability, juridical liability, corruption, mortality, captivity, alienation, or no ancestral inheritance at all. A theory of atonement must therefore name both the defect and the mechanism said to repair it. The two familiar structural objections in this section target penal substitution and its imputation-dependent relatives; the remaining models face a distinct necessity question rather than being collapsed into the penal case.

On the penal substitution model, sin incurs a penalty before divine justice, one that humans can’t pay. Christ, the sinless substitute, bears that penalty in their place. Justice is satisfied, and mercy is extended to the guilty, without justice being set aside. This is the Reformation account associated with Calvin. Its ancestor is the Anselmian satisfaction model, from *Cur Deus Homo*, written around 1098. Crisp’s analytic survey treats penal substitution and satisfaction as related but distinguishable accounts, alongside the other mechanisms separated below (Crisp 2020). The cross, on the penal account, is the point where divine justice and divine mercy meet.

It is this model, penal substitution and the satisfaction account behind it, that this section puts on trial, and only this model. The non-penal accounts are a separate family, and they aren’t on trial here. The Christus Victor tradition, on which the cross is a victory over captivity and death rather than a payment rendered, is one of them (Aulén 1931); so are Stump’s restoration and second-personal-union model (Stump 2018), the Eastern *theosis* tradition, and Swinburne’s repentance–reparation–penance account (Swinburne 1989). All of them locate the cross’s work somewhere other than the punishment of transferred guilt. (Theosis (Greek, “divinization” or “deification”) is the Eastern Orthodox doctrine that salvation consists in the believer becoming an actual participant in the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4) through union with Christ, rather than being acquitted of a legal penalty. On this model, the atonement’s work is restoring and deepening that union, not settling a debt—which is why, as the text notes, it isn’t touched by the two structural breaks aimed at penal substitution.) Payment, victory, transformation, forgiveness: the fork below runs on those four mechanisms, dividing payment into penal substitution and satisfaction because they incur different burdens. Neither of the two structural problems developed later applies to the non-penal mechanisms. The book’s own account of mercy is itself non-penal, and it stands with that family in refusing the transaction. What divides it from them isn’t the penal question, but a further one: whether a cross is necessary at all. That question is flagged at the close.

Two results from the account of righteousness bear directly here, and they hold where that account is granted (§11.9.2). Guilt attaches to the individual bearer whose act it tracks. It doesn’t transfer across separate bearers; the general result is laid out in §12.1.6. And mercy, on §11.9.2, is a gift beyond what is deserved, the remission of what is owed. It isn’t the redirection of what is owed to a third party.

The mechanism needs a transfer that doesn’t exist. Penal substitution requires the guilt of the many to become, in some real sense, the substitute’s, so that punishing the substitute discharges it. But guilt doesn’t move off the individual bearer whose act it tracks. Every device for making it move, reckoning, union, consent, or debt, either fails to transfer guilt at all, or transfers it only by stripping away the very thing that made it guilt in the first place: its connection to the agent who acted. There is no guilt of the right kind for the cross to carry.

The transaction destroys the very mercy it was meant to express. The model’s distinctive claim is that the cross lets mercy operate without justice being waived. But mercy, as already established, is the unearned remission of a debt. Once the debt isn’t remitted, but redirected, collected in full from a substitute, the structure of a gift beyond what is deserved has been replaced by the structure of transactional substitution. What the model preserves under the name mercy is no longer mercy. It is a rearrangement of who pays. The doctrine can’t have both a justice fully satisfied, every debt collected, and a mercy that is genuine, the debt forgiven. Satisfying the one this way removes the other.

**[Proposition]**

**A Redirected Debt Is Not a Remitted One** · *Proposition*

Penal substitution’s distinctive claim is that the cross lets mercy operate without justice being waived. Mercy, on the account the tradition itself uses, is a gift beyond what is deserved—the remission of what is owed. A debt that isn’t remitted but redirected, and then collected in full from a substitute, hasn’t been forgiven; the structure of a gift has been replaced by the structure of transactional substitution, and what the model preserves under the name of mercy is a rearrangement of who pays. The doctrine cannot hold both halves of its own claim at once: a justice fully satisfied with every debt collected, and a mercy that is genuine with the debt forgiven. Satisfying either this way removes the other.

*Scope.* This is the second of the two points and is independent of the first. It grants the transfer mechanism outright—whether guilt can move to a substitute at all is argued separately—and shows that even a transfer that worked wouldn’t deliver mercy in the sense the doctrine needs. Older moral objections to the cross aren’t being restated here; the pressure is on the model’s own definitions of justice and mercy.

There is a further problem for sets that combine the transaction with selective application, typically gated on belief. Even granting a coherent mechanism, if justice applies equally to every bearer of guilt, extending remission to some while withholding it from others requires a morally relevant difference between them. The mere fact that one satisfies an access condition doesn’t yet supply that difference. Universalist, election, inclusivist, sacramental, and direct-forgiveness accounts distribute the benefit differently and must be assessed under their own rule at §12.1.8; the objection here reaches only a set that calls the underlying liability universal while treating selective remission as self-justifying.

Forgiveness was never a transaction. The tradition’s own cases work against the model’s necessity. Forgiveness is at bottom an attitude: to remit a debt is to change how the wronged party stands toward the wrong. Changing an attitude takes no sacrifice to license it. Ordinary human beings do this unaided. A wronged party can simply decide to forgive, and often does, with no payment extracted from anyone. If forgiveness needs no transaction at the human scale, the tradition owes an account of why it would need one at the divine scale. The obstacles that might excuse a limited being from forgiving outright, cost, standing, capacity, are precisely the ones an omnipotent, perfectly loving God doesn’t face. The argument runs from the lesser case to the greater, not from any special evidence about God. The objection isn’t new: it is Socinus’s classical case against satisfaction (*De Jesu Christo Servatore*, 1578), that a God able to forgive outright needs no payment first. Defenders since have argued the two cases aren’t parity cases (see Lucas’s reply, discussed in the *Journal of Analytic Theology*, 2015). The sacrificial system itself isn’t a constraint God found waiting. It is a requirement he installed. Who made animals necessary for sin is the same party the cross is then credited with satisfying.

Scripture forgives without payment. Confronted by Nathan, David is told the Lord has put away his sin on confession alone, with no blood required (2 Sam 12:13). The Gospels repeat the same pattern from Christ’s own mouth, years before the cross is in view. He tells the paralytic lowered through the roof, “your sins are forgiven” (Mark 2:5), and tells the woman who anoints his feet, “your sins are forgiven... your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:48–50). Forgiveness is pronounced and completed by the very figure the penal model casts as the payment’s necessary instrument, on no security but the asking.

This isn’t an isolated proof text read against the tradition’s grain. It is the same structural pattern Judaism itself developed into a full atonement theology, one that never adopted a penal-substitution mechanism at all. What discharges sin on the Day of Atonement is confession and turning, teshuvah, not a transferred penalty (Lev 16), and the classical rabbinic view holds that teshuvah atones even without the Temple’s sacrifice (Mishnah Yoma 8:8–9). Islam reaches the same structural point by an independent line: tawba is direct repentance to God, requiring no intermediary and no sacrifice of any kind (Qur’an 4:110; 39:53). If sin can be remitted there by a word, the cross isn’t the mechanism that first makes forgiveness possible. It is a transaction laid over a forgiveness already within reach. What the penal model treats as structurally required, the tradition’s own practice treats as optional, and two related traditions never required it to begin with.

The penal defender will reply that this forgiveness was only provisional, that David’s pardon was credited prospectively to the cross, God having passed over former sins in his forbearance until justice was satisfied (Rom 3:25). Grant the reading; it doesn’t touch the objection. The complaint was never that forgiveness came too early. It was that no device moves guilt off the individual bearer whose act it tracks (§12.1.6). Prospective crediting reschedules the transaction; it doesn’t supply the transfer the transaction needs. At whatever date the cross is said to settle the account, it still requires a guilt that becomes the substitute’s, and there is none of the right kind to become his. The rejoinder secures, at most, that the impossible transaction was booked in advance, not that it can be performed.

The direct cases expose what the cross’s requirement actually is, once the transaction is set aside. Where confession and forgiveness needs only the two agents, the wronged party and the one asking, the penal model conditions its forgiveness on a third thing: that the recipient come to believe a particular event, the death and resurrection, occurred and accomplished what is claimed for it. That isn’t a lighter version of the direct relation but a different one, with a third party, the historical claim and one’s assent to it, standing where the tradition’s own counter-examples needed none. And the currency it is priced in is one the will doesn’t directly control: belief isn’t a switch the will throws (Williams 1973a; Alston 1988), though inquiry and attention remain within reach (§12.3.6). A forgiveness made available only to those who come to believe a specific claim about the past is gated on a state no asker can produce merely by asking for it. This relocates the problem the direct cases solve rather than escaping it, from a transaction sin supplies no material for, to a belief the will has no direct lever to install.

The requirement is gratuitous even granting the belief could be produced. Nothing about the stated end, right conduct toward others, calls for a historical claim as its content. A free-standing maxim, available to reason or conscience without reference to any particular time, place, or transmission chain, would secure that same end without incurring the costs the historical route carries: uneven access, the will’s non-control of belief, the transmission problem of §12.3.4–§12.3.5. Kant drew the line precisely here, distinguishing historical faith, belief tied to a particular revelation and narrative, from pure rational faith, the moral law legislating itself, and held that morality needs no religion at all, being “by virtue of pure practical reason... self-sufficient” (*Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone*)(Kant 1793). The diagnosis doesn’t require Kant’s larger apparatus. If the target is conduct, pegging access to it on a contingent historical claim adds a condition the target itself never asked for.

The escapes depart the penal model, which is just what they should be seen to do. The moves that relieve the pressure relieve it by dropping the penal logic. Recast the cross as the payment of a debt and it is no longer the punishment of the guilty but a payment on behalf of the guilty, a different structure wearing the same word. Recast it as the defeat of hostile powers (Aulén 1931) and the justice-language is gone entirely.
