Each such move purchases coherence not by rescuing penal substitution but by leaving it for the non-penal family already set aside, untouched by the two preceding problems, since it never needed the transfer they deny. That family isn’t refuted here; it simply isn’t the penal doctrine.

Penal substitution needs a guilt that transfers, which there isn’t, and a mercy that survives being turned into a transaction, which it doesn’t. What just and merciful actually name, on the book’s account, aren’t two competing things a single bearer must reconcile at the cross, but one structural feature seen from two sides: the right-ordering of subjects who keep one another in being, justice, the constitution side, and the same order restored where harm has displaced it, mercy, the restoration side. Read that way, there is nothing for the cross to transact. Mercy isn’t a debt redirected but an order repaired, and an order isn’t repaired by collecting its breach from the one party who never breached it. What falls, then, is the penal atonement, not the atonement as such, the cross read as the punishment of transferred guilt. The cross read instead as the repair of a broken order is left standing by the two preceding problems, which never touch it. The book’s disagreement with that reading is only the further question of whether a cross is needed at all for a repair that forgiveness, on the tradition’s own cases, asks no sacrifice to perform, a separate matter the two structural problems don’t settle.

**Not even that.** The further question doesn’t stay open long. Whatever the cross is asked to accomplish, forgiving sin, defeating death, or both, the necessity claim needs the same thing forgiveness’s necessity claim needed and didn’t have: some fact about God that rules out a direct route to the same end. Forgiveness needs no sacrifice, on the cases already given. Defeating death needs no sacrifice either, on the tradition’s own commitments about what its God can do. The same figure said to need his own death and resurrection to defeat death for others already defeats it directly, by a word, for Lazarus, no death of anyone required first (John 11:43–44).

A serious reply is that Lazarus’s case is mere resuscitation, not the pattern Paul has in view. Christ’s resurrection is claimed as the first instance of an imperishable kind that others come to share only by being joined to it (1 Cor 15:20–23; the recapitulation reading traced to Irenaeus), so the two events aren’t strictly parallel. Call this the recapitulation reply. It trades one claim, a debt needing a payment, for another, a pattern needing a root, and the second is no better established than the first: an assertion that this particular victory required this particular representative, not a demonstration of it, held here to the same standard as every other claimed constraint on omnipotence in this section. Nothing here says the cross accomplished nothing, or that its effects are unreal on the non-penal reading left standing by the preceding analysis. It says only that the tradition’s own text never shows the instrument was the only one available, sufficient, on its own telling, but nowhere shown necessary, for any job it has been asked to do.

**Which death, and how much of it.** The defeat-of-death claim has a further problem the necessity argument doesn’t reach: it isn’t clear the claimed victory matches the claimed injury. Genesis’s threat reads as bodily, dust returning to dust, exile before the tree that grants life forever (Gen 3:19, 22), and the tradition isn’t even settled on converting it into something else. Defenders of the doctrine have had to concede that the relevant death in Rom 5:12 must be spiritual, since a physical reading can’t explain why death reigns over those who broke no law of their own. The inaugurated-eschatological doctrine doesn’t claim that the resurrection immediately abolishes every bodily death. It claims that Christ’s resurrection is the firstfruits and representative beginning of a harvest still to come (1 Cor 15:20–23), that “the last enemy to be destroyed” is destroyed at the future consummation (15:26), and that spiritual deliverance is participation in that victory. Continued physical death is therefore not a direct contradiction of the doctrine.

**The payment doesn’t match the wage on permanence.** A separate mismatch sits alongside the question of which death, and it survives every answer to that question. The wage is stated in permanent terms: the death sin earns is the one the tradition contrasts with eternal life, a forfeiture that isn’t recovered (Rom 6:23). What the cross supplies is a death that is recovered, on the third day and by the doctrine’s own insistence—the resurrection isn’t incidental to the atonement but constitutive of it, since a Christ who stayed dead saves no one.

So the debt is denominated in a currency the payment doesn’t use. The difference is in what death takes: exactly the person’s continuation, which is why a loss that is restored and a loss that isn’t differ in kind and not merely in duration. The defender can’t close this by making the death spiritual rather than bodily, because the same asymmetry reappears in that register: whatever was surrendered was surrendered temporarily, and the tradition requires that it was. Nor can the transaction be rescued by the sufferer’s dignity, which is a claim about the magnitude of what was borne, not about whether what was borne is the kind of thing the wage names. A debt stated as permanent forfeiture and settled by recoverable loss hasn’t been paid; it has been substituted for.

That account changes the burden rather than removing it. If the diagnosis is physical, the present claim is a first instance and pledge whose decisive completion remains future. The direct-forgiveness argument still asks what makes the cross necessary for an omnipotent God to grant that completion, but present mortality alone doesn’t show that no victory was inaugurated. If the diagnosis is spiritual, the cure may be real for participants without yet being general: it is expressly conditional on belief, “whoever does not believe is condemned already” (John 3:18), which restricts the class over whom the victory is realized and ties access to a condition the will cannot install on demand. The warranted conclusion is therefore not that the cross simply failed to defeat death. Its necessity remains unestablished, while the full defeat-of-death claim depends on independent warrant for the resurrection, the promised eschatological consummation, and the accessibility of participation.

What reaches Salvation is therefore not one generic atonement verdict. Penal and imputation-dependent sets carry the guilt-transfer theorem and the redirected-debt result. Satisfaction sets carry the distinction between repayment and remission. Victor and recapitulation sets carry the necessity, identity, and promised-completion burdens. Restoration, union, moral-influence, and theosis sets carry a specified transformation and its means of participation. Direct-forgiveness sets carry no transactional requirement. Who receives the retained remedy, and on what condition, has still to be settled without substituting one mechanism for another (§12.1.8).

**[Disjunction]**

**The Atonement Diagnosis Problem** · *Disjunction*

What does atonement repair, and how?

- **If the defect is guilt or deserved penalty, repaired by penal substitution,** then culpability must pass from the acting bearer to an innocent substitute, and collecting the penalty must be reconciled with mercy. *Priced by* Guilt Does Not Travel (§12.1.6).
- **If the defect is dishonor or debt, repaired by satisfaction,** then satisfaction must explain why repayment is required rather than remission and whether punishment has really been left behind.
- **If the defect is captivity or death, repaired by victory or recapitulation,** then guilt transfer is unnecessary. But the necessity and efficacy of this particular victory remain owed.
- **If the defect is corruption or estrangement, repaired by transformation, union, or theosis,** then that model must specify how the cross produces the transformation and for whom.
- **If the defect is repaired by direct forgiveness,** then transactional problems recede. But the cross is no longer what first makes remission possible.

A mixed theory inherits every burden belonging to the mechanisms it combines. No branch may borrow the penal model’s satisfaction language after leaving its transfer, or a non-penal model’s immunity while continuing to claim that punishment was paid.

**Applies to:** any account on which Christ’s life, death, or resurrection repairs guilt, debt, captivity, corruption, alienation, mortality, or relation to God

**Depends on:** Guilt Does Not Travel (§12.1.6)

*Scope.* The dependency is active only on penal and imputation-dependent branches.

### 12.1.8 Salvation

What saves? The question looks elementary until the answers are placed beside one another. One branch says faith: believe in Christ, trust him, and the relation is restored. Another says grace, with faith following as gift or evidence rather than cause. Another places obedience, works, baptism, sacrament, perseverance, or repentance inside the saving relation. An inclusivist allows conscience or response to whatever light a person received to stand where explicit confession can’t. A universalist denies that the final relation is divided at all. These aren’t variations in emphasis around one gate. They are different gates, and some of them deny that there is a gate in the same sense.

That difference has to be fixed here because the sections downstream ask questions that apply selectively. Divine hiddenness bears where conscious relation is necessary and God remains unavailable to a willing seeker. Scripture and prophecy bear a heavier load where the saving condition depends on receiving their message. The account of will matters differently where belief is commanded, where grace produces belief, and where belief merely reports an election already made. Divine command theory enters where obedience is constitutive rather than evidential. Final judgment changes shape if loss is eternal, annihilative, remedial, or universally overcome. The closing reductions at §12.6 depend on these differences. An argument aimed at explicit-faith exclusivism can’t be spent against universalism, and an escape through election can’t later blame the unelected for failing to produce the faith the account said only grace could give.

The tradition’s texts supply the plurality rather than resolving it. Six passages set the gate in six different places. “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” puts it at belief (Acts 16:31). “By grace you have been saved through faith” puts grace before belief, and denies that the result is a work (Eph 2:8–9). “The one who endures to the end will be saved” adds perseverance (Matt 24:13). The judgment of the nations turns on what was done for the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and the imprisoned (Matt 25:31–46). Mark’s longer ending joins baptism to belief (Mark 16:16). And Paul allows Gentiles without the law to do what it requires, their conscience bearing witness (Rom 2:14–16). The universalist adds the texts in which God desires everyone to be saved (1 Tim 2:4), refuses pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11), and reconciles all things through Christ (Col 1:19–20), then argues that an omnipotent salvific will doesn’t finally fail of its object (Talbott 1999; Hart 2019). A verse can be made to sit at the center of any one of these accounts. The collection doesn’t tell us, without a theory of their relation, which statement is condition, means, evidence, fruit, ordinary route, or promised end.

So begin one level above the dispute. A salvation account must specify at least seven things. It must say what the defect is: guilt, corruption, alienation, bondage, mortality, disordered desire, or some conjunction. It must say what removes the defect: divine declaration, atoning payment, participation in Christ, healing, liberation, transformation, or restored relation itself. It must name any condition on the creature’s side and say whether that condition is necessary, sufficient, both, or neither. It must say how the condition reaches the person and what happens where the ordinary channel doesn’t. It must fix the scope of the remedy. It must say whether a lost state is final. And where the rule changes within history, it must identify the event that activates the new rule and what governs persons before the event, during its transmission, and after they receive it.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Salvation Specification Test** · *Diagnostic*

A doctrine of salvation isn’t yet specified by saying that salvation comes “by grace,” “through faith,” “in Christ,” or “through the Church.” A self-contained account must name: **(1)** the condition from which a creature is saved; **(2)** the agent and mechanism of repair; **(3)** every creature-side condition and whether it is necessary, sufficient, evidential, instrumental, or the fruit of something prior; **(4)** the channel through which that condition becomes available; **(5)** the scope of those reached; **(6)** whether loss is final; and **(7)** when the rule becomes operative, including what governs those who lived before it and those who die before its message reaches them. A later objection applies only to the branch whose specification contains the premise it tests.

*Scope.* This diagnostic doesn’t decide which salvation account is true. It fixes the set of commitments each account carries forward so that one account cannot answer an objection by borrowing a different account’s gate and then return to its original gate afterward.

*When the gate changes.* A condition introduced by an event in history needs an activation rule. The candidate moments aren’t identical: Christ’s death, the resurrection, Pentecost, the first proclamation, the public promulgation of the gospel, and each person’s actual reception of the message pick out different populations. People continue to die between every pair. If assent that God raised Jesus is necessary from the instant of resurrection, then persons dying before any witness reaches them are placed under a condition whose object was unavailable to them. A grace period postpones that result but only moves the boundary unless it says what ends the period and why someone on one side owes what someone on the other didn’t. If the condition activates only upon adequate reception, there is no single global starting moment; accessibility becomes part of the saving rule, and the account must define adequate reception rather than treating the calendar alone as decisive.

The classical Christian replies divide rather than converge. On a single-covenant or proleptic account, persons before Christ are saved through Christ’s future work under the revelation available to them: Abraham’s faith can be credited as righteousness without his assenting to a resurrection not yet reported (Rom 4; Heb 11). This can preserve the cross as the ontological ground of salvation across time, but it means explicit assent to the resurrection wasn’t the timeless creature-side condition. On descent or waiting-place accounts, the righteous dead don’t yet enter the final blessed state; Christ’s victory opens what had been closed. That supplies a temporal boundary, but it must identify the pre-cross condition for belonging among the waiting righteous and explain why an omnipotent remedy required the delay. On progressive-revelation or access-relative accounts, responsibility tracks what has actually been disclosed. That protects those before the message and those beyond its reach, but makes the operative condition vary with historical and geographical access rather than become universally binding at one instant.

The necessity question follows. If a prior rule already brought persons into the same final relation with God, a later, harder rule requiring assent to a newly reportable event needs an account of what good the replacement achieves. If the earlier rule worked only because Christ’s later act applied retroactively, the act may remain necessary as the account’s ground, but the older beneficiaries demonstrate that explicit knowledge of the act isn’t necessary for receiving its benefit. If no one could reach the final good before the act, the doctrine owes the status of every earlier person and the justice of withholding that good until the selected moment. The cross, resurrection, and proclamation can each be assigned a distinct role; what the account may not do is move the activation point among them whenever a different population comes into view. The mechanism carried from §12.1.7, the event tested at §12.2.4, and the belief condition tested at Faith and Belief (§12.3.7) must share one temporal rule.

Person-relative activation creates a further problem wherever the unexposed retain a real route through conscience, available light, or antecedent grace. Exposure isn’t automatically a benefit on that set. If hearing the claim creates a new liability for rejecting it, then a message delivered obscurely, coercively, inaccurately, or without adequate grounds can worsen the hearer’s position without giving them an epistemically adequate route to belief. The relevant state isn’t a decision to believe or disbelieve at will. It is whether the claim becomes credible within the person’s evidential field, a distinction made explicit later at §12.3.7. A mission that merely presents the proposition may therefore create risk without supplying the conditions needed to satisfy the gate.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Exposure-Risk Problem** · *Disjunction*

At what point does hearing the gospel raise the stakes?

- **If the stricter condition begins at mere exposure,** then an unclear or unconvincing presentation can create eternal liability without creating an adequate route to belief, making proclamation a possible harm.
- **If it begins only at adequate and intelligible exposure,** then that condition must define adequacy and may not blame the hearer where the messenger or evidence fails that standard. *Priced by* The Salvation Specification Test (§12.1.8).
- **If it never begins,** then the earlier route remains available, so explicit assent isn’t necessary for the hearer’s salvation.
- **If there was no safer route,** then the fork is escaped. But this reading inherits the separate burden of unequal access to the sole remedy. *Feeds into* The Uniform Requirement Problem (§12.3.6).

Proclamation may open a route, raise a risk, or leave the prior route untouched. It cannot be credited only as benefit until the activation rule is stated.

**Applies to:** salvation accounts combining a pre-exposure route with increased culpability for rejecting a later proclamation

**Still open:** the activation threshold, the recipient’s retained alternative, and whether proclamation can increase salvific risk

The channel field also inherits the Babel–Mission problem (§12.1.2). A branch that treats linguistic fragmentation as a historical divine judgment must say whether Pentecost or direct revelation universally repairs it, whether ordinary translation carries the message through it, or whether access-relative grace makes explicit receipt unnecessary. The salvation section doesn’t decide among those routes; it prevents a branch from treating linguistic plurality as divinely imposed when explaining Genesis and as a merely human obstacle when accounting for unequal access to salvation.

The same channel field is received downstream by the foreknowledge-and-selection dilemma (§12.3.1). A salvation account must distinguish a decreed outcome, a Molinist selection among feasible histories, circumstances chosen without using simple foreknowledge as a decision procedure, and an open future whose risks are divinely administered. Family, language, evidence, lifespan, and access to proclamation may not be treated as accidental to the salvific field where the providential branch says those circumstances were selected, decreed, or knowingly left at risk.

*Explicit faith and belief.* On the exclusivist branch, conscious belief in or trust toward Christ is ordinarily necessary. “No one comes to the Father except through me” supplies the exclusive object (John 14:6); condemnation for not believing supplies the stakes (John 3:18); and the commission to make disciples supplies the delivery project (Matt 28:19–20). The branch can distinguish bare assent from trust, and the current faith section does exactly that. It still carries three questions. Could a person identify the object of trust from the evidence available to them? Is belief directly chosen, indirectly cultivated, or received? What becomes of a person to whom the identifying message never arrives in a form they can recognize? Those questions belong to §12.3.4, §12.3.5, §12.3.6, and §12.3.7. They don’t bind a branch that denies explicit faith is necessary.

*Faith, obedience, and participation.* Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan, and other synergistic accounts resist the picture of a single belief-act opening a gate once. Grace initiates, but the creature responds; faith lives through love and obedience; baptism or sacramental participation may be an ordinary means; perseverance matters. The response can be constitutive, instrumental, evidential, or the fruit of grace, and those are different claims. If obedience is constitutive, the account owes the content and accessibility of the commands, the capacities required to answer them, and the standard under which failure becomes culpable. If sacramental participation is an ordinary rather than exceptionless means, the exception rule is part of the doctrine, not an embarrassment to be hidden. If the response is only evidence that grace has already done the saving work, failure of evidence can’t later become the cause of loss. This branch feeds the later treatment of divine command, moral capacity, Scripture, institutional transmission, and punishment; it isn’t exhausted by the question whether a proposition was believed.

*Grace and election.* The Reformed branch moves the decisive difference away from an unaided creaturely act. Faith itself may be a gift, regeneration may precede it, and perseverance may be secured by the same grace that begins the relation. Reformed epistemology supplies a corresponding account of belief: properly functioning faculties may produce warranted belief without inference (Plantinga 2000). This branch has real force against the claim that salvation asks a person to manufacture conviction by will. It also changes who bears the explanatory burden. If saving faith occurs because grace supplies it, then the difference between the saved and the lost isn’t explained by one person’s successful production of faith and another’s culpable refusal. The account owes its selection rule, or it accepts the selection as inscrutable; and an inscrutable selection can’t later be redescribed as a transparent judgment on a condition the creature was able but unwilling to meet.

*Inclusivism and conscience.* An inclusivist keeps Christ or grace as the ground of salvation while denying that explicit knowledge of that ground is necessary for every recipient. The person may answer conscience, seek the good available under another description, or receive grace through a channel they don’t identify correctly. This isn’t a small relaxation. It relieves the harshest distribution problem because ignorance of the Christian message is no longer automatically exclusion. It also narrows the work assigned to that message. If explicit confession is unnecessary, Scripture, prophecy, mission, and apologetic argument may still teach, form, or deepen relation, but they aren’t the sole bridge across which salvation can travel. The branch can’t invoke their universal necessity when defending their reach and then invoke inclusivism when their failure to reach is counted.

*Universal restoration.* The universalist keeps salvation’s object and removes the permanent division. Judgment may remain, and so may purification, freedom, repentance, and suffering; what disappears is a final class for whom the remedy never succeeds. Talbott and Hart press the branch from the conjunction of universal salvific desire, divine competence, and the refusal to make creaturely resistance eternally victorious over the good (Talbott 1999; Hart 2019). This route avoids no question about the means, duration, or justice of correction. It does change the later ledger decisively. Eternal-loss arguments no longer apply; the Greatest Loophole can’t run its guarantee against the hazard of irreversible damnation in the same form; and the Greatest Sacrifice can’t measure a permanent forfeiture no creature finally bears. A later section may test universalism, but it may not quietly price it with the permanent loss it denies.

*Conjunctive accounts.* Most lived theologies combine the branches. Grace produces the possibility of faith; faith issues in obedience; sacrament ordinarily mediates grace; perseverance confirms rather than purchases the relation; conscience governs exceptional cases; judgment corrects what earthly life leaves unfinished. A conjunction isn’t a loophole. It is simply a longer specification. Each part must be assigned its work, and the account must say what changes when one part is absent. If grace is sufficient, what does failure of belief add? If faith is necessary, what does invincible ignorance change? If obedience is evidence, why is its absence punished as cause? If sacrament is ordinary but not exceptionless, what licenses the exception? The price of a richer account isn’t incoherence. It is bookkeeping.

The ratchet begins there. Explicit-faith branches proceed into the problems of belief and transmission. Obedience and participation branches proceed into command, capacity, institution, and culpability. Election proceeds into providence, selection, and responsibility. Inclusivism proceeds into conscience and the reduced necessity of explicit revelation. Universalism proceeds into remedial judgment and a closing sequence without permanent loss. A reader may take any route. What the reader may not do is answer on one and arrive downstream carrying another.

## 12.2 Messiah and the Last Things

The second cluster begins on shared ground and branches at the messianic role. The promised role is first weighed against Jesus (§12.2.1). The doctrine of God that the Christian branch brings to that role is examined before the role is claimed (§12.2.2). Only the Christian branch then asserts that God entered the world in that claimant (§12.2.3) and that the same claimant was bodily raised (§12.2.4). Judaism exits those two claims by denying the identification; Islam assigns Jesus a messianic and eschatological role without the Nicene identity or the Christian death-and-resurrection sequence. The branches converge again over the last things: a life that doesn’t end (§12.2.5) and history closed in judgment (§12.2.6).

That structure prevents a tradition-specific doctrine from masquerading as an Abrahamic premise. Denying Incarnation doesn’t evade a test that Judaism or Islam had accepted; it records that the reader never entered that Christian branch. Conversely, a Christian defense can’t borrow the non-incarnational branch for one objection and quietly recover strict incarnation later. Non-Nicene, restorationist, and other modern movements are handled the same way: by the claims they actually retain, not by a label assigned to the movement.

Where a branch reaches a postmortem claim, the shared measure is the identity the doctrine promises to preserve. A continuation, resurrection, reward, or judgment must concern the same person who lived and died rather than a qualitatively similar successor. Chapter 11’s accounts of causality and interaction constrain any divine operation offered to secure that continuity (§11.7.2–§11.7.3). The sections ask whether the exact claim retained on each branch meets those burdens. They don’t assign every tradition the same doctrine to make the same objection land.

### 12.2.1 The Messiah
The messianic role is where the shared Abrahamic road first divides over Jesus. The Hebrew scriptures supply the role: a king descended from David who reigns from a permanent, unbroken throne (2 Sam 7:12–16; Jer 33:14–18), restores Israel’s judges (Isa 1:26) and gathers its scattered exiles (Isa 11:12), ends war by converting its instruments into instruments of agriculture and rules a peace spanning the earth (Isa 2:4; Zech 9:10), establishes a sanctuary and covenant that last forever (Ezek 37:24–28), and reigns where the knowledge of God becomes universal and predation and death themselves cease (Isa 11:6–9; 25:6–8). The mainstream Jewish branch holds that Jesus didn’t fill that role. Christianity identifies him as *ha-Mashiach* and reads the unmet public conditions through a first and second advent. Islam calls Jesus *al-Masīḥ* (Qur’an 3:45) while rejecting the incarnational identification and, on the dominant reading of Qur’an 4:157, the Christian crucifixion-and-resurrection sequence. These aren’t three answers to three unrelated questions. They are three sets of commitments formed around the same disputed role, and each carries a different Jesus into the forks that follow. Whether Jesus filled the role Christianity claims for him is therefore a historical and textual question, not merely a matter of private conviction. (On the Hebrew Bible’s messianic profile as a coherent, largely political and this-worldly role: (Collins 1995).)

The order matters. A reader who takes the Jewish branch doesn’t owe an account of Incarnation or Jesus’s resurrection; those doctrines were never retained. A reader who takes the Christian branch carries the messianic identification into both. A reader who takes the Islamic branch retains Jesus’s messianic title and eschatological role without carrying the Nicene identity claim. Incarnation and the resurrection of Jesus are therefore downstream branch tests, not Abrahamic entrance requirements.

The role bundles criteria with different degrees of candidate and narrator control. A person can arrange an entry into a city on a selected animal; a person can claim a lineage but can’t choose biological ancestry; no adult chooses birthplace, although a later author can place a birth narrative; public peace, gathered exiles, an enduring throne, and the defeat of death require conditions no claimant can stage alone. Evidential weight therefore cannot be assigned by a binary of “action” and “world-state.” Prior specificity, conjunction among independent signs, cost, hostile verification, source proximity, and the likelihood of later narrative accommodation all matter. Candidate control is one likelihood-reducing factor, not evidential nullity.

The passage places the contrast side by side (Zech 9:9–10). Verse 9 describes a humble king entering Jerusalem on a donkey; Matthew portrays Jesus deliberately arranging that entry (Matt 21:1–7). Deliberate enactment doesn’t make the episode worthless—it may express a public claim, and its evidential weight can increase with independent attestation or costly context—but it can’t authenticate the claim merely by matching an act the claimant selected. Verse 10 describes disarmament, peace among nations, and dominion from sea to sea. Those public outcomes didn’t obtain in the first century. The same distinction recurs across the profile, but with important intermediates: lineage and birthplace aren’t candidate-controlled, yet their evidential force depends on the sources reporting them and on whether the texts were being read as predictions before the reports were shaped. Ended war, gathered exiles, a continuing Davidic reign, universal knowledge of God, and the defeat of death have much lower accommodation risk because they are public states. The Christian case may rest on the conjunction, typology, resurrection, inaugurated fulfillment, and future completion; it can’t count the controllable matches at full strength while treating the unmatched public outcomes as though they had already confirmed the role.

The role even anticipates its own occupant’s fallibility in a way later theology has had to explain around rather than meet: the same oracle relied on for the throne’s permanence adds that when this king “commits iniquity, I will punish him with a rod such as mortals use, with blows inflicted by human beings” (2 Sam 7:14)—the description of a corrigible human ruler, not a sinless incarnate deity.

The mismatch also runs in the other direction. Alongside the criteria the role states, criteria Jesus’s followers couldn’t point to being met, the New Testament portrait adds an entire set of criteria the role never states at all: that the Messiah would die and rise, ascend, found a church, and return a second time to finish what the first arrival left undone. Those additions may be defended through typology, fuller sense, or progressive revelation rather than as direct predictions. That defense remains available, but it changes the evidential claim. The identification is then a later theological construal of the role, not an inference from the public completion of the role as originally described.

The tradition’s reply to all of this is the two-advent reading, and it is stronger than a bare deferral. Defenders don’t present the second coming as an amendment bolted on after the criteria went unmet; they locate the two-stage structure in the source texts themselves. Isaiah sets a servant who is despised, stricken, and cut off (52:13–53:12) beside the king who reigns in peace, and the tradition that reads both of a single figure has to distribute them across two arrivals. Zechariah puts them in one oracle a verse apart: a king who comes humble and riding on a donkey (9:9), and then a dominion from sea to sea with the war-horse cut off (9:10). Daniel’s son of man receives an everlasting dominion after being presented before the Ancient of Days (7:13–14), which reads naturally as a sequence rather than a single moment. On the *inaugurated* reading that follows, the kingdom is genuinely begun rather than merely promised—already, and not yet—so the criteria still outstanding are outstanding rather than failed. And the two-figure structure isn’t foreign to the source tradition: rabbinic material contemplates a suffering Messiah son of Joseph alongside the reigning Messiah son of David, so a tradition that splits the role across figures isn’t a Christian invention.

What the reading costs is checkability, and it costs it in the same coin every deferral does. A criterion that can be discharged at an unspecified later arrival can’t be failed at any particular time, so the role stops being the checkable job description the texts state and becomes a description no observation within any lifetime could count against. That is a real price rather than a decisive objection: the defender may accept it and hold that the role is simply not the sort of thing a single generation can adjudicate. What the defender can’t do is claim both—press the specificity of the prophecies as evidence that they were fulfilled, and then relocate the unfulfilled ones beyond the reach of evidence. The specificity was doing evidential work in the first move and is withdrawn from it in the second.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Foretold–Told-For Problem** · *Disjunction*

Were the qualifications foretold, or told for him?

- **If the fulfillment rests on candidate-controlled signs,** then acts such as arranging an entry into Jerusalem have little discriminatory force by themselves.
- **If it rests on public outcomes,** then ended war, gathered exiles, an enduring Davidic reign, universal knowledge of God, and the defeat of death did not obtain in the first century.
- **If the fulfillment is deferred,** then the Christian identification is preserved, but its decisive evidence is moved out of reach. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.
- **If it is typology, fuller sense, or progressive revelation,** then theological continuity may remain. But the identification is no longer a direct inference from the role’s public completion. *Feeds into* The Age-Old Problem (§12.1.2).

The Jewish branch may deny the identification; the Christian branch may retain it through deferred or re-described fulfillment; the Islamic branch may retain the title without the Nicene fulfillment set. Each route fixes what may count as fulfillment and when. *Feeds into* The Fulfillment Timing Problem (§12.3.5).

**Still open:** whether Jesus is denied, identified through deferred or typological fulfillment, or retained as Messiah without Nicene incarnation

This doesn’t show that no one could occupy a role described this way, reduce messianic hope to a checklist, or make every reported fulfillment evidentially inert. It shows that each criterion needs a case-specific likelihood assessment. Candidate-controlled enactments carry less discriminatory force; ancestry and birthplace depend on source reliability and accommodation risk; public outcomes remain deferred or theologically redescribed. The Christian identification may be cumulative, but its weight can’t be obtained by treating those different evidential relations as one kind of fulfillment.

### 12.2.2 The Trinity

The Trinity is the most distinctive metaphysical claim in Christian doctrine, and the one least like anything else the tradition asserts. Nicaea (325) fixed the Son as *homoousios* with the Father, of the same substance rather than a similar one; Constantinople (381) extended the same standing to the Spirit. The Athanasian formula states the result at its sharpest: “the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and yet there are not three Gods, but one God.” The Cappadocians gave the distinction its enduring form: the persons differ not in nature, will, power, or any perfection, but by *relations of origin* alone—the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding. The Latin tradition sharpened this into subsistent relations, on which each person just *is* a relation subsisting in the one simple essence (Aquinas, *ST* I.29–30). Two things are presupposed throughout, and they are the two examined here: that a real distinction can hold among the three, and that it can hold without dividing the one God.

The doctrine opens no new front against the structural account. Nothing in the argument of Chapters 1 through 9 turns on how many persons a divine ground would have; the Necessity of Nature is untouched either way. What the Trinity does is press the classical conception harder than any other doctrine, because it asks the divine essence to sustain a real internal distinction while remaining simple, and the resources that ordinarily make a distinction real have already been withdrawn by the attributes the same tradition affirms. The pressure here is internal: it comes from the tradition’s own commitments, and each branch below is closed by the tradition’s own rejections rather than by anything this book supplies.

*What makes a distinction real.* The difficulty isn’t that three is a strange number. It is that a distinction has to be made of something. Location, temporal trajectory, and material constitution are the ordinary resources by which one thing isn’t another, and classical theism withdraws all three from God deliberately and for good reason. Qualitative difference is withdrawn too: the persons are held to differ in no perfection, no power, no act of will. What remains is the relations of origin, and the weight of the doctrine rests on whether those relations can carry a load that nothing else is permitted to carry. That is the same bar applied to the count of *one* at §11.2.2: to fix a being as exactly one is already to hold the resource by which a second would have differed (Cardinality Presupposes Distinguishability). A doctrine that fixes the persons at exactly three needs that resource three times over.

*The relations-of-origin move, at its strongest.* Take the orthodox answer at full strength before examining it. It isn’t naive. Paternity, filiation and spiration aren’t accidents inhering in a substance, nor parts of it; they are *subsistent* relations, identical with the essence and distinguished from one another only by mutual opposition. On this account the persons aren’t three things that happen to be related, but three relations that are what they are wholly in relation. The move is elegant precisely because it locates the distinction in the only place classical simplicity leaves open. Whether it succeeds turns on one question: whether relative opposition supplies hyperintensional specifying content, or whether it distinguishes the persons only in the manner of describing them. That is the burden stated at §11.2.1 and not resolved there (The Discriminating-Content Burden): where the relata are each identical with one necessary essence, modal co-extension can’t be what makes them distinct, and the distinction must supply content or fail to be one.

*Generation and procession.* One further pressure is the same one the incarnation meets. *Begotten* and *proceeding* are directed terms; each names a *from* and a *to*, an order of derivation. The tradition is explicit that this order is eternal and involves no temporal succession and no change—the Son is begotten, not made, and there was no “when” he wasn’t. That reply is available, and it is the right one to make. What it costs is that the derivation must then be a relation of dependence carrying no transition at all, which is the account pressed at §11.3.3 on the divine attributes generally (Three Invariances, One Word). A dependence relation with no transition must still be asymmetric, or Father and Son aren’t distinguished by it.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Trinitarian Distinction Fork** · *Disjunction*

What makes the three persons three?

- **If it is located in the essence,** so that what is three is three beings rather than three persons of one being, then the distinction is secured and the resource securing it must be named. Location, temporal trajectory, material constitution, and qualitative difference are each withdrawn by the classical conception, and whatever is put in their place makes the divine essence countable. That is *tritheism*, and the tradition rejects it. *Priced by* Cardinality Presupposes Distinguishability (§11.2.2).
- **If it is located in a gradation of divinity,** so that one person is God in a fuller sense than another, then the distinction is real and rests on inequality of nature. That is *subordinationism*, and the tradition rejects it.
- **If it is located in the mode of appearance,** so that the three name ways the one God is presented rather than anything obtaining in God, then the distinction holds in the describing and the persons aren’t three in the sense the formula asserts. That is *modalism*, and the tradition rejects it.
- **If it is located in the relations of origin**—paternity, filiation, spiration, real in God and asymmetric without dividing the essence—then the distinction is where the tradition itself places it, and what it owes is content. Where each relatum is identical with one necessary essence and each is necessary, modal co-extension cannot be what makes them distinct; relative opposition must supply specifying content, and the derivation must be asymmetric while carrying no transition. *Priced by* The Discriminating-Content Burden (§11.2.1) and Three Invariances, One Word (§11.3.3).

The first three are the exits the tradition has already closed against itself. The fourth is the position it holds, and it isn’t closed here: the burden it carries is to supply the content, not to survive a refutation.

**Applies to:** Nicene Christianity and every account that affirms three persons in one God while retaining divine simplicity

**Still open:** subsistent relations with specifying content supplied, social trinitarianism with its count defended, a revised simplicity, or an explicit appeal to mystery

*The appeal to mystery.* A defender may answer that the doctrine is revealed rather than derived, and that its coherence isn’t ours to establish. That answer is available and it isn’t foolish; a tradition may hold something on authority that it can’t articulate. What it can’t then also do is treat the doctrine as explaining anything—as grounding divine love prior to creation, say, or supplying a reason the ground is personal. A claim held as mystery does no explanatory work, and the fork drawn at §10.2.1 applies here too: a predicate must be contrastive or it is empty (No Third Option Between Contrastive and Empty). Mystery is a legitimate resting place, but it is a resting place, and arguments elsewhere in the tradition that lean on the Trinity for content can’t be run from it.

*The reclamation.* The doctrine’s motivating intuition is real, and the difficulties above don’t answer it. What the tradition wants is a ground that isn’t solitary—one in which relation, otherness, and giving are there from the beginning rather than arriving with creation. That identifies something the bare classical conception doesn’t supply: a simple, timeless, relationless absolute has no room for relation at all, which is precisely why the Trinity was needed. If the proposed three-person solution fails, the motivating demand doesn’t fail with it. The instinct that the ground can’t be bare was right; what remains in dispute is whether relative opposition within one simple essence can satisfy that instinct without covertly reintroducing the differentiation it officially refuses.

None of this shows that no trinitarian account can be given. It locates what one owes: a resource by which the three persons are three. That resource can be neither a countable difference, which the tradition forbids, nor a distinction that holds only in the describing. The relations-of-origin account is where the tradition itself locates the distinction, and it remains open with that content supplied. What the doctrine can’t do is hold all three claims while declining to say what makes the distinction real, and then treat the result as available to explain anything further.

### 12.2.3 The Incarnation

The incarnation is the doctrine on which Christianity’s distinctive claim about God turns: that in Jesus of Nazareth the second person of the Trinity took on a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. “And the Word became flesh,” John’s Gospel says, “and lived among us” (John 1:14); the Council of Chalcedon (451) fixed the grammar: one person, in two natures, fully divine and fully human, united without confusion and without division. Stated at its most disciplined the claim runs: a single subject, the Logos, bears two complete natures at once, and the human life of Jesus (born, hungering, weeping, dying) is the life of that one divine subject. The analytic tradition has given the union three main models. The two-minds view (Morris 1986; Swinburne 1994) assigns the incarnate Word a divine consciousness and a distinct human one, the human contained within the divine. Kenotic christology (Crisp 2007) has the Word empty itself of, or restrict its use of, the strictly divine attributes for the span of the earthly life. Compositional christology (Crisp 2007) treats the person as a whole composed of the Word together with a human body and soul. Two things are presupposed throughout, the same two the miracle and the resurrection presuppose: a supernatural agent to do the assuming, and a standpoint outside Nature from which he descends into it.

The incarnation opens no wholly new front; like miracle and resurrection claims, it inherits the Chapter 11 questions about a determinate active God. A wholly structureless divine subject must explain how agency, relation, and becoming retain content, and an extra-natural source must specify what explanatory work it adds. These pressures don’t establish that every incarnation model is definitionally impossible, but they make its metaphysical commitments explicit. It is at the incarnation, as already noted at §11.7.3, that the doctrinal and narrative structures of interaction are least reconcilable, since the human nature interacts and the divine nature, by doctrine, doesn’t. To these is joined the result immutability turns on (§11.3.3): the *becoming* of John 1:14 is a directed transition, a *from* and a *to*, and a being that is timeless, immutable, and pure act has no transition to undergo. That governs what follows before any question of the historical Jesus is reached.

Take Chalcedon at its most literal: one subject, two complete natures, the divine one unchanged. The burdens divide by what the union claims. If *became* names a concrete assumption or entry into a human life, the operation is productive and relational work with determinate terms and a difference made at the contact. If all becoming is located in the human nature, as the classical reply holds (Aquinas, *ST* III.16), the account avoids intrinsic divine change but must explain what makes the one divine person—not merely the created nature—the subject of the birth, hunger, grief, and death. If the divine nature itself undergoes the assumption, strict immutability is revised. An atemporal grounding relation may explain the human nature’s dependence without temporal transmission, but dependence alone doesn’t yet establish the one-person identity Chalcedon asserts. The doctrine therefore owes an identity and predication account at exactly the point where it refuses both a second subject and change in the divine nature.

*The prophet-like-Moses text names an intermediary.* When Peter identifies Jesus in Acts 3, one text he uses is Deut 18: God will raise up “a prophet like me from among their own people; I will put my words in the mouth of the prophet” (Deut 18:18; Acts 3:22). Acts uses it to identify Jesus as that prophet, beside other titles in the same speech (“the Holy and Righteous One,” “the Author of life,” Acts 3:14–15); it isn’t offered as an argument for incarnation, which the tradition grounds in other texts. What the Deuteronomy passage does fix is the relation it names: a human being God speaks *through*, raised up from among the people, like Moses, and accountable for speaking what he wasn’t commanded (18:20). Putting words in a prophet’s mouth isn’t embodying him. This strand of the identification therefore supports the agency horn of the fork below rather than the identity horn. A defender may answer that the prophetic office is one role among several the same person holds, and that is right; the point is only that this role, taken by itself, describes an intermediary rather than a subject identical with the one who sends him.

The three models pay those prices differently. The two-minds view needs a divine consciousness standing alongside the human one and must explain both how the divine mind is realized and why two complete centers of consciousness constitute one person rather than two. Kenosis gives the earthly history real purchase by allowing self-limitation, but it thereby revises whichever strict divine attributes are surrendered or suspended. Compositional christology supplies a determinate unity through parts and relations, while qualifying the simplicity or non-composition otherwise attributed to the subject. Hick’s charge that literal content evaporates under pressure (Hick 1977) therefore succeeds only against a model that refuses every corresponding revision. A model may keep a determinate union, but it must state which classical commitment pays for it.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Incarnation Identity Fork** · *Disjunction*

What relation between God and Jesus does the doctrine keep?

- **If the doctrine retains strict two-natures identity,** then *became* must be reconciled with timelessness, immutability, and simplicity. One divine subject bears a complete human life, and that relation is real. *Priced by* Life Is the Modifier of an Extent (§11.3.2); Three Invariances, One Word (§11.3.3); The Discriminating-Content Burden (§11.2.1).
- **If it retains kenotic identity,** then human history is accommodated through self-limitation or change, revising part of the classical divine set.
- **If it retains indwelling, agency, adoption, or function,** then what is described is divine action through a human being rather than incarnation. A uniquely divine vocation may remain, but without numerical identity.
- **If it retains only symbolic identification,** then theological meaning remains without a metaphysical union.

**Applies to:** Christian, non-Nicene, and restorationist branches that retain some form of divine–human identification in Jesus

**Still open:** strict identity, revised divine attributes, divine agency without identity, or nonliteral identification

A literal incarnation doctrine must reconcile a determinate personal subject, real relation to a human life, and the transition named by “became” with the classical commitments to timelessness, immutability, and simplicity. Models that retain a real divine mind, kenotic change, or composition appear to reintroduce structural roles or revise the classical conception. That is a serious coherence burden, not a demonstration that every possible theological interpretation of incarnation has no referent. The human life, mind, hunger, grief, and death that the doctrine names remain real phenomena open to natural and historical explanation.

### 12.2.4 The Resurrection
The resurrection is the doctrine on which Christianity stakes everything, and it says so itself: “if Christ has not been raised,” Paul writes, “then our proclamation is in vain and your faith is in vain” (1 Cor 15:14). It is also the doctrine most often defended as history rather than dogma—not *believe because the Church teaches it* but *weigh the record and see*—and that evidential posture is taken seriously and, at the end, pressed. Stated at full strength the claim runs: (1) Jesus of Nazareth died and was buried; (2) his tomb was later found empty; (3) numerous people reported encountering him alive afterward; and (4) the best explanation of that cluster is that God raised him bodily. Habermas’s mature statement of the minimal-facts argument now occupies the first three volumes of *On the Resurrection*: *Evidences* develops the historical method, the minimal facts, the additional facts, and the Gospel data; *Refutations* answers the principal alternative explanations; and *Scholarly Perspectives* surveys the scholarly field on both (Habermas 2024a; Habermas 2024b; Habermas 2025).

The argument rests only on data Habermas takes to be conceded across critical scholarship and maintains that no naturalistic hypothesis accounts for them as well as a raising does. Volume 4 carries the claimed event into theology and practice rather than adding a fourth historical proof (Habermas 2026). Wright, in *The Resurrection of the Son of God*, adds that the abrupt mutation of Jewish resurrection belief into its early Christian shape is itself a fact needing explanation, one the resurrection best supplies (Wright 2003). Swinburne casts the whole as a Bayesian case in which a prior for a God who acts lifts an otherwise negligible probability (Swinburne 2003). Two things are presupposed throughout, the same two the miracle presupposes: a supernatural agent to do the raising, and a standpoint outside Nature from which it comes.

That is the historical-bodily branch examined below. A transformed resurrection body remains a bodily claim and owes an account of numerical continuity through transformation. A visionary or appearance-experience account may explain the reported encounters without claiming that a corpse returned to life; a spiritual-vindication reading may retain Easter’s theological meaning without treating the empty tomb as its evidential hinge. Those branches aren’t refuted by failing the bodily-history test, but neither may they later be cited as though they established a bodily raising. What each branch carries is therefore fixed at entry: an event in a body, an experience interpreted as an appearance, or a theological claim of vindication.

The resurrection needs no wholly new lever; it draws on Chapter 11’s questions about a determinate active divine agent. A proposed resurrection must specify a personal agent, a causal relation, and a mode of action adequate to the event. These are substantive burdens; the book doesn’t establish that every conceivable divine-action account is definitionally impossible. The lever here is the doctrine’s own identity claim. Death ends the life whose return is promised; if what later appears is only a replica carrying copied memories, the person who died has not been resurrected. A later body or consciousness must therefore be numerically continuous with that same person, not merely similar. The evidential passage is included because the resurrection is defended extensively on testimonial ground; it tests what the record establishes without treating the metaphysical and historical questions as one verdict.
 Two questions therefore have to be kept apart, and a reader who grants the event still faces the first. The conditional question asks what agent, causal route, and continuity relation would make a raised bearer the person who died, and what granting the raising would and wouldn’t establish. The historical question asks what a mediated record can bear. An answer to either leaves the other where it was.

*Where it breaks—the structural front.* Take the doctrine at its most literal: not a recovery from potentially reversible cardiac arrest, but a body that has died and been buried, then lives again on the third day. Cardiac arrest isn’t a counterexample to the relevant claim. It is an abrupt loss of heart function that may be treated if CPR and defibrillation restore a normal rhythm within minutes (American Heart Association 2025). Recovery in that window isn’t a return after irreversible death has been established. Death by neurologic criteria, by contrast, requires permanent loss of function of the entire brain, including the brainstem (Greer et al. 2023). The historical question is whether the sources establish the stronger condition the doctrine needs; the doctrine can’t assume what its historical case must show. But if the tradition’s own claims of death, burial, and later embodied presence are granted, the event isn’t resuscitation by another name. Begin with the model this section directly prosecutes—a wholly structureless divine agent, situated outside Nature, acting upon a person whose life has wholly closed. On that conjunction, each required relation has been removed. There is no determinate personal subject to author the raising, so the deed has no possible doer under the description supplied; there is no outside to Nature for the act to come from and no causal channel for it to come through. Death, on the account of mortality being used here, isn’t a condition in which an otherwise continuing person is detained. It is the cessation of the organizing activity that constituted that person.

Closure fixes a further burden that the agent-side objection doesn’t settle by itself. Reproducing the former body’s organization, memories, and character would establish qualitative continuity, but qualitative continuity isn’t yet numerical identity. If the same preserved information could produce two equally exact embodiments, both would satisfy the resemblance criterion, while both couldn’t be numerically identical to the one person who died. A resurrection model therefore needs an asymmetric continuity relation that selects this later bearer as that earlier person rather than as a perfect successor.

The candidate models divide at that point. A persisting soul or an uninterrupted divinely sustained bearer denies that the person wholly closed and must explain how the bearer remains the person through the interval. A bodily or causal-continuity model holds that enough of the original organism or its causal career persists through death and must identify the persistence relation that does the work. An information-preserving reconstruction supplies resemblance and memory but fails the duplication test unless some further non-duplicable continuity is added. Divine intention can’t substitute for that relation merely by applying the name of the earlier person to the later bearer; it must specify what the intention preserves that makes identity one-to-one.

The categorical result is therefore narrower than the claim that every conceivable resurrection is impossible, but it isn’t merely agnostic. Total closure followed only by later reconstruction doesn’t yield the numerical resurrection of the person who closed; it yields a successor. A model can avoid that result only by denying total closure or by supplying a continuity relation that survives it, and each option carries the distinct burden just named. The structureless-external-agent model supplies neither an agent nor such a relation, so resurrection on that model is structurally uninstantiable rather than merely improbable. Testimony may still be weighed after a defender supplies a different coherent model, but it cannot supply the missing metaphysics by itself.

*What resurrection alone wouldn’t establish.* Even setting every difficulty already identified aside and granting the raising as history, the inference to divinity doesn’t follow from the mechanism itself, because the tradition’s own text supplies non-divine cases of the same event. Jesus is reported raising Lazarus after four days in the tomb (John 11:38–44), and Matthew reports that at the crucifixion “many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised” and “came out of the tombs… and appeared to many” (Matt 27:52–53); neither Lazarus nor the unnamed saints is thereby credited with deity. If bodily return to life after death doesn’t make Lazarus or the Matthean saints divine, the same event happening to Jesus cannot by itself make him divine either; some further premise beyond the raising itself would have to carry that inference, and the case as stated doesn’t supply one.

*What granting it would cost.* There is a final price, internal to the tradition, that would fall due even if every difficulty above were waived and the raising granted as history. The resurrection doesn’t only crown the sacrifice; it specifies its recovery. A passion may remain terrible and costly while a resurrection certain in advance removes permanent death from what was staked. That doesn’t by itself show that the cross was no sacrifice under every ordinary use of the word. It creates the narrower comparative problem: on a metric that ranks sacrificial love by irrevocable loss, guaranteed recovery can’t outrank an unrecoverable loss merely by being called divine. That consequence is run in full at §12.6.2, including the tradition’s own statement of Christ’s expectation, its saintly counterexamples, and the reply from Christ’s limited human knowledge. The resurrection section needs only the local result: granting the raising doesn’t automatically secure every valuation built on it; it changes the description of what the cross permanently staked.

*The historical question.* The structural analysis doesn’t settle the historical question by itself. The resurrection is urged as a fact one is asked to weigh, so it is worth bracketing the metaphysical dispute and meeting the case where it actually stands—on the testimony. Set the prior structural claims aside, then, and ask only what the record could bear.

*Before the field—the company the claim keeps.* The defender presses that the appearances were shared, transformative encounters unlike ordinary grief experiences. Bereaved people nevertheless do sometimes see, hear, or sense those they have lost; among widowed populations in a heterogeneous review, reported rates are substantial, though samples and definitions vary (Castelnovo et al. 2015). Allison places the resurrection reports within a wider comparative record (Allison 2021). Those data neither diagnose a first-century claimant nor supply a numerical base rate for the particular evidence. They establish only that sincere experiences interpreted as encounters with the dead belong to the ordinary alternative set. Shared expectation, scriptural rereading, group experience, and subsequent transformation require further case-specific analysis. Their availability prevents the raising from being the only conceivable explanation; it doesn’t by itself rank the alternatives or fix the prior.

*The driving premise—the possibility field.* The claim reaches no one as an event; it reaches them as a report transmitted through fallible human hands. The relevant chain includes perception and memory, expectation and embellishment, oral transmission, anonymous composition and theological redaction, scribal copying, canon formation, translation, and the reader’s present assent. None need be the sole site of failure for the point to stand: the historical claim asks the reader to rely on every link’s preserving enough of what originated, while each supplies a familiar mechanism by which a report can change. Metzger and Ehrman document how copying and variant readings enter the textual record (Metzger and Ehrman 2005). Brown gives the standard critical picture of Gospel composition and Synoptic dependence (Brown 1997). Metzger records the later canonization process (Metzger 1987). Allison examines the role of memory and expectation in the formation of the accounts (Allison 2010).

The links aren’t strictly independent, and some may preserve their material accurately. It would be a mistake to assign a failure probability to each and multiply them as independent trials. The evidence to be explained is a mediated record, and perception, memory, oral transmission, composition, copying, and interpretation provide possible routes by which a sincere movement could produce such a record without a bodily raising. Listing routes establishes alternatives, not their likelihood relative to resurrection. A Bayesian verdict would require defended priors and likelihoods for the specific data under each hypothesis. The chain therefore establishes mediation and live underdetermination; it doesn’t identify a particular failed link or by itself prove that the record lacks every possible likelihood advantage.

*What the disagreements show.* The defender often turns the accounts’ variety into an asset: minor discrepancies, the argument runs, are the fingerprint of independent testimony, since a fabricator would have harmonized them away. But the empty-tomb narratives aren’t a file of independent eyewitness depositions. Mark, Matthew, and Luke are literarily related; on the common critical account Matthew and Luke use Mark, while John’s relationship to the Synoptics is more complex and contested (Brown 1997).

The four narratives aren’t transcripts authored by the women they portray. Critical scholarship commonly treats the Gospel titles and traditional authorship claims as later than the compositions, while defenders argue that early attribution and access to eyewitness tradition remain significant (Brown 1997). Anonymity within a text doesn’t prove that its author lacked eyewitness access. Luke explicitly describes research based on traditions handed down by eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–3), which claims mediated access rather than direct deposition. The historical task is therefore to assess source access and dependence, not infer their absence from anonymity alone. Mark names three women, Matthew two, Luke a larger group, and John begins with Mary; the accounts also vary over messengers, response, locations, and timing. Some variations may be complementary or ordinary narrative compression; others create sharper harmonization burdens. Their existence limits any simple treatment of the four texts as independent depositions but doesn’t show that no recoverable witness tradition stands behind them.

One sharp example concerns the stone. Mark, Luke, and John present it as already moved when the women arrive; Matthew narrates an earthquake, an angel’s descent, and the stone’s removal in proximity to their arrival (Matt 28:2–4). Many readers take Matthew’s sequence as something the women witness; harmonizers construe it as a prior event supplied in explanatory narration. The Greek and narrative sequencing must bear that dispute. The passage therefore creates a real harmonization burden, not an unqualified formal contradiction announced without the rival reading.

These variations don’t prove that no experience occurred. They show that the texts don’t supply the several independently preserved observations the apologetic reading asks them to supply.

On common critical datings, the narratives also display added material: Matthew adds a guard and an earthquake; John, writing latest among the four and with its distinctive theological program, presents a more extended sequence around Mary and the disciples and adds the Doubting Thomas episode (John 20:24–29), which functions less as a fifth independent sighting than as an answer to a specific objection—that the appearances were a ghost or a vision rather than a body—by having Thomas invited to touch the wounds. That pattern is compatible with literary development. It shouldn’t be treated as a mechanical line from Mark to John or as proof that any particular episode was invented; the source history of the Gospels remains more complicated than that.

Matthew’s guard tradition is objection-responsive in a more explicit way. Matthew acknowledges that the report *the disciples stole the body* was circulating when he wrote (Matt 28:15), then supplies a narrative explaining why it circulated: the authorities anticipate the theft, secure the tomb, receive the guards’ private report of the angelic opening, deliberate with the elders, pay the guards to report that they slept through a theft, and promise to manage the governor (27:62–66; 28:2–4, 11–15). The sequence closes the ordinary-theft route within Matthew’s story and explains why the contrary account survived despite the guards’ alleged knowledge. It also creates a source-access burden. The report, council, payment, instruction, and promise occur among guards and hostile authorities; Matthew identifies no route by which their private exchange reached his community. A guard, priest, elder, intermediary, or later convert could have disclosed it, so undisclosed access doesn’t prove invention. What the text independently establishes is narrower: the theft charge existed in Matthew’s polemical setting. The bribery account explaining that charge is preserved only in the narrative written to answer it.

A different tension sits inside the narratives rather than between them. In Matthew, the Twelve have watched Jesus restore the dead, have been commissioned to “raise the dead” themselves (Matt 10:8), and have repeatedly been told that Jesus will be killed and raised (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19). Yet resurrection reports still arrive as an event for which the followers appear to have no working expectation; the wider tradition sharpens the pattern through disbelief of the first reports and Thomas’s demand for touch (Luke 24:11; John 20:24–29). Delegated power to raise another doesn’t entail that a disciple should expect Jesus to raise himself, and temporary restoration need not be the transformed resurrection Paul describes. Grief and failed messianic expectation may also overwhelm an abstract possibility. Those distinctions block a formal contradiction. They don’t erase the cumulative expectation problem: the characters have been given direct demonstrations, delegated authority, and repeated prediction, yet the story presents their incredulity as though resurrection had not become a live possibility for them.

This development is one reason the familiar *liar, lunatic, or Lord* trilemma can’t govern the historical inquiry. The trilemma assumes that the decisive claims reached the sources substantially as Jesus made them. Legendary development, misattribution, redaction, and sincere misunderstanding leave further alternatives: Jesus need be neither deceitful nor deluded if the relevant formulation is later than him. Paul shows that resurrection belief and appearance claims arose early, so the point isn’t that Easter belief first appeared after Mark. It is that later surviving narratives increasingly supply objection-responsive authentication—secured tomb, angelic opening, narrated appearances, touchable wounds—absent from the earlier surviving narrative forms. That direction is evidence the development hypothesis predicts; independent tradition and selective authorial purpose remain competing explanations whose likelihoods require argument.

Synoptic dependence complicates a claim of four independent accounts. Traditional Matthean authorship doesn’t make source use impossible: an eyewitness author could employ an existing narrative for structure, shared wording, or communal authority and supplement it from other knowledge. Dependence means only that copied material can’t be counted again as independent attestation without identifying the independent contribution. Matthew’s revision of Mark 10:17–18 in Matt 19:16–17 is consistent with theological or rhetorical redaction (Ehrman 2014), but it doesn’t tell us that every changed or retained resurrection detail is invented. The narrower result is enough: literary relation reduces independence and keeps redaction and composition live; it doesn’t settle the authors’ access or the event.

*What the earliest source omits.* The empty tomb can be pressed from the other end, by asking what the earliest sources independently establish. The earliest witness to the resurrection isn’t a Gospel but Paul, writing within a couple of decades of the crucifixion. In the very passage where he lays out the case—the creed at 1 Cor 15:3–7 that the minimal-facts argument treats as bedrock—he recites death, burial, raising, and a list of appearances, and says nothing of an empty tomb, nothing of the women who found it, nothing of the discovery at all. That silence doesn’t demonstrate that no empty-tomb tradition existed. It does mean that the creed can’t independently corroborate the later tomb narrative. Critics accordingly read Mark’s narrative as a later literary development (Ehrman 2014). Defenders argue for an earlier, pre-Markan tradition. The narrower result is enough for the cascade: the earliest recoverable proclamation doesn’t supply the multiple independent witnesses the later story is asked to bear. On that critical reading, the tomb isn’t where the belief began; it is a later narrative whose relation to the earliest belief remains contested.

Mark is widely judged on textual-critical grounds to have originally ended at 16:8, with the women fleeing and no appearance narrated; 16:9–20 is later (Metzger and Ehrman 2005). That matters for what Mark independently attests: an empty-tomb narrative and an announced appearance, not a narrated encounter. Later Gospels contain appearance narratives, but chronology alone doesn’t show that they grew from legend rather than from other earlier traditions the authors used. The development hypothesis and the independent-tradition hypothesis both remain live, and their relative likelihood must be argued from more than sequence.

*What the appearance list establishes.* Paul relays an early tradition naming appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles, and finally Paul (1 Cor 15:5–8). Its earliness is important evidence that resurrection belief and named appearance claims arose quickly. It is still one transmitted list rather than preserved depositions from each named witness, and the five hundred receive no independent surviving report. Lüdemann’s proposal that a primary Petrine vision generated further experiences (Lüdemann 1994) and more recent naturalistic reconstructions (Ens 2024) show how the data might descend from fewer originating experiences, but possibility isn’t actuality. Conversely, the list’s number doesn’t by itself establish independence, shared sensory content, or bodily encounter. The historical question remains which hypothesis better predicts the early, multiple, and transformative claims once dependence and source access are specified.

Some replies try to cut the chain short. The minimal-facts strategy anchors to what it takes as bedrock—early creedal material (the formula Paul relays at 1 Cor 15:3–7) and Paul’s own claim to have met the risen Christ. Even the skeptical critic Lüdemann dates that formula to within two years of the crucifixion (Lüdemann 1994). Grant the early dating in full; it shortens the chain without changing its kind. The creed still reaches us only through the same manuscript and translation layers, and its early date speaks to *when* the belief formed, not to *what* formed it—an expectation-shaped conviction can form fast.

*What the early date buys.* The early date buys less than it appears to, because each of the ordinary mechanisms already named operates well inside the window an early dating protects. Memory for even the most vivid, high-confidence experiences degrades within months, not generations: tracked from days to years after the event, flashbulb memories—the kind people report for shocking, consequential news—show accuracy loss comparable to ordinary memory while confidence in their accuracy stays undiminished (Neisser and Harsch 1992; Talarico and Rubin 2003). A report also doesn’t need retelling across decades to lose its hedges; qualifying language is characteristically the first casualty of a single retelling, and the vivid, confidence-bearing content of a rumor is what reliably survives it (Allport and Postman 1947). A claim need not even pass between two people to firm up. A mind that merely entertains a hypothesis measurably raises its own later confidence that the entertained possibility was witnessed rather than supposed. The hypothesis need only be entertained: *maybe he is risen, maybe we didn’t really see him die, maybe he is out there still.* Judgments of a memory’s source rely on cues like vividness and familiarity, and repetition manufactures those whether or not the thing repeated is true (Johnson et al. 1993; Garry et al. 1996). Mere repeated exposure to a claim raises its felt truth, independent of any new evidence for it (Hasher et al. 1977; Dechêne et al. 2010). None of these mechanisms requires a liar, a lunatic, or a multi-generational game of telephone. Each is measured on the scale of days to a few years—the very window early dating is invoked to close.

Paul’s experience isn’t outside the field but well inside it: a reported vision, by a man who never met the living Jesus, is just what the perception-and-memory and expectation-and-embellishment links already cover—and the conversion of James, the brother of Jesus, urged as a further anchor because a onetime skeptic is said to have come to belief, gives way on the same reading. His skepticism rests on a couple of tendentious verses already inside the tradition (Mark 3:21; John 7:5), and the appearance credited to him (1 Cor 15:7) is one more vision of that same kind; grief for an executed brother and a movement gathering in his name are ordinary lines to conviction, and what both cases establish is that the man came to believe, not what he saw.
