A further, independent line of evidence supports the same reading of Paul’s report as an ordinary, situated product rather than an insulated channel: on an influential scholarly reading, Paul’s own letters handle inherited material inconsistently across the corpus—his treatment of the law worked out one way in one letter and reworked in another as the occasion demanded, rather than fixed in advance and applied uniformly (Räisänen 1986). That is what situational theologizing looks like from outside, not what an unmediated report would need to look like. The reading is contested—other scholarship treats the same texture as Paul using shared terms in different senses for different rhetorical occasions rather than genuinely disagreeing with himself—but either resolution serves the point made here: nothing in the record requires, or even suggests, a transmission link insulated from the ordinary pressures of memory, occasion, audience, and argument-in-progress that already do the work through every other link in the chain.

Claims of multiple attestation need source-by-source analysis. Matthew and Luke use Mark for substantial narrative material, but original Mark narrates no appearance, so later appearance traditions can’t simply be reduced to Mark’s appearance account. Paul, the Synoptics, and John have distinct but contested relations, and shared tradition can produce agreement without full independence. Habermas’s current survey is the large third volume of *On the Resurrection* (Habermas 2025), superseding reliance on the scale of the 2005 article (Habermas 2005). Scholarly agreement on crucifixion, early resurrection proclamation, and experiences interpreted as appearances isn’t yet agreement on bodily raising, but it is genuine evidence any alternative must explain. Willingness to suffer bears most directly on sincerity; martyrdom traditions vary in historical quality (Moss 2013). Sincerity neither proves truth nor becomes evidentially irrelevant. The comparative case must ask how well resurrection and each alternative explain the timing, multiplicity, content, and consequences together.

Wright is right that the rise and Jewish mutation of resurrection belief need explanation; listing psychological and social mechanisms doesn’t show that they predict that mutation as well as an event hypothesis. It keeps naturalistic explanation live and makes its bridge explicit. Swinburne’s Bayesian analysis depends on a prior for a God disposed to raise Jesus. Chapters 10–11 contest the simplicity and divine-action grounds used to raise that prior, but a reader who rejects those chapters will assign it differently. Cavin and Colombetti challenge Swinburne’s probabilistic case in detail (Cavin and Colombetti 2013). The evidential dispute is therefore not closed by either bare possibility or a prior imported without defense.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Resurrection Possibility Screen** · *Diagnostic*

Before a bodily resurrection can be compared with historical alternatives, identify three things: the determinate agent who performs the raising, the causal relation by which that act reaches the dead, and the continuity relation that makes the raised bearer numerically the person who died rather than a replica. A wholly structureless agent outside Nature acting on a life whose constituting activity has ceased supplies none of the three on the book’s account. A different model may pass the screen only by stating the agent, causal route, and identity bearer it adds or revises.

**Applies to:** bodily and transformed-body resurrection claims; visionary and spiritual-vindication branches carry different evidential claims

**Depends on:** One-Sided Interaction Is Not Interaction (§11.7.3)

The doctrinal claim needs a possibility screen before historical inference: it must specify a determinate agent, a causal relation, and an identity-preserving continuity relation. Recovery from potentially reversible cardiac arrest is a different description. The particular model directly prosecuted here fails the screen on the book’s prior account because it supplies neither the required doer nor continuity relation. That model is a wholly structureless, externally situated agent acting after the person’s closure. A revisionary proposal can contest those premises or supply another account. Even if a coherent alternative and nonzero prior are granted, the testimonial record remains mediated, contested, and compatible with several explanations. Mediation doesn’t prove that a witness or link failed, and alternative routes don’t rank themselves. Habermas’s mature evidences and refutations (Habermas 2024a; Habermas 2024b) therefore meet a live historical dispute rather than a record deductively closed here. The diagnostic carries the exact remaining questions: agent, causal route, identity bearer, priors, source dependence, and comparative likelihood.

### 12.2.5 Eternal Life

Eternal life is the promise that the person isn’t ended by death: the same self continues, on the classical Christian picture, in the beatific vision, the unclouded and unending life with God that the creeds name “the life of the world to come” (Aquinas, ST I-II.3). Substance dualism makes the soul a distinct immaterial substance that carries the mental life and departs the body intact at death (Swinburne 2013; Moreland and Craig 2003). Hylomorphism makes the soul the form of the body, able to subsist as a “separated soul” between death and a bodily resurrection (Aquinas, *ST* I.75–76) (Feser 2009). Bodily-continuity models preserve or transform the organism; re-creation models have God re-embody or reassemble the person after the original organism has ceased. Conditional immortality and universal restoration change who finally lives and whether loss remains possible, but they don’t remove the identity question for anyone said to return. Across the models one thing is fixed: the promise concerns this person, not merely a later bearer who resembles them.

Eternal life promises continued life for the person who would otherwise die. The promise itself therefore incurs an identity burden: a heavenly subject or divinely preserved consciousness must be numerically continuous with that person rather than a replacement sharing memories or character. A venue alone doesn’t secure that continuity, and neither does the bare assertion of preservation; the relevant causal relation has to be specified. No empirical account offered here independently rules out every transcendent venue. The resurrection, of which this is the special case, is taken up in its own right at §12.2.4, with the last judgment at §12.2.6; both turn on the same identity requirement.

The promise isn’t Christianity’s alone. Islam’s Jannah (Paradise) and Judaism’s Olam Ha-Ba (the World to Come) name related structures under different scripture: a persisting self, embodied or not, enjoying an unending blessed condition beyond ordinary earthly life. Each tradition supplies a different account of the bearer and venue. On the life-based identification used throughout this section, the bearer to be preserved is the same finite life. A concrete heavenly life remains a life within Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality even if it isn’t part of the present cosmic arrangement; an abstract or atemporal dependence relation doesn’t by itself supply an experiencing subject or a lived venue. The structural question is therefore what kind of bearer and continuation the selected doctrine asserts, not which tradition’s name the destination carries.

Take the promise at its most literal: the same self, alive again and unending. On the inherited account, the person is that finite life, not a passenger riding inside it. A later bearer therefore needs an identity relation that survives the prior life’s closure; duration and resemblance alone don’t supply it, since a perfect duplicate would satisfy both and still not be the same person. A defender may reject the life-based identification by positing a soul, organism, hylomorphic bearer, or divinely preserved relation. The doctrine then stands or falls with that bearer rather than with the word *eternal* alone.

The soul strategy carries its own burden. Substance dualism needs a bearer of mental life that persists once the body is gone (Swinburne 2013; Moreland and Craig 2003), while every mental process available to empirical inspection depends on organized realization. A separated soul must therefore explain how it bears this person’s consciousness, memory, and agency without that organization. If it remains an experiencing subject, its lived operations still require determinate ordering, differentiation, and bearing; if it is merely a subsisting form or capacity, the account must say what personal life continues during the interval. Hylomorphism acknowledges the second difficulty: the separated soul is an incomplete substance that can’t exercise its ordinary embodied functions (Aquinas, *ST* I.89) (Feser 2009). That is a substantive theory of the bearer, not a contradiction by definition, but it doesn’t let the phrase *the soul survives* discharge the identity and experience questions by itself.

Re-embodiment fares no better. A new body assembled in a new medium hosts a new life, and the connectedness carried into it (the values, the memories, the pattern) is a partial preservation of what mattered, real and admitting of degrees, but not yet the numerical continuation of this one. That genuine remainder is *legacy*: the causal and relational continuation of a person in other bearers after the person’s own life has closed. Legacy can preserve a representation, an influence, or a direction without preserving the same experiencing subject; it therefore can’t by itself discharge the stronger promise of eternal life. One reply is that God can make the later bearer the same person: by intending it, by constituting it as the continuation of the prior life, or by establishing a causal relation between the two. It is developed by philosophers defending the compatibility of a materialist metaphysics of persons with the doctrine (Van Inwagen 1978; Baker 1995; Corcoran 2001; Merricks 2009). But intention alone labels a new life without supplying the continuity in question; and a causal relation established after closure isn’t the ongoing self-producing process that made the earlier one this person rather than another. The defender must therefore identify a continuity that does more than reproduce the old pattern and memories, while still allowing the original life to have ended. The account offered here finds no such bearer: where the organizing activity has ceased, a later organized activity may inherit or resemble its history, but it begins a new first-person current rather than reopening the old one.

Reassembly after total closure therefore yields a duplicate unless some further one-to-one continuity relation is supplied. The venue is a separate question. If it hosts concrete lives, relations, memory, and experience, those operations require determinate subjects and relations; if it is only an atemporal ground, grounding alone doesn’t yet furnish a lived world (§11.7.2). Near-death experiences and the sense that the dead remain present can be explained by living brains and continuing relationships without deciding every survival claim; they aren’t, by phenomenology alone, discriminating evidence for one bearer model. Even if persistence is granted, the promise presses a further problem: the categorical desires that give a life its reasons to continue are finite, and an unending life may outrun them (Williams 1973b). A defender may answer through inexhaustible goods or transformed desire, but must say what keeps the resulting life both recognizably personal and worth continuing.

A second problem concerns the blessed condition itself. The state promised is one from which every tear is wiped (Rev 21:4), and the bearer promised is *this* person, history and all; memory is where the two specifications must be reconciled. Healing a memory past its original affective sting doesn’t by itself replace the person. A continuous self can reinterpret an event, alter its emotional valence, integrate it into a wider history, and still own it as what happened to them. The identity problem begins only where the promised condition requires erasure of constitutive history, destruction of the architecture that integrated it, or reconstruction without an adequate causal and mnemonic continuity relation. If the one in glory remembers the suffering and the lost while remaining wholly unclouded, the defender owes an account of how grief is transformed without the history being deleted; organic integration and postmortem completion are genuine answers to that first question, not verbal evasions. If instead the memory or its ownership is removed, the continuity problem sharpens: a successor spared what made the original who they were isn’t obviously this life carried across. The memory argument therefore doesn’t show that healing and identity are incompatible. It fixes the burden more precisely: the doctrine must explain transformation that preserves autobiographical ownership and numerical continuity through the prior closure, rather than purchasing blessedness through erasure or replacement. The dilemma is pressed against stronger erasure and replacement models at §12.5.3; here it reinforces the continuity question already carrying the section.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Living After Living Problem** · *Disjunction*

What lives on, and is it still you?

- **If an immaterial soul continues,** what carries your mind and history without the body?
- **If the body continues through transformation,** what survives death and total material change?
- **If God re-creates you,** what makes the re-created person you and not a copy?
- **If eternal life means being remembered,** what work is the word *life* doing?

Conditional immortality and universal restoration change who survives, not the continuity each surviving person requires.

**Still open:** What is supposed to carry your identity across death? And can that thing be lost for good?

Eternal-life doctrines face a demanding personal-identity problem: they must explain what makes a later bearer numerically the same person rather than a duplicate, and how that continuity survives the closure of the organism. The argument here is that substance-dualist, hylomorphic, and re-embodiment accounts bear substantial burdens on its account of mind and self, but those conclusions depend on the contested life-based identification. What doesn’t depend on it is the identity problem itself: the duplicate question is owed by any account of postmortem persistence, whatever theory of persons it runs on, and a reader who grants the structural theses nothing still has to say what makes the later bearer the same person rather than a copy. The human goods pictured by heaven—security, flourishing, freedom from loss, and continued relation—remain real aims for this-worldly institutions and communities, without implying that every afterlife interpretation is disproved.

### 12.2.6 Final Judgment

The last things arrive together in the creed: “he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead,” the dead are raised, and each receives a final verdict. The doctrine binds three events into one. The parousia is Christ’s return in power to close the age; the general resurrection raises all the dead, righteous and wicked alike, to be judged in the body; and the Final Judgment renders on each a final and irrevocable sentence, heaven or hell. Its most disciplined modern defenders treat the general resurrection as the hinge of Christian hope and a fact demanding explanation in its own right (Wright 2003), and read the whole as the consummation history is moving toward. Two things are presupposed, the same two every doctrine in this cluster presupposes: a personal agent who returns and judges, and a standpoint outside the age from which he breaks in to end it.

The Final Judgment is an eschatological concentration of prior questions. A literal returning and judging agent must be a determinate personal subject with a causal relation to the world; that raises Chapter 11’s burdens for a wholly structureless ground. The account must also say what explanatory work the proposed intervention performs. These pressures are serious but don’t establish, by stipulation, that every eschatological interpretation is impossible. The general resurrection is the resurrection (see §12.2.4) and eternal life (see §12.2.5) at the scale of everyone who has died, so it inherits the agent, causal-route, and personal-continuity questions already carried from those sections. A further question—what authorizes the judge to punish creatures for choices formed within a field that judge designed—belongs later at §12.3.12. The argument leaves that question there; it doesn’t borrow the later answer in advance.

Take the doctrine at full strength: a real return, a real raising, a real reckoning. The imported structural line asks for a determinate returning subject, a route by which the return occurs, and continuity between the dead and those raised for judgment. On the book’s account, a wholly structureless subject outside Nature supplies no determinate returner or causal channel, while a life that has closed supplies no persisting bearer to reopen; a later assembly would resemble the judged without yet being numerically the one whose acts are judged (see §12.2.4, §12.2.5). A reader who rejects those imported identifications still owes the same three specifications on another account. The disposition then branches. Eternal conscious punishment, annihilation, remedial judgment, and universal restoration (Hart 2019) don’t impose the same fate and must not be treated as interchangeable. The first two carry irreversible loss; remedial judgment makes punishment instrumental to restoration; universalism removes final loss. Each still requires a judge and judged subjects, but only the branches retaining punitive loss pass that moral authorization problem to Divine Punishment.

The structural front isn’t particular to the creed. Islamic accounts of the Day of Resurrection and Day of Judgment likewise retain raised subjects, a reckoning, and a final disposition; Jewish eschatological accounts vary more widely over resurrection, judgment, and the world to come, but every branch retaining a postmortem assize needs a judge, a judged subject, and an identity relation across death. The same specification questions therefore recur without pretending that every tradition carries the same timetable or outcome. One divergence matters immediately: the Qur’an explicitly declines to date the Hour—“they ask you about the Hour, when it will arrive; say: the knowledge of it is with my Lord alone” (Qur’an 7:187; also 33:63)—so the dated-forecast problem considered next belongs to Christian branches that use the Synoptic sayings for the future final event. It isn’t a general cost every Abrahamic eschatology pays.

The doctrine also carries a wound its own texts inflict. It was first delivered not as an open-ended hope but as a dated one: the end within the lifetime of those who heard it. “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see that the kingdom of God has come with power” (Mark 9:1; Matt 16:28); “you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes” (Matt 10:23); “this generation will not pass away until all these things have taken place” (Mark 13:30; Matt 24:34). The generation passed, and the age didn’t close. That the delay was a problem is visible inside the New Testament itself, where the scoffers already ask “Where is the promise of his coming?” and the reply relaxes the timescale to God’s own reckoning, on which a thousand years are as a day (2 Pet 3:3–4, 8). Two readings decline that face value, and they are the tradition’s real answers rather than evasions. A second question survives every redating: what the continuing interval is waiting to complete. The Grim Reaping Problem takes that question up where the greater good the delay is said to serve is fixed (§12.5.1).

*Preterism* holds that the predicted events did occur on schedule, and that the interpreter has misidentified them: the coming in question isn’t the close of the age but the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, with the temple destroyed within the generation exactly as the discourse says, and the apocalyptic imagery read as the standard prophetic idiom for the fall of a political order rather than as cosmic dissolution. On the partial-preterist version most widely held, some of the discourse was discharged then and a final coming remains outstanding, which lets the dated sayings be true as stated while preserving a future consummation. The second reading works on *this generation* itself, taking *genea* to mean the kind or lineage rather than the cohort then living, so that what is promised is survival to the end rather than an end within decades.

Each buys something and each is charged for it. Preterism keeps the timetable and pays in referent: if the coming with power was Jerusalem’s fall, then the sayings about it aren’t evidence for the doctrine this section examines, since a judgment on one city in one war isn’t the general resurrection and universal assize the creed confesses—and the partial version has to say, passage by passage, which clauses were discharged in AD 70 and which weren’t, on criteria the text doesn’t supply. The lineage reading keeps the referent and pays in content: a promise that the kind won’t pass away before the end is compatible with any date whatever, which is what makes it safe, and a prediction compatible with every outcome isn’t the urgent and checkable announcement the passages were doing their work as.

The historical reading takes the failure at face value: Jesus is intelligible as an apocalyptic prophet whose central prediction didn’t come to pass, and the doctrine’s later history is the long reworking of a dated forecast into an undatable one (Ehrman 2009; Allison 2010). But a prediction retooled until no observation could disconfirm it has bought its safety by surrendering its content: an end that is always imminent and never due is no longer a claim about what will happen.

*The petition, read structurally.* The most repeated request in Christian practice carries the same commitments in miniature, and it is worth reading slowly because familiarity has worn the words smooth. *Thy kingdom come.*

The obvious reading is territorial, and it is the one to set aside first, because it is the weakest and the tradition doesn’t need it. *Basileia* is closer to *reign* than to *realm*: what is asked for is that God rule, not that a country arrive. A defender is entitled to that reading and it costs the petition nothing.

It doesn’t, however, escape the verb. *Come* isn’t a description of a static condition but of a transition into one: a reign that comes is a reign that begins to obtain where it didn’t obtain before. That requires a before and an after, or the petition asks for nothing that isn’t already the case (T). It requires the two states to differ, or the arrival is a relabelling of the present (S at role level). And it requires that whatever it is that comes be the same reign on both sides of the transition, or nothing arrived and something else merely started. This holds on the metaphorical reading exactly as it holds on the literal one, which is why the retreat to *reign* doesn’t relieve the pressure: the loading was never in the noun.

The territorial reading, for those who keep it, adds a further question that the reign reading only postpones. If the kingdom is anywhere at all, there is a distance between the petitioner and it, since what is nowhere isn’t a place one could be brought into. So: is God in his kingdom? If he is, the kingdom is somewhere, and a God located somewhere isn’t the aspatial God the doctrine of divine simplicity was built to protect (§11.2.1). If he isn’t in it, the doctrine owes an account of where a God stands relative to a kingdom that is his and that he isn’t in. Neither branch is fatal to belief; both cost the classical attributes something, and the cost is the point.

None of this is an argument that the petition is empty. It is the ordinary result reached throughout: the language of the tradition is structurally loaded wherever it says anything determinate, and the loading is what makes it sayable. A prayer for a reign that comes is a prayer cast in succession, difference, and persistence. It asks, in the only vocabulary there is, for something to change.

**[Disjunction]**

**The No Apparent Future Problem** · *Disjunction*

Did Jesus name a date, an event, or nothing that could ever come due?

- **If “this generation” named the people listening to him,** then “this generation” and “some standing here” point at a real coming event. But that generation is gone.
- **If he meant the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70,** then the timetable holds. But the fall of a city isn’t the general resurrection and final judgment whose timing was at issue.
- **If “this generation” meant a people or a kind rather than a date,** then the coming event survives. But the deadline is gone, and a saying that fits any date predicts none. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.

A branch may keep the timetable, or the final event, or a saying that never expires. It may not treat one reading as supplying all three. *Feeds into* The Fulfillment Timing Problem (§12.3.5).

**Applies to:** Christian branches that use the Synoptic sayings as evidence for a future final return and judgment

**Still open:** Which timetable is claimed, and what event does it refer to? What final disposition follows from it?

A literal final-judgment doctrine must answer for a determinate returning judge, a causal mode of return, personal persistence across death, and an account of why anyone deserves the punishment the judgment would impose. The Synoptic timing passages additionally create a historical and interpretive problem for particular Christian formulations; that issue isn’t shared identically by every Abrahamic eschatology. The longing for final setting-right remains a real moral and political concern, and one this-worldly response is offered at §6. The argument is that the eschatological hypothesis bears substantial coherence and evidential costs; it doesn’t establish that no conceivable eschatological interpretation could survive.

## 12.3 Divine Governance, Authentication, and Moral Standing

The third cluster begins with governance: providence (§12.3.1), petitionary prayer (§12.3.2), and miracles (§12.3.3). These sections distinguish meticulous control, concurrence, general governance, noncoercive influence, petitionary intervention, formation of the petitioner, unusual providence, and publicly identifiable signs. What survives is a specification of how much causal control and publicly available intervention the retained God supplies.

Authentication comes next: Scripture (§12.3.4), prophecy (§12.3.5), and divine hiddenness (§12.3.6) test the message, its evidential markers, and the availability of the alleged speaker. Faith and Belief (§12.3.7) then applies only to accounts of salvation that make conscious assent, trust, or explicit belief necessary or evidentially central. The Four Insufficiencies (§12.3.8) asks which loads the retained message is actually required to bear. Authentication climbs four distinct rungs: that an event occurred, that its source was divine, that a given message is that source’s, and that a doctrine follows from the message. Evidence secured at one rung doesn’t carry the next, so each authentication claim is tested at the rung its evidence reaches. An inclusivist, election, conscience, sacramental, or universalist account may leave some of those pressures by revising the role assigned to explicit reception; it may not be treated as though it had retained exclusivism unchanged.

The final movement tests moral authentication and standing. The Moral Gap (§12.3.9) asks whether moral demand requires grace; Borrowed Moral Capital (§12.3.10) asks whether historical influence authenticates the faith; Divine Command Theory (§12.3.11) asks what makes a command binding; and Divine Punishment (§12.3.12) asks what standing the retained governor has to impose a final disposition. This order doesn’t assume the verdict of Chapter 11. It keeps the internal line available while allowing Chapter 11’s results to be applied conditionally where their premises are granted.

### 12.3.1 Providence
Providence is downstream of the sections around it, and the one place the tradition’s long-contested foreknowledge–freedom set-piece comes apart. Three theses travel under one head, and each is a relation between a personal God and the world: a governor and the governed, a knower and the known, an ordainer and the ordained. Governance is God conserving and directing all things to their ends. Foreknowledge is God knowing, infallibly and in advance, what will occur, the free acts of creatures included. Predestination is God ordaining the outcome, whether by the Reformed unconditional decree or by Molinist selection on the basis of middle knowledge (Molina, *Concordia* 1588).

The same three theses recur, under different names, across the other Abrahamic traditions that share the personal-God commitment the argument that follows targets. Islamic theology runs the identical dispute as *qadar* (decree), spanning Jabriyya determinism, Qadariyya libertarianism, and the Ash’arite middle position of *kasb* (God creates the act; the human merely ‘acquires’ it)—a solution that leans on the same occasionalism engaged at §11.7.1, where creaturely causal power is denied outright. Jewish philosophy holds the same tension between *hashgacha* (providence) and *bechira chofshit* (free choice); Maimonides’s own resolution denies that God’s knowledge of an outcome determines it (*Guide* III.20), a rescue some read as anticipating the open-theist move and others as a distinct fourth option (Seeskin 2000; Stern 2013). Different vocabulary, same three-way structure, and—if the argument that follows holds—the same dependence on a personal relatum none of the three traditions’ rescues can do without.

Providence also gathers several causal roles under one doctrinal name. Conservation may be stated as the created order’s continuing ontological dependence on God; governance toward ends is final-causal; concurrence attributes creaturely effects to divine and created causes at different explanatory levels; special intervention adds efficient or agent-causal work. The absence of temporal transmission isn’t an objection to grounding or final causation merely as such (§11.7.2). The question is which role a branch claims, and whether it later borrows control, responsiveness, or outcome-selection belonging to another role without supplying it.

The full engagement with the foreknowledge–freedom dilemma belongs to §11.4.2 and isn’t re-run here: Pike’s sharpening of it, and the Molinist, Ockhamist, atemporalist, and open-theist replies. Providence adds a different problem that bare foreknowledge doesn’t contain. Knowing an act doesn’t by itself cause the act. But a creator who knows possible histories and selects which complete history becomes actual does more than observe what creatures choose: the selection fixes which creatures exist and the circumstances in which their choosing occurs. Knowledge and actualization must therefore be separated before they can be recombined.

*The actual-history selection problem.* On a salvation account sensitive to belief, trust, obedience, sacramental access, or response to revelation, the selected circumstances aren’t neutral scenery. They include whether a person is born into a Christian, Jewish, Muslim, or nonreligious family; which language and scriptures they can read; which testimony reaches them; whether it arrives through love, coercion, distortion, or not at all; what evidence and defeaters enter their field; and how long they live with an opportunity to reconsider. None of those facts alone determines a libertarian response. Together they constitute much of the evidential and motivational field within which any response becomes possible. A providential account that selects the history therefore owes an account not only of freedom inside the field but of responsibility for selecting the field.

The deterministic branch answers directly. On Reformed decree, strong Thomist premotion, or an Ash’arite account on which God creates the act and the creature acquires it, the actual outcome belongs within providential determination. Compatibilism may preserve creaturely agency by locating freedom in action flowing from the creature’s own reasons and character rather than in an unconditioned alternative. It doesn’t make the outcome external to the decree. Salvation and loss remain among the states the providential order knowingly and intentionally contains, so the account bears the moral burden of that authorship rather than the libertarian burden of counterfactual freedom.

Molinism relocates rather than erases the selection. God doesn’t determine the counterfactuals of creaturely freedom; middle knowledge supplies what each possible creature would freely do in each circumstance, and the creative decree selects among the feasible worlds those truths permit (de Molina 1588; Flint 1998; Craig 1987). This preserves libertarian authorship of the response. It also makes the selection problem exact: in choosing one feasible world, God knowingly chooses the persons, families, languages, histories, evidential fields, and resulting pattern of salvation that world contains. The serious Molinist reply is feasibility. Perhaps no feasible world secures universal free acceptance, or every world with greater salvation sacrifices other goods or contains different persons. That reply is available, but it must identify the relevant feasibility constraint and the goods that justify this selection. The bare assertion that creatures would choose differently can’t do the work until the counterfactuals are grounded—the independent objection already recorded in §11.4.2—and the available alternatives compared.

Simple foreknowledge takes away the decision procedure. On that account God knows the actual future infallibly, but the knowledge is logically posterior to the creative decision and therefore can’t guide the choice of which world to create. This avoids the specifically Molinist picture of surveying counterfactual histories and choosing by their outcomes. Its cost is providential: foreknowledge supplies no explanation of why this history was selected rather than another, and can’t be invoked as the reason God chose these circumstances. Ockhamism addresses whether a past divine belief makes a later act unavoidable by treating the belief as a soft fact dependent on the later act. That may protect alternative possibility, but it likewise doesn’t answer why the creator actualized the circumstances in which the foreknown act occurs.

Atemporalism removes chronological priority, not the explanatory distinction. If one timeless act includes both complete knowledge and willing of the actual history, the account must still say whether the history is known because it is willed, willed in light of what is known, or known through the creatures’ acts without being selected according to them. The first approaches decree; the second reproduces selection; the third limits what complete knowledge contributes to providential choice. Declaring all three simultaneous doesn’t decide which dependence holds.

Open theism declines exhaustive definite foreknowledge of undetermined free acts. God knows every possibility and every settled fact, responds within history, and administers a creation whose creaturely branches are genuinely open (Hasker 1989; Boyd 2001; Mullins 2016). This protects the future from being selected as one already complete history. It changes the responsibility rather than eliminating it: God chooses the initial and continuing distribution of risks, evidence, capacities, interventions, and opportunities while knowing the possible losses. The relevant burden is prudent administration of an open field, not authorship of a settled outcome. It also gives up the classical claim that every future contingent is eternally known as a definite truth.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Chosen History Problem** · *Disjunction*

If God knows what creatures will do, what role does that knowledge play in selecting history?

- **If the creator selects history by determination,** then the outcomes remain within the decree even if compatibilism preserves creaturely agency. *Feeds into* The Divine-Judgment Specification (§12.3.12). *Priced by* Grip Requires a Domain (§11.7.4).
- **If the creator selects it by middle knowledge,** then God need not author creaturely responses, but selects the persons, families, languages, evidence, and circumstances known to accompany salvation or loss. Feasibility and competing goods must justify that selection. *Priced by* The Scope Sits in the Known (§11.4.2).
- **If the creator has only simple foreknowledge, which arrives once creation is already settled,** then it came too late to guide the choice, and cannot explain why these circumstances rather than others.
- **If the future is open,** then exhaustive definite foreknowledge is surrendered, and providence becomes the administration of known risks rather than the selection of a completed history.

Atemporality isn’t a fifth selection model. If knowledge and willing are one timeless act, the defender must still say whether history is known because it is willed, willed in light of what is known, or known through creaturely acts without being selected according to them. That dependence question applies within whichever non-open branch the defender retains.

**Applies to:** providential accounts combining divine knowledge, creative selection, creaturely freedom, and salvation-sensitive circumstances

**Still open:** What does God know at the moment of choosing? Which alternatives are actually available? Who decides what evidence a creature gets? And is the responsibility for a decreed outcome or for an administered risk?

These branches meet the upstream structural results differently. Governance is active power exercised selectively—this end rather than that—and *Three Prices for Active Power* (§10.2.1) sets out what selecting costs: differentiated content in God, or an unexplained brute *this rather than that*, or one necessary act with one necessary terminus and no contingency left in what is governed. Foreknowledge meets *Nothing for an Omniscient Ground to Make Sense Of* (§10.1.3), which reads intelligibility as a competence closing a gap: an omniscient knower has no gap to close, so the knowing relation the doctrine needs isn’t one it can stand in. A wholly structureless active-ground account must explain how those predicates retain determinate content without the role-level conditions identified in Chapter 11. If it can’t, the familiar problem isn’t resolved by that model. An embedded or revisionary theology may retain the predicates but pays a different cost in aseity, ultimacy, or the scope of foreknowledge. Providence is therefore not eliminated as a unit. Its branches retain different kinds of agency and knowledge while carrying different responsibility for the actual field of salvation.

### 12.3.2 Prayer
Petition is the most concrete doctrine here: not only a proposition to be believed but a practice to be performed. Someone in trouble asks in the confidence that the asking is heard and can bear on what happens next. That is transactive prayer’s distinctive claim. Contemplation, lament, praise, remembrance, confession, and the transformation of the one who prays may remain valuable without it. The question here is narrower: what must be true for a petition to make a difference beyond the petitioner?

Classical petition presupposes three things at once: a personal listener who can be addressed, responsiveness by which the request can count as a reason, and causal efficacy by which a response can bear on the world. Sophisticated accounts don’t imagine an omniscient being learning new information or an immutable being changing its mind. For Aquinas, prayer is among the means already contained in providence. Stump argues that even a perfect being might condition some goods on their being requested, preserving the relational good of asking; Swinburne extends the account to creaturely responsibility for others; and Molinist accounts place prayers and their answers within an eternal ordering of counterfactual circumstances (Stump 1979; Murray and Meyers 1994; Davison 2017). These models avoid a crude change-of-mind objection, but they don’t eliminate the need to say how the petition figures in the explanation of the outcome.

The empirical evidence bears only where the claim is operationalized. The STEP trial randomized 1,802 patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery among groups that did or didn’t receive remote intercessory prayer and that did or didn’t know whether prayer was certain. Complications occurred in 52 percent of the uncertain-but-prayed-for group and 51 percent of the uncertain-and-not-prayed-for group; the group certain of prayer had more complications, at 59 percent (Benson et al. 2006). The study therefore found no benefit attributable to prayer under that protocol. It didn’t test every kind of prayer, every proposed divine reason for acting, or the existence of an addressee. Its force is correspondingly exact: a specified, measurable intercessory claim failed in the setting designed to detect it. A theology that makes no comparable prediction isn’t refuted by STEP, but neither may it cite ordinary recovery as though the experiment had confirmed a causal transaction.

This specification blocks two easy overstatements. First, the alternatives aren’t merely inaction or coercion. Changed circumstances, persuasion, noncoercive influence, concurrence, and providential prearrangement are genuine middle positions. They preserve different amounts of creaturely agency and divine control, and they incur different burdens. A prayer for another person’s freely chosen reconciliation, for example, may be met by an opportunity, a reason, or an altered circumstance without guaranteeing the choice. The defender hasn’t thereby overridden the person; the defender has instead accepted that the petition’s requested result may still fail. If the result is guaranteed through determination, the agency cost returns.

Second, compatibility with every possible outcome isn’t automatically incoherence. A doctrine may distinguish granted, denied, delayed, or transformed requests by reasons unavailable to the petitioner. The evidential problem arises when those classifications have no independent criteria: success counts for the doctrine, failure can’t count against it, and the same outcome may be claimed as confirmation by adherents of incompatible traditions. In that case the experience may remain religiously significant, but its felt character alone doesn’t identify the addressee or establish that the petition caused the outcome. A contrastive criterion need not be a laboratory prediction; it does need to explain what the claim excludes.

The Abrahamic traditions don’t formulate this problem identically. Christian accounts range from prayer as a providentially appointed means to open-theist models on which some divine responses aren’t eternally settled. Jewish *tefillah* includes fixed communal petition, spontaneous request, lament, praise, and practices of *kavvanah* or directed attention; contemporary Jewish treatments therefore dispute both what an answer would be and what evidence petition could supply (Oren 2025). Islamic *du’a* is grounded in scriptural promises of response, while classical exegetes and Sufi writers distinguish response from the exact grant requested: an answer may instead avert harm, supply another good, be delayed, or consist in the relation enacted by asking. The same literature confronts the relation between supplication, divine decree, and acceptance of what God wills (Khalil 2011). These aren’t interchangeable doctrines. What they share, when an external answer is claimed, is the need to specify how asking figures in the explanation.

That shared burden reaches the metaphysics only conditionally. Under a wholly structureless active-ground model, a determinate listener, responsiveness, and causal relation can’t be treated as cost-free descriptions. A theology retaining them must meet the Chapter 11 burdens (§11.1; §11.7.3). A strict apophatic theology can’t withdraw every predicate and then rely on hearing, considering, or responding as positive explanatory features (§10.2.2; §10.3.2). Embedded, process, open, and other nonclassical models may retain a real relation by revising different portions of the classical inventory; the present argument doesn’t erase those differences.

*The reflexive petition.* One case sits apart from the rest, because it is the form in which petition is most often pressed on someone who doesn’t yet believe: a conditional request that the addressee, if real, disclose themselves and bring the petitioner to the truth. Its attraction is that it appears costless and appears to presuppose nothing. Two features complicate that.

First, the practice is ordinarily commended together with a prediction—that such a request isn’t refused—and a prediction has to be scored against the cases where the request was made and the disclosure didn’t follow. Those cases exist in quantity and aren’t collected. Petitioners who arrived where the practice recommends are visible, recount the arrival, and are counted; petitioners who asked over long periods and left leave no comparable record, and their departure removes them from the community that would otherwise register it. This is the denominator requirement that governs any selected-success argument (§10.1.16), applied to a practice rather than to a dossier. The replies available for the unanswered cases—insufficient sincerity, unacknowledged resistance, a different timetable, grace still operating unseen—are each compatible with the outcome either way, which by The Explanatory Burden is precisely what prevents the answered cases from being cited as evidence.

Second, this is the one petition whose success is measured by a change in the petitioner. Where a request concerns another person’s recovery, the transaction reading and the changes-only-the-petitioner reading predict different observables. Here they predict the same one. Sustained attention to a question, in a posture of openness, among people who hold the answer, is a process with well-understood effects on what comes to seem true, and those effects are expected on every account of what prayer is. The conversion that follows therefore doesn’t discriminate between the horns of the specification above.

**[Dissolution]**

**The Reflexive Petition Does Not Discriminate** · *Dissolution*

A petition asking that the addressee disclose themselves to the petitioner cannot serve as a test of the addressee’s existence or responsiveness. Its success condition is a change in the petitioner, which the transactive and petitioner-only readings both predict; its failures are unregistered, since those they befall characteristically leave the practice; and the explanations offered for those failures are available whatever the outcome. The practice may be recommended on other grounds and may be undertaken sincerely. What it cannot do is supply the discrimination its conditional framing appears to offer.

**Dissolves:** the use of conditional or exploratory petition as evidence bearing on the existence or responsiveness of the one petitioned

*Scope.* The dissolution concerns the evidential use of the practice, not its permissibility, its value to the petitioner, or whether any petition is answered. It doesn’t claim that those who report arriving by this route are insincere or mistaken about their own histories.

**Depends on:** The Explanatory Burden (§12); The Asking Problem (§12.3.2)

The boundary is therefore not between prayer and no prayer. It is between an external transaction and the wider practice in which petition occurs. Attention, alignment, lament, remembrance, and transformation can survive independently of a demonstrated external causal line. Where a tradition claims more—an outcome brought about partly because someone asked—the Petitionary-Prayer Specification identifies what must be supplied. It doesn’t pronounce a verdict in advance.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Asking Problem** · *Disjunction*

If petition affects something beyond the petitioner, what role does it play?

- **If petition contributes to the outcome,** then a good that was withheld until asked for was not being given on need—the asking did work the need alone did not, and a perfectly good giver has no reason to hold a good back for that. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.
- **If it operates within a fixed providential order,** then it must still say what the petition contributes and why that contribution belongs in the order. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.
- **If it influences without determining,** then agency is preserved. But the influence cannot by itself guarantee another person’s choice and still bears questions of permission and proportionality.
- **If it determines the choice or outcome,** then the result can be secured. But the choice was never really the petitioner’s to have gone otherwise—it was the decree’s. *Priced by* The Chosen History Problem (§12.3.1).
- **If it changes only the petitioner,** then alignment, consolation, or transformation may be genuine goods. But the claim is no longer one of external transaction.

External petition must make a specified difference, accept that the requested result may fail, or purchase the result with control. Without one of those, *answered* names the outcome after the fact rather than explaining it.

*Scope.* The disjunction doesn’t assume that divine action must compete with creaturely causation, nor that every answer must be publicly detectable. It requires only that a claimed external answer have some intelligible explanatory role. Contemplative and encounter dimensions of prayer are outside its target.

### 12.3.3 Miracles

Miracles complete the divine-action movement begun by Providence and Prayer. Providence fixed how a theology distributes control between divine and creaturely causes. Prayer fixed the possible role of a petition in an outcome. A miracle claim adds two further commitments: that an event departs from the relevant ordinary order because of divine action, and, where the event functions as a sign, that it identifies or authenticates a source, messenger, or message. A theology may retain both commitments, only the first, or neither. The burdens differ accordingly.

The classical account doesn’t reduce a miracle to whatever surprises an observer. Aquinas distinguishes events beyond the commonly observed order of nature from events whose cause is merely unknown, and ranks miracles by whether nature could never produce the effect, could produce its kind but not in that sequence, or could produce it naturally but didn’t do so in this instance (*SCG* III.101; *ST* I.105.7). The cause, on that account, is divine even where the effect—rain or recovery from fever—could otherwise occur naturally. Swinburne’s modern account likewise resists a crude violation model: a miracle may be a non-repeatable counter-instance to a law whose recurrence would instead prompt revision of the law (Swinburne 1970). The target is therefore not one doctrine. It includes an event beyond created powers, an exceptional exercise of providence through created causes, and a sign whose timing and context are held to disclose divine intention.

Hume’s question enters only after the claimed event is specified. His maxim isn’t that testimony is logically incapable of establishing a miracle. It is that testimony suffices only if its falsehood would be more extraordinary than the event reported; he then argues that religious miracle testimony has never met that comparative bar (Hume (1748) 1999, §X). A defender may reject Hume’s weighting, argue that background theism changes the prior probability, add independent physical or historical evidence, or contest whether a law has been violated at all. Those replies remain live here. The evidential task is still contrastive: the evidence must favor the reported event over mistake, embellishment, fraud, psychosomatic change, unknown ordinary causation, and other alternatives appropriate to the case. Establishing occurrence wouldn’t yet establish divine causation.

A law-anomalous event isn’t contradictory merely because it is anomalous. No doctrine tested here has to treat this universe’s observed regularities as exceptionless metaphysical truths. Walking on water, sudden healing, or a sea’s division would still be events with times, places, subjects, and changes to explain. The first question is therefore whether the event occurred; the next questions are what caused it and what, if anything, that cause authenticates. Calling the event unfamiliar settles none of the three.

The causal account then divides. If divine intervention is a temporal or responsive operation, it bears the Conditions at the operation and can’t be their exterior, self-subsistent ground. If the effect proceeds from one atemporal divine act, the event remains concrete while the proposed cause inherits the Grounding-Contact Trilemma: the theology must explain how that act is determinately related to this effect, here and now, rather than merely redescribing the whole order as eternally willed (§10.4). Concurrent and sacramental accounts may deny that God interrupts a closed natural sequence at all; they preserve divine causation by making it operate through or at another explanatory level from created causes. That avoids a competition model, but it still owes the contrast between an event that specially manifests divine action and an ordinary event equally sustained by God. Cessationism or a denial of public signs exits that burden by declining the present authentication claim.

Grant occurrence and divine causation, and authentication remains a further inference. The deed-type alone doesn’t identify its source. The Gospel tradition itself acknowledges rival exorcists (Matt 12:27; Luke 11:19) and warns that false messiahs and prophets may produce signs (Matt 24:24; Mark 13:22). The Torah instructs Israel not to follow a wonder-worker toward other gods even when the announced sign occurs (Deut 13:1–5). Josephus reports Eleazar performing an exorcism before a Roman audience, while Tacitus and Suetonius report Vespasian healing blindness with spittle, a medium also appearing in Mark’s healing narrative (Mark 8:23). (Josephus, *Antiquities* 8.46–48; Tacitus, *Histories* 4.81; Suetonius, *Vespasian* 7; Mark 8:23. The point is shared kinds of deed, not a biography of where Jesus learned them.) These comparisons don’t show that the Gospel deeds failed to occur or had an ordinary cause. They show that exorcism, healing, and wonder aren’t source-unique categories.

Islamic accounts make the distinction in another form. A *mu’jiza* isn’t merely an anomaly but a sign associated with prophetic truth, while the Qur’an resists treating a demanded spectacle as the prophet’s possession: signs belong to God, and the recited Book is offered as the standing evidence (Qur’an 29:50–51). Judaism, Christianity, and Islam therefore disagree about which signs authenticate which messengers, but none is well described by the bare inference *extraordinary event, therefore my doctrine*. Their own resources place antecedent revelation, moral and doctrinal fit, prophetic commission, or the character of the sign between event and identification. Those resources may strengthen a cumulative case. They also mean the event isn’t performing the identification alone.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Sign–Source Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

If a miracle is offered as proof, what identifies its source?

- **If the extraordinary deed itself identifies the source,** then the deed cannot discriminate among rival agents and traditions that report the same kinds of signs. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden. *Priced by* The Natural-Reach Fork (§10.1.16).
- **If independent features identify it,** then it is those features doing the work, not the event being extraordinary. Prior teaching, context, what was predicted, the character of the claimant, or independent witnesses may tell one source from another. Whatever weight they carry is the weight the case has. *Feeds into* The Concreteness Ceiling (§10.1.16).

A miracle may contribute to a cumulative case. It cannot authenticate a unique source merely by being called miraculous.

*Scope.* This dilemma grants that the event occurred and may even grant divine causation. It tests only the further use of the event as evidence for a uniquely identified messenger, revelation, or doctrine.

The argument therefore yields no universal verdict on miracles. An event beyond the Conditions is incoherent as an event; a law-anomalous event within them isn’t. A temporal intervener incurs the Conditions, while an atemporal cause owes the determinate contact. Historical occurrence remains an evidential question, and divine causation remains a causal one. Authentication succeeds only to the degree that the total evidence discriminates this source and message from the available alternatives. Keeping those stages separate preserves what a miracle claim may establish without letting one stage silently perform the work of all three. The positive evidential case is argued directly at §10.1.16: what religious experience and a cumulative miracle record can establish before the authentication question is reached.

### 12.3.4 Scripture

Revelation has two ends. God may speak, but a word only lands if someone is there to receive it, hold it, carry it, and read it, and every one of those is a human act. Doctrines of Scripture assign different strengths to that relation: inspired witness, providential canon, infallibility on saving matters, or comprehensive inerrancy, on which the text is true in all it affirms. The Princeton theologians Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield gave modern Protestant inerrancy a rigorous form, and the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) its confessional one, locating strict inspiration in the original autographs (the original manuscripts, before any copying). The argument therefore doesn’t ask whether one undifferentiated doctrine survived. It asks what is protected at the sending end, what is claimed at the receiving end, and what warrants the transfer between them.

The doctrine of Scripture relies partly on the account of revelation given at §11.8.4. That account argues that traditional deliveries bear recognizable human and historical mediation, while a proposed extra-natural source must show what distinctive explanatory work it adds. Human transmission introduces opportunities for fallibility and underdetermination; it doesn’t by itself prove that no divine source was involved. Scripture makes the question unusually explicit because the proposed delivery has separable stages: memory, testimony, composition, transmission, canonization, translation, and reading. Different doctrines protect different stages. Inerrancy of an autograph, preservation of a consonantal text, providential canon formation, and reliable translation aren’t one claim, and confidence warranted at one stage doesn’t automatically transfer to the next.

Christianity’s central revealer adds a prior design question at the sending end. No surviving canonical text presents itself as a document Jesus authored for later readers; even John depicts Jesus writing only unidentified marks on the ground (John 8:6–8). His teaching reaches the world through remembered speech, oral transmission, later composition, copying, canonization, and translation. An incarnational or ecclesial account may treat that human chain as the intended medium rather than a defect: a teacher forms witnesses and a community rather than depositing a manual, and an oral culture need not privilege private authorship as a modern reader does. The reply explains why an authored book wasn’t necessary. It doesn’t yet explain why a universally consequential message was better entrusted to a route that makes every later reader depend on disputed memories, authorship, selection, and interpretation when, on the doctrine’s own account, the revealer could have supplied a durable, publicly authenticated statement without those initial layers. The absence of such a statement isn’t evidence that Jesus was unable to write and doesn’t prove that the transmitted message is false. It makes the chosen delivery architecture part of the explanatory burden: what good the mediated route secures, why that good required leaving no authored standard, and what warrants confidence that the chain preserved the claims on which salvation or doctrine is made to depend.

Take comprehensive inerrancy: an inerrant Word, true in all it affirms. The Pentateuch doesn’t contain one blanket sentence asserting that Moses wrote every line. It repeatedly associates Moses with particular laws, speeches, and written materials, while also containing a notice of his death, the name Dan, and the retrospective phrase “before any king reigned over the Israelites” (Deut 34; Gen 14:14; 36:31). Later Jewish and Christian texts can conventionally ascribe the Torah or its law to Moses (Acts 3:22; 7:37; John 5:46–47; Mark 12:26) without thereby deciding the compositional history of every verse. Composite and post-Mosaic features therefore burden a doctrine of comprehensive Mosaic authorship or unmediated dictation; they don’t by themselves refute inspiration, Mosaic legal authority, or a providentially formed canon. Manuscript variation makes the same distinction necessary at the receiving end: wording is critically reconstructed from witnesses whose scribes sometimes erred or harmonized (Ehrman 2005), but that fact bears differently on exact verbal identity, substantial preservation, and theological reliability.

The same distinction is pressed from inside the narrative, at the other end of the citation. Where the Gospels report Jesus arguing from scripture, the wording quoted is frequently the Septuagint’s, and in several places that wording carries the argument while the Hebrew tradition doesn’t. Answering the Corban objection he charges his opponents with “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Mark 7:6–7), which is Isa 29:13 in Greek; the Hebrew of the verse says their fear of God is a commandment of men learned by rote, which doesn’t deliver that charge. Defending the children in the temple he cites “out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise” (Matt 21:16), where the Hebrew of Ps 8:2 has founded strength rather than prepared praise, and only praise answers the objection raised. The Nazareth declaration reads “recovery of sight to the blind” from Isa 61:1 (Luke 4:18), where the Hebrew has the opening of the prison to those who are bound.

Two constraints keep the observation from proving more than it does. The Septuagint isn’t simply a departure from an original: it sometimes translates a Hebrew text older than the Masoretic one—at Deut 32:43, in portions of Samuel, and behind the shorter Hebrew edition of Jeremiah—so which reading is prior has to be argued case by case rather than assumed. And the Gospels are Greek compositions throughout, so the form of a quotation is evidence about the evangelist’s text at least as directly as about the speaker’s. What survives both constraints is narrower, and is the part that bears here: the narrative presents divine speech whose force depends on a wording that one branch of the textual tradition carries and another doesn’t. A doctrine locating inspiration in the words rather than in the substance therefore owes an account of which words those were. Accommodation, genre, and joint divine and human authorship (traditionally, concursive authorship) are each available in reply—they are the same family of moves set out below—but each locates inspiration somewhere other than the wording the reported argument is using, which is the commitment comprehensive inerrancy was introduced to protect.

A second kind of check compares narrative scale with the external record. The exodus is a founding national narrative, while no Egyptian text independently records the mass departure described at its largest scriptural scale; the Merneptah stele instead attests a people called Israel in Canaan (Finkelstein and Silberman 2001). Silence isn’t disproof, especially for smaller or differently constituted movements, and Egyptian royal records weren’t neutral administrative archives of every loss. The pressure is proportional: the larger and more publicly disruptive the claimed event, the more historical work a no-trace account must do. A reduced historical core may remain possible, but it is then that reduced claim—not the largest narrative numbers—that has been defended.

The birth narratives supply a more localized historical test. Matthew places the birth under Herod the Great; Luke associates it with the census under Quirinius, conventionally dated to 6 CE, roughly a decade after Herod’s death in 4 BCE and later still than any birth placed earlier within Herod’s reign (Brown 1993). Matthew’s order that boys two and under be killed may allow an earlier birth, since the cutoff is keyed to the time Herod elicited from the Magi (Matt 2:7, 16), but it doesn’t fix Jesus’s age: the range may be precautionary, and Matthew gives no duration for the stay in Egypt. Neither the cutoff nor the flight can therefore be converted into a determinate number of additional years; they can widen the discrepancy under some reconstructions but can’t date it exactly. Defenders propose an earlier administrative role for Quirinius, translate Luke’s phrase as a census “before” his governorship, or distinguish the registration from the later census; those harmonizations are possible readings but require historical support beyond the narratives themselves. The two itineraries aren’t a formal contradiction. Matthew narrates a house in Bethlehem, flight to Egypt, and later settlement in Nazareth; Luke narrates temple observances and return to Nazareth without mentioning Egypt (Matt 2:11–23; Luke 2:4–39). Silence can conceal an interval. The evidential pressure is that each author constructs a different route connecting Bethlehem and Nazareth, not that omission alone makes their paths logically incompatible (Brown 1993).

The autographs aren’t the doctrine’s only resource, and interpretive commitments do much of the work. *Accommodation* holds that God addresses human capacity in the frame and idiom of an audience. *Phenomenological language* distinguishes description as observed from scientific assertion. *Genre* denies that poetry, apocalypse, hyperbole, approximation, and ancient historiography affirm what a flat literal reading assigns them. *Concursive* or dual authorship treats God and the human writer as authors at different explanatory levels. These are principled hermeneutical positions, not admissions of error, and the Chicago Statement itself invokes genre and ordinary language while locating strict inspiration in the autographic text (1978).

Taken singly each is reasonable, and the pattern only becomes visible when they are taken together. Inerrancy is the claim that scripture is true in all that it *affirms*, and each defense works by narrowing the affirmation set: accommodation moves the frame out of it, phenomenological language moves the observations out, genre moves the form out, and concursive authorship moves the human features out in advance. The doctrine is protected, and what it is protected by is a shrinking of what it says. The cost surfaces when one asks how the affirmation set is fixed. If it can be settled independently and in advance—here is what this text affirms, before we check—the doctrine remains testable and the defenses are legitimate refinements. If it is settled by what turns out to be the case, so that whatever survives inspection was affirmed and whatever doesn’t was accommodation, idiom, or genre, then the doctrine is preserved against every test by being placed beyond all of them.

Autographic inerrancy isn’t simply an ad hoc retreat: it follows from a doctrine on which inspiration attaches to the authors’ production rather than every later act of copying. The cost is epistemic rather than automatically logical. Because no autograph is extant, inerrancy is assigned to objects unavailable for direct inspection. The Chicago account replies that their wording can be recovered with great accuracy and that copies and translations carry authority insofar as they faithfully represent it (1978). The resulting question is therefore graded: how much uncertainty remains at each disputed reading, and does any load-bearing doctrine depend on the uncertain residue? Perfect originals wouldn’t warrant perfect confidence at the destination without a correspondingly reliable account of transmission, canon, translation, and interpretation.

A further question sits behind transmission: what communicative end the text was meant to secure. Sufficiency, clarity, inerrancy, and universal convergence are different theses. A canon might be sufficient for a church’s teaching office without being equally clear to every unaided reader; it might disclose enough for salvation while leaving metaphysics contested; it might form a tradition through argument rather than terminate argument. Persistent disagreement therefore doesn’t refute inspiration by itself. It presses sets claiming that a maximally competent source intended the text, without an indispensable interpretive authority or supplementary revelation, to secure clear and convergent belief on the very matters over which responsible readers remain divided.

Context dependence carries a related tradeoff. A historically embodied address can display particularity, narrative continuity, communal memory, and responsiveness to an audience that an abstract list of context-free propositions would lose. It also makes later understanding depend on linguistic, historical, and interpretive work. Omnipotence doesn’t entail that every communicative purpose is best served by maximal directness, and competence doesn’t entail maximizing one feature at every cost. The defensible question is comparative: given the ends a theology attributes to revelation, why was this balance of embodiment, clarity, accessibility, and dependence selected, and are the obscurities concentrated in matters the same theology calls necessary?

Source authentication adds another layer. Textual criticism, history, theology, communal authority, reported encounter, prophecy, miracle, and literary character are all used to identify a text as revelatory. Requiring interpretation or defense isn’t itself evidence against a divine source; much ordinary knowledge is mediated by expertise. Nor is a scientific fact embedded centuries early an obviously costless divine signature: its interpretation and provenance would themselves be contested. The narrower burden is discriminative. A claimed mark of source must favor the proposed source over literary achievement, communal formation, ordinary transmission, and rival revelation claims rather than merely coexist with them.

The dependency also falls unevenly on the audience. Text reaches literate readers before illiterate ones, readers of source languages before readers of translations, and readers with trained interpreters before those without the historical and doctrinal apparatus. That inequality isn’t automatically a communicative failure: oral recitation, communal teaching, translation, liturgy, and interpretive authority may be intended parts of the medium. It becomes a sharper problem for sets that make accurate explicit reception universally necessary while also claiming that the delivery was sufficient for all. For a set that attributes linguistic fragmentation to God’s act at Babel, the barrier is additionally priced by the Babel–Mission problem (§12.1.2). Pentecost, ordinary translation, and access-relative grace are distinct replies. Sufficiency can’t do more work than the selected model of audience, authority, and salvation allows.

The unevenness has a temporal axis as well. On an old-earth chronology, scriptural revelation arrives extremely late in cosmic history and long before technologies of near-instantaneous global distribution. That fact doesn’t by itself show mistiming: a Christian account may tie revelation to incarnation and a particular human history, a Jewish account to covenantal formation, and an Islamic account to a final recitation within an existing prophetic sequence. It does block one simple defense—that the date was selected because it maximized the message’s immediate reach.

One Christian answer appeals to the *fullness of time* (Gal 4:4), often glossed through Roman roads, widely used Greek, and imperial connectivity. Those conditions may explain unusually favorable first-century regional propagation; they don’t establish a global maximum. A fuller defense may instead claim that the timing balanced reach with incarnation, covenantal preparation, political conditions, or goods of ordinary human transmission. That is a legitimate multi-objective account, but it must name the ends being balanced. If people outside the message’s reach are saved through natural revelation, implicit faith, postmortem opportunity, or access-relative judgment, the access problem changes rather than disappears: the explicit message is no longer a universally necessary creature-side condition (§12.1.8).

**[Disjunction]**

**The Delivery Tradeoff** · *Disjunction*

Why was revelation delivered this way?

- **If the governing end is immediate reach,** then a first-century manuscript culture wasn’t the available maximum.
- **If it is historical embodiment or communal participation,** then the message arrives at the speed of history and community, so who receives it is settled by birthplace and era rather than by need or receptivity. Covenant, incarnation, community, or noncoercive transmission may justify a slower human channel; none of them makes the resulting distribution answer to anything about the people it reaches. *Feeds into* The Uniform Requirement Problem (§12.3.6). *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.
- **If it is an alternative route for the unreached,** then the access problem recedes. But explicit reception isn’t a universal creature-side condition.
- **If explicit reception is necessary,** then the distribution mechanism bears the resulting exclusion. *Feeds into* The Four Insufficiencies (§12.3.8).

The fork doesn’t show that revelation was impossible. It prevents one delivery advantage from being retained without its corresponding cost.

**Depends on:** The Salvation Specification Test (§12.1.8)

Warnings against trusting princes, flesh, or human wisdom aren’t bans on ordinary testimony or independent reasoning. In context they contrast ultimate or salvific reliance on human power with reliance on God; the same corpora routinely depend on witnesses, teachers, judges, scribes, and argument. They therefore don’t generate a contradiction merely because scripture reaches a reader through people. The real issue is calibration. A reader must rely provisionally on human authors, copyists, canonizers, translators, historians, and advocates before concluding that their product carries divine authority. The doctrine may justify that reliance through providence, communal authority, corroboration, or encounter, but it can’t erase the human evidential route by redescribing its endpoint as faith in God. Thomas and Paul show direct encounter within the Christian narrative (John 20:24–29; Acts 9:3–6); they establish that the narrative permits differentiated routes, not that every later believer was owed the same evidence.

The Christian testimony starts one step further back: Jesus left no known writing, and the accounts are works by later authors drawing on remembered, oral, and written materials. Luke’s prologue presents the Gospel as an investigation of earlier reports intended to give Theophilus assurance (Luke 1:1–4), which is neither a diary nor an admission of unreliability. Synoptic dependence means Matthew, Mark, and Luke cannot be counted as three wholly independent witnesses to every shared episode; it doesn’t make all their material one testimony or erase independent traditions proposed for Matthew and Luke. Historical confidence must therefore be assigned claim by claim, using date, source relation, genre, corroboration, and explanatory alternatives. The human shape of the evidence burdens a claim of self-authenticating certainty more directly than a modest claim of historically mediated testimony.

Jewish and Islamic scripture doctrines make different claims at these same stages. Maimonides’s eighth principle presents the Torah in Israel’s possession as received by Moses from God, with Moses writing as a scribe rather than composing on his own. That is a strong target for composite and post-Mosaic evidence. It isn’t the whole of Judaism: rabbinic discussion of the last verses of Deuteronomy and modern Jewish models of participatory, progressive, or historically mediated revelation distribute authorship differently (Sommer 2009). The pressure must therefore attach to the selected *Torah min HaShamayim* model, not to Jewish scripture as a single dictation theory.

In Islam, the Qur’an is recited as divine speech delivered through Muhammad, but preservation likewise has multiple objects: the recitation, the Uthmanic consonantal skeleton, canonical *qira’at*, or one exact vocalized wording. Early standardization and canonical reading plurality aren’t, within the tradition, simply scribal corruption. The lower text of the Sanaa palimpsest differs from the standard text in order and a number of readings (Sadeghi and Bergmann 2010), while the Uthmanic text became remarkably stable early. That evidence presses a model requiring one invariant written form before standardization more strongly than a model locating preservation in the authorized Uthmanic text and its canonical readings. It doesn’t by itself establish wholesale loss or disprove the Qur’an’s divine origin.

Strong doctrines of exact, inerrant, self-authenticating scripture face substantial historical and textual burdens. Weaker inspiration, providential-canon, communal-authority, and theological-witness models surrender some of those properties and must be assessed on what they retain. Human mediation doesn’t establish that no divine source was involved; it prevents source perfection from being transferred without argument to every stage of reception. Scripture remains available as literature, moral inheritance, theological witness, liturgical center, and an object of critical inquiry. Its moral and doctrinal claims can then be examined on their merits, while any stronger claim of divine speech carries the specific delivery, preservation, access, and discrimination burdens identified here (§11.8.4).

### 12.3.5 Prophecy
