Prophecy is the claim that a divine source can mark its word in advance of ordinary human knowledge. A text that genuinely foretold a specific event it couldn’t otherwise have known would be evidence of an author outside the human horizon, and could therefore be offered as authentication for revelation. The question isn’t whether ancient texts contain warnings, hopes, or imaginatively powerful anticipations. It is whether the cited cases have the historical form necessary for a prediction to function as evidence rather than as a later interpretation of an already known event.

Prophetic arguments carry a demanding sequence: the text must be demonstrably prior to the event; its meaning must be determinate before the event; the event must fit it more closely than competing events; and the correspondence must be neither self-produced nor selected from a larger field of failures. Any one condition can fail without showing that every prophetic utterance is worthless. But the argument needs enough successes under those conditions to make an extra-human source the best explanation.

The book’s account of revelation (§11.8.4) already removes the presumption that a humanly mediated message has a source outside the human field. Prophecy supplies a proposed exception: a pattern within the textual record that would require such a source. It is therefore assessed on its historical merits rather than dismissed by the general result alone. A genuine foretelling would matter. The issue is whether the texts cited actually bear that form.

A claim of fulfilled prophecy is an arrow in a target, and the question is whether the target was fixed before the arrow landed. Ezekiel’s Tyre oracle illustrates why each case needs its own textual model. Verses 7–11 name Nebuchadnezzar and use a singular agent; verse 12 shifts to a plural, which defenders relate to the “many nations” announced earlier and sometimes extend through Alexander’s later siege. On that corporate or sequential reading, the oracle need not assign every action to Nebuchadnezzar alone. The counterpressure comes from Ezek 29:17–20, which says his army received no wages from Tyre and assigns Egypt as compensation, and from the absolute language that Tyre would become bare rock and never be rebuilt. (Ezek 26:5, 7–14, 19–21; 29:17–20; (Block 1998). The oracle names Nebuchadnezzar (26:7). Chapter 29 is the text’s own record that he received no plunder. Alexander’s mole of 332 BCE is a later campaign by a king the oracle doesn’t name, against a city that was rebuilt and remains.) The case is therefore not a one-line failed prediction. Its evidential value turns on whether the plural naturally widens the agent in advance, how prophetic destruction idiom functions, and whether a centuries-later campaign and a continuing city satisfy the oracle more specifically than retrospective combination would.

The New Testament’s imminent-return sayings likewise remain a problem for readings that treat “this generation” as a dated forecast rather than apocalyptic rhetoric (Matt 24:34; Mark 13:30) (Allison 1985). The text supplies its own test for exactly this failure: a prophet who speaks in the Lord’s name and isn’t borne out by events has, on the law’s own terms, spoken a word the Lord didn’t command (Deut 18:20–22), and that test wasn’t written with an exemption for predictions later reinterpreted as figurative once the deadline passed. The signs offered as indicators of that end fail a prior condition. Wars and rumors of wars, nation against nation, famines, earthquakes, and false messiahs (Mark 13:7–8; Matt 24:6–8) are the standing weather of history, not a signature of one age. A forecast confirmed by whatever happens next hasn’t named the future; it has described the world as it already was.

Other cases raise the date question directly. On the dominant critical reading, Daniel’s visions track the Seleucid period with increasing specificity through the Maccabean crisis and then diverge from the history of Antiochus IV’s end, a pattern taken to locate the visions in the second century BCE. ((Collins 1993). On the critical reading of the seventy weeks (Dan 9:24–27) within the Antiochene crisis and the disputed decrees used as chronological starting points.) Traditional readings defend a sixth-century core and treat the accuracy as prediction. The argument from prophecy can’t simply assume either dating: manuscript evidence, language, historical allusion, genre, and the point at which the fit changes must carry it. The seventy weeks of Dan 9 adds disputed starting decrees and candidate referents. A countdown reaches Jesus only after those choices are defended rather than read off an uncontested timetable.

Still others are self-fulfilling: a figure who knows the script can stage the entry on the donkey to match it, and the citation is selective besides—Matthew quotes Zech 9:9 for the donkey but stops before verse 10, which describes the same king ending war and ruling from sea to sea, a reign the arrival didn’t bring (Zech 9:9–10).

Some proofs count the hits and set aside messianic criteria such as world peace, an ended exile, and a standing Davidic throne (Isa 2:1–4; 11:1–9; Ezek 37:24–28). One unmet promise doesn’t depend on the messianic question at all. The same oracle that guarantees David a man on the throne guarantees, in the next breath, that “the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to make grain offerings, and to make sacrifices for all time” (Jer 33:17–18). The sacrificial cult ended in 70 CE and hasn’t resumed. That is an unconditional promise, stated without an internal qualifier, and its failure bears on the text’s reliability whatever one concludes about any candidate.

Others depend on later Christological readings not uniquely fixed by the original setting. Isa 7:14 uses *almah* in Ahaz’s crisis, while Matthew follows the Septuagint’s *parthenos* (Brown 1993). Isa 49:3 names Israel as servant, yet nearby passages also distinguish a servant who restores Israel, leaving collective, individual, and representative readings in dispute. The perfect forms in Isa 53 don’t by grammar alone settle past versus future reference; Hebrew aspect and the so-called prophetic perfect must be interpreted with discourse and context. Ps 22:16/17 has a genuine textual problem: the Masoretic reading is commonly rendered “like a lion,” the Septuagint has “dug/pierced,” and Hebrew manuscript evidence has been invoked on both sides. Luke 4:18 follows the Septuagintal form of Isa 61:1. These facts don’t make Christological interpretation impossible. They prevent the source text’s prior, determinate sense from being treated as uncontested evidence without a textual and hermeneutical argument. (Isa 7:14; 23:4, 12; 47:1; 49:3; 53; 61:1; Ps 22:16; Luke 4:18; Matt 1:23; 2:15, 17–18, 23; Hos 11:1; Mic 5:2; Jer 31:15; Rom 1:3; Gal 4:4.)

The earliest letters don’t mention a virginal conception. Paul’s “born of a woman” and “seed of David according to the flesh” (Gal 4:4; Rom 1:3) are compatible with ordinary descent, but silence in occasional letters isn’t a denial, and legal or maternal descent can be proposed for Davidic lineage. The silence is therefore evidence to be weighed, not a contradiction that settles the tradition. The broader standard remains: date, prior sense, causal independence, and comparative fit must be established before a passage can authenticate revelation.

Matthew’s infancy citations are the same bar applied to a childhood itinerary. Hos 11:1 is Israel’s exodus, past tense, a nation already called; Mic 5:2 is a Davidic hope from Bethlehem under Assyria, not a birth notice; Jer 31:15 is Rachel weeping for the exile. None of them names a future child. “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matt 2:23) cites prophets who did not say it (Brown 1993).

Revelation applies the same bar from the other direction. The seven hills strongly evoke Rome, and 666—alongside the 616 variant—fits forms of *Nero Caesar* in Hebrew gematria; Nero-*redivivus* readings also make sense of a beast that “was, and is not, and is about to come” (Rev 17:8). ((Yarbro Collins 1984). 666 fits *Neron Kaisar* in Hebrew letters; 616 fits the Latinizing *Nero Caesar* without the final nun. The seven hills are Rev 17:9. Neronic and Domitianic datings affect how that symbolism is situated and don’t eliminate wider interpretive disputes.) Composition under Nero, under Domitian with a Neronic symbol, and more futurist or multilevel readings remain disputed. The Roman referent is therefore a strong historical anchor, not a demonstration that every image is exhausted by one emperor or that no future application is possible. What it blocks is scoring a modern fulfillment while ignoring a determinate first-century referent that already explains the identifying features.

The second condition is where the tradition pushes back, and it does so with a developed hermeneutic rather than a concession. On the *typological* reading, a prophecy need not have one determinate referent fixed in advance: an utterance can have a near fulfillment in its own setting and a fuller one later, the first standing to the second as pattern to realization, and a God who authors history as well as text can intend both. *Sensus plenior* names the same thought from the author’s side—a fuller sense present in the words and intended by their divine author, though not accessible to the human writer who wrote them. Neither is invented to rescue awkward cases; the New Testament uses the method openly, reading Hosea’s “out of Egypt I called my son” (11:1), a plain backward reference to the exodus, as spoken of Christ (Matt 2:15), which shows the writers weren’t claiming the single-referent model the objection assumes.

Granting the method changes what the argument can be used for. Typology isn’t unconstrained: traditions appeal to recurring patterns, canonical relations, and theological continuity rather than licensing any later association whatever. But a fuller sense unavailable before the event can’t independently predict that event for a public evidential test. It may support a retrospective theological interpretation once the divine-author premise is already in place; it can’t establish that premise by the same fit without circularity. A tradition may therefore retain both typology and prophecy, but it must identify which passages bear a prior predictive sense and which acquire their fuller evidential role only within an accepted canon.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Fulfillment Timing Problem** · *Disjunction*

Was the meaning there beforehand, or fixed by the event?

- **If the meaning was available beforehand,** then the prediction counts only once four further conditions are met. If the text predates the event, its relevant sense was already available, the fit discriminates this event from competitors, actors did not manufacture the correspondence by following the text, and misses are counted, the prediction supplies evidence whose strength tracks support for those conditions.
- **If it was fixed through the event afterward,** then the fulfillment is retrospective fit. Typology and *sensus plenior* may remain coherent theological readings, but a meaning disclosed only through the alleged fulfillment cannot also serve as its independent advance prediction. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.

Advance prediction must be available before the event. Meaning supplied by the event may remain theological fulfillment, but it cannot also be independent evidence for that event.

*Scope.* The dilemma tests prophecy as public evidence. It doesn’t deny the moral, political, liturgical, typological, or theological value of prophetic literature, and it doesn’t assume in advance that every cited case fails.

Islam’s corresponding authentication claim prominently includes *i’jaz*: the doctrine that the Qur’an exceeds human capacity and that its inimitability authenticates Muhammad’s prophethood, framed by the Qur’an’s own challenge to produce something comparable (Qur’an 2:23–24; 17:88). (Qur’an 2:23–24; 17:88; (Harb 2020).) Defenders don’t appeal only to private taste; they identify composition, rhetoric, semantic density, linguistic form, and the historical inability of challengers to match the text. The evidential burden is to state a comparison class, success criterion, competent judges, and possible defeater that don’t presuppose the authority being tested. Without them, admiration and unmatched status may be sincere and culturally consequential while remaining unable to discriminate divine from extraordinary human authorship. This is a different authentication problem from prediction, not a failed Christian prophecy argument under another name.

Prophecy can support a revelation claim only where its date, meaning, independence, and fit are independently established. The historical cases most often used as proof instead require late composition, a coded present sold as a future, nonspecific signs that obtain in every generation, selective fulfillment, self-fulfillment, or retrospective rereading to be ruled out case by case. This leaves prophetic literature available as moral, political, poetic, and theological inheritance; it doesn’t yield an automatic evidential bridge from ancient text to an external author.

### 12.3.6 Divine Hiddenness
The argument from divine hiddenness is, alongside the evidential argument from evil, one of the contemporary arguments against a perfectly loving God. It presses a God said to love as a parent loves and to want to be known, and asks why, on that description, the wanting isn’t evident to those who are looking for it—the case turning not on the obstinate but on the *non-resistant* unbeliever, who would believe if the evidence were there and doesn’t. The hiddenness case isn’t re-argued here from first principles. What is tested is the direct-refusal reply, against what the tradition’s own defenders of the demand to believe have already conceded about belief, and with indirect epistemic responsibility left in view. Two kinds of consideration run through the case and don’t support one conclusion. One is diagnostic: a genealogy of the inference from awe to a hidden author, bounded so that it doesn’t debunk belief indiscriminately, and evidence that the faculty said to make God plain is unevenly distributed. The other is Schellenberg’s internal argument, which turns on whether non-resistant nonbelievers exist and would stand if both diagnostics were set aside.

*What hiddenness names.* Before the argument is met on its own terms, what is the hiddenness in question? The believer and the unbeliever stand before one situation, not two: the grandeur of things is manifest and inescapable, and no God is visible within it. The hiddenness-arguer takes that silence to tell against a loving God; the believer takes the awe the grandeur provokes to be a *trace* of one. They split on the verdict but share the frame—each treats the situation as evidence bearing on a hidden author behind things, a sign that either points past itself or fails to. In neither case is the awe itself what hides—it is the most present datum a person has; what hides is the *explainer* the grandeur is taken to require, whether reached by inference or, on the reformed-epistemology variant, taken as given in the experience itself. Hiddenness is the hiddenness of a posited cause, not of a missing object.

It is that shared frame (that the grandeur, or its silence, points past itself to a transcendent author) that the book’s central result cancels. On the inversion the grandeur isn’t a pointer to a hidden source but the manifest face of the ground itself; and a ground that conditions every moment of existence, and does so necessarily (§11.1; §11.2.1), is the least hidden thing there is. The relocation isn’t foreign to the hiddenness-arguer’s own trajectory: a non-personal ultimate is what Schellenberg’s later ultimism names, and the inversion arguably reaches that destination by another line. Two senses of *hidden* must not be run together here: the ground is *ontologically* manifest (it conditions everything and couldn’t fail to) even where a *personal* God remains *epistemically* unevidenced; so ‘least hidden’ answers the awe-as-sign construal of hiddenness without yet touching the relationship-grade-evidence construal Schellenberg presses.

The religious response errs not in registering the greatness, which is real, but in posting it to a transcendent bearer rather than to the ground whose face it already is—the awe is veridical, responsive to something real, but its address is mistaken. The misaddressing isn’t an ad hoc charge but a predicted one: the native dispositions (a hair-trigger for agency, a bent toward purpose) deliver just this overshoot from felt grandeur to an inferred *person* (Barrett 2004; Kelemen 2004). Once that overshoot is seen as the dispositions’ own contribution, the awe’s standing as a *sign* falls with it.

Calling the address mistaken might still leave the grandeur looking like a message that merely reached the wrong recipient; the sharper point is that its message-character was never read off the grandeur in the first place. What the dispositions supply isn’t a destination but the sense that there is anything there to be addressed—that the grandeur points beyond itself, that it is *for* someone, that an author stands behind it who meant it. Strip that supplement and the splendor is undiminished and real, the manifest face of the ground it always was, yet inert as evidence of a person: a sunset loses none of its magnificence when one stops reading the sky as a message. What gets demoted isn’t the awe but its evidential role—so the inference from grandeur to a hidden someone isn’t merely misrouted but unfounded, undercut at its source by the very account of why it compels.

The debunking is bounded, not general: it bites an inference only where the disposition would fire whether or not its target were there *and* the target has no standing independent of the disposition. The awe-as-sign inference meets both conditions—the agency-sense fires on the grandeur whether or not any person stands behind it, and the posited person has no access to it except that very inference. Practices the book leans on elsewhere meet neither: moral discernment is given its own account rather than left to a bare disposition, and the modal intuitions the metaphysics runs on are constitutive of the field rather than reports about something outside it that a disposition might misrepresent. A genealogy that debunked indiscriminately would be the familiar overreach of the form; this one is held to the two conditions the awe-as-sign inference alone meets here. This doesn’t yet settle the dispute: Schellenberg’s argument is pitched at the absence of relationship-grade evidence for a *personal* God, and meeting it takes the will-result that follows, not a change of subject. But it relocates the disagreement before that engine engages—what presents as a God declining to appear is a demand for a hidden author behind a grandeur that was never a signature.

*The internal argument.* A perfectly loving God would want each person capable of relationship with God, and not resisting it, to be in a position to enter that relationship—which requires at least that they believe God exists. The scholastic tradition itself distinguishes these as separate stages: *assensus*, holding that God exists, and *fiducia*, trusting the God one holds to exist; the second is unavailable wherever the first hasn’t been secured. The exemplars the tradition reaches for confirm the point rather than complicate it. Heb 11’s roll of faith runs through exactly the figures who had the least need of *assensus*: Abraham receives the promise across direct visitations (Gen 12, 15, 18), and Moses speaks with God “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exod 33:11)—for these, that God exists was never the open question. What Hebrews commends in them is *fiducia* exercised from an *assensus* already secured: Abraham trusting the promise-giver’s character at the binding of Isaac, Moses enduring hardship “as seeing him who is invisible” (Heb 11:27), not enduring uncertainty about whether anyone was there at all.

The paradigm case is thus one stage short of the case it is made to justify: naming both achievements “faith” doesn’t make the non-resistant nonbeliever’s task, clearing a gate the exemplars walked through already open, the same task the exemplars performed. What follows targets only the gate, not the room behind it—the argument needs only that *assensus*, the precondition any *fiducia* would require, fails to arrive for the non-resistant through no fault of their own; whether they would go on to trust is a question that, for them, never gets asked. Yet there are *non-resistant nonbelievers* (Schellenberg’s later, more careful term for the inculpable nonbelief the argument turns on, Schellenberg 2007; Schellenberg 2015), people open to God, who would believe if the belief were available to them, and who nonetheless don’t believe. A perfectly loving God wouldn’t permit that gap. So, Schellenberg concludes, no such God exists (Schellenberg 1993).

The pattern isn’t static, either. On the tradition’s own record, direct address was once frequent—direct divine appearance, angelic visitation, a voice from a burning bush, a face-to-face friendship with Moses—before narrowing to a single incarnate appearance of limited scope and duration, and narrowing further still to the secondhand report of that appearance carried by others ever since. A God whose engagement was once immediate has, by the tradition’s own chronology, been retreating rather than merely remaining constant, and a retreat calls for an explanation a static hiddenness wouldn’t need: something changed, on the traditional account, between the God who walked and spoke and the God who does neither now. The argument doesn’t depend on this trajectory, but it sharpens what follows: the question isn’t only why a hidden God stays silent, but why a formerly present one grew progressively quieter.

The standard reply denies the second premise: there are no genuinely non-resistant nonbelievers. All nonbelief is at bottom culpable—a refusal, a turning-away, a suppression of what is plainly available (the Pauline charge that they “suppress the truth,” Rom 1:18–20). On this reading the hidden God is exonerated: the gap is the unbeliever’s doing, a fault in the will rather than a withholding by God.

The suppression charge already assumes what it needs to prove: that doubt is a moral failure rather than a cognitive one. Doubt isn’t manufactured by an unruly will; it is the ordinary output of a mismatch-detection faculty, the same mechanism that lets a person catch a bad argument, a false rumor, or an unsupported claim in any other domain, and one the tradition itself credits to God when it wants belief to look native (the *sensus divinitatis* analysis that follows; §11.8.4’s account of the cognitive faculties revelation depends on). A God who supplies that faculty for every other use and then classifies its ordinary operation, turned on himself, as sin rather than as the faculty functioning as designed is asking a creature to trust its cognitive equipment everywhere except the one place its own supplier has the most at stake. Calling that operation “suppression” only relabels the faculty doing exactly what a faculty built to flag unsupported claims is supposed to do.

The escape is a claim about the will—that unbelief is something a person *does*, a free refusal they could simply have reversed. That claim doesn’t survive contact with what believing is. Belief isn’t a lever standing beside a person’s picture of what’s possible; it is part of that picture. Whatever someone holds true is already among the possibilities they have to work with, and inference runs only from what the picture contains. Nobody selects into it a possibility it doesn’t hold. So belief isn’t contra-causally up to the will: a person believes what their evidence and formation deliver, and can’t by willing install a conviction they lack or dismiss one that compels them. That is doxastic involuntarism, and it is argued rather than assumed here—Williams and Alston each press it against the demand to “just believe” (Williams 1973a; Alston 1988). Pascal concedes it from the other side. The counsel to *cultivate* belief by acting as if until assent follows (§10.1.14) is a workaround, and a workaround is needed only because the will can’t install the conviction directly.

The direct-refusal version of culpable unbelief names nothing. If belief isn’t a contra-causal act, then unbelief can’t be a conviction the unbeliever simply chose and could reverse at will. Call a field that doesn’t deliver belief in God a map without that possibility—not, by that fact alone, a will withholding assent. The escape requires a volition answering to nothing the agent can see: a will choosing among possibilities it doesn’t hold is choosing among nothing, which is not a free act but no act at all. But doxastic non-control doesn’t by itself entail non-resistance. A person may exercise indirect epistemic agency by refusing inquiry, avoiding evidence, cultivating one-sided sources, or sustaining habits designed not to encounter a claim. Those acts can be culpable even though the resulting belief-state isn’t directly chosen. The hiddenness argument therefore owes actual cases in which neither direct refusal nor culpable indirect resistance explains the nonbelief.

“You could have sought” therefore names a real question but not a universal answer. Seeking is itself a selection over a field, and the same analysis governs it: inquiry can widen the field through attention, evidence, conversation, and self-correction, but it can’t guarantee what conclusion the widened field will deliver. A sincere inquirer can pursue the available routes, expose prior commitments to criticism, remain willing to revise, and still find that belief doesn’t obtain. Former believers who lose conviction despite wanting it, sustained seekers who would welcome relationship-grade evidence, and inquirers across traditions who apply comparable openness yet reach incompatible conclusions supply the relevant case class. A defender may challenge whether a particular case is fully non-resistant; the defender may not define resistance as whatever explains continued nonbelief, since that makes the premise unfalsifiable. Indirect agency is real, but once the available acts of inquiry and correction have been responsibly exercised, their failure to produce belief isn’t a further act the inquirer withheld.

Nor can the resistance reply be settled by treating the tradition as hostile to inquiry. The sayings at issue concern revelation to infants, worldly wisdom, and deceptive philosophy. They criticize status, pride, or reasoning governed by false premises (Matt 11:25; 1 Cor 3:19; Col 2:8); they don’t ban historical investigation or philosophy as such. Christian traditions have in fact built extensive philosophical and evidential arguments. The relevant question remains case-specific: whether a person culpably closed reasonable routes of inquiry, not whether the person employed an intellectual method the texts had already forbidden.

One boundary: the doxastic result stands on the book’s account of the will (§5.11), not on the modal argument alone. A reader who retains direct voluntary control of belief can refuse it at that contested frontier. Even within that account, indirect responsibility for inquiry remains, and the hiddenness argument requires actual non-resistant cases rather than treating every unbeliever as one. What the account of the will rules out is the simple demand that a person install assent by bare choice.

A further form of the escape, that belief is the field’s default, fails on its own. The suppression charge applies only if the truth was *plainly available* to begin with: belief in God as the natural state of a properly functioning mind, so that its absence must be a defect rather than a deprivation (the reformed-epistemology backstop—the *sensus divinitatis*, Plantinga 2000). That premise breaks twice over. Structurally it assumes the very thing at issue: no possibility sits in someone’s view by default, since what a person can see is fixed by the encounters that shaped them, not by a uniform endowment every mind carries—and “plainly available” only reinstates the standpoint-free deliverance the argument above has already ruled out. The structural break settles it; the empirical record only corroborates.

*The distribution diagnostic.* Were determinate belief in God the native default, its content wouldn’t track birthplace and century as closely as it does (Maitzen 2006), and the dispositions that do look native (a hair-trigger for agency, a bent toward purpose) yield promiscuous supernatural attribution, gods and ancestors and omens, rather than the determinate God the escape requires (Barrett 2004; Kelemen 2004). That a defender may answer that the faculty was only ever meant to seed a general sense of the divine which culture then completes doesn’t rescue the escape: a sense culture must complete isn’t the field-default deliverance the suppression charge needed—it concedes the content isn’t native after all, relocating the unauthored-field problem rather than dissolving it.

The further move that the faculty is real but merely *damaged* relocates it the same way: whether one’s faculty is intact or damaged is itself unauthored, one more feature of the field a current did not lay down. Nor is the variance only a matter of intact against damaged. The same dispositions the defender invokes aren’t uniform across minds either: like any cognitive disposition they vary in strength from person to person—agency-detection running hot in some and quiet in others, the pull toward purpose stronger here and fainter there, with no pathology to mark the difference and nothing the bearer chose. A mind built toward the systematizing end isn’t refusing a sign; the same grandeur arrives at a receiver tuned to register it less. The faculty meant to make God plain to all is, by the lights of the case made for it, distributed unevenly along an axis no one selects. That leaves the escape a fork with no safe tine: either the faculty is the access mechanism, and a loving God has graded that mechanism and faulted those issued its shallow end (the birthplace injustice moved inward from the map to the skull), or the faculty is too uneven to carry the claim that everyone already knows, and the suppression charge has no purchase on a mind built not to see.

The unevenness isn’t only geographic. One influential set of studies found an association among autism-spectrum traits, reduced mentalizing, and lower belief in a personal God, with mentalizing proposed as a mediator rather than general reasoning ability (Norenzayan et al. 2012). The proposed mediation is the contested part of that result, and the argument here doesn’t need it: what does the work is the association itself, not the mechanism offered to explain it. That finding is relevant to a faculty defense that specifically makes spontaneous attribution of mind the access mechanism. It doesn’t establish a universal causal pathway to religion, show that autistic people lack religious belief, or reduce every case of nonbelief to one cognitive trait. Its narrower force is enough: if one proposed route to naturally available theism varies for reasons a person didn’t choose, that route can’t by itself support the claim that every nonbeliever received the same unmistakable access and culpably suppressed it.

The consequence depends on the salvation rule. A defender may hold people responsible only for the light available to them, exempt those without relevant capacity, or deny that explicit belief is the gate at all. Those replies protect against a verdict based on inaccessible evidence; they don’t make the intervening life idle, since a life may contain relationship, formation, action, and goods independent of satisfying an explicit-belief condition. They instead establish that the condition is access-relative or non-universal. A view that retains one uniform belief requirement must explain why unchosen variation in a proposed access mechanism doesn’t make the requirement unequal.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Uniform Requirement Problem** · *Disjunction*

If minds differ in what they can register, how can awareness of God be required of everyone?

- **If the requirement is softened by access-relative judgment or capacity exemption,** then fairness is preserved. But explicit belief isn’t a universal condition.
- **If it is met by a different route of revelation,** then access may be restored. But the route’s availability and clarity must be shown rather than inferred from the disputed faculty. *Feeds into* The Four Insufficiencies (§12.3.8).
- **If it stays a uniform requirement,** then it must explain why unchosen differences in access don’t determine who can satisfy it.

Either the condition varies with access, access is independently supplied, or unequal access remains part of the judgment. Calling the missing capacity universal does not make a uniform demand fair.

**Depends on:** The Salvation Specification Test (§12.1.8)

The asymmetry cuts both ways. If the faculty’s uneven distribution makes fault an injustice for those it left blunt, the same distribution makes credit an accident for those it left sharp: a mind wired to register the pull toward purpose hotly no more earned that sensitivity than the muted mind earned its quiet. Whatever ledger the tradition would keep—credit for the believer’s ready assent, fault for the unbeliever’s absence of it—is drawn on an axis nobody selects, and it can’t discriminate credit from blame without discriminating on grounds neither party chose. The believer’s ease isn’t evidence of virtue any more than the unbeliever’s difficulty is evidence of vice; both report only where a given mind sat on a distribution laid down before either could have anything to say about it.

Evangelism and apologetics don’t contradict a natural-awareness claim. They may aim to render a general awareness explicit, correct suppression, identify the object more fully, communicate a salvific event unavailable through nature, or deepen trust rather than produce bare theism. Their existence therefore doesn’t show that Rom 1:19–20 or a *sensus divinitatis* account is false. It does force a specification the rhetoric of “plain to everyone” can obscure: what content is naturally available, what content requires historical proclamation, and which content the salvation rule actually gates. A general sense of divinity can coexist with a need for teaching; it can’t by itself establish that every person already possesses determinate belief in the particular God and event later proclamation supplies.

The two driving premises meet here without automatically closing every exit. The will-account narrows the *culpable-unbelief* reply to direct or indirect resistance that can actually be identified. A modest skeptical reply may still say that finite knowers shouldn’t expect to see every divine reason for distance. As established at §11.9.2, that move can undercut a confident inference without supplying a positive explanation; a stronger skepticism also limits favorable claims that hiddenness serves relationship, freedom, or formation unless an asymmetry is independently defended. A conditional burden falls on a wholly structureless transcendent person (§11.1; §11.2.1). The resulting case is cumulative, not a declaration that unknown reasons are impossible.

*Absence is the mild case.* Hiddenness, as the argument runs it, is a deprivation: the evidence a relationship would need never arrives, and the world is merely quiet. The tradition doesn’t describe a quiet world. It describes a contested one, in which a competent adversary—“the deceiver of the whole world” (Rev 12:9), able to disguise himself as an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14)—is permitted to work on the very faculty the economy grades. That is a different case rather than a louder version of the same one. A field that lacks the belief because nothing supplied it is unfortunate; a field that lacks it because something competent was licensed to work against it is a casualty of an arrangement rather than an accident within one. The permission is also precisely aimed: of everything an adversary might be allowed to damage, what he is allowed to damage is the one deliverable on which the judgment turns.

*The faculty argument inverts under interference.* The suppression charge was already answered by observing that doubt is mismatch-detection functioning as designed rather than a will withholding assent. Put that faculty into the world the tradition actually describes and the answer gets stronger rather than merely repeating. A detector built to flag unsupported claims, meeting counterfeit signs—lying wonders, ministers disguised as ministers of righteousness (2 Thess 2:9; 2 Cor 11:15)—flags them, which is the function performing correctly; but it can’t flag only the counterfeits when the tradition’s own account has the counterfeit issued in the same currency as the genuine article, which is why discernment is treated there as a gift rather than as standard issue. Raise the deceiver’s competence and the well-built faculty’s rational response is to lower its credence across the whole class of evidence, authentic instances included. The better the equipment works, the likelier it lands its bearer among the condemned. That isn’t the faculty failing. It is the faculty succeeding into the outcome the economy punishes.

*The delusion is sometimes described as sent, not merely permitted.* In the divine-council scene, a spirit proposes becoming “a lying spirit in the mouth of all [Ahab’s] prophets,” and the proposal is authorized (1 Kgs 22:19–23). Ahab isn’t innocent in the narrative: he already bears an extended record of wrongdoing, rejects unwelcome prophetic counsel, and receives Micaiah’s true warning before proceeding. The judicial-hardening reading therefore deserves priority over a reading on which deception creates guilt in a previously blameless person. The same qualification is explicit in 2 Thess 2:11–12, where delusion comes upon those said already to have refused the truth, and in Ezek 14:9’s setting of idolatrous inquiry. These texts still matter epistemically because they describe an environment in which religious error may be divinely used as judgment. They don’t establish that every mistaken seeker was entrapped or that Ahab’s guilt began with the lie.

The tradition’s replies include subtraction and judicial imposition, and they don’t stand or fall together. Aquinas holds that God infuses no malice and withholds only the grace that would have prevented fault, so hardening is privative rather than a positive production of evil (Aquinas, *ST* I-II, q.79, a.3). Calvin retains a stronger decree and calls it *decretum horribile* (Calvin, *Institutes* III.xxiii.7). Active judicial delusion fits the wording of the cited scenes better than pure withholding, but it also answers the charge that the delusion produced the antecedent guilt.

*The tradition raises the objection itself.* Rom 9 turns hardening from an incident into a stated policy—“he has mercy on whomever he chooses, and he hardens the heart of whomever he chooses” (Rom 9:18)—and then puts the present objection almost in its own words: “Why then does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (Rom 9:19). What follows isn’t an answer to it. “Who indeed are you, a human being, to argue with God?” and the potter’s right over the clay (Rom 9:20–21) concede the question’s force while denying the questioner standing to put it—a ruling about who may ask rather than about what is owed. A defender may take that as the proper creaturely posture rather than as evasion, and the reading is open; it is still not a justification. What remains when an economy answers by rank is allegiance rendered or withheld, in the vocabulary of justice.

*The ordinary case the doctrine has to overturn.* Strip the theology and the verdict isn’t in dispute. An elderly woman is telephoned by a man representing himself as an official, a relative in trouble, or a suitor; she believes him, because the presentation was built to be believed; she sends the money. No one proposes to fine her. The loss is already hers, the fault is the caller’s, and a court that added a penalty on top of her loss for having been credulous would be understood to have identified the wrong party. The verdict doesn’t turn on her being shrewd, or on her being free of the ordinary wish to be helpful that the scheme was designed to exploit; it turns only on the deception’s having been competent enough to work.

A general warning doesn’t disturb it either—a public notice that such calls occur doesn’t make the person who takes one at fault for its succeeding, least of all where the scheme’s whole design is to present as the exception the notice didn’t cover. What the theological case adds isn’t a reason to reverse that verdict but a further party to it. The judge isn’t a disinterested court that had no hand in the call: on the doctrine’s own account he supplied the faculties she answered with, licensed the caller to operate, and on the cited texts sometimes put the voice on the line. An analogy settles nothing on its own, and this one is offered to locate the ordinary intuition rather than to discharge the argument that has to earn it. What it does mark is the size of the request: the doctrine isn’t asking that a hard case be weighed but that an easy one be reversed, in favor of the party with the most involvement in how it came out.

*The cost falls on the tradition’s epistemology too.* A God who deceives isn’t only a difficulty for divine justice; it is a difficulty for every reconstruction of knowledge the tradition has built on divine veracity. Descartes’ rule that clear and distinct perceptions may be trusted is licensed by the premise that God is no deceiver, and without that premise the recovery from doubt doesn’t begin (Descartes, (1641) 1996). Plantinga’s warrant is the same dependence in contemporary dress—a belief is warranted when produced by faculties functioning properly, in a congenial environment, on a design plan successfully aimed at truth (Plantinga 2000)—and the *sensus divinitatis* backstop met above is an application of it. Sent delusion isn’t a marginal exception to those conditions but a counterexample to two of them at once: an environment in which a competent deceiver operates by permission isn’t congenial, and a design plan through which a powerful delusion is routed isn’t aimed at truth without qualification. The natural reply is that the delusion falls only on those already refusing the truth and leaves the sincere believer’s faculties intact—but whether one’s own faculties are among the intact ones is the single thing no believer can establish from the inside, since a delusion its bearer could detect in themselves wouldn’t be doing the work the text assigns it.

*What the deception case adds.* None of this requires treating the hardening texts as cases of deception that creates guilt, and one common reading survives untouched. On the judicial construal the delusion is a sentence rather than a snare, sent to those whose guilt is already fixed, and a defender who holds that consistently has answered the charge of injustice. It doesn’t answer the charge of deception, since a delusion justly sent is still a delusion sent; the epistemological cost accrues on the judicial reading exactly as on the other, and only the question of deserving turns on which is right. What remains is narrower and sufficient. The tradition’s own record doesn’t describe the neutral epistemic environment the culpability reply assumes when it locates the entire gap in the unbeliever’s will. Where that environment contains a permitted deceiver, and on these texts sometimes a divine one, it isn’t enough for the reply to say the truth was available. It has to say the truth was available through faculties the same tradition reports were worked against.

A further reply shifts to epistemic distance: some measure of hiddenness is said to preserve a noncoerced relationship, moral development, or trust rather than mere assent (Hick 1966). Angelic rebellion is sometimes offered as a counterexample, but it can’t carry the argument decisively. Rev 12:4 doesn’t itself state a developed doctrine of one-third of the angels freely rejecting God, and theological accounts differ over what angels knew and when. At most, an account on which some angels possessed certain awareness of God yet freely refused allegiance would show that certainty of existence need not compel loving trust. That pressures a defense aimed only at protecting *fiducia* by withholding *assensus*; it doesn’t refute every soul-making or noncoercion account of distance.

The defense must specify which good distance protects. Withholding evidence reduces the set of live, understood options; the buyer kept from viewing a house isn’t thereby better informed or able to choose among more alternatives. But evidence can exert psychological pressure without logically determining affection or allegiance, and some developmental accounts value discovery, trust under uncertainty, or morally formative searching. Those goods aren’t answered merely by counting options. The comparison must therefore ask whether relationship-grade evidence could preserve them with less non-resistant nonbelief, and why the selected degree and distribution of distance is proportionate to the good claimed.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Witness Protection Problem** · *Disjunction*

What freedom or good does divine hiddenness protect?

- **If hiddenness protects freedom to decide whether God exists,** then it withholds the option’s evidential availability—and a person can’t responsibly choose between alternatives they have no fair opportunity to recognize. Ignorance doesn’t widen that freedom; it removes a condition of exercising it.
- **If hiddenness protects freedom to trust or give allegiance,** then evidence that settles God’s existence need not determine that further response.
- **If it protects discovery, formation, or noncoercive relationship,** then the amount and the spread of hiddenness should track those goods—and neither does. It tracks birthplace and era, which no account of discovery, formation, or noncoercive relationship predicts or requires. *Feeds into* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1). *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.

The hidden God isn’t exonerated merely by redescribing every unpersuaded field as the sinner’s refusal. The deception texts add a set-specific complication: traditions that include permitted or judicial religious error must say how the sincere inquirer can discriminate it from revelation, while traditions reading those texts differently need not accept that burden in the same form. What remains is the original question, bounded to its proper target: a perfectly loving God said to seek relationship, and non-resistant persons for whom relationship-grade evidence never arrives. The defenses remain possible, but each must identify the good, mechanism, and distribution that justify the distance rather than appeal to hiddenness in the abstract.

*Calibrated evidence as a hypothesis.* A further reply runs hiddenness forward rather than defending against it. On this account divine self-disclosure is deliberately calibrated: enough evidence to make belief rationally available, enough counterweight to keep doubt psychologically open. The reply isn’t merely a defense of the distance but a prediction about the evidence, and its attraction is that it does two jobs at once. It explains why disconfirming material should be expected—apparent inconsistencies in a text held to be inspired, embarrassments beside otherwise strong reports—and, because it predicts them jointly, it withdraws their independence, so difficulties that would otherwise accumulate are said to share one cause and stop compounding. A defender may add that accommodations which look ad hoc case by case in fact follow from one antecedently reasonable posit, and so cost less in parsimony than their number suggests.

The correlating work is legitimate and is required elsewhere: a cumulative case must condition on common causes before counting its cases as independent (§10.1.16). What the reply can’t do is take the correlation without the price. A hypothesis that predicts ambiguous evidence has purchased its immunity by predicting ambiguity, and it must then hold that prediction fixed when the evidence runs favorably.

**[Dissolution]**

**Calibration Cannot Be Spent Twice** · *Dissolution*

An appeal to deliberately calibrated evidence may block an inference from apparent disconfirmation, and it may correlate difficulties so that they no longer compound. It cannot also count the resulting evidential situation as confirmation. The latitude that makes ambiguity expected makes clarity unexpected in the same measure, so a defender who cites the model to absorb the difficulties has spent the width that a favorable reading would need. Held evenly, the model predicts an evidential situation in which neither side’s reading is surprising, and it therefore discriminates between them less than either party wants.

**Dissolves:** the use of a calibrated-disclosure model both to neutralize disconfirming evidence and to treat the resulting ambiguity as evidence for the position it protects

*Scope.* The dissolution grants that a calibration model may be true, that a tradition may hold it for independent reasons, and that correlated difficulties genuinely don’t compound. It doesn’t make the model meaningless or settle whether any particular text is inspired. It fixes only that the two uses cannot be made together.

**Depends on:** The Explanatory Burden (§12)

### 12.3.7 Faith and Belief

Some salvation accounts present faith not as one virtue among others but as the gate: the condition without which the rest doesn’t count. “Without faith it is impossible to please him” (Heb 11:6). Asked directly what God requires, Jesus answers, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6:29)—belief directed at a person, not merely at a fact about one. The wisdom literature names the same posture: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not rely on your own insight” (Prov 3:5). Other Christian accounts deny that these texts make explicit belief the cause or universal condition of salvation: faith may be the fruit of election, the ordinary instrument of grace, trust responsive to an antecedently identified revealer, or one element in a conjunctive life of grace, sacrament, obedience, and perseverance. Which of these roles a retained set assigns to belief has to be fixed first (§12.1.8).

*What the requirement is defended as.* The tradition hasn’t left the requirement to stand on the texts alone, and four defenses of it run on different grounds. On the Thomist account, faith is assent to what isn’t seen, commanded by the will where the intellect isn’t compelled by sight, with First Truth as its object rather than a proposition held on inference (Aquinas, *ST* (1265–1274) 1947, II-II.1–7); the assent isn’t evidence-defying but evidence-underdetermined, and it is creditable to the believer for exactly that reason. Reformed epistemology denies the demand its premise instead: belief in God may be properly basic, warranted by a faculty functioning as designed in the environment it was made for, so that requiring an evidential argument before belief misdescribes how warrant works rather than exposing a failure to supply one (Plantinga 2000). James presses a third line from the ethics of belief: where an option is living, forced, and momentous, and the intellectual grounds don’t settle it, withholding assent until evidence arrives isn’t neutrality but a choice with its own costs, and the believer has the right to let the decision run ahead of the proof (1896). And Pascal supplies a fourth, in which the will is engaged before the intellect is satisfied and the practice of belief forms the belief itself, so the order of operations the objection assumes is reversed (1670). Each is answering a real question, and each will matter differently below, since they locate the requirement in different places: in the will, in the faculty, in the right to decide, and in the practice.

*Three things are called faith.* Trust in a person, belief that the person exists, and belief that a reported event involving that person occurred aren’t the same attitude, and they don’t stand in the same relation to evidence. Trusting someone is an attitude toward what they will do—their reliability, their character, their word. Believing they exist is assent to one proposition; believing that they died and were raised is assent to another. Trust ordinarily presupposes both the existence and the relevant history of its object: one comes to trust a friend by having encountered the friend and watched what they do. Neither prior assent is itself an act of trust, and in ordinary cases neither is the thing in question when trust is exercised.

The distinction matters because the standard defense of the requirement runs on interpersonal trust while some Christian accounts of salvation make assent to a historical proposition part of the gate. Rom 10:9 states the condition in exactly that form: confess that Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised him from the dead. Whatever further trust is directed toward Jesus, the immediate disputed object is therefore not only Jesus as a person but *the resurrection happened*. Faith of the religious kind is then defended by analogy to trusting a spouse, a friend, or a physician without proof. The analogy is exact in the wrong place. Ordinary trust begins after the person’s existence and the relevant history are available; it extends an observed record forward. The resurrection proposition reaches the believer only as testimony about an event the believer didn’t encounter, and the divine identity and character of its subject are among the conclusions the report is asked to establish. The analogy supplies trust after identification and history; it is offered to support assent before either has been independently secured.

The tradition’s own vocabulary marks the difference and then declines to hold it. Scholastic usage separates *fiducia*, trust placed in a person, from *assensus*, assent to a proposition—the distinction already in play at §12.3.6. The defense by analogy is a defense of fiducia; every ordinary case it cites is one of trust extended to someone whose existence no one doubts. The requirement, however, can’t be satisfied by fiducia alone, because fiducia has no object until assensus is in place. Nothing is trusted until something is taken to be there. So the requirement needs the very attitude the analogy never illustrates, and the analogy illustrates the very attitude the requirement can’t reach without it.

**[Dissolution]**

**The Trust Analogy Equivocates** · *Dissolution*

Where required faith is defended by analogy to ordinary interpersonal trust, ordinary trust is *fiducia*, extended to a person whose existence and relevant history are already available. An account of salvation that also requires assent that Jesus was raised asks for something prior: belief that a particular event occurred and identifies its subject as the set claims. The trust analogy cannot establish that historical proposition. Either it concerns *fiducia*, in which case the existence, event, and identity of its object must already have been established; or it is stretched to supply that prior *assensus*, in which case it is no longer the ordinary trust that made the analogy plausible. A set in which the revealer and event have been independently identified escapes this objection and carries the adequacy of those identifying grounds instead.

**Dissolves:** the defense of required faith by ordinary-trust analogy where the object hasn’t already been adequately identified

*The order of dependence.* A second difficulty concerns the route rather than the object. No later reader encounters the resurrection as an event; the reader encounters a humanly transmitted proposition about one. Before trust in Jesus can begin, the reader must rely on witnesses or traditions reporting the event, authors selecting and composing those reports, scribes preserving them, communities canonizing them, translators rendering them, and teachers or institutions presenting their significance. This need not mean blind confidence in every individual hand. Manuscript comparison, textual criticism, and historical method can detect some failures and sometimes reconstruct a reading despite them. The narrower point is about order: every available route to the supposedly direct divine object first depends on fallible human testimony and the human procedures used to assess it.

That order matters because divine supervision can’t certify the chain until the divine source has been identified, while the chain is often among the evidence used to identify precisely that source and its decisive act. To say the people and processes are trustworthy because God preserved the message, and that God is known to have preserved it because the message reliably reports God’s act, closes a circle unless some independent warrant enters. The warrant might be historical corroboration, miracle, prophecy, communal authority, internal testimony, or direct encounter; each is a real proposal and each bears its own argument. What the present section adds is the ordering. Human mediation isn’t an accompaniment encountered after faith in God; for a historically gated claim, it is the ordinary road by which a later believer reaches the alleged event and then its alleged divine author.

The order has a temporal edge fixed at §12.1.8. If resurrection-assent became necessary when the event occurred, the condition outran its own message and governed people who had no route to its object. If it became necessary only when adequately proclaimed, the saving rule activates person by person rather than at the cross or empty tomb, and the account owes a standard for adequate proclamation. If earlier and unreached persons receive the benefit without the assent, then the event may remain the ground of salvation while assent to its occurrence isn’t the universally necessary gate. The faith section inherits whichever activation rule Salvation selected; it may not supply a stricter one only after the message happens to arrive.

*What the warnings do and don’t forbid.* Biblical warnings against princes, flesh, worldly wisdom, or deceptive philosophy contrast ultimate reliance on human power and status with reliance on God, and warn against reasoning governed by premises hostile to the Gospel. They don’t prohibit ordinary testimony, historical investigation, philosophical argument, or every external check. The same corpus reasons in public, appeals to witnesses, and praises the Bereans for examining a proclamation (Acts 17:11). No anti-audit contradiction follows from those texts. A specific community may adopt a self-sealing rule, but that rule must be demonstrated rather than read into every warning about intellectual pride or bad philosophy.

The live issue isn’t whether inquiry is permitted but what authenticates the authority that guides it. An appeal to Scripture can test a new claim within a community that already accepts Scripture; it can’t, without further premises, authenticate Scripture’s own divine source to someone who doesn’t. Historical evidence can supply an external check, but then the strength of the faith claim is bounded by that evidence. Internal testimony or encounter may provide a different kind of warrant to the experiencer, but its availability and discrimination from rival experiences become the question. The routes aren’t forbidden. They simply can’t borrow one another’s warrant without argument.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Chain-of-Custody Problem** · *Disjunction*

What authenticates the human chain the faith had to travel?

- **If the chain is authenticated by independent historical or philosophical standards,** then those standards are doing the work, not the chain, and confidence must track their strength.
- **If it is authenticated by its own transmission of divine revelation,** then the divine source still needs an authentication that doesn’t presuppose the chain. *Feeds into* The Sign–Source Dilemma (§12.3.3). *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.
- **If it is authenticated by internal testimony, communal authority, or direct encounter,** then that route must explain its own reach and how it discriminates incompatible claimants. *Feeds into* The Sign–Source Dilemma (§12.3.3).

Human mediation is compatible with warranted faith. It isn’t self-authenticating merely because its reported object is divine.

**Depends on:** The Delivery Tradeoff (§12.3.4)

*What the method can reach.* Set the object aside and ask what the instrument discriminates. Faith is invoked where the evidential channels have been conceded insufficient, which means it is asked to do work the evidence isn’t doing—to warrant a conclusion the evidence doesn’t warrant on its own. An instrument of that description isn’t selective. Adherents of mutually exclusive traditions hold their own by faith, in the same sense and with the same sincerity, and the instrument returns each of them their own answer. It isn’t that faith *might* deliver incompatible conclusions; it demonstrably does, and the traditions it delivers them to are the standing demonstration. A route that yields every answer with equal facility can’t be what makes any one of them correct, and a believer who grants that another may reach the opposite conclusion by the same route has already conceded that the route isn’t what settled it.

The reply available here is the one that saves faith by relocating it: faith isn’t an evidence-substitute but a commitment made *downstream* of grounds one already has, the trusting response to a case independently made. That reply is coherent, and it isn’t free. It concedes that the grounds do the discriminating work and that faith adds only the posture toward them—which returns the entire burden to the channels the preceding sections have pressed (§12.3.4, §12.3.5, §12.3.3). Faith so understood can’t be what carries the belief when the evidential case is admitted to fall short, because on this construal it was never carrying it at all.

**[Dissolution]**

**Faith Discriminates Nothing** · *Dissolution*

Where faith is invoked as an independent warrant for what the evidence doesn’t warrant on its own, it must discriminate among candidates. Adherents of mutually exclusive traditions reach their own conclusions by a method described in the same terms and with the same sincerity, so the method alone doesn’t select among them. Either faith independently warrants a particular conclusion, in which case a discriminating account is still owed; or it is commitment downstream of grounds already had, in which case the grounds do the discriminating and faith cannot carry a belief the grounds are admitted not to support.

**Dissolves:** faith as an independent warrant for belief

**Depends on:** The Explanatory Burden (§12)

*Whether the requirement can be met at all.* One further consequence follows from how belief occurs, and it has a witness inside the tradition. A requirement is something a subject can satisfy or fail to satisfy, and satisfying it must be within reach of what the subject does. Belief isn’t like that, and at least one of the tradition’s own advocates conceded as much where it mattered most to him. Pascal, urging the wager, grants that one can’t simply decide to believe, and so proposes habituation—take the holy water, have the masses said—as the route to a belief the will can’t reach directly. That is the concession stated as a remedy: if belief were an act the will performs, no workaround would be needed. The strongest reply comes from Aquinas, whose assent of faith is commanded by the will—but by a will moved by grace (*ST* II-II, q.2, a.9), so the command is addressed to a will God is also moving. That reply is real, and it takes the exit the proposition below leaves open: faith produced by grace isn’t a condition met by bare compliance. What it does is relocate the question from the believer’s compliance to the distribution of the grace (The Chosen History Problem, §12.3.1). Inquiry and attention remain sites of indirect responsibility, and the point isn’t that a person can do nothing about what they end up believing. It is that the terminal state itself—belief arriving or failing to arrive—isn’t the sort of thing a demand reaches directly. A condition stated over that state isn’t a requirement anyone can comply with by complying; it is a description of how their field happened to resolve, addressed to them as though it were an instruction.

**[Proposition]**

**A Condition No One Can Meet by Meeting It** · *Proposition*

Where conscious belief is stated as a condition the subject must directly satisfy, the condition must be reachable by what the subject does. On the book’s account of belief (§12.3.6), which Pascal concedes from inside the tradition, belief is not an act the will performs, so the terminal state is not directly reachable by compliance. Indirect responsibility for inquiry and attention survives, and a grace-produced or evidential account of faith exits the direct-command objection. What does not survive is the set that addresses belief as a performed instruction while retaining the book’s account of how belief occurs.

The result isn’t that every theological use of faith fails. A set in which faith is grace-produced, evidential rather than causal, or trust downstream of an adequately identified object leaves at least one pressure stated here. What doesn’t survive unchanged is the set that treats explicit belief as a universally applicable gate, defends it by ordinary trust, uses it to supply what the identifying evidence doesn’t, and then addresses the terminal state of belief as though it were directly performed. The reader carries forward whichever narrower role remains.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Faith-Condition Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

If salvation turns on belief, what job is faith doing?

- **If faith is a condition the person must satisfy,** then that reading owes adequate access to faith’s object, and an action by which the condition can be met—access that different minds cannot register alike, which is exactly the uniform-requirement problem this reading inherits. *Feeds into* The Uniform Requirement Problem (§12.3.6).
- **If it is a state produced by grace or election,** then the direct-control objection recedes. But its distribution belongs to providence rather than to the recipient’s compliance. *Feeds into* The Chosen History Problem (§12.3.1).
- **If it is evidence of salvation already conferred,** then faith can identify a condition without causing it. But it cannot serve as the gate it was invoked to explain.
- **If it is interpersonal trust after identification,** then the trust may be coherent. But Scripture, prophecy, miracles, and hiddenness must identify its object before trust begins. *Feeds into* The Sign–Source Dilemma (§12.3.3).

These roles may coexist. A defender must distinguish which role is doing the work at each step, and a set combining roles inherits every applicable burden; it may not use one role’s advantages while disclaiming its costs.

**Applies to:** salvation accounts that make conscious assent, trust, or explicit belief necessary or evidentially central

### 12.3.8 The Four Insufficiencies

The preceding sections tested scripture, prophecy, hiddenness, and belief one at a time. The question here is what their defenses establish together. The controlling question is simple: *sufficient for what?* A document may be accurate without being widely available, available without being intelligible, intelligible without being credible to a responsible reader, and credible without the event it reports having occurred. The relations can also run in the other direction. No one property contains the others.

The Christian traditions distribute these loads differently. The Westminster Confession limits the promised clarity to what is necessary for salvation, says that those matters are clearly presented somewhere in scripture, and still requires the Spirit’s inward illumination for saving understanding (*WCF* I.6–7). Roman Catholic theology doesn’t assign the whole interpretive load to an ordinary reader confronting scripture alone: scripture, tradition, and the teaching authority of the Church form one transmission and interpretation structure (*Dei Verbum* 9–10). Ecclesial, sacramental, election, conscience, and inclusivist accounts add still other channels. These are real alternatives, not evasive restatements. Each changes the object being tested. If Spirit or Church supplies what unaided text doesn’t, the combined channel—not the text alone—bears the relevant load. If explicit reception is unnecessary, delivery and compellingness cease to be universal conditions of salvation.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Four Insufficiencies** · *Diagnostic*

Apply four independent tests to any message made necessary for salvation or culpable rejection: **delivery** asks whether an adequate presentation reaches the person; **clarity** asks whether the required content is intelligible through the set’s authorized interpretive channel; **compellingness** asks whether the available grounds make assent responsibly available rather than merely commanded; **historicity** asks whether the event asserted as indispensable occurred. A set fails only the tests whose loads it retains. An auxiliary channel may discharge a load, but then the sufficiency belongs to the combined channel. Passing one test supplies no result on the other three.

*Scope.* The diagnostic doesn’t assume that salvation always requires explicit belief, that scripture must operate without community or grace, or that disagreement by itself proves obscurity. It fixes what each selected set requires before testing whether the requirement is met.

**Depends on:** The Salvation Specification Test (§12.1.8); The Delivery Tradeoff (§12.3.4)

*Delivered.* Mark’s longer ending commands proclamation to the whole creation (Mark 16:15); it doesn’t say that proclamation was completed. First Timothy says that God desires everyone to be saved (1 Tim 2:4); it doesn’t identify one universally received message as the means by which that desire is realized. A delivery burden arises only when a set adds that explicit reception is necessary, that every accountable person has received an adequate presentation, or that non-reception is culpable. The relevant unit isn’t bare exposure to words. It is access sufficient for the creature-side condition fixed by the Salvation Specification Test. An inclusivist, conscience-based, election, or sacramental route may protect the unreached, but then explicit reception isn’t the universal gate. This is the tradeoff already isolated at §12.3.4, not a claim that a commission promised its own completion.

*Clear.* Second Timothy’s claim that scripture equips a person for every good work (2 Tim 3:16–17) is a claim about formation and equipment, not by itself a doctrine of clarity to ordinary readers. The clearer target is confessional: Westminster says that what must be known, believed, and observed for salvation is clearly presented somewhere in scripture, while denying that every passage is equally plain or equally clear to all (*WCF* I.7). That claim isn’t refuted merely by counting denominations. Disagreement may arise from background beliefs, language, competence, authority structures, interests, or noetic impairment. The test is whether the content made necessary by the selected set can be identified and understood through the channel that set authorizes. A Catholic account may answer through scripture, tradition, and magisterium together; a Protestant clarity claim bears the narrower text-centered test it actually makes.

*Compelling.* Rom 1:19–20 concerns what is manifest through created reality; it doesn’t say that the gospel, the resurrection, or one scriptural canon is compelling to every hearer. Natural revelation may support a general accountability claim while leaving the historical identification channel untouched. Compellingness becomes a message-load only where a set treats rejection of that message as culpable under the evidence actually available to the hearer. Because belief isn’t directly selectable at will, the test isn’t whether assent was commanded but whether responsible inquiry had an adequate route to it (§12.3.6; §12.3.7). An appeal to inward illumination or grace can explain why the same evidence lands differently, but it relocates the difference to the distribution of that aid and can’t simultaneously leave unaided evidence sufficient for everyone in the same respect.

*Historical.* Christian proclamation expressly stakes itself on an event: if Christ wasn’t raised, Paul says, the faith is futile (1 Cor 15:17). Contemporary resurrection apologetics doesn’t rest on Habermas’s earlier summaries alone. His four-volume *On the Resurrection* develops the evidential case, replies to alternative explanations, surveys scholarly positions, and draws the theological consequences (Habermas 2024a; Habermas 2024b; Habermas 2025; Habermas 2026). That is the relevant contemporary target. The historical question remains the one treated at §12.2.4: whether the evidence favors the event over its alternatives. For the present diagnostic, the entire historical case may be granted. The other three loads would remain separate.

The same diagnostic travels across Abrahamic traditions only after its object is changed. Judaism doesn’t ordinarily make universal receipt of one historical proclamation a condition of salvation, so the Christian delivery test can’t simply be transferred to Torah. Islamic accounts may assign clarity, preservation, and universal guidance to the Qur’an while distinguishing the accountability of those who received an adequate presentation from those who didn’t. Jewish covenantal transmission, Christian gospel proclamation, and Islamic *da’wa* therefore carry different combinations of the four loads. The diagnostic compares their structures; it doesn’t manufacture one Abrahamic message and test everyone against it.

The independence claim is the load-bearing result. Delivery concerns distribution and adequacy of access. Clarity concerns intelligibility under a specified interpretive practice. Compellingness concerns the relation between grounds and responsible assent. Historicity concerns the past. Evidence can bear on more than one when an argument supplies the bridge: early and geographically dispersed testimony, for example, may bear both on distribution among particular communities and on historical transmission. What doesn’t follow is propagation by label. Calling the event historical doesn’t make its report universal, plain, or convincing.

**[Dissolution]**

**Historicity Does Not Propagate** · *Dissolution*

Grant that the indispensable event occurred. Its occurrence doesn’t establish that an adequate report reached each person, that the required content is intelligible through the authorized channel, or that the available grounds make assent responsibly available. Those are claims about distribution, interpretation, and reception rather than the past. Each load retained by the account of salvation therefore requires its own bridge and evidence.

**Dissolves:** the assumption that establishing historicity secures any distinct message-load the retained set assigns

**Depends on:** The Four Insufficiencies (§12.3.8)

The diagnostic leaves every set the routes it actually retains. A universalist or inclusivist may release explicit delivery from the saving condition. A Spirit-assisted account may locate compellingness in grace rather than public evidence. An ecclesial account may place clarity in a community and teaching authority rather than in private reading. An exclusivist may retain all four and defend all four. What no set may do is leave through one of those revisions and later return carrying the unrevised claim. Four loads remain four loads. Their conjunction must be argued; it can’t be inherited from the success of one.

### 12.3.9 The Moral Gap

John Hare’s *The Moral Gap* begins from a Kantian structure: morality makes a categorical demand, ordinary human capacities are inadequate to it, and *ought implies can* requires some route by which compliance remains genuinely possible (Hare 1996). Hare doesn’t survey only two naturalist evasions and then overlook moral development. He examines three families of contemporary response: exaggerating natural capacity, diminishing the demand, and supplying a naturalistic substitute for divine assistance. He argues that the candidates he considers fail, then develops the Christian resources of repentance, forgiveness, atonement, justification, sanctification, providence, and grace. The argument deserves that full shape. Social formation belongs inside the natural-substitute family; calling it an unnoticed fourth category wouldn’t answer Hare.

The pressure nevertheless divides at two joints. First, what is the demand? Second, what changes a person from unable to able? A gap between present conduct and what morality requires establishes neither a completed infinite demand nor the identity of the enabling cause. Those require further premises. If the demand is Kantian and fixed while natural capacity is radically inadequate, assistance follows from *ought implies can*. Whether that assistance is divine grace, evolved sociality, habituation, institutional support, transformed attention, or some conjunction remains a comparative question. If no bridge is possible, then the demand, the incapacity thesis, or *ought implies can* must instead be revised. Rejecting several naturalistic proposals doesn’t establish the impossibility of their entire category unless the rejection reaches them by a shared criterion.

Two claims carry the weight at the first joint, and neither has to be imported. What is owed can exceed what an agent presently recognizes or reliably performs, because another person’s standing doesn’t wait on that agent’s moral education—a debt isn’t cancelled by the debtor’s failure to notice it. And what an agent can recognize and perform isn’t fixed: attention, testimony, encounter, correction, institutions, and practice all alter the field through which someone selects and acts. A gap between what is demanded and what is presently done is therefore unremarkable on its own. What the argument needs is a gap of a particular kind, and that is what the specification below asks it to state.

That account isn’t Hare’s gap closed on Hare’s own terms. It rejects the picture of one complete demand-total standing above every relation and a separately fixed natural capacity trying to reach it. Williams’s criticism of the modern “morality system” marks the cost: the book grounds particular claims and reasons within relations among subjects rather than preserving one blame-centered categorical total as ethics’ organizing object (Williams 1985).
