Hare may therefore classify the proposal as diminishing or revising the demand. The reply can’t simply deny that classification. It accepts the revision and owes the moral substance it claims to preserve: another subject’s standing must still bind when empathy fails, development is incomplete, or compliance is costly. Section 5.14 supplies that bridge through reciprocity and equal standing, while acknowledging that a reader may reject it without contradicting the upstream metaphysics.

The second joint remains even for a reader who rejects the book’s account and grants Hare’s demand. *Assistance* isn’t yet a source-identification. Christian grace may be understood as acting through ordinary means—community, sacrament, teaching, discipline, relationship, and habituation—rather than as a rival force inserted beside them. If those practices are sufficient under a natural description, the observed moral change doesn’t by itself discriminate between unaided formation and grace working through formation. If grace contributes something further, the account must say what difference it makes, how it bears on capacity, and what identifies the contribution as divine. The point isn’t that grace must be measurable as a separate physical cause. It is that the gap can’t authenticate its bridge merely by requiring one.

The Abrahamic comparison also divides rather than converges. Hare’s argument is a Christian moral theology, not a shared Abrahamic premise. Deuteronomy describes the commanded way as neither too hard nor far away, but near enough to perform (Deut 30:11–14). The Qur’an says that God doesn’t burden a soul beyond its capacity (Qur’an 2:286). Jewish and Islamic accounts still contain repentance, mercy, divine aid, formation, and practices ordered toward righteousness, but those resources don’t begin by granting the same incapacity thesis. A Christian doctrine of grace may affirm radical natural inability; a Jewish or Islamic account may locate divine assistance within a command already fitted to creaturely capacity. The shared question is how moral transformation occurs. The gap-structure itself is set-specific.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Gap–Bridge Specification** · *Diagnostic*

Before a moral gap can identify divine assistance, an account must specify **(1)** the moral demand allegedly exceeding present capacity; **(2)** whether the incapacity is natural, acquired, culpable, or universal; **(3)** what change would make compliance possible; **(4)** how the proposed assistance produces that change; and **(5)** what discriminates divine assistance from social formation, habituation, institutional support, revised understanding, or grace working through those same means. If the demand is revised, the original Kantian gap hasn’t been bridged but declined. If assistance is retained, the existence of the gap establishes a need for a bridge only conditionally; it doesn’t identify the bridge by itself.

*Scope.* This diagnostic doesn’t deny grace, reduce moral transformation to one natural mechanism, or establish the book’s relational account of morality. It prevents the distance between demand and present performance from serving as evidence for a uniquely divine remedy without the missing comparative argument.

Hare identifies a genuine pressure wherever a theology combines categorical demand, radical natural incapacity, and *ought implies can*. His work also prevents an easy naturalist answer: pointing to education or practice isn’t enough unless those means can plausibly produce the capacity the demand requires. The return pressure is equally exact. Naming grace isn’t enough unless the account specifies the assistance and explains why the gap identifies it. The book takes the premise-level route and offers a relational demand with developmental capacity. A reader may reject that route. What the moral gap can’t do, without more, is choose the Christian bridge on the reader’s behalf.

### 12.3.10 Borrowed Moral Capital

The civilizational argument begins with a serious historical claim. Modern Western commitments to the equal worth of persons, concern for victims, moral scrutiny of power, conscience, and universal obligation didn’t arrive without a history. They developed within societies formed for centuries by Christian texts, institutions, practices, disputes, and reform movements. Even people who reject Christian doctrine can inherit categories whose route to them passed through Christianity. Tom Holland’s *Dominion* presses this claim at civilizational scale: Christianity didn’t merely add several rules to an otherwise settled moral inventory; it transformed the imagination through which the West learned to describe weakness, dignity, sacrifice, oppression, and reform (Holland 2019).

That isn’t principally an origination thesis. Christianity could transform, select, combine, intensify, institutionalize, and transmit materials it did not independently invent. Nor is Holland’s history, simply as history, an argument that God exists or that Christian revelation is true. The apologetic use adds that final step. It moves from *these commitments reached us through a Christian history* to *their presence counts as evidence that the history’s theological claims are true*. The expression “borrowed moral capital” often carries both claims at once: secular moral judgment is said to depend genealogically on Christianity, then the dependence is treated as a debt to Christian truth.

The historical claim deserves its full strength before that inference is tested. The worship of a crucified victim placed an image of dishonor and state violence at the center of a civilization. Christian communities universalized membership across ethnic and political boundaries, developed institutions of care, supplied a vocabulary of conscience and charity, and repeatedly gave reformers the texts with which they accused Christian societies of betraying their own professions. Abolitionists and civil-rights leaders didn’t merely happen to use Christian language; for many of them the language supplied premises, communities, motives, and authority. A genealogy that omitted those channels wouldn’t become more secular. It would become less accurate.

The same accuracy prevents the genealogy from becoming single-source history. Reciprocity appears in Confucian, Greek, Jewish, Indian, Buddhist, and Egyptian traditions before or independently of its Gospel formulations; the convergence is well attested across those traditions independently. Hillel’s negative formulation and Lev 19:18 belong to the Jewish world from which Jesus spoke. Stoic cosmopolitanism, Roman jurisprudence, Hebrew prophecy, Greek philosophy, and ancient Near Eastern wisdom all entered the cultures later called Christian. Egyptian women could own property, make contracts, and initiate divorce under legal arrangements not produced by the Gospel (Rowlandson 1998). These antecedents defeat monopoly origination. They don’t show that Christian recombination and transmission were causally idle. A carrier can alter what it carries; a synthesis can be historically novel even when its components have histories.

Counterfactual dependence is harder still. From the fact that a commitment actually traveled through Christian institutions, it doesn’t follow that no other route could have produced or preserved it. That conclusion requires comparison with unrealized histories. Conversely, pointing to an antecedent doesn’t show that the modern form would have emerged without Christianity. The responsible historical question is therefore comparative and granular: which commitment, in which form, reached which population through which institutions, alongside which Jewish, classical, political, economic, and dissenting streams? “The West is Christian” and “the West is Stoic and Roman” are both too coarse to answer it.

The record also contains internal contest rather than one moral vector. Christian scripture and theology armed abolitionists; they also armed Christian defenders of slavery. Noll documents the resulting theological crisis among Christians who agreed on biblical authority while dividing over what the Bible authorized (Noll 2015). Christian accounts of conscience contributed to arguments for religious liberty; ecclesial authorities also resisted versions of that liberty before the Catholic declaration *Dignitatis Humanae* grounded civil religious freedom in the dignity of the person. (Pius VI, *Quod Aliquantum* (10 March 1791); Second Vatican Council, *Dignitatis Humanae* (1965). The point is development and contest within the tradition, not that Catholic teaching before and after the council can be reduced to one unchanged proposition.) This doesn’t cancel the tradition’s contribution by subtracting harms from benefits on an imaginary ledger. It shows why a genealogy must identify mechanisms and disagreements instead of assigning every later good to Christian essence and every contrary practice to accidental betrayal. Deciding which developments are faithful fruit already requires an interpretive and moral criterion.

The structural claim enters at that point. Moral standing arises among subjects capable of welfare, agency, exposure, and reciprocal claim. If that account succeeds, a community may discover, refine, suppress, or transmit moral knowledge, but it doesn’t create another subject’s standing by transmitting it. If the account fails, the historical genealogy doesn’t rescue it. A proposition’s route through history and the grounds of its truth are different questions. Inferring falsity from a belief’s human ancestry would be a genetic fallacy; inferring divine truth from a belief’s successful ancestry is the same mistake with the sign reversed.

The authentication step therefore owes a bridge. Cultural endurance by itself is non-discriminating: political power, literacy, institutions, education, family formation, law, art, coercion, persuasion, and genuine moral insight can all help a tradition shape its descendants whether or not its supernatural claims are true. Moral fruit is more selective only after the fruit has been identified as good. If Christian authority alone supplies that evaluation, the fruit can’t independently authenticate the authority. If reciprocity, welfare, dignity, reason, conscience, or another moral standard supplies it, that standard is already doing work not delivered by the genealogy. A providential account may connect truth to historical fruitfulness, but then it must explain why this pattern is more expected under Christian providence than under human cultural development, another Abrahamic providence, or a rival religious history containing its own reforming resources.

This isn’t a peculiarly Christian restriction. Jewish communities may credit covenantal teaching with preserving moral practices through dispersion; Islamic accounts may credit Qur’anic revelation and the *ummah* with legal, charitable, intellectual, or civilizational achievements. Those histories can be real and important. When any of them is offered as public authentication, the same distinction applies: influence identifies a causal inheritance; authentication must discriminate the alleged divine source from human transmission and incompatible sacred genealogies.

One Christian branch incurs an additional internal question. If Jesus is presented not only as transmitting or intensifying Israel’s moral tradition but as correcting a law that the Nicene set attributes to the same divine author, the account must specify the continuity. Fulfillment, accommodation, progressive revelation, and human misattribution are different routes. Each may preserve a Christian genealogy, but each carries a different account of what God originally commanded and why later moral judgment may criticize the earlier form. That issue belongs to §12.4.2; it can’t be settled merely by praising the later development.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Moral Credit Problem** · *Disjunction*

Does a tradition’s moral influence show it is true, or only that it came first?

- **If it establishes historical genealogy,** then the tradition selected, transformed, or transmitted particular commitments. That history is compatible with both true and false supernatural claims.
- **If it establishes religious authentication,** then the argument owes a bridge from valuable effects to this tradition’s truth. The argument needs an independent bridge showing why the valuable effects are more likely given this tradition’s divine truth than given human cultural development or rival sacred genealogies. Calling the effects *valuable* also requires a moral criterion that doesn’t presuppose the authority being authenticated. *Priced by* The Explanatory Burden.

Antecedents don’t erase genuine transformation, and genuine transformation doesn’t by itself authenticate revelation.

*Scope.* The magnitude and shape of Christian influence remain questions for comparative history. The dilemma governs only the evidential use of whatever influence that history establishes.

**Still open:** the extent of the retained historical genealogy; the proposed bridge from influence to divine truth; the moral criterion used to identify the relevant fruits

Christianity’s influence on the West can therefore be granted at the level this section needs: it is deep, constitutive, and still present in avowedly secular moral languages. Earlier parallels don’t make that influence unreal. They block exclusive invention, while the tradition’s internal disputes block a frictionless story of transmission. Neither point decides whether Christian doctrine is true. The civilizational history becomes apologetic evidence only when a further account explains why this history discriminates divine revelation from the ordinary—often morally serious—work by which cultures inherit, contest, and transform one another.

### 12.3.11 Divine Command Theory
Divine command theory begins from a feature a thinner moral naturalism can miss. Obligation doesn’t feel like a free-floating property attached to an act. It addresses someone, binds someone, and is answerable to someone. Robert Adams builds his modified divine command theory around that social character: moral wrongness consists in contrariety to the commands of a loving God, whose nature prevents the command from becoming the decree of an arbitrary tyrant (Adams 1999). C. Stephen Evans likewise treats divine commands as the ground of moral obligation while allowing goodness to be understood through God’s character (Evans 2013). The position isn’t merely “might makes right.” Its claim is that obligation is at home in a relation among persons and that the God–creature relation supplies the authority natural facts alone don’t.

That contemporary division matters. Goodness and obligation aren’t assigned the same explanatory job. God’s necessarily loving nature fixes the character of the commander and the range of what that God could command; the command makes an act obligatory. It therefore doesn’t follow that, because the nature carries evaluative content, the command is idle. Human normative life supplies ordinary counterexamples. A legitimate authority may select one traffic convention from several permissible alternatives; a promise may create a duty that didn’t exist before it was made; a judge may specify what compliance with an antecedent law now requires. In each case the directive changes what is obligatory without creating the entire moral order by fiat. Modified divine command theory occupies that space deliberately. The simple Euthyphro fork doesn’t remove it.

The repair begins one level earlier: authority can’t be inferred from personality alone. A command is *personal* because it issues from a will. It is *interpersonal* in the minimal sense that one person addresses another. Neither fact establishes that the addressee owes compliance. The relevant relation is second-personal: the commander must possess standing to make this demand of this subject about this matter. A stranger can address an order to me without acquiring authority over me. A legitimate official can bind within a role while having no authority over my worship, affection, or private convictions. Commands can generate duties where a prior normative relation authorizes specification; they don’t generate the authorizing relation merely by being issued.

Divine command accounts offer several candidates for that relation, and they shouldn’t be collapsed. *Creatorhood* establishes causal dependence, but causal production doesn’t by itself entail ownership or unlimited jurisdiction over a subject. *Ownership* would supply a stronger authority, but ownership of persons is itself a moral thesis and can’t be inferred from making them without argument. *Benefaction* can ground gratitude and some duties of response, yet a gift doesn’t ordinarily purchase unrestricted obedience. *Perfect goodness* makes a command maximally trustworthy if the attribute is established; reliability and jurisdiction remain different. *Covenant* can create special obligations through a constituted relationship, but its scope and conditions matter, and covenantal duties don’t automatically become duties of every person outside it. *Creaturely welfare* can support a fiduciary authority directed toward the creature’s good, but then welfare and standing already constrain what may be commanded and why.

The possibilities can combine. A Christian account may join creation, providence, perfect love, redemption, and covenant; a Jewish account may locate many commanded duties within the covenantal relation rather than a universal voluntarism; an Islamic account may join divine creation and sovereignty with a dispute over whether reason recognizes moral properties prior to revelation. Combination can strengthen the case. It also makes the source of authority more exact: whatever work is done by love, benefit, covenant, consent, welfare, or justice isn’t work done by bare command.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Command-Authority Specification** · *Diagnostic*

A divine-command account must distinguish the **goodness** of the commanded act from its **obligatoriness**, then specify **(1)** what gives the commander standing to bind the addressee; **(2)** whom that standing governs and over which matters; **(3)** whether the command creates a new duty, selects among permissible options, or declares a duty already grounded in another subject’s claim; **(4)** what limits follow from love, justice, welfare, covenant, consent, or the addressee’s own standing; and **(5)** how the commander and command are identified without presupposing the authority being tested. A command may genuinely specify an obligation. It cannot establish its own jurisdiction merely by being issued.

*Scope.* This diagnostic doesn’t restore the simple Euthyphro dilemma, deny that social relations can generate duties, or assume that every obligation must be reducible to welfare. It tests the distinct authority step on which modified divine command theory depends.

**Still open:** the proposed source and scope of divine authority; the work performed by the command rather than the antecedent relation; and the method by which the command is identified

**Depends on:** The Explanatory Burden (§12)

The Euthyphro question remains useful once aimed at the correct joint. If God’s nature fixes goodness while commands fix obligation, cruelty isn’t a possible command of the loving God; arbitrariness is blocked. The remaining question is why the nature-command relation gives God authority to impose an obligation rather than only a reliable reason to believe the act good. The modified theory can answer through the God–creature relation. It must then say which feature of that relation supplies jurisdiction and why its reach is categorical. That burden isn’t a disguised demand that obligation exist before the command. It is the ordinary distinction between possessing a good reason, possessing authority to direct another, and exercising that authority in a particular directive.

The classical Islamic dispute shows both the reach and the limits of the fork. Mu’tazilite theologians held that reason can recognize good and evil prior to revelation and that divine commands track an objective justice; Ash’arite voluntarism placed moral status under divine command (Hourani 1985). Maturidi positions complicate a two-school summary by allowing rational recognition of value while assigning revelation a distinctive role in obligation and accountability. These aren’t three labels for one theory. They distribute evaluative truth, divine legislation, epistemic access, and accountability differently. The common question is the specification question: what does the command add, and what prior relation gives it authority to add it?

The swapped-throne case can now be bounded. Suppose an apparently unlimited will demands allegiance under another name and another scripture. Sheer capacity to reward and punish doesn’t establish authority; otherwise the transfer of allegiance would be automatic. Modified divine command theory agrees, because it appeals to the loving divine nature rather than power alone. The case therefore tests identification and jurisdiction, not the coherence of the modified theory by itself. The believer must have a non-circular reason to identify this claimant as the loving creator whose relation allegedly supplies authority. Content, character, history, revelation, and encounter may jointly provide that reason; those channels are tested at §12.3.3 through §12.3.8. The throne scenario shows that unlimited power is insufficient, not that no divine claimant could be authenticated.

Abraham and Isaac sharpen the scope question. The narrative presents Abraham as trusting the commander even where the content appears to collide with the standing of another subject (Gen 22:1–18; Heb 11:17–19). A defender can appeal to divine ownership of life, unique revelatory warrant, the promised resurrection, typology, or the fact that the act is stopped. Those answers differ, but each recognizes that ordinary authority isn’t enough: the command claims jurisdiction over Isaac’s life and Abraham’s relation to him. The case can’t be settled by repeating that God commanded it. It asks which God–creature relation licenses one subject to be placed at risk through a command addressed to another.

That distinction exposes two classes of command relevant downstream. Some are principally *God-directed* and can be violated without a third-party victim: worship, allegiance, prayer, devotion, or an inward orientation toward God. Others govern how one creature treats another: prohibitions of killing, theft, sexual violation, deception, and dispossession. In the second class, the affected creature already has welfare, agency, and stakes that explain why the act matters. Divine command theory may hold that God’s directive converts those reasons into categorical obligation; the command-authority account must then explain what categorical force adds and why it belongs to God. In the first class, no third-party injury is required for obedience or culpability. That difference becomes decisive when suffering is later defended as the necessary price of morally significant choice (§12.5.2).

The Sermon on the Mount makes the separation sharper without requiring an inflated reading. Jesus places anger under judgment and treats lustful looking as adultery “in the heart” (Matt 5:21–22, 27–28); 1 John 3:15 calls hatred of a brother murder. Whatever further distinctions Christian ethics draws among temptation, entertained thought, settled intention, and completed act, the texts permit culpability before a victim bears the intended harm. A moral governor could therefore judge the inward orientation or attempted violation while preventing its completion. The command may regulate the heart; the victim’s suffering doesn’t thereby become necessary for the violation to be real.

One additional limit follows from the content of command. “Love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deut 6:5; Matt 22:37–38; Mark 12:30) doesn’t operate like a traffic convention. The book’s account of the will holds that love and belief aren’t terminal states installed by bare choice; they emerge from what encounter, attention, and conviction have formed (§12.3.6). A command may direct practices that cultivate love, prohibit conduct incompatible with it, or name the fitting orientation of a relationship. If it instead treats affection itself as immediately selectable, it demands what an addressee can’t produce by deciding. Divine authority doesn’t convert a non-voluntary terminal state into a voluntary act.

The book’s positive account enters without pretending to reproduce everything the theory wants. The positive account grounds other-regarding claims in subjects with welfare, agency, relationships, and stakes of their own, under an explicit reciprocity and equal-standing premise. It doesn’t derive a free-standing, blame-backed categorical institution from Chapters 1–3. A reader may reject that bridge and retain divine command theory without contradicting the upstream metaphysics. If the bridge is accepted, however, it explains why one subject has claims against another before a superior will speaks. Commands can still coordinate conduct, constitute roles and covenants, settle open specifications, and declare what those claims require. They aren’t idle. What they can’t do is erase the standing that limits their authority or create unlimited jurisdiction out of the fact of address.

Modified divine command theory therefore survives the simple Euthyphro objection. Grounding goodness in a loving nature and obligation in commands assigns different work to each. The live burden is more exact: identify the relation that gives God authority, establish its scope, show what the command adds, and authenticate the source. A personal will supplies an issuer. Only an adequately specified interpersonal relation supplies jurisdiction.

### 12.3.12 Divine Punishment
Divine judgment isn’t one doctrine with one purpose. A retributive account imposes what wrongdoing deserves. A protective account incapacitates or separates an agent to prevent further harm. A deterrent account addresses future conduct. A remedial account corrects, heals, or reconciles. An annihilationist account ends the wrongdoer’s existence; a universalist account makes judgment purgative and finally restorative; a self-exclusion account treats final loss as the creature’s continued refusal rather than a penalty externally imposed. Traditions combine these functions, and a single scriptural image may be read through more than one. The question “Does God have standing to punish?” cannot be answered until *standing* and *punishment* are specified.

The upstream branches arrive here with different subjects. Inherited corruption is separated from inherited culpability at §12.1.5. A corruption-only or nonhistorical-condition account brings no ancestral desert into judgment. An imputation or inherited-guilt account carries the burden identified at §12.1.6. Neither branch settles responsibility for a person’s own acts. The creature-side condition is separately fixed at §12.1.8, its activation point, and the rule for people who lack access or accountability. Judgment must use the same condition; it can’t punish under a gate whose content, effective date, or population changes when the argument moves sections.

Responsibility survives the fact that nobody authors themselves. Agents act from formations, reasons, convictions, capacities, and histories they didn’t choose from outside themselves—a point the tradition presses harder than most, in its own doctrines of inherited nature, concupiscence, and the circumstances a soul is born into. Their acts may nevertheless express who they are, respond to reasons with varying depth, alter other subjects’ possibilities, and create reparative responsibilities. Causal formation doesn’t by itself erase ownership or answerability, and a theology that said it did would have dissolved its own doctrine of sin along with the objection. Divine punishment therefore can’t be rejected merely because a creature didn’t author its own character. The question is whether a particular divine role changes the responsibility relation and, if so, how far.

Manipulation arguments identify one such change but have conditions. Pereboom’s designed agents and Mele’s zygote case are arranged so that a particular deliberative history and outcome occur while familiar compatibilist features remain (Pereboom 2001; Pereboom 2014; Mele 2006). They pressure the claim that reasons-responsiveness and identification are always sufficient for basic desert. Ultimate creation alone isn’t yet that arrangement. A creator may originate agents in a world containing other creatures, chance, secondary causes, social histories, and forms of self-modification without selecting each later outcome. Constitution isn’t outcome-specific intervention, and the difference cannot be erased by calling every causal contribution “field-authorship.”

The manipulation pressure attaches in proportion to the providential set retained at §12.3.1. A meticulous decree or deterministic concurrence account accepts comprehensive divine determination and must explain how creaturely ownership grounds retributive desert toward the determining source. Thomistic primary and secondary causation offers a real answer: the creature can be the complete secondary cause of an act even while God sustains its being as primary cause (Stump 2003). The remaining dispute is whether secondary sourcehood is enough for the penalty claimed, not whether the account simply forgot creaturely causation. A Molinist account preserves libertarian creaturely authorship while God selects among feasible worlds with knowledge of counterfactual choices; its pressure is selection of circumstances and outcomes, not causal production of the choice. Simple-foreknowledge accounts must distinguish foreseeing from using foreknowledge to select the history. Open theism reduces outcome-specific authorship by administering a genuinely open field and accepts the corresponding risk and control costs. General creation supplies responsibility for the kind of arena selected; only the stronger branches approach the designed-outcome cases.

Judicial standing must be separated from injury. A judge need not be the victim of a crime and need not gain from the sentence. Public jurisdiction can arise from a role ordered toward the standing of other subjects, the maintenance of a common field, the protection of the vulnerable, and the fair administration of law. Divine aseity therefore doesn’t remove judicial standing merely because God can’t be enriched, repaired, or made whole by punishment. It removes only one rationale: punishment can’t restore a loss to an impassible God if nothing creatures do can diminish that God. Protection, public justice, vindication of victims, and restoration remain distinct possible ends.

That is where The Command-Authority Specification (§12.3.11) enters. Creatorhood, sovereignty, perfect goodness, benefaction, covenant, and creaturely welfare are different proposed grounds of jurisdiction. They may combine, but the combination must establish more than power to impose consequences. It must explain why this authority governs this subject, why it covers the wrong at issue, and which limits love, justice, welfare, covenant, and the subject’s standing place on the response. The same authority that can specify an obligation need not possess an unlimited license to punish every failure without regard to capacity, notice, or proportion.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Divine-Judgment Specification** · *Diagnostic*

Before a divine consequence can be defended as just punishment, an account must specify **(1)** the wrong and whose standing it violated; **(2)** the agent’s capacity, knowledge, control, and contribution to that wrong; **(3)** God’s role as creator, circumstance-selector, outcome-determiner, injured party, lawgiver, public judge, protector, or healer; **(4)** the relation that gives God jurisdiction in that role; **(5)** whether the consequence is retributive, protective, deterrent, remedial, annihilative, restorative, or the result of self-exclusion; **(6)** how its severity, duration, distribution, and exit conditions answer to that purpose; and **(7)** whether the governing rule and stakes were adequately available to the person judged. Creation alone establishes neither outcome-specific manipulation nor unlimited punitive standing, and lack of personal injury establishes neither lack of public jurisdiction nor proportionality.

*Scope.* This diagnostic doesn’t deny divine judgment, assume libertarian sourcehood, or treat every consequence as retribution. It prevents causal authorship, public authority, desert, protection, and restoration from performing one another’s work without the required bridge.

**Still open:** the selected providential branch; the ground and scope of divine jurisdiction; the purpose of judgment; the responsibility conditions; and the proportionality and access rules

**Depends on:** The Command-Authority Specification (§12.3.11); §12.3.1; The Salvation Specification Test (§12.1.8)

*The Flood as a selected means.* The historical-local reading distinguished at §12.1.2 retains divine warning, a real inundation, rescue, and judgment without a planet-wide flood. Locality then creates a means problem of its own. The same advance warning that tells a six-hundred-year-old Noah to build a floating habitat can tell his household to leave the floodplain. Genesis itself supplies the precedent. The messengers warn Lot that Sodom will be destroyed, tell him to take his household out of the city, direct him toward refuge beyond it, and withhold the destruction until he reaches Zoar (Gen 19:12–22). The narrative therefore already knows how divine foreknowledge and selective rescue work when a doomed region has an outside: migration.

If the threatened flood region has an outside, the same means preserves Noah’s family and its dependent animals without the construction, confinement, and roughly year-long voyage. If it has no reachable outside, the local reading owes the barrier: why no route to safe land was available during the time in which an ark could be built, and how geographically limited the event remains once every accessible refuge has been removed.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Ark-or-Exit Problem** · *Disjunction*

If the flood was local, why build a world that floats instead of leaving the water’s path?

- **If safe land was reachable,** then the warning could have sent Noah’s household and its dependent animals there, just as Lot’s household is warned out of Sodom before its destruction. The ark and the year aboard weren’t needed for rescue.
- **If no safe land was reachable,** then the local reading owes what blocked migration during the same advance period in which the ark could be built. The farther the water must extend to close every exit, the more planetary scale the reading buys back.

Locality removes the need for a global flood. It also removes the clearest need for an ark.

**Applies to:** historical-local readings that retain divine warning and the ark as an actual means of rescue

The ark can still be assigned a further purpose: a public sign, a test of trust, an instrument of preaching, or the vehicle of a covenantal re-creation. But then flotation isn’t forced by the rescue problem. The account must explain why that further purpose required prolonged construction, confinement, and the drowning of the region rather than warning and migration. Symbolic work may explain why the story is told with an ark; it doesn’t by itself explain why a historical local rescue needed one.

The named end doesn’t require the means. Gen 6:5–13 charges human wickedness and then drowns “every living thing” but the ark’s pairs (7:21–23). Foreknowledge already picks out the guilty; the same narrative can bring animals to a boat (6:20) and later walk Lot out of a city’s ruin (Gen 19). The corpus already knows a strike without collateral. Onan refuses the duty to raise offspring for his dead brother, spills his seed rather than give Tamar a child, and is put to death; no one else drowns (Gen 38:8–10; so too Er, 38:7). Nadab and Abihu, Uzzah, Ananias and Sapphira are the same instrument used on a named offender while the rest remain standing (Lev 10:1–2; 2 Sam 6:6–7; Acts 5:1–10). A flood that leaves two of every kind isn’t the most precise tool this God is shown to have.

Retribution bears the heaviest sourcehood load because its justification is backward-looking desert. A hard-line compatibilist may hold that reasons-responsive ownership is enough even when a designer knowingly constitutes the agent and selects the history. That position remains available. A softer account may reduce desert where formation, coercion, impairment, ignorance, manipulation, or divinely selected circumstances reduce the agent’s control. The book’s account supports the second kind of calibration: responsibility tracks modal depth and actual contribution rather than ultimate sourcehood or its absence. The theological question is comparative. A peer wrongdoer can owe repair to the subject harmed even though neither authored itself. A creator or governor may also judge publicly, but any contribution that governor made to the particular outcome belongs inside the responsibility assessment rather than being converted into a universal immunity or ignored.

The act–defect distinction supplies another serious reply. On a Thomistic account, God causes the being of an act while sin lies in a privation or disorder attributable to the deficient secondary cause. The distinction blocks the inference from divine conservation to God’s positively causing sin *as sin*. It doesn’t end the inquiry where the retained providential set includes selection of circumstances, foreknown vulnerability, or determination of the act. Those facts may affect permission and proportionality without making God the sinner. The diagnostic asks for that allocation; it doesn’t assume that every occurrence-condition is equivalent to the wrongdoer’s intention.

Even when desert and jurisdiction are granted, magnitude requires a further argument. Finite agents act with bounded understanding, development, control, and temporal histories. A retributive penalty must explain how its severity and duration fit the wrong and the agent’s responsibility. Eternal conscious punishment is therefore a stronger claim than divine judgment generally (cf. Kvanvig 1993). An infinite-dignity account measures offense partly by the status of the one offended; an ongoing-rebellion account treats continuing punishment as answering continuing wrong rather than one finite act; a consequential account may invoke protection or deterrence; a self-exclusion account denies externally inflicted retribution; annihilationism, remedial judgment, and universal restoration revise the disposition itself. Each branch escapes some pressures and inherits others. None may cite the mere existence of divine authority as its proportionality rule.

The infinite-dignity route owes particular clarification. An offense can be aggravated by the standing of its patient without every difference in rank generating an unbounded penalty. The account must explain why divine dignity changes the measure infinitely, how a finite agent adequately apprehends the object offended, and why the resulting sentence remains proportionate to capacity and intent. Classical aseity blocks the idea that punishment repairs damage to God, but it doesn’t block God from judging injuries to creatures or violations of a public moral order. The argument therefore reaches the infinite-debt rationale more directly than it reaches divine judgment as such.

The self-exclusion model relocates rather than removes the agency conditions (Lewis 1940; Swinburne 1989; Walls 1992). Honoring a refusal can respect agency where the person understands the object, stakes, alternatives, and reversibility of the choice. Those conditions are made contestable at §12.3.6 and §12.3.7 where a finite person rejects an unclear revelation, a painful religious community, or an evidentially unpersuasive historical claim rather than God under the description *infinite good*. The model can answer through postmortem disclosure, continued opportunity, middle knowledge, or a claim that character eventually fixes itself. Each answer must state when refusal becomes adequately informed and why it becomes irreversible. “The door is locked from within” identifies the proximate mechanism; it doesn’t by itself establish comprehension or permanence (Talbott 1999).

Punitive threats create a distinct motivational pressure but not a universal defeater. Fear of punishment can coexist with concern for others, repentance, love, and principled restraint; mixed motives don’t make moral character unreadable. An unbounded threat can nevertheless dominate deliberation and make outward compliance poor evidence of inward transformation. If the proposed end is restored relationship or freely rendered love, the account must explain the role of fear and why the sanction doesn’t crowd out the response it is meant to elicit. If the end is public deterrence or restraint, fear may be functioning exactly as intended, and the defense should name that less intimate purpose.

People who die before accountability expose the need for branch consistency rather than a dilemma with only condemnation and automatic beatitude. Traditions have proposed inherited guilt, baptismal or covenantal grace, an age of accountability, divine mercy, limbo, postmortem formation, inclusivism, election, and universal restoration. These routes don’t all produce the same status or destination. The specification question is whether the doctrine’s responsibility condition, salvation condition, and disposition agree. A person lacking relevant capacity or notice can’t bear act-based retributive desert for failing that act or condition; an inherited-guilt branch must defend the different basis it invokes. A grace or postmortem route can preserve final good without an earthly trial, but then any claim that the trial is universally necessary must be revised. The result is a priced branch, not the conclusion that death before accountability is necessarily the surest passage to heaven.

The Abrahamic comparison remains set-specific. Jewish accounts of divine judgment include covenantal responsibility, repentance, mercy, temporal correction, *Gehenna*, and the world to come without one uniform doctrine of eternal conscious punishment. Christian accounts divide among eternal punishment, conditional immortality or annihilation, self-exclusion, remedial judgment, and universal reconciliation. Islamic accounts join judgment with divine justice and mercy while differing over the duration of punishment, the status of grave sin, the reach of intercession, and the relation between divine decree and acquired human action. What travels across the family isn’t one sentence about hell. It is the requirement that responsibility, divine jurisdiction, the purpose of judgment, and the disposition selected be made mutually consistent.

The book’s relational account supplies a standard without pretending to settle every theological branch. Wrongdoing can create responsibilities toward injured subjects and toward a shared field: repair, protection, restored agency, and prevention of renewed harm. Public judgment may administer those responsibilities without the judge being personally injured. Retribution adds the claim that suffering or deprivation is deserved independently of what it repairs, protects, or restores; eternal retribution adds a magnitude and duration beyond any finite civic analogue. Those additions bear the corresponding burden.

Divine punishment therefore doesn’t fail merely because God created the agent or cannot personally gain from the sentence. Creation becomes manipulation only under stronger outcome-shaping conditions, and public judges need not be victims. The live tests are more exact: whether the retained providence leaves sufficient creaturely ownership, whether the proposed God–creature relation supplies jurisdiction, whether the response serves the purpose named, whether its magnitude fits the agent and wrong, and whether the judged person could adequately encounter the rule and stakes. Strong retributive and eternal-punishment sets must satisfy the conjunction. Protective, annihilationist, remedial, universalist, and self-exclusion sets leave different parts of it by changing what judgment is claimed to do.

*The criterion cuts here too.* A defender of fine-tuning who adopts a sustaining criterion for tuned-for-conscious-life is committed to what that criterion certifies, and it certifies hell: conscious beings sustained indefinitely, which is more sustaining than this world manages for anyone (§10.1.9). That result is about the fine-tuning inference. What it leaves for a doctrine of judgment is a separate question, and it is asked here.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Certified Hell Problem** · *Disjunction*

If the criterion that certifies this world also certifies hell, what is hell?

- **If hell sustains conscious beings indefinitely,** then by the defender’s own criterion it is the best-tuned environment there is. It sustains what this world doesn’t manage to sustain for anyone. *Priced by* The Hell Is Fine Problem (§10.1.9).
- **If hell doesn’t sustain them,** then conditional immortality or universal restoration is taken, and endless conscious punishment is given up.
- **If the criterion is revised to exclude hell,** then some further difference between the two environments has to be named. Naming one is the open route out, and the named difference must not also exclude this world.

The doctrine and the criterion can be held separately. The box binds whoever holds both.

**Applies to:** accounts combining a sustaining criterion for divine tuning with a doctrine of endless conscious punishment

## 12.4 Problems of Good and Evil

The fourth cluster identifies the distinct forms of evil that a creator theology must answer before it can offer a defense. Teleological Evil (§12.4.1) concerns suffering built into the world’s design; Divinely Legislated Evil (§12.4.2) concerns harm written into standing law; and Divinely Commanded Evil (§12.4.3) concerns targeted harm ordered outright. These aren’t rival theodicies but the pressures a theodicy inherits.

These sections inherit what is already earned rather than relitigating the problem of evil from a standing start: the traditional classical God is already under pressure (Chapter 11), and one dilemma recurs across the cluster—suffering that is necessary constrains omnipotence, while suffering that isn’t necessary raises a question for benevolence. The following Theodicies cluster fixes the tradition’s proposed good and tests the escalating defenses offered in reply.

### 12.4.1 Teleological Evil

The theodicies gather under one heading—the problem of evil—but the evil they answer isn’t all of one kind, and the difference decides which of them can work. One kind issues from creaturely choice: the harm an agent works on another, the cruelty a will elects. This is *moral evil*, and it has a bearer other than the creator—the free creature whose act it is. The other kind waits on no one’s choosing. A gazelle is pulled down and opened while its heart still beats; a parasite completes itself by hollowing its host alive; an infant inherits a genetic course that will exhaust it before it can speak. None of this is done by anyone. It is simply what the natural order does, working exactly as built—predation, parasitism, disease, congenital disorder, famine, and the slow attritions of decay and age. This is *teleological evil*: suffering seated in the design of the world rather than in the misuse of a freedom within it. The literature more often calls it *natural evil*; the book’s name marks what is actually at stake—not merely that the suffering is natural rather than moral, but that it is built, a feature of how the world was purposively arranged. The term is fixed here because the sections that follow lean on it without stopping to establish it.

What makes the second kind harder is that it raises an authorship question. Moral evil can be laid, at least in part, at the creature’s door; teleological suffering often predates any relevant creaturely choice. A creator theology must therefore explain how the natural order, the capacities it gives creatures, and the suffering it permits relate to divine agency. An undirected-process account may treat that suffering as unwilled; a creator account can’t simply assume that the creator directly wills every feature, but must state its doctrine of creation, permission, law, and providence.

The accessibility claim must be disaggregated. The argument doesn’t need, and current physics doesn’t supply, a proof that every law or every suffering-bearing feature could be varied independently while preserving every good of this world. It needs a more bounded result: where the same stated end has an actually realized or otherwise independently possible less harmful implementation, the harsher implementation isn’t forced by that end.

The world supplies such witnesses for some central mechanisms. Autotrophic life converts light or chemical gradients into maintained living structure without killing sentient prey, so nourishment isn’t conceptually coupled to predation. Nociceptive signaling and phenomenal agony are physiologically dissociable—anesthesia and analgesia can suppress conscious suffering while damage detection, bodily regulation, and the agency of others continue—so protection isn’t conceptually identical to torment. These examples don’t prove that an entire biosphere could be replaced costlessly, and a defender may identify trade-offs. They do establish that the functions usually named in defense of these mechanisms have more than one realizer within the actual law-governed world. Under the creator theology being tested—an omnipotent agent selecting and sustaining a created order—an alternative already instantiated under that order can’t be dismissed as merely unimaginable. The burden is to name the relevant end and show why no less harmful available realizer could secure it at the required scale.

For the residual physical set, the conclusion is conditional rather than asserted. If a suffering-bearing feature follows from every creatable world capable of the specified good, then it is necessary relative to that good, and the question becomes whether choosing that good with its unavoidable cost is compatible with perfect goodness. If a less harmful world or mechanism was accessible, selecting the harsher one incurs the design-authorship burden. What a creator can’t do is move between those horns by calling the feature necessary without naming the end and establishing the necessity. That bounded fork, rather than a universal claim that every law is contingent, is the authorship argument developed here. To design something is to select or sustain the means by which its ends are realized; teleological evil is the suffering for which that selection must account.

This is why the burden falls where it does. To a world with no designer, the same suffering is no anomaly: an undirected selective process yields organisms that persist by consuming one another and that register damage as pain because registering it aids survival. Widespread suffering isn’t a difficulty for such a world; it is precisely what such a world would contain. Teleological evil is therefore not a problem for the world as such. It is a problem for one claim about the world—that it was made, and made by something good—and it presses on that claim alone.

The point is comparative, not a verdict that every particular suffering is gratuitous. The overall hedonic pattern is no surprise if sentient life emerges through unguided selection: pain often calibrated to survival, its failures and excesses where that calibration breaks, and no settled correlation between moral standing and earthly welfare. A perfectly good personal creator can offer a purpose for any element after the fact; but that isn’t yet a reason to expect the whole pattern in advance. The relevant question is which account makes the observed distribution less ad hoc, not whether a single case conclusively defeats theism (Draper 1989).

The oldest suffering of all is the remainder no reply through human agency can reach. Sentient life suffered for hundreds of millions of years before any human existed to choose, to be formed, or to deserve—suffering that answered to no choice, built no soul, and punished no fault, because there was as yet no one whose choice, soul, or fault it could involve. Teleological evil is at its hardest exactly where the tradition’s usual answers have nothing to take hold of.

*The three layers of design.* The theist who concedes that natural suffering is built in, not chosen, still hopes to keep it from being God’s intended feature. Three layers must each be cleared, and each is authored. The first is the *capacity* to suffer: a nervous system that registers damage as agony rather than as neutral signal. That capacity was designed: a creature could have been built to track injury as information without the felt torment. The second is the *inescapability* of that suffering for the creature that has it: the animal can’t opt out of its pain-signalling system, can’t revise its own design. Grant both, and the defender’s last move is that the suffering is inescapable *as such*, fixed by the nature of embodied life. But inescapability-for-the-creature isn’t inescapability-for-the-designer: what the animal can’t revise, the designer chose not to revise. The third layer is therefore *avoidable suffering at the design level*: a suffering escapable at the level of design but made inescapable for the creature isn’t a constraint the designer suffered but a feature the designer selected. Each layer the defender concedes pushes the authorship up one level, and the top level is the design itself.

*The appeal to law, and the fork it opens.* The standing reply is that the layers aren’t chosen but fixed: a law-governed world of the kind embodied life requires simply comes with damage, predation, and pain, and God could no more omit them than draw a round square. Ask where the necessity of these laws resides, and the reply forks. If God could have set different laws, then the law-set that makes suffering necessary was itself among his options, and choosing it is choosing the suffering it entails: the necessity is real, but it is the designer’s own stipulation, authored one level up. If God couldn’t, because the laws are a material he didn’t make and can’t alter, then he is a demiurge ordering a material given rather than the omnipotent creator ex nihilo the theodicy needs—the necessity is real, but the price is the very omnipotence the defense was built to protect.

There is a third reading, and it is the one classical theism actually holds: the laws couldn’t be otherwise because they flow necessarily from God’s own nature—binding on him, and in that sense unchosen, yet not imposed on him from outside. Pressed this far, the reply doesn’t break the dilemma but deepens it. If the laws, and the suffering they entail, follow necessarily from what God *is*, then that suffering is entailed by God’s very nature—not selected by his will, but authored beneath the level of will, in the divine essence itself; the believer who adopts this position doesn’t move the suffering away from God but roots it in him. So the fork closes from every side: laws God chose author the suffering by choice, laws flowing from God’s nature author it by nature, and only laws external to God break the authorship—at the price of the omnipotence the whole defense rests on.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Law Fork** · *Disjunction*

Why are the laws that build suffering into nature the way they are?

- **If God could have chosen different laws,** then selecting this law-set includes selecting the suffering it entails.
- **If the laws follow necessarily from God’s nature,** then the suffering is rooted in that nature rather than moved away from God.
- **If the laws are external constraints God couldn’t alter,** then design-level authorship recedes. But the creator is no longer omnipotent over the order being explained. *Priced by* Power Is a This-Rather-Than-That (§11.7.1).

The first two branches retain authorship by choice or nature; the third surrenders the power claim that made the defense a defense of creator theism.

**Still open:** authorship by selection, authorship by divine nature, or an external constraint on divine power

*The biological exhibit.* Autotrophs establish a narrower point than a complete alternative biosphere. Photosynthetic and chemosynthetic organisms show that metabolism and biological persistence don’t universally require consuming other organisms. They don’t demonstrate that a biosphere containing sentient, mobile, heterotrophic agents—or the same ecological goods the defender values—could be stable without predation, competition, death, or nutrient recycling through consumption. The evidence therefore defeats only the universal claim that *all life as such* must be consumptive. A stronger design alternative remains conditional: biology may support less harmful trophic organization, different balances of primary production and consumption, or reduced sentient predation, but its compossibility and ecological stability require an actual model rather than inference from autotrophs alone. A different necessity is sometimes pressed in its place: Swinburne’s argument that natural evil is required for *knowledge*, since significant free agency needs agents who can learn from regular natural processes how their actions bring benefit and harm, and that knowledge has to be bought with real instances of natural suffering (Swinburne 1998). Grant the connection in full; it doesn’t break the fork but chooses a horn within it. Autotrophs alone don’t show that a creator had available a complete agency-supporting world without built-in suffering. Swinburne’s knowledge defense must instead be tested comparatively: whether significant agency requires genuine harmful risk, whether less harmful lawlike arrangements were feasible, and whether the actual magnitude and distribution are proportionate. If the suffering-priced structure is shown to be one feasible option among less harmful equivalents, selection bears an authorship burden; that conditional can’t be treated as already empirically demonstrated.

*The anti-coercion exhibit.* The same test applies to a narrower and more exacting case: the vulnerability of an embodied reproductive system to insemination the bearer doesn’t consent to. If a body capable of sexual reproduction is thereby, of necessity, a body with no way to block that specific harm, the vulnerability is a cost of reproduction as such, not a further design choice layered on top of it. The claim is false on the same evidentiary ground the autotrophic case uses: contingent, currently existing lineages carry real defenses against exactly this harm, defenses too heterogeneous in mechanism and too uneven in distribution to be a side effect of anything reproduction as such requires. Waterfowl vaginal tracts have coevolved corkscrewing, dead-end pouches running counter to the male’s coiled phallus—structures that impede full penetration precisely in forced matings, and whose complexity tracks, across species, the rate at which females are subject to forced extra-pair copulation (Brennan and Prum 2015). Across primates and beyond, behavioral and physiological counter-strategies to sexual coercion—mate-guarding evasion, coalition formation, cryptic control of paternity—recur wherever the selective pressure that would favor them is present (Smit 2025). None of this is one mechanism generalized; it is convergent pressure answered independently, again and again, wherever a lineage’s circumstances favored it—and sometimes answered the other way: the copulatory tie of canids locks the pair together for the male’s benefit, not the female’s (Dewsbury 1972), confirming that the direction an arms race like this runs is itself a further design fact, not a forced outcome of embodiment.

The choice tracks no principle a defender could retreat to. Orangutans are great apes, among humanity’s nearest surviving relatives, and they face frequent forced copulation from unflanged males. Females deploy behavioral counter-tactics, seeking proximity to protective dominant males, but no anatomical mechanism comparable to the duck’s vaginal counter-morphology is documented in the lineage (Knott 2009). Phylogenetic closeness to humans, then, predicts nothing about whether the physiological layer of the defense is present. It is fixed lineage by lineage, which is what a design-level choice looks like and not what a nomological necessity does.

Applied to the three layers already distinguished: the capacity to be violated by forced insemination with no bodily recourse at all isn’t the only option a designer had; the option was demonstrably available, since it is instantiated right now in cousin lineages; and withholding it from the one lineage capable of reflecting on the fact is a design-level choice like any other—gratuitous unless it does the same justifying work the knowledge-buying reply claimed for suffering in general, which is the horn the fork already given has already closed.

*Why the line applies here and not elsewhere.* Against *moral* evil the theist has a real buffer: the free-will defense interposes a created will between God and the harm, so that the suffering traces to the creature’s choice rather than to the design (the book contests that defense on other grounds, but the buffer at least exists).

Natural evil has no such buffer. There is no free creature whose choice produced the earthquake or the parasite; there is no fallen will upstream of the Cambrian; there is no developing subject being formed by suffering that ran before subjects existed. Every device the other theodicies use to relocate authorship away from the design is unavailable, because the only candidate author left in the frame *is* the design. One move tries to restore the missing buffer: the Augustinian move Plantinga revives, as a defense rather than a theodicy, in *God, Freedom, and Evil* (Plantinga 1974), on which natural evil may trace to the free choices of nonhuman creatures—fallen angels whose rebellion predates and corrupts the natural order, supplying exactly the will upstream of the Cambrian that the design-authorship line says is absent. Grant the proposal in full. It still doesn’t relocate the authorship; it moves it up one agent and returns it unchanged. A created will, angelic or otherwise, acts in Time, occupies Space, and persists as a bearer—it stands inside the design, not behind it, and an agent inside the design can no more author the capacity to suffer, the inescapability of that capacity, or the law-set that fixes both than a creature can write its own pain-signalling system into being. What a fallen will could do is actualize cruelties the design already made available; what it couldn’t do is author the design that made them available. So the move faces the same fork as the appeal to law: either the angelic will works with a nature God set, and the three layers are authored exactly as before, or it works with a nature God didn’t set, which is the demiurge horn again, omnipotence traded away. The interposed will postpones the question by one agent; it doesn’t answer it.

So the dilemma this cluster shares (§12.4), taken in its gratuity-or-authorship form, doesn’t merely apply to natural evil—it has nowhere else to land: either the built-in suffering does no justifying work, in which case it is gratuitous, or it does, in which case it is a chosen feature of the design and authored by the designer.

*What this leaves the defender.* The honest fallback is to drop the necessity claim and own the design—to grant that the suffering is built in and intended, and to carry the burden of squaring an intended, creature-borne agony with the goodness the tradition ascribes to its author. That is the evidential problem of evil returned in full force, no longer softened by free will, by a fall, or by law. The skeptical-theist retreat to reasons past our grasp can block the inference from unseen reasons to no reasons, and that is a real achievement; what it can’t do is name the good the design serves, and a defense may not appeal to a good it also declares beyond assessment (§11.9.2). What remains, as with the soul-making theodicy, is suffering the design permits but can’t disown—except that here, with every buffer removed, it traces back to the designer.

*A second charge, independent of authorship.* The preceding charge runs on who designed the suffering. A defender who denies design-level intent outright—who holds that God sustains a natural order without specifying its harms in the way a craftsman specifies a blade—steps outside that argument entirely. It doesn’t follow that the charge is answered, because a separate result doesn’t need authorship to bind. Duty attaches to capacity, and the tradition states the principle in its own voice rather than borrowing it: the servant given much is required much (Luke 12:48), and the one who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it has sinned (Jas 4:17). Neither grounds the obligation in authorship, and that duty binds whether or not the duty-bearer chose the shape of the harm it could prevent. An omnipotent, omniscient sustaining agent has exactly the coercive and coordinating profile the duty-allocation premise names, at a limit no earthly institution reaches: total capacity, zero feasibility constraint, zero competing claim on scarce resources. A duty-bearer with that profile has no scarcity excuse: nothing is withheld from anyone else by holding the foundation, because there is no shortage of it to allocate. A designer who merely permits, rather than authors, what a nervous system suffers isn’t thereby released from that duty; permission by a capable duty-bearer is still non-provision. The authorship question and the duty question are independent tests, and a defense that survives the first must still clear the second.

**[Proposition]**

**A Duty-Bearer Need Not Have Designed the Harm** · *Proposition*

Duty follows capacity, and the tradition says so in its own voice rather than borrowing the principle. The servant given much is required much (Luke 12:48). The one who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it has sinned (Jas 4:17). The talents are judged by what each servant could do with what he was holding, not by what he had authored. None of these grounds obligation in authorship; each grounds it in what the agent was able to do. An omnipotent sustaining agent is that principle at its limit—total capacity, no feasibility constraint, no competing claim on scarce resources—so denying design-level intent doesn’t discharge the duty. Permission by a capable duty-bearer is still non-provision.

*Scope.* A defender who holds that these texts bind only creaturely servants, and that capacity in the divine case carries no answerability, can resist the charge. They then owe an account of why the principle their own scriptures state without qualification stops precisely where capacity is greatest.

The target is fixed, and the sections that follow are held to it. Natural evil raises an especially difficult authorship question for creator theism: a theology must explain the capacity for suffering, the relevant laws, and their distribution without simply relocating responsibility. The design-authorship argument applies with full force where a tradition attributes exhaustive creative control; it weakens where the theology revises omnipotence, adopts independent constraints, or disputes the proposed alternatives. The free-will defense addresses moral evil; soul-making and redemption theodicies address teleological suffering in different registers, but standard free-will and fall accounts don’t by themselves settle the natural-evil problem. A defense of the world’s suffering can’t answer only for harms caused by creatures and count the account closed; it must also address suffering built into natural history, borne before human choosers existed, and the relation that suffering has to any proposed creator or providential order (Draper 1989).

### 12.4.2 Divinely Legislated Evil

The standard theodicies sort evil into two species and post a defense at each. Moral evil—the harm creatures do to one another—is covered by the free-will defense (§12.5.2): a created will stands between God and the deed, and what the will does traces to the will that does it. Natural evil is the harm seated in the world’s design rather than in any creature’s choice, and it is prosecuted at §12.4.1, where the authorship argument runs on the physics. That taxonomy leaves one species unguarded: harm that God neither merely permits nor merely builds into the design but legislates—harm whose permitted forms, instruments, durations, and victims are specified in the law the tradition holds God gave.

The commitment isn’t incidental. The Torah’s case law is, on the shared floor of the Abrahamic family, divine legislation: given by God, to a named people, in words. That law regulates harm rather than prohibiting it. A slaveholder who beats a slave to immediate death is punished; one whose slave survives “a day or two” before dying isn’t, “for the slave is his money” (Exod 21:20–21). Foreign slaves may be bought, held as property, and bequeathed to children as a permanent inheritance (Lev 25:44–46). An ox that gores a free person to death costs its owner his life or a ransom; an ox that gores a slave to death costs the slave’s owner thirty shekels (Exod 21:28–32). Hammurabi 251–252 prices the same case by status—thirty shekels of silver for a free man gored to death, twenty for a slave—placing the rule within a Mesopotamian legal tradition whose relation to the Covenant Code is documented and debated (Wright 2009; Bowen 2021). Copan’s contemporary defense doesn’t deny what the texts say; it reframes what saying it was for. On the regulation-not-endorsement reading, the law meets a hardened people inside an institution it didn’t create, restrains harms within that institution, and points by stages toward the ethic the later revelation completes (Copan 2011; the redemptive-movement hermeneutic of Webb 2001), and behind both, the accommodation doctrine that runs back through Calvin. The tradition supplies the model itself: divorce was permitted “for your hardness of heart” (Matt 19:8) while the ideal stood waiting. Regulation, on this reading, is mercy in legal form—what its audience could bear at that stage. The critical literature denies that the texts can carry the reframe (Avalos 2011; Bowen 2021); this section doesn’t adjudicate the exegesis, but grants the defense its own reading and prosecutes it there.

*The audience the defense needs, and the audience the text gives it.* The regulation-not-endorsement reading needs a hardened people: a society already acquainted with slaveholding, for whom immediate abolition would have outrun what law could effectively teach or institutions could sustain. The text doesn’t permit the easier claim that Israel knew slavery only from below. The patriarchal narratives already describe household slaves, and the Passover law anticipates a slave “bought for money” before Sinai (Exod 12:44). The exodus nevertheless makes emancipation from bondage the people’s constitutive memory, and the law repeatedly appeals to that memory as a reason not to reproduce oppression (Exod 22:21; Deut 15:15; 24:18). That history doesn’t prove that immediate abolition was feasible, but it makes the accommodation burden unusually exacting: the defense must explain why remembered liberation could ground protections for some vulnerable classes while permanent, inheritable ownership of foreigners remained an acceptable divine concession. Nor is the corpus uniformly bound to regional precedent. It prohibits practices it attributes to surrounding nations, including child sacrifice and specified forms of divination (Lev 20:2–5; Deut 18:10–12), and it sometimes supplies rules more protective than neighboring law. The question is therefore not whether the audience had a slaveholding tradition. It did. The question is why that tradition fixed the limit of feasible reform here when the same revelation presents itself as capable of revising inherited practice elsewhere.

The argument inherits three results and adds no machinery of its own. From §12.4.1 it takes the authorship-vs-permission fork, relocated from physical design to legal institution: what an agent specifies, that agent authors. From the cluster’s shared dilemma it takes the necessity-or-gratuity engine: a harm justified by a good is either required for that good or gratuitous. A conditional pressure falls on the claim that the law flows necessarily from an absolutely simple divine nature (Chapter 11): the account must explain how this determinate legal content follows without differentiation, brute selection, or modal collapse (§11.1, §11.2.1). That pressure doesn’t replace the internal legal argument that follows.

The free-will buffer fails here by construction, not by degree. The defense’s whole content is that the harm traces to a created will and not to God: God permits the misuse of freedom without authoring what freedom does. A statute isn’t a permission of that kind. A law that fixes how long a beaten slave may linger before the beating is avenged has taken the harm out of the will’s hands and specified it—the instrument, the victim class, the survivable interval, the price. The slaveholder’s will chooses within terms; the terms are the legislator’s. Whatever the buffer protects, it doesn’t protect the author of the limits, and on the tradition’s own account the author of these limits is God.

The fork then runs as it ran on the design. Either a materially less harmful law compatible with the audience’s actual social and economic limits was available, or it wasn’t. If it was, the legislated harm is gratuitous, and gratuitous harm is exactly what a theodicy exists to rule out (cf. Morriston 2009, pressing the same fork against attempts—Copan’s included—to supply morally sufficient reasons for the parallel case of the Canaanite commands). If it wasn’t, accommodation owes a specific impossibility claim: which feature of the audience made which reform unworkable, and why less harmful legal mechanisms the same corpus uses elsewhere couldn’t be extended here. Omnipotence need not make a contradiction actual, but hardness of heart isn’t yet an argument that a particular reform was socially or economically impossible.

*The accommodation escape, priced twice.* Accommodation answers the second horn directly: the better law was unavailable not because God’s arm was short but because revelation that outpaces its audience fails as revelation. Ritual specificity alone can’t settle that defense. Leviticus’s detailed rules for offerings, infections, fabrics, and days demonstrate legislative attention and drafting capacity, not social or economic bearability. Nor does the Exodus narrative by itself prove that immediate universal abolition was feasible; it establishes the tradition’s willingness to treat one people’s enslavement as intolerable. Those comparisons still expose the moral priority the corpus assigns, but the feasibility evidence must come from the law’s treatment of slavery itself.

That evidence is narrower and stronger. Exodus requires manumission when a master destroys a slave’s eye or tooth (Exod 21:26–27), so release as a remedy for abuse was already legally intelligible, though Bowen (2021) notes the asymmetry runs deeper still: unlike the case of a free person’s eye, no talionic eye-for-eye claim against the master is available to the slave, because master and slave aren’t treated as legal equals under the same statute that supplies that remedy elsewhere. Deuteronomy requires a Hebrew debt-servant’s release in the seventh year and commands the former master to provide materially for the transition (Deut 15:12–15), so term limits and funded manumission were administrable within the same social world. The term is twice the length of the three-year release Hammurabi’s code sets for the same class of debt-bondage (Hammurabi 117, Bowen 2021), but the provision for the servant’s exit has no counterpart there, so the tradition was capable of out-legislating its neighbors when it chose to. Leviticus forbids treating an impoverished Israelite ruthlessly and requires release at the jubilee, then permits foreign slaves to be held permanently in the immediately following verses (Lev 25:39–46). The asymmetry is the tell: the law had working machinery for term limits, funded exit, and injury-triggered manumission, and applied all three selectively by the enslaved person’s ethnicity rather than by the severity of the harm. These provisions don’t prove that complete and immediate abolition was economically feasible. They establish the conclusion the fork needs: more protective mechanisms weren’t beyond the audience’s legal or social repertoire, they were in the same law, for a different class of victim.

The corpus already accepts a standing economic cost for a weekly rest: “the seventh day is a sabbath to the Lord your God; you shall not do any work—you, or your son or your daughter, or your male or female slave” (Exod 20:10). A legislator willing to idle every laborer, including the enslaved, one day in seven isn’t a legislator for whom disrupting the labor regime was uniquely unthinkable.

The accommodation defense therefore owes a differential feasibility argument—why manumission could remedy an eye or tooth but not a beating followed by death, why release and transition support could govern one class but not another, and why a prohibition on ruthless treatment could stop at the ethnic boundary. Without that argument, “the audience was not ready” names the disparity but doesn’t justify it, and the enslaved of the interval remain the identified bearers of its cost.

Even the Hebrew male’s six-year release, the provision the regulation reading treats as the law’s protective core, is converted by a second specification in the same chapter. If the master gives him a wife and she bears children, “the wife and her children shall be her master’s, and he shall go out alone” (Exod 21:4). The term limit is real. The family is the price of using it. Children born in the house are born as the master’s property, and the man’s love for them is the mechanism that turns a six-year term into service for life (21:5–6). Accommodation can’t call this a restraint it was too early to improve. The same statute that knows how to time a release also knows how to hold the children who would make the man take it.

The second price is deeper. A revelation disclosed by stages, each stage matched to what its audience can bear, is observationally indistinguishable from a moral understanding developing by ordinary cultural means. Same sequence. Same lag. Same direction of travel. (The underdetermination at Scripture (§12.3.4) presses on doctrinal development.)
