An escape that fits the evidence exactly as well as the tradition’s absence can’t be evidence for the tradition; it saves the doctrine only by making the doctrine invisible.

*The kidnapping exit.* A narrower defense grants the property law and points instead to Exod 21:16, “Whoever kidnaps a person... shall be put to death,” read as the corpus condemning slave-trading and therefore, at root, the institution it traded in. The law doesn’t bear that weight. A prohibition on kidnapping regulates the method of acquisition, not the legitimacy of the resulting status; it sits beside, not against, the same chapter’s provisions for acquiring slaves by purchase, by birth, by a father’s sale of a daughter, and by conquest (Exod 21:7–11; Deut 20:10–14; Num 31:17–18). A law against stealing cattle isn’t a law against owning cattle. The kidnapping statute protects existing owners’ property claims and free persons’ status from unauthorized seizure; it doesn’t touch, and was never aimed at, the standing legality of the trade it left every other door open to.

*The sexual-access statutes.* A distinct class of legislated harm sits beside the property law: statutes that allocate sexual and marital consequences through the woman’s status and household. Deut 22:28–29 is disputed. Its verbs have been read as forcible seizure, seduction, or intercourse whose legal significance doesn’t map neatly onto either modern category; Exod 22:16–17 is the clearer seduction parallel. The present argument need not decide among them. On any of those readings, the settlement pays the father, binds the man against divorce, and doesn’t make the woman’s authorization of the marriage an explicit legal condition. The preceding town-and-country cases are disputed as well: crying out functions as an evidentiary presumption in the text, while the country case expressly treats the woman as lacking rescue and assigns no guilt to her (Deut 22:23–27). The moral burden isn’t that the law unambiguously punishes every silent victim. It is that a location-based presumption can determine whether an accused woman faces death without the statute spelling out an inquiry into coercion beyond that proxy.

In the accusation-of-nonvirginity case, the parents spread the “evidence” or “tokens” before the elders (22:13–21). The text doesn’t expressly identify a bloodstained cloth, although that is a longstanding interpretation; on that reading the proposed sign is medically unreliable, while on a broader reading the interpreter must specify what exculpatory evidence the law contemplates. Either way, the woman’s life turns on evidence controlled and presented by her household. Lev 19:20–22 then assigns a different penalty where the woman is an unfreed slave, explicitly making legal status relevant to the disposition. Exod 21:7–11 likewise permits a father to sell a daughter into a relation the passage regulates through redemption, food, clothing, and marital rights rather than through the release rule for male servants. These texts don’t yield one uncontested modern offense label. They do yield the narrower structural claim: the law distributes sexual, marital, and penal consequences through paternal and proprietary status without stating the woman’s contemporaneous consent as the governing condition.

*The statutes that weren’t good.* Ezek 20:25–26 is an interpretive crux, not an uncontested confession that God legislated child sacrifice: “I gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live. I defiled them through their gifts, in causing every firstborn to pass over.” One family of readings takes the passage as judicial handing-over to corrupt practices Israel chose; another connects it to a distorted or punitive form of firstborn law; another hears Ezekiel making a severe claim about laws attributed to God. The firstborn texts elsewhere require consecration while also requiring redemption rather than human sacrifice (Exod 13:2, 12–15; 34:19–20; Num 18:15–16), and that canonical distinction prevents the argument from simply identifying Exod 22:29 with a command to kill children. The pressure is conditional. A handing-over reading carries a providential judgment in which the resulting defilement is punitive rather than ideal legislation. A Mosaic-law reading carries a divine statute the prophet himself calls not good. A human-distortion reading protects the divine law by conceding that an attributed command could be disastrously misconstrued. The passage therefore intensifies the source-and-authority fork; it doesn’t settle it by itself.

*The pregnancy statute and its translation fork.* Exod 21:22–25 describes fighting men who strike a pregnant woman so that “her children come out,” followed by a fine if there is no *ason*—harm or calamity—and talionic penalties if harm follows. The construction has long supported two readings. On the miscarriage reading, fetal loss receives a fine while further injury to the woman triggers life for life. On the premature-birth reading, the delivery itself may result in a living child, and the talion can apply to injury suffered by mother or child. The Hebrew doesn’t permit this section to announce one reading as though no rival existed. What follows is branch-relative: the miscarriage reading creates a valuation problem for a theology that elsewhere treats prenatal death as ordinary homicide; the live-birth reading avoids that result but can’t recruit the statute as evidence for it without defending the translation and the scope of *ason*. The text is a disputed test case, not an independent verdict.

*What the New Testament adds, and doesn’t.* A common move locates the difficulty in the Old Testament and treats the New as the moral advance the accommodation defense promised. No New Testament text abolishes the institution or names it as wrong. What it supplies instead is repeated instruction to the enslaved to obey, “with fear and trembling,” masters good or harsh alike (Eph 6:5; Col 3:22; 1 Tim 6:1; 1 Pet 2:18), and a matching instruction to masters to govern justly and stop threatening (Eph 6:9; Col 4:1), correction of manner, not of the arrangement. Glancy’s historical study places these texts within early Christian communities in which enslaved people and slaveholders were both present and the institution was generally accepted rather than rejected (Glancy 2002). Paul’s letter to Philemon, the New Testament’s one sustained engagement with a specific enslaved person, asks that Onesimus be received “as a beloved brother” and returns him to his owner; it doesn’t make manumission a condition of the request. Gal 3:28’s “no longer slave or free” states a standing before God, in the same breath as “no longer male and female,” a verse no one reads as dissolving sex, and which the letters carrying Paul’s name did not read as dissolving slavery either, since they go on instructing slaves to obey. Whatever moral trajectory progressive revelation claims to be tracking, it doesn’t reach the enslaved reader of either testament with an answer to why the arrangement itself was permitted to stand.

*Which move hits whom.* The prosecution is scoped by what a defender holds. It lands in full on any position for which the case law is divine legislation in the plain sense—the classical mainstream of the three traditions. A defender who relocates the law’s authority into a commanding will as such meets the structural account of obligation at §12.3.11 rather than this section. A reading that surrenders the premise—the law as Israel’s own legislation, humanly authored and humanly limited—escapes the species entirely, but at the price of the revelation claim itself, which is prosecuted at §12.3.4: a law that was never given can’t be evidence of a giver, and the escape forfeits downstream what it saves here.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Whose-Law Problem** · *Disjunction*

Whose law is it, and what authority does it keep?

- **If the law is God’s ideal will,** then the permitted harm is attributed directly to the divine legislator and cannot be assigned solely to creaturely misuse. *Priced by* The Command-Authority Specification (§12.3.11).
- **If it is an accommodation of an entrenched practice,** then the defender must identify the restrained evil, name the best feasible rule available within the claimed constraints, state the moral standard by which the temporary permission counts as an improvement, and price the victims of the rule retained. *Feeds into* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).
- **If it is a rule later corrected by progressive revelation,** then the earlier statute wasn’t the final moral norm and may not be cited as one elsewhere.
- **If it is culturally conditioned human legislation attributed to God,** then divine legislative authorship recedes. But the text surrenders the direct-revelation claim used to authenticate it.

**Still open:** ideal divine law, accommodated provisional law, corrected earlier law, or human legislation misattributed to God

On the branch retaining direct divine authorship, the two-species taxonomy loses the coverage it promised. Moral evil had its created-will buffer and natural evil its design-level trial; legislated evil crosses the division—the will that executes the harm is creaturely, but the terms on which it is permitted are attributed to the legislator. Accommodation and progressive revelation preserve a divine role only by carrying the provisional rule, its victims, and the standard by which it is later corrected. Human attribution escapes divine legislative authorship by relocating the law into the culture that produced it, and it carries that revised revelation claim forward. The argument doesn’t force those branches back into one verdict.

### 12.4.3 Divinely Commanded Evil

Legislated evil (§12.4.2) is the species the free-will defense and the authorship argument leave unguarded: harm neither permitted through a creature’s misuse of freedom (§12.5.2) nor built into the world’s design (§12.4.1) but written into standing law. That taxonomy still leaves one further species unguarded: harm neither permitted nor legislated as an ongoing institution but commanded outright, as a single targeted act against a named population, under the ḥerem—the ban of total destruction (Deut 20:17).

The command is explicit and repeated: against the seven nations of Canaan (Deut 7:1–2, 20:16–18), against Sihon and Og (Deut 2:33–34, 3:3–6), against Amalek (Exod 17:14; 1 Sam 15:2–3), against Midian (Num 31:1–18). Each specifies the same scope—“you must not let anything that breathes remain alive” (Deut 20:16)—and the conquest narrative reports compliance at the same scope (Josh 6:21, 10:40, 11:14). Unlike the case law of §12.4.2, the defense offered here isn’t a regulation of a hardened people’s existing institution but a deserving claim: the populations named merited the judgment. Deuteronomy gives the ground directly—the nations are marked so that Israel won’t learn “all the abhorrent things that they do for their gods” (20:18), the abhorrent thing named without euphemism a chapter earlier: they “would even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods” (12:31; cf. Lev 18:21, 20:2–5).

*The fork.* Two defenses must be separated. The first is preventive: the ban was required so that Israel wouldn’t learn the condemned practice. The second is retributive: the populations deserved judgment independently of what means prevention required. An alternative-means argument bears directly on the first defense. It doesn’t by itself disprove the second.

On the preventive claim, the text supplies the relevant comparison. Deuteronomy answers the risk of religious assimilation by prohibiting intermarriage and directing Israel to tear down altars, smash pillars, cut down sacred poles, and burn idols (Deut 7:3–5; 12:2–4). The law against child sacrifice directs punishment at those who give children to Molech, not at the children offered (Lev 20:2–5). These are measures aimed at transmission, institutions, and perpetrators. They don’t establish that every campaign could have ended without violence, but they do establish that preventing adoption of the practice doesn’t, by itself, entail killing its child-victims.

Num 31 adds a narrower point. In the Midian episode, the command distinguishes within a defeated population and leaves the virgin girls alive as captives (31:18). Captivity is itself a grave harm and isn’t offered here as a morally acceptable remedy. The episode shows only that killing every young person wasn’t treated as an operational prerequisite to victory or separation in that case; it doesn’t prove that captive-taking was feasible, morally equivalent, or adequate to every campaign’s stated aim. The independent bridge is the text’s own anti-assimilation program: where the preventive end is served by separating communities, dismantling cultic institutions, and directing sanction toward perpetrators, child-killing can’t claim necessity from that end alone. A defender who shifts from prevention to deserving must defend that claim directly, which is the burden the remaining argument takes up.

*The captives kept alive.* The ḥerem sections already given concern killing. A distinct commanded evil runs alongside it: not who was killed, but who was kept, and for what. After the Midianite ḥerem, the command distinguishes within the defeated population and directs that “all the young girls who have not known a man by sleeping with him, keep alive for yourselves” (Num 31:17–18). The total is recorded with the same accounting precision applied to the sheep and cattle taken in the same campaign: thirty-two thousand persons, “women who had not known a man by lying with him” (Num 31:35), a tribute of one in fifty rendered to the Levites alongside the tribute of oxen and donkeys (31:28–40). The virgin girls aren’t an incidental byproduct of victory left unaddressed by the command; they are a specified class, counted, divided, and distributed by the same procedure applied to livestock. Deuteronomy generalizes the mechanism beyond Midian: a soldier who desires a woman among war captives may take her home, impose a month of mourning and grooming on her, and then take her as a wife (Deut 21:10–14); if he later finds no delight in her, he must let her go rather than sell her, but the text nowhere asks whether she delighted in him. The consent of the woman isn’t a term in either provision. What is regulated is the soldier’s procedure and the timing of his access, not whether access was hers to grant.

*Why this can’t borrow the ban’s own defense.* The preventive and retributive defenses already offered for the killing commands don’t transfer to this provision, and the text itself marks the difference. The nations are to be destroyed, on Deuteronomy’s own account, so that Israel won’t learn what they do for their gods (Deut 20:18) or so that judgment falls on what they deserve. Neither ground applies to a virgin girl kept alive and distributed as spoil: sparing her can’t be explained by the need to prevent assimilation, since keeping her in the camp is the assimilation risk the destruction of her people was supposedly guarding against, and it can’t be explained by deserving, since deserving was the stated ground for killing the population she is drawn from, not for her individual survival and reassignment. The command doesn’t integrate her death into the ban’s logic and doesn’t integrate her survival into either defense. She is kept alive for a purpose the text states plainly and the accounting confirms: she is counted as plunder because she is plunder, and the ban’s own apologetic literature, built to answer for the killing, has nothing to say about the keeping.

A further commanded harm is neither ḥerem nor captive-taking. After David’s adultery, the Lord announces the sentence in the first person: “I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in broad daylight… I will do this thing before all Israel” (2 Sam 12:11–12). Absalom’s public violation of the concubines is then reported as that sentence carried out (16:22). The women aren’t the offenders. Desert can’t attach to them, and prevention of a condemned cult isn’t in view. The sexual harm is the punishment, assigned to people who didn’t commit the crime, in words that make God the one who takes, gives, and does. The ban’s apologetic literature, built to answer for killing named nations, has nothing to say about this either.

*What consent would require, and what the text withholds.* Set the theological defenses aside and ask what a permitted relation requires. The conditions fall out of what a *yes* has to do to count as one. Someone who doesn’t know what’s being agreed to hasn’t chosen the thing they’re then held to. Someone who can’t refuse hasn’t agreed; they’ve complied. Someone who can’t weigh what’s at stake hasn’t decided. A yes to one thing isn’t a yes to another. And a yes that can’t be taken back isn’t a permission but a forfeit. Informed, voluntary, competent, specific, revocable: absent those, the purported modification isn’t the subject’s rule for what may happen to them but another party’s rule imposed through the grammar of permission. The Numbers and Deuteronomy provisions don’t approach that foundation by any measure the text supplies. The woman is counted with the livestock in the same census (Num 31:35), assigned by a procedure she takes no part in (31:28–40), and in the Deuteronomic case granted only a delay before access, not a say in whether it occurs (Deut 21:10–14); the text is explicit that her own state isn’t consulted—only his. A regime that satisfies the form of a rule (a month’s mourning, a formal marriage, a right of eventual release) while leaving every condition of authorization absent hasn’t modified a right by consent; it has substituted procedure for the refusal procedure exists to protect. This is a distinct charge from the authorship and deserving arguments already given: it doesn’t ask whether the ḥerem was necessary or deserved, and doesn’t depend on either answer. It asks only whether the command, however justified as war-law, meets the minimum condition a permitted relation requires, and on the text’s own terms it doesn’t.

**[Proposition]**

**Captivity Forecloses the Modifier** · *Proposition*

A permitted relation requires consent that is informed, voluntary, competent, specific, and revocable; absent those conditions, a form of authorization is another party’s rule imposed through the grammar of permission, not the subject’s own. The captive-marriage provisions regulate the soldier’s procedure and the timing of his access without consulting the woman’s state at any point, so the textual conditions for a permitted relation are absent on the text’s own account—independent of whether the ban that produced the captivity was itself justified.

**Depends on:** Consent’s Conditions (§5.14); Consent as Right Modifier (§6.1)

*The hyperbole exit, and what it must explain.* Copan and Flannagan read the sweeping language as stock ancient Near Eastern conquest rhetoric—“leave nothing that breathes” as a genre convention rather than a literal census (Copan 2011; Copan and Flannagan 2014). That reading materially reduces the attributed command’s scope and must not be treated as though the literal reading had already won. It doesn’t, however, erase every retained harm, and it meets counterpressure in 1 Sam 15. Saul is condemned for sparing Agag and selected livestock after being told to strike Amalek without sparing (15:3, 9, 19, 26–28). A genre reading can answer that the narrative marks representative or cultically significant noncompliance rather than failure to achieve biological totality. It must then say which objects and persons the command still covered, why those retained targets were required, and how the account distinguishes conventional totalization from morally operative specification. The sequel pressures the hyperbole reading; it doesn’t by itself close it.

*The siege curse is a different category.* Jeremiah condemns Judah for burning children to Baal, something God says he did not command and that “did not enter my mind” (Jer 19:5), and then announces a siege so severe that parents will eat their children (19:9; cf. Lev 26:29; Deut 28:53). The juxtaposition is morally severe, but it isn’t an identity of acts. Child sacrifice is an intentional ritual killing offered as worship; siege cannibalism is described as a consequence or judicially imposed condition under which human agents do something horrific. The latter is neither a divine command to eat children nor an authorized sacrifice. Its proper burden belongs to providence, punishment, and proportionality: whether deliberately bringing about conditions foreseeably issuing in that horror can be justified as judgment, and whether announcing the human act as a sanction leaves enough creaturely distance for the free-will reply. That remains a substantial problem, but it can’t be made by holding the content fixed and changing only the divine addressee.

Jephthah supplies a different, explicitly limited comparison. He vows on his own initiative that, if granted victory, whatever first comes from his house will belong to the Lord and be offered up (Judg 11:30–31). The narrative grants the victory and reports that he acts according to the vow when his daughter emerges (11:32–39). It never says God requested, authorized, or accepted the vow, and Heb 11:32’s later inclusion of Jephthah among figures of faith doesn’t endorse every act attributed to him. The episode therefore can’t function as another divinely commanded sacrifice. Its narrower pressure is providential and revelatory: a narrative able to depict the victory as divine action leaves the disastrous condition uncorrected, unlike the interrupted sacrifice of Isaac. A defender may answer that silence is condemnation, that the vow was illicit, or that the daughter was dedicated rather than killed. Those readings preserve the ban on sacrifice by refusing to treat Jephthah’s act as authorized; they then carry the corresponding account of divine silence and the passage’s ambiguity.

The preventive reading needs the killing of each retained victim class to follow from the aim of preventing assimilation; the text’s own differentiated anti-assimilation measures prevent that entailment from being assumed. The deserving reading carries a separate burden of desert. Hyperbole may reduce the extension of the command without removing the harms its reading retains. The siege curse and Jephthah can’t be added to the commanded-evil ledger as though God ordered either human act, but they remain downstream tests for providence, punishment, and revelatory clarity. The resulting prosecution is narrower and stronger: each attributed command must be assessed according to what it actually commands, while predicted consequences, unauthorized vows, and narratorial silence must be carried under their own relations rather than made into commands by association.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Conquest Texts Problem** · *Disjunction*

What do the conquest and captivity texts attribute to God?

- **If the texts attribute literal divine directives to God,** then the defense must justify the means or establish desert for every class harmed, which Guilt Does Not Travel (§12.1.6) prices. A preventive defense must show why the named end required the commanded means; a retributive defense must establish the desert of every class subjected to killing or captivity. *Feeds into* What Makes the Verdict Right? (§11.9.2).
- **If they record conventional war hyperbole,** then the literal scope is reduced. But narratives treating incomplete destruction as disobedience and the harms retained by the non-total reading still require an answer. *Feeds into* The Age-Old Problem (§12.1.2).
- **If they record human wartime judgments later attributed to God,** then direct divine authorship recedes—and with it the revealed-authority claim the same texts are cited to support: material identified as human cannot be quoted back as divine law. *Feeds into* The Whose-Law Problem (§12.4.2).
- **If they record commands later corrected by progressive revelation,** then the later standard must be named, and the earlier command must remain provisional rather than being restored whenever convenient.

**Still open:** literal command with its preventive or retributive burden, hyperbolic command with its retained harms, human misattribution, or progressive correction

## 12.5 Theodicies

The fifth cluster stages the tradition’s attempts to account for evil as an escalation rather than a catalogue. It begins with Greatest Good (§12.5.1), which fixes the standard every reply must meet. Free-Will Theodicy (§12.5.2) and Soul-Making Theodicy (§12.5.3) offer instrumental accounts; Redemption Theodicy (§12.5.4) turns to non-instrumental defeat; and Skeptical Theism (§12.5.5) appeals to reasons beyond our knowledge. Evil God Redux (§12.5.6) then closes the arc by reversing the whole defensive repertoire and testing whether it can distinguish a good creator from an evil or indifferent one.

The sequence moves from a fixed target, through concrete explanations, to a non-instrumental rescue, an epistemic fallback, and a final comparative test. Each theodicy is assessed on its own claimed work rather than allowed to borrow an answer from a different theodicy.

### 12.5.1 Greatest Good

Many greater-good theodicies in this chapter spend the same currency: a good large enough that some suffering comes out justified or permitted. Not every Christian account is aggregative, and a rights-based account or one with several independently valuable final goods may deny that goods and evils can be summed into one maximizing ledger. The currency is rarely counted: left as *the greater good*, its greatness never specified—whatever the suffering, some good beyond our seeing is said to redeem it. But a good defined as beyond seeing can’t be weighed, and a good that can’t be weighed can’t be found wanting; the appeal is unfalsifiable by construction. So that construction must be refused and the good fixed, before any theodicy is permitted to draw on it.

**[Diagnostic]**

**The Greater-Good Specification Test** · *Diagnostic*

Before suffering can be justified by a greater good, the defense must identify: **(1)** the good produced or protected; **(2)** who receives it; **(3)** whether and how it may be compared with the suffering; **(4)** whether gains to one person may justify losses imposed on another; **(5)** the less harmful counterfactual alternatives being excluded; **(6)** any rights or side constraints that outcome improvement may not override; and **(7)** whether the suffering causes, enables, risks, accompanies, or is merely followed by the nominated good. An unspecified good, beneficiary, or relation cannot do justificatory work merely by being called greater.

**Applies to:** any theodicy that cites a good as explaining, permitting, outweighing, defeating, or redeeming suffering

**Still open:** the defense’s comparison rule, distribution rule, side constraints, and claimed relation between suffering and good

The fixing is done on the tradition’s terms, not the book’s. The account of goodness this book gives elsewhere holds that goodness isn’t a property conferred by a will standing above the order of persons, and nothing here retracts that. What follows is an *internal* lever: the good as the Christian tradition itself describes it, built from its own scripture, granted only so that the doctrines leaning on it can be held to their word. It grants the tradition’s premises and turns them, binding the position from the inside rather than measuring it against a standard it would reject.

The tradition doesn’t leave the good unspecified; it specifies it everywhere, then forgets it under pressure. God is said to want four things of his creatures, each asserted plainly in its own scripture well before any question of suffering arises: love, trust, obedience, and glory.

*Love.* It is named the great and first commandment: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deut 6:5), which Jesus repeats and ranks above every other (Matt 22:37–38; Mark 12:30). God asks for love, not bare assent.

*Trust.* Faith is set as the precondition of pleasing God at all—“without faith it is impossible to please him” (Heb 11:6)—and the faith in view is reliance on a person, not bare assent to a proposition: when asked what God requires, Jesus answers, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6:29)—belief directed at *him*, not merely at a fact about him. The wisdom literature names the same posture without qualification: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not rely on your own insight” (Prov 3:5).

*Obedience.* It is ranked above sacrifice itself—“to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Sam 15:22)—and bound directly to love by Christ: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15). The Preacher reduces the whole of human duty to it: “Fear God, and keep his commandments, for that is the whole duty of everyone” (Eccl 12:13).

*Glory.* God states that he made his people for this end—“everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory” (Isa 43:7)—and the end is universal in reach: “All the nations you have made shall come and bow down before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Ps 86:9). The creature’s whole activity is to be ordered to it: “whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor 10:31).

For the target family, the proposed greatest good isn’t a fifth thing hidden behind these four but their fullest joint realization. That proposal requires additional premises; the scriptural commitments alone don’t entail a single aggregative maximand.

The inference from what God wants to what the good is isn’t imported from outside the tradition. Christian universalism runs on it directly: God is said to desire that everyone be saved (1 Tim 2:4), the divine will isn’t the sort of thing that fails of its object, and the conclusion drawn is that all are in the end saved (Talbott 1999; Hart 2019). That is the same movement used here—read the good off the expressed desire—carried to a conclusion a large part of the tradition rejects. Its presence matters twice over. It shows the inference is native rather than imposed, since a live wing of the tradition already reasons this way about these verses. And it supplies the tradition’s own answer to the obvious reply.

That reply is the scholastic distinction between God’s *antecedent* and *consequent* will: God antecedently wills all to be saved, and consequently, taking sin and justice into account, wills otherwise, so that an expressed desire need not fix what is maximized. The distinction was developed on this very verse, and it is available. What the universalist presses against it is that a will divided this way leaves the antecedent half doing no work: what God is said to want, God doesn’t get, and an omnipotent will whose expressed desire is routinely overridden is a strange thing to call sovereign. The point here is narrower than the universalist’s. A theodicist may take the distinction and deny that maximal salvation is the maximand—but then owes an account of what overrides the antecedent will and why, and that account is the specification asked for here. Declining to give it returns the good to the condition the section opened by refusing: named, invoked, and never counted.

There is a further place the commitment is visible, and it isn’t a text at all. The tradition doesn’t merely state that God wants people saved; it organizes around getting them saved. Missions are funded, translators are sent, seminaries train apologists, and someone stands on a corner in the rain talking to strangers. None of that is intelligible unless more-saved is better than fewer-saved. A mission board doesn’t raise money on the view that the number reached isn’t a quantity worth increasing, and no one leaves home for a field they will likely die in on the understanding that the good in question can’t be weighed. The Great Commission is itself framed as a maximizing instruction—*all* the world, *whole* creation, *all* nations—and the practice built on it treats reach as something to be extended rather than merely occupied.

This isn’t a charge of hypocrisy, and nothing here suggests the believer is insincere; the point is about what the practice already takes for granted. The maximand under discussion isn’t a scale imported to embarrass the tradition. It is the scale the tradition’s own activity is organized on, held steadily everywhere except at the moment a theodicy needs it released. A defender is free to say the good can’t be summed and that maximal salvation isn’t what God is maximizing. What that costs is the rationale for the enterprise: on that view the apologist at the door and the translator in the field aren’t producing more of anything that can be said to be better, and the enterprise would need some other account of what it is for. The argument asks only that the same answer be given in both places.

And the four don’t pull apart at the limit: a creature that fully loves God, fully trusts him, fully obeys him, and fully returns him glory is, under each description, a creature in restored relation, which the tradition calls saved. Traditions weight faith and obedience differently in what *constitutes* being saved (the faith-and-works question) but not in its end-state: the fully restored creature loves, trusts, obeys, and glorifies God whether obedience is counted the road or its fruit. The ways converge on one state of affairs. Scripture is equally plain that God wills this of all, and not of some only: that none should perish but all come to repentance (2 Pet 3:9), that he desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4), that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but would have them turn and live (Ezek 33:11). Three bridge premises are therefore made explicit.

**[Premise]**

**The Bridge Premises** · *Premise · the greater-good target*

**Comparability.** The goods invoked can be compared with the evils they are said to justify.

**Aggregation.** At least some cross-person gains and losses may enter the same justificatory assessment.

**Monotonicity.** Adding a creature in restored relation at no cost to any other good is better, and losing one without compensating necessity is worse.

The three are stated as one premise because the section always spends them as a set: a theodicy accepts the bridge premises or is assessed by its own side constraints instead.

Greater-good theodicies that speak of suffering being outweighed accept some comparison and, where one person’s gain can justify another’s loss, some aggregation. Universalist or universal-salvific-desire formulations support monotonicity. A nonconsequentialist, rights-based theology or one recognizing several independently valuable final goods may reject one of these premises. It then leaves the single maximand and must supply person-affecting reasons or side constraints rather than justify suffering merely by a larger aggregate elsewhere. Some target sets order agency, virtue, and being of use to restored relation; others treat one or more as final goods with independent standing. The latter don’t escape assessment, but the balance must include the independent good rather than assume restoration exhausts value. Only where the set accepts all three bridge premises *and* orders the goods at issue to restored relation does the target resolve into maximizing creatures restored and minimizing creatures lost. Monotonicity by itself says only that adding a restored creature at no cost to any independently valuable final good is better; it doesn’t say every act that improves the salvation count is permitted or that earthly life has no standing. The argument therefore uses the maximand only for the specified aggregative, restoration-ordered target, not as a theorem about every Christian axiology or as a complete theory of right action.

The sections that follow apply this target where a theodicy accepts the bridge premises. Such a defense must show that the suffering it invokes tends toward restored relation rather than away from it. A theology that rejects aggregation is assessed instead by its own side constraints, person-affecting reasons, and independently valuable final goods; it may not borrow aggregate outweighing when convenient and disavow the maximizing structure when costs are counted. That is a claim that can be examined rather than assumed, and the soul-making and free-will sections examine it. What is set here is only the target the rest of the chapter aims at, and the theodicies are denied the move of leaving it unset.

Conditional on comparability, aggregation, and monotonicity, the specified greater-good and universal-salvific target has a determinate maximand: the greatest possible number of creatures in restored relation to God and the fewest possible lost. This is the tradition’s good read as an outcome for that target family, not a theorem about every Christian axiology.

The delay of the Parousia is defended in exactly that register. The martyrs are told to wait until the number of their fellow servants is complete (Rev 6:11); Paul names the fullness of the Gentiles (Rom 11:25); the Synoptic discourse waits on proclamation among all nations (Matt 24:14); and 2 Peter answers the charge of delay by saying that God is patient, wanting none to perish and all to repent (2 Pet 3:9). These texts need not name one trigger, and a tradition may read some symbolically. Where they are used to explain why the interval remains open, however, the waiting is said to serve a completion condition. Ask what is being completed.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Grim Reaping Problem** · *Disjunction*

What is the delay waiting to complete?

- **If it waits for a fixed tally of persons restored,** then the tally can state a stopping point. But it counts only the completed side. Under an aggregative mercy defense, the account must also include the persons lost during the interval and show why continuing improves rather than worsens the good invoked to justify it.
- **If it waits for a proportion of humanity,** then the denominator, target, and relevant time must be stated. A target already met no longer explains delay; an unmet target explains continued waiting only if the waiting is expected to move the proportion toward it rather than away.
- **If it waits for proclamation among all nations,** then geographic or communal reach can supply a mission condition. It does not by itself supply a number or ratio of persons restored, and the account must say why delivery rather than reception is the stopping fact.
- **If none of these is a public stopping condition,** then patience may remain a posture of mercy. But the appeal no longer explains why this interval continues rather than ending now.

Delay can be mercy only if what it waits for is specified and the waiting serves that end. A trigger with no stopping condition cannot explain why the interval remains open.

*Scope.* The disjunction applies only where completion, evangelization, or further repentance is offered as the reason for delay. It predicts no date, assumes no population estimate, and does not deny that a theology may refuse an aggregative measure or leave the timing undisclosed. A non-aggregative account owes its own reason for the interval rather than the calculation tested here.

**Depends on:** The Bridge Premises (§12.5.1); The No Apparent Future Problem (§12.2.6); The Salvation Specification Test (§12.1.8)

One pointer sits outside the remit. The maximand fixed here is the tradition’s good read as an *outcome*; the same blessed state (taken not as a venue beyond the world but as the widest field of live possibility a shared structure holds open) is developed elsewhere on the book’s own terms (§6). The lever stays internal: that relocation is named only so the two aren’t confused, and nothing in those sections is presupposed here.

### 12.5.2 Free-Will Theodicy
The free-will defense is the reflex answer to *moral* evil (the harms agents do to one another) and the tradition’s first line against the problem of evil. It is engaged internally throughout, on its own premises and on the commitments its own tradition already holds about freedom, foreknowledge and grace. The companion soul-making section (§12.5.3) takes up teleological evil (§12.4.1); the question here is exactly what ground freedom can cover and what it leaves unexplained.

Distinguish, with Plantinga, a *defense* from a *theodicy*. The free-will defense (Plantinga 1974; Plantinga 1974) claims only that the existence of evil is *logically compatible* with an omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good God, not that it states God’s actual reason. Its engine is a modal possibility: *transworld depravity*, the claim that *possibly* every creaturely essence is such that, in any world God could actualize in which that creature acts freely, it goes wrong at least once, so that creating significantly free agents who do evil may be the unavoidable price of any world with moral good in it. The picture is this: a world of creatures genuinely free to choose good or evil is more valuable than a world of automata compelled to the good; genuine love, courage, and virtue are possible only against live alternatives; so God’s creating agents who *can* and *do* choose evil is no defect. The defense needs only that this story is *possible*, not that it is true, a distinction that fixes what any objection must deliver to reach it: not merely that contra-causal freedom is *actually* absent, but that it isn’t so much as *possible*. The dependency sorting that follows traces which objections carry that far and which stop short.

The load-bearing skeleton of the theodicy form, which claims to explain actual suffering rather than bare logical compatibility:

(1) A world with genuinely free moral agents is a greater good than one of compelled goodness. (2) Genuine freedom requires the real possibility of choosing evil, and real choices must carry real consequences, including suffering. (3) Therefore suffering is the necessary price of free agency.

Two premises do the work; deny either and the price is unpaid.

Before either is tested, the response has to say which of two jobs it is doing, because they aren’t the same job and the arguments for them differ. It may claim only *permission*: that a world containing significant freedom is one in which suffering was left possible, which shows compatibility and no more. Or it may claim *explanation*: that this freedom is why the suffering that actually occurs, in its range and magnitude and distribution, occurs. The fork below runs only on that difference. Secondary-cause and compatibilist accounts answer different questions about mechanism and agency, so they are assessed after the job has been fixed rather than treated as further branches of the same choice.

Three results govern what follows, and the first two come from the tradition’s own commitments rather than from anything argued elsewhere in this book. The first is that the defense needs a particular account of the will, and it isn’t one the tradition agrees on. Premise 1 prizes *libertarian, contra-causal* freedom—the agent could have done otherwise, without qualification. Bañezian and Reformed compatibilist branches deny it, and Molinism keeps it only by adding middle knowledge, each for reasons internal to its own commitments about foreknowledge, providence, and efficacious grace. So the defense doesn’t merely assume a metaphysics of freedom; it takes one side of a dispute its own tradition has never settled, and owes an account of how contra-causal freedom coexists with the foreknowledge and sovereignty those branches were protecting. That burden is owed before the defense is available at all. The second is a symmetry the tradition imposes on God himself, whose omni-attributes leave him no alternative to the good, so that he *can’t* will evil: either contra-causal freedom is therefore *not* required for the highest goodness (God has goodness without it, and premise 1 fails) or God himself is unfree, and the defender can’t prize in creatures a freedom the supremely good being lacks. The third doesn’t close a *sui generis* divine liberty by definition. It fixes its price. If divine agency is concrete productive work, it incurs the operation-level burden; if it is an atemporal agency-making relation, it must say what makes the eternal fact an act rather than static entailment; if every differentiating feature is withdrawn, no liberty has been specified (§11.7.2, §11.10). Two fronts follow: the defense is pressed on its own premises, and its special divine-agency reply is required to supply the role it invokes.

*The driving premise: the good that suffering destroys.* One objection that follows is shared with the soul-making section. The defense nominates a good *G* (free moral agency) and sometimes presents suffering as its necessary price. But a foreseeable class of suffering can impair *G* itself: traumatic brain injury, severe anxiety, depression, and addiction may corrode deliberation, impulse control, and moral reasoning (Beauchamp et al. 2013; Beauchamp et al. 2019; cf. Sapolsky 2017). In those cases the token isn’t an instrument that exercises the agency it impairs. That establishes an explanatory burden, not gratuity by definition. A risk-based defense may say that a lawlike arena permissibly exposes agency to losses that aren’t themselves means to agency; it must then defend the type-level risk, its magnitude, safeguards, alternatives, and compensation. Put as the defender’s own question: if free will is valuable enough to justify the risk, what protection of that same freedom should a good designer build into the arena?

Take the defense front by front, on its own premises.

It doesn’t touch most of the evil there is. The defense ranges, at best, over *moral* evil: harm traceable to a free choice. It says nothing about teleological evil (predation, parasitism, congenital disease, earthquakes)—suffering built into the world’s ordinary functioning and willed by no creature—which the companion soul-making section engages directly. “The fall” doesn’t restore the range: it must then justify the spillover onto animals and geology, and as the Fall analysis argues (§12.1.4), the fall itself was an obedience test in a world without suffering.

The *experience* of suffering isn’t required for free action. Freedom is the capacity to choose and act; felt torment is a separable biological variable. Anesthesia and analgesia can remove pain while other agents continue to act, and congenital insensitivity to pain shows that pain experience and choice can come apart, though it also shows the protective importance of nociception. Grant that damage-signaling is useful to embodied agency; the defense still owes an account of intensity and duration. Agony that disorganizes deliberation or breaks the will does no token-level choice-enabling work. A type-level account may nevertheless classify it as a foreseeable risk of a useful system rather than a means. The relevant question is then whether a system with less destructive signaling, stronger safeguards, or reliable intervention could preserve the defended agency without the same losses. Mystery can block an inference from our failure to see a reason; it doesn’t by itself provide the positive explanation a theodicy claims to state.

*Culpability, consequence, and victimhood.* Divine command theory supplies an internal test of the claimed necessity. Some commands are principally *God-directed* and can be obeyed or violated without a third-party victim: prohibitions of rival worship and idolatry, requirements of allegiance and devotion, and the greatest commandment to love God (Exod 20:3–7; Matt 22:37). Calling the first tablet wholly victim-independent would be too broad, and on two counts rather than one—the Sabbath command expressly extends rest to children, servants, foreigners, and animals (Exod 20:10), and the sanction attached to the first commandments reaches past the worshipper to the third and fourth generation (Exod 20:5), so that on the text’s own terms a violation there does fall on third parties (that clause and its counter-texts are taken up at §12.1.6)—but the argument needs only one genuine class of morally significant God-directed choice. If obedience to God is itself a great good, worship, prayer, trust, restraint, and inward orientation already supply such a class.

The tradition also places culpability before completed injury. Jesus places anger under judgment and treats lustful looking as adultery “in the heart” (Matt 5:21–22, 27–28); 1 John 3:15 calls hatred of a brother murder. Temptation, passing thought, entertained desire, settled intention, attempt, and completed act need not be morally identical for the point to hold. On the weaker claim the texts plainly permit, a person can become culpable through an inward orientation or attempted violation before the intended victim bears the harm. A world can therefore permit wrongful selection while blocking wrongful completion. The agent’s failure remains attributable; another subject need not be made to receive it.

Four levels must remain separate. *Culpability* can be interior. *Relationship* requires other subjects, but not their injury: promise, consent, refusal, cooperation, loyalty, trust, and reconciliation are interpersonal exercises of agency. *Consequence* requires that a choice alter what follows, but not that the alteration become another subject’s agony; choices can change opportunities and relations, incur corrective duties, or be intercepted before injury while remaining the chooser’s acts. *Victimhood* begins when another subject is made to bear the harmful consequence. Embodied agency in a shared world supports the first three without granting unlimited access to the fourth.

The tradition’s own protology supplies the internal countermodel. On the set that treats pre-Fall Eden as free of creaturely suffering and death, Adam and Eve face a determinate command, can obey or disobey it, and are held responsible for the selection. The test can be passed without harm, and the violation can be complete as disobedience before suffering is imposed. The defender may say that threatened and realized consequences give the choice its seriousness. That reply changes the burden: suffering is no longer a constituent of freedom or obedience but a selected sanction and a policy for propagating one violation into the creaturely order. Its necessity must be defended separately. A nonliteral Eden, an Eden already containing natural suffering, or an account on which the pair lacks robust responsibility can leave this internal countermodel, but can’t continue citing the same scene unchanged as the paradigm of an original responsible choice.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Victimless-Agency Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

Does a choice only matter if someone actually gets hurt?

- **If morally significant choice doesn’t require successful victimization,** then the harm isn’t what the freedom required. If culpability can consist in God-directed disobedience, inward intention, or a prevented attempt, responsible agency is possible without another subject’s suffering.
- **If it does require it,** then that reading owes a reason why the cost had to fall on victims. It must explain why the required consequences include severe involuntary harm rather than changed relationships, lost opportunities, bounded corrective costs, or prevention after the agent’s intention and attempt are fixed. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).

On a literal suffering-free Eden set, the tradition itself supplies a responsible obedience test before suffering; treating the Fall’s harms as punishment or propagation therefore requires a further justification beyond freedom.

*Scope.* The dilemma doesn’t show that every interpersonal good is available without risk, that prevented attempts have every consequence completed acts have, or that a nonliteral Eden supplies a historical counterexample. It blocks the inference from the value of responsible agency to the necessity of victims.

**Still open:** victim-independent culpability or harm-required consequence; the proposed reason harmful completion must remain available; and the retained Eden set

**Depends on:** The Command-Authority Specification (§12.3.11)

Reactive goods provide no shortcut. Rescue, forgiveness after injury, and endurance under harm logically presuppose some adversity, but then freedom alone is no longer the justifier. The account has moved to soul-making or defeat and must show that the reactive good was unavailable through less harmful conditions, proportionate to the victim’s cost, and a good for the person bearing that cost rather than a benefit extracted from them. That further claim is taken up at §12.5.3.

The victim-independent point also travels beyond Christianity. Jewish covenantal commands and Islamic duties directed to God supply morally assessable relations that don’t require a third-party casualty, while their accounts of law and responsibility differ over what reason, revelation, and command each contribute. Divine Command Theory (§12.3.11) preserves those differences rather than treating every Lawgiver account as one voluntarism. (The Mu’tazilites and Ash’arites were rival schools of classical Islamic theology that clashed for centuries over whether justice is independent of God’s will: the Mu’tazilites held that reason alone can identify what is good, so God commands what is objectively just; the Ash’arites held that whatever God commands is just by virtue of his commanding it, with no independent standard he answers to. It’s the Islamic-tradition counterpart to the Divine Command Theory dispute run here in a Christian register.)

Heaven supplies the other internal comparison: redeemed persons love, worship, and relate with no pain or death (Rev 21:4; Isa 25:8). If the redeemed lack libertarian freedom, the highest state the tradition imagines is reached without the freedom premise 1 prizes. If they retain it, libertarian freedom stands without sin or suffering. Eden doesn’t by itself prove mature virtue without formation, and the soul-making defender may distinguish initial innocence from completed character. Together the two venues nevertheless separate responsible choice, developed goodness, and suffering rather than allowing the theodicy to treat them as one set. The burden is to explain why the interval required mutual suffering when the beginning contains accountable choice without it and the end contains perfected goodness without it.

Nor may free agency simply be announced as *the* greater good. The tradition’s good is already fixed as restored relation, so premise 1 must show that libertarian freedom serves that end rather than merely label it valuable. Whatever further goods risk supplies, the Victimless-Agency Dilemma prevents the value of agency alone from underwriting the victim’s cost.

*Premise 2 and alternative possibilities (Frankfurt).* Frankfurt cases (Frankfurt 1969) describe an agent who acts on their own reasons while a never-triggered intervener stands ready to force the same act had the agent begun to choose otherwise. They pressure the Principle of Alternative Possibilities: if responsibility survives in the actual sequence despite the unavailable alternative, responsibility may depend on sourcehood or guidance control rather than an all-things-considered ability to do otherwise. The cases don’t settle the issue. Libertarians dispute whether the agent retains a flicker of freedom, whether the intervener can be specified without presupposing a prior determining sign, and whether responsibility for character differs from responsibility for the particular act. Their conditional force is still important. If a defender accepts Frankfurt responsibility, it can’t infer from moral responsibility alone that God had to leave every harmful completion open. If it rejects the cases, it must state which alternative remains necessary and why prevention after intention is fixed would erase responsibility. Nor need ownership be cashed out through Frankfurt’s hierarchical descendants: an act can be the agent’s in the sense that matters here simply by issuing from what the agent is—their formation, their convictions, the reasons actually available to them.

*The will the defense needs is disputed inside the tradition.* Premise 1 prizes *libertarian* choice, and that freedom isn’t common ground among the traditions the defense speaks for: Molinism preserves it only by adding middle knowledge, Bañezianism subordinates it to physical premotion, and Reformed compatibilism denies it outright—each because of what foreknowledge, providence, or efficacious grace was taken to require. A defender who needs contra-causal freedom therefore can’t treat it as granted. They owe an account of what such freedom consists in, and the standing difficulty is the selection question: what explains one choice rather than another, when prior structure appears to determine the selection while no sufficient structure appears to leave it controlled rather than lucky? Naming an agent-cause relocates that question without yet answering it. A libertarian may deny the exhaustion, distinguish reasons from sufficient causes, or offer a non-event-causal account of agent control—but that account is owed here, alongside a reconciliation with the divine attributes their own branch was protecting when it rejected the freedom the defense now needs. Against an actual theodicy, the defender must supply a real freedom doing the proposed work; against Plantinga’s bare logical defense, the stronger modal conclusion follows only if the selection dilemma succeeds.

*A textual case: Pharaoh’s heart.* One narrative removes even the weaker fallback the freedom dispute leaves standing—that the resistant will, however determined, is at least the creature’s own. Exodus states the opposite directly and repeatedly: “I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go” (Exod 4:21; repeated at 7:3, 9:12, 10:1, 10:20, 10:27, 11:10, 14:4, 14:8) names God, not Pharaoh, as the cause of the very refusal the plagues are then addressed to. The narrative says the other thing too, and the order matters. In the early plagues Pharaoh’s heart “was hardened” with no agent named (7:13, 7:22; 8:19; 9:7), and three times Pharaoh hardens it himself (8:15, 8:32; 9:34); the first narrated divine hardening comes only at 9:12. That sequence is what the tradition’s judicial reading rests on: God confirms, as judgment, a refusal Pharaoh first made his own, withdrawing grace from a will already set rather than infusing malice into an innocent one (Aquinas, *ST* I-II, q.79, a.3). Paul, citing the case, stresses the other side, that God “hardens whomever he wills” (Rom 9:17–18). The judicial reading answers for Pharaoh’s first refusals, which the text does make his. The defense’s own scope claim—that it ranges over harm traceable to a free choice—still fails on the text’s own terms for the later refusals, which the narrative assigns to God, not by hypothesis but by its account of who is choosing; the objection needs no verdict on contra-causal freedom to land, so it stands independently of the freedom dispute already described. Two further features close the usual recoveries. The necessity premise is conceded away in the same chapters: the stated purpose of the hardening is demonstrative (“that I may multiply my signs,” “that my name may be declared throughout all the earth,” Exod 7:3–5; 9:16), and a display has no privileged claim to the harshest available means.

Non-lethal signs already in the same narrative (frogs, gnats, boils, hail) accomplish demonstrative work without a body count, and a beneficent register was equally available—abundant water, crops, and herds outperforming what Egypt’s own fertility and provision deities were credited with would have made the identical case against the Egyptian pantheon while manufacturing no victim at all; the chosen means isn’t merely unnecessary but dominated by an available alternative that reaches the same end. And the harm that does follow falls on parties absent from the dispute it is staged to settle: the firstborn of “the slave girl behind the handmill” and “all the firstborn of the livestock” (Exod 11:5) hold no role in the conflict between its two named parties and aren’t consulted by either. Nor does the judicial reading reach the end of the sequence. The refusal immediately before the death of the firstborn is narrated as God’s hardening (10:27; 11:10), and the prolonging is given a demonstrative purpose rather than a judicial one: “I have hardened his heart”—“that I may show these signs of mine among them, and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson” (10:1–2). Punishment presupposes that the punished originated what is punished. For the firstborn of the slave girl it fails on any reading, since she refused nothing. For Pharaoh’s final refusals it holds only if confirmation-as-judgment can be extended to acts the text assigns to the one confirming, and a defender taking that route owes an account of where Pharaoh’s own refusal ends and the display begins.

Nor is the directing confined to one tyrant. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Prov 21:1). Jeremiah is more general still: “the way of humans is not in their control; mortals as they walk cannot direct their steps” (Jer 10:23). The defense needs creaturely authorship of the harm. The tradition’s own texts treat the turning of the will as God’s ordinary work, not a special hardening reserved for Pharaoh.

*Moses isn’t exempted from the point; he sharpens it.* The narrative extends no hardening or softening to Moses, and elsewhere treats him as an ordinary responsible agent bearing his own consequences (Num 20:8–12, where his own conduct at Meribah costs him entry to the land, with no hardening invoked on either side). But nothing in the text obligates his errand to succeed, and God tells him in advance that it won’t, by its own stated terms: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart... Pharaoh will not listen to you” (Exod 7:3–4). Moses isn’t deceived about the outcome; he is briefed on it, then sent to perform the confrontation anyway, repeatedly, at real personal risk, so that a scripted refusal can occur on schedule. His courage and persistence are real and his own on the account already given, which only sharpens the wrong rather than relieving it: a will left genuinely free is used, its owner foreknowing what Pharaoh is never shown to foreknow, to stage an outcome that owner’s own effort was never positioned to affect.

*Which move bears on whom.* Against Plantinga’s bare *logical* defense, the book’s selection dilemma reaches the modal possibility only conditionally: if contra-causal selection collapses into determination or luck, transworld depravity loses the libertarian subject it presupposes. Frankfurt cases add a conditional pressure rather than a separate refutation: a defender who accepts responsibility without alternatives can’t use responsibility alone to require open harmful alternatives. Divine symmetry asks why the highest goodness lacks the power creatures allegedly need, but classical accounts may answer through analogical or sui generis divine freedom and thereby inherit the relevant Chapter 11 burdens. Even if the logical defense survives all three disputes, it establishes compatibility only. It names no actual reason for the actual range or magnitude of suffering.

Against the greater-good *theodicy*, the more direct burdens remain. Freedom has no immediate range over teleological evil; victim-independent culpability and prevented attempts separate responsibility from successful victimization; Eden and heaven, on the sets that retain them, separate agency and perfected goodness from suffering; and some realized harms impair the agency invoked to justify the arena. A type-level risk defense can absorb that last fact without calling the token an instrument. Its burden is comparative design: why meaningful agency required this exposure, severity, distribution, and level of safeguarding rather than a less destructive shared field.

Against the Divine-Command, obedience version, the interior-sufficiency line establishes that culpability and obedience need no victim or natural evil; the separate consequence analysis shows that freedom requires effects in a shared world but doesn’t by itself require severe involuntary suffering. Eden remains the tradition’s own case of an obedience test without suffering, and obedience sits comfortably with a non-libertarian will.

The Pharaoh’s-heart case, finally, needs none of the preceding objections to land and so survives every frontier the other objections stop at: it depends on none of the freedom dispute, the symmetry argument, or the Frankfurt result, only on the text’s own account of who is willing in the later refusals and who bears their cost, and it bears hardest on the greater-good theodicy specifically, since Exodus supplies, inside the same narrative, both the theodicy’s own stated demonstrative purpose and a dominated, less harmful alternative that would have served that purpose equally well.

The free-will defense faces several independent burdens: explaining why suffering beyond agency-preserving signaling is necessary, explaining teleological evil, reconciling freedom with suffering-free eschatological states, and defending a coherent account of libertarian freedom. The argument here is that its selection-dilemma gives strong reason to reject contra-causal freedom, but that argument remains contestable at the frontier it identifies. Plantinga’s bare logical defense may survive for readers who reject that dilemma or adopt a different modal account; the more direct conclusion concerns theodicies that claim to explain the actual range and magnitude of suffering. Those burdens don’t turn on the dilemma: freedom alone doesn’t entail the range and magnitude of suffering invoked in its defense, and the tradition’s own suffering-free eschatology is evidence against the entailment.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Free-Will Defense Fork** · *Disjunction*

What work does a free-will response claim to do?

- **If the response is only a logical defense,** then it cannot also serve as God’s actual reason for any particular suffering. A coherent possible model need only show that significant freedom and unavoidable risk are compatible with God.
- **If it is a theodicy,** then it must identify the freedom actually protected. It must then show why the range, magnitude, and distribution of suffering are necessary or proportionate to it. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).

A secondary-cause account may occupy either branch: under a defense it explains how harm remains possible, while under a theodicy it must additionally justify the actual risk, safeguards, preventable cases, and alternatives. A compatibilist account may also attempt either job, but it gives up Plantinga’s transworld-depravity engine and owes a different reason for retaining these risks.

**Still open:** compatibility only or actual explanation; libertarian or compatibilist agency; type-level risk or token-level instrumentality; and the safeguards and alternatives still owed

### 12.5.3 Soul-Making Theodicy
The soul-making theodicy is the theist’s reply to *teleological* evil (see §12.4.1)—the suffering built into the world’s design (predation, parasitism, disease, congenital disorder, disaster) that the free-will defense never touches. The argument engages it both *internally*, on its own premises, and *with the book’s earned results*, which constrain several of the theist’s recurring replies. The same instrumental structure recurs outside Christian doctrine—in Islamic *bala* (trial) theodicy and the Jewish frame of *yissurin shel ahavah* (“afflictions of love”)—and the objections pressed in the analysis that follows against suffering-as-instrument don’t depend on which tradition’s register frames the trial.

Hick’s Irenaean picture makes creation two-stage: we are made *in the image* of God (capable of growth) but must freely grow *into the likeness* of God (actual moral perfection). The world is a “vale of soul-making”—its hardships aren’t flaws but the conditions under which freely-won virtue becomes possible. Suffering isn’t good in itself; it is an *instrumental* good, the means to a greater end. Hick adds an epistemic distance: were God’s existence overwhelming, our responses would be compelled rather than free, so God stays partly hidden and the world’s difficulty sustains the distance across which free faith and growth occur (Hick 1966).

The argument’s structure:

(1) The possession of certain virtues is necessary for unity with God. (2) Those virtues require a process of development. (3) Suffering is necessary for that development. (4) Therefore, suffering is necessary.

Each premise is load-bearing: deny any one and the conclusion falls.

Two consequences of the book’s prior analyses govern the discussion. A transcendent, metaphysically simple God that retains determinate active predicates is under pressure (Chapter 11), while strict apophatic withdrawal bears a determinacy burden. The determinacy burden is the one established at §10.2.2, where the apophatic route is shown to have no position between saying something determinate and saying nothing; a theodicy needs the determinate side, since a God with no describable purposes has no soul-making program to defend. This means that simplicity, “God is goodness,” and analogical predication cannot be treated as cost-free exits. The theodicy is engaged on its own premises and through the book’s conditional analyses; no claim here depends on declaring every transcendent God-concept already void.

*The modal relations must be disaggregated.* A suffering token can relate to a proposed good in at least four ways. It may be an intended token-means; an instance of a type-level risk required by a law-governed arena; a constitutive condition of a practice without this token being required; or a foreseen side effect permitted within a structure selected for other goods. “Not strictly necessary” doesn’t by itself mean gratuitous, because a non-necessary token may be an unavoidable or proportionate side effect of a justified risk structure. “Necessary” doesn’t by itself mean that each realized token was intended as a means; the designer may intend the risky type while permitting particular outcomes. The theodicy’s burden is therefore more exact: specify which relation is claimed, show that the relevant type or token is proportionate and not replaceable by a less harmful structure, and explain why anti-developmental cases remain permissible. The replies sort under those relations, after one prior question that holds whichever relation is claimed: whether development needs suffering at all. Premise 3’s developmental case, Swinburne’s being-of-use, the praxis test, and the receipt claim the first relation; the stakes-virtue, epistemic-distance, and Eden–Heaven claims treat suffering as the third; and the double-effect and regularity defenses, van Inwagen’s minimum-dose reply, and the animal branches claim the second and fourth.

One boundary applies throughout. The objections bear directly on theodicies that nominate suffering as an *instrument* of virtue-development. Defeat models (Stump 2010; Adams 1999) assign different work: suffering may be integrated into the sufferer’s own union with God, defeated by an incommensurate good, or—on Stump’s medicinal strand—used to loosen willed resistance. The medicinal strand does make an instrumental claim and therefore meets the anti-developmental evidence where suffering damages the will it is meant to heal; Adams’s defeat account can instead combine defeat with a separate permission story without claiming that defeat explains why the suffering was imposed. Those distinctions belong to §12.5.4. The conclusions here are limited to the virtue-developing explanations actually analyzed and to the residual risk-design burdens carried by their lawlike-arena replies.

*Premise 1—belief or virtue?* What is “necessary for unity with God”? The answer forks, and both prongs are costly.

Horn 1, salvation by faith (*sola fide*): if unity is a gift received through faith in Christ (Eph 2:8–9, Rom 3:28), then virtue is the *fruit* of salvation, not its precondition (Gal 5:22–23)—the root is belief, not character. Then premise 1 is false, the soul-making virtues inconsequential to the end that matters: the deathbed convert with minimal virtue is saved, the lifelong saint who never believes isn’t, and suffering-as-virtue-forge becomes idle. Horn 2, virtue itself is required—and then we proceed to premises 2 and 3, where it breaks.

A theist can sit on either horn, but not escape between them: the more salvation rides on *belief*, the less it can ride on *developed virtue*, and vice versa.

*Are the soul-making virtues even good? (the Divine-Command problem)* Under Divine Command Theory the prized virtues invert into vices the moment they cut against obedience. Had Abraham chosen *compassion* over sacrificing Isaac, his compassion would have been the vice of disobedience; his obedience was the “virtue.” Uzzah’s courage in steadying the ark cost him his life; Peter’s courage in defending Jesus was rebuked. The apostate who walks away from real social cost shows the same “courage” the theodicy praises—in the wrong direction. A non-Christian may possess every soul-making virtue yet lack the one thing said to matter (belief). So the virtues are *conditional*, not unconditionally good—which means “developed virtue” isn’t reliably the good premise 1 needs it to be.

*Premise 2—the earned-vs-given dilemma.* Premise 2 says that “the virtues require a *process of development*.” It smuggles in a value-claim: that earned, hard-won virtue is superior to built-in, given virtue. That claim is the only thing that explains why God didn’t simply create us already virtuous. Call it (V). Turn (V) on God’s own virtues: God has them in maximal form, yet never developed or earned them—they are intrinsic, un-won, indeed *necessary* (he can’t be or do otherwise). So the defender is forked:

If (V) is true, God’s un-earned virtue ranks *below* a saint’s hard-won virtue, and a creature can exceed God in goodness—dethroning the [maximally great being](https://inversionofgreatness.org/glossary). Sharper for the libertarian: soul-making prizes virtue *freely chosen against live alternatives*, yet God has no alternative to the good, so by the defender’s own yardstick his *necessitated* goodness is the *least* meritorious of all. If (V) is false, God could have created us already virtuous at no loss—development is pointless, premise 2 fails, and the vale is idle.

Either God is dethroned or the soul-making is unnecessary. The same bind applies to angels, standardly created good with no vale.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Earned-Virtue Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

Is virtue developed through struggle better than virtue given complete?

- **If developed virtue is better than virtue given complete,** then God lacks a goodness creatures can have. Creatures can possess a kind of goodness unavailable to a necessarily good God, whose goodness was never earned against a live alternative. *Priced by* Character, Standard, and Exercise (§11.9.1).
- **If it isn’t better,** then the suffering wasn’t needed to produce it. Development cannot explain why creatures had to acquire goodness through suffering rather than receive it without loss. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).

The same choice applies to angels said to have been created good: either earned virtue outranks divine and angelic goodness, or earning cannot justify the vale.

**Still open:** whether developed virtue is superior to given virtue, and why an omnipotent creator couldn’t confer the relevant good without the ordeal

*The simplicity reply.* A classical theist can deny the comparison: God doesn’t *have* virtues as developed dispositions but *is* goodness. Chapter 11 prevents that reply from functioning as a cost-free stop. A univocal account still faces the comparison; an analogical account must state enough common content for *goodness* to justify soul-making; a strictly apophatic account can’t use an unspecified goodness as the reason the ordeal was selected (§11.2.1, §11.8.3). The reply may survive with a determinate analogy or an essence-prior account, but then that specification—not the bare word *simplicity*—must answer why developed creaturely virtue is worth the imposed cost.

No self-authorship escape. Relocating the value from adversity to free self-authorship changes no part of the dilemma: God never came to have goodness by an achievement of character over time. If self-authorship confers the relevant merit, divine goodness lacks it; if it doesn’t, it can’t explain why created virtue needs authoring. Aseity doesn’t help, because independence of existence isn’t the achievement of a character. The same symmetry therefore reaches every proposed value-conferring process—earning through suffering, free appropriation, or self-authorship: God has the good without the process, so the process either lowers divine goodness or proves unnecessary for creaturely goodness.

No scarcity escape either, and this one runs on the tradition’s own soteriology rather than on any political premise. Grace, on every branch that uses the word, is unmerited and prior to the capacity it produces—given before the recipient could earn it, which is exactly what distinguishes it from wages (Eph 2:8–9; Rom 4:4). A theodicy that requires a vale of earned virtue before the foundation is granted therefore runs the order backwards from the soteriology it sits inside: it asks the creature to demonstrate capacity to receive what its own doctrine insists is given before capacity exists. An omnipotent designer is the case where withholding costs nothing—no finite budget, no competing claimant, no feasibility ceiling any earthly institution must weigh—and a theology whose central claim is unmerited gift is the last one able to argue that the gift had to be earned first. This doesn’t turn on whether God’s own goodness is earned or given, so it survives a defender who bites the divine-symmetry bullet already conceded and calls God’s goodness incomparable to a creature’s: the foundation argument never compares the two goodnesses, only asks why a costless floor was conditioned at all.

**[Proposition]**

**No Scarcity Excuse for an Omnipotent Duty-Bearer** · *Proposition*

If the conditions required for agency can be held open without cost to the duty-bearer, conditioning them on demonstrated capacity needs a reason. An omnipotent designer is the limiting case: no feasibility ceiling, no competing claimant, no finite budget. Soul-making’s earned-vs-given structure therefore owes an answer independently of the divine-symmetry paradox already established. The question doesn’t turn on comparing God’s goodness to a creature’s, only on why a costless foundation was ever conditioned.
