*Scope.* The argument runs on a general capacity-and-cost premise rather than on political membership. A defender may deny that complete capacity to secure a costless agency floor generates any corresponding duty; the cost is an account of why it doesn’t.

*The driving premise—self-undermining instrumental goods.* Several of the following objections are one move wearing different clothes. A theodicy nominates some good *G* and offers suffering as the necessary price of *G*. The usual candidates are free agency, developed virtue, free faith, and the epistemic distance that makes faith free. But in a non-trivial, foreseeable class of cases suffering destroys the very *G* that is supposed to justify it:

Severe brain injury and disorder destroy the *free agency* the free-will defense prizes; trauma, depression, and anxiety destroy the *virtue-forming capacity* soul-making prizes; suffering drives *apostasy*, destroying the *faith* a belief-aimed God prizes; and the world delivers not clean *epistemic distance* but epistemic *confusion*, scattering sincere seekers—the opposite of what free faith needs.

The principle: an instrument that reliably destroys its own end in a foreseeable class of cases is, in exactly those cases, not instrumental toward that end. Each premise-3 move that follows is an instance. A risk-based account may still permit such a token as a side effect of a justified structure; it then owes the separate proportionality, alternatives, safeguards, and compensation case rather than calling the token soul-making.

The premise-3 case that follows doesn’t need the stronger claim that God could have made a world with no pain or no damage at all. It rests only on *gratuitous magnitude and avoidable predation*: surplus a soul-making world didn’t require, even granting a lawlike arena with real damage-signals.

*Premise 3—what development requires.* Even granting that virtue is the end (Horn 2) and that it must be developed, the claim that severe involuntary suffering is its necessary developer faces several independent comparisons. The unifying burden is whether the suffering exceeds what the nominated good requires. Skeptical theism may block an inference from “we see no sufficient reason” to “there is none,” but that is an inference-blocking defense rather than the positive soul-making explanation under examination. A theodicy that cites a particular developmental good must still show how the defended structure serves it; otherwise it has withdrawn from explanation to epistemic restraint.

Begin with multiply realizable virtue. Courage requires acting well under fear or risk, not war or a wounded body: a first speech before an audience, publishing work open to criticism, defending an unpopular truth, or entering an uncertain undertaking can realize the same capacity. Trust requires accepted vulnerability, not actual betrayal. Generosity can consist in voluntarily giving time, attention, comfort, or resources to someone whose life is thereby enlarged; it need not wait for deprivation. Perseverance can answer study, craft, athletic effort, or difficult inquiry. Cooperation and solidarity can be built through a shared project rather than a shared catastrophe. Self-restraint needs temptation, not a victim.

These aren’t costless goods. They involve effort, uncertainty, exposure, foregone alternatives, and sometimes chosen discomfort. That is precisely the distinction: challenge and voluntary cost can form a subject without assigning severe involuntary suffering to that subject or using another person’s agony as training material. Premise 3 therefore survives at most as “some resistance or vulnerability is needed” until the defender identifies a virtue whose acquisition requires *this kind* of suffering. Reactive goods such as rescue, forgiveness after injury, and endurance under harm do presuppose adversity. Their absence from a harmless world isn’t automatically a defect: a world without disease lacks medical rescue without becoming worse for lacking disease. To justify producing the occasion, the reactive good must be worth the victim’s cost, unavailable through a less harmful route, and a good for the victim rather than principally for the responder.

Then there is gratuitous affect: even granting that *some* challenge is needed, the *felt torment* of suffering is a variable separable from its function, and it overshoots—the internal-theodicy form of Draper’s evidential point that pain and pleasure track biological utility (what aids or threatens survival and reproduction) rather than moral or spiritual development, so their intensity and distribution are poorly explained by a soul-making end (Draper 1989). Pain’s biological job is to signal damage and motivate withdrawal—but the *intensity, duration, and persistence* of agony far exceed any signaling need: chronic pain, the agony of the terminally ill, pain that rages on long after it has told the sufferer everything it can. Grant the alarm; the theodicy still owes the *volume* of the alarm. The claim isn’t that God could have removed pain entirely—a lawlike world plausibly needs real damage-signals, and congenital insensitivity to pain maims and kills—the move isn’t against pain’s *existence* but against its gratuitous *magnitude*.

There is no window: development is gradual, needing time, reflection, and integration, yet suffering that culminates immediately in death (a child asphyxiating for hours under earthquake rubble) offers no such window and builds nothing. There is no subject: infants and the pre-cognitive lack the faculties to develop virtue at all, yet suffer congenital disease, starvation, abuse—suffering that falls entirely outside the theodicy’s own necessity criterion. There is a disparity double-bind: suffering is distributed grossly unevenly, by race, sex, orientation, class, geography (Commission on Social Determinants of Health (WHO) 2008; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2011; Institute of Medicine (US) et al. 2011), and if it does *not* aid soul-making, the disparity is gratuitous, an unjust burden apportioned through no fault of one’s own, while if it *does*, some souls get unjust *advantages* in development by accident of birth—either reading is intuitively unjust, and if two people reach comparable virtue through vastly different suffering, the surplus on the one is by definition unnecessary.

Then the self-undermining class, with its evidence. Severe anxiety, depression, addiction, and traumatic brain injury can constrict attention, motivation, trust, impulse control, deliberation, and moral reasoning—the capacities through which courage and developed agency must operate (Stefanopoulou et al. 2014 on generalized anxiety; Kern et al. 2021 on major depression and suicide; Beauchamp et al. 2013; Beauchamp et al. 2019 on TBI and moral reasoning). None of those conditions makes courage or growth universally impossible, and many sufferers exhibit extraordinary agency during and after them. The narrower result is enough: where the suffering impairs or destroys the relevant capacity in its bearer, it can’t be that person’s instrument for developing the same capacity.

Post-traumatic growth prevents a universal claim and sharpens the causal question. Growth after trauma may be mediated by later safety, care, therapy, community, interpretation, and the sufferer’s own work. Recovery from damage doesn’t by itself show that the damage was necessary for the recovered capacity. The theodicy must distinguish growth caused by the injury from growth achieved against it or through the repair of it. It needs no premise that suffering never builds virtue; it needs an account of the foreseeable class in which the nominated means reverses its own function.

*A neighboring theodicy—being of use.* Swinburne’s higher-order-goods defense relocates the good once more, not within the sufferer but in what her suffering makes possible for others: the justifying good is her *being of use*—that her suffering matters, occasions others’ compassion and serious moral responsibility, so that her life is woven into the moral fabric rather than left useless (Swinburne 1998). This is distinct from the regularity defense and from Hick’s sufferer-growth, so the objections to soul-making proper don’t automatically reach it; Swinburne presses, further, that being of use is a good *for her*—a dignity, not a degradation. Grant that being of use can be a genuine good, even a good for the one used. Three of the book’s results still converge on it. First, on the bridge premises and for a set that orders its goods to restored relation (§12.5.1), a good counts only as ordered to restored relation, so being-of-use can’t stand there as a free-standing justifier—suffering that drives the used party from God subtracts from the very end it must serve.

Second, grant Swinburne that being of use is a good even for one who never consents to or owns it. What can’t be granted is his further claim that the using is thereby a *dignity* rather than a degradation. That claim holds only where there is a standpoint from which the use is the sufferer’s *own*. It can’t reach the infant, the pre-cognitive, or the tortured-to-breaking, who are *used* without ever owning the use—and for them being-of-use is the instrumentalization charge in the open: one person’s agony made the raw material of another’s good and the world’s seriousness, a means to an end not their own. Third, the gratuity battery transfers intact: *this* magnitude and *this* distribution of agony aren’t needed for lives to matter to one another, milder occasions abounding, and the soul-destroying class isn’t even of use—suffering that breaks the sufferer makes her not useful but wasted. Being of use earns its keep only where the using is gentle, bounded, and ownable; the teleological high end is none of these.

*The praxis test.* If a theodicy claims that each suffering token is an intended and necessary soul-making means, alleviation appears to obstruct that means. Ordinary practices of medicine, charity, justice, and rescue count strongly against that token-instrumental version. A risk-based theodicy can avoid the contradiction: agents may be obliged to relieve harms even if a lawlike arena permissibly allows them. It then bears the narrower burden of explaining why the risk structure, rather than each token, is justified. Two corollaries make it worse:

First, instrumentalization: soul-making makes one person’s agony the *raw material* for another’s virtue (and the bystander’s compassion a good extracted *from* the sufferer’s ordeal). It treats the sufferer as a means to a moral end not their own, and it hands bystanders a perverse stake in suffering’s *continuation*—the precise inversion of the moral relation the virtues are supposed to honor. Second, corrupted moral perception: taken seriously, the theodicy reframes compassion as interference with a deserved or providential ordeal, so suffering becomes “deserved,” relief becomes presumption against God’s plan, and structural injustice becomes a soul-forge best left standing. (This is close to D.Z. Phillips’s line that theodicy is morally corrupting (Phillips 2004).)

*The clamp—the receipt.* The deepest internal point: the theodicy exists *to foster belief*—it is built to answer the suffering that drives people away from God. That purpose is an admission that suffering’s actual, widespread effect is *disunion* from God—soul-*destruction*, not soul-making. Disunion, in turn, is failure against the very good fixed at the outset: on the bridge premises, the greatest good read off the tradition’s own scripture is the largest number of creatures in restored relation and the fewest lost. A defender can parry that the theodicy answers an *intellectual* obstacle, the argument from evil: people are *argued* out of belief, not *hurt* out of it. The clamp is therefore weaker against the purely philosophical version and cuts hardest against *pastoral* soul-making, the theodicy offered to the grieving and the broken. There it rests on the empirical claim that *experienced* suffering is itself a leading driver of deconversion and disunion, and with that premise supplied the mechanism the theodicy sanctifies is the very one it was built to neutralize.

*The sharper form: the vale’s own exhibits are unavailable to God.* The earned-virtue fork grants the defender that God has the virtues and presses only on how he came by them. A whole class of them he can’t have at all. Soul-making’s leading exhibits are the stakes-virtues—courage, fortitude, patience, perseverance, compassion borne at cost—and each is constitutively tied to vulnerability. Courage isn’t a feeling but acting well while something is genuinely at risk; remove the risk and there is no act left to perform, not a safer version of the same act. Fortitude requires the live possibility of breaking, patience an unwilled duration one can’t simply end. Each of them tracks something at stake, and a stake requires a bearer for whom outcomes can go better or worse and who can lose what it holds. That isn’t a theory about virtue; it is what the words mean. Classical aseity and impassibility remove exactly that. A being to whom nothing can be added or lost, who can’t be moved by what a creature does (§11.3.4), has no stake in any outcome, and so has nothing for courage to be courage about. The defender is then worse off than the earned-virtue fork leaves him: it isn’t that God holds these virtues without earning them, but that the vale’s most celebrated products name conditions the maximally great being can’t satisfy.

**[Disjunction]**

**No Stakes, No Courage** · *Disjunction*

Are the stakes-virtues—courage, fortitude, patience, and perseverance—among the highest goods?

- **If they are,** then the maximally great being lacks them: aseity and impassibility leave nothing at stake, and without genuine vulnerability these are not acts a being can perform.
- **If they are not,** then a vale ordered to produce them is not producing the highest goods after all. It needs a further account of why lower goods justify the suffering it assigns.

The account must either revise what divine greatness contains or supply a higher good the vale actually serves.

**Depends on:** Being Heard Is a Structural Feature, Not a Register (§11.3.4)

*Epistemic distance overshoots and backfires.* Hick needs suffering to maintain the distance that makes faith free. But the distance doesn’t require *childhood cancer*—any number of milder veils would preserve free response (disproportionality again). And the distance the world actually delivers is the confusion already counted among the self-undermining goods: a veil that scatters honest seekers across contradictory faiths misdirects the faith it was supposed to enable.

*The Eden–Heaven bracket.* The two venues do different work and shouldn’t be made interchangeable. On a literal pre-Fall reading, Eden exhibits responsible obedience under a determinate test without antecedent creaturely suffering or death. It establishes morally significant agency, not completed character. The Irenaean reply is therefore live: Adam and Eve were innocent and immature, while courage, perseverance, compassion, and freely appropriated goodness require development. Heaven supplies the opposite end: perfected goodness with no continuing pain or death (Rev 21:4; Isa 25:8). The standard reply is that heavenly character retains what earthly formation produced, so maintenance without suffering doesn’t prove acquisition without it.

Grant both replies. The bracket still identifies the exact middle premise the theodicy must defend. Eden prevents suffering from being built into responsible choice as such; heaven prevents suffering from being built into perfected goodness as such. Suffering is left as a proposed route by which finite responsible agents acquire some indispensable goods. The account must name those goods, explain why benign formation couldn’t realize them, and show why actual victims rather than bounded challenge were required. The Victimless-Agency Dilemma (§12.5.2) supplies the first half of that separation; soul-making bears the second.

*The fast-pass question—the venue’s own occupants.* Traditions divide over those who die before moral accountability: Augustine assigns even unbaptized infants the *mitissima poena*, the mildest punishment of the damned (Augustine, *De peccatorum meritis et remissione* I.21); Aquinas develops limbo as natural happiness without the beatific vision (Aquinas, ST Suppl. App. I, q.1); the modern magisterium speaks of prayerful hope rather than certainty (International Theological Commission 2007); and many Protestant accounts infer infant salvation or an age of accountability from texts such as 2 Sam 12:23 and Matt 19:14. Only sets that actually admit the unformed to beatitude generate the comparison. They may answer that formation is divinely supplied, completed after death, unnecessary for agents lacking earthly opportunity, or included within merits they don’t personally earn. None of those answers simply proves that the same route is available under identical conditions to mature agents. Each does, however, qualify an unindexed claim that earthly suffering is necessary for every person fit for union with God. The account must state whether the vale is a universal means, an ordinary means with grace-governed exceptions, or one route among several—and why exposure to its risks is assigned so unequally.

*The creation-completeness fork.* A narrower literal set adds three claims: (A) the creation called “very good” was complete for its intended initial end (Gen 1:31); (B) suffering is necessary for the indispensable good of soul-built virtue; and (C) creaturely suffering and death entered only as consequences of the Fall. If *complete* means already containing every final perfection, A and C conflict with B. The Irenaean account avoids that conflict by reading initial goodness developmentally: creation was good as a beginning whose intended end had not yet been reached. That is a genuine exit, not a verbal evasion. Its cost is to relinquish Eden as completed perfection and to identify the developmental route God intended before the Fall. If that route was originally non-harmful, B remains unsupported; if the Fall introduced the suffering now used as the route, the account must explain why a contingent violation became the necessary curriculum for everyone else. If suffering was designed in from the first, C is surrendered and the Fall no longer explains its origin. The triad doesn’t bind evolutionary or nonliteral sets that reject C; those sets inherit the design-level problem of pre-human suffering instead.

*Double effect and risk permission.* Double effect, regularity, and risk-based defenses occupy genuine intermediate positions. They can distinguish intending a harmful token from selecting a lawlike structure in which harm is a foreseeable risk, provided the good is sufficiently important, the risk proportionate, agency isn’t used merely as a means, and no less harmful feasible structure secures the relevant goods. The Eden–Heaven bracket pressures claims of strict necessity within traditions that accept those venues. Autotrophs show that consumption isn’t universal to life, but they don’t demonstrate a complete sentient, mobile, ecologically stable biosphere without predation or harmful competition. The biological argument can support alternative or reduced trophic harm only conditionally. The live question is comparative design: what range of lawlike arenas was feasible, what goods require genuine risk, and whether the actual severity and distribution are proportionate.

The serious defender reply, and its cost. The regularity / real-hazard defense (Reichenbach 1982; Swinburne 1998; Hick 1966) holds that a law-governed arena with meaningful agency must permit processes that sometimes destroy—no real stakes without real downside. Grant it: this changes the thesis from token instrumentalism to type-level risk justification. A realized harm need not itself build a soul to be permissibly included as a foreseeable risk. The remaining evidential burden concerns proportionality, feasible alternatives, safeguards, compensation, and whether the actual severity and distribution exceed what the defended risk structure requires. Anti-developmental tokens are therefore counterevidence to a simple “each suffering builds” claim, not an automatic refutation of every risk-based theodicy.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Soul-Making Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

What good justifies the suffering, and who receives it?

- **If the suffering forms its bearer,** then cases that kill, incapacitate, traumatize, or deform that bearer can contradict the proposed function.
- **If the good is a world with real stakes, where stable laws make real harm possible,** then that explains why harm can happen at all. It doesn’t explain why it goes this far, falls where it does, or meets no limit. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).
- **If another person’s virtue is the good,** then the sufferer becomes the material of a benefit that may never become their own. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).
- **If the same virtue requires the more harmful route,** then a reason is owed for rejecting the gentler ones. Bounded challenge, voluntary cost, uncertainty, harmless temptation, and prevented wrongdoing were all available. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).
- **If formation is completed after death,** then formation does not require earthly damage after all, since it can be completed without it—so the damage needs a justification that formation itself no longer supplies, and those never completed suffered for an end they never received. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).

Formation can justify only suffering that can do the forming for the one whose suffering is used, where a less harmful route would not secure the same end. The rest needs another good.

**Still open:** who receives the developmental good, whether anti-developmental suffering is explained, and whether the same end was available by a less harmful route

**Depends on:** The Victimless-Agency Dilemma (§12.5.2); The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1)

A second serious reply targets the magnitude charge head-on. Van Inwagen presses that there is no non-arbitrary *minimum* dose of suffering a lawlike, morally serious world requires: for any proposed amount, a marginally smaller one may appear equally serviceable, so “God should have used less” risks either sliding to none or stopping arbitrarily (the *Problem of Air*) (van Inwagen 1991). This has real force against a purely quantitative charge. The qualitative distinction remains: suffering that destroys a person’s agency or developmental capacity isn’t that token’s instrument for producing the same capacity. But even this doesn’t establish that the token is gratuitous within every type-level account. A defender may treat it as a foreseeable casualty of a generally justified risk structure. The argument must therefore return to comparative design: whether a lawlike arena with meaningful stakes required risks of this kind and scale, whether safeguards could have reduced them without defeating the good, and what repair or compensation is owed when the risk destroys its proposed beneficiary.

*Animal suffering and pre-human time-depth (the most-contested front).* Billions of years of animal predation, disease, and injury preceded humanity—no human moral agents present to grow and no human beneficiaries then on the scene. A specifically human token-instrumental soul-making account therefore has no subject for those tokens. This front has several materially different replies, none of which should be collapsed into the task that Hick’s human formation account set itself:

Dougherty (*The Problem of Animal Pain*)(Dougherty 2014) treats animals as nascent persons capable of their own eschatological completion. That expands the population of soul-making subjects and owes an account of what the antemortem risks contribute, how postmortem defeat reaches the same animal, and what grounds the extension. Murray (*Nature Red in Tooth and Claw*)(Murray 2008), on the neo-Cartesian line, denies that animal pain has the morally relevant phenomenology; that route stands or falls with its account of the convergent neurological and behavioral evidence rather than with the human soul-making objection.

C.S. Lewis appeals to an animal fall or cosmic corruption, and Boyd (*Satan and the Problem of Evil*)(Boyd 2001) gives a warfare account on which pre-human angelic rebellion corrupts nature. An embodied-animal fall conflicts with a chronology in which predation precedes the candidate animals; a pre-cosmic angelic fall avoids that sequence but owes a causal and providential account of how created agents acquire authority to deform genetics and ecology, why the damage persists across deep time, and why divine permission of that risk is proportionate. Warfare relocates authorship; it doesn’t automatically settle permission.

Cutter and Swenson’s omission theodicy (Cutter and Swenson forthcoming) belongs to the same family and turns on a different act. Rather than corruption by rebellion, the proposal is delegation followed by failure: non-human moral agents were given responsibility for guiding the development of life, foresaw what would follow if they declined, and freely declined. The distribution of suffering then looks the way undirected development would look, which is the datum a warfare account has more trouble matching. The justification offered for divine non-intervention is where the account does its distinctive work. God doesn’t repair what the delegated agents omitted, because repairing it would remove the very difference their action made; their being genuine difference-makers requires that the creatures’ lives would in fact have gone worse without them, and the relational goods secured by exercising that responsibility well are said to aggregate across an unending afterlife until they outweigh the risked suffering.

Two things follow, and they aren’t the same. The chronology objection doesn’t touch this version: an omission needs no embodied fall and no corrupting act, so the sequence in which predation precedes any candidate agent is left intact. What the account inherits instead is the pricing question. The relational goods are cited as outweighing the suffering God risked, which makes this a greater-good claim and brings it under the specification test at §12.5.1: the good must be named, the connection to this suffering shown, and the aggregation defended, including across the animals who bore the cost and aren’t among the agents whose relationships are improved. The account also owes what any delegation account owes—how created agents acquire authority over the development of life, and why permitting that risk is proportionate to what was lost when it was declined.

The branches therefore carry different costs rather than one closed verdict. A nascent-person account must connect earthly experience to the animal’s eventual good and explain why postmortem completion is repair, development, or both. A sentience-denial account carries the empirical burden. An animal-fall account carries the chronology burden; an angelic-warfare account carries causal-authority and divine-permission burdens; an omission account sheds the chronology burden but must then price the aggregated relational goods it offers in exchange. A general ecological-risk account may instead claim that evolutionary regularity and creaturely goods justify animal vulnerability without making each injury a developmental means. That route leaves the comparative questions of severity, safeguards, and eschatological defeat. What the pre-human record rules out directly is only the claim that every such token was an instrument of human soul-making.

*Hick’s escape and its price.* Hick’s exit is universalism plus postmortem soul-making: everyone is completed after death, so no one’s suffering is finally undefeated. It slips the belief horn (no *sola fide*) and supplies a developmental horizon for no-window and no-subject cases. It doesn’t undertake to show that each earthly token was indispensable. Its remaining burden is to connect the earthly process to the completed person rather than letting postmortem formation do all of the explanatory work:

Universalism removes final loss as the price of unequal earthly exposure, but it may appeal to histories whose goods are integrated and defeated rather than erased. The question is whether the extreme disparity contributes to each person’s eventual good or is merely damage later overcome. Where postmortem repair restores a capacity earthly suffering destroyed, repair alone doesn’t show that the destruction was needed; where the person’s later agency appropriates and transforms the history, the account must explain why that same good couldn’t arise under safer conditions. The earned-versus-given fork becomes a specification question as well: which part of perfected character is freely appropriated, which is healed or given, and why the mixture required this earthly distribution.

Postmortem completion also faces a memory and compensation burden, but not a strict dilemma. If the redeemed person remembers with continuing grief, the account must explain how the promised defeat of suffering is complete. If the memory remains while its sting is healed, the healing doesn’t show that the original agony was separable from the suffering when it occurred; the account must explain how later transformation compensates the same person and why the earlier harm was permitted or required. If the event is forgotten, numerical identity need not disappear—people remain themselves despite forgotten experiences—but the account owes a bridge from a completion the subject no longer remembers to the harm that subject endured. Across persons the profiles differ: one redeemed person may carry the memory of childhood agony while another carries nothing comparable. That inequality isn’t pointless by definition, since an integrated and defeated history remains possible. What remains is the necessity and proportionality burden: why radically unequal earthly costs were required for persons who reach the same completed end.

The escape relocates the endpoint; it doesn’t answer why the process had to damage those it was meant to perfect.

*Which move bears on whom.* Against the hybrid *sola-fide* / virtue theist the moves apply one way; against Hick’s universalist, postmortem version they apply differently but bear just as directly. The belief-or-virtue dilemma (P1) undoes the hybrid view: virtue is fruit, not root, and the deathbed convert is saved. It also forces Hick to deny core Christian soteriology. The earned-vs-given fork (P2, God-symmetry) either dethrones God or makes development idle, and against Hick it convicts postmortem-perfected virtue of being given, not earned. The heaven corollary points out that perfected virtue with zero suffering already exists—for Hick, the eschaton simply *is* that suffering-free venue. The fast-pass corollary adds the venue’s occupants: souls admitted with no formation at all, so that either the necessity premise fails at the tradition’s own hand or the justice of the gate does.

On premise 3 the moves reach both theists alike. Multiply realizable virtue, gratuitous affect, and the no-window, no-subject, disparity, and anti-developmental cases leave the bridge from “some resistance may form virtue” to “this imposed suffering was required” still owed; universalism absorbs the no-window and no-subject cases only by making the earthly suffering do no work, and later repair isn’t proof that the injury was its instrument. The Divine Command point applies to the hybrid theist directly and to Hick less, and epistemic distance never needed childhood cancer to do its work. Animal time-depth defeats only a specifically human token-instrumental account of pre-human suffering; the other animal branches keep their own burdens. The praxis test reaches only the version on which each token is an intended developmental means, while a type-level risk account can affirm rescue and carries the narrower risk-design burden instead.

The instrumental soul-making theodicy faces sustained burdens: explaining why particular suffering is necessary for virtue, accounting for suffering that appears anti-developmental, and reconciling the appeal to suffering with the tradition’s own suffering-free eschatological images. These objections target the specific instrumental versions analyzed here; non-instrumental defeat models and alternative theological accounts remain separate positions. The argument here is that the evidence leaves much suffering without a clear soul-making role, not that it deductively excludes every possible redemptive interpretation.

### 12.5.4 Redemption Theodicy
The theodicies engaged so far often share an instrumental shape—suffering earns its place by what it produces: a soul formed, a freedom protected, a greater good secured downstream. Accounts of defeat and medicinal healing rearrange those relations. They must be taken up on their own terms because neither Adams nor Stump can be represented by the simple formula that an external greater good compensates for the evil.

For Marilyn McCord Adams, God defeats horrendous evil not by outweighing it with separable goods but by integrating it into the sufferer’s relationship with God, a good incommensurate with the horror and capable of making the person’s life a great good to them (Adams 1999). Defeat answers what becomes of the horror and can be paired with a distinct account of why God permits creaturely freedom and its risks; Adams need not pretend that defeat alone is the permission account. Eleonore Stump’s *Wandering in Darkness* is more explicitly medicinal: suffering can contribute causally by loosening a will’s resistance to the second-personal union that is good for the sufferer (Stump 2010). The union isn’t a separable prize paid to someone else, but the suffering may still function as a means to healing. The arguments must therefore divide. Non-instrumental defeat isn’t touched by the complaint that an omnipotent being needs no means; medicinal healing is touched only where the suffering is claimed to do the loosening; and neither relation substitutes automatically for an independent account of permission.

The defeat model needs a terminus: union with God, the personal intimacy into which suffering is gathered. A wholly structureless yet determinate personal apex is under pressure (Chapter 11), though that pressure doesn’t establish that every transcendent or relational theology has no bearer. The issue here is whether the proposed union can be made determinate while retaining the divine attributes it invokes. But that alone would make this section a result of §11.1, and the position deserves more—because it breaks from the inside, before the terminus is ever in view.

Before the question of who carries the evil arises, the relations must be fixed. Defeat explains how a horror need not remain undefeated within the sufferer’s life; by itself it doesn’t explain why God permitted the conditions under which it occurred. That isn’t a refutation of Adams where a separate freedom, lawlike-risk, or providential account is supplied. It is a division of labor: the independent account carries authorization, while defeat carries final integration. A *felix culpa* escalation makes a different claim—that horror is required for a uniquely greater union unavailable to an unsuffering creature. That instrumental or constitutive claim re-enters the comparative burden: what good is available only through horror, why maximal divine goodness doesn’t require the same history, and why a safer route couldn’t realize the creaturely good. Defeat may therefore complete a permission account, and medicinal suffering may form part of one, but redemption can’t silently be counted twice as both the healing and the reason the wound was allowed.

Defeat must be defeat *for the one who suffered*: numerical and autobiographical continuity matter. But healing a memory past its original affective sting doesn’t by itself replace the person. A person who continues, in the numerical sense, the same one and not a successor, can reinterpret an event, alter its affective valence, integrate it into a wider history, and remain numerically continuous through causal, mnemonic, bodily, and narrative links. The identity problem arises in stronger cases: erasure of constitutive history, destruction of the integrating architecture, or reconstruction with no adequate continuity relation. The defeat model therefore owes a theory of continuity through transformation; it isn’t refuted merely because genuine healing changes how the remembered evil feels.

Both Adams and Stump have an answer to that first horn, and each is owed a hearing on its own terms. Adams’s is *organic integration*: the horror isn’t removed but defeated in Chisholm’s sense, taken up as an organic part of a whole—the sufferer’s beatific intimacy with God—whose goodness is incommensurate with it, so that the person, possessing the whole, wouldn’t will the suffering away. Stump’s is *second-personal*: the continuity the redeemed self needs isn’t self-produced but sustained, the person held in being and known by God through the suffering, so that the self that is healed is the same self God never stopped being in relationship with. Both replies identify the real burdens. Organic integration requires a numerically continuous subject able to own the completed history as good on the whole; the question of personal continuity asks which causal, mnemonic, bodily, and narrative continuities are sufficient. Second-personal sustaining requires the determinate divine relation Stump’s theology posits; that relation is placed under structural and predicate burdens at §11.8.2, a structural line running alongside this section rather than standing in for it—its absence isn’t a premise here. These are conditional disagreements about personhood and theology, not a proof that transformation is replacement.

The hardest cases press the two models differently. Where Stump’s account runs medicinal, suffering that wrecks the will it is meant to loosen is evidence against token-level medicine; a type-level or indirect account may answer that later grace heals damage the suffering didn’t itself heal, but must not relabel repair as the token’s medicinal effect. Adams’s category of horrendous evil is designed precisely for cases capable of making a person’s life appear not worth living; it doesn’t assume that the sufferer’s present relational capacity remains intact. Divine defeat may restore that capacity. The resulting question is continuity through severe disruption: whether bodily, soul-based, causal, mnemonic, narrative, divine-memory, or second-personal relations suffice for the restored person to be the sufferer. The burden is real, but neither temporary incapacity nor altered affect alone proves replacement.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Redemption Authorization Problem** · *Disjunction*

Does eventual redemption license permitting the suffering in the first place?

- **If the suffering is gathered into eventual union with God,** then redemption after the harm is explained. But authorization to permit it isn’t. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).
- **If the suffering heals or loosens the will,** then the account becomes medicinal—and a medicine that destroys the agency it was given to restore has not treated the patient, which is what suffering does in the cases the account most needs to cover. *Priced by* The Soul-Making Dilemma (§12.5.3).
- **If horror is necessary for a uniquely greater union,** then the account becomes a *felix culpa* greater-good defense. It must show why that good was unavailable without horror. *Priced by* The Greater-Good Specification Test (§12.5.1).
- **If permission rests on an independent reason,** then that reason—not redemption—does the justificatory work and must be assessed separately.

In every branch, defeat must accrue to the numerically continuous person who bore the harm.

**Still open:** the independent reason for permission, the relation between suffering and healing, and the continuity criterion by which the redeemed subject is the sufferer

The defeat model isn’t dispatched by the instrumental reply—it was built to avoid that reply. It faces instead two conditional burdens: whether a postmortem or transformed self can be numerically continuous with the sufferer (§12.2.5), and whether the personal union it invokes can be made determinate on its theology. Those burdens depend on the book’s contested account of personhood and on its Chapter 11 predicate analysis. The prior objection doesn’t: that defeat redeems the suffering without supplying a reason for its imposition is an internal point about what the model accomplishes, owed by the defeat theorist whatever account of persons is correct, as is the case of the sufferer broken past the capacity to be reached. The argument is that the non-instrumental theodicies examined here haven’t yet supplied a satisfactory answer, rather than proving that no defeat account could do so.

### 12.5.5 Skeptical Theism

The good already named can still be defended from behind a single move: concede that we can’t see how a given evil is justified, but deny that this failure is strong evidence that no justifying reason exists. In its disciplined form this is *skeptical theism*, developed by Wykstra (1984), Alston (1991a), and Bergmann (2001). It is an inference-blocking defense, not a positive theodicy: it need not identify God’s actual reason and shouldn’t be criticized for declining that task. Its proper test is whether the restriction on our inference is principled, how far it extends, and which other claims remain warranted once it is accepted.

One version of the retreat can’t do the work by stipulation. If “good,” said of God, has no shared or analogically specifiable content with creaturely goodness, then the premise that God is good supplies no reason to expect this world rather than its opposite. A determinate analogical account is left under a specification burden rather than banned as such (§11.1, §11.2.1, §11.8.3). The epistemic version examined here accepts enough common moral content for goodness to remain a claim and narrows the skepticism to our access to the reasons for particular sufferings.

*The symmetry objection and its limits.* A restriction on our ability to infer divine purposes from apparently pointless suffering may also weaken some favorable inferences from apparent order, providence, or historical pattern. It doesn’t automatically defeat every belief grounded elsewhere. A defender may hold that revelation is independently warranted, that ordinary moral knowledge is reliable at the creaturely level, and that only inferences from our sample of goods to the complete divine ledger are restricted. That asymmetry is coherent if its independent warrant and domain can be stated without using the very purpose-reading under restriction. Likewise, local obligation need not wait on the cosmic ledger: an agent may be required to relieve a pro tanto evil on available evidence even if God has reasons that agent can’t survey. Moral paralysis follows only from versions that let unknown divine reasons override ordinary action-guidance, not from skeptical theism as such.

Bergmann presses just here: the doubt is confined to our inferences about God’s reasons, where inscrutability was antecedently to be expected, while moral practice carries on under its own commitments, owing nothing to the cosmic calculation. The reply is right about its target: obligation does track moral seeming rather than axiology, and a morality that waited on the final tally would never have begun. The quarantine can hold at one important point. A judgment that suffering is bad *pro tanto* and that an agent should relieve it from that agent’s epistemic position doesn’t entail an all-things-considered judgment that no justifying reason exists. Moral practice can therefore continue under ordinary duties, rules, and commands even if the cosmic ledger is inaccessible. Skeptical theism isn’t refuted merely by observing that local obligation and global justification concern the same event.

*The local/global reply.* The distinction is real and blocks the simple paralysis argument. Pro tanto badness is compatible with an outweighing good, and an obligation to intervene can be grounded in the agent’s limited role even if an omniscient agent would permissibly act otherwise. The evidential argument therefore needs an additional bridge: apparently pointless suffering counts against a perfect governor when, given the hypothesis, we would reasonably expect justifying connections to be sufficiently accessible, regular, or reflected in the distribution of goods and harms. Wykstra’s CORNEA-style reply denies that expectation because the cognitive distance is too large. The dispute is thus over the reliability and expected accessibility of the global inference, not over whether local badness itself proves gratuitousness.

Skeptical theism can preserve local duty by rule, command, or agent-relative evidence while undercutting global inference. Its cost is different and broader: the same restriction may weaken natural-theological, providential, and historical inferences that move from observed goods or patterns to claims about God’s purposes, unless an independent revelation or asymmetry is defended. The position is therefore not forced into moral paralysis, but it owes a principled account of why favorable global inferences remain available while apparently contrary global evidence doesn’t. Maitzen’s moral-skepticism concern remains a pressure on versions that let hidden reasons defeat ordinary action-guidance, not a consequence of every disciplined skeptical theism. If our moral sense can only ever confirm God’s goodness and never disconfirm it (if no conceivable state of the world is permitted to count against it), then the word has been emptied: he is “good” no matter what, which is to say the predicate has stopped doing any work. The move meant to protect God’s goodness from the evidence ends by severing it from evidence altogether.

*The abstraction bites on a real case.* Take an animal dying by increments in a predator’s grip with no rescuer in reach (see §12.4.1). Skeptical theism can say that the horror is locally bad while withholding the global verdict that no justifying reason exists. The evidential pressure is instead comparative: whether a world governed by perfect power and goodness should be expected to contain this scale, distribution, and opacity of apparently pointless suffering. The skeptical reply survives only by contesting that expectation and accepting the resulting limits on purpose-reading from the world.

*What the defense doesn’t discriminate.* The appeal belongs to no one faith. A Muslim can meet the problem of evil with the reminder that one may hate what is good or love what is bad while “God knows and you do not” (Qur’an 2:216), and Jewish and Christian traditions possess parallel disciplines of trust. That portability doesn’t make the defense worthless: a common defeater-defeater may protect beliefs whose positive warrant comes from different sources. It does mean that skeptical theism itself can’t identify which revelation, if any, is true. Discrimination must come from the independent warrant the defender pairs with it.

To answer “why this suffering?” by restricting our inference isn’t to supply an explanation; it is to deny that the missing explanation carries the evidential weight the critic assigns it. That can be the defense’s intended and legitimate role. It can’t then be credited as a theodicy that makes the suffering intelligible, and a fuller theodicy can’t alternate opportunistically between a named reason when the reason looks favorable and unrestricted mystery when counterinstances arise. The issue is consistency of epistemic role, not the defender’s rationality or sincerity.

**[Disjunction]**

**The One-Way Darkness Dilemma** · *Disjunction*

How far does skepticism about God’s reasons reach?

- **If the skepticism is modest,** then a confident inference to gratuitousness may be blocked. But no positive explanation of the suffering is supplied.
- **If it is strong,** then the same move disables the theist’s own inferences to divine purposes. Apparently pointless suffering may become evidentially inert, but so do inferences from apparent order, providence, answered prayer, or historical pattern to divine purposes.
- **If revelation supplies the asymmetry,** then revelation must be authenticated without relying on the purpose-reading now declared unreliable. *Priced by* The Sign–Source Dilemma (§12.3.3).

Skepticism can limit an inference or supply an independently warranted asymmetry. It cannot run only against the evidence the doctrine needs neutralized.

*Scope.* Local duties to prevent suffering remain intact. The trilemma concerns global evidence, not moral paralysis.

**Still open:** the strength and domain of the skepticism, which favorable inferences remain licensed, and the independent basis for any claimed asymmetry

*Scope.* An appeal to unknown reasons can block a confident inference to gratuitousness, but it isn’t itself a positive theodicy and can’t show how the suffering is justified. A defense that claims explanatory success must name enough of the good and its connection to suffering for assessment; a defender who remains skeptical may instead withhold explanation. The cost travels only as far as the restriction: natural-theological or providential inferences using the same disputed purpose-reading weaken, while independently warranted revelation, moral knowledge, or historical claims need not. If revelation supplies the asymmetry, its warrant must survive the separate revelation tests (§12.3.3–§12.3.8). The objection reaches special pleading only when counterevidence is made inaccessible by a restriction that favorable evidence of the same kind isn’t required to meet.

### 12.5.6 Evil God Redux
The theodicy sections have taken the defenses of a wholly good God one at a time. This one runs the whole arc in reverse. The *evil-god challenge* (Law 2010) begins from a hypothesis almost everyone rejects (that the world is the work of a wholly *malevolent* creator) and observes that this evil god faces a *problem of good* mirroring the believer’s problem of evil: if the creator is omnipotent and wholly evil, why is there love, beauty, kindness, laughter, health? The challenge isn’t that this hypothesis is true. It is that every move the theist makes to reconcile a good God with the world’s evil has an equal and opposite twin that reconciles an evil god with the world’s good—and if the reverse twins are too feeble to rescue the evil god, the originals are, by the same reasoning, too feeble to rescue the good one.

This isn’t a downstream doctrine like the sections around it; it borrows no single assumption the book has set aside. It is a closing argument about the goodness predicate itself—the capstone the theodicy arc has been building toward, since it asks not whether any one defense works but whether the defenses, taken together, could ever have been tracking a creator’s goodness at all.

*The mirror.* Run each defense backwards and it stands up about as well. The free-will defense (§12.5.2) reconciles a good God with moral evil by prizing freedom: a world of agents free to choose evil is held to be better than a world of automata. Reverse it: an evil god prizes freedom too, since freely-chosen cruelty is a greater evil than mere mechanical pain, so the kindness people freely show is the unavoidable price of a world with genuine malice in it. The soul-making theodicy (§12.5.3) makes suffering the instrument of virtue. Reverse it: comfort, pleasure, and love are the evil god’s instruments of corruption, breeding complacency, dependence, and the soft ruin of character—a vale of soul-*breaking*, in which every good is permitted for the deeper damage it enables. The appeal to second-order goods holds that evils are needed as the backdrop of higher goods—no courage without danger. Reverse it: goods are needed as the backdrop of higher evils—there is no betrayal without trust, no bereavement without love, so the evil god permits love precisely so that its loss can wound. Each reverse theodicy is about as plausible as its upright original, because each is the same machine run in the opposite direction.

The costs aren’t perfectly balanced. The good-god free-will defense doesn’t reach suffering no creature wills—congenital disease, earthquakes, predation—whereas precisely that suffering is unsurprising under a hostile creator. Soul-making must explain why suffering so often traumatizes, disables, or destroys the agency it was supposed to form; the reverse story needs only the familiar fact that real goods can be temporary and that losing love, safety, health, or standing can deepen the injury (§12.5.3). The order-of-value accounts are unequal in the same way. The benevolent defense must show that first-order evil is *needed* for the higher good that justifies it. Its malevolent twin need not show that every good is needed for some higher evil: first-order evils already produce further evils, while first-order goods add routes to jealousy, betrayal, fear of loss, and grief. None of this proves a malevolent creator. It shows that the reverse account sometimes incurs a weaker explanatory burden than the account it mirrors.

The pattern holds for hiddenness too, and it explains something the mirror alone doesn’t: why devotion to an evil god would look like devotion at all. Where salvation or punishment turns on belief, a good god’s ambiguous, unevenly distributed revelation creates an additional problem: persons begin with radically unequal access to the message, while the message travels through fallible human testimony rather than universal disclosure (§12.3.4; §12.3.6). The ambiguity is defended as preserving the freedom to seek or as keeping the choice genuine. Reverse it: an evil god has every reason to fragment revelation into many mutually exclusive, comparably difficult-to-verify traditions, each certain of its own access and each able to denounce the others, since the resulting confusion, authority contests, and conflict cost the evil god nothing. Selective interventions don’t break the pattern. Miracles reported to one community or period face both the evidential problem and rival traditions’ reports (§12.3.3); on the reverse hypothesis, incompatible revelations and an occasional apparent answer to prayer can strengthen the competing attachments rather than resolve them. And because such a god deals in real goods, not only privation, the attachment those goods produce—love, gratitude, answered prayer—functions the way any intermittent reward does: durable, costly to question, and more resistant to revision the more genuine the good feels. A trap built only of suffering is easy to leave. A trap that includes real love isn’t, and that is a fact about attachment, not about the god’s character. This doesn’t make religious pluralism intrinsically evil or every religious institution oppressive. It identifies the asymmetry relevant to the challenge: unequal access and unresolved rival claims are liabilities for a perfectly good revealer but available instruments for a deceiving one.

*The parity, and where the book already runs it.* The challenge’s force is the symmetry: one can’t accept the theodicies as defenses of a good God while dismissing their mirror images as too feeble to defend an evil one, not without special pleading. This even-handedness is the global form of a move the cluster has already made in the small. An appeal to reasons past our grasp can’t travel in one direction only (§12.5.5)—the darkness that blocks the inference from evil to no-good blocks the inference from good to goodness just as well. The evil-god challenge generalizes that result from the single mystery move to the whole theodicy repertoire: if the defenses are reversible, they aren’t the kind of thing that could discriminate a good creator from an evil one. The free-will section’s own *symmetry argument* is one instance of the pattern, counting the supremely good God as good with no freedom to do otherwise; this is the pattern at cluster scale.

*Where the symmetry might break—and what would be required.* The defender can answer the challenge by identifying an independently supported asymmetry that favors the good-god hypothesis. The world does contain candidate asymmetries, but none can simply be read off without specifying the hypotheses and their auxiliary commitments. Cooperation, affection, and pleasure can enhance survival and reproduction, so their presence is compatible with undirected evolution and doesn’t by itself identify a benevolent author. That point concerns a naturalistic process, not an “indifferent creator”; those are different hypotheses and must not be assigned the same expectations without argument. Natural evil supplies a distinct pressure. Predation is especially resistant to the free-will reply: it isn’t one creature’s culpable misuse of an otherwise harmless system but an energy ecology in which sentient life is organized around consuming and evading other life. A defender who holds that creation began perfect and free of suffering has already granted, from inside that set of doctrines, that living nature need not always depend on predation. Appealing to the Fall can relocate the change in time, but it cannot make animals the authors of the predatory drives, bodies, and dependencies installed afterward; what no creature authored remains a design-level question (§12.1.4, §12.4.1). The unclear distribution matters too: goods and evils falling without a legible relation to deserving or disclosure don’t transparently display perfect governance. These considerations may lower the comparative fit of some benevolent-governor sets, but a full likelihood ranking would require priors and explicit models of what benevolence, malevolence, indifference, and naturalism predict. The symmetry argument doesn’t supply that ranking. Its narrower result is enough: mirrorable defenses don’t themselves discriminate the creator’s moral character, and any proposed asymmetry must do that independent evidential work.

The scriptural moral record supplies a final, conditional asymmetry. Conditional, because the conduct counts as a creator’s conduct only if the defender maintains the texts’ divine attribution; a humanly authored text is evidence about its authors, not about God. But on the attribution the defense asks readers to accept, the Flood’s indiscriminate destruction (§12.1.2), punishment transferred across persons and generations (§12.1.6), laws permitting ownership and violence against enslaved people (§12.4.2), and commands of total destruction and sexual harm (§12.4.3) aren’t neutral data. A good-god account must redescribe or justify each; an evil-god account can take the attributed cruelty at face value. The point isn’t that these texts prove an evil god. It is the diagnostic question the challenge forces: if the same attributed acts are made compatible with perfect goodness by changing the moral description, what further conduct could still count as evidence of malevolence? A goodness on which no disclosed conduct can bear has been insulated from the record offered in its support.

*The predicate empties.* The reversibility makes a second point, the one the cluster’s groundwork was laid to reach. A defense that would acquit a wholly evil god as readily as a wholly good one isn’t registering the creator’s moral character at all; it is an all-purpose device that would reconcile any character whatever with any world whatever. A goodness defended by instruments that defend its opposite equally well is a goodness no arrangement of the world is allowed to count against—and a predicate insulated from every possible piece of evidence, as §12.5.5 found, has stopped doing any work. The theodicies don’t fail because the evil-god hypothesis is true; they fail because, working in both directions, they were never able to tell the difference. The solvent reaches only what it is poured on: the creator’s *moral character*, the goodness the theodicies were built to defend. It doesn’t touch the greatness the inversion relocates to Nature, because that greatness isn’t a character a defense could be run for in either direction—it is metaphysical fundamentality and necessity, what Nature is rather than how an agent behaves.

The reason is structural, not exemptive. The evil-god test reverses a polar evaluative predicate while holding the evidence fixed: good becomes evil, and each theodicy is asked whether it works unchanged. Necessity and fundamentality have no inverse character-pole that the same defense could protect. Their opposites—contingency and derivativeness—are modal relations that require independent arguments about what can fail to exist or what depends on what. The book’s claim is accordingly not inferred from the world’s appearing necessity-friendly in the way creator-goodness is inferred from its appearing benevolently governed; it is argued through the modal route of Chapters 1–3. Reverse the moral evaluation and that derivation is untouched; reverse the modal premises and one has changed the argument rather than mirrored its defense. The symmetry empties a defended goodness; it leaves untouched a greatness established in a different logical register.

**[Proposition]**

**A Mirrorable Defense Discriminates Nothing** · *Proposition*

The evil-god challenge begins from a hypothesis almost everyone rejects—that the world is the work of a wholly malevolent creator—and observes that such a creator faces a *problem of good* mirroring the believer’s problem of evil, answerable by mirror images of the same defenses. What the mirroring establishes is a constraint on what a defense can accomplish. A defense that runs equally well for an evil creator cannot by itself establish a good creator’s moral character, however successful it is at its own stated task of blocking an incompatibility charge. Defeating the charge that God and evil are logically incompatible is one achievement; discriminating a good creator from a malevolent or indifferent one is another, and the familiar theodicy forms are not shown to deliver the second by delivering the first.

*Scope.* The result is about what theodicies can settle, not a demonstration that the world is indifferent, and the symmetry argument is not offered as conclusive. A defender may identify genuine asymmetries in value, agency, revelation, or the evidence; the standing demand is that such asymmetries be independently defended rather than assumed, since assuming them is what the challenge exists to expose.

**Depends on:** The Explanatory Burden (§12)

The evil-god challenge shows that many familiar theodicy forms are evidentially non-discriminating: a defense that could be mirrored for an evil creator can’t by itself establish a good creator’s moral character. A defender may try to identify asymmetries in value, agency, revelation, or the evidence; the challenge is that those asymmetries must be independently defended rather than assumed. The argument is that theodicies alone don’t secure a good God against the evidence and that indifference may offer a simpler explanation of some data, not that the symmetry argument conclusively demonstrates an indifferent world.

## 12.6 The Passover of Christ

The sixth and final numbered cluster differs in kind from the five before it. Rather than pressing one doctrine at a time, its two sections form one paired construction. The Greatest Loophole (§12.6.1) first separates three questions: whether beatitude before accountability is guaranteed, how that outcome ranks against a life exposed to possible final loss, and what—if anything—authorizes a creature to act on the ranking. The Greatest Sacrifice (§12.6.2) then takes the branch that supplies the guarantee and the action bridge, gives it a willing agent who accepts permanent loss, and tests the resulting figure against irrevocability as one proposed measure of sacrificial greatness. The second argument is therefore downstream of a named branch of the first, not a free-standing verdict about every account of salvation or the cross.

The cluster sits last by design. Its sections presuppose the preceding sequence, drawing on results already established rather than introducing new machinery. A Novel God: The Final Retreat (§12.7) then asks the question the sequence leaves behind: if some mind stands behind the world, what would that mind have to want for this world to make sense? An argument that targets one doctrine belongs in the preceding clusters; the final question concerns the purpose attributed to a creator at all.

### 12.6.1 The Greatest Loophole

Exodus has weighed the theodicies one at a time; this section, the sequence’s last argument and a reductio in form, tests a specified plan of salvation against its own valuations. It is a construction and not a proposal. It grants the conditional maximand fixed at §12.5.1 for greater-good and universal-salvific accounts that accept comparability, aggregation, and monotonicity—the greatest number of creatures restored to God and the fewest lost—and adds commitments held by the target set: two final ends (Matt 25:46; Dan 12:2), divine justice, prenatal human value, and guaranteed beatitude before accountability. The outcome reversal follows from that conjunction. The stronger conclusion about what a creature may or ought to do requires a further action bridge and the absence of an overriding right or side constraint; those commitments are separated below rather than attributed to the whole tradition. Positions offering hope, limbo, punishment, non-aggregative goods, or deontic prohibitions therefore face different pressures. The core outcome problem has lately been pressed in the literature as the *afterlife dilemma* for the pro-life movement (Kerring 2022); what follows states its premise set, prices its exits, and identifies the additional branch on which it becomes a reversal of the atonement.

Two commitments frame the argument, and the strain is already visible between them. The first is that prenatal life bears the full value a human life has: on the tradition’s theology an ensouled person exists from conception, and on Marquis’s secular defense of the same verdict the fetus possesses a *future like ours* whose loss is the very thing that makes killing wrong (Marquis 1989). In either register the pro-life claim is that the one aborted is deprived of an incomparable good. The second commitment concerns those who die before they can be judged, and here the tradition has never held still. Augustine, holding original sin to condemn even the unbaptized infant, could allow them only the *mitissima poena*, the mildest of the punishments of the damned (Augustine, *De peccatorum meritis et remissione* I.21). Aquinas softened this to the *limbus infantium*: no beatific vision, but no suffering either—a natural happiness owed to those who bore no personal guilt (Aquinas, ST Suppl. App. I, q.1).

The modern magisterium has retreated further still: unable to reconcile inherited guilt with the universal salvific will of a just God, the International Theological Commission resolves the question into *hope*—“serious theological and liturgical grounds for hope” that such infants are saved, while conceding that these are “reasons for prayerful hope, rather than grounds for sure knowledge” (International Theological Commission 2007). Protestant thought reaches the warmer verdict by a shorter road, in an age of accountability below which none is condemned, read out of David’s confidence that he will go to his dead child (2 Sam 12:23) and Christ’s word that the kingdom belongs to such as these (Matt 19:14). The through-line isn’t a single verdict but the tradition’s inability to let the case rest: Augustinian punishment, Thomistic limbo, Catholic hope, and Protestant guarantee are competing answers to the same justice pressure. Only guaranteed beatitude supplies the full reduction that follows. The other positions block that arithmetic by paying a different price—punishment without personal guilt, exclusion from the highest good without personal fault, or uncertainty where the plan’s justice is supposed to govern.

*The reduction.* Grant guaranteed beatitude before accountability and a salvation-only ranking, and one comparison follows: secure beatitude outranks exposure to possible final loss. That comparison doesn’t yet show that earthly life has no value, that death confers no deprivation, or that anyone may cause it. Marquis’s *future like ours* can remain a genuine lost good even where beatitude follows (Marquis 1989); a theology may rank embodied vocation, relationship, agency, or obedience alongside salvation and may treat their wrongful deprivation as decisive. The reductio therefore targets the narrower set that treats the number securely saved as the complete outcome metric and assigns no independent value capable of reversing the comparison. Under that set, pre-accountability death secures the stipulated end more reliably than survival into risk. The result is an outcome-ranking pressure, not yet an all-things-considered evaluation of abortion or a license to act.

*What the argument doesn’t need.* The secular debate over abortion turns on a question this argument never asks. Whether the fetus is a person with a right to life—Thomson granting the right and severing the entailment (Thomson 1971), Warren and Tooley withholding personhood altogether (Warren 1973; Tooley 1972)—is the axis on which that literature moves. The reduction is indifferent to it. It neither needs the fetus to be a person nor needs to deny it; it borrows whatever status the tradition itself assigns—an ensouled subject bound for one of two eternities—and reasons from that alone. A defender escapes by neither conceding nor withholding personhood, because the argument runs on the soul the defender has already posited, not on any anthropology of the book’s. Its independence from the personhood question is what makes it awkward to meet: the standard replies are aimed at a claim it hasn’t made.

*Where the escape runs.* A strong age-of-accountability guarantee supplies the exemption; the ITC’s *hope* doesn’t, because hope is neither certainty nor a specified probability; Augustine’s punishment and Aquinas’s limbo block it through different accounts of the infant’s end. Even after guaranteed beatitude is granted, a defender may reject aggregation, include indispensable earthly goods in the outcome, or invoke rights, authority, and agent-relative duties. These are genuine exits, not evasions. The conditional pressure is therefore set-specific: guarantee beatitude and a salvation-only ranking, and the outcome comparison arises; deny the guarantee, revise the ranking, or deny the action bridge, and the corresponding justice, value, or deontic account carries forward.

*Outcome ranking and action authorization.* The maximand ranks outcomes; it doesn’t by itself authorize every act that would produce the highest-ranked one. Moving from “this state contains more creatures securely restored” to “a creature ought to bring it about” requires an additional action bridge: that agents should maximize that outcome, that no right or side constraint forbids the means, that creatures possess the relevant authority over life and death, and that no additional final good is lost. A theology may reject any of those claims while retaining the outcome ranking. The reduction reaches action-guidance only against the fuller set that accepts them.

On that fuller set, the pressure is severe. If every pre-accountability death secures beatitude, if fewer exposed to final loss is the complete ranking, and if creatures must maximize that ranking without an independent constraint on the means, the set generates an action implication it has decisive reason to reject. The reductio identifies the conjunction that must give way; it doesn’t issue the implication as an all-things-considered requirement or attach it to guaranteed beatitude alone.

The deontic response is therefore a genuine exit: grant that the outcome contains more guaranteed salvations while denying the license, because killing violates a right, uses a person as a means, or exceeds creaturely authority (Deut 32:39; Job 1:21). Its price isn’t logical inconsistency. It is the admission that maximal salvation isn’t the complete standard of right action: rights, authority, or obedience constrain what creatures may do even when the constrained act would improve the stipulated salvation outcome. The account must then explain why those constraints bind, and it may not use aggregate salvation as an overriding currency in theodicy while denying that currency whenever a side constraint becomes costly. But a consistently deontic theology can pay that price.

Nor does the divine-prerogative reply entail that the person killed suffers no wrong. A defender can hold that earthly life, agency, relationship, and the creature’s own vocation are goods whose deprivation wrongs the victim even if beatitude is ultimately secured. That reply gives those goods or rights independent standing; it thereby blocks the act inference while also denying that salvation alone exhausts the valuation. What remains from the reduction is the outcome reversal and the demand for a consistent action theory, not an unconditional recommendation of the deed.

*The census.* If personhood begins at conception and guaranteed beatitude covers every pre-accountability death, natural embryo loss and historical child mortality make the exempted population enormous. Estimates of loss from conception are model-sensitive, especially before clinically recognized pregnancy, but even cautious ranges plus high premodern child mortality prevent the exempted from being treated as a negligible edge case (Ord 2008; Volk and Atkinson 2013). The demographic conclusion remains conditional on conception-personhood, the scope of the exemption, and the empirical estimate; it doesn’t by itself establish the composition of heaven.

The demographic pressure concerns the explanatory role of earthly trial. If a large class reaches the highest end without it, the trial isn’t a universal necessary means. A defender may call earthly formation an ordinary good, a vocation for those who live, or one route among others rather than a condition of beatitude. Natural embryo loss can then remain a tragedy because it deprives persons of embodied goods even if their final end is secured. That reply blocks the inference from “heaven follows” to “there is no victim”; it also confirms that salvation alone doesn’t exhaust the value ledger. Nothing in the census authorizes deliberately causing the deprivation.

*The wager compared.* Under the stipulated guarantee, continued life introduces a possibility of final loss that pre-accountability death excludes. It also supplies embodied agency, relationships, vocation, temporal goods, and the opportunity for a person to own a history; causing death deprives the subject of those goods and may violate rights or reserved divine authority. The comparison therefore cannot be described as “birth versus heaven,” as though birth withheld heaven or death had no victim. It is secure final outcome plus deprivation on one side, and earthly goods plus risk to salvation on the other. A salvation-only metric ranks the first; a plural value theory may not. The point of the reduction is to force that ledger into the open, not to declare murder the only act that protects the beloved.

**[Disjunction]**

**The Beatitude Loophole Problem** · *Disjunction*

If dying before accountability guarantees heaven, may someone act to secure that outcome?

- **If guaranteed beatitude authorizes that act,** then the act is permitted, and the ranking that permits it has to be owned. That reading must rank secure beatitude above the earthly goods forgone and accept an action principle requiring that outcome despite any right, side constraint, or reservation of authority. Together those commitments pressure the very act it would otherwise condemn. *Feeds into* The Irrevocable Loss Problem (§12.6.2). *Priced by* The Bridge Premises (§12.5.1).
- **If it doesn’t authorize it,** then salvation isn’t the whole of what makes an action right. Maximal salvation isn’t the complete standard of creaturely action; the constraining right, duty, or authority must be stated and applied consistently.

Either beatitude exhausts right action and the authorization pressure stands, or something besides beatitude constrains action. The ranking cannot do both jobs.

**Still open:** whether beatitude is guaranteed, which goods enter the outcome ranking, and what principle authorizes or forbids creaturely action

*A narrower charge that doesn’t need aggregation.* Imposing a hazard on someone is licensed by their agreement to bear it, and an agreement is theirs only if refusal was available and the terms were known—the conditions set out at §12.4.3. Absent them, another party’s rule is imposed through the grammar of permission. No entrant can consent to entry itself, but ordinary birth isn’t therefore treated here as intrinsically wrongful. The comparison arises only on a set that guarantees the *same complete final good* to the pre-accountability dead and denies that earthly life contributes an indispensable additional final good. On those assumptions, the exemption displays a hazard-free route to everything the tried person finally receives, and the designer owes a reason for assigning the hazardous route to those who live. A defender exits by denying the identity of goods, treating earthly vocation as indispensable, or explaining why the exceptional route can’t be generalized. The charge doesn’t require aggregation, but it remains conditional on those exact sameness and availability claims.

**[Proposition]**

**Terms No One Could Consent To** · *Proposition*

If a salvation account guarantees the same beatitude without an earthly trial to those who die before accountability, then entry into a trial carrying possible final loss imposes a hazard no entrant could accept in advance. On that standard, a duty-bearer who can supply the same protected good without that hazard must justify choosing the hazardous route. The corollary does not assume that nonexistence itself requires consent: it applies only if the exempt and the tried receive the same final good and earthly life contributes no indispensable additional final good. Denying either condition exits the corollary and carries that difference forward for explanation.

**Depends on:** Captivity Forecloses the Modifier (§12.4.3)

### 12.6.2 The Greatest Sacrifice
The Greatest Loophole (§12.6.1) exposes a conditional reversal in a salvation economy that guarantees beatitude before accountability: within that construction, an act that sends a person to certain heaven can appear to maximize the tradition’s own stated end.
